[P1] The deadline in § 39.13(a) requiring FAA to receive public comments by Jan 19, 2018 is unreasonably short given the complexity of the AD; request extension of the comment period to at least 60 days after publication to allow stakeholders time to review figures and coordinate with POIs and manufacturers.

[P1] Legal counsel for small carriers will comment that the fixed January 19, 2018 deadline may be procedurally deficient if stakeholders did not get adequate notice; request reissuance with a new comment period to ensure due process.

[P2] Airlines will comment that the general obligation in § 39.13(f) to “comply within the compliance times specified” is vague absent a uniform compliance schedule across all paragraphs; request that the FAA specify exact calendar dates or a clear method for computing compliance deadlines relative to the AD effective date.

[P3] A major carrier will assert that the 120‑day compliance time in § 39.13(g) for Model 737 AFM revisions is too short for operators to incorporate, review, approval by the POI, and distribution across fleets, and request extension to 180 days.

[P4] Flight crew unions will state that the mandatory revision in § 39.13(g)(1) to AFM Section 1 (Fuel System Limitations) must be accompanied by FAA‑approved training guidance; request that the FAA require and fund standardized pilot guidance and training materials when AFM limitations change.

[P5] Several operators will note that the permission in § 39.13(g)(1) allowing insertion of a copy of the AD into the AFM is administratively burdensome and could lead to inconsistent AFMs; recommend instead allowing an FAA‑approved insert or operator template and clarify acceptable format and placement within the AFM.

[P6] Legal commenters will point out ambiguity in § 39.13(g)(1) where the clause permits inserting the AD into the AFM but does not state whether the AD insert is a permanent or temporary revision until incorporated into general AFM revisions; request clarification on retention/removal requirements and recordkeeping.

[P7] Operators will challenge § 39.13(g)(1) permission that general AFM revisions containing identical language may replace the AD copy, asking FAA to require documentation of equivalence and to specify the approval process and timing for removing the AD insert.

[P8] The obligation in § 39.13(g)(2) to revise AFM Section 3 Normal Procedures within 120 days raises concerns from training departments about the need to revise simulator and checkride syllabi; request an implementation grace period for training-related tasks following AFM revision.

[P9] Small operators will request that the permission in § 39.13(g)(2) to insert a copy of the AD into the AFM explicitly permit electronic AFM (eAFM) updates and mobile pilot applications to avoid logistical burdens of paper updates.

[P10] A 737 operator will comment that § 39.13(h) requiring Model 757 operators with certain line numbers to do actions within 120 days if service bulletin actions have not been done is unclear about whether compliance time is measured from AD effective date or receipt of the AD; request explicit measurement (e.g., calendar days after effective date).

[P11] Boeing and operators will note under § 39.13(h) the exception that service bulletin actions done after the AD effective date relieve the (h) actions but simultaneously create an obligation to perform paragraph (j) before further flight; request clarification of sequencing obligations and whether any grace period exists for paperwork updates after physical work is done.

[P12] Maintenance organizations will comment that § 39.13(h)(1) allowing AFM revision by inserting a copy of the AD is insufficient if operators have mixed fleets with varying AFM formats; request templates for figure 3 language in common AFM formats and clarification of required AFM sections to be annotated.

[P13] Flight standards offices will request that § 39.13(h)(1) and (h)(2) provide an alternative compliance path for operators that have already made equivalent AFM revisions under previous ADs or service bulletins—i.e., allow equivalency demonstrations rather than mandatory re‑insertion.

[P14] Model 757 operators will challenge the 120‑day MEL revision obligation in § 39.13(j) as impractical for carriers with centralized MEL systems requiring POI concurrence and multiple jurisdictional approvals; request extension to 180 days or exemptions for operators that can demonstrate an FAA‑approved schedule to implement.

[P15] Several operators will ask, regarding § 39.13(j) and similar MEL obligations (§§ 39.13(k)–(m)), for clarity about whether these MEL changes must be promulgated as permanent MEL items, or if Temporary Revisions/TCDS entries are acceptable pending long‑term MEL amendment.

[P16] The permission in § 39.13(j) that POIs may approve alternative MEL wording is useful but commenters will request formal criteria for POIs to evaluate alternatives, and whether centralized FAA guidance will be provided to ensure national consistency.

[P17] International carriers will comment that §§ 39.13(j)–(m) impact ETOPS dispatch; request coordination with EASA/foreign authorities and explicit guidance on acceptance of these MEL changes by non‑U.S. authorities.

[P18] 787 operators will comment under § 39.13(m) that the list of inoperative items (P36–P39) is incomplete because there are related valves and sensors in other ATA chapters that affect crossfeed operations; request expansion of figure 10 items or a catch‑all provision for equivalent inoperative items affecting fuel crossfeed.

[P19] Maintenance providers will assert that § 39.13(m) listing the Pressure Refueling System Main Tank Inboard Refuel Valve (P36) as an inoperative item requiring MEL change is confusing because the ATA reference (28–21–01–01) differs by operator manuals; request cross‑reference to Boeing IPC and standardize the part numbering or job card references.

[P20] Safety advocacy groups will argue that allowing removal of the prior AD AFM limitation after incorporation of these AFM revisions (§ 39.13(n)) could create gaps if operators incorrectly remove legacy limitations; request an FAA verification step or POI concurrence before removal is permitted.

[P21] Operators will request clarification in § 39.13(n) about recordkeeping: when an operator removes the prior AD limitation after incorporating the new AFM language, what documentation must be retained and for how long to demonstrate compliance during audits.

[P22] Industry commenters will request that the AMOC approval authority statement in § 39.13(o)(1) be broadened beyond the Seattle ACO Branch or that the rule explain coordination processes when an operator’s certification office is not Seattle to avoid delays.

[P23] Legal experts will comment that the AMOC procedural references in § 39.13(o)(1) and (o)(2) lack timelines for FAA decision on AMOC requests; request established FAA response times (e.g., 60 or 90 days) to prevent operational uncertainty.

[P24] Operators will request in § 39.13(o)(1) clarity on whether AMOC requests mailed to principal inspectors fulfill the requirement or whether the FAA will accept electronic submissions only at the specified email address in § 39.13(o)(1); request explicit allowed submission methods.

[P25] Flight standards organizations will comment that the instruction in § 39.13(o)(1) to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector may be impractical for foreign operators without a U.S. PI; request an alternative routing mechanism and contact information for international applicants.

[P26] Operators will comment that the email address provided in § 39.13(o)(1) (9‑ANM‑Seattle‑ACO‑AMOC‑Requests@faa.gov) may not be suitable for large attachments (e.g., engineering reports); request FAA acceptance of secure file transfer or dedicated AMOC portal.

[P27] Operators will request that § 39.13(o)(2) require that prior to using an approved AMOC, the operator notify the FAA in writing and receive written concurrence, rather than merely “notify” verbally, to ensure an auditable record.

[P28] Boeing and ODA holders will applaud § 39.13(o)(3) permitting use of ODA‑approved AMOCs but request clearer criteria on the necessary content of the ODA approval and a requirement that ODA approvals include explicit reference to this AD as stated in § 39.13(o)(3) to avoid confusion.

[P29] Legal commenters will note that § 39.13(o)(3) requires that repair/modification deviations meet the airplane’s certification basis and specifically reference this AD, but it is silent on how to handle modifications that were approved under previous certification bases; request guidance on grandfathering and acceptable equivalency demonstrations.

[P30] Pilot associations will request that any AFM Normal Procedures changes in §§ 39.13(g)(2), (h)(2), (i)(2) be subject to human factors review and that FAA circulate proposed figure language to pilot groups before finalizing mandatory inclusion.

[P31] A regional carrier will comment that the rule lacks an economic analysis of the cost of AFM and MEL revisions across fleets and training hours; request FAA include a detailed cost estimate and regulatory flexibility analysis for small entities.

[P32] A maintenance union will raise concern that the AD permits operators to insert the AD text into the AFM (§§ 39.13(g)(1), (g)(2), (h)(1), (h)(2), (i)(1), (i)(2)) without requiring an FAA stamp or approval; request that AFM insertions be approved by the POI and retained in the operator’s revision history.

[P33] Safety managers at airlines will request explicit guidance in § 39.13 on how to handle mixed‑configuration fleets where some airplanes have had the Boeing service bulletin actions performed and others have not (e.g., dispatch differences, threshold MEL differences).

[P34] International airlines will ask whether the MEL revisions required by §§ 39.13(j)–(m) will be accepted by foreign authorities for reciprocating ETOPS approvals, and request the FAA coordinate with ICAO/EASA and publish guidance for international acceptance.

[P35] An operations inspector will request that the AD include sample wording for POI‑approved alternative MELs (per §§ 39.13(j)(k)(l)(m)) to promote consistent safety outcomes and reduce review time.

[P36] An insurance industry commenter will express concern that the AD’s permission to use ODA‑approved AMOCs (§ 39.13(o)(3)) could create variability in safety standards across operators; request FAA oversight metrics or reporting requirements for ODA AMOC approvals related to this AD.

[P37] A Model 767 operator will seek clarification under § 39.13(i) whether the 120‑day AFM revision requirement applies to in‑service leased aircraft where the lessor controls the AFM revisions; request direction on lessor/lessee responsibilities.

[P38] Training providers will request that the FAA mandate a minimum lead time between AFM/MEL publication and when crews must be competent to operate under the new limitations (e.g., 30 days), to allow scheduled training without disrupting operations.

[P39] A maintenance engineering group will request that the AD explicitly state whether copies of the AD inserted into AFMs may be temporary (e.g., placard) or whether they must be added as official AFM revisions in the revision record and retained permanently.

[P40] Consumer safety advocates will request that the FAA require operators to notify affected passengers when aircraft are dispatching ETOPS with inoperative fuel crossfeed valves per the new MEL procedures (transparency regarding potential increased diversion risk).

[P41] A small charter operator will request relief or a phased compliance schedule for §§ 39.13(g)–(m) to prioritize safety‑critical airplanes first and allow operators with limited technical staff additional time to implement changes.

[P42] An avionics supplier will comment that the AD should explicitly allow electronic AFM updates distributed via company intranet and require operators to maintain proof of distribution (time/date stamp) to crewmembers, to be audit compliant.

[P43] An airport authority will request clarification whether AFM/MEL changes required by this AD affect airport planning (e.g., longer diversion distances for ETOPS) and ask FAA to publish modeling guidance if operational impacts are anticipated.

[P44] General counsel for an airline will request that the FAA explicitly state in § 39.13 whether compliance with the AFM/MEL revisions is required fleetwide or only for the specific line numbers/airplanes identified (to avoid misinterpretation and overcompliance).

[P45] An engineering trade association will recommend that the figures referenced in multiple paragraphs (figures 1–10) be incorporated by reference in the Federal Register and made available in machine‑readable format to facilitate operator compliance and reduce transcription errors.

[P46] A regulatory compliance consultant will request the FAA specify acceptable evidence to demonstrate compliance (e.g., annotated AFM revisions, MEL revision pages, training signoff sheets) to simplify audits and POI reviews.

[P47] A national pilots’ association will request that the FAA require operators to provide a notice to flight crews highlighting exact AFM/MEL changes and a signed acknowledgment from assigned PICs before flying under new limitations.

[P48] An environmental NGO will request analysis of whether MEL changes that allow dispatch with inoperative refueling/crossfeed items could lead to operational changes (e.g., payload restrictions) affecting emissions and request FAA consider environmental impacts.

[P49] A foreign regulatory body liaison will comment that the AD’s reliance on Boeing service bulletin compliance as an exception (P11, P20) requires coordination; request explicit FAA acceptance criteria for service bulletin implementation reports used to remove AFM/MEL obligations.

[P50] A university aviation safety researcher will recommend inclusion of a post‑implementation monitoring requirement (e.g., collect and report occurrences related to inoperative fuel crossfeed valve dispatch) to evaluate the safety effectiveness of the AFM/MEL revisions.

[P1] The 0.131 percent cellulosic biofuel standard for 2018 is unreasonably low and will discourage investment in cellulosic biofuel production; EPA should raise the percentage to reflect recent production increases and projected capacity.

[P1] Conversely, the 0.131 percent cellulosic value appears to exceed documented commercial cellulosic volumes for 2018; EPA should provide the underlying production and waiver accounting data demonstrating the basis for this precise figure.

[P1] The rule does not explain whether the cellulosic standard includes cellulosic renewable identification numbers (RINs) carried forward from prior years; EPA should clarify inclusion/exclusion and accounting methodology.

[P2] The 1.74 percent biomass-based diesel (BBD) standard for 2018 may understate obligated volumes given higher imports and domestic output; biodiesel producers request EPA increase the BBD requirement to avoid oversupply of carryforward RINs.

[P2] Fuel distributors and obligated parties contend that the 1.74 percent BBD standard is too high relative to actual BBD availability in some regions and will create market distortions and RIN price spikes; EPA should phase in increases or allow a geographic flex.

[P2] EPA must clarify whether the biomass-based diesel standard is expressed as a percentage of gasoline-equivalent energy or as a volumetric percentage of total transportation fuel; the legal text is ambiguous and affects compliance calculations.

[P3] The 2.34 percent advanced biofuel standard for 2018 fails to account for rapid growth in imported sugarcane ethanol and other qualifying fuels; refined fuel suppliers urge EPA to adjust the advanced biofuel percentage upward to incentivize domestic production.

[P3] Environmental advocacy groups support the 2.34 percent advanced biofuel standard but request EPA provide lifecycle greenhouse gas (GHG) analyses justifying that the included advanced fuels meet emissions reduction expectations.

[P3] Legal commenters note EPA must confirm whether cellulosic and biomass-based diesel volumes are included within the advanced biofuel percentage or treated as separate subtargets; clarify stacking and double-counting rules.

[P4] The 10.62 percent overall renewable fuel standard (RFS) for 2018 conflicts with statutory blends required by the Clean Air Act for the applicable fuel pool; EPA should publish the blending baseline (denominator) used to derive the percentage.

[P4] Refiners assert that a 10.62 percent RFS will impose significant compliance costs given limited access to blended fuel infrastructure; EPA should provide an economic impact analysis including regional cost differentials.

[P4] Small refinery trade groups request that EPA provide waiver or small-refinery exemption data tied to the 10.62 percent number, since exemptions materially change obligated gallons and thus the effective standard.

[P5] The requirement that "each insured credit union must include the official advertising statement in all of its advertisements, including on the main Internet page" is overly broad and could conflict with space-limited ad formats (e.g., banner ads); NCUA should allow a concise icon or hyperlink alternative.

[P5] Credit unions operating international or member-only intranet pages need clarification whether "main Internet page" refers only to publicly accessible websites or all online presences; propose limiting to publicly accessible consumer-facing pages.

[P5] Community credit unions with third-party marketing vendors raise concerns about enforcement and liability if vendors fail to include the statement; the rule should specify whether the insured credit union or the vendor is liable for omissions.

[P6] Limiting the official advertising statement to the specified forms removes flexibility for accurate, consumer-friendly variations (e.g., translations for non-English speakers); NCUA should permit translated versions where needed.

[P6] Consumer advocates argue that mandating specific phrasing is acceptable but NCUA should allow additional context (e.g., "deposits insured up to $250,000") adjacent to the statement to improve consumer understanding.

[P7] Some credit unions find the full wording "This credit union is federally insured by the National Credit Union Administration" too long for small ads and mobile displays; request that NCUA allow the abbreviated "Federally insured by NCUA" as the default or permit an icon.

[P7] Legal commenters note the long phrase in P7 could be considered redundant if the official sign reproduction per §740.4(b) is used elsewhere; NCUA should harmonize requirements to prevent conflicting obligations.

[P8] The permission to use "Federally insured by NCUA" is useful, but the rule should allow minor grammatical adjustments (e.g., "Federally insured by the NCUA") to accommodate different sentence structures without violating the rule.

[P8] Advertising agencies request explicit approval to include the "Federally insured by NCUA" statement in all-caps or stylized typography consistent with brand guidelines, provided legibility requirements are met.

[P9] The option "Insured by NCUA" may be too vague and could mislead consumers unfamiliar with the acronym; consumer protection groups recommend requiring the full agency name at least on the website main page.

[P9] Some multilingual credit unions request permission to use equivalent phrases in other languages (e.g., Spanish "Asegurado por NCUA") and ask for formal acceptance of validated translations.

[P10] Allowing a reproduction of the official sign in lieu of the text statements is appropriate, but the rule lacks specifications on minimum size, color contrast, and placement for the reproduced sign in different media; NCUA should add clear design standards.

[P10] Credit unions using co-branded or partner ads worry that the reproduced official sign requirement may conflict with third-party ad layouts; NCUA should permit placement flexibility if the sign remains clearly legible.

[P11] Permitting font size alteration for legibility of the official sign is necessary, but NCUA should specify maximum and minimum proportions relative to the sign's original design to avoid misleading enlargement.

[P11] Graphic designers request clarification whether altering font size is permitted across all digital responsive designs and whether scaling for accessibility (e.g., screen readers) is acceptable without formal alteration approval.

[P12] The mandate that the official advertising statement be "clearly legible" is subjective; NCUA should define measurable legibility standards (e.g., minimum font size in points/pixels, color contrast ratios) to ensure consistent compliance.

[P12] Disability advocates request that legibility standards align with WCAG accessibility guidelines to ensure visually impaired consumers can perceive the statement; specify provisions for screen-reader accessible text alternatives.

[P13] Requiring the official statement to be no smaller than the smallest informational font in the ad could unintentionally permit extremely small sizes if the ad uses tiny fonts elsewhere; propose instead a specific absolute minimum font size.

[P13] Advertisers caution that using the "smallest font elsewhere" metric could be gamed (e.g., placing tiny non-informational disclaimers) to force the statement to be small; NCUA should prohibit artifice and set objective minima.

[P14] Exempting radio ads under 30 seconds from the statement requirement ignores the reality that brief radio spots still convey financial claims; consumer groups recommend no exemption for any financial advertising, or at minimum require the abbreviated statement to be spoken.

[P14] Broadcasters and small credit unions support the radio exemption for under-30-second spots as necessary for practical spot limits and airtime cost; but they ask NCUA to permit a short audio tagline alternative (e.g., "Insured by NCUA") when time-limited.

[P14] Legal experts point out ambiguity about how to measure 30 seconds for radio ads that include pre- or post-roll content; NCUA should specify timing rules and whether cumulative runs count.

[P15] The television ad exemption for under 30 seconds may create unequal consumer protections because viewers of short TV spots won't see the insurance statement; industry suggests allowing on-screen logo-only displays as a compromise.

[P15] Public interest groups argue that the exemption for non-display TV ads under 30 seconds is inappropriate because many viewers watch without sound and will miss spoken statements; require the on-screen display or sign even in short spots.

[P15] Advertisers request clarity whether the 30-second rule applies per airing or per continuous creative element (i.e., if a 15-second spot airs twice back-to-back, does the exemption apply?) and whether different ad breaks change application.

Conversely, the 0.131 percent cellulosic value appears to exceed documented commercial cellulosic volumes for 2018; EPA should provide the underlying production and waiver accounting data demonstrating the basis for this precise figure.

The rule does not explain whether the cellulosic standard includes cellulosic renewable identification numbers (RINs) carried forward from prior years; EPA should clarify inclusion/exclusion and accounting methodology.

The 1.74 percent biomass-based diesel (BBD) standard for 2018 may understate obligated volumes given higher imports and domestic output; biodiesel producers request EPA increase the BBD requirement to avoid oversupply of carryforward RINs.

Fuel distributors and obligated parties contend that the 1.74 percent BBD standard is too high relative to actual BBD availability in some regions and will create market distortions and RIN price spikes; EPA should phase in increases or allow a geographic flex.

EPA must clarify whether the biomass-based diesel standard is expressed as a percentage of gasoline-equivalent energy or as a volumetric percentage of total transportation fuel; the legal text is ambiguous and affects compliance calculations.

The 2.34 percent advanced biofuel standard for 2018 fails to account for rapid growth in imported sugarcane ethanol and other qualifying fuels; refined fuel suppliers urge EPA to adjust the advanced biofuel percentage upward to incentivize domestic production.

Environmental advocacy groups support the 2.34 percent advanced biofuel standard but request EPA provide lifecycle greenhouse gas (GHG) analyses justifying that the included advanced fuels meet emissions reduction expectations.

Legal commenters note EPA must confirm whether cellulosic and biomass-based diesel volumes are included within the advanced biofuel percentage or treated as separate subtargets; clarify stacking and double-counting rules.

The 10.62 percent overall renewable fuel standard (RFS) for 2018 conflicts with statutory blends required by the Clean Air Act for the applicable fuel pool; EPA should publish the blending baseline (denominator) used to derive the percentage.

Refiners assert that a 10.62 percent RFS will impose significant compliance costs given limited access to blended fuel infrastructure; EPA should provide an economic impact analysis including regional cost differentials.

Small refinery trade groups request that EPA provide waiver or small-refinery exemption data tied to the 10.62 percent number, since exemptions materially change obligated gallons and thus the effective standard.

Community credit unions with third-party marketing vendors raise concerns about enforcement and liability if vendors fail to include the statement; the rule should specify whether the insured credit union or the vendor is liable for omissions.

Limiting the official advertising statement to the specified forms removes flexibility for accurate, consumer-friendly variations (e.g., translations for non-English speakers); NCUA should permit translated versions where needed.

Consumer advocates argue that mandating specific phrasing is acceptable but NCUA should allow additional context (e.g., "deposits insured up to $250,000") adjacent to the statement to improve consumer understanding.

Some credit unions find the full wording "This credit union is federally insured by the National Credit Union Administration" too long for small ads and mobile displays; request that NCUA allow the abbreviated "Federally insured by NCUA" as the default or permit an icon.

Advertising agencies request explicit approval to include the "Federally insured by NCUA" statement in all-caps or stylized typography consistent with brand guidelines, provided legibility requirements are met.

The option "Insured by NCUA" may be too vague and could mislead consumers unfamiliar with the acronym; consumer protection groups recommend requiring the full agency name at least on the website main page.

Allowing a reproduction of the official sign in lieu of the text statements is appropriate, but the rule lacks specifications on minimum size, color contrast, and placement for the reproduced sign in different media; NCUA should add clear design standards.

Legal experts point out ambiguity about how to measure 30 seconds for radio ads that include pre- or post-roll content; NCUA should specify timing rules and whether cumulative runs count.

The television ad exemption for under 30 seconds may create unequal consumer protections because viewers of short TV spots won't see the insurance statement; industry suggests allowing on-screen logo-only displays as a compromise.

Public interest groups argue that the exemption for non-display TV ads under 30 seconds is inappropriate because many viewers watch without sound and will miss spoken statements; require the on-screen display or sign even in short spots.

[P1] The comment deadline of October 23, 2020 is unreasonable and too short for international operators and small carriers to prepare substantive technical comments; request extension of the comment period by at least 60–90 days.

[P1] The FAA should provide an electronic docket link and direct mailing address in the provision text; simply stating the date without clear submission instructions will lead to lost or misfiled comments.

[P2] The applicability to all 737–600/700/700C/800/900/900ER series airplanes irrespective of modification/retrofit status is overbroad; request clarification whether airplanes with prior structural modifications or Supplemental Type Certificates (STCs) that alter STA 663.75 fittings are excluded.

[P2] The rule should specify applicability by serial number ranges or configuration codes because some 737s of the listed models have been modified to nonstandard configurations that may not be affected.

[P3] The blanket obligation to "comply within the specified compliance times unless already complied with" is vague; commenters request that the rule require holders to provide documentation proving prior compliance and specify acceptable forms of that documentation.

[P4] The requirement to perform a "detailed inspection" of STA 663.75 outboard chords and failsafe straps per Boeing MOM must define minimum inspection methods, access provisions, and eyelash magnification or borescope requirements; otherwise inspection consistency and repeatability will suffer.

[P5] The initial inspection deadline "prior to 30,000 flight cycles, or within 7 days after Oct 3, 2019, whichever is later" is retroactive and impractical for operators who exceeded 30,000 cycles before the AD effective date; request allowance for scheduling inspections within a reasonable window rather than an impossible retroactive date.

[P6] The alternate threshold in (g)(2) referencing 22,600 flight cycles or within 1,000 flight cycles after Oct 3, 2019 is ambiguous and conflicts with (g)(1); request explanation of when each threshold applies and whether operators closer to either limit may choose the more lenient schedule.

[P6] Operators will need an explicit algorithm for calculating "whichever is later" when effective dates and accumulated cycles interact; request illustrative examples with dates and cycles.

[P7] Requiring repair "before further flight" for any detected crack is operationally disruptive; request allowance for temporary repair or flight-limited special flight permits to reposition aircraft to a maintenance base, with detailed criteria for acceptable temporary measures.

[P8] The repetitive inspection interval "not to exceed 3,500 flight cycles until the initial inspection required by paragraph (i) is performed" could create overlapping inspection requirements and unnecessary duplication; request clarification on whether paragraph (i) initial inspection supersedes paragraph (g) repetitions immediately upon scheduling or only upon completion.

[P8] A 3,500 flight-cycle interval is burdensome for high-utilization operators; request consideration of alternate interval metrics (flight hours or calendar time) or operational relief for low-risk airframes with previous negative inspections.

[P9] The reporting requirement to submit all findings (positive and negative) from the initial inspection per Boeing MOM lacks clarity on the exact data elements required, acceptable electronic formats, and data privacy protections; request a reporting template and clear definition of required fields.

[P10] The requirement to submit the report within 3 days after inspection if done on/after Oct 3, 2019 is unworkable for large operators who perform many inspections; request extension to 14 or 30 days to allow consolidation, quality control, and secure transmission.

[P11] The requirement to submit reports within 3 days after Oct 3, 2019 for inspections done before that date imposes retroactive reporting obligations on historical inspections; request a phased compliance schedule allowing operators time to extract archived data.

[P12] Incorporating Boeing MOM tables by reference without including them in the AD or docket forces operators to obtain non-regulatory documents to ascertain compliance; request that all required MOM tables be included or summarized in the AD or made available in the public docket free of charge.

[P12] Relying on the Boeing Multi-Operator Message as the inspection standard raises conflict-of-interest concerns; request that the FAA independently endorse or validate the MOM procedures or replace MOM references with explicit, FAA-approved inspection instructions.

[P13] Requiring repairs "using a method approved in accordance with paragraph (n)" is appropriate but needs explicit timelines for FAA AMOC review and approval to avoid extended aircraft downtime; request a guaranteed FAA review turnaround (e.g., 30 days) for urgent repairs.

[P14] Repeating inspections at intervals specified only in Boeing MOM Tables creates uncertainty if Boeing revises the MOM; request that the AD lock in the specific table revisions referenced (by revision and date) and prohibit future MOM changes from altering regulatory obligations without a new AD.

[P15] The permission that completing the paragraph (i) initial inspection ends the paragraph (g) inspection requirement should be clarified: does completion of either inspection on one side of the airframe stop both, or must both left and right be completed? Request explicit language requiring both sides be inspected to terminate paragraph (g) obligations.

[P16] Replacing "original issue date" with "effective date of this AD" in the Boeing MOM may create unintended scheduling changes for operators who planned inspections around the MOM date; request examples and transitional guidance to avoid misinterpretation.

[P17] The duplicate reporting obligation in paragraph (k) (reporting findings from the paragraph (i) initial inspection) risks redundant submissions if (h) and (k) overlap; request consolidation of reporting requirements to a single, clearly timed submission to avoid double reporting.

[P18] The three-day reporting window after inspections done on/after the AD effective date is inconsistent between paragraph (h)(1) and (k)(1); request harmonization or explanation why two separate 3‑day obligations are necessary.

[P19] For inspections completed before the AD effective date, mandating reports within 3 days of the AD effective date creates a logistical burden for operators with large fleets; request an extended compliance period (e.g., 30–60 days) for retroactive reporting.

[P20] The allowance for special flight permits to ferry aircraft to repair locations requires unambiguous safety conditions and operational limits (e.g., maximum distance, weather minimums, payload restrictions); request the FAA publish default safe-lift conditions and criteria that the Manager will consider.

[P21] Requiring Manager (Seattle ACO Branch) concurrence for special flight permits centralizes decision-making and could delay urgent ferry flights; request delegation authority to local FSDOs or principal inspectors for routine ferry requests to reduce delays.

[P22] Requiring email requests to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov for concurrence does not account for secure transmission of sensitive safety data or attachments; request an alternative secure submission channel and confirmation-of-receipt procedure.

[P23] The PRA statements are boilerplate but the AD simultaneously makes responses mandatory (P26); request the FAA ensure the AD displays a valid OMB Control Number and include that number in the AD text to comply with the Paperwork Reduction Act.

[P24] The AD's statement that persons are not required to respond to PRA collections lacking a valid OMB Control Number (P24) conflicts with the later statement that responses are mandatory (P26); request the FAA reconcile these provisions and provide the OMB number before the AD becomes effective.

[P25] The prohibition on penalizing for PRA noncompliance prior to display of a valid OMB Control Number could be interpreted to allow operators to withhold reports; request FAA clarify that substantive safety-reporting obligations remain enforceable once the OMB number is published.

[P26] Since all responses to the collection are declared mandatory, operators request an explicit description of the penalties for noncompliance and the enforcement policy the FAA intends to apply.

[P27] The instruction to send PRA-burden comments to the Information Collection Clearance Officer lacks an email or web form; request contact details and acknowledgement procedures to ensure comments are considered.

[P28] The AMOC approval authority vested in the Seattle ACO Branch Manager is appropriate but AMOC procedures should allow for industry-standard submission formats and secure electronic transmission; request FAA publish an AMOC checklist and standard data package requirements.

[P29] Requiring AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO under 14 CFR 39.19 could cause confusion when operators have no principal inspector assigned (e.g., foreign operators); request guidance for foreign registrants and provision of a default FAA point of contact.

[P30] If AMOC information is sent directly to the certification office manager, the AD must identify that person by name and mailing address in paragraph (o)(1); request insertion of the current manager's contact or an updatable contact method.

[P31] Allowing AMOC requests by email to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is welcome, but operators ask for acknowledgement and target response times (e.g., 14 or 30 days) to plan maintenance schedules.

[P32] Requiring notification to the principal inspector or local FSDO before using an approved AMOC could delay implementation; request clarification whether notification may be done concurrently with AMOC use in urgent cases and whether electronic notifications satisfy the requirement.

[P33] Allowing Boeing ODA approval of AMOCs for repairs is efficient, but ODA approvals should require concurrent FAA notification and documentation; request a mandatory submission to FAA within 5 business days of any Boeing ODA AMOC approval for oversight.

[P34] The requirement that AMOC-approved repairs meet the airplane certification basis could be interpreted to exclude previously certified repair methods; request clarification on how to handle legacy repairs that were certified under prior rules.

[P35] Approving AMOCs previously approved for AD 2019–20–02 for corresponding provisions of this AD is practical, but commenters request a crosswalk table listing which specific AMOC approvals are carried forward to avoid uncertainty.

[P36] Similarly, carrying forward AMOCs from AD 2019–22–10 should be accompanied by a public list of approved AMOC IDs and their scope to allow operators to determine applicability.

[P4] Industry requests the FAA to allow accredited repair stations to perform the detailed inspections without additional FAA authorization and to specify whether non-destructive inspection technicians must hold specific qualifications or training records.

[P7] Advocacy groups request that "repair before further flight" be accompanied by mandatory reporting of repair methods and root-cause analyses to the FAA to support fleet-wide safety monitoring.

[P12] Legal experts note that incorporation by reference of Boeing MOM without making it available in the Federal Register record may violate rulemaking transparency principles; request the FAA provide the MOM in the public docket or incorporate the critical inspection steps into the regulatory text.

[P5] Small operators and lessors request an exception or extended compliance time for aircraft that are in storage or parked and cannot be inspected within the stated windows due to COVID-19 staffing and support limitations.

[P8] Labor unions representing maintenance technicians request the FAA require reasonable scheduling notice (e.g., 14 days) before mandated inspections to allow safe manpower planning and compliance with work-hour rules.

[P9] Privacy and data security advocates request that reports of inspection findings exclude personally identifiable information and that commercial-sensitive maintenance data be treated as confidential proprietary information, with the FAA publishing aggregated summary statistics instead.

[P20] International civil aviation authorities request harmonization guidance: confirm whether equivalent EASA ADs will be issued and whether compliance with one authority will satisfy the other to avoid duplicate inspections and reports.

[P1] The deadline in § 39.13(a) to submit comments by October 23, 2017 is inconsistent with other listed comment deadlines (e.g., May 14, 2018 in Docket No. FAA–2017–0792) and should be clarified or harmonized to avoid confusion among stakeholders about the actual comment period.

[P1] Requiring receipt of comments by October 23, 2017 may be insufficient time for small operators and foreign stakeholders to prepare meaningful responses; extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P2] § 39.13(f) obligates compliance “within the specified compliance times” but does not provide a consolidated table of those compliance times in the AD text; require that the AD include explicit compliance-time language (calendar days/cycles/flight hours) for each affected serial number.

[P2] The phrase in § 39.13(f) “unless already done” creates uncertainty whether actions performed under earlier service bulletins satisfy the AD; the AD should explicitly list acceptable prior actions and documentation that constitute compliance.

[P3] The exception in § 39.13(f) (“unless already done”) should require operators to submit proof of prior accomplishment (work orders, serial-numbered records) to avoid inconsistent interpretations by principal inspectors.

[P4] § 39.13(g) requires ultrasonic inspection at each piece-part exposure but does not define “piece-part exposure”; the FAA should define this term (e.g., removal to piece-part level for maintenance, repair, overhaul) to avoid enforcement variability.

[P4] Mandating UI at each piece-part exposure per § 39.13(g) will substantially increase shop labor and teardown time for MROs; provide an economic analysis or allow risk-based intervals rather than every exposure.

[P4] The requirement in § 39.13(g) to follow “the referenced GE service bulletin instructions” should be limited to instructions that are expressly incorporated by reference and available to the public at no cost, otherwise it violates notice requirements.

[P4] Performing ultrasonic inspections at every piece‑part exposure as required in § 39.13(g) is technically impractical for certain repair processes where disks remain assembled; provide acceptable alternative inspection techniques or AMOC pathways.

[P5] § 39.13(i)(1) gives the Manager authority to approve AMOCs but omits timelines for FAA response to AMOC requests; establish maximum FAA review times (e.g., 60 days) to prevent prolonged grounding or operational disruption.

[P6] The condition in § 39.13(i)(1) limiting AMOC approvals to requests made per 14 CFR 39.19 is reasonable, but the rule should explicitly allow simultaneous submission under manufacturer-established approval processes to streamline approvals.

[P7] Requiring AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO per § 39.13(i)(1) will burden operators without principal inspectors (e.g., certain repair stations); allow direct submission to the ECO Branch as an alternative.

[P8] § 39.13(i)(1) instructs senders to address direct submissions to the person named in paragraph (j)(1) but the AD duplicates contact blocks and may be confusing; include full name and mailing address in a single location and confirm that electronic submissions meet the requirement.

[P9] Permission to email AMOCs to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov (§ 39.13(i)(1)) is helpful, but the AD should specify acceptable file formats, maximum attachment sizes, and secure transmission options for proprietary data.

[P10] § 39.13(i)(2) obligates notification of the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC; require that the FAA provide written AMOC approval to the operator prior to operational use rather than relying solely on operator notification.

[P11] The exception in § 39.13(i)(2) allowing notification to the local FSDO/CHDO manager if no principal inspector exists is appropriate, but the AD should list contact procedures for foreign operators who do not have U.S.-based inspectors.

[P12] § 1216.11’s permission for the Board to determine an alternative fiscal year is overly broad; require that any alternative fiscal year adopted by the Board be approved in writing by the Secretary and publicly noticed at least 30 days before implementation.

[P13] The Secretary’s obligation in § 1216.11 to approve any Board-determined alternative fiscal year lacks criteria; provide objective factors (e.g., accounting consistency, stakeholder input) that the Secretary will use to evaluate alternatives.

[P14] § 1216.51(c) levies assessments on all farmer stock peanuts sold but does not clarify treatment of exempt sales (e.g., charity, on-farm consumption); include explicit exemptions or definitions to prevent unintended taxation.

raw_output:
[P1] The broad prohibition in §17.44(ff)(1) as written is vague because it applies to "persons under U.S. jurisdiction" without clarifying whether this includes federal contractors, state and local governments, tribal governments, and foreign entities operating in U.S. waters—request clearer definitional language or examples.

[P1] The rule should explicitly state whether incidental observers (e.g., recreational fishers who unintentionally net sickle darters) are criminally liable under §17.44(ff)(1) absent an exception; the current text could be read to impose criminal penalties for inadvertent, non-negligent conduct.

[P2] The import/export prohibition in §17.44(ff)(1)(i) lacks guidance on scientific transfers and museum loans across state lines or international borders that are non-commercial; recommend an explicit carve-out or streamlined permit process for bona fide scientific and conservation exchanges.

[P3] The take prohibition in §17.44(ff)(1)(ii) references §17.21(c)(1) but provides no clarity regarding activities such as electrofishing for population surveys conducted under state permits; request explicit cross-reference language allowing authorized survey methods when permitted under §17.32 or state agreements.

[P4] The possession prohibition in §17.44(ff)(1)(iii) could unintentionally prohibit temporary custody of injured sickle darters by wildlife rehabilitators; recommend an explicit exception or express inclusion of licensed rehabilitators under the §17.44(ff)(2)(i) permit pathway.

[P5] The interstate commerce ban in §17.44(ff)(1)(iv) will disrupt existing aquaculture or bait industries if sickle darter bycatch is transported across state lines; recommend narrow definitions, safe harbor procedures, or mandatory reporting and destruction protocols to avoid penalizing incidental commerce.

[P6] The sale prohibition in §17.44(ff)(1)(v) should clarify whether it applies to parts or derivatives (e.g., preserved specimens for teaching) and whether previously lawfully acquired specimens are grandfathered; request guidance or registration requirements for legacy collections.

[P7] The general exception framework in §17.44(ff)(2) is too fragmented; request a consolidated compliance flowchart and clear criteria so practitioners can determine whether an activity qualifies as an exception.

[P8] The permit authorization in §17.44(ff)(2)(i) referencing §17.32 should specify expected processing times, criteria for issuance, and conditions to ensure that agencies can issue permits quickly for time-sensitive conservation work.

[P9] The permission in §17.44(ff)(2)(ii) allowing certain takes per §17.21(c)(2)-(c)(4) should be clarified to state whether fatal takes are ever permitted and under what strict standards; conservation groups will seek strict limits, while industry will need certainty on acceptable incidental mortality rates.

[P10] The permitless take allowed under §17.44(ff)(2)(iii) via §17.31(b) requires specification of the minimal documentation or notification required to the Service to ensure transparency and enable enforcement; request mandatory post-activity reporting.

[P11] The incidental-take exception in §17.44(ff)(2)(iv) ties activities to specific project standards but lacks a required monitoring and adaptive-management component; recommend mandatory pre- and post-project monitoring to verify that the ecological outcomes (e.g., “ecologically functioning streams”) are achieved.

[P12] For §17.44(ff)(2)(iv)(A) channel restoration projects, the April 1–January 31 work window conflicts with typical construction windows and migratory timing in some states; request justification for these dates and consider regionally adjusted windows based on local spawning phenology.

[P13] §17.44(ff)(2)(iv)(A) requires creation of "natural, physically stable, ecologically functioning streams" but provides no measurable performance standards (e.g., bank stability metrics, native vegetation cover targets); recommend adding objective criteria and third-party verification.

[P14] The April 1–January 31 temporal restriction in §17.44(ff)(2)(iv)(A) is ambiguous about project initiation vs. in-water work; request clarification on whether multi-season projects that begin outside the window but have in-water phases are covered.

[P15] §17.44(ff)(2)(iv)(B) permits bioengineered streambank stabilization but prohibits sole use of rip-rap, rock baskets, or gabions; this could prohibit necessary emergency repairs where rock armoring is the only feasible alternative—request an emergency exception or allowance when bioengineering is infeasible.

[P16] The prohibition in §17.44(ff)(2)(iv)(B) on solely using quarried rock may increase costs and project timelines for municipalities that lack access to bioengineering expertise; recommend phased compliance, grant assistance, or technical support.

[P17] §17.44(ff)(2)(iv)(B) is vague about what constitutes "bioengineering techniques" and which materials or products are acceptable; request a non-exhaustive list of acceptable methods and certified practitioners.

[P18] For the bridge/culvert/dam removal projects in §17.44(ff)(2)(iv)(C), the rule should define "removal" vs. "replacement" and state whether temporary dewatering or short-term in-stream work windows beyond April 1–January 31 are permissible with mitigation measures.

[P19] §17.44(ff)(2)(iv)(C) lacks requirements for post-removal site stabilization and invasive species control, which are critical to ensure long-term habitat benefits; request mandatory restoration plans with monitoring and maintenance obligations.

[P20] The silviculture exception in §17.44(ff)(2)(iv)(D) that conditions eligibility on implementing State BMPs (§17.44(ff)(2)(iv)(D)(1)) creates uneven protection across states with varying BMP stringency; request minimum federal baseline BMP standards to ensure consistent protections.

[P21] Relying on State BMPs for §17.44(ff)(2)(iv)(D)(1) could create legal uncertainty for multi-state timber operators; request an explicit list of acceptable state BMP programs or a federal checklist confirming equivalency.

[P22] The temporal restriction in §17.44(ff)(2)(iv)(D)(2) that silviculture in spawning habitat must occur between April 1 and January 31 appears to allow activity during part of the spawning season—request confirmation of whether April 1 marks the start or end of the closing window, with justification based on life-history data.

[P23] §17.44(ff)(2)(iv)(E) permits transportation projects that provide fish passage but does not define minimum fish-passage design standards; transportation agencies need concrete design criteria (e.g., culvert slope, aperture, substrate) to plan projects without undue litigation risk.

[P24] The rule should clarify whether existing transportation projects scheduled before listing that include fish-passage measures automatically qualify for the incidental-take exception under §17.44(ff)(2)(iv)(E), or whether retroactive compliance review is required.

[P25] The possession allowance in §17.44(ff)(2)(v) for unlawfully taken wildlife per §17.21(d)(2) needs clarity on the chain-of-custody and reporting requirements to prevent illegal trade while allowing salvage and research uses.

[P26] Cross-references to §§17.4, 17.5, 17.21, 17.31, 17.32, etc., will be confusing to practitioners; recommend an integrated appendix summarizing all referenced definitions, standards, and examples specific to the sickle darter.

[P27] The rule lacks estimated economic impacts of prohibitions (P1–P6) and permissions (P7–P20) on local governments, transportation agencies, forestry industry, and conservation NGOs; request a Regulatory Impact Analysis with quantified costs and benefits.

[P28] The enforcement provisions and penalties for violation of §17.44(ff) are not included here; commenters request clarification on civil vs. criminal enforcement thresholds and intent requirements for violations.

[P29] Tribal governments should be explicitly consulted and included in exception pathways, particularly where tribal roads, fisheries, or restoration projects may be affected; request government-to-government coordination language.

[P30] Environmental NGOs will request that the incidental-take exceptions (especially §17.44(ff)(2)(iv)(A)–(E)) require mitigation sequencing (avoid, minimize, compensate) and measurable net conservation gain requirements rather than solely allowing take.

[P31] Recreational anglers and bait dealers will request clear protocols for handling incidental captures of sickle darter (e.g., live release techniques, reporting phone/email) to avoid inadvertent violations under the prohibitions in P1–P6.

[P32] The rule should specify recordkeeping and reporting obligations for project proponents invoking the incidental-take exceptions (P11–P19), including timelines, data elements, and availability to the public to ensure accountability.

[P33] Legal commenters will note potential vagueness challenges under the Administrative Procedure Act for terms like "ecologically functioning," "bioengineering," and "fish passage" and recommend adding objective standards to withstand judicial review.

[P34] The seasonal windows (April 1–January 31) repeat throughout multiple exceptions; request explanation of the biological basis for these dates and propose alternative regional windows where local data show different spawning and disturbance sensitivities.

[P35] Conservation researchers will request expedited, fee-exempt permitting under §17.44(ff)(2)(i) for monitoring and captive-propagation research necessary to recover the species, plus clear criteria that research permits will be granted when they demonstrably further recovery.

[P36] The rule should clarify how these exceptions interact with Section 7 consultation under the Endangered Species Act when federal actions are involved (e.g., transportation projects), to avoid duplicative processes or gaps in consultation.

[P37] Municipal stormwater and flood-control projects may be uncertain whether routine maintenance qualifies under the incidental-take exceptions; request explicit language addressing routine maintenance vs. new construction.

[P38] The prohibition on using rip-rap alone (§17.44(ff)(2)(iv)(B) limitation) may conflict with FEMA or state emergency management guidance after floods; request an emergency-use provision or coordination with disaster-relief agencies.

[P39] Industry commenters will ask for a clear process for obtaining determinations of eligibility for an incidental-take exception prior to committing funds to a project—e.g., pre-application consultations or written concurrence from the Service.

[P40] The rule should provide transitional provisions for projects currently permitted or in progress at the time of the rule’s effective date, specifying whether they are grandfathered and the documentation needed to qualify.

[P1] Industry commenters will argue that the phrase “unless already done” should require documentation of prior compliance (e.g., logbook entry or maintenance record reference) and request that the rule specify acceptable proof to prevent enforcement ambiguity.

[P2] Several stakeholders will assert that the comments due date of September 11, 2017 (§ 39.13(a)) provides an inadequate period for thorough technical and operational analysis and will request an extension of the comment period by at least 60 days to allow fleet operators, suppliers, and labor unions to prepare substantiated responses.

[P2] Legal commenters will state that because the proposed AD incorporates multiple service bulletins and AMOC pathways, the comment period should be kept open until after FAA posts the final approved methods referenced in paragraph (i) to permit meaningful review; they will request tolling of the deadline until related documents are available.

[P3] Operators will challenge the applicability (§ 39.13(c)) as potentially overbroad because it applies to “as identified in the service bulletin” without listing serial number ranges or configuration differences in the rule; they will request the AD include explicit serial-number applicability to avoid unnecessarily grounding airplanes not affected.

[P3] Maintenance organizations will request clarification whether airplanes modified under prior STCs or supplemental maintenance actions (other than the winglets referenced) remain in or out of applicability, since the reliance solely on the service bulletin identification may omit relevant field configurations.

[P4] Fleet operators will object that § 39.13(g)(1) mandates performing all RC-designated actions in Boeing Alert Service Bulletin 757–53A0108 without FAA review of the RC designations; they will ask the FAA to (a) publish the RC-designated steps in the docket and (b) allow operators to petition to reclassify certain steps from RC to non-RC when they pose no safety significance.

[P4] Legal and avionics suppliers will caution that requiring all RC steps without clarifying who may perform them (airline mechanics vs. OEM technicians) could restrict usual maintenance practices; they will request explicit language permitting appropriately certificated mechanic facilities to perform RC tasks.

[P5] Operators with blended or scimitar winglets will request that § 39.13(g)(2) explicitly state whether both the APB Alert Service Bulletin AP757–53–001 Rev 1 and Boeing Alert Service Bulletin 757–53A0108 must be incorporated into maintenance manuals, and how conflicting instructions between the two documents should be resolved.

[P5] Some commenters will point out a likely typo or truncated text in (g)(2) (“aeroplanes on which blended…” appears cut off). They will request the FAA correct and republish the full (g)(2) wording to ensure there is no ambiguity about which winglet configurations and STC numbers are covered.

[P6] Repair stations and legal counsel will object to § 39.13(h)(1)’s prescriptive instruction to use an FAA-approved method under paragraph (i) instead of contacting Boeing when the service bulletin directs contacting Boeing; they will contend that in some complex cases only OEM engineering solutions are practical and request that contacting Boeing remain an acceptable alternative or that the FAA provide a rapid approval pathway for Boeing-issued instructions.

[P6] Others will request that (h)(1) clarify acceptable timeframes for FAA review of methods “approved under paragraph (i)” to prevent delays in obtaining critical corrective actions when Boeing’s service bulletin directs contacting the manufacturer.

[P7] Many operators will request that § 39.13(h)(2) clarify how to measure compliance times when the service bulletin gives multiple baselines (e.g., “within 18 months after original issue or within 3,000 flight cycles after new revision”) — specifically asking the FAA to provide worked examples and confirm whether the AD’s effective date overrides all service bulletin baselines.

[P7] Legal commenters will argue that measuring compliance times from the AD’s effective date (h)(2) could create retroactivity problems for actions already scheduled per earlier service-bulletin issuance dates; they will request grandfathering language for tasks already completed or scheduled in accordance with prior compliance baselines.

[P8] Several operators will request that § 39.13(i)(1) expand the list of FAA contacts authorized to approve AMOCs beyond the Los Angeles ACO Manager, or provide an explicit delegation process, because some fleets’ principal inspectors or local FSDOs are in other geographic regions and the single-office approval may delay AMOC processing.

[P8] Trade associations will ask the FAA to publish estimated AMOC processing timelines and required documentation in the AD (or associated guidance) so operators can plan maintenance windows rather than facing unpredictable approval delays from the Los Angeles ACO.

[P9] Small operators and Part 145 repair stations will flag that § 39.13(i)(2) requires notifying the principal inspector or local FSDO/CHDO manager before using an AMOC but does not specify the minimum notice period; they will request a defined notification window (e.g., 48 hours) and a format for the notification to ensure compliance and avoid enforcement disputes.

[P9] Labor unions will seek assurance that the notification requirement in (i)(2) does not inadvertently require disclosure of proprietary maintenance procedures and will request confidentiality protections for AMOC details provided to principal inspectors.

[P10] Boeing and OEM commenters will support § 39.13(i)(3) allowing AMOC-approved repairs if approved by the Boeing ODA, but some legal commenters will request added specificity requiring that the ODA approval explicitly reference the AD number and the exact RC steps being addressed to avoid downstream ambiguity.

[P10] Conversely, some independent MROs will object to (i)(3) privileging Boeing ODA approvals, arguing it could disadvantage non-OEM repair providers; they will request equal treatment where the FAA or appropriately credentialed engineering organizations demonstrate equivalent authority to approve AMOC repairs.

[P11] Maintenance program managers will request that § 39.13(i)(4) explicitly state whether RC-labeled steps may require specific qualifications (e.g., certified inspectors, A&P with inspection authorization) and whether training records must demonstrate capability to perform RC steps.

[P11] Legal commenters will ask the FAA to clarify enforcement consequences for failing to follow paragraph (i)(4) — specifically whether an operator performing a non-RC-deviated step without an AMOC could be cited if the RC steps remain unaffected.

[P12] Operators will ask § 39.13(i)(4)(i) to permit limited deviations from RC steps during emergencies or where continuing airworthiness is at risk, with post-action reporting and an expedited AMOC procedure, rather than an absolute prohibition on deviations without prior AMOC.

[P12] Safety advocacy groups will argue that the strict requirement in (i)(4)(i) to complete all RC steps preserves safety and should be retained, but they will request that the AD include a mandatory reporting requirement for any proposed deviations to enable FAA tracking of deviations and safety impact.

[P13] Operators will welcome § 39.13(i)(4)(ii) allowing non-RC steps to be changed under an operator’s maintenance program but will request FAA guidance on acceptable documentation and recordkeeping to demonstrate that deviations did not impede performance of RC steps or return to an airworthy condition.

[P13] Some commenters will caution that (i)(4)(ii) could be misused to circumvent manufacturer guidance; they will request that the FAA require concurrence from the principal inspector for changes to non-RC steps that affect structural access, fastening patterns, or inspection intervals that could indirectly affect RC steps.
