[P1] The rule’s generic identification of “organic salt (PMN P-14-482)” without a CAS number or more specific identity will create uncertainty for downstream processors and importers about whether their substance is covered, leading to over- or under-reporting.

[P1] Industry comments will request that EPA add the specific PMN number cross-reference and any applicable synonyms/CAS to §721.11247 to avoid ambiguity about the regulated chemical.

[P2] Trade associations will challenge application of §721.80(j) to “industrial, commercial, and consumer uses” without defining the term “consumer use,” arguing this could unintentionally capture incidental household uses and onerously expand reporting burdens.

[P3] Worker safety advocates will support the provision that any manufacture, processing, or use that results in inhalation exposures is a significant new use, but will request clarification of what level of inhalation exposure (e.g., airborne concentration, duration, or likelihood) triggers reporting.

[P3] Chemical manufacturers will comment that the phrase “results in inhalation exposures” is vague and ask EPA to specify measurement thresholds, exposure scenarios, or control measures that differentiate routine contained operations from reportable inhalation exposures.

[P4] Commenters will argue that treating any exceedance of a PMN-stated confidential annual production volume as an automatic significant new use is unworkable where the PMN volume is confidential—requesting that EPA instead require notification only when a publicly specified threshold is exceeded or provide confidential mechanisms to notify EPA without public disclosure.

[P4] Legal experts will note potential due process and trade secret concerns if regulated entities cannot verify the confidential production volume benchmark and therefore cannot determine when reporting is required; they will request a mandatory confidential disclosure procedure.

[P5] Environmental NGOs will request that EPA clarify which Subpart A provisions are modified by paragraph (b) to ensure stakeholders understand any limitations on citizen suits, preemption, or other enforcement provisions.

[P6] Manufacturers and processors will request that EPA limit the scope of recordkeeping §721.125(a)-(c) and (i) to information they reasonably possess (e.g., exempting supplier-provided confidential business information) to avoid impossible information-gathering burdens.

[P6] Small business trade groups will request an extended compliance period and template recordkeeping forms for §721.125 obligations to reduce burden and compliance costs.

[P7] Commenters will ask EPA to specify how §721.185’s notification limitation and revocation process will be implemented for imports—particularly whether importers who relied on supplier representations can be held liable if a prior notification is later revoked.

[P8] Legal commenters will request clarification about the application of §721.1725(b)(1) determinations to paragraph (a)(2)(iii): specifically what criteria EPA will use to make determinations and whether affected entities will have an opportunity to respond before a determination is finalized.

[P9] For §721.11248’s generic identification of a substance (1,2-Cyclohexanedicarboxylic acid, 1-(phenylmethyl) ester...), industry will request inclusion of the CAS number and PMN number to ensure accurate identification.

[P10] Commenters will request that EPA define “application methods that cause inhalation exposures” in §721.11248(a)(2)(i), including whether low-pressure spraying, brushing, or heating processes are included, and request quantitative exposure metrics.

[P11] Municipal wastewater agencies will comment that the release-to-U.S.-waters threshold of 12 ppb (per §721.91 methods) in §721.11248(a)(2)(i) may be too low or too high depending on toxicity and persistence; they will request EPA provide toxicity benchmarks and rationale for selecting 12 ppb and an explanation of the testing frequency and analytic detection limits.

[P11] States will ask EPA to clarify the exception for “specified confidential use releases” — who qualifies, how confidentiality is claimed, and how such releases are monitored and enforced.

[P12] Environmental law practitioners will request that EPA append a crosswalk in §721.11248(b) summarizing which Subpart A provisions are in effect for stakeholders to avoid piecemeal interpretation.

[P13] Importers will request clarification on what additional record elements §721.125(k) requires (e.g., supply-chain information) and whether supplier confidentiality claims suffice to avoid disclosure.

[P14] Trade groups will request that EPA provide a safe-harbor for inadvertent late notifications under §721.185 to avoid punitive consequences for minor administrative errors.

[P15] Commenters will request that EPA provide the CAS or PMN reference for the polymeric quaternary ammonium/methoxypoly substance in §721.11249 to avoid mistaken applicability.

[P16] Worker safety groups will support §721.11249(a)(2)(i) regarding inhalation exposure but will ask EPA to mandate engineering controls and PPE as part of the SNUR conditions rather than only requiring notification.

[P17] Manufacturers will challenge the release-to-water requirement in §721.11249(a)(2)(ii) using N=1 (i.e., very low threshold) as impractical—requesting EPA to justify the choice of N=1, present supporting data, and consider a higher N that reflects realistic detection/monitoring capacity.

[P17] Public utilities and POTWs will request clarity on monitoring responsibilities for N=1 release thresholds: who must sample, sampling frequency, and analytical methods, and whether there will be funding support for small wastewater plants.

[P18] Commenters will request that EPA clearly indicate any deviations from standard Subpart A procedures in §721.11249(b) to avoid misapplication of the general SNUR framework.

[P19] Small businesses will request that recordkeeping obligations in §721.11249(b)(1) exclude redundant supplier or customer proprietary data and allow use of commercially reasonable estimates for historical volumes.

[P20] Legal commenters will request explicit treatment under §721.185 for situations where notifications are submitted by contractors on behalf of firms—clarifying whose revocation rights attach.

[P21] The generic polymer in §721.11250 lacks a CAS number; industry comments will request precise identity and any impurities or residual monomers the PMN identified.

[P22] Stakeholders will ask EPA to explain why §721.80(o) (rather than (j) or other subsections) was chosen for §721.11250 and what unique compliance requirements (e.g., worker protection, exposure controls) flow from §721.80(o).

[P23] Paint and coating manufacturers will argue that the spray-application trigger for reporting in §721.11250(a)(2)(i) is overly broad—requesting EPA to distinguish between high-velocity atomizing spray versus low-pressure aerosolization and to exempt closed-system spray booths with capture controls.

[P24] Chemical producers will object to the 20% residual isocyanate by weight trigger in §721.11250(a)(2)(i) as arbitrary; they will request EPA provide test methods, sampling plans, and a clear definition of “residual isocyanate” (free vs. total) and to allow averaging across blended lots.

[P25] POTWs and environmental organizations will ask EPA to justify N=33 for release-to-water in §721.11250(a)(2)(ii) (i.e., number of samples/events) and to explain statistical basis for choosing that N versus other values.

[P26] Commenters will request that EPA provide a phased compliance timeline for new N=33 monitoring obligations to allow facilities to budget and install required sampling infrastructure.

[P27] Industry will request that §721.11250(b)(1) recordkeeping requirements include an exemption for proprietary formulations already subject to confidentiality claims under TSCA and that EPA provide uniform templates.

[P28] Trade groups will request that §721.11250(b)(2) clarify interactions between SNUR notification revocation and other regulatory actions (e.g., TSCA Section 5(e) orders or state-level restrictions).

[P29] For the unsaturated polyfluoro ester (P–17–245) in §721.11251, environmental NGOs will request that EPA include the CAS number and provide a toxicity summary in the rule preamble to justify the proposed restrictions.

[P30] POTWs and environmental advocates will request clarification on the release-to-water requirements in §721.11251(a)(2)(i) (applying §721.90(a)(1),(b)(1),(c)(1)) including analytical detection limits, reporting thresholds, and whether bioaccumulation or persistence was considered in setting release criteria.

[P31] Industry stakeholders will ask EPA to clarify which aspects of §721.80(j) apply to the polyfluoro ester in §721.11251(a)(2)(ii), and whether consumer-use restrictions would effectively ban certain downstream products.

[P32] Waste management companies will support §721.11251(a)(2)(iii) that requires reporting for disposal other than sending via permitted hazardous waste incinerator, but will request EPA to provide a list of acceptable disposal pathways and whether permitted chemical-specific destruction technologies qualify.

[P33] Chemical waste generators will request an exception for legitimate recycling or reclamation operations that may not use permitted hazardous waste incinerators but can demonstrate equivalent destruction and containment.

[P34] Commenters will request that §721.11251(b)(1) explicitly detail retention periods for records under §721.125(i),(j),(k), as the current cross-reference does not state specific durations.

[P35] Trade associations will request harmonization between §721.11251(b)(2) notification rules and existing RCRA/TSCA reporting obligations to avoid duplicative reporting and potential conflicting deadlines.

[P36] Legal commentators will request transparency about how §721.1725(b)(1) determinations will be made for paragraph (a)(2)(ii) — including opportunity for notice-and-comment prior to final determinations that expand the SNUR.

[P37] For acetic acid, 2-(2-butoxyethoxy)- (P-18-48) in §721.11252, metalworking fluid formulators will challenge the restriction that use other than as an emulsifier for metalworking fluid is a significant new use, arguing that this unduly restricts potential beneficial alternative uses (e.g., as a solvent in industrial cleaners) without risk-based justification.

[P38] Downstream users will request a narrow definition of “emulsifier for metal working fluid” for §721.11252(a)(2)(i) and an exemption for minor ancillary uses (e.g., cleaning of equipment) that do not change exposure profiles.

[P39] Commenters will ask EPA to clarify which Subpart A provisions are modified in §721.11252(b) and to provide a compliance checklist for manufacturers, importers, and processors to implement §721.125 recordkeeping.

[P40] Small metalworking shops will request an exemption or simplified notification/recordkeeping process under §721.11252(b)(1) due to limited administrative capacity and low-volume use.

[P41] Industry will seek clarification of how §721.185 notification limits apply when suppliers reformulate or withdraw product lines, to avoid being trapped by prior notices tied to discontinued product codes.

[P42] For the organic salt in §721.11253, FIFRA stakeholders will request clarity about the interplay with FIFRA inert ingredient exclusions in §721.11253(a)(2)(i) — specifically how SNUR reporting will treat ingredients used in registered pesticide formulations and whether duplicative federal oversight is intended.

[P43] Pesticide manufacturers will request that EPA explicitly exclude FIFRA-regulated uses if those uses are already reviewed under FIFRA and provide a mechanism for cross-agency information exchange to avoid conflicting requirements under SNUR and FIFRA.

[P44] NGOs will request that EPA define “anti-scaling additive” and “FIFRA inert ingredient” in §721.11253(a)(2)(i) to avoid narrow loopholes where harmful uses could be claimed as exempt.

[P45] Commenters will request EPA to clearly list any deviations from Subpart A in §721.11253(b), particularly with respect to confidentiality protections and public notice.

[P46] Manufacturers will ask for more precise descriptions of the record types and retention periods required in §721.11253(b)(1) rather than simply cross-referencing §721.125.

[P47] Industry will ask EPA to specify whether §721.185 revocation will be retroactive and whether revocations can be appealed administratively or through judicial review.

[P48] Legal commenters will request transparency about the criteria EPA will use under §721.1725(b)(1) when applied to paragraph (a)(2)(iii) of §721.11253, and whether determinations will be published with rationale.

[P49] For the polymer in §721.11254, chemical industry commenters will request EPA to provide the PMN number, CAS (if any), and the impurity/residual profile that motivated the 1 ppb release-to-water threshold.

[P50] POTWs and environmental groups will request justification and a risk assessment for the 1 ppb water-release trigger in §721.11254(a)(2)(i) and explain detection limits and analytical methods per §721.91.

[P50] Chemical manufacturers will ask for an exemption for confidential intermediate uses (as noted) but will request criteria for claiming such confidentiality and how EPA will verify those claims without public disclosure.

[P51] Commenters will request EPA to provide examples of how Subpart A is modified by paragraph (b) in §721.11254 to ensure regulated parties understand differences from other SNURs.

[P52] Manufacturers and importers will request clarity on what additional record elements §721.125(k) requires, including whether chain-of-custody and shipping manifests must be retained.

[P53] Industry will ask for an appeals mechanism or administrative relief process if §721.185-based notification revocations are issued in error, to limit business disruptions.

Industry comments will request that EPA add the specific PMN number cross-reference and any applicable synonyms/CAS to §721.11247 to avoid ambiguity about the regulated chemical.

Trade associations will challenge application of §721.80(j) to “industrial, commercial, and consumer uses” without defining the term “consumer use,” arguing this could unintentionally capture incidental household uses and onerously expand reporting burdens.

Worker safety advocates will support the provision that any manufacture, processing, or use that results in inhalation exposures is a significant new use, but will request clarification of what level of inhalation exposure (e.g., airborne concentration, duration, or likelihood) triggers reporting.

Chemical manufacturers will comment that the phrase “results in inhalation exposures” is vague and ask EPA to specify measurement thresholds, exposure scenarios, or control measures that differentiate routine contained operations from reportable inhalation exposures.

Commenters will argue that treating any exceedance of a PMN-stated confidential annual production volume as an automatic significant new use is unworkable where the PMN volume is confidential—requesting that EPA instead require notification only when a publicly specified threshold is exceeded or provide confidential mechanisms to notify EPA without public disclosure.

Legal experts will note potential due process and trade secret concerns if regulated entities cannot verify the confidential production volume benchmark and therefore cannot determine when reporting is required; they will request a mandatory confidential disclosure procedure.

Environmental NGOs will request that EPA clarify which Subpart A provisions are modified by paragraph (b) to ensure stakeholders understand any limitations on citizen suits, preemption, or other enforcement provisions.

Manufacturers and processors will request that EPA limit the scope of recordkeeping §721.125(a)-(c) and (i) to information they reasonably possess (e.g., exempting supplier-provided confidential business information) to avoid impossible information-gathering burdens.
Small business trade groups will request an extended compliance period and template recordkeeping forms for §721.125 obligations to reduce burden and compliance costs.

Commenters will ask EPA to specify how §721.185’s notification limitation and revocation process will be implemented for imports—particularly whether importers who relied on supplier representations can be held liable if a prior notification is later revoked.

Legal commenters will request clarification about the application of §721.1725(b)(1) determinations to paragraph (a)(2)(iii): specifically what criteria EPA will use to make determinations and whether affected entities will have an opportunity to respond before a determination is finalized.

For §721.11248’s generic identification of a substance (1,2-Cyclohexanedicarboxylic acid, 1-(phenylmethyl) ester...), industry will request inclusion of the CAS number and PMN number to ensure accurate identification.

Commenters will request that EPA define “application methods that cause inhalation exposures” in §721.11248(a)(2)(i), including whether low-pressure spraying, brushing, or heating processes are included, and request quantitative exposure metrics.

Municipal wastewater agencies will comment that the release-to-U.S.-waters threshold of 12 ppb (per §721.91 methods) in §721.11248(a)(2)(i) may be too low or too high depending on toxicity and persistence; they will request EPA provide toxicity benchmarks and rationale for selecting 12 ppb and an explanation of the testing frequency and analytic detection limits.
States will ask EPA to clarify the exception for “specified confidential use releases” — who qualifies, how confidentiality is claimed, and how such releases are monitored and enforced.
Environmental law practitioners will request that EPA append a crosswalk in §721.11248(b) summarizing which Subpart A provisions are in effect for stakeholders to avoid piecemeal interpretation.
Importers will request clarification on what additional record elements §721.125(k) requires (e.g., supply-chain information) and whether supplier confidentiality claims suffice to avoid disclosure.
Trade groups will request that EPA provide a safe-harbor for inadvertent late notifications under §721.185 to avoid punitive consequences for minor administrative errors.
Commenters will request that EPA provide the CAS or PMN reference for the polymeric quaternary ammonium/methoxypoly substance in §721.11249 to avoid mistaken applicability.

Worker safety groups will support §721.11249(a)(2)(i) regarding inhalation exposure but will ask EPA to mandate engineering controls and PPE as part of the SNUR conditions rather than only requiring notification.

Public utilities and POTWs will request clarity on monitoring responsibilities for N=1 release thresholds: who must sample, sampling frequency, and analytical methods, and whether there will be funding support for small wastewater plants.

Small businesses will request that recordkeeping obligations in §721.11249(b)(1) exclude redundant supplier or customer proprietary data and allow use of commercially reasonable estimates for historical volumes.
Legal commenters will request explicit treatment under §721.185 for situations where notifications are submitted by contractors on behalf of firms—clarifying whose revocation rights attach.
The generic polymer in §721.11250 lacks a CAS number; industry comments will request precise identity and any impurities or residual monomers the PMN identified.

Stakeholders will ask EPA to explain why §721.80(o) (rather than (j) or other subsections) was chosen for §721.11250 and what unique compliance requirements (e.g., worker protection, exposure controls) flow from §721.80(o).

Paint and coating manufacturers will argue that the spray-application trigger for reporting in §721.11250(a)(2)(i) is overly broad—requesting EPA to distinguish between high-velocity atomizing spray versus low-pressure aerosolization and to exempt closed-system spray booths with capture controls.

Chemical producers will object to the 20% residual isocyanate by weight trigger in §721.11250(a)(2)(i) as arbitrary; they will request EPA provide test methods, sampling plans, and a clear definition of “residual isocyanate” (free vs. total) and to allow averaging across blended lots.

POTWs and environmental organizations will ask EPA to justify N=33 for release-to-water in §721.11250(a)(2)(ii) (i.e., number of samples/events) and to explain statistical basis for choosing that N versus other values.

[P1] The April 11, 2022 comments due date in P1 is unreasonably short and should be extended to at least 60 days from publication to allow operators, MROs, and unions sufficient time to analyze the technical requirements and coordinate industry-wide responses.

[P1] Small operators and independent repair stations will be disproportionately burdened by the April 11, 2022 deadline (P1); FAA should provide guidance and outreach along with an extended comment period.

[P1] The rule must clarify whether electronic comments and late submissions will be accepted if delivery interruptions occur before April 11, 2022 (P1); specify procedures for postmark/date-stamp acceptance.

[P2] The compliance obligation in P2 lacks clarity about whether "compliance times specified" are calendar times, flight-hour thresholds, flight-cycle thresholds, or calendar-plus-usage; the FAA should require the Bulletin's compliance metrics to be restated explicitly in the AD.

[P2] P2 should explicitly state whether previously completed actions using alternate procedures documented in supplier service bulletins or previous AMOCs are considered acceptable and documented for compliance credit; otherwise operators face inconsistent enforcement.

[P3] Requiring performance "at the specified times" per Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin (P3) makes compliance contingent on a non-regulatory manufacturer's document; the AD should embed the exact actions and times rather than rely on external Boeing material to ensure enforceability.

[P3] The AD should specify which versions of the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin are incorporated by reference; P3 refers to the bulletin but does not identify revision/version control or how later Boeing revisions will be treated.

[P3] For transparency and legal certainty, P3 must include the full text or a complete summary of the "Accomplishment Instructions" within the AD or confirm exact incorporation by reference citations and public availability.

[P4] The exception in P4 that replaces "original issue date" with the AD effective date is ambiguous regarding whether future revisions to Boeing's bulletin that retain "original issue date" language will be affected; the AD should state that any occurrence of "original issue date" in the bulletin is to be read as this AD's effective date (P4) to avoid confusion.

[P4] P4 should clarify whether "effective date of this AD" means the date specified in the Federal Register publication or the date the AD becomes enforceable for a particular operator; specify how to determine effective date for operators in different jurisdictions.

[P5] The requirement in P5 that any bulletin instruction to "contact Boeing" must instead use an FAA-approved method (per paragraph (i)) places an administrative burden on operators and Boeing; FAA should provide a pre-approved list of acceptable repair methods to reduce delay and inconsistency.

[P5] P5 is unclear whether contacting Boeing and implementing Boeing's repair instructions without FAA AMOC approval is prohibited; the AD should explicitly state that implementing Boeing-provided repairs requires AMOC approval unless the Boeing instructions are already FAA-approved.

[P5] The AD should require Boeing to submit standardized repair methods for common on-condition findings to FAA prior to the AD effective date so repairs referenced in P5 can be promptly approved under paragraph (i).

[P6] Limiting AMOC approval authority to the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch (P6) may delay approvals for operators outside the Seattle area; FAA should empower regional ACOs or provide a national streamlined AMOC review timeline.

[P6] Industry requests that P6 specify expected FAA decision timelines (e.g., 60 or 90 days) for AMOC approval to avoid operational disruption while AMOC requests await Seattle ACO action.

[P7] Requiring AMOC requests to go to "your principal inspector or responsible Flight Standards Office" (P7) is ambiguous for operators with multiple principal inspectors or for foreign operators; the AD should define which office is appropriate for multi-office operators and for non-U.S.-based operators.

[P7] The AD should allow operators to submit AMOC requests directly to FAA's central AMOC mailbox in P9 as an alternative to routing through principal inspectors to reduce administrative back-and-forth (P7).

[P8] P8's direction to send AMOC information directly "to the person named in paragraph (j)(1)" is problematic because paragraph (j)(1) is not reproduced in the AD excerpt—this creates procedural uncertainty; include the contact name and title in the AD text (P8).

[P8] If direct submission to the Manager is permitted (P8), the AD should require the FAA to acknowledge receipt within a defined timeframe and to provide a tracking number for each AMOC submission.

[P9] Allowing AMOC submissions by email to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov (P9) is practical, but the AD should also permit secure portals or web-based submission options to protect proprietary technical data and streamline processing.

[P9] The AD should require FAA to publish confirmation of receipt and estimated processing timelines for emails sent to the address in P9 to give requestors certainty and support planning for operational impacts.

[P10] The obligation in P10 to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC is vague about required evidence; the AD should specify the notification contents (AMOC reference number, scope, implementation date) and timelines (e.g., within 5 business days).

[P10] P10 should clarify whether notification to the principal inspector is required before initial use of an AMOC on an aircraft type not previously covered by that inspector (e.g., for third-party maintenance providers).

[P11] Allowing the Authorized Boeing ODA to approve AMOC-based repairs (P11) may create conflicts of interest; the AD should require independent FAA review or secondary FAA concurrence when ODAs approve deviations used to satisfy AD requirements.

[P11] P11 should require that any ODA approvals used under this AD be recorded and made available to the registry/owner/operator to ensure traceability and regulatory oversight.

[P12] The condition in P12 that repairs/modifications must meet the airplane's certification basis and explicitly reference this AD is appropriate, but FAA should provide a checklist or template for ODA and AMOC approvals to ensure consistent demonstration of conformance to certification basis.

[P12] P12 needs to clarify how differences between the airplane's certification basis and later supplemental type certificates (STCs) are to be handled for AMOC approval—specifically for modified fleets with STCs that affect affected systems.

[P13] The separate DATES requirement in P13 (Coast Guard comments due May 26, 2022) creates confusion when the FAA comment date in P1 is April 11, 2022; clarify whether stakeholders must submit duplicate comments to two agencies by different dates and provide consolidated submission guidance.

[P13] If the Coast Guard deadline of May 26, 2022 (P13) applies to related material, the AD should specify which aspects fall under Coast Guard jurisdiction and whether FAA comments submitted by April 11 will be shared or considered by the Coast Guard to avoid duplicative effort.

[General] The AD should include a regulatory flexibility analysis explaining impacts on small entities, repair stations, and lease operators given the compliance, AMOC, and repair approval processes (cross-references P2, P5, P6, P11, P12).

[Legal] Several provisions (P3, P5, P6, P11) create administrative delegation and reliance on non-federal documents; commenters request FAA to include legal basis and precedent citations to support these delegations and to explain oversight safeguards.

[Safety Advocacy] The AD should include a rationale for why Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin procedures are acceptable and how FAA verified their safety equivalence before mandating them in P3 and allowing ODA approvals in P11.

[P1] The en banc mandate may create conflicts of interest where a single judge has prior involvement; request authority to recuse individual judges without forfeiting a panel quorum.  
[P2] Allowing Judges unilateral discretion to choose in-person location or virtual format at their sole discretion lacks procedural safeguards; stakeholders request a notice-and-comment requirement or stakeholder input before format decisions.  
[P2] The provision does not guarantee reasonable accommodation for parties with resource constraints; require that virtual participation must be available and free of additional fees for remote participants.  
[P2] Holding hearings only at the Library of Congress could impose travel burdens on rural and tribal participants; the rule should mandate regional hearing locations upon showing of hardship.  
[P2] The Judges’ discretion to hold hearings virtually should include minimum technical standards (e.g., platform security, reliability, transcript capability) to protect due process.  
[P3] Conditioning TIP approval on an EPA TAS (Treatment in the Same Manner as a State) determination is appropriate but the rule fails to specify timelines or procedures for TAS decisions, creating uncertainty for tribes.  
[P3] Requiring tribes to meet “applicable regulations” without identifying which regulations apply creates vagueness; request an explicit list or guidance document detailing the TIP content requirements.  
[P3] The rule appears to treat TIP approval as contingent on federal determinations that may be duplicative of tribal processes; recommend streamlining federal review to respect tribal sovereignty.  
[P4] Requiring an MOA process for tribes to provide investigative leads to EPA/other agencies raises confidentiality and sovereignty concerns; request language protecting sensitive tribal law enforcement information.  
[P4] The MOA requirement lacks specificity on timeline expectations for providing leads “in a timely manner”; request clear definitions (e.g., within 24/72 hours) to avoid arbitrary enforcement.  
[P4] Mandating that tribes forward leads to federal agencies could chill tribal investigations if tribes fear federal intrusion; propose voluntary referral language except for imminent public safety risks.  
[P5] The provision that the federal government will assume primary criminal enforcement where tribes cannot exercise authority may disincentivize tribal capacity building; request a phased-assumption approach tied to capacity assessments.  
[P5] The rule does not define the criteria used to determine when a tribe is “precluded” from asserting criminal enforcement authority; request precise standards and appeal processes.  
[P5] Automatic federal assumption of criminal enforcement could create gaps in enforcement if EPA declines action; require contingency planning and joint enforcement protocols.  
[P6] The blanket prohibition on open burning on the Reservation is overly broad and could criminalize traditional low-impact activities not covered by exemptions; recommend narrowing the prohibition or expanding exemptions.  
[P6] The general prohibition may conflict with subsistence or agricultural practices; request explicit carve-outs or an expedited permit track for agricultural burns.  
[P7] The cultural/traditional/spiritual exemption lacks procedural guidance on how tribes will verify and authorize cultural burns, creating potential for inconsistent application; request an approval framework developed with tribal elders.  
[P7] The dimensional exemption (less than four feet diameter and three feet height) may be insufficient for certain customary practices; propose flexibility where cultural practices require slightly larger fires with safeguards.  
[P7] Clarify whether multiple small fires in proximity that cumulatively exceed dimensions are treated as a single large burn — without clarification, users may unintentionally violate the rule.  
[P8] Granting the Tribe the right to issue burn bans is appropriate, but the rule should require public notice protocols and criteria for declaration and termination of burn bans to protect affected residents.  
[P8] Burn ban authority should include appeal or emergency exceptions (e.g., for cultural ceremonies) with an expedited approval process.  
[P9] The prohibition on burning listed materials is necessary for air quality but lacks an explicit species/material list in the TIP; stakeholders request the list be attached or referenced clearly.  
[P9] The prohibition does not specify enforcement priority or gradation for accidental vs. intentional burning of listed materials; propose graduated penalties and remediation requirements.  
[P10] Allowing listed materials to be burned for training fires is acceptable, but the rule lacks controls on training frequency, monitoring, and emissions mitigation; require prior approval and emissions controls for training burns.  
[P10] The training fire exception should require the use of best practices (e.g., containment, air monitoring) and post-training reporting to prevent abuse.  
[P11] The permit threshold (four feet diameter or three feet height) is arbitrary; stakeholders request justification, and propose alternative threshold options (e.g., fuel load or emission potential-based thresholds).  
[P11] Requiring permits for burns meeting size thresholds could overwhelm the permitting office; request streamlined online permitting and clear processing timeframes (e.g., decision within 5 business days).  
[P12] Conditioning permit issuance on a determination “in consultation with the appropriate Bureau of Indian Affairs” may delay approvals; require timelines for BIA consultation and specify criteria BIA will apply.  
[P12] The involvement of BIA in permit decisions raises sovereignty concerns; request that consultation be advisory and not grant BIA veto authority over tribal permits.  
[P13] The mandatory minimum permit conditions (setbacks, equipment, wind limits, extinguishment) are reasonable, but the rule should provide quantitative specifications (e.g., minimum water volume, setback distances) rather than vague descriptors.  
[P13] Equipment and supply requirements may be cost-prohibitive for low-income residents; propose financial assistance, fee waivers, or flexible compliance alternatives for communities in need.  
[P14] Treating breach of permit terms as NCCAA violations exposes permittees to high civil penalties without graduated enforcement; request warning and cure periods for first-time or minor infractions.  
[P14] The rule should specify enforcement procedures for alleged permit breaches, including notice, opportunity to remedy, and standard of proof required.  
[P15] The two working-day advance notice to the Air Quality Administrator is reasonable but may be burdensome for unplanned or emergency burns; seek an emergency notification exception or same-day notification option.  
[P15] The rule does not specify the method of notification (phone, email, online portal) or confirmation requirements; require multiple acceptable channels and electronic receipt.  
[P16] The one-hour prior notification to Northern Cheyenne Fire Protection during business hours may be insufficient to mobilize resources; recommend at least two hours or require coordination with duty officers for after-hours burns.  
[P16] The restriction “during regular business hours” leaves unclear procedures for notifications for burns occurring outside those hours; clarify after-hours notification protocols.  
[P17] Granting the DEPNR Director authority to stop burns that will cause air standard exceedances is appropriate, but the rule lacks defined air quality thresholds and monitoring requirements used to make that determination.  
[P17] The determination to halt burns should require documented technical basis (e.g., modeled dispersion, monitoring data) and allow for immediate administrative review to avoid arbitrary stoppages.  
[P18] Empowering the Air Quality Administrator to issue compliance orders is standard, but the rule should require that compliance orders include findings of fact, legal grounds, and an explanation of remedies to satisfy due process.  
[P18] The Administrator’s authority to issue compliance orders must include procedural protections (notice, opportunity to respond) prior to imposition of penalties except in emergency cases.  
[P19] Civil penalties up to $5,000 per day per violation are high and could be disproportionate for small-scale or inadvertent violations; recommend a tiered penalty schedule tied to culpability and harm.  
[P19] The ability to recover DEPNR costs in compliance orders could create a perverse incentive for enforcement actions; require documentation of costs and limitation to reasonable, itemized expenses.  
[P20] Allowing the Administrator to file civil actions in Tribal Court is appropriate but the TIP should confirm availability of injunctive relief standards and include rules for service and enforcement of judgments.  
[P20] The TIP should clarify whether the Tribe will permit jury trials or other procedural rights in tribal court enforcement actions to protect defendants’ rights.  
[P21] The 30-day window to petition for administrative review may be too short for complex cases; recommend extending to 60 days or allowing tolling for good cause.  
[P21] The rule should specify the form and content requirements of a petition for administrative review to prevent dismissal on technical grounds.  
[P22] The Director’s duty to “promptly” review petitions is vague; require a specific deadline for decision (e.g., within 30 or 45 days) and criteria for extensions.  
[P22] The Director’s decision should include written findings of fact and legal conclusions to facilitate meaningful judicial review.  
[P23] Allowing alleged violators to file in Tribal Court is necessary, but the TIP should ensure independent judiciary procedures and protections against agency domination of the court.  
[P23] The TIP should clarify standards of review and available remedies in Tribal Court to ensure predictable outcomes for petitioners.  
[P24] The standard that Tribal Court must uphold Director decisions unless arbitrary and capricious or contrary to law may unduly defer to agency determinations; recommend adopting de novo review for mixed questions of law.  
[P24] The abbreviated “arbitrary and capricious” standard may be inappropriate in tribal courts lacking detailed administrative law precedent; propose training or appellate review mechanisms.  
[P25] EPA’s responsibility to pursue criminal enforcement when tribes lack criminal authority could leave enforcement gaps if EPA resources are constrained; request assurances of resourcing and prioritization.  
[P25] The provision should clarify the types of criminal violations EPA will prioritize and the criteria for EPA initiating prosecutions in Indian country.  
[P26] The MOA term requiring referral of violations beyond tribal authority to EPA Region 8 presumes EPA will act; the MOA should include timelines for EPA response and mechanisms for joint investigation.  
[P26] The MOA should protect tribal confidentiality and evidence sharing protocols and specify how jurisdictional disputes will be resolved.  
[P27] Preserving tribal authority to pursue criminal enforcement is essential; however, the rule should clarify interaction between tribal prosecutions and potential federal prosecutions to guard against double jeopardy and forum shopping.  
[P27] The TIP/MOA should establish coordination protocols to avoid conflicting prosecutions and to respect tribal sovereignty when tribes choose to prosecute.  
[P28] EPA enforcement authority over regulations in an approved TIP is necessary, but the scope and limits of EPA’s enforcement powers (e.g., civil vs. criminal, remedies) should be explicitly detailed in the TIP approval notice.  
[P28] The rule should require EPA to notify the Tribe before initiating enforcement under the TIP and to coordinate with tribal authorities to the maximum extent practicable.

raw_output:
[P1] Removing footnote 2 after "People's Republic of China" in § 381.196(b) will create ambiguity about the scope of imports subject to the provision because the footnote previously clarified whether the term included Hong Kong and Macau; the Agency should state explicitly how those territories are treated.

[P1] The rule does not explain why footnote 2 is being removed; FSIS should provide the legal and policy rationale for removing the footnote and an explanation of expected impacts on inspection or import controls.

[P1] Industry stakeholders (meat importers/traders) request a transition period before removal takes effect to update labels, customs paperwork, and compliance procedures that referenced the footnote.

[P1] Removing the footnote could unintentionally broaden or narrow enforcement discretion; FSIS should include sample enforcement scenarios or guidance to ensure consistent application across ports of entry.

[P1] Legal experts note that removing the footnote without amending cross-references elsewhere in the CFR may create internal inconsistency; FSIS should review and, if necessary, amend related citations to avoid regulatory conflict.

[P1] Consumer advocacy groups request that FSIS ensure the removal does not reduce transparency about country-of-origin distinctions consumers rely on; propose adding an alternative clarifying statement rather than simply deleting the footnote.

[P2] The deadline requiring comments to be received by July 31, 2017 is outdated and inapplicable to the current rulemaking record; FSIS should correct the date or remove the deadline reference to avoid confusion among current stakeholders.

[P2] Stakeholders seeking to file new comments now will be disadvantaged if the NPRM comment deadline is enforced; the agency must confirm whether new comments will be accepted and publish a current comment deadline.

[P2] Legal commenters argue that including a past date as an active regulatory text is procedurally improper and could be challenged for failing to provide meaningful notice and opportunity for public participation.

[P2] Trade associations request that FSIS explicitly reopen the comment period with a new, reasonable deadline to permit contemporary input from affected parties.

[P2] Small businesses request an extension of whatever current comment deadline the agency sets, arguing they need extra time to coordinate internal review and prepare technical responses.

[P3] The compliance obligation "within the specified compliance times" is vague where the AD references multiple documents with different timelines; the FAA should clearly enumerate the exact compliance dates in the AD text.

[P3] Operators request clarification whether partial compliance (e.g., modifying only some affected aircraft on a fleet) meets the AD's requirements, and whether staggered compliance across multiple maintenance cycles is acceptable.

[P3] Maintenance providers ask whether previous modifications performed to earlier revisions of the service bulletin count as "already complied" for the purposes of this AD; the AD should state how to document prior compliance.

[P3] Legal commenters note that the AD lacks an explicit provision for recordkeeping to demonstrate compliance within the specified times; the FAA should require and define acceptable records and retention periods.

[P3] Labor unions representing maintenance technicians request a safe-work provision or scheduling guidance to ensure compliance deadlines do not force unsafe rushed maintenance practices.

[P4] The two-year compliance window to modify and reidentify pilot and co-pilot seats is too long and could leave unsafe equipment in service; safety advocates urge a shorter compliance time (e.g., 90–180 days) for high-risk seating failures.

[P4] Conversely, some operators, particularly small airlines with limited maintenance resources, state that two years is insufficient to source parts and schedule modifications across fleets and request an extension to three or four years.

[P4] The requirement to use the specified Ipeco Service Bulletin's Accomplishment Instructions creates dependency on a manufacturer document; commenters request that the AD explicitly incorporate the SB by reference and provide free public access to the SB to avoid proprietary barriers.

[P4] Maintenance organizations request technical clarifications about acceptable deviations from the Service Bulletin (e.g., substitution of equivalent fasteners or alternative repair methods) and ask the FAA to pre-approve common equivalent measures.

[P4] International operators ask whether modifications performed outside the U.S. under equivalent national authority approvals will be accepted as compliant; the AD should clarify acceptance of foreign approvals and documentation.

[P4] Operators request an allowance for previously installed aftermarket seat modifications that achieve the same safety objective; the AD should include criteria for accepting alternative modifications as compliance.

[P5] The prohibition on installing any seat identified in paragraph (c) unless modified and reidentified should include a clear definition of "install" (e.g., temporary transfers, bench testing, or installation for ferry flights) to avoid enforcement uncertainty.

[P5] Aircraft leasing companies express concern that the ban on installation could impede aircraft transfers and request a limited exemption allowing temporary installation to facilitate safe repositioning, provided documentation of an installation prohibition is affixed.

[P5] Maintenance shops request guidance on how to handle replacement parts inventories that include unmodified seats produced before the AD effective date; they ask whether storage or sale for export is permitted.

[P5] Legal commenters warn the outright prohibition could create conflicts with existing repair station contracts and ask for transitional relief for aircraft undergoing scheduled heavy maintenance during which seats are removed and reinstalled.

[P5] Airlines request clarification whether the prohibition applies to installing reconditioned seats that have been previously modified and reidentified by third-party service centers and, if so, what documentation is required.

[P6] Stakeholders support the permission for the Boston Aircraft Certification Office Manager to approve AMOCs but ask for criteria and expected processing times so operators can plan compliance while a formal AMOC is pending.

[P6] Commenters recommend allowing other FAA offices or designated engineering representatives (DERs) to approve AMOCs when the Boston ACO is not timely available, to avoid operational delays.

[P6] Manufacturers request that the FAA publish examples of previously approved AMOCs for similar ADs to guide acceptable alternative methods and reduce submission back-and-forth.

[P6] Safety advocates caution that broad AMOC authority could undermine the AD's safety intent; they request that any AMOC must demonstrate an equivalent level of safety with transparent rationale and that approvals be publicly posted.

[P7] The requirement to follow 14 CFR 39.19 procedures to request an AMOC should include clear instructions for the documentation and substantiating data needed (e.g., engineering analysis, test results) to avoid repeated rejections.

[P7] Small operators and foreign registrants ask whether there is a waiver of the 14 CFR 39.19 fee or reduced administrative burden for AMOC submissions, and request FAA guidance on low-cost submission options.

[P7] Legal commenters note that 14 CFR 39.19 timelines for FAA response are not specified in the AD; they request that the FAA commit to a target response time to prevent prolonged uncertainty.

[P7] Industry requests that the AD clarify whether a previously granted AMOC for an earlier service bulletin or similar AD will carry forward or whether a new AMOC application is required specifically tied to this AD.

[P2] Requiring submission via regulations.gov identified by Docket ID EPA–HQ–OAR–2017–0548 unfairly excludes stakeholders without reliable internet access; EPA should permit alternative electronic submission paths or provide a temporary paper submission option.

[P2] The rule should clarify how to include the proper Docket ID in mailed or hand-delivered submissions to ensure they are properly associated with EPA–HQ–OAR–2017–0548.

[P3] The instruction to “follow the online instructions” at regulations.gov is vague—EPA should publish step-by-step guidance in the Federal Register notice to ensure consistent, compliant submissions.

[P4] The prohibition on editing or deleting comments after submission at regulations.gov is problematic because it prevents correction of inadvertent personal data disclosures; EPA should allow a limited editing window or a process to request redaction/removal.

[P4] The rule should define a mechanism and timeline for requesting removal or correction of comments containing sensitive personally identifiable information inadvertently posted.

[P5] The blanket prohibition on submitting CBI electronically is impractical for many businesses that only have electronic records; EPA should permit secure electronic submission channels that meet defined encryption standards.

[P5] EPA must define what “statutorily protected information” includes and provide a clear process for claim assertion so commenters know what not to submit electronically.

[P6] Requiring mailed CBI media to be labeled and to include an “electronic identification” inside the disk/CD is contradictory—EPA should allow a clearly labeled cover letter and a safe digital copy on encrypted media with instructions rather than undefined “electronically inside” labeling.

[P6] The provision should permit current commonly used media (e.g., encrypted USB drives) in addition to CD/DVD, and specify acceptable encryption standards and labeling practices.

[P7] Requiring both a complete CBI version and a redacted public copy imposes duplicative burdens; EPA should accept a single submission with a CBI claim plus a redacted public version submitted electronically, and clarify acceptable redaction methods.

[P7] The rule should specify formatting requirements (e.g., file types, OCR requirements) for the public redacted copy to ensure accessibility and usability in the public docket.

[P8] Restricting CBI submissions to a single EPA CBI Officer/address creates a single point of failure; EPA should provide alternative secure delivery points and an email/phone contact for confirmation of receipt.

[P9] Requiring multimedia submissions to include a written comment is reasonable, but EPA should specify minimum content or format for the written companion to ensure the multimedia material is adequately summarized.

[P9] The rule should clarify file size limits, acceptable formats, and instructions for submitting multimedia materials so submitters are not rejected for technical reasons.

[P10] Treating the written comment as the “official comment” risks discounting substantive content contained only in multimedia; EPA should require the written comment to summarize and reference all substantive multimedia content and provide a cross-reference protocol.

[P11] The rule’s statement that EPA “may publish any comment received” raises concerns about privacy—EPA should clarify its policies on redaction of personal data and provide an opt-out process for personal contact information.

[P12] The permission to inspect documents at EPA Region 6 is useful, but commenters outside that region need an alternative; EPA should ensure all materials are accessible online or through local regional offices.

[P13] EPA’s claim that documents are available online should include stable URLs and confirmation that archived materials (e.g., designation recommendations from Texas) are complete and machine-readable.

[P14] EPA’s invitation to provide input must be accompanied by clear timelines and the method by which input will be considered and referenced in the final decision.

[P15] The “ensure full consideration” condition tying consideration to the April 30, 2018 docket deadline is unfairly rigid—EPA should commit to considering late-filed substantial information if it is timely related and explains reasons for delay.

[P16] The guidance header lacks specific procedural details (acceptable file formats, page limits, signature requirements); EPA should include this detailed guidance in the supplementary information.

[P17] The obligation to identify the rule by docket number and other details is reasonable, but EPA should specify the exact text or metadata fields to include to prevent misfiling.

[P18] The generic “follow directions” obligation should be accompanied by a checklist of required submission elements to aid compliance by citizens and small organizations.

[P19] The encouragement to suggest alternatives is good, but EPA should specify whether alternative regulatory language will be posted and how it will be treated in the administrative record.

[P20] The request for comments addressing section 107(d)(1)(A) criteria should include a clear list of the specific criteria and data formats EPA will accept (e.g., emissions inventories, modeling outputs).

[P20] EPA should clarify whether modeling data submitted to support boundary recommendations must follow specified modeling protocols or peer-review standards.

[P21] Requiring commenters to describe assumptions and include technical data imposes an undue burden on low-resourced community groups; EPA should accept qualitative evidence and community testimony alongside technical data.

[P22] The obligation to provide specific examples and alternatives should include guidance on the level of detail necessary for EPA to act on boundary modification requests.

[P23] “Explain your views as clearly as possible” is not enforceable; EPA should provide examples of effective comments and poor comment examples to improve public input quality.

[P24] Redundant restatement of the comment deadline is confusing given later CMS extensions; EPA must reconcile the April 30, 2018 date with the extended deadlines discussed elsewhere in the rule.

[P25] The prohibition on considering materials located outside the primary submission may prevent EPA from considering relevant data housed in external databases; EPA should permit links to externally hosted datasets provided the primary submission contains sufficient instructions and a permanent copy is filed.

[P25] EPA should define “generally will not consider” more precisely—does EPA retain discretion to review externally-hosted data in exceptional circumstances?

[P26] EPA’s statement that marked CBI will not be disclosed except under 40 CFR part 2 procedures should include an explanation of how part 2 procedures will be implemented and the timeline for any disclosure determinations.

[P27] The rule should clarify the process and timeframe for Governors and tribal leaders to submit designation recommendations and whether EPA will provide technical assistance in preparing recommendations.

[P27] EPA should state how it will weigh governor and tribal leader recommendations in the record and whether failure to submit a recommendation will adversely affect a state’s interests.

[P28] The 120-day pre-notification obligation lacks detail about the content of the notice and whether it allows for a formal response period before promulgation; EPA should commit to a consultation window and public disclosure of notifications.

[P29] The obligation to include violating and contributing areas under section 107(d)(1)(A) requires clear criteria for “contribution”; EPA should publish quantitative thresholds or examples used to determine contributing areas.

[P29] EPA must clarify how mobile and transported pollution sources (interstate transport) are evaluated when establishing nonattainment boundaries.

[P30] The rule should specify the regulatory actions states, tribes, and EPA will be required to take post-designation and provide timeframes to implement required State Implementation Plan (SIP) changes.

[P30] EPA must clarify funding or technical resources that will be available to states and tribes to meet post-designation obligations, especially for economically disadvantaged areas.

[P31] Requiring petitions for review to be filed in the D.C. Circuit could limit access to justice for local parties; EPA should confirm whether venue exceptions exist and whether judicial notice of nationwide effects will be published.

[P32] The “nationally applicable” trigger for D.C. Circuit review needs clearer definitions so stakeholders can know where to file petitions.

[P33] EPA’s condition that locally applicable actions based on nationwide determinations be reviewable only in the D.C. Circuit requires the Administrator to clearly publish findings of nationwide scope; the rule should set standards for such findings.

[P34] The June 23, 2020 deadline for petitions challenging the denial of reconsideration must be accompanied by notice to affected parties and a clear statement of what constitutes the “final letter” to avoid disputes over filing dates.

[P35] The suspension of hand-delivered submissions to the EPA Docket Center imposes burdens on those who rely on in-person filing (e.g., people without internet); EPA must provide an alternative secure delivery method and explain the expected duration of the suspension.

[P36] The extension of the comment deadline to 5:00 PM EDT on June 23, 2020 conflicts with earlier deadlines in the document; EPA must reconcile and state which deadline governs and whether the extension applies to all docket items (including the 2018 items).

[P36] EPA should confirm whether the June 23, 2020 extension applies to submissions of CBI and whether the CBI delivery procedures and addresses remain the same for the extended period.

[P37] Permitting commenters to use methods outlined in the February 24, 2020 proposed rule is acceptable only if the earlier methods are still operational; EPA should list the permitted methods explicitly in this notice.

[P38] Requiring commenters to submit via only one listed method is overly restrictive— commentators may need to provide both an electronic and a physical CBI submission; EPA should allow dual submissions where necessary and explain how to indicate the authoritative version.

[P39] The obligation to make all timely comments available for public viewing should include a timeframe for posting (e.g., within X business days) and a process for notifying submitters when their comment is posted.

[P40] The policy to include personally identifiable information (PII) in posted comments raises privacy concerns; EPA should remove or redact PII by default and require explicit consent to post such information publicly.

[P41] EPA’s promise to post comments “as soon as possible after receipt” should be quantified (e.g., within 7 business days) so stakeholders know when comments become public and can monitor docket activity.

[P41] EPA must state how it will handle technically malformed submissions (e.g., unreadable files) and whether it will attempt to contact the submitter to obtain a usable copy before posting.

[P42] The instruction that users must follow website search instructions to view comments is inadequate—EPA should provide direct permalinks to individual comments and a guidance note for searching by docket ID.

[P43] The electronic signature authorization for Evell J. Barco Holland (CMS) should be accompanied by a chain-of-authority explanation so stakeholders know who to contact with procedural questions; otherwise this line is administrative and unnecessary for public comment.

raw_output:
[P1] The deadline in § 39.13(a) requiring the FAA to receive public comments by March 29, 2018 is procedurally deficient because it provides insufficient time for meaningful stakeholder review and should be extended by at least 60 days.

[P1] Small operators and maintenance facilities will be unable to prepare detailed, technical comments by the March 29, 2018 deadline; the FAA should publish the underlying service bulletin and provide a 90-day comment period.

[P2] The applicability list in § 39.13(c) appears incomplete or contains typographical truncation (ends with “–251N,”); the rule must clearly list all affected A320neo/A320ceo variants, including full model designators and serial number ranges if applicable.

[P2] Airbus and operators need clarification whether supplemental type certificates (STC) or freighter-conversion airplanes of the listed models are included or excluded by the applicability in § 39.13(c).

[P3] The compliance requirement in § 39.13(f) (“comply within the compliance times specified”) is vague because the NPRM does not explicitly restate the compliance time for each action; the FAA should insert explicit calendar deadlines into the AD text.

[P4] The 24-month inspection deadline in § 39.13(h) is unreasonably long for a potential battery retaining-rod safety issue and should be shortened (e.g., to 6 months) or prioritized for affected operators with higher utilization rates.

[P4] Conversely, for operators with limited maintenance access (remote regions), 24 months may be too short to schedule inspections fleetwide; the FAA should allow scheduling based on utilization or allow phased compliance.

[P5] § 39.13(i) requires replacement prior to next flight if an “SA” stamp is found but does not define “serviceable’ or acceptable alternatives; the AD should define acceptable replacement rod part numbers and sources.

[P5] The immediate “before next flight” replacement mandate in § 39.13(i) will ground aircraft unexpectedly and impose operational and economic burdens; the FAA should allow a short ferry/repair window or provide an on-wing temporary mitigation.

[P6] § 39.13(j) permits adding service information labels when no marking is found but does not require verification that unlabeled rods meet material/strength specifications; labeling alone is insufficient to establish airworthiness.

[P6] The requirement in § 39.13(j) to add a label when no marking is present should be accompanied by a mandatory traceability or material test (e.g., hardness or tensile check) before relying on labels rather than replacement.

[P7] The parenthetical in § 39.13(j) stating replacement is not required is ambiguous and could be interpreted to allow indefinite retention of unverified rods if labeled; FAA should clarify that labeling without further verification is only acceptable when other evidence confirms rod provenance.

[P7] Consumer/advocacy groups will likely object to the wording of § 39.13(j) parenthetical as undermining safety if rods of unknown manufacture are retained solely on label application.

[P8] The prohibition in § 39.13(k) banning installation of non-serviceable battery retaining rods as of the AD effective date is overly broad without defining “non-serviceable”; the AD should specify part numbers, condition criteria, or define “non-serviceable” per an established maintenance standard.

[P8] Suppliers and MROs need a clear process in § 39.13(k) for determining serviceability of replacement stock; otherwise supply-chain disruptions and grounding risks will arise.

[P9] § 39.13(l) terminates AD 2016–25–24 requirements upon compliance with (i) or (j), but does not explain interaction where only partial compliance (e.g., some rods replaced, some labeled) has occurred; FAA should clarify whether mixed actions fully terminate prior AD obligations.

[P9] Legal counsel will question whether the termination clause in § 39.13(l) creates retroactive effects or unintended relief for airplanes that previously complied with AD 2016–25–24 through other means; the FAA should include transition language.

[P10] The AMOC authority granted in § 39.13(m)(1) is limited to the Manager, International Section — industry stakeholders request delegation or expedited review channels for straightforward AMOCs to avoid operational delays.

[P11] § 39.13(m)(1) requires sending AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19; operators recommend adding an online submission/portal and a target FAA response time to reduce administrative delays.

[P12] Direct submission instructions in § 39.13(m)(1) third sentence requiring attention to the person in paragraph (n)(2) are confusing because paragraph (n)(2) is not included in this summary; the AD must include complete contact information and back-up contacts.

[P13] Permitting email submission to 9-ANM-116-AMOC-REQUESTS@faa.gov in § 39.13(m)(1) is helpful but lacks security and acknowledgment procedures; the FAA should confirm receipt and provide a tracking number for AMOC requests.

[P14] The notice requirement in § 39.13(m)(1) that operators must notify their principal inspector before using an approved AMOC lacks a required timeframe (e.g., 24 or 72 hours) — an explicit notification window should be added to prevent inconsistent implementation.

[P15] § 39.13(m)(2) requires corrective actions obtained from a manufacturer to be accomplished using a method approved by the FAA Manager, EASA, or Airbus DOA; this tri-party approval approach may create jurisdictional ambiguity and delays — FAA should allow approval by either the FAA or EASA to suffice if the other authority is notified.

[P15] Manufacturers request clearer documentation standards and timelines for approvals under § 39.13(m)(2), including whether previously issued manufacturer repair instructions are acceptable.

[P16] Requiring the DOA-authorized signature in § 39.13(m)(2) second sentence is acceptable but needs definition of acceptable electronic signatures and delegation procedures to accommodate global DOAs.

[P17] The RC designation requirement in § 39.13(m)(3) first sentence should specify how RC items will be identified in the service bulletin (e.g., boldface RC tag) to avoid misinterpretation by maintenance personnel.

[P18] Clarifying in § 39.13(m)(3) that non-RC procedures are recommendations is useful, but operators ask for examples of common non-RC tasks and guidance on documentation when they are intentionally omitted under operator maintenance programs.

[P19] Permission in § 39.13(m)(3) to deviate from non-RC procedures under an operator’s program without AMOC is sensible but should require a recordkeeping standard and inspector notification to ensure traceability during audits.

[P20] The requirement in § 39.13(m)(3) fourth sentence that substitutions to RC items require AMOC could be burdensome for routine adjustments; stakeholders request an expedited AMOC pathway for trivial, documented substitutions backed by engineering substantiation.

[P20] Legal experts will likely comment that the AD should define what constitutes a “substitution” versus a minor procedural deviation to reduce litigation risk and inconsistent FAA enforcement.

[P1] Industry commenter: Classifying medical image storage devices as Class I understates cybersecurity and data integrity risks; FDA should instead assign Class II to require special controls for encryption, access controls, and audit trails.

[P1] Hospital IT director: As a Class I device, manufacturers may not provide sufficient postmarket support and updates; hospitals request mandatory patching and vulnerability disclosure requirements be imposed.

[P1] Privacy advocacy group: Class I classification fails to protect patient privacy because it allows marketing of devices without demonstrating secure storage practices; recommend Class II or explicit security requirements.

[P1] Small manufacturer: Class I classification is appropriate and reduces regulatory burden, encouraging innovation and lowering costs for small businesses producing storage devices.

[P1] Legal expert: The rule lacks clarity on whether Class I general controls include specific labeling obligations related to storage format and retention; request explicit labeling requirements be added.

[P2] Radiology society: The 510(k) exemption conditioned on absence of irreversible compression is reasonable, but the provision should define "irreversible data compression" and list accepted codecs/standards to avoid uncertainty.

[P2] Manufacturer: The exemption condition will effectively force use of lossless compression only; request allowance for clinically validated lossy compression algorithms for non-diagnostic uses or provide a pathway for demonstrating equivalence without full 510(k).

[P2] Health IT interoperability group: The rule should clarify whether exception applies when devices support both reversible and irreversible compression modes; propose that devices default to lossless for diagnostic images but can enable lossy with clear labeling and user confirmation.

[P2] Patient safety advocate: Irreversible compression can alter clinical interpretation; supporting exemption only for non-compressed storage is protective, but enforcement and testing protocols to verify no irreversible compression are needed.

[P3] Industry commenter: Classifying image communications devices as Class I is appropriate for simple transfer devices but not for devices that perform format conversion, routing, or include embedded viewers—those functions merit Class II controls.

[P3] Cybersecurity expert: General controls are insufficient for communications devices exposed to networks; recommend mandatory encryption, authentication, and logging as special controls despite Class I classification.

[P3] Hospital CIO: Class I status reduces manufacturer obligations for interoperability standards compliance (DICOM, HL7); request explicit requirement to conform to recognized interoperability standards even as Class I.

[P4] Telemedicine provider: The 510(k) exemption only if no irreversible compression is transferred ignores that some network conditions necessitate lossy transfer; propose an exception allowing reversible compression or documented clinical validation to permit lossy transfer in constrained environments.

[P4] Network equipment vendor: The transfer exemption should address on-the-fly compression by third-party network appliances—clarify whether the device manufacturer is responsible when intermediate systems apply irreversible compression.

[P4] Clinical guideline developer: Recommend that the rule specify acceptable compression ratios and clinical testing requirements to demonstrate that irreversible compression does not degrade diagnostic quality if a manufacturer seeks exemption denial.

[P5] Manufacturer of image digitizers: Class II assignment with special controls is appropriate; request that FDA publish the proposed special controls (performance standards, labeling, calibration) to allow premarket planning.

[P5] Dental association: Image digitizers used for dental radiography have unique size/resolution requirements; request that special controls consider modality-specific performance criteria rather than one-size-fits-all requirements.

[P5] Standards organization: Special controls should reference specific international standards (e.g., DICOM, IEC 60601 series, ASTM resolution/linearity tests) to harmonize requirements and avoid redundant testing.

[P6] Printer/film output device manufacturer: Classification of hardcopy devices as Class II is reasonable, but FDA should define quality metrics (density range, grayscale reproducibility, resolution) and required calibration intervals in the special controls.

[P6] Environmental group: Special controls should include end-of-life disposal and chemical safety (e.g., for silver-based processing), including labeling and documentation for hazardous waste management.

[P6] Radiographer technician association: Require user instructions and warnings in the special controls on handling prints used for clinical diagnosis, including storage conditions to prevent image degradation.

[P7] PACS vendors: Assigning PACS to Class II is appropriate given system complexity; request clarity on which PACS functions (storage, retrieval, viewer, workflow) trigger specific special controls and whether modular certification is allowed.

[P7] Healthcare provider group: Special controls for PACS should mandate interoperability with EHRs, support for secure remote access, role-based access control, and audit logging to meet clinical workflow and privacy needs.

[P7] Legal/regulatory expert: The rule should clarify how legacy PACS already in clinical use will be treated — whether grandfathered, subject to retrospective compliance, or required to submit 510(k)s if they use irreversible compression or lack required features.

[P7] Patient safety organization: Recommend that PACS special controls require routine clinical quality assurance checks, backup and disaster recovery procedures, and recovery time objectives to prevent data loss and ensure continuity of care.

[P2] Legal counsel: The proposed text cuts off and is ambiguous ("when the device stores images without p"); request correction and full text to allow meaningful comment.

[P4] Legal counsel: Similarly, the truncated text for § 892.2020(b) prevents commenters from fully understanding the scope of the 510(k) exemption; request complete provision text before finalization.
