[P1] The blanket obligation in §63.7500(a) is overly vague about “subject to stated exceptions”; commenters will request a consolidated list or flowchart of applicable exceptions (paras b–e) to improve clarity for compliance planning.

[P1] Industry stakeholders will ask EPA to clarify whether §63.7500(a) applies per-unit or per-source when multiple boilers/process heaters share common support systems (fuel, controls, maintenance), because the phrase “whenever the affected unit is operating” could be read inconsistently.

[P2] Facilities will request explicit guidance on how to determine which specific tables (1–3, 11–15) apply to hybrid or multi-fuel boilers to avoid conflicting obligations under §63.7500(a)(1).

[P3] Cogeneration plants will comment that restricting output-based limits (lb/MMBtu steam output) “only for boilers/process heaters that generate or cogenerate steam” (§63.7500(a)(1) permission) needs a definition of “generate or cogenerate steam” and procedures to allocate steam vs. process heat when units have multiple functions.

[P4] Owners of electricity-only boilers will request clarification of how to convert generator output to MWh for the lb/MWh output-based option (§63.7500(a)(1) permission), including treatment of auxiliary loads and parasitic power.

[P5] Commenters will request example calculations or sample spreadsheets for using Equation 21 of §63.7575 as required by §63.7500(a)(1) to calculate total steam energy output for cogeneration/multi-header systems, to avoid different interpretations during enforcement.

[P6] Operators of units constructed/reconstructed between June 4, 2010 and May 20, 2011 will support the temporary option to comply with Table 11 or 14 until Jan 31, 2016 (§63.7500(a)(1)(i)), but will request an extension of the temporary compliance window or a grandfathering provision for projects delayed by permit/backlog issues.

[P7] Similar to P6, commenters will request EPA to clarify paperwork/notice required to elect the transitional option for units constructed between May 20, 2011 and December 23, 2011 (§63.7500(a)(1)(ii)) and to allow retroactive election where construction timelines spanned those dates.

[P8] Affected sources constructed between December 23, 2011 and April 1, 2013 (§63.7500(a)(1)(iii)) will request that the rule provide a clear mechanism to document the applicable construction date (permit issuance, groundbreaking, first fuel) to avoid disputes about eligibility for Table 13/14 temporary compliance.

[P9] New unit owners asking to use Table 1 or 14 temporarily (§63.7500(a)(1)(iv)) will request explicit notification and recordkeeping requirements to document that they are operating under the temporary limit and the date when the permanent Table 1 limit becomes effective.

[P10] Existing unit owners who may comply with Table 2 or 15 temporarily (§63.7500(a)(1)(v)) will request transitional relief for capital investments required to meet Table 2 limits and a clear definition of “existing” for units that were idle or reconstructed prior to the rule’s effective date.

[P11] Facilities operating limited-use boilers will request clarification of what counts as “limited-use” for the tune-up interval (§63.7500(c)): whether a specific annual operating-hour threshold applies and how to treat seasonal/backup units.

[P12] Environmental advocacy groups will object to exempting limited-use units from emission limits, annual tune-ups, energy assessment, and operating limits (§63.7500(c) exception), arguing this could create a loophole for high-emitting backup units; they will request a strict hours-per-year cap and reporting requirement to prevent misuse.

[P13] Small natural-gas-fired boilers in the gas 1 subcategory (≤5 MMBtu/hr) will request that the five-year tune-up frequency in §63.7500(e) be extended or harmonized with existing state/local tune-up programs to reduce duplicative regulatory burden.

[P14] Owners of slightly larger gas 1 units (>5 and <10 MMBtu/hr) will comment that the two-year tune-up interval in §63.7500(e) is unduly burdensome and request alignment with manufacturer-recommended maintenance intervals; they will also request flexibility to use condition-based tuning.

[P15] Industry groups will challenge the broad exemption of all units in the gas 1 subcategory from listed emission and operating limits (§63.7500(e) exception), asking EPA to provide data supporting the health and environmental safety of exempting these units and to consider size thresholds rather than fuel-only subcategory exemptions.

[P16] Testing laboratories and compliance managers will request detailed protocols and timelines for scheduling performance stack testing per §63.7505(c), including acceptable test methods, QA/QC, and allowance for seasonal operations that make immediate access difficult.

[P17] Companies relying on fuel-analysis compliance for HCl, mercury, or TSM (§63.7505(c) permission) will request clarification on representative sampling frequency and chain-of-custody requirements for fuel analyses to ensure defensible compliance demonstrations.

[P18] Operators of gas-fired units will point out the prohibition in §63.7505(c) on using fuel analysis for TSM alternative or HCl standards when burning gaseous fuels is appropriate, but will ask EPA to allow limited fuel analysis for gaseous fuel blends where constituent data is available from upstream suppliers.

[P19] Legal commenters will note that §63.7505(c) requires performance testing when fuel analysis isn’t allowed—requesting EPA to define “not allowed or not applicable” precisely (e.g., whether partial applicability triggers testing) to minimize disputes.

[P20] Facilities planning to elect stack testing under §63.7510(a) request more time and a clear sequencing process for initial compliance actions (notification, test plan approval, scheduling) to meet the initial test requirement without causing operational disruptions.

[P21] Sources using fuel analysis for HCl/mercury/TSM (§63.7510(b)) will request clarification on the requirement to set operating limits per §63.7530/Table 8, including how operating limits are established when fuel composition naturally varies seasonally.

[P22] Manufacturers and suppliers will seek explicit definitions of the fuels exempted from fuel analysis and operating limit requirements (§63.7510(b) exceptions) and request that commonly used fuel blends be included to reduce compliance burden.

[P23] Commenters will request that EPA expand the fuel categories exempted from chloride fuel analysis (§63.7510(b) specific exception) to include fuels with well-documented low-chloride content and established supplier certifications.

[P24] Operators electing mercury or HCl CEMS (§63.7510(b) exception) will support the exemption from performance testing and operating limit requirements but request detailed acceptance criteria, certification steps, and a timeline for approval to avoid delays.

[P25] Facilities subject to CO limits will request clearer instructions and standard test methods in §63.7510(c) about conducting CO performance tests per Table 5 versus performing CO monitor evaluations under §63.7525(a), and how to choose between them.

[P26] Sources using qualifying CO CEMS (§63.7510(c) exception) will request clarity on the definition of “qualifying” and whether previously installed CEMS that meet older performance specs are acceptable or must be upgraded.

[P27] New or reconstructed sources required to complete initial compliance by July 30, 2013 or within 180 days after startup (§63.7510(f)) will request grandfathering relief for units that missed that historical deadline or, where not applicable, request transitional deadlines proportional to startup date.

[P28] Commenters who initially elect less stringent limits (Tables 11-13) and must demonstrate compliance with Table 14 by July 29, 2016 (§63.7510(f)(1)) will request more time or an alternative phased schedule to accommodate installation of control technologies.

[P29] Those using Table 14 temporarily and required to meet Table 1 later (§63.7510(f)(2)) will ask EPA to provide quantitative cost estimates and technical feasibility analyses supporting the timeline for moving from Table 14 to Table 1 compliance.

[P30] Facilities that were idle and required to complete initial compliance within 180 days after restart (§63.7510(j)) will request explicit provisions for startup testing logistics and extension mechanisms when restart is unplanned or occurs in winter/weather-limited periods.

[P31] Sources subject to the initial tune-up timing after restart (§63.7510(j)) will request clarifications on the tune-up components listed in §63.7540(a)(10)(i)-(vi), including acceptable qualifications for the person performing the tune-up and recordkeeping requirements.

[P32] Facilities that historically comply with less frequent testing under §63.7515(b) will request clear documentation templates to demonstrate emissions ≤75% of the limit for two years and a clear definition of “operations haven’t changed” to avoid enforcement disputes.

[P33] Compliance managers will point out that the 37-month maximum between tests if electing every-third-year testing (§63.7515(b)) could create a timing trap and request a grace period or safe harbor when scheduling conflicts push a test slightly beyond 37 months.

[P34] Entities electing emissions averaging (§63.7515(b) obligation) will object that requiring continued annual testing after electing averaging is burdensome and duplicate monitoring; they will propose harmonizing testing frequency with the averaged group’s demonstrated performance.

[P35] Commenters will support the waiver in §63.7515(b) from testing at maximum input levels for chloride, mercury, and TSM unless specifically tested for those pollutants, but request guidance on what constitutes “maximum chloride/mercury/TSM input” for fuels with variable composition.

[P36] Owners will request that the rule allow use of alternative statistical techniques or bootstrapping rather than rigid consecutive-year thresholds in §63.7515(c) (annual tests after exceedance) to account for measurement uncertainty.

[P37] Facilities using fuel analysis for compliance (§63.7515(e)) will ask EPA to recognize upstream supplier certifications or third-party laboratory accreditation to fulfill the monthly fuel analysis requirement, reducing duplicative sampling.

[P38] Smaller sources will request that the “monthly” fuel analysis frequency in §63.7515(e) be relaxed for low-risk fuels or where historical data shows stability; they will propose semi-annual sampling rather than monthly.

[P39] Operators will ask for explicit instructions on how to perform a fuel analysis “before burning any new fuel type” (§63.7515(e)), including what constitutes a new fuel type and acceptable lead times for analysis to avoid operational delays.

[P40] Commenters will request explicit cross-references and examples that show how continuous compliance requirements in §63.7540 apply when demonstrating compliance via fuel analysis (§63.7515(e) obligation), to avoid contradictory demands.

[P41] Sources will recommend extending the allowance to reduce sampling to quarterly after 12 months of results ≤75% (§63.7515(e) permission) to include a 24-month demonstration period for greater statistical confidence.

[P42] Enforcement attorneys will request precise triggers and documentation requirements for returning to monthly sampling when a quarterly sample exceeds 75% (§63.7515(e) obligation), including notification timelines to the permitting authority.

[P43] Testing labs will request clarification on the 14-day minimum spacing for single monthly sampling events (§63.7515(e) condition), particularly when months have fewer than 28 days or when multiple samples are needed for QA/QC.

[P44] Sources that have been shutdown >1 year (§63.7515(g) obligation) will request clear definitions of “affected sources that have not operated since the previous compliance demonstration” and flexibility when supply-chain or economic conditions delay restart beyond 180 days.

[P45] Operators restarting after prolonged shutdowns will request that the subsequent tune-up requirements (§63.7515(g)) include allowance for staged recommissioning and partial operations when full tune-up within the prescribed schedule is not technically feasible.

[P46] Owners of boilers with CO CEMS (§63.7515(i) exception) will request clarity on the certification/QA/QC and performance specification documents they must maintain to claim the exemption from CO performance tests and oxygen limits.

[P47] Test method providers will request confirmation that each performance test must have three separate runs and meet minimum sampling times/volumes (§63.7520(d)), but ask EPA to permit truncated runs under documented emergency or safety conditions.

[P48] Fuel suppliers and operators will request detailed analytical method acceptance criteria and detection limits for chloride and mercury fuel analyses for solid/liquid fuels (§63.7521(a)) to ensure test result comparability.

[P49] Facilities electing the TSM alternative (§63.7521(a)) will request explicit definitions of the “total selected metals” list, the analytical methods to be used, and limits of detection required for compliance fuel analysis.

[P50] Gas 2 fuel users subject to mercury fuel analysis (§63.7521(a)) will request alternative approaches for compositional analysis when fuels are pipeline gas with variable constituents, including acceptance of supplier gas quality certificates.

[P51] Commenters will reiterate that prohibiting fuel analyses for gaseous fuels to comply with TSM alternative or HCl standards (§63.7521(a) prohibition) should include an express exception where continuous monitoring of the gas stream or supplier-provided compositional guarantees exist.

[P52] Operators of mixed gaseous fuel systems will object to being required to treat multiple gas streams as a single fuel type and sample only the combined fuel (§63.7521(a) obligation) because this could mask high-concentration substreams; they will request the option to sample individual streams when technically feasible.

[P53] Sources using fuels only for startup/shutdown/transient flame stability (§63.7521(a) exception) will request that EPA require documentation showing the fuel is used solely for those purposes and require hour-metering to verify exemption.

[P54] Facilities will request a clear rule that fuel analyses are required only for fuels/units actually subject to mercury, HCl, or TSM limits (§63.7521(a) obligation), including examples showing when ancillary boilers are excluded.

[P55] Commenters will seek clarification about the exemption of gaseous and liquid fuels from sampling requirements in paragraphs (c) and (d) (§63.7521(a) exception), and ask whether composite sampling and preservation rules still apply to liquefied fuels like LPG.

[P56] Testing labs will request that composite sampling requirements (§63.7521(c)(1)(ii)) be harmonized with existing ASTM procedures, and they will ask for a clear definition of “approximately equal intervals” for the three-sample composite.

[P57] Plant owners seeking flexibility will support the option to average PM/TSM/HCl/mercury among multiple existing units venting to separate stacks (§63.7522(b) permission), but ask EPA to clarify how facility boundaries and subcategory definitions affect eligibility.

[P58] Facilities electing emissions averaging (§63.7522(d) obligation) will challenge the 90% cap on averaged emission rates (must be ≤90% of Table 2 or 15 limits) as unnecessarily stringent given measurement uncertainty, and will request EPA to adopt a 95% threshold or incorporate confidence intervals.

[P59] Technical commenters will request worked examples for using Equations 1a/1b/1c (§63.7522(e)(1) obligation) to demonstrate compliance under emissions averaging, including units with mixed output-basis limits (heat input vs. steam vs. electric).

[P60] Commenters unable to determine maximum rated heat input for steam-generating boilers will support the permission to use Equation 2 (§63.7522(e)(2)) but request detailed instructions on calculating the variables and acceptable documentation when nameplate data is missing.

[P61] Sources venting to a common stack that wish to average emissions (§63.7522(h) permission) will request guidance on how to apportion emissions among units and how to handle differing control technologies and subcategory-specific limits.

[P62] Facilities where units from other subcategories vent to a common stack (§63.7522(j)(1) obligation) will request clarity on how to test in the common stack using §63.7520 and calculate group limits with Equation 6, and whether test results must be apportioned by fuel flow, output, or emission factor.

[P63] Sources subject to CO limits (§63.7525(a) obligation) will request explicit timelines for installing oxygen analyzers or CO/oxygen CEMS and whether temporary monitoring alternatives are allowed during commissioning or repair.

[P64] Owners electing the CO CEMS alternative (§63.7525(2) obligation) will request EPA to allow use of newer CEMS performance specifications or updated site-plan requirements rather than being restricted to older referenced documents.

[P65] Facilities that already have CO CEMS that meet Performance Specification 4/4A/4B (§63.7525(2) obligation) will request explicit language stating these existing systems are mandatory to use for compliance (as currently phrased) and guidance on upgrades if they partially meet the specs.

[P66] Operators will ask EPA to provide clear remediation/affirmative defense procedures for CO CEMS that fail to comply with §63.7525(a) and cannot be used to demonstrate compliance (§63.7525(2)(iv) prohibition), including temporary alternate monitoring or testing options.

[P67] Sources electing mercury or HCl CEMS (§63.7525(l) obligation) will request EPA to publish performance specifications, site-plan templates, and recommended vendors/methods given the complexity and relative scarcity of these CEMS technologies.

[P68] Units planning to use an SO2 CEMS to demonstrate HCl compliance (§63.7525(m) obligation) will request clarity on the required placement “downstream of controls” and confirm whether SO2-to-HCl correlations are acceptable only when supported by site-specific calibration and data.

[P69] Test method commenters will request clarification that using EPA Method 5 with three runs at highest expected load and minimum volumes (§63.7530(b)(4)(ii)(E)) should include guidance for situations when maximum expected load cannot be reached during test windows and allow extrapolation methods.

[P70] Owners of particulate wet scrubbers will request explicit calibration and QA/QC procedures for setting minimum pressure drop and liquid flow rate operating limits during performance tests as required in §63.7530(iii), and they will ask for tolerances to account for transient variability.

[P71] Commenters will request that EPA narrow or clarify which items in Table 3 apply during startup and shutdown and provide a definition of “startup” and “shutdown” to avoid inconsistent application of the work practice standards (§63.7530(h)).

[P72] Facilities electing efficiency credits (§63.7533(a) permission) will support the option but request more detail on acceptable energy conservation measures, the verification protocol for claimed savings, and whether third-party energy audits are required.

[P73] Existing boiler owners using the efficiency credit approach (§63.7533(a) permission) will request model Implementation Plan templates, standard benchmark formulas, and examples of acceptable documentation to demonstrate initial and monthly compliance.

[P74] Enforcement officials and affected sources will request that EPA clarify how adjusted emissions (with efficiency credits) must comply at all times after the compliance date (§63.7533(e) obligation), including treatment of short-term excursions and whether averaging windows apply.

[P75] Facilities will request worked examples of Equation 20 (§63.7533(f) obligation) showing how initial compliance is demonstrated when credits are applied, and how to document baseline efficiency and ongoing credit accumulation.

[P76] Commenters will request EPA to harmonize continuous compliance demonstration methods (§63.7540(a) obligation) with existing state Title V monitoring programs to reduce duplicate reporting and inspection burdens.

[P77] Sources using the alternative CO CEMS standard (§63.7540(a)(8) obligation) will request clear alarm/action level definitions, upset conditions, and required response procedures when CO exceeds the CO CEMS-based standard.

[P78] Operators will ask for clarification on the phrase “at all times” in §63.7540(a)(8)(ii) regarding maintaining CO emissions at or below the CEMS-based standard and whether short-term deviations during malfunctions qualify for affirmative defense provisions.

[P79] Owners using PM CPMS or PM CEMS (§63.7540(9) obligation) will request EPA to publish recommended performance specs, certification procedures, and accepted reference methods for calibration to ensure consistency across installations.

[P80] Facilities electing PM CEMS for compliance (§63.7540(19) obligation) will request clarification that using a 30-day rolling average for compliance should allow transparent submittal of daily/ hourly values and specify how missing data or downtimes are treated.

[P81] Sources will request that the deviation reporting obligation (§63.7540(b)) include reasonable timelines and de minimis thresholds for reporting minor exceedances to avoid an excessive administrative burden for trivial or transient deviations.

[P82] Facilities not using a CO CEMS will request explicit content and format for the required summary of maximum CO emission levels from performance tests (§63.7545(e)(3)), and whether raw test data must be submitted or only summarized results.

[P83] Affected sources will request sample recordkeeping checklists for the retention requirements in §63.7555(d) to ensure all required records are maintained and retrievable during audits.

[P84] Commenters exercising less-than-annual testing (§63.7555(d)(5)) will request explicit templates and minimum content for the records that document prior tests were <75% and that operations have not changed, including acceptable evidence of unchanged operations (e.g., fuel purchase records, process logs).

[P85] Environmental justice groups will request that EPA require public posting or electronic submittal of compliance records (tune-ups, fuel analyses, test reports) retained under §63.7555(d) to increase transparency for communities near facilities.

[P86] Legal commenters will urge EPA to incorporate explicit measurement uncertainty handling methods across all performance testing and fuel analysis provisions (e.g., §63.7520(d), §63.7521, §63.7515) to avoid inconsistent enforcement given laboratory variability.

[P87] State permitting authorities will request model permit language and delegation guidance to ensure consistent interpretation and enforcement of averaging, credits, and exemptions (e.g., §63.7522, §63.7533, §63.7500(c)/(e)) across jurisdictions.

[P88] Small business associations will request a small-entity compliance guide summarizing obligations, exemptions, and sample schedules for tune-ups, testing, fuel analyses, and CEMS installations referenced throughout §§63.7500–63.7555 to reduce compliance costs.

Commenters will request example calculations or sample spreadsheets for using Equation 21 of §63.7575 as required by §63.7500(a)(1) to calculate total steam energy output for cogeneration/multi-header systems, to avoid different interpretations during enforcement.

Operators of units constructed/reconstructed between June 4, 2010 and May 20, 2011 will support the temporary option to comply with Table 11 or 14 until Jan 31, 2016 (§63.7500(a)(1)(i)), but will request an extension of the temporary compliance window or a grandfathering provision for projects delayed by permit/backlog issues.

Similar to P6, commenters will request EPA to clarify paperwork/notice required to elect the transitional option for units constructed between May 20, 2011 and December 23, 2011 (§63.7500(a)(1)(ii)) and to allow retroactive election where construction timelines spanned those dates.

Affected sources constructed between December 23, 2011 and April 1, 2013 (§63.7500(a)(1)(iii)) will request that the rule provide a clear mechanism to document the applicable construction date (permit issuance, groundbreaking, first fuel) to avoid disputes about eligibility for Table 13/14 temporary compliance.

New unit owners asking to use Table 1 or 14 temporarily (§63.7500(a)(1)(iv)) will request explicit notification and recordkeeping requirements to document that they are operating under the temporary limit and the date when the permanent Table 1 limit becomes effective.

Existing unit owners who may comply with Table 2 or 15 temporarily (§63.7500(a)(1)(v)) will request transitional relief for capital investments required to meet Table 2 limits and a clear definition of “existing” for units that were idle or reconstructed prior to the rule’s effective date.

Facilities operating limited-use boilers will request clarification of what counts as “limited-use” for the tune-up interval (§63.7500(c)): whether a specific annual operating-hour threshold applies and how to treat seasonal/backup units.

Environmental advocacy groups will object to exempting limited-use units from emission limits, annual tune-ups, energy assessment, and operating limits (§63.7500(c) exception), arguing this could create a loophole for high-emitting backup units; they will request a strict hours-per-year cap and reporting requirement to prevent misuse.

Small natural-gas-fired boilers in the gas 1 subcategory (≤5 MMBtu/hr) will request that the five-year tune-up frequency in §63.7500(e) be extended or harmonized with existing state/local tune-up programs to reduce duplicative regulatory burden.

Owners of slightly larger gas 1 units (>5 and <10 MMBtu/hr) will comment that the two-year tune-up interval in §63.7500(e) is unduly burdensome and request alignment with manufacturer-recommended maintenance intervals; they will also request flexibility to use condition-based tuning.

Industry groups will challenge the broad exemption of all units in the gas 1 subcategory from listed emission and operating limits (§63.7500(e) exception), asking EPA to provide data supporting the health and environmental safety of exempting these units and to consider size thresholds rather than fuel-only subcategory exemptions.

Testing laboratories and compliance managers will request detailed protocols and timelines for scheduling performance stack testing per §63.7505(c), including acceptable test methods, QA/QC, and allowance for seasonal operations that make immediate access difficult.

Companies relying on fuel-analysis compliance for HCl, mercury, or TSM (§63.7505(c) permission) will request clarification on representative sampling frequency and chain-of-custody requirements for fuel analyses to ensure defensible compliance demonstrations.

Operators of gas-fired units will point out the prohibition in §63.7505(c) on using fuel analysis for TSM alternative or HCl standards when burning gaseous fuels is appropriate, but will ask EPA to allow limited fuel analysis for gaseous fuel blends where constituent data is available from upstream suppliers.

Legal commenters will note that §63.7505(c) requires performance testing when fuel analysis isn’t allowed—requesting EPA to define “not allowed or not applicable” precisely (e.g., whether partial applicability triggers testing) to minimize disputes.

Facilities planning to elect stack testing under §63.7510(a) request more time and a clear sequencing process for initial compliance actions (notification, test plan approval, scheduling) to meet the initial test requirement without causing operational disruptions.

Sources using fuel analysis for HCl/mercury/TSM (§63.7510(b)) will request clarification on the requirement to set operating limits per §63.7530/Table 8, including how operating limits are established when fuel composition naturally varies seasonally.

Manufacturers and suppliers will seek explicit definitions of the fuels exempted from fuel analysis and operating limit requirements (§63.7510(b) exceptions) and request that commonly used fuel blends be included to reduce compliance burden.

Commenters will request that EPA expand the fuel categories exempted from chloride fuel analysis (§63.7510(b) specific exception) to include fuels with well-documented low-chloride content and established supplier certifications.

Operators electing mercury or HCl CEMS (§63.7510(b) exception) will support the exemption from performance testing and operating limit requirements but request detailed acceptance criteria, certification steps, and a timeline for approval to avoid delays.

Facilities subject to CO limits will request clearer instructions and standard test methods in §63.7510(c) about conducting CO performance tests per Table 5 versus performing CO monitor evaluations under §63.7525(a), and how to choose between them.

Sources using qualifying CO CEMS (§63.7510(c) exception) will request clarity on the definition of “qualifying” and whether previously installed CEMS that meet older performance specs are acceptable or must be upgraded.

New or reconstructed sources required to complete initial compliance by July 30, 2013 or within 180 days after startup (§63.7510(f)) will request grandfathering relief for units that missed that historical deadline or, where not applicable, request transitional deadlines proportional to startup date.

Commenters who initially elect less stringent limits (Tables 11-13) and must demonstrate compliance with Table 14 by July 29, 2016 (§63.7510(f)(1)) will request more time or an alternative phased schedule to accommodate installation of control technologies.

Those using Table 14 temporarily and required to meet Table 1 later (§63.7510(f)(2)) will ask EPA to provide quantitative cost estimates and technical feasibility analyses supporting the timeline for moving from Table 14 to Table 1 compliance.

Facilities that were idle and required to complete initial compliance within 180 days after restart (§63.7510(j)) will request explicit provisions for startup testing logistics and extension mechanisms when restart is unplanned or occurs in winter/weather-limited periods.

Sources subject to the initial tune-up timing after restart (§63.7510(j)) will request clarifications on the tune-up components listed in §63.7540(a)(10)(i)-(vi), including acceptable qualifications for the person performing the tune-up and recordkeeping requirements.

Facilities that historically comply with less frequent testing under §63.7515(b) will request clear documentation templates to demonstrate emissions ≤75% of the limit for two years and a clear definition of “operations haven’t changed” to avoid enforcement disputes.

Compliance managers will point out that the 37-month maximum between tests if electing every-third-year testing (§63.7515(b)) could create a timing trap and request a grace period or safe harbor when scheduling conflicts push a test slightly beyond 37 months.

Entities electing emissions averaging (§63.7515(b) obligation) will object that requiring continued annual testing after electing averaging is burdensome and duplicate monitoring; they will propose harmonizing testing frequency with the averaged group’s demonstrated performance.

Commenters will support the waiver in §63.7515(b) from testing at maximum input levels for chloride, mercury, and TSM unless specifically tested for those pollutants, but request guidance on what constitutes “maximum chloride/mercury/TSM input” for fuels with variable composition.

Owners will request that the rule allow use of alternative statistical techniques or bootstrapping rather than rigid consecutive-year thresholds in §63.7515(c) (annual tests after exceedance) to account for measurement uncertainty.

Facilities using fuel analysis for compliance (§63.7515(e)) will ask EPA to recognize upstream supplier certifications or third-party laboratory accreditation to fulfill the monthly fuel analysis requirement, reducing duplicative sampling.

Smaller sources will request that the “monthly” fuel analysis frequency in §63.7515(e) be relaxed for low-risk fuels or where historical data shows stability; they will propose semi-annual sampling rather than monthly.

Operators will ask for explicit instructions on how to perform a fuel analysis “before burning any new fuel type” (§63.7515(e)), including what constitutes a new fuel type and acceptable lead times for analysis to avoid operational delays.

Commenters will request explicit cross-references and examples that show how continuous compliance requirements in §63.7540 apply when demonstrating compliance via fuel analysis (§63.7515(e) obligation), to avoid contradictory demands.

Sources will recommend extending the allowance to reduce sampling to quarterly after 12 months of results ≤75% (§63.7515(e) permission) to include a 24-month demonstration period for greater statistical confidence.

Enforcement attorneys will request precise triggers and documentation requirements for returning to monthly sampling when a quarterly sample exceeds 75% (§63.7515(e) obligation), including notification timelines to the permitting authority.

Testing labs will request clarification on the 14-day minimum spacing for single monthly sampling events (§63.7515(e) condition), particularly when months have fewer than 28 days or when multiple samples are needed for QA/QC.

Sources that have been shutdown >1 year (§63.7515(g) obligation) will request clear definitions of “affected sources that have not operated since the previous compliance demonstration” and flexibility when supply-chain or economic conditions delay restart beyond 180 days.

Operators restarting after prolonged shutdowns will request that the subsequent tune-up requirements (§63.7515(g)) include allowance for staged recommissioning and partial operations when full tune-up within the prescribed schedule is not technically feasible.

Owners of boilers with CO CEMS (§63.7515(i) exception) will request clarity on the certification/QA/QC and performance specification documents they must maintain to claim the exemption from CO performance tests and oxygen limits.

Test method providers will request confirmation that each performance test must have three separate runs and meet minimum sampling times/volumes (§63.7520(d)), but ask EPA to permit truncated runs under documented emergency or safety conditions.

Fuel suppliers and operators will request detailed analytical method acceptance criteria and detection limits for chloride and mercury fuel analyses for solid/liquid fuels (§63.7521(a)) to ensure test result comparability.

Facilities electing the TSM alternative (§63.7521(a)) will request explicit definitions of the “total selected metals” list, the analytical methods to be used, and limits of detection required for compliance fuel analysis.

Gas 2 fuel users subject to mercury fuel analysis (§63.7521(a)) will request alternative approaches for compositional analysis when fuels are pipeline gas with variable constituents, including acceptance of supplier gas quality certificates.

Commenters will reiterate that prohibiting fuel analyses for gaseous fuels to comply with TSM alternative or HCl standards (§63.7521(a) prohibition) should include an express exception where continuous monitoring of the gas stream or supplier-provided compositional guarantees exist.

Operators of mixed gaseous fuel systems will object to being required to treat multiple gas streams as a single fuel type and sample only the combined fuel (§63.7521(a) obligation) because this could mask high-concentration substreams; they will request the option to sample individual streams when technically feasible.

Sources using fuels only for startup/shutdown/transient flame stability (§63.7521(a) exception) will request that EPA require documentation showing the fuel is used solely for those purposes and require hour-metering to verify exemption.

Facilities will request a clear rule that fuel analyses are required only for fuels/units actually subject to mercury, HCl, or TSM limits (§63.7521(a) obligation), including examples showing when ancillary boilers are excluded.

Commenters will seek clarification about the exemption of gaseous and liquid fuels from sampling requirements in paragraphs (c) and (d) (§63.7521(a) exception), and ask whether composite sampling and preservation rules still apply to liquefied fuels like LPG.

Testing labs will request that composite sampling requirements (§63.7521(c)(1)(ii)) be harmonized with existing ASTM procedures, and they will ask for a clear definition of “approximately equal intervals” for the three-sample composite.

Plant owners seeking flexibility will support the option to average PM/TSM/HCl/mercury among multiple existing units venting to separate stacks (§63.7522(b) permission), but ask EPA to clarify how facility boundaries and subcategory definitions affect eligibility.

Facilities electing emissions averaging (§63.7522(d) obligation) will challenge the 90% cap on averaged emission rates (must be ≤90% of Table 2 or 15 limits) as unnecessarily stringent given measurement uncertainty, and will request EPA to adopt a 95% threshold or incorporate confidence intervals.

Technical commenters will request worked examples for using Equations 1a/1b/1c (§63.7522(e)(1) obligation) to demonstrate compliance under emissions averaging, including units with mixed output-basis limits (heat input vs. steam vs. electric).

Commenters unable to determine maximum rated heat input for steam-generating boilers will support the permission to use Equation 2 (§63.7522(e)(2)) but request detailed instructions on calculating the variables and acceptable documentation when nameplate data is missing.

Sources venting to a common stack that wish to average emissions (§63.7522(h) permission) will request guidance on how to apportion emissions among units and how to handle differing control technologies and subcategory-specific limits.

Facilities where units from other subcategories vent to a common stack (§63.7522(j)(1) obligation) will request clarity on how to test in the common stack using §63.7520 and calculate group limits with Equation 6, and whether test results must be apportioned by fuel flow, output, or emission factor.

Sources subject to CO limits (§63.7525(a) obligation) will request explicit timelines for installing oxygen analyzers or CO/oxygen CEMS and whether temporary monitoring alternatives are allowed during commissioning or repair.

Owners electing the CO CEMS alternative (§63.7525(2) obligation) will request EPA to allow use of newer CEMS performance specifications or updated site-plan requirements rather than being restricted to older referenced documents.

Facilities that already have CO CEMS that meet Performance Specification 4/4A/4B (§63.7525(2) obligation) will request explicit language stating these existing systems are mandatory to use for compliance (as currently phrased) and guidance on upgrades if they partially meet the specs.

Operators will ask EPA to provide clear remediation/affirmative defense procedures for CO CEMS that fail to comply with §63.7525(a) and cannot be used to demonstrate compliance (§63.7525(2)(iv) prohibition), including temporary alternate monitoring or testing options.

Sources electing mercury or HCl CEMS (§63.7525(l) obligation) will request EPA to publish performance specifications, site-plan templates, and recommended vendors/methods given the complexity and relative scarcity of these CEMS technologies.

Units planning to use an SO2 CEMS to demonstrate HCl compliance (§63.7525(m) obligation) will request clarity on the required placement “downstream of controls” and confirm whether SO2-to-HCl correlations are acceptable only when supported by site-specific calibration and data.

Test method commenters will request clarification that using EPA Method 5 with three runs at highest expected load and minimum volumes (§63.7530(b)(4)(ii)(E)) should include guidance for situations when maximum expected load cannot be reached during test windows and allow extrapolation methods.

Owners of particulate wet scrubbers will request explicit calibration and QA/QC procedures for setting minimum pressure drop and liquid flow rate operating limits during performance tests as required in §63.7530(iii), and they will ask for tolerances to account for transient variability.

Commenters will request that EPA narrow or clarify which items in Table 3 apply during startup and shutdown and provide a definition of “startup” and “shutdown” to avoid inconsistent application of the work practice standards (§63.7530(h)).

Facilities electing efficiency credits (§63.7533(a) permission) will support the option but request more detail on acceptable energy conservation measures, the verification protocol for claimed savings, and whether third-party energy audits are required.

Existing boiler owners using the efficiency credit approach (§63.7533(a) permission) will request model Implementation Plan templates, standard benchmark formulas, and examples of acceptable documentation to demonstrate initial and monthly compliance.

Enforcement officials and affected sources will request that EPA clarify how adjusted emissions (with efficiency credits) must comply at all times after the compliance date (§63.7533(e) obligation), including treatment of short-term excursions and whether averaging windows apply.

Facilities will request worked examples of Equation 20 (§63.7533(f) obligation) showing how initial compliance is demonstrated when credits are applied, and how to document baseline efficiency and ongoing credit accumulation.

Commenters will request EPA to harmonize continuous compliance demonstration methods (§63.7540(a) obligation) with existing state Title V monitoring programs to reduce duplicate reporting and inspection burdens.

Sources using the alternative CO CEMS standard (§63.7540(a)(8) obligation) will request clear alarm/action level definitions, upset conditions, and required response procedures when CO exceeds the CO CEMS-based standard.

Operators will ask for clarification on the phrase “at all times” in §63.7540(a)(8)(ii) regarding maintaining CO emissions at or below the CEMS-based standard and whether short-term deviations during malfunctions qualify for affirmative defense provisions.

Owners using PM CPMS or PM CEMS (§63.7540(9) obligation) will request EPA to publish recommended performance specs, certification procedures, and accepted reference methods for calibration to ensure consistency across installations.

Facilities electing PM CEMS for compliance (§63.7540(19) obligation) will request clarification that using a 30-day rolling average for compliance should allow transparent submittal of daily/ hourly values and specify how missing data or downtimes are treated.

Sources will request that the deviation reporting obligation (§63.7540(b)) include reasonable timelines and de minimis thresholds for reporting minor exceedances to avoid an excessive administrative burden for trivial or transient deviations.

Facilities not using a CO CEMS will request explicit content and format for the required summary of maximum CO emission levels from performance tests (§63.7545(e)(3)), and whether raw test data must be submitted or only summarized results.
Affected sources will request sample recordkeeping checklists for the retention requirements in §63.7555(d) to ensure all required records are maintained and retrievable during audits.

Commenters exercising less-than-annual testing (§63.7555(d)(5)) will request explicit templates and minimum content for the records that document prior tests were <75% and that operations have not changed, including acceptable evidence of unchanged operations (e.g., fuel purchase records, process logs).

Environmental justice groups will request that EPA require public posting or electronic submittal of compliance records (tune-ups, fuel analyses, test reports) retained under §63.7555(d) to increase transparency for communities near facilities.

Legal commenters will urge EPA to incorporate explicit measurement uncertainty handling methods across all performance testing and fuel analysis provisions (e.g., §63.7520(d), §63.7521, §63.7515) to avoid inconsistent enforcement given laboratory variability.

State permitting authorities will request model permit language and delegation guidance to ensure consistent interpretation and enforcement of averaging, credits, and exemptions (e.g., §63.7522, §63.7533, §63.7500(c)/(e)) across jurisdictions.

Small business associations will request a small-entity compliance guide summarizing obligations, exemptions, and sample schedules for tune-ups, testing, fuel analyses, and CEMS installations referenced throughout §§63.7500–63.7555 to reduce compliance costs.

raw_output:
[P1] The safety zone description in § 165.1319(b) is ambiguous and incomplete because the provision cuts off after “north of the points between Ba,” making it impossible for mariners and enforcement agencies to determine the exact geographic boundaries.

[P1] The proposed safety zone for Lake Washington south of the I-90 Floating West Bound Bridge could unreasonably restrict recreational boating and commercial water taxi operations during high-use summer months; the rule should specify times/dates or allow permits.

[P1] The regulation fails to include precise coordinates, navigation aids, or chart references for the safety zone, which is necessary for compliance by commercial operators, yacht clubs, and enforcement.

[P1] The rule does not explain the safety justification or risk assessment supporting designation of this portion of Lake Washington as a safety zone, preventing stakeholders from evaluating necessity and proportionality.

[P2] The comment deadline of June 17, 2019 is already expired (now retroactive) and therefore the agency should reopen the comment period with a new, reasonable deadline to allow meaningful public participation.

[P2] Even if the deadline is administratively correct, affected stakeholders (small businesses, local governments, tribal governments) need at least 60 days from a complete, unambiguous rule text to prepare substantive comments; the June 17, 2019 deadline is insufficient.

[P3] Requiring commenters to identify submissions by Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2016–0694 is fine, but the ADDRESSES text truncates alternative submission methods (“or the other methods iden…”); the agency should publish the full list of acceptable submission methods and contact details.

[P3] The agency’s preference for http://www.regulations.gov is acceptable, but reliance on that single portal disadvantages individuals and organizations with limited internet access; the ADDRESSES section should explicitly provide an email address and a mailing address.

[P4] The prohibition on editing or removing comments once submitted prevents commenters from correcting demonstrable typographical errors or removing inadvertently disclosed CBI; the agency should allow limited editing/removal or provide a process to request redaction.

[P5] EPA’s statement that it may publish any received comment to the public docket must be accompanied by clear guidance on redaction of personal contact information, and mechanisms to protect sensitive personal data; otherwise individuals may be deterred from commenting.

[P6] The prohibition on electronic submission of Confidential Business Information (CBI) is reasonable but the rule provides no secure alternative (e.g., instructions for submitting CBI physically or via secure portal); the agency should specify secure submission procedures.

[P7] Requiring multimedia submissions to be accompanied by a written comment is reasonable; however the agency should clarify acceptable file formats, maximum file sizes, and whether transcripts suffice for long-form oral testimony.

[P8] Identifying the written comment as the “official comment” is problematic when oral testimony at public hearings includes substantive material not reflected in the written comment; the agency should commit to accepting hearing transcripts as official comments if requested.

[P9] The EPA’s general refusal to consider comments located outside the primary submission (web/cloud links) may hamper submission of large technical appendices; the agency should allow supplemental materials hosted externally if the primary submission includes stable, permanent links and a brief summary.

[P9] The prohibition on external content consideration creates an accessibility barrier for commenters who use cloud-hosted datasets or GIS files; EPA should permit external data with DOIs or archived URLs and state how external materials will be preserved in the docket.

[P10] Offering two online public hearings is beneficial, but the rule should ensure multiple time slots to accommodate stakeholders in different time zones and to allow in-person testimony for local residents who lack reliable internet.

[P10] The agency should publish procedures for registering to speak at the online hearings, time limits, accommodation of translators or ASL interpreters, and how oral comments will be transcribed and associated with the docket.

[P11] EPA’s commitment to respond to substantive comments is welcome, but the rule should define what qualifies as “substantive,” outline response timelines, and indicate how grouped or form letters will be treated in the response document.

[P12] The recommendation that potentially affected entities examine the proposed rule is insufficient—EPA should provide an outreach plan and direct notice to known permittees, marina operators, tribal governments, and local ports likely affected by the Lake Washington safety zone.

[P13] Listing a single contact person for applicability questions is good practice; however the rule omits full contact details (phone, email, office hours) in the truncated text and should ensure multiple contacts for technical, legal, and public affairs inquiries.

[P14] The reference to CWA section 303(c) is accurate but the preamble fails to explain how federal safety zone action interacts with State water quality standards responsibilities under section 303(c); commenters request clarification of jurisdictional boundaries.

[P15] Invoking CWA section 303(c)(2)(A) obligations (designated uses and criteria) without specifying whether the safety zone could affect state-designated uses (e.g., recreation, aquatic life) is concerning; EPA should analyze and describe any anticipated effects on water quality designations.

[P16] 40 CFR 131.11(a)(1) requires scientifically justified criteria; commenters request EPA provide the scientific basis and data demonstrating that the safety zone will protect the most sensitive uses of Lake Washington, or confirm that the safety zone imposes no water quality criteria changes.

[P17] Under 40 CFR 131.10(b), the rule should discuss downstream water quality implications (e.g., flow through to Lake Union or Puget Sound) and show that the safety zone’s implementation will not impede attainment of downstream standards.

[P18] The rule references state obligations to review WQS every three years but does not indicate whether this action triggers state review or necessitates state rule changes; EPA should clarify timelines and responsibilities for Oregon/Washington (note: provision mix references Oregon elsewhere).

[P19] The requirement to submit revised WQS to EPA is noted, but the rule should state whether the safety zone designation will require any state WQS revision or submission, and if so, the expected schedule.

[P20] CWA section 303(c)(3)’s 90-day state adoption requirement after EPA disapproval is not relevant to this safety zone unless EPA intends to disapprove state criteria; the regulation should avoid conflating separate statutory processes and explain relevance.

[P21] The provision describing Administrator promulgation of federal WQS if states fail to adopt seems out of place in a safety zone rule; stakeholders request that the agency remove or clarify this language to avoid confusion about a federal takeover of state water quality regulation.

[P22] 40 CFR 131.11(b)(1) advice to use EPA 304(a) recommendations is fine in the abstract, but where the rule elsewhere references Oregon aluminum criteria, commenters request consistency and clarity about which technical guidance applies to Lake Washington.

[P23] Restating that criteria must be scientifically based (40 CFR 131.11(a)(1)) is redundant here; commenters suggest the agency streamline the preamble and focus on the specific safety justification and impacts of the Lake Washington safety zone.

[P24] The prohibition on exceeding acute (CMC) or chronic (CCC) criteria more than once every three years is standard, but commenters note the text duplicates later Alaska/Oregon aluminum provisions and may be confusing; recommend consolidating and clarifying numeric criteria applicability.

[P25] Requiring use of the 2018 Aluminum Criteria Calculator V.2.0 for site-specific CMC/CCC calculations (III.B) is overly prescriptive; states should be allowed to use updated software versions or equivalent scientifically validated models, with EPA approval.

[P26] Expressing CMC as a one-hour average and CCC as a four-day average (mg/L total recoverable) is scientifically specific; commenters request clarification on analytical methods, sampling frequency, and QA/QC standards required to demonstrate compliance.

[P27] Repeating the no-more-than-once-in-three-years exceedance frequency for CMC/CCC (III.B) raises implementation questions: how will episodic events (storms, dredging) be treated and what monitoring protocols will determine exceedances?

[P28] Requiring Oregon to use ambient pH, DOC, and total hardness data as model inputs (III.B) is appropriate, but the rule must specify acceptable data sources, minimum dataset durations, spatial sampling density, and statistical methods for representing variability.

[P29] Allowing Oregon discretion to reconcile model outputs is reasonable; however, commenters urge EPA to require transparent reporting of reconciliation methods, sensitivity analyses, and justification to ensure protectiveness and comparability across sites.

[P30] The obligation that criteria protect aquatic life across full spatial/temporal variability is necessary but vague—EPA should define “worst-case toxicity conditions,” require explicit modeling scenarios, and set benchmarks for acceptable uncertainty.

[P31] The EPA’s recommendation that the State prepare implementation materials is insufficient as a nonbinding suggestion; stakeholders request that EPA require and review a formal implementation plan before approving site-specific criteria.

[P32] Permitting the State to use EPA-suggested methods or alternate methods (III.B) is flexible, but commenters ask EPA to define criteria for accepting alternate methods (validation steps, peer review, documentation) to avoid arbitrary approaches.

The rule references state obligations to review WQS every three years but does not indicate whether this action triggers state review or necessitates state rule changes; EPA should clarify timelines and responsibilities for Oregon/Washington (note: provision mix references Oregon elsewhere).

The requirement to submit revised WQS to EPA is noted, but the rule should state whether the safety zone designation will require any state WQS revision or submission, and if so, the expected schedule.

CWA section 303(c)(3)’s 90-day state adoption requirement after EPA disapproval is not relevant to this safety zone unless EPA intends to disapprove state criteria; the regulation should avoid conflating separate statutory processes and explain relevance.

The provision describing Administrator promulgation of federal WQS if states fail to adopt seems out of place in a safety zone rule; stakeholders request that the agency remove or clarify this language to avoid confusion about a federal takeover of state water quality regulation.

40 CFR 131.11(b)(1) advice to use EPA 304(a) recommendations is fine in the abstract, but where the rule elsewhere references Oregon aluminum criteria, commenters request consistency and clarity about which technical guidance applies to Lake Washington.

Restating that criteria must be scientifically based (40 CFR 131.11(a)(1)) is redundant here; commenters suggest the agency streamline the preamble and focus on the specific safety justification and impacts of the Lake Washington safety zone.

The prohibition on exceeding acute (CMC) or chronic (CCC) criteria more than once every three years is standard, but commenters note the text duplicates later Alaska/Oregon aluminum provisions and may be confusing; recommend consolidating and clarifying numeric criteria applicability.

Requiring use of the 2018 Aluminum Criteria Calculator V.2.0 for site-specific CMC/CCC calculations (III.B) is overly prescriptive; states should be allowed to use updated software versions or equivalent scientifically validated models, with EPA approval.

Expressing CMC as a one-hour average and CCC as a four-day average (mg/L total recoverable) is scientifically specific; commenters request clarification on analytical methods, sampling frequency, and QA/QC standards required to demonstrate compliance.

Repeating the no-more-than-once-in-three-years exceedance frequency for CMC/CCC (III.B) raises implementation questions: how will episodic events (storms, dredging) be treated and what monitoring protocols will determine exceedances?

Requiring Oregon to use ambient pH, DOC, and total hardness data as model inputs (III.B) is appropriate, but the rule must specify acceptable data sources, minimum dataset durations, spatial sampling density, and statistical methods for representing variability.

Allowing Oregon discretion to reconcile model outputs is reasonable; however, commenters urge EPA to require transparent reporting of reconciliation methods, sensitivity analyses, and justification to ensure protectiveness and comparability across sites.

The obligation that criteria protect aquatic life across full spatial/temporal variability is necessary but vague—EPA should define “worst-case toxicity conditions,” require explicit modeling scenarios, and set benchmarks for acceptable uncertainty.

The EPA’s recommendation that the State prepare implementation materials is insufficient as a nonbinding suggestion; stakeholders request that EPA require and review a formal implementation plan before approving site-specific criteria.

Permitting the State to use EPA-suggested methods or alternate methods (III.B) is flexible, but commenters ask EPA to define criteria for accepting alternate methods (validation steps, peer review, documentation) to avoid arbitrary approaches.

[P1] The October 1, 2020 comment deadline is unreasonable and should be extended to at least 60 days from publication to allow small operators and public-interest groups adequate time to analyze and respond.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether postmarked or electronically submitted comments after October 1, 2020 will be accepted if attributable to the commenter prior to the deadline.

[P1] The requirement that the FAA "must receive comments by October 1, 2020" could be read to exclude late-filed comments for good cause; the preamble should explicitly allow the FAA to accept late comments on a showing of good cause.

[P2] The phrase "unless already complied with" is ambiguous — the AD should define what constitutes satisfactory prior compliance and what documentation is required to demonstrate it.

[P2] The AD should specify how operators document compliance timing when different serial-numbered parts or multiple engines are involved to avoid inconsistent interpretations of "the specified compliance times."

[P2] Legal commenters should note that tying compliance to "the specified compliance times" without repeating those times in the operative text could create administrative law issues; the AD should restate the precise deadlines within the mandatory regulatory text.

[P3] The dual threshold "250 flight hours or 270 days, whichever occurs first" fails to account for aircraft in storage or limited-use test aircraft; the rule should define how inactive time is counted toward the 270-day limit.

[P3] Operators will need clarification whether the 250 flight-hour limit applies per engine, per CT vane, or per aircraft; the AD should explicitly state the unit of measure for FHs.

[P3] The compliance period measured in flight hours or calendar days should include a provision for fleet-level scheduling — i.e., allow the 270-day alternative to be applied fleetwide to ease logistics during maintenance cycles.

[P4] Requiring removal of any CT vane repaired per STI–72–50–254 immediately within the 250 FH/270-day window will impose significant cost; the FAA should provide an economic justification and consider a phase-in or parts buy-back program.

[P4] The AD should require traceability documentation for CT vanes so operators can identify which vanes were repaired per STI–72–50–254; without mandatory marking or recordkeeping requirements the removal obligation will be impracticable to enforce.

[P4] The rule should permit continued operation of fleets where CT vanes repaired by STI have documented non-usage in the hot section (e.g., stored spares) to avoid unnecessary removals.

[P4] The AD should clarify whether "remove from service" means immediate physical removal at the first opportunity, or removal at the next shop visit, and whether the vane may be quarantined pending replacement.

[P5] Requiring removal of any CMSX–6 CT blade that has operated in an engine with an STI-repaired CT vane is overbroad — the causal link between STI repair and blade failure should be supported by service data or limited to blades showing evidence of damage.

[P5] The AD lacks a defined lookback period or operational threshold (hours or cycles) for identifying blades that "have been operated" with an STI-repaired CT vane; operators need clear criteria for which blades to remove.

[P5] The FAA must allow inspection-based alternatives (e.g., borescope or eddy-current inspection) before mandating blade removal to reduce unnecessary part scrappage and cost.

[P5] The AD should specify whether blades installed after an STI-repaired CT vane was removed but that previously operated with it are subject to removal, and how historical records must be kept to show chain-of-custody.

[P6] The absolute prohibition on installing CT vanes repaired per STI–72–50–254 after the effective date lacks a grandfather clause for parts already in sealed stores intended for non-airworthiness use (training, static display); the AD should exempt such non-installed uses.

[P6] The prohibition should be limited to installations on certificated aircraft in commercial service; private owners and experimental operators should be allowed to install these vanes with appropriate warnings.

[P6] The AD should define "install" (e.g., includes re-installation after storage, transfer between engines) to avoid enforcement ambiguity.

[P6] The FAA should require positive identification marking or tagging of STI-repaired vanes so that the prohibition on installation is enforceable.

[P7] Allowing only the Manager, ECO Branch to approve AMOCs centralizes authority and could create processing bottlenecks; the FAA should delegate initial AMOC review to designated representatives or regional offices to expedite approvals.

[P7] Stakeholders request a guaranteed timeline (e.g., 30 or 60 days) for decision on AMOC requests to provide regulatory certainty for operations planning.

[P7] The AD should clarify whether AMOCs approved previously for similar blade/vane issues may be applied by analogy, and whether those existing AMOCs remain valid or must be resubmitted.

[P8] Requiring AMOC requests to follow 14 CFR 39.19 procedures is appropriate, but commenters ask the FAA to summarize key submission content (data needed, test results, risk assessment) in the AD to reduce back-and-forth.

[P8] Legal commenters recommend that the AD include specific criteria the FAA will use to evaluate AMOCs (safety equivalence standards, acceptable test methods) to make the decision-making process transparent.

[P9] The obligation to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO may disadvantage operators absent a local principal inspector (e.g., foreign operators); the AD should provide alternative routing instructions for such operators.

[P9] The AD must clarify whether electronic submission to the principal inspector or FSDO satisfies the requirement and whether that triggers any additional local processing delays.

[P10] The requirement to address direct AMOC submissions to the person named in paragraph (j)(1) should include that person's name, title, and contact details in the AD; otherwise the instruction is meaningless.

[P10] The AD should permit copies of AMOC submissions sent to the ECO Branch manager to be routed simultaneously to the principal inspector or FSDO to ensure coordinated review.

[P11] Providing an email address (ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov) is helpful, but the FAA should confirm receipt and provide tracking numbers for emailed AMOC requests to aid operators in compliance planning.

[P11] The AD should require secure file-transfer options for large data-heavy AMOC submissions and specify acceptable file formats to avoid transmission failures.

[P11] Privacy and proprietary data protections should be described for emailed AMOC submissions, including whether proprietary commercial data will be released under FOIA.

[P12] Requiring notification to the principal inspector or FSDO before using an approved AMOC is reasonable, but the AD should define the required notice period (e.g., at least 48 hours) and the form of notification (email, NMS entry, logbook entry).

[P12] The obligation to notify "the manager of the local flight standards district office" where no principal inspector exists could create confusion for international operators; the AD should provide an alternative contact path for non-U.S. based operators.

[P12] The AD should state what documentation must be retained after notification (e.g., copy of AMOC approval, date/time of notification) and for how long, to ensure consistent oversight and auditability.

[P12] Civil penalty considerations: the AD should explain whether failure to notify before using an AMOC will be treated as an enforcement action and what remedies (grace periods, cure periods) are available.

raw_output:
[P1] The April 3, 2020 comment deadline is unreasonable and too short for operators, MROs, and foreign regulatory partners to analyze the AD, prepare technical comments, and coordinate with Boeing/APB; the FAA should extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] The proposed requirement that "The FAA must receive comments on this AD action by April 3, 2020" fails to provide an accessible electronic submission mechanism and should explicitly state acceptable submission methods and the email/contact address.

[P2] The applicability to "all Boeing 757–200, –200CB, and –300 series airplanes, certificated in any category" is overbroad — the preamble and compliance must clarify whether aircraft without the specific winglet/fairing installations or with prior modifications are in scope.

[P2] The AD should explicitly exclude airplanes that have already incorporated Boeing Alert Service Bulletin 757–53A0108 (original issue) or later approved alternative repairs to avoid redundant or conflicting requirements.

[P2] The scope phrase "certificated in any category" may inadvertently capture museum, ferry, or limited-use certificated 757s not operated in revenue service; the FAA should clarify applicability to operational fleets vs. those in storage/derivative certificates.

[P3] The general compliance obligation "Comply ... within the compliance times specified, unless already done" lacks clear default compliance intervals in the AD text for cases where the referenced service bulletin compliance table is ambiguous; the FAA should include explicit calendar or flight-cycle limits in the AD.

[P3] Operators need a clear statement about how compliance times are aggregated for fleets with mixed configurations or phased inspections; the AD should specify whether compliance times are per-airplane from the AD effective date or from each aircraft's specific threshold.

[P4] Requiring performance of all actions labeled "RC" in Boeing Alert Service Bulletin 757–53A0108 Rev 1 at the times in paragraph 1.E creates a dependency on Boeing service information that may change; the FAA should incorporate critical compliance tables into the AD to avoid future interpretive disputes.

[P4] The AD's reliance on Boeing Alert Service Bulletin 757–53A0108 Rev 1 for RC actions means operators without access to the full service bulletin cannot determine affected parts and labor — the FAA should make the relevant service bulletin or essential pages part of the docket.

[P5] Requiring RC actions in APB Alert Service Bulletin AP757–53–001 Rev 2 without including detailed compliance thresholds in the AD will impose unquantified costs on operators; the FAA should publish the compliance tasks and intervals within the AD.

[P5] APB service bulletin incorporation creates a potential conflict where APB and Boeing actions overlap; the AD should explain precedence rules where both service bulletins apply to the same airplane.

[P6] The provision requiring converted Group 1 airplanes to perform Group 2 actions is ambiguous: it does not identify which specific converted serial numbers or STC-modified airplanes are "specified converted Group 1"; the AD must list affected serial ranges or a clear identification method.

[P6] The AD should provide rationale (technical basis) for why converted Group 1 airplanes must perform Group 2 actions rather than the actions identified for their Group, and provide compliance time differentials if necessary.

[P7] Similarly, the requirement for specified converted Group 4 airplanes to perform Group 5 actions lacks clarity about which conversions are covered and whether STC holders or supplemental type certificate (STC) holders are responsible for corrective actions.

[P7] The AD should clarify whether operators of converted Group 4 airplanes can rely on the STC holder (conversion program operator) to perform or fund the Group 5 work, and whether credit is available for prior STC-required modifications.

[P8] Requiring that any instructions found in Boeing service bulletin that tell operators to "contact Boeing" be performed using an FAA-approved method under paragraph (i) delegates substantive repair approval to Boeing and creates potential delays; the FAA should provide a default approved repair table or expedite the AMOC process for such cases.

[P8] The AD should explicitly permit repairs provided in subsequent Boeing-released service bulletin revisions or Boeing-approved service letters to be acceptable without an AMOC provided they meet certain criteria, to avoid repeated AMOC cycles.

[P9] Replacing references to "the original issue date of this service bulletin" with May 3, 2018 may create inconsistency with operators' existing records that reference the actual original issue date; the FAA should explain the reason for this substitution and confirm it does not alter any compliance thresholds.

[P9] The exception that the May 3, 2018 substitution does not apply to notes or flag notes is vague; commenters request specific examples of where the original issue date must still be used.

[P10] Using "the effective date of this AD" in place of "the revision 1 date" could create a moving target for operators if the AD's effective date changes due to amendments; the FAA should specify the calendar date to avoid ambiguity.

[P10] The AD should confirm whether the effective date referenced is the date of publication in the Federal Register or the date of incorporation by reference entry, and whether operators may use the date of receipt to calculate compliance windows.

[P11] Mirroring P8 for the APB service bulletin, requiring that Boeing be contacted for repairs but then requiring FAA-approved methods may be circular where APB refers to Boeing; the AD should permit APB-approved repair methods that have been previously accepted by an FAA DER or ODA without requiring a new AMOC.

[P11] The AD needs to define the timeframe in which Boeing must provide repair instructions after being contacted, or require that APB/Boeing publish approved repairs to the public docket to avoid prolonged aircraft grounding.

[P12] Substituting May 3, 2018 for "revision 1 issue date" in the APB service bulletin may misalign APB's internal revision history with FAA compliance windows; the FAA should justify the substitution and confirm no change to required inspection intervals.

[P13] Using "the effective date of this AD" for APB "revision 2 issue date" references may cause confusion for international operators where AD effective dates differ by country — the FAA should include an absolute date or provide guidance for international conformity.

[P14] Granting the Manager, Los Angeles ACO Branch authority to approve AMOCs centralizes approvals and could create bottlenecks; commenters request decentralization or delegation options (e.g., authorized DERs/ODAs) to expedite operational compliance.

[P14] The AD should specify expected processing timelines for AMOC requests to the LA ACO Branch so operators can plan maintenance windows and avoid aircraft on ground (AOG) events.

[P15] The AMOC submission procedures should include the required content format, technical substantiation standards, and the acceptable electronic submission addresses; current language is too generic.

[P15] The AD should allow direct electronic submission to a dedicated AMOC mailbox and confirm confidentiality protections for proprietary repair data submitted as part of AMOC requests.

[P16] Requiring notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC may be impractical for foreign operators who do not have a US principal inspector; the AD should provide alternative notification procedures for foreign operators and state whether their authority having jurisdiction must also be notified.

[P16] The AD should clarify the timeframe for notifying the principal inspector "before using" an AMOC (e.g., 48 hours advance) and whether emergency uses are permitted with post-use notification.

[P17] Allowing AMOCs approved by an authorized Boeing ODA to satisfy repair/alteration requirements raises concerns about independent FAA oversight and potential conflicts of interest; commenters request that such ODA approvals also require FAA concurrence or subsequent FAA acceptance.

[P17] The AD must require Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to be submitted to the FAA for docketing and to include evidence of Boeing's analysis and limitations, rather than allowing silent reliance on ODA approvals.

[P18] Requiring repair/modification AMOCs to meet the airplane's certification basis may be interpreted to preclude compliant alternative methods that provide an equivalent level of safety but deviate from original certification — the FAA should explicitly accept equivalent level of safety (ELOS) demonstrations and outline acceptable analysis methods.

[P18] The requirement that AMOCs "explicitly reference this AD" is administratively burdensome; the FAA should allow AMOC approvals to reference both the AD number and the incorporated service bulletin number to avoid misinterpretation.

[P19] Prohibiting prior AMOCs approved for AD 2018–06–07 from being used creates uncertainty for operators who have implemented such AMOCs and relied upon them for years; the FAA must provide a transition path, grandfathering, or a rationale for why those AMOCs are insufficient.

[P19] The AD should identify specific differences between AD 2018–06–07 AMOCs and the new AD that justify invalidating prior approvals, and provide a process to expedite reapproval where differences are minor.

[P20] The provision governing RC-labeled steps should include guidance on how to interpret RC markings where service bulletins have inconsistent labeling between figures and text.

[P20] The AD should clarify whether future revisions of the incorporated service information that relabel RC steps will change the obligations under this AD or whether only the currently incorporated revision controls.

[P21] Requiring all RC steps and identified figures/substeps to be completed to comply with the AD may impose tasks (e.g., optional inspection traps or non-critical tasks) that are unnecessary for certain fleet configurations; the FAA should allow limited deviations where operators can demonstrate equivalent safety.

[P21] The AD must clarify recordkeeping requirements proving completion of each RC substep and figure (e.g., work cards, EO documentation) and whether maintenance release signatures are sufficient evidence of compliance.

[P22] The "RC Exempt" carve-out is helpful, but the AD provides no process for when an operator believes an RC-marked step should be reclassified as "RC Exempt"; the FAA should provide an expedited reclassification/AMOC pathway.

[P23] Requiring AMOCs for any deviation from RC steps, including figures, may be impractical for minor tooling or procedural deviations; the FAA should provide thresholds (e.g., de minimis changes) that operators can implement without AMOC while maintaining traceability.

[P23] The AD should allow DER-approved procedural deviations for RC substeps that do not affect structural integrity or human factors, with subsequent notification to the FAA rather than a full AMOC.

[P24] Allowing deviations from non-RC steps under an operator's maintenance program is appropriate, but the AD lacks detail on what "accepted methods" means — the FAA should provide examples of accepted methods and confirm whether SMS-based risk assessments suffice.

[P24] The AD must require operators to document any deviations from non-RC steps and retain records demonstrating that the airplane can be returned to an airworthy condition, to ensure auditability and consistent oversight.
