Using "the effective date of this AD" for APB "revision 2 issue date" references may cause confusion for international operators where AD effective dates differ by country — the FAA should include an absolute date or provide guidance for international conformity.

Granting the Manager, Los Angeles ACO Branch authority to approve AMOCs centralizes approvals and could create bottlenecks; commenters request decentralization or delegation options (e.g., authorized DERs/ODAs) to expedite operational compliance.
The AD should specify expected processing timelines for AMOC requests to the LA ACO Branch so operators can plan maintenance windows and avoid aircraft on ground (AOG) events.
The AMOC submission procedures should include the required content format, technical substantiation standards, and the acceptable electronic submission addresses; current language is too generic.
The AD should allow direct electronic submission to a dedicated AMOC mailbox and confirm confidentiality protections for proprietary repair data submitted as part of AMOC requests.

Requiring notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC may be impractical for foreign operators who do not have a US principal inspector; the AD should provide alternative notification procedures for foreign operators and state whether their authority having jurisdiction must also be notified.
The AD should clarify the timeframe for notifying the principal inspector "before using" an AMOC (e.g., 48 hours advance) and whether emergency uses are permitted with post-use notification.

Allowing AMOCs approved by an authorized Boeing ODA to satisfy repair/alteration requirements raises concerns about independent FAA oversight and potential conflicts of interest; commenters request that such ODA approvals also require FAA concurrence or subsequent FAA acceptance.

The AD must require Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to be submitted to the FAA for docketing and to include evidence of Boeing's analysis and limitations, rather than allowing silent reliance on ODA approvals.

Requiring repair/modification AMOCs to meet the airplane's certification basis may be interpreted to preclude compliant alternative methods that provide an equivalent level of safety but deviate from original certification — the FAA should explicitly accept equivalent level of safety (ELOS) demonstrations and outline acceptable analysis methods.

The requirement that AMOCs "explicitly reference this AD" is administratively burdensome; the FAA should allow AMOC approvals to reference both the AD number and the incorporated service bulletin number to avoid misinterpretation.

Prohibiting prior AMOCs approved for AD 2018–06–07 from being used creates uncertainty for operators who have implemented such AMOCs and relied upon them for years; the FAA must provide a transition path, grandfathering, or a rationale for why those AMOCs are insufficient.

The AD should identify specific differences between AD 2018–06–07 AMOCs and the new AD that justify invalidating prior approvals, and provide a process to expedite reapproval where differences are minor.
The provision governing RC-labeled steps should include guidance on how to interpret RC markings where service bulletins have inconsistent labeling between figures and text.

The AD should clarify whether future revisions of the incorporated service information that relabel RC steps will change the obligations under this AD or whether only the currently incorporated revision controls.

Requiring all RC steps and identified figures/substeps to be completed to comply with the AD may impose tasks (e.g., optional inspection traps or non-critical tasks) that are unnecessary for certain fleet configurations; the FAA should allow limited deviations where operators can demonstrate equivalent safety.

The AD must clarify recordkeeping requirements proving completion of each RC substep and figure (e.g., work cards, EO documentation) and whether maintenance release signatures are sufficient evidence of compliance.

Requiring AMOCs for any deviation from RC steps, including figures, may be impractical for minor tooling or procedural deviations; the FAA should provide thresholds (e.g., de minimis changes) that operators can implement without AMOC while maintaining traceability.
The AD should allow DER-approved procedural deviations for RC substeps that do not affect structural integrity or human factors, with subsequent notification to the FAA rather than a full AMOC.

Allowing deviations from non-RC steps under an operator's maintenance program is appropriate, but the AD lacks detail on what "accepted methods" means — the FAA should provide examples of accepted methods and confirm whether SMS-based risk assessments suffice.

The AD must require operators to document any deviations from non-RC steps and retain records demonstrating that the airplane can be returned to an airworthy condition, to ensure auditability and consistent oversight.

[P1] The requirement that FDA "make the fullest possible disclosure" is vague and should be clarified with concrete standards and examples to ensure consistent application across offices and FOIA officers.

[P1] Public interest advocates will request that "consistent with privacy, trade secret, and deliberative process considerations" be narrowly defined to prevent overbroad withholding under amorphous privacy or deliberative-process claims.

[P2] Industry commenters will urge that the phrase "all non-exempt FDA records must be made available" be reconciled with other statutory confidentiality obligations (e.g., FDCA, 301(j) authorities), otherwise it could create conflicts with existing laws.

[P3] Commenters representing transparency NGOs will support discretionary disclosure when no foreseeable harm exists but ask for a presumption in favor of disclosure and a requirement to document the harm analysis publicly.

[P3] Legal experts will request that FDA publish guidance on how "foreseeably harm" is assessed (timing, standard of proof, examples) to reduce arbitrary denials.

[P4] Trade groups will applaud the explicit exception for information "legally prohibited from disclosure" but ask FDA to list specific statutes or cite examples in preamble guidance to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P5] Public interest groups and journalists will insist that the procedures to identify and post records of general interest include mandatory proactive posting schedules and searchable metadata fields (e.g., subject, date, author, document type).

[P5] Disability advocates will demand that the "publicly accessible electronic format" requirement include accessibility standards (WCAG 2.1 AA) and machine-readable formats (CSV/JSON) for bulk reuse.

[P6] Requester organizations will support the rule that no justification is required for requests, but ask FDA to prohibit categorical denials based on requester identity (e.g., commercial vs. academic) except where statutorily permitted.

[P6] Industry commenters will warn that absolutely no justification requirement could lead to burdensome, fishing-request volume and request that FDA be allowed to require minimal specificity for large, burdensome requests.

[P7] FOIA practitioners will request specificity on how the "exemption(s) applied" must be noted (e.g., the exact FOIA exemption number, brief justification, and reference to legal authority) rather than a simple citation.

[P8] Requesters will ask that the required contact information for FOIA Public Liaison and OGIS include direct phone numbers and email addresses and be standardized in all denials/responses to improve access to dispute resolution.

[P9] Commenters will request that FDA explicitly allow FOIA submissions by secure electronic upload and clarify acceptable file formats, since relying on addresses/numbers "provided on FDA's website" can be burdensome if links change.

[P10] Privacy advocates will object to requiring telephone numbers and fee-payer names in all requests as unnecessary and potentially chilling, and ask FDA to make the contact and fee-payer information optional unless fees are likely to be assessed.

[P10] Industry trade groups will request an option for corporate requesters to provide a billing contact rather than a personal name and suggest allowing corporate email addresses to reduce privacy concerns.

[P11] Large requesters will argue that a single 10-working-day extension is insufficient for complex, multi-component requests and ask FDA to allow multiple extensions with specified limits, subject to notice and dispute rights.

[P11] Transparency advocates will caution that allowing an automatic 10-working-day extension could be abused and ask for a requirement that extensions be narrowly tailored and publicly logged with reasons.

[P12] Civil liberties groups will request that the written notice of extension must include a clear explanation of the reasons, an estimate of additional time required, and next-step remedies if the requester disagrees.

[P13] Requester support organizations will endorse FDA's permission to contact for clarifications and ask that such contacts be documented in writing and that tolling occur only after the requester confirms receipt of the clarification request.

[P14] Requesters will ask FDA to publish a list of the "specified conditions" under which the agency may toll the 20-day period to prevent misuse and to require prompt notification and status updates.

[P15] Commenters will request that the one-time toll for clarification be limited to a specific number of days (e.g., 10 business days) and require the Agency to give the requester a deadline for response when tolling.

[P16] Fee-paying organizations will seek limits on tolling for fee-assessment communications (e.g., maximum cumulative tolling days) and require FDA to provide detailed fee estimates before tolling.

[P17] Requesters will request that denial letters include not only the right to appeal to the HHS Deputy Agency Chief FOIA Officer, but also direct instructions and contact info for how to file the appeal and timelines.

[P18] Civil liberties advocates will ask for a definition of "exceptional circumstances" and for a requirement that FDA publicly report any court-ordered excusals of time limits to ensure transparency.

[P19] Requester groups will ask that the 10-day deadline for expedited processing determinations apply from the date the request is received (not from "all required information") or, if latter, require FDA to acknowledge receipt of missing items promptly.

[P19] Patient advocacy groups will request that the rule define "all required information" clearly and that the agency provide an immediate receipt acknowledging completeness or outstanding items to avoid delays.

[P20] Commercial entities will request clarity on how "commercial use" is determined (criteria, examples) to avoid disputes and suggest a safe-harbor definition for common business uses.

[P20] Transparency groups will warn that too-broad a definition of "commercial use" could deter investigative reporting and scientific reuse; they will ask for a narrow definition centered on direct commercial advantage.

[P21] FOIA practitioners will support the prohibition on charging search fees when FDA misses time limits but request an exception process for cases where lateness is due to requester's complicating conduct, with documentation requirements.

[P22] Large-scale requesters will criticize the >5,000 pages threshold as arbitrary and ask FDA to adopt a lower threshold (e.g., 2,500 pages) or to apply a proportionality test based on burden rather than fixed page counts.

[P22] Requester advocates will insist that FDA must actually conduct and document the three "good-faith attempts" to narrow requests (dates, methods) before charging, and require those contacts to be made in writing.

[P23] Requesters will demand a precise definition of "timely written notice" (e.g., within 10 business days of identifying unusual circumstances) and require proof of notice before fees are assessed.

[P24] FOIA practitioners will ask that the required discussions to narrow requests include a documented timeline and that telephone attempts be followed by written summaries to qualify as "good-faith attempts."

[P25] Educational and scientific institutions will support being charged only duplication costs but request that the rule define "noncommercial scientific institution" consistent with DOJ guidance to avoid unequal treatment.

[P26] Student and nonprofit organizations will welcome waiving copying costs for the first 100 pages but ask for exceptions (e.g., bulk electronic production) to be priced reasonably and for inflation adjustments over time.

[P27] Requesters will call for consistent application of the prohibition on duplication fees when time limits are missed and request a clear exception definition for "unusual or exceptional circumstances."

[P28] Commenters will note the inconsistency between duplication fee rules and the 5,000-page threshold and request that any waiver or charge provisions include proportionality and requester consultation.

[P29] Citizen requesters will ask for clarity on what counts as "other requests" and request examples to explain when only search and duplication charges apply.

[P30] Public interest lawyers will request that the “first 2 hours of search” and “first 100 pages” waivers be applied per request and not per component or sub-request to prevent fee gaming by agencies.

[P31] Legal commenters will request that the prohibition on assessing search fees after missed time limits be expanded to include administrative appeals and court-ordered deadlines to preserve requester remedies.

[P32] Large requesters will ask for transparent criteria for "unusual circumstances" that would permit charging after >5,000 pages, including requirement to provide cost estimates and alternatives like staggered productions.

[P33] Requester assistance groups will request that FOIA staff contacts offering help in reformulating requests be mandatory before invoking the unusual-circumstances fee rules, with documentation provided to the requester.

[P34] Labor and union representatives will request that the GS-grade hourly rate bands be updated annually and that lower-grade employee rates be used where appropriate to avoid overcharging for simple electronic searches.

[P35] FOIA fee experts will request that the 16% benefits addition be documented with current HHS or OPM data and that the rounding rule be explained to ensure predictable fee calculations.

[P36] Requesters will seek assurance that multi-grade searches will include detailed billing breakdowns showing hours per grade level and tasks performed to allow meaningful challenge of fee assessments.

[P37] Technology companies will request guidance on how "specialized programming" is defined and capped, and ask that charges for software/development be amortized or limited for requester-initiated one-off queries.

[P38] Civil liberties groups will call for denials to be signed by a senior official but also require the signatory to certify the factual basis for each exemption claim to deter boilerplate denials.

[P39] Requesters will ask that denial letters provide both legal and factual bases for each exemption applied, including citation to specific statutory text, and that appeals instructions be clear and hyperlinked in online releases.

[P40] Commenters will support including an estimate of the volume of denied records but caution that the "reasonable effort" standard must require a documented methodology or the estimate may be meaningless.

[P41] Transparency advocates will request that the "number of pages" estimate also be accompanied by an estimate of responsive file types and an approximate date range to help appellants assess the scope.

[P42] Industry submitters will request clarification when the volume is "indicated by deletions" — require FDA to state explicitly the number of pages withheld in addition to deletion markings to aid submitters' challenges.

[P43] Requesters will ask that contact information for FOIA Public Liaison and OGIS in denial letters include direct links to OGIS complaint forms and clear timelines for dispute resolution.

[P44] Submitters of confidential commercial information will object that a 10-working-day deadline to object is too short to prepare legal analysis and request at least 30 calendar days, especially for foreign or corporate submitters.

[P44] Trade associations will request that the rule permit submitters to request an extension as of right if they can show need for legal or technical review, instead of leaving extensions discretionary.

[P45] Conversely, public-interest requesters will caution that allowing too-frequent extensions for submitters could be used to delay disclosure and ask FDA to limit extensions and require FDA to document reasons.

[P46] Litigators will support the segregation requirement but urge FDA to provide examples and a checklist for "reasonably segregable factual information" to reduce overwithholding of mixed records.

[P47] Historians and archivists will applaud the 25-year limit on deliberative process privilege but recommend lowering it to 20 years or providing a public-interest override for historically significant materials.

[P47] Industry lawyers will warn that automatic loss of deliberative privilege after 25 years could expose sensitive tradecraft or legacy enforcement strategies and request limited exceptions where disclosure would cause demonstrable harm.

[P48] State and local regulators will support allowing Commissioner discretion for disclosure of exempt records but ask for inter-agency coordination and public reporting whenever the Commissioner exercises that discretion.

[P49] Transparency groups will request a presumption that discretionary disclosures are documented in a public log with the rationale and legal basis for transparency and to allow public oversight.

[P50] Commenters will ask FDA to define "public interest" and "FOIA objectives" and to require that deliberative needs, privacy, and trade secret interests be balanced through a written, reviewable test.

[P51] State/local agencies will support disclosure to other federal agencies but request clarity on whether such disclosures trigger any obligation for the receiving agency to process future FOIA requests for the same records.

[P52] Civil liberties groups will demand that the written agreements preventing further disclosure include penalties and audit rights for the receiving agency to ensure compliance.

[P53] Privacy advocates will request that the prohibition on further disclosure without FDA written permission include an obligation for the receiving agency to notify FDA promptly if compelled by court order or subpoena.

[P54] Industry commenters will accept limited disclosures in administrative/court proceedings but request that FDA seek protective orders and redactions by default and document efforts taken to minimize disclosures.

[P55] Trade secret holders will require that FDA be obligated to seek confidentiality protections (protective orders or in camera review) in any proceeding in which exempt data are revealed, not merely "will take or request" measures.

[P56] State/local public-health partners will support conditional disclosure to facilitate cooperative responses but ask for streamlined templates for the required written authority statements to reduce administrative burden.

[P57] State attorneys general will request clarity on what constitutes sufficient "authority to protect confidential info" and whether model confidentiality agreements will be provided by FDA.

[P58] Public health advocates will support allowing disclosure when the State/local agency can act faster but ask for safeguards to prevent unnecessary dissemination and to ensure sponsors are notified promptly.

[P59] Visiting State/local scientists will request standardized non-disclosure agreement (NDA) templates and standardized processes for obtaining written assurances to speed cooperative reviews and training.

[P60] Commenters will ask FDA to define "in the interest of public health" for joint reviews and provide examples to guide decisionmaking and avoid arbitrary denials of visitor access.

[P61] Industry submitters will insist that "FDA must retain physical control" be clearly operationalized (e.g., controlled reading rooms, no electronic copies offsite) and request written protocols for visitor reviews.

[P62] Visiting scientists and universities will request that confidentiality commitment forms be standardized and include clear, reasonable limitations on liability and data handling obligations.

[P63] Academic commenters will ask for a precise definition of "no disqualifying financial interest" and a process for disclosing potential conflicts to the submitter and FDA without deterring qualified experts.

[P64] Pharmaceutical manufacturers will support the prohibition on disclosing manufacturing-method trade secrets to State/local officials without submitter consent and ask FDA to strictly enforce it.

[P65] Conversely, some state public-health entities will request a limited, expedited process for obtaining submitter written authorization in urgent public health situations when manufacturing-method information is critical.

[P66] State regulators and international partners will support the Commissioner's authority to exchange nonpublic predecisional documents but ask for thresholds and public reporting when such exchanges occur.

[P67] Transparency groups will object to exchanges with State/local agencies unless there is a written public accountability mechanism and ask for mandatory written agreements to be published (redacted if necessary).

[P68] State/local agencies will request clear criteria the Commissioner will use to determine that an exchange is "reasonably necessary" to improve uniformity so that requests can be evaluated predictably.

[P69] Commenters will ask that the organization and individual authority statements required for exchanges be standardized, with model forms provided and a simple renewal process.

[P70] Foreign governments and trade associations will support exchanges for harmonization but ask FDA to list eligible countries or treaties that typically qualify to avoid uncertainty.

[P71] National security and legal experts will request that FDA require foreign partners to accept US-equivalent confidentiality protections and provide mechanisms to challenge disclosures by foreign governments.

[P72] Civil liberties groups will be concerned that exchanges with foreign officials could lead to wider disclosure abroad and ask for an audit trail and reporting when documents are shared internationally.

[P73] Transparency advocates will strongly object that exchanges under § 20.89(d)(2) "do not require making those records available to the public" and request that FDA publish a summary log of all such exchanges with redacted rationales.

[P74] Public users will request that public reading rooms' hours (9 a.m. to 4 p.m.) be extended or flexible hours be allowed (e.g., evening hours or weekend appointments) to accommodate working persons and different time zones.

[P74] Disability advocates will ask that FDA provide remote access or appointment-based assistance for those unable to visit reading rooms during stated hours.

[P75] Trade-secret claimants will request clarity on what constitutes "all of the data that are necessary" for FDA to determine a trade secret claim so petitioners know what to submit to avoid tentative denials.

[P76] Petitioners will request that when FDA states grounds for tentative denial, it must include specific legal citations and the factual deficiencies so petitioners can submit targeted rebuttals.

[P77] Petitioners will welcome the 60-day reconsideration window but ask for tolling exceptions (e.g., if submitter requests an extension or if international parties need more time) and for the ability to meet and confer with FDA during that period.

[P78] Trade associations will support the prohibition on disclosure or labeling requirements while litigation is pending if suit is filed within 30 days, but ask FDA to clarify whether oral disclosures or informal postings are also barred.

[P79] Consumer groups will urge that the 30-day period before release after a final determination not be used to delay access unduly and ask FDA to require prompt public notice of any suits filed and of final releases when no suit is filed.

Academic commenters will ask for a precise definition of "no disqualifying financial interest" and a process for disclosing potential conflicts to the submitter and FDA without deterring qualified experts.
Pharmaceutical manufacturers will support the prohibition on disclosing manufacturing-method trade secrets to State/local officials without submitter consent and ask FDA to strictly enforce it.

State regulators and international partners will support the Commissioner's authority to exchange nonpublic predecisional documents but ask for thresholds and public reporting when such exchanges occur.

Foreign governments and trade associations will support exchanges for harmonization but ask FDA to list eligible countries or treaties that typically qualify to avoid uncertainty.

National security and legal experts will request that FDA require foreign partners to accept US-equivalent confidentiality protections and provide mechanisms to challenge disclosures by foreign governments.

[P1] The two-criteria test in §590.102(p) is vague because it does not define whether aggregate exports across multiple applications or entities are considered when qualifying as small-scale natural gas exports.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether amendments to an approved small-scale export application trigger re-evaluation of the two qualifying criteria in §590.102(p).

[P2] The 0.14 billion cubic feet per day cap in §590.102(p)(1) is arbitrary and too low to meet industry commercial needs; stakeholders request an economic justification or raising the threshold.

[P2] LNG traders and exporters will be disadvantaged because the 0.14 Bcf/day limit in §590.102(p)(1) prevents combined shipments that are operationally typical for mid-size suppliers; propose an alternative metric (monthly/annual aggregate) instead of daily.

[P2] The technical specification in §590.102(p)(1) must include whether the limit applies per export point, per company, per application, or per contractual purchaser to avoid regulatory overlap.

[P3] Relying on DOE’s NEPA determination in §590.102(p)(2) to qualify an application creates circularity and unpredictability because NEPA thresholds are themselves subject to interpretation; request criteria for how DOE will determine when an EIS/EA is not required.

[P3] Environmental NGOs will object that §590.102(p)(2) allows small-scale exports to bypass environmental review simply by asserting no EIS/EA is required; recommend explicit baseline environmental screening criteria.

[P4] Automatic issuance of export authorization upon receipt of any complete small-scale application (§590.208(a)) removes DOE’s discretion and precludes case-by-case considerations of market or security impacts; request reinstatement of DOE review authority.

[P4] Industry supports §590.208(a) for reducing approval delays, but requests a defined timeframe for DOE to acknowledge receipt and completeness to ensure predictability.

[P5] Exempting small-scale applicants from the notice and application procedures (§590.208(a) exception) undermines transparency and public participation; request that at minimum a 7–14 day notice be required.

[P5] Legal experts will challenge the exemption in §590.208(a) as inconsistent with administrative procedures that mandate public notice for actions affecting interstate commerce.

[P6] The permission in §590.208(b) to export up to 100,000 cubic feet in a single shipment without prior authorization creates a loophole for repeated unregulated exports via multiple shipments; propose a per-entity or aggregate cap over time.

[P6] The provision in §590.208(b) should clarify whether the 100,000 cubic feet threshold applies to domestic-origin gas only and whether LNG/CNG in different states counts toward the limit.

[P6] Customs and border stakeholders request clarity in §590.208(b) on documentation requirements and reporting for the de minimis 100,000 cubic foot shipments to prevent smuggling and ensure tariff compliance.

[P7] The deadline in §39.13(a) (comments due October 16, 2017) is inconsistent with the current schedule and should be updated; stakeholders request an extension of the comment period to a current date.

[P7] Given the complexity of the AD, the comment deadline in §39.13(a) is too short for operators and maintenance organizations to conduct technical assessments; request at least 60 additional days.

[P8] The compliance requirement in §39.13(f) to follow specified compliance times without allowance for operational constraints is impractical for operators that cannot schedule engine shop visits within those times; request flexibility or alternative compliance timelines.

[P9] Requiring the one-time inspection at the next engine shop visit (§39.13(f)(1)) may allow an unreasonable delay if an operator schedules sparse shop visits; request a maximum calendar deadline (e.g., within 120 days) from the AD effective date.

[P9] Maintenance providers request clarification whether "next engine shop visit" for leased aircraft counts as the operator’s or the lessor’s scheduled visit under §39.13(f)(1).

[P11] Mandating the specific GE SB paragraph (§39.13(f)(1) method) could be problematic if GE revises the service bulletin; request that later approved revisions be permitted or that the AD reference the content rather than a single paragraph.

[P11] Airlines and MROs request that alternative approved inspection methods be explicitly allowed if they provide equivalent safety findings rather than mandating the proprietary GE procedure in §39.13(f)(1).

[P12] The replacement obligation in §39.13(f)(2) to replace retainers that show cracks or nonconformance may create supply chain issues if replacement parts are scarce; request allowance for temporary repair or part interchangeability pending parts availability.

[P12] Operators ask whether used or overhauled parts can qualify as "parts eligible for installation" under §39.13(f)(2), and request explicit criteria to avoid grounding aircraft.

[P13] The triggering condition in §39.13(f)(2) lacks quantitative tolerances for "dimensional nonconformance"; request the AD specify exact dimensional limits and measurement tolerances.

[P13] Technical commenters point out that nonconformance thresholds should reference manufacturing drawings and call-outs to avoid subjective determinations during inspections under §39.13(f)(2).

[P14] The AMOC authority in §39.13(h)(1) is appropriate, but the AD should specify expected response times from the FAA to AMOC requests to avoid operational delays.

[P14] Legal counsel requests clarification whether approved AMOCs will be published or otherwise made available industry-wide to ensure consistent compliance and avoid duplicate requests under §39.13(h)(1).

[P15] The requirement to route AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO (§39.13(h)(1)) may be burdensome for international operators without U.S.-based inspectors; request alternative submission pathways.

[P16] The instruction to address direct AMOC submissions to the person identified in paragraph (i)(1) (§39.13(h)(1)) should include contact name and phone/email in the AD text to avoid ambiguity.

[P17] Permitting email submission of AMOC requests (§39.13(h)(1)) raises cybersecurity concerns; request secure transfer protocols and acknowledgement receipts to ensure submissions are received.

[P18] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC (§39.13(h)(2)) could create operational delays if inspectors are unavailable; request a provision allowing operators to proceed after a set waiting period if no response is received.

[P19] Relying on GE to provide the service bulletin (§39.13(i)(2)) may limit access for small operators; request that GE be required to provide the SB at no cost or that the FAA post the SB publicly.

[P19] Intellectual property concerns: GE’s SB may be copyrighted or proprietary; operators request confirmation that referencing the SB in the AD does not infringe proprietary rights and that necessary information is made available.

[P20] Allowing viewing of the service information only at the FAA branch address (§39.13(i)(4)) is insufficient for remote operators; request that the FAA post the service bulletin online or provide electronic access.

[P1] The Find-and-Fix threshold of >0.015 mg/L is ambiguous because it does not specify whether results equal to 0.015 mg/L trigger the obligation; revise to "≥0.015 mg/L" or clarify intent.

[P1] Requiring Find-and-Fix at every sampling site above 0.015 mg/L will impose disproportionate operational burdens on small systems that must investigate many individual sites; provide phased implementation or flexibility for small systems.

[P1] Industry commenters will request clear definition and examples of the "Find-and-Fix" actions required by §141.82(j) (e.g., pipe replacement, flushing, aerator replacement) because the cross-reference alone is insufficient for compliance planning.

[P2] The obligation to provide follow-up sampling results per §141.85(d) lacks a specific timeline for delivering results to consumers; require a mandatory time frame (e.g., within 7 calendar days) to ensure timely public notice.

[P2] Consumer advocates will request that follow-up sampling results be mailed and posted online, not just "provided," to ensure accessibility for low-income and non-digital households; require multiple delivery methods.

[P3] Prohibiting pre-stagnation flushing or aerator removal before tap sampling may make certain samples unrepresentative of typical consumer exposure when faucets have prone-to-clogging aerators; allow explicit limited exceptions where aerators demonstrably affect sampling safety or accuracy with State approval.

[P3] Legal experts will challenge the prohibition as potentially conflicting with existing sampling protocols that recommend removal of debris to avoid contamination of sample bottles; the rule should explain scientific basis and reconcile with standard sampling guidance.

[P4] The requirement to use ≥55 mm wide-mouth bottles is prescriptive and may increase sample container costs and disrupt existing lab workflows; allow alternative validated bottle types if labs demonstrate equivalency.

[P4] Laboratories and suppliers will comment that the supply chain cannot reliably provide wide-mouth bottles to all systems within the transition period; request a compliance grace period and federal procurement guidance.

[P5] Requiring certification of full compliance with public notification within 10 days after completing public notification may be infeasible for systems that perform multiple staggered Tier 2/3 notices; allow certifications within 10 days after the final notice or extend the deadline.

[P5] Small systems will request that the 10-day certification requirement include an exemption for systems that use third-party contractors to distribute notices and may not receive distribution verification within 10 days.

[P6] Mandating representative copies of each type of Tier 2 and 3 notice with the certification will create administrative burdens; clarify what constitutes a "representative copy" and allow electronic copies or templates instead of each individualized notice.

[P6] Public health advocates will support requiring copies of notices to the primacy agency to enable oversight and recommend retention of original distribution proofs (e.g., mail receipts) as part of the submission.

[P7] The obligation to provide copies of any Tier 1 notice to EPA and the primacy agency "as soon as practicable and within 24 hours" is unrealistic for many systems that discover violations outside business hours; require "within 24 hours of discovery during normal business hours" or allow electronic submission the next business day.

[P7] Systems will ask for clarification on the method of submission (email, portal, fax) and request an official electronic portal to satisfy the 24-hour requirement.

[P8] The three-year compliance date for subpart requirements lacks a concrete calendar date in the proposed text ("[DATE THREE YEARS...]"); stakeholders request publication of the actual effective date and alignment with funding/grant timelines.

[P8] State primacy agencies will request additional time beyond three years for large-scale inventory and LSLR planning given staffing constraints; propose a staggered compliance schedule by system size.

[P9] The transition period provision that requires compliance with previous 40 CFR versions for 60 days until three years is confusing; stakeholders request clarity on which specific previous FR publications apply and how conflicts between old and new rules are reconciled.

[P10] Systems with exemptions being required to comply with old versions until exemption expiry could create regulatory inconsistency when the final rule is stronger; stakeholders ask for a provision allowing voluntary adoption of the new standard prior to exemption expiration.

[P11] Mandating school and child care facility sampling and public education "regardless of compliance sample results" will generate significant costs for systems that serve many facilities; request financial assistance, prioritization criteria, or phased implementation.

[P11] Parent and public health advocacy groups will support the unconditional sampling requirement, arguing it addresses vulnerable populations and that "regardless" is necessary to find intermittent problems.

[P12] Tying trigger and action levels to tap samples collected per §141.86 and analyzed per §141.89 requires immediate lab capacity; labs will comment on need for expanded accreditation and turnaround time standards to meet the rule's timelines.

[P13] Treating the highest sample result as the 90th percentile when fewer than five samples are allowed by the State could produce misleading statistical outcomes and unfairly penalize systems; recommend a different statistical adjustment or require a minimum sample count.

[P13] Legal commenters may argue that equating the single highest sample to the 90th percentile is arbitrary and could be challenged under arbitrary-and-capricious standards; request a more scientifically defensible approach.

[P14] Requiring all systems to install and operate corrosion control treatment meeting "optimal" definitions may be technically infeasible for some groundwater systems with naturally low corrosivity; request alternative compliance pathways or financial assistance.

[P15] The small system flexibility deeming small systems in compliance if they follow state-specified flexibilities should explicitly limit what flexibilities States may grant to avoid under-protection; consumer groups will ask for EPA oversight standards.

[P15] Small system associations will support the deemed-compliance approach but seek clear, published examples of acceptable State-specified flexibilities and timelines to implement them.

[P16] Mandatory lead service line replacement (LSLR) when the lead action level is exceeded must include specific timelines, prioritization of publicly owned vs. privately owned portions, and financial assistance mechanisms; commenters will request those details be added.

[P16] Property-rights advocates will object to mandatory replacement of privately owned portions without compensation or clear authority; request explicit legal basis and homeowner notification/consent requirements.

[P17] Goal-based LSLR for trigger exceedances lacks clear numeric targets or schedules in §141.84; stakeholders will request concrete, enforceable goals (e.g., X% replaced per year) rather than undefined "goal-based" language.

[P17] Environmental justice organizations will demand prioritization criteria within goal-based LSLR to address low-income and high-risk communities first.

[P18] Requiring service line inventories to include privately owned lines raises legal and practical issues regarding access to private property and accuracy; request clarification on methods (e.g., records review, customer surveys) and limits on enforcement actions against homeowners.

[P18] Municipal utilities will ask for federal funding to support inventory creation and propose phased deadlines tied to system size.

[P19] Obligation to notify persons served at tested taps of results per §141.85(d) should require delivery within a fixed timeframe (e.g., 5 days) and in the same language as service (multi-lingual notices); request specification.

[P19] Privacy advocates will ask that notices avoid publicly identifying individual households or sensitive locations when providing sample results.

[P20] Public education requirements triggered by action-level exceedances need detailed content standards (health effects, steps to reduce exposure) and minimum distribution channels; commenters will ask EPA to provide model materials.

[P20] Systems will request that public education obligations be limited to reasonable costs and allow use of state-provided templates to meet the requirement.

[P21] Requiring notification to all customers with lead service lines when the trigger is exceeded imposes burdens due to incomplete inventories; systems will request a safe-harbor provision for situations where ownership data are unknown.

[P21] Advocacy groups will support notification to all customers with lead service lines as an important consumer protection, and ask for mandated translation and accommodation for non-English speakers.

[P22] The public notification per subpart Q when action levels are exceeded must include explicit requirements on timing, methods, and penalties for failure to notify; request clarification to avoid inconsistent implementation.

[P23] Mandatory collection of lead samples from all schools and child care facilities (§141.92) is resource-intensive; commenters will request prioritization (e.g., based on building age, vulnerable populations) or federal funding to support required sampling.

[P23] School administrators will request longer lead time and coordination protocols with local education agencies to avoid disruption.

[P24] Defining noncompliance with §§141.80–141.93 as a violation requires clear penalty schedules and due-process protections; legal commenters will request explicit procedures for notice, opportunity to correct, and appeal.

[P24] Small systems will request that noncompliance be subject to graduated enforcement with technical assistance before formal penalties.

[P25] Deadlines in §141.81 for completing corrosion control treatment requirements are numerous and complex; request a consolidated timeline table in the rule and model schedules by system size.

[P26] Requiring large systems with existing treatment to complete §141.81(d) steps upon exceedance may duplicate prior optimization efforts; request recognition of prior validated optimization studies to avoid redundant work.

[P27] Large systems without treatment being required to complete §141.81(e) steps need access to technical assistance and funding; commenters will request EPA grants or state cost-sharing.

[P28] Permission for the State to require large systems that are not deemed optimized to complete §141.81(d) even absent exceedances could be used inconsistently; systems ask for objective criteria and appeals process for such State determinations.

[P29] Similarly, allowing States to force large systems without treatment to do §141.81(e) steps absent exceedances requires procedural safeguards and cost-recovery mechanisms.

[P30] The obligation for medium-size treated systems to complete §141.81(d) steps upon exceedance should be scalable—some medium systems lack in-house engineering capacity; require state-provided engineering assistance.

[P31] Medium untreated systems required to complete §141.81(e) steps need clearer definitions of "treatment recommendation" and allowable technologies; request an approved technologies list.

[P32] Requiring treatment recommendation steps when the lead trigger is exceeded for medium systems may cause unnecessary expense if not well-targeted; propose that recommendations be tied to exceedance magnitude.

[P33] The rule's requirement that subsequent exceedances force completion of remaining steps lacks clarity on cumulative timing and whether prior partial steps count; request explicit restart rules.

[P34] Small treated systems required to complete §141.81(d) steps upon exceedance will face budgetary strain; propose scaled timelines or funding prioritization.

[P35] Small untreated systems required to complete §141.81(e) steps upon action-level exceedance should be eligible for state technical assistance and extended compliance schedules.

[P36] Small systems exceeding the lead trigger being required to complete treatment recommendation steps should be allowed to rely on state-issued standard recommendations when local studies are impractical.

[P37] The requirement to complete remaining §141.81(e) steps upon later exceedance should allow previously completed work to count toward compliance to avoid duplicative studies.

[P38] The obligation to continue operating and maintaining optimal corrosion control treatment and meet State-required measures needs explicit recordkeeping and reporting requirements to ensure enforceability.

[P39] Following schedule for selected small system option under §141.81(f) needs to include mechanisms for extensions in emergencies (natural disasters, pandemics).

[P40] The requirement that systems without treatment complete treatment recommendation step to be deemed optimized should provide clear criteria for what constitutes an adequate recommendation and who reviews it.

[P41] The deeming of systems as optimized if they meet certain requirements and are not required to meet §141.87(d) parameters could create loopholes; consumer groups will ask EPA to require independent verification before deeming systems optimized.

[P42] Mandated continued tap monitoring at least once every three years using reduced sites for deemed optimized systems could miss localized spikes; request more frequent or randomized sampling alternatives.

[P43] Requiring written notice to the State of long-term treatment changes or new sources (§141.90(a)(3)) within the deemed-optimized provisions must include minimum lead time for notification (e.g., 90 days) and emergency exceptions.

[P44] States reviewing and approving proposed new sources or long-term treatment changes before implementation is appropriate but must include explicit maximum review timelines to prevent unreasonable delays.

[P45] The State's permission to require additional monitoring when approving changes should include cost-sharing if the State imposes tests beyond federal minima.

[P46] If systems that do not meet the copper action level are not deemed optimized and must implement corrosion control, the rule should clarify whether copper-only exceedances trigger the same LSLR and public notification obligations as lead exceedances.

[P47] Timelines that start from the sample date showing loss of deemed status may be problematic if notification to the system is delayed; require timelines to run from official written notice from the State, not the sample date.

[P48] Small systems selecting small-system options under §141.93 need clear definitions of monitoring requirements and thresholds for reverting to full requirements; request examples.

[P49] Allowing systems to stop treatment steps after Step 2 if meeting both action levels for two consecutive 6-month periods should require State verification of sampling quality and that the reductions are sustainable.

[P50] Mandatory completion of corrosion control treatment study and Step 4 regardless of prior compliance is redundant; request an exemption for systems that had already achieved both action levels before the study with documented evidence.

[P51] Requiring restart of treatment steps if later exceedances occur should permit credit for prior work and allow proportionate timelines rather than restarting the entire sequence.

[P52] The State's discretionary authority to require repetition of completed steps needs procedural due process — written justification and appeal rights — which the rule does include in part but should be emphasized.

[P53] The obligation that the State must notify systems in writing and explain the basis for requiring repeated steps should specify minimum content (data basis, corrective measures required) to make the notice actionable.

[P54] Systems required to stop after Step 2 under certain circumstances need clear documentation requirements to evidence that stopping is appropriate and protective.

[P55] If required to perform the treatment study under Step 3, the system must have access to qualified personnel; the rule should define minimum qualifications for study authors or allow state-provided contractors.

[P56] Restart obligations if systems later exceed action levels must include maximum acceptable timeframes for States to require reimplementation to avoid undue delay and public exposure.

[P57] Initial tap sampling obligations until exceedance or reduced monitoring must be accompanied by a clear schedule and sampling plan template to ensure consistent compliance.

[P58] Recommending optimal corrosion control treatment within six months after exceedance may be unrealistic for complex systems requiring bench or pilot testing; allow additional time for such studies with State approval.

[P59] The requirement for large systems to conduct re-optimization studies following exceedance should allow use of previously collected data where scientifically valid to avoid duplication.

[P60] The State's authority to require small/medium systems with treatment to perform re-optimization studies within 12 months is reasonable but must be tied to clear criteria to avoid arbitrary imposition of studies.

[P61] If the State does not require studies, specifying re-optimized control within 12 months for medium systems may be impractical without funding; request cost reimbursement options.

[P62] Specifying re-optimized corrosion control within 18 months for small systems absent required studies should be extended to 24 months for the smallest systems or those with limited staff.

[P63] Large systems required to complete re-optimization studies within 18 months should be permitted to negotiate milestone schedules with States for multi-phase studies.

[P64] If required by the State to complete studies within 18 months, systems should be allowed to petition for extensions based on demonstrated technical complexity.

[P65] States should have clear obligations and timelines to designate re-optimized control within six months after completion of Step 3 studies; lack of rigid timelines risks delayed protections.

[P66] When systems perform required studies, the State's six-month deadline to designate re-optimized control must be enforced with a remedy if the State misses the deadline.

[P67] The 12-month requirement for large systems to complete modifications to install re-optimized control after State designation may be technologically unrealistic for major infrastructure changes; allow multi-year phased installation schedules based on project scope.

[P68] Requiring small/medium systems to install re-optimized corrosion control within 12 months after designation may be infeasible without funding and contractors; propose extended timelines and grant programs.

[P69] Follow-up sampling within 12 months after installing re-optimized control is acceptable but should allow earlier sampling to document immediate improvements and expedite return-to-compliance decisions.

[P70] The State's obligation to review installed treatment and designate optimal parameters within six months after follow-up sampling should include minimum technical review criteria to ensure transparency.

[P71] The obligation to operate in compliance with State-designated optimal parameters and continue monitoring needs clarity on consequences of minor deviations and reporting burdens; call for tiered responses and clear recordkeeping templates.

[P72] Initial tap sampling requirements until exceedance or reduced monitoring should allow for substitution of sentinel site sampling in systems where representative sites are unavailable, subject to State approval.

[P73] The State's discretion to require studies within 12 months after exceedance should be coupled with an explicit right for systems to request technical assistance or federal funding to complete studies.

[P74] If the State does not require studies, the timelines for specifying optimal control for medium systems (18 months) must be extended when pilot testing or design work is necessary.

[P75] For small systems, the 24-month timeline to specify optimal control absent studies is more reasonable, but commenters will request additional flexibility for systems affected by natural disasters or workforce shortages.

[P76] Completing required studies within 18 months when the State requires them is desirable, but the rule must define acceptable study methodologies and quality assurance standards.

[P77] When systems perform required studies, the State's designation of optimal control must be accompanied by written rationale and an opportunity for systems to respond before final designation.

[P78] Removing the undesignated heading and entries from §52.1870(c) may have unintended regulatory cross-reference implications; request a redlined version showing downstream citation impacts and transition guidance for affected State rules.

raw_output:
[P1] The deadline in § 39.13(a) (comments due July 11, 2022) is unreasonably short and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow operators, MROs, unions, and international stakeholders time to prepare substantive technical and economic comments.

[P1] Request that the FAA clarify whether electronic submissions received after 11:59 PM ET on July 11, 2022, but bearing that date/time stamp, will be accepted, and propose a clear receipt policy to avoid inadvertent exclusion.

[P2] The applicability language in § 39.13(c) appears truncated (ends mid-list and omits some GE90 variants); the FAA should correct and publish a complete list of affected models and serial number ranges to avoid confusion about which engines are covered.

[P2] Industry requests explicit confirmation whether engines on lease, spares in storage, and engines installed on foreign-registered aircraft are included within the AD applicability in § 39.13(c).

[P3] § 39.13(f) requires compliance within specified times “unless already done,” but does not define acceptable evidence of prior compliance; request guidance on required documentation (work orders, shop reports, EASA approvals) acceptable to the FAA.

[P4] The 90-day requirement in § 39.13(g)(1) to revise the ALS and the operator’s maintenance program is unachievable for many airlines given contract review cycles and training requirements; request extension to 180 days or phased implementation tied to next scheduled program revision.

[P4] Require FAA to provide a sample ALS/maintenance-program amendment language and template to facilitate consistent incorporation of the mandated items within the 90-day window in § 39.13(g)(1).

[P5] For the rotating CDP seal P/N 2479M03P01 requirement (§ 39.13(g)(1)(i)), request that Table 1’s inspection intervals and life limits be justified with underlying data; ask FAA to publish the OEM’s service data and failure analyses used to derive those intervals.

[P5] If Table 1 imposes a hard life limit for P/N 2479M03P01, operators request an allowance for on-wing non-destructive inspections (NDI) to extend life in lieu of immediate replacement, with FAA-approved criteria.

[P6] For interstage HPT rotor seal P/N 2505M72P01 (§ 39.13(g)(1)(ii)), request clarification whether the Table 2 requirements apply to repaired or overhauled parts and what constitutes an eligible repair.

[P6] Concern that Table 2 inspection intervals may conflict with existing approved Continuous Airworthiness Maintenance Programs (CAMPs); request explicit instructions for harmonizing the new Table 2 items with operators’ existing programs.

[P7] For HPT rotor stage 2 disk P/N 2505M73P03 (§ 39.13(g)(1)(iii)), request economic impact analysis showing cost per shop visit and fleet-wide cost estimates for the added inspections or life limits in Table 3.

[P7] Safety advocates request that Table 3’s life limits for P/N 2505M73P03 be lowered further given possible catastrophic consequences of disk failure; ask FAA to consider conservative interim limits until longer-term data are collected.

[P8] The remove-and-replace requirement in § 39.13(g)(2) for interstage HPT rotor seal P/N 2629M47P01 (S/N NCU5430D) before 7,400 CSN imposes immediate operational disruptions—airlines request a phased compliance window or ferry-flight relief if replacements are unavailable.

[P8] MROs request clarity on whether the replace action in § 39.13(g)(2) may be performed using vendor-overhaul-reworked parts and whether parts re-identified with new part numbers remain compliant.

[P9] The 7,400 cycles-since-new threshold in § 39.13(g)(2) lacks context—request FAA to publish how cycles are to be counted (flight cycles, accumulated takeoff/landing, including training flights) and handling of engines with incomplete records.

[P9] Legal commenters note potential enforcement ambiguity where operators cannot determine exact CSN due to missing records; request an FAA-allowed reconstruction procedure and safe harbor for operators who reasonably estimate CSN.

[P10] While § 39.13(i)(1) permits AMOCs, operators and manufacturers request explicit timelines for FAA decisions on AMOC requests (e.g., 60 or 90 days) to avoid indefinite operational uncertainty.

[P10] Request that the FAA allow expedited AMOCs for operators demonstrating urgent safety or dispatch needs, with temporary relief pending full AMOC approval.

[P11] The requirement in § 39.13(i)(1) to submit AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO may add unnecessary administrative steps; suggest allowing direct electronic submission to the ECO Branch with concurrent notification of the principal inspector.

[P11] Small operators note they may not have a permanent principal inspector assigned; request explicit instructions and contacts for such cases to comply with the AMOC submission process in § 39.13(i)(1).

raw_output:
[P1] The February 10, 2023 comment due date is already past and therefore makes the proposed rule procedurally defective; the FAA must re-open a new comment period with a future deadline.

[P1] The AD should provide a clear electronic submission method and confirmation process; simply stating a calendar date is insufficient for stakeholders to know how to timely submit technical comments.

[P2] The applicability is overly broad—applying the AD to "all transport and commuter category airplanes equipped with a radio (also known as radar) altimeter" will capture models that never use radio altimeters for required operations and should be narrowed by make/model or function.

[P2] The term "radio (also known as radar) altimeter" is ambiguous and may cause confusion about which systems are covered (e.g., radio altimeter vs. barometric altimeter vs. radio altimeter components); the FAA should define covered equipment by part number, TSO, or installation configuration.

[P2] The AD fails to explain whether aircraft with multiple altimeter installations (redundant systems, flight-test modifications) are treated differently—clarify applicability for supplemental type certificates and modified fleets.

[P3] The Compliance provision lacks objective compliance timeframes keyed to each specific action (e.g., immediate, within X flight hours); simply saying "within the specified compliance times" without cross-referencing the specific timing for each paragraph impedes enforceability.

[P4] Requiring AFM Limitations revision "Before further flight" is impracticable for commercial operators that may have tight schedules and no centralized AFM revision process; allow a short operational grace period or temporary procedure for ferry flights to maintenance.

[P4] Mandating revision of the AFM Limitations to incorporate "figure 2" without providing the figure content in the rule text or making it easily accessible in the docket is procedurally unfair; include the full figure text in the regulatory preamble or AD body.

[P5] Permitting insertion of figure 2 as a compliance method is reasonable, but the AD should allow alternative formats (e.g., electronic AFM databases) and specify acceptable revision control/versioning practices.

[P6] The exception recognizing compliance with paragraph (g) of AD 2021-23-12 is ambiguous—commenters request cross-reference language and citation of the exact actions in AD 2021-23-12 that qualify as satisfying paragraph (h).

[P6] Operators who partially complied with AD 2021-23-12 need clarification whether partial compliance counts; the FAA should specify exactly which elements of paragraph (g) fully satisfy paragraph (h).

[P7] Figure 2's prohibition of ILS approaches, automatic landings, HUD guidance to touchdown, and EFVS-to-touchdown whenever a 5G C-Band NOTAM is active is overly restrictive and will cause widespread operational disruption at many airports; FAA must conduct and publish a detailed risk analysis and consider less severe mitigations.

[P7] The AD does not define the specific NOTAM content or criteria that will indicate 5G C-Band interference "is present"; operators need precise NOTAM language/format to determine compliance and avoid inadvertent violations.

[P7] Prohibiting EFVS-to-touchdown based on 5G NOTAMs negates a safety-critical capability for low-visibility operations and may increase diversion/cancel rates; the FAA should allow EFVS use when aircraft/airframe/airline demonstrate tolerance via testing.

[P8] Requiring different AFM actions for "non-radio altimeter tolerant airplanes" presumes the existence of an accepted tolerance standard; the AD must specify the technical criteria and test protocols used to determine tolerance.

[P9] The June 30, 2023 deadline to incorporate figure 3 is arbitrary and short; airlines need more time to coordinate AFM revisions, obtain approvals from authorities, and update procedures—extend the deadline and/or allow phased compliance.

[P9] Incorporation of figure 3 "terminates the paragraph (h) AFM revision requirement" could create confusion about which limitation set governs operations during the transition window; require explicit transition instructions and an effective date.

[P10] Requiring removal of the paragraph (h) AFM revision "before further flight" after incorporating figure 3 may create record-keeping and audit problems; request that FAA allow a documented change control and a short overlap period to prevent inadvertent removal.

[P11] The differentiation between radio-altimeter tolerant and non-tolerant airplanes imposes certification burdens on operators; the AD should provide guidance and a standardized pathway for operators to demonstrate tolerance.

[P12] The June 30, 2023 incorporation deadline for figure 4 for tolerant airplanes repeats the same impractical timing concerns as paragraph (i); request an extended compliance schedule tied to aircraft scheduled maintenance windows.

[P12] The rule should allow operators to use equivalent manufacturer-approved AFM language rather than literally inserting "figure 4" if the operator can demonstrate that the alternative language provides equal or greater safety.

[P13] The requirement to remove the paragraph (h) revision "before further flight" after adding figure 4 could create gaps during fleet transitions—FAA should permit an approved transition plan that retains necessary limitations until all aircraft are updated.

[P14] Figure 4's blanket prohibition of listed radio-altimeter-dependent operations in contiguous U.S. airspace except at FAA-designated mitigated airports is effectively a nationwide operational restriction and will materially harm network airlines; the FAA must publish the list of mitigated airports and the criteria for mitigation publicly and in advance.

[P14] The exception for "5G C-Band mitigated airports identified by FAA Domestic Notice" delegates critical operational determinations to a notice mechanism without minimum public notice period or comment; this may violate notice-and-comment requirements and should be incorporated into the AD or a formal Order.

[P14] The AD does not address how overflights, positioning flights, freight-only flights, or non-passenger operations are to be handled under the Figure 4 prohibitions; clarify applicability across flight types and operations under different parts (91, 125, 121).

[P15] Requiring part 121 operators to modify non-tolerant airplanes by Feb 1, 2024 is an aggressive mandate given supply chain, STC approval, and maintenance scheduling constraints; extend the modification deadline or allow approved AMOCs to provide staged compliance.

[P15] The AD lacks an estimated cost and burden analysis of the mandated modifications for part 121 fleets; provide economic impact data per aircraft and per operator in the final rule.

[P16] Requiring AFM Limitations revisions to incorporate figure 4 may conflict with foreign operator requirements and existing AFM approval processes—allow operators to obtain local authority validation prior to forced AFM changes.

[P17] Requiring removal of the paragraph (i) AFM revision as part of the part 121 modification process creates complexity for mixed-fleet operators; provide a matrix of required AFM texts for each aircraft configuration and operational authorization.

[P18] Allowing non-part-121 operators to optionally perform the part-121 modifications is good, but the AD should clarify whether voluntary modification confers operational privileges (e.g., access to mitigated airports) and how to document that privilege.

[P18] The rule should state whether voluntary modifications performed by non-part-121 operators require FAA acceptance, an STC, or paperwork beyond AFM revision; clarify approval pathway.

[P19] Empowering the Operational Safety Branch Manager to approve AMOCs is appropriate, but the AD should specify expected review timelines (e.g., 60 days) to ensure timely operational decisions.

[P20] Requiring AMOC requests to be routed through principal inspectors or Flight Standards Offices may delay review; allow direct submission to the Operational Safety Branch with concurrent notification to local FSO to expedite safety approvals.

[P21] The requirement to direct direct submissions to the person identified in paragraph (m) is acceptable, but paragraph (m) must be published in the AD; otherwise requesters lack a named contact.

[P22] Permitting email submission to AMOC@faa.gov is helpful; however, the AD should also allow secure file transfer for large technical packages and define file formats and maximum sizes.

[P23] Requiring prior notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC could create operational timing conflicts (e.g., last-minute operational contingencies); allow immediate use with retroactive notice to avoid safety/dispatch delays.

[P24] Recognizing AMOCs previously approved for AD 2021-23-12 as valid for paragraph (h) is helpful, but the FAA should publish a crosswalk of which specific AMOCs are covered and any limitations or conditional language attached to that acceptance.

[P7] The rule fails to describe enforcement consequences (civil penalties, certificate actions) for violations of the NOTAM-based prohibitions; operators need clarity on enforcement to assess compliance risk.

[P14] The AD does not explain coordination with the FCC and wireless carriers regarding power reductions, buffer zones, or technical mitigations at airports; request explicit interagency procedures and timelines for designating mitigated airports.

[P2] The AD must clarify how the rule applies to foreign-registered aircraft operating in U.S. airspace and whether foreign civil aviation authorities' approvals are acceptable to demonstrate radio altimeter tolerance.

[P15] For part 121 fleet commonality, the AD should allow dispatch exemptions for specific tail numbers that have completed modification so that partial fleet modification does not compel whole-fleet grounding or cancellations.

[P9] The AD should allow temporary operational relief via a carrier-specific operational risk assessment approved by the principal inspector while awaiting AFM revision incorporation, to avoid unnecessary cancellations.

[P12] The FAA must publish the technical criteria for "radio altimeter tolerant" (maximum allowable interference, detection thresholds, required mitigations) so that manufacturers and MROs can design compliant modifications and test plans.

[P7] The reliance on NOTAMs to trigger prohibitions is problematic because NOTAMs are not standardized globally and can be issued/withdrawn with little predictability; the FAA should use a more robust communication method with lead time and explicit content.

[P14] The AD neglects to account for cargo-only operators who perform many night/low-visibility operations at smaller airports that may not be designated as mitigated—this creates safety and economic impacts disproportionately affecting cargo carriers and should be addressed.

[P4] Requiring AFM revisions "before further flight" without specifying who may authorize a temporary operations letter or where such authorization should be documented leaves operators open to inconsistent interpretations by inspectors—provide a sample authorization form or process.

[P1] Given the February 10, 2023 date, many stakeholders may have already submitted comments—FAA should confirm whether previous comments were considered and publish a summary-response document when re-issuing a new comment period.

[P19] The AD should permit industry consensus standards (e.g., RTCA/DO documents) as an acceptable basis for AMOC approvals and reference those standards explicitly.

[P22] The rule should include expected confidentiality protections and handling procedures for proprietary technical data submitted in AMOC requests to AMOC@faa.gov.

[P14] The AD lacks an operational equivalency pathway for aircraft equipped with alternative sensors (e.g., enhanced GPS, synthetic vision) to perform otherwise prohibited operations when radio altimeter is degraded; provide criteria to use alternate equipment.

[P1] The May 29, 2018 comments due date is unreasonable and provides inadequate time for small operators and foreign stakeholders to prepare detailed technical comments; extend the comment period by at least 60–90 days.

[P1] The rule improperly uses an absolute calendar date (May 29, 2018) without specifying the AD effective date reference for calculation; clarify whether the deadline is relative to publication or effective date.

[P2] The blanket obligation "If actions have not already been done, perform the actions specified in (f)(1) and (f)(2)" fails to provide an explicit compliance window for operators who discover the AD late; add a clear compliance timeframe or grace period.

[P3] The requirement to inspect the aft face of the firewall "within the next 90 days after the effective date" is unclear for aircraft in storage, overseas, or under lease; clarify how the 90-day clock applies to aircraft not in U.S. registry or not accessible.

[P3] The inspection requirement references "specified service bulletin instructions" but does not identify the bulletin number or revision in the text of (f)(1); include a specific service bulletin reference and revision date to avoid ambiguity.

[P3] The 90-day inspection deadline is burdensome for operators with limited maintenance opportunities; permit inspection at the next scheduled heavy maintenance check within 180 days as an alternative for operators with scheduling constraints.

[P3] The AD does not define accepted inspection techniques (visual only, removal of panels required, borescope allowed); clarify acceptable methods and minimum qualifications for inspectors to ensure consistent compliance.

[P4] Requiring removal "before further flight" of black foam insulation found covering the firewall may ground aircraft unexpectedly; allow a short ferry period under operational safety limitations to reach a maintenance facility, with FAA-approved procedures.

[P4] The AD mandates removal "following the specified service bulletin instructions" but fails to state who authorizes deviations for safety or preservation of evidence; add an explicit provision allowing temporary measures for safe ferrying pending full compliance.

[P4] The AD does not specify whether replacement insulating materials are permitted or if any replacement is required; clarify approved materials and installation methods after removal to prevent reinstallation of noncompliant insulation.

[P5] Granting authority to the Manager, Small Airplane Standards Branch, to approve AMOCs without public transparency raises concerns; require that AMOC approvals for this AD be posted publicly with redacted proprietary information.

[P6] Requiring AMOC submission to a physical mailing address (901 Locust, Room 301, Kansas City) without clear acceptance of electronic submission is outdated; mandate acceptance of AMOC submissions by email and provide an email contact to expedite review.

[P6] The contact listed (Mike Kiesov) may change; include position-based routing (e.g., "Manager, Small Airplane Standards Branch") and provide a centralized mailbox to ensure continuity.

[P7] The obligation to notify the principal inspector (PI) or local FSDO before using an AMOC lacks a required timeframe for notification; specify a minimum notice period (e.g., 72 hours) to allow FAA oversight.

[P7] Operators without a designated PI may be uncertain whom to notify; define the default contact (local FSDO or certificate holding district office) and provide contact information or a lookup procedure.

[P8] Requiring corrective actions from a manufacturer to be approved by the named FAA manager or the New Zealand CAA creates potential jurisdictional conflicts and delays; permit manufacturer-approved repairs validated by a DER (designated engineering representative) or accredited organization as an interim measure.

[P8] The provision does not define the process or timeline for FAA or NZ CAA approval of manufacturer corrective actions; add explicit review timelines (e.g., 30–60 days) so operators can plan maintenance.
