[P1] The October 15, 2018 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonably short and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow stakeholders (airlines, MROs, labor unions, and general aviation operators) sufficient time to prepare detailed technical and economic comments.

[P1] Requiring receipt of comments by October 15, 2018 without specifying time zone or whether electronic submissions count as received on that date creates uncertainty; the FAA should clarify accepted submission methods and timestamp rules.

[P2] The blanket obligation in § 39.13(f) to “comply within the specified compliance times” lacks clarity about whether compliance timeframes are based on calendar days, flight cycles, flight hours, or scheduled maintenance opportunities; the FAA should specify units and baseline counters.

[P2] § 39.13(f) does not provide relief for operators unable to meet specified compliance times due to parts shortages or scheduling constraints; the rule should include explicit temporary extension procedures or allow immediate AMOC requests without penalty.

[P3] Requiring performance of all actions labeled “RC” in the Boeing Alert Service Bulletins (per § 39.13(g)(1)) without FAA incorporation by reference of the full Bulletin text or drawing set makes it difficult for operators to determine exact obligations; the FAA should incorporate the service bulletin by reference or publish the full instructions in the docket.

[P3] The cross-reference in § 39.13(g)(1) to “the applicable time specified in paragraph 5, ‘Compliance,’” of the Boeing Alert Service Bulletin is ambiguous as incorporated into the AD; the FAA should restate the compliance times in the AD to avoid reliance on external documents.

[P3] The reliance on Boeing Alert Service Bulletin B787–81205–SB290032–00, Issue 001, dated November 17, (year missing) is incomplete and creates uncertainty; the FAA must correct the citation to include the full date and revision history.

[P4] § 39.13(g)(2) requires Model 787–9 airplanes to install software and do other RC actions prior to or concurrently with other actions, but provides no specific software version or configuration control numbers; the FAA should specify the exact software release(s) required.

[P4] The requirement in § 39.13(g)(2) to perform software installation “prior to or concurrently” lacks metrics for “concurrently” and could force inefficient work sequencing; FAA should allow operators to complete software within a reasonable window after mechanical work if safety is not compromised.

[P5] The credit provision in § 39.13(h) for actions performed using Issue 001 before the effective date is helpful, but it does not state whether partial completion of tasks or earlier service bulletin revisions (other than Issue 001) qualify for credit; this should be clarified.

[P5] § 39.13(h) should explicitly require operators who claim credit for prior actions to document and submit proof (work orders, logbook entries, part serial numbers) to their principal inspector to avoid later enforcement disputes.

[P6] Using the AD effective date as the substitute for the service bulletin “Issue 001 date” per § 39.13(i) could retroactively change compliance timelines for operators who used the bulletin date as baseline; the FAA should explain why this approach is necessary and provide transitional relief.

[P6] § 39.13(i) may create inconsistent compliance determinations between operators who relied on the original bulletin Issue date and those who use the AD effective date; the FAA should allow operators to choose the earlier baseline that favors compliance.

[P7] Granting the Seattle ACO Branch Manager authority to approve AMOCs in § 39.13(j)(1) centralizes decision-making and may delay approvals for international operators; the FAA should allow designated FAA DERs or other ARTCC offices to process routine AMOCs to expedite relief.

[P7] § 39.13(j)(1) should specify expected turnaround times for AMOC decisions or require the Manager to publish processing time targets to avoid protracted grounding or work delays.

[P8] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO per § 39.13(j)(1) may be burdensome for operators without a principal inspector (e.g., foreign operators); FAA should permit direct submission to the Seattle ACO with copy to the local FSDO.

[P9] The instruction in § 39.13(j)(1) to address direct AMOC submissions “to the person named in paragraph (k)(1)” is circular because paragraph (k)(1) is not provided in the proposed rule text in the docket; the FAA should ensure the named contact is included and current.

[P10] Allowing AMOC information to be emailed to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is useful, but there is no statement about acceptable file formats, maximum attachment size, or security/confidentiality for proprietary information; FAA should provide guidance.

[P11] The obligation in § 39.13(j)(2) to notify the principal inspector or local FSDO “before using any approved AMOC” is ambiguous regarding timing (how far in advance?) and form of notice (written, electronic, phone); the FAA should specify timing and acceptable notification methods.

[P11] § 39.13(j)(2) should clarify whether notification of AMOC use must include copies of the AMOC approval and work instructions, and whether such notification constitutes FAA acceptance of the method for future audits.

[P12] Permitting Boeing ODA approval of AMOCs for repairs/modifications per § 39.13(j)(3) is appropriate for efficiency, but the AD does not require public disclosure or FAA oversight of Boeing ODA approvals; FAA should require reporting of ODA-approved deviations to the Seattle ACO.

[P12] Relying on Boeing’s ODA to approve AMOCs may raise conflict-of-interest concerns where Boeing is both the design approval holder and the approver; the FAA should require independent FAA review for AMOCs that affect safety-critical systems.

[P13] § 39.13(j)(3) requires that AMOC-approved deviations meet the airplane’s certification basis and reference this AD, but does not require evidence or engineering substantiation to be submitted for FAA review; the FAA should require documented substantiation and a clear path to appeal denials.

[P13] The phrase “meet the certification basis of the airplane” in § 39.13(j)(3) is vague for derivatives or special conditions; FAA should clarify how to address differences in certification basis across 787 models and export versions.

[P14] The obligation in § 39.13(j)(4)(i) that all RC-labeled steps “must be done” is strict; operators may need minor deviations for logistical reasons (tooling, access panels) and should be allowed limited deviations under an approved quality system without full AMOC process.

[P14] The inclusion of figures identified in RC steps as mandatory in § 39.13(j)(4)(i) could inadvertently make non-mandatory illustrative material enforceable; FAA should limit mandatory inclusion to written steps and key drawings only.

[P15] The exception for steps labeled “RC Exempt” in § 39.13(j)(4)(i) is reasonable, but the AD must clearly define whether an entire step labeled “RC Exempt” versus a substep labeled “RC Exempt” changes the compliance obligations for the entire procedure.

[P15] Operators may have followed the meaning of “RC Exempt” differently; FAA should require Boeing to clearly mark the service bulletin and publish an errata if any inconsistencies exist.

[P16] Requiring an AMOC for any deviation to RC steps in § 39.13(j)(4)(i) will create a heavy administrative burden for trivial deviations (e.g., torque wrench alternate) — the FAA should allow operators to use approved maintenance program repairs for non-safety-significant deviations with subsequent notification.

[P16] The AD should define the threshold for what constitutes an RC deviation requiring an AMOC (safety significance, system function) so operators and MROs can triage requests appropriately.

[P17] Allowing deviation from non-RC steps under an operator’s maintenance program without AMOC per § 39.13(j)(4)(ii) is appropriate, but the AD fails to require documentation or retention periods for such deviations; the FAA should mandate recordkeeping to demonstrate compliance during inspections.

[P17] § 39.13(j)(4)(ii) should require that any deviations from non-RC steps be reviewed by the operator’s accountable manager and that risk assessments be documented prior to implementation.

[P3][P4] The AD’s heavy reliance on Boeing Alert Service Bulletins to define the scope of mandated actions raises concerns about private standard-setting authority; the FAA should explicitly assert regulatory control and provide public availability of all incorporated material.

[P2][P11] The AD does not address enforcement or penalties for late compliance when AMOC requests are pending; the FAA should state enforcement discretion and allow continued operations under good-faith AMOC applications.

[P6][P5] Operators who completed actions based on earlier service bulletin issues other than Issue 001 should be given clear credit rules; otherwise inconsistent crediting will result in unnecessary rework and costs.

[P7][P12] Foreign civil aviation authorities (CAAs) should be allowed to accept FAA-approved AMOCs without duplicative approvals; the FAA should coordinate bilateral acceptance to prevent duplicated work for international operators.

[P10] The FAA should provide an alternative secure submission method for AMOC requests and sensitive technical data (e.g., SFTP or secure web portal) rather than only a public email address.

[P3] The AD should provide an economic impact statement or cost estimate for the mandated RC actions per airplane and fleet to enable commenters to evaluate cost reasonableness and propose alternatives.

[P1] The rule lacks clarity on what constitutes an "appropriate wage index" for adjusting the labor portion of the Federal per diem base rate and commenters request CMS define the specific wage index source (e.g., hospital wage index, CBSA-level BLS wage data) to ensure predictability.

[P1] Industry commenters will argue that using a single national or broad wage index without facility-level adjustments will misstate local labor costs for inpatient psychiatric facilities and request facility-specific or finer geographic wage measures.

[P1] State hospital associations will request that CMS allow use of state-level or locality-specific wage data where available, because the federal wage index may not reflect rural labor market disparities in psychiatric care.

[P2] Rural hospitals and rural health advocacy groups will comment that applying the wage index based only on the facility’s urban/rural designation under § 412.402 ignores intra-area wage variation and request that CMS permit adjustment at a sub-county or county level.

[P2] Legal experts will point out potential inconsistencies between how § 412.402 defines urban/rural and other CMS programs’ designations, asking CMS to harmonize definitions to avoid conflicting payment calculations.

[P3] Small inpatient psychiatric facilities will oppose the 95% cap on decreases as insufficiently protective, arguing that abrupt increases in labor index could still create cash-flow shocks and request a higher floor (e.g., 97.5% or hold-harmless for multiple years).

[P3] Budget-constrained payers will argue the 95% floor perpetuates legacy overpayments and ask CMS to provide analysis quantifying fiscal impact of the cap on federal expenditures and Medicare trust funds.

[P3] Labor unions will support the 95% cap on decreases, submitting that the cap prevents sudden, destabilizing pay reductions which could lead to staff turnover and reduced quality of psychiatric care.

[P4] Legal commenters will assert the prohibition (not less than 95% of prior year) may conflict with statutory mandates for wage index neutrality and request CMS provide legal authority and rationale for imposing the floor.

[P1] Technical commenters will ask CMS to specify the update frequency for the wage index (annual, biennial) and public posting schedule so facilities can plan budgets.

[P3] Health systems with psychiatric units in multiple facilities will request guidance on whether the 95% cap applies site-by-site or can be aggregated across facilities under common ownership to avoid perverse incentives.

[P1] The comment deadline of November 21, 2022 in § 39.13(a) is unreasonably short and should be extended to at least 60 days from publication to allow affected operators, unions, and manufacturers adequate time to prepare technical and economic comments.

[P1] The provision (§ 39.13(a)) does not state whether extensions to the comment period will be considered if new substantive data emerges; FAA should clarify extension policy or commit to reopening comment period if necessary.

[P2] The scope provision (§ 39.13(c)) is unclear whether the AD applies to Boeing airplanes modified by supplemental type certificates (STCs) or field-approved alterations; FAA should explicitly state whether STC-modified airplanes remain within scope.

[P2] § 39.13(c) lacks a clear definition of "as identified" (e.g., by serial number ranges or production line revisions); commenters should request that FAA include specific line numbers/serial ranges to avoid compliance confusion.

[P3] The identification in § 39.13(c)(1) of 737–600/–700/–700C/–800/–900/–900ER based on Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737–38A1072 RB is acceptable only if the bulletin's effectivity list is reproduced in the final rule; otherwise operators cannot verify applicability without purchasing proprietary Boeing documentation.

[P3] For § 39.13(c)(1): Small operators of passenger-to-freighter conversions of the listed 737 Classics may be uncertain if their unique configurations are covered; FAA should clarify applicability to freighter or converted airframes.

[P4] For § 39.13(c)(2), listing 737–8 and –9 via Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737–38A1073 RB without including the bulletin's effectivity text in the AD hinders transparency and may violate notice-and-comment expectations for affected parties.

[P4] The scope in § 39.13(c)(2) should explicitly address whether previously grounded or stored 737–8/–9 airplanes (temporarily deregistered) are within the compliance obligations when returned to service.

[P5] § 39.13(f) requires compliance "within the compliance times specified" but does not state whether calendar days, flight cycles, or flight hours are the controlling metric where the bulletin uses ambiguous language; FAA should clarify the time units for compliance.

[P5] The "unless already accomplished" clause in § 39.13(f) should require operators to maintain documentary evidence proving prior compliance; FAA should specify acceptable records and retention periods.

[P6] § 39.13(g)(1) mandates doing all applicable actions in Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737–38A1072 RB "except as specified by paragraph (h)" but provides no process for resolving conflicts between the bulletin and the AD beyond paragraph (h); operators need a clear hierarchy and conflict-resolution guidance.

[P6] Requiring incorporation of all actions from Boeing SBs or bulletins in § 39.13(g)(1) effectively delegates rulemaking to Boeing; commenters should object and ask FAA to ensure all mandated actions are FAA-adopted and legally enforceable with independent FAA justification.

[P7] Similarly, § 39.13(g)(2) references Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737–38A1073 RB; commenters should request that any required parts, tooling, or materials referenced in the bulletins be made available to third-party maintenance providers, not only Boeing-authorized repair stations.

[P7] § 39.13(g)(2) should clarify whether repetitive actions in the Accomplishment Instructions create ongoing maintenance requirements (IFR recurring inspections) or are one-time mitigations; ambiguity imposes compliance risk on operators.

[P8] § 39.13(h)(1) replaces the bulletin's original issue date with the AD effective date for compliance calculations; operators may have already scheduled work based on the bulletin's original issue date—FAA should allow credit for work done in reliance on the bulletin's dates and explicitly state that such work is acceptable.

[P8] The requirement in § 39.13(h)(1) to use the AD effective date could shorten compliance windows unexpectedly for operators who delayed action pending the AD; FAA should include a grandfathering provision for actions performed before the AD effective date but after bulletin issuance.

[P9] Identical to P8, § 39.13(h)(2) should also clarify how compliance time calculations handle airplanes with multiple bulletin revisions; FAA must indicate whether earlier revisions’ compliance times are preserved or superseded.

[P9] § 39.13(h)(2) fails to address time-in-service accrual for parked aircraft — commenters request guidance on counting flight cycles/hours accrued during storage for compliance time calculations.

[P10] § 39.13(i)(1) authorizes the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch to approve AMOCs but concentrates decision authority in a single office, which may delay urgent approvals for operators outside Seattle; FAA should permit delegation to local Flight Standards District Offices (FSDOs) or provide SLA timelines for AMOC decisions.

[P10] Legal commenters may argue that limiting AMOC approval authority to the Seattle ACO Manager may exceed FAA procedural norms for regionally based approvals and request clarification of the legal basis for centralizing authority.

[P11] § 39.13(i)(1) requires sending AMOC requests to the principal inspector or responsible Flight Standards Office per 14 CFR 39.19; commenters ask FAA to provide a standardized AMOC submission checklist to reduce processing errors and delays.

[P11] Operators note § 39.13(i)(1) should allow submission of AMOC requests electronically through a secure FAA portal rather than paper or email to better track status and records.

[P12] § 39.13(i)(1) instructs senders to address direct submissions to the certification office manager identified in paragraph (j)(1), but the NPRM does not reproduce paragraph (j)(1); commenters request the AD include the contact name and address to avoid misdirected requests.

[P12] Legal counsel points out that specifying a named individual in § 39.13(i)(1) may cause administrative problems if staffing changes; FAA should provide a position title and office contact rather than a personal name.

[P13] § 39.13(i)(1) permits emailing AMOC information to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov; commenters request confirmation that attachments up to specific sizes, acceptable file formats, and encryption protocols are supported.

[P13] Privacy advocates request that FAA disclose how emailed AMOC submissions will be protected under FOIA and whether proprietary or sensitive technical data will receive confidential treatment.

[P14] § 39.13(i)(2) requires notifying the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC but does not define timing (e.g., within 24 hours, prior to first flight). Commenters request a clear notification timeline and the required notification content.

[P14] Maintenance and operations organizations request an exception in § 39.13(i)(2) allowing post-use notification in emergency situations where immediate return-to-service is necessary for safety-of-flight.

[P15] § 39.13(i)(3) allows Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to be used for repairs/mods/alterations but conditions that approval on being "authorized by the Seattle ACO Manager"; this may duplicate bureaucracy—commenters ask FAA to clarify whether Boeing ODA approvals are effective immediately or require FAA concurrence.

[P15] Conflict-of-interest concerns: allowing the Boeing Company ODA to approve AMOCs for compliance with an AD that references Boeing bulletins raises the appearance of self-approval; commenters (public interest groups) ask FAA to explain safeguards against undue manufacturer influence.

[P16] § 39.13(i)(3) conditions AMOC approval on being authorized by the Manager, Seattle ACO, but does not specify the authorization process or standards; request that FAA publish the criteria and timeline for such authorization.

[P16] International operators question whether Boeing ODA approvals under § 39.13(i)(3) will be accepted by foreign civil aviation authorities; FAA should coordinate with ICAO partner authorities or provide guidance on mutual acceptance.

[P17] § 39.13(i)(3) requires that any AMOC repair/modification meet the airplane's certification basis and specifically reference this AD; commenters request FAA to define what constitutes sufficient technical substantiation that an alternative meets the certification basis.

[P17] Legal commenters point out that requiring specific reference to this AD in AMOC approvals could complicate future ADs that amend or supersede this AD; FAA should provide template language for referencing to avoid ambiguity.

[P17] Maintenance organizations ask FAA to confirm whether previously approved AMOCs for related Boeing bulletins will be automatically accepted under this AD if they already reference the certification basis and provide equivalent safety margins.

[P5] Economic stakeholders request FAA include an analysis or allow comment on the cost impact of compliance time demands in § 39.13(f), including labor, parts, and downtime estimates, since the AD imposes mandatory actions within specified times.

[P6] Airlines request clear instructions in § 39.13(g)(1) whether compliance actions must be performed by Boeing-authorized maintenance providers or whether certified third-party repair stations may perform the work.

[P7] For § 39.13(g)(2), pilot unions request clarity whether compliance actions will affect dispatch reliability or require operational limitations while repairs are pending; require FAA to define interim safety measures.

[P3] Environmental groups request FAA assess the environmental impacts of the mandated actions in Boeing bulletin 737–38A1072 RB and include any required NEPA analysis as part of the AD docket.

[P1] The deadline in provision P1 (comments due October 29, 2018) is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60–90 days to allow stakeholders, including small carriers and repair stations, to prepare informed comments and technical data.

[P1] Legal commenters will note that the proposed rule cites an October 29, 2018 comment deadline but the AD references effective dates in 2013; the agency should clarify whether the deadline is a clerical error and reissue the NPRM with correct dates if so.

[P2] Operators will object that P2’s vague phrasing “within the compliance times specified” without restating those times in the body of the AD forces reliance on outside documents and increases compliance risk; the AD should explicitly list the compliance times.

[P3] Many operators will request that provision P3’s 60-day window to revise the maintenance program after January 16, 2013 be updated to a forward-looking timeframe or provide relief for operators who could not have made changes retroactively.

[P4] Regional and low-utilization operators will challenge P4’s threshold requiring airplanes with ≤10,500 cycles as of 1/16/2013 to perform the AWL initial task before 12,000 cycles, arguing it unfairly penalizes aircraft that already schedule long intervals between heavy checks and that the agency should allow phased compliance tied to next scheduled maintenance.

[P5] For P5, operators with aircraft over 10,500 cycles as of 1/16/2013 will comment that the 1,500-flight-cycle compliance window is impractical for high-utilization aircraft and propose alternative metrics (e.g., calendar days or flight hours) or allow credit for accomplished inspections.

[P6] P6’s mixed thresholds (4360 or 1500 cycles, whichever is later) are confusing as presented; commenters will request that the FAA publish a clear table or calculator for determining the next AWL initial due date based on each aircraft’s inspection history.

[P7] Safety advocates will support P7’s termination provision but request clarification that doing (j) or (l) terminates paragraph (g) only for the repaired area and not for adjacent structure — and request language ensuring no loophole permitting termination where inspections are incomplete.

[P8] Legal commenters will ask P8 to define the scope of “accomplishment of (m)” that terminates paragraph (g): whether partial completion or only full completion of all tasks in (m) qualifies.

[P9] Industry will object to P9’s prohibition on using alternative actions or intervals after implementing paragraph (g) as overly restrictive and argue it prevents operators from using safety-based, data-driven alternatives developed after the AD; they will request broader AMOC pathways or performance-based alternatives.

[P10] Conversely, safety groups will support P10’s limited exception that alternatives be approved as AMOCs (P10) but request the FAA commit to expedited AMOC review timelines (e.g., 60 days) given the safety-critical nature of the requirements.

[P11] Operators will comment that P11’s allowance to insert Bombardier TR 2B–2187 into the MRM is helpful but request explicit permission to use equivalent approved service information (e.g., later TR revisions) without needing separate AMOC approval.

[P12] For P12, commenters will request the AD specify exact “times” for each action in (j)(1)–(j)(3) rather than referencing figure 1 only, because some operators cannot easily reconcile figure references with fleet scheduling software.

[P13] Regarding P13, NDT providers will request more detail on acceptable nondestructive inspection (NDI) methods allowed under AWL 53–61–153 (e.g., eddy current types, probe sizes) and ask the FAA to permit supplier-approved techniques when equivalent.

[P14] For P14, commenters will request engineering substantiation for the RPB modification required in (j)(2) and ask the FAA to publish the structural rationale and expected fatigue-life benefit to justify mandatory modification.

[P15] Operators will object to P15’s requirement to revise maintenance programs “before further flight” after accomplishing the modification in (j)(2) as impractical for line maintenance; they request a reasonable administrative window (e.g., 10 business days) to process program changes.

[P16] Maintenance organizations will request that P16 explicitly allow deferred temporary repairs approved by the FAA Manager or TCCA in emergency situations, provided final repair methods are later approved per P16’s approval authorities.

[P17] For P17, commenters will request that the REO referenced be provided in the docket and that FAA confirm whether alternative repair schemes approved by the TCCA DAO previously will be recognized without reapproval.

[P18] Operators with compliance histories will support P18’s allowance for airplanes that performed (j)(1) and (j)(2) before the AD to follow (l), but request clear eligibility criteria and documentation requirements to demonstrate they meet the “performed using the R…” (truncated in the proposal) standard.

[P19] For P19, inspectors will request clarification on the required depth and coverage of the “special detailed inspection for Zone B” and whether access panels or structural removal are required, plus a list of acceptable borescope and NDI techniques.

[P20] Regarding P20, commenters will note that using the REO’s threshold measured from its incorporation date creates potential for widely varying thresholds across operators; they will ask the FAA to standardize thresholds based on fleet age or cycles rather than program incorporation date.

[P21] For P21, Bombardier or the serial 7610 operator will request confirmation that the REO 601R–53–61–5828 Rev A reinforcement for serial 7610 has been validated and ask for fatigue test data confirming its adequacy as an alternative to (j).

[P22] Operators will object to P22’s requirement to revise the maintenance program “before further flight after accomplishing the reinforcement, or within 60 days” as duplicative and seek clarification which of the two (whichever is later) governs.

[P23] Commenters will challenge P23’s broad prohibition on alternative actions or intervals after revising the program per (j)(3), (l)(2), or (m), arguing that it removes operational flexibility and should be limited to safety-critical elements only or permit performance-based alternatives subject to FAA approval.

[P24] For P24, stakeholders will request a specific definition of “repaired area” to which termination of paragraph (g) applies, to avoid disputes about what constitutes the repaired area boundary.

[P1] The proposed action to amend Appendix B by revising B5.7 and reserving B5.8 lacks sufficient justification and analysis in the preamble; commenters request the DOE provide the administrative record and rationale supporting why these particular changes are necessary.

[P2] Revising section B5.7 (P2) to expand categorical exclusions should be accompanied by an explicit explanation of the environmental review history and evidence that past approvals under NGA section 3 had no significant environmental impacts; otherwise the rulemaking is arbitrary and capricious.

[P3] Removing and reserving section B5.8 (P3) without explaining what B5.8 currently covers raises concerns about regulatory gaps; DOE should publish the current text of B5.8 and explain how its removal will affect decisionmaking and environmental protection.

[P4] The categorical exclusion in B5.7 that would allow DOE to treat approvals/disapprovals of new exports under NGA section 3 as not requiring NEPA review (P4) is overly broad and could exempt projects with significant upstream greenhouse gas emissions from NEPA analysis.

[P5] The language in P5 that places approvals or disapprovals of new authorizations and amendments within a categorical exclusion fails to distinguish between projects with substantially different environmental footprints (e.g., small amendment vs. large new long-term export authorization), leading to an unlawful blanket exclusion.

[P6] Including transportation by marine vessel within the categorical exclusion (P6) is unlawful because marine transportation can produce direct environmental impacts (air emissions, ballast water, marine mammal strikes, coastal impacts) that warrant project-specific NEPA review.

[P7] Industry commenters will support P4–P6 if DOE clarifies that the categorical exclusion only applies to ministerial or narrow procedural determinations and will not apply to authorizations that would result in a significant increase in export volumes or new infrastructure.

[P8] Energy trade associations will request DOE to specify numeric thresholds (e.g., percentage change in authorized export volumes or tonnage/mmbtu) that trigger when an authorization is no longer categorically excluded, because the current text contains no such limits.

[P9] Environmental NGOs will object that the categorical exclusion ignores the reasonably foreseeable indirect effects of export approvals, namely increased domestic production, flaring, methane leakage, and life-cycle CO2 emissions; they will demand an explicit requirement to analyze upstream and downstream greenhouse gas impacts before applying the exclusion.

[P10] Coastal states and marine conservation groups will claim that including marine transport in the exclusion (P6) violates the Coast Guard and NOAA interest in assessing impacts on marine ecosystems and asked DOE to exempt any action involving new or expanded LNG tanker routes, increased vessel calls, or construction/modification of marine terminals from the categorical exclusion.

[P11] Legal experts will argue DOE lacks authority under NEPA to categorically exclude actions that have precedent of causing significant environmental effects, and must demonstrate with substantial evidence that the excluded actions do not individually or cumulatively have significant impacts.

[P12] Small public stakeholders and local governments near ports will request that DOE amend B5.7 to require consultation with local authorities and issuance of public notices before relying on the categorical exclusion for authorizations that will increase vessel traffic in their jurisdictions.

[P13] Commenters will ask DOE to add a “no extraordinary circumstances” clause to B5.7 that enumerates specific circumstances that would preclude use of the categorical exclusion (e.g., proximity to critical habitat, cultural resources, environmental justice communities, wetlands, designated marine protected areas).

[P14] Tribal governments will demand that DOE clarify that the categorical exclusion will not apply where actions may affect tribal treaty rights, cultural resources, or ancestral lands, and request mandatory government-to-government consultation before any exclusion is applied.

[P15] Public health advocates will claim the rule fails to consider cumulative air quality impacts from increased LNG exports and marine vessel emissions in nonattainment areas and urge DOE to require at least an Environmental Assessment (EA) in those cases.

[P16] State regulatory agencies will request DOE coordinate with state permitting and environmental review processes and clarify whether reliance on the categorical exclusion preempts state environmental review or reporting requirements.

[P17] Industry commenters will request DOE include a streamlined, predictable process and timeline for when DOE will determine to use the categorical exclusion, to avoid delays and legal uncertainty.

[P18] Renewable energy and climate advocates will recommend DOE exclude greenhouse gas-intensive export approvals from B5.7 and argue that life-cycle GHG accounting must be part of the review when export volumes exceed identified thresholds.

[P19] Legal counsel for potential project opponents will assert that removing sections C13, D8, and D9 (P7–P8) could eliminate useful procedural or analytical guidance formerly contained in those sections; DOE must publish the removed texts and explain replacements or alternative guidance.

[P20] Administrative law scholars will request DOE to explain how reserving sections (P1, P3, P7, P8) affects stakeholder rights — whether reserved sections will be reinstituted later and under what public process — and to commit to transparent follow-up rulemaking if content is to be reissued.

[P21] Environmental justice organizations will object that the proposed categorical exclusion lacks required analysis on disproportionate impacts to low-income and minority communities near production, transport, and export facilities; they will request specific EJ screening criteria to trigger NEPA review.

[P22] Port authorities will ask DOE to clarify that the categorical exclusion does not apply to authorizations that would require new onshore or offshore terminal construction, significant dredging, or other major infrastructure modifications.

[P23] Commenters will request DOE to include a mandatory check-list or screening form in B5.7 that project proponents must complete demonstrating absence of significant impacts before DOE may rely on the categorical exclusion.

[P24] Several parties will request that DOE conduct a retrospective review of prior NGA section 3 authorizations to compare actual environmental impacts to the agency’s assumptions supporting the proposed exclusion.

[P25] International trade advocates may claim that the categorical exclusion could speed exports and benefit trade objectives; they will request DOE affirm the rule’s intent to facilitate predictable export authorization processing while asking for safeguards to avoid environmental harm.

[P26] Academic experts will request DOE to provide data and modeling supporting the assertion that associated marine transport will not have significant cumulative impacts, including vessel emission inventories, route analyses, and species impact studies.

[P27] Procedural fairness advocates will demand that DOE explain how public participation rights will be preserved if NEPA documentation is not required for actions under B5.7, and propose alternative public notice/ comment steps where the exclusion applies.

[P28] Industry groups will request DOE define “amendments to existing authorizations” (P5) — whether short-term, seasonal, volume reallocations, or long-term term extensions — to avoid inconsistent application across cases.

[P29] Investors and finance stakeholders will warn that excluding NEPA review may increase litigation risk and ask DOE to provide indemnities or clear legal standards for when the exclusion is permissible to reduce project financing uncertainty.

[P30] Environmental law clinics will argue DOE must include an assessment of downstream end-use emissions (e.g., power generation, industrial uses abroad) when considering whether an export authorization might have significant effects and therefore cannot be categorically excluded.

[P31] Coastal municipalities will request DOE require coordination with local emergency response and spill-prevention plans before allowing reliance on the categorical exclusion for marine-associated exports.

[P32] Commenters will propose that DOE limit the categorical exclusion to decisions that do not involve new or expanded long-term export contracts exceeding a defined annual mcf/mmbtu threshold.

[P33] Government accountability advocates will ask DOE to include monitoring and post-authorization reporting requirements for authorizations processed under B5.7 so the agency can track environmental outcomes and reassess the categorical exclusion if harms emerge.

[P34] Labor organizations will raise concerns about worker safety and marine labor impacts associated with increased shipping and demand that those considerations be included in the screening for applicability of the categorical exclusion.

[P35] Legal commentators will request DOE to explicitly state whether the categorical exclusion applies to authorizations subject to interagency conditions or mitigations, and whether DOE will impose enforceable mitigation measures where potential impacts are identified.

[P36] Fisheries industry groups will object that the categorical exclusion disregards potential fishing gear conflicts and impacts on fish stocks from increased tanker traffic; they will request mandatory consultation with fishing communities before applying the exclusion.

[P1] Industry commenter: Requiring labor market determination solely by OMB MSA definitions will misclassify many rural and micropolitan service areas where hospices draw staff across county or state lines; we request allowance to use alternative commuting-area or county-based definitions for contiguous service patterns.

[P1] Legal expert: Using only OMB MSA definitions may raise Administrative Procedure Act concerns if CMS does not justify why other labor market definitions (e.g., CBSA subdivisions, county groupings) were rejected; CMS should include its rationale in the preamble.

[P1] Rural hospice advocacy group: MSAs exclude many rural populations; basing wage indices solely on MSAs will systematically understate rural wages and disadvantage rural hospices that recruit from broader regions.

[P2] Hospice provider association: Annual publication based on "most current available CMS hospital wage data" will create year-to-year volatility because hospital reporting lags; CMS should allow smoothing or multi-year averages to prevent abrupt changes.

[P2] Data privacy/accuracy advocate: Hospital payroll data are often incomplete for non-hospital-employed hospice staff; CMS should clarify data sources and methods to ensure the wage index reflects hospice workforce, not only hospitals.

[P2] State Medicaid agency: Requiring publication in the Federal Register annually may not be timely enough for states and contractors to update budgets; CMS should also provide advance draft indices and machine-readable files at least 90 days before FY start.

[P3] Medicare contractor association: The obligation to adjust payment rates to reflect local wage differences based solely on revised hospital wage data may be operationally burdensome without standardized adjustment protocols; CMS should issue detailed implementation guidance and deadlines for contractor updates.

[P3] Hospices in high-cost areas: Adjusting rates by contractor could produce inconsistent application across contractors; CMS must require national standardized formulas and audit requirements to ensure uniformity.

[P4] Hospices that would face large decreases: The cap on decreases starting 10/1/2022 creates transition relief but CMS should specify the phase-down methodology and whether cumulative multi-year decreases beyond the cap are allowed in subsequent years.

[P4] Fiscal watchdog group: Applying a decrease cap effective October 1, 2022 without retroactive budget-neutral adjustments could create budget shortfalls elsewhere; CMS must disclose the fiscal impact and offsets.

[P5] Taxpayer/Medicare affordability advocate: The prohibition that wage indices cannot fall below 95% of prior year may insulate hospices from legitimate local wage declines and perpetuate overpayments; CMS should tie the cap to demonstrated persistent cost differences or limit its duration.

[P5] Labor unions: The 95% floor may prevent necessary downward adjustments in areas with wage drops, but unions are concerned it could be used to justify wage stagnation; CMS should tie the index floor to labor market indicators to ensure wage adequacy.

[P6] Duplicate provision objection (from legal counsel): P6 repeats P1 verbatim; commenters ask CMS to consolidate redundant text to avoid confusion and ensure consistent cross-references.

[P7] Small hospice operator: Annual updates including MSA definition changes could reassign our hospice to a different MSA with higher costs; CMS should provide a mechanism for hospices to appeal or provide local data to contest MSA reassignments before the wage index is finalized.

[P7] Data transparency NGO: CMS must publish the full methodology, datasets, and weighting used to translate hospital wage data into a hospice wage index, including imputation methods for missing hospital data.

[P8] State contractor oversight group: The rule requires contractors to adjust payment rates but does not set timelines or error-correction procedures; CMS should mandate update windows and standardized reconciliation processes to prevent delayed payments.

[P8] Compliance officer for hospice chain: Clarify whether contractors must adjust historical claims already paid or only future payments; ambiguity could create audit risk for hospices.

[P9] Budget office analyst: The 95% cap effective Oct 1, 2022 could create significant cumulative costs; CMS should provide a detailed fiscal estimate, including impacts by MSA and net effect on Medicare spending.

[P9] Equity advocacy organization: The cap that prevents reductions below 95% may preserve higher funding for advantaged areas while doing little for low-wage regions; CMS should include targeted upward adjustments or reweighting for underserved regions.

[P10] Health policy researcher: The blanket 95% prohibition on reductions lacks an exit clause — commenters request that CMS set an evaluation period (e.g., sunset or review after 3 years) and metrics to assess whether the cap is achieving intended stability without skewing resource allocation.

[P10] Legal advocate for patients: The rule should expressly prohibit hospices from using the wage index floor to reduce service levels; CMS must monitor whether the wage index cap correlates with changes in beneficiary access or quality.

[P5] Auditor: The provision should clarify whether the 95% floor applies before or after any rural floor or other national adjustments (i.e., the sequence of wage index adjustments), to avoid double-counting protections.

[P3] Technical commenter: CMS must specify whether contractors should use hospital wage data at the MSA level or allow crosswalks when hospital data are suppressed; guidance absent will lead to inconsistent wage adjustments.

[P2] Hospital associations: Using hospital wage data to set hospice indices conflates hospital staffing patterns with hospice employment models; propose supplemental survey of hospice employer wages to validate and calibrate hospital-based index.

[P7] Coalition of small providers: Annual inclusion of OMB MSA definition changes could reassign providers frequently; CMS should grandfather hospice assignment to an MSA for at least two years following an OMB redefinition unless the hospice requests change.

[P4] State-level hospice regulators: If decreases are capped, CMS should also provide a symmetric cap on increases to control budget impact and maintain predictability for state budget planning.

[P1] Geographic equity advocate: OMB MSA boundaries do not reflect local cost-of-living differences; CMS should allow for sub-MSA adjustments or incorporate local CPI or rent indices to better reflect true local wages.

[P8] Contractor legal counsel: The rule lacks protections against erroneous contractor adjustments; require an appeals process allowing hospices to challenge contractor-applied wage adjustments before final payment reconciliation.

[P9] Congressional staffer: Request legislative clarity on whether appropriations implications of the 95% floor have been coordinated with congressional budget committees and that CMS provide classification of which MSAs will see increases or prevented decreases.

[P10] Data quality advocate: Require CMS to publish sensitivity analyses showing how the 95% floor changes allocations across MSAs, including identification of top beneficiaries and losers, to inform public comment and oversight.

[P1] State health agencies will object that allowing up to a 50% reduction in risk adjustment transfers for 2020–2023 will unfairly shift costs to smaller issuers and destabilize local markets, and request either narrower caps or mandatory mitigation protections for small carriers.

[P1] Health insurer trade associations will argue the rule lacks criteria for HHS review of state requests to reduce transfers for 2020–2023 and request clear, objective standards (e.g., market concentration, issuer financial impact thresholds) to prevent arbitrary approvals.

[P2] Consumer advocates will oppose limiting 2024 reduction requests to “prior participants,” contending this excludes states that did not participate previously but now face new market challenges, and request that all states be eligible for 2024 requests.

[P2] Legal experts will challenge the undefined term “prior participants” and request the rule define it precisely (e.g., participation in any prior HHS risk adjustment program year vs. specific years), to avoid inconsistent application.

[P3] Issuers will comment that the “de minimis impact” justification requirement for 2024 (P3) is vague and request HHS provide a quantitative threshold or methodology (e.g., maximum premium increase percentage or dollar amount) to demonstrate compliance.

[P4] Actuaries and issuers will assert the duplicate obligations in P3 and P4 to demonstrate de minimis impact create confusion and redundant burden; they will ask HHS to harmonize these provisions and specify the acceptable actuarial methods and data sources for the demonstration.

[P5] Issuers will raise operational concerns that the 15-calendar-day deadline to confirm or dispute second validation audit findings (P5) is too short given internal review processes and request extension to 30 or 45 calendar days.

[P6] Legal and issuer commenters will request clarification that the 30-calendar-day deadline to confirm or dispute the calculated risk score error rate (P6) begins upon receipt of complete documentation from HHS, and ask for tolling provisions if HHS data are incomplete.

[P7] Issuers will warn that P7’s reporting requirement to include disputed or reconsidered items could expose confidential pricing or proprietary information during open reporting and request limits on public disclosure and narrow scope to avoid duplicative reporting.

[P8] State Exchanges will state that requiring an approved or conditionally approved Blueprint and operational readiness assessment before open enrollment (P8) may delay state-run exchanges and ask for specified minimum timelines for HHS review and conditional approvals to prevent last-minute denials.

[P9] States proposing SBE–FP operation will request clarity about whether Blueprint approval criteria differ from state Exchange criteria (P9), and ask for a streamlined process when a state is transitioning to SBE–FP to avoid enrollment disruptions.

[P10] Agents/brokers industry groups will support the ability to submit rebuttal evidence during the 90-day suspension (P10) but will request HHS specify acceptable forms/manners (electronic submission, certified mail, evidentiary standards) to ensure due process.

[P11] Agents/brokers will comment that the 45-day review timeline (P11) for HHS to decide whether to lift a suspension is reasonable only if HHS commits to timely acknowledgment of receipt and to provide agents with status updates; they request such procedural guarantees.

[P12] Consumer protection organizations will warn that permitting termination of agreements for cause if rebuttal fails or is not submitted (P12) could lead to summary terminations harming consumers served by those agents; they request appeal rights beyond HHS reconsideration and interim protections for consumers.

[P13] Agents/brokers will request that the “final” reconsideration decision within 60 days (P13) be subject to an independent review or administrative appeal to preserve due process, noting that labeling it “final” may eliminate meaningful review.

[P14] Agents, brokers, and consumer advocates will raise privacy and logistical concerns about the requirement to provide correct info and document that consumers reviewed/confirmed eligibility before submission (P14), asking for safe harbor when systems error prevents recording and for clear limits on liability.

[P15] Small broker firms will object that requiring an action generating a maintainable record confirming consumer review (P15) (e.g., signature or recorded verbal confirmation) will be burdensome in field enrollments and remote assistance; they request acceptance of reasonable alternatives (email confirmation, portal checkbox) and exceptions for low-tech consumers.

[P16] Agents/brokers will object that the documentation elements (review date, consumer name, explanation of attestations, agent name) (P16) are too prescriptive and request templates and examples as well as an option to include these elements in system logs instead of separate forms.

[P17] Agents/brokers and small consumer assistance programs will strongly object to the 10-year retention requirement (P17) as excessive and costly, proposing retention periods of 3–5 years consistent with other federal programs and requesting HHS cover reasonable storage costs or allow de-identified data.

[P18] Consumer advocates and privacy advocates will insist that the requirement to obtain and document consent before assisting with enrollment or subsidy applications (P18) must include safeguards against coercive consent and require clear consumer-facing notices; they also request exceptions for urgent enrollments (e.g., loss of coverage) where consent mechanics may impede timely access.

[P19] Disability rights and community navigators will request that acceptable actions producing a record of consent (P19) explicitly include accessible formats (e.g., electronic signatures, verbal recordings with ASL interpreters, Braille confirmations) and exempt circumstances where the consumer lacks capacity, allowing authorized representative procedures.

[P20] Privacy advocates will object to the extensive consent documentation content requirement (P20) including scope, purpose, duration, rescission process, etc., as creating consumer confusion; they ask HHS to provide standardized consent forms and limit the duration detail to a maximum reasonably necessary (e.g., one year).

[P21] Community-based organizations and brokers will again object to the 10-year retention of consent documentation (P21) as disproportionate, and request alignment with HIPAA/state law retention requirements and clear destruction protocols to protect consumer privacy.

[P22] Low-income consumer advocates will object to the prohibition (P22) preventing Exchanges from determining APTC eligibility for tax filers with two consecutive years of unreconciled APTC, arguing it will create coverage gaps and harshly penalize filers who may be unaware of filing obligations; they request alternatives (outreach, conditional enrollment with lower APTC, or payment plans).

[P22] Legal groups will request clarification of the mechanics and due process before exclusion under P22 — specifically whether Exchanges must provide notice, appeal rights, and time to cure the failure to file before denying APTC eligibility.

[P23] Applicant assistance organizations will support the 60-day extension (P23) for verification but ask that HHS require Exchanges to proactively provide clear instructions and assistance to applicants asked for documentary income evidence to reduce churn.

[P24] Consumer advocates will support acceptance of attestation when tax return data not returned by Treasury (P24) but request safeguards to prevent fraud, such as random audits and cross-checks with alternative data sources, and urge HHS to publish guidance on when attestation will be accepted.

[P26] Consumer advocates will oppose automatic re-enrollment of non–CSR-eligible enrollees into the same plan (P26) without new premium comparison notices, arguing consumers should receive a clear disclosure when subsidies change.

[P27] Exchanges will request flexibility in P27 about re-enrolling CSR-eligible bronze enrollees into silver plans, asking HHS to permit re-enrollment only when actuarially equivalent and to require consumer consent before moving them to a silver plan that may change provider networks.

[P28] Consumer groups will support P28 (same plan for CSR-eligible non-bronze enrollees) but request explicit notice requirements and an opt-out process if the premium or benefits change materially.

[P29] Health plans will request technical guidance for implementing the “most similar network” standard (P29) and propose objective similarity metrics (e.g., ≥80% overlap of in-network primary care providers) to reduce disputes.

[P30] Parents and consumer advocates will applaud re-enrollment into same-product same-metal-level QHPs where possible (P30) but seek stronger protections when a “most similar” network materially reduces access to specialists or continuity of care.

[P31] Advocates for low-income consumers will insist that Exchanges must prioritize not increasing after-APTC premiums when choosing between bronze and silver plan re-enrollment options for CSR-eligible enrollees (P31) and request explicit language ensuring no increase in consumers’ net premiums.

[P32] Issuers and Exchanges will request clarification on the process for determining plan availability and what documentation constitutes a plan being “not available” (P32), including timelines for issuers to report product discontinuances.

[P33] Consumer advocates will ask HHS to require that when re-enrolling silver plan enrollees into silver under a different product or issuer (P33), Exchanges must verify parity in benefits and networks rather than rely solely on metal level and issuer.

[P34] Stakeholders will seek a definition of “most similar network” for P34 and request a dispute resolution process between issuers and Exchanges when network similarity determinations affect re-enrollment.

[P35] Consumers will request that if no same/adjacent metal level QHP exists in a product (P35), Exchanges prioritize choices that preserve providers and minimize out-of-pocket costs, and require clear communication about any coverage changes.

[P36] Consumer and issuer commenters will seek streamlined operational procedures and timelines for applying the issuer-product similarity rules in P36 to avoid last-minute reassignments and billing errors.

[P37] Issuers will request HHS provide a specific algorithm or priority list for evaluating “most similar product” and “most similar network” in same-issuer scenarios (P37) to standardize Exchange actions.

[P38] Small insurers will caution that mandatory re-enrollment options for CSR-eligible bronze enrollees into silver (P38) could create adverse selection; they request guardrails (e.g., limiting transfers to accounts with confirmed CSR eligibility and only if no premium increase).

[P39] Health plans will request that Exchanges be required to provide actuarial equivalence assessments and notifications to issuers when re-enrollment under P39 changes expected risk pools.

[P40] Issuers will request that Exchange staff be required to consult with the issuer before re-enrolling an enrollee into a QHP one metal level higher or lower under P40 to prevent network or formulary mismatches.

[P41] Issuers will object to re-enrollment into any other eligible QHP by the same issuer if it would materially change coverage (P41) and request that Exchanges obtain issuer confirmation that the substitute QHP meets continuity-of-care standards before assignment.

[P42] Consumer advocates will support the right to change to a silver QHP when someone becomes newly CSR-eligible (P42) but ask that Exchanges automatically offer and clearly explain the option, including cost comparisons and network impacts.

[P43] Consumer groups will oppose policies that allow an enrollee newly ineligible for CSRs to change plan metal level starting Jan 2022 (P43) without robust notification and an opportunity to consult with assisters, as this could result in coverage gaps.

[P44] Advocates will request clear timelines and consumer notice requirements tied to P44 (coverage effective date rules) to prevent confusion over when coverage begins after plan selection on or before a triggering event.

[P45] Consumers will request uniformity and predictability around P45 (Exchange option for effective dates when selection after triggering event) — asking HHS to require Exchanges to publish which option they will use and apply it consistently.

[P46] State Exchanges will ask for flexibility but request HHS define the “certain loss-of-coverage situations” (P46) in which the Exchange may accelerate effective dates, and require reporting when the option is used to prevent inconsistent application.

[P47] Consumers and assisters will support the general 60-day before/after window for special enrollments (P47) but caution that allowing Exchanges to shorten or limit via (c)(6) could reduce access in states that already constrain SEPs and ask for guardrails to prevent arbitrary narrowing.

[P48] Advocates will oppose one-sided timing options (P48) that give Exchanges discretion to allow only pre-event or only post-event windows, arguing it could reduce access; they request Exchanges be required to allow both unless they show data supporting a limitation.

[P49] State Exchanges will request flexibility under P49 (90-day option for Medicaid/CHIP leavers) but ask HHS to provide implementation guidance on outreach, verification of Medicaid/CHIP termination, and system changes needed to support the extended window.

[P50] Child advocates will strongly support the federal-platform prohibition against terminating dependent coverage based on age mid-plan year (P50) and request HHS require Exchanges to notify families proactively of this protection and correct issuer coding to prevent inadvertent terminations.

[P51] State Exchanges on their own platforms will seek clarity (P51) on whether their choice to prohibit age-based terminations requires any state-level statutory changes and request model contract language and implementation timelines.

[P52] Issuers will request explicit limited exceptions to the prohibition (P52) (e.g., fraudulent enrollment, death, loss of dependent status by legal change) and a clear process for disputing alleged violations, rather than a blanket prohibition without remedies.

[P53] Parties to eligibility appeals will request the 14-day window to request CMS Administrator review (P53) be extended to 30 days for complex cases where counsel or advocates need time to prepare filings.

[P54] Legal commenters will urge HHS to require that if the CMS Administrator declines to review an appeal within 30 days (P54), the Administrator must provide a written explanation and notice of any alternative remedy available to the party.

[P55] Parties will request that when the CMS Administrator renders a final decision within 30 days (P55), the decision include a clear statement of appeal rights, standard of review, and mechanisms for judicial review to avoid confusion.

[P56] Stakeholders will caution that the CMS Administrator option to “take no action” within 30 days (P56) could create prolonged uncertainty; they request defined follow-up timelines and interim protections for consumers whose eligibility remains in limbo.

[P57] Consumer advocates will request that when CMS initiates its own review within 14 days (P57), the affected parties be given notice and an opportunity to submit additional evidence, to preserve procedural fairness.

[P58] Legal experts will ask that when CMS may decline review after initiating it (P58), the rule require explanation of reasons and set a timeline for such declination to prevent administrative abuse.

[P59] Parties will request clarity on whether CMS’s 30-day timeline to render a final decision after initiating review (P59) may be tolled for good cause, such as exigent circumstances or missing records, and request a formal tolling mechanism.

[P60] Advocacy groups will object to CMS’s option to take no action within 30 days of initiating review (P60) and ask HHS to set outer limits on inaction and require status updates to the parties.

[P61] State Exchanges will note the new IPPTA data submission obligations (P61) create significant technical workload and request HHS provide transition funding, technical assistance, and realistic phased timelines.

[P62] State IT directors will request concrete schema standards and examples for the required data dictionary (P62) and ask HHS to allow reuse of existing state data dictionaries to avoid duplication.

[P63] State systems analysts will ask for clarification on the required detail and format of the entity relationship diagram (P63), and request HHS accept common modeling standards (e.g., ERD in XMI or PDF) to integrate with state design artifacts.

[P64] Exchanges will seek specificity about the scope of “business rules and related calculations” (P64), requesting HHS indicate whether proprietary, vendor-owned rules must be disclosed and how HHS will protect confidential business logic.

[P65] State Exchanges will object to the requirement to submit application data for at least 10 tax households and associated policy IDs (P65) if real consumer data are required, raising legal and privacy concerns; they request allowance for synthetic or de-identified test data.

[P66] States will ask HHS to publish the pre-testing and assessment plan timelines well in advance and to allow flexibility for states with concurrent system changes, asking for extensions without penalty under defined circumstances (P66).

[P67] State Exchanges will object to the one-calendar-year mandatory participation in IPPTA (P67) as too long for resource-limited states and request option for accelerated completion or phased participation tied to readiness milestones.

[P68] States will request that HHS provide orientation materials in multiple formats and schedule orientations at times accommodating state staff, as required by P68, and to provide documentation of orientation for audit purposes.

[P69] States will ask that HHS include in the jointly developed pre-testing plan measurable milestones, resourcing assumptions, and dispute resolution processes if the parties disagree on readiness (P69).

[P70] States will object to HHS keeping the State-specific plan internal and non-public (P70) and request at minimum that redacted summaries be published to provide transparency about expectations and timelines.

[P71] States will request timely and automated notifications per P71 with prescribed delivery channels (email, secure portal) and SLAs for HHS responses to ensure coordination during pre-testing.

[P72] States will request clear definitions of what constitutes an “operational, policy, business rule, IT, or other change” that must be reported (P72) and recommend materiality thresholds to avoid over-reporting trivial changes.

[P73] State IT teams will ask HHS to provide precise submission formats and endpoints (secure FTP, API specs) under P73 rather than leaving form/manner unspecified, to allow timely development.

[P74] States will request that HHS provide a tracking dashboard or portal for submitted materials as part of the coordination required in P74 to avoid lost documents and duplicate submissions.

[P75] States will welcome assistance to align data elements (P75) but request HHS publish the standardized set of data elements and mapping guidance well before required submissions to allow sufficient mapping and QA time.

[P76] States will request formal joint validation steps and acceptance criteria for HHS’s interpretation and validation of testing data (P76), including documented test cases and pass/fail criteria.

[P77] States will ask for commitments that HHS will not use submitted testing data for enforcement or penalties unrelated to pre-testing outcomes without prior notice and opportunity to correct (P77).

[P78] State Exchanges will request that the IPPTA checklist issued by HHS (P78) include clear completion criteria, timelines, and a mechanism to appeal checklist findings before they are considered final.

[P79] States will request HHS limit the required data documentation submissions to what is necessary (P79) and allow phased submission where legacy systems make immediate delivery of all documentation infeasible.

[P80] States will ask HHS to define the exact format, number, and structure of processing/testing data (P80) and permit use of de-identified synthetic test cases where privacy or practical constraints exist.

[P81] States will seek an explicit definition of “completion” of IPPTA processes (P81) and request HHS provide remediation plans and re-test windows rather than punitive determinations of failure.

[P82] States will object to HHS keeping the post-completion pre-testing report internal (P82) and request at least a redacted executive summary and specific remediation tasks be shared publicly to ensure accountability and allow stakeholders to plan.
