raw_output:
[P1] The rule fails to define the term "complete set of disclosures and statements" for the Live Poultry Dealer Disclosure Document, creating uncertainty about what documents dealers must include and risking inconsistent compliance.

[P1] Requiring dealers to provide the “complete set” without a standardized checklist will result in litigation over omissions and impose uneven burdens on growers and dealers.

[P2] Paragraph (a) should clarify whether electronic delivery (email, secure portal) satisfies the obligation to “provide” documents to prospective or current growers; as written it could be read to mandate only in-person or paper delivery.

[P2] The rule does not specify the language or reading level required for documents listed in paragraph (a), which may disadvantage limited-English-proficient or low-literacy growers.

[P3] The seven-day pre-execution delivery timeframe is unreasonably short for growers to obtain independent legal and financial advice, especially for complex arrangements requiring financing or contractor bids.

[P3] There is no explanation of how the seven-day requirement applies when growers and dealers negotiate amendments within the seven-day window; the provision should require seven days after the final, non-draft version is provided.

[P4] Requiring the Live Poultry Dealer Disclosure Document to be provided at least seven days before execution duplicates P3 and should be harmonized; commenters urge minimum 14-day review period for growers to secure counsel/financing.

[P4] The regulation does not state whether delivery of the Disclosure Document in a language other than English is required when the grower’s primary language is different; this omission burdens non-English-speaking growers.

[P5] Requiring simultaneous provision of specified documents with housing specifications when original capital investment is required is reasonable, but the rule fails to list all “specified documents” leading to compliance ambiguity.

[P5] The rule should require an independent cost estimate or third-party engineering specification be provided with housing specifications to help lenders and growers evaluate original capital investment needs.

[P6] Requiring a copy of the poultry growing arrangement affiliated with current housing specifications is problematic where multiple documents (IPAs, rider agreements) constitute the arrangement; the rule must define "copy" and which attachments are included.

[P7] Delivering the Live Poultry Dealer Disclosure Document concurrently with housing specifications is acceptable only if the disclosure includes lender-ready financial projections; the rule currently requires only a letter of intent.

[P8] The letter of intent "reliable to obtain financing" standard in (a)(2)(iii) is vague — lenders must be identified and minimum contents (loan amount, term, collateral acceptance) specified; otherwise lenders will not rely on such letters.

[P8] The rule should prohibit dealers from issuing letters of intent that create lender-facing misrepresentations or require that such letters be on lender letterhead or pre-approved templates.

[P9] The requirement to provide documents when modified housing specs could require additional capital investment does not set a reasonable notice period for growers; propose 30 days before implementation, not just “simultaneously.”

[P9] The phrase "could reasonably require" is subjective and will lead to disputes; the rule should define objective thresholds (e.g., >5% increase in square footage or >$X cost) that trigger disclosure.

[P10] Requiring a copy of the poultry growing arrangement affiliated with modified housing specs fails to address whether prior executed agreements remain valid and how amendments are executed; the rule should mandate a redline/summary of changes.

[P11] Providing the Disclosure Document with modified specs may be insufficient — dealers should also provide updated payment projection tables reflecting the modifications, not merely the static Disclosure Document.

[P12] A letter of intent for financing additional capital investment (a)(3)(iii) cannot be prepared "simultaneously" in many markets; lenders often require inspections and underwriting, so the rule should allow a phased or conditional timeline.

[P13] The cover page formatting and required order in (b) is overly prescriptive (title, contact info, term length first) and may prevent inclusion of other vital preliminary warnings; suggest allowing equivalent formats that meet readability standards.

[P14] Mandating the exact title in capital letters and bold could be burdensome for small dealers using templates; propose allowing equivalent prominent labeling in any legible font/style rather than an exact typographic requirement.

[P15] Requiring email addresses and parent company info on the cover page raises confidentiality and competitive concerns for dealers and may risk misuse of contact information; suggest optional inclusion of parent info or providing a secure contact point instead.

[P16] Stating the term length on the cover page is reasonable, but the rule must specify how to present variable terms (rolling, flock-to-flock, auto-renewal clauses) to avoid misleading growers.

[P17] The cautionary statement about farm income (b)(4) is useful, but its prescribed wording may be interpreted as agency endorsement of risk allocation; commenters request the ability to include an accompanying plain-language explanation tailored to local conditions.

[P18] Requiring disclosure of the "minimum number of placements" annually (b)(5)(i) is likely to be contested because dealers often reserve scheduling flexibility; the rule should allow dealers to disclose expected ranges and explain scheduling contingencies.

[P19] Stating the minimum stocking density per flock (b)(5)(ii) is necessary, but the rule should clarify whether density ranges, not single minimums, are acceptable when density varies by flock, house, or season.

[P20] The two alternative statements in (b)(6) about timing and accompanying documents are confusing; dealers need guidance on when each applies and whether additional explanatory text is permitted.

[P21] The statement preserving growers’ right to discuss terms despite confidentiality (b)(7) is appropriate; however, the rule should make clear that dealers may not enforce nondisclosure through indirect means such as retaliation or decreased flock placements.

[P22] The required USDA disclaimer in bold (b)(8) is redundant and could create liability confusion; request flexibility in placement and font while preserving prominence.

[P23] The roster of disclosures in (c) is extensive but lacks prioritization; commentators request an executive summary requirement to highlight the most significant economic and operational terms.

[P24] The six-year litigation summary (c)(1) intrudes on dealer confidentiality and will likely be resisted by dealers; disclosing "nature of litigation" and outcomes may be proprietary and result in false positives if suits were frivolous or dismissed.

[P24] The litigation disclosure raises concerns under privacy and defamation law for named parties; the rule should permit anonymized descriptions or aggregate statistics rather than case-level narratives.

[P25] Requiring disclosure of bankruptcy filings by parent, subsidiary, or related entities for six years (c)(2) is overly broad and may mislead growers about current creditworthiness; the rule should limit disclosures to filings that materially affect poultry operations.

[P26] The bankruptcy disclosure timeframe (six years) is excessively long relative to common credit cycles; propose reducing to three years or requiring disclosure only of active or pending insolvency proceedings.

[P26] The rule should specify the definition of "related entity" for bankruptcy reporting to avoid including unaffiliated corporate subsidiaries that have no operational connection.

[P27] The requirement to describe policies on sale or assignment of grower assets or arrangements (c)(3) is appropriate, but the rule must require specifics (purchase priority, valuation methods, right of first refusal) rather than a general statement.

[P28] The financial tables requirement (d) to include average annual gross payments per facility square foot for the previous year is useful but may reveal competitively sensitive compensation data; dealers will object that disclosure can be used by competitors or lenders to target growers.

[P29] Publishing payment tables by housing specification (d)(1) could mislead growers because payments vary by season, bird type, and local feed costs; require clear explanations of adjustments and limitations.

[P30] Grouping growers by housing specification (d)(2)(i) ignores other relevant stratifiers (feed contract, integrator-managed inputs) and may produce misleading comparators for growers with mixed arrangements.

[P31] Including both full-year contracted growers and flock-to-flock growers together (d)(2)(i)(A) will distort averages because these groups have materially different payment patterns; the rule should require separate tables for contract types.

[P32] Excluding growers whose housing specifications changed during the year (d)(2)(i)(B) will bias results and remove data from smaller operations; suggest including pro-rated data or flagging excluded growers in notes.

[P33] Summing all payments to determine a grower’s annual payments (d)(2)(ii) is straightforward, but the rule needs to specify treatment of non-recurring payments (signing bonuses, disaster payments) to avoid skewed per-square-foot figures.

[P34] Normalizing payments by facility square footage (d)(2)(iii) may disadvantage multi-house or multi-site growers whose payments are not linearly related to square footage; the rule should permit alternative normalizations (per bird space, per cycle).

[P35] Sorting normalized annual payments into quintiles (d)(2)(iv) is statistically arbitrary for small complexes with fewer than five growers; the rule should specify minimum sample sizes or use deciles/percentiles for large complexes.

[P36] Calculating quintile averages by summing normalized payments and dividing by number of growers (d)(2)(v) masks within-quintile variation; require disclosure of standard deviations and sample sizes for transparency.

[P37] The rule's requirement to provide projections when housing specs change or five-year averages are inaccurate (d)(3) is sensible, but dealers will challenge the standard for determining "inaccurate" averages — the rule should set objective criteria.

[P38] Projection tables (d)(3)(i) must specify the modeling methodology, price/feed cost assumptions, and confidence intervals; otherwise projections will be unreliable and potentially misleading to growers seeking financing.

[P39] The requirement to explain assumptions behind projections (d)(3)(ii) is appropriate; however, the rule must require that these assumptions be documented and auditable by USDA upon request.

[P40] Summarizing information the dealer collects on grower variable costs (d)(4) may require dealers to reveal proprietary supply-chain practices; the rule should limit required detail to cost categories rather than exact input prices.

[P41] Providing contact information for state extension or county farm advisors (d)(5) is positive, but the rule should allow inclusion of multiple sources, including USDA farm service or independent financial counselors for growers without reliable local extension services.

[P42] The processing threshold exemption (e) for dealers slaughtering fewer than 2 million live pounds weekly is arbitrary; small and mid-size dealers under this threshold can still exert market power and should not be categorically exempt.

[P42] The weekly threshold (2 million pounds) lacks adjustment for inflation or industry consolidation; propose indexing the threshold annually or using market share metrics instead.

[P43] The governance framework requirement (f) is broad and may impose significant compliance costs; suggest the rule provide a safe-harbor governance template or scalable requirements proportionate to dealer size.

[P44] Requiring CEO/principal officer review of a sample of Disclosure Documents during audits (f)(1)(i) is impractical for large firms with thousands of growers; recommend allowing delegated senior officers to certify on behalf of CEOs with documented policies.

[P44] The audit/testing requirement should clarify the frequency and scope of audits and whether third-party auditors or internal audit functions satisfy the requirement.

[P45] The obligation to ensure compliance with the Packers and Stockyards Act (f)(1)(ii) is duplicative since dealers already are subject to that Act; request harmonization language to avoid duplicative enforcement actions.

[P46] The required CEO certification (f)(2) that the document is not materially untrue or omitted imposes potential personal liability without safe-harbor protections; CEOs will resist unless the certification is limited to reasonable knowledge and due diligence.

[P46] The certification should include a statutory "good faith" and "reasonable inquiry" standard and specify remedies for inadvertent errors to avoid criminal or civil exposure.

[P47] The required signature page statement notifying growers of reporting avenues (g)(1) is useful but should be standardized and include phone, website, and multilingual options to be effective.

[P48] Obtaining the grower’s dated signature as evidence of receipt (g)(2) should not be construed as evidence of consent to contract terms; the rule must explicitly state the signature only acknowledges receipt of disclosures, not acceptance of the contract.

[P49] Requiring dealers to provide a copy of the dated signature page to the grower is reasonable but must allow electronic copies; the rule should accept emailed PDFs or secure portal downloads as valid copies.

[P50] Retaining signature pages for three years after expiration (g)(2) raises data retention and privacy concerns; dealers should be permitted to redact personal identifiers or store records securely with access controls.

[P51] The prohibition on confidentiality provisions preventing discussion of terms (h) is appropriate, but the rule must provide remedies and penalties for dealers who retaliate against growers for exercising this right.

[P51] The rule should define “discuss” to include sharing with legal counsel, lenders, financial advisors, USDA, and grower associations; otherwise, dealers may unduly restrict communications via overbroad nondisclosure clauses.

[P52] Listing minimum placements and minimum stocking density as dealer-controlled variables (i)(2) is accurate but could be expanded to include other dealer-controlled inputs (feed formulation, vaccination schedules) that materially affect payments.

[P53] For ranking systems, the obligation to produce records (201.214(a)) without specifying permitted formats and redaction rules will increase compliance costs; suggest accepting electronic records in standardized CSV/XML formats.

[P54] Maintaining ranking-system records for five years (201.214(a)) may be excessive for seasonal data; propose three years unless litigation or investigation requires longer retention.

[P55] The 24-hour requirement to provide placement information (201.214(b)) is operationally burdensome, particularly on weekends or holidays; request extending to "within one business day" or 48 hours for practical logistics.

[P56] Requiring disclosure of stocking density within 24 hours (b)(1) is reasonable but must allow for updates if deviations occur during placement or the grower makes post-placement alterations.

[P57] Providing breed names and all breed ratios within 24 hours (b)(2) could reveal proprietary breeding strategies; dealers may object and request ability to provide breed category (e.g., broiler strain A) rather than full ratios.

[P58] Disclosure of male/female ratios (b)(3) is often unknown at placement for some integrators; the rule should make this disclosure required only if sexing has been performed and data verified.

[P59] Requiring breeder facility identifiers within 24 hours (b)(4) may conflict with biosecurity protocols or breeder confidentiality; propose anonymized codes or consented disclosure to mitigate breeder concerns.

[P60] Providing breeder flock age (b)(5) is appropriate but the rule should clarify rounding conventions (weeks/days) and how to treat mixed-age breeder sources.

[P61] Requiring disclosure of known health impairments (b)(6) within 24 hours is critical for animal welfare, but the rule must define "known" (diagnosed vs suspected) and provide protections for preliminary information to avoid false alarms.

[P62] Disclosing potential pay adjustments based on placement inputs (b)(7) is necessary for transparency, but the rule should require the formulaic basis for adjustments to be provided, not just a statement that adjustments may occur.

[P63] Settlement documents for ranking-system payments (201.214(c)) must include clear definitions of all terms used (e.g., "grouping," "ranking") to ensure growers can meaningfully review and challenge settlements.

[P64] Furnishing a grouping/ranking sheet at settlement showing the grower’s exact position and the figures used (c)(1) is a meaningful transparency measure; however, the rule must ensure data is anonymized for other growers to protect privacy.

[P65] The requirement that grouping sheets show housing specifications and numerical figures (but not names) (c)(1) is helpful; commenters recommend this be provided in both paper and electronic formats for recordkeeping.

[P66] Reporting the distribution of dealer-controlled inputs to all ranking participants (c)(2) raises competitive concerns about revealing allocation strategies; dealers may seek an exception if disclosure would compromise proprietary management tools.

[P67] Disclosing stocking density for each placement to ranking participants (c)(2)(i) is operationally feasible and supports fairness but must include a tolerance for minor measurement errors and a correction process.

[P68] Revealing breed names and ratios to each participant (c)(2)(ii) could undermine breeder confidentiality agreements; propose permitting disclosure of breed classes or anonymized breed IDs.

[P69] Requiring disclosure of male/female ratios for ranking participants when sex is determined (c)(2)(iii) should be conditioned on accuracy verification and include an appeal process for growers who dispute the reported ratios.

[P70] Disclosing all breeder facility identifiers (c)(2)(iv) to ranking participants may increase biosecurity risks and unfair targeting; recommend controlled access to this data through USDA or anonymized identifiers.

[P71] Requiring breeder flock ages (c)(2)(v) to be shared is useful for benchmarking but must account for mixed-batch deliveries; the rule should specify how to report averages or ranges in such cases.

[P72] Reporting the number of feed disruptions of 12+ hours during the growout period to all ranking participants (c)(2)(vi) is appropriate for transparency but will require precise recordkeeping standards and dispute-resolution procedures to avoid gaming the system.

raw_output:
[P1] The April 24, 2017 deadline for submitting comments is unreasonably short and does not provide adequate time for small operators and third-party MROs to analyze the technical service bulletins and prepare meaningful comments.

[P1] The rule should specify whether extensions to the comment due date will be granted upon request, because stakeholders may need extra time if additional data requests are necessary.

[P2] The AD’s applicability language referring to paragraphs (c)(1)–(c)(3) is unclear — commenters request a concise, model-by-model list (including model years and serial number ranges) to determine whether a specific airframe is affected.

[P2] The phrase “certificated in any category” could inadvertently capture non-revenue and special category conversions; the AD should clarify whether experimental, restricted, or special flight permit statuses are included or excluded.

[P3] The compliance provision is vague about whether compliance times are measured from the AD effective date or from receipt of operator-specific notification; request explicit definition of “effective date” and any grace periods.

[P3] Operators request clarification whether “unless already done” applies only to the exact Boeing Service Bulletin procedures or to any equivalent prior inspections/replacements; legal counsel will need that for compliance credit interpretations.

[P4] The 8-year inspection compliance window for left and right engine fuel shutoff valve MOV actuators is excessively long and may leave aircraft operating with known-risk parts; safety advocates will urge a much shorter timeframe (e.g., 12 months to 2 years).

[P4] Conversely, some operators find the 8-year timeline too aggressive given maintenance scheduling constraints and request allowance for scheduling inspections within the interval aligned to existing heavy maintenance checks (D or C checks).

[P5] Allowing review of maintenance records in lieu of physical inspection is acceptable only if records are certified and traceable; recommend requiring sign-off by the accountable manager or an authorized inspector and retention of supporting evidence.

[P5] Maintenance-records-as-alternative should permit electronic records but require a chain-of-custody and cross-reference to part-tag numbers and historical maintenance events; the proposed language is silent on acceptable record formats.

[P6] The 8-year requirement in (g)(2) for engine and APU MOV actuators on (c)(2)/(c)(3) airplanes raises the same safety scheduling concerns as (g)(1); request harmonization of the compliance timeline across (g)(1) and (g)(2) with justification.

[P6] The AD references multiple Boeing service bulletins for the inspections; operators request that the FAA explicitly adopt those SB revisions by reference (including revision numbers and effective dates) to avoid ambiguity about acceptable procedures.

[P7] The maintenance-records alternative for (g)(2) should explicitly state what constitutes “conclusive” evidence — e.g., a part number on a part tag and an associated work order — to avoid inconsistent FAA interpretations.

[P8] Requiring replacement with P/N MA30A1017 within 8 years if specified part numbers are found is problematic: operators request a risk-based prioritization (e.g., immediate replacement for parts with known failure history, otherwise phased replacement) rather than a blanket 8-year mandate.

[P8] The AD should provide quantitative data supporting the necessity to replace the listed part numbers with MA30A1017; without failure-rate data or safety assessment, operators cannot justify replacement costs to stakeholders.

[P9] The Note allowing use of SB instructions if P/N MA20A1001–1 is found creates potential inconsistency — commenters request formal incorporation of that allowance into the regulatory text rather than a non-binding note.

[P10] Operators request clarity on whether partial replacements (e.g., replacing only actuators with serviceable tags) are permitted where access or parts supply is constrained, and whether temporary repairs are acceptable pending full replacement.

[P11] The note for (h)(2) referencing P/N MA20A1001–1 must specify whether the alternative SB procedures change the replacement part number requirement or only the method; legal certainty is needed to ensure ongoing compliance.

[P12] The (h)(3) replacement requirement for (c)(3) airplanes uses Boeing SB 767-28-0115 R1; commenters request the exact revision and date of that R1 document to ensure AMOC and compliance references match.

[P12] Request clarification whether the replacement obligation applies to MOV actuators installed on APUs as well as engines for (c)(3) airplanes, since the provision references “airplanes and APUs” elsewhere but is not explicit here.

[P13] The note for (h)(3) permitting SB instructions for P/N MA20A1001–1 should be extended to explicitly permit equivalent procedures approved via an AMOC, to avoid forcing separate approvals for commonly used alternate methods.

[P14] Requiring revision of the maintenance/inspection program “before or concurrently with” replacements or within 30 days is operationally infeasible for many operators who must coordinate with their FAA principal inspector and company maintenance program approval — request up to 180 days to revise programs.

[P14] The AD should state whether revisions to the maintenance/inspection program require a specific form of approval (e.g., FAA-approved MOE/CMP change) or can be self-implemented under an operator’s continuous airworthiness maintenance program.

[P15] The 6-year initial compliance threshold for AWL 28–AWL–24 measured “from the previous inspection” is ambiguous — commenters request definition of “previous inspection” (calendar date, last time task performed, or entry in logbook).

[P15] Operators request allowance for credit if the most recent inspection occurred earlier than the Boeing document’s baseline interval, to avoid penalizing operators who perform more frequent inspections.

[P16] Adding AWL No. 28–AWL–21 to the maintenance program without specifying exact inspection tasks, intervals, or acceptable techniques is insufficient; the FAA should incorporate the specific procedures from the referenced Boeing document by reference.

[P16] Maintenance technicians request that AWL No. 28–AWL–21 specify recordkeeping requirements for inspection findings (e.g., discrepancy codes, work orders) to ensure consistent compliance auditing.

[P17] AWL No. 28–AWL–22 addition must include allowable tooling, procedures for electrical bonding checks, and pass/fail criteria; without these, AMOs cannot standardize inspections across fleets.

[P17] Commenters request that the FAA provide an alternative acceptable source of procedures (e.g., OEM-approved CIP documents) in case operators do not have access to the referenced Boeing special compliance items.

[P18] AWL No. 28–AWL–24 inclusion and the referenced Boeing document must specify training requirements for maintenance personnel performing electrical bond and MOV actuator inspections; otherwise, the program revision is incomplete.

[P19] For (i)(2) airplanes, the requirement to revise maintenance programs prior to or concurrently with replacements should allow the use of an interim service bulletin or temporary inspection plan to maintain compliance until full program approval is processed.

[P20] The 6-year initial compliance time for AWL 28–AWL–25 in (i)(2) is unclear if it is cumulative with other AWL intervals; request a consolidated schedule showing how all AWL intervals interact.

[P21] The AWL additions listed in (i)(2)(i)-(iii) reference the Boeing 757 MPD — commenters request the exact MPD revision number and effective date to avoid discrepancies between operator documentation and the AD.

[P22] For (i)(3), operators request clarification whether the maintenance program revisions apply to airplanes with supplemental type certificates (STCs) that modify fuel system routing or electrical bonding, and if STC holders must provide compliance instructions.

[P23] AWL No. 28–AWL–23 as applied to Boeing 767s should specify whether checks are required for both original and retrofit actuator installations and whether retrofit kits installed per STC are exempt.

[P24] AWL No. 28–AWL–24 inclusion for Boeing 767s must address record retention periods for inspection data, recommended corrective actions, and coordination procedures with CAMOs for leased aircraft.

[P32] The requirement to route AMOC requests through the principal inspector or local FSDO (l)(1) may slow processing for foreign-registered operators; request allowance to submit AMOC requests directly to the Seattle ACO for non-U.S. operators.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement that premarket notifications for CDRH-regulated devices be addressed to "the current CDRH submission address on FDA's website" is vague and will cause compliance uncertainty when the website address changes; request adding an effective-date transition period and a clear definition of "current address."

[P1] Industry commenters will request that the rule allow electronic submission through FDA's established electronic submission gateway (e.g., ESG or Portal) without requiring reliance on a specific posted physical address for CDRH, to avoid mail/hand-delivery conflicts.

[P2] For CBER/CDER-regulated device submissions, directing submitters to the "current CBER address on FDA's website, or for CDER devices to the Central Document Room at the given address" is inconsistent and may create confusion about which center handles combination/overlap products; request consolidated routing guidance for combination products.

[P2] Clinical trial sponsors will ask the agency to explain whether the listed Central Document Room physical address remains acceptable for electronic-only submissions, and to explicitly state that electronic submissions to the FDA portal satisfy § 807.90(a)(2).

[P3] The mandate that inquiries be sent to "the address in this section or to one of the current FDA website addresses" is ambiguous about whether inquiries may be submitted by email or through FDA's online inquiry forms; recommend explicitly allowing electronic inquiry mechanisms and providing contact endpoints.

[P4] Requiring that premarket notifications "be submitted as a single version in electronic format" may be impractical for large submissions that require incremental attachments or proprietary master files; request clarification whether multi-part electronic submissions or zipped archives are permitted and what file size limits apply.

[P4] Small businesses will request an exception or alternative for submitters lacking the technical capability for a single consolidated electronic file (e.g., allow multiple electronic files or paper in limited circumstances) with a defined hardship waiver process.

[P5] The requirement to "request that FDA treat the intent to market as confidential commercial information and submit a certification to the Commissioner" lacks a template or standards for the certification; legal commentators will request sample language and clarification of burden of proof and confidentiality procedures.

[P5] Trade associations will argue that making a separate certification to the Commissioner for intent-to-market confidentiality adds administrative burden and duplicates existing FOIA/confidentiality frameworks; ask that routine confidentiality claims be handled through standard labeling and cover-letter designations.

[P6] Sending IDE correspondence for CDRH devices only to the current CDRH submission address on the website could disrupt ongoing active IDEs during an address change; sponsors will request explicit transitional procedures and confirmation that electronic IDE correspondence via FDA portals remains valid.

[P7] The rule should clarify whether CBER IDE correspondence must follow additional biologics-specific packaging or labeling requirements; CBER-regulated device sponsors will request harmonized formatting guidance.

[P8] Requiring a signed IDE application and accompanying materials in electronic format could conflict with statutory signature requirements for the "signed" application; sponsors will request acceptance of electronic signatures compliant with E-SIGN or an FDA-specified digital signature standard.

[P8] Clinical research organizations will request explicit technical specifications (file formats, encryption, submission schemas) for the requisite electronic IDE application to ensure interoperability and acceptance.

[P9] The obligation to send IDE applications only to addresses listed in §812.19 is circular if §812.19 points only to website addresses; request that the regulation permit submission through FDA's electronic portals and clearly list acceptable submission channels.

[P10] The requirement that eCopy be delivered by registered mail or by hand contradicts the electronic submission mandate and imposes unnecessary courier costs; industry will ask to eliminate the registered-mail/hand-delivery requirement for eCopy and allow secure electronic transfer only.

[P11] Requiring subsequent IDE correspondence to be submitted electronically but insisting that eCopy be sent by registered mail or hand creates confusion; request clarification about when physical delivery is required and harmonization so that follow-up correspondence can be fully electronic.

[P12] The blanket obligation that a PMA "shall include in electronic format" all specified items unless justified omission shown could disadvantage legacy PMAs or foreign applicants; request explicit allowances for paper or hybrid submissions during transition and clear standards for what qualifies as a justified omission.

[P13] The requirement for a table of contents specifying volume and page numbers may be incompatible with electronic-only submissions where pagination can vary; request that the agency accept internal document identifiers/bookmarks or PDF page numbers and provide guidance on acceptable pagination methods.

[P14] Mandating separate PMA sections for nonclinical and clinical investigations is reasonable, but commenters will seek templates and labeling conventions to ensure consistent organization across submissions.

[P15] Requiring the PMA to be "submitted as a single version" raises questions about resubmissions, corrected versions, and appendices; applicants will request guidance on versioning, amendment procedures, and whether a single container file (e.g., PDF portfolio) suffices.

[P16] The obligation to include and identify trade secret or confidential financial information in the PMA forces disclosure that could be inadvertently made public; trade groups will request a clear process for redaction, marking, and confidential treatment and confirmation that redactions will not impede substantive review.

[P17] Allowing incorporation by reference of pertinent FDA file information is helpful, but applicants will ask for a list of searchable/publicly available FDA files and the mechanics for citing internal FDA documents that may be non-public.

[P18] The provision that third-party master file material is not part of the PMA unless the third party authorizes reference will create negotiation burdens and potential delays; device makers will request standard master-file authorization forms and a process for timely consent.

[P19] Returning master files not referenced within 5 years could disrupt long-term supply chains and regulatory planning; manufacturers will request longer retention (e.g., 7–10 years) or notification prior to return, and the ability to request continued retention with justification.

[P20] The obligation to "periodically update" pending PMAs with new safety/effectiveness information is appropriate, but companies will request specific update intervals, definitions of "periodically," and examples of information that triggers an update to avoid overreporting.

[P21] Requiring that update reports "be consistent with the data reporting provisions of the protocol" assumes ongoing studies have harmonized reporting rules; sponsors will ask for guidance on resolving conflicts between clinical study protocols and FDA update requirements.

[P22] The requirement that update reports include the FDA-assigned PMA number presumes applicants will have the number for early pending applications; recommend allowing interim submissions to reference application identifiers if the PMA number has not yet been assigned.

[P23] Treating updates as amendments could unintentionally extend regulatory exposure; applicants will ask for clarification on what constitutes an amendment versus routine informational update and the procedural consequences of each.

[P24] FDA's statement that PMA review time will not be extended for updates unless they qualify as major amendments is helpful, but stakeholders will request a clear, objective definition of "major amendment" and examples to allow predictable planning.

[P25] Allowing color additive information to be included in the PMA instead of a separate part 71 petition is efficient, but color-additive manufacturers will ask for cross-reference procedures and confirm whether FDA fees or separate review timelines will apply.

[P26] Requiring that color additive information included in the PMA be in electronic format raises the same technical-file-format concerns; color-additive suppliers will request explicit format and submission instructions.

[P27] The rule that FDA will not approve a PMA until an associated section 721 color additive is listed could result in approval delays outside the applicant's control; applicants will request interim pathways (e.g., conditional approval) or timelines for FDA to process listing upon PMA submission.

[P28] Directing PMA submissions for CDRH devices to "the current CDRH submission address on FDA's website" repeats the ambiguity noted in P1 and raises concerns for electronic vs physical submissions; request explicit acceptance of FDA electronic submission gateways.

[P29] Similarly, requiring PMA submissions for CBER devices to the current CBER website address needs clarification that electronic portal submission is acceptable and that the website address serves as routing guidance only.

[P30] The requirement that all procedures for PMAs apply to PMA supplements but that supplements only include supporting change information could be interpreted inconsistently; applicants will ask for a checklist of mandatory elements for common supplement types to avoid unnecessary resubmissions.

[P31] The conditional summary requirement under §814.20(b)(3) for certain supplements (new indications or significant changes) is subjective; request clearer criteria or examples of what constitutes "significant changes in performance or design."

[P32] The obligation to submit PMA supplements electronically and include information relevant to proposed changes will require standardized eCTD-like structure; industry will request that FDA adopt or map to existing electronic submission standards (e.g., eCTD or Q-sub).

[P33] Requiring a separate section identifying each requested change and its reason is burdensome for minor administrative changes; urge an exception for administrative or editorial changes and provide a template for how to present multiple small changes efficiently.

[P34] The mandate to submit additional information requested by FDA electronically is reasonable, but parties will request realistic timeframes and recognition of circumstances where original data reside in legacy formats requiring time to convert.

[P35] Mandating that all original HDEs, amendments, supplements, and related correspondence be provided in electronic format and sent/delivered to specified addresses may conflict with statutory signature or verification requirements for HDEs; request electronic signature standards or allowance for wet-signed originals in limited cases.

[P36] Sending HDE submissions for CDRH devices to the current CDRH address on FDA's website raises the same website-change/transitional concerns repeatedly raised for PMA/IDE submissions; stakeholders will ask for a unified submission policy covering IDEs, PMAs, HDEs, and 510(k)s.

[P37] CBER HDE submitters will request confirmation that submission to the "current CBER address" includes electronic portal submissions and that FDA will not refuse filings based solely on routing to the web-posted contact address.

[P1] Legal experts will point out that relying on external website content in regulatory text may raise notice-and-comment concerns and recommend codifying specific submission channels within the regulation rather than referencing the website.

[P4] Patient advocacy groups will request that the electronic-format single-version requirement not impede inclusion of patient-reported outcomes or multimedia files (e.g., video of device use) and ask FDA to specify supported multimedia formats.

[P10] Small device developers will assert that the requirement to deliver eCopy by registered mail or by hand imposes disproportionate burden and cost compared with large manufacturers; request fee exemptions or postal alternatives.

[P16] Privacy advocates will request that the rule require explicit instructions on redaction of patient identifiers in PMAs and HDEs and mandate secure handling of identifiable health information in electronic submissions.

[P20] Institutional review boards and investigators will request clarification on how periodic updates for pending PMAs interact with ongoing investigator responsibilities and IRB reporting requirements to prevent duplication.

[P19] Regulatory consultants will ask for a notice-and-return process before FDA returns unreferenced master files after 5 years, including an opportunity for the original submitter to renew or update the master file to avoid loss of critical supplier information.

[P22] Commenters will request that the agency create a searchable public index or private docket system to track PMA numbers and associated updates to facilitate sponsor compliance and public transparency.

Requiring a signed IDE application and accompanying materials in electronic format could conflict with statutory signature requirements for the "signed" application; sponsors will request acceptance of electronic signatures compliant with E-SIGN or an FDA-specified digital signature standard.

Clinical research organizations will request explicit technical specifications (file formats, encryption, submission schemas) for the requisite electronic IDE application to ensure interoperability and acceptance.

The obligation to send IDE applications only to addresses listed in §812.19 is circular if §812.19 points only to website addresses; request that the regulation permit submission through FDA's electronic portals and clearly list acceptable submission channels.

The requirement that eCopy be delivered by registered mail or by hand contradicts the electronic submission mandate and imposes unnecessary courier costs; industry will ask to eliminate the registered-mail/hand-delivery requirement for eCopy and allow secure electronic transfer only.

Allowing incorporation by reference of pertinent FDA file information is helpful, but applicants will ask for a list of searchable/publicly available FDA files and the mechanics for citing internal FDA documents that may be non-public.

The provision that third-party master file material is not part of the PMA unless the third party authorizes reference will create negotiation burdens and potential delays; device makers will request standard master-file authorization forms and a process for timely consent.

Requiring that update reports "be consistent with the data reporting provisions of the protocol" assumes ongoing studies have harmonized reporting rules; sponsors will ask for guidance on resolving conflicts between clinical study protocols and FDA update requirements.

Treating updates as amendments could unintentionally extend regulatory exposure; applicants will ask for clarification on what constitutes an amendment versus routine informational update and the procedural consequences of each.

Allowing color additive information to be included in the PMA instead of a separate part 71 petition is efficient, but color-additive manufacturers will ask for cross-reference procedures and confirm whether FDA fees or separate review timelines will apply.

Requiring that color additive information included in the PMA be in electronic format raises the same technical-file-format concerns; color-additive suppliers will request explicit format and submission instructions.

The rule that FDA will not approve a PMA until an associated section 721 color additive is listed could result in approval delays outside the applicant's control; applicants will request interim pathways (e.g., conditional approval) or timelines for FDA to process listing upon PMA submission.

The obligation to submit PMA supplements electronically and include information relevant to proposed changes will require standardized eCTD-like structure; industry will request that FDA adopt or map to existing electronic submission standards (e.g., eCTD or Q-sub).

Patient advocacy groups will request that the electronic-format single-version requirement not impede inclusion of patient-reported outcomes or multimedia files (e.g., video of device use) and ask FDA to specify supported multimedia formats.

Small device developers will assert that the requirement to deliver eCopy by registered mail or by hand imposes disproportionate burden and cost compared with large manufacturers; request fee exemptions or postal alternatives.

Privacy advocates will request that the rule require explicit instructions on redaction of patient identifiers in PMAs and HDEs and mandate secure handling of identifiable health information in electronic submissions.

Regulatory consultants will ask for a notice-and-return process before FDA returns unreferenced master files after 5 years, including an opportunity for the original submitter to renew or update the master file to avoid loss of critical supplier information.
Commenters will request that the agency create a searchable public index or private docket system to track PMA numbers and associated updates to facilitate sponsor compliance and public transparency.

[P1] The 30-day deadline in §421.152(a) is unreasonably short for applicants who must gather medical records from multiple providers, and should be extended to 60 or 90 days to avoid denying meritorious requests for procedural reasons.

[P1] Requiring applicants to provide all evidence within 30 days will disproportionately burden low-income and rural applicants who rely on mail or limited internet access to obtain records; the agency should allow alternative electronic or telephone-assisted submission methods.

[P2] The permission to request an extension in §421.152(b) is welcome but insufficient unless the agency provides clear guidance and a standardized form for extension requests; otherwise applicants will submit inadequate requests and be denied.

[P3] The requirement in §421.152(b) that extension requests be submitted in writing is ambiguous as to whether electronic submissions (email, online portal) count as "in writing"; the rule should explicitly allow electronic filings and define acceptable formats.

[P4] Requiring applicants to "give the reasons" for needing an extension (§421.152(b)) without specifying the level of detail or supporting documentation will lead to inconsistent decisions; the agency should specify what constitutes adequate explanation and what supporting proof is required.

[P5] The "good cause" standard in §421.152(b) to extend the 30-day period is too vague; stakeholders request a non-exhaustive list of examples (e.g., provider delays, hospitalization, incarceration) that qualify as good cause to ensure uniformity.

[P6] Incorporating the standards of §404.911 (§421.152(b)) to determine good cause is problematic because §404.911 pertains to different program contexts and may not be appropriate here; the agency should tailor good-cause criteria specific to relief requests under this part.

[P6] Legal commenters will likely argue that cross-referencing §404.911 without adapting it risks confusing applicants and creating legal challenges based on misapplication of standards intended for disability benefit appeals.

[P7] The dismissal provision in §421.152(c) for failure to submit evidence within the 30-day or extended period is unduly harsh and could bar applicants from any meaningful review; the agency should provide a cure period or require a notice-and-opportunity-to-cure before dismissal.

[P7] Civil rights advocates will object that automatic dismissal for missed deadlines will disproportionately affect persons with mental disabilities or cognitive impairments, who may need assistive support to comply; reasonable accommodations procedures should be added.

[P8] The requirement to "prove unlikelihood of dangerous conduct" under §421.155 sets a high evidentiary burden without defining the standard (preponderance, clear and convincing); the agency must specify the burden of proof and acceptable types of evidence.

[P8] Mental health and disability advocacy groups will contend that requiring an applicant to "prove" lack of dangerousness re-stigmatizes disability and may be infeasible; the agency should permit a more holistic showing (current treatment, stability, support systems) rather than an adversarial proof requirement.

[P9] §421.160(a) giving the agency discretion to grant relief "to our satisfaction" raises due process concerns because it uses a subjective standard; stakeholders will request that the agency define objective criteria or a clear standard of review.

[P10] Requiring applicants to establish facts about disability, record, and reputation (§421.160(a)) without listing acceptable evidence types (medical records, provider statements, criminal background checks, third-party affidavits) will result in inconsistent outcomes; the rule should include a nonexclusive list.

[P11] The blanket prohibition in §421.160(b) that denies relief if state law prohibits firearm possession may conflict with federal preemption or create unequal treatment for applicants in different states; commenters will ask for clarification on interplay with federal law and whether restoration of rights under state law is required before federal relief.

[P11] Gun rights organizations will likely support §421.160(b) but seek clarification about the timing—whether the agency must independently verify current state-law prohibitions and how to treat applicants who have pending state petitions to restore rights.

[P12] §421.165(a)'s obligation to review submitted evidence is appropriate but the proposal lacks timeframes for intermediate steps (e.g., acknowledgment of receipt, timelines for follow-up requests); stakeholders request procedural timelines to ensure timely processing.

[P13] The requirement that a different decision maker review the request (§421.165(a)) is a positive safeguard, but commenters will ask for specific conflict-of-interest rules and qualifications for the reviewing official to ensure independence and expertise.

[P13] Disability rights groups will request that the rule prohibit participation by any official involved in the original representative payee determination or by those who directly benefit from the payee appointment.

[P14] §421.165(a) requires written notification of the agency's action, but the rule should specify acceptable delivery methods (mail, email, portal) and require proof of delivery to prevent later disputes about receipt.

[P15] The mandate to explain reasons for denial (§421.165(b)) should require a sufficiently detailed rationale tied to the evidence and criteria used, so applicants can meaningfully prepare for judicial review; boilerplate denials will not suffice.

[P16] Notifying denied applicants of the 60-day period to file a petition (§421.165(b)) is necessary, but commenters will ask that the agency also include instructions for obtaining counsel, filing fees, and links to pro bono resources to aid vulnerable applicants.

[P17] The obligation to explain reasons for granting relief (§421.165(c)) should include an explanation of what evidence was decisive, and any conditions attached to relief, so applicants understand the basis and scope of relief granted.

[P18] §421.165(c)'s promise to inform applicants that the agency will notify the Attorney General to remove NICS records is positive, but commenters will request a specified timeline for when the AG will be notified and when removal will occur.

[P19] The notice that applicants are "no longer prohibited under 18 U.S.C. 922(g)(4)" (§421.165(c)) must be tempered with guidance about remaining state prohibitions and practical steps (e.g., restoration certificates) the applicant may need to lawfully possess firearms in their state.

[P20] Notifying the Attorney General to remove NICS records (§421.165(c) & §421.165(c) duplicate) requires coordination; commenters will seek a required agency confirmation to the applicant when the AG has completed removal and an appeal path if removal is not timely.

[P21] The 365-day processing requirement (§421.165(d)) is consistent with the NIAA but commenters will insist on interim case status updates every 90 days to increase transparency and reduce applicant anxiety.

[P22] The provision that applications are deemed denied without cause if not resolved within 365 days (§421.165(d)) could incentivize administrative inaction or resource-based delays; stakeholders will request additional funding commitments or workload limits to ensure compliance rather than passive denials.

[P22] Legal advocates will note that deeming applications denied "without cause" may produce procedural fairness issues and recommend that the agency be required to provide an explanation whenever an application is deemed denied due to delay.

[P23] The de novo standard for judicial review (§421.165(d)) may expose the agency to increased litigation costs; commenters from the agency or budget-conscious stakeholders may recommend clarifying the scope of de novo review or promoting alternative dispute resolution first.

[P24] Making judicial review available under 18 U.S.C. 925(c) (§421.170(a)) requires the agency to provide clear notice in its decision letters about the applicable standard and the rights available under that statute to avoid confusion among applicants and courts.

[P25] Allowing petitions for judicial review in the plaintiff's district (§421.170(a)) is appropriate, but commenters will request that the agency provide sample federal-court complaint language and administrative record compilation guidance to aid pro se litigants.

[P26] The obligation in §421.170(b) to notify the Attorney General if a court grants relief is necessary; commenters will request that the rule require prompt notification (e.g., within 10 days of receiving the court order) and confirmation to the applicant when NICS removal is completed.

[P8] Concerns will be raised that §421.155 fails to account for dynamic risk factors (e.g., temporary crises) and thus could lead to inconsistent denial of relief based on outdated records; commenters will ask for a mechanism to weigh recent stabilization more heavily.

[P1] Industry stakeholders (e.g., medical records providers) will request that the agency permit direct provider-to-agency transmission of records to reduce burden on applicants and speed compliance with the 30-day rule.

[P5] Clarify whether unforeseen circumstances beyond applicant control (e.g., natural disasters affecting providers) qualify as good cause under §421.152(b); suggest adding explicit examples to prevent arbitrary denials.

[P7] Request that before dismissal under §421.152(c) the agency issue a final notice of deficiency with a short cure period (e.g., 7 days) and clear instructions on how to rectify the deficiency.

[P11] State governments will request guidance on how the agency will verify current state prohibitions—whether relying on state registries, certified court orders, or applicant attestations—and the acceptable evidence to demonstrate state law status.

[P12] Request that §421.165(a) specify that the agency will consider new or supplemental evidence submitted after the initial 30-day period if the applicant shows good cause, rather than categorically excluding late evidence.

[P15] Request that denial notices under §421.165(b) include the administrative record and the specific factual findings and legal standards applied so that subsequent judicial review is meaningful and efficient.

[P20] Advocacy groups will ask for public reporting metrics on NICS removals (e.g., time from grant to AG notification to actual removal) to allow oversight and identify bottlenecks in the interagency process.

[P21] Request that the agency include a remedial mechanism (e.g., temporary relief or stay of enforcement) for applicants whose applications are deemed denied because the agency missed the 365-day deadline due to agency error.

[P23] Constitutional law experts will likely challenge ambiguities in procedural protections and request explicit statements about applicant due process rights throughout the review, including representation, evidence standards, and cross-examination rights if any.

[P9] Request clarification whether "to our satisfaction" includes an evaluation of current mental health treatment adherence, medication compliance, or only static historical facts; recommend specifying weight to be given to each category of evidence.

[P18] Ask the agency to include language ensuring that notification to the Attorney General includes all necessary identifying information and the agency’s rationale so that the AG can promptly and accurately remove NICS records.

[P16] Request that the 60-day notice under §421.165(b) also explicitly state the deadline calculation rules (e.g., when receipt is deemed to occur for mailed vs. electronic notices) to prevent forfeiture of judicial rights due to technicalities.

[P3] Request that "in writing" (§421.152(b)) explicitly include requests made through an accessible agency online portal with an electronic signature to comply with ADA accessibility requirements.

[P8] Concern that §421.155’s requirement to prove lack of dangerousness may be interpreted to require a negative prediction (impossible to prove); ask the agency to adopt a reasonable-probability standard with defined evidentiary benchmarks.

[P22] Request that when an application is deemed denied due to agency delay, the agency must automatically provide an expedited administrative review option or seek to reopen the matter to avoid forcing immediate litigation.

[P1] The deadline of January 27, 2022 to receive comments on the AD (§39.13(a)) is unreasonably short and does not provide sufficient time for affected operators and MROs to analyze service information and prepare substantive technical comments.

[P1] Request to extend the comment deadline (§39.13(a)) by at least 60 days to allow airlines, unions, and engine manufacturers adequate time to evaluate operational and cost impacts.

[P2] The applicability language (§39.13(c)) is too vague by referencing paragraphs (c)(1) and (c)(2) without listing excluded serial numbers or production blocks; commenters request clarification of affected airframes by serial number ranges and line numbers.

[P3] The applicability in §39.13(c)(1) that limits affected 777–200 models to those with Pratt & Whitney PW4074, PW4074D, PW4077, PW4077D, PW4084D, PW4090, and PW4090–3 engines fails to address 777–200LR and -200ER subvariants explicitly, creating ambiguity about coverage for long-range variants.

[P3] Industry requests confirmation that aftermarket or field-modified engines (e.g., re-identified serial numbers or upgraded thrust rating kits) using the listed engine models are included in the AD applicability for §39.13(c)(1).

[P4] The inclusion in §39.13(c)(2) of only PW4090 and PW4098 for 777–300 models omits other engine variants or future thrust-rated modifications; commenters request language to capture any engine with the same core/LP compressor design regardless of suffix.

[P5] The compliance requirement (§39.13(f)) to comply "within the compliance times specified" is unclear because the AD does not summarize those times in a single table; request that the FAA provide a clear compliance timeline matrix in the AD preamble and regulatory text.

[P6] The requirement to perform actions "prior to further flight after the effective date" (§39.13(g)) is operationally burdensome for carriers with aircraft scheduled for immediate service; request allowance for phased compliance (e.g., within X flight hours) or ferry provisions to avoid heavy schedule disruption.

[P6] Legal commenters note that §39.13(g) must specify the effective date clearly in the rule text, and that retroactive requirements should be supported by a demonstrated imminent unsafe condition; request the FAA include safety rationale and risk assessment.

[P7] The repeated functional check interval of every 10 days (§39.13(g)(3) repeat) imposes high maintenance burden and potential aircraft downtime; operators request the FAA provide data supporting the 10‑day interval or allow longer intervals (e.g., 30 days) based on reliability demonstration.

[P7] Union/crew safety groups request that if the 10‑day interval remains, the AD require tracking and recordkeeping procedures for the functional checks, including who may perform them (licensed technician vs. pilot-crew-performed cockpit test).

[P8] The required installation of debris shields at specific thrust reverser inner wall locations (§39.13(g)(1)) lacks detailed installation instructions and referenced service bulletin numbers; request explicit incorporation by reference, parts lists, torque values, and post-installation inspection criteria.

[P8] MROs request that the AD allow the use of existing Pratt & Whitney or Boeing service bulletins for debris shield installations and provide AMOC pathways for alternative shield designs shown to meet equivalent protection.

[P9] The inspection for moisture ingress in fan cowl doors (§39.13(g)(2)) lacks objective acceptance criteria (what level or amount of moisture is considered ingress) and detection method specifics; request clear definitions and inspection procedures (visual, borescope, moisture detection stickers).

[P10] The requirement to repair any moisture ingression before further flight (§39.13(g)(2) condition) is overly restrictive for minor condensation findings that do not affect safety; request a threshold (e.g., presence of standing water or corrosion) or allow temporary mitigations until scheduled maintenance.

[P11] The functional check to verify hydraulic pump shutoff valves close with fire handle actuation (§39.13(g)(3)) requires clarity on the acceptable method to perform the test without introducing additional risk to systems; request a step-by-step procedure and identification of authorized personnel to perform the test.

[P11] Operators request that the AD explicitly state whether the functional check may be performed with the engine off or on APU power only, to avoid unnecessary engine starts and fuel burn.

[P12] The requirement to perform corrective actions before further flight if a valve fails to close (§39.13(g)(3) condition) could ground aircraft for extended periods; commenters ask for allowed temporary mitigations (e.g., placard limitations, ferry permits) and definition of "corrective actions."

[P13] The prohibition on special flight permits unless conditions in (h)(1) and (h)(2) are met (§39.13(h)) is too restrictive and could prevent safe repositioning or maintenance ferry flights; request that the FAA adopt a risk-based special flight permit policy allowing limited, supervised ferry flights under operational restrictions.

[P14] The flow-path UT inspection requirement in (h)(1) as a precondition for special flight permits is acceptable for safety but commenters note the AD should provide an alternative inspection method for operators lacking UT capability on short notice (e.g., borescope + dye-penetrant) and specify qualification of personnel.

[P15] The requirement that the functional check and repairs must have been performed within 10 days prior to a special flight (§39.13(h)(2)) is arbitrary; request that the FAA allow a longer window (e.g., 30 days) for ferry flights, or permit recheck at point of departure in lieu of the 10-day limit.

[P21] The requirement to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or Flight Standards Office (§39.13(j)(1) submission instruction) may cause procedural delays; request an expedited AMOC process for safety-critical deviations with specified maximum review timelines.

[P22] The instruction to address direct submissions to the certification office manager to the person in paragraph (k)(1) (§39.13(j)(1) attention) is fine, but the AD fails to list the contact in (k)(1); request that the AD include the name and contact details in the regulatory text for clarity.

[P23] Allowing AMOC requests via the specified FAA email (§39.13(j)(1) email option) is appropriate, but commenters request confirmation of receipt procedures and expected turnaround times, and secure transmission guidance for sensitive proprietary data.

[P24] The obligation to notify the principal inspector prior to using an approved AMOC (§39.13(j)(2)) should permit digital notification methods and define what constitutes adequate notice (email with read receipt, phone call log, etc.).

[P25] The NPRM comment deadline of February 11, 2022 (FAA–2021–1149) conflicts with the AD comment deadline of January 27, 2022 in §39.13(a); legal commenters ask the FAA to harmonize deadlines and explain the reason for differing dates.

[P26] Requirement to include docket numbers FAA–2021–1149/Airspace Docket No. 21–ASW–27 at the start of comments (NPRM submission) is overly prescriptive; request that the FAA accept any clear identification method and provide examples to avoid rejected submissions.

[P27] The option to submit comments online at regulations.gov (NPRM permission) is appreciated but commenters request assurance that large attachments (engineering reports, analysis, proprietary service data) will be accepted and kept confidential when requested.

[P28] Allowing in-person docket review at the Dockets Office (NPRM permission) is helpful, but request extended hours or appointment-based remote review options for stakeholders not located near Washington, DC.

[P29] The availability of FAA Order JO 7400.11F online (NPRM permission) should include a direct, permanent URL in the AD and citation to the exact revision date to prevent confusion over which version the FAA relied upon.

[P1] The 95% cap on decreases to the home health wage index (effective Jan 1, 2023) will artificially preserve wage index levels and may distort resource allocation by preventing full reflection of local wage declines.

[P2] Setting the wage index floor at 95% of the prior-year value unfairly advantages areas with previously high wage indices and disadvantages areas that have legitimate wage reductions due to economic changes.

[P3] Requiring the 5% cap on negative wage index changes to be implemented in a "budget-neutral" manner via wage index budget neutrality factors risks shifting payment reductions onto other providers or geographic areas without clear methodology described.

[P3] The rule lacks detail about how the wage index budget neutrality factors will be calculated and applied, creating unacceptable uncertainty for providers’ future reimbursement projections.

[P3] Budget neutrality implementation could result in cuts to base payment rates or to positive adjustments elsewhere; CMS must disclose modeling showing distributional impacts before finalizing the rule.

[P1] The effective date of January 1, 2023 is retroactive and administratively infeasible for providers to plan around; stakeholders request a prospective effective date or transitional guidance.

[P4] Allowing CMS to remove quality measures based on multiple factors is appropriate, but the rule does not require public notice-and-comment for each specific removal decision, undermining transparency.

[P5] The criterion that a measure may be removed if performance is "so high and unvarying" is vague; CMS should define specific quantitative thresholds (e.g., percentage ceilings, variance metrics) to justify removal.

[P6] Removing measures because improvements "do not result in better patient outcomes" requires clear evidence standards — the rule should specify analytic methods and patient outcome metrics to be used.

[P7] The provision permitting removal of measures not aligned with current clinical guidelines lacks a process for reconciling disagreements between CMS and professional societies about what constitutes "current" guidelines.

[P8] Removing a measure when a "more broadly applicable" measure exists may disadvantage specialized populations; CMS should require population-stratified analyses before substituting measures.

[P9] The concept of replacing measures with ones that are "more temporally close" to outcomes is reasonable, but CMS must specify acceptable time horizons and evidence linking the proximal measure to long-term outcomes.

[P10] Allowing removal when a measure "more strongly correlated with desired patient outcomes exists" could lead to overreliance on correlational evidence; CMS should require causal or predictive validation studies.

[P11] The allowance to remove measures because public reporting causes negative unintended consequences (excluding patient harm) is too broad — the rule should enumerate examples (e.g., gaming, patient selection) and require documentation before removal.

[P12] Permitting measure removal when costs outweigh benefits is valid, but CMS must define the cost and benefit metrics, including administrative burdens on small HHAs and data collection costs.

[P4] The rule does not require stakeholder input (e.g., public comment period or expert panels) prior to removal of measures under §484.245(b)(3); stakeholders request mandatory consultations.

[P5] Industry commenters will argue that designating a measure as "uniformly high" without considering statistical reliability across small HHAs could lead to premature removals that harm quality improvement.

[P6] Patient advocacy groups will oppose removing measures that are meaningful to patients even if broad outcome improvements are not directly demonstrable; CMS should require patient-centered input.

[P7] Clinical professional societies will request a formal appeals process to contest CMS decisions that a measure is not aligned with current clinical guidelines.

[P8] Researchers will request that CMS publish the analytic methods, datasets, and thresholds used to compare measures for broader applicability before using this as a basis for removal.

[P11] The exclusion of patient harm from the "negative unintended consequences" rationale is puzzling — if public reporting causes patient harm (e.g., worse access), CMS should explicitly allow removal on those grounds as well.

[P12] Health economists will demand that the cost-benefit analysis include consideration of long-term population health benefits, not just near-term program costs.

[P13] For new HHAs, defining the baseline year as the first full calendar year after certification could disadvantage agencies that begin late in a calendar year and request transitional adjustments — CMS should allow pro-rated baselines.

[P14] Defining the first performance year as the first full calendar year after the baseline could create a multi-year delay before new HHAs are evaluated; industry asks for clearer interim reporting requirements or accelerated performance measurement options.

[P15] Setting CY 2022 as the HHA baseline year for existing HHAs (certified before Jan 1, 2022) may be arbitrary and will freeze performance comparisons around pandemic-impacted data; commenters urge CMS to permit adjustment or exclusion of pandemic-affected data.

[P29] Existing HHAs will challenge using CY 2022 as baseline because staffing levels, patient mix, and service patterns during 2022 were atypical; CMS should allow alternative baseline selections or multi-year averages.

[P27] New HHAs request clarification on how partial-year data in the certification year are treated and whether providers can opt to use a subsequent year as baseline if the first full year is not representative.

[P28] The timing rules for baseline and first performance year do not address HHAs that change ownership or merge; CMS should provide guidance on baseline and performance year assignment in ownership transitions.

[P16] The repeated obligation that wage indices be no less than 95% of the prior year effectively creates a wage index floor that may perpetuate outdated geographic wage disparities and reduce incentives for efficiency.

[P17] Implementing the 5% cap via budget neutrality factors could trigger downstream adjustments to rural or low-wage area payments; rural providers request an impact analysis by rural-urban status.

[P3] Legal commenters will question whether imposing a budget-neutrality requirement for this cap is consistent with Medicare statute and payment update formulas; CMS should provide legal justification and cite statutory authority.

[P4] Consumer groups will request that any measure removal be accompanied by an explanation of how public reporting and patient decision-making will be preserved for the topic area.

[P6] There is a risk that removing measures for lack of outcome linkage will remove process measures that are still clinically meaningful; CMS should require preservation of necessary process measures unless evidence shows no utility.

[P11] The rule fails to specify monitoring and reintroduction procedures if removing a measure leads to unforeseen negative effects; commenters request a clear reinstatement process.

[P12] Small HHAs and Medicaid-focused agencies will argue that the cost threshold for removal should include disproportionate impacts on providers serving low-income or minority populations.

[P5] Quality improvement organizations will request that CMS provide variance-by-decile or by HHA-size analyses before deeming a measure "unvarying."

[P15] Quality reporting stakeholders will request transitional timelines and technical assistance for HHAs to adapt to the CY 2022 baseline designation, especially for reporting vendors and software upgrades.

[P1] Labor unions will oppose the wage index floor if it means that wage growth in lower-wage areas is capped indirectly through budget neutrality adjustments; they request protections for wage increases tied to local markets.

[P2] State Medicaid agencies will request coordination with state-level wage adjustments and implications for Medicaid payments if Medicare wage index floors distort local labor markets.

[P27] Accreditation bodies ask for clarity whether certification date refers to Medicare program eligibility date or state licensure date when determining the HHA baseline year.

[P28] Compliance officers point out the potential for gaming the certification date to manipulate baseline years; CMS should include anti-manipulation safeguards.

[P29] Legal experts will request explicit rules for HHAs that were certified before Jan 1, 2022 but had no Medicare claims activity in CY 2022 — whether CY 2022 still serves as the baseline.

[P17] The rule should require CMS to model and publish the effect of wage index budget neutrality factors on aggregate Medicare home health spending and on per-HHA payments by state.

[P4] Health IT vendors request advance notice (minimum 12 months) before any measure removal so vendor systems can be updated and claims/quality data flows adjusted.

[P6] Academic researchers recommend CMS publish the evidence base showing lack of linkage between measure performance and patient outcomes prior to removal.

[P11] Patient safety organizations urge that "other negative unintended consequences" be narrowly defined to avoid removal based on political or budgetary motivations.

[P12] Fiscal watchdog groups will demand that CMS consider the administrative cost savings to HHAs from removing burdensome measures as part of the cost-benefit analysis, and quantify them.

[P13] New HHAs argue that the baseline and performance year definitions should allow for appeals when the first full calendar year is materially atypical (e.g., natural disaster impacting services).

[P1] Some states contend that the 95% floor could be inconsistent with state-specific wage index adjustments and request coordination authority or exemptions for state-specific labor markets.
