raw_output:
[P1] The blanket application of all section 9(a)(1) prohibitions to the trispot darter is overly broad and will create uncertainty for landowners and local governments about routine activities that might be considered take.

[P1] The preamble should clarify whether lawful pre-existing permits and authorizations under other federal laws (e.g., Clean Water Act permits, state permits) shield permittees from enforcement under section 9 with respect to the trispot darter.

[P1] Legal experts will likely comment that adopting section 9(a)(1) in full without regulatory definitions invites litigation over scope and requires precise definitions of “harm,” “harass,” and “take” as applied to small aquatic species.

[P2] The exception for incidental take in §17.44(q)(2) is too vague because it does not establish a process for determining whether a given activity qualifies; commenters will request a formal verification or permit-like concurrence process.

[P2] Industry groups will request that the rule include an explicit safe-harbor mechanism (e.g., written concurrence by the Service) confirming that a specific project meets the exception conditions to avoid enforcement risk.

[P3] State wildlife agencies will applaud the broodstock and genetic sampling exception but will ask for clearer limits (e.g., maximum numbers, timing windows, handling protocols) to ensure practices remain protective and to prevent misuse.

[P3] Conservation NGOs will request mandatory reporting and monitoring requirements for State-led restoration activities under §17.44(q)(2)(i) to document impacts and ensure adaptive management.

[P4] The definition of “channel restoration projects” in §17.44(q)(2)(ii) is insufficiently specific; commenters will ask for design standards, measurable performance criteria, and timeframes to determine when a project “creates” a functioning stream.

[P4] Landowners and public works departments will request an appeals or project review process when the Service disputes whether a channel restoration project meets the exception.

[P5] The low shear stress requirement lacks quantifiable thresholds (e.g., specific shear stress values or accepted modeling methods); engineers will request numeric standards or recognized design guidance to implement consistently.

[P6] Requiring bank heights that “enable reconnection to the floodplain” is ambiguous—commenters (local floodplain managers) will ask for clear target elevations relative to stage-frequency (e.g., 1.5‑yr, 2‑yr, 10‑yr) or valley bottom criteria.

[P7] The perennial flow reconnection criterion should specify the minimum duration and return period of flows (e.g., baseflow percentages, months per year) required to qualify, otherwise managers cannot determine eligibility.

[P8] The restriction to using “existing materials” for riffles and pools is impractical in highly disturbed channels where imported substrate is necessary; construction contractors will request an allowance for engineered imported materials if they match local grain size and morphology.

[P9] The low soil compaction requirement in riparian areas lacks measurement methods; commenters will ask the Service to specify allowable bulk density values or compaction testing protocols.

[P10] Mandating riparian wetlands as a qualification could effectively bar many stream restoration projects in otherwise appropriate reaches; conservation practitioners will request alternative compensatory measures where wetland formation is infeasible.

[P11] The exception for bioengineering streambank stabilization should include a clear list of acceptable bioengineering techniques and materials (e.g., live staking, brush layering) and permit temporary disturbance windows to allow construction access.

[P12] The outright prohibition on stabilizing banks solely with quarried rock, rock baskets, or gabions is too restrictive for transportation agencies and utilities that face acute erosion threats; commenters will request limited-use exceptions where bioengineering is infeasible or fails.

[P12] Legal and engineering commenters will point out that the term “solely” is ambiguous—does it prohibit any use of rock as a component, or only exclusive reliance—and ask for clarification that mixed designs with rock and vegetation are allowed.

[P13] Timber industry stakeholders will support the silviculture exception in §17.44(q)(2)(iv) but will request precise definitions of “silviculture practices” covered and documentation requirements to demonstrate compliance with the exception.

[P14] The requirement to implement “highest-standard best management practices” for streamside zones, crossings, and roads is vague—commenters will ask the Service to identify specific, recognized BMP documents (state BMPs, NRCS standards) that meet this test.

[P15] The water quality guideline compliance condition needs clarity about which state or federal water quality standards apply and how compliance will be demonstrated during and after operations.

[P16] Allowing SFI, FSC, or ATFS certification as an alternative is helpful but insufficiently prescriptive; forest owners will request precise certification levels or modules that must be maintained (e.g., annual audits, chain-of-custody requirements) to qualify.

[P16] Environmental groups will comment that relying on third‑party certifications may not guarantee protection for the trispot darter and will request mandatory on-the-ground protections in addition to certification.

[P17] Transportation projects providing fish passage should not automatically qualify for the exception unless the fish passage design is proven effective for small-bodied species like trispot darter—engineers and ecologists will ask for species-specific passage design criteria.

[P17] Departments of Transportation will request that temporary impacts during construction (dewatering, diversions) be explicitly allowed if mitigation measures and timing windows minimize impacts, plus a procedure to verify that installed passage works.

[P18] The inclusion of NRCS Working Lands for Wildlife projects is welcome, but NRCS and landowners will ask for clear coordination procedures, approval timelines, and documentation requirements to ensure projects meet the rule’s intent.

[P18] Small private landowners participating in Working Lands programs will request assurances that participation will not create future land-use restrictions or trigger additional federal review beyond the exception.

[P2/P4] Several commenters will request that cumulative and indirect effects from eligible activities be addressed—e.g., whether repeated “qualified” projects could cumulatively degrade habitat and therefore lose protection.

[P4/P7] Conservation scientists will argue the rule must require pre- and post-project monitoring (e.g., hydrology, substrate, population surveys) to demonstrate perennial flows and habitat improvements are achieved and maintained.

[P3/P11] Animal welfare and scientific communities will request mandatory protocols for handling and transportation of broodstock and tissue samples (e.g., sterilization, quarantine) to prevent disease spread and genetic contamination.

[P5/P9] Contractors and restoration designers will ask the agency to provide or endorse recommended technical manuals and monitoring protocols (e.g., USDA, state manuals) for measuring shear stress and soil compaction to reduce project uncertainty.

[P12/P11] Permittees will ask for a waiver or variance process to allow use of engineered structures (rip-rap, gabions) in emergency stabilization situations where immediate public safety or infrastructure protection is necessary.

[P1/P2] Business associations will request an economic analysis supplement and regulatory flexibility for small entities, arguing the rule as written imposes compliance costs and legal uncertainty without adequate cost-benefit justification.

[P14/P15] Forest owners will request grandfathering or transition timelines for operations already planned or permitted before the rule’s effective date to avoid stranded investments.

[P4/P8] Local governments and engineers will ask the Service to allow imported materials when local materials are contaminated (e.g., heavy metals, excessive fines) or unavailable, provided material compatibility is demonstrated.

[P11] Environmental engineers will request clarity on whether temporary construction disturbances associated with bioengineering (e.g., access ramps) are allowed and, if so, under what mitigation measures.

[P17] Tribes and tribal fishery managers will ask to be explicitly included in consultation and implementation of fish-passage projects, and for recognition of tribal design standards and priorities.

[P3/P18] Conservation organizations will ask the Service to require public disclosure of projects claiming the incidental take exception (project descriptions, locations, monitoring results) to ensure transparency and accountability.

[P1/P2] Constitutional and administrative law experts will request that the rule specify enforcement mechanisms and penalties, and clarify how the exceptions interact with citizen-suit provisions under the Act.

[P2] Many commenters will request that the Service publish a concise checklist or decision tree showing which activities qualify for the incidental take exception and what documentation is required to rely on the exception.

[P1] The requirement in §87.8(a) that EPA publish a Federal Register document to enforce any other edition is ambiguous about the timing — commenters will request that the rule specify a minimum advance notice period (e.g., 60 or 90 days) before enforcement of a different edition to allow industry to adapt.

[P1] Legal experts will argue §87.8(a) should clarify whether the Federal Register document must include a detailed justification and comparison of editions, not just a citation, to satisfy notice-and-comment and due process concerns.

[P2] Industry commenters will request that §87.8(a)’s public availability obligation specify the formats and locations (e.g., Regulations.gov, EPA website, and libraries) to ensure manufacturers and certifiers can reasonably access the referenced material.

[P3] Aircraft manufacturers will challenge the absolute prohibition in §1030.1(a) that an airplane "may not exceed" GHG standards when seeking 14 CFR certification, asking the agencies to allow a limited tolerance or measurement uncertainty allowance (e.g., ±0.5% or established test uncertainty level).

[P3] Trade associations will request that §1030.1(a) explicitly allow conditional or provisional type certification where a design marginally exceeds the GHG metric but has a plan and timeline to meet the standard, to avoid grounding new designs.

[P4] Manufacturers and modification centers will request clarification in §1030.1(b) whether changes that reduce fuel efficiency (i.e., worsen the metric) due to mandatory safety equipment upgrades are exempt or eligible for exemption under §1030.10.

[P5] Legal commenters will assert §1030.1(b)’s prohibition that a modified airplane may not exceed the prior version's metric under §1030.30 is an impermissible retroactive restriction on previously certificated design baselines and conflicts with FAA authority unless tied to new type certification.

[P6] Small aircraft producers and general aviation advocates will assert that §1030.1(c)(1) and (2) MTOM exemptions (5,700 kg and 8,618 kg) are inconsistently low/high compared to international norms and request alignment with ICAO or FAA classifications or a justification for the chosen thresholds.

[P7] Operators of amphibious and specialized mission aircraft will comment that §1030.1(c)(3) and (4) exemptions are too broadly defined and propose clearer criteria and an objective approval process (e.g., a list of mission types or performance parameters) to prevent gaming of the exemption.

[P8] Manufacturers will request detailed procedures and timelines for EPA/FAA determination under §1030.1(c)(4) (specialized operations) including an appeal mechanism and publication of determinations so manufacturers know whether their designs qualify.

[P9] Commenters will question how "reference geometric factor of zero" in §1030.1(c)(5) can occur in practice and ask the agencies to define acceptable documentation and measurement methods to claim that exemption.

[P10] Firefighting operators will support §1030.1(c)(6) exemption but ask for clarity that retrofitted aircraft used seasonally for firefighting are covered and what documentation is required to establish firefighting use.

[P11] State environmental agencies and legal experts will challenge §1030.5's broad prohibition on state or local standards, urging clarification that states may implement complementary programs (e.g., reporting, incentives) and requesting a narrow preemption to avoid precluding non-standard but non-conflicting state actions.

[P12] State governments will request an explicit express preemption analysis and justification for §1030.5 under federalism principles and to clarify whether emission-related procurement or operational requirements (airport-level rules) are barred.

[P13] Industry commenters will seek a clear process and interagency timeline for FAA to consult with EPA on exemption applications per §1030.10, including a statutory maximum consultation period and who makes the final decision.

[P14] Aviation legal groups will request that §1030.10 specify whether FAA consultation with EPA is binding on FAA and whether EPA may veto exemptions, to avoid interagency confusion and litigation risk.

[P15] Manufacturers will object to the precision requirement in §1030.20 to round fuel efficiency metric values to three decimals as being unnecessarily burdensome; they will request alignment with measurement uncertainty and propose two-decimal precision instead.

[P16] Commenters will request that §1030.23(a)(2)(i) clarify the minimum quantity, flight envelope coverage, and statistical quality of SAR flight test data required to validate a performance model (e.g., number of flights, mass points).

[P17] Manufacturers will ask for specific criteria and timelines in §1030.23(a)(2)(ii) for FAA approval of performance models before SAR calculations can be made, including a reasonable review period (e.g., 120 days) and an opportunity to cure deficiencies.

[P18] Aircraft makers will request that §1030.23(b) list how MTOM should be treated for modular/convertible variants (e.g., convertible passenger/cargo) when establishing 1/SAR at reference masses.

[P19] Commenters will ask that §1030.23(b)(1) and (2) provide worked examples demonstrating calculation of high and low gross mass (92% MTOM and the formula) for typical MTOMs to reduce ambiguity.

[P20] Airframers will request clarification in §1030.23(c) excluding auxiliary power units: whether integrated APU performance that affects main-engine SAR indirectly must still be accounted for in overall airplane SAR determination.

[P21] International legal/industry commenters will request that §1030.23(d) explicitly allow updated ICAO Annex 16 procedures and provide a process for adopting newer Annex editions without requiring Federal Register publication for every minor procedural update.

[P22] Commenters will request that §1030.25 and subparts include CAD/3D modeling allowances, tolerances, and measurement uncertainty for fuselage projected area calculations for single- and multi-deck aircraft to avoid disputes over RGF measurements.

[P23] Aircraft OEMs will request examples and diagrams in guidance for applying §1030.25(b)(1) and (2) regarding cockpit exclusions and forward/aft pressure bulkheads to ensure consistent projected width determinations.

[P24] Industry will object to requiring division by exactly 1 m^2 to compute nondimensional RGF in §1030.25(c) if published CAD models use other units; they will ask for explicit unit conventions and rounding rules.

[P25] Commenters will request that §1030.25(d) allow the use of third-party accredited measurement labs and certify engineers to perform RGF measurements per ICAO Annex 16 rather than restricting who may perform them.

[P26] Multiple manufacturers will challenge §1030.30(b) numeric metric limits as overly prescriptive and request that the agencies publish the statistical basis, dataset, and regression methodology used to derive the MTOM-based formulae.

[P27] Industry will request transitional phase-in dates and lead times for compliance with the specific metric limits in §1030.30(b)(1)–(8), including grandfathering of in-production models for a set number of years.

[P28] Commenters will demand that §1030.30(b)(3) and (7) fixed numeric caps (0.764 and 0.797) include an allowance for small measurement or operational variances and explanation why fixed caps apply over a narrow MTOM band.

[P29] Small airplane manufacturers will ask that §1030.35(a) thresholds for modifications that trigger re-demonstration be clarified for common modification types (interior refits, systems upgrades) and include a de minimis threshold for non-performance modifications.

[P30] Industry will request clarity on how to calculate percent changes in the fuel efficiency metric for §1030.35(a)(2) when prior-version metrics were reported with lower precision or derived from different test methods.

[P31] Commenters will ask EPA/FAA to provide calculators or protocols for applying the linear threshold reductions in §1030.35(a)(2)(i)-(iii) across MTOM ranges to ensure consistent application.

[P32] Manufacturers will support §1030.35(b) permission to report prior metrics when modifications do not increase MTOM or metric beyond thresholds but will request confirmation that occasional minor production tolerances do not trigger re-testing.

[P33] For §1030.35(c), OEMs operating in the 2023–2028 window will ask for clarification of the retrospective application: whether modifications made prior to final adoption but after 1/1/2023 are subject, and request non-retroactivity.

[P34] Aircraft manufacturers will ask that §1030.90 annual reporting deadlines (February 28) include flexibility when that date falls on a weekend/holiday and request an electronic submission portal and an extension mechanism.

[P35] Commenters will object to §1030.90(a)’s requirement to include exempted airplanes in the report, arguing it undermines the point of exemptions and raises confidentiality and competitive concerns; they will request that exempt models be reported in aggregated form.

[P36] Industry will request that §1030.90(b) identify the "Designated EPA Program Officer" by office or provide a central submission address and an electronic filing process to avoid delivery issues.

[P37] Commenters will seek clarification in §1030.90(d)(1) whether "type certificates issued by any organization other than the FAA" includes foreign civil aviation authorities and what documentation suffices for foreign TC identification.

[P38] Manufacturers will request that §1030.90(d)(2) allow reporting of the date of application to certify to §1030.30 when such application is pending, and allow subsequent updates if certification occurs after the reporting deadline.

[P39] Airlines and OEMs will request that §1030.90(d)(3) permit reporting of applicable Annex 16 edition only by citation and URL and allow future edition updates without amending past reports.

[P40] OEMs will ask that §1030.90(d)(5) allow MTOM and RGF to be reported as specified ranges for multi-configuration models (e.g., convertible freighter) rather than a single value that could misrepresent variants.

[P41] Engine and propeller manufacturers will request confidentiality protections and redaction allowances for proprietary engine/propeller model names and type certificate details required under §1030.90(d)(6)–(7).

[P42] Commenters will request that §1030.90(d)(8) clarify whether "calculated GHG emission standard" is the numeric limit from §1030.30 or a per-airplane calculated limit after RGF/SAR inputs, and provide a formula example.

[P43] Manufacturers will request that §1030.90(d)(9) permit firms with zero production to submit a short form and to provide a waiver when the last manufacture date is proprietary, or allow aggregated reporting of end-of-production status.

[P44] OEMs seeking exemptions under §1030.10 will ask §1030.90(d)(10) to allow reporting of exemption approvals by docket number only and to permit delayed disclosure of the number of exempt airplanes where national security or proprietary concerns exist.

[P45] Corporate compliance officers will request that the signed attestation in §1030.90(e) include a defined authorized representative title list (e.g., CEO, VP Engineering) and allow electronic signatures to streamline filings.

[P46] Commenters will support the §1030.90(f) allowance to reuse prior-year information but ask the agencies to require a one-page affirmation rather than resubmitting full data, and to define what constitutes "valid and complete."

[P47] Manufacturers will ask that the three-year record retention requirement in §1030.95(a) be extended to five or seven years to align with FAA airworthiness recordkeeping or alternatively be coordinated to avoid duplicate retention burdens.

[P48] Commenters will request clarification in §1030.95(a) that the three-year restart rule only applies to data actually used in a new certification application and does not force indefinite retention through serial renewals.

[P49] Industry will propose that §1030.95(b) explicitly permit primary records in other languages and require only summary documentation in English, to accommodate multinational manufacturers and suppliers.

[P50] Trade groups will request that §1030.95(b) define "promptly" (e.g., 10 business days) for producing organized written records in English to avoid arbitrary enforcement.

[P51] Commenters will ask EPA to define the scope and limits of EPA's right to review records "at any time" under §1030.95(b) to prevent intrusive or duplicative audits, proposing reasonable notice and scheduled inspections except in emergencies.

[P52] Companies will request that §1030.98's application of 40 CFR 1068.10 on confidential information be accompanied by a process map and examples showing what company technical information can be withheld versus what must be disclosed in public reports.

[P53] Legal commenters will note that §1030.110(a) duplicates §87.8(a) and request consolidation or cross-reference language to avoid inconsistent implementation and reduce confusion about when Federal Register publication is required.

[P54] Public interest and environmental NGOs will argue that the Federal Register publication requirements in both §87.8(a) and §1030.110(a) should require EPA to provide analysis of the environmental and economic impacts of switching editions, not just notice.

[P55] International stakeholders will request the rule clarify whether enforcement of different editions via Federal Register under §1030.110(a) applies to adoption of future ICAO Annex 16 editions and propose a streamlined rulemaking procedure for routine international harmonization.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement that CMS or a contractor send written notice of intent to participate when electing to participate before receipt of a notice of hearing is vague about acceptable delivery methods (email vs. postal mail) and should specify permitted service methods and proof of delivery to avoid disputes.

[P1] Industry commenters will request a longer deadline or a conditional safe-harbor for sending notice of intent to participate when participation is elected prior to receipt of a hearing notice, to allow time for internal approvals and coordination with counsel.

[P2] Requiring notice to the “assigned ALJ or attorney adjudicator, or a designee of the Chief ALJ if not yet assigned” creates confusion about who constitutes a valid designee; CMS should list contact points or procedures to identify the designee to prevent misdirected notices.

[P2] Legal practitioners will object that sending notice to a designee of the Chief ALJ without a published roster or contact method risks due process defects if parties cannot verify the designee’s identity or receipt.

[P3] The rule obligates CMS/contractors to send notice to parties who received the notice of reconsideration or “relevant parties in escalated requests” but fails to define “relevant parties,” creating uncertainty and potential for exclusion of interested parties.

[P3] Patient advocacy groups will request that the rule explicitly require sending notice to the appellant’s designated representative (e.g., authorized representative) and to any party who filed an appeal, to protect beneficiaries’ rights.

[P4] The 10-calendar-day deadline for QIC/contractor notice of intent to participate after receiving a notice of hearing is unworkably short for complex claims that require coordination with counsel and internal review; CMS should extend this to 21 or 30 days.

[P4] Contractors may comment that the 10-day requirement could force rushed or inaccurate participation decisions and propose an exception where additional time may be requested if good cause exists.

[P5] The requirement to submit position paper or written testimony within 14 days of electing to participate (if no hearing scheduled) or no later than 5 days before the hearing is overly restrictive and does not account for complex medical records review; stakeholders request minimum page limits or an automatic extension for substantial records.

[P5] Health plans and contractors will request the rule permit submission of initial, non-final position papers with supplements permitted on a rolling basis to accommodate voluminous documentation.

[P6] Sending position papers before receipt of a notice of hearing to “the parties required to be sent a copy of the notice of intent” assumes those parties can be accurately identified—commenters will ask CMS to require contemporaneous proof of service and an electronic filing option.

[P7] The requirement that a notice of hearing be sent to all parties that filed an appeal or participated in reconsideration and any party found liable is administratively burdensome without standard electronic service protocols; industry requests a standardized electronic distribution list format.

[P7] Beneficiary advocates will caution that OMHA must ensure notice is sent to beneficiaries’ authorized representatives and in accessible formats (large print, translated languages) and request this be explicitly mandated.

[P8] The mandate to consider objections requesting in-person or VTC hearings is appropriate but should require ALJs to provide written reasons when such requests are denied to facilitate appellate review.

[P9] Requiring Chief ALJ concurrence for in-person hearings concentrates decisionmaking and may delay scheduling; commenters will propose allowing delegated concurrence thresholds or presumptive concurrence unless denied within a set period.

[P9] Parties will request clarification of the standard for “good cause” that ALJs must find to grant/reschedule in-person or VTC hearings to reduce inconsistent determinations.

[P10] The concurrence clause burdens the Chief ALJ with routine scheduling decisions and lacks criteria for when concurrence should be withheld; commenters recommend specifying objective concurrence criteria or allowing designees to act.

[P11] The “good cause” requirement to reschedule hearings is undefined and may be applied inconsistently; stakeholders ask CMS to enumerate non-exhaustive examples of circumstances that constitute good cause (illness, hospitalization, inability to travel).

[P12] The obligation to reschedule hearings to a time/place where the party can appear in person or by VTC should include an express requirement to consider participants’ disability accommodation needs and to provide assistive technologies.

[P13] The VTC exception that waives good cause for unrepresented beneficiaries who object to telephone hearings is beneficial but should ensure access by requiring ALJs to offer VTC infrastructure, technical support, and alternative locations for beneficiaries without broadband or devices.

[P14] Limiting official copies of adjudicative documents to CMS or its contractors could impede appellants’ ability to obtain records; patient and legal aid groups will argue that appellants or their authorized representatives must be entitled to obtain certified official copies upon request.

[P15] OMHA’s obligation to check for an electronic copy in the official record before requesting information from the QIC is sensible but should require OMHA to document efforts and timestamps in the administrative record to avoid delay and duplication.

[P15] Contractors may request a specified time limit (e.g., 5 business days) for OMHA’s check and acceptance of electronic copies to prevent unnecessary remands or scheduling pauses.

[P16] Dismissing or refusing to consider hearing requests where there is a previously binding determination on the same facts and issues risks precluding legitimate changes in law or new evidence; commenters will request an exception allowing consideration where a change in applicable law or newly discovered material evidence is shown.

[P16] Legal advocates will ask CMS to define “same facts and issues” and to require ALJs to issue written findings when dismissing based on prior determinations to permit meaningful review.

[P17] Permitting ALJs to deem appellants to have abandoned their requests where OMHA cannot contact them after “reasonable efforts” is potentially unfair to beneficiaries with unstable housing; commenters will demand a prescriptive set of required outreach attempts (number, modes, and time intervals) before abandonment may be found.

[P17] Civil legal aid groups will request that OMHA be required to attempt contact via the appellant’s listed authorized representative, electronic mail if available, and to use postal forwarding addresses before finding abandonment.

[P18] OMHA’s obligation to send written dismissal notices to many listed recipients and include the right to request vacatur is appropriate but should require use of multiple modes of contact (mail and email) and clear timelines for vacatur to ensure beneficiaries can rehearse mistaken dismissals.

[P19] Allowing vacatur within 180 calendar days if “good and sufficient cause” is shown is helpful, but 180 days may be too short for beneficiaries unaware of the dismissal; commenters propose extending to 1 year or permitting equitable tolling in extraordinary circumstances.

[P20] The 180-calendar-day time limit for vacatur should be accompanied by a definition of “date of the notice of dismissal” (mailing date vs. presumed receipt date) to avoid disputes over timeliness.

[P21] The obligation to remand cases to the QIC when the ALJ/attorney adjudicator determines the QIC’s dismissal was in error should include a deadline for the QIC to complete the readjudication to prevent prolonged appeals processing.

[P21] Parties will ask that remands identify the specific relief expected (e.g., conduct redetermination within X days) and require notice to the appellant of the remand and expected timeline.

[P22] Permitting remand when an official copy cannot be obtained is reasonable, but the rule should clarify when the ALJ may order production directly from non-CMS sources or accept alternative documentation to avoid unnecessary remands.

[P23] OMHA’s obligation to transmit remand notices and state the right to request Chief ALJ review is appropriate, but the exception (not required for remands under paragraph (d)(1)) risks depriving parties of review opportunities; commenters will seek clarification and justification for the exception.

[P24] Granting the Chief ALJ or designee final authority to review remands upon timely request centralizes review; commenters will request transparency requirements and timelines for Chief ALJ action to avoid indefinite delays.

[P25] The presumption that receipt of decisions/dismissals occurs 5 calendar days after notice date may be inaccurate for mailed notices and could prejudice appellants in filing deadlines; stakeholders request use of actual delivery confirmation or extended presumptive receipt (e.g., 7–10 days) for mail.

[P26] The right to an ALJ hearing only if the enrollee meets the amount in controversy thresholds may prevent low-income enrollees from accessing meaningful review; advocacy groups will challenge the adequacy of the thresholds and request an inflation-adjusted safety valve for hardship cases.

[P27] Requiring enrollees to meet amount in controversy requirements to be entitled to ALJ hearings may be inconsistent with due process where coverage or urgent care is denied; commenters will request exemptions (e.g., for medically necessary drugs) or alternative expedited procedures.

[P28] The minimum amount in controversy formula tied to a $100 base adjusted by the medical care CPI increase since July 2003 is opaque and could produce large year-to-year variability; stakeholders ask CMS to publish the current dollar amount in the preamble or a public table and to include an annual update schedule.

[P29] Rounding non-multiples of $10 to the nearest $10 without specifying rounding direction for .5 values could create ambiguity; commenters will request explicit rounding rules and timely publication of changes.

[P30] The $1,000 amount-in-controversy requirement for judicial review should be clarified whether it is similarly adjusted by the CPI and whether partial waivers are possible for systemic legal issues affecting many enrollees.

[P31] Using projected value of benefits (including refills) to compute amount in controversy for Part D plan refusals could inflate the amount and bar individual appeals; commenters will recommend using the demonstrable shortfall or a 12-month actual refill estimate, not indefinite projections.

[P31] Patient groups will point out that projecting future refill costs for non-maintenance or one-time drugs is speculative and may unfairly deny hearing rights.

[P32] For appeals based on at-risk determinations, computing amount in controversy using projected drug value including refills may be inaccurate and invite gaming; commenters will propose alternative methods (e.g., 6-month projection or actual past usage) and require supporting documentation.

[P33] Allowing aggregation of two or more appeals to meet the amount in controversy is beneficial, but the requirements (previous IRE reconsideration, timing, same enrollee or same drug) are restrictive; stakeholders will seek broader aggregation rules for related claims.

[P34] Requiring that appeals to be aggregated have been previously reconsidered by an IRE may prevent aggregation of newly identified but related claims; commenters will request permitting aggregation where reconsideration is pending or where claims were administratively combined.

[P35] The 60-day filing window for aggregation requests is short and unforgiving; beneficiaries often lack notice—CMS should allow aggregation requests to be filed within the appeal filing period for the latest reconsideration or permit an extension for good cause.

[P36] Requiring aggregated appeals to involve delivery of prescription drugs to a single enrollee limits aggregation of related administrative errors affecting multiple claims for the same enrollee (e.g., coverage denials across formularies); commenters will ask for broader criteria allowing aggregation of issues affecting the same treatment course.

[P37] Permitting multiple enrollees to aggregate appeals is useful for class-like matters, but procedural safeguards should be required (consent of all enrollees, shared counsel, confidentiality protections).

[P38] The condition that appeals aggregated by multiple enrollees must have been previously reconsidered by an IRE may be impractical for group actions; commenters will request an exception for mass denials where individualized reconsiderations are impractical.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The requirement that CMS or a contractor send written notice of intent to participate when electing to participate before receipt of a notice of hearing is vague about acceptable delivery methods (email vs. postal mail) and should specify permitted service methods and proof of delivery to avoid disputes.

Industry commenters will request a longer deadline or a conditional safe-harbor for sending notice of intent to participate when participation is elected prior to receipt of a hearing notice, to allow time for internal approvals and coordination with counsel.

Legal practitioners will object that sending notice to a designee of the Chief ALJ without a published roster or contact method risks due process defects if parties cannot verify the designee’s identity or receipt.

The rule obligates CMS/contractors to send notice to parties who received the notice of reconsideration or “relevant parties in escalated requests” but fails to define “relevant parties,” creating uncertainty and potential for exclusion of interested parties.

Patient advocacy groups will request that the rule explicitly require sending notice to the appellant’s designated representative (e.g., authorized representative) and to any party who filed an appeal, to protect beneficiaries’ rights.

The requirement that a notice of hearing be sent to all parties that filed an appeal or participated in reconsideration and any party found liable is administratively burdensome without standard electronic service protocols; industry requests a standardized electronic distribution list format.

Beneficiary advocates will caution that OMHA must ensure notice is sent to beneficiaries’ authorized representatives and in accessible formats (large print, translated languages) and request this be explicitly mandated.

Requiring Chief ALJ concurrence for in-person hearings concentrates decisionmaking and may delay scheduling; commenters will propose allowing delegated concurrence thresholds or presumptive concurrence unless denied within a set period.
Parties will request clarification of the standard for “good cause” that ALJs must find to grant/reschedule in-person or VTC hearings to reduce inconsistent determinations.

The concurrence clause burdens the Chief ALJ with routine scheduling decisions and lacks criteria for when concurrence should be withheld; commenters recommend specifying objective concurrence criteria or allowing designees to act.

The “good cause” requirement to reschedule hearings is undefined and may be applied inconsistently; stakeholders ask CMS to enumerate non-exhaustive examples of circumstances that constitute good cause (illness, hospitalization, inability to travel).

The obligation to reschedule hearings to a time/place where the party can appear in person or by VTC should include an express requirement to consider participants’ disability accommodation needs and to provide assistive technologies.

The VTC exception that waives good cause for unrepresented beneficiaries who object to telephone hearings is beneficial but should ensure access by requiring ALJs to offer VTC infrastructure, technical support, and alternative locations for beneficiaries without broadband or devices.

[P1] The requirement to set payment at 100% of ASP when ASP data are available fails to account for rapid price fluctuations and could overpay providers for drugs with recent price decreases, leading to increased program costs.

[P1] Hospitals and specialty pharmacies will contend that tying payment strictly to 100% of ASP removes incentives for efficient purchasing and could disadvantage providers that negotiate lower discounts, recommending a cap or blended rate instead.

[P1] Patient advocacy groups will argue that 100% of ASP may not reflect patient out-of-pocket affordability concerns and could result in higher coinsurance amounts for beneficiaries.

[P1] Legal experts will claim that mandating 100% of ASP without clear statutory authorization risks exceeding CMS’s regulatory authority and may be subject to challenge.

[P2] Manufacturers will object to reliance on voluntarily submitted ASP data, noting that voluntary submission creates data gaps and potential selection bias, and request mandatory reporting or alternative verified data sources.

[P2] Industry commenters will request clarifications on the phrase “calculated consistent with part 414, subpart J” — specifically how rebates, discounts, and marketplace price adjustments will be reflected in the ASP used for payment.

[P2] Data transparency advocates will argue that allowing manufacturers to voluntarily submit ASP data could enable manipulation or underreporting to influence Medicare payment rates, recommending audit and penalty provisions.

[P2] Pharmacy trade groups will ask for a timeline and process for how updated ASP submissions will be incorporated into payment rates and whether mid-year updates are permitted.

[P3] Stakeholders will request detailed definitions and triggers for paragraph (d)(2)(i)(B)(2) exceptions — the rule’s cross-reference is insufficient and creates uncertainty about when 100% ASP does not apply.

[P3] State Medicaid programs will express concern that the exception clause could lead to inconsistent application across payers and request coordination language to prevent divergent reimbursement policies.

[P4] Behavioral health providers will challenge the disparate fallback methodology — using TRICARE for methadone and NADAC for buprenorphine — asserting this creates inequitable payment treatment between medications treating the same condition.

[P4] Pharmacists will note operational complexity: switching basis for payment depending on ASP availability could complicate billing systems and claim adjudication, and request clear billing codes/edits.

[P4] Policy analysts will argue that relying on TRICARE and NADAC without adjustment factors may not reflect true commercial acquisition costs, potentially underpaying for methadone and buprenorphine.

[P5] Methadone treatment programs will state that TRICARE rates are often lower than commercial acquisition costs for methadone formulations and will lead to financial losses for opioid treatment programs, proposing provider exceptions or supplemental payments.

[P5] Veterans and military families advocates will point out that TRICARE rates are set for a different population and setting; using them as Medicare payment benchmarks is inappropriate and could create access issues.

[P6] Pharmacy associations will contend that NADAC does not always capture specialty pharmacy pricing or discounts for buprenorphine formulations, risking underpayment and reduced access to medication-assisted treatment.

[P6] Buprenorphine manufacturers will argue that NADAC-based payment could incentivize dispensing of lower-cost formulations only, reducing patient access to preferred delivery forms (e.g., films, long-acting injectables).

[P6] Clinical providers will request an adjustment mechanism to ensure NADAC-based payments reflect regional variations in acquisition costs, particularly in rural areas where acquisition costs are higher.

[P7] Advocates for program stability will support the CY2022 transitional provision but request that CMS extend the freeze beyond CY2022 if data volatility persists to prevent payment shocks.

[P7] Legal commentators will seek justification and rulemaking record for pegging CY2022 methadone payment to CY2021 levels, questioning whether this complies with notice-and-comment requirements and is appropriately temporary.

[P7] Providers will request retrospective reconciliation if CY2022 payments are later found inadequate compared to actual acquisition costs, asking CMS to permit cost-based adjustments or supplemental payments.

[P1] Economists will recommend adding a provision for periodic review (e.g., biennial) of the 100% ASP policy to assess impacts on access, utilization, and program spending.

[P2] Privacy and compliance officers will ask how CMS will verify the accuracy of voluntary ASP submissions and what penalties exist for fraudulent reporting.

[P4] State regulators will request coordination language to ensure Medicare’s fallback methodologies (TRICARE/NADAC) do not conflict with state Medicaid payment methodologies for methadone/buprenorphine.

[P5] Small, community-based opioid treatment programs will submit empirical data showing methadone acquisition costs exceed TRICARE rates and request an alternative reimbursement floor to avoid clinic closures.

[P6] Rural health advocates will claim NADAC’s urban-sourced data underestimates drug acquisition costs in rural retail and long-term care settings, calling for a rural adjustment factor.

[P1] Competitor manufacturers will warn that paying 100% ASP could inadvertently subsidize high list-price drugs with heavy rebates, recommending net-price or average net acquisition cost be used instead.

[P2] Pharmacy benefit managers will ask whether manufacturer-submitted ASPs will account for manufacturer-to-PBM rebates and whether such rebates should reduce ASP for Medicare payment purposes.

[P3] Consumer advocates will urge CMS to clarify that the exception in (d)(2)(i)(B)(2) cannot be used to systematically exclude coverage of certain formulations by manipulating data availability.

[P7] Payment integrity groups will demand that the temporary CY2022 provision include guardrails to prevent permanent entrenchment of outdated rates without future notice-and-comment rulemaking.

[P3] MROs request definition of “engine shop visit” (e.g., does borescope inspection requiring partial disassembly count?) because variable interpretations will lead to inconsistent compliance and enforcement.

[P3] Operators raise cost and downtime concerns with mandating removal/replacement at the next shop visit and request an allowance to defer replacement across a limited number of shop visits for parts availability or scheduling, provided interim inspections are performed.

[P8] Requiring AMOC requests be routed through the principal inspector or local FSDO imposes additional administrative burden for foreign operators and some part-145 repair stations; commenters ask for direct FAA AMOC submission options for non-U.S. operators.

[P8] Legal commenters note that 14 CFR 39.19 allows multiple submission routes; the AD should explicitly state that following 14 CFR 39.19 is sufficient and not add extra local routing requirements that could delay approvals.

[P9] Stakeholders request secure file transfer or PII protections for AMOC submissions sent via email to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov, as AMOC packages may contain proprietary technical data.

[P10] The requirement to notify the principal inspector or FSDO manager before using an approved AMOC is reasonable, but commenters request clarification on the acceptable notice period (e.g., 48 hours, 5 business days) to ensure operational planning.

[General] Commercial operators request the FAA include an economic analysis of parts, labor, and downtime costs for replacing the fuel hydraulic lines, and propose a parts-cost reimbursement mechanism or compliance credit for early replacements already performed.

[General] Foreign civil aviation authorities request that the AD explicitly allow their equivalent approvals for AMOCs and clarify how bilateral agreements (e.g., FAA-EASA) will treat compliance and approvals.

[P1] The August 12, 2019 comments due date is unreasonably short and prevents meaningful input from small operators and public interest groups; extend the deadline by at least 60 days.

[P1] The rule contains two different "Comments Due Date" provisions (P1 and P19) with different dates (Aug 12, 2019 and Jan 16, 2020); this creates confusion about the actual deadline—clarify which date controls.

[P19] If January 16, 2020 is the intended deadline, publish a corrected notice and extend the comment period to avoid depriving stakeholders of the full statutorily required comment opportunity.

[P2] The applicability text (P2/P20) is overly broad by applying to all 757–200/–200PF/–200CB/–300 airplanes irrespective of configuration or modification history; limit applicability to serial-number ranges or installations that actually have the affected structure/systems.

[P21] The STC ST01518SE exception (P21) is ambiguous: it does not explain why STC ST01518SE holders are exempt from a 'change in product' AMOC request—clarify the technical basis and scope of that exception.

[P24] The reduced compliance times for VTMAE STC ST03562AT converted freighters (P24) may be impractical and cost-prohibitive for operators; provide a risk assessment and allow phased compliance or alternative compliance schedules.

[P4] Requiring operators to "perform all applicable actions" per Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin (P4/P23) effectively delegates mandatory rulemaking details to a Boeing document; the FAA must incorporate by reference or publish the specific required actions in the AD itself for regulatory clarity.

[P5] Replacing "original issue date" with the AD effective date for compliance determinations (P5/P25) could change compliance time calculations for operators who relied on the bulletin's original dates; provide worked examples and transitional provisions.

[P6] The requirement that when the bulletin directs contacting Boeing, operators must perform the repair or alternatives "before further flight" using an FAA-approved method (P6/P26) is impractical in remote locations where immediate approved methods are unavailable; allow temporary ferry relief under conditions or permit interim safe-action guidance.

[P11] Requiring notification to the principal inspector or local FSDO before using an approved AMOC (P11/P31) duplicates 14 CFR 39.19 procedures and could create administrative delays; clarify timelines for notification and whether notification is retrospective or prior to use.

[P7] Concentrating AMOC approval authority in the Manager, Los Angeles ACO Branch (P7/P27) may be unduly centralized and slow; allow regional ACOs or designees to approve AMOCs to expedite resolution for affected operators nationwide.

[P8] The requirement to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 (P8/P28) is inconsistent with electronic submission options; clarify that electronic submissions to the listed FAA email satisfy the requirement and state acceptable formats.

[P9] The instruction to address direct submissions to the individual identified in paragraph (j)(1) (P9/P29) is unhelpful without including that person's name and contact information in the preamble; include full contact details to avoid misdirected AMOC requests.

[P10] Allowing AMOC requests by email (P10/P30) raises confidentiality and security concerns for proprietary repair methods; state whether encrypted submissions are accepted and how proprietary data will be protected.

[P12] Permitting AMOCs approved by an authorized Boeing ODA to be used (P12/P32) raises conflict-of-interest concerns because Boeing may approve methods that benefit the manufacturer; require FAA review/acknowledgment of Boeing ODA approvals or limit ODA use to non-safety-critical deviations.

[P13] Requiring AMOC repair methods to meet the airplane's certification basis (P13/P33) is appropriate, but the AD should specify the process and timeline for resolving conflicts when a proposed repair meets later supplemental basis or STC-derived bases.

[P14] Requiring that AMOC approvals explicitly reference this AD (P14/P34) is sensible, but the AD should state the required content of such references (e.g., AD number, paragraph) to avoid incomplete approvals.

[P15] The National Peanut Board composition limit of "no more than 13 peanut producers and alternates" (P15/P16) could exclude representation from emerging producing states; recommend an odd-numbered, more flexible composition or inclusion of at-large members to ensure broader geographic representation.

[P17] Requiring one member and alternate from each primary peanut-producing state to be selected from nominations by certified peanut producer organizations (P17) risks excluding independent producers not affiliated with such organizations; allow producers to self-nominate or include nominations from recognized individual producers.

[P18] The 3-year average production threshold of 10,000 tons to qualify as a primary peanut-producing state (P18) may freeze out states that have recently increased production; propose using the most recent single-year production figure or a sliding scale to reflect current changes.

[P22] The repeated obligation to "comply within the specified compliance times unless already done" (P3/P22) is redundant and may create uncertainty whether previous non-standard repairs count as "already done;" define what documentation is required to prove prior accomplishment.

[P23] Requiring operators to follow the Accomplishment Instructions in the Boeing Requirements Bulletin (P23) without FAA-approved revisions may prevent necessary operator-specific adaptations; permit operators to apply for alternative procedures when they can demonstrate equal safety.

[P24] The instruction to apply reduced compliance times to certain converted freighters (P24) fails to provide technical justification; publish the engineering rationale and expected risk differences that mandate the reduced intervals.

[P25] The AD's cross-references to the Requirements Bulletin "original issue date" exception (P25) are circular and could be misapplied in later revisions of the bulletin; require that any future revisions to the bulletin be explicitly addressed by the FAA before being effective for AD compliance.

[P26] Mandating that repairs/alternative inspections and any on-condition actions be completed "before further flight" when Boeing must be contacted (P26) effectively gives Boeing de facto operational control; allow continued operation under safe-limitation procedures with interim FAA-approved repairs when immediate compliance is infeasible.

[P30] The listed FAA email for AMOC submissions (P30) may not be monitored for complex engineering packages; require confirmation receipts and an expected processing timeline to ensure timely handling.

[P31] The obligation to notify the principal inspector or FSDO manager before using an approved AMOC (P31) should specify whether notification may be electronic and whether failure to notify within a specific timeframe voids the AMOC.

[P32] Allowing ODA-approved AMOCs to be used for required repairs (P32) should be conditioned on FAA concurrence for any deviation from structural criticality determinations; require FAA validation for structural repairs affecting certification basis.

[P33] The requirement that repair methods meet the airplane’s certification basis (P33) should include guidance on how to treat changes in certification basis over time (e.g., new rules, amendments) and whether grandfathering applies.

[P34] Requiring every AMOC approval to explicitly reference this AD (P34) could lead to administrative rejections of broader AMOC approvals; permit cross-referencing where appropriate and allow one approval to reference multiple related ADs if the technical basis overlaps.

raw_output:
[P1] The public comment deadline of August 6, 2018 is unreasonably short and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow affected operators, vendors, and maintenance organizations sufficient time to review the technical service bulletins and prepare detailed responses.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether electronic submissions received by 11:59 PM Eastern Time on August 6, 2018 will be accepted, and provide explicit instructions for time zone and format to avoid inadvertent late filings.

[P2] The compliance provision that requires owners/operators to meet the AD within the "specified compliance times" is ambiguous because the NPRM does not explicitly list the compliance-time table or examples for different utilization rates; the FAA should publish a clear compliance-time schedule tied to cycles/hours or flight hours.

[P3] The 15-month compliance time to modify aft belly fairing access panels is overly aggressive for smaller operators and for aircraft with tight maintenance schedules; FAA should allow longer compliance times (e.g., 24–36 months) or provide phased compliance based on ferry availability.

[P3] The AD should include an estimate of downtime and labor hours required to replace the aft belly fairing attachments so operators can plan maintenance windows and cost impacts; currently that cost data is missing.

[P4] Requiring specific Bombardier Service Bulletins (700–53–050 or 700–53–6008 Rev 01 dated Dec 16, 2016) for Model BD–700–1A10 airplane compliance is unduly prescriptive; the FAA should permit incorporation by reference of later-revised service bulletins or equivalent procedures approved via AMOC without requiring prior rule amendment.

[P4] The AD should clarify whether operators may use original (non-Revision 01) versions of the listed service bulletins with an FAA-approved AMOC, given that some operators already performed work to earlier SB versions.

[P5] For Model BD–700–1A11, listing two specific Bombardier SBs (700–1A11–53–025 or 700–53–5009 Rev 01 dated Dec 16, 2016) may create parts-supply and approval confusion; FAA should specify whether both are equally acceptable or whether one is preferred and explain differences.

[P6] The credit-for-previous-actions provision should explicitly state that all work done in accordance with the July 14, 2016 service bulletins (listed in h(1)-(h)(4)) will be accepted regardless of recordkeeping format, provided the maintenance records show SB number, task, and signature.

[P7] Crediting Bombardier Service Bulletin 700–1A11–53–025 dated July 14, 2016 is appropriate, but the AD should require that the specific revision/date used be documented in the aircraft logbook entry to prevent disputes during inspections.

[P8] Bombardier Service Bulletin 700–53–050 dated July 14, 2016 is listed for credit, but the AD must clarify whether partial compliance with that SB (e.g., only some attachment replacements) suffices or whether full SB compliance is required.

[P9] The credit for Bombardier Service Bulletin 700–53–5009 dated July 14, 2016 should be limited to actions performed exactly as noted in the SB; any deviations must be subject to AMOC to prevent inconsistent field modifications.

[P10] Crediting Bombardier Service Bulletin 700–53–6008 dated July 14, 2016 could create ambiguity if operators used later corrective steps; the AD should state that later approved revisions supersede or are also acceptable as credit.

[P11] The AMOC authority being centralized with the Manager, New York ACO Branch may delay responses for operators in other regions; FAA should allow delegated AMOC approval to regional ACOs or FSDO managers for routine, non-novel alternatives.

[P12] The requirement that AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 is fine, but the AD should provide an email address and online submission option to streamline timely AMOC processing.

[P13] The mailing/contact details to the Program Manager, Continuing Operational Safety, FAA New York office are incomplete in the NPRM; the AD should include complete mailing address, telephone, and email for submissions to avoid misdirected requests.

[P14] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC is burdensome if the AMOC was approved centrally and operators have fleet-wide implementation plans; allow a one-time notification plus periodic reporting rather than per-use notifications.

[P15] Requiring corrective actions obtained from the manufacturer to be approved by the FAA Manager, TCCA, or Bombardier's TCCA DAO may create jurisdictional conflicts and slow fixes; the AD should permit approval by the certifying authority for the operator's state of registry when TCCA or FAA resources are not available.

[P16] If a DAO approval is acceptable only with a DAO-authorized signature, the AD should define acceptable signatures (electronic signatures, stamped, designated representative) to accommodate modern workflows.

[P17] The Airbus AD comment deadline mirrors the Bombardier AD but should also be extended; operators who manage mixed fleets need additional time to analyze combined impacts.

[P18] The general compliance language for the Airbus AD referencing "specified compliance times" again lacks specificity for operators with varying utilization; please provide enumerated compliance times in the AD text.

[P19] The requirement to upgrade ELAC by loading L99 software or replacing with ELAC L99 P/N 3945128217 must include estimated mean time to perform (MTOP) and necessary tools/equipment listing, otherwise maintenance shops cannot plan.

[P20] The condition in (h)(1) that no ECAM warning/maintenance message is present before removing the ELAC unit is impractical in service where intermittent warnings occur; the AD should specify how long a unit must be free of warnings before removal or provide alternative verification procedures.

[P21] Requiring removal per AMM Task 27–93–34–000–001–A is acceptable, but the AD should permit equivalent procedures performed by appropriately qualified maintenance organizations (AME/part-145) with documented deviations approved via the AMOC process.

[P22] The requirement to verify ELAC by two different methods (LRU ID + label call up, or Alpha Call Up ELA1 and ELA2) is operationally onerous when the aircraft is not powered for Alpha Call Up; the AD should permit offline verification via serial number, batch records, or manifest when Alpha call-up is unavailable.

[P23] The reinstall step per AMM Task 27–93–34–400–001–A should include torque values and any post-installation functional tests required; the AD should reference those explicitly.

[P24] The prohibition on installing any affected ELAC on a modified airplane (i)(1) is overly broad — it should allow installation of affected ELACs that have been upgraded to L99 (or higher) software and verified per (j) to avoid unnecessary parts waste.

[P25] The prohibition in (i)(2) preventing installation of affected ELACs on airplanes whose ELAC units are not listed in the table, from the AD effective date, could create logistics problems for spare pool management; FAA should allow temporary installation under an AMOC if the unit has been upgraded to L99+ and verified.

[P26] The permission to install ELAC with software above L99 (j) is reasonable, but the AD must specify how operators demonstrate and document that the installed software level is above L99 (e.g., label, software readout, certificate) during line maintenance.

[P27] The requirement in (j)(1) that the ELAC part number be approved by FAA Manager, EASA, or Airbus DOA to count as compliance may unnecessarily restrict operators where national civil aviation authorities (CAAs) have delegated approval authority; add language recognizing approvals by the state of registry CAA when using EASA/FAA accepted findings.

[P28] The conditions in (j)(2) requiring modification instructions approved by listed authorities are appropriate, but the AD should allow manufacturer-approved instructions that have been submitted to and accepted by EASA/FAA equivalently.

[P29] The repeated need for absence of ELAC-related ECAM warnings before removal (j)(2)(i)) lacks guidance for transient faults; the AD should define acceptable monitoring period (e.g., 72 hours) or allow pre-removal functional tests to clear spurious warnings.

[P31] The obligation to verify ELAC by two methods prior to software loading (j)(2)(iii)) should permit qualified maintenance personnel to perform one method via documentation and a second via visual/label check where Alpha Call Up is infeasible.

The rule should clarify whether electronic submissions received by 11:59 PM Eastern Time on August 6, 2018 will be accepted, and provide explicit instructions for time zone and format to avoid inadvertent late filings.

The AD should include an estimate of downtime and labor hours required to replace the aft belly fairing attachments so operators can plan maintenance windows and cost impacts; currently that cost data is missing.

raw_output:
[P1] The June 25, 2018 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonably short and will prevent small operators and non-profit safety advocacy groups from preparing meaningful technical comments; the agency should extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] Because the AD references complex service bulletin content, the fixed June 25, 2018 deadline does not allow time to obtain and review Boeing Special Attention Service Bulletin 737–52–1170, Revision 1, and conduct necessary fleet impact analyses; the FAA should reopen the comment period after making the full service bulletin publicly available.

[P2] § 39.13(c) purports to apply this AD to “all” listed 737 Models in any category, but the preamble lacks explanation of why utility, restricted, or special‑authorisation certificated aircraft should be included; commenters request clarification or narrower applicability.

[P2] The phrase “as specified” in § 39.13(c) is vague—stakeholders request that the AD explicitly state whether it applies to production‑line, converted, and permanently modified airframes and clarify treatment of supplemental type certificated (STC) modifications.

[P3] § 39.13(c)(1) incorporates Boeing Special Attention Service Bulletin 737–52–1170, Revision 1, but does not provide the Revision 1 date fully in the regulatory text; commenters request that the exact revision date and document revision number be inserted into the regulation for clarity and administrative accuracy.

[P3] Operators request that the AD clarify how an airplane is to be categorized as Group 1 or Group 2 Configuration 1 when fleet records conflict with Boeing’s group designation tables, and request a mechanism for resolving discrepancies without delaying compliance.

[P4] § 39.13(c)(2) applies to Group 2 Configuration 2 airplanes but does not disclose the differences in required actions between Configuration 1 and Configuration 2 in the AD text; operators request the AD summarize the differing requirements or include a clear cross‑reference to the specific service bulletin tasks.

[P5] § 39.13(c)(3) attempts to limit Group 3 applicability by line‑number ranges tied to certificate dates, but the truncated line‑number range in the provision is incomplete (“4275 through 672...”), creating ambiguity; the AD must be corrected to show the full line‑number range.

[P5] The condition in § 39.13(c)(3) that ties applicability to line numbers based on certificate dates may be difficult for used airplane purchasers and lessors to apply; the FAA should provide an advisory tool or database lookup method to determine whether a specific tail number is within the affected range.

[P6] § 39.13(c)(4) makes applicability contingent on “original certificates dated after the AD effective date,” which could be interpreted to exclude re‑issued or amended certificates; legal counsel requests clear definition of “original Certificate of Airworthiness” and treatment of reissued documents.

[P6] The provision in § 39.13(c)(4) that applies to airplanes with original certificates dated after the AD effective date risks creating inconsistency for imported airplanes with different certifying authorities; commenters request explicit alignment with FAA policy on import airworthiness and export certificates.

[P7] § 39.13(f) requires compliance “within the compliance times specified” but does not restate those times in the AD; commenters request that all compliance timeframes be explicitly included in the regulatory text (or an FAA summary table) so operators do not have to rely solely on the Boeing service bulletin.

[P7] The AD should include allowance for operational exigencies (e.g., AOG status) when compliance windows are short; § 39.13(f) should permit temporary relief with FAA notification when compliance within the stated time would create undue operational risk.

[P8] § 39.13(g) mandates performing all actions labeled “RC” at times specified in the service bulletin but does not define “at the applicable time specified” when multiple calendar and flight‑hour intervals exist; commenters request clarification on precedence among intervals and the method for calculating compliance due dates.

[P8] Because § 39.13(g) makes RC actions mandatory, maintenance providers request that the AD explicitly allow credit for equivalent inspections documented in approved Continued Airworthiness programs, provided they meet or exceed the RC inspection scope.

[P9] § 39.13(h) replaces service bulletin original‑issue compliance dates with the AD effective date, but does not clarify how this interacts with voluntary earlier compliance performed under the original issue; commenters request explicit retention of credit language for earlier compliance and examples of how to compute deadlines when earlier work has been effectuated.

[P10] § 39.13(i) ends repetitive inspections only for modified MLG center door retention clip assemblies “for that clip only,” which may create confusion for assemblies with mixed‑state parts on the same airplane; operators request clarification on whether partial modifications on an airplane alter inspection intervals for the entire MLG center door assembly.

[P10] Maintenance organizations note that tracking inspection termination on a per‑clip basis (as in § 39.13(i)) will require changes to maintenance records systems; the FAA should provide recommended recording language and credit acceptance criteria.

[P11] § 39.13(i) states that paragraph (j) requirements remain in effect even if the modification is done, but does not describe the interaction of the prohibition in paragraph (j) with terminated inspections; commenters request a plain‑English explanation of the continuing obligations after modification.

[P12] § 39.13(j) prohibits installing an MLG center door assembly unless Group 3 RC actions have been completed; parts suppliers and MROs assert this effectively creates a parts‑traceability and aftermarket parts limitation and request an exception allowing installation of identical, new OEM parts accompanied by documentation demonstrating compliance.

[P12] The absolute installation prohibition in § 39.13(j) should be limited to installations on airplanes in Group 3 only; as drafted it could be read to bar installation of MLG center door assemblies on other groups—FAA should confirm the scope and add permissive language for non‑Group 3 airplanes.

[P13] § 39.13(j)’s condition that all Group 3 RC actions identified in the service bulletin be “accomplished within the compliance times specified” before installation creates practical supply chain delays—manufacturers ask for an interim allowance for installation if a documented one‑time inspection is performed at installation.

[P14] § 39.13(k) gives credit for prior work done using the July 29, 2014 Boeing service bulletin, but restricts credit to that exact bulletin edition; commenters who performed equivalent inspections under later Boeing revisions or under approved maintenance program revisions request that the AD allow credit for those actions as well.

[P14] Legal commenters request explicit recordkeeping requirements and acceptable evidence to substantiate claimed credit under § 39.13(k), e.g., what documentation satisfies the FAA that the July 29, 2014 service bulletin procedures were followed.

[P15] § 39.13(l)(1) delegates AMOC approval authority to the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch, but does not provide a timeline for FAA action on AMOC requests; operators request a 60‑day decision target to avoid prolonged business disruption.

[P16] § 39.13(l)(1) requires routing AMOC requests through the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19, which may be inefficient for international operators without a U.S. principal inspector; the AD should permit direct submission to the Seattle ACO with prior notice for foreign operators.

[P17] § 39.13(l)(1) directs direct submissions to the person in paragraph (m)(1) but paragraph (m)(1) is not shown in this excerpt; commenters ask the FAA to ensure contact information is complete, accurate, and included in the final rule.

[P18] § 39.13(l)(1) allows emailing AMOC information to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov, but there is no cybersecurity/PII guidance; submitters request encryption and file size guidance and confirmation that emailed requests will constitute formal FAA filings.

[P19] § 39.13(l)(2) obligates notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC, but offers no deadline for that notification; operators ask that the AD specify a timeframe (e.g., within 24 or 72 hours) and acceptable notification formats.

[P20] § 39.13(l)(3) permits Boeing ODA to approve AMOCs for required repairs if approved by the Manager and providing acceptable safety—manufacturers request further detail on the evidence and documentation the Boeing ODA must submit to the Manager to effect such delegation.

[P21] The approval criteria in § 39.13(l)(3) requiring that the AMOC “meets the certification basis of the airplane” and “explicitly references this AD” are vague; commenters ask the FAA to provide a checklist of required substantiation, analyses, and test data that demonstrate compliance with the certification basis.

[P22] § 39.13(l)(4)(i) makes all steps labeled “RC” and their substeps mandatory; maintenance providers are concerned that minor editorial or figure referencing differences between the service bulletin and shop process could be interpreted as noncompliance—request safe‑harbor language for clearly inconsequential clerical deviations.

[P23] The “RC Exempt” carve‑out in § 39.13(l)(4)(i) needs a definition of what qualifies as “RC Exempt” and examples; commenters request that the FAA publish a list of RC Exempt steps from the service bulletin and rationale for exempting them.

[P24] § 39.13(l)(4)(i) requires an AMOC for any deviations to RC steps, which will create administrative burden for minor deviations that do not affect safety; operators request an expedited or delegated AMOC process for trivial deviations (e.g., tolerances within ±X percent) and a clear definition of “deviation.”

[P25] § 39.13(l)(4)(ii) allows deviation from non‑RC steps using an operator’s accepted maintenance program but conditions it on the RC steps remaining doable; airlines request clarity on whether pre‑approval or post‑hoc FAA notification is required when relying on their maintenance program to deviate.

[P26] The condition in § 39.13(l)(4)(ii) that RC steps “can still be done as specified” is ambiguous—maintenance providers need explicit guidance on how to demonstrate that a non‑RC deviation will not impede RC task performance and request examples of acceptable analyses.

[P27] The second condition in § 39.13(l)(4)(ii) that the airplane “can be put back in an airworthy condition” should define the acceptable procedures and documentation demonstrating restoration to airworthiness; commenters request that this be tied to the operator’s approved maintenance program and include explicit recordkeeping requirements.

[P22] Safety advocates support strict mandatory RC steps (§ 39.13(l)(4)(i)) but request that the FAA include an auditable compliance metric (e.g., required logbook entries, work package signatures) to ensure RC tasks are performed exactly as required.

[P12] Consumer/travel groups are concerned that the installation prohibition in § 39.13(j) could ground aircraft awaiting compliance; they request that the FAA provide a temporary relief/alternate means (e.g., single‑flight ferry permit) for aircraft held out of service solely due to parts installation restrictions.

[P5] Legal commenters note that the AD repeatedly cross‑references Boeing service bulletin group definitions, which could conflict with regulatory definitions; recommend the FAA include its own definitions of “Group 1/2/3” and “Configuration 1/2” within the AD to avoid ambiguity.

[P8] Maintenance cost and labor burden estimates are missing for the mandatory RC actions in § 39.13(g); industry stakeholders request that the FAA publish an economic analysis (cost per airplane, fleet totals, downtime estimates) in the rulemaking record.

[P10] Aviation insurers request clarification of how terminating inspections for specific clips (per § 39.13(i)) will affect the airplane’s continued airworthiness determinations and ask whether insurers will accept partial inspection terminations without additional documentation.
