§ 39.13(j)’s condition that all Group 3 RC actions identified in the service bulletin be “accomplished within the compliance times specified” before installation creates practical supply chain delays—manufacturers ask for an interim allowance for installation if a documented one‑time inspection is performed at installation.

§ 39.13(k) gives credit for prior work done using the July 29, 2014 Boeing service bulletin, but restricts credit to that exact bulletin edition; commenters who performed equivalent inspections under later Boeing revisions or under approved maintenance program revisions request that the AD allow credit for those actions as well.

Legal commenters request explicit recordkeeping requirements and acceptable evidence to substantiate claimed credit under § 39.13(k), e.g., what documentation satisfies the FAA that the July 29, 2014 service bulletin procedures were followed.

§ 39.13(l)(1) delegates AMOC approval authority to the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch, but does not provide a timeline for FAA action on AMOC requests; operators request a 60‑day decision target to avoid prolonged business disruption.

§ 39.13(l)(1) requires routing AMOC requests through the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19, which may be inefficient for international operators without a U.S. principal inspector; the AD should permit direct submission to the Seattle ACO with prior notice for foreign operators.

§ 39.13(l)(1) directs direct submissions to the person in paragraph (m)(1) but paragraph (m)(1) is not shown in this excerpt; commenters ask the FAA to ensure contact information is complete, accurate, and included in the final rule.

§ 39.13(l)(1) allows emailing AMOC information to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov, but there is no cybersecurity/PII guidance; submitters request encryption and file size guidance and confirmation that emailed requests will constitute formal FAA filings.

§ 39.13(l)(2) obligates notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC, but offers no deadline for that notification; operators ask that the AD specify a timeframe (e.g., within 24 or 72 hours) and acceptable notification formats.

§ 39.13(l)(3) permits Boeing ODA to approve AMOCs for required repairs if approved by the Manager and providing acceptable safety—manufacturers request further detail on the evidence and documentation the Boeing ODA must submit to the Manager to effect such delegation.

The approval criteria in § 39.13(l)(3) requiring that the AMOC “meets the certification basis of the airplane” and “explicitly references this AD” are vague; commenters ask the FAA to provide a checklist of required substantiation, analyses, and test data that demonstrate compliance with the certification basis.

§ 39.13(l)(4)(i) makes all steps labeled “RC” and their substeps mandatory; maintenance providers are concerned that minor editorial or figure referencing differences between the service bulletin and shop process could be interpreted as noncompliance—request safe‑harbor language for clearly inconsequential clerical deviations.

The “RC Exempt” carve‑out in § 39.13(l)(4)(i) needs a definition of what qualifies as “RC Exempt” and examples; commenters request that the FAA publish a list of RC Exempt steps from the service bulletin and rationale for exempting them.

§ 39.13(l)(4)(i) requires an AMOC for any deviations to RC steps, which will create administrative burden for minor deviations that do not affect safety; operators request an expedited or delegated AMOC process for trivial deviations (e.g., tolerances within ±X percent) and a clear definition of “deviation.”

§ 39.13(l)(4)(ii) allows deviation from non‑RC steps using an operator’s accepted maintenance program but conditions it on the RC steps remaining doable; airlines request clarity on whether pre‑approval or post‑hoc FAA notification is required when relying on their maintenance program to deviate.

The condition in § 39.13(l)(4)(ii) that RC steps “can still be done as specified” is ambiguous—maintenance providers need explicit guidance on how to demonstrate that a non‑RC deviation will not impede RC task performance and request examples of acceptable analyses.

The second condition in § 39.13(l)(4)(ii) that the airplane “can be put back in an airworthy condition” should define the acceptable procedures and documentation demonstrating restoration to airworthiness; commenters request that this be tied to the operator’s approved maintenance program and include explicit recordkeeping requirements.

Safety advocates support strict mandatory RC steps (§ 39.13(l)(4)(i)) but request that the FAA include an auditable compliance metric (e.g., required logbook entries, work package signatures) to ensure RC tasks are performed exactly as required.

Consumer/travel groups are concerned that the installation prohibition in § 39.13(j) could ground aircraft awaiting compliance; they request that the FAA provide a temporary relief/alternate means (e.g., single‑flight ferry permit) for aircraft held out of service solely due to parts installation restrictions.

Legal commenters note that the AD repeatedly cross‑references Boeing service bulletin group definitions, which could conflict with regulatory definitions; recommend the FAA include its own definitions of “Group 1/2/3” and “Configuration 1/2” within the AD to avoid ambiguity.

Maintenance cost and labor burden estimates are missing for the mandatory RC actions in § 39.13(g); industry stakeholders request that the FAA publish an economic analysis (cost per airplane, fleet totals, downtime estimates) in the rulemaking record.

Aviation insurers request clarification of how terminating inspections for specific clips (per § 39.13(i)) will affect the airplane’s continued airworthiness determinations and ask whether insurers will accept partial inspection terminations without additional documentation.

[P1] The proposed amendment to incorporate FAA Order 7400.11A dated August 3, 2016 is unclear about whether subsequent revisions of that Order will be automatically incorporated; commenters request explicit language confirming whether future amendments are included or whether each update requires separate rulemaking.

[P1] Incorporation by reference of an outdated Order (2016) may conflict with newer airspace standards or recent amendments; request the FAA explain why the 2016 version is appropriate and provide the most current incorporated document.

[P2] Designating Class D airspace for Enid Woodring Regional Airport within a 4.5-mile radius up to 3,800 feet could impose new communication and equipment burdens on local general aviation pilots who currently operate without ATC services; request an economic impact analysis on GA operators.

[P3] Setting the vertical limit at 3,800 feet for both Enid and Vance raises safety concerns about interactions with nearby instrument procedures and traffic operating above that altitude; request supporting analysis showing 3,800 feet is the appropriate ceiling.

[P4] The 4.5-mile lateral radius around Enid Woodring may overlap with existing special use airspace or operations by nearby airports; request a charted depiction and conflict analysis with nearby airspace, heliports, and SUA.

[P5] The exclusion west of longitude 97°51′01″ W for Enid is ambiguous in geographic effect; request a map and clarification whether the exclusion creates a legal gap requiring pilots to change transponder/communication status when crossing the longitude.

[P6] Making Enid Class D effective only during dates/times established by NOTAM creates operational uncertainty for pilots relying on published charts; request that effective times also be clearly and promptly published in electronic flight information systems and the Chart Supplement with standard lead times.

[P6] Relying on NOTAMs for activation could lead to missed notifications and inadvertent noncompliance; request procedures for ensuring pilots receive timely NOTAMs, and consider fixed scheduled times rather than ad hoc NOTAM activations.

[P7] The 5.1-mile radius Class D for Vance AFB up to 3,800 feet appears to be larger than necessary for the airfield configuration and could unnecessarily constrain civil operators; request the FAA justify the 5.1-mile radius with traffic and procedure data.

[P8] Specifying the Vance AFB vertical limit to 3,800 feet may conflict with military training routes and high-performance military aircraft operations; request coordination documentation with the military and mitigation measures for mixed-use operations.

[P9] A 5.1-mile radius around Vance AFB potentially overlaps with Enid’s 4.5-mile radius; commenters request precise coordinates and a map showing the two Class D boundaries and their seamlines to ensure pilots can determine which tower/service to contact.

[P10] The exclusion of the portion east of long. 97°51′01″ W from Vance AFB airspace appears to create a discontinuous airspace shape that may confuse pilots; request graphic depiction and justification for using this meridian as the dividing line.

[P11] Excluding the 4.5-mile radius around Enid from Vance AFB Class D should be accompanied by explicit procedures for transition between the two Class D zones (e.g., frequency change points); request operational guidance.

[P12] Making Vance AFB Class D effective only by NOTAM may impede military scheduling and civilian planning; request regular published activation schedules (e.g., hours of tower operation) in addition to NOTAMs.

[P13] Publishing effective dates/times continuously in the Chart Supplement is helpful but commenters request a commitment to update digital charting vendors simultaneously and clarify update frequency and effective time lag.

[P14] Amending Class E surface area for Enid within a 4.5-mile radius and excluding west of 97°51′01″ W may displace uncontrolled VFR traffic into narrow corridors; request an assessment of VFR safety and recommended traffic advisories or pattern changes.

[P15] The 4.5-mile lateral limit for Class E surface at Enid will change the airspace where instrument approaches can be protected; request copies of the instrument approach procedures motivating this change and the benefit to IFR operations.

[P16] The longitudinal exclusion at 97°51′01″ W for Class E surface at Enid is an odd boundary to base exclusions on; request explanation for using a longitude rather than a radial or physical landmark, and whether GPS users may experience rounding/precision issues.

[P17] Using NOTAMs to govern effectiveness of Class E surface airspace will require pilots to check NOTAMs before every flight; request the FAA quantify how often activations are expected and consider scheduled publication in the Chart Supplement with dates to reduce pilot workload.

[P18] Creating Class E surface for Vance within a 5.1-mile radius but excluding east of 97°51′01″ W and excluding within 4.5-mile Enid radius may create a fragmented airspace that complicates IFR transitions; request an operations flowchart showing IFR routings and where controlled airspace begins/ends.

[P19] The 5.1-mile lateral limit around Vance for Class E should be harmonized with adjacent approach/departure procedures to avoid step-downs; request confirmation that instrument procedure containment analyses were performed.

[P20] Excluding the portion east of 97°51′01″ W from Vance Class E could push uncontrolled low-level traffic into populated areas east of Vance; request a noise and community impact assessment and public outreach documentation for affected towns.

[P21] Excluding the Enid 4.5-mile radius from Vance E2 airspace could leave a narrow uncontrolled gap between controlled airspace boundaries; request coordinate-based descriptions of any gaps and mitigation (e.g., extending boundaries slightly to eliminate holes).

[P22] Making Vance Class E surface effective only during NOTAM times and publishing in the Chart Supplement may create conflicts if NOTAM activations change frequently; request minimum lead times for NOTAM publication and automated alerts for subscribed pilots/operators.

[P23] The proposed E4 Enid extension along the 347° radial of Woodring VOR/DME with 2.4-mile each side from 4.5 to 7 miles may not accommodate modern RNAV procedures which do not use the VOR; request inclusion of RNAV waypoints or redesign using GPS fixes.

[P24] Limiting the E4 Enid extension to 7 miles north may be insufficient for protecting inbound instrument traffic on the 347° radial during high-altitude descent profiles; provide traffic and procedure analysis demonstrating the 7-mile limit is adequate.

[P25] The 2.4-mile lateral width each side of the 177° radial for the southern extension may be too narrow given navigation tolerances and crosswind dispersions; request that FAA consider increasing lateral protection or otherwise justify 2.4 miles.

[P26] Establishing a Vance E4 extension 1.3 miles each side of the 188° radial from 5.1 to 6.1 miles creates a very short 1-mile extension which may be unnecessary and complicates charting; request explanation for the 1-mile extension length and whether it could be combined with other classes for simplicity.

[P27] The narrow 1.3-mile lateral width of the Vance E4 extension may not provide adequate buffer for instrument approach tracks and navigation errors, especially for nonprecision approaches; request a safety analysis and potential widening.

[P28] Beginning the Vance extension at the 5.1-mile radius and ending at 6.1 miles south creates abrupt airspace edges near the airport; request smoothing of boundaries or use of continuous radials to reduce pilot confusion.

[P29] The E5 description expanding upward from 700 feet to large dimensions (8.7 miles east/west and 15.2 miles north/south of Vance) appears unusually large and could impose new IFR traffic handling obligations on controllers; request justification and an explanation of how this area interacts with adjacent ARTCC airspace.

[P30] The specified E5 rectangular-like dimensions (8.7 miles east/west and 15.2 miles north/south) are nonstandard relative to typical circular/radial descriptions; request coordinates and a map to understand the shape and how it aligns with instrument routes.

[P31] Beginning Class E at 700 feet above the surface within a 7-mile radius of Enid may extend controlled airspace into areas frequently used by ultralight, parachute, and agricultural operators; request outreach to these stakeholder groups and an assessment of practical impacts.

[P3] (legal) The rule lacks clear grandfathering language for existing operations and pilot certifications that assumed previous uncontrolled airspace; request clarification whether current operating authorizations remain valid and how compliance will be enforced during transition.

[P2] (economic) The FAA has not provided a quantified cost estimate of additional radio-equipped aircraft, training, and frequency congestion costs for small operators required to enter Class D; request a Small Entities Regulatory Flexibility Analysis.

[P14] (community) Local emergency medical helicopter operations that use visual corridors west of the airport may now fall inside the Class E surface; request assurances that medevac and law enforcement flights will retain access and a process for expedited coordination.

[P9] (charting) Charting vendors and avionics manufacturers need precise shapefiles; request that the FAA publish the airspace as georeferenced data (WGS84 polygons) upon final rule to allow timely updates to EFBs and GPS units.

[P5] (precision) The longitude coordinate 97°51′01″ W may be subject to rounding conventions across FAA publications; request specification of the coordinate datum and rounding rules to avoid small but operationally significant discrepancies.

[P13] (procedural) Continuous publication in the Chart Supplement must include effective-from and effective-to times for each activation; request standard formatting and retention of historical activation data for pilot planning.

[P21] (safety) The multiple exclusions between Enid and Vance create potential for mid-air conflicts at the seams if pilots are uncertain which facility controls descent/approach; request mandatory frequency change points and published recommended transition altitudes.

[P18] (military) Vance AFB likely has recurring temporary flight restrictions and training periods; request the rule explicitly coordinate with DoD procedures and state how conflicts between military operations and Chart Supplement activations will be resolved.

[P1] (administrative) The proposed rule text appears truncated ("effective S"); request a complete and legible rule text be provided for meaningful public review before final adoption.

[P1] The comment deadline in P1 (August 6, 2021) is internally inconsistent with P26 (§ 39.13(a) January 3, 2022) and must be clarified — stakeholders will be confused which deadline actually governs and may miss the correct comment period.

[P26] The January 3, 2022 comment due date in P26 conflicts with the August 6, 2021 date in P1; the FAA should reconcile and publish a single, clear comment deadline.

[P1] Industry requests an extension of the public comment period beyond the earlier of the two dates (Aug 6, 2021 / Jan 3, 2022) to allow technical analyses and coordination with manufacturers, proposing at least a 60-day extension from publication.

[P2] Operators object to the broad phrasing "within the specified compliance times" in P2 without explicit illustration of the specific compliance intervals for each affected airplane model; the rule should include or summarize the compliance timeframes or explicitly point to where they can be found.

[P3] Requiring strict compliance with all actions and compliance times of EASA AD 2021–0045 (P3) duplicates foreign directives and may impose unnecessary burden where U.S.-certified configuration or maintenance practices differ; the FAA should perform a U.S.-specific assessment rather than adopting EASA AD verbatim.

[P29] The cross-reference in § 39.13(g) to EASA AD 2021–0172 in P29 (and related cross-adoption approach) could create legal ambiguity if the EASA AD is revised; the FAA should incorporate the required actions and compliance times verbatim into the FAA AD to avoid future ambiguity.

[P4] Substituting the FAA AD effective date for any EASA effective-date references (P4) is reasonable, but the AD must state the actual FAA effective date in the regulatory text to avoid circularity.

[P30] The identical provision in § 39.13(h)(1) (P30) needs to specify whether "effective date of this FAA AD" means the date of publication in the Federal Register or the date the AD is made effective — please clarify.

[P5] Excluding the "remarks" section of the EASA AD (P5) may omit informative guidance that operators rely upon; the FAA should explicitly review that remarks material and either incorporate useful guidance or explain why it is excluded.

[P31] The § 39.13(h)(2) exclusion of the EASA AD remarks (P31) could eliminate safety-relevant context (e.g., rationale or background) — the FAA should state whether any content in the remarks that affects compliance or interpretation has been retained elsewhere.

[P6] The definition of "any discrepancy" in P6 (and mirrored in P32) expands the term to include a specific list of damage types; commenters ask for clarification whether this list is exhaustive or illustrative, and whether other forms of damage are included.

[P32] § 39.13(h)(3) (P32) should specify inspection thresholds (severity, dimensions, allowable limits) for the listed discrepancies (broken fittings, missing bolts, migrated bush, burred material, cracks) to ensure consistent findings between inspectors.

[P6] Aircraft lessors and operators request clarification whether discovery of any of the listed discrepancies triggers immediate grounding or whether corrective action may be deferred to the next maintenance opportunity; the AD should state the required operational status after discrepant findings.

[P7] The reporting timelines in P7/P8/P9 require submission within 90 days depending on inspection date; commenters request that the reporting mechanism (form, electronic portal) and required data fields be specified to reduce administrative burden.

[P8] For inspections performed on/after the FAA effective date (P8), the 90-day reporting window may be too short for small maintenance organizations; propose extending to 120 days or providing exemptions for resource-constrained operators.

[P9] For inspections done prior to the FAA effective date (P9), the requirement to report within 90 days after the AD effective date imposes retroactive obligations — legal counsel for operators may challenge retroactivity; FAA should provide legal justification or exempt historic inspections.

[P10] The AMOC authority granted to the Large Aircraft Section Manager in P10 is appropriate, but stakeholders request transparent criteria and target turnaround times (e.g., 60 days) for AMOC decisions to avoid prolonged operational impacts.

[P11] The routing requirement for AMOC requests in P11 to principal inspectors or the Flight Standards Office may delay requests for international operators that don't have a designated U.S. principal inspector; FAA should provide an explicit routing path for foreign operators.

[P12] Direct submission instructions in P12 referencing paragraph (j)(2) must include the named point of contact and mailing address in the AD text to avoid confusion and ensure proper routing.

[P13] Allowing email submission of AMOC information to the specified address in P13 (9-AVS-AIR-730-AMOC@faa.gov) raises cybersecurity and confidentiality concerns for proprietary manufacturer data; the FAA should provide secure submission alternatives and data protection assurances.

[P14] The requirement in P14 to notify the principal inspector prior to using an approved AMOC is unclear whether notification must be written and how long before use; commenters request explicit timing and acceptable notification methods.

[P15] Approving prior AMOCs from AD 2013–25–11 for corresponding provisions (P15/P39) is helpful but commenters request a list or mapping of which previous AMOCs are considered applicable to avoid uncertainty about equivalency.

[P16] The requirement in P16 that manufacturer instructions be approved by the FAA Manager, EASA, or Airbus's EASA DOA introduces potential delays when FAA approval is needed; operators ask whether OEM-approved service bulletins can be accepted immediately under an interim allowance.

[P17] The DOA signature requirement in P17 and P41 (must include DOA-authorized signature) is reasonable, but operators request confirmation that electronic signatures are acceptable and what constitutes acceptable DOA evidence.

[P18] The RC (Required for Compliance) provisions in P18/P42 make certain service procedures mandatory; commenters ask that the AD list which procedures in the referenced service documents are RC to avoid misinterpretation.

[P19] The non-RC provisions in P19/P43 allow deviation from recommended tasks; maintenance programs need clarification on documentation requirements when deviating from non-RC items under an operator’s program.

[P20] The permission in P20/P44 to deviate from non-RC items without AMOC is useful, but the AD should require a post-deviation audit or recordkeeping requirement to ensure continued airworthiness and traceability.

[P21] The requirement in P21/P45 that ANY substitution to RC procedures requires AMOC approval creates a heavy administrative burden; commenters ask whether minor editorial or tooling substitutions (e.g., equivalent torque wrench calibration) can be permitted under an operator’s quality system without full AMOC.

[P22] The mandatory nature of the information collection in P22 raises PRA concerns — commenters request that the FAA provide the OMB control number, estimate of average burden per response, and an explanation of confidentiality protections.

[P23] The instruction in P23 to send comments on the PRA burden estimate to a named FAA officer is fine but commenters request an electronic submission option and contact email for PRA comments.

[P24] Removing AD 2013–25–11 from § 39.13 (P24) may eliminate previously accepted compliance paths; commenters ask the FAA to identify any changes in compliance responsibilities or continuing AMOCs resulting from this removal.

[P25] Adding the new AD for Airbus SAS airplanes in § 39.13 (P25) must explicitly list the Model/Serial numbers or reference the exact EASA applicability paragraph(s) for clarity; current reference to "identified in paragraphs (c)(1) through (4)" requires explicit replication.

[P27] The applicability statement in § 39.13(c) (P27) referencing paragraphs (c)(1)-(4) should be reproduced in full within the FAA AD; commenters emphasize that simply referencing EASA paragraphs may omit U.S.-specific registration/serial issues.

[P28] The duplication of compliance language in § 39.13(f) (P28) is redundant with P2; commenters recommend streamlined language and avoidance of conflicting phrasing.

raw_output:
[P1] The January 23, 2023 comment deadline is unreasonable and unduly short given the complexity of the Boeing 777 fleet and requests an extension of at least 60 days to allow operators, MROs, labor unions, and manufacturers to submit substantive technical comments and data.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether the January 23, 2023 deadline is the USPS postmark date, the FAA receipt date, or the date of electronic submission, to avoid rejection of timely mailed comments.

[P1] The FAA must provide alternative methods to submit comments (e.g., an online portal and acknowledgement receipts) to ensure stakeholders receive confirmation that their comments were received by the January 23, 2023 cutoff.

[P2] The applicability referencing the Boeing bulletin is vague; the AD should explicitly list all affected Boeing Model 777 serial numbers and line numbers rather than only pointing to the referenced bulletin to prevent confusion about which airframes are covered.

[P2] The provision fails to specify whether aftermarket-modified or previously repaired 777s (e.g., re-winged or with supplemental type certificates) are included or excluded; request explicit inclusion/exclusion language.

[P2] The AD should clarify applicability to leased aircraft and aircraft with multiple certificates (e.g., U.S. versus foreign registration history) to avoid enforcement ambiguity for international operators.

[P3] The phrase "within the compliance times specified" lacks clarity on whether calendar days, flight cycles, flight hours, or landings are the governing metric; request explicit statement of the metrics used or direct cross-reference to the exact table rows.

[P3] The AD should include a provision allowing temporary relief for operators who cannot meet specified compliance times due to parts shortages or grounded fleets, with defined criteria for temporary extensions.

[P4] Incorporation by reference of the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin as the sole source of procedures creates a dependency on a manufacturer document that may not be readily available to all commenters; require FAA to publish or host the full bulletin text in the docket.

[P4] The AD should include explicit steps for operators when the Boeing bulletin's Accomplishment Instructions conflict with other FAA-approved maintenance data to prevent contradictory procedures.

[P4] Request that the FAA include a cost-estimate appendix for each required action in the Boeing bulletin so operators can assess economic impact during compliance planning.

[P5] Replacing "original issue date" with the AD effective date may shorten intended compliance windows for operators who already began work based on the bulletin’s original issue date; request that the AD grandfather in actions taken after the bulletin's issue date but before the AD effective date.

[P5] The rule should define "effective date of this AD" clearly (e.g., date of publication in the Federal Register versus the date of incorporation by reference) to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P6] Requiring operators to obtain FAA-approved repair methods when the bulletin instructs them to "contact Boeing" imposes burdens where Boeing's ODA or local repair stations already provide approved repairs; request that the AD accept Boeing ODA-approved repairs without additional FAA re-approval when previously FAA-accepted.

[P6] The AD’s requirement for repair methods to follow paragraph (i) approval procedures could delay repairs in service-critical situations; request a fast-track interim approval process for urgent repairs.

[P7] Centralizing AMOC approval authority exclusively with the Seattle ACO Branch Manager may create processing bottlenecks for non-West Coast operators; request delegation authority or regional ACO acceptance to expedite AMOC reviews.

[P7] The AD should allow designated engineering representatives (DERs) and Boeing's ODA to propose AMOCs directly to the FAA with a standardized checklist to expedite technical review.

[P8] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or responsible Flight Standards Office may be unclear for foreign operators without a U.S. principal inspector; request guidance for how foreign registrants should submit AMOC requests.

[P8] The rule lacks a specified timeframe within which the principal inspector or Flight Standards Office must forward AMOC requests to the FAA manager; request a defined processing timeline (e.g., 30 days) to prevent undue delays.

[P9] The identity of the person referenced in paragraph (j) is not provided in this excerpt; commenters will request that the AD include the specific name, title, and contact details for the manager to whom direct submissions should be addressed.

[P9] The AD should permit electronic submissions directly to the certification office manager with an automated receipt to satisfy documentation requirements rather than requiring paper or ad hoc methods.

[P10] Providing a single FAA email address for AMOC information may raise confidentiality and tracking concerns; request clarification on email security, file size limits, expected response times, and confirmation of receipt procedures.

[P10] The AD should permit submission of AMOC requests via the FAA's Web portal or secure file transfer, not only email, to accommodate large technical attachments and proprietary data.

[P11] The requirement to notify the principal inspector prior to using an approved AMOC is burdensome where multiple principal inspectors may be involved (e.g., multinational operators); request that notification be allowed to the responsible regional Flight Standards Office instead.

[P11] The AD lacks a required response time for principal inspectors to acknowledge notification of AMOC use; request that the FAA set a 10-business-day acknowledgment window to ensure regulatory oversight without operational delay.

[P12] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to satisfy repair requirements risks undermining independent FAA oversight unless the ODA approval must be explicitly accepted by the FAA; request requirement that ODA approvals be concurrently submitted to the FAA for review and filed in the AD docket.

[P12] The AD should require Boeing ODA AMOC approvals to include explicit documentation demonstrating equivalence to the AD's safety objectives and reference the specific AD paragraphs they satisfy.

[P13] Requiring that AMOC deviations meet the airplane's certification basis may be ambiguous for older 777 airframes with amended certification bases; request that the AD specify how to determine the applicable certification basis and handle cases with multiple or revised bases.

[P13] The rule should require that AMOC approvals explicitly cite the specific portions of the airplane's certification basis that are impacted, and include written findings that safety is maintained equal to or better than the original certification basis.

[P14] Mandating use of the listed service information "unless the AD specifies otherwise" could be read to preclude operator-developed equivalent procedures approved via AMOC; request explicit allowance for FAA-approved equivalent procedures to be used in lieu of the service information.

[P14] The AD must ensure that necessary service information is available free or at reasonable cost; commenters request the FAA to require Boeing to provide required service information to registrants and MROs at no charge for AD compliance.

[P15] The FAA viewing location in Des Moines, WA, is geographically inconvenient for many commenters (international operators, East Coast operators); request that the FAA also post the service information online or provide digitized copies accessible through the FAA docket.

[P15] Provide specific contact hours and an expected turnaround time for in-person inspections of the service information at the FAA location to prevent operational delays in arranging review appointments.

[P16] Requiring viewing at NARA without providing direct links or instructions to the exact incorporated documents is impractical; commenters request the FAA to include direct URLs and instructions for requesting copies from NARA.

[P16] The AD should explicitly state whether viewing the incorporated-by-reference service information at NARA satisfies operators' obligations to have immediate access to the procedures during maintenance, or whether they must obtain a personal copy for each maintenance event.

[P1] The blanket prohibition in § 17.41(k)(1) is overbroad because it fails to define the geographic scope of "persons subject to U.S. jurisdiction" with respect to cross-border ranching operations, creating uncertainty for foreign-owned agricultural firms operating in U.S. border counties.

[P1] Conservation NGOs will argue the general prohibition is appropriate but needs explicit language clarifying it applies to all activities whether intentional or negligent to ensure enforcement against indirect habitat destruction.

[P2] Export-dependent trade associations will claim that § 17.41(k)(1)(i) could inadvertently prohibit incidental movement of dead specimens (e.g., roadkill collected for scientific study) across state lines without a clarified research exemption.

[P3] Livestock and energy industry stakeholders will assert that the take prohibition in § 17.41(k)(1)(ii) is vague regarding incidental take arising from infrastructure maintenance and thus will chill routine maintenance unless the rule explicitly defines thresholds for "incidental" versus prohibited take.

[P3] Legal experts will claim that referencing § 17.21(c)(1) without restating the applicable definitions in this section creates interpretive problems and may conflict with other statutory definitions of "take" in case law.

[P4] Private landowners will object that prohibition on possession of unlawfully taken specimens (§ 17.41(k)(1)(iii)) could criminalize possession of specimens unknowingly obtained from prior owners; they will request an affirmative defense for good-faith purchasers.

[P5] Agricultural commodity groups will claim that the interstate commerce prohibition (§ 17.41(k)(1)(iv)) could be interpreted to bar sale or transport of agricultural products from properties where an incidental lesser prairie-chicken mortality occurred, and request a safe-harbor for commodity movement when no intent to harm the species exists.

[P6] Hunting and sporting organizations will argue the sale prohibition (§ 17.41(k)(1)(v)) needs clarification to ensure it does not prohibit lawful sale of already-registered captive-bred birds under state programs or exchanges for conservation breeding.

[P7] Permitting offices will request that § 17.41(k)(2) explicitly describe the process, timelines, and standards by which exceptions will be evaluated to avoid administrative delay and inconsistent application across regions.

[P8] Developers and renewable-energy companies will support § 17.41(k)(2)(i) allowing § 17.32 permits but will demand clarification on permit processing timeframes and cumulative-impact analysis requirements to plan projects reliably.

[P9] Farmers and ranchers will seek clarification of which specific types of take are allowed under § 17.41(k)(2)(ii) (§ 17.21(c)(2)-(c)(4)) and request inclusion of examples (e.g., vehicular strikes during harvest) so they can determine compliance without seeking agency guidance for every action.

[P10] State wildlife agencies will request that § 17.41(k)(2)(iii) (take as set forth at § 17.31(b)) be cross-referenced to state-authorized activities to ensure federal-state regulatory alignment and avoid duplicative permitting.

[P11] Industry groups will argue that the incidental take allowance in § 17.41(k)(2)(iv) must include clear, quantitative thresholds (e.g., number of mortalities per year per operation) and mandatory mitigation measures; otherwise it fails to provide regulatory certainty.

[P12] Agricultural associations will claim that § 17.41(k)(2)(iv)(A) permitting routine agricultural practices on "existing cultivated lands" is ambiguous about what constitutes "existing" (date-certain baseline) and may restrict new conversions or re-seeding of fallow fields unpredictably.

[P13] Crop producers will request that § 17.41(k)(2)(iv)(A)(1) explicitly exempt common harvest operations (combining, baling) and delayed-cut mowing practices during nesting season, or provide recommended seasonal timing to avoid incidental take.

[P14] Farmers will assert that § 17.41(k)(2)(iv)(A)(2) permitting routine support activities for agriculture should specifically allow replacement or upgrading of irrigation, fence, and drainage infrastructure even if those activities temporarily disturb nesting habitat, subject to best management practices.

[P15] Pesticide manufacturers and applicators will state that § 17.41(k)(2)(iv)(A)(3) permitting chemical use "according to label directions" is insufficiently protective unless the agency coordinates with EPA to identify specific chemicals and application practices that pose unacceptable risk to the lesser prairie-chicken.

[P16] Fire management agencies will support § 17.41(k)(2)(iv)(B) but request that the allowed activities be coordinated with state burn plans and permit processes to avoid conflicting requirements and to ensure firefighter safety.

[P17] Grazing permittees will ask that § 17.41(k)(2)(iv)(B)(1) clarify standards for constructing fuel breaks (width, restoration requirements) so that fuel break construction does not become a de facto long-term habitat loss.

[P18] Prescribed burn practitioners will request detail in § 17.41(k)(2)(iv)(B)(2) on what planning activities are covered (NEPA-level planning vs. operational burn plans) and whether prior environmental review satisfies the rule's intent.

[P19] Conservation scientists will urge that § 17.41(k)(2)(iv)(B)(3) include seasonal restrictions and protocols to minimize direct mortality during implementation of prescribed fire and require monitoring to measure impacts.

[P20] Ecologists will assert that § 17.41(k)(2)(iv)(B)(4) should require standardized monitoring metrics, reporting timelines, and data sharing to ensure follow-up actions effectively reduce adverse impacts, rather than allowing ad hoc monitoring.

raw_output:
[P1] The May 10, 2021 comments due date is unrealistically short for operators and MROs to evaluate the full MPD changes and prepare substantive technical comments; FAA should extend the comment period by at least 60–90 days.

[P1] Small operators and independent repair stations will not have adequate time to gather safety and cost data before May 10, 2021; FAA should provide a targeted extension or a separate longer comment period for non-manufacturer stakeholders.

[P2] The Applicability clause that limits the AD to line numbers 1 through 1609 appears to exclude later-produced 777s that may have identical wiring configurations; FAA should clarify whether later L/Ns are covered or provide rationale for the L/N cutoff.

[P2] The applicability language is ambiguous because it does not specify production blocks, options, or post-delivery modifications that could change wiring; request FAA clarify applicability for retrofitted/modified airplanes.

[P3] The Compliance provision lacks specifics on what constitutes compliance evidence (records, logbook entries, revised MPD pages); request FAA specify required documentation and acceptable record formats.

[P3] The phrase “unless already done” is vague; operators need clear criteria to determine when previously completed actions satisfy the AD (e.g., exact revision number/date of Boeing MPD) and how to document that to inspectors.

[P4] Revising the maintenance/inspection program within 60 days is impracticable for large fleets and for carriers operating internationally due to coordination with foreign authorities; FAA should extend the 60‑day timeframe to 120 days or allow staged compliance.

[P4] FAA should require submission of the revised program to the principal inspector for acceptance rather than simply instructing operators to revise internally; this will ensure consistent interpretation and enforcement.

[P5] The initial compliance times for AWL 28–AWL–01 (16,000 flight cycles or 3,000 days whichever occurs first) are insufficiently risk-based — FAA should provide technical justification (service history, failure rates) for these thresholds or consider a phase-in tied to utilization.

[P5] Using "whichever occurs first" for flight cycles vs. days can impose burdens on low-utilization aircraft (age-driven triggers); FAA should allow hours-based timing as an alternative for operators with known low cycle/high-day profiles.

[P6] The compliance time for AWL 28–AWL–03 uses the same 16,000 fc/3,000 day trigger as AWL–01 but lacks substantiation specific to FQIS wiring; FAA should provide data or allow AMOCs to tailor timing based on wiring material and environmental exposure.

[P7] For AWL 28–AWL–18, tying the initial compliance to the latest of multiple events (375 days after issuance, after specified service bulletins, or most recent inspection) creates administrative complexity; FAA should simplify and specify how operators must reconcile overlapping triggers.

[P7] The 375-day deadline for AWL–18 may create simultaneous maintenance demands across multiple tasks; FAA should allow scheduling flexibility to align with heavy maintenance visits without compromising safety.

[P8] AWL 28–AWL–21’s inclusion of a 365-day “or within 365 days after the effective date” clause imposes an aggressive backstop that could conflict with existing maintenance intervals; FAA should allow compliance at the next scheduled check within a reasonable window (e.g., 180 days).

[P9] AWL 28–AWL–26’s 30-day backstop in some cases is too short and could require unscheduled AOG-level interventions; FAA should permit operators to perform the action at the next maintenance opportunity within 90 days.

[P10] AWL 28–AWL–32 sets different compliance thresholds by line number but does not provide a matrix or table in the AD text — operators need a clear, unambiguous table mapping L/N ranges to the specific flight-day thresholds.

[P10] The L/N-based thresholds for AWL–32 risk being misapplied for reconfigured or re-serialed airframes; FAA should clarify treatment of frames that have undergone major repairs or reworks affecting L/N records.

[P11] AWL 28–AWL–101’s 7,500 flight-hour engine fuel suction feed operational test interval is potentially disruptive for high-utilization freighters; FAA should allow operators to perform the test at scheduled C-check intervals if those fall sooner.

[P12] AWL 47–AWL–04’s 108,000 flight-hour trigger lacks justification and will not capture many airplanes within a practical timeframe; FAA should consider a flight-cycle or calendar-based alternate to ensure earlier mitigation when warranted.

[P13] AWL 47–AWL–05’s 10,682 flight-hour threshold is oddly specific and unexplained; FAA should provide the basis for that number and consider rounding to a more administrable figure (e.g., 10,000 or 11,000 hours).

[P14] AWL 47–AWL–06 uses the same 10,682 flight-hour timing and may require ducting work that is time-consuming; FAA should permit coordination with scheduled maintenance events and allow AMOCs that demonstrate equivalent risk mitigation.

[P15] Paragraph (h) permits alternative wire types and sleeving but does not require FAA approval prior to using them; operators need clarity whether using the alternatives requires submission of an AMOC or is automatically acceptable under the AD.

[P16] The list of acceptable alternative wire types in (h)(1) omits part-number cross-references and supplier specifications; FAA should require the AD to include or reference the exact specs (e.g., MIL specs and acceptable manufacturers) to prevent OEM/operator disputes.

[P17] The acceptable sleeving materials in (h)(2) include materials whose long-term aging characteristics may differ from TFE–2X; FAA should require data demonstrating equivalent performance (flammability, abrasion, thermal aging) before an operator installs alternatives fleetwide.

[P18] The prohibition on alternative actions/intervals/CDCCLs in (i) is overly prescriptive and limits operators’ ability to use established safety management system (SMS) data to propose better intervals; FAA should broaden permitted alternatives via AMOC and streamline AMOC processing.

[P18] Prohibiting alternatives after the program revision could create conflicts with existing fleet-wide reliability programs; FAA must clarify whether previously-approved alternative CDCCLs remain valid or are superseded.

[P19] The exception allowing AMOCs per paragraph (k) provides a process but does not guarantee timely FAA response; FAA should commit to a review timeline for AMOC requests (e.g., 60–90 days) and provide interim acceptance procedures.

[P20] The terminating actions in (j) that remove obligations from prior ADs (2008–11–13 and 2014–09–09) should be explicitly tied to demonstrated equivalence of protection; request FAA to require operators to retain records showing that the new MPD revision indeed provides equal or better coverage.

[P21] For paragraph (j)(1), terminating all requirements of AD 2008–11–13 for certain models is appropriate only if the new AWLs fully address all failure modes; FAA should publish a mapping showing how each terminated requirement is replaced by specific AWL tasks.

[P22] For paragraph (j)(2), terminating AD 2014–09–09 requirements without owner/operator consultation may inadvertently remove mitigations still needed on certain serial-numbered airplanes; FAA should require a verification step before terminating prior AD obligations.

[P23] The delegation in (k)(1) to the Seattle ACO Branch Manager to approve AMOCs concentrates authority regionally and may slow decisions for non-US operators; FAA should allow other ACOs or delegated organizations to approve AMOCs or provide a central online AMOC portal.

[P24] The AMOC submission routing in (k)(1) referencing 14 CFR 39.19 is standard, but the AD should include a checklist of required technical data to reduce back-and-forth and speed approvals.

[P25] The requirement in (k)(1) to address direct submissions to the certification office manager as identified in (l)(1) is fine, but paragraph (l)(1) is not included in the AD text provided here; ensure cross-references are accurate to avoid misdirected requests.

[P26] Permitting AMOC requests via the 9-ANM email address is useful, but FAA must ensure secure, tracked submission and timely acknowledgement; request FAA publish an SLA (acknowledgement and review target times).

[P27] The obligation in (k)(2) that operators notify their principal inspector before using an approved AMOC is reasonable, but FAA should allow electronic notification and specify required content (AMOC approval reference, scope, effective dates).

[P28] Allowing AMOCs approved by the Boeing ODA (k)(3) is positive, but the AD must require Boeing to provide a public registry or copy of such ODA approvals to the FAA and affected operators to ensure transparency and consistency.

[P29] The requirement that repair/modification approvals meet the airplane's certification basis and explicitly reference this AD (k)(3) could cause confusion when an airplane's certification basis has been amended multiple times; FAA should provide guidance on determining the correct certification basis reference.

[P30] Duplicative comment deadlines: The separate DATES line for the Pratt & Whitney NPRM (also May 10, 2021) suggests multiple concurrent deadlines; FAA should coordinate comment periods to avoid stakeholder confusion and reduce administrative burden.

[P1] Administrative commenters will request that FAA correct the year references if the AD is issued in 2021 but effective dates or timelines reference different baseline dates; ensure consistency to avoid unintended early triggers.

[P4] Legal commenters will ask FAA to confirm whether incorporation of AWLs/CMRs into the maintenance program constitutes a rulemaking amendment requiring coordination under 49 U.S.C. 44701; request FAA provide legal basis and preemption analysis.

[P15] Industry groups will ask FAA to permit use of new industry-standard wire and sleeving materials developed after the Boeing MPD revision without requiring an AMOC, provided supplier test data are submitted to the principal inspector.

[P10] MROs will request detailed instructions for installations referenced in AWL 28–AWL–32 (torque values, clamp types, bracket part numbers) to avoid inconsistent workmanship and inspection findings across stations.

[P7] Safety advocates will challenge any extension of the 375-day or multi-trigger schedules, urging FAA to prioritize earliest practicable implementation for items addressing potential ignition sources near fuel tanks.

[P18] Legal experts will point out that the blanket prohibition on alternatives may be inconsistent with 14 CFR 39.19’s intent and ask FAA to clarify the interaction and ensure it does not unlawfully limit lawful AMOCs.

[P16] Materials engineering stakeholders will request that FAA require compatibility testing between the alternative wire insulations listed in (h)(1) and existing harness bonding/grounding practices to ensure no galvanic or thermal degradation issues.

[P12] International carriers will request FAA coordinate with EASA and other CAAs to harmonize compliance times (108,000 flight hours) to avoid duplicate regulatory requirements and potential differences in maintenance practice acceptance overseas.

[P11] Cargo operators will request an operational equivalency allowing engine suction feed operational tests (AWL 28–AWL–101) to be conducted using predictive monitoring (oil/wear/fuel system telemetry) in lieu of in-situ tests when validated.

[P20] Labor/technician unions will request FAA require training and certification requirements for technicians performing the new AWL/CMR tasks to ensure competence and reduce risk of improper wiring work.

[P4] Cost-sensitive commenters will demand FAA perform and publish a full regulatory flexibility analysis and cost estimate per Executive Order requirements, showing cost per airplane and total industry burden of the 60‑day revision deadline.

[P3] Airline legal departments will ask FAA to provide model compliance record language that demonstrates satisfaction of the AD for audit and enforcement purposes.

[P26] Privacy/security stakeholders will request that the FAA email address for AMOC submissions be evaluated for data protection and retention policy because AMOC submissions could include sensitive technical data.

[P2] The obligation in § 39.13(f) to "comply within the specified compliance times" is ambiguous—stakeholders request explicit guidance that operators may use scheduled heavy maintenance windows to meet compliance times without incurring operational penalties.

[P3] The scope in § 39.13(g)(1) is unclear whether airplanes that temporarily have part number BA–670–93465–1 installed (e.g., as a loaned part) are required to comply; request explicit language addressing transient installations.

[P4] The compliance timeframe in § 39.13(g)(1)/(g)(1) (800 flight hours or 4 months, whichever occurs first) is too short for many operators with limited maintenance access; request extension to 2,000 flight hours or 12 months or allow compliance at next scheduled maintenance.

[P5] The requirement in § 39.13(g)(1) to perform a "detailed visual inspection of the casing of the primary actuator for signs of chafing or missing paint" lacks an objective acceptance criteria; request that the AD specify measurable criteria or reference inspection illustrations.

[P6] § 39.13(g)(1) mandates replacement of RTL return springs but does not state whether overhauled or FAA-approved aftermarket equivalent springs are acceptable; request allowance for FAA-approved equivalent parts with AMOC provisions.

[P7] The eddy current inspections in § 39.13(g)(1) of the limiter arm lugs require specialized NDT capability not available at many line stations; request that the AD allow performance at certified repair stations within a reasonable geographic radius and specify required certification level.

[P8] Requiring that actions be accomplished "in accordance with Part A of Bombardier Service Bulletin 670BA–27–070, Revision B" (§ 39.13(g)(1)/P8) raises concern that the FAA is mandating a manufacturer's procedure without allowing operator deviations; request the AD explicitly permit alternative procedures via AMOC.

[P9] The explicit exclusion in § 39.13(g)(1) that SB 670BA–27–059 does not satisfy the requirement (P9) will cause confusion because many operators already performed SB 059; request an assessment/statement on which specific differences in SB 059 are unacceptable and whether supplemental actions can provide credit.

[P10] For § 39.13(g)(2) (8,000 fh compliance for part BA–670–93468–1), the AD does not provide interim mitigation measures for high-utilization operators who will exceed 8,000 fh quickly; request mandatory interim inspections at shorter intervals until compliance is carried out.

[P11] The 8,000 flight hours timeframe in § 39.13(g)(2)/(P11) is not tied to calendar time; operators with low utilization need a calendar-based alternate (e.g., X months) to avoid indefinite deferral—request addition of a calendar limit (e.g., 18 months).

[P12] The detailed visual inspection of RTL return springs for chafing (§ 39.13(g)(2)/P12) lacks definition of "detailed" and acceptance thresholds; request inclusion of torque/clearance/wear limits or reference photos.

[P13] § 39.13(g)(2) requires eddy current inspection and potential replacement/modification of limiter arm assemblies (P14) but does not estimate the expected economic burden or downtime; operators request the FAA include an economic cost estimate and allowance for access to loaner parts to minimize out-of-service time.

[P14] The credit paragraph (§ 39.13(h)/P17) permits credit for actions performed before the effective date if done per earlier SBs (P18, P19) but does not define acceptable documentation; request explicit documentation standards (work order, part numbers, signatures) to substantiate credit claims.

[P15] The list of acceptable service information for credit (§ 39.13(h)(1)/(h)(2) — P18, P19) omits other later-approved revisions or field-approved repairs; request FAA to include a catch-all clause allowing credit for later FAA-accepted revisions or TCCA-approved equivalents.

[P16] The AMOC approval authority limited to the Manager, New York ACO Branch (§ 39.13(i)(1)/P20) could delay approvals for operators outside that region; request delegation to regional ACOs or expedited electronic AMOC processing to prevent operational impacts.

[P17] The AMOC submission routing requirement (§ 39.13(i)(1)/P21–P23) is overly prescriptive and may conflict with corporate procedures; request allowance for electronic submissions to the manager with acknowledgments and timelines for FAA response.

[P18] § 39.13(i)(2) requires manufacturer corrective actions to be accomplished using a method approved by the FAA Manager, TCCA, or Bombardier's TCCA DAO (P24). Legal counsel requests clarification whether Bombardier service letter approvals alone are sufficient or FAA approval is always required.

[P19] The DAO signature requirement (§ 39.13(i)(2)/P25) could cause delays where DAOs are not available; request acceptance of equivalent documentation from Bombardier engineering with TCCA approval or temporary FAA concurrence.

[P20] The FDA-related deadlines (P26–P27, P33 etc.) shown in the rule language are inconsistent with the FAA AD deadlines and appear to be misplaced; request correction to remove FDA-specific submission instructions from this AD.

[P21] The requirement that electronic submissions be received by Feb 5, 2018 (P27) contradicts other stated dates; legal commenters request the agency reconcile all dates and republish the proposed rule with corrected DATES and ADDRESSES.

[P22] Prohibitions on late comments (P29, P42, P45) are standard, but stakeholders request that the FAA/FDA/EPA include an explicit policy for accepting late comments in exceptional circumstances (e.g., IT outages), rather than an absolute bar.

[P23] The electronic submission instructions (P30) are generic; small operators request clear step-by-step guidance and contact support for submitting comments and confidential attachments.

[P24] The obligation to avoid including confidential information in publicly posted comments (P31) and the complicated confidential submission process (P32, P35–P39) will deter small businesses from providing sensitive operational data; request simplified confidential submission procedures and a single point-of-contact for confidentiality determinations.

[P25] The requirement to submit two copies for confidential submissions (P36) and labeling conventions (P37–P39) seems archaic in an electronic era; request acceptance of a single PDF with encrypted confidential sections and an unredacted version via secure upload.

[P26] FDA's SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION statement that it will not grant any extensions on the comment period for the proposed delay (P42) is arbitrary and inconsistent with the Administrative Procedure Act's requirement for reasonable public participation; request discretionary extension authority be explicitly preserved.

[P27] The EPA docket instruction to submit comments to a specific email (P44) may be problematic for those wishing to use Regulations.gov; request confirmation that either method is acceptable and that emailed comments will be posted to Regulations.gov.

[P28] The EPA prohibition against submitting CBI electronically (P45) will prevent meaningful technical comments that contain proprietary data; request the EPA allow secure upload of redacted attachments with an unredacted confidential version submitted through a secure portal.

[P29] The multimedia submission requirement (P46) that a written comment accompany audio/video is reasonable, but request explicit formatting and file size limits and preferred codecs to avoid technical rejections.

[P30] For labeling obligations (§§ 201.128 and 801.4, P47–P51), manufacturers request clarification on the threshold that constitutes "intends" to market for different uses—specifically whether distributor marketing materials or sales incentives could be construed as intent.

[P31] The exception in § 201.128 and § 801.4 (P49, P52) that firms are not considered to intend a new use merely because they know providers prescribe off-label is helpful, but industry requests illustrative examples (e.g., promotional materials vs. passive knowledge) to reduce enforcement uncertainty.

[P32] The AD does not specify whether operators may use credit from actions performed per SB 670BA–27–070 dated Dec 17, 2015 (P18) if those actions omitted eddy current inspections that Revision B requires; request FAA to state whether missing elements require only the missing tasks or a full repeat of the SB.

[P33] The AD should include required training/qualifications for personnel performing the "detailed visual inspection" and eddy current inspections (P5, P12, P7, P14) to ensure consistency across providers; request specification of minimum technician certifications or training records.

[P34] The AD lacks an estimated parts lead-time and supply-chain risk analysis for replacement RTL return springs and limiter arms (P6, P7, P14); operators request the FAA coordinate with Bombardier to ensure adequate spares and consider phased implementation to avoid grounding fleets.

[P35] Aviation labor unions request that performance of the required inspections and modifications (P3–P7, P10–P15) be done by certificated maintenance technicians (A&P/AMT) and not outsourced without appropriate oversight.

[P36] Small air carriers request a provision allowing cost-recovery or temporary operational waivers where compliance would impose disproportionate economic hardship, especially for single-aircraft operators within the 800-fh/4-month window (P4).

[P37] Legal commenters request explicit incorporation of inspection and modification reporting requirements into the AD (e.g., submission of findings to FAA within X days), because the AD currently mandates actions but not reporting—this impedes FAA trend analysis.

[P38] The AD should state whether compliance with paragraphs (g)(1) and (g)(2) affects the airplane's dispatch or ETOPS status; operators request explicit language that completing these tasks does not require special ferry permits beyond standard maintenance releases.

[P39] The text mixing FAA, FDA, and EPA submission rules (P26–P46, P20–P23) creates risk of misfiling comments; request the agency separate and correct the administrative sections to the appropriate rulemaking agency before finalizing.

[P40] Airworthiness authorities and legal advisors request the FAA to clarify the interplay between TCCA approvals and FAA AMOC authority (P20, P24–P25) to avoid jurisdictional conflict and to specify timelines for TCCA concurrence.

[P41] The AD lacks definition of "as applicable" when instructing to modify or replace the RTL limiter arm assembly after eddy current inspection (P7, P14); request decision criteria (e.g., crack length, location) that trigger replacement vs. allowable repair/modification.

[P42] Operators request that the FAA provide model-specific applicability information (serial numbers/production blocks) for which the part numbers BA–670–93465–1, E0650–069–02750S, and BA–670–93468–1 were installed from the factory to better scope affected fleet and plan compliance.

[P43] Maintenance providers request copies of Bombardier Service Bulletin 670BA–27–070 Revision B be made publicly available in the docket (or incorporated by reference) so commenters can evaluate the mandated procedures before the comment deadline (relates to P8, P15, P18, P19).

[P44] The AD should permit temporary operational restrictions (e.g., reduced rudder authority limits) as an allowed interim mitigation while awaiting parts/repairs for airplanes that fail inspection, with FAA-approved procedures for ferry flights—request explicit allowance.

[P45] The AD's prohibition that SB 670BA–27–059 does not satisfy the requirement (P9, P16) may lead to duplicate work; request FAA coordinate with Bombardier to provide a bridging instruction that documents minimal additional tasks required for SB 059-compliant airplanes to meet Revision B requirements.

[P46] Commenters note inconsistent use of "flight hours" vs. "flight cycles" across the document (P4, P11) and request confirmation that all compliance times refer exclusively to flight hours and definition of what counts as a flight hour for ferry flights.

[P47] The AD should explicitly state whether records of compliance (inspection/part replacement) must be entered into the aircraft maintenance logbooks and what the acceptable form of the entry is—request explicit record-keeping language.

[P48] Consumer/public safety groups support the AD but request that the FAA adopt the shorter compliance interval (800 fh/4 months) for all affected part numbers rather than the longer 8,000 fh, arguing the safety risk of limiter arm lug cracks merits uniform urgency.

[P49] Conversely, business aviation operators argue that the disparity between 800 fh and 8,000 fh (P4 vs. P11) is unsupported by risk analysis in the NPRM and request the FAA publish the risk assessment and failure-rate data underpinning the different intervals.

[P50] Commenters request clarification whether compliance with the AD is required for aircraft in storage or preserved status and whether flight-hour accrual during storage counts toward compliance deadlines (relates to P4, P11).

[P51] The AD should clarify liability and warranty treatment for replacement parts installed to comply with the AD (P6, P7, P14)—operators want Bombardier or suppliers to warrant parts installed to satisfy the AD for a defined period.

[P52] Some legal commenters assert that provisions referencing FDA and EPA docket numbers and confidential submission rules (P26–P46) may be legally inapplicable to an FAA AD and could render portions of the document procedurally defective; request the agency correct or remove unrelated regulatory procedural text.

[P1] The rule's civil penalty formula lacks clarity on whether rounding of the manufacturer's average fuel economy to the nearest 0.1 mpg occurs before or after the difference is computed, creating uncertainty in penalty calculations.

[P1] Industry commenters will argue that applying the penalty "per 0.1 mpg" without specifying rounding rules could produce materially different penalties for small measurement variances and should specify rounding/truncation conventions.

[P1] Legal experts will claim that tying manufacturer liability directly to the government's fuel economy standard without explicit procedural safeguards may violate due process if notice and opportunity to contest the underlying average fuel economy determination are not detailed in the regulation.

[P2] Consumer and environmental advocates will request clarification about the interplay with 49 U.S.C. 32912(c), arguing the regulation must explicitly state the circumstances under which 32912(c) displaces the penalty and provide cross-references to the statutory text.

[P2] Manufacturers will assert that the provision is ambiguous because it says "Except as provided in 49 U.S.C. 32912(c)" but does not explain the administrative process to determine applicability, and they request an explicit adjudicatory or notice procedure.

[P3] Automotive trade associations will challenge the inflation adjustment mechanism for the $14 penalty, requesting the rule specify the index, base year, frequency, and formula for adjustments rather than leaving it implicit.

[P3] Small manufacturers will argue that the increase to $14 (plus inflation) beginning with model year 2019 represents a sudden and significant rise from $5.50 and request a phase-in, grandfathering, or hardship relief mechanism for small volume manufacturers.

[P3] State regulators and fiscal analysts will ask the agency to provide an economic impact analysis showing revenue projections under the $14-per-0.1 mpg penalty (with inflation) and the expected effect on manufacturer behavior.

[P4] Commenters will argue that retaining a $5.50-per-0.1 mpg penalty for pre-2019 model years raises statute-of-limitations and retroactivity concerns if applied to ongoing enforcement actions and seek confirmation that this is not retroactive beyond permitable limits.

[P4] Legal advocates will request clarification whether the $5.50 rate for pre-2019 model years is adjusted for inflation for penalties assessed after 2019, to avoid inconsistent treatment of older-model violations.

[P5] Manufacturers will request specification of the technical methodology and data sources used to compute the "manufacturer's average fuel economy under 49 U.S.C. 32904(a)(1)(A) or (B)" (e.g., how credits, off-cycle credits, footprint adjustments, and vehicle grouping are handled) to ensure reproducibility.

[P5] Compliance consultants will request that the rule define the reporting period, submission deadlines, and access to the government's calculations so manufacturers can reconcile and, if necessary, contest the computed averages prior to penalty assessment.

[P5] Environmental NGOs will argue that using only 32904(a)(1)(A) or (B) ignores other statutory calculation methods or flexibilities that could be used to understate noncompliance, and demand transparency on how all statutory options are applied.

[P6] Industry commenters will contest multiplying the per-0.1 mpg penalty by the number of applicable automobiles without capping the total penalty, arguing this could create disproportionate fines that are punitive rather than remedial, and request a per-manufacturer cap or proportionality limit.

[P6] Small-volume manufacturers will request an exemption or reduced multiplier for manufacturers producing below a certain threshold of applicable automobiles to avoid ruinous penalties for limited overages.

[P6] Legal commentators will question whether the "number of those automobiles" includes vehicles exempted under other statutes (e.g., low-volume, specialty, or exempted vehicle classes) and ask for a definition of "applicable automobiles."

[P7] Manufacturers will argue that the rule does not specify the sequencing and valuation of 49 U.S.C. 32903 credits when reducing penalties (e.g., vintage credits, projected credits, or banked credits), leading to uncertainty about available offsets.

[P7] Accounting and tax advisors will request that the regulation require the agency to accept manufacturers' certified credit ledgers and to provide an appeal mechanism if the agency disputes claimed 32903 credits prior to final penalty calculation.

[P7] Consumer advocates will caution that allowing broad use of 32903 credits to reduce penalties could undermine the deterrent effect of penalties and encourage credit banking instead of real-world fuel economy improvements; they will request limits on how credits can offset monetary penalties.

[P1] Commenters will request that the regulation require public disclosure of penalty calculations and associated data (standards, average mpg, production counts, credits used) to ensure transparency and promote public confidence in enforcement actions.

[P3] Industry associations will ask for clear applicability dates and transition rules specifying how model year determination is made for vehicles produced near the cutoff, to avoid double counting or gaps between model years.
