raw_output:
[P1] The requirement in § 60.5365(e) to calculate potential VOC emissions using “a generally accepted model/method” is unacceptably vague — the rule should specify which models (e.g., EPA AP-42, TCEQ, ISO methods) are acceptable or provide an approval process to avoid inconsistent enforcement across jurisdictions.

[P1] Industry requests clarification whether “maximum average daily throughput for a 30‑day production period” means (a) the single highest 30‑day rolling average in the facility’s history, (b) the highest projected 30‑day average in the prior 12 months, or (c) a permit‑authorized maximum; the rule should state the precise calculation method and look‑back period.

[P1] Small operators will be disproportionately burdened by the requirement to calculate a 30‑day maximum average daily throughput using potentially complex models; the agency should allow simpler, presumptive calculation approaches or provide free modeling tools/templates.

[P2] The recordkeeping obligation in § 60.5420(c)(5)(iv) to show number of consecutive days a skid‑mounted/premanently attached storage vessel is between wellhead and custody transfer is overly burdensome for mobile fleets (trucking/rail) because vehicles transit multiple sites daily; the rule should permit trip logs or GPS electronic records as sufficient documentation.

[P2] The phrase “permanently attached to something that is mobile (such as trucks, railcars, barges or ships)” is ambiguous — commenters ask the agency to clarify whether containers bolted to trailers but dismounted for storage count as skid‑mounted or as fixed, because classification affects compliance obligations.

[P3] The provision requiring inclusion of removal days when a vessel is returned or replaced within 30 days (§ 60.5420(c)(5)(iv)) creates perverse incentives to keep empty vessels offsite for 31 days to avoid counting — the agency should instead count only days physically present to reflect actual emissions potential.

[P3] Legal counsel notes that retroactive inclusion of removal days could conflict with ordinary meaning of “consecutive days present” and suggests the agency provide clear definition and examples (e.g., maintenance removals, emergency relocations) to avoid legal challenges.

[P4] § 60.5365a(e) duplicates § 60.5365(e) but without clarifying differences between unconventional and conventional well calculations; commenters request harmonization and clear cross‑references to avoid duplicate or conflicting compliance obligations.

[P5] Declaring installation of an additional compressor as a “modification” (§ 60.5365a(j)(1)) will subject routine capacity expansions to new source requirements — industry requests an economic de minimis threshold (e.g., <10% horsepower increase) to exempt small incremental capacity additions.

[P6] The rule’s classification of replacing compressors with greater total horsepower as a “modification” (§ 60.5365a(j)(2)) fails to consider situations where horsepower increases are for reliability/efficiency (not increased throughput); commenters request an alternative test based on emissions potential increase rather than horsepower alone.

[P7] Advocacy groups support § 60.5365a(j)’s exception that replacements with equal or smaller total horsepower are not “modifications,” but request the agency add a reporting requirement to document such replacements to prevent gaming.

[P8] § 60.5375a’s cross‑referencing to paragraphs (a)-(g) is unclear about whether recordkeeping, monitoring, and reporting found in those paragraphs apply to legacy wells; stakeholders request explicit phased implementation timelines for existing wells versus new wells.

[P9] Operators of wells that were hydraulically fractured before Nov 30, 2016 (§ 60.5375a) need clarification on which specific paragraphs apply pre‑ and post‑date, and whether wells that had subsequent workovers or refracturing are treated as “pre‑2016” or “post‑2016” for compliance.

[P10] For § 60.5380a, centrifugal compressor owners ask whether the standards in paragraphs (a)-(d) apply per unit, per station, or per facility when multiple compressors share a common wet seal degassing system; the agency should define the boundary for “centrifugal compressor affected facility.”

[P11] The 95% reduction requirement for wet seal fluid degassing systems (§ 60.5380a(a)(1)) may not be technically achievable for older compressors or certain process conditions — request a demonstrated infeasibility procedure, numerical performance testing options, or an alternative percent reduction tied to baseline performance.

[P12] Environmental groups urge that the 95% control requirement in § 60.5380a(a)(1) be accompanied by strict monitoring, continuous emissions monitoring (CEM), or periodic leak detection to ensure real‑world performance; otherwise the standard may be unenforceable.

[P13] § 60.5385a’s general obligation for reciprocating compressors lacks unit‑level numeric leak rate thresholds for rod packing and crankcase emissions; commenters request specific emission limits (e.g., g/hr or ppm) to make compliance measurable and enforceable.

[P14] The rod packing collection requirement (§ 60.5385a(a)(3)) demanding negative pressure and routing through a closed vent system meeting § 60.5411a(a) and (d) is technologically prescriptive and may prevent cost‑effective alternatives (e.g., enclosed combustion devices); suggest allowing performance‑based alternatives that achieve equivalent VOC reductions.

[P15] The provision (§ 60.5390a) allowing use of natural gas as a surrogate for VOC for pneumatic controllers should specify the surrogate conversion factors and test methods to avoid inconsistent surrogate application across companies and states.

[P16] Exempting certain pneumatic controllers under § 60.5390a(a) is appropriate but commenters request a clear list of qualifying controller designs and operational scenarios, plus required documentation to claim the exemption, to prevent misuse.

[P17] For pneumatic pumps (§ 60.5393a), the compliance date “on or after Nov 30, 2016” is confusing — owners/operators need to know whether retrofitting/backfitting is required immediately upon promulgation or only for new installations after that date.

[P18] § 60.5397a’s requirement that affected facilities under §§ 60.5365a(i) and (j) comply with paragraphs (a)-(j) should include clear applicability examples (e.g., compressor station expansions, unit swaps) and transitional provisions for facilities mid‑construction to avoid compliance gaps.

[P19] The Administrator’s discretion in § 60.5398a(a) to permit alternative means of emission limitation must be accompanied by transparent criteria and timelines for review, or stakeholders fear arbitrary or delayed approvals that create operational uncertainty.

[P20] § 60.5398a(d)(1)(xii) requires including operation & maintenance procedures in alternative means applications — commenters request that the rule specify minimal content (frequency, parameters, corrective actions) and allow use of existing O&M manuals to avoid duplicative paperwork.

[P21] Legal commenters note that § 60.5399a(c) requires the Administrator to decide “after notice and comment” whether an alternative fugitive emissions standard achieves equivalent reductions; they request statutory authority citations and a defined timeline for the notice‑and‑decision process to prevent indefinite delays.

[P22] The permission in § 60.5400a(c) to apply for alternative emission control approaches should include an expedited review path for widely adopted technologies or consensus standards (e.g., API, ISO) to reduce regulatory lag and promote deployment.

[P23] § 60.5402a(a) duplicates earlier authority for alternative means but does not limit the scope of conditions that may be imposed; industry requests explicit limits on retrospective conditions that could increase operational costs beyond what was proposed in the application.

[P24] The § 60.5402a(d)(2) application content requirement is extensive (references to (d)(1)(i)-(x)) and will be costly for small operators; recommend a two‑tiered application process with simplified requirements for small entities and a full application for major facilities.

[P25] § 60.5410a(a) initial compliance demonstration for well completions appears to require multiple sequential steps (a)(1)-(4) but does not state acceptable evidence (e.g., photo logs, wellhead pressure records); request explicit measurement, documentation, and certification templates.

[P26] The requirement in § 60.5410a(b)(1) to reduce centrifugal compressor wet seal degassing systems by 95% “and demonstrate per § 60.5413a” needs clarification about acceptable test methods, sample ports, and stack conditions; otherwise, demonstrating compliance may be technically infeasible.

[P27] § 60.5410a(d) references a list of requirements for pneumatic controller initial compliance but does not specify which are immediately enforceable versus those subject to monitoring/reporting timelines; request a compliance schedule and grandfathering for controllers already in service.

[P28] § 60.5410a(f) that onshore natural gas processing plants can demonstrate initial compliance by complying with § 60.5400a should be clarified to state whether use of Administrator‑approved alternative measures under § 60.5400a is automatically acceptable or remains subject to separate approvals.

[P29] The 95% by weight VOC reduction requirement in § 60.5412a(a)(1) for gases vented to control devices may be infeasible for very lean gas streams where VOC concentration is low but mass basis reduction is hard to meet; request an alternative ppm‑based or mass‑flow‑based standard for low‑concentration streams.

[P30] § 60.5412a(a)(2) obligating vapor recovery devices to be designed and operated for at least 95% reduction should permit design analyses in lieu of field testing (the rule allows this in § 60.5413a(c)) but request explicit parameters for acceptable design engineering analyses to avoid inconsistent approvals.

[P31] The option in § 60.5412a(a)(2) to demonstrate initial compliance by design analysis (§ 60.5413a(c)) needs clear engineer certification requirements and post‑installation monitoring to ensure design assumptions match field performance.

[P32] § 60.5413a(d)(11)(iii) requiring manufacturers to demonstrate 95% THC (as propane) destruction efficiency is overly prescriptive in test surrogate selection; manufacturers request allowance of other surrogates with validated equivalency and standardized test conditions.

[P33] Continuous reduction requirement in § 60.5415a(b)(1) to reduce wet seal fluid degassing VOCs by at least 95% continuously is technically challenging during transient operations and startups/shutdowns; request an allowance for temporary excursions with required corrective action and reporting.

[P34] § 60.5415a(f) permitting onshore natural gas processing plants to demonstrate continuous compliance via § 60.5400a compliance is useful but ambiguous — commenters request clear monitoring frequencies and data quality objectives that satisfy continuous compliance.

[P35] The recordkeeping requirement in § 60.5420a(c)(5)(iv) to maintain consecutive days records for skid‑mounted storage vessels at production/processing sites duplicates § 60.5420 and likely imposes double reporting for firms operating across segments; ask the agency to harmonize the two sections and permit a single consolidated record.

[P35] Counting removal days toward the consecutive total (§ 60.5420a(c)(5)(iv)) will penalize operators for temporary maintenance or transfer to another site; recommend deleting the inclusion of removal days or extending the threshold from 30 to 90 days to avoid penalizing normal operational practices.

[P11] Technical commenters request that the 95% control specification (§ 60.5380a(a)(1)) include an explicit test reference (e.g., EPA Method 25A, Method 18) and sample integrity requirements so that percent reductions are comparable and defensible.

[P28] Environmental NGOs argue that allowing demonstration of compliance for processing plants via § 60.5400a (§ 60.5410a(f)) could create loopholes if § 60.5400a permits alternatives; they urge the agency to require independent third‑party verification for alternative means used to demonstrate compliance.

[P19] Public interest groups request that the Administrator’s Federal Register notices under § 60.5398a(a) include an explicit public comment period of at least 60 days and criteria for revocation if real‑world performance is lower than projected.

[P21] State air agencies request explicit coordination provisions for § 60.5399a(c) decisions so state permitting authorities can incorporate Administrator decisions into state permits without duplicative reviews.

[P23] Small business representatives ask that the extensive application content requirements for alternatives (§ 60.5402a(d)(2)) be accompanied by a fee waiver or reduced filing fee for small entities, and that EPA provide a template application form.

[P31] Testing laboratories and manufacturers request that § 60.5413a(d)(11)(iii) define acceptable QA/QC procedures and accreditation (e.g., NELAP or ISO/IEC 17025) for the destruction efficiency demonstrations to ensure consistent test results.

[P13] Operators of aging reciprocating compressors note that the negative-pressure rod packing systems specified in § 60.5385a(a)(3) may require structural modifications to frame and seals of old units; request phased compliance timelines and financial assistance options.

[P12] Compliance auditors recommend that VOC standards for compressors (§§ 60.5380a, 60.5385a) require periodic independent audits every 3‑5 years to verify reported reductions, not just self‑monitoring, to ensure environmental integrity.

[P16] For pneumatic pump standards (§ 60.5393a), commenters request clarification on whether natural gas‑driven diaphragm pumps or nitrogen‑powered devices are included and the acceptable methods for demonstrating surrogate equivalency.

[P24] Public health advocates argue that the rule should adopt emission reduction metrics that account for co‑pollutants and toxic VOC species, not only total VOC or THC, because certain VOCs (e.g., benzene) drive health risks disproportionately.

[P1] The proposed maximum civil penalty of $41,484 per violation in § 578.6(h)(1) is arbitrary and should be adjusted for inflation or indexed annually to avoid rapid erosion of real-dollar deterrence.

[P1] The rule fails to specify whether the $41,484 cap applies per day when combined with P2’s daily-count rule, creating potential double-counting ambiguity that could expose defendants to unconstitutional excessive fines.

[P1] Industry commenters will request clarification whether the $41,484 penalty cap applies to natural persons, corporate officers, manufacturers, or other legal entities differently, since the provision currently says “person” without distinction.

[P1] Consumer advocacy groups will argue the $41,484 cap is too low to deter large manufacturers and request a higher statutory maximum for corporate actors whose violations yield substantial societal harm.

[P2] Counting each day a violation continues as a separate violation (P2) could result in penalties that are manifestly excessive when combined with P1’s per-violation cap, and commenters will request a daily maximum or a proportionality limit.

[P2] Automakers will request a clear definition of when a “day” begins and ends for continuing violations (e.g., midnight to midnight in local time, or based on notice date) to avoid enforcement uncertainty.

[P2] Legal experts will assert the cumulative-per-day approach conflicts with due process/penalty proportionality principles when applied to multi-year compliance issues and ask for a cap on aggregate liability per model year.

[P3] The $5.50 per 0.1 mpg penalty formula in § 578.6(h)(2) is inconsistent with historical penalty calculations and commenters will request explanation or justification of the dollar-per-0.1-mpg rate and whether it is subject to future adjustment.

[P3] Manufacturers will argue the formula lacks clarity on rounding rules (e.g., how to treat fractional 0.1 mpg differences) and request explicit rounding/truncation methodology to ensure consistent penalty computation.

[P3] Small-volume manufacturers will assert the linear per-vehicle multiplication in P6 combined with the $5.50 per 0.1 mpg rate could produce disproportional penalties for niche producers and request a de minimis threshold or graduated scale.

[P3] Environmental advocacy groups will argue the $5.50 per 0.1 mpg figure is too low to incentivize compliance and recommend increasing the per-0.1-mpg penalty to better reflect social costs of excess fuel consumption.

[P3] Automakers will request a formula example showing step-by-step calculation for a hypothetical manufacturer (including use of credits) to ensure predictable enforcement and compliance planning.

[P4] The rule’s statement that liability is “except as provided in 49 U.S.C. 32912(c)” (P4) should be expanded to explicitly list common exceptions (e.g., compliance extensions, hardship waivers) so regulated parties can readily determine applicability.

[P4] Legal commenters will ask the agency to provide interpretive guidance on how 49 U.S.C. 32912(c) interacts with the penalty calculation (e.g., whether statutory exceptions eliminate liability entirely or modify the penalty amount).

[P5] The reliance on 49 U.S.C. 32904(a)(1)(A) or (B) to determine manufacturer average fuel economy (P5) requires the agency to include the exact computational methodology (weights, model grouping, test procedures) in the rule text or supplemental guidance.

[P5] Manufacturers will request clarification whether the average fuel economy used is the certified value, adjusted in-use estimate, or another metric, and how post-production adjustments (e.g., recalls, EPA updates) affect the average.

[P5] Compliance consultants will ask whether vehicles imported, exported, or sold outside the U.S. during the model year are included in the average for purposes of P5, and request definitive inclusion/exclusion rules.

[P6] Multiplying the per-0.1-mpg penalty by the number of applicable automobiles (P6) requires precise definition of “applicable automobiles”; industry will seek clarity on whether truncated model lines, remanufactured vehicles, or fleet transfers are counted.

[P6] Commenters will request treatment guidance for vehicles manufactured in one model year but delayed for sale in a subsequent model year—whether they count under the manufacturing year (per P6) or sale year for penalty purposes.

[P6] Small manufacturers will request a cap on aggregate liability per manufacturer per model year to prevent bankruptcy risk from penalties calculated by simple multiplication without proportionality safeguards.

[P7] The rule reduces the calculated penalty by credits available under 49 U.S.C. 32903 (P7) but does not specify the order of operations where multiple credit types exist; commenters will ask for an explicit sequencing rule.

[P7] Environmental groups will object to allowing tradable credits to reduce civil penalties, arguing this weakens the deterrent effect, and will request that certain credits (e.g., carryforward credits) not be usable to abate penalties.

[P7] Manufacturers will request confirmation that only credits earned and available in the same model year may reduce that year’s penalty, and whether projected or banked credits from other years may be applied.

[P7] Accounting firms will ask the agency to require disclosure of the credit balances and calculations used to reduce penalties to ensure transparency and prevent manipulation.

[Overall] Commenters will request worked examples illustrating the entire penalty computation across P3–P7, including when P2’s per-day rule applies, to ensure predictable application and to identify any cumulative liability risks.

[Overall] Civil liberties and legal experts will request an administrative appeal and mitigation process be codified (e.g., ability to present good-faith compliance efforts or force majeure) before penalties are assessed under these provisions.

[Overall] Industry associations will request a phased implementation or grandfathering for vehicles already in production planning cycles to avoid sudden large penalty exposures caused by post-proposal regulatory changes.

[Overall] Commenters will urge the agency to publish a regulatory impact analysis showing estimated aggregate annual penalties, expected compliance cost impacts, and distributional effects across manufacturers, small businesses, and consumers.

[P21] Coho household allocation (10 +2 per household member) (P21) and similar species allocations will create enforcement complexity when multiple permits operate in same household; recommend limiting one permit per household or requiring household-level permits.

[P22] Pink salmon limit structure (10 +2 per household member) (P22) ignores the strong two-year cycle of pinks; suggest adjusting in-season manager authority to raise/lower limits based on expected odd/even year runs.

[P23] Allowing Ninilchik residents to take multiple salmon species by dip net or rod and reel on the upper Kasilof (P23) could conflict with state regulations on gear and space — request clear location boundaries (GPS) and gear specifications to prevent overlap and crowding.

[P24] Allowing up to two baited single or treble hooks for rod-and-reel users (P24) increases hooking mortality for species intended for release; request prohibition of treble hooks and restriction to single hooks only to reduce injuries.

[P25] The seasons in the Kasilof fishery (P25) and the trigger to close rainbow/steelhead take after 200 harvested lack clear basis and may be too permissive; ask for supporting escapement data and request a lower threshold or requirement to count released vs. retained separately.

[P26] Fish wheel permission for Ninilchik residents (P26) that allows one wheel only (P28) may create access bottlenecks and dependence on a single organization; small-boat fishers and households will request provision for rotating operation or multiple community-owned wheels.

[P27] Requiring a live box, monitoring, and prohibition on unattended fishing for fish wheels (P29) is appropriate, but enforcement in remote areas is challenging; request guidance on monitoring frequency and acceptable remote monitoring technology.

[P28] Awarding one fish wheel registration permit based on operational plan merits (P30) without a transparent selection process may favor certain organizations; recommend a published scoring rubric, appeal process, and periodic re-evaluation to ensure fairness.

[P29] Prohibiting renting/leasing the fish wheel for personal gain (P32) is vague — request definition of "personal gain" and whether cost-sharing among households or reimbursement for fuel/maintenance is permissible.

[P30] The requirement that the owner provide a pre-season operational plan describing allocation and distribution (P33) imposes substantial administrative burdens on community organizations; request template forms and a reasonable timeline for submission and amendments.

[P31] The 12x12 inch permanent plate requirement showing permit number and contact info on fish wheel (P34) risks vandalism/theft and may be impractical on small craft; request allowance for smaller labels or durable tags, and placement exceptions for safety.

[P32] Post-season reporting of operators, hours, and catch/retention/release counts by species (P35) is reasonable, but confidentiality concerns arise when small communities could be identified; request aggregated reporting options and data-use protections.

[P33] Requiring operators to remain onsite and remove fish at least hourly (P36) may be unsafe during extreme weather and impractical for volunteer operators; request flexibility for hourly removal when safe and documented exceptions for emergencies.

[P34] Requiring non-owner operators to attach a 12x12 plate with their permit info (P37) is redundant and could lead to multiple plates; propose a single clearly visible plate listing authorized operators or a laminated roster.

[P35] Allowing owner organizations to operate fish wheels on behalf of residents if permit identifies a responsible operator (P38/P39) raises liability questions — request clarification of legal liability, insurance requirements, and dispute resolution for distribution of catch.

[P36] The June 16–Oct 31 open period for Kasilof fish wheel (P40) may overlap with sensitive migration/escapement windows; recommend the in-season manager have explicit authority to shorten season dates based on escapement indicators.

[P37] The experimental community gillnet fishery expiration date of July 13, 2020 (P42) is obsolete and must be updated or removed; commenters will request correction to avoid legal ambiguity.

[P38] Limiting the experimental gillnet to ≤10 fathoms and not obstructing >half the river width (P43) is appropriate, but "half the river width" is ambiguous for braided or tidal reaches — request specification of measurement points and seasonal adjustments for flow changes.

[P39] The requirement to submit mesh size, times/locations, and allocation plans prior to season (P44) may not allow adaptive management in response to in-season conditions; request allowance for in-season amendments with short-notice manager approval.

[P40] Compliance with Kenai NWR rules for community gillnets (P46) should be enumerated or attached to the permit; otherwise applicants may be unaware of conflicting refuge restrictions — request explicit cross-references or incorporated provisions.

[P41] Allowing retention of incidental species but requiring release of rainbow/steelhead in fish wheels/gillnets (P27/48) will increase handling mortality; recommend mandatory use of gear and mesh sizes to minimize bycatch and clearer handling protocols.

[P42] The single gillnet allowed in Moose Range Meadows operated by the Ninilchik Traditional Council (P75/P84) concentrates stewardship but risks monopolization; recommend periodic community elections for operator authority and transparent allocation of benefits.

[P43] Counting fish taken in community gillnet toward household annual limits (P76) requires real-time recordkeeping to avoid overharvest; request mandatory daily reporting and cap per household to prevent exceeding limits.

[P44] The early-run Chinook provision that allows retention only if state preseason forecast predicts adequate escapement (P77) creates uncertainty; request definition of "adequate escapement," the forecast source/methodology, and a pre-published threshold to inform planning.

[P45] Closing the fishery when 50 early-run Chinook are retained/released or 200 late-run Chinook retained/released (P77/P78) may be inadequate protection given small run sizes; request adaptive lower closure triggers tied to in-season escapement counts and inclusion of release vs. mortality differentiation.

[P46] Requiring release of live incidentally caught rainbow and Dolly Varden but allowing dead fish retention, with closure after 100 rainbow or 150 Dolly Varden released/retained (P79), is confusing — commenters request that counts distinguish released alive versus dead and that thresholds reflect likely mortality rates.

[P47] Exception allowing Chinook under 20 inches to be retained and not count toward totals (P80) could be exploited to harvest juvenile fish; request scientific support and, if retained, require tagging/recording for population monitoring.

[P48] Counting incidental fish mortalities (except Chinook <20") toward totals (P81) is appropriate but will be difficult to measure accurately; recommend standardized reporting protocols and observer or photo verification for compliance.

[P49] The gillnet gear restrictions (≤10 fathoms, ≤5.25-inch mesh) (P82) may be insufficient to prevent escapement impacts on small Chinook; recommend a smaller maximum mesh and mandatory use of selective gears during sensitive periods.

[P50] The 200-foot separation requirement between stationary gillnets (P83) may not be enforceable in crowded fisheries; request a detailed marking and mapping requirement to help fishermen and enforcement locate and respect buffers.

[P51] Issuing a single registration permit to the Ninilchik Traditional Council with responsibility for post-season documentation (P84) centralizes management but lacks an oversight mechanism — request requirement for independent audit of reported data and public summary of allocations.

[P52] Allowing the Council to operate nets on residents' behalf if it requests permit (P85) could disadvantage households who prefer to fish independently; ask that permits also allow individual household participation under the community framework.

[P53] The rod-and-reel provision allowing two baited hooks in Kenai River lower reaches (P87) should limit bait types (e.g., barbless, single hooks) to reduce post-release mortality of protected species.

[P54] The annual combined limit of 4 Chinook per permit holder for Kenai River (P88) conflicts with earlier household Chinook limits (P66/P67) and per-permit versus per-household counting — request clarification whether permit holder and household limits operate cumulatively and how to account for multiple permit holders in one household.

[P55] The multiple and varying size thresholds across lower and upper Kenai (P91–P97) are highly complex and will confuse fishers and enforcement; propose simplified, geographically mapped limits and clear signage at access points.

[P56] The Hidden Lake special limit of 2 lake trout/day regardless of length (P95) may not reflect local population status; request the data supporting this unique limit and consideration of subsistence needs.

[P57] The under-ice gillnet check requirement every 48 hours (P60) may be inadequate to prevent predator captures, gear loss, or excessive mortality in ice conditions; recommend a 24-hour check interval or electronic alerts tied to net sensors.

[P58] Requiring name/address on a stake for unattended gear (P61) raises privacy and safety concerns for permittees in remote areas; suggest use of permit ID numbers or a secure contact phone instead of home addresses.

[P59] The permit reporting deadlines (P58/P59/P63) and the May 31 return date (P63) could jeopardize future permit eligibility for those who lack postal access; recommend multiple submission methods and a grace period for remote communities.

[P60] The rule lacks an explicit enforcement and penalty schedule tied to violations such as failure to mark fish, exceed limits, or improper gear (P5, P7, P63); legal commenters will request clear citation of penalties and due process protections.

[P61] Many provisions differentiate by residence (e.g., Ninilchik residents) (P23, P26, P75) but do not define residency criteria — stakeholders request a clear definition (length of residency, proof required) to avoid disputes.

[P62] The numerous cross-references to Federal in-season manager discretion (multiple provisions) concentrate authority without clear standards; request published decision criteria, timelines for actions, and opportunities for community input on special actions.

[P63] Cumulative impacts on Chinook and other at-risk stocks from multiple permitted fisheries across rivers (Kenai, Kasilof, Russian) are not addressed — request an aggregate biological impact analysis and explicit inter-fishery caps.

[P64] The permit and gear marking size requirements (12x12 in plates in P34/P37) are inconsistent with small gear boats and risk non-compliance; recommend proportional size ranges or alternative marking methods acceptable to managers.

[P65] The experimental and community fisheries (gillnet and fish wheel) lack clear anti-market provisions beyond "not for personal gain" (P32); request explicit prohibition on sale or barter, monitoring for illegal commercialization, and penalties for violations.

[P66] The rule requires many post-season reports (P35, P45, P84) but does not state how the information will be used or protected; request a data management plan, timeframe for public release, and protections for personal data and sensitive subsistence information.

[P67] The rule's complexity will disproportionately burden small rural households and community organizations with paperwork and monitoring costs; request funding for compliance assistance, training, and equipment (e.g., reporting tablets, tags).

[P68] Legal commenters will note potential preemption conflicts between state sport rules (incorporated by reference in P13) and federally declared subsistence priority — recommend legal analysis and explicit statements on primacy where differences exist.

[P69] The rule does not provide mechanisms for dispute resolution between households or organizations over allocation of community-caught fish (P33/P39/P44) — request mandatory allocation agreements and an appeal process administered by the Federal in-season manager.

[P70] For all fisheries using release-count triggers (P25, P77–79), the rule should specify measurement protocols (who measures length, method, and handling) to ensure consistent, enforceable counts rather than leaving determinations to field discretion.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The blanket permission to "take fish at any time" in Cook Inlet (P1) is overly broad and conflicts with existing state and tribal conservation measures; we request clear cross-references to applicable restrictions and explanation of hierarchy to avoid inadvertent violations.

Industry commenters will object that allowing fishing "at any time" (P1) creates enforcement ambiguity for patrols — recommend adding specific hours, dates, or sunset/sunrise language or a requirement to carry current permit terms.

Sport and conservation groups will challenge retention of incidentally caught rainbow/steelhead in subsistence net fisheries (P2) because it may increase mortality of vulnerable populations unless explicit handling/size/sex limits are included.

The annual limit of two rainbow/steelhead ≥20 inches for jigging or rod-and-reel in Kenai Peninsula fresh waters (P3) is inconsistent with other size/possession limits in the rule (e.g., P54/93) and should be reconciled to prevent confusion and double-counting.

Tribal advocates will argue that the 2-fish annual limit (P3) is too restrictive for communities reliant on rainbow/steelhead and ask for a community or household allocation alternative rather than per-permit limits.

The restriction that permit holders may take only salmon, trout, Dolly Varden, and other char (P4) appears to prohibit taking non-salmonid resident species (e.g., whitefish, pike) under federal permits — request clarification whether other subsistence species are covered elsewhere or should be expressly allowed.

Requiring that all fish taken under federal permits be marked and recorded before leaving the fishing site (P5) is burdensome and impractical in remote conditions; commenters will request an alternative timeline (e.g., within 24 hours) and define acceptable recording methods (paper, electronic).

The definition of "fishing site" as federal waters and adjacent shoreline (P6) could create jurisdictional confusion when fish are taken near mixed ownership boundaries; request maps or GPS coordinate guidance and procedures when harvest spans multiple sites.

Marking fish by removing the dorsal fin (P7) will likely render fish unsellable, impacts cultural practices for preparation/preservation, and increases handling mortality; commenters will propose alternative, less harmful marking methods (e.g., external tags, clips) or allow marking at home within a specified time.

The outright prohibition on taking grayling or burbot for subsistence (P8) will be contested by local subsistence users who rely on these species seasonally; request biological justification and consideration of limited household allowances with monitoring.

Limiting smelt dip net harvest to April 1–June 15 (P9) may not align with local run timing variability due to climate change; request the option for in-season manager to adjust dates regionally or language permitting closures/adjustments based on observed runs.

Having no harvest or possession limits for smelt (P10) could lead to overharvest, especially with high-effort dip netting; conservation groups will request at least a reasonable possession limit or guidelines to prevent waste/market diversion.

raw_output:
[P1] The public comment deadline of August 22, 2019 is unreasonably short for international operators and foreign competent authorities to coordinate technical reviews; extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] The proposed deadline does not account for the time required to consult OEM service bulletin details and maintenance records; FAA should allow comment submissions up to 90 days after publication of the full service bulletin.

[P2] Applying the AD to "all" 737-800, -900, and -900ER airplanes regardless of configuration or customer-specific modifications is overly broad and may capture aircraft that do not have the affected valve installation; the FAA should limit applicability to specific line numbers or N-Numbers shown to have the part installed.

[P2] The rule fails to clarify applicability for converted freighters, Boeing conversions, or supplemental type certificate (STC) installations; provide explicit guidance for airplanes modified under an STC.

[P3] The requirement to "comply within the specified compliance times" lacks clarity about whether repetitive inspections are required; specify whether compliance is a one-time action or subject to recurring checks.

[P3] The AD should include relief for aircraft grounded due to other maintenance needs that cannot schedule AD compliance within the compliance window; allow coordination or temporary extensions via AMOC without safety risk.

[P4] Requiring replacement of the left temperature control valve and control cabin trim air modulating valve within 60 months after July 20, 2017 effectively backdates the compliance clock; clarify whether operators who acquired airplanes after that date get a full 60 months from the AD effective date.

[P4] The 60-month compliance time for replacement is excessive for some operators who already planned near-term maintenance; FAA should allow operators to perform replacements at next heavy maintenance check with credit if installed earlier.

[P5] For airplanes not identified in (g) that have original certificates dated on or before the AD effective date, the two-step approach in (h) creates confusion about which aircraft are covered; clarify the population and provide a matrix (certificate date vs. prior service bulletin incorporation).

[P5] The provision in (h) appears to exclude aircraft certificated after the AD effective date; confirm whether newly certificated or imported airplanes that receive the affected part after the effective date are subject to (h) or (g).

[P6] A "general visual inspection" within 60 months to determine part numbers is too vague—define acceptance criteria, inspection access provisions, and who can perform the inspection (certified technician vs. licensed engineer).

[P6] The 60-month allowance for performing the inspection could allow unsafe valves to remain in service too long; require a shorter inspection interval (e.g., 12 months) or at next maintenance visit.

[P7] Allowing maintenance records instead of physical inspection is reasonable, but the rule should specify the minimum acceptable documentation (e.g., signed work order, parts traceability, vendor certification) to conclusively determine part numbers.

[P7] The AD must clarify how to handle incomplete or conflicting maintenance records (e.g., records indicating a part change but no part number listed); provide guidance on when a physical inspection becomes mandatory.

[P8] Replacing any valve with part number 398908-4 within 60 months is acceptable, but operators request a parts availability assessment and a transition schedule to avoid AOG situations; FAA should coordinate with Boeing on parts supply.

[P8] The rule should allow rework/repair of part 398908-4 as an alternative to replacement if the repaired item meets the certification basis, subject to Boeing or FAA approval, rather than mandating full replacement.

[P9] The prohibition on installing part number 398908-4 "as of the effective date" should be clarified to state whether existing spares with that part number may be consumed for non-aircraft uses, or whether surgical bench testing uses are restricted; provide disposition guidance for existing inventory.

[P9] The blanket ban on installing 398908-4 may conflict with legacy maintenance procedures for non-critical training aircraft; allow conditional installation for non revenue-service test rigs or ground-only training if documented.

[P9] The AD should define "install" (e.g., temporary installation for test purposes, installation for maintenance rigging) to avoid enforcement ambiguity.

[P10] Delegating AMOC authority solely to the Seattle ACO Branch Manager may disadvantage operators in other regions; allow regional ACO managers or the principal inspector to approve limited AMOCs to expedite compliance.

[P10] The rule should include timeframes for FAA action on AMOC requests (e.g., 60 days) to prevent prolonged delays that could ground aircraft or delay maintenance.

[P11] Requiring AMOC requests to go through the principal inspector or local FSDO may be redundant when the operator has an assigned certifying engineer or approved maintenance organization; permit direct submission by the operator's accountable manager with notification to the principal inspector.

[P12] The instruction to send information directly to the certification office manager identified in (k)(1) is unclear because paragraph (k)(1) is not provided in this excerpt; include full contact details and an alternate contact if the named person is unavailable.

[P13] Allowing AMOC requests by email to the specified address is helpful but the AD should also allow secure file transfer for large technical packages and confirm an automatic receipt/acknowledgment process.

[P14] Requiring notification to the principal inspector or local FSDO prior to using an approved AMOC could be operationally burdensome on short notice; allow notification within a short, specified timeframe (e.g., 48 hours) after first use.

[P15] Allowing Boeing ODA approval for AMOCs for repairs is practical, but approvals should be conditioned on FAA oversight and final acceptance to ensure no delegation exceeds ODA authority.

[P16] Requiring that AMOC deviations meet the airplane's certification basis is appropriate, but operators need guidance on how to determine the certification basis for older aircraft—provide reference to relevant certification records or a centralized FAA determination process.

[P17] The rule's handling of service information steps labeled RC needs clearer definition of what qualifies a step as RC and how Boeing will identify RC vs non-RC steps in revised service bulletins.

The proposed deadline does not account for the time required to consult OEM service bulletin details and maintenance records; FAA should allow comment submissions up to 90 days after publication of the full service bulletin.

Applying the AD to "all" 737-800, -900, and -900ER airplanes regardless of configuration or customer-specific modifications is overly broad and may capture aircraft that do not have the affected valve installation; the FAA should limit applicability to specific line numbers or N-Numbers shown to have the part installed.

The rule fails to clarify applicability for converted freighters, Boeing conversions, or supplemental type certificate (STC) installations; provide explicit guidance for airplanes modified under an STC.

The requirement to "comply within the specified compliance times" lacks clarity about whether repetitive inspections are required; specify whether compliance is a one-time action or subject to recurring checks.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement that every commercial fishing vessel be registered under a general HMS permit (§ 660.707(a)(1)) is overly broad and would impose unnecessary compliance costs on small-scale operators who rarely or incidentally encounter HMS species.

[P1] The rule lacks clarity on whether vessels that only transit the EEZ without fishing but carry DGN or other specified gear must be registered under the general HMS permit, creating enforcement uncertainty.

[P2] The condition requiring registration to fish for HMS in the EEZ off CA/OR/WA (§ 660.707(a)(1)(i)) will effectively expand federal jurisdiction over state-regulated nearshore fisheries and may conflict with existing state permits and management.

[P2] The rule does not define “fish for HMS” (e.g., target vs. incidental catch), leaving vessels uncertain whether they must obtain an HMS permit under § 660.707(a)(1)(i).

[P3] Requiring registration for vessels that land or transship HMS shoreward of the EEZ boundary (§ 660.707(a)(1)(ii)) could penalize port agents, processors, or transshipment vessels that never operated in the EEZ, creating burdens on non-fishing actors.

[P3] The provision fails to define “land or transship shoreward of the outer boundary of the EEZ,” particularly for mixed trips that offload at multiple ports; guidance is needed to avoid inconsistent application.

[P4] Limiting permit issuance only to persons eligible under 46 U.S.C. 12102(a) (§ 660.707(a)(4)) may exclude long-time small-boat fishers who operate state-registered but not federally-documented vessels, effectively disenfranchising these operators.

[P4] The cross-reference to 46 U.S.C. 12102(a) is ambiguous regarding corporate ownership and trusts; the rule should clarify whether entities (e.g., LLCs) or beneficiaries can hold permits.

[P5] NMFS’ obligation to issue permits to vessel owners identified from specified lists (§ 660.707(b)(1)) may lock in a snapshot list that omits vessels legitimately participating in the fishery because of registry timing; process for corrections should be specified.

[P5] The rule does not state an appeals or correction process for owners omitted from the initial NMFS list prior to permit issuance, risking denial of access to the fishery.

[P6] Requiring owners who did not receive a permit to apply to SFD (§ 660.707(b)(3)) places administrative burdens on transient vessel owners and should include expedited procedures for commercial operations needing immediate access.

[P6] The rule should specify acceptable proof of ownership for applicants who operate under lease, bareboat charter, or multi-owner arrangements when applying per § 660.707(b)(3).

[P7] The application completeness standard (§ 660.707(b)(3)(i)) is vague; the rule should list mandatory information fields and acceptable signature types (wet, electronic) to prevent arbitrary rejections.

[P8] The minimum 15-day processing timeframe (§ 660.707(b)(3)(ii)) is insufficient during peak seasons; commenters request a maximum processing time and expedited review for urgent commercial needs.

[P8] The 30-day cure period for deficiencies (§ 660.707(b)(3)(ii)) should require NMFS to provide a deficiency checklist and allow extensions for mail delays or documented extenuating circumstances.

[P9] Requiring SFD to state reasons for permit denials (§ 660.707(b)(3)(iii)) is appropriate but must also require citation of the specific regulatory or factual basis so applicants can meaningfully appeal.

[P10] The 30-day deadline to submit a written appeal (§ 660.707(b)(3)(iv)(A)) is too short for complex denials; appeals periods should be extended to 60 days to allow applicants to gather supporting documentation.

[P10] The appeal provision should explicitly allow electronic submission of appeals and recognize service by email given modern communications (§ 660.707(b)(3)(iv)(A)).

[P11] The Regional Administrator’s ability to request additional information (§ 660.707(b)(3)(iv)(B)) could be used to indefinitely delay appeals; the rule should set a limit on the number and type of supplemental requests.

[P12] The 30-day target for deciding appeals after sufficient information is received (§ 660.707(b)(3)(iv)(C)) is optimistic; the rule should provide a firm timeline with notice to the appellant if more time is required.

[P13] The informal hearing process (§ 660.707(b)(3)(iv)(D)) must guarantee the right to cross-examine witnesses and ensure the hearing officer is impartial; current language is silent on procedural safeguards.

[P14] The Regional Administrator’s discretion to adopt, modify, or reject hearing officer recommendations (§ 660.707(b)(3)(iv)(E)) could undermine the hearing’s value unless criteria for review are provided.

[P15] Allowing the Regional Administrator to extend time limits up to 30 days for “good cause” (§ 660.707(b)(3)(iv)(F)) is reasonable, but the rule needs to define “good cause” to prevent arbitrary or prejudicial extensions.

[P16] Two-year renewal terms (§ 660.707(b)(4)) may be too long for adaptive management needs; NMFS should retain authority to require annual reporting or shorter renewals when conservation concerns arise.

[P17] The per-vessel fee requirement (§ 660.707(e)) lacks transparency — the rule should publish the fee schedule or formula and an estimate of expected fees before finalizing the rule.

[P17] Tying fee calculation to the NOAA Finance Handbook (§ 660.707(e)) without an explicit cap or example figures risks unpredictable and potentially burdensome charges for small operators.

[P18] Requiring individuals who use large-mesh DGN to possess a Federal limited entry DGN permit (§ 660.707(f)(1)) will disrupt existing state-managed DGN fleets and may reduce employment if permits are limited.

[P19] The permission for California state limited entry DGN permit holders to obtain Federal permits upon final rule publication (§ 660.707(f)(2)) must be accompanied by a clear grandfathering timeline and transitional measures for non-California participants.

[P20] The March 31, 2018 postmark deadline (§ 660.707(f)(2)) for eligibility is arbitrary and retroactive; it unfairly penalizes holders who failed to timely renew a past state permit and should be removed or extended.

[P21] The documentation required to prove qualification (§ 660.707(f)(3)) is overly broad — listing specific acceptable documents and limiting SFD’s discretionary requests would reduce arbitrary denials.

[P21] Requiring contracts and “other evidence” (§ 660.707(f)(3)) without limiting categories could compel proprietary business information disclosure; confidentiality protections should be added.

[P22] The provision allowing SFD to request additional evidence (§ 660.707(f)(3)) should include a limit on the number of supplemental requests and a timeline for responses to protect applicants from indefinite processing delays.

[P23] Processing fees limited to actual service costs (§ 660.707(f)(4)) are appropriate, but the rule must require public posting of cost calculations and an audit mechanism to prevent excessive fee allocation.

[P24] Centralizing initial permit decisions in SFD (§ 660.707(f)(5)(i)) risks bottlenecks; consider delegating routine administrative approvals to regional offices with SFD oversight.

[P25] The requirement that adverse decisions state reasons (§ 660.707(f)(5)(ii)) must include citation to the specific regulations and factual findings relied upon, to allow meaningful judicial review.

[P26] The SFD’s discretion to decline to act on applications under sanction provisions (§ 660.707(f)(5)(iii)) should be narrowly defined and require notice explaining the sanction basis and how to resolve it.

[P27] Permits being vessel-specific and issued to individuals assigned to a vessel (§ 660.707(f)(6)) will complicate crew arrangements and inhibit vessel sales or temporary charters; allow flexible vessel assignment or short-term reassignment mechanisms.

[P27] Allowing permit holders to assign their permit to another vessel only once per permit year (§ 660.707(f)(6)) is too restrictive for legitimate operational needs (repairs, replacement vessels); increase allowed assignments or permit temporary vessel substitution.

[P28] The appealability of initial DGN permit decisions (§ 660.707(f)(7)) should include the same procedural protections requested for general permits — electronic filing, extended timeframes, and discovery privileges.

[P29] The three-year continuous holding requirement before transfer (§ 660.707(f)(8)) creates illiquidity and could reduce permit market value; shorter holding periods or alternative transferability mechanisms should be considered.

[P29] Requiring three consecutive years of holding ignores circumstances where permit holders have legitimate short-term ownership changes; propose allowing cumulative years rather than consecutive.

[P30] Counting time under California state DGN permits toward the federal three-year requirement (§ 660.707(f)(8)) is sensible, but the rule must specify documentation standards and a process to verify state-holding periods.

[P31] The serious illness/permanent disability exception (§ 660.707(f)(8)(i)) lacks a defined standard for “serious” and should specify acceptable medical documentation and a review procedure to avoid abuse or denial.

[P32] The six-month window for estate/heir transfers after death (§ 660.707(f)(8)(ii)) may be too short given probate timelines; extend to at least 12–18 months or allow extensions when probate delays are documented.

[P33] Allowing transfer upon dissolution of marriage where the permit is community property (§ 660.707(f)(8)(iii)) is appropriate but requires procedures to verify community property claims across different state laws.

[P34] Reliance on the permit holder’s “most recent address on file” for renewal notices (§ 660.707(f)(9)(i)) is insufficient safeguard; also require email/text notifications and public posting periods as secondary notice methods.

[P35] Placing sole responsibility for renewal on permit owners (§ 660.707(f)(9)(ii)) without robust proactive outreach risks inadvertent lapses; NMFS/SFD should implement reminder systems and grace periods.

[P36] The April 30 renewal deadline and annual renewal requirement (§ 660.707(f)(9)(iii)) may conflict with seasonal fishing operations; consider aligning renewal periods with fishing seasons or allowing staggered renewals.

[P37] The strict rule that expired permits won’t be renewed unless reissuance is requested by July 31 and NMFS finds proximate cause (§ 660.707(f)(9)(iv)) is unduly punitive; propose a longer reissuance window and clearer definitions of “proximate cause.”

[P38] The owner-on-board requirement during DGN fishing (§ 660.707(f)(10)(i)) will disproportionately harm owner-operators who rely on shore-based duties; consider allowing designated, qualified operators for routine operations beyond the limited substitute days.

[P39] Allowing substitutes for up to 15 days per year (§ 660.707(f)(10)(ii)) is insufficient for permit holders who need temporary relief for family or business reasons; increase substitute allowance and allow cumulative days under documented circumstances.

[P39] The 24-hour pre-trip notification to NMFS for substitute designation (§ 660.707(f)(10)(ii)) is operationally onerous; allow same-day or after-the-fact notification in emergencies.

[P40] NMFS authority to grant exemptions beyond 15 days for death/illness/injury (§ 660.707(f)(10)(iii)) must include an expedited review process for critically time-sensitive medical cases.

[P41] Requiring a death certificate for estate exemptions (§ 660.707(f)(10)(iv)) is reasonable, but the rule must accept interim documents (obituary, funeral home receipts) when the certificate is delayed and allow temporary authorization.

[P41] The estate exemption duration (until estate registers/transfers the permit or three years after death) (§ 660.707(f)(10)(iv)) could leave estates accountable for permit obligations for too long; shorten the maximum duration or require active estate progress reporting.

[P42] The medical letter requirement for illness/injury exemptions (§ 660.707(f)(10)(v)) must specify the level of medical detail required, privacy protections for medical information, and permit an independent medical review if NMFS disputes the claim.

[P42] Limiting illness/injury exemptions to a single fishing year (§ 660.707(f)(10)(v)) without allowing rolling extensions based on continuing medical evidence could force permit holders to choose between health and livelihood; allow multi-year extensions when medically justified.

[P3] The obligation to manage and dispose of residual solids that contain hazardous constituent levels under RCRA Subtitle C lacks specificity about acceptable interim storage, accumulation time limits, and permitted treatment standards prior to final disposal.  
[P3] State regulators will request clarification whether management under Subtitle C requires immediate transporter manifests and storage as D001–Dxxx codes or whether a specific hazardous waste code(s) should be assigned to these residual solids.  
[P4] The prohibition on disposing of residual solids as non-hazardous until verification sampling is completed could be administratively burdensome if EPA does not set a mandatory timeframe for completing verification sampling; commenters will request a clear deadline.  
[P4] A legal commenter will assert that delaying the exclusion's applicability until sampling is complete could conflict with the rule's statement that "the exclusion is effective upon publication" and ask EPA to clarify the interplay.  
[P5] The verification testing program lacks detail on sample frequency, number of composite samples, statistical confidence levels, and action levels — commenters will request explicit testing protocols to ensure representativeness.  
[P5] Public health advocates will demand that verification testing include leachate (TCLP) and total analyses for each listed constituent and that EPA require independent third-party labs for initial verification.  
[P6] The hard cap prohibiting generation of more than 20,000 cubic yards in any 12-month period is arbitrary; industry will request justification based on risk assessment data or a scalable threshold tied to demonstrated constituent concentrations.  
[P6] Blanchard or industry commenters will argue the 20,000 cubic yard limit is unworkable for normal operational fluctuations and request a volumetric averaging provision or a temporary exceedance allowance with expedited reporting.  
[P7] Requiring that any excess above 20,000 cubic yards be handled as hazardous waste and triggering a new petition is overly punitive and may force unnecessary hazardous landfilling; commenters will propose an interim management pathway with expedited review instead of immediate hazardous classification.  
[P7] Legal commenters will note that the requirement to file a new petition for any exceedance imposes significant costs and delays and request an administrative alternative (e.g., temporary notification plus risk-based handling) for modest, infrequent exceedances.  
[P8] The permission to dispose of solids as non-hazardous only after verification demonstrating meeting delisting levels should be conditioned on ongoing periodic testing; environmental groups will demand mandatory periodic re-verification (quarterly/annual) rather than a one-time demonstration.  
[P8] Municipal solid waste landfill operators receiving delisted material will want explicit liability protections and clear manifesting/acceptance procedures to avoid treating material as hazardous after receipt.  
[P9] The requirement to notify EPA in writing when starting and stopping disposal of delisted solids needs a specific timeline (e.g., within 7 days of start/stop) and a specified form or electronic filing method; commenters will request these procedural details.  
[P10] The obligation to notify EPA if Blanchard significantly changes the reclamation process or starts processes that could alter waste composition is too broad — commenters will ask for a clear definition of "significant change" to avoid over-notification.  
[P10] Industry will request that minor operational adjustments be excluded from the notification requirement and that only process changes that alter feedstock chemistry beyond defined thresholds trigger notification.  
[P11] The prohibition on treating solids from changed processes as non-hazardous until verification is complete could cause immediate shipment stoppages; commenters will request an interim handling protocol and express concern about supply chain disruptions.  
[P12] The prohibition tied to adding stabilization reagents lacks detail on which stabilization chemicals or loading rates trigger the prohibition, and commenters will ask EPA to list reagents or define "stabilization" for clarity.  
[P12] Technical commenters will note that addition of stabilization could reduce leaching and argue a presumption in favor of non-hazardous classification if stabilization is performed under an EPA-approved stabilization protocol and verified.  
[P13] The permission to resume normal operations after modified operations and meeting verification is reasonable, but commenters will request EPA to specify how long post-modification verification must continue before reverting to the prior testing regime.  
[P14] The allowance for Blanchard to periodically add chemical stabilization reagents should be constrained with operational limits and mandatory documentation each time reagents are used; commenters will request specific reporting and re-verification triggers.  
[P15] The five-year on-site records retention requirement is acceptable to some industry commenters but state agencies may request alignment with state record retention laws (which may be longer) or request EPA to permit electronic off-site storage with secure access.  
[P16] The instruction to retain all analytical and quality control data for five years should be expanded to require maintaining chain-of-custody documentation and method detection limits; laboratory accreditation requirements should be specified.  
[P17] The obligation to provide inspection copies of data to EPA or Texas representatives raises confidentiality concerns — Blanchard will request a protective order mechanism for confidential business information (CBI) and clear procedures for redactions.  
[P18] The requirement to file a new petition if generating more than 20,000 cubic yards imposes duplicative administrative burden; commenters will request an expedited petition review process or provisional authorization for temporary increases.  
[P19] The reopener/reporting procedure triggered by failing annual testing lacks transparency — commenters will request detailed steps EPA will take, timelines for corrective actions, and potential consequences, including whether off-site disposal must cease immediately.  
[P20] The obligation to report differing site conditions or testing failures to EPA within 10 days may be infeasible where confirmatory lab analysis is still pending; commenters will request a two-step reporting process (initial notification within 10 days, final report upon confirmation).  
[P21] The permission for EPA to take action on new information is overly broad; regulated entities and stakeholders will request criteria for what constitutes "new information" and procedural safeguards (notice, opportunity to respond) before reopening decisions.  
[P22] Legal commenters will seek clarification of the standards and burden of proof EPA will use to reopen a delisting decision to ensure due process and to outline opportunities for a hearing or public notice.  
[P23] The emergency rulemaking authority in the case of "immediate threat" is necessary but commenters will ask EPA to define "immediate threat" and to commit to posting a public justification and evidence when invoking good-cause emergency rulemaking.  
[P24] The one-time notification to state regulatory agencies that will carry or receive delisted waste should require EPA to provide a template notification and require Blanchard to keep proof of delivery; states will request a copy of the delisting decision and testing data with the notification.  
[P25] The 60-day advance notice to a relevant state agency before beginning transport or management in that state may impede timely operations if state review is slow; industry asks for a provision that allows transport after 30 days if the state does not respond.  
[P26] The obligation that EPA will initiate procedures to withdraw the exclusion upon violation lacks specificity on what constitutes a violation and what interim actions EPA will take pending withdrawal; commenters request a clear enforcement timeline and opportunity to cure.  
[P27] While EPA may assess enforcement for immediate threats, regulated entities request clarity on whether enforcement will be civil only, whether penalties will be retroactive to the start of the violation, and how EPA will coordinate with states.  
[P28] The expectation that Blanchard will perform required waste analyses and comply with delisting criteria should be accompanied by standards for laboratory accreditation (e.g., NELAP) and required QA/QC acceptance criteria; commenters will request these be mandatory.  
[P29] The obligation to obtain state delisting authorization before managing delisted waste in states with authority could effectively nullify the federal delisting in many states; Blanchard or industry will request a process and timeline for obtaining state concurrence and an alternative if a state refuses.  
[P30] The requirement that recycling plans comply with Hazardous Waste Recycling regulations needs clarification as to which specific regulatory provisions apply (e.g., 40 CFR 261.6, 266 subparts), and whether exemptions for reclaimed materials apply.  
[P31] The obligation that generators must continue verifying their wastes do not exhibit hazardous characteristics post-delisting should specify frequency and tests required; downstream generators and waste brokers will request clear testing intervals to minimize liability.  
[P31] Environmental groups will stress that continuing generator responsibility should be accompanied by a mandatory audit right for EPA and states to sample delisted material at receiving facilities to verify non-hazardous status.
