[P1] The $110 million combined annual sales threshold for “small manufacturer” is ambiguous as to whether non-U.S. parent company sales are included; the rule should explicitly state whether only U.S.-based parent company sales count.

[P1] The rule’s combined-sales test should allow aggregation across related entities only where there is majority ownership; as written it could inappropriately aggregate sales of minor investors and misclassify small firms.

[P2] The 45,400 kg/site production cutoff will disqualify many small firms with a single large product batch; EPA should clarify whether temporary spikes (e.g., one-time project production) count toward the annual site total.

[P2] Provision lacks guidance on how to apportion production at co-manufactured or toll-manufactured sites where multiple companies operate; clarify responsibility for determining whether a site exceeds 45,400 kg.

[P3] The alternative $11 million threshold (regardless of production) is confusing and potentially creates two inconsistent small business standards; EPA must explain when the $11 million test applies versus the $110 million test.

[P3] If the $11 million threshold applies to certain industries, EPA should specify the industries and rationale; otherwise the lower threshold will arbitrarily disqualify many mid-size manufacturers.

[P4] Reliance on BLS GDP deflators for adjusting sales thresholds could lag actual inflation experienced by chemical manufacturers; EPA should consider using industry-specific price indices or CPI adjustments instead.

[P5] The 20% GDP-deflator change trigger for adjusting thresholds is arbitrary; commenters request explanation why 20% was chosen and suggest annual review regardless of 20% to avoid outdated thresholds.

[P5] EPA’s discretion “may adjust…whenever the Agency deems it necessary” is overly broad; commenters request a mandatory schedule for adjustment or a requirement to publish a justification with each adjustment.

[P6] Notification in the Federal Register is necessary but insufficient; EPA should also provide direct notice to registered TSCA filers and publish plain-language guidance and a transition period before changes take effect.

[P7] The statement that failure to submit is unlawful must include reference to the penalties and due process protections; commenters request explicit citation of penalty provisions and opportunity to cure inadvertent omissions.

[P8] The requirement to keep and permit access to records should specify record retention periods, security/confidentiality protections for CBI, and procedures for inspection to avoid proprietary data exposure.

[P9] The inspection permission in § 711.1(c) should require inspectors to present warrants or credentials and limit inspections to reasonable hours; commenters urge safeguards to protect confidential business operations.

[P10] The subpoena authority should require notice to the affected person and an opportunity to seek protective orders for CBI; industry requests a clear process for challenging overbroad document requests.

[P11] The exempt substance categories list in § 711.6 is insufficiently defined; manufacturers seek a complete list with examples and clear criteria for partial versus full exemptions.

[P12] The carve-out that nominally exempt substances are nonetheless reportable if subject to other TSCA actions creates confusion; commenters request cross-references to the specific TSCA rules, orders, and court relief that trigger reporting.

[P13] The 25,000 lb (11,340 kg) site threshold should be harmonized with international reporting thresholds and other U.S. federal programs to reduce burdens of multiple, inconsistent reporting regimes.

[P13] The annual threshold should allow aggregation across production locations under common control for substances intentionally moved between sites; the rule should clarify whether such intra-company transfers count toward the per-site threshold.

[P14] Lowering the threshold to 2,500 lb for substances subject to certain TSCA actions is appropriate for targeted oversight, but EPA must clearly list which “subject to” statuses (proposed rule, consent order, SNUR, etc.) trigger the lower threshold.

[P14] There is risk of retroactive application where a substance becomes subject to a rule mid-year; EPA should clarify whether the 2,500 lb threshold applies only prospectively for the principal reporting year following promulgation.

[P15] The small manufacturer exemption in § 711.9 should explicitly define how to calculate combined sales across related affiliates to prevent inconsistent interpretations by firms and EPA.

[P16] The exception that small manufacturers are still subject to reporting for substances under certain TSCA actions undermines the small business relief; EPA should provide a de minimis exception or phased compliance for small entities.

[P17] The enumerated circumstances for exemption under § 711.10 are vague in places (e.g., “when: (then…)”); EPA must publish the full list and illustrative scenarios to avoid misapplication.

[P18] The R&D small-quantity exemption in § 711.10(a) lacks a quantitative definition of “small quantities” and clear boundaries between R&D and pilot/commercial production; commenters request numerical caps and criteria.

[P19] The article-import exemption in § 711.10(b) should be clarified to state whether imported articles containing trace amounts of a reportable substance (e.g., surface coatings) qualify for the exemption.

[P20] The byproduct exemption for materials “intended only for burning, disposal, or component extraction” leaves uncertainty about mixed-use byproducts; companies request guidance on byproducts that have multiple commercial uses.

[P21] The site-limited enclosed-system recycling exemption requires detailed recordkeeping and reporting instructions so firms can demonstrate eligibility; otherwise firms will be deterred from beneficial onsite recycling.

[P22] The byproduct exemption request procedure’s requirement for written requests with specified labeling is onerous; EPA should provide electronic submission templates and clarify the acceptable level of confidential information in requests.

[P23] EPA’s obligation to consider the “totality of available information” when reviewing byproduct exemption requests is too vague; requesters want a specific decision-making framework and timelines beyond the 120-day acknowledgment.

[P24] The criterion to consider whether the byproduct is recycled/used within an enclosed, same-process, same-site system is narrowly written and may exclude legitimate cross-process onsite recoveries; EPA should allow enclosed reuse at contiguous sites under common control.

[P25] Considering whether the site reports other chemicals (especially those made from the byproduct) creates circularity; firms request guidance on how to demonstrate innocuous downstream use to qualify for exemption.

[P26] The consideration of whether “EPA has a current interest” is subjective; stakeholders request criteria for what constitutes “current interest” and an appeal mechanism if EPA declines exemption on that basis.

[P27] Requiring that a byproduct “must have already been reported or would be expected to be reported” before granting exemption effectively nullifies the exemption for new processes; commenters request that EPA allow exemption for novel byproducts if other criteria are met.

[P28] EPA’s ability to initiate rulemaking to revise the exempt-byproduct list is appropriate, but the rule should commit to periodic review cycles (e.g., every 5 years) and stakeholder input sessions before rulemaking.

[P29] The 12-month pre-principal-year submission deadline for amendment requests is overly restrictive for small firms that discover a byproduct after that window; EPA should allow late petitions with expedited review under defined circumstances.

[P30] Exempting byproducts made solely in non-integral equipment is sensible, but the rule must define “not integral” and provide examples to prevent inconsistent application by inspectors.

[P31] The pollution control equipment exemption needs clarity on whether temporary upsets (e.g., startups/shutdowns) that produce reportable byproducts count toward exemption.

[P32] The boilers exemption for byproducts used to generate heat/electricity for the site should clarify whether exports of recovered fuel or heat to third parties negate the exemption.

[P33] The impurity exemption is too broad; EPA should specify concentration cutoffs or criteria for when an impurity becomes reportable (e.g., >0.X% by weight).

[P34] The exemption for byproducts not used for commercial purposes should define “commercial” (e.g., internal reuse, research vs. sale) and require documentation proving noncommercial status.

[P35] The exemption for substances formed incidentally by environmental exposure needs clearer boundaries, especially for post-manufacture transformations that result in persistent or toxic substances.

[P36] For substances formed during storage/disposal, EPA should require that firms maintain and produce documentation that the formation was truly incidental and not due to negligence or foreseeable reaction paths.

[P37] The end-use formation exemption should be limited to substances not distributed in commerce under any condition; clarifying transport and transfer scenarios would reduce confusion.

[P38] The exemption for substances formed during manufacture of articles but not further chemically changed needs examples and limits (e.g., surface treatments that wash off in use should be reportable).

[P39] The exemption for substances formed when additives function as intended creates potential loopholes where harmful reaction products are produced; EPA should require reporting when known hazardous transformation products form even if additive “functions.”

[P40] The nonisolated intermediate exemption requires clearer definitions of “nonisolated” and controls on residence time and containment; otherwise, firms may claim exemption for materials effectively isolated during processing.

[P41] The requirement to submit specified information for each substance meeting thresholds should include a machine-readable data schema to reduce reporting burden and errors.

[P42] Requiring a separate report for each chemical at each site will be administratively burdensome for multi-site, multi-chemical manufacturers; EPA should permit consolidated submissions with site-chemical line items.

[P43] Mandating use of e-CDRweb is reasonable but EPA must ensure the tool is accessible, secure, and provides batch upload capabilities for large filers; request for API documentation and test environment.

[P44] The requirement that submissions contain all information in paragraph (b) should allow partial submissions with explanations where information is not reasonably ascertainable, to avoid rejections for incomplete data.

[P45] The single Form U per site per chemical requirement is inflexible for co-manufacturing arrangements where multiple companies must report the same chemical; EPA should allow joint submissions or designate a single responsible party with attestation from others.

[P46] The obligation to provide information “known or reasonably ascertainable” is subjective; request guidance and a safe-harbor statement for diligent inquiries and good-faith attempts to obtain supplier data.

[P47] The detailed categories in (b)(1)-(b)(4) may conflict with supplier confidentiality and international privacy laws; EPA should provide clear CBI protection mechanisms and allow aggregated or coded reporting where necessary.

[P48] The processing/use exemption cross-reference to § 711.6 requires examples of when processing/use info is exempted to enable reporters to determine whether to submit (b)(4) data.

[P49] The certification signed by an authorized official should be accompanied by potential penalties for false statements, but EPA must allow delegation to qualified signatories for large firms; specify criteria for “authorized official.”

[P50] The requirement to report “currently correct” company and site information should permit reporting of parent-level contact when site-level contacts are unavailable, with follow-up rights for EPA to request corrections.

[P51] Requiring a D&B D-U-N-S® number for the highest-level U.S. parent is burdensome for companies without D&B identifiers; EPA should accept alternative identifiers (EIN, LEI) or provide assistance to obtain a D&B number.

[P52] The technical contact requirement must allow third-party consultants to serve and include attestations of authority; also allow multiple technical contacts for complex sites.

[P53] In co-manufacturing, requiring both controlling and producing site D&B numbers may expose proprietary contractual relationships; EPA should permit masked identifiers or alternative reporting methods to protect confidentiality.

[P54] The six-digit NAICS code requirement is unclear for diversified sites with multiple manufacturing lines; allow multiple NAICS codes and guidance on which to select as primary.

[P55] The chemical-specific information list is extensive; commenters ask for phased implementation, de minimis thresholds, or reduced data elements for low-volume substances.

[P56] The requirement to use CA Index names and CASRNs may be problematic for substances without CASRNs; EPA should accept alternative identifiers and provide a pathway for new substance registration.

[P57] Allowing metal compound category reporting as an alternative is helpful, but EPA must provide definitive lists of included compounds and clear exclusion rules to prevent ambiguity.

[P58] Determining thresholds for metal compound categories based on total amounts of all members may unfairly capture trace constituents; EPA should allow reporting by individual metal where analytical differentiation is practicable.

[P59] The joint-submission process where an importer requests a supplier to submit identity when supplier claims CBI is necessary, but the rule must define timelines, consequences if supplier refuses, and alternative documentation the importer can provide.

[P60] Similarly, when a manufacturer lacks identity of a confidential reactant, EPA should permit submission of functional description and analytical data in lieu of supplier identity, with a safe harbor for good-faith attempts to obtain upstream information.

[P61] Electronic-only acceptance of joint submissions via e-CDRweb/CDX is problematic where suppliers lack electronic access or are foreign entities; EPA should permit mailed requests or provide an intermediary filing mechanism.

[P62] The requirement to state whether a substance is manufactured domestically, imported, or both needs to account for substances produced by contract manufacturers; clarify how contractors should report manufacturing status.

[P63] Reporting total annual domestic and imported volumes to two significant figures raises rounding concerns for low-volume substances; EPA should provide rounding rules (e.g., minimum reporting unit) and allow metric units.

[P64] Reporting volumes used on-site and directly exported to two significant figures may require export-tracking systems some firms lack; EPA should allow estimates with specified confidence intervals or require best-available data only.

[P65] The designation of whether an imported substance is physically present at the reporting site needs definition for goods-in-transit, bonded warehouses, and off-site storage managed by third parties.

[P66] Requiring byproduct percentage rounded to nearest 10% (or 1% if under 5%) could obscure meaningful differences for regulatory decisions; commenters request reporting to fixed significant figures or an option for exact values when available.

[P67] The recycled vs. disposed designation should include definitions of “recycled” (e.g., energy recovery vs. material recovery) and examples, and require documentation where classification is ambiguous.

[P68] Number-of-workers-exposed codes W1–W8 may not capture contractor or intermittent worker exposure; EPA should require inclusion of contracted/temporary workers and provide guidance on estimating exposure headcount.

[P69] Reporting maximum off-site concentration with codes M1–M5 needs numeric concentration ranges tied to codes; stakeholders request explicit ranges and testing protocol references.

[P70] Physical form reporting when sent off-site should include guidance for multi-form shipments (e.g., slurry that separates) and allow selection of predominant form or multiple codes with percentages.

[P71] Requiring percentages of production by physical form rounded to nearest 10% is imprecise for certain processes; request option to report exact percentages where process controls provide them.

[P72] The processing/use information obligation for recipient and controlled sites “to the extent known or reasonably ascertainable” should permit suppliers to provide aggregate downstream use categories if specific customer end-uses are protected as CBI.

The rule’s combined-sales test should allow aggregation across related entities only where there is majority ownership; as written it could inappropriately aggregate sales of minor investors and misclassify small firms.

The 45,400 kg/site production cutoff will disqualify many small firms with a single large product batch; EPA should clarify whether temporary spikes (e.g., one-time project production) count toward the annual site total.

Provision lacks guidance on how to apportion production at co-manufactured or toll-manufactured sites where multiple companies operate; clarify responsibility for determining whether a site exceeds 45,400 kg.

The alternative $11 million threshold (regardless of production) is confusing and potentially creates two inconsistent small business standards; EPA must explain when the $11 million test applies versus the $110 million test.
If the $11 million threshold applies to certain industries, EPA should specify the industries and rationale; otherwise the lower threshold will arbitrarily disqualify many mid-size manufacturers.

Reliance on BLS GDP deflators for adjusting sales thresholds could lag actual inflation experienced by chemical manufacturers; EPA should consider using industry-specific price indices or CPI adjustments instead.
The 20% GDP-deflator change trigger for adjusting thresholds is arbitrary; commenters request explanation why 20% was chosen and suggest annual review regardless of 20% to avoid outdated thresholds.

EPA’s discretion “may adjust…whenever the Agency deems it necessary” is overly broad; commenters request a mandatory schedule for adjustment or a requirement to publish a justification with each adjustment.

Notification in the Federal Register is necessary but insufficient; EPA should also provide direct notice to registered TSCA filers and publish plain-language guidance and a transition period before changes take effect.

The statement that failure to submit is unlawful must include reference to the penalties and due process protections; commenters request explicit citation of penalty provisions and opportunity to cure inadvertent omissions.

The requirement to keep and permit access to records should specify record retention periods, security/confidentiality protections for CBI, and procedures for inspection to avoid proprietary data exposure.

The inspection permission in § 711.1(c) should require inspectors to present warrants or credentials and limit inspections to reasonable hours; commenters urge safeguards to protect confidential business operations.

The subpoena authority should require notice to the affected person and an opportunity to seek protective orders for CBI; industry requests a clear process for challenging overbroad document requests.
The exempt substance categories list in § 711.6 is insufficiently defined; manufacturers seek a complete list with examples and clear criteria for partial versus full exemptions.

The carve-out that nominally exempt substances are nonetheless reportable if subject to other TSCA actions creates confusion; commenters request cross-references to the specific TSCA rules, orders, and court relief that trigger reporting.
The 25,000 lb (11,340 kg) site threshold should be harmonized with international reporting thresholds and other U.S. federal programs to reduce burdens of multiple, inconsistent reporting regimes.

The annual threshold should allow aggregation across production locations under common control for substances intentionally moved between sites; the rule should clarify whether such intra-company transfers count toward the per-site threshold.

Lowering the threshold to 2,500 lb for substances subject to certain TSCA actions is appropriate for targeted oversight, but EPA must clearly list which “subject to” statuses (proposed rule, consent order, SNUR, etc.) trigger the lower threshold.

There is risk of retroactive application where a substance becomes subject to a rule mid-year; EPA should clarify whether the 2,500 lb threshold applies only prospectively for the principal reporting year following promulgation.
The small manufacturer exemption in § 711.9 should explicitly define how to calculate combined sales across related affiliates to prevent inconsistent interpretations by firms and EPA.

The exception that small manufacturers are still subject to reporting for substances under certain TSCA actions undermines the small business relief; EPA should provide a de minimis exception or phased compliance for small entities.
The enumerated circumstances for exemption under § 711.10 are vague in places (e.g., “when: (then…)”); EPA must publish the full list and illustrative scenarios to avoid misapplication.

The R&D small-quantity exemption in § 711.10(a) lacks a quantitative definition of “small quantities” and clear boundaries between R&D and pilot/commercial production; commenters request numerical caps and criteria.

The article-import exemption in § 711.10(b) should be clarified to state whether imported articles containing trace amounts of a reportable substance (e.g., surface coatings) qualify for the exemption.

The byproduct exemption for materials “intended only for burning, disposal, or component extraction” leaves uncertainty about mixed-use byproducts; companies request guidance on byproducts that have multiple commercial uses.

The site-limited enclosed-system recycling exemption requires detailed recordkeeping and reporting instructions so firms can demonstrate eligibility; otherwise firms will be deterred from beneficial onsite recycling.

The byproduct exemption request procedure’s requirement for written requests with specified labeling is onerous; EPA should provide electronic submission templates and clarify the acceptable level of confidential information in requests.

EPA’s obligation to consider the “totality of available information” when reviewing byproduct exemption requests is too vague; requesters want a specific decision-making framework and timelines beyond the 120-day acknowledgment.

The criterion to consider whether the byproduct is recycled/used within an enclosed, same-process, same-site system is narrowly written and may exclude legitimate cross-process onsite recoveries; EPA should allow enclosed reuse at contiguous sites under common control.

Considering whether the site reports other chemicals (especially those made from the byproduct) creates circularity; firms request guidance on how to demonstrate innocuous downstream use to qualify for exemption.

The consideration of whether “EPA has a current interest” is subjective; stakeholders request criteria for what constitutes “current interest” and an appeal mechanism if EPA declines exemption on that basis.

Requiring that a byproduct “must have already been reported or would be expected to be reported” before granting exemption effectively nullifies the exemption for new processes; commenters request that EPA allow exemption for novel byproducts if other criteria are met.

EPA’s ability to initiate rulemaking to revise the exempt-byproduct list is appropriate, but the rule should commit to periodic review cycles (e.g., every 5 years) and stakeholder input sessions before rulemaking.

The 12-month pre-principal-year submission deadline for amendment requests is overly restrictive for small firms that discover a byproduct after that window; EPA should allow late petitions with expedited review under defined circumstances.
Exempting byproducts made solely in non-integral equipment is sensible, but the rule must define “not integral” and provide examples to prevent inconsistent application by inspectors.
The pollution control equipment exemption needs clarity on whether temporary upsets (e.g., startups/shutdowns) that produce reportable byproducts count toward exemption.
The boilers exemption for byproducts used to generate heat/electricity for the site should clarify whether exports of recovered fuel or heat to third parties negate the exemption.
The impurity exemption is too broad; EPA should specify concentration cutoffs or criteria for when an impurity becomes reportable (e.g., >0.X% by weight).
The exemption for byproducts not used for commercial purposes should define “commercial” (e.g., internal reuse, research vs. sale) and require documentation proving noncommercial status.
The exemption for substances formed incidentally by environmental exposure needs clearer boundaries, especially for post-manufacture transformations that result in persistent or toxic substances.

For substances formed during storage/disposal, EPA should require that firms maintain and produce documentation that the formation was truly incidental and not due to negligence or foreseeable reaction paths.
The end-use formation exemption should be limited to substances not distributed in commerce under any condition; clarifying transport and transfer scenarios would reduce confusion.
The exemption for substances formed during manufacture of articles but not further chemically changed needs examples and limits (e.g., surface treatments that wash off in use should be reportable).

The exemption for substances formed when additives function as intended creates potential loopholes where harmful reaction products are produced; EPA should require reporting when known hazardous transformation products form even if additive “functions.”

The nonisolated intermediate exemption requires clearer definitions of “nonisolated” and controls on residence time and containment; otherwise, firms may claim exemption for materials effectively isolated during processing.
The requirement to submit specified information for each substance meeting thresholds should include a machine-readable data schema to reduce reporting burden and errors.

Requiring a separate report for each chemical at each site will be administratively burdensome for multi-site, multi-chemical manufacturers; EPA should permit consolidated submissions with site-chemical line items.

Mandating use of e-CDRweb is reasonable but EPA must ensure the tool is accessible, secure, and provides batch upload capabilities for large filers; request for API documentation and test environment.

The requirement that submissions contain all information in paragraph (b) should allow partial submissions with explanations where information is not reasonably ascertainable, to avoid rejections for incomplete data.

The single Form U per site per chemical requirement is inflexible for co-manufacturing arrangements where multiple companies must report the same chemical; EPA should allow joint submissions or designate a single responsible party with attestation from others.

The obligation to provide information “known or reasonably ascertainable” is subjective; request guidance and a safe-harbor statement for diligent inquiries and good-faith attempts to obtain supplier data.

The detailed categories in (b)(1)-(b)(4) may conflict with supplier confidentiality and international privacy laws; EPA should provide clear CBI protection mechanisms and allow aggregated or coded reporting where necessary.
The processing/use exemption cross-reference to § 711.6 requires examples of when processing/use info is exempted to enable reporters to determine whether to submit (b)(4) data.

The certification signed by an authorized official should be accompanied by potential penalties for false statements, but EPA must allow delegation to qualified signatories for large firms; specify criteria for “authorized official.”

The requirement to report “currently correct” company and site information should permit reporting of parent-level contact when site-level contacts are unavailable, with follow-up rights for EPA to request corrections.

Requiring a D&B D-U-N-S® number for the highest-level U.S. parent is burdensome for companies without D&B identifiers; EPA should accept alternative identifiers (EIN, LEI) or provide assistance to obtain a D&B number.
The technical contact requirement must allow third-party consultants to serve and include attestations of authority; also allow multiple technical contacts for complex sites.

In co-manufacturing, requiring both controlling and producing site D&B numbers may expose proprietary contractual relationships; EPA should permit masked identifiers or alternative reporting methods to protect confidentiality.
The six-digit NAICS code requirement is unclear for diversified sites with multiple manufacturing lines; allow multiple NAICS codes and guidance on which to select as primary.
The chemical-specific information list is extensive; commenters ask for phased implementation, de minimis thresholds, or reduced data elements for low-volume substances.
The requirement to use CA Index names and CASRNs may be problematic for substances without CASRNs; EPA should accept alternative identifiers and provide a pathway for new substance registration.
Allowing metal compound category reporting as an alternative is helpful, but EPA must provide definitive lists of included compounds and clear exclusion rules to prevent ambiguity.

Determining thresholds for metal compound categories based on total amounts of all members may unfairly capture trace constituents; EPA should allow reporting by individual metal where analytical differentiation is practicable.

The joint-submission process where an importer requests a supplier to submit identity when supplier claims CBI is necessary, but the rule must define timelines, consequences if supplier refuses, and alternative documentation the importer can provide.

Similarly, when a manufacturer lacks identity of a confidential reactant, EPA should permit submission of functional description and analytical data in lieu of supplier identity, with a safe harbor for good-faith attempts to obtain upstream information.

Electronic-only acceptance of joint submissions via e-CDRweb/CDX is problematic where suppliers lack electronic access or are foreign entities; EPA should permit mailed requests or provide an intermediary filing mechanism.

The requirement to state whether a substance is manufactured domestically, imported, or both needs to account for substances produced by contract manufacturers; clarify how contractors should report manufacturing status.

Reporting total annual domestic and imported volumes to two significant figures raises rounding concerns for low-volume substances; EPA should provide rounding rules (e.g., minimum reporting unit) and allow metric units.

Reporting volumes used on-site and directly exported to two significant figures may require export-tracking systems some firms lack; EPA should allow estimates with specified confidence intervals or require best-available data only.
The designation of whether an imported substance is physically present at the reporting site needs definition for goods-in-transit, bonded warehouses, and off-site storage managed by third parties.

Requiring byproduct percentage rounded to nearest 10% (or 1% if under 5%) could obscure meaningful differences for regulatory decisions; commenters request reporting to fixed significant figures or an option for exact values when available.
The recycled vs. disposed designation should include definitions of “recycled” (e.g., energy recovery vs. material recovery) and examples, and require documentation where classification is ambiguous.

Number-of-workers-exposed codes W1–W8 may not capture contractor or intermittent worker exposure; EPA should require inclusion of contracted/temporary workers and provide guidance on estimating exposure headcount.
Reporting maximum off-site concentration with codes M1–M5 needs numeric concentration ranges tied to codes; stakeholders request explicit ranges and testing protocol references.
Physical form reporting when sent off-site should include guidance for multi-form shipments (e.g., slurry that separates) and allow selection of predominant form or multiple codes with percentages.
Requiring percentages of production by physical form rounded to nearest 10% is imprecise for certain processes; request option to report exact percentages where process controls provide them.

The Table 7 letter codes for industrial processing/use operations must be published well in advance and include examples; otherwise reporters will miscode and face enforcement risk.

The byproduct exemption request must include CASRN and process ID, but EPA should allow submission of structural or descriptive identifiers where CASRNs are not assigned, and permit confidential attachments to avoid public disclosure of sensitive process details.

[P1] The provision allowing an inspector to cancel a controlled pre-stamping privilege orally creates unacceptable due-process risk because oral cancellations can be vague, inconsistent, and difficult for establishments to refute later.

[P1] Industry requests that § 327.10(d)(2) specify that only a written cancellation can take immediate effect on operations; if oral cancellation is used, it should be treated as a temporary suspension pending written confirmation.

[P2] The requirement to confirm oral cancellations "as promptly as circumstances allow" is unacceptably vague; commenters ask for a specific deadline (e.g., within 48 or 72 hours) for written confirmation.

[P2] Legal experts note that without a firm timeline for written confirmation of oral cancellations, establishments cannot timely prepare appeals under 9 CFR 500.9 and therefore their appeal rights are effectively undermined.

[P3] The cross-reference to 9 CFR 500.9 is appropriate, but commenters request explicit notice language required at the time of cancellation informing the person of their appeal rights and deadlines under 9 CFR 500.9.

[P4] The obligation that appeals "must state all of the facts and reasons" could be read to bar later supplementation of evidence; industry and legal advocates request explicit allowance for supplemental evidence submitted within a defined period (e.g., 14 days) after filing the initial appeal.

[P4] Civil liberties advocates argue that requiring complete factual statements at time of filing may unfairly penalize appellants who need agency records to assemble full facts; they request that appeals be permitted to incorporate documents obtained later or to request discovery.

[P5] Requiring appeals of any program employee decision to go to the employee's immediate supervisor risks conflicts of interest if that supervisor directly oversees the employee; commenters urge that appeals be directed to an independent appeals officer or higher-level official not in the direct supervisory chain for the employee making the decision.

[P6] Multiple commenters support retaining the ability to appeal inspector decisions under 9 CFR 500.9 but request clarification on the scope of appealable "decisions" (e.g., operational instructions vs. formal determinations) to prevent frivolous appeals and inconsistent enforcement.

[P7] For § 354.134, trade groups ask that the rule clarify whether appeals will stay enforcement action (i.e., whether the inspector's decision is stayed pending appeal) or whether appellants must continue to comply while appeal is pending.

[P8] Commenters note inconsistent phrasing across §§ 355.39, 381.35, and 381.202(d) and request harmonization to ensure the same appeal procedures apply across all inspection programs, including identical notice, timelines, and rights to present evidence.

[P9] Consumer safety organizations request that appeals not be used to delay enforcement where there is an imminent public health risk; they recommend the rule explicitly allow immediate enforcement action despite an appeal in such cases, with expedited appeal procedures.

[P10] For § 381.202(d) requiring retention tags and segregation pending appeal, industry comments that the costs and logistical burdens of segregating poultry/products and retaining U.S. tags should be quantified and that the Agency should provide guidance or financial relief mechanisms for small processors.

[P11] Small processors warn that the requirement to segregate products "in a manner approved by the inspector" is vague and could lead to inconsistent inspector-imposed burdens; they request objective standards or examples of acceptable segregation methods.

[P12] Import establishments object to oral cancellation authority under § 381.204(f)(2) mirroring § 327.10(d)(2) for the same due-process reasons and request that any cancellation that disrupts import operations be provided in writing with immediate explanation.

[P13] The repeated requirement across provisions that oral cancellations be "confirmed in writing, as promptly as circumstances allow" should be standardized with a single maximum timeframe (commenters suggest 72 hours) and uniform content requirements for the written confirmation.

[P14] Appellants request that the rule require written confirmations to include: the factual basis for cancellation, specific regulatory citations, the effective date/time of the cancellation, and instructions on appeal filing and timelines.

[P15] Legal commenters point out that appeals of cancelled pre-stamping privileges (§§ 327.10(d)(2), 381.204(f)(2)) should explicitly allow for temporary reinstatement or stay of cancellation where the appellant demonstrates likelihood of success on the merits and irreparable harm, to avoid disproportionate economic damage.

[P16] Regarding § 500.9(a), industry asks for clarification of what constitutes being "adversely affected"—whether procedural actions (e.g., requests for documentation) qualify—so businesses can determine appeal eligibility.

[P17] The 30-calendar-day deadline in § 500.9(a) to file initial appeals is too short when cancellations can occur orally and written confirmation may be delayed; commenters request that the 30-day clock start from receipt of the written confirmation, or extend the deadline to 60 days.

[P18] Advocacy groups argue that appeals should be permitted to include any arguments and evidence (as § 500.9(a) states) but the rule should also require the Agency to actively provide relevant inspection records and rationale to appellants promptly to ensure a fair process.

[P19] Commenters request that appeals to the immediate supervisor (§ 500.9(b)) include protections against bias by requiring supervisors with direct operational responsibility to recuse themselves or to forward appeals to an independent adjudicator.

[P20] For § 592.400 and similar cross-references allowing appeals, tribal and small-entity stakeholders request that the Agency provide plain-language appeal guides and filing templates to reduce procedural errors and ensure equitable access.

[P11] Consumer advocates request that the requirement to tag and segregate poultry/products pending appeal include chain-of-custody recordkeeping requirements and timelines for how long products may be held, to prevent unnecessary market disruption.

[P15] Food exporters and importers ask for an expedited appeal track specifically for cancellations of pre-stamping privileges to minimize port delays and increased storage/holding costs.

[P1] Several commenters recommend adding an internal notice-and-hearing requirement prior to cancellation for non-emergency compliance failures, reserving immediate oral cancellations for safety emergencies only.

[P3] Trade associations ask for clarification on whether third-party contractors or agents (e.g., customs brokers) acting on behalf of an establishment have standing to file appeals under 9 CFR 500.9 for cancelled pre-stamping privileges.

[P4] Appellants request that the rule specify whether failure to include every fact in the initial appeal will be treated as a jurisdictional defect (leading to dismissal) or whether the Agency will allow amendment of appeals.

[P12] Importers request that when pre-stamping privileges are cancelled, the Agency be required to provide alternative processing or inspection options to avoid cargo bottlenecks, with clear timelines for releasing detained goods.

[P9] Public health NGOs urge that when appeals concern labeling or product identity that pose potential consumer risk, the Agency must prioritize and resolve appeals within a set short timeframe (e.g., 10 business days).

[P17] Labor organizations request that employees and worker representatives be listed as potential appellants when inspector actions affect workplace safety or working conditions, clarifying their appeal rights under § 500.9.

[P6] Veterinary and scientific stakeholders ask that the rule allow for technical or scientific review panels to be consulted during appeals involving technical inspection determinations (e.g., residue testing), to ensure evidence-based outcomes.

[P1] The obligation to "consider" allowing use under a treatment IDE is too vague—stakeholders need clear standards and timelines for FDA decision-making rather than a discretionary "shall consider" standard.

[P1] FDA should be required to publish a written decision with specific reasons whenever it denies a request to use an investigational device under a treatment IDE, to ensure transparency and accountability.

[P1] The rule should specify an explicit timeframe (e.g., 30 or 60 days) for FDA to "consider" and respond to treatment IDE requests to avoid undue delay for patients with serious conditions.

[P2] The definition of "serious or immediately life‑threatening" is not provided; commenters will request that FDA adopt or cross‑reference existing statutory definitions (e.g., from 21 U.S.C. §360bbb or FDA guidance) to ensure consistent application.

[P2] Patient advocacy groups will argue that "serious" should include progressive diseases that significantly affect quality of life, not only imminent mortality, and ask FDA to clarify examples and criteria.

[P2] Industry will request explicit criteria and objective measures (e.g., mortality risk, morbidity scales, validated clinical endpoints) that FDA will use to classify a condition as "serious" or "immediately life‑threatening."

[P3] The provision requiring "no comparable or satisfactory alternative device or other therapy" is vague; commenters will ask FDA to define "comparable" and "satisfactory" and indicate how off‑label use, emergency use authorizations, or compassionate use access will be considered.

[P3] Manufacturers and clinicians will request that FDA clarify whether cost, accessibility, or patient-specific contraindications to existing therapies can make the investigational device eligible under the "no comparable alternative" criterion.

[P3] Patient advocates will argue that "no satisfactory alternative" should be interpreted broadly so that patients who have failed standard therapy or are intolerant of approved treatments can access investigational devices.

[P4] Requiring that the device be "under investigation in a controlled clinical trial" could exclude promising devices tested only in single‑arm studies or real‑world evidence; commenters will ask FDA to allow flexibility when randomized controlled trials are not feasible.

[P4] Academic researchers will request clarification of what constitutes a "controlled clinical trial" (randomized, historical controls, prospective controls) and whether international trials count.

[P4] Small device manufacturers will argue that the requirement to be "under investigation" may unduly delay access for devices ready for expanded use but not yet entered into formal controlled trials; they will request alternative pathways or conditional criteria.

[P5] The permission to use investigational devices "during the clinical trial or prior to final action on the marketing application" raises concerns about preserving trial integrity—commenters will request safeguards (e.g., limits on eligibility, separate data collection) to prevent bias or enrollment impact.

[P5] Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) and clinical investigators will request explicit requirements for informed consent language and additional oversight when devices are used outside the trial under a treatment IDE.

[P5] Ethicists will caution that allowing broad use during trials may create incentives for clinicians or sponsors to preferentially treat non‑trial patients, undermining recruitment; they will ask FDA to impose conditions to protect trial enrollment.

[P6] Permitting availability after completion of all clinical trials for "serious diseases" could be interpreted to allow widespread premarket access before FDA determines safety and effectiveness—commenters will ask for clear limits and post‑marketing surveillance requirements.

[P6] Payers will request clarity on evidence requirements for coverage decisions when devices are made available post‑trials but before marketing approval, to avoid inconsistent reimbursement policies.

[P6] Patient groups will support post‑trial availability but request mandatory registries and long‑term follow‑up obligations for sponsors to monitor safety once the device is used widely under a treatment IDE.

[P7] Allowing availability before completion of all clinical trials for immediately life‑threatening disease invites potential abuse; commenters will ask for strict eligibility criteria, independent review (e.g., expert panel), and time‑limited access tied to ongoing data collection.

[P7] Legal experts will note the need for explicit liability protections or clarification of sponsor/institution responsibilities when devices are used pre‑approval in immediately life‑threatening cases, including indemnification and reporting obligations.

[P7] Clinicians will request operational guidance on prioritization and allocation when supply of the investigational device is limited but multiple eligible patients request access under this provision.

[P1] Consumer safety advocates will demand that FDA articulate how it will weigh potential benefits vs. risks when "considering" use—e.g., minimum risk/benefit thresholds or quantitative risk‑benefit frameworks.

[P3] The rule should require sponsors to document and submit evidence that no comparable or satisfactory alternatives exist in the intended patient population, including literature reviews and expert statements.

[P4] The rule should permit devices in adaptive designs, platform trials, or other nontraditional "controlled" trial formats to qualify, and FDA should explicitly acknowledge these study designs.

[P5] Commenters will ask whether use "during the clinical trial" is limited to sites participating in the trial or can be extended to outside institutions; rule should clarify site eligibility and data reporting expectations.

[P1] The comment deadline of February 26, 2018 is unreasonable and inadequate because the AD was issued with an effective date of April 12, 2017, giving stakeholders insufficient time to review technical materials and prepare meaningful comments; FAA should extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] Legal experts will note that the provision's phrasing ("FAA must receive comments on this AD by February 26, 2018") is ambiguous about postmark vs. receipt — commenters request clarification that comments will be accepted if postmarked by that date or submitted electronically by 11:59 PM ET on that date.

[P2] Operators comment that the general compliance obligation ("must comply within the specified times unless already done") lacks clear grandfathering language for actions performed under previous AD 2017–07–10 or voluntary modifications, and request explicit recognition that prior compliance documentation satisfies this AD.

[P2] Maintenance organizations ask FAA to clarify whether "specified times" in the AD refer only to the times explicitly listed in paragraphs (h)(1)–(6) or whether other compliance times in referenced service letters also apply.

[P3] Several operators and pilot associations will object to the permanent restriction to non-aerobatic flight until required actions are completed, arguing the restriction is overly broad for aircraft used in utility or limited aerobatics operations and requesting FAA to define "aerobatic flight" consistent with 14 CFR 1.1 or permit limited maneuvering for flight training and competence checks.

[P3] Legal commenters will assert that retaining the effective date of April 12, 2017 for the aerobatic restriction (while issuing a new comment period to Feb 26, 2018) raises retroactivity concerns and request FAA justify why an effective restriction predates the current notice-and-comment opportunity.

[P4] Affected owners will object to the requirement to fabricate a placard "using at least 1/8 inch letters" without specifying materials, location tolerances, or whether machine-printed or hand-lettered placards are acceptable; they request specific placard material, color contrast, mounting method, and exact placement coordinates on the instrument panel be provided.

[P4] Some owners/operators request that FAA allow use of manufacturer-supplied placards or previously approved placards instead of requiring on-the-spot fabrication, to ensure durability and compliance with label standards.

[P5] Pilot groups and individual owner-operators will support allowing private pilot certificate holders to fabricate/install the placard but request clarification that the pilot must be the owner/operator of the aircraft (not merely the current temporary operator) and ask whether a certificated mechanic may perform the task instead.

[P5] Other commenters (maintenance shops and repair stations) will request that FAA explicitly permit certificated mechanics to perform the placard fabrication/installation and record the action, to avoid ambiguity about who may legally perform the work.

[P6] Maintenance record keepers and repair stations request clearer instructions on the required content of the entry under 14 CFR 43.9(a)(1)–(4) and 91.417(a)(2)(v), including whether the specific AD number, placard text, installer name, and signature are required; they ask FAA to provide a suggested sample entry.

[P7] Air carriers and commercial operators point out that referencing 14 CFR 121.380 and 135.439 without tailored guidance creates uncertainty about how to integrate the recordkeeping requirement into their existing maintenance control manuals and request an explicit statement about whether standard carrier logs suffice.

[P8] Several commenters (owners, maintenance providers) will argue the 10 hours TIS initial inspection requirement is overly burdensome and impractical for many operators — particularly those with limited access to maintenance facilities — and propose extending the inspection window to 25–50 hours TIS or allowing the inspection to occur at the next scheduled maintenance inspection if within 50 hours.

[P8] Industry commenters will also request clarification that ACAC SL No. 442 procedures are mandatory normative methods for the inspection versus recommended guidance, and ask that the AD incorporate critical procedural steps (e.g., inspection points, tools, magnification) directly to avoid misinterpretation.

[P9] Owners will request that FAA clarify whether removal of the placard (if no damage is found) requires any additional documentation besides the required record entry, and whether the removal can be performed by the same private pilot/owner or must be done by a certificated mechanic.

[P9] Some maintenance professionals will caution that allowing placard removal after a single inspection could risk reinstating aerobatic operation without adequate repeat verification; they request that FAA require a follow-up inspection after a set flight time or inclusion of a recurrent inspection schedule before removal.

[P10] Commenters will note the recurring-inspection interval "not to exceed 100 hours TIS" conflicts with common maintenance intervals (e.g., annual or 100-hour inspections) and request guidance for harmonizing with existing inspection schedules; they also ask whether calendar time limits apply in addition to hours-in-service.

[P10] Small operators will request an alternative of calendar-based intervals (e.g., every 12 months) for aircraft that fly infrequently, arguing that a strict hours-based recurring interval could leave aircraft out of compliance for long periods.

[P11] Work centers and parts suppliers will ask FAA to specify approved replacement parts and acceptable sources for replacement of cracked/damaged aileron hinge ribs/supports; they request FAA to allow installing FAA-approved parts manufactured per the referenced ACAC SL No. 444 or approved repair station parts.

[P11] Legal commenters will request clarification whether "before further flight" replacement can be performed under an operational ferry permit for maintenance purposes, and if so, what limitations apply; they also ask whether a special flight permit may be issued solely to reposition the aircraft for repairs despite paragraph (j).

[P12] Owners and operators will object to the 400-hour TIS deadline to install the reinforcement kit if not already done, seeking either extension (e.g., 800–1,000 hours) or an allowance to schedule installation at the next major maintenance event because the kit may require significant downtime and parts lead times.

[P12] Parts manufacturers will request explicit approval and incorporation by reference of the reinforcement kit part numbers and modification instructions so that contractors know exactly which kit to order and install to achieve AD termination.

[P13] Maintenance program managers request the exact text or PDF of "page 4–1 of the Airworthiness Limitations" to be incorporated by reference in the AD so they can insert precisely the required language into maintenance/service manuals, rather than rely on an ambiguous citation.

[P13] Operators will also ask FAA to confirm whether inserting the page into operator-specific maintenance programs requires FAA approval of the program change, or whether the insertion alone suffices under the AD.

[P14] Several industry commenters will challenge the statement that installing the reinforcement kit and inserting the manual page "terminates the requirements of this AD" on the basis that the revised limitations still include recurring inspections — they request FAA to clarify whether any AD obligations remain post-kit installation aside from the recurring inspections and whether the AD will be rescinded after a compliance demonstration period.

[P14] Advocacy groups will request FAA publish data supporting that the reinforcement kit plus manual insertion effectively mitigates the unsafe condition, including test results and inspection findings that justify terminating other AD requirements.

[P15] Consumer safety advocates will request FAA reconsider the exception that the AD does not require submission of information to the manufacturer (ACAC), arguing that data submission is critical for monitoring fleet-wide trends and should be mandated or at least strongly encouraged with an option to submit anonymized data to FAA.

[P15] Privacy advocates and some owners will support the exception, commenting that mandatory reporting to the manufacturer could raise proprietary or privacy concerns and that FAA consolidation of safety data is preferable to requiring owners to report to a manufacturer.

[P16] Operators and legal commenters will point out an apparent inconsistency: paragraph (j) prohibits aerobatic flight under a special flight permit, but paragraph (g)(3) permits the owner/operator to perform certain actions — they request clarification on whether a special flight permit may be issued to deliver the aircraft for maintenance when the placard remains in place, and whether aerobatic maneuvers remain prohibited during that ferry.

[P16] Flight schools and aerobatic training organizations will request an exemption process for limited aerobatic operations under supervised conditions (e.g., for training or certifications), arguing a blanket prohibition on aerobatics under special flight permits could impede necessary training and evaluations.

[P17] Industry and legal commenters will support AMOC authority vested in the Chicago ACO Branch manager but request FAA to publish expected processing times, required technical substantiation, and criteria for approval to ensure timely consideration of AMOC requests.

[P17] Operators in other regions will ask whether other ACO branches may be delegated authority to approve AMOCs in urgent cases and request a regional point-of-contact list to expedite submissions.

[P18] Commenters will request clarification on the form, content, and level of substantiation required for AMOC requests submitted to principal inspectors or local FSDOs under 14 CFR 39.19, including whether risk assessments, stress analyses, and service history must accompany initial submissions.

[P19] Several submitters will request that the person identified in paragraph (l) be named in the AD preamble or that contact information (name, email, phone) be included in the AD text, because the cross-reference makes it cumbersome to find the appropriate addressee.

[P19] Legal commenters will also request that FAA allow electronic submission of AMOC materials directly to the ACO manager and provide an official email address for receipt, and to confirm that electronic signatures and PDF attachments are acceptable.

[P20] Operators note that the requirement to notify the principal inspector or manager before using an approved AMOC is vague about acceptable notification methods and timing (e.g., prior to the first flight under the AMOC, within 24 hours of use); they request FAA specify acceptable timeframe and documentation proof of notification.

[P20] Some commenters will request that FAA require that AMOC approvals and associated notifications be entered into the aircraft maintenance records to ensure traceability and to remove ambiguity about who is responsible for notification and what documentation satisfies it.

[P1] The comments due date of July 21, 2017 is unreasonably short for international operators and non-U.S. stakeholders to assemble technical and economic feedback; extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] Small operators and independent maintenance organizations will need more time to coordinate data and submit meaningful comments; FAA should publish an extension or provide a mechanism for late submissions.

[P2] The broad requirement to "comply within the specified compliance times" lacks clarity for airplanes in storage or with deferred maintenance; the rule should specify how compliance times apply to parked, stored, or recently-acquired aircraft.

[P2] Airlines need explicit guidance on how compliance times apply when airplanes are leased across operators; require the FAA to clarify obligations for lessees versus lessors.

[P3] Requiring inspections "per the specified Boeing Alert Service Bulletin" effectively incorporates a manufacturer's non-federal document by reference; stakeholders request FAA publish the full inspection procedures within the AD or ensure free public access to the service bulletin.

[P3] The inspection requirement references only "general visual inspections" but does not define what qualifies as a GVI in this context; FAA should clarify the acceptable inspection level and required tools (e.g., mirror, borescope).

[P4] The 30-day inspection deadline for Group 1 airplanes after May 23, 2016 is retroactive and impractical for operators that took delivery after that date; propose that the 30-day clock start from the AD effective date for each operator.

[P4] Group 1 airplanes identified by Boeing's list may not match each operator's fleet records; require operators be allowed to use equivalent internal grouping if serial numbers differ.

[P5] The Group 2 compliance window ("within 180 flight cycles or within 90 days after May 23, 2016, whichever occurs later") is confusing and may create compliance determination ambiguity; FAA should provide examples and a clear method for calculating the trigger date.

[P5] For low-utilization aircraft, 180 flight cycles can take many months or years, making the "whichever occurs later" construct problematic—FAA should instead set a firm calendar deadline to ensure prompt inspections.

[P6] Mandating that inspections be done "in accordance with the Accomplishment Instructions" without acknowledging alternative equivalent procedures prevents flexibility; FAA should explicitly allow equivalent procedures through the AMOC process and clarify acceptance criteria.

[P6] The AD assumes operators have access to the Boeing Accomplishment Instructions; FAA should confirm the document is incorporated by reference and made available at no cost or provide a service bulletin copy in the docket.

[P7] The requirement to "repeat inspections at the intervals specified in the service bulletin until modification" creates ongoing operational burden and cost uncertainty; FAA should quantify expected inspection intervals and estimate recurring compliance costs.

[P7] The AD should permit temporary extension of inspection intervals in low-risk cases where prior inspections show no issues, subject to AMOC approval.

[P8] Reinstallation "before further flight" of any disengaged decompression panel may be impractical on transoceanic routes when maintenance resources or parts are not available at the next diversion airport; propose allowing temporary safe placarding or diversion procedures until reinstall can be performed.

[P8] The AD should specify acceptable temporary corrective actions and required documentation when immediate reinstallation is not possible, rather than a strict "before further flight" mandate.

[P9] The 22-month deadline to replace decompression panels and straps is burdensome for operators with limited downtime or maintenance slots; FAA should allow phased compliance based on fleet schedules or extend the compliance window to 36 months.

[P9] The replacement parts specified in the Boeing Alert Service Bulletin may have long lead times; require Boeing and FAA to coordinate and provide spare parts availability guidance prior to AD effective date.

[P10] While the terminating modification ends repetitive inspections, the AD does not require post-modification verification interval or a follow-up inspection; FAA should require a follow-up inspection after replacement to confirm correct installation.

[P11] The "except as provided by paragraph (j)" catchall is too vague; stakeholders request FAA to clearly enumerate all exceptions and their rationales in the AD preamble.

[P12] The requirement in (j)(1) to substitute P/N C412705–575 when Step 3 identifies C412705–577 could create parts interchangeability issues if not accompanied by engineering justification; provide rationale and compatibility data.

[P12] Operators will need documentation in the aircraft records showing the P/N substitution per (j)(1); FAA should specify the required recordkeeping and weight-and-balance or certification ramifications.

[P13] Similarly, (j)(2) requiring the opposite substitution (use C412705–577 when Step 4 identifies C412705–575) is confusing and risks installation errors; FAA should clarify the intended mapping and correct any typographical errors.

[P13] If (j)(1) and (j)(2) represent corrections to the service bulletin, FAA should ensure the corrected service bulletin is issued and incorporated into the AD instead of relying on operators to interpret conflicting steps.

[P14] Industry requests a defined SLA (service level agreement) for AMOC review timelines from the Seattle ACO to avoid prolonged groundings.

[P15] The AMOC request routing requirements are reasonable, but the AD's email contact should be validated and an alternative submission channel provided for secure or proprietary technical data.

[P16] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC is administratively onerous for large fleets with many local offices; allow centralized notifications for multi-base operators.

[P16] Clarify the timeline for notification (e.g., "within 24 hours" or "prior to first use") so operators know their obligations before employing the AMOC.

[P18] Requiring that AMOC repairs meet the airplane's certification basis is standard, but FAA should provide guidance on how to demonstrate compliance for legacy certification basis items (e.g., earlier amendments).

[P18] The AD should require that AMOC approvals specifically cite the AD paragraph(s) being addressed and be added to a central public registry for operator reference.

[P22] Requiring an AMOC for any deviation from RC steps is strict; operators request a de minimis allowance for clerical deviations (e.g., torque wrench calibration differences) that do not affect safety, or a simplified AMOC pathway.

[P22] The AD must clarify whether minor procedural deviations discovered during post-action compliance reporting will be treated as noncompliances requiring formal AMOCs or as reportable maintenance discrepancies.

[P23] Allowing deviations from non-RC steps under an operator's program is reasonable but raises oversight concerns; FAA should require operators to document deviations in their maintenance records and make them available for audits.
