raw_output:
[P1] The duplication of identical obligations across §§ 410.142(k), 414.68(j), 424.58(f), 488.1030(g), and 493.553(e) creates unnecessary redundancy and regulatory burden; request consolidation or cross-reference language to avoid repetitive compliance obligations for recognized accreditation organizations.

[P1] The provisions in § 410.142(k) are vague about timing and process when an AO contemplates a change of ownership; commenters request clarification that the § 488.5(f) requirements (including written notice and timelines) are the sole applicable procedures and that no additional agency-specific notifications will be required.

[P2] § 414.68(j) repeats the § 488.5(f) obligation but uses plural grammatical errors (“are”); recommend editing for consistency and legal clarity to avoid disputes over whether the rule applies to single-program AOs.

[P3] § 424.58(f) should specify which CMS office or contact point will receive the required § 488.5(f) notices to ensure timely and proper service; otherwise AOs may inadvertently miss the 90-day deadline.

[P4] Under § 488.5(f)(1), “contemplating or negotiating” is overbroad and could require notice for early-stage or exploratory discussions; request narrowing to binding agreements or material negotiations (e.g., executed LOI or exclusivity period) to avoid burdensome reporting.

[P5] § 488.5(f)(1)(ii) requires written notice but does not permit electronic notice methods; industry requests allowance for secure electronic submission (email with acknowledgement or portal filing) rather than only physical mail.

[P6] § 488.5(f)(1)(iii) mandates at least 90 days’ notice but provides no mechanism for expedited review where buyers need faster closings; request a defined expedited review path or waiver procedure when appropriate.

[P7] § 488.5(f)(2) places many obligations on purchasers but does not define “person(s) or organization(s)” (e.g., holding company, private equity fund, affiliate); request definition to avoid disputes about who must seek CMS approval.

[P8] § 488.5(f)(2)(i) requires CMS approval for transfer of the CMS approval but lacks clear criteria and timelines for CMS decision; commenters request a specific review timeframe (e.g., 60 or 90 days) and objective approval criteria to avoid indefinite transaction holds.

[P9] § 488.5(f)(2)(ii) requires compliance with (f)(2)(iii)-(f)(4) to show continuing compliance but does not state whether historical noncompliance findings against the target AO will automatically preclude approval; request guidance on how past performance is weighed.

[P10] § 488.5(f)(2)(iii) requires submission of specified information but does not protect confidential business information; purchasers request explicit CBI protection procedures (FOIA exemptions/process) for financial statements and transition plans.

[P11] § 488.5(f)(2)(iii)(A) requires legal name and address of new owner but should also require disclosure of ultimate parent entities, ownership percentages, and beneficial owners (including private equity investors) to permit CMS to evaluate conflicts of interest and fitness.

[P12] § 488.5(f)(2)(iii)(B) requires three audited financial statements demonstrating adequate staffing, funding, and resources; commenters ask CMS to define “adequate” with specific financial ratios or minimum staffing levels for varying sizes of AO programs to ensure consistent application.

[P13] § 488.5(f)(2)(iii)(B) imposing three years of audited financials may unfairly burden new entities formed by buyers that lack a three‑year audit history; request alternative acceptable documentation (pro forma financials, unaudited statements with CPA attestation) for startups or newly formed acquirers.

[P14] § 488.5(f)(2)(iii)(C) transition plan requirement is broadly worded; request a detailed template or checklist for the transition plan to ensure consistency and to reduce back-and-forth with CMS.

[P15] § 488.5(f)(2)(iii)(C)(1) requires management and governance changes and org charts but does not require disclosure of key personnel qualifications; request that CVs/resumes of key senior leaders and compliance officers be included to assess ability to operate accreditation functions.

[P16] § 488.5(f)(2)(iii)(C)(2) requires a list of CMS‑approved accreditation programs to be transferred but should require disclosure of any programs the AO intends to divest or add post‑transfer to assess continuity of services.

[P17] § 488.5(f)(2)(iii)(C)(3) requires reporting employee changes “if applicable” but does not define which employee categories trigger reporting; request clarification that key staff (surveyors, accreditation decision-makers, compliance staff) must always be disclosed.

[P18] § 488.5(f)(2)(iii)(C)(4) requires anticipated timelines but lacks required milestone granularity; request inclusion of specific milestones (e.g., survey continuity, data/system migration, notification to accredited providers) and contingency plans for delays.

[P19] § 488.5(f)(2)(iii)(C)(5) requires plans for notifying employees but mandates no minimum notice period to staff; commenters from labor/employee advocacy groups request provisions ensuring employees receive timely notice and protections for employee records and benefits.

[P20] § 488.5(f)(2)(iii)(C)(6) allowing “any other information CMS deems necessary” is unbounded; request CMS to either list likely additional items or limit this to reasonably related documentation to prevent arbitrary requests.

[P21] § 488.5(f)(3) requires a written acknowledgement containing multiple statements but does not prescribe a standard form; industry requests a model acknowledgement form to expedite compliance and prevent rejections for form issues.

[P22] § 488.5(f)(3)(i) obligates the purchaser to assume full responsibility “immediately upon finalization if CMS approves the transfer” but does not clarify whether any liabilities arising from pre‑transfer acts remain with the seller; request clear allocation of pre‑closing liabilities and indemnification expectations.

[P23] § 488.5(f)(3)(ii) requires purchasers to operate under all CMS-imposed terms and conditions, including program reviews and probationary terms, but is silent on whether CMS can impose new conditions as a condition of approval; legal commentators request due process protections and notice before imposition of additional conditions.

[P24] § 488.5(f)(3)(iii) prohibition on operating as CMS‑approved programs until effective date in CMS’s notice of approval could impair business continuity if CMS delays publication; request that CMS provide interim guidance and allow limited transitional operations under supervision to avoid disruptions to accredited providers.

[P25] § 488.5(f)(3)(iv) requires operation in accordance with §§ 488.5–488.9 but lacks transition guidance on how to handle active enforcement actions or pending appeals initiated under the seller; request guidance whether such actions survive transfer and how appeals are processed.

[P26] § 488.5(f)(4)(i) requires notification to affected providers and suppliers within 15 calendar days after CMS approval; request CMS clarify whether the 15‑day clock starts from CMS’s written notice to the new owner or from the Federal Register publication date.

[P27] § 488.5(f)(4)(i) 15‑day notification requirement could be burdensome for large AOs with thousands of accredited entities; request allowance for staged notification or electronic batch notices and a specified acceptable method (email, portal posting) rather than mail to every provider.

[P28] § 488.5(f)(4)(ii) requires acknowledgment to CMS if the acquired AO was under performance review or probation at time of notice; request clarity on what constitutes “under performance review” (open investigations, corrective actions, probation) and what evidence suffices.

[P29] § 488.5(f)(5) conditions Federal Register publication on written confirmation from new owner that change of ownership has occurred; request that CMS permit electronic certifications and define acceptable proof of occurrence (e.g., filed articles of merger, stock transfer documents).

[P30] § 488.5(f)(6) states CMS will notify all parties in writing if it disapproves; request CMS to specify the content of such notice (reasons, remediation steps, appeal rights, and timelines) to afford parties meaningful due process.

[P31] § 488.5(f)(7) contemplates outcomes if CMS was not notified or did not approve transfer but lacks an exact standard for when CMS will withdraw approvals; request clear, objective triggers and an opportunity to cure before withdrawal.

[P32] § 488.5(f)(7)(i) permitting the existing AO to continue operating if change of ownership was not completed could incentivize sellers to claim incomplete transactions to avoid withdrawal; request anticircumvention safeguards and audit rights for CMS.

[P33] § 488.5(f)(7)(ii) enabling CMS to withdraw approvals for unapproved transfers requires transparent procedures and notice periods to avoid sudden loss of accreditation for numerous providers; recommend minimum notice (e.g., 30–60 days) and remediation windows.

[P34] § 488.5(f)(8) states that if parties complete a transfer despite CMS disapproval and attempt to operate under previous owner’s approval CMS will withdraw the approved program; request clarity on whether CMS will hold purchasers liable for damages to accredited providers and on any enforcement penalties.

[P35] § 488.5(f)(9) allowing affected Medicare-certified providers to retain deemed status for 180 days after withdrawal is helpful, but the rule’s 60-day application deadline (f)(9)(i) may be impractical; request extension to 120 days to allow providers time to identify and apply to another AO.

[P36] § 488.5(f)(9)(i) requiring submission of an application to another AO within 60 days lacks clarity whether a complete application or just an intent-to-apply suffices to preserve deemed status; request that initial application filing date be the controlling factor if a bona fide application is submitted.

[P37] § 488.5(f)(9)(ii) requires written notice to the State Agency within 60 days; request specifying the information content required in that notice and whether electronic notice to SA is acceptable.

[P38] § 488.5(f)(9)(iii) shifts authority to the State Agency if timeframes are missed, but provides no guidance on how SAs will monitor or assess provider compliance; request CMS to coordinate with SAs and publish procedures for oversight during the transition.

[P39] § 488.5(f)(10) gives non‑certified suppliers one year of deemed status after withdrawal contingent on steps; this unequal treatment between certified providers (180 days) and non‑certified suppliers (one year) is arbitrary; request rationale or alignment of timeframes.

[P40] § 488.5(f)(10)(i) requires non‑certified suppliers to apply to another AO within 60 days; for small suppliers with limited administrative capacity this is onerous — request assistance options or a phased compliance schedule.

[P41] § 488.5(f)(10)(ii) requires written notice to CMS of application submission within 60 days; request that this notice suffice for both CMS and the State Agency to avoid duplicate filings.

[P42] § 488.5(f)(10)(iii) threatens de‑recognition for noncompliance with timeframes but does not provide an appeal or cure process; legal commenters request an administrative appeal process and opportunity to cure procedural deficiencies before de‑recognition.

[P43] § 488.5(f)(5) Federal Register publication dependency raises transactional uncertainty because many contracts require public notice; request CMS to provide an anticipated publication timeline or a mechanism to issue a private confirmation to counterparties once the change is effective.

[P44] Across §§ 488.5(f) and cross‑referenced provisions, CMS should clarify how data systems (surveyor databases, accreditation records) and IT access will be transferred securely and what responsibilities the buyer has for historical data privacy and HIPAA compliance.

[P45] Advocacy groups request that CMS require disclosure of any real or potential conflicts of interest introduced by the buyer (e.g., ownership interests in providers) as part of the transfer approval to preserve accreditation objectivity.

[P46] Small AOs and nonprofits request CMS to consider a scaled compliance approach for transfers involving small organizations (lower thresholds for financial documentation, longer notice windows) to avoid disproportionate burdens.

[P47] Legal commenters note potential preemption/anticompetitive concerns if CMS effectively blocks transfers without objective standards; request CMS to publish criteria and limit its discretion to avoid infringing on lawful transactions.

[P48] Request that CMS clarify whether a failure to notify (per f(1)) that is inadvertent or due to good-faith dispute over whether a transaction qualifies as a change of ownership will trigger immediate withdrawal or whether CMS will consider intent and allow cure.

[P49] Commenters request CMS provide guidance/examples of transactions that constitute “change of ownership” (stock sale, asset sale, management agreement, lease, joint venture) to reduce uncertainty and inconsistent reporting.

[P50] Request that CMS include explicit transitional protections for providers reliant on accreditation timelines (e.g., scheduled surveys, payment certifications) to prevent interruptions in Medicare billing if an AO transfer causes approval delays.

[P51] State Agencies request that CMS outline roles and responsibilities for SAs during transfers, including information sharing timelines and expectations for joint oversight or support when approvals are withdrawn.

[P52] Commenters ask CMS to include a clear statement about retroactivity: whether transfers completed before the effective date of this final rule will be grandfathered or subject to the new notice and approval requirements.

[P53] Industry stakeholders request CMS publish a FAQ and an electronic submission portal with status tracking for transfer applications, to provide transparency on application completeness, review progress, and expected decision dates.

[P54] Commenters ask CMS to coordinate with accreditation organizations' accreditees by establishing minimum notice periods for providers before any changes in accreditation operations take effect to allow providers to plan for potential re‑accreditation efforts.

[P55] Privacy and compliance officers request CMS require purchasers to certify compliance with data protection and confidentiality obligations for transferred staff and records, and to provide copies of BAAs (business associate agreements) where applicable.

[P56] Financial commenters request that CMS allow redaction of sensitive financial data in submitted audited statements, provided an unredacted version is available for CMS review under confidentiality protections, to protect competitive information.

§ 488.5(f)(6) states CMS will notify all parties in writing if it disapproves; request CMS to specify the content of such notice (reasons, remediation steps, appeal rights, and timelines) to afford parties meaningful due process.

§ 488.5(f)(7) contemplates outcomes if CMS was not notified or did not approve transfer but lacks an exact standard for when CMS will withdraw approvals; request clear, objective triggers and an opportunity to cure before withdrawal.

§ 488.5(f)(7)(i) permitting the existing AO to continue operating if change of ownership was not completed could incentivize sellers to claim incomplete transactions to avoid withdrawal; request anticircumvention safeguards and audit rights for CMS.

§ 488.5(f)(7)(ii) enabling CMS to withdraw approvals for unapproved transfers requires transparent procedures and notice periods to avoid sudden loss of accreditation for numerous providers; recommend minimum notice (e.g., 30–60 days) and remediation windows.

§ 488.5(f)(8) states that if parties complete a transfer despite CMS disapproval and attempt to operate under previous owner’s approval CMS will withdraw the approved program; request clarity on whether CMS will hold purchasers liable for damages to accredited providers and on any enforcement penalties.

§ 488.5(f)(9) allowing affected Medicare-certified providers to retain deemed status for 180 days after withdrawal is helpful, but the rule’s 60-day application deadline (f)(9)(i) may be impractical; request extension to 120 days to allow providers time to identify and apply to another AO.

§ 488.5(f)(9)(i) requiring submission of an application to another AO within 60 days lacks clarity whether a complete application or just an intent-to-apply suffices to preserve deemed status; request that initial application filing date be the controlling factor if a bona fide application is submitted.
§ 488.5(f)(9)(ii) requires written notice to the State Agency within 60 days; request specifying the information content required in that notice and whether electronic notice to SA is acceptable.

§ 488.5(f)(9)(iii) shifts authority to the State Agency if timeframes are missed, but provides no guidance on how SAs will monitor or assess provider compliance; request CMS to coordinate with SAs and publish procedures for oversight during the transition.

§ 488.5(f)(10) gives non‑certified suppliers one year of deemed status after withdrawal contingent on steps; this unequal treatment between certified providers (180 days) and non‑certified suppliers (one year) is arbitrary; request rationale or alignment of timeframes.

§ 488.5(f)(10)(i) requires non‑certified suppliers to apply to another AO within 60 days; for small suppliers with limited administrative capacity this is onerous — request assistance options or a phased compliance schedule.
§ 488.5(f)(10)(ii) requires written notice to CMS of application submission within 60 days; request that this notice suffice for both CMS and the State Agency to avoid duplicate filings.

§ 488.5(f)(10)(iii) threatens de‑recognition for noncompliance with timeframes but does not provide an appeal or cure process; legal commenters request an administrative appeal process and opportunity to cure procedural deficiencies before de‑recognition.

§ 488.5(f)(5) Federal Register publication dependency raises transactional uncertainty because many contracts require public notice; request CMS to provide an anticipated publication timeline or a mechanism to issue a private confirmation to counterparties once the change is effective.

Across §§ 488.5(f) and cross‑referenced provisions, CMS should clarify how data systems (surveyor databases, accreditation records) and IT access will be transferred securely and what responsibilities the buyer has for historical data privacy and HIPAA compliance.

Advocacy groups request that CMS require disclosure of any real or potential conflicts of interest introduced by the buyer (e.g., ownership interests in providers) as part of the transfer approval to preserve accreditation objectivity.

Small AOs and nonprofits request CMS to consider a scaled compliance approach for transfers involving small organizations (lower thresholds for financial documentation, longer notice windows) to avoid disproportionate burdens.

Legal commenters note potential preemption/anticompetitive concerns if CMS effectively blocks transfers without objective standards; request CMS to publish criteria and limit its discretion to avoid infringing on lawful transactions.

Request that CMS clarify whether a failure to notify (per f(1)) that is inadvertent or due to good-faith dispute over whether a transaction qualifies as a change of ownership will trigger immediate withdrawal or whether CMS will consider intent and allow cure.

Commenters request CMS provide guidance/examples of transactions that constitute “change of ownership” (stock sale, asset sale, management agreement, lease, joint venture) to reduce uncertainty and inconsistent reporting.

Request that CMS include explicit transitional protections for providers reliant on accreditation timelines (e.g., scheduled surveys, payment certifications) to prevent interruptions in Medicare billing if an AO transfer causes approval delays.

State Agencies request that CMS outline roles and responsibilities for SAs during transfers, including information sharing timelines and expectations for joint oversight or support when approvals are withdrawn.

Commenters ask CMS to include a clear statement about retroactivity: whether transfers completed before the effective date of this final rule will be grandfathered or subject to the new notice and approval requirements.

Industry stakeholders request CMS publish a FAQ and an electronic submission portal with status tracking for transfer applications, to provide transparency on application completeness, review progress, and expected decision dates.

Commenters ask CMS to coordinate with accreditation organizations' accreditees by establishing minimum notice periods for providers before any changes in accreditation operations take effect to allow providers to plan for potential re‑accreditation efforts.

Privacy and compliance officers request CMS require purchasers to certify compliance with data protection and confidentiality obligations for transferred staff and records, and to provide copies of BAAs (business associate agreements) where applicable.

Financial commenters request that CMS allow redaction of sensitive financial data in submitted audited statements, provided an unredacted version is available for CMS review under confidentiality protections, to protect competitive information.

raw_output:
[P1] Industry commenter: Section 1’s requirement that ATC inform operators via route planning information is unclear about who bears responsibility if the information is not transmitted; the rule should specify that ATC/FAA remains responsible for timely notification and cannot shift liability to operators.

[P1] Pilot association: Route planning information alone may not reach all operators (e.g., charter, GA, or foreign operators); the FAA should require redundant notification (NOTAMs and charts) in addition to route planning information.

[P1] Legal expert: The phrase “inform operators” is vague—please define “inform” (e.g., electronic flight plan updates, preflight briefings) and the time window for notification to avoid due-process and enforcement ambiguities.

[P2] Aircraft manufacturer: Section 2(a) references aircraft “comply with Section 2” but does not specify the certification standard or test procedures; request incorporation by reference of specific standards or an explicit list of acceptable compliance evidence.

[P2] International operator: The discretionary finding by “the Administrator” creates unpredictability for foreign operators; recommend objective criteria or an equivalency process to recognize foreign approvals.

[P3] Air carrier safety office: Requiring authorization in ops specs, LOA, or management specs is appropriate but the rule should clarify conversion procedures when operators change type certificate status or when multiple authorizations apply across operations (Part 121 vs Part 135).

[P3] Small operator: The options (ops specs, LOA, management specs) may impose different administrative burdens; request guidance on the least burdensome pathway for small/charter operators and timelines for FAA issuance.

[P4] Trade association: The requirement that aircraft be approved per Section 2 and operator complies with this section before authorization is redundant and could delay service; propose parallel processing (aircraft approval and operator compliance checks simultaneously) to reduce delays.

[P4] Legal counsel: The provision lacks an appeal or reconsideration process if the Administrator denies authorization; include a mechanism and timelines for reconsideration and emergency provisional authorizations.

[P5] Operator group: Section 3(b) requiring application “in the form and manner the Administrator prescribes” is overly open-ended; request that the FAA publish standard application forms and an online submission process before the rule becomes effective.

[P5] GA association: The rule should specify processing timelines and fees (if any) for applications; without timelines small operators could face prolonged grounding.

[P6] Operator safety manager: The list of specific information required in the application is referenced but not provided in the regulatory text excerpt; commenters request that the exact required items be published or incorporated by reference to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P6] Privacy advocate: If the application requires submission of crew rosters or personal data, the rule should include data-protection obligations and limits on FAA retention/sharing of sensitive information.

[P7] Airline: Section 3(c) obligates operators to provide “evidence” in a manner prescribed by the Administrator; request clarity on what types of evidence satisfy monitoring requirements (maintenance records, test reports, continuous monitoring system outputs).

[P7] Maintenance organization: The regulation should allow authorized third-party maintenance organizations to submit evidence on behalf of operators and specify acceptable lab/test standards.

[P8] Pilot union: The requirement that “each pilot has knowledge” of RVSM requirements lacks detail about training frequency and content; require standardized recurrent training intervals (e.g., initial plus annual refreshers) and specify minimum curriculum elements.

[P8] Flight school: For single-pilot and part-time operations, the training burden may be disproportionate; request an option for computer-based training and a competency-based alternative to fixed-hour mandates.

[P9] Legal expert: Section 4(b)(1) makes RVSM operations conditional on Administrator authorization per Section 3 or 9 but does not specify the consequences of operating without such authorization; recommend explicit civil penalty levels or corrective-action processes.

[P10] Charter operator: The dual path allowing aircraft approved under Section 2 or those complying with Section 9 is welcome, but the rule should clarify transition rules for mixed fleets where some aircraft meet Section 2 and others only Section 9.

[P10] Certification body: The phrase “approved and complies with Section 2” needs clarification on whether a type-certification basis approval is sufficient or whether individual aircraft must be traced to specific modification records.

[P11] Safety NGO: Requiring each pilot to have sufficient knowledge is necessary but insufficiently enforceable; propose requiring documentation of each pilot’s RVSM training and proficiency in the operator’s records for FAA audit.

[P12] Air carrier: Section 5 permitting deviations from §91.180/§91.706 for a specific RVSM flight could create safety risks if used frequently; request strict limitations (e.g., one-time emergency use only, with mandatory post-flight reporting).

[P12] Legal counsel for operators: The permission to deviate is useful for flexibility; ask for clear, published conditions under which the Administrator will grant such deviations, including timelines for decisions to avoid flight-planning uncertainty.

[P13] ATC labor union: Requiring ATC to determine at flight-plan filing that appropriate separation can be provided may create workload spikes and liability for controllers; recommend automated pre-flight conflict-checking tools and formal allocation of responsibility.

[P13] International airline: Flight-plan filing determination could vary between FIRs—seek harmonization with ICAO procedures and a clear standard operating procedure to avoid inconsistent approvals while crossing FIR boundaries.

[P14] Operator trade group: Section 7’s authority for the Administrator to prohibit or restrict operations if the operator is noncompliant is reasonable, but the rule should establish graduated remedies (notice, corrective action plan, suspension) rather than immediate prohibition.

[P14] Civil liberties group: The rule should require procedural protections (notice, opportunity to cure, appeal rights) before prohibiting operations to prevent arbitrary enforcement.

[P15] Legal scholar: Section 7’s reliance on the Administrator’s determination of noncompliance needs objective criteria and evidentiary standards; propose defining “noncompliance” thresholds (number of incidents, ASE exceedances) that trigger action.

[P16] ICAO-focused commenter: Section 8 permitting RVSM in all FIRs is overly broad; request language clarifying that application will follow bilateral/multilateral coordination and respect foreign state sovereignty and existing ICAO agreements.

[P16] Environmental NGO: Applying RVSM universally could change traffic flows and emissions; urge FAA to conduct an environmental assessment addressing potential impacts before broad implementation.

[P17] International ops manager: Section 9’s permission to conduct RVSM flights if listed conditions are met should include recognition of equivalent foreign standards and allow validated foreign approvals without duplicative FAA testing.

[P18] Aircraft manufacturer: Section 9(a)(1) requiring two independent operational altitude measurement systems is standard, but the rule should define “independent” (e.g., redundant sensors, separate pitot/static systems) to avoid interpretation disputes.

[P18] Vintage/legacy aircraft owner: For older aircraft, installing two independent systems may be impractical; request an exemption pathway with operational restrictions or a grandfathering clause for certain types.

[P19] Aerospace OEM: The requirement for at least one automatic altitude control system needs definition of acceptable system types (autopilot modes, auto-throttle integrated systems) and failure-mode tolerances.

[P20] Airline operations: The ±65-foot tolerance in Section 9(a)(2)(i) is very strict—seek data justification and whether this applies to climb/descend segments or only straight-and-level cruise; propose relaxation in specified conditions.

[P20] Safety analyst: The ±65-foot requirement may be unattainable in light turbulence — request allowance for transient deviations during turbulence with defined monitoring/reporting thresholds.

[P21] Manufacturer/legal counsel: The relaxed ±130-foot tolerance for older type-certification dates is arbitrary relative to safety — request evidence supporting the date cutoff April 9, 1997 and consider performance-based metrics rather than fixed dates.

[P21] Fleet operator: Operators with mixed fleets (older and newer type certifications) need guidance on dispatching limitations and whether mixed flights impose separation/ATC restrictions.

[P22] Avionics supplier: The altitude alert system requirement should specify performance, annunciation clarity, and crew interface standards to ensure alerts are actionable and not prone to nuisance alarms.

[P22] Human factors researcher: Recommend human-factors testing requirements for alert thresholds and presentation to avoid alarm fatigue leading to crew inattention in RVSM airspace.

[P23] Legacy aircraft operator: The ±300-foot alert threshold for pre-1997 aircraft is very wide compared to RVSM separation minima; request explanation how ±300 feet alerts ensure safety when RVSM separation is reduced.

[P24] Newer aircraft operator: The ±200-foot alert threshold for post-1997 aircraft may be inconsistent with the ±65/±130 autopilot tolerances — request clarification on how alert thresholds relate to control tolerances and monitoring requirements.

[P25] Equipment manufacturer: Mandating TCAS II TSO C-119b (v7.0) or later is acceptable but the rule should allow for planned upgrades and provide timelines for compliance, plus allowances for equivalent or better systems certified to alternative standards.

[P26] Foreign carrier: The Administrator’s ability to authorize exceptions to TCAS II requirements must be transparent and harmonized with foreign state authorities; request published criteria for granting exceptions.

[P27] Operators: The ADS-B Out requirement per §91.227 may be redundant with other surveillance mandates in some FIRs; ask for cross-reference guidance and whether alternative surveillance (e.g., Mode S) is acceptable where ADS-B coverage is absent.

[P27] Privacy/GA group: Mandating ADS-B Out raises privacy concerns for GA and business aircraft; request exemptions or limited-use modes for non-commercial operators operating in RVSM airspace.

[P28] International operator: Allowing ATC or the foreign country to authorize operation without ADS-B Out is necessary, but the rule must set minimum radar or surveillance capability that must exist for such authorizations to be safe.

[P29] Maintenance community: Requiring height-keeping performance monitoring “in a form and manner acceptable to the Administrator” is vague; request the FAA publish acceptable monitoring programs, frequency of checks, data retention, and audit procedures.

[P29] Safety auditor: The rule should require operators to report monitoring results to the Administrator periodically and define thresholds that trigger corrective maintenance or grounding.

[P30] Aircraft OEM/operator: The ASE limit of 200 feet should be supported by data showing that this threshold meets ICAO RVSM safety targets; if inconsistent with ICAO or international norms, harmonize the metric or provide justification.

[P30] Calibration service provider: The rule must specify ASE measurement methods, environmental conditions for testing, acceptable instrumentation accuracy for measurements, and allowable margins of error.

[P1] The FAA's requirement in § 39.13(a) that the agency "must receive comments by September 3, 2020" conflicts with the separate DATES provision (§ P15) that sets a September 18, 2020 deadline; the rule should clarify a single, correct comment deadline to avoid confusion.

[P15] The proposed DATES deadline of September 18, 2020 for receipt of comments is inconsistent with § 39.13(a)'s September 3, 2020 date, and commenters request the agency extend and harmonize the deadline to at least 30 days from publication to allow stakeholders adequate time.

[P1] Requiring comments to be received by September 3, 2020 (as written in § 39.13(a)) unduly shortens the comment period compared with normal practice; the FAA should provide a minimum 60-day comment period given the safety and economic impacts.

[P2] The applicability in § 39.13(c) that this AD applies to "all General Electric Company (GE) GEnx–1B64, –1B64/P1, –1B64/P2, –1B67, –1B67/P1, –1B67/P2, –1B70, –1B70/75/P1, –1B70/75/P2, –1B70/" appears to be truncated and incomplete; the FAA must correct and publish the full list of affected engine models and serial number range before finalizing the AD.

[P2] The scope in § 39.13(c) is overly broad if it captures all GEnx-1B variants regardless of installation or modification status; commenters request that the FAA limit applicability to engines with the specific outer fuel manifold P/N 2403M46G01 SIN 34302 (if that is the relevant affected part) or provide clear SN/part-level applicability.

[P3] § 39.13(f)'s blanket obligation to "comply with this AD within the compliance times specified, unless already done" is standard, but commenters ask for clarification on whether compliance times are counted from the AD effective date or from receipt of the AD by operators.

[P4] The 500 flight cycle initial inspection interval in § 39.13(g)(1) may be insufficiently protective; operators and safety advocates should see the risk analysis justifying 500 FCs and propose shorter intervals (e.g., 250 FCs) until reliability data are available.

[P4] Conversely, industry operators contend that a 500 FC inspection interval for the p-clamp is too frequent and would impose high maintenance burdens and downtime; they request the FAA provide data supporting the cycle threshold or allow extension based on fleet service data.

[P5] The continuing inspection interval in § 39.13(g)(1)(i) "not to exceed 500 FCs" lacks allowance for calendar-time-based limits (e.g., years) for low-utilization aircraft; commenters request adding a calendar-time cap (such as 12 months) for aircraft that do not accrue 500 FCs quickly.

[P6] § 39.13(g)(2) mandates a spot fluorescent penetrant inspection (FPI) of the outer fuel manifold "using the referenced SB instructions" if the p-clamp is out of limits or missing, but the proposed rule does not provide the Service Bulletin (SB) number in these provisions; commenters request explicit SB references and access instructions.

[P6] The requirement in § 39.13(g)(2) to perform spot FPI only "if the p-clamp is out of limits or missing" may miss progressive damage cases; safety groups recommend mandatory FPI for a sample percentage of engines even when clamps appear within limits.

[P7] § 39.13(g)(2)(i) requires removal of outer fuel manifold P/N 2403M46G01 SIN 34302 "before further flight" if a crack or fuel leakage is found; operators request clarification on allowable ferry-flight procedures and whether special flight permits may be issued to reposition aircraft for repair.

[P7] Legal counsel notes that § 39.13(g)(2)(i)'s instruction to remove P/N 2403M46G01 SIN 34302 before further flight must include guidance on sourcing eligible replacement parts and acceptable repair alternatives to avoid grounding aircraft indefinitely.

[P8] The mandated p-clamp replacement interval in § 39.13(g)(3) of "within 500 FCs after the effective date and thereafter at intervals not to exceed 500 FCs" creates potential operational scheduling burdens; commenters ask for transition relief for aircraft nearing the 500 FC threshold at AD issuance and request allowance for replacements during scheduled heavy maintenance.

[P9] The sequencing condition in § 39.13(g)(3) that replacement must be completed only after performing the visual inspections (per § 39.13(g)(1) and (g)(1)(i)) is reasonable, but operators seek explicit guidance on whether an immediate replacement may be performed in lieu of inspection when the part is known to be out of limits.

[P9] Maintenance organizations request clarification on recordkeeping: whether inspection findings required before replacement under § 39.13(g)(3) must be logged in the aircraft logbook or engine records, and whether photographic evidence is mandatory.

[P10] § 39.13(i)(1) permits the Manager to approve AMOCs, but industry requests clearer timelines for FAA responses to AMOC requests (e.g., 60 or 90 days) to avoid prolonged grounding or operational uncertainty.

[P11] The procedure in § 39.13(i)(1) requiring AMOC requests to go through a principal inspector or local FSDO may be inefficient for large international operators; commenters request explicit acceptance of requests from nominated company DERs/DOAs and a streamlined process for multinational fleets.

[P12] § 39.13(i)(1) instructs that AMOC information "when sending directly to the certification office manager, address it to the person identified in paragraph (j)(1)," yet the proposed text does not include paragraph (j)(1) details in the provided excerpt; commenters ask the FAA to publish the contact name, office, and mailing address to prevent misrouting.

[P13] The permission to email AMOC requests to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov (§ 39.13(i)(1) contact method) is helpful, but industry requests confirmation that emailed requests can include encrypted or large file attachments (e.g., inspection photos), and that receipt will be acknowledged with a tracking number.

[P14] § 39.13(i)(2) requires notifying a principal inspector or FSDO manager before using an approved AMOC; operators request clarity on what constitutes "before" (hours, days) and whether oral notification is acceptable prior to written confirmation.

[P14] Union representatives and maintenance technicians ask that § 39.13(i)(2) include a requirement that the approved AMOC be documented in the air carrier's maintenance program and made available to the technician performing the work to ensure compliance and safety oversight.

[P6] Non-U.S. operators request harmonization with EASA and other authorities regarding the required spot FPI in § 39.13(g)(2) to avoid duplicate inspections and conflicting methods.

[P1] The March 8, 2021 comment deadline is unreasonably short for stakeholders (airlines, MROs, and unions) to prepare technically detailed responses, and the FAA should extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] Small operators and foreign carriers were not given adequate notice of the March 8, 2021 deadline; the FAA must publish targeted outreach and extend the deadline to ensure inclusive participation.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether electronic, mailed, and hand-delivered comments received by March 8, 2021 will all be considered timely; otherwise stakeholders may risk exclusion.

[P2] The applicability in § 39.13(c) is too narrow/broad: commenters request clarification whether all production serial numbers of Boeing 737–9 are included or only specific S/Ns listed in Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737–57A.

[P2] The provision should explicitly state whether derivatives, modified, or supplemental type-certificated (STC) 737–9 airplanes (e.g., re-engined or major STC changes) are included or excluded from applicability.

[P2] The rule must clarify applicability for U.S.-registered versus foreign-registered 737–9 airplanes to avoid enforcement ambiguity for international operators.

[P3] The requirement to "comply within the specified compliance times" lacks a grace period for scheduling heavy maintenance; FAA should allow operators to coordinate compliance with existing maintenance checks within a defined extended window.

[P3] The FAA should provide relief language for unforeseen parts or tooling shortages that delay compliance beyond the specified times; without it operators face enforcement despite supply-chain issues.

[P3] The rule should specify whether "unless already accomplished" requires documented evidence of prior accomplishment and what records satisfy that requirement.

[P4] Incorporating all actions in the Boeing Requirements Bulletin by reference creates enforcement of manufacturer language without FAA modification; the FAA must ensure the bulletin was reviewed and explicitly adopt critical steps rather than wholesale incorporation.

[P4] The compliance times in the referenced Boeing Requirements Bulletin are not reproduced in the AD; the FAA should include the specific time thresholds in the AD text for transparency.

[P4] Operators request explicit acceptance of equivalent manufacturer service information updates (revisions) published after April 23, 2020, so they can rely on the latest Boeing instructions without submitting AMOCs.

[P5] Replacing the bulletin's "Original Issue date" with the effective date of the AD (§ 39.13(h)) creates confusion for operators using older revisions; FAA should explicitly define "effective date" and confirm that later bulletin revisions remain acceptable.

[P5] The cross-reference change may unintentionally shorten or lengthen compliance windows tied to the bulletin's Original Issue date; FAA should provide examples showing how compliance deadlines are recalculated.

[P6] The designation of the Seattle ACO Branch Manager as sole AMOC approver centralizes authority and could delay decisions; FAA should allow regional Flight Standards Offices to also approve AMOCs to expedite operator requests.

[P6] Legal commenters note that the provision should specify a statutory standard or criteria the Manager must use when approving AMOCs to ensure consistent decision-making and allow meaningful judicial review.

[P7] Requiring AMOC requests to go through the principal inspector or Flight Standards Office adds an administrative step that may duplicate FAA internal routing; allow direct submission to the Seattle ACO with a courtesy copy to the principal inspector to reduce processing time.

[P7] The rule should provide timelines for FAA response to AMOC requests submitted per 14 CFR 39.19 to prevent indefinite uncertainty for operators planning compliance.

[P8] The cross-reference to paragraph (j)(1) for the certification office manager's identity is opaque; the AD should explicitly name and provide contact details to avoid misdirected submissions.

[P8] Legal counsel requests that confidentiality and proprietary information handling be specified when sending AMOC information directly to the certification office manager.

[P9] Allowing AMOC submissions by email to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is helpful, but the FAA must confirm receipt and provide a trackable submission ID to requesters.

[P9] The AD should require secure file-transfer options for submitting large technical attachments or proprietary data rather than relying solely on email.

[P10] Requiring notification to the principal inspector "before using any approved AMOC" could be impractical for fleet-wide, recurring uses; FAA should allow batch notifications or pre-approval of repeated uses with periodic reporting.

[P10] The rule needs to define "appropriate principal inspector" and the timeframe for notification (e.g., number of days before first use) to avoid subjective enforcement.

[P11] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs for repairs/modifications is practical, but raises conflict-of-interest concerns; request the FAA require independent FAA review or oversight when Boeing ODA approves deviations affecting safety-critical systems.

[P11] Operators request clarification whether only Boeing-authorized ODA holders may approve AMOCs, or whether other delegated organizations (third-party DERs, other OEM ODAs) can approve, to avoid limiting repair options.

[P12] The requirement that AMOC-approved repair methods "meet the certification basis of the airplane" is vague; commenters request the FAA to list the applicable certification basis documents or provide a mechanism to determine compliance.

[P12] The AD should require that any AMOC approval explicitly reference the AD number and the specific bulletin paragraphs being deviated from, to ensure traceability and consistent enforcement.

[P12] Legal commenters ask the FAA to clarify whether previously approved AMOCs for the same modifications (for other ADs) remain valid for compliance with this AD or whether a new AMOC referencing this AD is always required.

[P1] The requirement that decisionmakers consider “whether more economical alternative facilities/services are available and feasible” is vague and will lead to inconsistent application across reviewers; request CMS provide concrete criteria or examples of what constitutes “economical” and “feasible.”

[P1] Hospitals and SNFs comment that requiring consideration of both patient condition and alternative availability in every “practical matter” determination will create additional documentation burden and delay discharge; ask CMS to limit the scope to cases where clinical staff identify potential alternatives.

[P1] Patient advocates support the obligation to consider patient condition and alternatives, but request CMS explicitly require that patient and caregiver preferences be documented as part of the “condition” consideration.

[P2] Providers note that prohibiting consideration of Medicare payment availability could force facilities to recommend care pathways that are unaffordable for beneficiaries; request CMS clarify how decisionmakers should account for beneficiary financial constraints without referencing Medicare payment.

[P2] Legal commenters argue the prohibition is appropriate to ensure clinical decisions are not determined by coverage rules; they request CMS reaffirm that commercial payer rules also may not be considered when making “practical matter” determinations.

[P3] Skilled nursing facilities (SNFs) state the example barring reliance on Part B non-enrollment as a basis for placing a patient in a SNF will create conflicts with admission processes where outpatient services are genuinely inaccessible; ask CMS to provide an exception when outpatient providers categorically refuse non-Part B patients.

[P3] Beneficiary advocacy groups assert the prohibition protects beneficiaries from being steered into higher-cost SNF care solely due to insurance status, and request CMS monitor and audit facilities for violations.

[P4] SNFs and industry groups comment that the performance levels required to earn VBP points are unspecified; request CMS publish the methodology and expected ranges for performance standards to allow facilities to plan quality improvement investments.

[P5] Hospitals and SNF associations request clarifying whether the 60-day announcement requirement applies equally to both baseline and performance period standards and whether electronic publication suffices for the 60-day notice.

[P6] Several commenters support CMS’s commitment to correct errors in published performance standards for FY2021 forward but request CMS define the timeframe and transparency requirements for those corrections (e.g., notice to affected SNFs, rationale, and impact analysis).

[P7] Industry commenters strongly oppose the prohibition on further updates after an initial correction for the same fiscal year, arguing that preventing subsequent corrections could lock in inaccurate benchmarks and unfairly penalize SNFs; they ask CMS to allow subsequent updates when material errors affecting scoring are found.

[P7] Legal experts warn that refusing to correct subsequent errors could expose CMS to legal challenges for arbitrary and capricious rulemaking if known inaccuracies remain uncorrected; recommend removing this limitation.

[P8] SNFs request clarity on the specific metrics, data elements, and format that will be included in the quarterly confidential feedback reports to ensure interoperability with facility quality systems.

[P8] Quality improvement organizations welcome quarterly confidential reports but ask CMS to commit to timely delivery (e.g., within X days of quarter end) and to provide technical assistance for interpreting the readmission measure.

[P9] SNFs object to the extended correction window (until March 31) for reports issued before Oct 1, 2019, because the longer lag may limit the utility of corrections; request CMS shorten the window or permit rolling updates.

[P10] SNFs and vendors generally support the 30-day correction window for performance period reports issued on or after Oct 1, 2019, but request CMS allow limited extensions for complex claims audits if SNFs can demonstrate good cause.

[P11] SNFs request that CMS clarify whether the 30-day window for baseline period reports issued on/after Oct 1, 2020, is calendar days or business days and to provide automated alerts to facilities when reports are posted.

[P12] SNFs and legal counsel request guidance on what constitutes “appropriate evidence” to support correction requests (e.g., specific claim forms, dates of service, clinician notes), and urge CMS to publish a checklist to standardize submissions.

[P12] Some commenters argue that requiring documentation with every correction request could disadvantage small SNFs with limited administrative resources; they request CMS permit attestation plus limited documentation for minor data issues.

[P13] Consumer advocates support public posting of the information on Nursing Home Compare but request CMS include contextual information (case counts, risk adjustment factors) so consumers can interpret readmission measures accurately.

[P13] SNF associations warn that posting performance data without clear caveats could mislead consumers; they request CMS provide clear explanations of the exclusions, low-volume designations, and the meaning of improvement vs. achievement scores on the public website.

[P14] Rural providers and small SNFs object to the rule that CMS will not report a SNF’s baseline readmission rate and improvement score when baseline stays <25 but performance period ≥25, arguing this asymmetry could obscure valid improvement and penalize facilities that recently expanded capacity.

[P14] Policy analysts request CMS consider lowering the 25-case threshold or provide disclosure of confidence intervals rather than suppressing baseline and improvement scores entirely.

[P15] SNFs state that suppressing public reporting when CMS classifies a facility as low-volume but assigns a performance score (under paragraph (d)(3)) will reduce transparency; they request CMS disclose the criteria for low-volume classification and the rationale for withholding specific score components.

[P15] Researchers request CMS make non-identifiable aggregate data available for low-volume SNFs to support policy evaluation, even if individual metrics are not published.

[P16] Patient advocates support the prohibition on public reporting when a SNF has zero eligible cases in the performance period, but request CMS explicitly state whether zero-case facilities will be exempt from any financial penalties under the VBP program.

[P16] SNFs ask CMS to clarify whether zero-case determinations are made prospectively or retroactively and how facilities can appeal a determination that they had zero eligible cases.

[P17] Hospitals request CMS define how “patient’s condition” should be documented and whether an interdisciplinary team assessment is required when making practical matter determinations.

[P17] Discharge planners argue that requiring consideration of “more economical alternative facilities and services” could incentivize under-provision of needed care; they request CMS require clinical justification whenever cost/availability considerations lead to recommending outpatient alternatives.

[P18] Legal commentators request clarification on whether the prohibition on considering Medicare payment availability extends to Medicare Advantage plans and other federal payer programs to avoid ambiguity in application.

[P19] Advocacy groups representing beneficiaries with limited Part B enrollment argue the prohibition against using Part B non-enrollment as a reason for SNF placement is essential, and request CMS issue guidance on how facilities should assist beneficiaries to obtain needed outpatient services (e.g., facilitating retroactive Part B enrollment or community resources).

[P19] Providers raise a practical concern: if outpatient providers decline to furnish daily therapy to uninsured beneficiaries, the rule may force hospitals to discharge to SNFs despite the prohibition; request CMS coordinate with HHS to identify funding or referral mechanisms for such beneficiaries.

[P20] SNF associations request CMS provide sample calculations showing how meeting or exceeding the specified performance standards translates to VBP points, so SNFs can model financial impacts and target improvements.

[P21] Quality stakeholders request CMS define the “start of the applicable performance period” precisely (e.g., fiscal year start date) and confirm whether the 60-day announcement requirement can be met by posting to a public CMS webpage.

[P22] SNFs and auditors request CMS commit to issuing individualized notices to facilities whenever published performance standard values are updated due to errors, including an assessment of how the updated values affect each SNF’s score.

[P23] Data specialists warn that prohibiting further updates after the first correction may permit residual calculation errors to persist and distort incentive payments; they ask CMS either remove the prohibition or limit it to non-material downstream rounding errors.

[P24] SNFs request clarity on how the confidential quarterly feedback reports will align with publicly reported measures and whether discrepancies will be reconciled before public posting.

[P25] SNFs favor permitting review of pre-Oct 1, 2019 reports through March 31 but request CMS publish an appeals escalation path if correction requests are denied or not acted upon by that date.

[P26] Vendors and facilities request CMS allow secure electronic submission of correction requests within the 30-day window and to provide a tracking system that confirms receipt and status.

[P27] SNFs request CMS define whether the 30-day correction window for baseline reports issued on/after Oct 1, 2020 applies even when the report distribution is delayed, and ask for assurances that late-provided reports will not prejudice SNFs’ ability to correct data.

[P28] SNFs and legal counsel ask CMS to specify the standard of proof for “appropriate evidence” (preponderance, clear and convincing) and whether CMS will permit sampling-based corrections where full documentation is impracticable.

[P29] Consumer groups request CMS ensure the Nursing Home Compare interface highlights which SNFs had suppressed metrics under the exceptions in (e)(3) so consumers understand why some scores are missing.

[P30] Rural health advocates reiterate that the <25 baseline / ≥25 performance-period suppression rule will disadvantage facilities in small markets; they recommend using statistical reliability adjustments rather than outright suppression.

[P31] SNFs challenge the policy of assigning a performance score to low-volume facilities (under paragraph (d)(3)) only to then withhold their specific performance metrics publicly; they argue this is inconsistent and request either full transparency or exclusion from scoring.

[P32] SNFs and policy analysts request CMS clarify the process and timeline for determining zero-eligible-case status and whether CMS will provide advance notice so SNFs can document reasons for zero cases (e.g., temporary closure, programmatic changes) to preserve data continuity.

Beneficiary advocacy groups assert the prohibition protects beneficiaries from being steered into higher-cost SNF care solely due to insurance status, and request CMS monitor and audit facilities for violations.

SNFs and industry groups comment that the performance levels required to earn VBP points are unspecified; request CMS publish the methodology and expected ranges for performance standards to allow facilities to plan quality improvement investments.

Hospitals and SNF associations request clarifying whether the 60-day announcement requirement applies equally to both baseline and performance period standards and whether electronic publication suffices for the 60-day notice.

Several commenters support CMS’s commitment to correct errors in published performance standards for FY2021 forward but request CMS define the timeframe and transparency requirements for those corrections (e.g., notice to affected SNFs, rationale, and impact analysis).

Industry commenters strongly oppose the prohibition on further updates after an initial correction for the same fiscal year, arguing that preventing subsequent corrections could lock in inaccurate benchmarks and unfairly penalize SNFs; they ask CMS to allow subsequent updates when material errors affecting scoring are found.

Legal experts warn that refusing to correct subsequent errors could expose CMS to legal challenges for arbitrary and capricious rulemaking if known inaccuracies remain uncorrected; recommend removing this limitation.
SNFs request clarity on the specific metrics, data elements, and format that will be included in the quarterly confidential feedback reports to ensure interoperability with facility quality systems.

Quality improvement organizations welcome quarterly confidential reports but ask CMS to commit to timely delivery (e.g., within X days of quarter end) and to provide technical assistance for interpreting the readmission measure.

SNFs object to the extended correction window (until March 31) for reports issued before Oct 1, 2019, because the longer lag may limit the utility of corrections; request CMS shorten the window or permit rolling updates.

SNFs and vendors generally support the 30-day correction window for performance period reports issued on or after Oct 1, 2019, but request CMS allow limited extensions for complex claims audits if SNFs can demonstrate good cause.

SNFs request that CMS clarify whether the 30-day window for baseline period reports issued on/after Oct 1, 2020, is calendar days or business days and to provide automated alerts to facilities when reports are posted.

SNFs and legal counsel request guidance on what constitutes “appropriate evidence” to support correction requests (e.g., specific claim forms, dates of service, clinician notes), and urge CMS to publish a checklist to standardize submissions.

Some commenters argue that requiring documentation with every correction request could disadvantage small SNFs with limited administrative resources; they request CMS permit attestation plus limited documentation for minor data issues.

Consumer advocates support public posting of the information on Nursing Home Compare but request CMS include contextual information (case counts, risk adjustment factors) so consumers can interpret readmission measures accurately.

SNF associations warn that posting performance data without clear caveats could mislead consumers; they request CMS provide clear explanations of the exclusions, low-volume designations, and the meaning of improvement vs. achievement scores on the public website.

Rural providers and small SNFs object to the rule that CMS will not report a SNF’s baseline readmission rate and improvement score when baseline stays <25 but performance period ≥25, arguing this asymmetry could obscure valid improvement and penalize facilities that recently expanded capacity.
Policy analysts request CMS consider lowering the 25-case threshold or provide disclosure of confidence intervals rather than suppressing baseline and improvement scores entirely.

SNFs state that suppressing public reporting when CMS classifies a facility as low-volume but assigns a performance score (under paragraph (d)(3)) will reduce transparency; they request CMS disclose the criteria for low-volume classification and the rationale for withholding specific score components.
Researchers request CMS make non-identifiable aggregate data available for low-volume SNFs to support policy evaluation, even if individual metrics are not published.

Patient advocates support the prohibition on public reporting when a SNF has zero eligible cases in the performance period, but request CMS explicitly state whether zero-case facilities will be exempt from any financial penalties under the VBP program.
SNFs ask CMS to clarify whether zero-case determinations are made prospectively or retroactively and how facilities can appeal a determination that they had zero eligible cases.
Hospitals request CMS define how “patient’s condition” should be documented and whether an interdisciplinary team assessment is required when making practical matter determinations.

Discharge planners argue that requiring consideration of “more economical alternative facilities and services” could incentivize under-provision of needed care; they request CMS require clinical justification whenever cost/availability considerations lead to recommending outpatient alternatives.

Legal commentators request clarification on whether the prohibition on considering Medicare payment availability extends to Medicare Advantage plans and other federal payer programs to avoid ambiguity in application.

Advocacy groups representing beneficiaries with limited Part B enrollment argue the prohibition against using Part B non-enrollment as a reason for SNF placement is essential, and request CMS issue guidance on how facilities should assist beneficiaries to obtain needed outpatient services (e.g., facilitating retroactive Part B enrollment or community resources).

Providers raise a practical concern: if outpatient providers decline to furnish daily therapy to uninsured beneficiaries, the rule may force hospitals to discharge to SNFs despite the prohibition; request CMS coordinate with HHS to identify funding or referral mechanisms for such beneficiaries.

SNF associations request CMS provide sample calculations showing how meeting or exceeding the specified performance standards translates to VBP points, so SNFs can model financial impacts and target improvements.

Quality stakeholders request CMS define the “start of the applicable performance period” precisely (e.g., fiscal year start date) and confirm whether the 60-day announcement requirement can be met by posting to a public CMS webpage.

SNFs and auditors request CMS commit to issuing individualized notices to facilities whenever published performance standard values are updated due to errors, including an assessment of how the updated values affect each SNF’s score.

Data specialists warn that prohibiting further updates after the first correction may permit residual calculation errors to persist and distort incentive payments; they ask CMS either remove the prohibition or limit it to non-material downstream rounding errors.
SNFs request clarity on how the confidential quarterly feedback reports will align with publicly reported measures and whether discrepancies will be reconciled before public posting.
SNFs favor permitting review of pre-Oct 1, 2019 reports through March 31 but request CMS publish an appeals escalation path if correction requests are denied or not acted upon by that date.
Vendors and facilities request CMS allow secure electronic submission of correction requests within the 30-day window and to provide a tracking system that confirms receipt and status.

SNFs request CMS define whether the 30-day correction window for baseline reports issued on/after Oct 1, 2020 applies even when the report distribution is delayed, and ask for assurances that late-provided reports will not prejudice SNFs’ ability to correct data.

SNFs and legal counsel ask CMS to specify the standard of proof for “appropriate evidence” (preponderance, clear and convincing) and whether CMS will permit sampling-based corrections where full documentation is impracticable.
Consumer groups request CMS ensure the Nursing Home Compare interface highlights which SNFs had suppressed metrics under the exceptions in (e)(3) so consumers understand why some scores are missing.

Rural health advocates reiterate that the <25 baseline / ≥25 performance-period suppression rule will disadvantage facilities in small markets; they recommend using statistical reliability adjustments rather than outright suppression.

SNFs challenge the policy of assigning a performance score to low-volume facilities (under paragraph (d)(3)) only to then withhold their specific performance metrics publicly; they argue this is inconsistent and request either full transparency or exclusion from scoring.

SNFs and policy analysts request CMS clarify the process and timeline for determining zero-eligible-case status and whether CMS will provide advance notice so SNFs can document reasons for zero cases (e.g., temporary closure, programmatic changes) to preserve data continuity.
