raw_output:
[P1] The establishment of a Softwood Lumber Board as an industry-run entity raises concerns about private agenda-setting for a sector-wide promotion program without sufficient independent public oversight; recommend clearer statutory limits on Board authority and public-interest safeguards.

[P1] The provision does not specify Sunshine/Open Meetings or FOIA applicability to Board meetings or records; commenters will request explicit transparency and public-records obligations for the Board.

[P2] The 15 million board feet eligibility threshold for Board membership effectively excludes small and mid-sized manufacturers and importers from serving, concentrating power among very large firms.

[P2] The 15 million board feet cutoff is arbitrary and lacks an economic justification in the rule text; commenters will ask for data showing how this threshold was chosen and for consideration of lower thresholds or a tiered representative model.

[P3] Apportioning seats strictly by production and import volume will underrepresent smaller operations and niche producers; commenters will request that non-volume factors (e.g., regional economic impact, employment, value-added) be considered.

[P4] Apportioning seats by size within geographic regions could freeze existing market concentration into governance and prevent representation of emerging businesses; commenters will urge mechanisms to ensure rotating small-business seats or term limits.

[P5] Allowing a seat to be filled by any-size nominee only when no eligible nominee exists could be used to circumvent intended size representation; commenters will ask for clear criteria and documentation required to demonstrate "no eligible nominee."

[P6] Allowing members to serve out terms after their size category changes could undermine the balance the size-based apportionment seeks to achieve; legal commentators will suggest requiring reassignment or replacement if size-category changes exceed a defined threshold.

[P7] Fixing Board size at 16 in 2020 and 14 thereafter seems arbitrary; commenters will ask for explanation of how these numbers optimize representation and governance efficiency and for flexibility tied to industry changes.

[P8] The allocation of 10–11 domestic manufacturer seats among three regions may not reflect current production geography; regional industry associations will request that initial apportionment be data-driven and publicly justified.

[P9] Requiring two large and three small South Region representatives in 2020 locks in a 3:2 small-to-large split that may not match actual operator distributions; Southern manufacturers will request the rule use current three-year averages before initial composition.

[P10] Making one South Region seat "any size" after 2021 creates ambiguity about how that seat will be filled; commenters will ask for clearer nomination eligibility and whether that seat is intended to be competitive.

[P11] The prescribed number of West Region members (five in 2020, four thereafter) may under/over-represent Western producers relative to national volumes; Western industry groups will request that regional seats be calibrated to actual production/import data.

[P12] The 2020 West Region requirement of four large and one small member will exclude most Western small producers from meaningful representation; small Western mills will object that this biases the Board toward consolidation interests.

[P13] For 2021 onward, permitting one West Region seat to be "any size" could permit dominance by large operators if nomination procedures are not controlled; commenters will request safeguards ensuring that "any size" seats do not consistently default to large firms.

[P14] Having only one Northeast and Lake States Region member (any size) risks systematic underrepresentation of that region; regional stakeholders will urge increasing seats or built-in rotating seats to ensure adequate voice.

[P15] Allowing four members in 2021 to be of any size could be used to pack the Board with large operators; small-business advocacy groups will request that "any size" seats be limited or that at least a minimum number be reserved for small businesses.

[P16] Allocating five importer seats in 2020 solely to defined Canadian regions may improperly privilege Canadian exporters and fails to account for imported softwood from other countries; importers of non-Canadian product will object.

[P17] The West-Region importer seat split (two large, one small) presumes importer-size categories align with Canadian sourcing regions; commenters will request clarification of how importer size is measured and documented.

[P18] Requiring one large and one small importer from the Canadian East Region may be impossible if importer business models or customs data do not clearly segregate by East/West sourcing; trade associations will ask for operational definitions and evidentiary requirements.

[P19] The 2021 importer composition (two large, one small, one any size) risks the "any size" slot being consistently filled by large importers; importers' groups will request proportional representation tied to import volumes, not arbitrary labels.

[P20] The requirement that at least three importer members import from specified regions may exclude importers with mixed sourcing or domestic brokers; commenters will ask the Board to allow multi-region importers to qualify and for clear percentage sourcing thresholds.

[P21] Mandating two importer members import from Canadian West Region could over-represent that sourcing region even if import volumes have shifted; commenters will ask that reapportionment account for up-to-date three-year averages.

[P22] Requiring one importer from Canadian East Region may be infeasible if market flows change (e.g., supply disruptions); commenters will ask for contingency procedures when region-specific importers are unavailable.

[P23] The five-year review required "but not more frequently than once in each three-year period" creates confusion—commenters will request clearer timing (e.g., must conduct at least once every five years but no more than once every three years is contradictory) and suggest harmonizing to "at least once every five years and no more often than once every three years."

[P24] Using a three-year average to review geographic distribution may mask sudden market shifts or one-off disruptions; commenters will request allowance for using shorter- or longer-term metrics when warranted and transparency on data sources.

[P25] Reviewing size-distributions by three-year averages similarly could disadvantage rapidly growing small businesses; small-business commenters will request that the Board consider year-to-year trends and provide a margin protecting small-firm representation.

[P26] The Board's authority to recommend reapportionment to the Secretary lacks an independent review standard; commenters will ask for objective triggers (numeric thresholds) for when reapportionment is "warranted."

[P27] The rule's requirement to consider volumes and size-distribution in reapportionment is vague; stakeholders will call for a published reapportionment methodology with weighting rules and examples.

[P28] Allowing the number of Board members to be changed as part of reapportionment could be used to manipulate board composition; legal commenters will request strict limits, thresholds, and public notice requirements before changing total membership.

[P29] Requiring Secretary-implemented rulemaking for composition changes may cause delays; industry commenters will ask for an expedited administrative process or interim measures to implement reapportionment in a timely way.

[P30] The nomination procedures lack timelines and required outreach metrics; commenters will request minimum outreach standards, public notice periods, and language access to ensure broad participation.

[P31] The Board's obligation to conduct outreach to "all segments" is undefined; civil-society commenters will request specific outreach requirements (e.g., notices to associations, independent mills, importers, trade unions) and documentation of outreach results.

[P32] Allowing only domestic manufacturers and importers to submit nominations excludes mill employees, value-chain actors (distributors, retailers), or consumer representatives; commenters will propose expanding nominators or creating advisory seats for other stakeholders.

[P33] The nominee eligibility requirement of 15 million board feet per fiscal year will exclude many domestic manufacturers and importers and may violate the Order's stated intent to represent industry segments; small firms will request inclusion of lower-volume nominees or reserved seats.

[P34] Permitting a short background statement is insufficient for vetting; commenters will request standardized disclosure forms on conflicts of interest, ownership, subsidiaries, and trade associations.

[P35] Allowing nominees to pursue any eligible seats could create strategic stacking; commenters will ask for rules preventing a single nominee from simultaneously being considered for multiple seats or requiring preference ranking.

[P36] The Board's duty to submit one primary and one additional nominee per seat may be inadequate if both nominees are from the same corporate family; commenters will call for prohibition of affiliated nominees or requirement that alternates be independent.

[P37] The rule requires designation of other qualified but not recommended persons as additional nominees, but does not require their qualifications be provided to the Secretary or public; commenters will request that full nominee records be transmitted.

[P38] Requiring nominations be submitted six months before term start could be burdensome, especially for new Board configurations after reapportionment; commenters will ask for flexibility or transitional timing provisions.

[P39] The Secretary's duty to select from Board-submitted nominations concentrates selection power on a potentially self-interested Board; commenters will recommend independent vetting by USDA or an advisory panel and require documented reasons for selections or rejections.

[P40] The prohibition on two members being employed by the same legal entity (including affiliates and subsidiaries) is positive but lacks an enforcement mechanism; commenters will ask for a clear disclosure process and penalties for violations.

[P41] Allowing the Board to recommend nomination-procedure modifications without a requirement for public comment could lead to opaque changes; commenters will request mandatory public comment periods before the Secretary considers such proposals.

[P42] Requiring the Secretary to implement nomination-procedure modifications via rulemaking provides accountability but may be slow; industry commenters will request an interim approval pathway for non-substantive changes.

[P43] The quorum requirement mandating at least two importers and five domestic manufacturers be present could paralyze meetings if importer seats are vacant; commenters will ask for contingency rules for temporarily filling or waiving these minima.

[P44] Counting remote participants as present for quorum and voting is appropriate but needs cybersecurity and authentication safeguards; commenters will request specific procedures to verify identity and protect vote integrity.

[P45] Allowing electronic voting is modernizing but leaves open questions about anonymity and auditability; commenters will ask for secure electronic voting standards, record retention, and independent audits.

[P46] Prohibiting proxy voting could hinder representation for geographically dispersed small operators; commenters will suggest allowing limited proxies under strict conditions and with authentication to improve participation.

[P47] The voting rule requiring majority plus two for assessments or budgets restricts decision-making but may protect minority interests; however, industry commenters will object to the supermajority and request clarifying whether "majority plus two" means two additional votes or two percentage points.

[P48] The "timely notice" requirement for meetings is vague; commenters will request minimum advance notice periods (e.g., 15 days for regular meetings, 48 hours for emergency meetings) and multilingual notices.

[P49] Allowing the Board to act outside convened meetings when the chair deems necessary centralizes power in the chair; commenters will request that the chair's determination be subject to majority approval or defined emergency criteria.

[P50] The requirement that all members and the Secretary be notified for off-meeting actions could be impractical on short notice; commenters will ask for a defined minimum notice period and proof-of-delivery standards.

[P51] Requiring a majority (or majority plus two) for off-meeting votes duplicates in-person thresholds but raises concerns about participation; commenters will request quorum verification and minimum participation rates for validity.

[P52] Prompt written confirmation and minute-recording of off-meeting votes is good practice but needs a defined timeline (e.g., within seven days) and public access to minutes; commenters will request these specifics.

[P53] The specified conversion factor for thousand board feet needs to be published and justified; commenters will ask for the exact factor, methodology, and how it accounts for different lumber dimensions and species.

[P54] A referendum every seven years to determine continuation may be too infrequent for industry changes; commenters will propose more frequent reviews or interim evaluations, particularly given market volatility and trade disputes.

[P55] Requiring both a majority of voting manufacturers and importers representing a majority of volume to favor continuation sets a high bar that could allow a small number of large-volume firms to defeat continuation; small manufacturers and worker advocates will argue this disenfranchises many producers.

[P56] Excluding domestic products that cannot be categorized under the referenced HTSUS numbers could create loopholes and inconsistent coverage; commenters will request clearer product definitions and examples to avoid disputes.

[P57] Treating U.S.-origin softwood exported and returned as covered if it fits HTSUS categories raises recording and jurisdictional questions; exporters/bers will request clear documentation requirements to avoid double-counting or improper assessments.

[P58] Exempting temporarily imported articles with subchapter XIII HTSUS exemptions is consistent with customs law but may create opportunities for evasion; commenters will request verification procedures and penalties for misclassified temporary imports.

[P1] The October 26, 2020 comment deadline is unreasonably short and will prevent small operators and public interest groups from preparing thorough technical comments; extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] The provision requiring FAA to "receive comments by October 26, 2020" fails to account for postal delays and does not clarify acceptance of electronically dated submissions received after that date; clarify receipt rules and permit postmarked-by dates.

[P2] The compliance obligation is vague because it references "specified compliance times" without summarizing them in the AD preamble; include a clear table of compliance deadlines in the AD text to avoid confusion.

[P2] The "unless already complied" carve-out lacks documentation requirements; require operators who claim prior compliance to produce maintenance records and serial numbers when asserting the exception.

[P3] The borescope inspection requirement applies to a long list of part numbers but omits a clear method to confirm part-numbered history for engines with incomplete records; require guidance on verifying part numbers and acceptable evidence for engines with incomplete traceability.

[P3] The list of diffuser case assembly part numbers (e.g., 2A0051, 2A2081–01, etc.) appears incomplete — the rule does not specify whether superseded or superseding part numbers are included; revise to include all superseded/replacement part numbers or reference a parts table in the service bulletin.

[P4] The threshold of 19,000 CSN to trigger immediate inspection is arbitrary and unsupported in the rule text; provide the risk assessment and data justifying the 19,000-cycle threshold.

[P4] Using CSN rather than cycles since last piece-part inspection (CSLFPI) when CSLFPI is unknown could misclassify components; require operators to exhaust all traceability avenues before resorting to CSN and describe acceptable methods to determine CSLFPI.

[P5] The requirement to perform initial BSI before reaching 20,300 CSN for parts under 19,000 CSN on the effective date imposes a narrow compliance window for high-utilization fleets; provide phased compliance or allow compliance at scheduled maintenance to reduce operational disruption.

[P6] The 250-cycle compliance window when CSN is unknown is too short for aircraft on long lease or in storage where cycles are infrequent; extend the window or allow an alternative verification procedure for stored/low-cycle engines.

[P7] Mandating use of specific paragraphs (2.A–2.G) of NMASB Revision 2 makes compliance contingent on a non-federal document that may change; incorporate the essential inspection steps into the AD or include the NMASB as a federal reference to avoid ambiguity.

[P7] Operators should be allowed to use equivalent inspection procedures performed by certificated repair stations using approved procedures rather than strictly the NMASB paragraphs; revise to permit equivalent procedures with FAA approval.

[P8] Requiring repeat BSIs at intervals not to exceed 2,100 cycles after a negative inspection may impose excessive maintenance costs for large fleets; justify the 2,100-cycle interval with supporting inspection interval analysis and consider allowing interval extension based on operational usage.

[P8] The rule does not address coordination with scheduled maintenance intervals; permit aligning the 2,100-cycle BSI with planned shop visits to minimize aircraft downtime.

[P9] If a crack is found, the AD requires either replacement or following NMASB tables to repeat inspections, but does not define acceptable crack sizes or acceptance criteria; include clear crack sizing limits and mandatory removal-to-service criteria.

[P9] Allowing repeated inspection in lieu of immediate replacement when a crack is found could permit continued operation with known damage; require mandatory replacement for cracks exceeding a conservative threshold and specify when repeated inspection is permissible.

[P10] Replacing the diffuser case M-flange at the next engine shop visit or before 20,000 CSN, whichever is later, could allow an engine to operate past 20,000 CSN if the next shop visit is scheduled late; change "whichever is later" to "whichever occurs earlier" to prevent operation beyond 20,000 CSN.

[P10] The "next engine shop visit" phrase is ambiguous — define "engine shop visit" (e.g., on-wing, removal for overhaul, major shop visit) to prevent inconsistent interpretations among operators.

[P11] Repeating replacement before accumulating 20,000 cycles since last replacement creates a recurring high cost; request analysis of life-cycle cost and consider extending life limit if inspections demonstrate low crack incidence.

[P11] The rule does not provide credit for recently replaced parts with documented low CSN; allow prorated credit or extend the replacement interval for newly installed M-flanges with traceable low-cycle histories.

[P12] Stating that replacement terminates the repetitive BSI requirement may be risky if replacement parts have variable histories; require that replacement M-flanges be new or documented as below a specified CSN threshold to qualify as terminating action.

[P12] The AD should require documentation of replacement (part number, serial, CSN at installation) be filed in the engine logbooks to qualify as terminating action; add specific recordkeeping requirements.

[P13] The installation prohibition banning installation of any diffuser case with more than 20,000 CSN after the effective date could create inventory issues for MROs that hold used parts above that CSN for spares; allow temporary use of such spares under an AMOC or require scrapping but provide a reasonable phase-out period.

[P13] The prohibition does not address the legality of installing over-limit parts to complete necessary ferry flights to reach maintenance facilities; add an exception for one-time ferry operations with conditions.

[P14] The credit-for-previous-actions permission references listed service documents but does not specify acceptable evidence to claim credit; require that operators provide dated service bulletin compliance records and associated sign-offs.

[P14] Clarify whether prior inspections/replacements conducted to earlier revisions of the listed service documents are acceptable for credit, or whether only Revision 2 actions qualify.

[P15] Granting the Manager the authority to approve AMOCs is appropriate, but the AD should set target timelines for FAA response to AMOC requests to prevent prolonged operational uncertainty; require FAA to respond within 60 days.

[P16] Requiring AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO may be inefficient for international operators without a U.S. principal inspector; allow direct submission to the certification office manager for foreign operators.

[P17] The obligation to send AMOC information to the person in paragraph (l)(1) lacks that person's contact details in the AD; include the name, title, mailing address, and email to ensure proper routing.

[P18] Permitting AMOC emails to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov is helpful, but the AD should also provide alternative secure transmission methods for proprietary technical data; allow encrypted attachments or a secure portal.

[P19] Requiring notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC may be impractical for large multi-base operators with many inspectors; provide streamlined notification processes or central FAA liaison contact options.

[P20] The parallel October 26, 2020 deadline for airspace comments duplicates P1 and may confuse stakeholders; consolidate comment deadlines or explain whether these are distinct dockets and whether separate submissions are required.

[P21] Requiring comments to be sent to a physical DOT Docket Operations address without acknowledging current electronic-only operations is outdated; explicitly state that electronic submissions via Regulations.gov satisfy the ADDRESSES requirement.

[P22] The requirement to identify docket numbers at the beginning of comments is reasonable, but the AD should provide clear instructions and examples for combined comments addressing multiple docket numbers to avoid misfiling.

[P23] While allowing Regulations.gov submissions is appropriate, the AD should clarify acceptable file formats and maximum file sizes for attachments to prevent rejection of large technical reports.

[P24] The direction to submit communications in triplicate to DOT Docket Operations is unnecessary given electronic filing and may impose burdens on commenters; dispense with the triplicate requirement or make it optional for physical mail only.

[P25] Requiring a self-addressed stamped postcard to receive acknowledgment is burdensome and unnecessary in the age of email confirmations; accept an email address for acknowledgment instead.

[P26] The general invitation to comment is appropriate, but the AD should proactively solicit data from small air carriers and repair stations on cost impacts; include a specific request for operational impact data.

[P27] Allowing in-person docket review is useful, but the AD should provide alternatives (digital copies) for international stakeholders who cannot visit; ensure all docket materials are available online.

[P28] The informal docket hours are limited to weekdays 8:00–4:30 and may not accommodate after-hours research by industry attorneys; provide a contact for scheduling or extend availability.

[P3] Legal experts will comment that the AD's heavy reliance on service bulletin procedures may raise preemption/consensus issues if the service bulletin contains operator-specific repair station procedures not vetted in rulemaking; recommend careful incorporation-by-reference and public availability of the NMASB.

[P9] Safety advocates will demand mandatory immediate grounding or suspensions of operations when certain crack sizes are found rather than permitting repeated inspections, to avoid catastrophic failure risk; specify immediate corrective actions for any through-thickness crack.

[P13] Leasing companies will object that the installation prohibition could render many leased engines unsupportable mid-lease; request transitional provisions protecting lessors and lessees or compensation mechanisms.

[P6] Maintenance organizations will seek a clear definition of "cycles" used for the 250-cycle requirement (flight cycles vs. engine cycles vs. takeoff/landing cycles) and request alignment with existing OEM definitions.

[P8] Airlines will request that the FAA permit incorporation of borescope inspections into scheduled C-checks to reduce aircraft downtime, and ask for explicit permission to count those inspections as compliant under the AD.

[P15] Manufacturers will request that the AD permit the engine OEM to propose AMOCs based on engineering data without requiring operator-specific substantiation for each request.

[P11] Financial stakeholders will request a regulatory flexibility analysis or small-entity compliance guide addressing the recurring replacement costs implied by the 20,000-cycle replacement rule.

[P3] Repair stations will request training and certification guidance for technicians performing the specified borescope inspections under NMASB Revision 2 to ensure inspection consistency and defensibility.

[P12] Require retention of inspection records for a minimum period (e.g., 5 years) and specify that records be made available to FAA upon request to ensure that replacement truly terminates inspection obligations.

[P1] Industry commenters will request clarification that the ban on aversive conditioning devices in § 882.5235(b) applies only when devices are used with the explicit intent to "reduce or stop" aggressive or self-injurious behavior, and not to other diagnostic, research, or non-behavioral applications of similar devices.

[P1] Disability-rights advocates will assert that the prohibition in § 882.5235(b) is too narrow because it only bans “use to reduce or cease aggressive or self-injurious behavior” and should also prohibit any use of aversive devices that may cause pain, distress, or long-term harm regardless of stated intent.

[P1] Facility administrators will claim the rule lacks a definition of “aversive conditioning devices,” creating uncertainty about whether commonly used sensory techniques, restraints, or mild stimuli are encompassed by the ban.

[P1] Legal experts will argue that § 882.5235(b) should include explicit grandfathering or transition provisions for ongoing individualized treatment plans to avoid sudden disruption of court-ordered or long-standing therapeutic programs.

[P1] Parent and guardian groups will contend the prohibition must include exceptions for emergency, life-saving situations where an aversive stimulus might be the only immediate option to prevent imminent harm.

[P2] Advocacy organizations will request an extension of the comments due date beyond July 7, 2016, arguing that the current deadline does not provide adequate time for stakeholders to prepare substantive responses given the complexity of the rule.

[P2] Industry associations will claim the July 7, 2016 deadline is procedurally defective if notice to affected parties was insufficient and ask the agency to reopen the comment period.

[P3] Air carrier operators or maintenance providers will ask for clarification of what constitutes the “specified compliance times” referenced in paragraph (f) and request that the AD include explicit calendar-based deadlines rather than only referring to external service documents.

[P3] Legal commenters will assert that paragraph (f) should provide relief or a phased compliance schedule for operators who can demonstrate that immediate compliance would create undue operational or safety hardship.

[P4] Operators and maintenance providers will request that the referenced Airbus Service Bulletin A300–54–0075, Revision 04, be incorporated by reference in the rule text or made available electronically so they can determine the “applicable time” for the pylon side panel inspection.

[P4] Safety advocacy groups will argue that the inspection at rib 8 specified in paragraph (g) may not be sufficient and request that the AD expand the inspection to adjacent ribs and additional pylon areas to ensure structural integrity.

[P5] Maintenance organizations will request that the rule specify acceptable HFEC equipment and calibration standards for the crack-confirmation inspection in paragraph (h) to ensure consistent inspection quality across operators.

[P5] Aircraft manufacturers will ask the FAA to allow a short ferry flight or limited flight privilege after a crack indication to reach a maintenance facility, instead of the absolute “before further flight” restriction, when the crack is below a specified size and subject to flight-limited procedures.

[P6] Operators will request that paragraph (i) explicitly state the inspection intervals in the regulatory text (rather than only by reference) to avoid ambiguity and ensure enforceability.

[P6] Some commenters will argue that the “either/or” choice in paragraph (i) (repeat inspections or modify pylons) should be tied to objective criteria (e.g., aircraft age, flight cycles, severity thresholds) rather than leaving the choice solely to operator discretion.

[P7] Operators will ask that the repeated inspection interval in paragraph (i)(1) be extended (lengthened) or allow risk-based intervals for low-utilization aircraft to reduce maintenance burden and cost.

[P7] Safety advocates will push back, requesting that the repeated inspection interval in (i)(1) be shortened for older aircraft or those with prior crack history.

[P8] Operators will request that the modification in paragraph (i)(2) be eligible for a one-time compliance credit if performed on multiple pylons simultaneously and that the rule allow scheduling flexibility for modifications.

[P8] Cost-concerned commenters will ask the FAA to provide an economic analysis of the required pylon modification in (i)(2) and to offer financial relief or extended compliance times for small operators.

[P9] Maintenance providers will request that the required post-modification HFEC inspection interval in (i)(2) be expressly specified in the AD text to avoid reliance on potentially superseded service bulletin intervals.

[P9] Technical commenters will recommend that, if modification is accomplished, the AD allow reduced HFEC frequency only when supported by damage-tolerance analysis submitted as an AMOC.

[P10] Operators and repair stations will seek clarity on acceptable repair methods in (i)(2)(third sentence) and request a pre-approved list or engineering criteria to streamline FAA Manager or EASA DOA approval.

[P10] Legal commenters will urge that the requirement to obtain FAA Manager, EASA, or EASA-DOA approval for repairs be accompanied by a defined, expedited approval timeline to prevent extended aircraft out-of-service time.

[P11] Maintenance organizations will request that paragraph (j) allow temporary repair measures with operational limitations (e.g., flight restrictions, weight or speed limitations) until a permanent repair approved by the FAA Manager or EASA is implemented.

[P11] International operators will ask the FAA to clarify whether repairs approved by EASA or Airbus's EASA DOA automatically satisfy FAA approval, and request a streamlined reciprocal acceptance process.

[P12] Operators will request clearer guidance on what specific service information qualifies for credit under paragraph (k) and whether earlier revisions or equivalent manufacturer-approved procedures are acceptable.

[P12] Regulatory lawyers will comment that paragraph (k) should require documentation standards for prior-completed actions (e.g., work orders, sign-offs) to establish credit and avoid future enforcement disputes.

[P13] Operators and repair stations will welcome the AMOC authority in (l)(1) but request a clear standard of review for AMOC approvals and an expectation-setting timeline for decision-making.

[P13] Safety advocates will caution that the AMOC provision must not be used to weaken inspection or repair standards and request that AMOCs be publicly posted with redacted proprietary information.

[P14] Commenters will ask for clarification about which office (principal inspector vs. local FSDO) is appropriate for operators that cross multiple districts or have relocated, and request a single point of contact option.

[P14] Small operators will request an electronic submission process for AMOC requests to their principal inspector or FSDO to reduce administrative burden and delay.

[P15] Commenters will request that the International Branch contact details in (l)(1) be updated to include a generic inbox and secure file-transfer option rather than relying on an individual (Dan Rodina) and a single fax number.

[P15] Security-conscious stakeholders will request assurance that email submissions to the specified address will be protected and that large data sets (inspection records, HFEC data) can be submitted securely.

[P16] Operators will request that the “notify before using an approved AMOC” requirement in (l)(1) be clarified to define the time window for notification (e.g., 24 hours before first use, within 5 business days after approval).

[P16] Airlines will propose that notification may be provided electronically via the principal inspector’s online portal as an acceptable method to satisfy the pre-use notification requirement.

[P17] Legal commenters will request that AMOC approval letters required to “specifically reference this AD” include a standardized citation format (AD number, effective date, and affected part numbers) to avoid ambiguity.

[P17] Operators will ask that the FAA allow AMOC approvals to reference groups of ADs where appropriate, to reduce paperwork when multiple ADs apply to a common repair or inspection.

[P18] Maintenance organizations will request that paragraph (l)(2) permit corrective-action methods approved by the manufacturer’s engineering authority outside EASA DOA if supported by FAA-approved substantiation, to accommodate non-EASA manufacturer approvals.

[P18] Commenters will ask the FAA to require manufacturers to provide a documented rationale and fatigue/damage-tolerance analysis when proposing corrective actions under (l)(2) so the FAA can evaluate long-term safety.

[P19] EASA and Airbus DOA representatives will request that the DOA-authorized signature requirement in (l)(2) be clarified to accept electronic signatures that meet DOA recordkeeping standards.

[P19] Legal commenters will point out that mandating a DOA-authorized signature without defining acceptable signature formats (wet ink vs. electronic) could slow approvals and request explicit acceptance criteria.

[P1] The requirement to publish the draft economic analysis "at the time" of the proposed critical habitat designation is ambiguous and should specify a minimum lead time (e.g., 60 days before the end of the comment period) so stakeholders have adequate time to review technical analyses.

[P1] Industry commenters will object that releasing only a "draft" economic analysis at proposal time without guaranteeing availability of supporting data and models impedes meaningful comment and request that the rule require publication of underlying data, assumptions, and model code.

[P2] Request that the Federal Register summary include key quantitative estimates (e.g., total projected costs, distribution of costs by sector, and range/uncertainty) rather than a qualitative summary so stakeholders can assess the draft analysis quickly.

[P3] Defense and national security stakeholders will demand clarification of how "national security impacts" will be identified and what interagency consultation process and protections (e.g., classified submissions) will be used before public disclosure.

[P3] Environmental NGOs will request that the Secretary be required to explain and document how identified national security impacts were weighed, with redaction only where legally necessary, to prevent overbroad claims of national security used to exclude habitat.

[P4] Landowners and local governments will support the requirement to identify and explain areas the Secretary is considering for exclusion but ask that the rule require the Secretary to publish the criteria and evidence supporting each proposed exclusion decision concurrently with the proposed designation.

[P5] Commenters will request that the phrase "at an appropriate scale" be defined (e.g., parcel-level, county-level, watershed-level) and that the rule require analysis at multiple spatial scales to capture localized impacts and cumulative regional impacts.

[P6] Some commenters will point out that permitting qualitative-only descriptions (without minimum quantitative thresholds) could allow agencies to downplay significant economic impacts and request that socioeconomic thresholds trigger quantitative analysis (e.g., impacts exceeding $5 million or affecting >100 jobs).

[P7] Conservation groups will argue that requiring consideration of probable impacts "before finalizing" is insufficiently prescriptive and request that the Secretary be required to respond to substantive comment on impacts in the final rule with written explanations for how comments changed (or did not change) the designation.

[P8] Commenters will challenge the open-ended "may choose" discretion to conduct exclusion analyses, urging that the agency should be required to conduct exclusion analyses whenever proponents submit credible information of impacts (i.e., eliminate discretionary refusal).

[P9] Legal commenters will request that § 17.90(c)(2) explicitly list timelines and standards for initiating and completing an exclusion analysis when the triggers in (c)(2)(i) or (ii) are met to prevent indefinite delays.

[P10] Permittee and industry groups will applaud that credible information from permittees triggers an exclusion analysis but will request clarification what constitutes "credible information" (e.g., sworn affidavits, economic studies by qualified economists) and require minimum evidentiary standards.

[P10] Environmental groups will warn that allowing permittees, lessees, or contractors to trigger exclusion analyses could incentivize gaming and request safeguards against fabricated or low-quality submissions.

[P11] NGOs will express concern that allowing the Secretary discretion to evaluate areas for exclusion (c)(2)(ii) could enable political influence; they will request transparency requirements and a public notice-and-comment period prior to initiating discretionary exclusion analyses.

[P12] Tribal commenters will support the explicit weighing requirement but ask the rule to require that Tribal information be solicited proactively and that Tribal sovereign submissions receive confidentiality protections where requested.

[P13] Commenters will request more detail on the standard for "assign[ing] weight" to outside experts' information and whether that weight is rebuttable only by "evidence" — asking the rule to require documented reasoned explanation when the Service departs from outside experts' conclusions.

[P14] Federally recognized Tribes will request specific procedures for how nonbiological impacts they identify will be solicited, evaluated, and afforded weight, including timelines for Tribal consultation and opportunities to submit supporting documentation.

[P15] State and local governments will request an explicit commitment that the Service will defer to binding state regulatory determinations and include those findings in exclusion analyses with defined evidentiary weight.

[P16] DOD/DHS or commenters concerned with security will request a classified-submission process so that national security agencies can convey impacts without public disclosure, with assurance the Service will consider classified impacts in exclusion determinations.

[P17] Permittee groups will request that personal business confidential information submitted by lessees/permittees be kept confidential (beyond general posting of comments) and outline an in-camera review process to protect proprietary data.

[P18] Economists will request that when the Service weighs economic impacts within its expertise it must use standard discounting, sensitivity analysis, and disclose benefit-cost comparisons quantitatively wherever practicable.

[P19] Conservation plan proponents will request clearer guidance on what will be considered "authorized" under section 10 so they can predict whether their plans will be favorably weighed under § 17.90(d)(3).

[P20] Developers and local governments will request objective criteria and documentation the Service will use to determine whether a permittee is "properly implementing" a conservation plan to avoid arbitrary determinations.

[P21] Plan authors will ask the Service to require demonstration—by measurable performance metrics—that a species is covered in a plan (e.g., explicit measurable conservation objectives) before counting that plan toward exclusion benefits under § 17.90(d)(3)(ii).

[P22] Commenters will ask that the Service define what it means for a plan to "meet its conservation needs in the planning area" and require the use of science-based biological endpoints rather than general or aspirational commitments.

[P23] Conservation NGOs will request that the permissive "may consider" factors (d)(4) for non-permitted plans be made mandatory to ensure consistent and thorough evaluation of voluntary or private conservation mechanisms.

[P24] Developers will argue that § 17.90(d)(4)(i) is appropriate but request the Service provide clear standards for concluding that designation would "impair expected benefits," including use of empirical projections and mitigation feasibility.

[P25] Public participation advocates will insist the Service must specify how it will evaluate "extent of public participation" (d)(4)(ii) and ensure disadvantaged communities and local stakeholders are meaningfully engaged in plan development.

[P26] States will request the Service give definitive weight to completed state regulatory reviews under (d)(4)(iii), and to coordinate timelines so pending state processes are not prejudiced by federal designations.

[P27] NGOs will say NEPA reviews described in (d)(4)(iv) should not substitute for species-specific science and ask the Service to not overvalue generic NEPA documentation when it lacks species/habitat specifics.

[P28] Proponents of conservation banking will request guidance on what constitutes "demonstrated implementation and success" (d)(4)(v), including minimum monitoring data or third-party audits required to prove success.

[P29] Scientists will request that (d)(4)(vi) require explicit mapping and measurable indicators of the "physical or biological features essential" to the species to avoid vague assertions that plans conserve essential features.

[P30] Commenters will ask that (d)(4)(vii) require binding commitments or funding assurances from plan proponents to create a "reasonable expectation" of implementation rather than relying on voluntary or aspirational language.

[P31] Conservation practitioners will insist that (d)(4)(viii) require detailed monitoring protocols, predefined adaptive triggers, and public reporting schedules for any plan to be weighed favorably.

[P32] Industry commenters will support § 17.90(e) (must exclude if benefits of exclusion outweigh inclusion) but request the rule require a quantified net-benefit test with standardized valuation methods to ensure predictable outcomes.

[P33] Environmental scientists will object to § 17.90(e) to the extent it mandates exclusion whenever non-economic benefits outweigh conservation benefits without requiring that extinction risks be centrally considered—urge stronger protection.

[P33] Many conservation commenters will stress that the exception in § 17.90(e) (do not exclude if failure to designate would result in extinction) needs a clear legal and scientific standard for when the Service may determine extinction risk, with thresholds and peer review.

[P34] Legal commenters will note the authority citation (P34) is standard but request cross-references be updated to reflect any statutory interpretations relied upon in the rulemaking discussion.

[P35] Conservation groups will strongly oppose deleting subpart I (§ 17.90) from part 17 (P35) if that deletion removes procedural safeguards; they request explanation and justification for removal and analysis of impacts of removing the regulatory text versus amending it.

[P36] Regulatory practitioners will support the redesignations in P36 and P37 for housekeeping but ask that all cross-references throughout the CFR and internal guidance be updated simultaneously to avoid confusion.

[P38] Chemical manufacturers will request more detailed hazard data and the rationale for the significant new use determination for PMN P–20–162 (P38), including toxicology, exposure scenarios, and whether low-volume exemptions were considered.

[P39] Workers and unions will request clarification of specific workplace protections referenced in § 721.63 for PMN P–20–162 (P39), including whether medical surveillance and training are required and at what frequency.

[P40] Industry will object that the rule's instruction to "consider and, where feasible, implement engineering or administrative controls" (P40) is vague and request mandatory hierarchy of controls language and examples of acceptable controls.

[P41] Downstream users will request clear labeling and SDS requirements tied to the hazard communication provisions in § 721.72 (P41), and timelines for updating labels if alternative GHS/OSHA statements are used (P43).

[P42] Trade associations will ask for harmonization language confirming that use of alternative hazard statements consistent with GHS and OSHA (P43/P56) will satisfy both TSCA/TSCA significant new use rule requirements and other federal requirements to avoid conflicting obligations.

[P43] Importers will object to the significant new use trigger for importing the substance not in solution except sealed ≤5 kg containers (P45), arguing that the ≤5 kg threshold is arbitrary and should be increased or tied to exposure risk assessments.

[P44] Process industries will challenge the "non-enclosed process generating dust/mist/aerosol" trigger (P46) as overly broad and request a de minimis exception for processes that generate trace aerosols below specified airborne concentration thresholds.

[P45] Manufacturers will request clarification of the 18-month manufacturing duration trigger (P47), including whether interruptions or batch manufacture count toward the 18 months and whether legacy inventories are covered.

[P46] Industry will request that recordkeeping requirements (P48, P59) explicitly allow for electronic records and specify retention periods and access protections for confidential business information.

[P47] Commenters will ask for clear procedures and timelines under § 721.1725(b)(1) (P50, P61) for determining whether listed uses are subject to the SNUR to avoid uncertainty for ongoing R&D projects.

[P48] Worker safety advocates will request that the respirator requirement with NIOSH APF ≥50 (P54) be accompanied by fit testing, medical evaluation, and program oversight requirements to ensure effective protection.

[P49] Environmental groups will request that release-to-water requirements (P58) specify numeric effluent limits and monitoring frequencies rather than simply cross-referencing § 721.90 to ensure adequate aquatic protection.

[P50] Small business representatives will request a regulatory flexibility analysis or small-entity compliance guide for the chemical-specific SNURs (P38, P51), as the rule imposes reporting and recordkeeping burdens without tailored support.

[P51] Procedural commenters will object to the duplication/contradiction in two identical comment-deadline provisions (P62 and P63) and ask the agency to correct any clerical errors and confirm the actual deadline.

[P52] Accessibility advocates will request that the agency provide alternative submission means and assistance beyond regulations.gov (contrary to the "request" to use only specified methods in P67/P75) to ensure participation by those with limited internet access.

[P53] Privacy advocates will object to the blanket statement that personal information will be posted (P68) and demand a presumption of redaction for personal phone numbers and addresses unless the commenter affirmatively consents to public disclosure.

[P54] Legal commenters will point out that the instruction not to resubmit prior comments (P72) is inappropriate—every commenter should be free to reiterate or update earlier comments and the rule should not discourage new submissions that add new information.

[P55] Commenters will request that the agency extend the comment period (deadline in P62/P63/P69) to allow stakeholders time to review the draft economic analyses and technical documents, proposing an extension of at least 60–90 days.

[P56] Trade groups will ask the agency to clarify whether mailed comments that are postmarked by the deadline but arrive late due to postal delays will be accepted, requesting a policy of accepting any mailed comments postmarked by the deadline (to avoid P70 confusion).

[P57] Civil-society organizations will request that the Service provide a searchable docket with data tables and GIS files for all proposed critical habitat maps and economic analyses rather than only PDFs, to facilitate independent analysis.

[P58] Commenters will request clarification on how the Service will "consider all relevant information" (P71) and demand a requirement that the Service produce a substantive response to major categories of comments in the final rule.

[P59] Confidential business information submitters will request clear instructions on how to request withholding of identifying information (P73), including examples of acceptable redaction requests and agency process/timeline for confidentiality determinations.

[P60] Procedural commenters will ask the agency to ensure that comments and materials "made available for public inspection" (P74) are posted in a timely manner and that any redactions are explained and appealable.

[P61] Accessibility commenters will request that the Federal Relay Service number provided (P76) be supplemented with an email or text alternative for TDD users and that notice of accommodations be included in the Federal Register notice.

raw_output:
[P1] The deadline for receiving comments by January 27, 2023 is unreasonably brief and should be extended to allow operators, suppliers, and labor unions adequate time to analyze the technical service bulletin and prepare substantive comments.

[P1] The AD should clarify whether the January 27, 2023 deadline is the postmark date, receipt date, or email timestamp to avoid procedural rejections of late comments.

[P1] Because the Compliance Instructions reference Boeing documentation published after the NPRM, the FAA should reopen the comment period beyond January 27, 2023 to allow review of any later Boeing revisions.

[P2] Applying this AD to "all" Boeing 787–8/–9/–10 airplanes certificated in any category is overbroad; the FAA should limit applicability to specific line numbers, configurations, or operators based on fleet differences identified in Boeing's data.

[P2] The AD’s blanket applicability to aircraft certificated in any category could inadvertently include special mission, experimental, or government-owned aircraft whose unique configurations make the mandated actions unnecessary or unsafe; include explicit carve-outs or tailored applicability.

[P2] The rule should require Boeing and the FAA to provide a clear parts/serial-number table so owners can readily determine whether each specific 787 variant and equipment configuration is affected.

[P3] The obligation to "comply within the specified compliance times" without a regulatory grace period for logistic constraints (parts, shop availability) imposes undue operational and economic burden; the FAA should allow phased compliance or provide longer windows.

[P3] The AD should define whether compliance times are calendar days, flight cycles, or flight hours where the Boeing bulletin uses potentially ambiguous terms; lack of clarity could lead to inconsistent implementation and enforcement.

[P3] The AD should explicitly permit credit for actions previously performed in accordance with earlier Boeing service instructions even if those instructions are not identical, provided they achieved the same safety outcome.

[P4] Requiring performance "in accordance with the Accomplishment Instructions" of the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin without allowing operator-engineered alternatives risks forcing unnecessary or non-optimal workscopes; FAA should allow documented equivalent procedures approved via AMOC.

[P4] The AD should identify which specific steps in the Boeing bulletin are mandatory versus recommended — the current cross-reference approach makes it difficult to determine enforceable requirements.

[P5] Replacing references to "Issue 001 date" with the AD effective date may create timing mismatches if Boeing revises the Requirements Bulletin after the AD effective date; the FAA should allow the use of the latest applicable manufacturer-issued revision unless specifically limited.

[P5] The exception that uses the AD effective date in place of "Issue 001 date" could cause confusion when operators hold revisions with different issue dates; the AD should provide explicit examples showing how to apply the compliance times in such scenarios.

[P6] The provision authorizing the Manager to approve AMOCs is appropriate, but the rule should specify maximum processing times for AMOC decisions to prevent grounding while awaiting FAA determination.

[P6] Stakeholders request publication of objective criteria that the Seattle ACO will use when evaluating AMOC requests to promote transparency and predictability.

[P7] Directing AMOC requests to the principal inspector or responsible Flight Standards Office may be impractical for globally based operators; allow requests to be submitted through the FAA Flight Standards District Office or via the Seattle ACO point of contact to accommodate international operators.

[P7] The AD should clarify whether industry AMOC submissions to delegated organizational representatives (DARs) or FAA-authorized service centers satisfy the requirement to submit via the principal inspector or Flight Standards Office.

[P8] The instruction to address information to the person identified in paragraph (j) when sending directly to the certification office manager is unclear without paragraph (j) content in the AD text; include the specific name or office contact in this rule to avoid delays.

[P8] Legal commenters will note that failing to include the specific addressee in the regulatory text may create administrative confusion and challengeability of AMOC submissions.

[P9] Allowing email submissions to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is helpful, but the AD should require the FAA to acknowledge receipt within a defined period and provide a tracking number for each AMOC request.

[P9] The AD should specify acceptable file formats, maximum file sizes, and secure transmission protocols for emailed AMOC information to protect sensitive technical data.

[P10] Requiring notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC is reasonable, but the AD should specify the form and timeline for that notification (e.g., written notice within 5 business days) to avoid inconsistent practices.

[P10] Clarify whether use of an AMOC is permitted immediately upon FAA approval or only after the principal inspector confirms applicability — ambiguous sequencing could ground work unnecessarily.

[P11] Permitting Boeing ODA approval of AMOCs for repairs is efficient, but the AD must require the ODA to document the rationale and provide the FAA with copies of approvals to ensure oversight and auditability.

[P11] There is a potential conflict of interest in allowing Boeing ODA to approve AMOCs that affect Boeing products; the FAA should require independent FAA concurrence or an oversight review for ODA-approved AMOCs used for AD compliance.

[P12] The requirement that deviations meet the airplane's certification basis is vague; the AD should define the certification basis (e.g., type certificate and amendments) or reference where operators can find the applicable certification basis for their airplane.

[P12] Legal commenters will assert that retrofitting repairs to meet a historical certification basis may be impractical for older aircraft; allow equivalency demonstrations showing an equal level of safety rather than strict adherence to the original certification basis.

[P13] Requiring AMOC approvals to specifically reference this AD is appropriate, but the AD should also allow batch approvals referencing multiple ADs where the same proposed AMOC would satisfy several directives to reduce paperwork.

[P14] Mandating use of the incorporated service information "unless the AD specifies otherwise" means deviations are automatically disallowed; the AD should explicitly list any acceptable alternative documents or define the process for proposing alternative service information.

[P14] Operators request that the FAA make electronically searchable, tagged versions of the incorporated Boeing service information available to avoid transcription errors and ensure accurate compliance.

[P1] The temporary permission to allow recertification face-to-face encounters via telecommunications only through December 31, 2024 (or the end of a PHE) is too short and should be extended permanently to provide continuity of care and accommodate persistent patient access issues.

[P7] Allowing telehealth for hospice recertification only when the encounter is “solely for hospice recertification” is ambiguous; commenters will request guidance on whether subsequent brief clinical issues discussed during the same visit would invalidate telehealth eligibility.

[P8] Tying the telehealth option’s temporal scope to the Public Health Emergency definition in § 400.200 creates legal uncertainty; commenters will urge CMS to detach the authority from PHE declarations and instead base it on evidence of benefit to patients.

[P9] Requiring the encounter to be “solely for hospice recertification” will create workflow inefficiencies and may force duplicative visits; hospices will ask for permission to address minor related clinical needs during the same telehealth recertification encounter without losing eligibility.

[P2] The 90% submission obligation for HIS records within 30 days is unduly burdensome for small and rural hospices with limited IT resources and staff; commenters will request a phased implementation, a lower threshold for small providers, or technical assistance funds.

[P11] The numeric 90% threshold lacks justification in the preamble; stakeholders will demand evidence that 90% is necessary and proportional and ask CMS to publish the analytic basis for selecting this cutoff.

[P12] The 30-day timeframe for submission of HIS records after admission or discharge is impractical for hospices passing through weekend admissions, delayed EHR exports, or patient/family consent processes; commenters will request an expanded window (e.g., 45 or 60 days) or exceptions for documented operational delays.

[P13] Requiring submission “through the CMS-designated data submission systems” without ensuring interoperability with widely used hospice EHR vendors will impose integration costs; hospices will request clear technical specifications, a vendor certification process, and a reasonable implementation timeline.

[P3] The 4-percentage-point reduction to the annual payment update as a penalty for missing the 90% threshold is excessive and will threaten financial viability of hospices serving disadvantaged populations; commenters will propose a graded penalty structure, alternative sanctions, or monetary penalties tied to severity.

[P14] Conditioning avoidance of the payment reduction on strict compliance with paragraph (j)(1) without allowances for good-cause exceptions (e.g., natural disasters, mass outages, cyberattacks) is unfair; stakeholders will ask CMS to define and include an explicit good-cause waiver process.

[P10] The duplicate listing of the 90% requirement in multiple paragraphs risks inconsistent enforcement; commenters will request consolidation and clarification to prevent misinterpretation by contractors and auditors.

[P4] The broad obligation in § 424.507(b) that a claim must “satisfy all listed requirements” to be payable is vague—commenters will request a non-exhaustive list of critical versus informational requirements and clarification whether documentation deficiencies constitute non-payment or audit adjustments.

[P5] Requiring ordering/certifying clinicians to meet unspecified “requirements (listed in the following subparts)” without cross-referencing up-to-date licensure and scope-of-practice rules may conflict with state laws; commenters (physician and advanced practice groups) will request explicit incorporation of current federal standards and reconciliation with state practice acts.

[P6] Applying paragraph (b) payment requirements to physicians identified in § 418.22(c) who made the certification for hospice claims may penalize hospices when certifications were made by out-of-state physicians with differing credentialing processes; hospices will request that CMS clarify acceptable documentation and recognize telemedicine-originated certifications.

[P15] The payment condition in § 424.507(b) could be read to allow claims denials for minor administrative errors (e.g., typo in NPI); providers will ask CMS to limit denial authority to substantive clinician eligibility failures and permit corrections for clerical errors without payment reductions.

[P16] The rule’s listing of eligible ordering/certifying clinicians (physicians, PAs, NPs, CNSs) should explicitly include recently-authorized categories (e.g., clinical nurse specialists where state law allows) and clarify supervision requirements for physician assistants to avoid inconsistent denials.

[P17] Applying paragraph (b) requirements to physicians described in § 418.22(c) may conflict with hospice physician delegation practices for recertifications; medical director organizations will request an exception when a qualified NP/PA conducted the encounter under physician supervision consistent with state law.

[P1] Patient advocacy groups will comment that telehealth recertification as permitted by § 418.22(a)(4)(ii) must include protections for beneficiaries with sensory, cognitive, or language barriers (e.g., requirement for interpreter services, captioning, and assistive technologies).

[P7] Technology access disparities mean many rural and low-income hospice patients cannot utilize telehealth for recertification; commenters will request that telehealth be optional and never mandated in lieu of an in-person option.

[P2] Quality measurement advocates will request that CMS tie the HIS submission requirement not only to payment but also to feedback loops—provide hospices with timely data reports and benchmarks to improve data quality rather than solely penalizing noncompliance.

[P11] Legal experts will challenge the rule for lacking notice-and-comment justification for a significant payment penalty (4 percentage points) tied to data submission, arguing that CMS must provide a more detailed regulatory impact analysis under the Administrative Procedure Act.

[P3] Fiscal intermediaries and MACs will request operational guidance on how to calculate the 4-percentage-point reduction (e.g., whether it applies before or after other adjustments) and whether partial compliance yields proportional reductions.

[P12] Hospices serving populations with high turnover (short lengths of stay) will argue the 30-day submission window is particularly burdensome and propose alternative submission triggers (e.g., within X days of record finalization) to account for rapid clinical changes.

[P13] Vendors will request a transition period and explicit test environments and validation tools before mandatory use of CMS-designated submission systems to avoid submission errors that could trigger payment penalties.

[P9] Clinician societies will seek explicit documentation standards for telehealth recertification visits (e.g., technology used, patient consent, location of clinician and patient) to ensure audits can verify that the encounter was “solely for hospice recertification.”

[P14] Small hospices will request that CMS include a de minimis exception (e.g., allow meeting 85% for one fiscal year following technical implementation) to avoid immediate harsh payment cuts during onboarding.

[P4] Privacy advocates will raise concerns that increased mandatory electronic submission of HIS records to CMS-designated systems could raise data security and HIPAA compliance issues; they will request explicit security standards and breach-notification protocols.

[P2] Labor unions and workforce advocates will note that meeting 90% submission within 30 days will require hiring more administrative staff; they will ask CMS to consider funding or grant programs to support compliance and not penalize hospices that cannot immediately expand staffing.

[P16] State Medicaid agencies and dual-eligible program administrators will request alignment language ensuring that Medicare billing/payment requirements here do not contradict state Medicaid hospice payment rules and documentation standards.

[P1] Hospice patient families will assert that some recertification assessments require physical examination elements that cannot be completed via telehealth, and request that CMS require a clinical determination that telehealth is clinically appropriate for each patient rather than allowing blanket telehealth recertifications.

[P3] Analysts will request modeling showing the aggregate fiscal impact of applying a 4-percentage-point reduction to hospices that fail the 90% requirement, including projected closures or service reductions, before finalizing the penalty.

[P11] Certification bodies will ask CMS to publish compliance error types that would count against the 90% numerator (e.g., late submission, incomplete fields, invalid patient identifiers) to allow hospices to target quality improvements.

[P7] Public commenters will ask for clarification whether telehealth encounters may be synchronous audio-only when video is unavailable, and whether audio-only encounters satisfy the “face-to-face” requirement for recertification.

[P13] Health IT associations will request that CMS accept automated batch uploads from certified EHR systems and provide a formal API specification to reduce manual reporting burden.

[P14] Consumer groups will argue that tying payment reductions to reporting compliance could incentivize hospices to prioritize data entry over direct patient care and request safeguards to prevent diversion of clinical resources to meet reporting thresholds.

[P9] Hospices will request guidance on how to document the “sole purpose” condition—for example, a required attestation field indicating the recertification-only nature of the telehealth visit to protect against incorrect denials.

[P2] Quality oversight organizations will request that CMS consider alternative incentives (bonus or technical support) for high-quality data submission rather than only punitive measures.

[P4] Billing consultants will ask CMS to clarify whether retroactive claim denials for failure to meet § 424.507(b) requirements are allowed and what appeal rights providers have if denied for missing documentation tied to certification rules.

[P6] Legal commenters will urge CMS to clarify how § 424.507(b)(3) interacts with existing delegation and supervision frameworks—particularly when a certification is initiated by one physician and finalized by another—to avoid improper claim denials.

[P1] Disability rights groups will request that CMS mandate accessible telehealth platforms (e.g., screen-reader compatibility) as a condition for allowing telehealth recertification to protect beneficiaries with disabilities.

[P1] The requirement to submit comments via Regulations.gov (identified by docket number) unfairly disadvantages stakeholders without reliable internet access; EPA should allow equivalently simple alternative electronic submission methods or extended paper submission windows.

[P1] The instruction to “follow the online instructions for submitting comments” is vague; EPA should publish an explicit step‑by‑step checklist in the preamble or on the docket landing page to avoid rejected submissions.

[P2] Requiring commenters to identify the docket number from a table adds an unnecessary procedural hurdle — EPA should allow commenters to search by site name or provide a direct link for each site’s comment form.

[P2] The proposed rule does not specify how to correct an incorrect docket number after submission; EPA should allow cross‑referencing or re‑tagging of comments to the correct docket.

[P3] The March 19, 2018 postmark deadline is already outdated and inflexible; EPA should extend the comment period to at least 60 days from publication or accept electronic comments until a date after the publication date to ensure adequate participation.

[P3] Relying on postmark date disadvantages commenters who use electronic submission — EPA should clarify whether electronic timestamps are treated the same as postal postmarks.

[P4] Prohibiting editing or removal of submissions on Regulations.gov may chill candid comments containing errors or sensitive inadvertent disclosures; EPA should permit an edit window or a removal request process for good cause.

[P4] The statement that comments cannot be removed is incorrect insofar as Regulations.gov currently allows request to redact personal contact information — revise to align with existing platform capabilities.

[P5] EPA’s permission to publish comments to the public docket lacks an explanation of redaction procedures for personal identifiers; EPA should commit to redacting sensitive personal data (e.g., SSNs, personal phone numbers) before public posting.

[P6] The prohibition on electronic submission of Confidential Business Information (CBI) is impractical for industry commenters who use electronic filing; EPA should provide a secure upload mechanism and clear instructions for CBI designation.

[P6] The rule does not explain how to designate information as CBI on Regulations.gov; EPA must add explicit labeling and guidance to prevent inadvertent public disclosure.

[P7] Requiring a written comment to accompany multimedia submissions is reasonable, but EPA should clarify whether a short written summary suffices when the substantive material is in a long video or audio file.

[P7] The rule should state whether transcripts of audio/video are acceptable as the written comment or whether additional analysis is required.

[P8] Calling the written submission “the official comment” conflicts with multimedia content being part of the record; EPA should explicitly state whether multimedia will be considered substantively or only for recordkeeping.

[P9] EPA’s refusal to consider material located outside the primary submission (e.g., cloud links) will unfairly exclude many technical appendices that are too large for direct upload; EPA should permit referenced external materials if submitted as stable, accessible links and with clear indexing.

[P9] The prohibition on considering outside material fails to account for third‑party hosted data repositories used by researchers; EPA should accept data hosted in recognized scientific repositories and allow citation to those datasets.

[P10] The USPS mailing address is provided but the rule does not state whether EPA will accept scanned mailed comments or notify receipt; EPA should confirm receipt procedures and whether mailed comments will be posted electronically.

[P10] Some rural commenters rely on USPS; EPA should state a cutoff for mailed submissions (e.g., postmark) and guarantee that mailed comments will be treated equivalently to electronic comments.

[P11] Restricting delivery verification to regular business hours for courier/hand delivery imposes burdens on working stakeholders; EPA should provide extended verification hours or accept courier delivery with electronic proof of delivery.

[P11] The Docket Center address should be provided in full in the rule text — the truncated address harms clarity and could lead to misdirected submissions.

[P12] Allowing in‑person inspection by appointment is helpful, but EPA should publish appointment scheduling procedures, any fees, and acceptable identification to lower barriers for public inspection.

[P13] EPA’s instruction to contact regional dockets for hours is insufficient; EPA should publish hours of operation and appointment availability for each regional docket online.

[P14] Permitting request of copies is important; EPA should specify whether copy fees will apply and the expected turnaround time for copying and mailing.

[P15] Encouraging informal requests instead of FOIA is reasonable, but EPA must clarify what constitutes an “informal” request and whether such requests carry the same legal protections as FOIA requests.

[P15] The rule’s suggestion to use informal requests risks deprioritizing lawful access timelines; EPA should affirm that formal FOIA remains available and that informal requests will not be used to circumvent statutory FOIA obligations.

[P16] Prohibiting copying or mailing of oversized maps and limiting viewing to in‑person prevents access by remote stakeholders; EPA should offer scanning on request or high‑resolution digital access under restricted conditions.

[P16] The inability to copy oversized maps may impede meaningful comment; EPA should commit to producing reduced‑scale reproductions suitable for public review.

[P17] Directing users to Regulations.gov for access is sensible, but EPA must ensure all docket documents are actually uploaded in a timely manner and provide a schedule for posting.

[P17] The rule should require that large technical documents be posted in machine‑readable formats (e.g., searchable PDFs) to facilitate review.

[P18] The obligation to submit comments to EPA Headquarters per ADDRESSES duplicates other provisions and may create confusion; EPA should clearly state whether regional dockets may also accept comments.

[P19] Requiring large submissions to indicate what EPA should consider and how it affects HRS scores is reasonable, but EPA’s rule should provide a template or minimum metadata fields for such submissions to ensure consistent evaluation.

[P19] The condition that commenters must point out specific impacts on HRS factor values favors parties with technical capacity; EPA should offer technical assistance or accept expert summaries for community commenters.

[P20] EPA’s refusal to address voluminous submissions not tied to HRS or listing criteria may exclude relevant contextual information (e.g., health studies) that inform risk; EPA should allow contextual materials while prioritizing HRS‑related content.

[P21] The prohibition on comments that fail to specify HRS components will likely lead to many rejected or unaddressed comments; EPA should adopt a liberal construction policy and ask for clarification before disregarding comments.

[P22] The policy of not responding to late comments and guaranteeing consideration only for timely postmarked comments is harsh; EPA should accept and consider late comments when fairness or practical obstacles (natural disasters, postal delays) justify them.

[P22] EPA should adopt a “good cause” standard for accepting late comments and provide an expedited process to include late submissions when they raise new, substantive information.

[P23] The statement that EPA generally will not delay final listing decisions to accommodate late comments undermines the right to meaningful participation; EPA should commit to delaying action when new evidence submitted late could change the outcome.

[P24] Making public comments available online “as received and without change” risks disclosure of personal or sensitive data; EPA must implement redaction protocols and notify commenters how to request redactions.

[P24] EPA should clarify whether it will convert submitted file formats and whether conversions may alter content (e.g., OCR errors), and provide an appeals process for commenters who find transcription errors.

[P25] The exception that comments containing copyrighted material, CBI, or statutorily restricted information will not be made public is necessary, but EPA should explain how such content will be handled in the decision‑making process and whether non‑public versions will be accessible to the agency and parties.

[P25] EPA should provide a mechanism for submitters to provide both a public redacted version and an unredacted version for the record, with instructions on labeling and secure submission.

[P26] Advising users to search the public dockets by docket ID is fine, but EPA should also allow search by site name, location, or keyword to aid public access.

[P27] The instruction to resubmit previously raised concerns during the formal comment period is burdensome; EPA should automatically include pre‑proposal site‑specific correspondence in the docket or at least notify prior correspondents when a site is proposed.

[P28] The policy of excluding pre‑proposal site‑specific correspondence from the docket may reduce transparency and waste prior input; EPA should include all site‑specific correspondence received and archive it with time stamps.
