The instruction to “follow the online instructions for submitting comments” is vague; EPA should publish an explicit step‑by‑step checklist in the preamble or on the docket landing page to avoid rejected submissions.

Requiring commenters to identify the docket number from a table adds an unnecessary procedural hurdle — EPA should allow commenters to search by site name or provide a direct link for each site’s comment form.
The proposed rule does not specify how to correct an incorrect docket number after submission; EPA should allow cross‑referencing or re‑tagging of comments to the correct docket.

The March 19, 2018 postmark deadline is already outdated and inflexible; EPA should extend the comment period to at least 60 days from publication or accept electronic comments until a date after the publication date to ensure adequate participation.
Relying on postmark date disadvantages commenters who use electronic submission — EPA should clarify whether electronic timestamps are treated the same as postal postmarks.

Prohibiting editing or removal of submissions on Regulations.gov may chill candid comments containing errors or sensitive inadvertent disclosures; EPA should permit an edit window or a removal request process for good cause.

The statement that comments cannot be removed is incorrect insofar as Regulations.gov currently allows request to redact personal contact information — revise to align with existing platform capabilities.

EPA’s permission to publish comments to the public docket lacks an explanation of redaction procedures for personal identifiers; EPA should commit to redacting sensitive personal data (e.g., SSNs, personal phone numbers) before public posting.

The prohibition on electronic submission of Confidential Business Information (CBI) is impractical for industry commenters who use electronic filing; EPA should provide a secure upload mechanism and clear instructions for CBI designation.

Requiring a written comment to accompany multimedia submissions is reasonable, but EPA should clarify whether a short written summary suffices when the substantive material is in a long video or audio file.

EPA’s refusal to consider material located outside the primary submission (e.g., cloud links) will unfairly exclude many technical appendices that are too large for direct upload; EPA should permit referenced external materials if submitted as stable, accessible links and with clear indexing.

raw_output:
[P1] The prohibition in 33 CFR Part 165 is overly broad because it does not define the geographic boundaries, duration, or typical activities covered by the "safety zone," creating uncertainty for commercial vessel operators about when authorization is required.

[P1] Industry commenters will object that prohibiting entry unless authorized by the Captain of the Port Charleston or a "designated representative" could delay routine transits and commercial operations if the rule does not set a maximum response time for authorization requests.

[P1] Recreational boaters and local marina operators will claim the blanket prohibition could criminalize inadvertent transits through popular waterways during events and ask for specific exemptions for ingress/egress to private docks, marinas, and emergency access.

[P2] Commenters will request that the provision permitting contact by telephone to request authorization include alternative contact methods (VHF channel, email, online portal) and provide full telephone number and hours of operation—current text truncates the phone number.

[P2] Mariners' associations will argue the rule should require the Captain of the Port to establish and publish clear procedures and timelines for processing authorization requests so vessels can plan safely.

[P3] Tug and barge operators will claim the obligation to "comply with instructions" lacks detail on what constitutes reasonable instructions and request an appeal or clarification process if instructions materially interfere with commercial obligations.

[P3] Legal commenters will argue that the rule should limit instructions to those that are necessary and proportionate for safety and that the COTP must provide written confirmation for complex or long-duration authorizations to avoid enforcement disputes.

[P4] Commercial shipping agents will comment that relying on Local Notice to Mariners, Broadcast Notice to Mariners, and on-scene representatives may be insufficient; they request mandatory advance publication timelines (e.g., at least 48 hours notice) and specifics on broadcast frequencies/channels.

[P4] Small businesses and local port users will request that notices include exact coordinates, expected duration, and contact information for the on-scene representative to reduce confusion and economic disruption.

[P5] Mine operators will object that requiring written safety programs for operators employing six or more miners creates an arbitrary threshold; they will request clarity on whether family-operated or seasonal operations count toward the six-miner threshold.

[P5] Small mine operators will request a delayed compliance timeline and phased implementation for the written safety program requirement to allow time to develop policies and train staff.

[P6] Commenters will ask that §56.23002(a) specify the "specified date" for developing and implementing the program and provide a realistic timeline (e.g., 12–18 months) rather than an ambiguous deadline.

[P7] Industry will request that §56.23002(b) clarify qualifications for the "responsible person" (e.g., required training, certifications, or experience) and allow delegation to qualified contractors rather than mandating an on-site employee.

[P7] Labor organizations will request that the designated responsible person cannot be the mine operator alone and should include input from miners or their representatives to ensure program effectiveness.

[P8] Safety advocates will support §56.23003(a) but will call for the rule to require specific minimum elements for the program (e.g., collision avoidance systems, blind-spot controls) rather than open-ended "actions."

[P9] Commenters will request that §56.23003(a)(1) require a formal hazard analysis methodology (e.g., job hazard analysis or risk matrix) and set risk-reduction performance metrics, instead of a vague "identify and analyze" mandate.

[P10] Maintenance contractors will ask that §56.23003(a)(2) clarify what constitutes an acceptable maintenance "schedule" and whether OEM recommended intervals must be followed; they will also request allowance for documented site-specific variations.

[P11] Tech vendors will support §56.23003(a)(3) but ask the agency to define "feasible" (cost-effectiveness, operational compatibility, technology maturity) and require a cost-benefit analysis threshold for adopting new technologies.

[P11] Small operators will object that requiring evaluation of "newly emerging" technologies could impose unrealistic burdens; they ask for a proportionality standard (e.g., review every 3 years unless capital investment planned).

[P12] Miner training providers will ask that §56.23003(a)(4) specify minimum training frequency, minimum topics, and documentation/recordkeeping requirements for training to ensure consistency and enforcement.

[P12] Labor groups will request that training be mandatory for contractors and visitors who operate or work near surface mobile equipment, not only miners "necessary to perform work."

[P13] The requirement in §56.23003(b) to evaluate and update the program "annually or as conditions change" will generate comments requesting the definition of "as conditions change" and whether minor operational changes trigger a full update.

[P14] Commenters will request flexibility in §56.23003(b) annual evaluation—suggesting a biennial evaluation option for low-risk operations, or streamlined annual reviews with full updates only when triggered by incidents or major changes.

[P15] Operators will seek clarity on what level of change in mining conditions or practices triggers an update and request examples (e.g., increase in haul road gradient > X%, new shift patterns, expansion of operation).

[P16] Safety advocates will insist that any accident or injury, even minor, should trigger an immediate review and update of the safety program and should be reported to the agency within a specified timeframe.

[P17] Equipment manufacturers will ask that §56.23003(b) define "changes or modifications" to surface mobile equipment (e.g., retrofits, software updates) and specify documentation required after such changes.

[P18] Labor representatives will strongly support §56.23004 requiring availability of the written safety program but will request that miners and their representatives be allowed to receive an electronic copy at no cost upon request within a set timeframe (e.g., 5 business days).

[P18] Operators will raise confidentiality concerns and request the rule clarify whether proprietary information, trade secrets, or sensitive security data may be redacted before sharing the program with miners or the public.

[P19] Commenters will request that §56.23004 require operators to provide copies upon request within a concrete timeline (e.g., within 7 business days) and specify acceptable formats (electronic or paper).

[P20] For §57.23000, underground metal/nonmetal surface-area operators will request harmonization with §56 requirements to avoid duplicative compliance obligations and ask the agency to explicitly cross-reference consistency between subparts.

[P21] Commenters will request that §57.23002(a) also include the same deadline clarity as requested for §56.23002(a), asking for a published "effective date" and staggered compliance schedule for small vs large operators.

[P22] Labor groups will request that §57.23002(b) require the responsible person to have specific mining safety credentials and to be independent of production pressures (e.g., not the site production manager).

[P23] Stakeholders will ask §57.23003(a) to require inclusion of traffic management plans and signage for surface areas of underground mines to reduce pedestrian-vehicle interface incidents.

[P24] Commenters will request that §57.23003(a)(1) require quantitative risk assessments for haul road interactions (e.g., vehicle separation distances, speed limits) rather than general hazard identification.

[P25] Maintenance contractors will request that §57.23003(a)(2) allow harmonization with existing maintenance management systems (CMMS) and permit operators to adopt OEM schedules where appropriate.

[P26] Technology vendors and safety advocates will request that §57.23003(a)(3) require timely review of telematics, proximity detection, and automated braking technologies and establish criteria under which adoption is recommended or required.

[P27] Training providers will ask §57.23003(a)(4) to require competency assessments and refresher training intervals after incidents or equipment changes, not merely initial training.

[P28] Commenters will reiterate that §57.23003(b)’s annual update requirement should include a written record of the evaluation findings and corrective actions, retained for a specified retention period (e.g., 3–5 years).

[P29] Operators will ask for an alternative to strict annual updates for stable operations, such as risk-based periodic reviews, to reduce administrative burdens.

[P30] The rule should specify thresholds of "mining conditions or practices" changes that require updates (e.g., changes in production rates >25%, new material handling methods).

[P31] Safety advocates will request mandatory reporting to the agency when an update is triggered by an accident, including submission of the updated program and corrective action plan.

[P32] For §57.23003(b) commenters will ask that equipment changes include software updates to control systems and require post-modification testing and verification procedures.

[P33] Commenters will request that §57.23004 include explicit rights for miners' representatives to request a copy and to discuss the program with the responsible person during normal working hours without retaliation.

[P34] Operators will request that §57.23004 allow reasonable redactions for proprietary information and require the agency to protect confidential business information (CBI) when operators submit programs for inspection.

[P35] Coal mine operators subject to §77.2100 will request alignment of definitions and timelines across §§56, 57, and 77 to avoid conflicting compliance obligations across different mine types.

[P36] Commenters will ask §77.2102(a) to spell out the "specified date" for compliance and propose staggered deadlines by operation size (e.g., >100 miners within 6 months, 6–99 miners within 12–18 months).

[P37] Labor and safety groups will object if §77.2102(b) allows the designated responsible person to be a production supervisor and will request independence and specific qualifications for that role.

[P38] Coal operators will request that §77.2103(a) recognize existing safety programs and allow operators to incorporate the new requirements into current documented systems rather than requiring wholly new documents.

[P39] Commenters will request that §77.2103(a)(1) require specific mitigations for typical coal-surface mobile equipment hazards (e.g., haul road berms, speed governors, seat-belt policies).

[P40] Maintenance personnel will seek clarification in §77.2103(a)(2) about recordkeeping for routine maintenance and non-routine repairs (what records, retention period, and format are required).

[P41] Technology vendors will support §77.2103(a)(3) but request that the rule provide guidance on evaluating feasibility, including cost thresholds and operational compatibility tests.

[P42] Training providers will ask §77.2103(a)(4) to include minimum training hours, certification criteria, and retraining triggers (after incidents, new equipment, or periodic intervals).

[P43] Commenters will reiterate that §77.2103(b) should require documentation of the annual evaluation and any changes made, including rationale and implementation timelines.

[P44] Coal operators will request flexibility to conduct more frequent targeted reviews rather than prescribed full annual rewrites if records show low risk and no incidents.

[P45] Commenters will ask for examples of "mining conditions or practices change" that would trigger updates (e.g., introduction of new ore processing, changes to haul road geometry).

[P46] Safety advocates will insist that any accident or injury triggers an immediate review and that findings be reported to MSHA within a set timeframe.

[P47] Equipment manufacturers will request that "equipment changes or modifications" explicitly include telematics, control software, retrofit kits, and third-party add-ons, and request a testing protocol be required post-change.

[P48] Labor representatives will strongly support §77.2104 but ask for explicit protections against employer retaliation when miners or their representatives request to inspect or obtain copies of the written safety program.

[P49] Operators will request that §77.2104 specify reasonable timelines (e.g., provide copies within 7 business days) and allow electronic transmission to satisfy the copy requirement to reduce administrative burden.

[P1] The Oct 30, 2006 compliance deadline in §63.9583(a) is obsolete and conflicts with later dates in the rule; EPA should clarify whether legacy sources that started before Dec 18, 2002 retain any phased-in obligations or are immediately subject to all current standards.

[P1] Industry requests a compliance extension for small taconite facilities subject to §63.9583(a), citing lack of funding and permitting delays; propose an alternate allowance of up to 24 additional months with a hardship demonstration.

[P2] The Oct 30, 2003 date in §63.9583(b) is already past; EPA should update these date references or provide transitional compliance language for affected sources with construction commenced on/after Dec 18, 2002.

[P3] §63.9583(c) requires compliance "upon initial startup" for sources starting after Oct 30, 2003 — this creates a potential impossibility for new plants that need time for performance testing and initial tuning; request a 180-day grace period after startup to complete testing and initial adjustments.

[P4] §63.9583(d)(1) makes new/reconstructed portions subject "upon startup" without distinguishing staged startups; request clarification that partial startups for commissioning do not trigger full-subpart compliance until commercial startup.

[P5] The three-year compliance window in §63.9583(d)(2) for other plant parts after becoming a major source is ambiguous about the triggering event; commenters request specifying whether "becomes a major source" refers to actual emissions increase date, permit issuance date, or discovery date by EPA/state.

[P6] §63.9583(e) requires multiple notifications before compliance date per §63.9640 and creates an administrative burden; industry asks EPA to publish a consolidated checklist and staggered schedule to avoid simultaneous submittals.

[P7] The 180-day compliance requirement in §63.9583(f)(1) for sources constructed before Sept 25, 2019 is too short for engineering changes; request alternatives of 1 year or allowance to demonstrate a compliance schedule with interim milestones.

[P8] §63.9583(f)(2) requires compliance "by the publication date of the final rule or by startup, whichever is later" for post-9/25/2019 construction — legal experts note this could impose retroactive obligations on plants nearing startup before final publication and request that obligations apply only to plants that commence construction after final publication.

[P9] §63.9590(b)(2) requires maintaining daily average scrubber water flow and fan amperage at or above minimums established during initial testing — operators request allowing site-specific upper and lower bounds, not only minimums, and request alternative metrics (e.g., particulate outlet concentration) where CPMS limitations exist.

[P10] §63.9622(b) requires establishing site-specific operating limits via the test procedures; industry requests guidance on acceptable statistical methods and allowances for operational variability (e.g., ramp-up/ramp-down) when setting limits.

[P11] §63.9622(b)(1) demands 15-minute CPMS measurements during each performance test run — commenters point out some existing CPMS cannot record at 15-minute intervals or are averaged differently; request allowance for equivalent averaging or demonstration of equivalency.

[P12] §63.9622(b)(2) requires using the lowest average values among runs to set operating limits — this penalizes normal variability and could set unachievable limits due to outlier low runs; suggest using the second-lowest run or the 95% confidence lower bound rather than absolute minimum.

[P13] §63.9600(a) general duty to operate consistent with good practices is duplicative of existing obligations and vague; legal commenters request deletion or rewording to avoid creating an independent enforceable standard separate from numeric limits.

[P14] §63.9600(a) exception that no further reductions are required once standard levels are met could be interpreted to bar innovative improvements; environmental advocates request removing or narrowing the exception to encourage continuous improvement.

[P15] §63.9600(b)(2) requires determining the cause of a bag leak alarm within 1 hour and beginning corrective action within 24 hours — operators state the 1-hour root-cause requirement is infeasible for remote or multi-site systems and request allowing a troubleshooting window (e.g., 4 hours) to diagnose.

[P16] The permissive corrective action list in §63.9600(b)(2) is useful, but commenters request EPA add an explicit allowance for temporary shutdown or reduced throughput as an acceptable corrective action when immediate repairs are unsafe or impractical.

[P17] §63.9610(a) demanding continuous compliance with paragraphs (a)(1)-(6) at all times lacks specificity about minor deviations during maintenance; industry requests de minimis carve-outs and a process for pre-approved scheduled maintenance that would not be considered noncompliance.

[P18] §63.9620(f) grouping criteria for representative testing are narrow; industry requests explicit allowance to group units with minor design differences when demonstrated by engineering equivalence to reduce testing burdens.

[P19] §63.9621(a) requirement to test under "normal maximum operating conditions" is ambiguous; operators request EPA define "normal maximum" with quantifiable parameters (e.g., 95th percentile hourly throughput) to prevent enforcement disputes.

[P20] The prohibition in §63.9621(a) against testing during malfunctions is appropriate, but testing windows and retest timelines are not specified; commenters request EPA include retest deadlines and acceptable documentation for postponements.

[P21] §63.9621(a) recordkeeping of process information to document normal operation during tests is necessary but the rule does not list minimum required parameters; commenters request EPA specify required process variables (throughput rate, fan speed, inlet concentrations) to ensure consistent reporting.

[P22] §63.9621(a) obligates providing records to the Administrator upon request without time limits; operators request a specified response timeframe (e.g., 15 business days) and provision for confidential treatment of proprietary process data.

[P23] §63.9621(a) references procedures in paragraphs (b) and (c) but does not harmonize with state-specific test methods; states request language allowing equivalent state-approved methods when approved by the Administrator.

[P24] §63.9621(b)(1) mandates listed test methods for PM concentration — commenters request EPA allow validated alternative test methods or new technologies (e.g., optical PM monitors) as equally acceptable when demonstrated equivalent.

[P25] §63.9621(b)(1)(i) requiring sampling ports at the control device outlet prior to atmospheric release may be infeasible for some stack designs with internal mixing; testing labs request allowance for the closest practicable sampling location with documented bias correction.

[P26] §63.9621(b)(1)(ii) requiring Method 2 series or 2G for volumetric flow is prescriptive; HVAC engineers request allowance for newer flow measurement technologies and specify calibration acceptance criteria.

[P27] §63.9621(b)(1)(iii) and (c)(1)(iii) permitting ANSI/ASME PTC 19.10–1981 Part 10 as an alternative only for manual procedures (not instrumental) is confusing; labs ask EPA to explicitly permit instrumental procedures in PTC 19.10 or reference a more recent standard.

[P28] §63.9621(b)(1)(iv) requiring Method 4 for moisture content may be impractical for high-temperature or corrosive stacks; request allowance for validated alternative moisture measurement methods.

[P29] §63.9621(b)(1)(v) and (c)(1)(v) requiring Method 5/5D/17 are resource-intensive and costly; smaller facilities request EPA allow performance testing by accredited third-party labs and permit split-sample testing to reduce cost.

[P30] §63.9621(b)(2) requiring three 1-hour runs for Methods 5/5D/17 may be insufficient to capture variability in batch processes; operators request flexibility to use longer runs or more runs when process variability demonstrates need.

[P31] Testing provisions in §63.9621(c)(1)-(v) treat stacks and non-stack points similarly though they have different flow characteristics; commenters request clearer distinctions and alternative procedures for low-flow or intermittent stacks.

[P32] §63.9621(c)(2) using detection limits for below-detection measurements and averaging three runs could bias compliance results; industry requests EPA allow use of method detection limits consistent with current EPA guidance and statistical treatment of nondetects (e.g., 1/2 MDL).

[P33] §63.9623(b)(2) requires site-specific operating limits and retention of scrubber performance records established during testing — operators request retention periods be aligned with other recordkeeping provisions, and request explicit retention length (e.g., 5 years).

[P34] §63.9625 introductory says meeting paragraphs (a)-(d) demonstrates initial compliance for control devices in §63.9590(b) but does not define what constitutes acceptable demonstration; commenters request a checklist and sample submittal template.

[P35] §63.9631(a) requires BLDS installation for each baghouse used to meet limits and inspections per §63.9632(a) — small facilities argue that older units with proven emission histories should be eligible for BLDS waivers or alternative monitoring (e.g., periodic stack tests).

[P36] The second sentence in §63.9631(a) mandates inspections for baghouses not required to have BLDS; commenters request explicit inspection frequencies and procedures rather than referring elsewhere, to avoid inconsistent state enforcement.

[P37] §63.9631(c) requires CPMS for dynamic wet scrubbers and daily average monitoring — many existing scrubber control systems lack CPMS capability; industry requests a phase-in period for CPMS installation and allowance for equivalent manual logging for a limited time.

[P38] §63.9632(a) introductory requiring BLDS for each exhaust stack of baghouses applied to meet particulate limits will be burdensome for multi-stack plants; request allowance to monitor representative stacks where cross-ducting and equalization can be demonstrated.

[P39] §63.9632(a)(1) certification thresholds for BLDS sensitivity (<=10 mg/m3 pre-9/25/2019, <=1 mg/m3 post-9/25/2019) create a steep technology jump; vendors and owners request a phase-in path or alternate performance demonstration for sites where 1 mg/m3 sensors are not available or reliable.

[P40] §63.9632(a)(3) requiring continuous recording of sensor output raises data storage and management concerns; smaller operators request allowance for aggregated hourly records or electronic data retention alternatives and clarification on retention duration.

[P41] §63.9632(a)(4) requires audible alarms audible to appropriate personnel — plants with remote control rooms or enclosed hearing protection regimes need allowance for visual or remote alarm transmission (e.g., to control center SCADA) rather than local audible alarms.

[P42] §63.9632(a)(5) site-specific monitoring plans must be submitted to Administrator for approval; commenters request EPA set a 90-day review deadline for approvals or deemed-approved language to avoid indefinite delays.

[P43] §63.9632(a)(5) plan consistency with manufacturer specs and EPA guidance may preclude site-specific adaptations; BLDS vendors request clearer reconciliation when manufacturer guidance conflicts with the EPA Fabric Filter Bag Leak Detection Guidance.

[P44] §63.9632(a)(7) prohibition on adjusting BLDS parameters without Administrator approval is overly rigid and could prevent routine seasonal tuning; operators appreciate the once-per-quarter allowance in (a)(7)(i) but request that minor adjustments to alarm set points for operational needs be allowed without prior approval if documented in the monitoring plan.

[P45] §63.9632(a)(7)(i) permitting quarterly sensitivity/range adjustments for seasonal effects requires following plan procedures; request clarity on whether post-adjustment notification to the Administrator is required and the documentation needed.

[P46] §63.9632(b)(3) requires performance evaluation procedures and treats failed calibration as CPMS inoperative until passing calibration — operators request allowance for temporary use of backup sensors or validated engineering estimates during short calibration failures without triggering inoperative status.

[P47] §63.9632(b)(4) O&M procedures and schedule must be consistent with §63.8 general requirements, but owners seek explicit minimum inspection intervals and a list of required preventive maintenance tasks to ensure consistency.

[P48] §63.9632(b)(5) data quality assurance procedures must be kept for life of source and superseded plans for 5 years — commenters request harmonization with other record retention rules (commonly 5 years) and propose limiting lifetime retention to physical impracticality exceptions for very old sources.

[P49] §63.9632(b)(6) requires ongoing recordkeeping and reporting per §63.10 but lacks explicit electronic format guidance prior to mandatory CEDRI dates; request temporary acceptance of paper and PDF submissions during transition to full electronic reporting.

[P50] §63.9632(f)(2) COMS quality control program requirements (daily drift checks, quarterly audits, annual zero alignment) are resource intensive; smaller sources request scaled requirements based on emission risk or allow semiannual drift checks for low-emission units.

[P51] §63.9632(f)(4) obligation to determine and record 6-minute average opacity when COMS is in control may be infeasible for low-concentration plumes where opacity methods are insensitive; request allowance to use alternative surrogate parameters or perform extended averaging.

[P52] §63.9633(a) requiring continuous monitoring/collection of data at all times the source is operating is broad; operators request explicit exceptions and guidance for brief planned outages, start-up/shutdown and stages of commissioning beyond the listed exceptions.

[P53] §63.9633(b) prohibition on using data from malfunctions/out-of-control/repairs/QA activities in averages raises compliance reporting difficulties when such periods are frequent; request EPA allow statistical adjustment methods or substitution with validated engineering estimates for short-duration events.

[P54] §63.9634(b)(3) applying representative unit operating limits to all units in the similar group may be unreasonable if units have different age/maintenance histories; commenters request allowance to demonstrate equivalency by engineering analysis or to set unit-specific limits where justified.

[P55] §63.9634(d) continuous compliance requirements for baghouses are prescriptive; facility managers request clearer examples of acceptable documentation to demonstrate conformance (inspection logs, photographs, vendor reports).

[P56] §63.9634(d)(2) requires written certification by a responsible official if BLDS sensitivity is adjusted beyond plan limits — industry requests a template certification form and clarification whether electronic signature via CEDRI satisfies the requirement.

[P57] §63.9634(d)(3) operating BLDS so alarms sound no more than 5% of operating time in any 6-month period is arbitrary; operators claim this benchmark may be inappropriate for processes with seasonal particulate spikes and request allowance to use rolling 12-month periods or adjust percentages based on demonstrated baseline performance.

[P58] §63.9634(d)(3)(i) exception not to count alarm time if inspection shows no corrective action needed could be abused; environmental groups request tightened criteria and independent verification requirements before excluding alarm time.

[P59] §63.9634(d)(3)(ii) counting each required-corrective-action alarm as at least 1 hour will artificially inflate alarm time for brief events; request allowing actual measured alarm duration to be counted when prompt corrective action documents show response time <1 hour.

[P60] §63.9634(d)(3)(iii) counting alarm time as actual time to initiate corrective action when initiation takes >1 hour is reasonable, but operators request clarity on what constitutes "initiation" and allow remote troubleshooting time not to be penalized.

[P61] §63.9634(f) dynamic wet scrubber continuous compliance demonstration requires completion of several items but lacks a standardized reporting template; industry requests a sample reporting form to ensure consistent submissions.

[P62] §63.9634(f)(1) reiteration of daily average thresholds for scrubber flow/fan amperage requires that daily averages be maintained; equipment OEMs request allowance for short transient dips during startup/shutdown that are not indicative of control failure.

[P63] §63.9634(f)(3) requiring collection/reduction/recording of monitoring data per §63.9632(c) — commenters note §63.9632(c) is not included in the provisions list and request EPA ensure cross-references are correct and provide the missing data reduction requirements.

[P64] §63.9634(f)(4) requiring corrective procedures when daily averages fall below limits — plant operators request clear definitions of "below" (single-day vs multi-day excursion) and thresholds before triggering corrective action timelines.

[P65] §63.9634(j)(1) requiring initiation/completion of initial corrective action within 10 calendar days and demonstration of success is impractical for repairs requiring long lead-time parts; propose an alternative: initiate planning within 10 days and complete repairs within a reasonable industry-specific timeframe with interim mitigations.

[P66] §63.9634(j)(2) requiring additional corrective action within 10 days if initial action fails is similarly infeasible for complex mechanical issues; request allowance for staged remedial plans with documented timelines approved by the Administrator.

[P67] §63.9637(a) requires reporting all deviations from emission limits/work-practice/O&M requirements; environmental groups support robust reporting but request that EPA require contemporaneous electronic notification for major deviations (e.g., those exceeding 24 hours or major PM releases).

[P68] §63.9640(e)(2) 60-day deadline to submit notification of compliance status including test results could be unrealistic given third-party lab turnaround and ERT formatting; request extending to 90 days or allowing a 60-day notification with a 180-day deadline for full results submission.

[P69] §63.9641(a)(2) first compliance report due by the earlier of July 31 or Jan 31 following the due date creates confusion; stakeholders ask EPA to fix a single calendar-driven deadline (e.g., Jan 31) to avoid "earlier of" ambiguity.

[P70] §63.9641(a)(4) subsequent semiannual report deadlines being the earlier of July 31 or Jan 31 again create ambiguity; commenters request clear deadlines tied to reporting periods (e.g., reports due within 30 days after the end of each semiannual period).

[P71] §63.9641(b) requiring inclusion of paragraphs (b)(1)-(8) in every compliance report is broadly described but lacks detail about what qualifies as "applicable"; industry requests an explicit list of mandatory elements for each report type to avoid overreporting.

[P72] §63.9641(b)(2) requiring a certified statement by a responsible official is acceptable, but legal experts request clarity that electronic signatures via CEDRI meet signature law requirements and that corporate delegations are valid.

[P73] §63.9641(b)(3) removing the report date when submitting via CEDRI may create recordkeeping gaps; commenters request that CEDRI automatically stamp report submission date into the filing and that facilities retain a copy for their files.

[P74] §63.9641(b)(7)(i) requiring total operating time hours for each affected source when not using CMS imposes a heavy recordkeeping burden on facilities with many small sources; request allowance to aggregate by process group or use reasonable estimates with methodology documentation.

[P75] §63.9641(b)(7)(ii) requiring emission estimates, start/stop times, cause and estimation method for deviations when not using CMS will be onerous; suggest allowing narrative summaries for minor deviations and reserving detailed calculation requirements for significant deviations exceeding defined thresholds.

[P76] §63.9641(b)(8)(ii) reporting CMS inoperative durations excludes routine checks — operators request clear definitions of what constitutes routine zero/high checks versus calibration checks to avoid inconsistent reporting.

[P77] §63.9641(b)(8)(iii) reporting CMS out-of-control periods must include §63.8(c)(8) information; commenters request EPA include an example of the required information and a template for consistency across sources.

[P78] §63.9641(b)(8)(iv)-(v) require granular reporting of deviations and totals as percent of operating time; privacy-sensitive business data and non-public operational metrics could be exposed — industry requests stronger CBI protections and clearer guidance on what information qualifies for CBI.

[P79] §63.9641(b)(8)(vi) requiring breakdown of deviation durations by cause categories may be subjective; operators ask EPA to provide standardized cause codes and definitions to ensure consistent categorization across facilities.

[P80] §63.9641(b)(8)(vii) total CMS downtime reporting as percent of operating time should allow rounding conventions and tolerances to account for clock sync issues and minor timestamp discrepancies.

[P81] §63.9641(b)(8)(ix) requiring reporting of monitoring equipment manufacturer and model and pollutant/parameter monitored is reasonable but vendors are concerned about CBI; request that model/manufacturer info be protected if it reveals trade secrets or competitive procurement strategies.

[P82] §63.9641(c) mandatory electronic submission via CEDRI starting 180 days after publication may be too fast for small sources with limited IT resources; request a staggered implementation (e.g., >90 TPY sources first, then smaller sources after 1 year) and acceptance of alternative electronic formats during transition.

[P83] §63.9641(c) requiring physical media submission of CBI files and a redacted electronic file via CDX imposes additional administrative burden and security risks; recommend accepting secure encrypted electronic transmissions for CBI files and eliminating the physical media requirement.

[P84] §63.9641(f) 60-day deadline for submitting performance test results is tight given ERT formatting and CBI handling; propose extending to 90 days and providing a detailed ERT conversion tool and technical assistance.

[P85] §63.9641(f)(1) requiring ERT-generated format or XML-consistent files for ERT-supported methods could disadvantage labs that do not use ERT; request EPA provide a free conversion utility and an interim acceptance of well-documented CSV files.

[P86] §63.9641(f)(2) submission procedures for non-ERT methods as attachments to ERT or XML-consistent files may be unclear; testing labs request clear examples of acceptable attachments and schema.

[P87] §63.9641(f)(3) requiring physical CBI-containing media to EPA for performance tests plus a CBI-omitted CDX submission creates duplicative work and possible data security vulnerabilities; propose that EPA accept encrypted electronic CBI submissions via a secure portal and allow certificate-based filings to satisfy requirements.

§63.9632(f)(4) obligation to determine and record 6-minute average opacity when COMS is in control may be infeasible for low-concentration plumes where opacity methods are insensitive; request allowance to use alternative surrogate parameters or perform extended averaging.

§63.9633(a) requiring continuous monitoring/collection of data at all times the source is operating is broad; operators request explicit exceptions and guidance for brief planned outages, start-up/shutdown and stages of commissioning beyond the listed exceptions.

§63.9633(b) prohibition on using data from malfunctions/out-of-control/repairs/QA activities in averages raises compliance reporting difficulties when such periods are frequent; request EPA allow statistical adjustment methods or substitution with validated engineering estimates for short-duration events.

§63.9634(b)(3) applying representative unit operating limits to all units in the similar group may be unreasonable if units have different age/maintenance histories; commenters request allowance to demonstrate equivalency by engineering analysis or to set unit-specific limits where justified.

§63.9634(d) continuous compliance requirements for baghouses are prescriptive; facility managers request clearer examples of acceptable documentation to demonstrate conformance (inspection logs, photographs, vendor reports).

§63.9634(d)(2) requires written certification by a responsible official if BLDS sensitivity is adjusted beyond plan limits — industry requests a template certification form and clarification whether electronic signature via CEDRI satisfies the requirement.

§63.9634(d)(3) operating BLDS so alarms sound no more than 5% of operating time in any 6-month period is arbitrary; operators claim this benchmark may be inappropriate for processes with seasonal particulate spikes and request allowance to use rolling 12-month periods or adjust percentages based on demonstrated baseline performance.

§63.9634(d)(3)(i) exception not to count alarm time if inspection shows no corrective action needed could be abused; environmental groups request tightened criteria and independent verification requirements before excluding alarm time.

§63.9634(d)(3)(ii) counting each required-corrective-action alarm as at least 1 hour will artificially inflate alarm time for brief events; request allowing actual measured alarm duration to be counted when prompt corrective action documents show response time <1 hour.

§63.9634(d)(3)(iii) counting alarm time as actual time to initiate corrective action when initiation takes >1 hour is reasonable, but operators request clarity on what constitutes "initiation" and allow remote troubleshooting time not to be penalized.

§63.9634(f) dynamic wet scrubber continuous compliance demonstration requires completion of several items but lacks a standardized reporting template; industry requests a sample reporting form to ensure consistent submissions.

§63.9634(f)(1) reiteration of daily average thresholds for scrubber flow/fan amperage requires that daily averages be maintained; equipment OEMs request allowance for short transient dips during startup/shutdown that are not indicative of control failure.

§63.9634(f)(3) requiring collection/reduction/recording of monitoring data per §63.9632(c) — commenters note §63.9632(c) is not included in the provisions list and request EPA ensure cross-references are correct and provide the missing data reduction requirements.

§63.9634(f)(4) requiring corrective procedures when daily averages fall below limits — plant operators request clear definitions of "below" (single-day vs multi-day excursion) and thresholds before triggering corrective action timelines.

§63.9634(j)(1) requiring initiation/completion of initial corrective action within 10 calendar days and demonstration of success is impractical for repairs requiring long lead-time parts; propose an alternative: initiate planning within 10 days and complete repairs within a reasonable industry-specific timeframe with interim mitigations.

§63.9634(j)(2) requiring additional corrective action within 10 days if initial action fails is similarly infeasible for complex mechanical issues; request allowance for staged remedial plans with documented timelines approved by the Administrator.

§63.9637(a) requires reporting all deviations from emission limits/work-practice/O&M requirements; environmental groups support robust reporting but request that EPA require contemporaneous electronic notification for major deviations (e.g., those exceeding 24 hours or major PM releases).

§63.9640(e)(2) 60-day deadline to submit notification of compliance status including test results could be unrealistic given third-party lab turnaround and ERT formatting; request extending to 90 days or allowing a 60-day notification with a 180-day deadline for full results submission.

§63.9641(a)(2) first compliance report due by the earlier of July 31 or Jan 31 following the due date creates confusion; stakeholders ask EPA to fix a single calendar-driven deadline (e.g., Jan 31) to avoid "earlier of" ambiguity.

§63.9641(a)(4) subsequent semiannual report deadlines being the earlier of July 31 or Jan 31 again create ambiguity; commenters request clear deadlines tied to reporting periods (e.g., reports due within 30 days after the end of each semiannual period).

§63.9641(b) requiring inclusion of paragraphs (b)(1)-(8) in every compliance report is broadly described but lacks detail about what qualifies as "applicable"; industry requests an explicit list of mandatory elements for each report type to avoid overreporting.

§63.9641(b)(2) requiring a certified statement by a responsible official is acceptable, but legal experts request clarity that electronic signatures via CEDRI meet signature law requirements and that corporate delegations are valid.

§63.9641(b)(3) removing the report date when submitting via CEDRI may create recordkeeping gaps; commenters request that CEDRI automatically stamp report submission date into the filing and that facilities retain a copy for their files.

§63.9641(b)(7)(i) requiring total operating time hours for each affected source when not using CMS imposes a heavy recordkeeping burden on facilities with many small sources; request allowance to aggregate by process group or use reasonable estimates with methodology documentation.

§63.9641(b)(7)(ii) requiring emission estimates, start/stop times, cause and estimation method for deviations when not using CMS will be onerous; suggest allowing narrative summaries for minor deviations and reserving detailed calculation requirements for significant deviations exceeding defined thresholds.

§63.9641(b)(8)(ii) reporting CMS inoperative durations excludes routine checks — operators request clear definitions of what constitutes routine zero/high checks versus calibration checks to avoid inconsistent reporting.

§63.9641(b)(8)(iii) reporting CMS out-of-control periods must include §63.8(c)(8) information; commenters request EPA include an example of the required information and a template for consistency across sources.

§63.9641(b)(8)(iv)-(v) require granular reporting of deviations and totals as percent of operating time; privacy-sensitive business data and non-public operational metrics could be exposed — industry requests stronger CBI protections and clearer guidance on what information qualifies for CBI.

§63.9641(b)(8)(vi) requiring breakdown of deviation durations by cause categories may be subjective; operators ask EPA to provide standardized cause codes and definitions to ensure consistent categorization across facilities.
§63.9641(b)(8)(vii) total CMS downtime reporting as percent of operating time should allow rounding conventions and tolerances to account for clock sync issues and minor timestamp discrepancies.

§63.9641(b)(8)(ix) requiring reporting of monitoring equipment manufacturer and model and pollutant/parameter monitored is reasonable but vendors are concerned about CBI; request that model/manufacturer info be protected if it reveals trade secrets or competitive procurement strategies.

§63.9641(c) mandatory electronic submission via CEDRI starting 180 days after publication may be too fast for small sources with limited IT resources; request a staggered implementation (e.g., >90 TPY sources first, then smaller sources after 1 year) and acceptance of alternative electronic formats during transition.

§63.9641(c) requiring physical media submission of CBI files and a redacted electronic file via CDX imposes additional administrative burden and security risks; recommend accepting secure encrypted electronic transmissions for CBI files and eliminating the physical media requirement.

§63.9641(f) 60-day deadline for submitting performance test results is tight given ERT formatting and CBI handling; propose extending to 90 days and providing a detailed ERT conversion tool and technical assistance.

§63.9641(f)(1) requiring ERT-generated format or XML-consistent files for ERT-supported methods could disadvantage labs that do not use ERT; request EPA provide a free conversion utility and an interim acceptance of well-documented CSV files.
§63.9641(f)(2) submission procedures for non-ERT methods as attachments to ERT or XML-consistent files may be unclear; testing labs request clear examples of acceptable attachments and schema.

§63.9641(f)(3) requiring physical CBI-containing media to EPA for performance tests plus a CBI-omitted CDX submission creates duplicative work and possible data security vulnerabilities; propose that EPA accept encrypted electronic CBI submissions via a secure portal and allow certificate-based filings to satisfy requirements.

raw_output:
[P1] The prohibition in § 17.46(d)(1) is overly broad because it applies to "any person subject to U.S. jurisdiction" without clarifying extraterritorial scope for U.S. persons acting abroad, which could create legal uncertainty for researchers and exporters operating outside U.S. territory.

[P1] The rule fails to define key terms used in § 17.46(d)(1) (e.g., "person," "subject to U.S. jurisdiction"), leaving regulated parties unsure whether corporate subsidiaries, contractors, or foreign affiliates fall within the prohibition.

[P2] Cross-referencing § 17.21(b) for import/export prohibitions in § 17.46(d)(1)(i) may inadvertently bar import of preserved museum specimens or loans for research unless an explicit research exemption is stated.

[P2] The import/export prohibition (§ 17.46(d)(1)(i)) does not provide clear procedures for customs declarations, permits, or temporary transit, imposing undue compliance costs on legitimate scientific exchanges.

[P3] The taking prohibition in § 17.46(d)(1)(ii) (via § 17.21(c)(1)) could criminalize routine sampling by universities and state agencies unless the exceptions are easier to obtain; commenters request clarity on whether standard research sampling constitutes "take."

[P3] Because § 17.21(c)(1) definitions are technical, duplicating them or summarizing key elements in § 17.46 would reduce confusion about what conduct qualifies as "taking" the Panama City crayfish.

[P4] Prohibition on possession of unlawfully taken specimens (§ 17.46(d)(1)(iii)) may impede museums and aquaria that unknowingly acquired specimens before listing; commenters ask for a narrow transitional safe harbor for pre-listing holdings documented with provenance.

[P4] The rule lacks a process for restoring legal possession status for specimens previously lawfully held but later determined to be unlawfully taken under new interpretation; request for amendment to permit registration of pre-existing collections.

[P5] The interstate/foreign commerce ban in § 17.46(d)(1)(iv) effectively prohibits commercial breeders and pet trade businesses without defining what constitutes "commercial activity"—request explicit thresholds (e.g., number of specimens, revenue) to distinguish hobbyists from commercial operators.

[P5] The commerce prohibition should clarify resale of captive-bred individuals or parts (e.g., shells) to avoid chilling of lawful commerce that does not threaten wild populations; commenters request a captive-breeding exception.

[P6] The sale/offer for sale prohibition (§ 17.46(d)(1)(v)) is too absolute and could criminalize low-risk transactions such as sales of captive-bred crayfish, educational specimens, or items previously lawfully acquired; propose an explicit captive-bred sale exception and labeling requirements.

[P6] Ambiguity about "offer for sale" may extend to online listings and social media posts, creating First Amendment and enforcement concerns; request guidance on de minimis offers and intent standards.

[P7] The general exception provision (§ 17.46(d)(2)) is vague because it delegates detailed exceptions to multiple cross-references, making compliance burdensome; suggest summarizing key exceptions directly within the section.

[P8] The permit exception (§ 17.46(d)(2)(i)) is useful but commenters request faster, predictable § 17.32 permit timelines and emergency permit procedures for urgent conservation research.

[P8] Industry and academic commenters request fee waivers or reduced fees for § 17.32 permits issued to public universities and state agencies conducting conservation-oriented research.

[P9] The regulatory take exceptions in § 17.46(d)(2)(ii) (cross-referencing § 17.21(c)(2)–(c)(4)) are not clearly applicable to incidental scientific handling; request illustrative examples showing which routine research activities qualify.

[P10] The § 17.46(d)(2)(iii) permission referencing § 17.31(b) should expressly confirm that previously authorized state agency control measures (e.g., nuisance species removal) remain permissible when coordinated with the Service.

[P11] The incidental-take permission (§ 17.46(d)(2)(iv)) is constructive but the criteria for what qualifies as "incidental" are not specified, risking uneven enforcement; request promulgation of an incidental-take screening checklist.

[P12] The conservation/restoration incidental-take allowance (§ 17.46(d)(2)(iv)(A)) is positive but requires clear authorization procedures, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements (e.g., number of specimens taken, GPS locations) to ensure transparency and accountability.

[P12] State wildlife agencies object to any implication that the Service's conservation activities can occur without state concurrence; request a statement that Service and state restoration activities will be coordinated and that state-approved methods suffice.

[P13] The development-practices incidental-take allowance (§ 17.46(d)(2)(iv)(B)) is too narrow in some subparts and too broad in others; developers request clear permitting thresholds and mandatory pre-construction surveys to reduce inadvertent take.

[P14] Allowing maintenance and work within existing footprints (§ 17.46(d)(2)(iv)(B)(1)) without a requirement for pre-activity surveys could allow cumulative habitat degradation; recommend mandatory baseline surveys and avoidance measures for ROW and powerline projects.

[P15] The allowance to build new small structures (<1,000 sq ft) within 100 feet of existing structures (§ 17.46(d)(2)(iv)(B)(2)) could be exploited to incrementally develop sensitive habitats; conservation groups request that proximity and footprint thresholds be tightened or require compensatory mitigation.

[P15] Private landowners support § 17.46(d)(2)(iv)(B)(2) but request clarification whether the 100-foot buffer is measured from original structure edge or property boundary and whether aggregate projects across contiguous parcels are restricted.

[P16] The culvert installation exception (§ 17.46(d)(2)(iv)(B)(3)) is reasonable but the criteria "not part of housing developments" is vague; commenters ask for a definition of "housing development" and whether small subdivisions are included.

[P16] Road and county public works departments request that culvert exceptions apply when projects are part of required public-infrastructure repairs regardless of parcel size, to avoid costly permit delays.

[P17] The recreational platform/boardwalk allowance (§ 17.46(d)(2)(iv)(B)(4)) relies on the vague standard "allow sufficient sunlight to maintain herbaceous groundcover"; request quantitative light-transmission criteria or clear BMPs to evaluate compliance.

[P17] Conservation organizations warn that boardwalks can fragment habitat; they request mandatory project-level review of cumulative impacts on Panama City crayfish habitat even for proposed platforms on conservation lands.

[P18] Permitting nonmotorized paths if project impacts alter no more than 5% of core/secondary soils (§ 17.46(d)(2)(iv)(B)(5)) is ambiguous because "core" and "secondary" soils are undefined in the rule text; request mapping and definitions before the rule is finalized.

[P18] Trail builders and park managers ask for guidance on how to calculate the "total project footprint" (temporary vs. permanent impacts) and whether multiple small projects on the same easement are aggregated for the 5% limit.

[P19] The land-management activities exceptions (§ 17.46(d)(2)(iv)(C)) are broadly protective but require harmonization with existing state forestry and agricultural programs to avoid duplicative compliance.

[P20] Silvicultural activities in secondary soils (§ 17.46(d)(2)(iv)(C)(1)) should be conditioned on adherence to specific, named state BMPs; commenters request incorporation by reference of the applicable BMP manuals to avoid confusion.

[P21] Allowing prescribed burning (§ 17.46(d)(2)(iv)(C)(2)) when following state BMPs or permits is appropriate, but agencies request clarity on whether smoke management and burn timing constraints are required to avoid indirect impacts.

[P22] Herbicide application exception (§ 17.46(d)(2)(iv)(C)(3)) must specify approved active ingredients, application rates, buffer zones, and monitoring requirements to ensure that herbicide use to control exotics does not harm crayfish populations.

[P23] The agricultural maintenance allowance for pre-1/3/2018 pasture/rangelands (§ 17.46(d)(2)(iv)(C)(4)) creates an arbitrary cutoff date that may penalize long-standing operators who cannot document establishment dates; request alternative criteria based on land-use evidence or grandfathering with simple affidavits.

[P23] Agricultural associations request clarification on what constitutes "indirectly impact adjacent Panama City crayfish habitat" and whether routine activities (manure spreading, irrigation) require consultation.

[P24] The utility actions exception (§ 17.46(d)(2)(iv)(D)) is helpful but utility companies ask for pre-approval pathways and emergency exemptions for unplanned outages and repairs that could otherwise be delayed.

[P25] Permitting ditch mowing and maintenance only when conducted outside critical habitat (§ 17.46(d)(2)(iv)(D)(1)) will impose increased costs for local governments continuing to manage roadside ditches—request clarification whether alternative mowing techniques inside critical habitat are allowed.

[P25] County road maintenance departments request mapping of critical habitat units and an explicit process to request authorization for necessary ditch work within critical habitat in emergencies (e.g., flood control).

[P26] The provision (§ 17.95(h)(4)) allowing the public to obtain field office location information via regional Service offices is inadequate; commenters request that the final rule include direct contact info (phone, email, web links) and designate local field contacts for quicker response.

[P26] NGOs and researchers ask that field office information be proactively published on the Service website and that staff responsible for Panama City crayfish consultation be identified to streamline communication.

[P1] Legal experts warn the rule's cross-references to many other sections without reproducing exemptions or procedures may violate the APA requirement for clarity and could be held arbitrary and capricious if not clarified.

[P12] Scientists request that any incidental take covered under § 17.46(d)(2)(iv)(A) include mandatory data-sharing and specimen deposition in accredited repositories to maximize conservation value.

[P15] Realtors and private landowners worry the small-house exemption (<1,000 sq ft) could be misapplied to accessory dwelling units and modular homes; they request a list of examples and whether temporary structures are included.

[P18] Conservation easement holders seek assurances that the 5% path-impact limit will not be applied retroactively to preexisting paths and that cumulative impact calculations will consider historical baseline conditions.

[P21] Fire management agencies ask the Service to provide training and standardized templates for burn plans that satisfy both state BMPs and the rule's expectations to avoid project-by-project disputes.

[P6] Animal welfare groups oppose any allowance of sale or transfer outside strict conservation or permitted research contexts; they recommend that the sale prohibition remain absolute except for accredited zoos and scientific institutions under tight conditions.

[P1] The proposed rule's broad application to all persons who manufacture, process, pack, or hold foods on the Food Traceability List is vague and could capture entities (e.g., small value-added producers, contract packers) not intended by FSMA without clear scope limits or illustrative examples.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether contract manufacturers/ co-packers and third-party storage providers are "persons who manufacture, process, pack, or hold" for purposes of §1.1300 to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P2] FDA must commit to a predictable update schedule and stakeholder notice process for the Food Traceability List published on its website (e.g., annual review and 60-day notice before changes), rather than leaving timing unspecified.

[P2] The rule should require FDA to publicize changes to the Food Traceability List via Federal Register notice and targeted stakeholder email lists in addition to posting on the website to ensure affected parties are aware.

[P3] Exempting farms that are "not covered farms" under part 112 may create confusion because many mixed-type facilities have both farm and non-farm activities; the rule should define how to determine which activities are "farm activities" for exemption purposes.

[P3] Legal commenters will note potential conflict with part 112 interpretations—FDA should provide cross-reference guidance and examples to delineate covered vs. non-covered farm activities.

[P4] The shell egg producer exemption threshold (<3,000 hens) is inconsistent with other FSMA size thresholds and may unfairly burden small family farms; FDA should harmonize with existing definitions or provide a phase-in.

[P4] The rule should clarify whether the hen count is per farm location or per corporate ownership across multiple farms to avoid circumvention or unintended aggregation.

[P5] The very small originator monetary threshold of $25,000 average annual sales is overly low and will exclude many small businesses that cannot bear traceability costs; recommend raising threshold or adding a tiered compliance schedule.

[P5] The rule should specify whether the $25,000 calculation includes affiliate/company-level sales, in-kind transfers, or intercompany sales to prevent gaming and to give certainty to small operators.

[P6] The direct-to-consumer farm sales exemption should be limited to on-site retail sales and clear when sales through CSA, farmers markets, or online ordering count as "direct" and exempt; the current language is ambiguous.

[P6] The requirement that sales be by the owner/operator/agent needs definition — the rule should state whether hired sales staff, cooperative marketing agents, or farmers market managers qualify as "agent."

[P7] The exemption for food produced and packaged on a farm is conditioned on packaging remaining intact until purchase; enforcement and verification of "packaging remains in place" will be difficult for preordered or subscription deliveries — guidance needed.

[P8] Requiring that packaging "maintains the integrity of the product and prevents contamination/alteration" is subjective; FDA should define objective criteria or standards (e.g., tamper-evident seals, material types) for what preserves integrity.

[P12] The shell egg processing exemption referencing §118.3 treatments must explicitly state whether on-farm pasteurization or third-party treatments qualify and how to document compliance.

[P13] The rarely consumed raw produce exemption should be updated with industry input and include a process for adding/removing items from the list with supporting consumption data and public comment.

[P14] The broad commingled raw agricultural commodity exemption risks severing traceability where commingling is extensive; FDA should require risk-based exceptions where commingling obscures source for high-risk commodities.

[P15] The requirement that registered persons handling commingled commodities keep records of immediate previous source and immediate subsequent recipient (per §§1.337 & 1.345) is administratively heavy for bulk commodity trades—consider allowing aggregated record approaches or electronic batching methods.

[P16] A two-year record retention period for commingled source/recipient records is short for some supply chain disputes and long for small operators—FDA should align retention times with other federal recordkeeping standards or permit electronic retention with backup.

[P17] The Option 1 exemption for retail establishments with ≤10 FTE employees is unclear about how to calculate FTE (seasonal staff, part-time, volunteers); define methodology and require documentation for claims to the exemption.

[P18] Under Option 2, exempting small retailers from only the spreadsheet availability requirement but requiring other traceability obligations may create unequal regulatory burdens; stakeholders will request a clear explanation of costs and benefits of both options.

[P19] The blanket exemption for retail establishments buying directly from farms (except as in h(2)) needs to define "directly" (e.g., via broker, cooperative) and whether intermediate logistics providers break the direct link.

[P20] Requiring retailers purchasing directly from farms to record the farm's name and address without specifying acceptable formats (e.g., receipt, invoice, purchase order) will lead to inconsistent compliance; FDA should list acceptable record types.

[P21] A 180-day retention period for retailer farm-source records is too short for some recall investigations that span longer periods; recommend aligning with the two-year retention for other records or explaining empirical basis for 180 days.

[P22] The exemption for schools/institutions in farm-to-school programs is helpful but should permit schools that contract with distributors to still claim the exemption when the food is procured under local procurement policies.

[P23] The requirement that schools record the farm's name and address when purchasing directly will impose administrative burdens on small school food authorities with limited staff; suggest permitting consolidated quarterly logs rather than per-delivery records.

[P24] A 180-day retention period for school procurement records may conflict with state recordkeeping policies for child nutrition programs—FDA should coordinate with USDA and permit longer retention where required.

[P25] The fishing-vessel owner/operator exemption is ambiguous about catch landed by multiple vessels or pooled landings through cooperatives; FDA should clarify applicability in cooperative offload scenarios.

[P26] Requiring registered fishing vessel operators to maintain records of immediate previous source and subsequent recipient for two years creates a heavy burden for small-scale fishers and buyer-seller relationships at landing — suggest scaled requirements or electronic templates.

[P27] Two-year retention for fishing vessel records should be harmonized with NMFS and state fisheries reporting requirements to avoid duplicative recordkeeping.

[P28] The transporter exemption is appropriate, but the rule must clarify whether transporters that perform cross-docking, repacking, or sorting remain exempt or become subject to the subpart.

[P29] The nonprofit exemption should specify whether social enterprises or mission-driven businesses that operate revenue-generating programs qualify, or whether the exemption is limited to tax-exempt 501(c)(3) entities.

[P30] The personal-consumption exemption should clarify whether community gardens, shared kitchens for friends/family, or barter systems fall within "personal consumption" to avoid unintended coverage.

[P31] The exemption for persons holding food on behalf of specific individual consumers is useful, but the condition that the holder not be a "party to the transaction" requires definition—does payment for storage or a storage contract make the holder a party?

[P32] The requirement that holders not be a party to the transaction (n)(1) could exclude storage lockers where customers pay monthly; FDA should clarify that incidental payment for storage does not automatically make the holder a party.

[P33] The "not in the business of distributing food" condition (n)(2) needs objective criteria (e.g., number of customers, revenue thresholds) so that small community groups can determine applicability.

[P34] The §1.1315(a) requirement to "establish and maintain" many types of traceability records lacks guidance on acceptable formats (paper, electronic, EDI) and data standards — stakeholders will request flexibility and optional standardized templates.

[P35] Requiring a description of reference records and how records are linked (§1.1315(a)(1)) may impose significant internal audit costs; recommend allowing summary descriptions and crosswalks rather than line-by-line mapping.

[P36] The obligation to maintain a list of shipped Food Traceability List items with traceability product identifiers (§1.1315(a)(2)) will require small businesses to implement SKU-level systems; propose phased compliance or a simplified list for small operators.

[P37] Documenting procedures for establishing and assigning traceability lot codes (§1.1315(a)(3)) could expose proprietary business practices—FDA should permit confidential treatment of detailed internal procedures while requiring limited high-level descriptions.

[P38] The requirement to provide codes, glossaries, and abbreviations (§1.1315(a)(4)) will necessitate ongoing updates and translation across trading partners; FDA should endorse use of existing industry standards (e.g., GS1) rather than creating new requirements.

[P39] Retaining traceability program records for two years after their use is discontinued (§1.1315(b)) is ambiguous — define "use is discontinued" (e.g., product sold, lot retired) to avoid inconsistent retention periods.

[P40] Mandating assignment of traceability lot codes at origination/transformation (§1.1320(a)) is reasonable, but the prohibition on creating new codes at other activities (§1.1320(b)) could conflict with necessary operational practices (e.g., repalletizing, repackaging) — request explicit permissible exceptions and procedures for reassignment.

[P41] The prohibition against new lot codes for activities other than origination/transformation (§1.1320(b)) could inhibit necessary product segmentation (e.g., for different customers or pack sizes); FDA should allow controlled secondary coding with trace back to original lot.

[P42] Growers' obligation to link traceability lot codes to growing information (§1.1325) requires GPS/lat-long data which may reveal sensitive landowner information or be unavailable for rented plots — allow alternative location descriptors or redaction for privacy.

[P43] Requiring GPS/latitude-longitude coordinates for growing areas (§1.1325(a)) raises privacy and security concerns for small producers and immigrant workers; FDA should permit farm field identifiers or parcel numbers as alternatives.

[P44] Sprout growers face onerous seed-and-lot recordkeeping (§1.1325(b)) — many small sprouters need compliance assistance, templates, and recognition of supplier-provided lot codes to avoid duplication.

[P45] Recording seed grower location identifier and seed lot codes (§1.1325(b)(1)) may be impossible where seeds are purchased in bulk from brokers; provide an alternative to capture supplier batch codes and supplier identity.

[P46] Recording seed conditioner/processor identifiers and conditioning dates (§1.1325(b)(2)) imposes tracking requirements beyond what many seed suppliers provide—recommend allowing sprouters to document supplier attestations when supplier data is limited.

[P47] Seed packinghouse lot code and packing/repacking date (§1.1325(b)(3)) requirements could conflict with existing supplier documentation practices—FDA should align with USDA or seed industry traceability norms.

[P48] Requiring seed supplier location identifiers (§1.1325(b)(4)) may be burdensome if seeds are sourced via multiple intermediaries; allow documentation of immediate supplier and linkages only as available.

[P49] The detailed seed description requirement (§1.1325(b)(5)) (taxonomic name, specs, antimicrobial treatments) could require seed testing or supplier guarantees; propose limiting mandatory items to those reasonably provided by suppliers.

[P50] Recordkeeping for seed supplier master and sub-lot codes (§1.1325(b)(6)) may be infeasible when supplier lot coding differs; recommend acceptance of supplier-provided codes and cross-reference guidance.

[P54] Recording the originator's location identifier and description (§1.1330(a)(1)) is reasonable but must allow use of supplier-provided identifiers (e.g., GS1 GLN) instead of new codes.

[P55] The obligation to record harvester business contact and harvest date/time (§1.1330(a)(2)) may not be available for some commodities harvested by independent contractors; clarify acceptable substitutes (e.g., crew codes, harvest ticket numbers).

[P56] Requiring recording of cooling location and date/time (§1.1330(a)(3)) creates challenges for decentralized cooling operations (e.g., roadside or mobile coolers); FDA should allow flexibility and reasonable proxies (e.g., receiving time at cooling facility).

[P57] Recording packing location and date/time (§1.1330(a)(4)) may conflict with industry practices where packing occurs multiple times—clarify which packing steps are required and permit consolidated records.

[P58] For vessel-caught seafood first receivers (§1.1330(b)), use of NMFS statistical area codes is appropriate but FDA should provide mapping tools and accept equivalent coordinate data to accommodate small harbors.

[P59] First receivers who must assign a traceability lot code if originator did not (§1.1330(c)) need clear instruction on code structure and how to notify downstream buyers; FDA should permit use of purchaser-assigned codes linked to origin data.

[P60] The comprehensive receiving record requirements (§1.1335) create significant data collection and storage burdens for midstream actors (wholesalers, aggregators); propose allowing industry-standard electronic data interchange formats and batch reporting.

[P61] Excluding transporters from "immediate previous source" reporting (§1.1335(a)) is reasonable but requires clarification when transporters operate under contract and exercise custody or repacking—define boundaries.

[P63] Recording precise date/time and location of receipt (§1.1335(c)) is feasible for large firms but difficult for small operations receiving multiple deliveries; recommend allowing day-level timestamps or delivery shift windows.

[P64] The requirement to record quantity and unit of measure (§1.1335(d)) should accept usual commercial measures (cases, pallets) and allow conversions rather than rigid weight-only standards.

[P65] Mandating traceability product identifier and product description (§1.1335(e)) without permitting standardized coding systems will cause inconsistencies; FDA should endorse GS1 GTIN, PLU, or similar standards.

[P72] The requirement to record product identifiers/descriptions for each input lot (§1.1340(a)(1)(ii)) should permit use of internal SKUs linked to external codes rather than requiring duplication of supplier naming conventions.

[P73] Recording quantities and units for each input traceability lot used (§1.1340(a)(1)(iii)) will be burdensome for continuous-process plants; FDA should permit aggregate batch yield records and recipe-level reconciliations.

[P76] New product identifier and description linkage to new traceability lot codes (§1.1340(a)(2)(ii)) should permit use of master product codes and packaging variation codes to avoid explosion of identifiers.

[P77] The requirement to record quantity/unit for each new traceability lot produced by transformation (§1.1340(a)(2)(iii)) should allow aggregating outputs produced over short time windows under a single traceability lot to reduce administrative burden when product is homogeneous.
