[P1] The December 22, 2017 deadline in § 39.13(a) is already past and therefore inconsistent with current rulemaking practice; request that the FAA correct the public-comment deadline to a current, realistic date and re-open the comment period if the date was mistakenly retained from an earlier draft.

[P17] The September 18, 2020 comment deadline in paragraph (a) conflicts with the December 22, 2017 date in P1; require the FAA to reconcile the two dates and publish a single, unambiguous comment deadline.

[P1] Industry commenters will claim that providing two different submission deadlines (2017 and 2020) creates legal uncertainty about whether the AD is procedurally valid and request withdrawal or reproposal until the administrative record and comment period dates are corrected.

[P2] Operators will state that the obligation to "comply within the specified compliance times unless already done" is vague because the rule does not explicitly state whether compliance accomplished under earlier service bulletins or similar ADs is acceptable as "already done"; request explicit language granting credit for prior compliance where equivalent work was performed.

[P18] Reiteration of P2: Commenters will request that the phrase "unless already done" be defined to specify what documentation is acceptable to demonstrate prior compliance (e.g., logbook entries, work orders, FAA Form 337).

[P3] Owners/operators will object that the initial inspection window of "within the next 100 hours TIS or within the next 12 months" (whichever occurs first) may be impractical for high-utilization or low-utilization aircraft and request that the FAA clarify whether "whichever occurs first" applies and consider alternative timing based on utilization or calendar age.

[P20] Maintenance organizations will comment that the recurring inspection interval of "not exceeding 7 years" is unusually long for corrosion-sensitive areas and argue that a shorter interval (e.g., 3–5 years) or a risk-based interval should be required, citing safety concerns and industry practice.

[P19] Maintenance providers will request clarification whether the 7-year repeat inspection interval applies from the initial inspection date, the effective date of the AD, or the date of any repair/CPP application, and ask FAA to specify the baseline for counting the interval.

[P21] Maintenance shops will request explicit acceptance criteria for the four visual-access methods (g)(1)(i)-(iv) to avoid varying inspector interpretations, and ask FAA to provide step-by-step guidance about when each access method is acceptable.

[P22] Owners will request that the AD clarify whether removing existing wing inspection access panels and fairings (g)(1)(i)) triggers additional airworthiness documentation (e.g., log entries, STC considerations) and who is authorized to reinstall panels after inspection.

[P23] Repair stations will request that the rule specify whether installing Inspection Access Hole Kit P/N 765–106V (g)(1)(ii)) requires a supplemental inspection authorization, STC, or repair-station capability beyond standard fabric/metal work, and request drawing/installation tolerances be referenced.

[P24] Operators will support allowing concurrent maintenance (g)(1)(iii)) to provide access but ask FAA to clarify whether an inspection performed during unrelated wing removal still meets the "initial inspection within 100 TIS/12 months" requirement or whether additional scheduled inspections are required afterwards.

[P25] Several commenters (maintenance, pilot groups) will ask for minimum borescope specifications for (g)(1)(iv)) beyond "10X or higher" (e.g., field-of-view, illumination, camera resolution) and request acceptance criteria for borescope images to determine pass/fail.

[P26] Maintenance engineers will request that the service bulletin steps referenced in (g)(2) be appended to the AD or incorporated by reference with explicit revision/version numbers to avoid ambiguity about cleaning methods and inspection standards.

[P29] Owners will request explicit procedural details about how prior inspections done "per the specified earlier service bulletin" qualify for credit—specifically which SB revision and what documentation is required to claim credit under (i).

[P5] Aircraft owners will request a clear definition of "evidence of corrosion" (e.g., pitting depth, percent of surface affected) for paragraph (i) to reduce subjectivity and inspector variability.

[P27] Repair stations will ask FAA to define "remove the corrosion and determine the component meets minimum thickness requirement" (h)(1) by providing specific minimum thickness values or a reference to an engineering document or repair manual with thickness limits.

[P28] Operators will request specification of acceptable corrosion preventive compounds (CPC) and application methods referenced in (h)(2) to ensure uniform compliance and avoid disagreements over material compatibility.

[P6] Aviation insurers and legal experts will comment that requiring "all necessary corrective actions and repairs" before further flight (j) is open-ended and potentially burdensome; they will request that the AD list allowable repair methods, limits of permissible in-service repairs, and when structural reinforcement or replacement is required.

[P31] Some commenters will urge that the AMOC submission procedure (j)(1)/(k)(1)) be simplified — allow direct electronic submission to the certification office manager in addition to local FSDO/principal inspector to speed review, and request defined turnaround times for AMOC responses.

[P7] Industry groups will request that the rule explicitly allow the Manager, Atlanta ACO Branch, to delegate AMOC approval authority to designated FAA engineers or the field office when workload requires, to avoid single-person bottlenecks.

[P8] Small operators will request clarification whether AMOC requests must always route through the principal inspector/local FSDO (k)(1)) or if manufacturers/repair stations may submit on behalf of operators with operator consent.

[P9] Legal commenters will point out ambiguity in directing AMOC information "to the person identified in paragraph (l)(1)" when paragraph (l)(1) is not included in this excerpt; request that the AD include the actual contact name, address, and email or explicitly reference the current contact list.

[P10] Operators will request that the AD require notification to the FAA of intended use of an AMOC after approval but define a specific timeline for notification (e.g., within 5 business days) rather than leaving it open-ended.

[P11] Maintenance organizations will express concern that labeling steps as RC (j)(3)(i)) makes certain procedural steps mandatory in a way that could conflict with existing maintenance programs, and ask the FAA to minimize RC labeling to only truly safety-critical steps.

[P12] Maintenance providers will request that the AD specify whether substeps and figures labeled RC are incorporated by reference and whether small, non-material deviations (e.g., torque values within tolerance) require formal AMOC.

[P13] Operators will request clarification on the AMOC requirement for deviations to RC steps (j)(3)(i)) — specifically whether minor alternative techniques accepted in standard maintenance practice must undergo full AMOC review or can be documented in the maintenance record with inspector concurrence.

[P14] Airlines and repair stations will support allowing deviations from non-RC steps (j)(3)(ii)) under their maintenance programs but request the FAA require that such deviations be recorded and made available for FAA audit to ensure accountability.

[P15] Safety advocates will object to allowing any deviation from non-RC steps if those deviations could indirectly impair the ability to perform RC steps; they will request the FAA require an engineer's determination that RC steps remain fully accomplishable prior to permitting deviations.

[P16] Pilot associations will request that the "airworthy condition" requirement (k)(3)(ii)) be explicitly tied to compliance with the applicable type certificate data and maintenance manual definitions of airworthiness, and that the AD specify what constitutes acceptable restoration to airworthiness.

[P30] Legal commentators will urge the FAA to publish criteria for evaluating AMOC requests (j)(1)/(k)(1)) so applicants know the standards and evidence required for approval rather than leaving approval to discretion without guidance.

[P32] Operators will ask FAA to codify the notification process in (j)(2)/(k)(2)) — specify the form, content, and timeline for notifying the principal inspector or local FSDO/CHDO before using an AMOC.

[P33] Maintenance organizations will request that any steps designated RC be accompanied by an explicit statement of the safety rationale for each RC step to allow commenters to assess proportionality and technical necessity.

[P34] Manufacturers (Piper) will request that the AD explicitly reference the exact Piper Service Bulletin revision(s) and include dates and part numbers for any kits or figures cited so that compliance does not rely on ambiguous references.

[P35] Trade groups will request that the FAA provide an estimate of the economic impact and labor hours associated with installing access panels (h) and performing inspections (g)/(i), and to include this in the final rule's regulatory flexibility analysis.

[P29] Some owners will request explicit allowance for credit where prior inspections used equivalent alternative techniques (e.g., different borescope magnification or non-Piper kits) and ask FAA to list acceptable equivalents or criteria to evaluate equivalence.

[P20] Maintenance/engineering commenters will request an immediate re-evaluation of the 7-year repeat interval for older aircraft models stored in corrosive environments and ask for a risk-based exception that mandates shorter intervals for aircraft that have been exposed to saltwater or high-humidity storage.

[P23] Repair stations will request that the AD allow use of aftermarket access kits other than P/N 765–106V if they are FAA-approved or meet defined engineering standards, rather than prescribing a single part number.

[P25] Pilot groups will ask FAA to permit remote inspection via acceptable imaging devices (e.g., high-resolution borescope with camera) and to define acceptance criteria for digital image submission in lieu of physical access when appropriate.

[P6] Owners will request that the AD specify whether any repairs performed "before further flight" must be performed by an FAA-certificated repair station, or if owner-performed repairs under owner-maintenance privileges are acceptable, and how those are to be documented.

[P27] Structural engineers will request that the AD incorporate or reference allowable repair drawings and thickness-limits tables so that shops know when a repair is structural vs. minor cosmetic corrosion removal.

[P11] Commenters will request the FAA to clarify whether any changes to the service bulletin after AD issuance that add or change RC steps will automatically become mandatory or require separate FAA action to incorporate new RC steps into the AD.

[P31] Airlines and operators will request that the FAA set service standards for AMOC review time (e.g., 60 days) and provide interim dispensation procedures if AMOC review is delayed and the aircraft would otherwise be grounded through no fault of the operator.

[P1] Industry commenter: The permission in §61.113(i) to act without a part 67 medical certificate should clarify whether it applies to commercial operations (e.g., flight instruction or rental-based paid services) to avoid unintended expansion beyond private non-commercial flights.

[P1] Legal expert: The rule must define "required flightcrew member" in the context of §61.113(i) to prevent ambiguity about which crewmembers (e.g., safety pilot, second-in-command in complex aircraft) can rely on the driver's-license pathway.

[P1] Medical advocacy group: Allowing pilots to substitute a valid U.S. driver's license for a medical certificate may reduce detection of medical conditions that impact safety; the FAA should publish risk assessments supporting this permission.

[P1] Individual pilot: The proposed §61.113(i) should explicitly state whether foreign-issued U.S.-equivalent driver’s licenses are acceptable when the pilot is a resident but holds a non-U.S. license.

[P2] Training providers: The 24-month window in §61.23(c)(3)(i)(C) is too short/frequent for recurrent training burden and cost; recommend extending to 36 months or allowing multi-year validity tied to the comprehensive exam cycle.

[P2] Small operator: The requirement to "retain the course completion certification" lacks format standards—request guidance on acceptable digital/printed proof and the FAA retention period for audits.

[P3] Medical community: Requiring a comprehensive medical exam by a State-licensed physician within 48 months (§61.23(c)(3)(i)(D)) conflicts with existing part 67 five-year intervals for certain classes; request harmonization to avoid duplicative exams.

[P3] Rural pilot association: The 48-month exam interval may be burdensome in areas with limited access to State-licensed physicians qualified under part 68—seek allowance for telehealth evaluations or alternative examers.

[P3] Legal counsel: Specify whether the "comprehensive medical examination" pursuant to §61.23(c)(3)(i)(D) must follow a particular checklist or form and whether physicians must submit results to the FAA or only retain in the pilot's records.

[P4] Disability rights group: The requirement in §61.23(c)(3)(i)(E) that a pilot with a diagnosed condition be "under the care and treatment" of a State-licensed physician is vague—define what constitutes adequate "care and treatment" and whether managed care plans meet this standard.

[P4] Individual pilot with chronic condition: Require exceptions for stable, well-managed chronic conditions with documented fitness-to-fly determinations so pilots are not unnecessarily grounded by blanket "under care" mandates.

[P4] Aviation safety NGO: Clarify enforcement and reporting responsibilities—if a pilot fails to maintain treatment for a condition, are physicians or treating clinics required or permitted to notify the FAA?

[P5] Course providers: §68.3(a) lacks specificity on curriculum depth, learning objectives, assessment standards, and minimum contact hours; request a detailed syllabus or baseline to ensure national consistency.

[P5] Consumer safety group: The content standards in §68.3(a) must include explicit modules on impairment from medications, cardiovascular and neurological warning signs, and cognitive decline screening to safeguard public safety.

[P5] Academic commenter: Require that the §68.3 course be accredited or periodically reviewed by an independent medical board to ensure scientific accuracy and currency.

[P6] Privacy advocates: §68.3(b) requires items be "electronically provided" and transmitted to the FAA—specify data security, encryption standards, consent mechanisms, and retention limits to protect personal health information.

[P6] Training vendor: Request clarification on the "specified items" to be transmitted to the FAA (§68.3(b))—identify required data fields, accepted file formats, and the transmission API or portal to avoid implementation delays.

[P6] Small flight school: Allow alternatives to electronic transmission (e.g., secure paper copies) for pilots without reliable internet access, or provide a delayed submission process to accommodate remote students.

[P7] Pilot rights group: The Special Issuance Authorization requirement in §68.9(a) for those seeking to operate under §61.113(i) could reintroduce medical gatekeeping; request clarity when Special Issuance is triggered and streamline the process for predictable, timely decisions.

[P7] Aviation physician: Define the evidence and documentation required for Special Issuance under §68.9(a), including which medical conditions mandate additional testing, to ensure standardized physician submissions.

[P7] Legal expert: The interplay between §68.9(a) Special Issuance and the driver's-license pathway must be explained—specify whether previously issued Special Issuance certificates under part 67 are grandfathered or require reapplication.

[P1] Insurance industry: Insurers will need clarity on liability exposure for pilots operating under §61.113(i); request the FAA coordinate with insurers and publish guidance to prevent coverage gaps.

[P2] Flight instructors: The timing requirement "during the 24 calendar months before acting" is ambiguous—does completion on the 24th month qualify? Request precise definitions of inclusive/exclusive timing.

[P3] State medical boards: Reaffirm whether "State-licensed physician" includes physicians licensed in the U.S. territories and clarify cross-state telemedicine licensure requirements for pilots who travel.

[P4] Public commenter: Require pilots to disclose any medication use to their treating physician as part of the "under care and treatment" condition, and provide guidance on which medications are disqualifying or require restrictions.

[P5] Small business association: Allow third-party approved course providers to develop the §68.3 course; request an FAA approval process and reasonable fees to avoid monopolistic pricing.

[P6] Records retention advocate: Specify how long course completion and transmitted records must be retained by both the individual and FAA, and whether they are subject to public records requests.

[P7] Regulatory compliance officer: Request a phase-in period and grandfathering rules for pilots who currently hold valid medical certificates to transition to the new Special Issuance requirements without disruption.

[P1] The rule’s statement that "FAA must receive comments by April 3, 2020" is confusing because it conflicts with the typical "postmark" vs. "received" language; request that the FAA clarify whether comments postmarked by April 3, 2020 but received later will be accepted.

[P2] The applicability in § 39.13(c) to "all Boeing 737–300, –400, and –500 series airplanes, certificated in any category" is overly broad and should be narrowed to only those airframes with the affected configuration/serial numbers or those within a specific maintenance configuration group.

[P2] Small commercial operators and private owners of 737–300/-400/-500s note that the AD's blanket applicability fails to account for earlier modifications or Service Bulletins that already address the unsafe condition; request a provision allowing operators to demonstrate through records that the AD does not apply.

[P3] The general compliance obligation in § 39.13(f) to "perform the actions within the specified compliance times" lacks clear phase-in scheduling for operators with limited maintenance resources; request staggered compliance windows or relief for fleet size.

[P3] Operators contend § 39.13(f) provides no exceptions for aircraft temporarily out of service for extended maintenance or storage, and request clarification that compliance times are measured from the AD effective date and allow credit for work done per earlier manuals.

[P4] Requiring that "at the specified times, perform all applicable actions in the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin" (§ 39.13(g)) makes compliance contingent on a manufacturer document that may change; request the FAA to incorporate the full required actions into the AD text to avoid dependence on external documents.

[P4] Maintenance providers request that § 39.13(g) explicitly allow performing Approved Data (e.g., FAA-approved engineering data) in lieu of literal adherence to the Boeing bulletin when it results in equal or greater safety, to avoid operational delays.

[P5] Paragraph § 39.13(g) terminating-action provision allowing the bulletin’s terminating actions to end AD requirements will be unworkable unless the bulletin clearly lists serial numbers and procedures; request FAA require Boeing to explicitly enumerate terminating actions and affected airplane serials.

[P5] Legal commenters note risk of ambiguity: if the bulletin’s terminating actions are later revised by Boeing, the AD should state whether those revised terminating actions are acceptable or require separate FAA approval.

[P1] The allowance in §205.601 of unspecified synthetic substances for organic crop production is overly broad and would erode the organic standard by permitting chemicals that are inconsistent with organic principles; the rule should list each synthetic substance explicitly and provide justification for each inclusion.

[P1] The provision permitting synthetic substances lacks required environmental and human health risk assessments for each listed synthetic; commenters request that the rule require disclosure of safety data, exposure limits, and environmental impact analyses for every synthetic allowed.

[P1] Industry commenters (organic certifiers and organic producers) will object that permitting synthetic substances without sunset reviews or periodic reevaluation risks permanent acceptance of materials that should be temporary or emergency-only; recommend adding review timelines and criteria for removal.

[P2] Allowing blood meal made with sodium citrate (§205.601(j)(2)) raises concerns about sodium citrate as a processing aid—commenters ask for clarity on whether sodium citrate residues are permitted and for maximum residue limits if allowed.

[P2] Animal welfare and religious groups will request documentation that the blood meal source is from animals slaughtered under humane practices and that blood meal production does not involve prohibited substances; ask for chain-of-custody and source verification requirements.

[P2] Food safety advocates will note that blood meal can harbor pathogens if not properly processed; they request mandatory processing standards (time/temperature) and pathogen testing for blood meal used in organic crop production.

[P3] The prohibition in §205.602 of nonsynthetic substances is ambiguous because many natural substances have synthetic analogs; commenters request the rule clarify whether naturally derived versus identically synthesized compounds are treated differently and provide examples.

[P3] Environmental NGOs will support the prohibition list but ask for transparency in criteria used to designate nonsynthetic substances as prohibited, and a clear appeals process for challenging listings.

[P4] The explicit prohibition of natamycin (§205.602(e)) should be accompanied by explanation of the scientific basis for the ban; manufacturers using natamycin in post-harvest preservation operations request data supporting the prohibition and an opportunity to propose alternative acceptable uses or mitigation measures.

[P4] Processors of organic dried fruits and cheeses (where natamycin is used as a surface mold inhibitor) will comment that banning natamycin could reduce shelf life and increase food waste; they request an exemption pathway for post-harvest treatments when supported by evidence that no organic-compliant alternative exists.

[P5] Permitting nonorganically produced agricultural ingredients in organic-labeled processed products (§205.606) risks consumer deception and dilution of organic integrity; consumer advocates request stricter limitations (e.g., 5% of product by weight) and conspicuous labeling of nonorganic ingredients.

[P5] Small organic processors argue that allowing nonorganic ingredients without strict criteria will disadvantage true-organic manufacturers; they request a formal list of allowed nonorganic ingredients with supply shortage documentation and supplier verification requirements.

[P6] Allowing tamarind seed gum (§205.606(s)) as a nonorganically produced ingredient raises an issue: tamarind seed gum is readily available from organic sources—commenters demand justification for listing it as nonorganic and request that organic tamarind seed gum be preferred or required when available.

[P6] Food formulators will request specification of purity, processing aids, origin labeling, and maximum allowable concentrations for tamarind seed gum when used in organic processed products to ensure consistent enforcement.

[P7] The invitation for written comments is standard, but stakeholder groups request additional public engagement mechanisms (e.g., public hearings, webinars) beyond written comments to ensure small producers and NGOs can participate effectively.

[P8] The methods for submitting comments are too narrow—commenters request inclusion of email, postal mail, and in-person submission options with clear instructions, and an extension of electronic submission windows for stakeholders with limited internet access.

[P9] Requiring that all written comments be included in the record is appropriate, but privacy-sensitive commenters request mechanisms to submit confidential business information (CBI) or redacted versions while providing a public summary, rather than full disclosure.

[P10] The statement that all written comments will be included in the official record should clarify whether attachments (large datasets, proprietary studies) will be hosted or summarized, and whether file size/type limits could exclude submissions; commenters request technical guidance.

[P11] Posting comments on regulations.gov raises confidentiality concerns; commenters request clear instructions on how to designate portions of comments as confidential or how to request redaction, consistent with FOIA and CBI rules.

[P12] The notice that commenter identities may be publicly disclosed will deter participation from individuals and small businesses worried about reprisal; commenters request an option to submit anonymous or pseudonymous comments or a process to request anonymity with justification.

[P12] Civil liberties groups will request explicit protections for whistleblowers and employees of large corporations who may submit comments criticizing industry practices, and assurance their identities will not be disclosed without consent.

[P13] The November 1, 2019 deadline to assure consideration is now past (or insufficiently long from publication) — commenters will seek an extension of the comment period to allow for data collection, stakeholder consultation, and translation into other languages for non-English-speaking producers.

[P13] Small farms and associations assert that the comment deadline does not provide adequate time to conduct empirical testing or economic impact analyses; request at least a 60–90 day extension to the comment period.

[P14] The prohibition on accepting comments not germane to the supplemental document appears overly restrictive; public interest groups request clear criteria for what is considered "germane" and an appeal process for rejected comments to avoid arbitrary exclusions.

[P14] Legal experts will warn that excluding off-topic comments could violate procedural fairness if topics are actually relevant to broader policy impacts; recommend allowing related comments and summarizing relevance decisions in the administrative record.

[P1/P5] Several commenters will point out a potential inconsistency: permitting synthetic substances in crop production (§205.601) while allowing nonorganic agricultural ingredients in processed organic products (§205.606) may create supply chain loopholes—request coherence between crop inputs and processed ingredient rules to preserve organic integrity.

[P2/P4] Food safety regulators will request harmonization between the blood meal provision and the natamycin prohibition to ensure pathogen control in post-harvest and soil amendments without enabling prohibited antimicrobial use in organic agriculture.

[P6/P11] Importers and exporters of tamarind seed gum request clarification on country-of-origin documentation requirements and whether FNS posting of comments will include proprietary supplier lists, which could harm competitiveness.

[P3/P1] Organic certifiers ask for explicit enforcement mechanisms and penalties for misuse of permitted synthetics and prohibited nonsynthetics (e.g., misuse of blood meal declared as sodium-citrate-processed), including audit requirements and sample testing protocols.

[P9/P11] Technical commenters request assurances that the regulations.gov posting will be accessible (ADA-compliant) and that submission metadata (IP addresses, email addresses) will be stripped before public posting to protect privacy.

[P7/P8] Nonprofit advocacy groups encourage FNS to provide translation services and outreach to historically underrepresented producers (e.g., tribal, minority-owned farms) about how to submit comments, plus extended hours for in-person assistance.

[P2] Public health advocates request that the rule specify labeling requirements if blood meal is used on crops destined for raw consumption, to inform consumers with dietary/religious restrictions.

[P5] Retailers and foodservice buyers object to the potential inclusion of nonorganic ingredients in products labeled "organic" without a clear threshold and demand that any product with nonorganic agricultural ingredients disclose the percent of nonorganic ingredients on package labeling.

[P4] Researchers request that FNS publish the scientific studies and criteria used to determine natamycin’s prohibition, and, if animal studies were used, provide summaries of methodologies and endpoints.

[P1] Trade associations ask FNS to evaluate trade implications of allowing new synthetics in organic production, including compatibility with international organic standards (EU, Codex) to avoid export disruptions.

[P13] State departments of agriculture request that the deadline align with state rulemaking timelines and ask for coordination meetings before finalization to address state-level implementation concerns.

[P14] Commenters will ask for transparency about how out-of-scope comments will be handled and whether they will still be acknowledged even if not considered germane, to maintain public trust in the process.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether the July 27, 2017 date is the postmark receipt date or the date the FAA must physically receive electronic comments, because ambiguity could cause dismissal of timely intent.

[P2] Applying the AD to "all Boeing 787–8 and 787–9 airplanes, certificated in any category" is overly broad; the FAA should limit applicability to transport-category aircraft used in revenue service or to specific certificated configurations affected by the PBM design.

[P2] The rule must specify whether foreign-registered 787-8/-9 aircraft operating to/from the U.S. are subject to this AD, and clarify coordination with foreign civil aviation authorities to avoid conflicting directives.

[P2] The phrase "certificated in any category" may inadvertently include parked, stored, or parts-only airframes; the FAA should explicitly exclude non-airworthy, non-operational aircraft to avoid unnecessary compliance burden.

[P3] The statement "Comply within the compliance times specified" lacks a specific baseline (effective date vs. AD publication date) for each compliance action; commenters request insertion of explicit calendar dates or a clear effective date reference.

[P3] The provision should allow credit for actions performed per earlier service bulletins even if not identical to the AD language, otherwise operators who complied in good faith may be forced to repeat work.

[P4] A 60-month compliance window to inspect PBMs is too long given potential safety implications; industry safety advocates and pilot unions will request a shorter inspection interval (e.g., 12–24 months) or an interim risk assessment justification.

[P4] Conversely, some operators (especially smaller carriers and lessors) will argue that 60 months is too short to schedule inspections across their fleets and request a phased compliance schedule or extended compliance time tied to heavy maintenance visits.

[P4] The provision fails to require documentation standards for the inspection outcome (e.g., form, data fields, and retention period); commenters will ask the FAA to mandate recordkeeping procedures to ensure traceability.

[P5] Allowing a records review in lieu of physical inspection is practical, but the rule must define "conclusively determined" (acceptable documents, signatures, tracing chain, and age of records) to avoid inconsistent interpretations and enforcement.

[P5] The FAA should require operators using records review to retain an auditable log (including copies of records relied upon) for a specified period (e.g., 3 years) and make those records available to the FAA upon request.

[P5] There is no provision for the accuracy of records that may be erroneous; commenters will request that if records are ambiguous or incomplete, a physical inspection be mandatory rather than optional.

[P6] The exception for PBM P/N 4260–0037–5 is appropriate, but the AD must require operators to document and retain evidence that the installed PBM is P/N 4260–0037–5 to prevent reinstallation of prohibited parts in the future.

[P6] Clarify whether PBMs that have been repaired or reworked retain the original P/N for the exception; request guidance on how modified units, with overhaul/repair tags, should be treated.

[P7] Requiring installation of PBM P/N 4260–0037–5 within 60 months for P/Ns -3 or -4 will impose significant parts and labor costs; industry commenters will request FAA cost-benefit analysis disclosure and potential financial relief or phase-in options.

[P7] The AD should allow the use of equivalent or improved PBM part numbers (developed after the AD) if they meet or exceed safety performance, rather than mandating only P/N 4260–0037–5.

[P7] Operators will request permission to coordinate installation during heavy maintenance checks to minimize downtime, and seek explicit language that allows scheduling installations at the next D-check or equivalent maintenance visit.

[P8] Requiring the PBM installation test within 60 months is vague about test acceptance criteria; commenters will request the FAA to incorporate or reference the specific Boeing/Rockwell Collins test procedures and pass/fail criteria.

[P8] The AD should allow the PBM installation test to be performed at a certified repair station or OEM facility and should specify qualifications/personnel authorized to perform/verify the test.

[P9] The requirement to perform "all applicable corrective actions" per the referenced Boeing service bulletin lacks specificity about what constitutes "applicable"; commenters will request that the FAA include a list or explanatory guidance, to avoid inconsistent application among operators.

[P9] Because the corrective actions reference a Boeing service bulletin, commenters will request the FAA to incorporate the exact revision number and date of the service bulletin into the AD to prevent confusion about which instructions apply.

[P10] Requiring that all applicable corrective actions be completed "before further flight" could ground airplanes unexpectedly if corrective parts are not available; air carriers and leasing companies will request allowance for temporary flight restrictions (e.g., ferry flight provisions) or conditional relief until parts are sourced.

[P10] The AD should specify an explicit process and approval path for temporary mitigations that permit safe ferrying to a maintenance base when immediate completion of corrective actions before further flight is impractical.

[P11] The prohibition on installing PBM P/Ns 4260–0037–3 or -4 as of the effective date should include a definition of "install" (e.g., includes reinstallation after bench testing, installation during modification) to avoid enforcement ambiguity.

[P11] Suppliers and MROs will request a limited grandfathering exception to allow installation for test, teardown, or loan purposes, provided the PBM is not returned to service on an airworthy airplane.

[P11] The AD should provide guidance on how to handle PBMs of the prohibited P/N that are in stock or in transit on the effective date, including return-to-vendor or scrap procedures.

[P12] Industry groups request published criteria and expected turnaround times for AMOC consideration by the Seattle ACO Manager to reduce operational uncertainty.

[P13] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 is standard, but commenters will request digital submission pathways be explicitly recognized to streamline processing.

[P14] The instruction to address direct AMOC submissions to the person identified in paragraph (j)(1) must be accompanied by that individual's name, phone number, and mailing address within the AD text; otherwise, it creates administrative confusion.

[P15] The option to email AMOC information to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is useful, but commenters will request confirmation of acceptable file formats, encryption requirements for proprietary information, and acknowledgement-of-receipt procedures.

[P15] Confidential business information protections for emailed AMOC submissions should be clarified, including how the FAA will handle proprietary attachments and whether redaction is permissible.

[P16] The requirement to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC lacks a timeframe (e.g., how many days before implementation notification must be given); operators will request a clear notification window to ensure compliance.

[P16] Small operators without an assigned principal inspector need guidance; commenters will request the FAA to specify exactly who constitutes "manager of the local FSDO/CHDO" and how to contact them.

[P17] Permitting Boeing ODA approval of AMOCs for repairs/modifications is efficient, but commenters will request that the AD require Boeing to document the ODA approval rationale and make summary findings available to operators and the FAA for transparency.

[P17] There should be limits on Boeing ODA’s authority to approve AMOCs if the proposed deviations affect systems beyond Boeing’s delegated scope; legal commenters will request guardrails to prevent inappropriate delegation.

[P18] Requiring repair/modification deviations to meet the airplane's certification basis is reasonable, but commenters will ask for instructions on how to interpret certification basis for older 787s that may have supplemental type certificates or previous AMOCs.

[P18] The AD should require the submitter to provide a compliance demonstration mapping the proposed deviation to the certification basis, including any acceptable means of compliance or test data.

[P20] Requiring performance of all RC-labeled steps, substeps, and figures is appropriate for safety; however, commenters will propose the FAA ensure that any RC annotations in the referenced service bulletin are unambiguous and that the AD lists the critical RC steps inline.

[P20] Legal commenters will request clarification about whether compliance with RC steps in earlier-revision service bulletins counts as compliance, and whether a positive compliance record from prior actions can be used to avoid re-performing RC steps.

[P21] The 'RC Exempt' carve-out is necessary, but the AD should define how RC Exempt steps are identified (e.g., bolding, separate list) and whether operators must document that a step is RC Exempt when using alternative methods.

[P22] Requiring AMOCs for any deviation from RC steps could create unnecessary administrative burden for minor procedural differences; commenters will request that the FAA allow minor, documented procedural deviations within the operator’s maintenance system provided safety equivalence is demonstrated.

[P22] The AD should provide examples of acceptable justification for AMOC requests that deviate from RC steps to guide applicants and reduce back-and-forth with the FAA.

[P23] Allowing deviation from non-RC steps under an operator’s program is practical, but the AD must explicitly require that such deviations be recorded in the operator’s maintenance records and be subject to FAA audit.

[P23] To avoid safety gaps, the FAA should require operators to assess and document that any non-RC deviations do not adversely affect the ability to perform RC steps and that the airplane can be returned to an airworthy condition before flight.

[P23] Clarify whether the operator’s internal acceptance criteria for non-RC deviations must be equivalent to FAA-accepted methods (e.g., EASA-compliant programs) when the operator is an international carrier.

raw_output:
[P1] The proposed rebuttable presumption in §208.33(a)(1) is overbroad because it applies to any alien entering at the southwest land border "without documents sufficient for lawful admission" after traveling through another country, which could sweep in asylum seekers who had no realistic opportunity to secure documents — request narrowing or clearer definitions of "documents sufficient for lawful admission."

[P1] The rule lacks clarity on the temporal scope of "after traveling through a" — commenters will argue the provision should specify whether a brief transit stops or prior residence in a third country count, to avoid arbitrary application.

[P2] §208.33(a)(1)(i) conditions avoidance of the presumption on having been "provided appropriate authorization to travel ... pursuant to a DHS-approved parole process," but the rule fails to define what counts as "appropriate authorization" or which parole programs qualify — ask for an explicit list or criteria and an appeal mechanism for denials.

[P2] Industry and legal aid groups will claim that relying on DHS parole processes as an exception disadvantages vulnerable populations because access to DHS-approved parole processes is limited, inconsistent, and often requires legal assistance; they will request expansion of acceptable authorizations (e.g., NGO referrals, refugee resettlement pathways).

[P3] §208.33(a)(1)(ii) creates an exception for presenting at a port of entry "pursuant to a pre-scheduled time and place" but does not provide standards for scheduling availability — commenters will assert DHS must ensure adequate scheduling capacity and publish scheduling availability and alternatives to avoid de facto denial of the exception.

[P3] The carve-out in §208.33(a)(1)(ii) for those who "demonstrate inability to use DHS scheduling" is vague and will be challenged as setting an overly burdensome evidentiary requirement; request explicit examples of acceptable proof (e.g., lack of internet, language barriers, time-sensitive threats).

[P4] §208.33(a)(1)(iii) conditions exception on having sought and received a "final decision denying" protection in a transit country; refugee and asylum advocacy groups will argue this is unworkable because many transit countries lack functioning asylum systems or issue no final determinations — request that DHS recognize documented attempts to seek protection even without formal denial.

[P4] Legal experts will claim that requiring a "final decision" in a transit country violates non-refoulement principles if transit systems are not fair or are hostile; they will request an exception where the transit country's process fails minimum protections.

[P5] The "preponderance of the evidence" standard in §208.33(a)(2) for rebutting the presumption of ineligibility may be too stringent given the often-limited documentary evidence available to asylum seekers; commenters will request lowering to a credible showing or clear-and-convincing standard adjustments for particular circumstances.

[P6] §208.33(a)(2)(i) lists "acute medical emergency at the time of entry" as an exceptionally compelling circumstance but does not define terms such as "acute," "at the time of entry," or acceptable medical documentation — health organizations will request definitions and acceptable forms of evidence, plus guidance for detained or unaccompanied minors.

[P6] Medical providers will comment that many migrants have chronic conditions that become acute intermittently; request that the rule explicitly include acute exacerbations of chronic conditions and permit medical affidavits where documentation from country of origin is unavailable.

[P7] §208.33(a)(2)(ii) includes "imminent and extreme threat" e.g., imminent rape/kidnapping/torture as exceptionally compelling, but the regulation lacks guidance on timeline and credibility assessment — survivors' advocates will request trauma-informed standards and protection from retraumatizing evidentiary demands.

[P7] Criminal justice groups will assert that the phrase "imminent and extreme threat" should encompass generalized gang or paramilitary threats where state protection is unavailable, and request explicit reference to non-state actor persecution with supporting guidance.

[P8] §208.33(a)(2)(iii) treats meeting the trafficking victim definition as an exceptionally compelling circumstance, but commenters will raise concerns that the trafficking definition in §214.11 is narrower than international standards; they will ask DHS to clarify that protections apply even where trafficking claims overlap with smuggling or coercion scenarios.

[P8] Anti-trafficking organizations will request specific procedures to identify trafficking victims at intake, ensure access to specialized services, and avoid burdening victims with the task of proving trafficking under high evidentiary thresholds.

[P9] §208.33(a)(3) requires that demonstration of any listed circumstance "shall necessarily" rebut the presumption — immigrant advocates will request that DHS clarify which evidentiary standards apply and ensure expedited processing for cases involving listed circumstances to prevent prolonged detention or removal.

[P10] §208.33(b) exempts unaccompanied alien children from the presumption, but commenters will insist the rule must affirmatively require child-appropriate procedures, counsel appointment, and non-detention alternatives — and demand alignment with existing child welfare statutes.

[P11] §208.13(f) and §1208.13(f) apply the rule to applications filed by aliens who entered during the 24-month window after the effective date — civil rights groups will argue retroactive or transition impacts may deny protections to those who entered prior to the effective date but filed later; request clarification on treatment of pending applications and fair notice.

[P12] §208.33(c)(1) requires asylum officers to determine presumption applicability first — legal practitioners will argue this prioritization could shortcut individualized protection determinations, leading to routinized negative credible fear findings; request requirements for individualized consideration and oversight metrics.

[P13] Under §208.33(c)(1)(i), failure to rebut the presumption requires entry of a negative credible fear determination — immigrant defenders will claim this creates a near-automatic denial pipeline for large classes of asylum seekers and request independent review or supervisory sign-off before issuing negative determinations.

[P14] §208.33(c)(1)(ii) requires asylum officers to follow §208.30 when presumption does not apply or is rebutted — commenters will ask DHS to explicitly require full consideration of non-asylum relief (CAT, withholding) in these proceedings and to provide training so officers evaluate all grounds consistently.

[P15] §208.33(c)(2)(i) directs asylum officers who enter negative credible fear determinations to assess reasonable possibility of persecution/torture in the prospective removal country(ies) — human rights groups will request that the rule prohibit return to countries where systemic torture or persecution is known, regardless of lack of individualized risk, to enforce non-refoulement obligations.

[P16] §208.33(c)(2)(ii) requires issuance of a Notice to Appear if the alien shows reasonable possibility — commenters will flag administrative capacity issues, arguing DHS must ensure timely issuance and access to counsel and hearings, and that delays should not result in prolonged detention without review.

[P17] §§208.33(c)(2)(ii) and (c)(2)(v)(B) permit aliens in removal proceedings to apply for asylum and other relief — immigrants' rights groups will stress the need to guarantee access to counsel, translation, evidence-gathering opportunities, and sufficient time to prepare, particularly for vulnerable populations.

[P18] §208.33(c)(2)(iii) requires written decisions and offer of IJ review where the alien fails to show reasonable possibility — due process advocates will demand that the written decision include detailed factual and legal bases, provide translation, and be given with adequate time to request review.

[P19] §208.33(c)(2)(iv) mandates that the alien indicate on a specified form whether they want IJ review — disability advocates and pro se litigants will argue that providing a single form may be inadequate for those with literacy, language, or cognitive disabilities and request alternative mechanisms and assistance in making the choice.

[P20] §208.33(c)(2)(v) conditions the service of a Notice of Referral to the IJ on the alien's affirmative request on the Record of Negative Fear — legal commentators will argue this creates an undue burden and potential for missed review due to confusion, coercion, or lack of counsel; request auto-referral or a low-threshold "mail-in" or later-request procedure.

[P21] §208.33(c)(2)(v) requires asylum officers/DHS to provide the IJ with the record of determination and related materials — judges and defense counsel will request strict timelines and accuracy requirements, and the opportunity to supplement incomplete records, plus protection of privileged or sensitive materials.

[P22] §208.33(c)(2)(v) directs IJs to evaluate cases under 8 CFR 1208.33(c) — immigration judges' associations will ask for clear training and resource allocations so IJs can fairly adjudicate de novo review under a new, complex presumption framework.

[P23] §208.33(c)(2)(v)(A)-(C) prescribes post-referral procedures but lacks timelines — stakeholders will request concrete deadlines for IJ hearings, decisions, and DHS removal actions to avoid indefinite limbo and to protect due process.

[P24] §208.33(c)(2)(v)(A) links positive IJ credible fear findings to §208.30(g)(2)(iv)(B) procedures — advocates will ask for confirmation that these procedures preserve access to full asylum merits hearings and remedies, including work authorization and release alternatives.

[P25] §208.33(c)(2)(v)(B) requires DHS to issue a Form I–862 when IJ finds positive credible fear — state court practitioners and defense attorneys will request that DHS be required to provide charging documents, evidence, and sufficient lead time before merits hearings.

[P26] §208.33(c)(2)(v)(B) and (c)(2)(v)(C) permitting application for asylum in removal proceedings — public defender organizations will insist the rule explicitly preserves eligibility for bond and parole, and does not mandate detention pending merits adjudication.

[P27] §208.33(c)(2)(v)(C) requires return to DHS for removal if IJ issues a negative credible fear finding — human rights groups will highlight risks of summary removal to danger and ask for a stay mechanism to allow review of changed circumstances or new evidence.

[P28] §208.33(c)(2)(v)(C) prohibits appeals from IJ decisions and submission of reconsideration requests to USCIS (except discretionary) — constitutional and due process scholars will argue this elimination of appeal violates statutory rights and request reinstatement of appeal rights or at minimum defined narrow grounds and a timeline for DHS reconsideration.

[P29] §208.33(c)(2)(v)(C) allows USCIS to "in its sole discretion" reconsider negative determinations — commenters will call this wording arbitrary and request objective standards and a petition process with timelines to prevent inconsistent or capricious exercise of discretion.

[P30] §1208.13(f) mirrors §208.13(f) applying the rule to entrants in the 24-month window — immigration clinics will request transitional protections for those who entered the U.S. in the covered period but whose circumstances (e.g., trafficking, medical emergencies) arise later.

[P31] §1208.33(a)(1) duplicates the presumption from §208.33 — civil liberties groups will request cross-references be harmonized and any duplicative language removed to prevent conflicting interpretations between USCIS and EOIR contexts.

[P32] §1208.33(a)(1)(i) referencing DHS-approved parole processes as an exception should be coordinated with CBP/ICE/USCIS guidance — commenters will ask for interagency protocols and public posting of eligible parole pathways and application procedures.

[P33] §1208.33(a)(1)(ii) exception for port-of-entry presentation includes an undefined "if t..." clause in the excerpt — commentators will point out that the draft appears truncated/unclear and request complete language and explanation of criteria for in-person port-of-entry exceptions.

[P34] §1208.33(a)(1)(iii) requiring "final decision denying" protection in transit countries duplicates concerns in §208.33(a)(1)(iii) — international law NGOs will urge DHS to accept credible attempts and evidence that an asylum application was futile or unavailable, not only a formal denial.

[P35] §1208.33(a)(2) reliance on preponderance of the evidence to show "exceptionally compelling circumstances" repeats the evidentiary concern — immigration law groups will request that certain circumstances (e.g., trafficking, acute medical emergency) be rebuttable on a lower or modified evidentiary showing.

[P36] §1208.33(a)(2)(i) includes acute medical emergencies but does not address access to independent medical evaluation — medical associations will request guaranteed access to independent medical exams and that detention not impede obtaining medical evidence.

[P37] §1208.33(a)(2)(ii) includes imminent threats such as rape/kidnapping/torture as qualifying — sexual violence and refugee organizations will request inclusion of gender-based persecution and family-based persecution explicitly, and trauma-informed interviewing and adjudication practices.

[P38] §1208.33(a)(2)(iii) references the trafficking definition in 8 CFR 214.11 but the text here differs between §208 and §1208 — request harmonization so trafficking victims get consistent treatment across DHS and EOIR processes.

[P39] §1208.33(a)(3) mandates that demonstration of any listed circumstance "shall necessarily" rebut the presumption — government accountability groups will request that DHS publish statistical reporting on how often the mandatory rebuttal is applied to ensure the provision is not being misapplied.

[P40] §1208.33(b) excludes unaccompanied alien children from the presumption but fails to address children accompanied by family who are nonetheless minors — child welfare advocates will ask for protections for all minors and dependent claimants, not just unaccompanied ones.

[P41] §1208.33(c) directs de novo IJ review of asylum officer negative credible fear determinations — court practitioners will request clear standards for de novo review scope, allowable new evidence, and procedures for remand if record is incomplete.

[P42] §1208.33(c)(2) requires IJs to determine presumption applicability first — defense counsel will argue this prioritization may bias judges toward presumption-based denials and request that IJs be required to consider individualized protection claims simultaneously.

[P43] §1208.33(c)(2)(i) instructs IJs to determine "significant possibility" of eligibility under §208.30 — request precise definition of "significant possibility" and uniform criteria to reduce inconsistent application across judges and courts.

[P44] §1208.33(c)(2)(ii) tasks IJs with determining whether a covered alien has a "reasonable possibility" of persecution/torture — legal commentators will demand alignment of "reasonable" and "significant" standards across USCIS and EOIR to prevent forum-shopping and confusion.

[P45] §1208.33(c)(3) refers cases back to procedures in 208.33(c)(2)(v)(A)-(C) after IJ determination — request that DHS/EOIR publish a clear flowchart and timeline so counsel and pro se litigants can understand next steps and deadlines.

[P46] §1208.33(d) treats ancillary spouses/children as rebutting the presumption when the principal would be granted asylum but for the presumption — family advocacy groups will praise this protection but request clarification as to what evidence is required to prove the principal's likely grant "but for" the presumption, and how derivative applicants will be protected from removal in the interim.

[P46] Commenters will also request that §1208.33(d) specify whether the rebuttal extends to all derivative family members (e.g., parents, adult dependents) and require continuity of benefits (work authorization, reunification) while claims are adjudicated.

§208.33(a)(1)(iii) conditions exception on having sought and received a "final decision denying" protection in a transit country; refugee and asylum advocacy groups will argue this is unworkable because many transit countries lack functioning asylum systems or issue no final determinations — request that DHS recognize documented attempts to seek protection even without formal denial.

Legal experts will claim that requiring a "final decision" in a transit country violates non-refoulement principles if transit systems are not fair or are hostile; they will request an exception where the transit country's process fails minimum protections.

The "preponderance of the evidence" standard in §208.33(a)(2) for rebutting the presumption of ineligibility may be too stringent given the often-limited documentary evidence available to asylum seekers; commenters will request lowering to a credible showing or clear-and-convincing standard adjustments for particular circumstances.

§208.33(a)(2)(i) lists "acute medical emergency at the time of entry" as an exceptionally compelling circumstance but does not define terms such as "acute," "at the time of entry," or acceptable medical documentation — health organizations will request definitions and acceptable forms of evidence, plus guidance for detained or unaccompanied minors.

Medical providers will comment that many migrants have chronic conditions that become acute intermittently; request that the rule explicitly include acute exacerbations of chronic conditions and permit medical affidavits where documentation from country of origin is unavailable.

§208.33(a)(2)(ii) includes "imminent and extreme threat" e.g., imminent rape/kidnapping/torture as exceptionally compelling, but the regulation lacks guidance on timeline and credibility assessment — survivors' advocates will request trauma-informed standards and protection from retraumatizing evidentiary demands.

Criminal justice groups will assert that the phrase "imminent and extreme threat" should encompass generalized gang or paramilitary threats where state protection is unavailable, and request explicit reference to non-state actor persecution with supporting guidance.

§208.33(a)(2)(iii) treats meeting the trafficking victim definition as an exceptionally compelling circumstance, but commenters will raise concerns that the trafficking definition in §214.11 is narrower than international standards; they will ask DHS to clarify that protections apply even where trafficking claims overlap with smuggling or coercion scenarios.

Anti-trafficking organizations will request specific procedures to identify trafficking victims at intake, ensure access to specialized services, and avoid burdening victims with the task of proving trafficking under high evidentiary thresholds.

§208.33(a)(3) requires that demonstration of any listed circumstance "shall necessarily" rebut the presumption — immigrant advocates will request that DHS clarify which evidentiary standards apply and ensure expedited processing for cases involving listed circumstances to prevent prolonged detention or removal.

§208.33(b) exempts unaccompanied alien children from the presumption, but commenters will insist the rule must affirmatively require child-appropriate procedures, counsel appointment, and non-detention alternatives — and demand alignment with existing child welfare statutes.

§208.13(f) and §1208.13(f) apply the rule to applications filed by aliens who entered during the 24-month window after the effective date — civil rights groups will argue retroactive or transition impacts may deny protections to those who entered prior to the effective date but filed later; request clarification on treatment of pending applications and fair notice.

§208.33(c)(1) requires asylum officers to determine presumption applicability first — legal practitioners will argue this prioritization could shortcut individualized protection determinations, leading to routinized negative credible fear findings; request requirements for individualized consideration and oversight metrics.

Under §208.33(c)(1)(i), failure to rebut the presumption requires entry of a negative credible fear determination — immigrant defenders will claim this creates a near-automatic denial pipeline for large classes of asylum seekers and request independent review or supervisory sign-off before issuing negative determinations.

§208.33(c)(1)(ii) requires asylum officers to follow §208.30 when presumption does not apply or is rebutted — commenters will ask DHS to explicitly require full consideration of non-asylum relief (CAT, withholding) in these proceedings and to provide training so officers evaluate all grounds consistently.

§208.33(c)(2)(i) directs asylum officers who enter negative credible fear determinations to assess reasonable possibility of persecution/torture in the prospective removal country(ies) — human rights groups will request that the rule prohibit return to countries where systemic torture or persecution is known, regardless of lack of individualized risk, to enforce non-refoulement obligations.

§208.33(c)(2)(ii) requires issuance of a Notice to Appear if the alien shows reasonable possibility — commenters will flag administrative capacity issues, arguing DHS must ensure timely issuance and access to counsel and hearings, and that delays should not result in prolonged detention without review.

§§208.33(c)(2)(ii) and (c)(2)(v)(B) permit aliens in removal proceedings to apply for asylum and other relief — immigrants' rights groups will stress the need to guarantee access to counsel, translation, evidence-gathering opportunities, and sufficient time to prepare, particularly for vulnerable populations.

§208.33(c)(2)(iii) requires written decisions and offer of IJ review where the alien fails to show reasonable possibility — due process advocates will demand that the written decision include detailed factual and legal bases, provide translation, and be given with adequate time to request review.

§208.33(c)(2)(iv) mandates that the alien indicate on a specified form whether they want IJ review — disability advocates and pro se litigants will argue that providing a single form may be inadequate for those with literacy, language, or cognitive disabilities and request alternative mechanisms and assistance in making the choice.

§208.33(c)(2)(v) conditions the service of a Notice of Referral to the IJ on the alien's affirmative request on the Record of Negative Fear — legal commentators will argue this creates an undue burden and potential for missed review due to confusion, coercion, or lack of counsel; request auto-referral or a low-threshold "mail-in" or later-request procedure.

§208.33(c)(2)(v) requires asylum officers/DHS to provide the IJ with the record of determination and related materials — judges and defense counsel will request strict timelines and accuracy requirements, and the opportunity to supplement incomplete records, plus protection of privileged or sensitive materials.

§208.33(c)(2)(v) directs IJs to evaluate cases under 8 CFR 1208.33(c) — immigration judges' associations will ask for clear training and resource allocations so IJs can fairly adjudicate de novo review under a new, complex presumption framework.

§208.33(c)(2)(v)(A)-(C) prescribes post-referral procedures but lacks timelines — stakeholders will request concrete deadlines for IJ hearings, decisions, and DHS removal actions to avoid indefinite limbo and to protect due process.

§208.33(c)(2)(v)(A) links positive IJ credible fear findings to §208.30(g)(2)(iv)(B) procedures — advocates will ask for confirmation that these procedures preserve access to full asylum merits hearings and remedies, including work authorization and release alternatives.

§208.33(c)(2)(v)(B) requires DHS to issue a Form I–862 when IJ finds positive credible fear — state court practitioners and defense attorneys will request that DHS be required to provide charging documents, evidence, and sufficient lead time before merits hearings.

§208.33(c)(2)(v)(B) and (c)(2)(v)(C) permitting application for asylum in removal proceedings — public defender organizations will insist the rule explicitly preserves eligibility for bond and parole, and does not mandate detention pending merits adjudication.

§208.33(c)(2)(v)(C) requires return to DHS for removal if IJ issues a negative credible fear finding — human rights groups will highlight risks of summary removal to danger and ask for a stay mechanism to allow review of changed circumstances or new evidence.

§208.33(c)(2)(v)(C) prohibits appeals from IJ decisions and submission of reconsideration requests to USCIS (except discretionary) — constitutional and due process scholars will argue this elimination of appeal violates statutory rights and request reinstatement of appeal rights or at minimum defined narrow grounds and a timeline for DHS reconsideration.

§208.33(c)(2)(v)(C) allows USCIS to "in its sole discretion" reconsider negative determinations — commenters will call this wording arbitrary and request objective standards and a petition process with timelines to prevent inconsistent or capricious exercise of discretion.

§1208.13(f) mirrors §208.13(f) applying the rule to entrants in the 24-month window — immigration clinics will request transitional protections for those who entered the U.S. in the covered period but whose circumstances (e.g., trafficking, medical emergencies) arise later.

§1208.33(a)(1) duplicates the presumption from §208.33 — civil liberties groups will request cross-references be harmonized and any duplicative language removed to prevent conflicting interpretations between USCIS and EOIR contexts.

§1208.33(a)(1)(i) referencing DHS-approved parole processes as an exception should be coordinated with CBP/ICE/USCIS guidance — commenters will ask for interagency protocols and public posting of eligible parole pathways and application procedures.

§1208.33(a)(1)(ii) exception for port-of-entry presentation includes an undefined "if t..." clause in the excerpt — commentators will point out that the draft appears truncated/unclear and request complete language and explanation of criteria for in-person port-of-entry exceptions.

§1208.33(a)(1)(iii) requiring "final decision denying" protection in transit countries duplicates concerns in §208.33(a)(1)(iii) — international law NGOs will urge DHS to accept credible attempts and evidence that an asylum application was futile or unavailable, not only a formal denial.

§1208.33(a)(2) reliance on preponderance of the evidence to show "exceptionally compelling circumstances" repeats the evidentiary concern — immigration law groups will request that certain circumstances (e.g., trafficking, acute medical emergency) be rebuttable on a lower or modified evidentiary showing.

§1208.33(a)(2)(i) includes acute medical emergencies but does not address access to independent medical evaluation — medical associations will request guaranteed access to independent medical exams and that detention not impede obtaining medical evidence.

§1208.33(a)(2)(ii) includes imminent threats such as rape/kidnapping/torture as qualifying — sexual violence and refugee organizations will request inclusion of gender-based persecution and family-based persecution explicitly, and trauma-informed interviewing and adjudication practices.

§1208.33(a)(2)(iii) references the trafficking definition in 8 CFR 214.11 but the text here differs between §208 and §1208 — request harmonization so trafficking victims get consistent treatment across DHS and EOIR processes.

§1208.33(a)(3) mandates that demonstration of any listed circumstance "shall necessarily" rebut the presumption — government accountability groups will request that DHS publish statistical reporting on how often the mandatory rebuttal is applied to ensure the provision is not being misapplied.

§1208.33(b) excludes unaccompanied alien children from the presumption but fails to address children accompanied by family who are nonetheless minors — child welfare advocates will ask for protections for all minors and dependent claimants, not just unaccompanied ones.

§1208.33(c) directs de novo IJ review of asylum officer negative credible fear determinations — court practitioners will request clear standards for de novo review scope, allowable new evidence, and procedures for remand if record is incomplete.

§1208.33(c)(2) requires IJs to determine presumption applicability first — defense counsel will argue this prioritization may bias judges toward presumption-based denials and request that IJs be required to consider individualized protection claims simultaneously.

§1208.33(c)(2)(i) instructs IJs to determine "significant possibility" of eligibility under §208.30 — request precise definition of "significant possibility" and uniform criteria to reduce inconsistent application across judges and courts.

§1208.33(c)(2)(ii) tasks IJs with determining whether a covered alien has a "reasonable possibility" of persecution/torture — legal commentators will demand alignment of "reasonable" and "significant" standards across USCIS and EOIR to prevent forum-shopping and confusion.

§1208.33(c)(3) refers cases back to procedures in 208.33(c)(2)(v)(A)-(C) after IJ determination — request that DHS/EOIR publish a clear flowchart and timeline so counsel and pro se litigants can understand next steps and deadlines.

§1208.33(d) treats ancillary spouses/children as rebutting the presumption when the principal would be granted asylum but for the presumption — family advocacy groups will praise this protection but request clarification as to what evidence is required to prove the principal's likely grant "but for" the presumption, and how derivative applicants will be protected from removal in the interim.

Commenters will also request that §1208.33(d) specify whether the rebuttal extends to all derivative family members (e.g., parents, adult dependents) and require continuity of benefits (work authorization, reunification) while claims are adjudicated.
