raw_output:
[P1] The proposed rule’s blanket classification of all devices "intended to treat insomnia and/or anxiety" as Class II fails to account for variation in risk profiles among device designs (e.g., low-energy wearable vs. implantable systems); the agency should allow for device-specific risk-based classification or a path for reclassification petitions.

[P1] Industry commenters will request clarification of whether devices with dual intended uses (e.g., general wellness for sleep improvement and medical treatment for insomnia) are subject to Class II special controls or exempt as low-risk wellness devices.

[P1] Academic stakeholders will argue that the proposed Class II designation for insomnia/anxiety devices contrasts with the stricter Class III for depression (P17) without explanation of the evidence base that justifies disparate classifications for related neurostimulation indications.

[P2] Small manufacturers will comment that the requirement to submit a "detailed summary of clinical testing demonstrating effectiveness" is unduly burdensome for incremental device modifications and request that the FDA define minimum acceptable study designs, sample sizes, endpoints, and statistical thresholds.

[P2] Clinical researchers will request that the rule specify acceptable clinical endpoints for insomnia (e.g., insomnia severity index score reduction, sleep latency measured by polysomnography) and anxiety (e.g., HAM-A, GAD-7) to ensure consistency in submissions.

[P2] Patient advocacy groups will request that the regulation require longer-term effectiveness data (minimum 6–12 months follow-up) rather than only short-term outcomes, to ensure sustained benefit is demonstrated.

[P3] Manufacturers will request explicit guidance on which ISO or FDA-recognized standards satisfy biocompatibility demonstration for skin-contact electrodes and adhesive materials, and whether prior biocompatibility data on equivalent materials can be referenced.

[P3] Hospital procurement officials will ask for clarity on expectations for transient vs. chronic contact materials (duration categorization) and whether devices intended for short-term home use are held to the same biocompatibility tests as implanted devices.

[P4] Device developers will request specification of relevant electrical safety and EMC standards (e.g., IEC 60601-1, IEC 60601-1-2) and whether testing must account for home-use electromagnetic environments (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, mobile phones).

[P4] Legal commenters will raise concern that the phrase "intended use environment" is vague and should be defined (hospital, clinic, home) because required EMC testing and labeling will differ substantially by environment.

[P5] Software vendors will ask the agency to clarify what constitutes "appropriate" software V&V and hazard analysis for firmware-driven stimulation control, including acceptance criteria, cybersecurity testing, and reliance on IEC 62304.

[P5] Cybersecurity experts will request that the rule explicitly require threat modeling and documentation of mitigations for remote-control or wireless-enabled devices, not only generic hazard analysis.

[P6] Manufacturers will request clear tolerances and test methods for each technical parameter (e.g., how to measure "maximum charge" and "maximum energy") and whether device-to-device variability must be demonstrated across production lots.

[P6] Biomedical engineers will call for standardization of measurement protocols (e.g., stimulus measurement instrumentation, calibration) and acceptance thresholds to avoid inconsistent submissions.

[P7] Patient groups will request that labeling requirements include clearer, patient-friendly summaries in addition to the technical details, because detailed clinical summaries and technical parameters may not be accessible to lay users.

[P7] Manufacturers will request confirmation on the acceptable format and length for the required labeling items (A)–(H), and whether digital labeling (online instructions) satisfies the requirement for over-the-counter or prescription home-use devices.

[P8] Clinicians will ask the agency to require that the labeling precisely define the intended patient population (e.g., age ranges, comorbidities, concurrent medications, severity thresholds) and intended use environment (clinical setting vs. unsupervised home use).

[P8] Disability advocates will request that labeling must address suitability and safety for older adults and those with cognitive impairment who commonly have insomnia or anxiety.

[P9] Physician societies will support the requirement that patients be monitored for worsening, but will request specificity on monitoring frequency, responsible parties (prescribing clinician vs. primary care), and criteria that mandate discontinuation and escalation of care.

[P9] Manufacturers will express concern that the warning to "monitor for signs of worsening" could be interpreted as a legal duty for ongoing surveillance and request language that balances safety with realistic expectations for outpatient monitoring.

[P10] Consumer advocacy groups will ask that the labeling not only instruct how to mitigate headaches but also quantify incidence rates observed in clinical trials and provide explicit threshold actions (e.g., stop treatment, seek medical attention if headache persists >24 hours).

[P10] Industry commenters will request flexibility in headache mitigation instructions to accommodate different stimulation parameters across devices, and ask whether standard analgesic guidance may be referenced rather than device-specific protocols.

[P11] Clinicians will ask that dizziness mitigation instructions include fall-risk mitigation strategies, especially for older users, and recommend advising against operating heavy machinery or driving for a specified period after treatment sessions.

[P11] Manufacturers will request evidence-based limits on duration of activity restrictions and whether dizziness warnings should vary by stimulation intensity.

[P12] Patient safety advocates will demand that the "detailed summary of clinical testing" in labeling include absolute numbers and rates of adverse events, stratified by severity and relatedness, rather than vague or aggregated statements.

[P12] Manufacturers will seek guidance on page/word limits and allowable use of hyperlinks for detailed clinical summaries to avoid overlong printed labels while making full details available online.

[P13] Clinician groups will request that instructions for electrode placement be accompanied by visual diagrams and parameter presets validated in clinical studies, and that the rule allow for clinician-programmable settings when supported by training.

[P13] Home-use device makers will request that the rule allow for simplified placement instructions for lay users when validated in usability testing, and ask whether remote clinician supervision can substitute for complex in-person training.

[P14] Technical commenters will ask that required technical parameter reporting be standardized (units, measurement methods, reporting templates) to ensure consistent interpretation across submissions and labeling.

[P14] Innovators will raise concern that publicly disclosing detailed waveform and energy parameters in labeling could facilitate off-label modification of devices by third parties; they may request that highly technical proprietary details be included in restricted submissions rather than consumer-facing labels.

[P15] Hospitals and reprocessors will request specification of accepted validation studies for reusable components (e.g., sterilization methods, number of reuse cycles, impact on electrode conductivity) and whether single-use labels may be required for certain parts.

[P15] Infection control experts will argue that the rule should mandate validated reprocessing protocols meeting recognized standards (e.g., AAMI, ISO 17665) and require instructions for monitoring reprocessing efficacy.

[P16] Manufacturers with legacy 510(k) clearances will object to the burden and short timelines implied by the required 510(k) amendments demonstrating compliance, and will request a phased compliance schedule and grandfathering provisions.

[P16] Legal commenters will request clarification on whether failure to submit the amendment by the effective date will cause immediate market removal or a grace period, and whether corrective action plans will be accepted in lieu of immediate amendment.

[P17] Multiple stakeholders (manufacturers, clinicians, patient advocates) will challenge the automatic assignment of all depression-intended devices to Class III PMA, asking the agency to define criteria by which some depression treatments could qualify for less burdensome pathways based on risk and prior evidence.

[P17] Innovators and venture capital investors will express concern that requiring PMA for depression indications will stifle innovation and small-company entry, and request a de novo or modular pathway for novel non-implant neuromodulation devices with robust safety profiles.

[P18] Manufacturers of legacy devices will request that the PMA/PDP filing deadline referenced be explicitly stated in the regulation and that a reasonable compliance window (e.g., 12–24 months) be provided after final rule publication.

[P18] Legal commentators will request clarification on the interplay between P18 and P16: whether devices requiring 510(k) amendments (P16) are also subject to PMA/PDP deadlines (P18) and how overlapping requirements are reconciled.

[P19] Companies selling devices that have been on the market for many decades will question how the agency will verify commercial distribution "before May 28, 1976" and request documentation standards or alternative evidence to establish eligibility.

[P20] Stakeholders will request that the unspecified date in (b) condition b (to be added 90 days after publication) be clarified now or that the agency commit to a transparent timeline, because the placeholder language creates regulatory uncertainty for manufacturers planning compliance.

[P20] Trade associations will request that the agency define "substantially equivalent" for the purpose of triggering PMA/PDP filing obligations, and whether equivalence to pre-1976 devices requires identical intended use or also includes substantial performance similarity.

[P21] Commenters will request clarification of the phrase "Any other device ... shall have an approved PMA or declared completed PDP in effect before being placed in commercial distribution" as to whether devices in development that plan to launch after the effective date must obtain an IDE, clinical data under an IDE, or can submit well-controlled pivotal studies concurrent with PMA.

[P21] Small device developers will request transitional enforcement discretion or a staggered compliance timeline for new devices in clinical development, arguing that immediate PMA requirements will halt ongoing trials and product launches.

[P2][P12] Independent clinical experts will comment that the rule should require reporting of both efficacy and safety outcomes in a standardized format (e.g., intent-to-treat, per-protocol, adverse event grading) to facilitate meta-analyses and comparative assessments.

[P4][P5] Standards organizations will recommend cross-referencing recognized consensus standards (IEC 60601 series, IEC 62304, ISO 10993) in the rule to reduce ambiguity and testing duplication.

[P1][P17] Mental health advocacy groups will caution that strict regulatory barriers for depression devices (Class III) with comparatively lower barriers for insomnia/anxiety could incentivize manufacturers to label devices for insomnia/anxiety to avoid PMA, potentially leading to misuse and off-label treatment of depression.

[P8][P13] Consumer safety organizations will request that labeling include contraindications (e.g., epilepsy, implanted electrical devices, pregnancy) and explicit instructions on interactions with medications (e.g., benzodiazepines, SSRIs) or comorbid psychiatric conditions.

[P5][P14] Clinical engineers will ask the agency to require that software change control and locked parameter lists be included in submissions and labeling to prevent unauthorized modification that could alter waveform/energy delivery.

[P16][P18] Commenters will request the FDA provide a clear, single compliance roadmap that explains how legacy 510(k) holders, devices from before 1976, and new entrants should proceed—identifying which submissions (510(k) amendment, PMA, PDP) apply in each scenario and timelines for each.

[P12][P15] Public health officials will request that adverse-event summaries in labeling include post-market surveillance commitments and clear instructions for reporting device-related adverse events to FDA (e.g., MedWatch), including phone/website info.

[P6][P14] Researchers will request that the agency specify acceptable tolerances for inter-session variability and cumulative dose limits (e.g., maximum total charge per day/week) to prevent excessive exposure from frequent self-administration.

[P11][P9] Geriatric medicine societies will request that labeling include age-specific safety data and monitoring recommendations for older adults, including fall risk assessments if dizziness is a common adverse event.

[P3][P15] Infection control and dermatology experts will request that the rule require testing for skin irritation and sensitization from reusable electrodes and adhesives across diverse skin types and pigmentation.

[P7][P12] Transparency advocates will request that the required clinical summaries be published in a publicly accessible FDA database (similar to 510(k) summaries) rather than only in device labeling, to aid independent evaluation.

[P17][P21] Legal and policy experts will warn that the PMA requirement for depression devices should be accompanied by clear guidance on the types and sufficiency of clinical evidence (randomized controlled trials, sham controls, blinding) to reduce uncertainty and litigation risk.

[P2][P5] Investigators will request that the FDA accept high-quality real-world evidence and pragmatic trial designs for demonstrating effectiveness in insomnia/anxiety when randomized controlled trials are not feasible, and to specify criteria for such evidence.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement that the physician or nonphysician practitioner be "immediately available" for direct supervision is vague and should be clarified with a precise definition (e.g., maximum response time, proximity, or communication standards) to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P2] The exception stating the supervisor need not be physically present in the room (P2) conflicts with longstanding patient expectations of in-person oversight for invasive procedures and should be rescinded or limited to low-risk procedures only.

[P3] Requiring direct supervision for pulmonary, cardiac, and intensive cardiac rehabilitation per §§ 410.47 and 410.49 (P3) duplicates and potentially conflicts with those sections; CMS should harmonize cross-references or provide a consolidated text to avoid confusion.

[P4] Allowing virtual presence via real-time audio/video (not audio-only) to satisfy direct supervision for rehabilitation services (P4) lacks minimum technical standards (latency, video resolution, redundancy) and should require certified platforms and contingency plans.

[P5] The prohibition on audio-only supervision (P4/P5) is overly restrictive for rural or low-bandwidth settings; commenters request allowance of secure audio-only under narrowly defined emergency or connectivity-failure exceptions.

[P6] The virtual supervision permissions for certain outpatient diagnostic services (P5) should specify documentation requirements (time-stamped recordings or logs) to demonstrate the clinician was virtually present throughout the procedure.

[P7] For virtual supervision permissions (P4/P5), CMS must require patient informed consent that clearly describes the supervisory modality (virtual vs. in-person) and associated risks.

[P8] The allowance for inpatient admissions for historically inpatient-only procedures to qualify for Medicare Part A regardless of expected duration (P6) could incentivize unnecessary inpatient billing; CMS should include utilization safeguards or medical necessity criteria.

[P9] Allowing procedures removed from the inpatient-only list to be paid under Part A according to other rules (P7) may create billing complexity and gaming; request clear examples and billing guidance to prevent improper payment.

[P10] The exemption from certain medical review activities for claims removed from the inpatient-only list until outpatient predominance is determined (P8) risks fraudulent inpatient billing during the transition and should be narrowed or include audit triggers.

[P11] The prohibition on accrediting organizations using criteria that promote or emphasize DEI characteristics for program approval (P9/P28/P29/P32/P34) is unlawful viewpoint discrimination that may conflict with federal non-discrimination obligations and should be withdrawn.

[P12] Banning DEI considerations as accreditation criteria (P9/P28/P29/P32/P34) will harm workforce diversity and patient outcomes; medical societies and minority health advocates will strongly oppose these provisions.

[P13] The restriction that listings in specified publications may not require programs to promote DEI (P10/P11/P30/P31) is ambiguous—commenters request CMS define "promote or emphasize DEI characteristics" to avoid chilling legitimate diversity-related educational content.

[P14] The carve-out that programs would qualify if they would be accredited except for an accreditor's DEI-reliant standard (P13/P33) creates an administrative quagmire requiring proof of "would be accredited" status—CMS should provide a clear evidentiary standard and process.

[P15] Capping ratings at 4 stars for hospitals in the lowest Safety of Care quartile in CY 2026 (P14) is punitive and arbitrary; hospitals with overall high performance in other domains could be unfairly penalized.

[P16] The policy to reduce hospitals in the lowest Safety quartile by one star beginning CY2027 (P15) effectively guarantees downgrades without an appeals process and may disincentivize safety improvement actions; request phased implementation with remediation opportunities.

[P17] CMS's provision to allow hospitals a preview of Star Ratings with at least 30 days (P16/P17) is welcome, but commenters request explicit procedures, timelines, and contacts to ensure meaningful review and correction.

[P18] The preview period should include a formal mechanism for hospitals to submit data corrections that will be reflected in the final published rating, not only an opportunity to "reach out" (P18).

[P19] The narrow list of qualifying reasons for suppressing Star Ratings (P19–P22) is appropriate but CMS should explicitly include major data-reporting vendor outages and state-level reporting changes as valid grounds for suppression.

[P20] CMS should provide an expedited and transparent process for hospitals to petition for suppression when upstream public health responses (e.g., local outbreaks) materially bias measures (P22).

[P21] Allowing CAHs to request withholding of their Star Ratings and public input files during the preview period (P23/P24) is reasonable; commenters request clarity on whether withholding affects public reporting obligations under other statutes.

[P22] The requirement that providers furnish patient service charge schedules and changes on contractor request (P25) imposes significant administrative burden; CMS should limit the frequency of requests and allow electronic submission in standardized formats.

[P23] Requiring providers to furnish median payer-specific negotiated charges by MS-DRG for Medicare Advantage payers (P26) risks violating contractual confidentiality clauses with MA plans; CMS should address confidentiality protections and legal risk.

[P24] The contractor obligation to evaluate charge schedules for usability for payment determinations (P27) needs clear methodological parameters and timelines to prevent arbitrary determinations that affect hospital reimbursement.

[P25] Repetition of prohibitions against DEI-centric accreditation standards in multiple provisions (P9, P28–P34) creates compliance complexity; request consolidation and harmonized definitions to avoid inconsistent application across GME, residency, and fellowship approvals.

[P26] The requirement that physicians consider enumerated safety factors before performing ASC procedures (P35–P42) is appropriate, but CMS must clarify whether these are mandatory checklists documented in the medical record or guidance to inform clinical judgment.

[P27] The safety factors include subjective terms (e.g., "significant safety risk," "major or prolonged invasion") (P36/P39); commenters request clinical definitions or examples to ensure consistent decision-making and avoid liability exposure.

[P28] CMS's process for adding procedures to the ASC list beginning Jan 1, 2026 (P43–P45) requires transparent timelines, stakeholder notice-and-comment opportunities, and publication of supporting safety evidence and utilization data.

[P29] Penalizing ASCs that fail quality reporting standards with a 2.0-percentage-point update reduction through 2026 and switching to CPI-U penalty from 2027 (P46–P48) is confusing; commenters request a single consistent approach and impact estimates.

[P30] The multifactor productivity adjustment plus a 2.0-percentage-point reduction applied to outpatient payment rates starting CY2026 (P57) imposes significant revenue cuts; hospitals and stakeholders request an economic analysis and transitional mitigation.

[P31] The exception exempting hospitals with CCN effective date Jan 2, 2018 or later from the 2.0-percentage-point reduction (P58) creates differential treatment that could be arbitrary; explain rationale and whether this creates incentives to game CCN dates.

[P32] CMS's extraordinary circumstance exception (ECE) policies for ASCs, hospitals, REHs (P50–P53, P59–P63, P66–P69) should include specific documentation thresholds and timelines for decision-making to ensure predictability.

[P33] The proactive ECE authority to grant exceptions to facilities that did not request them (P53/P73-style) is valuable but must include notice to facilities and an appeals process if scopes or durations are disputed.

[P34] The requirement to eliminate the inpatient-only list over three years beginning Jan 1, 2026 (P56) is a major system change; stakeholders request phased clinical and payment impact studies, transition funding, and explicit beneficiary protections.

[P35] The additional payment for Tc-99m doses when at least 50% of Mo-99 was produced in the U.S. (P64) is a positive domestic-manufacturing incentive, but the 50% threshold and documentation standards for provenance should be clearly defined.

[P36] Excluding Tc-99m doses where more than 50% of Mo-99 was processed outside the U.S. from the add-on (P65) could disadvantage hospitals in regions dependent on foreign suppliers; request grandfathering provisions or temporary waivers during supply transitions.

[P37] REH eCQM technical requirements mandating ONC-certified health IT and certified support for all eCQMs (P71–P73) may impose high costs on small REHs; request funding, phased compliance, or flexibility where equivalent interfaces are used.

[P38] The obligation that REHs must use the most recent eCQM specifications (P74) should include an exception window when vendors have not yet implemented updated specifications to avoid forced noncompliance.

[P39] The eCQM requirements applying only when a REH opts to report (P75) create ambiguity for hospitals required by other programs to report; clarify interplay with other reporting mandates.

[P40] The new machine-readable file attestation and CEO identification requirements beginning Jan 1, 2026 (P76–P79) impose legal exposure on executives; request safe-harbor language limiting personal liability and clarifying reasonable diligence standards.

[P41] Requiring hospitals to include Type 2 NPIs and all inpatient facility locations/standalone EDs in the MRF (P80) may be operationally difficult for hospital systems; request phased implementation and machine-readable schema examples.

[P42] The obligation to indicate whether standard charges are dollar amounts or algorithm-based and to provide derivation information and estimated allowed amounts, plus percentile allowed amounts and remittance counts by 2026 (P81–P83), imposes major data and analytics burdens; request technical guidance, de minimis thresholds, and transitional relief.

[P43] The 2025 requirement to encode an estimated allowed amount for algorithm-based standard charges (P82) is unrealistic for many hospitals lacking historical allowed-amount modeling; request CMS-provided calculation methodology or safe harbor.

[P44] Calculating and encoding 10th, median, and 90th percentile allowed amounts and remittance counts beginning Jan 1, 2026 (P83) raises patient privacy and contractual confidentiality concerns with payers; CMS should clarify data aggregation rules and permissible disclosure limits.

[P45] The 35% reduction in civil monetary penalties if a hospital waives its hearing within 30 days (P84) and the loss of future reductions and appeal rights (P85) may coerce waivers; request independent review to ensure hospitals are not pressured into forfeiting appeal rights.

[P46] The interplay between the MRF attestation requirements and anti-fraud statutes (P78) requires clarification to avoid criminal liability for inadvertent data errors; request explicit reliance protection for "good faith" efforts and correction windows.

[P47] The rule is silent on costs to small and rural hospitals of compliance across multiple provisions (MRF, eCQM, reporting, productivity reductions); request a small-hospital regulatory impact analysis and mitigations.

[P48] Legal commenters note potential conflicts between prohibitions on DEI-promoting accreditation criteria and existing federal civil rights statutes and grant conditions; recommend legal review and rescission of those prohibitions.

[P49] Patient advocacy groups object to limiting virtual supervision to non-audio-only options without recognizing accessibility needs for patients with sensory impairments; request accommodations and assistive-technology allowances.

[P50] The rule should include a clear grandfathering process for ongoing clinical trials, pilot programs, and existing contracted services affected by the inpatient-only list elimination (P56), to avoid disruption of patient care and research.

[P1] Industry commenter: The designation of tar acids (shale oil), C6–9 fraction, alkyl phenols, low boiling (PMN P–16–313) as a significant new use under §721.11507(a)(1) is overly broad because it fails to specify volume thresholds or concentration cutoffs that would trigger reporting, creating unnecessary burden for small-quantity manufacturers and processors.

[P1] Environmental NGO: The rule correctly designates tar acids (shale oil) as a significant new use, but EPA should clarify that downstream distributors and users who blend this substance into formulations at >0.1% are also required to report to prevent evasion of notification obligations.

[P2] Municipal wastewater authority: Requiring §721.90 requirements with N=14 for releases of the tar acids substance to water is insufficiently protective because the basis for selecting N=14 is not provided; EPA should justify the N value with ecotoxicity data and consider a lower N to trigger more stringent controls.

[P2] Industry compliance officer: The application of §721.90 with N=14 will impose monitoring and analytical requirements that are impractical for facilities lacking validated methods for this specific substance; EPA should provide guidance on acceptable analytical methods or allow surrogate monitoring approaches.

[P3] Legal analyst: Incorporating Subpart A by reference in §721.11507(b) without explicitly listing the modified or non-applicable Subpart A provisions risks ambiguity; EPA should publish a crosswalk identifying which Subpart A provisions remain effective and which are modified.

[P4] Small manufacturer association: The mandatory recordkeeping per §721.125(a)-(c) and (k) in §721.11507(b)(1) creates excessive retention periods and documentation requirements for SMEs; EPA should exempt manufacturers below a de minimis volume or allow electronic summaries rather than full records.

[P5] Industry safety officer: The application of §721.185 limitations and revocation provisions in §721.11507(b)(2) needs clarification about the process and timeline for revocation of notification privileges—stakeholders need due process and an appeal mechanism.

[P6] Chemical industry: The designation of 2-propenoic acid mixed esters (PMN P–17–333) as a significant new use in §721.11508(a)(1) is acceptable only if EPA clarifies whether incompletely characterized impurities and identifiers in the PMN are treated as part of the reporting obligation.

[P7] Environmental group: For PMN P–17–333, using N=1 for §721.90 water-release triggers (§721.11508(a)(2)(i)) is too lenient; the single-sample/threshold approach does not account for chronic low-level discharges—EPA should set a more protective monitoring frequency.

[P8] Regulatory practitioner: Reapplication of Subpart A in §721.11508(b) without explicit statement about enforcement priorities creates uncertainty; EPA should state whether inspections and enforcement will prioritize particular uses or sectors.

[P9] Trade association: Requiring §721.125(a)-(c) and (k) recordkeeping in §721.11508(b)(1) for PMN P–17–333 should allow centralized recordkeeping for contract manufacturers and toll processors to avoid duplicative burden; EPA should permit a single entity to maintain consolidated records with appropriate access for compliance verification.

[P10] Labor union: The application of §721.185 limitations to notification in §721.11508(b)(2) must ensure protection of workers’ health data confidentiality; EPA should require that revocation actions consider worker safety impacts first, and maintain confidentiality for sensitive business information only where justified.

[P11] Manufacturer: The generic identification for alkane, diisocyanato-(isocyanatoalkyl)- (PMN P–18–320) in §721.11509(a)(1) is too vague—diisocyanates vary widely in reactivity and hazard; EPA should require specification of molecular weight ranges or CAS RN(s) to avoid misapplication.

[P12] Occupational safety NGO: The workplace protection obligations imported by §721.11509(a)(2)(i) are appropriate, but EPA must require medical surveillance and mandatory training frequency for workers exposed to diisocyanates beyond the referenced paragraphs to ensure effective protection.

[P13] Industrial hygiene expert: The requirement in §721.11509(a)(2)(i) to “consider and, where feasible, implement engineering or administrative controls” is vague—EPA should convert “consider” to a concrete obligation to implement engineering controls unless infeasible and define criteria for infeasibility.

[P14] Employer association: The respirator requirement in §721.11509(a)(2)(i) mandating a NIOSH-assigned protection factor of at least 1000 is technically infeasible for most workplaces because few respirators are certified at PF 1000 and such equipment imposes excessive cost and fit-testing burdens; EPA should permit lower protection factors with combination controls or PAPR alternatives.

[P15] Chemical formulators: The cross-reference to §721.80(o) in §721.11509(a)(2)(ii) is ambiguous about whether consumer uses in finished articles are covered; EPA should specify whether finished goods containing trace levels of this diisocyanate are subject to §721.80(o) obligations.

[P16] Regulatory counsel: Applying Subpart A in §721.11509(b) except as modified without identifying modifications creates legal uncertainty; EPA should publish the specific Subpart A provisions that are modified for clarity and legal defensibility.

[P17] Manufacturer: Requiring expanded recordkeeping per §721.125(a)-(e), (i), and (k) in §721.11509(b)(1) for PMN P–18–320 will impose duplicative obligations on companies already subject to OSHA and state reporting systems; EPA should harmonize retention periods and content with existing OSHA requirements.

[P18] Environmental law center: The invocation of §721.185 in §721.11509(b)(2) must be accompanied by explicit timelines for limitation or revocation actions and clear criteria for when EPA will exercise these powers to satisfy due process concerns.

[P19] Polymer producer: The listing of phenol, polymer with formaldehyde... sodium salts (PMN P–?) in §721.11510(a)(1) as a significant new use without specifying molecular weight distribution or degree of substitution makes compliance identification impracticable—EPA should add physicochemical boundaries.

[P20] Water quality NGO: Using N=4 in §721.11510(a)(2)(i) for water-release monitoring is inadequate to detect episodic discharges that could harm aquatic life; EPA should set N based on mass flux or frequency-based sampling rather than a fixed N value.

[P21] Industry association: Subpart A application in §721.11510(b) should explicitly state that confidential business information (CBI) redactions allowed under Subpart A apply equally to data elements required under this section to protect proprietary process information.

[P22] Trade compliance manager: The §721.125(a)-(c) and (k) recordkeeping requirement in §721.11510(b)(1) should permit electronic recordkeeping standards (timestamped, tamper-evident) rather than paper only to reflect modern practices.

[P23] Public health researcher: The §721.185 applicability in §721.11510(b)(2) requires transparency—EPA must publish summaries of any limitations/revocations and the public-health rationale while protecting legitimate CBI.

[P24] Medical devices manufacturer: Designating N-Alkyl heteromonocyclic diphenolamide polymer (PMN in §721.11511) as a significant new use particularly for hollow fiber membrane applications (§721.11511(a)(2)(i)) could impede medical device development—EPA should exempt medical-grade polymer use where material is bound into final sterilizable membranes and not bioavailable.

[P25] Industrial user: The prohibition on uses other than as a polymer in hollow fiber membrane manufacture being considered significant new uses (§721.11511(a)(2)(i)) is unclear about intermediate processing steps—EPA should clarify whether polymer modification, coating, or compounding for membrane fabrication are treated as covered uses.

[P26] Legal expert: The cross-reference to §721.1725(b)(1) in §721.11511(b)(3) for determinations about whether a use falls under (a)(2)(ii) requires EPA to delineate the adjudicative process and timelines for such determinations to avoid unpredictability for manufacturers.

[P27] Small business: The §721.125(a)-(c) and (i) recordkeeping requirement in §721.11511(b)(1) may force small processors to retain proprietary supplier information indefinitely; EPA should limit retention to a reasonable period (e.g., 5 years) and allow redaction of extraneous supplier details.

[P28] Worker advocacy group: The application of §721.185 to notification requirements in §721.11511(b)(2) must ensure that revocations do not leave workers without protections; EPA should require contingency measures for worker safety during any procedural revocation.

[P29] Resin manufacturer: Listing 1,3,5-triazine trione tri-(oxiranylpropyl) (PMN P–20–38) as a subject under §721.11512(a)(1) without specifying epoxy equivalent weight or crosslink density makes compliance and hazard assessment impractical; EPA should provide technical identification criteria.

[P30] Occupational health expert: Designating any manufacture, processing, or use resulting in inhalation exposure as a significant new use (§721.11512(a)(2)(i)) is appropriate, but EPA should specify exposure concentration thresholds (e.g., airborne mg/m3) that trigger reporting to reduce ambiguity.

[P31] Environmental chemist: Using N=5 for water-release requirements in §721.11512(a)(2)(ii) may not align with environmental fate of epoxy-containing triazines; EPA should justify N with hydrolysis/biodegradation half-life data and consider downstream bioaccumulation.

[P32] Quality systems auditor: Applying §721.125(a)-(c), (i), and (k) recordkeeping in §721.11512(b)(1) should include an allowance for audits in which third-party auditors maintain records to avoid duplication, with EPA-accepted attestations from auditors.

[P33] Local emergency planner: The potential inhalation-triggered reporting in §721.11512(a)(2)(i) requires coordination with Local Emergency Planning Committees (LEPCs); EPA should require immediate notification to LEPCs for uses that create inhalation exposure risks above defined thresholds.

[P34] Coatings manufacturer: The generic identification of 2-Propenoic acid, cycloalkyl ester (PMN P–20–40) in §721.11513(a)(1) lacks detail on monomer composition and residual monomer limits—EPA should define allowable residual monomer thresholds to determine when product shipments must be reported.

[P35] Environmental regulator: For PMN P–20–40, setting N=7 for water-release (§721.11513(a)(2)(i)) seems arbitrary; EPA should align N with monitoring frequency standards used under NPDES permits and provide technical justification.

[P36] Trade association: Requiring §721.125(a)-(c) and (k) recordkeeping in §721.11513(b)(1) across multiple PMNs increases administrative burden—EPA should permit a single integrated TSCA compliance file covering multiple substances with cross-references to reduce duplication.

[P37] Public interest attorney: The repeated incorporation of §721.185 across sections (§721.11507(b)(2), .11508(b)(2), .11509(b)(2), etc.) demands that EPA define objective criteria for limitation/revocation (e.g., imminent hazard, noncompliance), timelines for action, and procedural safeguards to satisfy APA requirements.

[P38] Analytical laboratory: Many provisions require release-to-water monitoring with different Ns (1,4,5,7,14); EPA should provide validated analytical methods and detection limits for each substance and clarify sample matrix and holding time requirements to ensure practical compliance.

[P39] State regulator: EPA should clarify preemption interplay—whether state-level reporting or more stringent measures related to these PMNs remain enforceable and how §721 subpart A enforcement coordinates with state authorities.

[P40] Consumer product safety advocate: For substances where consumer activities are captured (e.g., §721.11509 referencing §721.80(o) and §721.11511 referencing §721.80(s)), EPA must require clear labeling and consumer safety information requirements when products containing these substances enter commerce.

[P41] Confidential business information counsel: The rule should clarify the process and standards for asserting CBI for chemical identity or use information required under these sections, including the evidentiary standard for trade secret claims and duration of protection.

[P42] Environmental justice group: EPA must assess and disclose the cumulative impacts of designating multiple PMNs in similar geographic regions (e.g., wastewater discharges with Ns of 4,5,7,14) on frontline communities and propose mitigation measures if burdens concentrate.

[P43] Transportation industry: The rule should state whether manifesting, labeling, or DOT hazardous materials requirements for transporting these PMNs are affected by their designation as significant new uses, to avoid conflicting compliance obligations.

[P1] The proposal to remove and reserve paragraph (t) of §1037.150 lacks an explanation of the regulatory effect and creates uncertainty for stakeholders who rely on the current text; EPA should provide the deleted text and rationale or retain the paragraph until a replacement is finalized.

[P1] Removing paragraph (t) without cross-referencing where any substantive requirements previously located in (t) are being relocated will likely cause noncompliance; EPA should publish a redline showing all consequential edits and references.

[P1] State and local agencies that reference §1037.150(t) in enforcement and permitting documents will need time to amend their regulations and should be given transitional guidance and at least 180 days before the change becomes effective.

[P2] Simply reserving §1037.150(t) (leaving it blank) is confusing and may be interpreted as an intention to add new substantive content later; EPA should either delete the paragraph number entirely or include a note explaining the reservation purpose.

[P2] Environmental advocacy groups will challenge the reservation as potentially hiding removal of protections; EPA should explain whether any obligations that formerly appeared under (t) are being relaxed, and if so justify the public-health impacts.

[P3] Removing §1037.635 in its entirety may eliminate critical compliance, reporting, or averaging provisions that regulated parties currently rely upon; EPA must provide the full text of §1037.635 and an analysis of impacts from its removal.

[P3] Manufacturers and fleet operators need assurance that removing §1037.635 does not eliminate any existing compliance flexibilities; EPA should clarify whether obligations previously implemented through §1037.635 will be moved elsewhere or permanently rescinded.

[P3] Legal commenters will flag potential statutory conflicts if §1037.635 removal undermines the Agency’s enforcement authority under the Clean Air Act; EPA should provide legal justification and demonstrate consistency with the Act.

[P4] Removing the definitions of "glider kit" and "glider vehicle" from §1037.801 will create ambiguity for manufacturers, rebuilders, and certifiers who currently rely on those terms to determine applicability of emissions standards; EPA should explain how affected parties should classify such vehicles after the change.

[P4] Revising "manufacturer" and "new motor vehicle" definitions without transitional provisions risks reclassifying many entities (e.g., small rebuilders, remanufacturers) as manufacturers subject to certification costs; EPA should include grandfathering or small-business exemptions.

[P4] Industry commenters will be concerned that deleting "glider" definitions is a backdoor ban on glider vehicles or a shift in liability; EPA must quantify the regulatory and economic impacts on businesses that build or operate glider-derivative trucks.

[P5] Deleting the "glider kit" definition will leave suppliers and purchasers uncertain whether glider kits remain subject to part 1037 requirements; EPA should state explicitly whether previously regulated glider kits are now treated as aftermarket parts, new vehicles, or something else.

[P5] Repair and aftermarket associations will request a clear definition or guidance document so that parts suppliers know when a kit triggers vehicle certification obligations, to avoid chilling commerce in replacement components.

[P6] Deleting the "glider vehicle" definition may inadvertently classify rebuilt trucks as new motor vehicles, imposing certification and labeling obligations that are infeasible and costly; EPA must clarify the regulatory treatment of rebuilt or remanufactured vehicles.

[P6] Legal experts will argue that removal of the "glider vehicle" definition could disrupt ongoing enforcement and litigation by changing the regulatory scope retroactively; EPA should clarify effective dates and non-retroactivity.

[P7] The proposed new "Manufacturer" definition references section 216(1) of the Act but truncates the illustrative examples; EPA should publish the full proposed text and explain any substantive change from current regulatory practice (e.g., who is deemed a manufacturer for rebuilt vehicles).

[P7] Small businesses and conversion-vehicle upfitters will likely be reclassified as manufacturers under the revised definition and thus face expensive certification burdens; EPA should perform and publish a Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act (SBREFA) analysis.

[P7] States and enforcement agencies need clarity whether importers, final-stage manufacturers, and remanufacturers are now unambiguously included; EPA should provide examples and compliance guidance.

[P8] The revised "New motor vehicle" definition that "generally means a motor vehicle meeting ..." appears truncated and ambiguous; EPA must supply the full text and explain whether rebuilt, remanufactured, or glider vehicles qualify as new motor vehicles under the new definition.

[P8] If the change expands the universe of "new motor vehicle," manufacturers of replacement engines and remanufacturers could be required to certify vehicles never previously subject to that status; EPA should provide cost estimates and a compliance timeline.

[P8] Consumer and trade groups will seek confirmation that existing title, registration, and warranty practices are not disrupted for vehicles currently sold as used or rebuilt; EPA should coordinate with DOT and state DMVs.

[P9] Revising §1068.120(f)(5) without clarifying the scope of "the standard-setting part" creates uncertainty about which programs (e.g., 1037, 86, 40 CFR parts) may impose additional restrictions when used engines are installed to repower equipment; EPA should list the parts that may impose such restrictions.

[P9] Manufacturers and repowerers need clear notice of what "additional restrictions" could include (e.g., engine model-year limitations, emissions certification, labeling, warranty requirements); EPA should provide an illustrative list or guidance.

[P9] The change may permit states or program parts to impose inconsistent restrictions on used-engine repower applications, creating multi-jurisdictional compliance burdens; EPA should require harmonization or preemption guidance.

[P10] Allowing the standard-setting part to impose further restrictions on used-engine repower activity could effectively ban cost-effective repowering using well-maintained used engines, harming operators of nonroad equipment who rely on repower cost savings; EPA should require a demonstration of environmental necessity before such restrictions are adopted.

[P10] Environmental NGOs may support stricter limits on repowering with used engines to prevent high-emitting engines from being reintroduced, but request EPA articulate criteria for when additional restrictions are justified (e.g., lifecycle emissions analysis, age/mileage thresholds).

[P10] The permissive language ("may apply") is overly broad and could be used to impose retroactive restrictions; stakeholders ask EPA to specify procedural safeguards, notice-and-comment requirements, and non-retroactivity clauses before restrictions are applied.

[P10] Repair shops and independent remanufacturers urge EPA to allow used-engine repowers with documentation, inspections, and tamper-evident labeling as an alternative to burdensome restrictions, preserving cost-effective compliance pathways.

[P4/P7] Several commenters will request consolidated examples showing how the revised "manufacturer" and "new motor vehicle" definitions apply to common scenarios (glider trucks, remanufactured chassis, engine swaps) to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P3/P1] Lawyers will request the administrative record and legal rationale for removal of §1037.635 and §1037.150(t), including cost-benefit analysis and statutory authority, to evaluate potential challenges under the Administrative Procedure Act.

[P5/P6] Historic-vehicle owners and hobbyist associations will request an exemption or explicit carve-out for specialty and low-volume builders that rely on glider kits or reconstructed vehicles, arguing that removal of definitions could jeopardize classic-vehicle restoration activities.

[P8/P9] State environmental agencies ask EPA to clarify whether the changes alter state implementation responsibilities under cooperative federalism and whether states must amend their SIPs or enforcement manuals.

[P7] Commenters will demand that EPA include a transitional compliance period and clear recordkeeping requirements if the "Manufacturer" definition expands obligations to a new set of entities, to allow businesses to budget for testing, certification, and administrative costs.

[P1] The comment due date of June 29, 2018 is unreasonably short and does not provide adequate time for operators and suppliers to analyze the technical service bulletin and prepare informed comments; extend the comment period by at least 60–90 days.

[P1] Small operators and private owners were not given specific direct notice; FAA should publish additional targeted outreach and extend the comment deadline to ensure broad participation.

[P2] The applicability is overly broad by including all 737–600/700/700C/800/900/900ER airplanes without limiting by configuration, serial number ranges, or installed horizontal stabilizer PN/SN — request clarity on whether previously modified or retrofitted airplanes are included.

[P2] The applicability should explicitly exclude airplanes that have had prior modification kits or replacement stabilizers installed per Boeing-approved Service Bulletins that already address the subject area; otherwise redundant actions and costs will occur.

[P3] The compliance provision lacks specificity about exactly which "specified times" apply to each affected configuration — request FAA to publish a clear table mapping affected serial numbers/configurations to specific compliance intervals.

[P4] Requiring all actions labeled 'RC' in the Boeing Alert Service Bulletin without FAA-owned alternate text gives Boeing de facto regulatory authority; request FAA to incorporate by reference only the mandatory text or reissue AD with FAA-determined mandatory actions.

[P4] Operators need an explicit list of which actions in the Boeing Alert Service Bulletin are RC; the AD should include an appendix or clear identification so operators can track mandatory tasks and costs.

[P5] Using the AD's effective date rather than the Service Bulletin revision date creates ambiguity for operators who began work using Revision 1 — FAA should clarify retrospective applicability and whether work begun before the AD effective date but after the SB revision date is compliant.

[P6] Requiring AMOC approval when the service bulletin instructs to "contact Boeing" for RC items effectively limits operators to a single OEM-approved solution; FAA should allow alternative approved methods from qualified repair stations or DERs when Boeing cannot respond in a timely manner.

[P6] The requirement that repairs specified as "contact Boeing" be approved through the AD AMOC process will create significant operational delays; FAA should permit use of Boeing ODA approvals per paragraph (k)(3) without separate FAA AMOC when the ODA approval records compliance to the airplane certification basis.

[P7] The prohibition on installing a horizontal stabilizer as of the AD effective date is overly restrictive and could ground aircraft awaiting parts; FAA should add a narrow grace period or permit installation with temporary/contingent inspection acceptance pending completion of required inspections.

[P7] The AD does not address whether installers, lessors, or MROs can be civilly liable under the prohibition if they install parts based on incomplete documentation — FAA should clarify legal liabilities and who bears responsibility to verify the inspection status before installation.

[P8] Allowing installation only if the identification plate inspection finds no affected serial number may be logistically impractical when plates are missing, illegible, or painted over; FAA should permit acceptable alternate means (e.g., traceable paperwork or supplier records) to verify part identity.

[P8] The inspection procedure referenced ('Part 2: Horizontal Stabilizer Identification Plate Inspection') must be incorporated by reference or summarized in the AD; otherwise operators cannot determine compliance criteria from the AD alone.

[P9] Permitting installation even if an affected serial number is found only if follow-on actions are completed presumes immediate availability of repair resources; FAA should require that parts be quarantined and traceable until inspections and corrective actions are done to prevent inadvertent installation.

[P9] The AD should specify whether a stabilizer found with an affected SN but with completed corrective actions retains serviceability limits or additional operational restrictions (e.g., flight-cycle limits) — current text is silent.

[P10] Requiring HFEC initial and repetitive inspections within the compliance times specified in paragraph (g) lacks explicit intervals; FAA should specify initial inspection thresholds in flight hours/cycles and repetitive intervals to ensure uniform compliance.

[P10] HFEC inspections necessitate specialized tooling and qualified personnel; FAA should allow a reasonable lead time for operators to procure equipment and train technicians before the compliance deadlines become mandatory.

[P11] The statement that all applicable corrective actions must be performed within the compliance times of paragraph (g) fails to define "applicable" — operators need objective criteria for applicability to avoid inconsistent interpretations by inspectors.

[P11] Some corrective actions may require major structural repair or part replacement not possible within short compliance windows; FAA should allow phased compliance or temporary operational limitations until permanent repairs can be scheduled.

[P12] The credit paragraph for previous actions references actions done under earlier service bulletin versions but does not list which specific tasks qualify; FAA should provide a clear equivalency table so operators can unambiguously claim credit.

[P12] The "credit for previous actions" should be extended to work performed under equivalent repairs approved via Boeing ODA or DER-approved repair methods, not only those performed strictly under the prior Boeing SB wording.

[P13] Centralizing AMOC approval authority in the Seattle ACO Manager may create processing bottlenecks for operators outside the region; FAA should permit regional offices to accept and act on AMOC requests when appropriate.

[P14] Requiring AMOC requests to go through the principal inspector or local FSDO may delay time-sensitive repairs; consider allowing direct submission to the Seattle ACO with notification to the principal inspector to expedite approvals.

[P15] The instruction to send information directly to the certification office manager per paragraph (l)(1) lacks a named contact in the AD; FAA should include the contact name, mailing address, and phone number to avoid misrouting.

[P16] Emailing AMOC requests to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov may raise security and record retention concerns — FAA should allow secure web portal submission or provide guidance on acceptable file formats and encryption for proprietary data.

[P17] The requirement to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC is redundant where the AMOC approval already includes operational conditions; FAA should define the required timing and method of notification (written/email) to create an auditable trail.

[P18] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved methods as AMOCs is appropriate, but the AD should require that Boeing ODA approvals be provided to the FAA concurrently and be retained in the aircraft maintenance records.

[P19] Requiring that proposed repairs meet the airplane's certification basis may be impossible to demonstrate practically for older modifications or when the certification basis is complex; FAA should provide guidance on acceptable substantiation and documentation for equivalency.

[P20] The requirement that AMOC approvals explicitly reference this AD is reasonable, but FAA should provide an AMOC template to ensure uniformity and avoid administrative rejection for clerical omissions.

[P21] Accepting previously approved AMOCs for AD 2016–13–16 may create safety gaps if those AMOCs were tailored to the prior AD's scope; FAA should require a brief re-validation statement for each prior AMOC confirming applicability to the new AD.

[P22] Mandating that all RC steps and substeps (including figures) be performed restricts operator flexibility for minor procedural deviations (e.g., tooling differences); FAA should provide a process for minor deviation approvals that do not require full AMOC complexity.

[P22] The AD must identify which specific figures are normative; as-printed figure numbering in the Boeing service bulletin may change, so the AD should include exact figure identifiers or incorporate the relevant pages.

[P23] The 'RC Exempt' exception should be clearly marked in the service bulletin version incorporated by reference; otherwise, operators may mistakenly treat exempt steps as RC and incur unnecessary costs.

[P24] Requiring an AMOC for any deviation to RC steps is appropriate for safety-critical steps but will be burdensome for trivial deviations (e.g., alternate fastener torque tool); FAA should define a threshold for what constitutes a deviation requiring AMOC versus standard maintenance judgment.

[P25] Allowing deviation from non-RC steps under an operator’s maintenance program is appropriate, but the AD should require that the operator document the rationale and concurrence of the principal inspector in the aircraft maintenance records for auditability.

[P25] The AD should explicitly state whether the operator's maintenance/inspection program deviations must be compliant with the Continuous Airworthiness Maintenance Program (CAMP) or can be temporary deviations pending permanent compliance.

[General] The AD references Boeing Alert Service Bulletin 737–55A1097, Revision 1 (Sept 20, 2017) but does not make that SB available in the docket; FAA should either incorporate the relevant mandatory text into the AD or ensure the SB is available to the public without subscription.

[Legal] Several provisions delegate substantive technical decisions to Boeing (e.g., "contact Boeing" RC items); commenters will challenge whether this delegation violates the Administrative Procedure Act by outsourcing rulemaking authority without adequate FAA oversight.

[Economic] The AD lacks a Regulatory Flexibility Analysis estimating costs to small entities and individual owners, including inspection, HFEC tooling, downtime, and potential part quarantines — FAA should publish a full economic impact assessment.

[Safety] The AD does not provide a risk-based prioritization for inspections by flight hours/cycles or phase of operation — suggest FAA add prioritized compliance windows for high-utilization aircraft to mitigate immediate safety risks.

[Implementation] Operators need an FAA-approved training plan or guidance for HFEC inspection acceptability and technician qualification; request FAA to include minimum qualification standards for personnel performing the inspections.

[Recordkeeping] The AD should require that completion of the RC steps and any AMOC approvals be recorded in the aircraft maintenance records with specific entries (date, signature, method used, and reference to AMOC) to ensure traceability during audits.
