raw_output:
[P1] The 180-day phase-out for consumer methylene chloride paint removers is unworkably short for manufacturers, distributors, and retailers to deplete inventories and reformulate products; request extension to at least 12–24 months or phased sell-through allowances.

[P1] Consumer advocacy groups will claim the prohibition is necessary and should be expanded to include any online marketplace sales exemptions to prevent continued consumer access.

[P2] Industry commenters will assert that the 180-day ban on manufacture/processing/distribution for commercial uses fails to account for existing long-term contractual obligations and inventory held by professional refinishers; ask for a sell-through or exemption period for existing contracts.

[P2] Legal experts will argue the rule must clarify liability for distributors who unknowingly sell to end-users engaged in prohibited commercial paint removal, and request a due-diligence safe harbor for ordinary commercial distributors who rely on purchaser declarations.

[P3] Military and defense contractors will support the narrow exception for commercial furniture stripping and critical military components but request explicit definitions of “commercial furniture stripping” and “critical corrosion-sensitive components” to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P3] Environmental NGOs will object to the military exception as too broad and urge that any exception be limited, time-limited, and subject to EPA reporting and independent oversight to prevent routine circumvention.

[P4] Defense contractors and military maintenance stakeholders will strongly object to the 10-year sunset of the exception, arguing it undermines long-term maintenance planning (airframe life cycles exceed 10 years) and request a permanent DOD exemption with conditions or a longer phase-out tied to validated alternatives.

[P4] Public health advocates will support the 10-year limitation removing military exceptions and request that the phase-out occur sooner than 10 years with mandatory transition plans for DOD to adopt safer alternatives.

[P5] Chemical distributors will challenge the prohibition on distributing methylene chloride in containers under 55 gallons as disruptive to legitimate commercial users who require smaller packaged volumes for safe handling; request allowance of smaller industrial pack sizes (e.g., 5–30 gallons) with certification and recordkeeping.

[P5] Labor unions and worker-safety groups will support the 55-gallon minimum distribution prohibition as a measure reducing small-quantity commercial use and accidental worker exposures, but ask for explicit enforcement guidance to prevent illicit small-batch repackaging.

[P6] DOD contractors will request that the DOD-specific 5-gallon minimum exception also permit smaller packaged sizes (e.g., 1–2.5 gallons) when specific maintenance tasks require them, coupled with stringent chain-of-custody controls.

[P6] Transparency advocates will demand that EPA require public reporting of volumes and recipients of DOD-exempt 5-gallon distributions to ensure the exception is not misused.

[P7] Employers and trade associations will argue that the 270-day delay for prohibition on commercial use is too short to implement alternative processes and procure compliant equipment; request longer compliance timelines or phased sector-specific compliance dates.

[P7] Worker-safety groups will claim the 270-day commercial-use prohibition is insufficiently protective and recommend accelerating the ban and increasing outreach to small businesses to prevent continued hazardous exposures.

[P8] Furniture-restoration small businesses will assert the exemption for commercial furniture stripping is vague and could create unfair market advantages; request explicit eligibility criteria, registration, or permit system for businesses claiming the exemption.

[P8] Local government hazardous-waste officials will request clarity on waste disposal and transport obligations for commercial furniture stripping operations that continue using methylene chloride under the exemption.

[P9] Military maintenance organizations will object to the final removal of the commercial-use exception after 10 years, asserting it will disrupt maintenance schedules and requesting either permanent limited exemptions or a transition fund for alternative process development.

[P9] Regulatory lawyers will note the 10-year removal of exceptions requires clear grandfathering language for works-in-progress and ask EPA to specify treatment of materials procured before the 10-year cutoff.

[P10] DOD and contractor commenters will request detailed technical specifications and permitted engineering controls referenced in § 751.107(d), arguing the current summary is insufficiently prescriptive to ensure safe, consistent implementation.

[P10] Public-interest law groups will demand that the “specified restrictions” include mandatory reporting, third-party audits, and worker protection measures to ensure the exception does not create undue risks.

[P11] Military bases and private maintenance yards will request explicit lists of acceptable “DOD-controlled” and “DOD-contractor” locations, including standards for contractor facilities (e.g., security, ventilation, training), and propose a site approval process.

[P11] Small defense subcontractors will claim that requiring use only at DOD-controlled or DOD-contractor locations will impose logistical burdens and increased costs; request allowance for mobile, certified containment units meeting EPA-approved standards.

[P12] Manufacturers and distributors will complain that the 45‑day deadline to provide written downstream notifications is impractically short for supply chains, and suggest at least 90 days and model notification language to ensure compliance.

[P12] Trade associations will request safe harbor language that downstream notifications delivered via standard business communication channels (e.g., email, EDI) qualify, and seek clarity on who constitutes “downstream companies” (distributors, retailers, end-users).

[P13] Companies will point out that requiring retention of documentation at company headquarters may be infeasible for decentralized distributors and ask that records be permitted to be maintained electronically at any accessible location with remote retrieval.

[P13] Privacy advocates will request redaction guidance for contact information in records when submissions are later provided to EPA, to balance transparency and privacy concerns.

[P14] Distributors will request specification about what constitutes adequate “contact” information (e.g., phone, email, authorized representative) and allow substitute identifiers (customer ID numbers) if included in company records.

[P14] Enforcement attorneys will ask EPA to clarify whether failure to collect recipient contact information triggers strict liability or if good-faith efforts suffice.

[P15] Industry commenters will request standardized downstream notification templates be provided by EPA to reduce compliance costs and disputes about sufficiency of the notification retained.

[P15] Worker-safety advocates will ask EPA to require distributors to certify that notifications include clear, plain-language hazard information, not just regulatory citations.

[P16] Manufacturers will ask for clarity on the granularity of “amount shipped” — whether it must be reported per SKU, batch, weight vs. volume, and how bulk shipments (railcar/bulk tanker) are to be recorded.

[P16] Small businesses will request aggregation allowances (monthly totals) rather than per-shipment records to reduce administrative burden.

[P17] Businesses will request extension of the 3-year records-retention requirement to match other federal recordkeeping cycles (e.g., 5 years) or harmonize with OSHA practices, or alternatively reduce it to 2 years if burdensome.

[P17] Compliance officers will ask whether the 3-year retention period runs from date of shipment or date of sale to end-user and request explicit examples.

[P18] Consumer-product manufacturers will object to Option 1's outright ban on NMP for consumer paint removal after 180 days and request a workable sell-through period and exemptions for small-volume specialty formulations.

[P18] Public-health organizations will support the Option 1 prohibition, arguing NMP poses reproductive and other serious risks and that a 180-day ban is justified.

[P19] Industry will request harmonization between the NMP commercial prohibition timelines and the methylene chloride provisions to avoid business confusion and compliance complexity.

[P19] Defense commenters will request that the same DOD exception provided for methylene chloride be explicitly mirrored for NMP commercial prohibitions and that definitions align cross-subpart.

[P20] Navy and Air Force depot maintainers will request a clear, narrow definition of “critical corrosion-sensitive components” and criteria for inclusion to prevent overbroad application of the military exemption.

[P20] Environmental groups will request documentation and reporting obligations for any NMP use under the military exception to ensure accountability and encourage transition to alternatives.

[P21] Contractors will challenge the 10-year prohibition on NMP manufacture/processing/distribution for critical components as too disruptive to long-term maintenance contracts and request a longer transition period or exemptions tied to availability of validated alternatives.

[P21] Health advocates will argue the 10-year limit should be shortened and that EPA should require DOD to submit transition plans within 1 year.

[P22] Chemical suppliers will object to the prohibition on distribution of NMP in containers under 55 gallons as commercially restrictive and ask that DOD and other verified industrial users be permitted to receive smaller containers with certified controls.

[P22] Worker and public safety groups will support the 55-gallon minimum as a deterrent to small-scale use and request anti-diversion monitoring.

[P23] DOD contractors will support the 5-gallon DOD exception but request that EPA allow the Department to authorize sub‑contractors to receive smaller packages under accountable chain-of-custody procedures.

[P23] Transparency advocates will ask for quarterly public reporting on volumes distributed under the DOD 5-gallon exception.

[P24] Commercial users will argue that the 270-day commercial-use prohibition for NMP does not provide sufficient time to implement the extensive worker protection programs required under Option 2, and request longer lead times or sector-specific phase-ins.

[P24] Worker-safety organizations will insist the 270-day timeframe is adequate and emphasize the need for early enforcement to protect workers.

[P25] Furniture-restoration small businesses will request clarity whether the commercial furniture stripping exception applies to artisan/restoration shops and whether registration or training is required to qualify.

[P25] Military maintenance commenters will request retention of the exception but with mandated PPE and monitoring requirements for users performing exempted NMP work.

[P26] Defense maintenance stakeholders will object to the 10-year commercial-use prohibition for critical components and request a schedule tied to validated alternative performance data to avoid aircraft downtime.

[P26] Legal commenters will ask whether equipment and materials procured before the 10-year cutoff may be used until exhaustion and request explicit grandfathering language.

[P27] DOD and contractor commenters will demand detailed, feasible operational restrictions in § 751.207(d) (e.g., ventilation rates, containment, waste handling), not just general statements, to ensure consistent compliance.

[P27] Labor and safety advocates will insist the restrictions include mandatory exposure monitoring, medical surveillance, and third-party audits.

[P28] Contractors will request ability to use certified off-site contractor facilities for NMP-based paint removal on military components and seek definition of acceptable DOD-contractor locations and approval process.

[P28] Union representatives will ask for mandatory worker-training standards and recordkeeping at approved DOD-contractor locations.

[P29] NMP manufacturers and distributors will reiterate that the 45-day notification window is too short and ask for model language and acceptance of electronic notice methods and batch-level notices.

[P29] Occupational health groups will request that downstream notifications must explicitly include worker-protection requirements and label warnings, not just regulatory citations.

[P30] Distributors will request that NMP record retention be permitted in electronic format off-site, and that small businesses be allowed aggregated reporting to reduce burden.

[P30] Regulatory compliance consultants will ask EPA to define “company headquarters” (domestic only? foreign?) and allow records to be stored at U.S.-based corporate agents.

[P31] Commenters will seek clarity whether recipient contact information must include individual names and direct telephone numbers or whether business contact centers suffice.

[P31] Privacy and data-security groups will ask EPA to provide guidance on protecting personally identifiable information included in retained records.

[P32] Industry will ask that copies of downstream notifications accepted for recordkeeping include stamped proof of delivery or date emailed to corroborate compliance.

[P32] Worker advocates will request that proof-of-notification records be made available to employees and labor representatives upon request.

[P33] Businesses will request guidance on acceptable units for “amount shipped” (e.g., gallons, liters, kilograms) and whether cumulative monthly totals suffice.

[P33] Enforcement agencies will request that EPA require shipment-level records for traceability in case of noncompliant distribution.

[P34] Companies will ask that the 3-year retention period align with statute of limitations for enforcement actions or be extended to 5 years to match other regulatory regimes.

[P34] Legal commenters will request clarity about retention when businesses go out of business, merge, or are acquired.

[P35] Under Option 2, chemical manufacturers will strongly oppose the outright ban on formulations >35% NMP after 180 days, arguing it is technically infeasible for many applications and request higher threshold or phased concentration-based compliance.

[P35] Health advocacy groups will argue the 35% cutoff is arbitrary and should be lower or replaced with a hazard‑based approach; alternatively, they will support the concentration cap as protective.

[P36] DOD and contractors will request the DOD-destined and contractor-use-only exceptions be broader to account for classified or logistics-sensitive projects, and ask for streamlined approval to expedite deliveries.

[P36] Transparency advocates will insist that any DOD exception require public reporting and independent verification that product use is genuinely limited to DOD projects.

[P37] Processors and employers will object to the glove-testing requirement for each distinct NMP formulation as unduly burdensome and costly, and request a tiered regime allowing acceptable glove types validated by manufacturers or certified third parties instead of per-formulation testing.

[P37] Occupational safety professionals will support glove testing but ask EPA to specify acceptable testing standards and accredited laboratories to avoid inconsistent results.

[P38] Employers will ask EPA to specify acceptable test methods and pass/fail criteria for demonstrating glove imperviousness and whether supplier test data are sufficient evidence.

[P38] Legal commenters will request shared liability language if employers rely on manufacturer/supplier glove data that later prove inadequate.

[P39] Employers will request guidance on how to simulate “expected exposure conditions” for glove testing (e.g., contact duration, temperature, solvents mixtures), and propose EPA-provided scenarios.

[P39] Safety consultants will ask for clarity whether worst-case solvent mixtures must be tested or only the product formulation as supplied.

[P40] Manufacturers will request explicit label size, font, and placement requirements and allow multi-lingual options; ask whether electronic labeling (QR codes) is permissible.

[P40] Consumer advocates will insist labels be clear, prominent, and include pictograms, not regulations-only text.

[P41] Employers will express concern that requiring label statements that commercial users must establish dermal and respiratory protection programs could create legal exposure for distributors; request model label language and conformity safe harbor.

[P41] Occupational-safety groups will support the label mandate but request it also require a cross-reference to training and program elements.

[P42] Reproductive-health advocates will support the consumer warning about fetal death and irreversible health risks but ask EPA to mandate that this warning be prominent and use plain-language, not just regulatory phrasing.

[P42] Industry will seek scientific justification for the specific wording and request that EPA provide standardized language to avoid litigation over phrasing.

[P43] Manufacturers will object to labeling that identifies formulation-specific gloves and instructs to use a new pair each use as potentially infeasible for some commercial operations; request allowance for reuse under documented decontamination protocols or provision of guidance on glove disposal costs.

[P43] Worker-safety advocates will insist on single-use gloves if product contact can cause dermal absorption and request EPA-funded guidance on cost-effective compliant gloves.

[P44] Small‑scale users will argue the “use outdoors or ventilate workspace” direction is inadequate for many indoor jobs and request clearer engineering control requirements or an explicit prohibition of indoor use.

[P44] Occupational hygienists will request EPA to specify ventilation rates or acceptable mechanical ventilation systems to make the instruction actionable.

[P45] Manufacturers will request an exemption for certain applicators where spraying is the only practical application method, conditional on use of engineering controls and PPE; otherwise they will accept the spray prohibition.

[P45] Environmental groups will support the spray prohibition to reduce aerosol exposures and off-site drift.

[P46] Employers will request clarity on what constitutes “clothing that covers exposed skin” and whether standard work clothes suffice versus impervious garments; ask for examples and certification pathways.

[P46] Safety advocates will request that the rule explicitly require impervious garments for all tasks with likely skin contact and provide a list of acceptable materials.

[P47] Industry will request clarification on the respirator APF 10 requirement applicability for consumers versus commercial users, and whether fit-testing and medical clearance requirements are waived for consumer use.

[P47] Respirator manufacturers will request specific references to accepted respirator models and equivalency testing procedures and ask EPA to coordinate with NIOSH guidance.

[P48] Employers will object to the Option 2 requirement that commercial use of >35% NMP be prohibited after 180 days unless comprehensive worker protection programs are in place, arguing that the programs are costly and require months to implement; request transition periods and financial-support mechanisms for small businesses.

[P48] Worker-safety groups will support stringent worker protection program requirements and request additional mandatory medical surveillance for exposed workers.

[P49] Industry will assert that the 10-year prohibition on >35% NMP formulations is arbitrary and request that the rule tie the prohibition to demonstrated availability of effective alternatives for specific applications rather than a blanket timeline.

[P49] Public-health commenters will request that the 10-year limit be shortened with interim milestones and mandatory reporting on efforts to replace NMP formulations.

[P50] DOD will request continued exemption for DOD-destined formulations beyond 10 years where no validated alternatives exist, but propose mandatory transition plans and periodic review by EPA and DOD.

[P50] Transparency advocates will request public reporting on DOD-exempt uses and independent reviews of necessity.

[P51] DOD and contractors will ask for precise operational restrictions for critical-component paint removal in § 751.205(b)(1) (e.g., work cell specifications, waste handling) and a certification process for compliant facilities.

[P51] Labor unions will demand that such work include mandatory health surveillance and that employees be covered by federal monitoring programs.

[P52] Contractors will request permission to conduct critical-component NMP work at off-site contractor facilities if those facilities meet DOD and EPA certifications, rather than only at DOD installations.

[P52] Regulatory lawyers will request a process and timeline for facility approval and re-certification, and appeals procedures.

[P53] Employers will seek flexibility in PPE procurement requirements and request EPA allow reliance on existing OSHA or other standards rather than duplicative specifications.

[P53] Safety consultants will request EPA to specify minimum quality standards and acceptance criteria for supplied PPE.

[P54] Employers will ask for model training curricula and allowable third-party trainers to meet the training requirement for every employee required to use PPE.

[P54] Labor representatives will insist on verification mechanisms (e.g., training records provided to employees and unions) and frequency requirements.

[P55] Employers will request that training content requirements be harmonized with OSHA HAZWOPER/HCS requirements to avoid duplication and regulatory conflict.

[P55] Worker advocates will request that training frequency be specified (e.g., annual) and that competency assessments be standardized.

[P56] Employers will request clarity on acceptable methods for demonstration of understanding (e.g., supervised performance, checklist) and documentation standards.

[P56] Labor groups will request that employees failing to demonstrate competence be removed from exposure until retrained and retested, and that records of failures be retained.

[P57] Employers will request limits on retraining triggers to avoid excessive retraining costs and ask EPA to define circumstances that render training “obsolete.”

[P57] Worker advocates will seek low thresholds for retraining to protect workers when any procedural or chemical change occurs.

[P58] Industry will request clearer criteria for who is “reasonably likely” to be dermally exposed to avoid overbroad PPE mandates and associated costs.

[P58] Safety advocates will support a broad interpretation and request conservative assumptions to protect workers.

[P59] Employers will strongly object to requirement for a new pair of formulation-specific gloves each use as financially burdensome and environmentally wasteful; ask for guidance on reuse protocols or exception for multi-task sessions within a shift.

[P59] Occupational hygienists will counter that single-use is necessary for high-permeation solvents and request EPA to identify scenarios where reuse may be acceptable.

[P60] Employers will request that “impervious clothing” be defined in terms of materials (e.g., laminated films) and performance specs so procurement is practicable.

[P60] Worker advocates will insist on impervious garments rather than standard cotton clothing for all operations with potential skin exposure.

[P61] Employers will ask EPA to accept manufacturer certifications or standardized test methods instead of requiring employers to perform independent testing of protective clothing.

[P61] Safety labs will request clarity on acceptable test methods and accredited laboratory requirements.

[P62] Employers will support the option to rely on manufacturer specifications but ask for minimum documentation required from suppliers.

[P62] Manufacturers will request clarity on acceptable manufacturer data and liability protections for suppliers.

[P63] Employers will raise concerns about providing NIOSH-certified respirators with APF 10 to all reasonably likely-exposed persons; request allowance for engineering controls to reduce reliance on respirators.

[P63] Worker-safety organizations will insist on respirator access plus fit-testing and medical clearance per OSHA-equivalent standards.

[P64] Employers will object to the detailed written respiratory program and recordkeeping as duplicative of existing OSHA programs and request cross-acceptance.

[P64] Occupational-safety professionals will ask EPA to provide a template respiratory program to reduce compliance costs.

[P65] Employers will request that EPA allow alternative respirator types where local conditions or supply constraints preclude listed models, provided they meet equivalent APF and certification standards.

[P65] Respirator manufacturers will request EPA coordinate with NIOSH to publish a definitive list of authorized models.

[P67] Safety professionals will request that EPA require full-face protection for any tasks with splash or high aerosol potential.

[P68] Trade groups will ask whether supplied-air respirators used intermittently require the same program rigor as continuous-use respirators.

[P69] Employers will question the feasibility of SCBA with a half mask for routine work and request guidance on when SCBA is required versus other options.

[P69] Emergency-response organizations will request clear protocols for use, training, and medical clearance for SCBA use.

[P70] Industrial hygienists will ask EPA to provide validated sampling and analytical methods and performance criteria for ECEL compliance.

[P71] Employers will challenge the 20 mg/m3 ECEL level as overly conservative or not based on consensus exposure limits and request EPA justify the derivation or align with existing occupational exposure limits (e.g., ACGIH, OSHA).

[P71] Worker-safety groups will support a conservative ECEL and request mandatory monitoring to ensure compliance.

[P72] Employers will raise cost concerns regarding the requirement for independent accredited laboratories to verify analytical methods and request acceptance of validated vendor methods or proficiency testing instead.

[P74] Safety professionals will argue initial monitoring is essential and request EPA to define reasonable timelines to conduct monitoring without halting operations.

[P75] Employers will request that employees with initial exposures below ECEL be allowed to choose respirator use and that the rule permit voluntary use policies consistent with OSHA exemptions.

[P75] Worker advocates will insist that no worker should be forced to work without respirators unless monitoring demonstrates safety and that worker choice must be respected.

[P76] Employers will ask for operational clarity on the number and timing of qualifying below-ECEL results required to remove respirator requirements and propose performance-based alternatives.

[P76] Safety consultants will request EPA to specify acceptable statistical confidence and sampling plans for these determinations.

[P77] Employers will request that the 15‑day timeframe to provide monitoring results be extended to 30 days given lab turnaround times, and seek model corrective action templates.

[P77] Labor groups will insist results be provided to employees promptly and require notification if exposures exceed ECEL with clear remedial timelines.

[P78] Employers will object to repeating monitoring every 6 months for intermediate exposures as costly and request risk-based frequency adjustments tied to exposure trend data.

[P78] Industrial hygienists will request clear numerical trigger bands and acceptance of automated real-time monitoring where validated.

[P79] Employers will argue that quarterly monitoring for high exposures is reasonable but request options for intensified controls to reduce monitoring frequency over time.

[P79] Worker advocates will ask that quarterly monitoring be minimum and that if exposures remain high more frequent monitoring be required.

[P80] Employers will request definition of what constitutes workplace changes that “may reasonably cause” increased exposures to avoid unnecessary monitoring.

[P80] Safety managers will ask for a checklist of changes that trigger re-monitoring to facilitate compliance.

[P81] Employers will request a flexible template for the written hazard communication program and allowance to incorporate existing HAZCOM or GHS programs.

[P81] Labor groups will demand that the written program include worker access rights and that it be provided in languages understood by the workforce.

[P82] Employers will ask that the program disclosure be limited to employees and designated representatives to protect proprietary information; labor groups will oppose restrictions.

[P83] Employers will welcome permission to use existing programs if they meet requirements but request EPA to publish a compliance checklist to demonstrate equivalency.

[P83] Compliance auditors will request that employers be able to certify equivalency in writing and maintain evidence.

[P84] Employers will ask whether the work-area list of NMP products can be maintained electronically and whether SDS identifiers suffice as unique product identifiers.

[P84] Safety managers will request guidance on frequency for updating the list and who is responsible in multi-employer worksites.

[P85] Contractors will request mandatory pre-job notifications in writing when contractor employees may be exposed and propose a standard form for use.

[P85] Employers will seek clarity on responsibility for informing contractors — host employer vs. contractors bringing products — and propose shared-responsibility frameworks.

[P86] Labor groups will insist on in-person, hands-on training where PPE and procedures are demonstrated.

[P87] Employers will ask EPA to allow cross-references to existing regulatory training content rather than duplicative materials.

[P87] Worker advocates will demand verification that training thoroughly covers the new requirements.

[P91] Labor groups will caution that reliance on existing programs must not dilute the new, specific protections required.

[P92] Trade groups will seek an exemption for R&D samples and small technical shipments under a de minimis threshold.

[P96] Enforcement agencies will request shipment-level granularity to facilitate tracing noncompliant uses.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The 180-day phase-out for consumer methylene chloride paint removers is unworkably short for manufacturers, distributors, and retailers to deplete inventories and reformulate products; request extension to at least 12–24 months or phased sell-through allowances.
Consumer advocacy groups will claim the prohibition is necessary and should be expanded to include any online marketplace sales exemptions to prevent continued consumer access.

Industry commenters will assert that the 180-day ban on manufacture/processing/distribution for commercial uses fails to account for existing long-term contractual obligations and inventory held by professional refinishers; ask for a sell-through or exemption period for existing contracts.

Legal experts will argue the rule must clarify liability for distributors who unknowingly sell to end-users engaged in prohibited commercial paint removal, and request a due-diligence safe harbor for ordinary commercial distributors who rely on purchaser declarations.

Military and defense contractors will support the narrow exception for commercial furniture stripping and critical military components but request explicit definitions of “commercial furniture stripping” and “critical corrosion-sensitive components” to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

Environmental NGOs will object to the military exception as too broad and urge that any exception be limited, time-limited, and subject to EPA reporting and independent oversight to prevent routine circumvention.

Defense contractors and military maintenance stakeholders will strongly object to the 10-year sunset of the exception, arguing it undermines long-term maintenance planning (airframe life cycles exceed 10 years) and request a permanent DOD exemption with conditions or a longer phase-out tied to validated alternatives.

Public health advocates will support the 10-year limitation removing military exceptions and request that the phase-out occur sooner than 10 years with mandatory transition plans for DOD to adopt safer alternatives.

Chemical distributors will challenge the prohibition on distributing methylene chloride in containers under 55 gallons as disruptive to legitimate commercial users who require smaller packaged volumes for safe handling; request allowance of smaller industrial pack sizes (e.g., 5–30 gallons) with certification and recordkeeping.

Labor unions and worker-safety groups will support the 55-gallon minimum distribution prohibition as a measure reducing small-quantity commercial use and accidental worker exposures, but ask for explicit enforcement guidance to prevent illicit small-batch repackaging.

DOD contractors will request that the DOD-specific 5-gallon minimum exception also permit smaller packaged sizes (e.g., 1–2.5 gallons) when specific maintenance tasks require them, coupled with stringent chain-of-custody controls.
Transparency advocates will demand that EPA require public reporting of volumes and recipients of DOD-exempt 5-gallon distributions to ensure the exception is not misused.

Employers and trade associations will argue that the 270-day delay for prohibition on commercial use is too short to implement alternative processes and procure compliant equipment; request longer compliance timelines or phased sector-specific compliance dates.

Worker-safety groups will claim the 270-day commercial-use prohibition is insufficiently protective and recommend accelerating the ban and increasing outreach to small businesses to prevent continued hazardous exposures.

Furniture-restoration small businesses will assert the exemption for commercial furniture stripping is vague and could create unfair market advantages; request explicit eligibility criteria, registration, or permit system for businesses claiming the exemption.

Local government hazardous-waste officials will request clarity on waste disposal and transport obligations for commercial furniture stripping operations that continue using methylene chloride under the exemption.

Military maintenance organizations will object to the final removal of the commercial-use exception after 10 years, asserting it will disrupt maintenance schedules and requesting either permanent limited exemptions or a transition fund for alternative process development.

Regulatory lawyers will note the 10-year removal of exceptions requires clear grandfathering language for works-in-progress and ask EPA to specify treatment of materials procured before the 10-year cutoff.

DOD and contractor commenters will request detailed technical specifications and permitted engineering controls referenced in § 751.107(d), arguing the current summary is insufficiently prescriptive to ensure safe, consistent implementation.

Public-interest law groups will demand that the “specified restrictions” include mandatory reporting, third-party audits, and worker protection measures to ensure the exception does not create undue risks.

Military bases and private maintenance yards will request explicit lists of acceptable “DOD-controlled” and “DOD-contractor” locations, including standards for contractor facilities (e.g., security, ventilation, training), and propose a site approval process.

Small defense subcontractors will claim that requiring use only at DOD-controlled or DOD-contractor locations will impose logistical burdens and increased costs; request allowance for mobile, certified containment units meeting EPA-approved standards.

Manufacturers and distributors will complain that the 45‑day deadline to provide written downstream notifications is impractically short for supply chains, and suggest at least 90 days and model notification language to ensure compliance.

Trade associations will request safe harbor language that downstream notifications delivered via standard business communication channels (e.g., email, EDI) qualify, and seek clarity on who constitutes “downstream companies” (distributors, retailers, end-users).

Companies will point out that requiring retention of documentation at company headquarters may be infeasible for decentralized distributors and ask that records be permitted to be maintained electronically at any accessible location with remote retrieval.
Privacy advocates will request redaction guidance for contact information in records when submissions are later provided to EPA, to balance transparency and privacy concerns.

Distributors will request specification about what constitutes adequate “contact” information (e.g., phone, email, authorized representative) and allow substitute identifiers (customer ID numbers) if included in company records.
Enforcement attorneys will ask EPA to clarify whether failure to collect recipient contact information triggers strict liability or if good-faith efforts suffice.
Industry commenters will request standardized downstream notification templates be provided by EPA to reduce compliance costs and disputes about sufficiency of the notification retained.
Worker-safety advocates will ask EPA to require distributors to certify that notifications include clear, plain-language hazard information, not just regulatory citations.

Manufacturers will ask for clarity on the granularity of “amount shipped” — whether it must be reported per SKU, batch, weight vs. volume, and how bulk shipments (railcar/bulk tanker) are to be recorded.
Small businesses will request aggregation allowances (monthly totals) rather than per-shipment records to reduce administrative burden.

Businesses will request extension of the 3-year records-retention requirement to match other federal recordkeeping cycles (e.g., 5 years) or harmonize with OSHA practices, or alternatively reduce it to 2 years if burdensome.
Compliance officers will ask whether the 3-year retention period runs from date of shipment or date of sale to end-user and request explicit examples.

Defense commenters will request that the same DOD exception provided for methylene chloride be explicitly mirrored for NMP commercial prohibitions and that definitions align cross-subpart.

Navy and Air Force depot maintainers will request a clear, narrow definition of “critical corrosion-sensitive components” and criteria for inclusion to prevent overbroad application of the military exemption.
Environmental groups will request documentation and reporting obligations for any NMP use under the military exception to ensure accountability and encourage transition to alternatives.

Contractors will challenge the 10-year prohibition on NMP manufacture/processing/distribution for critical components as too disruptive to long-term maintenance contracts and request a longer transition period or exemptions tied to availability of validated alternatives.
Health advocates will argue the 10-year limit should be shortened and that EPA should require DOD to submit transition plans within 1 year.

Chemical suppliers will object to the prohibition on distribution of NMP in containers under 55 gallons as commercially restrictive and ask that DOD and other verified industrial users be permitted to receive smaller containers with certified controls.
Worker and public safety groups will support the 55-gallon minimum as a deterrent to small-scale use and request anti-diversion monitoring.

DOD contractors will support the 5-gallon DOD exception but request that EPA allow the Department to authorize sub‑contractors to receive smaller packages under accountable chain-of-custody procedures.
Transparency advocates will ask for quarterly public reporting on volumes distributed under the DOD 5-gallon exception.

Commercial users will argue that the 270-day commercial-use prohibition for NMP does not provide sufficient time to implement the extensive worker protection programs required under Option 2, and request longer lead times or sector-specific phase-ins.
Worker-safety organizations will insist the 270-day timeframe is adequate and emphasize the need for early enforcement to protect workers.

Furniture-restoration small businesses will request clarity whether the commercial furniture stripping exception applies to artisan/restoration shops and whether registration or training is required to qualify.
Military maintenance commenters will request retention of the exception but with mandated PPE and monitoring requirements for users performing exempted NMP work.

Defense maintenance stakeholders will object to the 10-year commercial-use prohibition for critical components and request a schedule tied to validated alternative performance data to avoid aircraft downtime.
Legal commenters will ask whether equipment and materials procured before the 10-year cutoff may be used until exhaustion and request explicit grandfathering language.

Labor and safety advocates will insist the restrictions include mandatory exposure monitoring, medical surveillance, and third-party audits.

Contractors will request ability to use certified off-site contractor facilities for NMP-based paint removal on military components and seek definition of acceptable DOD-contractor locations and approval process.
Union representatives will ask for mandatory worker-training standards and recordkeeping at approved DOD-contractor locations.
NMP manufacturers and distributors will reiterate that the 45-day notification window is too short and ask for model language and acceptance of electronic notice methods and batch-level notices.
Occupational health groups will request that downstream notifications must explicitly include worker-protection requirements and label warnings, not just regulatory citations.
Distributors will request that NMP record retention be permitted in electronic format off-site, and that small businesses be allowed aggregated reporting to reduce burden.
Regulatory compliance consultants will ask EPA to define “company headquarters” (domestic only? foreign?) and allow records to be stored at U.S.-based corporate agents.
Commenters will seek clarity whether recipient contact information must include individual names and direct telephone numbers or whether business contact centers suffice.
Privacy and data-security groups will ask EPA to provide guidance on protecting personally identifiable information included in retained records.
Industry will ask that copies of downstream notifications accepted for recordkeeping include stamped proof of delivery or date emailed to corroborate compliance.
Worker advocates will request that proof-of-notification records be made available to employees and labor representatives upon request.
Businesses will request guidance on acceptable units for “amount shipped” (e.g., gallons, liters, kilograms) and whether cumulative monthly totals suffice.
Enforcement agencies will request that EPA require shipment-level records for traceability in case of noncompliant distribution.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement to "comply with certification procedures in 14 CFR part 21" is vague—request clarification on which specific sections of part 21 (e.g., §21.17, §21.21, §21.29) the FAA expects applicants to follow and whether any deviations or alternative procedures are acceptable for novel electric-propulsion architectures.

[P2] Requiring compliance with 14 CFR part 33 airworthiness standards "except those only for reciprocating and turbine engines" is unclear—stakeholders request an explicit list of Part 33 sections considered inapplicable to electrically driven rotors or hybrid systems to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P3] The additional requirements "beyond §33.7(a)" are broadly stated—industry seeks a consolidated, annotated matrix showing where existing §33 provisions remain applicable and where the special conditions add or modify requirements to prevent duplicative testing.

[P4] The obligation to "establish and include ratings and operating limits in the type certificate data sheet" lacks guidance on the granularity required (e.g., update intervals, transient limits, ambient conditions). Applicants request templates or examples of acceptable entries.

[P5] For P2(a)(1), specifying power/torque/speed/time for "rated maximum continuous power" without defining measurement reference conditions (temperature, pressure, electrical bus voltage, propeller load) will lead to inconsistent certification tests—request standard reference conditions.

[P6] For P2(a)(2), the requirement to set a "time limit for rated maximum temporary power" should specify maximum acceptable temporary durations or the methodology for selecting them; manufacturers need guidance on allowable transient durations and how those will be judged acceptable by the Administrator.

[P7] P2(b)'s duty cycle requirement and associated ratings are open-ended—manufacturers need criteria for how many duty cycles to declare for multi-mission aircraft (e.g., commuter, cargo, eVTOL) and how usage profiles affect certification.

[P8] The obligation in P2(b) to "declare the duty cycle(s) in the engine certificate data sheet" risks locking manufacturers into conservative limits that may not fit later operational use; propose allowing amendment processes post-certification based on service experience.

[P9] Mandating compliance with 14 CFR 33.15 materials requirements may impose legacy material testing irrelevant to novel electric motors or composite rotors—request an exemption mechanism or clarification about which materials provisions apply.

[P10] Requiring compliance with 14 CFR 33.17 fire protection (P10) without tailoring for electric propulsion systems is problematic; electrical fires differ from fuel fires—advocates request specific fire detection/suppression criteria for high-voltage systems rather than blanket application of turbine-engine rules.

[P11] P4's mandate that "high-voltage electrical wiring interconnect systems must be protected against arc-faults" is appropriate, but industry requests explicit performance metrics (e.g., detection time, maximum energy let-through) and allowed mitigation strategies (circuit breakers vs. arc-fault detectors).

[P12] The obligation to "analyze non-protected wiring to show arc-faults won't cause hazardous engine effects" (P12) invites excessive analysis scope—manufacturers request that the FAA limit this to wiring within identified high-energy zones and provide accepted analysis methods or representative failure scenarios.

[P13] P5's requirement to "minimize unsafe conditions between maintenance/overhaul/ICA actions" is conceptually sound but lacks quantifiable targets (e.g., MTBF, acceptable degradation rates); operators need objective performance thresholds to plan maintenance intervals and life-cycle costs.

[P14] Compliance with 14 CFR 33.21 cooling requirements (P14) needs adaptation for electric motors where thermal management relies on electronics and battery interactions—request guidance on allowable coolant types, redundancy, and monitoring requirements specific to electric propulsion.

[P15] The condition in P15 that cooling system monitoring features be documented in the installation manual when cooling is required (per special condition 17) should also require that monitoring alerting thresholds and pilot/maintenance actions be standardized in the ICA; otherwise installers will adopt inconsistent practices.

[P16] P16 and P17 reference compliance with 14 CFR 33.23 and 33.25 for mounting and accessory attachments—small integrators request illustrative load cases and installation envelope definitions to evaluate compatibility with multiple airframes.

[P17] The prohibition in P18 that rotor overspeed must not cause burst, growth, or damage leading to hazardous effects is appropriate, but the rule needs to state acceptable definitions of "hazardous engine effect" and whether containment alone is sufficient mitigation for high-energy failures.

[P18] The requirement in P19 to show overspeed compliance "by test, validated analysis, or both" should permit fair reliance on validated simulation tools for early-stage prototypes; industry requests FAA-accepted tool lists or qualification criteria for analytical methods.

[P19] P20's requirement to "declare and justify any assumed speeds used in overspeed compliance showing" could inadvertently require disclosure of proprietary design margins—manufacturers request confidentiality protections for declared assumptions or allow submission under protective order.

[P20] P21/P22 require rotors to have margin to burst above certified and failure-induced overspeed conditions and to demonstrate that margin—designers need specific margin factors (e.g., x% above maximum certified rpm) or a risk-based process to derive acceptable margins.

[P21] The prohibition in P23 that "engine must not exceed speed limits that could affect rotor structural integrity" duplicates other overspeed provisions and needs to clarify who sets operational speed limits (manufacturer vs. operator) and how speed-limiting hardware/software must be validated.

[P22] P24–P27 impose rigorous software/system assurance requirements (structured approach, verification acceptable to Administrator). Software developers ask FAA to adopt or reference existing DO-178C/ED-12C or DO-254 standards and explicitly state required assurance levels (DALs) for control system functions.

[P23] P26’s phrase "verification methodology acceptable to the Administrator" is vague—request explicit acceptance of common standards (DO-178C/DO-254/ARINC) and a clear process for obtaining approval of alternative methodologies.

[P24] The obligation in P27 to substantiate control system functions "throughout the declared envelope" will be onerous without guidance on envelope discretization and sampling—request that the FAA accept representative analysis points combined with worst-case margins instead of exhaustive testing.

[P25] P28's requirement to demonstrate environmental limits not covered by endurance via tests (special condition 27) needs a prioritized list of environmental threats (e.g., lightning, icing, salt spray) and acceptable test standards; otherwise applicants face uncertain testing scope and cost.

[P26] P29–P31's LOPC (Loss of Power Control) and single-fault tolerance requirements are ambiguous—are redundant hardware channels required, or can software fault-tolerant architectures with diverse algorithms satisfy single-fault tolerance? Request engineering alternatives be explicitly allowed.

[P27] The prohibition in P31 that "no single failure may result in hazardous engine effects" is a strict zero-failure tolerance that may be unattainable; safety engineers request alignment with probabilistic safety targets (e.g., catastrophic <= 1E-9 per flight hour) and guidance on acceptable residual risk.

[P28] P32–P36 concerning aircraft-supplied data: requiring the control system to detect and accommodate any single failure or corruption of aircraft-supplied data imposes complex integration/compatibility requirements; airframe manufacturers request standardized data interface protocols and required CRC/validation checks.

[P29] P37's obligation that loss or interruption of electrical power not cause hazardous effects needs clarification whether "electrical power" refers only to control electronics or total propulsion power; provide guidance on allowed fallback modes and required duration of electrical backup.

[P30] P38’s requirement to comply with 14 CFR 33.29(a),(e),(f),(g) should be accompanied by a cross-reference table showing how each subsection maps to the special conditions to prevent duplication or conflicts.

[P31] P39–P40's requirement to assess and prevent incorrect fit/configuration of sensors/connectors places heavy design-for-assembly burdens—manufacturers request practical design solutions (keying, color-coding) be accepted as sufficient when certain other constraints prevent full-proofing.

[P32] P41–P42 stress analysis obligations need explicit acceptance criteria and material property test methods for new materials (e.g., advanced composites, printed conductors) to avoid subjective Administrator determinations.

[P33] P43–P52 concerning classification and management of critical/life-limited parts plus the three plans (engineering, manufacturing, service) are comprehensive but will require significant post-certification obligations; small businesses request phased compliance timelines and acceptance of industry-standard quality systems (e.g., AS9100) in lieu of bespoke plans.

[P34] The explicit call-out in P48 that "magniX must perform damage tolerance assessments" appears to single out a specific company—commenters raise concerns about singling out a named entity in a general rule and request removal or clarification that this applies to any applicant.

[P35] Requiring that approved part life be published in the mandatory ICA (P49) is reasonable but the rule should allow proprietary life-assessment data to be submitted under confidentiality; operators need access to life limits but manufacturers need IP protection.

[P36] P50–P52 manufacturing and service plan prescriptions should allow delegation to approved suppliers/maintenance organizations; request that compliance can be satisfied by flow-down to suppliers accredited under recognized standards rather than manufacturer-conducted activities only.

[P37] P53–P55 lubrication system design/demonstration requirements are written for fluid-lubricated bearings—electric motor designs using solid lubricants or magnetic bearings need alternative means of compliance; request explicit allowance and test criteria for non-fluid lubrication systems.

[P38] The obligations in P56–P57 to enable controlled power increases across the full range raise questions about transient response requirements (maximum climb throttle ramp rate, in-flight surges) and allowable protective power management interventions; operators request defined maximum ramp rates and required annunciation to pilots.

[P39] The prohibition in P58 about continued in-flight rotation after shutdown must consider scenarios where windmilling provides necessary secondary functions (e.g., hydraulic/backup electrical generation); request an exception path where continued rotation is allowed if it does not cause hazardous effects and is demonstrated per P81.

[P40] P59–P63 referencing §33.75 and ingestion requirements should clarify standard test species and particle sizes for ingestion tests (e.g., bird sizes, ice particle criteria, hail energy) and whether computational methods may be used to bound risks.

[P41] The installation-manual documentation condition in P64 requiring installer-supplied features to be documented could shift certification burdens to airframe OEMs; request clear apportionment of certification responsibilities between engine and airframe manufacturers.

[P42] P65–P66 addressing liquid systems: for non-self-contained systems (interface to airframe), the requirement to define interfaces in the installation manual must include explicit data exchange formats, tolerance ranges, and failure modes so installers can verify system compatibility.

[P43] P67–P69 vibration design and survey requirements should define accepted instrumentation, duration of surveys, and pass/fail criteria for "acceptable vibration characteristics" to avoid subjective Administrator judgments.

[P44] The conditional approval path in P70 for transient overtorque requiring demonstration that the engine can continue operating "without the need for maintenance" is ambiguous—specify whether this means zero maintenance or only non-safety-critical inspections, and define acceptable restoration actions.

[P45] P71–P73 endurance, calibration, and limit capability demonstrations will be expensive and time-consuming; propose allowance for accelerated life testing protocols accepted by the Administrator to reduce cost/time while maintaining safety.

[P46] P74–P75 demand quantifying and justifying temperature margins for each rated condition and repeating demonstrations for all duty cycles—request acceptance of conservative analytical margins for early demonstrations with follow-on service-based refinement.

[P47] P76–P77 require demonstration of safe operating characteristics accounting for installation loads; large airframers request standardized installation load cases and a requirement that engine manufacturers provide interface-load envelopes to support integrators.

[P48] P78–P79 durability demonstrations must simulate start-stop cycles—operators of short-hop eVTOLs are concerned that the required cycle counts may be extraordinarily large; request risk-based scaling of cycle testing to reflect intended operations and acceptable extrapolation methods.

[P49] P80's blanket requirement that systems and components perform across all declared environmental and operating conditions needs a definition of "declared"—request that the declared envelope be jointly agreed to by applicant and Administrator and be amendable as service experience accrues.

[P50] The rotor-locking condition in P81 requires demonstration of reliable locking and absence of hazardous effects; request clarity on locking system qualification (cycles to failure, environmental exposure, inadvertent engagement prevention) and whether mechanical locks or active braking are preferred/acceptable.

[P51] P82–P86 teardown and life-limit provisions impose either full teardown or establishing life limits when no teardown is performed—manufacturers seek guidance on acceptable statistical bases and sample sizes for establishing life limits where teardown is impractical.

[P52] P87–P90 containment and fragment-energy documentation obligations should specify acceptable containment criteria (e.g., fragment energy absorption, residual fragment velocities at case boundary) and whether composite case materials have different thresholds.

[P53] P90’s requirement to document fragment energy/trajectory/size "in the installation manual" may require integrators to perform aircraft-level assessments—request that the engine applicant provide bounding data and that aircraft manufacturers be responsible for assessing aircraft vulnerability.

[P54] P91–P92 require functional demonstrations with representative propellers (feathering, negative/thrust) —propeller manufacturers request criteria for "representative" and whether scaled-inertia props or full-scale installations are required for certification.

[P55] P93–P96 permit maintenance during tests per proposed ICA but require that final engines be within serviceable limits after testing—operators ask for clear guidance on allowed maintenance extents during endurance tests so as not to invalidate durability demonstrations.

[P56] The administrator-triggered maintenance/testing conditions in P94 (when adverse conditions occur) are open-ended; applicants request a list of the "adverse conditions" referenced and objective triggers (e.g., exceeding vibration thresholds, component wear limits) that mandate additional tests.

[P57] P95–P97's post-demonstration serviceability and capability-to-operate-at-declared-ratings requirements should allow documented, limited repairs that preserve test validity; require clarification on what constitutes "serviceable limits" and "safe for continued operation."

[P58] Across the special conditions, numerous "acceptable to the Administrator" and "as determined by the Administrator" phrases create significant regulatory uncertainty—legal commentators request the FAA adopt clear acceptance criteria, allow pre-submission meetings to agree on methods, and define an appeals process for disputed determinations.

[P59] The cumulative testing and documentation burden implied by these provisions (endurance, teardown or life limit establishment, vibration surveys, temperature margin demonstrations, fragment analyses, software/system assessments) will be prohibitively expensive for small entrants; request phased requirements, scaled testing based on risk and production volume, and cost-impact analysis.

[P60] Request that the FAA explicitly state how compliance with these special conditions will be verified during production and continued airworthiness, including what elements will be audited, sampled, or reviewed in the TSO/TC/production approval processes.

P80's blanket requirement that systems and components perform across all declared environmental and operating conditions needs a definition of "declared"—request that the declared envelope be jointly agreed to by applicant and Administrator and be amendable as service experience accrues.

The rotor-locking condition in P81 requires demonstration of reliable locking and absence of hazardous effects; request clarity on locking system qualification (cycles to failure, environmental exposure, inadvertent engagement prevention) and whether mechanical locks or active braking are preferred/acceptable.

P82–P86 teardown and life-limit provisions impose either full teardown or establishing life limits when no teardown is performed—manufacturers seek guidance on acceptable statistical bases and sample sizes for establishing life limits where teardown is impractical.

P87–P90 containment and fragment-energy documentation obligations should specify acceptable containment criteria (e.g., fragment energy absorption, residual fragment velocities at case boundary) and whether composite case materials have different thresholds.

P90’s requirement to document fragment energy/trajectory/size "in the installation manual" may require integrators to perform aircraft-level assessments—request that the engine applicant provide bounding data and that aircraft manufacturers be responsible for assessing aircraft vulnerability.

P91–P92 require functional demonstrations with representative propellers (feathering, negative/thrust) —propeller manufacturers request criteria for "representative" and whether scaled-inertia props or full-scale installations are required for certification.

P93–P96 permit maintenance during tests per proposed ICA but require that final engines be within serviceable limits after testing—operators ask for clear guidance on allowed maintenance extents during endurance tests so as not to invalidate durability demonstrations.

The administrator-triggered maintenance/testing conditions in P94 (when adverse conditions occur) are open-ended; applicants request a list of the "adverse conditions" referenced and objective triggers (e.g., exceeding vibration thresholds, component wear limits) that mandate additional tests.

P95–P97's post-demonstration serviceability and capability-to-operate-at-declared-ratings requirements should allow documented, limited repairs that preserve test validity; require clarification on what constitutes "serviceable limits" and "safe for continued operation."

Across the special conditions, numerous "acceptable to the Administrator" and "as determined by the Administrator" phrases create significant regulatory uncertainty—legal commentators request the FAA adopt clear acceptance criteria, allow pre-submission meetings to agree on methods, and define an appeals process for disputed determinations.

The cumulative testing and documentation burden implied by these provisions (endurance, teardown or life limit establishment, vibration surveys, temperature margin demonstrations, fragment analyses, software/system assessments) will be prohibitively expensive for small entrants; request phased requirements, scaled testing based on risk and production volume, and cost-impact analysis.

Request that the FAA explicitly state how compliance with these special conditions will be verified during production and continued airworthiness, including what elements will be audited, sampled, or reviewed in the TSO/TC/production approval processes.
