raw_output:
[P1] Industry commenters will argue that permitting "any interested party" to file complaints against B Readers invites frivolous or harassing complaints from competitors, attorneys, or advocacy groups and should be narrowed to affected employers, miners, or qualified medical professionals.

[P1] Legal experts will claim the phrase "any interested party" is unconstitutionally vague and could chill clinicians from providing honest readings for fear of litigation or professional reprisal.

[P2] Pathologists and clinicians will object that requiring submission of original radiographs, ILO classifications, and a supporting medical professional letter creates privacy/HIPAA risks unless explicit instructions on de-identification and consent are added.

[P2] Rural providers and small hospitals will state the radiograph submission requirement (original images and paperwork) imposes excessive logistical and cost burdens, particularly for historical films, and request allowance for certified digitized copies and electronic submission.

[P3] Radiology societies will contend "more than a reasonable difference of opinion" is undefined and subjective; they will request objective, quantified standards or examples for what constitutes "more than reasonable."

[P3] Legal commentators will argue that using "more than a reasonable difference of opinion" substitutes an undefined administrative standard for established peer-review procedures and invites arbitrary dismissal of dissenting expert opinions.

[P4] Clinicians will protest that deeming incomplete complaints invalid with no preliminary opportunity to cure deficiencies is unfair; they will request a provision allowing complainants a fixed cure period (e.g., 14 days) to submit missing materials.

[P4] Patient advocacy groups will claim automatic invalidation and simple notice without guidance disproportionately harms miners and family members unfamiliar with procedural requirements; they will request mandatory assistance from NIOSH in assembling complete complaints.

[P5] B Reader professional associations will object that giving NIOSH unilateral discretion to initiate investigations without transparent criteria will lead to selective enforcement and request published investigation triggers and prioritization criteria.

[P5] Labor unions will support NIOSH discretion but will demand transparency about how investigations are prioritized and public reporting of investigations and outcomes to ensure accountability.

[P6] B Reader organizations will request that the panel size of "at least four B Readers" be expanded and include a requirement for geographic and practice-setting diversity to avoid groupthink or local bias.

[P6] Some commenters will argue that panels of at least four are duplicative and costly; they will propose a three-member panel with a designated tiebreaker to improve efficiency.

[P7] B Reader advocates will object to the rule that a single panelist finding the contested classification reasonable ends the matter, arguing this gives undue weight to one reviewer and can prevent identification of systematic misclassification; they will request a supermajority rather than any single concurring vote.

[P7] Medical-legal practitioners will claim that allowing one panelist to terminate enforcement creates perverse incentives for panel selection and call for anonymized, blinded reviews to prevent bias.

[P8] Worker safety advocates will support the unanimous-finding remedial threshold but request that remedial actions be triggered by a supermajority (e.g., 3 of 4) rather than unanimity to better capture patterns of error.

[P9] B Reader defendants will request that initial reports include detailed rationale, statistical analysis, and the identities/qualifications of reviewing panelists (or at least their credentials) to enable meaningful challenges.

[P10] Due process advocates will challenge the 30-day automatic finalization of an unchallenged initial report as too short, urging extension to 60–90 days to give B Readers reasonable time to obtain records and mount a response.

[P11] Professional organizations will request that the 90-day Program response timeline be strictly enforced with interim status updates and that failure to respond within 90 days triggers an automatic dismissal of the complaint.

[P11] Defense commenters will argue that a final Program decision within 90 days without an independent appellate body violates principles of impartial adjudication and request an external review board be available.

[P12] B Reader groups will warn that using the first final report as a "warning" that can lead to suspension without clear standards for what constitutes "further misclassification" is vague; they request defined thresholds and examples.

[P13] Commenters will request clarification that the "second complaint" requirement refers specifically to separate patient studies and not multiple readings of the same radiograph to avoid double-counting.

[P14] Civil liberties groups will argue again that a 30-day window to challenge an initial report is too short, particularly when months may be needed to gather records, and propose at least 60 days.

[P15] B Reader advocates will object to certification remaining "in good standing" during the 90-day challenge period if the consequence can be a 1-year suspension retroactive to the decision date; they will ask for provisional restrictions or a stay pending appeal.

[P15] Employers and insurers will urge that if certification remains in good standing during appeal, NIOSH should be allowed to flag the B Reader in databases to inform employers and clinics of pending investigations.

[P16] Training institutions will note that requiring passing the certification exam at the end of a one-year suspension may be impractical if exam cycles are limited and will request guaranteed exam access and remediation resources.

[P16] B Reader commenters will argue the requirement to retake the exam after suspension is punitive if the alleged misclassification arose from ambiguous films; they will request alternative remediation like supervised re-training.

[P17] Commenters will request explicit notice that "third complaint" counts only final adverse determinations and propose an appeals stay so that pending challenges cannot count toward automatic revocation unfairly.

[P18] Public commenters will again request extending the 30-day unchallenged-finalization deadline for the third initial report to permit thorough legal or scientific responses.

[P19] Constitutional and administrative-law experts will challenge the statement that the Program's decision "is final unless successfully appealed" if there is no independent adjudicator; they will request judicial or independent administrative review be available.

[P19] Professional groups will object to permanent revocation being effective on the date of the final decision letter without allowing for a stay pending appeal to an independent body or court.

[P20] Some commenters will argue that treating a single first complaint that "proves a pattern" as immediately invoking third-complaint procedures is arbitrary; they will call for clearly defined metrics and multi-case confirmation before escalating to potential revocation.

[P21] Medical societies will object to requiring radiographs from "three or more patients within one year" to demonstrate a pattern, noting that practice settings may have low volumes and asking for an alternative longer time frame (e.g., three patients within three years) or proportion-based metrics.

[P21] Privacy advocates will raise concerns that requiring multiple patient radiographs from a single B Reader could risk re-identification of miners and request strict de-identification standards and consent protocols.

[P22] Affected B Readers will comment that automatic decertification after three final adverse determinations ignores context (e.g., case mix, ambiguous films, evolving standards) and request a more nuanced remediation pathway before permanent removal.

[P23] Some commenters will support allowing appeal of revocation but will request a neutral, independent appeals panel rather than internal NIOSH review to avoid conflicts of interest.

[P24] Practitioners will point out that requiring appeals to be "postmarked" within 30 days is outdated and may disadvantage electronic submissions; they will request unequivocal acceptance of electronic submissions with clear timestamping rules.

[P24] Civil procedure experts will propose that the rule clarify standards for "signed" electronic submissions (e.g., digital signature types accepted) to prevent procedural rejections on technicalities.

[P25] B Reader appellants will request clearer guidance on what constitutes adequate "scientific and medical information" for appeals and opportunity to submit expert witness declarations and re-reads.

[P26] Commenters will urge including an explicit mailing address and an email upload portal in the regulation rather than leaving it to decertification letters, to avoid misdirected appeals.

[P27] Practitioners will say the Director's review should include a neutral hearing with opportunity for oral argument and cross-examination, rather than a purely paper review, to comply with due process norms.

[P28] B Readers will request that the Director's written notice include redaction options and clear confidentiality protections for proprietary or sensitive clinical information included in appeal records.

[P29] Pathologist groups will support compensation for autopsies but will request clearer limits on "at NIOSH's discretion" to ensure predictable payment rates and prevent de facto denial of customary fees.

[P30] Pathologists will request that the "prior authorization" requirement include a guaranteed response timeframe and that authorization not be retroactively denied after an autopsy is performed in good faith.

[P31] Pathologists will ask for clearer standards explaining what "in accordance with this subpart" means for autopsy technique to prevent denials of payment for minor deviations.

[P32] For the 180-day submission deadline, pathologists will request extension (e.g., 270–365 days) in complex cases requiring special stains or consultations and/or allowance for documented hardship extensions.

[P33] Submitting clinicians will support permitting multiple types of chest images but request explicit acceptance of CT scans and digital radiographs and standards for image quality and DICOM submissions.

[P34] Pathologist associations will seek a fee schedule or cap rather than the vague "ordinary, usual, or customary fee at NIOSH's discretion" to avoid arbitrary payment amounts and ensure fairness.

[P35] Pathologists will request clarification that compensation for radiographs within 5 years includes digitized copies and reimbursement for retrieval costs from hospitals or archives.

[P36] Pathologists and beneficiary representatives will support §37.202(c) prohibiting duplicate payments, but request explicit definitions of "specific payment" and safe-harbor rules to avoid repayment demands when payments were received in error.

[P37] Autopsy practitioners will request that the standard autopsy procedures referenced be published in full in the CFR or included as an appendix rather than only by reference, to ensure accessibility.

[P38] Several commenters will note that while copies may be "borrowed" from NIOSH, public access to referenced documents should be online and free to avoid undue burden.

[P39] Pathologists will argue that the long checklist of required examinations/specimens may be infeasible in certain cultural/religious contexts or when body condition precludes full sampling; they request exceptions or waivers with documentation.

[P40] Pathologists will request clarification that microscopic examination of tracheobronchial lymph nodes includes sampling method and minimum number of nodes to be examined.

[P41] Clinical pathologists will request allowance for weights measured in local hospital practice (e.g., grams) and a tolerance for minor deviations; they also request instruction on acceptable scales and calibration.

[P42] Cardiac pathologists will ask for more precise anatomical guidance and acceptable measurement protocols for cardiac valve circumferences to ensure consistency.

[P43] Commenters will request detailed measurement protocols and illustrations for ventricle thickness measurements to avoid inter-operator variability and denials for technical noncompliance.

[P44] Pathologists will ask for a standardized lesion reporting template to ensure required information (size, number, consistency, etc.) is consistently captured.

[P45] Practitioners will request more detail on how to "record the level of the diaphragm" (anatomic landmarks, units) to avoid inconsistent reporting.

[P46] Pathologists will challenge the minimum of three stained slides and three blocks per suspected lesion as potentially insufficient for complex histopathology and request allowance for additional slides/blocks when indicated.

[P47] Commenters will note that random sampling of three lung areas when no lesion is recognized may miss localized disease; they will request stratified sampling guidance (e.g., specific lobes and positions).

[P48] Some pathologists will object to blanket prohibition of needle biopsy techniques, noting that in some jurisdictions or cases, core needle sampling may be the only feasible option; they will request conditional acceptance with justification.

[P49] Pathologists will warn that requiring written authorization and payment agreement before performing the autopsy could delay time-sensitive autopsies and propose a retroactive authorization path in demonstrated urgent circumstances.

[P50] Pathologists will request that NIOSH clarify how "availability of payments" is determined and give advance notice before making the online authorization form inactive to avoid wasted efforts.

[P51] Pathologists will generally support a 3-working-day authorization response but will request a process for expedited emergency approvals (e.g., within 24 hours) in time-sensitive cases.

[P52] Commenters will request a clear electronic submission portal with receipt confirmations for all post-autopsy claim materials to avoid disputes over timeliness and completeness.

[P53] Pathologists will request explicit guidance on the form and content of the required signed statement that no other compensation is being received, including sample language and acceptable signatory authority.

[P54] Beneficiaries and legal advocates will request safeguards that assistance in completing the Consent, Release and History Form cannot be used to coerce or bias the documented history and that independence is preserved.

[P55] Pathologists will call for clear checklists cross-referencing the "information, slides, and blocks" required elsewhere to reduce claim denials for technical omissions.

[P56] Commenters will request limits on the scope of the clinical abstract requirement, with templates provided to standardize submissions and avoid excessive burdens on pathologists.

[P57] Pathologists will ask that the final summary requirement allow for provisional diagnoses and the inclusion of explanatory notes when pneumoconiosis findings are equivocal, rather than forcing a categorical yes/no statement that could be punitive.

[P1] The provision listing applicability only to "PPL Montana, LLC" is unclear and likely erroneous for a rule aimed at coal-fired EGUs; commenters will request clarification whether other Montana coal-fired EGUs are intentionally excluded and ask the Agency to correct or justify the narrow named-applicant scope.

[P1] Industry commenters will argue that naming a single corporate entity (PPL Montana, LLC) rather than using facility identifiers (plant name, unit numbers, ORISPL codes) creates enforcement ambiguity and request inclusion of specific unit identifiers and locations.

[P2] Cement industry stakeholders will contend that applying lb/ton-of-clinker limits (rather than stack concentration or lb/MMBtu) to all cement kilns could be inconsistent with existing EPA standards and request alignment or cross-reference to the applicable NSPS/MACT metrics.

[P2] Environmental NGOs will assert that the prohibition lacks explicit averaging periods for PM (only SO2/NOX specify rolling 30-day averaging), and request the rule state the averaging period for PM (e.g., 3-run stack test average or daily/hourly) to avoid loopholes.

[P3] Ash Grove will request that the rule include the complete formula and units — the provision truncates the formula text — and ask the Agency to provide worked examples showing limit calculations at representative process weight rates.

[P3] Legal commenters will argue that using a single threshold at 30 t/hr without justification is arbitrary; they will request the record show BART analysis supporting this breakpoint and the exponent 0.67 in the formula.

[P4] Ash Grove will request an explanation and supporting documentation for selecting a SO2 limit of 11.5 lb/ton clinker, including the baseline emissions, control technology assumed, and visibility benefit estimates underlying BART determinations.

[P4] Public health groups will assert that 11.5 lb/ton clinker for SO2 is likely insufficient to protect air quality and visibility and request a more stringent limit comparable to best-performing kilns nationally.

[P5] Industry will note that averaging NOX over a rolling 30-day period may hide short-term spikes and request either an additional 1-hour or 24-hour limit or continuous emissions monitoring (CEM) requirements tied to lb/hr or ppm.

[P5] State regulators will request explicit measurement methodology and conversion factors for computing lb/ton clinker for NOX from CEMs (which report ppm or lb/MMBtu), to ensure consistent compliance calculations.

[P6] Oldcastle (Trident) will challenge the PM limit of 0.77 lb/ton clinker as inconsistent with performance of their kiln configuration and ask for an allowance for process-specific baselines or an alternative compliance pathway (e.g., work practice standard).

[P6] Small cement producers will argue that compliance costs to meet 0.77 lb/ton could be disproportionate and request an economic impact assessment and consideration of financial assistance or longer compliance timeline.

[P7] Oldcastle will request documentation and technical basis for the 1.3 lb/ton SO2 limit, including whether fuel switching, fuel sulfur caps, or flue gas desulfurization was assumed, and whether monitoring requirements are feasible.

[P7] Legal commenters will question whether the SO2 limit aligns with the State Implementation Plan (SIP) and existing Title V permit terms; they will request clarification on permit modification procedures to implement the new limit.

[P8] Oldcastle will request clarity on the NOX averaging period (the provision references rolling 30-day elsewhere but should explicitly state it here) and whether seasonal variations (e.g., startup/shutdown) have separate provisions.

[P8] Industry will request allowance for predictive emissions monitoring systems (PEMS) in lieu of CEMs or lb/ton calculations, and request EPA accept alternative monitoring demonstrated equivalent.

[P9] Owners/operators will request that the rule specify how compliance obligations interact with existing Title V, NSR, and regional haze plan obligations, asking for a clear sequencing and preventing duplicative obligations.

[P9] Environmental groups will assert that labeling these units as BART sources triggers best available retrofit technology and that the rule must specify if further controls beyond the numeric limits are required should visibility improvements be inadequate.

[P10] Industry will object to the PM compliance deadline of November 17, 2012, as retroactive and unachievable (given current date); they will request updated, realistic deadlines consistent with time needed for procurement, permitting, and installation.

[P10] Legal counsel will point out that requiring compliance by a past date (2012) creates legal uncertainty and request the Agency to amend deadlines to prospective dates and provide transition relief.

[P11] Owners/operators will request clarification of the April 16, 2013 SO2/NOX deadline vs. the extended date, and ask for criteria the Agency will use to determine whether "additional controls must be installed" to qualify for the October 18, 2017 extension.

[P11] Project planners will request that if the later deadline applies, the rule explicitly allow timeline extensions for permitting delays, supply chain disruptions, or force majeure events for controls installation.

[P12] Environmental NGOs will oppose the long alternate compliance date (October 18, 2017) as undermining near-term visibility goals and request the Agency require interim emission reductions during the installation period.

[P12] Industry will request that the rule define "installation of additional emission controls" (e.g., physical installation commencement vs. startup) to avoid disputes over when the extended deadline applies.

[P13] Owners/operators will request that EPA allow stack testing frequency adjustments based on source performance history (e.g., biennial testing for consistently compliant sources) rather than mandatory annual tests.

[P13] Testing labs will request the provision specify acceptable EPA methods (method numbers) for PM testing during annual performance tests to avoid ambiguity and ensure valid data.

[P2] Industry commenters (ranchers, developers) will argue that the requirement for "well-drained sandy soil overlying strata of sandstone or indurated caliche" is overly narrow and may exclude nearby suitable habitats due to natural soil heterogeneity, leading to unnecessary land-use restrictions on adjacent private lands.

[P2] Agricultural stakeholders will claim the soil-layer specification (sand over sandstone/caliche) lacks clear survey protocols and thresholds (e.g., minimum sand depth, percent sand) so landowners cannot determine whether their property meets the criterion, creating uncertainty and regulatory burden.

[P3] Conservation scientists will claim that requiring "high soil gypsum concentration" without defining "high" (quantitative ppm or percent thresholds) makes the provision unworkable and legally vulnerable to challenge for vagueness.

[P3] Mining and mineral interests will argue that the inclusion of gypsum-rich areas as required habitat effectively precludes gypsum extraction on otherwise leaseable lands and constitutes an uncompensated taking risk.

[P4] Regional land managers and border-state officials will assert that restricting critical habitat to "open savannas and grasslands of the Tamaulipan shrubland ecological region" fails to recognize transitional or degraded habitats that can be restored and used for recovery, thereby limiting adaptive conservation opportunities.

[P4] Ecological restoration NGOs will state that excluding non‑Tamaulipan grasslands or historically altered areas prevents proactive restoration on marginal or recovering sites that could expand habitat connectivity.

[P5] Beekeeping associations and pollinator researchers will support the vegetation/pollinator requirement but will criticize the absence of metrics (e.g., minimum species richness, floral density, or bee/wasp population benchmarks) to implement and monitor compliance.

[P5] Agricultural pesticide applicators will claim the "healthy populations of native bee and wasp species" criterion may be used to challenge routine pesticide applications without a clear standard linking pesticide use to measurable pollinator health impacts.

[P6] Ranching and invasive species managers will contend that the "<20% cover of Pennisetum ciliare (buffelgrass)" threshold is arbitrary, not based on site-specific impact studies, and may be difficult to measure consistently over time (e.g., perennial tussock structure vs. percent cover).

[P6] Invasive species NGOs will argue the 20% buffelgrass cap is too lenient and should be lower or require active eradication programs in designated habitat to prevent fire regime changes that threaten Asclepias prostrata.

[P1] Legal experts will claim that listing highly specific physical and biological features in §17.96(a)(2) without delineating methods for field verification or dispute resolution invites administrative appeals and litigation over designation boundaries.

[P7] Private landowners and municipal planners will assert that excluding "manmade structures and the land on which they [sit]" is ambiguous as to whether surrounding yards, easements, or semi-developed parcels are included, creating regulatory uncertainty for redevelopment projects.

[P7] Infrastructure agencies (transportation, utilities) will request clarification that rights-of-way, pipelines, and linear infrastructure corridors are excluded only to the footprint of the structure and not to associated undeveloped corridor lands, to avoid unintended restrictions on maintenance.

[P8] Public interest groups will praise the permission to obtain field office location information but will request additional contact options (email, phone list) and faster electronic access to minimize delays in obtaining guidance.

[P9] Advocacy organizations and small stakeholders will claim that limiting submission methods to the listed options may disadvantage those without reliable internet access or familiarity with docket numbers and ask for expanded, plain‑language instructions and alternative submission pathways.

[P11] Frequent commenters and legal advocates will point out that the requirement to use the Federal e-Rulemaking Portal and to enter NOAA–NMFS–2022–0009 creates a single point of failure; they will request confirmation that submissions sent to agency staff via email referencing the docket will be accepted.

[P12] Community groups will object to the strict statement that comments sent by other methods or late "may not be considered," requesting a grace period or explicit administrative discretion to accept comments received shortly after the deadline or by alternative means in documented hardship cases.

[P10] Citizen commenters and civic groups will claim the March 2, 2022 deadline provides an insufficient comment window given the technical nature of the habitat criteria and request an extension of at least 60–90 days.

[P13] Privacy advocates will object to permitting anonymous comments while simultaneously warning that asking commenters to enter "N/A" offers little protection if other metadata (IP addresses) are retained, and will request explicit assurances about handling anonymity.

[P14] Small businesses and individuals will warn that the disclosure statement that personal identifying and sensitive information "will be publicly accessible" may deter participation and request a process for redaction of sensitive business data and addresses from public dockets.

[P15] Environmental organizations will request proactive public posting of the draft Framework 34, draft EA, and IRFA in machine-readable formats and that notice include summaries and maps of economic impact assumptions to allow meaningful review.

[P15] Fishing industry stakeholders will demand that all supporting documents cited as "available upon request and via the internet" be posted directly in the docket, not only "upon request," to ensure equal access to affected parties.

[P16] Fisheries management groups will object that committing to implement Framework 34 measures "as close as possible to April 1, 2022" without specifying how much later is acceptable creates planning uncertainty for quota holders and request a firm implementation deadline or interim guidance.

[P17] Commercial fishers will point out that the conditional statement that default allocation measures will take effect if implementation occurs after April 1 transfers risk to participants and may produce unfair economic outcomes; they will request exemptions or transitional relief if allocations change mid‑season.

[P1] Academics and botanists will request that the rule include a clear monitoring and adaptive-management protocol tied to the listed physical and biological features so that designated critical habitat can be updated in response to new science.

[P3] Soil scientists will request the rule include standardized soil-sampling depths, laboratory methods, and gypsum concentration thresholds for consistent application across sites.

[P6] Fire-management agencies will warn that buffelgrass cover can be highly patchy and seasonally variable, and will request guidance on temporal sampling windows and mapping methods to determine percent cover for enforcement.

[P4] Border security officials will request clarification whether existing border control activities within Tamaulipan shrubland will be exempted from critical habitat restrictions, or whether operations may require additional consultation, given national-security implications.

[P7] Real estate and land title professionals will ask for clarification that manmade structures in existence as of the rule's effective date are excluded, and whether future expansions or conversions of structures would bring land back into the critical habitat designation.

[P14] Trade associations will request an explicit procedure for submitting confidential business information (CBI) and an agency commitment to withhold commercially sensitive data from the public docket consistent with FOIA exemptions.

[P10] Legal clinics and public defenders will note the March 2, 2022 deadline appears inconsistent with typical 60-day public comment periods for rules of comparable complexity and will request the agency justify the shortened timeline under the Administrative Procedure Act.

[P1] The phrase "best available scientific and commercial information" in § 424.11(b) is too vague and invites arbitrary decisionmaking; the rule should define what constitutes "best available" and require disclosure of excluded data and reasons for exclusion.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether socioeconomic or industry-proprietary data qualify as "commercial information" and how confidentiality claims will be weighed against transparency under § 424.11(b).

[P2] § 424.11(c) places an implicit burden on petitioners and the Services to have comprehensive data — the rule should specify standards of evidence (e.g., statistical significance, confidence intervals) required to conclude a species "meets the definition" of endangered or threatened.

[P2] The requirement to base listings on "best scientific and commercial data available" could be used to delay listings by claiming insufficient data; the rule should add a presumption in favor of precaution when data are uncertain.

[P3] The text of § 424.11(c)(1) treats habitat modification as a factor but does not require quantitative thresholds (e.g., percent habitat loss, fragmentation metrics); commenters request that the rule require the Services to document and use quantitative habitat-loss thresholds when relying on this factor.

[P3] Industry commenters will be concerned that the broad formulation of "modification" in § 424.11(c)(1) could include routine land management; the rule should clarify that only modification that meaningfully impairs reproduction, survival, or resiliency supports listing.

[P4] § 424.11(c)(2) uses the term "overutilization" without distinguishing between sustainable use and unsustainable use; the rule should require demonstration that utilization is causing population-level declines before it can support listing.

[P4] Commercial fishing and timber industry stakeholders will argue that § 424.11(c)(2) must account for regulated, sustainable harvests and require the Services to consider management plans and quotas before treating use as a threat.

[P5] The inclusion of "disease or predation" in § 424.11(c)(3) as a standalone factor could lead to listing species affected by natural predator-prey dynamics; the rule should require evidence that such disease/predation is outside historical/expected ranges or exacerbated by human activity.

[P5] Wildlife managers will note the provision lacks guidance on attributing disease to anthropogenic causes (e.g., introduced pathogens) versus natural cycles; clarify standards for when disease/predation justify listings.

[P6] § 424.11(c)(4)'s "inadequacy of existing regulatory mechanisms" is open-ended; states and regulated entities request that the rule enumerate what constitutes "inadequate" (e.g., lack of enforceable measures, expired permits, insufficient coverage).

[P6] Legal commenters will point out that assessing regulatory inadequacy should require a showing that existing mechanisms are unlikely to reduce threats to levels compatible with species persistence, and the rule should require documented analysis of enforcement capacity.

[P7] The catch-all "other natural or manmade factors" in § 424.11(c)(5) is too broad and could encompass speculative threats (e.g., climate change projections without probabilistic assessment); the rule should require causal linkage and quantification before using this factor.

[P8] § 424.11(d) requires analysis of likelihood of becoming endangered within the "foreseeable future" but lacks a clear burden-of-proof standard (e.g., "likely," "probable"); commenters recommend adopting a specific probability threshold or clarifying how qualitative judgments should be documented.

[P9] The case-by-case description of "foreseeable future" in § 424.11(d) is appropriate, but the Services must be required to document the time horizons considered, the data supporting them, and sensitivity analyses showing how conclusions change with different time frames.

[P10] Allowing the Services to avoid specifying a concrete time period for the "foreseeable future" (§ 424.11(d)) undermines predictability; regulated parties request that the rule require the Services to provide an explicit numeric time horizon or a range whenever possible.

[P10] Conservation groups will argue that permitting non-specific foreseeability determinations could allow agencies to shrink time horizons to avoid listings; the rule should prohibit using artificially short timeframes that ignore long-term trends.

[P11] § 424.11(e) ties delisting to a status review "based on the best available data" but does not set minimum review intervals; stakeholders request mandatory periodic reviews (e.g., every 5 years) and timelines for delisting decisions once recovery criteria are met.

[P12] The criterion for delisting based on extinction (§ 424.11(e)(1)) requires clear standards for declaring extinction (e.g., survey effort, geographic coverage); the rule should adopt explicit survey protocols and burden of proof to avoid premature delisting.

[P13] § 424.11(e)(2) allows delisting when a species "does not meet the definition" of endangered or threatened — legal commenters request clarification that delisting requires demonstration that threats have been eliminated or reduced below statutory thresholds, not merely population increases in limited areas.

[P14] Requiring the same factors/standards in paragraph (c) for delisting (§ 424.11(e)(2)) is sensible, but the rule should require the Services to explain how recovered conditions satisfy each of the (c) factors and provide monitoring plans to ensure persistence post-delisting.

[P15] The delisting ground that the "listed entity is not a species" (§ 424.11(e)(3)) could be used to delist taxa after taxonomic revisions; commenters urge that taxonomic controversies should be resolved conservatively, with delisting only when there is robust peer-reviewed evidence and not solely on unpublished assessments.

[P16] § 424.11(f) permits treating CITES or similar protections as evidence a species is endangered or threatened; foreign governments and trade groups request clarity on how international listings will be evaluated and whether differing criteria (e.g., CITES Appendix II) will be equated to ESA status.

[P16] Conservation NGOs will argue that the Services should give substantial weight to CITES listings and State/foreign protections as triggers for prompt ESA protections, not merely "consideration" under § 424.11(f).

[P17] The obligation in § 424.11(f) to "give consideration" to species protected internationally or by States/foreign nations should require the Services to document how those protections influenced decisions, including any differences in criteria and enforcement.

[P18] § 424.11(g) requires considering conservation efforts by States and foreign nations when making listing/delisting decisions; commenters request that the rule specify how the existence, enforceability, and funding stability of these efforts will be evaluated and weighted.

[P18] Industry groups caution that relying on State or foreign conservation actions (§ 424.11(g)) should not substitute for federal protections unless those measures are legally binding, enforceable, and demonstrably effective; the rule should set minimum standards.

[P19] § 424.12(a)(1) gives the Secretary discretion to decide that a critical habitat designation is not prudent; conservation organizations will object and request that the rule limit this discretion and require formal justification and public review when prudency is declined.

[P20] The circumstance in § 424.12(a)(1)(i) that identification could increase threats is legitimate for sensitive species, but the rule should require clear evidence (e.g., documented illegal collection tied to maps) and limit secrecy to narrowly defined cases with periodic reassessment.

[P21] § 424.12(a)(1)(ii) allows non-prudency where habitat threats are not addressable by section 7(a)(2); however, commenters note that many threats can be addressed indirectly through consultation or voluntary measures; the Services should be required to document why section 7 measures are ineffective before declining to designate.

[P22] The "negligible conservation value" provision (§ 424.12(a)(1)(iii)) could be abused to avoid designating critical habitat for species that use transboundary or marginal U.S. habitats; the rule should require a quantitative analysis of U.S. contribution to global population persistence before invoking this ground.

[P23] § 424.12(a)(1)(iv) that "no areas meet the definition" must require the Services to publish the criteria used to determine whether areas meet the statutory critical habitat definition and to provide maps and analyses demonstrating why no areas qualify.

[P24] The catch-all § 424.12(a)(1)(v) allowing non-prudency "after analyzing the best scientific data" is overly broad; commenters want a requirement that such determinations undergo peer review and a formal public notice-and-comment process.

[P25] § 424.12(b)(2) permits designating unoccupied areas only if "essential" and at an "appropriate" scale determined by the Secretary; landowners and states request criteria for "essential" and constraints on how broad an "appropriate" scale can be (e.g., must relate directly to species life-history needs).

[P26] The requirement in § 424.12(b)(2) to first evaluate occupied areas is sensible, but the rule should mandate documentation showing why occupied areas are insufficient before unoccupied areas are designated.

[P27] The condition that unoccupied areas be considered essential only if designating only occupied areas would be inadequate or less efficient (§ 424.12(b)(2)) requires a comparative analysis; commenters request that the Services be required to produce and publish that comparative analysis and alternatives considered.

[P28] § 424.12(b)(2) requires a "reasonable likelihood" that an unoccupied area will contribute to conservation, but the rule fails to define "reasonable likelihood"; commenters suggest specifying a required probability range (e.g., >50% projected occupancy under defined scenarios) or modeling standards.

[P28] Conservation scientists will argue that "reasonable likelihood" determinations should be supported by transparent population viability analyses or habitat suitability models using peer-reviewed methods and publicly available data.

raw_output:
[P1] The establishment of multiple new restricted areas (R-2201A through R-2201J) concentrated around Fort Greely will significantly constrict low-altitude VFR corridor options for general aviation and flightseeing operators in the region; the rule fails to quantify expected lost access or propose mitigation.

[P2] The lateral boundary coordinates for R-2201A following Jarvis Creek are ambiguous because only three points are listed; commenters should request inclusion of the full polygon or a chart inset so pilots can determine exact boundaries and avoid inadvertent incursions.

[P3] Setting vertical limits of R-2201A from the surface to but not including 6,000 feet MSL will effectively prohibit all small fixed-wing and rotorcraft operations within the footprint during active times; the socioeconomic impacts on local operators were not analyzed.

[P4] Designating R-2201A active weekdays 0700–1900 local without weekend baseline protection alters normal civil flight patterns and will disrupt scheduled cargo and medevac flights that operate outside those hours; the rule should preserve essential civil flight exemptions.

[P5] Assigning FAA Anchorage ARTCC as the controlling agency for R-2201A without specifying procedures for real-time coordination between ARTCC and local flight service stations creates an operational gap that could delay approvals or create unsafe conflicts.

[P6] Designating USARAK (Commanding General, JBER) as the using agency for all restricted areas (A–J) without clarifying what missions trigger activation (e.g., live-fire, training flights, missile tests) is too vague; commenters will request specific activity types, frequency, and duration limits.

[P7] Establishing R-2201B with lateral coordinates following Granite Creek but supplying only three vertex points is insufficient for charting; the FAA should publish a GeoJSON/KML and include depiction on sectional and IFR charts.

[P8] Vertical limits for R-2201B from surface to but not including 6,000 feet MSL duplicate restrictions in R-2201A and will create overlapping low-altitude restricted space that could confuse pilots about safe VFR routes; request clarification on overlaps and lateral separation.

[P9] The weekday 0700–1900 activation period for R-2201B will conflict with scheduled aerial surveys and utility operations that frequently require daytime access; commenters representing those industries will request specific provisions for mission-specific exemptions or pre-coordination procedures.

[P10] FAA Anchorage ARTCC is named controlling agency for R-2201B but no communications frequencies, coordination points, or NOTAM formatting instructions are provided; operators need those operational details in the rule or an associated FAA order.

[P11] Assigning USARAK as the using agency for R-2201B without specifying safety requirements (e.g., transponder requirements, mandatory flight-following) risks inconsistent enforcement; stakeholders will request uniform minimum equipage and procedural standards.

[P12] Establishing R-2201C with lateral coordinates following Granite Creek again lists only three coordinates; small discrepancies in coordinate precision could produce large lateral errors in Alaska’s high-latitude mapping — request use of decimal degrees to six decimals and datum specification (NAD83/WGS84).

[P13] The vertical limits for R-2201C are inconsistent between provisions: some say surface to 6,000, others (P65/P69) say 6,000 to 11,000 MSL; commenters will demand correction and a single authoritative altitudinal range to avoid airspace classification errors.

[P14] Requiring R-2201C designation via NOTAM only (4 hours in advance) removes a predictable schedule for users and could force last-minute reroutes for commercial and general aviation; request a standing weekly schedule or advance published activation calendar for planned training.

[P15] Designating FAA Anchorage ARTCC as controller for R-2201C without addressing remote contingency control during outages (e.g., weather, communications) leaves uncertainty — commenters will ask for contingency control procedures and alternate contact points.

[P16] Using USARAK as the using agency for R-2201C without requiring safety risk management documentation or environmental impact assessments for sorties within the restricted area is procedurally deficient; request disclosure of risk mitigation measures and NEPA analysis.

[P17] For R-2201D, the lateral coordinates mirror R-2201A (Jarvis Creek) creating potential spatial overlaps among R-2201 segments; commenters will ask for a consolidated map showing all R-2201 series boundaries and identification of any overlaps or gaps.

[P18] The vertical limits for R-2201D are listed as 6,000 to 15,000 MSL in some items and 6,000 to 11,000 in others (P21 vs P69); this inconsistency must be resolved because it affects IFR routing, approach/departure procedures, and ARTCC responsibilities.

[P19] R-2201D’s weekday activation 0700–1900 with other times by NOTAM (4-hour notice) could preclude emergency medical flights at lower altitudes if NOTAM coordination delays clearance; request an explicit exemption process for emergency flights and medevac operations.

[P20] Naming FAA Anchorage ARTCC as controlling agency for R-2201D without specifying required coordination lead times between USARAK and ARTCC when activating by NOTAM may lead to missed 4-hour windows or confusion; request minimum lead-time and point-of-contact requirements.

[P21] Establishing R-2201E with lateral coordinates following Granite Creek duplicates concerns regarding mapping precision; stakeholders will request inclusion of legal descriptions and public access to GIS files and chart insets.

[P22] Vertical limits for R-2201E listed as 6,000 to 15,000 MSL (P27) but other provisions list different upper limits for adjacent sectors; commenters from the commercial aviation community ask for assurance there will be no negative impacts on low-altitude IFR routes or en route traffic flows.

[P23] The 0700–1900 Monday–Friday activation schedule across R-2201E (and all R-2201 areas) does not account for seasonal variations in daylight in Alaska; request that activation times be adjustable seasonally or tied to UTC to avoid unintended nighttime restrictions.

[P24] FAA Anchorage ARTCC is repeatedly named as controlling agency for R-2201E–J; however, Anchorage ARTCC’s workload and resources are not addressed — request statement on capacity, staffing, and training to manage these new restricted areas.

[P25] Using agency designation of USARAK for R-2201E and other areas without requiring publication of a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) between FAA and USARAK detailing activation procedures, responsibilities, and safety standards is inadequate; stakeholders will request an MOA before final rule.

[P26] Establishing R-2201F boundaries again with only three coordinates without explicitly stating polygon closure points increases risk of misinterpretation; request complete vertex list and depiction on appropriate aeronautical charts.

[P27] Vertical limits for R-2201F (6,000–15,000 MSL) may interfere with military training routes (MTRs) and civilian IFR traffic; request an analysis of impacts on existing MTRs, airway structure, and IFR minimum en route altitudes.

[P28] Recurrent requirement that NOTAMs be issued at least 4 hours in advance for activations in many sectors (P57, P62, P66, P70) may not be sufficient to protect both safety and operational flexibility for USARAK and civil operators; suggest alternatives such as 24-hour planning windows for scheduled activations and emergency immediate activations with defined protocols.

[P29] Assigning R-2201G altitudes from 15,000 MSL to FL220 creates a large upper layer of restricted airspace that may conflict with regional high-altitude routes used by turboprops and business jets; request traffic flow analysis and potential lateral reroutes or altitudinal reallocations.

[P30] The 15,000 MSL lower limit for R-2201G could push transiting aircraft into congested adjacent airspace or higher altitudes with fuel and performance penalties; request cost-impact analysis for affected operators.

[P31] Requiring NOTAM activation for R-2201G (0700–1900 M–F baseline) without indicating whether the restricted area will ever be used concurrently with adjacent R-2201 segments could create vertically stacked, concurrently active restricted volumes — request clarification on whether multiple segments may be active simultaneously and procedures for cross-segment coordination.

[P32] Designating R-2201H with 15,000–FL220 limits raises questions about interaction with domestic en route ATC routes and the presence of RNAV routes; request FAA to publish affected airway charts and propose reroutes if necessary.

[P33] The using agency being USARAK for R-2201H–J without disclosure of the types of weapon systems or activities anticipated (e.g., ballistic missile testing, air defense) raises environmental and public safety questions; request public disclosure of planned activities or a categorical exclusion justification.

[P34] Multiple provisions repeat control by FAA Anchorage ARTCC but do not indicate whether control includes issuance of clearances to enter the restricted area for civil aircraft under ATC control; request explicit language on when civil aircraft may be granted transit through inactive or active restricted areas.

[P35] The rule’s repetition of conflicting altitudinal bands across R-2201A–J (e.g., references to 6,000–11,000 MSL in some clauses and 6,000–15,000 in others) appears to contain drafting errors that could lead to unsafe operations; request a consolidated corrected table of altitudes.

[P36] The 4-hour NOTAM activation requirement for many segments does not include a maximum activation duration or required deactivation notifications; commenters will ask for limits on continuous activation time and mandatory deactivation NOTAMs to restore civil access.

[P37] There is no mention of procedures for GA flight schools or parachute operations in the area to obtain waivers or training windows; local aviation businesses request a formal waiver/approval process and contact procedures.

[P38] The proposed rule does not reference NEPA or environmental review for establishing these restricted areas over ecologically sensitive lands near Fort Greely (e.g., impacts on wildlife and subsistence activities); Tribal governments and environmental NGOs will request an environmental assessment or categorical exclusion documentation.

[P39] Local governments and airports were not identified as consulted parties; municipal commenters will request documentation of intergovernmental coordination and an analysis of economic impacts on local communities and tourism operators.

[P40] Emergency services (air ambulances, search and rescue) require guaranteed access; the rule must explicitly state that emergency flights retain priority access and the procedure to obtain immediate entry when areas are active.

[P41] The rule lacks a defined appeals or dispute resolution process if a civil operator believes ARTCC improperly denied access; legal commenters will request an appeal mechanism and timeline.

[P42] The using agency designation for USARAK is broad and does not require notification to pilots about specific training hazards (e.g., pyrotechnics, surface-to-air activity); request mandatory hazard advisories in NOTAM text.

[P43] There is no mention of required transponder or ADS-B equipage when transiting adjacent airspace near active restricted areas; ADS-B rule compliance and recommendations should be stated to enhance situational awareness and safety.

[P44] The effective times tied to local time can be confusing in Alaska where multiple time zones and daylight-saving observance vary; commenters suggest using UTC times in the regulatory text to avoid misinterpretation.

[P45] The designation of restricted areas with surface boundaries will affect landowners beneath the airspace; property owners and hunters may be impacted by low-altitude overflights being prohibited — request outreach to local stakeholders and compensation analysis where appropriate.

[P46] The proposed rule does not state whether temporary flight restrictions (TFRs) will be used in conjunction with these restricted areas; operators want clarity on how TFRs and restricted areas will interact and which takes precedence.

[P47] Charting lead times are not addressed: stakeholders need assurance that sectional, IFR en route, and special use airspace publications will be updated with adequate lead time before the effective date to avoid pilot confusion.

[P48] The rule should clarify whether pipeline patrols, wildlife surveys, and powerline inspections operating under FAA-authorized exemptions will maintain access or be required to obtain special clearances from ARTCC; industry groups will request streamlined coordination procedures.

[P49] The proposed text repeatedly states “other times by NOTAM” but later items specify “NOTAM 4 hours in advance”; commenters will ask the FAA to harmonize and standardize all NOTAM lead-time requirements across the R-2201 complex.

[P50] Legal experts will note that creating restricted areas that stack across multiple altitude blocks (surface–6k, 6k–15k, 15k–FL220) constitutes complex airspace redesign and requires justification demonstrating necessity and no reasonable less restrictive alternative; request that FAA provide that justification in the rulemaking record.

Requiring NOTAM activation for R-2201G (0700–1900 M–F baseline) without indicating whether the restricted area will ever be used concurrently with adjacent R-2201 segments could create vertically stacked, concurrently active restricted volumes — request clarification on whether multiple segments may be active simultaneously and procedures for cross-segment coordination.

Designating R-2201H with 15,000–FL220 limits raises questions about interaction with domestic en route ATC routes and the presence of RNAV routes; request FAA to publish affected airway charts and propose reroutes if necessary.

The using agency being USARAK for R-2201H–J without disclosure of the types of weapon systems or activities anticipated (e.g., ballistic missile testing, air defense) raises environmental and public safety questions; request public disclosure of planned activities or a categorical exclusion justification.

Multiple provisions repeat control by FAA Anchorage ARTCC but do not indicate whether control includes issuance of clearances to enter the restricted area for civil aircraft under ATC control; request explicit language on when civil aircraft may be granted transit through inactive or active restricted areas.

The rule’s repetition of conflicting altitudinal bands across R-2201A–J (e.g., references to 6,000–11,000 MSL in some clauses and 6,000–15,000 in others) appears to contain drafting errors that could lead to unsafe operations; request a consolidated corrected table of altitudes.

The 4-hour NOTAM activation requirement for many segments does not include a maximum activation duration or required deactivation notifications; commenters will ask for limits on continuous activation time and mandatory deactivation NOTAMs to restore civil access.

There is no mention of procedures for GA flight schools or parachute operations in the area to obtain waivers or training windows; local aviation businesses request a formal waiver/approval process and contact procedures.

The proposed rule does not reference NEPA or environmental review for establishing these restricted areas over ecologically sensitive lands near Fort Greely (e.g., impacts on wildlife and subsistence activities); Tribal governments and environmental NGOs will request an environmental assessment or categorical exclusion documentation.

Local governments and airports were not identified as consulted parties; municipal commenters will request documentation of intergovernmental coordination and an analysis of economic impacts on local communities and tourism operators.

Emergency services (air ambulances, search and rescue) require guaranteed access; the rule must explicitly state that emergency flights retain priority access and the procedure to obtain immediate entry when areas are active.
The rule lacks a defined appeals or dispute resolution process if a civil operator believes ARTCC improperly denied access; legal commenters will request an appeal mechanism and timeline.

The using agency designation for USARAK is broad and does not require notification to pilots about specific training hazards (e.g., pyrotechnics, surface-to-air activity); request mandatory hazard advisories in NOTAM text.

There is no mention of required transponder or ADS-B equipage when transiting adjacent airspace near active restricted areas; ADS-B rule compliance and recommendations should be stated to enhance situational awareness and safety.

The effective times tied to local time can be confusing in Alaska where multiple time zones and daylight-saving observance vary; commenters suggest using UTC times in the regulatory text to avoid misinterpretation.

The designation of restricted areas with surface boundaries will affect landowners beneath the airspace; property owners and hunters may be impacted by low-altitude overflights being prohibited — request outreach to local stakeholders and compensation analysis where appropriate.

The proposed rule does not state whether temporary flight restrictions (TFRs) will be used in conjunction with these restricted areas; operators want clarity on how TFRs and restricted areas will interact and which takes precedence.

Charting lead times are not addressed: stakeholders need assurance that sectional, IFR en route, and special use airspace publications will be updated with adequate lead time before the effective date to avoid pilot confusion.

The rule should clarify whether pipeline patrols, wildlife surveys, and powerline inspections operating under FAA-authorized exemptions will maintain access or be required to obtain special clearances from ARTCC; industry groups will request streamlined coordination procedures.

The proposed text repeatedly states “other times by NOTAM” but later items specify “NOTAM 4 hours in advance”; commenters will ask the FAA to harmonize and standardize all NOTAM lead-time requirements across the R-2201 complex.

Legal experts will note that creating restricted areas that stack across multiple altitude blocks (surface–6k, 6k–15k, 15k–FL220) constitutes complex airspace redesign and requires justification demonstrating necessity and no reasonable less restrictive alternative; request that FAA provide that justification in the rulemaking record.

[P1] The 60% cellulose-based fiber threshold in § 205.2 is too low to ensure meaningful compostability and soil incorporation; stakeholders representing composters and environmental NGOs will request raising the minimum to 80–100% cellulose for true biodegradability in field conditions.

[P1] The definition of "cellulose-based fiber" in § 205.2 is ambiguous and should specify included and excluded materials (e.g., pulp from agricultural residues, wood pulp, cotton linters) to avoid inconsistent enforcement and market confusion.

[P1] Seed companies and nursery growers will request clarity that coatings, labels, or plant ID tags attached to pots are excluded from the weight calculation of cellulose-based fiber to avoid penalizing common commercial practices.

[P1] Municipal composting operators will comment that the rule should require demonstration of breakdown in standard municipal/industrial composting conditions (time/temperature) because "suited to placement in or on the soil" is vague and may allow non-degrading products.

[P2] Allowing up to 40% nonsynthetic or certain synthetics under § 205.2 creates a loophole that could permit significant non-biodegradable synthetic-strengthening fibers (e.g., polypropylene) if misclassified; commenters will request a clear prohibition on conventional plastics and numeric limits on synthetic-strengthening fiber types.

[P2] Industry manufacturers will support the 40% allowance in § 205.2 as necessary to maintain product strength and usability, but will request an explicit list of permitted synthetic strengthening components and permitted adhesives to enable product development and certification.

[P2] Certification bodies and legal experts will ask that § 205.2 require suppliers to document and provide chain-of-custody declarations for any permitted synthetic ingredients used in the 40% allowance to ensure traceability and compliance.

[P3] The 80% biobased content requirement in § 205.2 is redundant with the 60% cellulose rule and may conflict with the 40% allowance in P2; commenters will request reconciliation (explain how both thresholds apply together) and a clear method for calculating weight- vs. carbon-based biobased content.

[P3] Testing burden: Small manufacturers will object that requiring third-party ASTM D6866 testing for 80% biobased verification imposes high cost and turnaround time; they will request alternative verification pathways such as supplier declarations, mass balance methods, or tiered/periodic testing.

[P3] Legal and standards organizations will request that the rule explicitly name acceptable test methods beyond ASTM D6866 (e.g., ISO equivalents) and define acceptable laboratories and accreditation requirements for "qualified third-party assessment" to avoid inconsistent interpretation.

[P4] Seed and pot manufacturers will seek clarification on how added nutrients in the material are evaluated under §§ 205.105, 205.203, and 205.206 — specifically whether trace micronutrient treatments used in seed-starting media are considered "added nutrients" and whether they trigger additional certification burdens.

[P4] Organic growers' associations will urge the agency to prohibit any added nutrients that are synthetic or not allowed under §§ 205.105, 205.203, and 205.206 to prevent contamination risks; they will request explicit language banning nonallowed nutrient fortification in paper-based planting aids.

[P4] Fertilizer manufacturers will ask for a clear compliance pathway when materials include permitted organic nutrient sources (e.g., compost or manure extracts), including documentation and limits, to avoid inconsistent denial of materials.

[P5] Mushroom growers will support the permission in § 205.601(o)(1) allowing microcrystalline cheesewax for log-grown mushroom production but will request guidance on acceptable application rates and any residue tolerance in harvested mushrooms.

[P5] Food safety advocates will request data demonstrating that microcrystalline cheesewax (CAS numbers listed) does not introduce food-safety hazards or undesirable residues in edible log-grown mushrooms and may ask for a maximum allowable residual concentration or application method restrictions.

[P6] Industry commenters will point out that banning ethylene-propylene co-polymer and synthetic colors in the cheesewax (P6) is enforceable only if composition testing is required; they will request method details and acceptable detection thresholds for these prohibited components.

[P6] Manufacturers of specialized wax formulations will ask for an explicit definition of "synthetic colors" (e.g., by CAS number or regulatory definitions) and whether naturally derived pigments processed with synthetic aids are considered synthetic colors under § 205.601(o)(1).

[P7] Seed-start retailers and greenhouse operators will welcome the permission for paper-based crop planting aids in § 205.601(o)(2) but will request explicit examples of covered products (seed tape, peat pots, paper plugs) to ensure consistent certification.

[P7] Environmental NGOs will praise allowing paper-based planting aids but will request that the allowance include requirements that materials be compostable in field or municipal compost systems within a specified timeframe (e.g., 12–24 months) to prevent persistent litter.

[P8] The restriction that paper must be virgin or recycled and not glossy or contain colored inks (§ 205.601(o)(2)) will be criticized by recycled-paper suppliers as overly restrictive because some post-consumer recycled papers contain small amounts of inks or coatings; they will request thresholds (e.g., <0.5% colored ink by weight) rather than absolute prohibitions.

[P8] Paper manufacturers will request clarity on what constitutes "glossy paper" (e.g., coated vs. uncoated, weight and coating specifications) and whether water-based varnishes or low-gloss coatings are permitted to ensure usable product options.

[P8] Certification bodies will ask for test methods and tolerances for detecting colored inks and glossy coatings to provide consistent determinations at certification time.

[P9] Processed-food manufacturers will support allowing nonsynthetic wood rosin (§ 205.605(a)) but will ask for labeling guidance and maximum use levels in 'organic' or 'made with organic' products to prevent misuse and consumer deception.

[P9] Consumer advocacy groups will request safety and allergen assessments for wood rosin used as a nonagricultural ingredient, including potential migration into food and any interactions with other ingredients, and may ask for clearance from FDA or independent toxicologists.

[P9] Resin suppliers will ask whether "wood rosin" includes derivatives or processed forms and request an explicit definition/CAS range to permit supply chain planning and certification.

[P10] Food manufacturers and ingredient suppliers will support allowing low-acyl gellan gum (§ 205.605(b)) but will request specification of permitted functional classes (e.g., gelling agent only) and maximum use levels in different food categories to ensure compliance with organic labeling rules.

[P10] Organic certifiers will ask that low-acyl gellan gum be limited to uses where no organic alternative exists and require documentation that organic alternatives were considered, consistent with the nonagricultural ingredient allowance framework.

[P10] Public-interest commenters will request disclosure of the permitted sources and manufacturing aids used in low-acyl gellan gum production (e.g., solvents, synthetic crosslinkers) to ensure manufacturing processes align with organic principles and § 205.605 requirements.

[P1] The requirement to "reduce and maintain employee airborne beryllium exposure at or below the PEL and STEL" is vague because the rule text truncates the PEL/STEL values; commenters will request explicit citation of numeric PEL (µg/m3) and STEL values to avoid enforcement confusion.

[P1] Industry commenters will argue that the obligation to use engineering and work practice controls "to the extent feasible" should include a clear feasibility assessment process and documentation requirements so employers know what evidence satisfies feasibility.

[P1] Labor and health advocacy groups will claim that allowing employers to "reduce exposures to the lowest feasible levels and supplement with respiratory protection" creates a loophole that permits reliance on respirators instead of achieving engineering controls; they will request stronger language prioritizing elimination/substitution and quantitative limits on permitted respirator reliance.

[P2] Small businesses will assert that the obligation to "ensure at least one listed control is in place for each operation that releases airborne beryllium" is overly prescriptive because single controls may be insufficient for some high-emission operations; they will ask clarification whether multiple controls are required for high-exposure tasks.

[P2] Legal commenters will request clarification of what constitutes an "operation" for sampling and control application (e.g., task-level vs. process-level) to avoid inconsistent interpretation across workplaces.

[P3] Manufacturers will comment that the "material and/or process substitution" requirement (P3) lacks guidance on acceptable substitutes, their evaluation for functional performance, and the regulatory timeframe for implementing substitution when technically feasible.

[P3] Environmental/worker safety NGOs will request that substitution be required whenever a technically and economically feasible non-beryllium alternative exists, and that the rule require documented justification when substitution is rejected.

[P4] Employers in fabrication and maintenance will point out that "isolation, such as ventilated partial or full enclosures" (P4) may be impracticable for large or mobile equipment; they will request recognition of alternative engineering practices and allowance for staged implementation timelines.

[P4] Occupational hygienists will request specific design performance criteria for enclosures (e.g., capture velocities, face openings, negative pressure differential) to ensure isolation is effective and enforceable.

[P5] Facilities operating legacy equipment will assert that requiring "local exhaust ventilation at points of operation, handling, and transfer" (P5) could entail significant retrofitting costs; they will ask for phased compliance schedules and financial assistance or alternative compliance options where retrofit is not feasible.

[P5] Worker advocates will ask that the rule include minimum performance standards (airflow rates, capture velocities) and routine inspection/maintenance requirements for local exhaust systems to ensure long-term effectiveness.

[P6] Automation vendors will support the "process control, such as wet methods and automation" (P6) but request explicit criteria for when wet methods are allowed (e.g., corrosivity, electrical hazards) and standards for automation safeguards to protect workers.

[P6] Trade unions will insist that automation cannot be used to justify workforce reductions without retraining/transition provisions; they will request a requirement to consult with affected employees/unions before implementing automation as a control.

[P7] Worker safety groups will object to the broad exemption framework (P7), contending it could be abused to avoid implementing controls; they will ask for strict evidentiary standards, third‑party oversight, and administrative approval for exemptions.

[P7] Employers will request that the rule explicitly permit written judgments documenting infeasibility to be relied upon during inspections, with a standardized template to reduce disputes.

[P8] Industry commenters will assert that the infeasibility exemption (P8) needs a clear definition of "not feasible" including technical, economic, and safety factors—otherwise OSHA inspections could second-guess cost-based decisions.

[P8] Labor representatives will oppose economic feasibility as a basis for exemption and argue that infeasibility should be limited to genuine technical impossibility, not cost barriers.

[P9] Industrial hygienists will challenge the sampling-based exemption (P9) because requiring "no fewer than two representative personal breathing zone samples taken ≥7 days apart per operation" may be insufficient to characterize variability in exposures; they will request guidance on sample number calculations based on process variability and statistical confidence intervals.

[P9] Employers will request that the rule allow use of historical exposure data and equivalent representative sampling schemes (e.g., composite sampling, task-based sampling) rather than mandating two samples per operation in all circumstances.

[P9] Legal experts will ask for definition of "operation" for sampling and clarification whether pooled sampling across shifts/locations is acceptable to establish exemption under (f)(2)(iii)(B).

[P10] Maintenance and laundry service operators will seek clarification of the prohibition on removal of beryllium from contaminated PPE/equipment by "blowing, shaking, or any method that disperses beryllium into the air," requesting specific prohibited techniques and permitted cleaning alternatives to avoid overbroad enforcement.

[P10] Worker safety advocates will request that the rule explicitly prohibit the use of compressed air for cleaning PPE and mandate engineering controls (e.g., ventilated changing rooms, gloveboxes) to prevent secondary exposure.

[P11] Foodservice and manufacturing facility operators will request more prescriptive standards for ensuring eating and drinking area surfaces are "as free as practicable" of beryllium (P11), including numeric surface contamination limits, testing frequency, and acceptable cleaning methods.

[P11] Public health commenters will argue that "as free as practicable" is subjective and request that OSHA adopt conservative surface contamination thresholds tied to health-based risk estimates.

[P12] Employees and unions will support the prohibition on entering eating/drinking areas wearing contaminated PPE (P12) but request clarity on enforcement, disciplinary measures, and accommodations for short-duration breaks during shifts that may make full decontamination difficult.

[P12] Employers will ask for permitted staging areas adjacent to eating areas to remove PPE and for clear procedures for verifying surfaces are decontaminated before allowing entry.

[P13] Industrial hygiene professionals will request specification of acceptable "non-dispersive methods" for removing surface beryllium (P13) — e.g., wet wiping with HEPA-filtered ventilation, HEPA vacuuming — and whether disposable coveralls that are sealed count as compliant removal.

[P13] Small business commenters will propose that laundering services certified to remove beryllium be considered an acceptable non-dispersive method and request guidance on labeling and tracking cleaned PPE.

[P14] Employers will request that the requirement to maintain all surfaces in beryllium work and regulated areas "as free as practicable" (P14) be tied to a written and auditable exposure control plan with defined cleaning schedules based on task frequency and measured contamination levels.

[P14] Compliance officers will request explicitly that failure to follow the written exposure control plan be the enforcement trigger rather than subjective judgments about "as free as practicable."

[P15] Facilities managers will ask for criteria that define "HEPA-filtered vacuuming or other methods that minimize airborne exposure" (P15), including certification requirements for HEPA vacuums, maintenance logs, and operator training standards.

[P15] Some commenters will recommend that only certified HEPA vacuums meeting specific filtration/efficiency standards be allowed, and that vacuum exhaust must be HEPA-filtered or ducted to appropriate capture systems.

[P16] Employers will argue that the prohibition on dry sweeping or brushing (P16) should include explicit exceptions for emergency spill response where dry methods may be the only immediate option, with required follow-up HEPA cleaning.

[P16] Occupational health organizations will support the prohibition but request clarity on what constitutes "not safe or effective" to trigger the exception allowing dry sweeping/ brushing (P17), and propose a required written justification and supervisor approval when the exception is used.

[P17] Emergency response groups will ask that the exception for dry sweeping/ brushing include approved alternate methods (e.g., wetting agents, specialized vacuums) and require after-action reporting to OSHA when the exception is invoked.

[P18] Recyclers and waste management firms will request clarification on the 0.1% beryllium threshold (P18) including analytical methods, sampling protocols, and measurement uncertainty to determine whether a material meets the regulated-concentration threshold.

[P18] Environmental compliance attorneys will note that the 0.1% threshold may conflict with other federal or state hazardous waste thresholds and request harmonization or guidance on interactions.

[P19] Logistics and waste contractors will seek more detail on the labeling required for sealed, impermeable enclosures (P19), including required signal words, hazard statements, and whether DOT or RCRA marking suffices.

[P19] Hazardous materials transporters will ask whether existing hazardous waste shipping paper and container marking requirements meet this labeling obligation or whether additional beryllium-specific labels are required.

[P20] Manufacturers seeking recycling options will request clarification of the standard's expectation that materials for recycling be "cleaned to be as free as practicable" (P20), including acceptable cleaning endpoints, verification sampling, and responsibility allocation between generator and recycler.

[P20] Recyclers will propose an alternative compliance path allowing sealed containment and labeled transport to a recycler without pre-cleaning, but request clear chain-of-custody documentation requirements.

[P21] Industry will ask for prescriptive cleaning methods and validated decontamination procedures for materials designated for recycling (P21), as well as acceptance criteria (e.g., surface concentration limits) that recyclers can rely upon.

[P21] Environmental advocates will urge that cleaning for recycling must be demonstrated by post-cleaning verification sampling and records retained for OSHA inspection.

[P22] Scrap processors will support the alternative allowing sealed, impermeable labeled enclosures (P22) but request clarity on storage duration limits, transport requirements, and whether secondary containment is required during transit to recyclers.

[P22] Some commenters will request that OSHA allow use of existing industrial packaging and labeling programs (e.g., RCRA, DOT) as compliant alternatives to avoid duplicative requirements.

Environmental advocates will urge that cleaning for recycling must be demonstrated by post-cleaning verification sampling and records retained for OSHA inspection.

Some commenters will request that OSHA allow use of existing industrial packaging and labeling programs (e.g., RCRA, DOT) as compliant alternatives to avoid duplicative requirements.
