[P1] The requirement that visible nutrition information “appear on the food label itself” is ambiguous for products sold without a traditional detachable label (e.g., items in clear packaging or printed directly on packaging film); request clarification that inkjet/thermal print on packaging qualifies.

[P1] Requiring the nutrition info to appear on the label itself will be infeasible for small, single-serve manufacturers who use shrink-sleeve or heat-transfer labels that lack space for additional mandated statements without redesign; propose an alternative compliance path for small businesses.

[P1] The rule should explicitly allow vending operators to display the required visible nutrition information on the vending machine in close proximity to the product when physically placing that information on the individual product label is technically impossible (e.g., bulk-packaged or repackaged items).

[P1] The provision fails to account for repackaged foods sold in vending machines (e.g., bakery or deli items repackaged by the operator); it should permit the vending operator to place the required visible nutrition info on the repackaging wrapper/label rather than on the original manufacturer label.

[P1] Legal commenters: Requiring information to be on the “food label itself” may conflict with existing federal labeling preemption and state law variations; request analysis of preemption implications and confirmation that this federal mandate supersedes conflicting state requirements if intended.

[P2] The requirement that nutrition information be “easily read on the article of food while in the vending machine” is impractical for products stacked behind glass or placed at an angle; request guidance on acceptable viewing distance/angle and lighting conditions.

[P2] Vending machine lighting, glare, and distance vary widely; the rule should allow the use of a machine-level display or adjacent placard when the package’s location or orientation prevents clear viewing, rather than mandating label redesign.

[P2] ADA/accessibility advocates: The phrase “easily readable” should include accessible formats for visually impaired consumers (e.g., tactile, large-print, or QR-code linking to a text-to-speech nutrition statement); request addition of accessibility provisions.

[P2] From industry: The requirement to be readable in the machine may force larger-format printing that increases packaging costs and waste; propose a performance-based standard (legible at X feet with Y luminance) rather than the absolute phrasing.

[P2] Retailers: Vending machines in low-light or outdoor settings may render on-package information unreadable; request an exception permitting machine-exterior signage with the required info for outdoor or dimly lit locations.

[P3] The 150% type-size mandate relative to the net quantity declaration is vague because many packages use different type sizes for multiple net quantity presentations (e.g., bold vs. small); request a specific absolute minimum font point size (e.g., 10 pt or 12 pt) instead of a percentage.

[P3] Small-pack single-serve products (e.g., gum, mints) cannot accommodate a nutrition statement at 150% of net-quantity type without reducing essential branding or exceeding package real estate; request exemptions or a scaled requirement based on package surface area.

[P3] Legal/design experts: The provision may lead to inconsistent enforcement because measuring “type size” across font families and proportional fonts is ambiguous; require specification of measurement method (x-height, cap height, point size) and permissible fonts.

[P3] Trade groups: The relative sizing rule could conflict with international labeling standards for exporters; request alignment with existing Codex or EU font-size requirements or an export exception.

[P3] Health advocates: A 150% requirement is laudable but should be paired with minimum contrast/color rules and placement standards (e.g., upper-right quadrant) to ensure actual visibility, not just larger type.

[P4] The mandate for “sufficient color and contrasting background” is subjective; provide objective contrast ratios (e.g., WCAG contrast ratio 4.5:1) to ensure consistent compliance and enforcement.

[P4] Packaging designers: Requiring higher contrast may force changes to brand color schemes and could be perceived as an infringement on trademarks and trade dress; request transitional flexibility and coordination with brand owners.

[P4] Small business concerns: Specifying color/contrast requirements without providing compliance testing guidance will create uncertainty; ask the agency to provide a safe-harbor methodology for determining sufficient contrast (e.g., use of defined color swatches or contrast-check tool).

[P4] Consumer advocates: Contrast requirements alone are insufficient; the regulation should prohibit placing the nutrition info over busy imagery, metallic finishes, or gradients that reduce legibility even when color contrast metrics are met.

[P4] Legal experts: The color/contrast requirement could trigger First Amendment challenges if applied to expressive elements of packaging; request legal analysis and narrow tailoring to avoid overbreadth.

[P5] The requirement to include at minimum the total number of calories “for the article as sold at the point of purchase” ignores that some vending items are offered in multiple sizes/serving options (e.g., fountain drinks, combo packages); clarify application for variable-portion items and require per-serving and per-package calories when applicable.

[P5] Nutrition labeling professionals: Providing only total calories is insufficient for consumers making informed choices; request that the visible information also include serving size, saturated fat, sugars, and sodium, or at least a link/QR code to full nutrition facts.

[P5] Industry: Calculating and printing per-item calories for assembled or freshly prepared vending items (e.g., made-to-order sandwiches) is impractical; ask for an exemption or allow machine-level consolidated calorie statements for such items.

[P5] Enforcement agencies: The phrase “as sold at the point of purchase” should be defined to prevent confusion about whether calories should reflect the packaged product, rehydrated forms, or prepared states (e.g., dried soup vs. prepared soup); request explicit definitions.

[P5] Public health groups: Limiting visible nutrition information to calories undermines broader nutrition goals; recommend expanding the mandatory visible elements to include calories, added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium to better guide consumer choices.

[P5] Small-format manufacturers: Adding calories to very small packaging will necessitate repackaging or stickers, raising costs and waste; request a phase-in period or allowance to use machine-displayed calories instead of on-package for items below a certain surface area threshold.

[P1][P2] Combined compliance concern: For small, transparent, or irregularly shaped packages sold in vending machines, the combined requirements (on-label, readable in machine, 150% type, color contrast, calories) are cumulatively impossible; request an alternative compliance mechanism using machine-level displays or shelf tags that link each product to its manufacturer nutrition data.

[P3][P4] Technical measurement: The proposal lacks standardized measurement protocols for font size and contrast; request adoption of ANSI or ISO measurement procedures and inclusion in guidance to ensure uniform enforcement.

[P2][P5] Accessibility/technology solution: Allow use of durable QR codes prominently displayed on the package (meeting size/contrast/type requirements) that link directly to calorie info and full nutrition facts as a permissible alternative when on-package print is constrained.

[P4][P5] Request that the agency conduct a consumer testing study to verify that the specified size/contrast/calorie-only approach actually improves consumer comprehension and choice before finalizing the rule.

[P1] Environmental groups: For products using compostable or recyclable packaging, print limitations may differ; request coordination with packaging standards to ensure the rule does not inadvertently increase non-recyclable inks or materials.

[P2] Enforcement practicability: Inspectors cannot reliably determine “easily readable” remotely; propose clear photographs or measurement criteria for compliance checks to reduce disputes.

[P5] Economic impact: Manufacturers will incur costs recalibrating packaging lines to add calorie statements at required size/contrast; request a Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis and small-business impact relief.

[P9] The requirement to submit AMOC proposals to the named FAA contact (James Blyn) (§ 39.13(f)(1)) is problematic if that individual changes position or leaves; request a generic, organizational address and incoming-mail tracking procedures instead of a single named individual.

[P10] The FAA's suggestion to "notify your principal inspector... before operating under an AMOC" (§ 39.13(f)(2)) is only advisory language ("suggests") and therefore creates regulatory uncertainty; stakeholders request mandatory notification and a defined timeline for acknowledgement.

[P13] The Leonardo AD requirement (§ 39.13, (g)(1)) to set and record a life limit of 600 hours TIS or 1,500 cycles within 5 hours TIS after May 3, 2012 is retroactive and impracticable for operators who were not notified in 2012; request grandfathering or alternative compliance for operators who lack historical records.

[P14] The rule's instruction to calculate unknown cycles as hours × 4 (§ 39.13, (g)(1) specification) is arbitrary and may misrepresent actual usage patterns (e.g., short-haul vs. long-haul); request validation data supporting the 4:1 ratio or allow alternative, documented cycle-count methods.

[P15] Requiring removal of specified T/R blades before they reach 600 hours TIS or 1,500 cycles (§ 39.13, Leonardo S.p.a. AD (g)(2)) will impose significant unexpected costs; request an economic analysis and consideration of phase-in or credit for condition-based monitoring.

[P16] The obligation in § 39.13, (g)(3) to determine total cycles within 5 hours TIS after the AD effective date for certain blade P/Ns is unworkable if records are incomplete; request extended compliance time and allowance for reasonable estimates verified by maintenance logs.

[P17] Repeating the same cycles=hours×4 rule for different blade part numbers (§ 39.13, (g)(3) specification) compounds the risk of inaccurate cycle counts; recommend allowing OEM or operator-specific cycle determination methodologies.

[P18] The requirement to remove blades that have reached or exceeded their life limit "before the next flight" (§ 39.13, (g)(3) - removal obligation) could ground aircraft immediately without notice, causing operational and safety management issues; request a grace period (e.g., up to 72 hours) to safely plan removals.

[P19] Setting life limits of 1,200 hours TIS or 3,200 cycles for certain blades (§ 39.13, (g)(3)(i)) appears inconsistent with prior manufacturer guidance; request the FAA provide technical justification and risk assessment for these specific thresholds.

[P20] The removal-before-40,000-cycles requirement for P/N 3G6410A00133 (§ 39.13, (g)(3)(ii)) seems excessive and likely unnecessary for many operators; request fracture mechanics data and service experience that support such a high-cycle limit being unsafe.

[P21] The limit of 4,033 hours TIS or 40,000 cycles for P/N 4G6410A00133 (§ 39.13, (g)(3)(iii)) is overly specific (4,033) suggesting possible typographical error; ask FAA to confirm intended value and provide rounding rationale.

[P22] The mandatory inspection interval "within 25 hours TIS and thereafter at intervals not to exceed 25 hours TIS" (§ 39.13, Leonardo S.p.a. AD (g)(4)) is excessively frequent and will impose heavy maintenance burdens on high-utilization operators; request extending to a more practicable interval or allowing condition-monitoring alternatives.

[P23] The requirement to remove any blade found with a crack "before further flight" (§ 39.13, Leonardo S.p.a. AD (g)(4) condition) is necessary for safety but may be ambiguous about acceptable defect sizing and allowable repair; request incorporation of specific crack-sizing criteria or reference to repair limitations.

[P24] The prohibition on installing certain blades unless prior actions completed (§ 39.13, Leonardo S.p.a. AD (g)(5)) could disrupt parts inventories and maintenance planning; request clear guidance on how to document compliance for installed spares and time limits for record updates.

[P25] Granting AMOC authority to the Manager, International Validation Branch (§ 39.13, Leonardo S.p.a. AD (h)(1)) without specifying SLAs will create delays; request defined response times (e.g., 30/60/90 days) for AMOC decisions.

[P26] The AMOC routing requirement to principal inspectors or local FSDOs (§ 39.13, Leonardo S.p.a. AD (h)(1)) may create duplication if operators also send requests to the manager; request simplified centralized submission options.

[P28] Allowing AMOC submissions via the specified email address (9-AVS-AIR-730-AMOC@faa.gov) (§ 39.13, Leonardo S.p.a. AD (h)(1) - email option) raises records-security and privacy concerns; request confirmation of receipt procedures, encrypted attachments support, and acknowledgement timelines.

[P29] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC (§ 39.13, Leonardo S.p.a. AD (h)(2)) should include a required format and timeframe for notification to ensure enforcement consistency.

[P31] The compliance statement in Airbus Helicopters AD § 39.13(f) that "certified operators must comply within specified compliance times" lacks necessary flexibility for operators with maintenance scheduling conflicts; request an explicit process for temporary operational relief (e.g., through special flight permits or AMOCs).

[P32] The 110 hours TIS visual inspection requirement for the LH fuel supply hose (§ 39.13, Airbus Helicopters AD (g)(1)) does not account for helicopters with low utilization where calendar aging may matter; request an alternative compliance that allows calendar-time triggers (e.g., within 90 days) for low-hour aircraft.

[P33] The requirement in § 39.13, Airbus Helicopters AD (g)(1)(i) to remove and replace any hose with internal twisting "before further flight" could cause immediate grounding if replacement hoses are unavailable; request allowance to ferry the aircraft to a maintenance facility under a special flight permit or provide temporary flight limitations.

[P34] The instruction to reinstall the hose per the Accomplishment Instructions if no internal twisting is found (§ 39.13, Airbus Helicopters AD (g)(1)(ii)) presumes the instructions are sufficiently detailed; ask the FAA to incorporate or reference the exact ASB revision and ensure public availability.

[P35] The prohibition on installing P/N 704A34416087 unless installed by following the ASB (§ 39.13, Airbus Helicopters AD (g)(2)) effectively bans any prior-installation methods; request clarity on acceptable prior installations and documentation needed to demonstrate compliance.

[P36] Limiting special flight permits to flights with "no passengers on board" (§ 39.13, Airbus Helicopters AD (h)) will impact medevac, law enforcement, and other public-service operations; request narrow exceptions for emergency public-service flights with FAA coordination.

[P41] The requirement to notify the principal inspector or local FSDO before using an approved AMOC (§ 39.13, Airbus Helicopters AD (i)(2)) should specify the time window for notification and form of acknowledgement; otherwise operators will face enforcement uncertainty.

[P44] The repetition of the 110 hours TIS LH hose inspection in § 39.13(g)(1) across multiple provisions suggests duplicative regulatory text; recommend consolidating and eliminating redundancy to reduce compliance confusion.

[P48] The mandate to remove P/N 704A34416087 and install improved P/N 704A34416101 within 1,200 hours TIS (§ 39.13(g)(2)) imposes significant logistics and parts-procurement burdens; request phased compliance, availability assurances from Airbus, and an estimate of replacement cost burden.

[P49] The installation prohibition on P/N 704A34416087 (§ 39.13(g)(3)) should specify whether previously produced stock in airline warehouses is immediately unusable or whether rework per the ASB can render them airworthy.

[P50] The "exception" that allows installation of P/N 704A34416087 only if installed per specific ASB paragraph (§ 39.13(g)(3) exception) is circular and may be unworkable if operators cannot access that ASB paragraph or if it conflicts with other maintenance manuals.

[P51] Providing credit for prior compliance when Revision 1 of the service bulletin was used (§ 39.13(h)) is helpful, but the AD should enumerate acceptable evidence (work orders, logbook entries) to substantiate prior compliance.

[P52] Allowing special flight permits only with no passengers (§ 39.13(i)) will disrupt commercial operations and passenger evacuation planning; request explicit carve-outs for repositioning flights with minimal risk and FAA concurrence.

[P54] The Manager's authority to approve AMOCs under 14 CFR 39.19 (§ 39.13(j)(1)) should be expanded to permit delegated AMOC approvals to regional FAA offices to speed responsiveness.

[P55] Requiring AMOC requests be sent to principal inspectors or local FSDOs per 14 CFR 39.19 (§ 39.13(j)(1) procedure) may delay processing if local offices lack technical expertise; request an option to submit directly to the technical branch with local notification.

[P57] Email submission to 9-AVS-AIR-730-AMOC@faa.gov (§ 39.13(j)(1) alternative) should require an automated acknowledgment receipt and tracking number; request the FAA implement such a system to avoid lost submissions.

[P58] The obligation to notify the principal inspector or local FSDO before using an approved AMOC (§ 39.13(j)(2)) must specify whether oral notification suffices and what constitutes proof of notification for enforcement; request a written-notice requirement with timestamped receipt.

raw_output:
[P1] Industry: Require clarification of the certification process referenced in §103.6(b)(1) — commenters request citation of the specific Treasury regulations or guidance implementing 31 U.S.C. 9304–9308 and the procedures/timeframe for obtaining and renewing a “Treasury-certified” surety certificate.

[P1] Legal experts: The rule should define “company holding a certificate” (e.g., domestic vs. foreign insurers, affiliate surety companies) to avoid downstream disputes about which entities qualify to post bonds.

[P2] Small-business/individual stakeholders: §103.6(b)(1) allowing deposits of “cash equivalents” such as postal money orders and certified checks should specify acceptable instruments and any required endorsement/holding period to prevent ICE from rejecting payments for formality reasons.

[P2] Consumer advocates: The rule should require ICE to accept modern electronic forms of cash-equivalent payment (wire transfers, ACH, prepaid escrow) in addition to paper instruments to avoid discriminatory barriers for remote detainees or families.

[P3] Surety industry: Granting ICE unfettered discretion under §103.6(b)(2) to “decline to accept” bonds risks arbitrary enforcement; commenters request objective standards and a required notice-and-hearing before discretion is exercised.

[P3] Civil liberties groups: The provision permitting ICE to decline Treasury-certified surety bonds should include protections so that bond refusals are not used to effectively detain individuals without individualized determinations.

[P4] Surety industry: The threshold of “ten or more past-due invoices simultaneously past due” in §103.6(b)(2)(i) is arbitrary; request empirical justification and suggest raising the threshold or using a sliding scale tied to the surety’s portfolio size.

[P4] Small/regional sureties: For small surety companies that issue relatively few bonds, ten simultaneous invoices could constitute a disproportionate penalty; request the rule exempt small volume sureties or apply a proportional threshold.

[P5] Surety industry and accountants: The $50,000 cumulative past-due invoice threshold in §103.6(b)(2)(ii) needs adjustment for inflation and for surety balance-sheet differences; request indexing to CPI or a percentage of the surety’s outstanding liability or surplus.

[P5] Financial regulators: Require ICE to detail whether the $50,000 threshold includes only principal or also interest/administrative fees, and to provide an accounting method for how fees and interest are calculated and accrued.

[P6] Surety trade associations: The 35% breach rate trigger in §103.6(b)(2)(iii) is unworkably high/low (depending on commenter) and fails to account for differences in bond types and case mix; request segmentation (e.g., by bond size, population served) or use of industry benchmarks.

[P6] Public defenders/advocacy groups: A 35% breach rate could disproportionately affect sureties who represent detained immigrants from high-flight-risk groups; urge ICE to consider root causes of breaches (e.g., counsel access, notice issues) before penalizing sureties.

[P7] Legal/technical commenters: The computation methodology in §103.6(b)(2)(iii) should be fully specified — define “breach” and “cancellation” precisely, explain treatment of multiple bonds for the same principal, time windows, and rounding rules used in January calculations.

[P7] Data transparency advocates: Require ICE to publish each surety’s underlying data (number of breaches, cancellations) and the calculation showing the breach rate so sureties can verify accuracy and the public can audit enforcement.

[P8] Surety industry: The phrase “ICE may initiate the process…when one or more (b)(2) standards apply” in §103.6(b)(4) grants too much discretion; propose limiting initiation to cases where multiple standards are met or where ICE finds systemic misconduct documented in a public report.

[P9] Due process advocates: §103.6(b)(4) requires that the written notice include “reasons” but should require specific factual findings and supporting evidence, not just conclusory statements, to allow a meaningful rebuttal by the surety.

[P9] Administrative law scholars: The regulation should specify deliverable methods and proof of receipt for the written notice (e.g., certified mail, electronic service) to prevent disputes about whether the notice was properly issued.

[P10] Surety trade groups: The notice’s requirement to inform the surety of an “opportunity to rebut and to cure” is vague — request a defined cure period, specific cure actions that will be accepted (e.g., payment plan, posting collateral), and objective criteria for what constitutes cure.

[P10] Public interest groups: The rule should bar ICE from declining bonds solely where cure measures are promptly initiated and in good faith by the surety, to promote access to bond for migrants and reduce undue detention.

[P11] Surety companies: Require that the provision specifying the surety must send responses “to the office that issued the notice” also permit delivery to a designated electronic submissions portal and to the surety’s counsel or registered agent to facilitate timely, documented responses.

[P12] Industry counsel: The 30-calendar-day deadline in §103.6(b)(5) is too short considering possible mail delays and the need to assemble legal and factual materials; request extension to 45 or 60 days, or allow tolling for good cause.

[P12] Due process advocates: If ICE keeps the 30-day deadline, it should allow requests for a prompt extension supported by a showing of good cause and require ICE to respond to extension requests within a short timeframe.

[P13] Legal commentators: The waiver consequence in §103.6(b)(5) (failure to timely respond = waiver) is harsh; propose a safe-harbor for late responses where the surety demonstrates excusable neglect or where ICE’s notice was deficient in content or delivery.

[P13] Small sureties and agents: Request explicit notice requirements (e.g., multiple attempts, electronic notice) before deeming a response “untimely” to avoid waiver due to administrative errors or misdirected mail.

[P14] Administrative law attorneys: §103.6(b)(6) should require ICE to include a written explanation of the basis for its determination and the administrative record considered, to allow meaningful judicial review of the final agency action.

[P15] Civil rights organizations: Declaring the written determination “final agency action” in §103.6(b)(6) without providing judicial review timelines risks truncating review rights; request confirmation that affected sureties retain the right to seek APA judicial review in federal court.

[P15] Legal defense groups: Ask ICE to clarify whether and how filing suit in federal court affects ICE’s declining of future bonds (e.g., stay pending judicial review) to prevent irreparable harm to principals and sureties.

[P16] Immigration advocates: If ICE declines future bonds from a surety under §103.6(b)(6), there should be a mechanism to ensure existing enrollees or bond principals are not forced into detention due to the surety’s delisting — e.g., allow a transition period or transfer of bond obligations.

[P16] Bonding industry: Request that ICE allow a grace period before declination takes effect to permit sureties to cure financial issues, to transfer outstanding bonds to acceptable sureties, and to avoid sudden market disruption.

[P17] Legal practitioners: The AAO decision being “final agency action” under §103.6(f)(1) should come with a clear description of the scope of review at the AAO and the record to be considered, to conform with APA requirements.

[P18] Surety/appeal counsel: Declaring initial breach determinations “inoperative” while appeals are pending is appropriate, but ICE should confirm whether enforcement actions (e.g., attempts to collect or list surety deficits) are stayed during appeal.

[P19] Procedural fairness advocates: For §103.6(f)(1)’s rule that an appeal dismissal is effective on the AAO decision date, ICE should require the AAO to provide written reasons for dismissal and proof of service to the surety.

[P20] Legal experts: The provision that an AAO decision becomes non-final only upon granting a motion to reopen/reconsider may conflict with other statutes of limitation; request clarification on how reopening/reconsideration interacts with judicial review or equitable tolling.

[P21] Surety industry: The rule in §103.6(f)(2) that failure to exhaust administrative appellate review or to file timely appeal constitutes waiver of all claims is overly broad; propose that ICE preserve defenses that could not have been raised earlier due to lack of notice or newly discovered evidence.

[P21] Due process advocates: Indicate concern that strict waiver rules may deprive sureties of meaningful review when ICE’s breach notices lack adequate factual detail; request that ICE supply complete investigatory files to enable exhaustion.

[P22] Bonding agents: The exception in §103.6(f)(2) stating failure to move to reconsider/reopen is not failure to exhaust remedies is confusing and may create inconsistent outcomes; ask ICE to clarify the interplay between appeals, motions, and the effect on waiver.

[P23] Sureties and counsel: Requiring sureties to raise “all issues and present all facts” in AAO appeals (§103.6(f)(3)) is unrealistic; request allowance for newly discovered evidence discovered after the appeal submission and a process for submitting such evidence.

[P23] Evidence/procedure experts: Propose that ICE adopt rules for supplementation of the administrative record at the AAO stage and permit limited discovery of factual matters bearing on breach determinations.

[P24] Legal commentators: The waiver of any untimely-raised claim under §103.6(f)(3) could bar meritorious defenses; request an express exception for claims involving constitutional issues or jurisdictional defects that may be raised at any time.

[P25] Surety trade associations: The consequence in §103.6(f)(4) that failure to timely file an AAO appeal creates a claim in favor of ICE on the bond needs limits — require notice of intent to collect and an additional short cure or appeal window before ICE seeks collection.

[P25] Immigration legal service providers: Warn that automatically creating a claim against the bond when a surety fails to appeal timely could lead to collection on bonds posted for vulnerable individuals whose surety lacked notice; urge procedural safeguards for principals.

[P26] Consumer protection groups: The automatic creation of a claim in favor of ICE (§103.6(f)(4)) should not be final without written notice to the bond principal and surety of the impending claim and an opportunity to contest it.

[P27] Financial/legal stakeholders: ICE’s permission to seek collection of the amount due on a breached bond (§103.6(f)(4)) must be accompanied by a clear administrative process for collection (billing, interest accrual, payment plans), limitations on fees, and protections against double recovery.

[P27] Small bond principals: Request that ICE be prohibited from pursuing collection actions against individual bond principals before it exhausts efforts to collect from the surety or before the agency’s breach determination is final after appeals.

[P6][P7] Data integrity advocates: Require ICE to exclude from breach-rate calculations any breaches that are later vacated or reversed on appeal, and to specify how pending appeals at the time of calculation are treated.

[P3][P14] Transparency advocates: Mandate publication of a redacted report each time ICE initiates the decline process under §103.6(b)(4), listing the factual bases and aggregate data so the public can assess whether ICE’s exercise of discretion is consistent and non-discriminatory.

[P10][P16] Immigrant rights groups: Request that the rule prohibit ICE from using declination authority in a way that results in increased detention (e.g., steering detainees to bond amounts they cannot meet); require ICE to consider alternatives like supervised release.

[P12][P13] Pro se or small agents: Ask ICE to allow electronic submission with time-stamped receipts and to accept submissions sent by registered agent or counsel as timely if ICE maintained prior contact details, to avoid forfeiture by clerical error.

[P21][P24] Legal scholars: Suggest adding a provision that preserves equitable tolling or excusable neglect principles for failure-to-appeal rules, consistent with federal appellate practice, to prevent harsh forfeitures.

[P5][P6] Economists/market analysts: Require ICE to model market impacts (e.g., concentration of surety market, bond price increases) of the decline provisions, and publish the economic impact analysis and invite comment before finalizing thresholds.

Small/regional sureties: For small surety companies that issue relatively few bonds, ten simultaneous invoices could constitute a disproportionate penalty; request the rule exempt small volume sureties or apply a proportional threshold.

Surety industry and accountants: The $50,000 cumulative past-due invoice threshold in §103.6(b)(2)(ii) needs adjustment for inflation and for surety balance-sheet differences; request indexing to CPI or a percentage of the surety’s outstanding liability or surplus.

Financial regulators: Require ICE to detail whether the $50,000 threshold includes only principal or also interest/administrative fees, and to provide an accounting method for how fees and interest are calculated and accrued.

Surety trade associations: The 35% breach rate trigger in §103.6(b)(2)(iii) is unworkably high/low (depending on commenter) and fails to account for differences in bond types and case mix; request segmentation (e.g., by bond size, population served) or use of industry benchmarks.

Public defenders/advocacy groups: A 35% breach rate could disproportionately affect sureties who represent detained immigrants from high-flight-risk groups; urge ICE to consider root causes of breaches (e.g., counsel access, notice issues) before penalizing sureties.

Legal/technical commenters: The computation methodology in §103.6(b)(2)(iii) should be fully specified — define “breach” and “cancellation” precisely, explain treatment of multiple bonds for the same principal, time windows, and rounding rules used in January calculations.

Data transparency advocates: Require ICE to publish each surety’s underlying data (number of breaches, cancellations) and the calculation showing the breach rate so sureties can verify accuracy and the public can audit enforcement.

Surety industry: The phrase “ICE may initiate the process…when one or more (b)(2) standards apply” in §103.6(b)(4) grants too much discretion; propose limiting initiation to cases where multiple standards are met or where ICE finds systemic misconduct documented in a public report.

Due process advocates: §103.6(b)(4) requires that the written notice include “reasons” but should require specific factual findings and supporting evidence, not just conclusory statements, to allow a meaningful rebuttal by the surety.

Administrative law scholars: The regulation should specify deliverable methods and proof of receipt for the written notice (e.g., certified mail, electronic service) to prevent disputes about whether the notice was properly issued.

Surety trade groups: The notice’s requirement to inform the surety of an “opportunity to rebut and to cure” is vague — request a defined cure period, specific cure actions that will be accepted (e.g., payment plan, posting collateral), and objective criteria for what constitutes cure.

Public interest groups: The rule should bar ICE from declining bonds solely where cure measures are promptly initiated and in good faith by the surety, to promote access to bond for migrants and reduce undue detention.

Surety companies: Require that the provision specifying the surety must send responses “to the office that issued the notice” also permit delivery to a designated electronic submissions portal and to the surety’s counsel or registered agent to facilitate timely, documented responses.

Industry counsel: The 30-calendar-day deadline in §103.6(b)(5) is too short considering possible mail delays and the need to assemble legal and factual materials; request extension to 45 or 60 days, or allow tolling for good cause.

Due process advocates: If ICE keeps the 30-day deadline, it should allow requests for a prompt extension supported by a showing of good cause and require ICE to respond to extension requests within a short timeframe.

Legal commentators: The waiver consequence in §103.6(b)(5) (failure to timely respond = waiver) is harsh; propose a safe-harbor for late responses where the surety demonstrates excusable neglect or where ICE’s notice was deficient in content or delivery.

Small sureties and agents: Request explicit notice requirements (e.g., multiple attempts, electronic notice) before deeming a response “untimely” to avoid waiver due to administrative errors or misdirected mail.

Administrative law attorneys: §103.6(b)(6) should require ICE to include a written explanation of the basis for its determination and the administrative record considered, to allow meaningful judicial review of the final agency action.

Civil rights organizations: Declaring the written determination “final agency action” in §103.6(b)(6) without providing judicial review timelines risks truncating review rights; request confirmation that affected sureties retain the right to seek APA judicial review in federal court.

Legal defense groups: Ask ICE to clarify whether and how filing suit in federal court affects ICE’s declining of future bonds (e.g., stay pending judicial review) to prevent irreparable harm to principals and sureties.

Immigration advocates: If ICE declines future bonds from a surety under §103.6(b)(6), there should be a mechanism to ensure existing enrollees or bond principals are not forced into detention due to the surety’s delisting — e.g., allow a transition period or transfer of bond obligations.

Bonding industry: Request that ICE allow a grace period before declination takes effect to permit sureties to cure financial issues, to transfer outstanding bonds to acceptable sureties, and to avoid sudden market disruption.

Legal practitioners: The AAO decision being “final agency action” under §103.6(f)(1) should come with a clear description of the scope of review at the AAO and the record to be considered, to conform with APA requirements.

Surety/appeal counsel: Declaring initial breach determinations “inoperative” while appeals are pending is appropriate, but ICE should confirm whether enforcement actions (e.g., attempts to collect or list surety deficits) are stayed during appeal.

Procedural fairness advocates: For §103.6(f)(1)’s rule that an appeal dismissal is effective on the AAO decision date, ICE should require the AAO to provide written reasons for dismissal and proof of service to the surety.

Legal experts: The provision that an AAO decision becomes non-final only upon granting a motion to reopen/reconsider may conflict with other statutes of limitation; request clarification on how reopening/reconsideration interacts with judicial review or equitable tolling.

Surety industry: The rule in §103.6(f)(2) that failure to exhaust administrative appellate review or to file timely appeal constitutes waiver of all claims is overly broad; propose that ICE preserve defenses that could not have been raised earlier due to lack of notice or newly discovered evidence.

Due process advocates: Indicate concern that strict waiver rules may deprive sureties of meaningful review when ICE’s breach notices lack adequate factual detail; request that ICE supply complete investigatory files to enable exhaustion.

Bonding agents: The exception in §103.6(f)(2) stating failure to move to reconsider/reopen is not failure to exhaust remedies is confusing and may create inconsistent outcomes; ask ICE to clarify the interplay between appeals, motions, and the effect on waiver.

Sureties and counsel: Requiring sureties to raise “all issues and present all facts” in AAO appeals (§103.6(f)(3)) is unrealistic; request allowance for newly discovered evidence discovered after the appeal submission and a process for submitting such evidence.

Evidence/procedure experts: Propose that ICE adopt rules for supplementation of the administrative record at the AAO stage and permit limited discovery of factual matters bearing on breach determinations.

Legal commentators: The waiver of any untimely-raised claim under §103.6(f)(3) could bar meritorious defenses; request an express exception for claims involving constitutional issues or jurisdictional defects that may be raised at any time.

Surety trade associations: The consequence in §103.6(f)(4) that failure to timely file an AAO appeal creates a claim in favor of ICE on the bond needs limits — require notice of intent to collect and an additional short cure or appeal window before ICE seeks collection.

Immigration legal service providers: Warn that automatically creating a claim against the bond when a surety fails to appeal timely could lead to collection on bonds posted for vulnerable individuals whose surety lacked notice; urge procedural safeguards for principals.

Consumer protection groups: The automatic creation of a claim in favor of ICE (§103.6(f)(4)) should not be final without written notice to the bond principal and surety of the impending claim and an opportunity to contest it.

Financial/legal stakeholders: ICE’s permission to seek collection of the amount due on a breached bond (§103.6(f)(4)) must be accompanied by a clear administrative process for collection (billing, interest accrual, payment plans), limitations on fees, and protections against double recovery.

Small bond principals: Request that ICE be prohibited from pursuing collection actions against individual bond principals before it exhausts efforts to collect from the surety or before the agency’s breach determination is final after appeals.

[P7] Data integrity advocates: Require ICE to exclude from breach-rate calculations any breaches that are later vacated or reversed on appeal, and to specify how pending appeals at the time of calculation are treated.

[P14] Transparency advocates: Mandate publication of a redacted report each time ICE initiates the decline process under §103.6(b)(4), listing the factual bases and aggregate data so the public can assess whether ICE’s exercise of discretion is consistent and non-discriminatory.

[P16] Immigrant rights groups: Request that the rule prohibit ICE from using declination authority in a way that results in increased detention (e.g., steering detainees to bond amounts they cannot meet); require ICE to consider alternatives like supervised release.

[P13] Pro se or small agents: Ask ICE to allow electronic submission with time-stamped receipts and to accept submissions sent by registered agent or counsel as timely if ICE maintained prior contact details, to avoid forfeiture by clerical error.

[P24] Legal scholars: Suggest adding a provision that preserves equitable tolling or excusable neglect principles for failure-to-appeal rules, consistent with federal appellate practice, to prevent harsh forfeitures.

[P6] Economists/market analysts: Require ICE to model market impacts (e.g., concentration of surety market, bond price increases) of the decline provisions, and publish the economic impact analysis and invite comment before finalizing thresholds.

raw_output:
[P1] The rule's restriction that experimental status is recognized only outside areas of overlap will create management confusion where populations naturally fluctuate seasonally; commenters request clarification on how temporary, predictable overlap (e.g., seasonal migration corridors) will be treated.

[P1] Industry stakeholders will argue that recognizing experimental status only outside overlap areas could unduly limit restoration projects that intentionally place individuals near existing populations to facilitate gene flow.

[P2] Conservation NGOs will contend that prohibiting recognition of specimens in overlap areas undermines adaptive management by preventing monitoring of released individuals when they enter mixed-use zones.

[P2] Private landowners will express concern that the prohibition could subject landowners to unexpected regulatory duties if experimental animals move into overlap areas on their property and lose experimental status.

[P3] Fisheries and wildlife managers will request a definition of “reasonably predictable” geographic separation, including quantitative criteria (e.g., frequency, duration, historical records) to ensure consistent application.

[P3] Tribal governments will comment that relying on “reasonably predictable” timing could ignore traditional ecological knowledge about cyclical movements and request explicit incorporation of TEK in determinations of predictability.

[P4] Scientists will object that excluding populations where separation might arise from random, unpredictable events (e.g., stochastic floods) will disqualify important reintroduction experiments that already factor in natural variability.

[P4] Legal experts will warn that the prohibition could be challenged as arbitrary if the Service fails to demonstrate how predictions about randomness were made for specific cases.

[P5] Advocacy groups will support Secretary authority to designate experimental populations but request transparency and minimum criteria for when the Secretary should exercise that discretion beyond the APA notice-and-comment requirement.

[P5] State wildlife agencies will request mandatory pre-designation coordination timelines and criteria to ensure state concerns are addressed before the Secretary issues regulations.

[P6] Conservation scientists will demand that “further the conservation of the species” be defined with measurable biological objectives (e.g., increase in viable subpopulations, genetic diversity targets) to prevent regulatory gaming.

[P6] Developers and agriculture associations will argue that the requirement to find releases will further conservation is vague and could be used to block economically important projects; they request clear balancing tests and timelines for decisions.

[P7] Several commenters will insist that “best available scientific and commercial data” explicitly require peer-reviewed analyses, population viability analyses where feasible, and documentation of data gaps and uncertainties.

[P7] Industry representatives will request that commercial data (e.g., harvest records, aquaculture data) be weighted appropriately and that proprietary data protections be clarified when such data inform findings.

[P8] Local governments and land managers will request explicit standards for containment measures (e.g., fence specs, buffer distances) and criteria for when isolating experimental populations is “appropriate” to avoid undue burdens on landowners.

[P8] Animal welfare organizations will support permitting isolation/containment but request safeguards to ensure containment measures do not cause undue stress or harm to animals and to mandate monitoring of containment effectiveness.

[P9] Conservation groups will request that issuance of 10(a)(1)(A) permits include public notice and opportunity for comment, and that permit conditions be publicly available and enforceable.

[P9] Private landowners will ask for clarity that permits under 10(a)(1)(A) do not impose perpetual land-use restrictions beyond the period necessary to establish the experimental population.

[P10] Tribal nations will emphasize the need for government-to-government consultation, not merely “consult with,” and request legally binding commitments to incorporate tribal management priorities and sovereign rights.

[P10] Local governments will request that the Service fund capacity-building or technical assistance for affected municipal authorities to engage effectively in consultation processes.

[P11] Conservation NGOs will call for a presumption in favor of public meetings (“shall” rather than “when appropriate”) because affected communities often lack other avenues to participate meaningfully.

[P11] Industry commenters may counter that public meetings can delay urgent releases and request virtual alternatives and strict time limits for public input.

[P12] Landowner groups will critique the “to the maximum extent practicable” language as too weak and request defined dispute-resolution processes when agreement among stakeholders cannot be reached.

[P12] Environmental law organizations will argue that promoting agreement among parties should not override statutory conservation standards and request an explicit statement that conservation objectives prevail when consensus cannot be achieved.

[P13] Taxpayers and conservation groups will request that species-specific rules and separate listings for experimental populations include unique codes and tracking to ensure monitoring and reporting are transparent and accessible.

[P13] Legal commenters will note potential confusion if experimental populations are separately listed; they ask how listing status interacts with existing catalogs and whether separate listings affect ESA protections and enforcement.

[P14] Conservation stakeholders will support authority to designate critical habitat for essential experimental populations but request explanation of the threshold for “essential” versus “nonessential.”

[P14] Private landowners will express concern about critical habitat designation for experimental populations and request compensatory mechanisms or mitigation when designation restricts land use.

[P15] State agencies will warn that following section 4 procedures for critical habitat may be time-consuming; they request interim protections or expedited processes for essential experimental populations needed urgently for species survival.

[P16] Conservation scientists will oppose the absolute prohibition on critical habitat for nonessential experimental populations, arguing that habitat protection can still be vital to long-term conservation even when populations are labeled nonessential.

[P16] Property rights advocates will support not designating critical habitat for nonessential populations but ask for clear criteria and public justification when the Service declares an experimental population nonessential.

[P17] Federal agencies will request guidance on how treating experimental populations as threatened for section 4(d) will alter standard permitting processes and rulemaking timelines.

[P17] Environmental lawyers will insist that the rule ensure full statutory protections applicable to threatened species under 4(d) are clearly enumerated in species-specific regulations to avoid regulatory uncertainty.

[P18] Conservation NGOs will request that species-specific protective regulations explicitly list prohibited take types and clearly define exceptions to prevent loopholes.

[P18] Industry groups will seek clarity that usual agricultural or development practices are not unintentionally prohibited unless specifically enumerated, and request safe-harbor provisions for ongoing lawful activities.

[P19] National Park and Refuge managers will ask for specific procedural requirements for treating essential experimental populations as threatened for section 7, including who bears responsibility for consultation and mitigation within park/refuge lands.

[P19] Conservation groups will argue that treating essential experimental populations in parks/refuges as threatened may be insufficiently protective and request that such populations be eligible for full endangered protections when warranted.

[P20] Federal project proponents will request clarification on how to conduct section 7 analyses treating experimental and nonexperimental populations as a single listed species—specifically whether separate population-specific baselines are required.

[P20] Legal practitioners will express concern that treating experimental and nonexperimental populations as a single listed species could expand the scope of Federal interagency consultation obligations unpredictably and request guidance examples.

[P21] Mollusk industry and scientists will request that any specific exceptions to § 17.31(a) and (b) be clearly and narrowly defined in the rule to avoid blanket application of ancient prohibitions to research and recovery actions.

[P21] Conservation advocacy groups will urge that the default application of § 17.31 prohibitions remain strict for mollusks and that any allowances be accompanied by monitoring, reporting, and enforcement measures to prevent inadvertent harm.

[P1] The January 25, 2021 public comment deadline in § 39.13(c) is internally inconsistent with paragraph (a)/§39.13(f) which sets a November 1, 2021 comment deadline; request clarification and consolidation of the correct comment deadline to avoid legal challenge.

[P1] If the FAA intends to require comments by January 25, 2021, stakeholders will not have had adequate time to review the full economic and operational impacts; request extension of the comment period to 60 days after publication of the final service information.

[P2] Paragraph (d)’s general obligation to “perform each action required by this AD within the specified compliance times” is vague as to whether it allows staged compliance across multiple actions; request explicit language permitting staggered compliance where the AD specifies different timelines.

[P3] Paragraph (e)(1) requires replacement “before further flight” for hoists with S/N not beginning with '4', but does not specify whether temporary grounding or ferry flights for maintenance are allowed; request clarification that non-passenger repositioning/ferry flights to perform replacements are permitted under an approved procedure.

[P4] The thresholds in (e)(1)(i) (12 months or before 55 hoist operating hours) appear inconsistent with the duplicate provision in paragraph (g)(1)(i) which refers to “55 total hoist operating hours” truncated in the text; request correction of the cut-off text and clear definition of “total” operating hours counting.

[P4] The 55 hoist operating hours limit in (e)(1)(i) is unworkably low for many SAR and utility operators who routinely operate hoists; request risk-based justification and consideration of extending the hours threshold to a higher, evidence-based value or allowing condition-based inspections in lieu of immediate replacement.

[P5] The 1,200-cycle threshold in (e)(1)(ii) lacks a tolerance for counting cycles performed during ground tests or training; request explicit exclusions or accounting rules for non-operational cycles to prevent premature replacements.

[P6] The 1,600 lifts threshold in (e)(1)(iii) does not define “lift” in a way that excludes training or maintenance lifts; request alignment with paragraph (g)(1)(iii) explicitly and clarity whether lifts with no load or simulated loads count.

[P7] Paragraph (e)(2) requires placards and RFM revisions “before further flight” but does not provide standardized text or format for the placards beyond “Figure” references; request the FAA to publish required placard templates and approved pen-and-ink RFM language to ensure consistent compliance.

[P8] The Figure 1 placard requirement for 500 lb hoists in (e)(2)(i) may conflict with occupant visibility and cockpit ergonomics for some aircraft models; request allowance for alternate placard placement if equal visibility is demonstrated.

[P9] Figure 2 placard mandate for 600 lb hoists in (e)(2)(ii) lacks specificity on material, size, and attachment method; request that the AD include requirements for durability and attachment to meet crashworthiness and environmental exposure standards.

[P10] The Figure 3 pilot-facing placard requirement in (e)(2)(iii) may interfere with existing instrumentation or obstruct pilot view in some helicopters; request a relief provision permitting equivalent labeling in a location that does not compromise safety-critical displays.

[P11] Figure 4 pilot-facing placard requirement in (e)(2)(iv) duplicates Figure 3 obligations for some fleets; request consolidation or clarification to avoid redundant placards and unnecessary maintenance burden.

[P12] Paragraph (e)(3)’s requirement to deactivate/remove a hoist after a partial peel out (≥20 inches) before further flight is appropriate for safety, but lacks guidance on permissible deactivation procedures and logbook entries; request standardized procedures and recordkeeping language.

[P12] The 20-inch threshold for a “partial peel out” in (e)(3) may be too low/too high depending on hoist drum size and cable diameter; request data supporting the 20-inch threshold or propose metric replacement threshold tied to drum circumference percentage.

[P13] The 30-day record review requirement in (e)(4) is administratively burdensome for large operators with extensive maintenance records; request extension to 90 days or allow phased compliance for fleets with more than 50 helicopters.

[P14] The condition in (e)(4) that any prior load test >1,500 lbs or of unknown weight requires cable replacement before next hoist operation is overly strict and will force replacement of otherwise serviceable cables without engineering evaluation; request allowance for engineering assessment or re-testing prior to mandatory replacement.

[P15] The repeated inspection intervals in (e)(5) — 30 days initially then every 6 months/400 lifts/300 cycles — create three concurrent limiting factors without specifying which is controlling when they conflict; request clarification which interval controls and an example of interval calculation.

[P16] The visual inspection of the first 18 inches for broken wires and necked sections in (e)(5)(i) lacks objective accept/reject criteria beyond the general replacement mandate; request inclusion of quantifiable acceptance criteria (e.g., number of broken wires per lay or percent reduction) to standardize judgments across inspectors.

[P17] The “replace before further flight” condition in (e)(5)(i) for any broken wire is impractical for some minor surface breaks that do not compromise integrity; request alignment with established cable inspection standards (e.g., NAS/ASA standards) rather than a zero-tolerance rule.

[P18] Measuring cable diameter at the most necked-down area (e)(5)(ii) with a pass/fail threshold of 0.185 inch is acceptable but the AD lacks required measurement method, tool calibration, and rounding rules; request specification of measuring tool accuracy, calibration intervals, and rounding methodology.

[P19] The 0.185 inch (4.7 mm) diameter replacement threshold in (e)(5)(ii) does not state whether core diameter or overall strand diameter applies; request clarification that the measurement is of the nominal outer diameter under no load and provide guidance for different cable constructions.

[P20] The requirement to use load check tool P/N 49900–889–104 in (e)(5)(iii) is unduly prescriptive if equivalent, calibrated tools exist; request allowance for equivalent tooling listed by part number or function plus a means to demonstrate equivalency.

[P21] The average-of-five-test-values pass/fail criterion in (e)(5)(iii) is reasonable, but the AD fails to specify the statistical handling of outliers or allowable variance; request guidance on how to handle anomalous single-test values (e.g., discard highest/lowest) and retest protocols.

[P22] The first 30 feet visual inspection in (e)(5)(iv) may be impractical in some installations where cable routing prevents inspection of full 30 feet without significant disassembly; request allowance for equivalent inspection coverage demonstrating that the critical cable sections are inspected.

[P23] The replacement-before-flight mandate in (e)(5)(iv) for any bird-caging or flattened area exceeding “allowable” limits references unspecified “allowable” limits; request that the AD include the numeric allowable limits or explicitly reference the specific paragraphs/tables in ASB 44301.

[P24] Requiring repetition of 18-inch visual and diameter checks in (e)(5)(v) without specifying whether the initial 30-day inspection counts toward the first interval creates ambiguity; request an explicit timeline example (e.g., initial within 30 days, next due at 6 months or per lift/cycle limits).

[P25] The mandatory reporting to Goodrich within 30 days after load test in (e)(6) and Appendix 1 raises privacy and competitive concerns about proprietary operational data; request that the FAA limit data fields to non-proprietary items and ensure anonymization for aggregated analyses.

[P26] Appendix 1’s specified data fields (P27) appear to require operator identifiers, serial numbers, and possibly operational data; request compliance with the Paperwork Reduction Act, explicit OMB control number inclusion, and justification for each data field’s necessity.

[P27] Paragraph (e)(7)’s prohibition on installing hoists without S/N starting with '4' as of the effective date lacks lead-time for manufacturers and suppliers; request a phase-in period (e.g., 180 days) to allow inventory management and avoid grounding replacement part stockpiles.

[P28] The exception in (e)(7) that permits installation only if the hoist has the improved overload clutch assembly S/N beginning with '4' lacks a method for verifying serial number authenticity; request requirement for traceable documentation (manufacturer’s release or label verification) and anti-tamper measures.

[P29] The Paperwork Reduction Act provisions in paragraph (f) (P30–P34) require an OMB control number but none is displayed in the AD; request the FAA publish the OMB Control Number and the PRA supporting statement in the docket before the final rule to comply with PRA.

[P30] The statement in (f) that “All responses to this collection of information are mandatory” (P33) conflicts with PRA protections; request legal justification for mandatory reporting to a manufacturer (Goodrich) and for FAA enforcement authority over such reporting.

[P31] Paragraph (f) asks commenters to send burden comments to the Information Collection Clearance Officer (P34) but does not include an email or phone number in the AD text provided; request contact details to enable meaningful burden comments.

[P32] Provision (g)(1)/(P35) granting the Manager authority to approve AMOCs is welcome, but the requirement to submit AMOCs to Kristi Bradley (P36) may not reflect current staffing; request inclusion of an FAA generic AMOC submission portal or updated contact in case of personnel changes.

[P33] The suggestion in (g)(2) to notify principal inspectors before using an AMOC (P37) should be a mandatory coordination step for public safety-critical AMOCs, not merely suggested; request elevating the notification to a requirement to ensure local oversight.

[P34] Paragraph (a)’s November 1, 2021 comment receipt date (P38) directly conflicts with other stated comment dates (January 25, 2021) and must be corrected; request immediate correction and republication of the NPRM with a single, consistent comment deadline.

[P35] The scope definition in paragraph (c) (P39) must explicitly list affected P/Ns and S/N ranges; request that the FAA include full P/N lists and serial number ranges so operators can unambiguously determine applicability.

[P36] The duplicate and overlapping obligations repeated across paragraphs (d), (f), and (g) (P2, P40, P48) create compliance confusion; request streamlining of language to a single set of enforceable compliance obligations with cross-references, and removal of duplicate text.

[P37] Paragraph (g)(1)(i)’s definition that hoist operating hours are counted “anytime the hoist motor is operating” (P43) may count motor operation during maintenance bench testing; request an exclusion for bench testing or maintenance operations not involving flight or loaded lift activity.

[P38] The cycle definition in (g)(1)(ii) requiring 16 feet extension/retraction (P45) could be ambiguous for operations conducted at ground-level or confined spaces where cycles are shorter; request allowance to count cumulative shorter movements that equal 16 feet or a redefinition to “one complete extend and retract to the extent normally used in operations.”

[P39] Paragraph (g)(1)(iii)’s lift definition (P47) including any time the cable is unreeled/recovered “with a load attached” regardless of length could count trivial loads (tools) and inflate lift counts; request that the AD define a minimum load threshold (e.g., 10% of rated load) to count as a lift.

[P40] The requirement in (g)(2) to revise the Rotorcraft Flight Manual Section 2 (P48) should allow incorporation by reference of FAA-approved service letters rather than pen-and-ink changes to each RFM; request an optional method to incorporate RFM revisions via an approved temporary revision insert.

[P41] The duplicative placard installation obligations in (g)(2)(i–iv) (P49–P52) impose material and labor costs; request FAA cost-benefit analysis in the docket and consideration of an alternative single mixed-view placard that satisfies both pilot and hoist operator requirements.

[P42] Paragraph (g)(3)’s deactivation/removal before further flight after a partial peel out (P53) should allow for one-time diagnostic flights solely to position the aircraft for maintenance, under a special flight permit; request allowance for special flight permits or maintenance flights with routing and operational restrictions.

[P43] The definition of partial peel out as 20 inches (0.5 m) in (g)(3) (P54) conflicts with earlier imperial/metric conversions elsewhere; request consistent use of metric and imperial values with matching precision across the AD.

[P44] The 30-day initial inspection and reporting windows in (g)(4) and (g)(6) (P55, P68) are short for operators overseas or in remote locations; request extension to 60 or 90 days for international operators or those without immediate access to required tools and reporting channels.

[P45] The “if prior tests were >1,500 lbs or unknown” replacement trigger in (g)(4) (P56) should be limited to instances where the operator cannot produce documentation to verify test loads; request that documented re-testing with calibrated equipment be allowed in lieu of mandatory replacement.

[P46] Paragraph (g)(5)’s criteria of “whichever occurs first” among time, lifts, or cycles (P57) is potentially confusing for tracking; request guidance and a standardized log format to facilitate compliance and audits.

[P47] The specified tools P/N 49900–889–103 or 49900–889–104 in (g)(5)(iii) (P62) may not be available globally; request acceptance of equivalent calibrated load-check tools and instructions for demonstrating equivalence.

The thresholds in (e)(1)(i) (12 months or before 55 hoist operating hours) appear inconsistent with the duplicate provision in paragraph (g)(1)(i) which refers to “55 total hoist operating hours” truncated in the text; request correction of the cut-off text and clear definition of “total” operating hours counting.

The 55 hoist operating hours limit in (e)(1)(i) is unworkably low for many SAR and utility operators who routinely operate hoists; request risk-based justification and consideration of extending the hours threshold to a higher, evidence-based value or allowing condition-based inspections in lieu of immediate replacement.

The 1,200-cycle threshold in (e)(1)(ii) lacks a tolerance for counting cycles performed during ground tests or training; request explicit exclusions or accounting rules for non-operational cycles to prevent premature replacements.

The 1,600 lifts threshold in (e)(1)(iii) does not define “lift” in a way that excludes training or maintenance lifts; request alignment with paragraph (g)(1)(iii) explicitly and clarity whether lifts with no load or simulated loads count.

Paragraph (e)(2) requires placards and RFM revisions “before further flight” but does not provide standardized text or format for the placards beyond “Figure” references; request the FAA to publish required placard templates and approved pen-and-ink RFM language to ensure consistent compliance.

The Figure 1 placard requirement for 500 lb hoists in (e)(2)(i) may conflict with occupant visibility and cockpit ergonomics for some aircraft models; request allowance for alternate placard placement if equal visibility is demonstrated.

Figure 2 placard mandate for 600 lb hoists in (e)(2)(ii) lacks specificity on material, size, and attachment method; request that the AD include requirements for durability and attachment to meet crashworthiness and environmental exposure standards.

The Figure 3 pilot-facing placard requirement in (e)(2)(iii) may interfere with existing instrumentation or obstruct pilot view in some helicopters; request a relief provision permitting equivalent labeling in a location that does not compromise safety-critical displays.

Figure 4 pilot-facing placard requirement in (e)(2)(iv) duplicates Figure 3 obligations for some fleets; request consolidation or clarification to avoid redundant placards and unnecessary maintenance burden.

Paragraph (e)(3)’s requirement to deactivate/remove a hoist after a partial peel out (≥20 inches) before further flight is appropriate for safety, but lacks guidance on permissible deactivation procedures and logbook entries; request standardized procedures and recordkeeping language.

The 20-inch threshold for a “partial peel out” in (e)(3) may be too low/too high depending on hoist drum size and cable diameter; request data supporting the 20-inch threshold or propose metric replacement threshold tied to drum circumference percentage.

The 30-day record review requirement in (e)(4) is administratively burdensome for large operators with extensive maintenance records; request extension to 90 days or allow phased compliance for fleets with more than 50 helicopters.

The condition in (e)(4) that any prior load test >1,500 lbs or of unknown weight requires cable replacement before next hoist operation is overly strict and will force replacement of otherwise serviceable cables without engineering evaluation; request allowance for engineering assessment or re-testing prior to mandatory replacement.

The repeated inspection intervals in (e)(5) — 30 days initially then every 6 months/400 lifts/300 cycles — create three concurrent limiting factors without specifying which is controlling when they conflict; request clarification which interval controls and an example of interval calculation.

The visual inspection of the first 18 inches for broken wires and necked sections in (e)(5)(i) lacks objective accept/reject criteria beyond the general replacement mandate; request inclusion of quantifiable acceptance criteria (e.g., number of broken wires per lay or percent reduction) to standardize judgments across inspectors.

The “replace before further flight” condition in (e)(5)(i) for any broken wire is impractical for some minor surface breaks that do not compromise integrity; request alignment with established cable inspection standards (e.g., NAS/ASA standards) rather than a zero-tolerance rule.

Measuring cable diameter at the most necked-down area (e)(5)(ii) with a pass/fail threshold of 0.185 inch is acceptable but the AD lacks required measurement method, tool calibration, and rounding rules; request specification of measuring tool accuracy, calibration intervals, and rounding methodology.

The 0.185 inch (4.7 mm) diameter replacement threshold in (e)(5)(ii) does not state whether core diameter or overall strand diameter applies; request clarification that the measurement is of the nominal outer diameter under no load and provide guidance for different cable constructions.

The requirement to use load check tool P/N 49900–889–104 in (e)(5)(iii) is unduly prescriptive if equivalent, calibrated tools exist; request allowance for equivalent tooling listed by part number or function plus a means to demonstrate equivalency.

The average-of-five-test-values pass/fail criterion in (e)(5)(iii) is reasonable, but the AD fails to specify the statistical handling of outliers or allowable variance; request guidance on how to handle anomalous single-test values (e.g., discard highest/lowest) and retest protocols.

The replacement-before-flight mandate in (e)(5)(iv) for any bird-caging or flattened area exceeding “allowable” limits references unspecified “allowable” limits; request that the AD include the numeric allowable limits or explicitly reference the specific paragraphs/tables in ASB 44301.

Requiring repetition of 18-inch visual and diameter checks in (e)(5)(v) without specifying whether the initial 30-day inspection counts toward the first interval creates ambiguity; request an explicit timeline example (e.g., initial within 30 days, next due at 6 months or per lift/cycle limits).
