raw_output:
[P1] The amendment to § 73.622(i) revising the Portland DTV allotment table lacks an explanation of interference analysis and could disrupt existing broadcasters’ channel protections; commenters request the technical justification and contour studies supporting channel reassignments.

[P2] Listing channel *10 for Portland without marking whether it is a reserved or protected channel creates uncertainty for broadcasters and the public — the rule should clarify the meaning of the asterisk and any operational restrictions for channel 10.

[P2] The addition of channels 8, 21, 40, 43, and 45 to the Portland allotment list may create co-channel or adjacent-channel interference with nearby markets (Salem, Vancouver, Eugene); commenters request coordination studies and mitigation measures before final adoption.

[P3] Requiring vehicles to comply with the 2013 California OBD requirements (§ 86.1806–17(a)) for all manufacturers nationwide effectively applies California standards to non-California vehicles and could conflict with federal preemption; legal commenters ask EPA to explain the authority to adopt California-based OBD in this federal regulation.

[P4] The provision allowing EPA to approve certification to a later California OBD version (§ 86.1806–17(a)) is too open-ended; industry requests a defined process, timeline, and objective criteria for evaluation of “compliance with the section's intent.”

[P5] The obligation in § 86.1818–12(c)(2)(i) to determine a CO2 target per passenger automobile lacks transitional guidance for vehicles designed to previous target frameworks; manufacturers request grandfathering rules or phase-in periods.

[P6] The footprint threshold at ≤41 sq ft in § 86.1818–12(c)(2)(i)(A) creates cliff effects for vehicles that differ only slightly in footprint; manufacturers request smoothing provisions or a tolerance for dimensional measurement variability.

[P7] The >56 sq ft threshold in § 86.1818–12(c)(2)(i)(B) for selecting table values does not address vehicles with variable footprints across trim levels; commenters ask for guidance on which footprint to use (base model, highest, or average).

[P8] The calculation and rounding to nearest 0.1 g/mi in § 86.1818–12(c)(2)(i)(C) may impose impractical precision requirements for manufacturers’ compliance systems; industry requests confirmation that standard rounding practices in existing certification tools are acceptable.

[P9] The cap preventing the calculated CO2 target from exceeding the model-year value in § 86.1818–12(c)(2)(i)(C) could result in inconsistent or non-monotonic target progression across footprints; policy analysts request worked examples showing impacts for multiple footprints and model years.

[P10] The separate light truck CO2 target determination (§ 86.1818–12(c)(3)(i)) treats passenger cars and light trucks differently but provides no explanation of the policy rationale; stakeholders request the underlying data and modeling used for this differentiation.

[P11] The ≤41 sq ft breakpoint for light trucks in § 86.1818–12(c)(3)(i)(A) is ambiguous for crossover vehicles and SUVs that may be classified differently by various agencies; commenters request cross-reference to vehicle classification rules and a clear method for classification.

[P12] The calculation framework in § 86.1818–12(c)(3)(i)(B) for light trucks with footprints >41 sq ft and ≤ maximum requires rounding to 0.1 g/mi but lacks specification of measurement protocols for footprint determination; manufacturers request explicit measurement standards and tolerances.

[P13] The prohibition that the calculated light-truck CO2 target cannot exceed the model-year maximum (§ 86.1818–12(c)(3)(i)(B)) could create situations where no feasible target exists for certain vehicle configurations; commenters ask for an exception or remediation process in such cases.

[P14] The requirement in § 86.1818–12(c)(3)(i)(C) to apply the specified equation between minimum and maximum footprints for each model year may produce discontinuities at the table endpoints; technical commenters request sample calculations and graphs across the full footprint range.

[P15] Selecting the CO2 target for light trucks greater than the minimum (§ 86.1818–12(c)(3)(i)(D)) from a table without guidance on interpolation for values between table entries is unclear; commenters request interpolation rules or an explicit continuous formula.

[P16] The statement in § 86.1865–12(k)(2) that nothing may be construed to limit EPA’s authority to terminate authorization appears overly broad and could undermine due process and reliance interests; legal commenters request limitation language or a required notice-and-comment termination process.

[P17] The obligation in § 86.1865–12(k)(3) for reporting and recordkeeping of CO2 credits (including early credits) lacks specificity about record retention periods, data formats, and confidentiality protections; manufacturers and trade groups request detailed regulatory guidance and assurance about confidential treatment of proprietary data.

[P18] The prohibition in § 86.1865–12(k)(6) barring use of credits older than five model years after generation is stricter than prior programs and will strand legitimate banked credits; auto manufacturers request extended banking life or a phase-out schedule to avoid sudden compliance shortfalls.

[P19] The exception preserving full value for 2016 credits through 2023 (§ 86.1865–12(k)(6)(i)) but disallowing use thereafter unfairly penalizes manufacturers who planned around previous rules; commenters request either conversion options, buy-back mechanisms, or transition relief for credits that will expire.

[P20] The rule in § 86.1865–12(k)(6)(ii) giving a six-year shelf-life for credits generated in 2017–2020 is arbitrary; industry asks for economic analysis demonstrating the rationale and for consideration of banking flexibility during market disruptions (e.g., supply chain, pandemic).

[P21] The permission for manufacturers to apply production multipliers (§ 86.1866–12(b)) for advanced technology vehicle credits is useful but the rule should clarify whether multipliers stack with other credits and the documentation required to substantiate eligibility.

[P22] The prohibition disallowing full-size pickups that use a production multiplier from claiming strong-hybrid or performance-based credits (§ 86.1866–12(b)) could force manufacturers into suboptimal credit strategies; commenters request an economic modeling of which credits will be most valuable and whether this restriction unfairly disadvantages certain technology pathways.

[P23] The obligation to use specified production multipliers for 2017–2025 (§ 86.1866–12(b)(1)) should be accompanied by a mechanism to update multipliers based on technological progress; trade associations request periodic review and rulemaking to adjust multipliers if advanced tech costs decline.

[P24] The credit caps on multiplier-based credits for 2022–2025 (§ 86.1866–12(c)(3)) may create a sudden constraint during the transition to higher advanced-technology production; manufacturers request phased caps or carry-forward provisions in case caps are reached.

[P25] The required computation of a nominal annual credit cap using an equation (§ 86.1866–12(c)(3)(i)) lacks the explicit formula text and examples in the preamble; commenters ask for worked numerical examples and clarification of rounding implications.

[P26] The obligation to compute g/mile equivalents (§ 86.1866–12(c)(3)(ii)) and cumulative sums (§ 86.1866–12(c)(3)(iii)) may create complexity and double-counting risks unless reporting templates are provided; stakeholders request standardized calculation spreadsheets and audit guidance.

[P27] The absolute cap that cumulative g/mile equivalent value cannot exceed 10.0 in any year (§ 86.1866–12(c)(3)(iv)) may be too constraining relative to the program’s greenhouse-gas objectives and could penalize early adopters; NGOs supporting stronger climate action may request a higher cap or justification for the 10 g/mi limit.

[P28] Requiring inclusion of nominal annual credit cap and cumulative g/mile equivalent values in the annual credit report (§ 86.1866–12(c)(3)(v)) is reasonable, but EPA should mandate electronic filing formats and clarify submission deadlines and public disclosure policies.

[P29] The fleet-average CO2 decrease caps in § 86.1869–12(b)(2) (10 g/mi through 2022 and 15 g/mi from 2023) risk restricting legitimate credit generation in years when manufacturers deploy many advanced vehicles; manufacturers request an appeals process or waiver for unexpected production changes.

[P30] Allowing a 15 g/mi default-credit reduction during 2020–2022 only if manufacturers meet certain definitions (§ 86.1869–12(b)(2) permission) creates unequal treatment; small-volume manufacturers may be unable to meet those definitions and seek parity provisions.

[P31] The formula to calculate combined fleet gram-per-mile decrease (§ 86.1869–12(b)(2)(i)) should be accompanied by a worked example illustrating how passenger car and light-truck fleets are aggregated, including treatment of nonconforming/multi-fuel vehicles.

[P32] The requirement to cap total credits in Mg if calculated fleet decrease exceeds limits (§ 86.1869–12(b)(2)(ii)) could create perverse incentives to manipulate vehicle classification to maximize credits; commenters request anti-avoidance rules and independent verification.

[P33] The provision allowing credits by category if the fleet decrease does not exceed the applicable limit (§ 86.1869–12(b)(2)(iii)) should detail which categories are eligible and how cross-category transfers are handled; manufacturers and auditors request clarity.

[P34] The prohibition limiting combined credits under paragraph (f) when limits are exceeded (§ 86.1869–12(b)(2)(iv)) may force disproportionate reductions affecting certain product lines; commenters request guidance on equitable allocation among vehicle categories and a dispute resolution mechanism.

[P35] The instruction to generally reduce credits from the vehicle category that caused the limit to be exceeded (§ 86.1869–12(b)(2)(iv)) lacks specificity on how to apportion reductions within that category; manufacturers request a precise algorithm or examples.

[P36] The optional treatment of “active transmission warm-up” systems as eligible through MY2019 (and optionally 2020–2022) (§ 86.1869–12(b)(4)(v)(A)) may create uncertainty for suppliers developing new systems after 2019; suppliers request certainty about optionality elections and retroactive application.

[P37] Expanding definition of active transmission warm-up from 2023 to include exhaust-waste-heat and potentially segregated coolant systems (§ 86.1869–12(b)(4)(v)(B)) is technologically favorable, but commenters ask for explicit test procedures and durability requirements to claim credits.

[P38] The similar permissions for active engine warm-up (§ 86.1869–12(b)(4)(vi)(A) and (B)) require validation protocols; engine manufacturers request test cycles, measurement methods, and end-of-life durability criteria to support credit claims.

[P39] The passive cabin ventilation definitions (§ 86.1869–12(b)(4)(x)(A) and (B)) broaden eligible technologies but could overlap with other credit categories; commenters request clarification on how passive ventilation credits interact with other thermal-management credits and any limits.

[P40] The requirement to include citations to previously approved methodologies and Federal Register notices in submissions (§ 86.1869–12(d)(2)(ii)(A)) is appropriate; however, EPA should provide a consolidated list of acceptable methodologies and a single reference appendix to reduce filing burdens.

[P41] The 20 g/mi strong-hybrid credit for full-size pickups (§ 86.1870–12(a)(2) permission) is a significant incentive, but the 10% production threshold (§ 86.1870–12(a)(2) obligation) may be unattainable for some manufacturers with diverse portfolios; commenters request a scaled credit or alternative thresholds for low-volume manufacturers.

[P42] The prohibition that vehicles earning strong-hybrid credits may not also claim production-multiplier credits (§ 86.1870–12(a)(2)) forces manufacturers to choose between incentives; commenters ask for analysis showing why stacking would be inappropriate and whether a blended approach could be allowed.

[P43] Allowing trucks that meet ≤0.80×target emissions to claim a 20 g/mi credit (§ 86.1870–12(b)(2)) is generous, but the metric and measurement protocol for “target emissions” must be explicitly defined to avoid disputes; commenters request the exact test procedure and tolerances.

[P44] The condition permitting a qualifying pickup to claim the 20 g/mi credit for up to five total years (§ 86.1870–12(b)(2)) hinges on emissions not increasing; manufacturers request a definition of “increase” (absolute vs. relative) and the measurement baseline.

[P45] The prohibition that the 20 g/mi credit cannot be claimed after 2025 (§ 86.1870–12(b)(2)) removes long-term predictability for product planning; manufacturers request an explanation of the policy goal and whether credits could be extended if technology adoption lags.

[P46] The production threshold requiring at least 10% of full-size pickup production meet emissions criteria to qualify for the credit (§ 86.1870–12(b)(2) obligation) should clarify how production is defined (domestic production vs. U.S. sales) and whether leased/demo vehicles count.

[P47] The permission to allow EPA-approved major redesigns to qualify for an additional five years (§ 86.1870–12(b)(2)) would benefit from a clear definition of “major redesign”; the “good engineering judgment” standard (§ 86.1870–12(b)(2) obligation) is too vague and could lead to inconsistent EPA decisions — commenters request objective criteria.

[P48] The arithmetic average calculation for natural gas dual-fuel model types for MY2012–2015 (§ 600.510–12(j)(2)(v)) rounded to nearest g/mi may be obsolete and irrelevant for current model years; affected manufacturers request retroactive compliance relief or confirmation this applies only historically.

[P49] Allowing MY2021+ natural gas dual-fuel models to use a utility factor of 0.5 or the prescribed UF (§ 600.510–12(j)(2)(vii)(A)) gives flexibility but could be gamed; regulators and environmental NGOs request documentation requirements proving real-world utility-factor usage and third-party verification.

[P50] Overall, the rule contains many cross-references and conditional permissions that increase compliance complexity; stakeholders request a consolidated compliance guide, machine-readable formulas, reporting templates, and a delayed effective date to allow systems updates.

The obligation in § 86.1818–12(c)(2)(i) to determine a CO2 target per passenger automobile lacks transitional guidance for vehicles designed to previous target frameworks; manufacturers request grandfathering rules or phase-in periods.

The footprint threshold at ≤41 sq ft in § 86.1818–12(c)(2)(i)(A) creates cliff effects for vehicles that differ only slightly in footprint; manufacturers request smoothing provisions or a tolerance for dimensional measurement variability.

The >56 sq ft threshold in § 86.1818–12(c)(2)(i)(B) for selecting table values does not address vehicles with variable footprints across trim levels; commenters ask for guidance on which footprint to use (base model, highest, or average).

The calculation and rounding to nearest 0.1 g/mi in § 86.1818–12(c)(2)(i)(C) may impose impractical precision requirements for manufacturers’ compliance systems; industry requests confirmation that standard rounding practices in existing certification tools are acceptable.

The cap preventing the calculated CO2 target from exceeding the model-year value in § 86.1818–12(c)(2)(i)(C) could result in inconsistent or non-monotonic target progression across footprints; policy analysts request worked examples showing impacts for multiple footprints and model years.

The separate light truck CO2 target determination (§ 86.1818–12(c)(3)(i)) treats passenger cars and light trucks differently but provides no explanation of the policy rationale; stakeholders request the underlying data and modeling used for this differentiation.

The ≤41 sq ft breakpoint for light trucks in § 86.1818–12(c)(3)(i)(A) is ambiguous for crossover vehicles and SUVs that may be classified differently by various agencies; commenters request cross-reference to vehicle classification rules and a clear method for classification.

The calculation framework in § 86.1818–12(c)(3)(i)(B) for light trucks with footprints >41 sq ft and ≤ maximum requires rounding to 0.1 g/mi but lacks specification of measurement protocols for footprint determination; manufacturers request explicit measurement standards and tolerances.

The prohibition that the calculated light-truck CO2 target cannot exceed the model-year maximum (§ 86.1818–12(c)(3)(i)(B)) could create situations where no feasible target exists for certain vehicle configurations; commenters ask for an exception or remediation process in such cases.

The requirement in § 86.1818–12(c)(3)(i)(C) to apply the specified equation between minimum and maximum footprints for each model year may produce discontinuities at the table endpoints; technical commenters request sample calculations and graphs across the full footprint range.

Selecting the CO2 target for light trucks greater than the minimum (§ 86.1818–12(c)(3)(i)(D)) from a table without guidance on interpolation for values between table entries is unclear; commenters request interpolation rules or an explicit continuous formula.

The statement in § 86.1865–12(k)(2) that nothing may be construed to limit EPA’s authority to terminate authorization appears overly broad and could undermine due process and reliance interests; legal commenters request limitation language or a required notice-and-comment termination process.

The obligation in § 86.1865–12(k)(3) for reporting and recordkeeping of CO2 credits (including early credits) lacks specificity about record retention periods, data formats, and confidentiality protections; manufacturers and trade groups request detailed regulatory guidance and assurance about confidential treatment of proprietary data.

The prohibition in § 86.1865–12(k)(6) barring use of credits older than five model years after generation is stricter than prior programs and will strand legitimate banked credits; auto manufacturers request extended banking life or a phase-out schedule to avoid sudden compliance shortfalls.

The exception preserving full value for 2016 credits through 2023 (§ 86.1865–12(k)(6)(i)) but disallowing use thereafter unfairly penalizes manufacturers who planned around previous rules; commenters request either conversion options, buy-back mechanisms, or transition relief for credits that will expire.

The rule in § 86.1865–12(k)(6)(ii) giving a six-year shelf-life for credits generated in 2017–2020 is arbitrary; industry asks for economic analysis demonstrating the rationale and for consideration of banking flexibility during market disruptions (e.g., supply chain, pandemic).

The permission for manufacturers to apply production multipliers (§ 86.1866–12(b)) for advanced technology vehicle credits is useful but the rule should clarify whether multipliers stack with other credits and the documentation required to substantiate eligibility.

The prohibition disallowing full-size pickups that use a production multiplier from claiming strong-hybrid or performance-based credits (§ 86.1866–12(b)) could force manufacturers into suboptimal credit strategies; commenters request an economic modeling of which credits will be most valuable and whether this restriction unfairly disadvantages certain technology pathways.

The obligation to use specified production multipliers for 2017–2025 (§ 86.1866–12(b)(1)) should be accompanied by a mechanism to update multipliers based on technological progress; trade associations request periodic review and rulemaking to adjust multipliers if advanced tech costs decline.

The credit caps on multiplier-based credits for 2022–2025 (§ 86.1866–12(c)(3)) may create a sudden constraint during the transition to higher advanced-technology production; manufacturers request phased caps or carry-forward provisions in case caps are reached.

The required computation of a nominal annual credit cap using an equation (§ 86.1866–12(c)(3)(i)) lacks the explicit formula text and examples in the preamble; commenters ask for worked numerical examples and clarification of rounding implications.

The obligation to compute g/mile equivalents (§ 86.1866–12(c)(3)(ii)) and cumulative sums (§ 86.1866–12(c)(3)(iii)) may create complexity and double-counting risks unless reporting templates are provided; stakeholders request standardized calculation spreadsheets and audit guidance.

The absolute cap that cumulative g/mile equivalent value cannot exceed 10.0 in any year (§ 86.1866–12(c)(3)(iv)) may be too constraining relative to the program’s greenhouse-gas objectives and could penalize early adopters; NGOs supporting stronger climate action may request a higher cap or justification for the 10 g/mi limit.

Requiring inclusion of nominal annual credit cap and cumulative g/mile equivalent values in the annual credit report (§ 86.1866–12(c)(3)(v)) is reasonable, but EPA should mandate electronic filing formats and clarify submission deadlines and public disclosure policies.

The fleet-average CO2 decrease caps in § 86.1869–12(b)(2) (10 g/mi through 2022 and 15 g/mi from 2023) risk restricting legitimate credit generation in years when manufacturers deploy many advanced vehicles; manufacturers request an appeals process or waiver for unexpected production changes.

Allowing a 15 g/mi default-credit reduction during 2020–2022 only if manufacturers meet certain definitions (§ 86.1869–12(b)(2) permission) creates unequal treatment; small-volume manufacturers may be unable to meet those definitions and seek parity provisions.

The formula to calculate combined fleet gram-per-mile decrease (§ 86.1869–12(b)(2)(i)) should be accompanied by a worked example illustrating how passenger car and light-truck fleets are aggregated, including treatment of nonconforming/multi-fuel vehicles.

The requirement to cap total credits in Mg if calculated fleet decrease exceeds limits (§ 86.1869–12(b)(2)(ii)) could create perverse incentives to manipulate vehicle classification to maximize credits; commenters request anti-avoidance rules and independent verification.

The provision allowing credits by category if the fleet decrease does not exceed the applicable limit (§ 86.1869–12(b)(2)(iii)) should detail which categories are eligible and how cross-category transfers are handled; manufacturers and auditors request clarity.

The prohibition limiting combined credits under paragraph (f) when limits are exceeded (§ 86.1869–12(b)(2)(iv)) may force disproportionate reductions affecting certain product lines; commenters request guidance on equitable allocation among vehicle categories and a dispute resolution mechanism.

The instruction to generally reduce credits from the vehicle category that caused the limit to be exceeded (§ 86.1869–12(b)(2)(iv)) lacks specificity on how to apportion reductions within that category; manufacturers request a precise algorithm or examples.

The optional treatment of “active transmission warm-up” systems as eligible through MY2019 (and optionally 2020–2022) (§ 86.1869–12(b)(4)(v)(A)) may create uncertainty for suppliers developing new systems after 2019; suppliers request certainty about optionality elections and retroactive application.

Expanding definition of active transmission warm-up from 2023 to include exhaust-waste-heat and potentially segregated coolant systems (§ 86.1869–12(b)(4)(v)(B)) is technologically favorable, but commenters ask for explicit test procedures and durability requirements to claim credits.

The similar permissions for active engine warm-up (§ 86.1869–12(b)(4)(vi)(A) and (B)) require validation protocols; engine manufacturers request test cycles, measurement methods, and end-of-life durability criteria to support credit claims.

The passive cabin ventilation definitions (§ 86.1869–12(b)(4)(x)(A) and (B)) broaden eligible technologies but could overlap with other credit categories; commenters request clarification on how passive ventilation credits interact with other thermal-management credits and any limits.

The requirement to include citations to previously approved methodologies and Federal Register notices in submissions (§ 86.1869–12(d)(2)(ii)(A)) is appropriate; however, EPA should provide a consolidated list of acceptable methodologies and a single reference appendix to reduce filing burdens.

The 20 g/mi strong-hybrid credit for full-size pickups (§ 86.1870–12(a)(2) permission) is a significant incentive, but the 10% production threshold (§ 86.1870–12(a)(2) obligation) may be unattainable for some manufacturers with diverse portfolios; commenters request a scaled credit or alternative thresholds for low-volume manufacturers.

The prohibition that vehicles earning strong-hybrid credits may not also claim production-multiplier credits (§ 86.1870–12(a)(2)) forces manufacturers to choose between incentives; commenters ask for analysis showing why stacking would be inappropriate and whether a blended approach could be allowed.

Allowing trucks that meet ≤0.80×target emissions to claim a 20 g/mi credit (§ 86.1870–12(b)(2)) is generous, but the metric and measurement protocol for “target emissions” must be explicitly defined to avoid disputes; commenters request the exact test procedure and tolerances.

The condition permitting a qualifying pickup to claim the 20 g/mi credit for up to five total years (§ 86.1870–12(b)(2)) hinges on emissions not increasing; manufacturers request a definition of “increase” (absolute vs. relative) and the measurement baseline.

The prohibition that the 20 g/mi credit cannot be claimed after 2025 (§ 86.1870–12(b)(2)) removes long-term predictability for product planning; manufacturers request an explanation of the policy goal and whether credits could be extended if technology adoption lags.

The production threshold requiring at least 10% of full-size pickup production meet emissions criteria to qualify for the credit (§ 86.1870–12(b)(2) obligation) should clarify how production is defined (domestic production vs. U.S. sales) and whether leased/demo vehicles count.

The permission to allow EPA-approved major redesigns to qualify for an additional five years (§ 86.1870–12(b)(2)) would benefit from a clear definition of “major redesign”; the “good engineering judgment” standard (§ 86.1870–12(b)(2) obligation) is too vague and could lead to inconsistent EPA decisions — commenters request objective criteria.

The arithmetic average calculation for natural gas dual-fuel model types for MY2012–2015 (§ 600.510–12(j)(2)(v)) rounded to nearest g/mi may be obsolete and irrelevant for current model years; affected manufacturers request retroactive compliance relief or confirmation this applies only historically.

Allowing MY2021+ natural gas dual-fuel models to use a utility factor of 0.5 or the prescribed UF (§ 600.510–12(j)(2)(vii)(A)) gives flexibility but could be gamed; regulators and environmental NGOs request documentation requirements proving real-world utility-factor usage and third-party verification.

Overall, the rule contains many cross-references and conditional permissions that increase compliance complexity; stakeholders request a consolidated compliance guide, machine-readable formulas, reporting templates, and a delayed effective date to allow systems updates.

[P1] The May 15, 2020 effective date in § 60.5474(a)(2) is infeasible for manufacturers given long production lead times and existing inventory commitments; we request a delayed effective date or phased-in compliance schedule.

[P1] The rule’s prohibition on manufacture or retail sale unless certified to the 2020 PM limit lacks clarity on whether prototype/demo units or display models require certification; request explicit exclusion for non-sale display/demo units.

[P1] The prohibition in § 60.5474(a)(2) fails to define “manufacturer” for foreign manufacturers importing through third-party distributors; request clarification that obligations attach to the U.S. importer of record.

[P1] The provision does not specify whether “sold at retail” includes online marketplace sales and marketplace facilitators; recommend explicitly including or excluding online sales platforms.

[P2] The allowed sale of 2015-certified hydronic heaters until May 15, 2022 creates an uneven market advantage for older models and disincentivizes compliance with 2020 limits; suggest shortening the sell-through period to 12 months.

[P2] The sell-through exception in § 60.5474(a)(2) should require manufacturers/retailers to report inventories of 2015-certified hydronic heaters as of May 15, 2020 to prevent circumvention and ensure transparency.

[P2] The exception does not limit geographic distribution — sellers could stockpile and sell 2015-certified units in areas with weaker enforcement; request limitation to existing channel inventory and proof of manufacture/import date.

[P3] The May 15, 2020 ban in § 60.5474(a)(6) for forced-air furnaces should be delayed to align with furnace replacement cycles and HVAC contractors’ purchasing cycles; propose a 12–18 month extension.

[P3] The rule’s prohibition does not address small-scale custom furnace builders or field-assembled units; request an exemption or tailored compliance path for field-assembled or custom units.

[P3] The provision lacks clarity on certification burden for small manufacturers of forced-air furnaces, including test costs and capacity; ask for a small-entity compliance analysis and potential financial assistance or longer compliance window.

[P4] The sell-through exception to May 15, 2022 for 2015-certified forced-air furnaces may create safety or performance risks if older models remain on market; recommend requiring labeling of such units as meeting 2015, not 2020, standards.

[P4] The exception should require dealers to maintain transaction records proving manufacture/import dates for exempted forced-air furnaces and make these records available to enforcement agencies.

[P5] The weighted-average 2.0 g/hr PM limit in § 60.532(b) may be technologically unattainable for several categories of affected wood heaters (e.g., low-cost, low-output units); request a feasibility study or tiered standard by unit class.

[P5] Using a weighted-average emission limit allows manufacturers to offset high-emitting models by producing low-emitting ones, potentially keeping some high emitters on the market; propose per-unit emission caps instead of a weighted average.

[P5] The 2.0 g/hr limit's calculation and averaging period are not specified; request explicit definitions of the averaging methodology, sample sizes, and whether rounding rules apply.

[P6] The exception referencing § 60.530(b) is vague; stakeholders request publication of the specific criteria for exemptions and a transparent process for applying for and granting exemptions.

[P6] The rule should require public posting of all granted exemptions under § 60.530(b) and the data supporting them to ensure accountability and prevent undue broad exemptions.

[P7] Allowing the cord wood alternative means of compliance creates enforcement complexity — how will inspectors verify wood species, moisture content, or usage consistent with the cord wood test? Request detailed implementation guidance and monitoring protocols.

[P7] The cord wood alternative could incentivize manufacturers to optimize for cordwood test conditions rather than real-world performance; propose requiring field testing or consumer-use testing in addition to cord wood lab tests.

[P8] Permitting retail sale of certain wood heaters manufactured/imported on or before May 15, 2020 until Nov 30, 2020 (shorter than other sell-through periods) creates inconsistency and potential stockpiling; request harmonizing sell-through dates across heater categories.

[P8] The November 30, 2020 sell-through date for wood heaters is too short relative to dealer inventory cycles; request a longer sell-through period or allowance for pre-existing committed orders.

[P9] Requiring compliance determinations using test methods in § 60.534 without allowing equivalent or updated test methods could lock in outdated procedures; request acceptance of internationally recognized equivalent test standards or a process for method approval.

[P9] § 60.534 test procedures need clear provisions on measurement uncertainty, sample sizes, and pass/fail criteria; request explicit statistical criteria (e.g., confidence intervals, outlier treatment).

[P9] The rule should permit third-party accredited labs and provide an accreditation standard for labs performing § 60.534 tests to ensure consistency and reduce conflicts of interest.

[P10] Deeming qualifying model lines to hold certificates of compliance until May 15, 2020 creates confusion for manufacturers about labeling and warranty obligations for units produced close to that date; request guidance on labeling and certificates for units produced in the final production window.

[P10] It is unclear whether the deemed certificate for previously certified model lines extends to minor design changes; request that any change that could affect emissions requires re-certification rather than automatic deeming.

[P11] Allowing retail sale of qualifying model lines until Nov 30, 2020 even if certificate validity describes ending May 15, 2020 could be misread by enforcement officials; request that manufacturers be provided a formal written extension document to carry in the chain of commerce.

[P11] The provision should require that model lines sold under the extended sell-through date be clearly labeled on packaging and in marketing materials as certified to the 2015 standards with sell-through eligibility through Nov 30, 2020.

[P1] The regulation lacks explicit civil penalty amounts or ranges for violations of the manufacture/sale prohibitions, leaving stakeholders uncertain about enforcement severity; request specification or reference to applicable penalties.

[P3] For forced-air furnaces, the rule does not address compliance obligations for replacement parts used in field repairs; request that replacement components not trigger re-certification unless they change emissions characteristics.

[P5] The weighted-average PM limit does not specify whether catalytic and non-catalytic technologies are treated equally; request clarification or separate limits for catalytic and non-catalytic heaters.

[P7] The cord wood alternative should require manufacturer instructions and consumer outreach on recommended fuel and operation to achieve compliance in the field; request mandatory consumer-use guidance.

[P2] The sell-through exception should prohibit relabeling or retroactive claims that 2015-certified models meet 2020 limits; include explicit prohibition on deceptive marketing.

[P9] The compliance testing requirement should include provisions for retest after failure, including timelines and who bears the cost; request explicit retest procedures and cost allocation.

[P6] The exemption process under § 60.530(b) must include a public comment period before granting any permanent exemptions, to ensure stakeholder input.

[P5] The rule should require periodic post-market surveillance testing of certified units to ensure ongoing compliance and prevent degradation over time.

[P3] The prohibition language should specify whether remanufactured or refurbished forced-air furnaces are considered “manufactured” and thus covered; request an explicit carve-out or rule for refurbishment.

[P1] The rule should allow temporary limited pilot manufacture of non-certified units for R&D or testing with prior notification to the agency to avoid stifling innovation.

[P8] The different sell-through deadlines across categories will complicate retail inventory management; request a single harmonized sell-through deadline for all residential heaters and furnaces.

[P11] The deemed extension for model lines should be accompanied by a requirement to notify retailers and distributors of the extension to avoid accidental removal from sale.

[P1] The requirement in §25.353 to design to ultimate loads from yaw maneuvers is unacceptably vague because it does not specify the load factor multipliers or safety margins to be applied, creating uncertainty for manufacturers about certification load levels.

[P1] Industry commenters will request clarification that "ultimate loads" means limit loads multiplied by the established safety factor (e.g., 1.5) consistent with other §25 structural provisions, otherwise there is inconsistency across certification standards.

[P1] Small aircraft manufacturers will argue that applying ultimate load design for all powered-rudder airplanes regardless of size or configuration imposes disproportionate cost and weight penalties and request scaling or applicability thresholds by maximum takeoff weight.

[P2] Requiring evaluation of yaw conditions with landing gear and speed brakes retracted ignores realistic failure scenarios during approach and landing; operators will request an additional required evaluation with landing gear and speed brakes extended.

[P2] Airworthiness authorities and safety advocates will challenge the restriction to retracted gear/spoilers because many rudder-related incidents occur near approach speeds; they will request the rule explicitly require assessment at landing configurations where pilot forces and control authority differ.

[P3] Allowing applicants to assume yawing velocity is zero when computing loads (§25.353 permission) will be opposed by flight test engineers and safety groups who argue that dynamic yaw rate can significantly change load cases, and they will request limiting or conditioning the permission (e.g., only for quasi-steady analyses, not for transient loading).

[P3] Aerospace structural analysts will request that if yawing velocity may be assumed zero, the agency must require a supporting justification and sensitivity analysis showing that nonzero yaw rates do not increase loads beyond those computed with zero yawing velocity.

[P4] The mandated 200-pound pilot force is unrealistic for international operations and pilots of varying sizes; pilot organizations will request either using a percentile-based anthropometric force (e.g., 95th percentile male) or providing alternate force cases for different crew sizes and seating layouts.

[P4] Human factors experts will point out that 200 pounds (~890 N) as a constant control input does not reflect the moment arms used in actual rudder pedals; commenters will request specifying how the 200-pound pilot force is to be applied (force vs. torque, pedal position) and whether it includes leg vs. foot application.

[P4] General aviation groups will argue that 200 pounds is excessive for light aircraft with manual rudder controls and may lead to overdesign; they will request differentiating between hydraulically/electrically actuated rudders and manual systems in applying the pilot force assumption.

[P5] Requiring the flight deck rudder control displacement per §25.351(a) and (b) for unaccelerated zero-yaw cases assumes availability of those referenced provisions; legal commenters will ask the agency to reproduce critical values or explicitly restate the referenced displacements to avoid cross-referencing errors.

[P5] Manufacturers will ask for clarification on how to apply §25.351 displacements in fly-by-wire systems with artificial feel and limiter laws, and whether simulated or commanded displacement counts as "flight deck rudder control is displaced."

[P6] The sudden opposite rudder displacement at the overswing sideslip angle (§25.353(b)) does not define the rate of displacement (time to deflect) — commenters will request specifying deflection rates or maximum time constants to ensure consistent load assessments.

[P6] Flight control system designers will request that the rule allow for credited control system rate limiting and servo dynamics in the analysis, rather than assuming instantaneous or infinite-rate displacements that are unattainable in real systems.

[P7] For §25.353(c) (opposite overswing sideslip angle), test labs will request explicit numeric definitions of "opposite overswing sideslip angle" or a procedure to compute it, otherwise different applicants will use inconsistent criteria leading to non-uniform safety levels.

[P7] Aerodynamicists will comment that the rule should require evaluation of both symmetric and asymmetric engine-out configurations in these overswing side-slip cases, because yawing moment capabilities differ with thrust asymmetry.

[P8] The "subsequent overswing sideslip angle" in §25.353(d) is ambiguous — legal and technical commenters will request the agency define "subsequent" (e.g., second maximum overswing in time sequence) or provide an example sequence of maneuvers to be analyzed.

[P8] Flight operations stakeholders will ask that the rule account for repeated oscillatory rudder inputs (multiple overswing cycles) since structural fatigue from repeated events could be critical even if single-event ultimate loads are met.

[P9] The sudden return-to-neutral scenario in §25.353(e) needs a specified return time or rate; manufacturers will ask for a quantitative return-to-neutral rate to avoid conservative assumptions that overstate loads.

[P9] Human factors and systems engineers will request that the rule permit incorporation of pilot reaction time and autopilot/autotrim interventions when modeling the sudden return to neutral, to reflect realistic control behavior.

[P10] The speed-range specification (from VMC or highest airspeed for max rudder deflection at zero sideslip up to VC/MC) is circular and operationally unclear; commenters will ask the agency to provide precise computational methods to determine the lower bound (VMC vs. highest airspeed for max rudder deflection).

[P10] Test pilots and certification engineers will request explicit definitions and computational procedures for "highest airspeed for which it is possible to achieve maximum rudder deflection at zero sideslip," including allowances for control system limits and aerodynamic loads that vary with altitude and center-of-gravity.

[P10] Operators will argue that using VMC as a lower bound may lead to overly severe load cases at very low speeds and request that the agency permit limiting the required evaluation speed range when operationally irrelevant (e.g., very light two-engine transports).

[P1] The annual re-interview requirement in § 200.89(b)(2) imposes an undue administrative burden on SEAs with small migratory student populations because re-interviewing a statistically valid random sample each year will consume disproportionate staff time and resources.

[P1] The rule should clarify the required sample size or sampling methodology for the annual validation in § 200.89(b)(2); as written, SEAs lack guidance on what constitutes an acceptable "random sample."

[P1] Requiring validation "for the current reporting period" in § 200.89(b)(2) is ambiguous—commenters request that the agency define the precise date range and cutoff used to determine which determinations are "current."

[P2] Permitting SEA or local operating agency staff to serve as re-interviewers creates a conflict of interest and risks biased results; only truly independent contractors or auditors should be allowed.

[P2] The permission in § 200.89(b)(2) to use "other trained persons" as re-interviewers is too open-ended; the rule must set minimum qualifications, training hours, and competency tests for non-SEA re-interviewers.

[P3] The requirement in § 200.89(b)(2)(i) to use independent re-interviewers at least once every three years until Sept 1, 2020 is obsolete and should be removed or updated to reflect current dates and transitional provisions.

[P3] The three-year frequency for independent re-interviewers in § 200.89(b)(2)(i) is insufficient to ensure ongoing program integrity; advocates recommend annual independent re-interviews rather than once every three years.

[P4] The definition of "independent re-interviewers" in § 200.89(b)(2)(i) should explicitly allow third-party contractors employed by SEAs so long as there is a written firewall preventing involvement in initial determinations, to address staffing realities.

[P4] Requiring independent re-interviewers to be trained to "apply program eligibility requirements" under § 200.89(b)(2)(i) necessitates a clear training curriculum and certification process; the rule currently lacks specificity.

[P5] The blanket prohibition in § 200.89(b)(2) barring anyone who worked on the initial determinations from serving as a re-interviewer is reasonable for independence, but must include an exception for remote oversight personnel who had incidental exposure but no decision-making role.

[P5] The prohibition in § 200.89(b)(2) could unfairly disqualify small agency staff who assisted in initial determinations but are the only qualified interviewers available; the rule should allow waivers where documented staffing constraints exist.

[P6] The mandate in § 200.89(b)(3) to use independent re-interviewers after major statutory or regulatory changes is appropriate, but "major statutory or regulatory change" must be precisely defined (e.g., citation, effective date, scope) to avoid inconsistent application.

[P6] Requiring independent re-interviewers "at least once within the first three full reporting periods" after a change under § 200.89(b)(3) will create auditing backlogs; commenters suggest a single validation within the first reporting period is sufficient.

[P7] Limiting the sample for post-change testing under § 200.89(b)(3) to children determined eligible after the change could ignore cross-cutting issues affecting determinations made shortly before the change; the sample should include a comparison cohort from before the change.

[P7] The provision in § 200.89(b)(3) that the entire independent re-interviewer sample be drawn only from post-change eligibles is operationally difficult when state records do not clearly tag determinations by effective-rule date; recordkeeping requirements must be specified.

[P8] The deadline in DATES (EPA-R09-OAR-2018-0535) requiring comments by June 23, 2022 is past and inconsistent with current rulemaking timelines; the preamble should be updated or the agency should reopen the comment period.

[P9] The requirement to submit comments at Regulations.gov with the specified docket ID (EPA–R09–OAR–2018–0535) is fine, but the agency should also publish direct email addresses for stakeholders with limited internet access.

[P10] The instruction in ADDRESSES to "follow the online instructions" on Regulations.gov is standard; however, commenters request the agency provide step-by-step guidance and examples for attachments to avoid submission errors.

[P11] The statement that comments cannot be edited or removed after submission on Regulations.gov (ADDRESSES, EPA-R09-OAR-2018-0535) discourages stakeholders from timely corrections; the agency should allow commenters to submit revised versions within the comment period and replace the original.

[P12] EPA's permission to publish received comments to the public docket raises privacy concerns; the agency should automatically redact personal contact information or provide an easy opt-out for public posting.

[P13] The prohibition on submitting CBI or restricted information electronically (ADDRESSES EPA-R09-OAR-2018-0535) is appropriate, but the rule must specify secure alternatives and the process for claiming confidentiality in mailed submissions.

[P14] The obligation that multimedia submissions include an accompanying written comment is reasonable, but the agency should accept multimedia as the primary content for commenters with disabilities and waive the written requirement when accommodations are requested.

[P15] Treating the written comment as the "official comment" (ADDRESSES EPA-R09-OAR-2018-0535) may disadvantage stakeholders who submit supplemental materials; the agency should allow referencing and incorporating by reference external reports hosted on stable third-party repositories.

[P16] The prohibition on EPA considering comments or content submitted outside the primary submission is overly restrictive; stakeholders should be able to submit supplementary documents hosted on secure cloud services, with the primary submission containing links and an explanation.

[P17] The 30-day public comment period (SUPPLEMENTARY INFO III) is inadequate for complex SIP and contingency measure proposals; commenters request at least a 60- to 90-day period to allow tribal, state, and public review and to prepare technical analyses.

[P18] The background obligation that states with nonattainment areas must submit SIP revisions after designation (SUPPLEMENTARY INFO) is legally correct, but EPA should provide technical assistance and templates to states for meeting the specific contingency measure requirements.

[P19] The requirement for states to implement the 2008 ozone NAAQS under Title I, part D is clear, but commenters ask EPA to reconcile how the current proposed actions interact with any subsequent ozone NAAQS updates or related litigation.

[P20] The obligation that "Serious" ozone nonattainment areas include contingency measures consistent with CAA sections 172(c)(9) and 182(c)(9) should be accompanied by detailed examples of measures that meet the requirement to reduce emissions by approximately one year's RFP.

[P21] The requirement to design contingency measures so they can be implemented prospectively (SUPPLEMENTARY INFO) is sensible, but the rule should require demonstration that the measures are enforceable and funding is available prior to SIP approval.

[P22] The prohibition on using previously implemented controls as contingency measures is ambiguous—commenters request clarification on whether enhancements to existing controls (e.g., tightening emission limits) count as "already implemented."

[P23] The SIP guidance that contingency measures include triggers, a schedule, and a statement they will be implemented without significant further action lacks a standard for what constitutes "significant further action" and should provide concrete examples.

[P24] The recommendation that contingency measures achieve emissions reductions roughly equal to one year's RFP is too prescriptive; commenters suggest allowing a reasonable range (e.g., 0.75–1.25 years) to account for measurement uncertainty.

[P25] The obligation to promulgate a FIP under section 110(c) if partial disapproval is finalized (II) is appropriately stated, but commenters urge EPA to provide timelines and coordination procedures with states to minimize disruption.

[P26] The imposition schedule for offset and highway funding sanctions (18 and 24 months as stated in II) is a significant policy consequence that warrants clearer explanation and notice procedures before sanctions take effect.

[P27] The exception that sanctions will not be imposed if a corrective SIP is submitted before the deadline (II) should be expanded to allow temporary relief where states demonstrate substantial progress toward correction even if formal SIP submission is delayed.

[P28] The DATES deadline (EPA-HQ-OLEM-2021-0609) of August 1, 2022 is inconsistent with other dockets and is outdated; the agency must ensure public materials show accurate current deadlines.

[P29] The permission to submit comments via multiple methods (EPA-HQ-OLEM-2021-0609) is helpful, but the agency should explicitly accept submissions from tribal governments via tribal government portals or designated tribal contacts.

[P30] The instruction to follow Regulations.gov online submission instructions (EPA-HQ-OLEM-2021-0609) should be supplemented with a contact helpdesk email/phone for users experiencing technical difficulties.

[P31] The prohibition on submitting CBI electronically (EPA-HQ-OLEM-2021-0609) creates operational burdens for businesses that need to submit proprietary technical data; EPA should offer secure electronic alternatives like encrypted uploads or secure portals.

[P32] Requiring every submission to include the docket ID number (ADDRESSES EPA-HQ-OLEM-2021-0609) is necessary, but the rule should specify consequences and remedies if a submission omits the ID but is clearly related to the rule.

[P33] The permission that EPA may post submitted comments without change including personal information (ADDRESSES EPA-HQ-OLEM-2021-0609) is a privacy risk; EPA should redline the default to redact personal identifiers and provide guidance on what personal data will be published.

[P34] Requiring scheduled appointments for hand deliveries and couriers (ADDRESSES EPA-HQ-OLEM-2021-0609) may impede large stakeholder groups; the agency should provide multiple appointment slots and remote deposit options.

[P35] The condition that access to the Docket Center requires appointment (ADDRESSES EPA-HQ-OLEM-2021-0609) could limit public review; EPA should ensure remote access to all docket materials with an easily navigable online reading room.

[P1] The applicability of the part to "every organizational element of the Forest Service" is overly broad and should be narrowed to exclude administrative units without operational control over on-the-ground actions (e.g., national headquarters program offices) to avoid redundant compliance burdens.

[P1] Applying the rule to every organizational element creates legal uncertainty about which internal units are "responsible officials" under § 220.4 and could lead to inconsistent application across regions; clarify definitions and responsibilities.

[P2] The phrase "trivial violations will not create an independent cause of action" is vague and could be used to dismiss legitimate harms; define "trivial" with objective criteria or remove the immunity language to preserve judicial review.

[P2] Legal experts will challenge the non-cause-of-action provision as potentially inconsistent with NEPA's citizen-suit and administrative-review doctrines; ensure this provision does not limit statutory rights to challenge failures to follow NEPA.

[P3] Requiring use "together with CEQ and USDA regulations" but not clarifying precedence may create conflicts where this part diverges from CEQ guidance; add a clause resolving conflicts and confirming CEQ/NEPA regulations control.

[P4] The rule's test for when NEPA applies is phrased in programmatic terms that could permit early-stage planning to avoid NEPA; require clearer triggers (e.g., issuance of a decision document or commitment of resources) so that NEPA review occurs before irreversible commitments.

[P5] The "goal and preparing to decide among alternatives" standard in § 220.4(a)(1) is subjective and may be manipulated to avoid NEPA by claiming no "decision" is imminent; provide objective milestones that trigger NEPA (scoping notice, funding request, contract solicitation).

[P6] The requirement that actions be "under Forest Service control and responsibility" mirrors 40 CFR 1508.18 but lacks examples for co-managed projects with states, tribes, or permittees; clarify how NEPA obligations apply to joint actions and delegated authorities.

[P7] The environmental-effects trigger in § 220.4(a)(3) lacks guidance on de minimis effects and cumulative context; define thresholds or provide examples to reduce inconsistent determinations about whether effects are meaningful.

[P8] The provision excluding statutorily exempt actions is appropriate, but commenters will request an explicit list of typical exemptions and procedures to document exemption determinations to prevent abuse.

[P9] The emergency determination standard in § 220.4(b) grants broad discretion to "responsible official" with little oversight; require documented criteria and post-action review to prevent routine bypass of NEPA under the emergency exception.

[P10] Permitting urgent actions to protect life and property is necessary, but stakeholders will request limits (timeframes, resource caps) and mandatory after-the-fact public notice and environmental documentation for transparency.

[P11] The obligation to consider environmental consequences during emergency actions is too vague—stakeholders want a requirement for a brief written environmental evaluation within a specified timeframe (e.g., 30 days) and publication to the project record.

[P12] Requiring an EA and FONSI for non-(b)(1) emergency actions that are not likely to have significant impacts could impede rapid response; suggest a streamlined template EA/FONSI process with expedited public notice to balance speed and transparency.

[P13] Consultation with the Washington Office about alternative NEPA arrangements is appropriate, but routing through regional offices (§ 220.4(b)(2) and (15)) could delay action; allow direct communication channels in time-critical situations and specify response time expectations.

[P14] Allowing the Chief or Associate Chief to authorize alternative NEPA arrangements centralizes discretion—advocacy groups will urge that any such authorization be documented publicly, include CEQ concurrence, and be subject to administrative review.

[P15] Coordination through the regional office for Washington Office consultations may create unnecessary bureaucracy; require maximum response times for regional coordination (e.g., 48–72 hours in emergencies).

[P16] The requirement to promptly consult with CEQ when emergency actions are likely to have significant impacts should specify timelines, the content of consultations, and whether CEQ concurrence or notification suffices.

[P17] Integrating NEPA review into decisionmaking is standard, but the rule should require that NEPA documents be completed and considered before any funding commitments, land allocations, or contract awards to prevent post hoc rationalization.

[P18] "Lead development" of proposals and analyses could be interpreted to limit interagency collaboration; clarify roles when other agencies lead or when Forest Service serves as cooperating agency.

[P19] The obligation to complete review of environmental documents prior to deciding on the proposal should explicitly prohibit commitments of funds or resources before decision completion and require certification in the administrative record.

[P20] Taking into account comments is appropriate, but require the responsible official to respond to substantive comments and document how comments influenced the decision to ensure meaningful public participation.

[P21] Including environmental documents and comments in the administrative record is necessary; add a requirement to post the administrative record online in a timely manner for public access.

[P22] The requirement to consider analyzed alternatives before decision could be circumvented by narrowing the range of alternatives; require justification in the record for eliminating any reasonable alternatives and include alternatives suggested by the public.

[P23] Ensuring decisions fall within the range of analyzed alternatives is appropriate—legal commentators will note this must be enforceable and recommend adding a non-arbitrary standard and examples of impermissible deviations.

[P24] Allowing local officials to expand public involvement is positive, but require minimum mandatory notice periods (e.g., at least 30 days for EAs, 45–60 for DEISs) and outreach to affected tribes and stakeholders.

[P25] Requiring publication to the Schedule of Proposed Actions (SOPA) is helpful, but commenters will request that SOPA entries include estimated timelines, applicable NEPA category (EA/EIS/CX), and contact information.

[P26] Ensuring SOPA is kept current is necessary; propose a requirement that updates occur at least quarterly and within 14 days of significant changes.

[P27] The duty to notify the public that SOPA is available should include proactive outreach (email lists, social media, direct tribal/agency notices) and that SOPA availability be prominently posted on local forest websites.

[P28] Mandatory scoping for all EISs is fine but need procedural specifics: minimum scoping periods, how input will shape alternatives, and documentation of scoping decisions.

[P29] Mandating cumulative effects analysis consistent with CEQ guidance is appropriate, but require explicit methodology (temporal/spatial boundaries, baseline selection) to ensure consistent, defensible analyses.

[P30] The obligation to determine what past-action information is relevant is vague; require use of publicly available data inventories and an explicit rationale for excluding otherwise relevant past actions.

[P31] Segregation of classified information "where practicable" may be abused to withhold material; require a formal review and court-available justification before withholding entire analyses.

[P32] Maintaining confidentiality of classified information must be balanced with public right to know; require that redactions be narrowly tailored and that non-classified summaries be provided.

[P33] Prohibiting classified information in public documents is standard, but commenters will request procedures for producing publicly releasable summaries and timelines for doing so.

[P34] Withholding entire analyses when segregation isn’t feasible could unfairly deny public participation; require the Forest Service to prepare a public summary and to seek CEQ/DOJ consultation before full withholding.

[P35] Allowing incorporation by reference is efficient, but the rule must require that referenced materials are accessible electronically and free of charge or available at minimal cost to ensure meaningful public review.

[P36] The obligation that incorporated materials be reasonably available and briefly described is good but should specify timeframes for making them available and formats (searchable PDFs) and prohibit reliance on unpublished proprietary studies without disclosure.

[P37] The requirement to provide policies or staff to advise applicants should include minimum service standards (response times, published checklists) and funding so applicants and small operators can obtain guidance.

[P38] Starting NEPA upon acceptance of an application per 36 CFR 251.54(g) is sound, but the rule needs a clear definition of "acceptance" and a requirement to notify applicants and the public when NEPA commences.

[P39] Evaluating whether prior NEPA suffices is practical, but the criteria are subjective; require use of a standardized DNA checklist and transparent documentation of each factor considered.

[P40] The "essentially similar" test for reusing prior analysis could be used to shortcut review; require quantitative comparison of effects, thresholds for similarity, and public notice when a DNA is used.

[P41] Assessing whether the prior range of alternatives remains adequate should demand demonstration that substantive new alternatives were considered or why they were infeasible; deny reliance on old analyses when baseline conditions have changed.

[P42] The standard to evaluate new information or circumstances that would substantially change prior analysis should list examples (climate impacts, species listings, land-use changes) and require updated consultation with agencies and tribes.

[P43] Comparing projected effects of the new action to prior analyses needs explicit metrics and should require documentation of uncertainties and cumulative interaction with new nearby projects.

[P44] Requiring a DNA in the project record is appropriate, but stakeholders will demand that DNAs be published for public review with a minimum comment period before decisions are finalized.

[P45] The statement that decisions relying on DNAs are subject to notice, comment, and administrative review must be enforced—clarify timelines for notice and appeal rights and whether DNAs themselves are subject to full public comment.

[P46] Permitting adaptive management in alternatives is reasonable, but environmental groups will insist on strict limits so adaptive management is not used to authorize environmentally harmful activities without upfront analysis and safeguards.

[P47] The requirement to identify adjustments triggered by monitoring is necessary—specify performance thresholds, monitoring frequency, and who validates trigger events (independent reviewer or agency biologist).

[P48] NEPA analyses must disclose effects of both planned action and adaptive adjustments; require quantitative modeling of plausible adjustment scenarios and worst-case impacts.

[P49] Describing monitoring to inform officials about effectiveness should include minimum monitoring standards, funding assurances, and public reporting of monitoring results.

[P50] Allowing condition-based management is useful, but require strict definition of triggering conditions and independent verification to prevent premature implementation of impactful actions.

[P51] Condition-based alternatives must specify actions and design elements tied to triggers—require clear, enforceable design criteria (e.g., buffer widths, equipment limitations) and thresholds for scaling up or halting actions.

[P52] NEPA analyses must disclose effects of condition-based actions considering limiting design elements—require disclosure of all plausible outcomes, not just the preferred limited scenario.

[P53] The duty to describe the process to validate triggering conditions prior to implementation must include who conducts validation, evidence standards, timeline, and opportunity for third-party review.

[P54] Supplement preparation obligations are appropriate; commenters will urge that the rule require objective criteria for "substantial change" and timelines for when a supplement is required.

[P55] The trigger for supplemental NEPA when the agency makes "substantial" environmentally relevant changes is vague; define "substantial" (percent changes, acres, emissions, habitat disturbance thresholds) to prevent arbitrary determinations.

[P56] The requirement to supplement when significant new circumstances/information arise needs an explicit list of examples (new species listings, discovery of cultural resources) and a rapid process to evaluate and, if necessary, prepare supplements.

[P57] Allowing supplemental information reports is reasonable but must require public posting of such reports with a comment period when the report affects decision outcomes.

[P58] Including supplemental information reports in the project record is appropriate; require that they also be posted online and that notices be sent to stakeholders.

[P59] Categorical exclusions (CXs) for proposed actions absent extraordinary circumstances risk overuse; recommend tightening CX criteria, requiring pre-decisional review of extraordinary-circumstance factors, and annual reporting of CX usage.

[P60] The list of resource-conditions to consider for extraordinary circumstances is comprehensive; however, the rule should require specific analysis methods and documentation explaining why each listed condition either is or is not implicated.

[P61] Considering listed or proposed T&E species and critical habitat is appropriate, but require mandatory consultation with USFWS/NOAA Fisheries when these species may be affected, not just internal determinations.

[P62] Inclusion of floodplains, wetlands, and municipal watersheds as extraordinary-circumstance considerations is welcome; require coordination with state/local agencies and adherence to Executive Order 11988/11990 procedures.

[P63] Considering congressionally designated areas is essential; require mandatory avoidance or heightened scrutiny for actions in or affecting wilderness, wild and scenic rivers, and other designated areas.

[P64] Roadless areas under 36 CFR part 294 are sensitive—CX usage should be prohibited in designated roadless areas unless a thorough environmental review is completed.

[P65] Research natural areas should trigger full NEPA review when actions may affect their integrity; prohibit CXs that could degrade research natural areas.

[P66] The requirement to consider American Indian and Alaska Native religious or cultural sites is necessary; require early tribal consultation, protection measures, and inclusion of Traditional Ecological Knowledge where appropriate.

[P67] Archaeological sites and historic properties must be treated as potential extraordinary circumstances; require compliance with NHPA section 106 and tribal consultation before any CX reliance.

[P68] Defining extraordinary circumstances based on substantial adverse effects is appropriate; require objective metrics for "substantial" and a presumption against CX reliance when listed conditions exist.

[P69] Allowing weighing of long-term benefits against short-term adverse effects when determining extraordinary circumstances opens the door to trade-offs that subordinate protected resources; require transparency in benefit calculations and prohibit discounting irreversible harms.

[P70] Authorizing additional public engagement beyond SOPA notice is beneficial—stakeholders ask that such engagement include public meetings, targeted outreach to disadvantaged communities, and translation services where needed.

[P71] Requiring proportional public involvement is vague; specify minimum engagement levels for different decision types (CX, EA, EIS) so the public can anticipate and rely on consistent processes.

[P72] Not requiring a project file and decision memo for listed categories risks lack of documentation and accountability; civic groups will request that at minimum a brief decision memo and supporting record be mandatory and posted online for all CX actions.

[P73] Conditioning clerical replacement special-use authorizations on compliance with prior terms makes sense, but clarify how compliance is verified and provide due process for disputed compliance findings.

[P74] The obligation to prepare a supporting record and decision memo for the paragraph (e)(1) categories is appropriate; request explicit content requirements for decision memos (rationale, alternatives considered, extraordinary-circumstance analysis).

[P75] Post-fire rehabilitation activities limited to 4,200 acres is an arbitrary cap that may be insufficient for large, severe fires; local managers and firefighting agencies will request flexibility to exceed the acreage cap with documented justification and expedited NEPA procedures.

[P76] Requiring conformity with Agency and Departmental procedures and land plans for post-fire rehab is appropriate, but when plans are outdated, require expedited plan amendments or a pathway to ensure timely rehabilitation.

[P77] Prohibiting herbicide/pesticide use and new permanent roads/infrastructure in post-fire rehabilitation could hinder effective restoration (e.g., invasive species control); request allowance for pesticide use under strict conditions and environmental safeguards, with public notice and monitoring.

[P78] The three-year completion requirement for post-fire rehabilitation may be infeasible for complex restoration requiring multi-year work; allow extensions with documented rationale and monitoring commitments.

[P79] The 70-acre limit and 1/2 mile temporary road cap for live-tree harvest are overly restrictive for some forest health projects; industry and forest managers will request higher acreages or clear criteria for when larger projects qualify for CX or require EA.

[P80] Allowing removal of individual trees for sawlogs, specialty products, or fuelwood under the 70-acre cap is reasonable, but require clear definitions (what constitutes "individual trees") to prevent conversion to larger commercial logging schemes.

[P81] Permitting commercial thinning to improve stand health is appropriate, but the rule should require performance standards (residual basal area, retention tree guidelines) to ensure thinning is ecologically beneficial.

[P82] Salvage harvest limits of 250 acres and 1/2 mile temporary road may be too small after large-scale disturbances—request scalable thresholds tied to severity of disturbance and landscape context.

[P83] Example salvage activities that allow short temporary roads need a definition of "short" and limits on total temporary road network created cumulatively across nearby projects.

[P84] Allowing harvest of fire-damaged trees is needed, but require protocols to protect soils, wildlife, and cultural resources and to coordinate with restoration objectives.

[P85] Sanitation harvests limited to 250 acres and 1/2 mile temporary road and allowing adjacent tree removal "as necessary" is vague; define "necessary" and require documentation and monitoring to guard against excessive removal.

[P86] Excluding plan amendments that approve or alter legal rights from this category is appropriate, but legal counsel will request detailed criteria to determine when a plan amendment "compels" or "alters" legal instruments.

[P87] Approving Surface Use Plans only if they stay within specified thresholds is sensible; industry will ask for clear measurement rules (how miles are counted, whether co-located pipelines count as one or multiple miles).

[P88] The one-mile new road construction threshold for Surface Use Plan approval needs clarification on whether it is cumulative across the plan term and across adjacent leases/operations.

[P89] The one-mile road reconstruction threshold must specify whether reconstruction that increases capacity or footprint counts and whether maintenance activities are included.

[P90] The three-mile pipeline/utility disturbance limit must clarify whether co-located, parallel pipelines count separately and whether temporary workspace disturbance is included in the mileage calculation.

[P91] The limit of four drill sites should define what constitutes a "drill site" (pad size, staging areas) and whether expansions or infill drilling during the authorization period are included; industry will seek flexibility for operational needs.

raw_output:
[P1] The January 1–May 15 submission window for quality measure data is too short and conflicts with many ASCs’ existing reporting schedules; CMS should extend the window to at least June 30 to accommodate data validation and vendor processing.

[P1] Requiring submission “in the year prior to the payment determination year” creates confusion for CY transition planning (e.g., CY 2017 reference); CMS should clarify whether calendar year collection or other reporting periods are acceptable and provide examples.

[P2] Allowing ASCs to request extensions or exemptions only within 90 days after an extraordinary circumstance is unduly restrictive; some circumstances (e.g., prolonged natural disaster recovery) may not be fully evident until later and CMS should permit requests up to 180 days.

[P2] The rule does not specify documentation standards or required evidence for an extension/exemption request after an extraordinary circumstance; CMS should specify acceptable supporting documentation and the standard of review to ensure consistent adjudication.

[P3] Mandating use of an approved OAS CAHPS survey vendor eliminates flexibility for ASCs that already operate validated patient-experience programs; CMS should permit alternative validated survey instruments or vendor-equivalency petitions.

[P3] Requiring an approved vendor for OAS CAHPS may increase costs and decrease competition; CMS should publish an annual list of approved vendors and their fee ranges, or allow direct submission by ASCs that demonstrate survey administration capacity.

[P4] The “Minimum Survey Requirements and Rules and agrees to comply with current protocols” criterion for vendor approval is vague; CMS should publish the full approval checklist, scoring rubric, and timelines for vendor application decisions to avoid arbitrary denials.

[P5] Reliance on requirements “found on the official OAS CAHPS Web site” without including them in the regulation delegations too much substantive rulemaking to a website; CMS should incorporate key Minimum Survey Requirements into the CFR or Federal Register guidance.

[P6] Requiring vendors to “agree to comply with current survey administration protocols” without a formal notice-and-comment process risks sudden protocol changes; CMS should commit to a public notice period before material protocol changes that affect vendor compliance.

[P7] The prohibition excluding payment for off-campus provider-based department services that are not “excepted” (effective Jan 1, 2017) will cause abrupt revenue losses for hospitals; CMS must provide a transition period or grandfathering for existing referrals and contracts.

[P37] The parallel requirement in paragraph (b)(3) for another set of yield measures duplicates (a)(3) and may cause confusion; CMS should consolidate measurement sets or explain when each set applies.

[P38] The “more than 10 fewer observed organs per 100 donors” criterion is nearly identical to P33 and repeats the same concerns about arbitrariness and lack of risk-adjustment, especially for OPOs serving populations with higher comorbidity burdens.

[P39] The <0.90 observed-to-expected ratio in (b)(3)(i)(B) again requires transparency about expected calculations and whether transplant center-level practices are considered.

[P40] The two-sided p-value <0.05 criterion in (b)(3)(i)(C) raises the same small-sample statistical concerns; CMS should permit alternative statistical measures for low-volume OPOs.

[P48] While CMS may permit extensions for good cause, the rule does not set standards for granting extensions; CMS should publish objective criteria and an expedited review timeline for extension requests.

[P49] Establishing Systems Improvement Agreements for up to 12 months may be insufficient for addressing systemic clinical issues; CMS should allow multi-year agreements tied to measurable milestones where necessary.

[P50] Allowing up to one 6-month extension at the hospital’s request is helpful, but CMS should clarify the process and criteria by which additional extensions (if needed) may be granted in extraordinary cases.

[P51] Keeping a signed Systems Improvement Agreement in effect even if compliance is restored can create ongoing administrative burdens; CMS should allow automatic suspension or termination of the agreement upon documented restoration with concomitant monitoring reduced to a limited probationary period.

[P53] Permitting entities in 2017 to opt into 2018 criteria creates complexity and potential gaming; CMS should require advance notification and ensure incentives/penalties are neutral across entities that choose differently.

[P84] Allowing Stage 3 measures to be calculated using only patients with CEHRT records is useful, but CMS must standardize the denominator rules and publish examples showing how mixed record environments should be handled.
