[P2] Requiring laminated product producers to follow fabricator requirements beginning June 1, 2018 in § 770.2(e)(1) fails to account for technical differences between lamination and fabrication processes; EPA should tailor requirements specifically for laminated product producers.

[P2] Laminated product producers need clarity on which specific fabricator provisions apply under § 770.2(e)(1); EPA should publish a crosswalk listing applicable sections to avoid variable enforcement.

[P3] Allowing sale and use of products manufactured before June 1, 2018 (§ 770.2(e)(4)) conflicts with § 770.12(a) prohibition on stockpiled inventory sales after June 1; EPA must reconcile the two provisions and clarify whether pre-June inventory is exempt from the stockpile ban.

[P3] The permission at § 770.2(e)(4) should be limited by reasonable sell-through timeframes and labeling requirements so downstream buyers can identify pre-June-1 products and make informed choices.

[P4] The 72-hour notification requirement in § 770.7(c)(4)(v)(C) is too short for TPCs to verify third consecutive QCL exceedances and prepare accurate notices; extend to at least 7 calendar days to avoid erroneous notifications.

[P4] The 72-hour window in § 770.7(c)(4)(v)(C) creates operational pressure on TPCs and panel producers that may lead to premature supply chain disruptions; allow for exception when additional confirmatory testing is pending.

[P5] Requiring inclusion of extensive technical data (product type, dates, test results, correlative values, QCL values, and QC method) in the 72-hour notice (§ 770.7(c)(4)(v)(C)) is burdensome and may disclose proprietary test methods; EPA should allow redaction of proprietary method details while still conveying compliance-relevant information.

[P5] The list of required notice elements in § 770.7(c)(4)(v)(C) does not specify format or limits, potentially causing inconsistent notices; EPA should provide a standard reporting template.

[P6] The broad applicability of emission standards from June 1, 2018 in § 770.10(a) to “any form” of composite wood products is ambiguous for finished goods with very small amounts of composite wood; EPA should include material thresholds or exemptions for incidental composite wood in finished goods.

[P6] § 770.10(a) should clarify whether emission standards apply to custom, one-off artistic items and small-quantity craft imports to avoid overregulation of small artisans and hobbyist commerce.

[P7] The flat prohibition on sale of stockpiled inventory after June 1, 2018 (§ 770.12(a)) will cause significant financial losses for distributors and retailers holding pre-existing inventory; EPA should adopt a sell-through provision with a compliance label or limited time window.

[P7] § 770.12(a) lacks an exception for inventory that was contractually obligated or in transit on June 1, 2018; EPA should permit sale if documentation shows goods left the foreign supplier prior to the effective date.

[P8] Requiring only certified composite wood products to be sold or manufactured beginning June 1, 2018 (§ 770.15(a)) will disrupt supply chains because certification capacity is limited; EPA should stagger certification requirements or allow temporary reliance on supplier statements while certification is pending.

[P8] The “unless specifically exempted” clause in § 770.15(a) is vague; EPA must list explicit exemptions and criteria for exemption to reduce uncertainty for importers and retailers.

[P9] Mandating submission of correlation data and linear regression equations for certification (§ 770.15(c)(1)(vii)) will force small panel producers to hire external labs and consultants, increasing costs disproportionately; EPA should allow simplified documentation or use of standardized correlations for common product types.

[P9] The requirement in § 770.15(c)(1)(vii) to submit statistical models (linear regression) raises intellectual property concerns because producers may view correlations as proprietary; EPA should permit confidentiality claims or limited-use protections.

[P10] The duplication of correlation data requirements between § 770.15(c)(1)(vii) and § 770.15(c)(2)(v) is unnecessary and could create inconsistent certification submissions; EPA should harmonize and consolidate these requirements.

[P11] Requiring three months and at least 13 QC tests including correlation (§ 770.17(a)(4)) for certification is excessive for small producers with low production volumes; EPA should allow smaller sample sizes proportional to production or permit aggregated testing across small producers.

[P11] The 13-test minimum under § 770.17(a)(4) will lengthen the certification timeline and increase costs; EPA should consider accepting validated historical data or third-party QC program data to reduce redundancy.

[P12] The six-month/26-test requirement in § 770.18(a)(4) is burdensome for producers seeking continuous certification renewal and could duplicate other QA/QC programs; EPA should allow streamlined renewal paths when prior performance has been consistently compliant.

[P12] § 770.18(a)(4) should clarify whether the 26 tests must be consecutive and over what time window samples must be collected to avoid interpretive disputes.

[P13] Allowing test results to be a single chamber value or the average of nine specimens (§ 770.20(c)(2)(iv)) is appropriate flexibility, but EPA must specify when averaging is required versus when a single chamber is acceptable (e.g., panel size, heterogeneity) to avoid inconsistent applications.

[P14] The requirement that nine specimens be tested in three groups of three and averaged to form one data point (§ 770.20(c)(2)(iv)) could mask intra-panel variability and reduce sensitivity to hot spots; EPA should permit statistical analysis of the three group values rather than collapsing to a single point.

[P15] Requiring annual demonstration of equivalence between ASTM E1333–14 and ASTM D6007–14 (§ 770.20(d)) is resource intensive; EPA should allow longer intervals (e.g., biennial) unless there is process change or noncompliance.

[P15] The phrase “upon significant change or reason to doubt equivalence” in § 770.20(d) is vague; EPA should define what constitutes a significant change (equipment modification, calibration drift thresholds, personnel changes).

[P16] Permitting equivalence demonstration across several similar apparatuses within the same lab (§ 770.20(d)) is sensible but EPA should require documentation of equipment models and calibration records to ensure comparability.

[P17] The requirement to re-demonstrate equivalence every two years only after three consecutive years of equivalence (§ 770.20(d)) creates a complex rolling schedule that will be difficult to track; EPA should adopt a fixed biennial schedule from the outset for administrative simplicity.

[P18] Mandating correlation between ASTM methods and any QC method before certification and on significant changes (§ 770.20(d)) lacks a de minimis allowance for minor QC method variations; EPA should provide an expedited correlation-validation process for minor method tweaks.

[P19] Allowing correlation between similar mill QC methods and TPC apparatus (§ 770.20(d)) is helpful, but EPA should require that mill QC labs meet minimum accreditation or competency standards to prevent false correlations.

[P20] The exception that correlation is not required if the TPC’s ASTM test chamber is used for producer QC (§ 770.20(d)) may be impractical for remote producers; EPA should clarify logistics and costs allocation when TPC chambers are used for producer QC testing.

[P21] Requiring at least five comparison sample sets in each tested range for equivalence (§ 770.20(d)(1)) may be statistically insufficient for robust equivalence assessment across variable materials; EPA should require more samples or allow power-based sample sizing.

[P22] The obligation to demonstrate equivalence in at least two of three emission ranges (§ 770.20(d)(1)(iv)) unfairly limits TPCs that only test one range; EPA should permit technical justification for single-range operation without auto-limiting certification scope.

[P23] Allowing TPCs to demonstrate equivalence in only one range if they only certify in that range (§ 770.20(d)(1)(iv) and (23)) is reasonable, but § 770.20(d)(1)(iv)(C) should allow expansion to other ranges later without redoing the whole equivalence program.

[P24] The requirement of at least five comparison sample sets when demonstrating equivalence in one range (§ 770.20(d)(1)(iv)) is duplicative with § 770.20(d)(1) and may be inadequate for narrow-range validation; EPA should harmonize and justify the five-sample minimum with a statistical rationale.

[P25] The Lower Range definition as ≤ 0.05 ppm (§ 770.20(d)(1)(iv)(A)) may conflict with existing state standards that use different cutoffs; EPA should clarify relationship to state programs and whether rounding rules apply.

[P26] Defining the Intermediate Range as >0.05 to ≤0.15 ppm (§ 770.20(d)(1)(iv)(B)) leaves ambiguous how values exactly at 0.05 ppm are treated (they fall in Lower Range per P25) — EPA should explicitly state the inclusive/exclusive boundaries to avoid confusion.

[P27] The Upper Range definition (>0.15 to 0.25 ppm) (§ 770.20(d)(1)(iv)(C)) caps at 0.25 ppm but does not specify treatment of values above 0.25 ppm; EPA should spell out that higher values are noncompliant and any consequences.

[P28] Requiring correlation to be shown by acceptable r-value or threshold approach (§ 770.20(d)(2)) without specifying acceptable r thresholds creates uncertainty; EPA should publish the minimum r-value and test acceptance criteria.

[P29] Mandating at least five data pairs and simple linear regression for correlation (§ 770.20(d)(2)(i)) may be statistically weak and ignores potential non-linearity; EPA should require diagnostic checks (residual analysis) and consider robust regression methods.

[P30] Allowing either composite wood products or reference materials to establish correlation (§ 770.20(d)(2)(i)) is flexible, but EPA should require that reference materials be certified and traceable to prevent inconsistent baselines.

[P31] Permitting panel producers to collaborate with their TPCs to develop correlations (§ 770.20(d)(2)(i)(A)) is beneficial, but EPA should require written agreements and conflict-of-interest safeguards to ensure independent verification.

[P32] Allowing use of the average of clustered data pairs as a QC limit instead of linear regression (§ 770.20(d)(2)(i)(B)) is potentially less protective and could be gamed; EPA should require statistical justification and minimum cluster sizes.

[P33] The requirement that the QC limit under the threshold approach be below the emission standard (§ 770.20(d)(2)(i)(B)) is appropriate, but EPA should define how much margin below the standard is required (e.g., safety buffer) to account for testing uncertainty.

[P34] The requirement that at least one representative test panel be randomly selected and not be top or bottom of a bundle (§ 770.22(c)(2)(i)) is good practice but EPA must define “random” and the randomization procedure to prevent biased selections.

[P35] Requiring panel sampling to follow the quarterly testing procedure in § 770.20(c)(2)(iv) (§ 770.22(c)(2)(i)) could be inconsistent with seasonal production variability; EPA should permit targeted sampling during different production runs when justified.

[P36] Allowing selection from properly stored samples set aside for retest (§ 770.22(c)(2)(i)) is reasonable, but EPA should set minimum storage conditions and chain-of-custody requirements to ensure sample integrity.

[P37] The exception in § 770.22(f)(1) that notifications need not apply when entities are notified after fabrication into component parts or finished goods unfairly shifts risk to fabricators, importers, distributors, and retailers; EPA should require suppliers to notify downstream users promptly and provide remediation obligations.

[P37] § 770.22(f)(1) should require that fabricators, importers, distributors, or retailers who receive late notification be entitled to remedies from the panel producer (e.g., replacement, recall support) rather than being left without options.

[P38] Requiring importers to retain records for three years and produce them within 30 days (§ 770.30(b)) may be unrealistic for small importers who use third-party logistics providers; EPA should allow 45–60 days or permit interim electronic access arrangements.

[P38] The 30-day production timeframe to EPA in § 770.30(b) conflicts with typical international document retrieval timelines; EPA should accept electronic production within 30 days if on-site originals require longer retrieval.

[P39] Mandating supplier written statements on bills of lading or invoices for three years (§ 770.30(b)) will require changes to international commercial practices; EPA must provide model supplier statements and allow electronic supplier declarations.

[P40] The requirement to make records available to EPA within 30 calendar days (§ 770.30(b)) should be accompanied by safe harbor language protecting importers who have made good-faith efforts to obtain documents from upstream suppliers.

[P41] Fabricators, distributors, and retailers being required to obtain supplier statements (§ 770.30(c)) imposes downstream verification duties that many retailers cannot practically perform; EPA should permit reliance on reasonable inquiry standards and provide sample verification procedures.

[P41] § 770.30(c) should clarify liability allocation when supplier statements are false — specifically whether downstream entities are liable if they reasonably relied on supplier documentation.

[P42] The labeling requirement in § 770.45(a) to include producer name, lot number, TPC number, and certification statement on panels/bundles is necessary but could be logistically difficult for very small panels or finished goods packaging; EPA should allow alternative electronic labeling or scannable codes.

[P42] § 770.45(a) should specify exact wording for the “TSCA Title VI certification/compliance statement” to avoid inconsistent or misleading claims by producers and suppliers.

[P43] Requiring an identification method linking unlabeled panels to supplier and label information (§ 770.45(a)) shifts the burden to downstream actors; EPA should permit common industry identification systems (e.g., barcodes, serialized invoices) and accept reasonable recordkeeping practices.

[P44] The obligation to provide supplier and label information to potential customers upon request (§ 770.45(a)) may create privacy and competitive concerns; EPA should permit anonymization of certain supplier details while still proving compliance.

[P45] Permitting labels to be applied by stamp, tag, or sticker (§ 770.45(a)) is flexible but needs standards for durability and legibility; EPA should require minimum font size, permanence, and location specifications.

[P46] Requiring that all panels and finished goods be properly labeled before importation (§ 770.45(f)) will complicate import logistics, especially for finished goods shipped in bulk; EPA should allow labeling at the first point of arrival in the U.S. under bonded customs control or permit consolidated shipment documentation for boxes/bundles.

[P1] The comment period deadline of May 26, 2022 (§ 39.13(a)) is unreasonably short given the technical complexity of the bulletin; stakeholders request an extension of at least 60 days to prepare meaningful comments.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether electronic comments submitted on May 26, 2022 at 11:59 p.m. ET will be accepted, because the provision does not specify a time-of-day cutoff.

[P2] The applicability (§ 39.13(c)) is overly broad by including all 757–200 and –300 series airplanes certificated in any category without regard to configuration or modification status; commenters request narrowing to affected line numbers or specific configurations.

[P2] Aircraft on which the referenced Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin actions have already been incorporated in later Supplemental Type Certificates (STCs) or modifications should be explicitly excluded from the applicability in § 39.13(c) to avoid redundant compliance.

[P3] The obligation to "comply within the compliance times specified" (§ 39.13(f)) lacks a mechanism for operators to document and receive approval for phased or prioritized scheduling across fleet assets; commenters request inclusion of scheduling flexibility and an exigent workload provision.

[P3] The provision (§ 39.13(f)) should require FAA to provide guidance on credit for previously performed actions performed to different standards, including an explicit acceptable level of deviation, rather than leaving it ambiguous.

[P4] Requiring operators to "perform all applicable actions and follow the Accomplishment Instructions" (§ 39.13(g)) without specifying acceptable deviations or tolerances could conflict with manufacturer repair practices; commenters ask for clear tolerances and acceptable alternate tooling/procedures.

[P4] The cross-reference in § 39.13(g) to the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin is too reliant on an external document; commenters request that critical steps (e.g., inspection intervals, torque values, part numbers) be incorporated directly into the AD to prevent interpretive errors.

[P1] The requirement that the design "must be the dominant feature" leaves too much ambiguity—please clarify quantitatively whether the live portrayal must cover a minimum percentage of the artwork area (e.g., 50% of the visible composition) or whether dominance is a qualitative judgment by judges.

[P1] Wildlife artists will be disadvantaged because many compelling stamp compositions rely on habitat, typography, or secondary elements; the rule should allow non-bird elements to share prominence so long as an eligible species remains clearly featured.

[P1] The phrase "one of the eligible waterfowl species" could be read to forbid hybrid or stylized representations—request explicit allowance for scientifically accurate hybrids or subspecies when applicable.

[P2] Permitting multiple eligible species is helpful, but the rule should state whether mixed-species group scenes must still maintain a single species as the dominant element under P1, or whether multiple species may jointly constitute the dominant feature.

[P2] Industry commenters worry that multiple-species depictions could complicate licensing and royalties if species-specific imagery affects state/federal marketing; request guidance on intellectual property/licensing implications for multi-species entries.

[P3] The judges’ mandate to select a design that will be "accepted" and "widely accepted" is inherently subjective—request objective selection criteria or a public-review step to validate "wide acceptance" before final selection.

[P3] Mandating judges to choose the "best design that will make an interesting, useful, and attractive duck stamp" could lead to exclusion of scientifically accurate but less stylistically conventional designs—ask for balancing language requiring conservation/scientific considerations be weighted equal to "attractiveness."

[P3] Legal experts will note that the phrase "accepted and pr" appears truncated in the text—request correction and full text to ensure enforceability.

[P4] Requiring original hand-drawn designs discriminates against artists who use mixed media or digital sketching as a primary artistic method—request allowance for digitally created art when it is the artist's original work and not generated by AI or automated devices.

[P4] The "hand-drawn" mandate imposes an accessibility burden on artists with disabilities who cannot produce hand-drawn work; propose an exception allowing equivalent original methods if the entrant documents a disability.

[P4] Clarify whether traditional uses of drafting aides (projectors, grids) or transfer techniques are permitted under "hand-drawn" or if those are considered mechanical reproduction.

[P5] The prohibition on copies/duplicates of previously published art includes photographs—this could unintentionally bar realistic drawings based on reference photographs; request a carve-out explicitly permitting an artist to use photographic references so long as the entry is an original creative work and not a trace/duplicate.

[P5] The term "previously published" is overbroad—does it include private portfolio websites, social media posts, or only commercially published works? Request definition of "published" and guidance on the look-back period.

[P5] Photographers and photo-based artists face uncertainty: if an artist published an earlier unrelated piece on social media, would that disqualify later artwork that references the earlier image? Request clear rules about prior self-publication and reuse.

[P6] The blanket prohibition on computer-generated art and prints will exclude many contemporary wildlife artists who use digital tablets and printers as part of their original practice; ask for an amendment permitting digitally created original art that is not generated by AI and is printed only for submission.

[P6] The exclusion of "art produced from a computer printer or other computer/mechanical output device" is vague—does scanning a hand-drawn piece and printing it for submission constitute disqualification? Request explicit guidance on acceptable submission formats (high-resolution scans vs. printer output).

[P6] Industry stakeholders warn that enforcement of the prohibition will be difficult and could lead to arbitrary disqualifications; request an objective test (e.g., file provenance, metadata, signed artist statement) to verify originality.

[P7] The airbrush exception creates an unjustified preference for a specific mechanical technique; request either removal of the exception or expansion to include other traditional mechanical aids (e.g., stippling pens, markers) used in fine art.

[P7] Clarify whether airbrush-produced works must be hand-painted originally and whether subsequent digital editing of airbrush art is permissible without disqualification.

[P8] Allowing previously submitted non-selected entries to be resubmitted is reasonable, but request a limit on how many times the same entry may be resubmitted (e.g., maximum two additional contests) to ensure the contest promotes new work.

[P8] The rule should clarify whether prior entries that were revised count as the "same entry"—if an artist substantially modifies a prior entry, will it be treated as new or resubmitted work? Request criteria defining "substantially revised."

[P9] The five-judge panel prerequisites are broad; request transparency requirements about how judges are selected, their qualifications, and disclosure of conflicts of interest to avoid cronyism.

[P9] Conservation organizations request that at least one seat on the five-judge panel be reserved for a recognized conservation scientist to ensure conservation values are represented.

[P10] "Recognized art credentials" is vague—ask the agency to list acceptable credentials (e.g., degrees, museum positions, professional memberships) or to define a minimum threshold of experience (years exhibiting, awards).

[P11] The requirement that judges have knowledge of waterfowl anatomy and habitat could be met superficially—request minimal standards or documentation (e.g., relevant coursework, publications, professional experience).

[P12] The inclusion of "understanding of the wildlife sporting world" may bias selection toward hunting-oriented aesthetics; request that the panel also include non-sporting viewpoints (birdwatchers, general public) to ensure broader acceptance.

[P13] Requiring awareness of philately privileges traditional collectors—request that judges be representative of modern stamp consumers and the general public, not just philatelists.

[P14] The criterion of "demonstrated support for conservation through active involvement" is reasonable, but ask for a clear definition of "active involvement" and acceptable evidence (e.g., volunteer hours, board membership, donations).

[P14] Small but highly knowledgeable artists who support conservation financially but lack formal conservation resumes would be unfairly excluded from judging roles; propose inclusive language that values different forms of conservation support.

[P15] The judging criteria list is helpful, but the rule should specify the relative weight of anatomical accuracy, artistic composition, and suitability for reduction so entrants and judges know how to prioritize elements.

[P15] Request publication of a scoring rubric and sample annotated examples so entrants understand how "artistic composition" and "suitability for reduction" are evaluated.

[P16] Emphasis on anatomical accuracy could penalize stylized or interpretive art that nonetheless captures the spirit of the species; ask that judges be instructed to allow stylistic interpretation provided the species remains identifiable.

[P16] Scientific experts urge that "anatomical accuracy" be defined with reference to current ornithological standards and that the agency provide guidance on allowable artistic liberties (e.g., simplified plumage patterns for small-format reproduction).

[P17] "Artistic composition" is subjective—request that the regulation require judges to record written justifications when composition is the deciding factor, to foster transparency.

[P17] Graphic designers point out that composition for a small stamp differs from large-format art; request specific composition guidelines (clear focal point, negative space for denomination/text) to guide entrants.

[P18] "Suitability for reduction" must be concretely defined—suggest measurable criteria such as legibility of key details at 1:4 reduction or color limits compatible with printing processes.

[P18] Printing industry commenters recommend the rule require finalists to submit a reduced-size mockup or a reproduction test to verify "suitability for reduction" before final selection.

[P1] The May 11, 2020 deadline is unreasonably short given the complexity of the CCL materials; request extension of the comment period to at least 60–90 days.  
[P1] The rule’s absolute phrasing “must be received on or before May 11, 2020” creates unfairness for mailed submissions subject to postal delays; allow for comments postmarked by May 11, 2020.  
[P2] The list of submission methods should explicitly include email to an agency inbox for stakeholders who cannot access regulations.gov or mail/hand deliver.  
[P3] Designating regulations.gov as the “preferred method” could disadvantage low-income, rural, or small community stakeholders without reliable internet access; request alternative accessible submission support.  
[P4] The portal’s online submission instructions should be summarized in the Federal Register notice to avoid confusion; commenters request that the agency include the key steps and file-size limits in the preamble.  
[P5] The Water Docket mailing address must include instructions about acceptable packaging and whether delivery receipts will be provided to confirm receipt.  
[P6] The hand-delivery location (EPA West Room 3334) should include hours and security requirements in the notice; clarify whether identification is required for entry.  
[P7] The limitation to “normal docket hours” and requirement for “special arrangements” for boxed deliveries is vague; request published normal hours and a contact person/process for arranging large or boxed deliveries.  
[P7] The rule should allow after-hours drop-off for stakeholders who cannot make daytime deliveries, or provide clear instructions for scheduling boxed deliveries to avoid deprivation of participation.  
[P8] Requiring the Docket ID on all submissions is reasonable, but the rule must clarify consequences if a submission omits the Docket ID (e.g., will it be accepted and docketed with administrative correction?).  
[P9] Posting comments “including any personal information” to the public docket raises privacy concerns; request explicit guidance on what personal data will be published and an option to redact contact information from public view.  
[P9] The EPA should provide an opt-out mechanism for publishing personally identifying information (home addresses, phone numbers) while still counting the comment in the record.  
[P10] Reiterating regulations.gov as preferred is acceptable but redundant; suggest consolidation of ADDRESSES language to reduce confusion.  
[P11] Prohibiting editing or removal after submission may chill participation; request a limited window (e.g., 48 hours) during which submitters can correct errors or withdraw submissions.  
[P11] The inability to remove or edit comments could inadvertently publish CBI or personal data; request an agency process to remove clearly inadvertent disclosures.  
[P12] EPA’s statement that it “may publish” received comments should be clarified to specify whether publication is mandatory and whether any screening for harmful content or privacy violations will occur before posting.  
[P13] The prohibition against submitting CBI electronically is too blunt; request clear instructions on how to submit CBI (e.g., certified mail to a secure address) and how the agency will handle such materials.  
[P13] Small businesses and municipalities need guidance on what constitutes CBI in this context; request examples and a form for marking submissions as CBI.  
[P14] Requiring a written comment with multimedia submissions is reasonable, but the rule should specify acceptable file formats and maximum file sizes for audio/video.  
[P15] Designating the written comment as “official” may disadvantage persons who can only speak or submit multimedia; request that the agency accept multimedia as primary where accompanied by a brief written summary prepared by the agency if necessary.  
[P16] The provision that EPA will generally not consider materials located outside the primary submission disadvantages commenters who host supporting datasets in repositories; request an exception allowing links to archived datasets with instructions for reliable access.  
[P16] If external links are disallowed, EPA should permit submission of large datasets on physical media and provide procedures and address for such submissions.

raw_output:
[P1] The blanket prohibition on “any person subject to U.S. jurisdiction” in § 17.46(b)(1) is overbroad and will create uncertainty for state and local governments, private landowners, and contractors performing routine land management and maintenance activities on or near streams that may host these crayfish.

[P1] Conservation NGOs support a strong general prohibition in § 17.46(b)(1) because it provides essential baseline protection for the crayfish across all jurisdictions and helps prevent loopholes that could undermine recovery.

[P2] The prohibition on import/export at § 17.46(b)(1)(i) will impose compliance costs on aquaculture suppliers and bait dealers who currently ship native crayfish between states; the rule should clarify notification, permitting, or transition procedures for existing commerce.

[P3] The broad prohibition on “activities that result in mortality” in § 17.46(b)(1)(ii) lacks a clear threshold for what constitutes “result in mortality” (direct vs. indirect, measurable mortality rates); agencies should define quantitative or qualitative thresholds to guide regulated parties.

[P4] Industry commenters (construction, mining, transportation) will object that § 17.46(b)(1)(ii)(A) effectively prohibits common project elements (low-water crossings, bridges, gravel mining) without specifying spatial buffers, timing windows, or mitigation standards, creating project delays and permitting uncertainty.

[P5] § 17.46(b)(1)(ii)(A)(1) (prohibiting construction of instream low-water crossings) fails to distinguish between temporary, properly designed low-water crossings that minimize impacts and poorly constructed crossings; the rule should permit best-practice designs or allow § 17.32 permitting pathways.

[P6] State departments of transportation will request an exemption or streamlined consultation for routine bridge maintenance/replacement referenced in § 17.46(b)(1)(ii)(A)(3) to avoid indefinite suspension of essential infrastructure projects.

[P7] § 17.46(b)(1)(ii)(A)(2) (destruction of riparian habitat causing excessive sedimentation) is vague because “excessive sedimentation” is not defined; the Service should adopt numeric turbidity or sedimentation metrics or cite existing standards (e.g., state water quality criteria).

[P8] Aggregate and gravel mining companies will challenge the prohibition in § 17.46(b)(1)(ii)(A)(4) as economically disruptive and ask for clear spatial restrictions, mitigation banking options, and a process for site-specific permits under § 17.32.

[P9] Mining industry and state regulators will argue that § 17.46(b)(1)(ii)(B) (prohibiting activities that introduce heavy metals) unfairly singles out heavy metal mining without accounting for modern mine water treatment and reclamation measures; request inclusion of conditional authorizations where best practices and effluent limits prevent species harm.

[P10] The explicit example listing heavy metal mining at § 17.46(b)(1)(ii)(B) (P10) will prompt mining stakeholders to seek clarification that regulated discharges meeting Clean Water Act/NPDES limits would not automatically constitute a violation.

[P11] Municipal wastewater authorities will request clarity on § 17.46(b)(1)(ii)(C) regarding “appreciably negatively affect water quality” and whether treated wastewater effluent that meets NPDES permit limits is considered prohibited; ask for safe harbor language for permitted discharges.

[P12] Agricultural organizations will raise concerns that § 17.46(b)(1)(ii)(C) and its example of agricultural runoff (P13) could criminalize routine farming practices absent clear thresholds or explicit exemptions for existing agricultural conservation practices.

[P13] The prohibition on altering hydrological flows (§ 17.46(b)(1)(ii)(D)) is ambiguous regarding small-scale water withdrawals or channel maintenance; irrigation districts request an exemption or an allowance for de minimis activities subject to best management practices.

[P14] Hydropower and water resources agencies will ask for an exemption or predictable permitting pathway for dam operation and maintenance activities (P15) that are essential for flood control and water supply but can be managed to avoid significant harm.

[P15] Flood control districts will request clarifying language regarding channel modification (P16) so routine dredging and bank stabilization authorized by existing permits are not per se prohibited.

[P16] Recreational anglers and bait retailers will object to the bait restrictions but also express support for the limited bait allowance (§ 17.46(b)(2)(iv)(D)) provided it is practically enforceable and accompanied by outreach; they will request an increase in the per-person possession limit or clarification about group or commercial baiting.

[P17] Conservation scientists will support the bait restriction conditions (P32–P33) but urge stronger monitoring and marking requirements to ensure bait is not moved between river systems, and request criminal penalties be paired with educational campaigns.

[P18] The exception allowing incidental take during restoration/remediation (§ 17.46(b)(2)(iv)(A)) is welcome, but federal agencies (EPA, USFS) and NGOs request explicit criteria for what constitutes an “overall benefit” and a transparent review process to prevent misuse.

[P19] State wildlife agencies will request that the specified agency programs named in § 17.46(b)(2)(iv)(A) be expanded to include state-led restoration projects, not only federal efforts, and that guidance be provided for cooperative funding scenarios.

[P20] Researchers and universities will support the research/education permit exception (§ 17.46(b)(2)(iv)(B)) but ask for a national model permit and reduced fees to facilitate noncommercial scientific study.

[P21] The condition in § 17.46(b)(2)(iv)(C) that crayfish captured for observation may not be removed from the site is unclear about temporary holding for educational displays; educators request an exception with biosecurity requirements and permit oversight.

[P22] The bait possession limit in § 17.46(b)(2)(iv)(D) (25 individuals) may be insufficient for guide services, tournaments, or group fishing events; guide associations ask for a commercial/guide-specific allowance with strict transport and disposal conditions.

[P23] The requirement that bait be used only in the river of collection (§ 17.46(b)(2)(iv)(D) condition) will be hard to enforce and could create hardship for anglers who move between connected waterways; commenters ask for a definition of “river” (watershed vs. named waterbody) and guidance on connected systems.

[P24] The disposal requirement that unused bait be returned to the source river or placed in a trash can (§ 17.46(b)(2)(iv)(D) condition) may increase disease/spread risks if anglers transfer bait between waters; conservation groups request mandatory decontamination and reporting when disposal is not possible.

[P25] Legal experts will note potential conflicts between the new prohibitions and existing state fishing and water use laws; they will request coordination language and preemption analysis explaining how state programs will be affected.

[P26] Private landowners and forestry companies will seek clarification on how § 17.46(b)(1)(ii)(A) and related habitat prohibitions apply to lawful silvicultural practices, logging road maintenance, and forest harvests adjacent to occupied streams.

[P27] Transportation and utility companies will request an emergency repair exception to the construction prohibitions (P5, P7) so critical repairs after storms or accidents are not delayed by endangered species prohibitions.

[P28] Environmental justice advocates will request that the Service analyze whether the rule’s restrictions on development, mining, or infrastructure maintenance will disproportionately affect low-income or rural communities and provide mitigation measures.

[P29] The rule should include clear, practicable compliance guidance and a map of occupied stream reaches; commenters will urge the Service to publish a geospatial dataset to reduce uncertainty about where prohibitions apply.

[P30] Industry commenters will request transitional flexibility (e.g., grandfathering) for projects with existing permits or projects in the planning phase to avoid stranded investments due to the sudden applicability of the rule.

[P31] Private citizens and anglers will ask for public outreach and signage requirements in affected river systems to inform the public of bait restrictions and prohibited activities and to reduce inadvertent violations.

[P32] State prosecutors and defense bar members will request clarity on enforcement: whether certain violations are civil or criminal, applicable penalties, and enforcement discretion to avoid disproportionate punishment for minor or inadvertent infractions.

[P33] The inclusion of possession/commerce prohibitions (§ 17.46(b)(1)(iii)–(v), P19–P21) may affect pet trade and aquaria; hobbyists and pet retailers request explicit exemptions or permitting pathways for captive, non-released specimens.

[P34] The exception in § 17.46(b)(2)(v) allowing possession of unlawfully taken wildlife pursuant to § 17.21(d)(2) is ambiguous; commenters request examples and a clear administrative pathway for surrendering such specimens to authorities without penalty.

[P35] The rule should include monitoring, reporting, and adaptive-management provisions tied to permitted incidental take under § 17.46(b)(2)(iv) so the Service can track impacts and adjust conditions if take exceeds expectations.

[P36] The proposed amendment to § 73.622(i) (P35) revising the Eugene DTV allotment table is unrelated to the crayfish protection rule; commenters request an explanation for its inclusion and whether it will have environmental or procedural interactions with the listed species rule.

[P37] Legal commenters will ask for the scientific basis linking each enumerated activity (e.g., bridge construction, gravel mining, wastewater discharge) to demonstrable harm to these specific crayfish species, including citations to site-specific studies used to justify categorical prohibitions.

[P38] Conservation groups will urge the Service to require mitigation sequencing (avoid, minimize, mitigate) and to authorize mitigation banking or habitat conservation plans as compliance pathways where limited impacts to habitat are unavoidable.

[P39] The Service should adopt clear definitions for key terms used throughout (e.g., “adjacent riparian areas,” “connecting habitat,” “appreciably,” “occupied”) to minimize litigation and inconsistent application among field offices.

[P40] Commenters will request that the Service coordinate this rule with Clean Water Act permitting, state water quality standards, and NEPA processes to create a single predictable compliance pathway for projects potentially affecting the species.

[P1] The February 24, 2020 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60 days to allow operators, suppliers, and labor groups adequate time to analyze the bulletin and submit substantive technical comments.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether the comment receipt date is the postmark date or the FAA’s actual receipt date to avoid premature rejections of mailed comments due to delivery delays.

[P2] The mandate in § 39.13(f) to "comply within the specified compliance times" lacks flexibility for operators facing scarce parts or limited shop availability; the FAA should allow relief for documented logistical constraints.

[P2] § 39.13(f) should require the FAA to publish explicit compliance-time metrics (flight hours, cycles, or calendar days) in the AD text rather than relying solely on the referenced Boeing service bulletin to avoid ambiguity.

[P3] Requiring all actions labeled RC in Boeing Service Bulletin B787–8120… per § 39.13(g) risks conflating manufacturer recommendations with regulatory mandates; the rule should clearly identify which actions are mandatory and which are advisory.

[P3] The cross-reference to "paragraph 5., 'Compliance,' of Boeing Service Bulletin B787–8120" in § 39.13(g) may not be consistent across revised service bulletin issues; the AD should list required tasks and times directly to prevent confusion if the service bulletin is revised.

[P4] § 39.13(h) substitution of "effective date of this AD" for "Issue 002 date" is unclear for actions already performed between Issue 002 date and AD effective date; the FAA should explicitly state how work done in that interval will be treated.

[P4] Legal counsel should review § 39.13(h) because replacing the service bulletin’s date with the AD effective date may create unexpected retroactive obligations for parts procurement and recordkeeping.

[P5] The prohibition in § 39.13(i) banning installation of CAC outlet check valves listed in paragraph 1.B on or after the AD effective date is overly broad; the rule should allow temporary use of identified spares under an approved AMOC until replacement parts arrive.

[P5] § 39.13(i) does not define a process for identifying and removing affected spares from inventory; operators need guidance on traceability, marking, and disposition to comply.

[P6] The credit provision in § 39.13(j) allowing work done to Issue 001 to count is helpful but should require documentation standards (logbook entries, work orders, service bulletin references) to ensure uniform acceptance.

[P6] § 39.13(j) should specify whether partial compliance under Issue 001 (e.g., some RC steps done) can be credited or whether only complete Issue 001 accomplishment qualifies.

[P7] § 39.13(k)(1) granting the Seattle ACO Branch manager authority to approve AMOCs concentrates decision-making geographically; operators outside the Seattle region should be concerned about response time and request a national-level AMOC process or delegated routes.

[P7] The rule should specify expected FAA response times for AMOC requests under § 39.13(k)(1) to avoid operational standstills while waiting for approval.

[P8] The procedural requirements in § 39.13(k)(1) for submitting AMOC requests per 14 CFR 39.19 are redundant; the AD should provide a single, clear point of contact with email, postal address, and required documentation checklist to streamline submissions.

[P8] Allowing email submissions in § 39.13(k)(1) without secure transmission standards risks disclosure of proprietary maintenance data; FAA should specify secure channels or allow encrypted attachments.

[P9] The notice requirement in § 39.13(k)(2) to inform the principal inspector or local FSDO before using an approved AMOC is vague about the timing (advance notice vs. immediate notification); the AD should set a specific notification timeframe (e.g., 48 hours prior).

[P1] The proposed application of section 9(a)(1) take prohibitions to the coastal Pacific marten is appropriately precautionary and stakeholders should be reminded that any ambiguity in enforcement will chill otherwise lawful activities without clear guidance.

[P1] Applying the full prohibitions of section 9(a)(1) to the coastal marten will impose significant regulatory burdens on private forest landowners and timber operators who lack clear permitting pathways for incidental take.

[P1] The rule needs to clarify whether the take prohibitions apply equally across public, private, and tribal lands and whether customary rights (e.g., tribal subsistence hunting) are affected.

[P1] The provision omits an explicit definition of "take" tailored to the coastal marten context; commenters request inclusion or cross-reference to the statutory/precedential definition to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P1] Legal experts will challenge blanket application of section 9(a)(1) without specifying available permits (e.g., incidental take statements under section 7, 10(a)(1)(B) incidental take permits), potentially rendering the rule arbitrary.

[P2] The exception for incidental take tied to specified activities is too narrow because it does not include other common land management practices (e.g., road maintenance, recreation facility work) that may incidentally take martens.

[P2] Conservation NGOs will argue that the carve-out for incidental take should require monitoring and mitigation conditions to ensure long-term viability — the proposed exception lacks explicit mitigation or monitoring requirements.

[P2] Industry stakeholders will request that the exception include a clear, administrative list of covered activities and standardized documentation requirements to expedite compliance and reduce litigation risk.

[P2] The proposed exception fails to state whether "incidental" excludes negligent or reckless conduct; commenters will ask the Service to clarify that only non-negligent, lawfully conducted activities qualify for the exception.

[P3] Wildfire-risk-reduction forestry activities should be explicitly limited to projects that demonstrably reduce fire risk and follow best-management practices to avoid misuse of the exception for broad commercial logging.

[P3] Firefighting and emergency suppression actions should be explicitly exempted from liability for take; however, the rule should require post-activity reporting to the Service to document impacts and adaptive measures.

[P3] Environmental groups will object if fuels reduction projects are allowed without requiring retention of adequate marten habitat (e.g., denning structures, understory complexity); the exception needs habitat-protection conditions.

[P3] The term "fuels reduction" is undefined and could be interpreted to permit clearcutting; the Service should define acceptable methods (e.g., thinning vs. clearcut) and limit removal thresholds (percent canopy cover removed).

[P3] Fire break and suppression activities often use heavy machinery and could destroy den sites; the rule should require seasonal restrictions to protect reproductive denning periods.

[P4] The exception tied to State-approved plans (California Department of Fish and Wildlife) risks creating uneven protections across jurisdictions and effectively delegates federal ESA protections to state processes without clear federal oversight.

[P4] Private landowners will request that the rule define which elements or minimum standards a Natural Community Conservation Plan or Habitat Conservation Plan must include for the exception to apply, to avoid arbitrary disapprovals.

[P4] Conservation groups will demand that any State-approved plan used to justify incidental take include enforceable, measurable conservation commitments (e.g., habitat retention percentages, monitoring, adaptive management triggers).

[P4] The provision does not specify whether grandfathered or legacy plans (approved prior to this rule) are eligible; commenters will ask for explicit treatment of existing plans and whether the Service will re-evaluate them.

[P4] Tribal governments will request recognition of tribal conservation plans and clarification whether State-only plan approval excludes tribal regulatory schemes from qualifying for the exception.

[P5] The broad phrase "consistent with the conservation needs of the coastal marten" in the formal-plan exception is vague and invites inconsistent application — commenters ask the Service to publish objective consistency criteria.

[P5] Forestry activities said to be "consistent with formal approved conservation strategies" should require demonstrable net conservation benefit (e.g., habitat improvement metrics), not merely compatibility.

[P5] Industry representatives will request a clear, expedited review timeline and checklist for determining whether a forestry activity is "consistent" with conservation strategies to avoid months-long uncertainty.

[P5] Conservation scientists will insist that the Service require baseline and post-activity population and habitat monitoring for any activity claimed to be consistent with conservation strategies.

[P6] The condition that the Service must determine that meeting plans/strategies would be consistent with this rule centralizes discretionary power without a transparent criteria set; commenters request publication of the Service's consistency-evaluation framework.

[P6] Legal experts will warn that allowing the Service to determine consistency "or portions thereof" invites piecemeal exceptions and could undermine comprehensive protections unless the Service publishes minimum standards and decision records.

[P6] Stakeholders ask for an appeal or administrative review mechanism for applicants whose plans are found inconsistent — the rule does not provide a process or timeline for challenging Service determinations.

[P6] The Service should commit to making all consistency determinations, supporting analyses, and any mitigation requirements publicly available and subject to public comment before finalizing exceptions for specific plans.

[P6] The Service must specify whether consistency determinations are reversible (i.e., can be withdrawn if new information shows higher take or declining populations) and provide notice procedures to affected landowners.

[P3][P6] Combined comment: Any exception for fuels reduction or wildfire management that relies on Service consistency determinations should require advance consultation, documented minimization measures, and a mandatory post-project survey submitted to the Service within a fixed timeframe.

[P2][P5] Combined comment: The rule should require that any incidental take exception (whether under state plans or formal strategies) include enforceable mitigation sequencing (avoid, minimize, compensate) and explicit monitoring and adaptive management triggers tied to marten population thresholds.

[P1][P4] Combined comment: Stakeholders request clarification on enforcement priorities and whether the Service intends to pursue civil/criminal penalties against landowners relying in good faith on State-approved plans that later are found deficient.

[P5] The Service should publish example scenarios or case studies showing what kinds of forestry activities would and would not be considered "consistent with the conservation needs" to guide practitioners and reduce litigation.

[P3] Request that the rule specify temporal protections: exclude incidental take exceptions during denning/pupping seasons (with defined dates) unless emergency measures justify otherwise.

[P4] Request that the Service define "State-approved" to confirm that only plans approved by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife qualify, and whether federal approval or concurrence is also necessary.

[P2] Request that the rule include mandatory recordkeeping and reporting requirements for parties relying on incidental take exceptions, including GPS locations, methods used, and any observed mortalities.

[P1] Comment that the rule should include language preserving the availability of incidental take permits under section 10(a)(1)(B) for activities not covered by the listed exceptions.

[P6] Request for an explicit timeline (e.g., 90 days) for the Service to make consistency determinations once a plan/strategy or application is submitted to prevent indefinite delays.

[P5] Conservation practitioners will ask that the Service require habitat connectivity and structural retention (e.g., legacy trees, coarse woody debris) as explicit conditions for any forestry activity to qualify as "consistent."

[P3] Fire management agencies will request language confirming that emergency wildfire suppression is automatically covered and cannot be second-guessed later as non-exempt incidental take, subject only to post-activity reporting.

[P4] Concern that relying on Natural Communities Conservation Plans transfers too much discretion to local governments; request that the Service set minimum statewide conservation standards for eligibility.

[P1] Request that the rule include non-waiver language clarifying that the application of section 9(a)(1) does not expand other authorities (e.g., CWA, state law) or create preemptive effects on state forestry regulation without consultation.

[P6] The dual threshold of 25,000 flight hours or 72 months is unclear regarding which metric controls when both are exceeded; request explicit "whichever occurs first/last" language be stated to remove ambiguity.

[P8] For AWL 28–AWL–20 in § 39.13(g)(4): tying the interval to Boeing service bulletin accomplishment makes compliance contingent on non-AD documents; request FAA to provide the exact service bulletin references, revision numbers, and acceptance criteria in the AD.

[P8] The 30-day catch-up window in § 39.13(g)(4) for unknown prior inspection is too short for widely distributed fleets—request an allowance for operators to document lack of records and obtain an AMOC for staged compliance up to 180 days.

[P9] For AWL 28–AWL–21 in § 39.13(g)(5): the 6-month catch-up period if no prior inspection is impractical for airlines with limited spare time and may force unscheduled maintenance; request extension to 12 months or permit inspection during next C-check.

[P9] The AD must clarify who may perform these bonding jumper installations—must they be Boeing-authorized repair stations, licensed avionics technicians, or may general certified mechanics perform them under 14 CFR part 145?

[P10] For AWL 28–AWL–27 in § 39.13(g)(6): the dependence on "specified Boeing service bulletin actions" again creates uncertainty unless the AD cites the exact Boeing SB numbers and effective revision dates; include SB references and credit.

[P10] The AD should specify acceptable test equipment, pass/fail criteria, and recordkeeping requirements for GFI testing to ensure consistent compliance across operators and MROs.

[P11] For AWL 28–AWL–28 in § 39.13(g)(7): require the FAA to publish the inspection procedures or reference the exact AWL revision so operators know the scope of inspection for the Override/Jettison pump protection system.

[P12] For AWL 28–AWL–35 in § 39.13(g)(8): requiring inspection of cushion clamps and Teflon sleeving every 144 months may be insufficient given aging-related degradation; request accelerated intervals for airplanes older than 20 years or those exposed to harsh environments.

[P13] For AWL 28–AWL–37 in § 39.13(g)(9): limiting the FQIS BITE test requirement to Model 767–300F L/N 1094 and subsequent is arbitrary—operators of earlier freighters request justification and either expansion to earlier L/Ns or technical rationale.

[P13] The 30-day catch-up requirement for AWL 37 is very short and could be infeasible for aircraft deployed overseas; request allowance for international operators to comply within 90 days or coordinate via AMOC.

[P16] For AWL 28–AWL–102 in § 39.13(g)(12): the 750 flight hour timeline is infeasible for long-haul operators between transoceanic legs; suggest allowing completion within the next scheduled maintenance visit not exceeding 6 months.

[P18] For AWL 47–AWL–05 in § 39.13(g)(14): clarify whether cross vent check valve inspections require removal/bench checks or can be accomplished via borescope; specifying acceptable methods will reduce unnecessary component removals.

raw_output:
[P1] The July 27, 2020 deadline for comments is unreasonable and impractical because operators need at least 60 days to assess fleet impacts and coordinate technical review across stakeholders.

[P1] The AD should clarify whether electronic comments submitted late due to system outages will be accepted if timestamped by July 27, 2020.

[P2] The phrase “Comply with all requirements of this AD within the specified compliance times unless already accomplished” is overly broad and should explicitly allow credit for equivalent inspections completed under approved AMOCs.

[P2] The rule should define “specified compliance times” precisely within the AD text rather than relying on cross-referenced service information to avoid ambiguity.

[P3] Requiring immersion USI at the next engine shop visit or before 6,500 CSN (whichever is first) will force some operators to perform unscheduled shop visits, increasing operational costs; the FAA should allow completion at the next scheduled heavy maintenance event within 12 months instead.

[P3] The 6,500 CSN threshold for GEnx–1B engines is not supported by presented risk analysis; FAA should provide data justifying why 6,500 CSN (rather than a higher or lower threshold) was selected.

[P3] The AD needs to define “engine shop visit” (e.g., levels of disassembly or on-wing capabilities) to avoid inconsistent interpretations by operators and inspectors.

[P4] Requiring removal and replacement “before further flight” for any rejectable indication may be technically infeasible if an alternate conforming disk is not immediately available; the AD should permit temporary operational relief with operational limitations until parts are sourced.

[P4] The AD should require GE to make eligible replacement parts available with a parts distribution plan and estimated lead times, otherwise grounding risks could disrupt airline schedules.

[P5] The identical timing requirement for GEnx–2B engines (next shop visit or 6,500 CSN) fails to account for differences in usage profiles across carriers; FAA should allow credit for equivalent non-immersion NDI methods when justified by a validated program.

[P5] The service bulletin referenced for the immersion USI on GEnx–2B should be incorporated by reference in the AD text or attached to avoid uncertainty about inspection procedures.

[P6] The “remove before further flight” mandate for GEnx–2B rejectable indications could create safety-of-flight interruptions at remote locations; FAA should permit ferry flights under strict conditions to reach maintenance facilities.

[P6] The AD should specify acceptance criteria and measurement tolerances for what constitutes a “rejectable indication” to reduce variability among inspection vendors.

[P7] The credit-for-previous-actions provision allowing earlier inspections per R00 SBs is helpful but limited; it should also accept inspections performed using subsequent minor revisions of those SBs if they are substantively equivalent.

[P7] Operators who performed inspections before the AD effective date using equivalent non-GE procedures or third-party approved NDI techniques should be eligible for credit; limiting credit to specific GE SB revisions is unduly restrictive.

[P8] Requiring that prior inspections must have used GE SB 72–0463 R00 or GE GEnx–2B SB 72–040 R00 excludes legitimate inspections done under other approved procedures and risks duplicative work — the AD should allow alternate documented procedures if records show equivalent coverage.

[P9] Granting the Manager, ECO Branch, FAA, sole authority to approve AMOCs centralizes approvals and may cause delays; the AD should permit regional certification offices to approve AMOCs for their operators to expedite responses.

[P9] The AD should publish expected turnaround times and criteria for AMOC approvals to provide predictability to operators requesting alternatives.

[P10] The requirement to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO may be inefficient for large international maintenance providers who centralize airworthiness communications; allow direct submission to the ECO Branch with copies to local authorities.

[P11] The instruction to address direct submissions to the person identified in paragraph (k)(1) is unclear because paragraph (k)(1) is not reproduced in the AD excerpt; include the manager’s name and contact details in the main AD text.

[P12] The option to email AMOC requests to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov should be accompanied by secure file transfer details for large non-text technical packages and confirmation procedures for receipt.

[P13] Notifying the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC could be administratively burdensome in multi-state operations; allow notification within a defined timeframe (e.g., 48 hours) rather than require advance notice.

[P13] The AD should clarify whether the notification requirement applies to temporary AMOCs or to every engine on which the AMOC is used, and what documentation is needed for the notification.

[P14] The duplicate July 27, 2020 deadline for Part 71 comments should be harmonized with the AD comment deadline and extended if necessary to allow integrated responses from airspace and engine stakeholders.

[P15] Requiring that comments include FAA Docket No. FAA–2020–0504; Airspace Docket No. 20–AAL–4 at the beginning of comments is unnecessarily prescriptive — allow placement in the subject line or form fields used by regulations.gov.

[P16] While online submission via regulations.gov is permitted, the AD must also explicitly allow electronic attachments of proprietary or Export-Controlled technical data under secure submission procedures.

[P17] The mailing address and phone numbers for the Department of Transportation Docket Operations should include guidance on COVID-era mail processing delays and alternative electronic submission if physical mail is delayed.

[P18] The provision that FAA Order 7400.11D can be viewed online is useful; however, the AD should provide a direct hyperlink to the specific amendment package referenced in the rule for ease of review.

[P19] The contact for the Rules and Regulations Group should include email and after-hours contact methods for international operators in different time zones.

[P20] The “Comments Invited” language should explicitly state whether confidential business information (CBI) can be submitted and the process for marking and handling such submissions.

[P21] The availability of referenced service information at the FAA office in Burlington should be paired with an option to request electronic copies for remote review, and a statement of expected response time for availability inquiries.

[P3] The AD lacks a defined applicability statement (list of affected serial numbers/part numbers) for the HPT rotor stage 2 disk — commenters will request precise applicability to avoid over-broad compliance.

[P4] The AD does not define “eligible part” — stakeholders will request a definition (e.g., part number, serial number ranges, manufacturing date, or repair state) to ensure compliant replacements.

[P5] There is no cost-impact analysis for the mandated inspections and potential replacements; airlines and MROs will demand a regulatory evaluation showing economic burden estimates.

[P6] MROs will request that the FAA coordinate with GE to produce training and qualification requirements for technicians performing the immersion USI to ensure consistency and reduce rework.

[P7] The AD should clarify recordkeeping obligations for completed inspections (how long to retain, format) and whether entries must be made in the engine logbooks or an alternative database.

[P9] Legal commenters will question whether the AMOC provisions comply with 14 CFR 39.19's criteria for equivalent safety and whether FAA must publish a rationale for any denied AMOC requests.

[P3] Labor and union stakeholders will request that the FAA consider the AD’s impact on workforce scheduling and include transition guidance to accommodate additional inspection workload without overtime penalties.

[P4] Safety advocacy groups will insist that “remove before further flight” remain as written but request that the AD require immediate grounding for any engine with documented crack propagation or multiple rejectable indications, not just single indications.

[P5] Freight carriers operating older GEnx engines may request a higher CSN threshold based on historical service experience demonstrating no incidents up to 10,000 CSN.

[P6] International operators will request clarification on how this AD harmonizes with EASA's airworthiness directives and whether reciprocal AMOCs will be accepted to avoid duplicative approvals.

raw_output:
[P1] The February 24, 2020 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonably short and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow operators, MROs, labor unions, and public-interest groups sufficient time to prepare technical and economic comments.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether comments submitted by overnight delivery or courier will be considered “received” if delivered after February 24, 2020 but bearing an earlier postmark/email timestamp.

[P2] § 39.13(f) should explicitly state that compliance times in the AD are mandatory and that failure to comply may result in enforcement actions; as written, the phrase “unless already complied” is ambiguous about past-compliance demonstrations.

[P2] The AD should provide a standard procedure for documenting and proving “already complied” status (e.g., required paperwork, acceptable records, retention period) to prevent disputes with inspectors.

[P3] The 500 engine flight hour (FH) window in § 39.13(g)(1) for engines with ≥17,500 FHs on the effective date is too short for many operators with high utilization; request extending the window to at least 1,000 FH or providing a risk-based assessment to justify 500 FH.

[P3] The AD must define whether the 500 FH compliance interval is calendar-time limited (e.g., 6 months) for low-utilization engines, to avoid indefinite exposure for aircraft that fly very few hours.

[P4] Requiring inspections per paragraphs 3.A.(4) and 3.A.(5) of GE ASB CF34–8C–AL S/B 72–A0335 in § 39.13(g)(1)(i) effectively mandates compliance with a private manufacturer service bulletin; the FAA should incorporate those procedures fully into the AD or make the ASB material available without paywall to ensure public access.

[P4] The AD should state whether any deviations from GE ASB CF34–8C–AL S/B 72–A0335 procedures (e.g., local tooling or equivalent inspection methods) require prior AMOC approval or may be used under accepted maintenance practice.

[P5] For § 39.13(g)(1)(ii) referencing GE ASB CF34–8E–AL S/B 72–A0221, commenters request clarification of the exact ASB revision/date being mandated and whether later GE revisions are automatically acceptable or must be incorporated by FAA approval.

[P6] The trigger in § 39.13(g)(2) that requires the initial inspection “within 500 engine FHs after it accumulates 17,500 FHs TSN or TSR” is unclear about how fractional hours or cycles are counted; request precise rounding rules and whether logging of partial hours is acceptable.

[P6] The AD must clarify whether both TSN and TSR are acceptable alternative metrics and, if the engine record shows different values (e.g., TSN vs TSR), which metric controls for the compliance trigger in § 39.13(g)(2).

[P7] The cross-reference in § 39.13(g)(2)(i) to GE ASB CF34–8C–AL S/B 72–A0335 should include the effective revision and date to avoid confusion; also request FAA to provide the referenced table and inspection criteria in the FAA docket.

[P8] Similarly, § 39.13(g)(2)(ii) should explicitly incorporate the GE ASB CF34–8E revision/date (June 27, 2019 is mentioned elsewhere) and clarify whether operators may use later GE service bulletin revisions without a separate AMOC.

[P9] § 39.13(g)(3)’s direction to use “engine flight hours since new” when TSN/TSR cannot be determined is impractical for engines with incomplete records; request guidance on acceptable methods to reconstruct FHs (e.g., operator logs, airframe records, estimates) and an AMOC pathway for engines with irretrievable data.

[P9] The rule should state a presumption of compliance relief (e.g., begin inspection at lower threshold) where records are missing, rather than requiring potentially unsafe delays while attempting to reconstruct hours.

[P10] § 39.13(g)(4) mandates repeat inspections using “the specified inspection criteria” but does not provide repeat intervals in the AD text; commenters request that the FAA incorporate the repeat intervals from the GE ASBs into the regulatory text or explicitly state the repeat schedule.

[P10] Operators need clarity whether repeat inspections are required for each removal/installation event or only at the Table-specified FH intervals; request examples to avoid inconsistent application.

[P11] § 39.13(g)(4)(i)’s reliance on Table 1 of GE ASB CF34–8C – without reproducing the table or summary in the AD – forces operators to obtain the ASB; request the FAA to include the table in the docket or summarize the inspection intervals and acceptance criteria in the AD.

[P12] The same concern for § 39.13(g)(4)(ii) (Table 1 of GE ASB CF34–8E) — industry requests that the FAA make the table and acceptance criteria publicly available and ensure compatibility between the two engine variants’ inspection programs.

[P13] § 39.13(h) prohibits installation of a combustion outer liner shell with greater than 17,500 FHs TSN/TSR without first inspecting per paragraph (g)(1); this will disrupt parts supply and return-shop logistics — suggest allowing pre-shipment inspections by certified repair stations as an alternative to onsite inspection at installation.

[P13] The AD should allow for documented, recent inspections performed within a defined time window (e.g., within 30 days or 50 FHs prior to installation) to be acceptable instead of re-inspecting at the installation location.

[P14] The condition in § 39.13(h) that the inspector “first inspect in accordance with paragraph (g)(1)” should permit equivalent inspection techniques approved via AMOC (e.g., borescope alternatives or enhanced NDT) without requiring a full paragraph (g)(1) procedure if safety is demonstrated.

[P15] The authorization in § 39.13(j)(1) for the Manager, ECO Branch to approve AMOCs should be expanded to allow delegation to other FAA certificated officers in high-volume regions to avoid processing backlogs.

[P15] Provide estimated AMOC processing times and a streamlined emergency AMOC procedure for operators needing temporary relief to avoid grounding aircraft pending approval.

[P16] The requirement in § 39.13(j)(1) to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 is standard, but commenters request clarity on whether electronic submission to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov satisfies this routing requirement.

[P17] § 39.13(j)(1) (direct submission specification) should identify the person in paragraph (k)(1) by name or title and include current contact information to avoid misdirected requests.

[P18] The permission to email AMOC requests to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov is appreciated, but commenters request confirmation of acceptable file formats, limits on attachment size, and acknowledgement-of-receipt procedures.

[P19] § 39.13(j)(2) requires notification to the principal inspector or local FSDO manager prior to using an approved AMOC; commenters ask whether email notification is adequate and what specific information must be included in that notice (AMOC reference number, effective dates, affected engines).

[P19] The AD should clarify whether using an AMOC approved for one operator automatically authorizes other operators with the same engine/part to use the AMOC, and if not, provide a procedure for multi-operator acceptance.

[P4] Legal commenters will challenge the AD’s reliance on non-public manufacturer service bulletin language without full incorporation into the regulatory text, arguing this raises notice-and-comment and public-accessibility concerns.

[P3] Labor/unions will submit that the short 500-FH compliance window increases technician workload and may create scheduling conflicts; request subsidies or workforce guidance to manage surge inspections.

[P13] MROs will comment that the prohibition in § 39.13(h) could increase scrap rates of used liners in the parts market and request an exception for parts installed in non-commercial or test aircraft where risk is lower.

[P9] Small operators and private owners will request an alternative compliance path for engines with inadequate historical records (e.g., accept a conservative inspection immediately regardless of hours rather than attempting to determine TSN/TSR).

[P11] Aviation insurers may request clarification whether inspections performed per the ASB but not recorded properly will affect coverage and suggest the AD require specific record-keeping elements for inspection results.

[P6] Commenters ask whether engines that have been subject to prior inspections similar to the ASB criteria may be credited toward the AD’s initial inspection requirement, and if so, what documentation will be accepted as credit.

[P8] Maintenance providers request clarification whether the June 27, 2019 date referenced for the GE CF34–8E ASB is the only applicable version or whether the FAA will issue an AD amendment if GE revises the ASB with improved inspection methods.

[P10] Environmental and community groups will request that the FAA assess the environmental impact of any required removals/replacements (disposal of parts) and include waste-handling guidance in the AD.

[P15] Legal commenters will ask the FAA to specify the standard of review and criteria the Manager will apply when evaluating AMOC requests to ensure consistent decision-making and defendability on appeal.

[P2] The AD should state explicit compliance record retention periods (e.g., keep inspection records for the remainder of the part’s service life plus 2 years) to avoid later disputes over whether compliance occurred “within the specified compliance times.”

[P1] Consumer/public-interest groups will request that the FAA reopen the comment period if substantive changes are made to the ASB references or when the full ASB materials are posted to the public docket.
