[P1] The prohibition on accepting elemental mercury in environmental media or consumer products is too broad and could prevent DOE from accepting contaminated waste streams where mercury has beneficial reuse potential after remediation.

[P1] Industry requests clarification on whether mixed-waste items containing elemental mercury below a specified mass or concentration threshold (e.g., trace contamination in equipment) are categorically excluded from DOE acceptance.

[P1] Environmental remediation contractors state that prohibiting elemental mercury in manufactured items (e.g., switches, thermostats, fluorescent lamp components) will complicate consolidation of mercury-bearing items for safe long-term management and increase disposal costs.

[P1] Hospitals and health-care facilities ask for an exception for elemental mercury contained in sealed medical devices or legacy instruments where removal poses safety risks, and request guidance on acceptable decontamination alternatives.

[P2] Chemical processors and recyclers object to the rigid 99.5% by volume purity requirement as impracticable for recovered mercury and request acceptance threshold flexibility (e.g., 99.0% or an alternate impurity specification) or allowance for pre-acceptance assay/processing.

[P2] Recyclers note that requiring 99.5% elemental mercury by volume will require additional on-site purification, imposing significant costs and delaying shipments, and request that DOE cover or reimburse reasonable pre-acceptance processing costs.

[P2] Legal experts request clarification of the term “by volume” versus “by weight” (mass) for mercury purity testing, as typical assays report concentration by mass; regulators should specify test methods and units.

[P2] Commenters ask DOE to specify approved analytical methods, sampling protocols, and acceptable laboratories for demonstrating the 99.5% purity to avoid disputes at the point of delivery.

[P3] Municipalities and industry request more detail on the fee schedule timing and whether fees are due at time of physical delivery, upon notice of DOE acceptance, or after DOE completes verification of purity, to avoid penalizing rejected shipments.

[P3] Community groups and small generators raise concern that immediate fee payment upon delivery will create cash-flow burdens and request invoicing options or staged payments tied to DOE acceptance and verification.

[P4] Several financial offices and grant-funded organizations request the option to remit fees via centralized agency billing or third-party invoicing rather than requiring payables to be made to the U.S. Department of Energy directly.

[P4] State environmental agencies request authority to pay fees on behalf of local generators and ask DOE to clarify whether state-administered funds (grants) are eligible to be used for fee payments.

[P5] International companies and exporters note the requirement for payments in U.S. funds may create foreign exchange barriers and request acceptance of major foreign currencies or specify acceptable conversion procedures.

[P5] Small businesses and non-profits request that DOE explicitly allow wire transfers and modern payment platforms in addition to ACH, checks, and credit cards to accommodate varied banking capabilities.

[P5] Privacy and security advocates request that DOE detail safeguards for ACH/EDI credit card transmissions and protections for payer financial data to prevent fraud or breaches.

[P6] Trade associations request transparency in fee calculations and an appeals process for disputing fees assessed under § 955.5(a), including timelines for dispute resolution and fee withholding during disputes.

[P6] Legal commenters ask DOE to define “person delivering” (owner, carrier, generator, broker) to determine who bears fee liability and to address joint and several liability where multiple parties are involved.

[P7] Industry stakeholders ask DOE to publish the specific formula components and assumptions (e.g., metric ton conversion factors, escalation indices, administrative overhead percentages) used to calculate receiving, storage, transport, and treatment/disposal costs.

[P7] Small generators and municipal governments assert that the inclusion of future-year transport and treatment/disposal costs in current fees (charged at delivery) will impose an unreasonable up-front charge and request that fees for post-storage transport/treatment be invoiced only in the year those services are rendered.

[P7] Environmental justice groups request that fee structure include reduced rates or fee waivers for community-based organizations and municipalities serving disadvantaged communities to avoid shifting financial burdens to those least able to pay.

[P7] Accounting firms ask DOE to clarify whether the storage cost escalation is compounded annually and to provide example fee calculations for common storage durations (1, 5, 10, 20 years).

[P8] Stakeholders support DOE’s authority to update fee components annually for cost recovery but request limits: require a minimum 60-day public comment period before substantial fee increases and cap annual increases to a specified percentage tied to CPI or another index.

[P8] Industry warns that unrestricted annual updates will create planning uncertainty and requests that DOE provide multi-year fee schedules or forecast guidance for at least five years.

[P9] Environmental NGOs request that DOE ensure the posted fee component values on the webpage include downloadable spreadsheets, historical fee data, and the calculation methodology so stakeholders can verify fees.

[P9] Several commenters note that reliance on a specific website requires redundancy and accessibility; they request DOE also maintain fee postings in an archived Federal Register notice and a machine-readable API.

[P10] Public interest groups request that DOE publish Federal Register notices with substantive detail when values change, not just a notice that values have changed, and that notices include the effective date, rationale, and impact analysis.

[P10] Legal commenters request that Federal Register notices provide sufficient lead time (e.g., 90 days) before new fee values become effective and require DOE to provide corrective actions if notice is not published timely.

[P1][P2] Industry seeks an appeals mechanism where the DOE can accept shipments that do not meet the 99.5% purity threshold provided the deliverer agrees to a supplemental treatment fee and DOE documents a remediation plan.

[P3][P7] Logistics providers ask DOE to clarify whether transport cost estimates used in fee calculations assume a typical point of origin or are distance-based, and request a distance-weighted fee model rather than a flat per-metric-ton transport cost.

[P2][P5] Chemical manufacturers request DOE accept certified statements of purity and chain-of-custody documentation in lieu of destructive sampling at DOE facility to avoid sample loss and exposure during verification.

[P6][P7] Commenters request that DOE provide an online fee calculator and pre-acceptance cost estimate tool based on declared purity, metric tonnage, and intended storage duration to help generators budget and comply.

[P4][P5] Accounting associations ask for receipts and standardized invoices for fee payments made to DOE, including a mechanism to obtain refunds for overpayment or rejected shipments.

[P1] Advocacy groups request an exception allowing DOE to accept elemental mercury in consumer products that are part of an approved stewardship program to facilitate safe recovery and avoid illegal disposal.

[P8][P10] Transparency advocates urge DOE to commit to publishing an annual fee-setting methodology report with stakeholder input and to hold a public webinar when significant methodology changes are proposed.

[P7] Industry requests clarification whether the fee components apply per metric ton of delivered material or per metric ton of accepted (post-verification) elemental mercury, and how impurities impact fee basis.

[P3] Poultry producers in the specified categories will argue that limiting indemnity to 25% is insufficient to cover the economic loss from depopulation and will request raising the payment percentage or providing a hardship waiver.

[P4] Legal experts will claim the rule’s definition of “participates in any Plan program in part 145 or 146” is ambiguous and may capture producers who only minimally interact with the Plan, unfairly subjecting them to the 25% rate.

[P5] Layer egg industry groups will challenge the threshold of 75,000 table-egg layers as arbitrary and request scaling formulas or regional adjustments for smaller high-density operations that face equal biosecurity risks.

[P6] Poultry integrators will comment that the weekly slaughter threshold of 200,000 chickens for slaughter plants (P6) unfairly privileges large processors and propose smoothing the threshold to a monthly or annual basis to avoid week-to-week gaming or sudden eligibility changes.

[P7] Turkey processors will argue the 2 million turkeys per 12-month threshold (P7) is excessively high, excludes many commercial operations, and recommend lowering the threshold or adopting a per-farm/per-plant proportional indemnity approach.

[P8] Waterfowl and upland game bird slaughter plants will object that the 50,000 birds annually threshold (P8) does not reflect regional industry structure and recommend geographic or market-share adjustments.

[P9] Raised-for-release game bird producers will assert that the 25,000 birds annually threshold (P9) excludes many legitimate commercial producers and request inclusion of smaller seasonal operations, or a tiered indemnity schedule.

[P10] Breeder flock operators will contest the 5,000 bird threshold (P10) for breeder flocks as arbitrary and ask for evidence justifying the cutoff or for an exception for high-value specialty breeders.

[P11] State animal health officials and producers in nonparticipating States will warn that imposing a 25% payment rate (P11) for States that do not participate in surveillance or lack an approved response plan will penalize farmers for State administrative decisions and could encourage underreporting rather than increasing State program participation.

[P12] Producers and accountants will request clarification of what constitutes “payments from other sources” (P12), asking whether business interruption insurance, private indemnity, third-party contracts, or other government relief programs will reduce APHIS payments and whether offsets will be applied before or after depreciation/appraisal.

[P13] Farm owners will assert that tying indemnity to “fair market value determined by an appraisal” (P13) may not reflect the specialized value of breeding stock or genetic lines and request statutory provision to consider replacement cost or genetic value premiums.

[P14] Producers will object that requiring use of APHIS appraisal calculator values when available (P14) may lock claimants into outdated or nonrepresentative values and request an appeal process and transparency about calculator inputs and update frequency.

[P15] Growers and contract growers will urge that the requirement to sign and submit an indemnity request form prior to destruction (P15) is impractical in emergency depopulation situations and will request clear timelines, an electronic submission option, and assurance that delayed submissions will not forfeit indemnity.

[P16] Industry and animal welfare groups will support the exception allowing immediate destruction if parties agree in writing (P16) but request model pre-authorized agreements that can be executed quickly during emergencies.

[P17] Producers will point out that appraisal reports requiring number of birds and value per head (P17) may be inadequate for flocks with mixed ages/values and request allowance for age-class breakdowns, genetic/production-value annotations, and documentation for layers vs. breeders.

[P18] Farmers will protest the requirement to provide complete inventory records prior to depopulation (P18) as unrealistic during outbreaks and request that APHIS accept contemporaneous inventories compiled during depopulation or allow State agencies to certify inventories where records are incomplete.

[P19] Claimants will request explicit lists of acceptable receipts/documentation for disposal compensation (P19), arguing current wording is vague and could lead to inconsistent claim denials.

[P20] Disposal contractors and producers will seek clarification that disposal performed under compliance agreements (P20) may include pre-approved third-party contractors and ask for streamlined contracting methods during emergencies.

[P21] States and contractors will ask for published criteria APHIS will use to review disposal compensation claims (P21) to ensure predictable approvals and to avoid ad hoc rejections.

[P22] Cooperating State Agencies will request explicit timelines and standard cooperative agreement templates for compensation when the State performs disposal (P22) to allow budgeting and prompt payment.

[P23] State agencies and legal commenters will request that the “initial State response and containment plan” referenced for destruction/disposal (P23) be required to be pre-approved, publicly available, and include environmental/safety mitigation to avoid conflicts between APHIS and local laws.

[P24] Small producers will welcome use of the APHIS flat-rate VE calculator for cleaning/disinfection (P24) but will ask for publication of all flat-rate amounts and the methodology for establishing them, and for exceptions where flat rates are inadequate.

[P25] Producers of niche premises not covered by flat-rate calculators will request clear standards for what receipts qualify for reimbursement and caps on reimbursable rates (P25) to prevent unrealistic or inconsistent expectations.

[P26] Claimants will ask that compliance agreements required for cleaning/disinfection compensation (P26) be permissible in electronic form and allow retroactive inclusion in emergencies where immediate action was necessary.

[P27] Industry and providers will request publication of the APHIS review checklist for cleaning/disinfection claims (P27) and an appeals process for denied claims.

[P28] Small operators will object that appraising materials for destruction when cleaning is impracticable (P28) will undervalue specialized equipment and ask that replacement cost or residual value be considered, not just depreciated fair market value.

[P29] Appraisal professionals will request standards, qualifications, and training requirements for APHIS official appraisers (P29) and the right for claimants to provide independent appraisals for comparison.

[P30] Claimants will ask for explicit guidance on what receipts/documentation are acceptable for material disposal compensation (P30) and whether invoices to third parties or destroyed-item photographs will suffice.

[P31] Owners will object to a requirement that appraisals be signed by owners to indicate agreement (P31), noting owners may dispute appraisals and should be able to sign under protest without forfeiting indemnity.

[P32] Producers will request that appraisals must not be a prerequisite to immediate emergency disassembly/destruction (P32) unless owner/admin/State agree, and seek stronger language protecting claimants who cannot obtain signatures in time.

[P33] Legal advocates will recommend that the exception permitting immediate destruction without prior appraisals only be allowed under narrowly defined emergency conditions and that a post-action appraisal and expedited dispute resolution be available (P33).

[P34] Claimants will seek a model compliance agreement (P34) and clarification that compliance agreements can be amended as actual costs become known during response operations.

[P35] Industry groups will request transparency on APHIS criteria for reviewing disposal compensation claims (P35), including timelines for review and payment.

[P36] Contractors and employers will request that required compliance agreement cost estimates (P36) allow for contingencies, overtime, and surge capacity costs, and that APHIS not arbitrarily reject reasonable contingency line items.

[P37] Contracting parties will ask that the requirement to identify responsible parties and estimated costs (P37) not impose personal liability on individual farm workers and clarify whether corporate entities or employers are the responsible parties.

[P38] Claimants will request that the requirement to forward receipts/documentation after completing work (P38) allow for phased submissions during ongoing operations and permit extensions in declared emergencies.

[P39] Producers will challenge the 30-day deadline to submit documentation after quarantine release (P39) as too short—requesting at least 60–90 days given complexities of accounting, insurance claims, and seasonal labor—and ask for administrative extensions.

[P40] Processors and farmers will oppose the prohibition on indemnity for poultry moved for controlled marketing (P40), arguing that controlled marketing may be the only feasible response option for biosecurity and that denying indemnity disincentivizes controlled marketing strategies that could reduce losses.

[P41] Public health and consumer advocates will support allowing cleaning/disinfection compensation for premises involved in controlled marketing (P41) but will ask APHIS to require strict documentation and oversight to prevent abuse.

[P42] Environmental and worker-safety groups will demand strict protocols and monitoring to ensure cleaning and disinfection of exposed premises/conveyances/materials (P42) are effective and pose no public health/environmental hazard.

[P43] Recycling and salvage firms will request clearer criteria for when materials should be destroyed because cleaning is impracticable or costs exceed value (P43), and a process for owners to appeal destruction determinations.

[P44] State environmental regulators will insist that initial State response plans (P44) must be coordinated with State environmental agencies and include measures to prevent water/soil contamination during virus elimination.

[P45] Environmental groups will insist that compliance with State and local environmental regulations (P45) be explicitly enforced and that APHIS provide guidance on reconciling federal response actions with differing State/local environmental standards.

[P46] Contractors will request confirmation that where livestock indemnity is 100% (P46), payment to eligible contractors can also be made promptly and that APHIS will publish contractor eligibility criteria and payment timelines.

[P47] Contractors will similarly request that where indemnity is 25% (P47), APHIS clarify whether contractor payments are limited to 25% of contracted amounts regardless of negotiations between owners and contractors.

[P48] Dealers in hatching eggs and poultry will ask for clarity on what constitutes “compliance with provisions of this part and NPIP Program Standards” (P48), and request an appeal or variance process for Administrator-approved alternatives.

[P49] Diagnostic laboratories will request that the list of Department- and State-approved ELISA kits (P49) be published and updated frequently, and ask for transition time when kits are added or removed.

[P50] Veterinary diagnostic labs will point out that the 48-hour timeline to perform AGID after a positive ELISA (P50) may not be feasible in rural areas or small labs and ask for flexibility or teleconference approval to transfer samples to reference labs.

[P51] Labs will request that the rule specify criteria for an “approved reagent” for AGID tests (P51) and provide a process for rapid approval during outbreaks.

[P52] Public health labs will ask that confirmatory testing pathways and turnaround times be specified (P52) to avoid delays in response decisions.

[P53] Federal Reference Laboratories will request clarity on what “appropriate tests for confirmation” entails (P53) and whether sequencing, PCR subtyping, or virus isolation is required in each instance.

[P54] State veterinarians will request explicit standards for when “further sampling and confirmatory tests” (P54) can be used instead of initial positive determinations to avoid unnecessary depopulation.

[P55] Diagnostic labs and industry will support use of agent detection tests for influenza A screening (P55) but will request explicit prohibitions on using them for subtype decisions and clear referral steps to confirmatory testing.

[P56] Field veterinarians will request guidance that samples for agent detection tests are not limited to mortality/clinically ill birds (P56) in certain surveillance contexts (e.g., routine surveillance in breeder flocks) and ask the rule to permit targeted sampling when epidemiologically indicated.

[P57] Multiplier flock operators will argue that requiring testing of up to 30 multiplier spent fowl per 90-day period and negative results within 21 days before movement to slaughter (P57) is onerous and suggest harmonizing with slaughter scheduling to reduce repeated testing.

[P58] State agencies will request procedural guidance for Official State Agency determinations for U.S. Newcastle Disease Clean classification (P58), including timelines and documentation required.

[P59] Breeder associations will request that the serologic monitoring requirements for vaccinated primary breeding flocks (P59) permit use of pooled sampling or validated alternative sampling strategies to reduce costs.

[P60] Small-scale unvaccinated breeders will request that the minimum 30-bird negative test requirement (>4 months old) (P60) allow for statistical sampling based on flock size for very small flocks.

[P61] Poultry health professionals will ask for clarification of what constitutes “response to vaccination is serologically compatible” (P61) and for numerical cutoff titers and lab interpretation guidance.

[P62] Veterinarians will ask for explicit definitions of acceptable “approved serological tests” (P62) and a public list of approved assays to avoid inconsistent state interpretations.

[P63] Producers will request flexibility in the requirement that serologic monitoring include at least 30 birds when >4 months old and prior to production, especially for small or hobby flocks (P63), proposing proportional sampling schemes.

[P64] Unvaccinated flock owners will highlight the burden of testing a minimum of 30 birds every 90 days (P64) and propose alternative risk-based testing intervals for low-movement, closed flocks.

[P65] Flock owners will support the allowance to test fewer than 30 birds at a time if all pens are equally represented (P65) but request explicit sampling protocols to ensure statistical validity.

[P66] Primary spent fowl owners will protest the requirement that up to 30 spent fowl must test negative within 21 days before movement to slaughter in each 90-day period (P66) as duplicative and costly; they will ask for alignment with slaughterhouse testing protocols.

[P67] Veterinarians and animal health advocates will endorse the requirement that licensed veterinarians report ND to State authorities (P67) but will ask for protections for client confidentiality and clear reporting forms and timelines.

[P68] Diagnostic labs will request resources and funding to handle the obligation to examine all submitted cases of unexplained respiratory disease, egg production drops, and mortality for ND (P68), arguing current lab capacity is insufficient.

[P69] Hobbyist and exhibition poultry keepers will request outreach and education resources to help them comply with general and special provisions for participating flocks (P69), noting that many operators are inexperienced with NPIP standards.

[P70] Raised-for-release waterfowl producers will request transitional assistance and phased compliance timelines for the requirement that all participating flocks be enrolled regardless of breeder status (P70).

[P71] Hatchery operators will request documented sanitation standards and reasonable timelines to bring facilities into compliance with hatchery sanitary provisions (P71), and ask that enforcement actions be delayed until guidance and funding are available.

[P72] Hatchery managers will challenge the obligation that an Authorized Agent collect and submit at least five hatchery samples every 30 days while operating (P72) as burdensome and costly, and request risk-based sampling frequency options tied to production scale.

[P73] Hatchery operators will ask for a detailed list of acceptable sample types and volumes (P73) and clarity on chain-of-custody and storage requirements for bacteriological Salmonella testing.

[P74] Pullet and breeder farms will request clarity on the scope and methods for annual environmental samples (P74), and whether pooled samples, swabs, or boot swabs are acceptable, and any lab turnaround expectations.

[P75] Industry groups will request definition and qualification criteria for a “qualified poultry health professional” (P75) and whether consultants, private veterinarians, or company-employed health specialists satisfy the requirement.

[P76] Processors and farms will ask for guidance on acceptable interventions developed from Salmonella monitoring results (P76) and whether APHIS will provide model intervention plans or funding to implement them.

[P77] Companies claiming the U.S. Salmonella Monitored classification will ask for audit protocols, recordkeeping expectations, and timelines to achieve compliance before they may market products under that claim (P77).

[P78] Chicken breeders will request uniform national standards and an appeals process for Official State Agency determinations of Newcastle Disease Clean classification (P78) to avoid interstate inconsistencies.

[P79] Vaccinated primary breeding flocks will ask that serologic monitoring schedules (P79) allow for harmonization with other required testing to reduce handling stress and costs.

[P80] Operators of small unvaccinated breeding flocks will request that the “minimum of 30 birds” requirement (P80) be scaled for flocks with fewer than 30 birds or allow whole-flock testing to meet the standard.

[P81] Poultry health professionals will request explicit guidance that the inactivated vaccine as final vaccination (P81) not be required where scientific evidence supports alternative vaccination schedules or where vaccine availability is limited.

[P82] Producers will ask that APHIS publish acceptable serologic test names and lab cutoffs (P82) so compliance can be demonstrated consistently across States.

[P83] Flock owners will propose that the 90-day maximum interval for serologic monitoring (P83) be adjusted to risk-based intervals for low-turnover or geographically isolated flocks to reduce unnecessary testing.

[P84] Unvaccinated flock owners will request a risk-based exception to the 90-day minimum testing interval for truly closed flocks with strict biosecurity (P84).

[P85] Owners will request standardized sampling protocols for testing fewer than 30 birds at a time (P85) to ensure pen-representation requirements are measurable and enforceable.

[P86] Primary spent fowl operators will seek alignment of the requirement that up to 30 birds test negative within 21 days before movement to slaughter (P86) with slaughterhouse entry testing to eliminate redundant sampling.

[P87] Laboratories and veterinarians will request funding, training, and technical assistance to ensure licensed veterinarians report ND to State authorities and that laboratories can examine relevant submissions (P87).

[P5] The prohibition on remaining within the regulated area (§100.T799–0631(c)(1)) could criminalize vessels that become trapped by weather or cannot safely exit, and the rule should expressly include exemptions for emergency situations.

[P1] The deadline to receive comments by September 27, 2021 is insufficiently publicized and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow small operators and public interest groups adequate time to prepare technical comments and economic analyses.

[P1] The provision placing the comment-receipt deadline on the FAA (§ 39.13(a)) should explicitly state acceptable methods of submission (online portal, email, mail) to avoid confusion and inadvertent missed deadlines.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether postmarked mail received after September 27, 2021 but delivered later will be accepted as timely — the current text only states that the FAA must receive comments by that date.

[P1] For transparency, FAA should publish a summary of substantive comments received by the September 27, 2021 deadline and explain how they influenced the final rule.

[P2] The phrase "within the specified compliance times" (§ 39.13(f)) is vague; the AD must list explicit calendar deadlines or flight-hour thresholds for each required action so operators can plan maintenance.

[P2] The provision should allow for hardship waivers or staggered compliance schedules for fleets with scheduling constraints, rather than a blanket requirement to comply within specified times.

[P2] The rule must require the FAA to publish the specific compliance time intervals in the AD text rather than deferring to referenced service documents, to ensure legal clarity and enforceability.

[P3] Requiring inspection "at the next engine shop visit" (§ 39.13(g)(1)) is ambiguous — the AD should define "engine shop visit" (e.g., any disassembly to the gearbox, engine removal, or scheduled depot-level maintenance) to avoid inconsistent interpretation.

[P3] The inspection requirement tied to "the next engine shop visit after the AD effective date" unfairly penalizes engines that recently had shop visits; FAA should add a maximum calendar-based backstop (e.g., within 180 days) to ensure timely inspections.

[P3] The AD should include minimum qualifications for the inspector and required documentation/photos for the visual inspection of the TGB radial gearshaft so that inspections are consistent and auditable.

[P3] The AD should permit operators to combine this inspection with other required TGB inspections to minimize operational disruption and cost, and the text should explicitly authorize combined work scopes.

[P4] The requirement to "replace the TGB radial gearshaft with an eligible part before further flight" (§ 39.13(g)(2)) is too absolute; FAA should allow temporary operational restrictions (e.g., ferry flight to repair facility) or ground-time repair options where replacement is impractical immediately.

[P4] The AD must define "eligible part" precisely (part number, serial number range, or approved modification status) to prevent disputes about acceptable replacements.

[P4] The rule should specify acceptable sources for eligible parts (OEM, approved repair stations) and require documentation of traceability to ensure counterfeit or unairworthy parts are not installed.

[P4] The AD should include alternative corrective actions (e.g., repair or rework instructions) in addition to replacement, approved by the manufacturer and FAA, to reduce costs and maintain supply-chain flexibility.

[P5] Allowing credit for prior inspections (§ 39.13(i)) only if performed using specified earlier service bulletin versions may be unduly restrictive; operators who used equivalent procedures with adequate records should also be allowed credit.

[P5] The rule should require the FAA to publish the exact service bulletin versions that qualify for credit and list acceptable equivalent inspection methods and documentation standards.

[P5] The provision should allow for retroactive acceptance of inspections performed shortly before the effective date if they meet the intent and criteria, even if service bulletin revision numbers differ by minor editorial changes.

[P6] Granting the Manager authority to approve AMOCs (§ 39.13(j)(1)) is appropriate, but the AD should outline criteria the Manager will use to evaluate AMOCs to provide predictability to operators and repair stations.

[P6] The AD should require the FAA to provide a target turnaround time (e.g., 60 days) for AMOC decisions to prevent prolonged grounding or operational uncertainty for affected aircraft.

[P6] The rule must ensure that AMOC approval criteria include consideration of international operators and ICAO-equivalent approvals to prevent unnecessary duplication for foreign operators.

[P7] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO (§ 39.13(j)(1)) could create delays due to resource constraints; the AD should permit direct submission to the Manager as an alternative.

[P7] The AD should clarify whether electronic submissions to the principal inspector or FSDO satisfy the procedural requirement and whether supporting technical data can be submitted later.

[P7] The rule must specify whether the principal inspector/FSDO can delegate initial review to contractors or external technical experts, and how confidentiality and proprietary data will be handled.

[P8] If applicants send AMOC information directly to the certification office manager (§ 39.13(j)(1)), the AD should include the full name, office, and mailing address in the Related Information section to avoid misrouting.

[P8] The AD should specify acknowledgement and tracking procedures when AMOC information is sent directly to the certification office manager, including confirmation of receipt and an assigned tracking number.

[P9] Allowing email submissions to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov (§ 39.13(j)(1)) is useful, but the AD must state acceptable file formats, maximum file size, and guidance on including protected proprietary information.

[P9] The FAA should provide an alternative secure upload mechanism for AMOC requests containing sensitive technical data rather than unsecured email.

[P9] The AD should require FAA to confirm receipt of email AMOC requests within a set time frame (e.g., 5 business days) and provide a single point of contact for follow-up.

[P10] The requirement to notify the principal inspector or local FSDO manager before using an approved AMOC (§ 39.13(j)(2)) should include a required notification timeframe (e.g., within 72 hours) and specify the form of notification (email, fax, log entry).

[P10] The obligation to notify "before using" an AMOC may be impractical for transient operations or unscheduled flights; the AD should allow notification within a short period after first use if prior notice is not operationally feasible, provided the AMOC approval is on record.

[P10] The AD should clarify what constitutes sufficient notification (brief statement vs. submission of the full AMOC approval) and whether operators must retain evidence of the notification for inspection.

[P13] The corrected part number instruction (§39.13(k)(2)) is necessary, but the rule should require Boeing to issue a formal corrected service bulletin to avoid confusion in supply chains.

[P14] Defining "40 drops or less" as a threshold (§39.13(k)(3)) is imprecise—request numeric definition of a "drop" and a clear decision matrix for required actions when findings equal 40 or fewer drops.

[P17] Clarify that individuals are not required to respond absent a valid OMB number (§39.13(m)), and identify which specific reports in this AD are subject to PRA and whether they were reviewed by OMB.

[P18] Reiterate that no penalties will be imposed for non-response without an OMB number (§39.13(m)), and specify whether penalties for regulatory noncompliance (not PRA) still apply.

[P19] §39.13(m) states responses to this specific information collection are mandatory, which conflicts with PRA prohibitions; reconcile and clearly identify which submissions are mandatory under the AD versus which would require OMB approval.

[P20] The burden comment address (§39.13(m)) uses the FAA headquarters address but should also include an email contact and instructions for PRA comments to facilitate participation.

[P24] Allowing AMOC requests by email (§39.13(n)(1)) is appropriate; request confirmation of receipt and estimated processing timelines to aid operational planning.

[P25] Define "before using an approved AMOC" (§39.13(n)(2)) with concrete timelines and emergency exception language to allow compliance with flight schedules in urgent safety scenarios.

[P26] Require Boeing to notify affected operators when their ODA approves AMOCs used for this AD (§39.13(n)(3)), including any operational limitations.

[P31] For RC deviations requiring AMOC (§39.13(n)(4)(i)), require FAA to provide a checklist of documentation required for AMOC submissions to reduce back-and-forth and processing time.

raw_output:
[P1] The allowance of Vitamins C and E as synthetic substances for use in organic crop production contradicts consumer expectations of "organic" and should be removed to preserve integrity of organic label.
[P1] If Vitamins C and E remain permitted synthetics, the rule must require labeling disclosure that these are synthetic inputs used in crop production so consumers can make informed choices.
[P1] Allowing synthetic Vitamins C and E could create unfair cost advantages for conventional farms converting to organic; the rule should require documentation that no organic alternatives were available.
[P1] The rule should specify maximum application rates, timing restrictions, and environmental safeguards for use of synthetic Vitamins C and E to prevent potential ecological or human health impacts.
[P2] The phrase "Only the following nonorganically produced agricultural products may be used" is vague without a full, final list and clear process for adding/removing items; request clarity on amendment procedures and notice-and-comment for list changes.
[P3] The cross-reference to "restrictions specified in this section" lacks specificity for many entries; commenters request that each permitted item include explicit, item-specific restrictions within the regulatory text rather than by reference.
[P4] The commercial availability test for using nonorganic ingredients lacks measurable standards (e.g., geographic market, timeframe, volume) and will lead to inconsistent determinations; propose a defined test (e.g., 12-month market survey, specified radius or national availability, documentation requirements).
[P4] Require certifiers to maintain and publish the evidence used to determine "not commercially available organically" for auditability and transparency to prevent inconsistent or biased decisions.
[P5] Carnauba wax is commonly produced outside organic systems; the rule must require sourcing transparency and that carnauba wax be free of prohibited synthetic contaminants (e.g., hexane residues).
[P5] Industry commenters request clarification whether carnauba wax used for surface coatings on organic produce requires additional inert carrier or solvent restrictions, and whether wax must be food-grade.
[P6] Allowing processed-intestine casings raises animal welfare concerns and should require that casings come only from animals raised under organic livestock standards, or explicitly permit nonorganic sourcing only when organic casings are unavailable.
[P6] The regulation should clarify whether processed-intestine casings may contain added preservatives or processing aids and whether those aids must be on the National List.
[P7] Celery powder is a high-nitrate ingredient with allergen and labeling implications; commenters request specification of acceptable processing methods and nitrate limits, and whether it must be sourced from specified species.
[P8] The prohibition on synthetic solvents/carrier systems/artificial preservatives for colors derived from agricultural products is appropriate, but enforcement will require clear analytical standards and testing protocols to detect prohibited processing aids.
[P9] Prohibiting synthetic solvents and carrier systems in color production may effectively bar many suppliers; request transition timeline and grandfathering for existing inventories and contracts.
[P10] The beet juice extract color prohibition on sugarbeets is scientifically unjustified — sugarbeet cultivars of Beta vulgaris produce similar pigments; request evidence basis or removal of the sugarbeet exclusion.
[P10] If sugarbeets remain excluded for beet juice extract color, the rule must define "sugarbeet" precisely (e.g., cultivar groups, processing origins) to avoid supply chain confusion.
[P11] The prohibition on sugarbeet-derived color will reduce domestic supply and raise costs for organic processors; request economic impact analysis and mitigation measures.
[P12] Allowing beta-carotene from carrots and Dunaliella salina but not other sources is arbitrary; request justification for excluding other agricultural or microbial sources and clarity on processing methods allowed for Dunaliella extraction.
[P12] For Dunaliella salina-derived beta-carotene, require documentation that cultivation and extraction avoid prohibited synthetic solvents and define acceptable extraction methods.
[P13] The permission for black/purple carrot juice color should specify permitted cultivars and whether concentrated or fermented forms are acceptable, and set limits on added processing aids.
[P14] For chokeberry (Aronia) juice color, request geographic sourcing guidance and disease/pesticide residue testing requirements because Aronia is sometimes treated with nonorganic inputs.
[P15] Elderberry (Sambucus nigra) sourcing should be restricted to species and parts specified; require testing to prevent contamination with toxic Sambucus species and specify acceptable drying/extraction methods.
[P16] Grape skin extract color from Vitis vinifera should require that grapes used are not treated with nonorganic post-harvest fungicides or vinification aids that are prohibited for organic production.
[P17] The allowance for purple sweet potato juice color derived also from Solanum tuberosum L. (potato) is confusing — request clarification if purple-fleshed potato varieties are intended, and specify acceptable cultivars and processing limits.
[P18] Red cabbage extract color permission should specify whether fermentation or enzymatic extraction is allowed and whether seeds or leaves are eligible source materials.
[P19] Red radish extract permission should define acceptable varietal sources and require testing for pesticide residues given conventional radish production practices.
[P20] Saffron extract color approval should include stringent provenance and adulteration safeguards due to saffron's high value and fraud risk; require traceability and testing protocols.
[P21] The stabilization requirement for fish oil is unclear: commenters ask whether "stabilized with organic ingredients" means antioxidants can only be organic or on the National List, and request a list of acceptable stabilizers or maximum allowed nonorganic stabilizer concentrations.
[P21] Fish oil CAS numbers are provided but the rule must clarify whether derived from wild-caught or aquaculture sources and whether sourcing must meet sustainability criteria to align with organic principles.
[P22] Fructooligosaccharides (FOS) are allowed but commenters request specification of acceptable production methods (enzymatic vs chemical synthesis) and substrate origins to ensure compliance with "not chemically synthesized" expectations.
[P22] Labeling requirements should be clarified for FOS when used: whether products must disclose the ingredient as nonorganic and provide justification of nonavailability of organic FOS.
[P23] Gelatin allowance should be limited to sources consistent with organic livestock standards where possible; otherwise require documentation of nonorganic sourcing only when organic gelatin is unavailable and require slaughterhouse sanitary and welfare standards.
[P23] Specify whether gelatin derived from fish, porcine, or bovine sources is acceptable and whether processing aids in gelatin manufacture must be on the National List.
[P24] Glycerin requirement to be from agricultural source materials and processed by biological or mechanical/physical methods is appropriate; request clear definition of acceptable feedstocks (e.g., soy, palm) and explicit prohibition of chemical hydrolysis or transesterification.
[P24] Require the rule to address sustainability concerns for glycerin feedstocks (e.g., palm oil deforestation) and encourage sourcing from low-environmental-impact crops.
[P25] Limiting gums to water-extracted forms is justified; regulators should add testing methods and supplier documentation standards to verify extraction method claims.
[P26] For inulin-oligofructose enriched, require clarity on source crops (e.g., chicory) and allowable extraction/enzymatic processing steps to ensure compliance with organic processing principles.
[P27] Specifying only de-oiled lecithin permitted is appropriate, but commenters request clarity on acceptable solvent use during deoiling and whether enzymatic degumming is allowed.
[P27] Require concentration or purity thresholds for "de-oiled" lecithin to avoid ambiguity in enforcement.
[P28] Dried orange pulp allowance should include limits on pesticide residues and specify acceptable drying methods (no synthetic anti-caking or preservatives) to prevent prohibited inputs.
[P29] Restricting orange shellac to unbleached only is appropriate; request confirmation that only natural solvents may be used in shellac dissolution and that coating additives must comply with National List.
[P30] Limiting pectin to non-amidated forms needs justification and explanation of functional impacts; processors may need guidance on how this affects gelling properties and labeling.
[P31] Potassium acid tartrate (cream of tartar derivative) allowance needs specification of sourcing and processing methods and whether it may be derived from conventional winemaking byproducts.
[P32] Pacific kombu seaweed inclusion should be limited to specified geographic harvest zones to prevent mislabeling of other kelp species and require testing for heavy metals (arsenic, iodine).
[P33] The broad listing of "starches" must be narrowed with explicit allowed types, processing methods, and allowed chemical modifications; otherwise processors will exploit ambiguity to use prohibited modified starches.
[P34] Native cornstarch authorization should explicitly prohibit chemically modified cornstarch and require that cornstarch be from non-GMO corn or require GMO disclosure consistent with organic standards.
[P34] Request requirement that native cornstarch suppliers document that wet- or dry-milling processes did not use prohibited chemical aids or enzymes not allowed on the National List.
[P35] The reserved item creates uncertainty; commenters ask whether this will be completed later and request NOIA (notice of intent to amend) and a timeline for filling reserved entries.
[P36] Tamarind seed gum allowance should require supplier documentation of water-only extraction and specify limits on microbial contamination and acceptable drying/preservation methods.
[P37] Tragacanth gum permission should include provenance requirements because overharvesting in some regions threatens sustainability; request sustainable harvest criteria and verification.
[P38] Wakame seaweed inclusion should be conditional on invasive species controls and harvesting best practices as Undaria pinnatifida can be invasive in some regions; require sourcing restrictions to avoid ecological harm.

[P1] The requirement that HLA, HPA, and HNA typing devices be Class II subject to these special controls will impose significant regulatory burden on small manufacturers and labs that currently operate under CLIA moderate complexity; FDA should quantify expected compliance costs and consider alternatives (e.g., scaled requirements for low-risk platforms).

[P1] The rule lumps together HLA, HPA, and HNA devices despite differing clinical risks and use-cases; FDA should stratify special controls by device type (e.g., transplant HLA typing vs. platelet antigen typing) rather than a one-size-fits-all Class II approach.

[P1] Requiring all such devices to meet these special controls could discourage innovation in research-use or emerging technologies; propose carve-outs or phased compliance for novel next-generation sequencing (NGS) platforms.

[P2] The premarket documentation list is overly prescriptive and may require proprietary information that is unreasonable to disclose publicly; FDA should allow redaction of confidential details and provide clear templates for submissions.

[P2] The rule lacks explicit timelines and sample size expectations for the required studies in premarket submissions; manufacturers need quantitative guidance (e.g., minimum number and diversity of samples) to design studies.

[P3] The accuracy study requirement to use "well-characterized samples that represent as many targets as possible" is vague and operationally unworkable for highly polymorphic HLA loci; FDA should define acceptable representativeness metrics (allele frequency coverage, ethnic diversity) and minimum allele counts per locus.

[P3] For rare alleles, requiring inclusion in accuracy studies is impractical; FDA should allow use of in silico analyses, synthetic constructs, or validated reference panels instead of physical samples for rare alleles.

[P3] Clinical laboratories and manufacturers need clarity on whether reference materials from external repositories (e.g., Coriell) satisfy "well-characterized" — FDA should list acceptable reference sources and characterization criteria.

[P4] Precision study expectations must define acceptable levels of intra-run, inter-run, inter-operator, and inter-lot variability and provide statistical methods; as written, the provision is qualitative and invites inconsistent interpretations.

[P4] The provision does not address proficiency testing or external quality assessment programs as part of precision evaluation; FDA should allow longitudinal data from PT programs to partially satisfy precision study requirements.

[P5] Comparison studies versus a predicate device are problematic for fundamentally different technologies (e.g., NGS vs. SSO/SSP); FDA should permit performance-based equivalence using well-established reference methods rather than strict predicate comparison.

[P5] The rule does not specify what constitutes an acceptable predicate for novel assays; clarify whether laboratory-developed tests (LDTs) or internationally marketed devices can be used as predicates.

[P6] Requiring information addressing false positive antibody reactivity (denatured/cryptic epitopes) seems targeted at serologic assays but is broadly applied; FDA should tailor this requirement only where antibody reagents or epitope recognition are used, and provide specific mitigation strategies.

[P6] The provision lacks guidance on acceptable experimental approaches to demonstrate mitigation of false positives (e.g., epitope mapping, adsorption studies); FDA should list validated methods or offer pre-submission meetings.

[P7] The requirement to describe assay cutoff establishment and validation needs quantitative expectations (e.g., ROC analysis, confidence intervals, cohort sizes); otherwise submissions will be inconsistent and reviewers will apply ad hoc standards.

[P7] For multiplex assays with continuous signal outputs, the rule should allow reporting of probabilistic or Bayesian thresholds rather than single binary cutoffs; current wording may force inappropriate dichotomization.

[P8] The comprehensive software documentation requirement (including architecture, algorithm description, hazard analysis, V&V) will pose intellectual property and cybersecurity disclosure concerns; FDA should allow submission of executable code under secure, confidential review and provide clear boundaries for cybersecurity vs. transparency.

[P8] The provision's EMC/wireless testing expectation is irrelevant for purely bench-top, non-connected analyzers; FDA should limit EMC/wireless requirements to devices with wireless or emitter components to avoid unnecessary testing.

[P8] The V&V expectations should be risk-based; for non-diagnostic decision-support software the full IEC 62304-style documentation may be disproportionate, and FDA should allow streamlined documentation for lower-risk software functions.

[P9] Requiring design specifications to prevent incorrect reactivity assignment in high-multiplex assays is reasonable, but the rule must provide specific validation strategies (barcoding, automated QC, primer/probe sequence traceability) that will be acceptable.

[P9] The provision does not acknowledge manufacturing realities where probe/primer panels are updated frequently; FDA should permit validated change-control processes rather than requiring revalidation for every panel update.

[P10] Mandating a plan to ensure unchanged performance as new HLA alleles are identified is necessary, but the rule should allow use of in silico reactivity assessment, database monitoring (e.g., IMGT/HLA), and post-market surveillance rather than routine revalidation for each novel allele.

[P10] The rule lacks requirements for the frequency and triggers for re-assessment when allele databases are updated; FDA should define routine review intervals and criteria that trigger analytical or clinical re-evaluation.

[P10] Small manufacturers will struggle to monitor worldwide allele discovery; FDA should accept reliance on public databases and peer-reviewed literature with a described monitoring plan rather than continuous active surveillance.

[P11] Required labeling statements should be limited in length and placement; the rule should specify where on packaging and IFU these statements must appear to ensure clarity and avoid cluttering critical instructions.

[P12] The mandatory limitation that results "should not be used as the sole basis for making a clinical decision" contradicts current clinical practice where some transplant matching decisions are driven primarily by typing results; FDA should allow context-specific labeling that clarifies appropriate uses rather than a blanket prohibition.

[P12] The restriction could be interpreted to undercut clinical autonomy and reimbursement coverage by payors who require FDA labeling; propose alternative wording that balances caution with clinical utility (e.g., "Results should be interpreted in the context of clinical and laboratory findings").

[P13] Requiring a warning that the device has not been cleared or approved as a companion diagnostic is confusing for devices never intended as CDx; FDA should instead require a succinct statement about intended use and limitations without implying deficiency.

[P13] The companion diagnostic warning may deter use in research and clinical practice and create liability concerns; FDA should clarify when such a statement is necessary (e.g., when a biomarker is linked to drug selection) rather than universally apply it.

[P1] The preamble and regulatory analysis lack an explanation of statutory authority and risk determination for downgrading or up-classifying devices to Class II with these specific controls; provide legal justification and risk assessment.

[P2] FDA should provide a transition period for devices already on the market to comply with the new special controls, with clear timelines and grandfathering provisions.

[P2] Regulators should offer an interactive Q&A and pre-submission templates/checklists aligning each special control to expected submission elements to reduce review delays and variability.

[P8] The rule should harmonize software and cybersecurity expectations with international standards (e.g., IEC 62304, ISO 27001) to avoid duplicative requirements for manufacturers selling abroad.

[P5] The rule does not address how discordant results between predicate and new devices should be resolved in clinical studies; require an adjudication plan using orthogonal methods.

[P3] Advocacy groups representing diverse patient populations request that FDA require demonstration of device performance across ancestries to prevent disparities due to allele frequency differences; specify required demographic breakdowns in accuracy studies.

raw_output:
[P1] The rule’s blanket requirement that all civil aircraft operations exceeding Mach 1 need a “special flight authorization” (§ 91.818) is overly broad and would unduly restrict non-harmful research or emergency operations by small operators; the regulation should exempt genuine in-flight emergencies and certain low-impact research flights.

[P1] The definition of “operato[r]” in § 91.818 is unclear — commenters will request that the rule explicitly define “operator” (owner vs. pilot-in-command vs. lessee) to avoid uncertainty about who must hold the special authorization.

[P1] Requiring a special authorization for any exceedance of Mach 1 could conflict with existing certificates of airworthiness or experimental flight-test approvals; the FAA should clarify how § 91.818 interacts with other FAA authorizations and 14 CFR parts for test/experimental aircraft.

[P2] Directing all applications to the FAA Office of Environment and Energy is procedurally problematic; industry will request that operational safety offices (e.g., Flight Standards or Aircraft Certification) be co‑recipients/reviewers or that a separate operational review path be prescribed.

[P2] The proposal lacks a timeline for FAA review of applications submitted to the Office of Environment and Energy — applicants will request a required decision deadline (e.g., 90 or 180 days) or deemed‑granted/denied construct to avoid indefinite delays.

[P3] The application-content requirements in § 91.818(a) are extensive but lack a standardized application form and data formats; commenters will request that the FAA publish a standardized application template and data submission standards (including confidential treatment process).

[P4] Requiring the operator’s name (§ 91.818(a)(1)) without requiring legal entity identifiers (e.g., DOT number, N-number, registration) is insufficient; applicants will ask the FAA to require aircraft registration and corporate/entity identifiers to prevent ambiguity.

[P5] The mandate to include “number and model(s) of the aircraft” (§ 91.818(a)(2)) should also require specific aircraft registration (N-number) and serial numbers, especially where multiple similar models exist, to ensure traceability — commenters will request this addition.

[P6] Requiring the number of proposed flights (§ 91.818(a)(3)) is reasonable, but commenters will ask the FAA to allow ranges or maximums (e.g., “up to X flights”) rather than exact counts when testing programs foresee adjustments; guidance on amendments should be provided.

[P7] The rule’s requirement for a date range (§ 91.818(a)(4)) is unclear about acceptable flexibility; industry will request allowance for rolling date ranges, contingency windows (weather delays), and a process for amending the date range without re‑submission of the entire application.

[P8] Requiring the time of day for flights (§ 91.818(a)(5)) is acceptable, but commenters will request that the FAA clarify whether time windows must be local time, UTC, and whether daylight saving adjustments are permitted.

[P9] The provision allowing the FAA to require additional justification for night operations (§ 91.818(a)(5)) is vague and could be applied arbitrarily; commenters (test centers, operators) will request a clear, objective standard for when additional justification is required and what specific information must be provided.

[P10] § 91.818(a)(6) requires a description of the flight area and environmental analysis per (c), but commenters will request explicit mapping standards (GIS shapefile/KML), coordinate formats, altitude layers, and required meteorological envelope to ensure consistent submissions.

[P11] The obligation to provide “all conditions and limitations” ensuring no measurable sonic boom overpressure reaches surface outside proposed area (§ 91.818(a)(7)) places an unrealistic burden on applicants because predicting sonic boom propagation with absolute certainty is scientifically difficult; commenters (industry and academic experts) will request that the standard be changed from “ensure” to “reasonably assure” and to define “measurable” numerically (e.g., >0.1 psf).

[P11] Environmental and community groups will counter that “no measurable sonic boom” is too permissive unless “measurable” is explicitly defined in terms of decibel levels or overpressure thresholds; they will request specific numerical thresholds and monitoring requirements.

[P12] The requirement to explain why supersonic operation is necessary (§ 91.818(a)(8)) is appropriate but needs guidance on the level of detail and types of evidence acceptable (mission necessity statement vs. technical justification); commenters will request illustrative examples of acceptable justifications.

[P13] The rule limits permissible authorizations to certain intended purposes (§ 91.818(a)(8)), but commenters will argue the list is incomplete — for example, it omits urgent public-interest operations (disaster response, medical delivery) and certain military-civil cooperative testing; request to add explicit carve-outs or permit case-by-case determinations.

[P14] Allowing authorizations for showing compliance with airworthiness requirements (§ 91.818(a)(8)(i)) is supported, but certification bodies will request explicit coordination procedures with the Aircraft Certification Office and clear evidence requirements to avoid duplication of NEPA/environmental review.

[P15] Permitting authorizations to determine sonic boom characteristics (§ 91.818(a)(8)(ii)) is supported by manufacturers, but they will ask for clearer test-design and monitoring standards and for preapproved sensor networks and modeling protocols the FAA will accept.

[P16] Allowing authorizations to establish methods to reduce/eliminate sonic boom effects (§ 91.818(a)(8)(iii)) is welcomed by industry; commenters will request that the FAA commit to expedited review for such research to encourage innovation.

[P17] The authorization purpose to demonstrate conditions/limitations under which supersonic flight will not cause measurable sonic boom (§ 91.818(a)(8)(iv)) duplicates § 91.818(a)(7) obligations and could create circular requirements; legal commenters will request harmonization and clarity about whether a single demonstration can support both application content and future authorizations.

[P18] Allowing measurement of noise characteristics (§ 91.818(a)(8)(v)) is fine, but communities will demand that applicants include community engagement plans and independent third-party noise monitoring to validate claimed results.

[P19] The requirement that applicants explain why they cannot operate far enough offshore (§ 91.818(a)(9)) is reasonable, but industry commenters will request clear numeric offshore-distance standards or safe‑harbor ranges (e.g., >200 nautical miles) to streamline applications and reduce arbitrary denials.

[P19] Environmental advocates will argue that the rule should presume operations must occur offshore unless applicants demonstrate a compelling public-interest reason to operate over land; request that the burden of proof be on the applicant with strict criteria.

[P20] Allowing flights outside a test area only upon a “conservative showing” (§ 91.818(b)) is vague — applicants need a clear definition of “conservative showing” and objective criteria for what constitutes sufficient evidence to conduct flights outside test areas.

[P21] Requiring prior flights within a test area under an (a)(8)(iv) authorization (§ 91.818(b)(1)) may be impractical for manufacturers with new designs; commenters will request that simulated or validated computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and wind‑tunnel data be accepted in lieu of initial test-area flights in certain cases.

[P22] The requirement that test results “demonstrate” supersonic speeds do not cause measurable sonic boom at the surface (§ 91.818(b)(2)) is scientifically challenging — commenters will request a defined statistical standard (e.g., confidence interval, sample size, measurement uncertainty) and numeric overpressure/noise thresholds for “measurable.”

[P23] Requiring that test-determined conditions cover “all foreseeable operating conditions” (§ 91.818(b)(3)) is unworkably broad; operators will request that the FAA define the set of “foreseeable conditions” (e.g., defined ranges of altitude, weight, temperature, speed, atmospheric profiles) and allow phased expansions as more data are collected.

[P24] The prohibition on granting authorizations if incompatible with protecting or enhancing the environment (§ 91.818(c)(1)) is proper, but commenters will ask the FAA to specify criteria and metrics used to make that environmental compatibility determination to avoid arbitrary or politically motivated rejections.

[P25] The Administrator’s obligation to determine whether issuance constitutes a “major Federal action” under NEPA (§ 91.818(c)(2)) will create lengthy procedural reviews; industry commenters will request categorical exclusions for narrowly scoped, low-impact test flights or a defined fast-track NEPA process.

[P26] Requiring applicants to supply information describing environmental impacts (§ 91.818(c)(2)) imposes substantial new analytic burdens; small operators will request scaled requirements depending on the size/scope of the operation and clear guidance on minimum content to prevent overbroad demands.

[P27] Allowing applicants to submit a newly prepared EIS (§ 91.818(c)(2)(i)) is reasonable, but commenters will emphasize the high cost and time of EIS preparation and ask that the FAA provide templates, standard methodologies, and an option for FAA-funded or shared environmental studies.

[P28] Permitting previously prepared EISs to be used if the FAA finds them adequate (§ 91.818(c)(2)(ii)) is helpful, but commenters will request a clear process and timeline for the FAA’s adequacy review and the standards the FAA will use to assess “adequacy, accuracy, validity, and timeliness.”

[P29] Allowing alternative environmental assessments (§ 91.818(c)(2)(iii)) is sensible; commenters will ask the FAA to publish an explicit list of acceptable assessment types and minimum content standards (acoustic modeling, population exposures, wildlife impacts).

[P30] Conditioning issuance on submission of required information and completion of environmental actions (§ 91.818(d)) could create a de facto prohibition due to NEPA delays; commenters will ask for interim authorizations for limited test flights while environmental reviews proceed, or for a clear expedited path.

[P31] The issuance condition that applicants must submit the described information (§ 91.818(d)) requires the FAA to specify completeness-check procedures and notice timelines so applicants know when their application is considered complete and the review clock starts.

[P32] The issuance condition that the Administrator has taken required environmental actions (§ 91.818(d)) gives broad discretion to the Administrator; commenters will request criteria and appeal rights when issuance is withheld on environmental grounds.

[P33] The indefinite, Administrator-determined duration of authorizations (§ 91.818(e)(1)) creates operational uncertainty; industry will request presumptive durations (e.g., up to 2 years for testing, renewable) and criteria for extensions.

[P34] The rule’s statement that an authorization remains effective until it expires or is surrendered (§ 91.818(e)(2)) needs clarification on what constitutes “expiry” and the process for voluntary surrender and partial revocation (e.g., for certain aircraft in a fleet).

[P35] Granting the Administrator unilateral authority to terminate, suspend, or amend an authorization whenever necessary to protect the environment (§ 91.818(e)(3)) is extremely broad and could be used unpredictably; commenters will request notice-and-comment procedures, minimum notice periods, and the ability to continue operations during appeal when safety is not at issue.

[P36] Allowing the holder 30 days to request reconsideration after administrative termination/amendment/suspension (§ 91.818(e)(4)) is insufficient for complex programs; operators will request a longer window (e.g., 60–90 days) and an expedited review timeline for the FAA to act on reconsideration.

[P37] The automatic permanent termination if the holder fails to request reconsideration and provide information (§ 91.818(e)(4)) is harsh; commenters will request that the rule allow the FAA discretion to reinstate or provide a cure period, and to set standards for what information must be submitted with a reconsideration request.

Requiring prior flights within a test area under an (a)(8)(iv) authorization (§ 91.818(b)(1)) may be impractical for manufacturers with new designs; commenters will request that simulated or validated computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and wind‑tunnel data be accepted in lieu of initial test-area flights in certain cases.

The requirement that test results “demonstrate” supersonic speeds do not cause measurable sonic boom at the surface (§ 91.818(b)(2)) is scientifically challenging — commenters will request a defined statistical standard (e.g., confidence interval, sample size, measurement uncertainty) and numeric overpressure/noise thresholds for “measurable.”

Requiring that test-determined conditions cover “all foreseeable operating conditions” (§ 91.818(b)(3)) is unworkably broad; operators will request that the FAA define the set of “foreseeable conditions” (e.g., defined ranges of altitude, weight, temperature, speed, atmospheric profiles) and allow phased expansions as more data are collected.

The prohibition on granting authorizations if incompatible with protecting or enhancing the environment (§ 91.818(c)(1)) is proper, but commenters will ask the FAA to specify criteria and metrics used to make that environmental compatibility determination to avoid arbitrary or politically motivated rejections.

The Administrator’s obligation to determine whether issuance constitutes a “major Federal action” under NEPA (§ 91.818(c)(2)) will create lengthy procedural reviews; industry commenters will request categorical exclusions for narrowly scoped, low-impact test flights or a defined fast-track NEPA process.

Requiring applicants to supply information describing environmental impacts (§ 91.818(c)(2)) imposes substantial new analytic burdens; small operators will request scaled requirements depending on the size/scope of the operation and clear guidance on minimum content to prevent overbroad demands.

Allowing applicants to submit a newly prepared EIS (§ 91.818(c)(2)(i)) is reasonable, but commenters will emphasize the high cost and time of EIS preparation and ask that the FAA provide templates, standard methodologies, and an option for FAA-funded or shared environmental studies.

Permitting previously prepared EISs to be used if the FAA finds them adequate (§ 91.818(c)(2)(ii)) is helpful, but commenters will request a clear process and timeline for the FAA’s adequacy review and the standards the FAA will use to assess “adequacy, accuracy, validity, and timeliness.”

Allowing alternative environmental assessments (§ 91.818(c)(2)(iii)) is sensible; commenters will ask the FAA to publish an explicit list of acceptable assessment types and minimum content standards (acoustic modeling, population exposures, wildlife impacts).

Conditioning issuance on submission of required information and completion of environmental actions (§ 91.818(d)) could create a de facto prohibition due to NEPA delays; commenters will ask for interim authorizations for limited test flights while environmental reviews proceed, or for a clear expedited path.

The issuance condition that applicants must submit the described information (§ 91.818(d)) requires the FAA to specify completeness-check procedures and notice timelines so applicants know when their application is considered complete and the review clock starts.

The issuance condition that the Administrator has taken required environmental actions (§ 91.818(d)) gives broad discretion to the Administrator; commenters will request criteria and appeal rights when issuance is withheld on environmental grounds.

The indefinite, Administrator-determined duration of authorizations (§ 91.818(e)(1)) creates operational uncertainty; industry will request presumptive durations (e.g., up to 2 years for testing, renewable) and criteria for extensions.

The rule’s statement that an authorization remains effective until it expires or is surrendered (§ 91.818(e)(2)) needs clarification on what constitutes “expiry” and the process for voluntary surrender and partial revocation (e.g., for certain aircraft in a fleet).

Granting the Administrator unilateral authority to terminate, suspend, or amend an authorization whenever necessary to protect the environment (§ 91.818(e)(3)) is extremely broad and could be used unpredictably; commenters will request notice-and-comment procedures, minimum notice periods, and the ability to continue operations during appeal when safety is not at issue.

Allowing the holder 30 days to request reconsideration after administrative termination/amendment/suspension (§ 91.818(e)(4)) is insufficient for complex programs; operators will request a longer window (e.g., 60–90 days) and an expedited review timeline for the FAA to act on reconsideration.
