[P1] The November 20, 2017 deadline for receipt of comments is arbitrary and unworkable for many stakeholders; request extension to at least 60 days from publication for meaningful public input.

[P1] The rule's requirement that comments "be received by November 20, 2017" should clarify whether comments postmarked by that date but received later will be accepted to avoid penalizing mail delays.

[P2] The phrase "follow the requirements of this AD within the specified compliance times unless already completed" is ambiguous about partial compliance—request clarification that partial completion actions count toward compliance and how to document them.

[P2] Industry requests explicit guidance on what documentation constitutes proof that an action was "already completed" prior to the AD effective date to avoid disputes during enforcement.

[P3] The obligation to "perform the applicable actions listed in paragraphs (g)(1)–(g)(4)" lacks a cross-reference mechanism for operators to determine which specific airplanes are affected; request clearer applicability criteria tied to aircraft registration/model/serial numbers.

[P3] Legal commenters note the exception "except as modified by paragraph (h)" could create conflicts; request the rule include an explicit precedence statement explaining how (g) and (h) interact in case of timing conflicts.

[P4] Requiring all actions marked 'RC' in Boeing Service Bulletin 747–52–2307 without incorporation by reference text raises concerns—request the FAA incorporate the full service bulletin into the rulemaking record or clearly adopt it by reference.

[P4] Operators request clarification of "At the applicable time specified in paragraph 1.E., 'Compliance,'" — specifically whether calendar date, flight cycles, or flight hours govern the timing, and how to calculate compliance for aircraft with atypical utilization.

[P5] Same as P4 for Boeing Service Bulletin 747–52–2308: request the service bulletin be incorporated by reference or appended in full to ensure enforceable, public text.

[P6] For Boeing Service Bulletin 757–52–0093 Rev 1, request explicit instructions on accepting earlier Revision 0 work and whether any differences between revisions affect RC steps and compliance.

[P6] Airlines ask for a compliance relief period for aircraft undergoing heavy maintenance that cannot schedule these actions within the specified times without operational disruption.

[P7] The 24‑month requirement to replace cargo door switches for airplanes identified in paragraph (c)(4) is too short for operators with limited access to parts and maintenance slots—request extension to 36 months or allow staged compliance tied to scheduled heavy checks.

[P7] Technical commenters request the rule specify part numbers, vendor specifications, and test criteria for the "improved switches" and "arm switches" to avoid equipment compatibility issues and procurement delays.

[P7] The requirement that some actions be done "in accordance with an FAA‑approved method" without stating acceptance criteria will cause delays; request publication of acceptable methods or an expedited approval process for commonly used methods.

[P8] The 24‑month blanket compliance period fails to accommodate differences in utilization across fleets (e.g., cargo vs passenger operators); request an alternative compliance metric based on flight cycles or door actuations.

[P9] Requiring approval by the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch centralizes decision-making and may create bottlenecks—request delegation to regional ACOs or authorization of Boeing ODA approvals under defined conditions.

[P9] Legal commenters argue the rule must provide a clear standard and timeline for the Manager's approval process to satisfy due process and avoid indefinite delays.

[P10] Changing service bulletin compliance time references to be measured from the AD effective date could unfairly shorten expected compliance windows for operators who already planned per-bulletin timelines; request a grandfathering clause for operators who scheduled work per bulletin issue dates before the AD.

[P10] Request that the AD explicitly state how to convert bulletin-based "within X months after issue" timings to "after AD effective date" for example aircraft to avoid miscalculation.

[P11] The credit provision for Boeing Service Bulletin 757–52–0093 (May 5, 2016) should be expanded to include other prior equivalent work accepted by operators' principal inspectors; otherwise, it may unfairly withhold credit for compliant earlier actions.

[P11] Request guidance on acceptable evidence to demonstrate that prior actions were performed in accordance with the earlier service bulletin to qualify for compliance credit.

[P12] The provision allowing the Manager to approve AMOCs per 14 CFR 39.19 does not address timelines — request a mandatory response timeframe (e.g., 60 days) for AMOC decisions to prevent operational uncertainty.

[P12] Operators request clarity on whether AMOC approvals issued to one operator are available for others to reference or rely upon, to promote consistency and efficiency.

[P13] Requirement to send AMOC requests to principal inspectors or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 may be confusing for foreign operators—request an explicit process for non‑U.S. operators and their national authorities.

[P14] The instruction to address information to the person in paragraph (k)(1) when sending directly to the certification office manager should include the manager's current name or functional title to avoid misrouting.

[P15] Allowing AMOC request information to be emailed to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov raises confidentiality concerns; request confirmation of secure handling and acknowledgement of receipt within a short timeframe.

[P16] The mandate to notify the principal inspector or local FSDO before using an approved AMOC is vague about the notice period; request a required minimum advance notice (e.g., 14 calendar days) and documentation content requirements.

[P16] Operators request that the rule permit immediate use of an AMOC in urgent situations with post‑use notification when delay would affect safety or operations, subject to FAA agreement.

[P17] Allowing Boeing ODA to approve AMOCs for repairs/modifications requires clear limitations—request that the ODA be required to document how its approval meets the airplane's certification basis and that the FAA retain final oversight.

[P17] Labor/worker groups request assurance that AMOC approvals by Boeing ODA do not bypass independent FAA review of safety implications for maintenance personnel.

[P18] Requiring that repair/modification deviations meet the airplane's certification basis may be impossible for older aircraft with ambiguous certification records; request guidance on how to determine certification basis and handle grandfathered design features.

[P18] Legal commenters request that approvals specifically reference the AD number be accompanied by a public index of those approvals to ensure transparency.

[P19] Making all 'RC' steps mandatory without exception risks operational inflexibility; request that the FAA allow narrowly tailored deviations via an expedited AMOC path when equivalent safety can be demonstrated.

[P19] Maintenance organizations request a clear, machine‑readable list of RC steps, substeps, and figures so maintenance tracking and compliance software can automatically identify mandatory actions.

[P20] The "RC Exempt" exception must be explicitly defined—request that the AD list which steps are "RC Exempt" in the body of the AD rather than relying solely on the service bulletin text.

[P21] Requiring an AMOC for any deviation to RC steps could impede minor, non‑safety‑affecting repairs; request that the FAA permit documented, inspector‑approved minor deviations with post‑action reporting.

[P22] Permission to deviate from non‑RC steps under an operator's maintenance program should include a requirement to notify the FAA when deviations are used more than a threshold (e.g., 5 times) to permit oversight.

[P22] Airlines seek clarification whether the operator's accepted methods must be pre‑approved by the principal inspector before using them to deviate from non‑RC steps.

[P23] The condition that RC steps remain accomplishable after deviations from non‑RC steps needs examples and objective criteria to prevent subjective enforcement actions; request illustrative scenarios in the AD preamble or guidance material.

[P23] Safety advocacy groups request that the FAA require operators to retain records demonstrating that deviations did not jeopardize the ability to perform RC steps, and that such records be made available during inspections.

[P1] The requirement that applicants address one or more listed priority areas is overly prescriptive and will exclude innovative projects that fall outside the enumerated priorities but still advance remote learning outcomes.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether applicants may propose projects that address cross-cutting issues spanning multiple priorities and how such multi-priority projects will be evaluated.

[P2] The definition of "technology-leveraging models" is vague; applicants need clearer definitions and examples beyond universal design for learning and competency-based education to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P2] Requiring adoption/support of technology-leveraging models may privilege vendors and commercially developed platforms; the Department should require open standards and procurement safeguards to prevent vendor lock-in.

[P2] The notice’s reference to competency-based education "as defined in this notice" lacks sufficient operational detail (e.g., time-to-competency metrics, mastery thresholds); applicants need explicit criteria to design assessments and interventions.

[P3] The obligation to provide "personalized, job-embedded professional learning" is undefined — the Department should specify minimum hours, credentialing expectations, or evidence standards to ensure comparability across applicants.

[P3] Smaller districts and community-based organizations cannot realistically scale intensive job-embedded professional learning without dedicated funding; the Department should allow partners or intermediaries to deliver this component.

[P4] The requirement to provide access to "reliable high-speed internet, devices, and software" does not specify minimum bandwidth, device specifications, or software accessibility standards, creating uncertainty for budgeting and procurement.

[P4] Funding projects that provide devices and internet with no sustainability plan risks temporary fixes; the Department should require applicants to include maintenance, replacement, and recurring service cost plans.

[P5] The cap limiting technology costs to 10% of total project activity costs is unworkable for projects whose primary activity is technology delivery (e.g., device provisioning or broadband buildout); the Department should exempt or raise the cap for infrastructure-heavy proposals.

[P5] The 10% technology cost limit will disincentivize high-quality digital content and necessary software licensing; commenters request clarification on whether technology-related implementation staff and training count as technology or non-technology costs.

[P6] The mandate to develop "valid, reliable performance-based assessments" for competency-based education requires technical expertise many applicants lack; the Department should permit use of validated third-party assessments and provide technical assistance funds.

[P6] The provision does not address data privacy or FERPA/GDPR considerations for performance-based assessments that collect granular student data; the rule should require explicit privacy protections and data minimization standards.

[P7] Supporting interoperable digital credentials is potentially beneficial, but the rule lacks specificity on governance, standards (e.g., Open Badges, W3C Verifiable Credentials), and liability for credential accuracy; applicants need clear standards to follow.

[P7] The requirement that students "control/share" achievements needs definition regarding age of consent, parent/guardian rights, and mechanisms for revocation or correction of erroneous credentials.

[P8] Mandating that credential information be publicly accessible in linked open data formats raises privacy concerns for minors and may conflict with FERPA if personally identifiable information is exposed; the Department must specify allowable fields and redaction requirements.

[P8] Many potential applicants lack the technical capacity to publish linked open data; the Department should fund tooling or permit alternative formats (e.g., machine-readable CSV/JSON with access controls) for smaller entities.

[P9] Targeting high-quality remote or competency-based education to several underserved subgroups without guidance on equity measurement will create inconsistent services; the Department should require disaggregated outcome metrics and culturally responsive approaches.

[P9] The list of underserved student subgroups appears to be truncated in the notice; commenters request the complete list and clarification whether projects must target only one subgroup or may serve multiple.

[P10] Requiring compliance with Section 504 and Title II is appropriate, but the rule should specify accessibility standards (e.g., WCAG 2.1 AA) and documentation applicants must provide to demonstrate compliance.

[P10] The Department should clarify whether legacy platforms will need remediation and whether remediation costs are allowable beyond the 10% technology cap (P5).

[P11] The language assistance requirement for English learners must include specific provisions for assessment accommodations, multilingual interfaces, and culturally appropriate pedagogy rather than generic "language assistance services."

[P11] Applicants need guidance on acceptable qualifications for language assistance providers and evidence of efficacy for remote language supports.

[P12] Granting the Secretary discretion to include whole priorities or parts creates unpredictability for applicants; the Department should publish criteria and timelines for how component parts will be selected in each competition.

[P12] This discretion could be used to pick and choose subcomponents in a way that advantages certain applicants; commenters request transparency and advance notice of which components will be used.

[P13] Requiring component (f) to be used only with at least one other component will disadvantage organizations whose core expertise is serving underserved subgroups remotely; the Department should allow standalone applications for component (f) where evidence shows focus fidelity.

[P13] The restriction may prevent targeted pilots focused solely on underserved populations; commenters urge flexibility to permit single-component competitions when justified.

[P14] Designating priority types via Federal Register notice is appropriate, but applicants need an earlier signals calendar so they can plan multi-year projects aligned with anticipated priority types.

[P15] Declaring an absolute priority will effectively bar worthy proposals that address other critical needs; the Department should avoid absolute designations for priorities that are rapidly evolving (e.g., technology standards).

[P16] The competitive preference priority mechanism must include transparency about the point values and how extent-of-meeting will be measured; applicants cannot budget or design proposals without knowing the scoring weight.

[P17] If additional points are awarded (P17), the Department should publish a rubric specifying criteria and scoring thresholds rather than leaving extent assessments to subjective reviewer judgment.

[P18] The authority to select an application meeting the priority over a comparably meritorious one (P18) risks undermining objective merit-based selection; commenters request that such tie-breakers be narrowly defined and used only with clear justification.

[P19] As stated, invitational priorities create no advantage; however, the Department should still provide feedback to applicants about how meeting an invitational priority might strengthen future applications.

[P20] The explicit prohibition on preferential treatment for invitational priorities is clear; however, applicants may misunderstand and invest resources accordingly — the Department should include explanatory guidance distinguishing types.

[P21] Publishing the final priority and definitions in the Federal Register is necessary, but the comment period timeline for changes seems unspecified; stakeholders request a minimum 60-day comment period on any substantive modifications.

[P22] While the Department will consider public comments, there is no commitment to respond to or justify material changes; commenters request that the Department publish a response-to-comments document explaining how input influenced final priorities.

[P23] Reserving authority to propose additional priorities or criteria in the future necessitates guardrails; commenters ask for notice-and-comment rulemaking for any substantive future additions that materially change application requirements.

[P24] Requiring application invitations via Federal Register notice is standard, but the Department should also use direct outreach to historically underrepresented applicants (small LEAs, community organizations) to ensure equitable awareness.

[P1] The requirement that OPM or a DEU "use one of the listed mechanisms to refer a sufficient number of candidates" is vague because "sufficient number" is undefined; request adding a numeric minimum or clear standard to avoid inconsistent application across agencies.

[P1] Industry commenters will object that the rule gives OPM/DEUs undue operational discretion to choose mechanisms without requiring coordination with hiring managers, which could slow hiring and reduce manager flexibility.

[P2] Requiring each agency to "establish a policy on the use of these procedures" will create duplicative paperwork and inconsistent practices across agencies unless OPM issues a model policy or minimum mandatory elements.

[P2] Small agencies and component offices request a phased implementation or template policy because they lack HR resources to develop bespoke policies immediately.

[P3] Allowing OPM/DEUs to "determine...which mechanism will best meet the hiring needs" without requiring consultation with hiring managers or stakeholders risks misalignment between assessment methods and mission needs.

[P3] The clause to "obtain at least three names" (minimum three) should be clarified when applicant pools are small or the position is highly specialized; agencies must be allowed to document good-faith efforts and proceed with fewer than three candidates in narrow circumstances.

[P4] Authorizing cut-off scores "based on the assessment(s) used, supported by job analysis data" is appropriate, but commenters request that the rule require documentation standards and validation evidence (e.g., predictive validity coefficients) for the job analysis and assessments.

[P4] Civil rights advocates caution that relying on assessment-based cut scores can have disparate impact; the rule should require adverse impact monitoring and remediation procedures when cut scores disproportionately exclude protected groups.

[P5] Permitting cut-off scores "based on business necessity" is too permissive and could be abused to justify subjective or exclusionary thresholds; commenters ask OPM to define acceptable evidence and a review process before business-necessity cutoffs are applied.

[P5] Legal experts note that "business necessity" is an EEOC legal standard; the rule should explicitly require agencies to document and retain the analysis demonstrating business necessity and lack of less discriminatory alternatives.

[P6] Allowing certification of a set number of highest-ranked applicants is reasonable, but the rule must require that set numbers be based on historical yield rates and hiring needs and justify the chosen number in the case file.

[P7] Certifying a set percentage of applicants could yield unpredictable candidate counts in small applicant pools; request a floor (e.g., at least three candidates) or alternate rule when percentages produce fewer than three names.

[P8] The tie rule that requires referring all applicants with the same score and veterans' preference category as the last candidate at the cut may produce very large certificates; agencies ask for an upper cap or guidance on handling many tied applicants to avoid operational burdens.

[P8] Veteran advocacy groups support the tie-and-veterans-preference provision but request clarification on how ties are resolved across multiple preference categories (e.g., 10-point vs. 5-point) and how groupings are determined.

[P9] The list of factors agencies "should consider" when selecting mechanisms is helpful but non-binding; commenters ask OPM to make certain factors (like assessment validity and historical applicant data) mandatory considerations.

[P9] Workforce diversity advocates request adding "impact on diversity and EEO outcomes" explicitly to the list of factors to ensure selection mechanisms advance inclusion.

[P10] Requiring the mechanism to be decided and stated in the job announcement may limit agencies' flexibility to adapt if applicant pools are unexpectedly small or assessments perform poorly; request a carve-out allowing amendment if justified and documented before certification.

[P10] Hiring managers fear that committing to a mechanism pre-announcement could hinder using newer validated assessments discovered after posting; ask for an expedited approval process to change the approach with notification.

[P11] The obligation to document the approach in the examining case file and make it available for reconstruction or third-party review raises confidentiality concerns for applicants; request guidance on redaction and data protections.

[P11] Compliance officers and legal counsel request that OPM specify retention periods, required data elements, and a standard format for documentation to enable consistent third-party review.

[P12] The requirement to provide hiring managers "when possible" with names to consider at least three candidates is ambiguous; agencies want a clear definition of "when possible" and guidance on documenting efforts when three candidates cannot be provided.

[P12] Hiring managers representing mission-critical components request that exceptions be allowed to proceed with fewer than three candidates when time-sensitive hiring is necessary, provided EEO counsel approves and the case file documents the exigent circumstances.

[P13] The mandate to decide beforehand how to expand candidates if certificates yield fewer than three (per the handbook) creates operational rigidity—request that the handbook be incorporated by reference into the regulation or that agencies get sufficient time to align processes.

[P13] Commenters ask OPM to publish the referenced "handbook" procedures concurrently with the final rule so agencies and applicants know expansion options in advance.

[P14] Requiring simultaneous listing of candidates on all applicable certificates could cause repeated outreach and multiple concurrent referrals that confuse candidates; suggest allowing agencies to coordinate offers to prevent multiple simultaneous job offers.

[P14] Privacy and candidate burden concerns: candidates may not want to be referred to multiple positions at once; request an opt-out mechanism for candidates who prefer one application per hiring action.

[P15] The exception permitting referring a candidate for only one vacancy at a time "in the interest of good administration" is excessively subjective; request clearer criteria and mandatory notification timing and format to candidates.

[P15] Candidates' advocates demand that any notification that limits simultaneous referrals be provided at application time and that candidates be given a reasonable period to accept or decline referrals.

[P16] The mandate that hiring managers "select any eligible candidate certified...based solely on merit and fitness" may be misconstrued; commenters request definition of "merit and fitness" and examples of permissible selection factors (e.g., mission-critical skills).

[P16] Legal commenters warn this could lead to litigation if agencies define "merit and fitness" inconsistently; request that OPM provide decision-making guidance and training materials.

[P17] The prohibition on passing over a preference eligible in favor of a lower-standing non-preference eligible unless pass-over procedures in § 332.406 are followed is essential; veteran groups ask that § 332.406 be included or cross-referenced explicitly, and request transparency requirements for pass-over decisions.

[P17] Agencies request clarification on timelines and review rights for preference eligibles who are passed over, and whether pass-over documentation must be provided to the affected candidate.

[P18] Allowing agencies to decline to consider an eligible who has been considered for three separate appointments may unfairly penalize persistent candidates; commenters ask for protections to ensure candidates are not excluded for exercising their appeal or reasonable persistence.

[P18] Disability advocates request accommodations in counting "considered" events — for example, if a candidate could not attend one interview due to a lack of reasonable accommodation, that event should not count toward the three-consideration limit.

[P19] The requirement that hiring managers must have made three valid selections and provided bona fide consideration before removing a candidate places significant documentation burden on hiring managers; agencies request templates for demonstrating "valid selection" and "bona fide consideration."

[P19] Opposing commenters argue the three-selection threshold could delay hiring for high-turnover occupations and suggest allowing agencies to apply the three-consideration rule flexibly for mission-critical roles with OPM approval.

[P20] Requiring consideration of application materials and an interview to count as a consideration could be interpreted to require in-person interviews for all candidates; request clarification that virtual interviews or structured phone interviews suffice if equivalent in rigor.

[P21] The rule's standard that interviews be of "the same rigor and thoroughness" as for other candidates is subjective; request standardized interview templates, scoring rubrics, or examples to ensure consistency and defensibility.

[P22] The document-and-explain requirement for removing a candidate imposes heavy recordkeeping; civil service reform groups ask OPM to define minimum required elements of the explanatory description to reduce variation.

[P22] Privacy advocates request guidance on redaction when these explanatory descriptions contain sensitive medical or other personal information.

[P23] Allowing agencies to remove one candidate starting with the fourth selection (and one per subsequent selection) appears to permit bypassing many candidates cumulatively; commenters ask for limits (e.g., a maximum total number removable per vacancy) to prevent circumventing veterans' preference and EEO protections.

[P23] Labor unions express concern that the three-consideration removal rule could be gamed to cycle out preferred candidates; recommend periodic audits and reporting requirements when agencies use the provision.

[P24] Applying veterans' preference as prescribed in the cited statutory provisions is appropriate, but request explicit crosswalk guidance so agencies can reconcile differences between those statutes and newer regulatory practices like category rating.

[P25] The prohibition on applying veterans' preference points in category rating (§ 337.304(b)) will reduce the numerical benefit veterans previously received and may disadvantage some qualified veterans; veteran service organizations request analysis of the expected impact and transitional protections.

[P25] Legal advocates argue that eliminating veterans' preference points in category rating could conflict with statutory intent in some cases; they request OPM to confirm the legal authority for this prohibition and provide implementation guidance.

[P26] Designating the cited statutory sections as the veterans' preference requirements for purposes of 5 U.S.C. 2302(b)(11)(A) and (B) requires clearer explanation of how this affects appeal rights and preference-protected processes; request examples and a statement of candidates' rights under the new cross-reference.

[P26] Commenters ask for OPM to clarify whether this designation changes which veterans are considered "preference eligible" for investigative or retention purposes and to provide scenarios showing application.

[P1] The blanket prohibition on any non-participant vessel entering, transiting, anchoring in, or remaining in the race area (§100.35T07–0195(c)(1)) is overly broad and fails to account for commercial fishing vessels that may need safe transit routes; it should include explicit exemptions or defined corridors for commercial fishing and subsistence navigation.

[P2] The exception allowing COTP or designated representative authorization (§100.35T07–0195(c)(1) exception) places too much discretionary power in a single office without required timelines; the rule should require the COTP to respond to authorization requests within a specified time (e.g., 30 minutes during events) to avoid unreasonable delays.

[P3] Permission to request authorization by phone or VHF-FM Channel 16 (§100.35T07–0195(c)(2)) is insufficient for mariners who rely on digital notice systems; the rule should also permit requests via VHF DSC, AIS text, or an email/online portal and state backup contact methods.

[P4] The permission provision (§100.35T07–0195(c)(2)) does not specify required information for authorization requests (vessel name, CG documentation, purpose, ETA); the rule should list mandatory data elements so applicants know what to provide and the COTP can adjudicate quickly.

[P5] The obligation to follow instructions from the COTP or designated representative while in the race area (§100.35T07–0195(c)(3)) is reasonable but needs a procedural limit: instructions should be lawful, reasonable, and documented in writing or via VHF to allow contesting unclear directives later.

[P6] Requiring written or recorded proof of authorization on board while in the race area (§100.35T07–0195(c)(3) implied by instruction compliance) is not included; the rule should require that any granted authorization be documented (written permit or broadcasted call sign) and kept onboard.

[P7] The comments deadline obligation (submit by Sept 6, 2018) is obsolete and will confuse readers of the final rule; the rule should update the DATES section to current dates or use relative language (e.g., "60 days from publication").

[P8] The ADDRESSES instruction to identify comments by Docket ID EPA–HQ–SFUND–2002–0001 (P6/P13) is inconsistent with the Coast Guard docket numbering and will misdirect comments; the regulation should correct the docket ID to reference the Coast Guard event docket and ensure alignment.

[P9] The requirement that submissions via Regulations.gov cannot be edited or removed after submission (P7) may discourage stakeholders from correcting errors or updating sensitive submissions; the agency should allow a short correction window (e.g., 7 days) for submitters to amend clerical mistakes.

[P10] The prohibition on submitting CBI or statutorily restricted information electronically (P10) is appropriate, but the rule fails to provide clear instructions for submitting sensitive information via secure channels or for requesting confidentiality designations; add explicit secure submission procedures and FOIA contact details.

[P11] Requiring multimedia files to be accompanied by a written comment and treating the written document as the official comment (P11/P12) is reasonable, but the rule should clarify whether transcripts of videos are sufficient and specify maximum file sizes and acceptable formats to avoid technical submission issues.

[P12] The electronic file guidance (P14) to avoid special characters, encryption, and viruses is fine, but the rule must specify accepted file formats (e.g., PDF/A, DOCX) and provide technical assistance contacts for stakeholders who encounter difficulties.

[P13] The mail and email submission permissions (P8/P9) list one EPA contact (Armando Saenz, Region 8) that appears unrelated to a race-area marine safety zone; clarify which agency and regional office is responsible for this rule and provide consistent contact information for the Coast Guard and EPA components.

[P14] The obligation that comments be identified by docket ID (P13) should also require inclusion of an organizational affiliation and contact information to facilitate follow-up; the current language does not discourage anonymous, potentially duplicative or automated mass comments.

[P15] The local excavation permit requirement (Operation and Maintenance P15) places a significant burden on small property owners by requiring permits for "restricted activities" without specifying thresholds (e.g., depth, volume); the ordinance should define exactly which excavation depths, areas, or volumes trigger the permit requirement.

[P16] The excavation disposition requirement (P16) forcing contaminated materials to be disposed at the open cell or capped with 18 inches of clean topsoil/road base is inflexible and may be technically infeasible for certain redevelopment projects; permittees should be allowed alternative proven remediation methods (e.g., off-site disposal under manifest, engineered barriers) with EPA/UDEQ approval.

[P17] The option to dispose excavated contaminated material in the open cell (P17) raises concerns about long-term containment, potential leachate, and transport costs; the rule should require engineering standards for the open cell, monitoring, and cost estimates or allow off-site licensed disposal where appropriate.

[P18] The capping option specifying 18 inches of clean topsoil or road base (P18) and the alternative 2-inch hard cover (P19) are inconsistent—there is no clarity when a 2-inch pavement cover is acceptable versus the 18-inch soil requirement; the rule should harmonize cover depth/quality requirements and provide performance standards (e.g., permeability, compaction).

[P19] The minimum 2-inch hard cover surface (P19) is insufficient for paved surfaces subject to vehicular traffic; require a structural design standard (e.g., minimum asphalt or concrete thickness based on traffic load) rather than an arbitrary 2-inch minimum.

[P20] The prohibition on disturbing or altering Response Action Structures (RASs) without EPA/UDEQ approval (P20) is appropriate for protection, but the rule should include an emergency exception allowing temporary disturbance for imminent safety repairs with immediate notice to EPA/UDEQ.

[P21] Requiring compliance with Eureka’s excavation ordinance as part of the environmental covenants (P21) could conflict with state or federal programs or create redundant permitting; clarify precedence and provide a streamlined approval process when overlapping jurisdictional permits are required.

[P22] Imposing obligations on subsequent owners via covenants that "run with the land" (P22) will deter property sales and redevelopment; the rule should require UDEQ/EPA to provide a clear covenant content template and offer mechanisms for covenant modification or termination when remediation levels are met.

[P23] Mandating statutory Five-Year Reviews because contaminants remain above unrestricted-use levels (P23) is legally required, but the rule needs to specify lead agency, review scope, stakeholder participation rights, and public notice procedures for the reviews to ensure transparency.

[P24] The O&M Plan assigning UDEQ and City of Eureka responsibility for implementing institutional controls and operating the open cell (P24) lacks defined funding and enforcement mechanisms; the rule should require a funding assurance plan, liability allocation, and clear triggers for corrective action if responsible parties default.

[P15] The permit requirement for restricted excavation activities (P15) lacks an appeal process or timelines for permit decisions; include an administrative appeal and guaranteed decision timeline (e.g., 60 days) to prevent project delays.

[P16] The requirement to cap contaminated material with "clean" topsoil is ambiguous—define "clean" with quantitative contaminant thresholds (e.g., below specific soil screening levels) to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P17] The permission to use the open cell for disposal of excavated materials (P17) should require prior chemical compatibility and volume limits to avoid overloading the cell with incompatible contaminants that could jeopardize long-term containment.

[P20] The prohibition on disturbing RASs without prior approval (P20) should include a defined approval timeframe and criteria; indefinite review timelines could prevent necessary property maintenance and emergency work.

[P21] The ECs forcing compliance with local excavation ordinances (P21) should not preclude reasonable residential gardening or minor landscaping; include de minimis exceptions (e.g., holes less than 12 inches deep) for homeowners.

[P22] The rule should require that environmental covenants include notice on property deeds and provide a standardized disclosure form for potential buyers to ensure informed transactions (relates to P22).

[P23] The Five-Year Review obligation (P23) should require that remedial performance data and monitoring results be made publicly available in an accessible format and that community members have the opportunity to request additional sampling.

[P24] The O&M responsibility allocation (P24) must include performance metrics, reporting frequency (e.g., annual reports), and enforcement provisions including penalties for non-compliance to ensure continued protection.

[P10] The prohibition against submitting CBI electronically (P10) should be accompanied by instructions for redacting confidential portions and a clear process for claim of confidentiality to prevent inadvertent public disclosure.

[P7] The statement that comments submitted to Regulations.gov cannot be removed (P7) conflicts with privacy interests where submitters might inadvertently post personal identifying information; allow limited removal or redaction requests post-submission.

[P1] The race-area prohibition (P1) lacks geographic specificity (coordinates, charted boundaries); the rule should include precise coordinates, chart references, and a map to prevent confusion and unintended violations.

[P3] Contacting the COTP by telephone or Channel 16 (P3) may not be feasible in severe weather or communication outages; require alternative authorization methods and specify procedures during communications failures.

[P11] Requiring multimedia to be accompanied by written comments (P11) is reasonable, but the rule must allow the multimedia itself to be the substantive submission when it includes the full argument (e.g., recorded testimony), or state how multimedia will be transcribed and used.

[P18] The capping option requiring 18 inches of clean topsoil or road base (P18) may be inconsistent with green infrastructure or stormwater practices; allow engineered vegetative caps or geotextile-integrated covers that meet protective performance standards.

The capping option specifying 18 inches of clean topsoil or road base (P18) and the alternative 2-inch hard cover (P19) are inconsistent—there is no clarity when a 2-inch pavement cover is acceptable versus the 18-inch soil requirement; the rule should harmonize cover depth/quality requirements and provide performance standards (e.g., permeability, compaction).

The minimum 2-inch hard cover surface (P19) is insufficient for paved surfaces subject to vehicular traffic; require a structural design standard (e.g., minimum asphalt or concrete thickness based on traffic load) rather than an arbitrary 2-inch minimum.

The prohibition on disturbing or altering Response Action Structures (RASs) without EPA/UDEQ approval (P20) is appropriate for protection, but the rule should include an emergency exception allowing temporary disturbance for imminent safety repairs with immediate notice to EPA/UDEQ.

Requiring compliance with Eureka’s excavation ordinance as part of the environmental covenants (P21) could conflict with state or federal programs or create redundant permitting; clarify precedence and provide a streamlined approval process when overlapping jurisdictional permits are required.

Imposing obligations on subsequent owners via covenants that "run with the land" (P22) will deter property sales and redevelopment; the rule should require UDEQ/EPA to provide a clear covenant content template and offer mechanisms for covenant modification or termination when remediation levels are met.

Mandating statutory Five-Year Reviews because contaminants remain above unrestricted-use levels (P23) is legally required, but the rule needs to specify lead agency, review scope, stakeholder participation rights, and public notice procedures for the reviews to ensure transparency.

The O&M Plan assigning UDEQ and City of Eureka responsibility for implementing institutional controls and operating the open cell (P24) lacks defined funding and enforcement mechanisms; the rule should require a funding assurance plan, liability allocation, and clear triggers for corrective action if responsible parties default.

The permit requirement for restricted excavation activities (P15) lacks an appeal process or timelines for permit decisions; include an administrative appeal and guaranteed decision timeline (e.g., 60 days) to prevent project delays.

The requirement to cap contaminated material with "clean" topsoil is ambiguous—define "clean" with quantitative contaminant thresholds (e.g., below specific soil screening levels) to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

The permission to use the open cell for disposal of excavated materials (P17) should require prior chemical compatibility and volume limits to avoid overloading the cell with incompatible contaminants that could jeopardize long-term containment.

The prohibition on disturbing RASs without prior approval (P20) should include a defined approval timeframe and criteria; indefinite review timelines could prevent necessary property maintenance and emergency work.

The ECs forcing compliance with local excavation ordinances (P21) should not preclude reasonable residential gardening or minor landscaping; include de minimis exceptions (e.g., holes less than 12 inches deep) for homeowners.
The rule should require that environmental covenants include notice on property deeds and provide a standardized disclosure form for potential buyers to ensure informed transactions (relates to P22).

The Five-Year Review obligation (P23) should require that remedial performance data and monitoring results be made publicly available in an accessible format and that community members have the opportunity to request additional sampling.

The O&M responsibility allocation (P24) must include performance metrics, reporting frequency (e.g., annual reports), and enforcement provisions including penalties for non-compliance to ensure continued protection.

The prohibition against submitting CBI electronically (P10) should be accompanied by instructions for redacting confidential portions and a clear process for claim of confidentiality to prevent inadvertent public disclosure.

The statement that comments submitted to Regulations.gov cannot be removed (P7) conflicts with privacy interests where submitters might inadvertently post personal identifying information; allow limited removal or redaction requests post-submission.

The race-area prohibition (P1) lacks geographic specificity (coordinates, charted boundaries); the rule should include precise coordinates, chart references, and a map to prevent confusion and unintended violations.

Contacting the COTP by telephone or Channel 16 (P3) may not be feasible in severe weather or communication outages; require alternative authorization methods and specify procedures during communications failures.

Requiring multimedia to be accompanied by written comments (P11) is reasonable, but the rule must allow the multimedia itself to be the substantive submission when it includes the full argument (e.g., recorded testimony), or state how multimedia will be transcribed and used.

The capping option requiring 18 inches of clean topsoil or road base (P18) may be inconsistent with green infrastructure or stormwater practices; allow engineered vegetative caps or geotextile-integrated covers that meet protective performance standards.

[P1] The requirement to "specify the analytical method used" when reporting test results is ambiguous about the level of detail required (e.g., method name and year, full protocol deviations, instrument models); request clarification to avoid inconsistent reporting across laboratories.

[P1] Requiring method specification without standardizing the format (e.g., a code or citation) will make electronic data aggregation and comparison difficult; propose a standardized method identifier (method number and year) for reporting.

[P2] Mandating MPN to resolve all controversies on chlorinated wastewaters unfairly precludes other validated confirmatory approaches (e.g., improved membrane filtration modifications or molecular confirmation); recommend allowing alternative resolution methods if validated equivalency to MPN is demonstrated.

[P2] The preamble claim that MF yields "low and variable recovery" from chlorinated wastewater is broad; require the agency to provide supporting data and define what constitutes a "controversy" that triggers mandatory MPN use.

[P2] Requiring MPN in disputes will increase time and cost for permittees and labs because MPN is labor- and time-intensive; request an economic analysis and consideration of thresholds (e.g., only require MPN when MF results differ by X% or regulatory limit is exceeded).

[P3] The obligation that laboratories "must perform tests that provide organism enumeration (density)" could conflict with qualitative presence/absence methods used under certain programs; ask the agency to clarify whether qualitative methods remain allowable in contexts where enumeration is unnecessary.

[P3] For low-resource or small-volume labs, the enumeration requirement may impose equipment and training burdens; request phased implementation, technical assistance, or allowance for accredited external labs to perform enumeration.

[P4] The requirement to "select appropriate tube/filtration configurations and dilutions/volumes based on sample quality and expected organism density" is subjective; propose prescribing specific default dilution schemes and decision criteria for turbidity and anticipated densities to ensure consistency.

[P4] This provision places the burden of predicting "expected organism density" on reporting labs without guidance; ask for validation guidance or conservatively broad dilution ranges to avoid over/under enumeration.

[P5] Allowing parallel multiple-tube tests "should" be interpreted as mandatory when MF was used on problematic samples to demonstrate applicability; industry requests that this be changed from discretionary ("should") to either mandatory or removed to avoid inconsistent practice. (or) Conversely, small labs request that "should" remain discretionary to avoid excessive workload.

[P5] Requiring parallel multiple-tube tests on historically problematic samples could double testing costs and turnaround times; request that the rule require parallel testing only when specific risk indicators are met (e.g., turbidity > X NTU, chlorine residual > Y mg/L).

[P6] The 25-parallel-test minimum and the <10% false-positive/false-negative threshold for substituting lactose broth are arbitrary; ask for justification and statistical basis, and propose alternative performance criteria based on confidence intervals or accepted validation standards.

[P6] Small or municipal labs may not be able to conduct 25 parallel tests (resource and sample availability constraints); request allowance for pooled inter-lab validation data or use of published equivalency studies in lieu of in-house 25 tests.

[P6] The restriction that lactose broth may only substitute LTB after meeting the 25-test standard could prevent use of more sustainable or locally available media; request provision for provisional approval with ongoing verification and reporting.

[P7] Forwarding all presumptive coliform tubes/bottles showing any gas, growth, or acidity for 9221F–2014 analysis could create excessive workload and cost for high-volume labs; request thresholds (e.g., amount of gas or growth) or risk-based prioritization.

[P7] The requirement presumes availability of method 9221F–2014 capacity; labs without accreditation for that method would be forced to send samples out, increasing turnaround time—request allowance for equivalent confirmatory methods when validated.

[P8] Mandating enumeration using multiple-tube or multiple-well procedures excludes membrane filter and other validated enumeration techniques; ask the agency to explicitly permit MF enumeration where appropriate and validated.

[P9] The obligation to "report the Most Probable Number (MPN)" when using multiple-tube procedures should specify rounding rules, significant figures, and how to report counts when beyond the test range (e.g., >2400); request reporting guidance to ensure uniform data.

[P9] The phrasing "appropriate tube and dilution configuration" is vague; request that the agency publish recommended configurations for typical concentration ranges and sample types to reduce inter-lab variability.

[P10] Requiring incubation of Colilert-18® at 44.5 ± 0.2 °C in a water-bath incubator is overly prescriptive—many labs use incubators with forced-air or calibrated dry block systems that maintain equivalent temperature accuracy; request allowance for validated alternative incubators with performance verification.

[P10] The ±0.2 °C tolerance is tighter than typical laboratory temperature control capabilities and may be impractical; propose widening to ±0.5 °C or tying tolerance to demonstrated method performance.

[P11] The monthly verification of at least ten blue colonies with LTB and EC broth may be burdensome for small laboratories that have few positive samples; request proportional requirements (e.g., verify all positives if <10 positives/month) or allow aggregation over longer periods.

[P11] Adjusting counts based on verification results requires clear statistical rules (e.g., when to apply correction factors); request explicit algorithms or examples to ensure consistent application.

[P11] The requirement references specific broths (LTB and EC) without allowing equivalent media that are validated; propose permitting equivalent media if equivalency is demonstrated and documented.

[P12] The suggestion that representative non-blue colonies "should" be verified in LTB needs clarity on what "representative" means; request defined selection criteria (randomization, proportion) to prevent biased verification.

[P13] Encouraging randomized sample sources for verifications is good practice but could be logistically difficult for routine monitoring with limited sample variety; ask for guidance on implementable randomization methods or acceptable alternatives (systematic selection).

[P14] Monthly verification of ten sheen colonies using LTB and brilliant green lactose bile is similarly burdensome and may be infeasible in months with few positives; request proportional verification schemes or alternate schedules tied to sample volume.

[P14] The requirement to "adjust counts based on verification results" must specify error propagation and reporting formats; without guidance this could produce inconsistent regulatory reporting.

[P15] The permission to verify non-sheen colonies with LTB should be expanded to allow other validated media or rapid confirmation technologies (e.g., MALDI-TOF, qPCR) as optional verification when equivalency is shown.

[P16] The "where possible" qualifier on randomized sources is too vague—stakeholders ask for clear minimum standards for randomization or acceptable deterministic selection rules to ensure audits can assess compliance.

[P17] Requiring all coliform-positive MF samples to be subjected to 9222I–2015 using NA–MUG media may be redundant when other confirmatory tests (e.g., chromogenic substrates or molecular assays) have equivalent sensitivity and specificity; request explicit allowance of validated alternative confirmatory methods.

[P17] The mandate to perform 9222I–2015 on all MF-positive samples will increase turnaround time and lab costs; request that confirmation be required only when regulatory decisions depend on the confirmation (e.g., exceedance of limit) rather than for every positive.

[P17] NA–MUG media can be costly and have supply chain limitations; request allowance for temporary use of equivalent media during shortages, with mandatory documentation.

[P18] Making incubation of BHI agar at 10 ± 0.5 °C optional is reasonable, but the rule should specify when optional verification is recommended (e.g., specific organism suspicion) to avoid inconsistent use across labs.

[P18] If optional verifications are used, the rule should require documentation of the rationale and results to support any discrepancies in reported counts; request adding a recordkeeping requirement for optional methods used.

[P1] The establishment of R‑2206A without accompanying justification or environmental analysis fails to explain the operational need and potential impacts on local aviation and should be withdrawn or supported with a detailed rationale.

[P2] The lateral boundary points for R‑2206A (beginning at lat. 64°19′44″ N, long. 149°15′42″ W to 64°19′44″ N, long. 149°10′18″ W and the described 100‑foot offset) are imprecisely described (incomplete sentence at “thence south, 100 feet west of and parallel to…”) and must be corrected to full, standard legal descriptions before finalization.

[P3] Designating R‑2206A from the surface to 8,800 ft MSL will effectively close significant airspace used by general aviation, air taxis, and medevac helicopters; the proposal lacks analysis of alternate routes and the burden on air ambulance response times.

[P4] Continuous time designation for R‑2206A (24/7) is overly broad; the agency should limit the designation to specific operating windows or provide mitigation (e.g., procedures for civil aircraft transit when activity is not occurring).

[P5] Designating FAA Anchorage ARTCC as the sole controlling agency for all R‑2206 areas could create single‑point coordination bottlenecks; the rule should specify coordination procedures, frequencies, and contingency handoff procedures to local ATC and Clear AFB when ARTCC is overloaded.

[P6] Designating the Commander 13th Missile Warning Squadron as using agency for R‑2206A without specifying the types of activities (e.g., missile defense tests, training) lacks transparency; public and environmental stakeholders need specificity on activities contemplated.

[P7] The creation of R‑2206B (new) without an explanation of overlap with existing R‑2206A raises concerns about redundant or unnecessary restrictions; the rule should justify the need for a separate adjacent restricted area.

[P8] The listed lateral boundaries for R‑2206B (beginning at lat. 64°20′13″ N, long. 149°13′12″ W through multiple points) appear to create complex non‑contiguous polygons; the FAA should provide clear maps and machine‑readable coordinate tables to avoid misinterpretation by pilots.

[P9] Excluding portions of R‑2206B wholly within R‑2206A (P9) creates confusing nested exclusions; the regulation should explicitly describe how pilots and ATC determine which restriction applies at a given location and altitude.

[P10] Setting R‑2206B vertical limits from 1,000 ft MSL to but not including 1,600 ft MSL creates a gap below 1,000 ft and between 1,600 ft and adjacent areas with different altitudes that could pose safety risks for VFR traffic; the FAA must analyze low‑level traffic patterns and ensure safe transition corridors.

[P11] Continuous designation of R‑2206B (P11) for altitudes 1,000–1,600 ft MSL will effectively ban low‑level local operations, including aerial surveying, agricultural flights, and emergency operations; exemptions or streamlined access procedures are needed for medevac, law enforcement, and life‑saving flights.

[P12] Assigning FAA Anchorage ARTCC as controlling agency for R‑2206B (P12) without specifying local communication frequencies or procedures for aircraft on short final or in the traffic pattern will create operational conflicts at Clear and surrounding airports.

[P13] Naming the Commander 13th Missile Warning Squadron as using agency for R‑2206B (P13) while R‑2206B excludes portions in R‑2206A suggests the Squadron operates in overlapping jurisdictions; clarify command and control and delegated authority between ARTCC and the Squadron.

[P14] The new R‑2206C establishment lacks justification and environmental review for airspace up to 32,000 ft MSL, which could affect overflight routes, fuel burn, and airline operations; provide an airspace efficiency analysis.

[P15] The lateral boundaries for R‑2206C defined by a 4.0 NM arc centered at lat. 64°20′22″ N, long. 149°11′2 (incomplete seconds) are missing full coordinate precision and must be corrected; incomplete coordinates render the regulation legally defective.

[P16] Excluding portions of R‑2206C wholly within R‑2206A (P16) creates a complex vertical/lateral mosaic that will be difficult for flight planning systems to depict; require publication of precise boundaries in ENR charts and digital databases (e.g., FAA ASRI).

[P17] Establishing R‑2206C altitudes from 1,600 ft MSL to 32,000 ft MSL will conflict with en route airway usage and could force airliners to alter filed routings; request a traffic impact study showing rerouting costs and emissions consequences.

[P18] Continuous designation of R‑2206C (P18) covering 1,600–32,000 ft MSL eliminates flexibility for civil flights; propose limiting continuous designation to necessary hours or providing a simple application/coordination process for transit.

[P19] Designating FAA Anchorage ARTCC as controlling agency for R‑2206C (P19) should include detailed NOTAM and coordination procedures for civilian aircraft requesting transit, including expected response times and contact points.

[P20] The Commander 13th Missile Warning Squadron as using agency for R‑2206C (P20) must commit to deconfliction procedures with civilian air traffic and to provide advance schedules of activities to FAA for publication to reduce flight disruptions.

[P21] The proposed R‑2206D establishment lacks an operational rationale that justifies its discrete patterned schedule (0200–0400 Tue/Thu/Sat); the FAA should explain why only those times are necessary.

[P22] The lateral boundaries for R‑2206D (beginning at lat. 64°20′13″ N, long. 149°13′12″ W with a 3.0 NM arc centered at 64°17′20″ N) include references that appear truncated; provide full coordinates and clarify whether arcs cross public highways and private property.

[P23] Excluding portions of R‑2206D wholly within R‑2206A (P23) without a clear depiction increases complexity for pilots performing low‑altitude operations at night (the 0200–0400 time span), potentially increasing risk.

[P24] Setting R‑2206D altitudes at 1,000 ft to but not including 1,600 ft MSL (P24) during 0200–0400 will restrict helicopter EMS and law enforcement night operations; specify an emergency access procedure that does not impose undue delay.

[P25] Designating R‑2206D only during 0200–0400 Tue/Thu/Sat (P25) but permitting designation at other times by NOTAM (P26) creates operational uncertainty; stakeholders need assurance that NOTAM activations will follow predictable criteria and minimum advance notice.

[P26] Allowing R‑2206D designation by NOTAM at unspecified times (P26) lacks standards for how much advance notice is required and whether short‑notice activations will be coordinated with local airports and emergency services; require minimum NOTAM lead times and coordination protocols.

[P27] FAA Anchorage ARTCC as controlling agency for R‑2206D (P27) should publish the specific frequencies and call signs to be used during NOTAM activations and the procedures for rapid coordination with Clear AFB operations.

[P28] Naming the Commander 13th Missile Warning Squadron as using agency for R‑2206D (P28) while the area is intermittently active raises questions about liability and responsibility in the event of an incident; clarify legal responsibilities and indemnities.

[P29] The creation of R‑2206E (new) without a quantified assessment of impacts on local airspace capacity and commercial operations is arbitrary; the FAA must include an aeronautical study showing no adverse effects.

[P30] The lateral boundaries for R‑2206E using a 4.0 NM arc centered at lat. 64°20′22″ N, long. 149°11′2 (incomplete seconds) are not fully specified in the proposal and must be corrected to full seconds and datum.

[P31] Excluding portions of R‑2206E that are fully inside R‑2206A (P31) will make charting and flight planning systems difficult to implement; require the FAA to supply digital boundary files and include these changes in FAA flight information publications well ahead of effective date.

[P32] Setting R‑2206E altitudes from 1,600 ft to but not including 2,100 ft MSL (P32) will affect low‑altitude practice areas, banner towing, and aerial work; the FAA should provide an exemption process for commercial aerial work with safety constraints.

[P33] Limiting R‑2206E active times to 0200–0400 Tue/Thu/Sat (P33) but allowing NOTAM activations (P34) repeats the earlier uncertainty problem; require predictable scheduling, shared calendars with local operators, and advance NOTAM timing standards.

[P34] FAA Anchorage ARTCC as controlling agency for R‑2206E (P35) must ensure coordination with local VFR pilots and flight schools that operate in the area during daytime; even if the area is mostly night‑time, transits and training flights need safe deconfliction protocols.

[P35] Naming the Commander 13th Missile Warning Squadron as using agency for R‑2206E (P36) should be accompanied by an operations safety assessment including mitigation of potential collisions with civilian traffic.

[P36] The proposed R‑2206F boundaries referencing Highway 3 and 4.0 NM arcs (P38) may implicate surface landowners and public roads; the FAA should clarify whether ground activities will affect highways and include an outreach plan to local authorities.

[P37] R‑2206F vertical limits from 2,100 ft to 3,200 ft MSL (P39) create a mid‑altitude block that overlaps with approach/departure profiles of nearby airports; the FAA must provide instrument procedure revalidation and ensure no degradation of airport access.

[P38] Designating R‑2206F only 0200–0400 Tue/Thu/Sat (P40) but permitting NOTAM activation at other times (P41) again raises timing unpredictability that could hamper scheduled airline and air taxi ops; require a NOTAM activation window and minimum notice.

[P39] FAA Anchorage ARTCC as the controlling agency for R‑2206F (P42) must ensure controllers have training and tools to manage dynamic activations across many contiguous restricted areas (R‑2206A–G) to prevent airspace deconfliction errors.

[P40] Command of using agency (Commander 13th Missile Warning Squadron) for R‑2206F (P43) requires a memorandum of agreement (MOA) with FAA Anchorage ARTCC outlining activation procedures, responsibilities, and risk mitigation; this MOA should be published or summarized in the rulemaking record.

[P41] Establishing R‑2206G (new) as continuous up to 32,000 ft MSL (P48,P49) will restrict en route altitudes for commercial and cargo flights; the FAA must include an economic impact assessment estimating increased fuel costs and delays.

[P42] The lateral boundaries for R‑2206G (4.0 NM arc centered at 64°20′22″ N, long. 149°11′2—P45) again contain truncated coordinates; the FAA must provide precise coordinates and the datum (NAD83/WGS84) to ensure consistent charting.

[P43] Excluding portions of R‑2206G wholly within both R‑2206A and R‑2206F (P46–P47) creates overlapping carve‑outs that will complicate flight planning systems and ATC display tools; require that digital boundary datasets indicate precedence and include visualization tools for stakeholders.

[P44] Continuous designation of R‑2206G covering 2,100 ft to 32,000 ft (P48–P49) likely eliminates normal military/civil shared use of the airspace; FAA should analyze whether scheduling R‑2206G for discrete times would minimize civil impact while preserving mission needs.

[P45] Assigning FAA Anchorage ARTCC as controlling agency for R‑2206G (P50) without specifying coordination with adjacent ARTCCs, military approach controls, and local flight service stations risks boundary coordination problems; include interagency coordination procedures in the rule.

[P46] The repeated incomplete coordinate notations across provisions (P2, P15, P22, P30, P38, P45) render the entire rule text ambiguous and legally deficient; the FAA must publish corrected full coordinates with degrees, minutes, seconds, and datum before seeking public comment closure.

[P47] The rule lacks any environmental assessment (NEPA) or statement of categorical exclusion regarding noise, wildlife (including migratory birds), subsistence hunting, and land use impacts for the Clear, AK area; request that the agency prepare an EA or EIS.

[P48] The proposed rule does not include procedures for emergency or lifesaving flights (air ambulances, fire suppression, law enforcement) to obtain immediate access to the restricted areas; require an expedited coordination and approval mechanism with guaranteed response times.

[P49] The cumulative effect of seven new/modified restricted areas (R‑2206A–G) around Clear, AK likely degrades airspace capacity and economic activity in the Fairbanks/Clear region; ask the FAA to prepare a regional airspace capacity and economic impact study.

[P50] The rule does not address how civil unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) operators should comply with these restricted areas; require explicit guidance on UAS operations, waivers, and enforcement.

The lateral boundary points for R‑2206A (beginning at lat. 64°19′44″ N, long. 149°15′42″ W to 64°19′44″ N, long. 149°10′18″ W and the described 100‑foot offset) are imprecisely described (incomplete sentence at “thence south, 100 feet west of and parallel to…”) and must be corrected to full, standard legal descriptions before finalization.

Designating R‑2206A from the surface to 8,800 ft MSL will effectively close significant airspace used by general aviation, air taxis, and medevac helicopters; the proposal lacks analysis of alternate routes and the burden on air ambulance response times.

Continuous time designation for R‑2206A (24/7) is overly broad; the agency should limit the designation to specific operating windows or provide mitigation (e.g., procedures for civil aircraft transit when activity is not occurring).

Designating FAA Anchorage ARTCC as the sole controlling agency for all R‑2206 areas could create single‑point coordination bottlenecks; the rule should specify coordination procedures, frequencies, and contingency handoff procedures to local ATC and Clear AFB when ARTCC is overloaded.

Designating the Commander 13th Missile Warning Squadron as using agency for R‑2206A without specifying the types of activities (e.g., missile defense tests, training) lacks transparency; public and environmental stakeholders need specificity on activities contemplated.

The creation of R‑2206B (new) without an explanation of overlap with existing R‑2206A raises concerns about redundant or unnecessary restrictions; the rule should justify the need for a separate adjacent restricted area.

The listed lateral boundaries for R‑2206B (beginning at lat. 64°20′13″ N, long. 149°13′12″ W through multiple points) appear to create complex non‑contiguous polygons; the FAA should provide clear maps and machine‑readable coordinate tables to avoid misinterpretation by pilots.

Excluding portions of R‑2206B wholly within R‑2206A (P9) creates confusing nested exclusions; the regulation should explicitly describe how pilots and ATC determine which restriction applies at a given location and altitude.

Setting R‑2206B vertical limits from 1,000 ft MSL to but not including 1,600 ft MSL creates a gap below 1,000 ft and between 1,600 ft and adjacent areas with different altitudes that could pose safety risks for VFR traffic; the FAA must analyze low‑level traffic patterns and ensure safe transition corridors.

Continuous designation of R‑2206B (P11) for altitudes 1,000–1,600 ft MSL will effectively ban low‑level local operations, including aerial surveying, agricultural flights, and emergency operations; exemptions or streamlined access procedures are needed for medevac, law enforcement, and life‑saving flights.

Assigning FAA Anchorage ARTCC as controlling agency for R‑2206B (P12) without specifying local communication frequencies or procedures for aircraft on short final or in the traffic pattern will create operational conflicts at Clear and surrounding airports.

Naming the Commander 13th Missile Warning Squadron as using agency for R‑2206B (P13) while R‑2206B excludes portions in R‑2206A suggests the Squadron operates in overlapping jurisdictions; clarify command and control and delegated authority between ARTCC and the Squadron.

The new R‑2206C establishment lacks justification and environmental review for airspace up to 32,000 ft MSL, which could affect overflight routes, fuel burn, and airline operations; provide an airspace efficiency analysis.

The lateral boundaries for R‑2206C defined by a 4.0 NM arc centered at lat. 64°20′22″ N, long. 149°11′2 (incomplete seconds) are missing full coordinate precision and must be corrected; incomplete coordinates render the regulation legally defective.

Excluding portions of R‑2206C wholly within R‑2206A (P16) creates a complex vertical/lateral mosaic that will be difficult for flight planning systems to depict; require publication of precise boundaries in ENR charts and digital databases (e.g., FAA ASRI).

The Commander 13th Missile Warning Squadron as using agency for R‑2206C (P20) must commit to deconfliction procedures with civilian air traffic and to provide advance schedules of activities to FAA for publication to reduce flight disruptions.
