raw_output:
[P1] The deadline of January 8, 2018 is unreasonably short given the complexity of issues raised by the Humane Society decision and stakeholders should be granted an extension of at least 60 days to prepare meaningful comments.

[P1] The rule's statement "accept comments received or postmarked by January 8, 2018" creates confusion about receipt versus postmark; the agency should clarify whether electronically submitted comments must be received by that date rather than merely postmarked.

[P2] The ADDRESSES provision listing a limited set of submission methods omits commonly used channels (e.g., email) and thus restricts public participation; NMFS/FWS should explicitly allow email submissions.

[P3] The physical mail/hand-delivery address for FWS comments (Public Comments Processing, ATTN: FWS–R6–ES–2017–0089, 5275 Leesburg Pike) may be inaccessible to rural or disabled commenters during the comment period; the agency should provide alternative in-person options or outreach.

[P3] The address listing truncates the city/state line ("Falls") and could confuse mail carriers; the rule should provide the full postal address including city, state, ZIP code to ensure delivery.

[P4] Requiring commenters to follow docket submission instructions on regulations.gov without summarizing essential steps in the Federal Register notice imposes an unnecessary barrier for less-savvy users; the agency should include brief step-by-step instructions in the notice.

[P5] The reference to the Federal Relay Service number is necessary, but the rule should also provide contact options for non-telephonic accommodations (e.g., email or TTY) to support persons with disabilities.

[P6] The promise to notify conclusions by March 31, 2018 is vague about the form of notification; the agency should commit to publishing a detailed response-to-comments document and final rule preamble by that date.

[P6] The March 31, 2018 target for responding to comments is unrealistic given the expected volume and complexity; the agency should not bind itself to that date or should explain contingency procedures if delayed.

[P7] The statement that the agency will consider all comments received by the specified date should clarify whether duplicate or form-letter submissions will be given equal weight to individualized technical comments.

[P8] Requiring submission by one of the listed methods (ADDRESSES) effectively prohibits late-filed or supplemental materials; the agency should allow supplemental submissions during administrative review if they are clearly marked.

[P9] The prohibition on considering comments sent by email or fax is arbitrary and may exclude substantive feedback from organizations that rely on email; the agency should accept email/fax submissions or explain why they are insecure/unacceptable.

[P10] Posting entire comments including personal identifying information to regulations.gov without redaction will chill public participation; the agency must provide a clear, easy mechanism to submit anonymous or redacted comments online.

[P11] Allowing requests to withhold personal identifying information only for hardcopy comments creates an unequal treatment between submission methods; the same withholding option should be available for electronic commenters.

[P12] The caveat that the Service "cannot guarantee" it will honor withholding requests is insufficient; the agency should detail the legal standard and circumstances under which identifying information might be disclosed.

[P13] The obligation to post all hardcopy comments on regulations.gov appears to contradict the privacy-protection option in P11; the agency must clarify how withheld identifying information will be treated when posting.

[P14] Making received comments available "online or by appointment" during normal business hours may disadvantage non-local stakeholders; the agency should offer a downloadable archive and extended access hours.

[P15] Inviting written comments only on how the Humane Society decision may affect the GYE grizzly bear final rule narrows the scope of comment and may preclude relevant adjacent issues (e.g., management mechanisms, monitoring); the agency should accept broader comments related to delisting decisions.

[P16] The limitation requesting comments "only on the issues raised in the preceding paragraph" unlawfully restricts public comment under the Administrative Procedure Act, which requires agencies to consider relevant comments beyond narrowly framed questions.

[P17] NMFS's separate January 8, 2018 deadline should be harmonized with the FWS deadline and clearly state whether joint or cross-agency comments will be accepted under both dockets.

[P18] NMFS's instruction to identify comments by docket number NOAA–NMFS–2017–0128 lacks cross-reference to the FWS docket and may create confusion for commenters addressing both agencies; the agencies should provide joint docket guidance.

[P19] Requiring all electronic comments to be submitted via regulations.gov (for NMFS) and not permitting other electronic channels is unnecessarily restrictive and risks excluding stakeholders with technical difficulties; the agency should allow email backups or provide technical support.

[P20] The proposed biennial catch limit applying to U.S. commercial fishing vessels in 2017 and 2018 lacks specificity about the actual numeric limit and geographic scope; NMFS must disclose the catch limit value, species covered, and management area used to justify trip limits.

[P21] The proposed 1-metric-ton trip limit for most vessels and 2-metric-ton limit for large-mesh drift gillnet vessels are arbitrary without supporting analysis of catch data, economic impacts, or bycatch consequences; NMFS must provide the data and modeling supporting these thresholds.

[P21] Applying a 2-mt trip limit specifically to large-mesh drift gillnet vessels while imposing 1-mt on others may be discriminatory absent demonstrated differences in gear capability; NMFS should justify the exception with operational evidence.

[P22] A flat 1-mt trip limit for "most vessels" fails to account for vessel size, gear types, and trip duration variability; NMFS should consider tiered limits or effort-based measures instead of a single-weight threshold.

[P23] The exception granting 2-mt to large-mesh drift gillnet vessels could incentivize gear-switching or concealment of vessel type; enforcement mechanisms must be described to prevent abuse.

[P24] Limiting trip limits "throughout 2018 or until the catch limit is reached and the fishery is closed" creates abrupt closures that could strand product or cause economic disruption; the agency should propose phased reductions, notice requirements, and grace periods for supply chains.

[P24] The rule does not specify the process, timing, or notification method for closing the fishery once the catch limit is reached; NMFS must commit to clear, real-time closure notices and protocols for observers and processors.

[P20] The application of a biennial limit covering 2017 and 2018 raises retroactivity concerns for fishing that already occurred in 2017; NMFS should clarify whether the 2017 portion will be applied retroactively or only prospectively.

[P8] Requiring supporting materials to be submitted by one of the listed methods (ADDRESSES) and not accepting large data files via email may impede submission of large datasets; NMFS should provide an FTP or data-upload mechanism for voluminous attachments.

[P10] The statement that entire comments will be posted on regulations.gov truncates mid-sentence ("will be posted on the Web s"); the agency must correct typographical errors to avoid ambiguity about public posting.

[P11] The option to request withholding of personal identifying information only applies to hardcopy submissions; the agency should explicitly instruct electronic commenters on how to request confidentiality and how such requests will be processed.

[P12] The claim that the Service "may be unable to honor" withholding requests is vague—legal standards (e.g., FOIA exemptions) determine disclosure; the agency should cite applicable statutes and FOIA exemptions that govern potential disclosure.

[P13] Posting all hardcopy comments online may result in dissemination of sensitive business information or proprietary data; the agency should allow redaction or confidential treatment for legitimately sensitive commercial information.

[P15] Soliciting comments on the Humane Society decision's impact on the GYE delisting without providing the decision text or a summary hinders meaningful comment; the agency should include the court decision and its legal analysis in the docket.

[P16] By restricting comments to only the issues raised about the Humane Society decision (P15), the agencies risk ignoring substantive scientific or socioeconomic concerns unrelated to that decision; the agencies should explicitly state they will consider other relevant issues.

[P17] NMFS's requirement that comments be "in writing" excludes oral comments from stakeholders who cannot submit written materials; the agency should provide procedures for submitting and transcribing oral comments or public hearings.

[P9] The rule's outright refusal to consider emailed comments is procedurally arbitrary and may be inconsistent with prior practice; the agencies should either accept email comments or explain the technical or legal rationale for exclusion.

[P21] The effective-through-2018 phrasing for the trip limits fails to specify whether the limits apply to trips that start in 2018 but land in 2019; NMFS should clarify trip attribution rules for multi-day or multi-calendar trips.

[P22] The proposed trip limits do not explain how they interact with state quotas, IFQs, or sector allocations; NMFS must describe coordination with existing state and federal management programs to avoid double-counting or conflicting limits.

[P23] The distinction for "large-mesh drift gillnet vessels" requires a clear definition (mesh size, target species, vessel characteristics); without a precise definition enforcement and compliance will be problematic.

[P14] Making comments available "by appointment, during normal business hours" for inspection does not accommodate stakeholders in other time zones or those with limited resources; the agency should extend hours or provide remote access.

[P6] The commitment to address comments by March 31, 2018 should include a schedule for interim updates if complex legal questions (e.g., court remand effects) delay the process.

[P20] The statement that "U.S. commercial fishing vessels are subject to a biennial limit for 2017 and 2018" must specify whether non-U.S. or charter/recreational vessels are affected; the scope of applicability should be clarified.

[P21] NMFS must provide an economic impact analysis estimating revenue loss, employment effects, and downstream processor impacts of the 1-mt/2-mt trip limits as required by the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

[P23] Granting a higher limit to large-mesh drift gillnet vessels may undermine bycatch reduction goals for protected species; NMFS must provide species-specific bycatch projections informing the exception.

[P10] Regulations.gov posts often strip attachments or render datasets unreadable; the agency should ensure attachments remain accessible and provide alternative access methods for large data files.

[P1] The May 22, 2023 comment deadline is unreasonably short; stakeholders such as foreign operators and public interest groups need a longer period (minimum 60–90 days) to prepare substantive technical and economic comments.

[P1] The rule should explicitly state whether late comments will be considered or how the FAA will handle supplemental information submitted after May 22, 2023, to avoid uncertainty for international operators gathering data.

[P2] The applicability to “all” Boeing 777–200/200LR/300/300ER/777F without differentiation by serial number, configuration, or operator flight hours is overbroad; the FAA should limit the AD to affected serial/production blocks or provide damage/failure criteria so unaffected airplanes are not unduly burdened.

[P2] The AD’s applicability to “certificated in any category” may unintentionally include special categories (e.g., government, corporate VIP, and cargo conversions); the FAA should clarify whether converted freighters or special mission derivatives are included and supply tailored compliance options.

[P3] The requirement to “comply within the compliance times specified” lacks clarity on whether compliance times are calendar days, flight cycles, or flight hours; the FAA must explicitly specify units and how to calculate elapsed time.

[P3] The AD should include relief for aircraft in storage or inactive fleets that cannot practically meet short compliance times, including provisions for extension or phased scheduling tied to return-to-service.

[P4] Requiring strict adherence to the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin except as specified in paragraph (h) risks importing non-mandatory manufacturer guidance wholesale into the AD; the FAA should identify any deviations or non-mandatory steps to avoid confusion.

[P4] The AD should incorporate by reference the exact Revision number and date of the Boeing Requirements Bulletin in paragraph (g) to ensure operators use the correct revision and avoid inconsistent compliance.

[P5] Replacing the bulletin’s “original issue date” with the AD effective date could shift compliance deadlines unexpectedly; operators need a clear rationale and an example showing how compliance times change under this substitution.

[P5] The rule should specify whether uses of “effective date” mean the FAA’s Federal Register publication date or the AD’s stated effective date in the regulatory text to prevent differing interpretations across jurisdictions.

[P6] Granting credit for actions done under the earlier bulletin revision is appropriate, but the AD should require documentation standards (e.g., work order references, part numbers) to prove prior compliance and avoid disputes during inspections.

[P6] The credit provision should explicitly state whether credit applies to corrective actions performed under non-U.S. approved alternative procedures, and whether foreign-approved equivalent documents will be accepted.

[P7] The prohibition on installing affected TE flap transmission or gearbox assemblies after the AD effective date is reasonable for safety, but the list of affected part numbers in the Appendix must be complete and verifiable; otherwise, operators cannot determine compliance.

[P7] The AD must clarify whether installations performed by third-party vendors overseas are subject to the prohibition and how operators should handle parts currently in logistics pipelines awaiting installation.

[P8] Allowing installation only if the assembly has been inspected and corrective actions completed requires clarity on who may perform the inspection and whether shop inspections (off-airframe) meet the requirement.

[P8] The AD should define acceptable non-destructive inspection techniques and minimum acceptance criteria for corrective actions to reduce differing interpretations by maintenance providers.

[P9] Centralizing AMOC authority with the Seattle ACO Manager may slow processing for non-U.S. operators; the FAA should state processing time expectations and whether delegated field approval is acceptable in urgent cases.

[P10] The requirement to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or Flight Standards Office may be problematic for operators lacking a domestic principal inspector (e.g., foreign carriers); the AD should provide an explicit path for foreign operators to submit AMOC requests.

[P11] Direct submission to the certification office manager requires naming the specific contact in paragraph (l), but the proposed text omits that name; the AD should include the named manager/contact to avoid misrouting.

[P12] Allowing AMOC information via email to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is helpful, but the AD should confirm whether encrypted or secure transmission is required for sensitive attachments and whether large data sets are accepted.

[P13] Requiring notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC could be impractical for airlines operating across multiple jurisdictions and bases; the AD should allow notification within a reasonable period after use (e.g., 72 hours) where prior notice is operationally infeasible.

[P13] The AD should specify the required content of the notification to the principal inspector (e.g., AMOC approval reference, affected tail numbers, and scheduled use dates) to ensure consistent recordkeeping.

[P14] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to be used raises potential conflict-of-interest concerns; the FAA should require independent oversight or secondary FAA verification for ODA approvals used to comply with this AD.

[P14] The AD must define the documentation required to demonstrate that a Boeing ODA-approved AMOC provides an “acceptable level of safety” and confirm whether those approvals will be posted or otherwise publicly available for transparency.

[P15] Requiring that repair/modification methods meet the airplane’s certification basis could impede novel fixes; the FAA should describe how equivalent safety findings will be assessed when the proposed fix was not envisioned in the original certification basis.

[P15] The AD should clarify how to handle situations where applying an AMOC would alter the certification basis (e.g., change airworthiness limitation requirements) and whether a separate certification action is required.

[P16] Mandating the use of specified service information “unless the AD states otherwise” implies that only the listed Boeing documents are acceptable; the AD should permit FAA- or EASA-approved alternative documents if they provide equivalent instructions.

[P16] The AD should specify revision levels and effective dates for each referenced Boeing service document to prevent ambiguity about which document version satisfies the requirement.

[P17] The contact information for obtaining service information is Boeing-centric and may create access delays for non-U.S. operators; the FAA should require Boeing to provide digital download access or airworthiness mail distribution procedures to expedite global compliance.

[P17] The AD should require that Boeing supply any required parts or replacement assemblies in a timely manner and disclose anticipated lead times to allow operators to plan compliance actions.

[P18] Stating that the service information may be viewed at the FAA Des Moines office is insufficient for international stakeholders; the FAA should provide online access or a public docket link to the exact documents referenced.

[P18] The AD should confirm whether viewing the service information at the FAA office constitutes permission to copy or reproduce the documents for in-house maintenance planning.

[P19] While NARA availability is useful, the AD should also provide direct electronic references or public docket numbers for the incorporated-by-reference documents so operators can verify requirements without NARA visits.

[P19] The rule must clarify which specific pages, figures, and tables are incorporated by reference and whether any non-incorporated parts of the Boeing bulletin are merely advisory and not mandatory under the AD.

[P1] The June 22, 2020 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonable and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow operators, suppliers, and airworthiness reps sufficient time to analyze the technical AWLs and prepare substantive responses.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether electronically postmarked comments submitted on June 22, 2020 but received by FAA systems after midnight will be accepted; as written § 39.13(a) creates uncertainty about time zone and submission method.

[P2] The phrase "unless already done" in § 39.13(f) is vague; commenters request that FAA define what record evidence constitutes proof that an action is "already done" (e.g., specific work orders, SB compliance tags, or logbook entries).

[P2] Operators seek clarification that compliance-time calculations in § 39.13(f) are based on the AD effective date, not the FAA publication date, and request worked examples for mixed-fleet transitions.

[P3] The 60‑day deadline in § 39.13(g) to revise maintenance/inspection programs is impractically short for large operators and MROs that must coordinate changes company‑wide; commenters recommend extending to 180 days or providing a phased implementation schedule.

[P3] The rule should require FAA to provide a template or sample maintenance program revision package for § 39.13(g) to ensure consistent and auditable incorporation of the specified Boeing AWL information.

[P4] The 120‑month interval in § 39.13(g)(1) for AWL No. 28–AWL–01 may be too long from a safety standpoint for certain wire degradation modes; safety advocacy groups request FAA to justify the 120‑month interval with failure‑rate data or shorten it.

[P4] Conversely, industry comments may state that 120 months after original certification is burdensome for older, hard‑to‑access wire bundles and request allowance for longer intervals with risk‑based justification.

[P5] For AWL No. 28–AWL–03 in § 39.13(g)(2), commenters request clarification whether the 120‑month clock resets after any partial inspection or only after the specific FQIS wiring inspection called out in the AD.

[P6] The 12‑month requirement in § 39.13(g)(3) for AWL No. 28–AWL–19 is ambiguous where service bulletin actions referenced are deferred; request explicit guidance on how the "whichever is latest" rule interacts with approved SB compliance extensions.

[P6] Maintenance unions and technicians request detailed procedural acceptability guidance for performing the AWL No. 28–AWL–19 tests (tools, test parameters, pass/fail criteria) rather than only mandating incorporation into programs via § 39.13(g)(3).

[P7] The exception in § 39.13(g)(3) referencing prior compliance with paragraph (s) of AD 2011–18–03 should require operators to furnish traceable records proving prior compliance; otherwise, ambiguity could lead to inconsistent application.

[P8] The 12‑month interval in § 39.13(g)(4) for AWL No. 28–AWL–20 may not be feasible for operators with limited maintenance downtime; request allowance to perform the actions at the next scheduled heavy maintenance check within a specified maximum window.

[P9] The § 39.13(g)(4) exception referencing AD 2011–20–07 paragraph (g)(2)(ii) should explicitly state how an operator documents eligibility for the operational test waiver to avoid post‑hoc disputes during inspections.

[P10] The 12‑month deadline for AWL No. 28–AWL–23 in § 39.13(g)(5) could conflict with other mandated ADs with overlapping shop visits; operators request that FAA permit consolidation of tasks and coordinated extensions consistent with safety.

[P11] The non‑applicability clause in § 39.13(g)(5) tied to AD 2011–18–03 paragraph (s) requires cross‑referencing guidance that explains exact configuration states that qualify for the exception.

[P12] The 72‑month interval in § 39.13(g)(6) for AWL No. 28–AWL–24 might leave known lightning/fault vulnerabilities unmitigated too long; request FAA provide analysis supporting the 72‑month period or shorten it.

[P12] MRO service providers ask that § 39.13(g)(6) specify whether partial accomplishment of the referenced service bulletin starts the 72‑month clock, and how to treat replaced components with new serial numbers.

[P13] For § 39.13(g)(7) requiring service bulletin actions for L/N 1–1754 within 120 months, operators request clarity whether "L/N 1–1754" is inclusive/exclusive of line number 1754 and how to handle airplanes with re‑numbered serials or production changes.

[P14] The dual compliance timing in § 39.13(g)(7) for L/N 1755 and subsequent (120 months or 48 months after AD effective date) is confusing; operators request precise examples of when the 48‑month option applies and how to calculate the later of the two.

[P15] The requirement in § 39.13(g)(8) to perform AWL No. 28–AWL–35 within 120 months after a service bulletin for airplanes that incorporated that SB should allow credit for equivalent alterations done under PMA or prior AMOC approvals; request explicit credit language.

[P16] The BITE test requirement in § 39.13(g)(9) (within 750 flight hours) for L/Ns 6987 and 7000 may create operational disruptions; airlines request flexibility to perform the test within 750 flight hours OR a specified calendar time (e.g., 90 days) to accommodate low‑utilization aircraft.

[P16] Avionics suppliers note that the BITE test interval in § 39.13(g)(9) should specify severity thresholds and data retention requirements for BITE failure records to ensure consistent follow‑up actions.

[P17] The long interval of 22,500 flight hours for AWL No. 47–AWL–04 in § 39.13(g)(10) may be too infrequent to detect thermal switch degradation; commenters request condition‑based monitoring alternatives and clear replacement criteria.

[P18] For AWL No. 47–AWL–06 in § 39.13(g)(11) with a 13,000 flight‑hour interval, operators request clarification whether flight hours are total aircraft time or flight cycles for mixed‑operation fleets.

[P19] The 6,500 flight‑hour interval in § 39.13(g)(12) for AWL No. 47–AWL–07 is inconsistent with other NGS checks; NGS manufacturers recommend harmonizing intervals (flight hours vs. calendar months) and providing risk analysis.

[P20] For AWL No. 47–AWL–09 in § 39.13(g)(13) the replacement thresholds based on flight hours/time should include explicit provisions for curtailed utilization (e.g., aircraft in storage) to avoid unintended expirations.

[P21] The operational test interval of 7,500 flight hours or 36 months (whichever is first) in § 39.13(g)(14) for AWL No. 28–AWL–101 may force frequent shop visits for high‑utilization aircraft; request an option to perform the test at the next scheduled heavy check if within a small window (e.g., 500 FH).

[P22] The optional changes allowed under § 39.13(h) (paragraphs (h)(1) and (h)(2)) should be expanded to include other commonly accepted wire and sleeving alternatives certified by major civil standards, not limited to the listed military/SAE types and brand names.

[P23] The allowance in § 39.13(h)(1) to use MIL‑W‑22759/16 and SAE AS22759 wire types as alternatives to BMS types must be accompanied by qualification criteria (temperature rating, insulation thickness) so operators can confirm equivalence without seeking AMOCs.

[P23] Wire manufacturers request that § 39.13(h)(1) include acceptance criteria and reference test methods (e.g., RTCA/DO, SAE) for the listed military/SAE wires to avoid inconsistent field substitutions.

[P24] The sleeving alternatives in § 39.13(h)(2) (Roundit 2000NX and Varglas) are narrow and brand‑specific; commenters recommend replacing brand names with material performance specifications to allow qualified equivalent products.

[P28] The blanket termination in § 39.13(j)(2) of all requirements of AD 2008–10–10 R1 may have unintended consequences for aircraft that only partially complied; request FAA to require an equivalency assessment before termination.

The rule should clarify whether electronically postmarked comments submitted on June 22, 2020 but received by FAA systems after midnight will be accepted; as written § 39.13(a) creates uncertainty about time zone and submission method.

Operators seek clarification that compliance-time calculations in § 39.13(f) are based on the AD effective date, not the FAA publication date, and request worked examples for mixed-fleet transitions.

The 60‑day deadline in § 39.13(g) to revise maintenance/inspection programs is impractically short for large operators and MROs that must coordinate changes company‑wide; commenters recommend extending to 180 days or providing a phased implementation schedule.

The rule should require FAA to provide a template or sample maintenance program revision package for § 39.13(g) to ensure consistent and auditable incorporation of the specified Boeing AWL information.

The 12‑month interval in § 39.13(g)(4) for AWL No. 28–AWL–20 may not be feasible for operators with limited maintenance downtime; request allowance to perform the actions at the next scheduled heavy maintenance check within a specified maximum window.

The § 39.13(g)(4) exception referencing AD 2011–20–07 paragraph (g)(2)(ii) should explicitly state how an operator documents eligibility for the operational test waiver to avoid post‑hoc disputes during inspections.

raw_output:
[P1] Commenters will request clarification on whether Table 17 grade limits apply to both domestic and import inspections, asking the agency to state explicitly that §800.86(c)(2) applies to all soybeans regardless of origin.

[P1] Industry stakeholders will argue Table 17 lacks methodology for measurement (sample size, sampling protocol, acceptable analytical methods) and request that the rule specify sampling procedures and tolerances to ensure reproducible grading.

[P2] Soybean processors will comment that the U.S. No. 1 damaged-kernel heat limit of 0.2% is overly stringent for current harvest/handling practices and will request raising the heat-damaged kernel breakpoint or providing a seasonal/region-specific adjustment.

[P2] Grain elevator operators will ask the agency to clarify whether the listed U.S. No. 1 “Total” 0.2 (presumably test weight or other metric) is a typographical error (duplicates “Damaged kernels (Total) 2.0”) and to correct ambiguous or inconsistent numeric entries in Table 17 and the regulatory text.

[P3] Farmers’ associations will object that the U.S. No. 2 foreign material maximum of 2.0% is ambiguous as to whether it includes dockage or field trash, and will request the definition of “foreign material” be cross-referenced or explicitly defined.

[P3] Exporters will request an appeals/reevaluation process for samples graded U.S. No. 2 due to small variations in damaged-kernel measurement and ask for defined laboratory proficiency requirements for graders assessing the heat-damaged kernel 0.5% breakpoint.

[P4] Commodity associations will comment that the U.S. No. 3 split limit of 30.0% will materially reduce the number of lots eligible for human food markets and request the agency add an allowance or exception for processing-grade soybeans destined for crushing/industrial uses.

[P4] Legal practitioners will note potential inconsistency between Table 17 and §810.1604 limits for U.S. No. 3 (both set splits at 30%), and will request reconciliation language to avoid conflicting interpretations between parts 800 and 810.

[P5] Small farmers will contend that allowing U.S. No. 4 foreign material up to 5.0% could mask safety hazards (glass, contaminated debris) and urge the agency to require that certain hazardous foreign material types automatically disqualify a lot regardless of percentage.

[P5] Public health advocates will request that the U.S. No. 4 damaged-kernel total limit of 8.0% be paired with mandatory testing for mycotoxins or other contaminants for lots graded U.S. No. 4, because higher damage correlates with safety risks.

[P6] Food-safety groups will urge clarifying whether purple mottled or stained beans that otherwise meet U.S. No. 2 numeric limits must nonetheless be downgraded to U.S. No. 3, and request objective thresholds (percent mottled/stained) rather than an unspecified visual standard.

[P6] Seed trade organizations will request a precise definition and measurement method for “purple mottled or stained” (e.g., percent of kernels affected, colorimetric standards) to prevent subjective downgrade by graders.

[P7] Crop advisors will request guidance on what constitutes “materially weathered” (e.g., visible cracking, weight loss percentage, moisture criteria) so producers can take appropriate post-harvest actions and avoid arbitrary downgrading to U.S. No. 4.

[P7] Commodity buyers will ask the agency to provide an appeals mechanism and sample photographic standards for “materially weathered” determinations to reduce inconsistent application across inspection offices.

[P8] Export-oriented traders will request confirmation that the 10.0% allowance for other colors in “yellow soybeans” applies per lot or per sample, and ask the agency to prescribe the sample size and counting method to determine the percent of other colors.

[P8] Specialty soybean growers will object that the 10.0% allowance for other colors undermines varietal purity claims for color-designated lots and will request an option for stricter certification for premium markets.

[P9] Seed certification bodies will request clarity on the exclusion of the hilum from seed coat color determination: specifically whether discoloration of the hilum-scar area adjacent to the coat is excluded, and whether colorimeter thresholds will be provided.

[P9] Laboratory standards organizations will ask the agency to include an explicit definition of “hilum” location/size and measurement guidelines to prevent inter-grader variability under §810.1602(a)(1).

[P10] Grain graders’ unions will request training requirements and proficiency testing for graders conducting determinations “based on the grain when free from foreign material,” since removing foreign material can change the proportional metrics drastically.

[P10] Legal commenters will point out potential circularity: if determinations are made on grain free from foreign material, but foreign material itself is a grade criterion, the rule should explain sequencing and whether dockage removal is permitted prior to grading.

[P11] Industry commenters will argue the phrase “grain as a whole” is vague and request examples and a list of determinations that are or are not covered, to avoid inconsistent treatment of attributes like moisture, odor, and varietal admixture.

[P11] Academic experts will request the agency publish a technical appendix defining “grain as a whole” and specify when metrics should be normalized to sample weight versus kernel count.

[P12] Commodity purchasers will request that §810.1604 explicitly cross-reference Table 17 or provide a consolidated table to remove duplication and potential inconsistencies between the two sections.

[P12] Auditors will ask for machine-automated measurement standards (e.g., calibrated optical sorters) to be recognized as acceptable methods for meeting the listed percent and count limits to modernize grading.

[P13] Processors will reiterate that the U.S. No. 1 foreign material 1.0% and split 10.0% limits are too restrictive for some regions and request allowance for processor-grade U.S. No. 1 when destined for crushing rather than food use.

[P13] Quality assurance managers will ask whether the U.S. No. 1 heat 0.2% and total damaged 2.0% limits apply on a per-lot basis or per sample, and request statistical acceptance criteria (AQL) for lot-level decisions.

[P14] Regional cooperatives will request modification that allows a buffer around the U.S. No. 2 split limit of 20.0% to account for measurement uncertainty, recommending +/- 1% or specification of counting error margins.

[P14] Export certification agencies will ask whether the U.S. No. 2 foreign material 2.0% includes prohibited seeds (e.g., noxious weeds) and request that the rule list materials that automatically disqualify regardless of percent.

[P15] Food-grade soy manufacturers will object to the U.S. No. 3 foreign material 3.0% and split 30.0% thresholds as permitting too much damage for human food products, and request a separate “food-grade” standard or label indicating suitability for food.

[P15] Statisticians will request that the rule specify rounding rules and reporting precision (e.g., two decimal places) for percent limits like damaged kernels 5.0% to avoid disputes over marginal samples.

[P16] Bulk carriers will request guidance on acceptable handling practices to avoid elevating splits to the U.S. No. 4 breakpoint (40.0%), and ask the agency to publish best-practice mitigation steps recognized in grading disputes.

[P16] Insurance companies will request that the agency clarify whether U.S. No. 4 thresholds trigger different loss-adjustment procedures and whether grades determined by private inspection services are admissible for claims.

[P17] Food-safety advocates will demand that items listed in maximum count limits (animal filth, castor beans, crotalaria seeds, glass) be treated as immediate safety red flags and not merely counted toward a total that could otherwise allow a lot to qualify.

[P17] Grain handlers will request clarification whether the “Total 10” other material limit is per sample or per 100 g (or other unit), and ask for a defined sample unit weight for count calculations.

[P18] Consumer advocates will ask for an expanded list of objectionable odors (beyond musty, sour) and for defined sensory thresholds (e.g., trained panel protocols) before a lot is assigned U.S. Sample grade under §810.1604(b).

[P18] Traders will request that the rule describe the remedies for lots graded U.S. Sample (e.g., reconditioning options, regrading intervals) to avoid de facto market exclusion without remediation pathways.

[P19] Grain processors will challenge the footnote that counts stones only if weight exceeds 0.1% of sample weight, arguing that many small stones cause equipment damage even below that weight threshold and requesting a separate equipment-safety threshold.

[P19] Scientific commenters will request that the agency specify the method for determining stone weight percentage (e.g., dried basis, as-received basis) to ensure consistent application of the 0.1% criterion.

[P20] Legal experts will note the footnote saying stone weight is not used in calculating total other material but is counted if above 0.1% creates inconsistency and ask the agency to explicitly describe the calculation steps and whether stones count toward the maximum count limits when over the weight threshold.

[P20] Grain safety advocates will request that glass and stones be treated separately from benign other material in total counts and propose that presence of glass always be an immediate disqualification regardless of the “total” calculation rules.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement that each operation selling or handling products represented as organic be certified (§205.100(a)) will impose undue cost and administrative burden on small-scale handlers who do minimal handling; recommend raising the exemption threshold or creating a micro-handler category.

[P1] Certification for “portion of an operation” is ambiguous and could force whole businesses to certify if a single employee or site handles organic product; clarify whether certification can be limited to discrete legal entities or physically separate facilities.

[P2] The introductory exemption (§205.101) states exempt operations must comply with subpart C and additional requirements, but the interplay between exemption status and full compliance obligations is unclear — request a plain-language matrix showing what exempt operations must and need not do.

[P3] Prohibiting exempt-operation products from being used as organic-identified ingredients in other handlers’ processed products (§205.101(a)) will disrupt existing supply chains (e.g., farmstands selling to local bakers); propose a limited-scope allowance with mandatory traceability for such transactions.

[P3] The ban in §205.101(a) could unfairly limit market access for small producers who sell to value-added processors; suggest permitting transfers to a certified handler with simple documentation rather than an absolute prohibition.

[P4] Requiring exempt operations to follow labeling provisions (§205.101(a) cross-ref §205.310) without the benefit of certifier guidance may lead to inconsistent labeling and enforcement; request USDA-provided labeling templates and training for exempt retailers and small producers.

[P5] The exemption for retail operations that only sell (not process) (§205.101(b)) should explicitly exclude online marketplaces that sell multiple sellers’ organic goods but do not process them — clarify applicability to e-commerce platforms and fulfillment centers.

[P6] Recordkeeping requirements for retail operations (§205.101(c)) to "prove organic origin and verify quantities" lack specificity on acceptable documentation (e.g., invoices, lot codes); request explicit examples and minimum data fields to reduce auditor discretion.

[P6] The burden of maintaining records sufficient to prove organic origin (§205.101(c)) for small retailers may be disproportionate; propose a simplified recordkeeping standard for businesses below a threshold annual revenue or volume.

[P7] Handling operations exempted under §205.101(d) are still required to comply with §§205.305 and 205.310 and maintain records — unclear whether cross-contamination prevention and handling protocols in §205.305 are fully applicable; ask USDA to clarify the scope of §205.305 for exempt handlers.

[P8] The exemption for storage/receiving/loading-only facilities (§205.101(e)) may still require certification under other provisions (e.g., if they commingle products) — request guidance on when passive storage triggers certification.

[P9] The 3-year record retention requirement (§205.101(f)) for exempt operations should be aligned with state business record requirements to avoid duplication; propose allowing shorter retention for microbusinesses or permitting digital retention in accepted formats.

[P10] The obligation for certified operations to fully disclose activities and transactions in auditable records (§205.103(b)(2)) is necessary but the proposed rule lacks clear standards for “sufficient detail”; recommend standardized record formats or minimum data elements.

[P11] Requiring audit trail documentation (§205.103(b)(3)) for every product handled could be duplicative where INTEGRITY already stores traceability data — request cross-recognition of INTEGRITY records to avoid redundant recordkeeping.

[P12] OSP monitoring practices requirement (§205.201(a)(3)) that mandates frequency and fraud-prevention measures is appropriate, but the rule should provide risk-based minimum frequencies or allow certifiers to approve alternative monitoring schedules.

[P13] Grower group OSP internal control system requirement (§205.201(c)) is comprehensive but may be overly prescriptive for small grower groups; propose scalable requirements tied to group size and complexity.

[P14] Requiring grower groups to define organizational structure and personnel roles (§205.201(c)(1)) is reasonable, but many informal cooperatives lack formal job titles — allow use of role descriptions rather than formal job descriptions.

[P15] Mandating identification of production unit locations (§205.201(c)(2)) may raise privacy and security concerns for independent growers; allow address obfuscation for public records while providing full locations confidentially to certifiers.

[P16] The geographical proximity criteria (§205.201(c)(3)) could exclude legitimate grower group members who farm in noncontiguous plots (common for leased land); recommend allowing flexible proximity definitions based on practical logistics rather than strict distance.

[P17] Requiring groups to describe characteristics that identify high-risk members (§205.201(c)(4)) may cause stigmatization and legal risks; request clear, objective criteria examples to prevent arbitrary profiling.

[P18] Requiring detailed description of shared production practices and inputs (§205.201(c)(5)) may force disclosure of proprietary supplier relationships; allow confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive information while ensuring certifier access.

[P19] The monitoring, surveillance, and auditing methods (§205.201(c)(6)) for grower groups should permit use of remote auditing, sampling, and statistical methods; ask AMS to provide acceptable audit methodologies and sample size calculators.

[P20] Sanctions and removal procedures (§205.201(c)(7)) must include due process protections, appeals procedures, and minimum notice periods; request explicit requirements to protect members’ legal rights.

[P21] Conflict-of-interest protections (§205.201(c)(8)) are essential, but the rule should define prohibited relationships and provide examples of acceptable mitigation measures to ensure consistent application.

[P22] The requirement to explain procurement and distribution of training/inputs to members (§205.201(c)(9)) may effectively force grower groups to act as centralized suppliers, which some groups cannot manage; request allowance for decentralized procurement with verification mechanisms.

[P23] Policies/procedures to verify member compliance (§205.201(c)(10)) should permit third-party verification and reciprocal recognition of equivalent certifier audits to reduce duplication.

[P24] The catch-all for additional Administrator-required terms (§205.201(c)(11)) is overbroad and could lead to unilateral imposition of unforeseeable obligations; request that any additional terms be subject to notice-and-comment rulemaking or specified criteria.

[P25] The import certification and labeling obligations (§205.273 intro) may slow trade if foreign certifiers lack timely access to INTEGRITY; request phased implementation and technical assistance to foreign certifiers.

[P26] Requiring exporters to request NOP Import Certificates for each physical shipment before export (§205.273(a)) could delay shipments due to time zone and processing constraints; recommend allowing issuance within a defined pre-export window (e.g., 7 days) or batch certificates for scheduled shipments.

[P27] Restricting NOP Import Certificates to USDA-accredited or authorized foreign certifiers (§205.273(a) permission) is appropriate but must include a clear process and timeline for foreign certifiers to seek authorization to avoid market disruption.

[P28] The 30-calendar-day review/issuance deadline for certifying agents (§205.273(b)) may be unworkable during peak seasons; propose a shorter target for routine shipments and an extended timeline for complex cases, with explicit consequences for missed deadlines.

[P29] Requiring uploading of NOP Import Certificates into ACE to declare organic (§205.273(c)) assumes all importers have ACE access and technical capacity; request alternative submission methods for small importers and technical support.

[P30] The importer-of-record verification duties (§205.273(d)) to verify no exposure to prohibited substances or ionizing radiation since export may be impossible to verify practically; propose that verification rely on certifier attestations and shipment seals rather than physical testing unless there is credible suspicion.

[P31] Requiring foreign-produced products for U.S. sale to be certified under subpart E and comply with §205.273 (§205.300(c)) may duplicate equivalence arrangements; clarify how this interacts with equivalence determinations (§205.511).

[P32] The blanket prohibition on processing organic products with ionizing radiation (§205.301(f)(2)) is consistent with consumer expectations but enforcement needs defined testing protocols for processors claiming no radiation was used.

[P33] The prohibition on using sewage sludge (§205.301(f)(3)) is clear; request guidance on acceptable fertilizers that may contain biosolids derivatives and testing thresholds.

[P34] The formula for calculating percent organic ingredients by weight excluding water/salt (§205.302(a)(1)) will disadvantage manufacturers of some processed foods (e.g., soups) — request worked examples for complex formulations and clarification on ingredient moisture basis (as-is vs. dry).

[P35] The liquid-volume calculation (§205.302(a)(2)) for liquids and concentrates could produce inconsistent results across certifiers; request standardized conversion factors for concentrates and clear rules for emulsions/suspensions.

[P36] The mixed-product calculation (§205.302(a)(3)) lacks direction on density conversions when combining solids and liquids; ask USDA to mandate use of specific gravities or provide conversion tables.

[P37] The nonretail container labeling requirement (§205.307(a)) is necessary for traceability but the mandated information (certifier statement, lot/shipping identification) should accommodate space-limited containers (e.g., small drums); allow use of affixed tags or accompanying shipping documents.

[P38] Permission to display handling instructions, USDA seal, producer/contact info on nonretail containers (§205.307(b)) is helpful but §205.311 restrictions on the seal need harmonization to avoid conflicting guidance.

[P39] Any use of the USDA seal on nonretail containers must comply with §205.311 (§205.307(b)(2)) — request clear technical specifications (size, color, placement) to avoid rejection at ports.

[P40] Allowing export-only labeling on shipping containers (§205.307(c)) if clearly marked and records maintained is reasonable, but the requirement to maintain proof per §205.101 may be burdensome; suggest a streamlined digital attestation system linked to INTEGRITY.

[P41] Requiring certifier certificates to be generated from INTEGRITY (§205.404(b)) will improve standardization but raises concerns about system reliability, downtime, and data portability; request contingency procedures and exportable certificate formats.

[P42] Permitting certifier addenda (§205.404(c)) is useful, but limitations on addenda expiration (not to exceed certificate expiration) may create administrative complexity; allow addenda with their own limited validity where justified.

[P43] Annual fee payment and reporting requirements to maintain certification (§205.406(a)) could disproportionately impact small operations; recommend fee scales based on operation size and minimize redundant reporting by leveraging INTEGRITY-stored data.

[P44] Mandating at least one on-site inspection per calendar year (§205.406(b)) is costly for remote producers and may be redundant for low-risk operations; propose risk-based inspection frequency allowing remote or hybrid inspections for low-risk certs.

[P45] The grower group inspection statistical sample requirement (at least 1.4×√N) (§205.403(a)(2)) is mathematically precise but may be onerous for large N; ask USDA to publish sample-size tables and allow stratified sampling and risk-based adjustments.

[P46] Requiring certifiers to conduct unannounced inspections of at least 5% of operations annually (§205.403(b)(1)) is important for integrity, but raising unannounced inspection minimums increases travel and labor costs; propose using risk-based criteria to select the 5% and allow remote surveillance technologies to supplement.

[P47] Certifying agents being required to be able to conduct unannounced inspections and to not certify operations in areas where they cannot (§205.403(b)(2)) could restrict market access in remote regions; recommend allowing partnerships with locally accredited inspection contractors subject to certifier oversight.

[P48] Inspection verification that quantities produced/purchased account for organic product sold (§205.403(d)(4)) is critical; request defined tolerances for minor variances (e.g., shrinkage, sampling loss) and acceptable reconciliation methods.

[P49] Traceability verification requirements (§205.403(d)(5)) could be satisfied by digital ledgers and INTEGRITY references; ask AMS to accept blockchain or equivalent systems and provide interoperability standards.

[P50] Certifying agents must continuously employ sufficient qualified personnel (§205.501(a)(4)) — require clarification on how “sufficient” is measured (caseload ratios, inspector-to-client ratios) to ensure consistent enforcement across certifiers.

[P51] The requirement for inspectors to maintain up-to-date knowledge of current USDA organic standards (§205.501(a)(4)(i)(A)) is appropriate, but AMS should supply standardized curricula and update notifications to ensure uniform competency.

[P52] The 20-hour minimum initial and annual training requirement for inspectors (§205.501(a)(4)(i)(B)) may be insufficient for complex scopes (multi-country, processing facilities); allow scope-adjusted training hours and require competency assessments, not just hours.

[P53] Requiring inspectors to have at least 1 year of field-based experience before assignments (§205.501(a)(4)(i)(C)) could limit certifier capacity; allow supervised apprenticeship inspections counted toward the experience requirement.

[P54] Certification reviewers’ training and experience requirements (§205.501(a)(4)(ii)) are essential but the rule should include recognition of equivalent professional credentials to avoid unnecessary retraining.

[P55] The 20-hour training requirement for certification review personnel (§205.501(a)(4)(ii)(B)) should permit blended learning and on-the-job modules; request AMS accreditation of private training providers.

[P56] Certifiers must maintain training procedures and records (§205.501(a)(4)(iii)) — request clarity on record retention timeframes and acceptable record formats (electronic signatures, LMS exports).

[P57] Demonstrating expertise for inspection/review personnel (§205.501(5)) needs objective criteria (degrees, certificates, years of experience) to prevent subjective certification decisions.

[P58] Annual performance evaluations and on-site observation at least once every three years (§205.501(6)) are reasonable, but the rule must define who qualifies as “qualified personnel” to conduct evaluations and acceptable evaluation metrics.

[P59] The confidentiality obligation (§205.501(10)) is important; however, the carve-outs for public disclosure and enforcement require clear boundaries and a process for client notice before disclosure.

[P60] Requiring certifiers to accept certification decisions by other USDA-accredited certifiers (§205.501(13)) promotes market fluidity, but there must be mechanisms for resolving disputes where certifiers disagree about scope or interpretation.

[P61] Maintaining current and accurate data in INTEGRITY (§205.501(15)) may impose IT burdens on smaller certifiers; request technical support, phased deadlines, and exemptions where data migration is in process.

[P62] Annual risk-based supply chain audits back to source (§205.501(21)) are a strong integrity measure, but certifiers need clear guidance on audit depth, acceptable documentation, and the frequency for different risk categories.

[P63] The 90-day notification requirement for beginning certification activities in a new office (§205.501(22)) is practicable but should allow retroactive notification where business exigencies caused delay; provide standardized notification templates.

[P64] Requiring applicants to submit procedures for sharing information and maintaining confidentiality (§205.504(b)(4)) is sensible; request sample procedures and confidentiality agreement templates to expedite accreditation.

[P65] Applicants must provide criteria to identify high-risk operations and procedures to report credible organic fraud (§205.504(b)(7)); request AMS-provided risk indicators and a secure reporting portal to standardize submissions.

[P66] Allowing foreign products to be certified by USDA-accredited certifiers (§205.511(a)) is beneficial, but AMS must ensure accredited certifiers have capacity and local presence to perform adequate oversight.

[P67] The process for countries to request equivalence (§205.511(b)) requires transparent timelines and published minimum technical documentation to avoid prolonged uncertainty for exporters.

[P68] AMS reviews of equivalence scope on a two-year cycle and reassessments every five years (§205.511(c)-(d)) may be resource-intensive for foreign systems; request risk-based review frequency or mutual recognition of competent foreign oversight to reduce burden.

[P69] AMS authority to terminate equivalence determinations (§205.511(e)) is necessary but should be coupled with a remediation process and transition period to prevent abrupt market exclusion.

[P70] The Program Manager’s authority to initiate enforcement for implying organic status when produced/handled in violation (§205.660(c)) should include notice and opportunity to cure for inadvertent labeling errors before formal enforcement.

[P71] The requirement to update INTEGRITY within 3 business days of suspension/revocation (§205.662(e)(3)) is reasonable, but certifiers need clear guidance on confirmation and electronic acknowledgement procedures to ensure compliance.

[P72] Permitting suspended operations to request reinstatement (§205.662(f)(1)) is fair; ensure the rule specifies documentation needed for reinstatement and reasonable timelines for review.

[P73] Civil penalties for knowingly selling/labeling as organic contrary to the Act (§205.662(g)(1)) must be proportionate and consider factors like intent and volume; request a penalty schedule with mitigating and aggravating factors.

[P74] Requiring certifying agents to include mediation acceptance criteria and mediator selection processes in administrative policies (§205.663(a)) is constructive; provide model mediation procedures to ensure consistency across certifiers.

[P75] Allowing mediation for certification denial or proposed suspension (§205.663(b)) is positive, but the rule should protect confidentiality of mediation communications and specify whether mediation results are binding.

[P1] Requiring comments to be received by Sept 21, 2020 creates legal ambiguity for this notice — the agency must correct the docket dates or reissue the NPRM with an accurate, current comment deadline.

[P2] The AD's general compliance statement is overly rigid; operators request clarification that compliance times may be adjusted consistent with approved AMOCs when safety considerations warrant temporary relief.

[P3] Mandating installation of FCC OPS software P12.1.2 (P/N 2274–COL–AC2–26) on both FCC A and B before further flight lacks allowance for staged installations during overnight maintenance windows; request permission to schedule install within a specified number of flight cycles.

[P3] The provision should explicitly allow installation of "later FAA-approved software versions" only if listed in the AD or approved via AMOC; otherwise it is ambiguous which later versions qualify as approved.

[P3] Operators request that the AD include acceptable methods for software loading and verification (e.g., specific test procedures, checksum values, or tool versions) to ensure consistent compliance across vendors and MROs.

[P4] Requiring corrective actions before further flight if the P/N is not shown during verification is reasonable, but the AD should define acceptable corrective actions and who is authorized to perform them to avoid inconsistent and potentially unsafe fixes.

[P4] The AD should allow a temporary dispatch with operational limitations if software P/N verification fails by virtue of a false negative (display issue), provided an AMOC is approved — current wording prohibits any flight.

[P5] Requiring AFM revisions "prior to further flight" is operationally burdensome for large fleets; request allowance for fleetwide AFM amendments to be accomplished within a specified compliance window (e.g., 30 days or next scheduled maintenance), accompanied by a mandatory pilot briefing.

[P6] Removing text labeled 'Required by AD 2018–23–51' from the AFM could eliminate important safety guidance in use; request the FAA confirm that the removed text is obsolete and will be replaced elsewhere, or provide rationale and transitional instructions.

[P7] The AD mandates revising the AFM General paragraph to include figure 1 material but does not provide electronic AFM change packages; operators request the FAA provide approved text in machine-readable format to expedite incorporation and maintain standardization.

[P8] Replacing the Airspeed Unreliable procedure (figure 2) may conflict with airline standard operating procedures (SOPs) or CRM practices; operators request confirmation that the new procedure is harmonized with ICAO/FAA pilot training guidance and that pilot training allowances are provided.

[P9] The Runaway Stabilizer paragraph replacement (figure 3) may require additional pilot training and simulator currency; request that the FAA fund or allow a grace period for recurrent training before mandatory AFM adoption.

[P10] The Stabilizer Trim Inoperative replacement (figure 4) should include explicit cross-references to checklist items and MEL limitations; current text requirement is ambiguous and may lead to inconsistent application in emergencies.

[P11] Adding figure 5 to the Operating Procedures without specifying font, formatting, or page placement may cause AFM numbering conflicts; request guidance on integrating figures while maintaining AFM pagination and revision control.

[P12] Adding figure 6 and P13 adding figure 7 may duplicate procedures already mandated by other ADs or service bulletins; request the FAA to coordinate and confirm there are no conflicting AFM instructions.

[P14] Adding figure 8 to AFM procedures could conflict with foreign authority requirements (EASA, TCCA) — request confirmation that the text is acceptable internationally or guidance for operators under other regulators.

[P15] Inclusion of figure 9 in AFM Operating Procedures should be accompanied by a compliance-cost estimate for AFM revisions and crew training; operators need these estimates for budgeting.

[P16] Allowing dispatch of airplanes with modified flight control functions inoperative only if the MEL incorporates figure 10 provisions is acceptable, but the AD should clarify whether temporary deviations to MEL wording require AMOC or can be handled under the operator's approved MEL process.

[P16] The AD must specify whether the figure 10 MEL provisions require operator-specific FAA approval or if the figure constitutes a blanket acceptable MEL relief.

[P17] Requiring completion of all RC actions in Boeing SB 737–31–1860 before further flight may create supply-capacity bottlenecks; request the FAA define acceptable interim measures or prioritized actions if parts or qualified personnel are unavailable.

[P18] The requirement to do all RC actions in Boeing SB 737–27–1318, Revision 1 before further flight should be clarified to state whether previous compliance to earlier revisions is acceptable without additional work; cross-crediting language is needed.

[P19] Mandating the AOA Sensor System Test per Boeing SB 737–00–1028 as RC before further flight demands that test equipment, calibrated sensors, and trained personnel be available; request guidance on acceptable test equipment and authorization to use equivalent procedures under an operator’s approved maintenance program.

[P20] Requiring all RC actions for the Operational Readiness Flight after completing (g)–(l) before further flight raises a sequencing issue: the AD should explicitly allow scheduling the ORF immediately after maintenance without additional ferry permits (though (m)(1) says no permit required) and clarify who may perform and sign off the ORF.

[P21] The exception that no special flight permit is required for the Operational Readiness Flight is helpful, but the AD should still specify minimum pilot experience, equipment, and operational limitations for that flight to ensure safety.

[P22] The requirement to resolve mechanical irregularities found during the ORF per the operator’s FAA-approved maintenance/inspection program before further flight is vague — request that the AD require documentation of corrective actions in the aircraft logbook and specify acceptable turnaround times.

[P23] The permission for special flight permits under 14 CFR 21.197/21.199 to move aircraft to a location where AD actions can be done must be reconciled with (m)(1) which disallows special permits for the ORF; request clarity on when special permits are permitted versus the ORF exception.

[P24] Granting credit for actions performed using an earlier service bulletin is appropriate, but the AD should list the exact service bulletin revision/date accepted and the documentation required to prove prior compliance.

[P25] Allowing the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch to approve AMOCs centralizes authority; operators request an option to route AMOCs through local Flight Standards District Offices (FSDOs) to expedite approvals and reflect operational realities.

[P26] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or Flight Standards Office may delay response for international operators; request an explicit alternative submission pathway for non-U.S. operators or those with certificating authorities in other countries.

[P27] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC is redundant and could slow operations; request that notification be allowed within a short timeframe after first use (e.g., 48–72 hours) rather than prior, where prior notice is impractical.

[P28] Prohibiting previously approved AMOCs for AD 2018–23–51 from being used for this AD is arbitrary if those AMOCs already provide equivalent safety; request the FAA review and grandfather equivalent AMOCs or provide a streamlined re-approval process.

[P29] The requirement that all steps labeled 'RC' are mandatory, including substeps and figures, is appropriate but needs clarification on whether tolerances, allowable torque intervals, and calibration intervals specified in referenced Boeing figures are mandatory or guidance.

[P30] The carve-out for 'RC Exempt' steps is helpful, but the AD should require a clear, searchable list of which steps are RC Exempt to avoid misinterpretation during maintenance.

[P31] Requiring an AMOC for any deviation to RC steps may be impractical for urgent on-wing corrective maintenance; request that the AD permit limited, documented deviations under the operator’s approved maintenance program with post-facto AMOC submission in safety-critical emergencies.

[P32] Allowing deviation from non-RC steps under the operator’s program is reasonable, but the AD must require operators to maintain records demonstrating that RC steps remain achievable and that deviations did not compromise airworthiness.

[P33] The condition that deviations to non-RC steps are allowed only if RC steps remain achievable should include a standardized assessment form and criteria so inspectors can uniformly evaluate compliance.

[P3] Legal counsel will likely comment that the AD must state whether software P/N labeling on maintenance displays is the definitive evidence of compliance or whether additional verification (e.g., evidence in maintenance logs) is acceptable.

[P17] Maintenance providers will comment that Boeing Special Attention Service Bulletins contain proprietary methods and tooling; the AD should permit equivalent procedures performed under an operator’s approved maintenance program and provide a path to document equivalency.

[P5] Labor unions and pilot groups will request that any AFM changes that alter emergency procedures must be accompanied by mandatory training and minimum notification periods before the AFM becomes operationally effective.

[P16] Some operators will request that the MEL provisions in figure 10 be applicable as temporary operations relief pending full AFM changes, with clear timelines for when AFM revisions must be incorporated fleetwide.

[P18] International operators will request confirmation that compliance with Boeing SB 737–27–1318 Revision 1 satisfies parallel requirements from their State of Registry and that the FAA will coordinate with other authorities to avoid conflicting directives.

[P21] Safety advocates will request the FAA to specify conservative limitations (e.g., weather minima, daylight-only, two-pilot crew) for ORFs conducted without a special flight permit to mitigate risk.

[P4] Airlines will ask the FAA to provide an expedited supply chain or parts waiver process for cases where corrective actions require unavailable hardware, or allow temporary operational limitations until parts become available.

[P19] Operators will request that the AD include acceptable intervals and retest requirements for the AOA Sensor System Test, and clarify whether repetitive AOA testing is required after an initial pass.

[P25] Legal experts will comment that delegating AMOC authority solely to the Seattle ACO Manager may conflict with 14 CFR 39.19 practice in other districts and request codified timelines for AMOC response and appeal.

[P1] The provision stating that previously submitted comments need not be resubmitted is confusing; stakeholders should be instructed whether previously submitted comments will be treated as part of the reopened record for each species-specific rule or only for the general docket.

[P1] Conservation groups will object unless the agency confirms that previously submitted comments will be considered with equal weight as newly submitted comments and that no filtering will occur because of the reopening.

[P2] The July 13, 2017 receipt deadline is arbitrary and unduly short given the 30-day reopened comment period and should be extended to at least 60 days to allow meaningful input from states, tribes, and researchers.

[P2] Industry commenters will request clarification whether comments must be received by midnight Eastern Time on July 13, 2017, and ask for time-zone and timestamp rules to avoid inadvertent late rejections.

[P3] The phrase “listed methods” is vague; commenters request the agency explicitly confirm that attachments (large datasets, GIS files, videos) are acceptable via regulations.gov and provide maximum file size and accepted file formats.

[P4] The regulations.gov submission instruction lacks the specific docket number(s) for each species; commenters request the agency publish the exact docket numbers and step-by-step instructions to avoid misfiling.

[P5] The mail/hand-delivery address is truncated in the text; commenters request the complete street address, room number, and mailing codes so mailed comments are routed correctly and receive docket numbers.

[P6] The agency’s request that commenters use only the listed methods is effectively a prohibition on other modes of submission; NGOs and small organizations ask for explicit allowance of alternative submission methods in exceptional circumstances (e.g., FTP for very large datasets).

[P6] Legal commenters will point out that “we request” is nonbinding but could deter submission; they urge the agency to clarify the legal effect of using an unlisted method and confirm such comments will be accepted if received.

[P7] The statement that the agency will post “any personal information you provide” is overly broad; privacy advocates will demand the agency specify exactly which categories of personal information will be posted and to provide an option to redact home addresses while preserving the substantive comment.

[P8] Researchers submitting raw data and confidential location coordinates for rare species will object to the blanket availability of supporting documentation and request a mechanism to submit sensitive geolocation data under protected/confidential treatment while still informing the agency.

[P9] The acceptance of written comments during the reopened period for Guadalupe fescue should be clarified to state whether electronic, mailed, and in-person comments are equally acceptable, and whether previously submitted data specific to this species will be incorporated.

[P10] Taxonomic evidence submissions for Guadalupe fescue: botanists request that the agency specify the preferred types of taxonomic evidence (e.g., voucher specimens, genetic sequence data, peer-reviewed publications) and any formatting/citation requirements.

[P11] Commenters on Guadalupe fescue will request clear guidance on how to submit precise location data for additional populations while protecting sensitive locality information from public release to prevent poaching or habitat disturbance.

[P12] For life-history and habitat information for Guadalupe fescue, landowners and agencies ask whether observational data from private lands can be submitted and whether landowner consent statements are required.

[P13] The reopened comment period for Tobusch fishhook cactus must specify whether surveys conducted since the original comment period will be accepted as “new information” and whether there is any cutoff date for field data.

[P14] Taxonomic assertions for Tobusch fishhook cactus: botanical societies will request that the agency accept DNA barcoding and raw sequence submissions and define how such data will be archived and used.

[P15] Requests for additional location records for Tobusch fishhook cactus raise concerns from landowners about public posting; commenters request a secure submission process for sensitive location and landowner-identifying information.

[P16] For Tobusch fishhook cactus ecology/life-history data, academic researchers request that the agency specify preferred metadata standards and required sampling protocols for data to be considered in the listing analysis.

[P17] The reopened period for Kuenzler hedgehog cactus needs clarification on whether the agency will solicit and accept Indigenous or traditional ecological knowledge and how such submissions will be credited and used.

[P18] Taxonomic classification submissions for Kuenzler hedgehog cactus should include instructions on whether unpublished taxonomic treatments or museum specimen re-identifications will be accepted and how they will be validated.

[P19] Commenters will request that the agency provide a template for reporting historical and current status, range, and population size for Kuenzler hedgehog cactus to ensure consistency across submissions.

[P20] For Kuenzler hedgehog cactus life history and habitat information, grazing permittees and ranchers request guidance on how land management data (e.g., grazing intensity records) can be submitted and used without exposing proprietary business information.

[P21] The reopened comment period for gypsum wild-buckwheat should state whether state natural heritage database records and unpublished survey reports are acceptable as new information.

[P22] For gypsum wild-buckwheat taxonomic and conservation evidence, botanists ask the agency to clarify whether morphological versus genetic evidence will be weighted differently and to publish the criteria for evidentiary sufficiency.

[P23] Commenters will request a clear protocol for submitting additional population locations for gypsum wild-buckwheat that balances scientific usefulness with protection of sensitive locations.

[P24] For gypsum wild-buckwheat life-history and habitat submissions, mining companies want assurance that the agency will consider industry-conducted baseline ecological studies and that such studies will be evaluated using transparent standards.

[P25] The cross-reference that comments concerning any proposed rules can be submitted by the listed ADDRESSES needs to be explicit that species-specific attachments will be associated with the correct docket and not lost in a general docket.

[P26] The advisory that personal identifying information may be made public should instruct commenters on how to submit anonymized contact information and whether organizational affiliation (versus personal name) suffices for docketing.

[P27] Posting of entire comments including personal identifying information submitted via regulations.gov will deter participation; privacy advocates request an automatic option at submission time to redact contact details from the public docket while still allowing the agency to know commenter identity.

[P28] The agency’s statement that it may not be able to honor requests to withhold personal identifying information is insufficient; commenters ask the agency to publish the legal standards and process the agency will use to evaluate such withholding requests.

[P29] For mailed/hand-delivered comments, the agency should provide a required cover-sheet template to request withholding and declare what confidentiality markings will be accepted and how they will be processed.

[P30] The requirement to post hardcopy submissions electronically creates a risk of inadvertent dissemination of confidential attachments; commenters request that the agency accept redacted versions for public posting while retaining unredacted originals under confidentiality protocols.

[P31] The provision allowing Federal Relay Service TTY calls 24/7 should be supplemented with an email or live-chat accommodation option for people who cannot use TTY or the relay service, and the agency should confirm response times.

[P32] The obligation to confirm the correct rulemaking/docket before submission is reasonable but commenters request that the agency add clear instructions and links on the agency website to prevent misdirected comments and provide remedy if a comment is mistakenly filed in the wrong docket.

[P33] Reopening the comment period for 30 days may not provide meaningful opportunity for input given the amount of new information being solicited for multiple species; conservation organizations and state agencies will request an extension to 90 days or at least 60 days.
