raw_output:
[P1] The March 18, 2019 deadline is unreasonably short for affected stakeholders (local governments, industry, and NGOs) to prepare technically supported comments on the proposed Sheboygan designation split; EPA should extend the comment period by at least 30–60 days.

[P1] Litigation counsel: Strict enforcement of a hard March 18, 2019 receipt deadline without clear time-zone or postmark rules could deprive parties of meaningful participation; EPA should accept timely mailed comments postmarked by March 18, 2019 or extend the deadline.

[P2] Industry commenter: Requiring identification of Docket ID No. EPA–R05–OAR–2018–0035 and submission via Regulations.gov or to aburano.douglas@epa.gov is acceptable, but EPA should allow alternative electronic portals for large file attachments (e.g., FTP or secure portal) for modeling datasets.

[P2] Privacy advocacy group: Posting the email address aburano.douglas@epa.gov invites spam and may expose personal accounts; EPA should require use of a general docket email or form to protect staff privacy and manage submissions.

[P3] Small nonprofit: Regulations.gov instructions are sometimes unclear for first-time users; EPA must publish step-by-step guidance specific to these dockets (including attachment size limits and file types) and provide a help contact.

[P4] Civil liberties organization: The inability to edit or remove comments on Regulations.gov raises concerns about correcting personal data or inadvertent disclosures; EPA should allow comment withdrawal or redaction requests and provide a mechanism to correct factual errors.

[P4] Legal expert: The ban on editing/removing comments could chill participation if commenters cannot correct mistakes; EPA should state a formal process for retraction, correction, or supplementing a comment after submission.

[P5] Concerned resident: EPA saying it "may publish" comments to the public docket should be clarified—will personal contact information be redacted? EPA must commit to redacting personal identifying information before public posting.

[P5] Industry trade association: EPA's right to publish comments could inadvertently publish confidential commercial information. EPA should clarify how it will handle business proprietary information and provide a clear CBI claim procedure.

[P6] Business commenter: The prohibition on submitting CBI electronically is impractical for companies with large proprietary datasets; EPA should provide secure electronic methods (encrypted upload, secure portal) for CBI submissions or explicitly accept properly marked encrypted files.

[P6] Legal practitioner: The provision is truncated ("restr") and unclear—EPA must fully define what constitutes "otherwise restricted information" and provide notice of acceptable formats and secure submission procedures.

[P7] Media organization: Requiring a written comment to accompany multimedia submissions is reasonable, but EPA should specify acceptable written formats and whether transcripts suffice for audio/video.

[P7] Accessibility advocate: For deaf or visually impaired commenters submitting multimedia (e.g., video testimony), EPA must require and accept captions, transcripts, and alternative formats to ensure accessibility.

[P8] NGO: Declaring the written comment as "official" could disadvantage commenters who intended to submit detailed datasets or linked appendices; EPA should allow incorporation by reference of external materials (with stable URLs) and clarify how those will be considered.

[P8] Research institution: EPA's rule that the written comment is the official comment must allow attachments and data files to be part of the official submission; clarify how large data attachments will be indexed and preserved.

[P9] Technology firm: EPA saying it will "generally not consider" content located outside the primary submission disadvantages stakeholders who host large files externally; EPA should permit external data if the primary submission contains a clear reference and stable access instructions and explain indexing/accessibility.

[P9] Privacy advocate: The "general" exclusion is vague—EPA should explicitly state circumstances under which externally hosted materials will be accepted or rejected to avoid arbitrary exclusions.

[P10] Local government: The summary of designation duties under CAA 107(d)(1) is accurate but the preamble should specify the timelines and criteria EPA will use to act after states submit recommendations to ensure predictability for local planning.

[P11] State environmental agency: The obligation for states to submit area designation recommendations needs clarity about whether EPA expects supporting modeling, monitoring data, and public outreach documentation as part of the submission.

[P12] Environmental health NGO: The use of a 0.075 ppm three-year design value threshold to determine attainment is consistent with the NAAQS, but EPA must explain how background ozone and transport from upwind sources are accounted for in the attainment evaluation.

[P12] Industry: Relying solely on design values may misrepresent local conditions influenced by episodic events (wildfire, exceptional events); EPA should clarify how exceptional events will be excluded and how that affects attainment status.

[P13] Data submitter: Requiring collection and QA per 40 CFR part 58 and recording in AQS is appropriate; EPA must provide explicit deadlines for uploading finalized quality-assured data into AQS to ensure it is considered for this action.

[P13] State agency: EPA should publish any QA/QC flags or issues discovered during its review and allow a period for states to correct or explain data before final determinations.

[P14] Monitoring network operator: The data completeness requirement for the three-year period must include explicit rules for missing days due to monitor outages or site relocations and provide procedures for data substitution or continuity.

[P15] Technical commenter: The 90% average completeness over three years and 75% minimum in any single ozone season are overly rigid for rural or small monitors that suffer seasonal outages; EPA should permit documented exceptions or apply a statistical completeness adjustment.

[P15] Public health organization: Lowering the bar for completeness would undermine confidence in design values; EPA should retain the 90%/75% thresholds but provide transparent documentation of any exceptions.

[P16] Citizen group: EPA's refusal to finalize attainment if any monitor's design value exceeds the standard after proposal/finalization is appropriate to protect public health; however, EPA should clarify how soon after a change in design value it will act and how affected parties will be notified.

[P16] Industry: This provision creates uncertainty for local industry planning because design values can fluctuate; EPA should define the administrative process and timeline for revising determinations based on updated design values.

[P17] State planning agency: EPA conditioning finalization of the clean data determination on completing the split of the nonattainment area creates circularity and delays; EPA should provide a clear schedule and criteria for the "split" action and consider provisional finalization with contingency procedures.

[P17] Legal commenter: Holding the clean data determination pending a separate administrative split may exceed EPA's discretion or improperly conflate two distinct actions; EPA should explain the legal basis for linking the two actions.

[P18] WDNR (or state commenter): The obligation for WDNR to submit attainment demonstrations, RACM, RFP, contingency measures, and other requirements needs a clear schedule and guidance about scope, modeling methods, emission inventory expectations, and public process.

[P18] Industry/regulated sources: EPA should provide clarity on what constitutes "reasonably available control measures" (RACM) for the WDNR submittal and allow economic feasibility analyses to be considered.

[P19] Environmental NGO: Suspending WDNR's planning requirements only while the area continues to attain the NAAQS risks complacency; EPA should require periodic verification and a rapid reactivation trigger if air quality degrades.

[P19] State agency: The suspension of planning requirements contingent on continued attainment is useful to avoid unnecessary planning burden, but EPA must define "continues to attain" (e.g., rolling three-year design value) and the notification/monitoring triggers for resumption.

[P20] The March 18, 2019 comment deadline for the Chicago rule is identical to P1; EPA should consider a unified extended comment period for all related dockets (Sheboygan and Chicago) to facilitate coordinated stakeholder input.

[P21] Regional planning organization: Requiring docket identification EPA–R05–OAR–2016–0496 is fine, but EPA should ensure cross-referencing between the Sheboygan and Chicago dockets for related technical analyses (ozone transport, background levels).

[P22] State small business ombudsman: Regulations.gov instructions often lack clarity on submitting confidential business impact statements; EPA should publish a specific FAQ for small businesses on submitting comments for the Chicago rule.

[P23] Several commenters: The inability to edit/remove comments on Regulations.gov (Chicago rule) again raises concerns—EPA should allow a comment amendment/addendum process and permit deletion requests for inadvertently disclosed personal information.

[P24] Transparency NGO: EPA's intention to publish submitted comments in the public docket (Chicago rule) is welcome for transparency, but EPA should explain redaction practice for personal data and verify consent before posting attachments containing third-party data.

[P25] Trade association: As with Sheboygan, prohibiting electronic submission of CBI for the Chicago docket is impractical; EPA must offer a secure electronic CBI submission mechanism and clearly describe marking procedures.

[P26] Accessibility group: Requiring a written comment for multimedia (Chicago rule) is acceptable, but EPA should explicitly state that alternative formats (Braille, large print) will be accepted and provide contact information for assistance.

[P27] Legal aid clinic: Declaring the written comment the official comment may disadvantage oral commenters or those who submit group multimedia; EPA should accept incorporation by reference of recorded oral testimony where the written summary identifies the audio file in the primary submission.

[P28] IT firm: EPA's general refusal to consider materials located outside the primary submission (Chicago) could prevent consideration of large modeling datasets hosted in cloud repositories; EPA should define a process to accept external datasets (with persistent identifiers) and ensure long-term access.

[P1] The requirement to apply the subpart for the "predominant activity" on mixed-substrate web coating lines is vague and will create enforcement uncertainty: EPA should define how "predominant" is measured (by mass coated, line hours, revenue, or throughput) and provide a clear, auditable metric.

[P1] Industry requests an explicit allowance for separate compliance for discrete coating stations on the same web coating line that coat different substrates (paper vs fabric), because line-level application may force facilities to use the more stringent standard for unrelated operations.

[P2] Manufacturers of printing-incorporated web coating lines oppose allowing lines modified to include printing to remain under this subpart without clear criteria; EPA should specify what scope of printing activities (e.g., spot prints, full web printing, colors) qualify to remain under this subpart rather than triggering subpart KK.

[P2] Printers request a permission clarification: if a web coating line adds printing occasionally (seasonal or pilot runs), the facility must be able to stay under this subpart rather than being reclassified to subpart KK, provided printing constitutes less than X% of annual operations (EPA should set the threshold).

[P3] Environmental groups object to language requiring emission limits "at all times, including SSM" without granting monitoring flexibility during brief, documented malfunctions; they urge EPA to retain a limited SSM affirmative defense or specify what monitoring adjustments are allowed during unavoidable events.

[P3] Legal experts warn that requiring limits "at all times, including SSM" may conflict with CAA case law on SSM and petition for EPA to specify how deviations during malfunctions, maintenance, or startups will be treated in enforcement (e.g., allow reporting but not automatic violations when good-faith efforts are documented).

[P4] Oxidizer operators note the 20 ppmv outlet organic HAP requirement plus a 100% capture efficiency condition is technically impossible: capture efficiencies cannot be literally 100%; EPA should revise to a practicable numeric capture efficiency (e.g., ≥95%) or clarify that 100% means "all emissions routed to the control device."

[P4] Process engineers request that EPA provide testing and monitoring protocols when using an oxidizer to demonstrate compliance with the ≤20 ppmv outlet requirement, including averaging period, correction to 3% O2, and procedures for low-flow exhausts where Method 25A has limits.

[P5] Small businesses note the pre-effective-date provision that allows SSM exemptions before [DATE+180 days] is ambiguous; they request EPA confirm whether facilities may rely on prior timelines and whether initial reports for that period are required.

[P6] Community health advocates oppose eliminating any allowance for noncompliance during SSM on and after [DATE+180 days]; they urge phased implementation tied to demonstrated availability of reliable monitoring and control, not a hard immediate "at all times" obligation.

[P7] Testing laboratories and facility owners highlight that requiring an initial periodic performance test by [DATE+3 years] may be infeasible for large fleets due to testing backlog; they request staggered compliance schedules or extensions for smaller sources.

[P7] Industry commenters request EPA provide explicit procedures to request time-limited extensions for the initial periodic test when test labs or access to stack/trains are constrained, without treating extension requests as violations.

[P8] Trade associations object to the electronic-only submission requirement for initial notifications, semiannual reports, and test reports, citing small facilities with limited internet access; they request a waiver or alternative paper submission process for small entities or during system outages.

[P8] Environmental advocates support electronic reporting but ask EPA to require public availability of submitted semiannual compliance reports to improve transparency and community oversight.

[P9] Equipment vendors warn that requiring new affected sources to meet emission limits "at all times, including SSM" immediately at startup is infeasible when commissioning control devices requires tuning and optimization; they request a short initial startup period (e.g., 30–90 days) for optimization before strict enforcement.

[P9] Legal commenters note immediate full compliance at startup may conflict with NSPS precedent and request EPA add a limited initial compliance period or a requirement to demonstrate "good-faith" commissioning activities in lieu of immediate numeric compliance.

[P10] Stakeholders request clarity on the §63.7(a)(2) time limits referenced for initial performance testing: provide explicit calendar deadlines (e.g., within 180 days of startup) to avoid inconsistent state interpretations.

[P11] Trade groups request that electronic submittal requirements under § 63.3330(b)(3) include secure file transfer guidelines, acceptable file formats, and an appeals process for submissions rejected due to system errors.

[P12] Facility operators request EPA clarify which semiannual compliance report elements are required immediately after [DATE+180 days] and which may follow on the regular semiannual cycle; they also seek transition guidance for reporting periods that cross the effective date.

[P13] Commenters request consistency: the pre-effective-date language in § 63.3340(a) refers to [DATE 181 DAYS AFTER PUBLICATION] while other provisions use 180 days; EPA should correct the typographical inconsistency to avoid compliance confusion.

[P14] Compliance officers ask EPA to explicitly describe how to treat overlapping obligations that become effective after [DATE+180 days], for example which provision governs when multiple new obligations kick in simultaneously; suggest a phased or priority list.

[P15] Manufacturers of newly constructed sources after Sept 19, 2019 highlight that retroactive applicability language could be interpreted to impose newer standards without allowance; they request an affirmation that sources that started after Sept 19, 2019 but before final effective date had ample notice and should be eligible for relief or staged compliance.

[P16] Operators request more concrete examples of what constitutes "operate and maintain in a manner consistent with safety and good air pollution control practices" per §63.6(e)(1)(i), including acceptable maintenance logs and training requirements, to reduce subjective enforcement.

[P17] Unions and safety advocates support the "safety and good practices" requirement but ask EPA to require written standard operating procedures (SOPs) and periodic staff training documentation to demonstrate compliance with § 63.3340(b).

[P18] Testing firms request EPA to clarify the scope of §63.3340(c): whether subparts allow reduced testing frequency if CPMS data demonstrate continuous compliance, and how waivers under §63.7(h) will be evaluated.

[P19] Test labs point out the prohibition on testing during SSM and nonoperation could delay establishing a representative baseline if the line has frequent startups/shutdowns; they request guidance on selecting representative operating windows and aggregating data across runs.

[P20] Industry legal counsel request clarification on the prohibition to test during malfunctions: define "malfunction" and require that provable documented malfunctions allow for rescheduling without triggering enforcement action.

[P21] Operators note the requirement to record and explain why test conditions were "normal" is subjective; they request a checklist of recommended parameters (web speed, coating viscosity, solvent content, dryer setpoints, exhaust flow) to use as supporting documentation.

[P22] Operators request EPA to specify what records related to performance tests are subject to confidentiality claims and how proprietary formulation information used to justify normal conditions will be treated in public disclosures.

[P23] Testing stakeholders request clearer numeric definitions of "representative flow rate" and "representative inlet concentrations" for capture/control testing, or alternatively provide percent ranges (e.g., within ±10% of nominal operating points).

[P24] Industry requests both performance-testing prohibitions during malfunctions and specific definitions of unacceptable capture/control device malfunctions; they urge EPA to include an objective metric (e.g., hours of downtime vs operating hours) that triggers retest.

[P25] Operators ask for a list of process and control device operating data points that must be recorded during control device tests (e.g., exhaust flow, temperature, pressure drop, inlet VOC), to ensure consistent compliance demonstrations.

[P26] States and enforcement agencies request that EPA specify an electronic format or template for records that must be provided to the Administrator upon request, to streamline audits and reduce record production burdens.

[P27] Facilities with intermittently-controlled work stations request clarification of the timing and frequency of monitoring and inspections required "following" initial or periodic performance tests per §63.3350(b): specify when monitoring must commence and acceptable intervals.

[P28] Operators of intermittently-controlled lines note that monitoring bypasses and mass applied during bypass will require new instrumentation and high recordkeeping expense; request EPA provide a de minimis bypass mass threshold below which monitoring exceptions apply.

[P29] Industry groups request that EPA allow use of engineering estimates or production records to demonstrate bypassed coating materials were compliant under §63.3370(o)/(p) rather than requiring full analytical testing of each never-controlled coating.

[P30] Facilities object to the requirement to use one of the enumerated bypass monitoring methods for each work station; they request EPA allow alternative methods demonstrated equivalent by performance testing and approved by the Administrator.

[P31] Operators request clarification on the 90% valid data requirement: define how "operating hours" are counted (calendar hours, hours when coating is applied, or hours when dryer is on) and how planned downtime is treated.

[P31] Compliance consultants warn that reporting missing or invalid data as deviations in the semiannual report could turn routine calibration and maintenance into frequent reportable violations; they request allowed maintenance windows that are excluded from the 90% calculation.

[P32] Control device users request that §63.3350(e) provide a grandfathering clause for existing CPMS that meet equivalent performance criteria but may not meet every specified element; allow performance-based acceptance testing rather than prescriptive equipment lists.

[P33] CPMS vendors support the 90% valid data requirement but urge EPA to clarify acceptable causes of invalid data (e.g., calibration checks) and define the allowed duration for temporary CPMS outages without a deviation.

[P34] Monitoring engineers find the 3-hour block averaging rule requiring at least two valid hourly averages per block problematic for intermittent operations with short runs; they request EPA allow averaging methods that better reflect the operational reality (e.g., mass-weighted averages).

[P35] Laboratories and owners request EPA provide specific content guidance for the required quality control program under §63.8(d), particularly for CPMS performance evaluation frequency and acceptable corrective action timelines.

[P36] Industry requests that the requirement to keep written QC procedures for the life of the source be balanced with an allowance to purge truly obsolete superseded versions after a reasonable records retention period (e.g., 10 years) to reduce record-keeping burdens.

[P37] Operators object to retaining superseded performance evaluation plans for 5 years after each revision (in addition to life-of-source retention), as this multiplies record volume; request consolidation or index requirements instead of complete plan retention.

[P38] EPA should clarify whether inclusion of a corrective action program in the performance evaluation plan is mandatory or guidance; industry prefers optional but recommended status with suggested minimum elements.

[P39] Oxidizer owners request EPA add alternative monitoring approaches (e.g., measuring CO as proxy) where temperature monitoring is unreliable for catalytic oxidizers, or allow performance-based demonstrations when temperature sensors cannot be installed at the exact specified locations.

[P40] Oxidizer manufacturers request detailed manufacturer-specification criteria for calibration and operation of temperature monitors; quarterly calibration of chart recorders/data loggers may be overly burdensome for small oxidizers and should be extendable to semiannual if justified.

[P41] Non-catalytic oxidizer operators request clarity on the required sensor placement "in the combustion zone" given diverse oxidizer designs; EPA should allow placement at a representative location with rationale documented.

[P42] Catalytic oxidizer operators request explicit guidance on how to compute temperature rise across the catalyst, including acceptable sensor spacing when direct inlet/outlet sensor placement is obstructed.

[P43] Operators request that quarterly validation of temperature sensors allow alternative schedules (semiannual) if historical data demonstrates sensor stability and maintenance logs support less frequent validation.

[P44] Manufacturers support the NIST-traceable device validation option but ask for specific accuracy tolerances, test procedures, and acceptable instrumentation models to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P45] Facilities request permission to use manufacturer's in-manual validation procedures only if the manual is publicly available or provided to the permitting authority during review, to ensure methods are auditable.

[P46] Operators request EPA clarify the circumstances under which manufacturer certification/re-certification of thermocouple electrical properties is acceptable evidence of calibration, including acceptable certification content.

[P47] Some facilities propose quarterly replacement of sensors (option D) is wasteful; request EPA allow replacement only upon failure or nonconformance rather than as a validation method.

[P48] Operators caution that the redundant sensor method requiring readings within 25°F may be too lax for low-temperature catalytic oxidizers where smaller deltas matter; suggest specifying relative tolerance (e.g., ±5% of operating temp) instead of absolute 25°F.

[P49] Facilities request EPA clarify the triggers for recalibration/validation when sensors exceed manufacturer ranges and require documentation templates for demonstrating such events and subsequent checks.

[P50] Owners request more specific inspection checklists for quarterly oxidizer component inspections to ensure consistency across facilities and inspectors; suggest EPA publish a sample checklist.

[P51] Coating formulators and users request clear laboratory guidance for determining organic HAPs and retained volatile matter content to avoid inconsistent methods across vendors; suggest EPA adopt a single preferred analytical method or narrow the alternatives.

[P52] Control device operators request EPA clarify whether initial performance tests for destruction/removal and capture efficiency must be performed simultaneously or can be staged, and whether capture efficiency testing can be done via engineering calculations in specific cases.

[P53] Facilities operating non-recovery control devices object to five-year periodic testing—some operators recommend shorter intervals (e.g., every 3 years) to ensure ongoing performance, while others argue for performance-based intervals where CPMS demonstrates stability.

[P54] Operators applaud the performance testing exemptions in §63.3360(b) but request a standardized format to document they meet exemption criteria (e.g., CEMS specs, capture efficiency determination) to streamline audits.

[P55] Facilities seeking the CEMS exemption request EPA provide minimum performance specifications for the CEMS (detection limits, calibration frequency, QA/QC) and clear rules for demonstrating capture efficiency calculation compatibility with CEMS outputs.

[P56] Commenters request EPA clarify the §63.7(h) waiver process timeline and criteria so sources can reliably use the waiver exemption in §63.3360(b)(2) without extended uncertainty.

[P57] Facilities using solvent recovery systems want clearer guidance on what constitutes an acceptable monthly liquid-liquid material balance (accuracy, documentation, tolerances) for the §63.3360(b)(3) exemption.

[P58] Chemical manufacturers note the 0.1 mass percent threshold for including organic HAPs from Table 3 may miss low-concentration toxic HAPs that are nevertheless health-relevant; they ask EPA to include a hazard-based exception requiring reporting of any HAPs of concern regardless of mass percent.

[P59] Coating producers support allowing Method 24 or consensus ASTM standards but ask EPA to state which standard is preferred or default when results differ, and require that manufacturer-submitted Method 24 results include QA/QC documentation.

[P60] Industry requests EPA update or allow recent revisions of ASTM D1963 be used rather than the 1985/1996 version cited, to reflect current test practice.

[P61] Similarly, request allowance for latest versions of ASTM D2111 and other standards to avoid conflicts with lab accreditation programs that use current standards.

[P62] Laboratories ask EPA to clarify whether reapproved dates (e.g., D2111–10 Reapproved 2015) are acceptable or if the original year must be used, to avoid confusion in referenced standard versions.

[P63] Commenters request EPA allow modern alternative test methods (e.g., instrumented headspace GC) as acceptable alternatives to Method 24 when validated against Method 24 for specific coating matrices.

[P64] Coating formulators request EPA allow manufacturer-provided formulation data to be used more broadly (beyond the thresholds) with certification statements and QA/QC to reduce testing burdens, not just as an alternate if Method 311 is required when mass fractions exceed thresholds.

[P65] Industry strongly supports permitting use of manufacturer formulation data when it accurately represents constituents, but requests EPA provide a standardized attestation form and allow third-party verification rather than full Method 311 in all cases.

[P66] Owners request clarification of calculation method & rounding for as-applied vs as-purchased HAP fractions where additions (solvents, diluents) are used, and ask EPA to provide example calculations for Equations 4–6.

[P67] Coating users ask EPA to allow use of representative formulation data for minor blend adjustments rather than treating each small change as a new test requirement, provided records document the change and emissions impact is negligible.

[P68] Facilities request an expedited Administrator approval process for alternative techniques when Method 24 cannot be applied (e.g., high solids, multi-component coatings) to avoid prolonged compliance uncertainty.

[P69] Trade groups request clarity that Method 24 or ASTM D3960 may be performed by manufacturers, but qualification/credential requirements for who may perform the analysis should be specified (accredited labs vs manufacturer QC labs).

[P70] Operators request EPA to specify conditions under which Method 25 vs 25A must be used for performance tests of oxidizers, including minimum concentrations, and to provide guidance for low-level detection corrections and ND (non-detect) treatment.

[P71] Testing laboratories request that the three-run, ≥1-hour requirement allow averaging of shorter runs when operations are intermittent (e.g., batch coating runs under 1 hour), or allow combining multiple consecutive batches to meet the method intent.

[P72] Stakeholders request explicit sample calculation examples for Equations 1–3 and the averaging procedures in §63.3360(e) to reduce inconsistent regulatory interpretation between facilities and permitting authorities.

[P74] Product manufacturers ask that EF developed be allowed to apply across production lines within the same facility if product formulation and process parameters are identical, rather than requiring separate tests per line.

[P75] Operators request clarity on the limitation that EF apply only to periods producing the same or similar product—EPA should define "similar" (e.g., ±X% solids or HAP content) to reduce disputes.

[P76] Facilities ask EPA to permit use of historical test data to support EF development where testing resources are limited, provided past tests meet method and QA/QC criteria.

[P77] Compliance managers request that monthly compliance demonstrations in §63.3370 allow line-level aggregation and demonstrate how grouped-line compliance aggregation should be calculated and reported to avoid inconsistent aggregation methods.

[P81] Compliance consultants urge EPA to reconcile the dual sets of HAP limits (by mass coating and by mass solids) to avoid double-counting and to clarify which limit governs when both are applicable.

[P86] Small entities request EPA perform a regulatory flexibility analysis showing cost impacts of quarterly sensor validation, CPMS installation, and frequent performance testing, and propose scaled requirements for small sources.

[P87] Academics and independent scientists recommend EPA require uncertainty analysis and detection limits be reported with all Method 25/25A and Method 24 results to provide a clearer picture of compliance confidence.

[P88] Trade groups request EPA allow use of appropriately validated predictive emissions monitoring systems (PEMS) as an alternative to some performance tests when correlated with periodic reference tests, to reduce costs and downtime.

[P89] Operators ask EPA to permit blending documentation and supplier declarations as interim compliance demonstrations during formulation transitions, with confirmatory testing scheduled within a specified time window.

[P90] Commenters request EPA provide an explicit enforcement policy for minor data gaps (e.g., less than 10% invalid CPMS hours) that are causally documented and promptly remediated, to avoid immediate enforcement while corrective action is underway.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The requirement to apply the subpart for the "predominant activity" on mixed-substrate web coating lines is vague and will create enforcement uncertainty: EPA should define how "predominant" is measured (by mass coated, line hours, revenue, or throughput) and provide a clear, auditable metric.

Industry requests an explicit allowance for separate compliance for discrete coating stations on the same web coating line that coat different substrates (paper vs fabric), because line-level application may force facilities to use the more stringent standard for unrelated operations.

Manufacturers of printing-incorporated web coating lines oppose allowing lines modified to include printing to remain under this subpart without clear criteria; EPA should specify what scope of printing activities (e.g., spot prints, full web printing, colors) qualify to remain under this subpart rather than triggering subpart KK.

Printers request a permission clarification: if a web coating line adds printing occasionally (seasonal or pilot runs), the facility must be able to stay under this subpart rather than being reclassified to subpart KK, provided printing constitutes less than X% of annual operations (EPA should set the threshold).

Environmental groups object to language requiring emission limits "at all times, including SSM" without granting monitoring flexibility during brief, documented malfunctions; they urge EPA to retain a limited SSM affirmative defense or specify what monitoring adjustments are allowed during unavoidable events.

Legal experts warn that requiring limits "at all times, including SSM" may conflict with CAA case law on SSM and petition for EPA to specify how deviations during malfunctions, maintenance, or startups will be treated in enforcement (e.g., allow reporting but not automatic violations when good-faith efforts are documented).

Oxidizer operators note the 20 ppmv outlet organic HAP requirement plus a 100% capture efficiency condition is technically impossible: capture efficiencies cannot be literally 100%; EPA should revise to a practicable numeric capture efficiency (e.g., ≥95%) or clarify that 100% means "all emissions routed to the control device."

Process engineers request that EPA provide testing and monitoring protocols when using an oxidizer to demonstrate compliance with the ≤20 ppmv outlet requirement, including averaging period, correction to 3% O2, and procedures for low-flow exhausts where Method 25A has limits.

Small businesses note the pre-effective-date provision that allows SSM exemptions before [DATE+180 days] is ambiguous; they request EPA confirm whether facilities may rely on prior timelines and whether initial reports for that period are required.

Community health advocates oppose eliminating any allowance for noncompliance during SSM on and after [DATE+180 days]; they urge phased implementation tied to demonstrated availability of reliable monitoring and control, not a hard immediate "at all times" obligation.

Testing laboratories and facility owners highlight that requiring an initial periodic performance test by [DATE+3 years] may be infeasible for large fleets due to testing backlog; they request staggered compliance schedules or extensions for smaller sources.

Industry commenters request EPA provide explicit procedures to request time-limited extensions for the initial periodic test when test labs or access to stack/trains are constrained, without treating extension requests as violations.

Trade associations object to the electronic-only submission requirement for initial notifications, semiannual reports, and test reports, citing small facilities with limited internet access; they request a waiver or alternative paper submission process for small entities or during system outages.
Environmental advocates support electronic reporting but ask EPA to require public availability of submitted semiannual compliance reports to improve transparency and community oversight.

Equipment vendors warn that requiring new affected sources to meet emission limits "at all times, including SSM" immediately at startup is infeasible when commissioning control devices requires tuning and optimization; they request a short initial startup period (e.g., 30–90 days) for optimization before strict enforcement.

Legal commenters note immediate full compliance at startup may conflict with NSPS precedent and request EPA add a limited initial compliance period or a requirement to demonstrate "good-faith" commissioning activities in lieu of immediate numeric compliance.

Stakeholders request clarity on the §63.7(a)(2) time limits referenced for initial performance testing: provide explicit calendar deadlines (e.g., within 180 days of startup) to avoid inconsistent state interpretations.

Trade groups request that electronic submittal requirements under § 63.3330(b)(3) include secure file transfer guidelines, acceptable file formats, and an appeals process for submissions rejected due to system errors.

Facility operators request EPA clarify which semiannual compliance report elements are required immediately after [DATE+180 days] and which may follow on the regular semiannual cycle; they also seek transition guidance for reporting periods that cross the effective date.

Commenters request consistency: the pre-effective-date language in § 63.3340(a) refers to [DATE 181 DAYS AFTER PUBLICATION] while other provisions use 180 days; EPA should correct the typographical inconsistency to avoid compliance confusion.

Compliance officers ask EPA to explicitly describe how to treat overlapping obligations that become effective after [DATE+180 days], for example which provision governs when multiple new obligations kick in simultaneously; suggest a phased or priority list.

Manufacturers of newly constructed sources after Sept 19, 2019 highlight that retroactive applicability language could be interpreted to impose newer standards without allowance; they request an affirmation that sources that started after Sept 19, 2019 but before final effective date had ample notice and should be eligible for relief or staged compliance.

Operators request more concrete examples of what constitutes "operate and maintain in a manner consistent with safety and good air pollution control practices" per §63.6(e)(1)(i), including acceptable maintenance logs and training requirements, to reduce subjective enforcement.

Unions and safety advocates support the "safety and good practices" requirement but ask EPA to require written standard operating procedures (SOPs) and periodic staff training documentation to demonstrate compliance with § 63.3340(b).

Testing firms request EPA to clarify the scope of §63.3340(c): whether subparts allow reduced testing frequency if CPMS data demonstrate continuous compliance, and how waivers under §63.7(h) will be evaluated.

Test labs point out the prohibition on testing during SSM and nonoperation could delay establishing a representative baseline if the line has frequent startups/shutdowns; they request guidance on selecting representative operating windows and aggregating data across runs.

Industry legal counsel request clarification on the prohibition to test during malfunctions: define "malfunction" and require that provable documented malfunctions allow for rescheduling without triggering enforcement action.

Operators note the requirement to record and explain why test conditions were "normal" is subjective; they request a checklist of recommended parameters (web speed, coating viscosity, solvent content, dryer setpoints, exhaust flow) to use as supporting documentation.

Operators request EPA to specify what records related to performance tests are subject to confidentiality claims and how proprietary formulation information used to justify normal conditions will be treated in public disclosures.

Testing stakeholders request clearer numeric definitions of "representative flow rate" and "representative inlet concentrations" for capture/control testing, or alternatively provide percent ranges (e.g., within ±10% of nominal operating points).

Industry requests both performance-testing prohibitions during malfunctions and specific definitions of unacceptable capture/control device malfunctions; they urge EPA to include an objective metric (e.g., hours of downtime vs operating hours) that triggers retest.

Operators ask for a list of process and control device operating data points that must be recorded during control device tests (e.g., exhaust flow, temperature, pressure drop, inlet VOC), to ensure consistent compliance demonstrations.

States and enforcement agencies request that EPA specify an electronic format or template for records that must be provided to the Administrator upon request, to streamline audits and reduce record production burdens.

Facilities with intermittently-controlled work stations request clarification of the timing and frequency of monitoring and inspections required "following" initial or periodic performance tests per §63.3350(b): specify when monitoring must commence and acceptable intervals.

Operators of intermittently-controlled lines note that monitoring bypasses and mass applied during bypass will require new instrumentation and high recordkeeping expense; request EPA provide a de minimis bypass mass threshold below which monitoring exceptions apply.

raw_output:
[P1] The mandatory use of standardized forms in both Phase I and Phase II (P1) will impose significant administrative burdens on small generators and municipal utilities that currently use established state or company-specific reporting formats; EPA should allow state or existing electronic forms where they provide equivalent data to avoid duplicate reporting.

[P1] Requiring a single national standardized form (P1) risks incompatibility with state permitting systems and computerized tracking (ATS) interfaces; EPA should publish machine-readable specifications (XML/CSV) and an implementation timeline to allow integration.

[P2] The instruction that meeting participants "should focus" only on form quality (P2) is vague and effectively discourages broader procedural or substantive feedback; EPA should explicitly permit and solicit comments on the regulatory context and implementation impacts of the forms.

[P3] EPA's request that the public submit completed forms using real unit data or hypothetical information (P3) raises confidentiality concerns for commercially sensitive fuel-sulfur and sales data; EPA must provide a clear confidentiality claim procedure and commitment to protect proprietary information submitted with comments.

[P3] Requiring submission of completed forms to the Air Dockets prior to the meeting (P3) disadvantages stakeholders without access to historical fuel or operational data (e.g., new developers); EPA should accept hypothetical entries and provide sample completed forms filled with redacted or fictionalized data.

[P4] Directing substantive comments only to public hearings or dockets separate from the forms meeting (P4) fragments the record and multiplies administrative burden; EPA should accept integrated submissions or cross-reference comments to ensure reviewers can evaluate form revisions in the context of substantive rule concerns.

[P5] The fixed registration deadline for oral presenters (Jan 3, 1991) (P5) is unreasonably short and inflexible for small entities and public-interest organizations that may need additional time to coordinate; EPA should extend the registration window and allow same-day registration with notice.

[P6] Limiting seating for non-preregistered attendees (P6) without alternative remote participation options discriminates against members of the public who cannot travel or preregister; EPA must provide teleconference or later webcast access.

[P7] First-come, first-served allocation for unregistered seats (P7) unfairly advantages those in close proximity and does not ensure representation from affected communities or small entities; EPA should reserve a portion of seating for stakeholders representing low-income communities and small businesses.

[P8] The 10-minute oral presentation limit (P8) is too restrictive for complex form critiques from technical experts or multi-stakeholder coalitions; EPA should allow 20 minutes for presenters submitting technical preprints or accept shorter oral remarks supplemented by written attachments.

[P9] Requiring units subject to an exemption nonetheless to comply with the listed sections (§72.6(b)(9)) (P9) creates uncertainty as to which specific recordkeeping/monitoring requirements apply to exempt units; EPA should provide an explicit checklist mapping each exemption category to the precise subsections that remain applicable.

[P10] Allowing certifying officials to petition the Administrator for a determination of applicability (§72.6(c)) (P10) is beneficial, but the rule lacks standards and timelines for EPA action; EPA should specify decision criteria and a statutory deadline (e.g., 60 days) to avoid prolonged regulatory uncertainty.

[P11] The petition content requirement (§72.6(c)(1)) that it be "in writing and include identification of the unit and relevant facts" (P11) is too minimal and will produce inconsistent petitions; EPA should prescribe a complete petition template and information requirements.

[P12] Requiring the certifying official to sign and certify the §72.21(b)(2) statement in the petition (§72.6(c)(1)) (P12) exposes individuals to criminal penalties without clarity on liability limits; EPA should clarify the legal standard for "knowing and willful" falsity and provide safe-harbor procedures for inadvertent errors.

[P13] The 10-business-day requirement to provide owners/operators a copy of the Administrator's determination (§72.6(c)(1)) (P13) may be impractical for certifying officials governing large multi-owner facilities; EPA should allow electronic distribution and permit a 15-business-day window.

[P14] Although petitions may be submitted anytime, recommending submission before permit issuance/renewal (§72.6(c)(2)) (P14) effectively pressures applicants to petition prematurely; EPA should clarify the consequences of late petitions and whether relief is retroactive.

[P15] The exemption for qualifying new units (§72.7(b)(1)) (P15) that are not allocated allowances in Tables 2/3 lacks clarity on whether partial allocations or conditional awards affect exemption eligibility; EPA should define "allocated" to include provisional or contested allocations.

[P16] Making the exemption effective on January 1 of the first full calendar year the unit meets criteria (§72.7(b)(2)) (P16) can create perverse incentives to delay start-up until the next calendar year; EPA should allow prorated or pro rata effective dates to reflect actual operation commencement.

[P17] The requirement that by Dec 31 of the first exemption year a signed statement be submitted to the permitting authority and possibly the Administrator (§72.7(b)(2)) (P17) imposes a narrow filing deadline that could be missed due to administrative delay; EPA should permit electronic filing and a cure period for late submissions.

[P18] The prescribed-format statement for exemptions (§72.7(b)(2)) must include generator capacities, fuels, sulfur contents, and a compliance pledge (§72.7(b)(2)) (P18), but the rule does not supply the prescribed format in the notice; EPA should publish the form and allow a public comment period on its fields.

[P19] Allowing an exempt new unit that is allocated allowances to still qualify if it meets requirements (§72.7(c)(1)) (P19) creates a mechanism for double-counting or gaming of allowances; EPA must explain how allowance allocation and subsequent surrender prevent market distortion.

[P20] The statement requirements when allowances are allocated (§72.7(c)(1)(i)) (P20) place onerous verification duties on designated representatives; EPA should permit third-party attestations or audit verification in lieu of full evidentiary submission.

[P21] Requiring identification of fuels and their sulfur content by weight for each generator (§72.7(c)(1)(i)(A)) (P21) is operationally difficult when fuel sources vary over short periods; EPA should allow use of fuel supplier certificates and averaging protocols.

[P22] The mandatory affirmation that owners/operators will comply with paragraph (e) (§72.7(c)(1)(i)(B)) (P22) lacks enforcement clarity; EPA should describe remedies for breaches and whether such affirmations create new civil penalty exposure.

[P23] Surrendering allowances equal to those allocated with same or earlier compliance/use dates (§72.7(c)(1)(i)(C)) (P23) effectively eliminates allocated allowances' utility and may create cash-flow burdens; EPA should allow operators to retain allowances but accept financial adjustments or escrow mechanisms instead.

[P24] The requirement to surrender any proceeds withheld for allowances (§72.7(c)(1)(i)(D)) (P24) is unclear about the timing and valuation method for proceeds; EPA must clarify how withheld proceeds are calculated and provide a standardized accounting methodology.

[P25] EPA's obligation to deduct surrendered allowances and close the ATS account (§72.7(c)(1)(ii)) (P25) is appropriate, but there is no timeline for EPA actions or notice to market participants; EPA should commit to specific processing times and provide automated ATS confirmations.

[P26] The exemption effective date provision (§72.7(c)(2)) making it Jan 1 of the first full calendar year (P26) repeats the calendar-year problem (see P16); EPA should permit exceptions where construction/commercial operation straddle calendar years.

[P27] The complicated compliance calculation rules for the 0.05% sulfur annual average (§72.7(c)(3)) (P27) create compliance and audit complexity; EPA should provide examples, software calculators, and tolerances for sampling and measurement uncertainty.

[P28] Treating natural gas-only burning as automatically compliant (§72.7(c)(3)(i)) (P28) may be abused if intermittent non-natural gas fuels are used without adequate reporting; EPA should require documentation or supplier attestations to substantiate natural gas-only claims.

[P29] The prescribed formula for averaging sulfur in mixed gaseous fuels (§72.7(c)(3)(ii)) (P29) must be published with units, rounding rules, and sampling frequency; otherwise regulated parties will face inconsistent enforcement.

[P30] For nongaseous fuels, the required annual average sulfur calculation or mass alternative (§72.7(c)(3)(iii)) (P30) places a heavy sampling burden on small units; EPA should allow representative sampling plans, supplier certification, or default values approved by permitting authorities.

[P31] Exempt units that must still follow paragraphs (d)(2) and (e) (P31) create a patchwork of partial obligations; EPA should provide a single consolidated summary of duties that apply to exempt units to avoid confusion.

[P32] The Dec 31, 1997 deadline to submit prescribed statements for exempt units allocated allowances (§72.7(d)(2)) (P32) is outdated and arbitrary in the proposed text; EPA must clarify if this is an editorial error or update the deadline to a practicable current date.

[P33] The requirement that owners/operators comply with Acid Rain requirements during non-exempt periods and for rules promulgated after exemption start (§72.7(e)(1)) (P33) could create retroactive obligations; EPA should limit retroactivity or specify grandfathering provisions.

[P34] Declaring that exempt units are not affected units or eligible opt-in sources but remain subject to parts 70 and 71 (P34) may lead to overlapping permitting requirements; EPA should provide guidance on reconciliation of part 70/71 obligations with exemption status.

[P35] The five-year on-site record retention requirement (§72.7(e)(3)) (P35) is burdensome for small operators with limited storage; EPA should allow electronic records with secure off-site backups and permit reduced retention where state laws require shorter periods.

[P36] Granting the Administrator discretion to extend the five-year recordkeeping period for cause (§72.7(e)(3)) (P36) is sensible, but the rule should define "for cause" and provide an expedited request process and default extension where enforcement action is pending.

[P37] Requiring records for each fuel delivery to include sulfur content or pipeline sample data (§72.7(e)(3)(i)) (P37) places an unreasonable verification burden when fuel is procured through spot markets; EPA should accept supplier certificates and representative sampling for spot buys.

[P38] Placing the burden of proof on owners/operators to demonstrate compliance with paragraph (a) (§72.7(e)(3)(ii)) (P38) flips the usual enforcement presumption; EPA should require that the agency bear initial proof burden for alleged noncompliance or at least allow shifting burden only after a prima facie showing.

[P39] The triggering events that cause an exempt unit to become an affected unit (P39) are numerous and could lead to inadvertent loss of exemption; EPA should require written notice to owners/operators before declaring loss of exemption and allow a cure period for minor, non-recurring breaches.

[P40] Using a 25 MWe combined nameplate capacity threshold to trigger loss of exemption (P40) is arbitrary and may disincentivize incremental capacity additions; EPA should consider a gross-output test over 12 months or a different threshold coordinated with grid interconnection requirements.

[P41] Loss of exemption if the unit burns coal or coal-derived fuels (P41) lacks definition for "coal-derived gaseous fuel" and its allowable sulfur content; EPA must define eligible coal-derived gaseous fuels and acceptable sulfur limits to avoid enforcement disputes.

[P42] The rule that exceeding the 0.05% sulfur annual average causes loss of exemption effective the following January 1 (P42) creates a lag that could allow ongoing non-compliant operation for months and complicates market behavior; EPA should make loss of exemption effective upon agency determination with an opportunity to remediate.

[P43] Requiring submission of a complete Acid Rain permit application within 60 days after loss of exemption or by Jan 1, 1998 (whichever later) (§72.7(d)(4)(ii)) (P43) is unworkable and contains obsolete dates; EPA must update deadlines and provide a reasonable timeframe (e.g., 180 days) to prepare complex permit applications.

[P44] Treating a unit losing exemption as a new unit for Part 75 monitoring with commencement date equal to the date exemption ended (§72.7(d)(4)(iii)) (P44) can impose immediate capital costs for monitoring equipment without transition allowances; EPA should allow phased compliance if monitoring installation requires procurement lead time.

[P45] Allowing permanent retirement exemptions (§72.8(b)(1)) (P45) is appropriate, but EPA should require independent verification of permanent cessation to avoid misuse as a temporary shutdown stratagem to evade obligations.

[P46] The Dec 31 deadline for submission of signed retirement statements for exemptions effective Jan 1 (§72.8(b)(2)) (P46) mirrors prior date problems (see P32); EPA must correct dates and allow filing flexibility and electronic submission.

[P47] The provision that retired units remain exempt except for certain provisions (§72.8(c)) (P47) needs a clear list of exceptions and required ongoing obligations (e.g., emissions leakage, demolition) to avoid confusion about ongoing liabilities.

[P48] The prohibition that an exempt permanently retired unit must emit no SO2 or NOx from the exemption effective date onward (§72.8(d)(1)) (P48) is unrealistic because fugitive emissions, startup testing, demolition, or residual emissions may occur; EPA should clarify that the prohibition applies to combustion-related emissions and allow short-term controlled activities under notification.

[P49] The requirement for Phase I units to submit Phase I permit applications and annual certification reports while retired (P49) is contradictory; if permanently retired, units should be exempted from recurring certifications unless they resume operation.

[P50] The obligation that a unit may not resume operation unless a complete permit application is filed at least 24 months before the later specified date and that resumption is conditioned on timely submission (§72.8(d)(2)) (P50) effectively bars timely returns to service for reliability reasons; EPA should allow emergency reactivation procedures with a shorter permit submission window and temporary operating authorizations.

[P51] Requiring compliance with Acid Rain requirements for periods when retirement exemption does not apply (§72.8(d)(3)) (P51) could impose retroactive obligations if EPA changes standards after retirement; EPA should ensure new requirements are prospective only.

[P52] Declaring that retired exempt units are not affected units or opt-in sources but remain subject to parts 70/71 (P52) risks regulatory overlap; EPA should publish specific crosswalk guidance to show which permitting requirements remain and which are suspended.

[P53] Five-year on-site retention of retirement proof records (§72.8(d)(5)) (P53) burdens small operators; EPA should permit electronic records and allow shorter retention if state archives require it, while ensuring accessibility for enforcement.

[P54] Treating the unit as losing exemption on the earlier of permit application submission or requirement to submit (§72.8(d)(6)(i)) (P54) effectively penalizes proactive carriers and could deter voluntary application; EPA should make loss of exemption tied to actual commencement of activities that contradict retirement, not mere paperwork.

[P55] The 60-day/Jan 1, 1998 submission requirement for units that lose exemption (§72.8(d)(6)(ii)) (P55) contains stale dates and an unreasonably short period; EPA must modernize and extend these deadlines to align with current permitting timelines.

[P56] Treating a unit losing retirement exemption as a new unit for Part 75 monitoring with commercial operation commencement on the date it resumes operation (§72.8(d)(6)(iii)) (P56) may create gaps where monitoring is required before operation resumes; EPA should require monitoring readiness before commercial operation and allow temporary monitoring alternatives.

[P57] Allowing submission of a complete petition for an industrial-unit exemption by the designated representative (§72.14(b)) (P57) is appropriate, but EPA should permit third-party submission on the representative's behalf and define acceptable evidence of authorization.

[P58] Requiring complete petition elements in a prescribed Administrator format (§72.14(b)) (P58) is fair, but EPA must publish the format and provide model petitions and a comment period so stakeholders can prepare compliant petitions.

[P59] The petition identification requirement (§72.14(b)(1)) (P59) should include Unit Identification Code (UCI) or ATS account number to avoid mistaken identity and streamline administrative review.

[P60] Requiring a statement that the unit is not a cogeneration unit (§72.14(b)(2)) (P60) is legally significant and may be subject to dispute; EPA should define "cogeneration" for these purposes and provide guidance on borderline cases.

[P61] The obligation to list historical owners/operators since the interconnection agreement date and state that none have electricity sale as principal business (§72.14(b)(3)) (P61) could be burdensome and raise privacy issues; EPA should permit redacted disclosure or a certification under penalty of perjury rather than exhaustive histories.

[P62] Demanding a summary of interconnection and power purchase terms, including required electricity amounts and expiration provisions (§72.14(b)(4)) (P62) may be commercially sensitive; EPA should allow confidential submission of contract copies with public redactions.

[P63] Requiring copies of the interconnection and power purchase agreements with the petition (§72.14(b)(5)) (P63) may conflict with non-disclosure commitments to counterparties; EPA should adopt procedures to protect confidential business information and allow submission of certified summaries where full disclosure is restricted by contract.

[P64] The need to state nameplate capacities of each generator served by the unit (§72.14(b)(6)) (P64) is reasonable but must account for deratings or seasonal variations; EPA should allow reporting of both nameplate and maximum demonstrated output.

[P65] Requiring annual data since 1985 on each generator's output and sales (§72.14(b)(7)) (P65) imposes an onerous record retrieval burden, especially for units with ownership changes; EPA should limit retroactive data requirements to a more recent and relevant baseline (e.g., last 5–10 years) or permit best-available estimates certified by the designated representative.

[P66] The petition must state that generators produced electricity for sale only as incidental sales (§72.14(b)(8)) (P66); however, the rule lacks a clear definition of "incidental sales" — EPA should quantify incidental thresholds or align with the 10% test used elsewhere.

[P67] Including special provisions of paragraph (d) in the petition (§72.14(b)(9)) (P67) creates circularity because petitioners must affirm compliance with provisions that are only explained later; EPA should provide the paragraph (d) requirements alongside the petition form.

[P69] Requiring denial of exemption if petitioners fail to demonstrate paragraph (a) requirements (§72.14(c)(1)(ii)) (P69) is appropriate but should include a procedural right to cure deficiencies before final denial.

[P70] Treating exemption petitions as permit applications using the same draft/proposed/final procedures (§72.14(c)(2)) (P70) is burdensome and may duplicate public comment processes; EPA should allow a streamlined review track for routine exemptions with public notice and limited review.

[P71] Making an issued exemption effective on January 1 of the first full year the unit meets requirements (§72.14(c)(3)) (P71) perpetuates the calendar-year timing problem and should be amended to allow the effective date to reflect actual start of compliance.

[P72] Leaving exemptions in effect until lost under paragraph (d)(4) (§72.14(c)(4)) (P72) is reasonable, but EPA should require annual reaffirmation to ensure continued eligibility and to capture changes in ownership or operations.

[P73] Obligating owners/operators to comply with Acid Rain requirements whenever the exemption is not in effect (§72.14(d)(1)) (P73) is reasonable but needs clarity regarding retroactive application of future requirements.

[P74] Clarifying that exempt industrial units are not affected units or opt-in sources but remain subject to parts 70/71 (§72.14(d)(2)) (P74) requires a practical cross-reference chart to avoid permit application errors.

[P75] The five-year on-site retention requirement for interconnection agreements and historical output/sales data (§72.14(d)(3)) (P75) is potentially duplicative of corporate archives; EPA should accept centralized electronic records and permit submission of certified copies.

[P76] Loss of exemption when ownership or related-entity status changes such that the principal business is electricity selling/transmitting/distributing (§72.14(d)(4)(i)) (P76) is appropriate but should include guidance on related-entity tests and exceptions for passive investment.

[P77] The rule that selling to anyone other than the purchaser specified in the interconnection agreement (P77) causes immediate loss of exemption creates risky cliff effects for incidental spot sales; EPA should adopt a de minimis safe harbor (e.g., <1% annual output).

[P78] The provision that sales not required under the agreement or causing annual sales to exceed 10% of nameplate×8760 cause loss of exemption (§72.14(d)(4)(i)(C)) (P78) uses the 10% metric tied to nameplate×8760 that is confusing — EPA should replace it with a clear percentage of annual generation to avoid miscalculation.

[P79] Loss of exemption if sales to the specified purchaser exceed 10% of the generator's actual annual output effective the following Jan 1 (§72.14(d)(4)(i)(D)) (P79) creates lagging enforcement that can be gamed; EPA should make the trigger effective upon discovery with an opportunity to appeal.

[P80] The trigger that expiration/termination of agreements causing sales leads to loss of exemption (P80) is reasonable but should allow a limited cure period for contract renegotiation (e.g., 90 days) to avoid immediate classification changes.

[P81] Requiring submission of a complete Acid Rain permit application within 60 days or by Jan 1, 1998 upon loss of exemption (§72.14(d)(4)(ii)) (P81) repeats obsolete deadlines and unrealistic timelines; EPA should modernize deadlines and permit phased application submittals.

[P82] Treating units losing industrial exemptions as new units for Part 75 monitoring with commencement on the date they are no longer exempt (P82) should include transitional monitoring arrangements and specified lead times for monitor procurement, installation, and certification to avoid forced noncompliance.

EPA's request that the public submit completed forms using real unit data or hypothetical information (P3) raises confidentiality concerns for commercially sensitive fuel-sulfur and sales data; EPA must provide a clear confidentiality claim procedure and commitment to protect proprietary information submitted with comments.

Requiring submission of completed forms to the Air Dockets prior to the meeting (P3) disadvantages stakeholders without access to historical fuel or operational data (e.g., new developers); EPA should accept hypothetical entries and provide sample completed forms filled with redacted or fictionalized data.

Treating units losing industrial exemptions as new units for Part 75 monitoring with commencement on the date they are no longer exempt (P82) should include transitional monitoring arrangements and specified lead times for monitor procurement, installation, and certification to avoid forced noncompliance.

[P1] An environmental law clinic claims the proposed removal violates the Administrative Procedure Act because the Service did not provide a reasoned explanation for reversing its prior determination of risk for this subspecies.

[P1] A federal land manager (BLM representative) supports delisting, claiming that existing federal land management plans and conservation agreements provide sufficient regulatory and management mechanisms to ensure the subspecies’ continued viability post-delisting.

[P1] A conservation NGO claims the proposal lacks a credible post-delisting monitoring plan or specific conservation commitments from landowners, and requests that delisting only be finalized contingent on a binding monitoring and contingency plan.

[P1] An endangered species scientist claims the Service’s threat analysis under the five-factor framework is incomplete because it understates impacts from climate change and invasive species to the subspecies’ microhabitats.

[P1] A private developer claims delisting will reduce regulatory burden and legal uncertainty on planned projects within the subspecies’ range and requests swift finalization of the rule.

[P2] An advocacy organization supports reopening the comment period for 30 days but argues 60 days are necessary to allow independent scientists and local stakeholders enough time to prepare substantive technical comments and data.

[P2] A small conservation group claims the 30-day reopened comment period is inadequate because notice was not widely distributed to local communities, requesting an additional extension and local outreach.

[P3] Several commenters note a conflict between the stated 30-day reopening and the December 1, 2017 deadline, claiming the Service must clarify whether the December 1, 2017 deadline or the 30-day window governs and ensure the comment period complies with statutory notice requirements.

[P3] A legal practitioner specializing in administrative law claims accepting comments postmarked by December 1, 2017 may prejudice electronic commenters if that date is sooner than 30 days from the notice publication, and requests the Service correct the dates to avoid confusion.

[P4] A civil liberties group requests additional submission methods (e.g., email to a direct docket inbox) because some rural stakeholders lack reliable internet access and cannot easily use regulations.gov or guarantee timely mail delivery.

[P5] Multiple commenters request clearer step-by-step guidance for submitting comments via regulations.gov, claiming the current instruction to click “Comment Now!” is insufficient for elderly or non-technical stakeholders.

[P6] A rural community association supports the availability of hardcopy submissions by U.S. mail or hand-delivery, but asks the Service to provide a PO Box with longer receipt hours because the current delivery address is located at a federal facility with restricted access.

[P6] A commenter warns that requiring hand-delivery to a specific processing center creates an undue burden on individuals who cannot travel, and requests the Service provide alternative, publicly accessible drop-off locations.

[P7] A public interest law firm challenges the phrase “send comments only by the methods described above,” asserting it could be read to preclude equitable late-filed comments and requests the Service explicitly state it will consider good-faith submissions by other methods or accept late comments in extraordinary circumstances.

[P7] A tech-access advocacy group requests explicit allowance for email submissions for parties who cannot use regulations.gov, arguing that “only” language unreasonably narrows means of participation.

[P8] A privacy advocate objects to posting all comments on regulations.gov, claiming blanket public posting of comments could chill participation from individuals who wish to report sensitive environmental harm or proprietary information.

[P8] An academic asks the Service to publish comments with metadata (date/time, submitter affiliation) to enhance transparency and enable better analysis of the public docket.

[P9] Several commenters object to the policy of posting personal information included in comments, requesting that the Service redact contact information or provide automated redaction options before public posting.

[P10] A privacy-focused NGO claims that the statement that entire comments submitted via regulations.gov will be posted (including personal identifying information) is inconsistent with privacy best practices and requests default redaction of phone numbers and addresses.

[P11] Multiple individuals request clear instructions and an easily accessible process for requesting withholding of personal identifying information that explains the criteria the Service uses to decide such requests.

[P11] A legal commenter notes that saying the Service “cannot guarantee” withholding is insufficient and asks the agency to commit to specific handling procedures (e.g., redaction within X days) and to inform requesters when their redaction cannot be honored.

[P12] A civil liberties organization claims the Service’s inability to guarantee withholding creates a real risk to vulnerable commenters (e.g., victims of harassment) and requests that at a minimum the Service not publish names/addresses of commenters who affirm they fear retaliation.

[P13] An attorney advising whistleblowers requests the Service adopt a standard header for mailed comments that triggers confidential handling, and asks for a public description of how hardcopy confidentiality requests will be processed.

[P13] A concerned citizen requests clarification on what constitutes an acceptable request in the top of a hardcopy comment to withhold personal information, and asks the Service to provide a sample statement.

[P14] A privacy advocate reiterates that the Service’s statement that it cannot guarantee withholding for hardcopy submissions is insufficient protection and urges removal of the requirement to publish hardcopy personal data.

[P15] An FOIA practitioner requests that when the Service posts hardcopy submissions to the electronic docket, it retain original file timestamps and provide scanned images to preserve the administrative record integrity.

[P15] A commenter warns that posting hardcopy submissions online without redaction could inadvertently expose sensitive personal or proprietary data and asks for a described redaction workflow before posting.

[P16] Several commenters state they will withhold personal contact information from their comments unless the Service provides assurances about redaction policies, claiming the current notice insufficiently protects privacy.

[P16] A public health researcher claims the “be aware” admonition is insufficient and requests explicit guidance on how to submit contact information privately to receive Service responses without public disclosure.

[P17] An environmental law group requests that the Service clarify how names and addresses will be used in the administrative record and whether such information will be accessible through FOIA requests; they ask for limits on dissemination to protect privacy.

[P18] A previous commenter points out that because prior comments will be considered, the Service should clearly identify which previous docket entries are being carried over and provide a summary of how prior comments influenced the proposed delisting.

[P18] A stakeholder asks for confirmation that prior commenters who submitted comments to earlier stages (e.g., scoping) are included and need not resubmit, requesting an itemized list of included prior submissions for transparency.

[P19] A commenter who uses a TDD appreciates the availability of the Federal Relay Service but requests that the Service include an email or text alternative for people with hearing impairments who do not use TDD.

[P19] A disability rights organization requests that the Service proactively offer accommodations beyond the Federal Relay Service (e.g., accessible web forms, large-print and braille materials) to ensure full participation in the comment process.
