[P1] Industry commenters will request clarification that allowing group health plans the option to pay premiums based on average enrollee premium amounts (§147.102(c)(3)(iii)(D)) must include standardized actuarial methods and disclosure requirements so plans do not shift costs to smaller employers or select enrollees.

[P1] Small-employer advocacy groups will argue the optional “average enrollee premium” payment method (§147.102(c)(3)(iii)(D)) could disadvantage employers with younger/healthier workforces and ask for a prohibition on premium adjustments that effectively surcharge based on demographic composition.

[P2] Consumer advocates will oppose permitting issuers to limit coverage availability to Nov 15–Dec 15 (§147.104(b)(1)(i)(B)), contending that a one-month enrollment window is too narrow and will harm people with scheduling, caregiving, or employment barriers; they will request extension to at least 45–60 days.

[P2] State regulators will seek explicit authority to set longer or alternative enrollment periods than Nov 15–Dec 15 (§147.104(b)(1)(i)(B)), arguing federal pre-emption of longer State windows would conflict with State consumer protection statutes.

[P3] Employers and brokers will request that the rule clarify how the quarter-based effective date option for small employers (§147.104(b)(1)(i)(C)) interacts with COBRA, employer plan year changes, and payroll cycles to avoid administrative disruption.

[P3] Labor unions will object that allowing small employers to choose a later effective date within a quarter (§147.104(b)(1)(i)(C)) could create gaps in coverage for employees and request a minimum protection guaranteeing no employee goes without coverage longer than 30 days.

[P4] Patient advocacy groups will request HHS define “initial” and “annual” open enrollment (§147.104(b)(1)(ii)) with specific start/end times and required notice periods to ensure individuals have meaningful ability to enroll.

[P4] Legal commenters will ask HHS to require issuers to provide real-time enrollment confirmation and standardized effective date disclosures when individuals purchase coverage during initial/annual open enrollment (§147.104(b)(1)(ii)).

[P5] Health plans will request clarification on the interaction between the limited SEP requirement (§147.104(b)(2)(i)) and off-Exchange coverage rules, specifically which triggering events are excluded for off-Exchange policies to avoid inconsistent practices.

[P5] Consumer groups will argue the exclusions for off-Exchange coverage in providing limited open enrollment (§147.104(b)(2)(i)) could create loopholes that deny consumers SEP protections and ask for alignment of Exchange and off-Exchange SEP rules.

[P6] Issuers will request specific timelines and secure transmission standards for providing enrollment, claims, encounter, and medical record documentation to auditors (§153.630(b)(6)) to avoid compliance uncertainty and privacy breaches.

[P6] Privacy and cybersecurity experts will demand that §153.630(b)(6) require encrypted transfers and minimum authentication methods when issuers furnish medical records to auditors, and request liability limits if HHS fails to specify standards.

[P7] Behavioral health providers will support allowing a signed mental/behavioral health assessment in lieu of full records (§153.630(b)(6)) but request a narrow, well-defined template and strict limits on what information can be included to protect patient privacy.

[P7] Civil liberties organizations will caution that permitting signed behavioral health assessments in place of full records (§153.630(b)(6)) risks coercing clinicians into disclosing sensitive information; they will request stricter limits on content and an appeals process.

[P8] Mental health providers will request clearer guidance on acceptable attestation language and legal basis when certifying they are “prohibited by privacy laws” from providing full records (§153.630(b)(6)) so providers are not exposed to legal risk.

[P8] Legal experts will warn that the required attestation (§153.630(b)(6)) could conflict with state mandatory reporting laws and request HHS add a safe-harbor for providers who furnish assessments in good faith.

[P9] Auditing firms will request that HHS publish the “manner and timeframe” for reporting inter-rater reliability (§153.630(b)(8)) in advance and provide a transition period so auditors can adapt methodologies and software.

[P9] Statisticians and methodological experts will request that HHS define the statistical methods, sample sizes, and confidence intervals required when measuring inter-rater reliability (§153.630(b)(8)) to ensure comparability across auditors.

[P10] Auditors and issuers will challenge the 95% required consistency in review outcomes (§153.630(b)(8)), calling it unachievable for complex clinical determinations; they will request a lower standard (e.g., 85–90%) or alternative risk-adjusted metrics outside the 2015–2016 exception.

[P10] Consumer protection advocates will argue the 95% consistency requirement (§153.630(b)(8)) is necessary to prevent audit variability and gaming, but will request clarity on remediation steps if auditors fail to meet the threshold.

[P11] Industry trade groups will request due process protections and a transparent penalty schedule if HHS imposes civil money penalties under §153.630(b)(9), including notice, cure periods, and appeal rights before penalties are levied.

[P11] Compliance officers will ask that HHS limit imposition of civil money penalties (§153.630(b)(9)) to cases of egregious or repeated violations and provide factors for downward adjustment (size of issuer, good-faith efforts, corrective action).

[P12] Issuers will request HHS allow grace periods or written extension authority before treating “failure to engage an initial validation auditor” (§153.630(b)(9)(i)) as a penalty trigger, noting contracting delays and auditor shortages.

[P13] Several issuers and State regulators will ask for clarity on what constitutes timely “submission of initial validation audit results” (§153.630(b)(9)(ii)), including acceptable electronic formats and handling of incomplete results due to technical failures.

[P14] Industry commenters will seek a narrow definition of “misconduct or substantial non-compliance” (§153.630(b)(9)(iii)) to avoid subjective enforcement and to align with existing audit standards and corrective action plans.

[P15] Legal groups will request HHS define “intentionally or recklessly misrepresents or falsifies information” (§153.630(b)(9)(iv)) with scienter standards and examples, and to require HHS prove intent before imposing the most severe penalties.

[P16] University legal clinics will request clarification that the exemptions (§154.103(b)) for grandfathered plans, excepted benefits, and student health plans apply consistently across other referenced parts to avoid conflicting obligations.

[P16] Consumer advocates will object that exempting grandfathered and excepted benefits (§154.103(b)) from these requirements could undermine consumer protections and request Congress-level policy justification or sunset provisions for the exemption.

[P17] Actuaries and insurers will ask HHS to provide worked examples and templates demonstrating the 15% federal threshold calculation (§154.200(a)) and explain whether the threshold applies per product, per market, or statewide.

[P17] State consumer advocates will request that HHS ensure the 15% federal threshold (§154.200(a)) applies to cumulative rate changes across all products in a rating area to prevent serial small increases that evade review.

[P18] State officials will seek clearer timelines, content requirements, and criteria HHS will use in evaluating State proposals to set higher State-specific thresholds by Aug 1 (§154.200(a)), including data standards and stakeholder input processes.

[P19] Insurers will request technical guidance and a prescribed formula for the premium-weighted average increase calculation (§154.200(b)) including treatment of enrollee churn, mid-year plan changes, and non-renewals.

[P20] Consumer groups will urge that §154.200(c) require HHS to aggregate increases across related filings and to publish methodology for combining increases so consumers can see when cumulative increases trigger review.

[P21] Transparency advocates will request HHS ensure that the public posting of Parts I and III of Rate Filing Justifications (§154.215(h)(2)) includes machine-readable data and redaction standards to prevent over-redaction of material non-confidential information.

[P22] States will request flexibility in the 5-business-day notification requirement (§154.301(b)(2)) when they plan to make rate information public sooner, proposing a mechanism for emergency disclosures or coordinated press releases with CMS.

[P23] States that want to run only an individual market Exchange using the Federal platform (§155.106(c)) will request clear cost-sharing arrangements and timelines for transition and for integrating State-specific requirements.

[P24] States will ask for detailed checklists and approval criteria for the listed steps required to operate a State Exchange on the Federal platform (§155.106(c)) including IT, privacy, and consumer assistance requirements.

[P25] QHP issuers and States will request a precise timetable and lead times for rate change submissions under the Federally-facilitated SHOP timeline (§155.200(f)(4)) to align carrier product development and renewal processes.

[P26] Consumer advocates will request HHS require at least one Navigator grant recipient to be a community-based or consumer-focused non-profit in each Exchange region (§155.210(c)(2)) to ensure representation of underserved populations.

[P26] Trade associations representing insurers will request HHS clarify whether issuers, agents, or brokers are eligible entities to be included under the specified categories for Navigator grants (§155.210(c)(2)) to avoid conflicts of interest.

[P27] National non-profits will applaud the prohibition on disqualifying Navigators due to out-of-area principal place of business (§155.210(e)(7)) but will ask HHS to clarify reasonable expectations for in-person outreach and staffing in service areas.

[P28] Organizations providing non-Navigator assistance will request clarification of the geographic neutrality prohibition (§155.215(h)) and ask whether virtual/remote assisters are subject to additional local credentialing.

[P29] Agents, brokers, and issuers will request HHS to clarify the scope and cost allocation rules for the required annual operational readiness third-party review under §155.221(a), including whether Exchanges or issuers may subsidize reviewer costs.

[P30] Commenters will object that the required third-party reviewer must be a downstream or delegated entity of the agent, broker, or issuer (§155.221(a)) because this creates conflicts of interest and request an independent third-party requirement instead.

[P31] Industry and audit firms will request HHS to publish the “specified standards” that third-party entities must meet (§155.221(b)) well before the rule’s effective date to allow firms time to obtain necessary credentials.

[P32] Third-party auditors will request more precise definitions of “relevant privacy and security standards” (§155.221(b)(1)) and whether HIPAA compliance alone suffices or additional Fed platform standards apply.

[P33] Agents and brokers will ask HHS to make the operational readiness specifications (§155.221(b)(2)) publicly available, including required test cases and acceptable remediation plans, so audits are consistent and predictable.

[P34] Industry will seek clarification on the data retention, format, and transmission requirements in §155.221(b)(3) and request that HHS limit the 10-year retention to audit artifacts only, not raw consumer data, to reduce storage burdens and privacy risk.

[P35] Commenters will request a narrow definition of “financial relationships” to be disclosed under §155.221(b)(4) to prevent overly broad reporting of routine market transactions and proprietary investor relationships.

[P36] Third-party entities will ask HHS to clarify what “all applicable Federal and State requirements” (§155.221(b)(5)) entail vis-à-vis conflicting State laws on contractor background checks and licensing.

[P37] Third-party firms will request HHS provide the operational readiness training curriculum and reasonable timelines for staff annual completion (§155.221(b)(6)) and ask for a grandfathering provision for staff who have completed equivalent training.

[P38] Audit firms will request that the access provision (§155.221(b)(7)) to books, contracts, and systems for 10 years be limited to materials directly related to the audit and include confidentiality protections for proprietary business information.

[P39] Business groups will request that HHS specify the “other minimum business criteria” (§155.221(b)(8)) by guidance and allow comment before enforcement, including minimum net worth, insurance, and staffing thresholds.

[P40] Large brokers and issuers will ask for flexibility in engaging multiple third-party entities (§155.221(c)) and request that HHS allow different entities to be used for IT, privacy, and operational testing provided each meets standards in (b).

[P41] Taxpayer advocates will support the prohibition (§155.305(f)(4)) on determining APTC eligibility for filers who failed to file required tax returns and reconcile credits, and will request automated exchange of delinquency data with IRS to improve enforcement.

[P41] Legal aid organizations will warn that the prohibition (§155.305(f)(4)) could lead to coverage termination for low-income households who lack representation, requesting procedural safeguards and appeal rights before APTC ineligibility is applied.

[P42] Applicants and enrollment assisters will request examples and scope of the conditions where an Exchange must accept attested increased household income without verification (§155.320(c)(3)(iii)(A)) to prevent inconsistent casework.

[P43] Compliance groups will ask HHS to define the verification steps in §155.315(f)(1)-(4) that must be followed when attested income falls between 100–400% FPL and is significantly above computed income (§155.320(c)(3)(iii)(D)), and to specify acceptable documentation.

[P44] States will request clarity and a cap on what constitutes the “reasonable threshold” that must be at least 10% and may include a dollar amount (§155.320(c)(3)(iii)(D)), and will ask HHS to publish a default national threshold for consistency.

[P45] Advocates for low-income households will support exempting applicants eligible under §155.305(f)(2) from verification (§155.320(c)(3)(iii)(D)) and request that HHS ensure outreach to such populations so they understand exemption criteria.

[P46] Enrollment assisters will request clear procedural guidance on how Exchanges must notify applicants and implement determinations when verification cannot be completed by the deadline (§155.320(c)(3)(iii)(E)), including standardized notice language and timelines.

[P47] Consumer groups will object to the requirement that the Exchange determine filer ineligible for APTC/CSRs if baseline info unavailable (§155.320(c)(3)(iii)(F)), requesting that HHS allow provisional APTC pending additional outreach to prevent sudden loss of subsidies.

[P48] Commenters will request that the “incompatible with other information” standard (§155.320(c)(3)(vi)(C)) be narrowly defined with examples to avoid subjective denials of attestation-based eligibility.

[P49] Legal advocates will request procedural safeguards before treating an attestation as “not reasonably compatible” with other information (§155.320(c)(3)(vi)(C)(1)), including notice, an opportunity to submit corroborating evidence, and a right to appeal.

[P52] Groups representing rural consumers will ask for flexibility and additional time under §155.320(c)(3)(vi)(F) if Exchanges cannot verify attested income due to lack of internet connectivity or delays in State data-sharing agreements.

[P53] Legal aid organizations will request that before determining tax filers ineligible and discontinuing advance payments (§155.320(c)(3)(vi)(G)), Exchanges provide individualized outreach and consider documented hardships or illness preventing response.

[P54] Exchanges will request detailed criteria and an upstream consultation process for determining they “do not reasonably expect to obtain sufficient verification data” (§155.320(d)(4)), and for the alternate procedures applicable 2016–2019.

[P55] Consumers will ask HHS to allow movement to any metal level QHP when qualifying for SEP (§155.420(a)(4)(iii)(A)) instead of limiting to same/adjacent metal levels, citing continuity of care and provider network differences.

[P56] Families will request that when adding a dependent who qualifies for SEP (§155.420(a)(4)(iii)(B)), Exchanges prioritize allowing the dependent to be added to the current QHP to avoid network disruption and minimize administrative barriers.

parsed_claims.claim_text: Industry commenters will request clarification that allowing group health plans the option to pay premiums based on average enrollee premium amounts (§147.102(c)(3)(iii)(D)) must include standardized actuarial methods and disclosure requirements so plans do not shift costs to smaller employers or select enrollees.

Small-employer advocacy groups will argue the optional “average enrollee premium” payment method (§147.102(c)(3)(iii)(D)) could disadvantage employers with younger/healthier workforces and ask for a prohibition on premium adjustments that effectively surcharge based on demographic composition.

Consumer advocates will oppose permitting issuers to limit coverage availability to Nov 15–Dec 15 (§147.104(b)(1)(i)(B)), contending that a one-month enrollment window is too narrow and will harm people with scheduling, caregiving, or employment barriers; they will request extension to at least 45–60 days.

State regulators will seek explicit authority to set longer or alternative enrollment periods than Nov 15–Dec 15 (§147.104(b)(1)(i)(B)), arguing federal pre-emption of longer State windows would conflict with State consumer protection statutes.

Employers and brokers will request that the rule clarify how the quarter-based effective date option for small employers (§147.104(b)(1)(i)(C)) interacts with COBRA, employer plan year changes, and payroll cycles to avoid administrative disruption.

Labor unions will object that allowing small employers to choose a later effective date within a quarter (§147.104(b)(1)(i)(C)) could create gaps in coverage for employees and request a minimum protection guaranteeing no employee goes without coverage longer than 30 days.

Patient advocacy groups will request HHS define “initial” and “annual” open enrollment (§147.104(b)(1)(ii)) with specific start/end times and required notice periods to ensure individuals have meaningful ability to enroll.

Legal commenters will ask HHS to require issuers to provide real-time enrollment confirmation and standardized effective date disclosures when individuals purchase coverage during initial/annual open enrollment (§147.104(b)(1)(ii)).

Health plans will request clarification on the interaction between the limited SEP requirement (§147.104(b)(2)(i)) and off-Exchange coverage rules, specifically which triggering events are excluded for off-Exchange policies to avoid inconsistent practices.

Consumer groups will argue the exclusions for off-Exchange coverage in providing limited open enrollment (§147.104(b)(2)(i)) could create loopholes that deny consumers SEP protections and ask for alignment of Exchange and off-Exchange SEP rules.

Issuers will request specific timelines and secure transmission standards for providing enrollment, claims, encounter, and medical record documentation to auditors (§153.630(b)(6)) to avoid compliance uncertainty and privacy breaches.

Privacy and cybersecurity experts will demand that §153.630(b)(6) require encrypted transfers and minimum authentication methods when issuers furnish medical records to auditors, and request liability limits if HHS fails to specify standards.

Behavioral health providers will support allowing a signed mental/behavioral health assessment in lieu of full records (§153.630(b)(6)) but request a narrow, well-defined template and strict limits on what information can be included to protect patient privacy.

Civil liberties organizations will caution that permitting signed behavioral health assessments in place of full records (§153.630(b)(6)) risks coercing clinicians into disclosing sensitive information; they will request stricter limits on content and an appeals process.

Mental health providers will request clearer guidance on acceptable attestation language and legal basis when certifying they are “prohibited by privacy laws” from providing full records (§153.630(b)(6)) so providers are not exposed to legal risk.

Legal experts will warn that the required attestation (§153.630(b)(6)) could conflict with state mandatory reporting laws and request HHS add a safe-harbor for providers who furnish assessments in good faith.

Auditing firms will request that HHS publish the “manner and timeframe” for reporting inter-rater reliability (§153.630(b)(8)) in advance and provide a transition period so auditors can adapt methodologies and software.

Statisticians and methodological experts will request that HHS define the statistical methods, sample sizes, and confidence intervals required when measuring inter-rater reliability (§153.630(b)(8)) to ensure comparability across auditors.

Auditors and issuers will challenge the 95% required consistency in review outcomes (§153.630(b)(8)), calling it unachievable for complex clinical determinations; they will request a lower standard (e.g., 85–90%) or alternative risk-adjusted metrics outside the 2015–2016 exception.

Consumer protection advocates will argue the 95% consistency requirement (§153.630(b)(8)) is necessary to prevent audit variability and gaming, but will request clarity on remediation steps if auditors fail to meet the threshold.

Industry trade groups will request due process protections and a transparent penalty schedule if HHS imposes civil money penalties under §153.630(b)(9), including notice, cure periods, and appeal rights before penalties are levied.

Compliance officers will ask that HHS limit imposition of civil money penalties (§153.630(b)(9)) to cases of egregious or repeated violations and provide factors for downward adjustment (size of issuer, good-faith efforts, corrective action).

Issuers will request HHS allow grace periods or written extension authority before treating “failure to engage an initial validation auditor” (§153.630(b)(9)(i)) as a penalty trigger, noting contracting delays and auditor shortages.

Industry commenters will seek a narrow definition of “misconduct or substantial non-compliance” (§153.630(b)(9)(iii)) to avoid subjective enforcement and to align with existing audit standards and corrective action plans.

Legal groups will request HHS define “intentionally or recklessly misrepresents or falsifies information” (§153.630(b)(9)(iv)) with scienter standards and examples, and to require HHS prove intent before imposing the most severe penalties.

raw_output:
[P1] The January 24, 2018 deadline for Michigan reopening comments is already past and the rule should clarify how late comments will be handled or provide an extended comment period to allow meaningful participation.

[P1] Requiring comments to be "received on or before January 24, 2018" creates uncertainty about time zone and electronic timestamping; the rule should specify the cutoff time (e.g., 11:59 PM EST) and how timestamps on Regulations.gov or emails will be interpreted.

[P2] The instruction to identify comments by Docket ID No. EPA–R05–OAR–2007–1092 should be reiterated in any email subject line requirements; the proposed text does not specify whether missing the docket ID will result in rejection.

[P2] Providing a single email contact (damico.genvieve@epa.gov) may create a bottleneck; commenters request alternate contacts or confirmation receipts for emailed submissions to ensure comments are received.

[P3] The requirement to "follow the online instructions" on Regulations.gov is vague; commenters request a link to the precise instructions or a brief description of acceptable file types and size limits.

[P4] The prohibition on editing or removing comments after submission on Regulations.gov raises privacy concerns for individuals who may inadvertently disclose sensitive information; the agency should allow limited redaction or withdrawal requests handled by staff.

[P5] EPA's permission to publish received comments should be accompanied by a clear policy on redaction of personal contact information and how to request non-public posting for sensitive identifiers.

[P6] The prohibition on submitting CBI electronically is unclear about the alternative secure submission methods; commenters request explicit instructions for submitting CBI (e.g., encrypted email, mail, hand-delivery) and how it will be handled.

[P7] Requiring multimedia submissions to include a written comment disadvantages some stakeholders (e.g., people with disabilities or those who speak only in audio formats); the rule should allow multimedia alone if accompanied by a transcript or acceptable alternate format.

[P8] Stating that the written comment is the "official submission" could discourage submission of supplemental materials elsewhere; commenters ask for clarification whether linked materials hosted off-site can be considered part of the record if the written comment references them.

[P9] EPA's general refusal to consider materials located outside the primary submission system could preclude submission of very large supporting datasets; commenters request an explicit exception and guidance on submitting large datasets (e.g., via FTP, physical media) and how they will be docketed.

[P10] The February 8, 2018 deadline for Oklahoma UST comments is in the past — the rule should state whether late comments will be accepted and, if not, provide an extension for adequate public participation.

[P11] The requirement to identify comments by docket EPA–R06–UST–2017–0504 is strict; stakeholders request confirmation that including the docket number in the body of the email or on mailed envelopes is sufficient.

[P12] The permission to submit via Regulations.gov should include guidance on what to do if the portal is down (e.g., alternative submission window or contacts).

[P13] Using a single email (lincoln.audray@epa.gov) as an alternative electronic submission route raises concerns about email security and retention; commenters ask whether emailed comments will be posted to Regulations.gov and how attachments will be handled.

[P14] Mailing comments to Audray Lincoln should include a snail-mail physical address in the rule text; the current summary is insufficient for mailed submissions and may lead to misdirected comments.

[P15] Requiring vessels and persons to "expeditiously transit" the danger zone when a small arms range is in use is vague; maritime operators request clear operational definitions (e.g., minimum transit speed or maximum permitted loiter time) to avoid enforcement uncertainty.

[P16] The prohibition on anchoring or loitering within the danger zone while the range is in use could interfere with legitimate maritime safety operations (e.g., disabled vessels); the rule should provide exceptions for vessels in distress and a process to request temporary waivers.

[P17] Requiring range activities to halt until all vessels are cleared imposes a duty on range operators to monitor and enforce vessel clearance; range operators request more specific procedures and timelines for clearing actions and notification responsibilities.

[P18] The obligation to allow normal maritime traffic, including anchoring/loitering when the range is not in use, is appropriate but needs specification of how the transition from "in use" to "not in use" is communicated to the public and mariners.

[P19] The requirement to display a red flag from a conspicuous shore location when the range is in use may be impractical at remote ranges without nearby shore infrastructure; the rule should allow alternative signaling methods and define "conspicuous and easily-seen location."

[P20] Mandating strobe lights at night in lieu of flags is acceptable but needs performance standards (e.g., strobe intensity, flash rate, visibility range) to ensure mariner safety.

[P21] Prohibiting range use when visibility is equal to or less than weapon maximum range is overly conservative and vague — commenters request a clear definition of "visibility" measurement method and whether weather instruments or human observation controls enforcement.

[P22] Assigning enforcement of public access restrictions to the Commander, Joint Region Marianas and delegated agencies lacks clarity about which agencies may be delegated and what enforcement authority they will possess; stakeholders request a list of potential delegable agencies and legal basis for delegation.

[P23] The Clean Air Act §110(a)(2)(C) requirement that SIPs include a permitting program for construction/modification is standard; environmental advocates will comment that the Michigan SIP submission must explicitly demonstrate how it assures attainment of each relevant NAAQS with quantitative modeling.

[P24] Rule 205's requirement that permits include limitations to restrict potential to emit below major thresholds should require uniform calculation methods and conservative assumptions; industry requests explicit guidance on what emission factors, capacity assumptions, and operating hours are acceptable.

[P25] The obligation that permits include practically enforceable emission limits and operational constraints needs specific examples of acceptable monitoring, recordkeeping, and testing to demonstrate enforceability; without that, SIP approvability is questionable.

[P26] Reference to Michigan Act 451's public participation process for draft permits requires confirmation that the state's 324.5511(3) procedure meets federal minimum public-participation requirements — commenters will demand a crosswalk showing equivalence to 40 CFR 124.

[P27] Granting MDEQ discretion to approve permits without following section 324.5511(3) if limits restrict potential to emit to less than 90% of thresholds undermines federal public notice principles; environmental groups will object and argue that any use of synthetic minor limits should still require full public notice and comment.

[P27] The 90% threshold allowing bypass of the public participation process is arbitrary and too high; commenters propose lowering it to 50% (or requiring public notice for any synthetic minor limitation) to prevent misuse.

[P28] Michigan's de minimis threshold of 50% for synthetic minor sources is inconsistent with federal practice and could improperly allow significant emissions increases; industry supports clarity that 50% is acceptable, but environmental groups will challenge its adequacy and request health-based justification.

[P29] Section 324.5511(3)'s 30-day public comment period and hearing timing requirements must be reconciled with EPA's requirement for "public participation" under the NSR program (often 30 days but with specific notification methods); commenters ask for clarity on whether Michigan's procedures meet federal standards for major sources.

[P30] Setting public comment periods to "at least 30 days" may be insufficient for complex permits with technical materials; community groups request longer comment periods (e.g., 45–60 days) for major source permits and for supplemental modeling.

[P31] The requirement of at least 30-day notice before hearings should specify who must be notified (e.g., adjacent communities, tribes, local governments) and the methods of notice (newspaper, website, direct mail).

[P32] EPA's policy requiring public participation for major source and major modification permitting must be explicitly incorporated into Michigan's SIP approval; legal commenters will demand that the SIP demonstrate procedural equivalence, including public notice, comment, and hearing availability.

[P33] Part 19/R 336.2817 obligations for Part 19 permits to meet federal NSR minima require that Michigan provide enforceable permit terms and PSD/nonattainment review procedures; commenters request the state to specify offsets, BACT/LAER procedures, and monitoring requirements.

[P34] The April 26, 2019 deadline for comments on this proposed rule should be extended if substantive permitting or SIP changes are made after initial notice; affected stakeholders will request a reopening of the comment period in that event.

[P35] The requirement to identify comments by Docket ID EPA–R05–OAR–2007–1092 in submissions should clarify acceptable variations (e.g., inclusion of hyphens or spacing) to avoid misfiling.

[P36] The obligation to follow Regulations.gov submission instructions should state how to handle large attachments and whether compressed files or hyperlinks are acceptable if file-size limits prevent uploading.

[P37] The prohibition on submitting CBI electronically is unclear whether redaction of CBI in electronic submissions is acceptable; businesses need explicit procedures on how to mark submissions partially CBI and how redacted public versions will be posted.

Requiring comments to be "received on or before January 24, 2018" creates uncertainty about time zone and electronic timestamping; the rule should specify the cutoff time (e.g., 11:59 PM EST) and how timestamps on Regulations.gov or emails will be interpreted.

The instruction to identify comments by Docket ID No. EPA–R05–OAR–2007–1092 should be reiterated in any email subject line requirements; the proposed text does not specify whether missing the docket ID will result in rejection.

Providing a single email contact (damico.genvieve@epa.gov) may create a bottleneck; commenters request alternate contacts or confirmation receipts for emailed submissions to ensure comments are received.
The requirement to "follow the online instructions" on Regulations.gov is vague; commenters request a link to the precise instructions or a brief description of acceptable file types and size limits.

The prohibition on editing or removing comments after submission on Regulations.gov raises privacy concerns for individuals who may inadvertently disclose sensitive information; the agency should allow limited redaction or withdrawal requests handled by staff.
EPA's permission to publish received comments should be accompanied by a clear policy on redaction of personal contact information and how to request non-public posting for sensitive identifiers.

The prohibition on submitting CBI electronically is unclear about the alternative secure submission methods; commenters request explicit instructions for submitting CBI (e.g., encrypted email, mail, hand-delivery) and how it will be handled.

Requiring multimedia submissions to include a written comment disadvantages some stakeholders (e.g., people with disabilities or those who speak only in audio formats); the rule should allow multimedia alone if accompanied by a transcript or acceptable alternate format.

Stating that the written comment is the "official submission" could discourage submission of supplemental materials elsewhere; commenters ask for clarification whether linked materials hosted off-site can be considered part of the record if the written comment references them.

EPA's general refusal to consider materials located outside the primary submission system could preclude submission of very large supporting datasets; commenters request an explicit exception and guidance on submitting large datasets (e.g., via FTP, physical media) and how they will be docketed.

The February 8, 2018 deadline for Oklahoma UST comments is in the past — the rule should state whether late comments will be accepted and, if not, provide an extension for adequate public participation.

The requirement to identify comments by docket EPA–R06–UST–2017–0504 is strict; stakeholders request confirmation that including the docket number in the body of the email or on mailed envelopes is sufficient.
The permission to submit via Regulations.gov should include guidance on what to do if the portal is down (e.g., alternative submission window or contacts).

Using a single email (lincoln.audray@epa.gov) as an alternative electronic submission route raises concerns about email security and retention; commenters ask whether emailed comments will be posted to Regulations.gov and how attachments will be handled.
Mailing comments to Audray Lincoln should include a snail-mail physical address in the rule text; the current summary is insufficient for mailed submissions and may lead to misdirected comments.

Requiring vessels and persons to "expeditiously transit" the danger zone when a small arms range is in use is vague; maritime operators request clear operational definitions (e.g., minimum transit speed or maximum permitted loiter time) to avoid enforcement uncertainty.

The prohibition on anchoring or loitering within the danger zone while the range is in use could interfere with legitimate maritime safety operations (e.g., disabled vessels); the rule should provide exceptions for vessels in distress and a process to request temporary waivers.

Requiring range activities to halt until all vessels are cleared imposes a duty on range operators to monitor and enforce vessel clearance; range operators request more specific procedures and timelines for clearing actions and notification responsibilities.

The obligation to allow normal maritime traffic, including anchoring/loitering when the range is not in use, is appropriate but needs specification of how the transition from "in use" to "not in use" is communicated to the public and mariners.

The requirement to display a red flag from a conspicuous shore location when the range is in use may be impractical at remote ranges without nearby shore infrastructure; the rule should allow alternative signaling methods and define "conspicuous and easily-seen location."
Mandating strobe lights at night in lieu of flags is acceptable but needs performance standards (e.g., strobe intensity, flash rate, visibility range) to ensure mariner safety.

Prohibiting range use when visibility is equal to or less than weapon maximum range is overly conservative and vague — commenters request a clear definition of "visibility" measurement method and whether weather instruments or human observation controls enforcement.

raw_output:
[P1] The 60-calendar-day compliance deadline in § 751.405(a) is unreasonably short for downstream manufacturers and importers to reformulate or identify alternative suppliers for DecaBDE-containing components and should be extended to at least 12–24 months.

[P1] The proposed blanket prohibition in § 751.405(a) does not provide a clear grandfathering mechanism for existing inventory in commerce at the time the rule becomes effective; commenters request explicit language allowing sale of pre-rule inventory produced before the effective date.

[P1] The rule fails to define "manufacture, processing, and distribution in commerce" for DecaBDE consistently with other statutes; commenters request definitions or cross-references to 15 U.S.C. § 2602 to avoid enforcement uncertainty.

[P2] The recycling exception in § 751.405(a)(1) lacks operational guidance on how recyclers must demonstrate that "no new DecaBDE is added during recycling"; commenters request specific testing protocols, chain-of-custody requirements, or certification procedures.

[P2] The exemption for recycled plastic in § 751.405(a)(1) should require labeling of recycled batches and downstream notification to purchasers to prevent inadvertent introduction of DecaBDE into consumer products.

[P2] Environmental justice and public health groups will comment that the recycling exception in § 751.405(a)(1) risks perpetuating environmental exposures in communities near recycling facilities and request the Agency conduct an EJ analysis and consider restricting recycling exemption in sensitive areas.

[P3] The allowance in § 751.405(a)(2) for finished products made from recycled plastic containing DecaBDE should be limited to non-consumer, industrial uses; as drafted it could permit DecaBDE in children's products and bedding, posing unacceptable risks.

[P3] Industry trade associations may applaud § 751.405(a)(2) but request clarification on whether blending recycled plastic with virgin material (where no new DecaBDE added) is covered and whether dilution affects applicability.

[P4] The replacement-parts exception in § 751.405(a)(3) for motor vehicles and aircraft is necessary but ambiguous: commenters ask whether aftermarket distributors, remanufacturers, and independent repair shops are covered and request explicit inclusion.

[P4] Safety and aviation stakeholders will request confirmatory language that parts subject to existing FAA or DOT safety mandates can continue to use DecaBDE when required, and ask for coordination with FAA to avoid grounding risks.

[P5] The three-year delayed allowance for DecaBDE in new aerospace vehicles (§ 751.405(a)(4)) is arbitrary; aerospace manufacturers ask for a longer phase-in (e.g., 5–7 years) to allow certification, testing, and redesign of parts.

[P5] Aviation safety groups will request that the Agency tie the § 751.405(a)(4) exception to specific certification requirements and provide an exemption process where safety-critical components can be reviewed on a case-by-case basis.

[P6] The 18-month delay for hospitality curtains (§ 751.405(a)(5)) is too short for the hospitality sector to transition inventory and existing contracts; hotel industry commenters request 36 months and clarity whether existing contracts for curtain supply are exempt.

[P6] Textile industry commenters ask whether flame-retardant performance standards that DecaBDE currently helps meet will require substitution by other chemicals and whether the Agency will issue guidance on acceptable alternatives for hospitality curtains under § 751.405(a)(5).

[P7] The three-year recordkeeping requirement in § 751.405(b)(1) imposes administrative burdens on small businesses; commenters request alignment with typical two-year retention schedules or provide a simplified compliance record template for SMEs.

[P7] Trade groups request clarification in § 751.405(b)(1) on the specific types of records required (e.g., purchase orders, test reports, certifications) and whether electronic records are acceptable; also request a safe harbor for de-identified aggregated records.

[P8] The exemption from recordkeeping in § 751.405(b)(2) for recycling activities is appropriate, but environmental NGOs argue that exempting recyclers from recordkeeping eliminates traceability and should be reconsidered or conditioned on facility-level reporting.

[P9] The 60-day prohibition deadline for PIP (3:1) processing and distribution in § 751.407(a)(1) is impracticable for industries that rely on long-term inventory and multi-step supply chains; industry asks for a 12–18 month compliance period.

[P10] The aviation hydraulic fluid exception in § 751.407(a)(1)(i) must require coordination with FAA and an explicit list of allowable formulations; aviation maintenance organizations request a petition process to add approved uses.

[P11] The lubricant and grease exception in § 751.407(a)(1)(ii) is overly broad and could allow PIP (3:1) in consumer automotive lubricants; commenters request limiting this exception to industrial and aviation-grade lubricants and adding concentration limits.

[P12] The allowance for use in new and replacement motor vehicle parts in § 751.407(a)(1)(iii) lacks temporal limits; auto manufacturers request a phasedown schedule or transition plan and clarification whether aftermarket importers are covered.

[P13] The prohibition on releasing PIP (3:1) to water in § 751.407(a)(2) is vague regarding what counts as a "release to water" (e.g., stormwater runoff from facilities, wastewater treatment effluent) and requests definitional clarity and compliance measurement methods.

[P13] Chemical manufacturers note that inadvertent trace discharges below analytical detection limits should be treated differently; they request de minimis thresholds or performance-based standards for § 751.407(a)(2).

[P14] The SDS notification requirement in § 751.407(b) to all recipients prior to or with shipment could conflict with downstream intermediaries that repack or reformulate; commenters request that distributors be allowed to include the text in transaction documents rather than amend SDSs immediately.

[P15] Requiring insertion of specified regulatory text into SDSs under § 751.407(b) may conflict with OSHA Hazard Communication Standard formatting and content requirements; legal commenters request confirmation that the SDS language is permitted and harmonized with OSHA.

[P16] Mandating the exact text in SDS Section 1.(c) (§ 751.407(b)(1)) may be legally problematic because Section 1(c) of SDS is typically supplier identification; commenters request allowance to place the required prohibition text in a different SDS section if necessary to comply with OSHA SDS format.

[P17] Requiring insertion of text in SDS Section 15 (§ 751.407(b)(2)) could create redundancy; downstream processors ask whether an electronic notification to immediate customers suffices for compliance instead of changing all SDS templates.

[P18] The three-year record retention for PIP (3:1) under § 751.407(c) duplicates other federal/state requirements and will impose extra burden; commenters request harmonization with existing recordkeeping periods (e.g., EPA TSCA or state programs) and template records.

[P19] The prohibition in § 751.409(a)(1) on distributing 2,4,6-TTBP in containers smaller than 55 gallons will disrupt small-scale formulators and aftermarket service providers who rely on 1–5 gallon containers; small businesses request an exemption or allow distribution in smaller containers for downstream professional users with documented controls.

[P19] Product stewardship advocates support § 751.409(a)(1) but ask the Agency to justify the 55-gallon threshold with data on exposure risk and to consider exceptions for sealed consumer end-use packaging that prevents exposure.

[P20] The ban on processing and distributing 2,4,6-TTBP for use as an oil and lubricant additive in § 751.409(a)(2) will eliminate a key additive for some high-temperature industrial applications; industry requests a limited-use exemption with required exposure controls and monitoring.

[P21] The three-year recordkeeping requirement for distributors of 2,4,6-TTBP (§ 751.409(b)) does not specify what constitutes "ordinary business records"; distributors request examples and acceptance of invoices and bills of lading as sufficient documentation.

[P22] The prohibition in § 751.411(a) on PCTP above 1% by weight lacks clear analytical methodology for determining concentrations in complex formulations and articles; manufacturers request standardized test methods and a tolerance for measurement uncertainty.

[P22] Small importers and retailers raise concern that § 751.411(a) will require reformulating a broad array of products; they request an exemption for sealed consumer products where migration studies show negligible exposure.

[P23] The conditional allowance in § 751.411(a) permitting ≤1% PCTP (by weight) is arbitrary; health advocates request a lower threshold (e.g., 0.1%) and stronger justification based on toxicological evidence.

[P23] Manufacturers ask whether the 1% threshold is per article, per component, or per finished product and request clarification that the limit applies to total PCTP concentration in the finished article.

[P24] The three-year retention requirement in § 751.411(b) for PCTP compliance records should allow electronic recordkeeping and remote access, and request an explicit provision that confidential business information may be redacted consistent with EPA procedures.

[P7] Legal experts will comment that the rule does not explain enforcement mechanisms or penalties for failure to maintain records under §§ 751.405(b)(1), 751.407(c), 751.409(b), and 751.411(b); commenters request the Agency include enforcement guidance and penalty ranges.

[P1] The rule should include an implementation FAQ and compliance assistance program for small businesses to interpret exemptions (P2–P6) and recordkeeping obligations (P7–P8).

[P1] The requirement that Part D sponsors and prescribers comply with the NCPDP SCRIPT Implementation Guide (Version 2017071) by Jan 1, 2021 is unworkable because it gives stakeholders insufficient lead time to implement and test system changes; we request at least a 12–18 month phased implementation period or a later effective date.

[P1] Requiring both Part D sponsors and prescribers to comply with the specified SCRIPT version creates unmatched timing and resource burdens for small provider practices and independent pharmacies that lack IT support; CMS should provide funding, technical assistance, or an exceptions process for small entities.

[P1] The rule lacks clarity about whether intermediaries (e.g., e-prescribing vendors, EHR vendors, pharmacy benefit managers) are required to be compliant or merely "encouraged"; we request explicit assignment of obligations to e-prescribing/EHR vendors and PBMs that facilitate prior authorization transactions.

[P1] Specifying a single dated version (2017071) of the SCRIPT standard without an automatic update mechanism will create obsolescence and interoperability gaps; the rule should adopt any subsequent NCPDP SCRIPT versions issued after a public-notice period or include a process for updating the referenced standard.

[P1] There is no description of acceptable compliance testing or certification criteria; the rule should require a formal conformance testing/certification process (or recognize existing certification bodies) so that sponsors and prescribers can demonstrate compliance.

[P1] The provision does not address handling of secure transmission, authentication, and patient privacy elements required by HIPAA; commenters request explicit requirements for secure transport (e.g., TLS), identity proofing, and auditing for PA transactions.

[P1] The rule fails to state whether the SCRIPT transactions will be mandatory for all prior authorizations or only for those "specified" in the preamble; CMS must clarify the scope — e.g., whether step therapy, quantity limits, formulary exceptions are included.

[P1] Imposing regulatory obligations on prescribers without addressing state laws that govern electronic signatures and prescription workflows may create conflicts; request coordination with state medical boards and a statement about preemption or accommodation.

[P2] Requiring support for PAInitiationRequest and PAInitiationResponse is reasonable in principle, but the rule does not define required response timeframes for sponsors to send PAInitiationResponses; commenters request explicit maximum processing times (e.g., within X business days) to avoid delays.

[P2] The rule should specify required and optional data elements within PAInitiationRequest/Response (e.g., clinical rationale, prior medications tried, lab values) to ensure uniformity; otherwise implementers will exchange inconsistent data, defeating interoperability.

[P2] There is no guidance on how to handle missing or incomplete data in PAInitiationRequest messages; the rule should require sponsors to request missing clinical info via a defined workflow and prohibit denial solely for missing optional elements.

[P2] The regulation does not address acknowledgement/error handling for PAInitiationRequest/Response transactions (e.g., what constitutes successful receipt, retry logic); commenters request explicit requirements for acknowledgements and error codes.

[P2] Small prescribers using third-party e-prescribing systems may incur costs to add support for PAInitiationRequest/Response; CMS should require vendors to certify low-cost implementation options or offer a hardship exemption for low-volume prescribers.

[P3] Mandating PARequest and PAResponse without clear content standards risks variability; commenters request that CMS define standardized clinical fields, codable fields (e.g., SNOMED, LOINC), and mapping expectations to avoid free-text narratives that impede automation.

[P3] The rule does not specify turnaround times for PAResponse after receipt of PARequest; commenters (patient advocates and providers) request binding time limits (e.g., 72 hours for urgent, 7 calendar days for standard) to prevent patient harm.

[P3] There is no prohibition on Part D sponsors using PAResponse messaging to provide generic or insufficient justification for denials; sponsors should be required to include denial rationale, applicable clinical criteria, and appeal instructions in the PAResponse.

[P3] The provision lacks guidance on concurrent processing across multiple payors or coordination when a patient has dual coverage; commenters request rules for reconciliation and which sponsor must reply when multiple plans are involved.

[P3] Technical interoperability issues (message size limits, attachments for clinical documents) are not addressed for PARequest/PAResponse; the rule should authorize or require support for document attachments (and specify acceptable formats) within SCRIPT messages.

[P4] Mandating PAAppealRequest and PAAppealResponse is positive, but the rule fails to define timelines for appeals adjudication once a PAAppealRequest is received; commenters request statutory timeframes consistent with existing Part D appeal deadlines.

[P4] The rule should require that PAAppealResponse include binding explanations tied to the plan’s clinical criteria and cite the evidence or guideline used; generic or templated responses will not protect patient rights.

[P4] There is no mention of an external review trigger if PAAppealResponse upholds a denial; commenters request that the regulation incorporate notification steps and a mechanism to escalate to external review or expedited appeals when clinically necessary.

[P4] The proposal does not address whether the submission of a PAAppealRequest tolls or extends existing time limits for patient access to medications; CMS should clarify the effect on coverage start dates and continuity of therapy during appeals.

[P4] The rule does not require audit logs or patient access to the content of PAAppealResponse messages; patient advocates request that patients have the right to receive copies of appeal communications electronically.

[P5] Requiring PACancelRequest and PACancelResponse is appropriate, but CMS must define acceptable reasons and authorization process for cancellations (e.g., prescriber-initiated, patient-requested, duplicate requests); without limits, cancellations could be abused.

[P5] The rule does not clarify how PACancelRequest interacts with in-progress PARequest/PAAppealRequest processing; commenters request rules to prevent race conditions (e.g., cancelling after an approval has been issued) and to require confirmation of status before cancellation.

[P5] The regulation should require that PACancelResponse include the current status and whether any prior authorizations already granted remain in force; otherwise prescribers and pharmacies could dispense medications wrongly assuming cancellation.

[P5] There is no security or authentication standard specified for PACancel transactions to prevent unauthorized cancellations; commenters request strong authentication of requestors (e.g., provider NPI + secure credentials) and logging.

[P5] Pharmacy stakeholders note that PACancelRequest could be used by sponsors to cancel PAs as a cost-containment tactic without notifying prescribers or patients; CMS should prohibit unilateral cancellations that interrupt therapy without clinician/patient notice and allow contestability.

General/comments across provisions:
[P1] The rule lacks a compliance enforcement mechanism and penalties for noncompliance; request clarity on enforcement, remedies, and whether civil monetary penalties or corrective action plans will be used.

[P1] The proposal does not include an implementation support plan (education, technical assistance, sample messages, test harness); CMS should fund a national testing environment to reduce deployment failures.

[P1] Legal commenters note potential HIPAA/BaAs implications when third-party vendors exchange PA transactions; request guidance on business associate responsibilities and liability when intermediaries process SCRIPT messages.

[P1] The regulation must address language/accessibility requirements (e.g., non-English messages, patients with disabilities) when appeal or denial information is exchanged electronically; request standards for translations and accessible formats.

[P1] The rule should include metrics and reporting requirements (e.g., rates of electronic PA adoption, average response times) and require CMS to publish periodic performance dashboards to monitor industry compliance and patient impact.

[P1] The requirement that shipping containers "must comply with the listed requirements" is unacceptably vague without dimensional standards, material specifications, or testing/inspection protocols; industry needs clear engineering criteria and acceptable certification processes.

[P2] Requiring containers to be "new or properly cleaned and disinfected" is economically burdensome for smaller exporters if acceptable disinfectants, contact times, and verification documentation are not specified; please list approved disinfectants and required log documentation.

[P2] The phrase "sufficiently reduces the risk" in §93.302(a)(1) is subjective and could lead to inconsistent enforcement; we request a quantitative or procedural standard (e.g., validated log reduction for specified pathogens, or EPA-registered disinfectants and procedures).

[P3] §93.302(a)(2) mandates containers be "of sufficient size and construction" but gives no minimum cubic feet per animal, headroom, door size, ventilation rates, or shoring requirements; specify measurable size and construction standards or reference an accepted industry standard.

[P4] The prohibition on stocking density that "impinges on safety" (§93.302(a)(3)) lacks numeric stocking density limits to ensure animal welfare; propose specific maximum density values by weight/class of equine or require compliance with recognized welfare standards.

[P5] Allowing the Administrator to approve alternatives to IATA LAR (§93.302(a)(4)) is reasonable, but commenters request transparency: publish criteria and a public docket for alternative guidance approvals to avoid arbitrary deviations from IATA.

[P6] §93.307's blanket prohibition on landing any horse-related articles (manure, fodder, equipment) is impractical for long-distance transports where removal of waste may be needed for biosecurity and sanitation; allow limited, inspected landing for sanitary disposal with proper containment.

[P7] The exception in §93.307 permitting inspector-directed restrictions lacks timeframes and procedures; importers need advance notice, standard operating procedures, and an appeals process if the inspector imposes restrictive measures that impede logistics.

[P8] Requiring Spanish Pure Breed horses to have been in Spain for 60 days (§93.301(d)(1)(ii)(A)) is unduly restrictive for owners who travel between EU countries; allow alternative demonstration of continuous residency in EU equivalently low-risk regions with supporting movement records and testing.

[P9] The certificate endorsement by a "salaried veterinary officer of the exporting national government" (§93.314(a)) will disadvantage countries that use accredited private veterinarians for export certification; permit recognized accredited veterinarians under standardized oversight when equivalent government signatories are unavailable.

[P10] The certificate content requirement (§93.314(a)) is extensive but does not specify a standardized form; request APHIS to provide model electronic and paper templates to minimize noncompliance and processing delays.

[P11] The 60-day regional residency requirement in certificates (§93.314(a)(1)) can be impossible to document for transient competition horses; propose acceptance of continuous movement records, entry/exit stamps, and validated stabling records as equivalent proof.

[P12] The gelding/castration rule (§93.314(a)(4)) that forbids gelding within 14 days unless accompanied by a castration certificate is impractical for emergency veterinary procedures performed during transit; allow retrospective veterinary reports for emergency castrations and clarify acceptable evidence.

[P13] Requiring a pre-export examination within 48 hours endorsed by a salaried veterinary medical officer (§93.314(a)(5)) will delay exports from countries lacking sufficient government staff; allow accredited private veterinarians with digital signatures and rapid electronic submission to APHIS.

[P14] The 12-month absence from CEM-affected regions (§93.314(a)(7)(i)) is overly broad and does not account for controlled biosecure facilities; allow exception where horses have been continuously housed in APHIS-approved isolation facilities with testing demonstrating absence of CEM.

[P15] Permitting electronic issuance/presentation of documents (§93.314(d)) is welcome, but the rule should require that the electronic system supports verifiable digital signatures, tamper-evident PDFs, and an API for border agencies to verify in real-time.

[P16] The EIA testing window of 180 days for horses from Canada (§93.317(a)) may not align with competition/test schedules; consider extending to 12 months with supplemental on-arrival testing, or allow recent negative tests plus EIA-free herd documentation.

[P17] Requiring blood draw within 180 days (§93.317(a)) without specifying time of laboratory reporting risks exports where testing turnaround is delayed; clarify that the draw date is controlling and require laboratory report upload before export.

[P18] The requirement that the EIA test be conducted in a laboratory approved by Canada's Department of Agriculture or USDA (§93.317(a)) may exclude accredited private labs; publish an explicit list of acceptable labs and the approval criteria, and allow equivalent third-country lab approvals with verification.

[P19] Certificates for Canadian horses must be issued and endorsed by a salaried Canadian Government veterinarian (§93.317(a)) — this will create bottlenecks at peak times; authorize CFIA-accredited veterinarians to sign when government staff are unavailable, with electronic attestation to CFIA.

[P20] The import permit requirement for horses from/transiting Central America or West Indies (§93.319) increases administrative burden and costs; request a streamlined permit process with expedited electronic approvals and clear timelines (e.g., decision within 5 business days).

[P21] Requiring two copies of the declaration (§93.319) is antiquated if electronic submissions are permitted (§93.314(d)); update cross-references to allow electronic submission in lieu of paper duplicate copies.

[P22] Quarantine facility import permits (§93.321) for horses quarantined at U.S. facilities create an additional bureaucratic step; clarify whether one permit may cover multiple horses of the same shipment and allow concurrent permit processing.

[P23] Mandatory quarantine at designated ports for horses from VEE-affected regions (§93.308(a)(1)) could shut off certain trade lanes; define which ports are designated, their geographic distribution, and provide cost estimates and timelines for quarantine processing.

[P24] Stating each imported horse must have an import permit at time of importation (§93.308(a)(1)) is unrealistic for transits with last-minute changes; allow conditional permits or electronic pre-approval with validated credentials to prevent denied entry at ports.

[P25] Maintaining a VEE-affected regions list on APHIS website (§93.308(a)(1)(i)) is sensible, but APHIS must commit to daily updates and email subscription alerts to notify stakeholders immediately when a region is added or removed.

[P26] Adding regions to the VEE list based on "reliable reports" (§93.308(a)(1)(ii)) requires transparency about what constitutes "reliable"; define required evidence (e.g., laboratory confirmation, OIE reports) and allow affected countries to submit data before listing.

[P27] The process for removing regions from the VEE list (§93.308(a)(1)(ii)) should include timelines and public criteria per §92.2; industry requests a maximum review period (e.g., 60 days) after receipt of official eradication data.

[P28] Allowing importation from screwworm regions only if requirements are met (§93.308(a)(3)) is appropriate, but the list of "other applicable parts" should be enumerated to avoid surprise obligations at ports.

[P29] The ivermectin treatment 3–5 days before export (§93.308(a)(3)(i)) should specify acceptable ivermectin formulations, doses (e.g., mg/kg), route of administration, and whether pour-on or injectable products are acceptable per label directions.

[P30] Requiring examination by a full-time salaried veterinary official within 24 hours before shipment for screwworm (§93.308(a)(3)(ii)) excludes exports from countries relying on accredited private vets; allow examinations by accredited veterinarians whose credentials are verified by the exporting government.

[P31] The requirement to treat detected screwworm infestation until elimination (§93.308(a)(3)(ii)) needs defined treatment protocols and time-to-clearance expectations to plan quarantine and export schedules.

[P32] Mandating treatment of visible wounds with 5% coumaphos dust at loading (§93.308(a)(3)(iii)) raises animal welfare concerns because coumaphos can be an irritant; provide alternative approved treatments and safety instructions for handlers, and require PPE specifications.

[P33] The certification signed by a "full-time salaried veterinary official" for screwworm (§93.308(a)(3)(iv)) may be infeasible in regions without such officials; allow equivalent signed attestations by authorized veterinary officers with an identification/credential verification mechanism.

[P34] Seven-day quarantine at designated ports for screwworm (§93.308(a)(3)(v)) plus mandatory holding at the animal import center for at least 7 days (§93.308(a)(3)(vii)) duplicates requirements and may double-charge owners; reconcile wording to clarify whether these are concurrent or cumulative and disclose quarantine fees.

[P35] The post-arrival 24-hour screwworm examination (§93.308(a)(3)(vi)) that includes external genitalia is invasive; require informed owner consent, veterinary sedation protocols, and specify who bears costs for sedation and potential injuries.

[P36] Holding horses at the animal import center for a minimum of 7 days (§93.308(a)(3)(vii)) will cause welfare and expense issues for competition horses; propose an accelerated protocol for horses with verifiable pre-export treatments and negative molecular testing on arrival.

[P37] On-day-7 examination costs borne by owner/broker (§93.308(a)(3)(vii)) should be capped or estimated in advance by APHIS; require APHIS to publish fee schedules and allow payment options to avoid detention due to unpaid fees.

[P38] Requiring male horses to be tranquilized/sedated for genital examination (§93.308(a)(3)(vii)) raises animal safety and liability concerns; require that sedation be performed only by licensed veterinarians, with written sedation protocols and monitoring, and specify drug classes/doses.

[P39] The rule should specify the actions and timelines for treatment and re-examination if screwworm is detected at day 7 (§93.308(a)(3)(vii)); without timelines, horses could be held indefinitely, increasing costs and animal stress.

[P40] Mandatory permanent identification of mares used to test stallions for CEM (§93.301(e)(4)(i)) is reasonable, but the rule should allow alternative modern identification methods (e.g., microchip) as APHIS-approved methods to reduce animal discomfort from hot iron branding.

[P41] Limiting applicators who apply permanent marks to inspectors, State inspectors, or accredited veterinarians (§93.301(e)(4)(i)) will slow testing programs in remote areas; permit trained and certified technicians under veterinarian supervision with audit controls.

[P42] The specified marking methods (hot iron, freezemarking, lip tattoo) (§93.301(e)(4)(i)) are archaic and have welfare impacts; request APHIS broaden the list to include microchipping and encourage noninvasive methods as primary options.

[P43] The 2-inch minimum size for hot iron/freezemarking (§93.301(e)(4)(i)) is excessive and visible scarring may affect sale value; allow smaller marks or alternative placements, and permit microchip plus certificate as equivalent identification.

[P44] The lip tattoo minimum size specifications (§93.301(e)(4)(i)) may cause pain and mucosal injury; require use of veterinary anesthesia/analgesia protocols and allow microchips as equivalent to lip tattoo.

[P45] Requiring State oversight during test breeding of quarantined stallions (§93.301(h)(4)) could be logistically impossible in states with limited veterinary inspectors; allow APHIS-certified private veterinarians to provide oversight under state authorization.

[P46] Maintaining a list of States approved to receive older stallions on the APHIS website (§93.301(h)(7)) is helpful, but APHIS must publish the approval criteria and provide an appeals mechanism for states denied listing.

[P47] Providing lists via postal mail, fax, or email upon request (§93.301(h)(7)) is insufficient; offer an automated subscription service with real-time updates and machine-readable formats (CSV, JSON) for industry systems.

[P48] The similar list requirement for mares (§93.301(h)(8)) should include anticipated capacity and biosecurity requirements for listed states so importers can plan logistics and avoid surprise rejections.

[P49] Requiring APHIS to provide lists by fax (§93.301(h)(8)) is outdated; remove fax as required delivery and emphasize secure electronic delivery with authentication.

[P50] Publishing a screwworm-affected regions list on the APHIS website (§93.308(a)(3)) is necessary, but APHIS must coordinate with OIE and neighboring countries to prevent unilateral listings based on unverified local reports.

[P51] The criteria for adding regions to the screwworm list (§93.308(a)(3)) should include a chance for the affected country to submit counter-evidence before listing and specify an appeals process to avoid trade disruptions.

[P52] The removal process from the screwworm list (§93.308(a)(3)) must include a defined review timeline and objective metrics (surveillance hours, negative trap counts, laboratory confirmations) so stakeholders know when restrictions might lift.

Quarantine facility import permits (§93.321) for horses quarantined at U.S. facilities create an additional bureaucratic step; clarify whether one permit may cover multiple horses of the same shipment and allow concurrent permit processing.

Mandatory quarantine at designated ports for horses from VEE-affected regions (§93.308(a)(1)) could shut off certain trade lanes; define which ports are designated, their geographic distribution, and provide cost estimates and timelines for quarantine processing.

Stating each imported horse must have an import permit at time of importation (§93.308(a)(1)) is unrealistic for transits with last-minute changes; allow conditional permits or electronic pre-approval with validated credentials to prevent denied entry at ports.

Maintaining a VEE-affected regions list on APHIS website (§93.308(a)(1)(i)) is sensible, but APHIS must commit to daily updates and email subscription alerts to notify stakeholders immediately when a region is added or removed.

Adding regions to the VEE list based on "reliable reports" (§93.308(a)(1)(ii)) requires transparency about what constitutes "reliable"; define required evidence (e.g., laboratory confirmation, OIE reports) and allow affected countries to submit data before listing.

The process for removing regions from the VEE list (§93.308(a)(1)(ii)) should include timelines and public criteria per §92.2; industry requests a maximum review period (e.g., 60 days) after receipt of official eradication data.

Allowing importation from screwworm regions only if requirements are met (§93.308(a)(3)) is appropriate, but the list of "other applicable parts" should be enumerated to avoid surprise obligations at ports.

The ivermectin treatment 3–5 days before export (§93.308(a)(3)(i)) should specify acceptable ivermectin formulations, doses (e.g., mg/kg), route of administration, and whether pour-on or injectable products are acceptable per label directions.

Requiring examination by a full-time salaried veterinary official within 24 hours before shipment for screwworm (§93.308(a)(3)(ii)) excludes exports from countries relying on accredited private vets; allow examinations by accredited veterinarians whose credentials are verified by the exporting government.

The requirement to treat detected screwworm infestation until elimination (§93.308(a)(3)(ii)) needs defined treatment protocols and time-to-clearance expectations to plan quarantine and export schedules.

Mandating treatment of visible wounds with 5% coumaphos dust at loading (§93.308(a)(3)(iii)) raises animal welfare concerns because coumaphos can be an irritant; provide alternative approved treatments and safety instructions for handlers, and require PPE specifications.

The certification signed by a "full-time salaried veterinary official" for screwworm (§93.308(a)(3)(iv)) may be infeasible in regions without such officials; allow equivalent signed attestations by authorized veterinary officers with an identification/credential verification mechanism.

Seven-day quarantine at designated ports for screwworm (§93.308(a)(3)(v)) plus mandatory holding at the animal import center for at least 7 days (§93.308(a)(3)(vii)) duplicates requirements and may double-charge owners; reconcile wording to clarify whether these are concurrent or cumulative and disclose quarantine fees.

The post-arrival 24-hour screwworm examination (§93.308(a)(3)(vi)) that includes external genitalia is invasive; require informed owner consent, veterinary sedation protocols, and specify who bears costs for sedation and potential injuries.

Holding horses at the animal import center for a minimum of 7 days (§93.308(a)(3)(vii)) will cause welfare and expense issues for competition horses; propose an accelerated protocol for horses with verifiable pre-export treatments and negative molecular testing on arrival.

On-day-7 examination costs borne by owner/broker (§93.308(a)(3)(vii)) should be capped or estimated in advance by APHIS; require APHIS to publish fee schedules and allow payment options to avoid detention due to unpaid fees.

Requiring male horses to be tranquilized/sedated for genital examination (§93.308(a)(3)(vii)) raises animal safety and liability concerns; require that sedation be performed only by licensed veterinarians, with written sedation protocols and monitoring, and specify drug classes/doses.

The rule should specify the actions and timelines for treatment and re-examination if screwworm is detected at day 7 (§93.308(a)(3)(vii)); without timelines, horses could be held indefinitely, increasing costs and animal stress.

Mandatory permanent identification of mares used to test stallions for CEM (§93.301(e)(4)(i)) is reasonable, but the rule should allow alternative modern identification methods (e.g., microchip) as APHIS-approved methods to reduce animal discomfort from hot iron branding.

Limiting applicators who apply permanent marks to inspectors, State inspectors, or accredited veterinarians (§93.301(e)(4)(i)) will slow testing programs in remote areas; permit trained and certified technicians under veterinarian supervision with audit controls.

The specified marking methods (hot iron, freezemarking, lip tattoo) (§93.301(e)(4)(i)) are archaic and have welfare impacts; request APHIS broaden the list to include microchipping and encourage noninvasive methods as primary options.

The 2-inch minimum size for hot iron/freezemarking (§93.301(e)(4)(i)) is excessive and visible scarring may affect sale value; allow smaller marks or alternative placements, and permit microchip plus certificate as equivalent identification.

The lip tattoo minimum size specifications (§93.301(e)(4)(i)) may cause pain and mucosal injury; require use of veterinary anesthesia/analgesia protocols and allow microchips as equivalent to lip tattoo.

Requiring State oversight during test breeding of quarantined stallions (§93.301(h)(4)) could be logistically impossible in states with limited veterinary inspectors; allow APHIS-certified private veterinarians to provide oversight under state authorization.

Maintaining a list of States approved to receive older stallions on the APHIS website (§93.301(h)(7)) is helpful, but APHIS must publish the approval criteria and provide an appeals mechanism for states denied listing.

Providing lists via postal mail, fax, or email upon request (§93.301(h)(7)) is insufficient; offer an automated subscription service with real-time updates and machine-readable formats (CSV, JSON) for industry systems.

The similar list requirement for mares (§93.301(h)(8)) should include anticipated capacity and biosecurity requirements for listed states so importers can plan logistics and avoid surprise rejections.
Requiring APHIS to provide lists by fax (§93.301(h)(8)) is outdated; remove fax as required delivery and emphasize secure electronic delivery with authentication.

Publishing a screwworm-affected regions list on the APHIS website (§93.308(a)(3)) is necessary, but APHIS must coordinate with OIE and neighboring countries to prevent unilateral listings based on unverified local reports.

The criteria for adding regions to the screwworm list (§93.308(a)(3)) should include a chance for the affected country to submit counter-evidence before listing and specify an appeals process to avoid trade disruptions.

The removal process from the screwworm list (§93.308(a)(3)) must include a defined review timeline and objective metrics (surveillance hours, negative trap counts, laboratory confirmations) so stakeholders know when restrictions might lift.
