raw_output:
[P1] The rule does not specify the exact data elements and formats required in the annual compliance report under § 80.1451(a)(1); commenters ask EPA to publish a detailed template or XML/CSV schema to ensure consistent submissions and interoperability with obligated parties' compliance systems.

[P1] Industry requests clarification whether proprietary or confidential business information in the annual compliance reports may be redacted or submitted under a confidentiality claim and, if so, the process and criteria for EPA treatment of such claims.

[P1] Environmental NGOs request that § 80.1451(a)(1) require inclusion of year-over-year RIN transaction histories, fuel pathway certifications, and lifecycle emissions assumptions so the reports enable independent verification of compliance and environmental outcomes.

[P2] The phrasing “latest of the specified dates” in § 80.1451(f)(1)(i)(A) creates ambiguity; commenters ask EPA to clarify precedence rules among the three deadlines and provide an algorithmic example for determinations.

[P3] March 31 deadline in § 80.1451(f)(1)(i)(A)(1) is too short for small entities to compile attestable data; trade associations request extending to May 1 or allowing an automatic 60-day extension for firms with fewer than X employees.

[P4] The “next quarterly reporting deadline” trigger in § 80.1451(f)(1)(i)(A)(2) is unclear when the subsequent compliance-year RFS standards are issued mid-quarter; commenters request explicit definition of “after the date” and examples for mid-quarter effective dates.

[P5] The cross-reference in § 80.1451(f)(1)(i)(A)(3) to the prior compliance year’s reporting deadline could create cascading delays if prior deadlines were extended; commenters request a prohibition on using extended prior-year deadlines to push current-year submissions later.

[P6] Small refinery staggered deadlines in § 80.1451(f)(1)(i)(B)(1) for the 2019 compliance year unfairly compress audit timelines and may conflict with previously issued compliance guidance; small refinery groups request grandfathering of prior deadlines or a uniform deadline across small refineries.

[P7] The sequential small refinery submission schedule in § 80.1451(f)(1)(i)(B)(2) for 2020 risks misalignment with state-level reporting and quarterly blending reports; state agencies request EPA coordinate deadlines to avoid conflicting reporting windows.

[P8] For § 80.1451(f)(1)(i)(B)(3) (2021 small refinery deadline), operators warn that requiring consecutive rolling quarterly deadlines without clear notice periods will increase compliance costs and may cause late submissions; they request an advance published calendar for affected years.

[P9] § 80.1451(f)(1)(ii) imposes a uniform March 31 deadline on non-obligated parties without regard to when their operations occur; trade groups representing importers and exporters request flexibility or an alternative filing window aligned with their fiscal year.

[P10] Relying on EPA to calculate and publish the deadline under § 80.1451(f)(1)(iii) places significant reliance on EPA’s website; commenters ask EPA to commit to publishing deadlines at least 90 days in advance and to provide machine-readable deadline feeds (e.g., API or CSV) to prevent missed filings.

[P11] § 80.1464(d)(1)(i) requires annual attest engagement reports by the “latest” of specified dates but does not define acceptable attest standards; auditors request explicit reference to a recognized standard (e.g., AICPA SSAE 18 or PCAOB standards) for the attest engagement.

[P12] The June 1 deadline in § 80.1464(d)(1)(i)(A) may not provide auditors adequate time after March 31 reporting deadlines to complete attest engagements; accounting associations request a minimum 90-day window after final compliance submissions.

[P13] The conditional June 1 deadline tied to “at least 60 days after the annual compliance reporting deadline” in § 80.1464(d)(1)(i)(B) is confusing — commenters ask EPA to clarify whether the 60-day count is calendar or business days and to provide examples when the compliance reporting deadline itself was extended.

[P14] Small refinery deadlines for the 2019 attest in § 80.1464(d)(1)(ii)(A) may conflict with auditors’ availability given pandemic-related disruptions in 2020–2021; small refinery associations request an alternative grace period or allowance for third-party audit extensions.

[P15] The 2020 attest deadline in § 80.1464(d)(1)(ii)(B) creates potential duplication if the same auditor must also perform attest work for state or voluntary programs; auditors request harmonization of attest timing and acceptance of a single combined report covering multiple programs.

[P16] For the 2021 attest deadline in § 80.1464(d)(1)(ii)(C), commenters request clarity whether attest reports may be submitted electronically via EPA’s existing portals and whether wet signatures are required for the auditor’s opinion.

[P17] § 80.1464(d)(2) requires non-obligated parties to submit attest engagement reports by June 1 but does not specify who qualifies as a “non-obligated party”; commenters ask EPA to provide a clear definition and illustrative examples (e.g., exporters, foreign refiners, blenders with no domestic obligations).

[P18] Similar to reporting deadlines, relying on EPA to publish the attest reporting deadline under § 80.1464(d)(3) requires a guaranteed publication schedule; commenters request EPA to publish deadlines and any deadline changes at least 90 days before they take effect and to provide email subscription alerts for affected parties.

[P1] Legal commenters warn that § 80.1451(a)(1)’s requirement to include “all the following information described in the rule” could be interpreted as delegating adjudicative discretion to EPA staff to expand required items without notice; they urge EPA to enumerate every required field in the regulatory text or incorporate a specific Federal Register guidance by reference.

[P2] Consumer and environmental advocates request that § 80.1451(f)(1)(i)(A) include consequences for late filing (e.g., penalty matrix or cure periods) because without transparent enforcement provisions the reporting deadlines may be ineffective.

[P3] Compliance officers request clarification under § 80.1451(f)(1)(i)(A)(1) on whether submissions received on March 31 in different time zones (e.g., Pacific vs. Eastern) will be considered timely and whether EPA will accept submissions timestamped by the sender’s email/server or EPA’s receipt system.

[P4] Accounting and IT commenters note that the “next quarterly reporting deadline” definition in § 80.1451(f)(1)(i)(A)(2) should include UTC or local time conventions and whether electronic system downtime at EPA constitutes an excuse for late filing.

[P5] Small refinery advocates argue that the 2019–2021 staggered deadlines in § 80.1451(f)(1)(i)(B)(1)-(3) and § 80.1464(d)(1)(ii)(A)-(C) effectively single out small refineries for different treatment without explaining the statutory basis; they request EPA provide the legal justification and economic analysis for differential deadlines.

[P6] Trade associations request that EPA provide a one-time transitional waiver or extension for the first year these deadlines are published (per § 80.1451(f)(1)(iii) and § 80.1464(d)(3)) to accommodate system updates and auditor capacity constraints.

[P7] Legal compliance groups ask whether electronic attest reports submitted under § 80.1464(d)(1)(i) must be accompanied by an electronic representation letter from management, and whether EPA will accept scanned PDFs with original signatures.

[P8] NGOs request that attest engagement reports under § 80.1464(d)(1) be required to include the auditor’s workpapers or a summary thereof, to allow EPA or third parties to assess the sufficiency of the attest procedures.

[P9] State environmental agencies request that EPA coordinate the timing of deadlines in § 80.1451 and § 80.1464 with state greenhouse gas reporting schedules to reduce duplicative reporting burdens and align verification/audit schedules.

[P10] Affected parties ask EPA to clarify in § 80.1451(f)(1)(i) and § 80.1464(d)(1)(i) whether extensions granted for natural disasters or emergencies will be automatic for registered entities in declared disaster areas, and to define the process for requesting emergency deadline relief.

[P11] Industry commenters raise concerns that publishing deadlines “on EPA’s website” (P10 & P18) without formal notice in the Federal Register could risk insufficient notice under the Administrative Procedure Act; they request that EPA also publish deadline determinations in the Federal Register or via direct notice to registered parties.

[P12] Accountancy boards ask EPA to indicate whether engagement reports under § 80.1464(d) may be performed by international firms not licensed in the U.S., and if so, what additional attestation requirements or cross-border certifications will be required.

[P13] Data security advocates request that EPA specify secure submission methods (e.g., encrypted SFTP or authenticated API) for both annual compliance and attest engagement reports to protect trade secrets and PII during electronic transmission.

[P14] Small businesses point out potential cumulative cost impacts of multiple staggered deadlines (P6–P8, P14–P16) and request EPA prepare a Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act (SBREFA) analysis quantifying compliance costs and auditor fees for 2019–2021.

[P15] Legal experts note that the deadlines for historic compliance years (2019–2021) create retroactive compliance obligations; they ask EPA to explain its authority to impose new filing dates for past compliance years and to provide notice-and-comment justification or a retroactive waiver mechanism.

[P16] Technology vendors ask EPA to publish a machine-readable schedule and sample submissions for each deadline scenario (standard, small refinery, delayed RFS standard effective date) so vendors can build automated validation and submission tools.

[P17] NGOs and transparency advocates request that EPA commit to publishing anonymized summary data from annual compliance and attest reports (consistent with confidentiality protections) to allow independent policy evaluation and academic research.

[P18] Interested parties request a clear appeals or dispute resolution process in the rule for contested EPA determinations of whether a filing met the deadline or whether the content satisfied § 80.1451(a)(1) requirements.

[P1] The May 24, 2019 comments due date is unreasonably short and does not provide sufficient time for international stakeholders and manufacturers to prepare technical comments; extend the comment period by at least 30–60 days.

[P16] There's duplication between § 39.13(a) and the Docket No. statement about the May 24, 2019 deadline; clarify that both refer to the same deadline and ensure consistent dates throughout the document.

[P2] The phrase "within the specified compliance times" is vague; the AD should specify absolute calendar deadlines (dates or flight-hour limits) rather than relying on the referenced EASA AD alone.

[P3] Requiring full compliance "in accordance with EASA AD 2019-0020" imports foreign regulatory text wholesale without harmonization; provide explicit FAA text of required actions rather than relying solely on EASA language to avoid legal uncertainty.

[P4] Substituting the FAA AD effective date where EASA references its effective date (h)(1) could create retroactive obligations for operators who relied on the EASA effective date—clarify whether compliance times measured from EASA effective date will be adjusted or tolled.

[P5] Excluding the "Remarks" section (h)(2) could omit important non-normative clarifications that operators use for interpretation; explain which specific remarks are excluded and provide any needed clarifications within the FAA AD.

[P6] The AMOC authority is delegated to the Manager, International Section—this centralization may slow approvals for U.S. operators; allow regional Flight Standards divisional managers to approve AMOCs for quicker response.

[P7] Requiring AMOC requests to go through the principal inspector or local FSDO (i)(1) may create inconsistencies; clarify whether requests routed through the principal inspector will be forwarded to the International Section or can be approved locally.

[P8] The instruction to send AMOC information to the person in paragraph (j)(2) lacks included contact details in the cited provisions; include the name, address, phone, and email explicitly in paragraph (j)(2) within this AD.

[P9] Emailing AMOC requests to 9-ANM-116-AMOC-REQUESTS@faa.gov may raise data security/privacy concerns for proprietary technical data; provide secure file-transfer alternatives and guidance on handling proprietary attachments.

[P10] The requirement to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC (i)(1) may be administratively burdensome if the approval process already involved the inspector; allow notification within a defined short period after first use (e.g., 48–72 hours) rather than prior to use.

[P11] Requiring manufacturer instructions to be "accomplished using a method approved by the Manager, International Section, FAA, or EASA, or Airbus’s EASA DOA" (i)(2) creates potential for conflicting approvals; specify the precedence among FAA, EASA, and DOA approvals or provide streamlined reciprocal recognition.

[P12] The DOA approval signature requirement (i)(2) may be impractical for urgent corrective actions where electronic approvals without a DOA-authorized signature are typical; allow accepted electronic attestations or other traceable approvals consistent with DOA practices.

[P13] Designation of certain service information procedures as Required for Compliance (RC) (i)(3) should be accompanied by a clear list of which tasks are RC; include an appendix or table enumerating RC procedures so operators can identify mandatory steps.

[P14] Allowing deviation from non-RC procedures without AMOC approval (i)(3) is appropriate, but require operators to document deviations in the aircraft maintenance records and to demonstrate equivalence to prevent inconsistent safety outcomes.

[P15] The requirement that any substitution to RC procedures requires AMOC approval (i)(3) may unacceptably delay routine maintenance; permit minor administratively equivalent changes (documented and validated) to be handled through the operator's approved maintenance data with post-change notification to FAA.

[P17] The proposed removal and replacement of energy absorber (EA) assemblies (B/E Fischer) could create significant grounding and logistic burden; provide an economic impact estimate, allowed time windows for fleet scheduling, and parts availability statements.

[P17] The AD should clarify whether the replacement EA assemblies are provided under warranty by the manufacturer and whether operators can use equivalent parts from other certified suppliers.

[P17] Provide a cost-benefit analysis and safety risk justification for mandatory removal/replacement of EA assemblies; absent quantified risk, the requirement may be overly prescriptive.

[P18] The cross-reference to 14 CFR 11.43 and 11.45 (addresses for comment submission) is appropriate, but offer clear guidance for commenters on how to mark confidential/proprietary information when using the electronic portal.

[P19] The Federal eRulemaking Portal instructions (regulations.gov) should include the Docket No. and Product Identifier prominently to prevent misfiling; consider including a direct permalink to the docket in the AD.

[P20] Accepting comments by fax to 202-493-2251 may be outdated and not secure; ensure fax submissions are treated equivalently and provide confirmation receipts for faxed comments.

[P21] For mailed comments, provide an estimated time allowance acknowledging postal delays so comments sent close to the deadline are accepted if postmarked by the deadline.

[P22] Hand-delivery hours (9 a.m. to 5 p.m.) may restrict stakeholders in different time zones or with operational duties; allow scheduled appointments outside these hours for parties with demonstrable need.

[P23] The FAA location for viewing service information in Burlington, MA may be inconvenient for international stakeholders; provide a redacted or public version online or list alternative viewing locations.

[P24] Clarify whether confidential business information (CBI) or proprietary service instructions submitted to the AD docket will be publicly viewable when examining the docket online or in person (AD Docket Examination).

raw_output:
[P1] The proposed 5.4-mile lateral radius for Class D around McChord Field is too large and will unnecessarily extend controlled airspace over populated neighborhoods west of the field; FAA should provide justification for that specific radius and consider reducing it.

[P1] The rule lacks an analysis of current and projected traffic patterns to support designating Class D up to 2,800 ft MSL around McChord Field; request FAA include traffic counts, IFR/VFR mix, and accident/incident data supporting the change.

[P2] Limiting the vertical extent to "up to and including 2,800 feet MSL" may conflict with local terrain and nearby airspace (e.g., surrounding Class E or special use airspace); request an airspace cross-section showing adjacent airspace interfaces and any needed shelfing.

[P2] The requirement to extend from the surface to 2,800 ft MSL will impose new communication and equipage burdens on small general aviation pilots who operate marginally above the surface—FAA should assess and quantify impacts on small operators.

[P3] Defining the lateral extent as a simple 5.4-mile radius ignores runway-specific procedures (arrival/departure corridors) and could capture airspace that is not operationally necessary; FAA should instead use procedure-based lateral boundaries.

[P3] The circular 5.4-mile radius will create unnecessary Class D overflying of the Nisqually River corridor and recreational areas frequented by light-sport and ultralight operations; FAA must assess safety vs. access tradeoffs for those communities.

[P4] The specification of boundary segments using bearings and coordinates appears truncated in the NPRM (text cuts off); commenters request complete, legible coordinates and bearings so stakeholders can map and evaluate the proposed boundaries.

[P4] The proposed boundary definition using bearings (315° to 162°) may create jagged or non-intuitive edges that complicate VFR navigation; FAA should provide geo-referenced shapefiles/KML for public review.

[P5] The comment deadline of September 9, 2021 is inadequate given the complexity of overlapping provisions (airspace, environmental review, and an unrelated AD); request extension of the comment period by at least 30–60 days.

[P6] The obligation for affected owners/operators to comply within specified compliance times for the AD lacks an analysis of fleet availability and spare parts supply—FAA must assess industry capacity to comply within the proposed timelines without grounding aircraft.

[P7] Requiring removal/replacement of the MGB lock nut within 100 hours TIS or at next overhaul may be infeasible for operators with dispersed maintenance schedules; recommend allowing compliance within 200 hours or a specified calendar time (e.g., 6 months) to avoid maintenance disruption.

[P7] The AD's requirement to remove and replace each MGB lock nut "within 100 hours TIS or at next scheduled MGB overhaul, whichever occurs first" could create operational safety gaps for helicopters that may exceed 100 hours before overhaul—FAA must permit ferry flights or limited operations under safety mitigations.

[P8] The note excepting the requirement to send removed parts to Leonardo Helicopters is welcome, but the AD is silent on proper disposition or retention of removed parts for traceability; request explicit retention/marking and recordkeeping guidance.

[P9] The prohibition on installing MGBs or MGB lock nut P/N 3G630A09151 "as of the AD effective date" is overly broad and could complicate pre-purchased spare inventories; recommend a limited sell-through period or grandfathering of parts already on order with supplier proof.

[P9] The AD forbids installation of any MGB with the specified lock nut P/N but does not address whether modified or reworked lock nuts with traceable inspection records are permitted; request clarification or an AMOC pathway for repaired parts.

[P10] Prohibiting special flight permits entirely is unduly restrictive and could impede safe repositioning or ferry to maintenance facilities; request that limited special flight permits be allowed with specific operating conditions (day VFR, max weight, altitude limits).

[P11] Delegating AMOC approval to the Manager, International Validation Branch, is acceptable, but the rule should specify expected turnaround times for AMOC decisions to avoid prolonged operational burdens.

[P12] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 may be confusing for internationally-based operators or those without a designated principal inspector; request process clarification for foreign operators and for operators whose inspector is unavailable.

[P13] Direct submissions to the Manager must reference the person in paragraph (j)(1), but paragraph (j)(1) contact information is not included in the public excerpt; request that full contact details be included and published.

[P14] The email address for AMOC submissions is provided, but there is no acknowledgment/receipt process described; request that FAA commit to electronic receipt confirmation and estimated review timelines.

[P15] The requirement to notify the principal inspector or local FAA manager "before using any approved AMOC" could be burdensome for operators doing urgent maintenance; request that FAA allow notification within 24 hours after use in emergency situations, provided safety isn't compromised.

[P16] The duplicated deadlines (14 CFR part 71 – DATES and §39.13(a)) create potential confusion; request that FAA harmonize and clearly state which deadline applies to which action (airspace comments vs. AD comments) and extend both consistently if one is extended.

[P17] The ADDRESSES provision requires mailed comments to Docket Operations, but provides no guidance about COVID-era mail delays; request acceptance of scanned, signed comment letters by email to the docket and confirmation that mailed comments received after the deadline due to mail delays will be considered.

[P18] Requiring commenters to identify both docket numbers at the beginning of comments may lead to misfiled submissions if omitted; request that FAA allow docket number inclusion anywhere in the submission and provide a simple online form that auto-populates docket IDs.

[P19] Allowing online submission via Regulations.gov is helpful, but the NPRM does not note accommodations for those without internet access; request that FAA provide alternative electronic submission methods (email) and telephone assistance.

[P20] The invitation to contact the Airspace Policy Group for more information should include a named contact, phone number, and expected response times; stakeholders need a single point of contact for technical mapping questions.

[P21] The "Comments Invited" language should explicitly encourage submission of environmental, economic, and equitable impacts analyses from community groups, not just technical comments; request FAA solicit specific data on noise, air quality, and socioeconomic effects.

[P22] Requiring submission of communications in triplicate is outdated in the digital era and creates unnecessary burden; request FAA eliminate the triplicate requirement and accept single electronic submissions.

[P23] The requirement that commenters include a self-addressed stamped postcard to receive an acknowledgment is burdensome and unnecessary; request FAA provide electronic acknowledgement of receipt for emailed or uploaded comments.

[P24] Regulations.gov availability is good, but FAA should also publish the proposed airspace maps/shapefiles (KML/GeoJSON) and the proposed AD support data in downloadable formats to enable third-party analysis.

[P25] The offer to review the public docket in person with restricted hours may impede community review; request extended public access hours and virtual docket review sessions for those unable to travel to Washington, DC.

[P26] The commitment to conduct an environmental analysis per FAA Order 1050.1F prior to final action is appropriate, but FAA should commit to releasing a draft environmental assessment (EA) for public comment before finalizing the airspace change.

[P26] The NPRM provides no schedule or timeline for completion of the environmental review; request that FAA publish an expected timeline and interim milestones so stakeholders can plan participation.

[P1] The NPRM does not discuss impacts on local emergency medical service (EMS) helicopter operations that rely on low-altitude routing; request FAA coordinate with EMS providers to ensure emergency response is not impeded.

[P3] The proposed Class D circle overlaps with existing training areas used by flight schools for touch-and-go practice; FAA should consult flight schools and consider designated VFR transition routes to minimize operational disruption.

[P9] The AD prohibition lacks a clear definition of "install" as applied to exchange/loaned MGBs during maintenance events; request FAA define whether temporary installations for testing are prohibited.

[P10] The absolute prohibition on special flight permits could force non-compliant aircraft to be grounded in remote locations; recommend permitting one-time special flight permits to ferry aircraft to approved maintenance facilities under strict conditions.

[P7] The AD does not include data on failure modes of the affected MGB lock nut or risk assessment that justifies the urgent 100-hour compliance; request FAA publish the underlying service difficulty reports or investigation findings.

[P8] The exception not to send removed parts to Leonardo Helicopters may hinder the manufacturer's ability to analyze failures for continued airworthiness—FAA should require submission of root-cause data to either the manufacturer or FAA in a traceable, anonymized manner.

[P11] The AMOC approval authority limited to the International Validation Branch may create bottlenecks for domestic operators; suggest allowing regional FAA offices limited authority to approve time-limited AMOCs.

[P12] The AMOC submission process should permit electronic signatures and scanned documentation; the rule's reliance on mailing to inspectors is outdated.

[P14] The single email address for AMOCs may not be secure for transmitting maintenance records with personal data; request FAA provide secure upload portal or guidance on redacting personal information.

[P21] Community groups will evaluate noise impacts from reconfigured traffic patterns due to the new Class D; urge FAA to include noise contour modeling and compare pre/post proposed change.

[P1] The NPRM should include an operational exemption or transition plan for flights that currently operate under uncontrolled airspace procedures to transition to contact/cleared operations without undue administrative burden.

[P4] The bearings-based lateral boundary description may not align with true north vs. magnetic north conventions; request FAA specify whether bearings are magnetic or true and ensure conversion is provided.

[P16] Because the NPRM mixes airspace procedural changes and an AD with overlapping comment deadlines, stakeholders may miss relevant comment periods; request FAA issue a consolidated notice clarifying which docket covers which provision and synchronized deadlines.

[P7] The AD's compliance trigger "within 100 hours TIS, or at next scheduled MGB overhaul" fails to account for helicopters with life-limited components scheduled by calendar time; request FAA allow compliance "whichever occurs first of 100 hours TIS or 6 months" to provide certainty.

[P25] For in-person docket review, FAA should post an appointment system and instructions for how to request paper copies for those with limited connectivity.

[P26] If the environmental analysis finds significant impacts, FAA should commit to holding at least one public hearing in the Tacoma/Thurston County area to solicit oral testimony.

[P1] The November 20, 2017 comment deadline is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60 days to allow affected operators, manufacturers, labor unions, and safety advocates sufficient time to analyze the AD and submit informed comments.

[P1] The rule must clarify whether electronic submissions received after 11:59 PM EST on November 20, 2017 but stamped by the FAA on that date will be considered timely; the current wording is ambiguous about time zones and receipt time.

[P2] The applicability paragraph lacks a clear method for identifying which specific line numbers or serial-numbered Boeing 787–8 and 787–9 airplanes are affected; commenters request that the AD explicitly list affected line numbers, serial numbers, or reference a specific parts/ATA list in the service information.

[P2] The AD should clarify whether airplanes modified to non-standard configurations or operated under foreign registry but maintained in the U.S. are included; the phrase "certificated in any category" needs explanation regarding foreign-registered operators.

[P3] The compliance statement should include an explicit provision that operators who have partial compliance (e.g., completed some but not all required actions) must document remaining work and obtain an extension or AMOC rather than facing immediate grounding.

[P4] The 36-month compliance time for installing new pack control unit software and hardware is too long given potential safety implications; industry safety groups request a shorter compliance interval (e.g., 12–18 months) or a phased requirement prioritizing high-risk fleets.

[P4] Conversely, several large air carriers and MRO providers will comment that the 36-month window may be insufficient to schedule aircraft downtime and obtain parts across global fleets; they will request flexibility to extend compliance times through the AMOC process or phased fleet scheduling guidance.

[P4] The AD should provide estimated parts availability and lead times for the specified hardware and a methodology for operators to request relief if manufacturers cannot supply kits within the compliance window.

[P5] Requiring related investigative and corrective actions to be completed "before the airplane is next flown" could force immediate grounding for some operators who discover findings during installation; commenters will ask for language allowing temporary flight with operational limitations pending corrective action if safety risk is low and with FAA approval.

[P5] The AD must define "related investigative and corrective actions" in more detail and specify which findings would necessitate grounding versus those that can be deferred with risk mitigation.

[P6] Mandating strict compliance "in accordance with the Accomplishment Instructions" without allowing minor deviations for equivalent procedures performed by an FAA-approved repair station is overly prescriptive; commenters will request explicit allowance for qualified repair stations to use equivalent procedures if they provide equal or greater safety and document them.

[P6] Legal commenters will assert that requiring strict adherence to manufacturer's service instructions may unlawfully delegate FAA judgment to Boeing if the AD does not independently state the required safety outcome; they will ask for FAA rationale showing the Accomplishment Instructions achieve the mandated safety objective.

[P7] For Model 787–8 airplanes, reliance on Boeing Service Bulletin Issue 003 dated March 29, 2017 should be accompanied by an analysis of changes from Issue 002; commenters will request a redline summary of differences and justification for making Issue 003 mandatory.

[P7] Operators that have implemented measures per Issue 001 or Issue 002 for 787–8 will request explicit confirmation (beyond paragraph h) that any deviations between Issue 002 and Issue 003 do not require additional work if the operator can demonstrate equivalence.

[P8] For Model 787–9 airplanes, making Boeing Service Bulletin Issue 003 (dated October 20, 2016) mandatory raises concerns because Issue 003 predates Issue 002 for some documents; commenters will ask the FAA to explain the rationale and ensure the correct date/version is cited.

[P1] The March 7, 2022 comments due date for the Bell Textron AD is unreasonable and provides insufficient time for small operators and repair stations to analyze the technical service information and prepare meaningful comments.

[P1] The rule should extend the Bell Textron AD comment period beyond March 7, 2022 to allow for coordination with Bell, suppliers, and foreign operators that operate affected helicopters.

[P2] The Applicability language for the Bell Textron AD is incomplete as provided (truncated part number text) and may lead to confusion about which tailboom left hand fin spar cap part numbers are subject to the AD.

[P2] The AD should list explicit model/serial ranges and the full part-numbered spar cap references so operators can determine applicability without contacting the FAA.

[P3] The generic Compliance requirement to “comply within the specified compliance times” lacks clarity where multiple interdependent actions exist; the AD should explicitly state whether repetitive inspections’ timelines supercede initial-action windows.

[P4] The 100 hours TIS initial and repetitive inspection interval for the Bell spar cap (P4) is overly burdensome for commercial operators and may impose excessive grounding/maintenance burden; FAA should consider a longer interval supported by risk analysis.

[P4] The AD should provide a grace period or phase-in for the 100-hour repeat interval to allow scheduling of maintenance events and avoid undue operational disruption.

[P5] Requiring 10x or greater magnification plus a flashlight (P5) is ambiguous about acceptable inspection methods (e.g., borescope, magnified inspection tools, approved eddy-current); the AD should explicitly permit equivalent non-visual NDI methods.

[P5] The magnification requirement may be impractical in the confined fin area; the AD should allow use of calibrated optical instruments or boroscopes and include acceptance criteria or reference figures.

[P6] Removing a spar cap from service before further flight if cracking/loose rivets/damage is found (P6) could strand aircraft; the AD should define acceptable temporary flight-limiting measures or ferry flight provisions for repositioning to a maintenance facility.

[P6] The directive to remove the spar cap from service before next flight does not define who is authorized to make that determination (pilot-in-command vs. certifying mechanic); the AD should clarify authorization.

[P7] The fin skin exterior inspection (P7) lacks defined inspection acceptance criteria (size of cracks, distortion thresholds, allowable rivet looseness); the AD should include or reference objective criteria.

[P8] Requiring removal of the spar cap before flight when fin skin shows cracking/distortion (P8) could be inconsistent where damage is confined to skin and not structural spar cap; the AD needs to allow repair of the skin where structural integrity is maintained, with approved repair instructions.

[P9] The AMOC authority assigned to the DSCO Branch manager (P9) should explicitly include timelines for AMOC disposition to prevent undue delays when operators request alternatives.

[P10] The AMOC request routing (P10) should permit electronic submission (email or portal) for the Bell AD, consistent with modern practice, rather than relying solely on in-person or postal channels.

[P11] Requiring notification of the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC (P11) may be burdensome for operators without assigned principal inspectors (e.g., foreign operators); the AD should specify acceptable alternate notification processes.

[P12] The March 7, 2022 comments due date for the Boeing AD duplicates the Bell timeline and similarly is too short for comprehensive industry and international operator input; the FAA should extend the comment period.

[P13] The Boeing AD applicability to all 757–200, –200PF, –200CB, and –300 series airplanes (P13) is broad; commenters will request clarification on any excluded serial number blocks, retrofit statuses, or supplemental type certificates that affect applicability.

[P14] The general compliance statement (P14) should clarify applicability to aircraft currently grounded, in storage, or under maintenance to avoid confusion about compliance timing for those aircraft.

[P15] The retained HFEC surface inspection of STA 1380 inner chord (P15) should include explicit probe settings, calibration standards, and personnel qualification requirements (e.g., level 2 NDT) to ensure inspection consistency across operators.

[P16] Requiring corrective actions to be completed before further flight (P16) is appropriate for safety but commenters will request that the AD include defined temporary repair/containment measures and ferry flight provisions when parts/materials are not immediately available.

[P17] The repeat intervals referenced to Boeing Service Bulletin paragraph 1.E. (P17) must be explicitly restated in the AD, because some operators may not have immediate access to the service bulletin and the AD must be self-contained for compliance planning.

[P18] The material identification task for Group 2 airplanes (P18) should specify acceptable identification methods (chemical test, lab analysis, part marking, supplier records) and the level of documentation required for compliance records.

[P19] The exception that 2024–T42 inner chord requires no further action (P19) needs an explanation and supporting data in the AD preamble so operators understand the basis and can trust the exception.

[P20] For 7075–T73 inner chord finding (P20), performing HFEC inspection before further flight may be impractical for operators operating remote routes; commenters will request permission for ferry to a maintenance base under defined conditions or allow temporary operational restrictions.

[P21] Using January 9, 2018 as the compliance reference for “after original issue date” (P21) may conflict with operators who used later revision dates for actions; the AD should specify whether actions performed after later revision dates meet compliance.

[P22] Requiring repairs per methods approved under paragraph (m) when Boeing directs “contact Boeing” (P22) could create delays for operators if Boeing’s response is slow; commenters will ask FAA to publish pre-approved repair methods or allow DER/ODA approvals within defined timelines.

[P23] Requiring compliance with the Boeing Requirements Bulletin 757–53A0118 RB (P23) but carving out paragraph (k) exceptions may create inconsistency; commenters will request the AD incorporate the full, updated service instructions into the regulatory text or append them for clarity.

[P24] Substituting the AD effective date for “original issue date” in the Requirements Bulletin (P24) may shorten compliance times unexpectedly for operators who relied on the bulletin’s original schedule; stakeholders will ask for grandfathering of actions already planned under the bulletin.

[P25] Requiring FAA-approved methods for Boeing-directed repair/alternative inspections (P25) but allowing ODA approval (P30) may be redundant; commenters will ask for clarity on whether Boeing ODA approvals satisfy paragraph (m) without separate FAA action, and request documented timelines for ODA approvals.

[P26] Declaring that accomplishment of initial inspections and corrective actions under the Requirements Bulletin terminates paragraphs (g) and (h) inspection obligations (P26) may be misinterpreted; commenters will request explicit language on whether repetitive inspections are terminated permanently or contingent on certain repair configurations.

[P27] The AMOC authority assigned to the Los Angeles ACO Branch manager (P27) should include delegation procedures to accommodate time-sensitive approvals for large operators with global fleets.

[P28] AMOC request procedure allowing email (P28) is useful but should mandate encrypted submission of sensitive data and provide a standardized electronic form to streamline review.

[P29] Requiring notification of the principal inspector before using an AMOC (P29) may delay urgent repairs when inspectors are not immediately reachable; commenters will ask for substitute notification options and maximum notification timeframes.

[P30] Allowing AMOCs approved by Boeing’s authorized ODA to be used (P30) is helpful, but commenters will request that the AD require the ODA approval be submitted to FAA for acceptance within a set timeframe and require public record of such approvals.

[P31] The AMOC approval condition that the method must meet the airplane’s certification basis and explicitly reference this AD (P31) is necessary, but commenters (especially legal counsel) will ask for clarification on how to determine the airplane’s certification basis for modified or re-engined airplanes.

[P32] The prohibition on using AMOCs previously approved for AD 2017–24–10 (P32) is concerning; operators will request a rationale and transition process to re-evaluate and re-submit previously accepted AMOCs to avoid duplicative work.

[P33] The requirement that steps labeled RC must be performed as written (P33) needs clearer definition of who may authorize deviations in emergency or unique situations and whether DERs can approve minor deviations without a formal AMOC.

[P34] Allowing deviations from non-RC steps under operator maintenance programs without AMOC (P34) is reasonable, but commenters will request guidance on acceptable documentation and risk assessment standards to demonstrate that non-RC deviations do not affect RC steps or overall airworthiness.

[P1] The permission limiting importation to the systems-approach conditions is overly vague without specifying which sections apply; request clarification of the exact treatments/standards referenced in § 319.56–78.

[P1] Industry requests clarification whether small-volume specialty brokers who consolidate produce from multiple Ecuadorian growers qualify as “commercial consignments” under § 319.56–78(a)(6).

[P2] Ecuador’s NPPO will need a clear timeline and format requirements for the operational workplan; request that APHIS publish a template and reasonable timeframe (e.g., 90 days) for submission.

[P2] Legal commenters note the rule does not specify consequences if the NPPO fails to submit an operational workplan by a deadline; request inclusion of explicit time frames and consequences.

[P3] Concern that APHIS approval standard for the operational workplan is not defined; request defined criteria and timeframe (e.g., 60–90 days) for APHIS review and approval to avoid indefinite delays.

[P4] Request that the rule require the operational workplan to include measurable performance metrics (e.g., trap density, acceptable fly thresholds) rather than just “describe” requirements to ensure enforceability.

[P5] Grower associations in Ecuador object that mandatory registration of “places of production” lacks definition of what constitutes a place (e.g., farm, field, orchard) and request precise definitions to avoid ambiguity and undue burdens.

[P5] Smallholder producers state registration costs and administrative burdens may exclude them from export; request fee waivers or phased registration assistance for small farms.

[P6] Requirement that packinghouses be “pest-exclusionary” and registered is vague; industry requests technical specifications for pest-exclusionary construction and a registration timeline and fee schedule.

[P6] Packinghouse operators request clarity whether mobile packing lines or temporary packing shelters are permissible and, if so, what registration and pest-exclusion standards apply.

[P7] NPPOs and trade groups oppose one-year record retention as insufficient for trace-back investigations; recommend extending retention to three years to align with other phytosanitary programs.

[P7] Privacy advocates request that the rule specify protections for sensitive commercial data in NPPO records before requiring provision to APHIS.

[P8] Request that APHIS specify the format, notice period, and frequency with which it may request records from the NPPO to prevent burdensome surprise audits.

[P9] Industry asks for detailed guidance on acceptable lot identity systems (barcodes, RFID, numbered field boxes) and tolerances for lot size to make compliance feasible.

[P10] Commenters request that the operational workplan specify acceptable traceability technologies and require interoperability with APHIS systems to allow electronic submission of lot identity.

[P11] Exporters request clarification that “commercial consignments only” excludes personal baggage but allows cross-border e-commerce shipments above a certain value/weight; propose threshold definitions.

[P12] Transporters raise concerns about the undefined requirements for “safeguarding during movement”; request explicit guidance on vehicle sealing, escort, documentation, and temperature control requirements.

[P12] Request for clear chain-of-custody procedures and allowed custody transfers (e.g., broker warehouses) while maintaining “safeguarded” status.

[P13] Trapping program obligations require specification of trap density, lure types, laboratory diagnostics, and who bears the cost of APHIS participation; request these be detailed in the workplan or rule.

[P14] The prohibition tied to trap count thresholds is punitive without stating exact numeric thresholds or statistical confidence levels; request disclosure of the trigger values for flies per trap per day and an appeals process.

[P14] Legal experts request due process protections for producers when sites are prohibited from exporting (notice, opportunity to remediate, timeline for appeal).

[P15] Request extension of trap record retention beyond one year to allow seasonal trend analysis and to align with P7’s recommendation for longer record retention.

[P16] Commenters ask that APHIS specify who bears costs for record transmission and whether data may be transmitted electronically and in what formats.

[P17] Farmers state that the requirement to remove fallen fruit per the workplan may be infeasible at scale without clear timelines and methods; request specification (daily collection, weekly) and permitted disposal methods.

[P18] Small growers warn that prohibition on placing fallen fruit in field containers could waste usable produce; request clarification of definition of “fallen” (ground-touch vs. fallen off plant) and an exception for fruit that can be sanitized and inspected.

[P19] Request definition of the inspection methods and sampling intensity for Tamarillo mosaic virus field inspections to ensure inspections are scientifically valid and non-arbitrary.

[P20] Plant pathologists request that the rule specify diagnostic protocols (visual symptoms vs. laboratory PCR/ELISA confirmation) required to declare a site free of Tamarillo mosaic virus.

[P21] Monthly inspections starting 60 days before harvest will be resource-intensive; request that APHIS allow alternate inspection frequencies based on risk assessments or pest pressure, or provide funding/assistance.

[P22] NPPO of Ecuador requests clear rules for APHIS monitoring of inspections (advance notice, number of APHIS observers allowed, costs, immigration/visa arrangements).

[P23] Request that “effective trapping and control measures” be defined with minimum standards (trap density, treatment frequency) and that APHIS publish accepted control guidelines.

[P24] Producers request that exclusion from the export program include a clear remediation pathway with defined corrective actions and timelines to return to compliance rather than open-ended exclusion.

[P25] Request that the joint APHIS-NPPO agreement requirement for reinstatement include an independent arbitration mechanism if the agencies disagree, to prevent indefinite exclusion.

[P26] Packinghouses note the restriction to accept only fruit from registered production sites may disrupt supply chains where multi-source packing is common; request allowance for segregated lines or quarantine holds for nonregistered sources under strict protocols.

[P27] The 24-hour packing requirement is operationally challenging in rural areas with long transport times; request extension to 48–72 hours or allow pre-cooling buffer steps if insect-proof containment is maintained.

[P27] Clarify who certifies that packaging is “insect-proof” and whether commercial cartons meet the standard without additional mesh.

[P28] Requirement that insect-proof packing remain intact until arrival in U.S. raises logistics issues for intermediate ports/transit; request specifics on acceptable handling during transshipment and liability for breaches during carrier handling.

[P29] The automatic denial of entry for compromised safeguards may be disproportionate; request remediation options at U.S. port of entry (on-site rewrapping, treatment) before destruction or refusal.

[P30] Request technical clarification that 1.6 mm screening applies to all mounting types and whether standard insect screening materials meet the specification; request tolerances for wear and tear.

[P31] Double-door entry requirement may be costly for older facilities; request a grandfathering/clawback period and financial assistance or alternatives (air curtains, vestibules) that achieve equivalent protection.

[P32] Disagreement that only NPPO or authorized officials may inspect biometric samples — industry requests acceptance of accredited private labs under NPPO oversight to expedite inspections.

[P33] Visual inspection alone for N. elegantalis and virus may miss latent infections; plant health scientists urge mandatory laboratory confirmation protocols rather than reliance on visual inspection.

[P34] Requiring cutting fruit to inspect for A. fraterculus and C. capitata is destructive and may not be statistically sufficient; request specified sample sizes and acceptance criteria (e.g., ISPM recommended sampling plans).

[P36] If quarantine treatments are allowed as an exception, APHIS must list approved treatments, capacity for monitoring, and who pays; request inclusion of treatment options and turnaround time estimates.

raw_output:
[P1] The required comment receipt deadline of August 22, 2022 is already past; the FAA must extend or reopen the comment period to allow meaningful stakeholder input instead of closing it retroactively.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether electronic comments submitted on or before August 22, 2022 but processed afterward will be considered timely to avoid rejecting valid submissions due to processing delays.

[P2] The phrase “unless already accomplished” is ambiguous; industry requests explicit criteria or recordkeeping requirements to demonstrate prior compliance (e.g., maintenance log entries, signed work orders).

[P3] The AD requires a “functional test of the specified cabin altitude pressure switches by the latest of the listed times using specified/equivalent adapters and matching hose”; commenters request the FAA publish the referenced “specified” adapter part numbers and test procedure step-by-step to avoid inconsistent testing.

[P4] The 2,000 flight-hour interval since the last test is too long for some high-utilization operators; business jet and regional operators request shorter intervals (e.g., 1,000–1,500 fh) or risk-based alternative intervals based on age/flight profile.

[P5] The option requiring the test “prior to accumulation of 2,000 total flight hours on the airplane” is confusing for in-service airplanes with >2,000 hours; the FAA should state applicability (e.g., only for new/overhauled switches or newly certificated aircraft).

[P6] The 90-day compliance option after the AD becomes effective may be infeasible for widebody fleets due to scheduling and parts availability; request extension to 180 days or allow phased compliance by tail number groups.

[P7] Repeating tests at intervals “not to exceed 2,000 flight hours” conflicts with existing maintenance programs for some operators; request permission to align interval with existing scheduled maintenance items (e.g., every A-check) when that interval is less than 2,000 fh.

[P8] The requirement to replace any switch that fails to activate between 9,000 and 11,000 ft “prior to the next flight” is operationally burdensome for remote or ferry flights; request allowance to defer replacement under an FAA-approved MEL with operational limitations and a defined repair window.

[P9] The allowance for equivalent adapters “as long as the mating side with the switch meets listed specifications” lacks a process for qualification; request inclusion of an approved-equivalency list or a formal verification procedure (e.g., dimensional drawing submission and FAA acceptance).

[P10] The numeric flareless end dimension tolerances (>=0.265 in and <=0.438 in) may be inconsistent with common industry fittings; manufacturers request confirmation that common spare part fittings meet these tolerances or provision of acceptable part numbers.

[P11] The AN4 flared end spec (<=0.5 in total with >=0.265 in thread) is imprecise regarding how to measure “total”; request definition (e.g., measure from shoulder to tip) and acceptable tolerance ranges to prevent misinterpretation.

[P12] Figure 1’s list of adapters and matching hose should include manufacturer part numbers, acceptable equivalents, and sourcing guidance so that small operators can source compliant test rigs without trial-and-error.

[P13] The requirement to use a 25–40 ft Barfield Pitot Hose or equivalent with #4 AN fitting may be excessive for ground tests in tightly spaced maintenance bays; request permission to use shorter hoses (e.g., 6–10 ft) when safe and equivalent test pressure stability can be demonstrated.

[P14] The mandate that the adapter's flat side (not the flared side) be connected to the switch should be clarified with an explanatory diagram and tolerance warnings to prevent damage to the switch inlet from improper mating.

[P15] The prohibition against connecting the flared side to the cabin altitude warning switch (NOTE) needs to be elevated from a note to an explicit regulatory sentence and accompanied by a rationale (damage risk/false readings) so maintenance personnel understand criticality.

[P16] The requirement that installed thread length be less than 0.5 inch to avoid bottoming out is ambiguous regarding where to measure; request precise measurement instructions and allowable tolerances, and specify tools/fixtures for measurement to ensure repeatability.

[P17] Allowing operation under an operator’s FAA‑approved MEL after a switch failure only if the MEL limits altitude to ≤10,000 ft MSL could be unsafe for certain operations (e.g., over-mountain flights, oceanic segments); request clarification whether ferry flights or delivery flights have an exception and whether ATC constraints are considered.

[P18] The condition that the MEL must include provisions limiting operation to ≤10,000 ft MSL should require operators to add standardized MEL language provided by the FAA to ensure uniformity across operators and expedite MEL approvals.

[P19] The designation that the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch, can approve AMOCs (per 14 CFR 39.19) may impede timely national approvals; request delegation or parallel processing options to local Certificate Holding District Offices (CHDOs) for faster response.

[P20] The requirement to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or responsible Flight Standards Office creates procedural duplication for operators that already have AMOC procedures; request ability to submit directly to the FAA AMOC email with cc to the principal inspector.

[P21] The instruction to address AMOC information to the person named in paragraph (j)(1) should include that person’s name/phone/email in this AD to avoid delays—commenters request the contact be explicitly repeated in the regulatory text.

[P22] The permitted email address for AMOC submissions is acceptable, but operators request guidance on acceptable file formats, maximum attachment sizes, and expected acknowledgment timelines to streamline compliance.

[P23] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using any approved AMOC may be impractical for international operators or ferries crossing jurisdictions; request alternative notification methods (email with timestamp) and explicit deadlines (e.g., within 24 hours prior to flight).

[P24] The permission to use AMOCs approved by the Boeing ODA for required repairs/modifications is welcome, but commenters request a requirement that Boeing provide a registry of current ODA-approved AMOCs referencing this AD to avoid duplication of approval efforts.

[P25] The condition that any repair/modification deviation must meet the airplane’s certification basis and specifically reference this AD is vague; request a clear template showing the minimum elements that must be included in an AMOC submission to demonstrate conformity with certification basis.

[P3] The AD should explicitly identify which part numbers/serial numbers of cabin altitude pressure switches are within scope to avoid unnecessary testing of compliant or redesigned switches.

[P8] Replacing a failed switch “prior to the next flight” may not be feasible if replacement parts are unobtainable; request allowance for one-time ferry with a maintenance release and altitude restriction under a letter of deviation authority until parts arrive.

[P7] The AD does not address how to account for ferry flights or non-revenue repositioning when calculating flight hours between tests — commenters request guidance on whether those hours are counted and how to document them.

[P4] For fractional ownership operators with cumulative logbooks spread across management companies, the 2,000 fh since last test requirement needs clarification on which entity is responsible for tracking and ensuring tests are performed.

[P13] The reference to “quick disconnect (if applicable)” creates uncertainty; request definition of circumstances when quick disconnects are required or prohibited and whether quick disconnect leakage rates affect test validity.

[P9] The AD should require calibration or verification of any “equivalent adapter” prior to first use (e.g., pressure leak check, dimensional inspection) and require documentation in the aircraft maintenance records.

[P16] Mandating installation of AN924-4 nut and a 7/16 spacer or washers should be accompanied by torque values and installation procedures to prevent improper assembly and potential damage to the switch or adapter.

[P11] The dimensional specs referencing both imperial and metric units could cause rounding issues; recommend specifying measurements to at least three decimal places and identifying which measurement controls in case of discrepancy.

[P17] The altitude limitation of ≤10,000 ft MSL during inoperative cabin altitude warning is insufficient safety mitigation for unpressurized flight segments at night or in IMC; safety advocates request grounding until repair or requiring a secondary warning system.

[P3] The phrase “using specified/equivalent adapters and matching hose” should include a requirement that the air data test set used meet a minimum accuracy/resolution to ensure test validity; request specification of acceptable air data test set models or performance criteria.

[P12] Figure 1 should include a parts list and recommended vendors for the adapters and hoses to ensure small operators can procure correct hardware without trial and error.

[P24] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to be used without FAA concurrence may create inconsistent safety outcomes; legal experts request an FAA review checkpoint before ODA AMOCs are accepted for AD compliance.

[P2] The AD should state recordkeeping obligations (how long maintenance records demonstrating compliance must be retained and what specific data is required) so operators can demonstrate compliance during audits.

[P14] The instruction to connect the flat side to the switch should also indicate permissible thread engagement depth to prevent thread damage and ensure a leak-tight connection.

[P16] The 0.5 inch installed thread length limit should include an explicit prohibition against using shims or washers that would result in exceeding that dimension after torqueing, and require a post-installation measurement.

[P7] The AD should permit prorating the repeat-test interval for aircraft with low utilization (e.g., per calendar time if flight hours are minimal) to ensure safety for aircraft parked or flying very infrequently.

[P5] Operators with newly manufactured airplanes that have accumulated more than 2,000 total flight hours before the AD’s effective date need a grandfathering clause or retrofit grace period to avoid immediate noncompliance.

[P13] The requirement for hose length 25–40 ft may introduce pressure lag or temperature effects that alter test results; request the FAA provide validation data supporting that hose length range for typical maintenance environments.

[P3] The AD fails to address training requirements for technicians performing the functional test; request mandatory training/qualification guidance and an allowance for training records to be kept in maintenance manuals.

[P8] Replace-before-next-flight requirement should specify acceptable replacement parts (manufacture part numbers and approved vendors) and whether PMA or overhauled parts are permitted.

[P19] Stakeholders request that the AD provide target turnaround times for AMOC decisions by the Seattle ACO Branch (e.g., 30/60/90 days) to allow operational planning.

[P22] Allowing email submissions of AMOC information is fine, but commenters request that encrypted email or secure portal options be offered for proprietary or sensitive technical data.

[P12] The AD should allow test rigs maintained at multiple operator bases to be certified once and recognized across the operator’s fleet, rather than requiring per-aircraft validation.

[P9] The equivalency language should include acceptance criteria for thread wear or damage on the switch inlet; worn threads might still “meet” dimensions but fail functionally.

[P25] The requirement that approvals reference this AD should include a standardized citation format to ensure traceability in maintenance records and future audits.

[P7] The AD does not specify how to count flight hours for rotary-wing conversions or special mission sorties; comment requests inclusion of a definition of “flight hour” for the purposes of the AD.

[P3] Clarify whether tests conducted in accordance with previous FAA or manufacturer Service Bulletins satisfy the AD requirements to avoid duplicate testing.

[P17] Operators request clarification whether the ≤10,000 ft MSL MEL limitation applies to all phases of flight including takeoff/landing in mountainous airports where airport elevation may exceed 10,000 ft.

[P1] The August 5, 2019 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60 days to allow affected operators, repair stations, labor unions, and consumer safety groups adequate time to prepare substantive comments and cost analyses.

[P1] The rule does not specify the time zone or received-by method for the August 5, 2019 deadline; FAA should clarify whether email submissions received before midnight EDT/PDT are acceptable and whether mailed comments must be postmarked by that date.

[P2] § 39.13(f) requires compliance “within the specified compliance times” but does not provide relief for parts shortages or limited availability of qualified maintenance technicians; FAA should include a hardship/waiver procedure or longer compliance windows tied to parts/skills availability.

[P2] The phrase “unless already accomplished” in § 39.13(f) is ambiguous about partial compliance; FAA should clarify how prior partial actions (e.g., inspections done to a different revision) satisfy the requirement.

[P3] § 39.13(g)(1) incorporates Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 757–53A0112 RB by reference for all airplanes except those in (g)(2); operators without access to the Boeing bulletin (proprietary or paywalled) cannot determine obligations — FAA must make the full bulletin publically available and incorporated material readily accessible.

[P3] The requirement in § 39.13(g)(1) to “perform all applicable actions” in the Boeing RB lacks clear applicability criteria for complex fleets; FAA should require an applicability matrix indicating which serial numbers/configurations require each action.

[P4] § 39.13(g)(2) defers to APB Alert Service Bulletin AP757–53–002 for airplanes with APB blended/scimitar winglets installed via STC, but does not address mixed fleets (airframes retrofitted after some inspections); FAA should clarify how to handle airplanes that received winglets after some AD-required actions were completed.

[P4] The rule does not specify whether AMOC or alternative instructions previously approved for the Boeing bulletin remain valid for APB-modified airplanes under § 39.13(g)(2); FAA should explicitly state whether prior approvals carry forward or must be re-evaluated.

[P5] § 39.13(h)(1) instructs substituting the AD effective date where the Boeing RB references its “original issue date,” but excludes notes and flag notes; this carve-out is confusing and risks inconsistent interpretations — FAA should provide concrete examples of where substitution applies and a redline of affected sentences.

[P6] § 39.13(h)(2) requires contacting Boeing for repair/alternative inspection instructions and mandates that such repairs be approved per paragraph (i); this effectively makes Boeing the gatekeeper for on-condition repairs, raising competitive and confidentiality concerns — FAA should permit independent repair stations and manufacturers to propose repairs approved through FAA AMOC procedures without Boeing consent.

[P6] Requiring Boeing-approved repair instructions in § 39.13(h)(2) may delay necessary repairs for operators that cannot obtain timely responses from Boeing; FAA should add a backstop requiring FAA to accept alternative procedures after a defined timeframe (e.g., 30 days) if Boeing does not respond.

[P7] § 39.13(h)(3) repeats the substitution of the AD effective date for APB service bulletin original issue date but again excludes notes; this increases legal uncertainty for organizations referencing the APB bulletin and should be clarified with examples and a statement about which dates control for compliance timing.

[P8] § 39.13(h)(4) directs operators to contact Boeing for repair instructions where APB bulletin says to do so; this appears to ignore APB’s role as the STC holder for winglets — FAA should require APB to provide repair/inspection alternatives for STC-modified airplanes or allow APB to approve ODA-level solutions instead of routing everything through Boeing.

[P9] § 39.13(i)(1) grants the Manager, Los Angeles ACO Branch, authority to approve AMOCs; industry requests that FAA permit requests to be reviewed by regional ACOs or provide a faster, centralized electronic AMOC intake to prevent bottlenecks at a single office.

[P10] § 39.13(i)(1) requires AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19; many operators currently use their ODA or corporate engineering for submissions — FAA should explicitly permit submission through those channels to streamline processing and reduce duplicative routing.

[P11] § 39.13(i)(1) instructs direct submissions to the certification office manager as identified in paragraph (j)(1), but paragraph (j)(1) is not included in the excerpt and may change; FAA should publish the named individual and include a fallback contact if that person departs to avoid lost requests.

[P12] § 39.13(i)(1) permits emailing AMOC requests to 9-ANM-LAACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov; however, the rule should require confirmation-of-receipt within 5 business days and an expected processing timeline (e.g., 60–90 days) to provide certainty to operators.

[P13] § 39.13(i)(2) mandates notifying your principal inspector prior to using an approved AMOC; legal counsel requests clarification whether “prior” means before the physical performance of the work or before returning the aircraft to service, and whether oral notification followed by written confirmation is acceptable.

[P14] § 39.13(i)(3) allows an AMOC approved by an authorized Boeing ODA to be used for required repairs/mods/alterations; labor and repair-station commenters will challenge delegating approval authority to the manufacturer’s ODA without independent FAA oversight as potentially creating conflicts of interest — FAA should limit ODA approval to minor deviations or require concurrent FAA concurrence.

[P15] § 39.13(i)(3) requires that any repair method used under an AMOC meet the airplane’s certification basis and explicitly reference the AD; legal commenters request that FAA define what constitutes adequate substantiation that a proposed repair meets the certification basis and require submission of supporting compliance demonstration data.

[P16] § 39.13(i)(4)(i) makes every step labeled “RC” mandatory; operators request that FAA provide a complete list of RC steps from the incorporated bulletins in the AD preamble or appendix so organizations can budget and plan manpower and tooling accordingly.

[P16] The RC obligation in § 39.13(i)(4)(i) should be accompanied by clear recordkeeping requirements (e.g., logbook entries, work order references) specifying what documentation constitutes compliance for inspections and RC repairs.

[P17] § 39.13(i)(4)(i) exempts steps labeled “RC Exempt” from RC requirements; commenters ask that FAA require the incorporated bulletins to conspicuously mark RC and RC Exempt steps and to publish a consolidated checklist to avoid inconsistent field interpretations.

[P18] § 39.13(i)(4)(i) states an AMOC is required to deviate from any RC-labeled steps; industry requests expedited AMOC pathways (e.g., limited-scope letters of deviation) for minor differences in technique that do not change the safety outcome, to avoid grounding aircraft pending full AMOC review.

[P19] § 39.13(i)(4)(ii) permits deviation from non-RC steps using accepted methods from the operator’s maintenance program without AMOC, provided RC steps remain performable; repair stations ask for explicit examples of acceptable deviations and confirm whether deviations that alter work sequencing but not outcomes are allowed.

[P19] The “return to an airworthy condition” standard in § 39.13(i)(4)(ii) is vague — FAA should define measurable criteria or cite acceptable maintenance program standards to reduce enforcement ambiguity.

[P6][P8] Consumer safety and FAA oversight groups object that multiple provisions (h)(2) and (h)(4)) shift decision-making to Boeing or proprietary bulletin authors for repair instructions; they argue FAA must retain ultimate authority and ensure repair instructions are independently reviewed for safety.

[P3][P4] Small regional carriers and leasing companies request clarification about applicability to airplanes in storage or on lease transitions; specifically, whether compliance must be performed by the current operator, the owner, or before lease return.

[P2][P3] Maintenance labor unions request that compliance times in the incorporated bulletins be adjusted to account for manpower constraints and that FAA coordinate with labor representatives when setting short compliance windows to prevent unsafe rushed work.

[P12] Data-security/privacy advocates request that the FAA not require inclusion of proprietary operator maintenance data in emailed AMOC requests to 9-ANM-LAACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov without secure transmission procedures and an option to submit redacted or encryption-protected files.

[P9][P14] Legal commenters note potential due-process concerns if AMOC approvals are routinely delegated to the Los Angeles ACO Manager or manufacturer ODAs without published criteria for approval, and request publication of AMOC approval standards and appeal procedures.

[P3][P16] Safety advocacy groups request FAA to require follow-up audits or spot checks on RC-labeled steps performed under this AD to ensure mandatory steps are in fact completed, and publish the results (redacted) to increase transparency.

[P1] Several commenters will note the August 5, 2019 date is already past and request the FAA reopen the comment period with a new, current deadline so stakeholders can submit timely comments on the proposed regulatory text.
