[P3] The 12-month inspection period in § 39.13(g) is too long for a potential safety issue tied to surveillance software; the FAA should shorten the inspection interval to 90 days for high-utilization operators.

[P3] The inspection requirement in paragraph (g) does not specify whether line stations may perform the inspection or if it must be done at a base maintenance facility; this should be clarified to avoid inconsistent implementation.

[P3] § 39.13(g) should specify the acceptable methods and tools to identify ISS OPS software part numbers (e.g., maintenance system printouts, software menus, checksum verification) to prevent disputes over inspection adequacy.

[P4] Allowing a records review in lieu of physical inspection (§ 39.13(g)) is appropriate, but the rule should require an auditable attestation from the person performing the records review to ensure the determination is “conclusive.”

[P4] The phrase “conclusively determined” in § 39.13(g) is vague; the FAA should define objective criteria (e.g., part-numbered software release records, vendor release notes) that satisfy conclusiveness.

[P5] Paragraph (h) mandates performing all applicable RC actions within 12 months but does not list the RC actions; the AD should either summarize those RC actions or explicitly incorporate the Boeing Alert Service Bulletin by reference, including revision/version limits.

[P5] Requiring all “applicable” RC actions in § 39.13(h) without a clear applicability matrix creates legal uncertainty; operators may be penalized for differing interpretations—FAA should provide a table mapping airplane groups to required RC actions.

[P6] The prerequisite in § 39.13(i) that Group 1 operators install new ISS OPS software and the DCA database “prior to” other RC actions could ground aircraft if parts or software are unavailable; FAA should allow concurrent compliance within a defined short window instead of strict precedence.

[P6] Paragraph (i) references Boeing Alert Service Bulletin B787–81205–SB340036–00 Issue 001 (dated June 30, 2017) but does not state whether later revisions are acceptable; the AD should permit using later FAA-approved service bulletin revisions to avoid unnecessary paperwork.

[P7] The prohibition in § 39.13(j) banning installation of ISS OPS part numbers COL40–0010–0100 and COL46–0007–0100 “as of the effective date” is overbroad and could invalidate routine maintenance that harmlessly re-installs legacy software; FAA should limit the prohibition to installations outside the controlled procedure specified in paragraph (i).

[P7] Paragraph (j)’s absolute ban creates supply-chain issues for aftermarket vendors and MROs who may have inventory of these software packages; the AD should provide a compliance pathway for inventory disposition.

[P8] The exception in § 39.13(j) permitting installation only as part of paragraph (i) actions should be expanded to allow installation for debugging or recovery purposes under an approved AMOC to avoid operational disruptions.

[P9] Paragraph (k) granting credit for installations done using the earlier Boeing service bulletin lacks explicit recordkeeping requirements; the FAA should require operators to submit records proving that the earlier actions are equivalent and specify acceptable documentation.

[P9] The credit provision should explicitly state whether voluntary installations performed by third-party MROs (not Boeing or the original operator) prior to the effective date qualify for credit.

[P10] The AMOC authority in § 39.13(l)(1) vested in the Seattle ACO Branch manager is appropriate, but the AD should allow delegated approval by other FAA offices for non-U.S. operators to avoid delays related to geographic jurisdiction.

[P10] The rule should require the FAA to publish standard criteria for AMOC approvals to enhance transparency and predictability rather than leaving decisions solely to the Manager’s discretion.

[P11] Requiring AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO (§ 39.13(l)(1)) will create unnecessary routing delays for international operators; allow direct submission to the Seattle ACO with concurrent notification to local offices.

[P11] The AD should provide an explicit timeline for FAA response to AMOC requests received through the principal inspector or FSDO to ensure operators can plan maintenance windows.

[P12] The instruction to send AMOC information directly to the certification office manager when appropriate (§ 39.13(l)(1)) is ambiguous because paragraph (m)(1) is not quoted; the AD should include the contact name and address in the body of the rule to prevent misrouting.

[P13] The option to email AMOC requests to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov (§ 39.13(l)(1)) should be complemented with an encrypted submission method or secure portal for attachments containing proprietary or export-controlled technical data.

[P14] The obligation to notify the principal inspector or local FSDO/CHDO manager before using an approved AMOC (§ 39.13(l)(2)) should specify minimum notification lead time (e.g., 48 hours) and required content of the notification.

[P14] The rule does not state whether notification under § 39.13(l)(2) must be written or can be verbal; written notification should be required to create an audit trail.

[P15] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs for repairs/modifications (§ 39.13(l)(3)) is efficient, but this creates a potential conflict of interest; the FAA should require independent FAA concurrence for ODA-approved AMOCs that change certification-basis features.

[P15] The AD should define the qualifications and documentation Boeing ODA must provide when approving AMOCs under paragraph (l)(3) to ensure consistency and traceability.

[P16] The requirement that repair/modification deviations meet the airplane’s certification basis (§ 39.13(l)(3)) is too vague; the AD should specify how to address older airplanes whose certification basis has changed or includes prior exemptions.

[P16] The rule should define the process for showing equivalence to the certification basis (e.g., required analyses, testing, and documentation) when seeking approval under paragraph (l)(3).

[P17] Requiring AMOC approvals to “specifically refer to this AD” (§ 39.13(l)(3)) is reasonable, but the FAA should permit consolidated AMOCs that address multiple ADs provided each AD is explicitly listed, to reduce administrative burden.

[P18] The statement that RC-step provisions apply (§ 39.13(l)(4)) needs clarification about how RC labeling in the Boeing service bulletin is identified and whether changes to RC labeling in later service bulletin revisions affect this AD.

[P19] Declaring RC-labeled steps mandatory (§ 39.13(l)(4)(i)) is appropriate for safety-critical tasks, but the AD should list which steps are RC to avoid disputes and to aid operators in planning.

[P20] The “RC Exempt” exception (§ 39.13(l)(4)(i)) needs a definition of how a step gets an “RC Exempt” label and whether that labeling requires FAA approval.

[P21] Requiring an AMOC for deviations from RC steps (§ 39.13(l)(4)(i)) is sound; however the AD must include expected FAA review timelines for AMOCs addressing RC deviations to prevent extended aircraft downtime.

[P22] Allowing deviations from non-RC steps using operator methods (§ 39.13(l)(4)(ii)) is helpful, but the AD should require operators to document deviations in their maintenance records and provide justification in case of audit.

[P22] The provision in § 39.13(l)(4)(ii) should clarify whether approved CMRs (Configuration Management Records) or approved company deviation procedures are sufficient to authorize deviation from non-RC steps.

[P23] The condition that RC steps can still be performed when deviating from non-RC steps (§ 39.13(l)(4)(ii)) is vague; the FAA should require a formal risk assessment demonstrating that RC step integrity is preserved.

[P24] The requirement that the airplane can be returned to an airworthy condition after deviation (§ 39.13(l)(4)(ii)) is basic but should specify what documentation must be produced to demonstrate restored airworthiness (e.g., functional checks, sign-offs, test flights).

[P24] The AD should clarify whether temporary deviations from non-RC steps that require later restoration actions are allowed and, if so, the maximum time allowed before full restoration is completed.

raw_output:
[P1] Industry commenter: Method 201A limited to “stationary sources only” (P1) is ambiguous for mobile or semi-stationary units (e.g., portable boilers, drilling rigs); request clarification that “stationary” excludes portable units used intermittently and specify criteria for stationarity.

[P1] Legal expert: The phrasing “stationary sources only” (P1) conflicts with other parts of the Clean Air Act definitions; recommend citing or reproducing the regulatory definition of “stationary source” to avoid inconsistent application.

[P2] Industry commenter: Allowing Method 201A to measure only filterable PM when filtration temperature > 29.4 °C (P2) could undercount total primary PM at sources where significant condensable PM forms above that temperature; request data justification and require tags/conditions when condensables are expected.

[P3] Environmental NGO: Requiring Method 201A be combined with Method 202 to measure both filterable and condensable PM when filtration temperature > 29.4 °C (P3) is appropriate but needs explicit sample collection, analytical QA/QC, and reporting requirements to ensure condensable fraction is not underreported.

[P3] Industry commenter: The requirement to measure both filterable and condensable PM when filtration temperature > 29.4 °C (P3) will substantially increase testing costs; request an economic impact analysis and phased compliance timeline or alternative thresholds.

[P4] Industry/regulator: The exception that Method 202 is not required if filtration temperature never exceeds 29.4 °C (P4) needs clear instruction on how to document and demonstrate that filtration temperature “never exceeds” 29.4 °C for the entire test period and long-term operations (e.g., continuous monitoring logs).

[P5] Testing labs: Permission to use Method 201A for PM10/PM2.5 sizing provided sampling is within 80–120% isokinetic flow (P5) is helpful, but the broad 80–120% band may affect size cut accuracy; request empirical validation or tightening to 90–110% for sizing applications.

[P6] Industry: The obligation to sample within 80–120% isokinetic flow for particle sizing (P6) is inconsistent with the more stringent 90–110% for total filterable particulate (P8); request harmonization or explanation why sizing can tolerate a wider range.

[P7] Industry/regulator: Permission to use Method 201A for total filterable particulate only if sampling meets flow, sampling-point, and filter-temperature conditions (P7) should explicitly list the “sampling-point” and “filter-temperature” criteria rather than cross-referencing multiple methods, to avoid confusion.

[P8] Testing organizations: The obligation that sampling must be within 90–110% isokinetic flow to obtain total filterable particulate (P8) is stricter than P6; request provision of acceptable correction procedures when small deviations occur and explicit procedures for documenting deviations.

[P9] Industry: Requiring the number of sampling points to match Method 5 or 17 (P9) may force >12 traverse points in large stacks (see P13); need clarity about how the fixed 12-point maximum in this method (P15) interacts with the cross-reference to Method 5/17.

[P10] Testing labs: The filter temperature requirement (P10) referencing “acceptable range for the referenced methods” lacks numeric bounds for several referenced methods; request inclusion of explicit temperature ranges for each applicable referenced method to prevent inconsistent interpretation.

[P11] Industry/QA: Specifying 120 °C as the “generally” acceptable filter temperature for Method 5 (P11) is not precise enough (“generally” ambiguous); request explicit allowable tolerance, e.g., 120 °C ± 5 °C, and conditions for when a different temperature is “specified.”

[P12] Industry/field techs: Permission to remove in-stack filters and use out-of-stack filters with PM recovery to satisfy Method 5 criteria (P12) should include validated recovery efficiency procedures and QA limits to prevent loss/contamination during transfer.

[P13] Industry: The permission to sample from >12 traverse points to satisfy Method 5 and 17 (P13) appears to conflict with Method 201A’s explicit maximum of 12 sample points (P14/P15); request resolution of this contradiction and specify which requirement governs.

[P14] Testing labs: Method 201A’s requirement for in-stack sampling using a maximum of 12 sample points, constant flow, and filter at stack temperature (P14) may be infeasible for stacks with highly nonuniform flow or large diameter; request allowance to use more traverse points or alternative approaches with approval.

[P15] Industry/regulator: The explicit cap “no more than 12 sample points” (P15) is impractical when Method 5 or 17 requires more points for accuracy in large stacks; ask EPA to allow exceeding 12 points when Method 5/17 would require it and to provide an approval process.

[P16] Testing labs: The obligation to operate the sampling train at constant flow to maintain cyclone size cuts (P16) should provide tolerances and corrective actions for transient flow variations and specify how to document constant-flow compliance.

[P17] Industry: Requiring the filter to be at stack temperature during sampling (P17) may not be achievable for stacks with very high temperatures; request acceptable temperature range and description of allowable engineering controls (e.g., heated housings) to meet requirement.

[P18] Industry/testing labs: Requirement to extend sampling time to collect minimum mass when using Method 201A instead of Method 5 or 17 (P18) should specify the minimum mass threshold, maximum allowable extension, and how extended sampling affects cross-contamination and measurement uncertainty.

[P19] All stakeholders: The obligation to obtain approval from the “establishing authority” before using Method 201A as an alternative to a regulatory test method (P19) needs definition of “establishing authority,” a timeline for approval decisions, and appeal procedures.

[P20] Testing labs: The Petri dishes requirement (glass, polystyrene, polyethylene) (P20) should permit other inert materials commonly used in field practice (e.g., polypropylene) or provide process for Administrator to approve equivalent materials.

[P21] Field technicians: Preheating the combined sampling head to stack temperature ±28 °C (±50 °F) (P21) allows a very wide tolerance; request tightening to ±10 °C or provide technical justification for ±28 °C given its potential impact on condensable capture.

[P22] Manufacturers/third-party certifiers: Requiring test labs to allow manufacturer, certifier, EPA, and delegated state agencies to observe certification testing (P22) is reasonable, but the rule should define observer roles, confidentiality protections, and limits on the number of observers to avoid interference.

[P23] Manufacturers: The prohibition on manufacturer participation in test conduct after the pretest burn begins (P23) is overly broad and could prevent necessary operational assistance in unsafe or emergency conditions; request an exception that allows manufacturer technical support for safety incidents if documented.

[P24] Manufacturers/test labs: Requiring operational communications be written and transmitted prior to the first pretest burn (P24) may be impractical for last-minute corrective actions; request allowance for written post-test clarification and a defined procedure for emergency verbal communications documented immediately thereafter.

[P25] Manufacturers/certifiers: Permitting manufacturers to communicate in writing with third-party certifier during tests to notify observed deviations (P25) is appropriate, but require that these written communications be time-stamped and incorporated into real-time test records to ensure traceability.

[P26] Test labs/legal: The requirement that all communications be included in test documentation and conform to the owner’s manual (P26) raises confidentiality and proprietary information concerns; request a process for redacting proprietary operational details while still providing sufficient documentation for regulators.

[P27] Landfill operators: Monthly monitoring of landfill gas temperature (P27) is operationally burdensome for small landfills; request allowance for alternative monitoring frequency tied to stability of prior measurements or use of representative sampling points.

[P28] Landfill operators: Annual calibration of the temperature measuring device per Method 2 (P28) is appropriate but the specified procedure in Method 2 Section 10.3 is designed for flow rate calibrations — request clarification that the referenced procedure is appropriate for temperature sensors and specify calibration tolerances.

[P29] Engineers/regulators: Requiring calibration at a minimum of two temperature points that bracket within 10% of landfill absolute temperatures (P29) could be impossible when landfill absolute temperatures vary widely; request alternative bracketing language or use of the ice/boiling fixed points exclusively (P30).

[P30] Small operators: The optional use of ice-bath and boiling-water fixed points corrected for barometric pressure for calibration (P30) should be allowed as a primary method for remote sites without access to calibration baths; request detailed correction procedures be included.

[P31] Source operators: Requiring establishment of a PM CPMS operating limit according to specified procedures if used for continuing compliance (P31) is acceptable, but the rule should explicitly allow use of existing CPMS calibration data when performing re-establishment to reduce redundant testing.

[P32] Stack test labs: Setting the operating limit as either the average CPMS output during the performance test or the output corresponding to 75% of the emission limit (P32) is unclear for tests that vary; request clear numeric examples and an algorithm for converting manual-run PM concentrations to CPMS mA values.

[P33] Industry: The requirement to verify or establish a new operating limit after each repeated performance test (P33) could cause frequent limit drift and regulatory uncertainty; request limiting re-establishment to when test results deviate by a predefined percent (e.g., >10%) from prior limits.

[P34] Operators: Annual performance tests and reassessment of site-specific operating limits (P34) create high recurring costs; request allowance for multi-year intervals when previous tests show consistent compliance and low variability, with EPA approval.

[P35] Instrument manufacturers: Requiring PM CPMS to provide 4–20 mA output (P35) may preclude newer digital-only instruments; request acceptance of digital outputs as long as a documented digital-to-analog conversion or standardized data format is provided.

[P36] Operators/engineers: PM CPMS must read zero up to at least two times allowable emission limit (P36) — for low allowable limits this may demand very high instrument dynamic range and accuracy; request allowance for ranges tied to instrument manufacturer specifications or mandatory auto-ranging verification procedures.

[P37] Test labs: Recording and averaging all PM CPMS outputs corresponding to compliance test runs (P37) is appropriate, but the method should specify averaging periods and handling of transient spikes or missing data to avoid penalizing short-term instrument anomalies.

[P38] Testing protocol experts: The requirement to calculate an operating limit by relating CPMS signal to PM concentration when average of three PM runs is below 75% of limit (P38) needs a prescribed statistical method and minimum data points to ensure robust regression and to avoid overfitting to low-concentration data.

[P39] Kiln operators: Annual performance testing for many pollutants for waste-burning kilns (P39) is costly and technically challenging; request that sources able to demonstrate reliable continuous monitoring (CEMS) be allowed to reduce or eliminate some annual tests.

[P40] Industry/environmental: The exception permitting use of CEMS instead of annual performance testing (P40) should be expanded and clarified to specify required CEMS performance standards, QA procedures, and acceptable downtime allowances so operators can make informed compliance choices.

[P41] Operators: Requiring HCl CEMS if no scrubber is present (P41) could be technically difficult for small kilns; request allowance for performance testing using validated sorbent methods as an alternative where HCl CEMS are not commercially available or economically feasible.

[P42] Kiln operators/regulators: Mandating mercury compliance be determined using mercury CEMS or integrated sorbent traps (P42) is acceptable, but sorbent trap analytical detection limits and QA/QC requirements should be specified given low mercury emission limits in tables (P59, P70, P81, P92).

[P43] Cement/waste operators: Requiring NOx and SO2 CEMS (P43) is standard but for small units cost-prohibitive; request tiered thresholds based on unit capacity below which periodic performance testing is allowed instead of continuous CEMS.

[P44] Operators: Requirement to use PM CPMS to demonstrate continuing PM compliance (P44) may be inappropriate for sources where CPMS technology is not validated for their process; request option to use a surrogate parameter (e.g., opacity) with EPA approval.

[P45] Industry: Permitting performance test results as alternative to installing CEMS/PM CPMS on certain bypass/inline stacks (P45) is useful, but the rule should specify minimum frequency and QA for such tests and limits on operational changes between tests.

[P46] Operators: The annual performance testing requirement “no later than 13 months after previous test” (P46) is reasonable, but the rule should allow extensions for unforeseen circumstances (e.g., pandemics, natural disasters) with a formal notification process.

[P47] All stakeholders: The general 13-month window for annual performance tests (P47) conflicts with some other program requirements tied to calendar-year reporting; request harmonization of test scheduling rules and clear instructions on reporting when tests fall outside a calendar year.

[P48] Permittees: The annual report inclusion of items (a) through (p) (P48) should be published as a consolidated checklist in the preamble or guidance to reduce administrative burden and ensure uniform reporting across jurisdictions.

[P49] Operators/advocates: Requirement to submit deviation reports for any deviation from operating limits or emission limitations (P49) must specify timelines for submission (e.g., within 30 days), required content, and whether minor deviations require the same level of formal reporting.

[P50] Energy recovery units: Requiring annual heat input and average annual heat input rate in the annual report for energy recovery units (P50) may be difficult when fuels are varied; request instruction on accounting for mixed fuels and acceptable estimation methods.

[P51] Operators/environment: Table 6 emission limitations for energy recovery units (P51) impose many new numeric limits; request transition timelines, demonstration-testing protocols, and consideration of fuel-specific operational realities before enforcement.

[P52] Industry/environmental labs: The cadmium limit in Table 6 (0.023 mg/dscm with fuel-specific values and 3-run averages) (P52) requires minimum sample volumes; request clarification of exact minimum volumes and detection limit demonstration protocols.

[P53] Operators: CO limits in Table 6 (35 ppm dv / fuel-specific values with 1-hour minimum sample time per run) (P53) need specification of reference oxygen correction basis and whether volume-based ppmdv is corrected to 7% O2 or other reference.

[P54] Environmental health groups: Dioxin/furans limits in Table 6 using TEQ but no total mass basis (P54) could allow high absolute mass of dioxins if TEQ skewed; request EPA to retain a complementary total mass cap or require species-specific reporting.

[P55] Toxicologists: The TEQ dioxin/furans limits (P55) require high-sensitivity sampling and analysis; request minimum laboratory QA/QC criteria and preparation protocols to ensure comparability of TEQ results across labs.

[P56] Community groups: Fugitive ash visible emission limit ≤5% of hourly observation periods using three 1-hour Method 22 observations (P56) is insufficiently protective because Method 22 is subjective; request continuous optical monitoring (e.g., cameras or PM sensors) and community-accessible reports.

[P57] Operators: HCl limits in Table 6 and elsewhere (P57) reference Method 26 with minimum volumes (e.g., 360 L) — need consistency across tables and clarification on sample volume differences between fuels and methods.

[P58] Environmental groups: Lead limits in Table 6 and Table 7 (P58,P69) rely on 3-run averages and minimum volumes; given lead’s toxicity, request lower limits and shorter averaging periods to better protect public health.

[P59] Public health advocates: Mercury limits listed (P59,P70,P81,P92) are very low and require highly sensitive sampling; request that EPA require third-party laboratory proficiency testing and method detection limit demonstration before relying on these values for compliance decisions.

[P60] Industry: NOx emission limits in Tables 6–8 (P60,P71,P82,P93) expressed as ppm dv may require clarification on reference oxygen or dry-corrected basis and whether conversion to mass-based units is permitted for tradeable compliance schemes.

[P61] Operators: The filterable PM limits (P61,P72,P83,P94) with high variability between fuel types (e.g., 5.1 mg/dscm biomass vs 130 mg/dscm coal) require explanation of the fuel categorization methodology and a process for reclassifying fuels with mixed composition.

[P62] Industry/environmental: SO2 limits in Tables (P62,P73,P84,P95) expressed as very high ppm values for coal (e.g., 850 ppm) appear inconsistent with control technology expectations; request clarification of reference conditions and whether these are interim or final numeric values.

[P63] Legal experts: Multiple cross-references to other appendices and methods create regulatory complexity and potential contradictions (e.g., P9 vs P15/P13); request consolidation of all Method 201A-related measurement rules into a single, self-contained section or explicit hierarchy of controlling provisions.

[P64] Small entities/small communities: The combined testing, CPMS, and CEMS requirements across the rule (P31–P44 and many table entries) impose substantial capital and operating costs; request a Small Entities Compliance Guide and possible tiered compliance options or extension of compliance deadlines for small sources.

parsed_claims.claim_text: Industry commenter: Method 201A limited to “stationary sources only” (P1) is ambiguous for mobile or semi-stationary units (e.g., portable boilers, drilling rigs); request clarification that “stationary” excludes portable units used intermittently and specify criteria for stationarity.

Legal expert: The phrasing “stationary sources only” (P1) conflicts with other parts of the Clean Air Act definitions; recommend citing or reproducing the regulatory definition of “stationary source” to avoid inconsistent application.

Industry commenter: Allowing Method 201A to measure only filterable PM when filtration temperature > 29.4 °C (P2) could undercount total primary PM at sources where significant condensable PM forms above that temperature; request data justification and require tags/conditions when condensables are expected.

Environmental NGO: Requiring Method 201A be combined with Method 202 to measure both filterable and condensable PM when filtration temperature > 29.4 °C (P3) is appropriate but needs explicit sample collection, analytical QA/QC, and reporting requirements to ensure condensable fraction is not underreported.

Industry commenter: The requirement to measure both filterable and condensable PM when filtration temperature > 29.4 °C (P3) will substantially increase testing costs; request an economic impact analysis and phased compliance timeline or alternative thresholds.

Industry/regulator: The exception that Method 202 is not required if filtration temperature never exceeds 29.4 °C (P4) needs clear instruction on how to document and demonstrate that filtration temperature “never exceeds” 29.4 °C for the entire test period and long-term operations (e.g., continuous monitoring logs).

Testing labs: Permission to use Method 201A for PM10/PM2.5 sizing provided sampling is within 80–120% isokinetic flow (P5) is helpful, but the broad 80–120% band may affect size cut accuracy; request empirical validation or tightening to 90–110% for sizing applications.

Industry: The obligation to sample within 80–120% isokinetic flow for particle sizing (P6) is inconsistent with the more stringent 90–110% for total filterable particulate (P8); request harmonization or explanation why sizing can tolerate a wider range.

Industry/regulator: Permission to use Method 201A for total filterable particulate only if sampling meets flow, sampling-point, and filter-temperature conditions (P7) should explicitly list the “sampling-point” and “filter-temperature” criteria rather than cross-referencing multiple methods, to avoid confusion.

Testing organizations: The obligation that sampling must be within 90–110% isokinetic flow to obtain total filterable particulate (P8) is stricter than P6; request provision of acceptable correction procedures when small deviations occur and explicit procedures for documenting deviations.

Industry: Requiring the number of sampling points to match Method 5 or 17 (P9) may force >12 traverse points in large stacks (see P13); need clarity about how the fixed 12-point maximum in this method (P15) interacts with the cross-reference to Method 5/17.

Testing labs: The filter temperature requirement (P10) referencing “acceptable range for the referenced methods” lacks numeric bounds for several referenced methods; request inclusion of explicit temperature ranges for each applicable referenced method to prevent inconsistent interpretation.

Industry/QA: Specifying 120 °C as the “generally” acceptable filter temperature for Method 5 (P11) is not precise enough (“generally” ambiguous); request explicit allowable tolerance, e.g., 120 °C ± 5 °C, and conditions for when a different temperature is “specified.”

Industry/field techs: Permission to remove in-stack filters and use out-of-stack filters with PM recovery to satisfy Method 5 criteria (P12) should include validated recovery efficiency procedures and QA limits to prevent loss/contamination during transfer.

Industry: The permission to sample from >12 traverse points to satisfy Method 5 and 17 (P13) appears to conflict with Method 201A’s explicit maximum of 12 sample points (P14/P15); request resolution of this contradiction and specify which requirement governs.

Testing labs: Method 201A’s requirement for in-stack sampling using a maximum of 12 sample points, constant flow, and filter at stack temperature (P14) may be infeasible for stacks with highly nonuniform flow or large diameter; request allowance to use more traverse points or alternative approaches with approval.

Industry/regulator: The explicit cap “no more than 12 sample points” (P15) is impractical when Method 5 or 17 requires more points for accuracy in large stacks; ask EPA to allow exceeding 12 points when Method 5/17 would require it and to provide an approval process.

Testing labs: The obligation to operate the sampling train at constant flow to maintain cyclone size cuts (P16) should provide tolerances and corrective actions for transient flow variations and specify how to document constant-flow compliance.

Industry: Requiring the filter to be at stack temperature during sampling (P17) may not be achievable for stacks with very high temperatures; request acceptable temperature range and description of allowable engineering controls (e.g., heated housings) to meet requirement.

Industry/testing labs: Requirement to extend sampling time to collect minimum mass when using Method 201A instead of Method 5 or 17 (P18) should specify the minimum mass threshold, maximum allowable extension, and how extended sampling affects cross-contamination and measurement uncertainty.

All stakeholders: The obligation to obtain approval from the “establishing authority” before using Method 201A as an alternative to a regulatory test method (P19) needs definition of “establishing authority,” a timeline for approval decisions, and appeal procedures.

Testing labs: The Petri dishes requirement (glass, polystyrene, polyethylene) (P20) should permit other inert materials commonly used in field practice (e.g., polypropylene) or provide process for Administrator to approve equivalent materials.

Field technicians: Preheating the combined sampling head to stack temperature ±28 °C (±50 °F) (P21) allows a very wide tolerance; request tightening to ±10 °C or provide technical justification for ±28 °C given its potential impact on condensable capture.

Manufacturers/third-party certifiers: Requiring test labs to allow manufacturer, certifier, EPA, and delegated state agencies to observe certification testing (P22) is reasonable, but the rule should define observer roles, confidentiality protections, and limits on the number of observers to avoid interference.

Manufacturers: The prohibition on manufacturer participation in test conduct after the pretest burn begins (P23) is overly broad and could prevent necessary operational assistance in unsafe or emergency conditions; request an exception that allows manufacturer technical support for safety incidents if documented.

Manufacturers/test labs: Requiring operational communications be written and transmitted prior to the first pretest burn (P24) may be impractical for last-minute corrective actions; request allowance for written post-test clarification and a defined procedure for emergency verbal communications documented immediately thereafter.

Manufacturers/certifiers: Permitting manufacturers to communicate in writing with third-party certifier during tests to notify observed deviations (P25) is appropriate, but require that these written communications be time-stamped and incorporated into real-time test records to ensure traceability.

Test labs/legal: The requirement that all communications be included in test documentation and conform to the owner’s manual (P26) raises confidentiality and proprietary information concerns; request a process for redacting proprietary operational details while still providing sufficient documentation for regulators.

Landfill operators: Monthly monitoring of landfill gas temperature (P27) is operationally burdensome for small landfills; request allowance for alternative monitoring frequency tied to stability of prior measurements or use of representative sampling points.

Landfill operators: Annual calibration of the temperature measuring device per Method 2 (P28) is appropriate but the specified procedure in Method 2 Section 10.3 is designed for flow rate calibrations — request clarification that the referenced procedure is appropriate for temperature sensors and specify calibration tolerances.

Engineers/regulators: Requiring calibration at a minimum of two temperature points that bracket within 10% of landfill absolute temperatures (P29) could be impossible when landfill absolute temperatures vary widely; request alternative bracketing language or use of the ice/boiling fixed points exclusively (P30).

Small operators: The optional use of ice-bath and boiling-water fixed points corrected for barometric pressure for calibration (P30) should be allowed as a primary method for remote sites without access to calibration baths; request detailed correction procedures be included.

Source operators: Requiring establishment of a PM CPMS operating limit according to specified procedures if used for continuing compliance (P31) is acceptable, but the rule should explicitly allow use of existing CPMS calibration data when performing re-establishment to reduce redundant testing.

Stack test labs: Setting the operating limit as either the average CPMS output during the performance test or the output corresponding to 75% of the emission limit (P32) is unclear for tests that vary; request clear numeric examples and an algorithm for converting manual-run PM concentrations to CPMS mA values.

Industry: The requirement to verify or establish a new operating limit after each repeated performance test (P33) could cause frequent limit drift and regulatory uncertainty; request limiting re-establishment to when test results deviate by a predefined percent (e.g., >10%) from prior limits.

Operators: Annual performance tests and reassessment of site-specific operating limits (P34) create high recurring costs; request allowance for multi-year intervals when previous tests show consistent compliance and low variability, with EPA approval.

Instrument manufacturers: Requiring PM CPMS to provide 4–20 mA output (P35) may preclude newer digital-only instruments; request acceptance of digital outputs as long as a documented digital-to-analog conversion or standardized data format is provided.

Operators/engineers: PM CPMS must read zero up to at least two times allowable emission limit (P36) — for low allowable limits this may demand very high instrument dynamic range and accuracy; request allowance for ranges tied to instrument manufacturer specifications or mandatory auto-ranging verification procedures.

Test labs: Recording and averaging all PM CPMS outputs corresponding to compliance test runs (P37) is appropriate, but the method should specify averaging periods and handling of transient spikes or missing data to avoid penalizing short-term instrument anomalies.

Testing protocol experts: The requirement to calculate an operating limit by relating CPMS signal to PM concentration when average of three PM runs is below 75% of limit (P38) needs a prescribed statistical method and minimum data points to ensure robust regression and to avoid overfitting to low-concentration data.

Kiln operators: Annual performance testing for many pollutants for waste-burning kilns (P39) is costly and technically challenging; request that sources able to demonstrate reliable continuous monitoring (CEMS) be allowed to reduce or eliminate some annual tests.

Operators: Requirement to use PM CPMS to demonstrate continuing PM compliance (P44) may be inappropriate for sources where CPMS technology is not validated for their process; request option to use a surrogate parameter (e.g., opacity) with EPA approval.

Industry: Permitting performance test results as alternative to installing CEMS/PM CPMS on certain bypass/inline stacks (P45) is useful, but the rule should specify minimum frequency and QA for such tests and limits on operational changes between tests.

Operators: The annual performance testing requirement “no later than 13 months after previous test” (P46) is reasonable, but the rule should allow extensions for unforeseen circumstances (e.g., pandemics, natural disasters) with a formal notification process.

All stakeholders: The general 13-month window for annual performance tests (P47) conflicts with some other program requirements tied to calendar-year reporting; request harmonization of test scheduling rules and clear instructions on reporting when tests fall outside a calendar year.

Permittees: The annual report inclusion of items (a) through (p) (P48) should be published as a consolidated checklist in the preamble or guidance to reduce administrative burden and ensure uniform reporting across jurisdictions.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement that comments be identified by Docket ID No. EPA–R10–RCRA–2018–0298 is overly rigid and may cause EPA to dismiss substantively important comments that fail to use the exact identifier; EPA should accept comments referencing the docket in any reasonable form.

[P1] Requiring submission by one of the listed methods (www.regulations.gov, email, mail, hand delivery) excludes stakeholders who rely on alternative digital platforms or public interest intermediaries; EPA should explicitly accept comments submitted through authorized third parties.

[P2] The instruction to follow online instructions at www.regulations.gov lacks guidance for users with disabilities; EPA should provide accessible step‑by‑step assistance and alternative submission formats for users who cannot use the website.

[P3] Directing comments to a specific individual email address (mccullough.barbara@epa.gov) creates a single point of failure and privacy risk; EPA should provide a general docket email address or confirmation that messages to this address are automatically routed into the docket system.

[P3] Using a personal-looking email for submissions raises concerns about long-term availability and staff turnover; EPA should confirm the address will be monitored and retained for the entire comment period and archived in the docket.

[P4] Mailing comments to the listed postal address may create delays that cause submissions to miss the October 5, 2018 deadline; EPA should clarify the mailbox postmark rule or accept any mail postmarked by the deadline.

[P5] The hand delivery option requires physical presence in Seattle, which is burdensome for rural, out‑of‑state, or disabled stakeholders; EPA should provide a timed pickup or courier alternative and extend business hours during the comment period.

[P6] Limiting hand deliveries to normal business hours disadvantages working commenters and community groups; EPA should offer extended or weekend hours or clear instructions on making "special arrangements" for after‑hours boxed deliveries.

[P6] The provision about "special arrangements" for boxed deliveries is vague — EPA must specify how to request arrangements, required lead time, and contact information to avoid lost submissions.

[P7] The prohibition on submitting CBI via www.regulations.gov or email is sensible for public transparency but fails to state the process for submitting redacted public comments while providing CBI to EPA; EPA should describe secure CBI submission procedures (e.g., physical submission or encrypted portal).

[P7] The rule does not specify how EPA will handle partially confidential submissions (public redacted version + confidential annex); commenters need clear instructions to avoid accidental public disclosure.

[P8] Requiring all comments be directed to the docket ID may be redundant with other identifiers; EPA should accept comments that reference the action title or Federal Register citation in addition to the docket number.

[P9] The obligation that electronic files avoid special characters/encryption and be virus-free is reasonable, but EPA should publish an acceptable file format list (e.g., PDF/A, .docx) and offer help for users whose software inserts characters automatically.

[P9] The prohibition on encrypted submissions conflicts with the need to submit CBI securely; EPA should provide an approved secure upload method for confidential materials rather than outright banning encryption.

[P10] Recommending that electronic comments include name and contact info in the body is insufficient; EPA should require a contact phone number and mailing address for follow‑up and specify whether organization affiliation should be listed.

[P10] The statement that including contact info is a recommendation — not a requirement — may allow anonymous comments; EPA should require minimum contact information to permit clarification under P11.

[P11] EPA's statement that unreadable comments may not be considered if EPA cannot contact the commenter creates due process concerns; EPA should commit to attempting at least two reasonable contact attempts before excluding a comment.

[P12] The firm deadline of October 5, 2018 does not accommodate stakeholders who receive the notice late; EPA should provide a mechanism for accepting late comments for good cause (e.g., postal delays, technical outages) or at least clarify the late‑comment policy.

[P12] The rule does not state the time zone for the deadline — commenters nationwide need EPA to specify deadline time (e.g., 11:59 pm ET) to avoid confusion.

[P13] The obligation that authorized States maintain hazardous waste programs "no less stringent" than Federal program is vague — EPA should define objective metrics for equivalence to prevent arbitrary enforcement.

[P14] Requiring States to update programs and request EPA authorization whenever the Federal program changes could impose significant administrative burden; EPA should set timeframes and prioritize material changes to reduce States' compliance costs.

[P15] Allowing Idaho to retain permitting responsibility for TSDFs except in Indian country could create regulatory gaps for facilities near reservation boundaries; EPA should clarify jurisdictional coordination procedures between State, EPA, and tribal authorities.

[P16] The provision that EPA will implement HSWA requirements in Idaho until authorization is granted lacks a clear timeline; EPA should specify estimated durations and criteria for transition to State authority.

[P17] Stating that facilities must follow authorized State requirements in lieu of Federal rules could create confusion where State and Federal texts diverge; EPA should require that authorized State rules be published with crosswalks to the Federal requirements.

[P18] Obligating facilities to comply with applicable Federal requirements that the State is not authorized for may create dual compliance burdens; EPA should identify which HSWA regulations remain EPA‑implemented and publish a consolidated compliance list.

[P19] Idaho's retention of enforcement authority raises concerns about enforcement consistency across States; stakeholders request EPA to publish enforcement performance benchmarks and oversight frequency for authorized States.

[P20] EPA's retention of authorities under RCRA sections 3007, 3008, 3013, and 7003 is broad; commenters seek clarification on how EPA will coordinate exercise of those authorities to avoid duplicative or contradictory actions with State enforcement.

[P21] The permission for EPA to require monitoring, tests, analyses, or reports lacks proportionality standards — EPA should indicate thresholds or criteria for imposing such requirements to prevent burdensome inspections.

[P22] The duplication between P21 and P22 (inspections may include requiring monitoring/tests/etc.) implies inconsistent drafting; EPA should consolidate and clarify the scope and limits of its inspection authority.

[P23] The EPA's authority to suspend, terminate, modify, or revoke permits is necessary, but commenters request notice, hearing, and appeal procedures to ensure fairness when EPA takes enforcement actions overlapping State actions.

[P24] Because enforcement actions may include permit revocation, commenters ask EPA to publish criteria and timelines for such actions and specify how they interact with State enforcement to avoid conflicting orders.

[P25] EPA may take enforcement regardless of Idaho's actions — industry stakeholders worry this could lead to duplicative penalties; EPA should commit to coordination and deconfliction procedures and explain how penalties will be allocated.

[P26] The prohibition suggesting there may be no further opportunity to comment is misleading; affected stakeholders may need additional notice once Idaho's final rulemaking occurs — EPA should commit to further notice if substantial changes arise.

[P27] Telling interested parties to submit comments now is reasonable, but EPA should provide outreach to communities and small businesses disproportionately affected to ensure meaningful participation.

[P28] The statutory prohibition on authorizing less stringent State laws is clear, but environmental groups will request EPA to define "less stringent" with examples and explain how it will evaluate equivalence.

[P29] The condition that less stringent State laws do not supersede Federal regulations needs enforcement mechanisms; commenters ask EPA to specify how it will prevent non‑authorized State rules from being applied in practice.

[P30] The prohibition on authorizing State laws broader in scope than the Federal program could prevent States from addressing local concerns; tribal governments and local advocates will argue that EPA should allow expansion where protective and consistent with RCRA.

[P31] Allowing authorization of State laws that are equivalent or more stringent is welcome; however, stakeholders request clarity on whether EPA will assume enforcement authority over State "more stringent" provisions after authorization and under what terms.

[P32] The obligation for Idaho to revise regulations to reflect the vacatur is vague on timing; EPA should set a clear deadline and provide technical assistance to ensure Idaho's revisions achieve equivalence.

[P33] The obligation that Idaho will keep issuing and administering permits for authorized provisions raises questions about permit processing capacity — EPA should require Idaho to demonstrate adequate staffing and resources before full authorization.

[P34] The condition that existing EPA permits remain in force until State action could cause overlapping permit obligations; EPA should clarify how permit conditions will be reconciled and whether facilities must comply with both until transition.

[P35] EPA's option to modify existing EPA permits to set earlier expiration dates when a State permit becomes effective could prejudice permittees; EPA should require notice and opportunity to contest earlier expirations.

[P36] The EPA's authority to terminate existing EPA permits "for cause" upon State permit issuance/denial must be defined; commenters seek a definition of "cause" and procedural safeguards for permit holders.

[P37] Allowing EPA permits to simply expire by their terms could create uncertainty about continuity of requirements — EPA should require that State permits be effective before EPA permits expire to prevent regulatory gaps.

[P38] The prohibition on EPA issuing new permits for provisions the State is authorized to implement may slow emergency responses if the State is not yet prepared; EPA should retain limited authority to issue permits in emergencies.

[P39] EPA's ongoing implementation of HSWA requirements for which Idaho is not authorized needs a published list of those requirements so facilities know which agency to contact for permits and enforcement.

[P40] The statement that Idaho is not authorized to implement its hazardous waste program in Indian country must be accompanied by explicit coordination requirements with tribes; tribal governments should be consulted and afforded opportunities to assume program responsibilities.

[P41] The obligation that the program revision does not apply in Indian country leaves potential gaps for non‑tribal lands within reservation boundaries; EPA should clarify jurisdictional boundaries and provide mapping resources.

[P42] EPA's requirement to submit the rule report to Congress and the Comptroller General prior to publication should be transparent to the public; commenters request that EPA post the submitted report and any communications with Congress to the docket.

[P43] The prohibition that major rules cannot take effect until 60 days after publication needs clarification whether this change is considered a "major rule"; commenters ask EPA to state explicitly whether the rule is a "major rule" and, if so, to confirm the effective date calculation.

Requiring all comments be directed to the docket ID may be redundant with other identifiers; EPA should accept comments that reference the action title or Federal Register citation in addition to the docket number.

The obligation that electronic files avoid special characters/encryption and be virus-free is reasonable, but EPA should publish an acceptable file format list (e.g., PDF/A, .docx) and offer help for users whose software inserts characters automatically.

The prohibition on encrypted submissions conflicts with the need to submit CBI securely; EPA should provide an approved secure upload method for confidential materials rather than outright banning encryption.

Recommending that electronic comments include name and contact info in the body is insufficient; EPA should require a contact phone number and mailing address for follow‑up and specify whether organization affiliation should be listed.
The statement that including contact info is a recommendation — not a requirement — may allow anonymous comments; EPA should require minimum contact information to permit clarification under P11.

EPA's statement that unreadable comments may not be considered if EPA cannot contact the commenter creates due process concerns; EPA should commit to attempting at least two reasonable contact attempts before excluding a comment.

The firm deadline of October 5, 2018 does not accommodate stakeholders who receive the notice late; EPA should provide a mechanism for accepting late comments for good cause (e.g., postal delays, technical outages) or at least clarify the late‑comment policy.
The rule does not state the time zone for the deadline — commenters nationwide need EPA to specify deadline time (e.g., 11:59 pm ET) to avoid confusion.

The obligation that authorized States maintain hazardous waste programs "no less stringent" than Federal program is vague — EPA should define objective metrics for equivalence to prevent arbitrary enforcement.

Requiring States to update programs and request EPA authorization whenever the Federal program changes could impose significant administrative burden; EPA should set timeframes and prioritize material changes to reduce States' compliance costs.

Allowing Idaho to retain permitting responsibility for TSDFs except in Indian country could create regulatory gaps for facilities near reservation boundaries; EPA should clarify jurisdictional coordination procedures between State, EPA, and tribal authorities.

The provision that EPA will implement HSWA requirements in Idaho until authorization is granted lacks a clear timeline; EPA should specify estimated durations and criteria for transition to State authority.

Stating that facilities must follow authorized State requirements in lieu of Federal rules could create confusion where State and Federal texts diverge; EPA should require that authorized State rules be published with crosswalks to the Federal requirements.

Obligating facilities to comply with applicable Federal requirements that the State is not authorized for may create dual compliance burdens; EPA should identify which HSWA regulations remain EPA‑implemented and publish a consolidated compliance list.

Idaho's retention of enforcement authority raises concerns about enforcement consistency across States; stakeholders request EPA to publish enforcement performance benchmarks and oversight frequency for authorized States.

EPA's retention of authorities under RCRA sections 3007, 3008, 3013, and 7003 is broad; commenters seek clarification on how EPA will coordinate exercise of those authorities to avoid duplicative or contradictory actions with State enforcement.

The permission for EPA to require monitoring, tests, analyses, or reports lacks proportionality standards — EPA should indicate thresholds or criteria for imposing such requirements to prevent burdensome inspections.

The duplication between P21 and P22 (inspections may include requiring monitoring/tests/etc.) implies inconsistent drafting; EPA should consolidate and clarify the scope and limits of its inspection authority.

The EPA's authority to suspend, terminate, modify, or revoke permits is necessary, but commenters request notice, hearing, and appeal procedures to ensure fairness when EPA takes enforcement actions overlapping State actions.

Because enforcement actions may include permit revocation, commenters ask EPA to publish criteria and timelines for such actions and specify how they interact with State enforcement to avoid conflicting orders.

EPA may take enforcement regardless of Idaho's actions — industry stakeholders worry this could lead to duplicative penalties; EPA should commit to coordination and deconfliction procedures and explain how penalties will be allocated.

The prohibition suggesting there may be no further opportunity to comment is misleading; affected stakeholders may need additional notice once Idaho's final rulemaking occurs — EPA should commit to further notice if substantial changes arise.
Telling interested parties to submit comments now is reasonable, but EPA should provide outreach to communities and small businesses disproportionately affected to ensure meaningful participation.

The statutory prohibition on authorizing less stringent State laws is clear, but environmental groups will request EPA to define "less stringent" with examples and explain how it will evaluate equivalence.

The condition that less stringent State laws do not supersede Federal regulations needs enforcement mechanisms; commenters ask EPA to specify how it will prevent non‑authorized State rules from being applied in practice.

The prohibition on authorizing State laws broader in scope than the Federal program could prevent States from addressing local concerns; tribal governments and local advocates will argue that EPA should allow expansion where protective and consistent with RCRA.

Allowing authorization of State laws that are equivalent or more stringent is welcome; however, stakeholders request clarity on whether EPA will assume enforcement authority over State "more stringent" provisions after authorization and under what terms.

The obligation for Idaho to revise regulations to reflect the vacatur is vague on timing; EPA should set a clear deadline and provide technical assistance to ensure Idaho's revisions achieve equivalence.

The obligation that Idaho will keep issuing and administering permits for authorized provisions raises questions about permit processing capacity — EPA should require Idaho to demonstrate adequate staffing and resources before full authorization.

The condition that existing EPA permits remain in force until State action could cause overlapping permit obligations; EPA should clarify how permit conditions will be reconciled and whether facilities must comply with both until transition.

EPA's option to modify existing EPA permits to set earlier expiration dates when a State permit becomes effective could prejudice permittees; EPA should require notice and opportunity to contest earlier expirations.

The EPA's authority to terminate existing EPA permits "for cause" upon State permit issuance/denial must be defined; commenters seek a definition of "cause" and procedural safeguards for permit holders.

Allowing EPA permits to simply expire by their terms could create uncertainty about continuity of requirements — EPA should require that State permits be effective before EPA permits expire to prevent regulatory gaps.

The prohibition on EPA issuing new permits for provisions the State is authorized to implement may slow emergency responses if the State is not yet prepared; EPA should retain limited authority to issue permits in emergencies.

EPA's ongoing implementation of HSWA requirements for which Idaho is not authorized needs a published list of those requirements so facilities know which agency to contact for permits and enforcement.

The statement that Idaho is not authorized to implement its hazardous waste program in Indian country must be accompanied by explicit coordination requirements with tribes; tribal governments should be consulted and afforded opportunities to assume program responsibilities.

The obligation that the program revision does not apply in Indian country leaves potential gaps for non‑tribal lands within reservation boundaries; EPA should clarify jurisdictional boundaries and provide mapping resources.

EPA's requirement to submit the rule report to Congress and the Comptroller General prior to publication should be transparent to the public; commenters request that EPA post the submitted report and any communications with Congress to the docket.

The prohibition that major rules cannot take effect until 60 days after publication needs clarification whether this change is considered a "major rule"; commenters ask EPA to state explicitly whether the rule is a "major rule" and, if so, to confirm the effective date calculation.

raw_output:
[P1] The 100-day waiting requirement before billing Medicaid for child support enforcement services (§ 433.139(b)(3)(ii)(B)) is vague about when the clock starts (date of claim submission to the third party vs. date of acknowledgement of receipt), creating legal uncertainty for providers.

[P1] Requiring providers to certify that they "did not receive payment" after 100 days (§ 433.139(b)(3)(ii)(B)) fails to account for partial payments or denials; the rule should allow certification where no payment or only partial payment was received and specify how partial payments affect Medicaid billing.

[P1] The provision lacks an appeal or cure process if a provider certifies compliance but later discovers a third-party payment; the regulation should permit retroactive adjustment rather than harsh sanctions.

[P2] The broad requirement that contracts include “specified requirements related to covered outpatient drugs” (§ 438.3(s)) is overly prescriptive and could interfere with contractual flexibility between States and MCOs/MCEs/PIHPs/PAHPs.

[P3] Imposing the statutory drug utilization review requirements directly on MCOs/MCEs/PIHPs/PAHPs (§ 438.3(s)(4)) without funding or technical assistance will create unfunded mandates and administrative burden for smaller managed care plans.

[P3] The rule does not clarify whether existing plan DUR programs that substantially comply will be grandfathered or must be restructured to exactly mirror section 1927(g), which is administratively impractical.

[P4] Requiring annual detailed descriptions of DUR activities (§ 438.3(s)(5)) will duplicate State reporting obligations and increase administrative costs; CMS should adopt a standardized template to minimize reporting burden.

[P5] The VBP bundled sale permission (§ 447.502 (Bundled sale (3))) lacks clear standards for what constitutes a valid outcome metric or performance requirement, risking inconsistent application across States and potential gaming by manufacturers.

[P6] The requirement that manufacturers ensure the "full value" of coupons is passed to the consumer (§ 447.504(c)(25)) is undefined — CMS must clarify how "full value" is measured and documented, especially for multi-tier pharmacy benefit designs.

[P6] Asking manufacturers to certify that pharmacies/agents receive no price concession for coupons (§ 447.504(c)(25)) is impractical because manufacturers often lack visibility into pharmacy reimbursement arrangements and PBM contract terms.

[P7] The three-condition test for free-goods programs (§ 447.504(c)(26)) is overly rigid and could eliminate legitimate patient assistance programs that rely on third-party distribution mechanisms where a pharmacy or agent may receive incidental compensation.

[P8] The non-contingency requirement for vouchers (§ 447.504(c)(26)(i)) could prohibit common manufacturer programs that require enrollment or prior authorization for program eligibility; CMS should limit the restriction to impermissible tied sales only.

[P9] The mandate that the "full value" of vouchers be passed to consumers (§ 447.504(c)(26)(ii)) ignores scenarios where pharmacy co-pay differentials or tiering reduce the consumer's realized value; guidance is needed on how to calculate and verify "full value."

[P10] Prohibiting any price concession to pharmacies/agents under free-goods programs (§ 447.504(c)(26)(iii)) may conflict with existing accreditation or dispensing fees; CMS must define "price concession" and allow reasonable dispensing fees unrelated to manufacturer programs.

[P11] Requiring manufacturers to ensure discount card full value passes to consumers (§ 447.504(c)(27)) places impractical monitoring obligations on manufacturers for discounts administered by third parties and PBMs.

[P12] The obligation that patient refund/rebate programs provide full/partial refunds to patients (§ 447.504(c)(28)(i)) lacks definition of timeliness and documentation required to substantiate refunds, potentially leading to disputes about compliance.

[P12] § 447.504(c)(28)(ii)'s requirement that pharmacies/agents receive no price concession for patient rebate programs is unworkable because many pharmacies receive administrative fees or reimbursements that could be characterized as concessions; CMS must provide safe harbors.

[P15] The rule’s insistence that copayment assistance benefits go entirely to the patient (§ 447.504(c)(29)) does not account for integrated programs where patient assistance is delivered via pharmacies or clinics that retain administrative fees.

[P15] Requiring manufacturers to ensure the pharmacy receives "no price concession" from copay assistance programs (§ 447.504(c)(29)(ii)) intrudes into pharmacy-manufacturer commercial relationships and may be preempted by contract law.

[P18] Repeating the coupon/discount restrictions in § 447.504(e)(13) without clarifying differences from (c)(25) creates duplicative and possibly inconsistent compliance obligations between best price and AMP exclusions.

[P19] The free-goods program conditions in § 447.504(e)(14) duplicate (c)(26) and risk conflicting interpretations between AMP and best-price contexts; harmonization and cross-references are needed.

[P24] The refund/rebate conditions in § 447.504(e)(16) again compel manufacturers to certify third-party behavior (pharmacies/agents receive no price concession), which is beyond manufacturers' control and may be unenforceable.

[P30] Requiring manufacturers to adjust best price when cumulative discounts later change prices (§ 447.505(d)(3)) will create significant retrospective accounting complexity and unpredictability in rebate liabilities, particularly for long-tail VBP arrangements.

[P31] Excluding authorized generic sales to wholesalers from the brand manufacturer’s AMP calculation (§ 447.506(b)) may encourage gaming by splitting authorized generic sales channels; CMS should clarify anti-evasion safeguards and documentation requirements.

[P32] The rule’s cap that rebates cannot exceed 100% of AMP (§ 447.509(a)(5)) is reasonable, but the regulation should clarify treatment of situations where additional fees or credits push net price below zero and whether negative net prices trigger clawbacks.

[P33] The additional rebate formula for noninnovator multiple source drugs (§ 447.509(a)(7)) is complex and could produce large retroactive liabilities; manufacturers need clear worked examples and data requirements.

[P34] Using the total number of units paid under the State plan as a factor (§ 447.509(a)(7)(i)) creates significant administrative burden on manufacturers to reconcile State-level dispensing data that may be incomplete or inaccurate.

[P35] Tying additional rebates to current AMP exceeding CPI-adjusted base date AMP (§ 447.509(a)(7)(ii)) could disproportionately penalize manufacturers when AMP rises for legitimate market reasons (e.g., shifts in distribution channels); CMS should provide safe harbors.

[P38] Calculating total rebate for noninnovator multiple source drugs as basic plus additional (§ 447.509(a)(8)) needs explicit guidance on rounding, timing, and coordination with State supplemental rebates to prevent duplicate adjustments.

[P39] The 100% cap for noninnovator multiple source drugs (§ 447.509(a)(9)) should not preclude States from seeking supplemental rebates outside the Medicaid drug rebate program; clarify the interplay with State supplemental rebate agreements.

[P40] Allowing exceptions to the 12-quarter rule for VBP arrangements (§ 447.510(b)(1)(vi)) is necessary, but the regulation lacks procedural requirements for demonstrating why an outcomes evaluation requires a longer lookback and how to document modifications.

[P41] The requirement that States submit quarterly drug utilization data to CMS (§ 447.511(b)) within 60 days duplicates existing reporting and will strain State IT resources; CMS should phase in stricter timelines with technical assistance.

[P42] The 60-day deadline for State submissions (§ 447.511(b) timing) is unrealistic for many States that depend on third-party vendors for data extraction; CMS should permit a short extension on a showing of good cause.

[P43] The business day rule (§ 447.511(b) (business day rule)) is reasonable, but the regulation should also allow for safe harbor if technical system outages prevent timely electronic submission.

[P44] Requiring States to transmit adjustments within the same reporting period (§ 447.511(b) (adjustments)) can be impossible when adjustments are identified after period close; CMS should permit inclusion in the next period with prompt notification.

[P45] Mandating certification of data submissions by high-level officials (§ 447.511(d)) may be impractical for States with limited senior staff availability; allow designated qualified signatories and require attestation procedures rather than prescriptive titles.

[P50] The specified certification language (§ 447.511(e)) imposes strict attestation obligations that may expose officials to legal risk; CMS should provide model language with narrower statements of reasonableness and allow qualified certifications.

[P51] The annual VBP reporting requirement by States (§ 447.518(d)(1)) will disclose commercially sensitive information about supplemental rebate arrangements and could chill VBP negotiations with manufacturers if confidentiality protections are not strong.

[P52] The 60-day deadline for VBP data submission after year end (§ 447.518(d)(2)) is too short given the complexity of calculating outcomes-based savings and reconciling pharmacy claims; a 120-day period is more realistic.

[P57] Requiring States to report administrative costs to implement VBP (§ 447.518(d)(2)(v)) may be administratively burdensome and subjective; provide a standardized cost-capture methodology and permissible cost categories.

[P58] Requiring States to report total savings generated by supplemental rebates attributable to VBP (§ 447.518(d)(2)(vi)) risks double-counting savings already claimed in other budgetary lines and may reveal proprietary rebate amounts; CMS should aggregate or anonymize data.

[P59] The DUR minimum standards (§ 456.703(h)(1)) are extensive but leave too many important parameters to State discretion without baseline national standards, leading to inconsistent protection across States.

[P60] Mandating prospective safety edit limits for opioids (§ 456.703(h)(1)(i)) without specifying maximum days' supply or exact morphine milligram equivalents invites wide variance and potential under-treatment of pain patients.

[P61] Requiring limits on days' supply for initial opioid prescriptions (§ 456.703(h)(1)(i)(A)) fails to account for clinical scenarios (e.g., post-surgical pain) where longer initial supplies may be appropriate; include clear clinical exceptions and provider override processes.

[P62] Safety edits limiting quantity for initial and subsequent opioid fills (§ 456.703(h)(1)(i)(B)) could disrupt continuity of care for patients stabilized on long-term opioid therapy if no individualized exemptions process is defined.

[P63] The duplication-prevention edits to avoid therapeutically duplicative opioid prescriptions (§ 456.703(h)(1)(i)(C)) must define which combinations are considered duplicative and how to handle opioid/long-acting plus short-acting combinations legitimately used in practice.

[P64] Rules on early refills for subsequent opioid fills (§ 456.703(h)(1)(i)(D)) may penalize patients with lost or damaged medication; require documented exception procedures for emergency replacements.

[P65] Mandating maximum daily MME limits for chronic pain (§ 456.703(h)(1)(ii)) risks undertreating some complex chronic pain patients; require individualized dose-justification and review procedures and an independent clinical appeals process.

[P66] The automated retrospective claims review requirement (§ 456.703(h)(1)(iii)) will necessitate significant IT investment by States; CMS should provide technical specifications, validation standards, and funding assistance.

[P67] Monitoring concurrent prescribing of opioids with benzodiazepines or antipsychotics (§ 456.703(h)(1)(iv)) is clinically sensible, but the rule must include provider notification protocols and safe, timely override and documentation procedures to avoid harmful abrupt discontinuation.

[P70] The requirement to monitor antipsychotic use among children (§ 456.703(h)(1)(v)) is appropriate, but the rule should prohibit discriminatory denials and ensure that monitoring leads to supportive interventions (care coordination), not automatic cessation.

[P71] The fraud/abuse identification process (§ 456.703(h)(1)(vi)) must include due process protections for prescribers, pharmacies, and beneficiaries to contest erroneous flags and prevent reputational harm from automated algorithms.

[P72] Identifying beneficiaries prescribed opioids under concerning circumstances to consider naloxone (§ 456.703(h)(1)(vii)) is important, but the regulation should require coverage of naloxone without prior authorization and reimbursement for co-dispensing.

[P73] The requirement to flag opioid prescriptions following MAT or OUD diagnosis (§ 456.703(h)(1)(vii)(A)) risks stigmatizing those in recovery; protocols must prioritize coordination with MAT providers and avoid interrupting MAT regimes.

[P74] The requirement to consider co-prescribing naloxone for high-risk beneficiaries (§ 456.703(h)(1)(vii)(B)) is laudable, but CMS should mandate coverage and reimbursement for naloxone, including take-home kits, and training support for prescribers.

[P75] The exemptions for hospice, palliative care, and cancer treatment (§ 456.703(h)(2) and (exemption A)) are appropriate, but States must be required to define and publish the criteria used to classify beneficiaries as exempt to prevent inconsistent application.

[P76] Allowing States the option to apply requirements to exempted individuals (§ 456.703(h)(2) (state option)) may create inequitable access to protective measures; CMS should require States that choose to apply them to include clear clinical safeguards and appeal rights.

[P78] Exempting residents of long-term care and similar facilities (§ 456.703(h)(2)(exemption B)) without requiring facility-level DUR oversight could leave vulnerable populations unprotected; require facility-specific monitoring protocols if exempted.

[P80] The public posting of all FFS and managed care DUR reports (§ 456.712(c)) raises confidentiality concerns and may include proprietary or sensitive patient/provider information; CMS must require redaction of proprietary data and ensure HIPAA compliance.

[P80] Public posting of DUR reports could be misused by advocacy groups or media without context, leading to misleading conclusions; CMS should accompany posted reports with explanatory summaries and caveats.

[P81] Expanding "States" to include five U.S. territories beginning April 1, 2024 (§ 447.502 States definition) is appropriate to extend benefits, but the rule must ensure territories receive proportional administrative support and funding for compliance.

[P82] Including the five territories in the "United States" definition (§ 447.502 United States) will increase reporting obligations on territories that may lack data infrastructure; CMS should provide phased implementation and technical assistance.
