raw_output:
[P1] The permission allowing physicians in a group practice to receive a share of group overall profits even if indirectly related to referral volume (§ 411.352(i)(1)) improperly creates an avenue for disguised referral-based remuneration and will undermine the anti-kickback intent of the Stark law.

[P1] Industry commenters will request clarifying examples and safe-harbor metrics showing when an “indirect” relationship to referral volume is permissible to avoid inconsistent enforcement across regions.

[P2] The requirement that overall profits be allocated in a “reasonable and verifiable” manner (§ 411.352(i)(1)(iii)) is too vague; stakeholders request specific documentation standards (e.g., audit trail, allocation formula, independent attestation) to satisfy “verifiable.”

[P2] Legal experts will argue the rule should define who bears the burden of proof and what standards (preponderance, clear and convincing) the Secretary will apply when assessing reasonableness and verifiability.

[P3] Permitting per-capita division of profits (§ 411.352(i)(1)(iii)(A)) could disproportionately benefit non-clinical physicians or those who make fewer patient-facing contributions; commenters will ask for safeguards tying per-capita splits to active medical staff status or minimum clinical participation.

[P3] Hospital and group-practice administrators will request guidance on whether part-time, locum tenens, or employed physicians count for per-capita distributions to prevent disputes.

[P4] Allowing distribution based on revenues from non-DHS services (§ 411.352(i)(1)(iii)(B)) risks manipulation of revenue coding to recharacterize DHS revenue as non-DHS; commenters will urge anti-fraud auditing requirements and explicit coding rules.

[P5] The 5 percent small-DHS-revenue threshold (§ 411.352(i)(1)(iii)(C) and related bonus provisions) is arbitrary; industry will request empirical justification for the 5% cutoff and either adjustment (e.g., lower threshold) or graduated safe-harbors.

[P5] Compliance officers will ask whether the 5% threshold is calculated on an annual or rolling basis and whether affiliates and related entities’ DHS revenues must be aggregated.

[P6] Allowing productivity bonuses that are indirectly related to referrals, while allowing direct relation for 'incident to' services (§ 411.352(i)(2)(i)), introduces inconsistency; physician groups request clear criteria distinguishing allowed indirect effects from impermissible direct incentive linking.

[P7] The requirement that productivity bonuses be “reasonable and verifiable” (§ 411.352(i)(2)(ii)) should be accompanied by sample documentation and acceptable methodologies (time-stamped encounter logs, EHR audit trails, RVU worksheets) to promote uniform compliance.

[P8] Basing productivity bonuses on total patient encounters or physician RVUs (§ 411.352(i)(2)(ii)(A)) may incent volume over value; patient-advocacy groups will object and request that quality measures be required as part of any productivity incentive.

[P9] Allowing bonuses based on non-DHS services (§ 411.352(i)(2)(ii)(B)) creates risk that services will be recoded as non-DHS to qualify; Medicare contractors should be required to validate service classifications and adjust payments when misclassification is found.

[P10] The 5 percent revenue threshold for bonuses (§ 411.352(i)(2)(ii)(C)) raises similar concerns as P5 — commenters will request that the threshold explicitly requires aggregation across related entities and specify the lookback period.

[P11] Requiring distribution of profits directly attributable to a physician’s VBE participation to that physician (§ 411.352(i)(3)) is reasonable, but commenters will seek a definition and methodology for attributing profits to an individual physician’s VBE participation.

[P11] VBE participants will request safe-harbor allocation formulas (e.g., attribution based on panel size, share of total VBE services) and dispute resolution procedures if an attribution is contested.

[P12] The obligation to provide supporting documentation to the Secretary on request (§ 411.352(i)(4)) is burdensome; commenters ask for limits on the scope of documents requested, protections for proprietary information, and reasonable timeframes for production.

[P12] Health systems will request a certification option (e.g., CFO attestation) to limit frequent exhaustive audits while still preserving oversight.

[P13] The absolute prohibition on Medicare payment for DHS furnished pursuant to a prohibited referral (§ 411.353(c)(1)) may lead to payment denials where a referral nexus is unclear; providers request a remedial grace period or ability to repay rather than automatic denial.

[P14] The statement that generally only §§ 411.355 and 411.357(p) exceptions apply to indirect compensation arrangements (§ 411.354(c)(4)(i)) may inadvertently limit other applicable exceptions; commenters ask for a crosswalk illustrating which common arrangements remain permissible.

[P15] When the chain includes a value-based arrangement to which the physician is a direct party (§ 411.354(c)(4)(ii)), the restriction to listed exceptions could disincentivize participation in multi-party VBEs; VBEs request expanded exceptions or explicit carve-outs to permit necessary downstream payments.

[P16] Treating unit-based compensation as not taking referrals into account if FMV and not variable by referral volume (§ 411.354(d)(2)) is appropriate, but commenters request illustrative calculations and acceptable valuation sources for FMV determinations.

[P17] The same FMV/variance limitation for not taking other business into account (§ 411.354(d)(3)) requires guidance on how to address productivity variance due to market conditions (e.g., pandemics) without triggering a violation.

[P18] The detailed requirements when compensation is conditioned on referrals (§ 411.354(d)(4)) are onerous; hospitals and physician recruiters request model contract language to meet these conditions and minimize transaction costs.

[P19] The obligation that compensation formulas be set in advance and any changes prospective (§ 411.354(d)(4)(i)) will hinder flexible pay structures (e.g., quarterly adjustments); commenters seek an allowance for objectively documented retrospective reconciliations or pre-specified adjustment mechanisms.

[P20] Requiring compensation be consistent with FMV (§ 411.354(d)(4)(ii)) is standard, but commenters request accepted valuation methods and a safe-harbor period during which valuations are deemed adequate if obtained from independent appraisers.

[P21] The obligation to comply with an applicable exception (§ 411.354(d)(4)(iii)) when referrals condition compensation is circular — commenters request explicit notice which exception is expected to be used in typical recruitment, managed care, and VBE contexts.

[P22] The writing and signature requirement for documented referral commitments (§ 411.354(d)(4)(iv)(A)) could impede oral, emergent patient transfers; commenters request clarification that emergency transfers and informal clinical directions are excluded.

[P23] The exception for patient preference, insurer choice, or physician judgment (§ 411.354(d)(4)(iv)(B)) must state who documents that exception and how retrospective reviewers should verify claims of medical necessity or patient preference.

[P24] Limiting referral requirements to services within the physician's scope and reasonably necessary (§ 411.354(d)(4)(v)) is appropriate, but physicians request a defined process for resolving disputes over “scope of employment” and “reasonably necessary” to avoid enforcement ambiguity.

[P25] The definition of when compensation is considered to “take into account” referral volume/value (§ 411.354(d)(5)(i)) is expansive and may capture standard performance measurements; employers will request clearer thresholds (e.g., correlation coefficients or materiality thresholds) before payments are treated as referral-based.

[P26] The rule that formulas using referrals as a variable that positively correlate with compensation constitute taking referrals into account (§ 411.354(d)(5)(i)(A)) could prohibit legitimate quality- or continuity-based incentives that inherently increase referrals; commenters request a carved-out list of permissible performance criteria.

[P27] Treating predetermined direct correlations between past referrals and future rates as taking referrals into account (§ 411.354(d)(5)(i)(B)) will chill the use of historical productivity data in compensation modeling; compensation consultants ask for safe-harbor modeling approaches.

[P28] The parallel provisions on “other business generated” (§ 411.354(d)(5)(ii)) are likewise overbroad and risk penalizing normal practice-building activities; practices request delineation between business development activities and impermissible referral inducement.

[P29] The negative-correlation provisions for physician-to-entity compensation (§ 411.354(d)(6)(i)(A) and (ii)(A)) are confusing — commenters request worked examples (e.g., recruitment subsidy decreasing when referrals drop) and clarification whether variable reductions tied to referrals are permissible.

[P30] Across sections (d)(5) and (d)(6), commenters will ask HHS to define acceptable statistical or contractual methodologies for proving absence of correlation (e.g., multivariate regressions, excluded confounders).

[P31] The provision allowing a writing/signature requirement to be deemed satisfied where the arrangement complies with an exception except for the writing (§ 411.354(e)(3)(i)) could create inconsistent application — commenters request objective criteria for invoking this relief and limits to prevent after-the-fact cure.

[P32] The 90-day cure period to obtain required writings/signatures after noncompliance (§ 411.354(e)(3)(ii)) may be insufficient for complex multi-party arrangements; hospitals request an extension (e.g., 180 days) and allowance for good-faith delays.

[P33] Medicare Advantage coordinated care plans qualifying under § 411.355(c)(5) (P40) should be explicitly permitted to use common network compensation structures; MA organizations will ask for cross-reference language to avoid local contractor denial.

[P34] The prohibition that academic medical center component total compensation not be determined based on referral volume or other business (§ 411.355(e)(1)(ii)(C)) may conflict with customary academic productivity-based compensation; AMCs request an exception for bona fide academic productivity metrics tied to teaching, research, and clinical work.

[P35] If compensation conditioned on referrals must meet §411.354(d)(4) (§ 411.355(e)(1)(ii)(D)), academic centers will request model compliance frameworks aligning academic metrics with the (d)(4) requirements.

[P36] The leased-space requirement that space be reasonable in size/necessity and exclusively used by the lessee when in use (§ 411.357(a)(3)) is vague; outpatient practices need concrete square-foot-per-FTE benchmarks or industry standards to evaluate reasonableness.

[P37] Allowing lessees to pay for common-area use provided payments do not exceed pro rata expenses (§ 411.357(a)(3) common areas clause) is welcomed, but property managers request guidance on calculating pro rata shares for mixed-use spaces and allocation of utilities/maintenance.

[P38] The lessor-invitee prohibition (§ 411.357(a)(3) lessor invitee prohibition) may create impractical restrictions for community hospitals with affiliated physicians who occasionally use practice space; hospitals request limited, documented exceptions for transient, clinically necessary uses.

[P39] The leased-equipment reasonableness and exclusive use requirement (§ 411.357(b)(2)) requires clarification on maintenance downtime or shared use with radiology/hospital departments — commenters request rules for incidental/shared clinical scheduling.

[P40] The lessor-invitee prohibition for equipment (§ 411.357(b)(2) lessor invitee prohibition for equipment) could prevent necessary vendor demonstrations or maintenance access; commenters request limited carve-outs for vendor personnel performing maintenance or training.

[P41] The broad prohibition that remuneration must not be determined by referrals (§ 411.357(c)(2)(ii)) will disrupt customary commercialization arrangements (e.g., outcomes-based contracting); industry asks for explicit exceptions for bona fide population-health or value-based compensation.

[P42] Requiring referral-conditioned remuneration to meet §411.354(d)(4) (§ 411.357(c)(5)) as repeated across multiple sections creates administrative redundancy; commenters request consolidation and harmonization across sections with a single compliance checklist.

[P43] The advance setting of compensation, FMV requirement, and prohibition on referral-determined compensation in § 411.357(d)(1)(v) will restrict innovative payment models; payers and providers request an innovation pathway permitting pilot arrangements under monitoring and pre-approval.

[P44] The physician incentive plan permission to base pay on referral volume/value if requirements are met (§ 411.357(d)(2)) is unclear — commenters ask for the complete list of “listed requirements” and sample compliant incentive plan clauses.

[P45] The repeated cross-reference that remuneration conditioned on referrals must meet §411.354(d)(4) (seen in P51, P53, P64, etc.) suggests §§ 411.354(d)(4) will be the primary compliance target; commenters request a central interpretive guidance document addressing common fact patterns.

[P46] The prohibition that remuneration amounts not be based on actual or anticipated referrals (§ 411.357(e)(1)(iii)) will chill hospital recruitment packages where productivity expectations are legitimately part of business planning; hospitals request examples of permissible recruitment compensation structures.

[P47] The requirement that physician practices sign the writing when remuneration is routed indirectly (§ 411.357(e)(4)(i)) is appropriate for transparency, but commenters request templates and clarity on when agent relationships (e.g., management companies) trigger the signature requirement.

[P48] The hospital prohibition that remuneration must not be based on referrals by the recruited physician/practice (§ 411.357(e)(4)(v)) will limit rural hospital recruitment incentives; rural hospitals request an exception or alternative compliance path for bona fide recruitment to underserved areas.

[P49] Applying paragraph (e) rules equally to FQHCs and RHCs (§ 411.357(e)(6)(i)) ignores the unique funding and mission of those clinics; FQHCs/RHCs request tailored standards or explicit carve-outs recognizing their federal grant/support structures.

[P50] The isolated financial-transaction FMV consistency requirement (§ 411.357(f)(1)(i)) is reasonable but needs guidance on acceptable valuation sources and whether retrospective market adjustments are permitted in volatile markets.

[P51] The six-month blackout period after an isolated financial transaction (§ 411.357(f)(3)) is administratively burdensome and may unintentionally prevent legitimate follow-on relationships; commenters request a narrower list of prohibited follow-ons or a 90-day period instead.

[P52] The prohibition that remuneration unrelated to DHS must not be determined by physician referral volume (§ 411.357(g)(1)) could be read to restrict community benefit or charitable assistance programs if not clarified; nonprofit hospitals request confirmation those programs remain permitted.

[P53] The condition that remuneration be for items/services not related to patient care (§ 411.357(g)(2)) is ambiguous — payers and providers ask whether nonclinical administrative services supporting patient care (e.g., billing, IT) count as “related to patient care.”

[P54] The FMV, per-unit fixed-in-advance, non-referral rule in § 411.357(h)(5) may preclude adaptive capitated arrangements used by ACOs; accountable care organizations request explicit cross-reference exceptions for bona fide population-based contracts.

[P55] The numerous cross-references to § 411.354(d)(4) across remuneration/lease/equipment exceptions create compliance complexity; compliance officers request a consolidated safe-harbor manual and a compliance checklist.

[P56] The fair market value provisions in § 411.357(i)(2)(i) and in the FMV definition section § 411.357(l) lack a prescriptive list of acceptable valuation experts or methodologies; commenters ask that CMS recognize board-certified health-care valuation professionals and provide an FMV safe harbor if a contemporaneous valuation is obtained.

[P57] The requirements that arrangements be written, signed, specify items, timeframes, and set compensation in advance (§§ 411.357(l)(1)-(3)) are administratively heavy for small practices; small-practice representatives ask for streamlined documentation options or template agreements.

[P58] The prohibition that rental compensation not be a percentage of revenue or per-unit charges tied to lessee referrals (§ 411.357(l)(3)(i)-(ii)) could disrupt common real estate practices (percentage rent for new practices); landlords and community developers request phased-in compliance and alternatives like graduated fixed rents.

[P59] The commercial reasonableness requirement (§ 411.357(l)(4)) needs objective criteria (benchmarks, market studies) to avoid subjective enforcement; commenters ask CMS to publish market-rate benchmarks by region and specialty.

[P60] The partial prohibition that services not involve counseling or promotion of business arrangements (§ 411.357(l)(6) partial) should include an explicit carve-out for legitimate vendor training and clinical education tied to patient care.

[P61] The addition of N-Ethylpentylone to Schedule I (§ 1308.11(d)(86)) (P76) will be opposed by harm-reduction and research groups unless accompanied by clear pathways for research and clinical exceptions; commenters request mechanisms for research exemptions and timelines for rescheduling if evidence supports medical use.

[P62] Removing and reserving § 1308.11(h)(36) (§ 1308.11(h)(36) removal) (P77) may have downstream impacts on previously scheduled substances; DEA-regulated laboratories request notice of which substance is being removed and transitional handling guidance for held inventories.

[P63] The extension of the target publication date for the final Medicare physician self-referral rule to August 31, 2021 (42 CFR Part 411 DATES) (P78) creates regulatory uncertainty; providers and health systems request interim guidance or non-enforcement policies until the final rule is published.

[P64] Overall, stakeholders request that CMS/HHS publish a comprehensive compliance toolkit — including model contract language, sample allocation spreadsheets, FMV valuation standards, and frequently asked questions — before finalizing the rule to reduce confusion and litigation risk.

The exception for patient preference, insurer choice, or physician judgment (§ 411.354(d)(4)(iv)(B)) must state who documents that exception and how retrospective reviewers should verify claims of medical necessity or patient preference.

Limiting referral requirements to services within the physician's scope and reasonably necessary (§ 411.354(d)(4)(v)) is appropriate, but physicians request a defined process for resolving disputes over “scope of employment” and “reasonably necessary” to avoid enforcement ambiguity.

The definition of when compensation is considered to “take into account” referral volume/value (§ 411.354(d)(5)(i)) is expansive and may capture standard performance measurements; employers will request clearer thresholds (e.g., correlation coefficients or materiality thresholds) before payments are treated as referral-based.

The rule that formulas using referrals as a variable that positively correlate with compensation constitute taking referrals into account (§ 411.354(d)(5)(i)(A)) could prohibit legitimate quality- or continuity-based incentives that inherently increase referrals; commenters request a carved-out list of permissible performance criteria.

Treating predetermined direct correlations between past referrals and future rates as taking referrals into account (§ 411.354(d)(5)(i)(B)) will chill the use of historical productivity data in compensation modeling; compensation consultants ask for safe-harbor modeling approaches.

The parallel provisions on “other business generated” (§ 411.354(d)(5)(ii)) are likewise overbroad and risk penalizing normal practice-building activities; practices request delineation between business development activities and impermissible referral inducement.

The negative-correlation provisions for physician-to-entity compensation (§ 411.354(d)(6)(i)(A) and (ii)(A)) are confusing — commenters request worked examples (e.g., recruitment subsidy decreasing when referrals drop) and clarification whether variable reductions tied to referrals are permissible.

Across sections (d)(5) and (d)(6), commenters will ask HHS to define acceptable statistical or contractual methodologies for proving absence of correlation (e.g., multivariate regressions, excluded confounders).

The provision allowing a writing/signature requirement to be deemed satisfied where the arrangement complies with an exception except for the writing (§ 411.354(e)(3)(i)) could create inconsistent application — commenters request objective criteria for invoking this relief and limits to prevent after-the-fact cure.

The 90-day cure period to obtain required writings/signatures after noncompliance (§ 411.354(e)(3)(ii)) may be insufficient for complex multi-party arrangements; hospitals request an extension (e.g., 180 days) and allowance for good-faith delays.

Medicare Advantage coordinated care plans qualifying under § 411.355(c)(5) (P40) should be explicitly permitted to use common network compensation structures; MA organizations will ask for cross-reference language to avoid local contractor denial.

The prohibition that academic medical center component total compensation not be determined based on referral volume or other business (§ 411.355(e)(1)(ii)(C)) may conflict with customary academic productivity-based compensation; AMCs request an exception for bona fide academic productivity metrics tied to teaching, research, and clinical work.

If compensation conditioned on referrals must meet §411.354(d)(4) (§ 411.355(e)(1)(ii)(D)), academic centers will request model compliance frameworks aligning academic metrics with the (d)(4) requirements.

The leased-space requirement that space be reasonable in size/necessity and exclusively used by the lessee when in use (§ 411.357(a)(3)) is vague; outpatient practices need concrete square-foot-per-FTE benchmarks or industry standards to evaluate reasonableness.

Allowing lessees to pay for common-area use provided payments do not exceed pro rata expenses (§ 411.357(a)(3) common areas clause) is welcomed, but property managers request guidance on calculating pro rata shares for mixed-use spaces and allocation of utilities/maintenance.

The lessor-invitee prohibition (§ 411.357(a)(3) lessor invitee prohibition) may create impractical restrictions for community hospitals with affiliated physicians who occasionally use practice space; hospitals request limited, documented exceptions for transient, clinically necessary uses.

The leased-equipment reasonableness and exclusive use requirement (§ 411.357(b)(2)) requires clarification on maintenance downtime or shared use with radiology/hospital departments — commenters request rules for incidental/shared clinical scheduling.

The lessor-invitee prohibition for equipment (§ 411.357(b)(2) lessor invitee prohibition for equipment) could prevent necessary vendor demonstrations or maintenance access; commenters request limited carve-outs for vendor personnel performing maintenance or training.

The broad prohibition that remuneration must not be determined by referrals (§ 411.357(c)(2)(ii)) will disrupt customary commercialization arrangements (e.g., outcomes-based contracting); industry asks for explicit exceptions for bona fide population-health or value-based compensation.

Requiring referral-conditioned remuneration to meet §411.354(d)(4) (§ 411.357(c)(5)) as repeated across multiple sections creates administrative redundancy; commenters request consolidation and harmonization across sections with a single compliance checklist.

The advance setting of compensation, FMV requirement, and prohibition on referral-determined compensation in § 411.357(d)(1)(v) will restrict innovative payment models; payers and providers request an innovation pathway permitting pilot arrangements under monitoring and pre-approval.

The physician incentive plan permission to base pay on referral volume/value if requirements are met (§ 411.357(d)(2)) is unclear — commenters ask for the complete list of “listed requirements” and sample compliant incentive plan clauses.

The repeated cross-reference that remuneration conditioned on referrals must meet §411.354(d)(4) (seen in P51, P53, P64, etc.) suggests §§ 411.354(d)(4) will be the primary compliance target; commenters request a central interpretive guidance document addressing common fact patterns.

The prohibition that remuneration amounts not be based on actual or anticipated referrals (§ 411.357(e)(1)(iii)) will chill hospital recruitment packages where productivity expectations are legitimately part of business planning; hospitals request examples of permissible recruitment compensation structures.

The requirement that physician practices sign the writing when remuneration is routed indirectly (§ 411.357(e)(4)(i)) is appropriate for transparency, but commenters request templates and clarity on when agent relationships (e.g., management companies) trigger the signature requirement.

The hospital prohibition that remuneration must not be based on referrals by the recruited physician/practice (§ 411.357(e)(4)(v)) will limit rural hospital recruitment incentives; rural hospitals request an exception or alternative compliance path for bona fide recruitment to underserved areas.

Applying paragraph (e) rules equally to FQHCs and RHCs (§ 411.357(e)(6)(i)) ignores the unique funding and mission of those clinics; FQHCs/RHCs request tailored standards or explicit carve-outs recognizing their federal grant/support structures.

The isolated financial-transaction FMV consistency requirement (§ 411.357(f)(1)(i)) is reasonable but needs guidance on acceptable valuation sources and whether retrospective market adjustments are permitted in volatile markets.

The six-month blackout period after an isolated financial transaction (§ 411.357(f)(3)) is administratively burdensome and may unintentionally prevent legitimate follow-on relationships; commenters request a narrower list of prohibited follow-ons or a 90-day period instead.

The prohibition that remuneration unrelated to DHS must not be determined by physician referral volume (§ 411.357(g)(1)) could be read to restrict community benefit or charitable assistance programs if not clarified; nonprofit hospitals request confirmation those programs remain permitted.

The condition that remuneration be for items/services not related to patient care (§ 411.357(g)(2)) is ambiguous — payers and providers ask whether nonclinical administrative services supporting patient care (e.g., billing, IT) count as “related to patient care.”

The FMV, per-unit fixed-in-advance, non-referral rule in § 411.357(h)(5) may preclude adaptive capitated arrangements used by ACOs; accountable care organizations request explicit cross-reference exceptions for bona fide population-based contracts.

The numerous cross-references to § 411.354(d)(4) across remuneration/lease/equipment exceptions create compliance complexity; compliance officers request a consolidated safe-harbor manual and a compliance checklist.

The fair market value provisions in § 411.357(i)(2)(i) and in the FMV definition section § 411.357(l) lack a prescriptive list of acceptable valuation experts or methodologies; commenters ask that CMS recognize board-certified health-care valuation professionals and provide an FMV safe harbor if a contemporaneous valuation is obtained.

The requirements that arrangements be written, signed, specify items, timeframes, and set compensation in advance (§§ 411.357(l)(1)-(3)) are administratively heavy for small practices; small-practice representatives ask for streamlined documentation options or template agreements.

The prohibition that rental compensation not be a percentage of revenue or per-unit charges tied to lessee referrals (§ 411.357(l)(3)(i)-(ii)) could disrupt common real estate practices (percentage rent for new practices); landlords and community developers request phased-in compliance and alternatives like graduated fixed rents.

The commercial reasonableness requirement (§ 411.357(l)(4)) needs objective criteria (benchmarks, market studies) to avoid subjective enforcement; commenters ask CMS to publish market-rate benchmarks by region and specialty.

The partial prohibition that services not involve counseling or promotion of business arrangements (§ 411.357(l)(6) partial) should include an explicit carve-out for legitimate vendor training and clinical education tied to patient care.

The addition of N-Ethylpentylone to Schedule I (§ 1308.11(d)(86)) (P76) will be opposed by harm-reduction and research groups unless accompanied by clear pathways for research and clinical exceptions; commenters request mechanisms for research exemptions and timelines for rescheduling if evidence supports medical use.

Removing and reserving § 1308.11(h)(36) (§ 1308.11(h)(36) removal) (P77) may have downstream impacts on previously scheduled substances; DEA-regulated laboratories request notice of which substance is being removed and transitional handling guidance for held inventories.

The extension of the target publication date for the final Medicare physician self-referral rule to August 31, 2021 (42 CFR Part 411 DATES) (P78) creates regulatory uncertainty; providers and health systems request interim guidance or non-enforcement policies until the final rule is published.

Overall, stakeholders request that CMS/HHS publish a comprehensive compliance toolkit — including model contract language, sample allocation spreadsheets, FMV valuation standards, and frequently asked questions — before finalizing the rule to reduce confusion and litigation risk.

raw_output:
[P1] The rule’s distinction in § 52.38(a)(6) that paragraph (a)(2)(i) ceases to apply only to sources subject to State SIP authority but continues to apply in Indian country will create regulatory fragmentation and enforcement complexity for multistate sources and should be revised to provide clear cross-jurisdictional coordination mechanisms.

[P1] Legal commenters will contend that applying paragraph (a)(2)(i) differently in State vs. Indian country may violate federal trust obligations and the EPA’s duty to consult with Tribal governments before imposing differential regulatory regimes.

[P2] The provision treating a partial FIP remedy as a partial SIP remedy unless the Administrator says otherwise (§ 52.38(a)(6)) is vague and grants unworkably broad discretionary authority to the Administrator; commenters will request objective criteria and a timetable for when the Administrator may reclassify a SIP revision as a full remedy.

[P2] Industry commenters will argue that treating SIPs as partial remedies by default when the FIP was partial creates long-term uncertainty for allowance markets and investment planning; EPA should require a fixed transition mechanism and clear milestone triggers.

[P3] § 52.38(a)(7)(ii) that allows the Administrator to finish allocation/recordation if already started despite SIP approval will be criticized by States as undermining State authority and creating dual allocation regimes mid-cycle; States will request that once a SIP is approved allocations be exclusively under the SIP except for narrow emergency circumstances.

[P3] Market participants will note that allowing post-approval recordation by the Administrator could retroactively alter market expectations and asset values, and they will request prohibitions on any actions that change allocations after public posting.

[P4] Requiring Subpart EEEEE coverage for 2017–2022 emissions (§ 52.38(b)(2)(C)) may impose retroactive compliance or reporting obligations on sources that did not plan for them; regulated sources will request clarification that no new retroactive penalties or liabilities will be assessed.

[P4] Environmental advocates will argue that continuing Subpart EEEEE for 2017–2022 is insufficiently protective and call for retrospective enforcement to correct past exceedances and deliver public-health benefits.

[P5] Applying Subpart GGGGG for 2023 and subsequent years (§ 52.38(b)(3)(B)) without adequate lead time for State implementation will be challenged by States and utilities as administratively impracticable; commenters will request phased implementation or delayed effective dates to allow program design and permitting.

[P6] Electric utilities will claim that applying Subpart GGGGG starting in 2023 creates compliance cost spikes and that EPA must provide modeling of allowance availability and expected prices under GGGGG before finalizing the rule.

[P7] The duplicate provisions (§ 52.38(b)(3)(C) and (B)) that apply Subpart GGGGG to the same populations are potentially redundant and confusing; legal commenters will request consolidation of these clauses to remove ambiguity about effective dates and scope.

[P8] § 52.38(b)(4) permitting States to adopt SIP revisions replacing specified Subpart BBBBB provisions should explicitly allow States to make broader changes where necessary for local circumstances; States will request that the “without substantively replacing other provisions” limitation be relaxed or clarified.

[P8] Conversely, environmental NGOs will object to allowing States to replace Subpart BBBBB provisions, asserting EPA must ensure replacement provisions are at least as stringent and preserve interstate air quality protections; they will request an explicit non-interop degradation standard.

[P9] § 52.38(b)(4) obligating EPA to approve State replacements of specified Subpart BBBBB provisions is premature; commenters will argue EPA must retain full discretionary review and not bind itself to an automatic approval promise without demonstrating equivalence in emissions reductions.

[P9] Legal experts will point out that promising approval in the regulatory text may exceed EPA’s statutory authority if State substitutions would frustrate attainment obligations in other States; they will request deletion or rephrasing to condition approval on demonstration of non-interference.

[P10] The allocation cap requirement in § 52.38(b)(8)(iii)(A) that allocations equal the cap minus multiple set-asides and prior allocations is complex and raises risks of double-counting set-asides; allowance administrators will request worked numerical examples and a prioritized ordering rule for applying multiple subtractions.

[P10] Market participants will also request clarification regarding which “previously allocated amounts” are included (e.g., prior years, multi-year banked allowances, reserved allowances) to avoid disputes over the cap calculation.

[P11] The June 1 deadline (TABLES 1–6 and § 52.39 tables; provisions P10–P15, P32–P35) for submission of allocations/auction results for 2025 and later is administratively burdensome for many States and market operators; States will request moving the deadline to September 1 or aligning with existing state budgeting and permit cycles.

[P11] Auction operators and third-party administrators will request minimum notice periods and a defined format for submissions tied to the June 1 deadline; absent such standards, they will face operational risk and potential invalidation of auctions.

[P12] Regulated entities will note that the uniform June 1 deadline across multiple tables lacks an exception for extraordinary circumstances (natural disasters, system failures) and will request force majeure or late-submission processes with clear remedial steps.

[P13] The tribal provision (§ 52.38(b)(9)(vii) and related P16/P26) allowing EPA to modify SIP approvals and FIPs if covered units are in Indian country not under State SIP authority is necessary but insufficiently protective of Tribal sovereignty; Tribal governments will demand mandatory Tribal consultation and an explicit requirement that EPA obtain Tribal consent before modifying approval.

[P13] States will argue that the provision could remove State regulatory tools without adequate notice; they will request a requirement that EPA coordinate with States and provide a transition plan if units in Indian country alter jurisdiction.

[P14] The electronic notification obligation in § 52.38(b)(10)(v)(A) to notify intent to submit a complete SIP revision by the final rule effective date using an EPA-specified format is too prescriptive without specifying the format and mechanisms; States will request sample forms, schema, and at least 60 days’ notice of the format.

[P14] Smaller states and those with limited technical capacity will request that EPA provide technical assistance and an alternative paper or assisted submission process for the electronic notification requirement.

[P15] The hard deadline for States to submit a complete SIP revision by Sept 1, 2023 (§ 52.38(b)(10)(v)(B)) is now impossible (relative to likely final rule timing) and will be deemed arbitrary; commenters will request extension to at least Sept 1, 2024, or a date measured from final rule publication.

[P15] Legal commenters will argue that a retroactive deadline predating the final rule effective date creates legal infirmities and may be invalid as it imposes obligations before rule adoption.

[P16] Requirements to allocate Group 3 allowances up to caps defined by §§97.1010/97.1021 minus set-asides (§§ 52.38(b)(11)(iii)(A), (b)(12)(iii)(A)) (P19, P22) will be contested by States and industry for lacking transparency on how set-asides are quantified and prioritized; commenters will ask EPA to publish explicit formulas and baseline datasets.

[P17] The prohibitions forbidding any changes to allocations after submission deadlines (§§52.38(b)(11)(iii)(D), (b)(12)(iii)(D)) (P21, P24) will be criticized by States and market operators as overly rigid; they will request limited corrective amendment procedures to fix clerical errors or to correct discovered double-counting, with strict time limits.

[P18] Market participants will stress that absolute prohibitions on post-deadline changes will produce perverse incentives (overly conservative initial allocations) and could lock in inequities; they will propose a narrowly tailored amendment window with independent audit verification.

[P19] The requirement that SIP revisions exclude requirements applying to units in Indian country not under State authority (§ 52.38(b)(12)(vi), P25) creates a complex split program; Tribal commenters will request that EPA instead develop a unified program or explicitly require Tribal-state-EPA coordination to avoid gaps.

[P20] § 52.38(b)(12)(vii) (P26) allowing EPA to modify approvals and FIPs if units in Indian country appear after approval leaves State-regulated sources exposed to shifting obligations; States will ask for a notification process (e.g., 120-day notice) and opportunity to negotiate modifications.

[P21] § 52.38(b)(13)(i) (P27) that ends application of certain paragraphs upon SIP approval but leaves them in Indian country will create unequal protection for communities depending on location; environmental justice groups will argue this perpetuates pollution disparities and demand measures to ensure equivalent protections in Indian country.

[P22] The narrow exception in § 52.38(b)(14)(ii) (P28/P3) letting the Administrator finish recording allocations already started should be tightly limited: commenters will ask EPA to restrict this to allocations begun within a clearly defined pre-approval window (e.g., 30 days before SIP approval) and to bar any substantive allocation changes.

[P23] § 52.38(b)(14)(iii)(F) and (G) (P29, P30) preserving conversion and recall provisions (97.826(e), 97.811(e)) for all allocated Group 1/2 allowances and holders raises concerns about retroactive adjustments to market holdings; market participants will request safeguards, including notice, appeal rights, and an escrow mechanism to prevent market disruption.

[P24] Paragraph (b)(16)(ii)(B) (P31) that prevents EPA from performing certain functions for specified States after Dec 31, 2022 (except limited exceptions) creates a cliff that may leave enforcement gaps; States and NGOs will request transitional responsibilities and clear definitions of the exceptions’ scope.

[P25] The large number of cross-references to subparts, tables, and sections in these provisions increase the risk of inconsistent implementation; legal commenters will ask EPA to include a consolidated implementation matrix in the preamble and guidance explaining interplay among provisions.

[P26] Multiple provisions tie obligations to the “final rule effective date” without specifying when that will be promulgated; commenters will request that EPA define the effective date or adopt language tying obligations to a calendar date or a specified number of days after publication.

[P27] Public transparency advocates will request that EPA require posting of all State allocation submissions and auction results in a standardized, machine-readable format upon receipt (and prior to final Administrator recording) to enable public review and prevent secret allocation deals.

[P28] Affected parties will ask EPA to include an appeals process or dispute-resolution mechanism when the Administrator modifies SIP approvals or records allocations (per P3/P16/P26) to ensure due process for States, Tribes, and market participants.

[P29] Small generators and community-based entities will request that EPA provide information and financial/technical assistance for participation in auctions and compliance programs created under Subparts EEEEE/GGGGG since fixed deadlines and allocation rules could disproportionately burden small actors.

[P30] Commenters will request that EPA analyze and disclose the economic impacts of the June 1 submission deadline (P10–P15, P32–P35) on State staffing, auction revenues, and compliance costs in the final regulatory impact analysis.

[P31] Environmental and public-health groups will insist that any State replacement of Subpart BBBBB provisions (§ 52.38(b)(4), P7-P9) be subject to a demonstration that interstate transport air quality benefits and ozone attainment projections are not degraded, with modeling posted for public comment.

[P32] Industry legal counsel will question whether the prohibition on changing allocations after submission (P21, P24) might conflict with statutory obligations to correct administrative errors and will request confirmation that administrative error correction consistent with administrative procedure law is permitted.

[P33] Tribal authorities will request that any provision allowing EPA to retain allocation or enforcement authority in Indian country (e.g., P1, P16, P26, P27) explicitly recognizes Tribal regulatory options, including Tribal Implementation Plans or Tribal trading programs, rather than defaulting to EPA unilateral action.

[P34] States listed in the various paragraphs (b)(2) categories will request an explicit, published list of which States fall into each subgroup (e.g., (b)(2)(i)(A), (b)(2)(ii)(C)), because the rule frequently references these categories without listing the member States in the regulatory text.

[P35] Commenters will request that EPA publish detailed technical guidance on how to calculate and report “previously allocated amounts” and “set-asides” used to determine allocation caps (§ 52.38(b)(8)(iii)(A), P9) including sample spreadsheets and data sources to ensure consistent, auditable accounting.

[P36] Market monitors and compliance auditors will request recordkeeping and reporting standards for allocation and auction submissions (P10–P15, P20, P23, P32–P35), including required metadata, validation checks, and retention periods to support future audits and potential recall actions (P29–P30).

[P37] Commenters will urge EPA to insert an express non-retroactivity statement clarifying that no civil penalties or enforcement actions will be initiated for historical emissions where allocations or conversion/recall provisions (P29–P30) change accounting treatment unless there is clear evidence of knowing fraud.

[P38] States will request an extended public-comment and consultation period on implementation guidance accompanying these provisions, because the regulatory text delegates key mechanics (formats, procedures, conversion rules) to subsequent EPA guidance documents not yet available.

Small generators and community-based entities will request that EPA provide information and financial/technical assistance for participation in auctions and compliance programs created under Subparts EEEEE/GGGGG since fixed deadlines and allocation rules could disproportionately burden small actors.

Commenters will request that EPA analyze and disclose the economic impacts of the June 1 submission deadline (P10–P15, P32–P35) on State staffing, auction revenues, and compliance costs in the final regulatory impact analysis.

Environmental and public-health groups will insist that any State replacement of Subpart BBBBB provisions (§ 52.38(b)(4), P7-P9) be subject to a demonstration that interstate transport air quality benefits and ozone attainment projections are not degraded, with modeling posted for public comment.

Industry legal counsel will question whether the prohibition on changing allocations after submission (P21, P24) might conflict with statutory obligations to correct administrative errors and will request confirmation that administrative error correction consistent with administrative procedure law is permitted.

Tribal authorities will request that any provision allowing EPA to retain allocation or enforcement authority in Indian country (e.g., P1, P16, P26, P27) explicitly recognizes Tribal regulatory options, including Tribal Implementation Plans or Tribal trading programs, rather than defaulting to EPA unilateral action.

States listed in the various paragraphs (b)(2) categories will request an explicit, published list of which States fall into each subgroup (e.g., (b)(2)(i)(A), (b)(2)(ii)(C)), because the rule frequently references these categories without listing the member States in the regulatory text.

Commenters will request that EPA publish detailed technical guidance on how to calculate and report “previously allocated amounts” and “set-asides” used to determine allocation caps (§ 52.38(b)(8)(iii)(A), P9) including sample spreadsheets and data sources to ensure consistent, auditable accounting.

Market monitors and compliance auditors will request recordkeeping and reporting standards for allocation and auction submissions (P10–P15, P20, P23, P32–P35), including required metadata, validation checks, and retention periods to support future audits and potential recall actions (P29–P30).

Commenters will urge EPA to insert an express non-retroactivity statement clarifying that no civil penalties or enforcement actions will be initiated for historical emissions where allocations or conversion/recall provisions (P29–P30) change accounting treatment unless there is clear evidence of knowing fraud.

raw_output:
[P1] The six-month prohibition on filing H-1B petitions (§214.2(h)(2)(i)(I)) is too restrictive for employers who need to secure visas well in advance for complex hiring processes and global transfers; we request extending the earliest filing date to 12 months prior to actual need.

[P1] The phrase "actual need date" in §214.2(h)(2)(i)(I) is ambiguous and should be defined (e.g., job start date, payroll start date, or date of beneficiary's relocation), otherwise it will invite inconsistent agency decisions and litigation.

[P2] Requiring electronic registration before filing (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(1)) imposes burdens on small employers and non-profits lacking IT capacity; USCIS should provide a paper alternative or vendor-assisted registration options.

[P2] The rule does not specify exceptions for third-party filing agents or law firms submitting registrations on behalf of multiple employers; §214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(1) should explicitly authorize accredited representatives or attorneys to register on petitioners' behalf.

[P3] Tying registration eligibility to strict compliance with 8 CFR 103.2(a)(1) and form instructions (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(1)) risks rejecting registrations for minor technical errors; USCIS should allow cure periods for immaterial defects.

[P4] The restriction that petitioners may file only after a registration is selected (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(1)) could delay urgent transfers and impede businesses' ability to preserve employment continuity — propose an expedited pathway for bona fide urgent needs.

[P5] The one-registration-per-beneficiary-per-fiscal-year requirement (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(2)) will harm beneficiaries with multiple legitimate employers or changing job offers; allow beneficiaries to be registered by more than one petitioner or permit multiple registrations if attested as bona fide separate offers.

[P5] Requiring a separate registration for each beneficiary (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(2)) creates high administrative costs for employers recruiting many beneficiaries (e.g., universities, tech firms); USCIS should permit batch registrations with individual named beneficiary data to reduce burden.

[P6] Mandating that every registration include the named beneficiary (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(2)) prevents employers from reserving spots for unnamed future hires and undermines workforce planning; allow anonymized or prospective-name placeholders with attestation and later validation.

[P7] The "one registration per beneficiary" permission (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(2)) is fine in principle but must explicitly address situations where the same beneficiary is represented by multiple authorized agents to avoid accidental invalidation.

[P8] The invalidation of all registrations if duplicate registrations are submitted by the same petitioner (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(2)) is unduly punitive for clerical errors; instead of deeming all invalid, USCIS should treat duplicates as a single registration or allow correction within a short cure window.

[P9] Requiring the initial registration period to last at least 14 days and start at least 14 days before earliest filing date (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(3)) is reasonable, but USCIS should commit to announcing dates at least 30 days before registration opens to allow employer planning.

[P10] Publishing registration start and end dates on the USCIS website (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(3)) is necessary but insufficient; USCIS should also notify registered employers via email, distribute an RSS feed, and coordinate with industry groups.

[P11] Restricting submissions during the initial registration period to requests with start dates on the first business day of the fiscal year (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(4)) is arbitrary and will disadvantage employers who need mid-year start dates; remove the restriction or allow multiple permissible requested start dates.

[P12] The allowance to request later start dates only if registration is extended or reopened (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(4)) could create uncertainty and inequity; instead permit any requested start date within a six-month window during initial registration.

[P13] Considering registrations that overlap the advanced degree exemption when determining the regular cap (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(5)) is appropriate but USCIS must publish reasoning and projections to ensure transparency.

[P14] If registrations are fewer than needed, notifying all properly registered petitioners that their registrations are selected (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(5)(i)) is efficient, but USCIS must clarify the timeline for such notification and whether selection is binding.

[P15] Keeping registration open past the initial period until the regular cap is met (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(5)(i)) could incentivize system gaming or create instability; USCIS must commit to concrete, published monitoring metrics and thresholds to prevent indefinite rolling openings.

[P16] Stopping acceptance of registrations once enough are received (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(5)(i)) is appropriate but USCIS must ensure high-availability systems to prevent legitimate registrants from being locked out during high traffic.

[P17] USCIS's obligation to publish the final registration date when the necessary number is received (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(5)(i)) should include timestamped system logs and an audit trail to enable public verification.

[P18] The use of computer-generated random selection on the final registration date (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(5)(i)) is fair in principle but the rule should require disclosure of the randomization algorithm, seed handling, auditability, and third-party verification to maintain confidence.

[P19] If registrations exceed the cap during the initial period, stopping acceptance and announcing a final registration date (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(5)(ii)) is reasonable but USCIS should commit to a precise time (including time zone) for the final date announcement to avoid confusion.

[P20] The required computer-generated random selection among initial-period registrations (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(5)(ii)) must be accompanied by transparency safeguards (public criteria, debugging logs, and independent audits); otherwise stakeholders will question fairness.

[P21] USCIS's obligation to assess advance-degree exemption eligibility only after closing regular-cap registrations (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(6)) may cause eligible advanced-degree beneficiaries to be disadvantaged if caps are met earlier; propose concurrent accounting for advanced-degree exemptions.

[P22] If remaining registrations are fewer than needed for the advanced degree exemption (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(6)(i)), notifying all properly registered petitioners is fair but USCIS should clarify how overlapping registrations (counted in both pools) are allocated.

[P23] Continuing to accept registrations until enough are received for the advanced degree exemption (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(6)(i)) requires clear deadlines and system capacity commitments to avoid arbitrary extensions.

[P24] Announcing the final registration date for the advanced-degree exemption when necessary number is received (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(6)(i)) must include disclosure of counting methodology (how double-counted registrations are handled).

[P25] Random selection for advanced-degree exemption registrations (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(6)(i)) should be subject to the same transparency and audit requirements urged for regular cap selection (algorithm publication, independent verification).

[P26] Stopping acceptance once advanced-degree exemption registrations exceed need (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(6)(ii)) is acceptable but USCIS should define "sufficient number" and how withdrawals or duplicates are treated.

[P27] The computer-generated random selection among remaining registrations for the advanced-degree exemption (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(6)(ii)) raises the same auditability concerns; require log retention and FOIA-accessible summaries.

[P28] Keeping unselected registrations on reserve for the fiscal year (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)) is beneficial, but USCIS must disclose the order and criteria for reserve selection to prevent unpredictability.

[P29] Selecting additional registrations from reserve if more are needed (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)) should be accompanied by a clear timeline and automated notice requirement to petitioners.

[P30] Allowing reopening of registration if reserve is exhausted (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)) could be abused to advantage certain petitioners; USCIS should set objective triggers for reopenings and provide advance notice of reopenings.

[P31] The continuous monitoring and announcement requirement when reopened (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)) should include precise reporting intervals and a public dashboard of registration counts.

[P32] Random selection among registrations submitted on the final registration date for reopened periods (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)) must follow the same transparency and audit rules as initial-period selections.

[P33] Announcing the start date of any reopened registration period on the USCIS website (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)) is necessary but insufficient; require direct notice (email/SMS) to all previously registered petitioners.

[P34] Electronic confirmation of registration acceptance (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(B)) must include a unique confirmation number, timestamp, and instructions for correcting errors; otherwise petitioners will lack proof in disputes.

[P35] Notification that registrations are selected and the filing period (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(C)) must include the exact start and end timestamps (including time zone), allowed methods of filing, and a clear list of required petition contents.

[P36] The permission to file only during the indicated filing period (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(C)) must be supplemented by a grace policy for technical filing failures (e.g., system outages) that prevent timely submission.

[P37] The rule that petitions may be filed only for selected registrations during the filing period (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(D)(1)) should clarify whether premium processing filings are permitted within that period and how premium processing interacts with selection timing.

[P38] The condition that the registration must have been selected in advance (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(D)(1)) requires USCIS to ensure its selection notices are delivered with sufficient lead time for employers to assemble complete petitions.

[P39] Limiting filing to the filing period shown on the selection notice (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(D)(1)) unfairly penalizes petitioners who receive notices late due to delivery errors; allow extensions when late notice is attributable to USCIS.

[P40] The blanket prohibition on substituting the named beneficiary or transferring the registration (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(D)(1)) is overly rigid — employers should be allowed to substitute beneficiaries in narrow circumstances (e.g., withdrawal of offer, beneficiary termination) with documentation and within a short cure window.

[P41] Denying or rejecting petitions filed on unselected registrations or for different beneficiaries (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(D)(1)) is appropriate, but USCIS should provide clear appeal or motion procedures and allow correction for inadvertent beneficiary name mismatches (typos) that do not change identity.

[P42] The requirement to properly file within the selection filing period (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(D)(2)) should be accompanied by a non-waivable list of required forms and evidence and an online checklist to reduce inadvertent rejections.

[P43] A minimum 60-day filing period (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(D)(2)) is helpful, but USCIS should make the filing period standard across years and publish it at least 90 days in advance for employer planning.

[P44] The threat of denial or rejection for failure to meet filing requirements (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(D)(2)) means USCIS must provide an administrative cure period for immaterial deficiencies, rather than immediate denial, to avoid unnecessary litigation.

[P45] Considering historical approvals/denials and other factors in computing needed registrations (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(E)) is reasonable, but USCIS must publish the models and assumptions used to prevent arbitrary projections.

[P46] The permission to increase projected numbers throughout the fiscal year (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(E)) should be accompanied by criteria and an objection/comment process, as mid-year increases can materially affect employers' recruitment strategies.

[P47] USCIS's discretion to suspend registration if inoperable (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(A)) is necessary, but the rule lacks standards for "inoperable"; define objective criteria (e.g., continuous outage >4 hours, security breach) to avoid arbitrary suspension.

[P48] When suspending registration, USCIS must provide immediate alternative filing procedures and a clear timeline for the petition-filing period announcement (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(A)); mere website announcement is insufficient notice for many employers.

[P49] If registration is suspended and USCIS conducts petition-based selection (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)), USCIS must ensure fairness by applying the same randomization, audit, and transparency safeguards as in registration-based selection.

[P50] USCIS's authority to deny petitions labeled as exempt if later found subject to the cap (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)) could result in unexpected denials; require USCIS to provide notice and opportunity to cure the exemption claim before denial.

[P51] The prohibition on returning or refunding filing fees for petitions denied under the suspended-registration provision (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)) is unfair to petitioners who acted in good faith; USCIS should refund fees when denials are based on agency error or unclear guidance.

[P52] When registration is suspended, using all properly submitted petitions to determine cap sufficiency (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(1)) is acceptable but USCIS must publish receipt-count methodologies and treatment of multi-beneficiary petitions.

[P53] Using historical data to calculate petition needs under suspension (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(1)) must be transparent; stakeholders need to see which historical years and metrics are used, and how changes in policy/practice are adjusted for.

[P54] Announcing the final receipt date once projected petition numbers are received (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(1)) should include the precise cut-off timestamp and a public reporting dashboard of daily receipt tallies.

[P55] Random selection among petitions on the final receipt date under suspension (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(1)) should be audited and have public summaries released post-selection to preserve public trust.

[P56] The requirement to randomly select from petitions received during the first five business days if the cap is met then (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(1)) is workable, but USCIS must define "first five business days" clearly (which calendar & time zone) and ensure equal access across time zones.

[P57] Rejecting petitions subject to the regular cap that were not selected or received after the final receipt date (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(1)) could disproportionately affect smaller employers who file later; USCIS should publish hourly receipt distributions and consider protections for small or rural employers.

[P58] Assessing whether remaining petitions suffice for the advanced-degree exemption after the regular-cap process (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(2)) risks advanced-degree applicants being disadvantaged; USCIS should permit parallel consideration or set-asides to protect advanced-degree beneficiaries.

[P59] The requirement to use historical data to calculate advanced-degree petition needs when registration is suspended (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(2)) must include correction factors for recent trends (e.g., STEM OPT changes) to avoid inaccurate projections.

[P60] Publishing the final receipt date for the advanced-degree exemption (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(2)) should likewise contain precise timestamps and a breakdown of counts by advanced-degree versus regular cap petitions.

[P61] Random selection for the advanced-degree exemption among petitions on the final receipt date (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(2)) needs transparency and access to randomized selection outputs for audit purposes.

[P62] The rule that if the advanced-degree exemption is reached in the first five business days USCIS will randomly select from those five days (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(2)) should include measures to ensure petition receipt systems are robust across different time zones and internet conditions.

[P63] Rejecting petitions not selected in the random draw or received after the final receipt date for advanced-degree exemption (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(2)) must be accompanied by administrative appeal or motion options and clear guidance on re-filing in subsequent years.

[P64] Allocating H-2B numbers by filing order (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)(vii)) disadvantages petitioners with slower internet or in different time zones; USCIS should consider a randomized allocation or weighted access to ensure fairness.

[P65] Projections of petitions needed to reach numerical limits (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)(vii)) must be transparent (model, inputs, confidence intervals); otherwise stakeholders cannot assess the reasonableness of USCIS actions like reopenings.

[P66] Tracking petition receipts and announcing the final receipt date (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)(vii)) should include beneficiary-level data and allow affected parties to verify counts, subject to privacy protections.

[P67] Random selection among petitions received on the final receipt date for H-2B numbers (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)(vii)) should be audited and described publicly (algorithm, seed, oversight) to avoid perceptions of unfairness.

[P68] Rejecting petitions subject to numerical limits that are not selected or arrive after the final receipt date (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)(vii)) should permit equitable relief where rejections were due to USCIS system outages or notice failures.

[P69] Denying petitions later found subject to numerical limitations after the final receipt date and refusing fee refunds (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)(vii)) is punitive; require fee refunds when denial results from USCIS error or ambiguous guidance.

[P70] Random distribution of numbers among petitions received during the first five business days when limits are reached (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)(vii)) is fairer than strict first-come-first-served, but USCIS must ensure postal/electronic receipt timestamps are synchronized and tamper-resistant.

[P71] The obligation for USCIS to consider all submitted evidence and any independently required evidence (§214.2(h)(9)(i)) should be coupled with a presumption that any missing non-material evidence can be requested via RFE rather than resulting in denial.

[P72] Requiring USCIS to send a Notice of Action when a petition is approved (§214.2(h)(9)(i)) is necessary; the rule should require delivery via email and online case status update in addition to mailed notice.

[P73] Approval notices must include beneficiary name(s), classification, and validity period (§214.2(h)(9)(i)); also require inclusion of any conditions, dependent allowances, and clear instructions on next steps (e.g., consular processing, change of status).

[P74] Allowing USCIS to approve petitions covering multiple beneficiaries or services in whole or in part (§214.2(h)(9)(i)) is practical but the rule should specify how pro rata approvals affect fee allocation, refunding, and beneficiary rights.

USCIS's discretion to suspend registration if inoperable (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(A)) is necessary, but the rule lacks standards for "inoperable"; define objective criteria (e.g., continuous outage >4 hours, security breach) to avoid arbitrary suspension.

When suspending registration, USCIS must provide immediate alternative filing procedures and a clear timeline for the petition-filing period announcement (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(A)); mere website announcement is insufficient notice for many employers.

If registration is suspended and USCIS conducts petition-based selection (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)), USCIS must ensure fairness by applying the same randomization, audit, and transparency safeguards as in registration-based selection.

USCIS's authority to deny petitions labeled as exempt if later found subject to the cap (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)) could result in unexpected denials; require USCIS to provide notice and opportunity to cure the exemption claim before denial.

The prohibition on returning or refunding filing fees for petitions denied under the suspended-registration provision (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)) is unfair to petitioners who acted in good faith; USCIS should refund fees when denials are based on agency error or unclear guidance.

When registration is suspended, using all properly submitted petitions to determine cap sufficiency (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(1)) is acceptable but USCIS must publish receipt-count methodologies and treatment of multi-beneficiary petitions.

Using historical data to calculate petition needs under suspension (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(1)) must be transparent; stakeholders need to see which historical years and metrics are used, and how changes in policy/practice are adjusted for.

Announcing the final receipt date once projected petition numbers are received (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(1)) should include the precise cut-off timestamp and a public reporting dashboard of daily receipt tallies.
Random selection among petitions on the final receipt date under suspension (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(1)) should be audited and have public summaries released post-selection to preserve public trust.

The requirement to randomly select from petitions received during the first five business days if the cap is met then (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(1)) is workable, but USCIS must define "first five business days" clearly (which calendar & time zone) and ensure equal access across time zones.

Rejecting petitions subject to the regular cap that were not selected or received after the final receipt date (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(1)) could disproportionately affect smaller employers who file later; USCIS should publish hourly receipt distributions and consider protections for small or rural employers.

Assessing whether remaining petitions suffice for the advanced-degree exemption after the regular-cap process (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(2)) risks advanced-degree applicants being disadvantaged; USCIS should permit parallel consideration or set-asides to protect advanced-degree beneficiaries.

The requirement to use historical data to calculate advanced-degree petition needs when registration is suspended (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(2)) must include correction factors for recent trends (e.g., STEM OPT changes) to avoid inaccurate projections.

Publishing the final receipt date for the advanced-degree exemption (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(2)) should likewise contain precise timestamps and a breakdown of counts by advanced-degree versus regular cap petitions.
Random selection for the advanced-degree exemption among petitions on the final receipt date (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(2)) needs transparency and access to randomized selection outputs for audit purposes.

The rule that if the advanced-degree exemption is reached in the first five business days USCIS will randomly select from those five days (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(2)) should include measures to ensure petition receipt systems are robust across different time zones and internet conditions.

Rejecting petitions not selected in the random draw or received after the final receipt date for advanced-degree exemption (§214.2(h)(8)(iv)(B)(2)) must be accompanied by administrative appeal or motion options and clear guidance on re-filing in subsequent years.

Allocating H-2B numbers by filing order (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)(vii)) disadvantages petitioners with slower internet or in different time zones; USCIS should consider a randomized allocation or weighted access to ensure fairness.

Projections of petitions needed to reach numerical limits (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)(vii)) must be transparent (model, inputs, confidence intervals); otherwise stakeholders cannot assess the reasonableness of USCIS actions like reopenings.

Tracking petition receipts and announcing the final receipt date (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)(vii)) should include beneficiary-level data and allow affected parties to verify counts, subject to privacy protections.

Random selection among petitions received on the final receipt date for H-2B numbers (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)(vii)) should be audited and described publicly (algorithm, seed, oversight) to avoid perceptions of unfairness.

Rejecting petitions subject to numerical limits that are not selected or arrive after the final receipt date (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)(vii)) should permit equitable relief where rejections were due to USCIS system outages or notice failures.

Denying petitions later found subject to numerical limitations after the final receipt date and refusing fee refunds (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)(vii)) is punitive; require fee refunds when denial results from USCIS error or ambiguous guidance.

Random distribution of numbers among petitions received during the first five business days when limits are reached (§214.2(h)(8)(iii)(A)(7)(vii)) is fairer than strict first-come-first-served, but USCIS must ensure postal/electronic receipt timestamps are synchronized and tamper-resistant.

The obligation for USCIS to consider all submitted evidence and any independently required evidence (§214.2(h)(9)(i)) should be coupled with a presumption that any missing non-material evidence can be requested via RFE rather than resulting in denial.

Requiring USCIS to send a Notice of Action when a petition is approved (§214.2(h)(9)(i)) is necessary; the rule should require delivery via email and online case status update in addition to mailed notice.

Approval notices must include beneficiary name(s), classification, and validity period (§214.2(h)(9)(i)); also require inclusion of any conditions, dependent allowances, and clear instructions on next steps (e.g., consular processing, change of status).

Allowing USCIS to approve petitions covering multiple beneficiaries or services in whole or in part (§214.2(h)(9)(i)) is practical but the rule should specify how pro rata approvals affect fee allocation, refunding, and beneficiary rights.
