[P1] Industry commenter: Allowing owners/operators to opt to comply with 40 CFR part 63, subpart WW for specified storage vessels is reasonable, but the rule should clarify exactly which storage vessel types and size thresholds are eligible to avoid inconsistent interpretation.

[P1] Environmental NGO: The permission to opt into subpart WW could weaken protections if subpart WW is less stringent for certain emissions; the preamble must justify that subpart WW provides equivalent or better emission reductions for all covered vessel types.

[P2] State air agency: Replacing subpart A of part 63 with this part’s subpart A when electing the option creates potential conflicts with state permitting programs that currently reference part 63 general provisions; EPA should explain how state implementation and delegation will be handled.

[P2] Industry compliance officer: We request explicit text confirming that any reporting deadlines and recordkeeping formats in this part’s subpart A take precedence, and an annotated crosswalk between the two subpart A sets of provisions to reduce administrative burden.

[P3] Industry legal counsel: The provision that this subpart’s definitions control where terms conflict with subpart WW could create ambiguity for terms not listed here; propose adding a rule that any undefined term retains its part 63 meaning and provide an explicit definitions appendix.

[P3] Environmental health organization: We object to prioritizing the less protective definition where this subpart’s definitions are narrower than part 63; EPA should ensure that chosen definitions are at least as protective as part 63 or require use of the more protective definition.

[P4] Industry operator: Requiring compliance with §60.116b monitoring requirements in addition to part 63 monitoring could duplicate efforts; request consolidation language allowing data collected under subpart WW monitoring to satisfy §60.116b unless specific gaps are identified.

[P4] Small business association: The monitoring obligations in §60.116b(a),(c),(e) may impose new capital costs on small facilities that previously followed part 63 monitoring schedules; request a small-entity impact analysis and consideration of phased compliance.

[P5] Industry records manager: Limiting “all records” to only §60.116b(c) records creates uncertainty about retention of other records generated under subpart WW; request clarification listing specific record types subject to the limitation.

[P5] Public interest law group: The “all records” limitation could inadvertently exclude records needed for enforcement or public transparency; recommend retaining broader record availability for EPA and public inspection except where confidentiality is demonstrably justified.

[P6] Industry: Removing the applicability of §60.116b(b) under the alternative option—if §60.116b(b) contains critical monitoring methods—could reduce measurement accuracy; request EPA justify omission and provide alternative required methods.

[P7] Compliance consultant: Excluding §60.116b(g) could eliminate required corrective action procedures; EPA should explicitly state what corrective actions are required under the alternative and where they are documented.

[P8] Industry: The recordkeeping and reporting list in (A)-(F) appears prescriptive; we request an itemized table mapping each required record/report to the corresponding requirement in part 63 to avoid duplicative submissions.

[P9] Facility operators: Requiring 30-day advance notice to EPA before the first subpart WW inspection is administratively burdensome for facilities with frequent turnover or short lead times; propose reducing notice to 7 days or allowing electronic immediate notifications.

[P9] State regulator: The 30-day pre-inspection notification could hinder coordinated state and local inspections; request a mechanism for states to be copied or for EPA to allow joint inspection scheduling.

[P10] Industry: The requirement to remain under the alternative standard until submitting new notification switching back effectively locks facilities into a regime; request a clearer process and timelines for reverting compliance regimes without penalties.

[P11] Industry legal counsel: Stating that switching between regimes does not reset the compliance schedule could penalize facilities that reasonably change approaches; recommend allowing a short transition window or resetting certain inspection due dates when switching to ensure fairness.

[P12] Industry: Requiring records for each facility using the alternative standard when conducting §63.1063(c)(1) inspections and inclusion in §63.1066 reports may duplicate data already submitted; request EPA allow cross-referencing of existing reports rather than duplicate attachments.

[P13] Industry: Similar to P12, inclusion of §63.1063(c)(2) inspection records in §63.1066 reports for alternative-standard facilities will increase report size; propose that EPA accept consolidated facility-level reports or electronic submittals.

[P14] Industry accountant: Extending retention of §60.115b(a)-(b) records for 2 additional years only for records not yet meeting the 2-year retention creates complex record retention schedules; recommend a single, uniform retention period starting from the date of notification to simplify compliance.

[P14] Records management NGO: Extending retention is reasonable for enforcement continuity, but EPA should require electronic submission of older records upon request to prevent burdensome onsite storage.

[P15] Industry manufacturing trade group: Requiring additional 5-year retention for §63.1065 records until a switch back notification is submitted could create indefinite retention if facilities fail to submit switching notifications; propose a maximum retention cap (e.g., 10 years) or automatic termination after a defined period.

[P15] Legal compliance expert: The interaction between §63.1065 five-year retention and the extended retention here creates potential conflicts with state records-retention laws; request guidance on resolving such conflicts.

[P16] Environmental NGO: The exceptions to §63.1066 reporting in (F) may narrow transparency; EPA should ensure exceptions (F)(1) and (F)(2) do not limit EPA’s or public’s access to critical startup and failure information.

[P17] Industry: Requiring initial startup notification under §63.1066(a)(1)-(2) to be attached to §60.7(a)(3) and §60.115b(a)(1) notifications may create submission format mismatches; ask EPA to permit separate but cross-referenced electronic submissions to accommodate existing systems.

[P17] State permitting authority: Attaching initial startup notifications to multiple different forms may create administrative duplication in state databases; request a single consolidated electronic submission that satisfies all requirements.

[P18] NGO: Tight deadlines for submitting inspection results after failures (60 days for gap measurements, 30 days for other inspections) may be insufficient to collect independent verification; request EPA allow extension where third-party testing labs have limited capacity.

[P18] Industry safety officer: Short submission deadlines after inspection failures could force rushed analyses and false negatives; propose allowing a documented extension process and acceptance of interim reports followed by final reports.

[P19] Chemical manufacturer: Designating the listed PMN chemical as subject to reporting for the significant new uses is appropriate, but EPA should publish the specific use limitations and any disposal or stewardship obligations to avoid market confusion.

[P19] Trade association: The rule should clarify whether imports of articles containing the PMN substance trigger the significant new use requirements, and if so, at what threshold.

[P20] Consumer product manufacturer: Triggering §721.80(f) and (o) for industrial, commercial, and consumer uses will impose broad obligations; ask EPA to specify whether formulation or incidental presence in mixtures counts as “use” and whether small concentration exemptions apply.

[P21] Water utilities: The release-to-water threshold for PMN chemical at N = 4 ppb may be below analytical detection limits for standard municipal monitoring; request EPA specify acceptable sampling/analytical methods and detection limits.

[P21] Environmental group: Requiring reporting for any release to water at or above 4 ppb is appropriate; however EPA should explain derivation of the threshold and potential ecological/human health risk basis.

[P22] Industry compliance manager: Applying Subpart A provisions except where modified is standard, but EPA should provide a consolidated, annotated version showing modifications to avoid misinterpretation.

[P23] Manufacturers: Requiring §721.125(a)-(c),(i),(k) recordkeeping could impose costly labelling and tracking for small processors; request clarification on whether de minimis quantities or R&D exemptions apply.

[P24] Manufacturer legal counsel: Applying §721.185 limitation and revocation provisions raises concerns about due process; request EPA clarify notice and appeal procedures prior to revocation and define “limitations” more precisely.

[P25] Chemical industry: Including PMN P–18–308 generic chemical under reporting is acceptable, but EPA should provide clearer identity or structural information where confidentiality claims hide key hazard attributes necessary for downstream users to assess risk.

[P26] Water quality NGO: The 3 ppb release-to-water threshold for PMN P–18–308 should be accompanied by monitoring guidance and a requirement to notify downstream public water systems if releases exceed the threshold.

[P27] Industry: As with P22, requesting consolidated regulatory text that shows how Subpart A is modified for P–18–308 to reduce compliance confusion.

[P28] Manufacturers/processors: Requiring §721.125(a)-(c) and (k) recordkeeping is acceptable, but EPA should specify retention periods, format (electronic vs paper), and whether aggregated/summary records are allowed.

[P29] Trade group: Application of §721.185 limitations/revocation to this generic PMN is a substantial compliance risk; request EPA to publish criteria that would trigger limitations or revocation so industry can implement preventative controls.

[P21] Legal expert: The phrase “where N= 4 ppb” and “N= 3 ppb” lacks definition of “N” (e.g., concentration, normalized measure); EPA should define N explicitly and cite measurement protocols to avoid legal challenges.

[P1] The blanket prohibition in § 50.20 on involving human subjects without “legally effective informed consent” is overly rigid and fails to account for emergency clinical research where subjects are incapacitated and no LAR is immediately available; request adding explicit emergency exception language or cross-reference to § 50.24.

[P1] The phrasing “legally effective informed consent” in § 50.20 is vague — commenters will request a defined standard (e.g., specify required elements, documentation, language comprehension standard, and standards for minors and diminished capacity) to avoid inconsistent IRB/investigator interpretation.

[P2] Requiring the investigator to obtain legally effective informed consent (§ 50.20) places unreasonable sole responsibility on the investigator when sponsors, study coordinators, or delegated staff often conduct consent; request clarification that delegation is permitted if documented in the investigator’s delegation log and supervised by the investigator.

[P2] § 50.20 should require documentation standards for “legally effective” consent (e.g., signed consent form with version/date, witness requirements, translation/interpretation documentation) to ensure compliance and auditability.

[P3] § 50.22 empowers IRBs to waive/alter consent but lacks procedural safeguards (e.g., required public justification, additional reporting to the agency, or time-limited waivers); request adding requirements for IRB to document rationale and to notify the agency for novel assessments.

[P4] The minimal risk threshold in § 50.22(a) is underdefined; industry and researchers will request illustrative examples and a risk-assessment rubric to achieve consistent IRB decisions across institutions.

[P4] Patient advocacy groups will argue that the “no more than minimal risk” criterion (§ 50.22(a)) is interpreted too broadly and request examples of unacceptable uses (e.g., collection of sensitive genetic data) to prevent erosion of consent protections.

[P5] § 50.22(b)’s requirement that a waiver “will not adversely affect the rights and welfare” is subjective; request adding mandatory community/stakeholder input or enhanced IRB scrutiny when vulnerable populations are involved.

[P6] The practicability standard in § 50.22(c) (that the research “could not practicably be carried out without the waiver or alteration”) is open to abuse; sponsors might claim impracticability to avoid consent — request adding a definition of “practicable” and examples of acceptable justifications (e.g., retrospective chart review vs. prospective enrollment).

[P7] The “whenever appropriate” language in § 50.22(d) is ambiguous — commenters will request criteria for when post-participation information must be provided, timeliness standards, and required content of such information.

[P3/P6] Legal experts will request that IRBs be required to document alternative measures attempted before granting waivers under § 50.22 (e.g., seeking consent from LARs, modifying consent process), to demonstrate that the practicability standard was meaningfully applied.

[P8] § 312.60’s obligation that investigators conduct the investigation “according to the signed investigator statement, the investigational plan, and applicable regulations” lacks specificity about allowable deviations and procedures for emergency deviations; request mandatory reporting timelines for deviations and a process for pre-approved minor deviations.

[P9] The duty in § 312.60 to “protect the rights, safety, and welfare of subjects” is broad; clinical investigators and sponsors request clarification of concrete expectations (e.g., monitoring frequency, adverse event management plans, staffing ratios) to avoid variable enforcement.

[P10] § 312.60’s requirement that investigators “maintain control of drugs under investigation” needs operational details about storage, accountability logs, shipment records, and permitted delegations to pharmacy services; otherwise industry will face inconsistent inspection findings.

[P11] Cross-references in § 312.60 to compliance with part 50 for informed consent should clarify how part 50’s waiver provisions apply to drug trials (e.g., can § 50.22 waivers be used in phase II/III drug trials), since sponsors need certainty on permitted consent modifications.

[P12] § 812.2(b)(1)(iii) places the sponsor responsible for ensuring investigators obtain informed consent — this is operationally unrealistic if sponsors cannot supervise day-to-day consent; sponsors request that “ensure” be clarified to mean reasonable oversight (training, monitoring) rather than absolute liability for each consent interaction.

[P12] Alternatively, industry will request safe-harbor language that compliance with sponsor-established training and monitoring programs satisfies the sponsor’s obligation under § 812.2(b)(1)(iii).

[P13] § 61.156’s requirement to present a graduation certificate from an “authorized training provider” lacks a process for how providers become authorized and how applicants can verify authorization; flight schools request an accreditation/authorization list and transition timeline.

[P14] § 61.160(a) permitting ATP application with 750 hours if required documentation is presented raises safety concerns from pilot unions and safety advocates who will argue 750 hours is too low for multiengine ATP privileges and request maintaining higher hour thresholds or stricter experience metrics.

[P15] § 61.160(b)’s alternative 1,000-hour pathway lacks detail on what “specified conditions” must be met; applicants and examiners will request explicit listing of those conditions (type of experience, cross-country, night, instrument time) to avoid inconsistent certification decisions.

[P16] The 1,250-hour pathway in § 61.160(c) may create multiple parallel routes to ATP that could be exploited; safety stakeholders will request harmonization with international standards and a requirement for recent multiengine experience (e.g., X hours within last 12 months).

[P17] § 61.160(d) that allows certain graduates with 30–59 semester hours to apply for ATP if other requirements are met is confusing; educational institutions request clarity on how credit hours map to required aeronautical experience and whether alternative competency-based assessments are accepted.

[P18] § 61.165(c)(2) requires completion of the ATP certification training program in § 61.156 — commenters will request that distance learning or hybrid courses be explicitly permitted/regulated, with defined minimum in-person training components.

[P19] § 61.165(f)’s requirements to add a multiengine class rating to an ATP certificate are not clear about concurrent versus separate training options; pilots and training providers ask for explicit curricula and minimum dual-control flight time requirements.

[P20] § 61.165(f)(2) requiring passing a knowledge test covering § 61.155(c) aeronautical knowledge areas relevant to multiengine airplanes should specify allowable test accommodations and retest policies, and request that test syllabi be published well in advance.

[P1/P2] Civil liberties groups will argue that the combined effect of P1 and P2 creates a consent-first regime that could impede low-risk public-health surveillance research; they will request explicit safe-harbors for de-identified data uses and retrospective record reviews.

[P3/P5] Community-based research organizations will request that IRBs consider community-level consent considerations and require community consultation before waiving consent under § 50.22(b) when vulnerable communities are disproportionately affected.

[P6] Institutional IRBs will request guidance on documentation that demonstrates that a study “could not practicably be carried out without the waiver” to withstand audit (e.g., sample size calculations showing infeasibility with consent).

[P8/P10] Clinical trial sponsors will request harmonization of § 312.60 drug control and recordkeeping expectations with 21 CFR Part 11 electronic records requirements and FDA guidance on drug accountability to reduce conflicting audit standards.

[P9/P11] Patient advocacy groups will request that investigator obligations (§ 312.60) include explicit requirements for language access services and accessible consent materials so that “protecting rights, safety, and welfare” includes linguistic and cognitive accessibility.

[P12] Bioethicists will comment that § 812.2(b)(1)(iii) should require sponsors to ensure investigators receive training in culturally competent consent procedures and conflict-of-interest disclosures as part of the sponsor’s oversight duties.

[P13/P17] Flight schools and universities will request a transition period to comply with new § 61.156/61.160(d) documentation requirements and clarity on how foreign or nontraditional academic credits are evaluated.

[P1] The proposed amendment text refers generally to "as described in the document" but does not include the full revised regulatory text for review; request publication of the complete amended 40 CFR part 372 language to allow precise legal review.

[P1] The proposal does not include an economic analysis (costs to reporters, enforcement burdens, state agencies) associated with the amendments to part 372; request a Regulatory Flexibility Analysis and cost-benefit assessment.

[P2] The preamble does not identify whether states that rely on part 372 (or state equivalents) will need to update their implementing regulations; request EPA discuss effects on state reporting programs and provide guidance.

[P3] Adding an alphabetized entry for "1321" to paragraph (a) is ambiguous because the numeric code alone lacks a description; request EPA confirm the meaning of code 1321 and provide the full textual entry to avoid interpretation errors.

[P3] If "1321" refers to a particular SIC or NAICS code, the rule should state the industry description and scope (e.g., include or exclude specific activities); request clarity so affected entities can determine applicability.

[P3][P5] The use of alphabetical insertion may create inconsistencies if code formatting (dash, hyphen, spacing) differs across listings; recommend EPA adopt standardized formatting and provide machine-readable tables to avoid misinterpretation by automated reporting systems.

[P1] The deadline in § 39.13(a) requiring the FAA to receive comments by June 24, 2021 is unreasonably short and should be extended to allow stakeholders (airlines, MROs, labor, and small operators) adequate time to analyze the technical AWL/CMR changes and prepare detailed comments.

[P1] The proposed comment deadline of June 24, 2021 does not account for stakeholders who require coordination with manufacturers or legal counsel; the FAA should provide at least a 60-day comment period from publication.

[P2] § 39.13(f) is ambiguous because it requires compliance “within the compliance times specified” without clarifying whether calendar time, flight hours, or cycles provided in the AWLs/CMRs govern; the rule should explicitly state that the specific units in each AWL/CMR control.

[P2] The obligation in § 39.13(f) should allow for documented operational constraints (e.g., aircraft grounded for reasons beyond operator control) to extend compliance windows through an AMOC process without punitive enforcement.

[P3] The 60-day timeline in § 39.13(g) to revise maintenance/inspection programs is infeasible for large operators and leasing lessors who must coordinate across fleets and obtain agreement from multiple airworthiness authorities; FAA should extend to 180 days or allow staged incorporation.

[P3] § 39.13(g) lacks required detail about who is responsible for updating the maintenance program when an aircraft is operated under multiple certificates (lessor vs. lessee); the FAA should clarify responsibilities.

[P3] The rule should require the FAA to provide the exact Boeing MPD document version and AWL/CMR pages to be incorporated, rather than referring generically to “specified AWL/CMR information,” to avoid inconsistent incorporation.

[P4] For AWL 28–AWL–01 in § 39.13(g)(1), the 120-month initial compliance interval is excessively long given the safety-critical nature of “External Wires Over Center Fuel Tank”; FAA should require a shorter interval (e.g., 36 months) or justify the 120-month basis with risk analysis.

[P4] Conversely, small regional carriers with lower utilization may need the 120-month interval expressed in flight hours/cycles; the rule should provide equivalent flight-hour/cycle thresholds rather than only calendar months.

[P5] For AWL 28–AWL–03 in § 39.13(g)(2), requiring initial compliance within 120 months after the most recent specified inspection could create gaps if records of “most recent inspection” are incomplete; FAA should require record reconciliation or mandate default compliance dates for missing records.

[P6] For AWL 28–AWL–14 in § 39.13(g)(3), FAA must provide detailed inspection/follow-up actions and acceptance criteria for “Fault Current Bond” revisions; without specifics, operators cannot reliably update their programs within 60 days.

[P7] § 39.13(g)(4) for AWL 28–AWL–20 ties compliance to service bulletin actions and inspections with a “whichever is later” clause; this could indefinitely delay compliance if operators defer service bulletin work—FAA should specify a firm outer limit to prevent indefinite postponement.

[P7] The 12-month interval in § 39.13(g)(4) relative to service bulletin actions may be insufficient to plan fleet-wide installations requiring line maintenance windows; FAA should allow phased compliance or temporary relief for scheduling burdens.

[P8] For AWL 28–AWL–21 (§ 39.13(g)(5)), the 12-month initial compliance timeframe for GFI functionality is not aligned with typical heavy maintenance schedules—FAA should permit credit for accomplishment during scheduled C-checks and clarify acceptable implementation checks.

[P9] The 72-month interval for AWL 28–AWL–25 in § 39.13(g)(6) appears arbitrary and the FAA must provide the technical rationale supporting why 72 months provides an acceptable level of safety for MOV actuator bonding.

[P10] For AWL 28–AWL–26 (§ 39.13(g)(7)), the 12-month requirement for "Power Failed On Protection System" may impose operational risk if performed incorrectly; FAA should mandate training or certification for maintenance personnel performing these system changes.

[P11] AWL 28–AWL–30 in § 39.13(g)(8) gives a choice of 24 months after AD effective date or 72 months after prior inspection—this “whichever is later” approach could permit operators to postpone safer earlier action; FAA should require the shorter of the two or justify the later threshold.

[P12] For AWL 28–AWL–33 (§ 39.13(g)(9)), the complex three-way “whichever is later” (24 months, 144 months after SB actions, 144 months after inspection) is confusing and invites inconsistent application; FAA must provide examples and a clear method for computing the applicable deadline.

[P12] The 144-month allowance for AWL 28–AWL–33 seems excessive for clamping and sleeving on out-of-tank wires; safety advocates will challenge this long interval without supporting service life data.

[P13] AWL 47–AWL–04 (§ 39.13(g)(10)) ties compliance to 17,300 flight hours which may disadvantage high-utilization aircraft; FAA should allow operators to convert to calendar time or cycles to match their scheduling needs.

[P14] § 39.13(g)(11) for AWL 47–AWL–05 also uses 17,300 flight hours—FAA must clarify whether flight-hour counters must be verified/calibrated and which flight hour source (airline flight log vs. aircraft FM) is the record of compliance.

[P15] AWL 47–AWL–07 (§ 39.13(g)(12)) establishes a 48,000 flight hour interval; maintenance planners need guidance on interim inspection requirements and risk mitigation for aircraft approaching this threshold.

[P16] § 39.13(h) allows alternatives in (h)(1) and (h)(2) but does not specify evaluation criteria for other potential alternatives; industry requests that FAA publish technical acceptance criteria for alternative materials to speed AMOC processing.

[P17] § 39.13(h)(1) permits specific wire alternatives in lieu of BMS 13–48/13–58/13–60; aircraft OEMs and wire manufacturers should be required to validate compatibility (temperature rating, insulation thickness, current capacity) before operators substitute—FAA should require documented engineering substantiation.

[P17] The permitted alternative wires in § 39.13(h)(1) (MIL–W–22759/16, SAE AS22759, etc.) appear to omit part numbers or insulation variants; this could lead to improper substitutions—FAA should list exact acceptable specifications or reference normative documents.

[P18] § 39.13(h)(2) permits Roundit 2000NX and Varglas as TFE–2X substitutes for sleeving; operators need material property comparisons (dielectric strength, flammability, abrasion resistance) and FAA should require supplier qualification data be retained.

[P18] Consumer/worker safety groups will request that FAA verify that allowed sleeving alternatives meet the same flammability and smoke/toxicity standards as TFE–2X; the rule should reference applicable flammability test standards (e.g., FAR/JAR material tests).

[P19] § 39.13(i) prohibition preventing use of alternative actions/intervals/CDCCLs once the maintenance program is revised is overly restrictive and could prevent necessary operational flexibility; operators ask for a provision allowing temporary deviations when safety dictates, pending AMOC approval.

[P19] Legal experts will assert that § 39.13(i)’s blanket prohibition may conflict with existing certificate-holder maintenance program authorities under 14 CFR Part 91/121 and that FAA should clarify interplay and enforcement policy.

[P20] The exception in § 39.13(i) permitting AMOCs per paragraph (k) is acceptable in principle, but the process is historically slow; FAA should commit to a time-bound AMOC review (e.g., 60–90 days) to avoid grounding aircraft or creating non-compliance.

[P21] § 39.13(j) states that completing paragraph (g) ends specified prior AD requirements—leasing companies need confirmation that compliance with (g) provides sole regulatory relief and that there are no lingering inspection recordkeeping or reporting obligations from the previous ADs.

[P22] Regarding § 39.13(j)(1), terminating all requirements of AD 2012–12–15 upon accomplishing paragraph (g) is acceptable only if FAA provides an assurance that safety equivalence has been validated; request the FAA publish an equivalence analysis.

[P23] For § 39.13(j)(2), terminating the requirements in paragraph (i)(2) of AD 2018–20–13 requires clear cross-references—operators need the exact text or amendment showing how the termination is achieved to avoid misinterpretation.

[P24] § 39.13(k)(1) authorizing the Seattle ACO Branch Manager to approve AMOCs centralizes authority geographically; operators outside the Seattle region request clarity whether delegation to other ACOs is possible and whether this will delay approvals.

[P25] The procedural obligation in § 39.13(k)(1) to send AMOC requests per 14 CFR 39.19 may be misunderstood by foreign operators; FAA should provide specific international submission guidance and contact points for non-U.S. operators.

[P26] Allowing email submission to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov (§ 39.13(k)(1) contact) is helpful, but stakeholders request confirmation of secure submission protocols for proprietary engineering data and an alternate mechanism for large file transfers.

[P27] § 39.13(k)(2) requires notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC; however, for operators without a principal inspector, the rule references the responsible Flight Standards Office but does not provide a directory—FAA should supply contact guidance.

[P28] The permission in § 39.13(k)(3) to use an AMOC approved by an authorized Boeing ODA raises conflict-of-interest concerns; independent validation or FAA concurrence should be required before accepting ODA-approved AMOCs for critical electrical/fuel system modifications.

[P29] The certification-basis requirement in § 39.13(k)(3)(condition 1) for AMOC approvals is appropriate, but FAA should provide examples of acceptable means of showing conformance to the airplane’s certification basis (e.g., service bulletin data, test reports).

[P30] Requiring that AMOC approvals specifically reference this AD (§ 39.13(k)(3)(condition 2)) is reasonable, but FAA should permit referencing by FAA approval number or provide a template wording to avoid administrative rejections for clerical errors.

[P3] Maintenance and repair organizations request that the FAA provide a compliance checklist or template for the required maintenance program revision under § 39.13(g) so that revisions are consistent across operators and acceptable to principal inspectors.

[P4] Labor organizations representing maintenance technicians request that FAA require documented training requirements and minimum qualifications for personnel performing the new AWL/CMR mandated tasks in § 39.13(g)(1) through (12).

[P11] Safety advocacy groups will challenge any “whichever is later” provisions that could extend compliance to 144 months or tens of thousands of flight hours without interim mitigations; they will request interim inspections or operational restrictions until compliance is achieved.

[P19] Small operators and regional carriers warn that the post-revision prohibition on alternative CDCCLs in § 39.13(i) could force fleet-wide immediate purchases of expensive parts (wiring/sleeving) and request phased implementation or financial assistance mechanisms.

[P17] Wire manufacturers will comment that the permissible alternatives in § 39.13(h)(1) reference industry standards (MIL/SAE) but may not cover modern wire constructions; they will ask FAA to allow equivalent modern-spec wires if substantiated.

[P18] Environmental groups may raise concerns about TFE/PFOA/PFAS content implications of allowed sleeving materials in § 39.13(h)(2) and request environmental assessment and disclosure of material chemistries for Roundit 2000NX and Varglas.

[P3] International aviation authorities (EASA, Transport Canada) will request harmonization language and seek consultation to ensure that incorporating Boeing MPD items under § 39.13(g) aligns with foreign continuing airworthiness requirements.

[P12] Maintenance recordkeeping burden: operators request that FAA specify documentation and reporting requirements for compliance with the multi-option deadlines in § 39.13(g)(9) (AWL 28–AWL–33) to ensure consistent auditability.

[P26] Privacy/commercial sensitivity: submitters request that FAA clarify whether emails to the AMOC address will be acknowledged with receipt and provide an estimated processing timeline to manage business planning.

[P24] Legal commenters will request that FAA publish the scope of the Seattle ACO Branch Manager’s authority in issuing AMOCs (e.g., limits, delegation options) and whether prior AMOC approvals for similar ADs will be considered acceptable precedent.

[P7] Operators request clarity on whether service bulletin “accomplishment” referenced in multiple subparagraphs (§ 39.13(g)(4), (5), (6), (7)) requires FAA-approved data or may be accomplished via company engineering orders with appropriate substantiation.

[P21] Lessors request explicit language confirming that termination of prior AD requirements (§ 39.13(j)) transfers airworthiness obligations appropriately between lessee and lessor and that lease contracts need not be amended solely because of this AD.

[P29] Engineering firms request that FAA allow use of equivalent analyses (finite element, test data) to demonstrate an AMOC meets the airplane’s certification basis per § 39.13(k)(3)(1) and ask the FAA to publish minimum content requirements for such analyses.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The deadline in § 39.13(a) requiring the FAA to receive comments by June 24, 2021 is unreasonably short and should be extended to allow stakeholders (airlines, MROs, labor, and small operators) adequate time to analyze the technical AWL/CMR changes and prepare detailed comments.

The proposed comment deadline of June 24, 2021 does not account for stakeholders who require coordination with manufacturers or legal counsel; the FAA should provide at least a 60-day comment period from publication.

§ 39.13(f) is ambiguous because it requires compliance “within the compliance times specified” without clarifying whether calendar time, flight hours, or cycles provided in the AWLs/CMRs govern; the rule should explicitly state that the specific units in each AWL/CMR control.

The obligation in § 39.13(f) should allow for documented operational constraints (e.g., aircraft grounded for reasons beyond operator control) to extend compliance windows through an AMOC process without punitive enforcement.

The 60-day timeline in § 39.13(g) to revise maintenance/inspection programs is infeasible for large operators and leasing lessors who must coordinate across fleets and obtain agreement from multiple airworthiness authorities; FAA should extend to 180 days or allow staged incorporation.

§ 39.13(g) lacks required detail about who is responsible for updating the maintenance program when an aircraft is operated under multiple certificates (lessor vs. lessee); the FAA should clarify responsibilities.

The rule should require the FAA to provide the exact Boeing MPD document version and AWL/CMR pages to be incorporated, rather than referring generically to “specified AWL/CMR information,” to avoid inconsistent incorporation.

For AWL 28–AWL–01 in § 39.13(g)(1), the 120-month initial compliance interval is excessively long given the safety-critical nature of “External Wires Over Center Fuel Tank”; FAA should require a shorter interval (e.g., 36 months) or justify the 120-month basis with risk analysis.

Conversely, small regional carriers with lower utilization may need the 120-month interval expressed in flight hours/cycles; the rule should provide equivalent flight-hour/cycle thresholds rather than only calendar months.

For AWL 28–AWL–03 in § 39.13(g)(2), requiring initial compliance within 120 months after the most recent specified inspection could create gaps if records of “most recent inspection” are incomplete; FAA should require record reconciliation or mandate default compliance dates for missing records.

For AWL 28–AWL–14 in § 39.13(g)(3), FAA must provide detailed inspection/follow-up actions and acceptance criteria for “Fault Current Bond” revisions; without specifics, operators cannot reliably update their programs within 60 days.

§ 39.13(g)(4) for AWL 28–AWL–20 ties compliance to service bulletin actions and inspections with a “whichever is later” clause; this could indefinitely delay compliance if operators defer service bulletin work—FAA should specify a firm outer limit to prevent indefinite postponement.

The 12-month interval in § 39.13(g)(4) relative to service bulletin actions may be insufficient to plan fleet-wide installations requiring line maintenance windows; FAA should allow phased compliance or temporary relief for scheduling burdens.

For AWL 28–AWL–21 (§ 39.13(g)(5)), the 12-month initial compliance timeframe for GFI functionality is not aligned with typical heavy maintenance schedules—FAA should permit credit for accomplishment during scheduled C-checks and clarify acceptable implementation checks.

The 72-month interval for AWL 28–AWL–25 in § 39.13(g)(6) appears arbitrary and the FAA must provide the technical rationale supporting why 72 months provides an acceptable level of safety for MOV actuator bonding.

For AWL 28–AWL–26 (§ 39.13(g)(7)), the 12-month requirement for "Power Failed On Protection System" may impose operational risk if performed incorrectly; FAA should mandate training or certification for maintenance personnel performing these system changes.

AWL 28–AWL–30 in § 39.13(g)(8) gives a choice of 24 months after AD effective date or 72 months after prior inspection—this “whichever is later” approach could permit operators to postpone safer earlier action; FAA should require the shorter of the two or justify the later threshold.

For AWL 28–AWL–33 (§ 39.13(g)(9)), the complex three-way “whichever is later” (24 months, 144 months after SB actions, 144 months after inspection) is confusing and invites inconsistent application; FAA must provide examples and a clear method for computing the applicable deadline.
The 144-month allowance for AWL 28–AWL–33 seems excessive for clamping and sleeving on out-of-tank wires; safety advocates will challenge this long interval without supporting service life data.

AWL 47–AWL–04 (§ 39.13(g)(10)) ties compliance to 17,300 flight hours which may disadvantage high-utilization aircraft; FAA should allow operators to convert to calendar time or cycles to match their scheduling needs.

§ 39.13(g)(11) for AWL 47–AWL–05 also uses 17,300 flight hours—FAA must clarify whether flight-hour counters must be verified/calibrated and which flight hour source (airline flight log vs. aircraft FM) is the record of compliance.

AWL 47–AWL–07 (§ 39.13(g)(12)) establishes a 48,000 flight hour interval; maintenance planners need guidance on interim inspection requirements and risk mitigation for aircraft approaching this threshold.

§ 39.13(h) allows alternatives in (h)(1) and (h)(2) but does not specify evaluation criteria for other potential alternatives; industry requests that FAA publish technical acceptance criteria for alternative materials to speed AMOC processing.

§ 39.13(h)(1) permits specific wire alternatives in lieu of BMS 13–48/13–58/13–60; aircraft OEMs and wire manufacturers should be required to validate compatibility (temperature rating, insulation thickness, current capacity) before operators substitute—FAA should require documented engineering substantiation.

The permitted alternative wires in § 39.13(h)(1) (MIL–W–22759/16, SAE AS22759, etc.) appear to omit part numbers or insulation variants; this could lead to improper substitutions—FAA should list exact acceptable specifications or reference normative documents.

§ 39.13(h)(2) permits Roundit 2000NX and Varglas as TFE–2X substitutes for sleeving; operators need material property comparisons (dielectric strength, flammability, abrasion resistance) and FAA should require supplier qualification data be retained.

Consumer/worker safety groups will request that FAA verify that allowed sleeving alternatives meet the same flammability and smoke/toxicity standards as TFE–2X; the rule should reference applicable flammability test standards (e.g., FAR/JAR material tests).

§ 39.13(i) prohibition preventing use of alternative actions/intervals/CDCCLs once the maintenance program is revised is overly restrictive and could prevent necessary operational flexibility; operators ask for a provision allowing temporary deviations when safety dictates, pending AMOC approval.

Legal experts will assert that § 39.13(i)’s blanket prohibition may conflict with existing certificate-holder maintenance program authorities under 14 CFR Part 91/121 and that FAA should clarify interplay and enforcement policy.

The exception in § 39.13(i) permitting AMOCs per paragraph (k) is acceptable in principle, but the process is historically slow; FAA should commit to a time-bound AMOC review (e.g., 60–90 days) to avoid grounding aircraft or creating non-compliance.

§ 39.13(j) states that completing paragraph (g) ends specified prior AD requirements—leasing companies need confirmation that compliance with (g) provides sole regulatory relief and that there are no lingering inspection recordkeeping or reporting obligations from the previous ADs.

Regarding § 39.13(j)(1), terminating all requirements of AD 2012–12–15 upon accomplishing paragraph (g) is acceptable only if FAA provides an assurance that safety equivalence has been validated; request the FAA publish an equivalence analysis.

For § 39.13(j)(2), terminating the requirements in paragraph (i)(2) of AD 2018–20–13 requires clear cross-references—operators need the exact text or amendment showing how the termination is achieved to avoid misinterpretation.

§ 39.13(k)(1) authorizing the Seattle ACO Branch Manager to approve AMOCs centralizes authority geographically; operators outside the Seattle region request clarity whether delegation to other ACOs is possible and whether this will delay approvals.

The procedural obligation in § 39.13(k)(1) to send AMOC requests per 14 CFR 39.19 may be misunderstood by foreign operators; FAA should provide specific international submission guidance and contact points for non-U.S. operators.

raw_output:
[P1] Industry commenters will request clarification that an SE Report may be submitted for combination products (e.g., tobacco product with a delivery device) and ask whether separate SE Reports are required for device components versus tobacco components when asserting substantial equivalence.

[P1] Public health advocacy groups will argue that permitting SE Reports risks circumventing robust premarket review and urge FDA to narrow the permission to only products with truly minor, well-documented changes to predicates.

[P1] Legal experts will request explicit guidance on whether an SE Report may rely on multiple predicate products (cross-referencing) or must compare a single new product to a single predicate as stated elsewhere (see P39/P44).

[P2] Manufacturers will comment that the 90-day minimum review clock is insufficient and request either a longer mandatory pre-submission period (e.g., 180 days) or that FDA provide expedited review pathways with guaranteed timelines.

[P2] Smaller manufacturers and importers will ask for an exception to the 90-day requirement for limited test-market introductions or very small-scale distribution, arguing that the rule as written would effectively bar small businesses from market entry.

[P2] Trade associations will request clarification on when the 90-day clock begins for amended SE Reports or resubmissions following an FDA deficiency letter (e.g., whether a new 90-day period restarts).

[P3] Industry commenters will challenge the prohibition on commercial distribution prior to an SE order, asking whether premarket marketing of limited quantities for research or product testing is allowed under any controlled exemption.

[P3] Consumer advocates will support the prohibition but request that FDA define and publish enforcement priorities and penalties for noncompliance to ensure the prohibition is meaningfully deterred.

[P3] Legal commentators will ask whether starting distribution before an SE order constitutes an automatic violation of the FD&C Act and request citation to statutory authority authorizing the specific prohibition and remedies.

[P4] Manufacturers will request explicit definition of “another premarket pathway” in the exception — e.g., whether enforcement discretion letters, marketing denial letters with conditions, or equivalent foreign authorizations count.

[P4] Public health groups will argue that the exception for products with another premarket authorization must not be used to circumvent substantive SE review and request that FDA require cross-referencing and provide the public record when an alternative authorization is relied upon.

[P5] Commenters from industry will request a clear list or template of the minimum “enough information” required for FDA to make a substantial equivalence determination to avoid inconsistent expectations.

[P5] Consumer safety organizations will urge that the rule require applicants to include independent third-party verification of key data elements in the comparison to ensure objectivity.

[P6] Industry will request that the rule define timelines for applicants to respond to deficiency citations and whether failure to respond within a specified time leads to refusal to accept or an adverse order under §1107.48.

[P6] Small businesses will request flexibility for iterative exchanges with FDA, arguing that the absolute obligation to provide requested information without procedural protections may be burdensome and should allow for negotiated data packages or partial submissions.

[P7] Industry and legal commenters will seek clarity on the circumstances under which FDA will choose to issue an order under §1107.48 versus allowing the review to remain open — request objective criteria and timelines for such decisions.

[P7] Public interest commenters will request notice-and-opportunity-to-cure before FDA issues an order under §1107.48, arguing that applicants should not face an immediate adverse order solely for initial noncompliance.

[P8] Industry will express concern that the broad refusal-to-accept standard could be used inconsistently and request publication of a refusal-to-accept checklist and appeal or reconsideration procedure.

[P8] Legal experts will request that FDA define what constitutes “comply with this section” in order to afford due process — e.g., whether minor formatting errors can lead to refusal to accept.

[P9] Applicant trade groups will request that FDA publish a fillable SE Report template covering all required items (the “following information”) to reduce submission errors and speed reviews.

[P9] Public health groups will argue that the required list of information must explicitly include independent toxicological and behavioral data to evaluate public health impact, not just product specifications.

[P10] Industry commenters will ask for detail on what the “general information as described in paragraph (c)” includes — request cross-references be explicit in the text to avoid ambiguity.

[P11] Consumer advocacy groups will request that the summary described in paragraph (d) include an executive summary of potential public health impacts and predicted youth appeal indicators.

[P12] Manufacturers will request an explicit list of the product description elements required in paragraph (e), including acceptable units and measurement methods for properties like ventilation and nicotine yield.

[P13] Industry will request that the rule permit reliance on publicly available predicate STNs and allow applicants to reference FDA’s predicate determinations without resubmitting proprietary underlying data.

[P13] Legal commenters will caution that requiring statements that the predicate has no adverse order or is grandfathered could create perverse incentives and recommend allowing applicants to explain predicate status where administrative records are ambiguous.

[P14] Independent labs and testing organizations will request specifications for acceptable comparative testing methodologies and validated analytical methods to be referenced in paragraph (g).

[P15] Industry will request explicit thresholds or comparability criteria for comparative testing information (e.g., acceptable variability ranges) to determine when differences raise different public health questions.

[P15] Public health commenters will insist that comparative testing must include both chemical constituents and emissions under realistic use conditions and behavioral/abuse liability data.

[P16] Manufacturers will request clarity on what constitutes “compliance with applicable tobacco product standards” — request a list of standards and acceptable evidence or certifications.

[P16] Standards organizations will request that FDA accept recognized consensus standard test reports (e.g., ISO) as evidence of compliance in lieu of custom testing.

[P17] Public health advocates will object to permitting a statement that health information will be made available only upon request, arguing that key health information summaries must be publicly posted to inform consumers and stakeholders.

[P17] Industry will request that the “health information summary” requirement define what content is required (constituent levels, emissions, toxicology) and allow confidential business information (CBI) redactions where appropriate.

[P18] Environmental and public health groups will request more detail on what demonstrating compliance with 21 CFR part 25 (NEPA-like requirements) entails for SE Reports and whether categorical exclusions are applicable.

[P18] Legal commenters will request that FDA specify whether environmental analyses are required for all product changes or only those with potential environmental impacts (e.g., disposal of new components).

[P19] Industry will request safe-harbor language for the certification statement required by paragraph (l), including model language to reduce liability concerns for inadvertent errors.

[P19] Consumer advocates will request that the certification include attestation to the completeness and accuracy of health-related data and identify responsible corporate officers.

[P20] Industry will request that the rule allow simultaneous submission of an SE Report and an application for marketing under another pathway, and clarify which submission date governs regulatory obligations.

[P20] Legal commenters will request guidance about electronic timestamping and whether the date of SE Report submission is the date of receipt by FDA or date of electronic transmission.

[P21] Applicants will ask whether amendments must be clearly labeled as such and whether an amendment resets any regulatory deadlines or the 90-day pre-introduction requirement.

[P21] Consumer advocates will request that amendments be publicly posted with redactions for CBI to ensure transparency about changes to submitted claims.

[P22] Industry will request confirmation that previously assigned FDA STNs can be referenced and that a single STN may cover multiple related SE Reports to reduce administrative burden.

[P22] Legal commenters will urge that failure to provide a prior STN should not be a sole basis for refusal to accept, provided the applicant supplies other identifying information.

[P23] Trade associations will request that references to meetings with FDA be non-binding and that the agency issue meeting minutes summarizing any substantive feedback relied upon in the SE Report.

[P23] Small businesses will request that informal communications with FDA not be used to hold applicants to unstated expectations unless memorialized in official meeting minutes.

[P24] Industry will request that third-party contract manufacturers be listed in addition to applicant name and address, with clear rules on liability and notification responsibilities.

[P24] Consumer groups will request that parent companies and brand owners be disclosed to aid enforcement and public accountability.

[P25] Foreign manufacturers will request clarification of the obligations for U.S. agents and whether a single U.S. agent can represent multiple foreign applicants on a single submission.

[P25] Legal commenters will request an explanation of whether failure to provide a U.S. agent for foreign applicants results in refusal to accept or grounds for an adverse order.

[P26] Industry will request examples of acceptable product identifiers when products are sold under different brand names in different markets (e.g., SKU-level guidance).

[P27] Trade groups will request that the manufacturer field allow third-party manufacturers and contract packagers to be identified separately to reflect modern supply chains.

[P28] Retailers and industry will request guidance on whether rebranding or private-labeling requires a new SE Report or can be covered by the original manufacturer’s SE order.

[P29] Industry will request precise definitions for each “product property” listed and dispute any requirement that attributes not present must be listed as “none” — arguing that exhaustive property lists may be burdensome.

[P30] Manufacturers will request that the product properties table be machine-readable and that FDA publish the table schema so applicants can prepare electronic submissions that map to FDA systems.

[P30] Public health groups will request that certain properties (e.g., characterizing flavors, ventilation) be required fields subject to specific test methods and detection limits.

[P31] Industry will request that FDA publish the mandatory form(s) referenced in §1107.18(b) well in advance of the rule’s effective date and provide a transition period for compliance.

[P31] Small entities will request that FDA provide alternative submission mechanisms (paper or assistance) during the initial rollout of the form requirement.

[P32] Industry will object to the “written in English” requirement for multinational companies and request translations be allowed with accompanying certified English translations rather than requiring original documents in English.

[P32] Civil rights and immigrant advocacy groups will request that FDA accept submissions and communications in multiple languages for non-English-speaking applicants, or at least provide translation support.

[P33] Industry will request that FDA publish the specific electronic formats and transmission standards (file types, container formats, encryption) the Agency can accept to avoid costly rework.

[P33] Small businesses will request flexibility or temporary waivers for electronic submission if they lack compatible IT systems, arguing the waiver mechanism (P34) needs clear criteria and timely processing.

[P34] Advocates for regulatory efficiency will request that the waiver process be automated and expedited, with clear standards and a presumption in favor of waivers for small entities or in cases of technical difficulty.

[P34] Enforcement groups will warn that waivers should be narrowly tailored to avoid undermining FDA’s ability to manage and review submissions efficiently.

[P35] Public health organizations will request that the introductory summary must include a plain-language public health impact statement intelligible to non-expert stakeholders.

[P35] Industry will request that the summary requirement include a mechanism to protect CBI and trade secrets from public disclosure while still meeting transparency goals.

[P36] Consumer advocates will request that the concise description include product emission yields under realistic use conditions, not just design specifications.

[P36] Manufacturers will request specification of acceptable units and test standards for describing characteristics to avoid inconsistent submissions.

[P37] Public health experts will request FDA guidance on the meaning of “different public health questions” and provide examples of differences that would and would not raise such questions.

[P37] Industry will request that the applicant’s belief statement be non-binding and not a basis for enforcement unless contradicted by FDA findings.

[P38] Consumer advocacy groups will request that similarities and differences include behavioral and appeal characteristics (e.g., youth appeal, marketing claims) that could affect public health.

[P38] Legal commenters will request that applicants be required to include a discussion of uncertainty and limitations in their similarity/difference assessments.

[P39] Industry will object to the one-to-one limitation (one new product compared to one predicate) and request allowance for master reports that compare multiple closely related new products to a single predicate to reduce redundant submissions.

[P39] Public health groups will support the one-to-one requirement, arguing it prevents applicants from “mix-and-match” predicates to minimize review of significant changes.

[P40] Manufacturers will request clear standards for acceptable drawings/schematics (scale, tolerances, file formats) and whether photographs or 3-D CAD files are required for complex components.

[P40] Security and IP counsel will request that detailed drawings be eligible for CBI protection and that the rule state the process for CBI claims for schematics.

[P41] Industry will request guidance on the depth of component-level disclosure required for proprietary accessory components (e.g., filters) and whether vendors’ confidentiality concerns can be accommodated with redactions.

[P41] Public health groups will argue that component functions affecting emissions or exposure (e.g., filter materials) must be fully disclosed and tested independent of vendor claims.

[P42] Manufacturers will request that the “concise overview of manufacturing process” permit reliance on high-level process descriptions for contract-manufactured products where the applicant does not control the entire process.

[P42] Environmental groups will request that manufacturing overviews include waste streams, solvent use, and emissions to assess environmental and public health impacts as part of 21 CFR part 25 compliance.

[P43] Industry will request examples of when manufacturing process changes are considered to affect product characteristics and therefore must be fully described versus when a statement that the process does not affect characteristics is acceptable.

[P43] Regulatory lawyers will request a safe-harbor checklist for asserting that manufacturing does not affect characteristics, including confirmatory testing requirements.

[P44] Industry will request clear guidance on how to document and verify that a predicate product is indeed grandfathered or previously found substantially equivalent, including what FDA records and certifications satisfy the requirement.

[P44] Public health advocates will caution that reliance on grandfathered predicates should be limited, and request that FDA require updated scientific evidence if the predicate determination is decades old or lacks modern testing.

Legal commenters will caution that requiring statements that the predicate has no adverse order or is grandfathered could create perverse incentives and recommend allowing applicants to explain predicate status where administrative records are ambiguous.
Independent labs and testing organizations will request specifications for acceptable comparative testing methodologies and validated analytical methods to be referenced in paragraph (g).

Industry will request explicit thresholds or comparability criteria for comparative testing information (e.g., acceptable variability ranges) to determine when differences raise different public health questions.
Public health commenters will insist that comparative testing must include both chemical constituents and emissions under realistic use conditions and behavioral/abuse liability data.
Manufacturers will request clarity on what constitutes “compliance with applicable tobacco product standards” — request a list of standards and acceptable evidence or certifications.
Standards organizations will request that FDA accept recognized consensus standard test reports (e.g., ISO) as evidence of compliance in lieu of custom testing.

Public health advocates will object to permitting a statement that health information will be made available only upon request, arguing that key health information summaries must be publicly posted to inform consumers and stakeholders.

Industry will request that the “health information summary” requirement define what content is required (constituent levels, emissions, toxicology) and allow confidential business information (CBI) redactions where appropriate.

Environmental and public health groups will request more detail on what demonstrating compliance with 21 CFR part 25 (NEPA-like requirements) entails for SE Reports and whether categorical exclusions are applicable.

Legal commenters will request that FDA specify whether environmental analyses are required for all product changes or only those with potential environmental impacts (e.g., disposal of new components).
Industry will request safe-harbor language for the certification statement required by paragraph (l), including model language to reduce liability concerns for inadvertent errors.
Consumer advocates will request that the certification include attestation to the completeness and accuracy of health-related data and identify responsible corporate officers.

Industry will request that the rule allow simultaneous submission of an SE Report and an application for marketing under another pathway, and clarify which submission date governs regulatory obligations.
Legal commenters will request guidance about electronic timestamping and whether the date of SE Report submission is the date of receipt by FDA or date of electronic transmission.
Applicants will ask whether amendments must be clearly labeled as such and whether an amendment resets any regulatory deadlines or the 90-day pre-introduction requirement.
Consumer advocates will request that amendments be publicly posted with redactions for CBI to ensure transparency about changes to submitted claims.
Industry will request confirmation that previously assigned FDA STNs can be referenced and that a single STN may cover multiple related SE Reports to reduce administrative burden.
Legal commenters will urge that failure to provide a prior STN should not be a sole basis for refusal to accept, provided the applicant supplies other identifying information.
Trade associations will request that references to meetings with FDA be non-binding and that the agency issue meeting minutes summarizing any substantive feedback relied upon in the SE Report.
Small businesses will request that informal communications with FDA not be used to hold applicants to unstated expectations unless memorialized in official meeting minutes.
Industry will request that third-party contract manufacturers be listed in addition to applicant name and address, with clear rules on liability and notification responsibilities.
Consumer groups will request that parent companies and brand owners be disclosed to aid enforcement and public accountability.
Foreign manufacturers will request clarification of the obligations for U.S. agents and whether a single U.S. agent can represent multiple foreign applicants on a single submission.
Legal commenters will request an explanation of whether failure to provide a U.S. agent for foreign applicants results in refusal to accept or grounds for an adverse order.
Industry will request examples of acceptable product identifiers when products are sold under different brand names in different markets (e.g., SKU-level guidance).
Trade groups will request that the manufacturer field allow third-party manufacturers and contract packagers to be identified separately to reflect modern supply chains.
Retailers and industry will request guidance on whether rebranding or private-labeling requires a new SE Report or can be covered by the original manufacturer’s SE order.

Industry will request precise definitions for each “product property” listed and dispute any requirement that attributes not present must be listed as “none” — arguing that exhaustive property lists may be burdensome.
Manufacturers will request that the product properties table be machine-readable and that FDA publish the table schema so applicants can prepare electronic submissions that map to FDA systems.
Public health groups will request that certain properties (e.g., characterizing flavors, ventilation) be required fields subject to specific test methods and detection limits.
Industry will request that FDA publish the mandatory form(s) referenced in §1107.18(b) well in advance of the rule’s effective date and provide a transition period for compliance.
Small entities will request that FDA provide alternative submission mechanisms (paper or assistance) during the initial rollout of the form requirement.

Industry will object to the “written in English” requirement for multinational companies and request translations be allowed with accompanying certified English translations rather than requiring original documents in English.

Civil rights and immigrant advocacy groups will request that FDA accept submissions and communications in multiple languages for non-English-speaking applicants, or at least provide translation support.
Industry will request that FDA publish the specific electronic formats and transmission standards (file types, container formats, encryption) the Agency can accept to avoid costly rework.

Small businesses will request flexibility or temporary waivers for electronic submission if they lack compatible IT systems, arguing the waiver mechanism (P34) needs clear criteria and timely processing.

Advocates for regulatory efficiency will request that the waiver process be automated and expedited, with clear standards and a presumption in favor of waivers for small entities or in cases of technical difficulty.

Industry will request that the summary requirement include a mechanism to protect CBI and trade secrets from public disclosure while still meeting transparency goals.

Manufacturers will request specification of acceptable units and test standards for describing characteristics to avoid inconsistent submissions.
Public health experts will request FDA guidance on the meaning of “different public health questions” and provide examples of differences that would and would not raise such questions.
Industry will request that the applicant’s belief statement be non-binding and not a basis for enforcement unless contradicted by FDA findings.
Consumer advocacy groups will request that similarities and differences include behavioral and appeal characteristics (e.g., youth appeal, marketing claims) that could affect public health.

Industry will request guidance on the depth of component-level disclosure required for proprietary accessory components (e.g., filters) and whether vendors’ confidentiality concerns can be accommodated with redactions.
Public health groups will argue that component functions affecting emissions or exposure (e.g., filter materials) must be fully disclosed and tested independent of vendor claims.

Manufacturers will request that the “concise overview of manufacturing process” permit reliance on high-level process descriptions for contract-manufactured products where the applicant does not control the entire process.

Environmental groups will request that manufacturing overviews include waste streams, solvent use, and emissions to assess environmental and public health impacts as part of 21 CFR part 25 compliance.

Industry will request examples of when manufacturing process changes are considered to affect product characteristics and therefore must be fully described versus when a statement that the process does not affect characteristics is acceptable.
Regulatory lawyers will request a safe-harbor checklist for asserting that manufacturing does not affect characteristics, including confirmatory testing requirements.

Industry will request clear guidance on how to document and verify that a predicate product is indeed grandfathered or previously found substantially equivalent, including what FDA records and certifications satisfy the requirement.

Public health advocates will caution that reliance on grandfathered predicates should be limited, and request that FDA require updated scientific evidence if the predicate determination is decades old or lacks modern testing.
