raw_output:
[P1] The permission in §52.38(a)(4) is vague about which specific subpart AAAAA provisions may be replaced; industry requests a definitive list to avoid regulatory uncertainty and litigation over scope.

[P1] Environmental groups will comment that allowing States to replace subpart AAAAA provisions undermines uniform federal emissions controls and may lead to a “race to the bottom” in emission reductions.

[P2] The June 1 submission deadlines in §52.38(a)(4)(i)(B)-(C) tied to “the fourth year before the year of the control period” are administratively infeasible for states that need to coordinate auctions and stakeholder allocation processes; the EPA should provide a later or flexible deadline.

[P2] Legal commenters will argue the deadlines for 2023 and 2024 allocations violate the Administrative Procedure Act if states cannot reasonably comply because the final rule’s effective date does not allow the statutorily prescribed lead time.

[P3] The permission in §52.38(a)(5) to adopt full SIP CSAPR NOX Annual Trading Programs will create inconsistency across states unless EPA requires submission of model rules or minimum standards; industry requests clear templates.

[P4] The Table 2 June 1 allocation submission requirement in §52.38(a)(5)(i)(B) imposes duplicative reporting when states also must submit auction results to regional market operators; EPA should allow submission via established market systems.

[P5] §52.38(a)(7)(i) obligates the Administrator to apply specified subpart AAAAA provisions under approved SIPs but does not clarify coordination between EPA and state allocation authorities during disputes; commenters request a dispute-resolution procedure.

[P6] Requiring the Administrator to apply the definitions in §97.402 (§52.38(a)(7)(i)(A)) may conflict with state statutory definitions; states ask for explicit preemption language or a process to reconcile conflicting definitions.

[P7] The obligation to apply §97.410(a) new unit set-asides (§52.38(a)(7)(i)(B)) could reduce available allowances for existing units; utilities request clarification of calculation methods and treatment of repowered units.

[P8] The cross-application of §§97.411 and 97.412 allocation and recordation procedures (§52.38(a)(7)(i)(C)-(F)) may inadvertently subject states to federal deadlines that conflict with state procurement and auction timelines; states request grandfathering of existing timelines.

[P9] §52.38(a)(7)(ii) preserves completion of allocation recording once begun by the Administrator, but does not protect against retroactive SIP changes; commenters worry this could lock in erroneous allocations and ask for correction mechanisms.

[P10] Making subpart EEEEE apply to listed states for emissions in 2017 and subsequent years (§52.38(b)(2)(iii)) raises retroactivity concerns because affected sources could be penalized for past conduct; regulated entities request safe-harbor for years prior to final approval.

[P11] The limited application of subpart EEEEE to 2017–2020 only for certain states (§52.38(b)(2)(iv)) creates compliance complexity for multistate generators that changed operations in 2021; owners request clear transition guidance and nonduplication of obligations.

[P12] Applying subpart GGGGG beginning in 2021 (§52.38(b)(2)(v)) without providing states or sources adequate notice of differing program mechanics will increase administrative burden; commenters ask for a detailed implementation schedule.

[P13] The permission in §52.38(b)(4) for abbreviated SIPs replacing subpart BBBBB is too permissive; environmental groups demand EPA specify minimum emission reduction outcomes that must be retained.

[P14] Table 3 deadlines in §52.38(b)(4)(ii)(B) for Group 1 allowance submissions (June 1) conflict with state budget cycles and auction processes; states urge EPA to allow up to a 90‑day extension upon showing of good cause.

[P15] §52.38(b)(6)(ii) makes approved SIPs immediately applicable to sources for designated control periods but lacks clarity about retroactive enforcement for emissions that occurred before EPA’s approval date; industry asks for non‑retroactivity language.

[P16] The permission at §52.38(b)(8) to replace subpart EEEEE provisions risks the loss of uniform monitoring and reporting standards; monitoring NGOs request that EPA require any state replacement to be at least as stringent and technically equivalent.

[P17] Allowing states to expand applicability beyond §97.804(a) and (b) (§52.38(b)(8)(ii)) could subject small cogeneration units to onerous obligations; small utilities and hospitals request a hardship exemption or tiered compliance schedule.

[P18] The Table 5 deadlines in §52.38(b)(8)(iii)(B) for Group 2 submissions (June 1) do not accommodate states that rely on auctions whose settlement occurs after June 1; auction administrators request an accommodation that accepts certified auction results submitted within a set post‑settlement window.

[P19] The permission at §52.38(b)(9) to adopt full Group 2 SIPs without specifying required provisions may lead to divergent allowance accounting rules; market participants request uniform accounting rules and EPA-issued model allocation methodologies.

[P20] Expanding applicability identical to §97.804(a)/(b) plus additional units (§52.38(b)(9)(ii)) could create double-counting risks if units participate in both state and federal programs; market auditors request mandatory reconciliations and anti‑double-counting provisions.

[P21] The corrective SIP revision permission for Group 3 in §52.38(b)(10) lacks clarity on what constitutes a “corrective” revision; states request examples and criteria for corrective actions to avoid arbitrary denials.

[P22] The requirement that any Group 3 SIP revision comply with paragraphs (b)(13)(i)-(viii) (§52.38(b)(10)(i)) imposes complex substantive constraints but the rule does not provide implementation guidance; legal counsel requests an explanatory preamble or guidance document.

[P23] §52.38(b)(10)(ii) applies approved Group 3 SIPs to subsequent control periods but does not address how changes in unit operations (mothballing, retirements, new builds) affect allocations; utilities request an amendment process for changed circumstances.

[P24] The §52.38(b)(11) permission letting states replace §97.1011(a) for 2022 by submitting a unit list and allocations is arbitrary because it limits this pathway to a single year; states seek the ability to use the mechanism for later years.

[P25] The requirement that units listed in §52.38(b)(11)(i) must have commenced commercial operation before Jan 1, 2019 excludes units that began operation in 2019 but were constructed under long lead times; plant owners request grandfathering for projects permitted before 2019.

[P26] The prohibition in §52.38(b)(11)(ii) capping total allocations to a specified portion of the Group 3 budget for 2022 lacks transparency on how the “specified portion” is calculated; states and utilities request publication of the precise numerical cap and methodology.

[P27] Requiring electronic submission in a format specified by the Administrator (§52.38(b)(11)(iii)) is reasonable, but EPA must publish the format specifications and provide test files and a helpdesk; small states and tribes request technical assistance.

[P28] The prohibition in §52.38(b)(11)(iv) forbidding any changes to units or allocations after approval removes flexibility to correct legitimate errors or respond to unforeseen retirements; states request an exception allowing limited post‑approval amendments with EPA concurrence.

[P29] The 60‑day “intent to submit” electronic notification deadline in §52.38(b)(11)(v)(A) is unreasonable for states that must secure legislative or regulatory approvals; states ask EPA to allow up to 120 days or to tie the date to the final rule’s effective date.

[P30] The 180‑day SIP submittal deadline in §52.38(b)(11)(v)(B) may be impossible for states that must conduct public hearings or allocate auctions; commenters request extension authority for demonstrated procedural requirements.

[P31] The permission in §52.38(b)(12) to adopt abbreviated SIP revisions replacing subpart GGGGG must require equivalent or better monitoring standards; environmental NGOs insist on nondiscretionary equivalency criteria.

[P32] Allowing a state to set a uniform lower MW applicability limit between 15–25 MWe (§52.38(b)(12)(i)) could be abused to raise the threshold to 25 MWe and exempt many smaller but significant emitters; public health groups request that states justify any threshold at or above 15 MWe with supporting emissions data.

[P33] The permission to expand applicability beyond §97.1004(a)/(b) (§52.38(b)(12)(ii)) may unintentionally bring in units subject to local efficiency constraints; regulated small-unit operators ask for clarity on how emissions baselines for newly included units will be established.

[P34] The allocation cap and auctioning limit in §52.38(b)(12)(iii)(A) that restricts total Group 3 allowances may force higher allowance prices and grid reliability impacts; utilities request a reliability impact assessment before EPA finalizes the limits.

[P35] The condition in §52.38(b)(12)(iii)(A)(1) limiting additional allowances to the highest seasonal NOX sums for added units excludes days with missing QA monitoring; commenters representing operators with sporadic monitoring gaps request an alternative method that prorates based on available data rather than excluding days.

[P36] The alternative cap method in §52.38(b)(12)(iii)(A)(2) using a portion of the State emissions budget could be manipulated if a state’s budget includes non‑comparable sources; environmental economists request standardized allocation formulas to prevent gaming.

[P37] The Table 7 submission deadlines (§52.38(b)(12)(iii)(B)) are not synchronized with other EPA deadlines (Tables 8 and earlier tables); affected parties ask EPA to harmonize all table deadlines across the rule to reduce compliance costs.

[P38] Requiring April 1 submissions after the control period for certain units (§52.38(b)(12)(iii)(C)) may conflict with internal financial reporting of utilities; utilities request an option to submit preliminary allocations by April 1 and final reconciled results by June 1.

[P39] The prohibition in §52.38(b)(12)(iii)(D) barring post‑submission changes to allocations removes necessary correction pathways for clerical or technical errors; legal experts request a narrowly defined correction window of at least 30 days after EPA’s recording.

[P40] The December 1 deadline in §52.38(b)(12)(iv) to submit a complete SIP revision for the first intended control period is inconsistent with state legislative calendars; states request a flexibility clause allowing submission as soon thereafter as the state regulatory process permits.

[P41] Allowing full Group 3 SIP adoption as corrective revisions (§52.38(b)(13)) without defining “correcting the determination of substituting” opens the door to broad reinterpretations; environmental plaintiffs warn this could be used to undo needed federal safeguards.

[P42] The permission under §52.38(b)(13)(i) to lower the applicability threshold to a uniform 15–25 MWe is ambiguous on whether states may choose any number in that range per unit type; commenters request that any chosen threshold be applied uniformly across all units in the state and documented in the SIP.

[P43] Expanding applicability identical to §97.1004(a)/(b) plus additional units (§52.38(b)(13)(ii)) again risks double-regulation or double-counting across trading groups; market participants ask for explicit anti‑double-counting rules and cross-program reconciliations.

[P44] The allocation methodology constraints in §52.38(b)(13)(iii)(A) that cap total allocations for 2023 and later could create stranded asset risk for generators that invested under previous allocation expectations; generator owners request transition allowances or phase-in.

[P45] The Table 8 deadlines in §52.38(b)(13)(iii)(B) for submission of allocations/auction results replicate timing concerns raised for other tables and should be harmonized and made flexible in case of auction delays.

[P46] The April 1 post-control-period submission requirement in §52.38(b)(13)(iii)(C) is too soon to reconcile continuous emissions monitoring system (CEMS) data for certain units; monitoring vendors recommend EPA allow submissions up to June 30 to ensure accurate data.

[P47] The prohibition in §52.38(b)(13)(iii)(D) forbidding changes to allocations after submission again removes error-correction capacity; accounting firms request at least a 60‑day amendment window to fix inadvertent allocation errors.

[P48] The combined cumulative effect of many near‑simultaneous deadlines across Tables 1, 2, 5, 7, and 8 will impose significant administrative and IT burdens on small states and tribes; EPA should offer centralized technical assistance and permit consolidated submissions.

[P49] Tribes are not explicitly referenced in many permissions and obligations; tribal governments will request explicit inclusion and tailored timelines/assistance for tribal authorities administering SIP-equivalent programs.

[P50] The rule relies heavily on electronic submissions in formats specified by the Administrator (§52.38(b)(11)(iii)), but lacks a transition plan for secure data transfer and privacy protections; commenters request detailed IT security standards and a testing period.

[P51] Several provisions lock in allocations and prohibit post-approval changes (§§52.38(b)(11)(iv), (b)(12)(iii)(D), (b)(13)(iii)(D)), which could contravene due process if stakeholders are improperly excluded; public interest groups request an administrative appeal mechanism.

[P52] The rule does not state how overlapping state SIP revisions will be reconciled when multiple states claim authority over the same multi-jurisdictional unit; regional grid operators and multi-state utilities request conflict-resolution language.

[P53] Legal commenters will request clarification whether EPA’s approval of state replacements or abbreviated SIPs constitutes a delegation of federal authority, and whether such delegations are revocable and subject to uniform federal oversight.

[P54] The permitting authorities are required to allocate or auction allowances under many provisions but the rule is silent on revenue treatment and transparency; civil society organizations request mandatory reporting of auction revenues and their use.

[P55] Any state option that expands applicability (multiple provisions) should require a cost-benefit analysis demonstrating that expanded coverage is necessary and will not negatively affect reliability or low-income communities; equity advocates will request an EJ (environmental justice) analysis requirement.

[P56] The rule lacks a clear enforcement framework for when states fail to submit allocations or auctions by the specified deadlines; regulated entities and states request a graduated set of remedies and clear timelines for EPA intervention.

[P57] Market operators request that EPA specify the validation and certification requirements for auction results submitted to meet the various table deadlines, including third‑party audit standards.

[P58] The frequent requirement that allocations may not exceed portions of trading budgets (multiple provisions) requires EPA to publish the computation templates and underlying emissions baselines; otherwise comments will challenge the opacity of budget calculations.

[P59] The rule does not clarify treatment of banked allowances or previously recorded trading balances when a state replaces federal provisions; generators request explicit transition rules to preserve or account for banked allowances fairly.

[P60] Because the rule contemplates several different control-period years and staggered applicability, grid reliability planners request that EPA require states to coordinate with regional transmission organizations (RTOs) to assess reliability impacts before approving SIP revisions that alter unit economics.

[P1] The requirement to "provide software performance and functional requirements and detailed design specifications" is overly broad and could force disclosure of proprietary algorithms and trade secrets without clear limits or confidentiality protections.

[P1] The rule should clarify the format, level of detail, and security classification for the required "detailed design specifications" to avoid inconsistent submissions and undue burden on manufacturers.

[P1] The regulation does not specify whether third-party contractors or subcontractors may submit the software design documentation on behalf of the device sponsor, creating ambiguity in contractual responsibility.

[P1] Request that the agency allow redaction or secure submission mechanisms for commercially sensitive material (e.g., proprietary control characteristics and algorithm details) rather than full public disclosure.

[P2] The obligation to "perform verification and validation testing and hazard analysis" lacks specificity about the standards to be used (e.g., IEC 62304, ISO 14971) — commenters ask that the rule reference recognized consensus standards to ensure consistency.

[P2] Small manufacturers and startups will be disproportionately burdened by V&V and hazard analysis requirements; request phased compliance timelines or scaled requirements based on device risk class.

[P2] The regulation should require documentation of test protocols, acceptance criteria, and traceability of test cases to requirements, not just a statement that testing was performed.

[P3] The labeling obligation is vague about the required format and whether labeling applies to packaging, user manuals, electronic labeling, or in-device displays; request explicit definitions.

[P3] The rule should define the acceptable language(s) for labeling and whether multiple languages are required for devices marketed in multilingual jurisdictions.

[P4] Requiring "software limitations" in labeling without defining "limitations" risks over-disclosure and liability exposure; propose a clear definition tied to safety-critical limitations only.

[P4] Patient advocacy groups will support explicit disclosure of limitations that affect safety or appropriate use, but manufacturers need guidance on the level of technical detail required so as not to mislead or confuse end users.

[P5] Mandating that labeling state "unresolved anomalies" and explain their safety/effectiveness impact could force disclosure of known but minor bugs that do not affect clinical performance; request a threshold for what qualifies as an unresolved anomaly that must be disclosed.

[P5] Legal experts will note that requiring disclosure of unresolved anomalies could create additional product liability exposure; ask the agency to provide safe-harbor language that limits liability where anomalies are documented and mitigated.

[P6] Requiring "revision history" in labeling is reasonable, but the rule should clarify whether this must include internal iterative builds or only public releases and major versions.

[P6] Device manufacturers need guidance on the retention period and format for revision histories — request that the agency specify a standard change-log format and minimum retention timeframe.

[P7] Including "hardware and peripheral specifications" in labeling could be excessive for modular systems with many optional peripherals; request that labeling require specifications only for hardware/peripherals necessary for safe operation.

[P7] The rule should clarify whether interoperability specifications (e.g., supported OS versions, network stacks) must be included in labeling or may be provided via a technical supplement.

[P8] The traceability matrix obligation must clarify the required elements (e.g., linkage between requirements, design, implementation, verification tests, and risk controls) and whether a specific tool or format is mandated.

[P8] Commenters request an exception or scaled requirement for legacy devices where creating a full traceability matrix would require disproportionate effort, proposing an alternative retrospective analysis approach.

[P9] The performance testing obligation should explicitly reference accepted test methods and pass/fail criteria to avoid inconsistent interpretations across manufacturers and reviewers.

[P9] The requirement to retest "when adding new functional requirements" is ambiguous about minor firmware updates or security patches; request a de minimis threshold for when retesting is required.

[P10] The examples (electrical safety, EMC, wireless coexistence) imply a broad retesting obligation that could require full formal lab testing for minor software changes; industry requests clear criteria for when such physical re-testing is actually necessary.

[P10] Wireless device makers request guidance on whether virtual or simulation-based coexistence testing is acceptable for software updates that alter wireless behavior, to reduce cost and time-to-market.

[P11] The prohibition barring all non-participating persons and vessels from entering the race area is unreasonably broad and may impede emergency responders, commercial traffic, and residents; request explicit exemptions for emergency services and pre-authorized commercial transit.

[P11] Local businesses and mariners will object that the prohibition lacks adequate public notice and navigation hazard mitigation plans, and ask for defined notification timelines and AIS/NOTAM procedures.

[P11] Legal commenters ask the agency to clarify enforcement mechanisms and the penalty structure for violations; the rule currently lacks due process detail for vessel operators cited for entering the race area.

[P12] The buffer zone prohibition that excludes all persons and vessels except enforcers unless authorized by the Captain of the Port will create operational burdens for routine harbor users; propose creating pre-authorized lanes or scheduled windows for transit.

[P12] Recreational boaters and charter operators request that the rule include an online or published map with coordinates and temporal schedules so mariners can plan routes instead of relying solely on ad hoc authorization.

[P13] The permission allowing the Captain of the Port to authorize entry should include objective criteria and timeframes for processing authorization requests to avoid arbitrary denials and delays.

[P13] Civil liberties groups will ask for a written appeals or review process when the Captain of the Port denies authorization, to protect against undue restriction of movement.

[P14] Allowing authorization requests by phone or VHF radio may be inadequate for modern operations; request that electronic authorization methods (email, web portal, VHF digital) be added and that receipt confirmations be mandatory.

[P14] The rule should require the Captain of the Port to publish expected response times and contact frequencies/channels so vessels know how far in advance to request authorization.

[P15] The obligation that authorized persons "comply with instructions" of the Captain of the Port is necessary, but the rule should define the scope and limits of such instructions to avoid overreach (e.g., orders that could create unsafe navigation conditions).

[P15] There should be safeguards against conflicting instructions from multiple authorities (e.g., race marshals vs Captain of the Port), and the rule should specify hierarchy of commands and communication protocols to reduce confusion.

[P2] Patient safety advocates request that V&V and hazard analysis reports be retained and made available to regulators for a defined period to enable post-market surveillance and incident investigation.

[P1] Cybersecurity stakeholders ask the agency to explicitly require documentation of cybersecurity-related software requirements and threat models in the software performance and design specification deliverables.

[P9] Emergency medicine providers request that performance testing include usability/human factors testing under realistic stress conditions, and that those test results be included in regulatory submissions or labeling.

[P8] Independent auditors ask for clarity about whether the traceability matrix must be independently audited or if manufacturer self-attestation is acceptable, and under what circumstances third-party verification would be required.

[P5] Patient groups request that unresolved anomalies materially affecting safety must be communicated to clinicians and users via urgent notifications, not only included in labeling, and that the regulation mandate timelines for such communications.

[P7] Hospitals and health systems request that hardware and peripheral specifications include maintenance and calibration intervals, so purchasers can adequately plan lifecycle costs.

[P4] Software developers ask the agency to allow high-level descriptions of algorithm behavior (e.g., intended clinical function and boundary conditions) instead of requiring source-level algorithm disclosure.

[P1] Requiring small refineries meeting § 80.1441(e)(2)(iii) to submit 2019 reports by Nov 30, 2021 conflicts with earlier EPA guidance and creates legal exposure for parties who reasonably relied on different timelines; EPA should clarify that no enforcement penalties will be assessed if reports are submitted within a reasonable cure period.

[P1] The provision does not specify the acceptable format or electronic submission method for 2019 reports due Nov 30, 2021; EPA should mandate an electronic upload portal and provide data schema to ensure consistent reporting and reduce administrative burden.

[P1] EPA should allow certified extensions or waivers for the Nov 30, 2021 deadline for small refineries demonstrating good cause (e.g., pandemic-related staffing shortages), otherwise the deadline penalizes vulnerable operators.

[P2] The January 31, 2022 deadline for 2020 annual compliance reports is too soon given widespread COVID-19 disruptions and supply-chain issues that delayed record-keeping; EPA should extend the deadline by at least 90 days.

[P2] The rule fails to define whether the Jan 31, 2022 deadline requires consolidated national-level reports or allows separate facility-level submissions; EPA should clarify to avoid inconsistent filings.

[P2] Industry requests that EPA permit submission of draft reports by Jan 31, 2022 with final reports accepted after comment resolution, since compiling complete 2020 data across affiliates will require additional time.

[P3] The June 1, 2022 deadline for 2019 reports under § 80.1464 is inconsistent with P1’s Nov 30, 2021 deadline for related compliance reports, creating confusion about which reports govern; EPA should harmonize deadlines or explain differences in scope.

[P5] Trade associations request that EPA confirm whether the June 1, 2022 RIN reporting requirement applies to retired or invalidated RINs, and if so, require inclusion of status codes to prevent miscounting.

[P1] Small refinery advocates ask for a safe harbor for reports filed by Nov 30, 2021 for 2019 if they include a statement of good-faith efforts and propose a remediation plan for any data gaps.

[P1] The rule’s blanket application of “all prohibitions and provisions” of §§ 17.31 and 17.32 to activities affecting the Louisiana pinesnake (except as noted) creates uncertainty because it does not identify which specific provisions are most relevant to typical forestry operations; we request the agency list or summarize the particular prohibitions that will apply in practice.

[P1] Legal experts will comment that incorporating §§ 17.31 and 17.32 wholesale into § 17.42(i)(2) may import provisions intended for other taxa and contexts, producing regulatory overreach and potential conflicts with existing state forestry statutes; the agency should reconcile or cross-reference specific provisions.

[P2] Conservation NGOs will object that the proposed incidental-take exemption for listed activities (P2) is overly broad and could undermine section 9 protections by effectively authorizing widespread harm absent an HCP or permit; they will request clear limits, monitoring, and mandatory reporting of all incidental take.

[P2] Industry commenters (timber, pipeline, utilities) will support the incidental-take exemption as necessary for routine operations but will ask for a streamlined, written confirmation process (e.g., a self-certification or agency acknowledgement) to avoid enforcement uncertainty when their activities fall under the exemption.

[P3] Forestry associations will argue that allowing clearcutting and replanting as exempt outside known EOHAs (P3) is essential for practical forest management and economic viability; they will request explicit definitions of “open canopy” and “maintain forest land use” to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P3] Environmental groups will challenge the inclusion of clearcutting in the exemption (P3), asserting that clearcutting has high potential to destroy habitat and should not be treated as automatically incidental-take exempt, even outside known EOHAs; they will request a prohibition on clearcutting within a specified buffer distance of EOHAs.

[P3] State forestry agencies will request explicit criteria and mapping standards for determining “outside known EOHAs” (P3), including use of the most recent range and habitat data and a clear process for updating EOHA designations to prevent accidental take.

[P4] Fire management agencies and prescribed-burn practitioners will support the exemption for prescribed burning outside known EOHAs (P4) but will request clarity that emergency wildfire suppression actions (already mentioned) are covered and that restrictions about firebreak construction (see P8) do not impede safe fire management.

[P4] Wildlife conservation commenters will urge that prescribed burns be subject to timing restrictions (e.g., avoid breeding season, hibernation) or pre-burn surveys in adjacent EOHAs because smoke, heat, and post-burn changes can affect snakes beyond the immediate burn footprint (P4).

[P5] Invasive species control advocates will support herbicide exemptions (P5) but ask for a precise definition of “minimal long-term impact” and “site preparation,” and for required use of least-toxic products and integrated vegetation management approaches to reduce non-target harm.

[P5] Pesticide safety and public health groups will insist that exempt herbicide applications (P5) must include buffer requirements near water bodies, residential areas, and sensitive species habitat; they will also request mandatory recordkeeping and public disclosure of products used and application rates.

[P6] Agricultural and chemical manufacturers will point out that requiring compliance with federal/state laws, EPA label restrictions, and manufacturer guidelines (P6) is redundant and unclear about enforcement responsibility—requesting that the rule specify whether deviations render an activity non-exempt and what penalties apply.

[P6] Environmental law groups will argue that mere adherence to label directions (P6) does not ensure protection of the Louisiana pinesnake and that the rule should require additional mitigation measures or case-by-case assessments where herbicide use overlaps with potential habitat.

[P7] Landowners with properties inside EOHAs will seek clarification about which “suitable or preferable soils” qualify (P7) and request that the agency publish soil maps and objective soil criteria so landowners can determine whether their lands are subject to the conditional exemptions.

raw_output:
[P1] The blanket presumption that all unsurveyed areas within 2 km of a known Fender’s blue population are “occupied” (§ 17.47(f)(1)(i)) is overly broad and will improperly restrict routine land management on large private properties where occupancy probability is negligible.

[P1] Assuming occupancy without requiring any minimum survey effort or protocol will create legal uncertainty for landowners who cannot afford professional surveys, effectively shifting the burden to landowners to prove absence.

[P1] The 2 km buffer distance is arbitrary and lacks citation to species-specific dispersal data; the rule should instead use scientifically justified dispersal thresholds or require evidence-based site assessment.

[P1] The presumption of occupancy for unsurveyed areas within 2 km will deter conservation-friendly activities (e.g., prescribed fire, invasive removal) because landowners will fear incidental take liability even when butterflies are absent.

[P2] Requiring a valid section 10(a)(1)(A) permit for any capture for identification (§ 17.47(f)(1)(ii)) is impractical for field technicians and citizen scientists conducting rapid visual inspections where brief netting is the only way to confirm identity.

[P2] The permitting requirement for capture will create significant administrative delays and costs for researchers and conservation practitioners, hampering time-sensitive surveys during flight windows.

[P2] The rule lacks a clear expedited or emergency permitting pathway for capture needed to confirm identification during short flight periods (§ 17.47(f)(1)(ii)).

[P3] The general prohibition provision (§ 17.47(f)(2)) is vague where it references other paragraphs and sections; commenters may be unable to determine which routine activities are lawful without cross-referencing multiple regulations.

[P4] The import/export prohibition (§ 17.47(f)(2)(i)) is appropriate but should explicitly carve out permitted scientific exchanges under existing § 17.32 permits to avoid chilling specimen sharing for research.

[P5] The take prohibition (§ 17.47(f)(2)(ii)) must clarify whether unintentional, incidental take during lawful activities is governed solely by the incidental take exceptions in (f)(3)(v) or also requires separate authorization.

[P6] The possession prohibition (§ 17.47(f)(2)(iii)) could criminalize common museum and research holdings unless expressly exempted; the text needs cross-reference to the possession exceptions in § 17.21(d)(2) and § 17.47(f)(3)(ii).

[P7] The interstate/commerce prohibition (§ 17.47(f)(2)(iv)) may unintentionally restrict noncommercial transfers of educational materials and images if not explicitly limited to commercial transactions; clarify that noncommercial exchanges are not targeted.

[P8] The sale prohibition (§ 17.47(f)(2)(v)) is necessary, but enforcement guidance is needed to distinguish prohibited commercial sales from permitted conservation breeding or restoration transfers under permit.

[P9] The list of exceptions in § 17.47(f)(3) is helpful, but the regulatory cross-references (e.g., § 17.32, § 17.21) make compliance difficult without a consolidated summary of permitted activities specific to Fender’s blue.

[P10] Allowing activities authorized by § 17.32 permits (§ 17.47(f)(3)(i)) is sensible, but the rule should require timely processing and provide guidance on when such permits are appropriate for restoration versus research.

[P11] The permission to possess unlawfully taken specimens under § 17.21(d)(2) (§ 17.47(f)(3)(ii)) is confusing; commenters request clarification when such possession is lawful and whether it applies retroactively to existing collections.

[P12] The references to take categories in § 17.21(c)(2)–(4) (§ 17.47(f)(3)(iii)) should be summarized within this species rule to avoid misinterpretation about allowable scientific or conservation-related takes.

[P13] The allowance of takes under § 17.31(b) (§ 17.47(f)(3)(iv)) should specify whether incidental take statements and safe harbor agreements under § 17.31 apply to small private landowners and under what conditions.

[P14] The incidental take permission for certain vegetation management methods (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)) is useful, but the rule's limitations (timing, buffers, consultation) are unevenly applied across methods and need harmonization to reduce confusion.

[P15] Allowing manual/mechanical invasive plant control outside the flight period if it avoids ground disturbance (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(A)) is reasonable, but the rule does not define “ground disturbance,” leaving enforcement discretion undefined.

[P16] Requiring landowners to “procure a qualified biologist” and implement a monitoring plan (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(A)(1)) may be financially burdensome for small landowners; the rule should allow alternative evidence-based protocols or agency-provided support.

[P17] The “best efforts” to avoid trampling and minimizing foot traffic near lupine (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(A)(2)) is vague and unenforceable; commenters request objective standards (e.g., maximum number of people, delineated paths) instead of subjective phrasing.

[P18] Tractor mowing allowed before Feb 15 and after Aug 15 in occupied habitat (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(B)) conflicts with local agricultural schedules and could be impractical for contractors; flexibility tied to phenology rather than fixed dates should be offered.

[P19] Allowing handheld mowers year-round (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(B)(1)) is helpful, but the required 8-meter buffer during flight season (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(B)(1) obligation) may be technically infeasible for many small parcels and needs exception criteria or adaptive buffer widths based on site conditions.

[P20] The mandated 8-meter (25-ft) buffer between handheld mowers and any lupine during flight season (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(B)(1) obligation) lacks basis and could prevent effective vegetation management in dense lupine stands; propose alternative protection measures (e.g., marked no-mow zones).

[P21] The “reasonable care” during mowing (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(B)(2)) that requires procuring and implementing technical assistance is ambiguous — commenters request definition of “technical assistance” and whether a single site visit satisfies this requirement.

[P22] Herbicide methods allowed (hand wiping, wicking, spot-spray) (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(C)) are appropriate, but requiring prior contact with the Oregon Fish and Wildlife Office (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(C) obligation) for acceptable chemicals/practices may delay time-sensitive invasive control and lacks a defined response timeframe.

[P23] The prior contact requirement with the Oregon Fish and Wildlife Office before herbicide use (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(C) obligation) should allow for electronic submission and an automatic provisional approval after a short period to avoid management delays.

[P24] The obligation to avoid broadcast spraying where drift into occupied habitat is possible (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(C)(1)) is reasonable but needs quantitative thresholds (e.g., wind speed limits, buffer distances) to guide applicators and enforcement.

[P25] The “best efforts” requirement to avoid trampling during herbicide application (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(C)(2)) is subjective; commenters request concrete measures such as designated access routes and signage requirements.

[P26] Allowing limited hand-based ground disturbance for planting native vegetation (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(D)) is positive, but the rule should define “limited” (maximum hole depth, area per acre, number of workers) to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P27] Requiring consultation with a qualified biologist during planting activities (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(D)(2)) again imposes cost burdens; the rule should permit use of standardized planting protocols or local extension service guidance as alternatives.

[P28] The footnote obligation to be aware of additional timing restrictions based on chemicals and to contact the Oregon FWO (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(E) footnote) places too much onus on landowners without providing an accessible centralized, regularly updated list.

[P29] The 5-calendar-day reporting requirement for injury or mortality (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(F) obligation) is unduly strict for rural landowners with limited internet/phone access; commenters request extension to 10 business days or allowance for emailed/temp storage until offices reopen.

[P30] The reporting requirement to the Service’s Office of Law Enforcement and the Oregon Fish and Wildlife Office and State Parks (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(F) obligation) duplicates notifications and could create confusion about which agency leads response; designate a single point-of-contact.

[P31] The disposal of specimens “only in accordance with directions from the Service” (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(F) condition) may prevent landowners from complying with biohazard or state wildlife disposal laws; request clarification and coordination with state agencies.

[P32] The rule’s allowance that the Service may permit additional reporting time if offices are closed (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(F) permission) is helpful but needs an explicit procedure for requesting extensions and a default deadline if no response is received.

[P33] Legal commenters will note that several obligations (e.g., “reasonable care,” “best efforts,” “qualified biologist”) create vague standards that could be challenged as arbitrary and capricious without definitional guidance or objective criteria.

[P34] Conservation NGOs support the incidental take allowances for targeted management techniques (manual removal, spot herbicide, hand planting) but request that the rule include mandatory best management practice (BMP) templates and training resources to ensure consistent application.

[P35] Private landowner groups will likely request a hardship exemption or cost-share program to help meet the consulting, monitoring, and reporting requirements (qualified biologist, monitoring plans, contacts with Oregon FWO) tied to permitted activities.

[P36] Agricultural stakeholders note that fixed seasonal dates for allowed tractor mowing (before Feb 15 and after Aug 15) may not align with local climate and butterfly phenology under climate change, and request adaptive management tied to biological indicators rather than calendar dates.

[P37] Permitting authorities should clarify whether volunteers and contractors working under landowner direction must individually meet the permit/qualification requirements (e.g., § 17.47(f)(1)(ii) permit to capture or “qualified biologist” consultation), as liability concerns will deter volunteer conservation work.

[P38] The rule should explicitly state whether compliance with state pesticide regulations and label instructions alone satisfies the “reasonable care” and “comply with applicable laws/guidelines” obligations during herbicide use (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(C)(1)).

[P39] Researchers request clarity on whether incidental mortalities discovered during permitted research must be reported within 5 days even if related to permitted takes under § 17.32 or § 10(a)(1)(A) permits, to avoid conflicting reporting obligations.

[P40] The rule should provide a clear map or GIS layer of known occupied areas and a searchable database to help landowners determine whether they fall within the 2 km presumption zone (§ 17.47(f)(1)(i)) to reduce inadvertent noncompliance.

[P41] Enforcement agencies should issue clear guidance on documentation required to demonstrate the “use of reasonable care” and “best efforts” (e.g., photographs, signed biologist reports) to prevent arbitrary enforcement actions.

[P42] The Service should quantify penalties or provide safe harbor for good-faith compliance with the specified BMPs (e.g., following the specified mowing windows, buffers, and herbicide contacts) to encourage proactive stewardship rather than defensive secrecy.

[P43] The rule should require the Service to publish the current list of “acceptable herbicides, application methods, timing, and BMPs” online and update it annually rather than requiring individual pre-contact for each project (§ 17.47(f)(3)(v)(C) obligation).

[P44] Tribal governments will seek explicit consultation and recognition of tribal land management needs and request that tribal practices be allowed exceptions or collaborative protocols where traditional management conflicts with some timing/buffer restrictions.

[P45] The definition of “qualified biologist” is absent; commenters request an explicit definition (education, experience, certifications) and whether state agency personnel qualify to reduce confusion and costs.

[P1] The prohibition in § 905.306(a) is overbroad because it bars any shipment from the production area to points outside it in the contiguous U.S. and DC unless fruit meets the Table I specs, which will prevent small-volume growers and direct-to-consumer sellers from selling marginal-grade fruit even when there is demand.

[P1] Industry commenters will argue the rule fails to define "production area" precisely, creating uncertainty about which shipments are covered by the § 905.306(a) prohibition and risking enforcement of shipments that should be exempt.

[P2] Requiring oranges to meet U.S. No. 2 and a minimum diameter of 2–4/16 inches (Table I) is too restrictive for specialty markets and processing customers who accept smaller or No. 3 fruit, harming market access and reducing returns to growers.

[P2] Growers will object that the 2–4/16 inch diameter threshold is impractical because packhouse sizing tolerances and natural fruit variation mean a significant percentage of mature, marketable oranges will fall marginally below the specified dimension and be rendered unsalable.

[P3] The requirement that seedless grapefruit meet U.S. No. 1 and a 3-inch diameter minimum is likely infeasible for some seedless cultivars that are commercially acceptable but typically smaller, effectively banning their interstate movement from the production area.

[P3] Researchers and citrus breeders will comment that the U.S. No. 1 grade requirement for seedless grapefruit does not account for varietal differences in peel or shape that affect grade determinations, causing inconsistent application and unfair rejections.

[P4] Mandating U.S. No. 2 grade and 2–6/16 inches for Fallglo tangerines will disproportionately impact small packers and niche processors that rely on smaller-sized fruit and may reduce cultivar diversity available to consumers.

[P5] The Honey tangerine minimums (U.S. No. 2; 2–6/16 inches) conflict with industry packing practices where tolerance bands and merchantable standards differ; commenters will ask for alignment with current commercial packing sizes or an alternative allowance for designated markets.

[P6] Sunburst tangerine size and grade requirements (U.S. No. 2; 2–6/16 inches) fail to account for seasonal and regional variation in fruit size; handlers may face waste and economic loss in years with smaller fruit sets.

[P7] Requiring tangelos to meet U.S. No. 1 and 2–8/16 inches will reduce availability for processors and increase grower disposal costs; commenters will request an exception for fruit destined for processing or juice.

[P8] The blanket exception for Ambersweet and Temple in § 905.306(a) is unexplained; industry will request the rationale and supporting data, and consumer advocates will ask why other cultivars are not similarly exempted.

[P8] Legal commenters will argue that carving out Ambersweet and Temple without objective criteria creates arbitrary classification risks and potential equal protection issues among growers of different cultivars.

[P9] Requiring all grapefruit shipped under § 905.306(a) to meet unspecified "minimum maturity requirements" in paragraph (e) is vague and invites inconsistent enforcement unless paragraph (e) is explicitly cross-referenced and clarified in the preamble.

[P9] Harvesting and testing for maturity (Brix, acid ratios, etc.) imposes additional costs and delays that small handlers cannot readily absorb; commenters will ask for clear, practicable maturity tests, sampling protocols, and cost allocation.

[P10] The prohibition in § 905.306(b) on shipments to destinations outside the contiguous U.S. and DC unless Table II standards are met will impede exports to U.S. territories (Puerto Rico, Guam) and create distribution disruptions because the rule treats those destinations differently without explaining plant health or market reasons.

[P10] Exporters will request clarification whether shipments to U.S. territories and insular areas are treated as "outside the 48 contiguous States and DC" and seek either harmonization of standards or explicit exemptions to avoid trade interruptions.

[P11] The Table II requirement that oranges shipped outside the contiguous U.S. meet U.S. No. 2 and 2–4/16 inches duplicates domestic standards but fails to consider importing country tolerances or port inspection practices; exporters need consistency with federal export certification to foreign markets.

[P12] Applying the same seedless grapefruit standard (U.S. No. 1, 3-inch minimum) for exports (Table II) could bar shipments to markets that accept smaller or lower-grade fruit, reducing competitiveness; exporters request flexibility to ship to designated foreign buyers with alternative standards.

[P13] The fallglo tangerine Table II minimums (U.S. No. 2; 2–6/16 inches) do not account for phytosanitary treatments or container-level segregation that could permit shipment of smaller fruit without plant health risk; commenters propose an alternative compliance pathway.

[P14] The honey tangerine export size/grade requirements (Table II) will raise packing costs and increase sorting labor for exporters, who ask for either adjustable tolerances or recognition of commercial grade tolerances for specific destination markets.

[P15] Sunburst tangerine export requirements (Table II) replicate domestic constraints and fail to provide an exceptions process for small consignments, specialty markets, or intercompany transfers; commenters will ask for a de minimis or sampling exception.

[P16] The Table II tangelo requirement (U.S. No. 1; 2–8/16 inches) may be infeasible for some export supply chains that mix varieties; exporters ask for labeling and segregation options rather than an outright shipping prohibition.

[P17] The identical exception for Ambersweet and Temple in § 905.306(b) raises trade concerns: allowing these varieties to bypass export standards could create competitive imbalances and circumvention opportunities that require justification and safeguards.

[P18] The requirement in § 905.306(b) that all grapefruit meet maturity requirements in paragraph (e) for export duplicates domestic testing and will require additional inspection/certification at packers’ expense; industry requests a streamlined certification process and clarity on who bears costs.

[P19] Incorporating terms and tolerances from U.S. Standards and Marketing Order No. 905 (§ 944.106(c)) without explicitly listing the applied tolerances creates regulatory uncertainty; commenters request the full text or exact cross-references to the specific standard versions and tolerances to be used.

[P19] Legal commenters will warn that relying by reference on external documents (United States Standards for Grades of Florida Grapefruit and Marketing Order No. 905) without making them part of the rulemaking record may violate notice requirements and impede meaningful comment.

[P20] Designating the Federal or Federal-State Inspection Service (§ 944.106(d)) as the inspection authority is appropriate only if sufficient inspectors, training, and laboratory resources are provided; state inspection agencies and packers request funding and staffing commitments to avoid certification delays.

[P20] Private sector commenters will request an option to use accredited third-party inspectors in lieu of Federal or Federal-State inspectors for timeliness and cost-efficiency, with USDA oversight, to prevent shipping bottlenecks.

[P1] Consumer advocates will argue the rule does not include carve-outs for donation programs or food banks; prohibiting shipping of substandard but safe fruit could increase food waste and impede charitable distribution.

[P2] Environmental groups will note the rule lacks consideration of how stricter size/grade standards increase food loss and associated environmental impacts; they will request impact assessment and mitigation measures.

[P3] Small growers and socially disadvantaged farmers will claim the grade and size minimums impose disproportionate burdens and request an economic hardship exemption or graduated compliance timeline.

[P9] Trade lawyers will request that the "minimum maturity requirements" in paragraph (e) be harmonized with international phytosanitary and quality standards (e.g., Codex, importing country rules) to avoid unnecessary barriers to trade.

[P19] Industry groups will ask for an administrative appeals process and clear inspection dispute resolution procedures when graders or Federal inspectors reject shipments under the referenced standards.

[P20] Exporters will request clarity on certification fees, turnaround times, and required documentation from the Federal or Federal-State Inspection Service to budget and plan logistics; the proposed rule does not provide this information.

[P1] Several commenters will request an effective date delayed by at least one crop season to allow packers, handlers, and exporters to adjust operations, update contracts, and train staff on new grading enforcement.

[P1] The blanket permission in § 205.601(a) to use “synthetic substances listed in this section” is overly broad and could be interpreted to allow additional, potentially harmful synthetics beyond those explicitly listed; request clarification that only substances individually named in the regulation are permitted.

[P1] Industry commenters will request a clear process and timeline for adding future synthetic substances to § 205.601(a), including criteria, scientific review standards, and stakeholder notice-and-comment opportunities before listing.

[P1] Organic certifiers and advocacy groups will argue that § 205.601(a) should require routine residue monitoring and reporting for all permitted synthetics to ensure compliance with organic principles and to detect cumulative exposure risks.

[P2] Growers and trade associations supporting the rule will submit that inclusion of potassium hypochlorite in § 205.601(a)(2)(iv) is appropriate for sanitation and disease control, and request guidance on allowable concentrations, application methods, and maximum residue limits.

[P2] Food safety advocates will request that the rule specify maximum application concentrations and pre-harvest intervals for potassium hypochlorite to prevent residues that could harm consumers and to provide enforceable standards for certifiers.

[P2] Legal experts will claim that the regulation must explicitly require labeling or recordkeeping for use of potassium hypochlorite in organic crop production so consumers and auditors can verify that its use complies with organic standards.

[P3] Sprout producers and public health advocates will support the explicit prohibition in § 205.601(a)(2)(iv) on potassium hypochlorite for edible sprout production, noting the unique microbiological risks with sprouts and the need for more stringent controls.

[P3] Conversely, some sprout industry commenters may request an exception process for potassium hypochlorite in edible sprout production when validated alternatives fail, accompanied by strict oversight, validated treatment protocols, and temporary approval criteria.

[P3] Certifiers and legal commenters will ask for clarification on the scope of “edible sprout production” (e.g., does it include sprout seeds, seed treatment, or sprouts used in animal feed) to avoid inconsistent enforcement of the potassium hypochlorite prohibition.

[P4] The permission for sodium hypochlorite in § 205.601(a)(2)(v) will prompt commenters to request explicit allowable concentrations, formulation types (stabilized vs. unstabilized), application methods, and required rinsing or pre-harvest intervals to prevent unacceptable residues.

[P4] Environmental and consumer groups will object that sodium hypochlorite allowance undermines organic principles due to potential formation of harmful byproducts (e.g., chlorinated organics) and will request toxicity and environmental impact assessments before finalizing permission.

[P4] Small-scale organic producers will request an explicit provision that sodium hypochlorite use must be documented in operation plans, with alternatives considered and used when effective (e.g., steam, peracetic acid), to preserve organic integrity.

[P5] Pineapple growers will praise § 205.601(k)(1) permitting ethylene gas to regulate flowering, but will request technical guidance on safe application rates, exposure times, worker safety protections, and monitoring measures to ensure compliant use.

[P5] Worker safety and labor groups will demand mandatory protective equipment standards, ventilation requirements, exposure limits, and training when ethylene gas is used under § 205.601(k)(1), and requester that these requirements be cross-referenced with OSHA rules.

[P5] Environmental groups will request an environmental assessment addressing potential off-target effects of ethylene application (e.g., effects on neighboring non-target crops and ecosystems) and mitigation measures before widespread adoption.

[P6] Tobacco industry stakeholders will support § 205.601(k)(2) allowing specified fatty alcohols (C6–C12) for sucker control, but request clarity on which exact compounds are permitted, concentration limits, and permissible formulations (emulsions, solvents).

[P6] Public health and anti-tobacco advocacy groups will object to providing any organic allowances for tobacco production, arguing that expanding organic inputs for a harmful product conflicts with public health goals and the spirit of the organic label.

[P6] Crop protection experts will request data demonstrating efficacy and environmental fate of the specified fatty alcohols in tobacco production, including effects on soil microbiota and non-target organisms, before final approval.

[P6] Legal commenters will request that § 205.601(k)(2) require documentation that fatty alcohols are used only for sucker control (not for other unpermitted purposes) and that their use be disclosed on farm plans to enable certification audits.

[P1/P2/P4] Multiple stakeholders will request cross-references between permissions for potassium hypochlorite and sodium hypochlorite and existing prohibitions (e.g., for sprouts) to prevent contradictory interpretations and to ensure consistent enforcement across commodity types.

[P2/P3/P4] Consumer groups will request that the rule require producers who use any hypochlorite (potassium or sodium) in organic production to disclose such use on product labels or on certifier websites to preserve consumer transparency.

[P1] Constitutional and administrative law experts will comment that the rule should specify the scientific standard (e.g., best available science, substantial evidence) the agency used to justify permitting these synthetics, to withstand judicial review.

[P4] Water quality and environmental regulators will raise concerns that increased use of sodium hypochlorite could lead to elevated chlorine residuals and byproducts in agricultural runoff and request mitigation, monitoring, and discharge limits be specified.

[P5] Trade associations will request harmonization with international organic standards (e.g., EU, Codex) regarding ethylene use on pineapples to avoid trade disruptions and differing import/export certification requirements.

[P6] Organic input suppliers will request a clear list of CAS numbers and purity criteria for the specified fatty alcohols (C6, C8, C10, C12) to avoid ambiguity in permitted raw materials and to prevent adulterated inputs entering the supply chain.

[P3/P4] Microbiologists will recommend that the prohibition on potassium hypochlorite for sprouts be accompanied by research funding and a timeline to develop and validate safer, effective alternatives (including whether sodium hypochlorite could be acceptable under controlled conditions).

[P2/P4] Certifiers will request standardized testing methods and action levels for residual hypochlorite on produce to determine compliance and to avoid inconsistent testing outcomes across labs.

[P1] Small farm advocates will request an explicit small-farm exemption or technical assistance program because implementation of new permitted synthetic substances (and related recordkeeping/testing) disproportionately burdens small organic operations.

[P1] The rule should clarify what constitutes a "complete" affidavit or declaration under § 7.37(a) by listing required fields and acceptable formats to reduce rejections for technical deficiencies.

[P2] The requirement in § 7.37(a)(1) that the holder file within the period set in § 7.36(b) is overly rigid; industry requests a 30-day grace extension to accommodate international time-zone and mailing delays.

[P3] § 7.37(a)(2) requires the verified statement to be executed "on or after the start of the filing period" — commenters ask for an explicit definition of "start of the filing period" (date of earliest permissible filing vs. calendar date) to avoid conflicting interpretations.

[P4] Permitting a person with "legal authority to bind the holder" to sign under § 7.37(a)(2)(i) is vague; businesses request a non-exhaustive list of acceptable corporate officers and documentation (e.g., corporate resolution) to prove authority.

[P5] The option in § 7.37(a)(2)(ii) to allow a person with "firsthand knowledge" and "actual or implied authority" to sign is legally risky — trademark owners and legal experts request elimination of "implied authority" or, at minimum, guidance on what evidence satisfies implied authority.

[P6] § 7.37(a)(2)(iii) allows attorneys to sign with "written, verbal, or implied power of attorney" — law firms and ethics groups object to allowing verbal or implied powers, urging that only written, signed powers be acceptable for evidentiary clarity.

[P7] The obligation in § 7.37(a)(3) to include the U.S. registration number should accommodate international registration filings lacking a U.S. registration number by allowing cross-reference to the international registration number when the U.S. number is pending.

[P8] § 7.37(a)(4) requires fees and follows multiple-class procedures but does not state accepted payment methods or currency — applicants request explicit payment methods and whether foreign currency or wire transfers will be accepted.

[P9] § 7.37(a)(4)(i) requires the fee per class as in § 7.6 — small businesses request a reduced or consolidated fee option for filings covering many classes to reduce financial burden.

[P10] The grace period surcharge in § 7.37(a)(4)(ii) should be capped or phased to prevent disproportionate penalties for honest filing delays; commenters request disclosure of surcharge amount in the rule text rather than cross-reference only.

[P11] Under § 7.37(a)(4)(iii) the Office may issue a notice when insufficient fees are submitted for multi-class registrations — industry asks for a minimum 30-day cure period and clear instructions on how to submit the missing fees electronically.

[P12] The permission in § 7.37(a)(4)(iii) to submit additional fees per § 7.39 should state whether acceptance of additional fees cures any late-filing surcharge or resets the filing date for evidentiary purposes.

[P1] The July 2, 2020 deadline for FAA to receive comments is unreasonably short and should be extended to at least 60 days from publication to allow meaningful stakeholder input.

[P1] The rule’s requirement that the FAA "receive" comments by July 2, 2020 could unfairly exclude timely mailed comments; the agency should clarify that comments postmarked by that date are acceptable.

[P1] The provision does not specify electronic submission methods or docket numbers tied to the July 2, 2020 deadline, creating ambiguity for commenters; require explicit instructions and alternative submission methods.

[P2] The phrase "within the specified compliance times" is vague; commenters request that the rule enumerate or summarize those compliance times in the AD itself rather than only referring to the Boeing bulletin.

[P2] Industry stakeholders assert that there should be a grace period for compliance in cases of parts backlog or scheduling conflicts, and request an allowance for FAA-approved phased compliance plans.

[P3] Reliance on the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin without incorporating it by reference into the AD denies regulated parties easy access to required steps; request incorporation by reference or full text inclusion in the rulemaking record.

[P3] Operators need clarity about which "applicable actions" apply to different airplane configurations; the AD should list applicability-by-configuration or provide a mapping table.

[P3] The requirement to "perform all applicable actions in the Accomplishment Instructions" creates potential liability for operators if the bulletin changes; commenters request that the AD specify that only the bulletin version dated November 15, 2019 is mandatory unless superseded by an FAA-approved AMOC.

[P4] Replacing "the original issue date" with the AD's effective date could alter compliance timing in unintended ways; industry requests an explanation and justification for this exception and proposes retaining bulletin issue dates for historical clarity.

[P4] Safety advocacy groups may object that substituting the AD effective date for the bulletin's "original issue date" could shorten time available for operators who relied on bulletin timing; they request confirmation that this exception does not accelerate unsafe compressed schedules.

[P5] The delegated authority to the Seattle ACO Branch Manager to approve AMOCs should be broadened to allow other FAA offices to approve AMOCs to avoid bottlenecks for operators not based in the Seattle region.

[P5] Legal commenters note that AMOC approvals must be processed consistently; request the FAA publish timelines and criteria used by the Seattle ACO Manager to approve or deny AMOCs.

[P6] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to a principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 may delay processing for non-part 121 operators; ask that the AD allow direct submissions to the Seattle ACO without routing through local offices.

[P6] Operators contend the provision should clarify whether electronic submission to the principal inspector satisfies 14 CFR 39.19 and whether acknowledgement timelines will be provided.

[P7] The instruction to address AMOC information to the person named in paragraph (j)(1) is circular because paragraph (j)(1) is not included in the text provided; request the AD include a complete citation or name to avoid misrouting.

[P7] Legal experts request that the AD explicitly identify the certification office manager (name/title/contact) to ensure proper delivery and to satisfy due process for applicants.

[P8] The specified email address for AMOC requests should be cross-checked for accuracy and redundancy; request alternative contact methods and confirmation that this mailbox is monitored and secure for technical data.

[P8] Privacy and security advocates request that the AD specify procedures for submitting sensitive proprietary information via the given email, including encryption or secure portal options.

[P9] The obligation to notify the principal inspector or FSDO manager prior to using an approved AMOC could be burdensome for operators with rapidly executed maintenance; request that notification may occur within a reasonable time after use (e.g., 48 hours) in urgent circumstances.

[P9] Operators ask for clarification on what constitutes adequate notification (written, electronic, acknowledgement required) to ensure compliance and avoid enforcement actions.

[P10] Allowing Boeing ODA approval of AMOCs for repairs/modifications raises conflict-of-interest concerns; request that the FAA require independent review or FAA concurrence rather than relying solely on Boeing ODA approval.

[P10] Operators and MROs want clarity whether approvals by Boeing ODA are sufficient for regulatory compliance across international registries, or if additional approvals are necessary by local authorities.

[P11] Requiring that AMOC-approved repairs "meet the certification basis of the airplane" is vague—commenters request that the AD define which version of the certification basis applies (original type certificate, amended, or latest FAA position).

[P11] Legal commenters argue that the requirement for the AMOC approval to "explicitly reference this AD" should be a formal condition of approval and propose model wording to be included in the AD to avoid ambiguity.

[P11] MROs request guidance on evidentiary documentation required to demonstrate that a repair meets the airplane's certification basis when seeking AMOC approval, including acceptable analyses and test data.

[P3] Industry commenters will request an explicit explanation of how compliance with Grant Assurances interacts with private lease arrangements and third‑party financings to avoid unintended liabilities for non-sponsor parties.

[P4] Appraisers and airport sponsors will ask for a defined timetable and process for FAA appraisal review—specify standards of review, acceptable appraisal methodologies, and appeal rights if FAA disputes a sponsor’s appraisal.

[P5] Sponsors will object to the "fair market value" requirement without defining valuation date or methodology for unique airport parcels (e.g., with aeronautical restrictions) and ask FAA to allow use of negotiated market mechanisms if justified.

[P5] Municipal fiscal officers will request guidance on allowable uses of sale/lease proceeds under Revenue Use Policy with concrete examples (capital projects, operations, debt service) to avoid future disputes.

[P6] Real estate developers and sponsors will seek clarification on what constitutes "sufficient authority" retained after disposal (e.g., easements, leaseback, covenants) and whether FAA approval of retention mechanisms is required.

[P9] Airport sponsors and privacy advocates will request limits on the scope and frequency of FAA audits and inspections, and ask for procedures protecting proprietary/confidential commercial information during FAA reviews.

[P9] Legal commenters will request due‑process protections for sponsors subject to FAA verification actions, including notice, an opportunity to cure, and an administrative appeal route before enforcement.

[P13] Sponsors and lenders will object to approval/consent letters that expire with lease terms because this undermines long-term financing; request that FAA allow multiyear or renewable approvals that align with typical commercial financing periods.
