raw_output:
[P1] The presumption that the contractor's 'Received' stamp or electronic delivery date is the date of receipt should be clarified to specify which takes precedence when both exist to avoid disputes about timeliness.

[P1] The rule lacks a mechanism for providers to challenge or appeal the contractor hearing officer’s presumption about date of receipt when no hearing officer is appointed, creating potential due process concerns.

[P2] Including the Office of the Attorney Advisor within the definition of "reviewing entity" could create a conflict of interest if the Office also participates in recommending agency positions; the rule should require firewalling or recusal rules.

[P2] The regulatory text should define the scope and limits of the Office of the Attorney Advisor’s authority as a "reviewing entity" to avoid overbroad application in procedural determinations.

[P3] Making the reviewing entity’s determination of date of receipt final and binding on all parties denies parties meaningful review and should instead be subject to de novo review by an impartial adjudicator.

[P3] The rule should require written justification and notice to parties when the reviewing entity determines a date of receipt, since binding determinations without explanation impede transparency.

[P4] The requirement to "send prompt written notice to the provider, and send a copy" is vague about to whom the copy must be sent; the rule should specify recipients (e.g., all parties, counsel, PRRB).

[P4] There is no timeframe defining "prompt"; commenters request a specific deadline (e.g., within 5 business days) to ensure timely receipt by providers.

[P5] The mandate that the decision be "sent promptly" lacks an objective timeline and acceptable delivery methods (mail, electronic), and should specify days and allowed formats.

[P6] Section §405.1814(c)(2) requires unspecified items to be sent "promptly" — the regulation must define which documents are covered and set an explicit deadline to prevent administrative delay.

[P7] Requiring all parties to familiarize themselves with PRRB instructions and electronic filing may burden small providers lacking IT resources; the rule should provide training resources or exemptions.

[P7] The obligation to familiarize oneself is not enforceable; instead, the agency should provide accessible guidance, deadlines, and technical assistance to ensure compliance.

[P8] Requiring the requesting party to promptly send subpoena requests to subpoenaed parties and other parties creates unnecessary duplicative service burdens and risks confidentiality breaches; the rule should allow central service by the Board.

[P8] The rule should define "promptly" for service of subpoena requests and permit electronic service for parties with prior consent to avoid certified mail delays.

[P9] Mandating certified mail for subpoena requests to nonparties imposes undue cost and delay; the rule should allow alternative reliable methods (overnight courier, electronic with proof of receipt).

[P9] The certified mail requirement may be infeasible for urgent subpoenas; commenters request an emergency exception permitting immediate electronic transmission and subsequent certified mail.

[P10] Allowing hospitals to retain surplus when prospective payments exceed costs (prospective payment surplus retention) could reduce incentives to control prices for private payers; CMS should monitor and report aggregate effects.

[P10] The permission to keep the difference between payment rate and costs could encourage upcoding or cost-shifting unless coupled with audit safeguards; commenters request anti-abuse provisions.

[P11] The rule making hospitals financially responsible for costs exceeding payment rate creates risk for safety-net hospitals treating high-cost patients; CMS should provide outlier payments or carve-outs.

[P11] The financial risk provision lacks transitional relief for hospitals facing pandemic-related cost surges; commenters ask for temporary mitigation or enhanced outlier thresholds.

[P12] CMS’s adjustment to the standardized amount to offset reasonable-cost payments for allogeneic stem cell acquisition must be budget-neutral across hospitals; commenters request disclosure of the adjustment methodology and estimated impacts.

[P12] The regulation does not specify the frequency or triggers for adjustments to the standardized amount; commenters request annual review and publication of adjustment factors.

[P13] The condition that payments for specified discharges on/after Oct 1, 2020 are adjusted per §412.85(c) appears retroactive; hospitals may face audit exposure for past cost reports — CMS should clarify implementation timing and transition relief.

[P14] Identifying MS-DRG 018 clinical trial discharges for special payment treatment will require clear coding guidance and audit criteria; commenters request detailed instructions on documentation and coding.

[P15] Adjusting the DRG weighting factor by a cost-ratio for clinical-trial vs non-clinical-trial MS-DRG 018 cases risks creating distortions if the sample of trial cases is small; CMS should require statistically robust sample sizes and publish methodology.

[P15] The regulation should require public posting of the cost-ratio calculation, data sources, and updates so hospitals can anticipate payment changes and verify accuracy.

[P16] Limiting CMS consideration for add-on payments to technologies with FDA authorization received by July 1 before the FY penalizes late-authorized, clinically important technologies; commenters suggest a later cutoff or rolling consideration.

[P16] The deadline may disadvantage small developers who obtain authorization after July 1; the rule should include an exception for technologies addressing unmet clinical needs or public health emergencies.

[P17] Permitting conditional approval of antimicrobial technologies under an alternative pathway is beneficial but should include clear criteria, performance milestones, and post-approval evidence requirements to avoid inappropriate payments.

[P17] CMS should require manufacturers receiving conditional add-on payments to report real-world effectiveness and maintain eligibility criteria, with clawback provisions if evidence is insufficient.

[P18] Requiring FDA authorization to be granted before July 1 for conditional approval contradicts the purported flexibility of paragraph (e)(3); commentators ask CMS to clarify how the two clauses interact and whether any late-authorizations are eligible.

[P18] The July 1 requirement for FDA authorization should allow documented extenuating circumstances (e.g., FDA delays) and provide a mechanism for late inclusion with retroactive payment adjustments.

[P19] Paying reasonable cost for allogeneic stem cell acquisition for certain hospitals is appropriate, but CMS must delineate which hospitals qualify as subsection (d) and provide clear cost reporting instructions.

[P19] The rule needs guardrails to prevent inflated reported acquisition costs; CMS should specify allowable cost categories, supporting documentation, and audit procedures.

[P20] The enumeration of donor acquisition cost categories needs more specificity (examples and limits) to ensure consistency across hospitals and prevent billing of unrelated donor services.

[P20] Commenters request that CMS confirm whether donor recruitment, testing, travel, and courier costs are included and whether caps or per-donor limits will apply.

[P21] The Medicare-share calculation using the ratio of Medicare transplants to total transplants should account for transfers and multi-site arrangements to avoid misallocation; CMS should provide rules for attribution.

[P21] There should be guidance on rounding, time windows, and how to handle transplants whose Medicare eligibility status changes between transplant and claim submission.

[P22] Requiring itemized statements with donor/recipient info raises HIPAA and donor privacy concerns; CMS should allow de-identified summaries or limit sensitive fields and require secure handling protocols.

[P22] The prospective recipient insurance number requirement may be impractical before final payer determination; CMS should permit provisional identifiers with subsequent reconciliation.

[P23] Requiring the Administrator review request to be sent "in care of the Office of the Attorney Advisor" may create confusion about proper address and delivery; CMS should publish a single submission address and acceptable electronic filing methods.

[P23] The rule should permit electronic submission directly to the Administrator with confirmation of receipt to streamline the process and reduce mailing errors.

[P24] The 15-day deadline for Administrator receipt of review requests is short and could be missed due to mail or email delays; commenters request extension to 30 days or allowance for filing under good-cause exceptions.

[P24] The rule should clarify whether weekends and federal holidays are included in the 15-day calculation and specify consequences of late filings and potential tolling provisions.

[P25] Mandating submission of an electronic copy to the Hospital and Ambulatory Policy Group creates duplicate filing burdens; commenters request that electronic submission to the Administrator suffice or that a single portal be used.

[P25] The rule must specify the required file formats, maximum file size, and secure transmission methods for the electronic copy to avoid technical rejection of filings.

[P26] Tying DRG weighting adjustments for clinical-trial cases to §412.85(c) requires alignment of data systems and retrospective reconciliation; hospitals need clear timelines for when the adjustments will be applied to claims.

[P26] The agency should publish transitional accounting guidance for FY2021 onward to prevent payment discrepancies when the adjusted weights take effect.

[P27] Payment for costs of sending patient records to the QIO should include a schedule of allowed formats and rates; otherwise hospitals may incur uncompensated expenses or inflate charges.

[P27] The rule should allow electronic transmission at standard rates and provide advance notice of eligible documentation formats and documentation of costs for reimbursement.

[P28] The broad obligation for providers to furnish information to contractors "upon request" could lead to overbroad or burdensome discovery; CMS should define scope, relevance standards, response times, and reasonable cost recovery.

[P28] Providers request a limit on the frequency and scope of information requests (e.g., no more than X requests per cost report) and an ability to seek review of overly burdensome requests.

[P29] Requiring copies of patient service charge schedules and updates on putting into effect could force publication of proprietary negotiated rates; CMS should limit the requirement to standard charge schedules, not confidential payer contracts.

[P29] There must be safeguards to protect competitively sensitive portions of charge schedules, with an option to file under protective order during audits.

[P30] Requiring median payer-specific negotiated charges by MS–DRG for MA and third-party payers is burdensome and may conflict with confidentiality obligations to payers; CMS should permit aggregated or de-identified reporting.

[P30] The methodology for calculating medians, handling outliers, and the MS–DRG mapping must be specified to ensure consistent reporting across providers.

[P31] Treating bad debts as implicit price concessions and recording them as part of net patient revenue for cost reporting periods beginning Oct 1, 2020 will materially alter hospital revenue recognition and may reduce Medicare allowable costs; CMS should provide detailed accounting guidance and transition relief.

[P31] The requirement to classify bad debts as price concessions may conflict with GAAP or provider accounting practices; CMS should coordinate with accounting standard setters or permit alternative acceptable accounting methods with disclosure.

[P1] The CONOPS requirement is vague about level of detail and format; industry needs clear templates and minimum page/section requirements to avoid inconsistent submissions and delays in FAA review.

[P1] Small UAS operators will be unable to compile a full CONOPS for multiple missions; the rule should allow a master CONOPS with modular mission appendices rather than a separate CONOPS per certification request.

[P2] Requiring a description of "intended type of operations" without defining categories (e.g., BVLOS, night, urban, cargo) creates uncertainty; the FAA should provide a closed list of operation types for standardized evaluation.

[P3] The UA specifications required in the CONOPS (e.g., dimensions, mass, payload) should explicitly include tolerances and units; otherwise manufacturers will receive inconsistent certification outcomes.

[P4] Requiring meteorological conditions in the CONOPS is burdensome for operators that plan to fly across variable climates; the FAA should permit a range-based or probabilistic description rather than fixed weather windows.

[P5] The personnel responsibilities field should clarify required qualifications/certifications for roles (remote pilot, observer, maintenance personnel); otherwise applicants cannot be assured what evidence to include.

[P6] The control station/support equipment description should allow reference to existing supplier documentation and COTS (commercial off-the-shelf) equipment rather than requiring bespoke engineering descriptions for each submission.

[P7] The C2 and communications description requirement should demand specific data (frequency bands, encryption, bandwidth, latency) to enable consistent cybersecurity and RF-spectrum review.

[P19] The cybersecurity protection obligation is broad; privacy and national-security stakeholders will ask the FAA to align with NIST cybersecurity frameworks and specify threat models, acceptable mitigations, and evidence types.

[P21] Automatic immediate execution of a predetermined action on C2 loss is a high burden for some operations (e.g., persistent surveillance over populated areas); operators request flexibility to allow time-delayed or graduated contingency behaviors tied to mission risk.

[P22] Including the predetermined C2-loss action in the Flight Manual is acceptable, but the rule must allow in-flight dynamic override by authorized controllers in certain contingencies; otherwise operational flexibility is lost.

[P23] Minimum C2 performance requirements in the Flight Manual should include measurable metrics (latency, packet-loss, BER, RSSI thresholds) and test methods; the current language is too high-level for enforcement.

[P24] Preventing takeoff when C2 is below minimum "by design or prohibited via operating limitation" could be burdensome—manufacturers need guidance on acceptable design interlocks and how FAA will validate they cannot be circumvented.

[P25] The lightning protection design requirement is costly and may be technically infeasible for small UAs; FAA should allow clearly defined operating limitations instead of an absolute design requirement.

[P26] If lightning protection is not shown, the operating limitation prohibition on flight into lightning-conducive weather must define how "lightning-conducive" is identified operationally (METAR, convective SIGMET, lightning detection systems).

[P27] Requiring design to operate in CONOPS-specified adverse weather (rain, snow, icing) without loss of control could exclude many useful UAS; FAA should allow limited approvals with clear operating limitations and mitigation strategies.

[P28] The two-option requirement for unapproved adverse weather (prevent inadvertent entry or provide detection/avoidance means) may be duplicative; operators request that detection capability be acceptable in lieu of complex operational limitations.

[P29] The obligation to develop operating limitations preventing inadvertent entry into adverse weather needs to specify how geofencing, sensor fusion, and preflight forecast checks satisfy that requirement.

[P30] The requirement to provide means to detect unapproved weather and demonstrate avoidance/exiting capability should include acceptance criteria for sensors (e.g., precipitation detectors, pitot icing warnings) and required reaction times.

[P31] Establishing a critical parts list when critical parts exist is reasonable; commenters request a definition of "critical parts" (safety effect thresholds) to avoid over-inclusion.

[P32] Mandatory maintenance instructions or life limits for critical parts impose lifecycle costs; industry asks for clear criteria on when life-limits vs. condition-based maintenance is acceptable.

[P33] Inclusion of mandatory maintenance/life limits in the Airworthiness Limitations Section is standard, but operators request that proprietary repair methods be allowed as referenced documents to avoid public disclosure.

[P34] Requiring a Flight Manual with each UAS is reasonable but burdensome for hobbyists and kit-built UAS; suggest proportional requirements or a simplified manual for small recreational UAS.

[P35] The operating limitations requirement in the Flight Manual must clarify whether operational waivers supersede manual limits and how updates to limitations post-certification are approved.

[P36] Normal and emergency procedures must be validated through simulator/human factors testing; the rule should require evidence of crew (remote pilot) training adequacy tied to these procedures.

[P37] Performance information in the Flight Manual should include established margins (e.g., 2-sigma performance uncertainties) rather than single-point numbers to reflect test variability.

[P38] Loading information should explicitly require maximum payload, center-of-gravity envelopes, and approved cargo configurations for external-load operations to avoid mis-loading risks.

[P39] The catch-all "any other information necessary for safe operation" is too vague and invites litigation; FAA should provide non-exhaustive examples to guide applicants.

[P40] FAA approval of Flight Manual portions requires predictable timelines; industry asks for formal review periods (e.g., 60–90 days) and criteria for expedited review for minor revisions.

[P41] ICA prepared per Appendix A to Part 23 will impose legacy aircraft standards on small UAS where they may be inappropriate; recommend tailoring Appendix A applicability to UAS size and complexity.

[P42] Allowing incomplete ICA at type certification only if completed before first delivery is reasonable, but FAA should require a security/assurance bond or escrow to ensure completion rather than relying solely on applicant promises.

[P43] Designing UAS durability/reliability "commensurate to maximum population density" is subjective; FAA should provide explicit population density bands and associated safety objectives or allowable risk levels.

[P44] The flight-test requirement with "no failures causing loss of flight, control, containment, or emergency landing outside recovery area" is an absolute standard that may be unattainable; industry requests allowance for minor non-safety-critical failures with rectification plans.

[P45] Requiring inclusion of all flights in the flight test report once testing begins is burdensome and could reveal proprietary test data; propose allowing anonymized summaries or a separation between developmental testing and certification testing.

[P46] The entire-flight-envelope testing mandate is appropriate, but FAA should permit representative sampling and statistical methods for routine verification rather than exhaustive testing of every conceivable combination.

[P47] Flight distance as a test metric should be correlated to CONOPS; commenters request clear minimum and maximum distance criteria for different operation types (BVLOS vs VLOS).

[P48] Flight duration test requirements should allow battery degradation curves and simulated endurance testing rather than continuous endurance flights for every configuration.

[P49] Route complexity testing is subjective; FAA should provide a definition (number of turns, waypoints density, obstacle proximity) and example scenarios.

[P50] Weight condition testing must allow use of worst-case mass margins rather than testing every intermediate weight; permit use of validated simulation tools to supplement flight tests.

[P51] Center of gravity test requirements should specify acceptable CG excursion ranges and test points (forward/aft limits) rather than an open-ended mandate.

[P52] Density altitude testing could be infeasible at extremes; FAA should accept augmented ground testing and analysis or testing at representative density altitudes with validated modeling for extremes.

[P53] Outside air temperature testing should define required temperature ranges based on CONOPS and geographic operation; allow lab environmental chamber testing for extremes.

[P54] Airspeed testing needs clarity on indicated vs true airspeed and calibration requirements for measuring instruments used in trials.

[P55] Wind condition testing must specify maximum gust/sustained wind levels and whether testing requires crosswind or tailwind scenarios; current language lacks actionable parameters.

[P56] Weather condition testing is duplicative with other weather provisions; propose consolidating weather testing requirements and permitting use of meteorological simulation tools.

[P57] Nighttime testing "if requested" creates uncertainty; operators seeking night approvals need objective criteria to know when night testing will be required—FAA should define triggering factors.

[P58] Energy storage system capacity testing must require characterization of worst-case cell degradation and mandatory reserve energy margins to ensure safe diversion/landing capabilities.

[P59] Aircraft-to-pilot ratio testing is essential but needs numerical thresholds (e.g., max 1:1, 3:1, etc.) for acceptable ratios and attendant monitoring requirements during operations.

[P60] Requirement to include most adverse combinations in testing may be impractically combinatorial; allow use of design-of-experiments and worst-case scenario analysis to bound testing burden.

[P61] Demonstrating a representative distribution of flight profiles tied to CONOPS is sensible; FAA should require justification metrics linking test profile distribution to expected operational frequency.

[P62] Conducting tests in CONOPS-consistent environmental conditions including EMI and HIRF is appropriate, but FAA should specify test levels and standards (e.g., MIL-STD-461, RTCA DO-160) to be used.

[P63] The prohibition on tests requiring "exceptional piloting skill or alertness" needs an operational definition and human-factors criteria; otherwise it's subjective and will impede testing of advanced systems requiring expert pilots.

[P64] Subjecting test UAS to worst-case ground handling/shipping loads is reasonable, but OEMs request definitions of "worst-case" and permitted use of representative sampling rather than every shipping configuration.

[P65] Maintaining and operating test UAS according to the ICA and Flight Manual before those documents are finalized may be impossible; FAA should allow phased implementation where provisional procedures are acceptable during testing under FAA oversight.

[P66] The prohibition on performing maintenance beyond ICA intervals to demonstrate compliance is unclear — applicants may need to perform extra maintenance to ensure safety during extended testing; FAA should allow documented, FAA-approved deviations during test campaigns.

[P67] Cargo/external-load testing for all critical weight/CG combinations is potentially extensive; allow use of analysis, ground tests, and scaled testing for certain cargo categories rather than full flight envelope testing for every load.

[P68] Demonstrating controllability with cargo/external loads at critical combinations is appropriate, but FAA should provide acceptance criteria (control margins, handling qualities) and pass/fail thresholds.

[P69] The requirement to demonstrate cargo retainability under critical conditions should allow certified cargo attachments and standardized release mechanisms as alternative evidence.

[P70] Designing UAS so probable failures do not cause loss of containment or control is appropriate; legal commenters will request definition of "probable" (quantitative failure probability) and acceptable residual risk.

[P71] Demonstrating by test that probable failures won't cause loss of containment/control requires clarity on test fault-injection levels and whether destructive testing is required; provide standardized fault models.

[P72] The list of equipment for which probable failures must be addressed is long; applicants ask for risk-based prioritization to focus most stringent requirements on highest-risk systems.

[P73] Propulsion system probable-failure mitigation must allow for single-engine designs where redundancy is impractical; permit alternative mitigations like restricted operating areas or immediate termination functions.

[P74] Requirements to address probable failures of the C2 link should allow use of redundant communication paths and spectrum diversity; FAA should accept documented mitigation strategies in lieu of physical redundancy in some cases.

[P75] Addressing probable GPS failures should allow usage of alternative navigation (INS, visual odometry, RTK, multilateration) and specify required performance of the alternative means.

[P76] Probable failures of single-point flight control components: the rule should require design diversity or safe failure modes but allow delegated assessment for small UAS where weight/cost constraints limit redundancy.

[P77] Control station probable-failure requirements need clarification on remote pilot hardware redundancy versus software/human procedures; remote pilots may operate from commercial devices—specify minimum resilience.

[P78] Addressing probable failures of any applicant-identified equipment invites applicants to list many items; FAA should require applicants to justify why any additional items are critical rather than permitting unlimited scope creep.

[P79] Operating test UAS in accordance with the Flight Manual when the Flight Manual may be provisional is impractical; FAA should permit controlled deviations during certification testing with FAA concurrence.

[P80] Conducting tests at the highest aircraft-to-pilot ratio may be costly and unsafe for initial tests; suggest progressive testing scaling ratios as confidence is established rather than jumping to worst-case immediately.

[P81] The broad list of capabilities in UAS.310 is comprehensive but lacks pass/fail performance metrics for each capability; applicants need quantitative criteria to design tests and demonstrate compliance.

[P82] Regaining command and control after C2 loss (UAS.310(a)(1)) should define timing limits (how long can C2 be lost), acceptable recovery methods (auto-reconnect vs. alternate station), and success criteria.

[P83] Electrical system power demonstration must include faulted conditions (e.g., single-bus failure) and prove reserve margins for diversion and emergency landing; require specified reserve energy percentage.

[P84] The requirement that "pilot can safely discontinue flight" needs a definition of "safely" and performance metrics (time to stop, steady-state descent rate) so testing is objective.

[P85] Demonstrating pilot ability to dynamically re-route the UA needs clarity on allowed latency and command upload methods; define maximum allowable reroute time and constraints during GPS-denied scenarios.

[P86] Ability to safely abort a takeoff must include defined rejected-takeoff distances and criteria; for VTOL or multirotor UAS, clarify metrics for safe abort.

[P87] Ability to safely abort landing/go-around should specify required climb gradients, thrust margins, and obstacle clearance criteria to be demonstrated.

[P88] Additional capabilities requested for approval (UAS.310(b)) should have clear test standards; without such standards approvals will be inconsistent and time-consuming.

[P89] Continued flight after propulsion degradation testing should define the degradation spectrum (partial thrust loss, propulsor failure) and minimum performance required to maintain controlled flight.

[P90] Geo-fencing that "contains the UA in all operating conditions" is technically challenging (GPS spoofing, sensor failure); FAA should accept redundant geofence enforcement mechanisms and define acceptable failure modes.

[P91] Positive transfer between control stations must include latency bounds, handshake/authentication requirements, and audit logging to ensure safe transfer; cybersecurity experts request specification.

[P92] Releasing external cargo to prevent loss of control must include safety constraints to prevent dropping hazardous materials over populated areas; require safety interlocks and emergency release procedures.

[P93] Detect-and-avoid capability testing requires standardized target detectability metrics (radar cross-section, RCS thresholds, sensor ranges) and defined separation minima for different airspace classes.

[P94] The design requirement to prevent inadvertent discontinuation of flight or inadvertent cargo release should be backed by human-factors validated interfaces and redundant actuators where required; propose specific reliability targets (MTBF, SIL).

[P95] Structural life requirement to withstand repeated loads needs a defined design life (flight hours/cycles) and fatigue analysis standards; otherwise applicants cannot determine acceptable life limits.

[P96] Airframe life limit establishment and test demonstration should permit scaling from subcomponent tests and be harmonized with expected maintenance program intervals to avoid premature retirement of UAs.

[P97] Demonstrating performance at least 5% over max gross weight (UAS.320) may be arbitrary and could penalize weight-constrained UAS; propose alternative metric based on required safety margins tied to handling qualities and performance under contingency.

[P3] The six-month removal requirement for each affected life jacket is operationally infeasible for some large fleets and should be extended to 12 months or allow phased compliance tied to scheduled maintenance checks.

[P3] The AD fails to define "remove" precisely — whether removal requires documentation, tag-out, and custody chain procedures — leading to enforcement ambiguity; the FAA should specify required recordkeeping.

[P6] The exception permitting installation only if repaired per SB 25–65–34 or FAA-approved method improperly makes the service bulletin mandatory; the FAA should explicitly explain the legal status of manufacturer service bulletins and allow equivalent procedures approved via AMOC.

[P7] The AD should explicitly permit installation of life jackets repaired under previously FAA-approved AMOCs (if the AMOC addresses the same defect) rather than insisting on compliance with a specific SB.

[P6] The exception allowing FAA-approved methods is appropriate but needs a streamlined approval path (e.g., pre-approved repair template) so operators can return aircraft to service quickly.

raw_output:
[P1] The one-year bar on accepting accreditation applications after three consecutive accreditation failures is unduly punitive and may force small facilities out of service; suggest reducing the period to 90 days or allowing a remediation plan to shorten the bar.

[P1] The rule lacks clarity on what constitutes a “consecutive accreditation failure” (e.g., does a facility that withdraws mid-review count?), creating unfair application denials; request clear definitions and examples.

[P1] Industry commenters will argue the prohibition fails to account for changes in ownership or management — a purchaser should be able to apply immediately even if the prior owner had three failures.

[P1] Legal experts will contend the provision may raise due process concerns by imposing a collateral bar to accreditation applications beyond the underlying failures; recommend an appeal process specific to the one-year prohibition.

[P2] The two-year ownership/operator prohibition after revocation will discourage investment and rehabilitation of facilities and should be limited to individuals directly responsible for the disqualifying act, not all owners/operators.

[P2] The text is ambiguous about partial owners (minority shareholders); stakeholders will request that the prohibition apply only to individuals with operational control or majority ownership.

[P2] Patient advocates may support a disqualification period but request that FDA define “owned or operated at the time of a disqualifying act” precisely to avoid overbroad application to historical investors.

[P3] Facilities will comment that indefinite maintenance of personnel records “relevant to MQSA qualification” is vague — request a specified retention period for active personnel beyond the minimums for former employees.

[P4] Compliance officers will warn that requiring instant availability of personnel records to MQSA inspectors without notice imposes unreasonable operational burdens; request a 48-hour production timeframe or allow secure electronic submission.

[P5] Requiring facilities to keep former employees’ records until the next annual inspection and FDA determination of compliance creates uncertainty for facilities that close between inspections; request a fixed retention period (e.g., 2 years) instead.

[P6] Personnel and privacy advocates will request explicit limits on information included in copies provided to former staff and require secure transfer mechanisms and redaction standards for sensitive data (e.g., social security numbers).

[P7] The obligation to arrange personnel access to MQSA records before facility closure is reasonable but lacks specifics about acceptable arrangements; commenters will request CMS/FDA-approved custodians or a national repository option.

[P8] Facilities will support the permission to permanently transfer records but will request technical guidance on chain-of-custody, data format standards, and liability for transferred records.

[P9] Manufacturers and facilities will request clarification on what constitutes “equivalent specifications” for digital accessory components cleared for non-mammography uses; propose an objective equivalence standard or an FDA checklist.

[P10] The requirement that digital accessories be FDA-cleared “specifically for mammography” may exclude widely used DICOM-compliant systems; commenters will ask FDA to explicitly accept devices cleared for diagnostic radiology when specifications match.

[P11] The alternative allowing clearance for a use that “could include mammography” with identical specifications is subjective; stakeholders will ask for a list of acceptable predicates or an expedited pathway for demonstrating equivalence.

[P12] Treating a converted unit as a new unit requiring equipment evaluation before clinical use is operationally burdensome and could interrupt patient care; request allowance for a limited grace period (e.g., 7 days) if validated QA testing is completed.

[P13] Facilities will request that accreditation bodies be required to provide expedited review processes and defined timelines for converted-unit accreditation applications to avoid service disruptions.

[P14] Screen-film facilities must use manufacturer-designated mammography film — commenters will ask for allowances if a specific film is discontinued or unavailable and request temporary substitution procedures.

[P15] The requirement that hardcopy prints use manufacturer-designated film that is printer-compatible is vague for mixed-vendor workflows; facilities will ask for interoperability guidance and testing procedures.

[P16] For non-screen-film image receptor systems, the mandated QA testing per (e)(6) must have clear pass/fail criteria and retesting intervals; request FDA to publish the specific test protocols and acceptance thresholds.

[P17] The requirement to present original-modality exams for interpretation (not copies/digitizations) will be challenged by teleradiology practices that routinely use transmitted DICOM copies; request FDA to permit lossless digital transfers that preserve original image fidelity.

[P18] Report requirement to include patient name and additional identifier is supported but commenters will seek guidance on which secondary identifiers are acceptable (DOB, MRN, SSN) and privacy protections.

[P19] The facility location requirement including ZIP and telephone number may be impractical for mobile units with no fixed city ZIP; mobile imaging providers will seek modified location reporting rules for mobile services.

[P20] Mandating the name of the interpreting physician in every report may conflict with buddy systems or multi-reader workflows; facilities will request guidance for reports reviewed by more than one physician and electronic signoff.

[P21] The mandated seven-category overall final assessment schema is prescriptive; radiology societies will request alignment with BI-RADS terminology to avoid duplication/confusion and recommend explicit crosswalks.

[P22] The “Negative” assessment subsection obliges interpretation of known clinical findings; clinicians will ask for clarity whether comorbidity or non-breast clinical findings must be described and how that affects coding.

[P23] The “Benign” category requires explanation of clinical findings if aware — practicing radiologists will request limits on the level of clinical detail required in the report to protect patient privacy and workflow efficiency.

[P24] The “Probably Benign” category’s use in screening versus diagnostic exams needs clarification; commenters request explicit instructions on follow-up timing and recommended management.

[P25] The “Suspicious” category definition may create medicolegal pressure toward biopsy recommendations; radiology groups will request guidance on language and management recommendations to standardize practice.

[P26] The “Highly suggestive of malignancy” label and associated obligations may trigger immediate reporting and patient notification obligations; facilities will ask for clear timelines and template notifications to avoid inconsistent messaging.

[P27] Reserving a category for “Known Biopsy Proven Malignancy” may be redundant; oncologists will request specification of when this category is appropriate vs. annotating prior pathology.

[P28] The “Post-Procedure Mammograms for Marker Placement” category could be misused; interventional radiologists will request criteria and examples to prevent overuse.

[P29] Requiring assignment of an “Incomplete” classification when work-up is incomplete is reasonable, but commenters will ask for definitions of “complete work-up” and acceptable timeframes to avoid excessive recalls.

[P30] For “Need additional imaging evaluation,” facilities will request standardized allowable tests and maximum time-to-complete before counting as an adverse performance metric.

[P31] For “Need prior mammograms for comparison,” commenters will object to the 30-calendar-day requirement for issuing a follow-up definitive assessment as unrealistic when prior films are held at other institutions; propose 60 days or expedited retrieval mechanisms.

[P32] The 30-day follow-up report deadline when prior films are needed (P32) will be considered impractical for patients with out-of-state priors; stakeholders request exceptions when reasonable efforts to obtain priors are documented.

[P33] The four-category breast density assessment requirement aligns with common standards but vendors will request precise numeric thresholds or imaging criteria to reduce inter-reader variability.

[P34] The language for the “almost entirely fatty” density category is acceptable, but commenters will request sample images or quantitative criteria to help radiologists classify consistently.

[P35] For “scattered fibroglandular density,” clinicians will ask for training resources to ensure accurate categorization and reduce misclassification.

[P36] The “heterogeneously dense” description requires guidance on when supplemental imaging should be recommended; patient advocates will push for clearer recommendations to ensure access to supplemental screening.

[P37] The “extremely dense” density statement triggers mandated lay-notification content; stakeholders will request evidence-based language and options for personalized risk-contextualized messaging.

[P38] Requiring recommendations for additional actions and addressing referrer clinical questions “to the extent possible” is vague; referring providers request standards for when the interpreting physician must contact the referrer directly.

[P39] The 30-calendar-day lay-summary deadline may be too long for patients with urgent results; patient advocates will urge expedited timelines for abnormal or suspicious findings (e.g., within 7 days).

[P40] Minimal content for lay summaries (patient name, facility contact, density) is insufficient; consumer groups will request inclusion of next-step instructions, timelines for follow-up, and resources for navigation assistance.

[P41] The requirement to provide lay summary within 7 days for “Suspicious”/“Highly suggestive” assessments and no later than 21 days from exam date is inconsistent with other timing provisions — commenters will ask for harmonization and clarification which deadline controls.

[P42] Sending the full report to patients within 30 days if they don’t name a provider (P42) may overwhelm patients with technical reports; patient advocates will request that the lay summary be provided first and the full report offered with contextual counseling resources.

[P43] Facilities that accept patients without a healthcare provider will object to the mandate to maintain a referral system (P43) without funding or defined standards; community clinics request federal support or model referral protocols.

[P44] The required low-density lay language (P44) is prescriptive and may conflict with state laws on patient communications; request model language and translations into common languages.

[P45] The high-density lay language (P45) requiring suggestion of supplemental testing may be interpreted as a mandate to offer costly additional services; insurers and facilities will ask FDA to clarify this is advisory and not a treatment mandate.

[P46] The 7-day/14-day provider notification timing for suspicious/highly suggestive reports (P46) will be operationally difficult for after-hours or weekend final interpretations; facilities request allowance for next-business-day compliance and electronic delivery methods.

[P47] The broad recordkeeping obligations (P47) will impose major IT and storage costs on small facilities; request a phased compliance schedule and cost analysis.

[P48] The minimum 5-year retention of mammograms and reports (10 years if no subsequent mammograms) (P48) may be inconsistent with some State laws that require longer; facilities request an explicit statement that the longest applicable retention period governs.

[P49] The obligation to implement policies minimizing loss of records (P49) is reasonable but needs specificity — commenters request required elements (backups, redundancies, encryption) and audit requirements.

[P50] Requiring retention of mammograms in the original modality and prohibiting copies/digitized originals (P50) is impractical for many facilities transitioning to digital systems; commenters ask FDA to permit validated, lossless digital archival copies as the “original” for electronic workflows.

[P51] The 15-calendar-day deadline to transfer original mammograms/reports on patient request (P51) is short for paper-film or remote archive retrieval; request extension to 30 days or allowance for reasonable delays with patient notice.

[P52] Prohibiting transfer of digitized copies (P52) will impede modern electronic health information exchange; health IT stakeholders request acceptance of certified digital transfers that preserve image metadata and fidelity.

[P53] Requiring original digital images to be provided electronically for transfers intended for final interpretation (P53) is appropriate but needs technical standards (file formats, transmission protocols); commenters ask FDA to reference DICOM/HL7 standards.

[P54] The 15-day deadline to provide copies upon patient request (P54) should include exceptions for extraordinary circumstances (e.g., record storage offsite, litigation holds); facilities request an extensions process.

[P55] The prohibition on charging more than documented costs for transfer/copy services (P55) is supported, but facilities want clear guidance on allowable cost components and documentation standards for audits.

[P56] The requirement to arrange for patient/provider access to records before closing (P56) is essential, but commenters want a standardized notice template and a list of approved custodians to reduce ambiguity.

[P57] Notifying accreditation body and certification agency in writing about closure record arrangements (P57) will require timing rules; facilities request a required notification timeline (e.g., 60 days before closure) and format.

[P58] The obligation to make “reasonable efforts” to notify all affected patients (P58) is vague; patient advocates want mandatory individual notifications (mail/email) in addition to public notices, with proof of attempts retained.

[P59] The requirement to collect and review outcome data for all mammograms (P59) will be resource-intensive; small practices will request minimum dataset requirements and a phased implementation timeline.

[P60] Calculating positive predictive value based on cancer diagnoses within 1 year (P60) may be skewed by patients receiving diagnosis elsewhere; commenters request guidance on data sources, linkages, and acceptable methods for attribution.

[P61] The cancer detection rate definition (P61) is unclear when applied to combined screening/diagnostic practices; facilities request separate reporting for screening vs. diagnostic mammograms.

[P62] The recall rate metric (P62) may penalize practices serving higher-risk populations; public health groups will ask for risk-adjusted benchmarks and stratified reporting.

[P63] The requirement to provide clinical images and relevant information to FDA/State when quality may be compromised (P63) raises patient privacy concerns; commenters request HIPAA-compliant procedures, a narrow scope of requested data, and protections for proprietary QA data.

[P64] Granting FDA/State authority to require patient notifications about deficiencies (P64) is appropriate for safety but must include criteria for when notifications are required and template language to prevent unnecessary alarm.

[P65] The requirement that notifications occur within agency-specified timeframes (P65) could conflict with legal counsel recommendations or active remediation; facilities request a chance to comment on draft notices to ensure accuracy.

[P66] Allowing FDA/State to notify patients via mass media if facility won’t do so (P66) risks broad public panic; commenters request that mass media be limited to instances of clear public health risk and require prior agency legal review.

[P67] FDA’s authority to suspend/revoke after notice and hearing (P67) is standard but stakeholders will seek clearer timelines for hearings and opportunities for interim corrective action to avoid abrupt service disruptions.

[P68] Designating failure to comply with reasonable records requests as grounds for suspension/revocation (P68) is acceptable but needs a definition of “reasonable” (scope, time) and an escalation process before revocation.

[P69] The provision making violating/aiding violations of 42 U.S.C. 263b a ground for revocation (P69) is redundant without examples; commenters request illustrative conduct categories and proportional remedies.

[P70] The ground for revocation for failing to comply with prior sanctions (P70) should require notice and reasonable opportunity to cure; legal commenters will urge a defined cure period and criteria for “failure to comply.”

[P71] Making failure to comply with personnel records requests grounds for revocation (P71) could produce harsh penalties for inadvertent noncompliance; recommend graduated enforcement (notice, civil penalty, probation) before revocation.

For “Need additional imaging evaluation,” facilities will request standardized allowable tests and maximum time-to-complete before counting as an adverse performance metric.

For “Need prior mammograms for comparison,” commenters will object to the 30-calendar-day requirement for issuing a follow-up definitive assessment as unrealistic when prior films are held at other institutions; propose 60 days or expedited retrieval mechanisms.

The 30-day follow-up report deadline when prior films are needed (P32) will be considered impractical for patients with out-of-state priors; stakeholders request exceptions when reasonable efforts to obtain priors are documented.
The four-category breast density assessment requirement aligns with common standards but vendors will request precise numeric thresholds or imaging criteria to reduce inter-reader variability.
The language for the “almost entirely fatty” density category is acceptable, but commenters will request sample images or quantitative criteria to help radiologists classify consistently.
For “scattered fibroglandular density,” clinicians will ask for training resources to ensure accurate categorization and reduce misclassification.

The “heterogeneously dense” description requires guidance on when supplemental imaging should be recommended; patient advocates will push for clearer recommendations to ensure access to supplemental screening.
The “extremely dense” density statement triggers mandated lay-notification content; stakeholders will request evidence-based language and options for personalized risk-contextualized messaging.

Requiring recommendations for additional actions and addressing referrer clinical questions “to the extent possible” is vague; referring providers request standards for when the interpreting physician must contact the referrer directly.
The 30-calendar-day lay-summary deadline may be too long for patients with urgent results; patient advocates will urge expedited timelines for abnormal or suspicious findings (e.g., within 7 days).

Minimal content for lay summaries (patient name, facility contact, density) is insufficient; consumer groups will request inclusion of next-step instructions, timelines for follow-up, and resources for navigation assistance.

The requirement to provide lay summary within 7 days for “Suspicious”/“Highly suggestive” assessments and no later than 21 days from exam date is inconsistent with other timing provisions — commenters will ask for harmonization and clarification which deadline controls.

Sending the full report to patients within 30 days if they don’t name a provider (P42) may overwhelm patients with technical reports; patient advocates will request that the lay summary be provided first and the full report offered with contextual counseling resources.

Facilities that accept patients without a healthcare provider will object to the mandate to maintain a referral system (P43) without funding or defined standards; community clinics request federal support or model referral protocols.
The required low-density lay language (P44) is prescriptive and may conflict with state laws on patient communications; request model language and translations into common languages.

The high-density lay language (P45) requiring suggestion of supplemental testing may be interpreted as a mandate to offer costly additional services; insurers and facilities will ask FDA to clarify this is advisory and not a treatment mandate.

The 7-day/14-day provider notification timing for suspicious/highly suggestive reports (P46) will be operationally difficult for after-hours or weekend final interpretations; facilities request allowance for next-business-day compliance and electronic delivery methods.
The broad recordkeeping obligations (P47) will impose major IT and storage costs on small facilities; request a phased compliance schedule and cost analysis.

The minimum 5-year retention of mammograms and reports (10 years if no subsequent mammograms) (P48) may be inconsistent with some State laws that require longer; facilities request an explicit statement that the longest applicable retention period governs.

The obligation to implement policies minimizing loss of records (P49) is reasonable but needs specificity — commenters request required elements (backups, redundancies, encryption) and audit requirements.

Requiring retention of mammograms in the original modality and prohibiting copies/digitized originals (P50) is impractical for many facilities transitioning to digital systems; commenters ask FDA to permit validated, lossless digital archival copies as the “original” for electronic workflows.

The 15-calendar-day deadline to transfer original mammograms/reports on patient request (P51) is short for paper-film or remote archive retrieval; request extension to 30 days or allowance for reasonable delays with patient notice.

Prohibiting transfer of digitized copies (P52) will impede modern electronic health information exchange; health IT stakeholders request acceptance of certified digital transfers that preserve image metadata and fidelity.

Requiring original digital images to be provided electronically for transfers intended for final interpretation (P53) is appropriate but needs technical standards (file formats, transmission protocols); commenters ask FDA to reference DICOM/HL7 standards.

The 15-day deadline to provide copies upon patient request (P54) should include exceptions for extraordinary circumstances (e.g., record storage offsite, litigation holds); facilities request an extensions process.

The prohibition on charging more than documented costs for transfer/copy services (P55) is supported, but facilities want clear guidance on allowable cost components and documentation standards for audits.

The requirement to arrange for patient/provider access to records before closing (P56) is essential, but commenters want a standardized notice template and a list of approved custodians to reduce ambiguity.

Notifying accreditation body and certification agency in writing about closure record arrangements (P57) will require timing rules; facilities request a required notification timeline (e.g., 60 days before closure) and format.

The obligation to make “reasonable efforts” to notify all affected patients (P58) is vague; patient advocates want mandatory individual notifications (mail/email) in addition to public notices, with proof of attempts retained.
The requirement to collect and review outcome data for all mammograms (P59) will be resource-intensive; small practices will request minimum dataset requirements and a phased implementation timeline.

Calculating positive predictive value based on cancer diagnoses within 1 year (P60) may be skewed by patients receiving diagnosis elsewhere; commenters request guidance on data sources, linkages, and acceptable methods for attribution.
The cancer detection rate definition (P61) is unclear when applied to combined screening/diagnostic practices; facilities request separate reporting for screening vs. diagnostic mammograms.
The recall rate metric (P62) may penalize practices serving higher-risk populations; public health groups will ask for risk-adjusted benchmarks and stratified reporting.

The requirement to provide clinical images and relevant information to FDA/State when quality may be compromised (P63) raises patient privacy concerns; commenters request HIPAA-compliant procedures, a narrow scope of requested data, and protections for proprietary QA data.

Granting FDA/State authority to require patient notifications about deficiencies (P64) is appropriate for safety but must include criteria for when notifications are required and template language to prevent unnecessary alarm.

The requirement that notifications occur within agency-specified timeframes (P65) could conflict with legal counsel recommendations or active remediation; facilities request a chance to comment on draft notices to ensure accuracy.

Allowing FDA/State to notify patients via mass media if facility won’t do so (P66) risks broad public panic; commenters request that mass media be limited to instances of clear public health risk and require prior agency legal review.

FDA’s authority to suspend/revoke after notice and hearing (P67) is standard but stakeholders will seek clearer timelines for hearings and opportunities for interim corrective action to avoid abrupt service disruptions.

Designating failure to comply with reasonable records requests as grounds for suspension/revocation (P68) is acceptable but needs a definition of “reasonable” (scope, time) and an escalation process before revocation.

The provision making violating/aiding violations of 42 U.S.C. 263b a ground for revocation (P69) is redundant without examples; commenters request illustrative conduct categories and proportional remedies.

The ground for revocation for failing to comply with prior sanctions (P70) should require notice and reasonable opportunity to cure; legal commenters will urge a defined cure period and criteria for “failure to comply.”

Making failure to comply with personnel records requests grounds for revocation (P71) could produce harsh penalties for inadvertent noncompliance; recommend graduated enforcement (notice, civil penalty, probation) before revocation.

[P1] The April 12, 2021 comment deadline is too short and should be extended by at least 60–90 days to allow affected operators, MROs, and unions adequate time to perform technical review, run CSN inventories, and coordinate consolidated industry responses.

[P1] The AD should provide clarification whether comments submitted electronically via email to the FAA address specified in paragraph (j)(1) count as timely if received by the close of business on April 12, 2021, to avoid confusion about receipt times.

[P2] The rule’s applicability text appears truncated (unfinished parenthetical after "part number ("); please correct and clarify exactly which P/N variants and serial numbers of the lower fuel manifold are included to avoid unintended applicability.

[P2] The applicability is ambiguous as to whether engines installed on in-service aircraft only or engines in spares pools and test stands are covered; the AD should explicitly state that spares and engines in storage are included/excluded.

[P3] The compliance clause "unless already done" lacks a definition of what constitutes "already done" (i.e., inspections performed to which standard, by which competent agency, and documented how); request explicit acceptance criteria for previously completed inspections and acceptable documentation.

[P4] Requiring operators to perform one of three different inspection methods without guidance on how to choose among them will create inconsistent risk outcomes and logistical burdens; the AD should prioritize a single preferred inspection method or provide objective criteria (e.g., accessibility, CSN ranges, maintenance interval alignment) for method selection.

[P4] The AD does not specify required qualifications, certification, or personnel (e.g., Level II USI technician, FPI certified personnel) for performing each inspection type; add explicit personnel qualification requirements to ensure consistent inspection quality.

[P5] Table 1 row 1's threshold triggers inspections "after it reaches 1,700 CSN, but before it exceeds 2,200 CSN" — this creates a window that could allow engines to go to 2,199 CSN without inspection if they accumulate cycles rapidly; recommend instead to require inspection within X cycles after the next scheduled shop visit or within Y months to prevent inadvertent exceedance.

[P5] The AD should clarify how to measure CSN for lower fuel manifolds that have been moved between engines or undergone component-level time accounting; specify required recordkeeping to track manifold-specific CSN.

[P6] The 500 flight cycle compliance window for parts with 1,700 CSN or more may be operationally disruptive for high-utilization fleets; request extension to 750–1,000 FCs or an option to perform inspections at the next scheduled maintenance event within that window.

[P6] The AD should address engine short-term storage/grounding scenarios — if an engine is not flown within 500 FCs after the effective date (e.g., in spares pool), clarify whether calendar time limits apply or whether the 500 FC clock remains paused.

[P7] The USI requirement referencing "paragraph 4. App…" of the service bulletin is truncated in the AD text; provide full reference and ensure the service bulletin revision date and complete procedure are incorporated by reference to avoid misinterpretation.

[P7] Ultrasonic inspection adjacent to support block pads may require disassembly or specialized fixtures; request FAA to provide guidance on allowable on-wing USI technique limitations and any torque/fastener removal allowances necessary to achieve reliable inspection.

[P8] The on-wing spot FPI procedure must specify allowable penetrant types, dwell times, surface preparation, and lighting/magnification standards; without these specifics inspections will be inconsistent and potentially unreliable.

[P8] Performing an on-wing spot FPI at brazed joints might require engine accessibility that conflicts with flight schedules; request the AD allow the on-wing FPI only when performed by qualified MROs with published procedures or allow the in-shop FPI as the default.

[P9] In-shop FPI implies removal and shop visit that is costly — the AD should provide cost-benefit justification and consider allowing deferred in-shop FPI until next scheduled shop visit for low-utilization engines.

[P9] The AD does not specify acceptable acceptance/rejection criteria for FPI indications (size, depth, location); add quantitative rejectable indication thresholds consistent with GE service bulletin to avoid subjective removals.

[P10] Requiring immediate removal and replacement "before further flight" for any crack or rejectable indication may be impracticable for remote operations; request allowance for temporary grounding, ferry permits, or one-flight ferry with operational restrictions if a non-propagating surface indication is identified and engineering evaluates risk.

[P10] The AD should allow for alternative corrective actions, such as repair per FAA-approved repair scheme, rather than mandatory replacement, provided a safe life and engineering substantiation exist.

[P11] The definition of "part eligible for installation" omits criteria for parts with unknown CSN or incomplete traceability; require that parts without verifiable CSN be treated as >=1,700 CSN and inspected before installation.

[P12] Allowing installation of manifolds with less than 1,700 CSN without inspection may be acceptable, but the AD should require that CSN documentation be attached to the part and verified during installation to prevent fraud or record-keeping errors.

[P13] The permission for manifolds with >=1,700 CSN that have been inspected and found free of cracks does not state the validity period of such an inspection; specify a re-inspection interval or that the clearance is only at time of inspection and does not exempt future inspections.

[P13] The AD should explicitly state whether an inspection performed by GE or a DER to an equivalent standard qualifies as an inspection "in accordance with paragraph (g)(1)(i),(ii), or (iii)."

[P14] The allowance to install an approved lower fuel manifold with a different part number needs a definition of "approved" — clarify whether that means FAA-PMA, OEM-approved alternative P/N, STC-approved parts, or parts approved via AMOC.

[P14] If alternate part numbers are permitted, require that their design be demonstrated to eliminate the brazed block joint cracking mode or have equivalent fatigue life substantiation; otherwise, the permission could encourage unauthorized deviations.

[P15] Removing the reporting requirement reduces data collection necessary to monitor fleet-wide crack incidence; recommend retaining at least anonymized or aggregate reporting to FAA to support future risk assessment and AD efficacy evaluation.

[P15] Alternatively, if reporting remains non-required, require operators to retain inspection records and make them available to FAA upon request for compliance monitoring.

[P16] While AMOC authority is delegated to the Manager, ECO Branch, FAA, the AD should include expected processing timeframes for AMOC requests (e.g., 60–90 days) so operators can plan and avoid grounding aircraft awaiting AMOC approval.

[P16] The AD should allow for limited-use provisional AMOCs (e.g., for specific fleet tail numbers) pending full AMOC approval to avoid unnecessary operational disruption.

[P17] The required routing of AMOC requests through principal inspectors or local FSDOs may delay submissions; request the FAA allow direct submission to the ECO Branch AMOC mailbox with a courtesy copy to the principal inspector to streamline review.

[P17] The AD should clarify whether email AMOC submissions require PDF attachments, signatures, and specific documentation (e.g., engineering substantiation, inspection forms) and provide a checklist to reduce incomplete submissions.

[P18] The requirement to notify the principal inspector or FSDO before using an approved AMOC is vague on timing (how much advance notice is required); specify timeline (e.g., within 48 hours prior to the first use) to provide administrative clarity.

[P18] The AD should permit electronic notification (email) of AMOC use and define the content of that notification (affected tail numbers, work scope, effective dates) to ensure consistent implementation tracking.

raw_output:
[P1] The deadline for receiving comments (May 9, 2022) is unreasonably short and should be extended to at least 60 days after publication to allow stakeholders sufficient time to prepare substantive technical and economic comments.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether the May 9, 2022 deadline applies to mailed, emailed, and hand-delivered comments and provide a clear timestamp standard (postmark vs. received).

[P2] The phrase "within the compliance times specified" is vague; commenters will request that the AD publish a clear table of compliance intervals for each affected model/line number rather than deferring to other documents.

[P2] The obligation to "comply ... unless already done" requires a method to document and accept prior compliance—commenters will request explicit guidance on what records constitute acceptable proof that actions were already done.

[P3] Requiring potable water system deactivation within 5 days after March 5, 2021 is retroactive and impractical for operators who did not receive earlier notice; commenters will argue the AD should set a compliance period measured from this AD's effective date or provide relief for operators that could not have complied earlier.

[P3] The deactivation requirement tied to March 5, 2021 conflicts with P1 comment deadline timing; commenters will request that the FAA avoid imposing retroactive compliance obligations and explicitly state whether civil penalties could apply for noncompliance during the retroactive period.

[P4] The applicability language for L/Ns 959 and earlier relies on prior accomplishment of Boeing Service Bulletin 777–38–0042, but does not define acceptable evidence or the date by which that SB must have been accomplished—commenters will request recordkeeping standards and an acceptable compliance log format.

[P4] Operators with partial or alternative modifications performed in accordance with earlier revisions of the service bulletin need clarification: does any deviation from the exact referenced Boeing Service Bulletin actions exclude an airplane from paragraph (g)(1)?

[P5] The inclusion of L/Ns 960 and subsequent without further qualification sweeps in a broad set of airplanes; commenters will request risk-based justification and Boeing fleet data supporting why all L/Ns 960+ must be deactivated immediately.

[P6] The prohibition on accomplishing Boeing Service Bulletin 777–38–0042 actions for airplanes not in paragraph (g) as of March 5, 2021 effectively freezes maintenance options for many operators and may prevent necessary safety fixes; commenters from industry will ask for an exception process to allow completing those actions under approved AMOCs.

[P6] The prohibition's effective date (March 5, 2021) creates legal uncertainty for actions performed between March 5, 2021 and the AD issuance—commenters will request a safe harbor for actions performed in good faith during that period and clarity on whether such actions will be grandfathered.

[P7] Removing the reporting requirement (contradicting Boeing MOM guidance) removes a valuable data-gathering tool; safety advocacy groups will request that the FAA either reinstate a mandatory reporting requirement or provide rationale and data showing reporting is unnecessary.

[P7] The AD's explicit statement that no reporting is required may prevent industry-wide trend analysis; commenters will ask the FAA to at least require optional centralized reporting or encourage voluntary submission of inspection findings to a designated FAA mailbox.

[P8] The obligation to follow the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin's Accomplishment Instructions "except as modified by paragraph (k)" needs specificity—commenters will demand a redline/summary of all differences between the bulletin and the AD to avoid confusion.

[P8] Reliance on Boeing's Alert Requirements Bulletin to define required actions risks creating a private standard; commenters (consumer advocates and legal experts) will request that all mandated steps be reproduced in the AD or the FAA ensure the bulletin is incorporated by reference and available free of charge.

[P9] Replacing "Original Issue date" with the AD effective date in compliance times could materially change compliance windows for operators who relied on the bulletin's original issue date; commenters will request examples demonstrating how this substitution affects compliance schedules for different airplanes.

[P9] The AD should explicitly state how the change in compliance date interacts with extensions, deferred maintenance, or previously approved AMOCs—legal commenters will request language preventing retroactive invalidation of prior AMO/DAO approvals.

[P10] The statement that completing the Bulletin's required actions ends the potable water system deactivation requirement should include confirmation on whether partial completion or staged completion would allow partial reactivation—operators will request guidance on phased return-to-service.

[P10] Commenters will request a clear post-action validation requirement (e.g., functional test, leakage check) to confirm potable water system safety before reactivation, and whether FAA needs to be notified of completion.

[P11] Granting AMOC approval authority only to the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch centralizes decision-making; commenters (large lessors/carriers) will request that other ACO branches be explicitly authorized or that timelines for AMOC review be specified to avoid delays.

[P11] Legal commenters will request clarification whether the Manager's authority is delegable and, if so, to whom, and what qualifications a delegate must possess.

[P12] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or Flight Standards Office may cause routing delays—operators request an option to submit directly to the Seattle ACO with an acknowledgement requirement and a service standard (e.g., 30-day response).

[P13] The instruction to address information to the person in paragraph (n)(1) lacks the named contact in the AD excerpt provided; commenters will request that the AD include the contact's name, title, and mailing address or that the AD specify how to find that information.

[P14] The permitted email address for AMOC requests is helpful, but commenters will request assurances on email security, confirmation of receipt, and an alternative secure upload method for large engineering data packages.

[P15] The requirement to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC could be burdensome where operators have multiple jurisdictions or international bases; commenters will request a standardized notification form and explicit timelines for notification (e.g., within 5 business days).

[P15] Operators without a principal inspector are required to notify the Flight Standards Office manager; commenters will ask FAA to describe how operators with international certificates should comply and which US-based office counts as "responsible."

[P16] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs for repairs/modifications raises conflict-of-interest concerns—safety advocacy groups will request transparency: FAA should require that Boeing provide the rationale and all test data used for ODA approvals and FAA confirm the ODA's independence.

[P16] Independent maintenance organizations will object that giving Boeing ODA authority could bypass FAA review and ask that any ODA-approved solution be subject to FAA concurrence and posted publicly for comment.

[P17] The requirement that AMOC approvals explicitly reference this AD and meet the airplane's certification basis is appropriate, but commenters will request that the AD specify the documentation that must accompany the approval to demonstrate compliance with certification basis (e.g., substantiation reports, certification data).

[P17] Certification experts will request a clear process and timeline for FAA validation when an AMOC includes alternative methods that affect the airplane's certification basis—specifically, whether a supplemental type certificate (STC) or other formal approval is required.

[P3] Airlines operating mixed fleets will request flexibility for reactivating potable water systems on a per-airplane basis depending on route and ground infrastructure, and want the AD to allow case-by-case exceptions when potable water is required for passenger health or international regulatory reasons.

[P4] Lessors will request explicit instructions on how the deactivation applicability tied to line numbers affects aircraft in lease transitions (e.g., between L/N<=959 and L/N>=960 aircraft) and whether lessors must notify lessees of deactivation obligations.

[P6] Maintenance providers will ask for clarification whether the prohibition on accomplishing SB 777–38–0042 for non-applicable airplanes includes performing partial tasks, inspections, or preparatory work, as that affects scheduling and tooling usage.

[P7] Flight crew and passenger advocacy groups will request that, if reporting is not required, the FAA at least require operators to maintain internal records of inspection findings for a defined period (e.g., 24 months) for audit and traceability.

[P8] Foreign regulatory authorities will likely comment that mandatory reliance on Boeing documents without harmonized EASA/ICAO language may create divergent compliance obligations internationally; they will request harmonization text or recognition statements.

[P1] Consumer groups will request that the FAA publish a summary of substantive comments received and the FAA's responses (a rulemaking docket) before finalizing the AD to ensure transparency.

The AD's explicit statement that no reporting is required may prevent industry-wide trend analysis; commenters will ask the FAA to at least require optional centralized reporting or encourage voluntary submission of inspection findings to a designated FAA mailbox.

The obligation to follow the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin's Accomplishment Instructions "except as modified by paragraph (k)" needs specificity—commenters will demand a redline/summary of all differences between the bulletin and the AD to avoid confusion.

Reliance on Boeing's Alert Requirements Bulletin to define required actions risks creating a private standard; commenters (consumer advocates and legal experts) will request that all mandated steps be reproduced in the AD or the FAA ensure the bulletin is incorporated by reference and available free of charge.

Replacing "Original Issue date" with the AD effective date in compliance times could materially change compliance windows for operators who relied on the bulletin's original issue date; commenters will request examples demonstrating how this substitution affects compliance schedules for different airplanes.

The AD should explicitly state how the change in compliance date interacts with extensions, deferred maintenance, or previously approved AMOCs—legal commenters will request language preventing retroactive invalidation of prior AMO/DAO approvals.

The statement that completing the Bulletin's required actions ends the potable water system deactivation requirement should include confirmation on whether partial completion or staged completion would allow partial reactivation—operators will request guidance on phased return-to-service.
