Legal commenters will request clarification whether the Manager's authority is delegable and, if so, to whom, and what qualifications a delegate must possess.

Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or Flight Standards Office may cause routing delays—operators request an option to submit directly to the Seattle ACO with an acknowledgement requirement and a service standard (e.g., 30-day response).

The instruction to address information to the person in paragraph (n)(1) lacks the named contact in the AD excerpt provided; commenters will request that the AD include the contact's name, title, and mailing address or that the AD specify how to find that information.

The permitted email address for AMOC requests is helpful, but commenters will request assurances on email security, confirmation of receipt, and an alternative secure upload method for large engineering data packages.

The requirement to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC could be burdensome where operators have multiple jurisdictions or international bases; commenters will request a standardized notification form and explicit timelines for notification (e.g., within 5 business days).

Operators without a principal inspector are required to notify the Flight Standards Office manager; commenters will ask FAA to describe how operators with international certificates should comply and which US-based office counts as "responsible."

Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs for repairs/modifications raises conflict-of-interest concerns—safety advocacy groups will request transparency: FAA should require that Boeing provide the rationale and all test data used for ODA approvals and FAA confirm the ODA's independence.

Independent maintenance organizations will object that giving Boeing ODA authority could bypass FAA review and ask that any ODA-approved solution be subject to FAA concurrence and posted publicly for comment.

The requirement that AMOC approvals explicitly reference this AD and meet the airplane's certification basis is appropriate, but commenters will request that the AD specify the documentation that must accompany the approval to demonstrate compliance with certification basis (e.g., substantiation reports, certification data).

Certification experts will request a clear process and timeline for FAA validation when an AMOC includes alternative methods that affect the airplane's certification basis—specifically, whether a supplemental type certificate (STC) or other formal approval is required.

Airlines operating mixed fleets will request flexibility for reactivating potable water systems on a per-airplane basis depending on route and ground infrastructure, and want the AD to allow case-by-case exceptions when potable water is required for passenger health or international regulatory reasons.

Lessors will request explicit instructions on how the deactivation applicability tied to line numbers affects aircraft in lease transitions (e.g., between L/N<=959 and L/N>=960 aircraft) and whether lessors must notify lessees of deactivation obligations.

Maintenance providers will ask for clarification whether the prohibition on accomplishing SB 777–38–0042 for non-applicable airplanes includes performing partial tasks, inspections, or preparatory work, as that affects scheduling and tooling usage.

Flight crew and passenger advocacy groups will request that, if reporting is not required, the FAA at least require operators to maintain internal records of inspection findings for a defined period (e.g., 24 months) for audit and traceability.

Foreign regulatory authorities will likely comment that mandatory reliance on Boeing documents without harmonized EASA/ICAO language may create divergent compliance obligations internationally; they will request harmonization text or recognition statements.
Consumer groups will request that the FAA publish a summary of substantive comments received and the FAA's responses (a rulemaking docket) before finalizing the AD to ensure transparency.

[P1] The February 12, 2020 comment deadline is unreasonably short given the technical complexity of the proposed AD and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow operators, MROs, and manufacturers to prepare substantive comments and data.

[P1] The rule text requires the FAA to receive comments by February 12, 2020, but does not state whether comments postmarked by that date are acceptable; the FAA should clarify receipt versus postmark rules to avoid unfair exclusion.

[P2] The AD’s applicability list omits several known LEAP-1B subvariants installed on retrofit or VIP configurations (e.g., in-service BBJ modifications); the FAA should explicitly confirm whether retrofited or modified serial-numbered engines fall within the scope.

[P2] The scope provision lists LEAP-1B models but does not clarify whether spare engines in storage, engines in spare pools, or engines installed on aircraft but not operated in U.S. service are subject; FAA should clarify territorial and status applicability.

[P2] The AD applies to multiple LEAP–1B models but fails to reference affected serial number ranges or S/N exclusions provided by the manufacturer; commenters request inclusion of specific S/Ns or a process to identify exempt engines to avoid over-compliance.

[P3] The requirement to "comply within the specified compliance times" lacks explicit language about whether compliance times are calendar days, flight cycles, or flight hours; request clarification and specific units for each action.

[P3] The AD does not provide alternative phased compliance for operators with large fleets who cannot meet short compliance windows; request graduated compliance windows based on fleet size or operational constraints.

[P4] The "unless already done" exception is ambiguous—CFM service bulletin compliance records are needed to substantiate "already done"; request FAA require documentation (work orders or EASA/other approvals) to prove prior compliance and avoid enforcement disputes.

[P5] The 15-day requirement to revise the ALS and maintenance program is unreasonably short for certificate-holders to coordinate program changes, revise manuals, obtain internal approvals, and file changes with the FAA; request extension to 60–90 days.

[P5] The AD mandates ALS revisions within 15 days but does not state whether operators must submit the revised ALS to the FAA for review/acceptance or merely retain them in company records; clarify submission and approval requirements.

[P6] Mandating insertion of ESM Data Module LEAP–1B–05–21–03–01A–281B–C Issue 002 dated Jan 9, 2020 into the ALS could create conflicts with existing national regulations (e.g., EASA) or operator programs; request assessment of cross-jurisdictional consistency and harmonization.

[P6] The AD requires inserting paragraph 6.B.(2) of the specific ESM module but does not reproduce the content or summarize the effect; operators need to know the substantive change (e.g., new life limits or inspections) to estimate cost and operational impact.

[P7] Requiring insertion of paragraphs 6.B.(1), 6.B.(2), and 6.C.(1) from ESM Module LEAP–1B–05–29–00–01A–281B–C Issue 001 may impose duplicative or conflicting tasks with previously mandated ALS items; request FAA to identify and reconcile overlaps with existing ALS requirements.

[P7] The AD references multiple ESM paragraphs in two distinct data modules; operators should be allowed to comply by referencing the complete ESM documents rather than extracting individual paragraphs to avoid transcription errors.

[P8] The absolute prohibition on using any alternative inspections, procedures, or intervals after revisions, absent an AMOC, is overly restrictive and could prevent operators from using previously-approved equivalent procedures under continuous airworthiness management; request modification to allow pre-existing approved alternatives to continue until FAA review.

[P8] The prohibition creates operational risk where urgent interim procedures used by operators or OEMs prior to issuance are no longer permitted; request grandfathering of OEM temporary procedures pending AMOC approval.

[P9] While the AD permits AMOCs, the rule does not provide expected timelines for FAA review and approval of AMOC requests; commenters request the FAA commit to specific review timelines (e.g., 60–90 days) to avoid grounding or noncompliance.

[P10] The provision giving authority to the Manager, ECO Branch, to approve AMOCs is acceptable, but stakeholders request clarity on delegation and whether regional Aircraft Certification Office managers may also approve AMOCs to expedite decisions.

[P11] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 may cause confusion since many principal inspectors are unfamiliar with engine-level AD AMOC technical review; suggest routing AMOCs directly to the certification office or ECO Branch for technical evaluation.

[P12] The instruction to address direct AMOC submissions to the person in paragraph (j)(1) is circular unless paragraph (j)(1) is repeated verbatim; request the FAA ensure paragraph references are correct and include the actual contact name in the main body for clarity.

[P13] Permitting email submission to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov is helpful, but the AD should confirm whether attachments of proprietary or export-controlled data are acceptable by email and whether secure transfer options are available.

[P14] The requirement to notify the principal inspector or local FSDO before using any approved AMOC could cause operational delays if the principal inspector is unavailable; request wording that allows prior notification within a reasonable timeframe (e.g., 24–72 hours) and permits electronic notification.

[P15] The contact information for Christopher McGuire lacks an email address in the AD text; commenters request inclusion of direct email and fax to facilitate timely technical inquiries.

[P15] Stakeholders request that Christopher McGuire’s duties and authority be clarified—whether he is the sole technical point of contact for interpretations or whether other ECO Branch engineers can provide guidance to avoid bottlenecks.

[P16] The AD directs parties to contact CFM in Cincinnati for service information but fails to state whether the referenced ESM Data Modules are publicly releasable or require a paid subscription; request that the FAA ensure the required service information is made available at no cost for compliance or provide FAA-copied versions.

[P16] The AD says service information can be viewed at the FAA branch "call for availability," which is not practicable for global operators; request electronic access links and confirmation of hours, language, and copy fee policies.

[P6] Legal commenters note the AD mandates incorporation of manufacturer ESM text by reference without following the formal Office of the Federal Register (OFR) incorporation-by-reference procedures; request confirmation that OFR procedures were followed and publicly accessible copies are available.

[P5] Maintenance organizations operating under foreign approvals cannot typically complete ALS revisions within 15 days because of internal approval processes and EASA/foreign authority notifications; request alignment of compliance timeframe with international approval processes.

[P3] The AD lacks a clear list of specified compliance times for each inserted paragraph and whether these are recurring inspection intervals or single actions; request a table mapping each ESM paragraph to explicit compliance time language (hours/cycles/days).

[P8] Small operators and part 145 repair stations rely on authorized deviations under their continuous airworthiness management; the no-alternative rule should allow previously-approved deviations to continue unless explicitly superseded.

[P10] Legal counsel requests clarification on whether an AMOC approval for one operator will be considered equally applicable to other U.S. operators or whether separate AMOC approvals must be obtained in each case.

[P7] Operators request that the FAA provide an impact analysis and estimated costs of mandating the insertion of the specified ESM paragraphs, including labor hours and potential downtime, as required under the Administrative Procedure Act for significant rulemaking.

[P2] Labor unions and maintenance personnel request clarification on whether these ALS revisions will change mandatory training, certification requirements, or create additional human performance burdens that affect staffing and shift patterns.

[P16] The AD should specify whether compliance with the ESM paragraphs requires use of CFM-authored tools or software and whether license fees apply; operators need this to budget for compliance.

[P14] Airlines request that notification of AMOC use be allowed via electronic logbook entries or equivalent recordkeeping systems rather than requiring direct contact with a principal inspector, to streamline operations.

[P1] Consumer and public-safety advocacy groups request the FAA extend the comment period to allow cross-border stakeholders (EASA, foreign operators) time to coordinate joint comments on harmonization and safety implications.

[P1] The proposed rule’s blanket requirement that both ozone and CO nonattainment areas implement I/M programs fails to account for areas where mobile source emissions are an insignificant contributor to violations; EPA should allow waiver/opt-out for areas with documented mobile-source insignificance.

[P2] Section 51.350(a)(1) will impose enhanced I/M on any MSA in an ozone transport region with 1990 population ≥100,000 — industry asks EPA to update the population baseline to a recent census (e.g., 2010/2020) to reflect current population patterns and avoid imposing outdated burdens.

[P2] Environmental groups support §51.350(a)(1) but request clarification that “portion of an MSA” means any county or census tract included in the MSA, and urge EPA to require contiguous suburban jurisdictions that share vehicle fleets to be included.

[P3] §51.350(a)(2)’s reliance on the “1990 urbanized area” for trigger thresholds is arbitrary and must be revised to use the most recent Census data; using 1990 misclassifies rapidly growing areas and undermines the rule’s environmental effectiveness.

[P4] Under §51.350(a)(3) requiring continued operation of previously SIP-approved I/M programs, states should be permitted to modernize testing methods (e.g., OBD-only testing) without being forced to maintain legacy hardware-oriented systems.

[P5] §51.350(a)(3) that any area previously required by the CAA to have I/M must implement a basic I/M should allow grandfathered jurisdictions to submit equivalency demonstrations using newer, less intrusive testing that achieve the same emission reductions.

[P6] §51.350(a)(4) mandating basic I/M in any 1990 urbanized area in a moderate ozone area could impose high costs on small jurisdictions — EPA should include a cost-effectiveness screen or de minimis economic impact exemption for urbanized areas under a specified vehicle population threshold (e.g., <10,000 vehicles).

[P7] §51.350(a)(5) requires basic I/M in 1990 urbanized areas for areas with population <200,000 — commenters request that the population threshold use current year figures and that EPA allow phased implementation for communities with limited administrative capacity.

[P8] §51.350(a)(6) requires implementation of basic I/M when boundaries change per §107(d)(4)(A); states need a clear timeline (e.g., at least 18 months after boundary change) to update systems, and EPA should permit temporary transition measures to avoid abrupt compliance requirements.

[P9] §51.350(a)(7) triggers enhanced I/M in newly included urbanized areas when 1980 urban population ≥200,000 — using 1980 population data is unjustifiable and must be replaced; this retroactive baseline will have inequitable fiscal impacts.

[P10] §51.350(a)(8) requires basic I/M upon reclassification from marginal to moderate — legal experts note that the rule should specify whether the reclassification effective date or the SIP revision approval date controls the start of the I/M requirement to avoid ambiguity.

[P11] §51.350(a)(8) (reclassification to serious or worse) makes enhanced I/M contingent on 1980 urban population ≥200,000 otherwise basic I/M applies — commenters request that EPA instead use contemporaneous population data and clarify treatment for multi-county urbanized areas split by political boundaries.

[P12] §51.350(a)(9) (moderate→serious) duplicates other reclassification provisions and creates confusion; EPA should consolidate reclassification rules and clarify which provision governs for ozone vs CO to avoid inconsistent state obligations.

[P13] §51.350(b)(1)’s allowance to exclude largely rural counties with density <200 persons/sq mile (1990 Census) could create enforcement and leakage problems at county borders; commenters ask EPA to require buffer-zone analysis and to permit exclusion only where commuting and vehicle travel patterns show minimal cross-boundary interactions.

[P14] §51.350(b)(2) permits some urban exclusions if equal numbers of non-urban residents are added — the “equal number” compensation rule is vague; states request guidance on how to measure “non-urban residents included” and whether vehicles per capita or VMT should be used instead.

[P15] Under §51.350(b)(3), credits from expanded coverage can be applied to RFP and offsets but not to enhanced I/M performance standard — states argue this penalizes voluntary expansions and request that expanded coverage be allowed to count toward both RFP and performance equivalency where demonstrated.

[P16] §51.350(b)(4) and (b)(4) second sentence requiring I/M in each state portion of a multi-state urbanized area with population ≥50,000 creates cross-jurisdictional implementation complexity; EPA should require coordination mechanisms and provide a harmonized model SIP template for multi-state areas.

[P17] §51.350(b)(4) further requiring enhanced I/M in portions with population ≥50,000 where the multi-state urbanized area meets 200,000 total population may force small states to run costly programs; commenters urge EPA to allow cost-sharing agreements and regional program administration.

[P18] §51.350(d) requiring SIPs to include legal authority to set program boundaries is appropriate, but municipal legal counsel request a sample set of statutory provisions or model enabling language to expedite state-level adoption.

[P19] §51.351(a) requires enhanced I/M to meet area-wide gpm performance standards — auto industry and testing contractors ask EPA to publish the numeric gpm target values and the baseline assumptions upfront and to allow states to run sensitivity analyses with EPA-approved tools.

[P20] §51.351(a) directing establishment of performance standards using specified model inputs and local characteristics could be administratively burdensome; states request EPA-provided default input datasets and an online equivalency tool to ensure consistent and efficient determinations.

[P21] §51.351(a)(1) model assumption of centralized testing is prescriptive — states with extensive decentralized inspection infrastructure should be allowed to adopt robust decentralized models if they can demonstrate equivalent effectiveness without the burdens of creating a centralized system.

[P22] §51.351(a)(2) model start dates (1983 for existing, 1994 for new) are obsolete; commenters ask EPA to replace these legacy dates with performance-based deadlines relative to SIP approval or area reclassification (e.g., within 24 months).

[P23] §51.351(a)(3) defaulting to annual testing (model assumption) conflicts with current best practices (e.g., biennial + OBD); many states request explicit allowance for OBD-based biennial regimes if equivalency is demonstrated.

[P24] §51.351(a)(4) model coverage of 1988+ vehicles may miss emission reductions possible from including pre-1988 vehicles; consumer groups request the option to expand coverage to older vehicles where cost-effective.

[P25] §51.351(a)(5) vehicle GVWR cutoff at 8,500 lb may exclude many light trucks/SUVs now used as personal vehicles; commenters ask EPA to re-evaluate GVWR thresholds to reflect current fleet composition and emissions contribution.

[P26] §51.351(a)(6) mandating IM240 for 1986+ vehicles is costly and may be unnecessary where OBD2 and remote sensing are available; testing vendors and states urge EPA to permit OBD-only or OBD+accelerated protocols as acceptable alternatives.

[P27] §51.351(a)(7)(i)-(vi) emission standards specified by model must be included in the preamble with numeric examples; SIP writers need the exact gpm values and how to apply them to mixed fleets to prepare approvable SIPs.

[P28] §51.351(a)(7)(vii)-(viii) specifying 1.2% CO and 220 ppm HC limits for 1981–1985 vehicles and dilution criteria require clarity on measurement methods and analyzer calibration standards — labs and regulators request explicit measurement protocols.

[P29] §51.351(a)(8) requiring visual inspections of catalysts and inlet restrictors for 1984+ vehicles raises privacy and mechanic-skill concerns; independent mechanics associations request training standards, inspector certification, and a list of acceptable inspection criteria.

[P30] §51.351(a)(9) evaporative system integrity and transient purge tests for 1983+/1986+ vehicles are technically complex; small jurisdictions ask EPA to provide test equipment specifications and funding assistance for purchasing expensive evaporative test rigs.

[P31] §51.351(a)(10)-(12) assumptions of a 20% failure rate for pre-1981 vehicles, 1% waiver rate, and 98% compliance appear optimistic/unsubstantiated — states ask for underlying data or allow states to propose realistic, locality-specific failure/waiver/compliance assumptions backed by local surveys.

[P32] §51.351(a)(13) requiring equivalence to the model program by 2000 (ozone) or 2001 (CO) is impossible for areas still designing programs; commenters demand revised milestone dates and transition provisions reflecting current calendar years.

[P33] §51.351(b) requiring on-road testing of at least 0.5% of the vehicle population is an important evaluator tool but may be logistically difficult and costly for small programs; EPA should permit pooled or regional on-road sampling to achieve statistical power cost-effectively.

[P34] §51.351(c) including OBD testing for vehicles certified to have OBD capability is appropriate, but manufacturers and states request details on pass/fail criteria, OBD connector protocols, and treatment of vehicles with malfunction indicator lamp (MIL) intermittency.

[P35] §51.351(d) requiring demonstration of equivalency using the most current EPA mobile source model creates potential administrative delays when model updates occur; EPA should allow states to use the model version current at the SIP submission date and provide a 12-month grace period after new model releases.

[P36] §51.351(d) exception that Administrator may exempt NOx reductions if not beneficial is vague — environmental groups request public criteria and thresholds for determining “not beneficial” and require transparent, documented economic and air quality analyses before any NOx exemption.

[P37] §51.351(e) special provisions for El Paso conditioned on prior SIP approval and milestones create unequal treatment and possible unfair precedent; other border areas request similar tailored relief and EPA to publish criteria for when special inputs are allowed.

[P38] §51.352(a) requiring basic I/M to meet area-wide gpm performance standards will be difficult for small rural programs lacking data; EPA should allow simplified performance measures or surrogate metrics (e.g., OBD fail rates) for basic programs.

[P39] §51.352(a)(1)-(5) basic model inputs (centralized testing, 1983 start, annual tests, 1968+ model years) are inconsistent with technological advances and current fleet characteristics; EPA should allow modernized basic models that incorporate OBD, remote sensing, and newer model year cutoffs.

[P40] §51.352(a)(7) mandating at least the stringency of 40 CFR part 85, subpart W is legally acceptable, but states request EPA to reconcile any conflicts between the new rule’s specific numeric limits and Subpart W to avoid contradictory SIP approval criteria.

[P41] §51.352(a)(8)-(11) assumptions of no control-device inspections for basic programs and a 0% waiver and 100% compliance rates are unrealistic; legal and programmatic commenters recommend EPA allow realistic waiver rates, and require states to justify any zero-waiver assumption with local data.

[P42] §51.352(a)(12) basic program equivalency deadlines (1997/1996) are obsolete; EPA must update milestone years and provide phased compliance timelines tied to SIP approval and funding availability.

[P43] §51.352(b) requiring OBD testing in basic programs for vehicles certified to have OBD capability is a reasonable modernization but needs detailed protocol specifications and retrofit/repair guidance for vehicles with inoperative OBD systems.

[P44] §51.352(c) equivalency demonstration using the current EPA model should include an appeal process and allow use of EPA-accepted third-party tools to reduce administrative burden.

Environmental groups support §51.350(a)(1) but request clarification that “portion of an MSA” means any county or census tract included in the MSA, and urge EPA to require contiguous suburban jurisdictions that share vehicle fleets to be included.

§51.350(a)(2)’s reliance on the “1990 urbanized area” for trigger thresholds is arbitrary and must be revised to use the most recent Census data; using 1990 misclassifies rapidly growing areas and undermines the rule’s environmental effectiveness.

§51.350(a)(5) requires basic I/M in 1990 urbanized areas for areas with population <200,000 — commenters request that the population threshold use current year figures and that EPA allow phased implementation for communities with limited administrative capacity.

§51.350(a)(8) requires basic I/M upon reclassification from marginal to moderate — legal experts note that the rule should specify whether the reclassification effective date or the SIP revision approval date controls the start of the I/M requirement to avoid ambiguity.

§51.350(a)(8) (reclassification to serious or worse) makes enhanced I/M contingent on 1980 urban population ≥200,000 otherwise basic I/M applies — commenters request that EPA instead use contemporaneous population data and clarify treatment for multi-county urbanized areas split by political boundaries.

§51.350(a)(9) (moderate→serious) duplicates other reclassification provisions and creates confusion; EPA should consolidate reclassification rules and clarify which provision governs for ozone vs CO to avoid inconsistent state obligations.

§51.350(b)(1)’s allowance to exclude largely rural counties with density <200 persons/sq mile (1990 Census) could create enforcement and leakage problems at county borders; commenters ask EPA to require buffer-zone analysis and to permit exclusion only where commuting and vehicle travel patterns show minimal cross-boundary interactions.

§51.350(b)(2) permits some urban exclusions if equal numbers of non-urban residents are added — the “equal number” compensation rule is vague; states request guidance on how to measure “non-urban residents included” and whether vehicles per capita or VMT should be used instead.

§51.350(b)(4) and (b)(4) second sentence requiring I/M in each state portion of a multi-state urbanized area with population ≥50,000 creates cross-jurisdictional implementation complexity; EPA should require coordination mechanisms and provide a harmonized model SIP template for multi-state areas.

§51.350(b)(4) further requiring enhanced I/M in portions with population ≥50,000 where the multi-state urbanized area meets 200,000 total population may force small states to run costly programs; commenters urge EPA to allow cost-sharing agreements and regional program administration.

§51.350(d) requiring SIPs to include legal authority to set program boundaries is appropriate, but municipal legal counsel request a sample set of statutory provisions or model enabling language to expedite state-level adoption.

§51.351(a) requires enhanced I/M to meet area-wide gpm performance standards — auto industry and testing contractors ask EPA to publish the numeric gpm target values and the baseline assumptions upfront and to allow states to run sensitivity analyses with EPA-approved tools.

§51.351(a) directing establishment of performance standards using specified model inputs and local characteristics could be administratively burdensome; states request EPA-provided default input datasets and an online equivalency tool to ensure consistent and efficient determinations.

§51.351(a)(1) model assumption of centralized testing is prescriptive — states with extensive decentralized inspection infrastructure should be allowed to adopt robust decentralized models if they can demonstrate equivalent effectiveness without the burdens of creating a centralized system.

§51.351(a)(2) model start dates (1983 for existing, 1994 for new) are obsolete; commenters ask EPA to replace these legacy dates with performance-based deadlines relative to SIP approval or area reclassification (e.g., within 24 months).

§51.351(a)(4) model coverage of 1988+ vehicles may miss emission reductions possible from including pre-1988 vehicles; consumer groups request the option to expand coverage to older vehicles where cost-effective.

§51.351(a)(5) vehicle GVWR cutoff at 8,500 lb may exclude many light trucks/SUVs now used as personal vehicles; commenters ask EPA to re-evaluate GVWR thresholds to reflect current fleet composition and emissions contribution.

[P1] Environmental groups will assert § 121.2 should require applicants to submit copies of all communications with the certifying authority, not just the final certification, to ensure transparency.

[P2] State agencies will object to the one‑year cap in § 121.4(a) as inflexible for complex projects and ask the agency to allow extensions beyond one year where justified and agreed by all parties.

[P2] Federal permitting offices will support § 121.4(a)’s one‑year cap as necessary to prevent indefinite delays, and urge retention of the categorical reasonable‑time approach for routine projects.

[P3] Project proponents will request § 121.4(b) include an explicit list of what constitutes “written notice” (e.g., electronic submission, certified mail) to avoid disputes about whether the Federal agency was properly notified.

[P3] Certifying authorities will request that § 121.4(b) be modified to permit them to require certain supporting documentation at time of notice to avoid multiple followups.

[P4] Industry and state agencies will insist that the 15‑day obligation in § 121.4(c) be extended (e.g., to 30 days) when Federal agencies are required to gather complex internal information or make categorical determinations, otherwise it is unworkable.

[P4] Legal commentators will claim § 121.4(c)’s 15‑day timeline may conflict with existing interagency review processes and request an ability to toll the period for mutually agreed reasons.

[P5] Project proponents will request that § 121.4(c)(1) require Federal agencies to state the basis for selecting a categorical vs. case‑by‑case reasonable period to promote predictability.

[P6] Certifying authorities will point out that § 121.4(c)(2) (providing date received) should require Federal agencies to use the certifying authority’s receipt date if earlier, to avoid manufactured waiver dates.

[P7] States will object that § 121.4(c)(3) (date waiver will occur) could be used strategically by Federal agencies to force premature waivers and request that waiver dates account for any pending legitimate information requests from certifying authorities.

[P8] Environmental groups will demand § 121.4(d)’s list of factors include consideration of cumulative impacts and climate change effects, not just project‑level complexity.

[P8] Industry will argue § 121.4(d) must require Federal agencies to document how each listed factor was weighed when setting the reasonable period, to avoid arbitrary deadlines.

[P9] Certifying authorities will request clarification in § 121.4(d)(1) on how “complexity” is defined and examples of complexity levels that would justify longer reasonable periods.

[P10] Environmental organizations will argue § 121.4(d)(2) (potential for any discharge) should mandate longer review periods for projects with transboundary or persistent pollutants.

[P11] Scientific reviewers will request that § 121.4(d)(3) require explicit criteria for when additional study/evaluation is necessary and that Federal agencies allow time for peer review of such studies.

[P12] Certifying authorities will support § 121.4(e) permitting modifications but request that any modification be based on a public, written justification and made available to applicants and the public.

[P12] Project proponents will request § 121.4(e) be amended to prevent Federal agencies from repeatedly modifying the reasonable period within the one‑year cap in a way that effectively delays decisions.

[P13] States will argue the absolute one‑year prohibition in § 121.4(e) is inconsistent with federalism and with statutory text that contemplates reasonable time, and ask for flexibility where state law prescribes longer review periods.

[P14] Both certifying authorities and project proponents will request that § 121.4(e)(1) allow oral emergency extension requests (with immediate written follow‑up) in urgent circumstances.

[P15] Stakeholders will request that § 121.4(e)(2) require Federal agencies to publish modifications to the reasonable period on a centralized public docket and explain the rationale.

[P16] Certifying authorities will challenge § 121.4(f)’s prohibition on requesting withdrawal as an infringement on routine administrative practice where a certifying authority needs a revised or supplemental submittal to complete review; they will ask for an exception allowing limited requests for voluntary withdrawal/re‑submission when agreed by the proponent.

[P17] Industry will warn that § 121.5(a)’s requirement that certification actions be completed within the established reasonable period will unfairly penalize certifying authorities that need to obtain additional legal or technical input, and request tolling options.

[P17] Legal commenters will assert § 121.5(a) must make clear that actions “within the scope of certification” include determinations about applicability of water quality standards and designated uses.

[P18] Certifying authorities will support § 121.5(a)’s permission to expressly waive certification but ask that waiver procedures include written explanations and public notice requirements to ensure accountability.

[P19] Environmental groups will oppose § 121.5(b)’s waiver option being used to avoid review; they will ask for strict limits and mandatory findings before a waiver can be accepted.

[P20] Industry and certifying authorities will request that § 121.5(c) require a standardized form or template for written grants to reduce litigation over sufficiency of the “statement that the discharge will comply.”

[P21] Legal advocates will ask that § 121.5(d) require that each condition include findings of fact and legal authority sufficient to allow judicial review, not just bare citations.

[P22] Environmental commenters will insist § 121.5(d)(1) require quantitative explanations (e.g., pollutant load limits or monitoring frequency) showing how the condition assures compliance, not just a narrative statement.

[P23] States will object that § 121.5(d)(2) forces them to disclose internal legal analyses by requiring a legal citation for each condition and request that the provision be limited to public statutes/regulations rather than internal policy citations.

[P24] Industry will support § 121.5(d)(3) but ask for a clear standard on what constitutes an adequate discussion of less stringent alternatives to avoid endless negotiation.

[P25] Project proponents will request § 121.5(e) require denials to include a clear and specific list of corrective measures the proponent could take to obtain certification, not just data requests.

[P26] Legal commenters will emphasize § 121.5(e)(1) must require citation to the exact provision of state or federal water quality standards alleged to be violated to satisfy due process.

[P27] Certifying authorities will request § 121.5(e)(2) allow the denial explanation to be supplemented if new information comes to light, rather than being final and unchangeable.

[P28] Industry will argue § 121.5(e)(3) should limit the specificity of required data identifications to avoid certifying authorities demanding burdensome, speculative data that cannot be obtained within the reasonable period.

[P29] Certifying authorities will support § 121.5(f) requiring grant or waiver where no water quality requirements apply but ask for guidance on how to document determinations that “no requirements apply” to avoid future challenges.

[P30] Project proponents will applaud § 121.6(a) allowing re‑submission after denial and request explicit instructions on how prior denials and information requests carry forward to subsequent submissions.

[P31] Federal agencies will request clarification in § 121.6(b) of the standard the agency uses to determine that a state denial “satisfies” CWA § 401, to avoid inconsistent application across agencies.

[P32] Environmental groups will contest § 121.6(b)’s prohibition on issuing the license/permit when a denial “satisfies” requirements, urging stricter deference to state determinations and non‑discretionary bar to issuance.

[P33] Industry groups will object to § 121.6(c) requiring the Federal agency to notify certifying authorities of insufficiency without a clear, expedited process for resolving disputes, and will request statutory timeline commitments.

[P34] Certifying authorities will welcome § 121.6(c)(1)’s opportunity to remedy deficiencies but ask for the right to a single, reasonable cure period tied to the original reasonable period rather than open‑ended negotiation.

[P35] Project proponents will object to § 121.6(c)(2)’s instruction to treat lack of satisfactory decision as a waiver, arguing this could incentivize certifying authorities to delay and then have their inaction be converted to a waiver without meaningful review; they will request safeguards.

[P36] Environmental advocates will challenge § 121.7(a)(1) allowing waiver by express written notice as inconsistent with some states’ laws that require substantive findings before waiving certification; they request cross‑reference to state law limitations.

[P37] States will request § 121.7(a)(1) require that any express waiver include a written explanation and public notice, not just a bare statement of waiver.

[P38] Environmental groups will object to § 121.7(a)(2) deeming failure/refusal to act a waiver and ask for protections that prevent waiver where the certifying authority has a pending good‑faith request for information or review.

[P39] Project proponents will request that § 121.7(b) require the Federal agency’s written notice of waiver to include a clear explanation of why the certifying authority’s inaction led to waiver to avoid abuse.

[P40] Industry will support § 121.7(c) that a Federal agency notice of waiver satisfies the applicant’s requirement, but will ask for a standardized waiver form and clear recordkeeping instructions.

[P41] Environmental groups will oppose § 121.7(d) permitting immediate issuance of a license/permit after agency waiver and request a short additional waiting period for certifying authorities to challenge the waiver.

[P42] States and legal commenters will insist § 121.8(a) require that incorporated certification conditions be enforceable by states/tribes as well as the federal government, or at minimum clarify the enforcement mechanisms.

[P43] Federal agencies will welcome § 121.8(a)(1) but ask for a defined, short timeline for notifying certifying authorities of deficient conditions and for the content of such notices to avoid disputes.

[P44] Certifying authorities will request that § 121.8(a)(2) allow them a meaningful cure period (not merely “prior to the end of the reasonable period” which may be impracticable) and require the Federal agency to state what remediation will be sufficient.

[P45] Project proponents will request § 121.8(b) require that permit/license root documents explicitly mark which conditions derive from the certification and include the certifying authority’s name and date, to avoid ambiguity in enforcement.

[P46] Certifying authorities will argue § 121.9(a) must allow remote or scheduled inspections and require the agency to pay reasonable inspection costs when the certifying authority initiates the inspection.

[P47] Industry will request § 121.9(b) require certifying authorities to provide written notice of alleged violations within a specified short timeframe after inspection and allow the proponent an opportunity to cure before federal enforcement is triggered.

[P48] Federal agencies will welcome § 121.9(c) but ask for clarity that federal enforcement responsibility applies only to conditions incorporated into the federal permit, not to state‑only conditions.

[P49] States will object to § 121.10(a)’s automatic notice to the Administrator upon receipt of application and certification as duplicative and burdensome, and ask for a threshold test (e.g., pollutant load or cross‑boundary effect) before notice is required.

[P50] Neighboring jurisdictions will support § 121.10(b) giving the Administrator 30 days to flag potential cross‑boundary effects and request that the Administrator be required (not discretionary) to review projects with potential interstate impacts.

[P51] Industry will warn that § 121.10(c) could be used by neighboring jurisdictions to delay projects and request that the federal license/permit not be stayed automatically pending resolution absent a specific showing of probable harm.

[P52] Neighboring states will request § 121.10(c)(1) require the Administrator to provide copies of specific technical materials and modeling data, not just identify “materials,” to enable meaningful review within 60 days.

[P53] Environmental groups will urge § 121.10(c)(1) to require public disclosure of the materials provided to neighboring jurisdictions and the Administrator to ensure transparency.

[P54] Neighboring jurisdictions will request § 121.10(c)(2) add a requirement that objections include proposed alternative conditions to mitigate impacts, not just identification of affected waters and standards.

[P55] Public interest groups will call for § 121.10(d) to require the hearing be held in the affected community (not remote) and to include meaningful opportunity for local stakeholders to present evidence.

[P56] Federal agencies will ask § 121.10(d)(1) to allow shorter notice than 30 days for emergency projects while preserving the 30‑day minimum for routine matters.

[P57] The Administrator’s office will request clarification in § 121.10(d)(2) on the scope of the “evaluation and recommendations” expected at the hearing and whether a written post‑hearing report is required.

[P58] Neighboring jurisdictions will insist § 121.10(d)(3) require the Federal agency to issue a written response showing how each recommendation/evidence was considered when deciding whether additional conditions are needed.

[P59] Environmental advocates will support § 121.10(d)(4) but request a clear standard for when additional conditions “cannot assure compliance” and require the sponsoring Federal agency to document why no conditions would suffice.

[P60] Tribal governments will emphasize § 121.11(a) must explicitly preserve tribal authority where tribes are the certifying authority under § 401, rather than defaulting to the Administrator.

[P61] The Administrator’s office will request § 121.11(b) clarify procedural standards the Administrator must follow when stepping in, including timelines and public notice.

[P62] Project proponents will object to § 121.12(a)’s mandatory pre‑filing meeting 30 days prior, arguing it adds cost and delay for small projects and requesting an exemption for minor activities.

[P63] Certifying authorities will support § 121.12(b) but ask for a defined maximum “timely” period for granting a pre‑filing meeting (e.g., 14 days) to prevent open‑ended delays.

[P64] Both sides will support § 121.12(c) requiring discussion of water quality effects but ask for a required pre‑meeting checklist so expectations are uniform.

[P65] Project proponents will request § 121.12(c) limit the extent of documentation required at pre‑filing to prevent premature demands for extensive studies before an application is filed.

[P66] Certifying authorities will ask § 121.12(d) to require Federal agencies to identify points of contact within a specific number of days (e.g., 10 days) after the meeting to facilitate coordination.

[P67] Industry will warn that § 121.13(a)’s 30‑day window to request additional information is too short for complex projects that require interagency technical consultation and ask for 45 or 60 days.

[P68] Certifying authorities will support § 121.13(b) limiting information requests to scope but request a definition of “directly related” to prevent fishing expeditions into unrelated project aspects.

[P69] Project proponents will assert § 121.13(c) must prohibit certifying authorities from requesting data that cannot reasonably be produced within the reasonable period, including multi‑season ecological surveys.

[P70] Certifying authorities will ask § 121.13(d) to specify minimum reasonable deadlines they must give applicants when requesting additional information, to account for time needed for consultants or labs.

[P71] Industry will challenge § 121.13(d)(1) that project proponents “shall comply” with all deadlines as unrealistic when third‑party testing is required; they will ask for a good‑cause standard for missed deadlines.

[P72] Certifying authorities will request § 121.13(d)(2) require Federal agencies to extend the reasonable period if certifying authorities need additional time to review unexpectedly voluminous supplemental data.

[P73] Project proponents will welcome § 121.13(e) but warn that it should not be used by certifying authorities to manufacture additional time by repeatedly requesting information and relying on proponent delays to extend review.

[P74] Public interest groups will support § 121.14(a) but ask that the 20‑day public notice requirement also include a public comment period of defined length (e.g., 30 days) and a public docket for submitted materials.

[P75] Environmental advocates will recommend § 121.14(b) require hearings where any substantial public objections are filed rather than leaving hearings to the Administrator’s discretion.

[P76] Federal agencies will welcome § 121.15(a) assistance provisions but request clear resource commitments (e.g., timelines for providing assistance) so requests are handled promptly.

[P77] Certifying authorities and project proponents will support § 121.15(b) but ask the rule to state that Administrator assistance is advisory and nonbinding, and to provide a timeline for responses to assistance requests.

raw_output:
[P1] The deadline scheme in §63.5990(a) is ambiguous because it references two nearly identical compliance dates (181 days before and 180 days after publication) — commenters should request clarification of the exact effective dates and which date applies to which provisions to avoid conflicting compliance obligations.

[P1] Industry commenters will assert that requiring continuous compliance "at all times" with emission limits in Tables 1–4 (both before and after the referenced dates) is infeasible during foreseeable maintenance activities and request explicit limited, defined allowances for routine maintenance periods.

[P2] Environmental advocacy groups will object to exempting SSM periods from the compliance requirement so long as a control device is "used," arguing this creates a loophole allowing elevated emissions during SSMs and urging that SSM emissions remain subject to numeric limits and reporting.

[P2] Legal commenters will request a definition of "using a control device to comply with an emission limit" to avoid disputes over whether partial operation, bypasses, or reduced-efficiency operation during SSM qualifies for the exception.

[P3] State air agencies will request harmonization of the two staged compliance deadlines in §63.5990(a) with state implementation plan (SIP) schedules, because the staggered language could conflict with SIP-approved schedules and enforcement actions.

[P4] Facilities will comment that the pre-effective-date requirement to "operate and maintain ... per §63.6(e)(1)(i)" lacks specificity about inspection frequency and preventive maintenance standards, and ask EPA to include measurable operation and maintenance (O&M) metrics or allow alternative O&M plans approved by the permitting authority.

[P5] Small business trade associations will argue that the post-effective-date requirement to "continuously operate and maintain ... using safety and good air pollution control practices" is unbounded and could be interpreted to require capital upgrades; they request that EPA clarify that the duty requires only reasonable, cost‑effective measures and does not require surpassing the applicable standard (see P6).

[P6] Industry commenters will welcome §63.5990(b)'s clarification that the general duty to minimize emissions does not compel reductions beyond the standard, but will ask EPA to explicitly state that this exception applies during SSM periods and to recordkeeping/inspection obligations to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P7] Commenters representing affected sources will state that the requirement to develop an SSMP before the earlier specified date is duplicative with existing SSM plans required under §63.6(e) and request EPA allow submission of previously approved SSM plans rather than new plans.

[P41] Small entities will request relief from immediate mandatory electronic submission of subsequent semiannual reports (P41) when CEDRI is challenging to access, and ask EPA to maintain the option for paper filings for a longer transition timeframe.

[P42] Operators who must follow SSMPs will ask EPA to clarify what constitutes "actions consistent with your SSMP" for inclusion in the pre-date compliance report (P42) to prevent inconsistent enforcement during SSM events.

[P43] Environmental groups will object to removing SSMP requirements post-date (P43), arguing that SSMPs are necessary for transparency and public protection during upsets, and ask EPA to retain at least limited SSMP and SSM reporting obligations.

[P46] Facilities will ask for an explicit methodology or examples for calculating "total operating time" of each affected source (P46) to ensure consistent reporting across operators.

[P47] Operators will seek clarification whether the post-date requirement to record number, date, time, and duration of each failure (P47) applies to only exceedances of numeric limits or to any operational deviation, and request threshold language to avoid over-reporting.

[P53] Report preparers will ask for explicit instructions and validation rules for the specified electronic CEDRI form (P53), including character limits, allowed units, and file attachment size/type restrictions.

[P54] Facilities will request that the fallback paper submission option for unavailable CEDRI forms (P54) explicitly allow submission to state agencies and require EPA to post notice when CEDRI is unavailable so regulated entities are not penalized.

[P55] Commenters will ask EPA to provide clear guidance on the "one year availability" rule (P55) including when the clock starts (date of form publication vs date form becomes operational) and whether EPA will provide interim extensions.

[P56] Industry will seek clarity that meeting the submission deadlines "regardless of method" (P56) will accept transmissions that are technically successful but later found to have format errors, subject to good-faith correction periods.

[P57] Trade associations will request detailed instructions for CBI physical media submittals (P57), including acceptable encryption, packing, and tracking requirements, to safeguard sensitive information and ensure receipt.

[P58] Facilities using control systems will request confirmation that the 5‑year performance test interval (P58) may be extended based on demonstrated continuous compliance and equipment stability, subject to Administrator approval, to reduce testing costs.

[P59] Labs will request that the 60-day submission timeline for performance test results (P59) apply only after data quality checks and ERT conversions are complete and ask for formal allowance for 30 additional days when complex QA is required.

[P60] Commenters will request that EPA publish the required ERT-generated file formats and XML schema for performance test submissions well in advance (P60) and provide a validation tool to check files before submission.

[P61] Sources using non-ERT-supported test methods will ask EPA to permit submission of results in commonly used formats (e.g., CSV, PDF) and to accept other electronic file types if they conform to an XML schema (P61), with a transition timeline.

[P62] Industry will reiterate the need for explicit procedures to protect CBI when submitting performance test data (P62), including templates for redacted CDX files and guidance for physical submissions to the CBI office.

[P63] Companies will ask EPA to clarify what documentation constitutes sufficient proof of system outage (P63) and to require EPA to post contemporaneous outage notices so that regulated entities are not disadvantaged.

[P64] Commenters will object to the narrow 5-business-day window for outage claims (P65) and force majeure claims (P72), recommending expansion to at least 10 business days to account for weekends/holidays and multi-day outages.

[P65] Legal commenters will note that permitting both planned and unplanned outages to qualify (P66) could encourage planned maintenance to coincide with reporting deadlines and request a prohibition on relying on planned, discretionary outages as a reason for late submissions.

[P66] Industry will request that the "prompt notification" obligations for outage and force majeure claims (P67, P73) include specific timelines (e.g., within 2 business days of knowledge) and allow email notice to a designated inbox to ensure receipt.

[P67] Commenters will request a standardized form or template for outage/force majeure written descriptions (P68, P74) to streamline EPA review and reduce administrative burden on both parties.

[P68] Regulated entities will seek an objective appeals process or time-bound EPA review for Administrator discretion to accept outage or force majeure claims (P69, P75), rather than leaving decisions entirely to unstructured discretion.

[P69] Facilities will request that the obligation to submit reports "as soon as possible" after an outage or force majeure (P70, P76) be defined (e.g., within 5 business days after restoration) to provide certainty.

[P70] Legal counsel will request clearer criteria EPA will use to evaluate force majeure claims (P71) including examples of acceptable events and thresholds for economic hardship versus physical impossibility.

[P71] Facilities will ask whether historical SSM records required pre-date (P77) must be retained for a fixed period (e.g., 5 years) beyond the facility lifespan and request harmonization with P15 retention requirements.

[P72] Trade associations will request confirmation that after the specified date the no-longer-required SSM recordkeeping (P78) does not preclude enforcement actions based on other recordkeeping provisions or existing SIP requirements.

[P73] IT managers will endorse the ability to maintain CEDRI-submitted records in electronic format (P79) but request EPA clarify acceptable electronic retention systems, metadata standards, and backup requirements to ensure auditability.

[P74] State and local agencies will reiterate that electronic recordkeeping does not remove on-site availability requirements (P80) and ask EPA to require an explicit timeframe (e.g., within 2 business days) to produce electronic records during on-site inspections.

[P75] Industry will request that Table 15 (P81) include cross-references to subpart-specific report examples and a consolidated report calendar to reduce confusion about overlapping deadlines.

[P76] Community groups will request that immediate reporting of SSM events (Table 15 item 2, P82) remain required after the specified date rather than being dropped, to ensure timely public notification and protect local health.

[P77] Facilities using control systems will request EPA to allow coordination of the 5-year performance test requirement in Table 15 item 3 (P83) with other regulatory testing schedules (NSPS, state rules) to reduce duplicative downtime and testing costs.

[P78] Aviation stakeholders will request that the amendment to 14 CFR 71.1 (P84) include a public availability statement and confirm the effective date for incorporating FAA Order JO 7400.11H to avoid confusion among pilots and airspace users.

[P79] Wilder Airport and local governments will request confirmation that the new Class E airspace (P85, P86) starting at 700 ft and extending 7 miles does not conflict with existing local airspace designations or impose inadvertent constraints on low-altitude operations (agricultural, emergency services).

[P80] Emergency services and agricultural operators will ask for an assessment of potential impacts from the new AGL SD E5 airspace (P85/P86) on crop-dusting, aerial firefighting, and medevac operations and request coordination procedures or waivers where necessary.

[P81] Environmental and health NGOs will request that EPA require public posting of enforcement actions, deviations, and performance test failures associated with the subpart on a publicly accessible website to improve transparency and community right-to-know.

[P82] Several commenters will urge EPA to provide a consolidated guidance document and compliance checklist addressing all cross-referenced electronic reporting (CEDRI/CDX), SSM, monitoring plan, testing, and retention requirements to reduce inconsistent interpretations among agencies, regulated entities, and the public.

[P1] The requirement in § 510.115(a) that specified hospitals submit a written participation election letter during the voluntary election period lacks clarity on whether a hospital may rescind or amend its election after submission; request explicit provisions for amendment and rescission and associated timelines.

[P1] The rule does not specify whether joint-venture hospitals or hospitals operating multiple CCNs must submit separate participation election letters for each CCN; request explicit instruction that each CCN requires its own letter or clarification that a single letter may cover multiple CCNs.

[P2] By including hospitals with a CCN primary address in voluntary MSAs at § 510.115(a)(1), CMS may unintentionally capture hospitals that primarily serve patients outside the MSA; request an operational definition of "CCN primary address" and propose an alternative criterion based on patient origin or majority of discharges.

[P2] Industry commenters will argue that excluding hospitals under § 510.100(b) is insufficiently delineated here — request CMS publish a list of CCNs in voluntary MSAs and identify which are excluded under § 510.100(b) before the election period.

[P3] The inclusion of "low-volume hospitals with a CCN primary address in a mandatory MSA" in § 510.115(a)(2) imposes the participation election requirement on small hospitals that may lack administrative capacity; request a waiver or simplified election process for low-volume hospitals and clarification of the threshold defining "low-volume."

[P3] Legal experts will question whether requiring low-volume hospitals in mandatory MSAs to submit election letters converts a nominally voluntary option into a de facto mandate; request CMS clarify that failure to submit does not produce punitive effects beyond exclusion from NPRA (or, if it does, to explicitly state those consequences).

[P4] Requiring rural hospitals in mandatory MSAs to submit election letters (§ 510.115(a)(3)) ignores connectivity and resource constraints in rural settings; request alternative submission methods (paper, fax) and extended deadlines for rural hospitals, plus technical assistance.

[P4] Rural hospital associations will request an exemption or extended timeline for rural hospitals facing staffing shortages, and data demonstrating whether rural hospitals in mandatory MSAs intended to be within scope.

[P5] The fixed voluntary participation election period of January 1–31, 2018 (§ 510.115(b)) is unreasonably short and falls during holiday/post-holiday staffing transitions; request extension of the window to at least 60 or 90 days and allowance for late submissions with good-cause.

[P5] Hospitals that learn of the rule late or whose boards meet infrequently will assert the Jan 31 deadline is arbitrary; request CMS provide an overnight mail receipt date or electronic timestamp acceptance and a grace period for mailed submissions.

[P6] The condition in § 510.115(c) that the election letter serve as the model participation agreement and be accepted only if it meets listed criteria creates significant risk that imperfectly formatted letters will be rejected; request CMS to provide an editable template, pre-submission validation, and an opportunity to cure defects before rejection.

[P6] Privacy advocates will request that CMS affirm whether the participation letter will be publicly posted and, if so, redaction rules for contact information included in the model participation agreement.

[P7] The requirement to include specific identifying information and CEHRT attestation (§ 510.115(c)(1)) may capture personally identifiable contact details of executives; request guidance on acceptable redaction or use of corporate contact points rather than individual e-mails/phone numbers.

[P7] Hospitals will request clarity on what constitutes acceptable CEHRT attestation language, especially for hospitals in the process of implementing or upgrading CEHRT but not yet fully certified.

[P8] The certification required in § 510.115(c)(2) is broad and open-ended ("will") — request CMS clarify what degree of future compliance is required (best efforts vs. strict guarantees) and whether inadvertent noncompliance exposes hospitals to sanctions.

[P9] The promise in § 510.115(c)(2)(i) to "comply with all applicable requirements of this part and all other laws and regulations" is overbroad; legal commenters will request specification of which statutes/regulations are intended and a reasonable compliance standard (e.g., "to the extent applicable and practicable").

[P10] The certification under § 510.115(c)(2)(ii) that hospitals will submit "accurate, complete and truthful" data invites criminal or civil exposure for honest errors; request safe-harbor for good-faith reporting errors and a correction process without immediate enforcement.

[P11] The signature requirement in § 510.115(c)(3) that the election letter be signed by the hospital administrator, CFO, or CEO may be impractical for corporate systems where an authorized representative signs on behalf of multiple hospitals; request allowance for electronically authenticated signatures by authorized delegates and clear corporate delegation documentation.

[P11] Compliance officers will request confirmation that scanned signatures and electronic signatures consistent with ESIGN/UETA are acceptable under § 510.115(c)(3).

[P12] The requirement that the election letter be "submitted in the form and manner specified by CMS" (§ 510.115(c)(4)) without specifying that form/manner in the rule creates legal uncertainty; request CMS publish the acceptable submission form/manner (portal URL, mailing address, file formats) well before the election period and allow alternate submission in emergencies.

[P13] The quarterly clinician engagement list requirement for hospitals choosing CEHRT (§ 510.120(c)) imposes significant administrative burden; hospitals and physician groups will request that CMS align this reporting with existing quarterly reporting cycles or allow semi-annual submission.

[P14] The requirement that clinician engagement lists include information "for the period of the performance year specified by CMS" (§ 510.120(c) following sentence) needs clarity on whether historical data must be backfilled and whether changes during the year require resubmission; request explicit instructions on update frequency and retrospective reporting.

[P15] For § 510.120(c)(1), hospitals must report every physician/nonphysician/therapist who is not a CJR collaborator — physician groups will object to reporting requirements that may duplicate other lists and request clarity on overlap, data sharing safeguards, and confirmation that employed clinicians vs independent contractors are treated consistently.

[P16] Requiring TIN and NPI for each clinician (§ 510.120(c)(1)(i)) raises privacy and tax-identity concerns; request that CMS limit collection to NPI only or provide secure transmission and narrow data-use policies to prevent unauthorized IRS/credentialing data linking.

[P17] The start and end date requirement for contractual relationships (§ 510.120(c)(1)(ii)) is likely difficult for hospitals with rolling or informal arrangements; request CMS allow approximate dates (month/year) or status indicators (active/inactive) and define "contractual relationship" for casual on-call arrangements.

[P18] The § 510.120(d) attestation if there are no individuals to report imposes a formal filing obligation even when nil — hospitals will request a simplified checkbox submission or waiver for hospitals that previously reported "no individuals" and permit annual rather than quarterly attestations.

[P19] The documentation maintenance requirement in § 510.120(e)(1) to retain CEHRT attestation and clinician lists imposes recordkeeping costs — request a specific retention period (e.g., 6 years consistent with Medicare) and allow electronic recordkeeping standards.

[P20] Requiring retention "in accordance with § 510.110" (§ 510.120(e)(2)) without summarizing key retention obligations may cause confusion; request CMS to reproduce or cross-reference the exact retention timeframe and access procedures in this rule or guidance.

[P21] The cancellation provisions in § 510.210(b) that exclude episodes from NPRA when certain events occur will create perverse incentives to delay or code events to avoid inclusion; request strong anti-manipulation safeguards and audit protocols to prevent gaming of cancellations.

[P22] Under § 510.210(b)(1)(i), episodes are canceled if the beneficiary ceases to meet criteria in § 510.205 — clinicians and patient advocates will request examples and borderline scenarios (e.g., transfer status changes) to avoid arbitrary cancellations.

[P23] The rule at § 510.210(b)(1)(ii) cancels episodes if the beneficiary is readmitted for another anchor hospitalization; hospitals point out this could unfairly penalize hospitals that receive necessary readmissions and request CMS to limit cancellation only when readmission is unrelated to initial care or to allow clinical review.

[P24] § 510.210(b)(1)(iii) excludes episodes if the beneficiary initiates an LEJR episode under BPCI — commenters representing hospitals in both models will ask how overlapping attribution and payments will be resolved and request coordination rules to avoid double-counting or gaps.

[P25] The death exclusion in § 510.210(b)(1)(iv) (episode canceled if beneficiary dies) could distort performance measurement by removing high-cost cases; patient safety advocates will request that CMS analyze and publish the impact of this exclusion on quality measurement and consider alternative risk adjustment rather than exclusion.

[P26] For PY3, § 510.210(b)(2) cancels episodes for hospitals that did not submit an accepted participation letter — hospitals that missed acceptance clerical requirements will request a cure process and argue that retroactive cancellation undermines reliance interests and financial planning.

[P27] The standardization methodology in § 510.300(b)(6) that excludes certain incentive programs and add-on payments from historical episode payments may undercount legitimate historical costs; provider groups request CMS to publish the full list of excluded incentives/add-ons and the precise adjustment algorithm for stakeholder review.

[P28] The reconciliation timeline in § 510.305(d)(1) requiring CMS actions "beginning 2 months after the end of each performance year" is aggressive for complex reconciliations; commenters will request that CMS provide interim statements, set deadlines for hospitals to submit disputes, and explain the timeline for final settlement.

[P29] The obligation in § 510.305(d)(1)(i) that CMS perform reconciliation calculations to establish an NPRA must be accompanied by transparency standards — hospitals will request that CMS provide the reconciliation worksheet and underlying data used to compute NPRA and a formal dispute resolution mechanism.

[P30] Under § 510.305(d)(1)(ii), CMS will account for reorganizations under a participant hospital's CCN, but the rule does not define "reorganization event"; hospital systems will request a clear definition (merger, acquisition, CCN reassignment, bankruptcy sale) and examples of documentation required.

[P31] The separate reconciliation requirement for predecessor hospitals (§ 510.305(d)(1)(ii)(A)) for episodes with anchor admissions before reorganization could create split financial liabilities; hospital legal counsel will ask how shared liabilities are allocated and whether successor hospitals assume predecessor NPRA obligations.

[P32] The reconciliation calculations for new or surviving hospitals (§ 510.305(d)(1)(ii)(B)) for episodes on/after reorganization effective date require CMS to explain how historical spending and benchmarks follow the CCN — request a detailed methodology and protections against double attribution or gaps during transition periods.

[P33] The provision at § 510.410(b)(1)(i)(G) that nonparticipation in CJR model-related evaluation activities is a failure subject to enforcement raises First Amendment and due-process concerns — academic researchers and hospitals will request that CMS limit enforcement to willful refusal and provide advance notice, a cure period, and narrowly tailored confidentiality protections for evaluation data.

[P33] Hospital associations will argue that mandatory participation in CMS-conducted evaluations could interfere with independent quality improvement initiatives and request that participation be limited to data provision, not forced involvement in surveys or on-site activities without compensation.

[P34] The waiver in § 510.65(c)(2) allowing distant-site payment for telehealth home visit HCPCS codes unique to this model is welcome, but telehealth providers request explicit payment rates, billing instructions, originating site rules, and crosswalks for modifier and place-of-service coding to ensure appropriate reimbursement.

[P34] Privacy and telehealth advocates will request that CMS clarify HIPAA and state licensure implications of allowing distant-site telehealth home visit payments, including whether cross-state encounters are permitted and whether additional consent or documentation is required.
