[P1] Industry commenters will request clarification of which "non-hospice providers" may request the addendum (e.g., treating physicians, DME suppliers, pharmacies, home health agencies) to avoid disputes about who has standing to request.

[P1] Legal advocates will argue the permission for "Medicare contractors" to request the addendum needs limits to prevent routine contractor fishing expeditions and request a definition and purpose limitation for contractor requests.

[P2] Hospices will comment that the 48-hour timeframe to provide the addendum when requested "at time of election" is unworkable for admissions that occur after-hours or on weekends and request extension to 72 hours or allowance for next-business-day delivery.

[P3] Hospices will assert that the requirement to "immediately" provide the addendum when requested during the election is ambiguous and seek a specific maximum timeframe (e.g., within 24 hours) to accommodate clinical workflow and verification.

[P3] Patient advocates will contend that "immediately" should mean immediate verbal disclosure plus written addendum within 24 hours, to ensure patients are adequately informed in urgent settings.

[P4] Hospices will request guidance on what constitutes a change "during the hospice election" triggering an updated addendum (e.g., only clinical diagnosis changes vs. changes in payer determinations or services requested).

[P4] Legal commenters will request a requirement that updates be delivered by the same method as initial addendum (paper or electronic) and documented in the medical record, and ask CMS to require proof of delivery.

[P5] Hospices and EHR vendors will ask for a standardized addendum template (machine-readable and human-readable) from CMS to ensure consistent content and to reduce administrative burden.

[P6] Hospices will request flexibility to use an equivalent title if translated for non-English speakers and ask CMS to permit adding the endorsed title in the patient’s language rather than strictly requiring the exact English phrase.

[P7] Hospices will request that the rule allow use of organizational DBA (doing-business-as) names and permit inclusion of facility locations when multiple hospices share a legal entity name.

[P8] Privacy advocates will request that the requirement to include "hospice medical record identifier" clarify acceptable identifiers (MRN, Medicare Beneficiary Identifier, last four of SSN) to avoid PHI overexposure on documents that might be sent off-site.

[P9] Clinicians will request clarification on the level of specificity required when "identify[ing] the individual's terminal illness and related conditions" — whether listing ICD codes is required or whether plain-language descriptions suffice.

[P10] Non-hospice providers and payers will object that listing all conditions present on admission and enumerating associated non-covered items creates an onerous documentation task and ask CMS to limit the list to conditions or items reasonably likely to be affected.

[P10] Patient advocates will request that the addendum require plain-language descriptions for each non-covered item/service/drug including likely clinical alternatives and expected out-of-pocket costs if obtained outside hospice.

[P11] Providers will request examples of acceptable "written clinical explanations" and an explicit prohibition on boilerplate language (e.g., "not related to terminal illness") without individualized clinical justification.

[P11] Legal commenters will argue that the clinical explanation requirement could create discoverable documentation in disputes and ask CMS to clarify confidentiality or define permissible content to avoid malpractice or coverage litigation escalation.

[P12] Advocates for racial equity and limited-English patients will request that the "general statement that relatedness decisions are made for each patient" include an explicit statement that determinations are individualized and may be reconsidered on request, to reduce perceptions of one-size-fits-all denial.

[P13] Patient groups will say the recommendation that individuals "should share the clinical explanation" is insufficient and propose a provision requiring hospices to provide a copy directly to any designated non-hospice provider upon patient authorization.

[P14] Clinicians and hospices will request examples or an approved list of "relevant clinical practice, policy, or coverage guidelines" and whether internal hospice policy suffices or CMS expects citation to national guidelines (e.g., NCCN, GOLD, CDC).

[P14] Payers will ask that references to third-party guidelines be limited to those relied upon in making the relatedness determination, to prevent overbroad citation.

[P15] Disability rights groups will request that the addendum require accessible formats (large print, Braille, audio) and translated versions for limited-English proficient beneficiaries.

[P16] Beneficiary advocates will object that the BFCC-QIO immediate advocacy statement may create false expectations about the scope of QIO review and request CMS to be required to include a brief description of what QIO advocacy can and cannot do.

[P16] Legal commenters will request that the rule specify timeframes for BFCC–QIO advocacy intake and expected response times to make the "immediate advocacy" claim meaningful.

[P17] Privacy and patient-rights advocates will object to a mandatory signature requirement when patients may be incapacitated or refuse to sign, and ask CMS to allow alternative acknowledgements (verbal with witness attestation) and to permit refusal to sign without adverse consequences.

[P17] Hospices will request direction on acceptable representatives and signatures (durable power of attorney, legal guardian, verbally authorized family member) and whether electronic signatures are permitted.

[P18] Patient advocates will request stronger language that the acknowledgement of receipt "is not necessarily agreement" must also inform patients that they may dispute determinations without penalty and that their care will not be discontinued during dispute resolution.

[P19] Patient advocates will request that the required acknowledgement that hospice is palliative not curative include a statement about potential implications for specific cancer-directed or disease-modifying treatments so patients can make informed decisions.

[P20] Clinicians and patient advocates will request a standardized script or worksheet to ensure consistent communication about waived Medicare services and examples of common services that would be waived.

[P21] Patient advocates will challenge the characterization that services unrelated to the terminal illness are "exceptional and unusual" and ask CMS to provide data supporting that assertion or to remove the language that may discourage needed care.

[P22] Hospices will object to the statement that hospices "should" provide virtually all care and request clarity on which services hospices are practically responsible for and the interplay with Medicare Advantage and other payers.

[P23] Beneficiaries will request that the cost-sharing information include dollar estimates or ranges for common non-covered services and explicit instructions on billing and appeals for those costs.

[P24] Hospices will request that the requirement to notify patients of the right to receive an addendum be integrated into existing election paperwork to avoid duplicative forms and reduce patient burden.

[P25] Legal commenters will request that the BFCC-QIO contact information be required in multiple modalities (phone, TTY, email, web) and for CMS to maintain an up-to-date centralized online resource hospices can reference.

[P26] Disability advocates will ask that the "full understanding" acknowledgement allow for iterative education and confirm that signing does not preclude future revocation of the hospice election.

[P27] Consumer advocates will request that the acknowledgement of waived Medicare services include explicit examples and a clear statement that patients retain the right to seek services outside of hospice at their own expense without losing hospice eligibility.

[P28] Hospices and compliance officers will request safe-harbor language clarifying that providing information about cost-sharing is informational only and does not create a billing obligation unless the beneficiary consents.

[P29] Legal commenters will seek a process requirement that the hospice document in the medical record when it notified the beneficiary of the right to an addendum and whether the beneficiary requested it, to create a clear audit trail.

[P30] Advocates for rural beneficiaries will request that BFCC–QIO information include local/regional contacts and specify how beneficiaries in areas without BFCC offices can access advocacy services.

[P31] Non-hospice providers (oncologists, surgeons) will request a mechanism to challenge the hospice determination other than BFCC–QIO (e.g., expedited medical director-to-medical director review) because contractor reviews can be slow and adversarial.

[P32] Hospices will request exemption or phased compliance for small or rural hospices that lack administrative capacity to produce individualized addenda within the mandated timeframes.

[P33] Hospices will ask for clarification whether the addendum must be generated each time a plan-of-care update occurs or only when new unrelated items/services/drugs are identified, to avoid repetitive paperwork.

[P34] Industry IT vendors will request that CMS adopt a standardized electronic data field specification for the addendum to permit EHR integration and automated generation, and ask for a compliance grace period.

[P35] Legal commenters will request that the rule explicitly prohibit retaliation or changes in hospice care for beneficiaries who refuse to sign the addendum or who file BFCC–QIO advocacy requests.

[P36] Consumer groups will request that the required title be accompanied by a clear short header (e.g., "Important: Items Hospice Will Not Cover") to ensure comprehension, especially among low-literacy populations.

[P37] Hospices will seek permission to include multiple hospice program names/locations on the addendum when a chain operates in multiple states and the patient receives services from more than one site.

[P1] The April 28, 2017 comment deadline for the FAA is unreasonably short given the technical complexity of the AD and referenced service bulletins; stakeholders request an extension of at least 60–90 days to prepare meaningful comments and data.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether postmarks or electronic timestamps will be accepted for comments received on April 28, 2017, to avoid administrative rejections.

[P2] The compliance requirement to "comply within the specified compliance times" lacks clarity about whether compliance times in the parent AD or in multiple referenced service bulletins control when they differ; please specify the controlling compliance time.

[P2] The rule should permit temporary operations under a maintenance program while parts are being scheduled for replacement; as written, it could ground aircraft before parts are available.

[P3] Requiring removal of listed hardware "before reaching the specified part cycles since new" is ambiguous: commenters request the rule explicitly state how to calculate cycles since new (e.g., flight cycles only, engine cycles, or including ground cycles) and require operators to document the calculation method.

[P3] The 50-cycle grace period after the AD's effective date is insufficient for international operators who must source eligible parts and schedule shop visits given logistical constraints; request an extended grace period or a tiered schedule based on geographic region.

[P4] The mandatory removal of HPT stage 2 air seal P/N 2A4157 per IAE NMSB V2500–ENG–72–0676 should be limited to parts with specific serial numbers or lot ranges identified as affected; as drafted it could force replacement of safe parts, imposing unnecessary cost.

[P4] The reference to Table 1 of IAE NMSB V2500–ENG–72–0676 should be included in full or appended to the AD record; otherwise operators may not be able to determine part applicability without purchasing the service bulletin.

[P5] The requirement to remove HPT 1st stage air seal P/N 2A3423 per NMSB V2500–ENG–72–0677, Revision 1, lacks a clear list of eligible replacement parts; request the AD specify approved part numbers or modification instructions.

[P5] The AD references a service bulletin dated January 11, 2017; operators outside the U.S. may have different revision distribution—please confirm that earlier or later revisions are or are not acceptable.

[P6] Removing HPT stage 2 ring plate P/N 2A3437 identified in IAE NMSB V2500–ENG–72–0682 could create a parts shortage; FAA should provide an economic impact analysis and mitigation plan, such as an AMOC process that allows extended use until replacements are available.

[P6] The AD should clarify whether rework of existing P/N 2A3437 parts to an approved configuration is acceptable as an "eligible part" to reduce disposal and procurement costs.

[P7] The requirement to remove specified hardware when the HPT module is disassembled and access is available is vague: commenters request a definition of "disassembled" (e.g., module removal from engine vs. full teardown) and "access to the part."

[P7] The rule should include a provision allowing coordinations with scheduled maintenance events so that operators are not compelled to disassemble HPT modules solely to comply, which would impose unnecessary maintenance costs.

[P8] The mandate to remove HPT 1st stage air seal P/N 2A3423 "when accessible" per NMSB V2500–ENG–72–0678, Revision 1, requires clearer thresholds for accessibility — such as specific maintenance tasks that would trigger removal — to prevent inconsistent enforcement.

[P8] Operators request the AD allow previously inspected but not removed P/N 2A3423 seals to remain in service until the next scheduled major shop visit rather than requiring immediate part change when merely accessible during routine inspections.

[P9] The instruction to remove HPT stage 2 ring plate P/N 2A3437 when accessible per NMSB V2500–ENG–72–0681, Revision 2 needs clarification on whether partial accessibility (e.g., ability to visually inspect but not remove without partial disassembly) qualifies as "accessible."

[P9] The AD should include an exception for parts already removed from service prior to the AD effective date to avoid confusion about whether those engines are compliant.

[P10] Granting the Manager, Engine Certification Office, authority to approve AMOCs is appropriate, but commenters request a transparent timeline (e.g., 60 days) for AMOC decisions to avoid prolonged grounding or operational uncertainty.

[P10] The AD should permit delegated AMOC approval by designated representatives of approved repair stations with documented capabilities to expedite necessary alternatives, subject to FAA post-approval oversight.

[P11] Requiring use of 14 CFR 39.19 for AMOCs is acceptable, but the rule should clarify whether abbreviated AMOC submissions (e.g., referencing existing equivalent approvals) are permitted to reduce administrative burden.

[P11] The rule should explicitly state what supporting data or test results are required with an AMOC request (e.g., fatigue analysis, teardown photos, traceability) to avoid repetitive requests and delays.

[P12] Allowing AMOC requests by email to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov is useful; however, commenters request confirmation of secure receipt acknowledgments and estimated processing times to ensure timely responses.

[P12] The AD should permit electronic submissions to the FAA's public docket as part of the AMOC record for transparency, not just email to a single inbox.

[P13] The proposed Coast Guard safety-zone prohibition on vessel or person entry without authorization from the Captain of the Port for Long Island Sound is overly broad and lacks defined spatial and temporal boundaries; commenters request publication of exact coordinates and times of enforcement.

[P13] The prohibition could interfere with commercial traffic and ferry operations; request an exemption process for scheduled commercial vessels with pre-approved transit corridors.

[P14] While the Captain of the Port may authorize entry, the AD should require publicly posted criteria and timelines for authorization requests, including emergency access procedures for search and rescue or critical supply deliveries.

[P14] The exception for authorized entry should explicitly permit pilots, salvage crews, and others performing emergency response functions without prior authorization if they notify the Captain of the Port as soon as practicable.

[P15] The Coast Guard's comment deadline of April 13, 2017 is earlier than the FAA's and may prevent integrated comments from stakeholders affected by both rules; request harmonization of comment deadlines.

[P15] The rule should clarify whether submissions to the Coast Guard docket by April 13, 2017 require duplicate submission to the FAA docket to be considered by both agencies.

[P16] The Coast Guard’s invitation to comment is appreciated, but the preamble lacks sufficient data on risk assessment and expected duration of the safety zone; commenters request the underlying analysis be posted to the docket.

[P16] Advocacy groups request the Coast Guard include an explicit statement of how public comments will be considered and where responses will be posted, to ensure transparency in final rule decisions.

[P17] Allowing submission via Regulations.gov with docket number USCG–2016–0825 is helpful; however, commenters request confirmation that large technical attachments (e.g., engine inspection reports, photo files) will be accepted and retained in the public docket.

[P17] The rule should also allow submission of confidential business information through a parallel process and clearly explain how redacted versions will appear in the public docket to protect proprietary maintenance data.

[P1] The prohibition in § 165.T09–0242(c)(1) is overly broad and vague because it does not define the geographic boundaries or coordinates of “this safety zone,” making compliance and enforcement impracticable for mariners.

[P1] Industry commenters will request that the rule include explicit start and end dates/times or triggers for when the prohibition is active, so commercial operators can plan transits and avoid unjustified delays.

[P2] The exception allowing authorization by the Captain of the Port (P2) lacks procedural detail (how to apply, expected turnaround time, and criteria for approval), which creates uncertainty and potential arbitrary denial of access to commercial and recreational vessels.

[P3] The blanket prohibition on “all vessel traffic” in § 165.T09–0242(c)(2) fails to account for essential navigation (e.g., ferries, emergency vessels, public utility workboats) and thus could disrupt critical services; commenters will ask for a list of exempted vessel categories or an emergency-access provision.

[P4] While P4 permits the Captain or on-scene representative to allow traffic, commenters will object that no standards or hierarchy are provided for granting exceptions (e.g., priority for lifesaving or commercial traffic), creating inconsistent enforcement across incidents.

[P5] The obligation in P5 to “contact the Captain” is reasonable but commenters will request that contact methods include telephone numbers and email addresses in addition to VHF, to ensure redundancy and accessibility during communications outages.

[P6] Reliance solely on VHF Channel 16 per P6 is problematic for small recreational boaters without VHF radios; commenters will request alternate notification and contact methods (phone/text, local harbor master, marina channels).

[P7] P7 requires operators granted permission to “comply with all directions” but does not constrain the scope of those directions; legal commenters will request that directions be limited to safety-related commands and be reasonable, with an appeals or clarification process for contested orders.

[P1] Recreational boating groups will claim that the prohibition (P1) should include a requirement that the Captain provide advance public notice (e.g., via Local Notice to Mariners) whenever the safety zone will be established, to avoid sleep disruption of recreational plans and economic harm to local marinas.

[P3] Commercial shipping interests will assert that closing the safety zone to “all vessel traffic” (P3) without minimum advance notice periods (e.g., 24–72 hours) could disrupt scheduled cargo operations and impose significant economic costs.

[P2] Environmental and fishing industry stakeholders will request that authorization criteria (P2) explicitly require balancing public-safety needs with access for commercial fishermen, scientific research vessels, and environmental response teams.

[P5] Port authorities will argue that P5 should require the Captain or representative to provide written confirmation (VHF broadcast plus written permit or POR) of any permission granted, including the permitted route, duration, and the identity of the authorized vessel(s).

[P6] Marina operators and small-boat users will point out that VHF Channel 16 is a distress and hailing channel; requiring routine permission requests on Channel 16 (P6) may conflict with radio etiquette and FCC rules — they will request use of a working channel or telephone number for non-emergency coordination.

[P7] Legal advocates will note that P7’s compliance mandate lacks procedural safeguards for due process when a vessel operator believes a direction is unlawful or unsafe; they will request a requirement that directions be promptly documented and that there be a mechanism for expedited review.

[P8] Public commenters will argue that the comment deadline (P8) of May 18, 2020 is inadequate because the proposed rule was published close to the deadline and affected stakeholders need more time to analyze marine-safety and economic impacts; they will request an extension of at least 30 days.

[P12] Privacy-conscious individuals and advocacy groups will insist that the requirement to include the Docket ID (P12) be paired with clearer guidance on how to submit comments anonymously or request redaction, because P13 allows posting of personal information.

[P13] Civil liberties organizations will object to P13’s statement that comments may be posted without change, including personal information, and will request that the agency implement an option to submit comments confidentially or to redact personal data before posting.

[P9] Some commenters will seek clarification of acceptable submission methods (P9): the provision lists methods but does not specify whether emailed attachments, multipart uploads, or mail-only supporting documents are accepted, leading to potential lost or improperly filed comments.

[P10] Technical users will support the regulations.gov preference (P10) but request assurances that the portal will remain secure and accessible, and that alternative submission channels remain available for those without internet access.

[P11] Civil-society groups will request that P11’s instruction to “follow online instructions” be supplemented by a plain-language guide and telephone help line to assist small organizations and the public in complying with submission procedures.

[P14] Due to the EPA Docket Center closure (P14), commenters will complain that closure diminishes meaningful public access to physical documents and in-person assistance; they will urge the agency to extend the comment period (P8) and provide remote alternatives (virtual reading rooms).

[P15] Organizations that rely on hand-delivery (P15) will object that the rule’s refusal to accept hand-delivered submissions and potential mail delays effectively disenfranchise stakeholders who cannot use electronic methods, and will demand explicit procedures for mailed comments and confirmation of receipt.

[P3] First-responder agencies will ask for explicit language exempting Coast Guard, police, fire, and medical-evacuation vessels from the “closed to all vessel traffic” prohibition (P3) to avoid uncertainty during multi-agency responses.

[P1] Property owners and marina businesses will request an economic-impact analysis be added, arguing the P1 prohibition could cause loss of business if applied frequently during peak recreational seasons.

[P2] Equity advocates will request that authorization procedures (P2) include outreach to limited-English-proficiency communities and clear multilingual guidance for obtaining permission to enter the safety zone.

[P6] Technology vendors will recommend allowing digital authorization (e.g., email or SMS confirmation) in addition to VHF (P6), to create auditable records and reduce radio congestion.

[P7] Compliance officers will propose that P7 require the Captain or representative to issue directions that are specific, time-limited, and physically reasonable (e.g., specifying speed limits, headings, or anchoring locations) rather than open-ended commands.

[P12] Legal commenters will note that failing to include the Docket ID (P12) should not automatically result in rejection of substantive comments; they will request that the agency accept and docket comments that lack the ID but clearly reference the rule.

[P13] Survivors and private individuals will urge the agency to provide explicit guidance on removing sensitive information (like phone numbers or addresses) before posting comments (P13), or to offer a redaction service.

[P8] Trade associations will point out that the May 18, 2020 deadline (P8) falls during the COVID-19 pandemic disruptions and will ask for an extension to accommodate remote work and delayed stakeholder consultations.

[P5] Commercial operators will request that the rule require the Captain of the Port to publish standard operating procedures for granting permissions (P5), including predictable hours of operation and response-time SLAs.

[P3] Environmental organizations will ask that the safety zone closure (P3) include clear environmental-mitigation protocols if closures force vessel rerouting that could increase emissions or disturb sensitive habitats.

[P1] Mariners will ask for an appeal or waiver process to contest a denial of authorization under P1/P2, including a requirement to provide written reasons for denial.

[P6] Recreational boating clubs will request that the rule expressly forbid using Channel 16 for lengthy administrative exchanges (P6) and require VHF hails on 16 be followed immediately by switching to a working channel for detailed communications.

[P11] Small nonprofits and individuals will request accessible instructions (P11) that are compatible with screen readers and meet ADA requirements for submitting comments online.

Industry commenters will request that the rule include explicit start and end dates/times or triggers for when the prohibition is active, so commercial operators can plan transits and avoid unjustified delays.

The exception allowing authorization by the Captain of the Port (P2) lacks procedural detail (how to apply, expected turnaround time, and criteria for approval), which creates uncertainty and potential arbitrary denial of access to commercial and recreational vessels.

The blanket prohibition on “all vessel traffic” in § 165.T09–0242(c)(2) fails to account for essential navigation (e.g., ferries, emergency vessels, public utility workboats) and thus could disrupt critical services; commenters will ask for a list of exempted vessel categories or an emergency-access provision.

While P4 permits the Captain or on-scene representative to allow traffic, commenters will object that no standards or hierarchy are provided for granting exceptions (e.g., priority for lifesaving or commercial traffic), creating inconsistent enforcement across incidents.

The obligation in P5 to “contact the Captain” is reasonable but commenters will request that contact methods include telephone numbers and email addresses in addition to VHF, to ensure redundancy and accessibility during communications outages.

Reliance solely on VHF Channel 16 per P6 is problematic for small recreational boaters without VHF radios; commenters will request alternate notification and contact methods (phone/text, local harbor master, marina channels).

P7 requires operators granted permission to “comply with all directions” but does not constrain the scope of those directions; legal commenters will request that directions be limited to safety-related commands and be reasonable, with an appeals or clarification process for contested orders.

Recreational boating groups will claim that the prohibition (P1) should include a requirement that the Captain provide advance public notice (e.g., via Local Notice to Mariners) whenever the safety zone will be established, to avoid sleep disruption of recreational plans and economic harm to local marinas.

Commercial shipping interests will assert that closing the safety zone to “all vessel traffic” (P3) without minimum advance notice periods (e.g., 24–72 hours) could disrupt scheduled cargo operations and impose significant economic costs.

Environmental and fishing industry stakeholders will request that authorization criteria (P2) explicitly require balancing public-safety needs with access for commercial fishermen, scientific research vessels, and environmental response teams.

Port authorities will argue that P5 should require the Captain or representative to provide written confirmation (VHF broadcast plus written permit or POR) of any permission granted, including the permitted route, duration, and the identity of the authorized vessel(s).

Marina operators and small-boat users will point out that VHF Channel 16 is a distress and hailing channel; requiring routine permission requests on Channel 16 (P6) may conflict with radio etiquette and FCC rules — they will request use of a working channel or telephone number for non-emergency coordination.

Legal advocates will note that P7’s compliance mandate lacks procedural safeguards for due process when a vessel operator believes a direction is unlawful or unsafe; they will request a requirement that directions be promptly documented and that there be a mechanism for expedited review.

Public commenters will argue that the comment deadline (P8) of May 18, 2020 is inadequate because the proposed rule was published close to the deadline and affected stakeholders need more time to analyze marine-safety and economic impacts; they will request an extension of at least 30 days.

Privacy-conscious individuals and advocacy groups will insist that the requirement to include the Docket ID (P12) be paired with clearer guidance on how to submit comments anonymously or request redaction, because P13 allows posting of personal information.

Civil liberties organizations will object to P13’s statement that comments may be posted without change, including personal information, and will request that the agency implement an option to submit comments confidentially or to redact personal data before posting.

Some commenters will seek clarification of acceptable submission methods (P9): the provision lists methods but does not specify whether emailed attachments, multipart uploads, or mail-only supporting documents are accepted, leading to potential lost or improperly filed comments.

Technical users will support the regulations.gov preference (P10) but request assurances that the portal will remain secure and accessible, and that alternative submission channels remain available for those without internet access.

Civil-society groups will request that P11’s instruction to “follow online instructions” be supplemented by a plain-language guide and telephone help line to assist small organizations and the public in complying with submission procedures.

Due to the EPA Docket Center closure (P14), commenters will complain that closure diminishes meaningful public access to physical documents and in-person assistance; they will urge the agency to extend the comment period (P8) and provide remote alternatives (virtual reading rooms).

Organizations that rely on hand-delivery (P15) will object that the rule’s refusal to accept hand-delivered submissions and potential mail delays effectively disenfranchise stakeholders who cannot use electronic methods, and will demand explicit procedures for mailed comments and confirmation of receipt.

First-responder agencies will ask for explicit language exempting Coast Guard, police, fire, and medical-evacuation vessels from the “closed to all vessel traffic” prohibition (P3) to avoid uncertainty during multi-agency responses.

Property owners and marina businesses will request an economic-impact analysis be added, arguing the P1 prohibition could cause loss of business if applied frequently during peak recreational seasons.

Equity advocates will request that authorization procedures (P2) include outreach to limited-English-proficiency communities and clear multilingual guidance for obtaining permission to enter the safety zone.
Technology vendors will recommend allowing digital authorization (e.g., email or SMS confirmation) in addition to VHF (P6), to create auditable records and reduce radio congestion.

Compliance officers will propose that P7 require the Captain or representative to issue directions that are specific, time-limited, and physically reasonable (e.g., specifying speed limits, headings, or anchoring locations) rather than open-ended commands.

Legal commenters will note that failing to include the Docket ID (P12) should not automatically result in rejection of substantive comments; they will request that the agency accept and docket comments that lack the ID but clearly reference the rule.

Survivors and private individuals will urge the agency to provide explicit guidance on removing sensitive information (like phone numbers or addresses) before posting comments (P13), or to offer a redaction service.

Trade associations will point out that the May 18, 2020 deadline (P8) falls during the COVID-19 pandemic disruptions and will ask for an extension to accommodate remote work and delayed stakeholder consultations.

Commercial operators will request that the rule require the Captain of the Port to publish standard operating procedures for granting permissions (P5), including predictable hours of operation and response-time SLAs.

Environmental organizations will ask that the safety zone closure (P3) include clear environmental-mitigation protocols if closures force vessel rerouting that could increase emissions or disturb sensitive habitats.
Mariners will ask for an appeal or waiver process to contest a denial of authorization under P1/P2, including a requirement to provide written reasons for denial.

Recreational boating clubs will request that the rule expressly forbid using Channel 16 for lengthy administrative exchanges (P6) and require VHF hails on 16 be followed immediately by switching to a working channel for detailed communications.
Small nonprofits and individuals will request accessible instructions (P11) that are compatible with screen readers and meet ADA requirements for submitting comments online.

raw_output:
[P1] The Phase I SIP submission limitation to project NOX emissions "no more than the State's Phase I NOX budget" is ambiguous regarding baseline year and accounting conventions; commenters request explicit specification of baseline year, treatment of growth, and whether banking or offsets are allowed in Phase I projections.

[P1] The October 30, 2000 deadline referenced for "Phase I SIP submission" is obsolete and creates legal uncertainty for states that submitted revisions late or seek corrective submittals; propose adding a procedure for late or corrected Phase I SIPs.

[P2] Alabama stakeholders will challenge the Phase I budget of 124,795 tons as insufficiently justified; industry and the State should be allowed to review and demand documentation of modeling and inputs used to derive that number.

[P2] Environmental groups will assert that Alabama's Phase I budget of 124,795 tons is too high to protect downwind nonattainment areas and request tightening the budget to reflect more stringent control assumptions.

[P3] Connecticut's Phase I budget of 42,891 tons appears inconsistent with more recent emission inventories; request that EPA reconcile this budget with 1999–2001 inventory data and provide recalculation methodology.

[P4] Delaware requests clarification whether the Phase I budget of 23,522 tons includes interstate transport reductions or only in-state emissions; if interstate contributions are excluded, the budget may be inadequate.

[P5] The District of Columbia's Phase I budget of 6,658 tons needs an explicit allocation methodology given DC's small geography and commuter-source emissions; commenters ask for delineation of mobile vs. stationary source shares.

[P6] Illinois industry groups will contest the Phase I budget of 278,146 tons as unrealistically low unless accompanied by specific control measures and implementation timelines; request an economic impact assessment.

[P7] Indiana requests documentation of the control technologies, cost assumptions, and growth factors used to set its Phase I budget of 234,625 tons and proposes a technical workshop before finalization.

[P8] Kentucky opposes the Phase I budget of 165,075 tons absent a clear demonstration that it will not impose retroactive control obligations on existing sources beyond previously adopted state rules.

[P9] Maryland environmental justice advocates claim the Phase I budget of 82,727 tons fails to address localized hotspots and ask for provisions ensuring reductions in overburdened communities.

[P10] Massachusetts requests that the Phase I budget of 85,871 tons be accompanied by an explicit list of included sources and any excluded categories (e.g., emergency generators, nonroad engines).

[P11] Michigan utilities assert the Phase I budget of 191,941 tons does not consider planned plant retirements and new generation capacity; request allowance for planned, documented structural changes.

[P12] New Jersey challenges the Phase I budget of 95,882 tons on grounds that the budget allocation between stationary and mobile sources is opaque; ask EPA to require breakdowns and separate sub-budgets.

[P13] New York environmental groups argue that the Phase I budget of 241,981 tons is too permissive given downwind impacts on New England and request a lower, health-protective budget.

[P14] North Carolina industry requests clarification whether the Phase I budget of 171,332 tons allows for the use of market-based trading across state lines or requires strictly in-state reductions.

[P15] Ohio state agencies ask for explanation of how Ohio's Phase I budget of 252,282 tons accounts for interstate transport obligations and whether reductions in adjacent states were credited.

[P16] Pennsylvania submits that the Phase I budget of 268,158 tons should be accompanied by a margin of safety provision and a reopener if ambient monitoring shows nonattainment or transport impacts.

[P17] Rhode Island requests data supporting the small Phase I budget of 9,570 tons and asks for guidance on allocating reductions among a small set of large sources versus many area sources.

[P18] South Carolina industry groups ask EPA to explain the derivation of 127,756 tons Phase I budget and to provide flexibility mechanisms (e.g., banking, offset provisions) to meet the budget cost-effectively.

[P19] Tennessee requests an economic and reliability impact analysis tied to its Phase I budget of 201,163 tons, asserting potential operational impacts on electric generation if strict controls are required.

[P20] Virginia seeks clarification whether its Phase I budget of 186,689 tons precludes use of EPA-administered cross-state trading programs or allows participation in future federal markets.

[P21] West Virginia coal and power industry groups argue that the Phase I budget of 85,045 tons underestimates the technical and economic feasibility of rapid NOX reductions and request phased compliance schedules.

[P22] The Phase II SIP submission requirement to limit projected NOX emissions to the State's final NOX budget lacks a definition of "projected emissions" (annual average, ozone-season only, tons per ozone season); request precise units and reporting format.

[P22] Legal commenters will request clarity on what triggers the obligation to submit a Phase II SIP "in compliance with paragraph (b)(1)(ii)" and whether affected parties can petition for extensions or adjustments.

[P23] Alabama objects to the reduction from Phase I (124,795) to Final budget (119,827) without transitional flexibility; ask for allowance to use remaining Phase I banked allowances or an adaptative compliance schedule.

[P24] Connecticut stakeholders note the minor difference between Phase I (42,891) and Final (42,850) budgets and ask whether the 41-ton change is within inventory uncertainty; request rounding rules and tolerance bands.

[P25] Delaware requests explanation for the reduction from Phase I 23,522 to Final 22,862 tons and whether that reduction was based on updated emissions controls or modeling corrections.

[P26] The District of Columbia objects to a single-ton decrement from 6,658 to 6,657 tons as administratively meaningless; request consolidation of precision and rounding to avoid trivial budget adjustments.

[P27] Illinois groups request that EPA provide the modeling files and inputs supporting the Final budget of 271,091 tons to permit independent review and potential legal challenge.

[P28] Indiana asks whether the Final budget of 230,381 tons allows credit for early reductions or only for measures implemented by the Phase II submission date.

[P29] Kentucky requests that the Final budget of 162,519 tons include an interim compliance pathway for facilities that need time to install controls, to avoid immediate enforcement actions.

[P30] Maryland reasserts that its Final budget of 81,947 tons must include targeted measures for urban hotspots and explicitly account for mobile-source strategies.

[P31] Massachusetts asks EPA to justify the downgrade from Phase I to Final (85,871 to 84,848) and provide evidence that the smaller budget will still attain air quality goals without disproportionate burdens.

[P32] Michigan utilities insist the Final budget of 190,908 tons should accommodate planned generation changes and request a process to adjust budgets if major capacity retirements or additions occur.

[P33] Missouri (newly included in Final budgets) stakeholders ask why Missouri appears only in the Final budgets (61,406 tons) and not in Phase I table; request clarification of inclusion criteria and implications for Missouri sources.

[P34] New Jersey points out the increase from Phase I 95,882 to Final 96,876 tons and asks for justification of the higher final allocation and whether it reflects modeling or legal settlements.

[P35] New York challenges the small decline from 241,981 to 240,322 tons and requests sensitivity analyses showing air quality outcomes under both budgets.

[P36] North Carolina requests that the Final budget of 165,306 tons permit the use of intrastate trading and include clear monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) standards to prevent double-counting.

[P37] Ohio utilities request that the Final budget of 249,541 tons be accompanied by specified compliance pathways and allowance allocation methodologies; otherwise, legal challenges may follow.

[P38] Pennsylvania demands transparency around the derivation of the Final budget of 257,928 tons and requests an independent technical review panel to assess modeling assumptions.

[P39] Rhode Island asks whether the reduction from 9,570 to 9,378 tons accounts for background concentrations and transport and whether the state can allocate budget flexibly across sectors.

[P40] South Carolina requests confirmation that its Final budget of 123,496 tons allows credit for federally enforceable regional controls and for early voluntary reductions.

[P41] Tennessee seeks a variance mechanism if compliance with the Final budget of 198,286 tons would threaten electric grid reliability, requesting conditional exemptions subject to mitigation.

[P42] Virginia requests explicit guidance on how the Final budget of 180,521 tons interacts with state-level regulations and existing SIP commitments to avoid regulatory duplication.

[P43] West Virginia industry groups question the technical basis for reducing Phase I 85,045 to Final 83,921 tons and request an appeals process if the state cannot feasibly achieve the lower final allocation.

[P44] States considering including monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting under 40 CFR part 75, subpart H need clarity whether requiring Part 75 MR&R for generators >25 MWe is mandatory or optional; propose explicit language confirming it is permissive.

[P44] Generator operators request that if Part 75 subpart H is required, EPA provide a timeline and funding support for small utilities to install compliant monitoring systems before enforcement begins.

[P44] Environmental groups support the authorization to require Part 75 monitoring for units >25 MWe and request the rule require continuous emissions monitoring (CEMs) rather than periodic testing.

[P45] Legal commenters note the proviso that this section does not create exceptions to Part 75 requirements under other legal authority—request cross-references to specific statutes and existing delegated authorities to avoid conflicts.

[P46] States are concerned that authorizing the Administrator to perform functions under Part 75 could be interpreted as preemption of state enforcement; ask for clarification that Administrator assistance is supplementary and voluntary.

[P46] Industry groups worry that Administrator-performed functions could lead to duplicative compliance obligations and request clear limits on EPA assuming enforcement responsibilities.

[P47] The prohibition on the Administrator carrying out functions in 40 CFR part 96 or SIP trading program provisions after Sept. 30, 2008 raises legal and operational concerns about the continuity of emissions trading markets; commenters request transitional rules and protection for existing compliance instruments.

[P47] Market participants argue the blanket prohibition could invalidate banked allowances and create significant stranded-assets risk; request non-retroactive treatment and grandfathering of existing allowances.

[P47] States request guidance on alternative federal assistance if Administrator functions under part 96 are prohibited, since some states rely on EPA to run interstate trading programs.

[P48] Mandating that states revise SIPs to adopt control measures achieving "the same portion of NOX emissions reductions" as previously approved trading programs is vague—commenters ask for a precise metric (tons reduced, percent reduction, or modeled air quality benefit) and methodology for calculation.

[P48] Legal experts warn that requiring equivalent reductions in the absence of trading mechanisms could force states to impose stringent command-and-control measures, raise cost and legality issues, and possibly exceed statutory authority without notice-and-comment rulemaking at the state level.

[P48] Utility and industrial commenters request allowance for economic equivalence (comparable cost-effectiveness) rather than strict ton-for-ton parity, and propose flexible compliance options including interstate crediting, to achieve the required portion of reductions.

[P48] Environmental advocates demand that SIP revisions required under §51.121(r)(2) include enforceable schedules, monitoring, and public reporting to ensure the purported "same portion" of reductions is actually realized.

raw_output:
[P1] The February 17, 2017 comments due date is unreasonably short and should be extended to at least 60 days from publication to allow operators and stakeholders sufficient time to analyze technical data and coordinate consolidated responses.

[P1] The rule text should clarify whether the Feb 17, 2017 deadline is the postmark date, received date, or electronic submission date to avoid premature rejection of late-submitted comments.

[P2] The phrase "within the specified compliance times" is vague; commenters will ask the FAA to require that the AD specify calendar dates or explicit flight-cycle/flight-hour thresholds rather than reference external tables only.

[P2] The AD should include relief for operators who can demonstrate good-cause reasons for delayed compliance (e.g., parts unavailability) or allow documented temporary deviations approved under an AMOC to avoid grounding.

[P3] The AD mandates inspections per Boeing Alert Service Bulletin 777–53A0081 but does not incorporate the ASB by reference; request that the FAA either incorporate the ASB by reference or include key inspection parameters (intervals, thresholds) in the AD itself for legal certainty.

[P3] Industry commenters will request that the AD specify which model years/configurations of 777 are affected and include a clear applicability statement rather than relying solely on the ASB to prevent misinterpretation.

[P3] Operators will ask for confirmation that performance of HFEC/ultrasonic inspections must be done only where specified in tables 1–6 and not universally, to avoid unnecessary cost for aircraft not in the affected configurations.

[P4] The option to perform "detailed inspections alone" versus "detailed plus HFEC/ultrasonic" is ambiguous; request that the FAA define objective criteria (e.g., damage thresholds, location, crack size) that determine when HFEC/ultrasonic is required.

[P4] Maintenance providers request clarification on acceptable personnel qualifications and equipment specifications for HFEC/ultrasonic inspections to ensure consistency across operators.

[P5] Requiring that investigative/corrective actions be completed "before further flight" may effectively ground aircraft when parts or approved repair methods are unavailable; commenters will request allowance for temporary operational relief (e.g., ferry flights under strict conditions or dispatch with operational restrictions) if an AMOC or equivalent authorization is in process.

[P6] The AD references repeat intervals in tables 1–6 of the ASB; commenters will request the FAA to publish those intervals in the AD or in an incorporated reference to avoid ambiguity about required repetition frequencies.

[P6] Operators will request explicit guidance on how to log and track repeat inspection intervals for aircraft with variable utilization (e.g., seasonal operators, leased aircraft) and whether intervals are calendar-based, flight-cycle-based, or hour-based.

[P7] The wording that replacing a longeron "ends the repetitive inspection requirement for that longeron only" should be clarified: commenters will ask whether the replaced longeron is considered a new part with a new inspection baseline or whether other structural interfaces still require inspections.

[P7] Repair stations and leasing companies will request that the AD permit installation of a serviceable longeron with traceable maintenance records from another aircraft or supplier and clarify whether that counts as a replacement ending repetitive inspections.

[P8] The requirement for post-replacement inspections at times in tables 7–14 is burdensome; operators will ask for rationale and data supporting those specific post-replacement intervals and request potential harmonization to reduce fleet disruption.

[P8] Commenters will request clarification whether post-replacement inspection tables 7–14 apply when a longeron is replaced as part of new-production spares installation, versus replacement after repair for damage.

[P9] As with paragraph P4, the choice between detailed-only versus detailed-plus-ultrasonic inspections for replaced longerons needs objective decision criteria and qualification standards for technicians and equipment.

[P9] Maintenance organizations will request that the AD explicitly permit use of equivalent non-ultrasonic NDT methods (e.g., phased-array ultrasonic) if demonstrated equivalent or better sensitivity, rather than being limited to the methods listed.

[P10] The requirement that corrective actions on replaced longerons be completed before further flight lacks provisions for contingency: commenters will ask the FAA to allow controlled, one-time repositioning or maintenance-only flights under an approved risk mitigation plan when parts or AMOC approvals are delayed.

[P11] The requirement to "repeat the inspections... at intervals not to exceed" tables 7–14 should state whether operators may perform more frequent inspections voluntarily without invalidating compliance, and how that affects scheduling and parts provisioning.

[P12] Changing ASB compliance times referenced to the service bulletin issue date to be relative to the AD effective date may shorten some operators' available time unexpectedly; commenters will request grandfathering for operators who have already begun work per the ASB and clear examples showing how the conversion is calculated.

[P12] Legal commenters will note that the conversion may create retroactive obligations for actions already scheduled under the ASB and ask the FAA to provide transition relief or credit for actions already performed in good faith prior to the AD effective date.

[P13] Requiring that any instruction to "contact Boeing" be complied with by obtaining an FAA-approved method before further flight is reasonable for safety, but commenters will request the FAA to provide a predictable timeline and review process for approval of such Boeing-proposed repairs to avoid extended aircraft downtime.

[P13] Boeing and operators will request explicit criteria for what constitutes an acceptable "method approved in accordance with the procedures in paragraph (j)" to ensure Boeing-approved dispositions can be processed efficiently without repeated clarification requests.

[P14] The delegation of AMOC approval to the Seattle ACO Manager will prompt requests for multiple regional FAA points of contact or a clearer escalation path, because operators outside the Seattle region may find single-point authority inefficient.

[P15] The instruction to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 should be accompanied by explicit timelines for FAA response and acceptance criteria; commenters will request a required FAA decision timeframe (e.g., 60 days) for AMOC requests.

[P16] When sending AMOC information directly to the ACO manager, commenters will ask the AD to specify a physical mailing address, fax number, and expected receipt confirmation process to prevent lost or delayed submissions.

[P17] Allowing AMOC information to be emailed is helpful, but commenters will request confirmation that emailed submissions constitute legal filings and that the FAA will provide automated acknowledgment of receipt with a tracking number.

[P18] The requirement to notify the principal inspector (or local FSDO/CHDO manager) before using an approved AMOC should be clarified whether that notification must be written and whether it triggers any additional FAA approval steps; commenters will request a simple written notification template.

[P19] Permitting Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to be used is practical, but commenters will request that the AD require the Boeing ODA approval to be accompanied by documentation demonstrating equivalence to the airplane's certification basis and to include explicit cross-reference to the AD in the ODA approval paperwork.

[P21] Legal commenters will recommend defining the term "RC" explicitly in the AD (including how manufacturers identify RC steps) and provide examples so that operators understand which service bulletin steps are mandatory.

[P22] The RC Exempt exception should be explained further — commenters will ask for a clear list of RC Exempt steps in the ASB and the rationale for exempting them to avoid inconsistent interpretation.

raw_output:
[P1] The binary choice in § 63.2840 (intro) forcing facilities to “choose and comply with either (a)-(d) or (e)” is ambiguous and could lead to inconsistent enforcement; EPA should clarify whether facilities may mix elements from both paths when technically necessary.

[P1] Industry commenters will object that requiring a single-path choice under § 63.2840 could penalize multi-line facilities that have different process trains better suited to different compliance approaches; EPA should allow source-by-source or equipment-by-equipment selection rather than facility-wide.

[P2] Requiring compliance with paragraph (g) in addition to choosing a path (§ 63.2840 (intro)) effectively makes the “choice” illusory; stakeholders will request justification for why § 63.2840(g) cannot be incorporated as an option within the (a)-(d)/(e) framework.

[P3] The trigger to comply with the work practice standard in (h) only “if you choose to operate your source under an initial startup period” is vague; commenters will ask EPA to define whether voluntary startup operations count and how to demonstrate the choice.

[P4] The 12-month rolling compliance ratio calculation in § 63.2840(a)(1) is burdensome and may penalize seasonal processors; commenters will request alternative shorter look-back periods or seasonal adjustments for facilities with atypical operating cycles.

[P4] Legal experts will raise that the compliance ratio method lacks an explicit margin of error or confidence interval for measurement uncertainty; EPA should provide guidance on how to account for measurement uncertainty in the ratio calculation.

[P5] The requirement in § 63.2840(b) to calculate the compliance ratio “by the end of each calendar month following an operating month” is administratively onerous; commenters will request extending the reporting/calculation deadline (e.g., to 45 or 60 days) to allow data validation.

[P6] The instruction to categorize a full-month shutdown as a “nonoperating month” (§ 63.2840(b)(3)) may create perverse incentives to shut down temporarily to improve compliance ratios; commenters will request safeguards against gaming (e.g., minimum run-duration rules).

[P7] Excluding nonoperating months entirely from the compliance ratio (§ 63.2840(b)(3)) could distort long-term emission accountability for intermittent sources; environmental advocacy groups will argue to require reporting of nonoperating months instead of exclusion.

[P8] The permission in § 63.2840(b)(4) to exclude initial startup period data only if the work practice standard is met could disadvantage new sources that cannot meet the standard for safety reasons; commenters will ask EPA to allow exclusion if documented good-faith safety or engineering reasons prevent meeting the work practice.

[P9] Allowing malfunction-period data exclusion only before a fixed date (§ 63.2840(b)(5)) and then removing that allowance (§ 63.2840(b)(5) & P10) creates a cliff that will surprise regulated entities; stakeholders will request an explanation and a longer phase-out or grandfathering for existing facilities.

[P10] Environmental groups will object that removing the ability to exclude malfunction periods after [date 181 days after publication] (§ 63.2840(b)(5)/(10)) will discourage accurate reporting during malfunctions and could unfairly penalize facilities for unexpected events; they will request retaining exclusion only with stringent documentation.

[P11] The obligation in § 63.2840(g) to “operate and maintain ... consistent with safety and good air pollution control practices” is vague; industry will request a clear, objective standard or referential guidance (e.g., ANSI standards) to avoid subjective enforcement.

[P11] Labor/safety groups will caution that § 63.2840(g)’s language could be interpreted to require unsafe operational practices to minimize emissions and therefore request explicit language prioritizing worker safety over emissions reductions.

[P12] The timing in § 63.2840(h) that the work practice standard applies “On and after [date 181 days...]” lacks clarity for sources that started startup periods just before that date; commenters will request transitional provisions specifying which rule version applies to overlapping periods.

[P13] The continuous operation requirement for the mineral oil absorption system during initial startup (§ 63.2840(h)(1)) is operationally unrealistic for some plant designs and may create safety risks; industry will request an exception for short, documented interruptions and a definition of “continuous.”

[P14] The identical continuous operation mandate for solvent condensers in § 63.2840(h)(2) fails to account for condenser bypasses used for safety or maintenance; commenters will request a permitted downtime allowance with notification requirements.

[P15] Requiring adherence to site-specific temperature and pressure limits for desolventizing and distillation units during startup (§ 63.2840(h)(3)) is reasonable, but operators need clear procedures for establishing and approving those limits; commenters will ask for an EPA template or criteria for technical justification.

[P16] Allowing site-specific operating limits based on manufacturer recommendations or “other site-specific values” (§ 63.2840(h)(3)(i)) is appropriate, but environmental groups will request that limits based solely on manufacturer specs be justified by exposure/emissions modeling before acceptance.

[P17] Permitting operating limits to be min/max/range (§ 63.2840(h)(3)(ii)) is good flexibility, but commenters will request EPA clarify whether excursions within tolerance bands during transient startup are considered violations.

[P18] The SSM plan requirement in § 63.2850(a)(3) being mandatory before [date] and then not required after that date (P18 & P56) is confusing; stakeholders will ask EPA to clarify whether SSM plans are permanently rescinded after the date or only for new instances.

[P19] The reporting obligations in § 63.2850(a)(5) are extensive; small processors will request consolidation or reduced-frequency reporting to lessen administrative burden.

[P20] Requiring initial startup period reports per § 63.2861(e) (§ 63.2850(a)(5)(iv)) may force disclosure of sensitive production details; industry will request options to file a confidential version and clarify CBI procedures.

[P21] Mandating existing sources under normal operation to meet Table 1 and Table 2 schedules (§ 63.2850(b)) without phase-in may impose immediate capital costs; industry will request staggered compliance deadlines or economic impact consideration.

[P22] The requirement that new sources upon initial startup meet full normal operation requirements (§ 63.2850(c)(1)) may be infeasible for commissioning activities; commenters will request a clearly defined commissioning/startup exemption period.

[P23] Allowing up to 6 months of initial startup treatment for new sources (§ 63.2850(c)(2)) but imposing the work practice standard after the [date] creates uncertainty; new-source developers will ask whether the 6-month period can be extended for complex facilities.

[P24] The rule’s different treatment of significant modifications with a 3-month initial startup period (§ 63.2850(d)(2)) versus new sources (6 months) may be arbitrary; stakeholders will request justification and parity or allow case-by-case extensions.

[P25] The requirement to choose a compliance option within 15 days of malfunction start (§ 63.2850(e) intro) is too short for complex events; industry will request 30 days to evaluate and notify regulators.

[P26] Requiring full compliance with paragraph (a) and Table 1 during malfunction periods (§ 63.2850(e)(2)) can be infeasible during emergency responses; commenters will ask for an explicit, narrowly tailored emergency exemption with retrospective reporting.

[P27] The reference error in Table 1 (§ 63.2850 (a)(2) referencing § 62.2840(g) per P33) is a drafting mistake that must be corrected to § 63.2840(g); legal commenters will request correction to avoid legal challenge.

[P28] The solvent loss measurement requirements (§ 63.2850 Table 1(b) / § 63.2853) lack specificity on allowed measurement technologies and tolerances; industry will request EPA provide acceptable methods and uncertainty allowances.

[P29] Requiring recording of HAP volume fractions >1% in shipments (§ 63.2850 Table 1(c)) could be impractical when suppliers don’t provide HAP fraction details; commenters will request supplier notification requirements or default conservative values.

[P30] The obligation to measure and record tons of each oilseed processed during normal operation (§ 63.2850 Table 1(d)) is straightforward but may be burdensome for mixed-batch or commingled shipments; commenters will request aggregation rules.

[P31] Computing weighted-average HAP fraction by the end of the following month (§ 63.2850 Table 1(e) / § 63.2854) may be administratively burdensome; processors request aligning that deadline with the compliance ratio calculation deadline.

[P32] The requirement in Table 1(f) to compute the 12-month compliance ratio “by the next calendar month” (for each 12-month period) duplicates § 63.2840(b) and increases confusion; commenters will request consolidation and a single clear deadline for all related computations.

[P33] Submitting NOCS or annual compliance certifications per Table 1(g) may require costly legal review; stakeholders will request a simplified certification form and clear instructions for small entities.

[P34] The deviation reporting trigger (compliance ratio >1.00) in Table 1(h)(1) is a strict cutoff that does not account for measurement error; stakeholders will request a de minimis buffer (e.g., 1.05) before a deviation is required.

[P35] Requiring deviation notification reports as described in § 63.2861(b) on and after the [date] (Table 1(h)(2)) without harmonization with other federal/state reporting systems will duplicate effort; regulated entities request EPA allow submission to a single portal acceptable to state agencies.

[P36] The periodic SSM reporting (§ 63.2850 Table 1(i)) and immediate SSM reporting (§ 63.2850 Table 1(j)) overlap in content and timing; commenters ask EPA to harmonize triggers and avoid multiple reports for the same event.

[P37] The requirement to keep the compliance demonstration plan in the Title V permit (§ 63.2851(a) intro) may require many permit modifications across jurisdictions; permit writers will ask EPA to allow incorporation by reference instead of physical attachment.

[P38] Requiring retention of prior versions of the compliance plan for five years (§ 63.2851(a)) will increase recordkeeping burdens; small processors will request permission to retain only summaries of changes.

[P39] The enumerated items required in the compliance plan (§ 63.2851(a)(last)) include potentially proprietary operational details; industry will request clearer CBI protection procedures beyond the general CBI submission requirements.

[P40] The obligation to include site-specific operating limits and their basis in the compliance plan (§ 63.2851(a)(8)(i)) may expose trade secrets; commenters will request explicit confidentiality protections for technical justifications.

[P41] The demand to include detailed measurement methods and frequencies for temperature and pressure (§ 63.2851(a)(8)(ii)) is reasonable, but EPA should allow cross-reference to existing monitoring programs to avoid duplication.

[P42] Requiring development of an SSM plan before the compliance date (§ 63.2852 intro) with no phased implementation is unrealistic; small businesses will request more time or simplified SSM templates.

[P43] The SSM plan requirement to reflect “best practices of the industry” (§ 63.2852) is vague and could be selectively enforced; stakeholders ask for a non-exhaustive list of acceptable standards or authoritative industry guidelines.

[P44] Requiring any other plan used as an SSM plan to meet all NESHAP requirements (§ 63.2852) could nullify existing company-wide emergency plans; compliance officers request a crosswalk showing how existing plans can be certified as meeting § 63.2852.

[P45] The complete removal of SSM plan obligations on and after the [date] (§ 63.2852 P56) contradicts other sections that continue to reference SSM reports and plans after that date; commenters will flag internal inconsistency and request clarification.

[P46] Categorizing operating status for each recorded time interval (§ 63.2853(a)(2)) will require high-resolution data logging; small processors will request allowed minimum interval durations (e.g., hourly vs. minute-by-minute).

[P47] Measuring and recording solvent inventory at the start and end of every normal operating period (§ 63.2853(a)(3)) is operationally heavy; commenters will propose acceptable surrogate measurements (metered receipts and shipments) and periodic reconciliation.

[P48] The permission to use control devices including incinerators, boilers, and flares (§ 63.2853(a)(5)(i)) should come with emission performance standards; environmental groups will request minimum destruction/removal efficiencies be specified.

[P49] The requirement to quantify gallons entering and destroyed in destructive control devices (§ 63.2853(a)(5)(i)) may be difficult for combined combustion systems; commenters will ask for specific accepted measurement and calculation approaches for combined fuel streams.

[P50] Allowing subtraction of solvent destroyed in a control device from total solvent loss (§ 63.2853(a)(5)(i)) could be misused to obscure fugitive emissions; environmental advocates will request mandatory stack testing or CEMS to verify destruction claims.

[P51] The allowance to use design evaluations instead of performance testing (§ 63.2853(a)(5)(i)) must be limited; commenters will request stringent documentation standards and periodic verification to ensure design evaluations reflect real-world performance.

[P52] Allowing substitution of a parametric monitoring plan (§ 63.2853(a)(5)(i) monitoring plan) instead of periodic performance testing is flexible, but commenters will request EPA pre-approval of parametric indicators and alarm thresholds.

[P53] The requirement that performance tests be conducted under Administrator-specified representative conditions on and after the [date] (§ 63.2853(a)(5)(i)(A)) raises due process concerns; industry will request clarity on what constitutes “representative” and an opportunity to propose test conditions.

[P54] The prohibition on conducting performance tests during malfunction periods (§ 63.2853(a)(5)(i)(A)) is appropriate, but commenters will request a definition of “malfunction period” consistent across the rule to avoid disputes.

[P55] The obligation to provide test records to the Administrator upon request (§ 63.2853(a)(5)(i)(A)) should include a reasonable response time and format guidance to avoid unreasonable administrative burdens.

[P56] Requiring measurement and recordkeeping of oilseed inventory at start and end of each normal operating period (§ 63.2855(a)(3)) duplicates solvent inventory rules and increases paperwork; commenters will ask EPA to harmonize oilseed/solvent inventory schedules.

[P57] The deviation report timing in § 63.2861(b) — submit by end of the following month — may not allow sufficient time to estimate excess HAP emissions accurately; stakeholders will request a 60-day deadline or allowance for preliminary then final reports.

[P58] The extensive content requirements for deviation reports (§ 63.2861(b)(5)-(7)) including counts, causes, affected equipment, and estimated excess emissions will require engineering-level analyses; small entities will request scaled requirements or tiered reporting based on deviation severity.

[P59] Requiring cause statements “or ‘unknown’” for each deviation (§ 63.2861(b)(5)) could invite second-guessing by regulators; commenters will request safe-harbor language that good-faith investigations suffice and will not automatically trigger enforcement.

[P60] The requirement to estimate excess HAP emissions and describe the estimation method for each deviation (§ 63.2861(b)(7)) is technically challenging; commenters will request EPA-provided calculators or default emission factors to ensure consistency.

[P61] Requiring records of work-practice deviations during initial startup (§ 63.2861(b)(8)) without clear confidentiality protections could reveal sensitive operational strategies; industry will push for CBI safeguards.

[P62] The monthly periodic SSM reports required before the date (§ 63.2861(c))—for initial startup and malfunction periods—are duplicative with deviation reports; commenters request consolidation into a single report type.

[P63] The immediate SSM report phone/fax within 2 working days and follow-up letter within 7 working days (§ 63.2861(d)) is unduly prescriptive in communication methods (phone/fax) and timelines; commenters will request allowance for modern electronic notifications and flexible timelines.

[P64] The initial startup report content required within 30 days after initial startup (§ 63.2861(e)) is extensive; operators will request ability to combine this with other required startup documentation to avoid duplication.

[P65] The performance test results submission requirements (§ 63.2861(f)(1)-(3)) mandating ERT/CEDRI/CDX electronic formats and physical CBI media are complex; commenters will request transitional flexibility and a clear step-by-step electronic submission guide.

[P66] The CBI submission workflow (§ 63.2861(f)(3)/(g)(CBI portion)) requiring physical media to the CBI office plus redacted electronic copies is onerous and costly; industry will request alternative secure electronic methods or acceptance of certified portal submissions.

[P67] The EPA system outage claim conditions (§ 63.2861(h)) are narrow (outage within 5 business days) and require prompt written notification (§ 63.2861(h)(4)); commenters will ask EPA to broaden the outage window and clarify acceptable proof/documentation.

[P68] The requirement that outage claims must be due to EPA system outages (§ 63.2861(h)(1)) may unfairly penalize submitters with local IT issues; commenters will request recognition of broader IT disruptions beyond EPA control when accompanied by evidence.

[P69] The rule should clarify whether state/local agencies will accept EPA’s CEDRI/CDX submissions and outage claims as satisfying state reporting obligations to avoid double filing; commenters will ask for coordination language.

[P70] Several cross-references appear incorrect (e.g., § 62.2840(g) vs § 63.2840(g)); legal commenters will demand correction of typographical and cross-reference errors before finalization to prevent compliance ambiguity.

[P71] The cumulative recordkeeping and reporting obligations across Tables and sections will impose significant costs for small entities; small business associations will request a small-entity compliance flexibility analysis and potential exemptions.

[P72] The rule does not include explicit enforcement discretion or affirmative defense language for deviations caused by unavoidable force majeure events; commenters will request a narrowly tailored force majeure provision.

[P73] Environmental justice advocates will request that EPA require public posting of deviation/S SM reports for facilities located in overburdened communities to ensure community right-to-know.

[P74] The rule lacks explicit requirements for calibration, validation, and QA/QC frequency for temperature/pressure sensors required under § 63.2851(a)(8)(ii); commenters will request minimum QA/QC procedures and acceptable calibration intervals.

[P75] Commenters will request that EPA provide sample templates for the compliance demonstration plan, SSM plan, deviation reports, and initial startup reports to ensure consistent submissions and reduce back-and-forth with regulators.

[P76] The rule should clarify whether violations discovered retrospectively (e.g., during an audit) that affect prior compliance ratios require retroactive deviation reports and potential penalties; stakeholders will request clear retroactive reporting rules.
