The timing in § 63.2840(h) that the work practice standard applies “On and after [date 181 days...]” lacks clarity for sources that started startup periods just before that date; commenters will request transitional provisions specifying which rule version applies to overlapping periods.

The continuous operation requirement for the mineral oil absorption system during initial startup (§ 63.2840(h)(1)) is operationally unrealistic for some plant designs and may create safety risks; industry will request an exception for short, documented interruptions and a definition of “continuous.”

The identical continuous operation mandate for solvent condensers in § 63.2840(h)(2) fails to account for condenser bypasses used for safety or maintenance; commenters will request a permitted downtime allowance with notification requirements.

Requiring adherence to site-specific temperature and pressure limits for desolventizing and distillation units during startup (§ 63.2840(h)(3)) is reasonable, but operators need clear procedures for establishing and approving those limits; commenters will ask for an EPA template or criteria for technical justification.

Allowing site-specific operating limits based on manufacturer recommendations or “other site-specific values” (§ 63.2840(h)(3)(i)) is appropriate, but environmental groups will request that limits based solely on manufacturer specs be justified by exposure/emissions modeling before acceptance.

Permitting operating limits to be min/max/range (§ 63.2840(h)(3)(ii)) is good flexibility, but commenters will request EPA clarify whether excursions within tolerance bands during transient startup are considered violations.

The SSM plan requirement in § 63.2850(a)(3) being mandatory before [date] and then not required after that date (P18 & P56) is confusing; stakeholders will ask EPA to clarify whether SSM plans are permanently rescinded after the date or only for new instances.
The reporting obligations in § 63.2850(a)(5) are extensive; small processors will request consolidation or reduced-frequency reporting to lessen administrative burden.

Requiring initial startup period reports per § 63.2861(e) (§ 63.2850(a)(5)(iv)) may force disclosure of sensitive production details; industry will request options to file a confidential version and clarify CBI procedures.

Mandating existing sources under normal operation to meet Table 1 and Table 2 schedules (§ 63.2850(b)) without phase-in may impose immediate capital costs; industry will request staggered compliance deadlines or economic impact consideration.

The requirement that new sources upon initial startup meet full normal operation requirements (§ 63.2850(c)(1)) may be infeasible for commissioning activities; commenters will request a clearly defined commissioning/startup exemption period.

Allowing up to 6 months of initial startup treatment for new sources (§ 63.2850(c)(2)) but imposing the work practice standard after the [date] creates uncertainty; new-source developers will ask whether the 6-month period can be extended for complex facilities.

The rule’s different treatment of significant modifications with a 3-month initial startup period (§ 63.2850(d)(2)) versus new sources (6 months) may be arbitrary; stakeholders will request justification and parity or allow case-by-case extensions.

The requirement to choose a compliance option within 15 days of malfunction start (§ 63.2850(e) intro) is too short for complex events; industry will request 30 days to evaluate and notify regulators.

Requiring full compliance with paragraph (a) and Table 1 during malfunction periods (§ 63.2850(e)(2)) can be infeasible during emergency responses; commenters will ask for an explicit, narrowly tailored emergency exemption with retrospective reporting.

The reference error in Table 1 (§ 63.2850 (a)(2) referencing § 62.2840(g) per P33) is a drafting mistake that must be corrected to § 63.2840(g); legal commenters will request correction to avoid legal challenge.

The solvent loss measurement requirements (§ 63.2850 Table 1(b) / § 63.2853) lack specificity on allowed measurement technologies and tolerances; industry will request EPA provide acceptable methods and uncertainty allowances.

Requiring recording of HAP volume fractions >1% in shipments (§ 63.2850 Table 1(c)) could be impractical when suppliers don’t provide HAP fraction details; commenters will request supplier notification requirements or default conservative values.

The obligation to measure and record tons of each oilseed processed during normal operation (§ 63.2850 Table 1(d)) is straightforward but may be burdensome for mixed-batch or commingled shipments; commenters will request aggregation rules.

Computing weighted-average HAP fraction by the end of the following month (§ 63.2850 Table 1(e) / § 63.2854) may be administratively burdensome; processors request aligning that deadline with the compliance ratio calculation deadline.

The requirement in Table 1(f) to compute the 12-month compliance ratio “by the next calendar month” (for each 12-month period) duplicates § 63.2840(b) and increases confusion; commenters will request consolidation and a single clear deadline for all related computations.

Submitting NOCS or annual compliance certifications per Table 1(g) may require costly legal review; stakeholders will request a simplified certification form and clear instructions for small entities.

The deviation reporting trigger (compliance ratio >1.00) in Table 1(h)(1) is a strict cutoff that does not account for measurement error; stakeholders will request a de minimis buffer (e.g., 1.05) before a deviation is required.

Requiring deviation notification reports as described in § 63.2861(b) on and after the [date] (Table 1(h)(2)) without harmonization with other federal/state reporting systems will duplicate effort; regulated entities request EPA allow submission to a single portal acceptable to state agencies.

The periodic SSM reporting (§ 63.2850 Table 1(i)) and immediate SSM reporting (§ 63.2850 Table 1(j)) overlap in content and timing; commenters ask EPA to harmonize triggers and avoid multiple reports for the same event.

The requirement to keep the compliance demonstration plan in the Title V permit (§ 63.2851(a) intro) may require many permit modifications across jurisdictions; permit writers will ask EPA to allow incorporation by reference instead of physical attachment.

Requiring retention of prior versions of the compliance plan for five years (§ 63.2851(a)) will increase recordkeeping burdens; small processors will request permission to retain only summaries of changes.

The enumerated items required in the compliance plan (§ 63.2851(a)(last)) include potentially proprietary operational details; industry will request clearer CBI protection procedures beyond the general CBI submission requirements.

The obligation to include site-specific operating limits and their basis in the compliance plan (§ 63.2851(a)(8)(i)) may expose trade secrets; commenters will request explicit confidentiality protections for technical justifications.

The demand to include detailed measurement methods and frequencies for temperature and pressure (§ 63.2851(a)(8)(ii)) is reasonable, but EPA should allow cross-reference to existing monitoring programs to avoid duplication.
Requiring development of an SSM plan before the compliance date (§ 63.2852 intro) with no phased implementation is unrealistic; small businesses will request more time or simplified SSM templates.

The SSM plan requirement to reflect “best practices of the industry” (§ 63.2852) is vague and could be selectively enforced; stakeholders ask for a non-exhaustive list of acceptable standards or authoritative industry guidelines.

Requiring any other plan used as an SSM plan to meet all NESHAP requirements (§ 63.2852) could nullify existing company-wide emergency plans; compliance officers request a crosswalk showing how existing plans can be certified as meeting § 63.2852.

The complete removal of SSM plan obligations on and after the [date] (§ 63.2852 P56) contradicts other sections that continue to reference SSM reports and plans after that date; commenters will flag internal inconsistency and request clarification.

Categorizing operating status for each recorded time interval (§ 63.2853(a)(2)) will require high-resolution data logging; small processors will request allowed minimum interval durations (e.g., hourly vs. minute-by-minute).

Measuring and recording solvent inventory at the start and end of every normal operating period (§ 63.2853(a)(3)) is operationally heavy; commenters will propose acceptable surrogate measurements (metered receipts and shipments) and periodic reconciliation.

The permission to use control devices including incinerators, boilers, and flares (§ 63.2853(a)(5)(i)) should come with emission performance standards; environmental groups will request minimum destruction/removal efficiencies be specified.

The requirement to quantify gallons entering and destroyed in destructive control devices (§ 63.2853(a)(5)(i)) may be difficult for combined combustion systems; commenters will ask for specific accepted measurement and calculation approaches for combined fuel streams.

Allowing subtraction of solvent destroyed in a control device from total solvent loss (§ 63.2853(a)(5)(i)) could be misused to obscure fugitive emissions; environmental advocates will request mandatory stack testing or CEMS to verify destruction claims.

The allowance to use design evaluations instead of performance testing (§ 63.2853(a)(5)(i)) must be limited; commenters will request stringent documentation standards and periodic verification to ensure design evaluations reflect real-world performance.

Allowing substitution of a parametric monitoring plan (§ 63.2853(a)(5)(i) monitoring plan) instead of periodic performance testing is flexible, but commenters will request EPA pre-approval of parametric indicators and alarm thresholds.

The requirement that performance tests be conducted under Administrator-specified representative conditions on and after the [date] (§ 63.2853(a)(5)(i)(A)) raises due process concerns; industry will request clarity on what constitutes “representative” and an opportunity to propose test conditions.

The prohibition on conducting performance tests during malfunction periods (§ 63.2853(a)(5)(i)(A)) is appropriate, but commenters will request a definition of “malfunction period” consistent across the rule to avoid disputes.

The obligation to provide test records to the Administrator upon request (§ 63.2853(a)(5)(i)(A)) should include a reasonable response time and format guidance to avoid unreasonable administrative burdens.

Requiring measurement and recordkeeping of oilseed inventory at start and end of each normal operating period (§ 63.2855(a)(3)) duplicates solvent inventory rules and increases paperwork; commenters will ask EPA to harmonize oilseed/solvent inventory schedules.

The deviation report timing in § 63.2861(b) — submit by end of the following month — may not allow sufficient time to estimate excess HAP emissions accurately; stakeholders will request a 60-day deadline or allowance for preliminary then final reports.

The extensive content requirements for deviation reports (§ 63.2861(b)(5)-(7)) including counts, causes, affected equipment, and estimated excess emissions will require engineering-level analyses; small entities will request scaled requirements or tiered reporting based on deviation severity.

Requiring cause statements “or ‘unknown’” for each deviation (§ 63.2861(b)(5)) could invite second-guessing by regulators; commenters will request safe-harbor language that good-faith investigations suffice and will not automatically trigger enforcement.

The requirement to estimate excess HAP emissions and describe the estimation method for each deviation (§ 63.2861(b)(7)) is technically challenging; commenters will request EPA-provided calculators or default emission factors to ensure consistency.

Requiring records of work-practice deviations during initial startup (§ 63.2861(b)(8)) without clear confidentiality protections could reveal sensitive operational strategies; industry will push for CBI safeguards.

The monthly periodic SSM reports required before the date (§ 63.2861(c))—for initial startup and malfunction periods—are duplicative with deviation reports; commenters request consolidation into a single report type.

The immediate SSM report phone/fax within 2 working days and follow-up letter within 7 working days (§ 63.2861(d)) is unduly prescriptive in communication methods (phone/fax) and timelines; commenters will request allowance for modern electronic notifications and flexible timelines.

The initial startup report content required within 30 days after initial startup (§ 63.2861(e)) is extensive; operators will request ability to combine this with other required startup documentation to avoid duplication.

The performance test results submission requirements (§ 63.2861(f)(1)-(3)) mandating ERT/CEDRI/CDX electronic formats and physical CBI media are complex; commenters will request transitional flexibility and a clear step-by-step electronic submission guide.

The CBI submission workflow (§ 63.2861(f)(3)/(g)(CBI portion)) requiring physical media to the CBI office plus redacted electronic copies is onerous and costly; industry will request alternative secure electronic methods or acceptance of certified portal submissions.

The EPA system outage claim conditions (§ 63.2861(h)) are narrow (outage within 5 business days) and require prompt written notification (§ 63.2861(h)(4)); commenters will ask EPA to broaden the outage window and clarify acceptable proof/documentation.

The requirement that outage claims must be due to EPA system outages (§ 63.2861(h)(1)) may unfairly penalize submitters with local IT issues; commenters will request recognition of broader IT disruptions beyond EPA control when accompanied by evidence.

The rule should clarify whether state/local agencies will accept EPA’s CEDRI/CDX submissions and outage claims as satisfying state reporting obligations to avoid double filing; commenters will ask for coordination language.

Several cross-references appear incorrect (e.g., § 62.2840(g) vs § 63.2840(g)); legal commenters will demand correction of typographical and cross-reference errors before finalization to prevent compliance ambiguity.

The cumulative recordkeeping and reporting obligations across Tables and sections will impose significant costs for small entities; small business associations will request a small-entity compliance flexibility analysis and potential exemptions.

The rule does not include explicit enforcement discretion or affirmative defense language for deviations caused by unavoidable force majeure events; commenters will request a narrowly tailored force majeure provision.
Environmental justice advocates will request that EPA require public posting of deviation/S SM reports for facilities located in overburdened communities to ensure community right-to-know.

The rule lacks explicit requirements for calibration, validation, and QA/QC frequency for temperature/pressure sensors required under § 63.2851(a)(8)(ii); commenters will request minimum QA/QC procedures and acceptable calibration intervals.

Commenters will request that EPA provide sample templates for the compliance demonstration plan, SSM plan, deviation reports, and initial startup reports to ensure consistent submissions and reduce back-and-forth with regulators.

The rule should clarify whether violations discovered retrospectively (e.g., during an audit) that affect prior compliance ratios require retroactive deviation reports and potential penalties; stakeholders will request clear retroactive reporting rules.

raw_output:
[P1] The rule’s blanket application of §§ 17.31 and 17.32 to the Atlantic pigtoe (§ 17.45(a)(1)) is ambiguous because it does not specify how existing permits issued under those sections will be modified or grandfathered; industry commenters will request explicit transitional language clarifying permit status for ongoing projects.

[P1] Conservation NGOs will claim that applying the full prohibitions of §§ 17.31 and 17.32 is appropriate and urge the Service to confirm that prohibitions on habitat modification under those sections extend to all tributaries and intermittent streams used by the Atlantic pigtoe.

[P2] State natural resource agencies will assert that the general statement in § 17.45(a)(2) allowing incidental take for listed activities lacks a required framework (e.g., monitoring, reporting, adaptive management) and request that the Service require standardized reporting for all incidental take allowed under paragraph (a)(2).

[P3] State wildlife agencies will support § 17.45(a)(2)(i) permitting incidental take during state species restoration (broodstock collection, tissue sampling, captive propagation, stocking) but will ask the Service to specify allowable sample sizes, frequency of broodstock collection, and handling protocols to minimize genetic or demographic impacts.

[P3] Academic geneticists will comment that the exception for tissue collection lacks safeguards against overcollection and recommend limiting tissue sample sizes, requiring non-lethal methods where possible, and instituting genetic monitoring to prevent erosion of genetic diversity.

[P4] Restoration engineers and consultants will welcome § 17.45(a)(2)(ii) allowing channel restoration incidental take when projects create “natural, physically stable, ecologically functioning streams” but will request a clear, objective definition and measurable performance standards for those terms to avoid subjective enforcement.

[P4] Local governments and permit applicants will request that the Service specify the required time horizon and metrics (e.g., bank stability for X years, macroinvertebrate indices, longitudinal connectivity measures) demonstrating that a restored channel is “ecologically functioning” to qualify for the exception.

[P5] Contractors and state DOTs will challenge the limitation in § 17.45(a)(2)(iii) permitting only specified bioengineering methods for bank stabilization, arguing it could prohibit proven hybrid approaches and requesting an allowance for alternative engineered solutions where bioengineering alone is insufficient, subject to Service approval.

[P6] Construction and quarrying industry groups will file comments opposing the exclusion of sole use of quarried rock (rip-rap), rock baskets, or gabions (§ 17.45(a)(2)(iii) specification/prohibition), arguing that in many high-energy sites rip-rap is the only viable method to protect infrastructure and requesting an exception process or the ability to use these materials when combined with vegetative techniques.

[P6] Environmental advocates will support the explicit prohibition on sole use of rip-rap, rock baskets, or gabions, asserting these materials degrade mussel habitat and requesting that the rule also restrict their use within a wider buffer zone around critical habitat.

[P7] Forestry trade associations will request clarification on the scope of “silviculture and forest management activities” in § 17.45(a)(2)(iv) (what practices qualify) and ask for an explicit list of covered activities (thinning, harvesting, prescribed fire, road maintenance) to reduce uncertainty.

[P8] Private landowners and timber companies will object that the requirement to “implement highest-standard best management practices” (§ 17.45(a)(2)(iv)(A)) is vague and potentially imposes an unbounded standard; they will request the Service define “highest-standard” (e.g., specify named BMP documents and versions) or instead require adherence to specific, enumerated BMPs.

[P9] Certification bodies and conservation groups will support § 17.45(a)(2)(iv)(B) requiring compliance with water-quality-related forest practice guidelines or recognized certification standards (SFI/FSC/ATFS) but will request the rule require independent third-party certification or audit frequency to verify compliance.

[P9] Small private landowners will raise concerns that requiring compliance with SFI/FSC/other certification standards (§ 17.45(a)(2)(iv)(B)) is cost-prohibitive and not available to all operators; they will request alternatives such as demonstrated adherence to state BMPs or technical assistance programs.

[P10] Public transparency advocates will support making critical habitat coordinates available at Regulations.gov (§ 17.95(f)(4)) but will caution that posting exact plot points may increase risk of illegal collecting and request either aggregated coordinate data or delayed release for sensitive subpopulations.

[P10] Recreational landowners and anglers will request clearer instructions for accessing the coordinate files referenced in § 17.95(f)(4), noting that not all stakeholders can navigate Regulations.gov and requesting downloadable GIS layers and contact points for assistance.

[P11] Local governments will ask that the requirement to contact a regional office for field office location information (§ 17.95(f)(4)) be accompanied by contact phone numbers and an online interactive map to avoid delays and inconsistent responses.

[P12] Legal experts will comment that the general prohibition in § 17.45(a)(1) should explicitly restate criminal and civil penalty consequences and the mens rea standards for violations to avoid confusion about enforcement thresholds and to ensure due process protections.

[P13] Aquarium industry and research institutions will request clarity on import/export prohibitions (§ 17.45(a)(1)(i)) — whether transboundary transfers for research or captive propagation programs are permissible under a § 17.32 permit and what conditions would apply.

[P14] Conservation hatcheries will ask whether “take” as prohibited in § 17.45(a)(1)(ii) encompasses temporary handling for captive propagation and request an explicit cross-reference that allowed take for propagation is governed by the § 17.32 permitting process.

[P15] Law enforcement and compliance NGOs will urge the Service to specify recordkeeping and chain-of-custody requirements for possession of specimens (§ 17.45(a)(1)(iii)) to prevent laundering of unlawfully taken individuals and to clarify evidentiary expectations.

[P16] Commercial businesses will ask whether the prohibition on interstate or foreign commerce (§ 17.45(a)(1)(iv)) applies to incidental inclusion of mussels in gravel or fill transported across state lines, and will request an exemption or safe-harbor for de minimis incidental transport subject to screening/inspection requirements.

[P17] Online marketplace operators will request guidance regarding § 17.45(a)(1)(v) (sale or offer for sale) to determine whether historic, taxidermy, or subfossil shells fall under the prohibition and if permits for educational sales are available.

[P18] Industry stakeholders will request that the list of exceptions in § 17.45(a)(2) explicitly include emergency actions (e.g., emergency bridge repairs, flood control) performed under governmental emergency authorities, or at minimum establish expedited consultation/permit procedures during declared emergencies.

[P19] Permit applicants will urge the Service to clarify how § 17.45(a)(2)(i) (conduct activities authorized by § 17.32 permit) interacts with the incidental take allowances under paragraph (a)(2)(v) to avoid duplication or conflicting requirements between general permits and project-specific authorizations.

[P20] Municipal stormwater managers will request detailed guidance on what constitutes qualifying “take as set forth at § 17.21(c)(3) and (c)(4)” (§ 17.45(a)(2)(ii)) to understand which project categories are presumptively covered and which require individual consultation.

[P21] State fish and wildlife agencies will support permitting possession and other acts under § 17.21(d)(2) (§ 17.45(a)(2)(iv)) but request the Service set standardized permit conditions for captive propagation to ensure consistent conservation outcomes across states.

[P22] Restoration practitioners will welcome the permission for incidental take tied to specified activities (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)) but will request that the Service provide templates for survey protocols, relocation procedures, and monitoring plans so that applicants can reliably meet obligations.

[P23] NGOs and scientists will insist that the survey and relocation requirement (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(B) and P26) include minimum survey effort, timing (seasonality), qualified personnel standards, and post-relocation monitoring to demonstrate survival and minimize harm, rather than just requiring relocation prior to project implementation.

[P23] Some commenters will argue that mandatory relocation of Atlantic pigtoe before restoration (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(B)/P26) could harm mussels if relocation sites are suboptimal; they will request the rule require Service approval of relocation sites and adaptive monitoring to confirm survival.

[P24] Riparian property owners will challenge the prohibition on sole use of rip-rap (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(C)/P28) as overly prescriptive and request an alternative permitting pathway where rip-rap is necessary for public safety or to protect infrastructure, provided mitigation and habitat offsets are implemented.

[P25] Watershed associations will request the Service further restrict the use of rock baskets and gabions beyond prohibition as sole methods (P6/P28) by also limiting partial use within SMZs because such structures can reduce benthic habitat quality.

[P26] Forestry practitioners will seek clarification on the measurement and enforcement of the Zone 2 width in the two-zoned SMZ requirement (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P31), asking whether Zone 2 width tables will be published for each stream order or watershed and how variability is calculated.

[P27] Timber companies will protest the absolute no-harvest rule for Zone 1 at a 50-foot minimum (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P32) as economically burdensome, requesting flexibility for low-impact selective harvests, insect/disease salvage operations, or other management activities via a case-by-case exemption process.

[P28] Road-building contractors will request technical specifications for the “properly designed” crossings required at right angles (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P33), including acceptable culvert sizes, bridge standards, fish-passage design criteria, and sediment control measures.

[P29] Environmental lawyers will argue that the right-angle crossing and prohibition on impeding fish passage or stream flow (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P33) must be reconciled with existing road geometry constraints and request a variance procedure for sites where right-angle installation is not feasible.

[P30] Forestry and logging operators will request the Service define what constitutes minimized visible sediment entering the waterbody (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P33) and propose measurable thresholds (e.g., NTU turbidity limits, percent fine sediment) and monitoring requirements.

[P31] Landowners and industry will seek clarification and guidance on the phrase “minimized” number of crossings (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P34), requesting numeric guidance (maximum crossings per mile or per harvest unit) or decision criteria for when crossings are allowed.

[P32] Conservation groups will urge the Service to require stream-crossing decommissioning and post-harvest rehabilitation as part of compliance with § 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P34 to reduce long-term impacts to Atlantic pigtoe habitat.

[P33] Small woodland owners will request cost-share, technical assistance, or exemptions given compliance burdens for establishing and maintaining a two-zoned SMZ (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P31–P34), arguing that the rule could disproportionately affect small landowners.

[P34] State forestry agencies will ask the Service to allow use of equivalent state BMPs that have been demonstrated effective in lieu of the specific SMZ configuration (50-foot Zone 1 minimum) (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P31–P32) where the state has well-documented, site-adapted practices.

[P35] Fisheries biologists will request the Service adopt a prescriptive timeline for pre-restoration surveys (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(B)/P26) (e.g., surveys within X months of construction) to ensure survey data reflect current conditions at the time of disturbance.

[P36] Legal commenters will point out a potential inconsistency: § 17.45(a)(1) bars possession of unlawfully taken specimens, but § 17.45(a)(2)(iv) permits certain possessory acts — they will request the Service clarify whether possession authorized under (a)(2)(iv) provides an affirmative defense to prosecution and how permittees should document authorization.

[P37] Tribes will request explicit recognition that tribal restoration programs qualify for the state restoration exception (§ 17.45(a)(2)(i)/P3) and ask for coordination procedures between the Service and sovereign tribes for broodstock collection and captive propagation.

[P38] Developers will request that the Service provide a standardized timeline for Service review and approval of required survey reports and relocation plans under the channel restoration exception (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(B)/P25–P26) to avoid project delays.

[P39] Scientists will urge the Service to require population-level impact assessments for all allowed incidental take activities (§ 17.45(a)(2)/P2), not just project-level avoidance measures, to ensure cumulative impacts do not jeopardize species recovery.

[P40] NGOs will recommend that the Service include mandatory compensatory mitigation for any authorized incidental take under § 17.45(a)(2)(v) (e.g., habitat restoration credits) to achieve net conservation benefits for the Atlantic pigtoe.

Permit applicants will urge the Service to clarify how § 17.45(a)(2)(i) (conduct activities authorized by § 17.32 permit) interacts with the incidental take allowances under paragraph (a)(2)(v) to avoid duplication or conflicting requirements between general permits and project-specific authorizations.

Municipal stormwater managers will request detailed guidance on what constitutes qualifying “take as set forth at § 17.21(c)(3) and (c)(4)” (§ 17.45(a)(2)(ii)) to understand which project categories are presumptively covered and which require individual consultation.

State fish and wildlife agencies will support permitting possession and other acts under § 17.21(d)(2) (§ 17.45(a)(2)(iv)) but request the Service set standardized permit conditions for captive propagation to ensure consistent conservation outcomes across states.

Restoration practitioners will welcome the permission for incidental take tied to specified activities (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)) but will request that the Service provide templates for survey protocols, relocation procedures, and monitoring plans so that applicants can reliably meet obligations.

NGOs and scientists will insist that the survey and relocation requirement (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(B) and P26) include minimum survey effort, timing (seasonality), qualified personnel standards, and post-relocation monitoring to demonstrate survival and minimize harm, rather than just requiring relocation prior to project implementation.

Some commenters will argue that mandatory relocation of Atlantic pigtoe before restoration (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(B)/P26) could harm mussels if relocation sites are suboptimal; they will request the rule require Service approval of relocation sites and adaptive monitoring to confirm survival.

Riparian property owners will challenge the prohibition on sole use of rip-rap (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(C)/P28) as overly prescriptive and request an alternative permitting pathway where rip-rap is necessary for public safety or to protect infrastructure, provided mitigation and habitat offsets are implemented.

Watershed associations will request the Service further restrict the use of rock baskets and gabions beyond prohibition as sole methods (P6/P28) by also limiting partial use within SMZs because such structures can reduce benthic habitat quality.

Forestry practitioners will seek clarification on the measurement and enforcement of the Zone 2 width in the two-zoned SMZ requirement (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P31), asking whether Zone 2 width tables will be published for each stream order or watershed and how variability is calculated.

Timber companies will protest the absolute no-harvest rule for Zone 1 at a 50-foot minimum (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P32) as economically burdensome, requesting flexibility for low-impact selective harvests, insect/disease salvage operations, or other management activities via a case-by-case exemption process.

Road-building contractors will request technical specifications for the “properly designed” crossings required at right angles (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P33), including acceptable culvert sizes, bridge standards, fish-passage design criteria, and sediment control measures.

Environmental lawyers will argue that the right-angle crossing and prohibition on impeding fish passage or stream flow (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P33) must be reconciled with existing road geometry constraints and request a variance procedure for sites where right-angle installation is not feasible.

Forestry and logging operators will request the Service define what constitutes minimized visible sediment entering the waterbody (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P33) and propose measurable thresholds (e.g., NTU turbidity limits, percent fine sediment) and monitoring requirements.

Landowners and industry will seek clarification and guidance on the phrase “minimized” number of crossings (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P34), requesting numeric guidance (maximum crossings per mile or per harvest unit) or decision criteria for when crossings are allowed.

Conservation groups will urge the Service to require stream-crossing decommissioning and post-harvest rehabilitation as part of compliance with § 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P34 to reduce long-term impacts to Atlantic pigtoe habitat.

Small woodland owners will request cost-share, technical assistance, or exemptions given compliance burdens for establishing and maintaining a two-zoned SMZ (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P31–P34), arguing that the rule could disproportionately affect small landowners.

State forestry agencies will ask the Service to allow use of equivalent state BMPs that have been demonstrated effective in lieu of the specific SMZ configuration (50-foot Zone 1 minimum) (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(D)/P31–P32) where the state has well-documented, site-adapted practices.

Fisheries biologists will request the Service adopt a prescriptive timeline for pre-restoration surveys (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(B)/P26) (e.g., surveys within X months of construction) to ensure survey data reflect current conditions at the time of disturbance.

Legal commenters will point out a potential inconsistency: § 17.45(a)(1) bars possession of unlawfully taken specimens, but § 17.45(a)(2)(iv) permits certain possessory acts — they will request the Service clarify whether possession authorized under (a)(2)(iv) provides an affirmative defense to prosecution and how permittees should document authorization.

Tribes will request explicit recognition that tribal restoration programs qualify for the state restoration exception (§ 17.45(a)(2)(i)/P3) and ask for coordination procedures between the Service and sovereign tribes for broodstock collection and captive propagation.

Developers will request that the Service provide a standardized timeline for Service review and approval of required survey reports and relocation plans under the channel restoration exception (§ 17.45(a)(2)(v)(B)/P25–P26) to avoid project delays.

Scientists will urge the Service to require population-level impact assessments for all allowed incidental take activities (§ 17.45(a)(2)/P2), not just project-level avoidance measures, to ensure cumulative impacts do not jeopardize species recovery.

NGOs will recommend that the Service include mandatory compensatory mitigation for any authorized incidental take under § 17.45(a)(2)(v) (e.g., habitat restoration credits) to achieve net conservation benefits for the Atlantic pigtoe.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement in §1.72 to "submit the required information elements in ACE when filing an import entry for FDA-regulated articles" lacks a phased implementation timeline and will impose immediate compliance costs and system changes on small importers; FDA should provide at least a 12–18 month phase-in and a small business compliance guide.

[P1] The rule does not specify liability or penalties for ACE filers or brokers if information submitted under §1.72 is inaccurate; commenters request clarification of enforcement consequences and an appeals process for inadvertent errors.

[P2] §1.72(a) requires "product identifying information" but the proposal does not list the exact field formats (character limits, codes vs free text); industry requests a machine-readable schema and field length/validation rules to avoid ambiguous rejections.

[P3] The FDA Country of Production requirement in §1.72(a)(1) will conflict with existing customs country-of-origin rules for multi-country production chains; the agency should harmonize definitions with CBP and clarify treatment of multi-step production in bonded facilities.

[P4] The definition in §1.72(a)(1) that the FDA Country of Production is where "meaningful manufacturing/processing" occurred is vague; commenters (manufacturers and legal experts) request a precise statutory definition or enumerated examples of what activities qualify as "meaningful manufacturing/processing."

[P4] The "meaningful manufacturing/processing" standard could be interpreted to require reporting the country of the component supplier rather than final assembly; suppliers and OEMs request examples for common supply chain scenarios (e.g., labeling, packaging, sterilization, blending).

[P5] The obligation to submit a "Complete FDA Product Code" in §1.72(a)(2) that "must agree with the invoice description" will create reconciliation disputes between customs brokers and suppliers; FDA should allow use of standardized product codes mapped to invoice descriptors and permit corrections within a defined cure period.

[P6] Requiring the "Complete FDA Product Code" to exactly match invoice descriptions (§1.72(a)(2)) will be operationally difficult for mixed loads or bulk shipments described generically on invoices; FDA should accept best-effort mapping and permit aggregate codes for bulk commodities.

[P7] The FDA Value requirement in §1.72(a)(3) and §1.73(a) (rounded to the nearest dollar and matching the invoice) will duplicate CBP valuation data and could be manipulated for regulatory screening; FDA should clarify whether declared value will be used for admissibility decisions or retained solely for screening.

[P6] §1.72(a)(3) rounding to the nearest dollar may distort low-value shipments or de minimis thresholds; request that FDA allow cents for values under $1,000 or align rounding with CBP practice.

[P7] The FDA Quantity obligations in §1.72(a)(4) requiring detailed packaging levels and smallest unit weight/volume will impose significant data collection burdens on exporters and brokers, especially for complex packaging hierarchies; FDA should permit simplified quantity reporting for pre-packaged consumer goods.

[P8] §1.72(b) requires entity identification including contact details "for a person related to importation"; this raises privacy and data protection concerns for individuals (e.g., manufacturer contacts) and cross-border privacy law conflicts—FDA should permit business contact points rather than personal emails/phones and specify data retention/security safeguards.

[P9] The requirement in §1.72(b)(1) to provide name, telephone, and email of one person related to the importation could be abused to target individuals for enforcement or harassment; trade associations request an option to supply a centralized corporate compliance contact instead.

[P10] §1.72(b)(2) mandating telephone and email of the importer of record may be redundant with ACE filer contact info and create duplicate data management; FDA should allow the ACE filer to affirm that importer contact info is on file with CBP rather than resubmitting.

[P11] §1.73(a) requiring FDA Value at time of entry filing for food could slow clearance for perishable goods if additional validation is required; FDA should permit provisional entries with an obligation to correct within a short timeframe to prevent spoilage.

[P12] The requirement in §1.73(b) to submit all §1.72 information at entry filing for food contact substances seems overly prescriptive for low-risk polymer components; industry requests risk-based exemptions for articles that are solely packaging materials with established low-risk profiles.

[P13] §1.73(c) requiring Food Canning Establishment Number, Submission Identifier, and can dimensions/volume at entry for low-acid canned foods is burdensome for small foreign canners that do not currently use FDA identifiers; FDA should provide a registry process and transition period for non-U.S. facilities to obtain and populate these identifiers.

[P14] §1.73(d) analogous requirements for acidified foods (§1.73(d)) do not address multi-ingredient products where acidification occurs at multiple steps; clarification needed on which establishment's number to report when acidification is performed by a co-packer.

[P15] §1.74 generally imposes many additional data fields for human drugs at entry without clear evidence of screening value; brand and generic drug importers request a cost-benefit analysis and a safe-harbor for identified authorized distributors.

[P16] §1.74(a) requiring both Drug Registration Number and Drug Listing Number for human drugs may be impossible for certain foreign manufacturers who do not have U.S. facility identifiers; request that FDA accept the foreign facility identifier or allow an importer to submit its UFI with a cross-reference process.

[P17] The definition in §1.74(a) that the Drug Registration Number is the UFI of the foreign establishment conflicts with current FDA registration timelines for foreign establishments; FDA should require submission only if the foreign facility is actually registered with FDA and provide an interim "pending" status code.

[P18] §1.74(b) requiring NDA/ANDA application numbers at entry for approved drugs raises confidentiality concerns for proprietary development-stage products and could disrupt clinical supply chains; request an alternative code or redaction mechanism for sensitive pipeline products.

[P19] §1.74(c) requiring submission of IND numbers for investigational drugs at entry could inadvertently block clinical trial material shipments when IND numbers are withheld for blinding; clinical researchers request an alternative secure transmission channel or exemption for qualified clinical shipments.

[P20] §1.75 imposing animal-drug specific data fields will complicate complex feed and medicated premix imports; agricultural stakeholders request harmonization with FDA Center for Veterinary Medicine data systems and flexibility for compounded or non-NDC-listed products.

[P21] §1.75(a) requiring Drug Registration Number and NDC for animal drugs will be impossible for many medicated feed ingredients and compounded formulations that lack NDCs; request an alternative identification pathway or temporary exception.

[P22] §1.75(b)-(d) requiring application, index file, or investigational numbers for animal drugs (approved/conditional/indexed/INAD) lacks a central searchable database; commenters request that FDA publish a machine-readable registry mapping those numbers to product names to enable accurate ACE submissions.

[P25] §1.76 imposing device-specific ACE data will require device manufacturers and importers to integrate regulatory databases (510/807) with their trade systems; small device firms request a one-year phased rollout and technical specifications for data exchange.

[P26] §1.76(a) requires Registration Number(s) and Device Listing Number for foreign manufacturers/exporters/domestic manufacturers—many foreign exporters are not FDA-registered; FDA should clarify whether importation will be refused if those numbers are absent and provide a pathway for late registration.

[P27] §1.76(b) obligating submission of IDE numbers at entry could halt importation of study devices for clinical trials due to timing mismatches between IDE issuance and shipment; clinical investigators request an option to submit IDEs through an alternative secure channel post-arrival.

[P28] §1.76(b) (NSR) requiring entry of "NSR" in the Affirmation of Compliance for nonsignificant risk or exempt studies is vague; request standard text and supporting documentation that must be retained to substantiate NSR status in audits.

[P29] §1.76(c) requiring Premarket Numbers (PMA, PDP, De Novo, 510(k), HDE) at entry presumes that all imported devices have such numbers; many components and accessories lack premarket numbers—request an exemption for components or explicit instructions for "no premarket number" entries.

[P30] §1.76(d) requiring an affirmation that an article is a component requiring further processing risks delays if importers are uncertain; recommend permitting a "component—intended for further processing" standardized code and guidance on documentation to avoid refusals.

[P31] §1.76(e) and §1.76(f) requiring specific affirmations of compliance (performance standard for electrode lead wires/patient cables and §801.410 for impact resistant lenses) are highly specific and will require manufacturers to verify compliance before shipment; industry requests acceptance of third-party attestations and a cure period for inadvertent omissions.

[P33] §1.76(g) requiring an Affirmation of Compliance for convenience kits is ambiguous—many kits are assembled in the U.S. from imported parts; FDA should clarify whether the affirmation applies to the kit assembler or the importer of individual components.

[P34] §1.76(h) requiring IND numbers for combination products when CDRH is primary jurisdiction may be unnecessary for devices with ancillary drug components and could expose sponsors' confidential IND data; request a confidential submission pathway or an exemption unless the IND relates directly to the device's primary function.

[P35] §1.77 mandating that all Form FDA 2877 declarations for radiation-emitting electronic products be submitted electronically in ACE may exceed current manufacturer capabilities, particularly for smaller electronics importers; request a transition period and template for electronic 2877 data.

[P36] §1.78 imposing a broad set of additional ACE fields for biological products, HCT/Ps, and related drugs/devices (CBER-regulated) will create complex mapping needs; blood/tissue banks and biologics manufacturers request specific field definitions, validation rules, and an API specification.

[P37] §1.78(a) requiring a product name that includes "established name/trade/brand/proper name or product description" could cause inconsistent naming conventions; request a controlled vocabulary or FDA-maintained product name registry to reduce mismatches.

[P38] §1.78(b)(1)-(2) requiring HCT/P Registration Numbers and affirmations of compliance for section 361 HCT/Ps will be problematic for foreign tissue establishments that are not currently registered under part 1271; FDA should provide registration instructions and a reasonable compliance deadline.

[P40] §1.78(c) asking for Submission Tracking Numbers or Biologics License Numbers for BLAs at entry will require sponsors to ensure the correct STN is applied to each lot; manufacturers ask for guidance on handling multi-lot shipments covered by a single BLA and whether a single STN suffices.

[P41] §1.78(d)-(f) duplicating drug registration/listing and NDA/ANDA/IND submission requirements create overlap with §1.74 and may impose conflicting validation rules; commenters request harmonized definitions and a single submission pathway for drugs that are also biologicals.

[P44] §1.78(g)-(i) duplicative device registration/IDE/premarket number requirements for biologics-associated devices will increase complexity for combination product importers; request a combined submission template for combination products to prevent duplicate entries.

[P47] §1.78(j) requiring an affirmation for device components needing further processing duplicates §1.76(d); commenters urge harmonization and a single code to indicate "component for further processing" across centers.

[P48] §1.79 requiring additional ACE information for tobacco product entries may capture sensitive marketing data (brand names) that could be misused; public health advocates request that brand name submission be used only for surveillance and not made public, while industry requests masking options during adjudication.

[P49] §1.79(a) requiring the brand name of tobacco products could be easily circumvented by generic descriptors on invoices; FDA should require product SKU or SKU-level identifiers rather than relying on brand text.

[P50] §1.79(b) requiring name and address of the ACE filer for tobacco could expose small retailers or brokers engaged in tobacco shipments to public disclosure; industry requests confidentiality protections and alignment with existing CBP reporting.

[P51] §1.80 mandating §1.72 data at entry for cosmetics may impose undue burden for low-risk cosmetic items and small importers; cosmetic industry trade groups request a simplified data set or de minimis exemption for shipments below a monetary threshold.

[P52] §1.90 requiring FDA to provide prompt notice to owner/consignee when a sample is requested is reasonable, but the rule lacks a maximum timeframe for "prompt" notification; owners request a definite deadline (e.g., within 24 hours of request) to avoid unexpected storage/detention costs.

[P53] §1.90 obligating the owner/consignee to hold the article until further notice creates storage liabilities; small businesses request that FDA specify maximum hold periods (e.g., 15 business days) and require FDA to compensate for reasonable storage fees if the hold extends beyond the period.

[P54] The prohibition in §1.90 on distributing the article after receiving notice until sample results are communicated could cause severe economic harm for perishable goods; request an expedited sampling timeline for perishable shipments or presumptive release procedures with conditions.

[P55] §1.94(a) requires a written/electronic notice stating reasons if the article may be refused admission or subject to destruction, but the rule does not set timing requirements for issuing such notice; importers request a requirement that notices be issued within a specific window (e.g., 5 business days) and include a clear explanation of the statutory basis.

[P56] §1.94(c) permits a single combined notice for refusal and destruction for certain drugs; legal experts caution that combining these notices may prejudice due process and request that FDA provide separate notices or an explicit explanation of rights and appeal processes within the combined notice.

[P57] §1271.420(a) requiring the importer of record to "notify the FDA district director before or at importation" of HCT/Ps and provide sufficient information (including ACE-submitted data) to make admissibility decisions imposes a duplicative notification burden on top of ACE filings; tissue establishments request that ACE filing be deemed adequate notice and that FDA limit separate email/fax notifications.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement to use Method 18 or 25A to determine compliance with ppmv TOC limits is overly prescriptive and should allow modern GC/MS or other validated instrumental methods without invoking Method 301 validation, because many facilities already use superior analytical techniques that are more sensitive and specific.

[P2] The permission to use ASTM D6420–18 in lieu of Method 18 only "under specified conditions" is ambiguous; the rule should explicitly list all allowed conditions and cross-reference the exact ASTM sections to avoid confusion during testing.

[P3] Allowing "any other method or data validated per Method 301" (P3) is acceptable in principle but the rule must specify the documentation, acceptance criteria, and review timeframe for EPA approval of Method 301 validations to prevent indefinite delays.

[P4] The obligation to use the procedures in paragraphs (e)(2)(iii)(A),(B),(D),(E) to calculate ppmv concentrations (P4) lacks clarity about rounding conventions, significant figures, and propagation of analytical uncertainty; EPA should add language specifying rounding rules and how to report measurement uncertainty.

[P5] Requiring correction of calculated concentrations to 3% oxygen for combustion control devices (P5) is reasonable, but the rule should allow facilities with continuous O2 trim systems to use measured O2 averaged over the test period rather than a fixed 3% reference when technically justified.

[P6] Mandating Method 3B or ANSI/ASME PTC 19–10–1981 Part 10 for oxygen determination (P6) may be impractical at some sites; EPA should permit calibrated continuous O2 analyzers meeting QA/QC criteria as an alternative.

[P7] The requirement that oxygen samples be taken at the same site and time as organic samples (P7) is operationally difficult for some large ducts; the rule should permit spatially proximate measurements with documented equivalence when sampling ports are not co-located.

[P8] Requiring Method 18 or ASTM D6420–18 to measure outlet TOC (P8) excludes other validated TOC methods (e.g., direct FID measurement with specified calibration) that are widely used; the rule should add a pathway for modern TOC methods without full Method 301 validation if equivalency is demonstrated.

[P9] The obligation to determine inlet regulated compounds by process knowledge or Method 18 screening (P9) places an undue burden on facilities with variable feeds; EPA should allow representative historical analytical data and vendor specifications to satisfy the inlet compound identification requirement.

[P10] Analyzing outlet samples only for compounds identified at the inlet (P10) risks missing degradation products or byproducts formed in combustion; the rule must require screening for unexpected compounds or a provision for broader analysis if process conditions change.

[P11] Limiting ASTM D6420–18 to the specific conditions in (D)(1)-(3) (P11) is appropriate, but the conditions are too restrictive (see methane/ethane and total VOC prohibitions) and could prevent efficient testing; EPA should consider allowing D6420 with supplemental methane/ethane quantification by other validated methods.

[P12] The condition that ASTM D6420–18 be used only if "all target compounds are known and listed as measurable" (P12) is unrealistic for many ethylene production streams where trace organics may be unknown; this will effectively bar D6420 in many cases.

[P13] The explicit prohibition on using ASTM D6420–18 for methane and ethane (P13) fails to address how methane/ethane should be measured contemporaneously; the rule should require an alternate approved method for methane/ethane and provide options and detection limits.

[P14] The ban on using ASTM D6420–18 as a total VOC method (P14) is logical given the method design, but EPA should clarify acceptable total VOC surrogate methods and how to combine results across methods for compliance determinations.

[P15] Requiring Method 18, 25, or 25A to determine percent reduction (P15) is prescriptive; the rule should allow equivalent validated methods (e.g., continuous emission monitors with performance specification) for percent reduction calculations.

[P16] Allowing ASTM D6420–18 for percent reduction under the same (D)(1)-(3) conditions (P16) transfers the same limitations noted above into percent reduction testing; commenters will request more flexible cross-method use and combined-method approaches.

[P17] The Method 301 alternative for percent reduction (P17) needs clearer timelines and acceptance criteria — specifically, the number of validation trials, statistical criteria, and EPA turnaround for approvals should be specified.

[P18] The requirement to use the listed procedures (e)(2)(iv)(A)-(I) to calculate percent reduction efficiency (P18) needs more guidance on how to handle non-detects, values below MDL, and data below the calibration curve when computing percent reductions.

[P19] The mandate to use Method 18 or ASTM D6420–18 to measure inlet and outlet total organic regulated material concentrations (P19) should explicitly permit split-sample analysis with alternate methods for quality assurance, e.g., one lab using Method 18 and another using GC/MS.

[P20] Requiring simultaneous collection of inlet and outlet samples (P20) may be technically infeasible for large, distributed systems or during upset conditions; the rule should allow near-simultaneous paired sampling with documented time offsets and justification.

[P21] For combustion control device tests, identifying inlet regulated compounds by process knowledge or Method 18 screening (P21) may omit low-level HAPs; EPA should require periodic comprehensive inlet screening (e.g., annual GC/MS) to capture changing feed composition.

[P22] Quantifying emissions of identified compounds at both inlet and outlet (P22) could be highly burdensome if dozens of compounds are present; EPA should permit grouping of similar compounds or use of TOC surrogates under certain thresholds.

[P23] The formaldehyde-specific testing requirement (P23) is appropriate given formaldehyde properties, but the threshold and approach are complex — stakeholders will request clarity on how to handle interferences and how to sample formaldehyde in high-temperature combustion exhaust.

[P24] Requiring Method 316 or 320 when formaldehyde is >50% of inlet (P24) is arbitrary; commenters will ask for justification of the 50% threshold and for allowance of other validated formaldehyde methods (e.g., DNPH cartridge with HPLC) where demonstrated equivalent.

[P25] For inlet formaldehyde >10% when complying with outlet TOC limit, requiring Method 316/320 and summing with other compounds (P25) will create method mixing issues and analytical incompatibilities; EPA should allow validated cross-calibration or surrogates to combine results.

[P26] Allowing ASTM D6348–12e1 in lieu of Methods 316/320 under specified situations (P26) is beneficial, but the referenced version year is inconsistent (12e1 vs 03 in other paragraphs); EPA should harmonize and reference a single, current ASTM version to avoid confusion.

[P27] The requirement that when using ASTM D6348 the %R value must be between 70% and 130% (P27) is excessively wide on the upper end and may mask serious recovery problems; commenters will request tightening the acceptability range or requiring investigation when %R deviates more than ±15%.

[P28] Declaring data unacceptable and requiring repeat testing if %R outside 70–130% (P28) could force multiple retests and operational downtime; the rule should allow corrective actions and documentation to salvage data where appropriate rather than automatic repetition.

[P29] Requiring reporting of %R and correction of field measurements by %R (P29) is technically okay but needs explicit instructions on propagation of uncertainty after correction and how to report corrected vs. uncorrected values in the test report.

[P30] The general compliance schedule cross-reference (P30) is fine but commenters will request a clear table mapping affected source categories to exact compliance deadlines rather than reliance on §63.1102(a) only.

[P31] Heat exchange systems constructed on or before Oct 9, 2019 must comply by initial startup or specified deadline (P31); industry will request grandfathering or extended compliance timelines for older units that would require costly retrofits.

[P32] Heat exchange systems built after Oct 9, 2019 must comply upon initial startup or specified publication date (P32) — commenters will ask for clarity about what constitutes "initial startup" and whether testing windows apply.

[P33] Waste streams from sources constructed on/before Oct 9, 2019 must meet flare requirements by initial startup or deadline (P33); affected facilities will request phased implementation and financial assistance due to capital costs.

[P34] Waste streams from sources constructed after Oct 9, 2019 must comply upon initial startup or publication date (P34) — operators will seek clarification on how to demonstrate compliance when startup coincides with other commissioning activities.

[P35] The exemption criteria for heat exchange systems (P35) are complex; facility engineers will request examples and a compliance flowchart to determine if their system meets (a)-(e) and the effect of (f).

[P36] The change in exemptions as of the compliance date (P36) — removing exemptions for systems meeting (c) or (d) — will create regulatory uncertainty and retroactive obligations; commenters will request grandfathering for systems constructed before the rule or phased compliance.

[P37] The requirement to meet §63.1085(a)-(f) if not exempt (P37) means many systems previously exempt will now be subject to prescriptive monitoring and repair; trade associations will request a cost-benefit analysis and less prescriptive performance-based alternatives.

[P38] Monitoring cooling water for leak-indicating substances per §63.1086(a)-(d) (P38) may be less protective than the new strippable hydrocarbon monitoring in (e); stakeholders need clear transition guidance on when to switch methods and how to reconcile historical data.

[P39] The repair requirements when a leak is detected (P39) are strict; many commenters will request reasonable repair timelines for complex exchangers and allowances for temporary mitigations without penalty.

[P40] Mandating monitoring for total strippable hydrocarbons per §63.1086(e) as of the compliance date while allowing opt-in earlier (P40) is acceptable but EPA should provide a standardized validation protocol for laboratories performing the Modified El Paso Method with FID.

[P41] Swapping repair requirements and delay rules (P41) as of the compliance date creates two separate repair regimes; regulated entities will request consolidated, simplified repair and delay rules to reduce confusion.

[P42] The monitoring choices in §63.1086 (P42) are numerous and may lead to inconsistent application between facilities; commenters will request EPA guidance on selecting monitoring approach (closed-loop vs once-through) and consistency checks.

[P43] The detailed procedures for total strippable hydrocarbon monitoring (P43) referencing the Modified El Paso Method with FID should include QC/QA acceptance criteria, calibration gas requirements, and method detection limits appropriate for ethylene plant matrices.

[P44] For closed-loop systems, requiring sampling from cooling tower return lines or representative risers (P44) may miss localized leaks; commenters will ask for directional guidance on when representative riser sampling is acceptable and how many risers constitute adequate coverage.

[P45] Monitoring at each cooling tower return line or representative riser prior to air exposure (P45) is operationally difficult for some designs; EPA should permit sampling after minimal air contact when demonstrated to be equivalent.

[P46] Allowing monitoring at selected heat exchanger exit lines to cover each exchanger or group (P46) requires clear rules for grouping exchangers — commenters will request flow-based grouping criteria and maximum allowed grouped flow rates.

[P47] Once-through system sampling at specified exit locations (P47) may be impractical for systems with numerous small exchangers; EPA should allow representative sampling with statistical justification when covering each exchanger individually is infeasible.

[P48] The combined monitoring allowance if combined flow ≤40,000 gpm (P48) uses an arbitrary threshold; commenters will request either justification or alternative thresholds based on facility size and risk.

[P49] Allowing inlet feed monitoring as an alternative and representative monitoring for multiple systems sharing the same feed (P49) is helpful, but the rule needs requirements for demonstrating that shared-feed monitoring is truly representative (e.g., hydraulic modeling or tracer tests).

[P50] Requiring calculation of total strippable hydrocarbon concentration as methane using the Modified El Paso Method with FID (P50) will underestimate heavier organics; commenters will request guidance on conversion factors or parallel analyses for multi-species mixtures.

[P51] The specified monitoring frequencies and leak action levels (P51) create significant operational obligations; commenters will request transition relief, particularly for legacy units, and alternative reduced-frequency schedules that maintain equivalent environmental protection.

[P52] Quarterly monitoring and a 6.2 ppmv action level for systems constructed on/before Dec 6, 2000 (P52) may be insufficiently protective for some high-risk facilities; environmental groups will push for monthly monitoring and lower action levels.

[P53] The monthly monitoring after completing initial weekly monitoring for 6 months (P53) is reasonable but the rule should clarify what constitutes "completion" and whether missing weekly events due to operational constraints resets the clock.

[P54] Requiring initial weekly monitoring for six months if not previously completed (P54) imposes heavy short-term burdens; commenters will propose a flexible schedule for completing the initial baseline that accounts for seasonal shutdowns and access constraints.

[P55] Weekly monitoring for the first 6 months upon startup for systems commencing after Oct 9, 2019 (P55) may be redundant for brand-new, leak-tested exchangers; commenters will ask for allowance of an engineering pressure test or hydrotest in lieu of six months of weekly sampling.

[P56] Defining a leak for inlet-monitored once-through systems as exit minus inlet ≥ action level (P56) seems appropriate, but the method must account for analytical variability; commenters will request use of statistically significant differences (e.g., accounting for MDL and two-sigma variability) rather than a simple subtraction threshold.

[P57] For other systems, defining a leak as any sample measurement ≥ action level (P57) may trigger false positives due to transient spikes; EPA should require confirmatory re-sampling within a short timeframe before requiring repairs.

[P58] The general requirement to comply with repair procedures unless delay applies (P58) is fine, but the interactions between §§1087, 1088, and 1089 are complex; stakeholders will request consolidated examples and a decision tree.

[P59] The 45-day repair deadline for leaks detected under §63.1086(e) (P59) is unachievable for many exchangers that require planned outages; commenters will request that the 45-day clock be suspended when shutdown scheduling is necessary and documented.

[P60] Re-monitoring after repair at the original location to verify concentrations are below action level (P60) is reasonable but should allow remote or reduced frequency follow-up when repairs are mechanical and demonstrably effective.

[P61] Allowing additional monitoring per paragraph (d) to verify repair effectiveness (P61) is useful; commenters will ask EPA to enumerate acceptable additional monitoring techniques (e.g., tracer tests, differential pressure checks).

[P62] Allowing physical modifications like welding or tube replacement as repair options (P62) is practical, but EPA should require welds and repairs to meet industry pressure/vibration standards and may require post-repair hydro/hydraulic testing.

[P63] Allowing blocking of leaking tubes (P63) is a common practice, but the rule should require documentation that blocking does not compromise heat exchanger performance or lead to process upsets.

[P64] Allowing pressure changes so water flows into process to address leaks (P64) could create safety and product contamination risks; commenters will urge EPA to restrict this option or require safety/risk assessments before using it.

[P65] The option to replace the heat exchanger or bundle (P65) is appropriate but the rule should allow credit for modular replacement plans and reasonable timelines for procurement and installation.

[P66] Isolating, bypassing, or removing leaking exchangers from service (P66) may not always be feasible without process interruptions; commenters will request that the rule require demonstration that isolation will not cause greater emissions or safety hazards.

[P67] The additional monitoring option for cooling tower return line leaks (P67) is beneficial, but EPA should clarify the spatial extent and number of associated exchangers that must be monitored and acceptable negative findings criteria.

[P68] The broad permission to delay repair under specified conditions (P68) is necessary; however, EPA must clearly define "isolated from the process" and acceptable evidence to support infeasibility claims to prevent misuse.

[P69] Allowing delay of repair when leak is below the delay action level with a 45-day determination window (P69) is reasonable but the rule should require EPA notification or recordkeeping demonstrating objective criteria for the delay decision.

[P70] The allowance to delay repair until the next scheduled shutdown if repair infeasible without shutdown and concentration remains below delay action level (P70) must include a maximum allowed delay (e.g., not exceeding 1 scheduled outage cycle or a fixed time) to avoid indefinite postponement.

[P71] Permitting a 120-day delay when parts/personnel unavailable (P71) is generous; commenters will request that facilities document exhaustive procurement attempts and provide timelines, and environmental advocates will argue 120 days is too long for known toxic emissions.

[P72] Defining the delay of repair action level as 62 ppmv (P72) appears arbitrary; commenters will demand a technical justification, exposure-risk assessment, and consideration of cumulative emissions across multiple leaks.

[P73] For once-through systems using inlet monitoring, defining exceedance as exit minus inlet ≥ 62 ppmv (P73) ignores variability in inlet concentrations and analytical uncertainty; commenters will request use of confidence intervals or limits of quantitation in determining exceedances.

[P74] For other systems, using single-sample measurement ≥ 62 ppmv to trigger action (P74) may be prone to transient false alarms; EPA should require confirmatory sampling or averaging across two consecutive samples.

[P75] The documentation requirements for delay of repair before compliance date (P75) are onerous but necessary; stakeholders will ask for standard forms/templates and electronic submission options to ease administrative burden.

[P76] Requiring recording reasons for delaying repair (P76) is reasonable but must be limited to objective, demonstrable reasons rather than subjective judgments, with required supporting evidence.

[P77] Requiring a schedule for completing repair as soon as practical (P77) should be tied to an explicit maximum allowable timeline and milestone reporting to prevent open-ended schedules.

[P78] Recording the date and concentration when leak was first identified and subsequent monitoring during delay (P78) is needed; commenters will request standardized reporting intervals and acceptable formats for data submission.

[P79] Requiring estimates of potential strippable hydrocarbon emissions for each delay monitoring interval (P79) is technically complex; facilities will request EPA-provided calculation spreadsheets, examples, and default values for missing flow or concentration data.

[P80] The conversion of ppmv methane to ppmw using molecular weight (P80) assumes methane-dominant composition; commenters will request guidance on using appropriate molecular weights for mixed-species leaks and on when more detailed speciation is required.

[P81] Requiring determination of cooling water mass flow rate using permitted measurement or conversion methods (P81) is practicable but will be challenging at locations without flow meters; EPA should allow engineering estimates with documented uncertainty and require installation of permanent meters when feasible.

[P82] The calculation of emissions as ppmw × mass flow × duration (P82) is straightforward but will produce large uncertainties when inputs are estimated; EPA should provide acceptable uncertainty quantification methods and criteria for conservative assumptions.

[P83] For the final interval ending with repair, using last pre-repair monitoring event flow rates (P83) could under- or over-estimate emissions if flow changed; commenters will request requirement to measure flow contemporaneously with final monitoring when feasible.

[P84] The obligation to keep validation test data for 40 CFR part 136 method validations before compliance date (P84) is appropriate, but the rule should provide a retention period (e.g., 5 years) and allow electronic recordkeeping.

[P85] Requiring semiannual reporting of delayed repairs and continuing until repair (P85) is necessary for transparency; industry will ask for clear templates and for allowance of consolidated reporting to avoid excessive paperwork.

[P86] For systems subject to §63.1085(e) and (f), the altered periodic report content (P86) shifts data burdens; commenters will request sample report formats and clarity on whether legacy data must be retroactively converted.

[P87] Requiring report of number of heat exchange systems subject to §63.1085(e),(f) (P87) may be ambiguous for complex plants with modular or partially-integrated systems — commenters will ask for definition of "heat exchange system" and counting rules.

[P88] Reporting the number of systems found leaking (P88) is reasonable but must be normalized (e.g., leaks per 100 systems) to provide meaningful trending; industry will suggest adding context requirements.

[P89] Reporting location ID, measured concentration, date first identified, and date source identified for each monitoring location meeting leak definitions (P89) is detailed; commenters will request secure reporting methods to protect sensitive plant layout information.

[P90] For leaks repaired during reporting period, reporting monitoring location, concentration during re-monitoring, and re-monitoring date (P90) is appropriate; stakeholders will ask for an extended timeframe to compile necessary verification data post-repair.

[P91] For each delayed repair, requiring monitoring location, date delay began, expected completion date, and concentration/date of each monitoring event (P91) creates heavy recordkeeping; facilities will request the ability to submit summaries or aggregated data for multiple delayed repairs.

[P92] The prohibition on entering the safety zone without authorization (P92) is standard, but maritime users will request clear signage and pre-notification requirements for planned operations near the zone to avoid accidental infractions.

[P93] Requiring vessels underway at activation to depart the zone (P93) could endanger small craft at night; commenters will ask for a transitional period or permit process for vessels unable to immediately vacate due to safe navigation constraints.

[P94] Requiring contact by telephone or VHF for entry permission (P94) is practical but the rule must ensure 24/7 staffing and alternative contact methods (e.g., email or digital notification) for redundancy.

[P95] Specifying VHF channel 16 for contacting enforcing Coast Guard vessels (P95) is fine; however, commenters will request backup radio channels and AIS messaging options for redundancy.

[P96] Requiring compliance with lawful orders from the Captain of the Port (P96) is standard; maritime legal experts will request inclusion of an appeals process or guidance on how to contest orders post-incident.

[P97] Allowing federal, state, and local agencies to assist in enforcement (P97) is appropriate, but commenters will ask for a delineation of roles and training requirements for assisting agencies to ensure consistent enforcement.

[P98] Stating the safety zone will be enforced during specified periods (P98) is necessary; affected commercial operators will request public notice timelines (e.g., at least 7 days notice) and broadcast notices (NOTMAR/Local Broadcast) to minimize disruption.

[P99] Requiring "FIREWORKS—DANGER—STAY AWAY" signage on both sides of the on-scene barge (P99) is reasonable; barge operators will request size, material, lighting, and placement specifications to ensure compliance.

[P100] Specifying the enforcement period from 11:00 p.m. Dec 31, 2019 to 1:00 a.m. Jan 1, 2020 (P100) is appropriate for a discrete event, but stakeholders will ask that the rule include procedures to amend enforcement times based on weather or operational changes and to provide rapid public notification of any changes.

For closed-loop systems, requiring sampling from cooling tower return lines or representative risers (P44) may miss localized leaks; commenters will ask for directional guidance on when representative riser sampling is acceptable and how many risers constitute adequate coverage.

Monitoring at each cooling tower return line or representative riser prior to air exposure (P45) is operationally difficult for some designs; EPA should permit sampling after minimal air contact when demonstrated to be equivalent.

Allowing monitoring at selected heat exchanger exit lines to cover each exchanger or group (P46) requires clear rules for grouping exchangers — commenters will request flow-based grouping criteria and maximum allowed grouped flow rates.

Once-through system sampling at specified exit locations (P47) may be impractical for systems with numerous small exchangers; EPA should allow representative sampling with statistical justification when covering each exchanger individually is infeasible.

The combined monitoring allowance if combined flow ≤40,000 gpm (P48) uses an arbitrary threshold; commenters will request either justification or alternative thresholds based on facility size and risk.

Allowing inlet feed monitoring as an alternative and representative monitoring for multiple systems sharing the same feed (P49) is helpful, but the rule needs requirements for demonstrating that shared-feed monitoring is truly representative (e.g., hydraulic modeling or tracer tests).

Requiring calculation of total strippable hydrocarbon concentration as methane using the Modified El Paso Method with FID (P50) will underestimate heavier organics; commenters will request guidance on conversion factors or parallel analyses for multi-species mixtures.

The specified monitoring frequencies and leak action levels (P51) create significant operational obligations; commenters will request transition relief, particularly for legacy units, and alternative reduced-frequency schedules that maintain equivalent environmental protection.
