parsed_claims.claim_text: Quarterly monitoring and a 6.2 ppmv action level for systems constructed on/before Dec 6, 2000 (P52) may be insufficiently protective for some high-risk facilities; environmental groups will push for monthly monitoring and lower action levels.

The monthly monitoring after completing initial weekly monitoring for 6 months (P53) is reasonable but the rule should clarify what constitutes "completion" and whether missing weekly events due to operational constraints resets the clock.

Requiring initial weekly monitoring for six months if not previously completed (P54) imposes heavy short-term burdens; commenters will propose a flexible schedule for completing the initial baseline that accounts for seasonal shutdowns and access constraints.

Weekly monitoring for the first 6 months upon startup for systems commencing after Oct 9, 2019 (P55) may be redundant for brand-new, leak-tested exchangers; commenters will ask for allowance of an engineering pressure test or hydrotest in lieu of six months of weekly sampling.

Defining a leak for inlet-monitored once-through systems as exit minus inlet ≥ action level (P56) seems appropriate, but the method must account for analytical variability; commenters will request use of statistically significant differences (e.g., accounting for MDL and two-sigma variability) rather than a simple subtraction threshold.

For other systems, defining a leak as any sample measurement ≥ action level (P57) may trigger false positives due to transient spikes; EPA should require confirmatory re-sampling within a short timeframe before requiring repairs.

The general requirement to comply with repair procedures unless delay applies (P58) is fine, but the interactions between §§1087, 1088, and 1089 are complex; stakeholders will request consolidated examples and a decision tree.

The 45-day repair deadline for leaks detected under §63.1086(e) (P59) is unachievable for many exchangers that require planned outages; commenters will request that the 45-day clock be suspended when shutdown scheduling is necessary and documented.

Re-monitoring after repair at the original location to verify concentrations are below action level (P60) is reasonable but should allow remote or reduced frequency follow-up when repairs are mechanical and demonstrably effective.

Allowing additional monitoring per paragraph (d) to verify repair effectiveness (P61) is useful; commenters will ask EPA to enumerate acceptable additional monitoring techniques (e.g., tracer tests, differential pressure checks).

Allowing physical modifications like welding or tube replacement as repair options (P62) is practical, but EPA should require welds and repairs to meet industry pressure/vibration standards and may require post-repair hydro/hydraulic testing.
Allowing blocking of leaking tubes (P63) is a common practice, but the rule should require documentation that blocking does not compromise heat exchanger performance or lead to process upsets.

Allowing pressure changes so water flows into process to address leaks (P64) could create safety and product contamination risks; commenters will urge EPA to restrict this option or require safety/risk assessments before using it.
The option to replace the heat exchanger or bundle (P65) is appropriate but the rule should allow credit for modular replacement plans and reasonable timelines for procurement and installation.

Isolating, bypassing, or removing leaking exchangers from service (P66) may not always be feasible without process interruptions; commenters will request that the rule require demonstration that isolation will not cause greater emissions or safety hazards.

The additional monitoring option for cooling tower return line leaks (P67) is beneficial, but EPA should clarify the spatial extent and number of associated exchangers that must be monitored and acceptable negative findings criteria.

The broad permission to delay repair under specified conditions (P68) is necessary; however, EPA must clearly define "isolated from the process" and acceptable evidence to support infeasibility claims to prevent misuse.

Allowing delay of repair when leak is below the delay action level with a 45-day determination window (P69) is reasonable but the rule should require EPA notification or recordkeeping demonstrating objective criteria for the delay decision.

The allowance to delay repair until the next scheduled shutdown if repair infeasible without shutdown and concentration remains below delay action level (P70) must include a maximum allowed delay (e.g., not exceeding 1 scheduled outage cycle or a fixed time) to avoid indefinite postponement.

Permitting a 120-day delay when parts/personnel unavailable (P71) is generous; commenters will request that facilities document exhaustive procurement attempts and provide timelines, and environmental advocates will argue 120 days is too long for known toxic emissions.

Defining the delay of repair action level as 62 ppmv (P72) appears arbitrary; commenters will demand a technical justification, exposure-risk assessment, and consideration of cumulative emissions across multiple leaks.

For once-through systems using inlet monitoring, defining exceedance as exit minus inlet ≥ 62 ppmv (P73) ignores variability in inlet concentrations and analytical uncertainty; commenters will request use of confidence intervals or limits of quantitation in determining exceedances.

For other systems, using single-sample measurement ≥ 62 ppmv to trigger action (P74) may be prone to transient false alarms; EPA should require confirmatory sampling or averaging across two consecutive samples.

The documentation requirements for delay of repair before compliance date (P75) are onerous but necessary; stakeholders will ask for standard forms/templates and electronic submission options to ease administrative burden.
Requiring recording reasons for delaying repair (P76) is reasonable but must be limited to objective, demonstrable reasons rather than subjective judgments, with required supporting evidence.
Requiring a schedule for completing repair as soon as practical (P77) should be tied to an explicit maximum allowable timeline and milestone reporting to prevent open-ended schedules.

Recording the date and concentration when leak was first identified and subsequent monitoring during delay (P78) is needed; commenters will request standardized reporting intervals and acceptable formats for data submission.

Requiring estimates of potential strippable hydrocarbon emissions for each delay monitoring interval (P79) is technically complex; facilities will request EPA-provided calculation spreadsheets, examples, and default values for missing flow or concentration data.

The conversion of ppmv methane to ppmw using molecular weight (P80) assumes methane-dominant composition; commenters will request guidance on using appropriate molecular weights for mixed-species leaks and on when more detailed speciation is required.

Requiring determination of cooling water mass flow rate using permitted measurement or conversion methods (P81) is practicable but will be challenging at locations without flow meters; EPA should allow engineering estimates with documented uncertainty and require installation of permanent meters when feasible.

The calculation of emissions as ppmw × mass flow × duration (P82) is straightforward but will produce large uncertainties when inputs are estimated; EPA should provide acceptable uncertainty quantification methods and criteria for conservative assumptions.

For the final interval ending with repair, using last pre-repair monitoring event flow rates (P83) could under- or over-estimate emissions if flow changed; commenters will request requirement to measure flow contemporaneously with final monitoring when feasible.

The obligation to keep validation test data for 40 CFR part 136 method validations before compliance date (P84) is appropriate, but the rule should provide a retention period (e.g., 5 years) and allow electronic recordkeeping.

Requiring semiannual reporting of delayed repairs and continuing until repair (P85) is necessary for transparency; industry will ask for clear templates and for allowance of consolidated reporting to avoid excessive paperwork.

For systems subject to §63.1085(e) and (f), the altered periodic report content (P86) shifts data burdens; commenters will request sample report formats and clarity on whether legacy data must be retroactively converted.

Requiring report of number of heat exchange systems subject to §63.1085(e),(f) (P87) may be ambiguous for complex plants with modular or partially-integrated systems — commenters will ask for definition of "heat exchange system" and counting rules.

Reporting the number of systems found leaking (P88) is reasonable but must be normalized (e.g., leaks per 100 systems) to provide meaningful trending; industry will suggest adding context requirements.

Reporting location ID, measured concentration, date first identified, and date source identified for each monitoring location meeting leak definitions (P89) is detailed; commenters will request secure reporting methods to protect sensitive plant layout information.

For leaks repaired during reporting period, reporting monitoring location, concentration during re-monitoring, and re-monitoring date (P90) is appropriate; stakeholders will ask for an extended timeframe to compile necessary verification data post-repair.

For each delayed repair, requiring monitoring location, date delay began, expected completion date, and concentration/date of each monitoring event (P91) creates heavy recordkeeping; facilities will request the ability to submit summaries or aggregated data for multiple delayed repairs.

The prohibition on entering the safety zone without authorization (P92) is standard, but maritime users will request clear signage and pre-notification requirements for planned operations near the zone to avoid accidental infractions.

Requiring vessels underway at activation to depart the zone (P93) could endanger small craft at night; commenters will ask for a transitional period or permit process for vessels unable to immediately vacate due to safe navigation constraints.

Requiring contact by telephone or VHF for entry permission (P94) is practical but the rule must ensure 24/7 staffing and alternative contact methods (e.g., email or digital notification) for redundancy.
Specifying VHF channel 16 for contacting enforcing Coast Guard vessels (P95) is fine; however, commenters will request backup radio channels and AIS messaging options for redundancy.

Requiring compliance with lawful orders from the Captain of the Port (P96) is standard; maritime legal experts will request inclusion of an appeals process or guidance on how to contest orders post-incident.

Allowing federal, state, and local agencies to assist in enforcement (P97) is appropriate, but commenters will ask for a delineation of roles and training requirements for assisting agencies to ensure consistent enforcement.

Stating the safety zone will be enforced during specified periods (P98) is necessary; affected commercial operators will request public notice timelines (e.g., at least 7 days notice) and broadcast notices (NOTMAR/Local Broadcast) to minimize disruption.

Requiring "FIREWORKS—DANGER—STAY AWAY" signage on both sides of the on-scene barge (P99) is reasonable; barge operators will request size, material, lighting, and placement specifications to ensure compliance.

Specifying the enforcement period from 11:00 p.m. Dec 31, 2019 to 1:00 a.m. Jan 1, 2020 (P100) is appropriate for a discrete event, but stakeholders will ask that the rule include procedures to amend enforcement times based on weather or operational changes and to provide rapid public notification of any changes.

raw_output:
[P1] The November 29, 2018 postmark/receipt deadline is unreasonably short given the complexity of the proposal; we request an extension of at least 60 days to allow full stakeholder review and data collection.

[P1] Requiring comments to be received or postmarked by the deadline unfairly disadvantages commenters who rely on slow mail or remote offices; the rule should clarify whether timely postmark is sufficient if actual receipt is delayed.

[P2] The 11:59 p.m. ET cutoff for electronic submissions discriminates against commenters in other time zones and should instead allow submission until 11:59 p.m. local time or accept submissions received the next business day.

[P2] The provision does not specify how system outages or portal downtime will be handled; commenters request an exception or contingency allowing timely submissions affected by technical failures.

[P3] Listing only the described submission methods limits participation from stakeholders who need alternative formats (e.g., mailed-on-disk, fax); the Service should explicitly accept reasonable alternative submission methods on request.

[P4] Directing commenters to use the "Comment Now!" function on regulations.gov without offering instructions for attaching large datasets or GIS files is impractical; the Service should provide guidance or an alternate portal for large scientific files.

[P4] The rule should clarify permitted file types and maximum upload sizes for electronic submissions to prevent rejection of substantive scientific data.

[P5] The hard-copy submission address includes a code (FWS–R1–ES–2007–0024) that may change; the Service should provide a failsafe contact or email to confirm correct mailing destinations and receipt.

[P5] The rule does not state whether hand-delivery hours or security procedures at the listed address will accept submissions after normal business hours; provide clear instructions for hand-delivered comments.

[P6] The wording "we request that you send comments only by the methods described above" reads as a prohibition; stakeholders need clarity that other methods will be accepted in exceptional circumstances and how to request such exceptions.

[P7] Posting all comments on regulations.gov without redaction may intimidate commenters; the Service should explicitly permit and explain how to request confidentiality or partial redaction when warranted.

[P8] Posting personal information contained in comments is a privacy risk; the Service must provide clear instructions and an easy process for redacting or withholding personal data, and explain the legal basis for posting.

[P9] Electronic submissions will be posted in full, including personal identifying information; the Service should allow electronic submitters to request that contact information be withheld from public posting, consistent with FOIA/privacy rules.

[P10] Allowing hardcopy submitters to request withholding of personal identifying information but not providing the same option for electronic submitters is inconsistent and discriminatory; the Service should permit the same withholding request for electronic comments.

[P11] Posting all hardcopy submissions to regulations.gov could cause transcription errors; the Service should commit to posting exact scanned copies and provide a mechanism to correct posting errors.

[P12] The statement that previously submitted comments "need not be resubmitted" creates confusion about how prior comments will be integrated; provide a clear summary of which prior comment periods and comment sets will be considered and how duplicates will be handled.

[P12] Legal commenters note that relying on past comments from 2008/2009/2014 without resubmission may violate notice-and-comment expectations if the new proposal materially differs; the Service should require resubmission if substantive changes are made.

[P13] The Service's promise to review "all comments received by the date and time specified" should be backed by a description of how comments will be considered in the decision record (e.g., how many comments, weighting of scientific vs. public comments).

[P14] The TDD Federal Relay Service number is helpful but the rule should also provide an email address and alternative accessible formats (braille, large print) for those with hearing or speech disabilities.

[P15] The mandatory minimum 5-year post-delisting monitoring program lacks detail on monitoring metrics, sampling design, roles of States vs. Service, and funding commitments; commenters request a specific, funded monitoring plan template.

[P15] Requiring cooperation "with the States" is vague; the rule should specify whether State concurrence is required, what happens if a State declines, and how monitoring will proceed in such cases.

[P16] The Service's ability to initiate listing procedures if monitoring indicates need is appropriate but must include explicit triggers, thresholds, and timelines for emergency listing versus standard listing to ensure predictability.

[P17] The draft PDM plan's proposed 5-year monitoring frequency over 20 years (i.e., surveys every 5 years) may be insufficient to detect rapid declines such as from disease or land-use change; recommend annual or biennial monitoring for the first 10 years.

[P17] Monitoring every 5 years for 20 years is likely underpowered statistically to detect population trends; request power analyses and minimum detectable change thresholds be included in the final plan.

[P18] The commitment to consider public and peer review comments is appropriate, but the Service should publish a response-to-comments document showing how each substantive scientific comment was addressed in the final PDM plan.

[P18] Peer reviewer selection criteria and conflicts of interest disclosures are not specified; the Service should require independent peer review panels with publicly disclosed expertise and COI statements.

[P19] The requested outreach to "native Hawaiian groups" is positive; however, the Service must ensure meaningful consultation with identified cultural practitioners and provide time and funding for participation.

[P19] Industry stakeholders (agriculture, biofuel producers) request clear timelines and formats for submitting economic and land-use data, and assurance that proprietary information will be protected if submitted.

[P20] The Service's list of requested topics is broad; stakeholders ask for prioritized research questions and standardized data formats (e.g., GIS projection, metadata standards) to ensure usable submissions.

[P21] The explicit request for new information on Rapid Ohia Death (ROD) is critical; forestry researchers request that the Service accept ongoing monitoring datasets and provide a mechanism to submit raw tree mortality and infection prevalence data with confidentiality protections.

[P21] Conservation groups request that the Service clarify whether ROD impacts on prey species will be considered as a threat multiplier in the delisting decision.

[P22] Requesting data on conversion of agricultural land to biodiesel crops is appropriate; agricultural stakeholders ask the Service to define the temporal window for "former and current crop types and acreage" and to accept state-level crop reporting datasets.

[P22] Biofuel industry commenters request that the Service define what constitutes "conversion" (e.g., change in crop type, land-use intensity, tillage) and whether fallow lands are included.

[P23] Permission to submit information by listed methods should include acceptance of supplementary submission via secure FTP or cloud links for large datasets; request explicit authorization for such methods.

[P24] The prohibition asking previous commenters not to resubmit is confusing and may suppress updated information; clarify that prior commenters may submit supplemental updates or rebuttals if there is new evidence.

[P24] Legal advocates argue that forbidding resubmission could impede commenters from addressing novel aspects of the current proposal; rescind or revise this instruction to encourage updated input.

[P25] The Service's promise to provide PRA comment opportunities for future information collections is welcome; request that any new survey or reporting requirements be accompanied by estimated burden hours and funding support for respondents.

[P25] Industry stakeholders request early notice of potential information collection so they can prepare compliance systems; ask the Service to publish anticipated PRA packages and timelines.

[P26] Encouraging previous commenters to provide additional comments "if appropriate" is vague; the Service should proactively notify prior commenters of the new proposal and the specific new issues for which updated input is sought.

[P27] The commitment to base final action on the best available scientific and commercial data is appropriate, but the Service should define the standard for "best available" and describe how it will resolve conflicting datasets or data gaps.

[P27] Legal commenters request that the Service document in the administrative record how it weighed commercial data (e.g., proprietary industry studies) versus peer-reviewed science to ensure transparency and defensibility.

[P7/P9] Privacy-conscious individuals request a redaction tool or form when submitting via regulations.gov so they can exclude personal identifiers without having to submit hard copy.

[P8/P10] Commenters worried about harassment request the ability to submit anonymously or under pseudonym for public posting while still providing verified contact information confidentially to the Agency.

[P11] Small organizations are concerned that posting hardcopy comments online will reveal organizational strategies and funding sources; request an option to withhold organizational affiliations or supporting attachments from public posting upon justification.

[P17/P15] State wildlife agencies request clear cost-sharing guidance and long-term funding commitments for PDM implementation, including who bears costs for unexpected emergency relisting actions prompted during monitoring.

[P16/P15] Conservation scientists request explicit procedures for rapid response if monitoring indicates decline — e.g., interim protective measures during listing proceedings to prevent irreversible harm.

[P4/P2] Technical commenters request that regulations.gov display a timestamp confirming receipt and provide an email confirmation to submitters; this should be stated in the ADDRESSES section.

[P12/P13] Transparency advocates request that the Service publish a timeline for how and when comments will be reviewed and when the agency expects to release the response-to-comments and final rule.

[P1] The requirement to “properly file” under 8 CFR part 103 and form instructions is vague and will create inconsistent rejections; DHS should specify what errors are curable versus fatal (e.g., missing signature, wrong filing fee, incorrect address).

[P1] Industry and legal aid providers will need clear guidance on constructive filing dates when multiple filings or corrected forms are submitted; request DHS add examples and a safe-harbor for minor clerical errors.

[P2] The rule implies the 365-day clock begins upon “receipt” by USCIS or the immigration court but does not clarify receipt for mailed vs. electronic filings; commenters will request explicit receipt standards and a timestamp rule.

[P2] Nonprofit legal clinics and pro se applicants will be disadvantaged if USCIS counts only agency timestamp instead of postage or courier proof; propose allowing mailed-date-of-postmark or electronic submission confirmation as receipt.

[P3] Granting discretionary leave to amend/supplement is appropriate but must include time limits and criteria; request DHS publish factors guiding the exercise of discretion to avoid arbitrary denials or limitless amendment windows.

[P3] Advocacy groups will request an explicit guarantee that amendments for newly discovered persecution evidence or changes in country conditions will be favored, not penalized as delays.

[P4] Treating amendment/supplement delays as applicant-caused delays will chill meritorious amendments; request exception for amendments based on newly discovered evidence, counsel substitution, or translation needs.

[P4] Legal experts will comment that labeling all amendment-related delays as applicant-caused is overbroad and conflicts with due process where agency or counsel delays force amendments.

[P5] The phrase “subject to listed restrictions” is too broad; employers and applicants need a clear, consolidated list of restrictions and how they interact with other employment-eligibility statutes.

[P6] Requiring use of USCIS-prescribed form and attendance at biometrics is standard, but commenters will ask for fee-waiver and free biometrics options for indigent applicants and fee-exemption clarity for those awaiting fee-waiver decisions.

[P6] Practitioners will request alternative options for applicants with disabilities who cannot attend biometrics in person (e.g., mobile biometrics or disability accommodation procedures explicitly referenced).

[P7] Prohibiting authorization during judicial review will create long work prohibitions; immigrant advocates will argue this could cause severe economic harm and request limited authorization during judicial stays or when remand is ordered.

[P7] Legal commentators will point out potential conflict with courts’ equitable powers and argue DHS should allow interim EADs during judicial review in cases of compelling hardship.

[P8] Granting initial EADs up to two years at USCIS discretion creates uncertainty; commenters will ask DHS to adopt a minimum initial period (e.g., 1 year) to provide stability for employers and workers.

[P8] Employers will request predictable EAD durations tied to case milestones rather than pure agency discretion to reduce workforce disruption when renewals are delayed.

[P9] The absolute 365‑day prohibition on filing for an initial EAD is unduly rigid for applicants who face urgent economic need; request an exception to file earlier with documented economic necessity or humanitarian need.

[P9] Small-business employers will note hiring complications if prospective employees cannot file until day 366 and propose allowing provisional EAD applications that trigger adjudication scheduling.

[P10] Denying EAD if asylum is denied before EAD adjudication could produce unfair outcomes where denials are administratively flawed; request DHS allow discretionary consideration where asylum denial is under appeal or based on technical grounds.

[P11] The broad categorical ineligibility list lacks proportionality; advocates will argue for individualized assessments, especially for minor offenses or old convictions.

[P12] The aggravated felony bar is standard, but commenters will request clear definitions and record standards for foreign convictions and plea-equivalency analyses.

[P13] The domestic felony bar (per 18 U.S.C. 3156(a)(3)) is sweeping — request clarification whether noncustodial misdemeanors in state court are treated as felonies and guidance on record review.

[P14] The foreign “serious non‑political crime” prohibition raises concern about disparate treatment due to differing foreign law standards; request a clear definition and standard of proof for such convictions.

[P15] The case‑by‑case consideration of foreign convictions requires transparent criteria; ask DHS to publish factors (nature of offense, sentencing, time elapsed, rehabilitation) and evidentiary burdens.

[P16] The public-safety offense categories are broad (domestic violence, child abuse, drugs, DUI); request definitions, thresholds (e.g., mens rea), and whether petty offenses or traffic misdemeanors qualify.

[P17] The domestic-violence exception (victim of extreme cruelty/not primary perpetrator) is appropriate in theory but needs implementing standards and evidentiary examples so survivors are not improperly barred.

[P17] Survivor advocacy groups will request that “extreme cruelty” be defined consistently with existing VAWA and U visa guidance and that DHS accept a wide range of documentary and attestation evidence.

[P18] A categorical bar for any conviction “against a child” is overbroad and may catch non‑willful conduct (e.g., negligent supervision); request narrow tailoring to sexually exploitive or severe child harm offenses.

[P19] The drug conviction bar should account for decriminalization in some states and minor possession offenses; propose mitigating factors for low-level possession and addiction-related conduct.

[P20] The DUI bar regardless of jurisdictional classification is disproportionately harsh for a nonviolent offense; recommend limiting to aggravated DUI or DUI causing serious injury, or allowing case-by-case mitigation.

[P21] Discretion for unresolved arrests/pending charges is necessary but needs timing rules; request that pending misdemeanor charges older than X months without prosecution be treated favorably.

[P22] Making applicants ineligible if asylum denied within 365 days or before EAD adjudication could incentivize rushed denials; ask DHS to permit preservation of EAD eligibility where delays were agency-caused or denial is appealed timely.

[P23] Automatically disqualifying late-filed applicants unless they obtain an exception is punitive for asylum seekers with traumatic delays; request specific enumerated exceptions and a low evidentiary threshold for demonstrating late filing cause.

[P23] Child advocates will emphasize that unaccompanied minors should be explicitly and broadly exempted from the late-filing bar beyond the limited mention.

[P24] The unlawful entry ineligibility unless three conditions are met is confusing and may replicate safe‑harbor issues; request clear burden-of-proof standards and acceptable proof for “presented without delay” and “good cause.”

[P25] “Presented without delay” is vague; request DHS define a reasonable time window (e.g., within 14 days) and acceptable evidence (CBP encounters, shelter intake) to prove prompt presentation.

[P26] Requiring an immediate statement of intent to apply for asylum or fear may be impossible for traumatized persons; request DHS accept later expressions of fear and substitute statements where applicants were incoherent or lacked counsel.

[P27] The “good cause” exclusion of evasion, convenience, or circumvention is lawful, but DHS should list non-exhaustive permissible good causes (e.g., trafficking victim, immediate physical danger).

[P28] Clarify how DHS will determine whether entry was for “circumvention of the orderly process” as this could be applied arbitrarily; ask for examples of disqualifying vs. qualifying conduct.

[P29] Applying ineligibility provisions retroactively to pending applications raises due process and reliance concerns; legal commenters will argue DHS cannot apply new substantive bars to applications already filed absent clear statutory authorization.

[P29] Practitioners will request a phased implementation or grandfathering clause for applicants who reasonably relied on earlier policies.

[P30] Denying EAD for unresolved applicant-caused delays at adjudication risks punishing those who attempted cure but were delayed by agency processing; request requirement that DHS provide applicants notice and an opportunity to cure before denial.

[P31] Treating amendment/supplement requests as applicant-caused delay that can lead to denial will deter applicants from correcting omissions; propose safe-harbor for amendments filed more than X days before adjudication or for material evidence.

[P32] Considering failure to appear to receive decision as applicant-caused delay is problematic for applicants lacking transportation or with disabilities; request DHS require good-faith outreach efforts and offer alternate receipt methods (mail, counsel acceptance).

[P33] Denial for requesting extension fewer than 14 days before the interview is unduly punitive for late-arriving evidence due to translation, medical emergencies, or counsel change; ask DHS to permit extensions for good cause shown.

[P34] Denial for missing interview (unless excused) must be coupled with strong notice requirements; request DHS adopt multiple notice methods (email/text/phone) and require proof of attempted service before treating as applicant-caused.

[P35] Denial for missing biometrics should require DHS to demonstrate proper notice and accessible locations; request DHS implement mobile/alternate biometrics for those in remote areas or with mobility issues.

[P36] Treating reschedule requests as applicant-caused delay regardless of reason is unfair; advocates will request an explicit exception for DHS‑initiated rescheduling, emergency medical reasons, or immigration detention transfers.

[P37] Denying EAD for requesting case transfer based on new address penalizes mobility (e.g., fleeing abuse); request that address-based transfers not be treated as applicant-caused delays if timely reported.

[P38] Labeling requests to provide additional evidence as applicant-caused delay will discourage applicants from submitting probative evidence; propose that only frivolous or repeatedly last‑minute requests be penalized.

[P39] Penalizing failure to provide a competent interpreter is reasonable only if DHS first offers interpreter services; request DHS clarify applicant responsibilities versus agency obligations to provide interpreters and accommodate limited-English-proficiency applicants.

[P40] The catchall “failure to comply with any other request” is vague and invites arbitrary determinations; request DHS list specific requests and require advance notice describing consequences and cure opportunities.

[P41] Renewing EADs at DHS discretion up to two years without guaranteed processing times will create employment gaps; request default automatic extensions of prior duration if renewal pending beyond X days.

[P42] Renewal form/fee requirement may be unfair when fee waivers are pending; request that pending fee-waiver motions preserve filing timeliness and that biometrics not be required when previous biometrics on file suffice.

[P43] Requiring proof of “continued pursuit” of asylum for renewal could be hard for those transferred or with pending appeals; request acceptance of alternate proof (appointments, counsel declarations) and automatic renewals when appeals are timely filed.

[P44] The enumerated items for proving pursuit (NTA, hearing notices, appeal filings) should explicitly include evidence of pending motions to reopen or remand and allow counsel affidavits where records are delayed.

[P45] Continuing EAD after asylum officer referral to IJ should be automatic; concern arises that DHS may later terminate—request explicit protection for EAD holders upon referral until final denial.

[P46] Allowing renewals during IJ review is positive but DHS should provide guidance on minimum renewal periods and adjudication timelines to prevent repeated short-term renewals.

[P47] Continuing EAD during the appeal period only while timely appeal is filed should be clarified to prevent inadvertent lapses from counsel errors; recommend safe-harbor where appeal was late due to agency delay.

[P48] Renewals during BIA review/remand should be treated presumptively favorably; request DHS not impose additional discretionary hurdles during appellate stays.

[P49] Automatic termination of EAD on asylum officer/IJ/BIA denial could cause sudden job loss; propose a wind-down period (e.g., 30–60 days) before termination to allow transition and challenge.

[P50] Allowing a limited applicant statement post-interview is reasonable but asylum officers should be required to consider it; request DHS set a minimum time/word limit and permit oral statements recorded in the transcript.

[P51] Requiring in‑person receipt/acknowledgment of decisions and treating failure as applicant-caused delay is burdensome—especially for detained or homeless applicants; request alternative methods (mail to counsel, electronic acknowledgment) and proof-of-service standards.

[P52] The 14-day documentary submission rule is overly rigid for applicants lacking access to foreign records; recommend allowing later submission with a showing of good cause and explicit guidance on acceptable proof of delay.

[P53] Asylum officer discretion to accept late evidence or grant brief extensions is helpful but labeling such extensions as applicant-caused delay will deter seeking extensions; request that DHS not treat discretionally granted extensions as applicant-caused for EAD purposes.

[P54] Failure to appear leading to multiple adverse consequences risks disproportionate harm; commenters will request mandatory individualized assessment and notice before dire consequences (dismissal, denial) are imposed.

[P55] Waiving interview rights for failure to appear should not be automatic; recommend DHS require demonstration of adequate notice and offer a reasonable cure period before waiver.

[P56] Dismissal of asylum application for failure to appear should be accompanied by reinstatement procedures, especially where failure to appear was due to emergencies or agency notice failures.

[P57] Referral to immigration court for failure to appear may prejudice asylum claims; request DHS coordinate with EOIR to ensure applicants are not disadvantaged by administrative notice errors.

[P58] Denial of employment authorization for failure to appear must require a showing that applicant’s conduct was willful and not caused by lack of notice or extraordinary circumstances.

[P59] USCIS being not required to notify an applicant of failure to appear before issuing a decision is contrary to due process; request mandatory notice and opportunity to cure before adverse decisions affecting asylum eligibility or EAD are issued.

[P60] Treating unfulfilled rescheduling requests as applicant-caused delays unfairly allocates delays caused by USCIS scheduling backlogs; request DHS place burden on agency to document reschedule status and not penalize applicant.

[P61] USCIS discretion to excuse failures and reschedule is appropriate but should be governed by published criteria and timelines to ensure consistent application.

[P62] “Exceptional circumstances” to reschedule an interview must be defined (e.g., serious illness, natural disaster, trafficking-related incapacity) and require minimal evidentiary threshold to avoid arbitrary denials.

[P63] Rescheduling biometrics “consistent with 8 CFR part 103” may be insufficient for applicants in remote or high‑caseload areas; request alternative biometric options and clear timelines for reschedules.

[P64] The definition of the class under 274a.12(c)(8) should explicitly confirm eligibility for applicants whose asylum cases were administratively complete but delayed by USCIS, including asylum officers’ threshold completeness determinations.

[P65] Repeated language granting EADs “in increments to be determined by USCIS” creates too much unpredictability; request either a default increment (12 months) or a rule that increments must equal remaining pendency length up to two years.

[P66] Mandating use of a designated form and fees for EAD applications should include explicit fee-waiver procedures and timelines so indigent applicants are not denied due to inability to pay.

[P66] Clarify whether initial EAD applications submitted on incorrect editions of the form are curable and whether DHS will accept corrected forms with an amended filing date.

[P67] The blanket grant of DHS discretion to approve or deny EADs requires publishing internal adjudicative factors; request DHS issue a policy memorandum listing discretionary factors to promote uniformity.

[P68] Requiring financial information when “economic necessity” is identified risks intrusive financial scrutiny; request DHS define “economic necessity,” limit the scope of financial inquiry, and protect sensitive data.

[P69] Reiterating form/fee requirements for asylum-related EADs should explicitly provide exceptions for those whose applications are pending with no biometrics or where biometrics were previously collected.

[P70] The automatic extension termination rule (up to 180 days) may leave gaps when USCIS denies renewal after protracted delay; request that extensions continue until final administrative exhaustion or allow interim work authorization during litigation.

raw_output:
[P1] The deadline to receive comments by August 16, 2021 is unreasonably short and should be extended to allow industry and public stakeholders adequate time to prepare technical and economic analyses.

[P1] The provision requiring FAA receipt of comments by August 16, 2021 fails to clarify whether electronic docket submissions received after that date but postmarked on or before that date will be accepted; request FAA to confirm acceptance criteria and time zone.

[P2] The AD’s blanket requirement to “follow all requirements...within the specified compliance times” is ambiguous because the rule does not clearly specify whether calendar days, flight cycles, or flight hours are the applicable time units for each compliance item.

[P2] Industry requests explicit tolerances/grace periods for the compliance times (e.g., a 10% tolerance in flight hours or 30-day administrative window) to accommodate maintenance scheduling and parts availability.

[P3] The RC designation of all Step 3.B.2 actions in the Boeing Alert Service Bulletin is overly prescriptive and creates operational risk if parts or trained technicians are not available within the specified windows; FAA should allow alternative compliance paths without prior AMOC in exigent circumstances.

[P3] The rule does not provide a consolidated list of the “applicable times specified in paragraph 1.E., 'Compliance,'” forcing operators to cross-reference multiple documents; request inclusion of the compliance table within the AD for clarity.

[P4] Designating Step 3.B.2 as RC only for Group 1 airplanes without defining how airplanes are to be positively identified as Group 1 in field records creates enforceability problems; request that the AD include a clear method to identify Group 1 applicability (e.g., by line number or configuration table).

[P4] Limiting the RC requirements for Step 3.B.2 to Group 1 airplanes as defined solely in Boeing Alert Service Bulletin Revision 2 risks disagreements if Boeing later revises group definitions; urge FAA to incorporate the Group 1 definition into the AD text.

[P5] Replacing references to “the Revision 1 date” with the AD effective date could create confusion for operators referencing previous revisions; recommend FAA require the bulletin to be revised to reflect the AD effective date to eliminate inconsistent references.

[P5] The exception permitting use of the AD effective date in place of “Revision 1 date” may unintentionally shorten compliance windows for operators who followed Revision 1 — request clarification that this substitution does not shorten any previously granted compliance credit periods.

[P6] The prohibition on contacting Boeing for repair instructions and requirement to use FAA-approved methods per paragraph (j) imposes an unnecessary administrative burden and delays safe repairs; request that FAA explicitly allow Boeing ODA-approved repair instructions to be acceptable without separate AMOC when Boeing is the design approval holder.

[P6] Forcing operators to obtain AMOC approval instead of following manufacturer instructions could create unsafe delays during urgent repairs; propose an interim allowance to use Boeing-issued repair instructions with notification to FAA pending formal AMOC processing.

[P7] Granting credit for actions performed using the June 3, 2004 service bulletin only to line numbers 1–1166 is arbitrary; operators of later line numbers that used the 2004 bulletin prior to the effective date should also receive credit if the work was equivalent — request equivalency criteria for credit.

[P7] The credit provision for line numbers 1–1166 lacks a requirement for documentation evidence; request FAA specify acceptable proof (work orders, logbook entries, service records) to substantiate credit claims.

[P8] The grant of credit for actions performed using Revision 1 (Sept 22, 2020) is helpful but needs explicit cross-references to which specific steps are credited; request FAA list the exact paragraph/step numbers that qualify for credit to avoid enforcement ambiguity.

[P9] Centralizing AMOC approval authority in the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch may create delays for operators located far from Seattle and increase workload bottlenecks; recommend delegating certain routine AMOCs to principal inspectors or regional ACOs.

[P9] Legal commenters may note that the AD must also specify timelines for FAA response to AMOC requests to comply with due process expectations; request FAA adopt a 60-calendar-day goal for AMOC disposition or provide interim relief procedures.

[P10] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or responsible Flight Standards Office per 14 CFR 39.19 is fine, but the AD should include contact information or web links to the appropriate offices to prevent misrouting and processing delays.

[P11] The requirement to address direct submissions to the certification office manager “to the person named in Related Information” is impractical if the named contact departs or changes; request an update mechanism and generic mail stop/email alias to ensure continuity.

[P12] Allowing AMOC requests by email is necessary; however, the AD should also permit secure file transfer for large technical packages and state file-size limits and acceptable formats (PDF, DWG, etc.) to avoid failed submissions.

[P13] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC could disrupt operations if immediate use is needed; request that notification be allowed to occur within a short reasonable period after use (e.g., 48 hours) in emergency situations.

[P13] Airlines seek clarification whether notification to the “manager of the responsible Flight Standards Office if none” requires written notice or may be accomplished electronically; request explicit acceptable notification methods.

[P14] Allowing AMOCs approved by an authorized Boeing ODA to be used is positive, but the AD must require that the Boeing ODA approval letter or document be included in maintenance records when an ODA-approved AMOC is used for auditability.

[P14] There is a legal risk if an ODA approval is later invalidated; request FAA require operators relying on Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to retain documentation and provide immediate notice to FAA if ODA approvals are withdrawn.

[P15] Requiring that AMOC repairs meet the airplane’s certification basis is appropriate but vague as to how to demonstrate conformity when certification bases differ across variants; request FAA specify the evidence required (analysis, test results) to establish equivalence.

[P15] The requirement that AMOC approval must “explicitly reference this AD” could be satisfied by ambiguous wording; recommend sample language or mandatory inclusion of AD number and specific paragraph reference in the AMOC approval text.

[P16] Accepting AMOCs previously approved for AD 2005–05–18 is efficient, but FAA should publish a crosswalk identifying which specific prior AMOCs correspond to which current AD provisions to reduce confusion during inspections.

[P16] Operators who relied on previously approved AMOCs may find them inconsistent with revised service information; request FAA confirm whether such legacy AMOCs remain valid without further review or if operators must revalidate applicability.

[P17] The rule’s treatment of RC and non-RC steps lacks a mechanism for operators to identify RC steps in the field easily; request FAA require service bulletins to mark RC steps prominently and include a one-page RC summary with step numbers.

[P18] The obligation that all RC-labeled steps (including figures) must be performed is reasonable but should include tolerance for minor, non-safety-affecting omissions (e.g., typographical figure numbering errors); request FAA to allow editorial errors to be corrected without AMOC.

[P19] The ‘RC Exempt’ exception needs clear criteria and should require that the service bulletin explicitly mark the affected steps as “RC Exempt” rather than relying on ambiguous text, to avoid enforcement disputes.

[P20] Requiring an AMOC for any deviation from RC steps will create operational challenges when a minor, equivalent alternative procedure exists; request FAA permit operators to use alternative methods approved under their maintenance control processes for truly equivalent deviations, with post-facto FAA notification.

[P20] Legal stakeholders may argue that automatic AMOC requirement for all RC deviations could conflict with operators’ statutory repair station authorities; request FAA coordinate with FAA Repair Station regulations to prevent regulatory overlap.

The provision requiring FAA receipt of comments by August 16, 2021 fails to clarify whether electronic docket submissions received after that date but postmarked on or before that date will be accepted; request FAA to confirm acceptance criteria and time zone.

The AD’s blanket requirement to “follow all requirements...within the specified compliance times” is ambiguous because the rule does not clearly specify whether calendar days, flight cycles, or flight hours are the applicable time units for each compliance item.

Industry requests explicit tolerances/grace periods for the compliance times (e.g., a 10% tolerance in flight hours or 30-day administrative window) to accommodate maintenance scheduling and parts availability.

The RC designation of all Step 3.B.2 actions in the Boeing Alert Service Bulletin is overly prescriptive and creates operational risk if parts or trained technicians are not available within the specified windows; FAA should allow alternative compliance paths without prior AMOC in exigent circumstances.

The rule does not provide a consolidated list of the “applicable times specified in paragraph 1.E., 'Compliance,'” forcing operators to cross-reference multiple documents; request inclusion of the compliance table within the AD for clarity.

Designating Step 3.B.2 as RC only for Group 1 airplanes without defining how airplanes are to be positively identified as Group 1 in field records creates enforceability problems; request that the AD include a clear method to identify Group 1 applicability (e.g., by line number or configuration table).

Limiting the RC requirements for Step 3.B.2 to Group 1 airplanes as defined solely in Boeing Alert Service Bulletin Revision 2 risks disagreements if Boeing later revises group definitions; urge FAA to incorporate the Group 1 definition into the AD text.

Replacing references to “the Revision 1 date” with the AD effective date could create confusion for operators referencing previous revisions; recommend FAA require the bulletin to be revised to reflect the AD effective date to eliminate inconsistent references.

The exception permitting use of the AD effective date in place of “Revision 1 date” may unintentionally shorten compliance windows for operators who followed Revision 1 — request clarification that this substitution does not shorten any previously granted compliance credit periods.

The prohibition on contacting Boeing for repair instructions and requirement to use FAA-approved methods per paragraph (j) imposes an unnecessary administrative burden and delays safe repairs; request that FAA explicitly allow Boeing ODA-approved repair instructions to be acceptable without separate AMOC when Boeing is the design approval holder.

Forcing operators to obtain AMOC approval instead of following manufacturer instructions could create unsafe delays during urgent repairs; propose an interim allowance to use Boeing-issued repair instructions with notification to FAA pending formal AMOC processing.

Granting credit for actions performed using the June 3, 2004 service bulletin only to line numbers 1–1166 is arbitrary; operators of later line numbers that used the 2004 bulletin prior to the effective date should also receive credit if the work was equivalent — request equivalency criteria for credit.

Centralizing AMOC approval authority in the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch may create delays for operators located far from Seattle and increase workload bottlenecks; recommend delegating certain routine AMOCs to principal inspectors or regional ACOs.

Legal commenters may note that the AD must also specify timelines for FAA response to AMOC requests to comply with due process expectations; request FAA adopt a 60-calendar-day goal for AMOC disposition or provide interim relief procedures.

The requirement to address direct submissions to the certification office manager “to the person named in Related Information” is impractical if the named contact departs or changes; request an update mechanism and generic mail stop/email alias to ensure continuity.

Allowing AMOC requests by email is necessary; however, the AD should also permit secure file transfer for large technical packages and state file-size limits and acceptable formats (PDF, DWG, etc.) to avoid failed submissions.

The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC could disrupt operations if immediate use is needed; request that notification be allowed to occur within a short reasonable period after use (e.g., 48 hours) in emergency situations.

Airlines seek clarification whether notification to the “manager of the responsible Flight Standards Office if none” requires written notice or may be accomplished electronically; request explicit acceptable notification methods.

raw_output:
[P1] The prohibition on assigning peer groups based on reagent lot number (§ 493.2) is ambiguous because it does not define “reagent system” vs. “reagent lot,” risking inconsistent enforcement across PT programs and labs.

[P1] Industry commenters will argue that banning reagent-lot-based peer groups could prevent meaningful comparisons for tests where lot-to-lot variability is the dominant source of inter-lab difference, reducing PT relevance and sensitivity.

[P2] Small laboratories will request clarification of the peer group size threshold language (peer group size ≥10) in § 493.2, asking whether participant counts are assessed per analyte, per instrument-model, or per reagent-manufacturer.

[P3] Manufacturers and reference labs will support allowing the participant-mean-after-outlier-removal (§ 493.2(i)) as a target value but request clear standardized outlier-removal procedures (e.g., definition of original SD, iterative vs. single-pass removal) to ensure reproducibility.

[P3] Statistical experts will comment that removing responses >3 SD from the “original” mean without specifying whether SD is robust (median absolute deviation) can be unduly influenced by non-normal distributions; they will request robust outlier rules or alternative methods.

[P4] Clinical laboratorians will support the option to use definitive/reference method means (§ 493.2(ii)) but demand specification of acceptable reference methods and accreditation/status criteria for those assays to prevent arbitrary designation.

[P5] For § 493.2(iii), stakeholders will request criteria for when “definitive methods or reference methods are not available” — e.g., how PT programs demonstrate lack of reference method and who adjudicates that determination.

[P6] Small or specialized labs will express concern about § 493.2(iv) applying the overall mean after outlier removal for peer groups <10, noting that means from very small N are unstable and suggesting alternative approaches (median, reference labs, or suspension of grading).

[P6] Academic statisticians will recommend that for peer groups <10, PT programs be allowed to use consensus expert-derived target values or to combine data across similar peer groups rather than rely on an overall mean.

[P7] Patient-advocacy groups will question the safety rationale for exempting compliance with §§ 493.801(a),(b)(7) and subparts J, K, M for waived tests (§ 493.20(c)), arguing this could create gaps in oversight for laboratories that perform both waived and non-waived testing.

[P8] Laboratories that perform waived tests will request examples or a list of the “required” provisions in § 493.20(c) (e.g., clarify scope of §§ 493.15(e), 493.801(b)(1)-(6), 493.1771, 1773, 1775) to ensure operational compliance and avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P9] Commenters will note the duplicative exception language in § 493.25(d) (same as § 493.20(c)) and request harmonization or consolidation to avoid confusion among labs about which waiver exceptions apply.

[P10] Clinical labs will point out that mandating compliance with §§ 493.15(e), 493.801(b)(1)-(6), and 493.1771/1773/1775 for waived tests (§§ 493.20(c) and 493.25(d)) imposes administrative burdens without clarifying enforcement or penalties; they will request examples of acceptable documentation.

[P11] Microbiology laboratories will request explicit guidance on what constitutes “the highest reporting level” for PT organism IDs (§ 493.801(b)(3)) — e.g., genus/species/subspecies/serotype — and whether reporting of “not identified to species” is acceptable when that is the patient-reporting practice.

[P11] Legal commenters will raise that requiring reporting at the highest level used for patient specimens (§ 493.801(b)(3)) could force labs to over-report or adopt practices beyond CLIA-certified test menus, creating regulatory liability.

[P12] PT providers will object to the minimum of ten laboratory participants before offering an analyte (§ 493.901(a)), citing market feasibility: some rare analytes or specialized tests will rarely reach 10 participants, potentially eliminating PT availability.

[P12] Patient-advocacy groups will counter that minimum participant thresholds are necessary to ensure statistical validity and request exceptions for analytes tied to rare but high-risk conditions, with alternate validation requirements.

[P13] PT programs will request technical specifications for the “mechanism to track electronic result changes and reasons” (§ 493.901(c)(6)): retention period, audit trail fields, timestamps, user IDs, and whether manual change logs suffice.

[P13] Privacy counsel will ask whether tracking changes to electronically submitted PT results (§ 493.901(c)(6)) implicates additional HIPAA or data-security obligations and request cross-reference to applicable data-protection standards.

[P14] PT programs will seek specificity on required response timeframes and escalation procedures for the “process to resolve technical, administrative, and scientific operational problems” (§ 493.901(c)(8)) to ensure consistent program operations.

[P15] Many commenters will oppose restricting administrative contractors to private nonprofits, Federal/State agencies, or designated agents (§ 493.901(c)(9)), arguing this exclusion of for-profit vendors will reduce competition, increase costs, and is arbitrary without demonstration that for-profits are less reliable.

[P15] Conversely, some advocacy groups may support § 493.901(c)(9) to reduce commercial conflicts of interest, but request clear conflict-of-interest rules and transparency rather than categorical exclusion of for-profits.

[P16] PT providers will request criteria and notice procedures for when HHS may require on-site visits for initial applications (§ 493.901(e)), including scope, frequency, cost recovery, and an appeals mechanism for burdensome or duplicative visits.

[P17] Programs will urge clarification of what constitutes “significant problems” that trigger a reapplication under § 493.901(f) and call for a defined remediation period and graduated sanctions before forcing reapplication.

[P18] PT program administrators will support the prohibition on altering laboratory-submitted PT data (§ 493.903(a)(3)) but ask for an allowed exceptions clause for clerical corrections with documented audit trail and laboratory notification.

[P19] PT programs and labs will ask § 493.905(a) to require CMS to provide affected programs with a specific deficiency notice and a remediation timeline before public notification or mandatory lab notification to reduce unnecessary alarm.

[P19] Enrolled laboratories will request clarity in § 493.905(a) on the required content of the program’s notice to enrolled labs within 30 days (e.g., specific reasons, interim measures, impact on grading), and whether labs have obligations to report program disapproval to accrediting bodies.

[P20] Programs will caution that CMS’s authority to disapprove for “false or misleading information” (§ 493.905(a)) needs procedural protections: definition of materiality, an opportunity to correct, and appeal rights.

[P21] PT programs will seek clearer timelines, standards of review, and confidentiality protections for the CMS reconsideration process (§ 493.905(b)); they will also ask whether reinstitution during appeal is possible.

[P22] Bacteriology PT providers will request justification and cost analysis supporting the minimum of five samples per event and at least three events/year (§ 493.911(a))—noting this may increase program costs and participant fees substantially.

[P22] Smaller labs will ask that the rule allow fewer samples per event or fewer events for low-volume tests or small labs to reduce burden while preserving quality.

[P23] Programs will ask for sample stability and shipping-condition standards if mailed shipments are used (§ 493.911(a) permission) and for allowances for international participants where mailing reliability varies.

[P24] Clinical microbiology labs will welcome the explicit inclusion of Gram stain, antigen/toxin detection, identification, and antimicrobial susceptibility samples in bacteriology PT (§ 493.911(a)(1)) but request flexibility where a lab’s scope does not include all categories.

[P25] PT programs will ask for clarification of the format and level of detail required in the annual sample description to HHS submitted six months in advance (§ 493.911(a)(2)), and whether changes after submission are permitted and how to document them.

[P26] Laboratories will question the requirement that at least 25% of bacteriology PT samples be mixed cultures (§ 493.911(a)(2)) as logistically challenging and potentially raising biosafety/shipping issues; they will request biosafety guidance and allowance for simulated mixtures.

[P27] For samples where labs report only principal pathogens (§ 493.911(a)(2)(i)), programs will request a written process for how the program “determines which isolates are reportable” to ensure transparency and avoid grade disputes.

[P28] For samples requiring reporting of all organisms (§ 493.911(a)(2)(ii)), labs will express concern that such samples may unrealistically penalize labs whose routine practice (or CLIA scope) does not include identification of minor flora; they request that grading reflect each lab’s reported patient scope.

[P29] Statistical and legal commenters will request detailed methodology and documentation for the two alternative 80% consensus rules (§ 493.911(b)(1)) and require that programs publish their attempts and rationale before electing not to grade a sample.

[P30] Repeating § 493.911(b)(2) claim: Labs will reiterate that requiring identification to the highest level they perform on patient specimens may penalize labs using limited identification workflows and request an explicit safe-harbor that PT grading align with declared test menus.

[P31] Labs will ask how to report routinely tested antimicrobial panels (§ 493.911(b)(8)) when hospital antibiograms and test panels vary by patient population, and request that PT programs accept “custom panel” declarations without penalty.

[P32] Clinical labs will request that § 493.911(b)(9)’s averaging method for bacteriology event scores include guidance on weighting components (b)(4)-(8) when some components are not applicable to a specific lab’s test menu.

[P33] Mycobacteriology PT programs will request justification for five samples per event and at least two events/year (§ 493.913(a)) and an explanation why fewer events are insufficient given biosafety and culture time constraints.

[P34] Mycobacteriology providers will seek clarity on the six-month advance sample description requirement (§ 493.913(a)(2)) and whether it must include BSL-level information and shipping/packaging plans.

[P35] Infection-control experts will ask for biosafety and shipping protocols associated with § 493.913(a)(4) requirement to include both acid-fast and non–acid-fast challenges, to prevent unintended exposure risks.

[P36] Mycobacteriology PT commenters will request the same clarity and publication of the 80% consensus process (§ 493.913(b)(1)) as requested for bacteriology PT programs.

[P37] Mycology PT programs will question the logistical and cost impacts of a minimum of five samples per event and three events per year (§ 493.915(a)), especially for laboratories in remote areas with infrequent mycology testing.

[P38] Mycology providers will ask whether the six-month planned-sample submission (§ 493.915(a)(2)) must include antifungal susceptibility challenge specifics since those can depend on emerging resistance patterns.

[P39] Laboratories performing antifungal susceptibility testing will seek clarification on the requirement to include at least two antifungal susceptibility challenges per event with predetermined patterns (§ 493.915(a)(4)) and request standardized interpretation criteria (breakpoints) to be specified.

[P40] Mycology PT programs will request that the 80% consensus rules (§ 493.915(b)(1)) be harmonized across microbiology disciplines (bacteriology, mycobacteriology, mycology, parasitology, virology, syphilis) to reduce complexity.

[P41] Parasitology PT providers will question the feasibility of providing five samples per event and three events per year (§ 493.917(a)) for rare parasites and request alternative validation mechanisms or combined analyte offerings.

[P42] Parasitology labs will request guidance on how mixed-structure or lifecycle-stage samples should be graded and whether identification to life stage counts toward accuracy for PT (§ 493.917(b)(1)).

[P43] Virology PT programs will ask whether the five-sample minimum and three-event requirement (§ 493.919(a)) are flexible for tests with rapid technological change (e.g., PCR panels) and for low-prevalence viruses.

[P44] Virology commenters will request explicit guidance on how consensus 80% rules (§ 493.919(b)(1)) apply to qualitative vs quantitative viral assays and to PCR Ct-value–based scoring.

[P45] Syphilis serology PT programs will support the inclusion of samples covering the full reactivity range (§ 493.923(a)) but request definitions of “highly reactive” and “non-reactive” tied to specific assay signal-to-cutoff metrics for comparability.

[P46] Clinical laboratories will request that syphilis PT grading (§ 493.923(b)(1)) account for algorithmic testing strategies (e.g., reverse sequence screening) and accept algorithm-appropriate responses rather than penalizing differing workflows.

[P47] TRICARE beneficiaries and providers will request clarification on the required scope of “prescribed and monitored by a physician or TRICARE-authorized allied health professional” (§ 199.4(c)(3)(x)(A)) — specifically whether telehealth supervision meets the oversight requirement.

[P48] Providers seeking fee-for-service TRICARE benefits will ask in § 199.6(c)(3)(iii)(K)(2) whether the required referral from a physician/allied professional may be electronic or must be an in-person evaluation, and whether standing orders are permitted.

[P49] TRICARE-authorized allied health professionals will request a clear list of who qualifies as “authorized” under § 199.6(c)(3)(iii)(K)(2) and whether the scope-of-license limitation permits supervision of programs across state lines for beneficiaries stationed in different states.

[P50] TRICARE providers will request clarity on what constitutes “continuing and ongoing oversight and supervision” (§ 199.6(c)(3)(iii)(K)(2))—frequency of review, documentation requirements, and liability exposure—so agencies can operationalize compliance.
