[P1] The March 1, 2016 deadline in P1 for submitting lists of exporting establishments is impossibly retrospective and should be removed or extended to a realistic future date because foreign authorities cannot comply with a past date.

[P1] Requiring documentation of establishments "that had been exporting and would continue exporting" by March 1, 2016 (P1) is ambiguous—FDA/FSIS must clarify whether previously exporting establishments that paused exports but intend to resume qualify.

[P2] The March 1, 2016 deadline in P2 for demonstrating legal authority and compliance with FDA GMPs, HACCP, sanitation, and 21 CFR part 123 is likewise unworkable and should be changed to a reasonable prospective compliance date.

[P2] P2's requirement that foreign countries show they regulate "fish production" to meet FDA GMPs/HACCP/21 CFR 123 is vague about scope; commenters request a clear definition of "fish production" (aquaculture farms, primary processors, secondary processors, cold chain handlers).

[P2] Industry requests that P2 explicitly allow phased submission of documentation (e.g., legal statutes then implementing regulations then on-site verification) rather than a single submission by the stated date.

[P3] The equivalence documentation requirement in P3 lacks specificity about the standards, data, and format required—FSIS should publish a detailed guidance checklist for equivalence submissions and acceptable evidence.

[P3] Legal experts will challenge whether FSIS may lawfully require foreign governments to demonstrate full "equivalence" of inspection systems as a precondition for trade without transparent, objective criteria and an appeals or reconsideration process.

[P4] P4 permitting continued exports pending determination if "complete" documentation submitted by Sept. 1, 2017 could create a loophole where countries submit superficial documentation—FSIS should define "complete" and require interim sampling/monitoring during the pendency.

[P4] Consumer advocates will request that P4 be conditioned on immediate intensified U.S. entry sampling for countries relying on the "continue exporting" permission during equivalence review.

[P5] Listing in the CFR (P5) as an eligibility condition is appropriate, but commenters request a timely and public process for adding/removing countries, including notice-and-comment or a prompt administrative process, so exporters have predictability.

[P5] Exporting businesses request clarity on the timeline from submission to publication in the CFR under P5—how long will FSIS take to decide and publish listings?

[P6] The certification obligation in P6 lacks specificity on the certifying authority and the form/content of certification; commenters request a model certificate and clarity whether private exporters or only national competent authorities may certify.

[P6] Foreign governments will seek a delegation option in P6 allowing competent authorities to certify establishments that meet requirements rather than requiring each exporter to certify individually.

[P7] P7 duplicates P3 and P2 and appears to impose multiple overlapping documentation obligations; FSIS should harmonize P7 with P2/P3 and eliminate redundant submissions.

[P7] Legal analysts will request an express statement in P7 on how FSIS will verify the submitted information (on-site audits, requests for additional information) and whether countries will have an opportunity to correct deficiencies before delisting.

[P8] The requirement in P8 that monitoring frequency "replicate" written sanitation procedures is overly prescriptive—establishments should be allowed to demonstrate equivalence of outcomes even if monitoring intervals differ due to operational realities.

[P8] Small processors may be unable to match the written monitoring frequency demanded in P8; FSIS should allow alternative, risk-based monitoring schedules approved by the competent authority.

[P9] The certification requirement for Vietnam in P9 (9 CFR 557.2(a)) appears to single out one country; commenters ask whether other countries will be required to make the same certification and request a consistent policy across all trading partners.

[P9] Exporters and the Vietnamese government will request an explicit process and timeline for the Vietnam certification under P9, and relief if certification cannot be completed immediately.

[P10] The broad requirement in P10 that imports originate from countries maintaining equivalence across multiple areas (inspection, sanitary, quality, species verification, residue standards, and FMIA provisions) is vague and may create trade barriers; commenters request objective criteria and measures for each listed area.

[P10] Seafood industry stakeholders ask that P10 explicitly permit equivalence determinations on a sector- or commodity-specific basis (e.g., culture-raised Siluriformes only), rather than requiring country-wide equivalence across all fish commodities.

[P11] The re-inspection list in P11 is open-ended ("but not limited to") and lacks granularity; commenters request a defined checklist and frequency for re-inspection to reduce administrative uncertainty and unnecessary detention.

[P11] Importers will request that FSIS publish standard operating procedures for U.S. point-of-entry re-inspection described in P11, including sampling protocols, holding times, and costs to importers.

[P12] P12 requires increased/ intensified sampling for further shipments from an establishment after a failure; commenters request a definition of "increased/intensified sampling" (what percent increase, number of lots, duration) and a process for returning to normal sampling.

[P12] Foreign competent authorities assert P12 should provide an appeals process or corrective-action plan timelines before indefinite intensified sampling or suspension occurs.

[P13] The permission in P13 to stamp products passing re-inspection is standard; importers request clarity on the mark's design and whether stamping at U.S. port-of-entry is mandatory or if foreign marks are acceptable.

[P14] The 45-day time frame in P14 for exporting, destroying, or converting refused product is too short for logistical realities and customs/port constraints; stakeholders ask for an extension to at least 90 days or a case-by-case extension process.

[P14] Converting refused product to animal food subject to FDA approval (P14/P17) is burdensome; feed industry stakeholders request clearer, expedited FDA pathways and documentation requirements for such conversions.

[P15] The obligation in P15 that refused product must be exported to country of origin within 45 days may be impossible for products from landlocked or otherwise constrained origins; commenters request exceptions or extensions in such circumstances.

[P16] The mandatory destruction within 45 days in P16 raises environmental and cost concerns; importers and environmental groups suggest allowing destruction under approved methods with oversight and possible use as rendered products where safe.

[P17] The conversion to animal food within 45 days in P17 is conditioned on FDA approval "when applicable"—commenters request clear criteria when FDA approval is needed and fast-track review timelines.

[P18] Adding the Socialist Republic of Vietnam to 9 CFR 557.2(b)(1) (P18) should be contingent upon satisfactory completion of the equivalence determination in P3—not automatic by administrative addition.

[P18] Human rights and labor advocates may object to adding Vietnam (P18) absent evidence FSIS considered labor and environmental standards in the supply chain; they request FSIS publicize any due diligence on these issues.

[P19] The eligibility in P19 tied to foreign inspection certificates (P20) requires model certificate templates; importing businesses request FSIS to publish the exact certificate format and attestations required.

[P20] The requirement in P20 that exporters provide foreign inspection certificates as required by § 557.4 imposes costs and administrative burdens; industry asks FSIS to provide an electronic submission option and limit data fields to necessary elements.

[P21] P21's requirement that products be inspected and marked "as required by applicable provisions of part 557" requires FSIS to publish a consolidated checklist mapping specific marking and inspection steps to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P22] Listing the People's Republic of China in P22 triggers calls from consumer safety groups to justify that country's inclusion given historic import violations; FSIS should publish the evidence supporting China's eligibility and any ongoing monitoring requirements.

[P23] The broad permission in P23 adding Vietnam to § 557.2(b)(1) is premature absent public disclosure of the equivalence evaluation report; stakeholders request FSIS publish the full equivalence assessment and inspection reports before listing.

[P23] Trade associations request clarity whether adding Vietnam under P23 applies to all Siluriformes products (fresh, frozen, processed) or only specified product types—FSIS should list covered product categories explicitly.

[P3] Food safety NGOs request that P3 require not only documentation but also timely FSIS on-site audits of foreign inspection systems before allowing continued exports after Sept. 1, 2017.

[P12] Importers ask that P12 specify notification timelines and modes (electronic notice) to the foreign competent authority when an imported product fails testing to ensure prompt corrective action.

[P6] Consumer advocates request that certifications required under P6 include traceability data (farm, establishment, lot/batch codes) to enable rapid recalls if problems arise.

[P8] Public health stakeholders request that P8 require that sanitation monitoring records be retained for a specified minimum period (e.g., 2 years) and be made available to FSIS upon request.

[P11] States with ports of entry request clarity on state vs. federal roles for re-inspection costs and responsibilities mentioned in P11, including who bears detention/holding expenses.

[P1] The deadline of May 24, 2021 for receiving comments is unreasonably short and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow operators, unions, and small businesses sufficient time to prepare substantive technical and economic comments.

[P1] The rule text should clarify whether postmarked comments or electronically submitted comments received after May 24, 2021 will be accepted, to avoid unfair rejection of late but timely-posted submissions.

[P2] The applicability to "all The Boeing Company Model 757–200, –200PF, –200CB, and –300 series airplanes, certificated in any category" is overbroad; the FAA should limit the AD to serial numbers or configuration groups with the affected structure rather than all 757-200/300s.

[P2] The AD should explicitly exclude 757s that have had prior affected structure replaced or modified per service bulletins, or provide a method to demonstrate that a specific airplane is not susceptible, rather than a blanket applicability.

[P2] The scope line fails to address leased or foreign-registered airplanes operated under U.S. continuing airworthiness responsibilities; the AD should state obligations for these operators to ensure clarity.

[P3] The phrase "within the compliance times specified" is ambiguous because the relevant compliance paragraph references multiple alternative intervals; the FAA should publish a single clear timeline table in the AD itself.

[P3] Compliance time relief is inadequately defined for aircraft that are out of service for extended maintenance or storage — the AD should state how the compliance clock is handled during storage or in MASPs.

[P4] Requiring strict adherence to Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 757–57A0074 RB without allowing operator deviations could conflict with existing maintenance programs; the FAA should allow equivalent procedures subject to AMOC approval.

[P4] The AD references Boeing's Requirements Bulletin but does not include the text of critical inspection criteria; the FAA should incorporate or summarize those inspection thresholds in the AD to ensure transparency.

[P5] The carve-out for airplanes with Aviation Partners Boeing (APB) blended winglets leaves unclear whether all APB STC installations are covered; the AD should list affected STC numbers or serial ranges to avoid interpretive disputes.

[P5] Requiring only actions marked 'RC' in APB Service Bulletin AP757–57–011 may omit other recommended actions necessary for airworthiness; the FAA should justify why non-RC actions are excluded from mandatory compliance.

[P6] Replacing references to the Requirements Bulletin "original issue date" with the AD effective date could cause confusion where operators rely on service bulletin revision history; the FAA should provide a crosswalk between bulletin revision dates and AD effective dates.

[P6] The provision that equates "original issue date" to the AD effective date may retroactively change compliance triggers; legal counsel should evaluate whether this change exceeds the FAA's statutory authority.

[P7] Mandating that Boeing-approved repair instructions be used "before further flight" but requiring approval per paragraph (i) could create operational grounding delays if Boeing is unavailable — the FAA should provide an alternate path or interim procedures for urgent repairs.

[P7] The phrase "using a method approved per paragraph (i)" is circular because paragraph (i) delegates approval authority to the FAA LA ACO manager and Boeing ODA; the AD should specify timelines and criteria for approval to prevent delayed repairs.

[P8] Similar to P6, substituting the APB service bulletin "original issue date" with the AD effective date is unclear and could misalign operators' maintenance records; the FAA should clarify how to document compliance in maintenance logs.

[P9] Requiring Boeing-approved repairs for APB-referenced instructions potentially forces reliance on a single manufacturer for repair methods; the FAA should permit alternative manufacturers or qualified repair stations to propose equivalent repairs subject to AMOC.

[P10] Concentrating AMOC approval authority solely in the Manager, Los Angeles ACO Branch may create bottlenecks and geographic inequities; the FAA should authorize regional ACO managers to approve AMOCs or specify service-level timelines.

[P10] The AD should define criteria that the Manager, LA ACO Branch will use to evaluate AMOCs to increase predictability for applicants.

[P11] Requiring AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or Flight Standards Office may be impractical for foreign operators or operators without assigned principal inspectors; the AD should provide an alternative routing path.

[P12] The AD refers to "the person identified in Related Information" but does not list that person in the regulatory text; the AD must explicitly name the certification office manager and contact details in the rule.

[P13] Allowing AMOC information to be emailed to 9-ANM-LAACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is useful, but the AD should also permit secure file transfer for large engineering packages and clarify maximum file size and accepted formats.

[P14] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC lacks a required timeframe (e.g., 24 or 48 hours); the AD should specify how soon notification is required to ensure oversight while allowing operational use.

[P14] For operators without a principal inspector, notifying "the manager of the responsible Flight Standards Office" is ambiguous — the AD should give contact details or a centralized FAA point of contact.

[P15] Allowing an AMOC approved by an authorized Boeing ODA to be used for required repairs gives Boeing potentially excessive de facto rulemaking power; the FAA should require FAA concurrence or a formal validation step before operator reliance.

[P15] The provision does not require the Boeing ODA approval to be documented in the aircraft's maintenance records; the AD should mandate recordkeeping language and retention periods for such ODA-approved AMOCs.

[P16] The requirement that the Boeing ODA be "authorized by the Manager, Los Angeles ACO Branch" should be backed by a published list of authorized ODAs to avoid uncertainty and to allow operators to confirm authorization.

[P16] The AD should prohibit delegation to sub-tier entities not covered by the ODA authorization unless specifically listed, to prevent unauthorized approvals.

[P17] Requiring that AMOC repairs meet the airplane's certification basis is appropriate, but the AD should specify whether showing equivalency to a supereceded rule part is acceptable and how to demonstrate compliance.

[P17] The AD should provide guidance about how to handle certification basis changes over time (e.g., amended type certificates) when evaluating whether an AMOC meets the airplane's certification basis.

[P18] The requirement that any AMOC approval "specifically reference this AD" should include an example of acceptable wording and require inclusion of the AD docket number to avoid ambiguous approvals.

[P18] The AD should require that AMOC approvals referencing this AD be posted to a searchable FAA database or docket so other operators can see precedent and reduce duplicate requests.

[P1] The rule’s division of the United States into exactly 31 geographic units for nominating and appointing producers lacks any stated statutory or empirical basis and appears arbitrary; commenters should request justification and the methodology used to determine 31 units.

[P1] Industry stakeholders will likely comment that using rigid geographic units instead of producer population or production volume data will distort representation and not reflect where most producers are located.

[P1] Agricultural producer associations will request that the rule include a mechanism for periodic review and adjustment of the 31 geographic units to account for demographic or market changes (e.g., every 5 years).

[P2] Several commenters will argue that the list-based assignment of Board membership by unit (the per-unit numbers) must be accompanied by the total Board size, quorum, and term limits; as drafted, the rule provides numbers but not governance detail, creating uncertainty about overall Board composition.

[P2] Legal experts may assert the rule should include a cross-check ensuring that the sum of members assigned across the listed units complies with any statutory cap on Board size; they will request an explicit total and citation to authorizing statute.

[P3] Procedural fairness advocates will contend that qualifying the assignment by paragraphs (d) and (e) without including those paragraphs in the public notice prevents meaningful comment on how the qualifications might alter the stated allocations; they will request publication of paragraphs (d) and (e) or an explanation of how they operate.

[P3] Commenters will request clarity on whether paragraphs (d) and (e) permit reallocation of seats among units based on census or production changes, and whether such reallocation requires a separate rulemaking or notice-and-comment.

[P4] South Dakota producers will challenge the assignment of 4 Board members as either insufficient or disproportionate depending on their state's producer population; they will request the data used to justify 4 seats and an equity analysis comparing seats per producer across states.

[P5] Ohio agricultural groups may argue that four seats do not reflect the state’s producer concentration and will request either additional seats or a formulaic adjustment tied to production metrics.

[P6] North Dakota producers are likely to submit a claim that assigning 4 members to North Dakota over-represents its producers relative to larger states, and they will request transparency on the allocation criteria.

[P7] Nebraska stakeholders will question why Nebraska receives 4 seats and will ask for data showing parity (e.g., seats per producer or per acreage) with other Midwestern states.

[P8] Missouri commenters may request assurance that the 4-member allocation will not dilute minority or small-producer voices within the state and ask for minority representation safeguards.

[P9] Minnesota organizations will request justification for 4 seats and ask whether alternatives (e.g., weighted voting or proportional representation) were considered.

[P10] Iowa producers will challenge the 4-member assignment if it conflicts with the statutory requirement to ensure fair representation of producers nationwide, asking for a proportionality analysis.

[P11] Indiana stakeholders will request detail on how nominations will be conducted within the state to ensure the 4 slots are competitively filled and representative of farm sizes and commodity types.

[P12] Illinois commenters will ask whether the 4-seat allocation accounts for the state’s large producer population, and if not, they will recommend a reallocation to prevent underrepresentation.

[P13] Wisconsin producers may assert that receiving 3 seats (instead of 4 like neighboring states) will marginalize the state’s producers and request an explanation for the lower allocation.

[P14] Tennessee groups will ask whether 3 seats adequately represent the state’s diverse agricultural sectors and request criteria for intra-state seat distribution (e.g., by region or commodity).

[P15] Mississippi stakeholders will express concern that 3 seats are insufficient to represent both large commercial and small diversified producers and ask for measures to ensure smallholder inclusion.

[P16] Michigan commenters will request the data supporting Michigan’s 3 seats and propose that Great Lakes regional issues require additional representation.

[P17] Kentucky organizations will ask whether the allocation accounts for specialty crop producers and request protection of niche producer representation among the 3 seats.

[P18] Kansas producers will question the 3-seat allocation relative to Kansas’ production of certain commodities (e.g., wheat, sorghum) and request an allocation tied to commodity output.

[P19] Arkansas commenters will request justification for 3 seats and propose safeguards to ensure equitable selection between row-crop and specialty-crop producers.

[P20] Virginia stakeholders will challenge the assignment of only 2 seats given the state’s agricultural diversity and proximity to major markets; they will request either additional seats or dedicated representation for certain producer classes.

[P21] Pennsylvania agricultural groups will argue that two seats will not allow adequate representation for both small family farms and larger operations and will request that one seat be reserved for small/limited-resource producers.

[P22] North Carolina commenters will request that the two seats reflect the state’s varied production (tobacco, poultry, greenhouse) and propose rule language requiring diversity of commodity representation among nominees.

[P23] Maryland stakeholders will seek clarification whether the two seats include representation from the Eastern Shore and urban agriculture producers, asking for guidance on nomination procedures.

[P24] Louisiana producers will submit comments asserting that two seats may not account for unique coastal or aquaculture producers and will request seat allocation or nomination guidance to ensure those interests are represented.

[P25] Alabama commenters will object to being assigned only one seat and argue that a single Board member cannot adequately represent the state’s geographic and commodity diversity, urging alternative mechanisms (e.g., regional alternates).

[P26] Texas stakeholders will strongly object to assignment of only 1 seat for Texas, the second-largest agricultural state by production and acreage, arguing this is grossly underrepresentative and likely violates the statutory requirement for equitable producer representation.

[P27] South Carolina producers will assert that a single seat is insufficient and ask for criteria that would enable additional seats if producer counts increase or to allow at-large members to represent the state’s interests.

[P28] Oklahoma commenters will request justification for only one seat given the state’s significant production in specific commodities (e.g., wheat, cattle), and propose combining Oklahoma with adjacent units rather than a single-seat allocation.

[P29] New York stakeholders will state that one seat cannot represent upstate and downstate agricultural interests and will ask for sub-state nomination procedures to ensure geographic balance.

[P30] New Jersey producers will highlight the diversity of specialty and urban agriculture in the state and argue that one member cannot represent these varied interests; they will request alternative representation mechanisms.

[P31] Georgia commenters will object to one seat and request that the rule include mechanisms for appointing alternates or at-large Board members to ensure broader representation for major commodities like poultry, peanuts, and peaches.

[P32] Delaware stakeholders will express concern that a single member will be overwhelmed by representing multiple producer types and request dedicated support or a guaranteed alternate from the Eastern Shore.

[P33] Eastern Region commenters will ask for clarification on the composition and boundaries of the “Eastern Region” unit (Connecticut, Florida, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Vermont, West Virginia, DC, and Puerto Rico) and challenge grouping such geographically and culturally disparate areas into a single one-member unit.

[P33] Puerto Rican agricultural advocates will strongly object to being grouped with distant Northeastern states and argue that one seat shared among those jurisdictions will fail to represent Puerto Rico’s unique production systems and legal status; they will request a separate seat or a different grouping.

[P33] Florida producers will oppose being grouped into the Eastern Region with New England states and Puerto Rico for a single member because Florida’s producer population is large and distinct, arguing this grouping dilutes their representation.

[P33] Legal experts will question the legitimacy of grouping a territory (Puerto Rico) and the District of Columbia together with disparate states into a single one-member unit without a clear statutory basis and will request reconsideration or legal justification.

[P33] Commenters will request that the rule explain how nominations will be solicited across the Eastern Region, how seat allocation among the included jurisdictions will be decided, and whether rotation or proportional nomination will be used.

[P34] Western Region stakeholders will challenge the aggregation of 13 large and diverse states (including California, Washington, and Alaska) into a single one-member unit, arguing this dramatically underrepresents Western producers and conflicts with statutory fairness requirements.

[P34] California agricultural organizations will file strong objections that California — with a substantial share of national specialty crop production — being collapsed into a single seat shared with other Western states is grossly disproportionate and unacceptable.

[P34] Alaska and Hawaii commenters will argue that including their unique production systems in a single Western unit with one seat ignores logistical and cultural differences and will request individual representation or a different grouping.

[P34] Commenters will request that the rule specify how nominees will be selected from within the expansive Western Region, whether rotational representation among the included states is required, and how conflicts among states will be resolved.

[P3/P34] Several legal and procedural commenters will demand publication of paragraphs (d) and (e) and an explanation of whether those paragraphs allow the Secretary to reallocate seats from single-member multi-state regions (Eastern/Western) to populous states — if such unilateral reallocation is contemplated, commenters will argue it must be subject to notice-and-comment.

[P2/P1] Civil rights and small-farm advocacy groups will comment that the unit-based seat allocations should be accompanied by demographic and socioeconomic analyses demonstrating they do not dilute minority, limited-resource, or socially disadvantaged producers’ representation.

[P1/P2] Commenters representing large commodity groups will request that allocation instead be based on objective criteria (e.g., number of producers, total production volume, acreage) with the methodology published, to avoid perceived political gerrymandering.

[P25–P34] Multiple state governments (especially Texas, California, Florida, New York) will submit claims that their single- or few-seat allocations raise federalism concerns and request consultations with state agriculture departments before finalizing seat numbers.

[P1] Procedural commenters will ask for transitional provisions describing how current Board members’ terms, staggering, and replacements will be handled after implementing the new 31-unit structure.

[P2] Transparency advocates will request that the agency publish a map and data table showing each geographic unit’s boundaries, the producer counts within each unit, and the math used to convert those counts into seat assignments.

[P3] Administrative law attorneys will assert that undefined qualifications in paragraphs (d) and (e) create vagueness that's reviewable under the Administrative Procedure Act and request that the agency define or incorporate those paragraphs directly into the notice for comment.

[P34] Western states’ producer cooperatives will request that the single Western seat be split into multiple seats (e.g., Pacific, Mountain, and Non-contiguous states) to adequately cover differences in production systems and distance.

[P33/P34] Commenters will propose alternative unit groupings or a population-weighted formula as a remedy — for example, reallocating seats to ensure no multi-state region has fewer than three representatives if it contains multiple large-state populations.

[P1/P2] Several commenters will request that the final rule include an appeals or dispute-resolution process for contested nominations or perceived malapportionment under the new 31-unit scheme.

[P2] Finally, academics and policy analysts will recommend a quantitative equity test (e.g., seats per 1,000 producers) and require the agency to demonstrate that the proposed allocations meet that standard before finalizing the rule.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The rule’s division of the United States into exactly 31 geographic units for nominating and appointing producers lacks any stated statutory or empirical basis and appears arbitrary; commenters should request justification and the methodology used to determine 31 units.

Industry stakeholders will likely comment that using rigid geographic units instead of producer population or production volume data will distort representation and not reflect where most producers are located.

Agricultural producer associations will request that the rule include a mechanism for periodic review and adjustment of the 31 geographic units to account for demographic or market changes (e.g., every 5 years).

Several commenters will argue that the list-based assignment of Board membership by unit (the per-unit numbers) must be accompanied by the total Board size, quorum, and term limits; as drafted, the rule provides numbers but not governance detail, creating uncertainty about overall Board composition.

Legal experts may assert the rule should include a cross-check ensuring that the sum of members assigned across the listed units complies with any statutory cap on Board size; they will request an explicit total and citation to authorizing statute.

Procedural fairness advocates will contend that qualifying the assignment by paragraphs (d) and (e) without including those paragraphs in the public notice prevents meaningful comment on how the qualifications might alter the stated allocations; they will request publication of paragraphs (d) and (e) or an explanation of how they operate.

Commenters will request clarity on whether paragraphs (d) and (e) permit reallocation of seats among units based on census or production changes, and whether such reallocation requires a separate rulemaking or notice-and-comment.

South Dakota producers will challenge the assignment of 4 Board members as either insufficient or disproportionate depending on their state's producer population; they will request the data used to justify 4 seats and an equity analysis comparing seats per producer across states.
Ohio agricultural groups may argue that four seats do not reflect the state’s producer concentration and will request either additional seats or a formulaic adjustment tied to production metrics.

North Dakota producers are likely to submit a claim that assigning 4 members to North Dakota over-represents its producers relative to larger states, and they will request transparency on the allocation criteria.
Nebraska stakeholders will question why Nebraska receives 4 seats and will ask for data showing parity (e.g., seats per producer or per acreage) with other Midwestern states.
Missouri commenters may request assurance that the 4-member allocation will not dilute minority or small-producer voices within the state and ask for minority representation safeguards.
Minnesota organizations will request justification for 4 seats and ask whether alternatives (e.g., weighted voting or proportional representation) were considered.
Iowa producers will challenge the 4-member assignment if it conflicts with the statutory requirement to ensure fair representation of producers nationwide, asking for a proportionality analysis.
Indiana stakeholders will request detail on how nominations will be conducted within the state to ensure the 4 slots are competitively filled and representative of farm sizes and commodity types.
Illinois commenters will ask whether the 4-seat allocation accounts for the state’s large producer population, and if not, they will recommend a reallocation to prevent underrepresentation.
Wisconsin producers may assert that receiving 3 seats (instead of 4 like neighboring states) will marginalize the state’s producers and request an explanation for the lower allocation.
Tennessee groups will ask whether 3 seats adequately represent the state’s diverse agricultural sectors and request criteria for intra-state seat distribution (e.g., by region or commodity).
Mississippi stakeholders will express concern that 3 seats are insufficient to represent both large commercial and small diversified producers and ask for measures to ensure smallholder inclusion.
Michigan commenters will request the data supporting Michigan’s 3 seats and propose that Great Lakes regional issues require additional representation.
Kentucky organizations will ask whether the allocation accounts for specialty crop producers and request protection of niche producer representation among the 3 seats.
Kansas producers will question the 3-seat allocation relative to Kansas’ production of certain commodities (e.g., wheat, sorghum) and request an allocation tied to commodity output.
Arkansas commenters will request justification for 3 seats and propose safeguards to ensure equitable selection between row-crop and specialty-crop producers.

Virginia stakeholders will challenge the assignment of only 2 seats given the state’s agricultural diversity and proximity to major markets; they will request either additional seats or dedicated representation for certain producer classes.

Pennsylvania agricultural groups will argue that two seats will not allow adequate representation for both small family farms and larger operations and will request that one seat be reserved for small/limited-resource producers.

North Carolina commenters will request that the two seats reflect the state’s varied production (tobacco, poultry, greenhouse) and propose rule language requiring diversity of commodity representation among nominees.
Maryland stakeholders will seek clarification whether the two seats include representation from the Eastern Shore and urban agriculture producers, asking for guidance on nomination procedures.

Louisiana producers will submit comments asserting that two seats may not account for unique coastal or aquaculture producers and will request seat allocation or nomination guidance to ensure those interests are represented.

Alabama commenters will object to being assigned only one seat and argue that a single Board member cannot adequately represent the state’s geographic and commodity diversity, urging alternative mechanisms (e.g., regional alternates).

Texas stakeholders will strongly object to assignment of only 1 seat for Texas, the second-largest agricultural state by production and acreage, arguing this is grossly underrepresentative and likely violates the statutory requirement for equitable producer representation.

South Carolina producers will assert that a single seat is insufficient and ask for criteria that would enable additional seats if producer counts increase or to allow at-large members to represent the state’s interests.

Oklahoma commenters will request justification for only one seat given the state’s significant production in specific commodities (e.g., wheat, cattle), and propose combining Oklahoma with adjacent units rather than a single-seat allocation.
New York stakeholders will state that one seat cannot represent upstate and downstate agricultural interests and will ask for sub-state nomination procedures to ensure geographic balance.

New Jersey producers will highlight the diversity of specialty and urban agriculture in the state and argue that one member cannot represent these varied interests; they will request alternative representation mechanisms.

Georgia commenters will object to one seat and request that the rule include mechanisms for appointing alternates or at-large Board members to ensure broader representation for major commodities like poultry, peanuts, and peaches.

Delaware stakeholders will express concern that a single member will be overwhelmed by representing multiple producer types and request dedicated support or a guaranteed alternate from the Eastern Shore.

Puerto Rican agricultural advocates will strongly object to being grouped with distant Northeastern states and argue that one seat shared among those jurisdictions will fail to represent Puerto Rico’s unique production systems and legal status; they will request a separate seat or a different grouping.

Florida producers will oppose being grouped into the Eastern Region with New England states and Puerto Rico for a single member because Florida’s producer population is large and distinct, arguing this grouping dilutes their representation.

Legal experts will question the legitimacy of grouping a territory (Puerto Rico) and the District of Columbia together with disparate states into a single one-member unit without a clear statutory basis and will request reconsideration or legal justification.

Commenters will request that the rule explain how nominations will be solicited across the Eastern Region, how seat allocation among the included jurisdictions will be decided, and whether rotation or proportional nomination will be used.

Alaska and Hawaii commenters will argue that including their unique production systems in a single Western unit with one seat ignores logistical and cultural differences and will request individual representation or a different grouping.

raw_output:
[P1] The April 2–June 30 subsistence season in the Northern Unit is too short for communities that rely on spring harvests; we request extending the start date to April 1 and the end date to July 7 to accommodate local harvest practices and travel conditions.

[P1] Industry (commercial guiding) comment: The Northern Unit season dates overlap with customary guiding operations; the rule must clarify whether licensed guides transporting subsistence hunters are authorized to operate during April 2–June 30 without additional permits.

[P2] Residents of the Northern Unit will be disproportionately harmed by the complete closure July 1–August 31 because many households depend on late-summer harvesting—request an exemption for eelgrass/shorebird egg gathering for personal use.

[P3] For the Central Unit, the split season (April 2–June 15 and July 16–August 31) fails to account for interannual variation in migration; commenters request a mechanism to shift the June 15 and July 16 dates by +/- 7 days based on biological indicators.

[P3] Legal expert: The Central Unit's listed dates are ambiguous as written; please specify whether inclusive dates mean harvest is allowed on June 15 and July 16 or whether closure begins at midnight—clarify time-of-day conventions.

[P4] Conservation group: The June 16–July 15 closure in the Central Unit is too short to protect nesting birds; recommend extending to July 31 for listed sensitive species, or at minimum adding a mandatory review of nest success data before reopening.

[P5] Local subsistence users around Izembek and Moffet lagoons: The August 16–31 Black Brant prohibition is arbitrary and restricts traditional late-August harvests; request exemption for tribal members with documented customary use.

[P5] Wetlands advocacy group: The targeted Black Brant closure in Izembek/Moffet lagoons is appropriate but needs signage and outreach to prevent inadvertent violations; require funding for on-the-ground outreach.

[P6] Hunters in Game Management Units 9(D) and 10: The absolute prohibition on tundra swan hunting and egg gathering lacks a process for emergency short-term harvest if swan populations recover; request trigger criteria and timeline for reopening.

[P6] Indigenous rights group: The blanket ban in Units 9(D) and 10 fails to accommodate cultural uses; request a limited ceremonial exception allowing egg gathering under tribal oversight.

[P7] For the Western Unit, the April 2–July 15 and August 16–August 31 seasons leave a one-month mid-summer closure—request clarification whether harvest on July 15 and August 16 is allowed and whether time zone considerations could affect those dates.

[P8] Western Unit commercial fisheries: The July 16–August 15 closure may conflict with peak fishing seasons and could increase wildlife depredation on gear; suggest coordinating closure dates with State fisheries managers.

[P9] Yukon/Kuskokwim Delta Region season April 2–August 31 is permissive but too broad given variable nest timings; conservation groups request seasonal staging points based on species-specific data rather than a single long season.

[P10] The obligation for the Regional Director to announce 30-day closure dates after consultation lacks a deadline—commenters request a fixed timeline (e.g., consultations completed and closure announced at least 14 days before effective date).

[P10] Procedural fairness: The consultation requirement for closure date announcements names field biologists but does not require tribal or community consultation; request mandatory consultation with affected villages and tribal councils before setting the 30-day closure window.

[P11] Media/communications groups: Requiring only forwarding a press release to regional newspapers, radio, and TV is insufficient—request using social media, local tribal channels, community bulletin boards, and dissemination in native languages.

[P12] The broad prohibition on hunting Black Brant and Cackling Canada Goose from egg laying until fledging is vague because "when egg laying begins" varies yearly; request that the rule define biological triggers and require public notice of the start date.

[P13] The obligation that the Director announce special closure dates after consultation with the Association is unclear as to which Association—request the rule identify full legal names and include a requirement to publish consultation minutes.

[P14] Requiring a press release alone for special closure dates is inadequate for remote communities—request funding and procedures for direct notification to village councils and posting at community stores and clinics.

[P15] Bristol Bay general season and seabird egg gathering dates (April 2–June 14 / July 16–August 31; eggs April 2–July 15) create overlapping and conflicting periods—commenters ask for a consolidated table and clear cross-references so users understand allowed activities on each date.

[P16] The Bristol Bay closures (June 15–July 15 general; July 16–August 31 seabird eggs) effectively ban seabird egg gathering during high egg availability—egg gatherers request the seabird egg gathering allowance be extended through July 31.

[P17] Stebbins/St. Michael Area season April 15–June 14 and July 16–August 31 excludes early-April spring hunts—local residents request opening April 1 to accommodate travel constraints and traditional calendars.

[P18] The June 15–July 15 closure for Stebbins/St. Michael fails to consider community subsistence cereals and staging—request an exemption for capture of molting/non-nesting waterfowl essential to some households.

[P19] The remainder-of-region scheme allowing waterfowl April 2–June 14 and July 16–August 31, but other birds April 2–July 19 and August 21–August 31, is confusing—request graphical calendar and examples to avoid enforcement mistakes.

[P20] The closures for waterfowl June 15–July 15 and other birds July 20–August 20 create two different closed intervals; enforcement officers may need species identification training—request mandatory training and distribution of ID guides to subsistence hunters.

[P21] Kodiak Island roaded area closure to harvesting migratory birds and eggs should be justified with data; commercial interests and Sportsmen groups request the biological rationale and impact study on local food security.

[P22] Closing marine waters within 500 feet of the water's edge adjacent to the Kodiak closed area could criminalize customary nearshore harvests—request narrowing buffer distance or exempting traditional shore-based harvest methods.

[P23] Offshore islands allowed to be open to harvest need clear access rules—commenters request clarification on whether motorized landing, permits, or seasonal restrictions apply for small boats landing on islands.

[P24] Kodiak Archipelago season dates for seabirds (April 2–June 30, July 31–August 31) and other birds have a 30-day seabird closure July 1–30—egg gatherers request an exception for Indigenous ceremonial needs between July 1–15.

[P25] The stated Kodiak closures (July 1–30 seabirds; June 21–July 21 other birds) overlap with tourism seasons; guide operators request clarity on liability and permitted guiding activities during closures.

[P26] Paragraph (f)(1) permitting various activities including seabird egg gathering May 20–July 12 lacks specified limits (bag limits, colony quotas); resource managers request numeric limits to prevent overharvest.

[P27] The general prohibition June 15–July 15 but exception for seabird eggs and molting/non-nesting waterfowl could be abused; enforcement agencies request criteria and documentation required to demonstrate a waterfowl is molting/non-nesting.

[P28] Allowing seabird egg gathering and molting/non-nesting waterfowl taking during closures is too permissive unless strict safeguards (seasonal quotas, species lists) are included—request that exceptions be limited to specified species and quantities.

[P29] Southern Unit seabird and other bird seasons have different start/end dates producing overlapping windows—communities need a single consolidated seasonal schedule to prevent inadvertent violations.

[P30] The Southern Unit closures (June 30–July 29 for seabirds; June 20–July 19 for other birds) will prevent customary harvests tied to family ceremonies—request a small number of permits for ceremonial subsistence uses.

[P31] The special Black Brant opening June 20–July 5 in the coastal area is too short for customary harvests and lacks clear mapping of the "open area"—request GIS maps and coordinates and a waiver for elders.

[P31] Environmental groups: Opening a coastal swath to Black Brant hunting June 20–July 5 risks disturbing staging flocks; recommend narrowing the open area to exclude high-density stopover sites and require buffer zones around colonies.

[P32] Northern Unit eider seasons (April 2–June 6 and July 7–August 31 for king/common eiders) differ from "all other birds" dates—request an explanation and species-specific harvest limits given conservation concerns for eiders.

[P33] The prohibition on king and common eiders June 7–July 6 is appropriate, but enforcement in remote areas is difficult—request increased funding for patrols and community-based monitoring programs.

[P34] Eastern Unit season April 2–June 19 and July 20–August 31 with closure June 20–July 19 fails to address climate-driven shifts in nesting; request adaptive management language allowing date changes when monitoring indicates shifts.

[P35] The Eastern Unit closure June 20–July 19 should be accompanied by compensation or alternative food support programs for communities relying on that period.

[P36] Allowing up to 20 yellow-billed loons annually to be kept if inadvertently entangled in nets is ambiguous on reporting: require immediate reporting to Service and community quotas be tracked transparently; request that the 20-loon cap be regional and annually audited.

[P37] The prohibition on possession of birds taken in violation of subparts C and D at any time may criminalize inadvertent possession (e.g., heirloom specimens); legal commenters ask for a de minimis exception for museum specimens or accidental possession with immediate reporting.

[P38] The obligation to present birds to Service law enforcement for species identification on request must be accompanied by protections for hunters' rights and privacy; request a warrant/administrative standard and prohibition on seizure absent probable cause.

[P39] Interior Region seasons and egg gathering dates (April 2–June 14 and July 16–August 31; egg gathering May 1–June 14) need clarification on collection limits per household and whether juveniles may gather eggs under adult supervision.

[P40] The Interior Region closure June 15–July 15 may disproportionately affect subsistence harvesters who travel during that period for other subsistence activities; request cross-season coordination and grandfathering for traditional harvests.

[P41] Upper Copper River Region season April 15–May 26 and June 27–August 31 with closure May 27–June 26 will create a 31-day interruption during migration—request data justifying the specific closure dates vis-à-vis nesting timings.

[P42] The closure May 27–June 26 in Upper Copper River could conflict with State hunting seasons—request harmonization language to minimize legal confusion and citizen risk of inadvertent violation.

[P43] Authorizing specified Copper River Basin communities to hunt in Unit 12 using paragraph (h) seasons should require a documented list and process for adding/removing communities; request criteria, notice, and appeal rights.

[P44] Prince William Sound Area West season April 2–May 31 and July 1–August 31 with June 1–30 closure is unusual—commenters request explanation and assessment of effects on migrating shorebirds.

[P45] The June closure in Prince William Sound Area West could concentrate hunting pressure before and after closure dates; request measures to avoid overharvest at closure boundaries, such as staggered openings.

[P46] Prince William Sound Area East restrictions separating hunting in April and gull egg gathering in May create enforcement complexity—request a consolidated permit covering both activities and clear signage at landing sites.

[P47] The Prince William Sound Area East closure periods (May 1–August 31 hunting; April 2–30 and June 1–August 31 gull egg gathering) effectively prohibit gull egg gathering most of the season—request justification and an allowance for tribal ceremonial uses in May.

[P48] The species list in § 92.31(j)(2)(iii) should be accompanied by a prohibited species list and current scientific names to avoid misinterpretation; request inclusion of Latin names and allowable bag limits per species.

[P49] The prohibition on hunting from motorized vehicles and any form of watercraft in the Prince William Sound East area may hinder safe transport for elderly harvesters who rely on boat-based access; request an exception for transport to/from permitted shore-based harvest sites.

[P50] Requiring an annual permit obtained from specific Cordova offices could be infeasible for remote residents; request online application, mailed permits, or local distribution through tribal offices and include a waiver for lack of access.

[P51] Kachemak Bay season dates (April 2–May 31; July 1–August 31) and June closure may not reflect migratory patterns—request species-specific rationale and consideration of shoreline access limits.

[P52] The June 1–30 closure in Kachemak Bay could conflict with commercial salmon operations and increase human-wildlife conflict; request coordination with fisheries managers.

[P53] Game Management Unit 16(B) limited seasons for specified portions should be accompanied by precise boundary coordinates (Skwentna River/Yentna River references are vague) and maps to avoid prosecution of well-meaning hunters.

[P54] The June 1–July 31 closure in parts of Unit 16(B) is a long window—request a temporary exception for molting geese and non-nesting waterfowl with community reporting requirements.

[P55] Hoonah glaucous-winged gull egg gathering May 15–June 30 is acceptable to local residents but enforcement must allow for customary collection techniques; request exemption from certain gear restrictions.

[P56] The July 1–August 31 prohibition in Hoonah may block community ceremonial needs; request a small number of permits for traditional feasts.

[P57] Craig and Hydaburg egg gathering May 15–June 30: request clarity whether commercial sale of gathered eggs is prohibited and penalties for inadvertent sale.

[P58] The July 1–August 31 closure in Craig and Hydaburg lacks flexibility for years with late nesting—request adaptive-opening language tied to nest monitoring.

[P59] Yakutat egg gathering season May 15–June 30 should include language allowing elders and persons with documented customary use to gather slightly earlier if weather delays would otherwise prevent safe access.

[P60] The July 1–August 31 Yakutat closure again raises concerns about lack of ceremonial exemptions—request narrowly tailored exceptions for documented traditional events.

[P61] Section 92.32 gives the Regional Director broad emergency authority to act upon an "imminent threat" to Steller’s eiders without defined thresholds—request clear biological criteria (e.g., x% decline in nesting success or population) and mandatory publication of the data supporting the finding.

[P62] The range of regulatory responses in § 92.32 (from small closures to statewide bans) is too open-ended; legal commenters request a required Environmental Assessment or EA/ EIS-level review before large-scale long-term closures are implemented, except in true emergencies with post-hoc review.

[P63] Leaving closures in effect until the Regional Director determines the risk no longer exists could create indefinite de facto restrictions without oversight—request mandatory periodic review intervals (e.g., every 90 days) and requirement to publish the scientific basis for continued closure.

[P36] The yellow-billed loon provision allowing up to 20 kept annually must specify who counts and how incidental takes must be reported (e.g., immediate notification to Service, mark/tag requirement); request reporting timeline and penalties for exceeding 20.

[P37] The absolute prohibition on possession of illegally taken migratory birds could criminalize family heirlooms or scientific specimens—request narrow safe-harbor for museum specimens with documentation and a process to regularize possession.

[P38] Hunters should be protected from arbitrary demands: presenting birds to Service law enforcement on request should be limited to reasonable suspicion or specific enforcement windows; request that compliance not be used for unrelated searches and require documentation of the request.

[P26] The dates for seabird egg gathering (e.g., May 20–July 12 in (f)(1)) do not specify colony-specific quotas or methods; request that the rule require colony stewardship plans developed with local communities before opening egg collection.

[P28] The exception in (f) for molting/non-nesting waterfowl needs a scientific definition of "molting/non-nesting" and a requirement that harvesters demonstrate these conditions (e.g., photographic record or inspection) to prevent misreporting.

[P11] The press release dissemination requirement should include translations into regional Indigenous languages and indigenous-run radio stations; request mandatory translation and distribution budgets.

[P50] The annual permit requirement in Prince William Sound East should include a fee waiver for low-income subsistence users—request explicit fee waiver language and alternate permit pickup locations.

[P31] For the Black Brant special opening in the Southern Unit, commenters request seasonal buffers around key drainages (Chinitna, Tuxedni, McArthur Rivers) to be precisely mapped and enforced to protect nesting waterfowl.

[P24] Kodiak Archipelago timelines should clarify whether "seabirds" includes all auklets and puffins—request species-specific lists, since some species are more vulnerable and may need longer closures.

[P21] Kodiak roaded area prohibition: request an exception for licensed research and authorized cultural harvests with prior notice to the Regional Director to ensure ongoing scientific work and cultural practices are not impeded.

Closing marine waters within 500 feet of the water's edge adjacent to the Kodiak closed area could criminalize customary nearshore harvests—request narrowing buffer distance or exempting traditional shore-based harvest methods.

Offshore islands allowed to be open to harvest need clear access rules—commenters request clarification on whether motorized landing, permits, or seasonal restrictions apply for small boats landing on islands.

Kodiak Archipelago season dates for seabirds (April 2–June 30, July 31–August 31) and other birds have a 30-day seabird closure July 1–30—egg gatherers request an exception for Indigenous ceremonial needs between July 1–15.

The stated Kodiak closures (July 1–30 seabirds; June 21–July 21 other birds) overlap with tourism seasons; guide operators request clarity on liability and permitted guiding activities during closures.

Paragraph (f)(1) permitting various activities including seabird egg gathering May 20–July 12 lacks specified limits (bag limits, colony quotas); resource managers request numeric limits to prevent overharvest.

The general prohibition June 15–July 15 but exception for seabird eggs and molting/non-nesting waterfowl could be abused; enforcement agencies request criteria and documentation required to demonstrate a waterfowl is molting/non-nesting.

Allowing seabird egg gathering and molting/non-nesting waterfowl taking during closures is too permissive unless strict safeguards (seasonal quotas, species lists) are included—request that exceptions be limited to specified species and quantities.
Southern Unit seabird and other bird seasons have different start/end dates producing overlapping windows—communities need a single consolidated seasonal schedule to prevent inadvertent violations.

The Southern Unit closures (June 30–July 29 for seabirds; June 20–July 19 for other birds) will prevent customary harvests tied to family ceremonies—request a small number of permits for ceremonial subsistence uses.

The special Black Brant opening June 20–July 5 in the coastal area is too short for customary harvests and lacks clear mapping of the "open area"—request GIS maps and coordinates and a waiver for elders.

Environmental groups: Opening a coastal swath to Black Brant hunting June 20–July 5 risks disturbing staging flocks; recommend narrowing the open area to exclude high-density stopover sites and require buffer zones around colonies.

Northern Unit eider seasons (April 2–June 6 and July 7–August 31 for king/common eiders) differ from "all other birds" dates—request an explanation and species-specific harvest limits given conservation concerns for eiders.
The prohibition on king and common eiders June 7–July 6 is appropriate, but enforcement in remote areas is difficult—request increased funding for patrols and community-based monitoring programs.

Eastern Unit season April 2–June 19 and July 20–August 31 with closure June 20–July 19 fails to address climate-driven shifts in nesting; request adaptive management language allowing date changes when monitoring indicates shifts.
The Eastern Unit closure June 20–July 19 should be accompanied by compensation or alternative food support programs for communities relying on that period.

Allowing up to 20 yellow-billed loons annually to be kept if inadvertently entangled in nets is ambiguous on reporting: require immediate reporting to Service and community quotas be tracked transparently; request that the 20-loon cap be regional and annually audited.

The prohibition on possession of birds taken in violation of subparts C and D at any time may criminalize inadvertent possession (e.g., heirloom specimens); legal commenters ask for a de minimis exception for museum specimens or accidental possession with immediate reporting.

The obligation to present birds to Service law enforcement for species identification on request must be accompanied by protections for hunters' rights and privacy; request a warrant/administrative standard and prohibition on seizure absent probable cause.

Interior Region seasons and egg gathering dates (April 2–June 14 and July 16–August 31; egg gathering May 1–June 14) need clarification on collection limits per household and whether juveniles may gather eggs under adult supervision.

The Interior Region closure June 15–July 15 may disproportionately affect subsistence harvesters who travel during that period for other subsistence activities; request cross-season coordination and grandfathering for traditional harvests.

Upper Copper River Region season April 15–May 26 and June 27–August 31 with closure May 27–June 26 will create a 31-day interruption during migration—request data justifying the specific closure dates vis-à-vis nesting timings.
The closure May 27–June 26 in Upper Copper River could conflict with State hunting seasons—request harmonization language to minimize legal confusion and citizen risk of inadvertent violation.

Authorizing specified Copper River Basin communities to hunt in Unit 12 using paragraph (h) seasons should require a documented list and process for adding/removing communities; request criteria, notice, and appeal rights.
Prince William Sound Area West season April 2–May 31 and July 1–August 31 with June 1–30 closure is unusual—commenters request explanation and assessment of effects on migrating shorebirds.

The June closure in Prince William Sound Area West could concentrate hunting pressure before and after closure dates; request measures to avoid overharvest at closure boundaries, such as staggered openings.

Prince William Sound Area East restrictions separating hunting in April and gull egg gathering in May create enforcement complexity—request a consolidated permit covering both activities and clear signage at landing sites.

The Prince William Sound Area East closure periods (May 1–August 31 hunting; April 2–30 and June 1–August 31 gull egg gathering) effectively prohibit gull egg gathering most of the season—request justification and an allowance for tribal ceremonial uses in May.

The species list in § 92.31(j)(2)(iii) should be accompanied by a prohibited species list and current scientific names to avoid misinterpretation; request inclusion of Latin names and allowable bag limits per species.

The prohibition on hunting from motorized vehicles and any form of watercraft in the Prince William Sound East area may hinder safe transport for elderly harvesters who rely on boat-based access; request an exception for transport to/from permitted shore-based harvest sites.

Requiring an annual permit obtained from specific Cordova offices could be infeasible for remote residents; request online application, mailed permits, or local distribution through tribal offices and include a waiver for lack of access.
Kachemak Bay season dates (April 2–May 31; July 1–August 31) and June closure may not reflect migratory patterns—request species-specific rationale and consideration of shoreline access limits.
The June 1–30 closure in Kachemak Bay could conflict with commercial salmon operations and increase human-wildlife conflict; request coordination with fisheries managers.

Game Management Unit 16(B) limited seasons for specified portions should be accompanied by precise boundary coordinates (Skwentna River/Yentna River references are vague) and maps to avoid prosecution of well-meaning hunters.
The June 1–July 31 closure in parts of Unit 16(B) is a long window—request a temporary exception for molting geese and non-nesting waterfowl with community reporting requirements.

Hoonah glaucous-winged gull egg gathering May 15–June 30 is acceptable to local residents but enforcement must allow for customary collection techniques; request exemption from certain gear restrictions.
The July 1–August 31 prohibition in Hoonah may block community ceremonial needs; request a small number of permits for traditional feasts.
Craig and Hydaburg egg gathering May 15–June 30: request clarity whether commercial sale of gathered eggs is prohibited and penalties for inadvertent sale.
The July 1–August 31 closure in Craig and Hydaburg lacks flexibility for years with late nesting—request adaptive-opening language tied to nest monitoring.

Yakutat egg gathering season May 15–June 30 should include language allowing elders and persons with documented customary use to gather slightly earlier if weather delays would otherwise prevent safe access.
The July 1–August 31 Yakutat closure again raises concerns about lack of ceremonial exemptions—request narrowly tailored exceptions for documented traditional events.

Section 92.32 gives the Regional Director broad emergency authority to act upon an "imminent threat" to Steller’s eiders without defined thresholds—request clear biological criteria (e.g., x% decline in nesting success or population) and mandatory publication of the data supporting the finding.

The range of regulatory responses in § 92.32 (from small closures to statewide bans) is too open-ended; legal commenters request a required Environmental Assessment or EA/ EIS-level review before large-scale long-term closures are implemented, except in true emergencies with post-hoc review.

Leaving closures in effect until the Regional Director determines the risk no longer exists could create indefinite de facto restrictions without oversight—request mandatory periodic review intervals (e.g., every 90 days) and requirement to publish the scientific basis for continued closure.

The yellow-billed loon provision allowing up to 20 kept annually must specify who counts and how incidental takes must be reported (e.g., immediate notification to Service, mark/tag requirement); request reporting timeline and penalties for exceeding 20.

The absolute prohibition on possession of illegally taken migratory birds could criminalize family heirlooms or scientific specimens—request narrow safe-harbor for museum specimens with documentation and a process to regularize possession.

Hunters should be protected from arbitrary demands: presenting birds to Service law enforcement on request should be limited to reasonable suspicion or specific enforcement windows; request that compliance not be used for unrelated searches and require documentation of the request.

The dates for seabird egg gathering (e.g., May 20–July 12 in (f)(1)) do not specify colony-specific quotas or methods; request that the rule require colony stewardship plans developed with local communities before opening egg collection.

The exception in (f) for molting/non-nesting waterfowl needs a scientific definition of "molting/non-nesting" and a requirement that harvesters demonstrate these conditions (e.g., photographic record or inspection) to prevent misreporting.
The press release dissemination requirement should include translations into regional Indigenous languages and indigenous-run radio stations; request mandatory translation and distribution budgets.
The annual permit requirement in Prince William Sound East should include a fee waiver for low-income subsistence users—request explicit fee waiver language and alternate permit pickup locations.

For the Black Brant special opening in the Southern Unit, commenters request seasonal buffers around key drainages (Chinitna, Tuxedni, McArthur Rivers) to be precisely mapped and enforced to protect nesting waterfowl.
Kodiak Archipelago timelines should clarify whether "seabirds" includes all auklets and puffins—request species-specific lists, since some species are more vulnerable and may need longer closures.

Kodiak roaded area prohibition: request an exception for licensed research and authorized cultural harvests with prior notice to the Regional Director to ensure ongoing scientific work and cultural practices are not impeded.
