raw_output:
[P1] The prohibition on disturbing or diluting media prior to characterization sampling (§761.3) is infeasible for many field sites where contamination is intermingled with debris or saturated soils that require removal to access representative samples; EPA should allow limited, documented disturbance under QA/QC procedures.

[P1] The as-found concentration rule should clarify whether standard construction activities (e.g., trenching for utilities) that unintentionally disturb media before sampling are considered violations or whether an after-the-fact characterization procedure is acceptable.

[P2] Requiring burners to burn used oil only in combustion facilities identified in §761.20(e)(1) and to identify the burner class is overly prescriptive and will limit legitimate small-scale burners (e.g., small industrial boilers) from accepting used oil; EPA should add an approval pathway for additional burner types.

[P2] The provision lacks detail on how burners should "identify the class of burner" (format, timing, record retention); industry requests standardized forms and retention periods aligned with 40 CFR Part 279 records to ensure enforceability and compliance.

[P3] Mandating that marketers include copies of analyses/documentation and certification notices in 40 CFR 279.72(b) and 279.74(b) records creates duplicative recordkeeping not contemplated under Part 279; EPA should harmonize recordkeeping requirements between Parts 761 and 279 to avoid conflicting obligations.

[P3] The rule should specify acceptable analytical detection limits and laboratory accreditation for the "no detectable PCBs" certification to prevent marketers from relying on non-validated low-sensitivity methods and to ensure consistency across suppliers.

[P4] Burners being required to keep copies of certification notices in 40 CFR 279.65 and 279.66 records imposes extra administrative burden without clear benefit; EPA should permit electronic retention and transmission consistent with Part 279 e-record provisions.

[P5] Requiring characterization of PCB contamination in natural gas pipelines by analyzing organic liquids from existing condensate collection points (§761.30(i)(4)) will not be protective where condensate points are infrequent or absent; EPA should allow alternative sampling locations or procedures (e.g., internal swabs or pigging samples).

[P5] The provision does not specify minimum sample volumes, preservation, or handling procedures for condensate-derived organic liquids, risking inconsistent and non-representative analyses; EPA should add detailed sampling and QA/QC requirements.

[P6] Requiring characterization of multi-phasic liquids to follow §761.1(b)(4) is ambiguous because §761.1(b)(4) may not address modern multi-phase sampling techniques; EPA should explicitly state methodologies for phase separation, homogeneity determination, and analyte partitioning.

[P7] Allowing characterization without liquids via standard wipe samples per subpart M when no liquids are present is acceptable only if wipe sampling detection limits and solvent/contact area are defined; otherwise it may under-detect PCBs on complex surfaces (e.g., porous metal, braided insulation).

[P8] Granting the Regional Administrator authority to require owners/operators to generate data to characterize risk (§761.50(b)(3)(i)(A)) is appropriate, but EPA should include timelines and limits on data requests to prevent open-ended demands that could be used to delay site closure.

[P9] The provision giving EPA authority to direct disposal per §761.61 upon finding an unreasonable risk lacks an objective risk threshold or criteria for "unreasonable risk"; stakeholders request a clear risk-based decision framework and an opportunity for the responsible party to propose alternatives.

[P10] The obligation that persons responsible for PCB waste meeting listed date/concentration conditions must dispose according to specified options (§761.50(b)(3)(ii)) needs clarity on how "date" conditions apply to legacy wastes and what documentation proves a waste meets a listed date criterion.

[P11] The Assistant Administrator's requirement to consider impacts on incentives to construct/expand PCB incinerators (§761.60(b)(2)(v)(C)) raises anti-competitive concerns and could bias permitting decisions; EPA should avoid language that could be interpreted as favoring incinerator development and instead require neutral assessment of disposal alternatives.

[P11] The rule should define the scope of "incentives" the Assistant Administrator will consider (financial, regulatory, market), and require documentation of the rationale to ensure transparency.

[P12] Mandating gas chromatography for chemical analysis of PCBs (§761.60(g)(1)(iii)) may be restrictive for matrices better analyzed by alternative validated methods (e.g., GC-MS/MS, LC-MS) — EPA should allow validated alternative techniques that meet method performance criteria.

[P13] While permitting appropriate gas chromatographic methods (including Method 608.3 and ASTM D4059–00) is helpful, EPA must explicitly approve modern instrumental methods (e.g., EPA 1668 Revision B for Aroclors/PCB congeners) and outline acceptance criteria for method modifications.

[P14] Allowing representative samples to be taken from common containers or individual electrical equipment (§761.60(g)(2)(ii)) is practical, but the rule must specify when container-level sampling is invalid (e.g., heterogeneous mixtures, poured-in service history) to avoid underestimating concentrations.

[P15] Declaring entire container contents ≥500 ppm if PCBs ≥500 ppm have been added (§761.60(g)(2)(ii)) may unfairly penalize containers with very small volumes of contaminated fluid in large volumes of clean fluid; EPA should allow destruction or segregation options if demonstrably feasible and supported by validated mixing/homogeneity analyses.

[P16] Requiring representative samples of mineral oil dielectric fluid per ASTM D923–86/D923–89 or from a thoroughly mixed container is reasonable, but these ASTM versions are outdated; EPA should reference current ASTM standards or permit modern sampling protocols with validation.

[P17] Requiring EPA Regional Administrator to respond in writing within 30 days to notifications for self-implementing cleanup (§761.61(a)(3)(ii)) is impractically fast for complex sites; EPA should allow longer review timelines or require acknowledgement followed by substantive response within an extended period.

[P18] Allowing the notifier to proceed if EPA does not respond within 30 days (§761.61(a)(3)(ii)) could lead to inconsistent cleanups and liability uncertainty; commenters request that proceeding without EPA approval be conditioned on meeting all notification requirements and subject to subsequent EPA review and corrective action if needed.

[P19] EPA's ability to require additional information if notification lacks required information (§761.61(a)(3)(ii)) is necessary, but the rule should set timelines for EPA requests and for notifier responses to avoid indefinite holds on cleanup.

[P20] The obligation that cleanup and disposal must meet requirements in paragraphs (a)(4)–(9) (§761.61(a)(3)(ii)) should be clarified to indicate which specific technical standards (sampling frequencies, QA/QC limits) apply, as the cross-references are extensive and may be interpreted inconsistently.

[P21] Requiring 14-days' written notice of proposed changes to a self-implementing cleanup once underway (§761.61(a)(3)(ii)) may be too short for emergency modifications; allow immediate verbal notice with a subsequent written submission when changes are needed to protect health/environment.

[P22] The requirement that EPA respond verbally within 7 days and in writing within 14 days to change notifications (§761.61(a)(3)(ii)) is operationally burdensome for regional offices and may not be feasible — request more realistic timeframes or an option for deemed approval if no response within a longer period.

[P23] Allowing proceeding with changes if EPA does not respond in specified timeframes (§761.61(a)(3)(ii)) should include an explicit protection for the notifier that EPA may later require corrective measures but not retroactive penalties if the notifier acted in good faith following approved procedures.

[P24] The obligation for generators to give 15-days' written notice before first shipment to specified off-site facilities including quantity and highest concentration (§761.61(a)(5)(i)(B)(2)(iv)) is overly prescriptive and may delay time-sensitive shipments; suggest reducing to 7 days or permitting electronic pre-notification.

[P25] Requiring generators to select extraction/analysis methods from a listed set to determine PCB concentration (§761.61(a)(5)(i)(B)(2)(iv)) could prevent use of newer validated methods; allow alternative validated methods under subpart Q or explicit EPA acceptance to encourage method modernization.

[P26] The permission to use modified or alternative methods if validated under subpart Q or authorized by §761.61(c) approval (§761.61(a)(5)(i)(B)(2)(iv)) is acceptable but the validation process under subpart Q must have clear timelines and criteria to avoid protracted approvals.

[P27] Mandating caps be designed per §264.310(a) and meet permeability/material parameters in §761.75 (§761.61(a)(7)) could conflict with state or site-specific engineered cover designs that are protective but not exactly per §264.310(a); EPA should allow performance-based equivalency demonstrations.

[P28] Minimum thicknesses for compacted soil caps (25 cm) and concrete/asphalt caps (15 cm) (§761.61(a)(7)) may not be protective for all climates, subsidence-prone sites, or vehicular loading; EPA should require site-specific engineering analysis to determine appropriate thicknesses.

[P29] The obligation that caps must be strong enough to maintain integrity during normal use/exposure (§761.61(a)(7)) is vague; EPA should specify design life, load-bearing standards, and maintenance inspection frequencies.

[P30] The prohibition that caps must not have PCB contamination ≥1 ppm (§761.61(a)(7)) is strict and may render reuse of some in-situ materials impracticable; offer an option for engineered barriers with leachate controls where minor contamination can't be removed but exposure risk is controlled.

[P31] Requiring repairs to cap breaches impairing integrity to start within 72 hours of discovery (§761.61(a)(7)) may be unrealistic in remote areas or when specialized contractors are needed; allow repairs to begin within 72 hours of mobilization or require temporary measures within 72 hours and permanent repairs per agreed schedule.

[P32] The perpetual maintenance obligation for fences or caps by site owners (§761.61(a)(8)) creates onerous long-term liability and may impede property transfers; EPA should allow financial assurance, institutional control mechanisms, or liability limitation if periodic inspections and funding for maintenance are secured.

[P33] The deed notation requirement to notify future purchasers of PCB remediation use and maintenance requirements (§761.61(a)(8)(i)(A)) is reasonable, but EPA must clarify interaction with state real property laws and provide model deed language to ensure consistency and avoid litigation.

[P34] Requiring the deed notation to state the land was used for PCB remediation waste disposal and any low occupancy restrictions (§761.61(a)(8)(i)(A)(1)) could stigmatize property and reduce its marketability; EPA should permit more neutral phrasing focused on required institutional controls and maintenance obligations rather than "disposal" terminology.

[P35] Mandating deed notation to state existence and requirement to maintain fence/cap (§761.61(a)(8)(i)(A)(2)) is appropriate but should allow flexibility where maintenance obligations are shared or delegated to a third party, with EPA acceptance.

[P36] Requiring the deed notation to state applicable cleanup levels left at site and in restricted areas (§761.61(a)(8)(i)(A)(3)) risks technical complexity in public land records; EPA should allow summary statements with reference to the administrative record or a publicly accessible registry for details.

[P37] The obligation to submit signed certification to EPA that the deed notation has been recorded (§761.61(a)(8)(i)(B)) is duplicative of state recording processes; allow submission of recording instrument ID or a link to the recorded document in lieu of owner-signed certification when state systems provide verification.

[P38] The permission to remove fence/cap/low occupancy designation after additional cleanup (§761.61(a)(8)(ii)) is positive, but the rule must clarify verification procedures, acceptable evidence of cleanup levels achieved, and whether independent third-party confirmation is required.

[P39] Allowing removal of deed notice no sooner than 30 days after achieving cleanup levels (§761.61(a)(8)(ii)) is acceptable, but EPA should require a formal notice period for neighboring property owners and a public comment opportunity before deed note removal for transparency.

[P40] The performance-based cleanup and disposal provision (§761.61(b) intro) is useful, but EPA must issue clear performance metrics, QA/QC standards, and templates for documentation to ensure consistent application and protect human health.

[P41] The statement that disposal under (b)(2) does not relieve site owner obligations for remaining PCBs (§761.61(b) intro) could create ambiguous ongoing liabilities for parties that conducted discrete disposal actions; recommend defining circumstances under which liability transfers or limitations apply.

[P42] Prohibiting the performance-based cleanup option for listed site types including surface waters and sediments (§761.61(b)(1)(i)(A)-(8)) is appropriate, but the list should be precisely defined (e.g., "surface waters" includes ephemeral streams?) to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P43] The exception that performance-based cleanup provisions do not bind cleanups under other authorities (§761.61(b)(1)(ii)(B)) should state explicitly that compliance with more stringent CERCLA/RCRA/Tribal requirements suffices and that states may adopt comparable but not less stringent requirements.

[P44] The obligation that on-site PCB remediation waste exceeding cleanup levels must be disposed or decontaminated per (b)(2) (§761.61(b)(1)(ii)) needs an exception for minimal quantities where institutional controls and monitoring may be more protective and practical; allow case-by-case EPA-approved alternatives.

[P45] Setting cleanup level for bulk PCB remediation waste and porous surfaces at ≤1 ppm (§761.61(b)(1)(ii)(A)) is a major tightening from some prior practice and will substantially increase remediation costs; EPA must provide economic impact analysis and consider tiered cleanup levels based on exposure scenario.

[P45] The 1 ppm cleanup level may be technically infeasible to achieve on many porous materials (e.g., concrete, brick) without demolition; EPA should allow performance-based containment or removal thresholds combined with land-use controls.

[P46] Referring liquid cleanup levels to §761.79(b)(1) and (b)(2) (§761.61(b)(1)(ii)(B)) is fine, but those sections should be cross-checked to ensure they provide clear analytical methods, holding times, and detection limits for enforcement.

[P47] Referring nonporous surface cleanup levels to §761.79(b)(3) (§761.61(b)(1)(ii)(C)) requires that Subpart P verification sampling be realistically achievable with documented detection limits; recommend explicit wipe area, solvent, and LOD requirements.

[P48] Requiring verification sampling per Subparts O/P and §761.269 for liquids (§761.61(b)(1)(iii)) is acceptable, but EPA should allow statistically justified alternate sampling plans for heterogeneous sites, with pre-approval from the Regional Administrator.

[P49] Mandating recordkeeping per §761.125(c)(5) (§761.61(b)(1)(iv)) should specify retention periods, electronic record standards, and whether records follow the property upon transfer.

[P50] Requiring notification within 14 days of final shipment of waste offsite (§761.61(b)(1)(v)) may be too short for entities shipping multiple lots to multiple facilities; allow consolidated notifications or electronic batch reporting within 30 days.

[P51] The required notification contents (§761.61(b)(1)(v)(A)-(D)) must include clear definitions of "final shipment," "site identification information," and standardized templates to ensure consistent reporting across sites.

[P52] The obligation to dispose of liquid PCB remediation waste per §761.60(a) or (e) or decontaminate per §761.79 (§761.61(b)(2)(i)) should include explicit acceptance criteria for decontamination and end-point verification methods to avoid disputes about adequacy.

[P53] Listing disposal options for non-liquid PCB remediation waste (§761.61(b)(2)(ii)) needs cost and capacity assessment; stakeholders note limited availability of high-temperature incineration and secure landfills and request transitional provisions for disposal capacity constraints.

[P54] Allowing management/disposal of dredged/excavated material <50 ppm PCBs under CWA §404 or MPRSA §103 permits is helpful, but EPA should require coordinated review with Army Corps and Marine Protection agencies to ensure consistent environmental protections and monitoring.

[P55] Requiring written application to conduct sampling/extraction/analysis/cleanup/disposal other than prescribed (§761.61(c)(1)) is reasonable but the application process must have defined review timelines and predictable decision criteria to prevent undue delays.

[P56] The requirement that applications include notification information and that EPA may request additional information (§761.61(c)(1)) should be balanced with limits on EPA's ability to repeatedly request information to delay approvals.

[P57] Prohibiting cleanup activities under §761.61(c)(1) before written EPA approval is received could prevent timely emergency responses; EPA should allow immediate protective actions in emergencies with prompt follow-up approval.

[P58] Requiring written application to EPA to handle PCB bulk product waste differently (§761.62(c)(1)) is appropriate, but applicants should have access to pre-application consultations to reduce uncertainty.

[P59] Applicants for §761.62(c)(1) must show proposed methods/locations will not pose unreasonable risk; EPA should provide quantitative screening criteria for "unreasonable risk" to ensure consistent decisions.

[P60] Prohibiting activities under §761.62(c)(1) without prior written EPA approval is reasonable but agencies must process approvals in a timely manner; propose statutory deadlines or deemed approvals if EPA fails to respond.

[P61] Permitting use of bulk product waste as daily landfill cover provided it remains in the landfill and is not dispersed (§761.62(d)) is pragmatic, but EPA should require monitoring and institutional controls to prevent future exposure during landfill reconfiguration or closure.

[P62] Requiring piles or non-leaking covered containers designed to control wind dispersal for storage (§761.65(c)(9)(i)) is appropriate; EPA should clarify acceptable control measures beyond wetting (e.g., wind fences, tarping) and allow flexible designs for different climates.

[P63] Storage sites' liner/container requirements to prevent migration and meet construction/foundation standards (§761.65(c)(9)(iii)(A)(1)-(3)) must be harmonized with state solid waste landfill liner standards and include specific permeability and chemical compatibility criteria.

[P64] The cover requirements to meet liner standards and be secured against expected winds (§761.65(c)(9)(iii)(B)) should include guidance on design wind speeds, anchoring methods, and inspection frequency to ensure compliance.

[P65] Requiring commercial storers to establish financial assurance for closure of each PCB storage facility they own or operate (§761.65(g) intro) is appropriate, but small businesses will need scaled financial assurance options; EPA should allow alternative instruments like escrow accounts or local government guarantees.

[P66] Allowing choice among listed financial assurance mechanisms (§761.65(g)(1)) is necessary; EPA should include clear templates, minimum funding levels tied to site-specific closure cost estimates, and periodic adjustments for inflation.

[P67] Deeming trust agreements with specified wording compliant unless Regional Administrator specifies modifications (§761.65(g)(1)(iv)) is helpful but Regional Administrators must provide written notice of required modifications and justification within a fixed timeframe.

[P68] Deeming use of specified surety bonds/instruments/standby trusts compliant (§761.65(g)(2)) should not preclude acceptance of modern financial instruments (e.g., corporate guarantees backed by rated parent company or insurance products) provided they meet security standards.

[P69] The submission and use of the specified surety bond instrument and standby trust being deemed compliant (§761.65(g)(3)(i)) is acceptable, but EPA should allow updated model bond language to reflect current financial market practices and include sample clauses for assignment upon change of ownership.

The Assistant Administrator's requirement to consider impacts on incentives to construct/expand PCB incinerators (§761.60(b)(2)(v)(C)) raises anti-competitive concerns and could bias permitting decisions; EPA should avoid language that could be interpreted as favoring incinerator development and instead require neutral assessment of disposal alternatives.
The rule should define the scope of "incentives" the Assistant Administrator will consider (financial, regulatory, market), and require documentation of the rationale to ensure transparency.

Mandating gas chromatography for chemical analysis of PCBs (§761.60(g)(1)(iii)) may be restrictive for matrices better analyzed by alternative validated methods (e.g., GC-MS/MS, LC-MS) — EPA should allow validated alternative techniques that meet method performance criteria.

While permitting appropriate gas chromatographic methods (including Method 608.3 and ASTM D4059–00) is helpful, EPA must explicitly approve modern instrumental methods (e.g., EPA 1668 Revision B for Aroclors/PCB congeners) and outline acceptance criteria for method modifications.

Allowing representative samples to be taken from common containers or individual electrical equipment (§761.60(g)(2)(ii)) is practical, but the rule must specify when container-level sampling is invalid (e.g., heterogeneous mixtures, poured-in service history) to avoid underestimating concentrations.

Declaring entire container contents ≥500 ppm if PCBs ≥500 ppm have been added (§761.60(g)(2)(ii)) may unfairly penalize containers with very small volumes of contaminated fluid in large volumes of clean fluid; EPA should allow destruction or segregation options if demonstrably feasible and supported by validated mixing/homogeneity analyses.

Requiring representative samples of mineral oil dielectric fluid per ASTM D923–86/D923–89 or from a thoroughly mixed container is reasonable, but these ASTM versions are outdated; EPA should reference current ASTM standards or permit modern sampling protocols with validation.

Requiring EPA Regional Administrator to respond in writing within 30 days to notifications for self-implementing cleanup (§761.61(a)(3)(ii)) is impractically fast for complex sites; EPA should allow longer review timelines or require acknowledgement followed by substantive response within an extended period.

Allowing the notifier to proceed if EPA does not respond within 30 days (§761.61(a)(3)(ii)) could lead to inconsistent cleanups and liability uncertainty; commenters request that proceeding without EPA approval be conditioned on meeting all notification requirements and subject to subsequent EPA review and corrective action if needed.

EPA's ability to require additional information if notification lacks required information (§761.61(a)(3)(ii)) is necessary, but the rule should set timelines for EPA requests and for notifier responses to avoid indefinite holds on cleanup.

The obligation that cleanup and disposal must meet requirements in paragraphs (a)(4)–(9) (§761.61(a)(3)(ii)) should be clarified to indicate which specific technical standards (sampling frequencies, QA/QC limits) apply, as the cross-references are extensive and may be interpreted inconsistently.

Requiring 14-days' written notice of proposed changes to a self-implementing cleanup once underway (§761.61(a)(3)(ii)) may be too short for emergency modifications; allow immediate verbal notice with a subsequent written submission when changes are needed to protect health/environment.

The requirement that EPA respond verbally within 7 days and in writing within 14 days to change notifications (§761.61(a)(3)(ii)) is operationally burdensome for regional offices and may not be feasible — request more realistic timeframes or an option for deemed approval if no response within a longer period.

Allowing proceeding with changes if EPA does not respond in specified timeframes (§761.61(a)(3)(ii)) should include an explicit protection for the notifier that EPA may later require corrective measures but not retroactive penalties if the notifier acted in good faith following approved procedures.

The obligation for generators to give 15-days' written notice before first shipment to specified off-site facilities including quantity and highest concentration (§761.61(a)(5)(i)(B)(2)(iv)) is overly prescriptive and may delay time-sensitive shipments; suggest reducing to 7 days or permitting electronic pre-notification.

Requiring generators to select extraction/analysis methods from a listed set to determine PCB concentration (§761.61(a)(5)(i)(B)(2)(iv)) could prevent use of newer validated methods; allow alternative validated methods under subpart Q or explicit EPA acceptance to encourage method modernization.

The permission to use modified or alternative methods if validated under subpart Q or authorized by §761.61(c) approval (§761.61(a)(5)(i)(B)(2)(iv)) is acceptable but the validation process under subpart Q must have clear timelines and criteria to avoid protracted approvals.

Mandating caps be designed per §264.310(a) and meet permeability/material parameters in §761.75 (§761.61(a)(7)) could conflict with state or site-specific engineered cover designs that are protective but not exactly per §264.310(a); EPA should allow performance-based equivalency demonstrations.

Minimum thicknesses for compacted soil caps (25 cm) and concrete/asphalt caps (15 cm) (§761.61(a)(7)) may not be protective for all climates, subsidence-prone sites, or vehicular loading; EPA should require site-specific engineering analysis to determine appropriate thicknesses.

The obligation that caps must be strong enough to maintain integrity during normal use/exposure (§761.61(a)(7)) is vague; EPA should specify design life, load-bearing standards, and maintenance inspection frequencies.

The prohibition that caps must not have PCB contamination ≥1 ppm (§761.61(a)(7)) is strict and may render reuse of some in-situ materials impracticable; offer an option for engineered barriers with leachate controls where minor contamination can't be removed but exposure risk is controlled.

Requiring repairs to cap breaches impairing integrity to start within 72 hours of discovery (§761.61(a)(7)) may be unrealistic in remote areas or when specialized contractors are needed; allow repairs to begin within 72 hours of mobilization or require temporary measures within 72 hours and permanent repairs per agreed schedule.

The perpetual maintenance obligation for fences or caps by site owners (§761.61(a)(8)) creates onerous long-term liability and may impede property transfers; EPA should allow financial assurance, institutional control mechanisms, or liability limitation if periodic inspections and funding for maintenance are secured.

The deed notation requirement to notify future purchasers of PCB remediation use and maintenance requirements (§761.61(a)(8)(i)(A)) is reasonable, but EPA must clarify interaction with state real property laws and provide model deed language to ensure consistency and avoid litigation.

Requiring the deed notation to state the land was used for PCB remediation waste disposal and any low occupancy restrictions (§761.61(a)(8)(i)(A)(1)) could stigmatize property and reduce its marketability; EPA should permit more neutral phrasing focused on required institutional controls and maintenance obligations rather than "disposal" terminology.

Mandating deed notation to state existence and requirement to maintain fence/cap (§761.61(a)(8)(i)(A)(2)) is appropriate but should allow flexibility where maintenance obligations are shared or delegated to a third party, with EPA acceptance.

Requiring the deed notation to state applicable cleanup levels left at site and in restricted areas (§761.61(a)(8)(i)(A)(3)) risks technical complexity in public land records; EPA should allow summary statements with reference to the administrative record or a publicly accessible registry for details.

The obligation to submit signed certification to EPA that the deed notation has been recorded (§761.61(a)(8)(i)(B)) is duplicative of state recording processes; allow submission of recording instrument ID or a link to the recorded document in lieu of owner-signed certification when state systems provide verification.

The permission to remove fence/cap/low occupancy designation after additional cleanup (§761.61(a)(8)(ii)) is positive, but the rule must clarify verification procedures, acceptable evidence of cleanup levels achieved, and whether independent third-party confirmation is required.

Allowing removal of deed notice no sooner than 30 days after achieving cleanup levels (§761.61(a)(8)(ii)) is acceptable, but EPA should require a formal notice period for neighboring property owners and a public comment opportunity before deed note removal for transparency.

The performance-based cleanup and disposal provision (§761.61(b) intro) is useful, but EPA must issue clear performance metrics, QA/QC standards, and templates for documentation to ensure consistent application and protect human health.

The statement that disposal under (b)(2) does not relieve site owner obligations for remaining PCBs (§761.61(b) intro) could create ambiguous ongoing liabilities for parties that conducted discrete disposal actions; recommend defining circumstances under which liability transfers or limitations apply.

Prohibiting the performance-based cleanup option for listed site types including surface waters and sediments (§761.61(b)(1)(i)(A)-(8)) is appropriate, but the list should be precisely defined (e.g., "surface waters" includes ephemeral streams?) to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

The exception that performance-based cleanup provisions do not bind cleanups under other authorities (§761.61(b)(1)(ii)(B)) should state explicitly that compliance with more stringent CERCLA/RCRA/Tribal requirements suffices and that states may adopt comparable but not less stringent requirements.

The obligation that on-site PCB remediation waste exceeding cleanup levels must be disposed or decontaminated per (b)(2) (§761.61(b)(1)(ii)) needs an exception for minimal quantities where institutional controls and monitoring may be more protective and practical; allow case-by-case EPA-approved alternatives.

Setting cleanup level for bulk PCB remediation waste and porous surfaces at ≤1 ppm (§761.61(b)(1)(ii)(A)) is a major tightening from some prior practice and will substantially increase remediation costs; EPA must provide economic impact analysis and consider tiered cleanup levels based on exposure scenario.

The 1 ppm cleanup level may be technically infeasible to achieve on many porous materials (e.g., concrete, brick) without demolition; EPA should allow performance-based containment or removal thresholds combined with land-use controls.

Referring liquid cleanup levels to §761.79(b)(1) and (b)(2) (§761.61(b)(1)(ii)(B)) is fine, but those sections should be cross-checked to ensure they provide clear analytical methods, holding times, and detection limits for enforcement.

Referring nonporous surface cleanup levels to §761.79(b)(3) (§761.61(b)(1)(ii)(C)) requires that Subpart P verification sampling be realistically achievable with documented detection limits; recommend explicit wipe area, solvent, and LOD requirements.

Requiring verification sampling per Subparts O/P and §761.269 for liquids (§761.61(b)(1)(iii)) is acceptable, but EPA should allow statistically justified alternate sampling plans for heterogeneous sites, with pre-approval from the Regional Administrator.
Mandating recordkeeping per §761.125(c)(5) (§761.61(b)(1)(iv)) should specify retention periods, electronic record standards, and whether records follow the property upon transfer.

Requiring notification within 14 days of final shipment of waste offsite (§761.61(b)(1)(v)) may be too short for entities shipping multiple lots to multiple facilities; allow consolidated notifications or electronic batch reporting within 30 days.

The required notification contents (§761.61(b)(1)(v)(A)-(D)) must include clear definitions of "final shipment," "site identification information," and standardized templates to ensure consistent reporting across sites.

The obligation to dispose of liquid PCB remediation waste per §761.60(a) or (e) or decontaminate per §761.79 (§761.61(b)(2)(i)) should include explicit acceptance criteria for decontamination and end-point verification methods to avoid disputes about adequacy.

Listing disposal options for non-liquid PCB remediation waste (§761.61(b)(2)(ii)) needs cost and capacity assessment; stakeholders note limited availability of high-temperature incineration and secure landfills and request transitional provisions for disposal capacity constraints.

Allowing management/disposal of dredged/excavated material <50 ppm PCBs under CWA §404 or MPRSA §103 permits is helpful, but EPA should require coordinated review with Army Corps and Marine Protection agencies to ensure consistent environmental protections and monitoring.

Requiring written application to conduct sampling/extraction/analysis/cleanup/disposal other than prescribed (§761.61(c)(1)) is reasonable but the application process must have defined review timelines and predictable decision criteria to prevent undue delays.

The requirement that applications include notification information and that EPA may request additional information (§761.61(c)(1)) should be balanced with limits on EPA's ability to repeatedly request information to delay approvals.

Prohibiting cleanup activities under §761.61(c)(1) before written EPA approval is received could prevent timely emergency responses; EPA should allow immediate protective actions in emergencies with prompt follow-up approval.

Requiring written application to EPA to handle PCB bulk product waste differently (§761.62(c)(1)) is appropriate, but applicants should have access to pre-application consultations to reduce uncertainty.

Applicants for §761.62(c)(1) must show proposed methods/locations will not pose unreasonable risk; EPA should provide quantitative screening criteria for "unreasonable risk" to ensure consistent decisions.

Prohibiting activities under §761.62(c)(1) without prior written EPA approval is reasonable but agencies must process approvals in a timely manner; propose statutory deadlines or deemed approvals if EPA fails to respond.

Permitting use of bulk product waste as daily landfill cover provided it remains in the landfill and is not dispersed (§761.62(d)) is pragmatic, but EPA should require monitoring and institutional controls to prevent future exposure during landfill reconfiguration or closure.

Requiring piles or non-leaking covered containers designed to control wind dispersal for storage (§761.65(c)(9)(i)) is appropriate; EPA should clarify acceptable control measures beyond wetting (e.g., wind fences, tarping) and allow flexible designs for different climates.

Storage sites' liner/container requirements to prevent migration and meet construction/foundation standards (§761.65(c)(9)(iii)(A)(1)-(3)) must be harmonized with state solid waste landfill liner standards and include specific permeability and chemical compatibility criteria.

The cover requirements to meet liner standards and be secured against expected winds (§761.65(c)(9)(iii)(B)) should include guidance on design wind speeds, anchoring methods, and inspection frequency to ensure compliance.

Requiring commercial storers to establish financial assurance for closure of each PCB storage facility they own or operate (§761.65(g) intro) is appropriate, but small businesses will need scaled financial assurance options; EPA should allow alternative instruments like escrow accounts or local government guarantees.

Allowing choice among listed financial assurance mechanisms (§761.65(g)(1)) is necessary; EPA should include clear templates, minimum funding levels tied to site-specific closure cost estimates, and periodic adjustments for inflation.

Deeming trust agreements with specified wording compliant unless Regional Administrator specifies modifications (§761.65(g)(1)(iv)) is helpful but Regional Administrators must provide written notice of required modifications and justification within a fixed timeframe.

Deeming use of specified surety bonds/instruments/standby trusts compliant (§761.65(g)(2)) should not preclude acceptance of modern financial instruments (e.g., corporate guarantees backed by rated parent company or insurance products) provided they meet security standards.

The submission and use of the specified surety bond instrument and standby trust being deemed compliant (§761.65(g)(3)(i)) is acceptable, but EPA should allow updated model bond language to reflect current financial market practices and include sample clauses for assignment upon change of ownership.

raw_output:
[P1] The blanket prohibition on credit purchases for dealers averaging over $100,000 annually will force many medium-sized dealers to cease normal credit terms, disrupting longstanding industry credit practices and causing supply chain liquidity issues.

[P2] The $100,000 threshold in §201.200(b) is arbitrary and insufficiently justified; it will sweep in dealers with marginally above-threshold purchases while exempting slightly smaller dealers, creating perverse incentives to restructure purchasing to fall just below the threshold.

[P2] The rule's use of "average annual purchases" is ambiguous — commenters will seek clarification on the averaging period (one year, three years, rolling average) and whether affiliated entities are aggregated.

[P3] Requiring dealers to obtain a written acknowledgment before purchasing on credit is impractical in fast-moving markets (e.g., livestock auctions, roadside purchases) and will slow transactions or prevent credit sales that sellers rely on.

[P3] The provision does not specify whether the acknowledgment can be electronic (e-signature) or must be a wet signature, creating legal uncertainty for modern business practices.

[P4] The mandated statement that sellers "will have no trust rights under section 318" is legally problematic and may be misleading to sellers because section 318's application can be fact-specific; prohibition of trust rights cannot be contracted away in some jurisdictions.

[P4] The specific wording required in the acknowledgment may violate state public policy or consumer protection laws if it attempts to waive statutory rights; the agency should allow alternative language or informational disclosures that accurately reflect legal consequences.

[P5] Requiring the acknowledgment to state whether the agreement is single-sale, multiple-sales with expiration, or until canceled is overly rigid; many dealer-seller relationships use open account terms that fluctuate and cannot be neatly characterized.

[P5] The rule does not explain how to handle rolling or evergreen agreements (e.g., "until canceled" combined with periodic modifications), nor what constitutes a valid "expiration date," risking litigation over technicalities.

[P6] The requirement to include the date the seller signed the agreement is reasonable but must allow for post-dated signatures and situations where the seller signs at a later time; the rule should expressly permit date corrections and electronic timestamping.

[P7] Requiring the seller's signature without clarifying acceptable signature methods (electronic, stamped, witnessed) will exclude commonly used contracting practices; the agency should accept electronic signatures compliant with ESIGN/UETA.

[P8] The retention obligation to keep acknowledgments and related documents "for not less than two calendar years after expiration" is unclear for agreements without a stated expiration; dealers need guidance on retention commencement for "until canceled" agreements.

[P9] The minimum two-year retention period may be too short for enforcement or for sellers asserting claims after business disruptions; trade groups may request extending retention to three to five years to align with other recordkeeping statutes.

[P8] The rule's requirement to retain "all other documents, if any, setting forth the terms of credit sales" is overly broad and could impose burdensome discovery/retention for informal communications (texts, emails); the agency should limit retained documents to defined core documents.

[P10] Requiring dealers to provide a copy of the acknowledgment to the seller creates logistical burdens at auctions and remote transactions; the rule should allow sending copies electronically within a reasonable timeframe after the sale (e.g., 5 business days).

[P11] Treating payment by any draft that is not a check as a credit sale is overly broad and may capture common instruments like certain money orders or cashier instruments; the rule should define "draft" and provide examples/exclusions.

[P11] The classification of drafts as credit purchases could unintentionally penalize dealers who accept widely used payment mechanisms (e.g., bank drafts, wire transfers initiated after sale) and impede common payment practices.

[P12] The obligation in §203.15(a) that sellers/growers must file notice with the Secretary within statutory timeframes is appropriate, but the rule must specify the exact filing mechanisms, addresses, and acceptable electronic formats to avoid rejections.

[P13] The rule references statutory timeframes (sections 206(b), 207(d), 318(b)) but fails to reproduce or summarize them, making compliance harder for non-lawyers; the agency should include the actual deadlines in the regulation text or guidance.

[P14] The "recommended" content for notices is presented as mandatory elsewhere; commenters will demand clarity whether the items in §203.15(a)(1)-(6) are required to preserve trust rights or merely recommended.

[P15] Stating that notices "should provide" that they preserve trust benefits could be interpreted as optional, risking denial of trust claims; agencies should make the essential elements mandatory or specify which elements are discretionary.

[P16] Requiring identification of the packer or dealer in notices may be difficult if sellers do not know legal entity names (e.g., transactions conducted by multiple affiliate names); the rule should accept common trade names and provide a mechanism to correct errors.

[P17] The requirement to identify the seller/grower in the notice is reasonable, but the rule should permit notices from authorized agents and specify documentation proving agency where necessary.

[P18] Requiring the transaction date in notices is reasonable but the rule must address situations where multiple dates are involved (delivery date vs. sale date) and which date controls for statutory timing.

[P19] The instruction to include the date the seller received notice of dishonored payment "if applicable" may create disputes about constructively received notices; the agency should define receipt standards (mail date, email delivery, in-person).

[P20] The requirement to state the amount due and to file a copy with PSD regional or headquarters offices needs clear filing addresses and acknowledgement procedures; commenters will request electronic filing portals and confirmation receipts.

[P21] The exception in §203.15(b) that a timely notice informing of non-payment is sufficient even if lacking details is necessary; however, commenters will request detailed safe-harbor language protecting sellers from procedural dismissals when minor notice details are missing.

[P21] Conversely, packers and dealers will object that §203.15(b) is too lenient and could lead to frivolous or ambiguous notices; they will request minimal required elements to prevent abuse.

[P1] Small dealers close to the $100,000 threshold will artificially restructure purchasing (use parent companies or third-party intermediaries) to avoid being classified as a covered dealer, undermining enforcement and market transparency.

[P3] Auction houses and livestock markets must be expressly exempted or given alternative compliance mechanisms because obtaining individual written acknowledgments for each credit transaction is infeasible in their operational model.

[P4] Consumer advocacy groups will argue the required waiver statement should be accompanied by plain-language explanations of trust rights and consequences, not just a legalistic sentence that many sellers may not understand.

[P8] Privacy and data-security concerns arise from mandatory retention of seller signatures and financial documents; the rule should require dealers to implement reasonable safeguards and limit retention of sensitive personal data.

[P10] Independent producers and smallholders lacking internet access may not receive electronic copies promptly; the rule should require paper copies on request and allow reasonable times for mailing.

[P2] Compliance costs (legal review, new forms, training, recordkeeping systems) will disproportionately burden small dealers near the threshold; the agency should conduct a regulatory flexibility analysis and consider higher thresholds or phased implementation.

[P11] Clarify whether wire transfers (where payment is initiated contemporaneously but settlement may occur later) count as credit sales under §201.200(c); industry will request an explicit carve-out for transfers that clear within 24-48 hours.

[P12] Grower contracts often involve intermediaries and corporate hierarchies; the rule should clarify how notices should be addressed when the immediate counterparty is an agent or affiliate.

[P15] Legal experts will note that the regulation cannot expand or narrow statutory rights under sections 206, 207, 318; any mandatory form language that purports to waive rights could be preempted or unenforceable.

[P9] Enforcement agencies should retain discretion to require longer retention where investigations are ongoing; commenters will request language preserving agency authority to demand records beyond the two-year minimum.

[P3] Emergency or disaster situations (e.g., animal disease outbreaks, natural disasters) will make pre-transaction acknowledgments impossible; the rule should provide an emergency exception or post-transaction cure period.

[P20] The rule lacks clear sanctions or consequences for failure to file notice with PSD offices (e.g., whether failure results in forfeiture of trust claim); stakeholders will request clarification on remedies and appeal procedures.

[P21] The alternative acceptance of bare notices in §203.15(b) should be limited to initial preservation of rights but require supplemental detailed notices within a short cure period to prevent prejudice to defendants.

[P5] The requirement to state whether the agreement "remains in effect until canceled in writing" could make routine amendments inadvertent breaches if parties orally modify arrangements; the agency should permit written modification records within a reasonable cure period.

[P7] Farmers and elderly sellers may have difficulty providing a signature or understanding the acknowledgment; the rule should permit agents, notaries, or witnessed attestations and require plain-language explanations.

[P8] The phrase "all other documents, if any, setting forth the terms of credit sales" could be read to include informal evidence (texts, voicemail transcripts); the agency should limit scope to executed contracts and business records to reduce litigation burden.

[P1] The regulation may conflict with existing state laws that govern livestock liens or UCC-based trust rights; commenters will request preemption analysis and coordination with state statutes.

[P3] The timing requirement "before purchasing on credit" should accommodate situations where the dealer issues credit contemporaneously at sale; define a narrow post-sale cure period (e.g., same business day) to avoid invalidating routine transactions.

[P14] The agency should publish model notice forms and templates for acknowledgments and seller notices to ensure uniform compliance and reduce disputes over form sufficiency.

[P20] Provide an electronic filing system with timestamps and read-receipts for §203.15 notices; stakeholders will request this to ensure timely preservation and avoid disputes over delivery.

[P10] Maintaining sulfur-by-weight records for each fuel oil shipment (§52.173(c)(5)(i)(A)) imposes an onerous administrative burden on small fuel suppliers; request that aggregate monthly certificates of analysis be allowed in lieu of per‑shipment records.

[P11] Permitting owner/operator, outside labs, or fuel suppliers to perform fuel sampling (§52.173(c)(5)(i)(A)) is reasonable, but the rule lacks minimum QA/QC standards for outside labs; request incorporation of specified laboratory accreditation (e.g., NELAP) or QA procedures.

[P15] The October 27, 2017 deadline to submit a report confirming the bark curve (§52.173(c)(5)(i)(B)) is unrealistic if the owner needs seasonal fuel availability to perform representative testing; request allowance for later submission contingent on demonstrated scheduling constraints.

[P16] Compiling daily fuel input records within 15 days after month‑end (§52.173(c)(5)(i)(B)) is administratively tight given current data systems; industry requests a 30‑day window or phased transition to avoid noncompliance solely on paperwork timing.

[P17] The specification that the 30‑day rolling average SO2 must be expressed in lb/day per boiler-operating-day (§52.173(c)(5)(i)(B)) conflicts with other sections that express rolling averages as lb/hr; request harmonization of units across the rule to prevent calculation errors.

[P18] The 15‑day requirement to compile and maintain daily total SO2 emission records (§52.173(c)(5)(i)(B)) should specify whether weekends and holidays count toward the 15 days and whether electronic recordkeeping is acceptable; request clarification.

[P20] Allowing an air permit revision to limit Power Boiler No.1 to pipeline-quality natural gas as sufficient to demonstrate SO2 compliance (§52.173(c)(5)(ii)) is acceptable only if the permit contains enforceable sulfur specifications and a testing or supplier certification requirement; request explicit permit language.

[P21] The exception removing paragraph (c)(5)(i) requirements when limited to pipeline gas (§52.173(c)(5)(ii)) undermines independent verification; environmental groups request retained periodic spot-testing or supplier certification to ensure gas quality meets the implied standard.

[P22] Requiring NOX stack testing using EPA Method 7E once every 5 years beginning Oct 27, 2017 (§52.173(c)(5)(iii)) is too infrequent to assure ongoing compliance for variable-operating boilers; public health groups request tests every 2–3 years or additional continuous monitoring.

[P23] Maintaining stack testing records and making them available upon request (§52.173(c)(5)(iii)) needs a specified retention period and electronic submittal requirements; stakeholders ask EPA to require submitting test reports to a public docket or state database.

[P24] Allowing NOX compliance demonstration by calculation using fuel usage and AP-42 factors if limited to pipeline gas (§52.173(c)(5)(iv)) may understate actual emissions because AP-42 factors are averages; request that EPA require periodic stack tests to validate AP-42 assumptions.

[P25] Compiling daily natural gas input records within 15 days (§52.173(c)(5)(iv)) duplicates other reporting regimes; industry requests allowance to use existing fuel metering data and to accept monthly aggregated submissions.

[P26] Requiring daily NOX emission calculation records within 15 days after month-end (§52.173(c)(5)(iv)) is administratively burdensome and subject to transcription errors; propose automated electronic submissions and a 30‑day compilation window.

[P27] Calculating 30‑day rolling average NOX per boiler-operating-day expressed in lb/hr (§52.173(c)(5)(iv)) is confusing because the paragraph expresses results in lb/hr whereas other sections use lb/day; request consistent units and worked examples.

[P28] Maintaining 30‑day rolling average NOX records and providing them on request (§52.173(c)(5)(iv)) should include a data quality requirement (e.g., audit trail) to ensure integrity when calculations replace CEMS.

[P29] The exception eliminating (c)(5)(iii) stack testing if limited to pipeline gas (§52.173(c)(5)(iv)) reduces independent verification; environmental commenters request at least initial stack tests after fuel switching and periodic audits.

[P30] October 27, 2021 SO2 and NOX compliance deadline for Boiler No.2 (§52.173(c)(7)) does not consider the unit’s scheduled outages and may force uneconomic retrofits; request phased compliance aligned with planned major maintenance outages.

[P31] The requirement to sum hourly emissions to determine daily NOX and SO2 and then compute 30‑day rolling averages in lb/hr (§52.173(c)(8)(i)) is unclear about how to treat partial-hour operation periods; request explicit treatment of partial hours and startup/shutdown periods.

[P32] The prohibition on using invalid hourly values in the rolling average calculation (§52.173(c)(8)(i)) lacks definition of “invalid” and the procedure to fill data gaps; request that EPA specify approved data substitution methods (e.g., Appendix F procedures) or provide missing-data allowance thresholds.

[P33] The obligation to maintain daily total SO2 and NOX emission records and provide them on request (§52.173(c)(8)(i)) should stipulate retention time and acceptable formats (paper vs. electronic); commenters request a minimum 5‑year retention and electronic reporting.

[P34] Maintaining 30‑day rolling average records for SO2 and NOX for each boiler-operating-day (§52.173(c)(8)(i)) may be duplicative of CEMS-generated reports; recommend allowing owners to provide exported CEMS daily/rolling reports in lieu of separate manual records.

[P35] The requirement to maintain and operate CEMS in accordance with cited 40 CFR requirements (§52.173(c)(8)(ii)) is appropriate, but the rule should explicitly reference the exact subparts and versions of 40 CFR part 60 to avoid ambiguity.

[P36] Compliance with CEMS QA procedures in 40 CFR part 60 (§52.173(c)(8)(ii)) is mandatory, but the rule should allow documented alternative QA procedures recognized by the state with EPA approval to accommodate newer monitoring technologies.

[P37] Using CEMS data to determine compliance (§52.173(c)(8)(ii)) is appropriate; however, the rule must allow reconciliation with fuel-based calculations in limited circumstances (e.g., prolonged CEMS outage with validated fuel records) with prior EPA approval.

[P38] Requiring continuous emissions monitoring during all boiler operation periods (§52.173(c)(8)(iii)) without specifying treatment of short excursions (e.g., <30 minutes) is inflexible; request allowance for planned maintenance windows and clear procedures for notification and reporting.

[P39] Mandating at least one CEMS cycle every 15 minutes (§52.173(c)(8)(iii)) is consistent with existing practice, but commenters ask EPA to clarify acceptable alternatives for low‑burn or intermittent units where 15‑minute cycles are technically infeasible.

[P40] The requirement to compute hourly averages with at least one data point in each 15‑minute quadrant of the hour (§52.173(c)(8)(iii)) may be impractical during certain calibration or maintenance activities; request defined missing-data substitution rules and maximum allowed missing quadrants.

[P41] Allowing hourly averages from at least two data points separated by 15 minutes (§52.173(c)(8)(iii)) when data are unavailable is reasonable, but EPA should limit the number of consecutive hours this method can be used and require documentation and cause investigation.

[P42] The alternate monitoring requirement when CEMS data are unavailable (§52.173(c)(8)(iii)) is vague about which EPA-approved alternative methods are acceptable and the minimum number of hours/days required; ask EPA to list approved alternative monitoring methods and reporting templates.

[P43] Treating a permit limit to pipeline-quality natural gas as sufficient for Boiler No.2 SO2 compliance (§52.173(c)(8)(iv)) should require specific sulfur limits and supplier certification in the permit; otherwise the presumed compliance is unenforceable.

[P44] Removing applicability of paragraphs (c)(8)(i)-(iii) for SO2 when limited to pipeline gas (§52.173(c)(8)(iv)) eliminates independent monitoring; environmental advocates request retained periodic verification testing or mandatory supplier QA to prevent circumvention.

[P45] Allowing NOX compliance by calculation using fuel records and AP‑42 factors for Boiler No.2 if permitted to burn pipeline gas and CEMS not required (§52.173(c)(8)(v)) risks underestimating emissions; recommend mandatory initial and periodic stack testing to validate AP‑42 factors.

[P46] Requiring daily natural gas input records within 15 days (§52.173(c)(8)(v)) should permit use of existing gas company measurement bills or SCADA exports; ask EPA to accept certified electronic meter data provided monthly.

[P47] Requiring daily NOX calculation records within 15 days after month-end (§52.173(c)(8)(v)) duplicates other reporting and is administratively burdensome; propose allowing quarterly summaries with retention of daily underlying data for audit.

[P48] Calculating 30‑day rolling average NOX per boiler-operating-day in lb/hr when demonstrating by calculation (§52.173(c)(8)(v)) is confusing; request worked examples and template spreadsheets to ensure consistent industry compliance.

[P49] Maintaining 30‑day rolling average NOX records and providing them on request (§52.173(c)(8)(v)) should include digital submission pathways and a standard data format (e.g., CSV) to facilitate state and EPA review.

[P50] The exception removing (c)(8)(i)-(iii) compliance determination requirements for NOX when pipeline gas and no CEMS (§52.173(c)(8)(v)) reduces transparency; public-interest commenters request at least annual reporting of calculated NOX emissions to the public.

[P51] The November 28, 2016 PM BART compliance deadline (§52.173(c)(10)) is already past and thus creates ambiguity about whether the source is in violation as of proposal publication; EPA should clarify that actions taken before proposal will be deemed compliant if documented.

[P52] The condition that limiting the permit to pipeline-quality natural gas suffices to meet PM BART (§52.173(c)(11)) ignores particulate emissions from combustion byproducts (e.g., ash carryover) and mechanical sources; request that PM monitoring or good combustion practice requirements remain.

[P53] Requiring all communications to be submitted to the Director, Multimedia Division, EPA Region 6 at a Dallas address (§52.173(c)(12)) is overly prescriptive and may impede electronic filing; request allowance for electronic submission to the EPA regional mailbox and state portal.

[P54] The catch-all obligation that owners/operators comply with listed requirements (§52.173(c)(12)) should include an explicit statement that state permit terms control where they are more stringent; legal commenters request a clause clarifying interplay between SIP and Title V permit obligations.

[P55] EPA’s finding that the Arkansas Regional Haze SIP revision satisfies BART (§52.173(g)) is premature without an independent analysis of visibility modeling and contribution; environmental groups request the underlying visibility improvement modeling and emissions inventory be placed in the docket for review.

[P56] The condition stating reasonable progress requirements are satisfied by listed SIP/FIP documents (§52.173(h)) lacks disclosure of the modeling assumptions, cost analyses, and visibility benefit calculations; stakeholders request full access to supporting documents and the opportunity to comment on the modeling.

[P1] The August 31, 2020 comment deadline is unreasonably short and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow operators, maintenance providers, and labor unions time to coordinate technical and economic feedback.

[P1] The rule incorrectly states the FAA "must receive comments by August 31, 2020" without providing guidance on electronic vs. mailed submissions or confirmation of receipt; request adding clear submission methods and acknowledgement procedures.

[P2] The requirement to "comply within the specified compliance times" is vague because compliance times in referenced documents vary; request that the AD explicitly list numeric deadlines for each affected model/configuration to avoid misinterpretation.

[P3] Requiring revision of the maintenance/inspection program within 14 days after Feb 22, 2019 is impossible for operators that were not notified or that acquired airplanes after that date; request the FAA amend this to 14 days after the AD effective date or provide relief for operators demonstrating good cause.

[P3] Legal experts will note that retroactive obligations to act within 14 days following a date in the past (Feb 22, 2019) are unenforceable; request correction to reference the AD effective date rather than a past AD effective date.

[P4] The 45-day initial compliance time measured from Feb 22, 2019 (a past date) creates legal and practical uncertainty; ask the FAA to restate the initial compliance time as 45 days from this AD's effective date.

[P5] The prohibition on using alternative actions or intervals after paragraph (g) revision, except via AMOC, is overly restrictive and may prevent use of industry-standard FAA-accepted inspection intervals; recommend clarifying that previously accepted equivalents remain allowed until the AMOC process is complete.

[P6] Requiring AMOC approval for any alternative action or interval without interim discretionary relief imposes operational risk for carriers with unique configurations; request an interim relief process or issuance of blanket AMOCs for common variants.

[P7] The requirement to perform all actions in Boeing Requirements Bulletin B787–81205–SB260008–00 RB without consideration of service history or previously-performed modifications may force redundant work; request allowance for credit where Boeing service history shows tasks already accomplished.

[P8] Reliance on the "Compliance" paragraph of the Boeing Requirements Bulletin as the sole source of timing is problematic because the bulletin may be revised; request that the AD specify which bulletin revision is mandatory and how superseding bulletins affect compliance.

[P9] Paragraph (i) says actions are required "except as specified by paragraph (j)" but paragraph (j) only addresses date phrase substitution; request clarification of any other exceptions and cross-references to avoid compliance confusion.

[P1] The November 6, 2020 comment deadline in P1 is unreasonably short for international operators and suppliers who require time to coordinate legal and technical review across jurisdictions; request extending the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] Small operators and independent maintenance organizations will not see adequate notice before the November 6, 2020 deadline; FAA should publish supplemental outreach and reopen the comment period to ensure meaningful participation.

[P2] Provision P2's applicability to "all" listed Boeing 747 variants is overbroad if the unsafe condition affects only specific production lots, serial numbers, or retrofit configurations; FAA should limit applicability to affected serial numbers or configurations.

[P2] The truncated list in P2 appears to be incomplete ("7" trailing text); clarify the complete list of affected models and confirm whether newer 747-8 variants are included or excluded.

[P3] P3 requires compliance "within the specified compliance times" but the AD fails to state those times explicitly in this document; request that the FAA include the exact compliance intervals in the AD preamble or regulatory text for clarity.

[P3] The phrase "unless already done" in P3 is ambiguous about acceptable record evidence for prior compliance; require FAA to specify documentation standards (logbook entries, SB compliance records) that will be accepted.

[P4] P4 mandates following Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin instructions "except as specified in paragraph (h)" but does not reconcile conflicts between the bulletin and this AD beyond (h); request FAA to state precedence rules if other bulletin language conflicts with AD.

[P4] Requiring strict adherence to Boeing's Accomplishment Instructions in P4 may impose proprietary or supplier dependencies; operators should be allowed to use equivalent methods demonstrated to provide equal safety, subject to AMOC approval.

[P5] P5 substitutes the AD effective date for "original issue date" in the Boeing bulletin; this could change compliance windows tied to the bulletin's issue date—request that FAA specify how this affects any time-based inspections or repetitive intervals.

[P5] Using the AD effective date in P5 may disadvantage operators who already began compliance based on the bulletin's original issue date; ask FAA to confirm that prior work performed between the bulletin issue date and AD effective date will be credited.

[P6] P6 requires Boeing-approved repair instructions before further flight when the bulletin says to contact Boeing; this creates a single-source approval pathway and could delay return-to-service if Boeing is unavailable—FAA should allow temporarily approved repairs by qualified repair stations subject to AMOC.

[P6] The "before further flight" mandate in P6 may be infeasible for aircraft in remote locations or in revenue service; request interim measures (e.g., flight restrictions, ferry permits) until approved repair instructions are provided.

[P7] P7's prohibition on installing original fiberglass fabric material TADD assemblies by part numbers listed in the appendix is overly broad if some assemblies have been inspected, modified, or reworked to be safe; propose an exception for assemblies that have passed FAA- or Boeing-approved inspection/repair.

[P7] The outright ban in P7 should specify whether the prohibition applies only to new installations or also to reinstallation of previously removed and inspected parts; clarify treatment of spares in inventory.

[P7] P7 fails to define "original fiberglass fabric material TADD assembly" for practical enforcement; request a technical definition or reference to specific part numbers and manufacturing revisions.

[P8] P8 centralizes AMOC authority in the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch; this may create delays for non-U.S. operators—suggest allowing other FAA certification offices or EASA/foreign authority delegations to approve AMOCs for affected international operators.

[P8] The delegation in P8 should clarify whether AMOCs approved by Boeing ODA (per P12) require subsequent FAA concurrence, to avoid duplication and uncertainty about approval validity.

[P9] P9 requires AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO, but many repair stations and leased operators do not have a principal inspector assigned; request guidance on the correct submission path for such entities.

[P10] P10 directs direct submissions to the person in paragraph (k)(1), but paragraph (k)(1) is not included here; request the AD include the specific name, office address, and contact information to avoid misdirected AMOC requests.

[P11] P11 requires notifying the principal inspector or local FSDO before using an approved AMOC; this could impose operational constraints on immediate safety fixes—request that notification may occur within a defined reasonable period post-use (e.g., 72 hours) for urgent operations.

[P11] The obligation in P11 should require the FAA to acknowledge receipt of notification within a set timeframe to provide regulatory certainty to operators using the AMOC.

[P12] P12 allows Boeing ODA-approved deviations to serve as AMOCs; stakeholders request clarity on the scope of ODA authority and whether ODA approvals will be automatically accepted by FAA without additional review.

[P12] Relying on Boeing ODA approvals per P12 may raise conflict-of-interest concerns; request that the FAA require independent technical review or concurrence for ODA-issued AMOCs affecting structural repairs.

[P13] P13 conditions AMOC approval on meeting the airplane's certification basis and explicitly referencing this AD; clarify how to apply this for older airplanes with multiple amendments to their certification basis and whether equivalency findings are acceptable.

[P13] The requirement in P13 to explicitly reference this AD in the AMOC approval could hinder cross-referenced AMOCs covering multiple ADs; request that referencing the AD be allowed by inclusion in the AMOC rationale rather than as a verbatim citation.

[P3][P4] The AD's compliance framework (P3 and P4) heavily relies on Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin format; request that the FAA publish the full text of the bulletin in the docket rather than only referencing it, to enable meaningful review and comment.

[P6][P12] The interplay between Boeing-provided repair instructions (P6) and Boeing ODA AMOC approvals (P12) creates potential for circular approval (Boeing both provides repair and approves AMOC); ask FAA to clarify checks to ensure independent validation.

[P7] The installation prohibition in P7 should include an implementation timeline for removal of prohibited TADD assemblies from service and supply chains, and specify whether operators must remove such assemblies immediately or at next scheduled maintenance.

[P1][P3] Because the AD's comment deadline (P1) precedes many operators' winter maintenance schedules, FAA should allow comments after November 6, 2020 if substantial new technical data emerge, or provide an extension mechanism.

[P2] Aircraft lessors and lessees need clarity on allocation of compliance responsibility under P3 and P4; request FAA to include explicit assignment rules for owners vs operators vs lessors in the AD.

[P9][P10] The AMOC submission procedures in P9 and P10 should allow electronic submission and establish receipt confirmation procedures; request FAA to accept secure email and provide tracking.

[P5] Changing "original issue date" to the AD effective date per P5 may unintentionally extend or shorten compliance windows for repetitive inspections; ask FAA to give worked examples showing the effect on compliance timing.

[P6] The requirement in P6 that repairs per Boeing instructions be done "before further flight" should be harmonized with international requirements (EASA, TCCA) to avoid conflicting operational directives for international carriers.

[P4] The AD should explicitly state whether following the Boeing bulletin's non-normative or advisory material (notes, non-mandatory figures) is required under P4, to prevent overreach into recommended practices.

[P12] Allowing ODA-approved AMOCs (P12) should be limited to ODAs with demonstrated recent experience on the affected 747 models; propose that the FAA publish criteria for acceptable ODA approvers.

[P7] Enforcement guidance is needed for P7: indicate whether installing prohibited assemblies inadvertently (e.g., through supply chain errors) will be treated as a civil penalty or if corrective actions can avoid penalties.

[P1] The AD should include a mechanism for late-filed comments to be considered if they present new data, despite the P1 November 6, 2020 deadline.
