[P1] The applicability in §531.3 is overly narrow because it limits the part to “manufacturers of passenger automobiles” and does not explicitly cover manufacturers that produce both passenger automobiles and other vehicle types, creating uncertainty about which provisions apply to multi-product manufacturers.

[P1] Clarify whether small-volume or niche manufacturers of passenger automobiles (e.g., specialty car builders) are covered by §531.3 or whether any exemptions apply.

[P2] The fleet average fuel economy obligations in §531.5(a) lack clarity about how manufacturers with joint ventures or common-control entities should aggregate fleets for compliance; request explicit aggregation rules.

[P2] The phrase “Except as provided in paragraph (f)” in §531.5(a) references an exception that is not included in the excerpt; commenters will request that the agency publish and justify paragraph (f) so stakeholders can evaluate compliance implications.

[P3] §531.5(b) requires compliance with a fleet average level “calculated using Figure 1 and Table 2 for MY 2011” but does not specify rounding rules or decimal precision for averaging; request specification of numerical rounding methods.

[P3] Manufacturers will ask for the underlying data and methodology (including vehicle footprints, weights, and test cycles) used to produce Figure 1 and Table 2 so they can validate the MY 2011 calculation.

[P4] For MYs 2012–2026, §531.5(c) ties standards to Figure 2 and Table 3; industry will request transition guidance for product planning and whether mid-model-year changes to fleet mix require recalculation.

[P4] Legal commenters will assert that the long span (2012–2026) of §531.5(c) standards raises separation-of-powers concerns if the agency intends to alter targets administratively without notice-and-comment rulemaking.

[P5] §531.5(d) imposes a domestically manufactured passenger automobile minimum fleet standard (Table 4); domestic manufacturers and labor groups will demand a clear definition of “domestically manufactured” and whether CKD/CKD assembly or partial domestic final assembly qualifies.

[P5] Import-dependent manufacturers will claim that the domestic minimum in Table 4 disadvantages firms that rely on global supply chains and request an economic impact analysis specific to Table 4 thresholds.

[P6] §531.5(e) names specific manufacturers with bespoke standards; manufacturers not listed will ask for the legal basis and objective criteria used to single out named manufacturers and for a process to petition for inclusion or amendment.

[P6] Named manufacturers will request assurance that the standards in subparagraphs (e)(1)-(15) reflect up-to-date product mixes and that there is a mechanism to petition for modification if their fleet composition changes materially.

[P7] The requirement in §531.6(a) to follow EPA procedures in 40 CFR part 600 for fleet-average calculations needs clarification on which edition/codification of part 600 applies and how future amendments to part 600 will affect current compliance.

[P7] Commenters will request that the rule explicitly state how test result variances, manufacturer-requested retests, and laboratory tolerances under 40 CFR part 600 are to be handled for fleet averaging.

[P8] §531.6(b) permits increases to fleet fuel economy using EPA procedures and allowed adjustments for MY 2017+, but lacks caps on total creditable adjustments; industry will request explicit caps or formulas to prevent gaming.

[P8] Environmental advocates will request that off-cycle and adjustment credits under §531.6(b) be restricted or phased down after a short window to ensure actual on-road gains rather than accounting devices.

[P9] The reporting obligation in §531.6(b) referencing 49 CFR 537.7 imposes deadlines; manufacturers will request the specific dates, required data formats, and confidentiality protections for competitively sensitive technology disclosures.

[P9] Legal commenters will request that the agency provide safe-harbor provisions for inadvertent late reports under §531.6(b) to avoid disproportionate penalties for minor administrative lapses.

[P10] §531.6(b)(1) requires compliance with 40 CFR 86.1868–12 for AC-efficiency technologies; manufacturers will request clarification whether compliance testing must be performed on certified production vehicles or on representative prototypes.

[P10] Air conditioning suppliers will request confirmation that manufacturer-submitted AC-efficiency data relying on supplier tests will be accepted and under what verification standards.

[P11] The specification in §531.6(b)(1) to determine fuel consumption improvements per 40 CFR 600.510–12(c)(3)(i) needs clarification about baseline reference cycles and whether manufacturer-requested baselines (older models) are allowed.

[P11] Commenters will ask how combined adjustments (e.g., AC efficiency plus off-cycle) are aggregated under 600.510–12(c)(3)(i) and whether additive stacking or multiplicative application is required.

[P12] §531.6(b)(2) requires following 40 CFR 86.1869–12 for off-cycle technologies; manufacturers will request a clear list of predefined off-cycle technologies and the criteria EPA uses to add or remove technologies from that list.

[P13] The permission in §531.6(b)(2) to obtain improvements per predefined off-cycle tech or via EPA 5-cycle testing needs timeline clarity: manufacturers will ask how long EPA takes to approve 5-cycle testing results and whether provisional credit is available while under review.

[P13] Test laboratories will request guidance on 5-cycle test protocols, required instrumentation, and data submission formats referenced in 40 CFR 86.1869–12(c).

[P14] §531.6(b)(2) ties off-cycle improvement calculations to 40 CFR 600.510–12(c)(3)(ii); manufacturers will request worked examples showing how off-cycle gains translate into fleet-average MPG credits under that subsection.

[P15] The permission in §531.6(b)(3) allowing alternative off-cycle methodologies via EPA application per 40 CFR 86.1869–12(d) creates administrative burden; small manufacturers will request a streamlined or expedited review pathway.

[P16] §531.6(b)(3)(i)’s eligibility condition requiring compliance with (A)–(C) is vague; commenters will request the text of (A)–(C) and whether partial compliance allows partial credits.

[P17] The applicability start date in §531.6(b)(3)(i) (A),(B),(D) beginning in MY 2024 raises transition concerns; manufacturers will request grandfathering rules for vehicles produced under contracts based on pre-2024 planning.

[P18] §531.6(b)(3)(i)(A) obliges manufacturers to submit and obtain EPA approval of a detailed analytical plan before the model year; commenters will request minimum content requirements, permitted modeling tools, and criteria EPA will use to evaluate the plan.

[P18] Data-sharing partners (suppliers, test labs) will request confidentiality assurances for analytical plans and supporting data submitted under (b)(3)(i)(A).

[P19] §531.6(b)(3)(i)(B) requires submission and EPA approval of an official credit application before September of the model year; manufacturers will ask whether applications received after September are categorically denied or subject to extension requests and penalties.

[P19] Trade groups will request a calendar of deadlines (including time zones) and guidance on what constitutes “approval” vs. “acknowledgement” for purposes of compliance.

[P20] §531.6(b)(3)(i)(C) mandates consultation with NHTSA and concurrent submission to NHTSA when seeking CAFE off-cycle values; manufacturers will request a joint EPA–NHTSA timeline and single submission portal to avoid duplicate filings.

[P20] Privacy and competition commenters will ask whether NHTSA will have access to proprietary technical details contained in EPA submissions and how interagency information sharing will be limited.

[P21] The permission in §531.6(b)(3)(i)(D) to request an extension from NHTSA for EPA approval creates uncertainty; manufacturers will request objective criteria and maximum extension lengths that NHTSA will grant.

[P22] The obligation in §531.6(b)(3)(i)(D) advising submission of extension requests 30 days before deadlines to cafe@dot.gov is administratively specific; manufacturers will ask for an electronic form and confirmation receipt process to avoid lost email disputes.

[P22] Industry commenters will request that the rule allow alternative submission methods (secure portal, certified mail) in addition to email, and clarification whether the 30-day advisory is a hard rule or guidance.

[P23] §531.6(b)(3)(ii) requires NHTSA to provide views to EPA on suitability of off-cycle technologies; manufacturers will request publication of NHTSA’s evaluative criteria and the timing of those views to ensure predictability.

[P24] The enumerated factors NHTSA must consider in §531.6(b)(3)(ii) include “relation to safety technologies”; automotive safety advocates will request that NHTSA place equal weight on potential safety tradeoffs and require independent safety testing before credits are granted.

[P24] Automaker safety engineers will ask for clear definitions of how NHTSA will measure “direct impact upon improving fuel economy” and how conflicting evidence will be reconciled between agencies.

[P25] §531.6(b)(3)(iii)(A) allows removal or adjustment of credits if technologies are defective; manufacturers want due process protections, timelines, and appeal rights before credits are removed.

[P25] Consumer safety advocates will request that NHTSA be empowered to remove credits immediately upon a credible safety defect finding to protect the public, with subsequent adjustment procedures.

[P26] The consultation requirement in §531.6(b)(3)(iii)(A) that NHTSA consults the manufacturer to determine adjustment amounts requires a transparent formula; commenters will request a default adjustment methodology if parties cannot agree.

[P27] §531.6(b)(3)(iii)(B) states that off-cycle credit approval does not exempt compliance with Vehicle Safety Act/FMVSs; manufacturers will request examples of circumstances where credit approval might conflict with FMVSS compliance to assess regulatory risk.

[P28] §531.6(b)(3)(iii)(B)(1) requires manufacturers to state that each vehicle with the technology will comply with all FMVSSs; manufacturers will ask whether this is a certification subject to civil/criminal penalties and whether pre-market test evidence suffices.

[P29] §531.6(b)(3)(iii)(B)(2) requires manufacturers to state whether the technology has a fail-safe or explain why not; commenters will request a standard definition of “fail-safe” and examples acceptable to EPA/NHTSA.

[P29] Safety advocacy groups will request that lack of a fail-safe be disqualifying unless an independent risk assessment shows no reasonable probability of safety harm.

[P30] The applicability in §533.3 to manufacturers of light trucks is ambiguous for crossover vehicles with passenger classification; manufacturers will request objective footprint/weight thresholds to classify a vehicle as a light truck under §533.3.

[P31] §533.5(a) imposes fleet-average standards for light trucks but does not specify whether small-volume manufacturers are eligible for alternate standards or credits; small manufacturers will request small-volume exemptions/adjustments similar to other regulatory programs.

[P32] §533.5(b)(1) permits MY1979 manufacturers to combine 2- and 4-wheel drive trucks or comply separately; retroactive application to longstanding model lines is unclear and commenters will ask whether this is a one-time election or applies annually.

[P33] §533.5(b)(2) confines the 4-wheel standard in MY1979 to “general utility” 4-wheel drive vehicles; manufacturers will request a clear statutory definition of “general utility” and examples to ensure consistent categorization.

[P34] §533.5(c) allows limited product line manufacturers for MYs1980–81 to choose standards; commenters will request the agency’s criteria for defining “limited product line” and whether this option applies to modern boutique manufacturers.

[P35] §533.5(d) for MYs1982–91 permits combining 2- and 4-wheel drive trucks with segregation of captive imports; manufacturers will request the required documentation and audit standards to substantiate segregation.

[P36] §533.5(e) for MY1992 requires segregation of captive imports; manufacturers with complex import arrangements will request guidance on tracing components and final assembly location rules.

[P37] §533.5(f) from MY1996 onward requires combining captive imports with other light trucks; manufacturers will raise concerns that blending captive imports could disadvantage global manufacturers and request transitional relief or crediting mechanisms.

[P38] §533.5(g) permits an irrevocable option for MYs2008–2010 to use Figure1/Table5; manufacturers will request clarification whether “irrevocable” means non-amendable after submission and what remedies exist if errors are discovered.

[P39] The reporting obligation in §533.5(g) referencing §537.8 requires timely reporting of the option; manufacturers will ask for the exact reporting format, timeline, and penalty structure for misreporting.

[P40] §533.5(h) obligates MY2011 compliance with Figure1/Table5 for light trucks; industry will request the technical inputs (e.g., vehicle footprints) used to generate Figure1/Table5 so they can benchmark compliance.

[P41] §533.5(i) for MYs2012–2016 ties standards to Figures2/3 and Table6; manufacturers will request an explanation of how these tables account for technology learning curves and changed fleet compositions.

[P42] §533.5(j) for MYs2017–2025 links standards to Figures2/4 and Table7; given the long horizon, manufacturers will request scheduled periodic reviews and an amendment process to reflect technological advances.

[P43] §533.6(a)(1) deems references to a class of light trucks to include trucks manufactured by entities under common control; commenters will request a precise definition of “under common control” and whether contractual or equity relationships trigger inclusion.

[P44] §533.6(a)(2) limits class inclusion to non-passenger vehicles per 49 CFR 523.5 “based on production measurements as sold to dealerships”; manufacturers will ask for guidance on vehicles sold through fleet channels or direct-to-business sales and whether they count.

[P45] §533.6(a)(3) excludes trucks exported within 30 days after the model year ends; exporters will request clarification on how export dates are determined (shipping date vs. customs clearance) and documentation required to substantiate exclusion.

[P46] §533.6(b) requires using EPA procedures in 40 CFR part 600 for light-truck fleet averaging; commenters will request coordination between EPA part 600 updates and NHTSA enforcement to avoid inconsistent methodologies.

[P47] §533.6(c) permits fuel-economy increases via AC efficiency, off-cycle, and hybridization for full-size pickups meeting 40 CFR 86.1803; pickup manufacturers will request clear eligibility criteria for hybridization/performance-based incentives and whether plug-in hybrids are included.

[P47] Environmental groups will request that hybridization credits for full-size pickups be limited to technologies that demonstrate real-world reductions in fuel consumption, not just certification-cycle improvements.

[P48] The reporting requirement under §533.6(c) referencing 49 CFR 537.7 requires deadlines; commenters will request consolidated reporting deadlines for passenger automobile and light-truck technology claims to reduce administrative burden.

[P49] §533.6(c)(1) mandates following 40 CFR 86.1868–12 for AC-efficiency on light trucks; commenters will request whether light-truck AC-efficiency credits are vehicle-class specific (e.g., cab size, payload) and examples of acceptable systems.

[P50] §533.6(c)(1) points to 40 CFR 600.510–12(c)(3)(i) for AC-fuel improvements; commenters will request clarity on how differences between vehicle test weights and in-use payload affect credited AC improvements.

[P51] §533.6(c)(2) requires following 40 CFR 86.1870–12 for hybridization/performance-based incentives for full-size pickups and measuring improvements per 600.510–12(c)(3)(iii); manufacturers will request worked examples showing how a hybridized full-size pickup’s credited MPG improvement is computed and how that translates to fleet averages.

raw_output:
[P1] Industry commenter: Requiring efficacy testing "through testing per label directions and accepted pest control practices" is vague; please define “commonly accepted pest control practices” and provide examples to ensure consistent study design across applicants.

[P1] Trade association: The obligation that “Each applicant must ensure through testing that their product is efficacious” imposes an open-ended burden on registrants; request clarification on who may perform testing (third-party labs, contract research organizations, academic partners) and whether previously conducted data may satisfy this requirement.

[P2] Registrant/legal commenter: The permission for EPA to require product performance data “on a case-by-case basis” could lead to arbitrary or duplicative requests; request a clear, transparent threshold and standardized criteria for when EPA will invoke this authority.

[P3] Industry and labs: Mandating that “All product performance testing is performed using the end-use product” may be impractical for certain formulations (e.g., bait matrices, in situ activated systems) and could require testing of large quantities; request allowance to test representative formulated mixtures or challenge matrices with agency approval.

[P3] Technical commenter: For products that rely on active ingredient conversion in the environment, requiring end-use product testing only could prevent meaningful mechanistic studies; request allowance to supplement end-use tests with formulated intermediate or active-ingredient-only studies.

[P4] Public health NGO: Requiring reporting of species used in testing is appropriate but should also require reporting of strain, colony origin, resistance status, and rearing conditions to ensure transparency and reproducibility.

[P5] Consumer advocacy group: The requirement to "test products to support labeling claims" should be expanded to require that negative or inconclusive test results be disclosed to EPA and reflected on label statements (e.g., limitations), to prevent misleading marketing.

[P6] Registrant: Referring applicants to “applicable sections of Subpart R” to determine required data is reasonable but the cross-references are numerous; request a consolidated guidance document or decision tree from EPA to simplify compliance.

[P7] Lawyers/regulatory experts: Requiring submission of product performance data to support any claim subject to this subpart is duplicative for products that already have peer-reviewed published efficacy studies; request explicit acceptance criteria for published data and non-U.S. studies.

[P8] Small business commenter: Requiring submission of product performance data "with any application for registration or amended registration" will increase costs and slow minor label changes; request an exemption or scaled requirements for minor labeling amendments that do not alter efficacy claims.

[P9] Vector control districts: The obligation to provide data specific to the species identified in pest-specific claims is scientifically sound, but for pest complexes with many regional species, this could require numerous tests; request allowance to use surrogate species with demonstrated equivalence and clear criteria for surrogate acceptance.

[P10] Industry: The requirement that the labeling claim determines the performance standard could create circularity where companies tailor labeling narrowly to avoid higher standards; request that EPA provide examples of allowable claim language and associated minimum standards.

[P11] Registrants: Defaulting to the performance standards in paragraphs (b) and (c) when no other standards exist may be overly rigid for novel or low-risk products; recommend an explicit pathway to propose alternate, scientifically justified standards during the registration review.

[P12] Consumer health groups: The 2-hour complete protection standard for skin-applied repellents may be too low for areas with high disease transmission; recommend increasing the minimum to 4 hours or adopting disease-vector-specific protection time requirements.

[P12] Industry/R&D labs: Achieving ≥2 hours complete protection in all conditions (e.g., sweating, water exposure) may not be feasible; request that EPA specify test conditions (e.g., sweating, water immersion) and allow conditional labeling statements for limited-use scenarios.

[P13] Human subjects advocates: Requiring compliance with 40 CFR part 26 for any testing involving human subjects is necessary; however, guidance is needed on how part 26 interacts with international human-subjects protections and multi-site studies.

[P14] Clinical researchers: Submitting human-subjects protocols to EPA for review before initiation is reasonable, but the rule must specify EPA’s review timeline to avoid unreasonable delays in study start.

[P15] Ethicists: The HSRB review requirement for intentional human exposure protocols is appropriate; request clarification on criteria EPA will use to determine which studies require HSRB review and the expected timeframe for HSRB feedback.

[P16] Small companies: The obligation to "contact EPA prior to initiating testing if uncertain" lacks procedural detail and could be burdensome; request a dedicated, expedited hotline or pre-submission consultation pathway with defined response times.

[P17] Pest control industry: The ≥90% performance standard for most claims is very high and could eliminate useful products that provide meaningful, but not near-perfect, control; request flexibility for integrated pest management (IPM) products or products intended as supplementary controls.

[P17] Public health NGOs: Conversely, industry may argue to lower standards; we support maintaining ≥90% for public-safety pests (mosquito vectors, ticks) but request specifying higher tiers for vector-borne disease control.

[P18] Registrants: Stating Subpart R controls over Harmonized Test Guidelines in conflicts is reasonable but ask EPA to publish a prioritized list of specific Harmonized Guidelines and anticipated conflict scenarios to guide study design.

[P19] Innovator companies: The permission for EPA to adjust data requirements for novel products is helpful; request that EPA publish a predictable framework and timelines for evaluating such modification requests.

[P24] State agriculture agencies: EPA’s discretionary authority to require data for invasive species claims case-by-case may lead to unequal treatment across regions; request standardized criteria for invasive species claims, including emergency pathways.

[P25] Forest service/municipalities: Requiring data for emerald ash borer and Asian longhorned beetle claims is appropriate; request that EPA accept regional efficacy data and allow collaborative testing programs given difficulties in maintaining these species in labs.

[P26] Vector control districts: For disease-vector claims, testing specified species is essential; request that EPA allow inclusion of local vector populations/strains with known insecticide resistance profiles to reflect field efficacy.

[P27] Registrants: EPA's authority to require testing on structural/wood-destroying pests not listed elsewhere is broad; request clear timelines and scoping procedures when EPA invokes §158.1710, and a mechanism for registrants to confer prior to data requests.

[P28] Ant and acarology researchers: Using labeling claims to determine mite test species is logical but the rule should require standardized test methods and environmental conditions for mite assays to ensure comparability.

[P29] Veterinary product manufacturers: Requiring tests on Demodex canis for dog follicle mite claims is appropriate, but culturing Demodex is technically difficult; request acceptance of field efficacy trials or adjusted protocols.

[P30] Allergy advocacy groups: Dust mite testing limited to D. farinae or D. pteronyssinus is appropriate, but request that standards also address allergen reduction, not only mite mortality, since labeling often implies allergen control.

[P31] Medical experts: Requiring Sarcoptes scabiei testing for scabies claims is appropriate; however, human scabies testing raises ethical concerns — request EPA clarify acceptable in vitro or animal model alternatives.

[P32] Consumer protection groups: A 100% performance standard for dog follicle mite claims is unrealistic given biological variability; request EPA justify the scientific basis and consider a lower threshold or conditional claims.

[P33] Medical/lab researchers: Requiring 100% for human itch/scabies mites may be infeasible and ethically problematic if human-subjects are involved; recommend acceptance of high-efficacy ranges (e.g., ≥95%) with post-market surveillance.

[P34] Outdoor product manufacturers: Mandating testing on Trombicula alfreddugesi for chigger claims may not cover regional chigger species; request acceptance of surrogate regional chigger species with justification.

[P35] Tick industry and vets: Using labeling claims to determine required tick species is reasonable, but the rule's lists should be updated periodically to reflect range expansions and emergence of new tick vectors.

[P36] Canine/feline product makers: Requiring testing on three hard tick species (including Ixodes scapularis and Amblyomma americanum) increases testing costs; request an option to use representative species and resistance profiles to reduce redundant testing.

[P37] Cattle industry: For cattle tick claims, testing on Rhipicephalus microplus or R. annulatus is acceptable, but in regions where other cattle ticks predominate, request EPA accept regional species or provide bridge studies.

[P38] Wildlife health groups: Testing on Ornithodoros hermsi for soft tick claims may not represent other soft ticks of concern; request guidance on when additional species testing is necessary.

[P39] Pet product industry: Requiring canine products to be tested on three tick species could double or triple study costs for each product; request allowance to use targeted claims (e.g., "effective against Ixodes spp.") to reduce testing burden or provide an accelerated pathway for multi-species claims after initial single-species approval.

[P40] Feline product manufacturers: Mandatory testing on specified tick species for cats is appropriate biologically but feline safety testing constraints require harmonized protocols and timelines that account for veterinary ethics and dosing differences.

[P41] Specialty pesticide manufacturers: Requiring testing on Centruroides vittatus for scorpion claims may not represent other medically significant scorpion species; request criteria for when other species should be tested or when one species suffices.

[P42] Spider product registrants: Using labeling claims to determine spider test species is appropriate; request standardized assays and acceptance criteria for venomous species handling safety.

[P43] Medical entomologists: For spider pest-group claims requiring Loxosceles reclusa and a black widow species, testing on L. reclusa is extremely difficult and dangerous; request acceptance of surrogate indicators of efficacy or in vitro neurotoxicity reduction endpoints.

[P44] Manufacturers: For black widow subgroup claims, allowing one specified species is reasonable, but request explicit guidance on sourcing and containment for Latrodectus species to avoid supply bottlenecks.

[P45] Public health stakeholders: Requiring testing on Loxosceles reclusa for brown recluse claims is appropriate for accuracy; request EPA define acceptable laboratory strains and testing endpoints (mortality vs. knockdown).

[P47] Toxicologists: Requiring tests on each black widow species for pest-specific claims is scientifically defensible but may be duplicative; request EPA allow phylogenetic rationale to justify cross-species extrapolation.

[P48] Centipede control product makers: Using labeling claim to set required centipede species is logical; request clarity on test endpoints (mortality vs. repellency) and exposure conditions.

[P49] Manufacturers: Allowing testing on one of several centipede species reduces burden; request explicit criteria for selecting which species is acceptable for a given geographic market.

[P50] Lice treatment companies: Using labeling claim to determine lice species and standards is appropriate; request uniform guidance on human clinical trial design to meet 100% standard.

[P51] Public health/education: Testing on head or body louse species should consider permethrin-resistant populations; request EPA require data addressing resistant strains or provide labeling language to reflect limitations.

[P52] Pediatric health advocates: A 100% performance standard for lice claims is unrealistic; demand evidence that 100% can be achieved and, if not, require labeling to disclose expected efficacy and retreatment intervals.

[P53] Flea product manufacturers: Label-determined test species is appropriate; request clear guidance on multi-host fleas and how results from cat flea testing translate to dog flea claims.

[P54] Pest control professionals: Requiring testing on Ctenocephalides felis for group flea claims is practical since it is the most common; request EPA clarify whether data from cat flea can support dog flea claims in multi-host formulations.

[P55] Veterinary public health: For pest-specific flea claims (e.g., dog flea), testing on C. canis may be difficult to obtain; request allowance for cross-validation using C. felis under specified conditions.

[P56] Cockroach product manufacturers: Label-determined species is sensible; request harmonized protocols for field vs. lab strains and acceptance criteria for bait versus residual insecticide claims.

[P57] Pest management industry: Requiring both American and German cockroach testing for group claims will increase costs but is required; request guidance on when data from one species may suffice due to similar susceptibility profiles.

[P59] Livestock industry: For keds, screwworms, and bot flies, some species are regionally restricted; request allowance for regional claim limitations and acceptance of field efficacy trials.

[P60] Equine product manufacturers: Requiring testing on horse bot fly species is appropriate; request clarity on test endpoints (larvicidal vs. adult control) and acceptable study durations.

[P61] Tropical health NGOs: Requiring Dermatobia hominis testing for human bot fly claims may be impractical in U.S.-based labs; request acceptance of validated surrogate models or field data from endemic countries.

[P62] Sheep/wool industry: Mandating Melophagus ovinus testing for ked claims is technically feasible but expensive; request funding assistance considerations or cooperative testing programs.

[P63] Livestock health agencies: Screwworm testing requirements are necessary for eradication programs but must be coordinated with APHIS and may require emergency exemptions during outbreaks.

[P64] Waste management operators: For filth fly claims, defining test species by label is appropriate; request clarity on acceptable blow/flesh fly species and how to handle evolving species distributions.

[P65] Public health entomologists: Requiring house fly plus one flesh or blow fly species is scientifically defensible; request EPA provide a standardized species list and test protocols for these groups.

[P66] Food industry: For pest-specific filth fly claims, the multiplicity of species may create heavy data burdens; recommend allowing representative species or cross-claiming under defined equivalency.

[P67] Mosquito control districts: The requirement to test across mosquito genera (Culex, Aedes, Anopheles) is appropriate for broad claims; request EPA accept regional vector species selection and include resistant strains in testing.

[P68] Repellent manufacturers: Requiring testing in Culex, Aedes, and Anopheles by selecting one species from each list is expensive; request options for tiered claims (e.g., genus-specific labels) to reduce testing loads.

[P69] Outdoor recreation NGOs: Label-determined biting fly species is sensible; request clarity on test conditions that reflect outdoor exposure (wind, humidity) for repellency claims.

[P70] Livestock product makers: Testing on stable fly plus one large and one small biting fly increases study complexity; request EPA allow representative species for region-limited products.

[P71] Researchers: For large biting fly subgroup claims requiring stable fly and one large species, standardization of trap/feeding assays is needed; request EPA publish validated protocols.

[P72] Public health groups: For small biting fly subgroup claims, species selection (Culicoides, Simulium, Leptoconops) has major behavior differences; request EPA provide species-specific endpoints and testing methods.

[P73] Vector control: For pest-specific biting fly claims, acceptance of field efficacy data under real-world conditions should be allowed in lieu of multiple lab species tests.

[P74] Hotel and lodging industry: Bed bug (Cimex lectularius) testing requirement is appropriate but obtaining and maintaining bed bug colonies is costly; request EPA accept validated field studies and standardized resistance profiling.

[P75] Consumer products industry: Mandating testing on Cimex lectularius for bed bug claims is logical; request clarified endpoints (mortality, ovicidal activity) and acceptance criteria for “control” claims.

[P76] Public health agencies: For conenose and kissing bug claims, lab testing standards should address nocturnal feeding behaviors; request EPA guidance on realistic exposure scenarios.

[P77] Vector control: Testing on Triatoma sanguisuga for conenose claims is reasonable for U.S. markets; request acceptance of regional species for labels intended for other geographies.

[P78] Registrants: Requiring Triatoma protracta for kissing bug claims may not cover all human disease vectors; recommend EPA permit species selection based on the target geography and disease risk.

[P79] Ant product manufacturers: Using label to determine ant test species is logical; request standardized colony-level endpoints and field trial requirements for colony claims.

[P80] Retailers/consumers: Requiring testing on pharaoh ant and red imported fire ant for group claims is burdensome because pharaoh ant behavior differs substantially from other common pests; request ability to make sub-grouped claims to reflect tested species.

[P81] Agricultural stakeholders: For fire/harvester ant subgroup claims, limiting testing to S. invicta may not address hybrid or regionally different species; request EPA accept regionally relevant species or hybrids for testing.

[P82] Pest management professionals: For pest-specific ant claims, the long list of species creates high testing burdens; request EPA allow data bridging across related species with demonstrated susceptibility equivalence.

[P83] Research institutions: For colony claims, allowing testing on S. invicta, S. richteri, or hybrids is reasonable; request definition of acceptable hybrid diagnostics and colony-level endpoints for demonstrating colony elimination.

[P84] Bait manufacturers: Requiring species-specific testing for bait/outdoor use claims and limiting group claims to foraging direct kill/residual surface claims may constrain marketing; request clarification on how bait matrix influences cross-species efficacy claims.

[P85] Beekeepers/environmental groups: Label-based species selection for bees/wasps/yellowjackets/hornets is critical; request that EPA require differential labeling to prevent misuse that could harm beneficial pollinators.

[P86] Municipal pest control: Requiring testing on two yellowjacket species and one Polistes for group claims may not reflect local pest complexes; request EPA accept data from other representative vespid species with justification.

[P87] Public safety entities: For pest-specific wasp/bee claims, clarify whether field colony-level suppression studies will be accepted in place of lab bioassays, given logistical constraints of working with social Hymenoptera.

[P88] Environmental advocacy: For colony claims requiring species-specific testing and 100% performance for Vespula colony claims, 100% is an unrealistic standard for colony elimination; request EPA reconsider the 100% threshold or provide rationale.

[P89] Construction/materials industry: Using labeling claims to set carpenter ant test species is reasonable; request clear guidance on wood types and exposure conditions for structural claims.

[P90] Pest control operators: Allowing testing on one of several carpenter ant species is practical; request EPA acceptance of regional species selection with defined protocols.

[P91] Building industry: The bait treatment performance standard requiring 95% prevention of wood damage for ≥3 years is onerous and may be unattainable due to complex infestation dynamics; request alternative efficacy metrics (e.g., reduction in gallery activity) or shorter warranty periods.

[P93] Architects/engineers: The structural protection requirement of 95% prevention of wood damage for ≥5 years imposes long-term testing burdens; request phased approval with post-market performance monitoring and label statements tied to demonstrated durations.

parsed_claims.claim_text: Industry commenter: Requiring efficacy testing "through testing per label directions and accepted pest control practices" is vague; please define “commonly accepted pest control practices” and provide examples to ensure consistent study design across applicants.

Trade association: The obligation that “Each applicant must ensure through testing that their product is efficacious” imposes an open-ended burden on registrants; request clarification on who may perform testing (third-party labs, contract research organizations, academic partners) and whether previously conducted data may satisfy this requirement.

Registrant/legal commenter: The permission for EPA to require product performance data “on a case-by-case basis” could lead to arbitrary or duplicative requests; request a clear, transparent threshold and standardized criteria for when EPA will invoke this authority.

Industry and labs: Mandating that “All product performance testing is performed using the end-use product” may be impractical for certain formulations (e.g., bait matrices, in situ activated systems) and could require testing of large quantities; request allowance to test representative formulated mixtures or challenge matrices with agency approval.

Technical commenter: For products that rely on active ingredient conversion in the environment, requiring end-use product testing only could prevent meaningful mechanistic studies; request allowance to supplement end-use tests with formulated intermediate or active-ingredient-only studies.

Public health NGO: Requiring reporting of species used in testing is appropriate but should also require reporting of strain, colony origin, resistance status, and rearing conditions to ensure transparency and reproducibility.

Consumer advocacy group: The requirement to "test products to support labeling claims" should be expanded to require that negative or inconclusive test results be disclosed to EPA and reflected on label statements (e.g., limitations), to prevent misleading marketing.

Registrant: Referring applicants to “applicable sections of Subpart R” to determine required data is reasonable but the cross-references are numerous; request a consolidated guidance document or decision tree from EPA to simplify compliance.

Lawyers/regulatory experts: Requiring submission of product performance data to support any claim subject to this subpart is duplicative for products that already have peer-reviewed published efficacy studies; request explicit acceptance criteria for published data and non-U.S. studies.

Small business commenter: Requiring submission of product performance data "with any application for registration or amended registration" will increase costs and slow minor label changes; request an exemption or scaled requirements for minor labeling amendments that do not alter efficacy claims.

Vector control districts: The obligation to provide data specific to the species identified in pest-specific claims is scientifically sound, but for pest complexes with many regional species, this could require numerous tests; request allowance to use surrogate species with demonstrated equivalence and clear criteria for surrogate acceptance.

Industry: The requirement that the labeling claim determines the performance standard could create circularity where companies tailor labeling narrowly to avoid higher standards; request that EPA provide examples of allowable claim language and associated minimum standards.

Registrants: Defaulting to the performance standards in paragraphs (b) and (c) when no other standards exist may be overly rigid for novel or low-risk products; recommend an explicit pathway to propose alternate, scientifically justified standards during the registration review.

[P2] Operators request explicit guidance on what constitutes "already complied" under § 39.13(f) — does compliance with similar non-U.S. ADs, manufacturer service bulletins, or prior company programs qualify?

[P2] Legal experts note ambiguity in § 39.13(f): require FAA to state how operators should document prior compliance to satisfy the "unless already complied" clause for audit/training purposes.

[P3] Airlines and MROs object to the requirement in § 39.13(h) to incorporate program revisions "prior to reaching the compliance times ... or within 12 months" as potentially forcing dual concurrent deadlines; request FAA clarify that the 12-month backstop applies uniformly and specify effective date.

[P4] Maintenance organizations request FAA to publish the exact text of Sections 5.0 and 6.0 from the referenced Boeing documents or include required procedures in the AD itself per § 39.13(h) to avoid ambiguity and reduce reliance on proprietary documents.

[P4] Flight safety advocates argue that mandating implementation "in accordance with" Boeing Sections 5.0 and 6.0 (§ 39.13(h)) may preclude operators from using equivalent, validated procedures developed by independent approved organizations — request FAA allow equivalent procedures with AMOC pathway.

[P5] Industry commenters note that the termination provision in § 39.13(h) (terminating actions in AD 2004–07–22 R1) could create gaps if Boeing revisions change scope; request FAA confirm that no previously required inspections will be omitted and provide a traceability matrix.

[P6] Non-LCF 747 operators state that requiring incorporation of all SSIs listed in D6–35022 Rev H (§ 39.13(h)(1)) may impose inspections on legacy SSIs that are inapplicable to certain fleet configurations — request an applicability table mapping SSIs to serial number ranges and options.

[P7] 747–400 LCF operators assert that adopting both D6–35022 Rev H and D6–35022–1 (§ 39.13(h)(2)) doubles administrative burden; request FAA clarify overlap handling and provide a consolidated SSI list for LCFs.

[P8] Operators request FAA confirm the precedence rule in § 39.13(h)(2) (use D6–35022–1 where SSI appears in both) applies only to inspection intervals/areas and not to repair methods, or explicitly state scope of precedence.

[P9] Maintenance unions express concern that the broad requirement in § 39.13(i) to "perform inspections of all structure identified" in D6–35022 Rev H is vague and may be interpreted to require fleet-wide teardown inspections; request FAA define inspection types and authorized techniques.

[P10] Airlines request explicit acceptance criteria and nondestructive inspection (NDI) techniques for repetitive inspections under § 39.13(i) (intro second sentence) to ensure uniform inspection quality across operators.

[P11] Operators point out § 39.13(i)(1) inspection timing (later of two specified times) is confusing — request a worked example showing how to determine the "later" date for a replaced component and for aircraft near both cycle and hour thresholds.

[P12] Airlines and leasing companies object to the 20,000 flight cycle / 100,000 flight hour threshold in § 39.13(i)(1)(i)(A) for certain 747 models as arbitrary — request FAA provide the damage-tolerance analysis that justifies these specific thresholds.

[P13] 747–400 operators challenge the 20,000 cycles / 115,000 hours threshold in § 39.13(i)(1)(i)(B) as inconsistent with existing fleet utilization (very long sector hours for some carriers) and request alternative hour/cycle equivalency guidance.

[P14] Small operators and cargo carriers say the alternative in § 39.13(i)(1)(ii) — inspect within 1,000 flight cycles measured from 12 months after the AD effective date — could force short-notice shop visits; request FAA allow flight-hour-based alternatives or phased ramp-up scheduling.

[P15] Non-wing structure owners ask FAA to clarify what is intended by "non-wing structure" in § 39.13(i)(2) and provide a list of included components to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P16] Operators request clearer guidance on applying the 20,000 total flight cycles initial compliance time in § 39.13(i)(2)(i) to aircraft with incomplete or partially missing records (e.g., derelict freighters).

[P17] Some commenters find the parallel alternative in § 39.13(i)(2)(ii) (1,000 cycles from 12 months after effective date) redundant and ask FAA to harmonize timing between wing and non-wing inspections to minimize downtime.

[P18] MROs ask for clarification on whether § 39.13(i)(3) (inspections for replaced SSI portions) applies to both OEM-part replacements and field repairs (e.g., doubler installation), and request explicit definitions of "replaced with new structure."

[P19] Leasing companies request that § 39.13(i)(3)(i) explicitly permit using the receiving airplane’s compliance clock for parts moved between operators, or else allow a documented transfer-of-life procedure.

[P20] Operators contend that § 39.13(i)(3)(ii)'s 10,000 flight cycle inspection interval after part replacement is excessive for frequently replaced components and should be adjusted based on part service life and damage-tolerance data.

[P21] 747–400 LCF operators request FAA to clarify whether the inspections mandated in § 39.13(j) supersede or supplement any inspections imposed by the LCF conversion STC.

[P22] Operators request that repetitive inspection intervals required by § 39.13(j) (intro second sentence) be published in the AD or an FAA-maintained reference to ensure transparency, rather than only in Boeing documents.

[P23] Legal commenters ask FAA to clarify the precedence clause in § 39.13(j) (intro precedence sentence) — whether D6–35022–1 takes precedence for intervals, inspection area, and corrective actions, or only for listed SSIs.

[P24] Airlines need clarification and examples for determining the "later of the two times" in § 39.13(j)(1) when an airframe both exceeds cycles thresholds and is nearing the 1,000-cycle-from-12-month mark.

[P25] Commenters request the technical basis and fleet usage data supporting the 20,000 cycles / 115,000 hours initial requirement in § 39.13(j)(1)(i) for LCF wing inspections.

[P26] Operators say the 1,000 flight cycle from 12 months alternative in § 39.13(j)(1)(ii) may produce unequal safety margins across operators with different utilization profiles; request FAA provide risk analysis or allow hour-based alternatives.

[P27] Maintenance planners request a consolidated schedule showing how § 39.13(j)(2)(i)(A) 20,000-cycle requirement interacts with the "applicable initial compliance time" under § 39.13(j)(2)(i)(B) so operators can prioritize inspections.

[P28] Boeing and repair stations ask FAA to define "applicable initial compliance time specified in Boeing Document..." (§ 39.13(j)(2)(i)(B)) and whether those times differ by SSI — request FAA append a table of initial compliance times for each SSI.

[P29] Operators request FAA to clarify in § 39.13(j)(2)(ii) whether the 1,000-cycle-from-12-month alternative may be measured in fractional cycles or whether cycles must be integer-counted.

[P30] MROs warn that § 39.13(k)'s requirement to "repair before further flight using an FAA-approved method" is ambiguous — request FAA to permit repairs done under existing approved repair data (e.g., manufacturer repair manuals, SRM) without separate FAA approval, provided records document compliance.

[P31] Repair stations request a defined timeline and approval process for emergency repairs discovered during inspections to comply with § 39.13(k) and avoid grounding aircraft for administrative approvals.

[P32] § 39.13(l) (first sentence): Operators ask how to track and validate SSI-specific cycles/hours when parts are removed and reinstalled across multiple aircraft — request permitted recordkeeping methods and acceptance of vendor certificates.

[P33] Record-keeping stakeholders point out that § 39.13(l) (second sentence) forcing use of airframe totals when SSI history is unknown will cause many components to be inspected earlier than necessary, increasing cost; request alternative presumptive life/crediting methods.

[P34] Operators and safety advocates highlight that the prohibition in § 39.13(m) on alternative inspections after program revision is overly restrictive and could prevent use of improved inspection technologies developed later; request FAA allow operator-proposed alternatives via expedited AMOC.

[P35] Industry supports the AMOC exception in § 39.13(m) only if the AMOC process is timely; request FAA commit to target review times (e.g., 60–90 days) and publish contact points.

[P36] Commenters request FAA publish guidance and examples for AMOC requests under § 39.13(p)(1), including data requirements, acceptable analyses, and sample submissions to reduce back-and-forth.

[P37] Operators require clarification under § 39.13(p)(2) about the notification process before using an approved AMOC — specify required content of the notification and whether it must be in writing.

[P38] Boeing requests FAA to permit AMOCs approved by Boeing’s ODA under § 39.13(p)(3) only if the ODA approval process and documentation are auditable by FAA and operators — request explicit record and traceability requirements.

[P39] Legal experts note § 39.13(p)(3)(second sentence) requires AMOC repairs meet the airplane's certification basis; request FAA clarify how to treat changes in certification basis due to later rule changes or STC installations.

[P40] Operators request FAA to provide a list of AMOCs previously approved for AD 2004–07–22 R1 that will be accepted under § 39.13(p)(4) to avoid re-submissions and to identify any that are now excluded due to expanded SSI areas.

[P41] Inspectors ask FAA to publish which SSIs have "expanded inspection area" per the § 39.13(p)(4) exception so operators know where prior AMOCs will not transfer.

[P42] Commenters request FAA include an explicit cost-estimate and paperwork burden justification for the PRA statements in § 39.13(o), asserting 5 minutes per response is unrealistically low for record searches and reporting.

[P43] Privacy advocates request clarification under § 39.13(o) whether the mandatory responses and associated records will be subject to FOIA and how proprietary information in Boeing documents will be handled.

[P44] Operators question the statement in § 39.13(o) that "All responses to this collection of information are mandatory" and ask FAA to confirm whether required reporting is limited to AD compliance records or includes additional reporting to FAA.

[P45] Commenters urge FAA to confirm the OMB Control Number 2120–0056 listed in § 39.13(o) remains valid for the entire AD implementation period and to publish renewal procedures if needed.

[P46] Small-operator groups request the comment address in § 39.13(o)(fifth sentence) be updated to include an email or electronic portal for burden-reduction comments to facilitate easier stakeholder input.

[P47] Operators request FAA specify whether AMOC approvals by the Seattle ACO Manager under § 39.13(p)(1) can be delegated regionally for operators based outside the Seattle jurisdiction to speed approvals.

[P48] Airlines request FAA clarify how to handle AMOC notifications under § 39.13(p)(2) during crew/operator organizational changes (e.g., if there is no “principal inspector” assigned).

[P49] Maintenance training organizations request FAA to allow use of OEM-approved training and certification for personnel performing inspections mandated in paragraphs (i) and (j) rather than new FAA-specific qualifications.

[P50] Safety advocates request FAA require operators to report all findings (including "no crack found") from the mandated inspections within a defined timeframe to a central database to improve industry-wide understanding of crack prevalence.

[P51] Manufacturers and operators request FAA explicitly allow use of newer nondestructive inspection technologies (e.g., phased-array ultrasonics) as equivalent, provided methods are validated, to avoid being constrained by Boeing Section 5.0/6.0 wording in § 39.13(h).

[P52] Airlines operating mixed fleets request FAA clarify how this AD interacts with foreign authorities' ADs and whether compliance with equivalent EASA/Japan ADs will satisfy § 39.13 requirements to avoid duplicate inspections.

[P53] Commenters request FAA add a provision addressing cost recovery or financial assistance for mandated inspections and repairs for small carriers disproportionately burdened by extensive SSI inspections.

[P54] Legal professionals request FAA to confirm that accomplishing the revision and initial inspections under § 39.13(n) fully terminates all obligations of AD 2004–07–22 R1, including any continuing reporting obligations, and to provide a written crosswalk.

[P55] Operators request FAA to provide a grace period for aircraft undergoing lease transitions to comply with the initial inspection times in paragraphs (i) and (j) so lessees/lessors can coordinate responsibility for compliance.

[P1] Removing AD 64–09–03 (Amendment 718) without clearly explaining why new AD language supersedes prior economic or safety assessments risks regulatory confusion for owners referencing the old directive in maintenance records.

[P2] Adding a new AD to § 39.13 for DHC–2 variants is appropriate but the proposed text lacks a clear economic impact analysis for small operators who predominantly fly DHC–2s.

[P3] The March 25, 2022 comment deadline is outdated and impossible to meet; the Agency should extend the comment period to allow stakeholders sufficient time to analyze technical data and prepare meaningful responses.

[P4] The applicability language referencing “Model DHC–2 Mk. I, DHC–2 Mk. II” is ambiguous — commenters request a complete serial-number range or explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria to avoid unintended coverage of modified or re‑serialed airframes.

[P5] The catch‑all “comply within the specified compliance times, unless already done” is fine in principle but must explicitly state that documented prior compliance meeting the new AD standards satisfies the requirement without further action.

[P6] The 8‑month deadline to establish an FAA‑approved corrosion prevention and control program in maintenance records is unreasonably short for small operators to develop, submit, and obtain FAA approval; request extension to 12–18 months.

[P7] The 8‑month time threshold (repeated) does not account for seasonal maintenance windows for floatplane operators and should be adjusted or allow staggered compliance based on operator maintenance schedules.

[P8] Requiring FAA approval for every operator’s corrosion prevention program could overwhelm the New York ACO Branch; the rule should allow approval of operator programs meeting an FAA‑published template or allow delegated organizational approvals (DAR/DOA) to streamline.

[P9] The mandated elements (initial inspections, repetitive intervals, corrective actions including repairs and corrosion inhibitors) are appropriate, but the AD should provide specific minimum inspection intervals and objective criteria for corrective actions to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P10] Requiring completion of all initial tasks “before further flight” after establishing the program could ground aircraft for extended periods; the AD should permit staged initial actions for items that do not affect immediate airworthiness, or provide relief when temporary measures mitigate risk until full repair.

[P11] Mandating that operators must contact the New York ACO Branch using paragraph (j)(3) information for FAA approval concentrates workload in one office and creates a single point of failure; permit contact with the local FSDO or principal inspector for program approval.

[P12] The 30‑day reporting requirement to Viking after finding corrosion is too short for operators who must compile technical findings and may be out of service; propose extending reporting to 60 days or allowing preliminary notification followed by a final report.

[P13] Requiring operator identity in corrosion reports is reasonable but raises confidentiality concerns for commercial operators; the AD should clarify how Viking will handle proprietary or commercially sensitive information.

[P14] Including the airplane serial number in reports is necessary; however, the AD must address reporting for aircraft that have been re‑serialized or registered under multiple jurisdictions and specify which serial should be used.

[P15] Requiring hours time‑in‑service at inspection in reports is appropriate, but AD should define whether Hobbs hours or tachometer hours are acceptable and require consistent units to ensure comparability.

[P16] Requiring inspection task number and inspection date in reports is fine; the AD should reference the exact PSM inspection task numbering scheme to avoid mismatched numbering between revisions.

[P17] Requiring the airplane operating environment in reports is ambiguous; the AD must define categories (e.g., marine, freshwater, saltwater, gravel operations, agricultural spray) or provide a standardized form to ensure consistent reporting.

[P18] Requiring type/extent/location/cause of corrosion is reasonable, but expecting operators to determine cause “if known” may lead to inconsistent or inaccurate attributions — the AD should provide guidance or allow Viking to request follow‑up investigations.

[P19] Granting the Manager authority to approve AMOCs is standard; commenters recommend including a predictable timeline (e.g., 60 days) for AMOC decisions to avoid operational delays.

[P20] Conditioning AMOC requests on following 14 CFR 39.19 procedures is acceptable but the AD should include a clear list of required documentation to accompany an AMOC request to reduce back‑and‑forth.

[P21] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO per § 39.19 is fine, but the AD should explicitly allow electronic submission methods for international operators whose principal inspector is outside the U.S.

[P22] Directing AMOC submissions addressed to the person in paragraph (j)(3) is acceptable, but the AD must publish that contact and provide backup contacts to avoid delays if that individual is unavailable.

[P23] Requiring notification to the principal inspector/local manager before using an approved AMOC is reasonable; however, the AD should permit immediate temporary use of AMOC under emergency circumstances with post‑use notification.

[P24] Allowing AMOCs approved specifically for this AD to satisfy repair/modification requirements is beneficial, but the AD should clarify whether previously approved AMOCs for other ADs are transferable or require re‑approval.

[P25] The condition that AMOCs must be specifically approved for this AD is acceptable but may create redundant approvals; request guidance for streamlined cross‑recognition of equivalent AMOCs.

[P26] The June 9, 2023 comment‑by date (duplicative) appears inconsistent with the earlier March 25, 2022 date — the rule needs one clear current comment deadline and notification to stakeholders when deadlines change.

[P27] Repeating compliance obligation multiple times creates unnecessary duplication and might create interpretive conflicts; suggest consolidating compliance language and specifying exact deadlines for each required action.

[P28] The requirement to establish FAA‑approved corrosion program in maintenance records within 8 months (repeated) should include a model program or acceptable baseline (e.g., Viking PSM revision) to expedite approvals and ensure consistency.

[P29] The requirement to complete all initial tasks before further flight after establishing the program (repeated) conflicts with typical maintenance prioritization; recommend allowing an FAA‑approved risk‑based prioritization so non‑critical tasks need not ground the aircraft.

[P30] Mandating contacting the New York ACO Branch in paragraph (j)(3) for program approval is redundant with other AMOC routing rules and unfairly centralizes authority; allow local FAA offices to accept documentation and issue provisional approvals.

[P31] Stating that the corrosion program must include initial inspections to find corrosion and cracking is vague — the AD should reference the specific inspection checklist and inspection methods (e.g., dye penetrant, borescope) to ensure repeatability.

[P32] Requiring repetitive inspection intervals without specifying minimum and maximum intervals leaves operators and inspectors uncertain; provide numeric baseline intervals by component or environment (e.g., every 100 flight hours for saltwater operations).

[P33] Mandating corrective actions including repairs and corrosion inhibitors is broad; the AD should specify acceptable materials, limits of allowable corrosion, and reference repair data or structural limits for rework versus replacement.

[P34] The requirement to report Level 2 or Level 3 corrosion to Viking within 30 days after inspections (post‑AD effective date) may conflict with operator confidentiality and foreign data transfer laws; request clarification on data handling and cross‑border reporting obligations.

[P35] Requiring operator identity in corrosion reports (repeated) raises competitive concerns and should allow redaction for public release or specify that Viking will treat operator identity as proprietary.

[P36] Requiring airplane serial number in reports (repeated) is necessary but the AD should define format and whether manufacturer serial number, FAA registration, or other identifier is required.

[P37] Including aircraft hours time‑in‑service at inspection in reports (repeated) should clarify accepted timekeeping source and whether cycles or landings count for float operations.

[P38] Requiring listing of inspection task number and date in reports (repeated) needs cross‑reference to the PSM revision used and instructions on how to report when using an operator‑modified inspection numbering system.

[P39] Requiring airplane operating environment in reports (repeated) should specify granularity and include options for mixed‑use aircraft (e.g., both saltwater and gravel island operations) and how to report predominant environment.

[P40] Requiring the type/extent/location/cause of damage in reports (repeated) should permit submission of photographs, measurement data, and non‑destructive inspection reports as attachments and allow preliminary reports with final follow‑up.

[P42] AMOC routing to principal inspector/local FSDO per § 39.19 (repeated) must accommodate modern electronic filing systems and international operators who may lack a U.S. principal inspector.

raw_output:
[P1] The Nov 27, 2020 comments due date is unreasonably short for affected operators and third-party stakeholders to perform necessary technical review and prepare meaningful comments; request extension of the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] The rule lacks clear notice of when the AD was issued and when the 30-day comment window began; clarify the AD effective date to ensure stakeholders know the exact available time to comment.

[P2] The compliance obligation is overly rigid and provides no grace for supply-chain delays or COVID-19 pandemic impacts; request inclusion of language allowing reasonable delays where parts, tooling, or qualified personnel are unavailable.

[P2] The phrase "unless already done" is vague regarding how operators document prior compliance; require explicit recordkeeping standards and acceptable evidence for previously completed work.

[P3] The 60-day deadline to revise maintenance/inspection programs to incorporate Bombardier Temporary Revision ALI–0721 is impracticable for large fleets that must coordinate program changes across multiple manuals and regulatory approvals; request extension to 120 days.

[P3] The provision fails to specify which version of operator manuals must be revised (e.g., continuous airworthiness maintenance program, scheduled maintenance manual, or both); clarify the exact manuals and sections to be updated.

[P4] Making the initial compliance time "whichever is later" between the Bombardier revision and 60 days after AD effective date could create ambiguity for tasks without explicit due dates in the Bombardier revision; require that tasks without dates be scheduled within 60 days of the AD effective date.

[P4] The rule does not address how to treat aircraft that enter the fleet after the effective date; request explicit compliance times for newly acquired or newly delivered aircraft.

[P5] The absolute prohibition on using alternative actions or intervals after program revision, absent AMOC approval, is unduly prescriptive and undermines operator flexibility; recommend allowing grandfathering of operator-established equivalent procedures that demonstrably provide an equivalent level of safety.

[P5] The prohibition could conflict with existing bilateral or national regulatory variations for foreign operators; request explicit harmonization language or allow recognized foreign regulatory approvals.

[P6] While AMOC exceptions are allowed, the AD does not provide expected timelines for FAA consideration of AMOC requests; request maximum processing time (e.g., 60–90 days) to avoid prolonged grounding or operational disruption.

[P6] The AMOC exception is conditioned on FAA approval but does not state evidentiary standards or data needed; request a checklist of required data to make AMOC submissions consistent and expedite review.

[P7] Centralizing AMOC approval authority in the New York ACO Branch may create bottlenecks for operators based elsewhere; request provision for regional ACOs to approve AMOCs for routine deviations to reduce administrative delay.

[P8] The requirement to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 lacks clarity about electronic submission options and secure channels; request explicit acceptance of secure electronic submissions and a contact email.

[P9] The direct submission address references an ATTN: Program Manager but the proposal does not include a mailing address or clear email/phone contacts in the preamble; require full contact details and an alternate point of contact for time-sensitive submissions.

[P10] Requiring notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC is reasonable, but the AD does not specify how much advance notice is required; request a standard notice period (e.g., 72 hours) and an emergency exception.

[P11] The requirement that manufacturer instructions be accomplished using a method approved by the FAA Manager (New York ACO), TCCA, or MHI RJ's TCCA DAO could create conflicts between authorities; request a prioritized approval pathway and dispute resolution process.

[P11] The AD does not allow for alternate accepted industry standards when manufacturer instructions are ambiguous; request clarification that industry-standard practices may be accepted where manufacturer guidance is silent.

[P12] Requiring the DAO-authorized signature for DAO approvals is appropriate, but the AD does not specify acceptable electronic signature methods; request acceptance of verifiable electronic signatures to streamline approvals.

[P13] The same Nov 27, 2020 comments due date for the Boeing AD duplicates timing concerns expressed for the MHI AD and should be extended to permit coordinated responses from operators affected by both ADs.

[P14] The Boeing AD's compliance requirement "unless already done" again lacks detail on acceptable documentation to prove prior compliance; request a recordkeeping format or examples of acceptable substantiation.

[P15] Incorporating Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 757–27A0158 RB by reference without publishing full task details in the NPRM limits stakeholders' ability to evaluate cost and feasibility; request that Boeing service information be included in the docket or summarized in the preamble.

[P15] The AD mandates "all applicable actions" at times in the Compliance paragraph but does not define "applicable" for mixed-configuration fleets; request guidance on how operators determine applicability for modified vs unmodified airframes.

[P16] The exception that replaces the bulletin's original issue date with this AD's effective date may inadvertently change task intervals; request explicit examples and a table mapping original dates to effective dates to avoid misinterpretation.

[P17] Allowing operation under an operator's FAA-approved MEL when the modified SIF is inoperable is sensible, but the AD should require that MEL relief be consistent with the specific failure modes introduced by the modification; suggest language requiring risk assessment documentation.

[P18] The MEL condition that the FAA-approved MEL must include provisions addressing the modified SIF needs clarification whether temporary MEL revisions or master MEL deviations are acceptable and what approval process is required.

[P19] Centralizing AMOC authority for the Boeing AD in the Los Angeles ACO Branch may delay approvals for operators outside the LA region; request delegation to regional ACOs for routine AMOCs.

[P20] The instruction to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or responsible Flight Standards Office should explicitly permit submission via the FAA's electronic AMOC submission portal to expedite processing.

[P21] The direct submission instruction references "the person identified in paragraph (k)(1)" but the proposed rule excerpt does not reproduce that identification; provide the actual name/contact to avoid confusion.

[P22] Allowing AMOC requests to be emailed to 9-ANM-LAACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is helpful, but the AD should state expected confirmation of receipt and typical processing timeframes to provide certainty to operators.

[P23] The requirement to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC lacks guidance on the form of notification (written, electronic) and required content; request a minimum content template and allowance for emergency situations.

[P24] Permitting Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to be used is efficient, but the AD does not require Boeing to submit their rationale or technical data to the FAA for transparency; request that Boeing ODA approvals used as AMOCs be documented in the FAA docket or made available to affected operators.

[P25] The condition that AMOC repair/modification methods must meet the airplane's certification basis could disadvantage in-service modifications that have no explicit certification basis; request guidance on how to demonstrate equivalence where the original certification basis is silent.

[P26] Requiring AMOC approvals to specifically reference this AD is standard, but occasionally cross-referencing multiple ADs is necessary; request allowance to reference multiple ADs when a single AMOC addresses several related AD requirements.

[P27] Automatically approving previously approved AMOCs from AD 2017–26–10 for corresponding provisions may be inappropriate if the new AD's scope or context differs; request an explicit review and validation step rather than blanket reauthorization.

[P27] The rule does not identify which specific AMOCs from AD 2017–26–10 correspond to provisions of this AD; require a cross-reference list for operator clarity.

[P3] The AD does not specify whether training on the new maintenance tasks is required for maintenance personnel; request an explicit training requirement or confirmation that existing qualifications suffice.

[P15] There is no economic analysis of the cost impact of performing all required actions from Boeing's bulletin; request a regulatory flexibility analysis and cost estimate for small operators.

[P3] For operators under foreign oversight, the AD should clarify whether incorporation of Bombardier Temporary Revision ALI–0721 satisfies equivalent national requirements or whether separate approvals are needed.

[P5] The prohibition on alternative intervals may conflict with approved operator reliability programs that use condition-based maintenance; request an explicit exception for programs with FAA- or foreign-authority-approved CMMS/CBM processes demonstrating equal safety.

[P11] Requiring TCCA or TCCA DAO concurrence for manufacturer instruction approvals may introduce international coordination delays; request parallel review timelines and a single-point contact to coordinate FAA/TCCA/DAO approvals.

[P12] The DAO-signature requirement should clarify whether delegation to a specific DAO role or a named individual is necessary, and whether updated DAO authorization lists will be published.

[P2] The AD lacks a provision addressing liability or insurance implications for operators who follow AMOCs approved under this AD; request clarification that use of approved AMOCs does not shift liability absent negligence.

[P7] Stakeholders request that the FAA publish historical AMOC approval metrics (turnaround times, denial reasons) for the New York ACO Branch to allow operators to plan resources and timelines.
