[P1] The June 18, 2018 initial comment deadline is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60 days to allow stakeholders time for technical and legal analysis.

[P1] The July 2, 2018 reply comment deadline does not provide sufficient time after the initial comments; reply comments should be due 45 days after the initial comment deadline.

[P1] The rule’s statement that comments are “due on or before June 18, 2018” creates uncertainty about whether postmarks count; the agency should clarify whether filings are considered timely based on receipt date, postmark date, or electronic timestamp.

[P2] The July 16, 2018 deadline to submit PRA comments to OMB is inconsistent with the June 18 and July 2 FCC deadlines and should be synchronized to avoid confusion about separate comment processes.

[P2] The provision permitting PRA comments to OMB lacks instructions on where and how to label such submissions; the FCC should provide a designated email address and OMB PRA control number to ensure proper routing.

[P3] The reference to WC Docket No. 17-144 should also require filers to include the docket number on the first page of any PDF or paper submission to prevent misfiling.

[P3] The methods listed for submitting comments identified by WC Docket No. 17–144 are not enumerated in the text; the rule should explicitly list acceptable methods (ECFS, mail, hand delivery, courier) in the provision itself.

[P4] The permission to request reasonable accommodations does not specify a reasonable advance notice period; the FCC should state a minimum notice (e.g., 7–10 business days) for accessible documents and interpreter services.

[P4] The rule should require the FCC to provide accessible versions of key rulemaking documents (e.g., Word or tagged PDF) automatically on request and to publish alternative formats on the docket without requiring individual requests.

[P5] Citing §§ 1.415 and 1.419 without summarizing their implications may confuse stakeholders unfamiliar with those rules; the provision should briefly explain what filings are permitted and any format requirements.

[P6] The ECFS link is provided, but the rule does not explain required metadata fields (e.g., docket number, contact info); the FCC should specify required ECFS filing fields to avoid rejected or miscategorized submissions.

[P6] The rule should confirm whether attachments to ECFS filings are subject to file size limits or file type restrictions and provide guidance for submitting large technical exhibits.

[P7] Requiring an original and one copy for each paper filing is outdated and burdensome; the Commission should accept a single paper copy or convert to entirely electronic filings to reduce paper waste.

[P7] The provision should clarify whether the “original” must be signed and whether electronic signatures are acceptable on paper filings.

[P8] The obligation to submit two additional copies for each additional docket or rulemaking number could create excessive duplication for large multi-docket filings; instead require a single extra paper copy per additional docket number or allow cross-reference to a master copy.

[P8] The rule should clarify whether the two additional copies must be identical paper copies, or whether photocopies or printed PDFs suffice.

[P9] While multiple delivery options are permitted, the rule should explain which delivery methods are considered timely if delivered on a deadline day (e.g., if USPS mail is used, is the postmark date controlling).

[P10] Requiring all filings to be addressed to the Commission’s Secretary may conflict with electronic submission procedures; the provision should clarify how electronic filers should format the “addressed to” requirement.

[P11] The specific delivery location (Room TW–A325) should include hours of acceptance and security procedures to prevent filers from being turned away or delayed.

[P11] The rule should provide alternative hand-delivery locations for filers located outside the DC area or specify whether courier companies may leave filings at a central mailroom.

[P12] Mandating that hand-delivered filings be secured with rubber bands or fasteners is unnecessary and could interfere with document handling; the FCC should allow reasonable means of bundling (e.g., binder clips) and not mandate rubber bands.

[P12] The provision should explain whether filings with multiple attachments should be stapled or clipped, and whether comb-bound submissions are acceptable.

[P13] Requiring that envelopes and boxes be disposed of before entering the building raises sanitary and environmental concerns; the FCC should clarify what disposal means and whether filers may use reusable containers at drop-off.

[P13] The rule should provide a secure place outside the building for sealed envelopes to be opened and scanned to protect confidential information rather than mandating disposal.

[P14] Directing commercial overnight mail (other than USPS Express and Priority) to 9050 Junction Drive, Annapolis Junction MD, requires filers to know which couriers are acceptable; the FCC should list accepted carriers and provide clear recipient names for delivery.

[P14] The proposal lacks guidance on liability and tracking for overnight deliveries sent to the Annapolis Junction address; the FCC should state whether deliveries there are considered received upon arrival and how to obtain proof of receipt.

[GENERAL] The rule contains many detailed physical delivery requirements but insufficiently emphasizes electronic filing as the preferred method; the FCC should explicitly encourage ECFS filings and phase out onerous paper requirements.

[GENERAL] Several provisions may conflict with current 47 CFR procedures or the Public Notice system; the FCC should perform a consistency review and cite cross-references to existing procedural rules to avoid confusion.

[GENERAL] The rule should include explicit accommodations and procedures for commenters located outside the United States, such as acceptable international courier addresses and time zone considerations for deadline compliance.

[P1] The rule lacks transparency and justification for grouping the 48 contiguous states into exactly three geographic areas rather than using more granular regions; request that the agency publish the data and methodology used under §1250.328(d)–(e) to support the three-area decision.

[P1] Grouping all states into three areas may dilute representation for states with unique production characteristics (e.g., egg type, seasonality); commenters request an impact analysis showing how producers in each state will be affected.

[P1] The proposed grouping process appears to be fixed; suggest including a periodic review provision (e.g., every 5 years) to re-evaluate geographic groupings based on shifts in egg production patterns.

[P1] Legal commenters: the rule may conflict with the Administrative Procedure Act if the grouping was made without adequate notice-and-comment analysis; request the agency provide the administrative record and alternatives considered.

[P2] Area I list appears to truncate “Virginia” as “Virgini”—typo needs correction to avoid ambiguity about which state is included.

[P2] Several northeastern states (e.g., New York, Pennsylvania) have substantially different production scales; placing them in the same Area I may unfairly advantage larger-state interests; request sub-area or seat weighting to address intraregional disparities.

[P2] Consumer/animal welfare advocates: Area I grouping fails to account for states with higher prevalence of cage-free facilities; urge that board composition reflect production practices, not just geography.

[P3] Area II omits several states typically considered central (e.g., Kansas is listed under Area III); commenters request clarification of the rationale for assigning Kansas to Area III rather than Area II.

[P3] Industry commenters: Area II as defined (Arkansas, Oklahoma, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Missouri, Ohio, Tennessee, and Wisconsin) clusters diverse producers (broiler-associated states vs. egg-specialized states); ask for data showing these ten states constitute the intended “central” production profile.

[P3] Legal comment: ensure that the list of states for Area II is complete with appropriate punctuation and that no states are accidentally omitted due to drafting errors.

[P4] Area III includes both large producers (California, Iowa) and small producers (Montana, Idaho); assigning them to the same area could skew representation—ask for seat allocation to reflect production concentration within Area III.

[P4] The rule lists Iowa in Area III (West) despite Iowa being geographically central/midwest; this anomalous placement raises concerns about arbitrary boundary drawing—request map and justification.

[P4] Environmental and rural advocates: Area III includes states with significant smallholder/independent producers; recommend safeguards to ensure these producers have access to Board nominations and are not dominated by large corporate producers.

[P5] The apportionment formula (area’s share of U.S. egg production × 18 seats) requires transparency—request the specific production percentages used and the date range/source of production data.

[P5] Commenters challenge use of a fixed 18-seat multiplier without rounding rules—need to specify how fractional seat allocations will be handled (e.g., rounding, largest remainder method) to avoid disputes.

[P5] Small-state producers: if an area’s calculated share yields fewer than one seat (after multiplication and rounding), the rule must specify minimum representation guarantees to comply with statutory fairness obligations.

[P5] Statistical/legal analysts: clarify whether the “share of U.S. egg production” is measured by number of eggs, dozens, shell eggs vs. processed eggs, or by value; the metric materially affects seat apportionment.

[P6] Assigning exactly 6 seats to each Area I, II, and III contradicts the apportionment formula in P5 and could produce malapportionment if production shares are unequal; request explanation for why the formula is overridden by equal allocation.

[P6] Equal 6-6-6 distribution could violate the statute’s requirement that representation reflect production proportions; recommend either adjusting the multiplier or providing legal justification for equal seats.

[P6] Industry stakeholders in high-production areas will object that equal seats dilute their influence; request sensitivity analysis showing representation outcomes under both equal-seat and production-weighted models.

[P6] Equity advocates: equal seats could underrepresent regions with historically underrepresented minority producers; ask for demographic analysis of how the 6-seat allocation affects board diversity.

[P7] Requirement for alternates to be appointed from the same area is reasonable, but the rule must clarify appointment process, qualifications, and whether alternates have voting rights only when primary members are absent.

[P7] Concern about potential for coordinated control: same-area alternates may be selected by the same nominators as principals, enabling single interests to effectively control both positions; propose conflict-of-interest safeguards and staggered terms for alternates.

[P7] Clarify whether alternates count toward quorum requirements and whether alternates may attend closed sessions; request explicit procedural rules to avoid governance disputes.

[P7] Legal commenters: specify whether alternates are subject to the same eligibility requirements, disclosure, and recusal obligations as primary board members to ensure transparency and compliance.

[P1] The prohibition in §17.41(a)(1) is overly broad because it extends all endangered-wildlife prohibitions to the streaked horned lark without tailoring to the lark’s specific conservation needs or population distribution, potentially criminalizing minor, non-harmful activities by private landowners.

[P1] The rule fails to define who is “subject to U.S. jurisdiction,” creating uncertainty for tribal governments, transboundary landowners, and contractors working on federal projects; this ambiguity should be clarified.

[P2] The import/export prohibition (§17.41(a)(1)(i)) is unnecessary for a predominantly local migratory bird and may unduly restrict scientific exchange of specimens and genetic material; the rule should explicitly allow transfers for bona fide scientific research under streamlined permitting.

[P2] The cross-reference to §17.21(b) in the import/export prohibition does not account for modern electronic transfers of genetic sequences or digital data; the Service should state whether digital/genomic transfers are covered.

[P3] Applying the general “take” standard at §17.21(c)(1) (§17.41(a)(1)(ii)) without specifying thresholds (e.g., incidental vs. purposeful, numbers, habitat vs. individual) will create enforcement uncertainty for farmers and landowners; the Service should specify numerical or contextual limits.

[P3] The take prohibition could criminalize routine land management (e.g., mowing) if a lark is present; the rule must include clear safe-harbor provisions or timing windows to avoid unintended liability.

[P4] The possession prohibition (§17.41(a)(1)(iii)) referencing §17.21(d)(1) could impede rehabilitation work by wildlife centers if it does not expressly allow licensed rehabilitators to possess injured larks; an explicit exemption for permitted rehabilitators is needed.

[P4] The rule should clarify whether dead specimens found on private property may be collected for scientific study by landowners or permitted entities without violating the possession ban.

[P5] The commerce prohibition (§17.41(a)(1)(iv)) may conflict with agricultural supply chains (e.g., sale of hay or seed from fields where larks nest); guidance is needed that routine commerce in goods is not prohibited absent intent to trade the bird.

[P6] The sale/offer-for-sale prohibition (§17.41(a)(1)(v)) is ambiguous regarding incidental inclusion of feathers or parts in estate collections or materials; the agency should define “sale” to avoid penalizing heirs or museums.

[P7] The general exceptions in §17.41(a)(2) are welcome but too dependent on references to other sections; the Service should consolidate critical exceptions within this rule for clarity to stakeholders.

[P8] The permit exception (§17.41(a)(2)(i)) should include expedited review timelines and lower fees for small landowners and conservation partners conducting habitat-preserving activities.

[P9] The take allowances at §17.41(a)(2)(ii) that reference multiple endangered-wildlife and migratory-bird sections are confusing; commenters request a plain-language summary of what types of take are permitted and under what circumstances (e.g., emergency removals, scientific take).

[P10] The §17.31(b) cross-reference (§17.41(a)(2)(iii)) should be explained in-line; otherwise landowners will not know when take described in §17.31(b) is lawful.

[P11] The incidental-take permission (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)) is crucial but currently too narrowly defined by activity lists; commenters request inclusion of other common lawful activities (e.g., utility maintenance, military training) or a mechanism to add activities without rulemaking.

[P12] The airport hazardous-wildlife management exception (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(A)) is appropriate, but the rule should require airports to follow an approved wildlife hazard management plan and recordkeeping to demonstrate that actions were necessary and minimized harm.

[P13] The hazing allowance (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(A)(1)) should specify acceptable hazing methods and prohibit inhumane techniques; airports need clear guidance on approved deterrents and training requirements for personnel/contractors.

[P14] The habitat modification allowance (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(A)(2)) for airports lacks required mitigation or monitoring standards; removing vegetation could degrade nearby lark habitat — the rule must require pre- and post-activity surveys and avoidance corridors.

[P15] The “routine repair and maintenance” permission for roads/runways (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(A)(3)) excludes upgrades/new construction, but the rule does not define “routine”; airports need definitions and examples to determine when a project crosses into “upgrade” and requires consultation/permit.

[P16] The explicit prohibition on upgrades/construction of new roads/runways under the airport exception (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(A)(3) exclusion) could freeze necessary safety improvements; the Service should allow upgrades if accompanied by compensatory mitigation and Service review.

[P17] The accidental aircraft strike exception (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(B)) is reasonable for non-Federal lands, but the distinction between Federal and non-Federal lands is unclear for airport operations on mixed-ownership properties; clarify applicability to joint-use airports and federally leased lands.

[P18] The agricultural practices exception (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(C)) limited to Washington and Oregon is geographically arbitrary; commenters from adjacent states or tribal lands request extension or explanation for the state-limited scope.

[P19] The crop-related activities allowed (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(C)(i)) should include timing constraints (nesting season windows) to prevent breeding-season losses; current text could permit planting/harvesting that destroys nests.

[P20] The road maintenance allowance for farms (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(C)(ii)) excludes improvement or construction of new roads, but the rule does not specify thresholds (e.g., widening by how many feet constitutes “improvement”); farmers need measurable criteria.

[P21] The prohibition on road improvements/new construction under the agricultural exemption (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(C)(ii) exclusion) could impede necessary farm access and modernization; permit pathways or mitigation options should be provided.

[P22] Allowing grazing at “normally acceptable and established levels” (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(C)(iii)) is vague — commenters request a mechanism to define “normally acceptable” (e.g., AUMs, stocking rates) and allow site-specific adjustments.

[P23] The hazing of geese or predators as an agricultural practice (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(C)(iv)) must be limited to non-lethal measures unless authorized under a permit; the rule should prohibit unauthorized lethal control.

[P24] Maintenance of irrigation and drainage (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(C)(v)) must include conditions to avoid destruction of nests during typical maintenance windows; require pre-maintenance nest searches and seasonal restrictions.

[P25] The noxious weed management permission (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(D)) allows herbicides, fumigation, and burning but the “avoid impacts to non-target plants to the maximum extent practicable” obligation (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(D) obligation) is vague and unenforceable without protocols; request explicit best-management practices and monitoring.

[P26] The list of allowed noxious-weed methods (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(D)(1)-(4)) omits integrated pest management (IPM) planning and alternatives assessment; the Service should require or encourage IPM and non-chemical controls before herbicide or fumigation.

[P27] The obligation to avoid impacts to non-target plants “to the maximum extent practicable” (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(D) obligation) could be interpreted to prohibit effective weed control in many cases; commenters ask for clear standards and an appeals process for operational managers.

[P28] The mowing allowance (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(D)(1)) should include seasonal timing to avoid destroying nests — require mowing outside the breeding season or after surveys confirm no nesting.

[P29] Allowing herbicide and fungicide use (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(D)(2)) without specifying approved compounds, application rates, buffer zones, and licensed applicator requirements risks collateral harm to larks and other species.

[P30] The fumigation permission (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(D)(3)) is alarming for conservation groups; fumigants can kill invertebrate prey and disrupt ecosystems — require strict limitations and alternatives analysis.

[P31] Burning as an allowed method (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(D)(4)) must require permits, seasonality constraints, smoke management, and post-burn monitoring to ensure burns benefit lark habitat and do not destroy nests.

[P32] The habitat restoration exception (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(E)) is valuable but conditioned on “formal approved conservation plans” — commenters worry plan approval could be slow or bureaucratic; propose a streamlined review for qualified conservation partners.

[P33] The phrase “determined by the Service to be consistent with this rule” in §17.41(a)(2)(iv)(E) is vague; commenters request objective criteria for Service consistency determinations and timelines for approvals.

[P34] The permit and exception structure heavily relies on cross-references to many other sections, which will be difficult for landowners, airports, and farmers to navigate; the Service should publish a single plain-language compliance guide with flowcharts.

[P35] Legal advocates note the rule should explicitly address interactions with state endangered-species laws and tribal authorities to avoid preemption conflicts and ensure collaborative conservation.

[P36] Law enforcement and legal-professional commenters request clarification of penalty provisions and evidentiary standards for alleged violations under the new prohibitions to ensure due process and consistent enforcement.

[P37] Small-business representatives request an economic exclusion or de minimis safe harbor for incidental, negligible impacts (e.g., one or two nests disturbed) to avoid disproportionate regulatory burden.

[P38] Conservation NGOs support exceptions for habitat restoration (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(E)) but request mandatory monitoring, adaptive management, and reporting requirements tied to any permitted incidental take to ensure measurable conservation outcomes.

[P39] Tribal governments request a specific consultation and co-management clause permitting tribal conservation practices and cultural uses consistent with the rule and exempting traditional activities when they do not threaten species recovery.

[P40] The rule does not specify monitoring, reporting, or recordkeeping requirements for activities relying on incidental-take exceptions (airports, farms, weed control); commenters ask the Service to require standardized reporting to evaluate impacts.

[P41] The restrictions on upgrades/new road construction across several exceptions (P15, P21) could impede infrastructure resiliency projects unrelated to habitat; commenters request a process for expedited review and mitigation when upgrades are necessary for safety or climate adaptation.

The rule fails to define who is “subject to U.S. jurisdiction,” creating uncertainty for tribal governments, transboundary landowners, and contractors working on federal projects; this ambiguity should be clarified.

The import/export prohibition (§17.41(a)(1)(i)) is unnecessary for a predominantly local migratory bird and may unduly restrict scientific exchange of specimens and genetic material; the rule should explicitly allow transfers for bona fide scientific research under streamlined permitting.

The cross-reference to §17.21(b) in the import/export prohibition does not account for modern electronic transfers of genetic sequences or digital data; the Service should state whether digital/genomic transfers are covered.

Applying the general “take” standard at §17.21(c)(1) (§17.41(a)(1)(ii)) without specifying thresholds (e.g., incidental vs. purposeful, numbers, habitat vs. individual) will create enforcement uncertainty for farmers and landowners; the Service should specify numerical or contextual limits.
The take prohibition could criminalize routine land management (e.g., mowing) if a lark is present; the rule must include clear safe-harbor provisions or timing windows to avoid unintended liability.

The possession prohibition (§17.41(a)(1)(iii)) referencing §17.21(d)(1) could impede rehabilitation work by wildlife centers if it does not expressly allow licensed rehabilitators to possess injured larks; an explicit exemption for permitted rehabilitators is needed.
The rule should clarify whether dead specimens found on private property may be collected for scientific study by landowners or permitted entities without violating the possession ban.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The commerce prohibition (§17.41(a)(1)(iv)) may conflict with agricultural supply chains (e.g., sale of hay or seed from fields where larks nest); guidance is needed that routine commerce in goods is not prohibited absent intent to trade the bird.

The sale/offer-for-sale prohibition (§17.41(a)(1)(v)) is ambiguous regarding incidental inclusion of feathers or parts in estate collections or materials; the agency should define “sale” to avoid penalizing heirs or museums.
The general exceptions in §17.41(a)(2) are welcome but too dependent on references to other sections; the Service should consolidate critical exceptions within this rule for clarity to stakeholders.
The permit exception (§17.41(a)(2)(i)) should include expedited review timelines and lower fees for small landowners and conservation partners conducting habitat-preserving activities.

The take allowances at §17.41(a)(2)(ii) that reference multiple endangered-wildlife and migratory-bird sections are confusing; commenters request a plain-language summary of what types of take are permitted and under what circumstances (e.g., emergency removals, scientific take).
The §17.31(b) cross-reference (§17.41(a)(2)(iii)) should be explained in-line; otherwise landowners will not know when take described in §17.31(b) is lawful.

The incidental-take permission (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)) is crucial but currently too narrowly defined by activity lists; commenters request inclusion of other common lawful activities (e.g., utility maintenance, military training) or a mechanism to add activities without rulemaking.

The airport hazardous-wildlife management exception (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(A)) is appropriate, but the rule should require airports to follow an approved wildlife hazard management plan and recordkeeping to demonstrate that actions were necessary and minimized harm.

The hazing allowance (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(A)(1)) should specify acceptable hazing methods and prohibit inhumane techniques; airports need clear guidance on approved deterrents and training requirements for personnel/contractors.

The habitat modification allowance (§17.41(a)(2)(iv)(A)(2)) for airports lacks required mitigation or monitoring standards; removing vegetation could degrade nearby lark habitat — the rule must require pre- and post-activity surveys and avoidance corridors.

[P1] The deadline to receive comments by November 29, 2021 is unreasonably short and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow affected operators, suppliers, unions, and independent maintenance organizations sufficient time to analyze the Boeing bulletin and submit technically informed comments.

[P1] Small operators and foreign operators will likely not see the NPRM in time to comment by November 29, 2021; the FAA should provide targeted outreach and an extended comment period to ensure equitable participation.

[P2] The requirement to "meet all requirements of this AD within the specified compliance times" lacks flexibility for unexpected supply-chain delays for parts and tooling; the rule should explicitly allow hardship relief or temporary extensions where parts are unavailable and safety is not compromised.

[P2] The phrase "unless already accomplished" is ambiguous — please clarify whether actions accomplished under earlier service bulletins issued by Boeing constitute compliance for the entire AD or only for specific tasks.

[P3] Requiring operators to "perform all applicable actions in the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin at the specified times" effectively incorporates by reference proprietary Boeing material; the FAA should either include the required actions in the AD text or make the full Boeing bulletin freely and publicly available in the docket.

[P3] Industry commenters request that the AD explicitly list which airplanes (by model, line number, and configuration) the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin applies to, since the current text may cause confusion and inconsistent application across fleets.

[P4] Replacing "Original Issue date of Requirements Bulletin" with "the effective date of this AD" may cause unintended changes to compliance timing calculations for operators who already started work under the bulletin; the FAA should provide worked examples showing how compliance times convert for in-progress actions.

[P4] Legal commenters note that substituting the effective date may shorten compliance windows compared to the bulletin's original intent; the FAA must explain the legal basis for this substitution and demonstrate it does not violate notice-and-comment rights.

[P5] The restriction that any instructions that would have required contacting Boeing must instead be performed only using methods approved under paragraph (i) could create a bottleneck if FAA resources for AMOC processing are limited; the FAA should permit Boeing ODA-approved instructions as an interim measure.

[P5] Independent MROs and third-party repair providers object to removal of direct Boeing contact for repair instructions because Boeing's engineering data may be necessary for safe repair; the AD should allow use of Boeing-approved instructions where the ODA certifies them and the operator documents compliance.

[P6] The delegation of AMOC approval authority to the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch concentrates discretion in a single office and may delay approvals for non-U.S. operators; the FAA should allow other FAA certification offices to approve AMOCs or provide a clear SLA for processing times.

[P6] Safety advocacy groups want assurance that the criteria used by the Seattle ACO Manager to approve AMOCs are transparent and publicly available; request publication of guidance on evaluation factors and precedent AMOC decisions.

[P7] Requiring AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or Flight Standards Office creates an extra administrative step that could be redundant; industry suggests allowing direct submission to the certification office with simultaneous notification to the principal inspector.

[P7] The provision does not specify acceptable formats or required technical content for AMOC submissions to the principal inspector; request the FAA to publish a checklist of information required to validate and expedite an AMOC review.

[P8] Direct submissions addressed to the certification office manager must identify the person in paragraph (j)(1), but paragraph (j)(1) is not included in this excerpt; commenters request that contact names, titles, and up-to-date contact information be included explicitly in the AD.

[P8] Privacy and FOIA concerns: operators may be reluctant to include proprietary technical data in direct submissions; the FAA should clarify how confidential/proprietary information will be handled and protected when sent to the certification office manager.

[P9] Allowing AMOC requests by email to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is helpful, but the rule should also permit secure file transfer for large engineering packages, and clarify whether encrypted attachments are accepted.

[P9] Cybersecurity teams request confirmation of maximum file size, accepted file formats, and acknowledgement/turnaround times for email-submitted AMOCs to avoid lost or delayed submissions.

[P10] The requirement to inform the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC could be impractical for international operators or for Part 129 operators without a U.S. principal inspector; the FAA should allow notice to the manager of the responsible Flight Standards Office or to a designated FAA representative via email as an alternative.

[P10] Operators request clarification of the acceptable timing for notification — e.g., how many days before implementing the AMOC the principal inspector must be informed — to prevent inadvertent noncompliance.

[P11] Permitting use of an AMOC for required repairs/modifications if approved by the authorized Boeing ODA is sensible, but the AD should require that Boeing ODA approvals be documented and submitted to the FAA for recordkeeping and auditability.

[P11] Consumer and safety advocates are concerned that reliance on Boeing ODA approvals may create conflicts of interest; they request that any ODA-approved alternative be independently reviewed by the FAA prior to widespread use.

[P12] Requiring that approved repairs/modifications meet the airplane's certification basis and explicitly reference this AD is appropriate, but operators seek clarification about how to demonstrate compliance with an earlier certification basis (e.g., if findings rely on earlier amendments or equivalent level of safety determinations).

[P12] Legal commenters note that the phrase "meet the certification basis of the airplane" may preclude novel but safe repair methods; request that the FAA provide a pathway for novel methods to be approved through an AMOC that documents safety equivalence.

[P5] Maintenance organizations request clarity on whether on-condition actions derived from contacting Boeing can be executed under the Boeing service provider network's authority, or if each repair must separately obtain FAA AMOC approval.

[P3] Labor unions representing maintenance technicians request that the AD specify training or qualification requirements for personnel performing the bulletin's required actions to ensure consistent and safe execution.

[P2] Operators note that some compliance times in the Boeing bulletin are calendar-based and others are flight-cycle based; the AD must specify which metric governs and how to account for aircraft with modified utilization profiles (e.g., during storage or ferry operations).

[P6] International civil aviation authorities will need to accept FAA AMOCs for continuing airworthiness oversight; the FAA should indicate how coordination with EASA and other authorities will be handled to avoid conflicting approvals.

[P1] Public interest groups request that the FAA reopen the comment period if substantive changes are made to the AD after November 29, 2021, to allow stakeholders to comment on revised provisions.

[P8] Airlines request that the FAA provide a single point-of-contact (name and phone) in paragraph (j)(1) for urgent technical discussions, not just an email address, to avoid delays during time-sensitive compliance windows.

[P12] Repair stations ask that the AD explicitly allow incorporation of previously FAA-approved repair data packages (e.g., STCs or minor alteration approvals) as satisfying the "must meet the airplane's certification basis" requirement, to avoid duplication of approvals.

[P1] The April 13, 2020 comment deadline is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60–90 days to allow operators, OEMs, unions, and independent MROs adequate time to analyze the AD and prepare technical comments.

[P1] The rule requires FAA to receive comments by April 13, 2020, but provides no mechanism for accepting late-filed substantive data; FAA should state a clear policy for accepting and considering late technical comments submitted within a reasonable grace period.

[P2] The applicability to all 737–600/–700/–700C/–800/–900/–900ER certificated in any category is overly broad; the FAA should exclude or differentiate cargo conversions, VIP/BBJ derivatives, and derivatives with modified avionics that do not use the referenced FCC OPS hardware.

[P2] The AD should explicitly list affected line numbers or serial number ranges rather than only model designations because many model 737s have varying avionics configurations that may not include the implicated FCCs.

[P3] The phrase "within the compliance times specified" is ambiguous because several compliance time references use different baselines (effective date vs. AD 2012 date); FAA should clarify the applicable baseline dates for each compliance action to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P4] The three-month inspection deadline measured from November 27, 2012 is impossible to meet for commenters today; FAA must clarify whether legacy compliance dates remain in effect or whether this AD repromulgates obligations with new effective dates.

[P4] Because paragraph (g) ties its 3-month inspection to an effective date in 2012, FAA should explain whether this AD is intended as a superseding or re-issuance and should provide a current compliance schedule consistent with the present AD effective date.

[P5] Requiring "before next flight" action when a listed OPS part number is found is operationally disruptive and could ground aircraft unexpectedly; FAA should allow a short operational window (e.g., 24–72 hours) for scheduled maintenance rather than an absolute "no flight" condition.

[P6] The mandate to install software listed in table 2 of ASB 737–22A1211 without allowance for operator-specific installation procedures raises safety and configuration-control concerns; FAA should require that installation follow the operator’s maintenance program and Boeing/rockwell-approved procedures, and allow time for change-control.

[P7] Requiring installation per Boeing ASB 737–22A1224 dated May 18, 2012 may be impracticable because some carriers no longer have access to legacy software packages or installation kits; FAA should permit equivalent Rockwell Collins/Boeing-specified installation media or updated packages.

[P8] The exception for OPS part numbers listed in table 2 is reasonable, but FAA must require documentation/certification demonstrating that the installed OPS version exactly matches table 2 — a general statement in the logbook is insufficient.

[P9] Termination of paragraph (g) requirements upon installation of an FCC OPS version approved after May 18, 2012 lacks a clear process for documenting termination in aircraft records and for demonstrating continued equivalence after future software updates.

[P10] Requiring approvals only by the Manager Seattle ACO, Manager BASOO, FAA, Boeing ODA, or international authority creates a narrow approval path that could delay urgent updates; FAA should allow other delegated ODA organizations or EASA equivalents to approve to expedite compliance.

[P11] The ODA-authorized signature requirement for approvals is overly prescriptive; FAA should accept electronic signatures and approvals issued via established ODA electronic workflows without requiring a specific pen-signed signature format.

[P12] The installation must be done in accordance with an approved method by the listed authorities, but FAA should explicitly allow the installation to be performed under an operator’s approved work card or MRO procedure when the method has been approved by one of the listed authorities.

[P13] Requiring the ODA-authorized signature for installation-method approvals duplicates P11 and could create administrative bottlenecks; FAA should accept ODA designees’ delegated approvals documented per established ODA procedures.

[P14] The 12-month window to inspect both FCC A and FCC B for vendor and version may be too long for operators with known configurations, yet too short for others; FAA should provide flexibility (e.g., allow record review or phased compliance for large fleets) and require compliance tied to scheduled maintenance events.

[P15] The allowance to use maintenance records in lieu of physical inspection is sensible but must require specific record elements (date of installation, software part number/version, approval certificate or work order reference) to ensure conclusiveness.

[P16] Requiring all actions in Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737–22A1322 RB within 12 months for Rockwell Collins FCCs with OPS P8.0 or P9.0 imposes significant workload on operators; FAA should provide an economic impact assessment and allow staged implementation for fleet operators with limited shop capacity.

[P16] The AD should clarify whether "all applicable actions" in the Requirements Bulletin includes optional non-mandatory insructions and should list critical versus recommended steps to avoid confusion during compliance.

[P17] The carve-out in (j)(2) is appropriate but the AD must mandate documentation in the aircraft maintenance records proving the airplane was not equipped with P8.0 or P9.0 at the time of the effective date.

raw_output:
[P1] The $0.41 per thousand board feet flat assessment unfairly burdens small domestic manufacturers who ship low-margin specialty products and should be graduated by company size or revenue.

[P1] The proposed $0.41/MBF rate lacks a published economic impact analysis demonstrating its necessity and proportionality to the Board’s stated program costs; the rule should include or reference that analysis.

[P2] The 15 million board feet annual exemption is too low to effectively exempt regional small producers; small mills that sell more than 15 MMBF only marginally above that threshold will face disproportionate new costs.

[P2] The exemption language “first 15 million board feet” is ambiguous for manufacturers with multiple affiliated entities — the rule should clarify whether the exemption is applied per legal entity, per parent company, or aggregated across related parties.

[P3] Calculating domestic manufacturers’ assessments based on volume “shipped within the United States” creates compliance complexity for manufacturers that both ship domestically and export; the rule should define “shipped” and how transfers to affiliates are treated.

[P3] The provision does not address how returns, defective shipments, or inventory transfers are credited; manufacturers need explicit rules for adjustments, refunds, and recordkeeping for shipped volumes.

[P4] For importers, basing assessments on “volume imported to the United States” without clarifying whether this refers to entries, shipments to bond, or final release creates customs administration conflicts; Customs Harmonized System (HTS) data reporting requirements should be specified.

[P4] The rule fails to designate who is the responsible party for imports involving multiple intermediaries (e.g., foreign seller, U.S. buyer, customs broker) — clarification is needed on which importer is obligated to pay.

[P5] Requiring the Board to review the assessment rate at least every 24 months is appropriate, but the rule should mandate that reviews include stakeholder notice, public comment, and transparent financials before any recommendation.

[P6] Allowing the Board to recommend rate changes to the Secretary without requiring an economic justification or impact statement could lead to arbitrary increases; recommendations should be accompanied by a cost-benefit analysis.

[P7] The vote threshold of “majority plus two” is unusual and could entrench existing Board leadership; the rule should justify this supermajority and assess whether it unduly shields rate changes from minority concerns.

[P7] It is unclear whether “majority of Board members plus two (exclusive of vacant seats)” requires a quorum calculation or absolute board-size calculation; the rule should specify the numeric vote requirement method.

[P8] The prohibition on rates below $0.35 and above $0.50 restricts flexibility; industry commenters will likely argue that the floor of $0.35 prevents the Board from lowering assessments in downturns, harming competitiveness.

[P8] Conversely, environmental and advocacy groups may comment that the $0.50 cap is too low to fund robust conservation, marketing, or research programs the Board might need; they will request a higher ceiling tied to demonstrated program needs.

[P9] Requiring Secretary rulemaking for any change in the assessment rate (even within the $0.35–$0.50 range) introduces a slow, potentially burdensome process; the rule should allow interim rate adjustments by the Board with subsequent Secretary approval in emergencies.

[P9] Legal experts will likely comment that the Secretary’s rulemaking obligation must adhere to APA notice-and-comment timelines; the regulation should clarify expected timelines to avoid operational uncertainty.

[P10] The conversion factors (1 m3 = 0.423776001 MBF; 1 m2 = 0.010763104 MBF) are overly precise and may create rounding disputes in reporting; the rule should provide rounding rules and acceptable tolerances.

[P10] Importers using metric invoices will be disadvantaged if alternate widely used conversion conventions differ; commenters will request recognition of alternative conversion practices or reconciliation procedures.

[P11] Assessing HTSUS 4407.11.00 at $0.1737/m3 and $0.004412/m2 appears inconsistent with the $0.41/MBF domestic rate once conversions are applied; importers will request an explicit formula and worked examples showing equivalence.

[P11] Customs brokers and importers will request confirmation that assessments for HTS 4407.11.00 are to be collected at entry based on declared quantity and that discrepancies discovered later will be subject to audit adjustments.

[P12] For HTSUS 4407.12.00, commenters will ask whether composite or mixed shipments containing multiple HTS lines should be prorated by line or aggregated, and how to treat misclassified entries.

[P13] For HTSUS 4407.19.05, exporters from Canada may request a waiver or reciprocal treatment given existing cross-border cooperative programs; they will highlight double-charging risks if both U.S. importers and Canadian exporters face assessments.

[P14] For HTSUS 4407.19.06, small-volume importers will seek clarification on minimum billing increments (e.g., fractional cubic meters) and how the assessment is invoiced and collected.

[P15] For HTSUS 4407.19.10, hardwood versus softwood mixed items may be misclassified; stakeholders will request guidance on species verification procedures to avoid incorrect assessments.

[P16] For HTSUS 4409.10.05, importers of finished goods containing softwood components will ask whether processed items with incidental softwood content are subject to the assessment and how de minimis rules apply.

[P17] For HTSUS 4409.10.10, commenters will request clear rules on treatment of treated, painted, or otherwise modified lumber that might fall into different HTS headings — is the assessment due on the base lumber or on the finished product?

[P18] For HTSUS 4409.10.20, logistics providers will highlight the administrative burden of tracking square meters versus cubic meters and will request allowance to report using HTS quantities as declared to Customs.

[P19] For HTSUS 4409.10.90, duty drawback, re-exports, and temporary imports (e.g., for exhibits) should be excluded; commenters will ask for explicit exemptions and refund procedures for such situations.

[P20] For HTSUS 4418.99.10, importers of engineered wood products will seek clarification whether composite products containing only trace amounts of softwood are still assessed at the specified per-unit rates.

[P1] Timber industry associations will comment that the assessment rate should be indexed to an inflation metric (e.g., CPI) or tied to lumber price indices to preserve program funding real value over time, instead of periodic discrete reviews.

[P2] Environmental NGOs will request that the 15 MMBF exemption be conditioned on demonstrated sustainable forestry practices to avoid exempting producers engaged in poor stewardship.

[P3] Legal commenters will note potential Commerce Clause or preemption issues if state-level assessments or programs conflict with this federal assessment scheme and request preemption clarification.

[P4] Small importers will request phased implementation or delayed compliance timelines for import-assessment reporting to allow IT systems and Customs reporting changes to be made.

[P5] Trade associations will ask the Board to publish methodology, data, and minutes from the 24-month review to ensure transparency and enable meaningful public comment on recommended rate changes.

[P6] Some commenters will urge that any recommended increase require a two-thirds supermajority rather than “majority plus two” to ensure broader consensus for higher assessments that affect price competitiveness.

[P7] Industry cost-accounting experts will demand clear reconciliation procedures between MBF-based domestic assessments and cubic-meter/square-meter import assessments to prevent double assessments or calculation errors.

[P8] Importers will ask whether the per-cubic-meter assessments apply to product blends or reconstituted wood and propose specific HTS carve-outs or subheadings to reduce ambiguity.

[P9] Customs law firms will request that the Secretary’s rulemaking be administratively streamlined with expedited processing for Board-initiated rate changes to minimize market disruption.

[P10] Trade unions and workers’ advocates may comment that funds generated should be earmarked for workforce training and safety programs; otherwise they will oppose the assessment as a general tax without worker protections.

[P11] State forestry agencies will request coordination language to avoid overlapping programs and to ensure collected funds support both national promotion and state-level forest health initiatives where appropriate.

[P12] Small businesses will request an appeals process for disputed assessments, including administrative review and binding arbitration options, which is not described in the proposed provisions.

[P13] Data privacy advocates will request that the Board publish only aggregated assessment payment data and protect confidential business information submitted during audits or reviews.

[P14] Some commenters will argue the per-unit import assessment rates ($0.1737/m3; $0.004412/m2) are inconsistent with the MBF conversion precision (P10) and recommend simplifying to fewer significant digits to reduce compliance errors.

[P15] International trade policy experts will raise concerns that the import assessments tied to HTS codes could be construed as a trade barrier if applied differently to trading partners and ask for WTO-consistency analysis.

[P1] The provision allowing obtaining incorporated materials from listed sources (§ 82.31(a)) is vague because it does not specify whether electronic copies or only physical copies are considered acceptable; request clarification that digital access is authorized.

[P1] Industry commenters will request that the rule explicitly permit obtaining incorporated materials from an official online Federal Register or EPA website mirror to avoid relying solely on physical sources.

[P1] Legal commentators will note that incorporation by reference must meet 1 CFR part 51 requirements and ask the Agency to confirm conformity and provide the exact edition, date, and publisher for each incorporated document.

[P2] The permission to inspect approved incorporated material only at the EPA docket or NARA (§ 82.31(a)) imposes an undue burdensome in-person inspection requirement for remote stakeholders; recommend adding remote inspection or downloadable electronic copies.

[P2] State and local agencies will request that the EPA maintain an up-to-date electronic docket with unredacted copies of incorporated materials to ensure timely access for compliance and enforcement purposes.

[P3] The definition of "properly using" (§ 82.32(e)(1)) is overly broad and might subject operators to unpredictable enforcement based on "recommended procedures;" ask EPA to narrow the definition or list the specific mandatory vs. advisory practices.

[P3] Manufacturers and repair shops will seek clarity on whether "recommended procedures" are mandatory under "properly using" or are only guidance, because treating recommendations as obligations could make compliance impracticable.

[P3] Legal experts will argue that including "but not limited to" in the list of items that constitute "properly using" creates vagueness and due process concerns; request the Agency adopt a more definite list or provide a safe-harbor.

[P4] The requirement to operate equipment according to the manufacturer's operation and maintenance guide (§ 82.32(e)(1)) may conflict with aftermarket modifications or third-party repair instructions; request an exception where manufacturers no longer support older equipment or where alternative procedures are certified equivalent.

[P4] Small repair shops will comment that proprietary manufacturer guides are sometimes unavailable or costly; ask EPA to provide standard industry operating/maintenance guidance for compliance or allow reliance on SAE/industry standards.

[P5] The obligation to use equipment only with the controlled substance for which the machine is designed (§ 82.32(e)(1)) will complicate shops that service multiple refrigerants; request an allowance for equipment retrofits certified by independent testing bodies to handle additional refrigerants.

[P5] Equipment manufacturers will request clear labeling and certification procedures to demonstrate the refrigerant(s) for which a machine is designed to prevent enforcement ambiguity.

[P6] The requirement to recycle refrigerant before returning it to any MVAC including the source appliance (§ 82.32(e)(1)) is technically difficult in some recovery scenarios (e.g., mobile roadside repairs) and could prevent prompt service; request an exception for emergency repairs with subsequent documented recycling within a specified timeframe.

[P6] Automotive service associations will request a defined standard or test to demonstrate that on-site "recycle" meets an accepted threshold of contamination removal before returning refrigerant to a source appliance.

[P7] The obligation to either recycle recovered refrigerant on-site or send it off-site for reclamation (§ 82.32(e)(1)) imposes substantial costs on small shops without on-site recycling capacity; request phased compliance deadlines or financial assistance/subsidies.

[P7] Reclamation facilities will warn that increased off-site shipments may strain existing reclaimers; recommend EPA provide guidance on approved transport, labeling, and chain-of-custody to prevent improper handling.

[P8] Requiring recover-only equipment to meet Appendix F standards for refrigerants other than CFC–12, HFC–134a, and HFO–1234yf (§ 82.36(a)(7)) may stifle innovation for emerging refrigerants because Appendix F appears tailored to a limited set; ask EPA to clarify how Appendix F applies to newly developed refrigerants or to create an alternative performance-based standard.

[P8] Test labs and manufacturers will request the Agency to publish Appendix F test protocols, pass/fail criteria, and acceptable tolerances to ensure reproducible certification results.

[P9] Appendix F, 3.1's requirement that equipment be capable of extracting a specific non-CFC–12/HFC–134a/HFO–1234yf refrigerant from MVAC systems could necessitate multiple dedicated units for shops servicing mixed fleets; request allowance for modular or multi-refrigerant-capable equipment certified under SAE J3030 instead of a separate dedicated unit per refrigerant.

[P9] Fleet operators will note that many vehicles may have mislabeling or retrofits; ask EPA to provide protocols for identifying the refrigerant present and addressing cross-contamination scenarios.

[P10] Mandating SAE J2843 compliance for equipment that recovers and recycles HFO–1234yf (§ 82.36(a)(8)) effectively incorporates a private standard; request EPA to explicitly identify the edition (including date) of SAE J2843 being incorporated and confirm public availability or provide equivalent EPA test methods.

[P10] Independent testing organizations will request clarity on whether minor deviations from SAE J2843 (for practical reasons) will be permissible if the equipment demonstrates equivalent performance.

[P11] Requiring recover-only equipment for contaminated HFC–134a and/or HFO–1234yf to meet SAE J2851 (§ 82.36(a)(9)) raises concerns about how "contaminated" is defined and measured; request numerical contaminant thresholds and acceptable analytical methods.

[P11] Service providers will ask for guidance on handling refrigerant streams that are partially contaminated with oils or other substances and whether a certain contamination level allows on-site recovery versus mandatory off-site reclamation.

[P12] The requirement that equipment handling both refrigerants meet SAE J3030 (§ 82.36(a)(10)) may be technologically challenging and expensive; request a cost-benefit analysis and phased implementation timeline for small businesses.

[P12] Equipment manufacturers will ask EPA to state which SAE J3030 edition applies and whether dual-capable equipment must pass combined tests or separate tests for each refrigerant.

[P13] Allowing independent testing organizations to apply for EPA approval to certify equipment (§ 82.38(a)) is positive, but commenters will request transparent criteria, timelines, and conflict-of-interest safeguards for EPA approval of such organizations.

[P13] Consumer and environmental NGOs will urge EPA to require approved testing organizations to publish test results and methodologies to ensure accountability and reproducibility.

[P14] The obligation that applications be sent to a specific EPA address (§ 82.38(a)) may be outdated (only a physical address shown and truncated in the text); request EPA to explicitly permit electronic submissions and provide the complete mailing address, email, and instructions for secure file delivery.

[P14] Applicants will request the EPA publish a standardized application form and checklist for certifications to reduce administrative errors and processing delays.

[P3] Environmental advocacy groups will argue that "properly using" should explicitly include leak detection and repair timelines and recordkeeping to ensure emissions reductions, and request adding these specific obligations.

[P6] Regulators will need clarity on whether "recycle" includes only mechanical filtration/drying or also chemical treatment; ask EPA to define acceptable recycling processes and performance metrics.

[P7] Transportation regulations (DOT) compliance questions: commenters will ask how shipping recovered refrigerant off-site for reclamation interacts with hazardous materials regulations and request cross-reference guidance.

[P9] Repair shops will request guidance on how to demonstrate compliance with Appendix F when recovering refrigerants from heavily modified or non-standard MVACs (e.g., custom or vintage vehicles).

[P11] Trade associations will seek an appeal or variance process for equipment that cannot meet SAE J2851 due to supply chain or technical constraints, asking EPA to allow temporary waivers.

[P1] The blanket prohibition in §17.40(t)(1) is overly broad and fails to clearly define "persons under U.S. jurisdiction," creating uncertainty for NGOs, researchers, and companies about whether incidental take aboard foreign-flag vessels or activities by U.S. persons abroad are covered.

[P1] The regulation does not define "specified acts regarding the Dolphin and Union caribou DPS," leaving stakeholders unable to determine what conduct triggers liability under §17.40(t)(1).

[P1] The cross-reference to "except as provided in paragraph (t)(2) and §§17.4–17.5" is confusing and may create gaps; the rule should explicitly list the allowed exceptions within §17.40 to avoid misinterpretation.

[P2] The prohibition on import or export per §17.21(b) could unintentionally prohibit the return of lawfully acquired personal property (e.g., museum loans, genetic samples) unless an explicit research or repatriation exception is added.

[P2] The rule should clarify whether import/export prohibitions apply to incidental transport of caribou parts (e.g., in baggage, as part of mixed shipments) to avoid enforcement of trivial or inadvertent infractions.

[P2] Industry commenters will request a clear permitting pathway and processing timeline for imports/exports under §17.21(b), which is not described in the proposed text.

[P3] The prohibition on interstate or foreign commerce in the course of commercial activity (§17.21(e)) could criminalize resale of legally obtained artifacts (e.g., hides, antlers) in private sales; the rule should clarify applicability to antique or historic items.

[P3] The provision lacks an explicit monetary threshold or definition of "commercial activity," leaving businesses uncertain whether barter, incidental sales, or nominal fees are covered.

[P3] State fish-and-game agencies will request coordination language to allow regulated subsistence commerce or trade authorized by indigenous governments that may cross state lines, to avoid conflict with local customary practices.

[P4] The ban on sale or offer for sale (§17.21(f)) is likely to burden small retailers, taxidermists, and online marketplaces; the rule should provide safe harbors for de minimis transactions and bona fide educational or scientific sales.

[P4] The regulation should clarify how digital listings (e.g., images or offers on online platforms) that reference Dolphin and Union caribou parts are treated under the prohibition on offers for sale.

[P4] Legal experts will challenge the lack of explicit intent requirement for offers for sale, arguing the prohibition could reach mistaken or ambiguous communications and should require knowing or willful conduct.

[P5] Paragraph (t)(2) permissions are too narrow; stakeholders will request additional express permissions for scientific research, museum exchanges, and indigenous subsistence uses that are not clearly covered.

[P5] The phrase "notwithstanding the prohibitions" suggests permissions override prohibitions only where expressly stated; commenters will ask the agency to incorporate a general authorization for pre-existing lawful holdings and activities consistent with conservation.

[P6] Allowing import of "personal sport-hunted trophies legally hunted in and exported from Canada with accompanying hunting tags" (§17.40(t)(2)(i)) may incentivize cross-border sport hunting that could harm the DPS; conservation groups will request strict quotas, documentation verification, and proof of sustainability.

[P6] Indigenous and northern communities will request explicit clarification that traditional harvests and transfers of trophies for family or cultural reasons are exempt or facilitated and will ask that the rule not impede customary practices.

[P6] Customs and border agencies will request more detail on required documentation format, authentication standards, and processes for verifying Canadian hunting tags to prevent fraud.

[P7] The allowance for activities authorized by a §17.32 permit (§17.40(t)(2)(ii)) needs clearer timelines and standards for permit issuance; research institutions and industry need predictable review criteria and expedited processing for non-lethal research.

[P7] Conservation NGOs will request that §17.32 permit criteria include stringent mitigation, monitoring, and reporting requirements to ensure permitted activities do not further jeopardize the DPS.

[P7] The rule should clarify whether incidental take authorizations under §17.32 cover actions by U.S. subsidiaries of foreign companies and whether permits can be conditioned on mitigation measures in home countries.

[P8] Permitting activities under a captive-bred registration (§17.40(t)(2)(iii)) is appropriate, but the rule must define "captive-bred" for this DPS (e.g., generational requirements, documented lineage) to prevent laundering of wild-taken animals.

[P8] Zoos, conservation breeders, and registrants will request grandfathering provisions for existing captive-held animals and clear procedures for registration, inspection, and compliance to enable conservation breeding programs.

[P8] Animal welfare organizations will request that captive-bred registrations include minimum husbandry standards and oversight to ensure captive programs prioritize conservation, not commercial exploitation.

[P1] The proposed language omits enforcement provisions and penalties for violations of §17.40(t)(1); commenters will seek clarity on civil vs. criminal enforcement, fines, and administrative remedies.

[P2] Exporters and importers will request guidance on how the rule interacts with CITES listings and whether dual reporting or permits will be required.

[P3] Online marketplace operators will urge the agency to issue safe-harbor guidance and compliance tools to avoid disproportionate liability for third-party sellers under §17.21(e) and §17.21(f).

[P4] Private citizens concerned about inadvertent violations will request an amnesty or compliance period after final rule promulgation to allow disposition of existing legally acquired items without penalty.

[P5] Tribal governments will request government-to-government consultation language and an explicit exemption or permitting mechanism for indigenous subsistence, ceremonial, and cultural uses not clearly authorized under (t)(2).

[P7] Academic institutions will ask the agency to allow multi-year research permits under §17.32 with flexible renewal options and clear criteria for data sharing to support conservation decisions.

[P8] Potential registrants will request clarity on whether offspring of registered captive-bred animals can be sold, transferred interstate, or used for reintroduction, and what documentation is required.

[P1] Constitutional law experts may assert that the extraterritorial application implied by "persons under U.S. jurisdiction" must be narrowly tailored to avoid overbroad application to non-U.S. activities.

[P2] Transport and logistics companies will ask for clear carrier liabilities and exemptions when transporting mixed cargo that may inadvertently include caribou parts, to prevent supply chain disruptions.

[P3] The proposed prohibition on commerce should be accompanied by a compliance checklist and examples to aid regulated parties in understanding what transactions trigger the prohibition.

[P4] E-commerce platforms request a safe-harbor notice-and-takedown procedure to address suspected listings while preserving due process rights for sellers accused of offering prohibited items.

[P6] Hunters’ associations will request consistency with Canadian provincial regulations and a mechanism for reciprocal recognition of tags to streamline lawful trophy importation.

The rule should clarify whether import/export prohibitions apply to incidental transport of caribou parts (e.g., in baggage, as part of mixed shipments) to avoid enforcement of trivial or inadvertent infractions.
Industry commenters will request a clear permitting pathway and processing timeline for imports/exports under §17.21(b), which is not described in the proposed text.

The prohibition on interstate or foreign commerce in the course of commercial activity (§17.21(e)) could criminalize resale of legally obtained artifacts (e.g., hides, antlers) in private sales; the rule should clarify applicability to antique or historic items.

State fish-and-game agencies will request coordination language to allow regulated subsistence commerce or trade authorized by indigenous governments that may cross state lines, to avoid conflict with local customary practices.

The ban on sale or offer for sale (§17.21(f)) is likely to burden small retailers, taxidermists, and online marketplaces; the rule should provide safe harbors for de minimis transactions and bona fide educational or scientific sales.

The allowance for activities authorized by a §17.32 permit (§17.40(t)(2)(ii)) needs clearer timelines and standards for permit issuance; research institutions and industry need predictable review criteria and expedited processing for non-lethal research.
Conservation NGOs will request that §17.32 permit criteria include stringent mitigation, monitoring, and reporting requirements to ensure permitted activities do not further jeopardize the DPS.

The rule should clarify whether incidental take authorizations under §17.32 cover actions by U.S. subsidiaries of foreign companies and whether permits can be conditioned on mitigation measures in home countries.

Permitting activities under a captive-bred registration (§17.40(t)(2)(iii)) is appropriate, but the rule must define "captive-bred" for this DPS (e.g., generational requirements, documented lineage) to prevent laundering of wild-taken animals.

Zoos, conservation breeders, and registrants will request grandfathering provisions for existing captive-held animals and clear procedures for registration, inspection, and compliance to enable conservation breeding programs.

Animal welfare organizations will request that captive-bred registrations include minimum husbandry standards and oversight to ensure captive programs prioritize conservation, not commercial exploitation.
The proposed language omits enforcement provisions and penalties for violations of §17.40(t)(1); commenters will seek clarity on civil vs. criminal enforcement, fines, and administrative remedies.
Exporters and importers will request guidance on how the rule interacts with CITES listings and whether dual reporting or permits will be required.
Online marketplace operators will urge the agency to issue safe-harbor guidance and compliance tools to avoid disproportionate liability for third-party sellers under §17.21(e) and §17.21(f).

Private citizens concerned about inadvertent violations will request an amnesty or compliance period after final rule promulgation to allow disposition of existing legally acquired items without penalty.

Tribal governments will request government-to-government consultation language and an explicit exemption or permitting mechanism for indigenous subsistence, ceremonial, and cultural uses not clearly authorized under (t)(2).
Academic institutions will ask the agency to allow multi-year research permits under §17.32 with flexible renewal options and clear criteria for data sharing to support conservation decisions.
Potential registrants will request clarity on whether offspring of registered captive-bred animals can be sold, transferred interstate, or used for reintroduction, and what documentation is required.

Constitutional law experts may assert that the extraterritorial application implied by "persons under U.S. jurisdiction" must be narrowly tailored to avoid overbroad application to non-U.S. activities.

Transport and logistics companies will ask for clear carrier liabilities and exemptions when transporting mixed cargo that may inadvertently include caribou parts, to prevent supply chain disruptions.
The proposed prohibition on commerce should be accompanied by a compliance checklist and examples to aid regulated parties in understanding what transactions trigger the prohibition.
E-commerce platforms request a safe-harbor notice-and-takedown procedure to address suspected listings while preserving due process rights for sellers accused of offering prohibited items.
Hunters’ associations will request consistency with Canadian provincial regulations and a mechanism for reciprocal recognition of tags to streamline lawful trophy importation.
