parsed_claims.claim_text: The annual attestation deadline of November 1 (§ 413.232(e)) is administratively burdensome for small and rural ESRD facilities that lack dedicated compliance staff and should be extended to at least December 15 to allow reconciliation of year-end cost reports.

Requiring an attestation each year regardless of unchanged status duplicates existing reporting and imposes unnecessary paperwork; allow multi-year attestations for facilities with stable low-volume status (e.g., 3-year attestations).
The special January 3, 2012 deadline for PY2012 (§ 413.232(e)(1)) is obsolete and confusing in the regulatory text; remove or clearly mark as historical to avoid misinterpretation.
The December 31, 2014 deadline for PY2015 (§ 413.232(e)(2)) should be clarified as historical and not applicable to current or future attestations to prevent compliance errors.
The December 31, 2015 deadline for PY2016 (§ 413.232(e)(3)) is outdated and should be removed from current regulatory language.

The December 31, 2020 deadline for PY2021 (§ 413.232(e)(4)) overlaps with the general November 1 rule and the COVID-19 PHE provisions; CMS should clarify whether this date remains an exception or has been superseded.

The attestation must include a statement that the facility meets the low-volume definition (§ 413.232(g)), but CMS should provide a standardized attestation form/template to reduce inconsistent statements and simplify MAC review.

The <4,000 treatments threshold in each of the three prior cost reporting years (§ 413.232(b)(1)) is too rigid and may unfairly exclude facilities with marginal exceedances (e.g., 4,050 treatments due to short-term population shifts); propose a de minimis tolerance (e.g., 1–2% overage).

For PYs 2021–2023, allowing an alternative attestation for facilities affected by the COVID-19 PHE (§ 413.232(g)(4)) is reasonable, but CMS must define criteria for being “affected by the COVID-19 PHE” to prevent inconsistent application across MACs.

The COVID-19 exception permitting attestation of <2,000 treatments in any six months of 2020 (§ 413.232(g)(4)) may be susceptible to gaming (selecting lowest 6 months); require documentation of COVID-related disruptions (e.g., local PHE declarations, facility-level infection rates, patient transfers).

Requiring facilities using the COVID-19 exception to also attest they furnished ≥4,000 treatments in the payment year because of temporary patient shifting (§ 413.232(g)(4)(i)) creates an illogical condition for truly low-volume facilities and will disqualify facilities that remained low-volume but were nonetheless impacted by COVID; offer an alternative pathway for facilities that remained low-volume but had pandemic-related service disruptions.

The MAC’s instruction to multiply the six-month treatment total by 2 when using the COVID-19 exception (§ 413.232(g)(4)(ii)) is an arbitrary extrapolation that can distort actual annual utilization; CMS should instead require documentation of patient-shift patterns or allow prorated calculations based on verified transfer records.

Relying solely on as-filed or final settled 12-consecutive-month cost reports for verification (§ 413.232(h) and § 413.232(g) verification data) disadvantages recently opened facilities or those with late-settled reports; MACs should be permitted to use alternative reliable records (e.g., payroll/EMR logs) when cost reports are not reflective.

The requirement that, upon third-year attestation, the MAC verify as-filed cost reports and then adjust rates or recoup payments (§ 413.232(h), (h)(1), (h)(2)) could result in significant retroactive recoupments that threaten facility solvency; limit recoupment to a capped amount or allow an appeals/payment plan process.

If a MAC determines a facility does not meet low-volume definition and reprocesses claims to recoup payments (§ 413.232(h)(2)), affected facilities must be given clear notice, a minimum 60-day cure period to provide corrective documentation, and an independent appeals process prior to recoupment.

Including payment for calcimimetics in the ESRD PPS base rate beginning Jan 1, 2021 (§ 413.234(f)) without a transition for facilities that had separate calcimimetic reimbursement may disrupt budgeting; CMS should phase in the change or provide an informational transition period.

Using Medicare ESRD facility claims (837 institutional bill type 072X) for 2018–2019 to derive calcimimetic utilization and paid hemodialysis-equivalent treatments (§ 413.234(f)(1)(i)) may undercount non-Medicare patients and commercial buy-and-bill practices; CMS should adjust methodology to capture all facility-administered calcimimetics or use supplemental data sources.

Relying on weighted average ASPs based on CMS determinations (§ 413.234(f)(1)(ii)) may not reflect acquisition cost differences across facilities (e.g., 340B, contract pricing); CMS should permit regional or facility-level adjustments or exclude 340B-impacted claims from the national average.

The multi-step methodology to compute per-treatment calcimimetic payment (§ 413.234(f)(2)) lacks transparency on handling anomalies, outliers, or missing data for 2018–2019; CMS should publish the dataset, code, and step-by-step calculations for public review.

Aggregating total units of oral and injectable calcimimetics to determine utilization (§ 413.234(f)(2)(i)) conflates drugs with different dosing schedules and clinical indications; CMS should present separate per-treatment amounts for oral versus injectable formulations or weight by therapeutic equivalence.

Using 100% of the most recent calendar quarter ASP values to set price (§ 413.234(f)(2)(ii)) fails to reflect rapid price shifts or manufacturer discounts; consider using a multi-quarter average (e.g., most recent 4 quarters) to smooth volatility.

Multiplying utilization by price to compute total expenditures (§ 413.234(f)(2)(iii)) assumes full Medicare payment capture and ignores patient cost-sharing and secondary payers; CMS should explain whether adjustments for non-Medicare payments are made.

Dividing total calcimimetic expenditures by total paid hemodialysis-equivalent treatments to derive an average per-treatment payment (§ 413.234(f)(2)(iv)) will dilute payments for facilities with higher calcimimetic use; propose an adjustment factor or separate add-on for high-utilization facilities.

raw_output:
[P1] The June 16, 2017 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60 days to allow operators, suppliers, and labor groups adequate time for technical and economic analysis.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether electronic submissions received by 11:59 PM ET on June 16, 2017 will be accepted, to avoid rejection of timely comments due to time-zone or system issues.

[P2] § 39.13(f) is unclear about whether compliance times are mandatory absolute deadlines or whether operators may use established inspection programs to manage scheduling; request explicit guidance on scheduling flexibility and recordkeeping.

[P2] The provision should require FAA to publish a grace/transition policy for aircraft currently undergoing overlapping maintenance so operators aren’t forced to interrupt maintenance to meet AD deadlines.

[P3] Requiring all RC actions "in accordance with" the Boeing Alert Service Bulletin (§ 39.13(g)) gives Boeing’s service document de facto regulatory force without FAA technical findings; commenters request FAA to more clearly state it has reviewed and accepted all RC procedures or to identify any FAA-approved deviations.

[P3] Boeing’s Alert Service Bulletin referenced in § 39.13(g) contains ambiguities in task wording and figures; the AD should either correct those ambiguities or explicitly allow FAA-approved clarifications before RC actions are required.

[P4] Interpreting "after the original issue of this service bulletin" as "after the effective date of this AD" (§ 39.13(h)(1)) changes retroactivity and could impose new burdens on operators who relied on the original bulletin’s timeline; request justification and impact analysis for this reinterpretation.

[P4] The redefinition in § 39.13(h)(1) may create legal uncertainty for past work done per the service bulletin; request explicit statement that work performed in good faith before the AD effective date will not be considered noncompliant.

[P5] § 39.13(h)(2) removes Boeing as the source of follow-on instructions for RC actions and instead requires methods approved under paragraph (k); operators express concern about losing the OEM technical path and request FAA to streamline approval of Boeing-issued repair instructions as AMOCs.

[P5] This provision could create operational delays because obtaining AMOC approvals under paragraph (k) can be time-consuming; request an expedited approval pathway for Boeing-originated instructions or allow Boeing ODA approvals to satisfy the requirement.

[P6] The complex three-threshold compliance scheme for replaced skin panels in § 39.13(h)(3) is confusing; request FAA to provide worked examples and a clear algorithm to determine which of the three thresholds applies to a given panel.

[P7] The 50,000 flight-cycle threshold in § 39.13(h)(3)(i) is excessively long for panels previously not inspected internally; safety advocates request shortening this to prevent latent fatigue cracks going undetected.

[P7] Conversely, some operators with high-cycle fleets note that a 50,000-cycle compliance window is unachievable for older, high-utilization aircraft and request an earlier mandatory inspection (e.g., 30,000 cycles) or phased approach.

[P8] Using July 14, 2003 as a reference date for a 20,000-cycle clock in § 39.13(h)(3)(ii) creates recordkeeping burdens, especially for international operators who may not have accessible logbooks back to that date; request alternative metrics (hours or calendar time) or requirement to accept reasonable evidence.

[P9] The 4,500 flight-cycle requirement after this AD’s effective date (§ 39.13(h)(3)(iii)) may be unnecessarily short for some operators who need lead time to plan dockings; request allowance for scheduling within maintenance checks as long as inspections occur before the next heavy maintenance.

[P10] § 39.13(i) states that replacing a skin panel per the service bulletin ends repetitive inspections at that panel; airlines request clarification whether partial-panel repairs or alternate repair methods approved as AMOC also terminate repetitive inspections.

[P10] Repair stations and MROs request explicit acceptance of approved repair drawings that differ slightly from the service bulletin as valid replacements that terminate repetitive inspections, provided an AMOC or Boeing ODA approval exists.

[P11] Termination of AD 2003–14–06 requirements (§ 39.13(j)) upon completion of initial inspections could prematurely relieve operators of needed safeguards if inspections are superficial; safety groups request FAA to specify minimum inspection depth and reporting requirements before terminating the earlier AD.

[P11] Legal commenters request documentation requirements be specified to prove completion of the initial inspections used to terminate AD 2003–14–06, to prevent disputes during audits and enforcement.

[P12] Granting the Manager, LA ACO authority to approve AMOCs (§ 39.13(k)(1)) centralizes decision-making; operators outside the LA office request either regional delegation or clear timelines for AMOC processing to prevent bottlenecks.

[P13] The requirement to send AMOC requests to a principal inspector or local FSDO per § 39.13(k)(1) will delay submissions for foreign operators without a U.S. principal inspector; request permission to submit directly to the LA ACO in such cases.

[P14] The instruction in § 39.13(k)(1) to address information to the person in paragraph (l)(1) when sending directly to the ACO manager needs the paragraph (l)(1) contact to be published in the AD text or made available online; commenters ask for direct contact details and backup contacts.

[P15] Allowing AMOC requests via the specified email (§ 39.13(k)(1)) is helpful, but commenters request confirmation of email receipt procedures, expected response times, and security/confidentiality protections for proprietary data.

[P16] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC (§ 39.13(k)(2)) could be operationally burdensome for international operators without a U.S. principal inspector; request alternative notification pathways (e.g., to the local FSDO or the LA ACO) for foreign operators.

[P17] Permitting Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to be used (§ 39.13(k)(3)) is beneficial, but OEM ODA approvals should be explicitly accepted as equivalent to FAA AMOC approvals for timely safety-critical repairs to avoid duplication and delays.

[P18] The requirement in § 39.13(k)(3) that repairs/modifications meet the airplane certification basis and explicitly reference this AD may be impossible for some legacy repairs whose substantiation documents predate the AD; request guidance on how to reference the AD in legacy paperwork.

[P19] The requirement to perform all steps labeled RC, including substeps and figures (§ 39.13(k)(4)(i)), may eliminate reasonable operator flexibility; request FAA to allow limited deviations where equivalent safety can be demonstrated without needing a formal AMOC.

[P20] The "RC Exempt" exception (§ 39.13(k)(4)(i)) must be clearly defined — commenters request an explicit list of RC Exempt steps in the service bulletin or the AD to prevent inconsistent interpretations.

[P21] Requiring an AMOC for any deviation from RC steps (§ 39.13(k)(4)(i)) could create excessive certification workload for trivial deviations (e.g., tool changes); request a risk-based threshold for deviations that would require AMOCs.

[P22] Allowing deviations from non-RC steps under an operator’s maintenance program (§ 39.13(k)(4)(ii)) is appropriate, but operators request FAA to confirm whether using standard approved alternative procedures (e.g., company-specific NDT methods) is acceptable without further FAA review.

[P22] Maintenance providers request clarification that deviation under § 39.13(k)(4)(ii) does not require immediate notification to FAA so long as RC steps remain achievable and records demonstrate return to airworthiness.

[P3] Legal commenters note the AD’s incorporation-by-reference of Boeing service material in § 39.13(g) raises FOIA and public-access concerns; request that all incorporated materials be made available publicly at no cost or included in the docket.

[P6] Small operators and regional carriers note that tracking the replaced skin panels identified in table 9 (per § 39.13(h)(3)) will require significant record searches and request FAA to provide a manufacturer-supplied list by N-number/serial number where feasible.

[P7] Labor unions representing maintenance technicians request additional training requirements or acceptable qualification standards be added before RC internal inspections are performed, given the complexity of Part 8 tasks referenced by § 39.13(h)(3).

[P8] International regulators and foreign operators ask FAA to coordinate harmonization with EASA/other authorities for the July 14, 2003 reference in § 39.13(h)(3)(ii) to avoid conflicting compliance calendars.

[P15] Aviation privacy advocates request clear rules on what proprietary technical data may be redacted when emailing AMOC requests to the specified email address under § 39.13(k)(1), and assurance that proprietary data will be protected.

[P12] Consumer/safety groups request transparency of AMOC approvals granted by the LA ACO under § 39.13(k)(1), including making redacted AMOCs publicly available so the public can evaluate safety equivalence.

raw_output:
[P1] The November 1, 2017 deadline is unreasonably short for stakeholders who require internal review and coordination across legal, regulatory, and technical teams; request an extension of at least 60 days for meaningful participation.

[P1] The rule's singular deadline for both electronic and paper comments could cause confusion; ask FDA to explicitly confirm that simultaneous receipt (electronic or paper) by Nov 1, 2017 is acceptable and to clarify time-zone handling.

[P2] Requiring electronic comments to be filed by November 1, 2017 is redundant with P1 and P3; suggest harmonizing language to avoid inconsistent enforcement and to state whether submission timestamps on Regulations.gov will govern timeliness.

[P2] Many small organizations and individuals lack reliable internet access or staff to file before Nov 1, 2017; urge FDA to accept electronic comments received within 24 hours of the deadline when technical failures on Regulations.gov are documented.

[P3] The paper comment timeliness rule relies on postal/courier postmarks or delivery receipts, but does not address lost mail; request that FDA accept documented proof of timely mailing (e.g., certified mail receipt) even if delivery is delayed.

[P3] Hand-delivery receipt procedures are not fully described (hours, address verification); ask FDA to publish detailed procedures and extended hand-delivery hours near the deadline to prevent inadvertent late filings.

[P4] Requiring use of Regulations.gov and following its instructions may exclude stakeholders unfamiliar with the portal; recommend step‑by‑step guidance and a dedicated helpdesk/phone line for submission assistance.

[P4] Regulations.gov has known file size/type limitations; request explicit guidance on accepted file formats and maximum attachment sizes and an alternate electronic route for large technical attachments.

[P5] The requirement that comments with confidential information be submitted as written/paper submissions may deter whistleblowers who fear mailing sensitive materials; propose an encrypted electronic upload option that ensures confidentiality without mailing.

[P5] The rule does not specify how FDA will verify confidentiality claims for paper submissions; ask FDA to outline the review process, timelines, and criteria for accepting confidentiality designations.

[P6] Specifying a single Dockets Management Staff address for paper submissions creates a single point of failure and delays; urge FDA to allow multiple mailroom locations or secure drop boxes at regional FDA offices.

[P6] The provision does not specify acceptable courier companies or whether signature-required services are necessary; request clarification to avoid rejected or delayed deliveries.

[P7] Posting paper comments and attachments to the public docket except for properly marked confidential information risks inadvertent disclosure of sensitive data; recommend a standardized confidentiality cover sheet template and pre-screening before public posting.

[P7] The exception for confidential information should require FDA to notify submitters when redaction or withholding occurs; ask for a notice-to-submitter policy and an appeal process for disputed confidentiality determinations.

[P8] Forcing all confidential submissions to be paper-based may expose them to physical security risks during transit; request an option for encrypted electronic submission to a secure FDA mailbox with access controls.

[P8] The requirement excludes those who need to include large confidential datasets—paper copies may be impractical; ask FDA to accept secure electronic media (e.g., encrypted USB) via courier with chain-of-custody documentation.

[P9] Requiring two copies (one confidential, one redacted) is burdensome and ambiguous about acceptable redaction methods; request guidance on acceptable redaction practices and whether electronic redacted versions are acceptable.

[P9] The rule should clarify whether the redacted copy may be submitted electronically to reduce mailing burden; propose permitting one paper confidential copy plus one electronic redacted version.

[P10] Requiring both copies to be submitted to a single Dockets Management Staff creates logistics issues; request confirmation that both copies must be simultaneous and whether one can be emailed to a docket contact after delivery.

[P11] Mandating specific docket numbers (FDA–2012–N–1210 and FDA–2004–N–0258) in all submissions is prone to typographical error; urge FDA to allow submissions referencing either docket number or to accept submissions that clearly identify the rule even if docket numbers are omitted, with a grace period to correct errors.

[P11] The rule does not state how missing or incorrect docket numbers will be handled; ask FDA to adopt a practice of treating submissions as timely if they can be reliably associated with the docket by staff, even if the submitter omitted the exact docket number.

[P12] Placing the burden solely on submitters to remove confidential/personal data is unfair; request that FDA provide clear instructions and examples of information considered personally sensitive and offer an FDA redaction assistance service prior to posting.

[P12] The obligation to ensure comments do not include confidential information could chill candid feedback; request a safe-harbor process where submitters can request FDA staff to review and redact personal data before public posting.

[P13] Allowing name/contact on a cover sheet to be withheld from public posting could be exploited by bad actors; ask FDA to define who can use this option and require a legitimate justification (e.g., trade secret, safety risk) rather than permitting blanket anonymity.

[P13] The cover-sheet confidentiality measure may conflict with transparency expectations for corporate commenters; request that corporate filings disclose at least company identity publicly, even if personal contact details are placed on a confidential cover sheet.

[P14] Requiring the cover-sheet information to be labeled "confidential" is vague; ask FDA to specify exact labeling language and placement to ensure consistent treatment and avoid accidental public posting.

[P14] The rule should require a certification statement that the submitter has legal authority to assert confidentiality over the cover-sheet information, to prevent frivolous confidentiality claims.

[P15] The prohibition on disclosure "except as allowed by applicable disclosure laws" is overly broad; request that FDA enumerate the specific statutes/regulations under which they may disclose confidential info and require notice to submitters prior to disclosure.

[P15] Legal experts will note that 21 CFR 10.20 includes provisions for FOIA disclosures; ask FDA to commit to notifying submitters and allowing them to contest releases before making disclosures beyond the docket.

[P16] The proposed compliance dates (≥$10M by Jan 1, 2020; <$10M by Jan 1, 2021) create a cliff that disadvantages mid-sized firms; request a graduated compliance schedule tied to more granular revenue bands or a phase-in by product complexity.

[P16] The $10 million sales threshold is arbitrary and lacks explanation of why it differentiates implementation burdens; ask FDA to justify the threshold using empirical cost estimates or consider adjusting it upward to reflect inflation and operational realities.

[P16] The two-tier compliance dates may incentivize artificial restructuring of companies to fall below $10M; request anti-avoidance provisions preventing firms from gaming the threshold through related-entity transfers.

[P16] The proposed dates may conflict with existing state requirements and supply-chain timelines; ask FDA to coordinate with states and provide transition guidance for labeling inventories produced before the compliance dates.

[P17] FDA's stated non-enforcement intention for the July 26, 2018 and July 26, 2019 dates lacks binding commitment; request a formal, written enforcement guidance or rule amendment that clearly confirms non-enforcement for those dates during rulemaking.

[P17] Industry needs clarity on how enforcement discretion will be applied (e.g., warnings vs. penalties); ask FDA to publish criteria and timelines for exercising discretion so regulated entities can plan.

[P18] Limiting comments to only the extension of compliance dates is unduly restrictive and may prevent stakeholders from addressing related implementation issues in context; urge FDA to accept substantive comments on any aspect of the underlying regulation to inform agency decision-making.

[P18] Legal commenters will argue that constraining the scope of responses violates public-participation best practices; request FDA explicitly state that substantive comments on other issues will still be considered in parallel dockets.

[P19] The VA comment deadline identical to FDA's Nov 1, 2017 may cause confusion among stakeholders who participate in both; request coordination and a consolidated submission option to avoid duplicative filings.

[P19] Veterans' advocacy groups may need more time to compile patient-impact data; ask VA for at least a 60‑day extension on the comment deadline to allow meaningful participation.

[P20] Requiring VA commenters to state the RIN (2900–AQ06) is prone to clerical error; ask VA to accept clear indicia of the rule (title and docket) and to not reject or discard comments for minor RIN mistakes.

[P20] The VA should provide a template or sample header for comments that ensures correct referencing of the RIN and reduces administrative burdens on submitters.

[P21] Requiring appointments to inspect comments in person is burdensome for public-interest groups and researchers; ask VA to provide remote access to comment files or extended viewing hours to accommodate different schedules.

[P21] The phone number-based appointment system may result in inconsistent access; request that VA publish an online scheduling tool and ensure staff are responsive, especially near deadlines.

[P22] The VHA obligation to ensure providers meet professional standards is broad; request that VA specify measurable quality metrics and credentialing procedures that will apply to telehealth providers under this rule.

[P22] Providers and unions need clarity on how standard-of-care expectations will be enforced across virtual encounters; ask VHA to issue detailed guidance outlining documentation, supervision, and malpractice coverage requirements.

[P23] The mandate for equal quality and access regardless of beneficiary or provider location within a State conflicts with existing state scope-of-practice laws and interstate licensure barriers; request VA guidance on how it will reconcile conflicts with state law and whether it will seek interstate compacts or federal preemption.

[P23] Rural service providers may lack resources to deliver identical levels of care; ask VHA to define "same high level of care" with realistic benchmarks and to provide funding or technical assistance to under-resourced facilities to meet that standard.

[P23] The requirement to ensure equal access "no matter where in a State" may impose disproportionate burdens on small community clinics; recommend phased implementation with metrics and support for clinics that need infrastructure upgrades.

[P1] The one-year compliance deadline in § 68.10(b) is unworkably short for many facilities and should be extended to at least 24–36 months to allow time for coordination with local responders and hiring/training of personnel.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether the “specified date” in § 68.10(b) is calendared from publication in the Federal Register or from the effective date of the final rule to avoid legal uncertainty.

[P2] Requiring development of exercise plans within four years under § 68.10(d) is too lenient for high-risk Program 3 facilities; EPA should require sooner completion (e.g., within 18 months) for Program 3 processes.

[P2] The provision at § 68.10(d) lacks a required content list for the exercise plans—EPA should specify minimum elements (objectives, participants, metrics, resources) to ensure consistency.

[P3] The two-year trigger for the public meeting requirement in § 68.10(e) for qualifying accidents creates an unnecessary delay in public disclosure; the timeframe should be shortened to 90 days to align with § 68.210(b).

[P3] § 68.10(e) should define “qualifying accident” precisely or cross-reference an explicit definition to prevent inconsistent interpretation by owners/operators.

[P4] The five-year compliance date in § 68.10(f) for §§ 68.160(b)(21) and 68.180 is too long given the potential public safety benefits; EPA should phase in a shorter schedule and require interim progress reports.

[P4] The rule should specify enforcement consequences if owners/operators fail to meet the § 68.10(f) deadline for complying with § 68.160(b)(21) and § 68.180.

[P5] § 68.54(a) obligates training/testing of current and newly assigned process employees but does not require documentation standards; EPA should mandate training records format, retention period, and proof of competency.

[P5] The requirement in § 68.54(a) should explicitly include contractors and temporary workers who operate or directly support covered processes.

[P6] The “at least every three years” refresher interval in § 68.54(b) is insufficient for high-turnover facilities and for processes with seasonal hazards; EPA should require risk-based refreshers (annual for high-risk).

[P6] The phrase “or more often if necessary” in § 68.54(b) is vague—EPA should define objective triggers (incident, near-miss, process change) that mandate immediate refresher training.

[P7] § 68.54(d) obligates training before startup after a major change but does not define “major change”; EPA should adopt the same definition used elsewhere in RMP/PSM guidance to ensure consistency.

[P7] The rule should require documented verification (e.g., sign-off) that operators received training on new/updated procedures under § 68.54(d) before restart.

[P8] The certification requirement in § 68.58(a) for triennial compliance evaluations must require the identity and qualifications of the certifying official and retention of supporting evidence.

[P8] § 68.58(a) lacks a requirement to correct deficiencies found during the triennial evaluations within a fixed timeframe; EPA should require corrective action plans and timelines.

[P9] The obligation in § 68.60(a) to investigate incidents that could have “reasonably” resulted in a catastrophic release is ambiguous; EPA should provide criteria or examples to reduce subjective under-reporting.

[P9] The rule should mandate that incident investigations under § 68.60(a) be conducted by personnel with specified qualifications and independence from affected operations to avoid conflicts of interest.

[P10] § 68.60(c) requires a summary with minimum content but omits required timelines for completion; EPA should require the summary be completed within 30–60 days of investigation close.

[P10] The regulation should require that investigation summaries under § 68.60(c) be made available to designated local emergency planning committees (LEPCs) and, except where CBI is validly asserted, to the public.

[P11] Requiring the date of the incident in § 68.60(c)(1) is appropriate, but EPA should also require timestamps and local time zone identification to aid cross-jurisdictional analyses.

[P12] § 68.60(c)(3) demands a description of the incident—EPA should require standardized incident classification codes to enable aggregated analysis across facilities.

[P13] The mandate in § 68.60(c)(4) to list contributing factors should require root cause analysis using recognized methodologies (e.g., 5 Whys, fault tree) and documentation of methodology used.

[P14] § 68.60(c)(5) requires recommendations from investigations but should also require assignment of responsible parties, deadlines, and verification of implementation.

[P15] The five-year retention period for investigation summaries in § 68.60(f) is too short for longitudinal safety analyses; EPA should extend it to at least ten years or align with OSHA PSM record retention.

[P16] § 68.65(a) requires completion of written process safety information before a PHA but does not define acceptable sufficiency—EPA should specify minimum technical data (e.g., process flow diagrams, safety limits, material properties).

[P16] The schedule cross-referenced in § 68.67 should be included in the regulatory text or guidance and must account for new facilities and transferred ownership scenarios.

[P17] The triennial certification of compliance in § 68.79(a) for the subpart should require submission to EPA or state agency, not just internal certification, to allow oversight and public accountability.

[P17] § 68.79(a) should require that the compliance evaluation include review of contractor performance and policies, not solely facility employees.

[P18] § 68.81(a) mirrors § 68.60(a) but for another subpart—EPA should harmonize investigation standards across both subparts to avoid duplicative or conflicting obligations.

[P18] The provision in § 68.81(a) should require notification to EPA or the appropriate state agency when an incident that could reasonably have resulted in a catastrophic release occurs, within a defined timeframe (e.g., 24 hours).

[P19] § 68.81(d) requires a report with minimum contents but needs deadlines for report completion and submission to agencies and LEPCs.

[P20] Including the date of incident under § 68.81(d)(1) is necessary; EPA should also require inclusion of precise location (coordinates) and affected process unit identifiers.

[P21] § 68.81(d)(2) requires date investigation began—EPA should require that investigations commence within a specified short period (e.g., 48–72 hours) after incident discovery.

[P22] The description requirement in § 68.81(d)(3) should mandate inclusion of photographs, diagrams, and measurement data where available to support findings.

[P23] § 68.81(d)(4) should require categorization of contributing factors into human, equipment, management, and external to facilitate trending and prevention strategies.

[P24] Recommendations required by § 68.81(d)(5) should be tracked to closure with documented verification and a deadline; otherwise recommendations may never be implemented.

[P25] § 68.93(b) requires providing emergency response plans and contact info to local organizations but does not require affirmative confirmation of receipt; EPA should require documented acknowledgment from LEPCs/fire departments.

[P25] The rule should require that emergency response plans provided under § 68.93(b) be current and updated within 30 days of any changes to contacts or procedures.

[P26] Requiring provision of an emergency response plan “if one exists” (§ 68.93(b) item) creates a loophole—EPA should require all covered stationary sources to have a written emergency response plan.

[P27] § 68.93(b) should require that the emergency action plan provided to local responders (§ 68.93(b) item) include clear roles, mutual aid agreements, and resource inventories.

[P28] Updated emergency contact information (§ 68.93(b) item) should have a required update frequency (e.g., annually and within 7 days of change) and require distribution verification.

[P29] The consultation obligation to establish exercise schedules (§ 68.93(b)) lacks a required minimum frequency for field exercises for Program 3 processes; EPA should set a minimum (e.g., biennial field exercises).

[P30] The requirement to request a meeting with LEPCs/fire departments (§ 68.93(b) item) should require these meetings to occur within a defined time window after the request (e.g., 60–90 days) to be effective.

[P31] § 68.93(d) states classified information disclosure is controlled by applicable law; the rule should provide a clear process mechanism for handling national security–classified process safety information in coordination with federal agencies.

[P32] The requirement in § 68.93(e) to provide a sanitized version of CBI to local responders is appropriate but needs clarity on what sanitization is acceptable and a process for emergency-only full-disclosure under secure conditions.

[P33] Asserting CBI using the same substantiation process as §§ 68.151–68.152 (§ 68.93(e)) will be burdensome; EPA should allow an expedited substantiation route for emergency responder use to avoid delays that could impede preparedness.

[P34] The prohibition against claiming five-year accident history information as CBI (§ 68.93(e)) is essential, but EPA should clarify whether aggregated or anonymized versions are permissible as non-CBI.

[P35] Requiring a generic category when chemical names are claimed as CBI (§ 68.93(e)) is acceptable but EPA must provide standardized category lists to prevent inconsistent or overbroad claims.

[P36] Annual notification mechanism exercises (§ 68.96(a)) are appropriate, but EPA should allow synchronous exercises across multiple nearby facilities to coordinate regional response and reduce responder fatigue.

[P36] § 68.96(a) should clarify whether exercises “before [specified date]” apply retroactively to exercises already conducted and whether facilities can credit recent exercises toward compliance.

[P37] The consultation to establish field exercise frequency (§ 68.96(b)(1)(i)) must require written agreements with local responders on scheduling and scope to avoid later disputes about adequacy.

[P38] The expectation that field exercises include multiple tests (§ 68.96(b)(1)(ii)) should be accompanied by minimum performance metrics and evaluation criteria to ensure quality of exercises.

[P39] Tests of public and agency notification procedures in § 68.96(b)(1)(ii) should explicitly require use of actual alerting systems (reverse-911, sirens) during exercises where permissible, not just tabletop simulations.

[P40] § 68.96(b)(1)(ii) requirement to test evacuations and medical treatment should include obligations to measure evacuation times and medical triage capability, with target benchmarks.

[P41] Tests of communications systems (§ 68.96(b)(1)(ii) item) must include interoperability with local public safety radio systems and backup communications; EPA should require demonstration of interoperability.

[P42] Mobilization of facility emergency personnel and contractors (§ 68.96(b)(1)(ii) item) should require verification of contractor availability under emergency contracts and documentation of response times.

[P43] Coordination with local emergency responders in field exercises (§ 68.96(b)(1)(ii) item) should require inclusion of mutual aid partners and regional hazmat teams where applicable.

[P44] Emergency response equipment deployment (§ 68.96(b)(1)(ii) item) testing should include functional testing of specialized containment and detection equipment and proof of maintenance logs.

[P45] The catch-all “any other actions identified” (§ 68.96(b)(1)(ii) item) could be abused to minimize exercise scope; EPA should require that any deviations from the core exercise elements be documented and justified.

[P46] The consultation requirement for tabletop frequency (§ 68.96(b)(2)(i)) should require written scheduling commitments and minimum frequency for Program 3 processes of once every two years, not once every three.

[P47] The requirement to conduct a tabletop exercise before [DATE 7 YEARS AFTER EFFECTIVE DATE] and every three years thereafter (§ 68.96(b)(2)(i)) is too delayed for many sources—EPA should shorten the initial deadline to within 24 months for Program 3 sources.

[P48] Tabletop exercises must include outside stakeholders (e.g., nearby community representatives, hospitals) as called for in § 68.96(b)(2)(ii) to ensure real-world planning and community preparedness.

[P49] Discussion of public and agency notification procedures in tabletop exercises (§ 68.96(b)(2)(ii) item) should require review of actual notification messages and translation/accessible communication planning for vulnerable populations.

[P50] Inclusion of evacuations and medical treatment procedures in tabletop exercises (§ 68.96(b)(2)(ii) item) should require coordination with local hospitals and EMS and verification that surge capacity plans were discussed.

[P51] Identification of facility emergency personnel and contractor responsibilities (§ 68.96(b)(2)(ii) item) should require documented role assignments and redundant backups to avoid single points of failure.

[P52] Discussion of coordination with local emergency responders (§ 68.96(b)(2)(ii) item) should require evaluation of responder capabilities (SCBA, decontamination, detection) and identification of capability gaps.

[P53] Procedures for deploying emergency response equipment (§ 68.96(b)(2)(ii) item) in tabletop exercises should require cost and logistic discussions for prolonged incidents and mutual aid activation thresholds.

[P54] The “any other actions” clause for tabletop exercises (§ 68.96(b)(2)(ii) item) should be limited and any additions publicly disclosed in exercise planning documents.

[P55] The 90‑day timeframe to prepare an evaluation report after each exercise (§ 68.96(b)(3)) is reasonable, but EPA should require interim after-action debriefs within 7 days to capture immediate lessons.

[P56] Evaluation reports (§ 68.96(b)(3) item) must protect personal privacy—requiring names and organizations of participants (§ 68.96(b)(3) item) raises personnel privacy and security concerns and should allow redaction or limited distribution.

[P57] The report requirement to include exercise scenario description (§ 68.96(b)(3) item) should not create security risks; EPA should allow sensitive tactical details to be sanitized before public release while ensuring LEPC/responder access.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The one-year compliance deadline in § 68.10(b) is unworkably short for many facilities and should be extended to at least 24–36 months to allow time for coordination with local responders and hiring/training of personnel.
The rule should clarify whether the “specified date” in § 68.10(b) is calendared from publication in the Federal Register or from the effective date of the final rule to avoid legal uncertainty.

Requiring development of exercise plans within four years under § 68.10(d) is too lenient for high-risk Program 3 facilities; EPA should require sooner completion (e.g., within 18 months) for Program 3 processes.
The provision at § 68.10(d) lacks a required content list for the exercise plans—EPA should specify minimum elements (objectives, participants, metrics, resources) to ensure consistency.

The two-year trigger for the public meeting requirement in § 68.10(e) for qualifying accidents creates an unnecessary delay in public disclosure; the timeframe should be shortened to 90 days to align with § 68.210(b).
§ 68.10(e) should define “qualifying accident” precisely or cross-reference an explicit definition to prevent inconsistent interpretation by owners/operators.

The five-year compliance date in § 68.10(f) for §§ 68.160(b)(21) and 68.180 is too long given the potential public safety benefits; EPA should phase in a shorter schedule and require interim progress reports.
The rule should specify enforcement consequences if owners/operators fail to meet the § 68.10(f) deadline for complying with § 68.160(b)(21) and § 68.180.

§ 68.54(a) obligates training/testing of current and newly assigned process employees but does not require documentation standards; EPA should mandate training records format, retention period, and proof of competency.
The requirement in § 68.54(a) should explicitly include contractors and temporary workers who operate or directly support covered processes.

The “at least every three years” refresher interval in § 68.54(b) is insufficient for high-turnover facilities and for processes with seasonal hazards; EPA should require risk-based refreshers (annual for high-risk).
The phrase “or more often if necessary” in § 68.54(b) is vague—EPA should define objective triggers (incident, near-miss, process change) that mandate immediate refresher training.
§ 68.54(d) obligates training before startup after a major change but does not define “major change”; EPA should adopt the same definition used elsewhere in RMP/PSM guidance to ensure consistency.
The rule should require documented verification (e.g., sign-off) that operators received training on new/updated procedures under § 68.54(d) before restart.
The certification requirement in § 68.58(a) for triennial compliance evaluations must require the identity and qualifications of the certifying official and retention of supporting evidence.
§ 68.58(a) lacks a requirement to correct deficiencies found during the triennial evaluations within a fixed timeframe; EPA should require corrective action plans and timelines.

The obligation in § 68.60(a) to investigate incidents that could have “reasonably” resulted in a catastrophic release is ambiguous; EPA should provide criteria or examples to reduce subjective under-reporting.
The rule should mandate that incident investigations under § 68.60(a) be conducted by personnel with specified qualifications and independence from affected operations to avoid conflicts of interest.
§ 68.60(c) requires a summary with minimum content but omits required timelines for completion; EPA should require the summary be completed within 30–60 days of investigation close.

The regulation should require that investigation summaries under § 68.60(c) be made available to designated local emergency planning committees (LEPCs) and, except where CBI is validly asserted, to the public.
Requiring the date of the incident in § 68.60(c)(1) is appropriate, but EPA should also require timestamps and local time zone identification to aid cross-jurisdictional analyses.
§ 68.60(c)(3) demands a description of the incident—EPA should require standardized incident classification codes to enable aggregated analysis across facilities.
The mandate in § 68.60(c)(4) to list contributing factors should require root cause analysis using recognized methodologies (e.g., 5 Whys, fault tree) and documentation of methodology used.
§ 68.60(c)(5) requires recommendations from investigations but should also require assignment of responsible parties, deadlines, and verification of implementation.

The five-year retention period for investigation summaries in § 68.60(f) is too short for longitudinal safety analyses; EPA should extend it to at least ten years or align with OSHA PSM record retention.

§ 68.65(a) requires completion of written process safety information before a PHA but does not define acceptable sufficiency—EPA should specify minimum technical data (e.g., process flow diagrams, safety limits, material properties).
The schedule cross-referenced in § 68.67 should be included in the regulatory text or guidance and must account for new facilities and transferred ownership scenarios.

The triennial certification of compliance in § 68.79(a) for the subpart should require submission to EPA or state agency, not just internal certification, to allow oversight and public accountability.
§ 68.79(a) should require that the compliance evaluation include review of contractor performance and policies, not solely facility employees.
§ 68.81(a) mirrors § 68.60(a) but for another subpart—EPA should harmonize investigation standards across both subparts to avoid duplicative or conflicting obligations.

The provision in § 68.81(a) should require notification to EPA or the appropriate state agency when an incident that could reasonably have resulted in a catastrophic release occurs, within a defined timeframe (e.g., 24 hours).

§ 68.81(d)(2) requires date investigation began—EPA should require that investigations commence within a specified short period (e.g., 48–72 hours) after incident discovery.
The description requirement in § 68.81(d)(3) should mandate inclusion of photographs, diagrams, and measurement data where available to support findings.
§ 68.81(d)(4) should require categorization of contributing factors into human, equipment, management, and external to facilitate trending and prevention strategies.
Recommendations required by § 68.81(d)(5) should be tracked to closure with documented verification and a deadline; otherwise recommendations may never be implemented.

§ 68.93(b) requires providing emergency response plans and contact info to local organizations but does not require affirmative confirmation of receipt; EPA should require documented acknowledgment from LEPCs/fire departments.
The rule should require that emergency response plans provided under § 68.93(b) be current and updated within 30 days of any changes to contacts or procedures.

raw_output:
[P1] The deadline to receive comments by February 11, 2022 is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60 days to allow carriers, MROs, and labor groups sufficient time to prepare technical and economic comments.

[P1] Request extension of the comment period because the AD references a Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin dated July 8, 2021, which operators need time to review against fleet maintenance records before commenting on compliance feasibility.

[P1] Small operators and private owners were not given adequate notice; the FAA should provide targeted outreach and extend the deadline so these stakeholders can submit meaningful comments.

[P2] The clause requiring performance "within the specified compliance times unless already done" is ambiguous about what constitutes "already done"; request clarification that any prior action must have been performed in accordance with the exact inspections and procedures in the referenced Boeing bulletin to count as "already done."

[P2] Seek an exception allowing temporary deferral of AD actions for aircraft on extended ferry or storage, with defined limits, because the current wording does not accommodate operational realities during disruptions.

[P3] The obligation to "perform all applicable actions ... in accordance with the Accomplishment Instructions" unduly locks operators to Boeing's procedures; request FAA allowance for FAA-approved equivalent procedures developed by qualified repair stations without going through the full AMOC process for routine tasks.

[P3] Clarify how operators should determine which actions are "applicable" when the Boeing bulletin contains condition-based tables—operators need explicit criteria to avoid inconsistent interpretations across the industry.

[P4] Replacing "original issue date" with the AD effective date may shorten some compliance windows for later-issued operators; request that the FAA instead allow the later of (a) AD effective date or (b) date of airplane delivery to the current operator.

[P4] Legal concern: Changing the compliance-time reference point from the bulletin's original issue date to the AD effective date may conflict with contractual maintenance programs and should be justified with regulatory analysis in the final rule.

[P5] The requirement that, when the bulletin says to contact Boeing for repair instructions, the repair must be done using an FAA-approved method under paragraph (i) creates an extra approval burden and could delay repairs; request that FAA explicitly permit use of Boeing ODA-approved repairs as immediately acceptable, pending FAA concurrence.

[P5] Request clearer procedures and timelines for approval when Boeing is the only source of repair instructions—operators need guaranteed expedited review procedures to avoid aircraft groundings.

[P6] The delegation allowing the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch to approve AMOCs centralizes approval authority geographically; request that other ACO managers or regional offices also be authorized to approve AMOCs to avoid bottlenecks.

[P6] Industry request: Provide published metrics (target review times) for AMOC decisions by the Seattle ACO Branch to ensure timely responses, especially for repairs that would ground aircraft.

[P7] The instruction to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector per 14 CFR 39.19 is unclear for international operators with U.S.-registered aircraft maintained abroad; request explicit guidance for foreign repair stations and the appropriate FAA points of contact.

[P7] Request clarification about how to proceed when the principal inspector is unavailable or when an operator has multiple principal inspectors across fleets—establish a default routing process.

[P8] If AMOC information is sent directly to the certification office manager, the rule references paragraph (j)(1) but does not reproduce or summarize the contact; request that the final rule include full contact details and acceptable delivery methods to avoid misrouting.

[P8] Concern about confidentiality: When sending AMOC information directly to the certification office manager, operators need assurance on treatment of proprietary data and a process for marking confidential business information.

[P9] Permission to email AMOC requests to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is helpful, but request confirmation that emailed submissions will be accepted as timely and guidance on required file formats, size limits, and security of attachments.

[P9] Request that the FAA also provide a secure web portal option for AMOC submissions to accommodate large technical files and protect sensitive data instead of relying solely on an email address.

[P10] The requirement to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC lacks a timeline—request that the FAA specify how far in advance notice must be given (e.g., 48 hours, 5 business days) and acceptable notification methods.

[P10] Clarify who is the "appropriate principal inspector" for leased aircraft operated under different principal inspector jurisdictions—operators need clear direction to ensure compliance with the notice requirement.

[P11] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to be used is practical, but the rule should require public disclosure or FAA oversight of ODA approvals used to comply with the AD to ensure transparency and consistent safety levels.

[P11] Concern that reliance on Boeing ODA approvals could create conflicts of interest; request that the FAA require independent technical review for ODA-approved AMOCs used to satisfy this AD.

[P12] The condition that repairs/modifications must meet the airplane's certification basis and explicitly reference this AD may exclude legacy repairs that are functionally acceptable; request guidance on how to demonstrate equivalence to the certification basis when proposing alternative repairs.

[P12] Request that the FAA publish an example AMOC approval letter template that explicitly shows the required language referencing the AD and the airplane certification basis to reduce back-and-forth during approvals.

[P5] Operators request that the AD explicitly allow the use of temporary "lower risk" repairs (with defined limitations and follow-up requirements) when immediate Boeing repair instructions are not available, to avoid grounding aircraft for safety-critical operations.

[P3] Maintenance organizations ask for clarification whether required actions include any mandatory post-repair inspections and recordkeeping beyond the Accomplishment Instructions, and if so, what the retention period for records should be.

[P2] Labor groups request that compliance timeframes account for required training and manpower constraints; if actions require specialized technicians, compliance times should be extended or phased to avoid unsafe rushed repairs.

[P4] Airlines request grandfathering for aircraft that have already undergone identical inspections or repairs based on service information issued after July 8, 2021 but before the AD effective date, to avoid duplicative work.

[P6] Legal commenters note that AMOC approvals are discretionary and request the FAA commit to objective criteria and nondiscriminatory processing of AMOC requests to meet administrative law standards.

[P9] Privacy advocates request that emailed AMOC requests containing employee or passenger data be subject to data minimization requirements and that the FAA provide encryption guidance for email submissions.

[P11] MROs recommend that the AD explicitly permit using AMOCs approved by foreign national aviation authorities for non-U.S. operators, provided they are accepted by the FAA under bilateral agreements, to prevent conflicting obligations.

[P12] Technical commenters request that the FAA clarify how to demonstrate that a proposed repair "meets the certification basis"—specify required analysis types (e.g., structural analysis, fatigue testing) and acceptable demonstration formats.

[P1] Citizen/environmental groups ask that the FAA reopen the comment period because public outreach materials were not widely distributed and because the AD may have downstream effects on community noise or emissions (through different maintenance patterns) that weren’t analyzed.

[P3] Request clarification whether mandatory actions in the Boeing bulletin that are marked as "optional" or "for future study" are considered "applicable actions" under paragraph (g), to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P5] Concern that requiring FAA-approved repair methods when bulletin instructs to contact Boeing could create delays in emergency repairs overseas; request an express emergency authorization process for repairs performed to return aircraft to service pending formal approval.

[P10] Operators ask for an explicit process to resolve disputes if a principal inspector opposes use of an FAA-approved AMOC—define the escalation path and timelines.

[P8] Aviation attorneys request inclusion of a statement in the AD that confirms appeals procedures and remedies if the certification office manager denies an AMOC submission, including timelines for reconsideration.

[P6] Request that the FAA publish a list of previously approved AMOCs for similar ADs as guidance material so that applicants can design proposals aligned with past acceptances.

[P12] Suggest that the FAA allow conditional approvals for repair methods that meet the certification basis subject to monitoring (e.g., enhanced inspections) until full data are provided, rather than outright denial if full data are not yet available.

[P3] Legal experts will challenge whether §17.41(l)(1)(ii) is consistent with existing incidental take permit frameworks and request harmonization language that avoids duplicative criminal liability for permitted incidental takes.

[P4] Private collectors and rehabilitation centers will ask for a defined process and timeframe in §17.41(l)(1)(iii) for determining and documenting whether specimens are "unlawfully taken" to avoid inadvertent violations when rescuing injured birds.

[P5] Commercial enterprises engaged in ecotourism will assert that the interstate/foreign commerce prohibition in §17.41(l)(1)(iv) could be interpreted to bar routine sale of guided-tour services and request an explicit carve-out or guidance that normal tourism services not involving sale of the animal itself are not covered.

[P6] Pet trade stakeholders will highlight that §17.41(l)(1)(v) banning sale or offer for sale could criminalize transfers among permitted scientific institutions and ask for cross-reference to §17.41(l)(2)(i) permit allowances (§17.32) to make that exemption explicit.

[P7] Conservation scientists will praise §17.41(l)(2) permitting framework but request the rule include processing timelines and fee waivers for research permits under §17.32 to avoid delays in time-sensitive studies.

[P8] Universities and researchers will request that §17.41(l)(2)(i) explicitly permit authorized transport of live pygmy-owls between accredited institutions under §17.32 without additional paperwork beyond the permit.

[P9] State wildlife agencies will seek clarification under §17.41(l)(2)(ii) on which parts of §17.21(c)(2)-(4) apply — specifically whether authorized "take" for conservation translocation and emergency rescue are included.

[P9] Developers and landowners will request that §17.41(l)(2)(ii) confirm that authorized take under §17.21(c)(6) and (7) for endangered migratory birds does not impose additional civil or criminal liability beyond existing MBTA/ESA authorizations.

[P10] Advocacy groups will push back that §17.41(l)(2)(iii) allowing take under §17.31(b) needs strict criteria to ensure any allowed take is truly negligible and monitored.

[P11] Rehabilitation centers will request that §17.41(l)(2)(iv) explicitly allow possession of lawfully rehabilitated pygmy-owls pending release and set maximum retention periods to reduce enforcement uncertainty.

[P12] Permitted incidental take under §17.41(l)(3) will prompt developers to demand an administrative appeal process and clear timelines for Service approval referenced in paragraph (l)(3).

[P13] Educators and zoos will praise §17.41(l)(3)(i) but request that the rule specify what constitutes an "appropriate, valid part 21 permit" (e.g., categories, conditions) and whether short-term display permits are covered.

[P13] Small non-profit education programs will request fee reductions or categorical authorizations under §17.41(l)(3)(i), since obtaining a full part 21 permit can be costly and time-consuming.

[P14] The condition in §17.41(l)(3)(i) requiring a part 21 permit should be clarified to allow emergency educational use (e.g., natural history outreach after a major wildfire) with post-activity reporting if prior permit acquisition is impracticable.

[P15] Conservation practitioners will support §17.41(l)(3)(ii)'s allowance for habitat restoration but request the Service publish clear, measurable criteria for "approval" so proponents know when projects meet the standard.

[P16] Landowners and restoration contractors will object that §17.41(l)(3)(ii)'s requirement for prior Service approval is administratively burdensome and request a de minimis category of low-impact restoration activities that can proceed with simple notification rather than full approval.

[P17] Restoration groups ask that §17.41(l)(3)(ii)(A) explicitly include active reforestation with native cacti and other native plants as covered habitat enhancement activities.

[P18] Fire management agencies will object to the exclusion in §17.41(l)(3)(ii)(B) of prescribed fire, arguing that in some Sonoran Desert contexts prescribed fire is a necessary tool to reduce invasive grass fuels and promote native community resilience; they request an exception for narrowly tailored fire prescriptions approved by the Service.

[P18] Conservation scientists will support the prohibition of actions leading to "more than minimal reduction/removal of tree cover" in §17.41(l)(3)(ii)(B) but request a quantitative definition (e.g., percentage canopy loss or basal area thresholds) to reduce enforcement ambiguity.

[P18] Invasive species managers will comment that the prohibition on promoting nonnative vegetation in §17.41(l)(3)(ii)(B) should specify whether use of nonnative species as nurse plants during restoration (temporary) is allowed under mitigation conditions.

[P19] Developers and project managers will request concrete guidance on what constitutes "reasonable care" in §17.41(l)(3)(iii) beyond the listed elements, including examples and compliance checklists.

[P20] The compliance element in §17.41(l)(3)(iii)(A) requiring adherence to all applicable Federal, State, and Tribal regulations may create conflicts where laws differ; stakeholders request a conflict-resolution provision and explicit priority rules.

[P21] Practitioners will request more detail on how to document that the "methods and techniques that, as feasible, cause the least harm" in §17.41(l)(3)(iii)(B) were chosen — e.g., requirement for alternatives analysis or demonstrating infeasibility.

[P22] Construction firms will ask for specifics on scheduling/seasonal avoidance under §17.41(l)(3)(iii)(C) — request defined nesting season dates or a process for obtaining a qualified biologist's determination to enable project planning.

[P23] The requirement in §17.41(l)(3)(iii)(D) to obtain technical assistance from a "qualified biologist" needs a definition of qualification (education, experience, certifications) to prevent inconsistent interpretations and to ensure availability in rural areas.

[P24] Small contractors will request that §17.41(l)(3)(iii)(D) allow tele-consultation with qualified biologists and provide a list of preapproved consultants to avoid delays.

[P25] Bird conservation groups will support §17.41(l)(3)(iii)(E) to "minimize the number of wild individuals disturbed" but ask for guidance on acceptable disturbance thresholds (e.g., number of flushes, proximity distances) and monitoring protocols.

[P26] Wildlife health organizations will request that §17.41(l)(3)(iii)(F) require specific biosecurity measures (disinfection protocols, quarantine periods, vaccination where feasible) and reporting of any disease events to the Service.

[P27] Geneticists and conservation biologists will applaud §17.41(l)(3)(iii)(G) to preserve genetic diversity but request the rule require genetic baseline assessments and explicit actions (e.g., restrictions on translocations of closely related subspecies) to operationalize the obligation.

[P28] Tribal governments will request explicit consultation requirements and recognition of Tribal conservation practices under §17.41(l)(3)(iii)(A)-(G), and ask that "qualified biologist" include Tribal biologists.

[P29] Environmental law practitioners will argue that the rule must provide a safe-harbor procedure for inadvertent, de minimis incidental take when all reasonable care has been practiced, to avoid criminalizing good-faith actors under §17.41(l)(1)(ii).

[P30] Private landowners will request incentives (e.g., expedited approvals, technical assistance funding) tied to §17.41(l)(3)(ii) approvals to encourage voluntary habitat restoration rather than litigating over prohibitions.

[P31] State agencies will request the Service produce guidance documents and standardized permitting templates to implement §17.41(l)(2) and §17.41(l)(3) uniformly across jurisdictions.

[P32] Rehabilitation and veterinary groups will ask for an explicit emergency exception to the prohibitions in P1–P6 to allow immediate rescue and treatment of injured pygmy-owls without prior permits, with prompt post-action notification requirements.

[P33] Attorneys will urge that the preamble address how these prohibitions and permissions interact with the Migratory Bird Treaty Act and with existing state endangered species laws to prevent conflicting enforcement.

[P34] Agricultural interests will seek clarification whether routine agricultural activities that inadvertently alter habitat (but are otherwise lawful) are subject to incidental take permitting under §17.41(l)(3) or are exempt.

[P35] Citizen scientists and birdwatching groups will request clear guidance that nonintrusive recreational observation and photography are not "take" under §17.41(l)(1)(ii) when conducted responsibly, and ask for recommended minimum approach distances.

[P36] The Service should specify enforcement priorities and penalties for violations of P1–P6 so stakeholders understand the consequences and can adjust compliance practices accordingly.

[P37] Applicants will ask the Service to publish criteria for evaluating "least harm" techniques in §17.41(l)(3)(iii)(B), including case studies and preferred methods for minimizing mortality during restoration or monitoring.

[P38] Conservation funders will request that the Service create a fast-track review process and dedicated funding support for restoration projects meeting §17.41(l)(3)(ii)(A) to expedite conservation outcomes.

[P39] Municipalities planning infrastructure projects will request that the Service provide coordination timelines and one-window permitting described in §17.41(l)(3) to avoid project delays.

[P40] Ethics and animal welfare groups will request that any allowed possession, display, or use under §17.41(l)(2)(i) and §17.41(l)(3)(i) include explicit animal welfare standards (housing, veterinary care, handling limits) and independent oversight.

[P1] The obligation in § 721.11556(a)(1) is vague because it generically identifies the substance as “rosin adduct ester, polymer with polyols, compd. with ethanolamine” without providing CAS numbers, synonyms, or structural identifiers; request inclusion of clear identifiers to avoid compliance uncertainty.

[P1] Industry commenters will assert that the reporting obligation for P–18–399 lacks a clear timeframe for submission after identification of a significant new use and should specify the exact notification deadline (e.g., 90 days) consistent with TSCA section 5.

[P2] Manufacturers and downstream users will challenge § 721.11556(a)(2)(i) as overly broad because it designates all “industrial, commercial, and consumer uses” as significant new uses without distinguishing low-exposure uses; they will request exemptions for closed-system industrial uses or processes that prevent releases.

[P2] Small businesses and consumer product manufacturers will claim that requiring compliance with § 721.80(s) for all industrial, commercial, and consumer activities creates disproportionate burdens and seek a de minimis threshold (e.g., volume or concentration) below which § 721.80(s) does not apply.

[P3] Legal commenters will argue that applying Subpart A by reference in § 721.11556(b) without reproducing key obligations obscures modifications and may lead to inconsistent interpretation; they will request that deviations from Subpart A be explicitly listed in full.

[P4] Trade associations will object to § 721.11556(b)(1) requiring recordkeeping under § 721.125(a)-(c) and (i) without clarifying retention periods and format (electronic vs. paper); they will request explicit retention periods (e.g., 5 years) and allowance for electronic records.

[P4] Privacy and confidentiality advocates will demand that § 721.11556(b)(1) explicitly address protection of confidential business information (CBI) within required records and outline procedures for claiming confidentiality consistent with TSCA section 14.

[P5] Commenters will note that § 721.11556(b)(2) references § 721.185 but does not state how revocation or limitation will be communicated to affected parties and request procedural safeguards and notice requirements before revocation of notification privileges.

[P6] Industry will request clarification of § 721.11556(b)(3)’s cross-reference to § 721.1725(b)(1), specifically asking how the determination process (who makes determinations, timelines, opportunity to rebut) will be implemented for uses in paragraph (a)(2)(ii).

[P7] The obligation in § 721.11557(a)(1) for P–18–400 (rosin adduct ester potassium salt) similarly lacks CAS or alternative identifiers; commenters will request precise chemical identifiers to prevent misapplication of the rule.

[P7] Environmental NGOs will argue that mandatory reporting under § 721.11557(a)(1) is appropriate but request that the agency require additional hazard characterization data as part of the report because the PMN record alone is insufficient to assess environmental fate.

[P8] Commercial formulators will contend that § 721.11557(a)(2)(i) treating all industrial, commercial, and consumer uses as significant new uses is arbitrary and seek guidance on what constitutes a “consumer” use (e.g., finished products vs. intermediate processing).

[P9] Regulatory compliance officers will request that § 721.11557(b) list any deviations from Subpart A explicitly and provide examples of how Subpart A provisions will be applied in practice to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P10] Small processors will assert that § 721.11557(b)(1) imposes burdensome recordkeeping (§ 721.125(a)-(c) and (i)) without cost estimates; they will ask EPA to conduct a small-entity compliance review and consider reduced requirements for small processors.

[P11] Legal commenters will challenge the incorporation by reference of § 721.185 in § 721.11557(b)(2) unless § 721.185’s procedures for limitation or revocation are tailored to ensure due process for regulated entities, including notice, opportunity to submit corrective actions, and appeal rights.

[P12] Commenters will request that § 721.11557(b)(3) clarify whether § 721.1725(b)(1)’s applicability determination is automatic upon filing or requires EPA notice, and ask for explicit timelines and procedures.

[P13] For § 721.11558(a)(1) (PMN P–20–68), industry will ask the agency to include the CAS No. 13431–57–7 in the regulatory text consistently to ensure unambiguous coverage of the chemical.

[P13] Product safety NGOs will request that reports required under § 721.11558(a)(1) include results of any available reproductive toxicity and chronic exposure studies given the diacetate functionality and potential for metabolic release of alcohols/acetate.

[P14] Manufacturers will argue that applying § 721.80(j) per § 721.11558(a)(2)(i) to all industrial, commercial, and consumer activities is inconsistent with the narrower § 721.80(s) used for the other two chemicals and request justification for the different subsection or harmonization across sections.

[P14] Downstream users will request specific examples of control measures and worker protection practices expected under § 721.80(j), and ask whether existing OSHA controls or state requirements will satisfy § 721.80(j) obligations to avoid duplicative compliance.

[P15] Commenters will request that § 721.11558(b) enumerate any modifications to Subpart A rather than merely stating that Subpart A applies except as modified, to provide clarity on which Subpart A provisions are altered.

[P16] Trade groups will request that § 721.11558(b)(1) clarify whether the recordkeeping items in § 721.125(a)-(c) and (i) include supplier information, concentrations, and use volumes, and whether aggregated reporting is acceptable to protect CBI.

[P17] Legal and procedural commenters will insist that § 721.11558(b)(2) explain the criteria under § 721.185 that will trigger limitation or revocation of notification rights and require EPA to publish any such determinations publicly with an explanation of the basis.

[P18] Industry and compliance attorneys will request that § 721.11558(b)(3) clarify the interplay between § 721.1725(b)(1) and paragraph (a)(2)(ii) uses when a use may be partially covered—e.g., when the same use in different facilities has different exposure profiles—and ask for a mechanism to obtain a written EPA determination.

[P7] The fifth vertex and return point (35°27′40″ N; 117°26′03″ W back to beginning) (P7) suggests a very large and irregular shape; stakeholders request the full ordered list of vertices and a published shapefile/KML for public review.

[P8] The vertical limits from 6,000 feet MSL up to but not including FL200 (P8) will affect both low-altitude GA and commercial flight operations conducting arrivals/departures in nearby terminals; FAA should analyze impacts on instrument procedures and minimum vectoring altitudes.

[P9] Designating the area intermittently only on weekdays 0700–1700 by NOTAM 7 days in advance (P9) imposes operational uncertainty because a single NOTAM is not adequate notice for airlines and air tour operators; FAA should require 30 days’ notice or a predictable recurring schedule.

[P9] The timing of designation (0700–1700, Monday–Friday) (P9/P10) disproportionately affects business aviation and cargo flights during peak daytime hours; commenters request the option to schedule activities outside of peak traffic windows or to allow conditional access.

[P11] Requiring NOTAM issuance 7 days in advance (P11) is insufficient for international operators and charter services that plan flights earlier; the rule should mandate multiple methods of notification (e.g., Chart Supplement, FAA website) and longer lead times.

[P12] Designating Joshua Control Facility at Edwards AFB as the controlling agency (P12) without specifying coordination procedures with adjacent TRACONs and ARTCC could create air traffic control confusion; commenters request formal coordination protocols and letter-of-agreement references.

[P12] The rule should clarify whether Joshua Control Facility has the staffing and technical capabilities to manage the restricted area intermittently, and whether contingency control (e.g., when Joshua is unavailable) is provided.

[P13] Naming the Naval Air Warfare Center Weapons Division, China Lake, as the using agency (P13) requires disclosure of the types of activities to be conducted and associated hazards (e.g., live munitions, electronic warfare) so the public can assess safety and environmental impacts.

[P13] The Using Agency’s operations (P13) may generate sonic booms, hazardous materials, or electromagnetic interference affecting communities and commercial services; require an environmental assessment and mitigation measures be attached to the rule.

[P1] The rule does not include exceptions or procedures for emergency medical flights, firefighting, search and rescue, or law enforcement; commenters request explicit emergency access provisions and immediate NOTAM cancellation procedures.

[P11] Relying solely on NOTAMs issued 7 days in advance (P11) without incorporation into aeronautical charts or the Digital - NOTAM system may lead to missed notices; require chart amendments or publication in the FAA Digital Products.

[P12] The rule should clarify the point of contact at Joshua Control Facility and provide a 24/7 phone/email for permission requests, activation/deactivation confirmations, and safety coordination.

[P1] The establishment of R–2511 without an accommodation procedure for overflight corridors or corridors at specific altitudes could create unnecessary flight plan rerouting; propose adding a conditional corridor through the area when activity is inactive.

[P8] The lower limit at 6,000 feet MSL (P8) will preclude aerial firefighting and agricultural aircraft operations that often operate below that altitude; require an exception process for state/local firefighting and agricultural operations.

[P3] The precise first vertex coordinate (P3) should be given in decimal degrees as well as DMS to avoid misinterpretation by civilian operators using different navigation systems.

[P9] The 0700–1700 local time designation (P9) does not account for daylight saving time changes; specify whether local time follows standard or daylight time or refer to UTC for clarity.

[P2] The rule should include a map and bearings/distances between vertices, as listing raw coordinates alone (P2–P7) is insufficient for many stakeholders to determine exact airspace impacts.
