[P1] The requirement that the design "primarily feature" a live portrayal of one eligible waterfowl species is vague and needs a quantitative threshold (e.g., percentage of image area) to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P1] Requiring a "live portrayal" as the dominant feature could preclude valuable stylized or interpretive art that still clearly depicts an eligible species and should be clarified to permit non-photorealistic representation.

[P2] Allowing depiction of more than one eligible species is appropriate, but the rule should specify whether mixed-species groupings must still have one species visually dominant to satisfy § 91.14(a).

[P3] The judges’ mandate to select the "best" design that appeals to various stakeholders is subjective; the regulation should provide objective criteria or a rubric to reduce arbitrariness and potential bias.

[P3] The provision that the stamp must be "accepted and pr" appears truncated/typoed and must be corrected to clarify the acceptance standard and obligations.

[P4] The absolute requirement that entries be original, hand-drawn works will exclude mixed-media pieces that incorporate hand-drawn elements plus permissible manual collage; the rule should specify acceptable mixed techniques.

[P4] Requiring exclusively hand-drawn work burdens artists who use assistive devices (for disability) — there should be an accommodation process or explicit allowance for assistive drawing tools if the work remains original.

[P5] The prohibition on designs copied from "previously published art, including photographs" is reasonable, but the rule should define "published" (e.g., public domain, private portfolio websites) and clarify treatment of reference photos taken by the entrant.

[P5] The ban on duplication of "images in any format published on the I..." is cut off and ambiguous; the agency must complete and clarify the sentence, especially regarding use of stock images and licensed photos as references.

[P6] The blanket disqualification of computer-generated art and art produced from printers will exclude widely accepted contemporary digital and hybrid art methods; the agency should reconsider or set a separate digital contest category.

[P6] The exception for airbrush but exclusion of other mechanical methods is arbitrary; if the concern is mechanical reproduction, the rule should define prohibited processes (e.g., direct output devices) rather than naming one allowed technique.

[P7] The airbrush exception is inconsistent with the ban on other mechanical outputs and may create an unfair advantage for artists who use airbrush; clarify why airbrush is allowed but other similar techniques (e.g., inkjet transfers) are not.

[P8] Allowing resubmission of prior non-selected entries is fair, but the rule must specify whether entries previously submitted to multiple state or federal contests are eligible and whether any past public display affects eligibility.

[P9] The condition that a previously submitted entry must meet current criteria creates uncertainty — entrants need explicit guidance on how changes in rules (e.g., 2018 hunting theme) affect the eligibility of older designs.

[P10] The 2018-only requirement to include hunting-related accessories or scenes unacceptably privileges hunting imagery and may alienate non-hunting stamp purchasers; this single-year thematic mandate should be reconsidered or balanced with conservation-focused themes.

[P10] Requiring hunting-related accessories in 2018 risks legal challenge for using a federal stamp design contest to promote a particular recreational activity; the rule should explain the statutory authority for a hunting heritage theme.

[P11] The non-exhaustive list of permitted hunting elements (dogs, equipment, decoys) is helpful, but the rule should clarify whether inclusion of humans engaged in hunting is permitted and whether depictions of weapons are allowed.

[P12] Requiring the winning design to "clearly meet" the hunting heritage theme is subjective; the agency should define measurable criteria for "clearly meet," for example listing mandatory visual elements or narrative coherence standards.

[P13] Mandating that 2018 judges have an "understanding and appreciation" of hunting heritage is vague and potentially exclusionary; the rule should define minimum qualifications or allow balanced panels including conservationists and artists.

[P13] The required ability of judges to "recognize hunting paraphernalia" favors judges with hunting backgrounds and could bias selection toward hunting-centric designs; the process should ensure representation of broader stakeholder perspectives.

[P14] Judging based on "anatomical accuracy, artistic composition, and suitability for reduction" is appropriate, but the regulation should provide scoring rubrics and examples to ensure consistent evaluation across judges.

[P14] The term "suitability for reduction" needs technical clarification (e.g., acceptable levels of detail, contrast, and linework) so entrants can prepare designs that reproduce well at stamp size.

[P15] Adding the hunting heritage evaluation in 2018 compounds subjectivity in judging criteria; the agency must specify relative weighting of anatomical accuracy versus thematic illustration to prevent unpredictable outcomes.

[P15] The extra 2018 criterion may conflict with longstanding emphasis on species depiction accuracy and could unintentionally deprioritize biological correctness; clarify how judges should balance theme vs. anatomical fidelity.

[P6] The disqualification of "photographs" might disallow photorealistic paintings made from an entrant's own photograph taken in the field; the rule should permit use of the entrant's own photos as references so long as the final work is hand-drawn and original.

[P5] The prohibition on copies of "previously published art" should clarify treatment of works in the public domain and of derivative works — can an original painting inspired by a public-domain illustration be submitted?

[P4] The requirement for original hand-drawn work raises copyright transfer questions — the rule should explain intellectual property rights, required assignments, or licenses upon submission and winning.

[P1] The limitation to one of the "five or fewer identified eligible waterfowl species" must be published in advance (list of eligible species) so artists can plan their entries and avoid disqualification.

[P2] The permission to depict multiple eligible species should specify whether non-eligible species or non-waterfowl may be included in background elements (e.g., marsh plants, other birds) and whether that affects compliance with the "dominant feature" rule.

[P13] Requiring judges in 2018 to recognize hunting paraphernalia could be challenged as imposing a political litmus test; the agency should ensure judges are appointed through transparent, merit-based processes.

[P10] The 2018-specific requirement creates administrative complexity and fairness issues for entrants unaware of the one-year theme; the agency should provide extended notice and outreach before the contest.

[P6] The allowance of airbrush but disallowance of computer-assisted airbrushing (digital airbrush tools) is ambiguous; clarify whether digital airbrush effects are permitted or prohibited.

[P8] The rule lacks a time limit for resubmission of prior entries — a previous entry from many years ago could be resubmitted; the agency should state whether there is a lookback period or limit on number of resubmissions.

[P12] The mandate that the selected design "will clearly meet the theme" might be unenforceable if the judging panel is split; the regulation should require documentation of how the winning entry meets the theme to ensure transparency.

[P14] Judges’ evaluation criteria do not address cultural sensitivity or representational accuracy for Indigenous peoples who have cultural ties to waterfowl hunting; the agency should include cultural review standards.

[P1] The phrase "dominant feature" may be interpreted as a composition rule that limits creative layout options (e.g., vignette or silhouette designs) and should be clarified to allow legitimate artistic variation.

[P4] The rule should explicitly prohibit tracing from another artist’s work even if traced by hand, to prevent circumvention of the "original hand-drawn" requirement.

[P6] Excluding works produced from "computer/mechanical output device" could be read to disqualify hand-drawn works that are scanned and printed for submission; the agency should specify acceptable submission file types and physical submission rules.

[P11] The list of acceptable hunting elements does not address depictions of endangered or protected species used as background — the agency should prohibit including non-eligible protected species that might trigger conservation or legal concerns.

[P15] The temporary 2018 criteria may create precedent; the agency should state whether future one-year themes are anticipated and how stakeholders will be consulted.

[P3] There is no conflict-of-interest policy described for judges charged with selecting a stamp "accepted and pr..." — the agency should require judges to disclose affiliations with entrants or sponsors.

[P5] The prohibition referencing "photographs" should clarify whether photo-based photogrammetry or 3D scans used as references constitute prohibited copying.

[P13] The requirement for judges to "appreciate" hunting heritage is subjective language that could be interpreted to exclude judges who favor conservation messaging; replace with objective qualifications like "experience with waterfowl-related history or culture."

[P10] Mandatory inclusion of hunting paraphernalia in 2018 may reduce marketability to non-hunting stamp collectors and could reduce sales revenue used for conservation; the agency should provide an economic impact analysis.

[P8] There is no procedure described for notifying entrants if a previously submitted design becomes ineligible under new theme requirements; the contest should provide pre-submission eligibility review or advisory services.

[P14] The rule should require that judges receive training on consistent application of "anatomical accuracy" to accommodate varying artistic styles (e.g., realism vs. stylization) to avoid penalizing valid artistic choices.

[P6] The exception for airbrush but prohibition of other mechanical outputs could create enforcement difficulties; the agency should describe how it will inspect and verify production methods without infringing on artist privacy.

[P1] The "five or fewer identified eligible waterfowl species" constraint needs to be publicly listed with the contest announcement and any rationale for the limitation provided to prevent perception of arbitrary species selection.

The condition that a previously submitted entry must meet current criteria creates uncertainty — entrants need explicit guidance on how changes in rules (e.g., 2018 hunting theme) affect the eligibility of older designs.

The 2018-only requirement to include hunting-related accessories or scenes unacceptably privileges hunting imagery and may alienate non-hunting stamp purchasers; this single-year thematic mandate should be reconsidered or balanced with conservation-focused themes.

Requiring hunting-related accessories in 2018 risks legal challenge for using a federal stamp design contest to promote a particular recreational activity; the rule should explain the statutory authority for a hunting heritage theme.

Adding the hunting heritage evaluation in 2018 compounds subjectivity in judging criteria; the agency must specify relative weighting of anatomical accuracy versus thematic illustration to prevent unpredictable outcomes.

[P1] The June 29, 2020 deadline in § 39.13(a) is now past; requiring the FAA to "receive comments by June 29, 2020" makes no practical sense and should be updated to a current, realistic comment period end date or removed from the final rule text.

[P1] Industry commenters will object that an absolute receipt deadline phrased as "the FAA must receive comments by June 29, 2020" is inflexible and does not account for postal delays or system outages; the rule should allow comments "postmarked by" or "submitted electronically by" the deadline to avoid unfair rejections.

[P2] Operators note § 39.13(f) lacks clarity on whether compliance times are measured from the AD effective date or from the date of notification to each operator; the AD should explicitly state the reference date for compliance times to avoid inconsistent interpretation.

[P3] The initial compliance window in § 39.13(g) (100 hours TIS or 12 months) is ambiguous because the provision text in the preamble and the regulatory text differ; the FAA should reconcile and clearly state the exact deadline (e.g., whichever occurs later) to avoid enforcement confusion.

[P4] The requirement in § 39.13(g) that the initial inspection be done "within 100 hours TIS or 12 months, whichever occurs later" is operationally burdensome for high-utilization aircraft and may permit operators to defer unsafe conditions for up to 12 months; commenters will ask FAA to make the initial inspection "whichever occurs first" to ensure timely safety action.

[P4] Small operators and Part 135 charter companies will request an extension of the initial compliance time beyond 12 months/100 hours TIS for aircraft that are in seasonal operation or in storage, or request a risk-based exception for aircraft with low hours since last inspection.

[P5] The recurring inspection interval of "every 500 hours TIS or 5 years, whichever occurs first" is unusually frequent for calendar-driven corrosion processes — commenters (especially maintenance providers and OEMs) will request the FAA provide supporting data justifying the 5-year cap and consider changing to "whichever occurs later" or to a condition-based interval.

[P5] Maintenance organizations will point out that tying the interval to whichever occurs first (500 hours or 5 years) imposes excessive inspection frequency on low-utilization aircraft; they will request the FAA adopt "whichever occurs later" to avoid unnecessary costs and downtime.

[P6] The list of components to inspect in § 39.13(g) (stabilizer hinge bracket, tailcone reinforcement angle, corner reinforcement, hinge reinforcement channel, etc.) appears incomplete relative to the referenced Textron service letter; commenters will request the FAA explicitly include all parts and figure numbers from the service document to prevent ambiguity.

[P6] Some commenters will request that the AD include clear part numbers and inspection zones (e.g., left/right, serial number ranges) because the broad wording could lead to inconsistent inspections across operators.

[P7] The obligation in § 39.13(g) to "remove any corrosion" is vague about acceptable removal methods, depths of material removal, and allowable surface condition post-cleaning; maintenance providers will request explicit guidance or reference to the service instructions and limits, and an allowance for non-destructive evaluation (NDE) to assess material loss.

[P7] Metalworkers and repair stations will request permission to use approved corrosion treatment and preservation techniques (e.g., anodic protection, primers) consistent with the manufacturer's structural repair manual, and to document acceptance criteria for removed corrosion.

[P8] The requirement to replace any cracked part following specific paragraphs of the Textron service letter is reasonable, but commenters will ask the FAA to explicitly allow approved alternative repair instructions (e.g., OEM-approved repairs or FAA-approved SRMs) and to clarify whether repairs (not replacements) are permitted under an AMOC.

[P8] Legal commenters will request the AD to state whether parts replaced under warranty or OEM service campaigns count as compliance and how to document such replacements in logbooks.

[P9] Requiring inspection for loose and sheared rivets is appropriate, but maintenance organizations will ask the AD to specify inspection methods (visual only, magnification, borescope, dye-penetrant) and acceptance criteria (maximum allowable looseness, gap sizes) to ensure consistent findings.

[P10] The "before further flight" rivet replacement mandate in § 39.13(g) for loose or sheared rivets may cause immediate grounding; operators will seek language allowing ferry flights under specific constraints or an expedited temporary repair procedure permitted by the principal inspector to avoid undue operational disruption.

[P11] The credit provision in § 39.13(h) allowing earlier inspections accomplished within the previous 5 years or 500 hours TIS to be credited is helpful, but commenters will request clarification on how to calculate the "most recent" metric when an inspection falls outside both thresholds (e.g., 4 years and 600 hours since last inspection).

[P11] Recordkeeping stakeholders will request the AD require specific documentation (dates, hours TIS at inspection, inspector signature, reference to inspection procedure) to show eligibility for credit under § 39.13(h).

[P12] The time-limit in § 39.13(h) that the interval between a credited inspection and the next required inspection may not exceed 500 hours TIS or 5 years is potentially confusing when combined with the recurring requirement in paragraph (g); commenters will ask for an example calculation and explicit bridging rules to prevent double-counting or gap in coverage.

[P13] The AMOC authority delegated to the Manager, Wichita ACO Branch, in § 39.13(i)(1) is appropriate, but commenters will request a faster, more transparent process (eg. target review times and required materials checklist) because the current 14 CFR 39.19 process can be slow and inconsistent across offices.

[P14] The routing requirement in § 39.13(i)(1) to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO adds administrative burden for small operators; commenters will ask the FAA to permit direct electronic submission to the certification office as an alternative route to streamline approvals.

[P15] The instruction in § 39.13(i)(1) to address direct AMOC submissions to the person named in paragraph (j) is meaningless unless paragraph (j) is updated with current contact information; commenters will ask FAA to include up-to-date contact details or a web link to the current manager.

[P16] The requirement in § 39.13(i)(2) to notify the principal inspector or local office manager before using any approved AMOC is unclear about the timing and method of notification (written, electronic, or verbal); operators will request that the FAA specify acceptable notification methods and a reasonable advance notice period.

[P16] Safety advocates will caution that notifying only the principal inspector may create inconsistencies; they will request that the AD require FAA concurrence or issuance of a formal approval letter before implementation of an AMOC to ensure proper oversight.

[P3] Several legal commenters will point out that overlapping and partially redundant language in (g) and (g) initial compliance paragraphs could lead to enforcement disputes; they will request the FAA consolidate and streamline the compliance time text for legal clarity.

[P5] Cost-sensitive operators will submit comments estimating the economic impact of 500-hour or 5-year recurring inspections on maintenance budgets and request the FAA perform and publish a formal cost-benefit analysis supporting the chosen intervals.

[P6] Aircraft owners with airplanes in storage will request an exemption or modified inspection schedule for airplanes that remain in controlled storage environments and do not accumulate TIS, since calendar-based intervals may be inappropriate for preserved aircraft.

[P7] Repair stations will request that the AD explicitly allow use of approved protective coatings after corrosion removal and provide acceptance criteria for repainting or resealing surfaces to avoid repeated corrosion cycles.

[P9] Some commenters will advocate for mandatory NDI (non-destructive inspection) for suspected cracks rather than relying solely on visual inspection, arguing that visual methods can miss subsurface cracking that could compromise structural integrity.

[P10] Air taxi and cargo operators will request an allowance for conditional continued operations with a placarded limitation (reduced maximum weight, lower gust envelope) if a rivet is suspected but replacement cannot be achieved before next flight due to parts or maintenance unavailability, subject to FAA approval.

[P13] Trade associations will ask FAA to clarify whether AMOCs that change inspection intervals or methods must be promulgated in a public docket (for transparency) or can be handled solely on a case-by-case basis without public notice.

[P11] Maintenance tracking software vendors will request that the FAA specify the acceptable formats for records that prove prior inspections (digital logs, signed PDF service records) to ensure electronic traceability for credit under paragraph (h).

[P1] Consumer advocates will argue that the outdated comment deadline undermines public participation and request that the FAA re-open or extend the comment period, ensuring stakeholders have an opportunity to comment on the final proposed compliance times and procedures.

[P1] The comment deadline of November 4, 2019 (§ 39.13(a)) is unreasonably short and deprives stakeholders of adequate time to prepare technical and operational responses; the FAA should extend the comment period by at least 60–90 days.

[P1] The rule fails to provide electronic submission details or an alternative extended timeline for international operators who may not have received the NPRM in time; request explicit electronic filing instructions and an extension.

[P2] § 39.13(c)(1) is overly broad by applying the AD to “all CFM” listed model turbofan engines with the affected HPT inner stationary seal without clarifying serial number ranges, manufacturing dates, or affected batches; this will create enforcement uncertainty.

[P2] The applicability in § 39.13(c)(1) lacks clarity on whether engines already removed from service, in storage, or exported are included; request explicit inclusion/exclusion language for engines not currently installed on U.S.-registered aircraft.

[P3] The exception in § 39.13(c)(2) for engines with seals repaired per a specified ESM after a listed year is ambiguous because the referenced ESM repair document and "listed year" are not specified in the AD text; provide the exact ESM revision/date and the year threshold.

[P3] The carve-out in § 39.13(c)(2) could be abused because it treats repaired parts as fully equivalent without requiring verification or traceability; require operators to produce repair records and serial-numbered evidence to claim the exception.

[P4] § 39.13(f) requires compliance "within the compliance times specified" but the AD does not list concrete deadlines or intervals in the regulatory text; include explicit shop-visit or flight-hour timelines in the AD itself.

[P5] The requirement in § 39.13(g)(1) to remove the affected HPT inner stationary seal at the "next engine shop visit" is vague—define "next engine shop visit" (e.g., next teardown, borescope inspection, or shop visit involving removal of the HPT module) to avoid inconsistent application.

[P5] Replacing seals only at the next shop visit (§ 39.13(g)(1)) may permit operation for many tens of thousands of flight hours in high-utilization fleets; propose an alternative compliance option to mandate a hard flight-hour or calendar-time replacement limit for high-utilization operators.

[P5] The mandated replacement with an "approved non-listed seal or an eligible repaired seal" (§ 39.13(g)(1)) should explicitly list acceptable part numbers, repair stations, and repair data references to avoid supply-chain and maintenance approval delays.

[P6] The inspection requirement in § 39.13(g)(2) references a service bulletin instruction but the AD should incorporate the inspection criteria and procedures (e.g., acceptance thresholds for honeycomb separation) into the regulatory text for clarity and enforceability.

[P6] The AD does not specify who is authorized to perform the honeycomb separation inspection in § 39.13(g)(2) (operator maintenance, certified repair station, OEM); clarify authorized personnel and required qualifications/certifications.

[P7] § 39.13(g)(3) requires corrective actions "before further flight" if honeycomb separation is found, but does not define acceptable repair means or provide allowed transient relief (e.g., ferry flights); request explicit allowances or prohibition of ferry flights with conditions.

[P8] The requirement in § 39.13(g)(3)(i) to remove and replace the rotating air HPT front seal "before further flight" is operationally burdensome and may ground aircraft unexpectedly; FAA should allow a limited, documented grounding period or approved ferry/repair flight under restricted conditions.

[P9] The inspection of HPT rotor blade internal cavities in § 39.13(g)(3)(ii) references CFM SB paragraph 3.C.(1)(a)(4) but does not provide the acceptance criteria for what constitutes hazardous "honeycomb metal debris"; the AD should specify debris size, quantity thresholds, or other objective metrics.

[P10] § 39.13(g)(3)(ii) mandates removal/replace of rotor blades if debris is found but does not account for potential rework or cleaning procedures that could render a blade serviceable; request allowance for OEM-approved cleaning/repair processes with documented nondestructive inspection demonstrating airworthiness.

[P11] The mandatory removal of the No. 3 ball bearing in § 39.13(g)(3)(iii) if honeycomb separation is found does not list acceptable replacement part numbers or life-limits, thereby creating ambiguity for maintenance planners; provide specific part numbers and airworthiness criteria.

[P12] The carve-out in § 39.13(i) that reporting requirements in the SBs are not required by the AD could reduce situational awareness for the FAA and OEM; oppose removal of reporting or request at least voluntary reporting mechanisms and encourage operators to report incidents to the FAA/OEM.

[P12] Legal experts may argue that excluding SB reporting (§ 39.13(i)) undermines the AD's ability to monitor compliance and fleet health; require data submission (anonymized if necessary) to inform future rulemaking.

[P13] While § 39.13(j)(1) allows AMOC approval by the Manager, ECO Branch, the AD should define standards and timelines for AMOC review to provide regulatory certainty; request a 60-day turnaround commitment for routine AMOCs.

[P14] § 39.13(j)(1) obligations to send AMOC requests to principal inspectors or FSDOs could create conflicting routing for international operators; allow direct AMOC submissions to the FAA certification office from foreign civil aviation authorities or their designees.

[P15] Requiring that AMOC submissions addressed to the certification office manager comply with paragraph (k)(1) (§ 39.13(j)(1)) without including the named contact in the AD text is impractical; include the name/contact information in the AD or reference a stable URL.

[P16] Authorizing AMOC email submissions to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov (§ 39.13(j)(1)) is helpful, but the AD should require receipt confirmations and specify maximum processing time and expected content/format for electronic AMOC filings.

[P17] The obligation in § 39.13(j)(2) to notify principal inspectors or FSDO managers before using an approved AMOC is redundant and may delay corrective actions in urgent situations; allow immediate use with retrospective notification in emergencies.

[P17] Require clear guidance in § 39.13(j)(2) about what constitutes "before using" (e.g., 24 hours prior, prior to first flight using AMOC) to avoid enforcement ambiguity.

[P18] § 39.13(k)(2) permits viewing of referenced service information at the FAA Engine & Propeller Standards Branch in Burlington, MA, but many stakeholders (including foreign operators) cannot access this office; require the FAA to make the SBs available electronically on a public docket or link.

[P18] The AD should specify if viewing the SB at the FAA office is free and whether copies can be made; currently the provision is silent on access fees or copying restrictions.

[P19] Providing a phone number for availability information (§ 39.13(k)(2)) is insufficient; request an email contact and a direct web link to obtain the referenced service bulletins to expedite compliance planning.

[P2] Industry stakeholders will request that the FAA include a definitive parts-traceability requirement so that operators can quickly determine applicability under § 39.13(c)(1) without extensive disassembly.

[P3] Consumer/advocacy groups will argue that the § 39.13(c)(2) exception must require independent verification from the OEM or FAA to prevent improperly performed repairs from escaping the AD.

[P5] Airlines will request a phased compliance schedule in § 39.13(g)(1) tied to scheduled heavy maintenance visits for each engine to avoid concentrated supply-chain impacts and unnecessary AOG events.

[P6] Maintenance organizations will request that the FAA incorporate alternative inspection techniques (e.g., borescope, eddy-current) into § 39.13(g)(2) as acceptable when the referenced SB method is not practicable.

[P10] Legal commenters will ask the FAA to clarify the burden of proof and recordkeeping required to demonstrate that a replaced rotor blade meets “eligible for installation” standards under § 39.13(g)(3)(ii) and (iii).

[P11] Suppliers and MROs will request that the AD include transition relief or a parts availability assessment because immediate replacement of No. 3 ball bearings (§ 39.13(g)(3)(iii)) and seals may exceed current inventory and disrupt ops.

[P12] Aviation safety advocates will argue that eliminating mandatory SB reporting (§ 39.13(i)) reduces transparency and recommend reinstating mandatory immediate notification to the FAA when honeycomb separation is detected.

[P13] Foreign civil aviation authorities will request reciprocal acceptance language for AMOCs (§ 39.13(j)(1)) to ensure approved deviations by other authorities are recognized for foreign-registered operators.

[P16] Operators will request confirmation that emailed AMOC submissions to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov (§ 39.13(j)(1)) will be accepted as legal filings and that sensitive proprietary attachments will be handled confidentially.

[P4] Request that the FAA include explicit enforcement language describing penalties or compliance consequences for failure to meet the obligations in § 39.13(f), (g), and (j).

[P6] Request clarification whether the inspections in § 39.13(g)(2) must be performed using the specific CBM tooling referenced in the SB or whether equivalent tools may be used with documented calibration.

[P7] Safety-certification experts will request that the AD include rationale and risk assessment (e.g., probability/severity of in-flight failure) to justify the "before further flight" corrective action requirement in § 39.13(g)(3).

[P5] Small operators will request cost-impact analysis and economic relief (e.g., compliance subsidies or extended timelines) because replacing seals at next shop visit (§ 39.13(g)(1)) may impose disproportionate costs.

[P2] Request that the FAA publish a searchable list of affected part numbers and engine serial numbers referenced in § 39.13(c)(1) to enable rapid applicability checks.

[P3] Request that the FAA require repaired seals claiming the § 39.13(c)(2) exception be accompanied by a new life-limit or inspection schedule to account for prior damage/repair.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The comment deadline of November 4, 2019 (§ 39.13(a)) is unreasonably short and deprives stakeholders of adequate time to prepare technical and operational responses; the FAA should extend the comment period by at least 60–90 days.

The rule fails to provide electronic submission details or an alternative extended timeline for international operators who may not have received the NPRM in time; request explicit electronic filing instructions and an extension.

§ 39.13(c)(1) is overly broad by applying the AD to “all CFM” listed model turbofan engines with the affected HPT inner stationary seal without clarifying serial number ranges, manufacturing dates, or affected batches; this will create enforcement uncertainty.

The applicability in § 39.13(c)(1) lacks clarity on whether engines already removed from service, in storage, or exported are included; request explicit inclusion/exclusion language for engines not currently installed on U.S.-registered aircraft.

The exception in § 39.13(c)(2) for engines with seals repaired per a specified ESM after a listed year is ambiguous because the referenced ESM repair document and "listed year" are not specified in the AD text; provide the exact ESM revision/date and the year threshold.

The carve-out in § 39.13(c)(2) could be abused because it treats repaired parts as fully equivalent without requiring verification or traceability; require operators to produce repair records and serial-numbered evidence to claim the exception.

§ 39.13(f) requires compliance "within the compliance times specified" but the AD does not list concrete deadlines or intervals in the regulatory text; include explicit shop-visit or flight-hour timelines in the AD itself.

The requirement in § 39.13(g)(1) to remove the affected HPT inner stationary seal at the "next engine shop visit" is vague—define "next engine shop visit" (e.g., next teardown, borescope inspection, or shop visit involving removal of the HPT module) to avoid inconsistent application.

Replacing seals only at the next shop visit (§ 39.13(g)(1)) may permit operation for many tens of thousands of flight hours in high-utilization fleets; propose an alternative compliance option to mandate a hard flight-hour or calendar-time replacement limit for high-utilization operators.

The mandated replacement with an "approved non-listed seal or an eligible repaired seal" (§ 39.13(g)(1)) should explicitly list acceptable part numbers, repair stations, and repair data references to avoid supply-chain and maintenance approval delays.

The inspection requirement in § 39.13(g)(2) references a service bulletin instruction but the AD should incorporate the inspection criteria and procedures (e.g., acceptance thresholds for honeycomb separation) into the regulatory text for clarity and enforceability.

The AD does not specify who is authorized to perform the honeycomb separation inspection in § 39.13(g)(2) (operator maintenance, certified repair station, OEM); clarify authorized personnel and required qualifications/certifications.

§ 39.13(g)(3) requires corrective actions "before further flight" if honeycomb separation is found, but does not define acceptable repair means or provide allowed transient relief (e.g., ferry flights); request explicit allowances or prohibition of ferry flights with conditions.

The requirement in § 39.13(g)(3)(i) to remove and replace the rotating air HPT front seal "before further flight" is operationally burdensome and may ground aircraft unexpectedly; FAA should allow a limited, documented grounding period or approved ferry/repair flight under restricted conditions.

The inspection of HPT rotor blade internal cavities in § 39.13(g)(3)(ii) references CFM SB paragraph 3.C.(1)(a)(4) but does not provide the acceptance criteria for what constitutes hazardous "honeycomb metal debris"; the AD should specify debris size, quantity thresholds, or other objective metrics.

§ 39.13(g)(3)(ii) mandates removal/replace of rotor blades if debris is found but does not account for potential rework or cleaning procedures that could render a blade serviceable; request allowance for OEM-approved cleaning/repair processes with documented nondestructive inspection demonstrating airworthiness.

The mandatory removal of the No. 3 ball bearing in § 39.13(g)(3)(iii) if honeycomb separation is found does not list acceptable replacement part numbers or life-limits, thereby creating ambiguity for maintenance planners; provide specific part numbers and airworthiness criteria.

The carve-out in § 39.13(i) that reporting requirements in the SBs are not required by the AD could reduce situational awareness for the FAA and OEM; oppose removal of reporting or request at least voluntary reporting mechanisms and encourage operators to report incidents to the FAA/OEM.

Legal experts may argue that excluding SB reporting (§ 39.13(i)) undermines the AD's ability to monitor compliance and fleet health; require data submission (anonymized if necessary) to inform future rulemaking.

While § 39.13(j)(1) allows AMOC approval by the Manager, ECO Branch, the AD should define standards and timelines for AMOC review to provide regulatory certainty; request a 60-day turnaround commitment for routine AMOCs.

§ 39.13(j)(1) obligations to send AMOC requests to principal inspectors or FSDOs could create conflicting routing for international operators; allow direct AMOC submissions to the FAA certification office from foreign civil aviation authorities or their designees.

Requiring that AMOC submissions addressed to the certification office manager comply with paragraph (k)(1) (§ 39.13(j)(1)) without including the named contact in the AD text is impractical; include the name/contact information in the AD or reference a stable URL.

Authorizing AMOC email submissions to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov (§ 39.13(j)(1)) is helpful, but the AD should require receipt confirmations and specify maximum processing time and expected content/format for electronic AMOC filings.

The obligation in § 39.13(j)(2) to notify principal inspectors or FSDO managers before using an approved AMOC is redundant and may delay corrective actions in urgent situations; allow immediate use with retrospective notification in emergencies.
Require clear guidance in § 39.13(j)(2) about what constitutes "before using" (e.g., 24 hours prior, prior to first flight using AMOC) to avoid enforcement ambiguity.

§ 39.13(k)(2) permits viewing of referenced service information at the FAA Engine & Propeller Standards Branch in Burlington, MA, but many stakeholders (including foreign operators) cannot access this office; require the FAA to make the SBs available electronically on a public docket or link.
The AD should specify if viewing the SB at the FAA office is free and whether copies can be made; currently the provision is silent on access fees or copying restrictions.

Providing a phone number for availability information (§ 39.13(k)(2)) is insufficient; request an email contact and a direct web link to obtain the referenced service bulletins to expedite compliance planning.

Industry stakeholders will request that the FAA include a definitive parts-traceability requirement so that operators can quickly determine applicability under § 39.13(c)(1) without extensive disassembly.
Consumer/advocacy groups will argue that the § 39.13(c)(2) exception must require independent verification from the OEM or FAA to prevent improperly performed repairs from escaping the AD.
Airlines will request a phased compliance schedule in § 39.13(g)(1) tied to scheduled heavy maintenance visits for each engine to avoid concentrated supply-chain impacts and unnecessary AOG events.

Maintenance organizations will request that the FAA incorporate alternative inspection techniques (e.g., borescope, eddy-current) into § 39.13(g)(2) as acceptable when the referenced SB method is not practicable.

Legal commenters will ask the FAA to clarify the burden of proof and recordkeeping required to demonstrate that a replaced rotor blade meets “eligible for installation” standards under § 39.13(g)(3)(ii) and (iii).

Suppliers and MROs will request that the AD include transition relief or a parts availability assessment because immediate replacement of No. 3 ball bearings (§ 39.13(g)(3)(iii)) and seals may exceed current inventory and disrupt ops.

raw_output:
[P1] Industry commenters will argue that requiring a 12-foot-wide test roadway for vehicles over 10,000 lb GVWR is impractical for many commercial test tracks and fleets, which commonly use wider lanes or multi-lane facilities, and request allowance for equivalent-width lanes or multi-lane setups.

[P1] Legal experts will claim the provision is ambiguous because it omits whether the 12-foot width applies per lane or to the total pavement width when testing on multi-lane roads, and request clarification.

[P2] Fleet operators will object that allowing burnish stops "on any surface" creates variability in results and will ask that burnish stops be standardized to specified surface types (e.g., clean concrete at specified PFC) to ensure repeatability.

[P2] Safety advocates will claim permitting burnish stops on any surface could mask poor brake performance on high-friction surfaces and ask for specifying acceptable surfaces and documenting surface PFC during burnish.

[P3] Test labs will note that restricting parking brake tests to "clean, dry, smooth Portland cement concrete" may be infeasible at many facilities and could increase costs; they will request acceptance of asphalt or other standardized surfaces with equivalent measured friction characteristics.

[P3] A state DOT will request clarity on acceptable maintenance and cleaning procedures to achieve "clean, dry, smooth" concrete and on acceptable tolerances for surface smoothness.

[P4] Truck manufacturers will contend that requiring a 500-foot-radius wet curved roadway with PFC 0.55 and water delivery per ASTM E1337–19 is not available at most proving grounds and will request permission to use instrumented flat-track simulators or skid slurry-applied surfaces that replicate the specified PFC.

[P4] Testing laboratories will request explicit tolerances (e.g., ±0.03 PFC) and frequency of PFC verification during the stability/control braking test, since maintaining 0.55 under water delivery is technically challenging.

[P5] Manufacturers will challenge the universal 1.02 PFC requirement for 60 mph stopping tests with specified loading, arguing that not all public roads or test tracks can sustain that high PFC and asking for an alternative accepted PFC range or allowance for normalized corrections.

[P5] Consumer groups will support the 1.02 PFC requirement as necessary to ensure consistent, conservative stopping performance metrics and urge strict enforcement.

[P6] Truck and bus OEMs will state that full-treadle brake application for the duration of the stop from 30 mph on a 500-ft radius wet curve at specified speeds is overly prescriptive and does not reflect real-world emergency braking, requesting allowance for modulation profiles or repeatable automated brake inputs.

[P6] Test labs will request clarification on "75% of maximum drive-through speed" calculation method and how it applies to variable vehicle geometries and tire sizes.

[P7] Legal commentators will assert that the requirement to stop at least once within Table II distances when stopped six times creates an unclear pass/fail statistical rule (one success out of six) and may allow too many failures; they will ask NHTSA to justify the sampling regimen and consider a higher success threshold.

[P7] Safety advocacy groups will argue that permitting only one compliant stop out of six is too lenient for emergency braking systems and request that a majority or all trials must meet Table II distances.

[P8] Emergency services and urban planners will point out that the "without any portion of the vehicle leaving the roadway" requirement is ambiguous for vehicles whose width approaches roadway width or for banked curves, requesting definition of "leaving the roadway" (e.g., tires beyond paved edge vs. curb contact).

[P8] Test operators will request allowance for minimal encroachment (e.g., <6 inches) due to steering geometry and tire deformation, with clear acceptance criteria.

[P9] Brake system manufacturers will strongly oppose allowing unlimited wheel lockup at any speed, arguing it undermines the effectiveness of ABS systems and could encourage designs that rely on wheel lock for stopping; they will request removal of the unlimited lockup permission or specification that prolonged lockup cannot damage safety systems or exceed skid-related metrics.

[P9] Legal experts will note potential conflict between unlimited wheel lockup permission and other standards or state laws prohibiting dragging wheels, and ask for harmonization language.

[P10] Automotive test facilities will raise cost and logistical concerns about maintaining multiple 12-foot-wide level straight roadways with PFC 1.02 and ask for acceptance of equivalent test layouts with documented lane centering procedures.

[P10] Vehicle manufacturers will request explicit tolerance for "level" (e.g., slope in percent) and for acceptable PFC measurement intervals before and during a testing session.

[P11] Test operators will request clarification on how to achieve precise "aligned in the center of the roadway" start positions for wide vehicles and multi-axle combinations, and whether automated centering equipment or markings are acceptable.

[P11] Plaintiffs' attorneys will note that centering requirement could bias tests in favor of vehicles with better straight-line stability and suggest randomizing start lateral position to replicate real-world conditions.

[P12] Tire manufacturers will request confirmation that the ASTM F2493–19 reference tire specification (including size, inflation pressure, and wear condition) must be used exactly and ask for documentation requirements when non-standard reference tires are used.

[P12] Testing labs will ask whether PFC measurement at 40 mph is required for all vehicle classes and whether speed variation (±2 mph) is permitted for large commercial vehicles.

[P13] Trucking industry stakeholders will demand full disclosure of Table II stopping distances and the derivation methodology and will request scaling or separate tables for multi-axle heavy vehicles, as existing distances may not be appropriate for varied GVWR classes.

[P13] Safety advocates will request that Table II values be set conservatively and supported by public crash-data analysis before finalizing.

[P14] Brake testing labs will object that the blanket requirement for high-friction surfaces for all dynamic brake tests (except ABS) fails to consider that some dynamic behaviors are best observed on intermediate-friction surfaces; they request explicit list of tests that can or cannot use high-friction areas.

[P14] OEMs will request that accelerated wear or heat buildup on high-friction surfaces be addressed with cooling or rest intervals to avoid confounding results.

[P15] Test track owners will request a quantitative definition of "level" and acceptable gradient tolerance beyond ≤1% (e.g., ±0.2%) and seek clarification on measuring gradient over what test segment length.

[P15] Some commenters will note that achieving ≤1% gradient over long test tracks is costly and ask for localized gradient measurement approaches.

[P16] Suppliers will question practicality of achieving and validating a PBC of exactly 1.02 and will request acceptable tolerance bands (e.g., 1.02 ±0.03) and frequency of verification during testing.

[P16] Technical commenters will ask whether PBC refers to wet or dry conditions and request alignment with PFC/PBC terminology across the rule to avoid confusion.

[P17] ABS test labs will request explicit definitions for "low-friction surface" materials (e.g., specific treatments or overlays) and standardized methods to produce reproducible surfaces across facilities.

[P17] Tire advocates will urge inclusion of procedures to prevent surface contamination between tests when switching from low- to high-friction surfaces.

[P18] Test facilities will ask for a definition of "clean" and whether light surface contaminants (e.g., rubber deposits) disqualify a surface, and they will request frequency and documentation requirements for surface cleaning.

[P18] Environmental groups will flag that permitting wet or dry low-friction areas may encourage use of excessive water for test conditioning and request water-conservation guidance.

[P19] Manufacturers will request that the ≤0.50 PBC requirement for low-friction surfaces include an allowed tolerance and method for achieving and verifying such low PBC reproducibly, particularly under varying ambient temperatures.

[P19] Some commenters will request allowance for using standardized low-friction overlay products with certification rather than on-site PBC measurement every test.

[P20] International vehicle makers will note that measuring PBC at 64 km/h (40 mph) may not be appropriate for vehicles designed for different speed regimes and will request provisions for alternative measurement speeds scaled for vehicle test speeds.

[P20] Testing labs will request allowance for metric/imperial rounding and clarify whether 64 km/h exactly or 40 mph exactly governs when equipment calibrations conflict.

[P21] Testing labs and manufacturers will express operational concerns about sequencing a low-friction surface immediately followed by a high-friction surface with PBC ≥0.90, citing difficulty ensuring clean transition zones and consistent PBC on the high-friction patch, and ask for defined transition length and tolerances.

[P21] Safety groups will support the low-to-high sequence as realistic for hazard recovery and request requirements for documenting PBC before each run.

[P22] Motorcycle and small-vehicle advocacy groups will ask whether the road test PFC 1.02 requirement at 40 mph without water delivery applies equally to motorcycles and small vehicles in §571.126, and if not, request explicit carveouts or scaled requirements.

[P22] Test track operators will request clarity on allowable measurement equipment and calibration certs to demonstrate the PFC 1.02 at 40 mph.

[P23] Commenters will request harmonization between §571.135, §571.126, §571.121, and §571.500 regarding PFC 1.02 requirements to avoid conflicting measurement speeds, water delivery requirements, and reference tire specifications.

[P23] Vehicle OEMs will propose a single, cross-referenced annex specifying testing speeds, reference tires, water delivery methods, and acceptable PFC tolerances for all affected standards.

[P24] Tire manufacturers will ask for empirical justification for setting PFC at "at least 1.02" for S7.4.3(f) and request performance-based alternatives where vehicles are evaluated relative to a benchmark rather than an absolute PFC value.

[P25] Test labs will request clarification whether PFC must be maintained at 1.02 for the entire test area used in S7.5.2 or only at the initiation point, and how to handle spatial PFC variability.

[P26] Commenters will note that specifying PFC 1.02 for numerous S7 tests (P24–P31) creates heavy burden on facilities and request an allowance for documented, recent PFC mapping across the entire test area rather than continuous measurement.

[P27] Research institutions will ask for data supporting the choice of 1.02 PFC for all those subtests and request that NHTSA provide surface-performance correlation studies in the docket.

[P28] Manufacturers of control systems will request clarification on how PFC requirements interact with electronic stability control and traction control calibrations during repeated runs.

[P29] Vehicle test engineers will ask whether test surfaces with PFC 1.02 must be homogeneous across lanes and what lateral PFC variation is acceptable when testing multi-axle or wide-track vehicles.

[P30] Tire-tech commenters will point out that PFC measurements can vary by tire temperature and wear; they will request guidance on reference tire conditioning (temperature, tread depth) prior to PFC measurement.

[P31] Commenters will assert that requiring the ASTM F2493–19 reference tire for PFC across many provisions could disadvantage regions where obtaining those tires is difficult, and ask for alternate accepted reference tires or an approval process for equivalent tires.

[P32] Trucking industry commenters will say duplicative PFC requirements across §§571.121, 126, 135, 136, and 500 create compliance complexity and request consolidation into a single testing-surface standard with cross-references.

[P33] Tire industry stakeholders will request clarification on the "traction index ≥112" threshold for snow tire definition: they will ask for rationale, data supporting the 112 cutoff, and whether regional snow conditions warrant multiple tiers or alternative tests.

[P33] Tire manufacturers will request explicit labeling tolerances and inspection protocols to verify Alpine Symbol marking and traction index calculations, including acceptable test labs.

[P34] Manufacturers will ask for consistency between §571.500 and other PFC 1.02 requirements and request explicit procedures if a test cannot reach 1.02 due to weather — e.g., postponement rules or allowed compensatory analysis.

[P35] Tire test consortiums will challenge the requirement to drive the convoy for 16 circuits (~6,400 miles) as excessively long and costly, and will request options for shorter validated endurance runs or use of accelerated wear protocols.

[P35] Consumer groups will support long-duration convoy testing to reveal durability/wear issues and oppose shortening the circuit requirement without demonstrated equivalence.

[P36] Tire manufacturers will raise logistical concerns about rotating tires after each ~400-mile circuit in large fleets and request flexibility for shorter intervals or rotational patterns that maintain test integrity while reducing downtime.

[P36] Some commenters will ask for explicit procedures and recordkeeping requirements for the visual inspections for treadwear anomalies performed after each circuit.

[P37] Convoy test operators will say that moving the last vehicle to the lead position every ~800 miles may create safety and operational issues (e.g., driver fatigue, convoy spacing) and request alternatives such as rotating only tire or vehicle roles without physically reordering the convoy.

[P38] Drivers’ unions and safety advocates will support prohibiting driver position rotation (P38) to promote consistent driver behavior as a variable, but also will raise concerns that forbidding rotation could create fatigue issues over long tests and request mandated rest breaks and maximum driving shift lengths.

[P39] Four-car convoy operators will request flexibility for non-standard convoy sizes and ask that the specified forward-rotation sequence (P39) be adaptable for three- or five-car convoys with equivalent rotation logic.

[P40] Test engineers will seek a definition of "manufacturer's midpoint specification" for wheel alignment adjustments and ask for a default procedure if manufacturer data are absent or ambiguous.

[P41] OEMs will support the exception allowing their recommended alignment when midpoint is not recommended, but request an explicit hierarchy of references (e.g., vehicle service manual, engineering spec sheet) to determine the "manufacturer's recommendation."

[P42] Alignment equipment vendors will request specification of acceptable "alignment machine manufacturer's specified tolerance" including numeric tolerances, calibration frequency, and whether third-party calibration certificates suffice.

[P43] Test labs will ask for detailed procedural guidance on implementing the 9-point tread depth measurement method, including equipment specs, measurement location maps, and acceptable averaging algorithms to ensure reproducibility.

[P44] Convoy test operators will raise practical concerns about moving full sets of tires between vehicles every ~1,600 miles (P44), including mounting/dismounting labor, risk of wheel torque variability, and request allowances for remounted wheel assemblies or equivalent rotational schedules.

[P45] Tire manufacturers and fleet test managers will request a defined method for verifying tire manufacture date and storage history to ensure the "no more than one-year-old" requirement for course monitoring tires is enforceable.

[P46] Testing organizations will request clarification on what constitutes "removal from storage" (e.g., from long-term warehouse vs. refrigerated storage) and how to document the 4-month in-use window for course monitoring tires.

[P47] Industry commenters will argue that rounding the NHTSA nominal treadwear grade percentage down to the nearest lower 20-point increment is arbitrary and will distort comparisons; they will request rounding to the nearest 5- or 10-point increment or using exact percentages with confidence intervals.

[P47] Consumer advocates will counter that rounding down to lower 20-point increments could understate performance and request instead that NHTSA disclose both raw percentages and rounded grades to improve transparency.

[P1] Small operators and independent maintenance providers will not receive adequate notice to respond by August 23, 2019 because of staffing and resource constraints; the FAA should publish a later deadline or provide a staggered schedule.

[P2] § 39.13(f) is vague about what constitutes “the specified compliance times” — commenters request the AD include explicit calendar deadlines or cross-references so operators can determine enforceable dates.

[P2] The phrase “unless the actions have already been done” in § 39.13(f) could create recordkeeping disputes; require that operators retain dated maintenance records proving prior compliance and specify acceptable proof.

[P3] Requiring performance of all actions labeled "RC" in the listed Boeing Alert Service Bulletins under § 39.13(g) without exception imposes prescriptive requirements that may conflict with existing operator maintenance programs; allow for AMOC pathways or clarify interactions with existing maintenance schedules.

[P3] The 36-month overall compliance window in § 39.13(g) may be too long for critical unsafe conditions; conversely, for some fleets the timing in the service bulletins may be impracticable — FAA should justify the 36-month period with risk analysis or allow fleet-specific phased compliance.

[P4] The “whichever occurs first” timing formula in § 39.13(g)/(time condition) is ambiguous when service bulletins specify recurring intervals; clarify whether recurring tasks governed by the bulletin must be accomplished at the first occurrence or can follow the bulletin’s periodicity.

[P4] For aircraft that are rarely flown, the “36 months or bulletin times, whichever is first” could force unnecessary early actions; request that the FAA allow operators to comply at the next scheduled heavy maintenance if within the 36-month window.

[P5] Requiring all replacements of affected AOA sensors prior to the next flight in § 39.13(g) is operationally disruptive and could ground aircraft unexpectedly; propose allowing a short ferry or maintenance flight with specific placard/operational limitations instead of mandatory no-further-flight in all cases.

[P5] The immediate “before further flight” replacement requirement lacks exception for remote locations or extended ferry operations; FAA should provide explicit ferry flight conditions and procedures so operators can move aircraft safely to a maintenance facility.

[P6] Using the AD effective date in place of the service bulletin “original issue date” under § 39.13(h) will alter compliance timing for operators who already complied to earlier bulletin dates; require grandfathering of earlier compliant actions and clear credit language.

[P6] The AD-mandated substitution for “original issue date” will create confusion across fleets that complied to different revision dates; the FAA should require that compliance credit be given when bulletin tasks were done before the AD effective date regardless of which date was used.

[P7] Granting AMOC authority to the Los Angeles ACO Branch Manager in § 39.13(i)(1) centralizes decision-making and may delay approvals for operators outside the LA region; allow delegated AMOC approval by regional ACOs or specify expedited timelines for decisions.

[P7] Petition to permit other FAA certification office managers, not only the Los Angeles ACO Branch Manager, to approve AMOCs to avoid bottlenecks and provide geographic parity.

[P8] The requirement in § 39.13(i)(1) to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO could create routing delays; allow direct submission to the LAACO AMOC email with copy to the principal inspector to streamline the process.

[P18] Clarify in § 39.13(i)(4)(ii) whether temporary deviations to non-RC steps that preclude immediate completion of an RC step are allowed if mitigations are put in place, and describe required documentation and oversight.

[P1] The May 1, 2017 comment deadline is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60–90 days to allow affected owners, maintenance organizations, unions, and safety advocates adequate time to prepare technical and economic comments.

[P1] If the FAA insists on the May 1, 2017 deadline, it should publish clear guidance on where and how to submit late technical data and substantive petitions for extension so stakeholders aren’t unfairly excluded.

[P2] The provision that owners/operators “must perform each action” within the specified compliance time lacks grandfathering language for parts already replaced under service bulletins; we request explicit credit language for prior compliant actions.

[P2] The phrase “unless it has already been accomplished” is ambiguous — commenters request the rule list acceptable evidence (maintenance logs, work orders, parts tags) to document prior compliance.

[P3] Requiring immediate removal from service of any spindle with 1,500+ TIS before next flight is overly burdensome for operators with limited spares and creates potential safety disruptions; allow a short operational ferry period (e.g., 24–72 hours) to reposition aircraft for maintenance.

[P3] The rule should specify whether removal from service requires part destruction, quarantine, or tagging procedures and who bears cost for removing and returning spindles to the manufacturer for inspection.

[P3] For helicopters that perform single-pilot or remote operations critical to emergency services, an exception or expedited replacement process should be allowed rather than a blanket before-next-flight grounding.

[P4] Using the helicopter’s TIS when spindle TIS is unknown will overstate usage for spindles that were recently installed; the rule should allow tracing of spindle installation records or affidavits from certified mechanics to establish true spindle TIS.

[P4] The FAA should require operators to make “reasonable efforts” to determine spindle-specific hours (e.g., parts tracking, shop records) before defaulting to helicopter TIS, and provide an appeal process if helicopter TIS overstates spindle life.

[P5] The mandate to remove spindles before they reach 1,500 hours needs clarification on whether “before” includes spindles at exactly 1,500.0 hours TIS; specify whether removal is required at 1,499.9 hours or at 1,500 hours.

[P5] The regulation should permit replacement during the next scheduled heavy maintenance if that occurs within a small buffer (e.g., 25 hours) rather than requiring immediate out-of-cycle removals that increase costs.

[P6] Conditioning subsequent inspection requirements on spindles with 500+ hours TIS is reasonable, but commenters request explicit instructions for spindles between 0–499 hours (e.g., initial inspection at 500 hours).

[P6] Clarify whether the 500-hour threshold applies cumulatively across multiple installations of the same spindle (i.e., total life) or only per-installation TIS.

[P7] Using helicopter hours when spindle hours are unknown will penalize operators who maintain reasonable part-tracking; propose a hierarchy of acceptable evidence (part tags, invoices, logbook entries, installer statements) before defaulting to helicopter TIS.

[P7] The FAA should permit use of time-on-condition tracking systems (electronic traceability) as valid proof of spindle TIS in lieu of helicopter TIS.

[P8] Requiring an MPI before the next flight for spindles with ≥500 hours, unless done within the last 500 hours, may be impractical for remote operators without access to Level II/III inspectors; request allowance for an extended compliance window (e.g., 72–120 hours) to obtain qualified inspection.

[P8] The AD should explicitly allow operators to use approved mobile NDT providers and clarify whether temporary ferry flights to inspection facilities are permitted under a special flight permit.

[P8] The “unless already done within the last 500 hours” language is vague: commenters request FAA to specify acceptable documentation proving an MPI occurred within the past 500 hours (report, inspector stamp, date and hours).

[P9] Requiring MPI by Level II or III inspectors qualified to EN4179 or NAS410 (or equivalent) may exclude many U.S. inspectors trained to other national standards; FAA should explicitly list acceptable equivalent qualifications or provide a process for equivalency approval.

[P9] The rule should clarify whether Level II/III qualifications must be specific to MPI in the aeronautics sector, or whether general magnetic particle inspection certification is acceptable when accompanied by aircraft-specific experience.

[P9] For international operators, requiring EN4179 may conflict with local certifying authority standards; allow NAS410, EN4179, or other ICAO-recognized equivalents and explain process for demonstrating equivalence.

[P10] Replacing any cracked spindle with an “airworthy spindle” before further flight should define “airworthy” — does this require new OEM parts, FAA-approved overhaul, or can refurbished/repaired spindles be used if certified?

[P10] The AD should instruct whether repaired spindles repaired per manufacturer repair schemes and returned to service with proper documentation meet the “airworthy” standard.

[P11] The 500-hour repetitive MPI interval could impose heavy recurring costs; operators request risk-based alternatives (e.g., condition monitoring, enhanced visual inspections at shorter intervals, or extension to 750 hours if additional nondestructive testing methods are used).

[P11] The FAA should require data collection on repeat inspection findings and consider adjusting interval length based on operational experience — propose a review after 12–24 months.

[P12] Centralizing AMOC approval authority to the Chicago Aircraft Certification Office may slow approvals for operators in other regions; request delegation of AMOC review to regional FSDOs or a fast-track process for routine, low-risk AMOCs.

[P12] The AD should define the criteria and expected timeline (e.g., 30 days) for AMOC review and approval to provide regulatory certainty.

[P13] Requiring submission of AMOC proposals to a single named individual (Monica Nemecek) and specific contact info is problematic if personnel change; the rule should provide a generic office address and functional mailbox/email/online portal as the official submission point.

[P13] The AD should allow electronic submission through the FAA’s existing online AMOC portal and provide confirmation-of-receipt procedures to prevent lost proposals.

[P14] The suggestion (not requirement) to notify the principal inspector or local FSDO before operating under an AMOC should be mandatory for certificate holders under parts 119 and 91K to ensure local oversight and consistent enforcement.

[P14] Clarify whether failure to notify the principal inspector will affect enforcement or validity of the AMOC — operators need certainty that notification is administrative, not a substantive condition of compliance.

[P15] Automatically approving AMOCs previously granted under AD 2015–08–51 could inadvertently approve AMOCs that only addressed differences specific to the prior AD; FAA should require confirmation that each prior AMOC fully addresses the corresponding requirements of this AD.

[P15] Request a list of all AMOCs approved under AD 2015–08–51 that the FAA intends to carry forward so stakeholders can assess their applicability and any necessary modifications.

[P5] § 39.13(h)(2) mandates “all applicable related investigative and corrective actions before further flight” but does not define “applicable,” creating enforcement uncertainty; add objective criteria or examples to guide inspectors and operators.

[P5] Requiring corrective actions “before further flight” in § 39.13(h)(2) may be operationally impracticable for airlines during irregular operations; allow temporary flight with specific mitigations where safety can be maintained and an AMOC is obtained.

[P6] § 39.13(h)(3) requires operators to obtain FAA/EASA/Airbus DOA-approved additional maintenance instructions within 6 months for airplanes modified prior to Table 2 thresholds; 6 months is insufficient for global operators to coordinate DOA approvals—request 12 months.

[P6] The provision in § 39.13(h)(3) should clarify whether the 6-month clock starts from the effective date of the FAA AD or from the date of notification to affected operators.

[P7] § 39.13(i) states this AD does not require submission of information to the manufacturer even if the EASA service information does; please confirm that not submitting information to the manufacturer will not impede tracking safety data or future corrective actions.

[P7] Removing the manufacturer reporting requirement in § 39.13(i) could impede trend analysis and fleet-wide safety monitoring; consider requiring submission to FAA or mandated reporting to a centralized FAA database instead.

[P8] The AMOC approval authority in § 39.13(j)(1) vests too much discretion in a single FAA Manager; require public posting of approved AMOCs or quarterly summaries to ensure transparency and consistent nationwide application.

[P9] § 39.13(j)(1) requires AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19, but many operators use centralized engineering — allow submissions from designated principal CAMO/continuing airworthiness organizations as well.

[P10] The instruction in § 39.13(j)(1) to send AMOC info directly to the person in paragraph (k)(2) needs the contact name and contact details included in the AD text to avoid delay.

[P1] The obligation in § 39.13(e) is vague about recordkeeping; commenters will request explicit recordkeeping and retention time (e.g., log entries, repair tags, or maintenance records kept for X years) to demonstrate compliance with "performed within the specified compliance time."

[P1] Industry commenters will request clarification that "already accomplished" means any action previously performed in accordance with the applicable Bell Alert Service Bulletins (ASBs) and signed off in the aircraft maintenance log by an FAA-certificated mechanic or repair station.

[P2] Operators will object that the 25 hours TIS or 30 days threshold in § 39.13(f)(1) is unworkably short for helicopters with limited downtime and will request extending the compliance time to a minimum of 50–100 hours TIS or 60–90 days to allow scheduling and parts availability.

[P2] Air ambulance and emergency operators will request an exemption or longer compliance time from § 39.13(f)(1) because taking aircraft out of service within 25 hours/30 days could impair critical public services.

[P3] Maintenance providers will request that § 39.13(f)(1)(i) explicitly permit removal of the T/R hub/blade assembly by certified repair stations only, to avoid liability and ensure consistent workmanship.

[P3] Commenters will request the ASB references in § 39.13(f)(1)(i) be incorporated by reference in the AD or included verbatim to avoid ambiguity regarding which Bell ASB revisions/procedures are acceptable.

[P4] Technicians will point out that requiring a "3x or higher magnifying glass" in § 39.13(f)(1)(ii) is ambiguous — commenters will ask whether other inspection aids (borescope, 10x loupe, microscope, dye-penetrant, eddy-current) are allowed or preferred and request explicit allowance of enhanced NDI techniques.

[P4] Legal/technical commenters will note that a visual inspection alone with only 3x magnification may be insufficient to detect subsurface corrosion/pitting and will ask the FAA to require or allow non-destructive testing (NDT) such as eddy current for more reliable detection.

[P5] Operators will request clarification of the phrase "before further flight" in § 39.13(f)(2) — whether it permits ferry flights to a repair facility under special flight permits or requires grounding until the action is completed.

[P5] Repair stations will request explicit language to permit issuance of an FAA special flight permit for repositioning if replacement parts are not immediately available, and to outline conditions for such permits.

[P6] Maintenance organizations will request that § 39.13(f)(2)(i) specify acceptable repair methods and repair limits (e.g., documented SRM/ASB repair instructions or repair station capability list) so that "repair the T/R blade" is not open to differing interpretations.

[P6] Operators will request that the AD explicitly permit blending/sanding up to the 0.003 inch limit only when performed per the ASB, with torque/inspections after repair; otherwise they will seek an AMOC for alternative repair procedures.

[P7] Several commenters will challenge the absolute replacement requirement in § 39.13(f)(2)(ii) for corrosion/pitting >0.003 inch as unduly conservative and costly, asking the FAA to allow approved repairs by certificated repair stations where material removal/patching can be shown reliable via NDT and fatigue analysis.

[P7] Legal commenters will ask for supporting data or risk assessment that justifies the strict >0.003 inch replacement threshold in § 39.13(f)(2)(ii), requesting the FAA publish the rationale or data used to set that limit.

[P8] Repair shops will request that § 39.13(f)(2)(iii) define "allowable repair limits" precisely (materials removed, residual thickness, taper geometry, life-limits after repair) and reference the specific Bell SRM or repair criteria to permit consistent repair acceptance.

[P8] Commenters will request that repairs involving parent material removal require post-repair NDT and fatigue-life limitations be specified (e.g., life extension or retirement-for-cause criteria).

[P9] Operators will ask § 39.13(f)(2)(iv) to clarify acceptable refinishing materials/primers/paints and curing processes for the refinish step and whether refinishing must follow a specific Bell ASB revision.

[P9] Maintenance providers will request that the AD explicitly require and describe functional checks (track and balance tolerances, flight checks) after reinstallation per the ASB, and whether log entry signatures suffice as completion evidence.

[P10] Several commenters will support the permission in § 39.13(g) that prior actions per AD 2011–12–08 count, but will request explicit cross-references to the exact paragraphs of AD 2011–12–08 that satisfy (f)(1)(i)/(ii) and (f)(2) to avoid compliance uncertainty.

[P10] Some will request transitional language confirming that compliance per earlier ASBs or service documents other than AD 2011–12–08 will also be accepted if materially equivalent and documented.

[P11] Industry and repair stations will request further detail in § 39.13(h)(1) about the criteria and expected turnaround time the Manager will use to approve AMOCs, to facilitate timely proposals.

[P11] Advocacy groups seeking safety conservatism will caution that AMOCs should be granted only with rigorous technical substantiation and request publication of accepted AMOCs for transparency.

[P12] Commenters will object that the AMOC submission route in § 39.13(h)(1) is too narrow and request email/online portal options with tracked receipts; they will also ask for a standard AMOC template to ensure submissions contain required data.

[P12] Small operators will request that the contact information in § 39.13(h)(1) include fax or secure electronic submission and confirmation to accommodate geographic dispersion and avoid mail delays.

[P13] Operators under parts 119 and 91K will request that § 39.13(h)(2) require, not just suggest, notification to the principal inspector or FSDO if using an AMOC, to ensure FAA oversight and consistency.

[P13] Some commenters will request that the rule define the timeline for notifying the principal inspector and the content required in that notification when an AMOC is used.

[P14] Multiple commenters will point out that the § 39.13(d) comment deadline of June 10, 2019 may be inadequate and request at least a 60-day comment period from publication to allow stakeholders to prepare technical comments and coordinate industry input.

[P14] Industry associations will request an extension of the comment period pending release of supporting data (service difficulty reports, inspection findings) that the FAA used to justify the AD so stakeholders can prepare informed comments.

[P1] Aviation safety advocates will request adding a requirement for fleet-wide reporting after inspections (e.g., submit findings and measurements to the FAA) so the agency can track corrosion prevalence and reassess the AD if necessary.

[P4] Some commenters will point out that the magnification requirement should specify measurement method for determining 0.003 inch depth (e.g., using calibrated depth micrometer or optical comparator), as a magnifier alone does not provide a quantitative measurement.

[P6] Maintenance industry commenters will request that the AD allow temporary repairs (with defined limitations) that permit limited operations to a maintenance base rather than immediate replacement when corrosion ≤0.003 in, provided a specific risk mitigant is in place.

[P2] Small helicopter owners will request that the FAA provide or allow loaner/overhauled T/R blades through a parts pooling program since the short compliance time could create immediate shortages and grounded aircraft.

[P7] Aircraft operators will ask that the AD include provisions for compensation or liability protections if replacement blades supplied under time pressure are later found defective or introduce other safety issues.

[P9] Pilots’ associations will request explicit post-action flight test requirements (e.g., hover and forward-flight checks, max gross weight conditions) following reinstallation and tracking/balancing to ensure operational safety before returning to revenue service.

[P11] Legal commenters will request that the AMOC authority be clarified whether it can approve deviations from mandated replacement thresholds (e.g., >0.003 in limit) and under what technical substantiation such deviations would be allowed.

[P8] Commenters will ask for an explicit quality-control acceptance standard for sanding operations to prevent inadvertent removal beyond allowable limits (e.g., use of depth-limiting sanding guides or templates).

[P3] Some commenters will request that the AD require tagging of removed hub/blade assemblies and tracking their serial numbers to ensure returned or newly installed blades are airworthy and traceable.
