[P1] Industry commenters (oncology drug manufacturers and infusion providers) will claim the rule is ambiguous because the code list is truncated in the text (ends with "J9230–") and does not clearly identify the full range of excluded codes, creating compliance uncertainty.

[P1] Patient advocacy groups will claim that excluding entire classes of chemotherapy drugs by code risks patient access to medically necessary oncology drugs during SNF stays, particularly for elderly cancer patients who require continuity of care.

[P2] Hospitals and SNFs will comment that excluding chemotherapy administration services identified as of July 1, 1999 (codes 36260–36262, 36489, 36530–36535, 36640, 36823, and 96405–965) fails to account for changes in administration techniques and newer HCPCS codes, potentially disincentivizing SNFs from providing essential administration services.

[P2] Clinical societies (oncology nurses, infusion medicine) will assert that excluding administration codes by date-authority (1999) ignores advances in practice and may force unnecessary patient transfers back to hospitals for administration, increasing readmissions and patient harm.

[P3] Providers will point out the phrase "(as subsequently modified by CMS), and any additional radioisot" is truncated and unclear, creating uncertainty about which radioisotope services are excluded and whether CMS will retroactively add codes.

[P3] Nuclear medicine and oncology stakeholders will argue that excluding radioisotope services under codes 79030–79440 without specifying modification rules could remove coverage for diagnostic or therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals developed after 1999 that are clinically indicated for Medicare beneficiaries.

[P4] Prosthetics manufacturers and SNF discharge planners will claim excluding customized prosthetic devices (HCPCS L5050–L5340, L550...) from SNF coverage when those devices are delivered during an SNF stay but intended for post-discharge use will create financial and logistical burdens, delaying timely patient discharge and increasing costs for beneficiaries.

[P4] Disability rights advocates will state that excluding customized prosthetic devices provided during SNF stays undermines reasonable continuity of care and may compel beneficiaries to pay out-of-pocket for essential mobility aids after discharge.

[P5] Hemophilia treatment centers and patient advocates will object to excluding specified blood clotting factors as of July 1, 2020 by HCPCS (text appears truncated), noting these products are life-sustaining and exclusion would limit access and increase morbidity for beneficiaries with bleeding disorders.

[P5] Legal experts will claim that excluding blood clotting factors by a fixed date (July 1, 2020) without a process to add newer factor products or to account for code revisions is arbitrary and may violate notice-and-comment rulemaking norms by failing to specify which exact HCPCS codes are affected.

[P6] SNF associations will support but seek clarification on the 90-day deadline to request an exception via email, requesting CMS confirm when the 90-day clock starts (date of event, date SNF learned of impact, or date of discovery of harm).

[P6] Smaller SNFs and rural providers will request alternative submission methods (fax, postal mail, web portal) in addition to email, arguing not all facilities have reliable email or the capacity to use the designated account within 90 days.

[P7] SNFs will object to the requirement that exception emails must include a completed Extraordinary Circumstances Request form hosted on qualitynet.cms.gov, asking CMS to permit inclusion of the form as an attachment in alternate formats and to allow late-submitted forms where evidence shows extenuating circumstances.

[P7] Advocacy groups will argue that requiring supportive evidence like photographs or media articles disadvantages facilities in low-pressure or privacy-sensitive incidents (e.g., infectious outbreaks where photos are restricted) and request CMS accept alternative attestations or certifications from public health authorities.

[P9] SNFs will ask CMS to provide a clear process timeline for when corrections, if accepted, will be reflected in public reports and payment adjustments to enable financial planning.

[P13] Quality measurement experts will contend that suspending the usual methodology undermines measure validity and comparability across years, making performance trends unreliable.

[P14] SNFs will object to assigning a performance score of zero to every SNF (except low-volume adjustments) for FY2022, arguing it will produce perverse incentives, inaccurately represent facility quality, and potentially harm facilities in public reporting and payment calculations.

[P16] SNF financial officers will request an explanation and worked examples of how CMS will compute the value-based incentive payment adjustment factor using a performance score of zero, and how this interacts with other payment adjustments.

[P16] Industry groups will warn that using zeros may result in unintended negative payment adjustments for facilities that actually had good performance, and request CMS model and publish projected payment impacts before finalizing.

raw_output:
[P1] The deadline of August 8, 2019 for public comments is unreasonably short and should be extended to allow stakeholders adequate time to analyze technical impacts and submit detailed comments.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether the August 8, 2019 date is the postmark date or the date FAA must receive comments, because many stakeholders rely on courier or agency docket-processing times.

[P2] The compliance clause is vague about whether operators who have partial work in progress are considered “already complied”; FAA should clarify how partial compliance is treated.

[P2] The rule must specify whether compliance times apply per engine, per aircraft, or per operator to avoid inconsistent interpretations among operators and maintenance organizations.

[P3] The initial inspection threshold “within 7,500 engine flight hours since new, or since the last inspection, or within 150 flight cycles after January 5, 2017” is confusing and appears to combine FH and FC benchmarks without clear sequencing — FAA should rewrite to state the exact triggering condition.

[P3] The January 5, 2017 date embedded in the compliance threshold creates retrospective compliance obligations that could be impossible to document for older engines; the FAA should allow operators to use best-available maintenance records or to perform an initial inspection immediately if records are incomplete.

[P4] Requiring use of paragraph (g)(3) procedures for the inspection without allowing incorporation of equivalent service bulletin procedures may prevent operators from using already-approved industry inspection methods; FAA should allow alternative approved procedures.

[P5] The repeating interval of every 7,500 engine FHs is onerous for high-FC but low-FH operators (e.g., short-haul fleets) and may not address fatigue driven by cycles; FAA should add an alternate repeat interval in flight cycles or a dual threshold (FH or FC), or justify why FH alone is appropriate.

[P6] Paragraph (g)(3) references “detailed steps that follow” but does not include tolerances, tool specifications, or training requirements; the lack of detail could lead to inconsistent inspections and should either include full SIs or explicitly incorporate a service bulletin by reference.

[P7] The visual inspection of seal face 22, seal support 23, and Zone A on the right side only appears to omit the left side — FAA must explain why inspections are required only on the right side and document evidence that left-side fairings are not susceptible.

[P7] The rule should define “visual inspection” (e.g., 3x magnification, lighting levels) to ensure consistent findings across shops and operators.

[P8] Requiring immediate grounding until repair/replacement when material release is found on seal face 22 (repair or replace prior to next flight) could impose safety and operational burdens; FAA should allow a risk-based deferred action procedure if the release is assessed as non-hazardous, or clarify that temporary placards/limitations are acceptable.

[P9] The prescribed repair window of 100 engine FCs or next shop visit for a single crack <6 mm may be insufficiently risk-based; commenters should be allowed to propose life-limited repairs or non-destructive evaluation intervals as AMOCs.

[P10] The very short compliance timeline of 15 engine FCs for single cracks >6 mm may not be practicable for engines in service with long intervals between shop visits; FAA should permit ferry flights or limited dispatch procedures with specific monitoring until replacement can occur.

[P11] Requiring replacement within 15 engine FCs for two or more cracks on seal face 22 could be logistically and financially burdensome for small operators; FAA should provide guidance on parts availability and consider a phased compliance schedule.

[P12] The absolute requirement to replace the fairing within 15 engine FCs for any cracking or material loss on seal support 23 does not allow for temporary repairs or spot fixes that may be approved by OEM engineering; FAA should allow OEM-approved temporary repairs with monitoring until replacement.

[P13] The rule’s mandate to conduct fluorescent penetrant inspection (FPI) if no visual cracks are found may be difficult to accomplish during line maintenance; FAA should clarify acceptable facilities, required cleanliness levels, and whether FPI can be deferred to the next shop visit.

[P13] FPI can produce false positives if contamination is present; the AD should provide contamination control guidance and specify acceptable FPI sensitivity levels and interpretation criteria.

[P14] The 100 engine FCs remedy interval for cracks <6 mm found by FPI mirrors the visual threshold but does not account for detection method differences; FAA should justify parity or create detection-method-specific intervals.

[P15] For cracks >6 mm detected by FPI, the 15 FC replacement requirement may not consider crack propagation rates and could be overconservative; FAA should provide root-cause analysis or fracture mechanics data supporting the chosen intervals.

[P16] Requiring modification of the upper bifurcation fairing assembly at the next engine shop visit after the AD effective date fails to define “next engine shop visit” (major/borescope/shop visit definition), leading to inconsistent application; FAA should define what constitutes a shop visit.

[P16] The mandatory terminating modification at the next shop visit could create a parts-supply bottleneck; FAA should include a compliance window (e.g., within X months) or allow staged implementation to avoid grounding due to part shortages.

[P17] Declaring installation of the modified fairing as terminating action for inspections is appropriate only if modification demonstrably mitigates the risk; FAA must provide the test data or service bulletin that justifies terminating inspection requirements.

[P17] The rule should require post-modification reporting or evidence of durability to ensure terminating action is valid; without such monitoring, removing inspections could create latent risk.

[P18] The outright prohibition on installing part number FK25470 after the effective date may strand inventory of new or overhauled parts held by MROs and OEMs; FAA should allow a sell-through or return-to-manufacturer pathway or grandfather parts for immediate replacement pending modification.

[P18] The installation prohibition lacks an exception for ferry or maintenance transfers where reinstallation of FK25470 may be necessary; FAA should allow temporary installation under an approved AMOC for limited operations.

[P19] The AMOC authority vested in the Manager, ECO Branch, is standard, but the AD should clarify expected review timelines for AMOC requests to prevent extended operational interruptions.

[P20] Conditioning AMOC approval on procedures in 14 CFR 39.19 without specifying acceptable supporting data creates uncertainty; FAA should list types of analyses and data (e.g., fatigue analysis, test reports) that will facilitate approval.

[P21] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or FSDO may be impractical for international operators without a U.S.-based inspector; FAA should provide an alternate submission route for foreign operators.

[P22] The instruction to address direct AMOC submissions to the person in paragraph (l) is unclear because paragraph (l) references contact information that may change; FAA should include up-to-date name/position and a mailing address directly in the AD.

[P23] The option to email AMOC requests to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov is helpful but the AD should also commit to acknowledging receipt and provide target response times for emailed AMOCs.

[P24] The requirement to notify the principal inspector prior to using an approved AMOC could be redundant when AMOC approval already comes from FAA; FAA should clarify whether notification suffices in lieu of local approval and define the timeline for notification.

[P25] Allowing parties to examine the referenced EASA AD in the docket is useful, but the AD should include a summary of differences between the FAA AD and the EASA AD to avoid misunderstandings.

[P26] Making service information available only at the FAA Engine and Propeller Standards Branch office in Burlington, MA is burdensome for remote stakeholders; FAA should provide electronic access or reference the OEM service bulletin number and a direct web link.

[P1] The requirement that registered handlers must pack tomatoes only in 10, 20, or 25 pound designated net weight containers is unduly prescriptive and will impose significant retooling costs on packers who currently use a wider variety of container sizes (e.g., 5 lb clamshells, 15 lb flats, 40 lb crates).

[P1] Small-scale and direct-market producers who sell to farmers markets and CSA programs will be disproportionately harmed because they commonly use nonstandard sizes (e.g., 5 lb, 8 lb) that the rule would prohibit, reducing market channels for small growers.

[P1] The rule fails to account for modern packaging formats (punnets, clamshells, consumer retail-ready multipacks) and therefore will disrupt retail and food service supply chains that rely on those different sizes.

[P1] The regulation does not provide a phased compliance timeline; requiring immediate adherence to only 10, 20, or 25 lb containers will create undue economic hardship for handlers who need time to order and inventory new containers.

[P1] The provision lacks an allowance or process for handlers to request approval for alternative container sizes when justified by market or logistical needs, which is necessary to avoid unnecessary waste and inefficiency.

[P1] The rule overlooks export and import considerations — international customers and foreign-flagged shipping containers use different sizing standards, so this packaging mandate may reduce export competitiveness.

[P1] The agency has not provided an economic analysis showing the cost-benefit of restricting container sizes to 10, 20, and 25 lb compared to current practice; without that analysis the mandate appears arbitrary and likely violates Administrative Procedure Act standards.

[P1] Retailers that require smaller consumer-ready packs (e.g., 1–5 lb) will be forced to repackage or reject shipments, increasing handling costs and food loss; the rule should permit consumer-sized packaging.

[P1] The rule could increase packaging material use and environmental impact by forcing single-purpose container inventories; an alternative that allows a range of sizes would better align with sustainability goals.

[P2] The strict prohibition that net weight shall not be less than the designated net weight gives no tolerance for minor shortfalls due to moisture loss or variability, creating an unrealistic compliance standard and potential for excessive penalties.

[P2] The rule does not specify acceptable methods or intervals for weighing/verification to ensure net weight compliance, leading to enforcement ambiguity and potential disputes between handlers and inspectors.

[P2] Requiring that contents never be under the designated net weight unfairly exposes handlers to strict liability for small, inadvertent underfills beyond their control; a reasonable de minimis tolerance (e.g., 1–2% underweight or fixed ounces) should be defined.

[P2] The prohibition could incentivize overfilling to avoid violations (subject to P3), but because P3 limits overfill only by two pounds, handlers may still be penalized due to measurement error — the interaction of P2 and P3 is unclear and needs clarification.

[P2] The rule does not account for weight loss during transit from packing to delivery (evaporation, respiration), particularly for tomatoes shipped long distances; the agency should allow for transit weight loss or mandate weighings at specified points.

[P3] Capping overfill at no more than two pounds above the designated net weight is arbitrary; large container sizes (e.g., 25 lb) may experience greater variance, so a percentage-based tolerance (e.g., ±8%) would be more appropriate and equitable.

[P3] The "not exceed by more than two pounds" limit creates practical packing issues for handlers using bulk-by-volume methods where weight variance is related to fruit density; a flat two-pound allowance may be insufficient and lead to unnecessary repacking.

[P3] The provision fails to specify whether the two-pound allowance is per container regardless of container size or whether it scales; this ambiguity will lead to inconsistent enforcement (e.g., two pounds on a 10 lb pack is more significant than on 25 lb).

[P3] Combined with P2's zero-tolerance for underweight, the two-pound overfill cap risks creating a narrow acceptable band that is smaller than normal packing variation, increasing compliance costs and the potential for disputes and enforcement actions.

[P3] There is no guidance on how rounding and weighing precision should be handled (e.g., scales tolerances, calibration frequency), which is critical when a two-pound threshold can determine compliance.

[P4] Excluding U.S. standard § 51.1863 from applicability creates legal uncertainty because handlers and inspectors currently rely on that standard for labeling and weight tolerances; removing it without clear replacements will cause confusion.

[P4] The rule does not explain why § 51.1863 is being excluded; stakeholders request justification and the expected practical effects of this exception, including whether other U.S. tomato standards will fill the gap.

[P4] Advocacy groups for consumer protection are concerned that removing § 51.1863 protections could reduce labeling clarity and consumer safeguards; the agency should confirm that consumer protections will be maintained.

[P4] The exception may conflict with state labeling laws or other federal standards that reference § 51.1863; the agency should evaluate preemption and harmonization to avoid regulatory conflicts.

[P5] The instruction that other terms shall have the same meaning as in Marketing Agreement No. 125, this part, and the U.S. tomato standards is too vague because stakeholders use different versions and amendments; the rule should cite the specific edition or amendment dates to avoid interpretive disputes.

[P5] Relying on Marketing Agreement No. 125 and unspecified "U.S. tomato standards" without incorporating them by reference deprives the public of clear notice about substantive obligations and may raise procedural and legal issues under the Administrative Procedure Act.

[P5] Legal practitioners note that cross-referencing multiple instruments (Marketing Agreement No. 125, "this part", and U.S. standards) without resolving inconsistencies will leave handlers uncertain which definition controls in case of conflict; the rule should include a hierarchy clause.

[P5] The rule must specify how future amendments to Marketing Agreement No. 125 or the U.S. tomato standards will affect meanings under § 966.323(g) — automatic incorporation could bind handlers to future standards without notice.

[P5] The agency should provide an accessible compilation of the referenced definitions (Marketing Agreement No. 125 and the cited U.S. tomato standards) alongside the final rule so handlers and inspectors have a single, authoritative source.

[P1/P2] Industry commenters will likely argue that the combined effect of forcing three container sizes and imposing zero-tolerance underweight creates operational incompatibilities — the rule should be revised to allow more container flexibility and reasonable underweight tolerances.

[P3/P5] Quality-control and compliance officers will request explicit weighing, calibration, and recordkeeping requirements (e.g., scale accuracy, calibration frequency, retention period) because the two-pound overfill limit and cross-referenced definitions require precise enforcement protocols.

[P1/P4] Organic and specialty tomato producers will request exemptions allowing alternative packaging and standards alignment with organic labeling rules, because the blanket exclusion of § 51.1863 and narrow container sizes may conflict with organic packaging practices.

[P2/P4] Consumer advocacy groups will request clarity that the prohibition on underweight containers is enforced in a manner that protects consumers from deceptive practices but also does not punish minor, unavoidable variances — proposing a defined consumer-facing tolerance.

[P1] Retailers and wholesalers request a stakeholder engagement process to adapt the specified container sizes to modern retail formats (e.g., resealable bags, multipacks) rather than forcing 10/20/25 lb-only packing.

[P1] The $85 filing fee for Form I-821D will create an undue financial barrier for low-income DACA-eligible applicants and should be waived or reduced for applicants who can demonstrate inability to pay.

[P1] Charging the $85 fee for renewals as well as initial I-821D filings is burdensome; the rule should clarify whether the fee applies to both initial and renewal requests and consider exempting renewals.

[P1] The rule provides no mechanism for fee waivers or partial waivers for minors or survivors of trafficking/abuse; USCIS should adopt explicit fee-waiver criteria for Form I-821D.

[P2] Requiring demonstration of "economic need" to apply for employment authorization (236.21(c)(2)) is vague and will produce inconsistent adjudications unless DHS defines acceptable proof and objective thresholds.

[P2] Conditioning ability to obtain work authorization on "economic need" conflicts with the rehabilitative and public-safety aims of employment and should be removed; employment authorization should be available without this extra gate.

[P3] The phrase "may consider" in §236.22(a)(1) gives USCIS too much uncertainty and could be read to allow arbitrary non-consideration; commenters request clear mandatory processing standards and timelines.

[P4] Prohibiting any interim benefits for pending DACA requests (§236.22(a)(2)) will leave applicants unable to work or travel while USCIS adjudicates their cases, causing severe hardship; at minimum USCIS should be allowed to grant interim EADs in prolonged delays.

[P5] Placing the full burden of proof "by a preponderance of the evidence" on applicants (§236.22(a)(3)) is appropriate, but USCIS must provide clear guidance on acceptable documentary evidence and alternative evidence for cases lacking typical records.

[P5] The preponderance standard without guidance will disproportionately harm applicants from rural areas or those who experienced family disruption; DHS should allow flexible evidentiary standards in close-call cases.

[P6] Granting DACA only upon a discretionary favorable exercise (§236.22(b)) makes approvals unforeseeable; DHS should publish objective discretion factors and weighted considerations so applicants understand likelihoods.

[P7] Requirement to show first residence before age 16 (§236.22(b)(1)) is appropriate but needs examples of acceptable proof (school records, affidavits); otherwise many who lack formal documentation will be unfairly denied.

[P8] Continuous residence from June 15, 2007 to filing (§236.22(b)(2)) is too strict for applicants who entered shortly after that date or had short gaps due to caregiving or health emergencies; DHS should allow minor gaps supported by evidence.

[P9] Treating any unauthorized travel after Aug 15, 2012 as interrupting continuous residence (§236.22(b)(2)) is overbroad and will penalize applicants for brief border crossings; the rule should align with prior guidance allowing brief, innocent departures.

[P10] The "brief and reasonably calculated" test for exceptions to interrupted residence (§236.22(b)(2)(i)) is subjective; DHS must provide concrete time standards or example scenarios so adjudicators apply it consistently.

[P11] Disqualifying absences resulting from orders of exclusion, deportation, or removal after June 15, 2007 (§236.22(b)(2)(ii)) may unfairly bar people who were subject to immigration proceedings as minors; DHS should permit relief where proceedings were later vacated or were erroneous.

[P12] Excluding absences tied to voluntary departure orders issued after June 15, 2007 (§236.22(b)(2)(iii)) ignores cases where voluntary departure was the only option under duress; DHS should permit consideration of coercion or ineffective assistance of counsel.

[P13] The requirement that conduct abroad must not be contrary to law (§236.22(b)(2)(iv)) is vague—does it include foreign traffic offenses or immigration infractions? DHS should specify which foreign laws would cause denial.

[P14] The physical presence requirement on June 15, 2012 and at filing (§236.22(b)(3)) should allow exceptions for medical emergencies that necessarily removed an applicant from the U.S. on that specific date.

[P15] The prohibition on having lawful status on June 15, 2012 (§236.22(b)(4)) is inconsistent with equitable outcomes because many youth were in short-term statuses (e.g., K-1, A-3) through no fault of their own; DHS should clarify how transient or temporary statuses are treated.

[P16] The requirement to show that prior lawful status expired or terminated before the relevant dates (§236.22(b)(4) condition) is burdensome when records are missing; DHS should accept credible affidavits and secondary evidence in lieu of official documents.

[P17] The education or veteran status requirement (§236.22(b)(5)) excludes caregiving youth who were unable to attend school due to responsibility for sick family members; DHS should add hardship or caregiving exceptions.

[P18] Requiring current enrollment in school (§236.22(b)(5) subpart) disadvantages those who cannot afford to continue education; alternative workforce training or proof of intent to enroll should be acceptable.

[P19] The graduation or certificate of completion requirement (§236.22(b)(5)) fails to recognize alternative education pathways—DHS must accept recognized diploma equivalents and documentation of completed coursework.

[P20] Requiring a GED (§236.22(b)(5)) as one alternative is reasonable but DHS must offer clear standards for equivalency from other countries and accept recognized foreign high school diplomas.

[P21] The veteran status provision (§236.22(b)(5)) should clearly define "honorably discharged" and what documentation suffices, especially for National Guard or Reserve service where records are sometimes incomplete.

[P22] The broad criminal-disqualification prohibition (§236.22(b)(6)) is overbroad—listing domestic violence, sexual abuse, burglary, firearm offenses, drug distribution, DUI as automatic disqualifiers will bar many applicants for minor or old offenses; DHS should limit disqualifiers to serious, recent threats.

[P23] Including DUI as a categorical disqualifier (§236.22(b)(6)(i)) is too punitive for isolated, nonviolent offenses; DHS should differentiate DUI severity (blood-alcohol level, injury) and allow waivers for distant convictions.

[P29] The rule should clarify whether biometric fees are included in the $85 or charged separately and whether fee waivers cover biometric costs.

[P30] Allowing concurrent requests for employment authorization (§236.23(a)(1)) is helpful, but the rule must specify whether the economic-need demonstration required under §236.21(c)(2) is needed at the time of filing or can be submitted later.

[P31] Limiting employment authorization after approval to no longer than the deferred action term (§236.23(a)(1) permission) is appropriate, but USCIS should allow earlier renewal filings to avoid employment gaps.

[P32] Mandating that all DACA requests be filed with USCIS, including by aliens in removal proceedings (§236.23(a)(2)), may deter applicants in EOIR proceedings from applying due to fear of negative consequences; the rule must reiterate confidentiality and protection from case referral.

[P33] Giving USCIS exclusive jurisdiction (§236.23(a)(2) condition) is sensible but should be accompanied by coordination protocols with EOIR to prevent duplicative proceedings and erroneous issuance of NTAs.

[P34] Prohibiting EOIR from considering or reviewing DACA requests or USCIS decisions (§236.23(a)(2) prohibition) removes judicial review at the immigration court level; the rule should preserve a limited review path or at least judicial review in federal court to protect due process.

[P35] Permitting individuals with voluntary departure or final removal orders to request DACA (§236.23(a)(2) permission) is positive, but the rule must specify how DACA interacts with underlying final orders and whether DACA halts enforcement of such orders.

[P36] Allowing aliens in administratively closed removal proceedings to request DACA (§236.23(a)(2)) is useful, but DHS should require coordination to prevent the reopening of those proceedings solely because of a DACA request.

[P37] Prohibiting approval of detained applicants unless released by ICE before decision (§236.23(a)(2) condition) effectively denies DACA to many detained youth; DHS should require ICE to promptly consider release for eligible applicants or allow USCIS to approve with DHS custody conditions.

[P38] USCIS's ability to request additional evidence by interview or appearance (§236.23(a)(3)) is necessary, but the rule should require that interviews be used sparingly and provide telephonic/video interview options.

[P39] Allowing denials without issuing an RFE or notice of intent to deny (§236.23(a)(3) permission) raises due-process concerns; commenters request that denials be preceded by an RFE in almost all cases and that summary denials be limited to clear fraud or absence of eligibility.

[P40] Two-year grants of DACA (§236.23(a)(4)) are shorter than prior administrative practice of two-year terms but should allow automatic, administratively efficient renewals for applicants with no new adverse factors.

[P41] Permitting USCIS to consult other agencies and law enforcement (§236.23(b)) without notice risks chilling applicants due to fear of referral; DHS must limit disclosures, require relevance standards, and include data-protection safeguards.

[P42] Requiring written notice to applicants and counsel (§236.23(c)(1) obligation) is appropriate; DHS should also require that notices include specific reasons for denial and list evidence relied upon.

[P43] Clarifying that denial does not bar other relief (§236.23(c)(1) permission) is helpful but DHS should add that USCIS will identify potential forms of relief available and provide referral resources.

[P44] Prohibiting issuance of NTAs or referrals to ICE based solely on DACA denial (§236.23(c)(2)) is crucial; however the carve-outs for fraud, national security, and public-safety must be narrowly defined and require supervisory sign-off.

[P45] The exception allowing NTA/referral for fraud or safety reasons (§236.23(c)(2) exception) must require a high evidentiary threshold (e.g., factual showing and corroboration) before ICE action and provide applicants notice explaining the basis.

[P46] Eliminating administrative appeal from a DACA denial (§236.23(c)(3) prohibition) removes an important check on discretionary denials; DHS should either restore an appeal right or permit motions to reopen/reconsider in certain circumstances.

[P47] Barring motions to reopen or reconsider under 8 CFR 103.5 (§236.23(c)(3) prohibition) conflicts with general immigration practice and could leave applicants without any administrative remedy; at minimum DHS should allow motions based on new evidence or misapplication of law.

[P48] Allowing USCIS to terminate grants at any time with or without notice (§236.23(d)(1) permission) is arbitrary and could cause sudden loss of work authorization; termination should require notice and an opportunity to respond except in exigent circumstances.

[P49] Automatic termination upon listed events (§236.23(d)(2) condition) must provide applicants with clear notice of what triggers termination and an opportunity to seek reinstatement in limited cases (e.g., inadvertent departure, administrative error).

[P50] Automatic termination when an NTA is filed (§236.23(d)(2)(i)) will result in abrupt loss of status for many; the exception for USCIS-issued asylum NTAs is narrow—DHS should allow temporary protections while status is adjudicated.

[P51] Termination for leaving the U.S. without advance parole (§236.23(d)(2)(ii)) is standard, but DHS must allow emergency humanitarian re-entry processes and clarify whether brief border crossings for emergencies count as unauthorized departures.

[P52] The asylum-exception to NTA-triggered termination (§236.23(d)(2)(i) exception) needs elaboration—what documentation will USCIS require to show the NTA is solely an asylum referral and not a general removal action?

[P53] Automatic termination of EADs when DACA terminates (§236.23(d)(3) condition) is logical, but USCIS should provide a short grace period to allow employers to transition and avoid employment disruptions.

[P54] Not requiring issuance of a notice of intent to revoke EADs when they automatically terminate (§236.23(d)(3) prohibition) is problematic—applicants and employers need formal written notice of revocation to comply with employment law and avoid liability.

[P55] The prohibition on using DACA request information to initiate enforcement (§236.23(e)(1) prohibition) is essential, but DHS must codify robust firewall protections, audit rights, and penalties for misuse to ensure compliance.

[P56] The exception allowing use of DACA request information for criminal, fraud, or security reasons (§236.23(e)(1) exception) is too broad; DHS should define the specific criminal offenses and evidence thresholds that permit enforcement use.

[P57] The promise not to use DACA filing information against family members or guardians (§236.23(e)(2) prohibition) should be expanded to include protection against use in civil immigration benefit adjudications affecting relatives.

[P58] Permitting deferred-action grantees to accept employment if they demonstrate economic necessity (§274a.12(c)(14)) duplicates and compounds the economic-need requirement elsewhere; DHS should standardize and simplify the economic-need test or remove it.

[P59] The cross-reference authorizing employment for DACA recipients if they establish economic necessity (§274a.12(c)(33)) lacks objective criteria—DHS must publish a list of acceptable evidence (pay stubs, household income thresholds, public benefits eligibility) and a clear standard of proof.

raw_output:
[P1] The September 27, 2018 deadline in § 39.13(a) is unworkably short for small operators and third-party maintenance providers who require more time to analyze the AD and prepare compliance plans; extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether Sept 27, 2018 is a postmark date, email receipt date, or physical receipt date to avoid disputes about late submissions.

[P2] The applicability in § 39.13(c) omits later 737 variants or newly certificated derivatives; the FAA should confirm whether amended or supplemental type-certificated 737–700/800 derivatives are included or excluded.

[P2] The phrase “certificated in any category” in § 39.13(c) could be read to include non-common carriage, private, and experimental categories; the FAA should explicitly limit applicability only to transport-category, type-certificated airplanes to avoid unintended coverage of homebuilt or experimental aircraft.

[P3] § 39.13(f) requires compliance “within the compliance times specified” but does not summarize those times in the AD; the absence of explicit calendar or flight-cycle deadlines in the AD itself creates ambiguity for operators and should be remedied by including the critical compliance intervals in the rule text.

[P3] The AD should clarify whether compliance times are measured from the effective date of the AD or from previous service bulletin issue dates to prevent differing operator interpretations.

[P4] § 39.13(g) incorporates RC-labeled actions in ASB 737–53A1368 by reference but does not provide the ASB in the docket; the FAA should make the specific Accomplishment Instructions readily available (free of charge) to ensure all operators can access RC steps.

[P4] Requiring compliance “at the applicable times specified in paragraph 1.E., ‘Compliance,’ of ASB 737–53A1368” ties regulatory obligations to a service bulletin that might be revised; the FAA should state that only the ASB revision specified in the AD is approved and that later revisions require AMOC or FAA approval.

[P5] The substitution in § 39.13(h)(1) of the AD’s effective date for the service bulletin’s original issue date could shorten or lengthen required intervals relative to operator expectations; the FAA should explain the policy rationale and provide examples of how this substitution affects specific compliance deadlines.

[P6] § 39.13(h)(2) mandates “repair before further flight” when the ASB directs contacting Boeing, but does not define acceptable interim mitigations; operators need guidance about allowable operational limitations (e.g., ferry flights) while awaiting approved repair methods.

[P6] The requirement in § 39.13(h)(2) that repairs be done using a method approved in paragraph (j) lacks a timeline for approval; the FAA should commit to expedited review timelines for critical “contact Boeing” cases to prevent grounding of aircraft.

[P7] § 39.13(i)(1) terminates PART 2 repetitive inspections after PART 4 repair, but does not specify required post-repair inspections or follow-up intervals to confirm durability; the FAA should require a one-time post-repair inspection at a defined interval and document retention requirements.

[P7] Operators may dispute that PART 4 repairs are equivalent across airframes; the AD should require that terminating repairs be recorded with specific part numbers, configuration data, and work order details to ensure consistent applicability.

[P8] § 39.13(i)(2) allows termination of repetitive inspections after PART 5 preventive modification, but does not require incorporation of modification design data into the aircraft configuration control records; the FAA should require amendment of the maintenance records and wiring diagrams.

[P8] The AD should specify whether PART 5 preventive modification costs and downtime are eligible for relief or financial assistance, as small carriers may face disproportionate burdens to perform the modification.

[P9] § 39.13(j)(1) delegates AMOC approval authority to the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch, but does not allow delegation to other ACOs in urgent cases; request that the FAA permit regional ACOs to approve AMOCs when the Seattle office is unavailable.

[P9] The provision should clarify whether industry-approved organizations (e.g., FAA-designated engineering representatives) can submit AMOC requests on behalf of operators and whether their approvals are accepted.

[P10] § 39.13(j)(1) requires sending AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19, but does not specify acceptable electronic submission formats other than the email address in (j)(1); request explicit permission to use AMOC submission portals or EFB-based workflows for timeliness.

[P11] § 39.13(j)(1)’s requirement to direct information to the person named in paragraph (k)(1) when sending directly to the manager needs to identify the name and contact in the AD text; as drafted it references paragraph (k)(1) which may not be present in the public AD text, creating confusion.

[P12] § 39.13(j)(1) authorizes emailing AMOC information to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov, which alleviates burden, but the FAA should confirm receipt procedures, expected response times, and whether passwords or encrypted attachments are permitted for sensitive technical data.

[P13] § 39.13(j)(2) requires notifying the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC, but does not prescribe required contents of that notification or timing (e.g., 48 hours prior); the FAA should specify notification timelines and the data elements to be provided.

[P13] The requirement in § 39.13(j)(2) to notify the principal inspector could create operational delays for unscheduled repairs; allow notification within a specified short window after use (e.g., within 24 hours) for emergency situations.

[P14] § 39.13(j)(3) permits AMOC use for repairs if approved by the authorized Boeing ODA, but does not require FAA concurrence of ODA approvals; request explicit confirmation whether ODA approvals are automatically acceptable to the FAA or if separate FAA approval is still required.

[P14] The rule should require the ODA approval to include the specific AD reference and include a certificate of conformance and technical substantiation to be retained in aircraft records.

[P15] § 39.13(j)(3) conditions AMOC approval on meeting the airplane’s certification basis but lacks guidance on how to demonstrate compliance for legacy airframes with amended certification bases; request examples of acceptable substantiation, tests, or analysis.

[P15] The AD should clarify whether equivalent safety findings or novel repair techniques that differ from the original certification basis can be approved, and what level of engineering analysis is required.

[P16] § 39.13(j)(4) subjects RC-labeled steps to special rules; commenters request that the FAA publish a precise list of all RC steps (and their figures/substeps) in the docket so operators know which steps are mandatory.

[P17] § 39.13(j)(4)(i) makes RC steps legally mandatory; legal counsel representing carriers note that this transforms manufacturer procedures into regulatory mandates and request the FAA to confirm whether contractors performing maintenance must be explicitly authorized to perform RC steps.

[P17] The AD should clarify recordkeeping obligations for completion of RC steps (e.g., logbook entries, signature, certificate of release to service) to ensure enforcement and traceability.

[P18] § 39.13(j)(4)(i) exempts “RC Exempt” steps from RC requirements; request that the FAA explain the criteria used to label a step “RC Exempt” and ensure no operationally critical steps are inadvertently exempted.

[P19] § 39.13(j)(4)(i) requires AMOCs for any deviation from RC steps, but does not provide expedited review pathways; operators request a fast-track AMOC process for minor deviations that have negligible safety impact.

[P19] Legal experts comment that the requirement for AMOCs for deviations to RC steps may create unreasonable rigidity for field repairs where identical safety is achieved with different tooling; ask for allowance of authorized DER or ODA-signed alternative approved methods without full FAA AMOC if accompanied by engineering substantiation.

[P20] § 39.13(j)(4)(ii) permits deviations from non-RC steps per the operator’s program, but operators request clarification on documentation required to justify such deviations and to demonstrate that they preserve ability to perform RC steps.

[P20] Maintenance providers ask whether deviations under (j)(4)(ii) that alter thresholds or intervals require formal revision to the operator’s maintenance program and whether those revisions must be submitted to FAA for approval.

[P21] § 39.13(j)(4)(ii) conditions deviation of non-RC steps on still being able to do RC steps and return to airworthy condition; request a more detailed definition of “airworthy condition” in this context and examples of acceptable deviations that meet this requirement.

[P3] Small carriers request a phased compliance schedule tied to heavy maintenance visits to minimize aircraft downtime and industry economic impact, rather than immediate compliance on the earliest possible date.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The September 27, 2018 deadline in § 39.13(a) is unworkably short for small operators and third-party maintenance providers who require more time to analyze the AD and prepare compliance plans; extend the comment period by at least 60 days.
The rule should clarify whether Sept 27, 2018 is a postmark date, email receipt date, or physical receipt date to avoid disputes about late submissions.

The applicability in § 39.13(c) omits later 737 variants or newly certificated derivatives; the FAA should confirm whether amended or supplemental type-certificated 737–700/800 derivatives are included or excluded.

The phrase “certificated in any category” in § 39.13(c) could be read to include non-common carriage, private, and experimental categories; the FAA should explicitly limit applicability only to transport-category, type-certificated airplanes to avoid unintended coverage of homebuilt or experimental aircraft.

§ 39.13(f) requires compliance “within the compliance times specified” but does not summarize those times in the AD; the absence of explicit calendar or flight-cycle deadlines in the AD itself creates ambiguity for operators and should be remedied by including the critical compliance intervals in the rule text.
The AD should clarify whether compliance times are measured from the effective date of the AD or from previous service bulletin issue dates to prevent differing operator interpretations.

§ 39.13(g) incorporates RC-labeled actions in ASB 737–53A1368 by reference but does not provide the ASB in the docket; the FAA should make the specific Accomplishment Instructions readily available (free of charge) to ensure all operators can access RC steps.

Requiring compliance “at the applicable times specified in paragraph 1.E., ‘Compliance,’ of ASB 737–53A1368” ties regulatory obligations to a service bulletin that might be revised; the FAA should state that only the ASB revision specified in the AD is approved and that later revisions require AMOC or FAA approval.

The substitution in § 39.13(h)(1) of the AD’s effective date for the service bulletin’s original issue date could shorten or lengthen required intervals relative to operator expectations; the FAA should explain the policy rationale and provide examples of how this substitution affects specific compliance deadlines.

§ 39.13(h)(2) mandates “repair before further flight” when the ASB directs contacting Boeing, but does not define acceptable interim mitigations; operators need guidance about allowable operational limitations (e.g., ferry flights) while awaiting approved repair methods.

The requirement in § 39.13(h)(2) that repairs be done using a method approved in paragraph (j) lacks a timeline for approval; the FAA should commit to expedited review timelines for critical “contact Boeing” cases to prevent grounding of aircraft.

§ 39.13(i)(1) terminates PART 2 repetitive inspections after PART 4 repair, but does not specify required post-repair inspections or follow-up intervals to confirm durability; the FAA should require a one-time post-repair inspection at a defined interval and document retention requirements.

Operators may dispute that PART 4 repairs are equivalent across airframes; the AD should require that terminating repairs be recorded with specific part numbers, configuration data, and work order details to ensure consistent applicability.

§ 39.13(i)(2) allows termination of repetitive inspections after PART 5 preventive modification, but does not require incorporation of modification design data into the aircraft configuration control records; the FAA should require amendment of the maintenance records and wiring diagrams.

The AD should specify whether PART 5 preventive modification costs and downtime are eligible for relief or financial assistance, as small carriers may face disproportionate burdens to perform the modification.

§ 39.13(j)(1) requires sending AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19, but does not specify acceptable electronic submission formats other than the email address in (j)(1); request explicit permission to use AMOC submission portals or EFB-based workflows for timeliness.

§ 39.13(j)(1)’s requirement to direct information to the person named in paragraph (k)(1) when sending directly to the manager needs to identify the name and contact in the AD text; as drafted it references paragraph (k)(1) which may not be present in the public AD text, creating confusion.

raw_output:
[P1] The scope in §60.390(a) is ambiguous because it cuts off after “each prime coat o…” — stakeholders will comment that the provision must clearly list all affected units (prime coat, guide coat, topcoat) and define whether multi-stage booths, flash-off stations, or pretreatment steps are included.

[P1] Automotive manufacturers will request clarification that the subpart applies only to continuous surface coating lines for complete vehicle bodies and not to separate specialty booths that coat small components or aftermarket parts.

[P2] Industry commenters will argue that the phrase “begins construction or modification after the listed date” in §60.390(b) is unclear: commenters will ask EPA to specify the exact promulgation or effective date used to determine applicability and whether “modification” follows the NSPS interpretation (physical change or change in method of operation).

[P2] Legal experts will assert that §60.390(b) must define “modification” and whether routine maintenance, tooling changes, or software updates that change paint mix recipes constitute a modification subjecting a facility to the subpart.

[P3] Trade associations will challenge the lack of grandfathering language for existing facilities that passed prior performance tests, requesting transitional compliance timelines and clarity on whether re-testing is required upon administrative changes (e.g., ownership).

[P3] Environmental groups will support the prohibition in §60.392 but will request EPA to add explicit monitoring and enforcement mechanisms and civil penalty guidance for exceedances.

[P4] Paint formulators and suppliers will comment that the 0.10 kg C/L limit for prime coats in §60.392(a) is technically impractical for certain anti-corrosion or zinc-rich primer chemistries and request an alternative compliance pathway or technology-specific exemptions.

[P4] Small body shops will state that the prime coat 0.10 kg C/L standard is unattainable without add-on controls or reformulation and ask for compliance flexibility (e.g., averaging across lines or a higher limit for low-volume operations).

[P4] Chemical industry experts will ask EPA to confirm whether the metric “kg carbon per liter of applied coating solids” accounts for oxygenated solvents differently and to provide conversion procedures for coatings reported as VOC by weight.

[P5] Detailing shops and guide coat product manufacturers will object that the 0.84 kg C/L limit for guide coats in §60.392(b) may restrict commonly used guide coat sprays and request a higher limit or an exemption for guide coats because of their limited use and volume.

[P5] Automotive paint operations will request clarity whether guide coat operations used only for inspection (very low usage) are subject to full testing and reporting requirements or eligible for de minimis treatment.

[P6] OEMs will raise concerns that the 0.84 kg C/L topcoat limit in §60.392(c) may not accommodate multi-stage clearcoats and basecoat systems that rely on higher-VOC solvents for appearance and performance, and they will request a provision allowing demonstration of equivalent performance through add-on controls or alternative metrics.

[P6] Paint suppliers will request that EPA allow use of certified low-VOC alternatives that achieve equivalent film properties, and that EPA publish an approved list or certification pathway for compliant topcoat formulations.

[P7] Commenters will request that §60.393(a) include a provision defining record retention periods, the format of records (electronic vs. paper), and availability to the public/Agency to avoid compliance disputes.

[P8] Incinerator manufacturers and facility engineers will ask for technical detail in §60.393(a)(1) about sensor placement, data logging frequency, calibration schedule, and acceptable methods for demonstrating the ±2°C accuracy certification by manufacturers.

[P8] Some stakeholders will argue that requiring manufacturer certification to ±2°C is overly prescriptive and request allowing third-party calibration labs or in-house calibration with documented procedures instead.

[P9] Facilities using EDP prime coat operations will request examples and worked numerical examples for the §60.393(a)(2) weighted-average VOC calculation and ask EPA to clarify handling of transient additions, partial tank makeups, and batch vs. continuous feed.

[P9] Operators will ask whether solvents that evaporate during storage or have variable VOC content between lots can be averaged or require separate testing each lot under §60.393(a)(2).

[P10] Spray-application operations will request clarification under §60.393(a)(3) whether “arithmetic average VOC content” must be mass-weighted by usage volume or coat-by-coat and how to treat multi-component systems mixed at the point of application (e.g., 2K systems).

[P10] Trade groups will ask EPA to allow use of supplier-provided certified VOC content statements for averaged calculations under §60.393(a)(3) rather than mandatory Method 24 testing for every batch.

[P11] Facilities will object that quarterly reporting in §60.393(b) is burdensome and request semi-annual reporting or electronic batch uploads; alternatively some environmental NGOs will ask for monthly reporting for higher transparency.

[P11] Commenters will request EPA to specify the reporting format, submission portal, and confidentiality protections for proprietary formulation data included in §60.393(b).

[P12] Owners/operators will submit that §60.393(b)(1)(i) — reporting any month where weighted average VOC in EDP prime makeup exceeds the value that “demonstrated compliance” — requires EPA to define “value that demonstrated compliance” (initial test value? rolling baseline?) and to allow short-term corrective action periods before mandatory reporting.

[P12] Legal commenters will request that EPA permit use of performance test confidence intervals when determining whether a month “exceeds” the demonstrated compliance value to avoid false positives from analytical variability.

[P13] For §60.393(b)(1)(ii), paint manufacturers will ask whether the “value that demonstrated compliance” is the single highest coating VOC used during the demonstration or an average; they will also request allowance for supplier formulation changes without immediate reporting if replaced materials meet equivalent certified VOC statements.

[P13] Small businesses will request a de minimis threshold in §60.393(b)(1)(ii) so that occasional use of specialty high-VOC coatings (e.g., emergency repairs) need not trigger full monthly reporting.

[P14] Incinerator operators will comment that §60.393(b)(2) requiring reporting of each >5-minute temperature excursion is overly strict due to normal fluctuations; they will ask for an averaging provision (e.g., excursions counted only if two consecutive 5-minute periods are below limit) or an allowance for startup/shutdown periods.

[P14] Technical commenters will request EPA to define “the level that demonstrated compliance” in §60.393(b)(2) as the minimum temperature established during the performance test and to allow tolerance for short transients caused by fuel switching or ramping.

[P15] Industry groups will seek removal or extension of the automatic sunset in §60.393(b)(3), arguing that reporting data remain valuable beyond five years and that automatic expiration creates regulatory uncertainty; they urge EPA to either make reporting permanent or specify criteria for expiration/extension.

[P15] Privacy advocates may ask EPA to explain how it will review the continued need for reporting prior to expiration, including public notice and comment procedures, to ensure transparency.

[P16] Laboratories and compliance consultants will request EPA to allow alternative validated analytical methods in §60.394(a) in addition to Appendix A methods, and to specify procedures for method approval under §60.8(b).

[P16] Commenters will ask EPA to provide tolerances and QA/QC requirements for using Appendix A reference methods, including instrument calibration, blanks, and recovery criteria.

[P17] Under §60.394(a)(1), manufacturers and suppliers will request clarification that Reference Method 24 sampling (1-L representative sample split in three aliquots) is impractical for some low-viscosity or particulate-laden coatings; they will ask for flexibility (larger samples, composite samples) or allowance to use supplier-certified VOC analyses.

[P17] Industry will request guidance on acceptable “representative” sampling methods for in-line mixed coatings and for two-component systems mixed at the gun, which complicate collection of a single 1-L representative sample.

[P18] Stakeholders will request that §60.394(a)(2) explicitly allow volume-weighted averaging (by liters used) instead of simple arithmetic mean when computing average VOC content for spray-applied systems to reflect emissions proportional to usage.

[P18] Technical commenters will ask EPA to provide examples demonstrating the averaging method under §60.394(a)(2) for variable-volume operations.

[P19] For §60.394(a)(3), EDP operators will request guidance on selecting the “one-month period” and whether rolling monthly windows or the month of the performance test must be used; they will seek allowance to use a representative 12-month average instead.

[P19] Commenters will request clarity on how to treat additives or solvent reclamation streams when computing weighted average VOC of makeup streams under §60.394(a)(3).

[P20] Under §60.394(a)(4), stakeholders will ask EPA to specify acceptable and default transfer efficiency (TE) values if real-time measurement is infeasible, and to provide procedures for measuring TE for automated vs. manual spray operations.

[P20] Industry will propose allowing use of manufacturer-certified transfer efficiencies supported by testing, instead of site-specific transfer efficiency measurement, provided documentation is maintained.

[P21] Multiple trade associations will request the transfer efficiency table in §60.394(a)(5) be accompanied by clear definitions (e.g., “electrostatic spray”, “airless spray”, “HVLP”) and measurement protocols; they will also ask for an appeals process if the Administrator rejects a weighted-average analysis.

[P21] Facilities that use several application methods will request that §60.394(a)(5) allow averaging across methods based on throughput with an explicit example and templates to standardize submissions.

[P22] Commenters will welcome the Administrator approval pathway in §60.394(a)(5) but will request a predictable approval timeline, criteria for justification, and an administrative review procedure to prevent arbitrary rejections.

[P23] Operators relying on add-on controls will ask §60.394(b) to permit use of EPA-approved continuous monitoring systems (CEMS) in lieu of periodic stack testing for demonstrating control device efficiency.

[P24] For §60.394(b)(1), stakeholders will request worked calculation examples showing how to compute ER and to clarify the units and rounding rules for E and ES used in the equation.

[P25] Under §60.394(b)(2) introductory language, testing laboratories will request that EPA permit use of other validated methods for specific VOC species (e.g., Method TO-17) and ask for criteria to gain Administrator approval for alternative methods.

[P26] In §60.394(b)(2)(i), commenters will request clarity on whether Method 25 sampling must be conducted simultaneously upstream and downstream for multi-stack systems or whether staggered tests are acceptable; they will also request explicit criteria for approving representative-stack testing.

[P26] Testing firms will indicate that simultaneous upstream-and-downstream Method 25 runs may be logistically impossible for large manifolds and ask EPA to allow multipoint averaging with demonstrated flow-weighted representativeness.

[P27] Commenters will argue that the minimum 60-minute sampling and 0.003 dscm volume in §60.394(b)(2)(ii) may be excessive for small stacks and request alternative minimums or a provision allowing shorter runs with statistical justification.

[P27] Environmental groups will oppose relaxing the 60-minute/0.003 dscm minimum, arguing that shorter sampling increases measurement uncertainty and may mask exceedances.

[P28] In §60.394(b)(2)(iii) and (iv), owners/operators will request detailed computational examples and spreadsheet templates for calculating EFF, fractions, and manifold sums to avoid inconsistent submissions and to reduce Administrator review burdens.

[P28] Operators will request that EPA allow use of approved flow-proportional composite sampling when multiple stacks feed a single control device, and clarify whether summing individual stack products requires measurement at the stack or may be based on process mass-balance.

[P29] Facilities will ask EPA to clarify the required frequency of Method 25/2 testing under §60.394(b)(2) — whether only during initial performance tests, annually, or after process changes — and to allow longer intervals when CEMS are used.

[P30] Commenters will request that §60.394(b)(2)(v) permit use of continuous emission monitoring results to compute EA instead of discrete stack tests, provided the CEMS are quality-assured and meet performance specifications.

[P31] Industry will request that the compliance condition in §60.394(b)(3) explicitly permit short-term excursions if EA is calculated over a defined averaging period and remains ≥ ER, rather than treating any single transient exceedance as noncompliance.

[P31] Enforcement/legal commenters will ask EPA to provide dispute resolution procedures if a facility’s calculated EA just barely falls below ER due to measurement uncertainty.

[P32] Manufacturers will support §60.395(a) exceptions but will ask EPA to clarify that model-year changeovers and shifts to larger car sizes are not modifications only if no increase in VOC emissions or change in coating process occurs; they will request burden-of-proof language for demonstrating non-modification.

[P33] OEMs will insist that §60.395(a)(1) explicitly permit model-year tooling changes and color-program adjustments without triggering NSPS modification, provided coating formulations and equipment remain unchanged.

[P34] For §60.395(a)(2), paint shops will request that increasing paint film thickness not be considered a modification only up to a defined percent increase (e.g., ±10%) or a maximum absolute thickness, and that increases done for safety or durability be excluded.

[P34] Worker-safety advocacy groups will caution that exempting increases in film thickness could lead to increased VOC emissions if unchecked and request that any such change be accompanied by notification and simple emissions check.

Industry will propose allowing use of manufacturer-certified transfer efficiencies supported by testing, instead of site-specific transfer efficiency measurement, provided documentation is maintained.

Multiple trade associations will request the transfer efficiency table in §60.394(a)(5) be accompanied by clear definitions (e.g., “electrostatic spray”, “airless spray”, “HVLP”) and measurement protocols; they will also ask for an appeals process if the Administrator rejects a weighted-average analysis.
Facilities that use several application methods will request that §60.394(a)(5) allow averaging across methods based on throughput with an explicit example and templates to standardize submissions.

Commenters will welcome the Administrator approval pathway in §60.394(a)(5) but will request a predictable approval timeline, criteria for justification, and an administrative review procedure to prevent arbitrary rejections.

Operators relying on add-on controls will ask §60.394(b) to permit use of EPA-approved continuous monitoring systems (CEMS) in lieu of periodic stack testing for demonstrating control device efficiency.
For §60.394(b)(1), stakeholders will request worked calculation examples showing how to compute ER and to clarify the units and rounding rules for E and ES used in the equation.

Under §60.394(b)(2) introductory language, testing laboratories will request that EPA permit use of other validated methods for specific VOC species (e.g., Method TO-17) and ask for criteria to gain Administrator approval for alternative methods.

Commenters will argue that the minimum 60-minute sampling and 0.003 dscm volume in §60.394(b)(2)(ii) may be excessive for small stacks and request alternative minimums or a provision allowing shorter runs with statistical justification.

In §60.394(b)(2)(iii) and (iv), owners/operators will request detailed computational examples and spreadsheet templates for calculating EFF, fractions, and manifold sums to avoid inconsistent submissions and to reduce Administrator review burdens.

Operators will request that EPA allow use of approved flow-proportional composite sampling when multiple stacks feed a single control device, and clarify whether summing individual stack products requires measurement at the stack or may be based on process mass-balance.

Commenters will request that §60.394(b)(2)(v) permit use of continuous emission monitoring results to compute EA instead of discrete stack tests, provided the CEMS are quality-assured and meet performance specifications.

[P1] The requirement that "each research facility, other than a Federal research facility, shall register" is ambiguous about hybrid institutions (e.g., privately operated labs on university campuses with Federal grants); commenters will request clarification on whether grant funding or federal affiliation exempts an otherwise nonfederal facility.

[P1] Industry commenters will argue the proposed mandatory registration form and filing process for every nonfederal “research facility” is duplicative of existing institutional animal care and use committee (IACUC) records and university institutional registrations, and request recognition of existing registrations to avoid redundant submissions.

[P1] Small research entities and individual investigators will request an exemption or simplified registration process for single-investigator labs or facilities that use very few animals per year to reduce administrative burden.

[P2] Requiring filing “with the Deputy Administrator” without an online electronic submission option is impractical; commenters will request explicit allowance for secure electronic filing and certify-receipt procedures rather than paper-only filing.

[P2] Legal experts will request that the rule specify processing timeframes and provide an automatic acknowledgement/receipt from the Deputy Administrator upon filing to prevent disputes about timely registration.

[P3] University administrators will challenge the provision that a school/department is to be “considered the research facility” in all such cases, arguing it may create multiple overlapping registrations within a single campus and request language allowing a single campus-level registration with departmental subidentifiers.

[P3] Academic commenters will request clarification on which entity — the department, the university, or a campus-wide office — bears legal responsibility under the rule when departments use shared animal facilities.

[P4] Organizations will object to requiring the signatory to be someone who “has the legal authority to bind the parent organization” without defining acceptable authority levels, and will request that signatories may include designated institutional officials (e.g., IACUC chairs or compliance officers) provided they have documented delegated authority.

[P4] Commenters will request an alternative electronic signature provision and clear standards for what documentation satisfies proof of authority, to avoid delays for institutions whose formal board approvals occur on different schedules.

[P5] The 10‑day certified-mail notification requirement for any change in name, address, ownership, or operational status is unreasonably short and burdensome; stakeholders will ask for a longer notice period (e.g., 30 days) and allowance for electronic notice or other courier methods.

[P5] Universities and multi-site research organizations will argue that "other change in operations affecting facility status" is overly vague (e.g., changes in IACUC membership, temporary closures, changes in principal investigators) and request a detailed list of what must be reported and which changes are exempt.

[P5] Commenters will assert that requiring certified mail for routine administrative changes imposes unnecessary cost and paperwork, and request that certified mail be optional if an electronic or secure portal with tracking is used.

[P6] While APHIS Form 7033 is allowed “may be used,” stakeholders will request mandatory acceptance of Form 7033 (or an online equivalent) for all change notifications to standardize submissions.

[P6] Commenters will request that APHIS publish and keep updated an electronic version of Form 7033 and provide guidance and examples to ensure consistent completion across diverse facilities.

[P7] Industry groups will request detailed instruction on what constitutes sufficient evidence when a facility “goes out of business or ceases to function” and how to demonstrate intent not to resume animal use to avoid inadvertent cancellation.

[P7] Smaller facilities will request that voluntary cancellation be allowed via electronic submission and that the rule permit a grace period before cancellation becomes effective to handle winding-down animal-care obligations.

[P8] Animal advocacy groups will express concern that allowing the Deputy Administrator to cancel registrations without written requests could result in premature cancellations that jeopardize animal welfare and call for procedural protections (e.g., notice, opportunity to respond) before cancellation.

[P8] Legal commenters will request due-process safeguards and an appeal process when the Deputy Administrator cancels registration on its own initiative, including a requirement to provide written notice and a defined timeline for response and reinstatement.

[P9] Commenters will demand that the rule define what constitutes “reason to believe” a facility has ceased functioning (e.g., lack of activity reports, failed inspections, unreturned communications) and require objective criteria and documentation before cancellation.

[P9] Research institutions will request an explicit requirement that APHIS provide advance written notice (e.g., 30 days) and multiple contact attempts before presuming a facility has ceased operations.

[P10] The 10‑day advance reregistration requirement before resuming animal activities is impractical for facilities whose resumed activities depend on unpredictable funding or project timelines; commenters will request shortening to 48–72 hours or allowing immediate temporary registration with subsequent full reregistration.

[P10] Commenters will ask for clarity on whether “at least 10 days prior” applies to minor activities (e.g., transporting a single animal) and propose a tiered approach based on scale or species.

[P11] Institutions will request an expedited emergency reregistration process for urgent research (e.g., outbreak response, public health emergencies) that may need to resume animal work with less than 10 days’ notice.

[P12] IACUCs and research institutions will ask the phrase “at appropriate intervals as determined by the IACUC, but not less than once every 3 years” be clarified to specify whether calendar years or continuous 36-month intervals apply and how to document the review schedule.

[P12] Animal welfare advocates will argue that a minimum triennial full review is insufficiently frequent for some high-risk activities and request mandatory annual full reviews for categories of research involving high pain, novel agents, or species with known welfare challenges.

[P12] Commenters will request guidance on what constitutes a “complete review” and whether expedited review procedures or limited reviews satisfy the requirement.

[P13] Researchers will request clarity on the timing phrase “at the end of the term” for providing written descriptions—specifying whether this means prior to protocol approval, at the end of the project term, or at each grant renewal—and suggest requiring submission at initial review and significant modifications rather than “end of term.”

[P13] Legal commenters will recommend including required elements for the “written description” (e.g., objectives, species, numbers, procedures, endpoints, analgesia) to ensure consistency and compliance.

[P14] Federal agencies and departments will request clarification that when a federal agency is the “reporting facility,” centralized reporting by an agency component is permitted, and ask how instrumentality delineation should be documented for complex federal organizations.

[P14] Universities with multiple colleges will request guidance on whether multi-department entities may consolidate reporting at the campus-level or must file separate reports for each department that uses animals.

[P15] Commenters will request that the December 1 annual report due date be shifted to a later date (e.g., January 31) to allow institutions to reconcile fiscal year closeouts and audited data, or at minimum provide a mechanism for extensions upon justification.

[P15] Stakeholders will ask for clarity on penalties for late or missing annual reports and for an administrative grace period to correct inadvertent late filings.

[P16] Many commenters will note a mismatch between the report due date (December 1) and the requirement that the report “cover the previous Federal fiscal year” (which ends September 30), and request explicit instructions on the reporting period to avoid confusion (e.g., confirm that Dec 1 submission covers Oct 1–Sep 30).

[P16] Institutions will request standardized templates and data definitions for the fiscal-year data elements to ensure consistent comparability across facilities.

[P17] Stakeholders will support allowing APHIS Forms 7023/7023A/7023B but request mandatory electronic versions and machine-readable formats, plus detailed instructions and examples to avoid inconsistencies.

[P17] Commenters will request that APHIS permit equivalent data submissions from other established reporting systems (e.g., OLAW, USDA PAS) to prevent duplicative reporting and allow crosswalks into the APHIS forms.
