raw_output:
[P1] The deadline in § 39.13(a) (receive comments by June 29, 2018) is unreasonable and should be extended to at least 60 days from publication to allow adequate stakeholder review, especially for international operators and unions.

[P1] Small operators and maintenance providers will not have sufficient time to analyze technical service bulletin impacts before the June 29, 2018 comment cutoff; the FAA should provide a targeted extension or additional outreach.

[P2] § 39.13(f) requires compliance "within the specified compliance times" but does not reconcile with operators' existing scheduled maintenance windows; the rule should allow reasonable flexibility to coordinate required work with scheduled heavy maintenance to avoid operational disruption.

[P2] The phrase "unless already done" in § 39.13(f) is ambiguous—commenters request explicit recordkeeping requirements (dates, work order references, service bulletin revision used) to document prior compliance and avoid enforcement uncertainty.

[P3] § 39.13(g) makes all 'RC' actions mandatory "at the applicable times specified" but does not state whether calendar or flight-hour thresholds govern repeated actions; the FAA should clarify whether repetitive RC tasks are time-based, cycle-based, or both.

[P3] The requirement in § 39.13(g) to perform all actions labeled 'RC' as in Boeing SB BASB 737–57A1327, R2 could impose conflicts with earlier ADs; the FAA should publish a crosswalk showing conflicts or precedence among related ADs and service bulletins.

[P4] § 39.13(h)(1) instructs use of September 22, 2017 when the SB says "the original issue date"—this will retroactively change compliance baselines for work done between the SB original issue and Sept 22, 2017; the FAA must explain rationale and whether crediting applies to work done earlier.

[P4] Legal experts will note that substituting a specific date for "original issue date" could create enforcement issues for non-U.S. carriers that used different SB issue dates; the rule should clarify applicability to foreign-approved maintenance actions.

[P5] § 39.13(h)(2) directs using this AD's effective date where the SB refers to "Revision 2 date"; commenters request that the AD specify the exact effective date in the AD text to avoid confusion during the interim period between publication and effectiveness.

[P5] Using the AD effective date for "Revision 2 date" could yield inconsistent compliance deadlines across operators depending on AD entry into force; FAA should instead use a uniform fixed calendar date to avoid staggered compliance obligations.

[P6] The prohibition in § 39.13(i) on installing Krueger flaps/bullnoses unless paragraph (g) actions are completed will disrupt scheduled parts provisioning and line maintenance; the FAA should provide a grace period or explicit inventory grandfathering for parts already on hand.

[P6] OEMs and MROs will face supply-chain impacts from § 39.13(i); the rule should clarify whether components in transit or owned by third-party lessors are subject to the installation prohibition.

[P7] The exception in § 39.13(i) that allows installation only if paragraph (g) actions have been accomplished on the bullnose is circular and unclear for operators installing serviceable overhauled parts; FAA should clarify whether a bullnose installed with documented prior RC compliance on another shipset is acceptable.

[P8] § 39.13(j)(1) grants credit for work done before Sept 22, 2017 using Boeing BASB 737–57A1327 original issue, but it does not require evidence standards; commenters request defined acceptable documentation (work order, SB revision, inspector signature, date) to claim credit.

[P9] § 39.13(j)(2) grants credit for work done before the AD effective date using Revision 2 of the Boeing SB, but it lacks a cut-off for partially completed actions or for work done under alternative methods—FAA should clarify how partial compliance and AMOC-based work will be credited.

[P10] § 39.13(k)(1) gives the Seattle ACO manager authority to approve AMOCs; commenters (airlines and legal counsel) request expanded AMOC delegation to regional offices to expedite time-sensitive approvals and reduce operational delays.

[P11] § 39.13(k)(1) requires AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19—operators note this duplicates procedures and propose a single centralized AMOC submission portal contact to reduce misrouting and processing delays.

[P12] § 39.13(k)(1) requires addressing direct manager submissions to the person in paragraph (l)(1); because paragraph (l)(1) may change, commenters ask the FAA to include a current named contact, phone and email in the AD to avoid lost requests.

[P13] § 39.13(k)(1) permits AMOC requests by email to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov; commenters request confirmation of receipt procedures, expected response timelines, and secure submission options for proprietary technical data.

[P14] § 39.13(k)(2) obligates notifying the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC—airlines ask whether prior verbal notification is sufficient or if documented written notification (email) is mandatory, and what constitutes timely notification.

[P15] § 39.13(k)(3) allows Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to be used for required repairs/modifications if they provide acceptable safety; third-party MROs and independent repair stations object that this appears to privilege Boeing ODA approvals over independent engineering approvals and request parity.

[P16] § 39.13(k)(3) condition that AMOCs must meet the airplane's certification basis and explicitly reference this AD is appropriate, but commenters request that the FAA publish a checklist of required certification-basis elements and the required wording for AD cross-reference to avoid rejection on clerical grounds.

[P17] § 39.13(k)(4) accepts AMOCs previously approved for AD 2017–16–05 for corresponding provisions of BASB 737–57A1327, R2; operators request FAA to publish a list of those specific AMOCs and any conditions that remain applicable so operators know which approvals they may rely on.

[P18] § 39.13(k)(5)(i) mandates completing all steps labeled 'RC' including substeps and figures; maintenance providers request clarification on whether tooling/facility-specific figures are normative or illustrative, and whether equivalent methods that achieve the same outcome require AMOC.

[P19] § 39.13(k)(5)(i) exception for steps labeled "RC Exempt" is useful, but commenters ask for explicit guidance in the AD identifying which specific steps in the Boeing SB are considered "RC Exempt" to reduce ambiguity.

[P20] § 39.13(k)(5)(i) requires an AMOC for any deviation to RC steps; industry commenters warn this will create administrative burden for minor, demonstrably equivalent deviations and request an expedited AMOC process or pre-approved deviations list.

[P21] § 39.13(k)(5)(ii) permits deviation from non‑RC steps using accepted methods without AMOC provided RC steps still completed and airworthiness restored; operators request FAA clarify what documentation is necessary to demonstrate their "accepted methods" and to show that RC steps remain unaffected.

[P21] Clarify whether deviations under § 39.13(k)(5)(ii) that involve vendor-supplied alternate parts require prior coordination with the FAA or simply operator maintenance program approval.

[P6] Legal counsel notes that the installation prohibition in § 39.13(i) could conflict with lease agreements requiring lessors to provide airworthy spares; FAA should resolve potential contractual conflicts or provide guidance for lessor-lessee responsibilities.

[P8] Maintenance organizations point out that crediting in § 39.13(j)(1) tied to the "original issue" may exclude compliant work performed to Boeing-recommended interim revisions—FAA should allow credit for work conforming to any FAA-accepted earlier engineering data.

[P3] Pilots' unions and safety advocates request the FAA justify why all 'RC' actions are made mandatory rather than allowing some RC items to be recommended, and provide data supporting the necessity and safety benefit of each RC item.

[P10] Legal experts request that the AMOC approval criteria in § 39.13(k)(1) be made transparent (e.g., acceptance criteria, review timeline, required substantiation) to ensure consistent decisionmaking and to avoid arbitrary denials.

[P14] Foreign civil aviation authorities request reciprocity guidance for before-use notification in § 39.13(k)(2) when an AMOC is approved by a non-U.S. authority—confirm whether that fulfills the notification requirement.

[P5] Aerospace suppliers request the FAA provide an implementation schedule showing how using the AD effective date for "Revision 2 date" aligns with production and retrofit timelines to avoid unnecessary part obsolescence.

[P18] The requirement to perform figures identified in an RC step may be impractical where figures depict measurements that vary by airplane serial number; the FAA should permit use of airplane-specific engineering data when equivalently demonstrated and documented under AMOC.

§ 39.13(k)(3) allows Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to be used for required repairs/modifications if they provide acceptable safety; third-party MROs and independent repair stations object that this appears to privilege Boeing ODA approvals over independent engineering approvals and request parity.

§ 39.13(k)(3) condition that AMOCs must meet the airplane's certification basis and explicitly reference this AD is appropriate, but commenters request that the FAA publish a checklist of required certification-basis elements and the required wording for AD cross-reference to avoid rejection on clerical grounds.

§ 39.13(k)(4) accepts AMOCs previously approved for AD 2017–16–05 for corresponding provisions of BASB 737–57A1327, R2; operators request FAA to publish a list of those specific AMOCs and any conditions that remain applicable so operators know which approvals they may rely on.

§ 39.13(k)(5)(i) mandates completing all steps labeled 'RC' including substeps and figures; maintenance providers request clarification on whether tooling/facility-specific figures are normative or illustrative, and whether equivalent methods that achieve the same outcome require AMOC.

§ 39.13(k)(5)(i) exception for steps labeled "RC Exempt" is useful, but commenters ask for explicit guidance in the AD identifying which specific steps in the Boeing SB are considered "RC Exempt" to reduce ambiguity.

§ 39.13(k)(5)(i) requires an AMOC for any deviation to RC steps; industry commenters warn this will create administrative burden for minor, demonstrably equivalent deviations and request an expedited AMOC process or pre-approved deviations list.

§ 39.13(k)(5)(ii) permits deviation from non‑RC steps using accepted methods without AMOC provided RC steps still completed and airworthiness restored; operators request FAA clarify what documentation is necessary to demonstrate their "accepted methods" and to show that RC steps remain unaffected.
Clarify whether deviations under § 39.13(k)(5)(ii) that involve vendor-supplied alternate parts require prior coordination with the FAA or simply operator maintenance program approval.

Legal counsel notes that the installation prohibition in § 39.13(i) could conflict with lease agreements requiring lessors to provide airworthy spares; FAA should resolve potential contractual conflicts or provide guidance for lessor-lessee responsibilities.

Maintenance organizations point out that crediting in § 39.13(j)(1) tied to the "original issue" may exclude compliant work performed to Boeing-recommended interim revisions—FAA should allow credit for work conforming to any FAA-accepted earlier engineering data.

Pilots' unions and safety advocates request the FAA justify why all 'RC' actions are made mandatory rather than allowing some RC items to be recommended, and provide data supporting the necessity and safety benefit of each RC item.

Legal experts request that the AMOC approval criteria in § 39.13(k)(1) be made transparent (e.g., acceptance criteria, review timeline, required substantiation) to ensure consistent decisionmaking and to avoid arbitrary denials.

Foreign civil aviation authorities request reciprocity guidance for before-use notification in § 39.13(k)(2) when an AMOC is approved by a non-U.S. authority—confirm whether that fulfills the notification requirement.

Aerospace suppliers request the FAA provide an implementation schedule showing how using the AD effective date for "Revision 2 date" aligns with production and retrofit timelines to avoid unnecessary part obsolescence.

The requirement to perform figures identified in an RC step may be impractical where figures depict measurements that vary by airplane serial number; the FAA should permit use of airplane-specific engineering data when equivalently demonstrated and documented under AMOC.

raw_output:
[P1] The Service's discretionary permission to postpone making specific regulatory proposals depending on available information and Flyway Council recommendations lacks clear deadlines and could be used to delay rulemaking indefinitely, reducing stakeholder predictability.

[P1] Industry commenters will request a formal timeline and criteria for when the Service may postpone proposals under P1 to ensure predictable regulatory planning for states and hunters.

[P2] Conservation groups will question relying on AHM for 2018–19 (P2) without disclosing the underlying models, assumptions, and recent calibration results; they request publication of model inputs and decision rules.

[P2] Sportsmen organizations will support the continued use of AHM (P2) but ask for clarification that stakeholder-recommended adjustments to AHM can be considered within the 2018–19 decision process.

[P3] The recommendation to use independent optimization for each mallard stock (P3) may lead to inconsistent, flyway-incoherent regulations that disadvantage migratory connectivity; commenters will request an analysis of cross-stock harvest spillover.

[P3] Scientists will request the technical documentation and validation for independent optimization (P3), including how trade-offs among stocks and cumulative impacts are evaluated.

[P4] Publishing a supplemental proposed rule in late July detailing the final AHM protocol (P4) is too late to allow meaningful public review before August finalization; stakeholders request the supplemental be published earlier or the finalization delayed.

[P5] The December publication of a proposed regulatory alternative for each Flyway (P5) after receiving status information is vague; state agencies need exact dates and data release schedules to prepare comments and rulemaking.

[P6] Allowing public comments on proposed alternatives only until July 15, 2017 (P6) is an unreasonably short comment period given the technical complexity; commenters request at least a 60-day period and advanced data access.

[P7] Finalizing Flyway regulatory alternatives in mid-August after public comment (P7) creates a narrow window between proposal and finalization, limiting stakeholder input and state administrative capacity; extend the finalization timeline.

[P8] The canvasback opening condition (P8) permitting a 1-bird daily bag nationwide if population and production meet criteria lacks publication of the numerical “specified criteria” and the harvest-rate model; request explicit thresholds and methodology.

[P9] Permitting a partial canvasback season if allowable harvest is below a 1-bird full-season threshold (P9) is ambiguous—stakeholders request definition of “partial season” (days, bag limits) and the decision rule for allocation among states.

[P10] The prohibition to close canvasback season nationwide if conditions are not met (P10) could disproportionately impact subsistence and local economies; commenters request contingency measures and compensation/transition support for affected communities.

[P11] Allowing a 2-bird daily bag for canvasbacks when predicted breeding population exceeds 725,000 (P11) needs justification—commenters request the conservation basis, model sensitivity, and risk of overharvest if predictions are uncertain.

[P12] The obligation to review current canvasback data (P12) should include a requirement to make the compiled dataset and analyses publicly available prior to Flyway meetings for independent review.

[P13] Presenting compiled canvasback information to Flyway councils in fall meetings (P13) should require simultaneous public posting of materials and a mechanism for written public input to Flyway councils.

[P14] The intent to adopt a decision framework for canvasback management in October for 2018–19 (P14) is too late relative to other deadlines; request alignment with Flyway schedules and transparency about appeal or revision processes.

[P15] Permitting limited take of trumpeter swans only during tundra swan seasons (P15) risks misidentification and unintended take of trumpeters; wildlife agencies and NGOs request mandatory species-identification training and stricter monitoring.

[P16] Requiring states to demonstrate >90% of swans in a proposed hunt area are tundra swans (P16) sets an extremely high evidentiary threshold that may be impractical; request guidance on the acceptable survey methods, sample sizes, and confidence levels.

[P16] Legal experts will question whether the 90% criterion (P16) is consistent with the Service’s statutory obligations and request language on how contested determinations are appealed.

[P17] Accepting comments on the swan DEA until October 15, 2017 (P17) may be insufficient; request an extension to allow tribal governments and NGOs to compile traditional knowledge and population data.

[P18] The obligation to prepare a final environmental assessment after comment (P18) should include mandatory disclosure of alternative analyses and a response-to-comments appendix.

[P19] The Service’s obligation to apply restrictions if the eastern mallard strategy indicates problems before the new framework (P19) should include clarity on what constitutes sufficient indication and require interim monitoring benchmarks.

[P20] The example that the Service may lower/change the Atlantic Flyway mallard daily bag limit (P20) requires procedural safeguards: pre-notice to states, reasonable transition period, and socioeconomic impact assessment.

[P21] Proposing to use the same regulatory alternatives for 2018–19 as 2017–18 (P21) ignores changing conditions; commenters request analyses showing why status quo alternatives remain appropriate given recent habitat and population trends.

[P22] Revising the National Dove Harvest Management Strategy (P22) should include a public review and peer review of the revised framework prior to adoption.

[P23] The obligation to review additional information on the EMU dove issue (P23) needs a defined scope and timeline and commitment to publish findings and data sources.

[P24] Requiring additional High Plains Mallard days to fall on/after the Saturday nearest December 10 (P24) could conflict with migration patterns and hunter availability; request biological rationale and flexibility to schedule earlier days if supported by data.

[P25] Permitting an additional 7 days in the Columbia Basin unit under all but the liberal alternative (P25) needs specification of the exact number of days and dates; the draft text leaves quantity unspecified and creates implementation confusion.

[P26] Specifying Alaska season length as 107 days and dates Sep 1–Jan 26 under all alternatives (P26) removes managerial flexibility to respond to unusual migratory timing; request allowance for limited adjustments in response to extreme conditions.

[P27] Allowing hunters to begin shooting 1/2 hour before sunrise (P27) raises safety concerns in certain habitats (waterfowl blinds in low visibility); request state discretion to set later opening times in populated or hazardous areas.

[P28] The prohibition on shooting after sunset (P28) should clarify enforcement mechanisms and exceptions (e.g., falconry) and ensure synchronization with state daylight-saving changes.

[P29] Permitting hunting to begin on the Saturday nearest Sept 24 (P29) could conflict with some state school calendars or religious observances; request state-level flexibility to choose nearby dates.

[P30] Permitting Oct 1 starts (P30) in some areas may be late for waterfowl migration; comment to allow states to choose between multiple opening date options based on local ecology.

[P31] Prohibiting hunting after the last Sunday in January (P31) may constrain management programs for late-season conservation actions; request ability for states to extend beyond that for population control under special permit.

[P32] Prohibiting hunting after Jan 20 (P32) in some areas conflicts with P31 other dates and creates inconsistent end-dates in the rule; request harmonization and clarity where both apply.

[P33] Limiting season length to specified days per flyway/alternative (P33) requires that the proposal publish the exact day counts by flyway/alternative in the rule text; stakeholders cannot evaluate impacts without that table.

[P34] Daily bag limits varying by flyway/alternative (P34) should be accompanied by a socioeconomic impact analysis showing how limits affect harvest, hunter satisfaction, and enforcement burden.

[P35] Species/sex mallard sublimits (P35) such as 3/1 or 4/2 need clearer labeling of female mallard legal take and improved hunter education to avoid inadvertent violations; request funded outreach materials.

[P36] Allowing additional High Plains unit days of 12 (restrictive) or 23 (moderate/liberal) (P36) demands habitat-based justification; NGOs will request modeling of how extra days affect mallard recruitment in that unit.

[P37] Reiterating that additional High Plains days must be on/after Saturday nearest Dec 10 (P37) should include an exception for abnormal environmental conditions (e.g., late freezing) with an expedited approval process.

[P38] The Columbia Basin provision (P38) lacks the exact number of additional days for each non-liberal alternative (placeholder “?”); this drafting error must be corrected before finalization.

[P39] Alaska bag limit ranges (5–8, 7–10) under alternatives (P39) are too broad and may create enforcement confusion; request fixed numeric limits per area and alternative with clear labeling.

[P40] The fixed Alaska season length and dates under all alternatives (P40) should allow the Alaska Department of Fish and Game to propose limited deviations in response to subsistence needs or climate-driven phenology shifts.

[P41] Default shooting and hawking hours (P41) should explicitly reconcile with P27/P28 and state exceptions, and allow falconers specified additional hours where biologically justified.

[P42] The possession limit being three times the daily bag (P42) could create large in-pocket storage for harvest and lead to illegal sales; request justification and consideration of lower possession limits for certain species.

[P43] Limiting federally authorized State-issued permits to the named individual (P43) is appropriate, but commenters request a process for replacing lost or damaged permits that preserves identity verification without reissuing a full permit.

[P44] Requiring permit holders to carry and present permits (P44) raises privacy concerns about displaying personal address; request allowance for redaction of street addresses or use of permit ID numbers.

[P45] Prohibiting transfer or sale of permits (P45) is necessary, but enforcement will be difficult; request guidance on penalties for violations and resources for monitoring permit markets (online resale).

[P46] Invalidating altered or defaced permits (P46) should require the Service to provide a mechanism for reissuance or verification to avoid penalizing hunters for minor wear-and-tear.

[P47] The prohibition on Sunday hunting in specified Atlantic Flyway States (P47) potentially conflicts with adjacent states’ rules and creates enforcement complexity for cross-border hunting; request harmonized cross-border guidance.

[P48] Allowing states to select two youth waterfowl days per zone (P48) is welcomed, but youth advocates will request guaranteed funding for outreach and youth mentor programs tied to those days.

[P49] Requiring youth days to be outside regular seasons and maximize participation (P49) may conflict with small states’ scheduling constraints; request flexibility to hold youth days within splits when needed.

[P50] Permitting youth days up to 14 days before/after regular seasons or within splits (P50) is appropriate, but states need a clear application process and timeline for notification to neighboring states to prevent enforcement confusion.

[P51] Requiring youth day bag limits equal to regular season (P51) could expose inexperienced youth to complex species limits; suggest simplified bag rules for youth days to reduce infractions while maintaining conservation.

[P52] Youth shooting hours matching regular hours (P52) should allow modification to earlier end-times in areas with safety concerns or limited daylight.

[P53] Allowing states to define youth age by established definitions (P53) will create inconsistency across states; youth organizations request recommended national standard ages to ease cross-state participation.

[P54] Prohibiting youth over 17 from participating (P54) may exclude 18-year-olds who are otherwise inexperienced; recommend allowing 18-year-olds who meet hunter education credentials to participate under youth provisions.

[P55] Requiring a supervising adult at least 18 to accompany youth into the field (P55) should clarify whether the adult must be physically present in the blind/boat or may supervise from a vehicle nearby.

[P56] Prohibiting the accompanying adult from duck hunting on the youth day (P56) limits mentor training opportunities; propose allowing the adult to model safe hunting behavior by participating under restricted bag not to exceed youth limits.

[P57] Requiring 16+ youth hunters to possess a Federal Duck Stamp (P57) could impose financial barriers; commenters request fee waivers or reduced-cost stamps for youth participants.

[P58] Restricting tundra swan take to permit holders (P58) is necessary, but enforcement will require clear permit markings and training for officers to distinguish tundra vs trumpeter swan; request funding for enforcement training.

[P59] Allowing certain states to select a special September teal season (P59) should require demonstrable population assessments supporting earlier harvest and contingency plans if teal numbers decline.

[P60] Limiting teal seasons to 16 consecutive days with a 6-bird bag (P60) may be biologically justified, but commenters request evidence that 6 birds/day is sustainable across all teal species included.

[P61] The South Carolina exception for shooting hours (P61) to sunrise-to-sunset may reduce hunting opportunity compared to half-hour before sunrise; request rationale and offer option for South Carolina to adopt earlier hours if desired.

[P62] Allowing FL, KY, TN to choose a 5-day combined teal/wood duck season (P62) necessitates clear enforcement guidance given wood duck identification challenges; recommend mandatory training and signage.

[P63] Capping wood ducks at no more than 2 within a 6-aggregate bag during the 5-day season (P63) is enforceable if hunters understand species limits; recommend public education campaigns prior to the season.

[P64] Iowa’s option to schedule up to 5 days of regular duck season in September (P64) should require monitoring to ensure those days do not negatively impact migratory staging or juvenile survival.

[P65] Allowing Atlantic Flyway seasons between Saturday nearest Sept 24 and last Sunday in January (P65) requires consistency with local conservation goals and coordination with neighboring jurisdictions to avoid cross-border enforcement issues.

[P66] The Atlantic Flyway baseline of 60 days and 6-duck daily bag with specific sublimits (P66) needs explanation of how these numbers align with AHM outputs and recent population data.

[P67] The closure on harlequin ducks (P67) is supported by conservation groups; request a monitoring plan and criteria for potential re-opening if populations recover.

[P68] The merganser limit of five with two hooded mergansers (P68) should clarify interaction with species-protection rules where hooded merganser populations are locally vulnerable.

[P69] Allowing specified states to select Special Sea Duck Seasons (P69) requires delineation of allowable harvest levels, monitoring programs, and stricter permitting to avoid overharvest of vulnerable sea duck species.

[P70] The condition that special sea duck take is allowed only in designated areas/dates (P70) must include a map and GPS coordinates of designated areas in state regulations before permitting such seasons.

[P71] Requiring states to describe and designate Special Sea Duck Areas in their regulations (P71) is appropriate; commenters request a deadline and minimum mapping standards to ensure consistency.

[P72] Obliging states to describe areas open to Canada goose hunting in hunting regulations (P72) should include standard geospatial data formats and public availability to reduce hunter confusion.

[P73] Extending shooting hours one-half hour after sunset for special early Canada goose seasons if other waterfowl seasons are closed (P73) raises safety and wildlife disturbance concerns; request limiting that extension to daylight-saving-consistent periods and only with state approval.

[P74] Allowing states to select among season lengths/daily bag options for white-fronted geese and brant (P74) needs population-specific harvest targets and monitoring to prevent local overharvest, especially for brant stocks of conservation concern.

[P75] Permitting up to 107-day light goose seasons with a 25-bird daily bag and no possession limit (P75) risks unsustainable harvest in areas with declining populations; request mandatory harvest monitoring and adaptive bag reductions if take exceeds modeled thresholds.

[P76] The closure for dusky Canada geese in OR/WA permit zones and requiring state permits for geese (P76) should include clear procedures for issuing permits and appeals for affected hunters, especially tribal hunters relying on customary harvest.

[P77] State-issued swan permits authorizing one swan per permit and per-hunter caps (P77) should be transparent about permit allocation mechanisms (lottery, first-come) and ensure equitable access for subsistence or rural communities.

[P78] Montana’s limit of 500 swan permits and December 1 season end and monitoring (P78) must include the details of the harvest-monitoring protocol and funding commitments to achieve compliance targets.

[P79] Utah’s conditions (2,000 permits, limit 10 trumpeter swans, season end Dec 9 or upon attainment of 10 trumpeters, MOA terms) (P79) are complex; NGOs request the MOA terms be published and subject to public comment before final approval.

[P80] Nevada’s conditions (650 permits, limit 5 trumpeter swans, season end Jan 6 or upon 5 trumpeters) (P80) require assurances that monitoring and rapid closure mechanisms are reliable and transparent to prevent overharvest.

[P81] Requiring Utah and Nevada to have harvest-monitoring programs to examine harvested swans or parts (P81) is reasonable but raises biosecurity/privacy issues; request clear chain-of-custody protocols and hunter compensation for submission burdens.

[P82] Encouraging states to maximize hunter compliance in providing harvested swans for examination (P82) should be strengthened into a requirement with concrete compliance tools (incentives, mandatory reporting).

[P83] The requirement that MT, NV, UT achieve at least 80% hunter compliance or face a 10% permit reduction (P83) may be punitive if compliance measurement is imperfect; request graduated penalties and a dispute resolution process.

[P84] Requiring MT, NV, UT to submit a June 30, 2019 report (P84) is appropriate but the Service should specify required report formats and provide technical assistance to ensure comparability across states.

[P85] Allowing states to issue tundra swan permits authorizing one swan and a second permit from unused permits (P85) needs procedural safeguards to prevent permit stockpiling and black-market resale.

[P86] Allowing Atlantic Flyway tundra swan seasons up to 90 days with North Carolina up to 6,250 permits and Virginia up to 750 (P86) demands justification—commenters request population impact analyses for such high permit numbers, especially in NC.

[P87] Central Flyway tundra swan permit caps (MT 625, ND 2,500, SD 1,875) (P87) must be supported by monitoring showing sustainable harvest; tribal and conservation groups request transparency in how caps were calculated.

Limiting teal seasons to 16 consecutive days with a 6-bird bag (P60) may be biologically justified, but commenters request evidence that 6 birds/day is sustainable across all teal species included.

The South Carolina exception for shooting hours (P61) to sunrise-to-sunset may reduce hunting opportunity compared to half-hour before sunrise; request rationale and offer option for South Carolina to adopt earlier hours if desired.
Allowing FL, KY, TN to choose a 5-day combined teal/wood duck season (P62) necessitates clear enforcement guidance given wood duck identification challenges; recommend mandatory training and signage.

Capping wood ducks at no more than 2 within a 6-aggregate bag during the 5-day season (P63) is enforceable if hunters understand species limits; recommend public education campaigns prior to the season.
Iowa’s option to schedule up to 5 days of regular duck season in September (P64) should require monitoring to ensure those days do not negatively impact migratory staging or juvenile survival.

Allowing Atlantic Flyway seasons between Saturday nearest Sept 24 and last Sunday in January (P65) requires consistency with local conservation goals and coordination with neighboring jurisdictions to avoid cross-border enforcement issues.
The Atlantic Flyway baseline of 60 days and 6-duck daily bag with specific sublimits (P66) needs explanation of how these numbers align with AHM outputs and recent population data.
The closure on harlequin ducks (P67) is supported by conservation groups; request a monitoring plan and criteria for potential re-opening if populations recover.
The merganser limit of five with two hooded mergansers (P68) should clarify interaction with species-protection rules where hooded merganser populations are locally vulnerable.

Allowing specified states to select Special Sea Duck Seasons (P69) requires delineation of allowable harvest levels, monitoring programs, and stricter permitting to avoid overharvest of vulnerable sea duck species.

The condition that special sea duck take is allowed only in designated areas/dates (P70) must include a map and GPS coordinates of designated areas in state regulations before permitting such seasons.
Requiring states to describe and designate Special Sea Duck Areas in their regulations (P71) is appropriate; commenters request a deadline and minimum mapping standards to ensure consistency.
Obliging states to describe areas open to Canada goose hunting in hunting regulations (P72) should include standard geospatial data formats and public availability to reduce hunter confusion.

Extending shooting hours one-half hour after sunset for special early Canada goose seasons if other waterfowl seasons are closed (P73) raises safety and wildlife disturbance concerns; request limiting that extension to daylight-saving-consistent periods and only with state approval.

[P1] The deadline in § 39.13(a) requiring the FAA to receive public comments by August 5, 2019 is impossible to meet now and should be updated to allow a current, reasonable comment period.

[P1] Requiring comments to be received by August 5, 2019 without providing an alternative effective date or reopening the comment period violates APA notice-and-comment norms; the agency must reopen the record.

[P2] § 39.13(c) excludes Model 737–100, –200, –200C, –300, and –400 but fails to explain why other legacy variants are included; the scope of applicability is ambiguous and needs justification and clearer definition.

[P2] The applicability text in § 39.13(c) should explicitly list all included 737 series model numbers and certificated configurations (passenger, cargo, combi) to avoid operator confusion.

[P3] § 39.13(f) requires compliance "within the specified compliance times" but does not state when those compliance times become effective if the AD's effective date is unclear; the rule should specify the effective date.

[P4] The exception "unless already done" in § 39.13(f) lacks documentation requirements — operators should be required to provide records proving prior compliance to avoid enforcement uncertainty.

[P5] The 24‑month initial inspection interval in § 39.13(g)(1) is too short/too long (industry commenters will argue both depending on risk assessment); FAA should provide the risk analysis justifying 24 months versus a shorter or longer interval.

[P5] § 39.13(g)(1) mandates a "general visual inspection" but does not define acceptance criteria or defect thresholds for "discrepancies"; the AD must include or reference pass/fail criteria to ensure consistent inspections.

[P5] Requiring inspections "per Boeing Service Bulletin Parts 1 and 2" (§ 39.13(g)(1)) without incorporating the bulletin by reference in the regulatory text raises legal concerns; the FAA should incorporate the SB or summarize mandatory steps.

[P6] § 39.13(g)(1) that mandates completion of investigative and corrective actions "before the airplane is next flown" could ground aircraft for extended periods pending parts availability; the FAA must provide allowed deviations or relief procedures to prevent disproportionate operational impacts.

[P7] The repeat inspection interval of 1,000 flight cycles in § 39.13(g)(1) may be inconsistent with typical maintenance intervals for some operators (e.g., fractional operators with high cycle rates); FAA should allow cycle-based tailoring or provide rationale.

[P8] The termination provision in § 39.13(g)(2) is unclear about required documentation to prove "attachments match post-reworked configuration"; the AD should require a specific method of verification and recordkeeping.

[P8] If the inspection shows post-reworked attachments and terminates repetitive inspections (§ 39.13(g)(2)), FAA should clarify whether future repairs or panel replacements re‑trigger the inspection requirement.

[P9] The 72‑month deadline in § 39.13(h) to accomplish rework or verification may be unreasonable for small operators with limited maintenance slots; FAA should allow phased compliance or extend the deadline for certain operators.

[P10] § 39.13(h)(1) requires rework "including accomplishment of all applicable related investigative actions and repairs per Part 3" without providing estimated man-hours or parts lists; operators need cost and logistics estimates to plan.

[P11] The before‑further‑flight requirement for investigations and repairs after rework (§ 39.13(h)(1)) could create operational disruptions if the rework uncovers extensive damage; FAA should allow interim flight with operational limitations when safe and documented.

[P12] § 39.13(h)(2) verification of "number and type of attachments" lacks objective measurement tolerances and acceptable documentation — the AD must specify acceptable evidence (e.g., hardware part numbers, rivet types) and inspection methods.

[P13] The prohibition in § 39.13(i) against installing fairing panel 194E unless attachments match post‑reworked configuration is overly broad and could prevent installation of FAA-approved aftermarket or repair parts; the AD should allow installation if an approved AMOC documents equivalency.

[P13] § 39.13(i) will create supply-chain issues because existing spares may not have the post‑reworked attachments; FAA should provide a parts compliance schedule or temporary relief for carriers using existing inventory.

[P15] Granting the Seattle ACO Manager sole authority to approve AMOCs (§ 39.13(j)(1)) concentrates decision-making and could delay time-sensitive approvals for operators outside the region; FAA should permit other ACOs or delegated offices to approve AMOCs.

[P16] § 39.13(j)(1) requires AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO, but many operators use centralized engineering; FAA should allow submission through operator engineering organizations as well as principal inspectors.

[P17] The instruction to address AMOC information to the person in paragraph (k)(1) (§ 39.13(j)(1)) is problematic because paragraph (k)(1) is not provided in this excerpt; the rule must identify the point of contact clearly in the AD.

[P18] Allowing AMOC information by email to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov (§ 39.13(j)(1)) raises cybersecurity and records-retention concerns; FAA should specify secure submission protocols and retention procedures.

[P19] § 39.13(j)(2) requires notifying the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC but provides no timeline for that notification; FAA should require prior notification and define acceptable windows (e.g., 72 hours prior).

[P20] § 39.13(j)(3) permitting Boeing ODA approval of AMOCs for repairs is appropriate but must be accompanied by mandatory FAA oversight and timely FAA concurrence to ensure independence.

[P21] The requirement in § 39.13(j)(3) that AMOC deviations meet the airplane's certification basis is ambiguous for modified airplanes with supplemental type certificates (STCs); the AD should explain how STC holders obtain AMOC approvals and which certification basis applies.

[P21] Requiring the AMOC approval to "specifically reference this AD" (§ 39.13(j)(3)) could cause administrative delays; FAA should allow cross-references when multiple ADs and SBs are implicated.

[P22] Incorporating Boeing Service Bulletin 737–53–1307 Parts 1 and 2 (§ 39.13(g)(1) and § 39.13(g)(1) repeated) without making the service bulletin publicly available in a usable form denies commenters the opportunity to review the exact inspection steps; FAA must place the SB in the docket or include essential steps in the AD.

[P22] The AD references Boeing Service Bulletin dated January 12, 2012 (§ 39.13(g)(1)/(22)), which may have been superseded; FAA should confirm the correct revision and allow operators to use later Boeing-approved revisions as acceptable means of compliance.

[P5] The AD does not state whether the "general visual inspection" requires removal of panels or can be done during routine maintenance checks; FAA should clarify inspection access and whether special equipment is necessary.

[P6] Requiring completion "before further flight" of investigative and corrective actions (§§ 39.13(g)(1), (h)(1)) without defining what constitutes "corrective action" invites inconsistent enforcement; FAA should include examples of acceptable repairs and temporary repairs.

[P9] The AD should include a provision for relief or extension of the 72‑month rework/verification deadline (§ 39.13(h)) if critical repair parts are backordered or if inspections reveal additional structural issues.

[P8] The termination condition (§ 39.13(g)(2)) should require operators to stamp logbooks or update maintenance records and the aircraft's configuration control documentation to prevent reversion to pre‑reworked configurations unknowingly.

[P13] The prohibition on installing panel 194E (§ 39.13(i)) may conflict with existing type design documents for some supplemental type certificates; FAA must coordinate with STC holders to resolve conflicts.

[P15] The AD should require the FAA to publish decisions on AMOC requests and rationales (redacted as necessary) to provide transparency and precedential guidance to other operators (relating to § 39.13(j)(1)).

[P18] The email address provided for AMOC submissions (§ 39.13(j)(1)) should be accompanied by an alternative submission method (fax or portal) for entities that cannot use that email system.

[P21] The language in § 39.13(j)(3) requiring that AMOC approvals "meet the certification basis of the airplane" should be clarified to state whether AMOCs invoking novel repair techniques require supplemental compliance demonstration (e.g., structural tests).

[P2] The AD should clarify applicability to converted freighter 737s and VIP-configured aircraft since the structural loads and attachment configurations may differ from passenger-certified versions referenced in § 39.13(c).

[P5] Boeing Service Bulletin Parts 1 and 2 are referenced for initial inspection (§ 39.13(g)(1)), but the AD must state whether compliance with equivalent foreign manufacturer's service instructions is acceptable for non‑U.S. operators.

[P11] The AD should explicitly allow use of temporary flight restrictions, such as "ferry flight" with operational limitations, where immediate repair "before further flight" is infeasible but flight is necessary for safe maintenance positioning (relates to §§ 39.13(g)(1),(h)(1)).

[P12] The verification procedure in § 39.13(h)(2) should specify acceptable verification methods (visual, borescope, part-number plate, or photographic evidence) and who is authorized to perform and sign off the verification.

[P7] The 1,000 flight-cycle repeat interval (§ 39.13(g)(1)) should be tied to flight hours where appropriate, or the AD should permit operators to substitute a flight-hour-based interval when cycle data is not tracked reliably.

[P13] The installation prohibition (§ 39.13(i)) needs an express grandfathering clause for panels installed per previous ADs or approved repairs, or authorized by an existing AMOC, to avoid retroactive noncompliance.

[P22] The AD must identify whether compliance with Boeing Service Bulletin 737–53–1307 satisfies any related maintenance manual mandatory inspection items, or whether the SB creates a new mandatory requirement beyond the MM.

[P18] The FAA should confirm receipt procedures and expected processing time for emailed AMOC requests to the address in § 39.13(j)(1) to help operators plan maintenance schedules.

[P16] The AD should clarify the role of principal inspectors versus local FSDOs in AMOC processing when multiple inspectors are assigned to a large operator — § 39.13(j)(1) is currently ambiguous.

[P1] The requirement to use calendar year 2019 as the baseline for PY2023–2024 (§413.178(d)(2)) is arbitrary and will produce misleading comparisons because 2019 pre-dates both the COVID-19 pandemic and major clinical practice changes; CMS should use a more recent baseline or provide justification and sensitivity analyses.

[P1] Using 2019 as the baseline disadvantages facilities that made legitimate improvements after 2019 (e.g., telehealth adoption or clinical protocol changes) because those improvements are not reflected; this will distort achievement thresholds and payments for PY2023 and PY2024.

[P1] Facilities that opened after 2019 or substantially reorganized will be unable to produce meaningful baseline data from calendar year 2019, causing unfair exclusions or unstable measures; CMS should allow alternative baselines or adjust attribution rules.

[P2] Setting PY2025 achievement/benchmark/mTPS baseline to calendar year 2021, while using 2022 for improvement threshold and 2023 as the performance period (§413.178(d)(2)), creates inconsistent and potentially confusing comparisons across metrics and may inflate improvement thresholds.

[P2] The staggered use of 2021, 2022, and 2023 for different components in PY2025 will disadvantage facilities that were disproportionately affected by the pandemic in 2021–2022; CMS should provide pandemic adjustment factors or exclude pandemic years from baselines.

[P3] Advancing baseline and performance periods by one year starting PY2026 (§413.178(d)(2)) is administratively reasonable, but CMS must specify transition rules for facilities with missing data in advancing windows (e.g., new facilities or mergers).

[P3] The rule to advance periods by one year each PY lacks detail on how CMS will handle ties, recalculation of benchmarks, and communication timelines; CMS should publish a clear schedule and recalculation methodology.

[P4] Calculating measure rates but not scoring or including them in TPS (§413.178(i)(1)) creates transparency without accountability; stakeholders request clarification on how CMS will use these calculated rates (public reporting, future scoring, model refinement).

[P4] If CMS calculates but does not score certain measures, facilities still incur reporting burden; CMS should explain how data collection burdens are justified and whether any reporting requirements will be reduced for these measures.

[P5] Calculating but not scoring the SHR clinical measure (§413.178(i)(1)) undermines incentives to reduce hospitalizations; hospital and patient advocacy groups request that SHR be fully scored or at least factored into non-financial recognition.

[P6] Not scoring the SRR clinical measure (§413.178(i)(1)) may discourage readmission reduction efforts; CMS should either include SRR in TPS or explain statistical reliability concerns and provide timelines for potential future inclusion.

[P7] Excluding Long-Term Catheter Rate from TPS scoring (§413.178(i)(1)) removes an important clinical quality signal related to infection risk; infection prevention advocates request that CMS phase this measure into TPS as reliability improves.

[P8] ICH CAHPS being calculated but not scored (§413.178(i)(1)) denies patient experience measures any role in performance payments; patient groups ask CMS to incorporate patient experience into TPS weighting or public reporting.

[P9] PPPW measure rates will be calculated but not scored (§413.178(i)(1)); transplant advocacy organizations contend that waitlisting is a key outcome and should influence TPS or at minimum be publicly benchmarked by facility.

[P10] Excluding Kt/V Dialysis Adequacy from TPS (§413.178(i)(1)) risks deprioritizing dialysis adequacy; nephrology societies ask CMS to provide a timeline and criteria for when Kt/V will be included in scoring.

[P11] The 95% cap on wage index decreases effective Jan 1, 2023 (§413.231(c)) is necessary to avoid sudden payment shocks, but stakeholders request clarity on cumulative caps over multiple years and whether the cap applies before or after other adjustments (e.g., reclassification).

[P11] Small and rural facilities with historic low wage indexes may still be harmed despite the 95% cap; CMS should model the impact and consider higher caps or transition funding for vulnerable providers.

[P12] The wage index floor of 0.6000 starting Jan 1, 2023 (§413.231(d)) will increase payments to low-wage geographies but may reallocate limited funds away from higher-need areas; stakeholders request impact analyses showing distributional effects.

[P12] Applying a 0.6000 floor could create perverse incentives for wage index gaming or facility relocation; CMS should include anti-manipulation safeguards and monitor for unintended consequences.

[P13] For MY5–MY10, assigning achievement scores for home dialysis or transplant rates only when aggregation group rate > 0 (§512.370(b)(3)) unfairly penalizes participants in areas with extremely low baseline transplant or home dialysis access and may lock them out of achieving improvements.

[P13] ETC participants in rural or underserved areas with zero baseline rates will be unable to receive achievement credit even if they implement large absolute improvements from zero; CMS should allow partial or alternative scoring for new or very low-baseline groups.

[P14] The condition that aggregation groups must have a >0 rate to be scored (§512.370(b)(3)) creates a disincentive to start counting or reporting small numbers (fear of being benchmarked); CMS should permit scoring when clinically meaningful denominators exist even if rates are initially zero.

[P15] The waiver permitting clinical staff to furnish kidney disease patient education under and incident to the Managing Clinician (§512.397(b)(1)) will expand access and is appropriate, but CMS must define supervision intensity, documentation requirements, and liability protections.

[P15] Waiving the statutory provider-type restriction could blur scopes of practice; professional licensing boards request that CMS require that services performed under the waiver comply with state scope-of-practice laws and provide guidance on delegation.

[P16] Requiring that clinical staff act under and incident to the ETC Participant Managing Clinician (§512.397(b)(1)) is appropriate, but CMS should clarify who qualifies as the Managing Clinician when multiple clinicians rotate or when telehealth is used.

[P17] Limiting services to "qualified staff" as defined at §512.310 (§512.397(b)(1)) is reasonable, but CMS should publish the full list of qualifications and training requirements and allow faster updates when workforce shortages arise.

[P18] Prohibiting staff leased from or provided by an ESRD facility or related entity from furnishing education beginning MY5 (§512.397(b)(1)) will constrain staffing models and may increase costs; ESRD providers and vendors request clarification and a rationale for excluding leased staff.

[P18] The restriction on leased staff in MY5 could prevent existing collaborative arrangements and worsen access in rural areas where independent staff are scarce; CMS should allow waivers or grandfathering for existing contracts.

[P19] Repeating the 2019 baseline requirement for PY2023–2024 (§413.178(d)(2)) without specifying handling of missing or low-volume data fails to account for facilities with insufficient 2019 data; CMS should allow alternate baseline selection or data imputation methods.

Using 2019 as the baseline disadvantages facilities that made legitimate improvements after 2019 (e.g., telehealth adoption or clinical protocol changes) because those improvements are not reflected; this will distort achievement thresholds and payments for PY2023 and PY2024.

Facilities that opened after 2019 or substantially reorganized will be unable to produce meaningful baseline data from calendar year 2019, causing unfair exclusions or unstable measures; CMS should allow alternative baselines or adjust attribution rules.

Setting PY2025 achievement/benchmark/mTPS baseline to calendar year 2021, while using 2022 for improvement threshold and 2023 as the performance period (§413.178(d)(2)), creates inconsistent and potentially confusing comparisons across metrics and may inflate improvement thresholds.

The staggered use of 2021, 2022, and 2023 for different components in PY2025 will disadvantage facilities that were disproportionately affected by the pandemic in 2021–2022; CMS should provide pandemic adjustment factors or exclude pandemic years from baselines.

Advancing baseline and performance periods by one year starting PY2026 (§413.178(d)(2)) is administratively reasonable, but CMS must specify transition rules for facilities with missing data in advancing windows (e.g., new facilities or mergers).

The rule to advance periods by one year each PY lacks detail on how CMS will handle ties, recalculation of benchmarks, and communication timelines; CMS should publish a clear schedule and recalculation methodology.

Calculating measure rates but not scoring or including them in TPS (§413.178(i)(1)) creates transparency without accountability; stakeholders request clarification on how CMS will use these calculated rates (public reporting, future scoring, model refinement).

If CMS calculates but does not score certain measures, facilities still incur reporting burden; CMS should explain how data collection burdens are justified and whether any reporting requirements will be reduced for these measures.

Calculating but not scoring the SHR clinical measure (§413.178(i)(1)) undermines incentives to reduce hospitalizations; hospital and patient advocacy groups request that SHR be fully scored or at least factored into non-financial recognition.

Not scoring the SRR clinical measure (§413.178(i)(1)) may discourage readmission reduction efforts; CMS should either include SRR in TPS or explain statistical reliability concerns and provide timelines for potential future inclusion.

Excluding Long-Term Catheter Rate from TPS scoring (§413.178(i)(1)) removes an important clinical quality signal related to infection risk; infection prevention advocates request that CMS phase this measure into TPS as reliability improves.

ICH CAHPS being calculated but not scored (§413.178(i)(1)) denies patient experience measures any role in performance payments; patient groups ask CMS to incorporate patient experience into TPS weighting or public reporting.

PPPW measure rates will be calculated but not scored (§413.178(i)(1)); transplant advocacy organizations contend that waitlisting is a key outcome and should influence TPS or at minimum be publicly benchmarked by facility.

raw_output:
[P1] The rule should clarify whether the labeling, color, outlet connection, reuse, and identification requirements apply to imported medical gas containers or only domestically manufactured containers to avoid international trade/conflict issues.

[P1] Industry commenters will request a phase-in period (e.g., 18–36 months) before §211.94(e) becomes enforceable to allow manufacturers and distributors to exhaust existing inventories and retool production lines.

[P1] The regulation should define “medical gas container and closure” precisely (size ranges, fixed vs. portable, tank vs. cylinder vs. cryogenic dewars) because the current language is vague and could be read to cover equipment not intended for medical use.

[P2] Requiring labels to state the “fraction/portion” of each gas on mixtures could be impractical for pre-filled cylinders that are filled at variable purities; the agency should permit tolerance ranges (e.g., ±X%) or permit concentration ranges rather than exact fractions.

[P2] Clarify whether fractions must be expressed as percentages, volume/volume, mole fraction, or other units — lack of a specified unit will create industry inconsistency and compliance burdens.

[P3] The term “standard name” should be defined to avoid confusion (e.g., “Medical Oxygen” vs. “Oxygen, USP” vs. chemical names); legal/labeling experts will request explicit examples and an approved name list.

[P3] The rule should allow alternate approved trade names or brand names to appear on the same label alongside the standard name rather than mandating exclusive use of the standard name presentation methods.

[P4] Allowing the standard name printed in the gas’s standard color on a white background could pose readability problems for certain color/contrast combinations (e.g., yellow on white). Commenters will request minimum contrast/legibility standards (e.g., WCAG contrast ratios) or permit an alternative when contrast is insufficient.

[P5] White lettering on color backgrounds may be unreadable on small cylinders or where colors fade; commenters will request specific minimum contrast and font weight specifications and testing requirements to ensure legibility.

[P6] The 2 3/4 inch minimum lettering height requirement is unrealistic for small/high-pressure cylinders or portable cryogenic containers where physical space is limited; request an alternative scaled requirement (e.g., minimum x% of circumference or minimum readable distance) or size tiers with proportional lettering heights.

[P6] Request an exemption or reduced lettering size for cylinders under a specified diameter (e.g., cylinders <4 inches in diameter) and for valves/parts that cannot accommodate 2 3/4-inch letters.

[P7] Printing the gas name “continuously around the label” may be technically infeasible for small cylinders or where safety and inspection markings must occupy that space; request allowing the name to appear on at least two opposite panels or a minimum continuous length covering X% of circumference.

[P8] Mandating labels “as close to the top as possible but below the top weld seam” may conflict with valve markings, inspection stamps, or physical features on many cylinder designs; request clearer vertical placement tolerances (e.g., within X cm below the weld seam) and allow alternate placement where impracticable.

[P9] The requirement that labels “cannot be easily detached or worn” needs measurable standards — specify acceptable attachment methods (metal stamping, embossing, fused paint) or minimum adhesion/durability test protocols (e.g., 1,000 hours UV + salt spray) to avoid variable enforcement.

[P9] Manufacturers will request guidance on which labeling methods count as “interfering with other labeling,” and whether DOT-required markings or serialized plate markings are considered “other labeling.”

[P10] Requiring the shoulder color to match paragraph (e)(5) for portable cryogenic containers may impose repainting costs and supply chain disruption; request a delayed compliance date for cryogenic container retrofitting and allowance for manufacturer-designated alternate marking when shoulder are not present.

[P11] The prohibition on using previously industrial gas cylinders for medical gases is overly broad and will significantly increase costs and waste; industry will argue this bans safe, common refurbishing practices and request a risk-based allowance if the cylinder passes inspection and reconditioning to medical specs.

[P11] Legal commenters will note potential conflict with DOT/PHMSA regulations that permit requalification and reuse of cylinders and request harmonization language or preemption clarification to avoid overlapping federal regimes.

[P12] The “converted before effective date” exception is vague about what constitutes “standard industry practice” and who certifies the conversion; commenters will ask the agency to specify objective criteria and documentation required to qualify for this grandfathering.

[P12] Request that the agency allow companies to certify conversions conducted before the effective date using documented conversion procedures and records, and define an acceptable retention period for such records.

[P13] The exception allowing post-effective-date use only if the container is used solely for medical gas and complies with other requirements needs a definition of “used solely” (does storage for sale count?) and how to prove exclusive medical use for previously industrial containers.

[P13] Suggest requiring a one-time conversion certification plus periodic audits rather than an absolute prohibition, to allow responsible reuse while ensuring safety and traceability.

[P14] Requiring gas-specific outlet connections “attached to the valve body so they cannot be readily removed or replaced (except by the manufacturer)” will create maintenance challenges — hospitals and third-party service providers need to replace damaged fittings; commenters will request an allowance for qualified service technicians with documented training and serial-numbered replacement parts.

[P15] The exclusive exception allowing only the manufacturer to remove/replace outlet connections will create single-source dependency, raise costs, and slow repairs. Industry will ask the agency to permit accredited third-party service centers to perform such work under approved procedures and certification.

[P15] Antitrust and procurement commenters will warn that manufacturer-only removal/replacement could violate federal contracting norms and reduce competition in the aftermarket.

[P16] The 360° wraparound label requirement for portable cryogenic containers could impede regulator-required inspection markings or DOT-required nameplates; request an exception allowing wraparound labels that leave a dedicated inspection window or integration with required markings.

[P16] Cryogenic insulation and frosted surfaces can prevent durable wraparound adhesion; request allowable alternative durable marking methods (e.g., engraved band, metal plate) when wraparound adhesive labels are impractical.

[P17] The rule should reconcile the FDA color identification scheme with existing international/ISO color systems and DOT color/marking codes to avoid confusion for multinational suppliers; request cross-reference and mapping.

[P18] Requiring non-aluminum cylinders to be entirely colored in the standard color will increase repainting and recoating costs and may conflict with DOT stenciling and data markings; industry will request permission to use a colored band scheme instead of full-body painting.

[P19] Coloring only the shoulder on aluminum cylinders may be insufficient for visual identification in storage and emergency settings; emergency responders and hospital clinicians will request larger colored areas or an accompanying high-contrast label to ensure rapid identification.

[P20] The durability requirements for coloring materials are vague — request specific ASTM/ISO test methods and minimum performance thresholds (UV exposure hours, salt spray cycles, abrasion resistance) so manufacturers know how to comply.

[P20] Clarify whether aftermarket re-coloring requires recertification of the cylinder by DOT/PHMSA or is limited to cosmetic repainting that does not affect structural integrity.

[P21] Coloring blended gas cylinders with component gas colors and applying proportionate color areas is ambiguous and will be logistically difficult for cylinders containing trace components; request objective rules for blends under X% (e.g., components under 5% need not be colored) and tolerances for “rough proportion.”

[P22] The visibility-from-top requirement for component colors may be impossible for many cylinder valve and cap designs; recommend an alternative that ensures a clearly visible top marker (e.g., colored valve cap) or allow exceptions where top visibility cannot be achieved.

[P23] “Rough proportion” is undefined and will be interpreted inconsistently; request a clear formula (e.g., percentage of circumference equal to % of component to nearest 5%) and tolerances for manufacturing.

[P24] The standard name-color table must include a comprehensive list of all medical gases and common mixtures; commenters will request adding gases such as xenon, argon, and specialty anesthetic blends or provide a process for adding new gases without rulemaking.

[P25] Identifying “Medical Air” solely by Yellow will conflict with facility piping color codes and some international standards; clinical groups will ask for crosswalk guidance to prevent confusion between cylinder color and pipeline color systems.

[P26] Gray for Medical Carbon Dioxide may be mistaken for inert or hazardous gas colors in certain settings; request confirmation that gray meets visibility standards and consider an alternate or high-contrast band.

[P27] Brown for Medical Helium conflicts with some industrial standards where brown indicates fuel gases; small hospitals and emergency responders will request an education and transition program to avoid misidentification.

[P28] Black for Medical Nitrogen could obscure stenciled data and be hard to read in low light; request permitted use of a high-contrast white band with a black stripe or exception for labeling methods that ensure legibility of required markings.

[P29] Blue for Nitrous Oxide is similar to existing nonmedical color uses; anesthesia societies will request additional labeling content (gas concentration, warnings) because color alone can lead to confusion in operating rooms.

[P30] Green for Medical Oxygen conflicts with green used for safe/oxygen piping versus compressed cylinders internationally; request harmonization with existing DOT and ISO standards and clarity on use of “Green” (specific Pantone or RAL reference).

[P31] For mixtures, coloring with each component’s standard colors could produce confusing multicolor cylinders; emergency medical services will request that mixtures have a standardized additional symbol/striping pattern or text label prioritized over multiple colors.

[P31] Add an alternative labeling option for complex blends (e.g., more than 3 components) that uses a standardized printed full-content label rather than attempting to proportion colors physically.

[P32] Waiving labeling reconciliation for 360° wraparound labels is appropriate but agencies should require manufacturers to maintain process controls showing how wraparound labels are reconciled during filling to prevent mislabeling — commenters will ask for minimum documentation requirements.

[P32] Clarify whether the waiver applies to all reconciliation activities (batch-level, cylinder-level) or only to the physical act of reconciling label placement; supply chain auditors will demand explicit recordkeeping expectations.

[P6] Legal commenters will flag that the 2 3/4-inch requirement may be vulnerable to challenge as arbitrary if no empirical basis is provided; request supporting data or a smaller, scaled requirement.

[P11] Environmental and waste-management groups will object to banning reuse of industrial cylinders without mandated recycling/repurposing programs, and will request guidance on environmentally responsible disposal or incentives to refurbish where safe.

[P14] Hospital biomedical engineers will request clear interoperability requirements so that outlet connections for medical gas equipment (regulators, flowmeters) remain compatible across suppliers; otherwise patient care may be disrupted.

[P21] Suppliers will need time to redesign manufacturing lines to apply multiple colors in proportion — ask for explicit tolerances and an extended compliance timeline for blended gas cylinder coloring.

[P17] Request that FDA coordinate with DOT/PHMSA, ANSI, and ISO to issue harmonized, non-conflicting color and outlet-connection standards to reduce dual compliance burdens.

[P5] For small portable devices where white lettering on a colored background is mandated, request an allowance to use black lettering if that provides better contrast and legibility instead of rigidly enforcing white.

[P9] Enforcement discretion should be articulated for minor label wear that occurs in normal field use so hospitals are not cited for labels that have faded but remain legible; request a de minimis wear standard.

[P24] Require the rule to specify exact color references (Pantone, RAL, or CMYK) for each named color (Yellow, Gray, Brown, Black, Blue, Green) to avoid manufacturer inconsistencies.

[P16] Emergency services groups will request that portable cryogenic containers carrying liquid oxygen or other cold gases include tactile or raised markings for identification in low-visibility or gloved-hand scenarios.

[P13] Request that transit/storage changes (e.g., being used temporarily for industrial gas in a nonmedical facility) not automatically disqualify a cylinder so long as there is documented medical-only use prior to filling for patient care.

[P11] Point out potential conflict with state regulations that currently permit reconditioning of industrial cylinders for medical use and request preemption language or coordination to avoid a patchwork.

[P3] Ask the agency to permit use of QR codes on labels linking to the standardized gas name, concentration, MSDS/SDS, and lot information as a supplement to the printed standard name, to improve traceability and digital workflow.

The visibility-from-top requirement for component colors may be impossible for many cylinder valve and cap designs; recommend an alternative that ensures a clearly visible top marker (e.g., colored valve cap) or allow exceptions where top visibility cannot be achieved.

“Rough proportion” is undefined and will be interpreted inconsistently; request a clear formula (e.g., percentage of circumference equal to % of component to nearest 5%) and tolerances for manufacturing.

The standard name-color table must include a comprehensive list of all medical gases and common mixtures; commenters will request adding gases such as xenon, argon, and specialty anesthetic blends or provide a process for adding new gases without rulemaking.

Identifying “Medical Air” solely by Yellow will conflict with facility piping color codes and some international standards; clinical groups will ask for crosswalk guidance to prevent confusion between cylinder color and pipeline color systems.

Gray for Medical Carbon Dioxide may be mistaken for inert or hazardous gas colors in certain settings; request confirmation that gray meets visibility standards and consider an alternate or high-contrast band.

Brown for Medical Helium conflicts with some industrial standards where brown indicates fuel gases; small hospitals and emergency responders will request an education and transition program to avoid misidentification.

Black for Medical Nitrogen could obscure stenciled data and be hard to read in low light; request permitted use of a high-contrast white band with a black stripe or exception for labeling methods that ensure legibility of required markings.

Blue for Nitrous Oxide is similar to existing nonmedical color uses; anesthesia societies will request additional labeling content (gas concentration, warnings) because color alone can lead to confusion in operating rooms.

Green for Medical Oxygen conflicts with green used for safe/oxygen piping versus compressed cylinders internationally; request harmonization with existing DOT and ISO standards and clarity on use of “Green” (specific Pantone or RAL reference).

For mixtures, coloring with each component’s standard colors could produce confusing multicolor cylinders; emergency medical services will request that mixtures have a standardized additional symbol/striping pattern or text label prioritized over multiple colors.
Add an alternative labeling option for complex blends (e.g., more than 3 components) that uses a standardized printed full-content label rather than attempting to proportion colors physically.

Waiving labeling reconciliation for 360° wraparound labels is appropriate but agencies should require manufacturers to maintain process controls showing how wraparound labels are reconciled during filling to prevent mislabeling — commenters will ask for minimum documentation requirements.

Clarify whether the waiver applies to all reconciliation activities (batch-level, cylinder-level) or only to the physical act of reconciling label placement; supply chain auditors will demand explicit recordkeeping expectations.
Legal commenters will flag that the 2 3/4-inch requirement may be vulnerable to challenge as arbitrary if no empirical basis is provided; request supporting data or a smaller, scaled requirement.

Environmental and waste-management groups will object to banning reuse of industrial cylinders without mandated recycling/repurposing programs, and will request guidance on environmentally responsible disposal or incentives to refurbish where safe.

Hospital biomedical engineers will request clear interoperability requirements so that outlet connections for medical gas equipment (regulators, flowmeters) remain compatible across suppliers; otherwise patient care may be disrupted.
Suppliers will need time to redesign manufacturing lines to apply multiple colors in proportion — ask for explicit tolerances and an extended compliance timeline for blended gas cylinder coloring.
Request that FDA coordinate with DOT/PHMSA, ANSI, and ISO to issue harmonized, non-conflicting color and outlet-connection standards to reduce dual compliance burdens.

For small portable devices where white lettering on a colored background is mandated, request an allowance to use black lettering if that provides better contrast and legibility instead of rigidly enforcing white.

Enforcement discretion should be articulated for minor label wear that occurs in normal field use so hospitals are not cited for labels that have faded but remain legible; request a de minimis wear standard.
Require the rule to specify exact color references (Pantone, RAL, or CMYK) for each named color (Yellow, Gray, Brown, Black, Blue, Green) to avoid manufacturer inconsistencies.

Emergency services groups will request that portable cryogenic containers carrying liquid oxygen or other cold gases include tactile or raised markings for identification in low-visibility or gloved-hand scenarios.

Request that transit/storage changes (e.g., being used temporarily for industrial gas in a nonmedical facility) not automatically disqualify a cylinder so long as there is documented medical-only use prior to filling for patient care.
Point out potential conflict with state regulations that currently permit reconditioning of industrial cylinders for medical use and request preemption language or coordination to avoid a patchwork.

Ask the agency to permit use of QR codes on labels linking to the standardized gas name, concentration, MSDS/SDS, and lot information as a supplement to the printed standard name, to improve traceability and digital workflow.
