[P1] The May 14, 2020 deadline for submitting public comments is unreasonable and should be extended to at least 60 days from publication to allow adequate stakeholder review and data collection.

[P1] The rule must clarify whether the May 14, 2020 deadline is the postmark date or the date comments are received by the FAA’s docket system.

[P2] The phrase “unless already done” in paragraph (f) is vague; request clarification on what documentation demonstrates that a requirement has “already been done” to avoid enforcement ambiguity.

[P2] Require explicit allowance for previously-performed work done to different but equivalent service instructions to be accepted without repeating the action.

[P3] The 24-month inspection timeframe is excessive for safety-critical components and should be shortened to 90 days (or at minimum 6 months) because cargo fire extinguishers affect in-flight fire suppression reliability.

[P3] Conversely, for small operators with limited maintenance resources, the 24-month inspection window may be insufficient; request a tiered compliance schedule based on operator size and MEL considerations.

[P3] The provision should specify whether the 24 months begins from the AD effective date or the date of publication in the Federal Register (the current text is truncated and ambiguous).

[P4] Allowing reliance on maintenance records only “provided they conclusively show” part/serial numbers is unclear; the rule should define what constitutes “conclusive” records (e.g., required fields, chain-of-custody).

[P4] Require that maintenance records used in lieu of inspection include a traceable source (work order, signature, date) and acceptable evidence of part provenance, rather than leaving acceptance to inspector discretion.

[P5] The requirement to replace affected parts “before further flight” creates operational burdens if discovered during turnaround; request clarification whether a special flight permit may be used to ferry the aircraft for replacement.

[P5] The AD should permit temporary placarding or operational restrictions where immediate replacement “before further flight” is impractical but where risk can be mitigated until replacement.

[P6] The rule requires Group 1 airplanes follow specified Accomplishment Instructions but does not list the cost or labor hours; request economic analysis and estimated downtime for Group 1 compliance.

[P6] Clarify whether approved alternative service documents issued after the bulletin dates are automatically acceptable for Group 1 replacements.

[P7] Mandating Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737–26A1150 RB (Sept 27, 2019) as an applicable document is acceptable only if the FAA confirms it has no proprietary restrictions and will be available free of charge in the docket.

[P7] Request that the AD explicitly allow later revisions of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737–26A1150 RB (if issued) to be used without requiring a new AMOC.

[P8] Same as P7: Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737–26A1151 RB must be made freely available and the AD should permit the use of later revisions.

[P8] The AD must identify which bulletin applies to which specific models/serial ranges within Group 1 to avoid operator confusion.

[P9] For Group 2 airplanes, the AD references “identified service information” but does not specify the exact document or revision; request insertion of the exact document titles, dates, and revision numbers.

[P9] Operators request FAA provide consolidated instructions for Group 2 to minimize divergence in interpretation between operators and repair stations.

[P10] The prohibition on installing affected parts unless stamped with a circled ‘G’ should define who is authorized to perform the stamping and what documentation must accompany the stamp.

[P10] The rule should provide a safe harbor allowing installation if accompanied by a manufacturer’s certificate of conformity or test report when a physical stamp is illegible or missing.

[P11] The exception permitting installation only when stamped with circled “G” fails to address legacy parts that have been tested/refilled but lack the stamp; propose an alternative verification pathway (e.g., manufacturer attestation).

[P11] Clarify whether re-stamping by an authorized maintenance facility is acceptable and what standards/procedures must be followed to apply the circled “G”.

[P12] The permission for special flight permits when low pressure or warnings occur should explicitly permit ferry flights to maintenance facilities and define required operational mitigations during such flights.

[P12] Require that the AD state whether special flight permits under 14 CFR 21.197 require preventative safety conditions (e.g., fire watch, minimum dispatch crewing) when operating with an affected extinguisher.

[P13] Granting AMOC authority to the Atlanta ACO Branch Manager should be accompanied by contact details and a timeline (e.g., 60 days) for FAA responses to AMOC requests.

[P13] Request that AMOC approvals be centrally logged and made public to ensure consistent application across operators.

[P14] The requirement to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO should include an alternative for foreign operators or non-U.S. registrants who do not have a U.S. principal inspector.

[P14] Clarify acceptable electronic submission methods for AMOC requests and whether email to the principal inspector satisfies the requirement.

[P15] If AMOC information is sent directly to the certification office manager as permitted, the AD must list the name, mailing address, and email of the person identified in paragraph (m)(1).

[P16] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC conflicts with operational confidentiality concerns; request that notification may be made via the operator’s approved electronic method and need not precede immediate operational use in emergencies.

[P16] Provide a reasonable timeline for notification (e.g., within 48 hours after first use) when immediate notification would delay safety-critical actions.

[P17] The treatment of RC-labeled steps requires clarification of how to identify RC steps in Boeing service documents; recommend the FAA include an annex listing RC steps for each referenced bulletin.

[P18] Mandating performance of RC-labeled steps in full prevents latitude for equivalent safe methods; request that the AD permit equivalent procedures where an operator’s approved maintenance program demonstrates equivalence without requiring an AMOC.

[P18] Legal commenters should note that binding RC labels effectively incorporate manufacturer procedures by reference; request the FAA to ensure the documents are available in the docket to satisfy notice-and-comment requirements.

[P19] The “RC Exempt” carve-out must be defined and examples provided so operators know which steps are exempt and can be reasonably omitted.

[P20] Requiring an AMOC for any deviations to RC steps imposes administrative burden; propose a streamlined AMOC process or a Fast-Track approval for minor deviations that do not raise safety risk.

[P20] The AD should define what constitutes a “deviation” to an RC step (material change vs. minor technique variation) to avoid inconsistent AMOC submissions.

[P21] The allowance to deviate from non-RC steps under an operator’s program should explicitly state that such deviations must still be documented in the maintenance log and be auditable by the FAA.

[P21] Request explicit guidance that deviations to non-RC steps do not invalidate compliance with the AD so long as RC steps are performed and the airplane is returned to an airworthy condition, to prevent enforcement actions over minor non-RC variances.

[P1] The 10.0 g/vehicle-mile cold CO limit for gasoline light-duty vehicles applied at both low and high altitude is unachievably stringent for many current engine calibrations without significant hardware changes, imposing disproportionate compliance costs on small manufacturers.

[P2] Allowing manufacturers to elect exemptions by whole engine family (§86.093-8(j)(2)) will create an incentive to group noncompliant vehicles into large families, undermining the environmental effectiveness of the standard.

[P3] The combined cap on exemptions (P3/P11) tied to the greater of 60% of production or 9,999 units effectively permits manufacturers to exempt a majority of their fleet, nullifying the benefits of the cold CO standards.

[P4] The 60% of combined production threshold (P4/P12) is administratively vague because “combined production” is not defined (calendar year, model year, or certification-year?), creating potential for gaming and enforcement difficulties.

[P5] The absolute 9,999-unit exemption threshold (P5/P13) is excessively high relative to many manufacturers’ annual sales and would allow small manufacturers to exempt nearly their entire production, defeating the rule’s intent.

[P6] The different exemption caps in §86.094-8(j)(2)(i) (20% production) (P21) for 1994-models but 60% elsewhere creates inconsistency and confusion about which threshold applies to which model years and may be unlawful arbitrary differential treatment.

[P7] The truck cold CO limits (12.0 g/mi and 15.0 g/mi) (P6/P7/P8/P24/P29) do not account for variability in payload/use cycles and will unfairly penalize truck models designed for towing or commercial use that inherently produce higher cold CO.

[P8] Applying the truck standards at both low and high altitude (P9/P25) without altitude-specific adjustment factors will disadvantage manufacturers that certify vehicles at high altitude or sell in mountainous regions.

[P9] Granting manufacturers the unilateral ability to elect exemptions by engine family for trucks (P10/P26) with combined national caps duplicates P2 concern and could lead to selective noncompliance concentrated in high-sales families.

[P10] The Administrator’s selection of the vehicle expected to have the highest cold-CO emissions for each engine family for testing (P14) is appropriate, but the regulation lacks transparent criteria or an appeal process for manufacturers to challenge the Administrator’s selection.

[P11] Requiring manufacturers to test the Administrator-selected vehicle using subpart C or Administrator-approved alternative procedures (P15) without specifying timelines for approval risks delaying certification and launches; a mandatory approval timeline should be included.

[P12] Labeling requirements that a vehicle is exempt from cold-temperature CO standards (P16/P17) may stigmatize exempt vehicles and create unfair market distortions; alternatively, mandatory consumer disclosure should be limited to compliance-relevant information without the word “exempt.”

[P13] The duplicative provisions across §86.093, §86.094, and §86.095 (P1, P18, P28 etc.) create regulatory redundancy and raise potential conflicts for manufacturers certifying multiple model years; the rule should harmonize cross-references and applicability.

[P14] Subpart C applicability to 1993+ models for 20°F tests (P30) is unclear for legacy certification records; manufacturers need explicit grandfathering language for vehicles certified prior to this rule’s effective date.

[P15] The dynamometer equipment requirements (P32/P33/P36) and constraints on roll specifications will impose significant capital costs; allowing broader equivalency pathways with clear objective performance metrics would reduce compliance burden.

[P16] Prohibiting increases in dynamometer settings to simulate air conditioning effects (P39) may lead to test results that underrepresent real-world CO emissions for vehicles whose emissions rise significantly with AC loads; the rule should allow optional AC simulation with correction factors.

[P17] The specified test fuel representing regular winter-grade unleaded fuel without oxygenates (P38) may not reflect regional winter fuel formulations (oxygenate-blended or varying volatility), biasing results; fuel specification ranges should accommodate regional variations.

[P18] The strict ambient temperature controls (P40–P43/P50/P56) (20°F±5°F, not below 10°F or above 30°F, and limits on excursions) are operationally onerous and likely to increase test failure rates due to minor, uncontrollable fluctuations; tolerances should be relaxed or allowed as averaged values with statistical allowances.

[P19] The prohibition on ambient temperature exceeding 25°F or falling below 15°F for more than three consecutive minutes (P41/P50) is technically unrealistic in many test cells and could lead to unnecessary retesting; a percentage-of-test allowance is more practical.

[P20] Measuring test cell temperatures at the intake of the fixed-speed cooling fan (P43/P49/P68) may not represent temperatures experienced at the engine or intake air, potentially mischaracterizing cold-start conditions; additional sensor locations should be permitted.

[P21] Requiring the vehicle to be “approximately level” during all test phases (P44) is vague; the rule should specify acceptable angle tolerances and how to measure them to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P22] The fuel handling and stabilization requirements (P45/P47) (e.g., fuel temperature ≤60°F, fuel stabilized at 20°F±10°F) are highly prescriptive and will necessitate specialized facilities; manufacturers seek flexibility to demonstrate equivalence using thermal modeling or alternate stabilization procedures.

[P23] Inflating drive wheel tires to 45 psi for vehicles stabilized at 68–86°F or to 40 psi at ~20°F (P46) may be unsafe for certain light trucks or overload tire specs; tire pressure settings should defer to vehicle manufacturer’s recommended maximum safe pressures.

[P24] The prohibition on using the test vehicle to set dynamometer horsepower (P48) could be infeasible for small manufacturers lacking secondary vehicles and add cost; allow instrumented, non-emission-critical runs on the test vehicle for dyno setup when properly documented.

[P25] Allowing heater/defroster use at any temperature and fan setting during the driving schedule (P51/P69) conflicts with the prohibition against simulating AC effects and could introduce test variability; the rule should specify standardized HVAC settings or document how variable use is accounted for.

[P26] The one-hour restabilization after cooling to 20°F±3°F (P60) and the 12–36 hour soak window (P56) combined with the ≤36 hour storage with max ambient ≤86°F (P57) create complex timing logistics that will increase testing time and costs; streamline soak and stabilization timing with performance-based endpoints (e.g., oil temperature) instead of rigid windows.

[P27] The force-cooling/fans requirement positioning and fan capacity limits (P61) (within 12 inches for front-engined vehicles and normally ≤5,300 cfm) may not be technically appropriate for certain vehicle designs (rear-engine, electric accessories) and should allow engineering justification for alternative setups.

[P28] Mandating vehicle speed measurement from dynamometer rolls (P62) excludes modern alternative speed measurement technologies (wheel speed sensors, GPS-based validation) that may be more accurate; allow validated alternate speed measures.

[P29] Practice runs permitted only when not sampling (P63) restrict manufacturer ability to perform necessary setup with emission monitoring tools; allow limited practice runs with sampling when accompanied by data-quality controls.

[P30] The humidity recommendation to prevent condensation on rolls (P64) should be upgraded from “recommended” to mandatory control limits with specific relative humidity ranges to ensure repeatable test conditions.

[P31] The requirement that the dynamometer be warmed per manufacturer recommendations and start the emission test within 10 minutes (20 minutes if bearings heated) (P65/P66) is operationally tight; allow documented procedural flexibility to account for facility constraints.

[P32] Manual dynamometer horsepower adjustments must be done within 1 hour before test (P67) but automatic-control dynamometers may be set anytime; this unequal treatment penalizes smaller labs with manual dynos and should be harmonized.

[P37] The obligation to prevent moisture condensation in sample collection bags (P75/P82) is reasonable, but the rule should provide acceptable engineering controls or mitigation practices to ensure consistent compliance.

[P45] Public health and environmental advocacy groups will object that labeling exempt vehicles (P16/P17) does not mitigate increased neighborhood CO exposure from concentrated exempted fleets in urban areas; regulators should require mitigation measures or localized caps.

[P46] States with high-altitude populations (e.g., Colorado) will request altitude-specific testing allowances or alternative standards because applying identical limits both low and high altitude (P1/P9/P18/P25/P28/P29) can be technologically challenging and may skew market availability.

[P47] Small-volume manufacturers and specialty vehicle makers will request a smaller absolute exemption cap (e.g., 500 units) instead of 9,999 units (P5/P13/P22/P23) to prevent a de facto blanket exemption for niche producers.

raw_output:
[P1] The permission to import fresh avocados from continental Ecuador only under the conditions of § 319.56–84 is overly restrictive and will effectively limit market access for Ecuadorian exporters without clear justification for each specific measure.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether the permission applies to all avocado cultivars or only the non-Hass and Hass varieties referenced elsewhere; current wording is ambiguous about scope.

[P2] Requiring the NPPO of Ecuador to provide an operational workplan subject to APHIS approval creates an open-ended approval process that could unduly delay shipments; the rule should require APHIS to provide written approval or denial within a defined timeframe (e.g., 60 days).

[P2] The obligation for the NPPO to provide an operational workplan lacks specific minimum content requirements and performance metrics; commenters request a template or minimum elements to ensure predictable, consistent plans.

[P3] Mandating that the operational workplan "include and describe the quarantine pest survey intervals and other specific requirements" without standardizing those intervals allows APHIS to demand differing survey frequencies across sites, imposing inconsistent burdens on exporters.

[P4] Restricting imports to commercial consignments only could exclude smallholders or small cooperatives who sell mixed small-lot shipments; the rule should define "commercial consignments" and allow small-producer aggregation mechanisms.

[P5] The requirement that all production sites be approved and registered with the NPPO per the operational workplan may be administratively burdensome for growers and could create backlog; propose phased registration or group certification options.

[P6] Monthly NPPO inspections beginning 2 months before harvest and continuing through the shipping season create high travel and labor costs for the NPPO and producers; commenters request alternative risk-based inspection intervals or the option for third-party accredited inspectors.

[P6] The rule should specify who bears the cost of monthly inspections (NPPO, producer, exporter) — lack of cost allocation could be a significant economic burden on small producers.

[P7] APHIS "may monitor" places of production if necessary but the rule does not set criteria for when monitoring is triggered; request objective triggers and notice requirements to protect producers from arbitrary inspections.

[P8] Prohibiting export from noncomplying production sites until investigation and remedial action are completed is reasonable but the rule lacks timelines for investigations and remediation; request maximum timelines (e.g., 30–90 days) and appeal procedures.

[P9] Requiring removal of fallen fruit at least once every 7 days from 2 months before harvest imposes unrealistic labor burdens during peak season for large acreages; request flexibility to base frequency on orchard size or provide mechanical removal alternatives.

[P10] Prohibiting fallen fruit from inclusion in field containers for export is reasonable for pest risk, but the rule should define "fallen fruit" (e.g., any fruit contacting ground for >X hours) to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P11] The 100-meter buffer prohibition against growing other hosts of A. fraterculus, A. serpentina, A. striata, or C. capitata near non-Hass production sites could be infeasible in mixed-farming landscapes; request scientific justification for 100 m and allowance for negotiated mitigation (e.g., baiting) where buffer impractical.

[P12] Mandatory fruit fly trapping beginning 2 months before harvest is acceptable, but the operational workplan must specify trap density, trap types, lure types, and maintenance protocols; without that, growers face uncertainty and potential noncompliance.

[P13] Requiring records of fruit fly detections for each trap each time traps are checked is administratively intensive; request acceptance of electronic consolidated logs or sampling-based recordkeeping to reduce paperwork.

[P14] The one-year retention period for trapping records may be insufficient for traceability in the event of multi-year pest investigations; request extending retention to two to three years or align with other APHIS retention policies.

[P15] The prohibition on exporting if trap thresholds are exceeded for more than two consecutive weeks needs clarity: the specific thresholds must be published in the operational workplan and be scientifically justified; also request an expedited testing/appeal process to lift prohibitions promptly.

[P16] Requiring field cartons to be marked to identify production site of origin raises data privacy and commercial confidentiality concerns for producers; request that marking requirements be limited to codes that APHIS can decode, rather than full producer names/addresses.

[P17] The requirement to move fruit to packinghouse within 3 hours of harvest or otherwise protect it from fruit fly infestation is logistically infeasible for remote farms; request an extended time window (e.g., 6–8 hours) or alternative validated protection methods (e.g., field cooling).

[P18] Packinghouse approval and registration with the NPPO per the operational workplan is necessary but the rule should allow multi-site consolidation centers and clarify cross-border third-party packinghouses are excluded/included.

[P19] Packing avocados within 24 hours of harvest in a pest-exclusionary packinghouse may be impractical for large harvest volumes and remote harvest sites; request alternative timelines tied to time-to-intervention (e.g., harvest-to-packing within 48 hours with additional safeguards).

[P20] Mandatory insect-proof mesh or tarpaulin during transit to packinghouse imposes additional packaging costs and could increase heat/humidity-related quality losses; request permitted alternatives (e.g., covered, ventilated transport with monitoring) validated by APHIS.

[P21] Requiring insect-proof cartons or coverings for transit to the U.S. increases material costs and potential environmental waste; seek allowance for reusable or recyclable materials and a list of acceptable materials meeting pest-exclusion performance standards.

[P22] Maintaining insect-proof safeguards intact until arrival at U.S. port is reasonable for phytosanitary integrity, but the rule must specify allowed handling procedures at intermediate stops, transshipment, and during fumigation — otherwise consignments risk denial for routine logistics events.

[P23] Denial of entry for consignments with safeguards not intact is appropriate but the rule should allow remedial measures at U.S. ports (e.g., approved treatments) rather than automatic refusal/destruction, to reduce economic losses.

[P24] Requiring screening ≤1.6 mm for all packinghouse openings is prescriptive; request performance-based alternatives (e.g., barrier that prevents entry of target pests) or allowance for proven alternative barriers where 1.6 mm screening is impractical.

[P25] Double doors at facility and interior packing area entrances could be expensive retrofits for existing facilities; request allowance for single airlock systems or proven alternative pest-exclusion entry systems.

[P26] Permitting packinghouses to accept avocados for U.S. export only from registered, approved production sites is necessary for traceability, but the rule should allow temporary acceptance under supervision when a production site is newly registered pending full approval.

[P27] Segregation of fruit intended for U.S. export from other markets is reasonable but needs clear, practical physical or labeling protocols and audited chain-of-custody procedures to prevent commingling.

[P28] Maintaining identity and origin information from packinghouse through export requires secure recordkeeping; request allowance for electronic traceability systems and clear minimum data elements to be retained.

[P29] Allowing ineligible consignments to be exported after APHIS-approved treatment under part 305 creates a useful flexibility, but the rule should specify which treatments are presumptively acceptable and provide expedited approval for commonly used treatments.

[P30] The biometric sample inspection requirement after post-harvest processing needs definition of sample size, sampling method, and acceptance/rejection criteria agreed in advance to avoid inconsistent application.

[P31] Visual inspections and cutting fruit when signs of internal-feeding pests are observed could lead to subjective determinations and excessive sample destruction; request clear diagnostic criteria and training requirements for inspectors.

[P32] Prohibiting consignments with detected quarantine pests unless treated under part 305 is appropriate, but the rule should allow treatment in the U.S. under APHIS supervision as an alternative to rejection or return.

[P33] Requiring shipping documents to identify the production site and packinghouse for each consignment at U.S. inspection is necessary, but the rule should permit coded identifiers accepted by APHIS to protect commercially sensitive information.

[P34] Maintaining identification in shipping documents until release is required but must accommodate electronic manifest systems; the rule should explicitly accept electronic records with secure access by APHIS.

[P35] Mandating a phytosanitary certificate stating compliance with § 319.56–84 is standard, but the rule should specify the exact certifying statement format to avoid delays due to inconsistent certificates.

[P36] The assertion that specified conditions mitigate Stenoma catenifer risk should be supported by the revised PRA data; request that APHIS publish the PRA and specific risk assessment details used to justify each condition.

[P37] Requiring pest-free places of production for Stenoma catenifer per international standards is appropriate, but the rule must state which international standard (e.g., ISPM number) will be used and how equivalence will be determined.

[P38] APHIS approval of the NPPO's survey protocol is reasonable; however, the rule should commit to timely technical assistance and a transparent review process for protocols to avoid implementation delays.

[P39] Mandating municipalities free of Stenoma catenifer be surveyed twice a year is costly; request risk-based survey frequency that considers pest biology, previous detections, and seasonality.

[P40] Surveys sampling "representative areas" including urban areas is vague; require precise minimum sampling units, trap densities, and spatial distribution criteria so surveys are statistically defensible.

[P41] Allowing site-level pest-free certification even if the municipality is not free is helpful, but the rule should define criteria and evidentiary requirements for site-level certification to prevent inconsistent approvals.

[P42] Requiring a 1-kilometer buffer zone in surveys for pest-free places of production may be infeasible in populated or island municipalities; request scientific justification and allowance for adjusted buffer sizes based on pest flight/dispersal data.

[P43] Monthly surveys of the production site and 1-km buffer from 2 months before harvest through harvest completion are onerous and costly; propose alternative survey schedules tied to pest phenology and orchard risk status.

[P44] Detecting any Stenoma catenifer and prohibiting exports until joint APHIS-NPPO mitigation is agreed could cause indefinite trade stoppages; request defined mitigation actions, timelines, and criteria for reinstatement to avoid long-term market disruptions.

[P45] The condition that export prohibition remains until joint agreement to mitigate risk lacks dispute resolution procedures if APHIS and NPPO disagree; request an arbitration or escalation mechanism with defined timelines.

[P46] The NPPO's obligation to record and update detections each survey is appropriate but should permit electronic reporting directly into an APHIS portal to streamline data sharing.

[P47] One-year retention of detection records seems short for epidemiological investigations; recommend extending retention to at least three years to support longitudinal analysis and traceback.

[P48] The operational work plan requirement detailing daily procedures is far too prescriptive and administratively heavy; request that the plan describe standard operating procedures at an appropriate summary level with annexes for detailed protocols.

[P49] The methods for submitting comments are standard, but the rule should also allow emailed comments to APHIS for stakeholders with limited access to regulations.gov.

[P50] Using regulations.gov is appropriate; request that APHIS ensure docket accessibility and that supporting scientific data (PRA) is clearly linked in the docket.

[P51] Postal mail submission option is fine but processing time and docket posting delays should be minimized; request confirmation receipts for mailed comments.

[P52] Allowing public viewing of documents and comments at regulations.gov and USDA reading room is important; request that APHIS also host public webinars summarizing key technical findings to facilitate informed comments.

[P55] The deadline for comments of June 15, 2021 may be insufficient for international stakeholders to fully assess and respond; request extension of the comment period by 60–90 days and translation of key documents into Spanish.

[P56] Requiring comments to be sent to a specified Docket Clerk or via regulations.gov is standard; request clear contact information for technical questions about implementation costs and timelines.

[P58] The offer for small businesses to request compliance information is helpful; request APHIS provide a dedicated hotline and outreach sessions in Ecuador (or virtual) to assist small producers.

[P60] The requirement to exhaust administrative proceedings before filing suit is noted; commenters request a clear description of administrative remedies and timelines in the preamble.

[P61] Allowing handlers to petition USDA for modification or exemption is important; request clarity on grounds for exemptions and expedited handling for perishable commodity disruptions.

[P62] The promise of an opportunity for a hearing on petitions is appropriate; request procedural timelines for filing, hearing scheduling, and decision timelines be included to ensure due process.

The 100-meter buffer prohibition against growing other hosts of A. fraterculus, A. serpentina, A. striata, or C. capitata near non-Hass production sites could be infeasible in mixed-farming landscapes; request scientific justification for 100 m and allowance for negotiated mitigation (e.g., baiting) where buffer impractical.

Mandatory fruit fly trapping beginning 2 months before harvest is acceptable, but the operational workplan must specify trap density, trap types, lure types, and maintenance protocols; without that, growers face uncertainty and potential noncompliance.

Requiring records of fruit fly detections for each trap each time traps are checked is administratively intensive; request acceptance of electronic consolidated logs or sampling-based recordkeeping to reduce paperwork.

The one-year retention period for trapping records may be insufficient for traceability in the event of multi-year pest investigations; request extending retention to two to three years or align with other APHIS retention policies.

The prohibition on exporting if trap thresholds are exceeded for more than two consecutive weeks needs clarity: the specific thresholds must be published in the operational workplan and be scientifically justified; also request an expedited testing/appeal process to lift prohibitions promptly.

Requiring field cartons to be marked to identify production site of origin raises data privacy and commercial confidentiality concerns for producers; request that marking requirements be limited to codes that APHIS can decode, rather than full producer names/addresses.

The requirement to move fruit to packinghouse within 3 hours of harvest or otherwise protect it from fruit fly infestation is logistically infeasible for remote farms; request an extended time window (e.g., 6–8 hours) or alternative validated protection methods (e.g., field cooling).

Packinghouse approval and registration with the NPPO per the operational workplan is necessary but the rule should allow multi-site consolidation centers and clarify cross-border third-party packinghouses are excluded/included.

Packing avocados within 24 hours of harvest in a pest-exclusionary packinghouse may be impractical for large harvest volumes and remote harvest sites; request alternative timelines tied to time-to-intervention (e.g., harvest-to-packing within 48 hours with additional safeguards).

Mandatory insect-proof mesh or tarpaulin during transit to packinghouse imposes additional packaging costs and could increase heat/humidity-related quality losses; request permitted alternatives (e.g., covered, ventilated transport with monitoring) validated by APHIS.

Requiring insect-proof cartons or coverings for transit to the U.S. increases material costs and potential environmental waste; seek allowance for reusable or recyclable materials and a list of acceptable materials meeting pest-exclusion performance standards.

Maintaining insect-proof safeguards intact until arrival at U.S. port is reasonable for phytosanitary integrity, but the rule must specify allowed handling procedures at intermediate stops, transshipment, and during fumigation — otherwise consignments risk denial for routine logistics events.

Denial of entry for consignments with safeguards not intact is appropriate but the rule should allow remedial measures at U.S. ports (e.g., approved treatments) rather than automatic refusal/destruction, to reduce economic losses.

Requiring screening ≤1.6 mm for all packinghouse openings is prescriptive; request performance-based alternatives (e.g., barrier that prevents entry of target pests) or allowance for proven alternative barriers where 1.6 mm screening is impractical.

Double doors at facility and interior packing area entrances could be expensive retrofits for existing facilities; request allowance for single airlock systems or proven alternative pest-exclusion entry systems.

Permitting packinghouses to accept avocados for U.S. export only from registered, approved production sites is necessary for traceability, but the rule should allow temporary acceptance under supervision when a production site is newly registered pending full approval.

Segregation of fruit intended for U.S. export from other markets is reasonable but needs clear, practical physical or labeling protocols and audited chain-of-custody procedures to prevent commingling.

Maintaining identity and origin information from packinghouse through export requires secure recordkeeping; request allowance for electronic traceability systems and clear minimum data elements to be retained.

Allowing ineligible consignments to be exported after APHIS-approved treatment under part 305 creates a useful flexibility, but the rule should specify which treatments are presumptively acceptable and provide expedited approval for commonly used treatments.

The biometric sample inspection requirement after post-harvest processing needs definition of sample size, sampling method, and acceptance/rejection criteria agreed in advance to avoid inconsistent application.

Visual inspections and cutting fruit when signs of internal-feeding pests are observed could lead to subjective determinations and excessive sample destruction; request clear diagnostic criteria and training requirements for inspectors.

Prohibiting consignments with detected quarantine pests unless treated under part 305 is appropriate, but the rule should allow treatment in the U.S. under APHIS supervision as an alternative to rejection or return.

Requiring shipping documents to identify the production site and packinghouse for each consignment at U.S. inspection is necessary, but the rule should permit coded identifiers accepted by APHIS to protect commercially sensitive information.

Maintaining identification in shipping documents until release is required but must accommodate electronic manifest systems; the rule should explicitly accept electronic records with secure access by APHIS.

Mandating a phytosanitary certificate stating compliance with § 319.56–84 is standard, but the rule should specify the exact certifying statement format to avoid delays due to inconsistent certificates.

The assertion that specified conditions mitigate Stenoma catenifer risk should be supported by the revised PRA data; request that APHIS publish the PRA and specific risk assessment details used to justify each condition.

Requiring pest-free places of production for Stenoma catenifer per international standards is appropriate, but the rule must state which international standard (e.g., ISPM number) will be used and how equivalence will be determined.

APHIS approval of the NPPO's survey protocol is reasonable; however, the rule should commit to timely technical assistance and a transparent review process for protocols to avoid implementation delays.
Mandating municipalities free of Stenoma catenifer be surveyed twice a year is costly; request risk-based survey frequency that considers pest biology, previous detections, and seasonality.

Surveys sampling "representative areas" including urban areas is vague; require precise minimum sampling units, trap densities, and spatial distribution criteria so surveys are statistically defensible.

Allowing site-level pest-free certification even if the municipality is not free is helpful, but the rule should define criteria and evidentiary requirements for site-level certification to prevent inconsistent approvals.

Requiring a 1-kilometer buffer zone in surveys for pest-free places of production may be infeasible in populated or island municipalities; request scientific justification and allowance for adjusted buffer sizes based on pest flight/dispersal data.

Monthly surveys of the production site and 1-km buffer from 2 months before harvest through harvest completion are onerous and costly; propose alternative survey schedules tied to pest phenology and orchard risk status.

Detecting any Stenoma catenifer and prohibiting exports until joint APHIS-NPPO mitigation is agreed could cause indefinite trade stoppages; request defined mitigation actions, timelines, and criteria for reinstatement to avoid long-term market disruptions.

The condition that export prohibition remains until joint agreement to mitigate risk lacks dispute resolution procedures if APHIS and NPPO disagree; request an arbitration or escalation mechanism with defined timelines.
The NPPO's obligation to record and update detections each survey is appropriate but should permit electronic reporting directly into an APHIS portal to streamline data sharing.
One-year retention of detection records seems short for epidemiological investigations; recommend extending retention to at least three years to support longitudinal analysis and traceback.

The operational work plan requirement detailing daily procedures is far too prescriptive and administratively heavy; request that the plan describe standard operating procedures at an appropriate summary level with annexes for detailed protocols.
The methods for submitting comments are standard, but the rule should also allow emailed comments to APHIS for stakeholders with limited access to regulations.gov.
Using regulations.gov is appropriate; request that APHIS ensure docket accessibility and that supporting scientific data (PRA) is clearly linked in the docket.
Postal mail submission option is fine but processing time and docket posting delays should be minimized; request confirmation receipts for mailed comments.

Allowing public viewing of documents and comments at regulations.gov and USDA reading room is important; request that APHIS also host public webinars summarizing key technical findings to facilitate informed comments.

The deadline for comments of June 15, 2021 may be insufficient for international stakeholders to fully assess and respond; request extension of the comment period by 60–90 days and translation of key documents into Spanish.
Requiring comments to be sent to a specified Docket Clerk or via regulations.gov is standard; request clear contact information for technical questions about implementation costs and timelines.
The offer for small businesses to request compliance information is helpful; request APHIS provide a dedicated hotline and outreach sessions in Ecuador (or virtual) to assist small producers.
The requirement to exhaust administrative proceedings before filing suit is noted; commenters request a clear description of administrative remedies and timelines in the preamble.
Allowing handlers to petition USDA for modification or exemption is important; request clarity on grounds for exemptions and expedited handling for perishable commodity disruptions.
The promise of an opportunity for a hearing on petitions is appropriate; request procedural timelines for filing, hearing scheduling, and decision timelines be included to ensure due process.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement that solo practitioners or groups of 10 or fewer must elect to participate in a virtual group before the performance period starts is unworkable for clinicians who only learn late in the year that they will need to change participation; request flexibility to allow elections up to the submission deadline.

[P1] Requiring the election prior to the start of the performance period unfairly penalizes clinicians whose staffing or practice arrangements change unexpectedly (e.g., sudden retirement, practice closure, merger) and prevents timely, reasonable responses.

[P2] The prohibition on changing a virtual group election during the performance period should be relaxed to allow changes in cases of bona fide emergencies (e.g., natural disasters, bankruptcy, unexpected loss of key personnel).

[P2] The rule's absolute bar on mid-period changes is legally problematic because it eliminates CMS discretion to approve administratively necessary adjustments and may violate due process by denying clinicians an appeal pathway.

[P3] Permitting membership in only one virtual group per performance period is too restrictive for clinicians who work in multiple distinct small practices or care settings; recommend allowing up to two groups or enabling pro rata reporting.

[P3] The one-virtual-group limit will disadvantage part-time clinicians and those practicing in multiple TINs/NPIs and may reduce care coordination; propose an exception for clinicians with documented work across multiple legitimate practice locations.

[P4] Binding the group's election to all MIPS eligible clinicians at the TIN level removes individual clinician autonomy; request clarification and an opt-out mechanism for NPIs within a TIN who have legitimate reasons not to participate in the group's election.

[P4] The provision fails to account for NPIs billing under a shared TIN but practicing independently (e.g., contracted locum tenens); require an administrative process allowing NPIs to confirm or contest group elections.

[P5] The December 1 submission deadline for virtual group elections is administratively burdensome, especially for newly formed groups late in the year; recommend extending the deadline to December 31 or allowing rolling formation with earlier notification.

[P5] Requiring a single-date election (December 1) will create administrative spikes for CMS and service centers and could increase errors; ask CMS to provide a phased window or staggered deadlines.

[P6] Allowing contact with designated assistance or Service Centers to determine eligibility is useful, but CMS must commit to providing timely responses (e.g., within 10 business days) and publish contact procedures and response time guarantees.

[P6] The permission to contact assistance centers must include an appeal mechanism when clinicians receive inconsistent eligibility determinations from different Centers; require standardized guidance and a central adjudication process.

[P7] The obligation to execute a written formal agreement among members before election may disadvantage informal collaboratives and solo practitioners forming ad-hoc groups; recommend allowing a provisional election with a 30-day cure period to submit the formal agreement.

[P7] Requiring the written agreement prior to election could be infeasible for groups negotiating contract terms late in the year; propose CMS accept electronic signature and dated drafts submitted by the representative with a later verified final agreement.

[P8] Repeating the December 1 submission requirement (for group representative) without accommodating holidays or mailbox delays is unreasonable; request CMS accept postmarks or electronic timestamps up to midnight ET on December 1 and allow limited late submissions for good cause.

[P9] The mandatory inclusion of TIN and NPI information and contact info in submissions raises privacy concerns; CMS should limit public disclosure and ensure secure electronic transmission (TLS, encryption) and specify data retention and access policies.

[P9] The rule does not state what happens if NPIs change after submission; require CMS to allow updates and provide clear procedures for NPIs added or removed after the election cut-off, including effective dates.

[P10] Requiring a one-time notification to CMS prior to the submission period for any election information changes that occurred during the performance period is unclear — request clarification whether this applies to past performance periods and practical guidance on the required content and timing.

[P10] The "one time prior to submission period" update requirement is ambiguous and may conflict with the obligation in P18 to notify within 30 days; request harmonization and an explicit timeline for notifications and whether CMS must acknowledge receipt.

[P11] The comprehensive contractual agreement requirement is overly prescriptive and may force groups to incur legal costs; suggest a CMS-provided template agreement and allowance for supplemental provisions tailored to practice realities.

[P12] Requiring the agreement to state that only the virtual group's TINs and NPIs are parties could preclude necessary participation by billing managers or administrators — propose language allowing designated agents to execute administrative functions while keeping TIN/NPI parties as primary.

[P13] Requiring signatures by individuals authorized to bind TINs and NPIs may be impossible for independent NPIs who lack signing authority at the TIN level (e.g., employed clinicians); request allowance for documented authorization (power of attorney) or delegated electronic signature.

[P14] The obligation that each member expressly agree to participate and comply with MIPS and applicable laws could be redundant and burdensome; ask CMS to permit attestation by the TIN representative that all NPIs were informed and agreed, with random audits rather than upfront signatures.

[P15] Requiring TINs to notify their NPIs about participation imposes an administrative burden and lacks a required method; ask CMS to specify acceptable notification methods and proof (email with read receipts, posted notices) and timelines.

[P16] Demanding the agreement describe NPIs' rights, obligations, reporting duties, and effects on outside participation is overly detailed; request CMS provide a safe-harbor checklist or model language to reduce negotiation costs and legal ambiguity.

[P17] The requirement to describe how payment adjustments incentivize quality improvement is speculative and could be difficult to operationalize; propose removing this requirement or narrowing it to a statement of intent rather than a detailed plan.

[P18] Requiring members to update Medicare enrollment and notify the virtual group within 30 days of changes may be infeasible in practices with limited administrative staff; ask for a 60-day window and clear examples of required updates.

[P19] Mandating a term of at least one performance period could lock clinicians into arrangements that become impractical; request provisions for early termination for cause with defined close-out procedures and timelines.

[P20] The close-out process requirement obligating TINs/NPIs to provide necessary data for aggregation upon termination needs clarity on data formats, deadlines, and liability for late submissions; ask CMS to define a 90-day data transfer window and acceptable formats (CSV, FHIR).

[P21] Assessing clinicians in participating TINs at the virtual group level eliminates individual accountability and may mask poor performance by specific clinicians; request CMS report both group-level and de-identified individual-level performance to aid quality improvement.

[P22] Requiring groups to meet the definition of a virtual group at all times during the performance period is rigid; propose allowing brief lapses (e.g., temporary reduction below threshold due to leave) with an administrative exception process.

[P23] Aggregating performance data across TINs risks blending disparate patient populations and could produce misleading scores; ask CMS to permit stratification by TIN or specialty and risk-adjustment transparency.

[P24] Assessing clinicians at the virtual group level across all four categories may harm clinicians whose ACI or improvement activities are better measured individually; recommend permitting category-level opt-outs or mixed attribution when clinically appropriate.

[P25] The obligation to adhere to CMS-established election processes requires CMS to publish detailed, machine-readable process guidance and a user-friendly portal; request CMS commit to a public timeline and practice-testing period prior to implementation.

[P26] Requiring selection of a specific submission mechanism for CAHPS and other quality information without recognizing resource constraints is burdensome; ask CMS to permit flexibility and phased adoption with technical assistance for small groups.

[P27] The requirement to report measures and activities using as many mechanisms as needed to meet category requirements increases administrative complexity and costs; propose consolidating allowed mechanisms and providing exception relief for small groups.

[P28] The permission to submit via multiple mechanisms must include safeguards against double-counting and clear instructions on precedence when the same measure is submitted through multiple channels.

[P29] Requiring the same identifier across all performance categories may conflict with TIN/NPI distinctions in different submission systems; ask CMS to allow mapping tables and transitional leniency when systems require different identifiers.

[P30] The requirement that groups of 25+ report on all CMS Web Interface measures is burdensome for heterogeneous groups; propose allowing measure selection aligned with group specialty mix or permitting sub-group reporting.

[P31] Reporting on the first 248 consecutively ranked beneficiaries for each measure is arbitrary and may introduce bias; request CMS justify the 248 threshold and consider random sampling or risk-stratified samples to improve representativeness.

[P32] The 50% data completeness threshold for 2020 may be unattainable for many practices during COVID-19 disruptions; ask CMS to delay implementation, lower the threshold for affected years, or permit attestation of extenuating circumstances.

[P33] Increasing the completeness threshold to 60% in 2021 presumes normal operations resume; request CMS adopt a phased approach tied to pandemic recovery metrics and provide hardship exemptions.

[P34] Requiring inclusion of at least 50% of applicable Medicare Part B patients in 2020 disregards telehealth visits and billing anomalies; clarify whether telehealth and remote services count and provide guidance for encounters not billed through Part B.

[P35] The 60% Part B patient inclusion requirement for 2021 similarly needs clarification about counting telemedicine, observation stays, and split/shared visits; ask CMS to publish definitive counting rules.

[P36] The multiple prescribed methods for submitting improvement activities data create complexity; recommend streamlining to two primary mechanisms and providing technical support and a grace period for adoption.

[P37] Applying an APM Entity's MIPS final score to each clinician and adjusting at the TIN/NPI level could lead to inequitable payment adjustments for clinicians with minimal APM participation; propose proportional application based on actual attributed patient share.

[P38] Treating each ACO participant TIN as a unique APM Entity if the ACO fails to report required quality data will create administrative chaos and sudden penalties; request CMS to provide notice, cure periods, and transitional relief rather than immediate reclassification.

[P39] Including clinicians in both virtual group and APM scoring and basing payments solely on the APM Entity score deprives virtual group participants of agency; demand clearer guidance on which score controls and propose an election hierarchy or clinician-level choice where feasible.

[P40] Calculating the APM Entity's quality score using CMS Web Interface and other CMS-specified measures should require CMS to publish scoring methodology, weighting, and public benchmarks in advance to ensure transparency.

[P41] The requirement to calculate a Quality Improvement Score beginning in 2018 for eligible APM Entities lacks specificity on the measures used; request CMS to publish the exact methodology and how historical data will be handled.

[P42] Defining the Total Quality Performance score as the sum of quality and quality improvement scores creates potential double-counting; ask CMS to clarify weighting and caps and provide worked examples.

[P43] Permitting ACO participant TINs to report MIPS quality data per MIPS if the ACO does not report is reasonable but CMS must clarify timelines, responsibilities, and liability — including whether ACO-level nonreporting triggers penalties or remedial obligations for TINs.

[P44] The four criteria for Other MIPS APM quality scoring (tied to payment, available, min 20 cases, benchmark) are too restrictive for small practices serving low-volume conditions; propose lowering the case minimum to 10 or allowing pooled multi-year measurement.

[P45] The "tied to payment" criterion is vague; require CMS to define precise standards for what constitutes a payment-linked measure and provide examples.

[P46] The "available for scoring" requirement should be clarified — specify whether availability requires public technical specifications, digital submission infrastructure, or historical use in CMS programs.

[P47] The 20-case minimum for measures used in APM quality scoring will exclude many legitimate quality measures for small specialties; request a lower minimum or alternative statistical techniques (e.g., hierarchical modeling) to include low-volume measures.

[P48] Requiring an available benchmark for measures used in APM scoring is appropriate but CMS must publish acceptable benchmark sources and procedures for developing provisional benchmarks when none exist.

[P49] The 2019 start of Quality Improvement Score calculation requires transitional guidance for APM Entities with incomplete prior data; ask CMS to allow a one-year transition with limited weighting for the improvement component.

[P50] Assigning an improvement activities score to each MIPS APM and applying it to each APM Entity may mask variance in activity performance across participating TINs; request CMS permit entity-level supplementation or opt-out where activities are not uniformly performed.

[P51] The permission for APM Entities to report additional improvement activities if assigned score is not maximal is positive but CMS should provide clear submission windows, evidence standards, and an appeals process for disputes over scoring.

[P52] Requiring each Shared Savings Program ACO participant TIN to report ACI performance data separately is duplicative and increases reporting burden; propose allowing ACO-level ACI reporting with TIN-level supplements only where justified.

[P53] CMS's reassignment of category weights when insufficient measures exist must be predictable; request CMS publish a fallback weighting schedule and allow stakeholder comment before application each year.

[P54] The specific reweighting (Quality to 0 → Improvement 25% and ACI 75%) could produce distorted incentives; ask CMS to model financial impacts and consider a more balanced re-weighting or clinician input before applying.

[P55] Reweighting ACI to 0 and setting Quality to 80% may unfairly advantage quality-focused groups while penalizing groups investing in health IT; request CMS provide grandfathering for groups that made ACI investments in good faith.

[P56] The permission to claim exclusions for measures with exclusion options should be limited to clinically appropriate cases; urge CMS to require documentation and audit thresholds to prevent overuse of exclusions.

[P57] Assigning zero points for failure to report required measures is harsh; recommend CMS provide a cure period, technical assistance for submission failures, and a narrowly defined exception for system outages.

[P58] The fallback scoring that awards 3 or 1 points when submitted measures cannot be scored is preferable to zeros, but CMS should publish how values are set and ensure small practices are not disadvantaged by lower fallback scores.

[P59] The exception treating administrative claims-based and Web Interface measures below case minimums as unscored (and some Web Interface under completeness as zero) is confusing; request clarification with flowcharts and examples, and consistency of treatment across mechanisms.

[P60] Requiring submission in accordance with § 414.1335 without aligning deadlines and data element definitions across referenced provisions risks inconsistent compliance; ask CMS to harmonize cross-references and provide consolidated submission guidance.

[P61] The policy to remove "topped out" measures after three consecutive years may prematurely eliminate clinically meaningful measures; urge CMS to publish criteria, allow stakeholder petition to retain measures, and ensure replacement measures are ready.

[P62] The requirement that measures meet case minimums, data completeness, and not have zero percent performance to qualify for bonus points disadvantages low-volume specialties; propose adjusted bonus eligibility rules or specialty-specific thresholds.

[P63] Capping high-priority measure bonus points at 10% of total available measure achievement points for 2019–2020 could limit incentives for important measures; request CMS reconsider the cap level and allow higher caps for meaningful public health priorities.

[P64] End-to-end electronic reporting bonuses capped at 10% and only once per measure even if submitted multiple ways may not sufficiently incentivize full electronic integration; recommend allowing stacking of end-to-end bonuses for multi-mechanism submissions where meaningful.

[P65] The condition that data used for improvement scoring be comparable across current and prior performance periods is reasonable, but CMS must provide precise comparability criteria and methods for when measure specifications change.

[P66] The cap on improvement percent score at 10 percentage points will blunt incentives for dramatic improvements, particularly for low baseline performers; propose either raising the cap or implementing a sliding cap that benefits larger relative improvements at lower baselines.

Including clinicians in both virtual group and APM scoring and basing payments solely on the APM Entity score deprives virtual group participants of agency; demand clearer guidance on which score controls and propose an election hierarchy or clinician-level choice where feasible.

Calculating the APM Entity's quality score using CMS Web Interface and other CMS-specified measures should require CMS to publish scoring methodology, weighting, and public benchmarks in advance to ensure transparency.

The requirement to calculate a Quality Improvement Score beginning in 2018 for eligible APM Entities lacks specificity on the measures used; request CMS to publish the exact methodology and how historical data will be handled.
Defining the Total Quality Performance score as the sum of quality and quality improvement scores creates potential double-counting; ask CMS to clarify weighting and caps and provide worked examples.

Permitting ACO participant TINs to report MIPS quality data per MIPS if the ACO does not report is reasonable but CMS must clarify timelines, responsibilities, and liability — including whether ACO-level nonreporting triggers penalties or remedial obligations for TINs.

The four criteria for Other MIPS APM quality scoring (tied to payment, available, min 20 cases, benchmark) are too restrictive for small practices serving low-volume conditions; propose lowering the case minimum to 10 or allowing pooled multi-year measurement.
The "tied to payment" criterion is vague; require CMS to define precise standards for what constitutes a payment-linked measure and provide examples.

The "available for scoring" requirement should be clarified — specify whether availability requires public technical specifications, digital submission infrastructure, or historical use in CMS programs.

The 20-case minimum for measures used in APM quality scoring will exclude many legitimate quality measures for small specialties; request a lower minimum or alternative statistical techniques (e.g., hierarchical modeling) to include low-volume measures.

Requiring an available benchmark for measures used in APM scoring is appropriate but CMS must publish acceptable benchmark sources and procedures for developing provisional benchmarks when none exist.

The 2019 start of Quality Improvement Score calculation requires transitional guidance for APM Entities with incomplete prior data; ask CMS to allow a one-year transition with limited weighting for the improvement component.

Assigning an improvement activities score to each MIPS APM and applying it to each APM Entity may mask variance in activity performance across participating TINs; request CMS permit entity-level supplementation or opt-out where activities are not uniformly performed.

The permission for APM Entities to report additional improvement activities if assigned score is not maximal is positive but CMS should provide clear submission windows, evidence standards, and an appeals process for disputes over scoring.

Requiring each Shared Savings Program ACO participant TIN to report ACI performance data separately is duplicative and increases reporting burden; propose allowing ACO-level ACI reporting with TIN-level supplements only where justified.

CMS's reassignment of category weights when insufficient measures exist must be predictable; request CMS publish a fallback weighting schedule and allow stakeholder comment before application each year.

The specific reweighting (Quality to 0 → Improvement 25% and ACI 75%) could produce distorted incentives; ask CMS to model financial impacts and consider a more balanced re-weighting or clinician input before applying.

Reweighting ACI to 0 and setting Quality to 80% may unfairly advantage quality-focused groups while penalizing groups investing in health IT; request CMS provide grandfathering for groups that made ACI investments in good faith.

The permission to claim exclusions for measures with exclusion options should be limited to clinically appropriate cases; urge CMS to require documentation and audit thresholds to prevent overuse of exclusions.

Assigning zero points for failure to report required measures is harsh; recommend CMS provide a cure period, technical assistance for submission failures, and a narrowly defined exception for system outages.

The fallback scoring that awards 3 or 1 points when submitted measures cannot be scored is preferable to zeros, but CMS should publish how values are set and ensure small practices are not disadvantaged by lower fallback scores.

The exception treating administrative claims-based and Web Interface measures below case minimums as unscored (and some Web Interface under completeness as zero) is confusing; request clarification with flowcharts and examples, and consistency of treatment across mechanisms.

Requiring submission in accordance with § 414.1335 without aligning deadlines and data element definitions across referenced provisions risks inconsistent compliance; ask CMS to harmonize cross-references and provide consolidated submission guidance.

The policy to remove "topped out" measures after three consecutive years may prematurely eliminate clinically meaningful measures; urge CMS to publish criteria, allow stakeholder petition to retain measures, and ensure replacement measures are ready.

The requirement that measures meet case minimums, data completeness, and not have zero percent performance to qualify for bonus points disadvantages low-volume specialties; propose adjusted bonus eligibility rules or specialty-specific thresholds.

Capping high-priority measure bonus points at 10% of total available measure achievement points for 2019–2020 could limit incentives for important measures; request CMS reconsider the cap level and allow higher caps for meaningful public health priorities.

The condition that data used for improvement scoring be comparable across current and prior performance periods is reasonable, but CMS must provide precise comparability criteria and methods for when measure specifications change.

The cap on improvement percent score at 10 percentage points will blunt incentives for dramatic improvements, particularly for low baseline performers; propose either raising the cap or implementing a sliding cap that benefits larger relative improvements at lower baselines.
