raw_output:
[P1] The March 13, 2017 written-comment deadline for the OSHA beryllium rule is unreasonably short and should be extended to allow stakeholders (small businesses, unions, medical experts) adequate time to prepare technical and economic analyses.

[P1] Requiring submissions to be postmarked, sent, or received by March 13, 2017 creates uncertainty for commenters using mail or courier services; OSHA should clarify whether "postmarked by" is acceptable and extend the receipt date accordingly.

[P2] The instruction to identify comments by Docket No. OSHA–H005C–2006–0870 is appropriate, but the rule should include an explicit statement that failure to include the docket number will not automatically result in rejection of substantive comments.

[P3] The Regulations.gov electronic submission option is necessary, but the agency should provide alternative electronic formats (e.g., direct email to a docket manager) for large technical appendices that exceed portal file-size limits.

[P4] Allowing fax submissions only if 10 pages or fewer is impractical for many stakeholders who rely on fax; OSHA should permit larger fax submissions or explicitly accept multi-part faxes without penalizing commenters.

[P5] The list of physical addresses for mail/hand delivery should include business hours, security procedures, and an email/telephone contact to confirm receipt, because current text omits practical delivery details and may deter in-person submissions.

[P6] Requiring all submissions to include the Agency name and Docket No. may lead to the exclusion of comments that omit that info; OSHA should state that substantive comments will be considered even if the docket number is inadvertently omitted.

[P7] The statement that comments will be placed in the public docket without change and may be posted online raises privacy concerns; OSHA should provide an easy mechanism for redacting personal contact information while retaining the substantive comment.

[P7] The provision that personal information "may" be made available online is vague; OSHA should specify what categories of personal information will be redacted (addresses, phone numbers, emails) to protect commenters.

[P8] Posting comments on Regulations.gov is standard, but OSHA should ensure that submitted supporting materials (large datasets, confidential business information) are handled properly and not automatically posted.

[P9] The EBSA warning not to include personally identifiable or confidential business information is appropriate, but the rule lacks guidance on how to submit confidential business information (CBI) in a protected manner — commenters request a clear CBI submission procedure.

[P10] The March 17, 2017 deadline for comments on the 60-day extension proposal is too brief; given the broad implications of extending fiduciary rule applicability dates, the Department should provide at least 60–90 days for comment.

[P11] The April 17, 2017 deadline for comments on the examination called for in the President’s Memorandum is acceptable only if the Department provides clear scope and sufficient background documents; otherwise it should be extended.

[P12] Identifying comments by RIN 1210–AB79 is necessary, but EBSA should confirm that simultaneous submission using multiple methods (portal + email) will not create duplicate docket entries that could confuse reviewers.

[P13] The Federal eRulemaking Portal (Regulations.gov) instructions should include guidance for submitting large exhibits (e.g., economic models) and confirm acceptable file formats to prevent technical rejections.

[P14] Allowing submission by email to EBSA.FiduciaryRuleExamination@dol.gov is useful, but the rule must specify maximum attachment sizes and security expectations (e.g., encryption for sensitive attachments).

[P15] Requiring RIN 1210–AB79 in the email subject line is reasonable, but EBSA should state whether failure to include the RIN will result in the comment being unprocessed or simply assigned manually.

[P16] The physical mail address for EBSA should include instructions on how to mark envelopes for "Attention: Fiduciary Rule Examination" to ensure timely routing; omission could delay docketing.

[P17] Requiring all submissions to include the agency name and RIN is redundant with other instructions and may cause confusion; EBSA should streamline its submission requirements to reduce formatting barriers to participation.

[P18] The statement that comments are public records and retrievable by search engines should be accompanied by guidance on how individuals can request redaction or removal of sensitive personal information after submission.

[P19] The STEL requirement in §1915.1000(a)(2) that exposure not exceed the listed STEL over a 15-minute sampling period needs clarification on sampling protocols, frequency, and compliance actions when short-term excursions occur due to non-routine tasks.

[P20] Requiring PEL determinations from breathing-zone air samples (Table Z footnote) is standard, but OSHA should define the specific breathing-zone sampling method, sampling height, duration for TWA versus STEL, and acceptable analytical methods.

[P21] The generic "compliance dates" provision should require OSHA to publish an implementation guidance document and compliance-assistance resources before any compliance date to aid employers in meeting obligations.

[P22] The March 12, 2018 compliance date for paragraphs (c), (d), (g), (k), and (l) is too soon for employers to implement comprehensive exposure control plans, medical surveillance, and recordkeeping; OSHA should phase in obligations or extend the date for small businesses.

[P23] The March 11, 2019 deadline to provide change rooms and showers is operationally challenging for many employers (especially small and construction employers); OSHA should allow a variance process or provide alternative hygiene controls.

[P24] The March 10, 2020 date to implement engineering controls in paragraph (f) may not be adequate for employers facing supply-chain constraints or needing to redesign processes; OSHA should allow documented extension requests when employers are actively pursuing feasible controls.

[P25] The December 12, 2018 deadline for all other obligations is overly compressed given overlapping dates; OSHA should harmonize dates to reduce administrative burden and confusion about phased compliance.

[P26] Requiring CBD diagnostic centers to have the capacity to perform pulmonary function testing, BAL, and transbronchial biopsy may be medically unnecessary and burdensome — transbronchial biopsy is an invasive procedure that should not be mandated as a capability for every diagnostic center.

[P27] The 24-hour requirement to transfer BAL samples to a laboratory for appropriate diagnostic testing is medically reasonable but needs specification of transportation standards, chain-of-custody, and acceptable laboratory qualifications.

[P28] Requiring the pulmonologist/pulmonary specialist to interpret biopsy pathology and BAL results assumes availability of local specialists with beryllium disease expertise; OSHA should allow use of remote expert consultation when local expertise is not available.

[P29] The same capacity requirements for construction-sector CBD diagnostic centers (§1926.1124(b)) are unrealistic for many rural or small community healthcare providers; OSHA should permit referral networks or telemedicine consultations.

[P30] The 24-hour transfer requirement in §1926.1124(b) is logistically difficult in remote areas; OSHA should allow a reasonable alternative timeframe if adequate preservation and shipping are used and documented.

[P31] Interpreting biopsy pathology and BAL results requires specialized pathology services; employers should be permitted to use certified laboratories and remote specialists rather than require on-site interpretation capability.

[P32] The obligation to use engineering and work practice controls to achieve TWA PEL and STEL (§1915.1024(f)(2)) is appropriate, but OSHA must provide an implementation hierarchy and examples of feasible controls for common industries.

[P33] The requirement that if controls cannot reduce exposures to PELs employers must implement "the lowest feasible controls" and supplement with respirators lacks an objective standard for "feasible"; OSHA should define technical and economic feasibility and require documented feasibility studies.

[P34] Mirroring §1915.1024(f)(2) in §1926.1124(f)(2) for construction is necessary, but the standard should explicitly address temporary and mobile operations where engineering controls may be impracticable and specify acceptable work-practice and PPE alternatives.

[P35] The obligation to document that controls cannot achieve PELs before relying on respirators (§1926.1124(f)(2)) requires a defined written justification format and review period; OSHA should require that employers update such justifications periodically.

[P36] Requiring employers to provide PPE at no cost and ensure employee use when exposures exceed limits (§1915.1024(h)(1)) is appropriate, but OSHA must clarify employer obligations for training, fit-testing, maintenance, and replacement schedules.

[P37] The mandate that employees remove PPE at shift end or after beryllium tasks (§1915.1024(h)(2)(i)) imposes logistical burdens on multi-task workers; OSHA should permit employers to designate storage and cleaning areas and provide guidance on cross-shift contamination controls.

[P38] The prohibition on removing PPE in ways that disperse beryllium airborne (§1915.1024(h)(2)(ii)) needs concrete examples and training requirements so employers can effectively enforce this provision without subjective interpretation.

[P39] The prohibition against blowing, shaking, or otherwise removing beryllium from PPE (§1915.1024(h)(3)(ii)) is sensible, but the rule should require employers to provide designated enclosed decontamination areas and mechanical methods (e.g., HEPA vacuums) as alternatives.

[P40] The requirement to use cleaning methods that minimize airborne exposure (§1915.1024(j)(1)) needs an explicit list of acceptable cleaning methods (e.g., HEPA-filtered vacuuming, wet methods) and performance expectations for cleaning efficacy.

[P41] The prohibition on dry sweeping or brushing where exposures may exceed limits (§1915.1024(j)(2)) is appropriate, but the regulation's exception is broad — OSHA should narrow the exception to clearly defined, documented circumstances and require supervisory approval.

[P42] The exception allowing dry sweeping or brushing when other methods are "not safe or effective" (§1915.1024(j)(2)) is vague and could be widely exploited; OSHA should require employers to document why other methods are unsafe/ineffective and to use respiratory protection when invoking the exception.

[P43] The absolute prohibition on compressed air cleaning if it causes or may cause exposures above limits (§1915.1024(j)(3)) is justified, but OSHA should define "may reasonably be expected to cause" with numerical or task-based criteria to enable compliance assessments.

[P44] Requiring employers to provide respiratory protection and PPE when dry sweeping, brushing, or compressed air are used (§1915.1024(j)(4)) is reasonable, but OSHA should specify the required assigned protection factors (APFs) and the respirator selection process tied to measured exposure levels.

[P45] The obligation to handle and maintain cleaning equipment to minimize airborne exposure and prevent re-entrainment (§1915.1024(j)(5)) needs prescriptive maintenance intervals, filtration efficiency requirements (e.g., HEPA), and recordkeeping expectations.

[P46] Requiring employers to provide a no-cost evaluation at a mutually agreed CBD diagnostic center (§1915.1024(k)(7)(i)) could create conflicts when employer and employee cannot agree; OSHA should define a dispute-resolution mechanism or list an independent referral process.

[P47] The requirement to provide pulmonary function testing, BAL, and transbronchial biopsy at no cost within a reasonable time if deemed appropriate by the CBD physician (§1915.1024(k)(7)(i)) lacks a definition of "reasonable time" and should set a maximum (e.g., within 30–60 days) for diagnostic procedures.

[P48] Mandating that the initial consultation with the CBD diagnostic center be provided within 30 days of triggering events (§1915.1024(k)(7)(i)) is reasonable, but OSHA should clarify the "triggering events" list and employer notification responsibilities.

[P49] Including beryllium in the employer's hazard communication program (§1915.1024(m)(1)(ii)) is consistent with HCS, but OSHA should require that beryllium SDSs explicitly reference beryllium-specific exposure controls and medical surveillance requirements in the standard.

[P50] The obligation that employees have access to labels and SDSs and training per HCS and paragraph (m)(3) (§1915.1024(m)(1)(ii)) is fine, but employers need model training modules and a minimum training frequency specified (e.g., initial + annual refresher).

[P51] Requiring a post-training record with employee name, job classification, training date, and topic (§1915.1024(n)(4)(i)) is appropriate, but OSHA should specify retention periods and whether electronic records meet the requirement.

[P52] The construction-sector requirement to provide PPE at no cost when exposures exceed limits (§1926.1124(h)(1)) should explicitly address multi-employer jobsite situations and clarify host/contractor responsibilities for providing and enforcing PPE use.

[P53] Ensuring employees remove PPE at shift end or after tasks involving beryllium (§1926.1124(h)(2)(i)) is challenging on transient construction sites; OSHA should allow portable changing facilities or permit off-site removal with employer-provided laundering/transport where feasible.

[P54] The prohibition on removing PPE in a manner that disperses beryllium airborne (§1926.1124(h)(2)(ii)) requires provision of suitable decontamination procedures and training for construction crews working in constrained spaces.

[P55] The ban on blowing/shaking PPE to remove beryllium (§1926.1124(h)(3)(ii)) should require employers to provide mechanical cleaning devices (e.g., HEPA vacs) and specify disposal or laundering protocols to prevent secondary exposures.

[P56] The cleaning-methods obligation in construction (§1926.1124(j)(1)) must account for on-site limitations; OSHA should permit approved mobile HEPA vacuum units and wet methods tailored for construction tasks.

[P57] The prohibition on dry sweeping/brushing in construction (§1926.1124(j)(2)) needs an operational definition of "brushing" vs. tool use (e.g., wire brushes on weld spatter) to avoid ambiguity for tradespeople.

[P58] The exception for dry sweeping/brushing in construction when other methods are unsafe or ineffective (§1926.1124(j)(2)) should require documentation, supervisory approval, and temporary use limits to prevent misuse.

[P59] The prohibition on compressed air for cleaning in construction (§1926.1124(j)(3)) must address scenarios where compressed air is integral to tasks (e.g., pneumatic tool maintenance) and clarify permitted engineering controls or local exhaust alternatives.

[P60] Obligating employers to provide respiratory protection and PPE when unsafe cleaning methods are used (§1926.1124(j)(4)) should include specific respirator types and fit-testing timetables appropriate for construction work cycles.

[P61] The requirement to handle and maintain cleaning equipment to minimize re-entrainment (§1926.1124(j)(5)) should include vendor certification of filters and maintenance logs as part of compliance evidence.

[P62] The obligation to provide no-cost CBD evaluations at a mutually agreed center in construction (§1926.1124(k)(7)(i)) must address multi-employer sites where employees are subcontractors — the rule should clarify which employer (host or contractor) bears responsibility.

[P63] The requirement to provide pulmonary testing, BAL, and biopsy at no cost within a reasonable time in construction (§1926.1124(k)(7)(i)) requires a maximum scheduling timeframe and provisions for covering travel costs for workers who must travel to specialized centers.

[P64] The 30-day initial consultation requirement for construction (§1926.1124(k)(7)(i)) needs clarity on counting days (calendar vs. business), and requirements for interim protective measures if diagnostic centers cannot schedule within 30 days.

[P65] The training record requirement in construction (§1926.1124(n)(4)(i)) should explicitly allow electronic rosters and require employers to make records available to employees, their representatives, and OSHA upon request.

[P66] Across the rule, OSHA should include small-business flexibility provisions (e.g., compliance schedules, model programs) because many obligations (engineering controls, medical diagnostics, facilities) impose disproportionate burdens on small employers.

[P67] The rule should provide explicit enforcement policy and penalty guidance for first-time, good-faith violations (e.g., during phased compliance periods) so employers and labor reps understand consequences.

[P68] The standards require numerous medical procedures (BAL, transbronchial biopsy) that pose risks; OSHA should consult with medical societies to ensure procedures are medically necessary and provide alternative diagnostic pathways.

[P69] OSHA should clarify recordkeeping retention periods for medical, training, and exposure monitoring records referenced across §§1915/1910/1926 to ensure uniform compliance and to address confidentiality of medical records.

[P70] The rule should specify acceptable analytical methods and labs for beryllium air and BAL testing, including accreditation requirements, to ensure consistency and reliability of compliance measurements.

The ban on blowing/shaking PPE to remove beryllium (§1926.1124(h)(3)(ii)) should require employers to provide mechanical cleaning devices (e.g., HEPA vacs) and specify disposal or laundering protocols to prevent secondary exposures.

The cleaning-methods obligation in construction (§1926.1124(j)(1)) must account for on-site limitations; OSHA should permit approved mobile HEPA vacuum units and wet methods tailored for construction tasks.

The prohibition on dry sweeping/brushing in construction (§1926.1124(j)(2)) needs an operational definition of "brushing" vs. tool use (e.g., wire brushes on weld spatter) to avoid ambiguity for tradespeople.

The exception for dry sweeping/brushing in construction when other methods are unsafe or ineffective (§1926.1124(j)(2)) should require documentation, supervisory approval, and temporary use limits to prevent misuse.

The prohibition on compressed air for cleaning in construction (§1926.1124(j)(3)) must address scenarios where compressed air is integral to tasks (e.g., pneumatic tool maintenance) and clarify permitted engineering controls or local exhaust alternatives.

Obligating employers to provide respiratory protection and PPE when unsafe cleaning methods are used (§1926.1124(j)(4)) should include specific respirator types and fit-testing timetables appropriate for construction work cycles.

The requirement to handle and maintain cleaning equipment to minimize re-entrainment (§1926.1124(j)(5)) should include vendor certification of filters and maintenance logs as part of compliance evidence.

The obligation to provide no-cost CBD evaluations at a mutually agreed center in construction (§1926.1124(k)(7)(i)) must address multi-employer sites where employees are subcontractors — the rule should clarify which employer (host or contractor) bears responsibility.

The requirement to provide pulmonary testing, BAL, and biopsy at no cost within a reasonable time in construction (§1926.1124(k)(7)(i)) requires a maximum scheduling timeframe and provisions for covering travel costs for workers who must travel to specialized centers.

The 30-day initial consultation requirement for construction (§1926.1124(k)(7)(i)) needs clarity on counting days (calendar vs. business), and requirements for interim protective measures if diagnostic centers cannot schedule within 30 days.

[P1] The exemption from 510(k) in § 878.4740(a)(2) is too broad: industry and patient safety advocates will comment that removing the 510(k) requirement (even subject to § 878.9) reduces FDA premarket review of design changes, and request that higher-risk staplers remain subject to 510(k) clearance.

[P1] Legal experts will argue that applying the general limitations in § 878.9 is insufficiently specific to ensure safety and request that the rule specify which § 878.9 limitations apply and how they will be enforced for staplers.

[P1] Hospitals and health systems will request an explicit grandfathering clause clarifying whether currently marketed staplers that would have required a 510(k) must now be relabeled or re-evaluated under this exemption.

[P2] Device manufacturers will ask for clearer definitions of “anticipated conditions of use” in § 878.4740(b)(2)(i) — specifically whether it includes off-label surgical scenarios, emergency use, or pediatric cases — because the scope affects testing burden.

[P2] Clinical societies will comment that the testing standard in § 878.4740(b)(2)(i) should require testing with commonly encountered comorbid tissue conditions (e.g., irradiated, inflamed, fibrotic tissue) and not just “normal” tissue analogues.

[P3] Manufacturers will request numeric tolerances or guidance for what constitutes “maximum and minimum tissue thicknesses” in § 878.4740(b)(2)(i)(A) (e.g., specific millimeter ranges by tissue type) to avoid inconsistent interpretations across submissions.

[P3] Surgeons and medical device testers will request that evaluations under § 878.4740(b)(2)(i)(A) include heterogeneous tissues and transitional interfaces (e.g., bowel mesentery to muscular wall), not only uniform thicknesses.

[P4] Industry commenters will ask FDA to define “worst-case deployment pressures” in § 878.4740(b)(2)(i)(B), specifying test methods, sample sizes, and acceptance criteria for stapler firing force.

[P4] Biomedical engineers will request that the rule require characterization of variability in deployment force across manufacturing lots and after simulated aging to capture reliability over shelf life under § 878.4740(b)(2)(i)(B).

[P5] Clinicians and patient-safety groups will demand that “measurement of staple line strength” in § 878.4740(b)(2)(i)(C) include quantitative thresholds (e.g., burst pressure in mmHg, tensile strength in N) tied to clinical outcomes, not just relative comparisons.

[P5] Testing labs will request standardized test methods (ASTM/ISO references) be specified for staple line strength measurements in § 878.4740(b)(2)(i)(C) to ensure comparability across manufacturers.

[P6] Commenters will seek clarification of “confirmation of staple line integrity” in § 878.4740(b)(2)(i)(D): whether this requires imaging, leak testing, histology, or a combination, and the acceptance criteria for passing.

[P6] Patient advocacy groups will request that staple line integrity testing include fatigue/cyclic loading to simulate postoperative stresses, and a minimum survival time post-procedure for in vivo tests under § 878.4740(b)(2)(i)(D).

[P7] Surgeons and regulators will challenge the in vivo hemostasis requirement in § 878.4740(b)(2)(i)(E) as potentially requiring animal studies for routine devices, and will request guidance on acceptable models, endpoints (e.g., immediate hemostasis vs. sustained), and when bench models suffice.

[P7] Animal welfare organizations will request that the rule allow validated ex vivo or benchtop simulations in lieu of in vivo testing where scientifically justified for § 878.4740(b)(2)(i)(E).

[P8] Clinician organizations will assert that the usability testing and labeling comprehension study in § 878.4740(b)(2)(ii) must include representative end users (attending surgeons, residents, OR nurses) across specialties and experience levels, and be conducted in simulated OR settings.

[P8] Small manufacturers will comment that the scope and sample size for labeling comprehension studies are unclear and burdensome; they will request minimum sample-size guidance and allowance for remote/electronic studies for § 878.4740(b)(2)(ii).

[P9] Biocompatibility experts will request that § 878.4740(b)(2)(iii) explicitly reference ISO 10993 standards and clarify when chemical characterization may substitute for full animal biocompatibility testing for device-contacting elements.

[P9] Allergy and patient groups will request that labeling require disclosure of all materials that contact patients (e.g., nickel content) and testing for sensitization in § 878.4740(b)(2)(iii).

[P10] Sterility assurance professionals will ask that § 878.4740(b)(2)(iv) specify acceptable sterility assurance levels (SAL), validated sterilization methods (e.g., EtO, gamma), and references to applicable standards (e.g., ISO 11135/11137) for sterility performance data.

[P10] Hospitals will request that the rule require documentation that packaging maintains sterility through expected supply-chain stresses in § 878.4740(b)(2)(iv).

[P11] Reprocessing service providers will request that validation requirements in § 878.4740(b)(2)(v) include worst-case soil loads, multiple reprocessing cycles, and validation for both manual and automated cleaning systems when applicable.

[P11] Infection control professionals will comment that the rule should require instructions that account for variability in hospital sterilization equipment and include reprocessing acceptance criteria for § 878.4740(b)(2)(v).

[P12] Supply chain stakeholders will request clarity on the accelerated aging protocols, sample sizes, and acceptance criteria for demonstrating shelf life under § 878.4740(b)(2)(vi), and whether real-time data will be required for longer shelf lives.

[P12] Clinicians will suggest that shelf-life testing include functional tests post-aging (e.g., firing force, staple formation) to meet the requirement that functionality be demonstrated over the labeled shelf life in § 878.4740(b)(2)(vi).

[P13] Professional societies will request that the required labeling list be harmonized with existing surgical device labeling guidance to avoid duplicative or conflicting requirements under § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii).

[P14] Manufacturers will seek specificity for contraindications under § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(A): they will ask for examples and evidence thresholds that would permit use on tissues currently listed as contraindications.

[P14] Surgeons will request that contraindications be evidence-based and not blanket prohibitions — for example, seeking ability to use staplers on certain vascular tissues when manufacturer data shows safety under § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(A).

[P15] Legal counsel will caution that the “unless available information demonstrates” language in § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(B) is vague; they will ask for a clear standard of proof and acceptable data types to avoid inconsistent labeling mandates.

[P15] Consumer safety groups will argue that the default should be conservative warnings and that manufacturers should bear the burden of proving warnings are unnecessary under § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(B).

[P16] Clinicians will support the warning in § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(B)(i) about obstructions and unintended stapling but will request example scenarios and recommended mitigation techniques (e.g., use of retractors, imaging) to be included in labeling.

[P16] Regulatory commenters will ask for clarity whether the obstruction warning in § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(B)(i) requires specific design features (e.g., tissue sensors) or only labeling.

[P17] Surgeons will request that the prohibition against clamping/unclamping delicate tissues in § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(B)(ii) be clarified — specifically which tissues are considered “delicate” and whether intraoperative exceptions (e.g., trauma surgery) are permitted.

[P18] Vascular surgeons will note that the warning against use on large vessels in § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(B)(iii) is appropriate but ask the rule to define “large vessels” (e.g., diameter thresholds) to avoid ambiguity.

[P19] Clinicians will support the requirement in § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(B)(iv) to establish and maintain proximal control before stapling but will request guidance on acceptable techniques and labeling language to instruct users.

[P20] Surgical societies will request that § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(B)(v) require detailed, stepwise instructions for management of stapler malfunctions crossing vessels (including algorithms), not just high-level warnings.

[P20] Risk managers will ask that the malfunction instructions in § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(B)(v) include required training elements and recommended emergency equipment to have available (e.g., vascular clamps, sutures).

[P21] Hospitals will insist that the compatibility warning in § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(B)(vi) be reinforced by requiring manufacturers to physically prevent incompatible staples from being loaded (design controls), not merely labeling, where technically feasible.

[P21] Procurement officers will request standardized labeling or connectors to prevent incompatible staple use across brands, as required by § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(B)(vi).

[P22] Professional societies will request that “measures associated with prevention of device malfunction” in § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(C) include recommended maintenance intervals, pre-use checks, and verification steps to be performed in the OR.

[P22] Human factors experts will request clear criteria for what constitutes sufficient “evaluation of tissue appropriateness” in § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(C), including decision aids or charts indicating tissue thickness ranges and staple selection guidance.

[P23] Manufacturers will request that the “list of staples the stapler is demonstrated compatible with” in § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(D) be permitted in an electronic format accessible to purchasers and that cross-referencing multi-brand compatibility be allowed if validated.

[P23] Competing staple manufacturers will object to listing only staples tested by the stapler manufacturer under § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(D) and request a mechanism for third-party compatibility testing and listing.

[P24] Biomedical engineers will ask that the “key performance parameters and technical characteristics” in § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(E) be explicitly enumerated (e.g., firing force range, staple closed height, cartridge gap tolerances) to avoid inconsistent disclosures.

[P24] Purchasing groups will request that key parameters in § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(E) be presented in a standardized table on labeling and packaging to enable quick device selection.

[P25] Clinical commenters will request that the “intended tissue types” information under § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(F) be accompanied by objective metrics (thickness, compressibility) and clinical indications/contraindications for each tissue type.

[P26] Patient-safety advocates will ask that the identification of stapler safety mechanisms in § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(G) include failure modes and limitations of those mechanisms (e.g., what they do not prevent) to avoid overreliance.

[P27] Sterilization and reprocessing professionals will request the validated reprocessing methods in § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(H) include step-by-step protocols, acceptable disinfectants/sterilants, and performance acceptance criteria after repeated cycles.

[P27] Infection preventionists will request that labeling explicitly state the maximum number of reprocessing cycles for reusable components, and require manufacturers to provide data supporting that limit per § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(H).

[P28] Supply-chain managers will ask that the shelf life/expiration date requirement in § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(I) include instructions for storage conditions (temperature/humidity) that were used to determine the shelf life.

[P28] Manufacturers will request flexibility to use both date-based and lot-based shelf life systems and clarity on what data is required to extend shelf life beyond initial claims under § 878.4740(b)(2)(vii)(I).

[P29] Purchasing clinicians will request that the “critical information/technical characteristics” required on package labels under § 878.4740(b)(2)(viii) be standardized (e.g., tissue thickness range, staple size, compatible cartridge codes) to support correct device selection in fast-paced OR environments.

[P29] Small device companies will request a size/format exception for package label content in § 878.4740(b)(2)(viii) when limited packaging area prevents full data display, allowing reference to a quick-access online datasheet or QR code containing required technical details.

[P1] Industry commenter: The Jan 1, 2023 sunset date in P1 is infeasible for firms that will need longer lead time to qualify and validate alternative blowing agents; request extension to a specific later date (e.g., Jan 1, 2025) or allow case-by-case extensions.

[P1] Legal commenter: P1 is ambiguous because it uses the phrase “reasonable efforts have shown” without defining the standard of “reasonable efforts”; request insertion of an objective standard or model checklist to reduce enforcement uncertainty.

[P1] Environmental advocacy group: Allowing continued use of blends containing up to 52% HFC-134a until Jan 1, 2023 undermines near-term GHG reduction goals; recommend prohibiting HFC-134a blends immediately or shortening the allowance period to 30 days from publication.

[P1] Small business association: The retroactive effective phrasing (“Acceptable from [insert date 30 days after date of publication] until January 1, 2023”) could be read to allow only a very short compliance window; request clarification of the exact start date and an implementation period of at least 180 days.

[P2] Industry compliance officer: P2’s recordkeeping obligation lacks specificity on retention period — request that the agency set a clear minimum retention period (e.g., 5 years) and clarify whether records must be submitted proactively or only upon request.

[P2] Privacy/legal counsel: P2 does not address protection of proprietary or confidential business information included in required documentation; request a CBI protection procedure and ability to redact competitively sensitive details.

[P3] Trade association: P3 requires “specific descriptive information” but does not list required data fields or format; request standardized templates or examples to ensure consistent compliance and reduce administrative burden.

[P4] Manufacturer: P4’s requirement to “Describe the process or product” should be limited to information necessary to establish technical infeasibility; otherwise regulators will request unnecessary proprietary process details. Request limiting description to functional requirements and performance metrics.

[P5] Environmental NGO: P5 demands listing of “other substitutes examined and rejected” but does not require that applicants consider low-GWP options first; request adding a requirement to document consideration of lowest-GWP feasible alternatives and justification if those were not prioritized.

[P6] Safety organization: P6’s requirement to explain why alternatives were rejected (performance, technical, safety) should require supporting test data where safety is cited; request explicit requirement to include test reports, third-party certifications, or engineering analyses when safety is claimed.

[P7] Industry R&D group: P7 asks for “anticipated date other substitutes will be available and projected time for switching” but does not account for supply-chain constraints; request that the rule permit inclusion of supplier lead-time documentation and phased transition plans.

[P8] Industry commenter: The identical sunset to Jan 1, 2023 in P8 for the HFO/water/CO2 blends is inconsistent given that these blends have lower HFC content; request that the agency allow these lower-GWP blends longer authorization or remove HFC-related cutoff.

[P8] Environmental advocacy group: P8 permits blends that still contain 40–52% HFC-134a; this allowance is inconsistent with the rule’s climate objectives and should be eliminated or tightened to a lower HFC cap.

[P9] Small manufacturer: P9 duplicates P2 but could double compliance burden if each authorized blend triggers separate recordkeeping; request cross-reference allowing one consolidated investigation record per production line rather than per blend.

[P10] Legal expert: P10’s “specific descriptive information” clause is vague and may be read to require voluminous technical submissions; request the agency set page or content limits and clarify that high-level descriptions suffice unless regulator reasonably requests more detail.

[P11] Product safety group: P11’s requirement to describe the process/product should require demonstration that the substitute’s use does not create new safety hazards (flammability, toxicity); request explicit inclusion of safety test results and mitigation measures.

[P12] Trade group: P12 requires listing rejected substitutes but does not require that the evaluation include cost and lifecycle GWP comparisons; request mandatory inclusion of cost, performance, lifecycle global-warming-potential, and flammability metrics for each considered substitute.

[P1] The June 15, 2020 comment deadline is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60 days to allow thorough review by industry and public-interest groups.

[P1] The rule’s mandatory statement “We must receive comments by June 15, 2020” is ambiguous about whether mailed comments postmarked by that date are acceptable; clarify accepted submission methods and postmark versus receipt rules.

[P2] The phrase “unless already done” in compliance times is vague; specify documentation required to demonstrate actions were “already completed” and acceptable evidence for compliance.

[P2] Requiring compliance “within the compliance times specified” without clear timelines in the FAA AD creates uncertainty for operators; the FAA should publish explicit calendar deadlines or compliance intervals.

[P3] Incorporating EASA AD requirements “except as specified in paragraph (h)” without reproducing full text of the cited EASA ADs makes compliance burdensome; the FAA should include the full text or a clear, consolidated summary of required actions.

[P3] Relying on foreign (EASA) ADs for required actions could create legal and operational conflicts with existing FAA-certified maintenance programs; the FAA should detail how conflicts will be resolved.

[P4] Substituting this AD’s effective date for EASA AD effective dates could create retroactive obligations for actions taken based on EASA schedules; clarify whether actions completed between EASA effective dates and this FAA effective date are treated as compliant.

[P5] Limiting required EASA paragraphs to only (5) and (6) while referencing the broader EASA AD may mislead practitioners; state clearly which procedures, parts, and intervals in paragraphs (5) and (6) are mandated.

[P5] The selection of only paragraphs (5) and (6) may omit essential preliminary inspections in (1)-(4) that ensure effectiveness of (5) and (6); justify why (1)-(4) are not required and assess safety impacts.

[P6] The requirement to “report insulation check results according to the timing in paragraphs (h)(4)(i) or (ii)” lacks a specified report format, required data fields, and submission point; the FAA should provide a standardized reporting template.

[P7] Requiring submission of inspection reports within 30 days after checks done on or after the AD effective date imposes an undue administrative burden on large operators; extend the deadline to 60 days or permit electronic batch submissions.

[P7] The 30-day reporting period in paragraph (h)(4)(i) may be impractical for checks performed during remote operations or outside of business hours; allow for exceptions when logistics prevent timely reporting.

[P8] For inspections done before the FAA AD effective date, requiring reports within 30 days after the AD effective date (h)(4)(ii) could result in duplicate reporting if operators already submitted reports to EASA; allow reliance on EASA submissions or accept EASA report copies.

[P8] Paragraph (h)(4)(ii) does not define whether previously-submitted reports to EASA satisfy the FAA reporting requirement; the FAA should accept existing EASA reports to avoid redundant work.

[P9] Removing the requirement to return parts to the manufacturer (h)(6) may hinder traceability and post-event analysis; request clarification about acceptable disposition and retention procedures for suspect parts.

[P9] While (h)(6) relieves operators from returning parts, the AD should mandate preservation, quarantine, and retention periods and require availability of parts for FAA or EASA inspection upon request.

[P10] The AMOC approval authority vested in the Manager Large Aircraft Section is appropriate, but the rule lacks service-level targets for FAA response times to AMOC requests; require a 60-day review timeline to provide predictability.

[P11] Requiring submission of AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO may create inconsistent handling; permit direct submission to the International Validation Branch with an option for local coordination.

[P12] The requirement to address direct AMOC submissions to the person in paragraph (j)(2) is administratively rigid; provide the named official’s contact information in the AD and allow for delegation.

[P13] Allowing AMOC submissions via the specified email is helpful, but the AD should also permit secure portals for large file attachments and confirm receipt/acknowledgment procedures to avoid lost submissions.

[P14] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC may delay operations if inspectors are unavailable; allow notification “as soon as practicable” and permit electronic notification methods.

[P15] Accepting AMOCs previously approved for AD 2018–17–05 is reasonable, but the AD should require that operators verify continued applicability given any technical differences between the ADs; require a documented equivalency assessment.

[P16] Requiring manufacturer instructions to be followed using methods approved by the FAA Manager, EASA, or Airbus DOA is appropriate, but the AD should explicitly permit use of equivalent approvals from other ICAO-recognized authorities in emergency situations.

[P16] Mandating that DOA approvals include a DOA-authorized signature creates paperwork friction; permit electronic signatures or a DOA-designated representative list to streamline verification.

[P17] Designating procedures/tests as Required for Compliance (RC) is necessary, but the AD must clearly identify which specific steps in the referenced service bulletins are RC; include an appendix mapping RC steps to service bulletin paragraph numbers.

[P18] Stating that non-RC procedures are recommended is beneficial, but operators need guidance on prioritizing non-RC tasks and examples of acceptable deviations; provide criteria for when non-RC deviations are acceptable.

[P19] Allowing deviation from non-RC procedures without AMOC if RC procedures can still be completed risks inconsistent quality; require documentation in the maintenance record describing the deviation and rationale.

[P20] Requiring AMOC approval for any changes to RC procedures is appropriate, but the AD should provide expedited AMOC pathways for minor administrative adjustments that do not affect safety margins.

[P21] The PRA prohibition is standard, but the AD simultaneously makes responses mandatory (see P24); clarify how the PRA rules interact with mandatory reporting to ensure legal compliance and avoid chilling effect.

[P22] The PRA permission that persons need not respond without a valid OMB Control Number conflicts with P24’s statement that responses are mandatory; specify the OMB Control Number or the mechanism by which the collection is authorized.

[P23] Prohibiting penalties for failure to comply absent a valid OMB number is appropriate; however, the AD should state whether any enforcement actions will be deferred until the OMB control number is visible.

[P24] Declaring all responses to the information collection mandatory (P24) conflicts with P21–P23 and invites legal challenge; the FAA must publish the OMB Control Number in the final rule and reconcile the statements.

[P24] The AD should estimate the reporting burden per submission (hours, number of staff, data elements) and provide guidance on acceptable methods to reduce burden (e.g., electronic upload).

[P25] The instruction to send comments on the burden estimate to the FAA Information Collection Clearance Officer should include an email address and an expected timeframe for FAA consideration of such comments.

[P6][P7][P8] The AD does not specify the destination address or portal for submitting insulation inspection reports; provide a single, centralized submission point and confirm security/confidentiality protections for potentially sensitive data.

[P5][P17] Because the AD only requires paragraphs (5) and (6) of EASA AD 2019–0301, but RC designations in the EASA documents may differ, the FAA should explicitly list which tasks are RC under the FAA AD to prevent misinterpretation.

[P10][P20] The AD should state whether AMOCs previously approved or newly approved will be publicly posted or logged to assist other operators in adopting equivalent compliance methods.

[P9] By not requiring return to manufacturer, the AD may shift costs and liabilities to operators; the FAA should clarify responsibility for defective parts and potential warranty/indemnity issues.

[P1][P7][P8] Given that the comment deadline and the 30-day reporting deadlines are both tight and overlapping, the FAA should coordinate timelines to avoid forcing operators to submit inspection reports before being able to comment on the rule’s reporting requirements.

[P3] The AD’s incorporation-by-reference approach to EASA ADs should include the method to obtain those EASA documents at no cost or specify the cost and ensure availability so that small operators can comply.

[P16] The requirement for EASA or Airbus DOA approval for manufacturer instructions could disadvantage non-European operators; clarify whether FAA-issued approvals or recognized bilateral agreements suffice.

[P13] Emailing AMOC requests to a public inbox raises concerns about sensitive IS/CM data being transmitted insecurely; require use of secure encrypted channels for proprietary technical data.

[P14] The AD should make clear whether notification to the principal inspector before using an AMOC is merely informational or if additional local approval is required.

[P6] The AD should require that insulation check reporting include follow-up corrective actions and timelines for remedying any deficiencies discovered, not just inspection results.

[P1] The rule’s general prohibition header in §17.41(f)(1) is overly broad and lacks definitions for key terms such as “activities” and “listed activities,” creating uncertainty for land managers and enforcement agencies about what conduct is actually prohibited.

[P2] The prohibition of “purposeful take” in §17.41(f)(1)(i) should clarify whether intentional, incidental, and negligent acts are distinguished and provide definitions for “capture” and “handling” to avoid criminalizing routine scientific monitoring conducted under authorization.

[P2] Industry and research organizations will need explicit language that permitted scientific research under §17.32 or other permits is not considered unlawful “purposeful take” under §17.41(f)(1)(i).

[P3] §17.41(f)(1)(ii) prohibits prescribed burns that result in incidental take without setting objective thresholds for what constitutes “incidental take,” making compliance and permitting unpredictable for fire managers.

[P4] The prohibition in §17.41(f)(1)(ii) fails to account for the ecological necessity of prescribed fire in many eastern black rail habitats and should allow prescribed burns when conducted under a certified burn plan that includes monitoring, not just BMPs.

[P5] §17.41(f)(1)(ii)(A) bans prescribed burns during nesting, brooding, or post-breeding flightless molt; commenters request the rule specify exact calendar dates or biologically based regional windows for these periods so managers can plan.

[P5] State wildlife agencies and landowners will need region-specific timing guidance because nesting and molt timing varies by latitude and habitat; the prohibition as written could unnecessarily restrict beneficial fire outside actual sensitive periods.

[P6] Listing “slow burn fires” as a BMP example in §17.41(f)(1)(ii) is vague; the rule should define “slow burn” operationally (e.g., flame length, rate of spread, ignition pattern) to be enforceable and useful to practitioners.

[P7] The BMP example in §17.41(f)(1)(ii) to “limit burned area to retain suitable dense cover” requires measurable metrics (percent of block retained, patch size, distance to refugia) so that land managers can demonstrate compliance.

[P8] The “patch or refugia” BMP example in §17.41(f)(1)(ii) should require minimum refugia size, spatial arrangement, and monitoring protocols to ensure those patches are functional for eastern black rails rather than aspirational.

[P9] The prohibition’s example to avoid “ring or perimeter fires” in §17.41(f)(1)(ii) needs clarification about whether containment line construction or backfiring done for safety/containment could be interpreted as ring fires and thus prohibited.

[P10] §17.41(f)(1)(iii) prohibits mowing, haying, and mechanical treatments in emergent wetlands during sensitive periods but does not define “emergent wetlands” or provide mapping guidance, creating implementation difficulties for agricultural producers and utilities.

[P10] The prohibition in §17.41(f)(1)(iii) should specify whether private landowners conducting agricultural harvests are subject to the same restrictions or whether agricultural exemptions apply; current language is ambiguous and could penalize routine farming operations.

[P11] §17.41(f)(1)(iv) prohibits grazing on public lands that results in incidental take but does not specify monitoring or stocking-rate thresholds to define “intensive” or “high-density” grazing, leaving managers unsure how to comply.

[P12] The grazing prohibition in §17.41(f)(1)(iv) needs an explicit treatment for pre-existing grazing allotments under valid existing rights; the rule should state whether grandfathering or adaptive management plans are allowed.

[P12] Legal experts will likely challenge the grazing prohibitions if they effectively nullify existing grazing permits without adequate compensation or procedural protections; the rule must address due process and permit modification procedures.

[P13] §17.41(f)(1)(iv)(A) prohibits grazing during nesting, brooding, or flightless molt — commenters request clear regional timing windows and an appeals or permitting pathway for unavoidable emergency grazing (e.g., drought-driven).

[P14] The prohibition on intensive/high-density grazing in §17.41(f)(1)(iv)(B) needs a quantitative definition (e.g., Animal Unit Months per acre) or reference to state-standard stocking rates to be enforceable and fair across landscapes.

[P15] §17.41(f)(1)(iv)(C)’s requirement to “maintain appropriate dense vegetation cover” lacks objective standards (height, percent cover, stem density) — the absence of measurable criteria will lead to inconsistent enforcement and litigation.

[P1] The requirement that comparator panels "match the color of the installed sheeting" is ambiguous — the rule should specify acceptable color tolerances (e.g., Pantone or spectral reflectance tolerances) to avoid subjective mismatches between comparator and installed sheeting.

[P1] Industry commenters will object that requiring comparator panels to conform to paragraph (c)(1) without reproducing those specifications in this provision leaves uncertainty about manufacturing and certification obligations for comparator panels.

[P2] Placing the comparator panel "directly adjacent to, or overlapping" the sheeting could damage vehicle or equipment paint/finish; the rule should permit a non-contact spacer or clamp method to avoid surface harm.

[P2] Emergency response organizations will request clarification that comparator panels may be temporarily attached by magnetic or Velcro methods and that overlapping is allowed only if it does not obscure safety-critical markings.

[P3] The phrase "cleaned, as necessary" is vague — commenters will ask for defined cleaning procedures and approved cleaning agents to prevent damage to sheeting during inspections.

[P3] Maintenance crews will request an explicit exemption allowing inspections to proceed without cleaning if cleaning is impracticable due to operational constraints and if documented.

[P4] The "preferably at 15 feet" perpendicular viewing requirement is impractical in confined spaces (ambulances, utility buckets); commenters will request explicit allowances for shorter distances and alternative perpendicularity criteria for tight conditions.

[P4] Measurement specialists will point out that "perpendicular" must be defined relative to the sheeting plane and recommend including an allowable angular deviation (e.g., ±5°) to ensure repeatability.

[P5] The 10–20 foot fallback range does not account for common field situations where only shorter distances (e.g., 3–8 feet) are possible; commenters will ask either to widen the permitted range or allow documented justification for outside-range evaluations.

[P6] Requiring the light source to be positioned adjacent to the inspector's eye may conflict with safety (eye exposure) and practical constraints; commenters will request specification of safe illumination levels and alternative allowed geometries (coaxial or fixed mount) with equivalency tests.

[P6] Legal experts will note that specifying "left or right" eye positioning could lead to inconsistent results between inspectors and request standardized instructions and training requirements rather than a left/right choice.

[P7] The subjective pass criterion "appears brighter" invites inconsistent decisions; commenters will urge replacing perception-based judgment with objective photometric thresholds or requiring photography/measurement for borderline cases.

[P7] Disability advocates will note that visual perception varies between inspectors (color vision deficiency, age) and request mandatory use of devices or dual-inspector verification for pass/fail calls.

[P8] The mandatory replacement before return to service for any non-brighter or indistinguishable sheeting is burdensome for operations with limited spares; fleet operators will request allowance for temporary marking with expedited replacement schedules or conditional service returns under risk mitigation.

[P8] Small operators will argue the rule should allow documented temporary limitations (e.g., reduced speed/operations) instead of immediate removal from service where replacement parts are unavailable.

[P9] Prohibiting evaluation of "damaged, obscured, or missing" sheeting with the comparator could be construed to prevent any assessment of degradation; commenters will ask that partial evaluations (e.g., intact sections) be permitted to prioritize replacements rather than blanket disqualification.

[P9] Operators will seek clarification of what constitutes "obscured" (dirt, frost, stickers) and request graded categories (cleanable obscuration vs. permanent obscuration) with different procedures.

[P10] Requiring replacement of damaged/obscured/missing sheeting before equipment returns to service is overly strict for temporary deployments; commenters will request permitted temporary remedies (e.g., reflective tape meeting standards) until permanent replacement is possible.

[P11] Allowing calibrated handheld retroreflectometers is positive, but commenters will request explicit calibration interval requirements, acceptable calibration authorities, and records retention requirements to ensure integrity.

[P11] Test labs will ask that the rule list approved device models or standards (e.g., ASTM or CIE references) and state whether third-party calibration certificates are acceptable.

[P12] Mandating an "annular device" excludes commonly used linear or directional retroreflectometers; manufacturers will comment that this limits available technologies and request acceptance of equivalent devices if they meet performance criteria.

[P12] Technical commenters will request a definition of "annular device" (e.g., geometry, entrance and observation angles) to avoid disputes about acceptable instrument forms.

[P13] Allowing a single measurement on a strip with an annular device may miss local defects or variability; commenters from safety advocacy groups will recommend multiple measurements across the panel with a specified sampling pattern and minimum n.

[P13] Fleet maintenance managers will ask for guidance on acceptable sample sizes based on sheeting area (e.g., one measurement per X square feet) to ensure inspections are defensible.

[P14] Placing the handheld device "directly against" the sheeting could contaminate or abrade delicate films; commenters will ask for permitted nondestructive spacing (e.g., up to 1 mm) and instruction on protective covers to prevent damage.

[P14] Device manufacturers will request allowance to follow manufacturer recommendations that may specify a small standoff for correct focusing, and for use of fixture adapters to ensure repeatable contact.

[P15] The specified minimum retroreflective values (150 cd/lx/m2 yellow, 250 cd/lx/m2 white at -4° entrance) should cite the exact measurement geometry (observer and source angles, observation plane) and the measurement standard (e.g., CIE, ASTM) to avoid inconsistent interpretation.

[P15] Several commenters will argue the thresholds are arbitrary and request supporting data demonstrating that these minimums correlate with safe visibility in operational conditions; alternatively, they will propose different thresholds for different vehicle types or operational speeds.

[P15] Manufacturers of colored sheeting other than pure yellow/white (e.g., orange, red) will request inclusion of minimum values for those common colors rather than limiting to yellow and white.

[P16] The replacement requirement when thresholds are not met lacks a grace period or conditional provisions; commenters will request a compliance window (e.g., 7-30 days) and allowance for documented sourcing issues before removal from service.

[P16] Legal commenters will point out potential conflicts with existing maintenance schedules and FMCSA/DOT rules and ask for harmonization language and cross-references.

[P17] Stakeholders will support the 30-day minimum waiting period for the record of decision but will request that the rule require notification to affected parties when the record is issued and provide an opportunity for short administrative challenge.

[P18] Disability advocates will endorse referencing 711 but request that additional contact modalities (email, web forms, video relay) be explicitly recognized to ensure broad accessibility.

[P19] International commenters will ask for clarification about acceptable international relay services, time zone considerations, and whether costs for international relay use will be reimbursed for participants in other countries.

[P20] Conservation groups opposed to lethal take will challenge the 10(j) provision permitting "allowable... take of gray wolves" in Colorado and request clear limits, monitoring requirements, public reporting, and adaptive management triggers to protect conservation goals.

[P20] Ranchers and hunting organizations supportive of local management will request clearer definitions of "allowable, legal, purposeful, and incidental take," including who may authorize take, permit processes, and liability protections for landowners.

[P21] Commenters will request that the docket link be supplemented with direct file names and a table of contents, and that offline access via mailed CDs or printed copies be provided for stakeholders with limited internet access.

[P21] Privacy advocates will request assurance that documents posted online will redact personal data of individuals and that submissions in the docket will be searchable and archived with metadata for transparency.

[P1] Requiring an accepted IRF‑PAI before processing the claim will effectively convert a data-submission compliance issue into a payment-forfeiture, which is disproportionate for single missing data elements or clerical errors.

[P1] The rule lacks clarity on the meaning of “accepted” IRF‑PAI (e.g., syntactic acceptance vs. full validation of all quality fields); commenters request CMS define acceptance standards and error-cycle timelines.

[P2] While CMS may waive consequences for failing to submit IRF‑PAI data due to extraordinary situations, the provision is silent on a prospective relief process; commenters request explicit timelines and expedited adjudication for waiver requests to prevent prolonged nonpayment.

[P2] Industry stakeholders will seek clarity that “extraordinary situation” includes widespread EHR vendor outages, cyberattacks, and national emergencies, and that waiver eligibility be applied consistently across similarly situated IRFs.

[P3] Legal experts will argue that exclusive CMS discretion must be bounded by objective criteria and request CMS publish examples of qualifying extraordinary circumstances.

[P4] The obligation that an IRF must “fully document” any extraordinary situation is vague; commenters ask CMS to specify required documentation types (logs, vendor outage reports, incident response reports, dated screenshots, certifications from third parties) and acceptable formats.

[P4] Small rural IRFs assert that the documentation burden for proving an extraordinary situation may be disproportionate to their resources and request CMS permit attestation under penalty of perjury or allow sworn vendor statements in lieu of extensive documentation.

[P6] Requiring submission “in the form, manner, and by the time CMS specifies” without publishing a predictable schedule or transition timeline grants CMS excessive unilateral control; commenters ask for at least 12 months’ notice before changes in form/manner/timing.

[P7] The permission for IRFs to request exceptions or extensions for one or more quarters is helpful, but commenters request clarification on the procedural steps, timing deadlines for requests, and whether requests can be retroactive.

[P7] Advocacy groups request that exception/extension requests be available to facilities experiencing sustained staffing shortages or natural disasters, and not limited to IT transmission failures.

[P8] CMS’s ability to grant exceptions/extensions for one or more quarters must include objective criteria and a presumptive grant for validated systemwide outages; commenters ask CMS to publish a list of presumptive events (e.g., declared federal emergency, national EHR vendor outages).

[P29] Likewise, changing the table heading to "Urban Facility B (Harrison Co., IN)" should trigger a review to ensure all cross-references in the preamble and RIA are consistent; commenters request CMS confirm no downstream impacts on cost estimates or policy conclusions.

raw_output:
[P2] The November 1–January 31 2016–2017 annual open enrollment window is overly long and will increase adverse selection and premium uncertainty for insurers and should be shortened or paired with stricter risk-adjustment/funding protections.

[P3] The November 1–December 15 annual open enrollment period for 2018 onward is too short to allow adequate consumer shopping and could reduce enrollment; CMS should extend it through December 31 or reinstate later deadlines for special circumstances.

[P3] Requiring a December 15 close for 2018+ will create operational burdens on state-based Exchanges and carriers for plan setup, premium reconciliation, and notices; more lead time or a phased implementation timeline is needed.

[P1] The limited open enrollment requirement tied to §155.420(d) triggering events lacks clarity on which events are excluded, risking inconsistent issuer implementation; cross-reference language should be explicit in issuer-facing guidance.

[P21] The issuer-level obligation to provide a limited open enrollment for enumerated triggering events (§147.104/§155.420) may conflict with state-mandated enrollment windows; the rule must clarify preemption and coordination with state laws.

[P4] §155.420(a)(3) requires Exchanges to allow qualified individuals and dependents not enrolled through the Exchange to enroll when a triggering event occurs, but the rule does not define processes for verifying eligibility for non-Exchange enrollees; CMS must prescribe documentation standards and timelines.

[P24] The obligation to allow non-Exchange enrollees to enroll through the Exchange after a triggering event raises questions about carrier billing and retroactive premium allocation — guidance is needed to prevent gaps or double-billing.

[P5] Allowing added dependents to be placed on the enrollee's current QHP conflicts with some carrier network/underwriting rules; the rule should require carriers to modify business rules to accept dependents rather than forcing plan changes.

[P6] The mandate to add a gained dependent to the current QHP (§155.420(a)(4)(i)) should be conditional on the dependent meeting plan eligibility rules (e.g., enrollment periods, family tiers); the current text could be interpreted as eliminating all carrier discretion.

[P7] If business rules prevent adding a dependent, allowing a change only within the same metal level (or adjacent) may limit consumer access to needed benefits; the rule should permit change to any available QHP unless actuarial value differences would materially harm risk pools.

[P29] Permitting a one-level up/down metal change only when no same-level QHP is available could force enrollees into plans with substantially different cost-sharing; the regulation should require consumer consent and clear disclosure of differences.

[P8] Allowing enrollment of the dependent in a separate QHP (rather than adding to the primary enrollee’s QHP) may lead to family members housed on plans with different networks and coordination-of-care problems; the rule should require coordination-of-benefits and network compatibility standards.

[P30] The option to enroll a dependent in a separate QHP must address premium tax-credit allocation and how the Exchange will assign APTC when family members are on different policies.

[P9] Allowing movement into silver plans for newly CSR-eligible enrollees is appropriate, but the rule should require Exchanges to automatically present CSR options and highlight net premium differences to avoid consumer confusion.

[P31] The requirement that enrollees newly eligible for CSRs may change only if they elect to change enrollment risks low take-up due to complexity; CMS should require proactive outreach and simplified one-click plan change functionality.

[P10] The provision allowing changes to same-QHP or same-metal-level QHPs "if other QHPs at that level are available" (§155.420(a)(4)(iii)) creates unequal access where insurers exit markets; the Exchange should allow cross-level changes if same-level options are limited.

[P12] Conditioning the ability to change QHPs on the availability of other QHPs at that metal level is arbitrary and will disadvantage consumers in thin markets; the rule should permit changes to the closest actuarial equivalent regardless of metal-label availability.

[P11] Excluding triggering events (d)(4),(d)(8),(d)(9),(d)(10) from the change-of-QHP allowance is not justified in the preamble and may leave consumers unable to secure appropriate coverage after important life events — CMS should justify each exclusion.

[P13] The permitted methods to demonstrate prior coverage (one day of MEC or one day living abroad) are too narrow and may exclude people with legitimate short gaps (e.g., incarceration release, deployment); CMS should allow alternate proofs such as past-payroll deductions or veteran/Medicaid records.

[P33] Permitting either MEC for 1+ days or residence outside the U.S. for 1+ days as proof of prior coverage is reasonable, but the rule must specify acceptable documentation and the process for consumers who cannot produce paperwork.

[P14] Allowing consumers to elect a coverage effective date up to one month later to avoid owing 2+ months retroactive premium is consumer-protective, but the rule lacks clear instructions for premium reconciliation and retrospective liability — CMS should require standardized notice and calculation methods.

[P16] The condition that the enrollment be delayed pending eligibility verification (§155.420(b)(5)) could incentivize Exchanges to delay and thus push consumers into later effective dates; safeguards and timelines for verification are needed.

[P17] The threshold "2 or more months of retroactive premium" to trigger the delayed effective date is arbitrary; commenters request analyses showing why 2 months was chosen and suggest a lower threshold (e.g., 1 month) or a sliding scale.

[P15] Limiting the alternative effective date to no more than one month after the specified effective date may still result in coverage gaps for consumers who need immediate access to care — CMS should permit a retroactive effective date in some hardship cases.

[P18] §155.420(d) requires Exchanges to allow enrollment or changes when triggering events occur "subject to (a)(3)-(5)" but the layering of conditions is confusing; the rule should include a consolidated flowchart showing how special enrollment interacts with metal-level switches, prior coverage proofs, and effective dates.

[P37] The overall structure of special enrollment rules (§155.420(d)) duplicates obligations across provisions and will create inconsistent implementation across states; commenters ask for a unified, plain-language special enrollment rule set.

[P19] Requiring at least one spouse to have MEC for 1+ days in the prior 60 days to qualify for marriage-triggered SEP (§155.420(d)(2)(i)(A)) will unfairly bar newly married couples where both were uninsured; CMS should allow marriage SEPs regardless of prior coverage.

[P38] The marriage-triggering-event prior-coverage requirement could encourage people to obtain short-duration coverage to preserve SEP access; CMS should instead permit marriage-based SEP without prior MEC or offer a transitional SEP with limited benefits.

[P20] The allowable AV variation (-4/+2) generally and -4/+5 for certain bronze plans could permit materially different value plans being marketed under the same metal label; CMS must require clearer labeling and consumer-facing disclosures of how a plan deviates from standard AV.

[P39] The AV corridor for bronze plans (-4/+5) for those that cover at least one major service pre-deductible or meet HDHP rules will create consumer confusion if premium differences are not explained; regulators should require an "AV deviation" notice at point of sale.

[P40] The exception allowing greater AV variance for bronze plans that pay pre-deductible major services or qualify as HDHPs may be gamed by insurers to design plans that appear richer but shift costs differently; CMS should limit this exception or require actuarial equivalency testing.

[P36] The consumer option to postpone effective dates due to verification delays must be accompanied by a guaranteed simple opt-in mechanism and clear deadlines; without operational standards, Exchanges will inconsistently apply this consumer safeguard.

[P22] Requiring November 1–January 31 for 2016–2017 while shifting to November 1–December 15 afterward creates transitional complexity for multi-year plan designs and SEP handling; CMS should provide explicit transitional rules for enrollments bridging 2017–2018.

[P23] The 2018+ change to a shorter enrollment period should be accompanied by a robust outreach plan to minimize disenrollment and ensure consumers understand new deadlines; commenters request funding/metrics for outreach effectiveness.

[P25] The mandate to allow adding gained dependents in the circumstances described (d)(2)(i) should explicitly cover newborns and adoptees and spell out retroactive enrollment and premium rules for those situations to prevent coverage gaps.

[P26] The requirement to add gained dependents to the enrollee's current QHP must clarify treatment of age-banded premiums and family tiers — Exchanges and carriers need instruction on premium recalculation and billing cycles.

[P27] The fallback that Exchanges must allow switching when "QHP business rules do not allow the dependent to enroll" lacks a definition of "business rules"; CMS should enumerate acceptable reasons (e.g., insurer residency network restrictions) and disallow arbitrary denials.

[P28] Allowing changes only within the same metal level as a remedy to business-rule rejections could disproportionately harm low-income enrollees whose APTC/cost-sharing subsidies are tied to specific plan choices; rule should permit any plan that preserves subsidy calculations.

[P34] The 1+ day MEC demonstration option relies on the ACA's technical definition of MEC in 26 CFR 1.5000A–1(b); consumers and navigators will need specific examples of acceptable MEC to avoid erroneous denials.

[P35] The option to show residence outside the U.S./territory for 1+ days should include guidance on acceptable travel documentation and exceptions for short-term medical travel to ensure consistent verification.

[P1] The general issuer obligation to provide a limited open enrollment for triggering events (§147.104/§155.420) should include penalties for noncompliance and a consumer appeal process so affected individuals have remedies when an issuer denies SEP access.

[P21] Requiring issuers to offer limited open enrollment in the individual market may increase administrative costs; commenters from industry request a regulatory impact analysis quantifying expected cost and proposed transitional amortization of these costs.

[P32] The provision in §155.420(a)(4)(iii) allowing changes to same-level QHPs if available should be revised to require Exchanges to display all available QHPs across metal levels and recommend actuarially closest options when same-level choices are unavailable.

[P11] The list of excluded triggering events (d)(4),(d)(8),(d)(9),(d)(10)) should be published with justification and examples of how excluded events will be treated in practice to avoid arbitrary denial of SEPs.

[P17] The rule lacks safeguards to prevent gaming the "2 or more months retroactive premium" requirement (e.g., delaying verification intentionally); CMS should set strict verification timelines and penalties for unjustified delays.

[P15] The one-month cap on delayed effective dates complicates continuity-of-care for patients undergoing pre-authorized treatments; CMS should permit plan issuers to offer retroactive coverage for a defined set of medically necessary services pending verification.
