raw_output:
[P1] The requirement in § 424.516(g)(1) to disclose "specified ownership, governance, and related party information" upon initial enrollment and revalidation is overly broad and vague; the rule should list all required data fields explicitly to avoid inconsistent interpretations by CMS contractors and suppliers.

[P1] Skilled nursing facilities (SNFs) will face significant administrative burden and cost to compile the comprehensive ownership and related-party data at every revalidation cycle; CMS should provide an estimate of paperwork/time costs and consider phased implementation.

[P1] Requiring disclosure "in addition to all other applicable reporting requirements" creates redundancy with state survey/certification and other federal reporting (e.g., Medicare PECOS, CMS-855), risking duplicate submissions and confusion; CMS should harmonize forms and allow cross-referencing of existing submissions.

[P2] The obligation in § 424.516(g)(1)(i) to provide names, titles, and service periods for each governing body member raises privacy concerns for board members who are not public officials; CMS should limit required fields to business contact and role rather than full service dates or provide a confidentiality safeguard.

[P2] Many nursing homes have large governing boards whose composition changes frequently; requiring precise service periods for each member will be administratively burdensome and error-prone—CMS should allow reporting of service periods in years (e.g., 2019–2022) rather than exact dates.

[P3] § 424.516(g)(1)(ii) requires listing every officer, director, partner, trustee, or managing employee as defined in § 424.502, but the definitions are complex and may unintentionally capture frontline managers; CMS should clarify thresholds (e.g., compensation or decision-making authority) that qualify someone as a "managing employee."

[P3] Inclusion of "each person or entity" who is an officer, director, etc., may require disclosure of investors or passive limited partners; the rule should exclude purely passive, non-managing investors below a specified ownership threshold (e.g., <5%).

[P4] § 424.516(g)(1)(iii) obligates identification of "additional disclosable party" without clarifying how far downstream affiliates must be traced; hospitals and multi-facility chains request a safe harbor that limits required disclosure to entities with direct ownership or management control (e.g., >10% ownership or direct board control).

[P5] Requiring the organizational structure of each additional disclosable party and descriptions of relationships (§ 424.516(g)(1)(iv)) will force companies to produce corporate family trees and contractual relationships that may contain confidential commercial information; CMS should allow submission of redacted diagrams or a standardized hierarchy template.

[P5] The rule's requirement to describe "relationships to the facility and to each other" could be interpreted to require disclosure of supplier, vendor, or contractual relationships beyond ownership; CMS should limit required relationships to ownership, management, and control arrangements only.

[P6] The exception in § 424.516(g)(2) not to repeat the same disclosure on the same enrollment application is helpful but insufficient; SNFs want an explicit cross-reference mechanism permitting CMS to pull previously submitted data (from PECOS or state databases) instead of re-entering data for revalidation if nothing has changed.

[P7] § 424.516(g)(3) requires reporting changes to disclosed information "within the applicable timeframes in paragraph (e)," but the proposed rule does not restate those timeframes here; stakeholders request that CMS explicitly list notification deadlines (e.g., 30 days from change) or clarify if different change types have different deadlines.

[P7] The change-reporting obligation may conflict with corporate disclosure schedules (e.g., board appointment effective date vs. reporting date); the rule should allow a reasonable cure period or grace period (e.g., 60 days) to reconcile corporate records before penalty.

[P8] Duplicate obligations in § 455.104(e)(1) for nursing facilities (Medicaid) that mirror Medicare provisions create duplicative state and federal reporting burdens; states request CMS allow reliance on a single federal filing or permit electronic data sharing between Medicaid and Medicare enrollment systems.

[P9] § 455.104(e)(1)(i) requiring names, titles, and service periods for each governing body member for Medicaid-enrolled facilities duplicates state requirements and raises state privacy concerns; states ask CMS to align content and timing with existing state licensure databases.

[P10] The requirement in § 455.104(e)(1)(ii) to list "managing employees" per § 455.101 risks inconsistent application across states because § 455.101 definitions vary in interpretation; CMS should issue a national guidance document and examples to ensure uniform compliance.

[P11] § 455.104(e)(1)(iii) demands disclosure of "additional disclosable party" entities without addressing foreign entities or offshore owners; commenters recommend clarifying scope for foreign ownership and allowing alternate documentation where foreign corporate records are confidential or governed by foreign law.

[P12] The obligation in § 455.104(e)(1)(iv) to provide organizational structure and inter-relationships could trigger anti-trust or competitive concerns for multi-facility chains; industry asks for a certification alternative (attestation that information exists and will be provided upon lawful request) rather than public disclosure.

[P13] The § 455.104(e)(2) exception that "The State need not require the facility to disclose the same information more than once on the same enrollment application" should be expanded to require states to accept a facility’s attestation that previously submitted information remains unchanged to avoid redundant data entry during combined Medicare/Medicaid applications.

[P1] Legal experts note that the requirement to disclose "related party information" may inadvertently create liability for inadvertent nondisclosure by facilities unaware of complex LLC or trust structures; CMS should include safe-harbor protections for good-faith disclosures and a remediation pathway.

[P2] Advocacy groups representing residents request that CMS require disclosure of board member conflicts of interest, beyond names and service periods, so families can assess whether governance decisions are influenced by related-party financial ties.

[P3] Financial auditors comment that the rule needs to specify acceptable documentation (e.g., corporate minutes, IRS filings, state business registrations) to substantiate claims about officer/director service periods; otherwise, enforcement will be subjective.

[P4] Small non-profit nursing facilities express concern that the added disclosure of "additional disclosable parties" could expose donor or subsidiary information unnecessary for payer oversight; CMS should carve out bona fide nonprofit donors or require minimal disclosure in those cases.

[P5] Privacy advocates object to publication or public access to the required disclosures if CMS posts them online; they request that CMS limit public access and only share sensitive ownership data with authorized oversight bodies to prevent doxxing or harassment of individuals.

[P6] Trade associations request that CMS provide a standardized, machine-readable template (XML/JSON) for reporting organizational structure and relationships to reduce manual labor and ensure consistency across submissions.

[P7] State Medicaid agencies request a transition period (e.g., 18 months) before full enforcement of § 455.104(e) to update state systems, train staff, and coordinate with providers.

[P8] Nursing home operators ask CMS to clarify whether disclosure obligations apply to management companies that provide services under contract but do not have ownership — specifically whether management contracts create "related party" status under §§ 424.516(g) and 455.104(e).

[P9] Commenters note contradictory definitions between § 424.502 and § 455.101 for "managing employee" and "organizational structure"; CMS should harmonize definitions across subparts or explain which control in cases of conflict.

[P10] Corporate compliance officers request that CMS permit consolidated reporting for multi-facility chains (one master filing plus facility-specific updates) rather than repeating identical corporate charts for each facility to reduce duplication.

[P11] Hospital-based SNFs ask whether the parent hospital’s board members must be listed as the facility's governing body under § 424.516(g)(1)(i); CMS should provide guidance for hospital-owned facilities to avoid double-reporting the same individuals across entities.

[P12] Providers ask for clarity on the consequences for late or inaccurate disclosures; the rule should detail whether recoupment, enrollment denial, civil monetary penalties, or other sanctions apply and allow a cure period for unintentional errors.

[P13] Consumer advocacy organizations request that CMS require disclosure of beneficial owners and ultimate beneficial owners (UBOs) of any entity with control, not just nominal officers or directors, to ensure transparency where ownership is layered through trusts or shell companies.

[P14] Banking and investment stakeholders warn that full disclosure of organizational structures could reveal sensitive strategic or financial arrangements; they request the option to submit a certified summary of ownership percentages and control rather than detailed corporate diagrams.

[P15] Rural facilities indicate that identifying every "additional disclosable party" may capture local lenders, landlords, or service providers with minor interests; CMS should limit disclosures to parties with governance or control roles and owners of equity interests above a specified threshold (e.g., ≥5% or ≥10%).

[P16] Health law practitioners recommend adding a mandatory standardized attestation statement that the information provided is true and complete under penalty of perjury to prevent inconsistent reporting and facilitate enforcement.

[P17] State survey agencies suggest CMS provide training and a Q&A dossier about borderline cases (e.g., family trusts, nominee trustees) to ensure consistent application of the disclosure requirements across jurisdictions.

[P18] Commenters request an appeals process or administrative review mechanism for facilities that are accused of nondisclosure, to allow correction and prevent abrupt termination of payment rights based on disputed corporate structure interpretations.

[P19] Organizations representing persons with disabilities urge CMS to prioritize disclosures about conflicts of interest that could affect patient care (e.g., related-party contracts for staffing or pharmacy services) and not only list names and titles.

[P20] Law firms note that the rule should specify the format and lifecycle of submitted organizational charts (e.g., maximum file size, acceptable file types, whether changes require full resubmission) to ensure technical feasibility for electronic enrollment systems.

[P1] The requirement that manufacturers install OBD systems on all new LDVs and LDTs is appropriate, but the rule should clarify whether small-volume manufacturers (e.g., low-production specialty vehicle makers) receive phased compliance timelines or exemptions.

[P1] The regulation should define "install" to specify who is responsible for integration testing and final verification — manufacturers, tier-1 suppliers, or final assemblers — to avoid enforcement disputes.

[P2] Requiring detection of "at least catalyst and O2 sensor" deterioration is insufficiently specific — commenters will ask EPA to list all minimum sensors/components that must be detectable (e.g., EGR, NOx sensors on diesels, turbocharger boost sensor) for parity across technologies.

[P2] The phrase "accurately identifying for the vehicle's useful life" is vague; stakeholders will request a clear numerical accuracy performance standard and test protocol for detection sensitivity and false positive/negative rates across the defined useful life.

[P3] The obligation to "alert owners/operators when maintenance or repair is likely needed" should specify the alert modality (MIL only, dashboard message, smartphone app, or dealer notification) and the minimum lead time before emission exceedance to enable timely repairs.

[P3] Consumer advocates will request that alerts include plain-language diagnostic information and possible repair cost estimates to prevent needless dealer visits and help independent repair shops.

[P4] The rule to store and allow retrieval of fault codes "as specified by the Administrator" requires EPA to publish the fault-code spec concurrently with the final rule; manufacturers and aftermarket tool makers need that spec well before compliance.

[P4] Legal commenters will argue that EPA must ensure stored fault-code data is standardized (format, naming, semantic definitions) to prevent proprietary obfuscation that would impede independent repair and inspection.

[P5] "Provide access to stored diagnostic information in the manner specified by the Administrator" invites concerns about data access controls and cybersecurity; industry will request explicit limits on what data must be exposed over the interface to protect trade secrets and vehicle safety.

[P6] Requiring all 1994 and subsequent model-year vehicles to have OBD systems appears retroactive; manufacturers or secondhand sellers may seek clarification whether the rule applies only to new production vehicles going forward and not to remanufactured/repowered vehicles.

[P6] Historic vehicle collectors and small restorers will request an exemption or alternate compliance pathway for bona fide collector vehicles and limited-production recreations where OBD retrofits are impractical.

[P7] The monitoring requirement for "components for malfunctions or deterioration that could cause emissions to exceed thresholds" must define the emission threshold numerically and provide test procedures and confidence levels used to determine when a monitored change "could cause" exceedance.

[P8] Requiring the MIL to light and store codes upon detection is standard, but repair shops will comment that the rule needs to ensure stored codes persist through power cycles and for a specified minimum retention period (e.g., 30 days or X ignition cycles) to support roadside inspection.

[P9] The requirement that manufacturers provide "timely repair information to any person sufficient for accurate repair" should be explicit about delivery channels (web, printed manual, paid subscription) and timelines (e.g., within X days of vehicle sale or on continuous online access).

[P9] Aftermarket and independent repair advocates will insist that "any person" include independent repair shops and consumers with no paywalls or forced registration, and that data be machine-readable for third-party diagnostic tools.

[P10] Mandating catalyst and O2 sensor monitoring is necessary, but manufacturers may need flexibility for alternative emissions control architectures (e.g., NOx adsorbers, lean-NOx catalysts); commenters will request clarifying language to cover equivalent monitoring for those systems.

[P11] The requirement to detect "significant engine misfire" must define "significant" numerically (e.g., misfire rate per minute or misfire percentage of firing events) and provide threshold test cycles and cold/hot conditions.

[P12] The proposed shutoff of fuel to a misfiring cylinder for sequential fuel-injected vehicles raises concerns about drivability, unintended catalyst overheating, and limp-home modes; manufacturers will request clear safety exceptions and transition timing for vehicles without sequential systems.

[P12] Vehicle safety advocates will ask EPA to require safeguards to prevent fuel shutoff actions from causing loss of control (e.g., sudden torque changes) and to require torque-limiting strategies where fuel shutoff is employed.

[P13] Requiring monitoring for electrical disconnects of emission-related components that interface with the vehicle computer should include an explicit list of monitored circuits and allowable detection latency to prevent nuisance codes from momentary connector movement.

[P14] Requiring conformance to SAE and ISO standards and access via a standard handheld tool is constructive, but the rule should specify the exact versions of SAE/ISO standards and commit to a schedule for updates to prevent perpetual uncertainty.

[P14] Tool manufacturers will request that the standard interface pinout, connector mechanical spec, and communications protocol be made available in the final rule so aftermarket tool makers can ensure interoperability.

[P15] The obligation to provide specified diagnostic and engine data "if available to the on-board computer" is ambiguous — commenters will push EPA to require that certain critical data elements (e.g., freeze-frame, readiness status, MIL status, pending codes, VIN) must be made available regardless.

[P16] Requiring bi-directional diagnostic control capability via the standard serial port raises cybersecurity and safety concerns; commenters will seek explicit cybersecurity requirements, authentication mechanisms, and restrictions on which actuators can be commanded via the public port.

[P16] Repair industry and OEMs will request clarity on whether manufacturers can require authentication or commercial licensing to access bi-directional functions and whether independent shops must be able to perform routine bidirectional operations.

[P17] The freeze-frame requirement should specify the minimum set of parameters to be captured (e.g., engine speed, load, vehicle speed, MAF, fuel trim, throttle position, ambient temp) and minimum resolution and retention count (e.g., last 5 events).

[P18] The requirement to protect on-board computers against tampering necessitates a clear, narrow definition of "tampering" and guidance on manufacturer obligations so that legitimate aftermarket repairs and diagnostics are not impeded.

[P18] Civil liberties and right-to-repair advocates will warn that overbroad anti-tampering measures could be used to lock out independent repairers; they will ask for anti-lockout provisions and oversight to ensure compatibility.

[P19] Requiring write-protect features for flash-memory OBD systems is reasonable, but commenters will request the technical spec: which memory regions must be write-protected, when write-protection may be temporarily disabled for authorized updates, and secure update mechanisms.

[P20] The single MIL requirement may confuse consumers who are used to multiple lights (e.g., engine, ABS, airbag); consumer groups will request that the rule permit secondary informative indicators or text messaging while preserving the single MIL for emissions.

[P21] While the rule permits separate warning lights for safety/engine-damage conditions, consumer advocates will ask EPA to require clear labeling distinguishing MIL (emissions) from other warnings so drivers understand the difference.

[P22] Requiring MIL illumination during key-on each start is sensible for inspection, but privacy advocates may raise concerns if that mechanism is used to infer vehicle status remotely; commenters will request confirmation that this requirement does not require any telemetry.

[P23] The MIL extinguishing after engine start unless malfunction present should include tolerances for transient detection events during cold start or transient ECU learning so as not to create misleading MIL behavior.

[P24] Mandating a readiness code is needed for inspection programs, but inspection authorities will request standardized readiness codes and a defined set of monitors required to be "ready" for model years to ensure harmonized emissions testing.

[P25] The compatibility requirement for aftermarket parts is broad; commenters from the aftermarket industry will ask for objective compatibility tests and a certification program to avoid subjective enforcement against legitimate parts.

[P25] Aftermarket parts manufacturers will request safe-harbor design guidelines so they can produce parts that meet compatibility without being exposed to arbitrary tampering allegations.

[P26] Treating installation of aftermarket parts that disable OBD as tampering should be limited to intentional disabling; commenters will ask EPA to clarify the distinction between defective aftermarket parts and intentional circumventing modifications, and to provide a de minimis exception for non-emissions-related cosmetic/structural parts.

[P27] Requiring all monitored components be evaluated "at least once per trip" is technically challenging for some subsystems and certain driving patterns; manufacturers will seek permission to use alternate time/operational triggers or extended monitoring windows where operand limitations exist.

[P28] Counting one CVS-72 driving cycle as a trip is useful for certification tests, but commenters will note that many real-world trips are shorter and ask for guidance on how monitoring requirements apply to short trips and low-mileage urban use to avoid false ready/not-ready states.

[P29] The permission for more frequent monitoring if needed is fine, but consumer groups will request EPA oversight to ensure that manufacturers do not over-monitor in ways that degrade component life or cause unnecessary MIL illuminations.

[P30] The "prompt" MIL illumination requirement upon detection needs a quantitative timing standard (e.g., within X seconds or Y engine revolutions) to ensure consistent behavior and to guide enforcement.

[P31] Requiring the MIL to stay lit until cleared by a technician or until repeated evaluations show problem no longer occurs raises questions about owner self-service; repair shops and DIYers will request the ability for qualified owners to reset codes under specified conditions.

[P32] Allowing extinguishment if repeat-driving verification criteria are met is reasonable, but independent testers will ask EPA to publish the exact repeat-driving algorithms and tolerances so that neutral verification is possible.

[P33] The prohibition on extinguishing in fewer than three sequential driving cycles should be clarified whether those are three "trips," three CVS-72 cycles, or three engine start/stop cycles, and how interrupted or partial trips are counted.

[P34] The California-derived ±10% speed/load matching requirement for extinguishment is technically difficult to measure in the field; commenters will ask EPA to provide explicit algorithms and tolerances for how matching is determined, including allowable sensor noise.

[P34] Small fleets and rental companies will request guidance on how to comply when drivers cannot reproduce near-identical speed/load profiles, seeking an alternate verification pathway.

[P35] The recall-and-repair requirement for in-use noncompliant vehicle classes lacks a quantitative definition of "substantial number of vehicles"; commenters will demand a concrete threshold (e.g., percent of fleet, absolute number) and clear remedial timelines and remedies.

[P35] Manufacturers will request procedural due process protections, such as notice and opportunity to demonstrate corrective measures before mandatory recall determinations.

[P36] The obligation to make emission-related maintenance and repair information available must include a requirement that such information be provided in machine-readable formats and at reasonable cost (or free) to prevent paywalls that exclude independent repair shops.

[P36] Intellectual property-holding OEMs will request protections for proprietary calibrations and require that EPA define the boundary between necessary repair information and protected trade secrets.

[P37] The Standard No. 209 ELR 50,000-cycle test with at least 10,000 lockups may be burdensome for small seat-belt suppliers; suppliers will ask EPA to allow validated alternative test methods or staged compliance schedules.

[P38] The 10,000-cycle test requirement for ALR devices should specify cycle parameters (speed, temperature) more precisely and allow accelerated or equivalency testing methods to reduce test burdens while preserving safety performance.

Legal commenters will argue that EPA must ensure stored fault-code data is standardized (format, naming, semantic definitions) to prevent proprietary obfuscation that would impede independent repair and inspection.

"Provide access to stored diagnostic information in the manner specified by the Administrator" invites concerns about data access controls and cybersecurity; industry will request explicit limits on what data must be exposed over the interface to protect trade secrets and vehicle safety.

Requiring all 1994 and subsequent model-year vehicles to have OBD systems appears retroactive; manufacturers or secondhand sellers may seek clarification whether the rule applies only to new production vehicles going forward and not to remanufactured/repowered vehicles.

Historic vehicle collectors and small restorers will request an exemption or alternate compliance pathway for bona fide collector vehicles and limited-production recreations where OBD retrofits are impractical.

The monitoring requirement for "components for malfunctions or deterioration that could cause emissions to exceed thresholds" must define the emission threshold numerically and provide test procedures and confidence levels used to determine when a monitored change "could cause" exceedance.

Requiring the MIL to light and store codes upon detection is standard, but repair shops will comment that the rule needs to ensure stored codes persist through power cycles and for a specified minimum retention period (e.g., 30 days or X ignition cycles) to support roadside inspection.

The requirement that manufacturers provide "timely repair information to any person sufficient for accurate repair" should be explicit about delivery channels (web, printed manual, paid subscription) and timelines (e.g., within X days of vehicle sale or on continuous online access).

Aftermarket and independent repair advocates will insist that "any person" include independent repair shops and consumers with no paywalls or forced registration, and that data be machine-readable for third-party diagnostic tools.

Mandating catalyst and O2 sensor monitoring is necessary, but manufacturers may need flexibility for alternative emissions control architectures (e.g., NOx adsorbers, lean-NOx catalysts); commenters will request clarifying language to cover equivalent monitoring for those systems.

The requirement to detect "significant engine misfire" must define "significant" numerically (e.g., misfire rate per minute or misfire percentage of firing events) and provide threshold test cycles and cold/hot conditions.

The proposed shutoff of fuel to a misfiring cylinder for sequential fuel-injected vehicles raises concerns about drivability, unintended catalyst overheating, and limp-home modes; manufacturers will request clear safety exceptions and transition timing for vehicles without sequential systems.

Vehicle safety advocates will ask EPA to require safeguards to prevent fuel shutoff actions from causing loss of control (e.g., sudden torque changes) and to require torque-limiting strategies where fuel shutoff is employed.

Requiring monitoring for electrical disconnects of emission-related components that interface with the vehicle computer should include an explicit list of monitored circuits and allowable detection latency to prevent nuisance codes from momentary connector movement.

Requiring conformance to SAE and ISO standards and access via a standard handheld tool is constructive, but the rule should specify the exact versions of SAE/ISO standards and commit to a schedule for updates to prevent perpetual uncertainty.

Tool manufacturers will request that the standard interface pinout, connector mechanical spec, and communications protocol be made available in the final rule so aftermarket tool makers can ensure interoperability.

The obligation to provide specified diagnostic and engine data "if available to the on-board computer" is ambiguous — commenters will push EPA to require that certain critical data elements (e.g., freeze-frame, readiness status, MIL status, pending codes, VIN) must be made available regardless.

Requiring bi-directional diagnostic control capability via the standard serial port raises cybersecurity and safety concerns; commenters will seek explicit cybersecurity requirements, authentication mechanisms, and restrictions on which actuators can be commanded via the public port.

Repair industry and OEMs will request clarity on whether manufacturers can require authentication or commercial licensing to access bi-directional functions and whether independent shops must be able to perform routine bidirectional operations.

The freeze-frame requirement should specify the minimum set of parameters to be captured (e.g., engine speed, load, vehicle speed, MAF, fuel trim, throttle position, ambient temp) and minimum resolution and retention count (e.g., last 5 events).

The requirement to protect on-board computers against tampering necessitates a clear, narrow definition of "tampering" and guidance on manufacturer obligations so that legitimate aftermarket repairs and diagnostics are not impeded.

Civil liberties and right-to-repair advocates will warn that overbroad anti-tampering measures could be used to lock out independent repairers; they will ask for anti-lockout provisions and oversight to ensure compatibility.

Requiring write-protect features for flash-memory OBD systems is reasonable, but commenters will request the technical spec: which memory regions must be write-protected, when write-protection may be temporarily disabled for authorized updates, and secure update mechanisms.

The single MIL requirement may confuse consumers who are used to multiple lights (e.g., engine, ABS, airbag); consumer groups will request that the rule permit secondary informative indicators or text messaging while preserving the single MIL for emissions.

While the rule permits separate warning lights for safety/engine-damage conditions, consumer advocates will ask EPA to require clear labeling distinguishing MIL (emissions) from other warnings so drivers understand the difference.

Requiring MIL illumination during key-on each start is sensible for inspection, but privacy advocates may raise concerns if that mechanism is used to infer vehicle status remotely; commenters will request confirmation that this requirement does not require any telemetry.

The MIL extinguishing after engine start unless malfunction present should include tolerances for transient detection events during cold start or transient ECU learning so as not to create misleading MIL behavior.

Mandating a readiness code is needed for inspection programs, but inspection authorities will request standardized readiness codes and a defined set of monitors required to be "ready" for model years to ensure harmonized emissions testing.

The compatibility requirement for aftermarket parts is broad; commenters from the aftermarket industry will ask for objective compatibility tests and a certification program to avoid subjective enforcement against legitimate parts.
Aftermarket parts manufacturers will request safe-harbor design guidelines so they can produce parts that meet compatibility without being exposed to arbitrary tampering allegations.

Treating installation of aftermarket parts that disable OBD as tampering should be limited to intentional disabling; commenters will ask EPA to clarify the distinction between defective aftermarket parts and intentional circumventing modifications, and to provide a de minimis exception for non-emissions-related cosmetic/structural parts.

Requiring all monitored components be evaluated "at least once per trip" is technically challenging for some subsystems and certain driving patterns; manufacturers will seek permission to use alternate time/operational triggers or extended monitoring windows where operand limitations exist.

Counting one CVS-72 driving cycle as a trip is useful for certification tests, but commenters will note that many real-world trips are shorter and ask for guidance on how monitoring requirements apply to short trips and low-mileage urban use to avoid false ready/not-ready states.

The permission for more frequent monitoring if needed is fine, but consumer groups will request EPA oversight to ensure that manufacturers do not over-monitor in ways that degrade component life or cause unnecessary MIL illuminations.
The "prompt" MIL illumination requirement upon detection needs a quantitative timing standard (e.g., within X seconds or Y engine revolutions) to ensure consistent behavior and to guide enforcement.

Requiring the MIL to stay lit until cleared by a technician or until repeated evaluations show problem no longer occurs raises questions about owner self-service; repair shops and DIYers will request the ability for qualified owners to reset codes under specified conditions.

Allowing extinguishment if repeat-driving verification criteria are met is reasonable, but independent testers will ask EPA to publish the exact repeat-driving algorithms and tolerances so that neutral verification is possible.

The prohibition on extinguishing in fewer than three sequential driving cycles should be clarified whether those are three "trips," three CVS-72 cycles, or three engine start/stop cycles, and how interrupted or partial trips are counted.

The California-derived ±10% speed/load matching requirement for extinguishment is technically difficult to measure in the field; commenters will ask EPA to provide explicit algorithms and tolerances for how matching is determined, including allowable sensor noise.
Small fleets and rental companies will request guidance on how to comply when drivers cannot reproduce near-identical speed/load profiles, seeking an alternate verification pathway.

The recall-and-repair requirement for in-use noncompliant vehicle classes lacks a quantitative definition of "substantial number of vehicles"; commenters will demand a concrete threshold (e.g., percent of fleet, absolute number) and clear remedial timelines and remedies.
Manufacturers will request procedural due process protections, such as notice and opportunity to demonstrate corrective measures before mandatory recall determinations.

The obligation to make emission-related maintenance and repair information available must include a requirement that such information be provided in machine-readable formats and at reasonable cost (or free) to prevent paywalls that exclude independent repair shops.
Intellectual property-holding OEMs will request protections for proprietary calibrations and require that EPA define the boundary between necessary repair information and protected trade secrets.

The Standard No. 209 ELR 50,000-cycle test with at least 10,000 lockups may be burdensome for small seat-belt suppliers; suppliers will ask EPA to allow validated alternative test methods or staged compliance schedules.

The 10,000-cycle test requirement for ALR devices should specify cycle parameters (speed, temperature) more precisely and allow accelerated or equivalency testing methods to reduce test burdens while preserving safety performance.

raw_output:
[P1] The May 23, 2019 comments due date is unreasonably short and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow affected operators, unions, and international stakeholders time to prepare detailed technical and economic comments.

[P1] The rule’s repetition of the May 23, 2019 deadline in multiple places (P1 and P27) creates confusion; the FAA should consolidate and clarify a single, consistent comment deadline.

[P27] The NPRM for VOR Federal Airways uses the same May 23, 2019 date; if commenters intend to respond to both the AD and the VOR NPRM, the agency must coordinate deadlines or provide cross-reference guidance to avoid missed comments.

[P2] The requirement to “comply within the specified compliance times” without a hardship relief mechanism or phased compliance option may be infeasible for smaller operators with limited maintenance capacity; the FAA should allow phased compliance or provide relief for capacity-constrained carriers.

[P3] Requiring AFM Abnormal Procedures to be revised “at the applicable time” per paragraph (g)(1)/(g)(2) is ambiguous; the AD should specify calendar dates or precise triggering events to eliminate operator uncertainty.

[P4] Allowing insertion of TR 113 Issue 1.0 into the AFM (P4) is acceptable, but the AD must require document control procedures (revision log, page numbering) to ensure inserted TR pages are treated as official AFM pages and not inadvertently removed.

[P5] Permitting replacement of TR 113 with general AFM revisions only “when the relevant information matches TR 113” lacks a defined equivalence standard; the FAA should require a formal cross-reference checklist or validation procedure to demonstrate the general revision is equivalent.

[P6] The obligation to operate the airplane according to TR 113 procedures (P6) effectively makes TR 113 regulatory material; the FAA should explicitly publish TR 113 text in the AD docket or incorporate it by reference to ensure enforceability and public access.

[P7] The provision that AFM overrides ECAM when discrepancies exist (P7) raises safety concerns because ECAM is the primary flightcrew alerting system; operators and flightcrew unions request justification and risk assessment supporting AFM precedence over ECAM.

[P7] For discrepancies between ECAM and AFM, the AD should require Airbus/DOA to issue a definitive harmonization bulletin or ECAM software change rather than instruct crews to follow AFM as the sole remedy.

[P8] The 30-day compliance time after the AD effective date for airplanes modified by Airbus mods 113758 and 113760 (P8) is too short for scheduling maintenance during heavy operations; the FAA should allow extensions or provide ferry allowances until the next scheduled heavy maintenance check.

[P9] Requiring AFM revisions within 30 days after Nov 23, 2018 for other airplanes (P9) is retroactive and effectively obligates compliance in the past; the AD should clarify whether operators that have not done the revision by that date are noncompliant immediately or have a new 30-day window from the AD’s effective date.

[P10] The 6-month deadline to perform modification actions (P10) lacks consideration of parts availability and shop capacity; the FAA should permit documented scheduling to the next C-check if within a reasonable extended timeframe (e.g., 9–12 months).

[P11] The mandate to install the ATQC per subparagraphs (P11) does not describe required parts kits or verify global parts supply; the AD should include an estimated parts lead time and an allowance for AMOCs if parts are unavailable.

[P12] The requirement to install ATQC standard V4 per Service Bulletin A350–31–P028 for FWS S4/2.0 airplanes (P12) makes incorporation of a service bulletin essential — the AD should clarify whether compliance with non-mandatory service bulletin steps is required and identify any deviations.

[P13] Similarly, installation per Service Bulletin A350–31–P029 for FWS S5/2.2 airplanes (P13) must be approved for operators outside the U.S.; the AD should specify whether EASA approvals or DOA authorizations are acceptable without separate FAA AMOC.

[P14] Activating ECAM temporary change code No. 27AF per SB A350–31–P030 (P14) could conflict with existing airline ECAM configuration management processes; the AD should require coordination procedures and state whether the activation affects historical flight data or maintenance logs.

[P15] The authority granted to the Manager, International Section, to approve AMOCs (P15) centralizes AMOC approvals; commenters request clearer SLAs (service-level agreements) and timeframes for AMOC decisions to avoid operational delays.

[P16] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO (P16) duplicates 14 CFR 39.19 and may conflict with international operators who do not have a U.S. principal inspector; the FAA should provide an alternate routing for foreign operators.

[P17] The instruction to address direct International Section submissions to paragraph (j)(2) contact (P17) should include the name, email, and mailing address in the AD text for clarity and to avoid delays.

[P18] Permitting email submission of AMOC information to 9-ANM-116-AMOC-REQUESTS@faa.gov (P18) is useful, but the AD should confirm acceptable attachment formats and encryption/privacy expectations for proprietary data.

[P19] The requirement to notify principal inspector or FSDO before using an approved AMOC (P19) could cause practical delay if the inspector is unavailable; the FAA should allow electronic notification and define acceptable timing (e.g., within 48 hours of implementation).

[P20] Approving previously granted AMOCs for AD 2018–22–13 as approved for corresponding provisions of this AD (P20) is sensible, but the AD should publish a crosswalk of equivalencies to help operators determine applicability.

[P21] Requiring manufacturer corrective actions to be approved by the FAA Manager, EASA, or Airbus DOA (P21) may create duplication when EASA has already approved a fix; the FAA should accept EASA approvals automatically under bilateral agreements to avoid redundant reviews.

[P22] The DOA approval requirement to include the DOA-authorized signature (P22) is reasonable, but the AD should specify an acceptable digital signature or electronic approval method to expedite submissions.

[P23] Designating certain procedures/tests as Required for Compliance (RC) (P23) significantly narrows operator flexibility; the FAA should publish the RC-designated items in the service information and justify RC designations with safety risk data.

[P24] Labeling non-RC items as recommended but not required (P24) is appropriate, but operators need guidance on how performing only RC items affects future airworthiness recordkeeping and warranty coverage.

[P25] Allowing deviation from non-RC items under the operator’s maintenance program without AMOC (P25) could create inconsistent implementations; the FAA should require operators to document deviations in the maintenance records and notify the principal inspector.

[P26] Requiring AMOC approval for any changes to RC procedures/tests (P26) is necessary for safety but the AD should define the expected review timeline for AMOC requests for RC changes (e.g., 60/90 days) to avoid operational disruptions.

[P28] The requirement to send comments to DOT Docket Operations at the specified physical address and phone numbers (P28) is outdated; the FAA should emphasize electronic submissions via regulations.gov and confirm acceptance of email comments.

[P29] Insisting that comments identify FAA Docket No. FAA–2019–0241 and Airspace Docket No. 18–AEA–18 at the beginning of comments (P29) is overly prescriptive; the agency should accept docket identification anywhere in the submission body to avoid rejecting comments for formatting errors.

[P30] While the AD permits electronic comments via regulations.gov (P30), the notice should include instructions for submitting large technical attachments and how confidential/proprietary material can be protected.

[P31] The “for further information contact” provision pointing to the Airspace Policy Group (P31) is the wrong point of contact for AD-technical questions; the FAA should provide a technical contact in the International Section or the Aircraft Certification Office.

[P32] Inviting interested parties to submit written data, views, or arguments (P32) is standard, but the AD should clarify whether stakeholders may request a public hearing and the process/timing for such requests.

[P3] The AD should explicitly state whether operators who have already incorporated TR 113 into their AFM prior to the AD must reissue the AFM pages to reflect the AD or whether existing pages remain compliant.

[P4] TR 113 Issue 1.0 dated Aug 17, 2018 is incorporated by reference via permission to insert a copy (P4); the FAA must place TR 113 in the public docket and provide a redline of any later revisions so operators can track mandatory changes.

[P6] Forcing flight operations to follow TR 113 (P6) without providing training guidance or mandated recurrent training hours could increase risk; the FAA should require or at least recommend training syllabi and minimum simulator/CBT time.

[P7] The instruction that AFM procedures supersede ECAM (P7) may create legal liability for crews who follow ECAM in the heat of an emergency; the FAA should provide transitional guidance, checklists, and crew decision aids to prevent confusion.

[P11] The AD should provide an explicit parts and labor cost estimate for installing the ATQC per (h)(1) (P11) to support economic impact analysis and to allow carriers to budget for compliance.

[P12] Service Bulletin A350–31–P028 referenced in (P12) must be explicitly incorporated by reference in the AD or made available free of charge in the docket; otherwise operators may face copyright barriers to compliance.

[P13] The AD should clarify whether compliance with Airbus service bulletins A350–31–P028 and A350–31–P029 is required exactly as written, or whether operator-furnished minor procedural optimizations are acceptable under non-RC allowances.

[P14] Activating ECAM temporary change code No. 27AF (P14) should include rollback instructions if unintended ECAM behavior occurs; the AD should require Airbus to provide deactivation steps and conditions.

[P15] The Manager’s sole authority to approve AMOCs (P15) risks bottlenecks; the FAA should permit delegated AMOC approvals to regional Aircraft Certification Offices for routine, low-risk AMOCs.

[P16] Sending AMOC requests through principal inspectors (P16) risks jurisdictional delays for foreign repair stations; the AD should allow direct submission by FAA-certificated repair stations to the International Section.

[P18] The specified AMOC email address (P18) must be staffed and monitored; the FAA should commit to acknowledging receipt within a defined period (e.g., 3 business days).

[P21] Requiring DOA-signed approvals (P22/P21) begs the question of what constitutes an acceptable DOA signature — the AD should accept electronic signatures consistent with EASA DOA practice and clarify authentication requirements.

[P23] The AD should explicitly list the RC-identified procedures/tests in the AD body or associated service documents so operators can immediately identify compliance-critical tasks without obtaining full service documents.

[P25] The statement that non-RC deviations may be made without AMOC (P25) should be constrained so that safety-significant deviations still require FAA notification; otherwise critical safety work could be informally bypassed.

[P26] The AD should define what constitutes a “substitution” versus a minor procedural clarification for RC items to give operators clear boundaries on when AMOC is required.

[P3] Paragraph (g) references “applicable time specified in paragraph (g)(1) or (g)(2)” but (g)(2) refers to a date that preceded the AD effective date (P9); the FAA must reconcile this retroactivity issue or provide a waiver mechanism.

[P10] The AD imposes concurrent obligations: AFM revision within 30 days and hardware/software changes within 6 months (P8/P10). Operators need clarity if aircraft may continue to operate under AFM/TR 113 interim procedures pending completion of the 6-month modifications.

[P14] The AD should clarify whether activation of ECAM temporary change code No. 27AF requires software load validation and whether activation can be done via ground update or requires removal from service for reconfiguration.

[P4] The allowance to insert a paper copy of TR 113 into the AFM (P4) may violate some operators’ electronic AFM configuration control; the FAA should allow electronic AFM inserts provided they are documented per the operator’s configuration control program.

[P28] The physical mailing address for comments (P28) lacks instructions for submitting confidential business information (CBI); the FAA should provide a CBI submission procedure and a point of contact for redaction requests.

[P30] Regulations.gov submissions (P30) do not guarantee immediate docket posting; the FAA should commit to timely docket updates and provide a receipt confirmation system for comments.

[P32] The AD invites comments (P32) but does not state the weight given to comments from different stakeholders; the FAA should describe how comment input will be used in final rule determinations.

[P1] The rule’s blanket statement that the UIC program “is composed of the listed elements submitted in the state's revision application” is ambiguous and could allow the state to later claim additional materials are part of the federally-approved program without a separate EPA notice-and-comment approval; EPA should specify that only the exact documents listed in the docket and incorporated by reference are enforceable.

[P1] The provision does not require EPA to publish a complete, dated inventory of the “listed elements” in the Federal Register or the docket; commenters request that EPA publish a clear, dated index of every element and version incorporated so regulated parties and the public can determine precisely what is in effect.

[P1] Industry stakeholders will object that incorporation of unspecified “elements” from the state application could create compliance uncertainty and recommend that EPA limit incorporation to specific named documents with version and signature dates.

[P2] The incorporation-by-reference of state statutes and regulations into the federal UIC program (§ 147.1751(a)) without reproducing key provisions in the CFR may impede judicial review and enforcement because the text is not in the CFR; legal commenters will argue EPA should reproduce critical statutory language or provide permanent online access to the exact statutory text cited.

[P2] Environmental advocacy groups will challenge incorporation of state statutes that may be less protective than federal requirements, requesting EPA to identify any deviations from federal minimums and explain how the incorporated statutes meet SDWA §1422(c) criteria.

[P2] The provision names the “binder entitled ‘EPA-Approved North Dakota SDWA § 1422 Underground Injection…’” but truncates the title; commenters will request the full binder title, the binder’s docket number, and the effective dates of the cited state statutes and regulations to avoid confusion.

[P2] Regulated operators request that EPA clarify whether later amendments to the incorporated North Dakota statutes and regulations become part of the federal program automatically or only upon separate EPA approval, to avoid retroactive obligations.

[P3] The rule allows inspection of incorporated regulations at EPA, docket, and NARA locations, but does not require that the documents be available electronically and free of charge; commenters will request that EPA ensure downloadable, machine-readable versions are posted on Regulations.gov and the EPA regional web page.

[P3] Rural and tribal stakeholders will point out that physical inspection locations (EPA Region VIII office and NARA) are geographically distant for many North Dakota residents; they will request additional local access points or guaranteed digital access to the documents.

[P4] Providing a phone number and URL for obtaining materials (§ 147.1751(a)) is insufficient for timely public access; commenters will request a dedicated email address and that all incorporated documents be posted on the EPA public docket with clear file names and version dates.

[P4] Small businesses and public interest groups will ask EPA to confirm whether there is any cost associated with obtaining materials from the Regional Office, the Headquarters Library, or NARA, and to require that no-fee digital copies be made available.

[P5] Incorporating the Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) between EPA Region VIII and the North Dakota Industrial Commission (§ 147.1751(e)) raises concerns about delegation of enforcement authority; legal commenters will request that the MOA be published in full in the docket and that EPA explain which enforcement authorities remain with EPA and which are delegated to the state.

[P5] Environmental organizations will claim the MOA may contain provisions that limit EPA oversight or impose state discretion inconsistent with the SDWA; they will request EPA to disclose the MOA’s specific terms regarding monitoring, inspection frequency, and corrective action triggers.

[P5] Industry parties will request clarity in the MOA about the process and timeline for obtaining permits under the Class VI program, and whether state timelines supersede any federal deadlines.

[P6] Incorporation of the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between state agencies (§ 147.1751(f)) could affect inter-agency roles (e.g., DMR Oil and Gas Division vs. Industrial Commission); commenters will demand the MOU include specifics on lead agency for permits, review timelines, data-sharing protocols, and dispute resolution mechanisms.

[P6] Tribes and local governments will request that the MOU disclose procedures for consultation with federally recognized tribes and whether the state will coordinate with tribal governments on siting and monitoring of Class VI wells.

[P6] Public interest attorneys will argue that the MOU should explicitly state that state agency personnel will follow federal confidentiality and public records standards when handling data submitted under the federal UIC program, and request that the MOU be revised if it conflicts.

[P7] Incorporation of the Attorney General’s Statement of Legal Authority (§ 147.1751(g)) should include the exact language and scope of the legal opinion; commenters will request the full text and any caveats the AG included about enforcement, funding, or limitations in state law.

[P7] Legal experts will assert that the Attorney General’s Statement may be insufficient to establish adequate legal authority for the state to carry out all Class VI authorities required by the SDWA; they will request EPA to evaluate and publish whether any gaps exist and how they will be addressed.

[P7] Industry commenters will want confirmation that the Attorney General’s Statement covers the state’s authority to require financial responsibility, corrective action, and indefinite monitoring for Class VI wells, and will ask EPA to identify any limits.

[P8] Incorporating the Class VI Program Description and “any other materials submitted” (§ 147.1751(h)) is overly broad and could assimilate informal correspondence or non-binding drafts into the federal program; commenters will request that EPA limit incorporation to final, signed program descriptions and explicitly exclude drafts, internal notes, or emails.

[P8] Environmental groups will demand that the Class VI Program Description include detailed procedures for site characterization, monitoring, well construction, and corrective action, and will ask EPA to confirm that each of these specifics is present in the incorporated description.

[P8] Operators will ask EPA to publish the exact Class VI Program Description document with version/date and to state whether state-specific standards (e.g., casing specifications or pressure testing criteria) differ from EPA’s Class VI guidance and why.

[P8] Citizens and public health advocates will request that any future supplements to the program be subject to separate public notice-and-comment before incorporation into the federal program, rather than being automatically included by reference.

[P1] Administrative law commenters will assert that the provision should specify the effective date of each incorporated element and whether the state or EPA may amend incorporated elements, to avoid legal uncertainty about when obligations start.

[P2] The rule should identify conflicts between incorporated state regulations and federal Class VI requirements and state how such conflicts will be resolved; stakeholders ask EPA to include a conflict-resolution clause.

[P3] Several commenters will raise accessibility concerns: provide searchable OCR text versions of incorporated documents, and ensure that materials are accessible to people with disabilities in compliance with Section 508.

[P5] Industry and environmental commenters alike will request that the MOA specify performance metrics and reporting requirements for the state’s implementation of the Class VI program so EPA and the public can assess program effectiveness.

[P6] Public transparency advocates will ask that the MOU require publication of inspection reports, well logs, monitoring data, and enforcement actions on a public website in a timely manner.

[P7] The AG’s Statement should be accompanied by a legal sufficiency review by EPA; commenters request that EPA publish its legal analysis concluding the state has the required authority under SDWA §1422.

[P8] Commenters request that EPA clarify whether "any other materials submitted" includes technical appendices, economic analyses, or modeling results, and if so, require those be made publicly available in the docket.

[P1] The establishment of R–2509E as a new restricted area will create significant airspace impacts for general aviation pilots who routinely use VFR routes through the Twentynine Palms area; the rule fails to analyze or mitigate diversion distances and additional fuel/time burdens.

[P1] The rule does not provide a mitigation plan for emergency medical flights (MEDEVAC) that could be blocked when R–2509E is active from the surface to FL400, which could endanger patient outcomes.

[P2] The proposed horizontal boundary coordinates for R–2509E overlap existing VFR reporting points and published visual corridors used by local GA pilots, but no coordination or alternative routing is described.

[P2] The polygon defined for R–2509E lacks a reference datum beyond the coordinate list (e.g., NAD83), creating ambiguity about precise boundaries for charting and navigation.

[P3] Designating R–2509E from the surface up to FL400 is excessively broad and will unnecessarily restrict civilian IFR traffic that transits the area at cruise altitudes; the FAA should limit the vertical extent or adopt a higher lower limit to reduce impacts.

[P3] A surface-to-FL400 vertical limit for R–2509E is inconsistent with standard restricted area practice where higher altitudes are commonly used only when required; the proposal lacks justification for extending to FL400.

[P4] Activating R–2509E only intermittently by NOTAM between August 7–26, 2017 is insufficiently transparent for planning; NOTAMs can be missed by pilots, and the FAA should require advance publication in the Chart Supplement and enhanced outreach.

[P4] The very short, date-limited activation window (Aug 7–26, 2017) suggests temporary operations; commenters request clarification whether this is a test period and whether continuing or recurring activations will be sought, as no sunset/renewal process is described.

[P5] Assigning control responsibility to Los Angeles ARTCC is appropriate, but the rule does not specify procedures for coordination between ARTCC and nearby approach/center facilities or how handoffs will be managed when the restricted area is active.

[P5] The proposal does not specify communications frequencies or clearance procedures between ARTCC and MCAGCC when R–2509E is active; absent these details, controllers and airspace users may face confusion.

[P6] Granting use authority to the Commanding General, MCAGCC is acceptable, but the rule lacks constraints on the types of activities (e.g., live munitions, low-altitude maneuvering) permitted within R–2509E, preventing stakeholders from assessing risk.

[P6] The rule should require MCAGCC to publish schedules of planned training activities to minimize conflicts with civil aviation and to allow airport operators and flight schools to plan around activations.

[P7] The creation of R–2509W will further fragment the airspace around Twentynine Palms and needs a cumulative impacts analysis considering R–2509N, R–2509E, and R–2509W simultaneous activations.

[P8] The horizontal boundaries of R–2509W as proposed may overlap with existing SUA or TFR areas; commenters request a map overlay and cross-reference to existing restricted/MOA/TFRs to assess conflicts.

[P9] Excluding the 3.4-mile radius cylinder (surface to 1,500 ft AGL) from R–2509W is ambiguous because the exclusion's point coordinates are given but no named airport/reference point is cited; stakeholders cannot determine which local operations benefit from the exclusion.

[P9] The exception for the 3.4-mile radius to 1,500 ft AGL could be insufficient to protect helicopter operations and flightseeing tours if adjacent restricted airspace activates; commenters ask for clarification on lateral and vertical buffer requirements.

[P10] Limiting R–2509W vertically to surface–8,000 ft MSL will still constrain numerous regional VFR and IFR operations (including approach/departure paths of nearby public-use airports); the FAA must analyze impacts on those procedures.

[P10] The rule fails to state whether altitudes within R–2509W will be available for transit with prior permission (e.g., corridors or transit lanes), which would allow reduced disruption to civil traffic.

[P11] Activating R–2509W intermittently by NOTAM during Aug 7–26, 2017 raises the same concerns about NOTAM reliability and pilot awareness; the FAA should require pre-published activation windows and coordination with flight planning vendors.

[P12] As with R–2509E and R–2509N, assigning control to Los Angeles ARTCC requires clear procedures for coordination with adjacent facilities and with military range control; the rule does not describe these coordination mechanisms.

[P13] Identifying MCAGCC as the using agency for R–2509W does not include any safety oversight or reporting requirements; commenters ask that MCAGCC be required to report unusual incidents, airspace violations, and after-action safety reviews to the FAA.

[P14] Establishing R–2509N as a new restricted area extending to 16,000 ft MSL overlaps national airspace used by general aviation cross-country flights and could force altitude adjustments; the FAA must provide a safety and economic impact assessment.

[P15] The horizontal boundary description for R–2509N references coordinate points that may not form a closed polygon in the order listed; the FAA should provide precise ordered vertices and a chart depiction to remove ambiguity.

[P16] A vertical limit of surface–16,000 ft MSL for R–2509N could interfere with turbine-powered aircraft en route at cruise altitudes; the FAA must justify this altitude based on documented military training needs and risk assessments.

[P17] Making R–2509N active intermittently by NOTAM during Aug 7–26, 2017 without specifying likely times/durations (daily hours or single continuous events) prevents airports and GA pilots from effective planning and may lead to unnecessary cancellations or diversions.

[P18] Control by Los Angeles ARTCC should include explicit coordination requirements with military controllers at MCAGCC when R–2509N is activated, including pre-activation coordination and deconfliction of IFR flight plans; such requirements are absent.

[P19] Granting MCAGCC use authority for R–2509N permits a range of military training without restrictions; commenters request limits on types of weapons employment, minimum lateral/vertical separation from civil routes, and mitigation for noise impacts on surrounding communities.

[P1] The rule does not include any environmental review summaries (noise, wildlife, cultural resources) associated with establishing three restricted areas; commenters request an Environmental Assessment (EA) or reference to one already completed.

[P2] The coordinate precision (seconds) is adequate, but without a graphical depiction and electronic dissemination format (e.g., GIS shapefiles), charting vendors and GA navigation systems may implement incorrect boundaries.

[P3] The lack of a mechanism for emergency transits through R–2509E (e.g., MEDEVAC, law enforcement) is a safety concern; the rule should require predefined emergency transit procedures with immediate coordination paths.

[P4] Limiting activation to Aug 7–26, 2017 appears to reflect a specific training exercise; the FAA must confirm whether this rule is temporary and, if permanent designation is intended later, publish additional opportunity for public comment.

[P6] Civilian flight training schools based in nearby airports should be explicitly included in consultation and provided with revised training areas or waivers during activations to avoid economic harm.

[P9] The exclusion of the 3.4-mile radius cylinder may create lateral "choke points" where traffic concentrates just outside the exclusion; the FAA should analyze potential congestion and collision risk.

[P10] The inconsistent vertical limits among the three restricted areas (FL400, 16,000 ft, 8,000 ft) increase complexity for pilots and controllers; commenters request justification for the differing ceilings and recommendation for harmonization where possible.

[P11] The reliance on NOTAMs for intermittent activations is problematic given known issues with NOTAM formatting and distribution; the FAA should require supplemental publication in Flight Service briefings and on aeronautical charts for the activation dates.

[P13] MCAGCC should be required to fund and coordinate outreach to local airports, fixed-base operators, and flying clubs to explain operational impacts and provide real-time activation information.

[P16] Raising R–2509N to 16,000 ft MSL without corridor allowances could push IFR traffic into congested adjacent airways; the FAA must analyze downstream air traffic flow effects and file-flow management implications.

[P5] The rule does not specify which air traffic control facility will issue clearances or coordinate intercepts for nonparticipating aircraft inadvertently entering an active restricted area; this operational gap could delay response to airspace violations.

[P1] Affected parties request that the FAA incorporate waiver procedures enabling transient civil flights to transit restricted areas with prior permission when safe, rather than blanket prohibition.

[P14] Local businesses relying on aerial tourism and flightseeing ask for assurances that scheduled tourist flights will receive prioritized coordination or compensation if frequent cancellations occur due to activations.

[P2] The lack of notice about how often the restricted areas will be activated during the listed period (number of activations, anticipated daily schedule) prevents meaningful assessment of economic impacts on local aviation-dependent businesses.

[P19] Community groups near Twentynine Palms request noise monitoring and public reporting when the restricted areas are used for low-level or high-intensity training, which the proposed text does not require.

[P7] Emergency services (firefighting, law enforcement) request guaranteed immediate access protocols to ensure their aircraft can respond to incidents within the restricted area footprint at any time.

[P8] Airlines and cargo operators request an analysis of potential rerouting fuel and crew costs if R–2509 areas are active at times of routine flights, particularly given the proximity to scheduled westbound traffic corridors.

[P15] Aviation legal experts note the rule lacks a clear legal basis or reference to Department of Defense coordination agreements; the FAA should cite interagency Memoranda of Agreement (MOAs) that define control and use responsibilities.

[P4] The August 7–26, 2017 activation period has already passed; commenters ask whether this proposed regulatory text is retroactive, and if so, how that complies with notice-and-comment requirements and pilot rights.

[P1] Private pilots request that the FAA provide proposed charting updates and timeline for incorporation into VFR sectional charts and the Digital—Chart Supplement to prevent inadvertent entry.

[P13] The proposed rule does not include an incident reporting or enforcement policy for violations inside the restricted areas; commenters urge clear consequences and an educational first-offense policy for inadvertent entrants.

[P10] The rule should clarify altitude reference for the R–2509W ceiling (MSL is stated, but how this interacts with terrain in the Mojave Desert and surrounding airports should be explained for safe vertical separation planning).

[P6] The MCAGCC should be required to maintain an online, machine-readable schedule and NOTAM cross-reference for activations so flight planning systems can automatically flag affected routes.

[P1] The deadline in § 39.13(a) (August 27, 2018) is unreasonablely short and should be extended to allow more stakeholder review and technical assessment.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether the August 27, 2018 date is the date comments must be postmarked, received, or submitted via the FAA docket system, to avoid confusion about timeliness.

[P2] § 39.13(f) is vague about what constitutes the "specified compliance times" and commenters request that the rule include explicit calendar times (e.g., flight hours, cycles, or calendar days) rather than cross-referencing undefined figures.

[P2] Industry commenters will object that § 39.13(f) provides no grace period for scheduling maintenance downtime and request language allowing “as soon as reasonably practicable” within a specified maximum delay to avoid operational disruptions.

[P3] The mandatory replacement of each MLG OST per Bombardier SB 670BA–32–058 (§ 39.13(g)) should be accompanied by published parts availability estimates; airlines and MROs are concerned about supply chain capacity and potential grounding.

[P3] Operators will request that the FAA explicitly allow installation of FAA- or TCCA-approved equivalent parts or repair designs in lieu of strict adherence to Bombardier SB 670BA–32–058, to accommodate aftermarket parts and approved repairs.

[P3] Legal commenters may argue that incorporation by reference of Bombardier SB 670BA–32–058 without providing access to the full text in the docket could violate public participation norms and request that the service bulletin be made freely available in the rulemaking docket.

[P4] The phrase in § 39.13(g) “within the compliance times specified in figure 1 to paragraph (g)” is unclear; stakeholders request that figure 1 be included in the regulatory text or docket with explicit numeric thresholds (e.g., hours/cycles/calendar months) to avoid interpretive disputes.

[P4] Operators will ask for a tiered compliance schedule in figure 1 (e.g., fleets with higher cycles subject to shorter compliance times) if that is the intent; if not intended, the FAA should state so to avoid uneven enforcement.

[P5] The 90‑day deadline in § 39.13(h) to revise maintenance/inspection programs is too short for some operators (especially smaller carriers) to incorporate and get approval for Bombardier Temporary Revision ALI–0593; request extension to 180 days.

[P5] Commenters will request that the rule specify the approval path for revised maintenance programs (e.g., does the FAA need to approve the program revision or is operator incorporation sufficient) to reduce regulator/operator uncertainty.

[P6] The initial compliance time rule in § 39.13(h) that defers to the Bombardier temporary revision or 90 days, whichever is later, may create inconsistent schedules; commenters request that the FAA set a single, uniform initial compliance baseline or require Bombardier to specify precise calendar limits.

[P6] Safety advocates will request that if Bombardier’s temporary revision provides longer initial compliance times for some aircraft, the FAA adopt the shorter timeframe to ensure safety and uniformity.

[P7] § 39.13(i) prohibition on alternative actions once the program is revised is overly restrictive; commenters from operators and MROs will request that limited flexibility be retained for unavoidable circumstances (e.g., emergent repairs) without requiring an AMOC.

[P7] Small operators will note that the AMOC process is burdensome and time-consuming; they will request that certain pre-approved alternative inspection techniques be allowed without individual AMOCs.

[P8] The exception in § 39.13(i) allowing AMOCs per paragraph (j)(1) is conditioned on procedures that appear to centralize approval with the NY ACO Branch; regional operators request explicit delegation options or quicker provisional approvals to avoid operational delays.

[P9] § 39.13(j)(1) granting authority to the Manager, New York ACO Branch to approve AMOCs may create a single point of bottleneck; commenters recommend allowing other appropriate FAA offices or designated engineering representatives to approve AMOCs to speed responses.

[P9] Legal commenters will ask the FAA to clarify the legal standard and evidentiary requirements the Manager will use to grant AMOCs (e.g., what data, analyses, or substantiation are required).

[P10] The routing requirement in § 39.13(j)(1) to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 is potentially inconsistent with the direct-to-manager submission option; commenters ask for a clear, step-by-step process flow and expected timelines for each path.

[P11] The direct submission address in § 39.13(j)(1) should include an email and electronic docket submission option; commenters note that physical mail alone is slow and unreliable.

[P12] The requirement in § 39.13(j)(1) to notify the principal inspector or FSDO before using an approved AMOC (§ 39.13(j)(1) notification before use) is vague about timing (e.g., how many days prior) and the method of notification (written, electronic); commenters request specification (e.g., at least 5 business days in writing).

[P12] Operators will request a process for emergency use of AMOCs (e.g., immediate temporary use for safety reasons) with subsequent retroactive notification to the FSDO within a specified short window.

[P13] § 39.13(j)(2) requiring corrective actions from a manufacturer to be approved by the Manager (NY ACO), TCCA, or Bombardier’s TCCA DAO creates jurisdictional ambiguity—commenters request clarification on whether concurrent approvals are required and how conflicts between authorities will be resolved.

[P13] Foreign operators and their national authorities will request reciprocal recognition language to avoid repeated approvals by TCCA and the FAA when one competent authority has already approved a corrective action.

[P14] The DAO signature requirement in § 39.13(j)(2) lacks clarity on acceptable formats (electronic signature, stamped signature, etc.); commenters ask FAA to accept documented electronic approvals consistent with EASA/TCCA practices.

[P14] Commenters will request that the rule specify what constitutes adequate documentation from a DAO (e.g., DAO approval letter reference number, date, scope) to ensure consistent acceptance.

[P3] Maintenance organizations will ask whether compliance with Bombardier SB 670BA–32–058 requires use of Bombardier-serviced parts only, or whether OEM-approved vendor parts and standard MRO practices are acceptable.

[P3] Financial stakeholders will point out the rule does not estimate cost impacts of replacing each MLG OST and will ask the FAA to include a regulatory flexibility analysis, including impacts on small entities.

[P5] Labor unions and workforce groups will ask for lead time beyond 90 days to schedule training and staffing needed to incorporate Bombardier Temporary Revision ALI–0593 into their maintenance programs.

[P7] Consumer/passenger advocacy groups will argue that prohibiting alternative intervals without AMOC might delay beneficial more-frequent inspections proposed by operators, and suggest the rule allow operators to adopt more stringent inspections without AMOC.

[P9] Commenters will ask the FAA to publish expected turnaround times for AMOC reviews by the NY ACO Branch to enable operators to plan maintenance schedules.

[P1] Historic preservation or transparency advocates will request that the docket remain open past August 27, 2018 if substantive new data emerge, and that the FAA seek supplementary comments if the service bulletin is updated.

[P4] Legal counsel will warn that referencing "figure 1 to paragraph (g)" without including figure content creates interpretive risks in enforcement actions and request the FAA include that figure in the Federal Register publication.

[P2] Nursing home associations are likely to assert that the 8th-day initial assessment deadline in §413.343(b) is too strict for patients with complex discharges and that CMS should allow initial assessment by the 8th calendar day or the 8th Medicare day (clarify whether hospital discharge day counts) to avoid penalizing providers for administrative delays.

[P2] Advocates for rural SNFs will likely comment that the §413.343(b) 8th-day requirement fails to account for staffing shortages and limited clinician availability in rural areas and request a reasonable extension or an exception for facilities with documented staffing constraints.

[P3] Long-term care providers will likely welcome the permission to perform additional interim assessments (§413.343(b)) but request CMS to define reasonable limits (e.g., maximum number of interim assessments per 90-day stay) to avoid audit exposure for frequent, clinically driven reassessments.

[P3] Legal experts may claim that the phrase “as the SNF determines are necessary” in §413.343(b) is unbounded and could lead to inconsistent use for financial optimization; they will likely request guardrails requiring clinical documentation standards to justify interim assessments to prevent gaming.

[P4] Hospitals and SNFs will likely comment that the §413.360(a) requirement to begin reporting by the first day of the calendar quarter at least 30 days after CCN notification is administratively burdensome and request a 60–90 day implementation window to configure systems and train staff.

[P4] Small SNFs and new entrants may point out that the “first day of the calendar quarter” timing could force a facility to start reporting immediately after notification even when the 30-day buffer crosses quarter boundaries; they will request CMS to allow the later of (a) 30 days after notification or (b) the first day of the subsequent quarter to avoid confusion.

[P5] Provider groups will likely contest the penalty in §413.360(a) (two-percentage-point reduction to the market basket percentage) as disproportionate and economically punitive for an administrative reporting lapse, asking CMS to instead implement graduated sanctions or cure periods before applying the reduction.

[P6] SNF trade associations will likely state that §413.360(d)(1) should require a minimum notice period (e.g., 60 days) between non-compliance notification and application of any penalty so facilities have meaningful time to cure reporting errors.

[P7] Legal organizations may request clarity that the 30-day reconsideration period begins from the date of receipt (or date of posting in an electronic portal) rather than the date on the letter, to account for mailing delays.
