[P10] Patient advocacy groups will argue that the §413.343(b) requirement for an initial assessment by day 8 should explicitly require that the assessment be comprehensive (cover physical, cognitive, and social needs) and include patient/caregiver input, not merely a billing-oriented form.

[P10] Facility compliance officers will request clarification whether the “8th day of posthospital SNF care” counts partial days, observation days, or readmissions, and ask CMS to provide concrete examples and a start-of-care definition.

[P11] Quality oversight organizations will request that §413.343(b)’s allowance for “other interim payment assessments” include documentation standards (who can perform them, required clinical justification, timing relative to significant status changes) to ensure consistency and quality.

[P12] Commenters will request that CMS publish an implementation timeline with milestones (test data submission, certification, pilot phase) so SNFs can plan to meet the reporting start date in §413.360(a).

[P1] The June 4, 2020 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonably short and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow affected operators and suppliers time to prepare meaningful technical comments.

[P1] The rule’s requirement that "FAA must receive comments by June 4, 2020" is ambiguous about postmark/email timestamps; clarify whether comments postmarked or emailed by June 4, 2020 but received later will be accepted.

[P1] Require alternative electronic submission channels (e.g., secure upload, docket portal) in addition to email for the June 4, 2020 deadline because the single method may impede large-file technical data submissions.

[P2] § 39.13(c) applies the AD to "all Boeing 737-8 and 737-9 airplanes certificated in any category" without exemptions for foreign-registered aircraft operating under bilateral agreements — clarify scope for non-U.S. operators.

[P2] The AD's blanket applicability to all 737-8/9 airplanes, regardless of configuration or existing modifications, is overly broad; request carving out airplanes that already have corrective modifications or deterministic inspections showing compliance.

[P2] The phrase "certificated in any category" may inadvertently include prototype, ferry, or experimental configurations; provide explicit examples or exclusions to avoid enforcement confusion.

[P3] § 39.13(f) mandates compliance "within the compliance times specified" but the AD does not specify a uniform compliance time; request that the FAA publish a clear table of deadlines by action and fleet segment.

[P3] The obligation allowing "unless already done" lacks guidance on what documentation constitutes proof of prior compliance — request a list of acceptable records and retention period.

[P4] § 39.13(g) requires performing "all applicable actions" per Boeing Special Attention Requirements Bulletin 737–71–1911 RB (Nov 26, 2019) but the rule text appears truncated ("except as specified by paragraph (" ) — this drafting error must be corrected to identify exceptions.

[P4] Mandating strict adherence to Boeing's Requirements Bulletin without FAA-approved deviations shifts normative authority to the manufacturer; request FAA clarification that only FAA-approved procedures are mandatory.

[P4] The AD should specify whether operators may use later-revised Boeing bulletins or only the Nov 26, 2019 issue; request permission to use Boeing-revised procedures once FAA has reviewed and accepted them.

[P5] § 39.13(h) substitutes the AD's effective date for the bulletin's "original issue date," but fails to define "effective date" (publication vs. compliance effective) — clarify which calendar date operators should use.

[P5] Replacing "original issue date" with the AD effective date could shorten operator timelines unexpectedly if the bulletin was issued recently — request grandfathering where operators already initiated actions based on the bulletin date.

[P6] § 39.13(i) prohibits installing SDOS actuators BOE–2001–901F or BOE–2001–901H "as of the effective date," but does not address installed actuators before the effective date — request explicit instructions on required removal, quarantine, or continued operation of already-installed units.

[P6] The installation prohibition lacks an exception for operational testing, maintenance, or ferry flights where replacement parts are unavailable; propose a limited-time exemption with mandatory risk mitigations.

[P6] The rule forbids installation on "any airplane" without distinguishing part condition; request clarification whether remanufactured or reworked actuators with the same part numbers but updated serial numbers are also prohibited.

[P7] § 39.13(j)(1) grants the Seattle ACO Branch Manager sole AMOC approval authority; this centralization may cause processing delays for operators outside Seattle — recommend allowing regional certification offices to approve AMOCs to expedite relief.

[P7] Provide criteria and expected turnaround times for AMOC approvals by the Seattle ACO Manager so operators can plan maintenance.

[P8] § 39.13(j)(1) requires sending AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19, but does not specify acceptable formats or required technical content — request a template and list of required analysis/data.

[P8] For foreign operators without a U.S. principal inspector or local FSDO, the rule should specify the appropriate submission path for AMOC requests to avoid jurisdictional uncertainty.

[P9] § 39.13(j)(1) directs AMOC information to the certification office manager named in paragraph (k)(1), but paragraph (k)(1) is not present in the provided text — correct the cross-reference and provide the named contact.

[P10] Allowing email submissions to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is helpful, but the rule should require an acknowledgment of receipt and tracking number to avoid disputes about timeliness.

[P10] Emailing AMOC requests may raise security/confidentiality concerns for proprietary data; request acceptance of encrypted submissions or a secure portal and assurance of non-disclosure protections.

[P11] § 39.13(j)(2) obligates notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC but does not require written confirmation of notification or state what constitutes sufficient notice — request written approval/acknowledgment be required.

[P11] For operators without a principal inspector, notifying the manager of the local FSDO/CHDO may be impractical for international fleets; request an alternate notification path (e.g., to the FAA certificate-holding district office managing the operator).

[P12] § 39.13(j)(3) permits Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs only if the ODA has authority delegated by the Seattle ACO Manager; this introduces potential conflicts of interest and inconsistent determinations — request FAA oversight requirements and public disclosure of ODA approvals.

[P12] The provision allowing Boeing ODA to approve AMOCs for repairs/modifications required by the AD may raise safety-of-flight impartiality concerns; ask that final FAA concurrence be required for ODA-approved AMOCs.

[P12] Clarify whether all Boeing ODA units are eligible or only specific ODAs with designees for the 737-8/9 program and provide a list of authorized ODAs.

[P13] § 39.13(j)(3) requires repairs/modifications to meet the airplane certification basis, but the rule lacks guidance for legacy airplanes whose certification basis may be complex; request procedures for determining the applicable certification basis and handling equivalent safety findings.

[P13] Demand clarity on how compliance with the certification basis will be demonstrated and documented when AMOCs propose novel repair methods.

[P14] § 39.13(j)(3) requires AMOC approvals to "specifically refer to this AD" — this is vague about the level of specificity (AD number, paragraph, or full text) — request exact referencing requirements (e.g., docket number, AD citation).

[P14] Require that AMOC approvals referencing this AD be posted to a publicly accessible FAA docket so other operators can evaluate precedent and promote consistency.

[P4] The AD relies on Boeing Special Attention Requirements Bulletin 737–71–1911 RB (Nov 26, 2019); stakeholders request incorporation by reference be completed in the NPRM with full bulletin text or clear instructions on how to obtain it without cost.

[P6] The prohibition of installing specified SDOS actuator part numbers could disrupt supply chains for ground test spares; request transitional allowances for non-operational spares used only for depot-level teardown and analysis.

[P2] Small operators with single 737-8/9 airplanes will face disproportionate compliance burdens; request cost-benefit analysis or phased compliance schedules to reduce economic impact.

[P3] The "unless already done" carve-out should require operators to submit supporting documentation within a specified timeframe to claim the action was completed prior to the AD effective date.

[P7] Provide an expedited AMOC review process for safety-critical items with defined SLA (e.g., 15 business days) to reduce operational disruptions.

[P5] If the bulletin's "original issue date" differs across Boeing documents incorporated by reference, substituting the AD effective date may create inconsistencies; request uniform approach across all referenced Boeing documents.

[P12] Define "acceptable level of safety" for Boeing ODA approvals to avoid arbitrary determinations; include measurable criteria or references to FAA guidance.

[P1] The Secretary’s unilateral authority to designate information as CEII under §1004.13(d) is overbroad and lacks clear standards; commenters will request explicit, narrow criteria and examples to constrain designation power consistent with FPA §215A.

[P2] Allowing the Secretary to delegate CEII designation authority to “any DOE Office” (§1004.13(d)) risks inconsistent application across offices; commenters will urge limiting delegation to specific offices with demonstrable mission need and security capacity.

[P3] Requiring the CEII Coordinator to be the “primary contact” for all designation submissions (§1004.13(e)) may create a bottleneck; industry commenters will request provisions for regional or functionally based points-of-contact with clear escalation paths.

[P4] The list of delegated duties for the CEII Coordinator (§1004.13(e)(1)) is too broad and centralizes decision-making without due process safeguards; commenters will call for independent oversight or multi-office review panels for contentious designations.

[P5] The obligation for the CEII Coordinator to “receive and review all incoming CEII designation requests” (§1004.13(e)(1)(i)) lacks a statutory timeline for initial review; requesters will ask for explicit review timelines and acknowledgement-of-receipt deadlines.

[P6] The requirement that the CEII Coordinator make “initial determinations” about whether information fits the CEII definition (§1004.13(e)(1)(ii)) should require written explanation of the factual basis for initial determinations to enable meaningful reconsideration.

[P7] Assistance to DOE Offices in assessing requester “need for and ability” to protect CEII (§1004.13(e)(1)(iii)) is vague; commenters will request objective security standards and minimum technical controls that a requester must demonstrate.

[P8] The CEII Coordinator’s authority to “set reasonable conditions” for release requests (§1004.13(e)(1)(iv)) is too discretionary; commenters will ask for a pre-defined menu of permissible conditions and a requirement to justify any additional conditions in writing.

[P9] The CEII Coordinator’s power to make final determinations on non-Federal entity CEII requests (§1004.13(e)(1)(v)) concentrates finality outside of an independent legal review; legal commenters will request that final determinations be subject to review by the Office of General Counsel or an appeals panel.

[P10] Requirement to notify the CEII submitter when a non-Federal entity requests their CEII (§1004.13(e)(1)(vi)) must specify the content of the notice (e.g., requester identity, intended use) and timeline; submitters will request this be clearly defined.

[P11] The five-business-day requirement to convene a call between affected DOE Office and submitter (§1004.13(e)(1)(vii)) is unrealistic in complex cases; stakeholders will propose a flexible timeline with the obligation to document reasons for any delay.

[P12] Oversight duties to set handling, storage, and international sharing guidance (§1004.13(e)(1)(viii)) should require publication of binding DOE-wide CEII handling standards and mandatory training for personnel and contractors.

[P13] The annual meeting requirement among DOE Offices with delegated authority (§1004.13(e)(2)) should be more frequent (quarterly) or require documented minutes and implementation plans to ensure consistent designations.

[P14] Semi-annual meetings with FERC (§1004.13(e)(3)) are appropriate but should be mandatory (not “at the discretion of the CEII Coordinator”) to ensure regular alignment; commenters will request a fixed schedule and public summary of outcomes.

[P15] Annual meetings with Commerce, NTIA, and other agencies (§1004.13(e)(4)) should include DHS and CISA for cybersecurity alignment; omission of these agencies will be criticized by security stakeholders.

[P16] Requiring all CEII designation requests to be submitted to the CEII Coordinator (§1004.13(f)(1)) should allow electronic submission through a secure portal with automatic receipt confirmation and tracking numbers.

[P17] The labeling requirement “CEII—DO NOT RELEASE” on cover pages (§1004.13(f)(1)(i)) may be insufficient for mixed-document submissions; industry will request standardized labeling formats and metadata tagging requirements for digital files.

[P18] Requiring indication of the DOE Office(s) from which designation is requested (§1004.13(f)(1)(ii)) may be burdensome when multiple offices touch a submission; submitters will seek guidance on when multiple-office identification is necessary.

[P19] The segregation requirement for CEII portions (§1004.13(f)(1)(iii)) is infeasible in some integrated technical documents; commenters will request flexibility to submit redacted public versions and annotated copies instead of physical segregation.

[P20] Obligation to provide a public redacted version (§1004.13(f)(1)(iv)) must include explicit standards for acceptable redaction and a process for resolving disputes about sufficiency of the redacted public copy.

[P21] The parallel requirements for DOE personnel/contractors to submit CEII requests (§1004.13(f)(2)) should clarify how classified or controlled unclassified information intersect with CEII to avoid duplicative processes.

[P22] Mandating DOE submitters to label DOE-generated CEII (§1004.13(f)(2)(i)) should not preclude DOE from retroactively designating legacy files; commenters will request clear retroactive procedures and notice obligations.

[P23] The segregation requirement for DOE-generated CEII (§1004.13(f)(2)(ii)) must consider operational difficulties in archival records; commenters will ask for exemptions where segregation is impracticable and alternate protections.

[P24] DOE’s obligation to provide a public/redacted version of DOE-generated info (§1004.13(f)(2)(iii)) should include an internal quality-control review to ensure redactions do not over-withhold and must be subject to FOIA oversight.

[P25] Permission to designate internally-generated information as CEII at any time (§1004.13(f)(2)(iv)) raises concerns of retroactive secrecy; civil liberties groups will request a prohibition on retroactive designation for information already lawfully released.

[P26] The pre-designation review for specified categories upon receipt (§1004.13(f)(3)(i)) needs a clear list of “specified categories” and objective triggers for immediate pre-designation to prevent arbitrary withholding.

[P27] Holding submissions non-public while DOE determines designation (§1004.13(f)(3)(ii)) should be time-limited; requesters will ask for a maximum automatic confidentiality period (e.g., 30 or 60 days) unless extended with written justification.

[P28] DOE’s obligation to decide designation status before responding to requests (§1004.13(f)(3)(iii)) must be paired with firm deadlines for deciding so FOIA timelines are not indefinitely stayed.

[P29] The requirement that the CEII Coordinator “execute evaluation” with appropriate DOE Office (§1004.13(f)(4)(i)) should require written findings and evidentiary record to facilitate meaningful reconsideration and judicial review.

[P30] The Secretary or delegated office making the CEII determination (§1004.13(f)(5)(i)) must provide a written determination citing the legal and factual basis, not just an internal conclusion, to satisfy transparency and due process.

[P31] Notification of the submitter after determination (§1004.13(f)(5)(i)) should include notice of appeal rights, timelines, and the redacted rationale for the decision to enable effective reconsideration.

[P32] DOE’s ability to review CEII designations at any time (§1004.13(f)(5)(ii)) could be abused to retroactively remove public access; commenters will request that such reviews be limited to material changes in circumstances or periodic review schedules.

[P33] Mandatory review of CEII designation upon FOIA request (§1004.13(f)(5)(ii)(A)) should require DOE to publish a written explanation of why exemption (b)(3) applies rather than withholding by rote.

[P34] Mandatory review upon reconsideration requests (§1004.13(f)(5)(ii)(B)) should include a requirement that DOE produce the administrative record relied upon for the designation.

[P35] If voluntary submitter-provided info is not granted CEII, DOE’s promise to return or destroy it upon request (§1004.13(f)(5)(iii)) must include specific timelines and certification of destruction; submitters will request liability protections for inadvertent prior disclosures.

[P36] The prohibition against removing electronic files “in the ordinary course of business” (§1004.13(f)(5)(iii)) is unclear; commenters will ask DOE to define “ordinary course” and processes to expunge improperly retained copies.

[P37] Allowing required submitters to request review if designation is denied (§1004.13(f)(5)(iii) permission) is appropriate but should not be limited to “required” submitters; voluntary submitters need equivalent review rights.

[P38] Requirement that all CEII include the date of designation and be clearly labeled (§1004.13(f)(6)(i)) should also require version-control metadata and an index to facilitate records management and eventual de-designation.

[P39] For CEII that cannot be physically labeled, storage in secure electronic environments (§1004.13(f)(6)(i)) must meet defined NIST or federal security standards; commenters will ask DOE to specify acceptable technical controls.

[P40] Asserting exemption under FOIA (b)(3) for CEII (§1004.13(f)(6)(ii)(A)) is legally significant; FOIA advocates will request that DOE specify the statutory basis and cite the specific statute(s) that preclude disclosure.

[P41] The prohibition on making CEII available under laws requiring public disclosure by state/local/tribal authorities (§1004.13(f)(6)(ii)(B)) may conflict with state transparency obligations; state governments will request preemption analysis and coordination procedures.

[P42] The secure storage obligation for requested-CEII (§1004.13(f)(6)(iii)) must require logs, access controls, and audit trails; requesters will ask for mandatory periodic third-party audits.

[P43] Allowing CEII designations to remain up to five years (§1004.13(h)) is reasonable, but commenters will urge shorter default terms (e.g., 3 years) with extensions only upon documented need.

[P44] Requiring the Secretary or delegated office to set the duration at designation (§1004.13(h)(1)(i)) should mandate that the duration be justified in writing based on specific nexus to infrastructure risk.

[P45] The right for submitters to reapply starting one year before expiration (§1004.13(h)(1)(ii)) should allow earlier applications in special circumstances and should provide a streamlined re-designation process.

[P46] Permitting removal of designation at any time if disclosure would no longer impair security (§1004.13(h)(2)) should also require affirmative periodic reviews (e.g., every 3 years) and transparent criteria for removal.

[P47] The 10-business-day notice and comment opportunity before removal (§1004.13(h)(2)) is too short for complex records; submitters will request at least 30 business days to provide substantive input.

[P48] Separate 20-business-day notice before actual disclosure after removal (§1004.13(h)(2)) conflicts with the 10-business-day comment period (§1004.13(h)(2) and (48)); commenters will request alignment of these timelines and clarification whether they run concurrently.

[P49] The requirement to explain briefly why submitter objections don’t justify retaining designation (§1004.13(h)(2)) should demand a detailed, reasoned explanation with references to the criteria used, not a “brief” justification.

[P50] Return/destruction of expired CEII upon submitter request (§1004.13(h)(3)) must include certification, chain-of-custody, and preservation of minimal metadata for legal/operational continuity; submitters will ask for a documented process.

[P51] Treating backup electronic files as CEII until destroyed per retention schedules (§1004.13(h)(3)) is acceptable but DOE must commit to expedited destruction if requested and if no legal retention obligations remain.

[P52] DOE’s obligation to consult submitters when a FOIA request arrives before return/destruction (§1004.13(h)(3)) should require DOE to provide submitters with the FOIA requester identity, requested records, and proposed redactions within a short timeframe.

[P53] The reconsideration right for submitters (§1004.13(i)(1)(i)) with a 10-business-day filing deadline (§1004.13(i)(1)(i)) is too short; commenters will ask for at least 30 business days from notice to file reconsideration.

[P54] The electronic filing requirement for reconsideration (§1004.13(i)(1)(i)) should include alternative methods for submitters lacking secure electronic capabilities and confirmation procedures.

[P55] The requirement to submit a supporting statement within 20 business days of determination (§1004.13(i)(1)(i)) should be combined with the request to file reconsideration so that the initial stay period is meaningful; commenters will request alignment of deadlines.

[P56] Treating reconsideration submissions as filed upon receipt by OGC (§1004.13(i)(1)(i) condition) should include time-stamping and acknowledgement to prevent disputes over timely filing.

[P57] The 20-business-day decision deadline for reconsideration (§1004.13(i)(1)(iii)) may be unrealistic for complex matters; requesters will seek an initial 20-day decision timeline with a single permissible extension only for documented reasons.

[P58] Requiring reconsideration before judicial review (§1004.13(i)(1)(iv)) is appropriate but should not be jurisdictionally fatal if DOE fails to timely decide; commenters will request that failure to decide within the 20-business-day period be treated as denial for purposes of judicial review.

[P59] The automatic stay on the underlying decision when reconsideration is filed (§1004.13(i)(1)(v)) should be clarified to specify which actions are stayed and to provide a mechanism to seek expedited DOE action when the stay impedes critical operations.

[P60] The emergency and necessary-sharing exceptions to the stay (§1004.13(i)(1)(v) exceptions A–C) are broad; commenters will request strict definitions (including approval tiers and required written justifications) for what qualifies as “law enforcement,” “reliable operation/maintenance,” or “threats/emergencies.”

[P61] The law enforcement exception (§1004.13(i)(1)(v)–A) should require a written law-enforcement request signed by a senior official and subject to post-hoc review to prevent over-broad invocation.

[P62] The “ensure reliable operation/maintenance” exception (§1004.13(i)(1)(v)–B) must be narrowly defined to prevent routine operational sharing from circumventing protections; utilities will request objective criteria and an approval log.

[P63] The “infrastructure security/threats/emergencies” exception (§1004.13(i)(1)(v)–C) needs clear activation thresholds, duration limits, and mandatory after-action reports to preserve accountability.

[P64] Requiring Federal entities requesting CEII to follow procedures in §1004.13(k) (§1004.13(j)(1)) should be calibrated to preserve interagency emergency sharing protocols and national-security exemptions.

[P65] DOE’s permission to share CEII with affected agencies while imposing additional restrictions (§1004.13(j)(1) permission) should require written MOUs that specify allowed uses and audit rights.

[P66] The Secretary/Coordinator’s final determination on sharing CEII with eligible non-Federal entities (§1004.13(j)(2)) must be accompanied by a written risk assessment explaining why sharing is necessary and how risks are mitigated.

[P67] The requirement that non-Federal requesters execute an NDA with “minimum requirements” (§1004.13(j)(2)) must include the text of required NDA provisions in the rule or guidance to avoid inconsistent NDAs.

[P68] The NDA minimums obliging requesters to limit use, secure protection, destruction/return, and bar prohibited parties (§1004.13(j)(2)(i)-(iv)) should specify technical and administrative safeguards (e.g., encryption at rest/in transit, background checks) rather than broad terms.

[P69] The DOE audit right in NDAs (§1004.13(j)(2)(v)) must outline frequency, scope, and remedy for audit findings to be meaningful and not arbitrary.

[P70] The absolute prohibition on further sharing without DOE permission (§1004.13(j)(2)(vi)) is reasonable but should include limited exceptions for downstream contractors who sign equivalent NDAs and who are disclosed to DOE in advance.

[P71] The mandate that entities receiving CEII execute an NDA or participate in an approved sharing program (§1004.13(j)(3)) should allow recognition of industry-standard information-sharing programs (e.g., ISACs) that meet DOE security criteria.

[P72] Maintaining copies of each NDA with CEII Coordinator (§1004.13(j)(3)) must observe privacy and trade-secret protections and should not require sharing commercially sensitive NDA terms publicly.

[P73] If DOE facilitates voluntary CEII sharing and imposes extra restrictions (§1004.13(j)(3) and (78)), those extra restrictions must be published and subject to public comment prior to being applied broadly.

[P74] Delegation of authority to develop international CEII sharing protocols after consultation with Canada and Mexico (§1004.13(j)(4) permission) should require consultation with relevant domestic stakeholders (utilities, tribes) and explicit safeguards against foreign disclosure beyond Canada/Mexico.

[P75] Assistance by the CEII Coordinator in international protocol development (§1004.13(j)(4) obligation) must ensure that international sharing complies with U.S. export-control and counterintelligence laws.

[P76] The 10-business-day electronic notice to submitters before releasing non-DOE CEII (§1004.13(j)(5)) should require that DOE include the identity of the recipient and the purpose for release so submitters can meaningfully evaluate risks.

[P77] If prior notice cannot be provided (§1004.13(j)(5)), DOE’s obligation to notify “as soon as practicable” is too vague; commenters will request a defined maximum (e.g., within 48–72 hours) and reporting on why prior notice was impracticable.

[P78] The five-day call requirement after electronic notice (§1004.13(j)(5)) should allow for documented scheduling conflicts and substitute written explanations when the submitter cannot participate.

[P79] DOE’s final authority to decide whether to share non-DOE CEII (§1004.13(j)(5) permission) must include an obligation to document the decision rationale and to provide the submitter with redacted determinations to support appeal rights.

[P80] The required materials list for CEII requests (§1004.13(k) intro) must be accompanied by templates and examples to prevent procedural denials for formatting errors.

[P81] The contact-information requirement for requesters (§1004.13(k)(1)) should allow designated points-of-contact for organizations and permit use of secure mailing addresses when necessary for sensitive requests.

[P82] The detailed explanation of need and intended use (§1004.13(k)(2)) should be narrowly tailored, time-limited, and subject to confidentiality; requesters will ask for guidance on what constitutes sufficient detail.

[P83] Requiring an executed NDA/Acknowledgement with every request (§1004.13(k)(3)) may burden legitimate academic and research users; commenters will request tiered access levels with proportionate protection measures.

[P84] The CEII Coordinator’s duty to consult the maintaining office and deny/share decisions with reconsideration rights (§1004.13(k)(4)) should require written rationale and a record available to the requester to permit meaningful reconsideration.

[P85] DOE’s right to remove CEII designation if the submitter publicly discloses it (§1004.13(l)(1) permission) may create perverse incentives for third parties to “force” de-designation; submitters will request safe-harbor notification windows and opportunity to seek re-designation if disclosure was inadvertent.

[P86] Sanctions for DOE employees/contractors who knowingly disclose CEII (§1004.13(l)(2)) should include specified disciplinary ranges and criminal referral criteria; unions and contractors will ask for due-process protections and clear investigative procedures.

[P87] The rule lacks a clear definition of who qualifies as a “submitter” for notification and appeal rights across provisions (e.g., §1004.13(e)(1)(vi), (j)(5), (h)(2)); commenters will request a definition and proxy authorization mechanisms.

[P88] The interplay between CEII designations and other confidentiality regimes (e.g., classified information, Sensitive Security Information, Critical Energy/Electric Infrastructure Information under other statutes) is not addressed; legal commenters will ask DOE to map overlaps and conflict-resolution protocols.

[P89] Tribal governments should be explicitly included in consultation and notice provisions when CEII involves tribal infrastructure (§1004.13(e)(2), (j)(1)); tribal commenters will request government-to-government consultation requirements.

[P90] The rule should require publication of an annual CEII transparency report (redacted) summarizing number of designations, removals, sharing incidents, and appeals to enable public oversight.

[P91] There is no stated process for handling disputes when multiple parties claim submitter status or ownership of a record; commenters will request an interparty dispute-resolution procedure before de-designation or release.

[P92] The rule does not address FOIA fees or cost-recovery procedures when DOE reviews CEII requests or executes redactions; requesters will ask for fee-waiver guidance and timelines for fee-related delays.

[P93] The rule should mandate training requirements and certification for any non-Federal personnel authorized to possess CEII (background checks, security awareness training) rather than leaving those details to NDAs.

[P94] The rule must clarify whether state or local utilities that are privately held fall within the FPA §215A eligible non-Federal categories referenced in §1004.13(j)(2), to avoid denial of essential operational sharing.

[P95] The process and standards for “attempting to remove copies from DOE files” when submitters request return/destruction (§1004.13(f)(5)(iii), (h)(3)) lack specifics; commenters will ask for an obligation to search identified systems and produce a written account of actions taken.

[P96] The rule should require that any sharing with foreign entities (per §1004.13(j)(4)) be limited to Canadian and Mexican governmental entities and exclude private foreign corporations unless explicitly approved at the Secretary level.

[P97] The absence of explicit privacy-protection standards for CEII databases (e.g., retention limits, minimization) raises concerns; privacy advocates will request Privacy Impact Assessments and minimization rules.

[P98] The rule should specify remedies available to submitters and requesters in the event of unauthorized disclosure (e.g., injunctive relief, statutory damages, corrective measures) rather than leaving consequences unspecified.

[P99] The broad delegation authorities throughout the rule (§1004.13(d), (j)(4), etc.) should require public posting of any delegation memos and designation policies to ensure accountability and consistent application.

[P100] The rule should require that all CEII-related decisions—designations, removals, sharing approvals, and reconsideration outcomes—be documented in an indexed registry maintained by the CEII Coordinator and made available in redacted form to the public to enable oversight.

The law enforcement exception (§1004.13(i)(1)(v)–A) should require a written law-enforcement request signed by a senior official and subject to post-hoc review to prevent over-broad invocation.

The “ensure reliable operation/maintenance” exception (§1004.13(i)(1)(v)–B) must be narrowly defined to prevent routine operational sharing from circumventing protections; utilities will request objective criteria and an approval log.
The “infrastructure security/threats/emergencies” exception (§1004.13(i)(1)(v)–C) needs clear activation thresholds, duration limits, and mandatory after-action reports to preserve accountability.

Requiring Federal entities requesting CEII to follow procedures in §1004.13(k) (§1004.13(j)(1)) should be calibrated to preserve interagency emergency sharing protocols and national-security exemptions.
DOE’s permission to share CEII with affected agencies while imposing additional restrictions (§1004.13(j)(1) permission) should require written MOUs that specify allowed uses and audit rights.

The Secretary/Coordinator’s final determination on sharing CEII with eligible non-Federal entities (§1004.13(j)(2)) must be accompanied by a written risk assessment explaining why sharing is necessary and how risks are mitigated.

The requirement that non-Federal requesters execute an NDA with “minimum requirements” (§1004.13(j)(2)) must include the text of required NDA provisions in the rule or guidance to avoid inconsistent NDAs.

The NDA minimums obliging requesters to limit use, secure protection, destruction/return, and bar prohibited parties (§1004.13(j)(2)(i)-(iv)) should specify technical and administrative safeguards (e.g., encryption at rest/in transit, background checks) rather than broad terms.
The DOE audit right in NDAs (§1004.13(j)(2)(v)) must outline frequency, scope, and remedy for audit findings to be meaningful and not arbitrary.

The absolute prohibition on further sharing without DOE permission (§1004.13(j)(2)(vi)) is reasonable but should include limited exceptions for downstream contractors who sign equivalent NDAs and who are disclosed to DOE in advance.

The mandate that entities receiving CEII execute an NDA or participate in an approved sharing program (§1004.13(j)(3)) should allow recognition of industry-standard information-sharing programs (e.g., ISACs) that meet DOE security criteria.
Maintaining copies of each NDA with CEII Coordinator (§1004.13(j)(3)) must observe privacy and trade-secret protections and should not require sharing commercially sensitive NDA terms publicly.

If DOE facilitates voluntary CEII sharing and imposes extra restrictions (§1004.13(j)(3) and (78)), those extra restrictions must be published and subject to public comment prior to being applied broadly.

Delegation of authority to develop international CEII sharing protocols after consultation with Canada and Mexico (§1004.13(j)(4) permission) should require consultation with relevant domestic stakeholders (utilities, tribes) and explicit safeguards against foreign disclosure beyond Canada/Mexico.

Assistance by the CEII Coordinator in international protocol development (§1004.13(j)(4) obligation) must ensure that international sharing complies with U.S. export-control and counterintelligence laws.

The 10-business-day electronic notice to submitters before releasing non-DOE CEII (§1004.13(j)(5)) should require that DOE include the identity of the recipient and the purpose for release so submitters can meaningfully evaluate risks.

If prior notice cannot be provided (§1004.13(j)(5)), DOE’s obligation to notify “as soon as practicable” is too vague; commenters will request a defined maximum (e.g., within 48–72 hours) and reporting on why prior notice was impracticable.
The five-day call requirement after electronic notice (§1004.13(j)(5)) should allow for documented scheduling conflicts and substitute written explanations when the submitter cannot participate.

DOE’s final authority to decide whether to share non-DOE CEII (§1004.13(j)(5) permission) must include an obligation to document the decision rationale and to provide the submitter with redacted determinations to support appeal rights.
The required materials list for CEII requests (§1004.13(k) intro) must be accompanied by templates and examples to prevent procedural denials for formatting errors.

The contact-information requirement for requesters (§1004.13(k)(1)) should allow designated points-of-contact for organizations and permit use of secure mailing addresses when necessary for sensitive requests.

The detailed explanation of need and intended use (§1004.13(k)(2)) should be narrowly tailored, time-limited, and subject to confidentiality; requesters will ask for guidance on what constitutes sufficient detail.

Requiring an executed NDA/Acknowledgement with every request (§1004.13(k)(3)) may burden legitimate academic and research users; commenters will request tiered access levels with proportionate protection measures.

The CEII Coordinator’s duty to consult the maintaining office and deny/share decisions with reconsideration rights (§1004.13(k)(4)) should require written rationale and a record available to the requester to permit meaningful reconsideration.

DOE’s right to remove CEII designation if the submitter publicly discloses it (§1004.13(l)(1) permission) may create perverse incentives for third parties to “force” de-designation; submitters will request safe-harbor notification windows and opportunity to seek re-designation if disclosure was inadvertent.

Sanctions for DOE employees/contractors who knowingly disclose CEII (§1004.13(l)(2)) should include specified disciplinary ranges and criminal referral criteria; unions and contractors will ask for due-process protections and clear investigative procedures.

The rule lacks a clear definition of who qualifies as a “submitter” for notification and appeal rights across provisions (e.g., §1004.13(e)(1)(vi), (j)(5), (h)(2)); commenters will request a definition and proxy authorization mechanisms.

The interplay between CEII designations and other confidentiality regimes (e.g., classified information, Sensitive Security Information, Critical Energy/Electric Infrastructure Information under other statutes) is not addressed; legal commenters will ask DOE to map overlaps and conflict-resolution protocols.

Tribal governments should be explicitly included in consultation and notice provisions when CEII involves tribal infrastructure (§1004.13(e)(2), (j)(1)); tribal commenters will request government-to-government consultation requirements.
The rule should require publication of an annual CEII transparency report (redacted) summarizing number of designations, removals, sharing incidents, and appeals to enable public oversight.

There is no stated process for handling disputes when multiple parties claim submitter status or ownership of a record; commenters will request an interparty dispute-resolution procedure before de-designation or release.

The rule does not address FOIA fees or cost-recovery procedures when DOE reviews CEII requests or executes redactions; requesters will ask for fee-waiver guidance and timelines for fee-related delays.

The rule should mandate training requirements and certification for any non-Federal personnel authorized to possess CEII (background checks, security awareness training) rather than leaving those details to NDAs.

The rule must clarify whether state or local utilities that are privately held fall within the FPA §215A eligible non-Federal categories referenced in §1004.13(j)(2), to avoid denial of essential operational sharing.

The process and standards for “attempting to remove copies from DOE files” when submitters request return/destruction (§1004.13(f)(5)(iii), (h)(3)) lack specifics; commenters will ask for an obligation to search identified systems and produce a written account of actions taken.

The rule should require that any sharing with foreign entities (per §1004.13(j)(4)) be limited to Canadian and Mexican governmental entities and exclude private foreign corporations unless explicitly approved at the Secretary level.

The absence of explicit privacy-protection standards for CEII databases (e.g., retention limits, minimization) raises concerns; privacy advocates will request Privacy Impact Assessments and minimization rules.

The rule should specify remedies available to submitters and requesters in the event of unauthorized disclosure (e.g., injunctive relief, statutory damages, corrective measures) rather than leaving consequences unspecified.

The broad delegation authorities throughout the rule (§1004.13(d), (j)(4), etc.) should require public posting of any delegation memos and designation policies to ensure accountability and consistent application.

The rule should require that all CEII-related decisions—designations, removals, sharing approvals, and reconsideration outcomes—be documented in an indexed registry maintained by the CEII Coordinator and made available in redacted form to the public to enable oversight.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement to base critical habitat designations on "best scientific data" lacks a clear standard; we request clarification of what qualifies as "best" and whether unpublished local monitoring data or traditional ecological knowledge will be accepted and weighted equally with peer‑reviewed studies.

[P1] Industry commenters will object if economic impacts are only "considered" and not given commensurate weight with scientific factors; propose that the rule explicitly require quantitative economic cost‑benefit analysis to be given substantial weight in final designations.

[P2] Rural landowner groups will argue that the Secretary's discretion to exclude areas when benefits of exclusion outweigh designation benefits is too vague and could be applied inconsistently; request specified factors and a transparent scoring rubric for exclusion decisions.

[P2] National security stakeholders will request that areas near military bases or testing ranges be presumptively considered for exclusion unless the Service demonstrates that designation would not impair readiness.

[P3] State governments and regulated entities will request explicit deadlines and procedural timelines for issuing rules to complete designations or revisions to prevent indefinite delays under "must issue a rule."

[P3] Conservation groups will caution that requiring a formal rule to complete designations could introduce unnecessary procedural hurdles; they will request expedited rulemaking authority or an administrative process for minor revisions.

[P4] Agricultural and development interests will challenge the "maximum extent prudent and determinable" standard as legally indeterminate and seek guidance on what factual thresholds render habitat "determinable."

[P4] Environmental NGOs will assert that the obligation to designate critical habitat for every listed species must be interpreted to include unoccupied areas essential for recovery, and they will oppose any narrowing of this obligation.

[P5] Federal agencies will request clarifications on the scope of "not likely to destroy or adversely modify critical habitat," including whether de minimis impacts and cumulative impacts trigger consultation.

[P5] Legal experts will point out that prior caselaw on "adverse modification" is unsettled; they will request the agency adopt a clear regulatory definition consistent with court precedent to guide interagency consultations.

[P6] Private landowner associations will support the explicit prohibition on access to private lands solely due to designation and request the rule include enforcement language to prevent misuse by third parties seeking access.

[P6] Conservation organizations will caution that while designations do not grant access, the rule should clarify that this does not prevent voluntary conservation easements or incentive programs that involve access for habitat management.

[P7] Non‑Federal landowners will request an explicit statement that critical habitat designation does not create new affirmative obligations (e.g., fencing, restoration), and seek assurance that private property rights will not be diminished.

[P7] Restoration advocates will argue that absolving non‑Federal landowners of restoration responsibilities undermines recovery; they will request clarity that incentives and voluntary agreements can be used to encourage restoration.

[P8] Landowners and developers will seek a narrow interpretation of when proposed actions "may affect" listed species or critical habitat to avoid triggering burdensome section 7 consultations for unrelated projects.

[P8] Tribal governments will request that consultations explicitly account for tribal actions and that the rule clarify how section 7 applies to projects on tribal lands and to federal funding to tribes.

[P9] Environmental lawyers will challenge the provision that agencies and landowners must implement reasonable and prudent alternatives (RPAs) rather than restore or recover species, arguing this could weaken recovery obligations and may conflict with statutory duties.

[P9] Federal action agencies will request guidance on criteria for acceptable RPAs, including cost, feasibility, temporal scope, and monitoring requirements, to avoid open‑ended obligations.

[P10] Conservation commenters will object to the statement that agency and landowner are not required to restore or recover the species after an adverse modification finding, arguing that this undermines the recovery purpose of the Act and request removal or qualification of this exception.

[P10] Industry stakeholders will welcome that restoration is not mandatory after an adverse modification finding and will request confirmation that monetary mitigation or alternative conservation measures can satisfy obligations.

[P11] Environmental NGOs will request detailed standards for what constitutes "reasonable and prudent alternatives," including examples and minimum performance criteria tying RPAs to measurable conservation outcomes.

[P11] Permit applicants will ask for a timeline and dispute resolution mechanism for implementing RPAs to prevent indefinite delays of authorized actions while conservation measures are negotiated.

[P12] Public interest groups will point out that the comment receipt date of February 4, 2019 is in the past and request an extension of the comment period to allow for fresh review of updated data and analyses.

[P12] State agencies will request an extension of the comment period, citing that the draft economic analysis was released late in the comment window and stakeholders need additional time to prepare substantive economic comments.

[P13] Rural communities with limited broadband access will object to the requirement that electronic comments be received by 11:59 p.m. ET; request alternative receipt acknowledgments for those submitting near the deadline via mail.

[P14] Stakeholders will request that the deadline for requests for public hearings (January 22, 2019) be extended and that hearings be held in multiple locations, including in affected rural counties and tribal lands.

[P15] Commenters will request that the agency accept additional submission methods (e.g., email to a designated inbox) beyond those listed to increase accessibility for constituents.

[P16] Some commenters will raise concerns about the "Comment Now!" function on regulations.gov not preserving attachments correctly and request confirmation that uploaded supporting documents will be posted in their entirety and in accessible formats.

[P17] Civic groups will request clear instructions and confirmation processes for hand‑delivered hard copies to ensure they are logged and posted timely on regulations.gov.

[P18] Commenters will object to the agency's request that commenters use only the described methods, arguing the agency should accept reasonable alternative submission methods if technical issues arise with the listed portals.

[P19] Privacy advocates will request the agency publish comments in a searchable, machine‑readable format and ensure redaction protocols protect sensitive personal data beyond what is mandatory.

[P20] Privacy and domestic violence survivors will strongly object to the agency's statement that it will post entire hard‑copy comments "including personal identifying information" and request that the agency redact addresses, phone numbers, and signatures by default unless the commenter explicitly consents to disclosure.

[P21] Commenters will request clarification on the agency's ability to withhold personal information — specifically the standard the agency will use to grant or deny such requests and how to request redaction after submission.

[P22] Request that the agency post supporting documentation used to prepare the proposed rule (including GIS shapefiles, species occurrence records, and economic model inputs) online contemporaneously with the proposed rule to enable meaningful review.

[P23] The scientific community will urge the agency to solicit targeted input from universities and state wildlife agencies with recent field data on the Sonoyta mud turtle and to provide compensation or data‑sharing agreements where proprietary data are used.

[P23] Industry will request that the Federal Highway Administration, Department of Defense, and other relevant federal agencies be formally consulted as "concerned government agencies" given potential impacts on infrastructure and operations.

[P24] Recreational user groups will submit comments arguing designation will restrict access and increase enforcement, and will ask the agency to analyze whether human recreational threats would increase or decrease because of designation.

[P24] Conservation scientists will provide the opposite claim: designation will reduce threats by triggering conservation measures, and they will submit scientific rationale showing that benefits of designation outweigh prospective increases in targeted human activity.

[P25] Commenters will urge that subparts (a)–(e) require submission of georeferenced habitat maps, data collection protocols, and raw monitoring data, not just summary statements, so the Service can verify claims.

[P26] Local watershed groups will submit precise, quantitative data on the current extent (acres and stream kilometers) and spatial distribution of Sonoyta mud turtle habitat and will challenge any Service estimates that omit seasonal or ephemeral water sources.

[P27] Scientists will identify specific occupied spring and stream reaches containing the physical or biological features for the subspecies and provide peer‑reviewed evidence supporting inclusion of those areas in the designation.

[P28] Climate adaptation NGOs will request that proposed critical habitat include corridors and higher‑elevation refugia and ask for specific management recommendations such as riparian shading or groundwater recharge to maintain habitat suitability.

[P29] Recovery planners will identify unoccupied areas (with coordinates) that are essential for long‑term conservation—e.g., potential translocation sites—and provide demographic models showing necessity.

[P30] Mexican conservation partners will submit transboundary habitat information for the Rio Sonoyta watershed and argue that cross‑border areas are essential and should be included or at minimum inform U.S. designation decisions.

[P31] Local governments will submit current land use designations, planned developments, and an assessment of how designation would interact with zoning and water rights to avoid unintended regulatory conflicts.

[P32] Climate scientists will provide projections (with scenarios and models cited) on how temperature and precipitation changes will affect the Sonoyta mud turtle and argue that designation must be dynamic and include climate‑resilient areas.

[P33] Chambers of commerce and economic development agencies will submit detailed economic impact estimates (lost development revenue, permit costs, employment effects) and argue the draft economic analysis underestimates localized impacts.

[P33] Conservation economists will challenge the draft economic analysis, asserting it overstates costs by failing to account for avoided costs and the benefits of ecosystem services provided by conserved habitat.

[P34] Industry commenters will state that the draft economic analysis does not reasonably estimate indirect and cumulative economic impacts (e.g., on groundwater‑dependent agriculture) and request a revised, peer‑reviewed analysis.

[P34] Environmental groups will argue the draft economic analysis fails to quantify non‑market benefits (biodiversity, cultural values) and request inclusion of these benefits in the final economic assessment.

[P35] Landowners will identify specific parcels they believe should be excluded under section 4(b)(2), providing economic and national security rationales, and will request the Service adopt a presumption of exclusion for private lands with existing conservation agreements.

[P35] Conservation groups will oppose broad exclusions and will identify specific areas that should not be excluded—particularly headwaters and perennial springs—arguing their exclusion would jeopardize recovery.

[P36] Social scientists will submit evidence on likely adverse social reactions (e.g., retaliatory killings, vandalism, reduced cooperation with conservation agencies) and argue the Service must account for these social costs in its benefit–cost balancing.

[P36] Local elected officials will contend that adverse social reactions described in the draft economic analysis are overstated and request the Service present mitigation strategies rather than excluding habitat based on social reaction likelihood.

[P37] Civic groups will propose specific process improvements: longer notice periods, public webinars, local field workshops, and transparent posting of all datasets and modeling assumptions to increase participation and trust.

[P37] Legal advocates will request procedural changes to ensure meaningful public participation, such as requiring in‑person hearings when a threshold number of written requests are received and providing translation services for Spanish‑language stakeholders.

[P1] The addition of the "Hellbender, eastern [Missouri DPS]" to §17.11(h) is appropriate and necessary to protect the genetically and geographically distinct Missouri population, which faces unique threats not addressed by the rangewide listing.

[P1] Listing the Missouri DPS separately will create regulatory confusion with existing range-wide listings for eastern hellbenders unless the preamble clarifies that protections apply only within Missouri and identifies interactions with adjacent-state populations.

[P1] The rule should include a clear boundary map or watershed delineation for the Missouri DPS; the proposed text does not specify precise geographic limits and may lead to enforcement uncertainty for landowners and agencies.

[P1] The Service must ensure that listing the Missouri DPS will not preclude future actions under State conservation plans; recommend adding language encouraging coordination with Missouri Department of Conservation recovery efforts.

[P2] Specifying the common name as "Hellbender, eastern [Missouri DPS]" is confusing to the public and could be simplified to "Missouri eastern hellbender (DPS)" to improve clarity in outreach materials.

[P2] The bracketed DPS notation in the common name may be misleading; common names should be accessible to non-experts — recommend dropping "[Missouri DPS]" from the common name and instead indicating the DPS in the scientific or geographic line.

[P2] Advocacy groups support the common name as proposed because it emphasizes the eastern hellbender species while signaling the distinct Missouri population that requires protection.

[P3] The scientific name Cryptobranchus alleganiensis alleganiensis is correct for the eastern hellbender; commenters urge the Service to cite the taxonomic sources used to assign this name in the preamble to avoid challenges.

[P3] Legal commenters note potential conflict if future taxonomic revisions change subspecies classification; request the rule include a mechanism for updating scientific names without re-promulgating the listing.

[P3] Research institutions request that the Service publish the genetic and morphological data supporting DPS designation alongside the listing to allow independent scientific review.

[P4] Listing "Where listed: Missouri" is ambiguous about whether the listing covers the entire state or specific river systems; request the rule specify counties, river basins, or HUC codes to avoid overbroad application.

[P4] Landowner and industry groups are concerned that a statewide "Where listed: Missouri" could be interpreted to restrict activities across the whole state; recommend narrowing the geographic scope to documented occupied stream reaches.

[P4] Conservation groups support the statewide designation if it allows proactive protections for un-surveyed but potentially occupied habitats within Missouri's portion of the species' range.

[P5] Designating the Missouri DPS as Endangered (E) is warranted given documented declines, habitat degradation, and disease threats; commenters support the Endangered status rather than Threatened.

[P5] Recreational and development interests request the Service justify the Endangered designation with explicit criteria (e.g., population trend thresholds, habitat loss percentages) because an Endangered status triggers stricter prohibitions and greater regulatory impacts.

[P5] Municipalities and infrastructure agencies warn that Endangered status could significantly affect federally funded projects in Missouri; they request guidance on Section 7 consultation timelines and anticipated compensatory mitigation expectations.

[P5] Agricultural stakeholders express concern that Endangered designation may limit routine farm activities adjacent to streams; request clarification that normal agricultural practices, when conducted in compliance with best management practices, will not constitute unlawful take.

[P1] The rule should include targeted exceptions or special rules for conservation activities (e.g., translocations, captive breeding) to enable recovery actions without triggering take prohibitions.

[P2] Fishers and anglers request educational outreach materials clarifying that the listing does not pertain to any other hellbender populations outside Missouri to avoid unnecessary concern.

[P3] Academic commenters recommend including a reference to voucher specimens or museum collections validating the presence of the subspecies in Missouri to strengthen the scientific basis of the rule.

[P4] Emergency response agencies ask for explicit language on allowable emergency actions (e.g., pollution control, dam breach responses) in areas where the DPS occurs to avoid delays during crises.

[P5] Environmental law organizations request that the Service outline expected timelines and milestones for producing a recovery plan following listing, as required under the ESA, and seek adequate funding commitments.

[P1] The requirement in § 710.25(a) that “any person who manufactured” during the lookback period submit Form A could be interpreted to include small, one-time contract manufacturers and subcontractors who never owned the substance — this provision should clarify whether toll manufacturers and contract packagers are covered.

[P1] The rule does not define “manufactured” for purposes of § 710.25(a) with regard to chemical intermediates produced solely for on-site consumption vs. production for commerce; EPA should specify whether on-site intermediate production triggers Form A.

[P2] § 710.25(b) is permissive (“may submit”) but the rest of the rule treats processors as required reporters elsewhere; industry requests explicit confirmation that processors who choose not to submit under § 710.25(b) will not be subject to penalties if another entity files.

[P3] The obligation in § 710.25(c) to submit Form B “prior to manufacturing or processing” could block just-in-time manufacturing; EPA should allow submission up to a specified short window (e.g., 5 business days) prior rather than strictly prior to any activity.

[P3] § 710.25(c) lacks guidance on de minimis quantities and small-volume pilot runs; request exemption or reduced reporting requirements for productions below a de minimis tonnage threshold.

[P4] The catch-all in § 710.27(a) that lists exceptions should include a requirement that EPA publish guidance interpreting those exceptions to reduce inconsistent application by inspectors and litigants.

[P5] The R&D exemption in § 710.27(a)(1) is ambiguous about scale — commenters request a clear quantitative threshold (e.g., batch size, annual aggregate quantity) that qualifies as “small quantities for research and development.”

[P6] § 710.27(a)(2) excludes “import as part of an article” but does not define “article” for mixed-material consumer products; trade groups request alignment with the statutory TSCA article definition and examples (e.g., finished electronics with chemical-containing components).

[P7] § 710.27(a)(3) references § 720.30(g) or (h) but those provisions are not summarized here; importers request cross-referenced definitions and examples of covered activities to avoid inconsistent claims of exemption.

[P8] The exemptions for naturally occurring chemical substances in § 710.27(b) lack clarity on processed derivatives — industry asks EPA to clarify whether chemically modified derivatives of naturally occurring substances are exempt or reportable.

[P9] § 710.27(b)(1) exempts manufacture described in § 710.4(b) “unless manufactured by other means or made from a naturally occurring chemical substance” — this conditional language is confusing; request examples showing when the exemption is lost (e.g., biosynthetic vs. chemical synthesis).

[P10] The limited processing exemption in § 710.27(b)(2) (manual/mechanical, dissolution in water, flotation, etc.) should explicitly state whether minor heating, filtering, or addition of non-reactive solvents during processing preserves the exemption.

[P11] The requirement in § 710.29(a) that all submissions (including substantiation of confidentiality) must use e-NOA, CISS, and CDX unfairly burdens small businesses without secure IT access; request alternative submission methods (e.g., secure paper with verified signature) or a hardship waiver process.

[P11] EPA should provide a timeline and testing sandbox for e-NOA/CISS/CDX capacity before the rule’s effective date to ensure systems can handle volume and third-party joint submissions, per § 710.29(d)(4)(iii).

[P12] The cross-references in § 710.29(a) to paragraph (b) and (c) must be accompanied by machine-readable schema and a sample completed Form A and Form B so reporters can ensure completeness and avoid enforcement for technical errors.

[P13] § 710.29(a) mandates a separate form for each chemical substance; for mixtures with dozens of trace reportable constituents this will be administratively burdensome — request allowance to group trace constituents under a single submission with attachments.

[P14] The permission in § 710.29(a) to report multiple substances in one session but transmitted as separate forms needs clarification on whether EPA will assign a single tracking number for the session or separate tracking for each form to facilitate audits.

[P15] § 710.29(b) requires “the information described in this paragraph for each reportable chemical substance” during the submission period but lacks an explicit list of required fields for Form A in the preamble; stakeholders request EPA to publish the full data dictionary and validation rules.

[P16] The requirement in § 710.29(b)(1) to provide § 710.29(d) information for Form A may be burdensome for importers without supplier cooperation; request protection from enforcement when importers provide all information reasonably available and document supplier refusal.

[P17] § 710.29(b)(2) obligates reporting whether a substance was manufactured domestically, imported, or both — commenters urge EPA to permit reporting at the facility level (site of manufacture or entry) rather than at corporate level to improve accuracy.

[P18] The obligation in § 710.29(b)(3) to report first and last dates of manufacture/import during the lookback period may be impossible for legacy substances where recordkeeping is incomplete; industry requests an alternative such as best-available estimates with attestation and a safe harbor.

[P19] For Form B under § 710.29(c), the obligation to provide all listed information for each inactive substance should allow conditional submissions when the substance identity is legitimately unknown to a downstream processor (with supplier contact included), rather than forcing inaccurate data.

[P20] § 710.29(c)(1) requiring § 710.29(d) information for Form B must be harmonized with section § 710.37 confidentiality substantiation timing to avoid conflicting deadlines.

[P21] The requirement in § 710.29(c)(2) to state the intended commercial activity for inactive substances is vague about mixed activities; request guidance on how to report intended manufacture+processing+import combinations and whether multiple intended activities require multiple submissions.

[P22] § 710.29(c)(3)’s requirement to provide the actual date by which the inactive substance will be manufactured/imported/processed is too rigid — commenters suggest allowing an intended date range or a “within X days” estimate to accommodate supply chain variability.

[P23] § 710.29(d) lists company, contact, and chemical-specific information but does not address privacy concerns for personal contact information; commenters request that personal mobile numbers be optional and a secure contact mechanism be provided.

[P24] § 710.29(d)(1) requires the name of the submitting company but does not account for distributors submitting on behalf of multiple principals; request allowance to list both submitting entity and principal owner of the activity.

[P25] § 710.29(d)(2) requires name and address of an authorized official — legal experts note potential liability exposure and request clarity on who qualifies as an “authorized official” and whether a corporate officer’s signature can be electronically delegated.

[P26] The technical contact requirement in § 710.29(d)(3) to provide telephone numbers able to answer questions is reasonable, but EPA should permit email-first contact and specify business hours/time zone expectations.

[P27] § 710.29(d)(4) requires correct CA Index name and CASRN, but CASRNs may not exist for certain UVCBs or confidential substances; request guidance for reporting such substances (e.g., use of TSCA Accession Number or provisional identifiers).

[P28] The importer-supplier joint-submission process described in § 710.29(d)(4)(i) is impracticable when suppliers are foreign and unwilling to share confidential identities; request creation of a secure, brokered submission process and explicit safe harbor for importers who follow the “ask supplier” procedure but receive no supplier cooperation.

[P29] Similarly, § 710.29(d)(4)(ii) requiring manufacturers/processors to request suppliers to provide confidential reactant identity directly to EPA could expose suppliers’ confidential business information outside contractual protections; request an alternative in which suppliers can provide information under a confidentiality protective agreement.

[P30] The electronic-only joint submissions condition in § 710.29(d)(4)(iii) unfairly penalizes small foreign suppliers without access to EPA systems; request an exception allowing third-party service providers or authorized representatives to submit on suppliers’ behalf.

[P31] § 710.29(d)(5) requires certification that submissions are complete and confidentiality claims are true “under penalty of law” — legal counsel requests more precise language about criminal vs. civil penalties and a statement of intent standard (good faith) for legacy reporting.

[P32] The signature and date requirement in § 710.29(d)(5)(i) for the authorized official should allow electronically authenticated signatures via EPA’s CDX system rather than wet signatures to enable timely filings.

[P33] The mandated certification language in § 710.29(d)(5)(ii) is overly broad; request modification to permit certification attesting to “best knowledge, information, and belief” to avoid liability for inadvertent historical record errors.

[P34] § 710.30(a) requires submission within the “applicable submission period” but the proposed start dates tied to publication are undefined here; stakeholders request explicit calendar deadlines in the final rule (e.g., 180 days from publication is X date) to plan compliance.

[P35] The manufacturer submission window in § 710.30(a)(1) (publication to 180 days after) is too short for entities with decentralized record systems and overseas subsidiaries; recommend extending to 270–365 days for manufacturers.

[P36] The processor submission window in § 710.30(a)(2) (publication to 360 days after) may be adequate, but EPA should allow staggered submissions for large processors with many sites and substances to avoid system overload and compliance errors.

[P37] § 710.30(b) requires Form B submission no more than 30 days prior to the actual date; this 30-day maximum may be problematic for planned multi-month contracts and long-lead-time imports — ask EPA to allow earlier notifications (e.g., up to 180 days) with an option to update the date.

[P38] § 710.33(a) allowing parties to decide who will submit Form A is helpful, but the condition that EPA will hold each qualifier liable if no notice is submitted (§ 710.33(a) condition) creates duplicative risk; request EPA to adopt a safe-harbor mechanism for cooperating parties who document the agreed reporter.

[P39] The liability provision in § 710.33(a) that “EPA will hold each such person liable” if no notice is submitted is harsh when parties have good-faith agreements; legal commentators urge EPA to adopt a “first-filed” safe harbor or the ability to reassign liability when evidence shows a different party filed.

[P40] § 710.33(b) similarly allows parties to decide who will submit Form B, but the residual liability for all persons if no notice is submitted (per § 710.33(b) condition) may deter cooperative agreements; recommend a joint reporting plan template EPA will accept to limit exposure.

[P41] § 710.35’s record-retention obligation should permit electronic recordkeeping and require EPA to issue clear acceptable formats (PDF, CSV, etc.); otherwise, firms may be punished for using agency-standard record systems.

[P42] The 5-year retention period in § 710.35 for Form A records (beginning last day of submission period) may be insufficient for substances with long latent effects; public health advocates recommend a 10-year retention minimum or retention tied to the substance’s regulatory review lifecycle.

[P43] Similarly, the 5-year retention period in § 710.35 for Form B records beginning the day the notice was submitted should be extended to 7–10 years to align with other EPA/OSHA recordkeeping regimes.

[P44] § 710.37(a)’s limitation that an existing confidentiality claim for specific chemical identity may be maintained only if it is listed as confidential on the Inventory “at time of submission” unfairly penalizes firms who relied on pending petitions; request that the rule allow maintenance of claims if they were confidential at any time during the lookback period.

[P45] The requirement in § 710.37(a) that confidentiality maintenance requests be made at time of submission is administratively burdensome when supplier identity is unknown until after initial filing; ask EPA to permit follow-up substantiation within a reasonable window (e.g., 60 days) without losing protection.

[P46] § 710.37(a) condition that no request to maintain confidentiality results in moving the identity to the public Inventory is a significant commercial risk; industry requests that EPA notify affected claimants and provide an appeal window before making identities public.

[P47] The multi-step requirements in § 710.37(a)(1)(i)–(ii) for maintaining confidentiality (early answers and 30-day substantiation) create conflicting timelines with Form B’s 30-day submission rule; request harmonization to avoid impossible compliance (e.g., needing substantiation before filing Form B).

[P48] The rule’s provision in § 710.37(a)(1)(i) that early answers received within five years of the substantiation due date will be deemed substantiations is ambiguous — request explicit definition of “received” (EPA’s inbound date vs. submission transmission time) and what constitutes “required detail.”

[P49] The 30-day deadline in § 710.37(a)(1)(ii) to submit detailed substantiation is unrealistic for confidential business information requiring legal review and internal approvals; request extension to 90 days or allowance for staged substantiation with a good-faith attestation.

[P50] The consequence in § 710.37(a)(1)(ii) that failure to substantiate within 30 days results in treating identity as not confidential is severe — request a cure period and notification from EPA before public disclosure.

[P51] § 710.37(a)(2) requires marking any asserted confidential information in substantiation answers; confidentiality advocates request clear labeling protocols and examples to avoid inadvertent public disclosure of sensitive trade secrets.

[P52] The allowance in § 710.37(a)(1)(i) to submit early detailed written answers “signed and dated by an authorized official” should permit electronically signed submissions and designate acceptable signature authentication procedures.

[P53] § 710.37(b) permits confidentiality claims for non-identity information only if claims are made at time of submission — commenters request that EPA allow amendment of confidentiality claims within a short window (e.g., 14 days) when new information emerges.

[P54] The prohibition in § 710.37(b) against claiming confidentiality for fields left blank or marked unknown is reasonable but could penalize reporters who in good faith lack historical data; request a mechanism to assert “confidential limited access” for unknown fields with documentation of attempts to obtain the information.

[P55] The procedural substantiation steps in § 710.37(b) are extensive; small businesses will need standardized templates and clear examples from EPA to comply — request that EPA release sample substantiations and a pre-submission review option.

[P56] § 710.37(b)(1) mandates detailed written substantiation answers at time of submission signed by an authorized official — legal experts caution that making signatory personally liable without safe harbor could chill legitimate confidentiality claims; ask for limited liability if claims are made in good faith and later overturned.

[P57] The rule lacks an explicit confidential treatment timeline or process for EPA review of confidentiality substantiations; commenters request EPA to state target review timelines (e.g., 180 days) and an interlocutory stay of public posting during review to avoid premature disclosures.

[P58] Environmental and public-interest groups will object if § 710.37 permits undue delay in moving identities to the public Inventory; request that EPA default to public disclosure if substantiation is not compelling and publish a redaction-only policy when necessary for personal data.

[P59] The interplay between joint submissions (§ 710.29(d)(4)(i)-(iii)) and confidentiality substantiation creates potential for suppliers to refuse cooperation and strategically force disclosure by importers; request EPA to adopt a mediation process and enforcement tools to require supplier cooperation when reasonably requested.

[P60] The proposed rule does not discuss penalties or enforcement discretion for minor or clerical errors in submissions (e.g., transposed dates in § 710.29(b)(3)); request that EPA adopt a cure process allowing corrected resubmissions within a set time without penalty.

[P61] Consumer product manufacturers request an explicit safe harbor clarification that reporting obligations under this subpart do not duplicate obligations under other TSCA sections (e.g., premanufacture notices), and request cross-references to avoid double reporting.

[P62] Small entities request that EPA conduct a final regulatory flexibility analysis and provide compliance assistance materials (webinars, checklists, template forms) before the compliance windows in § 710.30(a)(1)-(2) open.

[P63] Legal commenters note that the certification penalty language (§ 710.29(d)(5)(ii)) should be harmonized with the Paperwork Reduction Act requirements and request EPA estimate per-submission burdens and include OMB control numbers in the final rule.

[P64] The rule should explicitly state whether substances covered only by the outdated or superseded CA Index names must be reported with current Inventory names per § 710.29(d)(4) or if aliases are acceptable; industry requests an alias mapping table from EPA.

[P65] Public health organizations ask EPA to require reporting of downstream use categories or functional use in § 710.29(d) submissions to support exposure assessment rather than limiting chemical-specific identity only.
