§ 710.33(b) similarly allows parties to decide who will submit Form B, but the residual liability for all persons if no notice is submitted (per § 710.33(b) condition) may deter cooperative agreements; recommend a joint reporting plan template EPA will accept to limit exposure.

§ 710.35’s record-retention obligation should permit electronic recordkeeping and require EPA to issue clear acceptable formats (PDF, CSV, etc.); otherwise, firms may be punished for using agency-standard record systems.

The 5-year retention period in § 710.35 for Form A records (beginning last day of submission period) may be insufficient for substances with long latent effects; public health advocates recommend a 10-year retention minimum or retention tied to the substance’s regulatory review lifecycle.
Similarly, the 5-year retention period in § 710.35 for Form B records beginning the day the notice was submitted should be extended to 7–10 years to align with other EPA/OSHA recordkeeping regimes.

§ 710.37(a)’s limitation that an existing confidentiality claim for specific chemical identity may be maintained only if it is listed as confidential on the Inventory “at time of submission” unfairly penalizes firms who relied on pending petitions; request that the rule allow maintenance of claims if they were confidential at any time during the lookback period.

The requirement in § 710.37(a) that confidentiality maintenance requests be made at time of submission is administratively burdensome when supplier identity is unknown until after initial filing; ask EPA to permit follow-up substantiation within a reasonable window (e.g., 60 days) without losing protection.

§ 710.37(a) condition that no request to maintain confidentiality results in moving the identity to the public Inventory is a significant commercial risk; industry requests that EPA notify affected claimants and provide an appeal window before making identities public.

The multi-step requirements in § 710.37(a)(1)(i)–(ii) for maintaining confidentiality (early answers and 30-day substantiation) create conflicting timelines with Form B’s 30-day submission rule; request harmonization to avoid impossible compliance (e.g., needing substantiation before filing Form B).

The rule’s provision in § 710.37(a)(1)(i) that early answers received within five years of the substantiation due date will be deemed substantiations is ambiguous — request explicit definition of “received” (EPA’s inbound date vs. submission transmission time) and what constitutes “required detail.”

The 30-day deadline in § 710.37(a)(1)(ii) to submit detailed substantiation is unrealistic for confidential business information requiring legal review and internal approvals; request extension to 90 days or allowance for staged substantiation with a good-faith attestation.

The consequence in § 710.37(a)(1)(ii) that failure to substantiate within 30 days results in treating identity as not confidential is severe — request a cure period and notification from EPA before public disclosure.

§ 710.37(a)(2) requires marking any asserted confidential information in substantiation answers; confidentiality advocates request clear labeling protocols and examples to avoid inadvertent public disclosure of sensitive trade secrets.

The allowance in § 710.37(a)(1)(i) to submit early detailed written answers “signed and dated by an authorized official” should permit electronically signed submissions and designate acceptable signature authentication procedures.

§ 710.37(b) permits confidentiality claims for non-identity information only if claims are made at time of submission — commenters request that EPA allow amendment of confidentiality claims within a short window (e.g., 14 days) when new information emerges.

The prohibition in § 710.37(b) against claiming confidentiality for fields left blank or marked unknown is reasonable but could penalize reporters who in good faith lack historical data; request a mechanism to assert “confidential limited access” for unknown fields with documentation of attempts to obtain the information.

The procedural substantiation steps in § 710.37(b) are extensive; small businesses will need standardized templates and clear examples from EPA to comply — request that EPA release sample substantiations and a pre-submission review option.

§ 710.37(b)(1) mandates detailed written substantiation answers at time of submission signed by an authorized official — legal experts caution that making signatory personally liable without safe harbor could chill legitimate confidentiality claims; ask for limited liability if claims are made in good faith and later overturned.

The rule lacks an explicit confidential treatment timeline or process for EPA review of confidentiality substantiations; commenters request EPA to state target review timelines (e.g., 180 days) and an interlocutory stay of public posting during review to avoid premature disclosures.

Environmental and public-interest groups will object if § 710.37 permits undue delay in moving identities to the public Inventory; request that EPA default to public disclosure if substantiation is not compelling and publish a redaction-only policy when necessary for personal data.

The interplay between joint submissions (§ 710.29(d)(4)(i)-(iii)) and confidentiality substantiation creates potential for suppliers to refuse cooperation and strategically force disclosure by importers; request EPA to adopt a mediation process and enforcement tools to require supplier cooperation when reasonably requested.

The proposed rule does not discuss penalties or enforcement discretion for minor or clerical errors in submissions (e.g., transposed dates in § 710.29(b)(3)); request that EPA adopt a cure process allowing corrected resubmissions within a set time without penalty.

Consumer product manufacturers request an explicit safe harbor clarification that reporting obligations under this subpart do not duplicate obligations under other TSCA sections (e.g., premanufacture notices), and request cross-references to avoid double reporting.

Small entities request that EPA conduct a final regulatory flexibility analysis and provide compliance assistance materials (webinars, checklists, template forms) before the compliance windows in § 710.30(a)(1)-(2) open.

Legal commenters note that the certification penalty language (§ 710.29(d)(5)(ii)) should be harmonized with the Paperwork Reduction Act requirements and request EPA estimate per-submission burdens and include OMB control numbers in the final rule.

The rule should explicitly state whether substances covered only by the outdated or superseded CA Index names must be reported with current Inventory names per § 710.29(d)(4) or if aliases are acceptable; industry requests an alias mapping table from EPA.

Public health organizations ask EPA to require reporting of downstream use categories or functional use in § 710.29(d) submissions to support exposure assessment rather than limiting chemical-specific identity only.

[P1] The October 12, 2017 comments due date is unreasonably short and does not provide sufficient time for international stakeholders and small carriers to prepare substantive comments; extend the deadline by at least 60 days.

[P1] Requiring that "We must receive comments by October 12, 2017" without clarifying postmark vs. receipt creates legal uncertainty; specify whether comments postmarked by that date but received later will be accepted.

[P2] The compliance obligation is ambiguous about operators who have partially complied; clarify whether partial completion of referenced tasks counts as "already complied with."

[P3] The 72-month compliance window for inspecting for mask P/N MLD20–626–1 is overly long for a safety-related issue affecting crew oxygen equipment; require a shorter inspection interval (e.g., 90–180 days).

[P3] The applicability clause tying the inspection requirement to airplanes with original certificates issued on or before the AD effective date is unclear—request clarification whether aircraft that had certificates reissued or amended after the effective date are included.

[P4] The option to use maintenance-records review in lieu of physical inspection should require specific record elements (date installed, P/N, serial number, maintenance action signature/date) to ensure conclusiveness; without this, records review may be unreliable.

[P4] Allowing records review "if the part number can be conclusively determined" places an undue burden on small operators with decentralized recordkeeping; propose alternative acceptable evidence (supplier invoices, OEM shipping records).

[P5] Requiring completion of all applicable 'RC' actions within 72 months if the prohibited mask is found fails to identify what "all applicable" means and whether partial compliance is permitted; require detailed compliance steps and interim mitigation options.

[P5] The AD should require immediate removal or grounding upon discovery of P/N MLD20–626–1 rather than allowing up to 72 months to complete RC actions given the potential safety risk.

[P6] The prohibition on installing P/N MLD20–626–1 "as of the effective date" should include a grandfathering clause for masks installed as spares in sealed packaging with traceable provenance, or permit use if proven airworthiness through testing.

[P6] The parts-installation prohibition lacks guidance on disposition of existing stock and vendor obligations—request provisions for return, quarantine, or reimbursement to suppliers and operators.

[P7] Concentrating AMOC approval authority solely with the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch may create bottlenecks; permit delegation to regional ACOs or provide expected processing timelines to avoid operational delays.

[P8] Requiring AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO may be inappropriate for certificate holders whose principal inspector lacks expertise in Boeing/oxygen-mask issues; allow direct submission to the Seattle ACO as an alternative.

[P9] The cross-reference to paragraph (j)(1) for the certification office manager creates procedural complexity if paragraph (j)(1) is changed; recommend including the actual name/position and contact information within paragraph (i)(1) to avoid ambiguity.

[P10] Allowing AMOC information to be emailed to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov raises security and proprietary data concerns; require an encrypted submission option or secure portal and confirm receipt/acknowledgment procedures.

[P11] The obligation to notify the principal inspector or FSDO manager before using an approved AMOC should define a timeframe (e.g., within 24 or 48 hours) and the required notification content; without this, compliance may be inconsistent.

[P12] Allowing an AMOC approved by the Boeing ODA to be used is acceptable, but the rule must require FAA concurrence or documentation of the ODA’s authority and provide transparency about the ODA approval criteria.

[P13] Requiring that any repair/modification deviation meet the airplane's certification basis and specifically reference this AD is appropriate, but the rule should provide a process for updating documentation when the certification basis has been amended.

[P14] Requiring all steps labeled RC (including figures) to be performed as written may be impractical for operators with alternate tooling or access constraints; allow minor non-substantive deviations (e.g., alternate torque tools) without needing an AMOC, if validated by engineering data.

[P15] The RC Exempt exception is useful, but the AD must clearly list which steps are RC Exempt in the service bulletin or the AD itself; otherwise operators cannot reliably identify exemptions.

[P16] Requiring an AMOC for any deviation to RC steps—even for typographical errors or minor non-safety changes—will overwhelm the AMOC process; distinguish between substantive safety-related deviations (require AMOC) and editorial/administrative errors (permit local correction with recordkeeping).

[P17] The permission to deviate from non-RC steps via accepted methods in the operator's program should require the operator to document the deviation rationale and retain records for FAA inspection; otherwise oversight will be hindered.

[P17] Clarify what constitutes "acceptable methods" under an operator’s program for non-RC deviations—reference specific maintenance program standards (e.g., 14 CFR part 121/145 policies) to avoid inconsistent application.

[P18] The duplicate listing of the October 12, 2017 comment deadline in the VOR airways NPRM section could cause confusion for commenters—consolidate and harmonize deadlines across documents.

[P19] The ADDRESSES requirement to send comments to the Docket Operations physical address should include instructions for handling confidential/privileged material and an option for secure electronic submission beyond regulations.gov.

[P20] Requiring commenters to identify both FAA and Airspace docket numbers at the beginning of comments is reasonable, but provide an explicit template or sample header to prevent misfiling.

[P21] While permitting electronic comments via regulations.gov is helpful, the AD should state whether large technical appendices or supporting datasets can be submitted via alternative electronic means and how to reference them in the docket.

[P22] The permission to review the public docket in person at the Dockets Office should include hours for persons outside the Washington, DC area and whether appointments are required; clarify accessibility for persons with disabilities.

[P23] The provision to view FAA Order 7400.11A online is useful, but the AD should cite the specific version/date of the Order and a permanent URL or DOI to avoid confusion if the page is updated.

[P24] The contact information for the Airspace Policy Group should include alternative contacts (email/phone) for technical questions outside normal business hours and for stakeholders in different time zones.

[P25] Making the Order available at NARA is compliant with recordkeeping, but the AD should state whether there is a fee for NARA inspection/copies and provide guidance for remote access to the Order.

[P26] The invitation to submit written data, views, or arguments should explicitly welcome alternative compliance proposals backed by data (e.g., safety assessments, cost-benefit analyses) and clarify evaluation criteria.

[P27] The AD’s solicitation for comments on environmental and energy-related aspects should request more specific guidance on the scope of environmental analysis expected from commenters (e.g., noise, emissions, hazardous materials disposal of removed parts).

[P28] Requiring that communications be submitted in triplicate to the Docket Management Facility is outdated given electronic filing; allow single electronic submissions via regulations.gov to satisfy the triplicate requirement.

[P3] The applicability limiting inspection to airplanes with original certificates issued on or before the AD effective date could be interpreted to exclude imported or re-exported aircraft; clarify applicability to avoid inadvertent noncompliance by international operators.

[P6] Prohibiting installation of P/N MLD20–626–1 "on any airplane" should clarify whether this includes non-flight operations (training rigs, simulators) and whether installation for non-operational purposes is allowed.

[P5] The AD should require operators who find the prohibited mask to report the finding to the FAA and Boeing (including quantity and serial numbers) within a specified timeframe to support fleet-wide safety tracking.

[P10] Provide an expected response timeframe for emailed AMOC submissions and require automated acknowledgment of receipt to prevent lost submissions.

[P12] If Boeing ODA approvals are accepted, require public disclosure of the ODA approval documents in the docket (redacted as necessary) so that other operators can rely on the precedent.

[P14] Require that any required RC steps that reference figures include CAD-readable figures or dimensioned drawings in the service bulletin so operators can verify compliance; blurry or low-detail figures are insufficient.

[P4] When permitting records review in lieu of physical inspection, the AD should require an independent audit or spot physical verification by a qualified inspector for a sample of aircraft to validate records accuracy.

[P11] The notification requirement before using an AMOC should state whether the notification must be prior to the work start date or prior to the first flight using the AMOC remedy; ambiguity could lead to inadvertent noncompliance.

[P16] Provide expedited AMOC pathways for operators proposing time-limited deviations necessary to maintain operations (e.g., parts scarcity) if accompanied by temporary mitigations and risk assessments.

[P6] Clarify whether the parts-installation prohibition applies to maintenance performed under foreign regulatory approvals where the foreign authority has not adopted this AD; provide guidance for coordination.

[P5] The AD should include instructions for labeling or placarding aircraft where prohibited masks are found and pending completion of RC actions, to prevent inadvertent reuse during maintenance.

[P2] Clarify whether compliance times specified elsewhere in referenced service bulletins prevail over the AD-specified compliance table if there is a conflict, and provide a conflict-resolution rule.

[P14] Require that any RC-designated task that involves consumable parts explicitly list approved part numbers and suppliers, to avoid delays while operators verify acceptable parts.

[P21] For electronic submissions via regulations.gov, provide guidance on acceptable file types and maximum file sizes for technical attachments relevant to this AD to avoid rejection of comments.

[P26] Encourage submission of operational data (flight hours, cycles) to support any proposed alternative compliance timelines and state how the FAA will weigh such operational data in its decision-making.

[P13] Define what constitutes meeting the airplane’s "certification basis" for older aircraft with multiple amendments—require referencing specific amendments or showing equivalence analysis.

[P15] Require that the service bulletin explicitly mark which steps are "RC Exempt" and explain the rationale for exempt status to help operators prioritize work.

[P3] Confirm whether the 72-month clock for inspection starts from the AD effective date for all operators equally, including those who may receive notification later (e.g., due to international mailing delays), or whether operators will be given an alternative compliance window from receipt of the AD.

[P1] The deadline to receive comments by December 9, 2019 is inconsistent with later-stated November 2020/May 7, 2021 comment deadlines (see P16); please clarify which public-comment due date applies and re-notice if necessary.

[P16] The May 7, 2021 comment deadline conflicts with the December 9, 2019 date in § 39.13(a); this creates legal uncertainty about the required comment period and should be corrected before adoption.

[P2] The statement “Comply with the AD within the specified compliance times unless already complied” lacks an explicit statement about credit for previous corrective actions documented under approved repair schemes; the rule should expressly allow documented earlier compliance as meeting requirements.

[P17] The duplicative obligations in P2 and P17 create redundancy and potential inconsistency; consolidate language so operators know whether these are separate obligations or identical restatements.

[P3] Requiring removal within 50 cycles after July 5, 2019 or before further flight (whichever later) for seals with ≥7,000 cycles since reconfiguration is unworkable for in-service fleets because it effectively mandates immediate removals with inadequate logistics lead time; extend the window to allow scheduled maintenance planning.

[P19] The July 5, 2019 effective date reference in (g)(1)(i) is obsolete for operators who discovered the AD later; the FAA should provide a procedure to rebase compliance times to the actual AD effective date or the date of engine/operator notification.

[P4] The 500-cycle window for seals with 6,001–6,999 cycles is too short for many carriers and MROs to source eligible replacement parts and perform shop visits; request extension to at least 1,500 cycles or allow phased compliance with documented parts availability.

[P20] The cap of “not past 7,050 cycles since reconfiguration” is ambiguous—please clarify whether the 7,050-cycle cap applies to the 500-cycle window only or also to prolonged operation under AMOCs.

[P5] The blanket requirement to remove seals before 6,500 cycles (for –5B/–7B) irrespective of engine usage profile or inspection findings may be overly conservative; propose allowing condition-based removal if nondestructive inspection demonstrates acceptable integrity.

[P21] The requirement to remove seals before 6,500 cycles or within 50 cycles after the AD effective date fails to provide a transition allowance for engines on long-term lease or in storage; ask FAA to add exceptions for engines not in commercial service.

[P6] For CFM56–5C engines, requiring removal within 25 cycles for seals ≥4,250 cycles since reconfiguration (g)(2)(i) is infeasible for international operators not notified promptly; propose harmonization with international authorities and a minimum 90-day compliance window.

[P23] The multiple alternative timings in (g)(2)(i) (“within 25 cycles, within 1,500 cycles since last FPI, or before further flight...whichever later”) are confusing and could be interpreted inconsistently by inspectors; request clear, prioritized sequencing and examples.

[P7] For seals with 3,751–4,249 cycles requiring removal within 250 cycles (g)(2)(ii), the rule should clarify how to account for cycles on loaned engines or engines with incomplete maintenance records.

[P24] The clause “within 1,500 cycles since last FPI” in (g)(2)(ii) is inappropriate without defining “last FPI” (first piece inspection?)—provide a definition and acceptable record sources to establish the FPI date.

[P8] The requirement to remove CFM56–5C seals before 4,000 cycles or within 50 cycles after the AD effective date (g)(2)(iii) could force AOG situations for carriers with multiple affected spare engines; request allowance for temporary deviations when safety can be ensured.

[P25] The uniform cycle thresholds (4,000 for –5C; 6,500 for –5B/–7B) appear arbitrary in the absence of supporting damage-tolerance analysis in the docket; provide and justify the risk assessment and failure-rate data underlying these thresholds.

[P9] The prohibition on assembling any rotating air HPT front seal with >0 cycles on a different HPT disk (i.e., pairing seals only to original disk S/N) imposes an operational burden on MROs and the spare-parts supply chain; request an exception for reassembly following inspection demonstrating full serviceability.

[P27] The explicit prohibition tied to serial numbers (para i) will complicate parts pooling and engine shop practices worldwide; FAA should permit reassembly to a different disk if traceability and nondestructive inspections confirm no damage.

[P28] The limited exception allowing reassembly only onto the same S/N disk is impracticable where disks are replaced; request an alternate-path provision allowing transfer if documented in an approved data package and after passing prescribed inspections.

[P26] Paragraph (g)(3) requiring seals originally for –5B/–7B that have been operated in –5C to be removed per (g)(2) creates recordkeeping burdens; require operators to maintain clear engine-flow records or permit reconfiguration inspection to establish cycles on each engine model.

[P29] Empowering the Manager, ECO Branch to approve AMOCs (j)(1) is useful, but FAA should commit to a specific turnaround time for AMOC decisions (e.g., 30 days) to avoid operational disruption.

[P10] The AMOC approval permission (j)(1) lacks required content elements for a complete submittal; provide a clear checklist of the technical data and substantiation required so operators submit complete requests.

[P30] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to principal inspectors or local FSDOs per 14 CFR 39.19 (j)(1) may delay handling; permit direct submission to the ECO Branch with concurrent notification to the principal inspector to expedite technical review.

[P12] The condition that direct submissions to the certification office manager must be addressed to the person in paragraph (k)(1) is fine, but the rule should include full contact details in the regulatory text to avoid routing errors.

[P13] Allowing AMOC requests by email to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov is appropriate, but the AD should also accept encrypted or secure file transfer options for large engineering files and specify any file-size or format constraints.

[P31] The instruction to address material to the person named in Related Information when sending information directly to the certification office manager should be updated if those personnel change; include a website link for current contact information.

[P14] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC (j)(2) should allow for emergency use if the PI is unreachable, with a requirement to notify within 48 hours thereafter.

[P33] The requirement to notify the PI or, if none, local FSDO/CHDO before using an AMOC should clarify whether notification must be written, electronic, or may be verbal in urgent circumstances.

[P15] Permitting viewing of referenced service information only at the FAA Engine & Propeller Standards Branch (Burlington, MA) is impractical for non-U.S. commenters; require that referenced service documents be made available electronically in the rule docket.

The July 5, 2019 effective date reference in (g)(1)(i) is obsolete for operators who discovered the AD later; the FAA should provide a procedure to rebase compliance times to the actual AD effective date or the date of engine/operator notification.

raw_output:
[P1] The 0.10 percent by weight limit for any organic HAP in Table 5 of §63.3092(a)(2) is infeasible for standard electrodeposition primer formulations and will force reformulation or product discontinuation without realistic lead time or technical guidance.

[P1] The rule does not specify an averaging period or testing frequency for verifying the 0.10% organic HAP limit in electrodeposition primer, creating enforcement uncertainty and potential disputes over conformance.

[P1] Limiting any single organic HAP to 0.10% by weight is ambiguous as to whether trace impurities below reporting thresholds are included; EPA should clarify detection limits and rounding/truncation rules.

[P1] The provision should allow use of supplier formulation data as presumptive compliance evidence for the 0.10% organic HAP limit (as in §63.3151(a)(4)), to avoid costly confirmatory testing.

[P2] Requiring compliance with operating limits in Table 1 for any controlled coating operation without defining “controlled coating operation” in the subpart will cause interpretive disputes; request EPA to define the term clearly.

[P3] Applying the operating limits specifically to emission capture and add-on control systems (§63.3093(b)) will impose significant retrofitting costs for facilities whose capture systems were sized for previous standards; request economic impact analysis and phased implementation.

[P4] Mandating that operating limits be set only through performance testing per §63.3167 is overly rigid — small facilities should be allowed to use engineering assessments, manufacturer specifications, or equivalent demonstrated methods when testing is impractical.

[P5] Requiring continuous adherence to established operating limits “at all times after you establish them” (no allowance for transient deviations) is unduly strict and could lead to enforcement for brief, unavoidable excursions; recommend a de minimis allowance or cure period.

[P6] The compliance date scheme in §63.3100(b) (181 days after publication) is too short for facilities that need to install add-on control or capture modifications to meet Table 1 limits; request at least 12–24 months and a phased schedule tied to facility size.

[P7] Allowing startup/shutdown/malfunction (SSM) exceptions prior to the compliance date but removing them after the compliance date (§63.3100(b) & (d)) creates regulatory cliffs and incentives to delay necessary improvements; suggest retaining appropriately tailored SSM provisions or transition relief.

[P8] The elimination of the SSM defense on and after the compliance date (§63.3100(b) and (d)) conflicts with §63.6(e)(1)(i) and safety requirements — operators may need to temporarily deviate for safety reasons; recommend explicit narrow emergency exception for safety.

[P9] The requirement to operate and maintain affected sources per §63.6(e)(1)(i) before the date (§63.3100(d)) duplicates existing obligations and should be cross-referenced rather than restated; suggest harmonizing to avoid conflicting language.

[P10] Requiring operation and maintenance “consistent with safety and good air pollution control practices” after the date (§63.3100(d)) is subjective and could be interpreted inconsistently; request elaboration or illustrative examples of acceptable practices.

[P11] The carve-out in §63.3100(d) that once emission levels required by the standard are achieved no further efforts are required (P12) could be read to bar continuous improvement and is inconsistent with the general duty to minimize emissions; recommend rewording to say “no additional beyond-the-standard measures are required, provided the owner/operator continues to maintain required practices.”

[P13] The SSMP requirement prior to the date (§63.3100(f)) imposes burdens on small sources that use capture systems and add-on devices; suggest a de minimis exemption for small facilities or an abbreviated SSMP template.

[P14] Requiring SSMPs to follow §63.6(e)(3) (§63.3100(f)) may be inappropriate for coating operations with unique process characteristics; request flexibility to tailor SSMP content to specific capture/control technology.

[P15] The proposed SSMP element requiring corrective actions for malfunctions of capture/control equipment (§63.3100(f)) lacks specificity on acceptable corrective timelines and documentation; recommend defining expected response times and recordkeeping.

[P16] Removing the SSMP requirement on and after the compliance date (§63.3100(f) exception) (i.e., discontinuing SSMP) could reduce operational transparency and weaken readiness for malfunctions; ask EPA to justify why SSMPs are no longer necessary and consider retaining at least a simplified plan requirement.

[P17] Semiannual report requirement to include a statement that there were no deviations (§63.3120(a)(4)) is redundant if a full electronic submission is already required via CEDRI; request EPA to allow a checkbox or short code to reduce reporting burden.

[P18] The requirement in §63.3120(a)(4) to state that CPMS were never out-of-control, if control devices were used, should permit reliance on CPMS calibration/validation logs and exclude brief instrument anomalies that do not indicate loss of control.

[P19] The post-date expansion of semiannual reporting for deviations from adhesive/sealer/deadener limits (§63.3120(a)(5) new item (v)) to require counts, affected equipment, and estimated excess emissions will impose substantial estimation and recordkeeping burdens; EPA should provide standardized estimation procedures and templates.

[P20] Requiring reporting of the “reason or cause (or unknown)” for each deviation (§63.3120(a)(5)(iv), (a)(7)(iii), (a)(8)(xii)) will lead to speculative cause assignments; suggest allowing “under investigation” status for initial reports and an update within a defined period.

[P21] New after-date requirement to report counts, affected equipment, estimated excess emissions, and estimation methods for each deviation (§63.3120(a)(5)(v), (a)(6)(xv), (a)(7)(iv), (a)(32)) is duplicative of existing recordkeeping and may risk revealing confidential business information (CBI) — EPA should allow redaction or CBI procedures and provide standardized calculation tools.

[P22] The detailed reporting of CPMS inoperative/out-of-control events with causes and corrective actions (§63.3120(a)(6)(vi)–(vii), (a)(8)(v)–(vi)) may discourage proactive maintenance if operators fear enforcement; recommend allowing a “maintenance window” category or safe harbor for documented preventive maintenance.

[P23] Requiring reporting of each bypass of add-on control devices and whether it occurred during startup/shutdown/malfunction (§63.3120(a)(6)(viii) and (a)(8)(vii)) will capture legitimate operational bypasses for maintenance; request that temporary, documented maintenance bypasses be excluded from enforcement if pre-authorized and notified.

[P24] The categorized breakdown of total duration of deviations/bypasses by cause categories (§63.3120(a)(6)(x) and (a)(8)(ix)) uses different categories before and after the date — EPA should harmonize categories and provide guidance to ensure consistent reporting across facilities and time.

[P25] Reporting requirements for deviations from work practice standards (§63.3120(a)(6)(xiii), (a)(9)) that expand after the date to include counts and affected equipment will be administratively burdensome; suggest allowing facilities to submit aggregated data for repetitive minor deviations.

[P26] The requirement that deviation descriptions include “actions taken to minimize emissions per §63.3100(d)” (§63.3120(a)(6)(xiii)(A), (a)(29)) is subjective and will lead to inconsistent enforcement; request standardized examples of acceptable minimization actions.

[P27] Semiannual reporting of performance test results via electronic formats (CEDRI/ERT/XML) (§63.3120(d)(1)-(3)) is acceptable in principle, but EPA must provide sufficient lead time, training, and testing of templates to avoid submission errors and inadvertent noncompliance.

[P28] The requirement to submit full CBI-containing electronic files on a physical medium to the EPA CBI Office (§63.3120(d)(3), (e)(3), (f)(59)) is burdensome and anachronistic; request allowance for secure electronic CBI transmission protocols rather than physical media.

[P29] Mandating initial notifications and notifications of compliance status via CEDRI on and after the date (§63.3120(e)) may disadvantage facilities in regions with limited internet access or IT capacity; request alternative electronic submission options or a waiver process.

[P30] The rule’s requirement that once the CEDRI template has been available for 1 year all subsequent semiannual reports must be submitted via CEDRI (§63.3120(f),(57)) fails to consider updates/interruptions to templates — EPA should allow temporary paper or email submission when CEDRI is undergoing maintenance.

[P31] The option to assert EPA system outage to justify late reporting (§63.3120(g)) places a heavy documentation burden on the facility to prove the outage; recommend EPA publish a straightforward outage verification process or accept EPA outage notices as presumptive proof.

[P32] Requirements to notify the Administrator in writing “as soon as possible” when asserting EPA outage or force majeure (§63.3120(g),(h)) are vague; EPA should define specific timeframes (e.g., within 7 calendar days) to ensure fairness.

[P33] The force majeure provision (§63.3120(h)) that leaves acceptance of the claim to the Administrator’s discretion creates legal uncertainty — commenters request objective criteria for acceptance and an appeal process.

[P34] The recordkeeping requirements to retain estimates of excess emissions and the method used (§63.3130(g)(3)) demand technical expertise and may require third-party consultants; EPA should provide default estimation methodologies to reduce costs and improve consistency.

[P35] The required records of actions taken to minimize emissions (§63.3130(g)(4)) are nebulous—EPA should provide a non-exhaustive list of qualifying minimization actions and a template for documentation.

[P36] Allowing records submitted via CEDRI to be kept electronically (§63.3130(p)) is reasonable, but requiring physical availability during on-site evaluations (§63.3130(p)) may be burdensome if access to the electronic system is limited; recommend allowance for remote access or provision of printed copies upon request within a defined timeframe.

[P37] The obligation to make electronic records available to delegated agencies during on-site compliance evaluations (§63.3130(p),(77)) raises cybersecurity and confidentiality concerns—EPA should specify secure access protocols and limits on copying.

[P38] The requirement to count and report organic HAPs present at 0.1% and 1.0% and to truncate mass fractions to four decimal places (§63.3151(a)(1)(i)) is precise but may be inconsistent with laboratory detection limits; request rounding conventions and minimum detection limits be specified.

[P39] Permitting use of EPA Method 24 or ASTM D2369–10 as substitutes for organic HAP mass fraction for coatings (§63.3151(a)(2)) is appropriate, but EPA should clarify when VOC-based proxies are not acceptable (e.g., for HAPs with low volatility).

[P40] Allowing reliance on supplier/manufacturer formulation data (§63.3151(a)(4)) is necessary, but the provision that testing prevails unless the facility convinces the enforcement authority otherwise sets an impractical burden on facilities; suggest a rebuttable presumption framework where supplier data is presumed accurate unless objective evidence indicates otherwise.

[P41] The density determination requirement using ASTM D1475–13 (§63.3151(b)) will require batch-level testing for some materials; EPA should allow use of manufacturer-stated densities if accompanied by a supplier certification to reduce testing burden.

[P42] The rule lacks explicit procedures for how to estimate “quantity of each regulated pollutant emitted over any applicable emission limit” for short-duration deviations (§63.3130(g)(3), §63.3120(a)(6)(xv)), which will lead to inconsistent methods and enforcement — request EPA provide calculation examples and spreadsheets.

[P43] The new heavy reliance on electronic reporting (CEDRI/CDX) across many provisions (§63.3120(d),(e),(f),(g),(h),(52–57)) raises data security and reliability concerns; EPA should include requirements for data encryption, authentication, and data retention policies.

[P44] The regulatory text does not specify whether deviations and associated excess emissions must be reported gross or net of baseline emissions controls; clarify whether reported excess emissions should reflect control device performance reductions.

[P45] Several provisions require reporting of “unknown cause” for deviations (§63.3120(a)(5)(iv), (a)(7)(iii), (a)(8)(xii)), which could be interpreted to penalize facilities that cannot immediately determine cause — recommend allowing interim “investigation pending” status and final follow-up within a reasonable period.

[P46] The cumulative effect of expanded reporting, testing, and recordkeeping (many provisions) will disproportionately impact small businesses, and EPA should include a small entity compliance guide, model templates, and potential reduced reporting frequencies for low-risk sources.

[P47] Legal commenters: The combination of absolute product formulation limits (P1) and rigorous mandatory performance testing (P4) could be challenged as arbitrary and capricious if EPA has not demonstrated that the 0.10% limit is technologically and economically achievable across the sector; request EPA include the technical basis and economic feasibility analysis in the record.

[P48] Industry commenters: The requirement to report estimated excess emissions and the method used (multiple provisions) could expose companies to third-party litigation and should be limited to regulatory enforcement use or CBI protection.

[P49] Environmental advocacy commenters: The removal of SSM exceptions after the compliance date (P8) is appropriate and necessary to prevent emissions spikes; however, EPA should ensure robust monitoring and prompt public disclosure of deviations to improve accountability.

[P50] State/local air agencies: The rule’s electronic reporting mandate may not be compatible with some state programs’ databases; EPA should coordinate with states to ensure data interoperability and avoid duplicative submissions.

[P51] Worker safety advocates: Prohibiting SSM exemptions post-compliance date without an explicit safety exception (P8) could create conflicts between compliance and worker safety — rule should explicitly allow immediate shutdowns for worker protection and require prompt reporting rather than treating as violations.

[P52] Technical commenters: The rule should clarify what constitutes a “malfunction” versus “start-up/shutdown” for capture and control systems (many reporting provisions reference these terms) to ensure consistent reporting.

[P53] Legal commenters: The phrase “operate and maintain... in a manner consistent with safety and good air pollution control practices” (P11) is vague and may raise due process concerns because it delegates broad discretion; request adding objective benchmarks or examples.

[P54] Trade associations: EPA should publish standard test protocols, CPMS performance specifications, and data quality objectives to support the extensive CPMS-related reporting and out-of-control criteria in the rule (multiple provisions).

[P55] Environmental justice groups: EPA should require public availability of non-CBI elements of deviation reports (counts, durations, estimated excess emissions) because cumulative impacts from repeated deviations can disproportionately affect nearby communities.

[P56] Compliance officers: The requirement to maintain records “suitable and readily available for expeditious review” (§63.3131(a)) conflicts with normal archival practices for some companies; suggest defining “expeditious” (e.g., within 3 business days) and acceptable file formats.

[P57] Manufacturers of capture/control equipment: The rule should permit use of vendor-specified performance curves and validated engineering models to establish Table 1 operating limits during performance testing (§63.3093(b),(d)), rather than forcing repeated on-site full-stack testing.

[P58] Petition: For provisions that require extensive post-date reporting (many P20–P44 entries), EPA should phase in enhanced reporting requirements over time to allow industry and states to adapt their IT systems and processes.

[P59] Request for clarification: Multiple provisions reference “date …” (181 days after publication) but do not provide concrete calendar dates in the regulatory text; EPA should include explicit compliance dates or a clear method for calculating them.

[P60] Privacy/Cybersecurity commenters: The CEDRI/C DX dissemination of detailed deviation and emissions-estimate data (many provisions) could pose security risks; EPA should implement role-based access controls and limit public display of sensitive facility-level performance data unless required by statute.

New after-date requirement to report counts, affected equipment, estimated excess emissions, and estimation methods for each deviation (§63.3120(a)(5)(v), (a)(6)(xv), (a)(7)(iv), (a)(32)) is duplicative of existing recordkeeping and may risk revealing confidential business information (CBI) — EPA should allow redaction or CBI procedures and provide standardized calculation tools.

The detailed reporting of CPMS inoperative/out-of-control events with causes and corrective actions (§63.3120(a)(6)(vi)–(vii), (a)(8)(v)–(vi)) may discourage proactive maintenance if operators fear enforcement; recommend allowing a “maintenance window” category or safe harbor for documented preventive maintenance.

Requiring reporting of each bypass of add-on control devices and whether it occurred during startup/shutdown/malfunction (§63.3120(a)(6)(viii) and (a)(8)(vii)) will capture legitimate operational bypasses for maintenance; request that temporary, documented maintenance bypasses be excluded from enforcement if pre-authorized and notified.

The categorized breakdown of total duration of deviations/bypasses by cause categories (§63.3120(a)(6)(x) and (a)(8)(ix)) uses different categories before and after the date — EPA should harmonize categories and provide guidance to ensure consistent reporting across facilities and time.

Reporting requirements for deviations from work practice standards (§63.3120(a)(6)(xiii), (a)(9)) that expand after the date to include counts and affected equipment will be administratively burdensome; suggest allowing facilities to submit aggregated data for repetitive minor deviations.

The requirement that deviation descriptions include “actions taken to minimize emissions per §63.3100(d)” (§63.3120(a)(6)(xiii)(A), (a)(29)) is subjective and will lead to inconsistent enforcement; request standardized examples of acceptable minimization actions.

Semiannual reporting of performance test results via electronic formats (CEDRI/ERT/XML) (§63.3120(d)(1)-(3)) is acceptable in principle, but EPA must provide sufficient lead time, training, and testing of templates to avoid submission errors and inadvertent noncompliance.

The requirement to submit full CBI-containing electronic files on a physical medium to the EPA CBI Office (§63.3120(d)(3), (e)(3), (f)(59)) is burdensome and anachronistic; request allowance for secure electronic CBI transmission protocols rather than physical media.

Mandating initial notifications and notifications of compliance status via CEDRI on and after the date (§63.3120(e)) may disadvantage facilities in regions with limited internet access or IT capacity; request alternative electronic submission options or a waiver process.

The rule’s requirement that once the CEDRI template has been available for 1 year all subsequent semiannual reports must be submitted via CEDRI (§63.3120(f),(57)) fails to consider updates/interruptions to templates — EPA should allow temporary paper or email submission when CEDRI is undergoing maintenance.

The option to assert EPA system outage to justify late reporting (§63.3120(g)) places a heavy documentation burden on the facility to prove the outage; recommend EPA publish a straightforward outage verification process or accept EPA outage notices as presumptive proof.

Requirements to notify the Administrator in writing “as soon as possible” when asserting EPA outage or force majeure (§63.3120(g),(h)) are vague; EPA should define specific timeframes (e.g., within 7 calendar days) to ensure fairness.

The force majeure provision (§63.3120(h)) that leaves acceptance of the claim to the Administrator’s discretion creates legal uncertainty — commenters request objective criteria for acceptance and an appeal process.

The recordkeeping requirements to retain estimates of excess emissions and the method used (§63.3130(g)(3)) demand technical expertise and may require third-party consultants; EPA should provide default estimation methodologies to reduce costs and improve consistency.
The required records of actions taken to minimize emissions (§63.3130(g)(4)) are nebulous—EPA should provide a non-exhaustive list of qualifying minimization actions and a template for documentation.

Allowing records submitted via CEDRI to be kept electronically (§63.3130(p)) is reasonable, but requiring physical availability during on-site evaluations (§63.3130(p)) may be burdensome if access to the electronic system is limited; recommend allowance for remote access or provision of printed copies upon request within a defined timeframe.

The obligation to make electronic records available to delegated agencies during on-site compliance evaluations (§63.3130(p),(77)) raises cybersecurity and confidentiality concerns—EPA should specify secure access protocols and limits on copying.

The requirement to count and report organic HAPs present at 0.1% and 1.0% and to truncate mass fractions to four decimal places (§63.3151(a)(1)(i)) is precise but may be inconsistent with laboratory detection limits; request rounding conventions and minimum detection limits be specified.

Permitting use of EPA Method 24 or ASTM D2369–10 as substitutes for organic HAP mass fraction for coatings (§63.3151(a)(2)) is appropriate, but EPA should clarify when VOC-based proxies are not acceptable (e.g., for HAPs with low volatility).

Allowing reliance on supplier/manufacturer formulation data (§63.3151(a)(4)) is necessary, but the provision that testing prevails unless the facility convinces the enforcement authority otherwise sets an impractical burden on facilities; suggest a rebuttable presumption framework where supplier data is presumed accurate unless objective evidence indicates otherwise.

The density determination requirement using ASTM D1475–13 (§63.3151(b)) will require batch-level testing for some materials; EPA should allow use of manufacturer-stated densities if accompanied by a supplier certification to reduce testing burden.

The rule lacks explicit procedures for how to estimate “quantity of each regulated pollutant emitted over any applicable emission limit” for short-duration deviations (§63.3130(g)(3), §63.3120(a)(6)(xv)), which will lead to inconsistent methods and enforcement — request EPA provide calculation examples and spreadsheets.

The new heavy reliance on electronic reporting (CEDRI/CDX) across many provisions (§63.3120(d),(e),(f),(g),(h),(52–57)) raises data security and reliability concerns; EPA should include requirements for data encryption, authentication, and data retention policies.

The regulatory text does not specify whether deviations and associated excess emissions must be reported gross or net of baseline emissions controls; clarify whether reported excess emissions should reflect control device performance reductions.

Several provisions require reporting of “unknown cause” for deviations (§63.3120(a)(5)(iv), (a)(7)(iii), (a)(8)(xii)), which could be interpreted to penalize facilities that cannot immediately determine cause — recommend allowing interim “investigation pending” status and final follow-up within a reasonable period.

The cumulative effect of expanded reporting, testing, and recordkeeping (many provisions) will disproportionately impact small businesses, and EPA should include a small entity compliance guide, model templates, and potential reduced reporting frequencies for low-risk sources.

Legal commenters: The combination of absolute product formulation limits (P1) and rigorous mandatory performance testing (P4) could be challenged as arbitrary and capricious if EPA has not demonstrated that the 0.10% limit is technologically and economically achievable across the sector; request EPA include the technical basis and economic feasibility analysis in the record.

Industry commenters: The requirement to report estimated excess emissions and the method used (multiple provisions) could expose companies to third-party litigation and should be limited to regulatory enforcement use or CBI protection.

Environmental advocacy commenters: The removal of SSM exceptions after the compliance date (P8) is appropriate and necessary to prevent emissions spikes; however, EPA should ensure robust monitoring and prompt public disclosure of deviations to improve accountability.

State/local air agencies: The rule’s electronic reporting mandate may not be compatible with some state programs’ databases; EPA should coordinate with states to ensure data interoperability and avoid duplicative submissions.

Worker safety advocates: Prohibiting SSM exemptions post-compliance date without an explicit safety exception (P8) could create conflicts between compliance and worker safety — rule should explicitly allow immediate shutdowns for worker protection and require prompt reporting rather than treating as violations.

Technical commenters: The rule should clarify what constitutes a “malfunction” versus “start-up/shutdown” for capture and control systems (many reporting provisions reference these terms) to ensure consistent reporting.

Legal commenters: The phrase “operate and maintain... in a manner consistent with safety and good air pollution control practices” (P11) is vague and may raise due process concerns because it delegates broad discretion; request adding objective benchmarks or examples.

Trade associations: EPA should publish standard test protocols, CPMS performance specifications, and data quality objectives to support the extensive CPMS-related reporting and out-of-control criteria in the rule (multiple provisions).

Environmental justice groups: EPA should require public availability of non-CBI elements of deviation reports (counts, durations, estimated excess emissions) because cumulative impacts from repeated deviations can disproportionately affect nearby communities.

Compliance officers: The requirement to maintain records “suitable and readily available for expeditious review” (§63.3131(a)) conflicts with normal archival practices for some companies; suggest defining “expeditious” (e.g., within 3 business days) and acceptable file formats.

Manufacturers of capture/control equipment: The rule should permit use of vendor-specified performance curves and validated engineering models to establish Table 1 operating limits during performance testing (§63.3093(b),(d)), rather than forcing repeated on-site full-stack testing.

Petition: For provisions that require extensive post-date reporting (many P20–P44 entries), EPA should phase in enhanced reporting requirements over time to allow industry and states to adapt their IT systems and processes.

Request for clarification: Multiple provisions reference “date …” (181 days after publication) but do not provide concrete calendar dates in the regulatory text; EPA should include explicit compliance dates or a clear method for calculating them.

Privacy/Cybersecurity commenters: The CEDRI/C DX dissemination of detailed deviation and emissions-estimate data (many provisions) could pose security risks; EPA should implement role-based access controls and limit public display of sensitive facility-level performance data unless required by statute.

raw_output:
[P1] The rule lacks specificity about the "specified components" for a required warning in §1141.10(a); stakeholders need the full text/layout requirements (font size, typeface, border, color palette) to assess compliance costs.

[P2] Requiring manufacturers to choose "one of the listed textual warning statements" (§1141.10(a)(1)) without allowing custom or updated statements limits flexibility to reflect new scientific findings and could impede public health messaging.

[P3] The statement "WARNING: Tobacco smoke can harm your children." (§1141.10(a)(1)(i)) is vague and may be challenged for insufficient causal specificity; public health advocates will argue for inclusion of explicit harms (e.g., SIDS, asthma exacerbation).

[P4] The phrase "causes fatal lung disease in nonsmokers" (§1141.10(a)(1)(ii)) could be fact-checked and litigated by industry as overstating evidence; request for citation of underlying scientific basis to support this exact wording.

[P5] The macular degeneration warning (§1141.10(a)(1)(iii)) may be seen as less salient to younger smokers; public health commenters should request rotation frequency emphasize the most impactful statements for target demographics.

[P6] The diabetes wording (§1141.10(a)(1)(iv))—"raises blood sugar"—could be misleading because type 2 diabetes is multifactorial; medical groups may request clarification that smoking increases risk rather than directly "causes" diabetes.

[P7] The amputation warning (§1141.10(a)(1)(v)) is medically specific and may require graphic depiction guidance to avoid sensationalism; manufacturers will request standards for the accompanying color graphic to prevent arbitrary FDA rejections.

[P8] Requiring the cataracts/blindness statement (§1141.10(a)(1)(vi)) without age/context may dilute impact; ophthalmology societies might request inclusion of prevalence data or specifying population risk.

[P9] The bladder cancer wording (§1141.10(a)(1)(vii)) referencing "bloody urine" could be considered unduly graphic for ads visible to children; retailers and civil liberties groups may object to graphic content in public spaces.

[P10] The erectile dysfunction warning (§1141.10(a)(1)(viii)) raises concerns about decency standards in certain advertising venues; retailers and trade groups will request exemptions for ads in family-oriented locations or clarification on "public" advertisement scope.

[P11] The head and neck cancer warning (§1141.10(a)(1)(ix)) is broad; oncological societies may request inclusion of examples (e.g., oral cancer) or evidence to support the plain-language phrasing.

[P12] The heart disease and stroke wording (§1141.10(a)(1)(x)) uses "clogging arteries" which is colloquial; medical stakeholders may request technically accurate alternatives to avoid confusion and legal challenges.

[P13] The pregnancy/fetal growth warning (§1141.10(a)(1)(xi)) could conflict with state pregnancy anti-discrimination policies or lead to stigmatization; maternal health advocates may request supportive cessation resource referrals be required alongside this warning.

[P14] The COPD fatality warning (§1141.10(a)(1)(xii)) may be redundant with other statements; industry will argue for limiting the number of rotating warnings to reduce packaging complexity and inventory burdens.

[P15] Requiring a color graphic to accompany each textual warning (§1141.10(a)(2)) dramatically increases printing costs and complicates production lines; small manufacturers request a phased compliance timeline or monetary impact assessment.

[P16] Mandatory reproduction "exactly from the electronic files" (§1141.10(b)) will force costly software and quality control changes; manufacturers request the electronic files be provided in multiple scalable vector formats and color profiles (CMYK/Pantone) to ensure reproducible fidelity.

[P17] The broad prohibition on manufacturing/selling cigarettes without required warnings (§1141.10(c)) creates severe supply chain liability risks for importers and distributors when foreign-sourced cartons arrive without compliant warnings; importers request a grace period and clear enforcement policy.

[P18] The requirement that warnings be printed on the package and visible under clear wrapping (§1141.10(c)(1)) prohibits common retail practices of adding point-of-sale sleeves; retailers request an exception for shrink-wrapping added post-distribution or permission to affix approved external labels.

[P19] The 50% coverage requirement of front and rear panels (or left 50% on cartons) (§1141.10(c)(2)) will necessitate complete redesign of packaging artwork; small brands argue this will impede market entry and seek smaller size thresholds or tiered application based on sales volume.

[P20] Requiring the warning text orientation to match other panel information (§1141.10(c)(3)) is too rigid for innovative packaging designs; designers request flexibility for vertical text or dual-orientation where shelf display orientation varies.

[P21] The prohibition on advertising without a required warning (§1141.10(d)) may conflict with state constitutions or First Amendment protections for commercial speech; legal experts will likely challenge this as overbroad and request tailored restrictions consistent with Supreme Court precedent.

[P22] Mandating the warning appear "directly on visual advertisements" (§1141.10(d)(1)) could be technically infeasible for some digital ad formats (animated banners, video overlays); digital advertisers request alternative compliance methods (pre-roll static frames, click-to-view warnings).

[P23] The 20% ad area requirement and prominent top placement (§1141.10(d)(2)) will disrupt ad creative and may be impossible for constrained formats (billboards, transit shelters); advertising associations request exemptions for specified ad types or a different placement rule (e.g., bottom-right).

[P24] Requiring English text for all required warnings (§1141.10(d)(3)) could reduce comprehension among non-English speakers and create public health inequities; immigrant advocacy groups will ask that warnings be bilingual or in predominant local languages by default.

[P25] The "non-English medium" exception (§1141.10(d)(3)(i)) lacks guidance on determining the "predominant language" of the medium for multi-language platforms (e.g., social media feeds); advertisers request objective criteria or a safe-harbor list.

[P26] The exception for an English medium with a non-English ad (§1141.10(d)(3)(ii)) may create enforcement ambiguity for mixed-language ads; marketing firms ask for examples and a clear rule when multiple languages appear.

[P27] Requiring English and Spanish warnings to be reproduced from specified electronic files (§1141.10(d)(4)) centralizes control and could delay ad campaigns if FDA file distribution is slow; advertisers request an API or ftp distribution and timely updates with version control.

[P28] For non-Spanish non-English warnings, the requirement to use FDA electronic files with accurate translations (§1141.10(d)(5)) places translation burden on manufacturers/distributors and could create liability for mistranslation; international trade groups ask that certified translation services and accepted glossaries be provided.

[P29] Requiring warnings to be "indelibly printed or permanently affixed" (§1141.10(e)) may prohibit certain packaging technologies (e.g., peel-off tax stamps, resealable pouches); packaging manufacturers request clarification on what constitutes "permanent" and acceptable adhesives.

[P30] The ban on placing warnings on removable clear outer wrappers (§1141.10(e)) will invalidate current practices where retailers add wrap-around promotions and could force repackaging; retailers ask for limited exceptions when wrappers are sold with the product and not removed by consumers.

[P31] The broad prohibition against dealing in cigarettes with noncompliant packages/ads (§1141.10(f)) could impose strict liability across complex distribution chains; distributors request a due-diligence safe harbor if they can prove they procured products from compliant suppliers in good faith.

[P32] The requirement for random display distribution annually per an FDA-approved plan (§1141.10(g)(1)) imposes complex inventory tracking and reporting burdens; manufacturers request detailed recordkeeping standards and an electronic reporting option.

[P33] The quarterly rotation requirement for advertisement warnings (§1141.10(g)(2)) will increase creative and trafficking workload for advertisers and may be impracticable for long-term campaigns; ad agencies request flexibility to change warnings on campaign milestones rather than rigid quarters.

[P34] FDA review and approval of rotation/display plans (§1141.10(g)(3)) creates regulatory uncertainty and potential delays; manufacturers request a presumptive approval process if plans meet clear, published criteria or a deemed-approved time limit.

[P35] The plan condition requiring equal distribution on packaging (§1141.10(g)(3)(i)) could be infeasible for small-batch SKUs and varying regional sales; manufacturers request proportional distribution allowances based on sales volume and SKU availability.

[P36] The condition that "all required labels will be displayed at the same time" (§1141.10(g)(3)(ii)) is ambiguous: is simultaneous display on a single pack required or across the market? Manufacturers and legal counsel will request clarification that it means simultaneously available in the marketplace, not on individual packs.

[P37] The four-year retention requirement for approved plans (§1141.10(g)(4)) is burdensome for small manufacturers with limited administrative capacity; industry requests a shorter retention period or electronic archive acceptance to reduce record storage costs.

[P38] The retailer non-violation exception (§1141.1(c)) provides limited protection because it requires the package to be supplied by a licensed manufacturer/distributor (§1141.1(c)(2)); small retailers sourcing from informal channels (e.g., small wholesalers) may still be exposed to liability.

[P39] The condition that packaging "contains a warning" (§1141.1(c)(1)) could be interpreted narrowly; retailers request explicit guidance that a compliant external band supplied by a licensed distributor fulfils this condition when permanent package changes are not feasible.

[P40] The requirement that packaging supplied by license/permit-holding manufacturer/distributor qualifies for retailer exception (§1141.1(c)(2)) puts retailers at risk when suppliers fail to maintain permits — retailers request a safe-harbor relying on good-faith supplier representations and documentation.

[P41] The "not materially altered" condition (§1141.1(c)(3)) is undefined and will generate disputes about what counts as material; retailers want enumerated examples of material vs. non-material alterations (e.g., price stickers vs. removal of warnings).

[P42] Limiting §1141.10(d) applicability to retailers only when they are responsible for or direct ad warnings (§1141.1(d)) is appropriate, but the rule should specify how responsibility is determined for in-store displays created by third-party vendors.

[P43] The carve-out that retailers remain liable if they display or alter public advertisements so they lack warnings (§1141.1(d)) could chill legitimate in-store promotions; retailers ask for a compliance checklist to avoid inadvertent liability.

[P44] Deeming a package without a required warning to be misbranded under FD&C §903(a)(1) (§1141.12(a)) increases enforcement penalties and civil exposure; manufacturers request a phased enforcement with notice-and-cure opportunities before misbranding findings.

[P45] Treating advertisements lacking required warnings as misbranding under FD&C §903(a)(7)(A) (§1141.12(a)) may expand FDA enforcement into speech areas traditionally regulated by FTC and states; request interagency coordination and limits on federal preemption.

[P46] The clause that any advertisement bearing a required warning will be deemed to include a brief statement of relevant warnings for FD&C purposes (§1141.12(b)) is unclear — stakeholders need to know which additional statements are deemed included and whether this creates new liabilities.

[P47] Requiring inclusion of warnings in all advertisements and descriptive printed matter or the product becomes misbranded (§1141.12(b)) could sweep in retailer shelf tags, promotional flyers, and online product descriptions not authored by manufacturers; organizations representing retailers request limiting the scope to manufacturer-originated materials.

[P48] The cross-application of these cigarette-specific labeling rules to tobacco product categories not explicitly covered (e.g., e-cigarettes, cigars) is ambiguous and may lead to enforcement overreach; industry requests explicit scope definition excluding other product classes unless stated.

[P49] The customer records safeguards (§160.30 and subparts) appear unrelated to tobacco labeling provisions; agencies should explain the relevance and avoid duplicative compliance burdens for small entities already subject to privacy laws.

[P50] The general requirement to adopt administrative, technical, and physical safeguards (§160.30) needs specificity about standards (e.g., NIST 800-53, encryption levels) so covered entities know how to comply without excessive cost.

[P51] The obligation to ensure policies reasonably protect against anticipated threats (§160.30(b)) is open-ended; financial and trading entities request a risk-based framework with examples of acceptable controls to satisfy the rule.

[P52] The requirement to protect against unauthorized access that could cause "substantial harm or inconvenience" (§160.30(c)) is vague; commenters request a definition or threshold for "substantial harm or inconvenience" to prevent overbroad enforcement.

[P1] The requirement that veterinarians be licensed in the State where they perform accredited duties will create unnecessary barriers for mobile or relief veterinarians who routinely cross state lines to respond to emergencies or provide temporary services.

[P1] Requiring state licensure for all accredited duties duplicates existing federal accreditation and will increase administrative burden and costs for veterinarians and APHIS without measurable animal health benefits.

[P1] State licensure requirements disproportionately impact rural communities that rely on out-of-state practitioners for specialized services, potentially reducing access to accredited veterinary services.

[P1] The rule fails to acknowledge telemedicine and remote services; requiring an in-state license for veterinarians performing accredited duties remotely from another State is impractical and could hinder disease surveillance.

[P1] The provision should specify whether temporary, emergency, or disaster-response credentials (e.g., interstate compacts) satisfy the in-state licensure requirement to avoid confusion during crises.

[P1] The rule should allow National Veterinary Accreditation Program (NVAP) accreditation to substitute for state licensure for routine accredited duties to streamline multi-state operations.

[P2] Allowing unlicensed veterinarians to practice with written State authorization is useful, but the rule lacks a standardized process or timeline for obtaining such authorization, leaving applicants subject to arbitrary delays.

[P2] The regulation should require States to publish clear, objective criteria and timelines for granting written authorizations to ensure consistency and prevent denial for non-meritorious reasons.

[P2] There is potential for uneven implementation across States—some states may deny written authorizations for protectionist reasons, undermining the rule’s intent to permit cross‑state practice.

[P2] The rule should specify whether written authorization granted by one State can be recognized by neighboring States during multi-state disease events to facilitate coordinated responses.

[P2] The rule must require that written authorizations be provided in a standard format (electronic and printable) and remain available for inspection by APHIS and producers to avoid disputes about validity.

[P3] Allowing States to restrict geographical areas and activities in written authorizations is necessary for public safety, but the proposed text is too vague and could be used to unduly limit practice beyond legitimate concerns.

[P3] The provision should require that any geographical or activity-based restrictions be narrowly tailored, based on public health or safety reasons, and documented with a written explanation from the State.

[P3] There should be an appeals mechanism defined for veterinarians who believe a State’s restrictions on activities or areas are arbitrary or overly broad.

[P3] The rule should prohibit States from imposing restrictions that effectively nullify the authorization (e.g., limiting practice to an area where no relevant producers are located), to prevent de facto denials.

[P3] The regulation should clarify whether restrictions may be temporary (e.g., for specific outbreaks) and require States to provide start/end dates and justification for temporary restrictions.

[P4] Requiring APHIS to verify licensing by contacting State boards is reasonable, but the rule should allow APHIS to rely on State online license verification databases to reduce administrative delays.

[P4] The provision should set a clear timeline (e.g., 10 business days) within which APHIS must complete verification to avoid delaying practitioners’ ability to perform accredited duties.

[P4] APHIS verification by contacting State boards raises confidentiality concerns; the rule should limit the personal data APHIS may request/retain and specify data protection measures.

[P4] The regulation should permit automatic, reciprocal verification agreements with State boards to streamline renewals and multi-state practice, rather than manual contacts for each applicant.

[P4] The rule lacks a process for resolving discrepancies between a veterinarian’s claim of licensure and the State board’s record; APHIS should be required to notify the veterinarian and provide a remediation timeframe.

[P5] The prohibition on performing accredited duties without license or documentation is appropriate to protect animal health, but the rule needs to define the penalties for violations (civil fines, de-accreditation, criminal) to provide due process.

[P5] The regulation should allow for emergency exceptions where an accredited veterinarian can perform duties without immediate documentation during declared animal health emergencies, with a requirement to produce documentation within a short window.

[P5] The blanket prohibition could impede mutual aid and disaster response where accredited veterinarians from other states are urgently needed; the rule should include clear emergency waivers or fast-track authorization processes.

[P5] The rule should define what constitutes “possession of documentation authorizing practice” (original paper, electronic copy, State confirmation) to avoid enforcement confusion.

[P5] Enforcement discretion must be clarified: will APHIS or State boards enforce the prohibition, and how will jurisdictional conflicts be resolved when an accredited veterinarian is accused of unauthorized practice?

[P1/P5] The interplay between state licensure requirement (P1) and the prohibition (P5) creates legal risk for accredited veterinarians who reasonably relied on prior guidance—APHIS should provide transitional relief and grandfathering for accreditations issued before the rule’s effective date.

[P2/P4] If APHIS verification is a prerequisite to recognizing written authorizations (P2 & P4), the procedure should be synchronized to prevent situations where a State has granted authorization but APHIS verification is delayed, leaving the veterinarian effectively barred.

[P3/P5] States’ ability to restrict activities (P3) combined with prohibition (P5) may allow States to indirectly ban out-of-state accredited veterinarians; commenters request guardrails to prevent protectionist use of restrictions.

[P4] Legal commenters will likely challenge APHIS’ authority to require direct verification from State boards for accreditation purposes without establishing standard operating procedures in a notice or memorandum of understanding.

[P1] Academic and professional associations will request clarity on whether specialty board-certified veterinarians practicing under limited-scope accredited duties must hold a full general license in the State or whether limited/specialty licenses are acceptable.

[P2] Private practice groups will ask that the rule expressly allow corporate or clinic-level authorizations (where the employer obtains a state authorization for multiple unlicensed veterinarians) to reduce administrative overhead.

[P5] Animal welfare advocates will support strict enforcement of the prohibition but will request that APHIS create an anonymous reporting mechanism and require timely investigations into suspected unauthorized practice.
