[P1] The January 27, 2022 comment deadline is insufficient time for affected operators, OEMs, labor unions, and international civil aviation authorities to analyze the technical attachments and prepare coordinated technical and economic comments; extend the comment period by at least 60–90 days.

[P1] The rule does not state whether the comment deadline is the postmarked date or received date for mailed submissions and does not provide alternate electronic submission instructions; clarify acceptable submission methods and whether extensions will be considered.

[P2] The applicability language referencing “The Boeing Company airplanes, certificated in any category, as specified in paragraphs (c)(1) and (2)” is vague and may create uncertainty for leased, stored, or special-configuration airframes; require clarification that leased aircraft and those with supplemental type certificates (STCs) are included or excluded explicitly.

[P3] The Model 777–200 applicability (c)(1) lists specific Pratt & Whitney engine models but omits engine serial number ranges, thrust ratings, or retrofit states; provide more precise applicability (by engine serial numbers, production blocks, or modification status) to avoid overbroad application.

[P3] Operators of 777–200s with PW4077D engines modified under STC or service bulletin X may be incorrectly included; require FAA to confirm whether modified engines are within applicability or provide exclusion language for engines that have previously incorporated blade or inlet reinforcement retrofits.

[P4] The Model 777–300 applicability (c)(2) includes PW4090 and PW4098 engines but does not address derivative or re-engined variants (e.g., engines re-rated or re-bearing); request clarification whether these variants are covered.

[P5] The compliance provision "within the compliance times specified" lacks explicit timing in the extracted text; commenters will request that the FAA clearly publish specific compliance intervals (e.g., before next flight, within X flight hours/cycles, or within Y days) and justify those intervals with safety risk analysis.

[P6] Requiring the engine inlet modification "prior to further flight" (g) imposes immediate grounding unless an FAA-approved method is available and repair capacity exists; operators will request a phased compliance schedule or a limited extension with risk-mitigation measures to avoid widespread grounding and severe economic disruption.

[P6] The modification requirement lacks an implementation standard or reference service bulletin describing the design, test criteria, and acceptance thresholds for withstanding fan blade failure loads; require the FAA to include or reference the approved modification design package or minimum performance criteria.

[P7] Limiting approval authority for the modification method to the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch (g) centralizes decision-making and may create bottlenecks and delays; request that the FAA delegate approval authority to other appropriate regional ACO branches or accept approvals from EASA or Transport Canada to expedite compliance.

[P8] The prohibition on special flight permits (h) except for aircraft meeting (h)(1) and (h)(2) effectively prevents ferry flights for maintenance or repositioning; operators and lessors will request that the FAA allow conditional special flight permits with explicit risk mitigations (e.g., single-engine ferry, altitude restrictions) approved on a case-by-case basis.

[P9] Requiring a flow path UT inspection of 1st-stage LPC blades as a precondition for special flight permits (h)(1) within an unspecified timeframe or without clear access to inspection facilities may be impractical for some operators; request clear timelines (e.g., within 72 hours prior to the intended flight) and recognition of equivalent approved NDT methods performed by qualified facilities.

[P9] The AD references a Pratt & Whitney procedure for the UT inspection but does not state whether other qualified service providers or third-party NDT facilities can perform the inspection; request explicit acceptance of inspections by certified commercial NDT providers and airlines' internal NDT groups, provided they follow the referenced procedures.

[P10] The requirement for functional checks of hydraulic pump shutoff valves within 10 days prior to flight (h)(2) is overly restrictive for scheduling and may not be feasible for ferries from remote locations; suggest expanding the window (e.g., 30 days) or allowing in-flight functional verifications under controlled conditions.

[P10] The AD does not define "all applicable corrective actions" arising from the hydraulic valve checks; request the FAA to enumerate acceptable corrective actions, acceptable repair methods, and reporting requirements to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P11] Granting credit for prior inspections (i) only if performed using specific Pratt & Whitney Special Instructions may unfairly reject equivalent work performed per other approved procedures or earlier revision versions; request that the FAA accept equivalent inspections if documented, performed by qualified personnel, and approved by the principal inspector.

[P12] Accepting only Special Instruction No. 85F–21 paragraph 2 as credit (i)(1) may exclude inspections performed under other manufacturing or airline-developed procedures that achieve the same detection sensitivity; request that the FAA provide criteria for equivalency and allow operators to apply for credit with proof of equivalence.

[P13] The credit provision for Special Instruction No. 130F–21 paragraph 1.a (i)(2) should clarify whether interim revisions, translations, or operator-tailored procedures are acceptable; request explicit acceptance of later-reissued service instructions or operator-adopted procedures if they meet the inspection objectives.

[P14] For credit of 130F–21 Rev A paragraph 2.a (i)(3), request that the FAA specify required documentation to prove when, by whom, and how the inspection was performed to qualify for credit, including NDT reports and sign-offs.

[P15] Allowing AMOCs to be approved by the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch (j)(1) is appropriate, but the process timeline is unspecified; request the FAA publish target review times (e.g., 30/60/90 days) for AMOC applications and an expedited review path for emergency or operational necessity requests.

[P16] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the requester's principal inspector or responsible Flight Standards Office (j)(1) may conflict with operators whose principal inspector is unavailable or where international operators have different oversight structures; request the FAA clarify procedures for international operators and provide a direct AMOC submission path.

[P17] The paragraph requiring direct submissions to the certification office at a specified attention line and email (j)(1) should include the specific contact name from paragraph (k)(1); without that, applicants cannot be sure they are addressing the correct person — request the FAA publish the contact name and backup contacts.

[P18] The requirement to notify principal inspectors or Flight Standards Office managers before using any approved AMOC (j)(2) is reasonable, but the rule should clarify whether prior written notification or telephonic notification suffices and whether notification can be contemporaneous with first use; request procedural details and timelines for such notifications.

[P6] The language "withstand fan blade failure event loads" lacks quantitative load cases, safety factors, or testing standards; ask FAA to publish the failure load envelope, analysis basis, test methodology (static/dynamic), and required factor of safety so modifications are engineered consistently.

[P3] Labor organizations representing maintenance personnel will request training guidance and required qualifications for personnel performing the flow path UT inspections and inlet modifications, which are not specified in the AD.

[P8] Airport authorities and insurers will ask the FAA to assess and publish the operational and insurance implications of disallowing special flight permits, including guidance for diversion, disruption, and passenger rights.

[P5] Small carriers and cargo operators will request a cost and economic impact assessment accompanying the compliance timeline, including availability of parts, skilled labor, and depot capacity for inlet modifications.

[P7] Foreign regulators (EASA, TCCA) and non-U.S. operators will request reciprocal recognition of AMOCs and approvals issued by their civil aviation authorities to avoid duplicated approvals and delays.

[P6] The AD should provide interim mitigations for aircraft awaiting modification (e.g., operational restrictions like flight altitude ceilings, speed limits, or engine run limits) that reduce risk while enabling limited operations; request the FAA issue such operational mitigations.

[P9] The requirement that blades be "found serviceable" for special flight permits is ambiguous; define clear acceptance/rejection criteria (e.g., crack sizes, location, and repair criteria) to ensure consistent decision-making.

[P1] Because the comment due date is in the past (January 27, 2022), request the FAA confirm whether this is a typographical error and, if so, reissue the NPRM with corrected dates to ensure an open and lawful comment period.

[P15] Legal commenters will request that the FAA clarify appeal and reconsideration procedures if an AMOC is denied and provide statutory or regulatory citation of the FAA's authority to grant AMOCs in this specific context.

[P11] Airlines that performed voluntary inspections using proprietary techniques or non-P&W instructions before the effective date should be allowed to submit evidence for credit determination on a case-by-case basis rather than being categorically excluded.

[P6] The AD should include explicit post-modification inspection intervals and life-limits for modified inlets (e.g., overhaul intervals or repetitive inspections) — request the FAA define ongoing airworthiness requirements for the modification.

[P8] Emergency medical flight operators and government/military users may require exceptions to the special flight permit prohibition; request explicit provisions allowing critical medical/evacuation flights subject to strict risk controls and operational limitations.

[P3] Clarify whether freighter conversions of 777–200 or 777–300 series (P2 applicability) with altered pylons, nacelles, or modified engines remain within the applicability or whether conversion STCs change applicability.

[P17] Provide a public docket link or email alias for AMOC-related public records; multiple commenters requested transparency on previously approved AMOCs for similar ADs to guide applicants.

[P9] The AD should specify the minimum acceptable UT equipment sensitivity and calibration standards, including probe frequency, acceptance criteria, and certification of technicians, to ensure consistent detection capability across operators.

[P10] The 10-day window for hydraulic valve functional checks should be tied to the planned special flight date rather than any flight within 10 days; request clarification that the check must be within 10 days before the specific intended flight to qualify.

[P2] Aviation lessors request explicit guidance on responsibilities for compliance (operator vs owner) when an aircraft is between operators or in storage at the AD effective date.

[P6] The requirement to modify "before further flight after the effective date" implies immediate grounding risk; request FAA to publish a list of approved repair stations and design organizations authorized to perform the modification to prevent capacity shortages.

[P15] Safety advocates will request transparency on the criteria the Manager will use to evaluate AMOCs, including safety case expectations, evidence requirements, and whether prior-similar AMOCs will be used as precedents.

[P1] Stakeholders request confirmation that comments submitted after January 27, 2022 will be accepted and considered if accompanied by justification (e.g., newly discovered data), and that the FAA will publish how late submissions will be handled.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement that CBP publish notice at least 30 days before any new fees takes effect is insufficient for businesses that need to renegotiate contracts or update billing systems; commenters request a 60–90 day notice period instead.

[P1] The proposed annual determination obligation is vague about the criteria CBP will use to decide whether an adjustment is “necessary”; request that CBP specify factors (e.g., projected revenue needs, staffing, program costs) and publish the supporting calculations with the Federal Register notice.

[P2] Maintaining fees and limitations only on CBP’s website is inadequate: stakeholders request archived historical fee tables and machine-readable (CSV/JSON) formats so automated systems can ingest and reconcile fee changes.

[P3] The prohibition on collecting additional fees when a user prepaid before a fee change should explicitly require CBP to provide a clear, searchable record (online ledger) showing which prepaid accounts qualify to prevent disputes at ports.

[P3] The rule should clarify whether prepayments are tied to vehicle VINs, carrier EINs, transponder IDs, or other identifiers; industry will comment that lack of specificity risks inconsistent application across ports.

[P4] Requiring users who have not prepaid to comply with adjusted limits on the effective date may create retroactive obligations for transactions initiated before notice; request a safe-harbor for transactions in progress as of the Federal Register publication date.

[P5] The obligation that the driver/person in charge must tender fees on arrival should allow alternative tender methods (e.g., electronic billing to carrier account) and clarify acceptable payment forms at all ports, including remote crossings.

[P6] The exception for prepaid fees (c)(3) should require CBP to publish detailed registration and prepayment procedures and timelines so drivers/carriers can reliably comply; otherwise prepayment as an exception is illusory.

[P7] The prohibition exempting trucks transported by non-ferry vessels from fees could create avoidance incentives (moving goods via vessel segments to escape fees); request clarification on multi-modal journeys and rules to prevent fee circumvention.

[P8] The $100 annual prepayment threshold that exempts further arrival fees may be unfairly high for small carriers or owner-operators; small-business commenters will request a lower threshold or a prorated option.

[P8] Clarify whether the $100 prepayment and transponder requirement applies per truck, per EIN, or per transponder serial number; ambiguity will cause enforcement inconsistency.

[P9] The $5.50 passenger fee (adjustable) should be assessed for legality and for impact on tourism and travel industries; airlines and cruise lines will likely object to fee increases without demonstrated cost causation.

[P9] Request that CBP specify who is responsible for collecting and remitting the $5.50 fee (airlines, vessel operators, or CBP at point of arrival) and whether it may be collected as part of an existing passenger facility charge to avoid duplicate billing.

[P10] The exception for journeys originating in U.S. territories needs clearer definitions of “originates” (point of first embarkation vs. itinerary); carriers will request examples to ensure correct fee application.

[P11] The exception for journeys originating in the United States but not limited to territories and possessions is ambiguous and may be redundantly worded; legal commenters will request plain-language clarification and examples of when each passenger fee applies.

[P12] The $1.93 fee for passengers from U.S. territories should be compared to existing travel promotion agreements with territories; territorial governments will request consultation and economic impact analysis before implementation.

[P13] The annual customs broker fee of $138 (adjustable) per district or national permit will disproportionately burden small brokers and those with multiple district permits; brokers will request a cap on aggregate fees per broker or a multi-permit discount.

[P13] Clarify whether the fee applies to inactive or suspended permits; brokers will ask that CBP exempt permits not in active use to avoid charging for dormant authorizations.

[P14] Requiring brokers to pay the district permit fee to the port that granted the permit may be administratively burdensome for brokers with permits granted by multiple ports: request option to centralize payments electronically to CBP rather than multiple ports.

[P15] For national permits, the instruction to submit fees to the port “through which their license was delivered” is ambiguous for electronic deliveries; request an option to remit nationally via a single CBP portal.

[P16] The repeated obligation to publish adjusted amounts at least 30 days prior duplicates P1; stakeholders will request consolidation and that adjustments be accompanied by a public explanation and spreadsheet of the calculation.

[P17] The mandated CPI-based computation method should be supplemented with an option to use other appropriate inflators (e.g., PPI or wages) if CBP demonstrates CPI is not reflective of program cost drivers for specific fee categories.

[P18] Using the CPI–U arithmetic average for June–May without explanation raises concerns that seasonal effects could distort adjustments; commenters will request justification and request that CBP model alternative averaging windows.

[P19] The use of 236.009 as the FY2014 CPI–U baseline should be justified and documented; legal commenters will question whether selecting FY2014 is arbitrary and ask whether statutory authority requires this base year.

[P20] The process for using the last adjusted year’s CPI average as the comparison-year (C) needs to address chained or multiple adjustments over time and require CBP to publish the comparison-year value in each notice to ensure transparency.

[P21] Rounding and difference calculations (D = A − C) should be accompanied by worked examples in the Federal Register notice to allow stakeholders to verify CBP’s math for each annual adjustment.

[P22] Rounding D to the nearest whole number (E) may create material step changes from small CPI movements; request that CBP instead round to one decimal or provide rationale for whole-number rounding to avoid over- or under-adjusting fees.

[P23] The step computing F = (E ÷ C) × 100% produces an approximation; commenters will request CBP publish both precise unrounded and rounded values and the exact formulas used in computer-readable form.

[P24] The 1% threshold for making any adjustment is arbitrary; industry groups will argue for a lower threshold (e.g., 0.5%) to keep fees aligned with inflation, while regulated entities that pay fees may request maintaining the threshold to reduce small frequent changes—request CBP justify the policy choice with cost-benefit analysis.

[P25] Calculating G = A − B (current vs FY2014) and then using H to adjust fees annually could compound rounding effects over time; request that CBP include anti-distortion safeguards and publish cumulative impact analyses.

[P26] Computing H = (G ÷ B) × 100% using the fixed FY2014 baseline will produce large nominal increases the longer the rule remains unchanged; stakeholders ask CBP to model multi-year scenarios and cap annual increases (e.g., no more than X%) to avoid sudden cost shocks.

[P27] Adjusting fees upward by H percent without any downward adjustment provision is one-sided; consumer advocates and regulated parties will request symmetry allowing downward adjustments if CPI falls, or at minimum a review mechanism.

[P27] The requirement to round adjusted fees to the second decimal could create cent-level anomalies (e.g., rounding up for many transactions); request CBP state rounding rules for cumulative billing and whether fractions of cents accrue or get carried forward.

[P28] § 24.23’s 30-day publication requirement for merchandise processing fee adjustments is inadequate for importers who must update pricing and contractual terms; importers will request a 60-day notice and transitional rules for entries already in transit.

[P29] The $1.00 per air waybill/bill of lading fee for express/centralized hub facilities may be passed through to consumers; carriers will request a detailed cost justification and statutory authority showing the fee is reasonable and cost-caused.

[P30] The ad valorem fee for entries valued at $2,500 or less needs clarity on which ad valorem rate applies and whether it interacts with other de minimis thresholds; small importers will request examples and confirm that low-value shipments will not be subject to duplicative fees.

[P31] Quarterly payment requirements that must “cover all applicable transaction fees for the quarter” impose cash-flow burdens on carriers/operators; industry will request monthly or flexible payment options and interest-free short grace periods.

[P32] The per-waybill fee floor ($0.35) and cap ($1.00) being adjustable creates uncertainty; stakeholders request CBP specify the mechanism and limits for future adjustments and require impact analyses before adjusting the band.

[P33] The prohibition on exceeding $1.00 per waybill must clarify whether the cap applies per document, per house waybill, or per master waybill in consolidated shipments to prevent double-charging.

[P34] The minimum fee of $0.35 could be confiscatory for extremely low-value, high-volume transactions that are already marginal; small shippers will request an exemption or alternate low-volume threshold.

[P35] The electronic payment requirement via Fedwire or pay.gov may exclude small carriers without access to those systems; request alternative low-cost electronic payment options (ACH, credit card) and explicit accommodations.

[P36] The required information to be included with quarterly payments (facility identity, port code, allocation) will increase administrative burden; carriers ask for a standardized template and machine-readable upload facility to streamline compliance.

[P37] Requiring identification of the calendar quarter on payments is reasonable but must allow corrections for amended quarterly reports; carriers request a formal amendment procedure and deadline.

[P38] The obligation to allocate payments among multiple facilities needs safe-harbored allocation methods and audit tolerance thresholds to avoid penalties for minor allocation variances.

[P39] The requirement to provide a breakdown by entry procedure type may be infeasible for carriers that do not control entry procedures (importer-driven); request that CBP permit carriers to provide the data they maintain or accept importer-supplied breakdowns.

[P40] The refund request process requiring a written letter to an address is outdated; carriers will request an electronic refund submission portal and automated acknowledgements to expedite overpayment refunds.

[P41] The one-year deadline to request refunds is unduly short given complex reconciliation cycles; carriers request extending the refund claim window to three years or at least to match the statute of limitations for tax/fee claims.

[P42] Interest on underpayments accruing from the original due date could impose punitive costs for inadvertent errors; request a grace period or reduced interest rate for first-time or minor underpayments and a clear interest-rate formula tied to a published benchmark.

[P43] The provision allowing assessment of penalties and liquidated damages for underpayment lacks specificity on penalty amounts, appeal rights, and calculation methods; carriers and trade associations will request a detailed penalty schedule, notice-and-cure periods, and administrative appeal procedures.

[P43] CBP should commit to exercising enforcement discretion for inadvertent clerical errors and provide training and outreach before imposing penalties to avoid disproportionate sanctions on small carriers.

[P5/P6] Port-level variations in fee collection practices require CBP to issue uniform operational guidance to all ports; industry commenters will request this to prevent inconsistent enforcement of the tender-on-arrival and prepayment exception.

[P8/P5] The requirement to affix a transponder as a condition of the $100 prepayment exemption raises privacy and equipment-cost concerns; small carriers will ask CBP to cover transponder costs or permit alternative electronic identifiers.

[P13/P14] Brokers object to the administrative burden of routing fees to the specific port that granted a permit rather than allowing centralized electronic remittance and consolidated annual invoicing.

[P29/P31] Express consignment carriers argue that quarterly remittance timing (payment due last day of month following quarter) could create liquidity issues; request monthly settlement or the option to net against monthly revenue.

[P24/P27] Legal commenters will question whether the CPI adjustment methodology and 1% trigger meet the Administrative Procedure Act's requirements for reasoned decisionmaking and request CBP include a regulatory flexibility analysis and economic impact statement.

raw_output:
[P1] The October 21, 2019 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonably short and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow operators, MROs, and unions adequate time to analyze cost and safety impacts.

[P1] The rule fails to provide clear instructions on how to submit late comments if the October 21, 2019 deadline is missed due to industry-wide outreach needs; the FAA should publish a formal late-comment policy for this AD.

[P2] § 39.13(f) improperly precludes operators from using compliance time flexibilities for unrelated maintenance scheduling constraints; the FAA should explicitly allow coordination with existing scheduled overhauls where safety is not compromised.

[P2] The phrase “unless the actions have already been done” in § 39.13(f) lacks a recordkeeping standard for proving prior compliance; the FAA should require acceptable evidence (logbook entries, parts tags, maintenance release references) to be specified.

[P3] The 40,000 flight-hours threshold in § 39.13(g)(1) for HMU removal is arbitrary and unsupported by publicized service history or risk assessment; the FAA must publish the data supporting this threshold or consider a lower threshold.

[P3] The alternative compliance of “within 180 days after the AD effective date, whichever is later” in § 39.13(g)(1) creates operational uncertainty for high-utilization operators and could allow unsafe HMUs to remain in service longer; the FAA should change to "whichever is earlier" or provide utilization-based escalators.

[P3] § 39.13(g)(1) does not define what constitutes a “part eligible for installation,” leading to potential inconsistent interpretations; the FAA should specify approved part numbers, PMA/overhaul criteria, and inspection certificates required.

[P4] The conditional replacement requirement in § 39.13(g)(1) when FHs are unknown places an unreasonable burden on lessor/lessee chains and older aircraft owners who cannot obtain historical records; the FAA should provide a safe-harbor process (e.g., teardown inspection) or longer compliance time.

[P4] Requiring replacement within 180 days when FHs cannot be determined (§ 39.13(g)(1) condition) effectively mandates immediate expensive parts replacement for some operators; the FAA should allow non-destructive testing or borescope inspections as an alternative to full replacement.

[P5] § 39.13(g)(2)’s recurring requirement to remove HMUs before 40,000 FHs after the initial action will impose significant lifecycle costs without demonstrated reliability data; FAA should allow life-extension via approved inspection intervals or set a longer interval tied to demonstrated HMU service.

[P5] The rule does not clarify whether FHs “since last overhaul” are reset by a bench overhaul performed by an FAA-certified repair station versus a non-certified overhaul; § 39.13(g)(2) should define acceptable overhaul documentation and who can sign-off.

[P6] Granting the ECO Branch Manager authority to approve AMOCs in § 39.13(i)(1) centralizes discretionary power and may slow approvals; the FAA should allow delegation to regional certification offices to expedite operator requests.

[P6] § 39.13(i)(1) should permit AMOC approval by the operator’s principal inspector for low-risk deviations to reduce administrative overhead, rather than require ECO Branch Manager involvement for all AMOCs.

[P7] The AMOC submission routing in § 39.13(i)(1) (to principal inspector or local FSDO) is confusing for large, multi-base operators; the FAA should allow a single point of contact and electronic portal submission to avoid misrouting.

[P7] The rule lacks a specified timeline for FAA response to AMOC requests submitted per § 39.13(i)(1); commenters request a mandatory 30- or 60-day decision deadline to avoid prolonged operational disruption.

[P8] § 39.13(i)(1)’s instruction to address direct submissions to the person in paragraph (j)(1) is problematic because paragraph (j)(1) is not included in the NPRM text provided to the public; the FAA should ensure contact details are published in the final rule.

[P8] The requirement to address direct AMOC submissions to a named certification office manager (per § 39.13(i)(1) conditional) creates single-person dependency; the FAA should allow addressing to a position title or office to avoid delays if personnel change.

[P9] Allowing email submissions to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov in § 39.13(i)(1) is useful, but the rule must state acceptable file formats, maximum attachment sizes, and security requirements for proprietary data submitted in AMOC requests.

[P9] The FAA should clarify whether email AMOC submissions to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov satisfy the regulatory requirement to send requests to principal inspectors; the interplay between email option and routing to local FSDO must be explicit.

[P10] § 39.13(i)(2) obligates notifying the principal inspector or local FSDO/CHDO manager before using an approved AMOC, but provides no timeframe for that notification; the FAA should require notification at least 48 hours before use, or immediately upon implementation, depending on safety risk.

[P10] The rule should specify the form and content of the notification required under § 39.13(i)(2) (e.g., AMOC approval number, scope, affected tail numbers) to ensure consistent oversight by inspectors.

[P10] For operators without a principal inspector, § 39.13(i)(2) should permit notification via the same email address used for AMOC submission (ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov) to streamline compliance and create an electronic audit trail.

[P3] The compliance timing in § 39.13(g)(1) does not account for aircraft grounded due to parts shortages; the FAA should include language allowing extensions where parts are unavailable, subject to inspection and risk mitigation.

[P5] § 39.13(g)(2) fails to address credit for time-in-service on replacement HMUs installed as spares with unknown FHs; the FAA should provide a method to document and accept traceable records for spares to prevent premature removals.

[P2] The obligation in § 39.13(f) to “follow the AD within the specified compliance times” should explicitly allow concurrent accomplishment with other mandatory ADs or service bulletins when safe to do so to reduce repetitive shop visits.

[P3] The AD should require operators to provide compliance status and HMU FH records to the FAA upon request; the current provisions do not obligate reporting, which impedes post-implementation safety monitoring.

[P4] The rule must prescribe acceptable methods for determining unknown FHs (logbook search protocols, engine data recorder outputs, or maintenance database queries) to ensure consistent application of the 180-day conditional replacement in § 39.13(g)(1).

[P6] The AMOC authority granted in § 39.13(i)(1) should explicitly state that previously-approved, equivalent AMOCs for related ADs are acceptable to avoid redundant submissions.

[P7] The procedure in § 39.13(i)(1) does not address confidentiality claims over proprietary repair procedures submitted as part of AMOC requests; FAA should include a process to protect confidential business information.

[P1] The rule should have used a future-effective comment deadline rather than October 21, 2019 (a past date) — commenters question whether the docket text contained an error and request correction and republication of the NPRM with accurate dates.

[P8] Paragraph (j)(1) referenced by § 39.13(i)(1) should include contact phone numbers and alternate points of contact to accommodate urgent AMOC submissions when email is impractical.

[P5] The recurring replacement requirement in § 39.13(g)(2) should include an exception for HMUs that have been monitored with an approved health-usage monitoring program demonstrating acceptable condition, rather than automatic removal at 40,000 FHs.

[P3] Operators request a phased compliance plan for § 39.13(g)(1) allowing smaller regional carriers longer lead time (e.g., 12 months) due to limited MRO capacity and parts supply chain constraints.

[P9] The FAA should confirm whether attachments emailed to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov will be treated as official submissions under 14 CFR 39.19, and whether receipt confirmations will be sent automatically.

parsed_claims.claim_text: § 39.13(g)(1) does not define what constitutes a “part eligible for installation,” leading to potential inconsistent interpretations; the FAA should specify approved part numbers, PMA/overhaul criteria, and inspection certificates required.

The conditional replacement requirement in § 39.13(g)(1) when FHs are unknown places an unreasonable burden on lessor/lessee chains and older aircraft owners who cannot obtain historical records; the FAA should provide a safe-harbor process (e.g., teardown inspection) or longer compliance time.

Requiring replacement within 180 days when FHs cannot be determined (§ 39.13(g)(1) condition) effectively mandates immediate expensive parts replacement for some operators; the FAA should allow non-destructive testing or borescope inspections as an alternative to full replacement.

§ 39.13(g)(2)’s recurring requirement to remove HMUs before 40,000 FHs after the initial action will impose significant lifecycle costs without demonstrated reliability data; FAA should allow life-extension via approved inspection intervals or set a longer interval tied to demonstrated HMU service.

The rule does not clarify whether FHs “since last overhaul” are reset by a bench overhaul performed by an FAA-certified repair station versus a non-certified overhaul; § 39.13(g)(2) should define acceptable overhaul documentation and who can sign-off.

Granting the ECO Branch Manager authority to approve AMOCs in § 39.13(i)(1) centralizes discretionary power and may slow approvals; the FAA should allow delegation to regional certification offices to expedite operator requests.

§ 39.13(i)(1) should permit AMOC approval by the operator’s principal inspector for low-risk deviations to reduce administrative overhead, rather than require ECO Branch Manager involvement for all AMOCs.

The AMOC submission routing in § 39.13(i)(1) (to principal inspector or local FSDO) is confusing for large, multi-base operators; the FAA should allow a single point of contact and electronic portal submission to avoid misrouting.

The rule lacks a specified timeline for FAA response to AMOC requests submitted per § 39.13(i)(1); commenters request a mandatory 30- or 60-day decision deadline to avoid prolonged operational disruption.

§ 39.13(i)(1)’s instruction to address direct submissions to the person in paragraph (j)(1) is problematic because paragraph (j)(1) is not included in the NPRM text provided to the public; the FAA should ensure contact details are published in the final rule.

[P1] The March 11–August 31 window for state management and control activities is too narrow for northern states where snowmelt and nesting occur earlier or later; states need flexibility based on local phenology.

[P1] Restricting take to March 11–August 31 will hinder timely responses to nuisance or safety situations (e.g., geese at schools or parks) that occur before March 11.

[P1] The proposed start date of March 11 conflicts with existing state permits and programs already authorized to take resident Canada geese earlier in the year; the rule should include a grandfathering clause.

[P1] The end date of August 31 may be insufficient to address late-season broods and molting geese that create public-safety or agricultural damage through September and October.

[P1] The fixed date range (March 11–August 31) is arbitrary and unsupported by biological evidence; the agency should require date ranges tied to local nesting phenology rather than a single federal date.

[P2] Allowing egg and nest manipulation at any time is appropriate and necessary for effective population control and should be maintained.

[P2] The exception permitting egg and nest manipulation year-round lacks safeguards to prevent misuse (e.g., destruction outside nesting season when eggs are absent); the rule should require documentation of active nests before destruction.

[P2] The rule should require reporting and recordkeeping for egg and nest manipulations conducted year-round to ensure transparency and monitor impacts on population dynamics.

[P3] The April 1–September 15 window for airports and military airfields is too short for some regions; airports face hazards from nonbreeding flock behavior outside these dates and need broader authority.

[P3] Airports require urgent, flexible authority to remove problem geese whenever aircraft safety is threatened; limiting take to the April–September period could increase strike risk during migration overlaps.

[P3] Military airfields operate year-round and may face mission-critical safety risks from geese outside April 1–September 15; the rule should allow year-round emergency take authority for active runways under strict reporting.

[P4] Permitting nest and egg destruction at any time for airports and military airfields is acceptable but must include verification requirements (nest checks) and limits on the number destroyed to prevent unnecessary population impacts.

[P4] The exception allowing destruction of nests and eggs year-round at airports lacks a requirement to avoid disturbance during migratory staging—this could unintentionally disrupt nonresident geese.

[P5] Allowing registrants to destroy nests and eggs year-round is reasonable for property managers, but registrants should be defined precisely and required to obtain training or certification.

[P5] The rule should require registrants to obtain landowner consent (similar to P6) before destroying nests and eggs on private property to protect property rights and avoid disputes.

[P5] Registrants destroying nests and eggs year-round should be required to maintain records of actions, locations, and evidence of nesting to enable oversight.

[P6] Requiring homeowners' associations and local governments to obtain landowner consent is appropriate; however, the rule must specify evidence required (written consent) and process for disputed ownership.

[P6] The consent requirement may be impractical for large multifamily or condominium associations where common areas are owned collectively; the rule should clarify who qualifies as "landowner."

[P7] The obligation to comply with all state and local laws is redundant but necessary; the rule should explicitly state that federal authorization does not preempt stricter state/local protections.

[P7] The rule should provide guidance when state/local law prohibits nest destruction year-round so associations and local governments know they cannot rely solely on federal permission.

[P8] The May 1–August 31 window for agricultural producers is too late in some regions where nesting and grazing conflicts begin earlier; growers need access beginning in March or April.

[P8] Agricultural producers need emergency authority outside May–August when geese cause acute crop damage at vulnerable growth stages (e.g., early spring planting and seedling establishment).

[P8] The rule should require agricultural producers to use nonlethal deterrence before resorting to take during the permitted window to minimize impacts.

[P9] Allowing nest and egg destruction year-round for agricultural producers is necessary but must include limits and verification to avoid overuse and to protect migratory populations.

[P9] The exception for agricultural nest destruction should not permit destruction of nests of migratory subspecies; the rule needs a clear method to differentiate resident versus migratory nests.

[P10] The April 1–August 31 window for state and tribal wildlife agencies lacks flexibility for tribal authorities whose local cultural practices or ecological conditions may require different timing.

[P10] State and Tribal agencies should be authorized to act when immediate public safety or human-health threats occur outside the April–August window; an emergency clause should be added.

[P10] The rule should specify reporting requirements and population monitoring obligations for State and Tribal agencies conducting takes during the allowed period.

[P11] The year-round exception for destruction of nests and eggs by State and Tribal agencies is reasonable, but must include procedures to verify residency status of geese and avoid impacting migratory birds.

[P11] Tribal authorities should retain sovereign discretion; the rule must explicitly recognize tribal jurisdiction and allow tribes to set different timing consistent with cultural practices.

[P11] The exception allowing year-round nest destruction for State and Tribal agencies should require public notification and transparency to allow community input, especially in urban areas.

[General] The proposed rule does not clearly define "resident Canada geese," creating legal uncertainty; commenters request a precise biological definition or screening criteria to distinguish resident from migratory geese.

[General] The rule lacks an adaptive management framework requiring monitoring of population-level impacts from the increased year-round nest destruction; recommend mandatory surveys and adaptive thresholds.

[General] The rule should include clear enforcement provisions and penalties for unauthorized take or nest destruction, including civil and criminal penalties for noncompliant entities.

[General] The rule should require coordination among federal, state, tribal, and local authorities to prevent duplicative or conflicting actions and ensure humane, evidence-based practices.

[General] Legal experts note potential conflicts with the Migratory Bird Treaty Act for actions affecting migratory individuals; the rule should include safeguards to ensure no take of migratory geese occurs.

[General] Animal welfare and conservation NGOs will object to unbounded year-round nest destruction absent strict limits, oversight, and humane standards; propose mandatory best-practice protocols and independent audits.

[P1] The allowance to use listed synthetic substances as slug or snail bait in organic crop production conflicts with the organic principles of minimizing synthetic inputs and will erode consumer trust in the organic label.

[P1] The rule lacks criteria for when slug/snail baits may be used (e.g., thresholds of pest damage, integrated pest management requirements), potentially permitting routine prophylactic use rather than limited, last-resort use.

[P1] The rule does not require recordkeeping or reporting specific to synthetic slug/snail bait applications, making enforcement and transparency impossible; commenters request mandatory treatment logs and justification for each use.

[P1] Allowing synthetic slug/snail baits without specifying application rates, timing restrictions, or buffer requirements risks environmental contamination of nearby waterbodies and non-target organisms, including amphibians and beneficial invertebrates.

[P1] The provision gives no direction on labeling treated crops or informing certifiers when synthetic slug/snail baits are used, which would prevent consumer awareness and impede market differentiation.

[P2] Ferric phosphate is permitted but the rule fails to specify acceptable formulations or concentration limits (e.g., ppm), which could allow highly toxic additives or attractants that increase non-target impacts.

[P2] The rule should require that ferric phosphate products used in organic production be certified or documented as free from prohibited co-formulants (e.g., other synthetic pesticides, heavy metals); the current text does not.

[P2] Ferric phosphate is toxic to some non-target species (earthworms, beneficial mollusc predators) at certain doses; the proposal does not include environmental risk assessments or mitigation measures for ferric phosphate.

[P2] Industry (molluscicide manufacturers) will request clear guidance on maximum application rates and allowable bait matrices; without that, inconsistencies across certifiers will arise—request insertion of specific rate limits and application method standards for ferric phosphate.

[P2] The provision omits worker safety protections (personal protective equipment, re-entry intervals) for ferric phosphate use; comment recommends adding such requirements to protect farmworkers and handlers.

[P3] Elemental sulfur is permitted as a slug/snail bait, but sulfur is widely used as a fungicide/soil amendment; the rule does not clarify cumulative application limits or interactions with other organic-approved sulfur uses, creating risk of excessive sulfur loading.

[P3] The efficacy and safety profile of elemental sulfur as a molluscicide is not well established in the rulemaking record; commenters request publication of scientific evidence supporting its inclusion or removal of sulfur until data are provided.

[P3] Elemental sulfur dusts can cause respiratory irritation and create drift concerns; the rule should include mandated application methods (granules vs. dust) and PPE requirements to mitigate worker and bystander exposure.

[P3] Allowing elemental sulfur for mollusc control may increase sulfur residues on food crops; commenters request residue limits or monitoring requirements to ensure food safety.

[P4] Permitting Polyoxin D zinc salt lacks specification of allowable use patterns (crops, rates, pre-harvest intervals), raising concerns about residues, impacts on non-target fungi, and development of resistance; request detailed use parameters.

[P4] Polyoxin D zinc salt is an antifungal antibiotic-like compound; its use could conflict with prohibitions on antibiotics or pharmaceutical agents in organic systems—request clarification on compatibility with organic standards and whether microbial resistance monitoring is required.

[P4] The rule does not require that Polyoxin D zinc salt inputs be produced without genetically engineered organisms or contain no prohibited biocides; commenters request supply-chain certification and source disclosure.

[P4] Environmental fate and ecotoxicity data for Polyoxin D zinc salt are not cited; commenters demand a risk assessment for soil microbial communities, aquatic toxicity, and accumulation before allowing it in organic production.

[P5] Allowing specified nonorganic substances as ingredients in “organic” or “made with organic” processed products risks broadening the range of nonorganic additives permitted without clear limits, diluting the organic label — request stricter limitations and full disclosure on labels.

[P5] The proposed §205.605(a) lacks a list of specific allowed nonorganic substances and criteria for inclusion (availability, essentiality, or processing necessity); commenters urge that any additions must meet a demonstrated nonavailability test and be transparently listed.

[P5] The provision does not require certification or traceability for nonorganic ingredients used in “organic” processed products, which could permit fraud or inclusion of prohibited substances—request chain-of-custody and supplier documentation requirements.

[P5] Processed-food consumer advocates will object that §205.605(a) should require labeling that identifies which ingredients are nonorganic within “organic” and “made with organic” products to enable informed choices.

[P5] Small processors may be disproportionately burdened by administrative requirements if the provision later adds complex approval processes for nonorganic ingredients; request phased implementation or exemptions for small businesses.

[P6] Magnesium chloride is permitted as an ingredient in or on processed products labeled as “organic” or “made with organic,” but the rule fails to specify maximum allowable levels or functional uses (e.g., firming agent, coagulant), which could lead to overuse.

[P6] The allowance of magnesium chloride is problematic for certain diets (e.g., sodium-restricted consumers) and may have functional overlaps with prohibited additives; commenters request specification of permitted functional categories and labeling requirements.

[P6] The regulation does not address the source of magnesium chloride (synthetic vs. mined, contaminants like heavy metals), nor require purity specifications or testing—request minimum purity standards and contaminant limits.

[P6] Approving magnesium chloride without a demonstrated nonavailability determination is inconsistent with organic policy that nonorganic materials be allowed only when organic equivalents are unavailable; request documentation that organic alternatives are not feasible.

[P6] Food manufacturers and certifiers seek clarity on whether magnesium chloride is allowed in both “organic” and “made with organic” products and whether its use affects the percentage of organic content calculation; request explicit cross-references and accounting rules.

[P1] The six-month automatic suspension timeline in § 59.24(a) is unreasonably short for many communities to enact or transmit required floodplain-management regulations, and FEMA should extend the period or allow documented good-faith extensions.

[P1] The rule does not specify what constitutes "required regulations" for triggering the suspension; stakeholders request explicit definitions or a checklist to avoid arbitrary determinations.

[P2] The condition in § 59.24(a) that relies solely on receipt of copies by the Administrator is problematic — the rule should accept electronic filing, certified mail proof of local adoption, or third‑party verification as proof of compliance.

[P2] The provision lacks a process for resolving disputes about whether submitted regulations are "adequate"; commenters ask for an appeal or informal review process before suspensions are finalized.

[P3] Requiring written notice "no later than 30 days before the six‑month period expires" creates a narrow window for communities to respond; FEMA should require notice as soon as possible and allow longer response time.

[P3] The rule does not require that the written notice identify the specific deficiencies in the community's regulations; commenters request that notices include clear citations to statutory/regulatory requirements and the actions needed to cure the deficiency.

[P4] Publishing loss of eligibility "on the internet or by a comparable method" may not reach affected property owners or lenders; the rule should require direct notice to registered NFIP policyholders and mortgage lenders in the community in addition to online publication.

[P4] The term "comparable method" is vague and could permit inadequate notification; FEMA should define acceptable alternative publication methods (e.g., local newspaper, mailed notice, email to registrants).

[P5] The provision that suspension becomes effective automatically at six months could unfairly penalize communities that have taken corrective steps but whose submissions are delayed in agency processing; FEMA should condition effectiveness on actual agency determination rather than a hard time trigger.

[P6] § 59.24(c)'s requirement that the Administrator "shall inform" the community 30 days prior to suspension needs to specify the mode of delivery and provide proof of receipt to prevent disputes about whether notice was received.

[P6] The rule must clarify whether the 30‑day prior written notice can run concurrently with the public online publication or whether separate actions are required; timing ambiguity could lead to procedural challenges.

[P1] The January 6, 2020 comment deadline is already expired and therefore this provision should be revised to provide a new, reasonable comment period; stakeholders did not have an opportunity to submit meaningful comments under that deadline.

[P1] If the agency retains a January 6, 2020 deadline, the rule is procedurally invalid under the Administrative Procedure Act for failing to provide adequate notice and an opportunity to comment — FAA should reissue the NPRM with a fresh comment period.

[P2] The requirement to "follow the requirements of this AD within the specified compliance times" is ambiguous because "specified compliance times" are not consistently defined across the AD; FAA must explicitly list compliance times for each affected engine/part.

[P2] The compliance clause should include a grandfathering exception for engines that have undergone equivalent inspections or mitigations prior to the effective date — otherwise operators who have already taken action may be redundantly burdened.

[P3] Requiring removal of listed LPT 3rd-stage blades "at the next engine shop visit" is operationally unclear for leased engines, and FAA should clarify obligations when shop visits are scheduled by lessors versus operators.

[P3] "At the next engine shop visit" could force unplanned maintenance and economic hardship for operators with long on-wing intervals; FAA should provide an alternative compliance window (e.g., within X flight cycles or hours) rather than tying compliance to potentially distant or irregular shop visits.

[P3] The AD does not account for spare engines in storage that are not scheduled for a shop visit; FAA should clarify when and how blades in stored/spare engines must be removed.

[P4] For P/N 5387343, removal at next shop visit lacks a definition of "remove from service" (scrap, quarantine, send to manufacturer) — FAA should specify disposition and credit provisions for removed parts.

[P4] Operators need guidance on documentation and traceability requirements when removing P/N 5387343 blades; the AD should require or permit tagging and recordkeeping instructions.

[P5] For P/N 5387493, the AD should state whether rework/repair that changes the P/N is permitted to avoid removal — current wording may unintentionally prohibit legitimate repairs.

[P5] The AD does not estimate the fleetwide quantity of P/N 5387493 blades or provide an economic impact analysis specific to replacing this P/N; FAA must supply cost and availability information.

[P6] For P/N 5387473, there is no phase-in option or allowance for operators to use serviceable inventory until the next planned shop visit if the shop visit will not occur for many flight hours; FAA should allow a defined grace period.

[P6] The AD should identify whether modified P/N 5387473 blades (e.g., that have been processed per a specific service bulletin) remain subject to removal — ambiguity will create enforcement issues.

[P7] For P/N 5387503, the AD fails to indicate whether blades with serial-numbered modifications or parts approval documents that render them non-conforming P/Ns are exempt; FAA should provide serial-number or modification-based guidance.

[P7] The requirement to remove P/N 5387503 at next shop visit fails to consider supply chain constraints — replacement "eligible parts" availability may be limited, and FAA should include a temporary relief provision or ordered phasing.

[P8] The "engine shop visit" definition excludes flange separation solely for transportation, but does not address other transient flange separations (e.g., for non-maintenance inspections); FAA should clarify borderline cases to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P8] The flange-separation criterion may be ambiguous for MROs that perform limited disassembly; FAA should add examples of qualifying and non-qualifying activities to reduce dispute.

[P8] The requirement tied to "induction into the shop" could be interpreted to permit operators to delay compliance by claiming no shop induction — FAA should clarify enforcement mechanisms to prevent gaming.

[P9] Defining "part eligible for installation" simply as any LPT 3rd-stage blade not having the listed P/Ns may allow substitute aftermarket parts lacking proper certification; FAA should require that "eligible parts" meet specific certification or traceability standards.

[P9] The AD should clarify whether reworked or repaired blades that are assigned new P/Ns remain eligible for installation, to avoid legal uncertainty for MROs performing authorized repairs.

[P10] Granting the Manager AMOC approval authority centralizes discretion without providing objective criteria; commenters request publication of standards or factors the Manager will consider when approving AMOCs to ensure consistency.

[P10] The rule should permit applicants to seek AMOC approval from the manufacturer’s DER (designated engineering representative) or equivalent delegated authority in addition to the Manager to expedite approvals.

[P11] The routing requirement to send AMOC requests to a principal inspector or local FSDO may delay review when the engine is operated internationally or by non-U.S. operators; FAA should allow direct submission to the ECO Branch in such cases.

[P11] The AD should permit electronic submission to the ECO Branch as an alternative to routing through the principal inspector to streamline multinational operator compliance.

[P12] The instruction to address AMOC submissions to the person named in paragraph (j)(1) is circular because paragraph (j)(1) is not included in the preamble excerpted; FAA must ensure contact names and addresses are present and updated.

[P12] FAA should provide a published checklist and preferred submission format for AMOC materials when sending directly to the certification office manager to avoid rejection for noncompliance with administrative requirements.

[P13] Allowing AMOC requests via ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov is helpful, but the AD must guarantee acknowledgment timelines and estimated review times so operators can plan maintenance schedules.

[P13] The AD should permit encrypted file transfer or a secure portal for AMOC submissions rather than standard email to protect proprietary engineering data included in requests.

[P14] Requiring notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC may be impractical for small operators without a principal inspector; FAA should explicitly permit notification to the manager of the local FSDO or CHDO (as parenthetical suggests), and define acceptable notice lead times.

[P14] The AD should clarify whether “before using” means prior to commencing the maintenance action or prior to returning the engine to service after using the AMOC — this timing ambiguity can affect operational planning.

[P15] The applicability provision lists many IAE PW1000G variants but the excerpt is truncated; commenters request that the FAA publish the full list and ensure that all affected submodels and serial-number ranges are clearly identified.

[P15] The applicability should explicitly state whether engines installed on specific airframes (e.g., A320neo family, Embraer variants) are included or excluded, to avoid confusion among operators and lessors.

[P15] Legal commenters will likely argue that the AD must include a clear applicability table mapping P/Ns to specific engine serial numbers, kit configurations, and production blocks to avoid overbreadth.

[P3] Industry commenters will request an allowance for credit for prior actions: if an operator replaced listed blades per a manufacturer SB before the AD effective date, that should be explicitly accepted as compliance.

[P4][P5][P6][P7] MROs and parts suppliers will request FAA to include guidance on financial compensation, parts return processes, and whether removed blades are eligible for return-to-manufacturer credit.

[P9] Consumer/aviation-safety advocates will request that FAA require inspections of adjacent stages when removing 3rd-stage blades to ensure no collateral damage or wear compromises safety.

[P2][P3] Operators will request an economic impact analysis quantifying downtime, parts cost, and labor per engine to justify the immediate removal-at-shop-visit requirement.

[P10][P13] Legal and industry commenters will ask FAA to set maximum review timelines for AMOC requests (e.g., 60 days) and to publish backlog statistics for AMOC processing to provide transparency.

[P8] Maintenance organizations will request an explicit statement whether transient test stands or bench tests that separate flanges count as "shop visit" to avoid unintended compliance triggers.

[P3] International operators will request harmonization language to accept equivalent EASA or other foreign authority directives as compliance to prevent duplicative actions.

[P9] Aftermarket parts manufacturers will request an explicit pathway for new blade part numbers to be certified as "eligible for installation" under the AD, including acceptance criteria and documentation requirements.

[P1] Public-interest groups will request that FAA re-open the comment period to allow stakeholders to address supply chain and safety implications in light of current global maintenance disruptions (e.g., COVID-19 impacts as of early 2020).

[P2] Safety advocates will request that the AD include interim flight restrictions or operational mitigations (such as reduced thrust settings or inspection intervals) until blades can be replaced at the next shop visit.

[P3] Some operators will challenge the safety basis presented for immediate removal only at shop visit and request that FAA provide the underlying data (fracture rates, failure modes, risk assessment) used to justify the action.

[P7] Parts distributors will request clarification on whether the prohibition on installing listed P/Ns applies to parts already purchased but not yet installed, and whether sale or transfer of such inventory is restricted.

[P11] Small operators will request that FAA permit a simplified AMOC submission route for routine, low-risk alternatives (such as extending inspection intervals) to reduce administrative burden.

[P13] Security-conscious commenters will ask FAA to confirm that submissions to the public ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov address will not trigger export control or ITAR issues for foreign-origin engineering data, and to provide guidance accordingly.

[P14] Flight standards personnel will request standard operating procedures for receiving notifications about AMOC usage to ensure consistent acceptance and recordkeeping across FSDOs.

[P15] Environmental groups will request that the AD include a disposition plan for removed blades to prevent improper disposal of hazardous materials and ensure environmental compliance.

[P1] The rule’s classification test in §800.30(a) is ambiguous because it references paragraphs (c)-(f) without defining an objective compliance procedure, creating uncertainty for manufacturers about when a device is OTC versus prescription.

[P1] Industry commenters will request clarification that meeting paragraphs (c)-(f) must be demonstrated by documented testing records and labeling submission to FDA, not merely self-attestation.

[P2] The provision that any air‑conduction hearing aid not meeting §520(q) or the specified requirements is a prescription device (§800.30(a)) could unintentionally classify many hybrid or software‑driven devices as prescription without a clear rubric for borderline cases.

[P2] Trade associations will ask for examples or a decision flowchart showing how devices with partial compliance (e.g., compliant hardware but non‑compliant software features) should be classified.

[P3] Audiology clinics and dispensers will support §800.30(b)’s prohibition on deeming a device “used” simply because a prospective user tried it, but request that the rule also provide a clear permissible evaluation timeframe and sanitation standards to avoid infection risks.

[P3] Consumer safety advocates may argue that the prohibition should be limited—if a device is tried in multiple ears or returned after trial without adequate reprocessing, it should be treated as used and subject to cleaning/inspection requirements.

[P4] Manufacturers will request the full text or a template for the “specified labeling content” required by §800.30(c) to ensure uniform compliance and avoid differing interpretations by FDA inspectors.

[P5] Retailers will ask that §800.30(c)(1)’s outside‑package requirements include minimum font size, language, and placement standards to ensure feasible packaging design for small form‑factor devices.

[P6] Pediatric health advocacy groups strongly support the explicit prohibition in §800.30(c)(1)(i)(A) (no use under 18) but will request an exception or pathway for pediatric audiologists to access OTC devices under controlled clinical programs.

[P7] Some hearing professionals will object to the mandatory warning that under‑18s “should go to a doctor” as insufficiently specific—requesting that the rule list which specialists (ENT, pediatric audiologist) and recommended timeline for evaluation.

[P8] The permission in §800.30(c)(1)(i)(C) to seek assistance from a hearing professional is vague; hearing professionals will request that the rule explicitly allow them to provide fitting/support services for OTC devices without converting the device to a prescription product.

[P9] Consumer advocates will request that §800.30(c)(1)(ii) require language indicating that “used or rebuilt” items must meet specific refurbishment and sterilization standards, not merely a declaration on the package.

[P10] Manufacturers object to the burden in §800.30(c)(2) to include a printed brochure in every package plus maintain an electronic version freely accessible, citing cost and environmental impact—request allowance for QR code linking to the brochure without printing for multi‑unit retail packs.

[P11] Disability rights groups will insist that the electronic brochure requirement (§800.30(c)(2)) include accessibility standards (WCAG, large print, formats for screen readers) and multiple language translations.

[P12] Consumer groups will challenge §800.30(c)(2)(i) ordering requirement for warnings (appearance “prior to any content except the cover page”), arguing it could push important operational instructions below mandatory warnings and confuse users—request that operational safety instructions also be front‑and‑center.

[P13] Medical societies will support §800.30(c)(2)(i) (red‑flag warnings) but ask that the list of conditions requiring a physician be evidence‑based and limited to avoid over‑referral and unnecessary medical visits.

[P14] Retailers and e‑commerce platforms will request that §800.30(c)(2)(i)(E)’s phone‑request option for paper copies include a reasonable fulfillment window (e.g., 7 business days) and allow fulfillment via in‑store pickup to avoid shipping costs.

[P16] Small manufacturers will ask for clarity in §800.30(c)(2)(iii) about the permitted order and prominence of cautions/notices to avoid subjective enforcement and recall risk.

[P17] Pediatric advocates reiterate that duplicative warnings banning use under 18 in §800.30(c)(2)(iii)(A) are necessary but request that packaging include a clear path for parents seeking professional evaluation and guidance on pediatric devices.

[P18] Consumer safety groups will request §800.30(c)(2)(iii)(B) (consult physician prior to purchase if certain conditions are present) include a brief definition of “sudden hearing loss” and examples to prevent consumer confusion.

[P19] Patient advocates will demand that §800.30(c)(2)(iii)(C) require manufacturers to provide a toll‑free number with trained personnel for reports of pain/discomfort, not just contact information for the manufacturer.

[P20] Occupational safety organizations will support the hearing protection caution in §800.30(c)(2)(iii)(A) but request an explicit prohibition on marketing OTC hearing aids as “hearing protection” or “noise reduction” unless certified.

[P21] Consumer groups will argue that the caution about excessive sound output (§800.30(c)(2)(iii)(B)) should require default maximum volume limits in the device firmware and not rely solely on labeling.

[P22] Hearing specialists will request that the “Note: If you remain concerned, consult a professional” (§800.30(c)(2)(iii)(D)) be accompanied by guidance on how to find licensed professionals and whether packaged devices must include a list or link.

[P23] Manufacturers will object to requirements in §800.30(c)(2)(iv)-(ix) (illustrations, functions, accessories, side effects, technical specs) as overly prescriptive for small or generic devices and ask for thresholds (e.g., only for devices above certain complexity) or template language.

[P24] Engineers and testing labs will request more specific measurement protocols and tolerances for the technical specifications required in §800.30(c)(2)(ix) and (c)(4) to ensure reproducible reporting across labs.

[P25] Manufacturers will ask for clarification on what constitutes “known physiological side effects” in §800.30(c)(2)(viii) and whether anecdotal user complaints must be included if not causally linked.

[P26] Manufacturers and repair networks will welcome §800.30(c)(2)(xii) but request that the required repair information include privacy safeguards (not publishing customer addresses) and allow a centralized repair portal instead of a single street address.

[P27] Companies that conducted supporting studies will ask for specifics on the summary content required by §800.30(c)(2)(xiii), including word limits and whether proprietary data can be redacted.

[P28] Device designers will request clearer tolerances and permissible exceptions for permanent markings (§800.30(c)(3)), e.g., font size or placement for in‑ear micro‑devices where durable markings are impractical.

[P29] Battery‑powered device makers seek an alternative to the “+” marking requirement (§800.30(c)(3)(ii)) for designs that physically prevent reverse insertion, requesting an allowance for pictograms or packaging markings instead of on‑device markings.

[P35] The exception in §800.30(d)(2) allowing 120 dB SPL for devices with input‑controlled compression and user volume control will draw requests from engineers to define the required compression parameters and to clarify how user volume control must be limited (e.g., max increment steps).

[P39] Test labs will ask that §800.30(e)(2)’s prohibition on noise‑floor‑lowering methods during self‑noise measurement include explicit definitions of prohibited features (e.g., noise gates, adaptive filters) and standard disablement procedures.

[P50] Legal experts will warn that the statement in §800.30(h)(2)(C) that representing oneself as a servicer/etc. creates no specialized obligations may conflict with existing state consumer‑protection obligations and seek harmonizing language.

[P51] Standards organizations will request that the incorporation by reference in §800.30(i) include the full ANSI/CTA–2051:2017 text, effective date, and instructions for public access and amendment procedures.
