raw_output:
[P1] The comment deadline of May 5, 2022 is unreasonably short and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow operators and OEMs to prepare technical data and economic impact analyses.

[P1] The rule does not state whether electronic comment submissions will be accepted after business hours on May 5, 2022; clarify acceptance window to avoid rejecting timely-but-late-in-day filings.

[P2] The general compliance obligation lacks grandfathering language for work already performed to equivalent standards; request explicit recognition that equivalent inspections accomplished per other approved SB revisions satisfy the AD.

[P3] Requiring BSIs for all Group 1 engines with affected blades is overbroad; ask FAA to limit mandatory inspections to engines that meet the specific service bulletin serial-number or life-cycle criteria rather than all Group 1 units.

[P3] The AD should clarify responsibility for scheduling and performing borescope inspections when engines are operated by third-party MROs under lease arrangements (airframe operator vs. lessor vs. MRO responsibility).

[P4] The initial BSI timing reference is internally inconsistent and appears truncated ("before the HPT rotor stage 1 blade accumulates 1,7…"); the FAA must correct the numeric threshold (confirm whether it is 1,700 FCs or 17,00 CSN) before final rulemaking.

[P4] The requirement to perform the initial inspection within "100 FCs after accumulating 800 MENA takeoffs" is ambiguous: define whether the 100 FCs are counted globally, per-engine, or per-airframe and whether takeoffs in non-MENA regions count toward the 800 threshold.

[P5] Repetitive BSI interval of "not to exceed 150 FCs" for Group 1 may impose excessive maintenance burdens; request risk assessment justifying 150-FC frequency and consideration of longer intervals for low-deterioration environments.

[P6] The grouping criteria distinguishing Group 1 and Group 2 engines are not provided in the AD text; include clear definitions (engine models, modifications, serial ranges) to avoid misclassification.

[P7] The Group 2 initial BSI timing contains conflicting numeric limits ("before the HPT rotor stage 1 blade accumulates 2,600 CSN, or withi…") and appears truncated; correct the rule to include full thresholds and the exact triggering conditions.

[P7] The combination of 100 FCs after 800 MENA takeoffs or before 2,600 CSN creates an operational conflict for many operators; FAA should provide example scenarios to show which threshold takes precedence.

[P8] A 300-FC repetitive interval for Group 2 may still be burdensome for short-haul operators; request allowance for condition-based extension if prior inspections show no degradation and to permit an AMOC process for interval extension.

[P9] The disposition criteria in (g)(3) rely on a referenced service bulletin, but the AD does not incorporate the SB by reference with revision/version number; specify exact SB revision to ensure consistent compliance.

[P9] The AD should detail mandatory reporting formats and data elements for replacement vs. re-inspection actions to avoid inconsistent implementation across operators.

[P10] The conditional sister-engine action within 50 FCs is operationally unrealistic for some fleets with limited ground time; request clarification whether ferry flights or maintenance events count toward the 50-FC limit and whether extensions can be authorized.

[P11] Requiring inspection or replacement of sister engines within 5 FCs after the affected engine inspection is excessively tight and could conflict with scheduled operations; propose extending the sister-engine window to 50 FCs or allowing a risk-based alternative with FAA approval.

[P11] The AD does not clarify which party bears cost for unscheduled sister-engine removals/repairs on leased aircraft; require allocation guidance or compensation mechanisms for lessors/operators.

[P12] Mandating replacement when the SB specifies engine removal is disproportionate—if the SB allows engine removal for off-wing repair, the AD should permit rework or repair in lieu of replacement, provided the repair meets FAA-approved procedures.

[P12] Requiring physical replacement rather than engine removal (for off-wing repair) could require unnecessary spare engines and increase costs; FAA should allow on-wing remedial repairs that restore airworthiness per approved methods.

[P13] The 30-day reporting requirement to CFM for any unserviceable finding is too short for operators in remote locations or with limited connectivity; extend reporting to 60 days or permit alternate reporting channels (fax, postal) with acknowledgement.

[P13] The AD should specify the confidentiality and use of proprietary data submitted in reports to CFM, and whether those reports will be available under FOIA; operators may be reluctant to submit sensitive maintenance data without assurances.

[P14] The designation of the Manager, ECO Branch, as sole AMOC approver centralizes authority and may create bottlenecks; propose allowing delegated approval by regional FAA offices for non-controversial AMOCs to speed compliance.

[P15] AMOC request routing requirements are inconsistent: sending to principal inspectors, local FSDOs, or directly to the certification manager should include standardized forms and an expected response timeline (e.g., 45 days) to provide predictability.

[P15] Require that AMOC submissions sent by email to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov receive an automated receipt and tracking number so applicants can monitor status.

[P16] Notifying the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC could delay operations if the inspector is unavailable; allow operators to implement AMOC once FAA approval is granted and notify the inspector within a defined timeframe (e.g., 48 hours) rather than obtain pre-use permission.

[P16] Clarify who is the "appropriate principal inspector" for operators with multiple jurisdictions or for leased aircraft operating across regions to avoid confusion about notification obligations.

[P3] The AD should require training and qualification standards for technicians performing the borescope inspections to ensure consistent detection of the specified defects.

[P5] Specify acceptance criteria and photographic documentation requirements for BSIs so that different maintenance providers produce comparable findings.

[P9] The AD's reliance on the referenced SB for re-inspect/replace criteria without mandating that only FAA-approved SB revisions apply creates legal uncertainty; mandate that only the SB revision cited in the AD (or FAA-approved later revisions) be used.

[P13] Require that reporting include root-cause analysis for unserviceable findings and not just the defect description, to allow fleet-wide safety assessment.

[P4] The AD must define "MENA takeoffs" precisely (routing, airport boundary, or pairings) to ensure consistent counting across operators.

[P7] For engines near the 2,600 CSN threshold, the AD should allow credit for prior non-FAA inspections that used equivalent techniques (e.g., detailed visual inspections) to avoid redundant work.

[P11] The AD needs to define "sister engine" (same aircraft, same flight number, same engine model) to prevent misinterpretation when fleets mix engine types on similar airframes.

[P2] Request inclusion of an economic impact section estimating direct costs per inspection, replacement, downtime, and reporting burden for affected operators to comply with the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

[P3] Operators request an AMOC pathway specifically allowing remote borescope video review by OEM or FAA experts in lieu of immediate on-site decision-making when findings are ambiguous.

[P13] The AD should state whether reporting to CFM satisfies any FAA reporting obligations, or whether separate reports to FAA Service Difficulty Reporting (SDR) are also required.

[P12] Legal commenters will argue that requiring replacement where an SB directs engine removal may exceed FAA authority under 14 CFR 39 absent a safety justification; provide legal rationale and risk assessment supporting this mandate.

[P1] Because May 5, 2022 has passed, the AD should withdraw and reissue with current dates rather than enforce an expired comment period.

The combination of 100 FCs after 800 MENA takeoffs or before 2,600 CSN creates an operational conflict for many operators; FAA should provide example scenarios to show which threshold takes precedence.

A 300-FC repetitive interval for Group 2 may still be burdensome for short-haul operators; request allowance for condition-based extension if prior inspections show no degradation and to permit an AMOC process for interval extension.

The disposition criteria in (g)(3) rely on a referenced service bulletin, but the AD does not incorporate the SB by reference with revision/version number; specify exact SB revision to ensure consistent compliance.
The AD should detail mandatory reporting formats and data elements for replacement vs. re-inspection actions to avoid inconsistent implementation across operators.

The conditional sister-engine action within 50 FCs is operationally unrealistic for some fleets with limited ground time; request clarification whether ferry flights or maintenance events count toward the 50-FC limit and whether extensions can be authorized.

Requiring inspection or replacement of sister engines within 5 FCs after the affected engine inspection is excessively tight and could conflict with scheduled operations; propose extending the sister-engine window to 50 FCs or allowing a risk-based alternative with FAA approval.

Requiring physical replacement rather than engine removal (for off-wing repair) could require unnecessary spare engines and increase costs; FAA should allow on-wing remedial repairs that restore airworthiness per approved methods.

The 30-day reporting requirement to CFM for any unserviceable finding is too short for operators in remote locations or with limited connectivity; extend reporting to 60 days or permit alternate reporting channels (fax, postal) with acknowledgement.

The AD should specify the confidentiality and use of proprietary data submitted in reports to CFM, and whether those reports will be available under FOIA; operators may be reluctant to submit sensitive maintenance data without assurances.

AMOC request routing requirements are inconsistent: sending to principal inspectors, local FSDOs, or directly to the certification manager should include standardized forms and an expected response timeline (e.g., 45 days) to provide predictability.

Clarify who is the "appropriate principal inspector" for operators with multiple jurisdictions or for leased aircraft operating across regions to avoid confusion about notification obligations.
The AD should require training and qualification standards for technicians performing the borescope inspections to ensure consistent detection of the specified defects.
Specify acceptance criteria and photographic documentation requirements for BSIs so that different maintenance providers produce comparable findings.

The AD's reliance on the referenced SB for re-inspect/replace criteria without mandating that only FAA-approved SB revisions apply creates legal uncertainty; mandate that only the SB revision cited in the AD (or FAA-approved later revisions) be used.
Require that reporting include root-cause analysis for unserviceable findings and not just the defect description, to allow fleet-wide safety assessment.
The AD must define "MENA takeoffs" precisely (routing, airport boundary, or pairings) to ensure consistent counting across operators.
For engines near the 2,600 CSN threshold, the AD should allow credit for prior non-FAA inspections that used equivalent techniques (e.g., detailed visual inspections) to avoid redundant work.
The AD needs to define "sister engine" (same aircraft, same flight number, same engine model) to prevent misinterpretation when fleets mix engine types on similar airframes.

Request inclusion of an economic impact section estimating direct costs per inspection, replacement, downtime, and reporting burden for affected operators to comply with the Regulatory Flexibility Act.
Operators request an AMOC pathway specifically allowing remote borescope video review by OEM or FAA experts in lieu of immediate on-site decision-making when findings are ambiguous.
The AD should state whether reporting to CFM satisfies any FAA reporting obligations, or whether separate reports to FAA Service Difficulty Reporting (SDR) are also required.

Legal commenters will argue that requiring replacement where an SB directs engine removal may exceed FAA authority under 14 CFR 39 absent a safety justification; provide legal rationale and risk assessment supporting this mandate.
Because May 5, 2022 has passed, the AD should withdraw and reissue with current dates rather than enforce an expired comment period.

raw_output:
[P1] The February 11, 2019 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonably short and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow operators and unions time to prepare informed responses and for affected suppliers to provide technical data.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether electronic comments submitted on Feb 11, 2019 at 11:59 PM ET will be accepted as timely to avoid potential rejection of late-in-the-day submissions.

[P2] § 39.13(c) should explicitly state whether Boeing 767-200F (freighter conversions) and other supplemental type certificated (STC) derivatives are included, since some STC-modified -200/-300 series airplanes may have modified seat installations.

[P2] The applicability in § 39.13(c) is overly broad by covering “certificated in any category” without addressing military, cargo-only, or governmental-exempt operations — request carve-outs or clarifications for government-operated aircraft and exempt categories.

[P3] § 39.13(f) lacks specificity on whether compliance times are counted from the AD effective date or some other date; cross-reference to the AD effective date should be added to avoid ambiguity.

[P3] The obligation in § 39.13(f) should allow for relief where operators have compelling supply-chain issues preventing timely compliance; request inclusion of temporary extensions or interim mitigations pending parts availability.

[P4] The 36-month inspection deadline in § 39.13(g) is too long for a potential safety-critical seat part/serial-number inspection — safety advocates request a shorter compliance interval (e.g., 180 days) for initial inspections.

[P4] Airlines and MROs request permission to combine the § 39.13(g) inspection with scheduled heavy maintenance checks (C or D checks) when within the 36-month window to reduce operational disruption; request an explicit allowance.

[P4] § 39.13(g) must define what documentation constitutes acceptable evidence of part/serial numbers (photos, maintenance records, OEM parts tags) to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P5] § 39.13(h) incorporates Boeing service bulletin RC actions but does not provide FAA-approved alternative performance standards; request FAA validation of the Boeing acceptance and explicit listing of required corrective actions in the AD text.

[P5] There is insufficient clarity in § 39.13(h) about whether mandatory “RC” actions include both inspection and replacement; commenters request an enumerated list of the RC actions from the Boeing service bulletin in the AD.

[P6] The substitution in § 39.13(i) replacing “original issue date” with the AD effective date could unintentionally shorten or lengthen compliance windows compared to the manufacturer’s intent; request examples and a table showing equivalent dates.

[P6] Legal experts request that § 39.13(i) clarify how the AD effective date interacts with previously issued Boeing SB revisions and whether operators who complied to the SB before the AD effective date are considered compliant.

[P7] § 39.13(j)(1) should specify the qualification and traceability requirements for a “serviceable Captain’s seat” (approved parts number, maintenance status, life-limited parts) to ensure consistent interpretation across operators.

[P7] Industry commenters request that § 39.13(j)(1) permit installation of an FAA-accepted PMA or STC replacement Captain’s seat that meets equivalent safety standards, not only the exact seats specified in the Boeing SB.

[P7] Labor/unions express concern that allowing installation to end repetitive inspections (§ 39.13(j)(1)) may incentivize temporary seat swaps that compromise human factors or ergonomics; request human-performance review before deeming seats “serviceable.”

[P8] Parallel to P7, § 39.13(j)(2) must define what constitutes a “serviceable First Officer’s seat” and whether refurbished seats with replaced subcomponents meet the criterion to terminate repetitive checks.

[P8] Cargo operators request confirmation that installing a serviceable First Officer’s seat per § 39.13(j)(2) on single-pilot ferry flights or ferry configurations still meets the intent of the AD.

[P9] The authority in § 39.13(k)(1) concentrating AMOC approvals with the Seattle ACO Manager creates a single point of bottleneck; commenters request delegation alternatives or guaranteed response timelines for AMOC decisions.

[P9] Legal commenters request the AD specify the criteria the Seattle ACO Manager will use to approve or deny AMOCs to ensure transparency and fair process.

[P10] § 39.13(k)(1) requires sending AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO under 14 CFR 39.19; commenters ask for a clear flowchart and contact list to reduce misdirected AMOC submissions.

[P10] Operators request explicit acknowledgement that electronic submission to the email in § 39.13(k)(1) satisfies the requirement to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector/local FSDO.

[P11] § 39.13(k)(1) instructs senders to address information to the person named in paragraph (l)(1) when sending directly to the certification office manager, but paragraph (l)(1) is not included in the proposed excerpt; commenters request that the full contact be published in the final rule.

[P11] Confidential business information considerations: if senders must direct AMOC materials to a named person, the AD should include procedures for marking confidential attachments and handling proprietary technical data.

[P12] § 39.13(k)(1) allows email submissions to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov, but commenters raise cybersecurity and privacy concerns — request guidance on encrypted submission methods and confirmation receipts.

[P12] Operators request confirmation that attachments up to a certain file size (e.g., 25 MB) will be accepted via the provided email address or alternative secure portals should be offered.

[P13] § 39.13(k)(2) requires notification to the principal inspector or FSDO/CHDO before using an approved AMOC; commenters ask for timing requirements (how far in advance) and whether oral notification is sufficient.

[P13] Legal commenters note the burden and potential operational disruption of requiring prior notification before implementing an AMOC and request the rule allow retrospective notification when immediate action is necessary to maintain operations.

[P14] § 39.13(k)(3) allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to be used for repairs raises independence concerns; commenters request that any ODA approvals be subject to FAA concurrence and documentation proving equivalent safety.

[P14] Independent AMOC option: industry commenters request the AD allow OEM-authorized maintenance organizations other than Boeing ODA to approve equivalent AMOCs when they can demonstrate equivalent expertise.

[P15] § 39.13(k)(3) requires that AMOC-approved repair methods meet the airplane’s certification basis and explicitly reference this AD — commenters request a template for the necessary reference language to ensure consistent approvals.

[P15] Certification lawyers warn that the requirement to meet the original certification basis could unduly restrict innovative repair methods; request FAA provide a process for showing equivalent level of safety that is not strictly limited to the original certification basis.

[P16] Requiring all RC-labeled steps per § 39.13(k)(4)(i) to be accomplished is appropriate, but commenters request the AD include acceptance criteria and measurable standards for each RC step to avoid subjective enforcement.

[P16] MROs request clarification whether performing RC steps using non-standard tooling or using alternative qualified personnel requires prior AMOC approval, even if the steps themselves are unchanged.

[P17] The RC Exempt exception in § 39.13(k)(4)(i) needs a list or cross-reference to indicate which steps in the Boeing SB are RC Exempt to prevent confusion.

[P17] Operators request an explanation of the rationale used to designate specific steps as “RC Exempt” to assess risk tradeoffs.

[P18] § 39.13(k)(4)(i) requires AMOCs for deviations from RC steps; commenters request expedited AMOC review pathways for minor deviations caused by parts obsolescence or tooling limitations.

[P18] Airlines ask whether temporary deviations from RC steps in emergency situations (safety of flight) can be taken without prior AMOC and reported afterward; propose explicit allowance for emergency deviations with immediate reporting requirements.

[P19] § 39.13(k)(4)(ii) permitting deviations from non-RC steps under an operator’s maintenance program should require operators to document the basis for deviation and risk assessment — commenters request mandatory recordkeeping requirements be added.

[P19] Maintenance program managers request the FAA to clarify whether a deviation under § 39.13(k)(4)(ii) requires submitting a revision to the operator’s approved maintenance program or can be treated as a one-off practice.

[P20] The condition in § 39.13(k)(4)(ii) that RC steps must still be accomplishable after deviating from non-RC steps is vague — commenters request objective metrics or examples demonstrating acceptable deviations that preserve RC step accomplishability.

[P20] Commenters ask that the FAA define what constitutes “accomplished as specified” for RC steps (tolerances, torque values, sequence requirements) to prevent enforcement disputes.

[P21] § 39.13(k)(4)(ii)’s requirement that the airplane can be returned to an airworthy condition after deviations must be accompanied by explicit criteria for what documentation and certification are needed to demonstrate return to airworthiness.

[P21] Legal and operations commenters request clarification whether post-deviation return-to-service actions require sign-off by a certificated mechanic with inspection authorization (IA) or the principal inspector, and whether ferry flight conditions are permitted.

[P1] Industry commenters will argue that §97.1’s broad permission to prevent “using the variety in producing hybrids or different varieties” is overly expansive and could bar routine breeding research and should be narrowed to exclude bona fide research and breeding exceptions.

[P1] Plant breeders’ advocacy groups will claim §97.1 lacks clarity on whether farmers’ traditional practices (e.g., saving seed for on-farm selection) are covered and request explicit carve-outs for farm-saved seed and breeder research.

[P1] Seed trade associations will assert that §97.1’s list of prohibited acts (selling, reproducing, conditioning, stocking, using) duplicates other statutes inconsistently and ask the agency to align terminology with the Plant Variety Protection Act (PVPA) and provide definitions for “using” and “conditioning.”

[P2] Small breeder groups and legal practitioners will request that §97.5(c) specify timelines, electronic formats, and public availability for the Commissioner-issued application and exhibit forms to avoid delays and inconsistent form versions.

[P3] Applicant organizations will comment that requiring payment of filing, examination, and certificate issuance fees with initial filing (§97.6(c)) imposes cash-flow burdens on small breeders and request an option to pay issuance fees later or an installment schedule.

[P3] Legal commenters will request that §97.6(c) include a provision permitting fee waivers or reductions for public breeders, universities, and small entities, consistent with other USDA fee programs.

[P4] Hybrid seed companies will object to §97.6(d)(3)’s requirement to establish vegetative plots for each parent in a Commissioner-approved public depository, arguing this raises confidentiality and IP theft risks and asking for alternative private deposit options or protective measures.

[P4] Public depository operators and public researchers will request clarification under §97.6(d)(3) about who bears the cost of maintaining vegetative plots and what security and access protections the Office will require.

[P5] Asexually-propagated variety developers will argue §97.6(d)(4)’s mandatory deposit in a Commissioner-approved public depository could be impractical for long-lived or clonal material that cannot be preserved easily and ask for alternative acceptable deposit methods (e.g., DNA sequence deposit).

[P6] Transparency advocates will request that §97.7(c)(5) require the PVPO notice of depository recognition/default/discontinuation include the reason for action and a transition plan for affected deposits, not just a bare posting.

[P7] Applicants will object that §97.7(d) imposing a three-month original deposit deadline for seed-reproduced plants after filing is too short given international phytosanitary and shipping delays, and ask for a minimum six-month period or automatic extensions.

[P8] Asexual/tuber crop breeders will say §97.7(d)’s three-month deadline after notice of certificate issuance for tuber/asexually reproduced plants is unworkable for crops with seasonal production windows and request flexibility tied to crop seasonality.

[P9] Importers and international breeders will support §97.7(d)’s waiver authority for phytosanitary delays but request the rule specify documentary evidence required and a presumptive grant period to avoid discretionary denials.

[P10] Practitioners will request §97.7(d)(1) clarify who qualifies as “a person in a position to corroborate” the voucher (e.g., licensed lab, university researcher) and propose an explicit list or standards to avoid inconsistent rejections.

[P11] Commenters will ask that §97.7(d)(1)(i) require the corroborating statement to include not only depository name/address but also depository contact information and accession URL to facilitate verification.

[P12] Applicants will request §97.7(d)(1)(ii) specify acceptable date formats and documentary proof for the date of deposit to prevent administrative rejections for technicalities.

[P13] Depositories and applicants will ask §97.7(d)(1)(iii) to allow alternate identifiers if an accession number is not immediately assigned, and to permit later supplementation without penalty.

[P14] Asexually propagated variety owners will question the practical standard in §97.7(d)(1)(iv) that the deposit be “capable of reproduction,” requesting objective criteria or testing protocols to determine reproducibility.

[P15] Applicants relying on technical-deposit waivers under §97.7(d)(2) will seek explicit maximum extension lengths and required evidence when a waiver is requested, to avoid indefinite uncertainty.

[P16] Civil society and breeders will challenge §97.7(d)(2)’s abandonment consequence (certificate considered abandoned if specimen not provided) as draconian and ask for cure periods, notice requirements, and an appeal process before abandonment is declared.

[P17] Horticultural applicants will request that §97.9(b) allow high-resolution digital color images submitted electronically in lieu of printed color drawings/photographs when color is distinguishing, given modern filing practices.

[P18] Commenters will ask §97.9(b) to accept alternative color standards (e.g., Pantone, digital color profiling) in addition to Nickerson, Munsell, or RHS charts, and to allow colorimetric values as supplemental data.

[P19] Artists, archives, and applicants will request that §97.9(c) clarify acceptable dimensions, media, and digital submission standards for drawings, and confirm whether scanned images suffice if originals are mailed flat.

[P20] Applicants will request §97.12(a) include a guaranteed timeframe (e.g., within 3 business days) for issuance of the application number and effective filing date notification, and to require electronic acknowledgement receipts.

[P21] Commenters will ask §97.12(a) to require that the Office notify applicants by email and provide an online portal update, not just mail, to speed communications and reduce lost mail problems.

[P22] Joint owners filing under §97.14(d) will support the remaining owner’s authority to file but request explicit safe-harbor procedures and standards for demonstrating “diligent effort” to locate the missing owner.

[P23] Civil liberties groups will ask §97.14(d) to require the written explanation and last known address provided by the filing owner to be accompanied by declarations under penalty of perjury to deter fraud.

[P24] Commenters will request §97.14(d) that the Office’s forwarding notice to the missing owner include information on how to contest the filing and a reasonable response period before certificate issuance.

[P25] Legal practitioners will ask §97.14(d) to expand publication methods beyond a single PVPO website posting (e.g., Federal Register, mailing list) when notice is undeliverable, to increase likelihood of informing missing owners.

[P26] Joint owners will request §97.14(d) to stipulate a deadline and required form for a missing owner to join prior to issuance and to clarify whether late joinders can alter ownership shares.

[P27] Public interest groups will request §97.19 require scheduled periodic publication intervals (e.g., monthly) so stakeholders can reliably monitor pending applications, rather than leaving frequency to Commissioner discretion.

[P28] Industry users and researchers will request §97.19(c) to extend the PVPO website display beyond “name of the crop” to include variety breeder name, applicant, and brief description to improve transparency.

[P29] Applicants will argue §97.20(a)’s 30-day active-advancement rule is too short for complex applications and request a longer baseline (e.g., 90 days) and an automatic short extension mechanism without abandonment.

[P30] Small entities will object to §97.20(a)’s no-refund policy for filing and examination fees upon abandonment and ask for partial refunds or credit toward refiling if abandonment results from procedural confusion or Office error.

[P31] Applicants will support §97.23(c) returning original voluntarily withdrawn applications but request the Office also return accompanying exhibits and clarify timelines for returns.

[P32] Commenters will challenge §97.23(c) requiring refiling and payment of new fees to reconsider a voluntarily withdrawn original application, proposing a grace period for reinstatement without full new fees.

[P33] Applicants will request §97.101’s notice of allowance to include a checklist of required items (e.g., deposit confirmation, owner verifications) and to specify permissible methods of delivering verification.

[P34] Some applicants will ask §97.101 to clarify that the opportunity to withdraw after notice of allowance is not time-barred by other deadlines (e.g., deposit deadlines) to avoid forced issuance.

[P35] Applicants will request extending the §97.101 30-day response period for notice of allowance where international coordination or owner verification involves time zones and foreign mail, or allow electronic response to toll the deadline.

[P36] Practitioners will ask §97.101 to cap the delayed response fee (§97.175(f)) or provide a sliding scale for late responses to avoid disproportionate penalties for minor delays.

[P37] Applicants will support §97.103(a)’s prompt issuance but request the rule define “promptly” (e.g., within 10 business days) after specification of sale classification to provide certainty.

[P38] Seed companies will object to §97.103(a)’s prohibition on later amending a certificate to remove a “sale by variety name only as certified seed” restriction, asking for limited post-issuance amendment rights in cases of changed market conditions.

[P39] Depository operators will request clarity in §97.104(a) on the accounting and invoicing process for replenishment handling fees and timelines for owners to respond to requests.

[P40] Depositories and applicants will request that §97.104(a) mandate transparent retention/destruction policies and notice to owners before destroying samples related to abandoned applications or certificates.

[P41] Owners will challenge §97.104(a)’s three-month replenishment deadline as too short (especially for international owners) and request a minimum six-month cure period or multiple notices before declaring abandonment.

[P42] Farmers and seed companies will say §97.104(a) publishing abandonment notices no sooner than one year after request is appropriate but ask that notices include clear information on when the ‘certified seed only’ restriction is removed and any remaining obligations.

[P43] Applicants will seek automatic reinstatement relief under §97.104(b) when seed/propagating material is submitted within 9 months, but request explicit criteria and documentation needed to qualify for the “as though no abandonment occurred” treatment.

[P44] Commenters will request §97.104(b) define “good cause” for extensions more specifically (e.g., extreme weather, quarantine) and prescribe a maximum aggregate extension period to limit uncertainty.

[P46] Owners will request §97.104(c) require the Commissioner to notify the owner by email and mail prior to publishing the voluntary abandonment notice, to prevent inadvertent loss of rights.

[P47] Certificate holders will request guidance under §97.141 on acceptable label placement, font size, and required language for the “Unauthorized Propagation Prohibited” notice to ensure enforceability and avoid trade barriers.

[P48] Retailers and seed distributors will ask §97.141 that adding “PVPA 1994” to labels be optional and that the Office provide sample label templates to avoid compliance mistakes.

[P49] Applicants releasing material for testing under §97.142 will request safe-harbor language allowing explicit limited-use testing/increase exemptions and model label language to prevent inadvertent forfeiture of rights.

[P50] Stakeholders will request that §97.175 include a fee schedule summary and a public comment on proposed fee amounts to ensure fees are reasonable and transparent.

[P51] Applicants will object to §97.175(e) requiring full reimbursement of PVPO travel costs calculated under government travel regs when inspections could be done virtually; they request a presumption of remote inspection unless infeasible.

[P52] Small entities will comment that the $97 per employee hour cap in §97.175(f) may be inadequate or excessive depending on service; they request the Commissioner provide justification and periodic inflation adjustments tied to an index.

[P53] Applicants and finance officers will ask §97.177 to require that the electronic PVPO payment system provide transaction receipts and confirmation numbers and to require secure ACH options to reduce reliance on mail.

[P54] International applicants will request §97.177 foreign remittance rules (payable and immediately negotiable in U.S.) to allow common instruments like SWIFT transfers and to provide guidance on acceptable banks and intermediary fees.

[P55] Commenters will ask §97.177 to clarify liability allocation for mailed payments beyond “sender bears the risk,” and request recommended tracked mailing services be allowed or mandatory for fee payments.

[P56] Applicants will request §97.178 clarify procedures and timelines for refunds of mistaken or excess payments and require electronic refund options to the original payer account when feasible.

[P57] Small applicants will ask §97.178 to ensure the refund of examination fees (§97.178) applies even if the Office caused processing delays or errors leading to voluntary withdrawal, and propose a dispute resolution process.

[P58] Applicants will request §97.178 specify the timeframe for refunding certificate issuance fees when withdrawn after examination but before issuance to avoid prolonged cash tie-ups.

[P59] Commenters will object to §97.178’s $1-or-less nonrefund rule as petty and request all overpayments be refunded automatically to reduce administrative burden and improve fairness.

[P60] Pro se filers and other stakeholders will request §97.403(d) require that website-only service be used only after reasonable attempts at other methods and include an email alert to affected parties, not just a single website posting.

[P61] Appellants and civil litigators will request §97.500 clarify deadlines, procedural steps, and the scope of review in appeals to the Federal Circuit or district court to avoid procedural confusion.

[P62] Appellants will request §97.500 require the Secretary to provide the certified record promptly and at reasonable cost, and to provide electronic certified records where possible to reduce appellant burden.

[P63] Appellants will ask §97.500 to clarify the appellant/plaintiff’s obligation to bear the expense of forwarding the certified record and whether fee waivers or caps apply for indigent public interest plaintiffs.

[P64] Public variety proponents will support §97.800’s voluntary publication program but ask the Office to provide standardized submission formats, review timelines, and a disclaimer policy for published public variety descriptions.

raw_output:
[P1] The August 31, 2020 deadline in §257.101(a)(1) is infeasible for many owners/operators given procurement, permitting, and construction lead times for retrofits; EPA should extend the deadline or provide a clear, objective extension process.

[P1] The rule does not define "retrofitting" clearly in §257.101(a)(1); owners/operators need a precise definition (e.g., liner types, performance standards) to determine what actions satisfy the retrofit option.

[P2] §257.101(b)(1)(i) requires cessation by Aug 31, 2020 if a unit hasn't demonstrated location-standard compliance, but the rule lacks a clear process and timeline for owners to demonstrate compliance with the location standard prior to that date.

[P3] §257.103 introductory language conditions continued receipt on meeting (a),(b),(e),(f) requirements, but it is unclear whether multiple alternatives can be combined; EPA should clarify whether owners may use a mix of provisions to qualify.

[P4] §257.103(a)(1) allows continued receipt at a CCR landfill with a certification of lack of alternative capacity, but does not specify required evidence standards or third-party verification; EPA should require standardized documentation and allow state review.

[P5] The trigger in §257.103(a)(2) — "once alternative capacity is available" — is ambiguous; the rule should define "available" (permitting complete, contract executed, physical capacity ready) to prevent disputes and delay.

[P6] §257.103(a)(3)'s five-year outer limit for continued receipt without alternative capacity is arbitrary for large regions where disposal capacity development takes longer; EPA should allow site-specific extensions with transparent criteria.

[P7] §257.103(b)(1) permits continued landfill receipt if boilers will cease within specified timeframes, but the provision lacks specificity about what constitutes adequate proof of boiler cessation (e.g., decommissioning permit, binding corporate commitment).

[P8] §257.103(b)(1) interim-use requirement that facility must "continue to use the CCR unit because no alternative capacity exists" creates enforcement difficulty; EPA should require contemporaneous documentation of outreach and negotiations for alternatives during the interim.

[P9] The documentation requirement in §257.103(b)(1) is too vague about the level of detail required; EPA should publish templates or examples for the necessary documentary evidence.

[P10] §257.103(c)(1) requires a "notification of intent" in the operating record, but the rule fails to prescribe required contents beyond a general description; EPA should require a standardized form and minimum elements to ensure transparency.

[P11] The Aug 31, 2020 deadline for placing the notification in the operating record under §257.103(c)(1)(i) is too soon for facilities preparing complex demonstrations and should be extended to avoid administrative noncompliance.

[P12] Requiring the same Aug 31, 2020 operating-record notification for units closing under §257.101(b)(1) per §257.103(c)(1)(ii) could unfairly penalize owners who are actively disputing location standard findings; EPA should allow a short tolling period while appeals are pending.

[P13] The six-month window in §257.103(c)(1)(iii) after a noncompliance determination to prepare the notification is too brief when complex corrective actions are under consideration; EPA should permit a flexible timeframe based on the complexity of corrective measures.

[P14] §257.103(e)(1) short-term permission through Nov 30, 2020 is arbitrary and may be insufficient for operators who face legal, logistical, or contractual impediments to locating alternative capacity; EPA should allow case-by-case extensions with expedited review.

[P15] §257.103(e)(1)(i) explicitly excluding cost and inconvenience as grounds for "no alternative capacity" is reasonable, but the rule should recognize situations where extraordinary cost (bankruptcy, market collapse) effectively precludes capacity and allow a narrowly tailored exception.

[P16] The continuous-effort obligation in §257.103(e)(1)(ii) to make and "continue making" efforts to obtain capacity imposes an open-ended burden without defining acceptable levels of effort; EPA should specify minimum outreach and documentation requirements.

[P17] §257.103(e)(1)(ii)'s requirement to "arrange to use such capacity as soon as feasible" is vague; EPA should define "feasible" (e.g., within X days of availability) to prevent protracted delays.

[P18] §257.103(e)(1)(iii) places the burden of demonstrating compliance on the owner and ties noncompliance to loss of authorization, but the rule lacks procedural protections (notice, opportunity to cure) before authorization is withdrawn.

[P19] The Nov 30, 2020 hard stop in §257.103(e)(3) for lack of alternative capacity is too soon and does not account for unavoidable delays in siting and permitting new facilities; EPA should allow an administrative extension process.

[P20] §257.103(e)(4)(i) requires an Aug 31, 2020 notification in the operating record for short-term alternative users, but does not require concurrent public notice; EPA should require immediate public posting and state notification for community awareness.

[P21] §257.103(e)(4)(ii) requiring the §257.102(g) notification of intent to close is duplicative with other required notices; EPA should harmonize notice requirements to avoid redundant filings.

[P22] The site-specific infeasibility provision in §257.103(f) (intro) grants broad discretion to continue receiving wastes but lacks objective criteria for denial; EPA should publish evaluation criteria to ensure consistent decision-making.

[P23] §257.103(f)(1)(i) demands a demonstration including many documents, but the rule provides no page limits or data confidentiality protections — owners will be reluctant to provide proprietary business information without strong FOIA and confidentiality rules.

[P24] §257.103(f)(1)(i)(A) repeats that cost/inconvenience alone is insufficient for demonstrating no alternative capacity; however, EPA should clarify whether reasonable cost differentials (e.g., 3x) may be considered in combination with other factors.

[P25] §257.103(f)(1)(i)(B) certification that managing wastes in the impoundment is necessary because obtaining alternative capacity by Nov 30, 2020 was infeasible appears self-certified; EPA should require independent verification or state concurrence.

[P26] §257.103(f)(1)(i)(C) requires certification of compliance with the subpart, but does not indicate whether historical violations (even if corrected) disqualify a facility; EPA should clarify whether past noncompliance affects eligibility.

[P27] The detailed workplan requirement in §257.103(f)(1)(i)(D) (and subparts D1-D5) is reasonable, but EPA should require these be prepared by a qualified professional and provide minimum content standards to avoid superficial submissions.

[P28] The schedule and visual timeline in §257.103(f)(1)(i)(D)(2) will be difficult to produce credibly without permitting timelines; EPA should allow inclusion of contingent milestones tied to permitting and contract milestones.

[P29] §257.103(f)(1)(i)(D)(4) requires narrative of progress to date, but the rule should specify what documentary proof (emails, contracts, meeting minutes) is sufficient to substantiate progress claims.

[P30] §257.103(f)(1)(ii) requires immediate use of alternative capacity once available, but lacks enforcement mechanisms to verify timeliness; EPA should require proof of transfers and receipts within a defined period (e.g., 30 days).

[P31] §257.103(f)(1)(iii)'s cap disallowing operation past Oct 15, 2023 is arbitrary for large impoundments with complex closure logistics; EPA should allow phased closures or alternative remedial measures for those where closure within that date is infeasible.

[P32] The all-stop deadline of Oct 15, 2023 in §257.103(f)(1) does not account for natural disasters, litigation holds, or force majeure events; EPA should include a force majeure provision.

[P33] §257.103(f)(1)(iv) imposes automatic loss of authorization for any noncompliance without an opportunity to correct; EPA should provide procedural safeguards and a cure period before automatic termination.

[P34] The notice and progress-reporting obligations in §257.103(f)(1)(v) are extensive; EPA should streamline required content and allow consolidation with other periodic reporting to reduce administrative burdens.

[P35] §257.103(f)(1)(vi)-(vii) require operating-record entries upon submission and decision; EPA should require that these documents be provided in a machine-readable format and be accessible to the public.

[P36] §257.103(f)(1)(viii) requires prompt notification upon need for additional time after approval; EPA should define "promptly" (e.g., within 7 days) to ensure consistent compliance.

[P37] The semi-annual progress reporting requirements in §257.103(f)(1)(ix)-(x) are onerous and duplicative of other EPA/state reporting; EPA should permit a single joint report to satisfy multiple obligations and allow electronic submittal.

[P38] §257.103(f)(1)(ix)(A)(2) asks whether the owner is on schedule; the rule should require independent verification or an auditor attestation for "on schedule" statements to prevent self-serving reports.

[P39] The public posting schedule in §257.103(f)(1)(x)(A)-(B) (April 1 and October 1) needs to allow flexibility for facilities that receive approval near those dates; EPA's "soonest after approval" rule could result in very short posting windows — clarify grace periods.

[P40] §257.103(f)(1)(xi) reiterates the §257.102(g) closure notification requirement; EPA should coordinate timelines so the closure notification and alternative-demonstration processes are not contradictory.

[P41] §257.103(f)(2)(i) requires a mitigation plan to address human health and environmental risks, but the rule does not specify minimum elements, performance objectives, or independent review requirements for such plans.

[P42] The timeframes for impoundments ≤40 acres in §257.103(f)(2)(ii)(A) (complete by Oct 17, 2023) and >40 acres in §257.103(f)(2)(ii)(B) (complete by Oct 17, 2028) are arbitrary size cutoffs; EPA should justify the 40-acre threshold with supporting analysis or consider alternative metrics tied to risk.

[P43] §257.103(f)(2)(ii)(B) allowing up to Oct 17, 2028 for large impoundments may imperil communities near large impoundments; EPA should require heightened monitoring and interim risk-reduction measures for units operating under the extended deadline.

[P44] §257.103(f)(2)(iii) makes qualification demonstration continuous and links noncompliance to automatic loss of authorization; owners need clear procedures for demonstrating compliance and for appealing authorization revocations.

[P45] §257.103(f)(2)(vii)'s annual report requirement lacks a required template and timeline for submission to EPA/state agencies; EPA should supply a standardized report form and submission deadlines.

[P46] §257.103(f)(3)(i)(A) requiring submission at least two months before a unit's cease-receiving deadline may be too short for facilities that need to assemble complex demonstrations; EPA should allow a longer minimum lead-time.

[P47] The prohibition in §257.103(f)(3)(i)(B) that no facility may operate past Oct 15, 2023, even with new demonstrations, conflicts with §257.103(f)(2)(ii) which allows closures as late as Oct 17, 2028 for large impoundments; EPA must resolve this inconsistency.

[P48] §257.103(f)(3)(i)(C) requires submission by May 15, 2020 for f(2)(i) demonstrations — an impractically early date relative to rule adoption and notice; EPA should reset submission windows relative to promulgation date.

[P49] §257.103(f)(3)(ii)'s provision that EPA may request additional information is necessary, but EPA should define maximum timeframes for EPA's requests and for owner responses to prevent indefinite tolling.

[P50] The tolling rule in §257.103(f)(3)(ii) that only "complete" demonstrations toll the deadline lacks standards for completeness; EPA should publish a checklist and process for completeness determinations and allow an initial 15-day cure period for incomplete submissions.

[P51] §257.103(f)(3)(iii) calls for a 15-day public comment period on EPA's proposed decision — this is too short for meaningful public input especially for complex demonstrations; EPA should require at least 30, preferably 45, days and mandate public notice in the local community.

[P52] §257.103(f)(3)(iv)'s 4-month deadline for EPA final decision after a complete demonstration is reasonable, but the provision allowing proposed decisions to become effective 5 days after close of comments if no substantive comments received is arbitrary and could expedite decisions without adequate review; EPA should require an explicit review of comments before effectiveness.

[P53] §257.105(i)(14)-(21) and §257.106(i)(14)-(21) place extensive operating-record and provision obligations on owners; EPA should allow consolidation of records and permit electronic central filing to reduce duplication.

[P54] The redundancy across §257.105 and §257.106 obligations (multiple identical cites) creates administrative confusion; EPA should streamline and consolidate recordkeeping and submittal requirements.

[P55] §257.107(i)(14)-(21) public posting requirements are appropriate for transparency, but the rule should require machine-readable formats, accessible design for the disabled, and prominent local notice for affected communities without internet access.

[P56] The rule does not specify penalties or enforcement mechanisms for failure to post materials on the public website as required by §257.107; EPA should clarify enforcement and allow states to impose additional penalties.

[P57] Environmental justice groups will comment that continuations of operation until 2023/2028 under §§257.103(f)(1) and (f)(2) allow prolonged exposure risks to nearby low-income and minority communities; EPA should require enhanced monitoring, community notification, and interim remediation measures.

[P58] Trade associations will argue that the rule's strict prohibition on relying on cost/inconvenience alone (e.g., §§257.103(e)(1)(i), (f)(1)(i)(A)) fails to account for legitimate economic realities in some regions and will request allowance for documented, demonstrable economic hardship to be considered in combination with other factors.

[P59] Legal experts will note that automatic loss of authorization upon any noncompliance (multiple provisions) raises due-process concerns; EPA should adopt formal procedures for notice, hearing, and appeal before authorization is revoked.

[P60] Community groups will request that EPA require public hearings before approving any site-specific demonstration under §257.103(f), not just online posting and a short comment period, to ensure meaningful local participation.

[P61] State regulators will request that EPA clarify the role of "Participating State Director" in §§257.103(f)(1)(vi)-(vii) and elsewhere, including criteria for state participation, timelines for state review, and deference standards between EPA and the state.

[P62] The recordkeeping retention periods for the various operating-record items (e.g., §§257.105 and .106) are not specified; EPA should state minimum retention periods and whether they run from closure or final decision dates.

[P63] The obligations to post semi-annual and annual reports (e.g., §§257.103(f)(1)(x), (f)(2)(vii), §§257.107(i)(18),(21)) should include requirements to notify the local community by mail or newspaper to reach stakeholders without internet access.

[P64] The rule should require that any demonstration relying on future availability of off-site capacity include binding contracts or letters of intent, not mere negotiations, to prevent speculative claims of forthcoming capacity under §§257.103(a),(e),(f).

[P65] The definitions section should clarify what counts as "non-CCR wastestreams" across multiple provisions to avoid ambiguity about permitted receipts during the alternative-authorization periods.

[P66] The provisions that allow continued receipt while boilers are scheduled to cease (e.g., §§257.103(b) and (f)(2)) should require setbacks on new fills and prohibit expansion of footprint to minimize increased long-term liability.

[P67] The rule lacks language addressing groundwater monitoring expectations and interim corrective measures for units allowed to continue operations under alternatives (e.g., §§257.103(e),(f)); EPA should require enhanced monitoring and immediate corrective action triggers.

[P68] Operators will request clarity on whether closure according to §257.102(e),(f) requires immediate capping and final cover, or whether phased closure is permitted; the rule should specify acceptable closure sequencing.

[P69] The public posting and operating-record requirements must include a requirement to provide translations into languages commonly spoken in affected communities to satisfy environmental justice and accessibility concerns.

[P70] EPA should require independent third-party audits of the semi-annual and annual progress reports (§§257.103(f)(1)(ix), (f)(2)(vii)) to ensure accuracy and avoid conflicts of interest where owners self-certify progress.

[P71] The rule's multiple cross-references to §257.102(g) and §257.105/.106/.107 are confusing and could lead to inconsistent compliance; EPA should publish a consolidated compliance checklist with deadlines for each obligation.

[P72] The deadlines that reference dates in 2020 and 2023/2028 are unlinked to the rule's effective date; EPA should clarify whether these calendar dates are fixed or whether they phase relative to the rule's final effective date to avoid legal challenges.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The August 31, 2020 deadline in §257.101(a)(1) is infeasible for many owners/operators given procurement, permitting, and construction lead times for retrofits; EPA should extend the deadline or provide a clear, objective extension process.

The rule does not define "retrofitting" clearly in §257.101(a)(1); owners/operators need a precise definition (e.g., liner types, performance standards) to determine what actions satisfy the retrofit option.

§257.101(b)(1)(i) requires cessation by Aug 31, 2020 if a unit hasn't demonstrated location-standard compliance, but the rule lacks a clear process and timeline for owners to demonstrate compliance with the location standard prior to that date.

§257.103 introductory language conditions continued receipt on meeting (a),(b),(e),(f) requirements, but it is unclear whether multiple alternatives can be combined; EPA should clarify whether owners may use a mix of provisions to qualify.

§257.103(a)(1) allows continued receipt at a CCR landfill with a certification of lack of alternative capacity, but does not specify required evidence standards or third-party verification; EPA should require standardized documentation and allow state review.

The trigger in §257.103(a)(2) — "once alternative capacity is available" — is ambiguous; the rule should define "available" (permitting complete, contract executed, physical capacity ready) to prevent disputes and delay.

§257.103(a)(3)'s five-year outer limit for continued receipt without alternative capacity is arbitrary for large regions where disposal capacity development takes longer; EPA should allow site-specific extensions with transparent criteria.

§257.103(b)(1) permits continued landfill receipt if boilers will cease within specified timeframes, but the provision lacks specificity about what constitutes adequate proof of boiler cessation (e.g., decommissioning permit, binding corporate commitment).

§257.103(b)(1) interim-use requirement that facility must "continue to use the CCR unit because no alternative capacity exists" creates enforcement difficulty; EPA should require contemporaneous documentation of outreach and negotiations for alternatives during the interim.
The documentation requirement in §257.103(b)(1) is too vague about the level of detail required; EPA should publish templates or examples for the necessary documentary evidence.

§257.103(c)(1) requires a "notification of intent" in the operating record, but the rule fails to prescribe required contents beyond a general description; EPA should require a standardized form and minimum elements to ensure transparency.

The Aug 31, 2020 deadline for placing the notification in the operating record under §257.103(c)(1)(i) is too soon for facilities preparing complex demonstrations and should be extended to avoid administrative noncompliance.

Requiring the same Aug 31, 2020 operating-record notification for units closing under §257.101(b)(1) per §257.103(c)(1)(ii) could unfairly penalize owners who are actively disputing location standard findings; EPA should allow a short tolling period while appeals are pending.

The six-month window in §257.103(c)(1)(iii) after a noncompliance determination to prepare the notification is too brief when complex corrective actions are under consideration; EPA should permit a flexible timeframe based on the complexity of corrective measures.

§257.103(e)(1) short-term permission through Nov 30, 2020 is arbitrary and may be insufficient for operators who face legal, logistical, or contractual impediments to locating alternative capacity; EPA should allow case-by-case extensions with expedited review.

§257.103(e)(1)(i) explicitly excluding cost and inconvenience as grounds for "no alternative capacity" is reasonable, but the rule should recognize situations where extraordinary cost (bankruptcy, market collapse) effectively precludes capacity and allow a narrowly tailored exception.

The continuous-effort obligation in §257.103(e)(1)(ii) to make and "continue making" efforts to obtain capacity imposes an open-ended burden without defining acceptable levels of effort; EPA should specify minimum outreach and documentation requirements.
§257.103(e)(1)(ii)'s requirement to "arrange to use such capacity as soon as feasible" is vague; EPA should define "feasible" (e.g., within X days of availability) to prevent protracted delays.

§257.103(e)(1)(iii) places the burden of demonstrating compliance on the owner and ties noncompliance to loss of authorization, but the rule lacks procedural protections (notice, opportunity to cure) before authorization is withdrawn.

The Nov 30, 2020 hard stop in §257.103(e)(3) for lack of alternative capacity is too soon and does not account for unavoidable delays in siting and permitting new facilities; EPA should allow an administrative extension process.

§257.103(e)(4)(i) requires an Aug 31, 2020 notification in the operating record for short-term alternative users, but does not require concurrent public notice; EPA should require immediate public posting and state notification for community awareness.
§257.103(e)(4)(ii) requiring the §257.102(g) notification of intent to close is duplicative with other required notices; EPA should harmonize notice requirements to avoid redundant filings.

The site-specific infeasibility provision in §257.103(f) (intro) grants broad discretion to continue receiving wastes but lacks objective criteria for denial; EPA should publish evaluation criteria to ensure consistent decision-making.

§257.103(f)(1)(i) demands a demonstration including many documents, but the rule provides no page limits or data confidentiality protections — owners will be reluctant to provide proprietary business information without strong FOIA and confidentiality rules.

§257.103(f)(1)(i)(A) repeats that cost/inconvenience alone is insufficient for demonstrating no alternative capacity; however, EPA should clarify whether reasonable cost differentials (e.g., 3x) may be considered in combination with other factors.

§257.103(f)(1)(i)(B) certification that managing wastes in the impoundment is necessary because obtaining alternative capacity by Nov 30, 2020 was infeasible appears self-certified; EPA should require independent verification or state concurrence.

§257.103(f)(1)(i)(C) requires certification of compliance with the subpart, but does not indicate whether historical violations (even if corrected) disqualify a facility; EPA should clarify whether past noncompliance affects eligibility.

The detailed workplan requirement in §257.103(f)(1)(i)(D) (and subparts D1-D5) is reasonable, but EPA should require these be prepared by a qualified professional and provide minimum content standards to avoid superficial submissions.

The schedule and visual timeline in §257.103(f)(1)(i)(D)(2) will be difficult to produce credibly without permitting timelines; EPA should allow inclusion of contingent milestones tied to permitting and contract milestones.
§257.103(f)(1)(i)(D)(4) requires narrative of progress to date, but the rule should specify what documentary proof (emails, contracts, meeting minutes) is sufficient to substantiate progress claims.

§257.103(f)(1)(ii) requires immediate use of alternative capacity once available, but lacks enforcement mechanisms to verify timeliness; EPA should require proof of transfers and receipts within a defined period (e.g., 30 days).

§257.103(f)(1)(iii)'s cap disallowing operation past Oct 15, 2023 is arbitrary for large impoundments with complex closure logistics; EPA should allow phased closures or alternative remedial measures for those where closure within that date is infeasible.
The all-stop deadline of Oct 15, 2023 in §257.103(f)(1) does not account for natural disasters, litigation holds, or force majeure events; EPA should include a force majeure provision.

§257.103(f)(1)(iv) imposes automatic loss of authorization for any noncompliance without an opportunity to correct; EPA should provide procedural safeguards and a cure period before automatic termination.

The notice and progress-reporting obligations in §257.103(f)(1)(v) are extensive; EPA should streamline required content and allow consolidation with other periodic reporting to reduce administrative burdens.

§257.103(f)(1)(vi)-(vii) require operating-record entries upon submission and decision; EPA should require that these documents be provided in a machine-readable format and be accessible to the public.
§257.103(f)(1)(viii) requires prompt notification upon need for additional time after approval; EPA should define "promptly" (e.g., within 7 days) to ensure consistent compliance.

The semi-annual progress reporting requirements in §257.103(f)(1)(ix)-(x) are onerous and duplicative of other EPA/state reporting; EPA should permit a single joint report to satisfy multiple obligations and allow electronic submittal.

§257.103(f)(1)(ix)(A)(2) asks whether the owner is on schedule; the rule should require independent verification or an auditor attestation for "on schedule" statements to prevent self-serving reports.

The public posting schedule in §257.103(f)(1)(x)(A)-(B) (April 1 and October 1) needs to allow flexibility for facilities that receive approval near those dates; EPA's "soonest after approval" rule could result in very short posting windows — clarify grace periods.

§257.103(f)(1)(xi) reiterates the §257.102(g) closure notification requirement; EPA should coordinate timelines so the closure notification and alternative-demonstration processes are not contradictory.

§257.103(f)(2)(i) requires a mitigation plan to address human health and environmental risks, but the rule does not specify minimum elements, performance objectives, or independent review requirements for such plans.

The timeframes for impoundments ≤40 acres in §257.103(f)(2)(ii)(A) (complete by Oct 17, 2023) and >40 acres in §257.103(f)(2)(ii)(B) (complete by Oct 17, 2028) are arbitrary size cutoffs; EPA should justify the 40-acre threshold with supporting analysis or consider alternative metrics tied to risk.

§257.103(f)(2)(ii)(B) allowing up to Oct 17, 2028 for large impoundments may imperil communities near large impoundments; EPA should require heightened monitoring and interim risk-reduction measures for units operating under the extended deadline.

§257.103(f)(2)(iii) makes qualification demonstration continuous and links noncompliance to automatic loss of authorization; owners need clear procedures for demonstrating compliance and for appealing authorization revocations.
§257.103(f)(2)(vii)'s annual report requirement lacks a required template and timeline for submission to EPA/state agencies; EPA should supply a standardized report form and submission deadlines.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement to "install an IPSB that resists intrusion into the flightdeck whenever the flightdeck door is opened" is unclear about which aircraft types, retrofit schedules, and operators are covered; commenters will request clarification of applicability (e.g., regional turboprops, commuter jets, cargo-only aircraft, small fractional operators).

[P1] Industry commenters will assert the rule fails to provide a compliance timeline or phase-in schedule for retrofitting the entire fleet and will request a multi-year compliance period tied to maintenance schedules (e.g., phased in over heavy checks).

[P1] Operators will claim the proposal does not estimate labor hours, parts cost, or downtime associated with installing IPSBs and request an economic analysis and cost-benefit justification.

[P1] Labor unions and maintenance organizations will request specification of who is authorized to install the IPSB (certificated mechanics vs. manufacturer technicians) and whether major modifications require Supplemental Type Certificates (STCs).

[P1] Legal commenters will argue that mandating an IPSB "whenever the flightdeck door is opened" could conflict with existing safety regulations for emergency egress and must be reconciled to avoid liability for blocking escape routes.

[P2] Commenters will demand that the rule define “deployed” precisely (stowed vs. extended states, transitional movement) so testing and compliance are objectively measurable.

[P2] Certification organizations will request standardized test procedures and instrumentation to demonstrate compliance with the "when deployed" performance requirements rather than leaving methods to applicants.

[P3] Aircraft manufacturers will comment that a 250-pound static load at “most critical locations” lacks definition of testing locations and attachment points; they will request diagrams or a standard mapping of critical locations for each IPSB design.

[P3] Structural engineers will assert that a 250 lb static load requirement toward the passenger cabin may be insufficient to stop dynamic loads (kicks, pushes, surges) and recommend that the rule specify dynamic impact testing or a higher static/dynamic equivalence.

[P3] Small aircraft operators will argue that the 250 lb requirement could be excessive for lightweight aircraft, potentially overloading surrounding structure, and ask for weight-scaled or size-based exceptions.

[P3] Legal commenters will request clarification whether the 1,113 Newtons figure is a minimum or target and whether a safety margin is required for manufacturing tolerances and wear.

[P4] Airlines and manufacturers will challenge the 600-pound static load toward the flightdeck as unrealistic for door/frame attachments on some aircraft, requesting structural analysis guidance and possibly alternative compliance showing equivalent resistance.

[P4] Certification engineers will point out the asymmetry (600 lb toward flightdeck vs. 250 lb toward cabin) needs rationale in the rulemaking record and request crash or intrusion scenarios that justify those load values.

[P4] MRO providers will ask whether the 600 lb load must be sustained indefinitely or only for a specified duration during testing, and request a duration/deflection acceptance criterion.

[P4] Aircraft owners will request that the rule allow alternative means of compliance (AMOCs) that demonstrate overall flightdeck protection without meeting the 600 lb static load at discrete points (e.g., energy-absorbing structures or active locking systems).

[P5] Flight crew associations will object that the required minimum 5-second delay is too short to ensure safety in real intrusion scenarios and will request a longer minimum (e.g., 10–15 seconds) tied to standard door operation times with one hand.

[P5] Manufacturers will counter that requiring a delay "no less" than the time for a crewmember to open and reclose the flightdeck door creates circular compliance requirements and request the agency specify a numeric delay requirement (e.g., minimum 5 seconds, maximum X seconds).

[P5] Human factors experts will request the rule define the test procedure for measuring "delay a person attempting to access" (e.g., single attacker vs. multiple attackers, tools used) and whether mechanical breach tools must be considered.

[P5] Legal commenters will note ambiguity over who counts as a “person attempting to access” (adult vs. child) and request that the rule specify anthropomorphic test device profiles (sizes, forces) to standardize testing.

[P6] Security advocacy groups will praise the prohibition on reaching through and touching the flight deck door but will request detailed probe tests and clearance dimensions (maximum allowable gaps) be specified so designs can be objectively measured.

[P6] IPSB designers will ask for exact dimensional tolerances for “prevent reaching through” (e.g., maximum opening width, Sherwood probe dimensions) consistent with existing international standards, and request harmonization with EASA/ICAO guidance.

[P6] Operators will seek an explicit exception for situations where crewmembers must pass items through the door (medications, documents) and request allowed small apertures or passthrough procedures be defined.

[P7] Flight crew and safety advocates will request the rule list or exemplify “necessary crewmember activities” that must be permitted when the IPSB is deployed (e.g., reaching controls, viewing instruments, communicating with cabin crew, passing paperwork), to avoid designs that impede safety tasks.

[P7] Human factors commenters will require performance criteria ensuring IPSB does not interfere with emergency egress, communication, or safety equipment access, and ask for ergonomic testing standards.

[P7] Pilots’ associations will request that the rule prohibit IPSB designs that obstruct the view, access, or operation of emergency equipment (e.g., fire extinguishers, masks) and require that deployed IPSB still allow immediate door operation by trained crew.

[P8] Aircraft manufacturers and operators will demand specificity about which airplanes “required by paragraph (f)” are covered and whether newly certified designs must include IPSB at type certification or only retrofit.

[P8] Legal commenters will request clarification whether the line-of-sight requirement applies under all lighting and turbulence conditions, and whether electronic video systems could satisfy the line-of-sight requirement as an alternative.

[P8] Accessibility advocates will ask whether providing a line-of-sight requirement could conflict with privacy or medical confidentiality for crew members in the crew rest compartment and request guidance on acceptable camera use and data retention.

[P9] Operators and maintenance organizations will comment that the proposed AFM amendment mandating abnormal propeller vibration instructions lacks specificity on the content, formatting, and mandatory use of those procedures and will request model AFM text or required elements.

[P9] Repair stations will request clarification whether the visual and NDT inspection of the propeller hub is required at every A-check, only upon abnormal vibration, or at set intervals; they will request inspection methods and acceptance criteria be published.

[P9] Aircraft owners will request that the AD provide approved NDT methods (e.g., eddy current, dye penetrant, ultrasound) and reference service bulletins so the inspections are uniformly applied.

[P10] Maintenance organizations will assert the maintenance records review requirement is vague about the review period (e.g., life of the propeller, last 5 years) and request the FAA specify exact dates or events to review.

[P10] Operators will request that the rule state who is authorized to perform the records review (operator maintenance personnel vs. certificated repair station) and whether documentation of the review must be submitted to FAA.

[P10] Small operators will ask for relief provisions if historical maintenance records are missing or incomplete, requesting alternative initial inspections instead of an impossible records review.

[P11] Maintenance providers will request the AD specify the exact torque values for the propeller blade retention nuts and the torque method (manual torque wrench, calibrated tools, multipliers) instead of leaving values unspecified.

[P11] Legal and industry commenters will request clarification whether tightening to specified torque values applies only once (as remedial action) or requires periodic re-torquing at maintenance intervals.

[P11] Manufacturers will ask whether retorquing is allowed on-service or whether replacement of hardware is required if torque cannot be achieved; request acceptance criteria for threads and nuts.

[P12] Operators will request the AFM/NDT AD clarify the required technique and threshold for "shake" inspections of propeller blades (e.g., acceptable axial/play limits in mm/inches) to ensure consistent enforcement.

[P12] Maintenance organizations will request guidance on whether shake inspections must be done on-wing or require propeller removal and whether specialized jigs/tools are required.

[P13] Owners will object to a mandatory removal-from-service requirement for any detected axial play without distinguishing between serviceable wear limits and catastrophic indications; they will request quantified allowable axial play thresholds and repair options.

[P13] Safety advocates will support immediate removal if axial play exceeds a conservative threshold but will ask the FAA to publish numeric limits that trigger removal versus those that warrant monitoring.

[P14] NDT providers will request the AD specify acceptable NDT techniques, acceptance criteria for hub flaws, and reporting formats rather than a generic requirement to "perform an NDT inspection."

[P14] Commenters will ask who bears the cost of NDT inspections (operator vs. manufacturer) and whether the FAA will allow alternative proven inspection methods as AMOCs.

[P15] Several stakeholders will request an extension of the comment deadline beyond September 15, 2022 (e.g., additional 30–60 days) to allow time for industry to prepare technical comments, especially given the economic and safety implications.

[P15] International operators and foreign registrants will request the FAA coordinate comment period timing with EASA and other authorities to avoid conflicting schedules and to allow cross-jurisdictional technical input.

[P16] Consumer and advocacy groups will request clear instructions on how to submit confidential business information (CBI) and whether redacted public versions are acceptable under the listed comment procedures.

[P16] Small entities will request multiple, simplified submission methods (email upload without required PDF formatting) and clarification on file size limits and acceptable attachments.

[P17] Industry commenters will note that allowing review of service information only at the FAA office in Burlington, MA is burdensome and request that the service information be posted online or made available at multiple regional FAA offices.

[P17] Legal commenters will ask whether the service information is incorporated by reference and, if so, request that the referenced material be made available without charge for review during the comment period.

[P18] Several commenters will support online docket access but will request longer in-person hours or appointment-based access given pandemic constraints and remote work realities.

[P18] Technical experts will request that the docket include all referenced service bulletins, test reports, and data used to derive the load and delay thresholds to enable meaningful technical review.

[P19] Commenters will object to the rigid requirement to include the specified docket identifier at the start of comments and request that the FAA accept submissions that clearly reference the docket elsewhere in the text to avoid procedural rejection.

[P19] Civil liberties groups will request the FAA accept anonymous comments or comments with redactions for privacy concerns while still associating them with the docket number.

[P20] Several commenters will note that while the FAA invites data, views, and arguments, the proposal lacks technical substantiation for key parameters (250 lb, 600 lb, 5 seconds) and request the FAA publish the risk assessment, threat modeling, and test data used to derive these numbers so commenters can provide informed critiques.

[P20] Industry commenters will request the FAA to solicit an advisory circular or consensus standard development with stakeholders (manufacturers, airlines, pilots, certifiers) to refine performance criteria and testing protocols before finalizing the regulation.
