Manufacturers will counter that requiring a delay "no less" than the time for a crewmember to open and reclose the flightdeck door creates circular compliance requirements and request the agency specify a numeric delay requirement (e.g., minimum 5 seconds, maximum X seconds).

Human factors experts will request the rule define the test procedure for measuring "delay a person attempting to access" (e.g., single attacker vs. multiple attackers, tools used) and whether mechanical breach tools must be considered.

Legal commenters will note ambiguity over who counts as a “person attempting to access” (adult vs. child) and request that the rule specify anthropomorphic test device profiles (sizes, forces) to standardize testing.

Security advocacy groups will praise the prohibition on reaching through and touching the flight deck door but will request detailed probe tests and clearance dimensions (maximum allowable gaps) be specified so designs can be objectively measured.

IPSB designers will ask for exact dimensional tolerances for “prevent reaching through” (e.g., maximum opening width, Sherwood probe dimensions) consistent with existing international standards, and request harmonization with EASA/ICAO guidance.

Operators will seek an explicit exception for situations where crewmembers must pass items through the door (medications, documents) and request allowed small apertures or passthrough procedures be defined.

Flight crew and safety advocates will request the rule list or exemplify “necessary crewmember activities” that must be permitted when the IPSB is deployed (e.g., reaching controls, viewing instruments, communicating with cabin crew, passing paperwork), to avoid designs that impede safety tasks.
Human factors commenters will require performance criteria ensuring IPSB does not interfere with emergency egress, communication, or safety equipment access, and ask for ergonomic testing standards.

Pilots’ associations will request that the rule prohibit IPSB designs that obstruct the view, access, or operation of emergency equipment (e.g., fire extinguishers, masks) and require that deployed IPSB still allow immediate door operation by trained crew.

Aircraft manufacturers and operators will demand specificity about which airplanes “required by paragraph (f)” are covered and whether newly certified designs must include IPSB at type certification or only retrofit.

Legal commenters will request clarification whether the line-of-sight requirement applies under all lighting and turbulence conditions, and whether electronic video systems could satisfy the line-of-sight requirement as an alternative.

Accessibility advocates will ask whether providing a line-of-sight requirement could conflict with privacy or medical confidentiality for crew members in the crew rest compartment and request guidance on acceptable camera use and data retention.

Operators and maintenance organizations will comment that the proposed AFM amendment mandating abnormal propeller vibration instructions lacks specificity on the content, formatting, and mandatory use of those procedures and will request model AFM text or required elements.

Repair stations will request clarification whether the visual and NDT inspection of the propeller hub is required at every A-check, only upon abnormal vibration, or at set intervals; they will request inspection methods and acceptance criteria be published.
Aircraft owners will request that the AD provide approved NDT methods (e.g., eddy current, dye penetrant, ultrasound) and reference service bulletins so the inspections are uniformly applied.

Maintenance organizations will assert the maintenance records review requirement is vague about the review period (e.g., life of the propeller, last 5 years) and request the FAA specify exact dates or events to review.

Operators will request that the rule state who is authorized to perform the records review (operator maintenance personnel vs. certificated repair station) and whether documentation of the review must be submitted to FAA.
Small operators will ask for relief provisions if historical maintenance records are missing or incomplete, requesting alternative initial inspections instead of an impossible records review.

Maintenance providers will request the AD specify the exact torque values for the propeller blade retention nuts and the torque method (manual torque wrench, calibrated tools, multipliers) instead of leaving values unspecified.

Legal and industry commenters will request clarification whether tightening to specified torque values applies only once (as remedial action) or requires periodic re-torquing at maintenance intervals.
Manufacturers will ask whether retorquing is allowed on-service or whether replacement of hardware is required if torque cannot be achieved; request acceptance criteria for threads and nuts.

Operators will request the AFM/NDT AD clarify the required technique and threshold for "shake" inspections of propeller blades (e.g., acceptable axial/play limits in mm/inches) to ensure consistent enforcement.
Maintenance organizations will request guidance on whether shake inspections must be done on-wing or require propeller removal and whether specialized jigs/tools are required.

Owners will object to a mandatory removal-from-service requirement for any detected axial play without distinguishing between serviceable wear limits and catastrophic indications; they will request quantified allowable axial play thresholds and repair options.

Safety advocates will support immediate removal if axial play exceeds a conservative threshold but will ask the FAA to publish numeric limits that trigger removal versus those that warrant monitoring.
NDT providers will request the AD specify acceptable NDT techniques, acceptance criteria for hub flaws, and reporting formats rather than a generic requirement to "perform an NDT inspection."
Commenters will ask who bears the cost of NDT inspections (operator vs. manufacturer) and whether the FAA will allow alternative proven inspection methods as AMOCs.

Several stakeholders will request an extension of the comment deadline beyond September 15, 2022 (e.g., additional 30–60 days) to allow time for industry to prepare technical comments, especially given the economic and safety implications.

International operators and foreign registrants will request the FAA coordinate comment period timing with EASA and other authorities to avoid conflicting schedules and to allow cross-jurisdictional technical input.

Consumer and advocacy groups will request clear instructions on how to submit confidential business information (CBI) and whether redacted public versions are acceptable under the listed comment procedures.
Small entities will request multiple, simplified submission methods (email upload without required PDF formatting) and clarification on file size limits and acceptable attachments.

Industry commenters will note that allowing review of service information only at the FAA office in Burlington, MA is burdensome and request that the service information be posted online or made available at multiple regional FAA offices.

Legal commenters will ask whether the service information is incorporated by reference and, if so, request that the referenced material be made available without charge for review during the comment period.
Several commenters will support online docket access but will request longer in-person hours or appointment-based access given pandemic constraints and remote work realities.
Technical experts will request that the docket include all referenced service bulletins, test reports, and data used to derive the load and delay thresholds to enable meaningful technical review.

Commenters will object to the rigid requirement to include the specified docket identifier at the start of comments and request that the FAA accept submissions that clearly reference the docket elsewhere in the text to avoid procedural rejection.
Civil liberties groups will request the FAA accept anonymous comments or comments with redactions for privacy concerns while still associating them with the docket number.

Several commenters will note that while the FAA invites data, views, and arguments, the proposal lacks technical substantiation for key parameters (250 lb, 600 lb, 5 seconds) and request the FAA publish the risk assessment, threat modeling, and test data used to derive these numbers so commenters can provide informed critiques.

Industry commenters will request the FAA to solicit an advisory circular or consensus standard development with stakeholders (manufacturers, airlines, pilots, certifiers) to refine performance criteria and testing protocols before finalizing the regulation.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement to ensure the control device is operating whenever tank gases/vapors are routed to it (§63.1404(c)) is vague about what constitutes "operating" — request clarification whether brief transient downtimes, ignition/relay cycles, or reduced efficiency modes count as non‑operating.

[P1] The rule should allow a short startup/shutdown period (e.g., up to 5 minutes) when the control device is coming online or going offline without treating those moments as violations under §63.1404(c).

[P2] The permission to bypass for planned routine maintenance (§63.1404(c)(1)) lacks a required notice to the permitting authority and nearby communities — commenters will request mandatory prior notification and public posting for planned bypasses.

[P3] The condition that bypass is permitted only when maintenance cannot be performed while emissions are vented to the control device (§63.1404(c)(1)(i)) is unworkable for many facilities because vendors often require isolation of the device for safety — request allowance for documented vendor/contractor safety requirements as a valid reason to bypass.

[P4] The 240‑hour per year cap on routine maintenance bypass time (§63.1404(c)(1)(ii)) is overly restrictive for large complex control devices that require lengthy scheduled outages; industry requests a phased in approach or ability to apply for site‑specific extensions based on documented engineering justification.

[P5] The prohibition on increasing tank material levels during bypass (§63.1404(c)(1)(iii)) is impractical for operations with variable inventory and could force production curtailment; request clarification of "increase" (relative to what baseline) and an exemption for unavoidable operational needs with required mitigation.

[P6] The permission to route tank gases to an alternate control device (§63.1404(c)(2)) should require pre‑approval and equivalency demonstration to ensure the alternate device meets emissions reduction and monitoring requirements, but the provision lacks explicit approval procedures.

[P6] The provision allowing alternate control devices (§63.1404(c)(2)) should require continuous monitoring and same data reporting as primary devices to prevent gaming through lower‑performance alternates.

[P7] Requiring compliance with either (a)(1) or (a)(2) for each continuous process vent at new sources (§63.1405(a)) may create duplicative obligations when vents are already covered by other instruments; commenters ask for cross‑reference language to allow reliance on existing equivalent permits or MACT standards.

[P8] The option to elect paragraph (c)(1) instead of (a) (§63.1405(a) permission) is helpful but needs clear timelines and transition provisions detailing how/when an owner may switch compliance paths without penalty.

[P9] The 85% by weight reduction requirement (§63.1405(a)(2)) is ambiguous for complex streams with multiple organic HAPs of differing molecular weights; commenters request specification whether reduction is measured as mass of total organic HAP or as TEQ, and methods to account for variable stream composition.

[P10] The requirement to achieve the 85% reduction by venting through closed‑vent systems to subpart SS devices (§63.1405(a)(2)) may force expensive retrofits; industry requests allowance to use equivalent control technologies demonstrated by performance testing instead of strict subpart SS device lists.

[P11] The requirement that existing sources comply with either (b)(1) or (b)(2) for each vent (§63.1405(b)) could be infeasible for small/remote facilities that cannot route to flares or meet the numeric limit; commenters request a size‑based de minimis exemption or extended compliance timeline.

[P12] The option to elect paragraph (c)(2) instead of (b) (§63.1405(b) permission) must include a clear definition of “existing affected source” for eligibility to avoid regulatory uncertainty and litigation.

[P13] Requiring routing all organic HAP emissions to a flare for existing sources (§63.1405(b)(1)) is impractical in regions with bans on flaring or for facilities lacking space and permits for flares; commenters request allowance for enclosed combustion or other high‑efficiency thermal oxidizers as alternatives.

[P14] The emission limit of ≤4.3 kg per megagram of resin produced for back‑end vents (§63.1405(b)(2)) appears to be based on specific technology and may not be achievable across all resin types and product grades — request disaggregation by resin type or allowance for product‑specific factors.

[P15] The permission to choose alternative compliance in (c) (§63.1405(c)) is welcome, but (c) lacks clear criteria for when alternative standards are appropriate and how to get Administrator approval; commenters request explicit application and demonstration requirements.

[P16] The alternative standard for new vents requiring outlet concentrations ≤20 ppmv (combustion) or ≤50 ppmv (non‑combustion) (§63.1405(c)(1)) relies on ppmv which can be temperature/pressure dependent and not mass‑based; commenters urge inclusion of equivalent mass‑based limits or correction procedures.

[P16] The numeric alternative outlet concentration limits (§63.1405(c)(1)) are extremely stringent for certain compounds with low detection limits using FTIR; request demonstration that test method detection limits and interference issues allow reliable compliance determination at 20/50 ppmv.

[P17] The requirement that vents not meeting the alternative standard must be controlled under (a)(1) or (a)(2) (§63.1405(c)(1) permission) creates a potential compliance trap if monitoring equipment QoL issues produce false exceedances; commenters request allowance for confirmatory testing and temporary corrective action plans before reclassification.

[P18] Requiring existing vents to meet the same outlet concentration thresholds as new vents (§63.1405(c)(2)) is financially burdensome; industry requests grandfathering or longer phase‑in for existing sources.

[P19] The cross‑reference that vents not meeting (c)(2) must comply with (b)(1) or (b)(2) (§63.1405(c)(2) permission) could lead to unintended duplicative controls; commenters request clarification that operators need only meet one set of requirements and how to demonstrate selection.

[P20] The TRE ≤4.0 trigger requiring either measurements or compliance with §63.1405(a) (§63.1412(k)(2)) is ambiguous regarding acceptable measurement frequency and methodology; commenters ask for explicit protocols and burden estimates.

[P21] The three‑stage compliance framework for each emission point (§63.1413(a)) (test/design/continuous) is comprehensive but places heavy administrative burdens on multi‑unit facilities — request options for facility‑level instead of per‑point compliance in certain cases.

[P22] Allowing design evaluations as equivalent to performance tests for uncontrolled vents (§63.1413(a)(1)(iii)) risks underestimating emissions; environmental groups will comment that design evaluations must be strictly limited and require conservative assumptions and independent review.

[P23] The design evaluation content requirements (§63.1413(a)(3)) are appropriate but lack clarity on acceptable sources for emission factors and bench data; commenters request a non‑exhaustive list of acceptable data sources and minimum quality criteria.

[P24] The requirement to establish parameter monitoring limits using specified procedures (§63.1413(a)(4)) should allow statistical approaches (e.g., 95th percentile) to set control parameter bounds rather than single fixed values to account for operational variability.

[P25] The obligation to operate control devices to keep monitored parameters within established limits (§63.1413(a)(4)) does not provide a pathway for the use of predictive maintenance or temporary deviations during start‑up/shutdown; commenters request explicit approved exceptions and reporting requirements for planned deviations.

[P26] Requiring initial compliance demonstration for flares per paragraph (g) (§63.1413(c)(2)) should include acceptable surrogate monitoring and combustion efficiency testing methods for small flares where continuous CO monitoring is impractical.

[P27] Mandating continuous compliance with flare requirements via §63.1415 monitoring (§63.1413(c)(4)) is technically challenging for intermittent vents; commenters request alternatives for intermittent operations such as duty cycle adjusted averaging.

[P28] The production‑based emission limit compliance demonstration procedures (§63.1413(c)(5)) will impose heavy recordkeeping on facilities with multiple products and varying formulations — request allowance for product family grouping and representative sampling.

[P29] The dual procedures for demonstrating emission rate limits (§63.1413(c)(6)) create complexity; commenters request a clear decision tree and simplified default pathway for facilities without in‑house measurement capabilities.

[P30] The requirement to follow subpart SS procedures when using closed vents and control devices (§63.1413(c)(6)(i)) may force duplication of monitoring requirements if subpart SS already applies — request harmonization to avoid double‑counting monitoring and reporting obligations.

[P31] For facilities using alternative methods to meet emission rate limits (§63.1413(c)(6)(ii)), the (h)(2) procedures are onerous and lack clarity on acceptable modeling approaches — request explicit modeling standards and validation requirements.

[P32] The requirement to demonstrate alternative‑standard compliance using paragraph (f) procedures (§63.1413(c)(7)) should allow use of third‑party accredited labs for testing per §63.1414 to reduce conflicts of interest.

[P33] The daily average outlet concentration test method thresholds in §63.1413(f) (20 ppmv combustion, 50 ppmv non‑combustion) could be affected by calibration drift and matrix interferences with FTIR; request mandatory zero/span checks, calibration gas specs, and QA/QC frequency.

[P34] Mandating use of the test method in §63.1414(a)(6) and compliance with monitoring provisions in §63.1415(e) by initial compliance date and daily thereafter (§63.1413(f)) imposes continuous FTIR operation and data handling burdens; commenters request an allowance for periodic spot checks plus continuous surrogate parameter monitoring rather than daily FTIR operation.

[P35] The mass emission limit compliance procedures (§63.1413(h)(1)) rely on certified production records; trade groups will request clear guidance on acceptable certification language, third‑party audits, and retention periods.

[P36] The comparison of performance test or design evaluation results to the mass emission limit for initial compliance (§63.1413(h)(1)(i)) should allow confidence intervals and statistical uncertainty treatment so small measurement uncertainties do not trigger noncompliance.

[P37] Calculating daily average emission rates beginning with the first 24‑hour period after the compliance date (§63.1413(h)(1)(ii)) could unfairly penalize facilities during startup transients; commenters request that an initial stabilization period (e.g., 7 days) be allowed before daily averages are enforced.

[P38] Requiring engineering assessments to substitute for direct measurements of vent flow and concentration (§63.1413(h)(4)(iii) & (h)(4)(ii)) is reasonable, but the rule must specify minimum documentation, assumptions, and uncertainty bounds for engineering assessments to be acceptable.

[P39] Permitting the use of previous tests, bench data, permit limits, and design analysis as engineering assessments (§63.1413(h)(4)(iii) and §63.1413(h)(4)(ii)) risks allowing outdated data; commenters will request maximum age limits (e.g., 5 years) and circumstances requiring re‑testing after process changes.

[P40] The continuous monitoring requirement using FTIR Method PS‑15 for outlet organic HAP concentration (§63.1415(e)) raises concerns about method applicability to complex multicomponent streams and ambient interference; request allowance for alternative validated continuous monitors (e.g., GC‑MS with appropriate calibration) where FTIR is not suitable.

[P41] The monitoring requirement to calculate a daily average outlet concentration (§63.1415(e)) should specify how to handle data gaps, failed QA checks, and analyzer downtime to avoid inadvertent noncompliance; commenters request explicit data substitution or exception protocols.

[P42] The TRE record retention requirement to include all data, assumptions, and procedures for engineering assessments (§63.1416(f)(1)) is appropriate but needs a specified minimum retention period (e.g., 5 years) and confidentiality protections for proprietary engineering data.

[P43] Requiring recording of organic HAP concentration as measured or determined via engineering assessment (§63.1416(f)(3)) should clarify required frequency and resolution of records (e.g., 1‑minute, 1‑hour) to avoid inconsistent reporting across facilities.

[P44] The records required for demonstrating compliance with the mass emission limit (§63.1416(f)(5)) must be allowed to be maintained electronically and signed electronically; commenters request explicit acceptance of electronic records and formats.

[P45] The obligation to identify the operating day period in records (§63.1416(f)(5)(ii) & (f)(6)(ii)) is ambiguous — commenters request a definition of "operating day" (calendar day, 24‑hour rolling period, or shift basis) and whether facilities can define their own operating day in permit applications.

[P46] The requirement to retain daily organic HAP emissions determined per §63.1413(h)(3) (§63.1416(f)(5)(iii)) will be burdensome for facilities with numerous vents; request allowance for aggregated reporting and retention at reasonable intervals (e.g., monthly summaries) with detailed records kept on‑site.

[P47] The records required for average hourly organic HAP emissions (§63.1416(f)(6)(iii)) should permit use of validated data loggers and data compression algorithms rather than storing every raw datapoint for every hour indefinitely.

[P48] The flare recordkeeping requirements when complying by venting to a flare (§63.1416(f)(7)) should be synchronized with existing NSPS/Title V flare monitoring obligations to prevent conflicting records and redundant monitoring.

[P49] The requirement to include measures adopted to prevent future pressure releases in incident reports (§63.1416(g)(5)(v)(E)) is reasonable, but confidentiality concerns arise — request redaction allowances for security‑sensitive details while still demonstrating corrective actions.

[P50] The Precompliance Report submission requirement for requests (extensions, alternatives, etc.) (§63.1417(d)) lacks a clear timeline and process for EPA review and approval; commenters request defined EPA response deadlines to avoid indefinite uncertainty.

[P51] The detailed content requirements for Precompliance Reports (§63.1417(d)(2)‑(11)) may contain proprietary process information; stakeholders request an explicit confidential business information (CBI) procedure to protect trade secrets.

[P52] The requirement to submit a sample of production records in the Precompliance Report when complying with the mass emission limit (§63.1417(d)(8)) is acceptable, but commenters request clarification on sample size, selection method, and whether redacted samples are allowed.

[P53] The reporting requirements to include results of applicability determinations, tests, inspections, and monitoring system performance (§63.1417(e)(1)) should be standardized into a single electronic template to reduce reporting burden and facilitate EPA review.

[P54] The semiannual periodic report deadline (no later than 60 days after each 180‑day period) (§63.1417(f)) may not align with facilities' existing reporting cycles; request flexibility to align with Title V reporting to reduce duplicate submissions.

[P55] Allowing a simple statement that no compliance exceptions occurred during the period (§63.1417(f)(2)) is reasonable, but commenters request a required attestation signed by a responsible official under penalty of law to ensure accuracy.

[P56] The detailed reporting requirements following mass emission limit deviations (§63.1417(f)(5)) could expose proprietary operational data; request limited public disclosure and a CBI claim process for sensitive items.

[P57] The quarterly reports requirement to include detailed information for the emission point (§63.1417(f)(12)(ii)) will create significant paperwork for facilities with many vents — request consolidation options such as annual summaries with quarterly flags for deviations only.

[P58] Requiring inclusion of daily average emission rates for each operating day with a deviation (§63.1417(f)(14)) may allow enforcement to second‑guess legitimate short‑term excursions; request that the rule require EPA to consider root causes and corrective actions before initiating enforcement.

[P59] The requirement to include calculated average hourly rates and underlying hourly data when reporting deviations (§63.1417(f)(15)(i) & (ii)) imposes heavy data‑handling needs; commenters request that only the affected period data be required and that older archived data can be provided on request.

[P60] The 60‑day reporting requirement after a vent becomes newly subject to §63.1405 due to a process change (§63.1417(h)(7)) is too short for facilities performing complex assessments and control modifications; request extending to 120 days and allowing a Preliminary Notice followed by a full report.

Permitting the use of previous tests, bench data, permit limits, and design analysis as engineering assessments (§63.1413(h)(4)(iii) and §63.1413(h)(4)(ii)) risks allowing outdated data; commenters will request maximum age limits (e.g., 5 years) and circumstances requiring re‑testing after process changes.

The continuous monitoring requirement using FTIR Method PS‑15 for outlet organic HAP concentration (§63.1415(e)) raises concerns about method applicability to complex multicomponent streams and ambient interference; request allowance for alternative validated continuous monitors (e.g., GC‑MS with appropriate calibration) where FTIR is not suitable.

The monitoring requirement to calculate a daily average outlet concentration (§63.1415(e)) should specify how to handle data gaps, failed QA checks, and analyzer downtime to avoid inadvertent noncompliance; commenters request explicit data substitution or exception protocols.

The TRE record retention requirement to include all data, assumptions, and procedures for engineering assessments (§63.1416(f)(1)) is appropriate but needs a specified minimum retention period (e.g., 5 years) and confidentiality protections for proprietary engineering data.

Requiring recording of organic HAP concentration as measured or determined via engineering assessment (§63.1416(f)(3)) should clarify required frequency and resolution of records (e.g., 1‑minute, 1‑hour) to avoid inconsistent reporting across facilities.

The records required for demonstrating compliance with the mass emission limit (§63.1416(f)(5)) must be allowed to be maintained electronically and signed electronically; commenters request explicit acceptance of electronic records and formats.

The obligation to identify the operating day period in records (§63.1416(f)(5)(ii) & (f)(6)(ii)) is ambiguous — commenters request a definition of "operating day" (calendar day, 24‑hour rolling period, or shift basis) and whether facilities can define their own operating day in permit applications.

The requirement to retain daily organic HAP emissions determined per §63.1413(h)(3) (§63.1416(f)(5)(iii)) will be burdensome for facilities with numerous vents; request allowance for aggregated reporting and retention at reasonable intervals (e.g., monthly summaries) with detailed records kept on‑site.

The records required for average hourly organic HAP emissions (§63.1416(f)(6)(iii)) should permit use of validated data loggers and data compression algorithms rather than storing every raw datapoint for every hour indefinitely.

The flare recordkeeping requirements when complying by venting to a flare (§63.1416(f)(7)) should be synchronized with existing NSPS/Title V flare monitoring obligations to prevent conflicting records and redundant monitoring.

The requirement to include measures adopted to prevent future pressure releases in incident reports (§63.1416(g)(5)(v)(E)) is reasonable, but confidentiality concerns arise — request redaction allowances for security‑sensitive details while still demonstrating corrective actions.

The Precompliance Report submission requirement for requests (extensions, alternatives, etc.) (§63.1417(d)) lacks a clear timeline and process for EPA review and approval; commenters request defined EPA response deadlines to avoid indefinite uncertainty.

The detailed content requirements for Precompliance Reports (§63.1417(d)(2)‑(11)) may contain proprietary process information; stakeholders request an explicit confidential business information (CBI) procedure to protect trade secrets.

The requirement to submit a sample of production records in the Precompliance Report when complying with the mass emission limit (§63.1417(d)(8)) is acceptable, but commenters request clarification on sample size, selection method, and whether redacted samples are allowed.

The reporting requirements to include results of applicability determinations, tests, inspections, and monitoring system performance (§63.1417(e)(1)) should be standardized into a single electronic template to reduce reporting burden and facilitate EPA review.

The semiannual periodic report deadline (no later than 60 days after each 180‑day period) (§63.1417(f)) may not align with facilities' existing reporting cycles; request flexibility to align with Title V reporting to reduce duplicate submissions.

Allowing a simple statement that no compliance exceptions occurred during the period (§63.1417(f)(2)) is reasonable, but commenters request a required attestation signed by a responsible official under penalty of law to ensure accuracy.

The detailed reporting requirements following mass emission limit deviations (§63.1417(f)(5)) could expose proprietary operational data; request limited public disclosure and a CBI claim process for sensitive items.

The quarterly reports requirement to include detailed information for the emission point (§63.1417(f)(12)(ii)) will create significant paperwork for facilities with many vents — request consolidation options such as annual summaries with quarterly flags for deviations only.

Requiring inclusion of daily average emission rates for each operating day with a deviation (§63.1417(f)(14)) may allow enforcement to second‑guess legitimate short‑term excursions; request that the rule require EPA to consider root causes and corrective actions before initiating enforcement.

The requirement to include calculated average hourly rates and underlying hourly data when reporting deviations (§63.1417(f)(15)(i) & (ii)) imposes heavy data‑handling needs; commenters request that only the affected period data be required and that older archived data can be provided on request.

The 60‑day reporting requirement after a vent becomes newly subject to §63.1405 due to a process change (§63.1417(h)(7)) is too short for facilities performing complex assessments and control modifications; request extending to 120 days and allowing a Preliminary Notice followed by a full report.

[P1] The requirement that Category I drugs have "no withdrawal period at the lowest use level in each approved major species" is ambiguous about whether it applies per individual product label or per active ingredient across all formulations; industry requests clarification to avoid conflicting obligations for different formulations of the same active ingredient.

[P1] Animal drug manufacturers will be unable to register necessary therapeutic drugs for multi-species use if the no-withdrawal requirement for Category I is interpreted strictly, thereby reducing available treatments for food-producing animals.

[P1] The phrase "lowest use level" in P1 lacks a clear definition (e.g., per dose, per mg/kg, per day), which creates legal uncertainty for sponsors determining compliance and calculating residue studies.

[P1] Agricultural producer groups object that requiring no withdrawal periods for Category I drugs in every approved major species is overly restrictive and may force sponsors to seek approval only for minor species, limiting farm-level treatment options.

[P1] Legal experts note that P1 could conflict with existing statutory standards for drug safety and efficacy because it effectively prohibits approval of drugs that necessitate any withdrawal even if scientifically justified; the rule should allow case-by-case determinations.

[P1] Public health advocates support the intent of P1 to minimize drug residues but request an explicit mechanism (e.g., transition timeline or waiver process) for existing Category I products that currently have withdrawal periods.

[P2] P2's requirement that Category II drugs must have a withdrawal period "for at least one approved major species" is vague about how long the withdrawal must be and what residue endpoints and tolerances must be met.

[P2] Food industry commenters warn that P2 will create supply-chain complexity if some major species require withdrawals and others do not, complicating label instructions, on-farm management, and monitoring programs.

[P2] Veterinarians argue P2 may force choice of less appropriate drugs for certain species because a sponsor may decline approval for a species to avoid creating a withdrawal period, reducing veterinarians' therapeutic options.

[P2] Consumer safety groups request that P2 clarify scientific standards and testing protocols for establishing the withdrawal period at the "lowest use level," including required study designs and statistical criteria.

[P3] P3 duplicates P2 but lacks guidance on when a withdrawal for one species is considered sufficient to classify a drug as Category II; regulators should specify whether a single major species withdrawal is adequate regardless of other uses.

[P3] Trade associations point out that requiring only one species to have a withdrawal could perversely incentivize sponsors to seek approval solely for a species with favorable pharmacokinetics, leaving other species unregulated or without appropriate label warnings.

[P3] Legal commenters recommend adding an appeals or petition process for sponsors to contest a Category II classification based on scientific residue evidence that supports a no-withdrawal designation.

[P4] The alternative in P4 that allows "no-residue" or "zero tolerance" regulation for carcinogenic concerns is too broad; commenters request a clear definition of "carcinogenic concern" and the scientific threshold (e.g., IARC classification, FDA/ EPA determinations) that triggers zero-tolerance regulation.

[P4] Pharmaceutical companies caution that the "zero tolerance because of carcinogenic concern" posture could result in de facto prohibition of useful drugs based on marginal or preliminary carcinogenicity signals without standardized risk assessment procedures.

[P4] Public health NGOs support P4 but request that the rule require transparent publication of the evidence and risk assessment methodology used to invoke "no-residue/zero tolerance" status for a drug.

[P4] Academic toxicologists ask the agency to specify whether mechanistic, genotoxicity, or long-term carcinogenicity data will be weighted in determining zero-tolerance and whether acceptable daily intake (ADI) calculations will ever permit non-zero residues for carcinogens.

[P5] P5 states the "no-residue/zero-tolerance regulation applies irrespective of whether any species has a withdrawal period" — industry warns that this could render withdrawal data irrelevant and nullify sponsors' investments in residue depletion studies if an unrelated species triggers zero-tolerance.

[P5] Food processors and exporters express concern that P5 could cause trade disruptions if imported products are tested under zero-tolerance for certain residues despite internationally accepted tolerances in major trading partners.

[P5] State agriculture departments request explicit coordination procedures between federal zero-tolerance determinations and state-level enforcement to avoid inconsistent regulatory actions under P5.

[P5] Legal advocates argue that applying zero tolerance "irrespective" of withdrawal periods raises due process concerns and should include notice-and-comment steps before an active ingredient is re-classified to no-residue status.

[P2/P4] Several commenters note an internal inconsistency: P2 allows regulation "on a no-residue/zero-tolerance basis" as an alternative to a withdrawal requirement, yet P4 and P5 make no-residue determinations independent of species withdrawals; stakeholders request a unified decision framework explaining when each pathway applies.

[P1/P3] Small animal veterinarians point out that the rule appears to focus on food-producing species ("major species") and may inadvertently restrict approvals for companion animal products containing similar active ingredients, calling for explicit carve-outs or alignment.

[P1] Farmers request an implementation timeline (e.g., multi-year phase-in) for existing Category I products that would need label changes to remove withdrawal periods, to avoid disruptions to farm operations and beef/pork/poultry supply.

[P3] Analytical laboratories ask for guidance on detection limits and analytical methods that will be required to verify compliance with withdrawal periods established "at the lowest use level" under P3.

[P4] Consumer groups ask that any no-residue/zero-tolerance designations include mandatory monitoring programs and public reporting of detection events to ensure enforcement and transparency.

[P5] Export-oriented producers warn that unilateral zero-tolerance rules under P5 could cause inconsistent maximum residue levels with Codex Alimentarius and recommend alignment or a process for equivalence recognition.

[P2] Commenters request clarification whether combination products containing multiple active ingredients are assessed per active ingredient (so Category II applies if any active requires withdrawal) or per product.

[P1] Environmental groups recommend that the rule require environmental residue assessments when removing withdrawal periods under P1 because on-farm excretion can lead to environmental exposure.

[P4] Industry seeks clarity on whether a no-residue determination because of carcinogenic concern is permanent or subject to revision if new evidence emerges, and requests a defined re-evaluation process.

[P1] The requirement that plans have a contract meeting §422.107(c) and satisfy integration criteria beginning 1/1/2021 is retroactive and imposes unfair obligations on plans whose contracts and operations were executed before that date; CMS should provide a prospective compliance date or transition period.

[P1] Industry commenters will request clarification whether the “one or more specified integration criteria” must be satisfied continuously or only at the time of contract execution and how CMS will monitor ongoing compliance.

[P2] State Medicaid agencies will request explicit specification of which elements of §422.107(d) satisfy the integration criteria and whether partial compliance with §422.107(d) counts.

[P3] Plans proposing to be “highly integrated D‑SNPs” ask for a clear, objective definition and measurable thresholds for “highly integrated” (e.g., minimum overlap of governance, shared financial risk, data exchange standards) to avoid inconsistent State/CMS interpretation.

[P4] For fully integrated D‑SNPs, stakeholders seek clarification whether “fully integrated” requires a single managed care contract or whether a legally affiliated but separate Medicaid MCO is sufficient.

[P5] Beneficiary advocates will challenge the single-entity requirement that Medicare and Medicaid are under one entity, arguing it may limit beneficiary choice in states where separate MA and Medicaid contractors provide better local access.

[P5] Plans request CMS to clarify whether holding an MA contract and a separate Medicaid managed care contract through a related but distinct legal entity (e.g., parent/subsidiary) satisfies the “single entity” obligation.

[P6] Long-term care providers and plans note that the 180‑day minimum nursing facility services coverage per plan year is arbitrary; they request evidence supporting the 180‑day threshold or ask CMS to allow State-specific adjustments based on local practice patterns.

[P6] States caution that mandating inclusion of 180 days of nursing facility services in capitated contracts may conflict with existing State Medicaid actuarial assumptions and request flexibility to negotiate duration in the State contract.

[P7] Plans ask CMS to further define “aligned care management” and “specialty care network methods,” including minimum staffing ratios, required types of care managers, and data exchange standards for high‑risk beneficiaries.

[P8] Advocacy groups request that CMS require beneficiary-facing coordination policies to be available in plain language and multiple languages and to include measurable timeframes for responses to grievances/appeals.

[P8] Legal commenters ask CMS to clarify the scope of CMS- and State-approved policies—whether approval is limited to content or includes operational validation—and how often approvals must be renewed.

[P9] States request examples of acceptable evidence that an MA organization or related entity “has” a capitated Medicaid contract that includes LTSS or behavioral health to qualify as highly integrated.

[P9] Plans argue that requiring the parent or related entity to hold the Medicaid contract could disadvantage smaller MA organizations and reduce market competition; they request allowance for contractual partnerships to qualify.

[P10] Consumer advocates support allowing additional supplemental benefits but request stronger guardrails on CMS approval criteria and timing to ensure enrollees can access benefits at plan start dates.

[P10] Plans request a clear, published standard for the “minimum performance/quality standards” to avoid ad hoc CMS decisions and permit advance operational planning.

[P11] MA organizations note the statutory requirement to have a State contract to offer a D‑SNP but request clarity on whether Memoranda of Understanding or other collaborative agreements satisfy the contract requirement in cases where State law prohibits single contracts.

[P12] States and plans seek more detail on the specific responsibilities for coordinating LTSS and behavioral health in §422.107(c)(1), including division of care management responsibilities and financial accountability.

[P13] Advocates request that the contract eligibility categories and criteria (§422.107(c)(2)) must be narrow enough to prevent unwarranted denials and broad enough to capture clinically appropriate dual eligible subpopulations; they ask CMS to require public posting of these criteria.

[P14] Plans ask for precise guidance on how to list benefits “covered under a capitated contract or via risk contract arrangements by affiliated managed care organizations,” particularly how to reflect carve‑outs and pass‑through payments in bids.

[P15] Non‑integrated D‑SNPs express concern that the required hospital and SNF admission notifications for at least one group of high‑risk full‑benefit duals could create burdens if States set very short notice timeframes; they request CMS-set minimum and maximum notice windows.

[P16] Plans and States request detailed minimum standards and acceptable modalities (electronic, fax, phone) for the notice methods the State may establish under §422.107(d) to ensure interoperability and timeliness.

[P17] Legal commenters caution that holding SNPs strictly liable when they authorize others to perform notices (but cannot control those entities) may be unreasonable; they request a “reasonable efforts” standard or safe harbor if authorized entities fail.

[P18] Plans point out that the compliance effective date of 1/1/2021 for paragraph (d) is in the past; they request retroactive safe harbor language or explicit guidance on enforcement and penalties for the retroactive period.

[P19] Consumer groups support the comprehensive written pre‑enrollment statement requirement (§422.111(b)(2)(iii)) but request CMS to mandate standardized templates and plain-language readability scores to ensure comprehension by low‑literacy beneficiaries.

[P19] Plans request clarification on the scope of “cost‑sharing protections” and examples of what must be disclosed (e.g., state Medicaid spend‑down rules, copay maximums) to avoid inconsistent disclosures.

[P20] Telehealth advocates strongly support allowing clinically appropriate telehealth as Part B basic benefits for Part C purposes but request criteria clarifying which services are “clinically appropriate” and whether asynchronous services count.

[P21] Plans note the prohibition on treating electronic-exchange services as basic benefits if requirements are unmet and request a clearly defined corrective action process and timeline for bringing services into compliance rather than immediate downgrading to supplemental benefits.

[P22] Plans request CMS to specify the “required actions” in §422.135(c) with objective metrics, timelines, and enforcement procedures to enable operational planning.

[P23] Beneficiary advocates insist that the in‑person option must not be used to coerce enrollees away from telehealth offerings and that plans must provide transportation assistance when in‑person visits are required and the enrollee lacks means.

[P24] Consumers request that Evidence of Coverage language about telehealth be required to include examples, technical requirements (device/internet), and instructions for requesting reasonable accommodations.

[P25] Plans object to the requirement to identify in provider directories whether providers offer telehealth or telehealth-only services, citing frequent provider changes; they request flexibility on update frequency and acceptable directory timestamps.

[P26] Providers request explicit guidance on interstate licensing: while plans must require providers to meet state laws where enrollee is located, telehealth across state lines needs clearer reciprocity rules or reliance on telemedicine compacts.

[P27] Plans note the credentialing and selection rules in §422.204 may not align with existing telehealth vendor onboarding processes and request CMS to allow alternate credentialing pathways for telehealth‑native providers.

[P27] Legal commenters request specification of acceptable documentation that satisfies credentialing requirements for remote providers and CMS acceptance of electronic credentials.

[P27] Plans request an exception allowing contracted telehealth vendors to rely on the credentialing of an in‑network supervising provider when permitted by state law.

[P27] Consumer advocates request confirmation that plans may not use telehealth provider credentialing to limit access unlawfully to services in certain languages or by culturally competent providers.

[P27] Organizations representing rural providers request clarification whether state licensing limitations could bar out‑of‑state telehealth providers and whether CMS will allow waivers in shortage areas.

[P27] Plans request CMS guidance on liability and malpractice coverage expectations for telehealth services, particularly for providers located in different states.

[P27] Plans and providers request CMS to define the scope of “other applicable laws” providers must meet where the enrollee is located (e.g., prescribing controlled substances via telehealth) so that plans know when to restrict services.

[P27] Plans ask for CMS to allow use of telehealth vendor attestations and centralized credentialing to avoid duplicative credentialing across multiple MA plans.

[P27] Consumer advocates request protections ensuring telehealth providers who fail credentialing cannot continue seeing enrollees in the interim without notice and transition plans.

[P27] Telehealth vendors ask CMS to permit contracted platforms that enable provider‑patient electronic exchange to be considered contracted providers for the purpose of §422.135(d) when they meet privacy/security standards.

[P27] Privacy advocates request that any information CMS requires under §422.135(c)(5) for telehealth coverage include strict de‑identification and data minimization standards to protect beneficiary privacy.

[P27] Plans request clarity on the periodicity and data elements CMS may request about telehealth utilization to avoid unexpected reporting burdens.

[P28] Plans note the condition that additional telehealth as basic benefits be provided only through contracted providers may limit emergent telehealth access via hospital systems or urgent care that are not contracted; they request an exception for emergency services.

[P29] Consumer groups urge that coverage of non‑contracted providers as supplemental benefits should not be used to impose prohibitive cost sharing that effectively denies access.

[P30] Plans request explicit instructions for including additional telehealth benefits in basic benefits bids and sample actuarial treatment to avoid bid submission errors.

[P31] Consumer advocates and some state regulators object to permitting differential cost sharing for in‑person versus electronic exchange services if it results in barriers to telehealth for low‑income or rural beneficiaries; they request limits on higher telehealth cost sharing.

[P31] Plans support the flexibility to set different cost sharing but ask CMS to require actuarial justification and non‑discrimination (e.g., not imposing higher telehealth cost sharing on enrollees with disabilities).

[P32] Plans and legal experts request detailed criteria and transparency regarding what constitutes “data integrity concerns” for measure exclusions under §422.164(f)(1)(v) and an appeal process for measures excluded for data integrity.

[P33] MA organizations object to automatic reduction to 1 star for appeals measures if Timeliness Monitoring Project data are not submitted; they request graduated penalties, justification thresholds, and the ability to cure missing submissions.

[P34] Plans request that the June 30 deadline for requesting CMS or IRE review of appeals data (§422.164(h)(1)) include an exception for reasonable cause (e.g., documented systems outage) and clarity on acceptable "supporting documentation."

[P35] Similarly, plans request that the June 30 deadline for CTM review requests be extended or made flexible in years where plan financial cycles or audits delay internal reconciliation.

[P36] Plans seek a clear definition and examples of “extreme and uncontrollable circumstances” under §422.166(i) (e.g., pandemic, natural disaster) and predictable workflows for obtaining relief and required proofs.

[P37] Contracts request clearer standards for the CAHPS administration exemption—what documentation suffices to “demonstrate the required sample cannot be contacted” and whether displacement due to disaster qualifies in more ambiguous situations.

[P38] Stakeholders urge CMS to publish a streamlined, expedited process for approving CAHPS/HOS/HEDIS exemptions and to commit to specific CMS decision timelines to avoid uncertainty.

[P39] Plans ask for confirmation that receiving prior-year CAHPS/HOS/HEDIS measure stars due to exemptions will not trigger downstream regulatory consequences tied to quality improvement obligations.

[P40] Plans and consumer advocates request clarification of the 25% FEMA IA threshold—whether it’s based on enrollment on the date of the disaster, cumulative enrollment, or another metric—and how CMS will verify FEMA IA designations.

[P41] Providers and plans object to the provision that CMS will not adjust call center measures generally (§422.166(i)(6)(ii)) and request a detailed list of circumstances under which the communications exception applies and an expedited petition process.

[P42] Plans ask for transparency on the specific call center measures excluded from adjustment and the statistical methodology CMS will apply to adjust those measures in qualifying instances.

[P43] Plans request clear guidance on how measures reverted to prior-year data (per §422.166(i)(7)) will be treated in plan improvement calculations and any retroactive payment/reward calculations.

[P44] Analytics vendors and actuaries request the technical appendix describing the cut point recalculation methodology when affected contracts’ numeric values are excluded (§422.166(i)(9)) to model financial implications.

[P45] Plans request clarification of the threshold mechanics at 60% and 25% (different provisions) to ensure consistent application and to prevent perverse incentives for enrollment shifts.

[P46] Small MA organizations argue that exclusion of numeric values for contracts with ≥60% enrollees in FEMA IA areas may penalize them if their enrollment is concentrated in one disaster area; they request a more nuanced, per-measure approach.

[P47] Plans request detail on the Reward Factor calculations and proof that affected contracts will not be disadvantaged financially when CMS excludes numeric values as described in §422.166(i)(10).

[P48] Providers and compliance officers raise due process concerns about the preclusion list provisions: they request an opportunity for notice and temporary payment continuation when inclusion is tied to OIG exclusion dates (per §422.222(a)(3)(ii) and (a)(5)).

[P49] Patient advocates object to §422.222(a)(4) barring beneficiary appeals of payment denials based on preclusion list inclusion; they request at minimum an information-only appeal right so beneficiaries can challenge factual errors that impact care continuity.

[P50] Legal commenters request clarity about the interplay between CMS preclusion duration for felony convictions (10 years, §422.222(a)(5)(iii)) and State credentialing or licensing sanctions and how CMS will consider rehabilitation and petition processes.

[P51] Professional associations ask CMS to define the “specified factors” it will consider to shorten preclusion periods for felony convictions so affected individuals have predictable remediation paths.

[P52] Organizations representing formerly incarcerated providers request procedural safeguards and transparent criteria for CMS determinations on shorter preclusion periods under §422.222(a)(5)(iii).

[P53] MA organizations request explicit guidance and timelines for the 30‑day beneficiary notice obligation after posting an updated preclusion list (§422.222(a)(1)(ii)(A)), including model notice language and permitted delivery methods.

[P54] MA organizations note the obligation to make “reasonable efforts” to notify newly precluded providers (§422.222(a)(1)(ii)(B)) is vague; they request a definition of “reasonable efforts” (e.g., number of contact attempts, documented methods).

[P55] Plans request that §422.222(a)(1)(ii)(C)’s prohibition on denying payment solely because a provider was newly added to the list during the 60‑day notice window be clarified to permit denial when there is independent evidence of fraud or imminent patient safety risk.

[P56] Providers request that CMS clarify procedures for joint appeals of preclusion and contemporaneous Medicare revocations under part 498 (§422.222(a)(2)(ii)(B)) and ensure sufficient time and resources to prepare joint appeals.

[P57] Plans request CMS to clarify whether inclusion on the preclusion list affects only Medicare payments or whether plans must also deny Medicaid payments and whether dual‑eligibility billing implications have been coordinated with States.

[P58] MA organizations ask CMS to publish a standard reconciliation timeline and methodology for remitting improper payments identified by RADV audits (§422.310(e) and §422.311), including installment/offset options to mitigate cash‑flow impacts.

[P59] Plans request that CMS publish technical specifications and statistical methodologies it will use for RADV extrapolation to PY 2011 forward (§422.310(e), §422.311) so plans can model potential liabilities and challenge methodologies before audit.

[P60] Industry stakeholders urge CMS to limit the retrospective extrapolation window or provide a phase-in of recovery amounts to avoid destabilizing large recoveries based on very old data (Payment Year 2011 forward).

[P61] Legal commenters ask whether CMS will apply interest, administrative cost offsets, or allow appeals timelines when recovering improper payments under the Secretary’s extrapolation methodology (§422.311).

[P62] MA organizations request clarification on the confidentiality and use of medical records submitted for RADV validation (§422.310(e)), including limits on redisclosure and provider notification requirements.

[P63] Plans request CMS to clarify penalties for submission of false data (§422.310(e) condition) including the range, due process for contesting CMS findings, and whether penalties apply only to intentional misconduct.

[P64] State Medicaid agencies request coordination guidance between CMS RADV activities and State audits to avoid duplicated record requests and conflicting remediation demands.

[P65] Plans ask for an express rule that CMS will not extrapolate RADV findings to affect payments for years beyond reasonable statute-of-limits or will apply equitable tolling policies for older years.

[P66] Consumer advocates request that the MA enrollee financial protection provision (§422.504(g)(1)(iv)) be made explicit to prohibit balance billing in all forms and require plans notify enrollees promptly if an in-network provider becomes precluded.

[P67] Plans and provider groups request clarity on the truncated text of §422.504(g)(1)(iv) to ensure mutual understanding of the prohibition on enrollee financial liability and any exceptions (e.g., out-of-network emergency care).

[P68] Stakeholders across sectors request that CMS publish the final rule required by the Act within the 3‑year timeframe referenced (§1871 and related provisions) and provide a timetable and milestones for any permitted extensions under Section 1871.

[P69] Advocacy organizations request that any extension of final rule publication (per §1871(a)(3)(B)) include public notice and an opportunity for supplemental comment, as well as clear justifications beyond generic “complexity.”

[P70] Regulatory experts request that CMS specify examples of “exceptional circumstances” that would justify setting a publication timeline longer than 3 years to ensure transparency and prevent unnecessary delay.

[P71] Public stakeholders request CMS to release all modeling, impact analyses, and state‑level fiscal estimates relied upon to extend the deadline for finalizing the November 1, 2018 proposed rule until November 1, 2022 (§94) and to allow comment on those analyses.

[P72] Industry commenters ask CMS to confirm whether the extension in §94 interacts with statutory deadlines for plan bid submissions and contract changes and to provide transitional compliance plans for affected MA organizations.

[P73] Plans request explicit transitional compliance guidance for provisions with retrospective effective dates, including enforcement discretion and good‑faith compliance safe harbors for technical violations.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The requirement that plans have a contract meeting §422.107(c) and satisfy integration criteria beginning 1/1/2021 is retroactive and imposes unfair obligations on plans whose contracts and operations were executed before that date; CMS should provide a prospective compliance date or transition period.

Industry commenters will request clarification whether the “one or more specified integration criteria” must be satisfied continuously or only at the time of contract execution and how CMS will monitor ongoing compliance.
State Medicaid agencies will request explicit specification of which elements of §422.107(d) satisfy the integration criteria and whether partial compliance with §422.107(d) counts.

Plans proposing to be “highly integrated D‑SNPs” ask for a clear, objective definition and measurable thresholds for “highly integrated” (e.g., minimum overlap of governance, shared financial risk, data exchange standards) to avoid inconsistent State/CMS interpretation.

For fully integrated D‑SNPs, stakeholders seek clarification whether “fully integrated” requires a single managed care contract or whether a legally affiliated but separate Medicaid MCO is sufficient.

Beneficiary advocates will challenge the single-entity requirement that Medicare and Medicaid are under one entity, arguing it may limit beneficiary choice in states where separate MA and Medicaid contractors provide better local access.

Plans request CMS to clarify whether holding an MA contract and a separate Medicaid managed care contract through a related but distinct legal entity (e.g., parent/subsidiary) satisfies the “single entity” obligation.

Long-term care providers and plans note that the 180‑day minimum nursing facility services coverage per plan year is arbitrary; they request evidence supporting the 180‑day threshold or ask CMS to allow State-specific adjustments based on local practice patterns.

States caution that mandating inclusion of 180 days of nursing facility services in capitated contracts may conflict with existing State Medicaid actuarial assumptions and request flexibility to negotiate duration in the State contract.

Plans ask CMS to further define “aligned care management” and “specialty care network methods,” including minimum staffing ratios, required types of care managers, and data exchange standards for high‑risk beneficiaries.

Advocacy groups request that CMS require beneficiary-facing coordination policies to be available in plain language and multiple languages and to include measurable timeframes for responses to grievances/appeals.
Legal commenters ask CMS to clarify the scope of CMS- and State-approved policies—whether approval is limited to content or includes operational validation—and how often approvals must be renewed.
States request examples of acceptable evidence that an MA organization or related entity “has” a capitated Medicaid contract that includes LTSS or behavioral health to qualify as highly integrated.

Plans argue that requiring the parent or related entity to hold the Medicaid contract could disadvantage smaller MA organizations and reduce market competition; they request allowance for contractual partnerships to qualify.
Consumer advocates support allowing additional supplemental benefits but request stronger guardrails on CMS approval criteria and timing to ensure enrollees can access benefits at plan start dates.
Plans request a clear, published standard for the “minimum performance/quality standards” to avoid ad hoc CMS decisions and permit advance operational planning.

MA organizations note the statutory requirement to have a State contract to offer a D‑SNP but request clarity on whether Memoranda of Understanding or other collaborative agreements satisfy the contract requirement in cases where State law prohibits single contracts.

States and plans seek more detail on the specific responsibilities for coordinating LTSS and behavioral health in §422.107(c)(1), including division of care management responsibilities and financial accountability.

Advocates request that the contract eligibility categories and criteria (§422.107(c)(2)) must be narrow enough to prevent unwarranted denials and broad enough to capture clinically appropriate dual eligible subpopulations; they ask CMS to require public posting of these criteria.

Plans ask for precise guidance on how to list benefits “covered under a capitated contract or via risk contract arrangements by affiliated managed care organizations,” particularly how to reflect carve‑outs and pass‑through payments in bids.

Non‑integrated D‑SNPs express concern that the required hospital and SNF admission notifications for at least one group of high‑risk full‑benefit duals could create burdens if States set very short notice timeframes; they request CMS-set minimum and maximum notice windows.

Plans and States request detailed minimum standards and acceptable modalities (electronic, fax, phone) for the notice methods the State may establish under §422.107(d) to ensure interoperability and timeliness.

Legal commenters caution that holding SNPs strictly liable when they authorize others to perform notices (but cannot control those entities) may be unreasonable; they request a “reasonable efforts” standard or safe harbor if authorized entities fail.

Plans point out that the compliance effective date of 1/1/2021 for paragraph (d) is in the past; they request retroactive safe harbor language or explicit guidance on enforcement and penalties for the retroactive period.

Consumer groups support the comprehensive written pre‑enrollment statement requirement (§422.111(b)(2)(iii)) but request CMS to mandate standardized templates and plain-language readability scores to ensure comprehension by low‑literacy beneficiaries.

Plans request clarification on the scope of “cost‑sharing protections” and examples of what must be disclosed (e.g., state Medicaid spend‑down rules, copay maximums) to avoid inconsistent disclosures.

Telehealth advocates strongly support allowing clinically appropriate telehealth as Part B basic benefits for Part C purposes but request criteria clarifying which services are “clinically appropriate” and whether asynchronous services count.

Plans note the prohibition on treating electronic-exchange services as basic benefits if requirements are unmet and request a clearly defined corrective action process and timeline for bringing services into compliance rather than immediate downgrading to supplemental benefits.
Plans request CMS to specify the “required actions” in §422.135(c) with objective metrics, timelines, and enforcement procedures to enable operational planning.

Beneficiary advocates insist that the in‑person option must not be used to coerce enrollees away from telehealth offerings and that plans must provide transportation assistance when in‑person visits are required and the enrollee lacks means.

Consumers request that Evidence of Coverage language about telehealth be required to include examples, technical requirements (device/internet), and instructions for requesting reasonable accommodations.

Plans object to the requirement to identify in provider directories whether providers offer telehealth or telehealth-only services, citing frequent provider changes; they request flexibility on update frequency and acceptable directory timestamps.

Providers request explicit guidance on interstate licensing: while plans must require providers to meet state laws where enrollee is located, telehealth across state lines needs clearer reciprocity rules or reliance on telemedicine compacts.

Plans note the credentialing and selection rules in §422.204 may not align with existing telehealth vendor onboarding processes and request CMS to allow alternate credentialing pathways for telehealth‑native providers.
Legal commenters request specification of acceptable documentation that satisfies credentialing requirements for remote providers and CMS acceptance of electronic credentials.
Plans request an exception allowing contracted telehealth vendors to rely on the credentialing of an in‑network supervising provider when permitted by state law.
Consumer advocates request confirmation that plans may not use telehealth provider credentialing to limit access unlawfully to services in certain languages or by culturally competent providers.
Organizations representing rural providers request clarification whether state licensing limitations could bar out‑of‑state telehealth providers and whether CMS will allow waivers in shortage areas.
Plans request CMS guidance on liability and malpractice coverage expectations for telehealth services, particularly for providers located in different states.

Plans and providers request CMS to define the scope of “other applicable laws” providers must meet where the enrollee is located (e.g., prescribing controlled substances via telehealth) so that plans know when to restrict services.
Plans ask for CMS to allow use of telehealth vendor attestations and centralized credentialing to avoid duplicative credentialing across multiple MA plans.
Consumer advocates request protections ensuring telehealth providers who fail credentialing cannot continue seeing enrollees in the interim without notice and transition plans.

Telehealth vendors ask CMS to permit contracted platforms that enable provider‑patient electronic exchange to be considered contracted providers for the purpose of §422.135(d) when they meet privacy/security standards.

Privacy advocates request that any information CMS requires under §422.135(c)(5) for telehealth coverage include strict de‑identification and data minimization standards to protect beneficiary privacy.
Plans request clarity on the periodicity and data elements CMS may request about telehealth utilization to avoid unexpected reporting burdens.

Plans note the condition that additional telehealth as basic benefits be provided only through contracted providers may limit emergent telehealth access via hospital systems or urgent care that are not contracted; they request an exception for emergency services.
Consumer groups urge that coverage of non‑contracted providers as supplemental benefits should not be used to impose prohibitive cost sharing that effectively denies access.
Plans request explicit instructions for including additional telehealth benefits in basic benefits bids and sample actuarial treatment to avoid bid submission errors.

Consumer advocates and some state regulators object to permitting differential cost sharing for in‑person versus electronic exchange services if it results in barriers to telehealth for low‑income or rural beneficiaries; they request limits on higher telehealth cost sharing.

Plans support the flexibility to set different cost sharing but ask CMS to require actuarial justification and non‑discrimination (e.g., not imposing higher telehealth cost sharing on enrollees with disabilities).

Plans and legal experts request detailed criteria and transparency regarding what constitutes “data integrity concerns” for measure exclusions under §422.164(f)(1)(v) and an appeal process for measures excluded for data integrity.

MA organizations object to automatic reduction to 1 star for appeals measures if Timeliness Monitoring Project data are not submitted; they request graduated penalties, justification thresholds, and the ability to cure missing submissions.

Plans request that the June 30 deadline for requesting CMS or IRE review of appeals data (§422.164(h)(1)) include an exception for reasonable cause (e.g., documented systems outage) and clarity on acceptable "supporting documentation."
Similarly, plans request that the June 30 deadline for CTM review requests be extended or made flexible in years where plan financial cycles or audits delay internal reconciliation.

Plans seek a clear definition and examples of “extreme and uncontrollable circumstances” under §422.166(i) (e.g., pandemic, natural disaster) and predictable workflows for obtaining relief and required proofs.

Contracts request clearer standards for the CAHPS administration exemption—what documentation suffices to “demonstrate the required sample cannot be contacted” and whether displacement due to disaster qualifies in more ambiguous situations.
Stakeholders urge CMS to publish a streamlined, expedited process for approving CAHPS/HOS/HEDIS exemptions and to commit to specific CMS decision timelines to avoid uncertainty.
Plans ask for confirmation that receiving prior-year CAHPS/HOS/HEDIS measure stars due to exemptions will not trigger downstream regulatory consequences tied to quality improvement obligations.

Plans and consumer advocates request clarification of the 25% FEMA IA threshold—whether it’s based on enrollment on the date of the disaster, cumulative enrollment, or another metric—and how CMS will verify FEMA IA designations.

Providers and plans object to the provision that CMS will not adjust call center measures generally (§422.166(i)(6)(ii)) and request a detailed list of circumstances under which the communications exception applies and an expedited petition process.
Plans ask for transparency on the specific call center measures excluded from adjustment and the statistical methodology CMS will apply to adjust those measures in qualifying instances.
Plans request clear guidance on how measures reverted to prior-year data (per §422.166(i)(7)) will be treated in plan improvement calculations and any retroactive payment/reward calculations.

Analytics vendors and actuaries request the technical appendix describing the cut point recalculation methodology when affected contracts’ numeric values are excluded (§422.166(i)(9)) to model financial implications.
Plans request clarification of the threshold mechanics at 60% and 25% (different provisions) to ensure consistent application and to prevent perverse incentives for enrollment shifts.

Small MA organizations argue that exclusion of numeric values for contracts with ≥60% enrollees in FEMA IA areas may penalize them if their enrollment is concentrated in one disaster area; they request a more nuanced, per-measure approach.
Plans request detail on the Reward Factor calculations and proof that affected contracts will not be disadvantaged financially when CMS excludes numeric values as described in §422.166(i)(10).

Providers and compliance officers raise due process concerns about the preclusion list provisions: they request an opportunity for notice and temporary payment continuation when inclusion is tied to OIG exclusion dates (per §422.222(a)(3)(ii) and (a)(5)).

Patient advocates object to §422.222(a)(4) barring beneficiary appeals of payment denials based on preclusion list inclusion; they request at minimum an information-only appeal right so beneficiaries can challenge factual errors that impact care continuity.

Legal commenters request clarity about the interplay between CMS preclusion duration for felony convictions (10 years, §422.222(a)(5)(iii)) and State credentialing or licensing sanctions and how CMS will consider rehabilitation and petition processes.
Professional associations ask CMS to define the “specified factors” it will consider to shorten preclusion periods for felony convictions so affected individuals have predictable remediation paths.
Organizations representing formerly incarcerated providers request procedural safeguards and transparent criteria for CMS determinations on shorter preclusion periods under §422.222(a)(5)(iii).

MA organizations request explicit guidance and timelines for the 30‑day beneficiary notice obligation after posting an updated preclusion list (§422.222(a)(1)(ii)(A)), including model notice language and permitted delivery methods.
