raw_output:
[P1] The prohibition in § 52.1189(b)(1)(i) is vague because it does not specify the method of aggregation or averaging for multi-stack units (e.g., “all stacks combined” in P2) — commenters will request clear averaging periods and stack aggregation methodology.

[P2] The 55.00 lbs/hr limit for Boilerhouse 1 (P2) is infeasible given current fuel sulfur content and historic throughput; the facility requests EPA to provide technical justification and throughput basis or to raise the limit.

[P3] The 0.31 lbs/hr limits for each Hot Strip Mill Slab Reheat Furnace 1–5 (P3–P7) are unrealistically low and would effectively require fuel switching to ultra‑low sulfur fuels or installation of SO2 control that these furnaces cannot physically accommodate.

[P4] For Hot Strip Mill Slab Reheat Furnaces (P3–P7), EPA should allow alternative compliance methods (e.g., averaged hourly/rolling average or mass emission limits) rather than a strict instantaneous hourly cap of 0.31 lbs/hr.

[P5] No. 2 Baghouse limit of 3.30 lbs/hr (P8) appears inconsistent with particulate control device performance — the rule should clarify whether this is a stack concentration, stack flow‑adjusted emission rate, or an averaged value.

[P6] Main Plant Boiler No. 8 and No. 9 limits of 0.07 lbs/hr each (P9–P10) are effectively zero and do not account for startup/shutdown emissions; the rule lacks a startup/shutdown/malfunction (SSM) provision or exemptive methodology.

[P7] The A1 Blast Furnace limit of 0.00 lbs/hr (P11) is legally and technically problematic — an absolute zero emission limit is impossible to demonstrate and unenforceable; EPA should change to a practicable numerical floor or specify decommissioning is required.

[P8] The 40.18 lbs/hr limits for B2 and D4 Blast Furnaces (P12–P13) do not indicate if these are based on calendar day averages or hourly instantaneous values; commenters will ask EPA to specify averaging period and basis for the numbers.

[P9] The A/B Blast Furnace Flares and D Furnace Flare limits of 60.19 lbs/hr (P14–P15) fail to identify whether flare purge flows, pilot flames, or periods of venting are included; commenters will request clarity on calculation methods and excluded flows.

[P10] The two‑year delayed applicability for Boilerhouse 2 (P16) is arbitrary and the rule does not explain or justify the staged timeline — industry will request either immediate applicability or explanation of the rationale.

[P11] The conditional Boilerhouse 2 limits (P17–P18) — 750.00 lbs/hr when only unit operating vs. 81.00 lbs/hr when others operate — create operational complexity and potential for gaming by idling/starting other units to relax limits; commenters will request anti‑gaming safeguards and objective criteria for determining “only unit operating.”

[P12] Requiring a combined Boilerhouse 2 stack at least 170 feet above ground (P19) raises safety, engineering, and local zoning concerns and may be infeasible at the existing site; the facility will request reasoned alternatives (e.g., emission controls) or a site‑specific height variance.

[P13] The 90‑day deadline to submit a construction permit application to the State of Michigan for the stack (P20) is unduly tight given design, engineering, and stakeholder coordination needs; commenters will request extension to 180–365 days.

[P14] The obligation to timely and completely obtain any other state or local permits (P21) is vague and could be interpreted to shift state/local permit lapses to federal noncompliance; commenters will ask for clarification that state/local permit processing delays are not absolute violations if a good‑faith application is filed.

[P15] The prohibition that only Boilerhouse 2 emissions may come from the specified tall stack after two years (P22) is inflexible and does not allow for temporary bypass during emergencies or forced maintenance — commenters will request limited, clearly defined exceptions and reporting requirements.

[P16] Requirement to install and continuously operate an SO2 CEMS on Boilerhouse 2 within two years (P23) needs clarification on required quality assurance, span ranges, calibration frequency, and data substitution protocols consistent with 40 CFR part 75 or 60; commenters will ask EPA to align with existing federal CEMS standards.

[P17] Mandating mass balance determinations for all other units per (b)(4) (P24) while requiring a Boilerhouse 2 CEMS creates disparate monitoring requirements and potential inconsistencies; facilities will seek allowance to use CEMS or validated PEMS for other units as equivalent.

[P18] The initial compliance test for Boilerhouse 2 using EPA Test Method 6 within 180 days of CEMS installation (P25) should allow alternative EPA‑approved methods when Method 6 is not appropriate for high flow or variable composition streams; commenters will request flexibility for Method 6A/6C or other validated methods.

[P19] The mass balance calculation requirement (P26–P27) assuming 100% sulfur-to‑SO2 conversion is overly conservative and not physically accurate for many processes; regulated entities will request EPA permit use of process‑specific conversion factors substantiated by testing or engineering analysis.

[P20] The CAP requirement (P28) to be implemented and submitted within 30 days of the FIP effective date is unreasonably short for complex methodology development; commenters will request at least 90 days and an opportunity for iterative review with EPA.

[P21] Requiring submission of a list of idled units within 30 days (P29) and CAPs for idled units before resuming operations (P30) could discourage necessary temporary shutdowns and create administrative burdens; industry will request that resumption be allowed with rapid CAP submission (e.g., 7–14 days) and interim controls.

[P22] The five‑year records retention requirement (P31–P37) should explicitly permit electronic records and allow shorter retention for proprietary operational data; commenters will request permission for electronic storage and confidentiality protections.

[P23] The production records requirement (P32) is overly broad — commenters will request EPA to limit required production data to parameters necessary for SO2 calculation to protect trade secrets and competitively sensitive information.

[P24] The requirement to maintain hourly emissions calculated per the CAP for five years (P33) must permit aggregation and reasonable rounding rules; operators ask EPA to clarify acceptable formats and the handling of missing data.

[P25] The CEMS data retention requirement (P34) should align with existing CEMS recordkeeping rules (e.g., 40 CFR part 75) and allow use of validated backup data substitution procedures; commenters will request explicit alignment.

[P26] QA/QC records requirement (P35) should allow use of manufacturer and third‑party QA reports rather than imposing duplicative test protocols; commenters will request cross‑reference to applicable QA/QC provisions rather than creating new obligations.

[P27] The requirement to retain records of major maintenance activities (P36) for five years needs a definition of “major maintenance”; commenters will request a clear definition or threshold (e.g., activities costing over $X or downtime exceeding Y hours).

[P28] Quarterly report submission to a specified EPA address (P38) should include secure electronic submittal and acknowledgements; commenters will request permission to use EPA’s electronic reporting tools (e.g., CDX/Compliance Tracker) and for confirmation receipts.

[P29] The CAP submission deadline restated in (P39) (30 days) conflicts with the complexity of CAP development (P28); commenters will request harmonization and extension to 90 days.

[P30] Quarterly reporting of CEMS data and hourly mass balance calculations due 30 days after quarter end (P40) imposes heavy data validation burdens; commenters will request phased reporting (e.g., initial submissions followed by certified final reports) and allowance for data corrections.

[P31] Requiring initial compliance test reporting within 60 days (P41) is acceptable, but commenters will seek clarity on EPA review timelines and the effect of tentative/conditional passes pending EPA acceptance.

[P32] The quarterly excess emissions report content requirements (P42) are comprehensive but will be administratively burdensome; commenters request standardized report templates and the ability to submit a single consolidated report for co‑located units.

[P33] Quarterly CEMS performance reports (P43) and CEMS performance test result submission (P44) should be consolidated with other required CEMS reporting obligations (40 CFR parts 60/75) to avoid duplication.

[P34] The requirement to state that no excess emissions occurred if none did (P45) is unnecessary administrative burden; commenters will request that a single quarterly statement suffice and that minor formatting be acceptable.

[P35] The Underfire Combustion Stack EUCoke‑Battery limits (P46–P49) — specifically the mix of 3‑hour average, annual tonnage, and 1‑hour concentration limits — can produce compliance conflicts during normal operational variability; commenters will request harmonized averaging and clear measurement methodology (mass vs. concentration) and reference conditions.

[P36] Requiring CERM operation in conformance with 40 CFR part 60 Appendix F for the EUCoke-Battery (P50–P52) should allow temporary CERM downtime with approved data substitution methods; commenters will ask EPA to adopt Appendix F data substitution protocols.

[P37] Several Cleveland‑Cliffs limits (P54–P61) use “calendar day average” without defining how calendar day is determined relative to shifts — commenters will request a definition (e.g., midnight–midnight or plant shift) and explicit rounding/averaging procedures.

[P38] The combined mass and hourly limits for Cleveland‑Cliffs units (P56–P61) create complex allocation questions across stacks; operators will request explicit stack‑level allocation rules and the option to manage compliance at the facility rather than per‑stack.

[P39] The CERM and CEMS requirements for Cleveland‑Cliffs baghouse/stove stacks (P62–P64) should permit use of validated predictive monitoring (PEMS) where appropriate; commenters will request EPA to allow PS‑16 PEMS alternative (as allowed in P71) and provide acceptance criteria.

[P40] The DIG boilers combined daily and annual limits (P66–P69) lack clarity on whether flare contributions are normalized by heat content; commenters will request definition of included sources and method to apportion emissions between boilers and flares.

[P41] The PEMS alternative protocol reference (P71) should be applicable for all units where CEMS installation is infeasible; commenters will ask EPA to explicitly permit PS‑16 PEMS in lieu of CEMS across affected units, with clear validation and performance criteria.

[P42] The rule does not include clearly defined procedures for handling unavoidable malfunctions and force majeure events (e.g., power outages, natural disasters) — legal commenters will request a narrowly tailored SSM exemption and reporting/verification requirements.

[P43] Several limits are expressed to multiple decimal places (e.g., 0.702 lb/1000 scf in P49, 60.19 lbs/hr in P14/P15) — commenters will request EPA to round limits to a reasonable number of significant figures for operational practicality and permit rounding rules for reporting.

[P44] The enforcement consequences and potential penalties for minor exceedances during validated startup/shutdown or monitoring downtime are not explained; commenters will request that EPA commit to a compliance assistance period and a corrective action‑based enforcement approach for early implementation.

[P45] The rule lacks cost and technology feasibility analysis for each expressed limit (especially the near‑zero values); industry will request publication of the technical support document and an opportunity to comment on EPA’s cost/BSER assumptions.

[P46] Environmental justice advocates will comment that the FIP should include additional community monitoring, public notice, and health impact assessment given the multiple facility changes and potential for localized SO2 exposure.

[P47] Public health stakeholders will assert that some limits (e.g., the Underfire Combustion Stack 1‑hour concentration P49 and 3‑hour average P47) might still allow short‑term peaks harmful to sensitive populations and will request more stringent short‑term caps or fenceline monitoring with public access to data.

[P48] Legal commenters will challenge the A1 zero‑emission requirement (P11) as potentially arbitrary and capricious absent explanation of practicability and legal authority to impose a zero emissions limit on an operating blast furnace.

[P49] State regulators will request coordination language recognizing that state permitting decisions or stack height approvals (P19–P21) are subject to local zoning and state environmental statutes, and that the FIP should not preempt procedural requirements for local approvals.

[P50] Trade associations will request that EPA provide compliance flexibilities such as averaging across identified groups of units, emissions trading within the facility, or use of emission reduction credits to meet these tight per‑unit limits.

[P51] Commenters will request modeled demonstration of ambient impacts showing that proposed stack height (170 ft) plus emissions limits actually achieve the intended ambient SO2 reductions in surrounding communities, before requiring construction.

Main Plant Boiler No. 8 and No. 9 limits of 0.07 lbs/hr each (P9–P10) are effectively zero and do not account for startup/shutdown emissions; the rule lacks a startup/shutdown/malfunction (SSM) provision or exemptive methodology.

The A1 Blast Furnace limit of 0.00 lbs/hr (P11) is legally and technically problematic — an absolute zero emission limit is impossible to demonstrate and unenforceable; EPA should change to a practicable numerical floor or specify decommissioning is required.

The 40.18 lbs/hr limits for B2 and D4 Blast Furnaces (P12–P13) do not indicate if these are based on calendar day averages or hourly instantaneous values; commenters will ask EPA to specify averaging period and basis for the numbers.

The A/B Blast Furnace Flares and D Furnace Flare limits of 60.19 lbs/hr (P14–P15) fail to identify whether flare purge flows, pilot flames, or periods of venting are included; commenters will request clarity on calculation methods and excluded flows.

The two‑year delayed applicability for Boilerhouse 2 (P16) is arbitrary and the rule does not explain or justify the staged timeline — industry will request either immediate applicability or explanation of the rationale.

The conditional Boilerhouse 2 limits (P17–P18) — 750.00 lbs/hr when only unit operating vs. 81.00 lbs/hr when others operate — create operational complexity and potential for gaming by idling/starting other units to relax limits; commenters will request anti‑gaming safeguards and objective criteria for determining “only unit operating.”

Requiring a combined Boilerhouse 2 stack at least 170 feet above ground (P19) raises safety, engineering, and local zoning concerns and may be infeasible at the existing site; the facility will request reasoned alternatives (e.g., emission controls) or a site‑specific height variance.

The 90‑day deadline to submit a construction permit application to the State of Michigan for the stack (P20) is unduly tight given design, engineering, and stakeholder coordination needs; commenters will request extension to 180–365 days.

The obligation to timely and completely obtain any other state or local permits (P21) is vague and could be interpreted to shift state/local permit lapses to federal noncompliance; commenters will ask for clarification that state/local permit processing delays are not absolute violations if a good‑faith application is filed.

The prohibition that only Boilerhouse 2 emissions may come from the specified tall stack after two years (P22) is inflexible and does not allow for temporary bypass during emergencies or forced maintenance — commenters will request limited, clearly defined exceptions and reporting requirements.

Requirement to install and continuously operate an SO2 CEMS on Boilerhouse 2 within two years (P23) needs clarification on required quality assurance, span ranges, calibration frequency, and data substitution protocols consistent with 40 CFR part 75 or 60; commenters will ask EPA to align with existing federal CEMS standards.

Mandating mass balance determinations for all other units per (b)(4) (P24) while requiring a Boilerhouse 2 CEMS creates disparate monitoring requirements and potential inconsistencies; facilities will seek allowance to use CEMS or validated PEMS for other units as equivalent.

The initial compliance test for Boilerhouse 2 using EPA Test Method 6 within 180 days of CEMS installation (P25) should allow alternative EPA‑approved methods when Method 6 is not appropriate for high flow or variable composition streams; commenters will request flexibility for Method 6A/6C or other validated methods.

The mass balance calculation requirement (P26–P27) assuming 100% sulfur-to‑SO2 conversion is overly conservative and not physically accurate for many processes; regulated entities will request EPA permit use of process‑specific conversion factors substantiated by testing or engineering analysis.

The CAP requirement (P28) to be implemented and submitted within 30 days of the FIP effective date is unreasonably short for complex methodology development; commenters will request at least 90 days and an opportunity for iterative review with EPA.

Requiring submission of a list of idled units within 30 days (P29) and CAPs for idled units before resuming operations (P30) could discourage necessary temporary shutdowns and create administrative burdens; industry will request that resumption be allowed with rapid CAP submission (e.g., 7–14 days) and interim controls.

The five‑year records retention requirement (P31–P37) should explicitly permit electronic records and allow shorter retention for proprietary operational data; commenters will request permission for electronic storage and confidentiality protections.

The production records requirement (P32) is overly broad — commenters will request EPA to limit required production data to parameters necessary for SO2 calculation to protect trade secrets and competitively sensitive information.

The requirement to maintain hourly emissions calculated per the CAP for five years (P33) must permit aggregation and reasonable rounding rules; operators ask EPA to clarify acceptable formats and the handling of missing data.

The CEMS data retention requirement (P34) should align with existing CEMS recordkeeping rules (e.g., 40 CFR part 75) and allow use of validated backup data substitution procedures; commenters will request explicit alignment.

QA/QC records requirement (P35) should allow use of manufacturer and third‑party QA reports rather than imposing duplicative test protocols; commenters will request cross‑reference to applicable QA/QC provisions rather than creating new obligations.

The requirement to retain records of major maintenance activities (P36) for five years needs a definition of “major maintenance”; commenters will request a clear definition or threshold (e.g., activities costing over $X or downtime exceeding Y hours).

Quarterly report submission to a specified EPA address (P38) should include secure electronic submittal and acknowledgements; commenters will request permission to use EPA’s electronic reporting tools (e.g., CDX/Compliance Tracker) and for confirmation receipts.
The CAP submission deadline restated in (P39) (30 days) conflicts with the complexity of CAP development (P28); commenters will request harmonization and extension to 90 days.

Quarterly reporting of CEMS data and hourly mass balance calculations due 30 days after quarter end (P40) imposes heavy data validation burdens; commenters will request phased reporting (e.g., initial submissions followed by certified final reports) and allowance for data corrections.

Requiring initial compliance test reporting within 60 days (P41) is acceptable, but commenters will seek clarity on EPA review timelines and the effect of tentative/conditional passes pending EPA acceptance.

The quarterly excess emissions report content requirements (P42) are comprehensive but will be administratively burdensome; commenters request standardized report templates and the ability to submit a single consolidated report for co‑located units.

Quarterly CEMS performance reports (P43) and CEMS performance test result submission (P44) should be consolidated with other required CEMS reporting obligations (40 CFR parts 60/75) to avoid duplication.

The requirement to state that no excess emissions occurred if none did (P45) is unnecessary administrative burden; commenters will request that a single quarterly statement suffice and that minor formatting be acceptable.

The Underfire Combustion Stack EUCoke‑Battery limits (P46–P49) — specifically the mix of 3‑hour average, annual tonnage, and 1‑hour concentration limits — can produce compliance conflicts during normal operational variability; commenters will request harmonized averaging and clear measurement methodology (mass vs. concentration) and reference conditions.

Requiring CERM operation in conformance with 40 CFR part 60 Appendix F for the EUCoke-Battery (P50–P52) should allow temporary CERM downtime with approved data substitution methods; commenters will ask EPA to adopt Appendix F data substitution protocols.

Several Cleveland‑Cliffs limits (P54–P61) use “calendar day average” without defining how calendar day is determined relative to shifts — commenters will request a definition (e.g., midnight–midnight or plant shift) and explicit rounding/averaging procedures.

The combined mass and hourly limits for Cleveland‑Cliffs units (P56–P61) create complex allocation questions across stacks; operators will request explicit stack‑level allocation rules and the option to manage compliance at the facility rather than per‑stack.

The CERM and CEMS requirements for Cleveland‑Cliffs baghouse/stove stacks (P62–P64) should permit use of validated predictive monitoring (PEMS) where appropriate; commenters will request EPA to allow PS‑16 PEMS alternative (as allowed in P71) and provide acceptance criteria.

The DIG boilers combined daily and annual limits (P66–P69) lack clarity on whether flare contributions are normalized by heat content; commenters will request definition of included sources and method to apportion emissions between boilers and flares.

The PEMS alternative protocol reference (P71) should be applicable for all units where CEMS installation is infeasible; commenters will ask EPA to explicitly permit PS‑16 PEMS in lieu of CEMS across affected units, with clear validation and performance criteria.

The rule does not include clearly defined procedures for handling unavoidable malfunctions and force majeure events (e.g., power outages, natural disasters) — legal commenters will request a narrowly tailored SSM exemption and reporting/verification requirements.

Several limits are expressed to multiple decimal places (e.g., 0.702 lb/1000 scf in P49, 60.19 lbs/hr in P14/P15) — commenters will request EPA to round limits to a reasonable number of significant figures for operational practicality and permit rounding rules for reporting.

The enforcement consequences and potential penalties for minor exceedances during validated startup/shutdown or monitoring downtime are not explained; commenters will request that EPA commit to a compliance assistance period and a corrective action‑based enforcement approach for early implementation.

The rule lacks cost and technology feasibility analysis for each expressed limit (especially the near‑zero values); industry will request publication of the technical support document and an opportunity to comment on EPA’s cost/BSER assumptions.

Environmental justice advocates will comment that the FIP should include additional community monitoring, public notice, and health impact assessment given the multiple facility changes and potential for localized SO2 exposure.

Public health stakeholders will assert that some limits (e.g., the Underfire Combustion Stack 1‑hour concentration P49 and 3‑hour average P47) might still allow short‑term peaks harmful to sensitive populations and will request more stringent short‑term caps or fenceline monitoring with public access to data.

Legal commenters will challenge the A1 zero‑emission requirement (P11) as potentially arbitrary and capricious absent explanation of practicability and legal authority to impose a zero emissions limit on an operating blast furnace.

State regulators will request coordination language recognizing that state permitting decisions or stack height approvals (P19–P21) are subject to local zoning and state environmental statutes, and that the FIP should not preempt procedural requirements for local approvals.

Trade associations will request that EPA provide compliance flexibilities such as averaging across identified groups of units, emissions trading within the facility, or use of emission reduction credits to meet these tight per‑unit limits.

Commenters will request modeled demonstration of ambient impacts showing that proposed stack height (170 ft) plus emissions limits actually achieve the intended ambient SO2 reductions in surrounding communities, before requiring construction.

raw_output:
[P1] The November 16, 2017 deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonably short and should be extended to at least 60 days from publication to allow small operators and third-party stakeholders sufficient time to prepare substantive comments.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether the November 16, 2017 deadline is a postmark-by date or received-by date for mailed submissions to avoid inadvertent rejection of late-arriving comments.

[P2] § 39.13(c) appears to limit applicability to Boeing 737–600/–700/–700C/–800/–900/–900ER with original airworthiness certificates issued on or before the AD effective date; commenters request clarification whether airplanes that have had a change in type certificate status or supplemental type certificates (STCs) remain subject.

[P2] The applicability language should explicitly state whether re‑issued or re‑validated original airworthiness certificates (e.g., after export/import actions) change the compliance-clock triggers for affected 737s.

[P3] § 39.13(f) requires compliance "within the specified compliance times unless already accomplished" — commenters request that the AD define how operators can demonstrate prior accomplishment (acceptable records, documentation timeframe).

[P3] Operators request clarification whether accomplishment performed under previous ADs or service bulletins counts as "already accomplished" for § 39.13(f), and what evidence the FAA will accept.

[P4] The 60‑day deadline in § 39.13(g) to revise maintenance/inspection programs is too short for carriers to complete engineering analysis, training, and CASS/maintenance program revision submittals; extend to 180 days.

[P4] Commenters ask the FAA to confirm whether the 60‑day maintenance program revision deadline applies to both Part 121 and Part 135 operators and whether certificated repair stations performing maintenance must also comply within the same timeline.

[P5] § 39.13(g)(1) requires AWL No. 28–AWL–01 within 120 months measured from original certificate issuance or most recent inspection; industry requests clarification whether calendar months or months-in-service are intended, and what constitutes the "most recent inspection" for restarting the clock.

[P5] Airlines request an option to use the date of incorporation of prior equivalent actions (service bulletin compliance) as the baseline for the 120‑month interval for AWL No. 28–AWL–01 when documented evidence exists.

[P6] The 120‑month interval for AWL No. 28–AWL–03 in § 39.13(g)(2) is overly long given the safety issues addressed; consumer safety groups request a shorter interval (e.g., 36 months).

[P6] Electrical maintenance providers request technical detail on the acceptable test equipment/procedures to demonstrate compliance with AWL No. 28–AWL–03, because without such details compliance verification may be inconsistent.

[P7] The 12‑month requirement for AWL No. 28–AWL–19 in § 39.13(g)(3) conflicts with operational scheduling for some operators; commenters request the FAA provide credit for in‑progress modifications or allow phased compliance windows tied to heavy checks.

[P7] Legal commenters note that measuring the 12‑month period from either original certificate issuance, service bulletin accomplishment, or most recent inspection is ambiguous and may create different compliance dates across fleets — propose a single, uniform compliance trigger.

[P8] The exception in § 39.13(g)(3) excluding airplanes that complied with paragraph (s) of AD 2011–18–03 is unclear about the required equivalency of previous compliance — request FAA to specify documentation necessary to prove prior compliance.

[P8] Consumer safety advocates argue that the carve-out in § 39.13(g)(3) might create gaps if earlier AD compliance was limited in scope; they request FAA verification that prior paragraph (s) compliance is substantively equivalent to the new AWL requirement.

[P9] § 39.13(g)(4) sets a 12‑month schedule for AWL No. 28–AWL–20; operators request clarification whether partial compliance steps performed earlier (e.g., pre-modification testing) can be credited toward the 12‑month requirement.

[P9] Maintenance organizations request that the FAA publish the criteria used to determine that 12 months is sufficient for the "Boost Pump GFI" actions given varying MRO capacities worldwide.

[P10] The exception in § 39.13(g)(4) that waives operational testing for R54/R55 for airplanes that complied with AD 2011–20–07(g)(2)(ii) should require explicit cross‑reference and documentation proving the exact test procedures used previously.

[P10] Airlines warn that relying on compliance with AD 2011–20–07(g)(2)(ii) as a blanket exemption risks accepting non‑equivalent tests; they request the FAA publish the minimum test criteria for R54/R55 to confirm equivalency.

[P11] § 39.13(g)(5) requires AWL No. 28–AWL–23 within 12 months for "Power Failed On Protection System"; carriers request detailed procedural guidance and acceptable test pass/fail criteria, currently missing from the AD text.

[P11] Labor unions representing maintenance technicians request additional time or staged compliance for AWL No. 28–AWL–23 due to workforce training needs to correctly perform the new tasks.

[P12] The exception in § 39.13(g)(5) excluding airplanes that complied with paragraph (s) of AD 2011–18–03 again lacks specificity; commenters ask the FAA to list exactly which modifications or records will be accepted as proof.

[P13] The 72‑month interval in § 39.13(g)(6) for AWL No. 28–AWL–24 may be too long for electrical bonding tasks; safety advocates want the FAA to justify the extended interval with risk assessment data.

[P13] MROs request that § 39.13(g)(6) clarify whether the "service bulletin accomplishment" date refers to the operator's service bulletin compliance date or Boeing's service bulletin release date.

[P14] § 39.13(g)(7) establishes different deadlines based on line numbers (L/N 1–1754 vs L/N 1755+); commenters ask how operators with mixed‑line-number fleets should manage fleet scheduling and whether L/N is the only determinant.

[P14] Airlines request that the FAA provide a definitive list or method to determine an airplane's line number in maintenance records if not readily available.

[P15] § 39.13(g)(8) requires AWL No. 47–AWL–04 within 22,500 flight hours; operators request an option to convert flight‑hour thresholds into calendar time for aircraft with low utilization to ensure timely compliance.

[P15] NGS system suppliers request FAA to supply the technical acceptance criteria for "Thermal Switch" integrity checks to avoid inconsistent test interpretations across MROs.

[P16] § 39.13(g)(9) sets a 13,000 flight‑hour interval for AWL No. 47–AWL–06; commenters ask whether hours are tracked per airplane or fleet and whether partial hours already accrued under other ADs can be counted.

[P16] Operators request clarification whether hours measured "after the date of issuance of the original standard airworthiness certificate" can be reset by major structural repairs, major alterations, or re-certification actions.

[P17] The 6,500 flight‑hour interval in § 39.13(g)(10) for AWL No. 47–AWL–07 may be burdensome for small carriers; propose allowing phased compliance aligned with scheduled maintenance events.

[P17] Maintenance unions ask for explicit training and certification requirements for personnel performing NEA ducting integrity inspections under AWL No. 47–AWL–07.

[P18] § 39.13(g)(11) requires AWL No. 28–AWL–101 operational test within 7,500 flight hours or 36 months, whichever occurs first; commenters request a clear rule for operators that have high cycles but low hours (which metric to prioritize).

[P18] Airlines request an allowance to perform AWL No. 28–AWL–101 during scheduled heavy maintenance visits if such visits occur within the required interval, to minimize AOGs.

[P19] § 39.13(h) permits optional changes to AWL No. 28–AWL–05 when accomplishing paragraph (g); Boeing and industry support this flexibility but request that the AD include engineering rationale and equivalency data for the optional changes.

[P20] § 39.13(h)(1) allows adding MIL‑W wire types; wire manufacturers request the FAA include specific part numbers, temperature ratings, and installation limitations to prevent improper substitutions.

[P20] Some commenters raise safety concerns that adding MIL–W–22759 and similar wires as acceptable may change fire propagation or arcing behavior; they request test data demonstrating equivalence to the BMS wire types listed.

[P21] § 39.13(h)(2) permits Roundit 2000NX and Varglas materials as sleeving alternatives; operators request temperature, abrasion, and flammability performance specifications to ensure those materials meet AWL intent.

[P21] Maintenance technicians ask for approved installation instructions for the new sleeving materials (e.g., overlap, bonding, routing) to ensure correct implementation across shops.

[P22] § 39.13(i) prohibits alternative actions, intervals, or CDCCLs after revising the maintenance program unless approved as an AMOC; industry requests an expedited AMOC review process to avoid operational disruptions given the volume of potential requests.

[P22] Legal commenters warn that prohibiting use of previously approved CDCCLs without an AMOC could create regulatory uncertainty for operators who have historically used CDCCLs; recommend grandfathering existing CDCCLs that provide equivalent safety.

[P23] § 39.13(j) states that accomplishing the paragraph (g) revision terminates specified prior AD requirements; commenters request transitional guidance explaining recordkeeping: how to document termination and whether prior AD compliance records must still be retained.

[P23] Some operators worry that terminating prior AD requirements could inadvertently remove redundant safety layers; request FAA to confirm continued applicability of non‑terminated safety tasks.

[P24] With regard to § 39.13(j)(1), clarify how operators demonstrate that the new revision satisfies the former requirements of AD 2008–06–03(h)/(h)(1) — request a crosswalk document showing equivalency.

[P25] For § 39.13(j)(2), terminating all requirements of AD 2008–10–10 R1 may have unforeseen maintenance planning impacts; operators request a detailed mapping of tasks that are rendered unnecessary.

[P26] Concerning § 39.13(j)(3), clarify whether termination of the paragraph (g) requirement from AD 2008–17–15 covers both the maintenance program revision and any associated inspection tasks.

[P27] For § 39.13(j)(4), termination of paragraph (k) of AD 2011–18–03 should be accompanied by guidance on how that affects previously granted AMOCs or approvals issued under that AD.

[P28] Regarding § 39.13(j)(5), terminating all requirements of AD 2013–15–17 requires FAA to publish a cross-reference list to prevent confusion during maintenance planning and audits.

[P29] § 39.13(k)(1) gives the Seattle ACO Branch Manager AMOC authority; operators outside the Seattle jurisdiction request an option for local ACOs to approve AMOCs to reduce administrative delays.

[P29] Legal experts request clarity on the scope of the Seattle ACO Branch Manager's authority — whether it can be delegated and what timelines apply to AMOC decision-making.

[P30] § 39.13(k)(1) requires AMOC requests be sent to principal inspectors or local FSDOs; operators want the FAA to confirm whether electronic submission via the email in (k)(1) fulfills the "sent to principal inspector" requirement.

[P31] § 39.13(k)(1) email address is provided; commenters request confirmation of security, acknowledgement receipts, and maximum review times for AMOC submissions sent to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov.

[P32] § 39.13(k)(2) obligates notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC; operators ask whether written or electronic notice suffices and whether prior approval documentation must be carried on the aircraft.

[P33] § 39.13(k)(3) allows AMOCs approved by the authorized Boeing ODA for repairs/modifications; third‑party repair stations request that the AD clarify procedures for obtaining ODA approvals and whether Boeing ODA approvals are automatically accepted by the FAA.

[P33] Consumer safety groups request transparency: if Boeing ODA approvals are used as AMOCs, FAA should post all ODA‑approved methods used to comply with this AD to the public docket.

[P34] § 39.13(k)(3) requires that an AMOC meet the airplane's certification basis and explicitly reference this AD; commenters request a template for the necessary content to ensure AMOC requests meet FAA expectations and avoid unnecessary rework.

[P34] Legal commenters note that requiring AMOCs to meet the "certification basis" may be difficult for legacy airplanes with multiple amendments; request FAA to provide guidance on determining the appropriate certification basis for AMOC approval.

[P1] Requiring strictly electronic submissions may disadvantage states with limited IT resources; ask EPA to provide funding, technical assistance, and transition timelines to avoid imposing unfunded mandates.

[P1] The rule should specify acceptable file formats, size limits, and metadata standards for electronic submissions under §60.23a(a)(1) to avoid inconsistent or unreadable filings.

[P2] EPA should clarify whether use of an "analogous electronic reporting tool" requires formal EPA certification and publish the certification criteria and timeline for states to switch.

[P2] Small or resource-constrained states and territories may lack the capacity to onboard to SPeCS within proposed deadlines; request phased implementation, optional pilot testing, and training.

[P3] The prohibition on transmitting CBI through SPeCS will create practical difficulties because many state plan materials necessarily include sensitive business information; EPA must provide a secure alternative submission route for CBI and define what constitutes CBI in this context.

[P3] The rule lacks a procedure for redacting CBI in documents uploaded to SPeCS or for marking CBI-submitted materials; request clear guidance on CBI handling, confidentiality claims, and appeals.

[P3] Prohibiting CBI transmission via SPeCS without providing an integrated secure option could force states to submit incomplete plans or delay submissions; suggest EPA implement an encrypted CBI module within SPeCS.

[P4] The 15-month deadline for state plan submissions after final EG publication is too short for states that need new rulemakings, public comment periods, or legislative changes; recommend extending to 24 months or allowing extensions for documented cause.

[P4] The proposed 15-month submission period does not account for EPA’s potential delays in publishing the final EG or for overlapping regulatory actions; request clarification on when the clock starts and options for tolling.

[P4] States with existing SIP/plan backlog or limited staff will be unfairly penalized by a 15-month deadline; recommend phased deadlines based on state size or available resources.

[P5] Reducing EPA's completeness determination timeframe from six months to 60 days may be unrealistic given complex submissions and could lead to cursory reviews; ask for a minimum extension mechanism for complex plans.

[P5] The proposed 60-day completeness determination lacks transparent criteria and process for supplemental information requests; request EPA publish objective completeness checklists and timelines for state responses.

[P5] Shortened completeness review could increase dispute risk over "complete" determinations; suggest an independent appeal or mediation process for contested completeness findings.

[P6] Requiring EPA to take final action on a complete state plan within 12 months may compress necessary interagency coordination and public involvement; request flexibility for EPA to extend deadlines with notice and justification.

[P6] The 12-month final action timeframe should be tied to resource commitments within EPA to avoid rushed or inadequate review; request EPA commit to staffing and priority scheduling.

[P6] The rule must clarify consequences if EPA fails to take final action within 12 months (e.g., automatic approval, deemed disapproval); request explicit default outcomes to avoid legal uncertainty.

[P7] The 12-month deadline for promulgating a Federal plan after state failure or disapproval is too aggressive given rulemaking procedural requirements under the APA; recommend extending to 18–24 months or providing an interim Federal plan option.

[P7] EPA must define "failed to submit a complete plan" precisely and describe notice procedures before invoking a Federal plan; otherwise states may be unfairly preempted.

[P7] The proposed timing should permit coordination with affected states and stakeholders; require EPA to publish draft Federal plans for comment prior to final promulgation.

[P8] Requiring increments of progress when final compliance occurs later than 16 months after the plan submission deadline is appropriate, but the rule does not define the minimum frequency or enforceability of such increments; request specific timelines and enforceable milestone requirements.

[P8] States should be allowed to justify alternative progress schedules where physical or permitting constraints exist; propose criteria for waiver or modification of increments of progress.

[P8] The regulation should require penalties or corrective measures for missed increments of progress to ensure they are meaningful rather than advisory.

[P9] For states invoking RULOF, stakeholder engagement should include notice to affected communities and an opportunity for formal comment; require publication of engagement summaries in plan submissions.

[P10] Requiring supporting materials showing state legal authority for each plan component is reasonable but may expose confidential deliberative legal opinions; request EPA clarify whether legal work product can be submitted under protective procedures.

[P10] The rule should specify acceptable forms of legal demonstration (statutes, regulations, attorney general letters) and the level of detail required to avoid inconsistent denials.

[P10] Given that legal authority can be contested in court, EPA should provide guidance on sufficiency standards to prevent arbitrary disapprovals based on differing legal interpretations.

[P11] Allowing standards to be established via state permits or administrative orders is flexible, but EPA must require templates or minimum permit conditions so standards are enforceable and uniformly applied.

[P11] If states use permits or administrative orders to satisfy plan requirements, the rule should require that such permits include direct EPA oversight or review to ensure consistency with EGs.

[P11] The provision could allow backdoor weakening of substantive standards via individual permits; recommend prohibiting lower-case-by-case standards and requiring statewide or category-wide conditions where practicable.

[P12] The obligation that states demonstrate legal authority to set standards through permits/orders is necessary; however, EPA should provide a clear checklist of the legal showings required (statutory citations, enabling legislation, enforcement mechanisms).

[P12] The rule should permit EPA to accept model permit language or statewide administrative orders as presumptively sufficient evidence of authority to streamline completeness reviews.

[P1] The April 8, 2021 deadline for submitting comments is unreasonably short and should be extended to at least 60 days from publication to allow operators, parts suppliers, labor unions, and international stakeholders time to prepare meaningful technical comments.

[P1] The rule does not state the date of publication in the Federal Register; therefore the April 8, 2021 deadline is ambiguous for foreign operators — the FAA should clarify the comment period start and end dates in calendar form.

[P1] The AD should allow electronic acknowledgement of receipt if comments are submitted near the deadline; currently small operators risk having submissions rejected due to mail or processing delays.

[P2] The applicability list appears to contain a typographical duplication ("CF6–80C2A5, CF6–80C2A5"); the FAA should correct and confirm the intended engine model list to avoid confusion about covered engines.

[P2] The AD as written does not include CF6–80C2B variants widely used on certain U.S.-registered aircraft; the FAA must explain the basis for excluding CF6–80C2B models or expand applicability if they share the same HPT thermal shield/disk design.

[P2] The AD should explicitly state whether engines in storage, on ground test stands, and on exported aircraft remain subject to the AD to avoid enforcement uncertainty across operators and MRO facilities.

[P3] The phrase "within the compliance times specified" is vague because the AD summary does not list specific inspection intervals or time-in-service thresholds; commenters request complete compliance time tables in the regulatory text.

[P3] The AD must provide transition relief for engines currently in the middle of scheduled shop visits so that operators can plan maintenance cycles without forced out-of-service events that disrupt airline schedules.

[P4] Requiring a fluorescent penetrant inspection (FPI) at every piece-part exposure of stage 1 disk, stage 2 disk, or thermal shield will substantially increase shop labor and turnaround times; the FAA should provide an economic analysis of added labor hours and downtime per engine.

[P4] The AD should allow use of equivalent NDT methods (e.g., eddy current, ultrasonic) where demonstrated to be equally effective for the HPT thermal shield geometry; limiting to visual + FPI may be unnecessarily prescriptive.

[P4] The AD does not define "piece-part exposure" (e.g., whether partial disassembly for borescope access qualifies); the FAA should define the term to prevent inconsistent application among MROs.

[P5] The requirement to remove stage 1 and stage 2 disks from service if a crack extends through the forward or aft flange of the thermal shield appears overly broad — removal of expensive rotor disks may not be necessary if the crack is confined to the shield and root cause can be addressed; the FAA should provide repair or restoration criteria and allowable service limits.

[P5] The AD does not permit return-to-service after a documented repair of the thermal shield and rotor disks; commenters request technical guidance on acceptable repairs, life-limits, and required tests to return components to service.

[P6] The absolute prohibition on reinstalling HPT rotor stage 1 or stage 2 disks removed under paragraph (g)(2) fails to account for validated rework/overhaul processes; accredited repair stations should be allowed to refurbish and return disks to service if repairs meet FAA-approved standards.

[P6] Because removed disks are expensive and may be serviceable after proper corrective action, the FAA should allow disposition under an approved AMOC rather than an outright prohibition.

[P7] The delegation of AMOC approval authority solely to the Manager, ECO Branch may create bottlenecks; the FAA should permit delegation to additional qualified officials or regional ECO representatives to expedite determinations for urgent safety-of-flight situations.

[P7] The AD should publish objective criteria for what constitutes an acceptable AMOC for this issue so that applicants know the technical justification and testing data required.

[P8] Requiring AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO first may delay responses; industry requests that the AD allow direct submission to the ECO Branch with a courtesy copy to the principal inspector to streamline the process.

[P8] The AD should clarify whether foreign repair stations and non-U.S. principal inspectors may submit AMOC requests through their civil aviation authority or must use the U.S. FSDO/principal inspector pathway.

[P9] The Related Information section does not currently identify a named person or contact details; the AD should be amended to include the specific ECO Branch manager name and mailing address to ensure timely receipt and to comply with the requirement in paragraph (j)(1).

[P10] Permitting AMOC requests via email to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov is helpful but insufficient; the FAA should explicitly confirm acceptable file formats, encryption for proprietary data, and an automated receipt confirmation to reduce lost submissions.

[P10] The AD should allow for secure portal submission of AMOC technical data (e.g., large FEA models, test reports) rather than relying solely on email which may be limited by attachment size and pose confidentiality concerns.

[P11] The requirement to notify the principal inspector or, if none, the local FSDO/CHDO manager before using an approved AMOC is vague about timing — the AD should specify whether notification is required prior to first use, within 24 hours, or another defined window.

[P11] For international operations without a U.S. principal inspector, the AD should define "manager of the local flight standards district office" responsibilities and provide contact procedures to ensure operators overseas can comply with the notification requirement.

[P11] The AD should permit batch notifications for operators applying an AMOC across a pool of engines, rather than requiring individual notifications for each engine installation, to avoid administrative burden.

[P4] The AD fails to provide illustrative acceptance criteria for FPI indications (e.g., maximum crack length, depth, or location thresholds) resulting in inconsistent disposition decisions among repair stations.

[P5] The AD does not require root-cause analysis reporting to the FAA when a thermal shield crack is found; operators recommend mandatory incident reporting to allow the FAA to assess fleetwide trends and consider further action.

[P2] The applicability table should cross-reference affected service bulletins and part numbers for thermal shields and rotor disks to help MROs quickly identify impacted hardware.

[P6] The AD's prohibition could conflict with existing lease agreements and return-to-service obligations between lessors and lessees; the FAA should consider transition rules addressing leased aircraft engines.

[P3] There is no grandfathering provision for engines that have recently passed a shop visit but would next be inspected after the compliance times; the FAA should clarify applicability to in-process maintenance to avoid double inspections.

[P7] The AD should clarify whether emergency AMOCs for safety-of-flight are permitted and the expected FAA turnaround time for such requests to prevent operational disruptions.

[P4] The requirement to perform inspections "after the effective date" at every piece-part exposure could be interpreted to require re-inspection of components that have already been inspected to a higher standard; the FAA should allow credit for prior documented inspections meeting equivalent standards.

[P2] The AD should explicitly state whether spare HPT thermal shields and rotor disks in overhaul stock are subject to the inspection requirements prior to installation, to avoid accidental installation of noncompliant parts.

[P1] For transparency, the FAA should extend the comment period and reopen it if substantive changes (e.g., corrected applicability list or added compliance times) are made after April 8, 2021.

[P10] The FAA must commit to acknowledging receipt of emailed AMOC requests and provide a tracking number; without this, companies cannot reliably track pending approvals and plan maintenance.

[P3] Small operators will request flexibility in compliance schedules (e.g., phased compliance based on next scheduled inspection) arguing that immediate compliance within short hours could ground fleets unexpectedly.

[P4] Operators and maintenance providers will challenge the 25 engine operating hour removal requirement in P4 as unduly burdensome and request extension to at least 50–100 hours to allow scheduled maintenance planning.

[P4] Aircraft owners will assert that 25 engine operating hours is insufficient time to obtain replacement parts and coordinate maintenance, and request an allowance for non-service-hour compliance measured in calendar days (e.g., 30 days).

[P4] Repair stations will request an exception or prioritized parts distribution mechanism for aircraft engaged in commercial operations to avoid disproportionate economic harm from the 25-hour removal mandate.

[P4] Some commenters will request a risk-based exemption for engines that have additional inspection data showing no immediate hazard, rather than mandatory removal within 25 hours.

[P5] Operators will request clarification of the process and timeline for applying for the one-time special flight permit described in P5, including expected FAA review time and required documentation.

[P5] Emergency-service operators (e.g., medevac, law enforcement) will request that the FAA allow multiple flight permits or special consideration beyond a one-time ferry flight in cases where safe repair facilities are not locally available.

[P5] Legal commenters will ask whether the one-time special flight permit can be issued after the 25-hour removal deadline if used only to ferry to maintenance, to avoid conflict between P4 and P5.

[P6] Air ambulance and charter operators will object to P6's blanket prohibition on carrying passengers during the ferry flight, requesting carve-outs for essential personnel (e.g., a single required mechanic or crew) under strict conditions.

[P6] Pilot associations will request clarification on whether the prohibition on passengers includes non-revenue positioning of company personnel or deadhead pilots who may be necessary for subsequent operations.

[P6] Safety advocates will support P6, arguing that no-passenger restriction is necessary given the known crankshaft risk, and request strict enforcement guidance.

[P7] Operators will request that P7 be modified to allow instrument flight rules (IFR) ferry flights under constrained circumstances (e.g., when weather or airspace constraints make VFR impractical), with additional safety mitigations.

[P7] Weather service organizations will ask FAA to define VFR minima required for the special flight permit (visibility, cloud ceilings) rather than relying on ambiguous "VFR day" language.

[P8] Pilots and operators will request objective thresholds for "areas of known turbulence" in P8 — for example, avoidance of forecast moderate-or-greater turbulence, or designated SIGMET areas — so pilots know what to avoid.

[P8] Some commenters will point out that turbulence can be encountered unexpectedly and request FAA guidance on acceptable deviation procedures if moderate turbulence is encountered during the ferry flight.

[P8] Legal counsel will request that the FAA clarify enforcement standards for P8 and whether failure to avoid an unforeseen turbulence encounter would be grounds for enforcement action.

[P9] Industry commenters will request that AMOC approvals be allowed from other FAA offices (not only Fort Worth) for operators based outside the region to avoid delays.

[P9] Legal experts will request that the FAA provide an appeal or review process if an AMOC request is denied by the Fort Worth ACO Branch Manager.

[P1] The proposal to remove AD 2022–05–04 from § 39.13 (Provision P1) is unclear whether any residual compliance obligations or grandfathered approvals from AD 2022–05–04 will remain applicable; request explicit statement that removal does not reintroduce risk or leave gaps.

[P1] Removing AD 2022–05–04 without a clear cross-reference to the new AD (P2) may cause confusion for operators and maintenance providers who use consolidated regulatory lists; request that the FAA include a note in § 39.13 linking the removed AD entry to the new AD entry.

[P2] Adding a new AD to § 39.13 (Provision P2) without publishing the full text of the AD in the NPRM text excerpt may prevent meaningful review; request that the FAA publish the full AD text and figures in the docket for comment.

[P3] The comment deadline of May 23, 2023 (Provision P3) is inadequate for operators and industry groups to perform operational and legal reviews of the proposed AFM revisions and potential AMOCs; request a 60-day extension of the comment period.

[P4] Provision P4’s applicability excludes 737–200 and –200C with SP–77 but otherwise includes a wide range of 737 series aircraft; request the FAA to provide a clear rationale and technical basis for excluding only those specific SP–77-configured aircraft.

[P4] The applicability language in P4 appears truncated and ambiguous (cut-off sentence); request the FAA correct and provide complete applicability text to avoid misinterpretation about which serials/configurations are included.

[P5] The general compliance requirement to comply within specified times (P5) needs to be accompanied by explicit tolerances and effective dates for each affected operator type (air carriers, part 91 owners, lessors); request clarification of applicability by operating certificate type.

[P6] Requiring AFM Limitations revisions within 2 days after Feb 24, 2022 (P6) is unreasonable and retroactive given this proposed AD is being added now; operators cannot retroactively comply and need confirmation that meeting the later June 30, 2023 deadlines (P11, P16, P21) will suffice to replace the 2-day obligation.

[P6] The 2-day deadline in P6 duplicates the earlier AD and could be redundant if the new AD requires later compliance; request the FAA explicitly rescind or reconcile the 2-day requirement to avoid conflicting compliance obligations.

[P7] Permitting insertion of Figure 3 into the AFM (P7) should specify acceptable insertion methods (loose-leaf, electronic AFM update procedures) and require version control language; request clear instructions acceptable to operators with electronic AFMs.

[P8] The requirement to revise AFM Operating Procedures within 2 days (P8) is operationally impracticable for widely distributed fleets and could create inconsistent AFM versions across operators; request extension or allowance for fleet-wide software/electronic AFM update processes.

[P9] The permission in P9 to insert Figure 4 or 5 lacks specification of which operators get Figure 4 vs Figure 5; request FAA publish clear eligibility criteria and examples for selecting the applicable figure.

[P10] The separate obligations for “non-radio altimeter tolerant airplanes” (P10) and “radio altimeter tolerant airplanes” (P15) will create confusion unless the AD defines “radio altimeter tolerant” with objective, verifiable criteria; request the FAA include a precise definition and acceptable verification methods.

[P11] The June 30, 2023 deadline for revising AFM Limitations for non-radio altimeter tolerant airplanes (P11) may be infeasible for small operators and private owners to process and distribute AFM revisions by that date; request a phased compliance schedule or an extension for part 91 operators.

[P12] Allowing compliance by inserting Figure 6 into the AFM (P12) should require operators to annotate AFM revision records and maintain a compliance log; request the FAA require documentation standards and retention periods.

[P13] The statement that incorporating Figure 6 terminates the earlier AFM revision required by P6 (P13) should explicitly state whether any operational limitations triggered under the earlier revision can be lifted immediately or only after the required removal (P14); request clarification to avoid inadvertent noncompliance.

[P14] The requirement to remove the AFM revision required by P6 before further flight after incorporating Figure 6 (P14) is operationally risky if an operator lacks immediate access to the physical AFM to remove the previous page; request allowance for electronic means to mark the prior revision as superseded and a short grace period.

[P15] Provision P15’s bifurcation (radio altimeter tolerant airplanes) does not identify how an operator demonstrably proves radio altimeter tolerance to inspector satisfaction; request a list of acceptable evidence (manufacturer data, STC, lab test results).

[P16] The June 30, 2023 deadline for Figure 7 incorporation (P16) for radio altimeter tolerant airplanes may conflict with international operational approvals (EASA, CAAC); request harmonization timeline statements or acceptance of foreign approvals.

[P17] Allowing insertion of Figure 7 (P17) should include a requirement to include the date and AD number on the inserted page and to notify the operator’s principal inspector; request that FAA add labeling and notification requirements to the permission.

[P18] The cancellation of the prior AFM revision upon incorporation of Figure 7 (P18) should state whether aircrew training/briefing requirements associated with the earlier AFM revision are also terminated immediately; request explicit instruction about training records.

[P19] Requiring removal of prior AFM revision before further flight (P19) could cause grounding if the physical AFM is not onboard (e.g., distributed across fleet); request permission to use an approved temporary flight authorization with electronic AFM until physical removal is completed.

[P20] The obligation for all operators to perform the actions in P20 lacks clarity whether maintenance organizations, lessors, or operators are responsible for making AFM insertions and removals; request assignment of responsibility and notification obligations.

[P21] The June 30, 2023 requirement to revise Operating Procedures using Figure 8/9 (P21) should be accompanied by sample crewmember guidance and training checklists; request FAA provide standardized text and training advisory material to ensure consistent procedures.

[P22] The permission to insert Figures 8 or 9 (P22) must specify format and legibility requirements for electronic AFMs and EFBs to avoid enforcement issues; request that FAA permit high-resolution PDF inserts for EFBs and define acceptable print size/resolution.

[P23] The termination of the earlier Operating Procedures revision (P23) when Figures 8/9 are incorporated needs to clarify whether flight crew briefings or SOP compliance demonstrations tied to the earlier text are also obsolete; request guidance on decommissioning the prior revision.

[P24] Requiring removal of prior AFM Operating Procedures before further flight (P24) raises the same practical concern as other removal provisions; request that FAA allow removal to be accomplished in electronic AFM systems and provide a 72-hour window for physical documentation updates.

[P25] Authorizing the Manager to approve AMOCs (P25) is standard, but stakeholders request the FAA publish a predictable AMOC approval timeline (e.g., 30/60/90 days) and a public docket of AMOCs already approved to avoid duplicate requests.

[P26] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or responsible Flight Standards Office (P26) may delay national consistency; request a parallel centralized FAA AMOC submission and tracking portal in addition to local routing.

[P27] If AMOC information is sent directly to the manager (P27), the AD should identify the contact person by name or title in paragraph (m) and provide a mailing address; request insertion of complete contact information in the AD.

[P28] Permitting emailing AMOC information to AMOC@faa.gov (P28) is helpful but the AD should also state security requirements, encrypted transmission expectations, and confirmation-of-receipt procedures; request explicit email handling procedures and expected response timelines.

[P29] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC (P29) could create delays in emergency or time-critical operational adoption; request allowance for immediate use with retroactive notification in emergencies and specify acceptable notification methods.

[P30] Allowing AMOCs previously approved for AD 2021–23–12 to satisfy paragraph (h) requirements until June 30, 2023 (P30) should make clear whether those AMOCs are automatically extended or require re-application; request that FAA confirm automatic authorization and list which AMOCs are covered.

[General] The AD frequently references figures (Figures 3–9) but the NPRM text does not include the content of those figures; request that FAA publish all figures and any underlying analysis in the docket so commenters can assess operational impacts.

[Legal] Several provisions impose effective retroactive obligations (e.g., P6 and P8 effective Feb 24, 2022) that may conflict with the Administrative Procedure Act’s notice-and-comment requirements; request legal analysis and justification for retroactivity or revision of effective dates to prospective only.

[Small business] Small operators and part 135 on-demand carriers will incur material administrative burdens complying with AFM changes by the stated deadlines; request a regulatory flexibility analysis and consideration of cost-minimizing alternatives.

[International] Foreign operators of U.S.-certificated 737s need confirmation of acceptance by non-U.S. authorities if they comply with AMOCs or AFM changes; request FAA coordinate with EASA and other major authorities and state acceptance language.

[Safety] If the AFM revisions change minima or approach procedures based on radio altimeter capability (P11–P19), the FAA should provide safety justification data showing reduced risk and metrics used to derive the specific procedural changes; request underlying safety assessment and risk analysis.

[Compliance records] The AD should require operators to document AFM revisions, AMOC approvals, and communications with inspectors in maintenance records and make them available for DOT audits; request explicit recordkeeping requirements and retention periods.

[Enforcement] Because the AD permits insertion of figures into AFMs (P7, P9, P12, P17, P22) but also requires removal of prior revisions (P14, P19, P24), FAA should state enforcement tolerances for inadvertent paperwork errors during the transition period; request a 90-day administrative tolerance for documentation discrepancies.

[Clarity] The AD text includes truncated sentences and cross-references that could lead to misinterpretation (e.g., cut-off applicability text in P4); request editorial corrections and republication of the corrected AD for comment.

Requiring removal of prior AFM Operating Procedures before further flight (P24) raises the same practical concern as other removal provisions; request that FAA allow removal to be accomplished in electronic AFM systems and provide a 72-hour window for physical documentation updates.

Authorizing the Manager to approve AMOCs (P25) is standard, but stakeholders request the FAA publish a predictable AMOC approval timeline (e.g., 30/60/90 days) and a public docket of AMOCs already approved to avoid duplicate requests.

Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or responsible Flight Standards Office (P26) may delay national consistency; request a parallel centralized FAA AMOC submission and tracking portal in addition to local routing.

If AMOC information is sent directly to the manager (P27), the AD should identify the contact person by name or title in paragraph (m) and provide a mailing address; request insertion of complete contact information in the AD.

Permitting emailing AMOC information to AMOC@faa.gov (P28) is helpful but the AD should also state security requirements, encrypted transmission expectations, and confirmation-of-receipt procedures; request explicit email handling procedures and expected response timelines.

The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC (P29) could create delays in emergency or time-critical operational adoption; request allowance for immediate use with retroactive notification in emergencies and specify acceptable notification methods.

Allowing AMOCs previously approved for AD 2021–23–12 to satisfy paragraph (h) requirements until June 30, 2023 (P30) should make clear whether those AMOCs are automatically extended or require re-application; request that FAA confirm automatic authorization and list which AMOCs are covered.

[General] The AD frequently references figures (Figures 3–9) but the NPRM text does not include the content of those figures; request that FAA publish all figures and any underlying analysis in the docket so commenters can assess operational impacts.

[Legal] Several provisions impose effective retroactive obligations (e.g., P6 and P8 effective Feb 24, 2022) that may conflict with the Administrative Procedure Act’s notice-and-comment requirements; request legal analysis and justification for retroactivity or revision of effective dates to prospective only.

[Small business] Small operators and part 135 on-demand carriers will incur material administrative burdens complying with AFM changes by the stated deadlines; request a regulatory flexibility analysis and consideration of cost-minimizing alternatives.

[International] Foreign operators of U.S.-certificated 737s need confirmation of acceptance by non-U.S. authorities if they comply with AMOCs or AFM changes; request FAA coordinate with EASA and other major authorities and state acceptance language.

[Safety] If the AFM revisions change minima or approach procedures based on radio altimeter capability (P11–P19), the FAA should provide safety justification data showing reduced risk and metrics used to derive the specific procedural changes; request underlying safety assessment and risk analysis.

[Compliance records] The AD should require operators to document AFM revisions, AMOC approvals, and communications with inspectors in maintenance records and make them available for DOT audits; request explicit recordkeeping requirements and retention periods.

[Enforcement] Because the AD permits insertion of figures into AFMs (P7, P9, P12, P17, P22) but also requires removal of prior revisions (P14, P19, P24), FAA should state enforcement tolerances for inadvertent paperwork errors during the transition period; request a 90-day administrative tolerance for documentation discrepancies.

[Clarity] The AD text includes truncated sentences and cross-references that could lead to misinterpretation (e.g., cut-off applicability text in P4); request editorial corrections and republication of the corrected AD for comment.
