raw_output:
[P1] States may object that the specified date range (Sept 1, 2023–Mar 10, 2024) is too restrictive for local ecological conditions and request flexibility to extend or shift dates regionally within the flyway for conservation or hunter access reasons.

[P1] Conservation NGOs will request a justification for why the 2023–2024 single-year date range is being fixed in the framework rather than adopting a recurring annual framework with adaptive date-setting.

[P2] Hunting organizations will urge clarification that “maximum number of hunting days” permits multiple nonconsecutive segments as long as the total does not exceed the maximum, to avoid regulatory uncertainty about segmenting.

[P3] States and legal experts will ask for explicit treatment of inadvertent administrative errors (e.g., clerical miscounts) to prevent automatic violation findings if the aggregate days slightly exceed the season length due to record-keeping mistakes.

[P3] Industry groups (outfitters, retailers) will request language clarifying whether days closed for weather/emergency count against the total allowed season length if a State cancels days after publishing.

[P4] Several States will ask for criteria defining when “unless otherwise specified” applies, demanding transparency about what circumstances would negate zone-based selection.

[P5] Flyway Councils will request clarity and timelines on the phrase “in years the Service allows” for zone-based duck seasons — specifically, the notification deadline and criteria used by the Service to allow zone use.

[P6] States will comment that the obligation to “describe, delineate, and designate areas” lacks minimum mapping standards and ask for a required GIS format, datum, and submission deadline to the Service to ensure consistency.

[P6] Hunting access advocates will request that delineation requirements include public notice procedures and outreach to ensure hunters are aware of designated areas before seasons open.

[P7] Several States and legal commenters will challenge the requirement to publish areas in the Federal Register as a frameworks final rule (except early teal), arguing it creates an unnecessary administrative burden and delay and requesting an alternative streamlined notice process (e.g., Federal Register notice of availability or posting on the Service website).

[P8] Recreational hunters will request clarification whether “one-half hour before sunrise to sunset” applies when daylight-saving time adjustments are in effect and ask that times be provided in local time zones in State regulations.

[P8] Safety advocates will request retention of the default shooting hours be qualified to allow States to shorten hours for safety or conservation reasons without a separate approval process.

[P9] Hunters and retailers will request an explicit mechanism for States to set different possession limits (e.g., two times daily limit) and ask whether those deviations must be published and approved by the Service.

[P10] Waterfowl conservation groups will support permit authorization but request explicit guidance on species for which permits will be used and the scientific standards for when permits are required.

[P11] Tribes and States will ask for transparency on the Service’s method for “determining the amount of harvest” (models, inputs, population thresholds) and request publication of the harvest allocation methodology.

[P12] States will object that requiring State-issued permits to be “set at levels expected to produce the Service-authorized take” shifts scientific and administrative burden to States without funding and request federal support or clear delegation of modeling responsibilities.

[P13] States will request a timeline and emergency procedures if the Service fails to approve the authorized take before hunting seasons begin, to avoid invalidating State permits and creating legal exposure for hunters.

[P14] Individuals will ask for clarification on name/address changes after issuance (e.g., how to correct minor errors) and whether digital permits can be updated without reissuing.

[P15] Hunters will request an accepted list of proof (physical copy, digital permit on phone, license printout) and guidance for officers on electronic presentation and offline verification.

[P16] Some commenters will support the nontransferability prohibition but request clear penalties for improper transfer and guidance on family situations (e.g., lending permit during multi-day hunt) to avoid criminalization of minor transgressions.

[P17] Permit administrators will request a clear definition of “altered or defaced” (e.g., wet smudges, phone case scratches on digital permits) and procedures for issuing replacement permits without penalty.

[P18] Civil liberties and hunting groups in Atlantic Flyway States will request a preemption analysis clarifying the interplay between State Sunday-hunting bans and federal authority, asking whether the Federal rule effectively codifies State prohibitions and how conflicts will be resolved.

[P19] Youth organizations will support two youth days but ask whether the 2-day allocation is per zone per year or per zone per hunter cohort, and request guidance when zones straddle State boundaries.

[P20] States will request guidance on permitting concurrent scheduling of youth and veterans days (e.g., whether the same day can simultaneously count toward both allocations) and any reporting differences required.

[P21] Advocates for rural youth hunting access will request specific definitions of “holidays” and “other non-school days,” and request flexibility for areas with year-round schooling or nontraditional schedules to maximize participation.

[P22] States will request clarification whether the “up to 14 days before or after” window is counted within the outer date ranges for regular duck seasons or is in addition to them.

[P23] Several commenters will seek species-level clarification on whether mergansers, coots, gallinules, and swans are treated as part of duck/day limits in special days, and ask for cross-references to the duck-limit provisions.

[P24] States that implement hybrid scaup seasons will request a clear definition of “hybrid scaup season” and the specific scaup daily limit logic so State regulations are consistent and enforceable.

[P25] Flyway councils will request that the rule specify which existing flyway species and area restrictions continue to apply and require cross-references or an appendix listing applicable restrictions.

[P26] States will request limits on how broadly they may alter their youth age definition and ask for examples of acceptable State definitions consistent with safety and conservation goals.

[P27] Some youth-hunting advocates will request raising the youth age limit to under 21 in certain jurisdictions or allowing States flexibility for older youth programs; conversely, some safety advocates will request lowering the maximum age.

[P28] Public-safety commenters will request more specificity about the supervising adult’s role, minimum distance from youth while hunting, and training or licensing requirements for the adult supervisor.

[P29] Hunting rights groups will challenge prohibiting the adult from duck hunting while supervising, arguing it unduly burdens family hunts and request an exception for multi-adult groups or split responsibilities.

[P30] States will request clarification about what “participate in other concurrently open seasons” means practically (e.g., can the adult hunt geese or doves while accompanying a youth duck hunter on the same outing) and whether equipment sharing is allowed.

[P31] Waterfowl managers will request the process for verifying swan permits on-site during youth and veterans days and whether swan harvesting by special-day participants is subject to additional reporting.

[P32] Veterans’ advocacy groups will request clear proof of veteran or active-duty status required at check-in, and accommodations for veterans who lack documentation.

[P33] Same as P31 but veterans-specific: request cross-jurisdictional recognition of swan permits for veteran participants, especially if they travel between States for special days.

[P34] States not listed in the designated Areas for early teal will request rationale and population data supporting area selection and ask for an appeals or petition process to request inclusion in future years.

[P35] States and hunters will request explanation for limiting outside dates for early teal to Sept 1–30 and whether those dates align with teal migration timing across all designated Areas.

[P36] Hunting organizations will object to the 16-day maximum early teal season in areas that historically had longer seasons and ask for data showing 16 days provide adequate recreation without harming populations.

[P37] Conservation groups will support the six-teal daily limit but ask for clarity on species counted as “teal” (e.g., blue-winged, green-winged, cinnamon) and whether subspecies distinctions (if any) matter.

[P38] States listed with sunrise-to-sunset hours will request a rationale and the authority for the different hours, and ask whether hunters in those States may receive a waiver or petition to revert to the default hours.

[P39] Some States will ask for guidance on how choosing a 5-day teal–wood duck season interacts with existing wood duck bag limits in overall duck limits (i.e., accounting for aggregate duck limits across seasons).

[P40] Conservation scientists will request explanation of the 2-wood-duck cap rationale and modeling that supports that cap to protect wood duck populations when aggregated with other seasons.

[P41] States considering the adjacent 4-day teal-only season will ask whether the 4-day season counts toward the 16-day maximum for early teal seasons (i.e., combined-season accounting).

[P42] Atlantic Flyway States will request clarity on the start date: “Saturday nearest Sept 24 (September 23)” is ambiguous — commenters will ask whether the Saturday nearest Sep 24 in 2023 is Sep 23 or 30 and request a deterministic rule tied to calendar dates.

[P43] Atlantic Flyway States will request explicit species sublimit schedules (e.g., mallard sex split timing) and modeling supporting the 60-day length and 6-duck daily limit to ensure compatibility with population objectives.

[P44] States will request operational guidance for implementing the 40-day/20-day scaup split, including how the segments must be scheduled and how harvest reporting must separate the two segments for compliance and monitoring.

[P45] States that count mergansers under duck limits will request confirmation of enforcement priorities — whether possession-check counting rules differ (e.g., how to count a mixed bag) — and instructions to hunters.

[P46] Waterfowl biologists will request the scientific basis for the coot daily bag limit of 15 and whether the limit remains when coots are taken concurrently with ducks and other species.

[P47] Hunting groups and some conservationists will request justification and alternatives for the harlequin duck closure, including data on population trends and whether limited, permit-based take could be sustainable.

[P48] Listed States seeking to split seasons will request explicit procedures and deadlines for notifying the Service and hunters of segmented seasons and guidance on ticketing/enforcement across segments.

[P49] Connecticut, Maryland, North Carolina, and Virginia will request specification of study methods, reporting timelines, and funding for the required evaluation of zones and split seasons for 2021–25, and ask whether the evaluation window is sufficient.

[P50] Environmental groups will request strict conditions for use of powered craft in Sea Duck Areas (e.g., speed limits, gear restrictions) to avoid disturbance of non-target species and safety hazards.

[P50] Marine safety groups will request collision-avoidance and operator-training requirements for powered craft permitted to be used for shooting/retrieval in Sea Duck Areas.

[P51] States and hunters will request clarity on the 15-geese aggregate bag limit: whether that is per day, per hunter, or per permit, and how Canada and cackling geese are distinguished in reporting.

[P52] Some States will object to allowing shooting 30 minutes after sunset in early goose seasons, citing concerns about visibility, safety, and enforceability, and will request strict local approvals before extending hours.

[P53] Pacific Flyway States and tribal groups will request a clear swan permitting process timeline and criteria for permit issuance to ensure fair and transparent allocation.

[P54] States will request federal funding or technical assistance obligations to administer swan permit programs given the Service’s role in setting quotas and monitoring.

[P55] Animal protection groups will oppose numerical permit caps in ID, MT, NV, and UT as arbitrary and request the biological basis for the listed numbers and mechanisms to adjust them if populations decline or increase.

[P56] Hunters will request clarification whether permits authorizing “no more than one swan” allow retention of whole birds or require submission of parts for species determination (consistent with monitoring obligations).

[P57] Nevada hunters will request explanation and fairness justification for allowing two permits per hunter in Nevada but only one in MT and UT, and request parity or a rationale tied to population data.

[P58] Tribes, States, and hunters will request real-time reporting procedures and enforcement policies once the trumpeter swan harvest quotas (20 UT, 10 NV) are reached, including who bears the responsibility to close seasons and how public notice will be given.

[P59] States will request standardized monitoring protocols and sample forms for measuring bill parts or providing species-determinant parts to ensure consistent data across jurisdictions.

[P60] Hunting organizations will support states being “advised” to maximize compliance but request examples of “appropriate measures” and whether failure to use recommended measures creates enforceability consequences.

[P61] State agencies will object to the 80% hunter compliance threshold as unattainably high in some areas, request graduated sanctions rather than an automatic 10% permit reduction, and ask for an appeals process before penalization.

[P62] Oregon and California will request biological justification for mandating brant season closure no later than December 15 and request consideration of interannual variation in migration timing and abundance.

[P63] Adjacent state agencies will support the recommendation for consistency between matching zones but request whether consistency is mandatory or advisory and pathways for resolving unavoidable mismatches.

[P64] Tribes will support the explicit permission to establish independent tribal regulations but ask for detail on how federal enforcement will recognize Tribal regulations and avoid conflicting enforcement actions.

[P65] Tribes will request clarification on how compliance with “this section’s regulations and applicable Tribal hunting regulations” will be measured in cases of conflict between Tribal and Federal rules.

[P66] Tribes with reserved rights will request a clear definition of the “specified lands” where tribal special regulations apply and a process for notifying the Service and States of Tribal regulations.

[P67] States will request dispute-resolution mechanisms where Tribes apply Tribal regulations to nontribal members on reservation lands in manners that differ from State seasons.

[P68] Tribal legal counsel will request detailed guidance on how the March 11–Aug 31 closed season must be integrated with Tribal regulations and whether Tribes may set shorter closed seasons within that window.

[P69] Tribes will ask for confirmation that setting different on-reservation seasons for nontribal members does not invoke State licensing requirements and request clarity on license reciprocity.

[P70] States will request an explicit list of allowable deviations for nontribal members’ regulations on reservations and whether the Service must preapprove such regulations as within the annual frameworks.

[P71] Nontribal hunters and State enforcement will request clarification on enforcement authority and which Federal regulations apply to nontribal hunters on reservations in practice.

[P72] Tribes will request explicit authority to choose identical seasons for simplicity and administrative ease, and request federal guidance on recordkeeping and reporting when Tribes elect identical or different regimes.

[P73] Tribal governments will ask for clarity on whether establishing Tribal-member-only seasons affects nontribal subsistence or ceremonial access and how intergovernmental coordination will occur.

[P74] States and conservation groups will request limits and review standards on Tribes setting seasons outside Service frameworks for Tribal members only, to ensure conservation objectives are not compromised.

[P75] Legal experts will request clarification as to what “All Federal hunting regulations in this part apply” means in practice — whether exemptions exist for Tribal cultural practices and how conflicts are reconciled.

[P76] Tribes and the Service will need to define the scope and process for “short-term experimental hunts,” including timelines, monitoring requirements, and how § 20.21 will be formally overridden.

[P77] Tribes and public commenters will request a mandatory timeline and public notice for Service publication of formal agreements on experimental methods of take, and mechanisms for public review and comment.

[P78] Tribes will request clarity on the geographic extent of “ceded lands,” the process for determining which off-reservation lands qualify, and procedures for coordination with affected States.

[P79] States and Tribes will request a specific deadline and format for providing Tribal regulations to State offices before the season opens and ask for a dispute-resolution mechanism if States find Tribal regulations inconsistent with conservation needs.

[P2] Health care workforce and patient advocacy groups will argue that the 0.5 percentage point reduction starting in 2025 will exacerbate staffing shortages and reduce access to outpatient services unless CMS phases in the reduction or ties it to demonstrated productivity gains.

[P2] Legal commentators may claim CMS lacks clear statutory authority to impose a uniform 0.5 percentage point reduction without rulemaking that explicitly demonstrates compliance with the Administrative Procedure Act’s requirement for reasoned explanation; CMS must provide a more detailed legal justification.

[P3] The exception excluding hospitals with a CCN effective January 2, 2018 or later from the 0.5 percentage point reduction (§ 419.32(b)(1)(iv)(B)(12)) appears arbitrary and raises equal-protection concerns—CMS should explain the policy rationale for a CCN-based cutoff date and consider less arbitrary, need-based criteria.

[P3] Smaller or newly certified hospitals not meeting the CCN cutoff will claim the exclusion creates an unfair competitive distortion and encourages artificial changes in CCN dates; CMS should instead use objective measures (e.g., rurality, Medicaid share) to determine exceptions.

[P3] Commenters representing manufacturers or suppliers will note the explicit exclusion of separately payable drugs from the 0.5 percentage point reduction may cause cost-shifting to drug billing or influence coding practices; CMS should clarify coding and billing expectations to prevent gaming.

[P4] The provision that the 0.5 percentage point reduction and its exception remain effective until estimated payment reductions total $7.8 billion (§ 419.32(b)(1)(iv)(B)(12)) lacks transparency—CMS must disclose the methodology for estimating cumulative payment reductions and publish periodic tallies so stakeholders can track when the $7.8 billion threshold is reached.

[P4] Hospitals will demand that CMS clarify whether the $7.8 billion cap is nominal or inflation-adjusted and whether any repayments, offsets, or reconciliation mechanisms will adjust the running total.

[P4] Advocacy groups will argue that tying the duration of the policy to an aggregate dollar threshold could result in unpredictable year-to-year rate changes; CMS should set clear timelines or caps per year to allow provider budgeting.

[P1] The 30-day comment period ending March 8, 2021 is insufficient for international operators and affected suppliers to prepare informed responses given COVID-19 disruptions; extend the comment deadline by at least 60–90 days.

[P1] The rule references two separate ADs (Rolls‑Royce and Boeing) with identical comment due dates; the FAA should stagger deadlines to reduce administrative burden on stakeholders who must comment on both.

[P2] The compliance language "within the specified compliance times unless already done" is vague — request clarification that documented prior compliance (with date and service bulletin reference) satisfies the requirement without additional paperwork.

[P3] The requirement to remove and replace affected HPT stage 1 disks before exceeding 2,840 FCs or within 60 days could ground fleets unexpectedly; propose allowing phased compliance tied to scheduled shop visits to avoid operational disruption.

[P4] The 2,840 flight-cycle threshold lacks supporting risk assessment in the preamble; provide the data and analysis demonstrating why 2,840 FCs is the safe limit rather than a higher/lower threshold.

[P5] The alternative 60‑day after effective date compliance trigger could be infeasible for operators with many engines; request an option to comply within 180 days if parts lead time or MRO capacity prevents 60‑day replacement.

[P6] The 8‑year cap when using flight cycles (P6) is unclear — request explicit examples showing how compliance is calculated for disks already exceeding 2,840 FCs at AD effective date and how the 8‑year limit interacts with that.

[P7] The installation prohibition (P7) lacks an exception for part transfers to non-airworthy uses (e.g., training, ground test stands) or for use as spares pending modification — request an explicit carve‑out to allow non-flight use.

[P8] The AMOC authority centralized with the Manager, ECO Branch (P8) may cause delays; suggest delegating limited AMOC authority to regional ACOs or permitting a fast‑track review for routine, low‑risk relief.

[P9] Requiring AMOC requests to go through the principal inspector or local FSDO (P9) duplicates the 14 CFR 39.19 process and may slow submission; permit direct submission to the ECO Branch with cc to the local FSDO as an alternative.

[P10] Direct submission routing (P10) says send to the person in Related Information but that section may change; require the AD to include a named position and contact details to avoid misdirection.

[P11] Providing an email address for AMOCs (P11) is helpful, but the AD should also permit encrypted file transfer for proprietary technical data and confirm receipt procedures/timelines for emailed AMOCs.

[P12] The notification-before-use requirement for AMOCs (P12) is reasonable, but request clarification on timing (e.g., how many business days before use) and the acceptable method of notification (fax, email, logbook entry).

[P13] The identical March 8, 2021 comment deadline for the Boeing AD (P13) should be extended for the same reasons cited for P1 — industry needs more time to coordinate multinational responses.

[P14] The generic compliance phrase in Boeing AD (P14) should require operators to maintain records evidencing compliance times and any deviations, with a specified retention period (e.g., 3 years) to ensure enforcement consistency.

[P15] The 27‑month window to determine modification status of rudder pedal covers (P15) is excessively long for in‑service safety mitigation; shorten to 90–180 days or require interim inspections until modification status is determined.

[P16] Allowing records review to determine modification status (P16) is appropriate but must require a standardized acceptable records format and minimum fields (work order number, STC/Service Bulletin reference, technician name/date) to avoid ambiguous determinations.

[P17] Requiring modification per Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletins (P17) without incorporating those documents by reference leaves uncertainty; incorporate the exact Revision and Issue date of the Bulletins into the AD regulatory text to prevent interpretation variance.

[P18] The exception substituting the AD effective date for "original issue date" in the bulletins (P18) could inadvertently shorten compliance windows; publish an explicit mapping table that shows the resultant compliance dates for typical production batches.

[P19] Credit for previous actions (P19) should require submission of verification to the FAA (e.g., logbook entry or maintenance release) to prevent fraudulent claims of prior compliance.

[P20] The post-certification parts installation prohibition (P20) could disrupt supply chains for new-build aircraft; allow manufacturers to ship uninstalled parts to final assembly lines with an FAA‑approved process to ensure parts will be modified prior to installation.

[P21] The exception allowing installation if part has been modified (P21) needs a clear definition of what constitutes acceptable modification — reference the exact Boeing modification instructions and acceptance criteria.

[P22] The pre‑effective certificate installation limitation (P22) forbids installation of unmodified parts after modification is performed on the aircraft; clarify if this prohibits using existing unmodified spares to replace removed parts during field maintenance prior to completing AD modification.

[P23] The reinstallation allowance for temporarily removed unmodified parts (P23) must be limited in time and accompanied by inspection requirements; allow temporary reinstallation only for up to 7 days and require placarding and maintenance log entries.

[P24] Granting AMOC authority to the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch (P24) centralizes decisions; request further delegation to Boeing ODA for routine, well-documented AMOCs to expedite approvals consistent with safety.

[P25] Routing AMOC requests through principal inspectors or FSDOs (P25) may delay multinational operators; permit operators to submit AMOCs through their U.S. principal design approval holder or ODA with notification to FAA.

[P26] Direct submission to the person in paragraph (m)(1) (P26) needs a published contact name, phone, and backup in case of staff turnover; otherwise AMOC requests risk being lost.

[P27] Emailing AMOC requests to the Seattle ACO address (P27) should include automatic acknowledgement and target review timelines (e.g., 30 days) so operators can plan maintenance.

[P28] The pre‑use notification requirement for AMOCs (P28) is unclear about whether the FAA must affirmatively approve use or simply be notified; clarify whether notification is a notice-only obligation or requires concurrence.

[P29] Permitting Boeing ODA‑approved AMOCs to be used (P29) is efficient, but require transparency: Boeing ODA approvals used as AMOCs should be submitted to the Seattle ACO archive and made available to operators upon request to ensure consistent application.

[P30] The condition that the ODA approval must be authorized by the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch (P30) is circular and administratively burdensome; allow ODA approvals made under existing delegation scopes without separate FAA authorization for each AMOC.

[P31] Requiring that AMOC deviations meet the airplane's certification basis (P31) is appropriate but may block practical field fixes; provide guidance on how to demonstrate equivalence to certification basis for common deviations.

[P32] AMOC approval must reference the AD (P32) — recommend that FAA provide a standard approval template to ensure consistent referencing and prevent ambiguity about applicability.

[P33] Disallowing use of AMOCs previously approved for AD 2017‑14‑13 (P33) could waste previously validated solutions; explain the technical rationale and consider grandfathering AMOCs that remain technically applicable.

[P34] Making RC‑labeled steps mandatory (P34) is standard but the AD must list which specific steps are RC in the regulatory text rather than leaving it only in the service bulletin, to avoid interpretation disputes.

[P35] The RC Exempt exception (P35) must be clearly identified in the service information; request that the FAA publish an annex listing all RC Exempt steps to avoid confusion during maintenance.

[P36] Requiring AMOCs for deviations from RC steps (P36) should allow for emergency deviations where safety or operational necessity requires immediate action, with requirement to submit AMOC request within 72 hours after the action.

[P37] Allowing deviation from non‑RC steps per operator programs (P37) is reasonable, but require that operator methods be documented and auditable, and that they demonstrate equivalent or better safety than the manufacturer procedures.

[P38] The condition that RC steps remain achievable after non‑RC deviations (P38) is subjective; request objective acceptance criteria (e.g., specified dimensional tolerances, required tools, or functional tests) to verify RC step performability.

[P39] Requiring airplane be returned to an airworthy condition after non‑RC deviations (P39) should define acceptable evidence of airworthiness (e.g., release to service by certified mechanic, specific functional checks) so inspectors can uniformly enforce the requirement.

[P3] The petition content requirement (§ 171.130(b)) that assertions be "supported by data" is vague; the rule should define the minimum types and quality of data (e.g., GLP, peer-reviewed, raw study reports) required to avoid arbitrary rejections.

[P3] Academic and public-interest commenters will argue that the term "new information" must include credible epidemiological and post-market surveillance data, not just manufacturer-submitted toxicology studies.

[P3] Small business stakeholders will request an exception or reduced data burden when petitions concern abandonment of uses rather than novel toxicity claims, to prevent excessive cost barriers to petitions.

[P3] Legal experts will assert that requiring data in petitions should not foreclose petitions relying on properly framed legal, economic, or market-experience arguments; the rule should allow non-scientific evidence where relevant.

[P4] Requiring new data to be furnished in the exact forms specified by 21 CFR 171.1 and 171.100 could be unduly technical; the agency should allow equivalent electronic formats and provide templates to reduce submission errors.

[P4] Commenters will request explicit guidance on how proprietary/confidential business information in data submissions will be handled under FOIA and the public docket to protect trade secrets.

[P4] Researchers will ask that the regulation explicitly permit submission of supplemental datasets and code (e.g., for reproducibility) and specify acceptable file types and metadata standards.

[P5] The permission for petitioners to seek amendment based on abandonment (§ 171.130) could be abused to remove safe allowances from the market; the rule should require affirmative evidence of non-use over a defined period (e.g., 5 years) and notice to affected stakeholders before final action.

[P5] Manufacturers will request that the rule clarify whether abandonment determinations consider niche or limited-volume uses (e.g., specialty foods), and propose a quantitative threshold (e.g., <0.1% market share) rather than an absolute "abandoned" standard.

[P5] Public health groups will argue that abandonment alone should not be sufficient to repeal an additive allowance if safety information is incomplete; the rule must preserve ability to maintain low-level allowances for safety or contamination control.

[P6] The condition that abandonment must be "complete" with respect to intended U.S. uses (§ 171.130) is unworkably strict; many additives have sporadic or seasonal uses, so FDA should allow evidence of sustained non-use (e.g., 3–5 consecutive years) rather than an absolute standard.

[P6] Industry commenters will request that importation and minor uses be explicitly considered when determining "complete" abandonment to avoid unintended trade disruptions.

[P6] Trade associations will seek clarity on how FDA will determine intended uses — whether based on labeling, import entries, production volume, or other metrics — and ask for a published methodology.

[P7] The obligation to "adequately define" abandoned uses for scope clarity is reasonable, but the rule should specify what level of specificity is required (e.g., specific food categories, concentration ranges, processing conditions) to avoid disputes.

[P7] Petitioners will request a standardized form or checklist for defining uses (including food matrices, processing steps, exposure routes) so petitions meet the adequacy requirement and reduce agency rejections.

[P7] Legal commenters will warn that vague definitions of uses could result in overbroad amendments that unintentionally affect lawful uses; the regulation should require FDA to provide a proposed amendment text showing exact regulatory language changes.

[P8] Requiring commenters who claim certain uses have not been abandoned to identify specific ortho-phthalates (or other named substances) is reasonable, but the rule should allow collective or category-based submissions when exact chemical identity is proprietary or unknown.

[P8] Manufacturers and trade groups will object to the requirement that commenters name ortho-phthalates when confidentiality concerns exist; the agency should permit confidential identifiers or in-camera submissions for proprietary formulations.

[P8] Environmental and public-health NGOs will request that the rule require commenters contesting abandonment to also supply quantitative evidence (e.g., sales, import, or analytical testing data) for the named phthalates to substantiate continued use.

[P9] Small businesses and consumer advocates will ask for clear templates and examples for the recommended product descriptions to reduce the burden of compliance and ensure consistent submissions.

[P9] Commenters will ask FDA to accept and encourage third-party testing results (e.g., market surveillance analytical data) as part of product descriptions to demonstrate continued use or abandonment.

[P1][P7] Public commenters will ask that the new procedural regulation include explicit standards for how FDA will evaluate competing petitions (e.g., first-in-time, completeness, public-interest priority) to promote transparency and fairness.

[P6][P8] Importers and distributors will request explicit guidance on the transition period and compliance enforcement if FDA finds uses abandoned and amends regulations; they need time to adjust inventories and labeling.

[P3] Consumer-safety organizations will demand that "new toxicity data" include non-animal and high-throughput screening data where scientifically validated, and that FDA not exclude these data types a priori.

[P4][P9] Academic researchers will ask that data submissions be made available in anonymized form for independent reanalysis to foster transparency while protecting proprietary information.

[P5][P6] Trade associations will propose a rebuttable presumption standard (e.g., presumption of non-abandonment unless petition shows <X volume or no commercial distribution for Y years) to avoid arbitrary rulings based on incomplete information.

[P3][P7] Petitioners seeking amendments based on abandoned uses should be required to publish public notice to former users and offer a comment period specifically targeting those parties before FDA finalizes changes.

[P8] NGOs will request that the rule require more than identification of specific ortho-phthalates — commenters alleging continued use must submit analytical detection thresholds and methods to avoid spurious contentions based on trace contamination.

[P1] Constitutional and administrative-law scholars will request an explanation of how the new regulation under section 409(i) interacts with existing delegation doctrines and whether any new rulemaking constraints on FDA decisionmaking are implied.

[P2][P3] Public-health stakeholders will encourage FDA to retain broad authority to act on petitions and sua sponte where emergent science indicates risk, and to set low procedural barriers for whistleblower or third-party safety petitions.

[P4] IT and e-filing stakeholders will ask that FDA provide an online portal for petitions and data submissions conforming to 21 CFR 171.1 and 171.100 to reduce processing delays and transcription errors.

[P1] The deadline in § 39.13(a) (comments due by October 24, 2022) is unreasonably short given the technical complexity of the Boeing 737 structural inspections referenced; request an extension of at least 60–90 days to allow affected operators, MROs, and labor organizations to prepare substantive comments.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether extension of the comment period will be considered if stakeholders request more time; the regulation currently mandates a hard deadline without process for extension.

[P2] § 39.13(c) should clarify whether airplanes modified by supplemental type certificates (STCs) or previously re-winged/altered 737–600/700/800/900 series remain subject to the AD as written, or whether STC holders/operators must demonstrate applicability exceptions.

[P2] The applicability in § 39.13(c) is incomplete because it omits production line suffixes, export variants, and international registrations; request explicit language confirming that all certificated-in-any-category 737–600/700/700C/800/900/900ER airplanes worldwide are covered.

[P2] Request that the FAA supply a mapping table cross-referencing Boeing line numbers and serial numbers to the model designations in § 39.13(c) to help operators determine applicability without ambiguity.

[P3] § 39.13(f) states “comply within the compliance times specified, unless already done,” but does not specify whether repeated or recurring inspections already performed under previous service bulletins count as “already done”; request explicit credit language for prior actions and for actions done to previous revisions of the referenced bulletin.

[P3] The compliance-time language should provide relief for aircraft with maintenance programs that had inspections performed earlier than the start of the compliance window (i.e., a grace period or credit so operators are not required to reperform recently completed equivalent inspections).

[P4] § 39.13(g) cross-references the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin but does not reproduce critical procedural steps; operators need the FAA to explicitly state that following the Boeing Requirements Bulletin exactly satisfies the AD, or identify any FAA-required deviations beyond paragraph (h).

[P4] The AD should specify whether tasks in the referenced Requirements Bulletin that are labeled as “optional” or “for future consideration” are mandatory when incorporated by reference via § 39.13(g).

[P5] The substitution in § 39.13(h)(1) (use this AD’s effective date wherever the bulletin references its original issue date) is ambiguous: commenters ask the FAA to confirm that this substitution applies to all compliance-time rows and any time-limited repetitive intervals, and to provide an example of how compliance dates shift.

[P5] Operators request that the FAA explicitly state whether using the AD effective date may shorten or lengthen the compliance window compared to the bulletin and whether any previously scheduled maintenance events are disrupted by this substitution.

[P6] § 39.13(h)(2) prohibits simply contacting Boeing for repair instructions and requires AMOC-type approval instead; industry commenters argue this removes an efficient existing pathway (Boeing ODA repairs) and request FAA to allow Boeing-authorized repair instructions without separate AMOC where Boeing ODA approval already exists.

[P6] Clarify whether Boeing Service Bulletin repair instructions that previously required contacting Boeing are now prohibited unless approved via paragraph (i) procedures, and whether this change will delay repairs due to AMOC processing times.

[P7] While § 39.13(i)(1) grants the Seattle ACO Manager authority to approve AMOCs, commenters request clarity whether other FAA ACOs or the Director-level office may approve AMOCs in urgent cases, and what the expected review timeframe will be.

[P7] Legal commenters request explanation of the standard the Manager will apply when approving AMOCs (e.g., “acceptable level of safety” criteria) and whether decisions will be published or precedential.

[P8] § 39.13(i)(1) requires sending AMOC requests to the principal inspector or responsible Flight Standards Office; smaller operators request guidance on what constitutes the “responsible Flight Standards Office” and how to proceed when their principal inspector is no longer assigned.

[P8] Request that the FAA provide a clear, centralized intake process and contact list for AMOC submissions to prevent misdirected requests and processing delays as implied by § 39.13(i)(1).

[P9] The instruction in § 39.13(i)(1) to address AMOC submittals to the person named in paragraph (j)(1) lacks the named individual in the excerpt; request that the final AD include the full name, title, and contact details to ensure proper routing.

[P10] § 39.13(i)(1) permits emailing AMOC information to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov, but commenters raise cybersecurity and confidentiality concerns about sending proprietary Boeing repair data via that address; request secure submission alternatives (encrypted portal, upload system).

[P10] Operators request confirmation that emailed AMOC submissions will be acknowledged with a timestamp and tracking number and that receipt will be considered the filing date for compliance-timing purposes.

[P11] § 39.13(i)(2) requires notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC; union and labor commenters ask whether this notification suffices for operational approval or if additional local regulatory approvals (e.g., ops specs) are needed before returning an aircraft to service.

[P11] Request clarification on the timeline required between FAA AMOC approval and the mandatory notification to the principal inspector — i.e., whether notification must be prior to the first flight after repair or within a defined number of days.

[P12] § 39.13(i)(3) allows Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to be used if approved by the Manager; Boeing and OEM commenters request a faster-track process recognizing Boeing ODA approvals as presumptively acceptable, subject to FAA verification, to avoid duplicative approvals.

[P12] Conversely, consumer-safety and labor groups object to automatic deference to Boeing ODA approvals and request that FAA retain full independent review authority before accepting ODA-approved AMOCs for safety-critical repairs.

[P13] § 39.13(i)(3) requires that repair/modification deviations meet the airplane’s certification basis and that approval explicitly reference this AD; commenters ask the FAA to define “meet the certification basis” (e.g., list of regulations, special conditions) and whether showing equivalence is sufficient.

[P13] Request that the FAA provide a template for approval letters that explicitly reference the AD and list the certification basis findings to improve transparency and uniformity across AMOC approvals as required by § 39.13(i)(3).

[P6] MROs warn that requiring AMOC approval for any repair that the Boeing bulletin directs to “contact Boeing” may create bottlenecks and grounded aircraft while AMOCs are reviewed; request interim repair authorization procedures to keep aircraft serviceable.

[P4] Airlines request that the FAA incorporate by reference the latest revision of the Boeing Requirements Bulletin or explicitly state which revision (July 2, 2021) is mandatory, to avoid future disputes about which bulletin version applies under § 39.13(g).

[P3] Commenters request inclusion of relief provisions for operators that cannot meet the specified compliance times due to parts availability, manpower shortages, or COVID-related constraints, with a process for expedited temporary extensions under § 39.13(f).

[P2] International operators request coordination language indicating whether foreign civil aviation authorities (e.g., EASA, Transport Canada) will be notified or given an opportunity to harmonize AD applicability dates for the models listed in § 39.13(c).

[P1] Consumer-safety advocates request that the FAA keep the comment period open beyond October 24, 2022 if substantive new data (e.g., additional incident reports) emerges during the comment window, rather than closing the docket on a fixed date per § 39.13(a).

[P1] The requirement to maintain cabin pressure altitude at or below 8,000 feet in normal operations is overly prescriptive and fails to account for legitimate operational tradeoffs on long-range flights (fuel/weight/engine performance) — request allow performance-based compliance or altitude/time-averaged metrics.

[P1] The standard does not define "normal operations" (e.g., climb/cruise/descent, diversion, emergency) and therefore creates regulatory uncertainty for operators regarding when the ≤8,000 ft obligation applies.

[P1] Aircraft manufacturers request an extended implementation timeline and grandfathering for existing type-certificated airplanes that cannot meet a strict ≤8,000 ft cabin altitude without major redesign.

[P2] The required warning indication at the pilot/flight engineer station lacks specificity on format (visual, aural, discrete vs. integrated) and could create ambiguity about acceptable installations — propose specifying minimum performance and prioritization (e.g., distinct, attention-getting aural plus visual).

[P2] Flightcrew unions support the warning requirement but ask that the rule require the warning to be continuous and latched until acknowledged, to ensure crew awareness during high workload.

[P3] Allowing markings on the pressure differential indicator to satisfy the differential-limit warning is inadequate — markings are passive and may not be noticed during abnormal conditions; require an active alerting element in addition to markings.

[P3] Legal commenters note that the phrase "appropriate warning markings" is vague; request explicit criteria (size, color, wording, location, illumination) to ensure uniform compliance and avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P4] The provision that an alert that warns when cabin altitude exceeds 10,000 ft satisfies the warning requirement should be clarified to mandate both visual and aural components, as visual-only alerts may be missed during pilot distraction.

[P4] Safety advocates argue that 10,000 ft is too high for an initial alert given hypoxia risk, and recommend lowering the alert threshold to 8,000–9,000 ft or requiring a two-tiered alert (advisory at 8,000, caution at 10,000).

[P5] The permission to set cabin pressure equal to airport elevation for airports ≥8,000 ft is reasonable for mountain operations, but operators request clarification whether this applies to both arrival and departure segments and to transient ground operations.

[P5] Public health and passenger advocacy groups oppose routinely equating cabin pressure to high-altitude airport elevation because prolonged passenger exposure (e.g., long taxi, boarding delays) could exceed safe limits for vulnerable passengers.

[P6] The condition limiting the high-elevation operation permission to airplanes being operated at or below 25,000 ft is problematic for turboprops and regional jets that routinely operate near or above that ceiling — ask for justification of the 25,000 ft cutoff or propose alternative altitude-dependent criteria.

[P6] Aircraft operators suggest the 25,000 ft limit imposes unnecessary constraints for aircraft certified for higher flight levels; propose allowing use up to certified maximum cruising altitude with mitigation measures.

[P7] The requirement that the pressurization system be designed to minimize occupant exposure time above 8,000 ft is vague — request a measurable metric (e.g., maximum cumulative minutes above 8,000 ft per flight segment) or validated design criteria to demonstrate compliance.

[P7] Medical and disability advocates request a requirement to minimize exposure especially for medically vulnerable passengers (pregnant, cardiac, respiratory) and ask for mandated preflight crew briefings and accommodations when operating to/from high-elevation airports.

[P8] Allowing the cabin altitude warning to be shifted to 15,000 ft (or 2,000 ft above field elevation) when operating into/out of airports >8,000 ft may create confusion and increased hypoxia risk for passengers and crew — request retaining the 10,000 ft baseline or requiring enhanced mitigation.

[P8] Operators supporting flexibility argue the provision is necessary to avoid nuisance alarms at high-elevation airports and request clear operational procedures and training to ensure safe use.

[P9] The requirement that an alert "clearly show" the pilot that the high-altitude warning threshold has been shifted is subjective — commenters request specific display and annunciation requirements (e.g., dedicated MIL/MASTER annunciator plus cockpit log entry) to avoid misinterpretation.

[P9] Human factors experts recommend training and standardized symbology for the shift indication; without standardization, different airplane types could present the shift in conflicting ways, increasing error risk.

[P10] The need for an alert to notify flightcrew to take action if the automatic shift function fails is sensible, but operators request clarity on what constitutes "take action" — specify required actions (don oxygen, descend, reset system) and timeframes.

[P10] Maintenance and avionics suppliers request guidance on testability and fault annunciation requirements for the automatic shift function so that in-service failures are readily detectable and reportable.

[P11] Allowing either an alerting system or AFM procedures to satisfy the requirement to notify crew when to don oxygen is insufficiently protective — AFM procedures alone, without automatic alerts, risk delayed donning during high workload; recommend requiring both.

[P11] Pilot associations request that any AFM procedures required under this paragraph be standardized across operators and include mandatory immediate donning times and checklist verbiage to avoid variations in practice.

[P1] The June 9, 2022 comment deadline is unreasonably short and should be extended to at least 60 days from publication to allow affected operators and unions to prepare meaningful technical and economic comments.

[P1] The rule fails to provide notice of the methods by which comments will be accepted (portal, mail, docket number); the FAA should clarify submission procedures and confirm extensions if technical portals fail.

[P2] The applicability to “all” Boeing 767–2C series airplanes is overly broad; the FAA should limit the AD to specific serial-number ranges or production configurations known to be affected, or explain the data supporting universal applicability.

[P2] The AD’s applicability language does not clarify whether U.S.-registered leased aircraft or aircraft operated under foreign registry but operated within the U.S. are covered; clarify applicability to leased and foreign-registered aircraft.

[P3] The phrase “within the compliance times specified” is vague because some referenced compliance times vary by configuration; the AD should reproduce the specific compliance times for each action in the regulatory text for legal clarity.

[P3] The AD should include a provision allowing relief/extension of compliance times where parts or shop capacity are unavailable, especially for airlines experiencing supply-chain delays, rather than relying solely on AMOC requests.

[P4] Requiring strict adherence to all actions in Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 767–27A0240 RB without providing those service bulletin details in the rule creates dependence on manufacturer material; the FAA should summarize critical actions and intervals in the AD itself.

[P4] The cross-reference to paragraph (h) is confusing; paragraph (h) alters dates and actions, but the AD should explicitly list any deviations from the bulletin so operators can assess obligations without parsing multiple documents.

[P5] Incorporating Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 767–27A0243 by reference may make compliance dependent on a document under copyright; the FAA must ensure full public access to the bulletin or restate required actions in the rule.

[P5] The AD does not specify whether Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 767–27A0243 revisions or later issue dates are acceptable without a new AD or AMOC; request clarification whether later Boeing revisions can be used and under what approval process.

[P6] The termination provision allowing installation of two new drain holes to end repetitive inspections should include explicit inspection intervals and a validation requirement to show that the modification permanently mitigates the failure mode.

[P6] The AD does not require recordkeeping proof that the two drain holes were installed; require documentation in the maintenance log with specific work-order references to ensure inspectors can verify termination eligibility.

[P7] The 90-day inspection requirement for 767–2C airplanes is too short for operators with heavy maintenance backlogs; propose a staggered compliance schedule or allowance for consolidation with planned heavy checks.

[P7] The AD’s inspection scope for LSPTMs, wiring, drain holes, and leveling compound is not described in sufficient technical detail (methods, borescope vs. open inspection); the AD should define acceptable inspection techniques or include them in the regulatory text.

[P7] Requiring Manager-approved methods for on-condition actions (see P8) without defined acceptance criteria creates enforcement uncertainty; the AD should provide baseline acceptable repair options or sample approval criteria.

[P8] Concentrating approval authority for on-condition methods in the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch creates potential bottlenecks; allow delegated approvals to principal inspectors or a centralized FAA online AMOC portal to expedite responses.

[P8] The AD should specify a timeline for Manager review of proposed on-condition methods (e.g., 30 days) to prevent indefinite delays and operational disruptions.

[P9] Replacing the bulletin’s “original issue date” with the AD effective date may unintentionally change compliance windows that referenced intervals measured from bulletin issuance; the FAA must demonstrate that this substitution does not shorten operator compliance time.

[P9] The AD should clarify whether operators that complied with actions measured from the bulletin original issue date prior to the AD effective date are considered in compliance, to avoid double compliance burdens.

[P10] Same comment as P9: Using the AD effective date in lieu of the bulletin’s original issue date could shorten allowable time for operators who have been scheduling actions based on the bulletin — FAA must provide grandfathering language for prior compliance planning.

[P11] Forcing Action 1 timing to follow paragraph (g)(1) rather than bulletin-specified timing could conflict with operator maintenance programs; the FAA must justify the change with safety data or allow operators to follow the bulletin when it provides equal or greater safety.

[P11] The AD should list the specific compliance interval for Action 1 in the text so operators do not need to cross-reference multiple documents to determine required actions.

[P12] Allowing the Manager to approve AMOCs is appropriate but the AD should include an expedited AMOC process for repetitive, minor deviations that do not affect safety, such as alternate inspection tools or surface-cleaning techniques.

[P12] The AD does not explain whether AMOCs approved by other FAA ACOs (not Seattle) will be recognized; request explicit cross-recognition policy to avoid repeat submissions.

[P13] Requiring AMOC requests to be routed through the principal inspector or Flight Standards Office adds administrative steps that may delay urgent compliance; permit direct submission to the Seattle ACO with mandatory simultaneous notification to the principal inspector.

[P14] The paragraph (j)(1) designee referenced for direct submissions is not named in the AD; include the specific contact name and title or a current contact point to avoid misrouting.

[P15] The email address for AMOC submissions should be confirmed as secure for transmission of proprietary repair data; the FAA should provide an encrypted upload portal or guidance for submitting sensitive information.

[P16] The obligation to notify the principal inspector prior to using an approved AMOC could be impractical for foreign operators or for flights in remote locations; allow notification within a defined period (e.g., 72 hours) instead of prior notification in such cases.

[P16] The AD should state whether a written record of the notification to the principal inspector is required and how it should be documented in maintenance records.

[P17] Permitting AMOCs approved by an authorized Boeing ODA to be used is efficient, but the AD must require that Boeing ODA approvals be provided to the FAA for audit and include criteria for FAA review to ensure independence.

[P17] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs may create a conflict of interest if Boeing both issues the bulletin and approves deviations; require FAA oversight or concurrence on Boeing ODA approvals for this AD.

[P18] Requiring that repair approvals meet the airplane’s certification basis and specifically reference this AD is appropriate, but the AD should require the approval letter to document the certification-basis substantiation and provide it to the operator for records.

[P18] The AD does not specify how deviation approvals that affect multiple operators will be promulgated or shared; require that AMOCs or ODA approvals be posted to a public docket or FAA website so other operators can adopt them.

General/legal

[P2] The AD lacks a regulatory economic analysis demonstrating cost impacts on small air carriers and cargo operators that primarily operate 767–300F/767–2C aircraft; submitters will request a Small Entity Compliance Guide and cost estimates.

[P4/P5] Operators will request that the FAA issue a compliance cost estimate that separates labor hours, parts cost (drain hole kits), and downtime per model series to evaluate economic feasibility and whether an extended compliance timeline is warranted.

[P6] Safety benefit justification for terminating repetitive inspections upon installation of two drain holes is not included; stakeholders will demand technical data showing that the drain holes fully mitigate corrosion/water intrusion risks.

[P7] Labor qualifications for required inspections and on-condition repairs are not specified; commenters will ask that the AD clarify whether certified mechanics with inspection authorization, repair stations, or Boeing ODA personnel may perform specific tasks.

[P8/P12] The rule should clarify whether alternative inspection techniques (e.g., eddy current, ultrasound) require AMOCs or are acceptable methods under the AD to reduce unnecessary shop visits.

[P1] The AD should commit to reopening the comment period if substantive clarifications or changes are made to the bulletin incorporation or compliance times before final rule issuance.

[P1] Consumer advocates will object that permitting terms like "zero fat" or "no fat" without strict analytical criteria risks misleading consumers due to trace fat naturally present in some dairy-derived products.

[P1] Public health groups will demand that the rule require standardized serving sizes and testing methods when manufacturers use "fat-free," "skim," or similar claims so comparisons across products are meaningful and enforceable.

[P1] Legal commenters will note that the truncated text of § 101.62(b)(1) appears inconsistent with existing NLEA standards and request explicit cross-references to existing nutrient content claim definitions to avoid regulatory conflict.

[P2] Dairy manufacturers will support the alternative blending method in § 131.149(a) as providing manufacturing flexibility but will ask for explicit allowable blend ratios or compositional parameters to ensure uniformity across producers.

[P2] Small dairy processors will request transitional compliance guidance and testing protocols for certifying cream produced by blending defined milks and creams, arguing current laboratory methods may not readily demonstrate equivalence.

[P3] Consumer protection organizations will challenge the vague "equivalent in composition" criterion in § 131.149(a) as unenforceable unless the rule specifies which compositional metrics (fat content, solids-not-fat, moisture, protein, acidity) must match and allowable tolerances.

[P3] Industry commenters will ask that the agency provide objective analytical specifications and acceptable tolerance bands (e.g., ±0.2% milkfat, ±0.5% solids-not-fat) to operationalize "equivalent in composition."

[P3] Legal experts will warn that without defined equivalence criteria the provision invites inconsistent enforcement and potential litigation over whether a blended cream is lawful.

[P4] Dairy industry trade associations will strongly oppose removal of the standard of identity for sweetened condensed skimmed milk (§ 131.122), arguing it creates marketplace uncertainty and undermines product naming protections.

[P4] Consumer safety advocates will request that, if § 131.122 is removed, the rule include labeling requirements to prevent misleading use of the name "sweetened condensed skimmed milk" and protect consumers with allergies or dietary needs.

[P5] Manufacturers of lowfat dry milk will object to removal of § 131.123, noting that elimination of the standard of identity could allow products with substantially different composition to be marketed under the same name, confusing buyers and foodservice purchasers.

[P5] State regulators will seek federal guidance on how the removal of § 131.123 affects state-level procurement specifications that currently refer to the CFR standard.

[P6] Milk processors will express concerns that removing the standard for evaporated skimmed milk (§ 131.132) could lead to product substitution and variability affecting recipes and institutional buyers (e.g., schools, hospitals).

[P6] Food technologists will request that the agency publish recommended compositional and processing criteria or allow voluntary grade specifications to preserve quality expectations after § 131.132 is removed.

[P7] Nutrition advocates will oppose deletion of the lowfat milk standard (§ 131.135), asserting it weakens consumer protection by permitting inconsistent use of "lowfat milk" across products.

[P8] Producers of acidified lowfat milk will request clarifying labeling and compositional criteria if § 131.136 is removed, particularly to distinguish acidified products from fermented cultured products in the absence of a standard.

[P9] Manufacturers and food safety officials will caution that removing the cultured lowfat milk standard (§ 131.138) could obscure whether live cultures are present and affect probiotic claims; they will ask for explicit labeling safeguards.

[P10] Consumer groups will object to elimination of the skim (nonfat) milk standard (§ 131.143), requesting that the agency maintain a defined milkfat maximum (e.g., ≤0.5% milkfat) for products labeled "skim" to prevent consumer confusion.

[P11] Producers of acidified skim (nonfat) milk will request transitional allowances and explicit labeling rules if § 131.144 is removed to distinguish acidified vs. fermented products.

[P12] Stakeholders will ask that removal of cultured skim (nonfat) milk standard (§ 131.146) be accompanied by guidance on probiotic labeling and identity of culture strains to avoid misleading statements.

[P13] Dairy and foodservice purchasers (e.g., restaurants, cafeterias) will oppose removal of the sour half-and-half standard (§ 131.185), arguing the change could alter product performance in coffee/culinary applications and disrupt contracts that reference the CFR standard.

[P14] Industry commenters will request that removal of the acidified sour half-and-half standard (§ 131.187) be delayed until acceptable product descriptions and labeling conventions are published to avoid market disruption.

[P15] Yogurt industry groups will strongly object to deleting the lowfat yogurt standard (§ 131.203), arguing standard removal may permit products with differing nutritional profiles to share the "lowfat" descriptor and mislead consumers seeking lower-fat options.

[P15] Nutrition researchers will ask for retention of minimum live culture requirements and maximum fat limits associated with lowfat yogurt if § 131.203 is removed.

[P16] Producers of nonfat (skim) yogurt will request that § 131.206 not be removed absent precise compositional limits (e.g., ≤0.5% milkfat) and clear standards for stabilizers and added solids to preserve product identity.

[P17] Cottage cheese manufacturers will oppose elimination of the lowfat cottage cheese standard (§ 133.131), warning that it could allow increased fat content while retaining the "lowfat" label unless explicit maximum fat percentages are maintained.

[P18] Housing and consumer advocates will support permitting federal credit unions to make up to 40-year residential loans (§ 701.21(g)(1)) but will request consumer protection safeguards—caps on total interest, prepayment penalty restrictions, and mandatory RESPA/TILA disclosures tailored to longer maturities.

[P18] Financial regulators and risk analysts will warn that allowing loans "up to 40 years or longer as permitted by the NCUA Board" (§ 701.21(g)(1)) creates uncertainty; they will request limits, supervisory oversight language, and capital/reserve requirements to address interest-rate and credit risk.

[P18] Affordable housing groups will express concern that extremely long maturities may increase interest paid over the life of the loan and recommend mandatory amortization schedules and examples on disclosures.

[P19] Federal credit unions will request clarification that loans secured or guaranteed by federal/state agencies (§ 701.21(e)) are exempt from maturity limits only to the extent the underlying program permits and that the agency’s acceptance letter constitutes sufficient documentation.

[P19] Legal commenters will ask for explicit procedures for documenting the existence and terms of guarantees/insurance (e.g., FHA/VA commitment letters) to rely on § 701.21(e) permissibility.

[P20] Credit unions will support the general allowance for 20-year loans (§ 701.21(f)(1)) but will request clarifying language on how such loans affect concentration limits, underwriting standards, and loan-to-value requirements.

[P21] Consumer advocates will oppose allowing 20-year loans for mobile homes (§ 701.21(f)(1)(i)) unless there are robust appraisal, title, and affixation standards to ensure the mobile home is permanently affixed and eligible for mortgage interest deduction treatment.

[P21] Manufactured housing industry will welcome the 20-year mobile home financing (§ 701.21(f)(1)(i)) but request clarification of documentation required to prove permanent affixation (e.g., recording fixture filing, certificate of title surrender) and permissible collateral remedies.

[P22] Borrower protection groups will ask for limits or underwriting safeguards on 20-year second mortgages (§ 701.21(f)(1)(ii)) to prevent predatory lending and ensure borrowers understand cumulative debt obligations on their residences.

[P22] Credit unions will ask whether the 20-year exception for second mortgages applies when the first mortgage is held by an affiliate or in cases of subordinate liens with different priority language; they request clarifying examples.

[P23] Home improvement lenders and credit unions will support allowing 20-year loans to finance repair/alteration (§ 701.21(f)(1)(iii)) but request a clear definition of "repair, alteration, or improvement" and caps on the loan amounts relative to property value.

[P23] Consumer protection groups will request that loans under § 701.21(f)(1)(iii) include conditions on escrow, contractor verification, and post-disbursement inspection to protect borrowers from misuse of funds.

[P24] Recreational vehicle, house trailer, and boat owners will object to the broad definition of "mobile home" in § 701.21(f)(2), arguing inclusion of RVs and boats could permit financing for inherently non-permanent dwellings under 20-year terms and request a stricter permanence test (e.g., property tax classification, certificate of affixation).

[P24] Legal commentators will note that including RVs and boats in the "mobile home" definition may conflict with tax and mortgage interest deduction rules and ask the agency to harmonize definitions with IRS and state law to avoid unintended tax consequences.
