[P1] Industry commenter: Require clarification of what objective criteria will be used to determine whether a pseudo-patient “demonstrates key characteristics” (age, frailty, functional status, cognitive status, care goals) to avoid subjective enforcement and inconsistent survey findings under §418.3.

[P1] Patient advocate: The rule should prohibit use of pseudo-patients who have active infectious diseases or vulnerabilities that increase risk to trainees or staff; the provision currently lacks safety protections for pseudo-patients.

[P1] Legal expert: Request definition of “capable of responding to and interacting” in §418.3 and guidance on accommodations for pseudo-patients with communication impairments to ensure compliance with ADA and consent requirements.

[P1] Labor/education association: Recommend allowing trained actors or standardized patients as pseudo-patients and specify minimum training/certification standards so hospices are not forced to recruit actual vulnerable patients.

[P2] Pharmacy/provider group: Supportive comment that non-hospice providers and Medicare contractors may request the addendum (§418.24(c)), but ask for a process timeline and secure transmission method to protect patient privacy when third parties request the list.

[P2] Privacy advocate: Express concern that permitting Medicare contractors and non-hospice providers to request the addendum (§418.24(c)) could increase unnecessary disclosure of sensitive patient information; request explicit limits and HIPAA-aligned safeguards.

[P3] Hospice association: Seek the full text or list of the “specified required items” in §418.24(c) referenced in the preamble so hospices can assess administrative burden; recommend publishing a template addendum.

[P4] Consumer advocate: Support requirement that the addendum include name, signature, date, and statement that signing is only acknowledgment (§418.24(c)(9)) but request that the statement language be standardized and patient-friendly (plain language, large font).

[P4] Legal expert: Question whether the required signature in §418.24(c)(9) may be obtained electronically and request explicit authorization for e-signatures and procedures for representatives signing on behalf of incapacitated individuals.

[P5] Non-hospice provider: Request clarification that the exception in §418.24(c)(9) explicitly allows external providers and Medicare contractors to receive the addendum without signing; ask for confirmation that recipients may rely on the addendum without signature.

[P6] Hospice compliance officer: Ask for guidance on what format and time-stamped documentation satisfies the “date the hospice furnished the addendum” requirement in §418.24(c)(10) (e.g., mailed date, electronic delivery receipt).

[P7] Hospice operator: Object to the five-day turnaround for furnishing an addendum requested within the first 5 days (§418.24(d)(1)) as administratively burdensome during admissions; request extension to 7–10 business days or allowance for immediate electronic delivery.

[P7] Patient advocate: Argue that the 5-day requirement (§418.24(d)(1)) is appropriate to ensure patients and caregivers have timely notice of items/services deemed unrelated; oppose extending the deadline.

[P8] Hospice operator: Request clarification whether the 3-day timeframe in §418.24(d)(2) applies to calendar days or business days and propose changing to business days to accommodate weekends/holidays.

[P9] Clinician group: Seek specification of what constitutes a “change to the plan of care” that triggers the update obligation in §418.24(d)(3) (minor vs. major changes) to avoid excessive, frequent addendum updates.

[P9] Family caregiver organization: Recommend requiring hospices to proactively provide addendum updates whenever an item/service previously deemed related becomes unrelated (and vice versa) so families are fully informed (§418.24(d)(3)).

[P10] Hospice association: Request clarification of the scope of the exception in §418.24(d)(4) — if the patient dies/revokes/discharges before addendum furnished, does the hospice still need to notify non-hospice providers who requested it?  

[P10] Legal expert: Ask that §418.24(d)(4) require hospices to use best efforts to furnish the addendum prior to discharge/revocation/death and to document what steps were taken, to prevent arbitrary failure to furnish.

[P11] CMS auditor: Support the documentation requirement in §418.24(d)(4) that hospices note reasons for not furnishing the addendum, but request standardized documentation fields for auditability and comparability across hospices.

[P12] Health records manager: Clarify how addenda completed before discharge become part of the medical record (§418.24(d)(4)) — specify whether scanned copies, electronic admission modules, or separate forms meet record retention and accessibility requirements.

[P13] Patient rights group: Concern that §418.24(d)(5) exception (not required to furnish if beneficiary dies/revokes/discharged before signing) could deprive families and other providers of important information; request that hospices still be required to furnish unsigned addenda to authorized representatives when feasible.

[P14] Compliance officer: Ask for a required taxonomy or codes for documenting reasons why an addendum was not signed in §418.24(d)(5) to facilitate monitoring and reduce ambiguous entries like “not available.”

[P15] Health information management society: Recommend retention and access rules when addendum becomes part of patient’s medical record (§418.24(d)(5)), including minimum retention period and patient access rights.

[P16] Training program director: Support requirement that competency evaluations cover all subjects in §418.76(b)(3) (§418.76(c)(1)) but request that CMS publish the precise subject list and standardized competency checklists to ensure consistent evaluations.

[P17] Nursing association: Ask for clarification of what tasks are encompassed by paragraphs (b)(3)(i),(iii),(ix),(x),(xi) that must be evaluated by direct observation, and request flexibility to use simulation when direct patient observation is unsafe.

[P17] Safety advocate: Insist that direct observation requirements in §418.76(c)(1) not force trainees to perform invasive or distressing tasks on vulnerable patients; allow trained pseudo-patients or high-fidelity simulation instead.

[P18] Hospice educator: Support permission to use written/oral exams or simulation for remaining subject areas (§418.76(c)(1)) but request guidance on minimum pass thresholds and validation of written/oral exam content.

[P18] Labor union: Request that competency evaluation methods allowed in §418.76(c)(1) include a requirement for periodic re-evaluation frequency and that simulation scenarios be standardized.

[P19] Surveyor organization: Ask for examples or criteria of how an “area of concern” is to be identified during on-site visits (§418.76(h)(1)(iii)) to promote consistent survey determinations.

[P20] Hospice provider: Concern that the obligation in §418.76(h)(1)(iii) to conduct competency evaluation of all related skills when one deficiency is found is overly broad and could require re-testing of unrelated skill sets; request limiting “related skills” to a narrowly defined set.

[P20] Patient safety group: Support the requirement in §418.76(h)(1)(iii) that deficits trigger evaluation of related skills, but ask CMS to define “related” to ensure critical competency gaps are not missed.

[P21] Workforce advocate: Request that §418.76(h)(1)(iii) include timelines for when the aide must complete the competency evaluation after deficiency verification to avoid prolonged placement of underqualified aides.

[P21] Legal counsel: Ask whether aides may be restricted from performing certain tasks pending completion of the competency evaluation under §418.76(h)(1)(iii), and request guidance on temporary work restrictions to protect patients and reduce liability.

[P22] Fiscal policy group: Question the rationale for using CPI medical care for inflation adjustment in §418.309(a)(1) for certain accounting years and request analysis showing that CPI-Medical Care accurately reflects hospice cost inflation versus other indices.

[P22] Hospice association: Oppose changing the inflation adjustment mechanism in §418.309(a)(1) without transitional guidance; request impact estimates on aggregate cap levels for affected accounting years.

[P23] Economist: Request clarification of why CPI change is measured from March 1984 to the fifth month of the cap year (§418.309(a)(1)) and ask CMS to provide worked examples for multiple cap years.

[P24] Fiscal watchdog: Support §418.309(a)(2) linking cap updates to the hospice payment rate percentage, but request transparency about how productivity adjustments are applied and whether they will reduce cap levels.

[P24] Small hospice operator: Warn that productivity or other adjustments referenced in §418.309(a)(2) could create unpredictability in cap calculations for accounting years after 2016; request multi-year schedules or advance notice.

[P25] Quality improvement organization: Support requirement to submit admission and discharge HIS for each patient (§418.312(b)(1)) but request explicit guidance on exclusions (e.g., very short stays, readmissions) to reduce duplicative reporting.

[P25] Small rural hospice: Express concern about administrative burden and resource strain of completing both admission and discharge HIS for every patient regardless of payer or age (§418.312(b)(1)); request phased implementation or funding for smaller providers.

[P26] Data privacy advocate: Question the statement that administrative data used for hospice quality measures “are required and automatically satisfy HQRP requirements” (§418.312(b)(2)) — ask CMS to describe data de-identification safeguards and how patient consent is handled.

[P27] Measure developer: Support CMS authority under §418.312(b)(3) to remove measures but request transparent, public criteria and stakeholder notice periods before removal to allow feedback and re-tooling.

[P28] Consumer group: Concern that removal criterion §418.312(b)(3)(i) (uniformly high performance) could mask disparities among subpopulations; request that CMS analyze measure performance stratified by race, geography, and hospice size before removal.

[P29] Clinician society: Request that CMS require evidence that removing a measure under §418.312(b)(3)(ii) (no link to patient outcomes) will not inadvertently reduce focus on important aspects of care; demand publication of supporting analyses.

[P30] Professional guideline body: Endorse removal under §418.312(b)(3)(iii) when a measure is no longer aligned with current clinical guidelines, but request a formal crosswalk process to demonstrate non-alignment.

[P31] Health services researcher: Recommend that before invoking §418.312(b)(3)(iv) (availability of a more broadly applicable measure), CMS provide psychometric comparisons showing superior validity and reliability of the broader measure.

[P32] Quality metric expert: For §418.312(b)(3)(v) (timing), request definition of “proximal” and criteria for judging temporal association with outcomes; ask for evidence thresholds required for removal.

[P33] Outcomes researcher: For §418.312(b)(3)(vi) (stronger association), ask CMS to publish statistical methods and minimum effect sizes that would support replacing a measure.

[P34] Policy analyst: For §418.312(b)(3)(vii), ask CMS to provide examples of “negative unintended consequences” (other than patient harm) and a process for stakeholders to appeal a removal decision based on claimed unintended consequences.

[P35] Small hospice operator: For §418.312(b)(3)(viii), request that CMS include cost-benefit templates and allow hospices to submit cost burden data before removing measures on cost grounds.

[P36] Hospital system/non-hospice provider: Request clarification on scope of items/services/drugs that can be designated “unrelated” (§418.24(c)) and whether determinations are clinical, administrative, or both, plus an appeals process for providers who disagree.

[P37] Patient advocate: Insist the election statement addendum required under §418.24(c) include plain-language explanations of what “unrelated” means and how beneficiaries can contest determinations.

[P38] Legal advocate: For §418.24(c) obligations to contain specified information, request that CMS publish a standard form to prevent variability and to ensure legal sufficiency in documenting beneficiary choices.

[P39] Health plan: Reiterate that non-hospice providers and Medicare contractors should not be required to sign the addendum (§418.24(c)(9)), but ask that recipients acknowledge receipt electronically for tracking while preserving the no-signature rule.

[P40] Records manager: For §418.24(c)(10), request that the rule explicitly permit automated electronic time stamps and specify acceptable audit trails to verify date furnished.

[P41] Patient rights organization: Urge CMS to clarify whether the 5-day real-time requirement in §418.24(d)(1) permits immediate electronic delivery at admission and whether verbal delivery plus later written confirmation satisfies the rule.

[P42] Hospice chain: Request that the 3-day requirement in §418.24(d)(2) be measured in business days and include an exception for extraordinary circumstances (e.g., natural disasters, mass-casualty events).

[P43] Clinical director: Ask for examples of plan-of-care changes that trigger §418.24(d)(3) updates and propose that only clinically material changes require a new addendum to minimize administrative churn.

[P44] Ombudsman: Concern that exceptions in §418.24(d)(4) allowing non-furnishing if death/revocation/discharge occur may be abused; request that hospices be required to notify authorized representatives and document attempts to deliver the addendum.

[P45] Quality auditor: Recommend CMS require a standardized reason-code list for documenting why an addendum was not furnished (§418.24(d)(4)) to permit consistent auditing.

[P46] EHR vendor: Request technical specifications for integrating the addendum into electronic medical records so that when completed before discharge it automatically becomes part of the chart as required by §418.24(d)(4).

[P47] Patient/family: Seek an exception to §418.24(d)(5) so that even if a beneficiary dies or revokes before signing, the hospice must provide the completed addendum to the surviving designated representative or primary care provider.

[P48] Compliance consultant: Ask for guidance on minimal acceptable documentation for reasons an addendum was not signed under §418.24(d)(5), including required timestamps and witness statements.

[P49] Health information management: Request clarity on access controls and retention scheduling when an unsigned addendum “becomes part of the patient’s medical record” under §418.24(d)(5).

[P50] Educator association: Urge CMS to publish the full list of subjects in §418.76(b)(3) and to permit blended assessment approaches as long as every listed subject is evaluated (§418.76(c)(1)).

[P51] Surveyor/training program: Ask that CMS permit validated simulation or objective structured clinical examinations (OSCEs) as equivalent to direct observation for the subject areas in §418.76(b)(3)(i),(iii),(ix),(x),(xi) when patient access is not feasible.

[P52] Accreditor: Recommend standardized acceptable methods (written/oral/observation) and minimum scoring rubrics for the remaining subject areas under §418.76(c)(1) to ensure comparability across hospices.

[P53] State agency: Request clarification of the triggers and evidentiary standard for verifying an “area of concern” during on-site visits (§418.76(h)(1)(iii)) and whether third-party complaints must be corroborated.

[P54] Hospice provider: Object that conducting competency evaluations of all “related skills” under §418.76(h)(1)(iii) may require re-testing of broad skill sets; ask CMS to limit scope to skills with reasonable clinical connection and provide examples.

[P55] Financial analyst: Request CMS to model and publish the fiscal impact of the CPI-based cap adjustments (§418.309(a)(1)) and the alternative percentage-update method (§418.309(a)(2)) on hospice revenues across multiple years.

[P56] Data vendor: Seek precise technical specifications and transmission standards for submission of admission and discharge HIS files (§418.312(b)(1)), including allowable formats, error tolerances, and resubmission rules.

[P57] Privacy officer: For §418.312(b)(2) stating administrative data “are required and automatically satisfy HQRP,” request clarification that required administrative data used are limited to de-identified or minimum necessary elements and that patient consent/notice obligations are observed.

[P58] Stakeholder coalition: Request that CMS publish a public process (timeline, notice, public comment) for any measure removals under §418.312(b)(3) rather than relying solely on internal CMS determinations.

[P59] Equity advocate: When considering removal under §418.312(b)(3)(i) for uniformly high performance, ask CMS to analyze whether high performance is universal across demographics and geographies to avoid masking inequities.

[P60] Outcomes researcher: For removals under §418.312(b)(3)(ii), request that CMS define the evidence standard (e.g., randomized data, observational studies) required to prove lack of outcome association.

[P61] Clinician guideline group: Recommend that before removing measures under §418.312(b)(3)(iii), CMS convene clinical experts to vet the guideline misalignment and publish rationale.

[P62] Measure alignment specialist: Suggest CMS require demonstration that the broader measure in §418.312(b)(3)(iv) has been validated in hospice populations prior to replacing a hospice-specific measure.

[P63] Quality improvement working group: For §418.312(b)(3)(v), ask CMS to define acceptable temporal windows that constitute “more proximal” measures and provide examples.

[P64] Health economist: For §418.312(b)(3)(vi), request CMS to quantify the minimum strength of association (e.g., correlation or predictive value) required to justify removal in favor of an alternative measure.

[P65] Policy researcher: For §418.312(b)(3)(vii), ask CMS to enumerate specific non-harm unintended consequences (e.g., gaming, resource diversion) that could justify removal and provide monitoring strategies to detect them.

[P66] Small provider coalition: For §418.312(b)(3)(viii), request that CMS accept provider-submitted cost data and perform transparent cost-benefit analyses before deciding to remove measures on cost grounds.

Labor/education association: Recommend allowing trained actors or standardized patients as pseudo-patients and specify minimum training/certification standards so hospices are not forced to recruit actual vulnerable patients.

Pharmacy/provider group: Supportive comment that non-hospice providers and Medicare contractors may request the addendum (§418.24(c)), but ask for a process timeline and secure transmission method to protect patient privacy when third parties request the list.

Privacy advocate: Express concern that permitting Medicare contractors and non-hospice providers to request the addendum (§418.24(c)) could increase unnecessary disclosure of sensitive patient information; request explicit limits and HIPAA-aligned safeguards.

Hospice association: Seek the full text or list of the “specified required items” in §418.24(c) referenced in the preamble so hospices can assess administrative burden; recommend publishing a template addendum.

Consumer advocate: Support requirement that the addendum include name, signature, date, and statement that signing is only acknowledgment (§418.24(c)(9)) but request that the statement language be standardized and patient-friendly (plain language, large font).

Legal expert: Question whether the required signature in §418.24(c)(9) may be obtained electronically and request explicit authorization for e-signatures and procedures for representatives signing on behalf of incapacitated individuals.

Non-hospice provider: Request clarification that the exception in §418.24(c)(9) explicitly allows external providers and Medicare contractors to receive the addendum without signing; ask for confirmation that recipients may rely on the addendum without signature.

Hospice compliance officer: Ask for guidance on what format and time-stamped documentation satisfies the “date the hospice furnished the addendum” requirement in §418.24(c)(10) (e.g., mailed date, electronic delivery receipt).

Hospice operator: Object to the five-day turnaround for furnishing an addendum requested within the first 5 days (§418.24(d)(1)) as administratively burdensome during admissions; request extension to 7–10 business days or allowance for immediate electronic delivery.

Patient advocate: Argue that the 5-day requirement (§418.24(d)(1)) is appropriate to ensure patients and caregivers have timely notice of items/services deemed unrelated; oppose extending the deadline.
Hospice operator: Request clarification whether the 3-day timeframe in §418.24(d)(2) applies to calendar days or business days and propose changing to business days to accommodate weekends/holidays.

Clinician group: Seek specification of what constitutes a “change to the plan of care” that triggers the update obligation in §418.24(d)(3) (minor vs. major changes) to avoid excessive, frequent addendum updates.

Family caregiver organization: Recommend requiring hospices to proactively provide addendum updates whenever an item/service previously deemed related becomes unrelated (and vice versa) so families are fully informed (§418.24(d)(3)).

Hospice association: Request clarification of the scope of the exception in §418.24(d)(4) — if the patient dies/revokes/discharges before addendum furnished, does the hospice still need to notify non-hospice providers who requested it?

Legal expert: Ask that §418.24(d)(4) require hospices to use best efforts to furnish the addendum prior to discharge/revocation/death and to document what steps were taken, to prevent arbitrary failure to furnish.

CMS auditor: Support the documentation requirement in §418.24(d)(4) that hospices note reasons for not furnishing the addendum, but request standardized documentation fields for auditability and comparability across hospices.

Health records manager: Clarify how addenda completed before discharge become part of the medical record (§418.24(d)(4)) — specify whether scanned copies, electronic admission modules, or separate forms meet record retention and accessibility requirements.

Patient rights group: Concern that §418.24(d)(5) exception (not required to furnish if beneficiary dies/revokes/discharged before signing) could deprive families and other providers of important information; request that hospices still be required to furnish unsigned addenda to authorized representatives when feasible.

Compliance officer: Ask for a required taxonomy or codes for documenting reasons why an addendum was not signed in §418.24(d)(5) to facilitate monitoring and reduce ambiguous entries like “not available.”

Health information management society: Recommend retention and access rules when addendum becomes part of patient’s medical record (§418.24(d)(5)), including minimum retention period and patient access rights.

Training program director: Support requirement that competency evaluations cover all subjects in §418.76(b)(3) (§418.76(c)(1)) but request that CMS publish the precise subject list and standardized competency checklists to ensure consistent evaluations.

Nursing association: Ask for clarification of what tasks are encompassed by paragraphs (b)(3)(i),(iii),(ix),(x),(xi) that must be evaluated by direct observation, and request flexibility to use simulation when direct patient observation is unsafe.

Safety advocate: Insist that direct observation requirements in §418.76(c)(1) not force trainees to perform invasive or distressing tasks on vulnerable patients; allow trained pseudo-patients or high-fidelity simulation instead.

Hospice educator: Support permission to use written/oral exams or simulation for remaining subject areas (§418.76(c)(1)) but request guidance on minimum pass thresholds and validation of written/oral exam content.
Labor union: Request that competency evaluation methods allowed in §418.76(c)(1) include a requirement for periodic re-evaluation frequency and that simulation scenarios be standardized.
Surveyor organization: Ask for examples or criteria of how an “area of concern” is to be identified during on-site visits (§418.76(h)(1)(iii)) to promote consistent survey determinations.

Hospice provider: Concern that the obligation in §418.76(h)(1)(iii) to conduct competency evaluation of all related skills when one deficiency is found is overly broad and could require re-testing of unrelated skill sets; request limiting “related skills” to a narrowly defined set.

Patient safety group: Support the requirement in §418.76(h)(1)(iii) that deficits trigger evaluation of related skills, but ask CMS to define “related” to ensure critical competency gaps are not missed.

Workforce advocate: Request that §418.76(h)(1)(iii) include timelines for when the aide must complete the competency evaluation after deficiency verification to avoid prolonged placement of underqualified aides.

Legal counsel: Ask whether aides may be restricted from performing certain tasks pending completion of the competency evaluation under §418.76(h)(1)(iii), and request guidance on temporary work restrictions to protect patients and reduce liability.

parsed_claims.claim_text: Fiscal policy group: Question the rationale for using CPI medical care for inflation adjustment in §418.309(a)(1) for certain accounting years and request analysis showing that CPI-Medical Care accurately reflects hospice cost inflation versus other indices.

Hospice association: Oppose changing the inflation adjustment mechanism in §418.309(a)(1) without transitional guidance; request impact estimates on aggregate cap levels for affected accounting years.
Economist: Request clarification of why CPI change is measured from March 1984 to the fifth month of the cap year (§418.309(a)(1)) and ask CMS to provide worked examples for multiple cap years.

Fiscal watchdog: Support §418.309(a)(2) linking cap updates to the hospice payment rate percentage, but request transparency about how productivity adjustments are applied and whether they will reduce cap levels.

Small hospice operator: Warn that productivity or other adjustments referenced in §418.309(a)(2) could create unpredictability in cap calculations for accounting years after 2016; request multi-year schedules or advance notice.

Quality improvement organization: Support requirement to submit admission and discharge HIS for each patient (§418.312(b)(1)) but request explicit guidance on exclusions (e.g., very short stays, readmissions) to reduce duplicative reporting.

Small rural hospice: Express concern about administrative burden and resource strain of completing both admission and discharge HIS for every patient regardless of payer or age (§418.312(b)(1)); request phased implementation or funding for smaller providers.

Data privacy advocate: Question the statement that administrative data used for hospice quality measures “are required and automatically satisfy HQRP requirements” (§418.312(b)(2)) — ask CMS to describe data de-identification safeguards and how patient consent is handled.

Measure developer: Support CMS authority under §418.312(b)(3) to remove measures but request transparent, public criteria and stakeholder notice periods before removal to allow feedback and re-tooling.

Consumer group: Concern that removal criterion §418.312(b)(3)(i) (uniformly high performance) could mask disparities among subpopulations; request that CMS analyze measure performance stratified by race, geography, and hospice size before removal.

Clinician society: Request that CMS require evidence that removing a measure under §418.312(b)(3)(ii) (no link to patient outcomes) will not inadvertently reduce focus on important aspects of care; demand publication of supporting analyses.

Professional guideline body: Endorse removal under §418.312(b)(3)(iii) when a measure is no longer aligned with current clinical guidelines, but request a formal crosswalk process to demonstrate non-alignment.

Health services researcher: Recommend that before invoking §418.312(b)(3)(iv) (availability of a more broadly applicable measure), CMS provide psychometric comparisons showing superior validity and reliability of the broader measure.
Quality metric expert: For §418.312(b)(3)(v) (timing), request definition of “proximal” and criteria for judging temporal association with outcomes; ask for evidence thresholds required for removal.
Outcomes researcher: For §418.312(b)(3)(vi) (stronger association), ask CMS to publish statistical methods and minimum effect sizes that would support replacing a measure.

Policy analyst: For §418.312(b)(3)(vii), ask CMS to provide examples of “negative unintended consequences” (other than patient harm) and a process for stakeholders to appeal a removal decision based on claimed unintended consequences.
Small hospice operator: For §418.312(b)(3)(viii), request that CMS include cost-benefit templates and allow hospices to submit cost burden data before removing measures on cost grounds.

Hospital system/non-hospice provider: Request clarification on scope of items/services/drugs that can be designated “unrelated” (§418.24(c)) and whether determinations are clinical, administrative, or both, plus an appeals process for providers who disagree.
Patient advocate: Insist the election statement addendum required under §418.24(c) include plain-language explanations of what “unrelated” means and how beneficiaries can contest determinations.

Legal advocate: For §418.24(c) obligations to contain specified information, request that CMS publish a standard form to prevent variability and to ensure legal sufficiency in documenting beneficiary choices.

Health plan: Reiterate that non-hospice providers and Medicare contractors should not be required to sign the addendum (§418.24(c)(9)), but ask that recipients acknowledge receipt electronically for tracking while preserving the no-signature rule.
Records manager: For §418.24(c)(10), request that the rule explicitly permit automated electronic time stamps and specify acceptable audit trails to verify date furnished.

Patient rights organization: Urge CMS to clarify whether the 5-day real-time requirement in §418.24(d)(1) permits immediate electronic delivery at admission and whether verbal delivery plus later written confirmation satisfies the rule.

Hospice chain: Request that the 3-day requirement in §418.24(d)(2) be measured in business days and include an exception for extraordinary circumstances (e.g., natural disasters, mass-casualty events).

Clinical director: Ask for examples of plan-of-care changes that trigger §418.24(d)(3) updates and propose that only clinically material changes require a new addendum to minimize administrative churn.

Ombudsman: Concern that exceptions in §418.24(d)(4) allowing non-furnishing if death/revocation/discharge occur may be abused; request that hospices be required to notify authorized representatives and document attempts to deliver the addendum.
Quality auditor: Recommend CMS require a standardized reason-code list for documenting why an addendum was not furnished (§418.24(d)(4)) to permit consistent auditing.

EHR vendor: Request technical specifications for integrating the addendum into electronic medical records so that when completed before discharge it automatically becomes part of the chart as required by §418.24(d)(4).

Patient/family: Seek an exception to §418.24(d)(5) so that even if a beneficiary dies or revokes before signing, the hospice must provide the completed addendum to the surviving designated representative or primary care provider.
Compliance consultant: Ask for guidance on minimal acceptable documentation for reasons an addendum was not signed under §418.24(d)(5), including required timestamps and witness statements.
Health information management: Request clarity on access controls and retention scheduling when an unsigned addendum “becomes part of the patient’s medical record” under §418.24(d)(5).
Educator association: Urge CMS to publish the full list of subjects in §418.76(b)(3) and to permit blended assessment approaches as long as every listed subject is evaluated (§418.76(c)(1)).

Surveyor/training program: Ask that CMS permit validated simulation or objective structured clinical examinations (OSCEs) as equivalent to direct observation for the subject areas in §418.76(b)(3)(i),(iii),(ix),(x),(xi) when patient access is not feasible.

Accreditor: Recommend standardized acceptable methods (written/oral/observation) and minimum scoring rubrics for the remaining subject areas under §418.76(c)(1) to ensure comparability across hospices.

State agency: Request clarification of the triggers and evidentiary standard for verifying an “area of concern” during on-site visits (§418.76(h)(1)(iii)) and whether third-party complaints must be corroborated.

Hospice provider: Object that conducting competency evaluations of all “related skills” under §418.76(h)(1)(iii) may require re-testing of broad skill sets; ask CMS to limit scope to skills with reasonable clinical connection and provide examples.

Financial analyst: Request CMS to model and publish the fiscal impact of the CPI-based cap adjustments (§418.309(a)(1)) and the alternative percentage-update method (§418.309(a)(2)) on hospice revenues across multiple years.

Data vendor: Seek precise technical specifications and transmission standards for submission of admission and discharge HIS files (§418.312(b)(1)), including allowable formats, error tolerances, and resubmission rules.

Privacy officer: For §418.312(b)(2) stating administrative data “are required and automatically satisfy HQRP,” request clarification that required administrative data used are limited to de-identified or minimum necessary elements and that patient consent/notice obligations are observed.

Stakeholder coalition: Request that CMS publish a public process (timeline, notice, public comment) for any measure removals under §418.312(b)(3) rather than relying solely on internal CMS determinations.

Equity advocate: When considering removal under §418.312(b)(3)(i) for uniformly high performance, ask CMS to analyze whether high performance is universal across demographics and geographies to avoid masking inequities.
Outcomes researcher: For removals under §418.312(b)(3)(ii), request that CMS define the evidence standard (e.g., randomized data, observational studies) required to prove lack of outcome association.
Clinician guideline group: Recommend that before removing measures under §418.312(b)(3)(iii), CMS convene clinical experts to vet the guideline misalignment and publish rationale.
Measure alignment specialist: Suggest CMS require demonstration that the broader measure in §418.312(b)(3)(iv) has been validated in hospice populations prior to replacing a hospice-specific measure.
Quality improvement working group: For §418.312(b)(3)(v), ask CMS to define acceptable temporal windows that constitute “more proximal” measures and provide examples.

Health economist: For §418.312(b)(3)(vi), request CMS to quantify the minimum strength of association (e.g., correlation or predictive value) required to justify removal in favor of an alternative measure.

Policy researcher: For §418.312(b)(3)(vii), ask CMS to enumerate specific non-harm unintended consequences (e.g., gaming, resource diversion) that could justify removal and provide monitoring strategies to detect them.

Small provider coalition: For §418.312(b)(3)(viii), request that CMS accept provider-submitted cost data and perform transparent cost-benefit analyses before deciding to remove measures on cost grounds.

[P1] The electronic-only registration requirement on the USCIS website imposes undue burdens on small employers and pro se petitioners who lack access to reliable internet or tech support; request alternative paper or assisted filing options.

[P1] Requiring registration by the petitioner or its attorney/accredited representative excludes employees or third-party recruiters who commonly prepare registrations; clarify whether authorized agents and staffing firms can register on behalf of employers.

[P1] The rule should require USCIS to provide multi-language guidance and accessible interfaces (e.g., screen-reader compatibility) for the mandatory electronic registration to avoid discrimination against non-English-speaking petitioners.

[P2] The cross-reference to paragraphs (h)(8)(iii)(A)(5) and (6) for ranking and selection is vague; commenters should request explicit, consolidated criteria and examples in the regulation text rather than by reference.

[P3] Ranking registrations solely by the highest OES wage level that the proffered wage equals or exceeds will disadvantage entry-level positions and industries where wages are compressed; ask USCIS to consider factors beyond OES level such as occupation-specific demand.

[P3] Using the “highest corresponding OES wage level” as a determinative ranking metric may create perverse incentives to inflate proffered wages solely to increase lottery odds, distorting labor market practices.

[P4] Treating proffered wages based on other legitimate sources as equivalent to OES level I (when below OES I) penalizes employers in areas or occupations where OES is outdated or unrepresentative; request allowance for other reliable prevailing wage determinations to be used for ranking.

[P4] The provision that downgrades non-OES prevailing wage-based offers below OES Level I creates inconsistency with DHS’s acceptance of alternative prevailing wage sources for LCA purposes; recommend harmonization.

[P5] For multiple work locations/positions, ranking by the lowest OES wage level the proffered wage equals or exceeds will unfairly penalize assignments with a minor remote component in a low-wage area; propose allowing weighting or separate registrations per worksite.

[P5] The rule lacks guidance on how employers should handle hybrid or telework arrangements for ranking by multiple locations; request clear definitions and examples to avoid inconsistent USCIS adjudications.

[P6] Ranking based on the OES wage level "matching the position's requirements" when no current OES data exists is ambiguous and invites arbitrary determinations; demand a transparent methodology and appeals process.

[P6] Where no current OES data exists, USCIS should permit use of contemporaneous Department of Labor or certified prevailing wage determinations rather than an undefined matching process.

[P7] Ranking/selecting by descending OES wage level (IV to I) on oversubscription effectively prioritizes higher-paid beneficiaries and may disadvantage U.S. workers and lower-wage sectors; challenge the policy rationale and request empirical justification.

[P7] The abrupt preference for higher OES wage levels risks concentrating cap numbers among large employers who can pay more, disadvantaging startups and nonprofits; propose set-asides or corrective mechanisms.

[P8] When no current OES data exists, defaulting to a wage level tied to “position requirements” could be administratively unworkable; request defined standards for how position requirements translate to OES levels.

[P9] Random selection within a wage level lacks transparency — request that USCIS publish the randomization algorithm, seed handling, and independent audit procedures to ensure fairness.

[P9] The rule should require notice to registrants whose entries were in a wage level that underwent random selection, including their random draw number and selection probability.

[P10] Applying the same wage-level descending ranking during the initial registration period duplicates concerns that wealthier employers are favored; request modeling of impacts and consideration of alternative prioritization (e.g., degree-based, country caps).

[P11] If no OES data during the initial registration period, ranking based on position requirements without a defined process will create inconsistent outcomes between different adjudicators; ask for standardized guidance.

[P12] Random selection among many registrations at a wage level needs safeguards to prevent gaming (e.g., coordinated filings by related entities); request anti-fraud rules to detect and treat related-party bulk filings as one unit.

[P13] Prioritizing the advanced degree exemption registrations by highest OES wage level favors higher-paying institutions and sectors with many advanced-degree holders; law schools, hospitals, and universities should request explicit protection for nonprofit and research employers.

[P14] Where no OES data exists for advanced degree exemption registrations, the "matching" process is undefined; request that USCIS accept academic classifications or DOL determinations to set wage-level equivalents.

[P15] Randomly selecting among advanced-degree registrations at a wage level may disadvantage international students from lower-paying disciplines; suggest including educational priority or geographic diversity adjustments.

[P16] Ranking remaining initial-period registrations that may be counted again toward advanced-degree exemption by wage level may reduce transparency; request disclosure of which registrations are considered "remaining" and how USCIS determines eligibility for recounting.

[P17] The fallback to position-requirements-based ranking for remaining advanced-degree registrations without current OES data lacks clear standards; demand explicit rules and an appeal mechanism.

[P18] Random selection among remaining advanced-degree registrations should be accompanied by publicly available logs and auditing procedures to ensure randomness and guard against manipulation.

[P19] Keeping unselected registrations on reserve for the fiscal year creates uncertainty about selection timing for employers and beneficiaries; request mandatory periodic status updates and an expected timeline for reserve usage.

[P19] Registrations “on reserve” may unfairly tie up employers' ability to recruit and plan; ask USCIS to permit employers to withdraw and replace reserve registrations without penalty.

[P20] When selecting additional registrations from reserve, USCIS should be required to follow the same ranking and selection standards with public notice about which reserved registrations are being selected and why.

[P21] The authority to reopen the registration period if reserves are exhausted could be abused to favor later filers; request strict criteria, advance notice periods, and stakeholder consultation before any reopening.

[P21] Reopening registration should not be left discretionary; ask for objective triggers (e.g., exact exhaustion metrics) and a fixed minimum public notice window before reopening.

[P22] USCIS monitoring and public notification when necessary number received is essential, but the rule should require real-time or near-real-time public dashboards with counts by wage level, registrations received, and projected shortfalls.

[P22] Require USCIS to publish historical registration volumes and wage-level distributions to allow employers to make informed decisions prior to filing.

[P23] When selecting additional registrations, applying the same ranking rules is logical, but commenters should demand that USCIS explain how prior selections and demographic impacts are accounted for to avoid compounding inequities.

[P24] The rule should mandate advance notice (e.g., 72 hours) on the USCIS website before any reopened registration period begins, and provide the exact opening time in Eastern Time to avoid confusion.

[P25] Allowing filing only on the basis of a valid selected registration is reasonable, but USCIS must clarify the validity period of the selection and whether beneficiaries can change employers between selection and filing.

[P26] The requirement to file the petition within the filing period in the selection notice needs clarity on time-zone, receipt vs. postmark rules, and acceptance of courier or overnight deliveries.

[P27] The prohibition on substituting the beneficiary or transferring the registration prevents legitimate business reorganizations or acquisitions from using a selected registration; request exceptions for mergers, asset transfers, and bona fide successor employers.

[P27] Preventing transfer of registration to another petitioner will disadvantage staffing agencies and employers using agents; propose narrowly tailored exceptions allowing transfers when there is an employer-of-record or documented contractual relationship.

[P28] USCIS's authority to reject/deny petitions based on unselected or invalid registrations should be coupled with a mandatory pre-decision notice and an opportunity to cure minor technical defects in the registration.

[P29] Treating a registration as invalid if its fee is declined/rejected/canceled after submission is harsh for technical payment failures; request USCIS permit a short cure period to remedy payment issues before invalidation.

[P29] Non-refundable fee policy combined with immediate invalidation for payment problems could penalize small employers subject to bank payment delays; ask for refund exceptions for system errors and incorrect fee processing by USCIS.

[P30] The non-refundable registration fee due at submission may discourage legitimate employers from participating, especially non-profits and universities; ask for fee waivers or reduced fees for qualifying small or nonprofit entities.

[P30] Require USCIS to disclose fee amount, refund policies, and dispute mechanisms prior to registration opening to avoid surprise and litigation.

[P31] USCIS may reject or deny petitions if registration contains inaccurate or fraudulent facts, but the rule should set standards for materiality and provide notice and an opportunity to correct inadvertent errors.

[P31] Clarify whether factual errors in the employer identification number, job title, or wage amount that are non-material will result in denial, and if so, provide a cure window.

[P32] The discretionary authority to deny or revoke petitions that appear intended to unfairly decrease proffered wages allows broad agency action; request clear, objective criteria and examples of what constitutes “unfair” behavior.

[P32] USCIS should impose penalties (e.g., debarment) for bad-faith manipulation of wage levels, but only after a formal investigation and adjudicative process with appeal rights.

[P33] The non-denial clause (will not deny solely because proffered wage differs if not corresponding to a lower OES level) is helpful, but needs clarification on how USCIS will determine whether a change “corresponds” to a lower level.

[P33] Request guidance on acceptable documentation to show that a different proffered wage does not correspond to a lower OES level to protect employers from arbitrary denials.

[P34] The rule's selection of petitions if cap met within first five business days should be revisited; forcing selection based on the first five days advantages employers who can mobilize filings immediately and disadvantages smaller employers.

[P35] Ranking/selecting petitions by highest OES wage level when over-subscribed at receipt stage duplicates earlier concerns about favoring high-wage employers; ask for socioeconomic impact analysis.

[P36] For petitions lacking current OES data, the fallback to position-requirements-based ranking again risks inconsistent treatment; demand uniform guidance and opportunity for employers to submit supporting evidence.

[P37] Ranking petitions with proffered wage below OES level I into Level I category may mask the true wage and fail to protect beneficiaries from underpayment; suggest USCIS require additional attestations when proposed wages are below OES I.

[P38] Ranking petitions the same way even when using non-OES prevailing wage sources may create conflicts with DOL wage methodologies; recommend harmonization and a mechanism for resolving discrepancies.

[P39] Random selection among petitions at a wage level should exclude petitions filed by related entities to prevent gaming; propose rules treating common-control employers as one entity for random draws.

[P40] The process to determine sufficiency for advanced degree exemption after regular cap processing lacks transparency; request that USCIS publish the formula and historic conversion rates used in projections.

[P41] Using historical approvals, denials, and revocations to calculate numbers needed for the advanced degree exemption could perpetuate prior biases; ask USCIS to use neutral projections and to disclose the data and assumptions used.

[P42] Requiring USCIS to monitor and announce the projected advanced degree receipt date is useful, but USCIS should commit to real-time dashboards and email subscription alerts for registrants.

[P43] Selecting petitions for advanced degree exemption if cap met within first five business days has the same fairness concerns; request alternative windows or rotational priorities for small employers and nonprofit research institutions.

[P44] Ranking/selecting for advanced degree exemption by descending OES wage level will concentrate slots among high-paying employers of advanced-degree holders; propose a percentage of the exemption reserved for non-profit educational and research institutions.

[P45] For advanced-degree petitions with no OES data, adopting an opaque “position requirements” standard is unacceptable; demand explicit acceptance of university job classifications and certified wage determinations.

[P46] Ranking advanced-degree petitions with proffered wage below OES I into Level I may undermine labor protections for advanced-degree beneficiaries; recommend USCIS require additional LCA attestations and DOL sign-off for such petitions.

[P47] Treating non-OES prevailing wage sources the same for ranking may induce inconsistent cross-agency standards; ask DHS to coordinate with DOL to adopt a single prevailing wage framework.

[P48] Random selection among advanced-degree petitions must include safeguards against manipulation by large employers filing many petitions across related entities; request affiliation rules and aggregation limits.

[P49] The discretionary denial authority for inaccurate registration statements should be tied to defined standards of intent — negligent versus willful misstatement — with proportional remedies.

[P50] Automatic denial for fraudulent or materially misrepresentative statements is acceptable, but USCIS must define "material" and ensure due process with notice and opportunity to rebut before denial.

[P51] Denial of petitions not based on a valid registration should allow equitable relief where employers relied on USCIS errors or where third-party agents made unauthorized filings; require cure procedures.

[P52] The requirement that registrations represent legitimate job offers is vague; request concrete criteria and examples of what constitutes a legitimate offer to avoid arbitrary determinations.

[P53] USCIS discretion to deny new/amended petitions intended to unfairly increase selection odds must be balanced with a clear process, evidentiary standards, and appeal rights to prevent misuse.

[P54] The prohibition against denying solely because a proffered wage differs if it does not equate to a lower OES level needs clear rules on how level equivalence is measured and documented.

[P55] Identifying untrue/inaccurate statements in forms as grounds for action should include standards for harmless versus material misstatements and provide opportunities to correct clerical errors.

[P56] Labeling filing of new/amended petitions intended to unfairly increase selection odds as grounds for action may chill legitimate employment changes; define "intended to unfairly increase" and provide safe-harbor procedures.

[P57] The clause preventing revocation solely because of wage differences absent a lower OES level must be accompanied by a transparent process for wage-level comparisons and evidentiary requirements to protect employers from arbitrary revocation.

Random selection among many registrations at a wage level needs safeguards to prevent gaming (e.g., coordinated filings by related entities); request anti-fraud rules to detect and treat related-party bulk filings as one unit.

Prioritizing the advanced degree exemption registrations by highest OES wage level favors higher-paying institutions and sectors with many advanced-degree holders; law schools, hospitals, and universities should request explicit protection for nonprofit and research employers.

Where no OES data exists for advanced degree exemption registrations, the "matching" process is undefined; request that USCIS accept academic classifications or DOL determinations to set wage-level equivalents.

Randomly selecting among advanced-degree registrations at a wage level may disadvantage international students from lower-paying disciplines; suggest including educational priority or geographic diversity adjustments.

Ranking remaining initial-period registrations that may be counted again toward advanced-degree exemption by wage level may reduce transparency; request disclosure of which registrations are considered "remaining" and how USCIS determines eligibility for recounting.
The fallback to position-requirements-based ranking for remaining advanced-degree registrations without current OES data lacks clear standards; demand explicit rules and an appeal mechanism.
Random selection among remaining advanced-degree registrations should be accompanied by publicly available logs and auditing procedures to ensure randomness and guard against manipulation.

Keeping unselected registrations on reserve for the fiscal year creates uncertainty about selection timing for employers and beneficiaries; request mandatory periodic status updates and an expected timeline for reserve usage.
Registrations “on reserve” may unfairly tie up employers' ability to recruit and plan; ask USCIS to permit employers to withdraw and replace reserve registrations without penalty.

When selecting additional registrations from reserve, USCIS should be required to follow the same ranking and selection standards with public notice about which reserved registrations are being selected and why.

The authority to reopen the registration period if reserves are exhausted could be abused to favor later filers; request strict criteria, advance notice periods, and stakeholder consultation before any reopening.
Reopening registration should not be left discretionary; ask for objective triggers (e.g., exact exhaustion metrics) and a fixed minimum public notice window before reopening.

USCIS monitoring and public notification when necessary number received is essential, but the rule should require real-time or near-real-time public dashboards with counts by wage level, registrations received, and projected shortfalls.
Require USCIS to publish historical registration volumes and wage-level distributions to allow employers to make informed decisions prior to filing.

When selecting additional registrations, applying the same ranking rules is logical, but commenters should demand that USCIS explain how prior selections and demographic impacts are accounted for to avoid compounding inequities.
The rule should mandate advance notice (e.g., 72 hours) on the USCIS website before any reopened registration period begins, and provide the exact opening time in Eastern Time to avoid confusion.

Allowing filing only on the basis of a valid selected registration is reasonable, but USCIS must clarify the validity period of the selection and whether beneficiaries can change employers between selection and filing.
The requirement to file the petition within the filing period in the selection notice needs clarity on time-zone, receipt vs. postmark rules, and acceptance of courier or overnight deliveries.

The prohibition on substituting the beneficiary or transferring the registration prevents legitimate business reorganizations or acquisitions from using a selected registration; request exceptions for mergers, asset transfers, and bona fide successor employers.

Preventing transfer of registration to another petitioner will disadvantage staffing agencies and employers using agents; propose narrowly tailored exceptions allowing transfers when there is an employer-of-record or documented contractual relationship.

USCIS's authority to reject/deny petitions based on unselected or invalid registrations should be coupled with a mandatory pre-decision notice and an opportunity to cure minor technical defects in the registration.

Treating a registration as invalid if its fee is declined/rejected/canceled after submission is harsh for technical payment failures; request USCIS permit a short cure period to remedy payment issues before invalidation.

Non-refundable fee policy combined with immediate invalidation for payment problems could penalize small employers subject to bank payment delays; ask for refund exceptions for system errors and incorrect fee processing by USCIS.

The non-refundable registration fee due at submission may discourage legitimate employers from participating, especially non-profits and universities; ask for fee waivers or reduced fees for qualifying small or nonprofit entities.
Require USCIS to disclose fee amount, refund policies, and dispute mechanisms prior to registration opening to avoid surprise and litigation.

USCIS may reject or deny petitions if registration contains inaccurate or fraudulent facts, but the rule should set standards for materiality and provide notice and an opportunity to correct inadvertent errors.
Clarify whether factual errors in the employer identification number, job title, or wage amount that are non-material will result in denial, and if so, provide a cure window.

The discretionary authority to deny or revoke petitions that appear intended to unfairly decrease proffered wages allows broad agency action; request clear, objective criteria and examples of what constitutes “unfair” behavior.
USCIS should impose penalties (e.g., debarment) for bad-faith manipulation of wage levels, but only after a formal investigation and adjudicative process with appeal rights.

The non-denial clause (will not deny solely because proffered wage differs if not corresponding to a lower OES level) is helpful, but needs clarification on how USCIS will determine whether a change “corresponds” to a lower level.
Request guidance on acceptable documentation to show that a different proffered wage does not correspond to a lower OES level to protect employers from arbitrary denials.

The rule's selection of petitions if cap met within first five business days should be revisited; forcing selection based on the first five days advantages employers who can mobilize filings immediately and disadvantages smaller employers.
Ranking/selecting petitions by highest OES wage level when over-subscribed at receipt stage duplicates earlier concerns about favoring high-wage employers; ask for socioeconomic impact analysis.

For petitions lacking current OES data, the fallback to position-requirements-based ranking again risks inconsistent treatment; demand uniform guidance and opportunity for employers to submit supporting evidence.

Ranking petitions with proffered wage below OES level I into Level I category may mask the true wage and fail to protect beneficiaries from underpayment; suggest USCIS require additional attestations when proposed wages are below OES I.
Ranking petitions the same way even when using non-OES prevailing wage sources may create conflicts with DOL wage methodologies; recommend harmonization and a mechanism for resolving discrepancies.
Random selection among petitions at a wage level should exclude petitions filed by related entities to prevent gaming; propose rules treating common-control employers as one entity for random draws.

The process to determine sufficiency for advanced degree exemption after regular cap processing lacks transparency; request that USCIS publish the formula and historic conversion rates used in projections.

Using historical approvals, denials, and revocations to calculate numbers needed for the advanced degree exemption could perpetuate prior biases; ask USCIS to use neutral projections and to disclose the data and assumptions used.
Requiring USCIS to monitor and announce the projected advanced degree receipt date is useful, but USCIS should commit to real-time dashboards and email subscription alerts for registrants.

Selecting petitions for advanced degree exemption if cap met within first five business days has the same fairness concerns; request alternative windows or rotational priorities for small employers and nonprofit research institutions.

Ranking/selecting for advanced degree exemption by descending OES wage level will concentrate slots among high-paying employers of advanced-degree holders; propose a percentage of the exemption reserved for non-profit educational and research institutions.

For advanced-degree petitions with no OES data, adopting an opaque “position requirements” standard is unacceptable; demand explicit acceptance of university job classifications and certified wage determinations.

Ranking advanced-degree petitions with proffered wage below OES I into Level I may undermine labor protections for advanced-degree beneficiaries; recommend USCIS require additional LCA attestations and DOL sign-off for such petitions.
Treating non-OES prevailing wage sources the same for ranking may induce inconsistent cross-agency standards; ask DHS to coordinate with DOL to adopt a single prevailing wage framework.

Random selection among advanced-degree petitions must include safeguards against manipulation by large employers filing many petitions across related entities; request affiliation rules and aggregation limits.

Automatic denial for fraudulent or materially misrepresentative statements is acceptable, but USCIS must define "material" and ensure due process with notice and opportunity to rebut before denial.

Denial of petitions not based on a valid registration should allow equitable relief where employers relied on USCIS errors or where third-party agents made unauthorized filings; require cure procedures.
The requirement that registrations represent legitimate job offers is vague; request concrete criteria and examples of what constitutes a legitimate offer to avoid arbitrary determinations.
USCIS discretion to deny new/amended petitions intended to unfairly increase selection odds must be balanced with a clear process, evidentiary standards, and appeal rights to prevent misuse.
The prohibition against denying solely because a proffered wage differs if it does not equate to a lower OES level needs clear rules on how level equivalence is measured and documented.
Identifying untrue/inaccurate statements in forms as grounds for action should include standards for harmless versus material misstatements and provide opportunities to correct clerical errors.

Labeling filing of new/amended petitions intended to unfairly increase selection odds as grounds for action may chill legitimate employment changes; define "intended to unfairly increase" and provide safe-harbor procedures.

The clause preventing revocation solely because of wage differences absent a lower OES level must be accompanied by a transparent process for wage-level comparisons and evidentiary requirements to protect employers from arbitrary revocation.

[P1] The deadline to "receive comments by April 24, 2017" is unreasonable and should be extended because the proposed AD was released with insufficient lead time for operators, manufacturers, and labor unions to coordinate technical analyses and cost estimates.

[P1] The rule text requiring receipt of comments by April 24, 2017 lacks any explanation of whether late comments will be considered; clarify that substantive late comments will be accepted and considered in the FAA's decision.

[P2] The required initial compliance timeframe of "within 12 months" is too short for large commercial operators with extensive fleets and limited maintenance capacity; we request an extension to 18–24 months or a phased schedule by fleet size.

[P2] The regulation does not provide credit for inspections already performed if they occurred more than 12 months but less than 24 months prior to the AD effective date; clarify that recent inspections that meet the AD's procedures satisfy the initial compliance requirement.

[P3] The inspection for the "RP031" marking is ambiguous because the provision does not specify acceptable methods of verification (visual only, borescope, or part-tag records); clarify acceptable inspection techniques and recordkeeping requirements.

[P3] The "RP031" marking exception should allow reliance on maintenance records or parts traceability documentation instead of physical marking when the marking is missing but documentation proves the part is compliant.

[P4] The AD requires "initial pull force checks" of stages 1–3 without specifying measurement procedure, instrument calibration, or ambient conditions; the rule should reference a specific test method or service bulletin to ensure repeatability.

[P4] There is no allowance for tooling downtime or spare part availability; operators should be allowed to schedule the initial pull force checks at the next heavy maintenance visit if they can demonstrate equivalent risk mitigation until then.

[P5] The threshold "more than 100 lbs" to trigger reaming and coating is overly conservative/unvalidated; provide supporting data or allow alternative corrective actions such as clearing and lubrication before reaming.

[P5] Mandating ream and anti-corrosion coating "before next flight" if pull force >100 lbs is operationally impracticable for in-service flights; require that the ream/coating be completed within a specified number of flight hours or cycles (e.g., 10 flight cycles) instead of before next flight.

[P5] The rule does not specify approved materials, coating standards, or process controls for the anti-corrosion coating; require specification of acceptable coatings, application standards, and post-process inspection criteria.

[P6] Requiring a repeat inspection within 3 months when pull force is >75 and ≤100 lbs may cause excessive maintenance burden; request that the FAA allow an alternative of closer monitoring via flight data and conditional operation limits rather than mandatory shop visits.

[P6] The AD fails to indicate whether the 3-month interval is calendar months or flight-cycle months; clarify that intervals are calendar months from the date of the last inspection.

[P7] The 12-month repetitive interval for pull forces ≤75 lbs is acceptable only if combined with a clear requirement to document forces and maintain records; the AD should require log entries with measured forces and inspector identity.

[P7] The 75 lb threshold lacks justification and may not reflect performance across different engine variants; publish the basis for threshold selection or allow fleet-specific thresholds based on trend monitoring.

[P8] The provision to "continue to perform repetitive pull force checks" is indefinite; request the FAA define a maximum duration (e.g., until a terminating action is performed or until a service bulletin provides a design fix) and require periodic review of continuing necessity.

[P8] There is no provision allowing reduced inspection frequency based on demonstrated low-risk history; include a risk-based relief mechanism to lengthen intervals for engines with multiple consecutive low-force inspections.

[P9] Declaring reaming and coating as "terminating action" is appropriate only if long-term effectiveness is demonstrated; require submission of lifecycle data showing reamed/coated bores remain compliant for a specified interval (e.g., 5 years or X cycles) before allowing termination.

[P9] The AD should clarify whether partial reaming/coating (e.g., only affected stages) terminates repetitive inspections for all stages or only for those reamed/coated; the current text implies all stages but needs explicit wording.

[P9] The rule must specify acceptable shop approvals and qualifications for performing the terminating ream and coating work; limit performing these actions to OEM-approved shops or provide AMOC guidance for other facilities.

[P10] Granting the Manager authority to approve AMOCs is standard, but the AD should specify expected turnaround times for AMOC decisions to prevent prolonged operational uncertainty.

[P10] The provision allowing AMOCs by the Manager should explicitly state whether relief can be granted for initial inspection intervals, thresholds, or terminating actions to enable operational flexibility.

[P11] Requiring use of 14 CFR 39.19 for AMOC requests is appropriate, but the AD should also provide clear guidance on the technical substantiation required with an AMOC request (e.g., test data, analysis, alternate procedures).

[P11] The cross-reference to 14 CFR 39.19 alone may be insufficient for international operators; include explicit instructions for operators outside the U.S. on coordination between their civil aviation authority and the FAA for AMOC approval.

[P12] Allowing AMOC requests via email to ANE–AD–AMOC@faa.gov is helpful, but the AD should permit submission via EASA/other authority channels and provide a trackable web portal or confirmation procedure to ensure receipt.

[P12] The AD does not address confidentiality/sensitive business information in AMOC communications sent by email; provide secure submission options and a statement about handling proprietary data.

[P3] The inspection requirement does not state whether marking "RP031" applies to legacy parts or only parts produced after a certain date; clarify applicability by serial number, production date, or shop order history.

[P5] The AD omits instructions for discrepant actuation rings that are stuck but show pull forces below thresholds; provide additional criteria for assessing binding versus false readings due to contamination or tooling.

[P4] The AD should specify whether pull force checks may be conducted on-wing (in-service) with the engine installed, or whether engine removal is required; clarify to avoid inconsistent practices among maintenance organizations.

[P6] The AD's reliance on discrete lb-force thresholds may produce measurement variability between technicians; require use of calibrated load-measuring devices and specify calibration intervals.

[P2] The AD does not provide any cost or burden estimation per aircraft/operator; include an economic analysis and small-entity impacts to comply with the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

[P8] The rule lacks a provision for immediate grounding or operational restrictions if an engine repeatedly exceeds thresholds but the operator cannot obtain prompt ream/coating capacity; include temporary operational limitations or dispatch rules to mitigate safety risk.

[P9] The AD should clarify whether reamed coated bores require any post-action verification (e.g., pull tests) to confirm efficacy; require a post-processing pull force check before returning to service.

[P10] The AD should permit the use of Alternative Methods of Compliance by non-U.S. CAAs when an equivalent safety case is presented, to avoid duplication and trade impediments.

[P3] For engines without external access to see the "RP031" marking, allow acceptance of parts records or a one-time borescope inspection procedure; otherwise, inspection may be impossible without disassembly.

[P5] The AD does not address potential adverse effects of reaming (e.g., loss of material, change in clearances) on engine life; require OEM engineered ream specifications and confirm no negative impact on structural integrity.

[P1] The March 27, 2020 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonably short and should be extended to allow affected stakeholders (airlines, MROs, labor unions, and suppliers) adequate time to prepare technical and economic comments.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether the March 27, 2020 deadline is a firm cutoff or whether late comments will be accepted and considered, given distribution and notice delays.

[P2] § 39.13(f) requires compliance “within the specified compliance times” but does not define whether calendar days, flight cycles, or flight hours control; the AD must specify the metric used to avoid inconsistent compliance.

[P2] The provision should explicitly allow relief for operators who can demonstrate that required work was performed to equivalent standards before the AD effective date (clarify “unless already accomplished”).

[P3] The required “detailed inspection” in § 39.13(g) for thumbnail and mid strut fairing panels lacks an objective acceptance/rejection criterion for “excessive rework”; the AD should include measurable thresholds or reference detailed inspection criteria.

[P3] Inspectors performing the detailed inspection need specified training and tooling; the rule should state or reference the required inspector certification/qualification and allowed inspection methods (e.g., visual only, borescope, NDT).

[P3] The time window “before further flight” for the inspection is operationally infeasible for aircraft scheduled for immediate departures; FAA should allow a defined grace period (e.g., next overnight maintenance opportunity) or permit special flight permits under defined conditions.

[P4] Requiring the specific steps of Boeing Special Attention Service Bulletin 737–54–1056 (Steps 4, 6–9, 11, 12) without incorporation by reference details may create ambiguity; the AD must incorporate the exact procedures or include them in the docket.

[P4] The AD should allow alternative accomplishing instructions when the Boeing service bulletin steps cannot be performed exactly (different fleet configuration or improved techniques) subject to AMOC approval, and clarify the expected turnaround time for such approvals.

[P5] Allowing special flight permits under § 39.13(h) is appropriate, but the rule should state whether limitations (e.g., ferry-only, passenger carriage prohibited) apply to permits issued under this AD.

[P6] Requiring concurrence by the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch, for every special flight permit creates a single-point bottleneck; FAA should permit delegated concurrence to regional ACO managers or local FSDO in urgent cases to avoid operational disruption.

[P7] Requiring a description of electromagnetic field (EMF) radiation sources along the planned route in special flight permit requests is overly burdensome and vague — the rule fails to define the level of detail, acceptable format, or why EMF source description is relevant to fairing rework issues.

[P7] The EMF information requirement could implicate security-sensitive information (e.g., locations of critical infrastructure); the AD should allow operators to provide a high-level summary or confidential submission procedures.

[P8] Sending special flight permit requests to the person in paragraph (j)(1) without providing alternative contacts or an online portal risks delayed processing; the AD should include backup contacts and an electronic submission process.

[P9] The authority given to the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch, to approve AMOCs (§ 39.13(i)(1)) should be broadened to permit other appropriate FAA offices to act to expedite approvals for operators outside the Seattle region.

[P10] The requirement to submit AMOC requests to a principal inspector or local FSDO (§ 39.13(i)(1)) may be inefficient for foreign operators or non-U.S. registrants; the AD should specify procedures for these operators and allow direct submission to the certification office.

[P11] When sending AMOC information directly to the manager, requiring it to be addressed to the person in paragraph (j)(1) (§ 39.13(i)(1)) is too prescriptive — the AD should allow general submission to the Seattle ACO office with electronic tracking.

[P12] Allowing AMOC submissions by email (§ 39.13(i)(1)) is appropriate, but the AD should require an acknowledgement receipt and a target response timeframe to ensure timely processing.

[P13] The obligation to notify the principal inspector or local FSDO before using an approved AMOC (§ 39.13(i)(2)) lacks a required notification timeframe; the AD should specify the minimum advance notice (e.g., 48 hours) and required content of the notification.

[P13] Operators need clarity whether notification of AMOC use may be done electronically and whether an operator’s maintenance control organization may give the notice on the operator’s behalf.

[P14] Permitting Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs for repairs (§ 39.13(i)(3)) may improperly delegate FAA safety determinations to a manufacturer; the AD should specify oversight requirements and confirmation of continued FAA authority.

[P14] Clarify whether an AMOC approved by Boeing ODA must still be submitted to and accepted by the FAA manager for recordkeeping and audit, or whether Boeing ODA approval alone is sufficient to proceed.

[P15] Requiring that approvals meet the airplane’s certification basis and specifically reference this AD (§ 39.13(i)(3)) is appropriate, but the AD should provide guidance on acceptable means to demonstrate equivalence to the certification basis and required documentation format.

[P15] The AD should state who is responsible for maintaining the AMOC approval records (operator, Boeing ODA, or FAA) and for how long, to ensure compliance and inspection readiness.

[P3] The inspection and modification requirements appear to apply to all affected 737 sub-models but do not list part numbers or serial ranges; the AD should identify affected part numbers, affected serial numbers, or configurations to prevent inconsistent application.

[P4] The AD’s mandatory reliance on a Boeing service bulletin may create cost and access issues for third-party MROs who cannot obtain full technical data; the FAA should ensure service bulletin availability in the docket or allow equivalent data.

[P6] Requiring Manager concurrence for each special flight permit may not be lawful under the FAA’s delegation order if the Manager cannot delegate; legal commenters should review whether the rule improperly narrows delegation.

[P7] The EM field radiation description requirement lacks technical justification in the preamble; FAA should provide the safety basis and risk assessment demonstrating why EM fields affect the inspection/modification tasks.

[P5] The AD should explicitly state whether special flight permits may be granted for repositioning with passengers onboard, or only for non-revenue ferry flights.

[P2] Operators request an exemption mechanism or phased compliance schedule if fleet capacity constraints prevent simultaneous compliance within the specified compliance times.

[P12] The email address provided for AMOC submissions should be audited for cybersecurity/privacy compliance; the AD should advise how sensitive proprietary data will be protected when emailed.
