[P1] The requirement that IPFs include a valid ECT procedure code on claims is vague because the rule does not specify which CPT/HCPCS codes are "valid" for ECT, risking inconsistent reimbursement and denials.

[P1] Industry commenters will request a list of acceptable ECT procedure codes and guidance on modifiers and units to avoid claim rejections.

[P17] Duplicate with P1: Requiring a "valid ECT procedure code" without clarifying billing for ECT-related anesthesia or monitoring services will cause underpayment; commenters ask CMS to confirm whether anesthesia codes billed by separate providers are payable in addition to the ECT per-treatment payment.

[P6] Requiring up to 24 additional ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes on discharge claims is administratively burdensome for small and rural IPFs that lack coding staff; commenters ask for a phased implementation, additional training funds, or an exception for facilities below a size threshold.

[P24] The instruction to record up to 24 additional diagnosis codes does not clarify whether blank fields beyond actual coexisting diagnoses are allowed or whether omitting codes will trigger audits; commenters request clarification that only present and affecting conditions should be entered and that unused slots may remain blank.

[P2] Mandating strict adherence to "code first" sequencing per ICD-10-CM for psychiatric diagnoses may produce clinically inaccurate primary diagnoses in cases where manifestation codes better reflect the active problem; clinical advocates request an appeals mechanism when sequencing per guideline conflicts with clinical documentation and medical necessity for IPF payment.

[P16] The CMS claims processing system's automatic treatment of primary non-psychiatric "code first" situations (by searching secondary psychiatric codes for DRG assignment and comorbidity adjustments) may produce unintended DRG assignments and payment errors; commenters ask for pre-release testing results and an edit file to help submitters validate expected grouping logic.

[P25] Requiring coders to sequence underlying etiology first when manifestations exist is appropriate, but CMS must provide examples specific to common psychiatric presentations (e.g., substance-induced mood disorder vs. primary mood disorder) to avoid inconsistent coding and denied payments.

[P3] The prohibition on reporting diagnoses that relate only to prior episodes and do not affect the current stay is overly broad—many prior conditions (e.g., histories of self-harm, past psychotic episodes) influence current risk assessment and treatment planning; clinicians request guidance on when historical diagnoses should be reported as relevant comorbidities.

[P19] Duplicate with P3: Auditors may use this prohibition to deny legitimate comorbidity adjustments by retroactively deeming conditions "prior" even when they meaningfully influenced the current stay; commenters request explicit documentation standards to justify inclusion of prior conditions.

[P7] The requirement that a comorbid condition must affect treatment or LOS to qualify for an adjustment is subjective; providers ask for objective examples and a non-exhaustive list of qualifying conditions and documentation examples to reduce variability and appeals.

[P20] Duplicate with P7: Clinical advocates note that some conditions (e.g., chronic pain, nicotine dependence) may not change LOS but materially affect treatment complexity; CMS should clarify whether "affect treatment" includes care coordination, monitoring, or medication adjustments.

[P4] Allowing only one comorbidity adjustment per comorbidity category per claim will undercompensate for multiple distinct comorbidities within the same category that each materially increase cost (e.g., multiple significant cardiac conditions); industry requests reevaluation of category definitions or a tiered approach.

[P21] The combined permission/limitation that an IPF may receive only one adjustment per category but multiple across categories leads to gaming concerns where comorbidities are arbitrarily split across categories to maximize adjustments; commenters ask CMS to publish category definitions and mapping logic.

[P22] Duplicate with P4: Legal commenters warn that limiting to one adjustment per category may conflict with clinical reality and could invite litigation alleging arbitrary payment caps; they recommend CMS conduct a recalibration study before finalizing.

[P5] Allowing adjustments from multiple categories is reasonable, but CMS must clarify aggregation rules—whether adjustments are additive, multiplicative, or capped—and provide examples of calculation for common multi-comorbidity scenarios.

[P23] Duplicate with P5: Payment administrators request sample paid-claim scenarios that demonstrate how multiple category adjustments interact with per diem declining factors to allow accurate financial forecasting.

[P8] The declining per-diem adjustment through day 21 may not reflect actual cost trajectories for long-stay psychiatric patients whose intensity may increase in later days (e.g., due to complications or comorbidity onset); behavioral health advocates request an evidence basis and sensitivity analysis showing costs by day.

[P9] Applying a 1.31 multiplier to day 1 per diem for IPFs with a qualifying ED disproportionately favors facilities with ED designation; rural advocates say many psychiatric patients present through non-designated EDs or transfer processes and request parity or transitional adjustments.

[P10] The 1.19 multiplier for IPFs without a qualifying ED may undercompensate for initial intake resource use in facilities that cannot meet the qualifying ED definition due to local hospital organization; commenters ask CMS to define "qualifying ED" and permit waiver/temporary exceptions.

[P11] The statutory 2-percentage-point reduction to annual updates for failure to report quality data is harsh for small facilities with limited reporting infrastructure; commenters propose a graduated penalty, lookback period, or technical assistance before applying reductions.

[P18] Duplicate with P11: Commenters request clarification whether reporting failures due to data transmission errors attributable to CMS systems will nevertheless trigger the 2-point reduction and ask for an administrative appeals process.

[P12] CMS's application of a -0.15 percent payment rate and a separate budget-neutrality factor for IPFs failing IPFQR requirements lacks transparency; commenters request the methodology, calculation worksheets, and the legal authority cited for combining these factors.

[P13] Applying reduced updates and budget-neutrality factors to the ECT per-treatment payment for reporting failures may disincentivize provision of ECT in facilities that serve vulnerable populations; specialty psychiatric societies urge CMS to exempt ECT per-treatment payment from such reductions or provide an alternative remediation pathway.

[P14] If psychiatric principal diagnoses that do not map to the 17 MS-DRGs receive no MS-DRG adjustment, some legitimate psychiatric presentations may be underweighted—commenters ask for a list of excluded diagnoses and justification, plus transitional payments until mapping is refined.

[P15] The wage index obligation to use "best Medicare data" and an "appropriate wage index" is too vague; hospitals and labor economists request specification of data sources, base period, and the treatment of frontier/rural wage anomalies and wage index floor/ceilings.

[P16] Duplicate with earlier: CMS's automated search for secondary psychiatric codes to assign DRGs must be transparent; commenters request pre-publication of grouping logic, including tie-breaking rules when multiple secondary psychiatric codes exist.

[P26] Repeating the "code first" requirement for psychiatric primary codes, commenters representing clinical coders ask CMS to produce training modules, Frequently Asked Questions, and sample claim-level coding scenarios to ensure uniform application.

[P6/P24] Requiring up to 24 additional diagnosis codes raises EHR interoperability concerns—vendors need a clear schema for code fields, field lengths, and whether present-on-admission (POA) indicators are required for each of the 24 codes.

[P3/P19] Patient advocates worry that excluding prior but relevant diagnoses from claims will reduce visibility of patients' longitudinal needs in administrative data, undermining research and quality oversight; they request a separate optional field for historical diagnoses not affecting current stay.

[P7/P20] Disability rights groups argue that the "affect treatment or LOS" standard may systematically exclude psychosocial factors (housing instability, lack of community supports) that increase resource needs but are not coded as medical conditions; they ask CMS to allow social determinants codes to be counted for adjustments.

[P4/P21] Health plans and auditors request a crosswalk mapping specific ICD-10-CM codes to comorbidity categories so payers and providers can consistently determine eligibility for only one adjustment per category.

[P8] Quality advocates request analysis showing whether declining per-diem adjustments create incentives to discharge patients earlier, potentially harming clinical outcomes; they urge CMS to include monitoring metrics and safeguards.

[P9/P10] Clarify whether the day 1 multiplier applies when the stay is less than 24 hours or when an IPF stay crosses midnight; providers ask for guidance on partial-day stays and transfers.

[P11/P18] Clarify timing and scope of the reporting failure penalty: whether the 2-percentage-point reduction applies to the entire facility's federal per diem base rate retroactively for that rate year or only to discharges after the determination date.

[P12/P13] CMS should publish examples showing how the -0.15 percent update and 1.0078 wage index budget neutrality factor combine to affect both base per diem and ECT per-treatment payments, including rounding rules.

[P14] Legal commenters ask whether appeals of MS-DRG non-mapping decisions are allowed and what the administrative remedy process is when a psychiatric principal diagnosis should legitimately map but was excluded due to grouping software errors.

[P1/P17] Hospitals request grace periods for claims with missing or incorrect ECT procedure codes, along with clear instructions for corrected/resubmitted claims and whether prior retroactive payment adjustments will be allowed.

[P6/P24] Request clarification whether the "develop later" language requires updating already-filed admission claims if a new comorbidity manifests after submission and whether supplemental claims must be filed.

[P16/P21] Vendors ask for test files and sample transactions for the claims-processing logic that finds secondary psychiatric codes to validate their billing systems before enforcement begins.

[P2/P26] Clinical coding societies recommend CMS coordinate with NCHS/CDC on ICD-10-CM interpretation where psychiatric "code first" instructions conflict with specialty coding practice, and request joint guidance to avoid conflicting instructions.

[P3/P19] Hospitals request safe-harbor documentation elements to show why a historical diagnosis was excluded to shield against future audit penalties when auditors contest non-reporting of prior conditions.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement that physician supervision be provided only by a “rehabilitation physician” is ambiguous and will exclude experienced hospitalists or neurologists who currently supervise IRF patients; CMS should clarify the required credentials or permit other physicians with equivalent rehabilitation experience.

[P1] Narrowing supervision to “rehabilitation physician” will exacerbate workforce shortages in rural areas where no rehabilitation physician is available; propose allowing physician supervision by other qualified physicians under documented consultation with a rehabilitation physician.

[P2] Requiring face-to-face visits by the rehabilitation physician at least 3 days per week is clinically unnecessary for stable patients and will divert physician time from higher-acuity care; recommend a risk-based standard (e.g., intensity-based or patient complexity) rather than a flat 3 visits/week.

[P2] The 3-days-per-week in-person visit mandate will significantly increase operating costs (physician FTEs and travel time) for IRFs, particularly small and rural facilities; CMS must provide cost estimates or a rural exemption.

[P2] The rule does not specify whether the “3 days per week” must be consecutive or can be spread across the week; request clarification and allow non-consecutive scheduling to accommodate physician availability.

[P3] Allowing the post-admission physician evaluation to count as one visit is helpful, but CMS should explicitly state that it must meet the same substantive requirements as other face-to-face visits (documentation, assessment elements).

[P3] The provision should permit other documented physician encounters (e.g., telemedicine visits) to count as one of the required visits when in-person is not feasible, especially in rural/telehealth contexts.

[P4] The requirement that a licensed/certified clinician “designated by a rehabilitation physician” conduct preadmission screening within 48 hours unduly centralizes authority and could create delays in transfers; allow the facility's clinical leader to designate screeners when a rehabilitation physician is not immediately available.

[P4] The 48-hour pre-admission screening window is too narrow for patients transferred from long-term acute care or other settings where logistics may delay documentation; propose extending to 72 hours or allowing documented clinical rationale for longer intervals.

[P5] The condition that CMS will accept a screening older than 48 hours only if an update is performed is reasonable, but the rule fails to define the required content of the “update”; request specification of minimum elements that must be updated and documented.

[P5] The rule should permit electronic health record (EHR) reconciliation or review (with documentation) as sufficient for the 48-hour update when in-person/telephone contact is impractical.

[P6] Requiring the update to be in-person or by telephone within 48 hours preadmission is inflexible — it should allow secure video visits and EHR review as acceptable methods, given telehealth technology.

[P6] The mandate to document the update within the medical record within the 48-hour window may conflict with admission processes that finalize records after admission; request clarification on acceptable timing and retroactive documentation.

[P7] Requiring the rehabilitation physician to develop the required plan with interdisciplinary team input within 4 days is appropriate, but CMS must clarify whether the physician must personally draft the plan or may sign a team-prepared plan.

[P7] The 4-day timeframe may be too long for high-acuity patients who need individualized plans sooner; recommend that an initial plan be completed within 48 hours with a comprehensive plan by day 4.

[P8] Mandating that interdisciplinary team meetings be led by a rehabilitation physician will be operationally difficult in facilities without on-site rehabilitation physicians daily; allow alternate qualified team leaders (e.g., physiatrist via teleconference, nurse practitioner with supervision) when a rehabilitation physician is not available.

[P8] The specified required attendees (specialized RN, social worker/case manager, and licensed/certified therapists from each discipline treating the patient) may be impractical for small IRFs treating few disciplines; request flexibility to include team members based on the therapies actually provided to the patient.

[P9] Requiring that every team member “maintain current knowledge” of the patient's status is vague and unenforceable; CMS should define what documentation or activities demonstrate “current knowledge” (e.g., attendance, updated notes, signoffs).

[P10] Permitting the rehabilitation physician to lead team meetings remotely is essential; commenters recommend explicitly allowing remote leadership to count toward the leadership requirement and specifying minimum technological standards to ensure clinical engagement.

[P10] CMS should clarify whether remote leadership means real-time audio-video participation is required, or whether telephone-only leadership suffices, and whether asynchronous input (e.g., shared notes) may be used.

[P11] The deadline to begin IRF QRP reporting by the first day of the calendar quarter following 30 days after CCN notification is administratively burdensome for new providers; request a phased-in reporting timeline or grace period for initial data submission.

[P11] The rule should specify whether partial-quarter reporting is acceptable for facilities whose CCN notification occurs mid-quarter and how CMS will prorate reporting deadlines.

[P12] CMS’s methods for written notification of non-compliance include the CMS system, USPS, or MAC email — the rule should require CMS to use at least two methods to ensure receipt, given the consequences of non-compliance.

[P12] Specify timelines for when CMS will send non-compliance notices and deadlines for IRFs to respond or remediate; current language lacks procedural timeframes.

[P13] For reconsideration decisions, CMS must provide a clear appeals timeline (e.g., number of days to issue final decision) and state whether the written notice will include reasoning and evidence relied upon.

[P13] CMS should require simultaneous electronic delivery of reconsideration decisions (secure email) in addition to USPS to expedite resolution.

[P14] The obligation to meet two data completeness thresholds is reasonable, but the rule should allow for legitimate data interruptions (EHR downtime) with an excused-event process.

[P15] The 95% completeness threshold for IRF-PAI data is very high and may penalize larger facilities with complex caseloads; recommend lowering to 90% or providing risk-adjusted expectations.

[P15] Clarify whether the 95% denominator excludes cases exempted from IRF-PAI (e.g., short stays, early deaths) and how partial assessments are treated.

[P16] The 100% completeness requirement for CDC NHSN submissions is unrealistic given reporting downtimes and evolving definitions; request that CMS change this to a high but achievable threshold (e.g., 98%) and allow exceptions for documented technical failures.

[P16] CMS must clarify which specific NHSN measures are subject to the 100% requirement and whether there is an appeals process for disputed missing submissions.

[P17] (duplicate of P1) The repeated insistence on a rehabilitation physician for supervision without allowing delegation to APRNs/physician assistants with appropriate training could worsen access to care; propose permitting delegation under defined supervision protocols.

[P18] (duplicate of P2) The in-person 3-days/week requirement does not account for team-based models where non-physician clinicians (PT/OT/RN/APRN) perform much of monitoring; request recognition of interdisciplinary monitoring activities as complementary to physician visits and allow reduced physician visit frequency for low-risk patients.

[P19] (duplicate of P3) Clarify whether the post-admission physician evaluation counted as a face-to-face visit may be conducted via telemedicine when appropriate and whether it must be documented with the same assessment elements.

[P20] (duplicate of P4) The requirement that the preadmission screening be done by a clinician “designated by a rehabilitation physician” could delay transfers from acute care where the rehab physician is off-site; allow designation by a facility medical director or documented protocol.

[P21] (duplicate of P5) For preadmission screenings older than 48 hours, requiring an in-person or telephone update may be clinically unnecessary for very stable patients; propose allowing a documented clinical review of the medical record as sufficient when accompanied by a brief attestation.

[P22] (duplicate of P7) The 4-day deadline for the interdisciplinary plan should specify whether weekends/holidays count and whether the “development” date is the physician’s signature date or when team input was completed.

[P23] (duplicate of P8) The requirement to include therapists from each discipline treating the patient should be clarified to mean only those disciplines actively treating during the relevant time, not every discipline the IRF offers.

[P24] (duplicate of P9) Define “current knowledge” for team members (e.g., read and initial of last progress note within 24 hours) to create an auditable standard.

[P25] (duplicate of P10) Require that when the rehabilitation physician leads remotely, the meeting minutes document the physician’s participation (time-stamped) to prevent disputes.

[P26] (duplicate of P11) New IRFs need technical onboarding time to CMS QRP submission systems; propose allowing the first required quarter after CCN notification to be a preparation quarter without penalty.

[P27] (duplicate of P12) Request that CMS provide sample non-compliance notices and a remediation checklist so facilities can quickly correct deficiencies.

[P28] (duplicate of P13) For fairness, CMS should require that reconsideration decisions include instructions for further appeal and timelines to request judicial review if applicable.

[P29] (duplicate of P14) Provide an exception process for data completeness thresholds for facilities experiencing major natural disasters or cyberattacks that impede reporting.

[P30] (duplicate of P15) Explain whether the 95% requirement applies to each measure individually or to aggregate completeness across all required measures.

[P31] (duplicate of P16) For NHSN 100% completeness, require that CMS accept “not applicable” designations where measures clearly do not apply to a patient or facility (e.g., specialty populations).

[P32] The unrelated maritime prohibitions in §100.1701(b) appear misplaced in this regulatory text governing IRFs; confirm whether inclusion is an error and remove or relocate to the correct part.

[P33] (re: §100.1701(c)) Requiring entrants to obtain permission from on-scene patrol on VHF Channel 9 is irrelevant to IRF operations; if this is included accidentally, CMS must rescind or correct cross-references to avoid compliance confusion.

The 3-days-per-week in-person visit mandate will significantly increase operating costs (physician FTEs and travel time) for IRFs, particularly small and rural facilities; CMS must provide cost estimates or a rural exemption.

The rule does not specify whether the “3 days per week” must be consecutive or can be spread across the week; request clarification and allow non-consecutive scheduling to accommodate physician availability.

Allowing the post-admission physician evaluation to count as one visit is helpful, but CMS should explicitly state that it must meet the same substantive requirements as other face-to-face visits (documentation, assessment elements).

The provision should permit other documented physician encounters (e.g., telemedicine visits) to count as one of the required visits when in-person is not feasible, especially in rural/telehealth contexts.

The requirement that a licensed/certified clinician “designated by a rehabilitation physician” conduct preadmission screening within 48 hours unduly centralizes authority and could create delays in transfers; allow the facility's clinical leader to designate screeners when a rehabilitation physician is not immediately available.

The 48-hour pre-admission screening window is too narrow for patients transferred from long-term acute care or other settings where logistics may delay documentation; propose extending to 72 hours or allowing documented clinical rationale for longer intervals.

The condition that CMS will accept a screening older than 48 hours only if an update is performed is reasonable, but the rule fails to define the required content of the “update”; request specification of minimum elements that must be updated and documented.
The rule should permit electronic health record (EHR) reconciliation or review (with documentation) as sufficient for the 48-hour update when in-person/telephone contact is impractical.

Requiring the update to be in-person or by telephone within 48 hours preadmission is inflexible — it should allow secure video visits and EHR review as acceptable methods, given telehealth technology.

The mandate to document the update within the medical record within the 48-hour window may conflict with admission processes that finalize records after admission; request clarification on acceptable timing and retroactive documentation.

Requiring the rehabilitation physician to develop the required plan with interdisciplinary team input within 4 days is appropriate, but CMS must clarify whether the physician must personally draft the plan or may sign a team-prepared plan.
The 4-day timeframe may be too long for high-acuity patients who need individualized plans sooner; recommend that an initial plan be completed within 48 hours with a comprehensive plan by day 4.

Mandating that interdisciplinary team meetings be led by a rehabilitation physician will be operationally difficult in facilities without on-site rehabilitation physicians daily; allow alternate qualified team leaders (e.g., physiatrist via teleconference, nurse practitioner with supervision) when a rehabilitation physician is not available.

The specified required attendees (specialized RN, social worker/case manager, and licensed/certified therapists from each discipline treating the patient) may be impractical for small IRFs treating few disciplines; request flexibility to include team members based on the therapies actually provided to the patient.

Requiring that every team member “maintain current knowledge” of the patient's status is vague and unenforceable; CMS should define what documentation or activities demonstrate “current knowledge” (e.g., attendance, updated notes, signoffs).

Permitting the rehabilitation physician to lead team meetings remotely is essential; commenters recommend explicitly allowing remote leadership to count toward the leadership requirement and specifying minimum technological standards to ensure clinical engagement.

CMS should clarify whether remote leadership means real-time audio-video participation is required, or whether telephone-only leadership suffices, and whether asynchronous input (e.g., shared notes) may be used.

The deadline to begin IRF QRP reporting by the first day of the calendar quarter following 30 days after CCN notification is administratively burdensome for new providers; request a phased-in reporting timeline or grace period for initial data submission.
The rule should specify whether partial-quarter reporting is acceptable for facilities whose CCN notification occurs mid-quarter and how CMS will prorate reporting deadlines.

CMS’s methods for written notification of non-compliance include the CMS system, USPS, or MAC email — the rule should require CMS to use at least two methods to ensure receipt, given the consequences of non-compliance.
Specify timelines for when CMS will send non-compliance notices and deadlines for IRFs to respond or remediate; current language lacks procedural timeframes.

For reconsideration decisions, CMS must provide a clear appeals timeline (e.g., number of days to issue final decision) and state whether the written notice will include reasoning and evidence relied upon.
CMS should require simultaneous electronic delivery of reconsideration decisions (secure email) in addition to USPS to expedite resolution.
The obligation to meet two data completeness thresholds is reasonable, but the rule should allow for legitimate data interruptions (EHR downtime) with an excused-event process.
The 95% completeness threshold for IRF-PAI data is very high and may penalize larger facilities with complex caseloads; recommend lowering to 90% or providing risk-adjusted expectations.
Clarify whether the 95% denominator excludes cases exempted from IRF-PAI (e.g., short stays, early deaths) and how partial assessments are treated.

The 100% completeness requirement for CDC NHSN submissions is unrealistic given reporting downtimes and evolving definitions; request that CMS change this to a high but achievable threshold (e.g., 98%) and allow exceptions for documented technical failures.
CMS must clarify which specific NHSN measures are subject to the 100% requirement and whether there is an appeals process for disputed missing submissions.

(duplicate of P1) The repeated insistence on a rehabilitation physician for supervision without allowing delegation to APRNs/physician assistants with appropriate training could worsen access to care; propose permitting delegation under defined supervision protocols.

(duplicate of P2) The in-person 3-days/week requirement does not account for team-based models where non-physician clinicians (PT/OT/RN/APRN) perform much of monitoring; request recognition of interdisciplinary monitoring activities as complementary to physician visits and allow reduced physician visit frequency for low-risk patients.

(duplicate of P3) Clarify whether the post-admission physician evaluation counted as a face-to-face visit may be conducted via telemedicine when appropriate and whether it must be documented with the same assessment elements.

(duplicate of P4) The requirement that the preadmission screening be done by a clinician “designated by a rehabilitation physician” could delay transfers from acute care where the rehab physician is off-site; allow designation by a facility medical director or documented protocol.

(duplicate of P5) For preadmission screenings older than 48 hours, requiring an in-person or telephone update may be clinically unnecessary for very stable patients; propose allowing a documented clinical review of the medical record as sufficient when accompanied by a brief attestation.

(duplicate of P7) The 4-day deadline for the interdisciplinary plan should specify whether weekends/holidays count and whether the “development” date is the physician’s signature date or when team input was completed.

(duplicate of P8) The requirement to include therapists from each discipline treating the patient should be clarified to mean only those disciplines actively treating during the relevant time, not every discipline the IRF offers.
(duplicate of P9) Define “current knowledge” for team members (e.g., read and initial of last progress note within 24 hours) to create an auditable standard.
(duplicate of P10) Require that when the rehabilitation physician leads remotely, the meeting minutes document the physician’s participation (time-stamped) to prevent disputes.

(duplicate of P11) New IRFs need technical onboarding time to CMS QRP submission systems; propose allowing the first required quarter after CCN notification to be a preparation quarter without penalty.
(duplicate of P12) Request that CMS provide sample non-compliance notices and a remediation checklist so facilities can quickly correct deficiencies.
(duplicate of P13) For fairness, CMS should require that reconsideration decisions include instructions for further appeal and timelines to request judicial review if applicable.
(duplicate of P14) Provide an exception process for data completeness thresholds for facilities experiencing major natural disasters or cyberattacks that impede reporting.
(duplicate of P15) Explain whether the 95% requirement applies to each measure individually or to aggregate completeness across all required measures.
(duplicate of P16) For NHSN 100% completeness, require that CMS accept “not applicable” designations where measures clearly do not apply to a patient or facility (e.g., specialty populations).
The unrelated maritime prohibitions in §100.1701(b) appear misplaced in this regulatory text governing IRFs; confirm whether inclusion is an error and remove or relocate to the correct part.

(re: §100.1701(c)) Requiring entrants to obtain permission from on-scene patrol on VHF Channel 9 is irrelevant to IRF operations; if this is included accidentally, CMS must rescind or correct cross-references to avoid compliance confusion.

raw_output:
[P1] The October 29, 2018 comment deadline is unreasonably short and does not provide adequate time for small carriers and trade associations to analyze the technical service bulletin and prepare informed comments; request extension to at least 60 days after publication of the service bulletin.

[P1] The rule text should clarify whether the October 29, 2018 deadline is inclusive of mailed comments received by that date or if it is the postmark date; request explicit specification (received vs. postmarked vs. electronic timestamp).

[P2] The applicability language is overbroad because it applies to all 737–600/700/700C/800/900/900ER airplanes "certificated in any category" without regard to configuration or fleet usage; request narrowing to only those airplanes with the affected PSU/life vest panel part numbers or serial numbers identified in the Boeing Service Bulletin.

[P2] The AD should explicitly include or exclude converted freighters and other supplemental type certificate (STC) configurations — current text "certificated in any category" is ambiguous for STC-modified airplanes; request clarification to prevent inconsistent interpretation.

[P3] The compliance provision lacks a mechanism for phased compliance for operators with heavy maintenance scheduling constraints; request allowance for phased compliance tied to base maintenance checks or a defined extension process.

[P3] The phrase "unless already performed" should require documentation standards to prove prior compliance (e.g., signed work order referencing Boeing SB revision and serial numbers); ask FAA to specify acceptable evidence.

[P4] The 60-month compliance time for accomplishing all "RC" actions is excessively long given potential safety risks (lanyard failures could affect passenger evacuation); request justification for 60 months and consider shortening to 18–36 months.

[P4] Conversely, small regional carriers with limited maintenance access to spares contend 60 months may be insufficient to retrofit their entire fleet and request a flexible compliance schedule tied to heavy maintenance visits.

[P4] The AD should specify whether the 60-month clock starts from the AD effective date or from the date of operator receipt of the Boeing Service Bulletin; request explicit wording to avoid dispute.

[P5] The prohibition on installing a PSU or life vest panel unless its lanyard has been updated could create parts logistics issues for MROs and parts suppliers; request a grandfathering exception for parts on contract if installation is performed during a single maintenance event that immediately updates the lanyard.

[P5] The prohibition should define who is responsible for verifying lanyard update status at installation (operator, installer, or supplier) and require documentation standards; the current text is silent and creates liability uncertainty.

[P6] Paragraph (h)(1) is confusing: it appears to prohibit installation of non-updated PSUs on airplanes "after modification of the airplane as required by this AD," which could unintentionally bar temporary use of serviceable spare units during retrofit periods; request clarification or exception for temporary replacements subject to onboard compliance within X days.

[P6] For airplanes currently without updated lanyards, the rule should permit installation of new PSUs provided the lanyard is updated at the same maintenance visit; the present wording could be read to prohibit necessary replacement parts during the retrofit window.

[P7] Paragraph (h)(2) implies immediate prohibition as of the AD effective date for airplanes already having updated lanyards; this may prevent transfer of components between aircraft of mixed status — request clarification on inter-aircraft transfer rules and required paperwork.

[P7] Operators who have some installed updated lanyards but spares without updated lanyards need guidance: does (h)(2) prohibit installing a spare part onto an aircraft that already has updated assemblies? Request explicit allowance or prohibition and documentation requirements.

[P8] The granting of AMOC authority to the Manager, Seattle ACO is appropriate, but commenters request publication of typical processing times and criteria for approval to ensure predictability for operators seeking AMOCs.

[P8] Legal commenters request clarification whether the Manager’s AMOC authority is limited to alternative means providing an "acceptable level of safety" or can consider cost and logistical practicability.

[P9] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO may impose undue procedural burden; recommend allowing direct submission to the Seattle ACO for complex technical AMOCs to avoid delays.

[P9] The rule should allow electronic submission through a centralized FAA AMOC portal in addition to local offices to standardize handling and provide tracking numbers; current reference only to 14 CFR 39.19 and local offices is outdated.

[P10] Paragraph (i)(1) that requires sending information to the person identified in (j)(1) should include that person’s name, mailing address, and phone number in the AD itself to avoid ambiguity and misdirected requests.

[P11] Permitting email of AMOC information to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is helpful, but commenters request confirmation that encrypted attachments containing proprietary data will be accepted and guidance on acceptable file formats and size limits.

[P12] The obligation to notify the principal inspector or manager before using any approved AMOC is burdensome if the AMOC was approved centrally; request that notification be allowed contemporaneously rather than prior if operationally impracticable, or permit notification within a short time window (e.g., 48 hours).

[P12] Operators request clarification on what constitutes adequate "notification" — written email, phone call documented in maintenance records, or formal letter — and recommend allowing electronic notification to satisfy the requirement.

[P13] The permission to use Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs for repairs is reasonable, but commenters urge that the AD require Boeing to provide written documentation of ODA approval tied to this AD so operators have audit evidence.

[P13] Independent repair stations and third-party MROs are concerned this favors manufacturer ODAs and may limit competition; request FAA confirm that AMOCs approved by other qualified organizations are acceptable if they meet certification basis.

[P14] Requiring repair methods to meet the airplane's certification basis could create uncertainty where the certification basis has changed over time; request FAA to list acceptable means to demonstrate compliance or allow reference to the current Aircraft Certification Office baseline.

[P14] Legal commenters suggest including an explicit process for resolving disputes where an operator believes a proposed repair meets the certification basis but FAA disagrees — e.g., mediation timeline or escalation path.

[P15] Requiring approval to explicitly reference this AD is reasonable, but commenters request model wording or an approval template to ensure consistent cross-referencing and avoid inadvertent invalidation of AMOCs.

[P16] The requirement to complete all RC steps, substeps, and identified figures for compliance is precise, but commenters request that the AD publish the Boeing Service Bulletin revision and figure numbers in the docket to avoid uncertainty about which figures are "identified in an RC step."

[P16] Maintenance organizations request clearer guidance on whether RC-labelled steps that reference normative industry standards (e.g., torque values) allow use of equivalent tools/methods that meet those values without prior AMOC.

[P17] The RC Exempt exception needs clearer definition — commenters ask whether "RC Exempt" labeling in Boeing's service bulletin is allowed to be applied post-issuance and whether operators can rely on a later revision that designates steps RC Exempt.

[P17] Advocacy groups request FAA to provide a public rationale for why certain steps are RC Exempt to ensure those exemptions do not undermine safety.

[P18] Requiring an AMOC for any deviation from RC steps could be administratively burdensome for complex repairs that require minor deviations; request allowance for pre-approved minor deviations documented in the operator’s maintenance program that do not require full AMOC review.

[P18] Legal commenters point out that the AD should define the threshold for what constitutes a "deviation" from an RC step (e.g., alternate fastener type vs. alternate sequence) to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P19] Allowing deviations from non-RC steps under the operator’s accepted program is appropriate, but commenters request FAA clarification that these deviations must still be documented in the aircraft maintenance records and be subject to audit.

[P19] Operators ask for explicit language that deviations from non-RC steps must not compromise the ability to accomplish the RC steps and must ensure the airplane can be returned to an airworthy condition without additional FAA approval.

[P19] Safety advocates request that any operator-level deviations from non-RC steps be reported to FAA for trend analysis to ensure systemic issues are identified, rather than being left solely to operator discretion.

[P4][P5] MRO industry commenters note potential supply-chain impacts: if installations are prohibited absent updated lanyards, suppliers will need to stock only updated lanyard assemblies; request lead time guidance and transition allowances to prevent grounding of aircraft awaiting parts.

[P2][P4] International operators request clarification on how this AD interacts with foreign airworthiness directives and whether compliance with an equivalent EASA AD or Boeing Service Bulletin will be accepted as showing compliance.

[P8][P11] Privacy-conscious commenters request clarity on how proprietary or sensitive information submitted via the AMOC email address will be protected and whether FOIA protections apply to certain submissions.

[P1][P4] Several commenters request that the FAA hold a stakeholder meeting/webinar prior to the comment deadline to explain the AD's technical basis, compliance timeline, and AMOC process to facilitate higher-quality comments.

[P1] The exemption of the FRTIB-13 system of records from multiple Privacy Act requirements is overly broad and lacks justification; stakeholders request a detailed explanation of the harms that would result if sections (c)(3), (d), (e)(1), (e)(4)(G)-(I), and (f) were applied.

[P1] Privacy and civil liberties groups will challenge the proposed blanket exemption for FRTIB-13 as creating an unacceptable risk of misuse of personally identifiable information without agency accountability or opportunity for individuals to access or amend records.

[P1] Legal experts will request citation to statutory authority enabling this specific scope of Privacy Act exemptions and demand redaction-limited alternatives (e.g., only exempting targeted records or fields rather than the entire system).

[P1] Industry commenters (e.g., firms contracting with FRTIB-13) will ask for clarity on what categories of records and what downstream contractors will be covered by the exemption and for assurances of contractual privacy safeguards.

[P2] Trading partners and foreign government representatives will welcome permission for an authorized national representative to request APHIS recognition but will request clearer definitions of who qualifies as an “authorized national government representative” to avoid diplomatic confusion.

[P2] Exporters’ associations will request procedures to allow subnational authorities or competent regional agencies to submit requests when national governments are unable or unwilling to make requests, or to allow written delegation from national authorities.

[P3] Exporting countries will object to the requirement that requests be submitted only in English, arguing it creates an unnecessary barrier and favors English-speaking countries; they will request acceptance of requests in other UN languages or permitting certified translations.

[P3] Legal practitioners will request that APHIS provide a secure electronic submission option in addition to the specified postal address and clarify whether emailed or portal submissions meet the requirement.

[P4] Foreign veterinary services will request more specificity regarding page limits, format templates, and whether electronic or standardized data formats (e.g., XML, spreadsheets) are acceptable for the information required under paragraph (b).

[P5] Requesting governments will ask for a clear definition of “scope of the requested evaluation,” including whether requests may be disease-specific, commodity-specific, or apply to multiple diseases simultaneously.

[P6] Veterinary associations will request that APHIS specify which veterinary control and oversight documentation is required (e.g., legal statutes, staffing levels, certification of personnel) and whether third-party audits suffice.

[P7] Countries will ask for precise requirements for “disease history and vaccination practice information,” including the time periods to cover, acceptable record types, and whether aggregated vs. individual-level data is required.

[P8] Industry and traceability vendors will request specificity on acceptable livestock demographic fields (e.g., herd-level vs. individual animal IDs), accepted traceability systems, and whether unique identifiers are mandatory.

[P9] Requesting parties will ask APHIS to define standards or metrics for demonstrating “epidemiological separation,” including geographic buffer widths, quarantine protocols, and modelling expectations.

[P10] Commenters will request that APHIS specify required surveillance performance metrics (e.g., sensitivity, sampling intensity, reporting timeliness) and acceptable surveillance methodologies.

[P11] Laboratories and national reference centers will request clarity on minimal diagnostic laboratory capability standards, accreditation requirements (e.g., ISO/IEC 17025), and proficiency testing expectations.

[P12] Emergency-response organizations will ask APHIS to define the elements of “emergency preparedness and response,” including response timelines, outbreak investigation procedures, and compensation mechanisms for affected producers.

[P13] Wildlife conservation groups will object to the 25-year domestic/10-year wildlife absence thresholds for “historically free” status as arbitrary and inconsistent with OIE standards for some diseases; they will request alignment with OIE or disease-specific epidemiology.

[P13] Some exporting governments will argue that the 25-year requirement for domestic livestock is excessively long for certain diseases with short incubation and transmission windows and request disease-specific, science-based timeframes.

[P14] Non-English-speaking countries will reiterate that requiring detailed historical-free requests in English is burdensome and request acceptance of submissions in other major languages with certified translations.

[P15] Commenters will request that APHIS provide templates for scope-of-historical-free evaluations to ensure consistent, efficient submission and review.

[P16] Veterinary NGOs will request that APHIS specify whether historical veterinary control changes (e.g., reforms) must be documented and how to present historical versus current control measures for the historically free determination.

[P17] Requesting parties will seek specificity about what constitutes acceptable documentation of past vaccination practices (e.g., vaccine brand, lot, coverage rates) for historical-free claims.

[P18] Public health and animal health stakeholders will ask APHIS to require documentation of legally mandated disease notification systems, timelines, and enforcement mechanisms in historically free requests.

[P19] Epidemiologists will request APHIS to require quantitative disease detection metrics (surveillance sensitivity, diagnostic turnaround times) for historical-free requests rather than qualitative assertions.

[P20] Requesting governments will ask for guidance on what constitutes adequate “barriers to disease introduction” (e.g., physical borders, import controls, vector control) and acceptable evidence to demonstrate them.

[P21] Industry groups will request standardized templates and data exchange formats for compartment recognition requests to avoid repetitive bespoke submissions.

[P22] Commenters will ask APHIS to clarify whether the scope of a compartment evaluation may be limited to specific commodities, single farms, corporate networks, or multi-site production systems.

[P23] Companies seeking compartment recognition will request clear criteria for compartment-level veterinary control (e.g., required SOPs, on-site veterinary staffing, oversight audits) and whether private veterinary oversight is acceptable.

[P24] Requesting entities will ask for explicit guidance on acceptable disease history and vaccination documentation at the compartment level, including timeframes and record retention requirements.

[P25] Producers and trade groups will seek definition of acceptable traceability systems for commodity movement into, within, and out of a compartment, and whether electronic traceability with interoperable identifiers is mandatory.

[P26] Agricultural stakeholders will request examples of acceptable epidemiologic separation measures for compartments (e.g., double fencing, controlled access zones) and evidence thresholds to demonstrate effectiveness.

[P27] Commenters will request APHIS to specify surveillance expectations for compartments, including minimum sampling plans, frequency, and laboratory confirmation pathways.

[P28] Diagnostic laboratories will request clear standards for compartment-related lab capabilities, including accreditation, minimum biosecurity levels, and turnaround-time expectations.

[P29] Applicants will request clarity on required emergency preparedness elements for compartments, including contingency plans, outbreak notification triggers, and access to indemnity funds.

[P30] Stakeholders will request that APHIS define the threshold of evidence used to conclude that a request “can be safely granted” and to disclose the internal evaluation criteria or scoring rubric to improve transparency.

[P30] Trade groups will request timelines for APHIS’ review and a commitment to meet deadlines to avoid undue market disruption for applicants seeking recognition.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The exemption of the FRTIB-13 system of records from multiple Privacy Act requirements is overly broad and lacks justification; stakeholders request a detailed explanation of the harms that would result if sections (c)(3), (d), (e)(1), (e)(4)(G)-(I), and (f) were applied.

Privacy and civil liberties groups will challenge the proposed blanket exemption for FRTIB-13 as creating an unacceptable risk of misuse of personally identifiable information without agency accountability or opportunity for individuals to access or amend records.

Legal experts will request citation to statutory authority enabling this specific scope of Privacy Act exemptions and demand redaction-limited alternatives (e.g., only exempting targeted records or fields rather than the entire system).

Exporters’ associations will request procedures to allow subnational authorities or competent regional agencies to submit requests when national governments are unable or unwilling to make requests, or to allow written delegation from national authorities.

Exporting countries will object to the requirement that requests be submitted only in English, arguing it creates an unnecessary barrier and favors English-speaking countries; they will request acceptance of requests in other UN languages or permitting certified translations.

Legal practitioners will request that APHIS provide a secure electronic submission option in addition to the specified postal address and clarify whether emailed or portal submissions meet the requirement.

Foreign veterinary services will request more specificity regarding page limits, format templates, and whether electronic or standardized data formats (e.g., XML, spreadsheets) are acceptable for the information required under paragraph (b).

Requesting governments will ask for a clear definition of “scope of the requested evaluation,” including whether requests may be disease-specific, commodity-specific, or apply to multiple diseases simultaneously.

Veterinary associations will request that APHIS specify which veterinary control and oversight documentation is required (e.g., legal statutes, staffing levels, certification of personnel) and whether third-party audits suffice.

Countries will ask for precise requirements for “disease history and vaccination practice information,” including the time periods to cover, acceptable record types, and whether aggregated vs. individual-level data is required.

Industry and traceability vendors will request specificity on acceptable livestock demographic fields (e.g., herd-level vs. individual animal IDs), accepted traceability systems, and whether unique identifiers are mandatory.
Requesting parties will ask APHIS to define standards or metrics for demonstrating “epidemiological separation,” including geographic buffer widths, quarantine protocols, and modelling expectations.
Commenters will request that APHIS specify required surveillance performance metrics (e.g., sensitivity, sampling intensity, reporting timeliness) and acceptable surveillance methodologies.

Laboratories and national reference centers will request clarity on minimal diagnostic laboratory capability standards, accreditation requirements (e.g., ISO/IEC 17025), and proficiency testing expectations.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement that comments "must be received by May 30, 2017" (§ 39.13(a)) conflicts with the separate deadline of December 26, 2017 in § 39.13(a)/(P40) and is confusing; the agency should clarify and harmonize the public comment deadline.

[P40] The alternate comment deadline of December 26, 2017 (§ 39.13(a)) contradicts the May 30, 2017 deadline (P1); stakeholders request explicit correction to a single, consistent docket submission date.

[P2] The phrase "Must comply with the AD within the specified times unless already accomplished" (§ 39.13(f)) is circular and ambiguous about whether previously completed work documented informally is considered "already accomplished"; request clarification of acceptable evidence.

[P44] Requiring a records review "within 50 hours TIS after the effective date" (§ 39.13(g)/P44) imposes an impractically short compliance window for owners without immediate access to maintenance records; request extension to a minimum of 90 days or 100 hours TIS.

[P7] The initial-replacement trigger for couplings with <500 hours TIS (§ 39.13(h)(1)/P7) is unclear where the coupling has had partial documented repairs; ask the FAA to define how partial repairs or prior non-standard work affect the hours TIS determination.

[P8] The requirement to replace couplings within 50 hours if TIS ≥500 or unknown (§ 39.13(h)(2)/P8) is overly burdensome for operators with multiple aircraft and limited spares; request a phased compliance schedule or longer lead time.

[P5] Referencing compliance times "in paragraphs (g)(1) and (g)(2)" (§ 39.13(g)/P5) is confusing because the rule text uses (h)(1)/(h)(2) elsewhere; request correction of paragraph cross-references to avoid misinterpretation.

[P3] The mandate to replace specific part numbers N4211–375–M and 5322C–375–Z with "a new exhaust tailpipe v-band coupling" (§ 39.13(g)/(i)(1)/P3/P55) does not specify approved replacement P/Ns or OEM source; request listing of acceptable replacement part numbers and acceptable manufacturers.

[P61] Allowing installation of the one-piece coupling P/N NH1000897–40 as terminating action (§ 39.13(i)(2)(i)/P61) should include explicit airworthiness approval and service bulletin reference; request the FAA include certification basis and any supplemental instructions for installation.

[P34] The prohibition on installing used v-band couplings after the effective date (§ 39.13(h)(4)/P34) may create supply issues for owners of vintage aircraft; request an allowance for properly documented used parts that meet inspection criteria or provide a parts supply plan.

[P31] The limitation that removed-coupling inspections only apply to reinstalling the same coupling (§ 39.13(h)(3)/P31) is ambiguous about couplings removed from one airplane and reinstalled on another after inspection; request explicit prohibition or allowance with documentation requirements.

[P33] The statement that removed-coupling inspections do not restart the 500-hour replacement clock (§ 39.13(h)(3)/P33) conflicts with language elsewhere that resets TIS when a new coupling is installed; request clarity on how TIS is tracked after removal/reinstall and after installing new vs. used parts.

[P4] The specific installation torque procedure "tighten to 40 in-lbs, tap, and torque again to 40 in-lbs" (§ 39.13(g)/(i)(1)/(i)(56)/P4/P56) lacks tolerance bands and acceptable torque tool calibration requirements; request the FAA specify torque tolerances and tool calibration frequency.

[P59] Specifying a 60 in-lbs torque for P/N U4211–375–M (§ 39.13(i)(2)(i)/P59) without indicating acceptable torque measurement method or whether inch-ounces are acceptable is incomplete; request torqueing method (e.g., inch-ounces vs. in-lb torque wrench) and calibration standards.

[P60] The instruction for P/N 4404C375–M to "add 20 in-lbs after running torque is overcome" (§ 39.13(i)(2)(i)/P60) is vague about how to identify "running torque" and whether the additional 20 in-lbs is absolute or relative; ask for step-by-step procedure and numeric thresholds.

[P6] Note 2's recommendation to run the engine and recheck torque after installation (§ 39.13 Note 2 to (g) and (h)(2)/P6/P54) is advisory only and could be interpreted inconsistently; request this become a mandatory post-installation verification to ensure flight safety.

[P72] The annual inspection torque requirement "torque to 40 in-lbs" for certain P/Ns (§ 39.13(j)(2)(vii)(A)/P72) lacks tolerances and does not address potential thread lubrication effects; request specification of torque measurement conditions (dry vs lubricated) and acceptable ± tolerance.

[P74] The complex procedure for P/N 4404C375–M during annual inspection (§ 39.13(j)(2)(vii)(C)/P74) that requires loosening, verifying running torque, then adding 20 in-lbs is operationally unclear and time-consuming; request that FAA provide a clear step sequence and rationale or allow replacement with a one-piece clamp as an alternative.

[P63] Requiring visual inspection "at the next annual or within 12 months and then every 12 months" (§ 39.13(j)/P63) may conflict with operators on alternative inspection schedules under continuous airworthiness maintenance programs; request allowance for equivalent inspections under approved maintenance programs.

[P64] The permission to perform the removed-coupling inspection instead of the installed inspection if removed during annual (§ 39.13(j)(1)/P64) should mandate documentation of the removed-coupling inspection in logbooks; request explicit logbook entry requirements.

[P15] The flatness criterion requiring gap <0.062 inches with a straight edge (§ 39.13(h)(1)(iii)/(k)(1)(iii)/P15/P79) is too precise for field measurement without specifying straight edge thickness and measurement method; request standardized measuring tools and method description.

[P16] The prohibition to reinstall if gap >0.062 inches (§ 39.13(h)(1)(iii)/P16) may lead to many replacements because small measurement variability could exceed the threshold; request a tolerance band (e.g., 0.062 ±0.010 in) or requirement for repeat measurements.

[P11] Mandating cleaning with "crocus cloth and Stoddard solvent" (§ 39.13(h)(1)(i)/(k)(1)(i)/P11/P77) may conflict with local environmental or shop policies that prohibit Stoddard solvent; request acceptable alternative cleaning agents listed or equivalent cleaning standards.

[P12] Requiring a 10X magnifier for visual inspection (§ 39.13(h)(1)(ii)/(k)(1)(ii)/P12/P78) does not specify whether optics must be illuminated or if borescopes are acceptable for hard-to-see areas; request allowance for equivalent magnification tools and illumination requirements.

[P18] The inspection with t-bolt at 12 o'clock to check attachment (§ 39.13(h)(1)(iv)/(k)(1)(iv)/P18/P80) may be physically difficult on some installations; request diagrams or photos to show the required orientation and acceptable alternative positions.

[P19] The recommendation to use backlighting (§ 39.13(h)(1)(iv)/P19) should be made mandatory where lighting conditions prevent adequate inspection; request that the FAA require adequate lighting or specify lumen/illumination standards.

[P20] Prohibiting reinstallation if gaps between outer band and v-retainer are found (§ 39.13(h)(1)(iv)/P20) requires a clear definition of "gap" measurement; request specification of minimum gap depth that constitutes a reportable defect.

[P21] Requiring installation of new coupling "before further flight" when gaps are found (§ 39.13(h)(1)(iv)/P21) could ground aircraft on short trips; request allowance for ferry flights under special flight permits to reach maintenance facilities.

[P22] Inspecting bend radii "throughout the length of the segment" (§ 39.13(h)(1)(v)/P22) is subjective; request objective criteria or examples of cracks that are permissible vs. not permissible.

[P23] The prohibition on reinstalling if any crack is found in bend radii (§ 39.13(h)(1)(v)/P23) should define crack size threshold (e.g., length or depth) and allow non-destructive testing (NDT) as an alternative; request NDT allowance and threshold guidance.

[P25] Inspecting the outer band opposite the t-bolt for "distortion, creases, bulging, or cracks" (§ 39.13(h)(1)(vi)/P25) is highly subjective; request photographic examples and objective measurement tolerances for each defect type.

[P26] The prohibition to reinstall if any damage is found opposite the t-bolt (§ 39.13(h)(1)(vi)/P26) may be overly conservative for minor cosmetic defects; request classification of severity levels that permit safe continued use until next scheduled maintenance.

[P28] Allowing reinstall of a removed coupling only if it passes all inspections (§ 39.13(h)(2)/P28) needs an explicit acceptance criteria checklist that can be filed in the aircraft logbook; request inclusion of an inspection form that technicians must sign.

[P29] The post-reinstallation requirement to "verify there is space between each v-retainer segment below the t-bolt" (§ 39.13(h)(2)/P29) lacks a minimum gap specification; request numeric gap requirement or measurement method.

[P30] Requiring replacement "before further flight" if no space between segments exists after reinstallation (§ 39.13(h)(2)/P30) should allow for special flight permits/ferry flights and clarify whether the aircraft can be moved to a maintenance facility under specific conditions.

[P36] The AMOC approval authority assigned to the Wichita ACO Manager (§ 39.13(i)(1)/(l)(1)/P36/P86) may limit access to AMOC processing for operators in other regions; request multiple regional points of contact or national-level AMOC processing guidance to expedite requests.

[P37] Requiring AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 (§ 39.13(i)(1)/P37) may delay urgent AMOC approvals; request the FAA provide an expedited AMOC process for safety-critical compliance or a temporary relief path.

[P39] The obligation to notify your principal inspector before using an approved AMOC (§ 39.13(i)(2)/P39) should require written notification with a 48-hour timeline rather than ambiguous "notify"; request standardized notification procedures and timelines.

[P42] The exemption for airplanes with one-piece coupling P/N NH1000897–40 (§ 39.13(c)(2)/P42) does not state whether that part must have been installed by the manufacturer or whether a field-mod installation qualifies; request clarification and documentation requirements.

[P41] The applicability statement listing specific Textron models (§ 39.13(c)(1)/P41) should include explicit serial number ranges or clarify "all serial numbers" to avoid ambiguity about remanufactured airframes or derivative models.

[P85] The prohibition in § 39.13(k)(4) on installing used couplings except as inspected is broadly phrased; request the FAA define "used" and whether parts remanufactured to OEM spec are considered "new" or "used."

[P75] Stating that visual inspections do not terminate the 500-hour replacement requirement (§ 39.13(j)(3)/P75) may confuse maintenance record-keeping; request explicit instructions on how to log inspections versus replacements and how to track the 500-hour replacement interval.

[P46] The cross-reference in § 39.13(h) to perform repetitive replacements per paragraph (i) (P46) is confusing because paragraph (i) contains replacement installation steps and part lists; request clearer structuring so compliance times and actions are unambiguous.

[P76] The general requirement to perform removed-coupling inspections if coupling is removed during visual inspection (§ 39.13(k)/P76) needs an explicit list of authorized personnel (A&P, IA) who may perform the inspections and sign off; request clarification.

[P77] The instruction to clean corrosion/pitting "pay particular attention to spot weld areas" (§ 39.13(k)(1)(i)/P77) should provide acceptance criteria for pitting depth beyond which replacement is mandatory; request numeric limits or acceptance charts.

[P81] The requirement to inspect bend radii for cracks (§ 39.13(k)(1)(v)/P81) should allow use of dye penetrant or other NDT methods when visual inspection is inconclusive; request inclusion of acceptable NDT methods and criteria.

[P83] Allowing reinstallation if the removed coupling passes checks (§ 39.13(k)(2)/P83) should require recordation of the removed-coupling inspection results in the aircraft maintenance log with the technician's certificate number; request mandatory logbook entries.

[P86] Granting AMOC authority only to the Wichita ACO Manager (§ 39.13(l)(1)/P86) could create inequity or processing delays; request delegation to multiple ACOs or to the national AD office to streamline AMOC approvals.

[P87] The submission instructions for AMOCs (§ 39.13(l)(1)/P87) require direct submissions to named FAA managers but do not provide email or electronic submission standards; request provision of email addresses, secure upload instructions, and expected turnaround times.

[P88] The obligation to notify principal inspector before using an approved AMOC (§ 39.13(l)(2)/P88) should specify acceptable methods of notification (email, fax, logbook entry) and required timing (e.g., prior to the next flight or within 48 hours); request concrete notification procedures.

The prohibition to reinstall if gap >0.062 inches (§ 39.13(h)(1)(iii)/P16) may lead to many replacements because small measurement variability could exceed the threshold; request a tolerance band (e.g., 0.062 ±0.010 in) or requirement for repeat measurements.

Mandating cleaning with "crocus cloth and Stoddard solvent" (§ 39.13(h)(1)(i)/(k)(1)(i)/P11/P77) may conflict with local environmental or shop policies that prohibit Stoddard solvent; request acceptable alternative cleaning agents listed or equivalent cleaning standards.

Requiring a 10X magnifier for visual inspection (§ 39.13(h)(1)(ii)/(k)(1)(ii)/P12/P78) does not specify whether optics must be illuminated or if borescopes are acceptable for hard-to-see areas; request allowance for equivalent magnification tools and illumination requirements.

The inspection with t-bolt at 12 o'clock to check attachment (§ 39.13(h)(1)(iv)/(k)(1)(iv)/P18/P80) may be physically difficult on some installations; request diagrams or photos to show the required orientation and acceptable alternative positions.

The recommendation to use backlighting (§ 39.13(h)(1)(iv)/P19) should be made mandatory where lighting conditions prevent adequate inspection; request that the FAA require adequate lighting or specify lumen/illumination standards.

Prohibiting reinstallation if gaps between outer band and v-retainer are found (§ 39.13(h)(1)(iv)/P20) requires a clear definition of "gap" measurement; request specification of minimum gap depth that constitutes a reportable defect.

Requiring installation of new coupling "before further flight" when gaps are found (§ 39.13(h)(1)(iv)/P21) could ground aircraft on short trips; request allowance for ferry flights under special flight permits to reach maintenance facilities.
Inspecting bend radii "throughout the length of the segment" (§ 39.13(h)(1)(v)/P22) is subjective; request objective criteria or examples of cracks that are permissible vs. not permissible.

The prohibition on reinstalling if any crack is found in bend radii (§ 39.13(h)(1)(v)/P23) should define crack size threshold (e.g., length or depth) and allow non-destructive testing (NDT) as an alternative; request NDT allowance and threshold guidance.

Inspecting the outer band opposite the t-bolt for "distortion, creases, bulging, or cracks" (§ 39.13(h)(1)(vi)/P25) is highly subjective; request photographic examples and objective measurement tolerances for each defect type.

The prohibition to reinstall if any damage is found opposite the t-bolt (§ 39.13(h)(1)(vi)/P26) may be overly conservative for minor cosmetic defects; request classification of severity levels that permit safe continued use until next scheduled maintenance.

Allowing reinstall of a removed coupling only if it passes all inspections (§ 39.13(h)(2)/P28) needs an explicit acceptance criteria checklist that can be filed in the aircraft logbook; request inclusion of an inspection form that technicians must sign.

The post-reinstallation requirement to "verify there is space between each v-retainer segment below the t-bolt" (§ 39.13(h)(2)/P29) lacks a minimum gap specification; request numeric gap requirement or measurement method.

Requiring replacement "before further flight" if no space between segments exists after reinstallation (§ 39.13(h)(2)/P30) should allow for special flight permits/ferry flights and clarify whether the aircraft can be moved to a maintenance facility under specific conditions.

The AMOC approval authority assigned to the Wichita ACO Manager (§ 39.13(i)(1)/(l)(1)/P36/P86) may limit access to AMOC processing for operators in other regions; request multiple regional points of contact or national-level AMOC processing guidance to expedite requests.

Requiring AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 (§ 39.13(i)(1)/P37) may delay urgent AMOC approvals; request the FAA provide an expedited AMOC process for safety-critical compliance or a temporary relief path.

The obligation to notify your principal inspector before using an approved AMOC (§ 39.13(i)(2)/P39) should require written notification with a 48-hour timeline rather than ambiguous "notify"; request standardized notification procedures and timelines.

The exemption for airplanes with one-piece coupling P/N NH1000897–40 (§ 39.13(c)(2)/P42) does not state whether that part must have been installed by the manufacturer or whether a field-mod installation qualifies; request clarification and documentation requirements.

The applicability statement listing specific Textron models (§ 39.13(c)(1)/P41) should include explicit serial number ranges or clarify "all serial numbers" to avoid ambiguity about remanufactured airframes or derivative models.

The prohibition in § 39.13(k)(4) on installing used couplings except as inspected is broadly phrased; request the FAA define "used" and whether parts remanufactured to OEM spec are considered "new" or "used."

Stating that visual inspections do not terminate the 500-hour replacement requirement (§ 39.13(j)(3)/P75) may confuse maintenance record-keeping; request explicit instructions on how to log inspections versus replacements and how to track the 500-hour replacement interval.

The cross-reference in § 39.13(h) to perform repetitive replacements per paragraph (i) (P46) is confusing because paragraph (i) contains replacement installation steps and part lists; request clearer structuring so compliance times and actions are unambiguous.

The general requirement to perform removed-coupling inspections if coupling is removed during visual inspection (§ 39.13(k)/P76) needs an explicit list of authorized personnel (A&P, IA) who may perform the inspections and sign off; request clarification.

The instruction to clean corrosion/pitting "pay particular attention to spot weld areas" (§ 39.13(k)(1)(i)/P77) should provide acceptance criteria for pitting depth beyond which replacement is mandatory; request numeric limits or acceptance charts.

The requirement to inspect bend radii for cracks (§ 39.13(k)(1)(v)/P81) should allow use of dye penetrant or other NDT methods when visual inspection is inconclusive; request inclusion of acceptable NDT methods and criteria.

Allowing reinstallation if the removed coupling passes checks (§ 39.13(k)(2)/P83) should require recordation of the removed-coupling inspection results in the aircraft maintenance log with the technician's certificate number; request mandatory logbook entries.

Granting AMOC authority only to the Wichita ACO Manager (§ 39.13(l)(1)/P86) could create inequity or processing delays; request delegation to multiple ACOs or to the national AD office to streamline AMOC approvals.

The submission instructions for AMOCs (§ 39.13(l)(1)/P87) require direct submissions to named FAA managers but do not provide email or electronic submission standards; request provision of email addresses, secure upload instructions, and expected turnaround times.

The obligation to notify principal inspector before using an approved AMOC (§ 39.13(l)(2)/P88) should specify acceptable methods of notification (email, fax, logbook entry) and required timing (e.g., prior to the next flight or within 48 hours); request concrete notification procedures.
