raw_output:
[P1] The effective date of January 1, 2019 creates retroactive obligations for clinicians who furnished items/services earlier in 2019; CMS should clarify transitional relief for clinicians who could not reasonably know they were subject to MIPS at the start of the year.

[P1] The rule should specify how payments that cross calendar-year service dates (e.g., services starting in December 2018 and ending in January 2019) are attributed to the 2019 MIPS payment year to avoid double-counting or omission.

[P2] The exclusions list in §414.1310(b)(1) is incomplete because it does not address clinicians who are on temporary leave, sabbatical, or are deceased midyear; CMS should add transient-status exceptions.

[P3] The Qualifying APM Participant (QPP) exclusion (§414.1310(b)(1)(i)) must clarify timing — whether QP status determined after the performance period or during it controls eligibility for that performance year.

[P3] CMS should state how QP status calculated for different APMs with non-calendar reporting periods (e.g., quarterly APMs) will interact with the calendar-year MIPS performance period.

[P4] The provision excluding Partial QPs who elect not to report (§414.1310(b)(1)(ii)) could create gaming by Partial QPs opting out strategically; CMS should require documentation of the election and limit retroactive elections.

[P4] CMS should clarify whether Partial QPs who elect not to report still count towards group-level assessments and TIN aggregation under §§414.1310(e)(2)-(e)(4).

[P5] The low-volume threshold exclusion (§414.1310(b)(1)(iii)) lacks transparency about the exact numerical thresholds and look-back period; stakeholders request publication of the precise dollar/service thresholds and the data source.

[P5] Providers near the low-volume threshold need a mechanism to appeal CMS determinations of threshold status or opt in voluntarily; the rule should allow voluntary participation for excluded clinicians.

[P6] The prohibition on treating new Medicare-enrolled clinicians as MIPS eligible until the next year (§414.1310(c)) unfairly delays quality accountability for clinicians who begin practice early in the year; CMS should consider prorating or allowing partial-year participation.

[P6] CMS must clarify the definition of “new Medicare-enrolled eligible clinician” (e.g., new NPI vs. new TIN affiliation) and whether clinicians transferring practices are treated as new for purposes of §414.1310(c).

[P7] The prohibition on applying MIPS adjustment factors to non-MIPS clinicians (§414.1310(d)) needs procedural safeguards — specify how CMS will prevent erroneous adjustments in claims processing and how clinicians can seek correction.

[P8] The continuous group definition requirement (§414.1310(e)(2)) is overly rigid — groups frequently change membership, mergers occur, and TIN arrangements shift; CMS should allow short interruptions or provide safe harbors (e.g., 30-day grace periods).

[P8] CMS should define what constitutes “meeting the definition of a group at all times” (e.g., continuous shared TIN, formal legal entity status, tax filings) to reduce ambiguity and disputes.

[P9] The requirement to aggregate performance data across the group's TIN (§414.1310(e)(3)) will unfairly penalize clinicians who bill under the same TIN but practice independently; CMS should allow sub-TIN reporting or opt-out for clinically independent practitioners.

[P9] Aggregating across a TIN fails to account for multi-site practices with different patient mixes; CMS should permit risk adjustment or stratification within TINs before aggregation.

[P10] Requiring that a group assessed as a group be assessed across all four categories (§414.1310(e)(4)) removes flexibility for groups that are ready to report in some categories but not others; CMS should allow hybrid assessments or partial group participation.

[P11] The CMS-required election process for group assessment (§414.1310(e)(5)) must be detailed publicly well before the performance period with timelines and consequences for missing deadlines; otherwise groups cannot plan operationally.

[P11] CMS should provide an electronic interface and confirmation receipts for group election submissions and permit corrections within a defined window.

[P12] Mandating submission of quality, CPIA, and advancing care information (§414.1325(a)) creates significant reporting burden; CMS should allow small practices (e.g., ≤15 clinicians) flexibility or simplified reporting requirements.

[P12] CMS should publish standardized data schemas and testing environments for each submission mechanism so clinicians can validate their submissions in advance.

[P13] Allowing individual clinicians to choose among data submission mechanisms (§414.1325(b)) creates potential inconsistency; request clarification on whether clinicians may switch mechanisms year-to-year and the deadlines for changing mechanisms.

[P14] The qualified registry option (§414.1325(b)(1)) should include certification criteria and a public list of approved registries; CMS must require registries to demonstrate data security and auditability.

[P15] The EHR submission mechanism (§414.1325(b)(2)) must require EHR vendors to support standardized reporting formats and to provide attestation that data submitted on behalf of clinicians is complete and unaltered.

[P16] QCDR submission (§414.1325(b)(3)) should be limited to QCDRs that have publicly available measure specifications and transparent benchmarking; CMS should require QCDRs to publish exclusion logic and sampling methods.

[P17] Using Medicare Part B claims to submit quality data (§414.1325(b)(4)) risks undercounting quality because claims lack clinical detail; CMS should require supplemental documentation or limit claims-only reporting to specific measures validated for claims.

[P18] Attestation for CPIA and advancing care information (§414.1325(b)(5)) may be vulnerable to inaccuracies; CMS should require supporting documentation be retained and subject to audit for a specified period (e.g., 6 years).

[P19] Groups' choice among submission mechanisms (§414.1325(c)) should permit different clinicians within a group to use different mechanisms only if the group is not electing group assessment; clarify interplay with §414.1310(e)(3).

[P20] Qualified registries for groups (§414.1325(c)(1)) should be required to accept batch uploads and provide feedback reports within a defined timeframe to allow groups to correct errors.

[P21] EHR vendor submissions for groups (§414.1325(c)(2)) must ensure that vendors have explicit authorization from the group and that data provenance is preserved; CMS should prohibit vendors from charging excessive fees for submissions.

[P22] QCDRs for groups (§414.1325(c)(3)) should be required to support aggregated TIN-level reporting and provide comparative benchmarking to help groups improve performance.

[P23] The CMS Web Interface limitation to groups of 25+ clinicians (§414.1325(c)(4)) is arbitrary; smaller groups should have access to a Web Interface option or an alternative lightweight web reporting tool.

[P24] Allowing attestation for CPIA and advancing care information at group level (§414.1325(c)(5)) raises accuracy concerns; CMS should require attestations to include named responsible officials and require periodic audits.

[P25] Requirement to use a CMS-approved survey vendor for CAHPS (§414.1325(c)(6)) should include vendor qualifications, conflict-of-interest rules, and fee caps; smaller groups may be priced out and need subsidy or a low-cost alternative.

[P26] Requiring groups using CAHPS to also choose another mechanism for other quality data (§414.1325(c)(6) / §414.1325(a)(3)(B)) increases burden and cost; CMS should permit CAHPS plus a simplified claims-based measure set for smaller groups.

[P27] Allowing multiple submission mechanisms (§414.1325(d)) can produce inconsistent identifiers and mapping errors; CMS should mandate a single canonical identifier in CMS systems and require reconciliation procedures.

[P28] Requiring the same identifier across all performance categories (§414.1325(d)) is reasonable, but CMS must specify the acceptable identifier (NPI, TIN+NPI) and provide guidance for clinicians with multiple NPIs.

[P29] Limiting submissions to one mechanism per performance category (§414.1325(d)) is inflexible — if a submission fails (e.g., registry rejects file), clinicians should be allowed to submit via an alternative mechanism within the submission window.

[P30] Mandating CMS-approved survey vendor for CAHPS (§414.1325(e)) without listing approved vendors or the approval timeline prevents groups from timely vendor contracting; CMS should publish the vendor list and procurement schedule.

[P31] Permitting other quality data to be reported using any single available mechanism (§414.1325(e)) requires clearer rules on how to combine measures submitted via different mechanisms for the same clinician when not reporting as a group.

[P32] Exempting resource use from clinician submission and having CMS calculate it via claims (§414.1325(f)) is appropriate, but CMS must publish detailed measure specifications, risk-adjustment models, and attribution rules before the performance period.

[P33] The March 31 deadline (§414.1325(g)(1)) for qualified registry, QCDR, EHR, and attestation submissions is too soon after the close of the performance period for small practices to reconcile data; CMS should extend the deadline or provide a phased submission window.

[P34] Requiring Part B claims to have dates of service during the performance period (§414.1325(g)(2)) is logical, but CMS should clarify handling of late claims reopens and resubmissions after the 90-day processing window.

[P35] The 90-day processing requirement for Part B claims (§414.1325(g)(2)) may be unrealistic given current Medicare claims processing backlogs; CMS should either lengthen the processing window or provide a failsafe allowing late claims in exceptional circumstances.

[P36] An eight-week CMS Web Interface submission window (§414.1325(g)(3)) that must begin no earlier than January 1 and end by March 31 compresses reporting into a busy time of year; CMS should stagger Web Interface windows regionally or extend the end date.

[P37] The requirement that the Web Interface period not begin before January 1 (§414.1325(g)(3)) is unnecessary; earlier windows could ease bandwidth and vendor load — allow CMS discretion to open earlier if operationally feasible.

[P38] Ending the Web Interface by March 31 (§414.1325(g)(3)) conflicts with the March 31 deadline for other mechanisms and leaves no time for cross-mechanism reconciliation; CMS should align and possibly extend all mechanisms to a single shared deadline.

[P39] The quality measure selection (§414.1330(a)) should include a mechanism for clinicians to propose new measures or contest measure specifications before finalization; transparency is required for measure retirement and addition.

[P40] Using the final MIPS list (§414.1330(a)(1)) is acceptable only if CMS publishes measure technical specifications, numerator/denominator logic, and exclusions sufficiently in advance (at least 120 days prior to the performance period).

[P41] Including QCDR measures (§414.1330(a)(2)) raises comparability concerns; CMS must ensure QCDR measures are harmonized, validated, and risk-adjusted comparable to MIPS final list measures before their inclusion in scoring.

[P42] The shifting weight percentages for the quality category (§414.1330(b)) create instability; CMS should provide multi-year notice of weight changes and grandfathering rules to allow clinicians to plan investments.

[P43] Setting quality at 50% for 2019 (§414.1330(b)(1)) will heavily penalize clinicians unable to report quality in their first MIPS year; CMS should allow temporary reweighting for small and new practices.

[P44] Reducing quality to 45% in 2020 (§414.1330(b)(2)) and further to 30% thereafter (§414.1330(b)(3)) must be accompanied by transparent methodology for how reweighting will occur and how the vacated weight is reallocated.

[P45] The downward trajectory of quality weighting (§414.1330(b)(3)) may de-emphasize clinical outcomes over cost/IT metrics; patient advocates should be allowed to comment on the policy rationale.

[P46] Requiring submission of quality measures via specified methods (§414.1335(a)) is acceptable only if CMS provides clear allowable codes, data formats, and validation rules for each method.

[P47] The 12-month reporting period requirement (§414.1335(a)(1)) is burdensome for clinicians with short-term contracts or locum tenens; CMS should permit shorter reporting intervals for such clinicians with prorated scoring.

[P48] The requirement to report at least six measures including one cross-cutting and one outcome (§414.1335(a)(1)(i)) may be infeasible for many specialties that lack outcome measures; CMS should expand the list of acceptable outcome/high-priority measures per specialty.

[P49] The exception allowing another high priority measure if no outcome exists (§414.1335(a)(1)(i)) needs a defined hierarchy and definitions of “high priority” to avoid arbitrary CMS determinations.

[P50] The fallback requiring reporting all applicable measures if fewer than six apply (§414.1335(a)(1)(i)) could disadvantage clinicians in narrow specialties; CMS should implement an adjustment to scoring when fewer than six measures are applicable so clinicians are not penalized.

[P51] Allowing selection from the full MIPS list or specialty subsets (§414.1335(a)(1)(ii)) is positive, but CMS must publish specialty subsets and the process/timeline for requesting addition or modification of subsets.

[P52] The ability to choose measures from the complete MIPS list (§414.1335(a)(1)(ii)) requires clarity about cross-specialty applicability — whether measures outside a clinician’s specialty can be used and how scoring accounts for relevance.

[P53] CMS-designated specialty-specific measure sets (§414.1335(a)(1)(ii)) should be developed with specialty societies and contain measures validated for comparability and clinical relevance.

[P54] Requiring groups to report via the Web Interface for 12 months (§414.1335(a)(2)) assumes groups can maintain consistent data capture across sites; CMS should permit site-level exceptions when CMS Web Interface measures are not feasible at all locations.

[P55] The requirement that groups of 25+ report on all CMS Web Interface measures (§414.1335(a)(2)(i)) is burdensome — CMS should allow a subset selection if a measure is demonstrably inapplicable to the group’s patient population.

[P56] Requiring reporting on the first 248 consecutively ranked beneficiaries per measure (§414.1335(a)(2)(i)) is arbitrary; groups need the option of randomized sampling and the ability to oversample for specialty areas.

[P57] The rule that groups must report 100% of assigned beneficiaries when sample < 248 (§414.1335(a)(2)(ii)) could create undue burden for very large or complex patient panels; CMS should permit statistically valid sampling methodologies when sample sizes are small.

[P58] The CAHPS survey vendor requirement for CAHPS participation (§414.1335(a)(3)(i)) requires CMS to ensure geographic coverage and linguistic accessibility; smaller/rural groups may have difficulty accessing approved vendors.

[P59] Counting CAHPS as one measure and satisfying cross-cutting requirements (§414.1335(a)(3)(A)) is useful, but CMS should clarify how CAHPS survey response rate thresholds affect measure scoring and whether nonresponse adjustments are applied.

[P60] The requirement that groups using CAHPS select another submission mechanism for other quality data (§414.1335(a)(3)(B)) increases cost and operational complexity; CMS should allow certain small groups to substitute a validated claims-based measure set.

[P61] Excluding non-patient-facing clinicians from cross-cutting reporting (§414.1335(b)) is appropriate, but CMS should clarify the exact thresholds and documentation needed to demonstrate non-patient-facing status.

[P62] Requiring reporting on at least 90% of patients meeting denominator criteria for QCDR/registry/EHR (§414.1340(a)) is excessively high and may be unattainable for practices with fragmented records; CMS should lower the threshold (e.g., to 70–80%) or permit representative sampling.

[P63] The 80% threshold for Part B claims reporting (§414.1340(b)) is similarly high given historical claim variability; CMS should adopt an 80% benchmark only for measures validated on claims and provide exceptions for low-volume clinicians.

[P64] Requiring groups submitting via Web Interface to meet CMS-provided sample requirements (§414.1340(c)) is acceptable only if CMS publishes the sampling methodology, randomization process, and allows appeals for demonstrably unrepresentative samples.

[P65] CMS specifying resource use measures (§414.1350(a)) must include full transparency of methodology, attribution, and risk adjustment; otherwise resource use scoring will be contested.

[P66] Reweighting authority for resource use (§414.1350(b)) must be constrained; CMS should publish triggers for reweighting and provide notice and comment prior to substantial changes in category weights.

[P67] Setting resource use at 10% for 2019 (§414.1350(b)(1)) may underemphasize cost control, while later increases to 30% could be abrupt; CMS should phase weight changes more gradually and give two years notice before major changes.

[P68] Increasing resource use to 15% in 2020 (§414.1350(b)(2)) requires clinicians to have access to resource use reports and benchmarks well before the performance period; CMS must commit to distributing actionable reports.

[P69] Jumping resource use to 30% after 2020 (§414.1350(b)(3)) could disproportionately affect specialties with inherently higher costs; CMS should apply specialty-level normalization or caps on year-to-year score swings.

[P70] The CPIA inventory requirement (§414.1355(a)) must include an open process for stakeholders to propose activities and realistic timelines for CMS to vet and approve activities.

[P71] Fixing CPIA at 15% of CPS (§414.1355(b)(1)) is acceptable if CMS allows flexibility to reweight CPIA for small practices or when advancing care information cannot be reported due to EHR limitations.

[P72] The list of CPIA inclusion criteria (§414.1355(c)) is comprehensive but CMS should prioritize clarity on how activities are scored (binary yes/no vs. scaled points) and how multiple activities combine to produce a CPIA score.

[P73] The “relevance to subcategory” criterion (§414.1355(c)(1)) needs examples and mapping to existing CPIA subcategories so clinicians can design activities that clearly meet the requirement.

[P74] The requirement that activities demonstrate importance toward improved beneficiary outcomes (§414.1355(c)(2)) must not require prohibitive levels of clinical evidence; CMS should accept high-quality process measures and plausible logic models.

[P75] The requirement that CPIA activities help reduce disparities (§414.1355(c)(3)) is commendable, but CMS must define metrics for disparity reduction and provide weight for activities targeting social determinants.

[P76] Alignment with patient-centered medical home (§414.1355(c)(4)) should not limit CPIA credit to only PCMH-recognized models; small practices implementing PCMH principles without formal recognition should be eligible.

[P77] The criterion that activities be performable by multiple provider types (§414.1355(c)(5)) risks excluding specialty-specific innovations; CMS should allow a portion of the CPIA inventory to include specialty-specific activities.

[P78] The feasibility and provider burden criterion (§414.1355(c)(6)) should include explicit protections for small (≤15), rural, and HPSA practices, including simplified reporting pathways and higher weighting for low-burden activities.

[P79] CMS’s ability to validate CPIA activities (§414.1355(c)(7)) must be defined — what documentation will CMS require, what audit methods will be used, and what sanctions apply for non-validation.

[P80] Evidence supporting likely improvement in outcomes (§414.1355(c)(8)) should allow for emerging practices and pilot programs; CMS should permit provisional CPIA credit for innovative activities with a plan for evaluation.

[P81] CMS stating it will assess CPIA performance using inventory-listed activities (§414.1355(d)) should also explain scoring rules, minimum thresholds for credit, and how partial completion of activities is treated.

[P82] The requirement that clinicians submit CPIA data using listed mechanisms (§414.1360(a)) should be accompanied by detailed data element definitions and standardized attestation forms.

[P83] Listing administrative claims as an acceptable CPIA submission mechanism only “if technically feasible” (§414.1360(a)) lacks clarity — CMS should define technical feasibility and provide a timetable for claims-based CPIA implementation.

[P84] Because administrative claims may not capture CPIA activities well (§414.1360(a)), CMS should invest in modifying claims forms (e.g., adding G-codes) before relying on claims for CPIA submissions.

[P85] Qualified registry submission for CPIA (§414.1360(a)) must require registries to accept small-volume submissions and provide error reports; CMS should publish registry certification requirements.

[P86] EHR submission mechanisms for CPIA (§414.1360(a)) must be standardized via certified APIs, and CMS should require EHR vendors to support CPIA exports without additional proprietary fees.

[P87] QCDRs accepting CPIA submissions (§414.1360(a)) should be required to publicly disclose their CPIA mappings and scoring algorithms to ensure transparency and comparability.

[P88] CMS Web Interface as a CPIA mechanism (§414.1360(a)) should be available to groups of all sizes when feasible, not only large groups, especially for CPIA activities that cannot be captured in claims/EHR.

[P89] Allowing attestation for CPIA submissions (§414.1360(a)) must be coupled with a clear audit schedule, retention requirements, and penalties for falsified attestations.

[P90] The truncated provision requiring yes/no responses for activities performed at least 90 days (§414.1360(a) truncated) is unclear; CMS should publish complete reporting instructions, define the 90-day threshold precisely, and indicate whether partial completion (e.g., 60 days) receives partial credit.

The EHR submission mechanism (§414.1325(b)(2)) must require EHR vendors to support standardized reporting formats and to provide attestation that data submitted on behalf of clinicians is complete and unaltered.

QCDR submission (§414.1325(b)(3)) should be limited to QCDRs that have publicly available measure specifications and transparent benchmarking; CMS should require QCDRs to publish exclusion logic and sampling methods.

Using Medicare Part B claims to submit quality data (§414.1325(b)(4)) risks undercounting quality because claims lack clinical detail; CMS should require supplemental documentation or limit claims-only reporting to specific measures validated for claims.

Attestation for CPIA and advancing care information (§414.1325(b)(5)) may be vulnerable to inaccuracies; CMS should require supporting documentation be retained and subject to audit for a specified period (e.g., 6 years).

Groups' choice among submission mechanisms (§414.1325(c)) should permit different clinicians within a group to use different mechanisms only if the group is not electing group assessment; clarify interplay with §414.1310(e)(3).
Qualified registries for groups (§414.1325(c)(1)) should be required to accept batch uploads and provide feedback reports within a defined timeframe to allow groups to correct errors.

EHR vendor submissions for groups (§414.1325(c)(2)) must ensure that vendors have explicit authorization from the group and that data provenance is preserved; CMS should prohibit vendors from charging excessive fees for submissions.
QCDRs for groups (§414.1325(c)(3)) should be required to support aggregated TIN-level reporting and provide comparative benchmarking to help groups improve performance.

The CMS Web Interface limitation to groups of 25+ clinicians (§414.1325(c)(4)) is arbitrary; smaller groups should have access to a Web Interface option or an alternative lightweight web reporting tool.

Allowing attestation for CPIA and advancing care information at group level (§414.1325(c)(5)) raises accuracy concerns; CMS should require attestations to include named responsible officials and require periodic audits.

Requirement to use a CMS-approved survey vendor for CAHPS (§414.1325(c)(6)) should include vendor qualifications, conflict-of-interest rules, and fee caps; smaller groups may be priced out and need subsidy or a low-cost alternative.

Requiring groups using CAHPS to also choose another mechanism for other quality data (§414.1325(c)(6) / §414.1325(a)(3)(B)) increases burden and cost; CMS should permit CAHPS plus a simplified claims-based measure set for smaller groups.

Allowing multiple submission mechanisms (§414.1325(d)) can produce inconsistent identifiers and mapping errors; CMS should mandate a single canonical identifier in CMS systems and require reconciliation procedures.

Requiring the same identifier across all performance categories (§414.1325(d)) is reasonable, but CMS must specify the acceptable identifier (NPI, TIN+NPI) and provide guidance for clinicians with multiple NPIs.

Limiting submissions to one mechanism per performance category (§414.1325(d)) is inflexible — if a submission fails (e.g., registry rejects file), clinicians should be allowed to submit via an alternative mechanism within the submission window.

Mandating CMS-approved survey vendor for CAHPS (§414.1325(e)) without listing approved vendors or the approval timeline prevents groups from timely vendor contracting; CMS should publish the vendor list and procurement schedule.

Permitting other quality data to be reported using any single available mechanism (§414.1325(e)) requires clearer rules on how to combine measures submitted via different mechanisms for the same clinician when not reporting as a group.

Exempting resource use from clinician submission and having CMS calculate it via claims (§414.1325(f)) is appropriate, but CMS must publish detailed measure specifications, risk-adjustment models, and attribution rules before the performance period.

The March 31 deadline (§414.1325(g)(1)) for qualified registry, QCDR, EHR, and attestation submissions is too soon after the close of the performance period for small practices to reconcile data; CMS should extend the deadline or provide a phased submission window.

Requiring Part B claims to have dates of service during the performance period (§414.1325(g)(2)) is logical, but CMS should clarify handling of late claims reopens and resubmissions after the 90-day processing window.

The 90-day processing requirement for Part B claims (§414.1325(g)(2)) may be unrealistic given current Medicare claims processing backlogs; CMS should either lengthen the processing window or provide a failsafe allowing late claims in exceptional circumstances.

An eight-week CMS Web Interface submission window (§414.1325(g)(3)) that must begin no earlier than January 1 and end by March 31 compresses reporting into a busy time of year; CMS should stagger Web Interface windows regionally or extend the end date.

The requirement that the Web Interface period not begin before January 1 (§414.1325(g)(3)) is unnecessary; earlier windows could ease bandwidth and vendor load — allow CMS discretion to open earlier if operationally feasible.

Ending the Web Interface by March 31 (§414.1325(g)(3)) conflicts with the March 31 deadline for other mechanisms and leaves no time for cross-mechanism reconciliation; CMS should align and possibly extend all mechanisms to a single shared deadline.

The quality measure selection (§414.1330(a)) should include a mechanism for clinicians to propose new measures or contest measure specifications before finalization; transparency is required for measure retirement and addition.

Using the final MIPS list (§414.1330(a)(1)) is acceptable only if CMS publishes measure technical specifications, numerator/denominator logic, and exclusions sufficiently in advance (at least 120 days prior to the performance period).

Including QCDR measures (§414.1330(a)(2)) raises comparability concerns; CMS must ensure QCDR measures are harmonized, validated, and risk-adjusted comparable to MIPS final list measures before their inclusion in scoring.

The shifting weight percentages for the quality category (§414.1330(b)) create instability; CMS should provide multi-year notice of weight changes and grandfathering rules to allow clinicians to plan investments.

Setting quality at 50% for 2019 (§414.1330(b)(1)) will heavily penalize clinicians unable to report quality in their first MIPS year; CMS should allow temporary reweighting for small and new practices.

Reducing quality to 45% in 2020 (§414.1330(b)(2)) and further to 30% thereafter (§414.1330(b)(3)) must be accompanied by transparent methodology for how reweighting will occur and how the vacated weight is reallocated.
The downward trajectory of quality weighting (§414.1330(b)(3)) may de-emphasize clinical outcomes over cost/IT metrics; patient advocates should be allowed to comment on the policy rationale.
Requiring submission of quality measures via specified methods (§414.1335(a)) is acceptable only if CMS provides clear allowable codes, data formats, and validation rules for each method.

The 12-month reporting period requirement (§414.1335(a)(1)) is burdensome for clinicians with short-term contracts or locum tenens; CMS should permit shorter reporting intervals for such clinicians with prorated scoring.

The requirement to report at least six measures including one cross-cutting and one outcome (§414.1335(a)(1)(i)) may be infeasible for many specialties that lack outcome measures; CMS should expand the list of acceptable outcome/high-priority measures per specialty.
The exception allowing another high priority measure if no outcome exists (§414.1335(a)(1)(i)) needs a defined hierarchy and definitions of “high priority” to avoid arbitrary CMS determinations.

The fallback requiring reporting all applicable measures if fewer than six apply (§414.1335(a)(1)(i)) could disadvantage clinicians in narrow specialties; CMS should implement an adjustment to scoring when fewer than six measures are applicable so clinicians are not penalized.

Allowing selection from the full MIPS list or specialty subsets (§414.1335(a)(1)(ii)) is positive, but CMS must publish specialty subsets and the process/timeline for requesting addition or modification of subsets.

The ability to choose measures from the complete MIPS list (§414.1335(a)(1)(ii)) requires clarity about cross-specialty applicability — whether measures outside a clinician’s specialty can be used and how scoring accounts for relevance.
CMS-designated specialty-specific measure sets (§414.1335(a)(1)(ii)) should be developed with specialty societies and contain measures validated for comparability and clinical relevance.

Requiring groups to report via the Web Interface for 12 months (§414.1335(a)(2)) assumes groups can maintain consistent data capture across sites; CMS should permit site-level exceptions when CMS Web Interface measures are not feasible at all locations.

The requirement that groups of 25+ report on all CMS Web Interface measures (§414.1335(a)(2)(i)) is burdensome — CMS should allow a subset selection if a measure is demonstrably inapplicable to the group’s patient population.

Requiring reporting on the first 248 consecutively ranked beneficiaries per measure (§414.1335(a)(2)(i)) is arbitrary; groups need the option of randomized sampling and the ability to oversample for specialty areas.

The rule that groups must report 100% of assigned beneficiaries when sample < 248 (§414.1335(a)(2)(ii)) could create undue burden for very large or complex patient panels; CMS should permit statistically valid sampling methodologies when sample sizes are small.

The CAHPS survey vendor requirement for CAHPS participation (§414.1335(a)(3)(i)) requires CMS to ensure geographic coverage and linguistic accessibility; smaller/rural groups may have difficulty accessing approved vendors.

Counting CAHPS as one measure and satisfying cross-cutting requirements (§414.1335(a)(3)(A)) is useful, but CMS should clarify how CAHPS survey response rate thresholds affect measure scoring and whether nonresponse adjustments are applied.

The requirement that groups using CAHPS select another submission mechanism for other quality data (§414.1335(a)(3)(B)) increases cost and operational complexity; CMS should allow certain small groups to substitute a validated claims-based measure set.

Excluding non-patient-facing clinicians from cross-cutting reporting (§414.1335(b)) is appropriate, but CMS should clarify the exact thresholds and documentation needed to demonstrate non-patient-facing status.

Requiring reporting on at least 90% of patients meeting denominator criteria for QCDR/registry/EHR (§414.1340(a)) is excessively high and may be unattainable for practices with fragmented records; CMS should lower the threshold (e.g., to 70–80%) or permit representative sampling.

The 80% threshold for Part B claims reporting (§414.1340(b)) is similarly high given historical claim variability; CMS should adopt an 80% benchmark only for measures validated on claims and provide exceptions for low-volume clinicians.

Requiring groups submitting via Web Interface to meet CMS-provided sample requirements (§414.1340(c)) is acceptable only if CMS publishes the sampling methodology, randomization process, and allows appeals for demonstrably unrepresentative samples.
CMS specifying resource use measures (§414.1350(a)) must include full transparency of methodology, attribution, and risk adjustment; otherwise resource use scoring will be contested.
Reweighting authority for resource use (§414.1350(b)) must be constrained; CMS should publish triggers for reweighting and provide notice and comment prior to substantial changes in category weights.

Setting resource use at 10% for 2019 (§414.1350(b)(1)) may underemphasize cost control, while later increases to 30% could be abrupt; CMS should phase weight changes more gradually and give two years notice before major changes.

Increasing resource use to 15% in 2020 (§414.1350(b)(2)) requires clinicians to have access to resource use reports and benchmarks well before the performance period; CMS must commit to distributing actionable reports.

Jumping resource use to 30% after 2020 (§414.1350(b)(3)) could disproportionately affect specialties with inherently higher costs; CMS should apply specialty-level normalization or caps on year-to-year score swings.
The CPIA inventory requirement (§414.1355(a)) must include an open process for stakeholders to propose activities and realistic timelines for CMS to vet and approve activities.
Fixing CPIA at 15% of CPS (§414.1355(b)(1)) is acceptable if CMS allows flexibility to reweight CPIA for small practices or when advancing care information cannot be reported due to EHR limitations.

The list of CPIA inclusion criteria (§414.1355(c)) is comprehensive but CMS should prioritize clarity on how activities are scored (binary yes/no vs. scaled points) and how multiple activities combine to produce a CPIA score.
The “relevance to subcategory” criterion (§414.1355(c)(1)) needs examples and mapping to existing CPIA subcategories so clinicians can design activities that clearly meet the requirement.

The requirement that activities demonstrate importance toward improved beneficiary outcomes (§414.1355(c)(2)) must not require prohibitive levels of clinical evidence; CMS should accept high-quality process measures and plausible logic models.

The requirement that CPIA activities help reduce disparities (§414.1355(c)(3)) is commendable, but CMS must define metrics for disparity reduction and provide weight for activities targeting social determinants.

Alignment with patient-centered medical home (§414.1355(c)(4)) should not limit CPIA credit to only PCMH-recognized models; small practices implementing PCMH principles without formal recognition should be eligible.

The criterion that activities be performable by multiple provider types (§414.1355(c)(5)) risks excluding specialty-specific innovations; CMS should allow a portion of the CPIA inventory to include specialty-specific activities.

The feasibility and provider burden criterion (§414.1355(c)(6)) should include explicit protections for small (≤15), rural, and HPSA practices, including simplified reporting pathways and higher weighting for low-burden activities.
CMS’s ability to validate CPIA activities (§414.1355(c)(7)) must be defined — what documentation will CMS require, what audit methods will be used, and what sanctions apply for non-validation.

Evidence supporting likely improvement in outcomes (§414.1355(c)(8)) should allow for emerging practices and pilot programs; CMS should permit provisional CPIA credit for innovative activities with a plan for evaluation.

CMS stating it will assess CPIA performance using inventory-listed activities (§414.1355(d)) should also explain scoring rules, minimum thresholds for credit, and how partial completion of activities is treated.
The requirement that clinicians submit CPIA data using listed mechanisms (§414.1360(a)) should be accompanied by detailed data element definitions and standardized attestation forms.

Listing administrative claims as an acceptable CPIA submission mechanism only “if technically feasible” (§414.1360(a)) lacks clarity — CMS should define technical feasibility and provide a timetable for claims-based CPIA implementation.
Because administrative claims may not capture CPIA activities well (§414.1360(a)), CMS should invest in modifying claims forms (e.g., adding G-codes) before relying on claims for CPIA submissions.
Qualified registry submission for CPIA (§414.1360(a)) must require registries to accept small-volume submissions and provide error reports; CMS should publish registry certification requirements.
EHR submission mechanisms for CPIA (§414.1360(a)) must be standardized via certified APIs, and CMS should require EHR vendors to support CPIA exports without additional proprietary fees.
QCDRs accepting CPIA submissions (§414.1360(a)) should be required to publicly disclose their CPIA mappings and scoring algorithms to ensure transparency and comparability.

CMS Web Interface as a CPIA mechanism (§414.1360(a)) should be available to groups of all sizes when feasible, not only large groups, especially for CPIA activities that cannot be captured in claims/EHR.
Allowing attestation for CPIA submissions (§414.1360(a)) must be coupled with a clear audit schedule, retention requirements, and penalties for falsified attestations.

The truncated provision requiring yes/no responses for activities performed at least 90 days (§414.1360(a) truncated) is unclear; CMS should publish complete reporting instructions, define the 90-day threshold precisely, and indicate whether partial completion (e.g., 60 days) receives partial credit.

[P1] The proposal to extend all prohibitions that apply to endangered plants to whitebark pine effectively uplifts the species to near-endangered status without a separate analysis of socioeconomic impacts, and commenters request a regulatory flexibility analysis demonstrating necessity.

[P1] The rule lacks clarity on whether hybrid or nursery-grown whitebark pine individuals are covered by the prohibitions; industry stakeholders will request an explicit definition excluding cultivated stock used for restoration and commercial nurseries.

[P1] Conservation NGOs support applying endangered-plant-style prohibitions to whitebark pine but ask the agency to include explicit guidance showing how these prohibitions interact with existing forest-management plans and statutory authorities like the Healthy Forests Restoration Act.

[P2] Exporters and nursery associations will object to the blanket prohibition on import/export (§17.61(b) analog) without a streamlined permitting pathway for certified seed, cones, seedlings, and germplasm used exclusively for restoration and research.

[P2] Tribal governments will request an exception or expedited permit process for tribal trade and cultural exchanges of whitebark pine materials (cones, seeds) that are essential to tribal traditional practices and subsistence.

[P2] Legal commenters will note the regulation as drafted does not specify documentation or chain-of-custody requirements for permitted interstate/international transfers, and will request that the agency define required certifications to avoid enforcement vagueness.

[P3] Recreational users and campground operators will request clarification on what constitutes “removal” or “possession” on federal lands—e.g., whether collecting a displaced cone or branch found on the ground is prohibited—because the provision as written could criminalize benign activities.

[P3] State forestry agencies will challenge the clause prohibiting removal/damage when done “in knowing violation of state law” as creating uncertainty about enforcement cooperation; they request a clear standard describing how state law violations trigger federal prohibition applicability.

[P3] Logging and timber industry commenters will argue that the prohibition on removal from federal lands must be reconciled with lawful timber sale contracts and fuel-reduction projects, and request an explicit carve-out or permitting route to avoid contract breaches.

[P4] Commercial seed and nursery businesses will contend that prohibiting interstate or foreign commerce “in the course of commercial activity” could unintentionally ban sale of commercially produced whitebark-pine seedlings used for restoration, and ask for an exemption for certified, disease-free nursery stock.

[P4] Trade associations will request that the rule specify whether noncommercial interstate transfers (e.g., private sale between hobbyists across state lines) are treated differently from commercial transactions, and ask for monetary threshold or intent-based criteria.

[P5] Online marketplaces and small-business sellers will ask the agency to clarify whether offering whitebark pine for sale via e-commerce platforms triggers criminal liability, and to describe takedown/notice procedures and safe-harbor for third-party platforms.

[P5] Botanical gardens and arboreta will request an explicit exception permitting sales or transfers to other accredited institutions for conservation or educational purposes, or at least a streamlined inter-institutional permit.

[P6] The prohibition on solicitation or causing others to commit prohibited acts may chill legitimate scientific collaboration and outreach; researchers request an explicit safe-harbor for educational solicitation (e.g., seeking volunteers for restoration activities) when conducted under permits or cooperative agreements.

[P6] Civil liberties organizations will raise concerns that the attempt/solicitation language is broad and could expose citizens to prosecution for discussing whitebark pine translocations online; they request narrowing to require specific intent and a substantial step toward committing an offense.

[P7] States and counties will request clarity on the procedure and timeline for obtaining exceptions under paragraph (a)(2), including appeal rights if a requested exception is denied, to ensure predictable implementation.

[P7] Environmental NGOs will support the inclusion of limited exceptions but ask that exceptions be conditioned on strict monitoring, reporting, and mitigation requirements to ensure activities under exceptions do not harm wild populations.

[P8] Conservation practitioners will welcome the §17.72 permit pathway but request the agency publish the criteria, expected timelines, fee structure, and minimum application requirements now, so restoration projects can plan.

[P8] Some commenters will urge that permits under §17.72 be available for multicounty or multiyear restoration projects with blanket/annual coverage rather than project-by-project application to avoid administrative burdens.

[P8] Legal commenters will request that the agency clarify enforcement discretion and the legal effect of having a §17.72 permit—i.e., whether permitted activities provide an affirmative defense to criminal charges and civil penalties.

[P9] Federal land managers (e.g., Forest Service, BLM) will object to limiting forest management exceptions only to activities “conducted or authorized by the Federal agency with jurisdiction,” asking that cooperator-led projects (e.g., multijurisdictional fuels reduction) be clearly included when done pursuant to interagency agreements.

[P9] Private landowners adjacent to federal land will request clarification whether federal-authorized restoration activities that cross property boundaries (e.g., planting seed zones) are covered, or whether they need separate authorization for off-unit work.

[P9] Environmental groups will demand that any forest management exception include requirements to use disease-free stock and adhere to best practices (limiting seed transfer, sanitation protocols) to avoid spreading pathogens like white pine blister rust.

[P10] State conservation agencies will request to expand the “qualified employee or agent” definition to include Tribal employees and vetted non-governmental conservation partners engaged under cooperative agreements.

[P10] NGOs and academic researchers will ask for transparent qualification standards and training requirements for “designated qualified” personnel authorized to remove or destroy whitebark pine on federal lands, and for mandatory reporting of such actions.

[P10] Civil liberties and property-rights advocates will ask the agency to clarify whether the authority for Service or State agents to remove/destroy trees on federal lands includes entering adjacent private lands, and to explicitly prohibit any action off federal jurisdiction without owner consent or separate legal authority.

[P10] Some commenters will request an independent appeal or oversight mechanism for removals performed by agency agents under cooperative agreements to prevent misuse or unnecessary destruction for administrative convenience.

[P1] The blanket exclusion of most Class I devices from § 820.30 design control requirements is overly broad and risks patient safety by removing design documentation and verification requirements for devices that, while Class I, may still cause harm if poorly designed.

[P1] Clarify the scope of the § 820.30(a)(2) exceptions referenced — stakeholders need a specific list or criteria to know which Class I devices remain subject to design controls, rather than a vague cross-reference.

[P2] The proposed reliance on “risks and the regulatory controls needed” to classify accessories lacks clear, objective criteria and will create unpredictability for manufacturers; FDA should publish a detailed risk matrix or examples.

[P2] The rule should require FDA to publish the data and analysis used to assess an accessory’s risk profile when assigning classification so affected parties can meaningfully comment and plan.

[P3] The criterion that an accessory is “eligible” for distinct Class I only if it meets listed criteria is circular unless the proposed criteria are fully enumerated and operationalized; the proposal fragment “if the accessory: (1) Is not for us…” is incomplete and confusing.

[P4] The prohibition on Class I for accessories “for use in supporting or sustaining human life, or of substantial importance in preventing impairment to human health” is appropriate, but FDA should define “substantial importance” and provide examples to avoid inconsistent application.

[P4] Professional societies (e.g., surgeons, biomedical engineers) need the opportunity to comment on borderline accessories (e.g., certain fixation tools) that could be argued both ways on “supporting or sustaining life.”

[P5] The standard that an accessory “does not represent a potential unreasonable risk of illness or injury” is vague; FDA should define “unreasonable risk” and provide quantitative or qualitative thresholds for assessment.

[P6] Requiring that “general controls alone” be sufficient for Class I distinct classification ignores many accessories where general controls plus special controls (labeling, performance testing) are necessary; FDA should allow tailored special controls rather than forcing a binary decision.

[P7] Limiting design controls for Class I devices only to those automated with computer software or listed under § 820.30(a)(2)(ii) will exempt many devices with embedded electronics or simple firmware that nonetheless require design controls; FDA should extend design control applicability to devices with any software/firmware that affects performance.

[P7] The phrase “automated with computer software” is ambiguous — commenters need clarification whether devices with firmware, microcontrollers, or mobile app connectivity are covered.

[P8] The rule’s statement that non-automated accessories that would require design controls are ineligible for this final action could lead to inconsistent treatment of accessories across product lines; FDA should establish a clear path for reclassification or tailored controls in such cases.

[P9] The invitation for commenters to propose additional accessories for distinct Class I classification is valuable but insufficient without a transparent review timeline and criteria for how FDA will evaluate and respond to such petitions.

[P10] Requiring commenters to “briefly explain why general controls alone are sufficient” is reasonable, but FDA must state what level of evidence (bench testing, clinical data, failure mode analyses) will be required to support such assertions.

[P11] The requirement that those who disagree explain why additional controls (e.g., 510(k), PMA) are necessary is fair, but FDA should commit to providing a rebuttal and rationale if it rejects such evidence, to preserve due process.

[P12] Classifying orthopedic manual surgical instruments as Class I and exempting them from premarket notification is broadly acceptable for simple hand tools, but FDA must limit the exemption with clear “exemption limits” (e.g., materials, sterility, intended use) to avoid exempting higher-risk instruments.

[P13] The historical practice of reviewing device-specific instruments together with the parent device should be retained for any device-specific orthopedic instruments to ensure system-level safety evaluation; separating classification risks missing interactions.

[P14] The requirement that device-specific instruments have “precise technical specifications or design characteristics” implies FDA will still expect design documentation when instruments are device-specific; this position should be explicitly stated to avoid manufacturer confusion.

[P15] Stating that Class I orthopedic manual surgical instruments do not require the discussed design controls must be qualified: instruments intended to be sterile, single-use, or with cutting edges should still be subject to appropriate manufacturing and design controls.

[P16] Requiring manufacturers to describe orthopedic instruments in parent device premarket submissions should be mandatory only when those instruments are necessary to achieve the parent device’s intended performance; otherwise the rule places unnecessary burden on manufacturers of stand-alone instruments.

[P17] The permission to classify non-device-specific orthopedic instruments under § 888.4540 should include a clear checklist of factors (e.g., absence of unique sizing, no mechanical interfacing with implants) to help stakeholders self-determine eligibility.

[P18] Allowing device-specific orthopedic accessories to be eligible under section 513(f)(6)(D)(ii) if they meet the definition is appropriate, but FDA must clarify the procedural steps and evidence required to demonstrate eligibility under that section.

[P19] The proposed list of accessories suitable for distinct Class I classification must be published in full with specific device names, product codes, and intended uses so manufacturers and clinicians can verify applicability.

[P20] FDA’s intention to classify listed accessories into Class I upon final publication raises due process concerns — affected parties should have an opportunity for notice-and-comment on the final list before automatic reclassification takes effect.

[P21] Assigning accessories to Parts 876, 878, or 886 without publishing crosswalks to existing product codes will create administrative confusion; FDA should publish mapping tables and transitional guidance.

[P22] Exempting listed accessories from 21 CFR part 807 premarket notification, “subject to exemption limits,” requires that those exemption limits be disclosed now so manufacturers can assess regulatory burden and compliance costs.

Clarify the scope of the § 820.30(a)(2) exceptions referenced — stakeholders need a specific list or criteria to know which Class I devices remain subject to design controls, rather than a vague cross-reference.

The proposed reliance on “risks and the regulatory controls needed” to classify accessories lacks clear, objective criteria and will create unpredictability for manufacturers; FDA should publish a detailed risk matrix or examples.
The rule should require FDA to publish the data and analysis used to assess an accessory’s risk profile when assigning classification so affected parties can meaningfully comment and plan.

The criterion that an accessory is “eligible” for distinct Class I only if it meets listed criteria is circular unless the proposed criteria are fully enumerated and operationalized; the proposal fragment “if the accessory: (1) Is not for us…” is incomplete and confusing.

The prohibition on Class I for accessories “for use in supporting or sustaining human life, or of substantial importance in preventing impairment to human health” is appropriate, but FDA should define “substantial importance” and provide examples to avoid inconsistent application.

Professional societies (e.g., surgeons, biomedical engineers) need the opportunity to comment on borderline accessories (e.g., certain fixation tools) that could be argued both ways on “supporting or sustaining life.”

The standard that an accessory “does not represent a potential unreasonable risk of illness or injury” is vague; FDA should define “unreasonable risk” and provide quantitative or qualitative thresholds for assessment.

Requiring that “general controls alone” be sufficient for Class I distinct classification ignores many accessories where general controls plus special controls (labeling, performance testing) are necessary; FDA should allow tailored special controls rather than forcing a binary decision.

raw_output:
[P1] The prohibition making it unlawful to fail or refuse to submit information (§ 713.1(d)) is overbroad because it does not define a reasonable good-faith standard or provide an opportunity to cure unintentional omissions, exposing reporters to criminal or severe civil penalties for minor clerical errors.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether the "person" referenced in § 713.1(d) includes corporate officers, contractors, subsidiaries, or only the legal entity that manufactures/imports or stores mercury to avoid ambiguous personal liability.

[P1] The regulation should include a safe-harbor for inadvertent non-submission due to software/technical failure (e.g., CDX outages), but § 713.1(d) currently creates strict liability without such an exception.

[P2] The requirement that persons must keep records and permit access (§ 713.1(d)) is vague about the scope of "permit access" (on-site inspection, remote access, copies) and lacks procedural protections (notice, warrant, confidentiality during inspection).

[P2] The unlawful-failure-to-keep-records prohibition should be limited to records required by the part; the rule must specify which documents constitute required records to avoid criminalizing routine business documents not contemplated by EPA.

[P3] Requiring reporters to "certify accuracy" (§ 713.1(e)) without allowing for qualifiers (e.g., "to the best of my knowledge") or requiring reasonable efforts to verify data could subject certifiers to perjury-like exposure; the rule should allow good-faith certifications.

[P3] The certification requirement should permit delegation to qualified corporate officers or designated compliance officers; § 713.1(e) is silent on who may legally sign and certify.

[P4] The obligation to keep records documenting reported information (§ 713.1(e)) should specify the minimum content, format, and provenance required (e.g., sampling logs, invoices, lab analyses) — the current text is too vague and creates compliance uncertainty.

[P4] The rule requires retention of underlying raw data (§ 713.1(e)) but does not accommodate third-party proprietary data or confidentiality claims; EPA should clarify how confidential business information (CBI) is treated for retained records.

[P5] Allowing EPA access and copying of reported records (§ 713.1(e)) must include limits to protect trade secrets and personal data; commenters request a clear process for contesting overly broad document requests and redaction of non-relevant proprietary material.

[P6] The exception for mercury generated as a byproduct not used for commercial purposes (§ 713.7(a)) is ambiguous — the rule should define "byproduct" and "not used for commercial purposes" to avoid inconsistent application and ensure intended waste streams are captured.

[P6] Industry will request affirmation that trace-level mercury generated incidentally in manufacturing (ppm levels in process residues) qualifies for the byproduct exception in § 713.7(a).

[P7] The exemption for mercury-containing waste (§ 713.7(b)) conflicts with other disclosure goals; environmental advocates will ask EPA to narrow this exception to ensure that waste handlers who recover, treat, or export mercury-bearing waste still report.

[P7] The rule should require reporting when mercury-containing waste is transferred across state lines or exported, even if characterized as waste, to close potential reporting loopholes under § 713.7(b).

[P8] The 2,500-lb threshold for elemental mercury (and corresponding thresholds for compounds) in § 713.9(a) is arbitrary — stakeholders will ask EPA to justify the threshold with risk-based analysis and consider lower thresholds for public health protection.

[P8] Small and medium manufacturers near the 2,500-lb threshold require transitional guidance; the rule should provide pro-rated or de minimis reporting obligations rather than an abrupt reporting obligation under § 713.9(a).

[P9] Reporting stored pounds of mercury (§ 713.9(a)(1)) must clarify whether "stored" includes in-transit, warehoused, or contained within devices/components (e.g., switches) and whether concentration thresholds apply.

[P10] "Distributed in commerce" (§ 713.9(a)(2)) is undefined — commenters will request clarity on whether internal transfers between parent/subsidiary entities or sales to affiliates count as distribution.

[P11] The catch-all § 713.9(b) ("all other persons... shall report, as applicable") is vague; regulated parties will request examples of "as applicable" to determine which subparagraphs apply and avoid duplicative reporting.

[P12] Reporting pounds manufactured excluding imports (§ 713.9(b)(1)) should allow use of production accounting systems and reconciliation across fiscal vs. calendar year; the rule must state preferred accounting methods.

[P13] For imported mercury (§ 713.9(b)(2)), commenters will request whether bonded warehouse receipts, temporary imports, or imports for re-export count, and whether customs data may be used to satisfy reporting.

[P14] The export reporting exclusion for mercury prohibited by 15 U.S.C. 2611(c)(1) and (7) (§ 713.9(b)(3)) requires cross-reference language and examples (which countries/uses are prohibited) to avoid inconsistent interpretation.

[P15] The requirement to report stored pounds (§ 713.9(b)(4)) duplicates § 713.9(a)(1) and may create double-counting risk — the rule should harmonize storage reporting across categories.

[P16] The requirement to report distributed-in-commerce pounds (§ 713.9(b)(5)) should clarify whether distribution to non-U.S. entities, transfers to tolling partners, and distribution of components containing trace mercury are included.

[P17] Sellers in IMERC Notification states (§ 713.9(c)) will request coordination and data-sharing provisions to avoid dual reporting to IMERC and EPA; small retailers need simplified procedures.

[P17] The carve-out "except a product that contains a component that is a mercury-added product" in § 713.9(c) is ambiguous — manufacturers of assembled products need guidance whether reporting the mercury in components is required.

[P18] Reporting pounds of mercury in domestically manufactured products (§ 713.9(c)(1)) must allow use of representative sampling and engineering estimates rather than requiring product-level destructive testing.

[P19] Imported product reporting (§ 713.9(c)(2)) should permit importers to rely on manufacturer declarations and Certificates of Conformity rather than independent testing; otherwise supply chain disruption may occur.

[P20] Exported product reporting (§ 713.9(c)(3)) should be coordinated with export control regimes to avoid conflicts and should allow reliance on customs/export documentation.

[P21] The phrasing in § 713.9(d) for "all other persons who manufacture (including import) mercury-added products" may capture distributors and contract manufacturers inadvertently; the rule should exclude entities that do not alter product mercury content.

[P22] Reporting pounds of mercury in domestically manufactured mercury-added products (§ 713.9(d)(1)) should be prorated for products with components sourced from multiple suppliers; suppliers should be able to jointly allocate mercury content.

[P23] Reporting imported mercury-added products (§ 713.9(d)(2)) must address when importers lack visibility into component-level mercury — the rule should permit importers to require supplier attestations.

[P24] Reporting exported mercury-added products (§ 713.9(d)(3)) should clarify whether exports to U.S. military uses or diplomatic shipments are exempt or treated differently.

[P25] Reporting pounds of mercury in products distributed in commerce (§ 713.9(d)(4)) should exclude products in long-term storage and products sold for research purposes; the rule lacks these limiting provisions.

[P26] Processors who intentionally use mercury (§ 713.9(e)) are captured broadly — chemical processors who use trace mercury as part of catalysts request exemption when mercury is bound in process matrices and not released.

[P27] The obligation to report pounds of mercury intentionally used (§ 713.9(e)(1)) must define "intentionally" (added deliberately vs. present as contaminant) to avoid capturing contamination-level amounts.

[P28] Reporting stored mercury by processors (§ 713.9(e)(2)) should be harmonized with inventory accounting and allow aggregation across facilities under common control.

[P29] Reporting mercury in exported final products (§ 713.9(e)(3)) should allow processors to rely on downstream manufacturer reports if processors do not control export decisions.

[P30] Reporting mercury in final products distributed in commerce (§ 713.9(e)(4)) should provide de minimis thresholds for products with trace mercury and allow reporting in ranges to protect confidential supplier information.

[P31] The requirement to select specific mercury compounds from Table 1 (§ 713.11(a)) is burdensome if the table lacks CAS numbers or clear chemical identifiers; stakeholders request inclusion of CAS numbers and synonyms for each listed compound.

[P31] The rule should permit reporting "mixtures" or "unidentified compounds" where exact speciation is unknown and require EPA to provide a pathway for submitting best-available identification.

[P32] Identifying categories/subcategories from Table 2 for mercury-added products (§ 713.11(b)) will be difficult where products straddle categories; commenters request an appeals process or crosswalk guidance.

[P33] Table 2 must be comprehensive and updated periodically; manufacturers worry products may not fit pre-selected categories and the rule does not describe how to request new categories.

[P34] Processors required to specify processes and uses from Tables 3 and 4 (§ 713.11(c)) will need clear definitions of each process/use; otherwise inconsistent coding across firms will compromise data quality.

[P35] Table 3 selections (§ 713.11(c)(1)) should allow multi-select where mercury is used in multiple steps; the rule should allow reporting percentages of total use by process.

[P36] Table 4 use categories (§ 713.11(c)(2)) (e.g., catalyst, reactant, reagent) require precise definitions; otherwise legal risk exists if companies misclassify uses and face enforcement.

[P37] The contextual reporting thresholds in § 713.13(a) tied to the 2,500-lb threshold create perverse incentives to remain below thresholds rather than reducing mercury use; commenters will urge lower thresholds or sliding-scale reporting.

[P38] Requiring countries of origin for imported mercury (§ 713.13(a)(1)) must allow use of customs/entry data and permit consolidated reporting for multi-source shipments.

[P39] Reporting countries of destination for exported mercury (§ 713.13(a)(2)) raises confidentiality concerns where exports are to a small number of purchasers; commenters request aggregation rules or CBI protections.

[P40] Requiring NAICS codes for mercury distributed in commerce (§ 713.13(a)(3)) will be problematic for diversified firms with multiple codes; the rule should allow multiple NAICS codes and explain how EPA will use them.

[P41] The "as applicable" language in § 713.13(b) again is overly vague — parties need explicit criteria for which contextual elements are required for different actors (manufacturers vs. sellers vs. processors).

[P42] For imported products (§ 713.13(c)(1)), sellers may lack knowledge of countries of origin; the rule should allow reliance on supplier declarations and require EPA to accept reasonable due diligence.

[P43] For exported products (§ 713.13(c)(2)), sellers request alignment with export control and customs documentation to avoid duplicative reporting burdens.

[P44] NAICS code reporting for products distributed (§ 713.13(c)(3)) should permit confidential submission where codes reveal sensitive business strategy; EPA should state how it will treat such CBI.

[P45] The broad coverage of § 713.15 (header) listing who is required to report is helpful, but the definitions are unclear — the rule should include concrete examples (e.g., toll manufacturers, contract packagers) to identify scope.

[P46] § 713.15(a)-(c) conditions are ambiguous regarding controlled subsidiaries and contract manufacturers; legal experts will request explicit guidance on allocating reporting responsibility between original manufacturer, importer, and contract processor.

[P47] The waste-management exception in § 713.17(a) could be exploited by entities that purposely characterize activities as "waste management" while recovering mercury — EPA should require any recovery, reclamation, or distillation operations to report.

[P48] The trade-only exception (§ 713.17(b)) should clarify whether wholesale distributors who perform minor processing (e.g., repackaging) are exempt; ambiguity could lead to underreporting.

[P49] The requirement to report for the submission period in § 713.19 without a clear mechanism for amendments or corrections is problematic; commenters request a formal correction/amendment window after submission.

[P50] The obligation in § 713.19(a) to report quantities per activity (as in § 713.9) should allow reporting in ranges and estimated values with documented methodologies to protect confidential unit-level data.

[P51] § 713.19(b) requiring reporting of specific compound/category/process information should permit use of aggregated categories for CBI protection and allow submission of redacted details with EPA review.

[P52] Contextual information (§ 713.19(c)) such as NAICS and country codes can be commercially sensitive; EPA should provide strong CBI protections, including limited internal disclosure and aggregated public reporting.

[P53] The requirement to submit reports according to § 713.25 procedures (§ 713.19(d)) will be burdensome for small businesses if the electronic application (§ 713.25(a)) is inflexible or incompatible with existing enterprise systems; commenters ask for bulk upload APIs and templates.

[P54] Defining the 2020 reporting year as Jan 1–Dec 31, 2018 (§ 713.21(a)) is confusing and appears to create a retrospective reporting year — legal commenters will request explanation/justification and alignment with calendar years to avoid legal challenges.

[P55] The 3-year interval reporting schedule (§ 713.21(a) subsequent years) may be too infrequent to capture rapid changes in supply chains or accidental releases; environmental NGOs will request annual reporting.

[P56] The July 1 deadline (§ 713.21(b)) following reporting years may create conflicts with other compliance deadlines and tax reporting cycles; industry requests flexibility or staggered deadlines for large firms.

[P57] For the 2020 submission deadline (July 1, 2019) (§ 713.21(b)), stakeholders will request a substantial lead time and phased compliance to allow system upgrades and data collection (more than the proposed timeline suggests).

[P58] The 3-year recurring submission deadlines beginning in 2022 (§ 713.21(b) subsequent deadlines) conflict with the 2020/2018 reporting year definitions and need harmonization and a clear compliance calendar.

[P59] The 3-year records retention period (§ 713.23 second sentence) is too short for parties who must defend against long-latency claims or retrospective liability; commenters propose extending retention to 5–7 years.

[P60] § 713.23 requires retention of documents but does not specify electronic recordkeeping standards (formats, encryption, chain of custody); regulated entities need technical guidance for compliance.

[P61] Requiring use of a specific electronic application (§ 713.25(a)) without naming it or describing interoperability (§ 713.25(a) second sentence) creates uncertainty; commenters request that EPA publish the exact application name, system requirements, and testing schedule.

[P62] Mandating submissions through CDX (§ 713.25(b)) may be burdensome for small entities without CDX accounts; EPA should provide alternatives (secure file upload, paper exception) or technical support for CDX onboarding.

[P63] The web access method (§ 713.25(c)(1)) and hotline CD-ROM option (§ 713.25(c)(2)) are inadequate modern options — stakeholders request downloadable machine-readable templates (CSV/XML) and secure bulk upload endpoints rather than CD-ROMs.

[P64] The rule lacks clarity on whether reports submitted to interstate programs (e.g., IMERC) can satisfy EPA reporting (§ 713.25 interplay with § 713.9(c)); commenters ask for data-sharing agreements to avoid duplicative submissions.

[P65] The rule lacks an explicit procedure for confidential business information claims for each required field (quantities, NAICS, country) — commenters demand a formal CBI submission process and timeline for EPA determinations.

[P66] The proposed rule does not specify enforcement metrics, penalties, or a warning/cure period for noncompliance with reporting obligations, certifications, or recordkeeping; commenters request clarity to ensure proportional enforcement.

[P67] Small businesses and tribal entities request a hearing or stakeholder session to discuss how the burdens (reporting, electronic filing, recordkeeping) can be reduced; the rule should include a small-entity compliance guide.

[P68] Legal experts note potential preemption or conflict with state IMERC or other state-level mercury reporting programs; the rule should clarify whether EPA reporting supersedes or is coordinated with state obligations.

[P69] The rule’s definitions of "manufacture," "import," "distribute in commerce," and "intentional use" are not provided here — commenters will demand precise definitions in the regulatory text to avoid inconsistent application.

[P70] The rule should allow phased implementation and a limited penalty moratorium for the first reporting cycle to allow regulated entities to adapt systems and processes to the new requirements.
