[P1] Industry commenter: Requiring inter-handler transfers of inshell pecans to be reported on APC Form 4 will impose duplicative recordkeeping where handlers already maintain bills of lading and transfer invoices; request exemption when equivalent documentation is retained electronically.

[P1] Legal expert: The rule does not specify sanctions or penalties for failure to file APC Form 4; request clarification on enforcement and due process rights for alleged noncompliance.

[P2] Small handler association: The deadline "by the tenth day of the month following the first transfer between two handlers" is ambiguous for handlers with multiple transfers in a month — request clarification whether the ten-day clock restarts after each first transfer between any pair of handlers or only after the fiscal-year first transfer.

[P2] Industry commenter: Ten days after the first transfer may be infeasible for companies with high transaction volumes and limited administrative staff; request extending the filing deadline to 20 business days.

[P3] Trade group: The weekend/holiday exception moving the deadline to the next business day creates uncertainty when the tenth falls on a federal holiday that is observed on a different day by private businesses; request defining "holiday" as federal legal holidays and provide a calendar or automated notice.

[P4] Handler: Annual renewal requirement for inter-handler transfer reports each fiscal year will create redundant filings when no transfers occurred in the prior year; request an option to file a nil/no-transfer certification instead of a full renewal.

[P5] Accounting firm: §986.162(a)(1) requires the fiscal year covered by the report but lacks a specified fiscal year definition (calendar vs. marketing year); request the regulation define "fiscal year" reference or allow company fiscal-year identification.

[P6] Compliance officer: Requiring names and signatures for both transferring and receiving handlers may be impractical for electronic submissions; request acceptance of electronic signatures or delegated agent signatures and standards for authentication.

[P7] Exporter: The obligation to identify the handler who assumes reporting and assessment obligations for transferred pecans is unclear when obligations are split (e.g., assessments vs. storage); request guidance on partial assumption and joint liability.

[P8] Processor association: The year-end inventory report due after August 31 each fiscal year conflicts with many handlers' fiscal-year ends; request flexibility to align year-end reporting to the handler's accounting year or clarify if the fiscal year is fixed by the Council.

[P9] Small business: The September 10 filing date for year-end inventory leaves only ten business days for reconciliation after month-end close; request extending to September 30 to allow proper audit and reconciliation.

[P10] Handler: The weekend exception for September 10 should explicitly recognize state-observed holidays and provide allowance where local business days differ; request harmonization with the executive branch business-day definition.

[P11] Auditor: APC Form 5 content requirements are not enumerated in the text; request the agency publish the exact form fields and validation rules in the preamble and allow 60 days for implementation.

[P12] Large handler: Monthly summary reports due by the tenth for receipts, shipments, inventory and committed inventory will create heavy monthly administrative burdens; request aggregation allowance for handlers below a specified volume threshold (e.g., under 500,000 lbs/month).

[P13] Small cooperative: The weekend/holiday exception for the monthly report should permit filings on the next business day even if the next business day is state-observed holiday; request consistent national business-day definition.

[P14] IT manager: Requiring APC Form 1 for monthly summaries without specifying an electronic submission mechanism will hinder compliance; request mandatory online portal, API specs, and privacy/security standards.

[P15] Grower-processor: Reporting total weight and type of inshell pecans received each period is reasonable, but the regulation fails to define "type"; request the Council define categories (variety, grade, moisture) to avoid inconsistent reporting.

[P16] Commodity group: Year-to-date received totals may create cumulative errors if prior reports had corrections; request allowance to file corrected year-to-date figures and a mechanism to submit revisions.

[P17] Export logistics firm: Reporting weights of all shipments and inter-handler transfers for both inshell and shelled pecans requires consolidation across carriers; request guidance on whether weights from third-party warehouses/carriers suffice and acceptable proof (BOL, customs docs).

[P18] Trade association: Requiring previous-month and year-to-date shipment weights creates redundant data requests already captured in monthly and year-end reports; request streamlining to avoid duplication between §986.177(a)(6) and (7).

[P19] Handler: "Total inventory held by handler" is vague about whether consigned, in-transit, or third-party stored pecans must be included; request clear definitions and thresholds (e.g., include only inventory under contractual title).

[P20] Exporter: Requiring reporting of "committed inventory" including sold or otherwise obligated pecans for domestic sale or export will force disclosure of confidential commercial contracts; request an exception for proprietary contract details or aggregation above a de minimis threshold.

[P21] Buyer: Reporting weights of pecans under contract for purchase from other handlers could chill contract negotiations by exposing pipeline purchasing commitments; request that reporting be limited to aggregated bands (e.g., 0-10k lbs, 10k-50k lbs).

[P22] Importer: The import summary report due by the tenth of the following month duplicates customs filings; request acceptance of CBP (Customs) import/export documents in lieu of APC Form 2 when they contain required data.

[P23] International trade counsel: The weekend/holiday exception for import reports should accommodate time zone differences for handlers operating across borders; request the Council apply the handler's principal place-of-business local holiday calendar.

[P24] Customs broker: APC Form 2 likely requires data that brokers already submit to multiple agencies; request the Council adopt existing international trade data standards (e.g., ACE, EDI) to avoid rekeying.

[P25] Exporter to Mexico: Requiring reporting of the weight of inshell pecans exported to Mexico for shelling is necessary for tracking but needs clarity on processing tolling arrangements where the exporter does not retain title; request instruction for tolling vs. sale transactions.

[P26] Processor: Reporting the date shelled pecans returned to the U.S. after shelling in Mexico may be unknown to the original handler when third-party logistics handle return shipments; request ability for returning processor or importer to file the return date.

[P27] Trade compliance group: Reporting weight of shelled pecans returned from Mexico may conflict with privacy/competitiveness concerns; request aggregation or a confidentiality provision to prevent disclosure of buyer identities.

[P28] Agricultural economist: Year-to-date totals for exports to Mexico and returns must allow corrections and re-statements; request an appeals/correction procedure and specify deadlines for adjustments.

[P29] Exporter: The export report due by the tenth following shipment is consistent with other deadlines but adds another monthly filing (APC Form 3); request consolidation so exporters can submit a single consolidated monthly submission covering exports, imports, and inventory.

[P30] Legal counsel: The same weekend/holiday exception across reports should specify which time zone applies for the due date for handlers operating in multiple states/time zones; request clarification (Council HQ time vs. handler local time).

[P31] Compliance manager: APC Form 3 content fields are not provided in the rule; request sample forms, electronic schema, and a 90-day implementation window before compliance is required.

[P32] Handler: Requiring the handler's name and address on export reports is redundant when other identifiers (handler ID) could be used; request use of unique handler identifier instead of full address to streamline electronic processing.

[P33] Export agent: Stating the month covered by the export report will be ambiguous when shipments span months (e.g., sea freight); request guidance on whether to report by shipment date, departure date, or date of title transfer.

[P34] Trade group: Reporting total weight of pecans shipped for export, including substandard pecans, could encourage underreporting of lower-quality shipments to avoid market impacts; request a neutral confidentiality treatment and clear quality definitions.

[P35] Economist: Providing export weights for the previous period and year-to-date duplicates other reports; propose the Council minimize redundant fields across APC Forms 1–3 to reduce reporting burden.

raw_output:
[P1] The provision allowing the Secretary to consider disease symptoms, contacts, or originating-place prevalence (§ 208.13(c)(10)) is overly broad and could permit public health status to be used as a pretext to exclude migrants based on nationality or perceived health risk without individualized medical evaluation.

[P1] Industry and travel-sector commenters will argue that relying on originating-place prevalence as a factor is vague and could lead to sudden travel bans or restrictions that disrupt commerce and supply chains.

[P2] Requiring a joint determination by the Secretary and Attorney General that presence of aliens from specified places would cause danger to U.S. public health (§ 208.13(c)(10)(ii)(A)) concentrates too much discretionary power in two officials without procedural safeguards or required public notice.

[P2] Public-health experts will contend that the standard “cause danger to U.S. public health” is undefined and should require clear epidemiological thresholds (e.g., R0, case prevalence per 100k, demonstrated community transmission) before restrictions apply.

[P3] The joint-designation requirement to identify countries/regions/periods or circumstances (§ 208.13(c)(10)(ii)(B)) lacks criteria for how long a designation may last and what evidence triggers termination, risking indefinite restrictions against nationals of listed places.

[P3] Human-rights groups will argue the rule’s ability to designate political subdivisions or regions could lead to discriminatory targeting of minority populations within countries without adequate justification.

[P4] The absolute denial of withholding of removal applications if statutory disqualifying provisions apply (§ 208.16(d)(2)) may produce arbitrary results when applied alongside the new disease-related security criteria, and the rule should require individualized determinations rather than categorical denial.

[P5] Treating any alien convicted of a “particularly serious crime” as a danger to the community (§ 208.16(d)(2)) without defining that term in the regulation invites inconsistent adjudications and constitutional due-process concerns.

[P5] Criminal-justice reform advocates will note that labeling classes of offenses as “particularly serious” without clear, narrow standards could disproportionately affect noncitizen populations and deny protection to otherwise eligible refugees.

[P6] Shifting the burden to applicants to prove by a preponderance that statutory grounds for denial do not apply (§ 208.16(d)(2) burden of proof) is inconsistent with international refugee-protection norms and will disadvantage asylum seekers who lack access to counsel or documents.

[P6] Legal organizations will argue that the preponderance standard is too onerous when government evidence of ineligibility is minimal or based on health presumptions, and request that the agency clarify evidentiary rules and standards of proof.

[P7] Allowing the Secretary to consider disease symptoms, contacts, and origins in withholding-of-removal danger assessments (§ 208.16(d)(2) disease consideration) risks conflating medical conditions with security threats and could violate anti-discrimination laws (e.g., ADA, Title VII analogues).

[P7] Medical associations will warn that non-clinicians making determinations about disease status without medical testing or due process could create public-health harms by stigmatizing individuals and disincentivizing treatment-seeking.

[P8] Requiring joint determinations by the Secretary and Attorney General before disease-based considerations apply to withholding cases (§ 208.16(d)(2)(ii)(A)) is a positive procedural limitation, but the rule must specify timelines, required interagency consultation, and opportunity for public comment on such determinations.

[P9] The joint-designation of places and periods/circumstances for withholding determinations (§ 208.16(d)(2)(ii)(B)) should require publication in the Federal Register and a required scientific rationale; without this, the designations lack transparency and are subject to political manipulation.

[P10] The Department’s authority to remove an alien requesting protection to a third country (§ 208.16(f)(1)) is permissive and risks refoulement if the third country is not a safe refuge; commenters will demand strict safe-third-country criteria and monitoring.

[P10] Refugee-rights organizations will demand that the regulation explicitly prohibit third-country removal to nations where persecution or torture risk exists, or where effective protection or durable solutions are unavailable.

[P11] Allowing removal to a third country before adjudication if the alien hasn’t established lack of threats or likely torture there (§ 208.16(f)(2)) creates a fait accompli that undermines non-refoulement obligations and denies meaningful review.

[P12] The requirement that the Department advise the alien at the time of request that the alien could be removed to a third country prior to adjudication (§ 208.16(f)(2)(i)) is necessary but insufficient; commenters will request standardized, translated advisals and proof of receipt to ensure informed consent.

[P13] The obligation to provide the alien an opportunity to withdraw the withholding/deferral request to avoid third-country removal (§ 208.16(f)(2)(ii)) must include a minimum period to consider withdrawal and access to counsel — otherwise the “opportunity” is illusory.

[P14] The severability clause (§ 208.25) that keeps remaining provisions in effect if any provision is invalidated could allow unlawful or unconstitutional provisions to persist; commenters will urge that the agency commit to reevaluating remaining provisions’ validity and public notice obligations post-litigation.

[P15] The requirement that asylum officers create a written record of credible-fear determinations with detailed contents (§ 208.30(e)(1)) is appropriate, but the rule should mandate that copies be provided to applicants and retained for a specified period for FOIA/accountability purposes.

[P16] Defining credible fear of torture as showing a “significant possibility” of eligibility for withholding of removal (§ 208.30(e)(3)) is ambiguous; legal and medical experts will ask for a clearer threshold or examples to reduce inconsistent decisions across officers.

[P17] The asylum officer’s duty to consider whether a case presents novel or unique issues warranting a full IJ hearing (§ 208.30(e)(4)) is positive, but commenters will request explicit criteria for what constitutes “novel or unique” to avoid arbitrary denials.

[P18] Placing aliens who establish credible fear but appear subject to mandatory bars into § 240 proceedings (§ 208.30(e)(5)(i)(A)) may expose them to prolonged detention and denial of timely protection; commenters will request safe alternatives and bond eligibility.

[P19] The DHS option to either place an alien in § 240 proceedings or remove the alien to another country when torture-likelihood conditions are met (§ 208.30(e)(5)(i)(B)) is problematic because it authorizes removal instead of providing protection, and must be limited to cases where third-country safety is independently verified.

[P20] Requiring IJs to review all issues de novo, including torture risk, when an alien is placed in proceedings (§ 208.30(e)(5)(i)(B)(1)) is an important safeguard but will be undermined if record development standards and access to evidence/counsel are not specified.

[P21] The requirement that removal to another country comply with section 241 and not send the alien to countries where life/freedom or torture risk is established (§ 208.30(e)(5)(i)(B)(2)) must be accompanied by mandatory country-condition reports and individualized assessments before removal.

[P22] Advising aliens at the time of request of the possibility of removal to a third country prior to adjudication (§ 208.30(e)(5)(i)(B)(2)(i)) must require interpretation services, written notice in the alien’s language, and confirmation of comprehension.

[P23] The obligation to provide aliens an opportunity to withdraw requests to prevent third-country removal (§ 208.30(e)(5)(i)(B)(2)(ii)) must include counseling on the consequences of withdrawal and a minimum decision period to ensure the choice is informed.

[P24] Requiring a written notice of decision if the alien fails to establish torture likelihood during the interview (§ 208.30(e)(5)(i)(B)(3)) should include a clear statement of appeal rights, legal remedies, and next steps; otherwise the notice will not be meaningful.

[P25] Automatically entering a negative credible-fear determination as to asylum intent if the alien is ineligible under § 208.13(c)(4) (§ 208.30(e)(5)(iii)) removes the possibility of individualized assessment of changed circumstances or rehabilitative evidence; commenters will request exceptions and review mechanisms.

[P26] Allowing DHS to place an alien in § 240 proceedings or remove to another country when the alien establishes reasonable fear or more-likely-than-not torture under specified conditions (§ 208.30(e)(5)(iii)(A/B)) risks circumventing non-refoulement protections and should require independent verification of third-country safety.

[P27] The IJ’s de novo review obligation in § 240 proceedings including torture likelihood (§ 208.30(e)(5)(iii)(1)) must be paired with mandatory disclosure of DHS evidence and adequate time for defense preparation to ensure meaningful review.

[P28] Requiring third-country removals to follow statutory/regulatory protections and only after advising the alien and providing an opportunity to withdraw (§ 208.30(e)(5)(iii)(2)) is appropriate, but commenters will insist on explicit safeguards — e.g., prohibition on removal to countries with poor human-rights records regardless of advisals.

[P29] The duty to advise aliens at the time of requesting withholding/deferral about the possibility of third-country removal prior to adjudication (§ 208.30(e)(5)(iii)(2)(i)) should mandate standardized scripts, written translations, and logging of the advisal in the record.

[P30] The requirement to provide an opportunity to withdraw withholding/deferral requests to prevent removal (§ 208.30(e)(5)(iii)(2)(ii)) should prohibit coercive practices and guarantee access to counsel and independent advice before the withdrawal decision is accepted.

[P31] Mirroring § 208.13(c)(10) in § 1208.13(c)(10) (Attorney General consideration of disease symptoms, contacts, or origin) duplicates authority without clarifying coordination, creating the risk of inconsistent determinations between the Secretary and Attorney General.

[P31] Civil-liberties groups will argue that allowing the Attorney General to consider disease-related factors in asylum adjudication conflicts with asylum’s humanitarian purpose and risks discriminatory application.

[P32] The Attorney General/Secretary joint-determination requirement for public-health danger (§ 1208.13(c)(10)(ii)(A)) should require an evidence-based public-health determination (e.g., CDC concurrence) and an opportunity for independent scientific review before designations are made.

[P33] The joint-designation authority over places/periods/circumstances (§ 1208.13(c)(10)(ii)(B)) must be subject to notice-and-comment or at least a requirement to publish determinations, including the scientific basis and termination criteria, to ensure transparency.

[P34] Denial of withholding of removal if statutory disqualifications apply in § 1208.16(d)(2) duplicates concerns about categorical exclusions and will disproportionately affect vulnerable asylum seekers without due process protections.

[P35] The requirement that applicants prove by a preponderance that statutory grounds for denial do not apply (§ 1208.16(d)(2) applicant burden) will be difficult for applicants lacking documentation; commenters will request presumptions in favor of vulnerable applicants and expanded access to legal representation.

[P36] Allowing the Attorney General to consider disease symptoms and origin in withholding-of-removal danger assessments (§ 1208.16(d)(2) disease consideration) risks stigmatization and violates medical privacy; commenters will demand that medical evidence be evaluated by qualified health professionals and that disease status alone not be treated as criminality or a security threat.

[P37] DHS’s authority to remove asylum-seekers to third countries (§ 1208.16(f)(1)) needs stringent safe-third-country protections, oversight, and reporting requirements to ensure compliance with non-refoulement and international obligations.

[P38] Allowing DHS to remove an alien to a third country before adjudication if the alien hasn’t established no-threats or lack of torture there (§ 1208.16(f)(2)) creates perverse incentives for expedited removals without adequate fact-finding; commenters will call for a prohibition on pre-adjudication third-country removal except with judicial authorization.

[P39] The procedural obligations that such third-country removal can only occur if the alien was advised and provided an opportunity to withdraw (§ 1208.16(f)(2)(i)-(ii)) are insufficient unless the rule mandates linguistic assistance, written notices, and a meaningful waiting period.

[P40] The severability provision (§ 1208.25) should not be used to salvage unlawful provisions; commenters will request a commitment to review remaining provisions and reopen public comment if any substantive part is struck down to ensure ongoing legitimacy.

[P41] The provision that an IJ must find no credible fear of persecution for aliens ineligible under specified provisions and that the decision is final and not appealable (§ 1208.30(e)) removes an important appellate safeguard and could violate due process; commenters will urge permitting at least limited administrative or judicial review.

[P42] If an IJ concurs with an asylum officer’s negative credible-fear determination and lack of torture likelihood, the rule requiring return to DHS for removal with the IJ decision final and not appealable (§ 1208.30(g)(2)(iv)(A)) effectively eliminates appellate review and may contravene statutory protections — commenters will request preservation of appeal rights.

[P43] The requirement that if an IJ finds credible fear they vacate the asylum officer’s order and DHS may commence § 240 proceedings (with IJ de novo review) (§ 1208.30(g)(2)(iv)(B)) is appropriate as a matter of procedure, but commenters will demand deadlines for de novo review, access to counsel, and protections against prolonged detention during proceedings.

Civil-liberties groups will argue that allowing the Attorney General to consider disease-related factors in asylum adjudication conflicts with asylum’s humanitarian purpose and risks discriminatory application.

The Attorney General/Secretary joint-determination requirement for public-health danger (§ 1208.13(c)(10)(ii)(A)) should require an evidence-based public-health determination (e.g., CDC concurrence) and an opportunity for independent scientific review before designations are made.

The joint-designation authority over places/periods/circumstances (§ 1208.13(c)(10)(ii)(B)) must be subject to notice-and-comment or at least a requirement to publish determinations, including the scientific basis and termination criteria, to ensure transparency.

Denial of withholding of removal if statutory disqualifications apply in § 1208.16(d)(2) duplicates concerns about categorical exclusions and will disproportionately affect vulnerable asylum seekers without due process protections.

The requirement that applicants prove by a preponderance that statutory grounds for denial do not apply (§ 1208.16(d)(2) applicant burden) will be difficult for applicants lacking documentation; commenters will request presumptions in favor of vulnerable applicants and expanded access to legal representation.

Allowing the Attorney General to consider disease symptoms and origin in withholding-of-removal danger assessments (§ 1208.16(d)(2) disease consideration) risks stigmatization and violates medical privacy; commenters will demand that medical evidence be evaluated by qualified health professionals and that disease status alone not be treated as criminality or a security threat.

DHS’s authority to remove asylum-seekers to third countries (§ 1208.16(f)(1)) needs stringent safe-third-country protections, oversight, and reporting requirements to ensure compliance with non-refoulement and international obligations.

Allowing DHS to remove an alien to a third country before adjudication if the alien hasn’t established no-threats or lack of torture there (§ 1208.16(f)(2)) creates perverse incentives for expedited removals without adequate fact-finding; commenters will call for a prohibition on pre-adjudication third-country removal except with judicial authorization.

The procedural obligations that such third-country removal can only occur if the alien was advised and provided an opportunity to withdraw (§ 1208.16(f)(2)(i)-(ii)) are insufficient unless the rule mandates linguistic assistance, written notices, and a meaningful waiting period.

The severability provision (§ 1208.25) should not be used to salvage unlawful provisions; commenters will request a commitment to review remaining provisions and reopen public comment if any substantive part is struck down to ensure ongoing legitimacy.

The provision that an IJ must find no credible fear of persecution for aliens ineligible under specified provisions and that the decision is final and not appealable (§ 1208.30(e)) removes an important appellate safeguard and could violate due process; commenters will urge permitting at least limited administrative or judicial review.

If an IJ concurs with an asylum officer’s negative credible-fear determination and lack of torture likelihood, the rule requiring return to DHS for removal with the IJ decision final and not appealable (§ 1208.30(g)(2)(iv)(A)) effectively eliminates appellate review and may contravene statutory protections — commenters will request preservation of appeal rights.

The requirement that if an IJ finds credible fear they vacate the asylum officer’s order and DHS may commence § 240 proceedings (with IJ de novo review) (§ 1208.30(g)(2)(iv)(B)) is appropriate as a matter of procedure, but commenters will demand deadlines for de novo review, access to counsel, and protections against prolonged detention during proceedings.

raw_output:
[P1] The exemption in §63.8985(f) that excludes HCl production facilities if all gaseous streams containing HCl and Cl2 are recycled or routed for process purpose is ambiguous because it does not define what constitutes “routed for process purpose,” creating enforcement uncertainty for facilities and regulators.

[P1] The all-or-nothing condition in §63.8985(f) is impractical for many HCl producers because occasional maintenance, breakdowns, or minor purging events may temporarily vent streams, which would then subject an entire facility to the subpart despite otherwise continuous recycling.

[P1] Industry requests a clear de minimis threshold or allowance for occasional, short-duration deviations from full recycling before a facility loses the §63.8985(f) exemption (e.g., permitting intermittent venting up to X hours per month).

[P1] Environmental advocates oppose broad use of §63.8985(f) because recycling/rerouting that still results in eventual release (e.g., via downstream processes or periodic purge vents) could evade emissions control requirements; the rule should require proof that recycled streams never lead to uncontrolled emissions.

[P2] The compliance deadline in §63.9005(a) (181 days after publication) is too short for existing sources to retrofit or install required controls and conduct necessary testing; industry requests at least 12–18 months for planning, permitting, and installation.

[P3] The near-immediate requirement in §63.9005(a) to be “in compliance at all times” after the 180‑day date leaves no transition for operational learning curves; commenters request phased compliance or interim emission limits to avoid immediate noncompliance exposure.

[P4] Requiring new/reconstructed sources with construction commencing after Feb 4, 2019 to comply at all times (P4) is unfair when those sources may have been designed to meet prior standards; request grandfathering for facilities permitted under earlier rules or an applicability clarification tied to actual start-up dates.

[P5] The obligation in §63.9005(b) to operate and maintain control and monitoring equipment per §63.6(e)(1)(i) before the deadline appears to import SSM-related flexibilities that the rule removes elsewhere; legal commenters request reconciliation to avoid internal contradiction.

[P6] The requirement in §63.9005(b) after the date to “operate and maintain at all times consistent with safety and good practices to minimize emissions” (P6) is subjective; stakeholders request a more concrete standard or examples of practices that demonstrate compliance.

[P7] The pre-deadline mandate in §63.9005(c) to develop a written SSM plan (P7) will impose administrative burdens on small HCl producers; small business commenters request a simplified template or scaled requirements.

[P8] The removal of the SSM plan requirement after the specified date in §63.9005(c) (P8) is legally problematic because it eliminates an established compliance tool and could impair transparency; states and NGOs request retention of SSM plan obligations or at least recordkeeping of SSM events.

[P9] For P9, industry requests clarification whether new/reconstructed sources that began construction after Feb 4, 2019 but before promulgation are categorically exempt from SSM plan obligations, and whether that affects liabilities for SSM deviations.

[P10] The pre-deadline O&M procedural requirements in §63.9005(d)(4) (P10) referencing §63.9025 are resource-intensive; commenters ask for phased implementation and a clear list of minimum required elements to reduce compliance cost.

[P11] Post-deadline differences in O&M requirements (P11) are unclear—stakeholders request a redline comparison of pre- and post-deadline obligations to assess new monitoring burdens.

[P12] The data QA procedures required before the deadline in §63.9005(d)(5) that adopt §63.8(d) (P12) could impose RATA and other testing frequency requirements that are costly; request flexibility for facilities using modern continuous monitors validated by performance evaluations.

[P13] The carve-out in §63.9005(d)(5) excluding SSM‑tied §63.8(d)(3) requirements after the specified dates (P13) may create inconsistencies in QA expectations; laboratories and testing bodies request clarification of which QA elements remain mandatory.

[P14] The life-of-source retention requirement for written data QA procedures (P14) is disproportionate for facilities that expect to change operations; request that records be retained for a defined period (e.g., 5 years) rather than the life of the source.

[P15] Requiring retention of superseded performance evaluation plans for 5 years (P15) is reasonable but should be harmonized with existing state record retention rules to avoid conflicting obligations.

[P16] The advisory to include a corrective action program in the QA plan (P16) should be made mandatory to ensure consistent responses to QA failures; environmental groups support making corrective action programs binding rather than advisory.

[P17] The pre-deadline recordkeeping/reporting per §63.10(c) and (e)(1),(2)(i) (P17) duplicates many existing reports; facilities request consolidation to avoid duplicate submissions and to allow using state reporting portals where permitted.

[P18] The expanded post-deadline recordkeeping/reporting in §63.9005(d)(6) (P18) imposes new data elements; industry requests an implementation guide and pilot period for electronic reporting templates to prevent submission errors.

[P19] The requirement in §63.9020(a)(2) to perform performance tests under representative conditions before the date (P19) needs clearer definition of “representative,” particularly for batch processes and variable-load operations; commenters request examples and acceptance ranges.

[P20] The ongoing obligation to test under normal operations after the date (P20) (i.e., no testing during abnormal periods) may make it impossible to demonstrate compliance for units that rarely operate at a single steady-state; request allowance for averaged data or alternative compliance demonstrations.

[P21] The mandate to record process information during performance tests and explain representativeness (P21) creates proprietary concerns—companies request explicit confidentiality protections for detailed process data submitted to EPA.

[P22] Requiring facilities to provide test condition records to the Administrator upon request (P22) without a timeframe or format could impose administrative burdens; request that EPA specify response timelines and accept electronic submissions in standard formats.

[P23] The prohibition on conducting performance tests during SSM periods (P23) could prevent facilities from demonstrating compliance for units that start up infrequently; request allowance to certify normal-operation tests that bracket SSM transitions or to perform alternate test methods.

[P24] The CMS data validity requirement in §63.9025(a)(3) to obtain valid monitoring data for at least 75% of operating hours per 24‑hour day (P24/P25) is impractically stringent—especially for intermittent-operation units—and should be relaxed to a weekly or monthly validity percentage.

[P25] The mandate that valid data include at least 4 equally spaced valid periods each hour (P26) is technically burdensome for many monitor types (e.g., monitors with response times >15 minutes); request alternative spacing criteria or allowance for equivalent monitoring plans.

[P26] Small facilities and those with intermittent operations argue that both the 75% daily coverage and the 4-per-hour requirement (P24–P26) will result in frequent out-of-control findings and unintended violations; request a business-size exemption or phased approach.

[P27] The NOCS submission requirements before the date (P27) and the 180‑day NOCS timing in §63.9045(f) (P31) create overlapping deadlines; commenters ask EPA to harmonize and provide a single clear timeline for initial submissions.

[P28] The post-deadline expansion of NOCS content to include §63.9050(d) (P28) increases reporting burden; industry requests standardized electronic templates and the ability to submit confidential business information under the CBI procedures.

[P29] The pre-deadline provision in §63.9040(e) allowing SSM deviations to not be violations if the owner demonstrates compliance with §63.6(e)(1) to the Administrator’s satisfaction (P29) is vital for legal certainty and should not be removed as in P30.

[P30] Removing the SSM deviation exemption after the specified dates (§63.9040(e) P30) exposes facilities to strict liability for unavoidable malfunctions and is likely unconstitutional; legal commenters request the provision be retained or replaced with narrower criteria.

[P31] The requirement to submit NOCS with performance test results within 180 days after applicable compliance dates (P31) may be infeasible if test labs and EPA scheduling are constrained; request flexibility or extension authority.

[P32] The compliance report content obligations in §63.9050(a) and (c)-(e) (P32) are extensive; suggest EPA provide a machine-readable template and a checklist to reduce submission errors.

[P33] Requiring inclusion of §63.10(d)(5)(i) SSM-plan reporting elements in compliance reports when an SSM occurred and actions were consistent with the SSM plan (P33) is unnecessary if SSM plans are being eliminated (see P8/P34); request removal or harmonization of this cross-reference.

[P34] The post-deadline removal of SSM reporting requirements (P34) will reduce transparency about SSM events and emissions; community groups request retention of SSM event reporting even if formal SSM plans are not required.

[P35] The obligation to state “no deviations” when none occurred (P35/P75) is redundant but low burden; nevertheless, request EPA allow a standardized checkbox in electronic reports to improve consistency.

[P36] The requirement to include CMS deviation information for each deviation including SSM periods (P36) conflicts with the removal of immediate SSM reports (P39); request clarity on reporting format and timing for deviations that occur during SSM.

[P37] The mandate to submit immediate SSM reports for SSMs not consistent with SSM plans (P37) is obsolete once SSM plans are no longer required (P39); EPA should clarify whether immediate reporting still applies to any events and what triggers are required.

[P38] The procedural timing in §63.9050(f) that requires reporting according to (f)(1) and (f)(2) unless Administrator approves a different schedule (P38) centralizes discretion with EPA; commenters request appeal or petition processes and predictable default timelines.

[P39] Eliminating the requirement for immediate SSM reports after the specified date (P39) will delay community notification of significant releases; local governments and environmental justice groups oppose removal and request immediate notification requirements remain.

[P40] The 60‑day submission requirement for performance test results (P40) is reasonable, but EPA should accept extensions for validated cause with documentation, and allow electronic submission exceptions when ERT is unavailable.

[P41] The obligation to submit ERT-supported test methods via CEDRI in ERT format or XML (P41) may be burdensome for smaller facilities lacking IT capacity; request acceptance of CSV or other common formats and transition assistance.

[P42] For test methods not supported by ERT (P42), requiring attachment submission in the ERT is workable but EPA should clarify maximum file size, acceptable file types (PDF, CSV), and secure submission protocols.

[P43] The CBI submission process (P43) requiring physical media to EPA’s CBI Office and electronic non-CBI submission is burdensome and outdated; request secure electronic CBI portals in lieu of physical media and harmonization with other EPA CBI procedures.

[P44] The 60‑day deadline to submit CMS performance evaluations (P44) should be aligned with performance evaluation schedules (e.g., annual) and allow for combined submissions where multiple evaluations occur close together.

[P45] When CMS RATA pollutants are supported by ERT (P45), the required formats should be published well in advance with schema examples and validation tools to avoid rejection of submissions.

[P46] For CMS RATAs not supported by ERT (P46), the same concerns about acceptable file types and attachments apply; EPA should publish guidance on formatting to ensure consistent acceptance.

[P47] The CBI procedure for CMS evaluation submissions (P47) again requiring physical media is obsolete; stakeholders request secure online CBI submission options and clear decryption/handling processes.

[P48] The requirement to begin electronic submission of compliance reports after [DATE 181 DAYS AFTER PUBLICATION] (P48) should be delayed until EPA verifies CEDRI capacity and provides training; otherwise, many regulated entities risk missed deadlines.

[P49] The mandatory electronic submission of performance evaluations beginning on the specified date (P49) risks data loss or misformatting; request a phased enforcement policy and acceptance of paper submissions with good cause.

[P50] Requiring NOCS submissions electronically after the specified date (P50) (with same concerns as P48/P49) necessitates that EPA guarantee CEDRI uptime and provide alternative submission routes during outages.

[P51] The requirement in §63.9050(l) to submit reports via CEDRI using the appropriate template and to submit CBI on physical media (P51) is procedurally complex; request combined CBI/non‑CBI secure electronic workflow and single submission confirmation.

[P52] Allowing EPA system outage claims for late reporting (P52) is reasonable, but the strict requirement that the outage occur within 5 business days before the due date (P54) is arbitrary and could penalize users impacted by earlier outages that delayed preparation; request expanding the outage window to 10 business days.

[P53] Allowing planned outages to qualify for outage claims (P55) could be abused if EPA schedules planned maintenance without adequate notice; request that claims for planned outages require EPA to have posted notice at least X days in advance.

[P54] The obligation to promptly notify the Administrator when you first knew an event may cause delay (P56) should specify acceptable means of notification (email, CEDRI message, certified mail) and include a standard acknowledgement timeframe from EPA.

[P55] The written description requirements for outage claims (P57) are reasonable, but EPA should allow templated forms to streamline submissions and reduce disputes about sufficiency.

[P56] Vesting sole discretion with the Administrator to accept outage claims (P58) or force majeure claims (P64) creates legal uncertainty; commenters request objective criteria and an appeal mechanism for denied claims.

[P57] The requirement that reports be submitted electronically as soon as possible after an outage (P59) is vague; request defined maximum extension days proportional to the outage length.

[P58] The force majeure claim provisions (P60–P65) are useful, but the 5-business-day timing window (P61) is too narrow for events with lingering impacts; suggest allowing claims for events up to 30 days before due date and reasonable aftermath periods.

[P59] The notification and written description obligations for force majeure (P62–P63) should allow the use of third-party declarations (e.g., utility outage reports, emergency declarations) as supporting documentation.

[P60] The post-deadline elimination of SSM record retention requirements (P66–P67) conflicts with other obligations that continue to require deviation records; request EPA specify which SSM-related records must still be retained and for how long.

[P61] The requirement after the date to keep deviation records with date/time/duration and pollutant estimates (P68–P70) imposes heavy estimation burdens (particularly quantifying emissions during transient events); request EPA-approved emission estimation protocols and default factors.

[P62] The obligation to record corrective actions taken to minimize emissions (P71) is appropriate but should be tied to practicability standards—small facilities may not have extensive corrective action documentation; request a scaled requirement.

[P63] Allowing records submitted via CEDRI to be maintained electronically (P72) is sensible, but the rule should permit cloud-based storage with specified security and backup controls.

[P64] The on-site availability requirement despite electronic storage (P73) may be duplicative; request permission to provide electronic access (secure remote login) during on-site compliance evaluations to reduce paper copying.

[P65] The 99% control efficiency or ≤120 ppmv outlet concentration standard for specified HCl storage tank streams (P74) is technologically challenging for some existing retrofit situations; industry requests allowance of alternative equivalent emission limits based on mass emissions (e.g., lb/day) or phased compliance.

[P66] Environmental groups support the stringent requirement in P74 (99% or ≤120 ppmv) but request EPA specify enforceable test methods, sampling locations, and QA procedures to ensure consistent measurement.

[P67] The compliance report table items that require statements of no deviations or no CMS out-of-control periods (P75–P76) should include definitions for “deviation” and “out-of-control” tied to measurable thresholds to avoid subjective determinations.

[P68] The obligation to report LDAR plan noncompliance per Table 6 row 6 (P80) must specify what constitutes “procedures not followed” (e.g., missed inspections, failed repairs) and required corrective action timelines to avoid inconsistent state enforcement.

[P69] The interaction of SSM elimination, CMS reporting of SSM-period deviations (P36/P39), and the prohibition on testing during SSM (P23) creates potential gaps where emissions during SSM may neither be tested nor promptly reported; stakeholders request rule edits to close this compliance and transparency gap.

[P70] Legal commenters note potential conflict between the removal of SSM defenses (P30) and the general duty to avoid strict liability for malfunctions under the Clean Air Act; request EPA include an express, narrow affirmative defense for unforeseeable malfunctions with notification and mitigation requirements.

[P71] States implementing their own programs request that EPA clarify delegations and allow submission of required reports to state electronic systems where state portals meet EPA data standards, to avoid duplicative submissions to both EPA and states.

[P72] The rule should include an explicit grandfathering clause for facilities currently subject to permits based on previous NESHAPs to avoid triggering permit reopenings solely due to administrative changes in reporting format (electronic vs. paper).

[P73] Commenters request EPA publish a comprehensive compliance guide, examples of acceptable monitoring plans, and sample templates for NOCS, compliance reports, CMS performance evaluations, SSM notifications, and outage/force majeure claims to reduce interpretive disputes.

[P1] The May 23, 2019 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonable and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow affected operators, repair stations, labor unions, and foreign regulators sufficient time to prepare meaningful technical and legal comments.

[P1] The rule should include an explanation of why the May 23, 2019 deadline is necessary; without justification, stakeholders cannot assess the urgency and therefore cannot prioritize resources to meet the deadline.

[P2] The scope in § 39.13(c) is overbroad because it includes 747–8 series airplanes without demonstrating the unsafe condition exists on all listed models; the FAA should provide model-specific risk evidence or limit applicability to only affected variants.

[P2] The AD’s applicability to all 747–400D and 747–400F airplanes is ambiguous because the service bulletin references configuration differences; the rule should clarify whether specific line numbers, production blocks, or retrofit statuses are excluded or included.

[P3] § 39.13(f) lacks explicit compliance timeframes within the AD text (it merely references "specified compliance times"); the AD should state absolute compliance deadlines in the regulation so operators know enforceable timing without referring only to the service bulletin.

[P3] The provision that operators "must comply ... within the compliance times specified" imposes a strict mandate without accommodating scheduling constraints (e.g., maintenance checks); the FAA should allow credit for accomplishing actions at the next scheduled maintenance event within a defined window.

[P4] Requiring performance of all actions labeled RC in the Boeing service bulletin (per § 39.13(g)) effectively incorporates detailed manufacturer procedures by reference; the FAA should publish the critical RC steps in the AD itself or ensure the service bulletin is readily available free of charge.

[P4] The phrase "except as specified in paragraph (i)" in § 39.13(g) creates uncertainty about which deviations are permitted; commenters request the FAA explicitly list paragraph (i) exceptions in the preamble to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P5] Limiting the end of repetitive inspections in § 39.13(j) to only the seats where a serviceable seat is installed could incentivize partial modifications and create record-keeping burdens; the FAA should allow fleet-wide termination or provide clearer criteria for what constitutes a "serviceable" seat.

[P5] The rule does not define "serviceable" for Captain’s and First Officer’s seats in § 39.13(j); industry needs a precise definition (e.g., part number ranges, modification kits, specific maintenance release) to ensure consistent compliance.

[P6] The 36-month period in § 39.13(h) for inspecting seat nameplates is excessively long given potential immediate safety concerns; safety advocates and labor organizations will request a shorter compliance time (e.g., 6–12 months) for initial inspections.

[P6] Conversely, some operators will claim that the 36-month inspection window in § 39.13(h) is too short for international fleets with limited access to OEM parts and request extensions or phased compliance (e.g., larger operators 24 months, small operators 36 months).

[P6] § 39.13(h) requires "on-condition" follow-up actions based on nameplate inspections but does not specify the nature, compliance time, or acceptance criteria for those on-condition actions; the AD must detail required corrective actions and allowable deferred-action processes.

[P7] Allowing maintenance record review in § 39.13(h) to determine part/serial numbers is reasonable, but the AD should specify what constitutes "conclusive" determination (acceptable documentation types, chain-of-custody requirements) to prevent inconsistent acceptance by different inspectors.

[P7] The rule should permit use of maintenance records only when verified by a qualified inspector; an operator declaration alone should not be sufficient to avoid physical nameplate inspection.

[P8] § 39.13(i) that substitutes the AD effective date for the service bulletin’s original issue date may create retroactive compliance ambiguities; legal counsel will request confirmation that no actions performed between the service bulletin issue date and the AD effective date become invalid or nonconforming.

[P9] The AMOC authority in § 39.13(k)(1) is centralized to the Seattle ACO Branch manager; foreign operators and non-U.S. EASA/Transport Canada regulators may request reciprocity language or delegation procedures so that local certification authorities can approve AMOCs to avoid operational delays.

[P9] The AD should clarify timelines and criteria the Seattle ACO will use to evaluate AMOC requests to avoid indefinite waiting periods that ground aircraft.

[P10] § 39.13(k)(1) requires AMOC requests to be sent to principal inspectors, local FSDOs, or certification office managers and provides an email address; commenters will request redundancy (fax, secure file transfer) and an acknowledgement-of-receipt requirement to document timely submissions.

[P11] The obligation in § 39.13(k)(2) to notify the principal inspector or local FSDO before using an approved AMOC is vague about timing (how far in advance must notification occur) and the acceptable form of notice; operators request explicit notice windows (e.g., 72 hours prior) and permitted communication methods.

[P12] The permission in § 39.13(k)(3) allowing an approved AMOC to be used for any repair/modification if approved by the Boeing ODA raises conflict-of-interest concerns; independent approval by the FAA or a neutral party should be required in addition to Boeing ODA concurrence.

[P13] The requirement in § 39.13(k)(3) that repair/modification deviations meet the airplane’s certification basis lacks guidance on how to treat older aircraft with amended certification bases (grandfathered findings); commenters request a process for determining equivalence and grandfathering.

[P14] Mandating that any AMOC approval "must specifically refer to this AD" in § 39.13(k)(3) is appropriate, but the rule should require that AMOC approval letters include explicit implementation instructions and applicability statements to avoid misapplication across fleets.

[P15] § 39.13(k)(4)(i) requires performing all RC-labeled steps including figures and substeps; industry will request clarification whether human-factor tasks depicted only in figures (e.g., torque values, orientation) are considered RC and whether tooling calibration records are required.

[P16] The "RC Exempt" exception in § 39.13(k)(4)(i) must be clearly identified in the service bulletin; operators will request that the FAA publish a list of any RC-exempt steps in the AD to prevent inconsistent interpretations among maintenance providers.

[P17] The AMOC requirement for any deviation from RC steps (§ 39.13(k)(4)(i)) could create operational inflexibility for urgent repairs; commenters ask the FAA to permit post-action AMOC submissions for emergency deviations provided the operator documents the justification and notifies the principal inspector within a short timeframe.

[P18] The permission in § 39.13(k)(4)(ii) allowing deviation from non-RC steps using accepted operator methods should be expanded to explicitly include approved maintenance program procedures (e.g., MSG-3 tasks) and continuous airworthiness procedures to avoid conflict with existing programs.

[P18] The condition in § 39.13(k)(4)(ii) that the airplane can be returned to an "airworthy condition" after non-RC deviations is vague; the AD should define measurable acceptance criteria or reference specific airworthiness standards to guide inspectors.

[P1] The AD should include instructions on how late-filed comments submitted after May 23, 2019 will be handled (e.g., will they be considered, entered into docket) to avoid discouraging substantive late submissions.

[P2] Labor unions representing flight crews will comment that the AD should require crew training or briefings if seat replacements or modifications change seat adjustment procedures, restraint configurations, or emergency egress behavior for Captain/First Officer seats.

[P6] Passenger and crew safety advocates will request that the AD require physical verification of seat part numbers during routine heavy maintenance rather than permitting record-only determinations, due to risk of record inaccuracies.

[P12] Small repair stations and third-party modifiers will object that requiring Boeing ODA approval for AMOC uses (per § 39.13(k)(3)) creates a bottleneck and may be inconsistent with 14 CFR 121/135 repair station privileges; recommend allowing appropriately authorized repair stations to approve limited deviations subject to FAA oversight.

[P3] The AD should provide explicit credit language for actions done voluntarily before the effective date (e.g., service bulletin accomplishment) to avoid disputes about whether prior work satisfies compliance requirements.

[P15] Legal commenters will raise that treating figures in service information as RC steps (per § 39.13(k)(4)(i)) may turn illustrative material into legally binding requirements; the FAA should limit RC designation to discrete procedural steps, not illustrative drawings.

[P7] Operators managing international recordkeeping systems will request that the AD permit use of digitized/migrated maintenance records (with audit trail) to satisfy § 39.13(h) instead of requiring original paper nameplate records.

[P11] The requirement to notify principal inspectors before using an AMOC (§ 39.13(k)(2)) should explicitly allow notification via the AMOC approval document uploaded to the FAA’s AD Portal to streamline compliance for large fleets.

[P1] Allowing synthetic substances generally in organic livestock production undermines the fundamental organic principle of minimizing synthetic inputs and will cause consumer confusion about the meaning of the organic label.

[P1] The rule fails to specify limits, conditions, or documentation requirements for which synthetic substances may be used in organic livestock production, creating enforcement and auditing gaps for certifiers.

[P1] Synthetic allowances should be narrowly defined and limited to specific use cases (e.g., emergency or therapeutic use) and include reporting, withdrawal periods, and approval by the certifying agent.

[P1] Industry commenters support some limited synthetic use but request a clear list of permitted synthetics, permitted purposes (disease treatment vs. routine use), dosage limits, and required veterinary oversight to prevent routine prophylactic use.

[P1] Animal welfare advocates worry that permitting synthetics without veterinary oversight could lead producers to choose cheaper synthetic treatments over higher-welfare management practices.

[P2] Allowing elemental sulfur to treat both livestock and livestock housing is scientifically questionable because sulfur products can be toxic when applied to animals; the rule must clarify application methods, concentrations, and safety protocols.

[P2] The provision does not set residue limits or withdrawal periods for elemental sulfur used on livestock, risking contamination of organic meat, milk, and eggs and inconsistent certification decisions.

[P2] Request for evidence: commenters ask the agency to provide scientific studies demonstrating the safety and efficacy of elemental sulfur for direct treatment of livestock (not only housing), including impacts on animal health and product residues.

[P2] If elemental sulfur is permitted, require labeling, worker safety training, PPE requirements, and explicit restrictions preventing inhalation exposures to animals and humans.

[P2] Housing-only use of elemental sulfur would be more appropriate; permitting direct application to animals should be removed unless supported by clear toxicology data.

[P3] Removing potassium acid tartrate from § 205.605(b) (the list of allowed nonsynthetics?) creates inconsistency with other sections and may inadvertently prohibit its use where it has been accepted historically; the agency must explain rationale and cross-reference other provisions.

[P3] Legal commenters: The amendment to § 205.605(b) appears to create a regulatory conflict with § 205.606(o) which separately allows potassium acid tartrate as a nonorganically produced ingredient; the rule should be reconciled to avoid ambiguity.

[P3] If removal is intended to change status (from allowed to prohibited), the agency must provide notice of change, scientific justification, and transition time for manufacturers to reformulate products.

[P4] Allowing nonorganically produced agricultural products as ingredients in products labeled "organic" risks weakening organic standards unless limited to unavoidable ingredients and subject to strict access exception criteria.

[P4] The rule must clarify that nonorganically produced ingredients are only permitted when an equivalent organic ingredient is not commercially available (NOP's commercial availability criteria) and require documentation and annual justification.

[P4] Consumers will be misled if processed products labeled "organic" contain nonorganic agricultural ingredients without clear disclosure; require on-package disclosure when nonorganic agricultural ingredients are used.

[P4] Enforcement commenters: Certifiers need clear procedural requirements for approving nonorganic ingredients, including proof of effort to source organic alternatives, documentation retention periods, and auditing protocols.

[P5] Allowing potassium acid tartrate as a nonorganically produced agricultural product ingredient in organic processed foods is acceptable only if it meets the NOP criteria for unavoidable ingredients and has a clear supply-chain verification process.

[P5] Potassium acid tartrate is commonly used in winemaking and processed foods; permitting it without restrictions could allow widely available nonorganic versions to replace organic tartaric acid—must require demonstration that organic potassium acid tartrate was unavailable.

[P5] Food safety commenters request assurance that potassium acid tartrate used is produced to food-grade standards and that its production process does not use prohibited synthetic processing aids that would conflict with organic handling requirements.

[P5] Legal risk: Because § 205.605(b) is being amended to remove potassium acid tartrate while § 205.606(o) would allow it, the rule as drafted creates legal uncertainty; commenters urge the agency to consolidate treatment of potassium acid tartrate in a single provision and clarify intent.

[P1] Request for regulatory impact analysis: commenters ask for an economic analysis of permitting synthetics in livestock production, including effects on small-scale organic producers, market prices, and export market acceptance.

[P2] Worker safety and environmental groups request an environmental assessment of increased sulfur use (runoff, air emissions), and cumulative exposure analysis for farmworkers and neighboring communities.

[P4] Advocacy groups demand public reporting of all approved nonorganic ingredient uses in organic-labeled products (a publicly available registry) to maintain transparency and consumer trust.

[P1] Certification consistency concern: Certifiers will interpret broad synthetic permissions differently; the agency should issue guidance and model standard operating procedures to ensure uniform implementation.

[P5] Manufacturers ask for a transition period and grandfathering provisions if potassium acid tartrate’s status changes, to allow reformulation, supplier contracts, and label changes without market disruption.

[P2] Veterinary groups request clear distinctions between therapeutic uses of elemental sulfur (if any) and environmental/biocidal uses, with veterinary prescription requirements for animal treatments.

[P3] Procedural comment: The proposed removal of potassium acid tartrate from § 205.605(b) lacks adequate notice and rationale; the agency should publish supporting data and the administrative record justifying the amendment.

[P2] Including "certificated in any category" could unintentionally capture aircraft that are permanently retired or amateur-built derivatives; the FAA should exclude permanently decommissioned or major-modification-recertified airframes.

[P3] The AD's catch-all “perform the following ... unless already done” is vague; it should state how prior actions are documented and acceptable proof (work orders, logbook entries, manufacturer service bulletin compliance) that will satisfy the "already done" condition.

[P4] The 30-day compliance time to insert temporary POH revisions for POH AIR 2825 is impractically short for operators in remote locations or with limited maintenance access; extend to 90 days or allow electronic temporary revisions distribution with a 60-day compliance.

[P4] The AD does not specify whether installation of the temporary POH revision must be recorded in the aircraft logs or how operators should document compliance; add explicit logbook entry requirements and acceptable forms of record.

[P5] The identical 30-day insertion requirement for POH AIR 3237 (P5) raises the same concerns as P4; the FAA should harmonize compliance times for both POH types and permit electronic placarding pending formal POH insertion.

[P6] Requiring replacement of the low-oil-pressure-light pressure switch within 100 hours TIS or 12 months (whichever first) may be burdensome for high-utilization fleets; the FAA should allow a risk-based alternative interval (e.g., 300 hours) supported by service data or condition monitoring.

[P6] The AD does not provide required parts availability or approved part numbers for the replacement switch; without guaranteed supply, compliance within the timeframe may be impossible — the FAA must coordinate with Pacific Aerospace to ensure parts availability and publish P/Ns.

[P6] The compliance metric "100 hours TIS or 12 months (whichever first)" should clarify how hours are counted ( Hobbs vs. tach ) and whether partial-hour accumulation prior to the effective date counts toward the 100-hour limit.

[P7] The requirement to replace the oil pressure/temperature indicator within 100 hours TIS or 12 months lacks guidance on acceptable replacement units — the AD should reference approved part numbers or service bulletin Part B procedures to avoid non‑conforming replacements.

[P7] For aircraft not currently fitted with PIN INS 60–8 indicators, the AD's applicability language is unclear whether the requirement is inapplicable or whether retrofitting is required; clarify applicability for differently fitted aircraft.

[P8] Granting the Manager authority to approve AMOCs is routine, but the AD should clarify expected timing for AMOC responses (e.g., 60 days) to prevent operational uncertainty for operators seeking alternatives.

[P9] Requiring AMOC submissions to be mailed to a single FAA contact in Kansas City may impede timely processing; the FAA should explicitly accept electronic submissions and provide a tracking mechanism and confirmation of receipt.

[P1] The deadline in § 39.13(a) (March 19, 2018) is already passed and therefore the rule text should be updated to reflect a current, realistic comment period; as written it creates confusion for stakeholders submitting comments now.

[P1] If the FAA intends to retain a fixed calendar deadline, the agency should extend the comment deadline or reopen the comment period because affected operators did not receive adequate notice before the March 19, 2018 date.

[P2] § 39.13(f) requires compliance “within the specified compliance times” but does not define how temporary operational restrictions (e.g., limited-use ferries) interact with those times—request clarification that ferry flights permitted under other provisions do not constitute “noncompliance.”

[P3] The requirement in § 39.13(g)(1) to remove bearing assembly P/N 2544198 “in accordance with the compliance times in Figure 1…or within 90 days” is ambiguous where the AD effective date is unclear; request that the FAA explicitly define the “AD effective date” in the preamble and regulatory text.

[P3] § 39.13(g)(1) does not specify acceptable methods for documenting removal of P/N 2544198 (logbook entries, maintenance records, electronic records); operators need a clear recordkeeping standard to demonstrate compliance.

[P4] Figure 1’s requirement that PTGs with 0–750 hours be removed “not later than 750 hours” effectively allows some aircraft to operate up to 750 hours post-AD without action; this creates safety concern for high-utilization operators and should be shortened for helicopters used in commercial air ambulance, offshore, or emergency operations.

[P4] The compliance banding in Figure 1 (0–750 hours) is too broad—operators at 740 hours will only have 10 hours to comply, which is infeasible for scheduling; propose adding a minimum advance-notice window (e.g., 30 days) or setting compliance in calendar days after AD effective date.

[P5] For PTG time 751–1000 hours, Figure 1’s “not later than 1,000 hours” deadline does not account for partial-flight-hour accumulation or in-service scheduling; request that FAA allow compliance by calendar days as an alternative for aircraft with unpredictable hour accumulation.

[P6] The 1,250-hour deadline for PTGs with 1001–1250 hours lacks any allowance for maintenance shop capacity; many MROs will not be able to meet the surge; FAA should include a temporary relief mechanism or allow staggered deadlines by operator size.

[P7] The 1,500-hour deadline for PTGs with 1251–1500 hours in Figure 1 fails to consider end-of-life contingencies where operators plan PTG overhaul—FAA should permit removal at scheduled overhaul dates earlier than the deadline without penalty.

[P8] For PTGs with >1501 hours, the “at the next PTG removal for any reason” requirement could permit indefinite continued operation if an operator delays PTG removal; FAA should set an absolute calendar backstop (e.g., remove within X days) to avoid unbounded risk.

[P8] The clause “next removal for any reason” is vague regarding whether consequences such as unscheduled removals triggered by unrelated failures qualify—request illustrative examples and a definition of “removal for any reason.”

[P9] The “alternative condition” in § 39.13(g)(1) that allows removal within 90 days if that is later than the figure’s compliance time could inadvertently lengthen exposure for many operators; stakeholders ask FAA to justify the safety basis for allowing a 90‑day extension beyond the hour thresholds.

[P9] The interplay of the 90-day alternative with Figure 1 could create inconsistency across operators (some get longer compliance windows); request that FAA instead apply the 90-day alternative only as a one-time exception for specific hardship cases via AMOC.

[P10] § 39.13(g)(2) requires installation of an “eligible replacement” before further flight but fails to list approved part numbers or specify the standard of eligibility—industry needs explicit acceptable part numbers, certificate of conformity requirements, or reference documents.

[P10] The rule should clarify whether overhauled or reconditioned bearing assemblies are “eligible replacements,” and what documentation (ETOPS/TSO-like traceability, vendor stamp) is required to prove eligibility.

[P11] Allowing the Chicago ACO Branch Manager to approve AMOCs (§ 39.13(h)(1)) centralizes authority in one office; suggest permitting delegated AMOC authority to other ACOs or the local FSDO to avoid processing delays for geographically distributed operators.

[P12] The AMOC submission procedure (§ 39.13(h)(1)) mandating routing via the principal inspector or local FSDO may delay urgent requests; request an expedited electronic submission pathway and a specified FAA response timeframe (e.g., 30 days).

[P12] 14 CFR 39.19 routing requirements should be clarified for foreign operators and foreign repair stations—specify whether submission through the operator’s State of Registry is acceptable.

[P13] The instruction in § 39.13(h)(1) to address direct submissions to the Chicago ACO Branch to the person in paragraph (i)(1) is incomplete in the NPRM excerpt; ask FAA to include the full point-of-contact, mailing address, email, and phone so stakeholders can comply.

[P14] § 39.13(h)(2) requires notification of the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC, but does not require concurrent notification to the certificate holder’s accountable manager; recommend adding that requirement to ensure organizational awareness.

[P14] The obligation in § 39.13(h)(2) is silent on the time window for notification prior to using an AMOC; request that FAA define a minimum advance notice (e.g., 48 hours) and acceptable forms of notice (email, automated system).

[General] The AD does not include an economic analysis of costs to operators for removing and replacing P/N 2544198 across the staged compliance bands; request FAA provide a detailed cost-benefit assessment and consider cost relief for small operators.

[General] Legal commenters should note that the AD’s effective dates, compliance windows, and AMOC routing create potential due-process concerns if operators are penalized for ambiguous deadlines; recommend the FAA revise language to be clear and administrably enforceable.

[General] Maintenance providers request that FAA publish recommended service bulletin procedures (step-by-step removal/installation torques, inspection criteria) to standardize work scope and minimize varied interpretations during inspections.

[P1] The requirement that commenters "choose only one" submission method is unduly restrictive for organizations that collect comments via multiple channels (online portal, mail, and overnight) and may prevent legitimate duplicate submissions on behalf of different constituents — please allow coordinated multi-method batch submissions or clarify how organizations representing multiple individuals should submit.

[P1] Prohibiting submission by more than one method could disenfranchise individuals whose electronic submissions fail due to technical issues; request language permitting a secondary submission method if the primary method fails, with a mechanism to de-duplicate paired submissions.

[P2] Allowing electronic submissions via Regulations.gov is helpful, but the rule should specify supported file formats, maximum file size, and accessibility accommodations (e.g., for screen readers) to ensure equitable participation.

[P2] The rule should explicitly permit attachments containing large datasets or exhibits via Regulations.gov or provide an alternative transfer method; otherwise complex commenters cannot submit necessary supporting evidence.

[P3] Restricting regular mail to the single specified P.O. Box address may burden commenters in remote areas; request inclusion of a physical street address for hand-delivered or in-person submissions during business hours.

[P3] Mailing only to the specified P.O. Box may create processing delays and ambiguity about postmark versus received dates; clarify whether postmark date or received date governs timeliness for mailed comments.

[P4] Limiting express/overnight mail to a single specified address without including recipient name and suite number could cause delivery refusals; request provision of full street address, recipient name, and receiving hours for courier deliveries.

[P4] The rule should clarify whether tracking/confirmation numbers from express carriers will be accepted as proof of timely submission if delivery is delayed, to protect commenters.

[P5] The deadline "received by October 12, 2021" creates an unacceptable urgency and may exclude stakeholders who rely on organizational review cycles; request extending the deadline by at least 30 days and clarifying whether postmark or received date applies.

[P5] The assurance-of-consideration standard tied to a single date is ambiguous for mailed comments; request explicit acceptance of comments postmarked by the deadline but received shortly after, or at minimum an exception for postal delays.

[P6] Requiring reference to file code CMS–5528–P on all submissions is reasonable, but the rule should state that failure to include the code will not automatically result in rejection and provide a mechanism to associate mis-coded comments with the record.

[P6] The rule should clarify where to place the file code in multi-page mailed submissions and whether it must appear in email subject lines or on attachments.

[P7] Posting all comments publicly, including PII and confidential business information (CBI), raises privacy and trade-secret concerns; request clear instructions and an easy process for submission of redacted public comments and separate confidential attachments with claim-of-confidentiality procedures.

[P7] The statement that PII and CBI will be visible to the public conflicts with federal privacy statutes and FOIA practices; ask CMS to adopt a process to flag and protect sensitive information and to provide commenters notice before public posting.

[P8] Posting comments "as soon as possible after receipt" is vague; request a specific timeframe (e.g., within 10 business days) and confirmation of posting so commenters can verify that their input is in the public docket.

[P8] CMS should commit to redacting obvious sensitive identifiers (SSNs, medical record numbers) before posting rather than posting raw submissions and then trying to address privacy concerns reactively.

[P9] The prohibition on posting comments that "make threats" is sensible, but the rule must define the standards CMS will use to determine what constitutes a threat and provide an appeals process for comments removed as threatening.

[P9] CMS should clarify whether comments that criticize institutions or propose strong enforcement actions (but do not contain explicit threats) could be mistakenly categorized as threats and removed; request clear examples and guardrails.

[P10] The request that individuals avoid submitting duplicate comments is reasonable, but given the value of mass comments to demonstrate public support, CMS should explicitly state how mass-submission campaigns will be treated and whether signature lists are acceptable.

[P10] The encouragement against duplicates conflicts with P11 which says identical comments from unique commenters will be posted; request harmonization and clarity so grassroots campaigns know their submissions will be accepted.

[P11] Committing to post acceptable comments from unique commenters even if content is identical is important for democratic participation, but CMS should define "acceptable" and explain how it will validate uniqueness to prevent fraudulent mass submissions and gaming.

[P11] The rule should state how CMS will handle thousands of identical comments in terms of docket usability (e.g., aggregation or tagging) so the public record remains navigable.

[P12] Requiring users to "follow the site's search instructions" to view comments is not sufficient guidance; CMS should include direct links and step-by-step instructions in the preamble and accommodate users unfamiliar with Regulations.gov.

[P12] Accessibility concerns: the search instructions on Regulations.gov must be accessible for users with disabilities; request CMS to confirm compliance with Section 508 and provide alternative ways to obtain comments (e.g., downloadable docket ZIP).

[P13] Requiring strict adherence to Regulations.gov "Submit a comment" instructions is acceptable, but CMS should list common errors and troubleshooting tips (e.g., attachment naming, character limits) and provide helpdesk contact information.

[P13] The rule should allow submission via email as a fallback when Regulations.gov is unavailable due to technical outages, with clear guidance on how such submissions will be handled and de-duplicated.

[P14] For commenters in states with known postal delays, this condition may be insufficient; suggest CMS accept electronic copies as supplemental evidence of timely mailed submissions.

[P15] Requiring commenters to choose only one submission method (duplicate of P1) may be unenforceable and inconsistent with commenters who want to preserve proof of submission; request explicit exception permitting simultaneous submission via an alternate method solely to confirm receipt.

[P15] The rule should clarify whether organizational submissions on behalf of multiple individuals count as one submission or multiple submissions and how the single-method rule applies in such cases.

[P17] Stakeholders should be assured that CMS will consider late-filed comments under exceptional circumstances; request CMS to adopt a formal procedure for accepting and documenting such requests.
