[P2][P13] Industry stakeholders will ask for assurances that Regulations.gov will accommodate submission of proprietary economic models and that CMS will accept encrypted attachments or a secure upload mechanism for sensitive business data.

[P9][P7] Legal commenters will ask CMS to reconcile the prohibition on posting threatening comments with First Amendment jurisprudence, ensuring removal standards are narrowly tailored and content-neutral.

[P3][P4] Non-profit and small-entity commenters will request acceptance of donations-paid courier services or pre-paid return envelopes to facilitate mailed submissions and avoid burdening low-resource stakeholders.

[P2][P8] Request that CMS implement an automatic confirmation email with a unique docket tracking number when comments are successfully uploaded, and that this confirmation be accepted as proof of filing.

raw_output:
[P1] The 30-boiler operating day initial performance test requirement is unreasonably burdensome for small and seasonal units that cannot operate continuously for 30 days; request an alternate shorter test period or allowance for combined multiple shorter tests.

[P1] Requiring 90 boiler operating days for Hg CEMS initial testing (where applicable) creates excessive delay and cost; propose allowing prior high-quality Hg test data (see P4) to satisfy the requirement when recent and representative.

[P2] Cross-referencing §63.10007 and Table 5 without clarifying which test methods prevail creates regulatory uncertainty; request insertion of an explicit prioritized list of acceptable methods for initial performance tests.

[P3] Allowing stack flow and moisture to be derived from data collected during Method 5/5D/6/26A/29 tests is helpful, but the provision should specify acceptable temporal alignment (e.g., concurrent sampling windows) to prevent bias from nonconcurrent measurements.

[P3] Industry commenters will request explicit guidance on how to adjust flow/moisture when stack conditions vary during the test (e.g., ramping loads), including averaging conventions and acceptable interpolation.

[P4] The option to use prior performance test data for initial compliance should be limited to tests conducted within a specified recent timeframe (e.g., 12 months) and under similar operating and fuel conditions; the rule as written lacks an explicit recency and representativeness requirement.

[P4] Environmental groups will object that allowing prior test data undermines the purpose of an initial performance test and could permit outdated data that underestimates current emissions; propose restricting prior-data use to cases with documented continuous controls and no fuel or equipment changes.

[P5] Requiring weighted average emissions rate calculations to include data from units that operated fewer than the averaging-period days may unfairly penalize peaking or backup units with atypical high emissions during limited operation; recommend allowing exclusion or separate treatment for rare-use units.

[P6] The requirement to use all data collected during boiler operating hours except for specific exclusions is reasonable, but the rule should clarify handling of intermittent missing data (e.g., brief telemetry outages) to avoid automated exceedances.

[P7] Excluding data during monitoring system malfunctions is appropriate, but the provision lacks a definition of "malfunction" and criteria for validating that the malfunction legitimately affected data quality; request a clear definition and documentation requirements.

[P8] Reporting monitoring system malfunctions as deviations in §63.10031(c)/(g) may create duplicative reporting burdens with existing CEMS QA reports; recommend harmonizing malfunction reporting formats and eliminating redundancy.

[P9] The out-of-control period exclusion in (h)(6)(ii) should be limited in duration and require pre-approval or prompt notification to EPA; otherwise sources might claim extended out-of-control periods to avoid compliance consequences.

[P10] Requiring reporting of out-of-control periods as deviations is appropriate, but the rule should specify the content and timing of such deviation reports (e.g., within 10 business days) to ensure timely corrective action.

[P11] Excluding data during QA/QC activities that temporarily interrupt PM CPMS measurement is reasonable, but the rule should require that the duration of such interruptions be minimized and recorded to prevent abuse.

[P12] Excluding startup and shutdown data from compliance assessment is necessary, but the proposal lacks clear, objective definitions of "startup" and "shutdown" durations for different unit types; recommend standardized presumptive durations or an alternative justification process.

[P13] Requiring recording and reporting of PM CPMS performance audit results per §63.10031(k) is appropriate; compliance entities request sample report templates to streamline submittals.

[P14] Making dates and durations of PM CPMS out-of-control periods available upon request is reasonable, but stakeholders urge that requests be limited to EPA and delegated authorities to protect confidential business information.

[P15] Allowing installation of PM CEMS to meet PM limits in lieu of metal HAP limits is attractive to industry; however, the provision should require demonstration that PM is a valid surrogate for the specific metal HAPs at affected units, or else environmental protections could be weakened.

[P16] Determining PM compliance on a 30-boiler operating day rolling average creates potential for short-term excursions being masked; environmental groups will argue for a shorter averaging period or an additional daily cap to prevent high short-term releases.

[P17] Requiring PM CEMS installation and certification per appendix C section 4 is reasonable, but stakeholders request clarity on acceptable vendors, certification timelines, and grandfathering of existing certified PM CEMS.

[P18] The operation, maintenance, and QA requirements in appendix C section 5 must allow for practical QA schedules (e.g., when outages prevent daily checks); request inclusion of contingency procedures for extended shutdowns.

[P19] Reducing PM CEMS data to hourly averages per section 6.1 may obscure sub-hour spikes; environmental advocates will request retention and reporting of higher-resolution (e.g., 1-minute) raw data for incidents.

[P20] The obligation to collect PM CEMS data whenever the unit operates, except for listed excluded periods, imposes continuous monitoring burden; small operators ask for a de minimis exemption for very small EGUs or during short-term maintenance.

[P21] Using all PM CEMS data from boiler operating hours to assess compliance means every transient counts; industry requests clear interpolation rules when data are missing or flagged during excluded activities.

[P22] Excluding data during monitoring system malfunctions for PM CEMS is necessary, but the rule should specify the acceptable documentation (repair logs, vendor reports) to substantiate the exclusion.

[P23] Requiring reporting of monitoring system malfunctions as deviations duplicates P8 concerns and increases paperwork; ask EPA to allow inclusion of malfunction details in routine QA/QC quarterly reports instead of separate deviation reports.

[P24] The out-of-control period exclusion for PM CEMS should require that corrective actions be completed within a specified timeframe (e.g., 30 days) or else data resume being counted; otherwise it could be used to evade compliance.

[P25] Excluding QA/QC and maintenance interruptions that temporarily interrupt emissions measurement must be tightly defined so routine preventive maintenance isn't exploited to mask high emissions.

[P26] Excluding startup/shutdown data for PM CEMS lacks specificity on what emission reporting is still required during those periods; request that operators still log emissions and operational parameters to allow EPA assessment of frequency/duration.

[P27] The recordkeeping and reporting requirements in section 7 of appendix C (P27) are extensive; operators request EPA provide standardized data schemas and an implementation timeline aligned with ECMPS capabilities.

[P28] Requiring operators to make PM CEMS out-of-control date/duration information available upon request indefinitely is a confidentiality concern; recommend retention for a defined period (e.g., 5 years) and protections for business-sensitive data.

[P29] Calculating 30-boiler operating day rolling averages in units of the applicable limit per appendix C 6.2.4 should include explicit rounding rules, handling of missing days, and treatment when boilers in a group have different duty cycles.

[P30] Requiring continuous collection of HAP metals CEMS data whenever the unit operates (P30) may be unattainable for some technologies; propose phasing in HAP metals CEMS requirements with alternative methods allowed during the transition.

[P31] Using all HAP metals CEMS data for compliance assessment (P31) without specifying how to handle detection limits and non-detects could bias results; request explicit treatment (e.g., substitute half MDL) and QA procedures.

[P32] The exclusion for monitoring malfunctions for HAP metals CEMS (P32) needs clear documentation standards and timelines for corrective actions to prevent prolonged unreportable data gaps.

[P33] Out-of-control exclusions for HAP metals CEMS (P33) should require pre-notification to EPA for prolonged out-of-control periods and a cap on allowable exclusion days per year.

[P34] Excluding QA/QC interruptions for HAP metals CEMS (P34) is fine if EPA requires logging of all QA/QC activities and demonstration that interruptions are necessary and limited in duration.

[P35] The startup/shutdown exclusion for HAP metals CEMS (P35) again raises the need for standardized definitions and reporting of the number, duration, and emissions during such periods (even if excluded from averages).

[P36] Recording and reporting HAP metals CEMS performance audits per §63.10031(k) (P36) should include prescriptive timing (annual, biennial) for audits to ensure consistency across sources.

[P37] Making HAP metals CEMS out-of-control periods available upon request (P37) raises confidentiality and administrative burden concerns; set a reasonable retention period and restrict requests to enforcement authorities.

[P38] The Notification of Compliance Status requirement to include initial compliance demonstration results (P38) is appropriate, but EPA should provide a checklist and electronic form fields to reduce inconsistent submissions.

[P39] Requiring reporting of emissions data recorded during startup and shutdown (P39) conflicts with the exclusions at P12/P26/P35; the rule should reconcile whether excluded data must still be reported for informational purposes.

[P40] For those relying on the alternative startup definition, requiring supplementary startup/shutdown information for incidents on/ before Dec 31, 2023 in semiannual reports (P40) imposes a retroactive paperwork burden; request an extension or simplified reporting for historical incidents.

[P41] Requiring quarterly PDF submission of startup/shutdown info for incidents on/after Jan 1, 2024 (P41) is burdensome; recommend allowing these reports to be included within the ECMPS XML quarterly report to avoid duplicate filing.

[P42] The pre-2024 requirement to report tune-up date electronically in semiannual PDF and in hard copy if requested (P42) is inconsistent and unclear; clarify when hard-copy submissions will be requested and whether electronic submission suffices by default.

[P43] On/after Jan 1, 2024 requiring tune-up dates in quarterly reports per ECMPS (P43) is acceptable, but operators need clear XML data element definitions and a grace period to implement ECMPS integration.

[P44] Defining the tune-up report date as the date when tune-up requirements are completed (P44) may be ambiguous for multi-step tune-ups; ask EPA to allow reporting of both start and completion dates and a brief checklist of completed tasks.

[P45] Mandating electronic submission using the ECMPS Client Tool (P45) could disadvantage smaller operators lacking IT resources; request alternate secure upload options or EPA-provided training and transitional support.

[P46] Extending deadlines that fall on weekends and federal holidays to the next business day (P46) is reasonable; request explicit definition of "business day" and confirmation that state holidays are not included.

[P47] Automatic deadline extension when ECMPS is offline (P47) is fair, but stakeholders ask EPA to publish real-time outage notices and maintain a public outage log to substantiate extensions.

[P48] Clarifying that ECMPS submissions satisfy related subpart A requirements (P48) is helpful; operators request explicit confirmation that state/local agencies will accept electronic submittals through ECMPS as well.

[P49] Requiring alternative-startup electing sources to include startup/shutdown reports in semiannual PDF for incidents on/ before Jan 1, 2024 (P49) duplicates P40 and should be harmonized to avoid double reporting.

[P50] For incidents on/after Jan 1, 2024 requiring quarterly PDF submission of startup/shutdown info via ECMPS (P50) duplicates P41 and creates uncertainty; request consolidation into a single ECMPS data flow.

[P51] The Notification of Compliance Status must include all applicable information (P51); industry asks EPA to publish a standard NOCS template mapping each (e)(1)-(8) element to ECMPS fields.

[P52] Requiring identification for each existing EGU of which Table 2 emissions limit you plan to comply with initially (P52) could lock operators into suboptimal choices; request ability to change choice without onerous justification, provided recent testing demonstrates compliance.

[P53] The note allowing switching emission limits after initial notification but imposing procedures and conditions (P53) seems overly restrictive; operators want a streamlined, transparent process with a clear timeline for approvals.

[P54] The 45-day requirement to include performance stack test results or valid CMS data obtained within 45 days prior to a switch request (P54) is impractical for scheduling tests and obtaining results; propose extending to 90 days or allowing existing continuous CMS data with QA flags to qualify.

[P55] The catch-all obligation to submit each applicable report in §63.10031 (P55) should be accompanied by a consolidated reporting calendar and example sequences to help compliance planning.

[P56] Requiring electronic reporting of continuous Hg monitoring per appendix A (P56) is appropriate; request EPA to provide guidance on acceptable Hg CEMS vendors and data format validation rules.

[P57] Mandating electronic reporting for continuous HCl/HF monitoring per appendix B (P57) is reasonable, but HCl monitors have known interferences—EPA should allow validated alternative monitoring technologies and provide clear QA acceptance criteria.

[P58] The transitional provision for HCl monitors certified per Performance Specification 18 (P58) that delays some reporting until 2024 is helpful, but operators need a clear list of which records are required now versus later and a timeline for retaining the QA records.

[P59] For PM continuous monitoring, starting electronic reporting at the later of Jan 1, 2024 or after initial correlation test completion (P59) could create split reporting periods; request transitional guidance and examples to ensure correct quarter assignment.

[P60] For PM CPMS, beginning electronic reporting at the later of Jan 1, 2024 or after initial stack test (P60) similarly needs clarity on handling data collected before the reporting start date and whether that data must be submitted.

[P61] If monitoring SO2 as an HCl surrogate (P61), the requirement to use ECMPS for all plan and QA data is appropriate, but the surrogate approach must require site-specific validation and periodic re-evaluation to ensure SO2 remains a valid surrogate.

[P62] The requirement to submit monitoring plan information for SO2 CEMS and additional monitors (P62) should specify what constitutes "additional monitors" and provide templates for the conversions to standard units.

[P63] Submitting certification, recertification, QA, and diagnostic test results per §75.64(a)(5) (P63) may create duplication with Acid Rain Program reporting; request EPA coordinate to accept existing §75 submissions in lieu of duplicate submissions where applicable.

[P64] The quarterly electronic report timing requirement (P64) to submit within 30 days after each quarter could be burdensome; request alignment with standard ECMPS 60-day windows used elsewhere in Part 63 to reduce administrative complexity.

[P65] Including operating data specified in §75.57(b) (P65) in quarterly reports duplicates Part 75 obligations for units already reporting under Acid Rain/CSAPR; EPA should accept cross-referenced Part 75 submissions rather than requiring duplicate data entry.

[P66] Requiring hourly unadjusted SO2 concentration streams rounded to one decimal (P66) may conflict with CEMS native resolution; request tolerances for rounding and clear guidance on conversion methods.

[P67] The hourly SO2 emission rate data stream in lb/MMBtu or lb/MWh (P67) calculated per §63.10007(e) needs a clear algorithm and allowed default heat content values to avoid inconsistent calculations between sources.

[P68] Including results of all required daily QA tests for SO2 monitor (P68) will generate large datasets; operators request that daily QA pass/fail summaries be allowed instead of full datasets when daily values show no anomalies.

[P69] The signed compliance certification by a responsible official (P69) should allow electronically authenticated signatures and designate responsible official roles more flexibly for corporate entities.

[P70] The semiannual compliance report obligation (P70) is clear; stakeholders request consolidated reporting for groups of EGUs under common control to reduce administrative burdens.

[P71] The first compliance report period timing (P71) is complex and may be confusing for sources with varied compliance dates; EPA should provide an automated tool or flowchart to determine exact reporting periods.

[P72] The deadline to submit the first compliance report electronically by July 31 or Jan 31 (P72) could create confusion across time zones and receipt dates; clarify that EPA receipt date determines timeliness.

[P73] Subsequent semiannual report deadlines at July 31/Jan 31 (P73) may conflict with state reporting schedules; request harmonization with state deadlines to avoid multiple parallel filings.

[P74] Transitioning from semiannual reports ending Dec 31, 2023 to quarterly reports starting Q1 2024 (P74) imposes a significant early-2024 reporting surge; EPA should phase in the quarterly reporting or provide extended deadlines for the initial quarter.

[P75] The contents required in semiannual compliance reports (P75) are extensive; request sample report templates and a machine-readable XML schema to ensure consistent submissions.

[P76] Requiring inclusion of malfunction number, duration, and brief description when malfunctions may have caused exceedances (P76) is appropriate, but EPA should limit "brief description" to a standardized code list to reduce subjectivity.

[P77] The change in reporting content for CMS-reliant EGUs (P77) — ceasing excess emissions/downtime summary in 2024 and moving to appendix E elements for deviations — may be confusing; request a side-by-side mapping of old to new reporting elements.

[P78] Title V permit holders must report all deviations in the semiannual monitoring report (P78); operators request clarity on whether ECMPS quarterly reports satisfy Title V reporting requirements and whether state authorities will accept ECMPS uploads.

[P79] The requirement to submit PDF test reports for performance stack tests completed before Jan 1, 2024 within 60 days (P79) may be impossible for historical tests; request grandfathering of previously submitted tests or extended deadlines for older tests.

[P80] The RATA/RRA/RCA/correlation test PDF submission timing (P80) is complex; propose harmonizing all test-report submission deadlines to one uniform period (e.g., 60 days after test completion) regardless of date.

[P81] Quarterly PDF reporting of 30-boiler rolling averages through Q4 2023, then integrating into quarterly reports after Q1 2024 (P81), creates dual-reporting windows; request EPA provide clear examples and machine-readable templates for transition quarters.

[P82] The requirement to submit semiannual compliance reports and Notifications of Compliance Status as PDFs through Dec 31, 2023 and switch to XML in 2024 (P82) imposes a technology transition that will require training and validation; ask EPA for a six-month voluntary pilot before mandatory XML.

[P83] The overarching requirement to submit all specified reports via ECMPS in required formats (P83) is administratively heavy; small sources request temporary exemptions or assistance, and vendors request sample ECMPS test accounts for integration.

[P84] Requiring entry of PDF report type into ECMPS at submission (P84) is a minor administrative burden but needs clear dropdown options and validation rules to avoid rejected submissions for clerical errors.

[P85] Entering performance test completion date and test number into ECMPS with PDF submission (P85) should allow retrospective entry for tests completed before ECMPS integration, with documentation to avoid penalizing early testers.

[P86] Starting mandatory ECMPS quarterly electronic compliance reports in Q1 2024 with 60-day submission windows (P86) is aggressive; recommend aligning with established ECMPS quarterly reporting cycles and providing a built-in 30-day grace period during the first year.

[P87] On/after Jan 1, 2024 initial Notifications of Compliance Status submitted as PDF via ECMPS with specific data elements entered (P87) duplicates prior concerns about transition and requests for templates and validation tools.

[P88] The alternative startup definition reporting requirements (P88) across two time periods add complexity; recommend consolidating startup/shutdown reporting rules into a single coherent schedule applicable to all electing sources.

[P89] The PM CEMS correlation test submission requirements (P89) with varying timing based on when data were recorded create confusing cutoffs; request EPA to allow correlation reports to be submitted within 60 days of test completion uniformly, independent of other dates.

[P90] Quarterly PDF QA/QC activity reports for PM CPMS or HAP metals CEMS beginning Q1 2024 (P90) may duplicate appendix-specific electronic reporting; request consolidation of QA/QC reporting into the same ECMPS quarterly submission to minimize duplication.

[P91] The extensive recordkeeping obligations (P91) that require appendix-specific records, §63.7(g) elements, and appendix E elements will impose high storage and retrieval costs; stakeholders request a minimum retention period and allowance for electronic storage with searchable metadata.

[P92] The specific recordkeeping requirement to keep copies of each notification/report and supporting initial compliance documentation (P92) is reasonable but should allow electronic copies and permit confidential business information redaction when appropriate.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The 30-boiler operating day initial performance test requirement is unreasonably burdensome for small and seasonal units that cannot operate continuously for 30 days; request an alternate shorter test period or allowance for combined multiple shorter tests.

Requiring 90 boiler operating days for Hg CEMS initial testing (where applicable) creates excessive delay and cost; propose allowing prior high-quality Hg test data (see P4) to satisfy the requirement when recent and representative.

Cross-referencing §63.10007 and Table 5 without clarifying which test methods prevail creates regulatory uncertainty; request insertion of an explicit prioritized list of acceptable methods for initial performance tests.

Allowing stack flow and moisture to be derived from data collected during Method 5/5D/6/26A/29 tests is helpful, but the provision should specify acceptable temporal alignment (e.g., concurrent sampling windows) to prevent bias from nonconcurrent measurements.

Industry commenters will request explicit guidance on how to adjust flow/moisture when stack conditions vary during the test (e.g., ramping loads), including averaging conventions and acceptable interpolation.

The option to use prior performance test data for initial compliance should be limited to tests conducted within a specified recent timeframe (e.g., 12 months) and under similar operating and fuel conditions; the rule as written lacks an explicit recency and representativeness requirement.

Environmental groups will object that allowing prior test data undermines the purpose of an initial performance test and could permit outdated data that underestimates current emissions; propose restricting prior-data use to cases with documented continuous controls and no fuel or equipment changes.

Requiring weighted average emissions rate calculations to include data from units that operated fewer than the averaging-period days may unfairly penalize peaking or backup units with atypical high emissions during limited operation; recommend allowing exclusion or separate treatment for rare-use units.

The requirement to use all data collected during boiler operating hours except for specific exclusions is reasonable, but the rule should clarify handling of intermittent missing data (e.g., brief telemetry outages) to avoid automated exceedances.

Excluding data during monitoring system malfunctions is appropriate, but the provision lacks a definition of "malfunction" and criteria for validating that the malfunction legitimately affected data quality; request a clear definition and documentation requirements.

Reporting monitoring system malfunctions as deviations in §63.10031(c)/(g) may create duplicative reporting burdens with existing CEMS QA reports; recommend harmonizing malfunction reporting formats and eliminating redundancy.

The out-of-control period exclusion in (h)(6)(ii) should be limited in duration and require pre-approval or prompt notification to EPA; otherwise sources might claim extended out-of-control periods to avoid compliance consequences.

Requiring reporting of out-of-control periods as deviations is appropriate, but the rule should specify the content and timing of such deviation reports (e.g., within 10 business days) to ensure timely corrective action.

Excluding data during QA/QC activities that temporarily interrupt PM CPMS measurement is reasonable, but the rule should require that the duration of such interruptions be minimized and recorded to prevent abuse.

Excluding startup and shutdown data from compliance assessment is necessary, but the proposal lacks clear, objective definitions of "startup" and "shutdown" durations for different unit types; recommend standardized presumptive durations or an alternative justification process.
Requiring recording and reporting of PM CPMS performance audit results per §63.10031(k) is appropriate; compliance entities request sample report templates to streamline submittals.

Making dates and durations of PM CPMS out-of-control periods available upon request is reasonable, but stakeholders urge that requests be limited to EPA and delegated authorities to protect confidential business information.

Allowing installation of PM CEMS to meet PM limits in lieu of metal HAP limits is attractive to industry; however, the provision should require demonstration that PM is a valid surrogate for the specific metal HAPs at affected units, or else environmental protections could be weakened.

Determining PM compliance on a 30-boiler operating day rolling average creates potential for short-term excursions being masked; environmental groups will argue for a shorter averaging period or an additional daily cap to prevent high short-term releases.

Requiring PM CEMS installation and certification per appendix C section 4 is reasonable, but stakeholders request clarity on acceptable vendors, certification timelines, and grandfathering of existing certified PM CEMS.

The operation, maintenance, and QA requirements in appendix C section 5 must allow for practical QA schedules (e.g., when outages prevent daily checks); request inclusion of contingency procedures for extended shutdowns.

Reducing PM CEMS data to hourly averages per section 6.1 may obscure sub-hour spikes; environmental advocates will request retention and reporting of higher-resolution (e.g., 1-minute) raw data for incidents.

The obligation to collect PM CEMS data whenever the unit operates, except for listed excluded periods, imposes continuous monitoring burden; small operators ask for a de minimis exemption for very small EGUs or during short-term maintenance.

Using all PM CEMS data from boiler operating hours to assess compliance means every transient counts; industry requests clear interpolation rules when data are missing or flagged during excluded activities.
Excluding data during monitoring system malfunctions for PM CEMS is necessary, but the rule should specify the acceptable documentation (repair logs, vendor reports) to substantiate the exclusion.

Requiring reporting of monitoring system malfunctions as deviations duplicates P8 concerns and increases paperwork; ask EPA to allow inclusion of malfunction details in routine QA/QC quarterly reports instead of separate deviation reports.

The out-of-control period exclusion for PM CEMS should require that corrective actions be completed within a specified timeframe (e.g., 30 days) or else data resume being counted; otherwise it could be used to evade compliance.
Excluding QA/QC and maintenance interruptions that temporarily interrupt emissions measurement must be tightly defined so routine preventive maintenance isn't exploited to mask high emissions.

Excluding startup/shutdown data for PM CEMS lacks specificity on what emission reporting is still required during those periods; request that operators still log emissions and operational parameters to allow EPA assessment of frequency/duration.

The recordkeeping and reporting requirements in section 7 of appendix C (P27) are extensive; operators request EPA provide standardized data schemas and an implementation timeline aligned with ECMPS capabilities.

Requiring operators to make PM CEMS out-of-control date/duration information available upon request indefinitely is a confidentiality concern; recommend retention for a defined period (e.g., 5 years) and protections for business-sensitive data.

Calculating 30-boiler operating day rolling averages in units of the applicable limit per appendix C 6.2.4 should include explicit rounding rules, handling of missing days, and treatment when boilers in a group have different duty cycles.

Requiring continuous collection of HAP metals CEMS data whenever the unit operates (P30) may be unattainable for some technologies; propose phasing in HAP metals CEMS requirements with alternative methods allowed during the transition.

Using all HAP metals CEMS data for compliance assessment (P31) without specifying how to handle detection limits and non-detects could bias results; request explicit treatment (e.g., substitute half MDL) and QA procedures.
The exclusion for monitoring malfunctions for HAP metals CEMS (P32) needs clear documentation standards and timelines for corrective actions to prevent prolonged unreportable data gaps.
Out-of-control exclusions for HAP metals CEMS (P33) should require pre-notification to EPA for prolonged out-of-control periods and a cap on allowable exclusion days per year.
Excluding QA/QC interruptions for HAP metals CEMS (P34) is fine if EPA requires logging of all QA/QC activities and demonstration that interruptions are necessary and limited in duration.

The startup/shutdown exclusion for HAP metals CEMS (P35) again raises the need for standardized definitions and reporting of the number, duration, and emissions during such periods (even if excluded from averages).
Recording and reporting HAP metals CEMS performance audits per §63.10031(k) (P36) should include prescriptive timing (annual, biennial) for audits to ensure consistency across sources.

Making HAP metals CEMS out-of-control periods available upon request (P37) raises confidentiality and administrative burden concerns; set a reasonable retention period and restrict requests to enforcement authorities.

The Notification of Compliance Status requirement to include initial compliance demonstration results (P38) is appropriate, but EPA should provide a checklist and electronic form fields to reduce inconsistent submissions.

Requiring reporting of emissions data recorded during startup and shutdown (P39) conflicts with the exclusions at P12/P26/P35; the rule should reconcile whether excluded data must still be reported for informational purposes.

For those relying on the alternative startup definition, requiring supplementary startup/shutdown information for incidents on/ before Dec 31, 2023 in semiannual reports (P40) imposes a retroactive paperwork burden; request an extension or simplified reporting for historical incidents.

Requiring quarterly PDF submission of startup/shutdown info for incidents on/after Jan 1, 2024 (P41) is burdensome; recommend allowing these reports to be included within the ECMPS XML quarterly report to avoid duplicate filing.

The pre-2024 requirement to report tune-up date electronically in semiannual PDF and in hard copy if requested (P42) is inconsistent and unclear; clarify when hard-copy submissions will be requested and whether electronic submission suffices by default.

On/after Jan 1, 2024 requiring tune-up dates in quarterly reports per ECMPS (P43) is acceptable, but operators need clear XML data element definitions and a grace period to implement ECMPS integration.

Defining the tune-up report date as the date when tune-up requirements are completed (P44) may be ambiguous for multi-step tune-ups; ask EPA to allow reporting of both start and completion dates and a brief checklist of completed tasks.

Mandating electronic submission using the ECMPS Client Tool (P45) could disadvantage smaller operators lacking IT resources; request alternate secure upload options or EPA-provided training and transitional support.

Extending deadlines that fall on weekends and federal holidays to the next business day (P46) is reasonable; request explicit definition of "business day" and confirmation that state holidays are not included.
Automatic deadline extension when ECMPS is offline (P47) is fair, but stakeholders ask EPA to publish real-time outage notices and maintain a public outage log to substantiate extensions.

Clarifying that ECMPS submissions satisfy related subpart A requirements (P48) is helpful; operators request explicit confirmation that state/local agencies will accept electronic submittals through ECMPS as well.

Requiring alternative-startup electing sources to include startup/shutdown reports in semiannual PDF for incidents on/ before Jan 1, 2024 (P49) duplicates P40 and should be harmonized to avoid double reporting.

For incidents on/after Jan 1, 2024 requiring quarterly PDF submission of startup/shutdown info via ECMPS (P50) duplicates P41 and creates uncertainty; request consolidation into a single ECMPS data flow.
The Notification of Compliance Status must include all applicable information (P51); industry asks EPA to publish a standard NOCS template mapping each (e)(1)-(8) element to ECMPS fields.

Requiring identification for each existing EGU of which Table 2 emissions limit you plan to comply with initially (P52) could lock operators into suboptimal choices; request ability to change choice without onerous justification, provided recent testing demonstrates compliance.

The note allowing switching emission limits after initial notification but imposing procedures and conditions (P53) seems overly restrictive; operators want a streamlined, transparent process with a clear timeline for approvals.

The 45-day requirement to include performance stack test results or valid CMS data obtained within 45 days prior to a switch request (P54) is impractical for scheduling tests and obtaining results; propose extending to 90 days or allowing existing continuous CMS data with QA flags to qualify.
The catch-all obligation to submit each applicable report in §63.10031 (P55) should be accompanied by a consolidated reporting calendar and example sequences to help compliance planning.
Requiring electronic reporting of continuous Hg monitoring per appendix A (P56) is appropriate; request EPA to provide guidance on acceptable Hg CEMS vendors and data format validation rules.

Mandating electronic reporting for continuous HCl/HF monitoring per appendix B (P57) is reasonable, but HCl monitors have known interferences—EPA should allow validated alternative monitoring technologies and provide clear QA acceptance criteria.

The transitional provision for HCl monitors certified per Performance Specification 18 (P58) that delays some reporting until 2024 is helpful, but operators need a clear list of which records are required now versus later and a timeline for retaining the QA records.

For PM continuous monitoring, starting electronic reporting at the later of Jan 1, 2024 or after initial correlation test completion (P59) could create split reporting periods; request transitional guidance and examples to ensure correct quarter assignment.

For PM CPMS, beginning electronic reporting at the later of Jan 1, 2024 or after initial stack test (P60) similarly needs clarity on handling data collected before the reporting start date and whether that data must be submitted.

If monitoring SO2 as an HCl surrogate (P61), the requirement to use ECMPS for all plan and QA data is appropriate, but the surrogate approach must require site-specific validation and periodic re-evaluation to ensure SO2 remains a valid surrogate.

The requirement to submit monitoring plan information for SO2 CEMS and additional monitors (P62) should specify what constitutes "additional monitors" and provide templates for the conversions to standard units.

Submitting certification, recertification, QA, and diagnostic test results per §75.64(a)(5) (P63) may create duplication with Acid Rain Program reporting; request EPA coordinate to accept existing §75 submissions in lieu of duplicate submissions where applicable.

The quarterly electronic report timing requirement (P64) to submit within 30 days after each quarter could be burdensome; request alignment with standard ECMPS 60-day windows used elsewhere in Part 63 to reduce administrative complexity.

Including operating data specified in §75.57(b) (P65) in quarterly reports duplicates Part 75 obligations for units already reporting under Acid Rain/CSAPR; EPA should accept cross-referenced Part 75 submissions rather than requiring duplicate data entry.
Requiring hourly unadjusted SO2 concentration streams rounded to one decimal (P66) may conflict with CEMS native resolution; request tolerances for rounding and clear guidance on conversion methods.

The hourly SO2 emission rate data stream in lb/MMBtu or lb/MWh (P67) calculated per §63.10007(e) needs a clear algorithm and allowed default heat content values to avoid inconsistent calculations between sources.

Including results of all required daily QA tests for SO2 monitor (P68) will generate large datasets; operators request that daily QA pass/fail summaries be allowed instead of full datasets when daily values show no anomalies.
The signed compliance certification by a responsible official (P69) should allow electronically authenticated signatures and designate responsible official roles more flexibly for corporate entities.
The semiannual compliance report obligation (P70) is clear; stakeholders request consolidated reporting for groups of EGUs under common control to reduce administrative burdens.

The first compliance report period timing (P71) is complex and may be confusing for sources with varied compliance dates; EPA should provide an automated tool or flowchart to determine exact reporting periods.

The deadline to submit the first compliance report electronically by July 31 or Jan 31 (P72) could create confusion across time zones and receipt dates; clarify that EPA receipt date determines timeliness.
Subsequent semiannual report deadlines at July 31/Jan 31 (P73) may conflict with state reporting schedules; request harmonization with state deadlines to avoid multiple parallel filings.

Transitioning from semiannual reports ending Dec 31, 2023 to quarterly reports starting Q1 2024 (P74) imposes a significant early-2024 reporting surge; EPA should phase in the quarterly reporting or provide extended deadlines for the initial quarter.
The contents required in semiannual compliance reports (P75) are extensive; request sample report templates and a machine-readable XML schema to ensure consistent submissions.

Requiring inclusion of malfunction number, duration, and brief description when malfunctions may have caused exceedances (P76) is appropriate, but EPA should limit "brief description" to a standardized code list to reduce subjectivity.

The change in reporting content for CMS-reliant EGUs (P77) — ceasing excess emissions/downtime summary in 2024 and moving to appendix E elements for deviations — may be confusing; request a side-by-side mapping of old to new reporting elements.

Title V permit holders must report all deviations in the semiannual monitoring report (P78); operators request clarity on whether ECMPS quarterly reports satisfy Title V reporting requirements and whether state authorities will accept ECMPS uploads.

The requirement to submit PDF test reports for performance stack tests completed before Jan 1, 2024 within 60 days (P79) may be impossible for historical tests; request grandfathering of previously submitted tests or extended deadlines for older tests.

The RATA/RRA/RCA/correlation test PDF submission timing (P80) is complex; propose harmonizing all test-report submission deadlines to one uniform period (e.g., 60 days after test completion) regardless of date.

Quarterly PDF reporting of 30-boiler rolling averages through Q4 2023, then integrating into quarterly reports after Q1 2024 (P81), creates dual-reporting windows; request EPA provide clear examples and machine-readable templates for transition quarters.

The requirement to submit semiannual compliance reports and Notifications of Compliance Status as PDFs through Dec 31, 2023 and switch to XML in 2024 (P82) imposes a technology transition that will require training and validation; ask EPA for a six-month voluntary pilot before mandatory XML.

The overarching requirement to submit all specified reports via ECMPS in required formats (P83) is administratively heavy; small sources request temporary exemptions or assistance, and vendors request sample ECMPS test accounts for integration.

Requiring entry of PDF report type into ECMPS at submission (P84) is a minor administrative burden but needs clear dropdown options and validation rules to avoid rejected submissions for clerical errors.

Entering performance test completion date and test number into ECMPS with PDF submission (P85) should allow retrospective entry for tests completed before ECMPS integration, with documentation to avoid penalizing early testers.

Starting mandatory ECMPS quarterly electronic compliance reports in Q1 2024 with 60-day submission windows (P86) is aggressive; recommend aligning with established ECMPS quarterly reporting cycles and providing a built-in 30-day grace period during the first year.

On/after Jan 1, 2024 initial Notifications of Compliance Status submitted as PDF via ECMPS with specific data elements entered (P87) duplicates prior concerns about transition and requests for templates and validation tools.

The alternative startup definition reporting requirements (P88) across two time periods add complexity; recommend consolidating startup/shutdown reporting rules into a single coherent schedule applicable to all electing sources.

The PM CEMS correlation test submission requirements (P89) with varying timing based on when data were recorded create confusing cutoffs; request EPA to allow correlation reports to be submitted within 60 days of test completion uniformly, independent of other dates.

Quarterly PDF QA/QC activity reports for PM CPMS or HAP metals CEMS beginning Q1 2024 (P90) may duplicate appendix-specific electronic reporting; request consolidation of QA/QC reporting into the same ECMPS quarterly submission to minimize duplication.

The extensive recordkeeping obligations (P91) that require appendix-specific records, §63.7(g) elements, and appendix E elements will impose high storage and retrieval costs; stakeholders request a minimum retention period and allowance for electronic storage with searchable metadata.

The specific recordkeeping requirement to keep copies of each notification/report and supporting initial compliance documentation (P92) is reasonable but should allow electronic copies and permit confidential business information redaction when appropriate.

raw_output:
[P1] The January 23, 2023 deadline for submitting comments is unreasonably short and does not provide stakeholders sufficient time to analyze the technical service bulletin and operational impacts; the FAA should extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] The AD's comments due date does not account for holiday-season staffing and industry slow-down; the agency should reopen the comment period or accept late comments received shortly after January 23, 2023.

[P2] The requirement to "comply within the specified compliance times" is vague because the AD references multiple compliance time rows in the Boeing bulletin; the FAA should clearly restate each compliance time in the AD itself to avoid ambiguity.

[P2] There is no mechanism described for what constitutes "already accomplished" work for compliance credit; the AD should define acceptable prior actions and recordkeeping to demonstrate prior compliance.

[P3] Requiring installation "in accordance with the Accomplishment Instructions of Boeing Requirements Bulletin 767–25–0589 RB" without incorporating the full necessary details into the AD risks ambiguity if Boeing issues revisions; the FAA should incorporate the exact task steps and any critical part numbers into the regulatory text.

[P3] The AD relies entirely on Boeing Requirements Bulletin 767–25–0589 RB for placard installation actions; operators request that the FAA clarify whether any deviations in the bulletin's figures or part numbers are acceptable and how to request relief.

[P4] Substituting the AD effective date for the bulletin's "original issue date" could unintentionally shorten or lengthen compliance windows for some fleets; the FAA must explain the rationale and provide examples of how the substitution affects compliance times.

[P4] The exception in paragraph (h) could create inconsistencies for operators who already complied to dates referenced to the bulletin issue date; the FAA should allow operators to elect which date basis they used when documenting prior compliance.

[P5] Requiring AFM Section 3.1 revision "within 12 months" is too long for safety-critical procedure updates that affect occupant briefing before pushback or engine start; safety advocates urge a shorter compliance time (e.g., 90 days).

[P5] Conversely, some operators state that 12 months is too short given scheduling constraints for large fleets and request a compliance extension to 24 months or allow staged compliance tied to scheduled maintenance checks.

[P6] Allowing insertion of a copy of figure 1 into the AFM as an alternative is acceptable, but the AD must specify formatting and permanence requirements (e.g., approved change pages, revision logs) so airlines maintain compliant and auditable AFM documentation.

[P6] Clarify whether inserting figure 1 as a placard or temporary page requires approval from the operator's AWO/CM or whether a simple administrative AFM amendment suffices.

[P7] Delegating AMOC approval authority to the Seattle ACO Branch Manager is standard, but operators outside that geographic area request clear guidance on timeline expectations for AMOC review and decisions.

[P7] Legal commenters request that the AD specify whether the Manager's AMOC approvals can be issued with conditions, and whether such conditional approvals are binding across all operators.

[P8] Requiring AMOC requests to follow 14 CFR 39.19 is appropriate, but the AD should restate the specific documentation and substantiation elements expected to speed consistent review and avoid unnecessary back-and-forth.

[P9] The instruction to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or responsible Flight Standards Office lacks clarity for foreign operators or leased aircraft; the FAA should add guidance for non-U.S. operators on the proper submission channel.

[P10] Direct submission to the certification office manager per paragraph (k) is contingent on paragraph (k) identification, but paragraph (k) is not reproduced in the AD preamble; include full contact name/role to avoid misdirected requests.

[P11] Allowing email submission of AMOC requests to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is helpful, but parties are concerned about sensitive proprietary attachments transmitted by email; the FAA should provide secure upload instructions for large or confidential files.

[P12] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC is burdensome when operators have no assigned principal inspector; the AD partially addresses this by mentioning the Flight Standards Office manager, but operators request a clear standardized notification template and allowable lead time for notification.

[P12] Clarify whether the notification requirement is procedural only or whether failure to notify prior to use would constitute noncompliance subject to enforcement action.

[P13] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to be used is efficient, but independent repair stations and third-party design approval holders object to perceived favoritism and request parity: the AD should enable AMOCs approved by other authorized DER/ODA organizations, subject to equivalent substantiation.

[P14] Requiring that AMOC deviations “meet the certification basis of the airplane” is a high-level standard but ambiguous in practice for older 767 variants with differing certification bases; the FAA should describe how to handle differences among Model subtypes and amended certification bases.

[P15] Mandating that AMOC approvals "specifically refer to this AD" is reasonable, but legal commenters recommend standard wording or citation format to avoid administrative errors that could invalidate AMOC applicability.

[P16] Mandating use of identified Boeing service information "unless the AD specifies otherwise" risks locking in OEM procedures that may become obsolete; commenters request a process for timely revision of incorporated-by-reference documents and explicit allowance for later-released revised Boeing bulletins if they provide equal or greater safety.

[P16] Operators ask the FAA to clarify whether operators may use later-revised versions of the Boeing Requirements Bulletin without first obtaining an AMOC, and if not, what expedited path exists to approve newer revisions.

[P17] Providing viewing access at the FAA Des Moines office is necessary, but many stakeholders (including international operators) request that the FAA post the full incorporated service information publicly online or provide a direct link to reduce travel/administrative burden.

[P18] The FAA phone number for availability inquiries (206–231–3195) is given, but commenters request an email contact and online ordering instructions for the incorporated materials and hours of operation.

[P19] Allowing viewing at NARA is useful for record-keeping, but the National Archives access procedures are slow; stakeholders request that the FAA additionally make the materials available via eCFR or the regulations.gov docket.

[P20] Requiring briefings of non-flight-crew occupants prior to pushback/engine start on seat positions for taxi/takeoff/landing imposes additional workload on flightcrew and ramp staff; operators request clarification about who is the "appropriate flight crew member" and whether ground personnel (e.g., loadmasters) may conduct the briefings for freighter operations.

[P20] The AFM figure 1 occupant briefing requirement could conflict with existing company SOPs and labor agreements concerning who conducts pre-pushback briefings; carriers ask the FAA to allow delegation to appropriately qualified non-flight crew (e.g., loadmasters) and to specify minimum training.

[P20] Safety advocates support the occupant briefing requirement but ask the FAA to mandate that placards be installed in freighter cabins corresponding to the AFM guidance and to require a standard wording for the brief to ensure consistency across operators.

[P20] Private owners and small freighter operators request clarification regarding applicability: whether the occupant briefing and AFM revision requirements apply to all 767 freighter variants including private/corporate freighters, and whether relief exists for aircraft with permanently reconfigured cabins.

General/Legal

[P3/P16] Legal commenters note that the AD cites Boeing special procedures and incorporates them by reference but does not include those documents in the docket; the FAA should ensure full public availability of the service bulletin and any referenced figures at the time of final rule to satisfy notice-and-comment obligations.

[P5/P6/P20] Labor and safety unions request consultation on the AFM revision text and the occupant briefing content to ensure the new duties do not create unsafe single-person workload spikes during critical phases (e.g., pushback).

[P11/P17] International operators request confirmation that emailed AMOC submissions and viewing at FAA offices satisfy foreign data-protection requirements and that FAA acceptance of electronic submissions is equivalent to signed originals for compliance purposes.

[P13/P14] Maintenance/repair industry stakeholders request clear criteria for Boeing ODA approvals to be accepted without independent FAA review, and ask for transparency into the ODA approval records to ensure consistent safety determinations.

[P1/P2] Small operators with limited administrative staff request staggered compliance/reporting deadlines and an exemption pathway or fee relief for administrative burdens associated with AMOC requests and AFM revisions.

raw_output:
[P1] The permission to change an IPF unit's exclusion status "at any time during a cost reporting period" lacks limits and could encourage frequent status changes purely to manipulate reimbursement; CMS should add a minimum interval between changes (e.g., one year) or require substantive justification to prevent gaming.

[P2] The 30-day written notice requirement to the fiscal intermediary and CMS Regional Office is administratively burdensome for hospitals that operate multiple IPF units and may be inadequate to effectuate system changes; CMS should allow electronic/expedited notice and clarify acceptable methods of delivery.

[P3] The rule's requirement to "maintain the information needed to accurately determine costs" is vague—hospitals need explicit recordkeeping standards (which cost elements, allocation methods, retention periods) to ensure compliance and consistent audits.

[P4] Requiring that a status change remain effective for the remainder of the cost reporting period could unfairly trap hospitals that discover an error shortly after a change; CMS should permit rescission within a short corrective window (e.g., 14 days) when the change was inadvertent and corrected documentation is provided.

[P5] The proposed 2.0 percentage-point reduction to the annual update for failing to submit required quality data is disproportionate for small IPFs and could threaten financial viability; CMS should adopt a scaled penalty based on IPF size or the degree/duration of noncompliance.

[P6] CMS should clarify whether the 2.0 percentage-point reduction applies per measure, per reporting period, or only once per year—ambiguity will create uncertainty in financial forecasting and enforcement.

[P7] The obligation to register on QualityNet before reporting (b)(1) should include transitional provisions and technical support timelines; smaller IPFs may not have the IT capacity to register quickly and will need onboarding assistance.

[P8] The requirement to identify and register a QualityNet security official (b)(2) does not address staffing burden or qualifications; CMS should allow designation of an external vendor or shared security official across hospital networks.

[P9] The Notice of Participation (NOP) mechanism (b)(3) must permit bulk or network-level NOP filings for hospital systems that operate multiple IPFs to reduce administrative duplication.

[P10] Allowing withdrawal from the IPFQR Program via QualityNet up to August 15 (c) could incentivize late withdrawals to avoid public reporting while still reaping program benefits early in the fiscal year; CMS should require advance notice (e.g., by June 30) or require a minimum participation period.

[P11] The condition that a withdrawn IPF will have its annual payment update reduced (c) needs specification of the effective year and the calculation method; commenters request an illustrative example showing how the penalty is computed and applied.

[P12] Requiring a withdrawn IPF to re-register and meet all (b) obligations to participate in future years (c) imposes redundancy; CMS should allow a streamlined re-enrollment process for recent participants to limit administrative costs.

[P13] The requirement in (d) that data be submitted "in the form, manner, and at the time specified by CMS" is overly open-ended—stakeholders request publication of the form/manner/time specifications at least 180 days before the reporting period with machine-readable technical specifications.

[P14] The exceptions in paragraph (f) are too discretionary; hospitals need a clear, objective standard and timeline for CMS responses to exception requests, including appeal rights if an exception is denied.

[P15] Examples of extraordinary circumstances (f)(2) should explicitly include cyberattacks, vendor outages, and public health emergencies (e.g., pandemics); stakeholders ask CMS to codify these examples rather than leaving them to ad hoc determinations.

[P16] CMS granting exceptions without an IPF request (f)(2) raises due process concerns; CMS should notify affected IPFs in writing and provide an opportunity to accept or decline the exception or to supplement the record.

[P17] The 30-day review period prior to public posting (g)(36/72) may be insufficient for IPFs with complex datasets to identify CMS calculation errors; stakeholders request a 45- to 60-day review window and clearer guidance on the correction process.

[P18] CMS must define what constitutes a "CMS calculation error" versus disagreement over data interpretation; the review and correction process should allow substantive challenges to CMS-run calculations, not just clerical fixes.

[P19] The public posting obligation (g) should allow IPFs to request temporary suppression of provider-identifiable or patient-sensitive elements while corrections or appeals are pending, with a clear time-limited process.

[P20] Rulemaking for substantive measure specification updates (e)(1) is appropriate, but CMS should commit to multi-stakeholder technical expert panels before proposing changes, especially for clinical measures that require clinical input.

[P21] Retaining prior-year measures by default (e)(2) may perpetuate obsolete or low-value measures; CMS should require periodic formal review cycles (e.g., every 3 years) with public reporting on measure validity and burden.

[P22] The list of factors CMS will consider for measure removal/modification (e)(3)(i) is comprehensive but lacks weighting or procedural guidance; stakeholders request CMS to publish how these factors will be empirically assessed and what thresholds (e.g., percent of IPFs at ceiling performance) will trigger consideration.

[P23] Factor 1 (e)(3)(i)(A) (uniformly high performance) needs a numerical definition (e.g., 95th percentile or mean >90%) so measures aren't removed prematurely or arbitrarily.

[P24] Factor 2 (e)(3)(i)(B) (alignment with clinical guidelines) must include a process for reconciling conflicting guidelines and timelines for CMS to update measures when guidelines change.

[P25] Factor 3 (e)(3)(i)(C) (replaceable by broader or more proximal measures) should require pilot testing of replacement measures across diverse IPFs before full adoption to prevent unintended consequences.

[P26] Factor 4 (e)(3)(i)(D) (performance does not lead to better outcomes) requires CMS to specify the evidence standard (e.g., randomized trials, observational studies, magnitude of effect) for linking process measures to outcomes.

[P27] Factor 6 (e)(3)(i)(F) (negative unintended consequences from reporting) is subjective; CMS should solicit and publish evidence of such harms and provide a mechanism for real-time mitigation when harms are identified.

[P28] Factor 7 (e)(3)(i)(G) (measure feasibility) should include consideration of disparities—measures that are infeasible mainly for safety-net IPFs should be adapted rather than removed.

[P29] Factor 8 (e)(3)(i)(H) (costs outweigh benefits) requires CMS to conduct a formal cost-benefit or burden analysis and make it publicly available when proposing removal.

[P30] The retention permission (e)(3)(ii) allowing CMS to keep measures that meet removal factors if aligned with policy goals is too open-ended and could be used to retain low-value measures for political reasons; CMS should require a strong justification and a periodic sunset for retained measures.

[P31] The rule does not specify penalties or remediation for repeated or willful misreporting of data that is later corrected during the 30-day review period; commenters request graduated sanctions and an appeals process.

[P32] The interplay between IPF unit exclusion status changes (P1/P38) and quality reporting obligations is unclear—if an IPF unit becomes excluded mid-year, CMS should clarify whether that unit's data must still be submitted for the reporting period and how penalties are apportioned.

[P33] Hospitals operating multi-unit psychiatric services need clarity on cost allocation methodologies when an IPF unit's exclusion status changes during the cost reporting period to avoid double-counting or omitting costs.

[P34] The rule lacks a safe harbor for inadvertent data submission errors made in good faith during QualityNet submission; CMS should adopt a one-time cure period for first minor reporting errors without penalty.

[P35] QualityNet technical requirements and security official registration (b)(2) pose HIPAA and cybersecurity compliance responsibilities; CMS should provide clear guidance on the acceptable qualifications and liability protections for designated security officials.

[P36] The ability to withdraw by changing the NOP on QualityNet (c) should be accompanied by confirmation receipts and audit logs; commenters request that CMS maintain records showing who initiated withdrawals and when.

[P37] CMS should clarify whether the 2.0 percentage-point reduction (a) is subject to equitable relief if an IPF demonstrates reasonable cause (e.g., catastrophic event) for failing to submit data, separate from paragraph (f) exceptions.

[P38] The rule should explicitly exempt IPFs with fewer than a defined minimum number of discharges (e.g., <25) from certain reporting burdens to avoid privacy risk and statistical unreliability.

[P39] Legal commenters note that the rule's frequent use of discretionary language ("may," "at the discretion of CMS") could raise arbitrary-and-capricious concerns if CMS fails to articulate consistent criteria when denying exceptions or retaining measures.

[P40] Advocacy groups request that CMS require public posting of the raw measure specifications, value sets, and risk-adjustment methodologies used to calculate public measure scores to promote transparency and reproducibility.

[P41] The 30-day pre-publication review applies only to corrections "resulting from CMS calculations"; IPFs should also be able to submit contextual information (e.g., data caveats, case-mix anomalies) for inclusion in the public posting.

[P42] The rule should establish timelines for CMS to process registration, NOP, and exception requests (e.g., within 30 days) and require notice if processing will be delayed.

[P43] There is no mention of how composite measures or cross-setting measures will be handled; CMS should clarify how measures that overlap with other programs (e.g., HQA, hospital inpatient measures) will be harmonized to avoid duplicative reporting.

[P44] Hospitals request sample data submission templates and a testing environment on QualityNet well before the first required reporting cycle to validate data extraction from EHRs and billing systems.

[P45] The rule should require CMS to provide a small-grants program or technical assistance for safety-net and rural IPFs to upgrade IT systems necessary for electronic reporting and security official registration.

[P46] CMS should clarify whether public reporting will include risk adjustment for case mix and social determinants of health; without adjustment, rankings could penalize IPFs serving more complex or disadvantaged populations.

[P47] The rule lacks detail on data security and patient privacy protections for published datasets; CMS should commit to de-identification standards and certify HIPAA-compliance of published outputs.

[P48] Professional psychiatric organizations request that measure removal decisions (e)(3) involve clinical specialty societies to ensure clinical validity and feasibility, not solely CMS-conducted technical reviews.

[P49] The rule should define the consequences of failing to register on QualityNet—does failure to register equal automatic non-participation and trigger the 2.0 percentage-point reduction? Clarify intent and timeline.

[P50] CMS should specify whether participation in the IPFQR Program is mandatory for all IPFs paid under IPF PPS or whether small or newly certified IPFs have temporary exemptions; current text is ambiguous.
