raw_output:
[P1] The requirement to "submit a written request to the Director" lacks clarity on acceptable transmission methods (email, electronic portal, certified mail), creating uncertainty and potential delay for agencies and applicants.

[P1] The rule does not specify a deadline or acknowledgement timeframe for the Director to confirm receipt of the written request, which could lead to disputes over when consultation formally began.

[P2] The phrase "sufficient to assess effects" is subjective and could be interpreted to require burdensome levels of detail beyond what is feasible at project planning stages; the rule should specify minimum data elements or tiered standards.

[P2] Industry commenters will object that requiring measures to "offset" effects (not just avoid/minimize) effectively mandates mitigation commitments before consultation, imposing legal and financial obligations prematurely.

[P3] Requiring agencies to include "the purpose of the action" could subject sensitive national security or proprietary project goals to public disclosure; the rule should allow redaction or a confidential filing mechanism.

[P4] The obligation to include "duration and timing" of the action is impractical for phased projects or programs with adaptive schedules; the rule should allow ranges or worst-case timing scenarios.

[P5] The location requirement is vague about spatial resolution (parcel, watershed, coordinates). The rule should require GIS-compatible coordinates and standard map scales to avoid inconsistent submissions.

[P6] The mandate to describe "specific components of the action and how they will be carried out" could force preliminary contractors or permittees to disclose proprietary construction methods; propose allowing high-level descriptions where details are commercially sensitive.

[P7] Requiring maps, drawings, or blueprints may be infeasible for preliminary proposals; the substitution provision (P14) partially addresses this, but the rule should state minimum acceptable schematic quality and acceptable file formats.

[P8] "Any other available information" is overly broad and could be used to demand extensive data collection; the rule should limit this to information reasonably obtainable by the agency or applicant without extraordinary cost.

[P9] The expanded definition of "action area" to include all areas indirectly affected could dramatically widen consultation scope and impose analyses of diffuse, remote impacts (e.g., downstream effects), creating heavy burdens—agencies seek clearer limiting language or examples.

[P9] Conservation groups will support including indirect areas but request explicit guidance on the spatial and temporal boundaries for indirect effects to ensure consistent application across projects.

[P10] Requiring provision of all information "in the agency's or applicant's possession" could force agencies to undertake extensive records searches and disclose third-party data; suggest narrowing to information reasonably known or readily accessible.

[P10] Academic researchers and NGOs will push that the rule require agencies to use existing survey and monitoring datasets (including citizen science) and to document data sources and quality in the initiation package.

[P11] The rule's mandate to "analyze any cumulative effects" without defining the appropriate temporal or spatial scale creates legal uncertainty and nearly unbounded analytical obligations; propose criteria for what constitutes reasonably foreseeable cumulative effects.

[P12] The requirement to summarize applicant-provided information "if available" invites inconsistent treatment; applicants request a clear statement that failure to provide such information will not delay consultation if it is not reasonably obtainable.

[P13] Listing EISs and EAs as required available information could duplicate NEPA documents and produce lengthy packages; agencies ask for allowance to incorporate NEPA analyses by reference rather than restating.

[P14] Allowing substitution of NEPA analyses is useful, but the rule should mandate that substituted documents be of a certain recency and relevance to prevent use of outdated analyses.

[P15] The written summary locating initiation-package elements within substituted documents creates an extra administrative task; agencies request a standardized checklist or template to satisfy this requirement efficiently.

[P16] Prohibiting initiation of formal consultation until a required biological assessment (BA) has been completed could delay consultations for actions where the need for a BA is ambiguous; suggest clarifying thresholds for when a BA is required under §402.12.

[P16] Legal commenters will argue that this prohibition conflicts with programmatic or tiered consultation practices where early consultation without a full BA is beneficial; recommend an explicit exception for programmatic consultations.

[P17] Allowing a single request to encompass multiple actions "subject to Director approval" centralizes discretion and could result in arbitrary denials; stakeholders ask for objective criteria the Director will use to approve programmatic or grouped consultations.

[P18] The clarification that effects must be considered "as a whole" when grouping actions is appropriate, but agencies ask for guidance on how to aggregate effects (e.g., summing emissions, habitat acres) and how to treat uncertainty in cumulative assessments.

[P19] The requirement to "assess the current status and environmental baseline" is standard, but commenters request explicit instruction on acceptable data sources, baseline temporal windows, and treatment of climate change trends.

[P20] Mandating incorporation of project and cumulative effects "into the environmental baseline" raises legal concerns because historically baselines exclude future actions; legal experts will request clarification on whether reasonably certain future actions should be included and how.

[P21] The "best available scientific and commercial data" standard is appropriate but ambiguous regarding incorporation of unpublished or proprietary data; parties seek procedures for handling confidential business information and weighting of different data types.

[P21] Industry stakeholders will urge that the requirement to give "appropriate consideration" to beneficial actions proposed by applicants should create presumption in favor of crediting on-site mitigation measures, with clear evidence standards.

[P22] The list of required elements in the biological opinion is helpful, but litigators will argue the rule should require Service explanations for key determinations of fact and law to satisfy judicial review.

[P23] Requiring "a summary of the information" underlying the opinion may be insufficient—NGOs will request that the full datasets and models used be appended or made publicly available to allow independent review.

[P24] The "detailed discussion" of effects should include uncertainty analyses and quantitative impact estimates where practicable; the rule should require documentation of assumptions and model parameters.

[P25] The statement that the Service must state whether the action is likely to jeopardize or adversely modify critical habitat needs clear definitions of "likely" (e.g., probability thresholds) to avoid inconsistent application.

[P26] For jeopardy opinions, stakeholders request guidance on the standard of proof and whether "likely to jeopardize" requires a more-likely-than-not finding, consistent with other agency standards.

[P27] For "no jeopardy" opinions, industry requests safe-harbor language that protects agencies relying on a Service no-jeopardy opinion from subsequent enforcement actions absent new information.

[P28] Requiring "reasonable and prudent alternatives" in jeopardy opinions is standard; however, the rule should set deadlines and standards for formulating alternatives and clarify when the agency must adopt them.

[P29] The obligation to state that no reasonable and prudent alternatives exist "to the best of its knowledge" is appropriate, but petitioners will request a requirement that the Service document the search/analysis undertaken to reach that conclusion.

[P30] Allowing the Service to adopt an agency's initiation package could expedite consultation, but stakeholders worry the Service may selectively adopt favorable parts while ignoring critical uncertainties; request standards for when adoption is appropriate.

[P31] Agencies want explicit timelines for the Service to indicate acceptance or request additional information if it intends to adopt the initiation package, to avoid consultation delays.

[P32] Adoption of the Service's own section 10(a) analysis into a biological opinion (P32) may blur distinctions between ESA consultation and incidental take permitting; commenters seek clarification on legal effects and cross-references.

[P33] The optional collaborative process is promising, but NGOs request that opportunities for public participation be preserved when an agency and Service agree to this process for significant actions.

[P34] The requirement to consider action characteristics when choosing collaborative process appropriateness needs objective criteria; agencies request examples of actions suitable for collaboration to encourage consistent application.

[P35] Creating coordination procedures is useful; stakeholders ask that such procedures be promulgated as templates or model MOUs to prevent negotiation delays for each consultation.

[P36] The expedited consultation option is beneficial for time-sensitive projects; however, environmental groups caution against using expedited processes for high-impact actions and request explicit exclusions for major federal actions or those impacting critical habitat.

[P37] The factors to determine expedited consultation appropriateness should include resource capacity and public interest; commenters ask that the rule require public notice when expedited consultation is used for actions with significant potential impacts.

[P38] Requiring establishment of expedited timelines is sensible, but the rule should set maximum permissible timelines for different complexity tiers to prevent unjustified short schedules that compromise science.

[P39] The requirement that expedited consultation packages include all initiation information could duplicate expedited timelines' intended efficiencies; agencies request a streamlined minimal package option for low-risk actions.

[P40] Encouraging—rather than requiring—coordination when developing initiation packages undermines the goal of efficiency; agencies propose a stronger presumption or requirement to engage Service staff early for complex actions.

[P41] The Service's additional responsibilities in expedited consultations must come with resource commitments; the Service should be required to designate staff and commit to staffing levels to meet expedited timelines.

[P42] The obligation for the Service to provide species information and guidance is critical; stakeholders request that such guidance be timely, standardized, and made publicly available to ensure transparency.

[P43] The promise to conclude expedited consultations within agreed-upon timeframes should be enforceable; agencies want a mechanism to extend timelines by mutual written agreement, and applicants want penalty or dispute-resolution provisions if the Service misses deadlines.

[P44] The reinitiation requirement where discretionary involvement is retained is appropriate, but federal land management agencies request clearer guidance on what constitutes sufficient "discretionary involvement or control" to trigger reinitiation.

[P45] The prohibition on reinitiation after land management plan approval (e.g., 43 U.S.C. 1712) if actions are addressed separately risks leaving newly listed species unconsidered across broad plans; conservation groups oppose this exception and request that agencies must consider species listings that arise post-plan approval at the plan level.

[P46] The condition that authorized actions affecting newly listed species must be addressed through separate action-specific consultation could fragment cumulative effects analyses; commenters argue that this undermines landscape-scale protections and request that plans be subject to adaptive reanalysis when listings occur.

[P46] Practitioners warn that reliance on action-specific consultations may create inconsistent mitigation across similar actions covered by a plan; they recommend a mechanism to ensure consistency (e.g., plan-level guidance or mandatory conditions).

[P9] Small municipalities and tribes note that inclusion of indirect impacts in the action area (P9) could require assessments of regional downstream or migratory impacts beyond their resources—request scaled requirements or additional funding/technical assistance.

[P21] The "commercial data" acknowledgment in best available data should include specific instructions for handling proprietary datasets (e.g., data-use agreements), otherwise applicants may refuse to share key information, undermining consultation quality.

[P15] The written summary locating required elements in substituted NEPA documents should be subject to Service review within a short timeframe to verify completeness rather than leaving agencies uncertain whether their substitution suffices.

[P11] Renewable energy developers request that cumulative effects analyses recognize planned mitigation and conservation actions (public and private) and provide standardized methods for crediting landscape-scale conservation to avoid double-counting impacts.

[P24] Commenters recommend requiring biological opinions to include adaptive management triggers and monitoring requirements in the "detailed discussion of effects" to ensure accountability for uncertainty and changing conditions.

[P25] Environmental lawyers will request that the rule explicitly requires the Service to articulate the causal link between specific action components and predicted harms in its jeopardy/adverse modification determination to meet administrative law standards.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The requirement to "submit a written request to the Director" lacks clarity on acceptable transmission methods (email, electronic portal, certified mail), creating uncertainty and potential delay for agencies and applicants.
The rule does not specify a deadline or acknowledgement timeframe for the Director to confirm receipt of the written request, which could lead to disputes over when consultation formally began.

The phrase "sufficient to assess effects" is subjective and could be interpreted to require burdensome levels of detail beyond what is feasible at project planning stages; the rule should specify minimum data elements or tiered standards.

Industry commenters will object that requiring measures to "offset" effects (not just avoid/minimize) effectively mandates mitigation commitments before consultation, imposing legal and financial obligations prematurely.

Requiring agencies to include "the purpose of the action" could subject sensitive national security or proprietary project goals to public disclosure; the rule should allow redaction or a confidential filing mechanism.
The obligation to include "duration and timing" of the action is impractical for phased projects or programs with adaptive schedules; the rule should allow ranges or worst-case timing scenarios.

The location requirement is vague about spatial resolution (parcel, watershed, coordinates). The rule should require GIS-compatible coordinates and standard map scales to avoid inconsistent submissions.

The mandate to describe "specific components of the action and how they will be carried out" could force preliminary contractors or permittees to disclose proprietary construction methods; propose allowing high-level descriptions where details are commercially sensitive.

Requiring maps, drawings, or blueprints may be infeasible for preliminary proposals; the substitution provision (P14) partially addresses this, but the rule should state minimum acceptable schematic quality and acceptable file formats.

"Any other available information" is overly broad and could be used to demand extensive data collection; the rule should limit this to information reasonably obtainable by the agency or applicant without extraordinary cost.

The expanded definition of "action area" to include all areas indirectly affected could dramatically widen consultation scope and impose analyses of diffuse, remote impacts (e.g., downstream effects), creating heavy burdens—agencies seek clearer limiting language or examples.
Conservation groups will support including indirect areas but request explicit guidance on the spatial and temporal boundaries for indirect effects to ensure consistent application across projects.

Requiring provision of all information "in the agency's or applicant's possession" could force agencies to undertake extensive records searches and disclose third-party data; suggest narrowing to information reasonably known or readily accessible.

Academic researchers and NGOs will push that the rule require agencies to use existing survey and monitoring datasets (including citizen science) and to document data sources and quality in the initiation package.

The rule's mandate to "analyze any cumulative effects" without defining the appropriate temporal or spatial scale creates legal uncertainty and nearly unbounded analytical obligations; propose criteria for what constitutes reasonably foreseeable cumulative effects.

The requirement to summarize applicant-provided information "if available" invites inconsistent treatment; applicants request a clear statement that failure to provide such information will not delay consultation if it is not reasonably obtainable.

Listing EISs and EAs as required available information could duplicate NEPA documents and produce lengthy packages; agencies ask for allowance to incorporate NEPA analyses by reference rather than restating.
Allowing substitution of NEPA analyses is useful, but the rule should mandate that substituted documents be of a certain recency and relevance to prevent use of outdated analyses.

The written summary locating initiation-package elements within substituted documents creates an extra administrative task; agencies request a standardized checklist or template to satisfy this requirement efficiently.

Prohibiting initiation of formal consultation until a required biological assessment (BA) has been completed could delay consultations for actions where the need for a BA is ambiguous; suggest clarifying thresholds for when a BA is required under §402.12.

Legal commenters will argue that this prohibition conflicts with programmatic or tiered consultation practices where early consultation without a full BA is beneficial; recommend an explicit exception for programmatic consultations.

Allowing a single request to encompass multiple actions "subject to Director approval" centralizes discretion and could result in arbitrary denials; stakeholders ask for objective criteria the Director will use to approve programmatic or grouped consultations.

The clarification that effects must be considered "as a whole" when grouping actions is appropriate, but agencies ask for guidance on how to aggregate effects (e.g., summing emissions, habitat acres) and how to treat uncertainty in cumulative assessments.

The requirement to "assess the current status and environmental baseline" is standard, but commenters request explicit instruction on acceptable data sources, baseline temporal windows, and treatment of climate change trends.

Mandating incorporation of project and cumulative effects "into the environmental baseline" raises legal concerns because historically baselines exclude future actions; legal experts will request clarification on whether reasonably certain future actions should be included and how.

The "best available scientific and commercial data" standard is appropriate but ambiguous regarding incorporation of unpublished or proprietary data; parties seek procedures for handling confidential business information and weighting of different data types.

Industry stakeholders will urge that the requirement to give "appropriate consideration" to beneficial actions proposed by applicants should create presumption in favor of crediting on-site mitigation measures, with clear evidence standards.

The list of required elements in the biological opinion is helpful, but litigators will argue the rule should require Service explanations for key determinations of fact and law to satisfy judicial review.

Requiring "a summary of the information" underlying the opinion may be insufficient—NGOs will request that the full datasets and models used be appended or made publicly available to allow independent review.

The "detailed discussion" of effects should include uncertainty analyses and quantitative impact estimates where practicable; the rule should require documentation of assumptions and model parameters.

The statement that the Service must state whether the action is likely to jeopardize or adversely modify critical habitat needs clear definitions of "likely" (e.g., probability thresholds) to avoid inconsistent application.
For jeopardy opinions, stakeholders request guidance on the standard of proof and whether "likely to jeopardize" requires a more-likely-than-not finding, consistent with other agency standards.
For "no jeopardy" opinions, industry requests safe-harbor language that protects agencies relying on a Service no-jeopardy opinion from subsequent enforcement actions absent new information.

Requiring "reasonable and prudent alternatives" in jeopardy opinions is standard; however, the rule should set deadlines and standards for formulating alternatives and clarify when the agency must adopt them.

The obligation to state that no reasonable and prudent alternatives exist "to the best of its knowledge" is appropriate, but petitioners will request a requirement that the Service document the search/analysis undertaken to reach that conclusion.

Allowing the Service to adopt an agency's initiation package could expedite consultation, but stakeholders worry the Service may selectively adopt favorable parts while ignoring critical uncertainties; request standards for when adoption is appropriate.
Agencies want explicit timelines for the Service to indicate acceptance or request additional information if it intends to adopt the initiation package, to avoid consultation delays.

Adoption of the Service's own section 10(a) analysis into a biological opinion (P32) may blur distinctions between ESA consultation and incidental take permitting; commenters seek clarification on legal effects and cross-references.
The optional collaborative process is promising, but NGOs request that opportunities for public participation be preserved when an agency and Service agree to this process for significant actions.

The requirement to consider action characteristics when choosing collaborative process appropriateness needs objective criteria; agencies request examples of actions suitable for collaboration to encourage consistent application.
Creating coordination procedures is useful; stakeholders ask that such procedures be promulgated as templates or model MOUs to prevent negotiation delays for each consultation.

The factors to determine expedited consultation appropriateness should include resource capacity and public interest; commenters ask that the rule require public notice when expedited consultation is used for actions with significant potential impacts.

Requiring establishment of expedited timelines is sensible, but the rule should set maximum permissible timelines for different complexity tiers to prevent unjustified short schedules that compromise science.

The requirement that expedited consultation packages include all initiation information could duplicate expedited timelines' intended efficiencies; agencies request a streamlined minimal package option for low-risk actions.

Encouraging—rather than requiring—coordination when developing initiation packages undermines the goal of efficiency; agencies propose a stronger presumption or requirement to engage Service staff early for complex actions.

The Service's additional responsibilities in expedited consultations must come with resource commitments; the Service should be required to designate staff and commit to staffing levels to meet expedited timelines.

The obligation for the Service to provide species information and guidance is critical; stakeholders request that such guidance be timely, standardized, and made publicly available to ensure transparency.

raw_output:
[P1] The deadline of January 23, 2023 for receiving comments is insufficient and improperly short given the technical complexity of the proposed AD; request an extension of the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] The rule text appears inconsistent about the effective date vs. the comment deadline; clarify which date triggers the 30‑day inspection and compliance timelines and extend the comment period if dates conflict.

[P2] The phrase “unless already done” is vague — request clarification on what constitutes adequate prior compliance documentation and whether previous inspections/replacements performed under different ADs or manufacturer service bulletins count.

[P3] The 30‑day inspection requirement to determine date of manufacture is unworkable for operators with large fleets and poor traceability; request allowance of 90 days or acceptance of serial number lookup with manufacturer assistance.

[P3] The provision limits inspection to part numbers 117080‑02, ‑03, and ‑04 but the truncated text may omit additional part numbers; request confirmation of the complete list of affected P/Ns and if spares in storage are included.

[P4] Allowing maintenance record review “provided the date can be conclusively determined” is too narrow — request explicit acceptable evidence (manufacturer trace, serial number registry, production lot records) and permission to use multiple corroborating records if no single document is conclusive.

[P4] Maintenance record systems vary internationally; request that digital records and third‑party MRO records be explicitly accepted as valid documentation for date determination.

[P5] Requiring replacement before units exceed 10 years since manufacture imposes significant cost and logistical burden; request a risk‑based alternative (e.g., condition inspection or test) rather than strict age limit.

[P6] The requirement to replace units manufactured in 2008 or earlier within 6 months or by 15 years since manufacture, whichever is earlier, creates a compliance trap for very old items that already exceeded 15 years — request explicit instruction for units already beyond 15 years and allowance for immediate grounding/technical directive instead of ambiguous timing.

[P6] The 6‑month replacement window for 2008 or earlier units is too short for operators with global supply chain and limited depot capacity; request extension to 12 months and allowance for phased compliance based on aircraft routing.

[P7] The 12‑month replacement requirement for 2009–2010 units does not account for seasonal maintenance schedules; request coordination with scheduled C‑checks and permission to replace at next heavy maintenance within 18 months.

[P8] The 24‑month allowance for 2011–2013 units may be overly permissive given safety concerns; conversely, it could be burdensome to smaller operators if replacements are scarce — request FAA to publish estimated replacement part availability and allow prioritization based on risk ranking.

[P9] The prohibition on installing any passenger chemical oxygen generator unless it is a “serviceable unit” is broadly stated; request that the AD define “install” to clarify whether installation on ground equipment or storage racks is included and whether transfers between operators are affected.

[P9] The prohibition fails to address installation of generators on international lease returns or ferry flights; request exemption language for temporary installation to safely ferry an aircraft to maintenance, subject to operator approval.

[P10] The AD’s definition of “serviceable unit” is not provided in the extracted provisions — request that the FAA publish the precise definition and acceptance criteria (e.g., date ranges, markings, certifications).

[P11] Allowing the Seattle ACO Manager to approve AMOCs centralizes decision making; request that other FAA certification offices be explicitly authorized to process AMOCs to avoid bottlenecks for non‑West Coast operators.

[P12] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or Flight Standards Office may delay processing; request clear timelines for FAA response to AMOC requests and electronic submission routes.

[P13] The instruction to address direct AMOC submissions to the person identified in paragraph (l)(1) is circular given the NPRM; request that the AD include the actual name and contact information or a stable title for submissions.

[P14] Emailing AMOC requests to 9‑ANM‑Seattle‑ACO‑AMOC‑Requests@faa.gov is helpful, but comment that email acceptance must include S/MIME or secure upload options for attachments containing proprietary data; request alternative secure submission methods.

[P15] Requiring operators to notify their principal inspector before using an approved AMOC could be impractical for operators without a standing principal inspector; request a streamlined process for foreign operators and leased aircraft to notify the responsible FAA office.

[P16] Permitting Boeing ODA approval for AMOCs related to repairs/modifications allows industry expertise to be used; however, request that approvals by Boeing ODA also require FAA concurrence and public posting of approved AMOCs to ensure transparency.

[P17] The condition that repairs/modifications must meet the airplane’s certification basis is appropriate but may be unclear for altered or supplemental type certificated (STC) airplanes; request guidance for aircraft with amended certification bases and for modernized fleets.

[P18] Requiring any AMOC approval to specifically reference this AD is reasonable, but request template language and citation format to reduce processing errors.

[P19] The NPRM date requirement duplicates P1 and could confuse commenters; request consolidation of deadlines and removal of redundant language to avoid inconsistent submissions.

[P20] Requiring submission of comments in triplicate to a physical address is outdated and burdensome; request that electronic submissions via the docket system (e.g., Regulations.gov) be explicitly accepted as sufficient and that triplicate hard copies be optional.

[P21] The requirement to include a self‑addressed, stamped postcard to receive acknowledgment is unnecessary and should be replaced with automated email acknowledgments upon electronic submission.

[P22] Allowing electronic download of the document is helpful; request that the FAA also post any referenced service information, supporting data, and risk assessment to the docket for public review.

[P23] The broad invitation for comments should explicitly invite data from international regulators and operators, particularly on fleet composition and generator inventories, to ensure decisions reflect global operations.

[P24] The FAA specifically requests comments on economic impacts — stakeholders request that the FAA provide a quantitative cost estimate (parts, labor, downtime) and regulatory flexibility analysis to inform comments.

[P24] Stakeholders request environmental and energy impact information to be included in the docket (e.g., disposal/recycling plan for replaced chemical oxygen generators) so commenters can assess environmental consequences.

[P3] The AD does not clarify whether spares in airline stockrooms, manufacturer warehouses, or MRO facilities are subject to the 30‑day inspection; request explicit inclusion/exclusion of stocked spares and interstate/international storage.

[P5] The AD does not address safe disposal of replaced chemical oxygen generators containing hazardous materials; request mandatory disposal/transport instructions and costs recovery options.

[P7] For leased aircraft, responsibility for replacement (lessor vs. lessee) is not specified; request clear assignment of responsibility and instructions for lease transitions.

[P16] Allowing Boeing ODA to approve AMOCs may create a conflict of interest if Boeing has commercial incentives; request independent FAA review of ODA‑approved AMOCs in safety‑critical cases.

[P3] The inspection requirement assumes labeling or markings are legible; request an alternative method (manufacturer verification) if markings are missing or illegible.

[P9] The prohibition does not explicitly prohibit installing refurbished or reconditioned oxygen generators; request explicit inclusion of refurbished units under the prohibition unless they meet “serviceable” criteria.

[P11] The AMOC approval authority should be broadened to include other OEM ODAs (not only Boeing) if they hold relevant delegation for particular airframes; request cross‑recognition or a process for OEMs other than Boeing.

[P15] The notification requirement prior to using approved AMOCs lacks a timeline for how far in advance notification must be provided; request specification (e.g., at least 5 business days before use).

[P6] The “whichever is earlier” clause for the 2008 or earlier items could force replacement sooner than necessary; request clarification and option to use a risk‑based timeline where life remaining is demonstrated.

[P5] Operators request a grandfathering clause for generators installed on aircraft that will be retired or otherwise permanently withdrawn from service within the replacement window to avoid unnecessary expenditure.

[P8] For units manufactured 2011–2013, the 24‑month replacement schedule may conflict with international airworthiness directives; request coordination language to align compliance across jurisdictions.

[P20] Identification of “both docket numbers” in communications is ambiguous — request that the FAA specify the exact docket numbers and provide instructions for commenting on multiple related dockets.

[P21] The SASE requirement is impractical for large corporate commenters who submit hundreds of pages; request the FAA adopt electronic acknowledgement and waive the postcard requirement for electronic filers.

[P14] The public should be allowed to request redacted versions of confidential AMOC submittals; request a clear process for submitting proprietary or sensitive information with confidentiality claims.

[P22] Request that the downloadable electronic copy include hyperlinked references to related ADs, service bulletins, and the docket to facilitate thorough review.

[P24] Economic stakeholders request the FAA conduct a regulatory flexibility analysis addressing impacts on small air carriers and provide compliance alternatives (e.g., extended phase‑in schedules) to mitigate disproportionate burdens.

[P3] Airlines operating older fleets may lack maintenance records for earlier decades; request that the FAA allow the manufacturer to determine date of manufacture via serial number lookup as acceptable proof.

[P1] Industry commenters will argue that requiring specified risk materials only from cattle “inspected and passed” in official or certified establishments (§ 310.22(d)(1)(i)) is overly burdensome for small exporters who use custom or small proprietary facilities not currently certified, and request an allowance or phased certification timeline.

[P1] Legal experts will claim the cross-reference to import eligibility under § 327.1(b) in § 310.22(d)(1)(i) is ambiguous and ask the Agency to clarify whether retrospective imports (inspected/passed abroad before a country’s listing changed) remain eligible.

[P1] Agricultural exporters will request explicit guidance on what documentation constitutes proof that the cattle were “inspected and passed” in an official or certified establishment, and urge acceptance of electronic certificates and authenticated digital seals.

[P2] Trade associations will contend that the blanket prohibition in § 327.2(a)(4) on meat from countries “not deemed eligible” is too rigid and will request a streamlined emergency-entry waiver process for time-sensitive products and research materials.

[P2] Consumer advocacy groups will support § 327.2(a)(4) and argue that the prohibition should be expanded to explicitly include meat derived from animals in zones within a country that are affected by transboundary animal diseases.

[P3] Exporting countries’ governments will request clear, published criteria and timelines for the Administrator’s discretionary withdrawal authority in § 327.2 to avoid unpredictable trade disruptions and potential due process concerns.

[P3] Trade law experts will assert that § 327.2’s open-ended “may withdraw” language without required notice or opportunity to cure could be arbitrary and ask for procedural safeguards (notice, findings, opportunity to remediate, and right to appeal).

[P4] Foreign inspection authorities will challenge the standard in § 327.2 (that their system “does not assure compliance with equivalent requirements”) as vague and call for a specific equivalence framework and measurable benchmarks rather than subjective determinations.

[P4] Industry stakeholders will request that equivalence assessments under § 327.2 be limited to aspects directly affecting public health, rather than including ancillary regulatory or facility design differences.

[P5] Foreign governments and exporters will object to § 327.2’s condition permitting withdrawal where “reliance cannot be placed upon certificates” and ask the Agency to specify what types of certificate irregularities (e.g., fraud, improper signatures, inconsistent lot data) would trigger withdrawal.

[P5] Legal commenters will emphasize the need for protocols for notification and remediation before using lack-of-reliance on certificates as grounds for withdrawal under § 327.2.

[P6] Exporting countries will request that the “lack of current information” ground in § 327.2 be defined with explicit timelines for information requests, response windows, and consequences, to avoid permanent delisting for temporary reporting delays.

[P6] Public health NGOs will support the § 327.2 condition that countries must maintain up-to-date information, but will advocate that the Agency specify minimum surveillance and reporting metrics required to demonstrate currency.

[P7] Importers will request clarification in § 327.2(b) about the precise form, content, and format of the country-of-origin meat inspection certificates required by § 327.4, including acceptance of translations and electronic copies.

[P7] Customs brokers will request that § 327.2(b) include an explicit provision allowing provisional entry when certificates are delayed but verifiable through authenticated electronic systems, to prevent port congestion and economic loss.

[P8] Animal health advocates will ask that the § 327.2(b) exception for certain products from disease-affected countries be narrowed so fresh/chilled/frozen imports remain ineligible, arguing current language could be interpreted too broadly.

[P8] Trade groups representing processed meat manufacturers will request broader use of the § 327.2(b) exception to allow certain heat-treated or shelf-stable products from disease-affected countries to enter after inspection and marking, noting low risk when safety treatments are validated.

[P9] Poultry exporters will seek specificity about the criteria in § 381.195(c) and § 381.196(b) that determine which countries are “found eligible” so they can plan investments and certifications accordingly.

[P9] Public health commenters will support § 381.195(c) but urge that the Agency require ongoing audits and unannounced inspections of eligible foreign poultry processors to ensure continued compliance.

[P10] Importers and retailers will challenge the restriction in § 381.195(c) that imported slaughtered poultry must be “ready-to-cook,” asking for clarity on allowable processing steps (e.g., marination, cut-up, deboning) that still meet the ready-to-cook definition.

[P10] Consumer safety groups will argue that the “ready-to-cook” limitation in § 381.195(c) is appropriate but ask the Agency to define the term clearly to prevent circumvention (e.g., minimally processed items labeled ambiguously).

[P11] Foreign governments will object to the § 381.196(a)(4) prohibition on poultry from countries not deemed eligible and request a temporary conditional import program (with additional safeguards) rather than outright exclusion in early stages of equivalence assessment.

[P11] Legal commentators will seek clarity on the “except as provided” carve-outs referenced in § 381.196(a)(4), asking the Agency to list the specific sections that might permit exceptions to avoid confusion.

[P12] Exporting countries will ask that the Administrator’s withdrawal authority under § 381.196 include transparent criteria and an appeals process and that withdrawal be subject to timed notice and opportunity to demonstrate corrective action.

[P12] Poultry industry groups will request that withdrawals under § 381.196 be proportionate (e.g., applied by establishment or region) rather than country-wide, to avoid punishing compliant processors in a country with localized problems.

[P13] Foreign inspection agencies will argue that the § 381.196 condition about “assuring compliance with equivalent requirements” should allow for recognition of functional equivalence rather than identical regulatory texts.

[P13] Food safety advocates will counter-request that equivalence assessments under § 381.196 incorporate performance data (e.g., pathogen prevalence, residue testing) rather than relying solely on paper-based regulatory comparisons.

[P14] Trade lawyers will demand that § 381.196 specify the evidentiary standard and types of verification that would constitute “reliance cannot be placed upon certificates,” to prevent arbitrary rejection of legitimate paperwork.

[P14] Industry compliance officers will ask that § 381.196 include remedies short of withdrawal (e.g., intensified sampling, targeted audits) when certificate reliability is questioned.

[P15] Exporting governments will request clear deadlines and procedural steps in § 381.196 for how they can reestablish eligibility after being deemed to lack current information, including required documentation and timelines.

[P15] Consumer safety organizations will support the “current information” requirement in § 381.196 and push for a public list and periodic updates showing which countries are under information reviews to enhance transparency.

[P16] Importers will ask § 381.196(b) to explicitly permit electronic submission and verification of inspection certificates required by § 381.197, to modernize processes and reduce paperwork delays.

[P16] Enforcement agencies will request that § 381.196(b) clarify responsibilities and liabilities when certificates are forged or incorrect, including where the economic burden falls (importer vs. foreign authority).

[P17] Industry stakeholders will ask that § 381.196(b)’s requirement for inspection and marking prior to entry include explicit standards for marks and seals, and allow approved electronic traceability systems as equivalent to physical marking.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement that materials may be incorporated by reference only with the approval of the Director of the Federal Register creates unnecessary procedural delay and should include a timeframe (e.g., 60 days) for the Director to act on incorporation requests.

[P1] Incorporation by reference of technical standards without providing full text in the docket undermines public participation; the rule should require that any incorporated NFPA or other standards be posted in the docket or made freely available.

[P2] Providing TTY access only via the Federal Relay Service toll-free number is insufficient for non-English speakers or deafblind individuals; the rule should require multiple alternative-access methods (e.g., captioned telephone, video relay service, real-time text).

[P2] The rule should specify whether the Federal Relay Service call is toll-free from all devices and whether callers may expect bilingual relay operators, otherwise persons with hearing or speech impairments could be effectively excluded.

[P3] The exclusion of underground pipelines from the definition of "hazard" appears to conflict with varying State standards; the rule should clarify which specific Federal, State, and local safety standards apply and whether minimum federal safety design criteria are required.

[P3] Allowing pipelines that merely "comply with applicable Federal, State, and local" standards to be excluded could create uneven protections; the rule should require pipelines to meet specific federal pipeline safety regulations (e.g., PHMSA standards) to qualify for exclusion.

[P4] Limiting the NFPA 58 compliance exclusion to containers of 250 gallons or less for liquefied propane gas (LPG) may be ambiguous — the rule should clarify whether capacity is measured per vessel, per aggregation on-site, or per installation.

[P4] The rule's incorporation of NFPA 58 by reference for LPG containers should ensure the exact edition referenced is specified, and that the text is made accessible in the docket; otherwise regulated parties cannot determine compliance obligations.

[P5] The January 9, 2019 comment deadline is outdated (and already passed); the rule's dates must be updated or clarified to avoid rejecting timely comments and to comply with the Administrative Procedure Act's notice-and-comment requirements.

[P5] Requiring comments to be received by a fixed date without specifying receipt method or time zone (local to EPA) can lead to unfair rejections; the rule should state the deadline in Eastern Time and that comments submitted via regulations.gov by 11:59 pm ET on the deadline will be accepted.

[P6] Requiring submitters to follow detailed instructions in a specific September 17, 2018 FR document burdens late or new stakeholders who may not have access; the rule should summarize key submission requirements in this document rather than deferring entirely.

[P6] The cross-reference to 83 FR 47004 (FRL–9983–14) is not sufficiently specific for electronic docket searching; the rule should provide a direct link or attach the ADDRESSES instructions within the docket for clarity.

[P7] Listing a single technical contact (Kenneth Moss) may create bottlenecks; EPA should provide backup contacts and specify expected response times for technical inquiries.

[P7] The rule should clarify whether Kenneth Moss can provide interpretations binding on EPA or whether only published guidance constitutes official positions, to avoid reliance on informal communications.

[P8] Providing the TSCA-Hotline contact information with an ABVI-Goodwill address is confusing; the rule should provide direct email and phone contact and clarify hours of operation and expected response times for general inquiries.

[P8] The TSCA-Hotline contact information appears to be for an external organization (ABVI-Goodwill); the rule should confirm data privacy protections when contacting an outsourced hotline.

[P9] The requirement that comments must be received by January 9, 2019 makes participation impossible for stakeholders who were not previously notified; EPA should reopen the comment period with a current deadline and adequate notice.

[P10] Requiring submission at regulations.gov under a specific docket ID is acceptable, but the rule should also explicitly allow mailed or hand-delivered comments for those without internet access and provide addresses.

[P11] The instruction to follow online submission instructions is too vague; the rule should list common pitfalls (file size limits, acceptable file types) to prevent inadvertent missing submissions.

[P12] The prohibition on editing or removing comments after submission may chill dissent or correction of inadvertent personal data disclosure; EPA should permit commenters to request redaction or removal of their own comments in cases of sensitive information or typos.

[P12] Because comments cannot be removed once posted, EPA must provide a clear confidential business information (CBI) submission pathway and strong instructions to avoid accidental disclosure, otherwise submitters may be deterred from commenting.

[P13] The prohibition on submitting CBI electronically without alternative guidance is burdensome; the rule must provide clear procedures, addresses, and formats for submitting CBI by mail or secure upload.

[P13] The rule should explicitly state how EPA will handle inadvertent electronic submission of CBI and what remedies (e.g., redaction, removal) are available to submitters.

[P14] Requiring multimedia submissions to be accompanied by a written comment may disadvantage stakeholders who wish to submit audiovisual demonstrations; EPA should accept multimedia as primary submissions if clearly referenced and ensure accessibility (transcripts, captions).

[P14] The rule should specify acceptable multimedia formats and maximum file sizes, and whether the multimedia will be made publicly accessible or only summarized in the written comment.

[P15] Declaring the written comment as the official submission is reasonable but the rule must permit attachments and appendices to be considered part of the official submission and explain how multi-file submissions are processed.

[P16] The general prohibition on considering comments outside the primary submission could exclude substantive materials hosted on other platforms; the rule should allow hyperlinks in the primary submission to external files and explain how EPA will archive and consider linked materials.

[P16] EPA should allow limited inclusion of cloud-hosted datasets by reference, provided the primary submission contains a stable identifier (e.g., DOI) and clear instructions for access, otherwise technical commenters cannot provide large supporting datasets.

[P17] The permission to visit an EPA webpage for additional submission methods is helpful but the rule should provide the exact URL in the regulation text to ensure stable access and avoid broken links.

[P17] The rule should require EPA to maintain the referenced web guidance for the entire comment period and for a defined archival period after final action to facilitate legal review and transparency.

[P18] The obligation that authorized states must maintain programs "equivalent to, consistent with, and no less stringent than" the federal program needs clearer metrics for "equivalent" and "consistent" to prevent arbitrary federal rejections of state programs.

[P18] Stakeholders request that EPA provide a standard checklist or template that states can use to demonstrate equivalence and consistency, reducing uncertainty and administrative burden.

[P19] Requiring states to update their programs and request authorization for federal changes imposes a short timeline; EPA should set minimum time windows (e.g., 12 months) for states to submit authorization requests after each federal change.

[P19] The rule should clarify which federal changes trigger the requirement to seek authorization (major rulemakings only, or also technical and guidance changes) to reduce undue administrative load on states.

[P20] EPA's obligation to implement new federal requirements in states until state authorization is approved could create dual enforcement uncertainty; EPA should detail coordination procedures to avoid duplicative or conflicting permits.

[P20] The rule should require EPA to provide state agencies with advance notice and an implementation plan before EPA issues permits implementing new requirements in the state to allow for smooth transitions.

[P21] Assigning Alabama responsibility for permitting TSD facilities "except in Indian country" requires clarification on which lands are considered Indian country for regulatory purposes; stakeholders request a map or list of affected areas.

[P21] The rule should specify how Alabama will coordinate with EPA regarding HSWA limitations and what enforcement responsibilities remain with EPA to avoid gaps in oversight.

[P22] EPA's retention of authorities under specified RCRA sections is appropriate, but the rule should outline how EPA will exercise those retained authorities to avoid perceived federal overreach into authorized state programs.

[P22] The rule should establish thresholds or criteria for EPA's exercise of retained authorities (e.g., imminent risk, pattern of noncompliance) to provide predictability to regulated parties and states.

[P23] The permission for EPA to require monitoring, tests, analyses, or reports should be bounded by reasonableness standards and cost considerations; the rule should require that EPA justify monitoring requests and consider small entities' burdens.

[P23] EPA should commit to using standardized test methods and data quality standards when requiring monitoring or analyses to ensure comparability and avoid duplicative sampling.

[P24] EPA's authority to suspend or revoke permits must be accompanied by due process protections and clear criteria for suspension or revocation actions to protect permittees' rights.

[P24] The rule should require EPA to coordinate with the state before suspending or revoking a state-issued permit, providing notice and an opportunity to cure noncompliance where feasible.

[P25] The provision allowing EPA to take enforcement irrespective of state action could create timing conflicts; the rule should require EPA to notify the state and allow the state an initial opportunity to act, except in emergencies.

[P25] Stakeholders request EPA to describe how it will avoid duplicative penalties for the same violation when both EPA and a state take enforcement actions.

[P26] The obligation that comments on the authorization must be submitted "at this time" is vague; the rule should define the precise comment period dates in each notice rather than refer to "this time" to prevent confusion.

[P25] The identical 24-month-from-May-20-2013 timetable in § 39.13(g) is obsolete; the agency should replace it with a practicable timeline tied to this AD’s actual effective date and provide alternative compliance schedules for aircraft placed in service after 2013.

[P4] Allowing records review in lieu of inspection (AD paragraph (g) records alternative) is appropriate, but the rule fails to define what constitutes “conclusive” evidence in maintenance records; FAA should specify acceptable documents and the standard of proof required.

[P26] The records-review permission in § 39.13(g) needs explicit procedures for when records are ambiguous, including acceptance of electronic records, chain-of-custody requirements, and what constitutes a qualified person to certify the records.

[P5] The requirement to replace any unit with a Table 1 serial number “before further flight” (AD paragraph (g)(1)) is overly burdensome for airlines operating multiple aircraft during overnight operations; FAA should permit a short, defined MEL (minimum equipment list) or temporary grounding window to allow scheduled maintenance replacement.

[P27] The identical § 39.13(g)(1) replacement-before-next-flight requirement is unnecessarily strict and may lead to operational disruptions; FAA should allow a maximum repair period (e.g., 10 days or next A-check) if safety risk assessment justifies.

[P11] The replacement mandate in AD paragraph (i)(1) (for airplanes other than those in paragraph (g)) repeats the same “before further flight” threshold and poses identical operational hardship; FAA must provide risk-based prioritization or relief.

[P34] § 39.13(i)(1)’s exception for unreadable serial numbers tied to manufacturing date is reasonable, but the rule does not define acceptable evidence for “conclusively determined” manufacturing dates; FAA should list acceptable sources (manufacturer’s records, shipping manifests, certs).

[P35] The manufacturing-date exception (§ 39.13(i)(1)) is ambiguous about the permissible date range; the FAA should explicitly state the date range that triggers the exception so operators can apply it consistently.

[P6] Requiring operators to add the letter “I” to serial number labels for Table 2 units (AD paragraph (g)(2)) may violate existing marking/labeling regulations and could compromise label readability; FAA should specify font, size, placement, and methods (permanent marker vs. label) to ensure compliance and traceability.

[P36] § 39.13(g)(2) lacks guidance on whether the “I” marking must be applied by a certificated technician or recorded in maintenance logs; FAA should require a signed maintenance entry and provide form guidance.

[P12] The identical requirement in AD paragraph (i)(2) to mark Table 2 units before further flight is impractical if the marking process necessitates removal to access the label; FAA should clarify whether in-situ marking is permitted or outline procedures for swift removal/reinstallation.

[P37] The prohibition on installing Table 1 units (AD paragraph (h) and § 39.13(j)(1)) needs an express exception for emergency replacement parts when a serviceable equivalent cannot be sourced, with FAA approval, to avoid grounding aircraft indefinitely.

[P31] The effective-date-based prohibition (as of May 20, 2013) in AD paragraph (h) is retroactive and penalizes operators who lawfully installed parts prior to the effective date; FAA must clarify that the prohibition applies prospectively from this AD’s effective date or provide amnesty for pre-existing installations documented in records.

[P8] The AD’s blanket prohibition on installing listed serial-number units lacks a parts disposition/traceability procedure; operators need instructions on how to quarantine, tag, and disposition prohibited units to ensure compliance.

[P14] § 39.13(j)(2)’s prohibition on installing Table 2 units unless modified per (i)(2) creates supply chain complications because it fails to provide an FAA-acceptable modification form or a method for verifying modifications performed overseas; FAA should permit acceptance of foreign repair station documentation when accompanied by FAA Form 8100-2 or equivalent.

[P38] The distinction between aircraft in paragraph (g) and those outside it is unclear in the applicability criteria; FAA should define which airplane models/serial ranges are “identified in paragraph (g)” to ensure operators know which timeline applies.

[P9] Requiring the same 24-month inspection for airplanes not covered by paragraph (g) (AD paragraph (i)) with the same May 20, 2013 start date creates inconsistent compliance expectations; the FAA should harmonize schedules and provide credit for previously completed inspections.

[P32] § 39.13(i) does not address aircraft operated under continuous maintenance programs (e.g., CAMP) and whether previously logged inspections under those programs satisfy the AD; the FAA should explicitly allow credit for equivalent documented inspections.

[P7] The instruction to reinstall the stowage box unit “before further flight” when no serial number is identified and records review was not done (AD paragraph (g)(3)) is unclear — it appears to require removal/reinstallation for no change; FAA should explain the safety rationale and provide step-by-step installation instructions or waive the reinstall requirement if no defect is found.

[P29] § 39.13(g)(3) conflicts with § 39.13(g)(3) exception (P30); FAA must explicitly state when reinstall is required and when records review obviates reinstall to eliminate contradictory readings.

[P13] AD paragraph (i)(3) and § 39.13(i)(3) require reinstalling units before further flight if serial number not identified, which could lead to unnecessary work; FAA should clarify whether “reinstall” means reinstalling the same unit after inspection or installing a replacement, and if returning the same unit requires any functional tests.

[P30] The records-review exception (§ 39.13(g)(3) exception) should explicitly state the qualifications of personnel performing the records review and whether third-party audits of records are acceptable for compliance.

[P15] Granting the Seattle ACO Manager authority to approve AMOCs (AD paragraph (k)(1) / § 39.13(k)(1)) is acceptable, but the rule should provide timelines for AMOC decisions (e.g., 60 days) to avoid undue operational delays.

[P16] The procedure to send AMOC requests to principal inspectors or FSDOs (AD paragraph (k)(1) procedures) should allow electronic submission via a secure portal, not only email, and the FAA should commit to acknowledging receipt within a defined period.

[P17] Allowing AMOC requests by email to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is fine, but the rule should advise acceptable file formats, maximum file sizes, and whether encrypted attachments are allowed for proprietary technical data.

[P18] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC (AD paragraph (k)(2)) needs a timeline (e.g., notify within 48 hours of first use) and should specify required notification contents to ensure consistent oversight.

[P43] § 39.13(k)(2) should clarify whether advance notice or post-approval notice is required and provide standardized notification templates for operators to reduce administrative burden.

[P19] Permitting Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs for repairs/modifications (AD paragraph (k)(3)) is acceptable but raises concerns about independence; the FAA should require that Boeing ODA approvals be reviewed by the FAA and submitted to the docket for transparency.

[P44] § 39.13(k)(3) should require that any AMOC approved by a Boeing ODA include a statement of ODA authority and be countersigned by the FAA certification office to ensure public accountability.

[P20] Requiring AMOC repair methods to meet the airplane’s certification basis (AD paragraph (k)(3) approval conditions) is standard, but the rule should provide guidance on how to address certification-basis changes for older aircraft where records are incomplete.

[P45] § 39.13(k)(3)’s obligation that AMOC approvals must specifically reference this AD is reasonable; however, FAA should require that AMOC approvals be posted to a searchable public registry to help operators determine whether prior AMOCs apply to their aircraft.

[P21] The requirement that AMOC approvals specifically reference this AD (AD paragraph (k)(3) approval reference) should also require inclusion of the AMOC approval date and expiration (if any) to prevent indefinite or ambiguous approvals.

[P22] Accepting previously approved AMOCs from AD 2013–07–09 (AD paragraph (k)(4)) is necessary; FAA should publish a list of those AMOCs and the corresponding provisions they cover so operators can readily identify applicability.

[P46] § 39.13(k)(4) should clarify whether previously approved AMOCs require revalidation due to any changes in the service bulletin revisions or differences between the old and new AD language.

[P40] The repeated authorization of the Seattle ACO Branch Manager to approve AMOCs (§ 39.13(k)(1)) should be expanded to allow delegation to experienced designees in high-volume regions to prevent bottlenecks.

[P41] The requirement to send AMOC requests to principal inspectors or local FSDOs (§ 39.13(k)(1)) should explicitly permit submission through a central FAA AMOC portal to streamline processing and create an auditable trail.

[P42] Directing AMOC submissions to the certification office manager (if sent directly) (§ 39.13(k)(1)) needs the current point-of-contact name and address (paragraph (l)(1) reference) included in the AD to prevent misdirection.

[P33] The records-review permission in § 39.13(i) must explicitly allow reliance on electronic maintenance records (e.g., AMOS, CAMP) and specify that electronic signatures are acceptable to determine serial numbers.

[P28] The requirement to mark Table 2 units with an “I” and reinstall before further flight (§ 39.13(g)(2) / § 39.13(i)(2)) should allow that marking and reinstallation to be deferred to the next scheduled maintenance event when a documented risk assessment demonstrates negligible safety impact.

[P39] The exception to § 39.13(j)(2) permitting installation of Table 2 units only if modified per (i)(2) is vague about who may perform the modification and whether field-modification kits or STCs are required; FAA should clarify approved modification methods and authorized providers.

[P5] The mandated replacement “with a new or serviceable unit” (AD paragraph (g)(1) and § 39.13(g)(1)) should define “serviceable” in the context of parts with no serial numbers or parts reworked by non-original manufacturers to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P11] The cross-references to Intertechnique Service Bulletin MXP1/4–35–175 Revision 2 are essential; the AD should incorporate by reference the exact revision and date to avoid ambiguity if newer revisions are published.

[P27] § 39.13(g)(1) should state whether operator-incurred costs (parts and labor) will be eligible for consideration under FAA economic hardship relief programs, as replacement of multiple units may impose significant unexpected cost.

[P1] The AD paragraph (a) obligation to receive comments by August 9, 2019 should include instructions for submitting confidential/proprietary information and how the FAA will treat redacted submissions.

[P23] § 39.13(a) should provide a mechanism for stakeholders to request an extension of the comment period if new, substantive supporting data (e.g., revised service bulletin) is issued during the comment window.
