[P1] The requirement that the application form "comply with CMS instructions regarding content and format and be approved by CMS" (§ 417.430(a)(1)) is unworkable on CMS's current approval timeline and will delay applicants; we request defined CMS review timelines and expedited review for time-sensitive enrollments.

[P1] Requiring CMS approval of the application form under § 417.430(a)(1) gives CMS unilateral control over content and format that may conflict with state licensing forms and should include a mechanism to resolve conflicts with state-required language.

[P2] The obligation that the applicant "complete the application" and be an HMO or CMP eligible (or soon to become eligible) individual (§ 417.430(a)(1)) is vague with respect to "soon to become eligible"; please define the timeframe and documentary evidence required.

[P2] Requiring applicants to include authorization for disclosure between HHS/designees and the HMO/CMP in every application (§ 417.430(a)(1)) may run afoul of state privacy laws and should include a specification of the scope, retention limits, and a model authorization form.

[P3] Requiring all section 1876 cost contracts to agree to be rated under MA and Part D quality rating systems (§ 417.472(k)) imposes significant measurement burdens on small cost contracts that historically did not report MA measures; CMS should phase in this requirement or provide technical assistance and funding.

[P4] The exception that cost contracts need not submit data on measures CMS deems inapplicable (§ 417.472(k)) lacks clear criteria for "inapplicable" and "lacking available data"; CMS should publish objective criteria and a predictable process for determinations.

[P5] Extending payment-preclusion list prohibitions to HMOs and CMPs (§ 417.478(e)(1)) is appropriate for fraud prevention but the rule fails to specify the timeline or process for notifying HMOs/CMPs of additions/removals to the preclusion list they must act on.

[P6] The instruction in § 417.478(e)(2) to read references to part 422 as part 417 and MA organizations as HMOs/CMPs creates interpretive complexity; stakeholders request a crosswalk table illustrating exactly which provisions and definitions apply after substitution.

[P7] The prohibition against payments to precluded individuals/entities (§ 417.484(b)(3)) is too absolute: it may prevent payment to entities with outstanding disputes; request an exception allowing temporary payment under escrow pending appeal with CMS-defined safeguards.

[P8] Requiring CMS approval for continuation area, communications, and access assurances (§ 422.54(c)(1)(i)) will lengthen plan implementation timelines; request a defined review period and a "deemed approved" remedy if CMS fails to act within X days.

[P9] The requirement that organizations describe advance-notice procedures in communication materials (§ 422.54(d)(4)(ii)) should require CMS template language to ensure consistency and avoid misleading instructions to beneficiaries.

[P10] The permissive authority for CMS to implement passive enrollment (§ 422.60(g)(1)) is broad; consumer advocates will comment that CMS must apply strict safeguards and limit usage to narrowly defined emergencies with oversight and reporting requirements.

[P11] Conditioning passive enrollment into MA–PD plans only for plans meeting listed requirements (§ 422.60(g)(2)) is reasonable, but stakeholders will seek clarification on how CMS will verify "substantially similar" networks and benefits (§ 422.60(g)(2)(ii)).

[P12] The obligation that eligible plans operate as fully integrated dual-eligible SNPs or meet a "high standard of integration" (§ 422.60(g)(2)(i)) is under-specified; request a clear definition, objective criteria, and examples of acceptable evidence of integration.

[P13] The requirement that provider/facility networks and Medicare/Medicaid-covered benefits be "substantially similar" (§ 422.60(g)(2)(ii)) is subjective; industry requests a quantitative standard (e.g., X% overlap of primary care providers and Y% overlap of institutional providers).

[P14] The 3-star minimum requirement for passive-enrollment eligibility (§ 422.60(g)(2)(iii)) could exclude many plans serving rural or high-need populations where ratings lag due to data limitations; request allowance for regional adjustments or exception for low-enrollment/new plans beyond the limited carve-outs.

[P15] The prohibition on plans that have CMS-imposed prohibitions on new enrollment being eligible for passive enrollment (§ 422.60(g)(2)(iv)) may be redundant; legal commenters will request clarity on whether temporary corrective action plans constitute a "prohibition on new enrollment."

[P16] The obligation that plans have premiums and cost-sharing limits "appropriate to full-benefit dual eligible beneficiaries" (§ 422.60(g)(2)(v)) lacks specificity; request CMS publish numeric thresholds or an algorithm used to determine appropriateness.

[P17] Requiring operational capacity and agreement to receive passively enrolled beneficiaries (§ 422.60(g)(2)(vi)) is reasonable but CMS should require plans to demonstrate capacity with documented staffing, network capacity metrics, and acceptance protocols before passive enrollment occurs.

[P18] The requirement that individuals must decline the CMS-selected plan "in a form and manner determined by CMS" to avoid passive enrollment (§ 422.60(g)(3)(i)) may pose accessibility barriers for limited-English-proficient, low-literacy, or disabled beneficiaries; CMS should require multiple modalities (phone, mail, in-person, electronic) and language assistance.

[P19] Permitting individuals to request enrollment in a different plan to avoid passive enrollment (§ 422.60(g)(3)(ii)) is beneficial but the rule must clarify timing, whether requested alternative plans must meet the same eligibility criteria, and how premium/benefit differentials are handled.

[P20] The obligation that MA organizations receiving passive enrollments must provide notices describing costs/benefits, access procedures, and how to decline or choose another plan (§ 422.60(g)(4)) should require CMS-approved plain language templates and translations for LEP populations.

[P21] The requirement that notice be provided prior to the enrollment effective date (or promptly after if impractical) in a CMS-specified form/manner (§ 422.60(g)(4)) is problematic: "as soon as possible after" is vague and could leave beneficiaries without timely information; require a maximum number of days (e.g., 14 days post-effective date) and tracking of timely delivery.

[P22] Granting a special election period to individuals passively enrolled who otherwise lack one (§ 422.60(g)(5)) is appropriate, but the rule must state the length of that special election period and whether it includes Part D actions.

[P23] The once-per-year MA election allowance during the first three months (§ 422.62(a)(3)(i)) could create churn and administrative burden; industry commenters will ask CMS to clarify exceptions and coordination rules with Part D elections to avoid duplicate processing.

[P24] Allowing the accompanying Part D coordinating election when switching MA plans during the first three months (§ 422.62(a)(3)(i)) needs clearer guidance on retroactive effective dates for Part D enrollment and how late-enrollment penalties are handled.

[P25] For newly MA-eligible enrollees allowed one change during the three-month entitlement window (§ 422.62(a)(3)(ii)), CMS should clarify interaction with employer group plans and COB (coordination of benefits) situations where mid-period changes could disrupt coverage.

[P26] The exception that single-election limits do not apply during the annual coordinated election period or special election periods (§ 422.62(a)(3)(iii)) requires clearer cross-referencing to list all qualifying special election periods to avoid confusion.

[P27] Allowing institutionalized MA-eligible individuals to change elections at any time (§ 422.62(a)(4)) is important, but CMS should require facilities to provide in-person assistance and ensure residents are free from undue influence; propose anti-steering safeguards.

[P28] The grandfathered option to elect Original Medicare once between Jan 1–Feb 14 through 2018 (§ 422.62(a)(5)) is obsolete; request deletion or clarification if any legacy processes still rely on this text.

[P29] Deeming individuals who fail to elect during the initial coverage election period as having elected Original Medicare (§ 422.66(c)(1)) may unintentionally disenroll individuals who intended to join an MA plan; recommend default outreach and an opt-in notice prior to deeming.

[P30] Allowing default enrollment into MA SNPs during the initial coverage election period only if all enumerated conditions are met (§ 422.66(c)(2)) is potentially fraught; consumer groups will request explicit safeguards and documentation requirements for each condition, especially regarding beneficiary consent.

[P31] The condition that the individual remain enrolled in an affiliated Medicaid managed care plan at time of deemed election (§ 422.66(c)(2)(A)) requires clarity about timing and what constitutes "affiliated" (same parent org, same network, contractual affiliation).

[P32] Requiring state approval and provision of information to identify eligible individuals for default enrollment (§ 422.66(c)(2)(B)) risks variability across states; request uniform data transfer standards and explicit data security and consent requirements.

[P33] The requirement that MA organizations issue the required notice to individuals prior to default enrollment (§ 422.66(c)(2)(C)) must specify minimum delivery methods, language access, and proof-of-delivery mechanisms.

[P34] Condition that individuals must not decline default enrollment or choose other coverage prior to effective date (§ 422.66(c)(2)(D)) should explicitly state how declines are documented and how CMS handles conflicting indications (e.g., returned mail plus verbal decline).

[P35] CMS approval for MA organizations to implement default enrollment (§ 422.66(c)(2)(E)) should require public posting of approvals and an appeals process for states or plans denied approval.

[P36] The obligation that MA organizations obtain CMS approval before implementing default enrollment and that CMS may suspend/rescind approval for noncompliance (§ 422.66(c)(2)(ii)) necessitates clear compliance standards, timelines for corrective action, and notice to impacted beneficiaries.

[P37] The requirement to provide detailed notification at least 60 days before default enrollment (§ 422.66(c)(2)(iv)) is a strong consumer protection, but CMS should require that the notice include plain language comparisons with prior coverage and be available in preferred languages and accessible formats.

[P38] The obligation that MA plans must accept any individual meeting enrollment-period and eligibility conditions (§ 422.66(d)(1)) needs clarity about documentation requirements and timelines for acceptance; also confirm ESRD-related protections asserted in the provision.

[P39] Allowing use of a simplified election process for seamless continuation (§ 422.66(d)(5)) is useful, but CMS should publish the simplified forms and ensure they comply with disability-accessible formats and language translation requirements.

[P40] MA local plans' cap on out-of-pocket maximums for Parts A and B not to exceed the CMS annual FFS-derived limit (§ 422.100(f)(4)) should include a clear methodology for how FFS data are translated to plan-level limits and allow for public comment on the annual limit calculation.

[P41] The special rule for local PPOs that separates network versus total catastrophic limits (§ 422.100(f)(5) parent) may create beneficiary confusion; require that plan marketing materials clearly and prominently explain in-network vs out-of-network catastrophic limits.

[P42] The requirement that the total catastrophic limit not exceed the annual CMS FFS-based limit (§ 422.100(f)(5)(ii)) may constrain network design for PPOs; insurers request transition relief when CMS revises the annual FFS-based limit.

[P43] The obligation that cost sharing for Part A/B must not exceed CMS-determined discriminatory thresholds and that CMS may use FFS and encounter data to set those thresholds (§ 422.100(f)(6)) needs transparency: CMS must publish the thresholds, methodology, and opportunity for stakeholder comment before they are applied.

[P44] Requiring MA regional plans to set in-network catastrophic out-of-pocket limits no greater than CMS's annual FFS-based limit (§ 422.101(d)(2)) could disadvantage plans serving high-cost regions; industry requests regional adjustments or risk corridors.

[P45] The obligation that MA regional plans establish a total catastrophic out-of-pocket limit covering both in-network and out-of-network benefits (§ 422.101(d)(3) parent) may cause narrow network plans to increase in-network cost sharing to meet financial targets; request guardrails to prevent discriminatory plan design.

[P46] The rule that the total out-of-pocket catastrophic limit may exceed the in-network limit but cannot increase the in-network limit and must be no greater than CMS's annual FFS-based limit (§ 422.101(d)(3)(i)) requires clear disclosure requirements so beneficiaries understand worst-case exposure when using out-of-network providers.

[P47] Allowing MA organizations to package supplemental benefits (§ 422.102(d)) raises antitrust/competition concerns if packaging limits consumer choice; consumer advocates request standards to ensure transparency of what is bundled and an unbundled price for each service.

[P48] The obligation that MA organizations disclose specified information in CMS-specified manner (§ 422.111(a)) should require CMS to provide standardized electronic data feeds (machine-readable) in addition to consumer-facing formats to facilitate third-party comparison tools.

[P49] Requiring disclosures at enrollment and annually by the first day of the annual coordinated election period (§ 422.111(a)(3)) could create duplication; industry requests flexibility to send consolidated materials and to rely on posted updates with notice instead of full re-mailings.

[P50] The obligation to provide hard copies of evidence of coverage, summary of benefits, and network information upon enrollee request even if posted online (§ 422.111(h)(2)(ii)) is appropriate, but CMS should limit the frequency of free hard-copy requests (e.g., one per year) to control administrative costs while ensuring access.

[P51] The data collection obligation for MA organizations to measure health outcomes and quality indices (§ 422.162(b)(2)) will require significant IT investments; smaller organizations request phased implementation, technical assistance, and clear measure specifications.

[P52] The requirement to provide unbiased, accurate, and complete quality data to CMS timely when requested (§ 422.162(c)(2)) must include explicit standards for timeliness, acceptable formats, and penalties only for willful noncompliance, not for data system failures.

[P53] CMS's authority to add/update/remove Star Ratings measures annually and publish Technical Notes (§ 422.164(a)) is necessary, but stakeholders demand a formal comment period and advance notice (e.g., 60 days) before new measures are used for payment or enrollment consequences.

[P54] The obligation that CMS review data quality before using the data to score or rate measures (§ 422.164(b)) should require CMS to publish data quality thresholds and a remediation process for measures that fail quality checks rather than simply excluding them ad hoc.

[P55] Reiterating that the application form must follow CMS instructions (§ 417.430(a)(1)) (duplicate of P1) — industry requests a single consolidated instruction document and machine-readable templates to reduce compliance costs.

[P56] The obligation that the application must be completed by an HMO or CMP eligible (or soon to become eligible) individual (§ 417.430(a)(1)) (duplicate of P2) should specify acceptable proof of eligibility and whether proxies (e.g., legal representatives) may sign.

[P57] Requiring authorization for disclosure between HHS/designees and HMO/CMP on the application (§ 417.430(a)(1)) (duplicate of P2) should include model language and limit the authorization to information necessary for enrollment and program integrity.

[P58] Requiring cost contracts to agree to be rated under MA quality systems (§ 417.472(k)) (duplicate of P3) — request that CMS clarify whether Part D-specific measures apply to cost contracts that do not offer Part D.

[P59] The exception to exclude inapplicable measures for cost contracts (§ 417.472(k)) (duplicate of P4) should be accompanied by an appeals process if CMS determines a measure is applicable.

[P60] Extending payment-preclusion rules to HMOs/CMPs (§ 417.478(e)(1)) (duplicate of P5) — legal commenters will analyze preclusion notice and due-process rights and request codified procedures for HMOs/CMPs to contest erroneous listings.

[P61] The interpretive substitution rule for applying part 422 provisions to part 417 (§ 417.478(e)(2)) (duplicate of P6) creates a need for consolidated guidance and example scenarios demonstrating application to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P62] The payment prohibition to precluded entities (§ 417.484(b)(3)) (duplicate of P7) — propose that CMS allow emergency payments to prevent interruption of beneficiary services when a provider is newly listed, paired with later recovery if preclusion is upheld.

[P63] The "substantially similar" network/benefit requirement for continuation area/MA organizations (§ 422.54(c)(1)(ii)) (duplicate of P13) may be impossible in some Medicaid-managed care transitions; suggest objective metrics (provider counts, geographic coverage percentage) for "substantially similar."

[P64] The requirement to obtain CMS approval for continuation area, communications, and access assurances (§ 422.54(c)(1)(i)) (duplicate of P8) should allow conditional approvals with required remediation plans rather than flat denials.

[P65] The requirement that organizations describe advance-notice procedures in communications (§ 422.54(d)(4)(ii)) (duplicate of P9) should mandate that notices be sent in multiple modalities and include a toll-free number for assistance.

[P66] The permissive listing that CMS may use passive enrollment under defined circumstances (§ 422.60(g)(1)) (duplicate of P10) — request CMS publish an annual passive-enrollment plan and post-implementation evaluations.

[P67] The enumeration of circumstances where passive enrollment may be applied, including immediate terminations and potential harm (§ 422.60(g)(1)(i)-(iii)) (duplicate of P67) requires defined thresholds for "potential harm" and a beneficiary-level risk assessment standard.

[P68] The limitation that passive enrollment under (g)(1)(iii) applies only to MA–PD plans that satisfy requirements (§ 422.60(g)(2)) (duplicate of P11) should include CMS verification steps and a public list of eligible receiving plans.

[P69] The requirement that recipient plans have at least a 3-star rating or qualify as low-enrollment/new plans (§ 422.60(g)(2)(iii)) (duplicate of P14) — propose that CMS allow appeals or exceptions for plans improving quality metrics with documented action plans.

[P70] The condition that plans must have no CMS-imposed prohibition on new enrollment (§ 422.60(g)(2)(iv)) (duplicate of P15) should clarify if plans under informal remediation but without formal new-enrollment prohibition are still eligible.

[P71] The obligation that plans have premiums/cost-sharing appropriate to full-benefit dual eligibles (§ 422.60(g)(2)(v)) (duplicate of P16) demands CMS publish numeric ceilings or an actuarial equivalence standard.

[P72] The requirement that plans be operationally ready and agree to accept passively enrolled beneficiaries (§ 422.60(g)(2)(vi)) (duplicate of P17) should include certification timelines and penalties for plans that later refuse enrollees.

[P73] The default-deemed election approach unless beneficiaries take specified actions (§ 422.60(g)(3)) (duplicate of P73) raises due process concerns; consumer advocates request opt-out reminders via trusted intermediaries (e.g., State Medicaid agencies) and independent beneficiary advocates.

[P74] The permission for individuals to decline the CMS-selected plan only in CMS-specified form/manner (§ 422.60(g)(3)(i)) (duplicate of P18) — require CMS to accept verbal declinations via recorded phone line and in-person forms at Title XIX/XX agencies.

[P75] The permission to request enrollment in another plan to avoid default enrollment (§ 422.60(g)(3)(ii)) (duplicate of P19) — CMS should ensure alternative plan selection tools are accessible and updated in real time.

[P76] The obligation for MA organizations to provide notices describing costs/benefits/access and options (§ 422.60(g)(4)) (duplicate of P20) — require inclusion of provider continuity information (whether current PCP and specialists are in-network) in the notice.

[P77] The timing requirement that the notice be provided prior to the effective date or as soon as possible thereafter (§ 422.60(g)(4)) (duplicate of P21) — request a requirement that notices be provided at least 30 days prior when passive enrollment is not due to an immediate termination.

[P78] The obligation to provide a special election period for passively enrolled individuals without an otherwise-available SEP (§ 422.60(g)(5)) (duplicate of P22) — request CMS define the SEP start and end dates and permit auto-termination of passive enrollment if SEP timely used.

[P79] The once-per-year election during first three months permission (§ 422.62(a)(3)) (duplicate of P23) — consumer groups warn this could be exploited by brokers and request strong anti-steering rules and conflict-of-interest disclosures.

[P80] The condition that failure to elect during the initial coverage election period results in default to Original Medicare (§ 422.62(c)(1)) (duplicate of P29) — request CMS require proactive outreach to new eligibles (e.g., welcome calls) before defaulting them.

[P81] The permission allowing newly eligible individuals one change during their entitlement-period window (§ 422.62(c)(1)(ii)) (duplicate of P25) — ask CMS to clarify coordination with employer/union coverage and retroactive entitlements.

[P82] The cumulative condition set (A–E) for default enrollment into MA-SNPs during initial coverage (§ 422.62(c)(2) / § 422.66(c)(2)) (duplicate of P82) — legal commenters will request that CMS require beneficiary affirmative consent in addition to the enumerated conditions for ethical and constitutional reasons.

[P83] The obligation that MA organizations obtain CMS approval for default enrollment and face suspension/rescission for noncompliance (§ 422.66(c)(ii)/ (iii)) (duplicate of P36) — request a transparent process for CMS approvals, public posting, and opportunity to cure prior to suspension.

[P84] The 60-day prior notice obligation for default enrollment (§ 422.66(c)(iv)) (duplicate of P37) — ask CMS to require that notices include an individualized cost estimate comparing default plan to current coverage.

[P85] The obligation that MA plans accept any eligible individual requesting enrollment during initial coverage (§ 422.66(d)(1)) (duplicate of P85) — request CMS clarify how this interacts with network adequacy limits and provider panel capacity.

[P86] The permission to use a CMS-approved simplified election process for seamless continuation (§ 422.66(d)(5)) (duplicate of P86) — request CMS publish simplified election forms and ensure they allow for authorized representatives to act.

[P87] The rules about effectiveness dates for elections during initial coverage periods (§ 422.68(a)(1)-(2)) (duplicate of P87) — ask CMS to clarify retroactivity when elections and entitlement months overlap and provide examples for beneficiaries and enrollment brokers.

[P88] The obligation that MA regional plans set in-network catastrophic OOP limits no greater than CMS's FFS-based limit (§ 422.101(d)(2)) (duplicate of P88) — request explicit treatment for emergency services obtained out-of-network and how those amounts apply to the OOP limit.

[P89] The obligation that MA regional plans set a total catastrophic limit for all benefits not to exceed the in-network annual limit set by CMS (§ 422.101(d)(3)) (duplicate of P89) — request a prohibition on plans structuring non-covered supplemental benefits in a way that shifts costs to beneficiaries to avoid OOP limits.

[P90] The local PPO total catastrophic limit obligation with network-use limit applying only to network providers (§ 422.101(f)(5)) (duplicate of P90) — request explicit disclosure examples in Summary of Benefits showing in-network vs total catastrophic scenarios.

[P91] The prohibition that cost-sharing must not exceed CMS-determined discriminatory thresholds (§ 422.101(f)(6)/(f)(6) duplicate of P43/P91) — legal advocates request details on how CMS defines "discriminatory" and the appeal rights for beneficiaries who experience disparate impacts.

[P92] The permission to package supplemental benefits (§ 422.102(d)) (duplicate of P47) — consumer groups request that when benefits are grouped, plans must provide an itemized alternative price so consumers can compare value.

[P93] The obligation to disclose required information at enrollment and annually in CMS-specified manner (§ 422.111(a)/(a)(3)) (duplicate of P48/P49/P93) — request that CMS require machine-readable standardized data elements for all required disclosures to facilitate third-party tools and audits.

[P94] The obligation to provide hard copies upon request (§ 422.111(h)(2)(ii)) (duplicate of P50/P94) — advocates request that "upon request" includes proactive offer of paper to beneficiaries over age 85 and those identified as digitally disadvantaged.

[P95] The quality data collection obligation (§ 422.162(b)(1)/(b)(2)/(b)(3) duplicates of P51/P95/P96/P97) — call for clear guidance on data submission formats, protection of PHI, and timeline for consolidated reporting changes when contracts consolidate.

[P96] The obligation that MA organizations supply unbiased, accurate, complete quality data that reflect enrollment post-consolidation (§ 422.162(b)(1)/(b)(3)/P96) — ask CMS to publish the enrollment-weighted methodology and examples used for QBP and consolidated rating calculations.

[P97] The specified method for calculating QBP status for consolidated contracts using enrollment-weighted means in year one and consolidated Star Ratings later (§ 422.162(b)(3)(ii)-(iv)/P97) should have an appeal mechanism for plans that believe weighting misstates performance due to extraordinary events (e.g., hurricane-related enrollment shifts).

[P98] The obligation in § 423.128(a)(3) to provide applicable information at enrollment and annually by the first day of the annual coordinated election period (P98) should require harmonization with § 422.111 timing to avoid duplicate mailings and beneficiary confusion; request CMS provide consolidated timing rules.

[P99] Across multiple provisions, CMS relies on undefined terms ("substantially similar," "appropriate," "operational capacity," "timely") — request CMS include a definitions section with objective metrics or examples to ensure consistent application.

[P100] Many provisions create potential beneficiary confusion (e.g., passive/default enrollment, default SNP enrollment, special election periods); recommend CMS fund a robust beneficiary education campaign, stakeholder webinars, and a public FAQ to accompany the final rule.

Requiring CMS approval of the application form under § 417.430(a)(1) gives CMS unilateral control over content and format that may conflict with state licensing forms and should include a mechanism to resolve conflicts with state-required language.

The obligation that the applicant "complete the application" and be an HMO or CMP eligible (or soon to become eligible) individual (§ 417.430(a)(1)) is vague with respect to "soon to become eligible"; please define the timeframe and documentary evidence required.

Requiring applicants to include authorization for disclosure between HHS/designees and the HMO/CMP in every application (§ 417.430(a)(1)) may run afoul of state privacy laws and should include a specification of the scope, retention limits, and a model authorization form.

Requiring all section 1876 cost contracts to agree to be rated under MA and Part D quality rating systems (§ 417.472(k)) imposes significant measurement burdens on small cost contracts that historically did not report MA measures; CMS should phase in this requirement or provide technical assistance and funding.

The exception that cost contracts need not submit data on measures CMS deems inapplicable (§ 417.472(k)) lacks clear criteria for "inapplicable" and "lacking available data"; CMS should publish objective criteria and a predictable process for determinations.

Extending payment-preclusion list prohibitions to HMOs and CMPs (§ 417.478(e)(1)) is appropriate for fraud prevention but the rule fails to specify the timeline or process for notifying HMOs/CMPs of additions/removals to the preclusion list they must act on.

The instruction in § 417.478(e)(2) to read references to part 422 as part 417 and MA organizations as HMOs/CMPs creates interpretive complexity; stakeholders request a crosswalk table illustrating exactly which provisions and definitions apply after substitution.

The prohibition against payments to precluded individuals/entities (§ 417.484(b)(3)) is too absolute: it may prevent payment to entities with outstanding disputes; request an exception allowing temporary payment under escrow pending appeal with CMS-defined safeguards.

Requiring CMS approval for continuation area, communications, and access assurances (§ 422.54(c)(1)(i)) will lengthen plan implementation timelines; request a defined review period and a "deemed approved" remedy if CMS fails to act within X days.

The requirement that organizations describe advance-notice procedures in communication materials (§ 422.54(d)(4)(ii)) should require CMS template language to ensure consistency and avoid misleading instructions to beneficiaries.

The permissive authority for CMS to implement passive enrollment (§ 422.60(g)(1)) is broad; consumer advocates will comment that CMS must apply strict safeguards and limit usage to narrowly defined emergencies with oversight and reporting requirements.

Conditioning passive enrollment into MA–PD plans only for plans meeting listed requirements (§ 422.60(g)(2)) is reasonable, but stakeholders will seek clarification on how CMS will verify "substantially similar" networks and benefits (§ 422.60(g)(2)(ii)).

The obligation that eligible plans operate as fully integrated dual-eligible SNPs or meet a "high standard of integration" (§ 422.60(g)(2)(i)) is under-specified; request a clear definition, objective criteria, and examples of acceptable evidence of integration.

The requirement that provider/facility networks and Medicare/Medicaid-covered benefits be "substantially similar" (§ 422.60(g)(2)(ii)) is subjective; industry requests a quantitative standard (e.g., X% overlap of primary care providers and Y% overlap of institutional providers).

The 3-star minimum requirement for passive-enrollment eligibility (§ 422.60(g)(2)(iii)) could exclude many plans serving rural or high-need populations where ratings lag due to data limitations; request allowance for regional adjustments or exception for low-enrollment/new plans beyond the limited carve-outs.

The prohibition on plans that have CMS-imposed prohibitions on new enrollment being eligible for passive enrollment (§ 422.60(g)(2)(iv)) may be redundant; legal commenters will request clarity on whether temporary corrective action plans constitute a "prohibition on new enrollment."

The obligation that plans have premiums and cost-sharing limits "appropriate to full-benefit dual eligible beneficiaries" (§ 422.60(g)(2)(v)) lacks specificity; request CMS publish numeric thresholds or an algorithm used to determine appropriateness.

Requiring operational capacity and agreement to receive passively enrolled beneficiaries (§ 422.60(g)(2)(vi)) is reasonable but CMS should require plans to demonstrate capacity with documented staffing, network capacity metrics, and acceptance protocols before passive enrollment occurs.

The requirement that individuals must decline the CMS-selected plan "in a form and manner determined by CMS" to avoid passive enrollment (§ 422.60(g)(3)(i)) may pose accessibility barriers for limited-English-proficient, low-literacy, or disabled beneficiaries; CMS should require multiple modalities (phone, mail, in-person, electronic) and language assistance.

Permitting individuals to request enrollment in a different plan to avoid passive enrollment (§ 422.60(g)(3)(ii)) is beneficial but the rule must clarify timing, whether requested alternative plans must meet the same eligibility criteria, and how premium/benefit differentials are handled.

The obligation that MA organizations receiving passive enrollments must provide notices describing costs/benefits, access procedures, and how to decline or choose another plan (§ 422.60(g)(4)) should require CMS-approved plain language templates and translations for LEP populations.

Extending payment-preclusion rules to HMOs/CMPs (§ 417.478(e)(1)) (duplicate of P5) — legal commenters will analyze preclusion notice and due-process rights and request codified procedures for HMOs/CMPs to contest erroneous listings.

The interpretive substitution rule for applying part 422 provisions to part 417 (§ 417.478(e)(2)) (duplicate of P6) creates a need for consolidated guidance and example scenarios demonstrating application to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

The payment prohibition to precluded entities (§ 417.484(b)(3)) (duplicate of P7) — propose that CMS allow emergency payments to prevent interruption of beneficiary services when a provider is newly listed, paired with later recovery if preclusion is upheld.

The "substantially similar" network/benefit requirement for continuation area/MA organizations (§ 422.54(c)(1)(ii)) (duplicate of P13) may be impossible in some Medicaid-managed care transitions; suggest objective metrics (provider counts, geographic coverage percentage) for "substantially similar."

The requirement to obtain CMS approval for continuation area, communications, and access assurances (§ 422.54(c)(1)(i)) (duplicate of P8) should allow conditional approvals with required remediation plans rather than flat denials.

The requirement that organizations describe advance-notice procedures in communications (§ 422.54(d)(4)(ii)) (duplicate of P9) should mandate that notices be sent in multiple modalities and include a toll-free number for assistance.

The permissive listing that CMS may use passive enrollment under defined circumstances (§ 422.60(g)(1)) (duplicate of P10) — request CMS publish an annual passive-enrollment plan and post-implementation evaluations.

The enumeration of circumstances where passive enrollment may be applied, including immediate terminations and potential harm (§ 422.60(g)(1)(i)-(iii)) (duplicate of P67) requires defined thresholds for "potential harm" and a beneficiary-level risk assessment standard.

The limitation that passive enrollment under (g)(1)(iii) applies only to MA–PD plans that satisfy requirements (§ 422.60(g)(2)) (duplicate of P11) should include CMS verification steps and a public list of eligible receiving plans.

The requirement that recipient plans have at least a 3-star rating or qualify as low-enrollment/new plans (§ 422.60(g)(2)(iii)) (duplicate of P14) — propose that CMS allow appeals or exceptions for plans improving quality metrics with documented action plans.

The condition that plans must have no CMS-imposed prohibition on new enrollment (§ 422.60(g)(2)(iv)) (duplicate of P15) should clarify if plans under informal remediation but without formal new-enrollment prohibition are still eligible.

The obligation that plans have premiums/cost-sharing appropriate to full-benefit dual eligibles (§ 422.60(g)(2)(v)) (duplicate of P16) demands CMS publish numeric ceilings or an actuarial equivalence standard.

The requirement that plans be operationally ready and agree to accept passively enrolled beneficiaries (§ 422.60(g)(2)(vi)) (duplicate of P17) should include certification timelines and penalties for plans that later refuse enrollees.

The default-deemed election approach unless beneficiaries take specified actions (§ 422.60(g)(3)) (duplicate of P73) raises due process concerns; consumer advocates request opt-out reminders via trusted intermediaries (e.g., State Medicaid agencies) and independent beneficiary advocates.

The permission for individuals to decline the CMS-selected plan only in CMS-specified form/manner (§ 422.60(g)(3)(i)) (duplicate of P18) — require CMS to accept verbal declinations via recorded phone line and in-person forms at Title XIX/XX agencies.

The permission to request enrollment in another plan to avoid default enrollment (§ 422.60(g)(3)(ii)) (duplicate of P19) — CMS should ensure alternative plan selection tools are accessible and updated in real time.

The obligation for MA organizations to provide notices describing costs/benefits/access and options (§ 422.60(g)(4)) (duplicate of P20) — require inclusion of provider continuity information (whether current PCP and specialists are in-network) in the notice.

The timing requirement that the notice be provided prior to the effective date or as soon as possible thereafter (§ 422.60(g)(4)) (duplicate of P21) — request a requirement that notices be provided at least 30 days prior when passive enrollment is not due to an immediate termination.

The obligation to provide a special election period for passively enrolled individuals without an otherwise-available SEP (§ 422.60(g)(5)) (duplicate of P22) — request CMS define the SEP start and end dates and permit auto-termination of passive enrollment if SEP timely used.

The once-per-year election during first three months permission (§ 422.62(a)(3)) (duplicate of P23) — consumer groups warn this could be exploited by brokers and request strong anti-steering rules and conflict-of-interest disclosures.

The condition that failure to elect during the initial coverage election period results in default to Original Medicare (§ 422.62(c)(1)) (duplicate of P29) — request CMS require proactive outreach to new eligibles (e.g., welcome calls) before defaulting them.

The permission allowing newly eligible individuals one change during their entitlement-period window (§ 422.62(c)(1)(ii)) (duplicate of P25) — ask CMS to clarify coordination with employer/union coverage and retroactive entitlements.

The cumulative condition set (A–E) for default enrollment into MA-SNPs during initial coverage (§ 422.62(c)(2) / § 422.66(c)(2)) (duplicate of P82) — legal commenters will request that CMS require beneficiary affirmative consent in addition to the enumerated conditions for ethical and constitutional reasons.

The obligation that MA organizations obtain CMS approval for default enrollment and face suspension/rescission for noncompliance (§ 422.66(c)(ii)/ (iii)) (duplicate of P36) — request a transparent process for CMS approvals, public posting, and opportunity to cure prior to suspension.

The 60-day prior notice obligation for default enrollment (§ 422.66(c)(iv)) (duplicate of P37) — ask CMS to require that notices include an individualized cost estimate comparing default plan to current coverage.

The obligation that MA plans accept any eligible individual requesting enrollment during initial coverage (§ 422.66(d)(1)) (duplicate of P85) — request CMS clarify how this interacts with network adequacy limits and provider panel capacity.

The permission to use a CMS-approved simplified election process for seamless continuation (§ 422.66(d)(5)) (duplicate of P86) — request CMS publish simplified election forms and ensure they allow for authorized representatives to act.

The rules about effectiveness dates for elections during initial coverage periods (§ 422.68(a)(1)-(2)) (duplicate of P87) — ask CMS to clarify retroactivity when elections and entitlement months overlap and provide examples for beneficiaries and enrollment brokers.

The obligation that MA regional plans set in-network catastrophic OOP limits no greater than CMS's FFS-based limit (§ 422.101(d)(2)) (duplicate of P88) — request explicit treatment for emergency services obtained out-of-network and how those amounts apply to the OOP limit.

The obligation that MA regional plans set a total catastrophic limit for all benefits not to exceed the in-network annual limit set by CMS (§ 422.101(d)(3)) (duplicate of P89) — request a prohibition on plans structuring non-covered supplemental benefits in a way that shifts costs to beneficiaries to avoid OOP limits.

The local PPO total catastrophic limit obligation with network-use limit applying only to network providers (§ 422.101(f)(5)) (duplicate of P90) — request explicit disclosure examples in Summary of Benefits showing in-network vs total catastrophic scenarios.

The prohibition that cost-sharing must not exceed CMS-determined discriminatory thresholds (§ 422.101(f)(6)/(f)(6) duplicate of P43/P91) — legal advocates request details on how CMS defines "discriminatory" and the appeal rights for beneficiaries who experience disparate impacts.

The permission to package supplemental benefits (§ 422.102(d)) (duplicate of P47) — consumer groups request that when benefits are grouped, plans must provide an itemized alternative price so consumers can compare value.

The obligation to disclose required information at enrollment and annually in CMS-specified manner (§ 422.111(a)/(a)(3)) (duplicate of P48/P49/P93) — request that CMS require machine-readable standardized data elements for all required disclosures to facilitate third-party tools and audits.

The obligation to provide hard copies upon request (§ 422.111(h)(2)(ii)) (duplicate of P50/P94) — advocates request that "upon request" includes proactive offer of paper to beneficiaries over age 85 and those identified as digitally disadvantaged.

The quality data collection obligation (§ 422.162(b)(1)/(b)(2)/(b)(3) duplicates of P51/P95/P96/P97) — call for clear guidance on data submission formats, protection of PHI, and timeline for consolidated reporting changes when contracts consolidate.

The obligation that MA organizations supply unbiased, accurate, complete quality data that reflect enrollment post-consolidation (§ 422.162(b)(1)/(b)(3)/P96) — ask CMS to publish the enrollment-weighted methodology and examples used for QBP and consolidated rating calculations.

The specified method for calculating QBP status for consolidated contracts using enrollment-weighted means in year one and consolidated Star Ratings later (§ 422.162(b)(3)(ii)-(iv)/P97) should have an appeal mechanism for plans that believe weighting misstates performance due to extraordinary events (e.g., hurricane-related enrollment shifts).

The obligation in § 423.128(a)(3) to provide applicable information at enrollment and annually by the first day of the annual coordinated election period (P98) should require harmonization with § 422.111 timing to avoid duplicate mailings and beneficiary confusion; request CMS provide consolidated timing rules.

Across multiple provisions, CMS relies on undefined terms ("substantially similar," "appropriate," "operational capacity," "timely") — request CMS include a definitions section with objective metrics or examples to ensure consistent application.

Many provisions create potential beneficiary confusion (e.g., passive/default enrollment, default SNP enrollment, special election periods); recommend CMS fund a robust beneficiary education campaign, stakeholder webinars, and a public FAQ to accompany the final rule.

[P1] The deadline of September 29, 2017 to receive comments (P1) is obsolete and confusing given the AD's effective date; extend or clarify the comment period to allow current stakeholders adequate time to respond.

[P1] Stakeholders may have missed the September 29, 2017 deadline (P1); the FAA should reopen the comment period or explicitly accept late submissions received for good cause.

[P2] The blanket obligation to "comply with all requirements within the specified compliance times" (P2) lacks guidance about how operators should document compliance when multiple, overlapping compliance windows exist.

[P2] The AD should clarify whether compliance time tolerances and known maintenance scheduling practices (e.g., maintenance checks spanning days) are acceptable under P2, or whether discrete completion dates are required.

[P3] Requiring electrical power deactivation "at the latest of" several dates (P3) creates operational uncertainty; the FAA should allow the earliest applicable date to be used instead of the latest.

[P4] The 120‑day window after the "last deactivation per MOM" (P4) is vague because operators may not have access to Boeing MOM records; the AD should define what constitutes the "last deactivation" and how to document it.

[P4] Compliance deadline in P4 should be counted from the operator's performance log date, not from proprietary Boeing MOM records that operators may not control.

[P5] The 120‑day requirement after issuance of the original certificate of airworthiness (P5) is unfair to older aircraft where that issuance date occurred long before this AD; clarify intent or provide an alternative reference date.

[P6] The requirement to accomplish deactivation within 7 days after May 1, 2015 (P6) is impossible to meet for operators who received the AD after that date; provide relief or acknowledge prior compliance credit explicitly.

[P7] Repeating electrical power deactivation every 120 days until software installation (P7) imposes significant operational and maintenance burdens and potential dispatch reliability impacts; request extension of intervals or allowance to align with scheduled maintenance checks.

[P7] The AD should provide explicit allowances for scheduling the recurring deactivations to coincide with overnight maintenance to minimize operational impact (P7).

[P8] Permitting APU and main batteries to remain connected during deactivation (P8) may not mitigate the safety issue the AD intends to address; require disconnect or provide engineering rationale and risk assessment justifying this exception.

[P8] Operators need explicit procedural guidance (lockout/tagout, safety checklists) if batteries can remain connected (P8); the AD's silence creates ambiguity and potential safety risk.

[P9] The 12‑month deadline to install new OPS into all six GCUs (P9) is aggressive for small carriers and third‑party maintenance providers given parts lead times and limited ODA capacity; request extension to 18–24 months or allow staged compliance by serial number groups.

[P9] The AD should state whether one GCU software update can be installed at a time during scheduled checks, or whether all six must be completed in the same maintenance event (P9).

[P10] Requiring all corrective actions to be completed before further flight (P10) is reasonable for safety, but the AD should define which corrective actions may be deferred under approved AMOCs to avoid grounding aircraft for non‑critical items.

[P11] Termination of recurring deactivation obligation upon completion for all six GCUs (P11) is appropriate, but the AD should allow termination when a documented acceptable combination of hardware/software changes is installed (e.g., if an STC changes configuration), not only the six‑GCU OPS.

[P12] Requiring Group 1 airplanes to perform (i)(1) actions "before or concurrently" with paragraph (h) (P12) could force operators to sequence complex maintenance in one visit; allow flexibility to perform related installs within a short window (e.g., 30 days) rather than strictly simultaneous.

[P13] Installation of the new fuel quantity management program and software checks (P13) must be accompanied by clear acceptance test criteria; the AD should specify expected test results or reference the exact test procedures from the Boeing SB.

[P14] The requirement to perform corrective actions and repeat checks until software passes (P14) is acceptable, but the AD must clarify what constitutes an acceptable corrective action and whether software rollbacks to previous versions are permitted pending resolution.

[P15] Requiring installation of CICD 9.3 software (P15) may have unintended interoperability effects with airline‑specific avionics; request validation data showing compatibility and any required configuration changes.

[P16] The "repeat checks until pass" requirement for CICD 9.3 (P16) should include allowable troubleshooting steps and an approved path for flight with restrictions (e.g., ferry flight) if immediate rectification is impossible.

[P17] For Group 2 airplanes, mandating CICD 9.3 installation before or at the same time as paragraph (h) (P17) may duplicate work already done under prior service actions; the AD should more clearly identify which serial numbers are affected and accept prior equivalent actions.

[P18] The AD's requirement to do corrective actions before further flight after failed checks for Group 2 (P18) may be clearer if the AD defines an explicit process for applying for ferry or maintenance‑only flights under an AMOC.

[P19] Granting credit for prior actions done under Boeing SB Issue 001 for Group 1 and 3 (P19) is helpful but should be extended to any operator who can demonstrate equivalency via maintenance records even if a slightly different SB revision was used.

[P20] The conditional credit for Group 2 prior actions (P20) imposes a 12‑month follow‑up burden; request the FAA allow a reasonable extension (e.g., 180 days) for operators who face part or labor scheduling constraints.

[P21] The condition that additional actions in the other service bulletin must be done within 12 months (P21) lacks an exception for aircraft out of service or stored; permit extensions for parked or stored aircraft.

[P22] Centralizing AMOC approval authority with the Seattle ACO Branch Manager (P22) is reasonable but may create processing delays for international operators; allow delegation or specify expected turnaround times for AMOC requests.

[P23] Requiring submission of AMOC requests through principal inspectors or local FSDOs (P23) may be burdensome for non‑US operators; clarify acceptable direct submission channels for foreign operators and maintenance organizations.

[P24] When sending information directly to the certification office manager, the AD should provide full contact details and an electronic submission process to avoid delays (P24).

[P25] Permitting AMOC requests to be emailed (P25) is useful; request that the FAA publish the expected acknowledgment timeline and processing SLAs for emailed AMOC submissions.

[P26] The obligation to notify principal inspectors before using an approved AMOC (P26) should clarify required documentation and timelines for such notification to ensure regulatory compliance.

[P27] Allowing Boeing ODA to approve AMOCs for repairs/modifications required by the AD (P27) raises potential conflict‑of‑interest concerns; request FAA oversight requirements and documentation standards for Boeing ODA approvals.

[P28] The requirement that Boeing ODA approvals meet the airplane certification basis and specifically reference the AD (P28) should include guidance for operators if airplane certification basis has been amended by previous STCs.

[P29] Recognizing previously approved AMOCs for AD 2015–09–07 as acceptable for corresponding paragraph (g) provisions (P29) is logical, but the AD should require operators to revalidate that the previously approved AMOC remains applicable to any changed configuration.

[P30] The mandatory requirement to perform all steps labeled "RC" (P30) should be accompanied by a clear list in the AD of which steps are RC; operators must have unambiguous identification to avoid inadvertent noncompliance.

[P31] The "RC Exempt" labeling exception (P31) could be abused if OEM documentation is inconsistent; require that the AD explicitly list RC‑Exempt steps or include the referenced service bulletin pages.

[P32] Requiring an AMOC for any deviations to RC steps (P32) is necessary for safety, but the AD should specify an expedited AMOC process for minor, time‑critical deviations to avoid grounding aircraft.

[P33] Allowing deviation from non‑RC steps using operator maintenance program methods (P33) is reasonable, but the AD should require operators to document such deviations and retain records for FAA audit.

[P34] The condition that RC steps remain achievable and airplane can be returned to airworthy condition (P34) should be clarified to allow temporary deviations that do not impact critical safety functions, with appropriate recordkeeping and oversight.

[P1] Industry commenter: Requiring the wage index to be applied based on facility urban/rural location (§413.337(b)(4)(i)) will disadvantage SNFs that serve mixed or catchment-area populations; CMS should clarify how facilities that span urban and rural designations will be categorized and whether a blended wage index is permitted.

[P1] Labor union: Tying standardization to the wage index (§413.337(b)(4)(i)) without updating the underlying occupational wage data annually risks undercounting real wage growth; CMS should require more frequent wage index updates or an adjustment factor to reflect recent labor market changes.

[P2] Rural SNF association: The 95% floor on year-to-year wage index decreases (§413.337(b)(4)(ii)) starting Oct 1, 2022 is insufficient to prevent funding instability in rural SNFs experiencing multiple-year declines; CMS should consider a higher floor (e.g., 97.5% or 100%) or multi-year smoothing.

[P2] Budget advocacy group: The cap that prevents wage index declines below 95% of prior FY (§413.337(b)(4)(ii)) will perpetuate disparities by delaying needed reallocations of Medicare funds to higher-cost areas; CMS should justify the fiscal impact and distributional consequences.

[P3] Provider trade group: Standardizing cost data for facility case-mix using case-mix indices (§413.337(b)(4)(iii)) requires full transparency on which case-mix indices and other facility data will be used; CMS should publish the full algorithm and weighting before implementation.

[P3] Clinical advocates: Reliance on existing case-mix indices (§413.337(b)(4)(iii)) may not capture social risk factors or dual-eligible patients who increase resource use; CMS should incorporate an adjustment for socio-economic status or dual-eligibility.

[P4] Legal expert: The statement that the SNF VBP Program applies to “facilities described in section 1888(e)(7)(B)” (§413.338(b)) needs explicit cross-references and definitions in the regulation to avoid ambiguity about inclusion of specialized SNFs (e.g., LTCH-affiliated or hospital-based units).

[P5] Small facility operator: Excluding SNFs from VBP for a fiscal year if they lack the minimum number of cases for each measure (§413.338(b)(1)) could disproportionately exclude small and rural providers; CMS should publish the minimum case thresholds and provide an appeals process.

[P6] Patient advocacy group: Excluding SNFs that lack the minimum number of measures (§413.338(b)(2)) will remove incentives for quality improvement in facilities serving small populations; CMS should create alternative reporting pathways or composite measures to include low-volume SNFs.

[P7] Fiscal watchdog: Setting aside “at least 60%” of the reduction for value-based incentive payments (§413.338(c)(2)(i)) lacks precise accounting controls; CMS must define “at least” and provide annual public accounting of withheld amounts and distribution.

[P8] Rural health coalition: Increasing the total VBP pool to account for assigning performance scores to low-volume SNFs (§413.338(c)(2)(i) specification) is appropriate, but CMS must specify the methodology and magnitude of the increase to ensure predictability for providers.

[P9] SNF association: Fixing the FY2023 VBP pool at 60% of the reduction (§413.338(c)(2)(i) FY2023 specification) without phase-in analyses of payment impacts could create sudden payment changes; CMS should provide facility-level impact estimates before finalizing.

[P10] Compliance officer: Assigning a performance score to low-volume SNFs for FY2019–FY2022 that produces a payment equal to the adjusted Federal per diem rate (§413.338(d)(3)) requires clarity on whether other payment adjustments (e.g., facility-level add-ons under §413.337(f)) are applied subsequently; provide worked examples.

[P11] Quality measurement expert: CMS’s authority to designate measures annually (§413.338(d)(5)) should be accompanied by objective criteria for measure selection (validity, reliability, risk-adjustment adequacy) and a formal public notice-and-comment process before measures are adopted each year.

[P12] Provider association: Announcing performance standards only 60 days before a performance period (§413.338(d)(6)(i)) is insufficient lead time for SNFs to implement process changes; CMS should extend the notice period to at least 120 days.

[P13] Data integrity advocate: The policy to correct discovered calculation errors in published performance standards (§413.338(d)(6)(ii)) is necessary, but CMS must commit to a transparent correction log showing what changed and why for stakeholder review.

[P14] Legal observer: The prohibition on making further updates if additional errors are discovered for the same fiscal year (§413.338(d)(6)(ii) exception) is arbitrary and could lock in erroneous standards; CMS should instead allow iterative corrections with clear versioning and justification.

[P15] Facility quality officer: Requiring SNFs to meet minimum case counts to receive points on a measure (§413.338(e)(1)) compounds exclusions and reduces comparability; CMS should allow partial credit or statistical shrinkage methods for low case volumes.

[P16] Measurement specialist: Awarding 1–9 achievement points between achievement threshold and benchmark (§413.338(e)(1)(i)) needs specification of the scoring scale (linear or non-linear) and rounding rules; CMS must publish exact point allocation formulas.

[P17] Consumer group: Awarding 10 achievement points only when a benchmark is met (§413.338(e)(1)(ii)) may create cliff effects; CMS should consider graduated bonus above the benchmark to reward continuous improvement.

[P18] Quality improvement network: Awarding 0–9 improvement points (§413.338(e)(1)(iii)) should account for regression-to-the-mean and random variation; CMS must use reliability weighting when calculating improvement points.

[P19] Statisticians: Not awarding improvement points if the SNF fails to meet baseline case minimums (§413.338(e)(1)(iv)) will penalize facilities with historically low volumes; CMS should allow pooling of multiple baseline years to reach the minimum.

[P20] Policy analyst: Using the higher of achievement and improvement scores as the measure score (§413.338(e)(1)(v)) is reasonable, but CMS should explain tie-breaking and how this interacts with composite scoring across measures.

[P21] Auditor: The multi-step method to calculate a SNF performance score (§413.338(e)(2)) needs full transparency, including weighting of measures, treatment of missing measures, and normalization procedure to 100 points.

[P22] Legal counsel: Summing points across measures to calculate a point total (§413.338(e)(2)(i)) raises fairness concerns if measures are correlated; CMS should disclose whether measures are weighted equally or adjusted for redundancy.

[P31] Rural SNF: Withholding any public information if a SNF lacks the performance-period case minimum (§413.338(f)(4)(ii)) will leave consumers without data on small providers; CMS should allow reporting with statistical caveats or pooled aggregates.

[P34] Quality expert: Calculating SNF readmission measure rates for each SNF using FY2023 data (§413.338(i)(1)(a)) requires that CMS disclose the readmission definition, risk adjustment variables, and the claims look-back window.

[P38] Quality improvement group: Providing confidential feedback reports on the SNF readmission measure for FY2023 (§413.338(i)(3)) is useful, but CMS should permit SNFs to submit corrections for claims-based readmission flags given known claims coding variability.

[P39] Public reporting advocate: Publicly reporting SNF readmission performance in accordance with paragraph (f)(3) for FY2023 (§413.338(i)(4)) should include clear notices indicating that FY2023 scores are not used for incentive payments (or explain if they are), to avoid misinterpretation by consumers.

[P40] Medicare Administrative Contractor (MAC) organization: Requiring MACs to validate claims-reported SNFRM information beginning FY2023 (§413.338(j)(1)) imposes significant operational burdens; CMS should provide funding, technical specifications, and a phased implementation timeline.

[P41] SNF IT director: The dual data completeness thresholds (80% MDS and 100% NHSN) (§413.360(f)(1)) create an unrealistic expectation—100% NHSN reporting is practically unattainable for facilities with EHR integration issues; CMS should allow a realistic tolerance (e.g., 95%) during the first two years.

[P42] Infection control association: Requiring 100% completion of CDC NHSN measures (§413.360(f)(1)) is appropriate to ensure complete infection surveillance, but CMS must provide resources and training to SNFs to meet the threshold beginning FY2023.

[P43] Small SNF operator: Applying the 80% and 100% thresholds to all QRP measures (§413.360(f)(2)) will disproportionately penalize small facilities with staffing shortages; CMS should permit exclusions for certain measures where reporting is unfeasible.

[P45] Legal analyst: The requirement to standardize cost data to remove geographic and case-mix variation (§413.337(b)(4)) must comply with the statutory mandate; CMS should provide a legal justification and show that standardization methodology does not result in impermissible reallocation of statutory payments.

[P50] Small SNF coalition: Beginning FY2023 exclusion conditions (§413.338(b)) should include an exception for facilities under active merger, ownership change, or major reconstruction that disrupts case volumes; otherwise stable facilities could be penalized.

[P51] Data transparency NGO: The thresholds that determine exclusion for lacking minimum cases for each measure (§413.338(b)(1)) should be publicly posted with the exact numeric minima at least 180 days before the performance period.

[P52] Ombudsman program: Excluding SNFs for not having the minimum number of measures in a fiscal year (§413.338(b)(2)) could remove protections for vulnerable residents; CMS should require public notice to residents when a facility is excluded from VBP for a year.

[P56] Provider counsel: Announcing performance standards only 60 days before performance periods (§413.338(d)(6)(i)) could violate due process principles for materially affected parties; extend notice or permit an administrative reconsideration period.

[P61] Consumer advocate: Granting full 10 points at benchmark (§413.338(e)(1)(ii)) without capping maximum total points per domain could let one measure dominate composite scores; CMS must cap measure influence or employ domain-level weighting.

[P64] Policy implementer: Using the higher of achievement or improvement scores (§413.338(e)(1)(v)) can be gamed if facilities simply focus on measures where they can maximize either strategy; CMS should monitor for strategic behavior.

[P65] Statutory compliance commenter: The multi-step SNF performance score calculation (§413.338(e)(2)) must be published as regulatory text or technical guidance to meet notice requirements; CMS should issue an accompanying technical manual.

[P66] Provider association: Summing points across measures (§413.338(e)(2)(i)) without weighting for measure importance will reward minor process measures; CMS should weight measures by clinical importance and reliability.

[P67] Data scientist: Normalizing points to 100 (§413.338(e)(2)(ii)) should preserve interpretability across years; CMS must define whether normalization is based on absolute maximum points or distributional scaling (percentile-based).

[P68] SNF quality director: Quarterly confidential feedback with 30-day corrections (§413.338(f)(1)) must include machine-readable data files and a standardized correction portal; otherwise the process will be administratively burdensome.

[P69] Provider counsel: The 30-day review window for corrections (§413.338(f)(1) SNF review period) should be tolled when CMS delays sending reports or when technical problems impede access; define procedures for such tolling.

[P70] Compliance group: Prohibiting review of administrative claims data (§413.338(f)(1) administrative claims data) leaves SNFs unable to correct billing mistakes that affect measures; CMS should permit corrections for clear clerical or coding errors with MAC adjudication.

[P71] Records manager: Requiring evidence with correction requests (§413.338(f)(1) correction requests) should specify acceptable formats and a minimum evidentiary standard; otherwise adjudicators will apply inconsistent standards.

[P72] Transparency NGO: Public reporting on Nursing Home Compare (§413.338(f)(3)) should include confidence intervals and case counts alongside rates to prevent misinterpretation by consumers.

[P75] Legal group: Not publicly reporting any data for SNFs lacking minimum measures in the performance period (§413.338(f)(4)(iii)) may conflict with transparency mandates; allow redacted or aggregated reporting instead.

[P78] Consumer advocate: Assigning zero performance scores to all SNFs for FY2023 (§413.338(i)(1)(c)) will mask relative facility performance; CMS should reconsider or at minimum publish relative rankings for consumer information even if payments are frozen.

[P80] Quality improvement organization: Providing confidential readmission feedback for FY2023 (§413.338(i)(3)) is helpful, but CMS should permit collaborative learning sessions and offer technical assistance to facilities with high readmission rates.

[P81] Public reporting advocate: Public reporting of FY2023 readmission performance (§413.338(i)(4)) must be accompanied by explanatory text that FY2023 performance scores are not used for VBP payouts and any methodological differences from other years.

[P82] MAC contractor union: Requiring MACs to validate SNFRM claims data beginning FY2023 (§413.338(j)(1)) may require additional staffing and training; CMS must fund these activities and revise MAC contracts to cover the workload.

[P85] Ombudsman: Linking both thresholds to a 2-percentage-point reduction in annual payment update (§413.360(f)(3)) could reduce quality of resident care due to funding losses; CMS should replace or accompany the penalty with remediation and support.

[P86] Policy analyst: CMS should perform and publish an equity impact analysis showing how the wage index cap, VBP pool rules, exclusions, and reporting thresholds will affect SNF funding by geography, facility size, ownership type, and resident socioeconomic status before final rule publication.

raw_output:
[P1] The 30-day comment period ending August 17, 2017 is unreasonably short for affected operators and maintenance organizations to analyze the technical service letter and prepare substantive comments, and the FAA should extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] Small operators and private owners will not realistically be aware of this AD in time to submit meaningful comments by August 17, 2017; the FAA should provide direct notice to all registered owners of affected aircraft and extend the comment deadline.

[P2] The blanket statement to "follow this AD within the specified compliance times" lacks clarity about whether compliance times are mandatory or advisory in the presence of approved AMOCs; the FAA should clarify that compliance times are mandatory unless an AMOC is approved in writing.

[P2] The provision fails to state consequences for noncompliance (e.g., grounding vs. enforcement discretion); the FAA should clarify enforcement policy to allow temporary relief for operators with scheduling constraints.

[P3] Requiring upgrade of the TSSA–4100 FLS to specific RCPNs within the earlier of 12 months or 750 hours TIS imposes an undue operational burden on high-utilization fleets; the FAA should allow a single fixed compliance timeframe (e.g., 12 months) rather than the shorter 750 hours TIS trigger.

[P3] The dual-trigger compliance (12 months or 750 hours TIS) creates ambiguity for aircraft close to the 750-hour threshold at the AD effective date; the FAA should specify how fractional hours and planned upcoming flights are to be counted.

[P3] The phrase "as applicable" in referencing RCPN 810–0052–013 or 810–0052–102 is ambiguous; the AD should include a clear identification table mapping serial numbers or hardware versions to the applicable RCPN to avoid inconsistent upgrades.

[P4] Requiring completion "within the next 12 months after the effective date" does not account for lead times to obtain parts and schedule certified technicians; the FAA should allow an extension where parts are backordered or approved repair stations have wait lists.

[P4] The 12-month deadline may conflict with scheduled maintenance windows for large commercial operators, forcing out-of-cycle downtime; the FAA should permit compliance to be scheduled at the next heavy maintenance check within a specified maximum interval.

[P5] The 750 hours TIS alternative is overly restrictive for aircraft used intensively (e.g., air taxi, EMS), potentially requiring multiple unplanned maintenance events; the FAA should provide proportional compliance based on utilization bands or allow consolidation with other required maintenance.

[P5] The AD does not define how to calculate time-in-service for fractional-day operations or for partial-time leasing arrangements; the FAA should define TIS accounting rules to prevent disputes.

[P6] Mandating use of Rockwell Collins Service Information Letter TSSA–4100–SIL–10–1, Revision No. 9 (Mar 31, 2017) without incorporation by reference in the regulatory text may impede access for commenters and operators; the FAA should incorporate the document by reference or provide the full SIL text in the docket.

[P6] The AD should allow use of later revisions of the service information if they address the same unsafe condition, rather than locking in Revision No. 9 only, to avoid requiring AMOCs for minor editorial updates.

[P6] The service information letter may include non-normative instructions (recommendations) that conflict with mandatory AD language; the FAA should identify which SIL steps are mandatory actions required by the AD.

[P7] Granting credit for prior upgrades performed under earlier SIL revisions is beneficial, but the AD's list of accepted revisions (Rev 6–8) may not include all previous acceptable methods; the FAA should explicitly state whether any earlier revisions (e.g., Rev 1–5) or alternative documented methods can receive credit if they achieved the required RCPN.

[P7] Operators who performed field modifications using equivalent engineering data (e.g., DER-approved drawings) prior to the effective date may be unfairly excluded from credit; the AD should permit credit where the resulting modification can be documented to achieve the same RCPN outcomes.

[P8] Conditioning credit on having used Revision No. 6, 7, or 8 of the SIL is unduly narrow; many operators may have used an airline maintenance engineering bulletin or internal procedure based on Rev 5 — the FAA should accept demonstrated equivalence rather than restrict to specific revision numbers.

[P8] The AD does not specify acceptable documentary evidence required to prove that a prior upgrade was performed in accordance with Rev 6–8; the FAA should require that operators produce work orders, forms, and signoffs, and state acceptable formats.

[P9] Requiring that the prior upgrade resulted in RCPN 810–0052–013 or 810–0052–102 to receive credit ignores situations where an operator installed an equivalent part number or software level with the same safety effect; the FAA should allow credit for equivalent configurations documented by the manufacturer.

[P9] The AD fails to explain how to handle mixed installations where some components meet one RCPN and others meet the alternate; the FAA should provide guidance on what combination constitutes compliance.

[P10] Centralizing AMOC approval authority solely in the Wichita ACO Manager may create bottlenecks and delays for operators in other regions; the FAA should permit delegated authority to regional ACOs or to principal inspectors for routine AMOCs.

[P10] The AD does not provide decision timelines for AMOC requests to the Wichita ACO Manager; the FAA should commit to reviewing standard AMOCs within a specific timeframe (e.g., 60 days) to avoid operational disruption.

[P11] Requiring submission of AMOC requests to a principal inspector or local FSDO may be impractical for operators without assigned principal inspectors (e.g., foreign operators); the FAA should allow direct submission to the Wichita ACO with a specified process for foreign operators.

[P11] The AD cites 14 CFR 39.19 but does not summarize supporting documentation required for AMOC requests (e.g., substantiating data, test results); the FAA should specify the minimum data package to streamline reviews.

[P12] Addressing AMOC request submissions "to the person listed in paragraph (j)(1)" creates a brittle reference if contact information changes; the AD should include direct contact details (name, phone, email) or a current FAA web page link for AMOC submissions.

[P12] The AD should permit electronic submission of AMOC requests (email or web portal) rather than requiring physical mail to the Wichita ACO Manager to expedite processing.

[P13] Requiring notification to the principal inspector or local FSDO before using an approved AMOC is reasonable, but the AD does not provide a required lead time for such notification; the FAA should specify a minimum notification period (e.g., 48 hours) to allow oversight.

[P13] The AD should clarify whether notification before use of an approved AMOC can be done electronically and what information must be included in that notification (AMOC reference number, affected tail number, planned work dates).

[P13] The requirement to notify "or, if none, the local FSDO/CHDO manager" creates uncertainty for operators in non-U.S. jurisdictions; the FAA should specify procedures for foreign authorities and operators to coordinate notifications.

[P3] The AD lacks an economic analysis of the cost impact of upgrading every TSSA–4100 FLS to the specified RCPNs within the stated timeframes; the FAA should publish an estimate of labor, parts, and downtime costs and solicit comments on those estimates.

[P6] The Service Information Letter Revision No. 9 was dated March 31, 2017 but the AD effective and comment dates are in August 2017; stakeholders need assurance that there have been no subsequent safety-critical changes — the FAA should require Rockwell Collins to certify that Rev 9 is current and complete.

[P3] The AD should require that installation be performed only by certificated repair stations or appropriately qualified personnel; as written, it does not expressly limit who may perform the upgrade, which could lead to inconsistent work quality.

[P5] The dual compliance metric could be gamed by operators who manipulate flight logs to delay the 750 hours trigger; the FAA should require independent verification of TIS calculations with maintenance release stamps.

[P7] The allowance of credit for prior actions should require that those actions were recorded in the aircraft logbook and that the logbook entries reference the specific RCPN installed; the AD should state this explicitly to avoid recordkeeping disputes.

[P6] Revision No. 9 of the SIL may contain proprietary or copyrighted material from Rockwell Collins not freely available to the public; the FAA must ensure public access consistent with the Administrative Procedure Act before making SILs a mandatory reference.

[P10] The AD should define criteria under which an AMOC would be approved (safety equivalence, data required) to give stakeholders predictability, rather than leaving the wide discretion with the Wichita ACO Manager.

[P4] For internationally registered aircraft operated under bilateral agreements, the 12-month compliance date may conflict with foreign authority directives; the FAA should coordinate with bilateral partners or allow operators to comply under their State of Registry's timelines if equivalent.

[P3] The AD should include a list of affected aircraft models and serial numbers; as currently drafted it references only the FLS hardware without making clear which airframes are subject to the AD.

[P9] The AD should provide an approved parts list (APL) or drawing references for RCPN 810–0052–013 and 810–0052–102 to ensure maintenance personnel can identify the correct hardware unambiguously.

[P6] The SIL reference to "follow" without specifying mandatory steps could be interpreted as allowing deviation for safety or practicality; the FAA should explicitly identify which SIL paragraphs are mandatory to comply with the AD.

[P1] The AD should re-open the comment period if substantive changes are made to the service information or compliance times following the original August 17, 2017 comment deadline.

[P3] For leased aircraft with lessor/lessee maintenance responsibilities split, the AD should clarify which party is responsible for performing and paying for the upgrade and for recordkeeping to avoid contractual disputes.

[P13] The AD should allow emergency use of an AMOC without prior notification when unforeseen in-flight issues require immediate deviation, provided notification is given as soon as practicable afterwards.
