raw_output:
[P1] Industry comment: The requirement that device design and materials "match intended use" and "include a sharps injury prevention feature" is vague; please define objective acceptance criteria and examples of compliant SIP features to avoid inconsistent review and costly redesigns.

[P1] Legal expert: The rule does not specify how FDA will determine whether materials are "consistent with the intended use"—request clarification on whether ISO 10993 or other standards are required to demonstrate conformity.

[P2] Manufacturer: Requiring that the SIP feature "irreversibly disables device after one use" will effectively ban any reusable components for many point-of-care lancets; please clarify whether replaceable single-use cartridges within reusable housings are permitted and under what testing standard.

[P2] Industry: The mechanical testing requirement to show irreversible disablement after one use lacks specified test methods, sample sizes, and acceptance criteria—request FDA to adopt specific ASTM/ISO test standards and provide performance thresholds.

[P3] Clinician group: The biocompatibility demonstration requirement should explicitly allow use of existing biocompatibility data (ISO 10993) for materials already cleared in similar devices to avoid duplicative testing.

[P4] Small business: Sterility testing requirements are unspecified (SAL, method, validation). Request clarification whether ethylene oxide, gamma, or aseptic processing validation is acceptable and what sterility assurance level (SAL) is expected.

[P5] Patient advocate: The broad requirement to "include specified content in device labeling" should mandate that labeling be available in multiple languages common to the intended US user population, not just English.

[P6] Home users: The requirement for "illustrated, detailed instructions" should ensure illustrations meet low-literacy and accessible-design standards; ask FDA to require pictograms and 7th-grade reading level for home-use labeling.

[P7] Public health group: Mandating handwashing instructions before and after use is appropriate, but labeling should also advise on use of alcohol-based hand sanitizer when soap/water are unavailable; request inclusion.

[P8] Infection control experts: Skin cleaning/disinfection instructions should reference specific antiseptic agents and contact times (e.g., 70% isopropyl, chlorhexidine concentrations) or allow manufacturers to reference CDC guidance—ask for clarity.

[P9] Waste management NGO: "Safe disposal instructions" must include direction on sharps container standards, local disposal options, and environmental guidance; request FDA to require disposal options for consumers without access to medical waste programs.

[P10] Hospital procurement: Requirement that labeling be "suitable for the device's intended use environment" is subjective—request examples and acceptance criteria differentiating clinical versus home settings.

[P11] Health-care facility commenter: For health-care-intended devices, labeling must explain facility use and PPE use (e.g., gloves)—request clarity whether the agency expects specific glove types, donning/doffing guidance, and compatibility statements with standard PPE.

[P12] Consumer group: For home-use devices, requiring "understandable to lay users" should be operationalized (e.g., readability scores, user testing with lay participants). Request FDA to require human factors/usability testing results demonstrating comprehension.

[P13] Trade association: The "prominently include specified warning/usage statements" requirement duplicates existing labeling practices; request flexibility in placement and formatting to allow compliance with device size constraints for small packaging.

[P14] Manufacturer: The mandated statement "For use only on a single patient. Discard the entire device after use." will preclude some multi-component designs that safely segregate single-use parts; request allowance for devices with replaceable, verifiably single-use elements.

[P15] Infection control advocate: The labeling warning that lancets are not for multiple patients is necessary but should also require a brief explanation of why (risk of bloodborne pathogen transmission) and link to CDC guidance.

[P16] Industry: §878.4850(b)(2)(i) repeats design/materials consistency and mitigation obligations similar to P1—request consolidation to avoid redundant submissions and streamline premarket documentation.

[P17] Testing lab: Mechanical testing to show devices withstand forces encountered during use needs specified load cases, force magnitudes, and cycles—request FDA publish required test protocols or accept published ASTM standards.

[P18] Regulatory consultant: The biocompatibility clause in (b)(2)(iii) should explicitly permit use of predicate device data and reference ISO 10993 testing matrices to reduce unnecessary animal or in vitro testing.

[P19] Small manufacturer: Sterility testing in (b)(2)(iv) should permit different sterilization methods and not require terminal sterilization for all device types; ask for criteria when aseptic processing is acceptable.

[P20] Advocacy group: Labeling content in (b)(2)(v) must include clear contraindications and populations at increased bleeding or infection risk (e.g., anticoagulated patients, immunocompromised) — request addition.

[P21] Home health providers: Illustrations required in (b)(2)(v)(A) should depict step-by-step device use, common misuse scenarios, and troubleshooting; request FDA to require inclusion of common error warnings observed in real-world use.

[P22] Consumer safety group: Handwashing instructions (b)(2)(v)(B) must specify duration/evidence-based methods (e.g., 20 seconds) to avoid ambiguity.

[P23] Infection preventionist: Skin cleaning/disinfection instructions in (b)(2)(v)(C) should include contact times and acceptable agents consistent with local practice; request explicit allowance to reference the EPA/CDC lists.

[P24] Environmental group: Safe disposal instructions (b)(2)(v)(D) should require manufacturers to include a take-back program or prepaid disposal option for home users to reduce improper disposal.

[P25] Legal counsel: The "appropriate for the intended use environment" labeling phrase is vague—ask FDA to provide concrete labeling templates for hospital, clinic, and home environments.

[P26] Healthcare system: For facility-use labeling (b)(2)(v)(E)(1), request clarification on whether the label must include integration instructions with facility sharps disposal systems and regulatory citations (OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard).

[P27] Consumer advocate: For home-use labeling (b)(2)(v)(E)(2), require inclusion of a quick-start card and online video resources (with accessible captions) to aid lay users.

[P28] Clinical risk manager: The "prominently include specified statements" requirement (b)(2)(vi) should allow font and color flexibility but insist on signal word hierarchy per ANSI Z535—request FDA to align with ANSI standards.

[P29] Manufacturer: The single-patient/discard statement (b)(2)(vi)(A) may conflict with reusable-base designs where only blades are single-use; request explicit allowance for removable single-use elements if overall labeling explains reuse limitations.

[P30] Public health attorney: The warning in (b)(2)(vi)(B) should be drafted in plain language and avoid duplicative statutory language to reduce litigation risk from ambiguous instructions.

[P31] Device designer: §878.4850(c)(2)(i) device-specific design requirements should clarify whether automated blade-change mechanisms (triggering a storage unit) must themselves be single-use or can be part of reusable base—request detailed guidance.

[P32] Sterile processing department: The requirement in (c)(2)(i)(A) that the blade can be changed every use "manually or by triggering a blade storage unit" raises questions about contamination control during the change—request performance criteria and validation protocols.

[P33] Materials scientist: The materials/structure clause (c)(2)(i)(B) that requires permitting validated cleaning/disinfection should specify acceptable materials (e.g., autoclavable polymers, stainless steel) and limits on porosity to ensure cleanability.

[P34] Test lab: Mechanical testing in (c)(2)(ii) should include lifecycle testing for reusable bases (e.g., number of reload cycles) and specify accelerated aging protocols—request FDA to include such requirements.

[P35] Biocompatibility consultant: The biocompatibility clause (c)(2)(iii) should allow use of chemical characterization and cytotoxicity tests for low-risk reusable bases rather than full ISO 10993 batteries.

[P36] Manufacturer: Sterility testing in (c)(2)(iv) for reusable systems with single-use blades is ambiguous—does sterility only apply to blades? Request FDA clarify sterilization expectations for blades versus reusable bases.

[P37] Infection control expert: The validation requirement in (c)(2)(v) to show reusable base can be cleaned and low-level disinfected must define "low-level disinfection" and acceptable EPA-registered disinfectants, including required contact times.

[P38] Home-care providers: Labeling for reusable single-patient devices in (c)(2)(vi) should require step-by-step decontamination checklists appropriate for non-clinical staff to minimize misuse.

[P39] Manufacturer: Requiring EPA-registered disinfectant contact times in labeling (c)(2)(vi)(B) may be impractical due to changing EPA registrations—request allowance to reference current EPA lists and not hardcode contact times.

[P40] Consumer health organization: Handwashing instructions (c)(2)(vi)(C) for reusable single-patient devices must include guidance for caregivers who assist non-ambulatory patients; request additional caregiver-specific instructions.

[P41] Infection prevention committee: Skin cleaning instructions (c)(2)(vi)(D) should include warnings for patients with skin conditions, infants, and elderly—request inclusion of contraindications.

[P42] Manufacturer: Instructions for cleaning and disinfecting the device (c)(2)(vi)(E) must allow validated wipe-down procedures and not require sterile reprocessing for non-critical reusable components; request explicit validation pathways.

[P43] Environmental health group: Safe disposal instructions (c)(2)(vi)(F) should address environmental impact of refill blades and propose recycling or take-back where possible.

[P44] Hospital safety officer: Instructions addressing safe storage of reusable base and storage/disposal of refill blades (c)(2)(vi)(G) must specify maximum storage times and conditions (temperature, humidity) to prevent microbial growth—request guidance.

[P45] Clinical educator: Labeling appropriateness for intended environment (c)(2)(vi)(H) should include font sizes and durability requirements for labels used in clinical settings with barrier precautions—request minimum standards.

[P46] Manufacturer: Facility-use labeling requirements (c)(2)(vi)(H)(1) should clarify expectations around PPE recommendations—does FDA expect manufacturers to require glove use or simply to advise on typical PPE?

[P47] Consumer rights group: Home-use labeling (c)(2)(vi)(H)(2) must require usability testing with diverse lay populations (limited English proficiency, low literacy, seniors) to ensure comprehension—request FDA to require documented testing.

[P48] Regulatory affairs: The prominent single-patient-use and disinfection statement (c)(2)(vii)(A) that requires disinfection "between each use" may conflict with single-patient reusable bases used multiple times per day—request clarity on frequency and method.

[P49] Safety advocacy: The mandated statement that "Used lancet blades must be safely discarded after a single use" (c)(2)(vii)(B) should require manufacturers to specify acceptable sharps containers and disposal pathways for both facility and home users.

[P1] The rule’s assertion that the FAA "must receive" comments by January 4, 2021 could be read to bar late-filed comments; the provision should clarify that late comments will be accepted and considered to the fullest extent practicable.

[P1] The provision should specify acceptable methods of submission (mail, email, docket portal) and time-zone handling for the January 4, 2021 deadline to avoid confusion about when comments are considered timely.

[P2] § 39.13(f) obligates operators to comply "within the compliance times specified" but does not provide a mechanism for temporary relief for operators unable to meet those times due to supply chain constraints; the rule should add explicit allowance for extensions or interim mitigations.

[P2] The phrase "unless actions already done" in § 39.13(f) is vague — the rule should require operators to retain and submit documented evidence of prior compliance to avoid enforcement ambiguity.

[P3] § 39.13(g) requires performing all applicable actions "as identified in the referenced Boeing Requirements Bulletin" but does not include the bulletin text in the regulatory docket; the FAA should incorporate the bulletin by reference in the rule or attach it to ensure enforceability and transparency.

[P3] Relying on a manufacturer bulletin (Boeing Requirements Bulletin) for mandatory actions raises due process concerns; the rule should specify how conflicts between the AD and the bulletin will be resolved.

[P3] The provision lacks guidance on applicability determinations (how operators determine which "applicable actions" apply to particular serial-number aircraft); the FAA should add clear applicability criteria or examples.

[P4] § 39.13(h)(1) instructs using the AD effective date where the bulletin refers to its original issue date, but does not define "effective date" — the rule should state the exact effective date or clarify whether it is the date of publication in the Federal Register.

[P4] Substituting the AD effective date for the bulletin original issue date may change compliance intervals or inspection thresholds; the FAA should analyze and explain any resulting changes in compliance deadlines or intervals.

[P5] § 39.13(h)(2) requires contacting Boeing for repair instructions or alternative inspections but then mandates approvals per paragraph (i); this creates circularity and potential delays — the rule should permit use of approved FAA-accepted repair data from independent authorized providers, not only Boeing.

[P5] The requirement to use Boeing contact instructions could unfairly privilege the manufacturer and create anti-competitive barriers; the FAA should explicitly allow equivalent repair instructions from qualified third parties or FAA-approved data.

[P6] § 39.13(i)(1) grants the Seattle ACO Branch Manager authority to approve AMOCs, but geographic concentration of approval authority may create bottlenecks; FAA should permit multiple ACOs or regional designees to approve AMOCs for operators based outside Seattle.

[P6] The rule should set explicit timelines for the Seattle ACO Branch Manager to respond to AMOC requests (e.g., 60 days) to ensure predictable processing and avoid grounding or compliance delays.

[P7] § 39.13(i)(1) requires sending AMOC requests to the principal inspector or Flight Standards Office "as appropriate" but does not define criteria for "appropriate" — commenters ask for clarification of routing rules, particularly for operators with multiple certificates or international bases.

[P7] The rule should provide a standardized cover sheet or checklist for AMOC submissions to principal inspectors to reduce inconsistent requests and processing delays.

[P8] § 39.13(i)(1) instructs that AMOC information sent directly to the certification office manager be addressed to the person in paragraph (j)(1), but paragraph (j)(1) is not included in the excerpt; commenters request that the rule include the name, title, and contact details to avoid misdirected submissions.

[P8] The rule should permit electronic submission directly to the certification office manager in addition to physical mail to expedite AMOC review, and should publish the exact email address/contact for that manager.

[P9] Permitting AMOC requests by email to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov (§ 39.13(i)(1)) is helpful, but the rule should also allow secure file-transfer for large attachments and confirm email acknowledgement and tracking procedures.

[P9] The rule should require the FAA to acknowledge receipt of emailed AMOC requests within a set time (e.g., 5 business days) and provide a tracking number so requesters can monitor progress.

[P10] § 39.13(i)(2) obligates operators to notify their principal inspector before using an approved AMOC but does not require documentation of that notification; the FAA should require written notification and retention of records to demonstrate compliance during audits.

[P10] The rule should clarify the acceptable timeframe for the required notification to the principal inspector before using an AMOC (e.g., 48 hours, 5 business days) to avoid uncertainty.

[P11] § 39.13(i)(3) allows use of an AMOC for repairs/modifications if approved by Boeing's authorized ODA, which appears to delegate approval to Boeing — commenters object that this improperly shifts FAA safety determinations to the manufacturer and request that FAA explicitly retain final approval authority or require concurrent FAA concurrence.

[P11] Relying on Boeing ODA approval for AMOCs could raise conflict-of-interest concerns; the rule should require transparency regarding ODA approvals and permit independent review by FAA engineers.

[P12] § 39.13(i)(3) requires any AMOC-approved repair/modification to "meet the certification basis of the airplane" and reference this AD, but provides no specification about documentation standards or how equivalence to certification basis is demonstrated; commenters ask for explicit acceptance criteria and required substantiating analyses.

[P12] The rule should require that AMOC approvals that claim to meet the airplane's certification basis include a conformity statement mapping each changed item to the certification regulation(s) and be available in the public docket (with appropriate redactions for proprietary data).

[P12] The AD should specify whether previously-approved AMOCs for related ADs remain valid for the repairs/modifications here, or whether operators must seek a new AMOC that explicitly references this AD as required.

[P5] The instruction to "contact Boeing for repair instructions" conflicts with international operators' regulatory duties to comply with local authority requirements; the FAA should add language ensuring that following Boeing's instructions does not override local civil aviation authority approvals.

[P3] Because the AD makes the Boeing Requirements Bulletin mandatory, the FAA should estimate and disclose the economic impacts and burden on operators of each required action in the bulletin (man-hours, parts, downtime).

[P2] The phrase "comply with this AD within the compliance times specified" should include an allowance for human factors — e.g., relief for operators if necessary maintenance personnel are unavailable due to pandemic-related staffing shortages.

[P6] The FAA should publish criteria the Seattle ACO Branch Manager will use to evaluate AMOC requests (safety acceptance criteria, required analysis) so applicants can submit complete packages initially.

[P9] The single email address in § 39.13(i)(1) may create security and privacy risks for submission of proprietary data; the FAA should offer a secure submission portal and specify acceptable encryption practices.

[P1] The public comment deadline of January 4, 2021 should be accompanied by at least one public hearing or webinar so stakeholders can ask clarifying questions about the AD language and referenced Boeing bulletin.

[P1] The comment period deadline of May 9, 2022, is unreasonably short for carriers and MROs to compile fleet data and technical analyses and should be extended by at least 60 days.

[P1] Small operators and foreign air carriers were not given adequate notice of the May 9, 2022 comment deadline; FAA should republish the NPRM with a longer comment period to ensure meaningful participation.

[P2] The applicability to all 777–200, –200LR, –300, –300ER, and 777F models is overly broad; commenters request clarification whether specific line-fit options, retrofit kits, or serial-number ranges are excluded/included.

[P2] The AD should explicitly state whether factory-converted or supplemental type certificated (STC) 777s (e.g., freighter conversions) are included, because "certificated in any category" may create ambiguity for operators of converted aircraft.

[P2] The proposed applicability may inadvertently capture 777 variants no longer in service or those with modified systems; FAA should permit model/serial-number-based applicability or include an appendix listing affected serial numbers.

[P3] Compliance times are not reproduced in the NPRM text; the requirement to “comply within the compliance times specified” without restating those times in the AD notice prevents stakeholders from assessing operational impact.

[P3] The phrase “unless already done” is vague; AD should require operators to provide documented evidence (maintenance records) demonstrating that the work was previously completed and acceptable to the FAA.

[P4] Requiring performance “in accordance with the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin” without incorporation by reference details or publicly available copies limits transparency; FAA should fully incorporate the bulletin into the rulemaking docket.

[P4] The AD should allow operators to use equivalent procedures from other approved maintenance data if they provide equal or greater safety, rather than mandating strict adherence to Boeing's Accomplishment Instructions.

[P5] The terminating-action provision references Boeing Bulletin 777–57A0122 RB but does not describe the terminating action; FAA should describe or summarize what counts as terminating action so operators can plan long-term compliance.

[P5] There is potential for confusion if terminating actions in the Requirements Bulletin are later revised by Boeing; AD should clarify whether later revisions also terminate the AD or require separate FAA approval.

[P6] Requiring use of the AD effective date in interpreting compliance times may shorten operators’ available time if Boeing’s bulletin used an earlier original issue date; FAA should justify this change and provide transitional relief where it shortens compliance windows.

[P6] The rule should specify how to compute compliance windows when AD effective date differs materially from the bulletin original date (calendar days vs flight cycles vs flight hours) to avoid inconsistent interpretation.

[P7] Where the Requirements Bulletin tells operators to contact Boeing for repair instructions, the AD requires FAA-approved methods per paragraph (i), but does not specify timelines for FAA review/approval — risking prolonged grounding; FAA should commit to expedited review timelines for such repair approvals.

[P7] Relying on Boeing for repair instructions could create conflicts of interest; FAA should permit repairs approved by independent repair stations or third-party engineering organizations if they meet certification basis.

[P8] Granting the Seattle ACO Branch Manager sole authority to approve AMOCs centralizes decision-making and could create bottlenecks; FAA should allow other ACOs or the national office to approve AMOCs for operators outside the Seattle region.

[P8] The AD should specify objective criteria the Seattle ACO will use to evaluate AMOCs to ensure consistency and transparency in approvals.

[P9] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or Flight Standards Office may delay review when the principal inspector is unfamiliar with complex structural repairs; FAA should allow direct submission to the certification office in such cases.

[P10] If AMOC information is sent directly to the certification office manager, the AD references paragraph (j)(1) but that paragraph is not included here; commenters request the specific contact name/role be included in the AD to avoid misrouting.

[P11] While email submission of AMOC requests is permitted, the AD should also authorize secure upload to FAA docket systems and provide guidance on acceptable file formats and maximum attachment sizes for large engineering packages.

[P11] The AD must state acknowledgement/receipt timelines for emailed AMOC submissions to ensure operators know when the FAA has received their safety-related requests.

[P12] The requirement to notify the principal inspector prior to using an approved AMOC could be impractical for international operators or for operators without an assigned principal inspector; FAA should allow notification to the responsible Flight Standards office or local FAA designee.

[P12] The AD should clarify how and to whom foreign operators should provide the required notification, particularly for non-U.S. operators under ICAO oversight.

[P13] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs for repairs creates potential conflicts because Boeing represents the design approval holder; FAA should require independent FAA concurrence for AMOCs approved solely by Boeing ODA for AD compliance.

[P13] The AD should require that Boeing ODA approvals for AMOCs include submission of the ODA evaluation to the FAA for recordkeeping and potential audit.

[P14] Requiring that repair methods meet the airplane’s certification basis could be impractical for legacy airplanes with incomplete certification records; FAA should allow alternative means of compliance that demonstrably achieve equivalent safety without strict reliance on historic certification baselines.

[P14] The AD should define “meet the certification basis” — e.g., which amendments, special conditions, or exemptions are considered — to avoid inconsistent AMOC interpretations.

[P15] Mandating that any approval must specifically reference this AD may be overly prescriptive for minor repair deviations; FAA should permit cross-referencing when appropriate and provide a template for required referencing language.

[P15] Legal commenters may argue that requiring specific reference to the AD in every approval could create recordkeeping burdens and potential for inadvertent noncompliance; FAA should allow retrospective linkage of approvals to the AD if adequate traceability is maintained.

[P2/P13] Industry commenters will request an explicit process for foreign regulatory acceptance of Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs and how bilateral agreements will be used to avoid duplicate approvals for the same repair.

[P4/P7] MRO trade associations will request that Boeing's Accomplishment Instructions be approved as acceptable data under 14 CFR Part 43.3 or otherwise allow licensed repair stations to adapt procedures under organizational limits without separate FAA approval for each deviation.

[P3/P6] Airlines request that FAA provide a compliance schedule that considers maintenance planning windows, parts lead times, and scheduled heavy checks so the AD doesn't force out-of-cycle maintenance or aircraft removals from service.

[P5/P7] Safety advocates request that terminating actions be verified by FAA engineering analysis, not solely by compliance with Boeing instructions, to ensure the terminating action truly mitigates the identified unsafe condition.

[P8/P11] Legal commenters request that the AD include an explicit appeals process and timeline if AMOC requests are denied or delayed by the Seattle ACO Branch Manager, to protect operators from prolonged operational impacts.

[P1/P4] Several commenters will assert that because the comment deadline has passed (May 9, 2022), the FAA must reopen the docket to accept late-submitted data (e.g., post-field findings) before issuing a final rule.

[P2/P4] Consumer/worker-safety groups will ask FAA to confirm that applicability includes aircraft leased or operated under wet-lease agreements and that lessee/operator responsibilities for compliance are clearly assigned.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The comment period deadline of May 9, 2022, is unreasonably short for carriers and MROs to compile fleet data and technical analyses and should be extended by at least 60 days.

Small operators and foreign air carriers were not given adequate notice of the May 9, 2022 comment deadline; FAA should republish the NPRM with a longer comment period to ensure meaningful participation.

The applicability to all 777–200, –200LR, –300, –300ER, and 777F models is overly broad; commenters request clarification whether specific line-fit options, retrofit kits, or serial-number ranges are excluded/included.

The AD should explicitly state whether factory-converted or supplemental type certificated (STC) 777s (e.g., freighter conversions) are included, because "certificated in any category" may create ambiguity for operators of converted aircraft.

The proposed applicability may inadvertently capture 777 variants no longer in service or those with modified systems; FAA should permit model/serial-number-based applicability or include an appendix listing affected serial numbers.

Compliance times are not reproduced in the NPRM text; the requirement to “comply within the compliance times specified” without restating those times in the AD notice prevents stakeholders from assessing operational impact.

The phrase “unless already done” is vague; AD should require operators to provide documented evidence (maintenance records) demonstrating that the work was previously completed and acceptable to the FAA.

Requiring performance “in accordance with the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin” without incorporation by reference details or publicly available copies limits transparency; FAA should fully incorporate the bulletin into the rulemaking docket.

The AD should allow operators to use equivalent procedures from other approved maintenance data if they provide equal or greater safety, rather than mandating strict adherence to Boeing's Accomplishment Instructions.

The terminating-action provision references Boeing Bulletin 777–57A0122 RB but does not describe the terminating action; FAA should describe or summarize what counts as terminating action so operators can plan long-term compliance.

There is potential for confusion if terminating actions in the Requirements Bulletin are later revised by Boeing; AD should clarify whether later revisions also terminate the AD or require separate FAA approval.

Requiring use of the AD effective date in interpreting compliance times may shorten operators’ available time if Boeing’s bulletin used an earlier original issue date; FAA should justify this change and provide transitional relief where it shortens compliance windows.

The rule should specify how to compute compliance windows when AD effective date differs materially from the bulletin original date (calendar days vs flight cycles vs flight hours) to avoid inconsistent interpretation.

Where the Requirements Bulletin tells operators to contact Boeing for repair instructions, the AD requires FAA-approved methods per paragraph (i), but does not specify timelines for FAA review/approval — risking prolonged grounding; FAA should commit to expedited review timelines for such repair approvals.

Relying on Boeing for repair instructions could create conflicts of interest; FAA should permit repairs approved by independent repair stations or third-party engineering organizations if they meet certification basis.

Granting the Seattle ACO Branch Manager sole authority to approve AMOCs centralizes decision-making and could create bottlenecks; FAA should allow other ACOs or the national office to approve AMOCs for operators outside the Seattle region.
The AD should specify objective criteria the Seattle ACO will use to evaluate AMOCs to ensure consistency and transparency in approvals.

Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or Flight Standards Office may delay review when the principal inspector is unfamiliar with complex structural repairs; FAA should allow direct submission to the certification office in such cases.

If AMOC information is sent directly to the certification office manager, the AD references paragraph (j)(1) but that paragraph is not included here; commenters request the specific contact name/role be included in the AD to avoid misrouting.

While email submission of AMOC requests is permitted, the AD should also authorize secure upload to FAA docket systems and provide guidance on acceptable file formats and maximum attachment sizes for large engineering packages.
The AD must state acknowledgement/receipt timelines for emailed AMOC submissions to ensure operators know when the FAA has received their safety-related requests.

The requirement to notify the principal inspector prior to using an approved AMOC could be impractical for international operators or for operators without an assigned principal inspector; FAA should allow notification to the responsible Flight Standards office or local FAA designee.
The AD should clarify how and to whom foreign operators should provide the required notification, particularly for non-U.S. operators under ICAO oversight.

Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs for repairs creates potential conflicts because Boeing represents the design approval holder; FAA should require independent FAA concurrence for AMOCs approved solely by Boeing ODA for AD compliance.
The AD should require that Boeing ODA approvals for AMOCs include submission of the ODA evaluation to the FAA for recordkeeping and potential audit.

Requiring that repair methods meet the airplane’s certification basis could be impractical for legacy airplanes with incomplete certification records; FAA should allow alternative means of compliance that demonstrably achieve equivalent safety without strict reliance on historic certification baselines.
The AD should define “meet the certification basis” — e.g., which amendments, special conditions, or exemptions are considered — to avoid inconsistent AMOC interpretations.

Mandating that any approval must specifically reference this AD may be overly prescriptive for minor repair deviations; FAA should permit cross-referencing when appropriate and provide a template for required referencing language.

Legal commenters may argue that requiring specific reference to the AD in every approval could create recordkeeping burdens and potential for inadvertent noncompliance; FAA should allow retrospective linkage of approvals to the AD if adequate traceability is maintained.

/P13] Industry commenters will request an explicit process for foreign regulatory acceptance of Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs and how bilateral agreements will be used to avoid duplicate approvals for the same repair.

/P7] MRO trade associations will request that Boeing's Accomplishment Instructions be approved as acceptable data under 14 CFR Part 43.3 or otherwise allow licensed repair stations to adapt procedures under organizational limits without separate FAA approval for each deviation.

/P6] Airlines request that FAA provide a compliance schedule that considers maintenance planning windows, parts lead times, and scheduled heavy checks so the AD doesn't force out-of-cycle maintenance or aircraft removals from service.

/P7] Safety advocates request that terminating actions be verified by FAA engineering analysis, not solely by compliance with Boeing instructions, to ensure the terminating action truly mitigates the identified unsafe condition.

/P11] Legal commenters request that the AD include an explicit appeals process and timeline if AMOC requests are denied or delayed by the Seattle ACO Branch Manager, to protect operators from prolonged operational impacts.

/P4] Several commenters will assert that because the comment deadline has passed (May 9, 2022), the FAA must reopen the docket to accept late-submitted data (e.g., post-field findings) before issuing a final rule.

/P4] Consumer/worker-safety groups will ask FAA to confirm that applicability includes aircraft leased or operated under wet-lease agreements and that lessee/operator responsibilities for compliance are clearly assigned.

raw_output:
[P1] The rule fails to explain the data and methodology used to set the total salable quantities and allotment percentages for the 2018 marketing year, leaving stakeholders unable to assess the fairness or accuracy of the figures.

[P2] The specified salable quantity of 760,660 pounds for Class 1 (Scotch) oil is unreasonably low given recent production trends and will likely force Scotch oil producers to leave the market or suffer significant revenue losses.

[P2] The 35% allotment percentage for Class 1 (Scotch) oil does not reflect regional production differences and will disproportionately harm small-scale Scotch oil growers in less productive districts.

[P2] The rule does not include an adjustment mechanism if actual production exceeds or falls short of the 760,660 pound salable quantity for Class 1, creating market rigidity and potential supply shortages or surpluses.

[P3] The 1,307,947 pound salable quantity for Class 3 (Native) oil and its 53% allotment percentage appear to privilege Native oil at the expense of other classes without justification; the rule lacks an economic impact analysis comparing class-specific outcomes.

[P3] The 53% allotment for Class 3 (Native) oil may incentivize overproduction of Native-type spearmint, distorting crop diversity and increasing farmers' exposure to market volatility for that class.

[P4] The instruction to remove §§ 985.234 and 985.235 is procedurally unclear because the proposal does not state whether those sections contained critical administrative or enforcement provisions; removing them without replacement could create regulatory gaps.

[P4] Deleting §§ 985.234 and 985.235 may eliminate existing producer protections or dispute-resolution procedures; the agency should publish the text of the removed sections and explain the consequences.

[P5] The comment deadline of August 13, 2018, is unreasonably short for stakeholders (especially small producers and cooperatives) to analyze the proposed allotments, conduct economic modeling, and prepare meaningful comments.

[P6] The PRA-related deadline for comments on information collection burden (also August 13, 2018) does not provide sufficient time for businesses to gather the necessary data to assess recordkeeping or reporting burdens.

[P7] While the proposal invites written comments, it fails to provide guidance on what supporting data (e.g., production records, price impacts) the agency expects, impairing commenters' ability to submit useful evidence.

[P8] Allowing online comments via Regulations.gov is helpful, but the agency should also confirm that large file uploads (datasets, economic models) will be accepted and retained in the docket without format conversion that could corrupt data.

[P9] The option to submit comments by mail to the Promotion and Economics Division is acceptable, but the rule should provide a full street address (the text is truncated) and clarify mailroom handling to ensure timely docketing.

[P10] Accepting comments via facsimile at (202) 205–2800 is outdated and insecure; stakeholders should be encouraged to use electronic submission methods only to protect confidential business information.

[P11] Requiring commenters to reference the docket number and Federal Register page is standard, but the proposal should provide the exact docket number and page citation in the preamble to avoid misfiling.

[P12] The agency requests comments on burden minimization but does not provide its current burden estimate or sample forms, preventing informed feedback on ways to reduce respondent workload.

[P13] Directing PRA-related comments to the OMB Desk Officer is appropriate, but the rule omits the full OMB mailing address and contact email, making it harder for commenters to comply.

[P14] The separate August 27, 2018 deadline for the proposed airworthiness directive is unrelated to this spearmint oil rulemaking and risks confusing stakeholders; the agency should clearly segregate unrelated dockets and deadlines.

[P15] The cross-reference to 14 CFR 11.43 and 11.45 in permission to use listed procedures is irrelevant to this USDA rule and could mislead commenters about applicable procedural requirements.

[P16] Recommending use of the Federal eRulemaking Portal (Regulations.gov) is fine, but the proposal should include step-by-step submission instructions and a help contact for first-time users.

[P17] The inclusion of an alternate fax number (202–493–2251) in a different section creates inconsistency; the rule should standardize the fax contact to avoid misdirected submissions.

[P18] Mailing comments to the Department of Transportation Docket Operations address (listed elsewhere) is inappropriate for USDA rulemaking; the agency should ensure only the correct USDA docket address is used to prevent loss or misrouting of comments.

[P19] The hand-delivery hours (9 a.m. to 5 p.m.) for Docket Operations may be impractical for rural producers who must travel long distances; consider allowing after-hours drops or electronic verification of timely submission.

[P1] The proposal lacks an economic analysis showing projected price impacts on downstream users (flavor and fragrance industries) resulting from the specified allotments for each class.

[P2] The Class 1 allotment fails to account for 2017 weather-related crop losses; producers who already contracted on the assumption of higher allotments will face breach-of-contract risk.

[P3] By allotting a majority share (53%) to Class 3 (Native) oil, the rule may contradict statutory objectives to balance producer and consumer interests; legal review is needed to confirm statutory compliance.

[P1] The rule provides no transitional provisions for producers who bought or contracted for spearmint oil under prior allotment structures; this omission risks unfair windfalls or losses.

[P1] The agency should include monitoring and reporting requirements tied to these salable quantities, including quarterly production disclosure, so stakeholders can assess real-time compliance and market effects.

[P4] If §§ 985.234 and 985.235 contain enforcement provisions, their removal without replacement could impede the agency's ability to ensure compliance; the agency must state what enforcement framework will govern after removal.

[P6] The PRA notice should quantify expected annual responses and hours per response from individual producers and clarify whether cooperative or third-party submissions count separately.

[P12] The rule should propose specific automated collection techniques (e.g., online forms, API submission) to minimize burden as required by the PRA rather than merely soliciting comments.

[P2] The proposal should allow voluntary transfers or pooled allotments among producers of Class 1 to accommodate variability in yields; the current fixed salable quantity prevents efficient reallocation.

[P3] Similarly, the agency should permit temporary reallocation between classes if market conditions change during the marketing year, rather than leaving rigid class percentages for the entire year.

[P1] The agency must clarify whether the salable quantities are nationwide totals or allocated by production area, as lack of geographic detail will create uncertainty for individual districts and growers.

[P2] The rule should disclose how carryover stocks from prior marketing years were treated when calculating the 760,660‑pound figure for Class 1.

[P3] For transparency, the agency should publish the underlying production, demand, and inventory data used to derive the 1,307,947‑pound salable quantity for Class 3.

[P1] Stakeholders request a public hearing or webinar to explain the proposed numeric allotments and allow Q&A, especially given the numerical specificity and imminent implementation date.

raw_output:
[P1] The rule’s prohibition on take only when it occurs on “suitable American burying beetle habitat in specified areas” is ambiguous and will create enforcement confusion—define “suitable habitat” and the geographic “specified areas” precisely in the regulation or preamble.

[P1] Industry commenters will argue that limiting the take prohibition to “suitable habitat” and “specified areas” could create perverse incentives for developers to avoid surveys only outside mapped areas, so the Service should require pre-activity surveys across a broader area rather than relying solely on area boundaries.

[P2] Farmers and construction contractors will request clarification of what constitutes “soil disturbance” in the New England and Northern Plains Analysis Areas—specifically whether routine activities such as tilling, grazing, fence-post holes, or vehicle track creation are covered.

[P2] Legal experts will comment that prohibiting incidental take only when it “results from soil disturbance” could be read to exclude other common sources of incidental take (e.g., removal of carrion, vegetation clearing, off-road vehicle use), and suggest amending the text to list all covered disturbance types or use broader language.

[P3] Ranchers and private landowners in the Southern Plains will challenge the scope of “defined conservation lands,” requesting a clear list or mapping of lands included and the criteria used to designate them to avoid unexpected criminal exposure.

[P3] Conservation NGOs will support the prohibition of incidental take on defined conservation lands in the Southern Plains but will request that the rule also prohibit incidental take on other high-quality habitats not formally designated as “conservation lands.”

[P4] Agricultural and energy industry commenters will assert that the exception allowing incidental take if in compliance with a Service-approved conservation plan (on conservation lands in the Southern Plains) is unrealistic because the Service’s plan approval process timeframe and requirements are undefined and burdensome—request explicit timelines and streamlined approval criteria.

[P4] State wildlife agencies will request that the rule allow for the use of State-developed conservation plans that meet Service-equivalency standards and ask for clear criteria for “Service-approved” to avoid duplicative reviews.

[P5] Recreational collectors and citizen scientists will assert that the prohibition on possession and other acts involving unlawfully taken beetles is overbroad and may criminalize inadvertent possession; they request an affirmative safe-harbor for persons who promptly report an accidentally taken specimen.

[P6] Pet trade and museum stakeholders will request clarification of the criminal liability for possessing any beetle “taken in violation of federal or state law,” asking whether bona fide scientific specimens collected under state permits would be affected and how to validate lawful provenance.

[P7] State and Federal law enforcement agencies will support the explicit permission allowing officers to possess, transport, and ship unlawfully taken beetles for official duties but ask for language permitting cooperation with universities and forensic labs for evidence analysis and chain-of-custody provisions.

[P8] Exporters and importers will object to a blanket prohibition on import and export of the American burying beetle, asking for a permitting pathway for scientific exchange, captive-breeding programs, and bona fide conservation translocations.

[P8] Academic researchers will request an explicit exception or permitting mechanism for import/export in the context of cooperative conservation breeding and genetic rescue, with safeguards to prevent commercial exploitation.

[P9] Commercial carriers and businesses will request clarification whether incidental transit (e.g., beetles found in shipped goods or vehicles) constitutes a violation of the prohibition on interstate or foreign commerce during commercial activity, and ask for a de minimis exception and reporting procedure.

[P9] Postal and logistics companies will request a clear procedure to follow if an American burying beetle is discovered in shipment to avoid criminal liability for carriers and to set handling/notification requirements.

[P10] Online marketplaces and retailers will request that the prohibition on selling or offering for sale in interstate or foreign commerce include a compliance safe-harbor for sellers who can document due diligence and provenance, and ask for penalties to be proportional to intent.

[P11] State conservation agencies will support permitting Service or State employees to take beetles during official duties but request clear recordkeeping and reporting requirements to ensure transparency and to prevent misuse.

[P12] Several State agencies will object that requiring State conservation agency personnel to be covered by an “approved cooperative agreement” to take beetles is too restrictive and will delay needed conservation actions—ask for temporary emergency authorization procedures or a simplified approval process.

[P13] Wildlife management agencies will request more detail about what qualifying “wildlife management activities” are for incidental take in the Northern Plains Analysis Areas (e.g., predator control, population surveys, habitat restoration) and whether those activities require prior notification or consultation with the Service.

[P13] Tribes will request explicit inclusion of Tribal wildlife agencies in the permission for incidental take during wildlife management activities, or at minimum parity with State agencies.

[P14] Ranchers and grazing associations will praise the allowance for incidental take resulting from ranching and grazing but will request explicit definitions (e.g., what constitutes “ranching and grazing activities”), and ask whether customary range management practices (prescribed burns, brush control) are protected.

[P14] Conservation organizations will caution that allowing incidental take from ranching and grazing without conditions risks habitat degradation—recommend conditionality tied to best management practices, monitoring, and mitigation.

[P15] Public commenters will object to the short comment period deadline (October 9, 2019) and request an extension to allow affected stakeholders and Tribal governments sufficient time to prepare technical comments and coordinate responses.

[P16] Commenters submitting electronically will request clarification and flexibility about the 11:59 p.m. ET receipt deadline given cross-time-zone access issues and potential site outages at regulations.gov; suggest acceptance of submissions with server timestamps or acknowledgments.

[P17] Rural stakeholders relying on mail services will request that the Service accept comments postmarked by the deadline even if delivered later due to postal delays and ask the Service to provide a contingency for documented mailed submissions.

[P18] Disabled individuals and those without reliable internet will express concern that the described submission methods may disadvantage them and request additional outreach channels (fax, phone comments) or in-person assistance.

[P19] Technical commenters will request that the docket number FWS–R2–ES–2018–0029 be prominently displayed in all outreach to avoid misfiling and to ensure comments are attributed to the correct rule.

[P20] Several commenters will report past experience of misfiled electronic comments and ask the Service to implement a confirmation email or web receipt to verify the correct document prior to finalizing submissions.

[P21] Frequent commenters will urge the Service to ensure the comment box can accept long-form submissions and attachments without truncation and to publicly document maximum file sizes and acceptable formatting.

[P22] Large stakeholder groups submitting attachments will request the Service also accept PDF attachments without conversion to Word, arguing that converting files can corrupt formatting and exhibits.

[P23] Advocacy groups planning mass comment campaigns will object to requiring multiple comments be submitted in Excel spreadsheets (for form letters), saying that this preferential format may be a technical barrier for smaller organizations and individuals—request alternatives.

[P24] Commenters sending hard copy submissions will ask for a precise street address and hours for hand-delivery to avoid delivery failures and request acknowledgement of receipt for mailed/hard-copy comments.

[P25] Attendees at the public hearing will request an on-site process for obtaining a copy of the administrative record and for submitting supplemental materials after the hearing if technical issues prevented immediate submission.

[P26] Civil liberties groups will object to the Service’s request that comments be submitted only by described methods and ask for acceptance of other reasonable means (e.g., email to field office) when technical or access barriers make the specified methods impracticable.

[P27] Privacy advocates will urge the Service to adopt stronger protections than simply posting “substantive comments,” recommending redaction of personal identifying information by default unless the commenter affirmatively consents to public posting.

[P28] Individuals will express concern that the statement that entire submissions (including personal identifying information) will be posted on regulations.gov will chill comment participation and request an online mechanism to request redaction equivalently to the hardcopy provision.

[P29] Hardcopy submitters will support the option to request withholding of personal identifying information but request guidance on what qualifies as “personal identifying information” and how the Service will treat such requests.

[P30] Commenters will ask for assurance that hardcopy submissions will not be scanned and posted in a way that exposes redaction requests, and request confirmation of how redaction requests will be processed before posting.

[P31] Researchers and legal counsel will request timely posting of the supporting documentation used to develop the proposed rule so commenters can analyze and respond with accurate technical critiques, and ask for machine-readable data where applicable.

[P32] Small businesses and NGOs will ask the Service to explicitly confirm that all submitted supporting studies and data will be available in the docket in native (non-proprietary) formats to facilitate independent review.

[P33] Scientists and economists will remind the Service of its statutory obligation under Act §4(b)(1)(A) to base determinations solely on best scientific and commercial data and request disclosure of the data sets, modeling code, and methods used to map analysis areas and habitat suitability.

[P34] Organizations that previously submitted comments on May 3, 2019 will question the instruction not to resubmit prior comments and request confirmation that earlier submissions have been incorporated into the record and considered; they also request a clear process to update prior comments with new information.

[P35] Stakeholders will ask for guidance on what level of specificity the Service expects in comments and for examples of acceptable supporting information to ensure submissions meet the Service’s standards for “specific as possible.”

[P36] Academic commenters will note that the request to include supporting information so the Service can verify assertions is reasonable, but ask the Service to commit to a process that allows confidential proprietary data to be submitted under FOIA-protected terms.

[P37] Members of the public planning to speak at the hearing will request details on how oral comments will be transcribed and posted and whether supplemental materials referenced during oral testimony will be appended to the hearing record.

[P38] Interested parties will request the Service publish the hearing agenda, speaker sign-up procedures (including remote/telephonic testimony options), and estimated time allocations in advance to facilitate participation.

[P39] Frequent public meeting attendees will request that if the Service limits oral statement time because of attendance, they provide a fair allotment and an opportunity for written follow-up to avoid abridging substantive testimony.

[P40] Oral presenters will support the recommendation to provide written copies of statements but request assurance that those written copies will be uploaded to the docket and indexed with the speaker’s name and affiliation.

[P41] Local stakeholders will request the Service allow pre-registration for speakers at the hearing to avoid long lines and last-minute denials to participate.

[P42] Advocacy groups will reaffirm that the unlimited written comment length is positive but request practical guidance on how best to structure long submissions for review (e.g., executive summary plus appendices).

[P43] Persons with disabilities will appreciate the reasonable accommodation provision but request detailed accessibility information for the hearing location, virtual options, and contact methods other than telephone.

[P44] Disability advocates will request that the 3-business-day accommodation request deadline be extended or that late requests be accepted when good cause is shown to avoid excluding those who learn of the meeting late.

[P45] Deaf and hard-of-hearing commenters will request that sign language interpreter requests be accepted later than September 18, 2019, or that remote captioning/CART services be provided as an alternative.

[P46] Commenters will request transparency on how the Service will weigh written versus oral comments in its final determination and ask for an explanation of how the record will be used in the decision-making process.

[P47] Multiple stakeholders will request that the Service explicitly confirm whether comments submitted after the closing date but before publication of the final rule will be considered and, if so, under what circumstances.

[P48] Legal experts will query whether the rule’s permitting of incidental take for ranching/grazing (P14) and wildlife management (P13) creates a de facto regulatory takings exposure for landowners whose land-use is restricted, and request a legal analysis of takings implications be included in the record.

[P49] State attorneys general will ask for clarity about preemption—whether the federal prohibitions (P5–P10) supersede conflicting state laws, and request language describing interplay with state permitting schemes.

[P50] Tribal governments will request government-to-government consultation documentation be included in the record and express concern that the rule does not explicitly address Tribal lands or Tribal authority regarding conservation plans and incidental take permissions.

Legal experts will comment that prohibiting incidental take only when it “results from soil disturbance” could be read to exclude other common sources of incidental take (e.g., removal of carrion, vegetation clearing, off-road vehicle use), and suggest amending the text to list all covered disturbance types or use broader language.

Ranchers and private landowners in the Southern Plains will challenge the scope of “defined conservation lands,” requesting a clear list or mapping of lands included and the criteria used to designate them to avoid unexpected criminal exposure.

Conservation NGOs will support the prohibition of incidental take on defined conservation lands in the Southern Plains but will request that the rule also prohibit incidental take on other high-quality habitats not formally designated as “conservation lands.”

Agricultural and energy industry commenters will assert that the exception allowing incidental take if in compliance with a Service-approved conservation plan (on conservation lands in the Southern Plains) is unrealistic because the Service’s plan approval process timeframe and requirements are undefined and burdensome—request explicit timelines and streamlined approval criteria.

State wildlife agencies will request that the rule allow for the use of State-developed conservation plans that meet Service-equivalency standards and ask for clear criteria for “Service-approved” to avoid duplicative reviews.

Recreational collectors and citizen scientists will assert that the prohibition on possession and other acts involving unlawfully taken beetles is overbroad and may criminalize inadvertent possession; they request an affirmative safe-harbor for persons who promptly report an accidentally taken specimen.

Pet trade and museum stakeholders will request clarification of the criminal liability for possessing any beetle “taken in violation of federal or state law,” asking whether bona fide scientific specimens collected under state permits would be affected and how to validate lawful provenance.

State and Federal law enforcement agencies will support the explicit permission allowing officers to possess, transport, and ship unlawfully taken beetles for official duties but ask for language permitting cooperation with universities and forensic labs for evidence analysis and chain-of-custody provisions.

Exporters and importers will object to a blanket prohibition on import and export of the American burying beetle, asking for a permitting pathway for scientific exchange, captive-breeding programs, and bona fide conservation translocations.

Academic researchers will request an explicit exception or permitting mechanism for import/export in the context of cooperative conservation breeding and genetic rescue, with safeguards to prevent commercial exploitation.

Commercial carriers and businesses will request clarification whether incidental transit (e.g., beetles found in shipped goods or vehicles) constitutes a violation of the prohibition on interstate or foreign commerce during commercial activity, and ask for a de minimis exception and reporting procedure.

Postal and logistics companies will request a clear procedure to follow if an American burying beetle is discovered in shipment to avoid criminal liability for carriers and to set handling/notification requirements.

Online marketplaces and retailers will request that the prohibition on selling or offering for sale in interstate or foreign commerce include a compliance safe-harbor for sellers who can document due diligence and provenance, and ask for penalties to be proportional to intent.

State conservation agencies will support permitting Service or State employees to take beetles during official duties but request clear recordkeeping and reporting requirements to ensure transparency and to prevent misuse.

Several State agencies will object that requiring State conservation agency personnel to be covered by an “approved cooperative agreement” to take beetles is too restrictive and will delay needed conservation actions—ask for temporary emergency authorization procedures or a simplified approval process.

Wildlife management agencies will request more detail about what qualifying “wildlife management activities” are for incidental take in the Northern Plains Analysis Areas (e.g., predator control, population surveys, habitat restoration) and whether those activities require prior notification or consultation with the Service.
Tribes will request explicit inclusion of Tribal wildlife agencies in the permission for incidental take during wildlife management activities, or at minimum parity with State agencies.

Ranchers and grazing associations will praise the allowance for incidental take resulting from ranching and grazing but will request explicit definitions (e.g., what constitutes “ranching and grazing activities”), and ask whether customary range management practices (prescribed burns, brush control) are protected.

Conservation organizations will caution that allowing incidental take from ranching and grazing without conditions risks habitat degradation—recommend conditionality tied to best management practices, monitoring, and mitigation.

Public commenters will object to the short comment period deadline (October 9, 2019) and request an extension to allow affected stakeholders and Tribal governments sufficient time to prepare technical comments and coordinate responses.

Commenters submitting electronically will request clarification and flexibility about the 11:59 p.m. ET receipt deadline given cross-time-zone access issues and potential site outages at regulations.gov; suggest acceptance of submissions with server timestamps or acknowledgments.

Rural stakeholders relying on mail services will request that the Service accept comments postmarked by the deadline even if delivered later due to postal delays and ask the Service to provide a contingency for documented mailed submissions.

Disabled individuals and those without reliable internet will express concern that the described submission methods may disadvantage them and request additional outreach channels (fax, phone comments) or in-person assistance.
Technical commenters will request that the docket number FWS–R2–ES–2018–0029 be prominently displayed in all outreach to avoid misfiling and to ensure comments are attributed to the correct rule.

Several commenters will report past experience of misfiled electronic comments and ask the Service to implement a confirmation email or web receipt to verify the correct document prior to finalizing submissions.

Frequent commenters will urge the Service to ensure the comment box can accept long-form submissions and attachments without truncation and to publicly document maximum file sizes and acceptable formatting.
Large stakeholder groups submitting attachments will request the Service also accept PDF attachments without conversion to Word, arguing that converting files can corrupt formatting and exhibits.

Advocacy groups planning mass comment campaigns will object to requiring multiple comments be submitted in Excel spreadsheets (for form letters), saying that this preferential format may be a technical barrier for smaller organizations and individuals—request alternatives.

Commenters sending hard copy submissions will ask for a precise street address and hours for hand-delivery to avoid delivery failures and request acknowledgement of receipt for mailed/hard-copy comments.

Attendees at the public hearing will request an on-site process for obtaining a copy of the administrative record and for submitting supplemental materials after the hearing if technical issues prevented immediate submission.

Civil liberties groups will object to the Service’s request that comments be submitted only by described methods and ask for acceptance of other reasonable means (e.g., email to field office) when technical or access barriers make the specified methods impracticable.

Privacy advocates will urge the Service to adopt stronger protections than simply posting “substantive comments,” recommending redaction of personal identifying information by default unless the commenter affirmatively consents to public posting.

Individuals will express concern that the statement that entire submissions (including personal identifying information) will be posted on regulations.gov will chill comment participation and request an online mechanism to request redaction equivalently to the hardcopy provision.

Hardcopy submitters will support the option to request withholding of personal identifying information but request guidance on what qualifies as “personal identifying information” and how the Service will treat such requests.

Commenters will ask for assurance that hardcopy submissions will not be scanned and posted in a way that exposes redaction requests, and request confirmation of how redaction requests will be processed before posting.

Researchers and legal counsel will request timely posting of the supporting documentation used to develop the proposed rule so commenters can analyze and respond with accurate technical critiques, and ask for machine-readable data where applicable.

Small businesses and NGOs will ask the Service to explicitly confirm that all submitted supporting studies and data will be available in the docket in native (non-proprietary) formats to facilitate independent review.

Scientists and economists will remind the Service of its statutory obligation under Act §4(b)(1)(A) to base determinations solely on best scientific and commercial data and request disclosure of the data sets, modeling code, and methods used to map analysis areas and habitat suitability.

Organizations that previously submitted comments on May 3, 2019 will question the instruction not to resubmit prior comments and request confirmation that earlier submissions have been incorporated into the record and considered; they also request a clear process to update prior comments with new information.

Stakeholders will ask for guidance on what level of specificity the Service expects in comments and for examples of acceptable supporting information to ensure submissions meet the Service’s standards for “specific as possible.”

Academic commenters will note that the request to include supporting information so the Service can verify assertions is reasonable, but ask the Service to commit to a process that allows confidential proprietary data to be submitted under FOIA-protected terms.

Members of the public planning to speak at the hearing will request details on how oral comments will be transcribed and posted and whether supplemental materials referenced during oral testimony will be appended to the hearing record.

Interested parties will request the Service publish the hearing agenda, speaker sign-up procedures (including remote/telephonic testimony options), and estimated time allocations in advance to facilitate participation.

Frequent public meeting attendees will request that if the Service limits oral statement time because of attendance, they provide a fair allotment and an opportunity for written follow-up to avoid abridging substantive testimony.

Oral presenters will support the recommendation to provide written copies of statements but request assurance that those written copies will be uploaded to the docket and indexed with the speaker’s name and affiliation.
Local stakeholders will request the Service allow pre-registration for speakers at the hearing to avoid long lines and last-minute denials to participate.

Advocacy groups will reaffirm that the unlimited written comment length is positive but request practical guidance on how best to structure long submissions for review (e.g., executive summary plus appendices).

Persons with disabilities will appreciate the reasonable accommodation provision but request detailed accessibility information for the hearing location, virtual options, and contact methods other than telephone.

Disability advocates will request that the 3-business-day accommodation request deadline be extended or that late requests be accepted when good cause is shown to avoid excluding those who learn of the meeting late.

Deaf and hard-of-hearing commenters will request that sign language interpreter requests be accepted later than September 18, 2019, or that remote captioning/CART services be provided as an alternative.

Commenters will request transparency on how the Service will weigh written versus oral comments in its final determination and ask for an explanation of how the record will be used in the decision-making process.

Multiple stakeholders will request that the Service explicitly confirm whether comments submitted after the closing date but before publication of the final rule will be considered and, if so, under what circumstances.

Legal experts will query whether the rule’s permitting of incidental take for ranching/grazing (P14) and wildlife management (P13) creates a de facto regulatory takings exposure for landowners whose land-use is restricted, and request a legal analysis of takings implications be included in the record.

State attorneys general will ask for clarity about preemption—whether the federal prohibitions (P5–P10) supersede conflicting state laws, and request language describing interplay with state permitting schemes.

Tribal governments will request government-to-government consultation documentation be included in the record and express concern that the rule does not explicitly address Tribal lands or Tribal authority regarding conservation plans and incidental take permissions.
