raw_output:
[P1] The requirement in §1904.41(a)(1) to electronically submit OSHA Form 300A for any establishment that had 250+ employees "at any time during the previous calendar year" is overbroad and will capture establishments that only briefly exceeded 250 employees due to short-term seasonal spikes, imposing undue reporting burden.

[P1] Clarify whether the 250+ employee threshold is based on a single payroll snapshot, average monthly employment, or headcount on any day — the current phrasing "at any time" creates uncertainty and inconsistent application across employers.

[P2] The annual submission deadline in paragraph (c) is not specified in the proposed text; commenters will request a concrete date (e.g., March 2) and an explicit time zone to avoid confusion and late-submission penalties.

[P2] Requiring submission "by the deadline listed in paragraph (c) for the year after the covered calendar year" gives employers insufficient time to finalize records after year-end; request that OSHA allow at least 90 days after year-end for compilation and review.

[P3] Requiring the Employer Identification Number (EIN) for each establishment raises privacy and security concerns if OSHA publishes or otherwise disseminates EINs; request limitations on public disclosure and protections against identity theft.

[P3] Clarify whether multi-establishment employers must provide separate EINs for each physical site or whether a corporate EIN is acceptable when establishments do not have unique EINs.

[P4] The phrase "only two specified categories are required to routinely submit" (§1904.41(b)(1)) is ambiguous — the rule should explicitly list those two categories in the body of the regulation rather than relying on cross-references to reduce compliance uncertainty.

[P5] Requiring annual submission from all establishments that had 250+ employees and "must keep records" duplicates existing federal and state obligations; request an analysis of incremental burden and justification under the Paperwork Reduction Act.

[P6] Mandating submission for establishments with 20–249 employees in industries listed in Appendix A will disproportionately burden small businesses in certain NAICS codes; request a phased implementation or exemption for employers under 50 employees.

[P6] The rule should clarify how Appendix A will be maintained and updated, and provide a process for employers to challenge incorrect industry categorization that triggers the 20–249 submission requirement.

[P7] Requiring submission "by the paragraph (c) deadline in the year after the covered calendar year" without grace periods or cure windows could lead to harsh enforcement for minor delays; request an administrative grace period (e.g., 30 days) before penalties apply.

[P8] The conditional requirement that employers not in the two categories only submit when OSHA notifies them is acceptable, but commenters will ask for a mandatory minimum notice period (e.g., 60 days) and a clear description of what information will be requested.

[P9] Counting every individual employed "at any time during the year" as one employee (including part-time, seasonal, and temporary workers) may inflate employment counts compared to the common FTE measure; request that OSHA allow use of full-time equivalents (FTEs) or clarify the rationale for headcount versus FTE.

[P9] The rule should provide examples of how to count workers who switch between establishments, are on loan from staffing agencies, or are contractors, to avoid inconsistent employer counts.

[P10] OSHA's requirement to notify employers by mail for individual data collections (§1904.41(b)(3)) may be slow and unreliable; request allowance for email notification and confirmation, and specification of what constitutes "mail" (first-class vs. certified).

[P11] Announcing individual data collections via the Federal Register, newsletter, and website is insufficient outreach for small employers; suggest additional outreach via industry associations and state plan agencies to ensure awareness.

[P12] Not sending notifications to employers who are already required to submit routinely (§1904.41(b)(3)) could lead to confusion about changes in submission format or deadlines; request that OSHA still provide annual reminders and software/interface change notices to routine submitters.

[P13] When OSHA notifies an employer for an individual data collection, the employer must follow "the notification's specifications" — commenters will request that those specifications include data fields, formats, secure transmission methods, and sample template files in advance.

[P14] The electronic-only submission requirement (§1904.41(b)(5)) may disadvantage small employers or those in rural areas with limited internet access; request alternative submission methods (e.g., secure fax, mailed encrypted storage) or at minimum a hardship waiver process.

[P15] OSHA's commitment to provide a secure website for submissions is necessary but commenters will request detailed security standards (e.g., TLS 1.2+, encryption at rest, SOC 2 compliance), independent security audits, and annual security assessments made public.

[P16] OSHA must specify that notifications for individual data collections will include the secure website URL and clear login/instruction procedures, and that phishing safeguards will be communicated to prevent spoofing.

[P17] The exemption for employers partially exempt from recordkeeping under §§1904.1/1904.2 (so they are not required to routinely submit) is appropriate, but commenters will ask for clarity on which partial exemptions qualify and for examples (e.g., low-hazard office employers).

[P18] Requiring partially exempt employers to submit if OSHA provides written notification (§1904.41(b)(6)) could impose retroactive obligations; commenters will ask whether OSHA can require those employers to begin recordkeeping only after notification (i.e., not retroactively) and whether records prior to notification must be reconstructed.

[P19] The obligation in (b)(6) that employers "must keep the required records and submit the requested information as directed" upon written notification needs a clear timeline for when recordkeeping must commence and what retrospective periods must be covered.

[P20] Applying the same requirements to employers in State Plan States (§1904.41(b)(7)) without harmonization could conflict with state-specific reporting schedules and formats; request coordination language and transition timelines to avoid duplicative reporting.

[P20] State Plan States should be allowed to accept submissions through their state systems and forward consolidated data to OSHA to minimize employer burden; OSHA should formalize data exchange protocols with State Plans.

[P21] Allowing enterprise or corporate offices to collect and submit information on behalf of establishments (§1904.41(b)(8)) is sensible, but the rule must require that the corporate submitter certify accuracy for each listed establishment and provide contact points at each establishment for verification.

[P21] Clarify liability allocation when a corporate office submits for multiple establishments — who is responsible for errors or omissions, the corporate submitter or the individual establishment?

[P3] Require guidance on EIN validation — OSHA should state acceptable evidence if an establishment lacks a unique EIN (e.g., single EIN used across locations) to avoid submission rejections.

[P14] The rule should include provisions for temporary system outages or technical failures of OSHA's electronic submission site, including an automatic extension and alternative secure upload procedures to prevent enforcement for inability to submit.

[P6] Appendix A's industry lists likely rely on NAICS codes; commenters will request precise mapping to NAICS 2017/2022 codes and examples of common misclassifications to assist employers in self-identifying.

[P1] Employers that merged, spun off, or changed ownership during the year need guidance on which entity is responsible for submission when employee counts shift across legal entities.

[P9] Temporary staffing agencies supply workers to client establishments — request clarification whether the client or the staffing agency counts those workers for the establishment's headcount when determining the 20/250 thresholds.

[P3] Given concerns about using EINs as an identifier, request that OSHA allow alternative unique identifiers (e.g., OSHA establishment ID) where privacy or contractual reasons prevent sharing EINs.

[P11] Asking OSHA to provide an estimated number of anticipated individual data collections per year and expected sample sizes would help employers plan for possible notifications and administrative resource needs.

[P5] Request that OSHA publish a small-business impact analysis and regulatory flexibility analysis quantifying compliance costs per establishment for the 20–249 and 250+ categories as required under the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

[P15] Request clear retention and destruction policies for submitted Form 300A data, including how long OSHA will retain personally identifiable information and whether aggregate data may be shared with third parties.

[P6] For employers around the 20–249 cutoff, request a de minimis exception or a rolling average test to prevent employers from toggling in and out of submission obligations due to temporary hiring fluctuations.

[P8] For employers subject only to individual data collection notifications, request the right to appeal or request additional time if the requested information is no longer available or if records were not kept due to prior exemption.

[P13] Insist that OSHA publish a complete data dictionary and machine-readable submission schema (e.g., JSON/XML schema) well in advance of the first required submission so employers and software vendors can prepare.

[P2] Ask OSHA to synchronize the submission deadline with other federal reporting deadlines (e.g., EEO-1) where possible to reduce administrative burdens from multiple, closely timed filings.

[P1] Employers will ask for a safe harbor for inadvertent reporting errors (e.g., minor numeric transcription mistakes) and a correction process without enforcement for first-time, good-faith mistakes.

[P14] Suggest that OSHA provide low-cost or free technical assistance and a helpdesk for small businesses to assist with registration, EIN linkage, and file submission to promote compliance.

[P17] Clarify treatment of multi-establishment employers where some establishments are partially exempt under §§1904.1/1904.2 and others are not — request that exemptions apply at the establishment level and that corporate-level submission reflect that distinction.

[P1] The proposal to exempt 40 CFR 2.201–2.215 entirely for information covered by confidentiality determinations in 40 CFR part 1068 (§ 2.301(j)(1)) is overly broad and will undermine transparency by preventing routine CBI procedures, including requester appeals and procedural safeguards, from applying to a wide range of information.

[P1] Legal experts will comment that removing 40 CFR 2.201–2.215 protections for part 1068 information could conflict with FOIA and administrative law principles because those parts implement statutory procedures and appeal rights that cannot be unilaterally displaced without clear statutory authorization.

[P2] Industry stakeholders will request clarification of the scope of § 2.301(j)(2): specifically, what categories of part 1068 data are covered (e.g., test data, design drawings, formulations) because removing 2.201–2.208 could eliminate basic confidentiality claim filing and substantiation procedures they rely on.

[P2] Confidential business information (CBI) submitters will object that § 2.301(j)(2) eliminates established notice and contest procedures (e.g., opportunity to submit substantiation) afforded by 2.201–2.208, increasing risk that proprietary information will be withheld or mishandled without procedural recourse.

[P3] Commenters will object that § 2.301(j)(3) requiring mandatory FOIA denials under Exemption 4 for all information previously determined by rulemaking to be confidential lacks flexibility for case-by-case assessments when statutory circumstances change or when redacted release could be appropriate.

[P3] Civil liberties and transparency advocates will assert that the requirement to include only a regulatory citation in denial notices under § 2.301(j)(3) is insufficient — denial notices must also state the factual basis and provide guidance on appeal/administrative review rights to satisfy FOIA requirements.

[P4] Environmental NGOs will challenge § 2.301(j)(4) to the extent it permits long-lasting confidentiality determinations absent periodic review; they will ask for explicit mandatory periodic reassessment timelines (e.g., every 5 years) rather than indefinite continuation unless EPA acts.

[P4] Industry commenters will support § 2.301(j)(4) on grounds it provides predictability, but will request more explicit criteria and timelines for EPA action to modify determinations to avoid indefinite uncertainty.

[P5] Trade associations will request that § 2.301(j)(4)(i) specify the procedural steps and notice requirements for making a new confidentiality determination in rulemaking, including stakeholder notice, comment periods, and timelines, to ensure procedural fairness.

[P5] Legal commenters will argue that § 2.301(j)(4)(i) must confirm that reversal of confidentiality determinations via rulemaking remains subject to judicial review and the Administrative Procedure Act's notice-and-comment requirements.

[P6] Manufacturers will seek clarity in § 2.301(j)(4)(ii) about the standard used to deem information "emission data" vs. CBI, and request examples and a definition to avoid arbitrary reclassification that could force public disclosure of competitively sensitive information.

[P6] Public interest groups will insist that converting information to "emission data" under § 2.301(j)(4)(ii) should trigger public disclosure whenever it meaningfully informs environmental impacts, and request a presumption favoring disclosure unless a clear harm finding is made.

[P7] The Office of General Counsel’s power in § 2.301(j)(4)(iii) to revisit determinations "based on a change in law or facts" needs tighter definition — commenters will request specific triggering events and a required written explanation to ensure transparency and predictability.

[P7] Industry will request that § 2.301(j)(4)(iii) prohibit retrospective application of new legal interpretations to past submissions without advance notice to affected businesses.

[P12] Manufacturers will request that § 60.4202(g) explicitly allow continued certification to previous tiers for engines normally subject to Tier 4 when used only at the designated locations, but also ask for temporal limits or conditions (e.g., maximum deployment hours) to prevent abuse.

[P13] Regulated entities will ask that § 60.4218(a) (Table 8) include a clear, searchable mapping of which General Provisions apply to which types of sources and provide examples to reduce compliance ambiguity.

[P14] Engine manufacturers will welcome § 60.4218(b)'s application of 1068.10/1068.11 but will request confirmation that trade-secret procedures and timelines in part 1068 satisfy the notification and appeal rights otherwise in part 2.

[P15] Similarly, under § 60.4246(b) engine manufacturers will ask for harmonization language to avoid inconsistent confidentiality obligations between different EPA programs; small-volume manufacturers ask for guidance tailored to their capacity.

[P16] Importers will request further detail in § 85.1501(a) about which EPA regulations trigger applicability to nonconforming vehicles and streamlined procedures for certification/determination to avoid undue delays at ports.

[P17] Consumer advocacy groups will emphasize that § 85.1501(a)'s statement that compliance with this subpart does not exempt compliance with other Clean Air Act provisions must be supported by an explanation of how conflicts between standards will be resolved.

[P18] Manufacturers and remanufacturers will request clarification in § 85.1501(a) about the exclusion of heavy-duty engines certified under parts 86/1036 — specifically whether replacement engines for older vehicles are affected and how labeling must reflect these distinctions.

[P19] For § 85.1514, submitters will request procedural detail on how 1068.10/1068.11 apply to submissions under this subpart, including submission formats, redaction guidance, and handling of third-party requests.

[P20] Vehicle importers and compliance labs will request that § 85.1515(a)(2)(ii)(A) clarify whether measuring emissions over the FTP and highway cycles per 1066.801 applies to vehicle-level testing only or also to powertrain-level testing and whether laboratory accreditation is required.

[P21] Remanufacturers will request clarification under § 85.1515(a)(2)(ii)(A) that requiring the same test procedures used by the original manufacturer for certification does not preclude validated alternative procedures that are technologically equivalent.

[P22] Small testing labs will object to the electric dynamometer requirement in § 85.1515(a)(2)(ii)(A) as costly and request clear, objective criteria for EPA approval of alternative dynamometers, including a cost threshold and an appeal process for denials.

[P23] For § 85.1515(a)(2)(ii)(A), manufacturers who propose non-electric dynamometers will ask that the required certification statement (that the family would meet standards if tested on an electric dynamometer) be allowed to be supported by equivalency studies and not necessarily full retesting.

[P24] Stakeholders will point out that § 85.1701(a)(1)'s transition to 1068 subpart C beginning Jan 1, 2014 should include retroactivity language and guidance for compliance for vehicles produced during the transition period to avoid ambiguity.

[P25] Emergency services and retrofit businesses will assert in response to § 85.1701(a)(1) that the continued applicability of emergency vehicle field modifications (§ 85.1716) must be preserved with explicit procedures to expedite emergency conversions without lengthy waiver processes.

[P26] For § 85.1701(b), commenters will request harmonized confidentiality claim procedures and an explicit reference to how confidentiality claims under this subpart interact with state-level disclosure requirements.

[P27] Manufacturers certifying under part 86 subpart S will request § 85.1701(c) include a definition of "durability groups" and "test groups" and examples to ensure consistent application of engine family terminology.

[P28] For § 85.1808, submitters will request that the application of 1068.10/1068.11 include explicit timelines for EPA review of confidentiality claims to avoid indefinite withholding of information.

[P29] Commenters will request that § 85.1901(a) specify the practical effect and transition mechanics when certain heavy-duty engines/vehicles move to 1068.501 starting Jan 1, 2018, including whether prior certifications remain valid.

[P30] For § 85.1909, small manufacturers will ask for an explicit procedure and deadlines for asserting confidentiality claims under 1068.10/1068.11 so that importers and remanufacturers know when data will be available.

[P31] Vehicle owners and consumer advocates will support § 85.2103(a)(3) requiring manufacturers to remedy nonconformities that cause owners to bear penalties, but will request clearer definitions of "penalty or other sanction" and procedures for owners to demonstrate causation.

[P32] Manufacturers will seek clarification of the 24-month/24,000-mile limitation in § 85.2103(a)(3) exception and request that the rule specify how mileage and time are determined (owner logs, odometer records, or vehicle service records).

[P33] Under § 85.2104(a), consumer advocates will warn that permitting denial of warranty claims for failure to follow written maintenance instructions could be abused; they will request that manufacturers bear the burden of proving that owner failure directly caused the emission failure.

[P34] Related to § 85.2104(h), manufacturers will request a definitive list of prohibited bases for warranty denial and ask EPA to interpret the prohibition narrowly to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P35] For § 85.2106(b), owners will request that the list of authorized locations to submit emission warranty claims include non-franchised independent repair facilities and online submission options to improve access in rural areas.

[P36] Under § 85.2106(c), aftermarket and independent repair industry groups will seek assurance that, where federal or state law requires it, manufacturers must provide timely access to parts, training, tools, and diagnostic information to non-franchised repair facilities.

[P37] Consumer groups will request that § 85.2106(d) require manufacturers to publish their procedures for processing emission warranty claims publicly and provide average timelines for claim adjudication to prevent unreasonable delays.

[P38] For § 85.2106(d)(2), dealers and repair facilities will ask for a clear, time-limited obligation for forwarding claims to an authorized office (e.g., within 5 business days) and for an owner’s explicit written waiver form to be standardized.

[P39] Manufacturers will support § 85.2106(g) that they must pay all costs for valid claims, but will request explicit guidance on cost categories covered (e.g., towing, rental cars, diagnostic time) to avoid disputes.

[P40] Under § 85.2107(a), consumer advocates will ask that the manufacturer obligation to ensure EPA emission compliance and safety for the useful life be clarified to include software updates and remote remediation where feasible.

[P41] Industry commenters will request that § 85.2107(a)(1) and related post-24-month limitations be harmonized with state lemon laws and other warranty regimes to avoid conflicting obligations and duplicate remedies.

[P42] For § 85.2107(a)(2), repair shops will ask for examples of "other components" the manufacturer must repair to enable major components to function, and request a dispute-resolution mechanism when parties disagree about coverage.

[P43] Under § 85.2107(b), manufacturers will ask EPA to confirm that state or local caps on labor rates or parts prices for warranty repair do not reduce the manufacturer's obligation to pay the total cost, but request guidance on reasonable rate standards.

[P44] Consumer groups will request that § 85.2109(a) require that the full emission warranty explanation be provided in plain language, both paper and electronic formats, and in multiple languages appropriate for the market.

[P45] For § 85.2109(a)(6), commenters will ask that the warranty explanation include direct contact information (phone, email, web) and a clear description of reporting procedures to the EPA Compliance Division cited in the permission.

[P46] Regarding § 85.2111 introductory prohibition, manufacturers will request a detailed list of the acts that will be considered prohibited to reduce uncertainty and potential overbroad enforcement.

[P47] With respect to § 85.2111(b), manufacturers will ask for clear standards for what constitutes "failing or refusing" to comply with warranty terms (e.g., will reasonable delays or disputes count?) and request an administrative dispute resolution process prior to civil penalties.

[P48] Concerning § 85.2111(c), aftermarket parts suppliers and independent service providers will support the prohibition on conditioning warranty coverage on use of brand-name components, and request that EPA clarify the scope of permitted waivers and the process for obtaining the Office Director’s written waiver.

[P49] For § 85.2123, commenters will request a cross-reference table showing how confidentiality procedures in 1068.10/1068.11 apply specifically to submissions under this subpart, including timelines for EPA decisions.

[P50] Manufacturers selling in territories listed in § 86.007-11(f) will ask EPA to explain how the alternate standards under 1036.655 interact with federal fleet-counting, certification, and compliance obligations to avoid market segmentation issues.

[P51] For § 86.007-11(g), specialty vehicle manufacturers will seek clarity on eligibility criteria, documentation requirements, and limits on the number of engines qualifying for alternate standards under 1037.605.

[P52] Similarly, for § 86.008-10(g), manufacturers of Otto-cycle specialty vehicle engines will request transitional provisions and harmonized test procedures for demonstrating compliance with alternate standards.

[P53] For § 86.010-18(a) OBD requirements, manufacturers will ask for precise technical specifications, test methods, and fault-detection thresholds for each emission-related system to avoid subjective enforcement.

[P54] Regarding § 86.010-18(a) and the MY2027 shift to 1036.110, manufacturers request phased implementation details (e.g., reporting/data format differences, certification submission processes) and an extended lead time for software and hardware redesign.

[P55] On § 86.010-18(a)'s requirement that OBD detect all specified malfunctions, manufacturers will request allowance for integrated monitoring strategies where one monitor assesses multiple malfunctions, accompanied by demonstration protocols.

[P56] For § 86.016-1 applicability, stakeholders will request more explicit lists of engine/vehicle types covered, and the interplay between this subpart and other subparts to reduce duplicate testing and certification burdens.

[P57] Commenters will object to § 86.016-1(a)/(j) largely ceasing to apply starting MY2027 without transitional relief; they will request phased compliance, grandfathering of existing certifications, and clarified grandfathering criteria.

[P58] Manufacturers will support the option in § 86.016-1(a) to comply with either this subpart or subpart S but will request an explicit equivalency table showing where requirements differ and how to demonstrate compliance with the alternative set.

[P59] OEMs of heavy vehicles >14,000 lb GVWR will request precise guidance in § 86.016-1(d)(4) about how 1037 standards apply to vehicles without propulsion engines, including how crediting, testing, and labeling obligations are handled.

[P60] Clean-vehicle advocates will object to the prohibition in § 86.016-1(d)(4) preventing electric heavy-duty vehicles from generating PM credits, arguing that electrification reduces real-world PM and should be eligible for credits to accelerate deployment.

[P61] Relatedly, stakeholders will request clarification and exception mechanisms for NOX credits in § 86.016-1(d)(4) to account for noncombustion technologies that deliver real NOX benefits but fall outside 1037's express allowances.

[P62] Commenters will ask in response to § 86.016-1(j) for a consolidated crosswalk showing which specific provisions of 1036 and 1037 replace each provision of this subpart starting MY2027, to aid compliance planning.

[P63] For § 86.090-5(b)(4), engine manufacturers using vanadium-based SCR catalysts will request specific design and test protocols demonstrating prevention of vanadium sublimation and temperature protections, and ask for realistic durability test durations.

[P64] For § 86.450, submitters will request that EPA commit to specific response timelines for confidentiality claims under 1068.10/1068.11 to ensure timely processing of proprietary material.

[P65] Under § 86.1117(a) label requirements, manufacturers will request sample label text and acceptable supplemental label formats and materials, and ask for allowances for electronic owner notification where physical label placement is impractical.

[P66] Regarding § 86.1117(a)(1), manufacturers will request that the "within 10 days after PCA completion" labeling requirement include exception provisions for supply-chain delays and a cure period before enforcement.

[P67] For § 86.1117(a)(2), commenters will request that the required statement about nonconformance penalty payment include precise definitions of "compliance level" and instructions on how affected owners can obtain more information.

[P68] On § 86.1117(a)(3), commenters will request standard procedures and timelines for providing required labels to owners when engines/vehicles are introduced before the compliance level determination, including penalties for delayed owner notification.

[P69] Manufacturers will request that § 86.1117(b) give broad authority for pre-approval of alternative label content/formats and provide a streamlined approval process (e.g., 30-day constructive approval if EPA does not respond).

[P70] For § 86.1301(b), hybrid powertrain manufacturers will request clarification on when using 1036 test procedures is permissible, whether credits or averaging calculations differ, and documentation required to use the hybrid-only test option.

[P71] If choosing hybrid testing under § 86.1301(b), manufacturers will request harmonized SET duty cycle selection criteria and a clear method for selecting between § 86.1362 or 1036.505 to ensure consistent compliance demonstrations.

[P72] Laboratories and manufacturers will ask for technical details in § 86.1362(b) about the ramped-modal dynamometer duty cycle (e.g., cycle durations, speed/power bins, sampling rates) and for allowance of equivalent dynamometer cycles validated by correlation studies.

raw_output:
[P1] Industry commenter: The definition of attending physician in §418.3(1) is overly restrictive by limiting qualifying clinicians to only state-licensed MD/DOs, NPs meeting §410.75(b), and PAs meeting §410.74(c); we request adding certified clinical nurse specialists and certified nurse midwives who provide comparable services in some states.

[P2] State hospital association: Requiring that doctors be "legally authorized by the State to practice medicine and surgery in the State in which services are performed" (§418.3(1)(i) / P2) will create barriers for multi-state telehealth and locum tenens arrangements; we ask for clarification that valid licensure in the state where the patient is located is sufficient for telemedicine.

[P3] Hospice provider group: The cross-reference to §410.75(b) for nurse practitioners (§418.3(1)(ii) / P3) fails to account for state-level scope-of-practice variations; we request CMS clarify that NPs who practice within their state-authorized scope meet the criterion even if their training/credentialing does not precisely mirror §410.75(b).

[P4] Physician assistant professional association: The rule's reliance on §410.74(c) for PAs to qualify as attending physicians (§418.3(1)(iii) / P4) should explicitly permit PAs who are state-licensed with required supervision agreements, even if their federal credentialing differs; please add explicit language that state PA licensure plus the §410.74(c) components suffice.

[P5] Rural health advocates: The payment authorization in §418.304(f)(1) for PAs (P5/P17) is welcome, but CMS must confirm whether this payment applies when the PA provides services via telehealth from a different state than the beneficiary.

[P6] Labor union / clinician group: §418.304(f)(1) payment eligibility "regardless of whether they are hospice employees" (P6) raises billing and employment ambiguity; request guidance on employer billing responsibilities, payroll tax treatment, and who is the "employer" when PAs are contracted through physician groups.

[P7] Compliance officer at a hospice chain: §418.304(f)(2) requires the employer or contractor to bill and receive payment only if conditions are met (P7); we request CMS publish sample billing scenarios and modifiers to ensure consistent claims submission and auditability.

[P8] Legal expert: The requirement that the PA be the beneficiary's attending physician as defined in §418.3 (§418.304(f)(2)(i) / P8/P19) is circular because §418.3 refers to §410.74(c); we request CMS clarify whether prior patient-physician relationship documentation is required and what documentation suffices.

[P9] Medicare audit defense attorney: The "medically reasonable and necessary" standard (§418.304(f)(2)(ii) / P9/P20) is vague and invites denials; propose CMS specify examples of hospice attending services by PAs that meet this standard and issue safe-harbor guidelines.

[P10] Physician group: The condition that services be performed by a physician in the PA's absence and that PA services be furnished under general supervision (§418.304(f)(2)(iii) / P10/P21) conflicts with state laws where physician supervision may be more limited; request alignment with state supervision standards and clarification of "general supervision" in hospice settings.

[P11] Advocacy group for patients with serious illness: Excluding services related to certification of terminal illness from PA billable services (§418.304(f)(2)(iv) / P11/P22) will limit patient choice and continuity of care; we urge CMS to allow PAs to perform and be paid for terminal illness certifications if state law authorizes them.

[P12] Small hospice provider: The 85% payment rate for PA attending services (§418.304(f)(3) / P12/P23) reduces revenue and may disincentivize hiring PAs; request CMS adopt parity (100% of physician fee schedule) or at minimum 95% to reflect comparable clinical value and operating costs.

[P13] Academic health center: The flat 85% payment (§418.304(f)(3)) does not account for specialty complexity or time-based codes commonly used in hospice; request CMS allow differential payment or an add-on when PAs provide complex care management equivalent to physician complexity.

[P14] State Medicaid agency: CMS should clarify whether the 85% Medicare payment to employers/contractors under §418.304(f)(3) will be treated as the Medicare physician fee schedule amount for crosswalks used by state Medicaid programs and managed care.

[P15] Billing services vendor: The rule lacks instruction on which NPI or billing provider type must submit claims when an employer or contractor bills for PA services per §418.304(f)(2); request sample claim forms, required modifiers, and NPI guidance.

[P16] Quality improvement organization: The restriction that PAs cannot be paid for services "related to the certification of terminal illness specified in §418.22" (P11/P22) may compromise timely certification; recommend establishing an exception for emergency or remote certifications when no physician is available.

[P17] Patient rights organization: The proposed provisions do not require informing beneficiaries of the PA’s role, supervision arrangement, or difference in payment rate (85%); request a disclosure requirement at election of hospice and at first visit.

[P18] Defense counsel for hospices: We are concerned that the rule's supervisory requirement (general supervision under a physician) creates liability ambiguity for hospices; request CMS clarify supervisory documentation and limits of physician responsibility.

[P19] Telehealth provider: Since §418.3 requires clinicians be "authorized by the State in which he or she performs that function" (P2/P14), CMS must state whether the clinician's physical location or the patient’s location determines the state for licensure compliance in telehealth hospice care.

[P20] Medicare beneficiary representative: Request clarification whether the beneficiary must explicitly "select" the PA as attending physician in writing to trigger payment under §418.304(f)(1) (P5/P17), and if so, what form and timing are required.

[P21] Ethics / legal scholar: The rule omits how conflicts are resolved when an employer/contractor bills under §418.304(f)(2) but the PA is also employed by another entity; request conflict-of-interest disclosure and rules for dual employment situations.

[P22] State medical board: The cross-references to §410.74(c) and §410.75(b) (P3/P4/P15/P16) may include federal requirements that duplicate or conflict with state credentialing processes; ask CMS to coordinate with state boards and allow state credentialing equivalence to suffice.

[P23] Hospice financial officer: Asking employers/contractors to bill for PA services (P7/P18) could shift reimbursement disputes onto hospices; request CMS specify payment recoupment protections and timelines for appeals when services are retrospectively denied.

[P24] Rural PA practitioner: The rule should confirm that PAs in solo rural practice who meet §410.74(c) and have patient elect hospice may serve as attending physicians and bill without a hospice employment relationship (P6/P19), and request an explicit statement to avoid local contractor denials.

[P25] Health policy researcher: CMS should provide an impact analysis of the 85% payment rate on access to hospice care, particularly in underserved areas, and include projected effects on workforce composition before finalizing the rule.

[P26] Attorney specializing in Medicare billing: The phrase "medically reasonable and necessary" (P9/P20) should be defined with specific examples of allowed CPT/HCPCS codes in hospice contexts for PA-attending services to reduce inconsistent adjudication.

[P27] Consumer health coalition: The exclusion of certification-related services from PA billable services (§418.304(f)(2)(iv)) could cause delays in hospice enrollment if physicians are unavailable; propose permitting temporary PA certification with subsequent physician validation.

[P28] Managed care organization: Request clarification whether the 85% payment for PA attending services applies when the beneficiary is enrolled in a Medicare Advantage plan contracting with a hospice, and whether plan-level rates supersede this provision.

[P29] Hospital system legal counsel: The regulation does not state whether hospitals that employ PAs may bill for PA-attending hospice services when the hospice election is made and the PA serves as attending; request explicit permission and billing instructions for hospital-employed PAs.

[P30] Disability rights advocate: Ask CMS to ensure that the rule does not unintentionally reduce in-person attending visits by encouraging lower-paid remote PA coverage, which could disadvantage patients with disabilities who need in-person care.

[P1] The requirement in § 710.43(a) to submit substantiation as specified in §§ 710.45 and 710.47 is unclear about whether previously submitted partial substantiations will be accepted, creating uncertainty for companies with incomplete records.

[P1] The obligation in § 710.43(a) to submit substantiation for every Notice of Activity Form A confidentiality claim will impose significant administrative burden on small manufacturers that routinely file Form A for numerous low-volume chemicals.

[P2] The exemption in § 710.43(b)(1) for those who completed the voluntary substantiation under § 710.37(a)(1) should be broadened to explicitly cover substantiations submitted under similar state or foreign programs to avoid duplicative work.

[P2] The text of § 710.43(b)(1) is ambiguous about whether voluntary substantiations submitted more than once (amended or corrected) still qualify for the exemption; EPA should clarify that corrected voluntary submissions remain exempt.

[P3] § 710.43(b)(2) conditions allowing a prior substantiation to exempt a person lack guidance on what constitutes the “same” specific chemical identity (e.g., stereoisomers, salts, mixtures), risking inconsistent application.

[P4] The date requirement in § 710.43(b)(2)(i) that a prior substantiation must have been submitted “on or after [insert date five years before the date that is 90 days after effective date of final rule]” is unduly restrictive and could invalidate legitimate prior substantiations submitted just before that window.

[P4] The retroactive cutoff date in § 710.43(b)(2)(i) is arbitrary; industry requests EPA either remove the date limitation or adopt a reasonable grandfathering period to avoid forcing re-submissions for longstanding claims.

[P5] § 710.43(b)(2)(ii) obligates reporting prior submission identifiers by the § 710.47 deadline but provides no standardized format for the identifiers (case number vs transaction ID), leading to potential processing delays.

[P5] Requiring the submission of case numbers or transaction IDs in § 710.43(b)(2)(ii) may be impossible for foreign firms or for submissions made under legacy systems where such identifiers are not retained; EPA should accept alternative proof of prior submission.

[P6] § 710.45’s requirement to submit signed and dated answers to § 710.37(c)(1) and (2) and the certification in § 710.37(e) should explicitly permit electronic signatures to accommodate modern filing practices and reduce paper burdens.

[P6] The certification statement required by § 710.45 may expose corporate officers to undue liability if the rule does not specify the standard of knowledge or intent when signing; EPA should limit certification language to reasonable knowledge.

[P7] Requiring claimants to mark any claimed confidential information in the substantiation as CBI under § 710.45 could incentivize overbroad CBI markings; EPA should require justification for each CBI marking to prevent overclaiming.

[P7] The instruction in § 710.45 to “clearly mark” confidential portions lacks specificity about label placement and file naming conventions for electronic submissions, creating potential processing errors.

[P8] The 90-day deadline in § 710.47(a) for all required substantiations is unworkable for companies with large portfolios and limited resources; EPA should provide a phased schedule or extension mechanism.

[P8] § 710.47(a) does not account for supply chain disruptions or third-party data sources needed to compile substantiations; EPA should permit documented extensions for good cause.

[P9] The deadline in § 710.47(b) for submitting exemption information under § 710.43(b)(2) tied to the same 90-day period is too compressed for entities needing to locate prior submission records, especially multinationals.

[P10] § 710.49’s consequence that a missing substantiation will result in the chemical identity not being treated as confidential is disproportionately severe — EPA should require notice and an opportunity to cure before public disclosure.

[P10] The rule’s treatment in § 710.49 of “deficient” claims does not define procedural safeguards or appeal rights prior to loss of confidentiality, raising due process concerns.

[P11] The permission in § 710.49 for EPA to disclose information publicly “without further notice” is legally and practically problematic; stakeholders request at least 30 days’ notice and an opportunity to request reconsideration.

[P11] EPA’s ability under § 710.49 to immediately disclose imposes business risks and could result in inadvertent public release of legitimately protected trade secrets due to clerical errors; EPA must adopt additional verification steps.

[P12] § 710.51’s cross-reference to § 710.39 lacks any explanation of acceptable electronic formats and metadata standards, which will impede consistent data intake.

[P13] The record retention requirement in § 710.53 to retain documentation of reported information is reasonable but needs an explicit allowance for records kept in electronic systems with routine backup and disaster-recovery practices.

[P14] The five-year retention period in § 710.53 starting on the last day of the submission period is insufficient; industry recommends a minimum of seven years to align with common corporate retention and statute-of-limitations practices.

[P14] Conversely, some small businesses may prefer a shorter retention period for CBI records; EPA should consider allowing petition-based shorter retention where justified.

[P15] § 710.55(a) requiring review “according to 40 CFR part 2, subpart B” should specify how conflicts between part 2 procedures and this subpart will be resolved to avoid inconsistent confidentiality adjudications.

[P16] The 10-year protection period in § 710.55(b) for approved specific chemical identities is disproportionately long given rapid innovation cycles; third parties and public-interest groups will object to blanket 10-year confidentiality.

[P16] The rule should clarify whether the 10-year protection period renews automatically upon continued assertion or whether claimants must re-substantiate at renewal to prevent perpetual secrecy.

[P17] § 710.55(b) allows claimants to withdraw protection prior to expiration, but there is no mechanism described for partial withdrawal or redaction; EPA should permit partial declassification of specific components or uses.

[P18] The exception in § 710.55(b) that EPA will follow TSCA section 14(g)(2) procedures when determining information does not qualify lacks a clear timeline for those procedures, potentially delaying necessary disclosures.

[P19] § 710.55(c)’s requirement to periodically update the TSCA Inventory based on review results is positive but lacks defined frequency and transparency metrics; stakeholders request quarterly updates and a public log of changes.

[P20] Publishing an annual review goal and prior year completed reviews as required by § 710.55(d) is appropriate, but EPA must also publish resource allocation and staffing plans to demonstrate feasibility.

[P21] The target completion date in § 710.55(d) to aim for completion of all reviews by Feb 19, 2024 is unrealistic for EPA given current caseloads; stakeholders request elimination of hard target dates or a phased multi-year schedule.

[P22] The permission in § 710.55(e) to extend the target by up to two years with a Federal Register notice should be constrained by mandatory interim reporting requirements so stakeholders can track progress during extensions.

[P22] EPA should commit to stakeholder consultation before invoking a two-year extension under § 710.55(e), as extensions materially affect business planning.

[P23] The comment submission deadline of December 9, 2019 is historical and confusing to stakeholders reviewing the proposed text now; EPA should allow an updated, clearly stated comment period in any supplemental notice.

[P24] Requiring docket ID EPA–HQ–OPPT–2018–0320 on all comment submissions (per § 710.24) is fine but agencies should accept bulk submissions with an index to simplify large multi-entity comments.

[P25] The requirement to use regulations.gov (per § 710.25) is acceptable, but EPA must ensure the portal will accept large file sizes and provide confirmation receipts that include attachments’ checksums.

[P26] The prohibition against submitting CBI via electronic methods (per § 710.26) conflicts with modern secure-file-transfer capabilities; EPA should allow secure portal uploads or encrypted email with defined standards.

[P27] Mailing comments to the Document Control Office as required in § 710.27 imposes unnecessary delays and costs; EPA should encourage electronic secure submissions for non-public CBI under defined encryption protocols.

[P28] The hand-delivery arrangement instructions in § 710.28 lack clarity on contact persons and business hours, which can cause missed deadlines for urgent filings.

[P29] § 710.29’s obligation to identify and mark CBI is appropriate, but EPA must provide a template and examples of acceptable CBI markings to reduce overbroad claims.

[P30] Guidance is needed for § 710.30’s requirement to label mailed electronic media externally and identify CBI electronically inside, including acceptable file-naming conventions and encryption recommendations.

[P31] Requiring both a full CBI version and a redacted public version for the docket (per § 710.31) could create duplication for multi-file submissions; EPA should permit a single submission with both versions linked and cross-referenced.

[P32] The assurance in § 710.32 that EPA will not disclose marked CBI except under 40 CFR part 2, subpart B is appreciated, but EPA should publish its procedures for timely protection determinations to avoid inadvertent disclosure.

[P33] The new reverse-engineering questions in 40 CFR 710.37(c) substantially broaden EPA’s inquiry into proprietary formulation details and may effectively eliminate meaningful trade-secret protection for many formulations.

[P33] Legal experts will note that mandating answers about reverse-engineering methods in 710.37(c) may conflict with trade-secret protections under state law and common-law standards; EPA should conduct a legal review and provide stronger justification.

[P34] The obligation in 710.37(c) to supplement previously submitted substantiations by answering the new reverse-engineering questions unfairly penalizes companies that relied in good faith on earlier guidance and submitted complete substantiations at the time.

[P34] EPA should allow previously submitted substantiations to be amended opportunistically rather than require blanket supplementation, to reduce burden on firms with thousands of legacy substantiations.

[P35] Requiring Group 1 and 3 reporters to submit responses to the additional questions (per P35) without defining Group membership in the rule text will cause confusion; EPA must clearly identify which reporters fall into each group.

[P36] Excluding Group 2 from the additional requirements (per P36) creates an uneven regulatory field and may incentivize reporters to seek reclassification into Group 2; EPA should justify the differential treatment.

[P37] The inclusion of NOA Form B reporters in the 40 CFR part 710 amendments (per P37) means processors with short turnaround times must comply within 30 days (per P40/P43), which is an unreasonable timeline for obtaining proprietary supplier data.

[P38] Combining the two new reverse-engineering questions with the rest of the substantiation (per P38) creates a composite filing that may inadvertently reveal competitive information; EPA must allow segmented submissions with protective markings.

[P39] The 90-day filing requirement for NOA Form A substantiations (per P39 and P42) will create a sudden spike in filings that EPA must be resourced to process; otherwise, automatic denial or disclosure under § 710.49 will unfairly affect submitters.

[P40] The existing 30-day requirement for NOA Form B substantiation (per P40 and P43) should be extended where the NOA Form B reporter is dependent on third-party suppliers for information required to answer the reverse-engineering questions.

[P41] Requiring previously voluntarily submitted substantiations to be supplemented (per P41) should be limited to newly asserted claims made after the final rule; retroactive supplementation is unfair.

[P42] The requirement that earlier substantiations must fully respond to all final-rule questions (per P44) to qualify for the exemption is vague — EPA should describe acceptable equivalency criteria and provide a checklist.

[P43] Treating CDR- or NOC-based substantiations as responsive to the new 710.37(c) questions (per P45) is helpful, but EPA must publish clear mapping guidance showing which CDR/NOC fields correspond to the new questions to streamline exemptions.

raw_output:
[P1] The December 16, 2019 deadline for receiving comments is unreasonably short and should be extended to at least 60 days from publication to allow affected operators, maintenance providers, and trade associations time to review technical details and submit meaningful comments.

[P1] Requiring the FAA to "receive" comments by December 16, 2019 could exclude late-postmarked mail; clarify whether comments postmarked by that date but received later will be accepted or whether electronic submissions are preferred.

[P2] The compliance statement is too vague—operators need clarity whether compliance times are hard deadlines or can be met by previously performed equivalent inspections; request explicit allowance for previously accomplished actions supported by records.

[P2] The rule should explicitly state whether compliance times are calendar-based from the effective date or measured in flight hours/cycles from issuance; lack of specificity creates ambiguity for scheduling.

[P3] Requiring RFM revisions "before further flight" is overly prescriptive; for aircraft grounded for maintenance it is unnecessary—allow a limited administrative window (e.g., next scheduled flight within 24–72 hours) to avoid operational disruption.

[P3] The provision mandates adding either Figure 1 information or a copy of the AD to the RFM; clarify which exact text/figure is acceptable, and whether a digital copy kept with the RFM is permissible.

[P4] Allowing owner/operators with a private pilot certificate to perform the RFM revision is acceptable, but the rule should require that the person be the current registered owner/operator and that the revision be logged with a signed entry—clarify identity and documentation requirements.

[P4] The FAA should explicitly prohibit unqualified persons (non-pilots) from making the RFM entry; current wording could be read to allow anyone to perform the action if supervised—clarify.

[P5] The mandatory use of 14 CFR 43.9(a)(1)–(4) and 91.417(a)(2)(v) for the record entry may be inconsistent with some operators' record systems; request model language for the required entry and confirm electronic logbooks satisfy the requirement.

[P5] For Part 135 and 121 operators, the cross-reference to 43.9 and 91.417 may not be sufficient—request confirmation that company maintenance control systems and electronic records meet the entry requirements without additional paperwork.

[P6] The rule lists multiple recordkeeping regulations (91.417, 121.380, 135.439); commenters request clarification which applies to mixed-use helicopters (e.g., some hired for air tour under Part 135) and whether duplicate entries are required.

[P6] Maintaining records "as required" under 91.417 et al. could impose burdensome long-term storage; request clarity on retention period for this specific AD-related entry and whether it must be retained for the life of the helicopter.

[P7] The 25-hour TIS initial compliance window is impractically short for many operators (especially those with low utilization); request extension to 100 hours TIS or 30 days to allow scheduling with authorized maintenance facilities.

[P7] The rule should allow credit for recent inspections performed using an approved inspection program if those actions are equivalent and documented, rather than mandating a fresh inspection within 25 hours for all helicopters.

[P8] Opening the oil cooler/baggage compartment door on the right-hand side may require specific tools or training; request specification of necessary access panels, required tools, and whether an A&P mechanic is required for safe access.

[P8] For helicopters modified by STC or operator-specific equipment, the specified compartment door may not provide access; request guidance on acceptable alternative access methods when the standard door is not present.

[P9] The requirement to remove paint and stray sealant and clean eight attachment fittings and specified areas is vague regarding approved solvents, abrasives, and acceptable cleaning methods; request a list of permitted materials and processes to avoid damage to bonded structures.

[P9] Removing topcoat paint in those areas risks changing corrosion protection or bonding surfaces; require that the AD specify acceptable paint removal limits and surface preparation standards to prevent inadvertent damage.

[P10] Allowing primer and edge/fillet sealant to remain is helpful, but the rule should define "primer" and acceptable sealant types; operators need assurance that leaving certain coatings will not hinder inspection or create noncompliance.

[P11] Requiring reapplication of primer/sealant "before further flight" if removed effectively mandates on-the-spot rework; that may not be possible at remote fields—request allowance to ferry the helicopter to a maintenance facility under a special flight permit or extend the time before flight to accomplish reapplication.

[P12] The push inspection requires "an additional person" to push at a very specific rivet line; this creates safety and manpower issues—request alternative approved techniques (e.g., use of calibrated jacks or test fixtures) or allowance for a mechanic to perform equivalent loading.

[P12] The borescope and bright light inspection criteria lack objective defect sizing thresholds and acceptance standards; request that the FAA include measurable criteria or reference an industry inspection standard to reduce subjective enforcement.

[P13] The requirement to repair defects "within allowable limits" before further flight is vague without defined repair limits or reference documents; request that the AD include or reference the allowable damage criteria and approved repair methods.

[P14] The removal-from-service criteria for defects exceeding limits or for cracks/buckling are appropriate, but operators need a list of approved repair stations or repair manuals; request that the FAA identify acceptable repair data or approve specific procedures.

[P15] Re-bonding before further flight after bond separation may require specialized tooling and ovens; request allowance to ground the helicopter and perform re-bonding at a qualified facility, or provision of a ferry permit to move the aircraft.

[P16] The exception for 39-inch extended landing gear STC SR01742NY helicopters is narrow; operators with different STCs or similar gear extensions need guidance on applicability—request clarification and a process to petition for similar exceptions.

[P16] The rule should require the STC holder to notify affected owners/operators of the inspection modification applicability; otherwise many operators may be unaware they are excepted and perform unnecessary checks.

[P17] The exposed thread tolerance (less than one full thread or more than three threads exposed) lacks rationale; industry requests supporting data and asks whether thread engagement limits differ based on bolt grade or length—request allowance for alternative acceptable-thread engagement documented in engineering data.

[P17] Inspecting for "less than one full thread" could vary with bolt design; request that the AD permit measurement in millimeters and specify measurement methodology to ensure consistent interpretation.

[P18] The torque/movement check allowing only tightening-direction torque could hide undertorque conditions that manifest under alternating tightening/loosening; request that the FAA permit applying installation torque per the maintenance manual (both directions if specified) and allow use of calibrated torque wrenches and documented torque values.

[P18] Reliance on observing torque stripe movement is subjective; request allowance for measured torque verification and documentation by qualified mechanics rather than visual stripe checks alone.

[P19] Re-torquing a replaced bolt "in tightening direction only" after a flight may leave residual preload issues; request justification and engineering data for this method and ask that the FAA allow full torque procedure per manufacturer instructions.

[P19] The requirement to apply a torque stripe after retorque is fine, but the AD should allow equivalent marking methods (e.g., tamper-evident fastener markers or electronic maintenance records) for operators using digital maintenance systems.

[P20] The 25-hour recurring interval limited to the upper left attachment is too frequent and inconsistent with manufacturer interval recommendations; request data supporting the 25-hour interval and ask that the FAA harmonize intervals with the 100-hour all-bolt inspection cadence.

[P20] Limiting the 25-hour inspections to only one attachment may be confusing for maintenance personnel; request that the AD include a clear diagram indicating which attachment is the "upper left" relative to forward flight.

[P21] The 100-hour inspection interval for all four attachments may be unworkable for low-utilization helicopters that fly many short flights; request interval expressed in calendar days as alternative (e.g., every 90 days) or allow flight-hour based flexibility.

[P21] Operators performing progressive inspections as part of approved maintenance programs should be allowed to incorporate these AD actions into those programs rather than repeat redundant procedures; request explicit allowance for approved continuous airworthiness programs to substitute.

[P22] The blanket prohibition on special flight permits prevents ferrying aircraft to qualified maintenance facilities when immediate repair cannot be accomplished locally; request that the FAA allow special flight permits with operating limitations (e.g., day VFR, minimum crew) or issue specific ferrying guidance.

[P22] Prohibiting special flight permits is disproportionate where only administrative RFM changes are needed; ask the FAA to carve out exceptions for non-airworthiness-limiting conditions to permit safe repositioning flights.

[P23] Limiting AMOC approval authority to the Denver ACO Manager centralizes decision-making and could delay urgent alternatives; request regional AMOC authority or expedited timelines for AMOC consideration.

[P24] Routing AMOC requests through principal inspectors or local FSDOs adds bureaucratic steps; industry requests a streamlined electronic submission portal and defined processing time (e.g., 30 days) for AMOC responses.

[P25] The direct submission contact is a named individual and physical address; request inclusion of an email and phone contact for AMOC submissions and clarification about acceptable electronic formats.

[P26] Requiring notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC may be redundant if the AMOC was approved centrally; request that the FAA permit concurrent notification within a defined period (e.g., within 72 hours) rather than prior notice, to avoid operational delays.

For Part 135 and 121 operators, the cross-reference to 43.9 and 91.417 may not be sufficient—request confirmation that company maintenance control systems and electronic records meet the entry requirements without additional paperwork.

The rule lists multiple recordkeeping regulations (91.417, 121.380, 135.439); commenters request clarification which applies to mixed-use helicopters (e.g., some hired for air tour under Part 135) and whether duplicate entries are required.

Maintaining records "as required" under 91.417 et al. could impose burdensome long-term storage; request clarity on retention period for this specific AD-related entry and whether it must be retained for the life of the helicopter.

The 25-hour TIS initial compliance window is impractically short for many operators (especially those with low utilization); request extension to 100 hours TIS or 30 days to allow scheduling with authorized maintenance facilities.

The rule should allow credit for recent inspections performed using an approved inspection program if those actions are equivalent and documented, rather than mandating a fresh inspection within 25 hours for all helicopters.

Opening the oil cooler/baggage compartment door on the right-hand side may require specific tools or training; request specification of necessary access panels, required tools, and whether an A&P mechanic is required for safe access.

For helicopters modified by STC or operator-specific equipment, the specified compartment door may not provide access; request guidance on acceptable alternative access methods when the standard door is not present.

The requirement to remove paint and stray sealant and clean eight attachment fittings and specified areas is vague regarding approved solvents, abrasives, and acceptable cleaning methods; request a list of permitted materials and processes to avoid damage to bonded structures.

Removing topcoat paint in those areas risks changing corrosion protection or bonding surfaces; require that the AD specify acceptable paint removal limits and surface preparation standards to prevent inadvertent damage.

Allowing primer and edge/fillet sealant to remain is helpful, but the rule should define "primer" and acceptable sealant types; operators need assurance that leaving certain coatings will not hinder inspection or create noncompliance.

Requiring reapplication of primer/sealant "before further flight" if removed effectively mandates on-the-spot rework; that may not be possible at remote fields—request allowance to ferry the helicopter to a maintenance facility under a special flight permit or extend the time before flight to accomplish reapplication.

The push inspection requires "an additional person" to push at a very specific rivet line; this creates safety and manpower issues—request alternative approved techniques (e.g., use of calibrated jacks or test fixtures) or allowance for a mechanic to perform equivalent loading.

The borescope and bright light inspection criteria lack objective defect sizing thresholds and acceptance standards; request that the FAA include measurable criteria or reference an industry inspection standard to reduce subjective enforcement.

The requirement to repair defects "within allowable limits" before further flight is vague without defined repair limits or reference documents; request that the AD include or reference the allowable damage criteria and approved repair methods.

The removal-from-service criteria for defects exceeding limits or for cracks/buckling are appropriate, but operators need a list of approved repair stations or repair manuals; request that the FAA identify acceptable repair data or approve specific procedures.

Re-bonding before further flight after bond separation may require specialized tooling and ovens; request allowance to ground the helicopter and perform re-bonding at a qualified facility, or provision of a ferry permit to move the aircraft.

The exception for 39-inch extended landing gear STC SR01742NY helicopters is narrow; operators with different STCs or similar gear extensions need guidance on applicability—request clarification and a process to petition for similar exceptions.

The rule should require the STC holder to notify affected owners/operators of the inspection modification applicability; otherwise many operators may be unaware they are excepted and perform unnecessary checks.

The exposed thread tolerance (less than one full thread or more than three threads exposed) lacks rationale; industry requests supporting data and asks whether thread engagement limits differ based on bolt grade or length—request allowance for alternative acceptable-thread engagement documented in engineering data.
Inspecting for "less than one full thread" could vary with bolt design; request that the AD permit measurement in millimeters and specify measurement methodology to ensure consistent interpretation.

The torque/movement check allowing only tightening-direction torque could hide undertorque conditions that manifest under alternating tightening/loosening; request that the FAA permit applying installation torque per the maintenance manual (both directions if specified) and allow use of calibrated torque wrenches and documented torque values.
Reliance on observing torque stripe movement is subjective; request allowance for measured torque verification and documentation by qualified mechanics rather than visual stripe checks alone.

Re-torquing a replaced bolt "in tightening direction only" after a flight may leave residual preload issues; request justification and engineering data for this method and ask that the FAA allow full torque procedure per manufacturer instructions.

The requirement to apply a torque stripe after retorque is fine, but the AD should allow equivalent marking methods (e.g., tamper-evident fastener markers or electronic maintenance records) for operators using digital maintenance systems.

The 25-hour recurring interval limited to the upper left attachment is too frequent and inconsistent with manufacturer interval recommendations; request data supporting the 25-hour interval and ask that the FAA harmonize intervals with the 100-hour all-bolt inspection cadence.

Limiting the 25-hour inspections to only one attachment may be confusing for maintenance personnel; request that the AD include a clear diagram indicating which attachment is the "upper left" relative to forward flight.

The 100-hour inspection interval for all four attachments may be unworkable for low-utilization helicopters that fly many short flights; request interval expressed in calendar days as alternative (e.g., every 90 days) or allow flight-hour based flexibility.

Operators performing progressive inspections as part of approved maintenance programs should be allowed to incorporate these AD actions into those programs rather than repeat redundant procedures; request explicit allowance for approved continuous airworthiness programs to substitute.

The blanket prohibition on special flight permits prevents ferrying aircraft to qualified maintenance facilities when immediate repair cannot be accomplished locally; request that the FAA allow special flight permits with operating limitations (e.g., day VFR, minimum crew) or issue specific ferrying guidance.

Prohibiting special flight permits is disproportionate where only administrative RFM changes are needed; ask the FAA to carve out exceptions for non-airworthiness-limiting conditions to permit safe repositioning flights.

Limiting AMOC approval authority to the Denver ACO Manager centralizes decision-making and could delay urgent alternatives; request regional AMOC authority or expedited timelines for AMOC consideration.

Routing AMOC requests through principal inspectors or local FSDOs adds bureaucratic steps; industry requests a streamlined electronic submission portal and defined processing time (e.g., 30 days) for AMOC responses.
The direct submission contact is a named individual and physical address; request inclusion of an email and phone contact for AMOC submissions and clarification about acceptable electronic formats.

Requiring notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC may be redundant if the AMOC was approved centrally; request that the FAA permit concurrent notification within a defined period (e.g., within 72 hours) rather than prior notice, to avoid operational delays.
