raw_output:
[P1] FEMA’s exclusive administration and oversight of “all FEMA-related hazard mitigation programs and grants” as stated in §77.3(a) is overly broad and could preempt effective state, local, and Tribal program administration models that have proven successful; request narrowing or clarification of scope and interaction with non‑FEMA programs.

[P1] The rule imposes a significant administrative burden on FEMA to oversee “all FEMA‑related” programs without specifying staffing or resource requirements; request an analysis of FEMA capacity and funding to meet this duty.

[P2] §77.3(a)(1) should require minimum timelines for issuance of program implementation procedures and funding availability information (e.g., X days after appropriation) to avoid delaying applicants; as written “as needed” is vague and risks arbitrary delays.

[P2] The provision lacks a requirement that program implementation procedures be published publicly in an accessible format and include appeal timelines; request explicit publication and transparency standards.

[P3] §77.3(a)(2) grants the Administrator discretion to “prioritize properties” but does not specify criteria or a nondiscrimination requirement; stakeholders request defined prioritization factors and an anti‑discrimination clause.

[P3] The obligation to award grants “after evaluating subaward applications for eligibility and ensuring compliance” lacks a maximum review timeframe; recommend a statutory clock (e.g., 90 days) to prevent five‑year denials under §77.4(c).

[P4] §77.3(a)(3) requires FEMA to provide technical assistance and training but does not specify frequency, formats, or cost; request explicit minimum assistance levels and provisions for remote/tribal outreach.

[P4] Tribal governments and rural communities will need culturally and linguistically appropriate training; request mandatory tailoring and direct Tribal funding to support participation.

[P5] §77.3(a)(4) obligates FEMA to review and approve plans under part 201 but lacks timelines and objective approval standards; request clear review deadlines and criteria to reduce inconsistent approvals.

[P6] §77.3(a)(5) permits FEMA to “review and supplement” state/subrecipient environmental analyses—this may duplicate NEPA and State processes and create conflicts; request coordination standards and an advance notice requirement before supplementation.

[P6] The rule should state that FEMA will not use supplementation to second‑guess scientifically supported state EHP assessments without providing a written scientific rationale.

[P7] Requiring quarterly reports under §77.3(a)(6) for FEMA monitoring is appropriate but the provision does not specify report content or format; request template and allowance for consolidated reporting to reduce recipient burden.

[P8] §77.3(a)(7) allows FEMA to request additional closeout documentation but does not cap the number or timeframe for requests; recommend limiting follow‑up requests to one 60‑day cure period to avoid indefinite closeout.

[P9] §77.3(b) obligates recipients to have “working knowledge” of NFIP goals—this is vague; request definition of required competencies or minimum training hours and that FEMA fund recipient training.

[P10] Requiring a FEMA‑approved mitigation plan under §77.3(b)(1) at the recipient level duplicates §77.6(b) requirements; request harmonization and grandfathering of recently approved plans.

[P11] §77.3(b)(2) requires recipients to provide technical assistance to communities but does not provide funding; request an explicit allocation for recipients to finance this obligation or allow costs as eligible administrative expenses beyond the 10% cap.

[P12] §77.3(b)(3) makes recipients responsible for prioritizing subaward applications using unspecified “other evaluation criteria”; request transparency requirements: publish criteria, scoring, and appeals process.

[P13] §77.3(b)(4) obligates recipients to award FEMA‑approved subawards but does not address conflicts when recipient budget constraints prevent awards; request procedures for amendments and communication when a recipient cannot fund approved subawards.

[P14] §77.3(b)(5) requires recipient quarterly monitoring in alignment with approved scope/budget—request clarity on whether recipients may use FEMA’s quarterly report templates and whether remote monitoring is acceptable.

[P15] §77.3(b)(6) mandates closeout per 2 CFR 200.343/.344 but should also specify timelines for recipients to complete closeout actions to avoid FEMA recapture for administrative delays beyond recipient control.

[P16] §77.3(b)(7) and §77.3(c)(4) require compliance with 2 CFR parts 200/3002; legal commenters will request explicit cross‑references to the specific applicable provisions and clarification on which version of 2 CFR applies.

[P17] §77.3(c) obligates subrecipients to complete and submit subaward applications to recipients but does not set minimum notice periods for solicitation; request a required solicitation window (e.g., 60 days) to allow adequate local participation.

[P18] §77.3(c)(2) mandates implementation of approved subawards but lacks exceptions for force majeure or permitting delays; request incorporation of excusable delay provisions and guidance on amendments.

[P19] §77.3(c)(3) requires subrecipient quarterly reporting mirroring recipient obligations—this duplicates reporting for small subrecipients; request scaled reporting frequency or simplified reports for grants under $X.

[P20] §77.3(c)(4)/(5) and §77.8(a) require compliance with grant laws—nonprofits and small jurisdictions request additional technical assistance and a de minimis exceptions for certain administrative requirements.

[P22] §77.4(a)(1) gives the Administrator allocation discretion “based upon criteria established for each application period” but does not require publication of those criteria before application periods open; request mandatory pre‑publication and public comment on allocation criteria.

[P23] §77.4(a)(1) permissive factors (NFIP policies, SRL/RL counts) may disadvantage growing jurisdictions with few existing policies; suggest adding population vulnerability, economic impact, and future risk as mandatory factors to avoid perpetuating coverage disparities.

[P24] §77.4(a)(2) caps planning grants at $50,000 (State) and $25,000 (community); many states and communities assert these amounts are insufficient to develop compliant FEMA mitigation plans under part 201 and request increases tied to community population or complexity.

[P24] Legal aid and Tribal commenters will request that Tribal planning grant caps be adjusted (or specified) separately; current language only references States and communities and could underfund Tribal planning.

[P25] §77.4(b)(1)(i) allows FEMA to pay up to 100% for SRL structures “if technically feasible and cost‑effective” but does not define “cost‑effective” or required cost‑benefit thresholds; request explicit CBA methodology and discount rate.

[P26] §77.4(b)(1)(ii) permitting FEMA to contribute up to expected NFIP savings for acquisition/relocation may create perverse incentives to overstate projected savings; request independent NFIP savings verification and audit rights.

[P27] §77.4(b)(2) capping FEMA contribution for repetitive loss structures at 90% could prevent low‑income homeowners from participating; request a hardship waiver or sliding cost‑share for disadvantaged households.

[P28] §77.4(b)(3) 75% cap for other mitigation activities may be insufficient for small or fiscally constrained jurisdictions; request authority for up to 90% in high‑need or low‑capacity communities.

[P29] §77.4(b)(4) references mixed projects cost‑share calculations but provides no formula; request a clear allocation methodology and examples so applicants can budget and meet cost‑share requirements.

[P30] §77.4(c) treating applications not awarded within 5 years as denied and reallocating funds creates risk of losing long‑term projects stuck in review or environmental permitting; request tolling provisions for applications delayed due to FEMA requests, permit processes, or legal challenges.

[P30] Commenters ask FEMA to require notice to applicants at 4 years and a chance to update/refresh applications before automatic denial at 5 years.

[P31] §77.5(a)(1) reliance on 2 CFR 200.202/.203 for funding notifications is fine but request FEMA to require broadcast via multiple channels including direct email to registered applicants and posting on Grants.gov with standardized notice language.

[P32] §77.5(a)(2) makes applicants responsible for soliciting and prioritizing subapplications; small states and counties request financial support or technical templates to conduct equitable solicitation and outreach to non‑English speaking and under‑served communities.

[P33] §77.5(b) requires subapplicants to develop and submit subapplications within FEMA timeframes but does not require reasonable notice; request minimum submission window and extension authority where applicants face permitting/backlog issues.

[P34] §77.6(a)(1) conditions NFIP participation on being neither suspended nor withdrawn but does not account for communities that have been suspended for administrative reasons beyond control; request transitional eligibility or assistance to reinstate NFIP participation.

[P35] §77.6(a)(2) requires NFIP insurance on impacted structures prior to application opening and maintained for the structure’s life—this may exclude low‑income homeowners who cannot afford premiums; request allowance for escrowed premium assistance, phased compliance, or alternative proof of intent to maintain coverage.

[P36] §77.6(b)(1)/(b)(1 Tribal) requiring FEMA‑approved mitigation plans at both application and award time may unfairly penalize applicants in the process of plan updates; request grandfathering for plans under active revision if they meet stated minimums.

[P37] §77.6(b)(2) requiring subapplicants to have approved mitigation plans to be eligible for project grants effectively bars communities that could use project grants to complete plans; recommend allowing planning grants to proceed concurrently with project applications when feasible.

[P39] §77.6(c)(1) allowing FMA planning grants to develop/update plans is positive but needs clarity whether the $25k/$50k caps (§77.4(a)(2)) apply and if match is required; request explicit match and cap guidance.

[P40] §77.6(c)(2) conditioning funded projects to reduce flood damage to NFIP‑insured properties excludes projects that reduce communitywide risk but do not directly benefit insured properties (e.g., stormwater system upgrades); request expansion to include community flood risk reduction projects with documented NFIP nexus.

[P41] §77.6(c)(2) prohibition on activities started/completed before award will disadvantage communities that act rapidly after major events; request an exception for pre‑award emergency actions taken with documented need and prior notification to FEMA.

[P42] §77.6(c)(2)(i) enabling acquisition outside the floodplain is positive but raises questions about relocation affordability and environmental justice; request guidance on displacement impacts, tenant protections, and affordable replacement housing requirements.

[P43] §77.6(c)(2)(ii) elevation eligibility requires compliance with base flood elevations or higher “if required” — stakeholders request clarification whether locally higher freeboard ordinances are eligible costs and whether variances affect eligibility.

[P44] §77.6(c)(2)(iii) floodproofing eligibility limited to non‑residential structures needs clarification for mixed‑use buildings with ground‑floor commercial and upper‑floor residences; request eligibility for floodproofing occupied residential components when safe and feasible.

[P45] §77.6(c)(2)(iv) floodproofing historic structures per §59.1 is positive but request explicit standards for balancing preservation with mitigation and allowance for alternative treatments with SHPO concurrence.

[P46] §77.6(c)(2)(v) demolition and rebuilding to required elevations should require that replacement dwellings be affordable to displaced households; request anti‑displacement safeguards and relocation assistance specifics.

[P47] §77.6(c)(2)(vi) limiting eligible projects to “localized” flood risk reduction and excluding large‑scale or non‑localized projects could prevent regional solutions; request definition of “localized” and criteria for regional projects to be eligible when they demonstrably protect NFIP properties.

[P48] §77.6(c)(2)(vii) elevation/relocation/floodproofing of utilities is eligible but the rule should clarify when utility projects duplicative of other Federal/state funding are ineligible under §77.6(d)(6).

[P49] §77.6(c)(2)(viii) allowing other activities described in mitigation plans is flexible but requires FEMA guidance on acceptable documentation to demonstrate plan conformity; request required plan language and documentation templates.

[P50] §77.6(c)(3) offering up to $50,000 technical assistance for recipients awarded $1M+ last year creates a perverse incentive structure and disadvantages small recipients; request eligibility for technical assistance grants based on current capacity, not previous award size.

[P51] §77.6(d) listing additional minimum criteria is appropriate but many criteria are subjective (e.g., “technically feasible”); request objective definitions and a rubric or checklist for applicants.

[P52] §77.6(d)(1) requiring conformance with approved mitigation plans prevents modifications to address new risks; request a streamlined plan amendment process to permit alignment with evolving hazards.

[P53] §77.6(d)(2) requiring compliance with EHP laws is necessary, but applicants request clear guidance and timelines for EHP reviews to prevent project hold ups.

[P54] §77.6(d)(3) “technically feasible and cost‑effective” standard or elimination of NFIF payments for SRL acquisitions lacks quantifiable thresholds; request adoption of the standard used under BRIC or Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (e.g., BCR≥1.0) and clarity on NFIF elimination calculations.

[P55] §77.6(d)(4) requiring assurance of completion for multi‑phase projects demands documented funding and schedules; local governments may not have binding commitments—request allowed forms of assurance (letters of intent, legislative appropriations) and acceptable timelines.

[P56] §77.6(d)(5) requiring “consideration” of long‑term changes and maintainability is reasonable, but subrecipients should be allowed to propose maintenance plans with defined funding sources; request FEMA to allow maintenance costs to be eligible as a match or provide separate O&M grants.

[P57] §77.6(d)(6) prohibition on duplicating benefits from other sources favors agencies with primary programs; request clarification on what constitutes “more primary” federal programs and an appeals mechanism when determinations exclude parallel but complementary funding.

[P58] §77.7(a)(1)(i) permitting up to 10% management costs for recipients is likely insufficient for small recipients administering multiple subawards; request higher caps or allowance for documented cost-based indirect rates above 10%.

[P59] §77.7(a)(1)(ii) subapplicant 5% management cap may be inadequate for Tribal governments and small communities; request an economy of scale adjustment or waiver process.

[P60] §77.7(a)(2) stating indirect costs are eligible within management cost caps could conflict with recipients that have approved indirect cost rates exceeding these percentages; request an option to use an approved indirect rate instead of the flat cap or to claim de minimis under 2 CFR 200.414.

[P61] §77.7(b) FEMA’s discretion to fund pre‑award costs creates uncertainty; request a presumption in favor of reimbursing pre‑award costs that comply with program requirements and an application for pre‑award reimbursement at time of application.

[P62] §77.7(c) prohibition on duplication requires applicants to notify FEMA of other benefits; privacy concerns arise for individual homeowners asked to disclose insurance or assistance; request limits on data collection and clear process for reducing awards that protects recipients from undue liability.

[P63] §77.8(a) cross‑compliance with 2 CFR is necessary but small jurisdictions need simplified compliance pathways; request optional streamlined reporting for awards under $250,000.

[P64] §77.8(b)(1) FEMA’s consideration of overruns only if funds are available is reasonable but applicants need priority rules when funds are scarce; request transparent criteria for how FEMA prioritizes overrun funding.

[P65] §77.8(b)(2) allowing offset of overruns with underruns in the same award may penalize well‑run projects; request that reallocation authority require recipient notice to subrecipients and consent where reallocation would materially alter scope.

[P66] §77.8(b)(3) requiring written justification to the Regional Administrator for overruns is appropriate but require a standard form and maximum decision timeframe (e.g., 30 days) to ensure timely award amendments.

[P67] §77.8(c) FEMA recapture at closeout if matching funds are not provided or projects not completed could be unduly harsh when delays are caused by permitting or federal agency review; request cure periods and allowance for documented exceptional circumstances.

[P68] §77.8(d) FEMA may terminate awards per 2 CFR—request that FEMA provide graduated remedies (technical assistance, corrective action plan) before termination for non‑material noncompliance.

[P69] §77.8(e) reconsideration requests must be filed within 60 days; this window may be too short for Tribal governments or under‑resourced jurisdictions; request extension to 120 days and publication of reconsideration procedures and decision timelines.

[P70] §80.9(b) duplicative text on pre‑award costs should be harmonized with §77.7(b); request clear, consistent guidance across parts to avoid confusion.

[P71] §80.9(c) duplication prohibition requires notification of other benefits to subapplicants and FEMA—request privacy protections, minimal disclosure requirements, and clear examples of reportable benefits.

[P72] §80.11(a) voluntariness of property owner participation and prohibition on eminent domain is appropriate, but the clause allowing negotiation failure to prevent acquisition may hinder community buy‑outs where owners refuse; request guidance on dealing with holdouts while respecting property rights.

[P73] §80.13(a)(3) requiring deed restrictions consistent with FEMA model language and local government recording is legally appropriate but the requirement that variations need Office of Chief Counsel approval creates delay; request delegated regional authority to approve minor variations within a set timeframe.

[P74] §80.17(a) prohibiting acquiring contaminated properties unless certified clean, and prohibiting FEMA funds for cleanup, will prevent beneficial acquisition of low‑value contaminated parcels; request allowance for limited FEMA remediation funding or explicit coordination with EPA/state brownfields programs.

[P75] §80.17(b) requiring title insurance and fee simple transfer by general warranty deed may be cost‑prohibitive in some jurisdictions (e.g., Tribal trust land); request alternative acceptable evidences of title for Tribal lands and waiver process.

[P76] §80.17(c)(3) ineligibility for pre‑event market value offers for owners who did not own at the relevant event or are not nationals/qualified aliens could produce inequitable results for surviving household members; request clarification on treatment of heirs and tenants with long occupancy history.

[P77] §80.17(c)(4) entitling tenants to URA relocation benefits is appropriate but requires clarity on timing and funding responsibilities between recipients and subrecipients; request examples and required notices.

[P78] §80.17(c)(5) allowing additional payments when offers are insufficient is appropriate but requires defined Administrator criteria; request caps and objective measures for when supplemental payments are allowable.

[P79] §80.17(c)(6) mandating written owner notification of valuations and voluntary participation is good consumer protection—request model notice language and requirement for translator availability for non‑English speakers.

[P80] §80.17(d) 90‑day removal requirement for incompatible facilities after settlement may be unrealistic where asbestos/lead or permitting constraints exist; request allowance for environmental abatement timelines and an explicit exception process with standard extension periods.

[P81] §80.17(e) requiring deed notices of restrictions at settlement is reasonable but jurisdictions with paper record systems may face administrative delays; request temporary electronic filing acceptance and deadlines for physical recording.

[P82] §80.19(a) perpetual dedication and maintenance as open space imposes long‑term stewardship obligations that may be challenging for small communities; request clear guidance on eligible stewards, funding for perpetual maintenance, and alternatives such as endowments or conservation easements.

[P83] §80.19(a)(3) improvements requiring floodproofing/elevation per FEMA/ordinance and Administrator criteria need explicit technical standards and a variance process for limited accessory uses to ensure consistency across regions.

[P84] §80.19(b) requiring prior written approval for conveyance of property interests creates administrative bottlenecks; request delegation thresholds (e.g., conveyances under $X or to local governments) and maximum review periods.

[P85] §80.19(b)(1) requiring transferee statements and conservation documentation is acceptable but the provision should specify acceptable evidence of conservation status and templates for transferee statements.

[P86] §80.19(b)(2) limiting conveyance only to public entities or qualified conservation organizations may prevent innovative public‑private partnerships; request allowing conveyance to private entities subject to binding conservation easements and monitoring requirements.

[P87] §80.19(b)(3) requiring conservation easements when transferred to non‑conservation public entities is appropriate but needs model easement language and a list of necessary enforcement rights to ensure compliance.

[P88] §80.19(b)(4) requiring reference to original deed restrictions and a reversion provision is necessary; request clearer default mechanisms for enforcement if a transferee ceases eligible status and guidance on triggering reversion.

[P89] §80.19(c) FEMA’s right to inspect with “reasonable notice” is appropriate but recipients request clear notice periods (e.g., 10 business days), and limits on frequency and scope to respect privacy and operations.

[P90] §80.19(d) requiring triennial certification that the property was inspected within the prior month imposes a recurring administrative burden; request alternative acceptable inspection schedules for low‑risk properties and electronic certification processes, and allow certified third‑party inspections to reduce costs.

§77.4(a)(1) gives the Administrator allocation discretion “based upon criteria established for each application period” but does not require publication of those criteria before application periods open; request mandatory pre‑publication and public comment on allocation criteria.

§77.4(a)(1) permissive factors (NFIP policies, SRL/RL counts) may disadvantage growing jurisdictions with few existing policies; suggest adding population vulnerability, economic impact, and future risk as mandatory factors to avoid perpetuating coverage disparities.

§77.4(a)(2) caps planning grants at $50,000 (State) and $25,000 (community); many states and communities assert these amounts are insufficient to develop compliant FEMA mitigation plans under part 201 and request increases tied to community population or complexity.

Legal aid and Tribal commenters will request that Tribal planning grant caps be adjusted (or specified) separately; current language only references States and communities and could underfund Tribal planning.

§77.4(b)(1)(i) allows FEMA to pay up to 100% for SRL structures “if technically feasible and cost‑effective” but does not define “cost‑effective” or required cost‑benefit thresholds; request explicit CBA methodology and discount rate.

§77.4(b)(1)(ii) permitting FEMA to contribute up to expected NFIP savings for acquisition/relocation may create perverse incentives to overstate projected savings; request independent NFIP savings verification and audit rights.

§77.4(b)(2) capping FEMA contribution for repetitive loss structures at 90% could prevent low‑income homeowners from participating; request a hardship waiver or sliding cost‑share for disadvantaged households.
§77.4(b)(3) 75% cap for other mitigation activities may be insufficient for small or fiscally constrained jurisdictions; request authority for up to 90% in high‑need or low‑capacity communities.
§77.4(b)(4) references mixed projects cost‑share calculations but provides no formula; request a clear allocation methodology and examples so applicants can budget and meet cost‑share requirements.

§77.4(c) treating applications not awarded within 5 years as denied and reallocating funds creates risk of losing long‑term projects stuck in review or environmental permitting; request tolling provisions for applications delayed due to FEMA requests, permit processes, or legal challenges.
Commenters ask FEMA to require notice to applicants at 4 years and a chance to update/refresh applications before automatic denial at 5 years.

§77.5(a)(1) reliance on 2 CFR 200.202/.203 for funding notifications is fine but request FEMA to require broadcast via multiple channels including direct email to registered applicants and posting on Grants.gov with standardized notice language.

§77.5(a)(2) makes applicants responsible for soliciting and prioritizing subapplications; small states and counties request financial support or technical templates to conduct equitable solicitation and outreach to non‑English speaking and under‑served communities.

§77.5(b) requires subapplicants to develop and submit subapplications within FEMA timeframes but does not require reasonable notice; request minimum submission window and extension authority where applicants face permitting/backlog issues.

§77.6(a)(1) conditions NFIP participation on being neither suspended nor withdrawn but does not account for communities that have been suspended for administrative reasons beyond control; request transitional eligibility or assistance to reinstate NFIP participation.

§77.6(a)(2) requires NFIP insurance on impacted structures prior to application opening and maintained for the structure’s life—this may exclude low‑income homeowners who cannot afford premiums; request allowance for escrowed premium assistance, phased compliance, or alternative proof of intent to maintain coverage.

§77.6(b)(1)/(b)(1 Tribal) requiring FEMA‑approved mitigation plans at both application and award time may unfairly penalize applicants in the process of plan updates; request grandfathering for plans under active revision if they meet stated minimums.

§77.6(b)(2) requiring subapplicants to have approved mitigation plans to be eligible for project grants effectively bars communities that could use project grants to complete plans; recommend allowing planning grants to proceed concurrently with project applications when feasible.

§77.6(c)(1) allowing FMA planning grants to develop/update plans is positive but needs clarity whether the $25k/$50k caps (§77.4(a)(2)) apply and if match is required; request explicit match and cap guidance.

§77.6(c)(2) conditioning funded projects to reduce flood damage to NFIP‑insured properties excludes projects that reduce communitywide risk but do not directly benefit insured properties (e.g., stormwater system upgrades); request expansion to include community flood risk reduction projects with documented NFIP nexus.

§77.6(c)(2) prohibition on activities started/completed before award will disadvantage communities that act rapidly after major events; request an exception for pre‑award emergency actions taken with documented need and prior notification to FEMA.

§77.6(c)(2)(i) enabling acquisition outside the floodplain is positive but raises questions about relocation affordability and environmental justice; request guidance on displacement impacts, tenant protections, and affordable replacement housing requirements.

§77.6(c)(2)(ii) elevation eligibility requires compliance with base flood elevations or higher “if required” — stakeholders request clarification whether locally higher freeboard ordinances are eligible costs and whether variances affect eligibility.

§77.6(c)(2)(iii) floodproofing eligibility limited to non‑residential structures needs clarification for mixed‑use buildings with ground‑floor commercial and upper‑floor residences; request eligibility for floodproofing occupied residential components when safe and feasible.

§77.6(c)(2)(iv) floodproofing historic structures per §59.1 is positive but request explicit standards for balancing preservation with mitigation and allowance for alternative treatments with SHPO concurrence.

§77.6(c)(2)(v) demolition and rebuilding to required elevations should require that replacement dwellings be affordable to displaced households; request anti‑displacement safeguards and relocation assistance specifics.

§77.6(c)(2)(vi) limiting eligible projects to “localized” flood risk reduction and excluding large‑scale or non‑localized projects could prevent regional solutions; request definition of “localized” and criteria for regional projects to be eligible when they demonstrably protect NFIP properties.

§77.6(c)(2)(vii) elevation/relocation/floodproofing of utilities is eligible but the rule should clarify when utility projects duplicative of other Federal/state funding are ineligible under §77.6(d)(6).

§77.6(c)(2)(viii) allowing other activities described in mitigation plans is flexible but requires FEMA guidance on acceptable documentation to demonstrate plan conformity; request required plan language and documentation templates.

§77.6(c)(3) offering up to $50,000 technical assistance for recipients awarded $1M+ last year creates a perverse incentive structure and disadvantages small recipients; request eligibility for technical assistance grants based on current capacity, not previous award size.
§77.6(d) listing additional minimum criteria is appropriate but many criteria are subjective (e.g., “technically feasible”); request objective definitions and a rubric or checklist for applicants.
§77.6(d)(1) requiring conformance with approved mitigation plans prevents modifications to address new risks; request a streamlined plan amendment process to permit alignment with evolving hazards.
§77.6(d)(2) requiring compliance with EHP laws is necessary, but applicants request clear guidance and timelines for EHP reviews to prevent project hold ups.

§77.6(d)(3) “technically feasible and cost‑effective” standard or elimination of NFIF payments for SRL acquisitions lacks quantifiable thresholds; request adoption of the standard used under BRIC or Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (e.g., BCR≥1.0) and clarity on NFIF elimination calculations.

§77.6(d)(4) requiring assurance of completion for multi‑phase projects demands documented funding and schedules; local governments may not have binding commitments—request allowed forms of assurance (letters of intent, legislative appropriations) and acceptable timelines.

§77.6(d)(5) requiring “consideration” of long‑term changes and maintainability is reasonable, but subrecipients should be allowed to propose maintenance plans with defined funding sources; request FEMA to allow maintenance costs to be eligible as a match or provide separate O&M grants.

§77.6(d)(6) prohibition on duplicating benefits from other sources favors agencies with primary programs; request clarification on what constitutes “more primary” federal programs and an appeals mechanism when determinations exclude parallel but complementary funding.

§77.7(a)(1)(i) permitting up to 10% management costs for recipients is likely insufficient for small recipients administering multiple subawards; request higher caps or allowance for documented cost-based indirect rates above 10%.
§77.7(a)(1)(ii) subapplicant 5% management cap may be inadequate for Tribal governments and small communities; request an economy of scale adjustment or waiver process.

§77.7(a)(2) stating indirect costs are eligible within management cost caps could conflict with recipients that have approved indirect cost rates exceeding these percentages; request an option to use an approved indirect rate instead of the flat cap or to claim de minimis under 2 CFR 200.414.

§77.7(b) FEMA’s discretion to fund pre‑award costs creates uncertainty; request a presumption in favor of reimbursing pre‑award costs that comply with program requirements and an application for pre‑award reimbursement at time of application.

§77.7(c) prohibition on duplication requires applicants to notify FEMA of other benefits; privacy concerns arise for individual homeowners asked to disclose insurance or assistance; request limits on data collection and clear process for reducing awards that protects recipients from undue liability.
§77.8(a) cross‑compliance with 2 CFR is necessary but small jurisdictions need simplified compliance pathways; request optional streamlined reporting for awards under $250,000.

§77.8(b)(1) FEMA’s consideration of overruns only if funds are available is reasonable but applicants need priority rules when funds are scarce; request transparent criteria for how FEMA prioritizes overrun funding.

§77.8(b)(2) allowing offset of overruns with underruns in the same award may penalize well‑run projects; request that reallocation authority require recipient notice to subrecipients and consent where reallocation would materially alter scope.

§77.8(b)(3) requiring written justification to the Regional Administrator for overruns is appropriate but require a standard form and maximum decision timeframe (e.g., 30 days) to ensure timely award amendments.

§77.8(c) FEMA recapture at closeout if matching funds are not provided or projects not completed could be unduly harsh when delays are caused by permitting or federal agency review; request cure periods and allowance for documented exceptional circumstances.
§77.8(d) FEMA may terminate awards per 2 CFR—request that FEMA provide graduated remedies (technical assistance, corrective action plan) before termination for non‑material noncompliance.

§77.8(e) reconsideration requests must be filed within 60 days; this window may be too short for Tribal governments or under‑resourced jurisdictions; request extension to 120 days and publication of reconsideration procedures and decision timelines.
§80.9(b) duplicative text on pre‑award costs should be harmonized with §77.7(b); request clear, consistent guidance across parts to avoid confusion.

§80.9(c) duplication prohibition requires notification of other benefits to subapplicants and FEMA—request privacy protections, minimal disclosure requirements, and clear examples of reportable benefits.

§80.11(a) voluntariness of property owner participation and prohibition on eminent domain is appropriate, but the clause allowing negotiation failure to prevent acquisition may hinder community buy‑outs where owners refuse; request guidance on dealing with holdouts while respecting property rights.

§80.13(a)(3) requiring deed restrictions consistent with FEMA model language and local government recording is legally appropriate but the requirement that variations need Office of Chief Counsel approval creates delay; request delegated regional authority to approve minor variations within a set timeframe.

§80.17(a) prohibiting acquiring contaminated properties unless certified clean, and prohibiting FEMA funds for cleanup, will prevent beneficial acquisition of low‑value contaminated parcels; request allowance for limited FEMA remediation funding or explicit coordination with EPA/state brownfields programs.

§80.17(b) requiring title insurance and fee simple transfer by general warranty deed may be cost‑prohibitive in some jurisdictions (e.g., Tribal trust land); request alternative acceptable evidences of title for Tribal lands and waiver process.

§80.17(c)(3) ineligibility for pre‑event market value offers for owners who did not own at the relevant event or are not nationals/qualified aliens could produce inequitable results for surviving household members; request clarification on treatment of heirs and tenants with long occupancy history.

§80.17(c)(4) entitling tenants to URA relocation benefits is appropriate but requires clarity on timing and funding responsibilities between recipients and subrecipients; request examples and required notices.

§80.17(c)(5) allowing additional payments when offers are insufficient is appropriate but requires defined Administrator criteria; request caps and objective measures for when supplemental payments are allowable.

§80.17(c)(6) mandating written owner notification of valuations and voluntary participation is good consumer protection—request model notice language and requirement for translator availability for non‑English speakers.

§80.17(d) 90‑day removal requirement for incompatible facilities after settlement may be unrealistic where asbestos/lead or permitting constraints exist; request allowance for environmental abatement timelines and an explicit exception process with standard extension periods.

§80.17(e) requiring deed notices of restrictions at settlement is reasonable but jurisdictions with paper record systems may face administrative delays; request temporary electronic filing acceptance and deadlines for physical recording.

§80.19(a) perpetual dedication and maintenance as open space imposes long‑term stewardship obligations that may be challenging for small communities; request clear guidance on eligible stewards, funding for perpetual maintenance, and alternatives such as endowments or conservation easements.

§80.19(a)(3) improvements requiring floodproofing/elevation per FEMA/ordinance and Administrator criteria need explicit technical standards and a variance process for limited accessory uses to ensure consistency across regions.

§80.19(b) requiring prior written approval for conveyance of property interests creates administrative bottlenecks; request delegation thresholds (e.g., conveyances under $X or to local governments) and maximum review periods.

§80.19(b)(1) requiring transferee statements and conservation documentation is acceptable but the provision should specify acceptable evidence of conservation status and templates for transferee statements.

§80.19(b)(2) limiting conveyance only to public entities or qualified conservation organizations may prevent innovative public‑private partnerships; request allowing conveyance to private entities subject to binding conservation easements and monitoring requirements.

§80.19(b)(3) requiring conservation easements when transferred to non‑conservation public entities is appropriate but needs model easement language and a list of necessary enforcement rights to ensure compliance.

§80.19(b)(4) requiring reference to original deed restrictions and a reversion provision is necessary; request clearer default mechanisms for enforcement if a transferee ceases eligible status and guidance on triggering reversion.

§80.19(c) FEMA’s right to inspect with “reasonable notice” is appropriate but recipients request clear notice periods (e.g., 10 business days), and limits on frequency and scope to respect privacy and operations.

§80.19(d) requiring triennial certification that the property was inspected within the prior month imposes a recurring administrative burden; request alternative acceptable inspection schedules for low‑risk properties and electronic certification processes, and allow certified third‑party inspections to reduce costs.

[P1] The rulemaking text revising paragraph (5) and adding paragraph (8) is vague about whether other parts of the Spring Pygmy Sunfish entry (such as occupied vs unoccupied habitat descriptions) remain unchanged; commenters should request the agency publish the full, consolidated revised regulatory text rather than only noting amendments to specific paragraphs.

[P1] Revising paragraph (5) and adding paragraph (8) without a clear regulatory preamble explaining the biological and administrative rationale will impede meaningful public review; the agency should provide a clear explanation of why Unit 3 is being added and how the revision affects existing critical habitat boundaries.

[P1] The proposed change should explicitly state the effective date of the revisions to § 17.95(e)(5) and (8); absence of an effective date creates legal uncertainty for landowners and project proponents.

[P2] Maintaining the existing authority citation is a procedural action but the preamble should reaffirm the legal authorities relied upon (e.g., specific ESA sections) rather than merely restating the citation number to ensure the administrative record supports the regulatory change.

[P2] Legal commenters should request clarification that no additional statutory authorities are being invoked beyond those currently cited, and that no delegation changes occur as a result of this amendment.

[P3] The inclusion of an “index map” in § 17.95(e)(5) as rule text raises formatting and accessibility concerns; maps in the CFR must be legible in print and machine-readable for electronic users — the agency should commit to publishing high-resolution, georeferenced map files (e.g., GIS shapefiles) on its website.

[P3] The regulation must specify the map datum/projection and scale used for the index map to avoid ambiguity in interpreting legal boundaries for landowners, counties, and regulators.

[P3] Commenters representing private landowners will request that the index map include clear demarcations between critical habitat boundaries and adjacent private properties, and include parcel-level overlays where available so owners can determine impacts.

[P3] Environmental NGOs will request that the index map explicitly indicate which areas are occupied vs unoccupied, the presence of primary constituent elements (PCEs), and seasonality of habitat use, because an index map alone is insufficient to understand conservation obligations.

[P3] Industry commenters (utilities, developers, transportation agencies) will demand that the rule clarify whether the index map is determinative for section 7 consultations or whether the regulatory text or geospatial data in the administrative record controls in case of any discrepancies.

[P4] Adding Unit 3 (Blackwell Swamp/Run, Madison County, AL) without providing accompanying biological survey data in the preamble or administrative record makes the designation arbitrary — commenters should request disclosure of survey methods, dates, population estimates, and justification for including this unit.

[P4] Local governments in Madison County will object unless the economic analysis for designation of Unit 3 is provided and demonstrates compliance with the ESA’s regulatory flexibility considerations and the requirement to consider economic impacts during designation of critical habitat.

[P4] Landowner and agricultural stakeholders will request that the agency identify specific land parcels within Unit 3, list any federal actions likely to trigger section 7 consultation, and provide guidance on anticipated restrictions or conservation measures.

[P4] Conservation organizations will support adding Unit 3 but will request that the rule specify the PCEs for Spring Pygmy Sunfish within Unit 3 and include measures to protect spring flow, water quality, and surrounding riparian vegetation.

[P4] Commenters should ask the agency to clarify whether inclusion of Unit 3 creates any new prohibitions for private incidental take under section 9, and to explain the interplay between critical habitat designation and take prohibitions.

[P4] Tribal governments or indigenous groups (if present in Madison County) should request consultation and clarification whether Unit 3 overlaps any tribal lands or culturally important sites and how the designation will affect tribal rights and activities.

[P4] Emergency service providers and infrastructure agencies will request confirmation that critical habitat designation for Unit 3 will not obstruct legally required emergency or safety activities, and ask for explicit regulatory language or guidance to that effect.

[P5] The requirement to include a map of Unit 3 in the rule text (§ 17.95(e)(8)(ii)) raises concerns about the legal precision of map-based boundaries; commenters should demand that the rule incorporate a legal textual description (metes and bounds or coordinates) in addition to the map.

[P5] The rule should specify the coordinate system and provide latitude/longitude coordinates (decimal degrees) for the perimeter of Unit 3 so regulated parties can determine exact boundaries for compliance and consultation.

[P5] GIS and municipal planners will request that the agency provide downloadable shapefiles and KML files for the Unit 3 map, as images embedded in the CFR are insufficient for planning and section 7 analysis.

[P5] Property owners within or adjacent to Unit 3 should request that the unit map explicitly indicate any existing developed areas, roadways, and non-habitat lands that are being excluded or considered exempt from the critical habitat designation.

[P5] Legal commenters should warn that including complex cartographic images within the CFR text may create challenges for codification and recommend that the regulatory text reference maps posted in the docket and on the agency website, with clear statements that the digital map governs.

[P5] Commenters should request a discrepancy-resolution process be described in the rule for cases where on-the-ground markers or landowner maps conflict with the Unit 3 map in the CFR (e.g., how the agency will resolve contestations of boundary placement).

[P3][P5] Multiple stakeholders will request clarification about whether the index map (P3) and the Unit 3 map (P5) are the sole authoritative boundary sources, and if not, which data set (CFR-embedded map, published GIS layer, or descriptive coordinates) governs for enforcement and consultation.

[P4][P5] Environmental compliance consultants will ask the agency to provide transitional guidance on how ongoing or pending section 7 consultations in Madison County will be treated with respect to the new Unit 3 map — whether re-initiation is required and how to account for new critical habitat.

[P1][P3] Procedural due process commenters will assert that the agency must provide additional public outreach (local hearings in Madison County) because adding Unit 3 is a substantive change with localized impacts, not just a technical amendment to paragraph numbering.

[P4] Commenters will request disclosure of any mitigation or conservation plans (e.g., Safe Harbor, candidate conservation agreements) that the agency intends to promote or require inside Unit 3 and how those programs will interact with critical habitat protections.

[P3] Scientific reviewers will ask that the index map include hydrological connectivity features (springs, seeps, groundwater recharge zones) because the Spring Pygmy Sunfish depends on spring systems; omission of hydrology undermines the utility of the map.

[P4] Business associations (homebuilders, developers) will challenge the need for Unit 3 inclusion if historical occurrence records are sparse; they will request the agency provide a clear threshold of evidence it used to designate the unit.

[P5] Commenters will request that any map published in the CFR be accompanied by an accessible legend, scale bar, north arrow, and other cartographic elements required by standard map publication practices to avoid misinterpretation.

[P3][P5] Several commenters will request that the agency state whether the addition of maps will be archived in the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) in a readily accessible format, to ensure the maps are part of the permanent rulemaking record.

[P4] Conservation scientists will request that the agency specify management actions or regulatory triggers associated with Unit 3 (e.g., protective buffers, groundwater withdrawal limits) so the designation has practical conservation effect beyond boundary delineation.

[P2] Administrative law experts will comment that simply “maintaining the existing authority citation” does not absolve the agency from providing a full statement of basis and purpose showing how the authority supports the specific changes being made to § 17.95(e).

[P1] The June 1, 2021 comment deadline is unreasonable and too short for international operators and small entities to prepare meaningful technical comments; extend the comment period by at least 60–90 days.

[P1] The rule does not state whether the comment due date is the postmark date or received-by date; clarify that comments postmarked by June 1, 2021 will be accepted.

[P2] The compliance requirement "within the compliance times specified" is vague because the AD references multiple actions with different timelines; provide a consolidated compliance schedule and examples to avoid misinterpretation.

[P2] The AD should include explicit relief or a phased compliance plan for operators that cannot meet all specified compliance times due to supply-chain constraints for replacement parts.

[P3] The 120‑day deadline to revise an FAA‑approved MEL for GEnx‑1B engines is burdening for foreign and small operators that require internal approvals and FAA coordination; extend to 180 days or allow temporary operational procedures until MEL revision is completed.

[P3] The AD does not specify whether the 120‑day MEL revision starts from the AD issuance date or the effective date; clarify the start point to avoid enforcement ambiguity.

[P4] Allowing the principal operations or maintenance inspector to approve alternative MEL wording (Note 1) could create inconsistent mitigations across jurisdictions; require FAA regional guidance or model alternative wording to ensure uniform safety levels.

[P4] Note 1 should require the inspector to document any alternative MEL wording and make that documentation subject to FAA oversight and audit.

[P5] The 120‑day MEL revision requirement for GEnx‑2B engines mirrors P3 concerns; request extending to 180 days or permitting temporary dispatch procedures when operators demonstrate equivalent safety.

[P6] Note 2 permitting inspector‑approved alternative wording needs the same constraints as Note 1 — require submission of alternative wording to the FAA for recordkeeping and consistency.

[P7] The dispatch prohibition tied to EICAS "ENG EEC C 1 X" is too broad; operators seek clarification whether the prohibition applies when the message appears only transiently or requires persistence for a defined time.

[P7] The AD should clarify whether the dispatch prohibition applies to multi‑engine dispatch scenarios (e.g., ferry flights with one engine inoperative) and whether ferry permits can be issued.

[P8] Figure 1 condition i (no CMCF maintenance messages correlating with EICAS) could generate false positives due to data transmission delays; require allowance for confirmation checks (e.g., verify after power cycle) before prohibiting dispatch.

[P9] The condition in Figure 1 ii tying dispatch prohibition to specific maintenance fault code combinations lacks guidance on how maintenance personnel should retrieve and interpret CMCF messages; include diagnostic procedures and examples.

[P10] The exact fault code combinations in Figure 1 ii (e.g., {TLA out of range fault} {76-1953X (CH-A)} AND {73-3204X OR 73-3121X OR 73-1205X OR 73-1122X}) are highly specific and may differ by software/database versions; require FAA to publish a mapping of codes across CMCF software revisions and EEC software versions.

raw_output:
[P1] The March 12, 2018 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonably short given the complexity of the AD and should be extended to allow operators and OEMs enough time to assess impacts and prepare meaningful comments.

[P1] Requiring comments to be received by March 12, 2018 without clear time zone or receipt method raises procedural ambiguity; specify the exact time (e.g., 11:59 p.m. EST) and acceptable delivery methods.

[P2] § 39.13(f) is unclear whether "comply within the specified compliance times" permits phased compliance across fleets with staggered shop visits; request explicit allowance for staged compliance schedules tied to operational constraints.

[P2] The obligation in § 39.13(f) lacks an exception for emergency maintenance or temporary deviations necessary for safety or operational continuity; propose a narrowly tailored temporary exemption process.

[P3] § 39.13(g)(1) references multiple ASBs and tables but does not provide these documents in the rule text; commenters request that the FAA include or directly reference the exact service bulletin revision numbers and dates to avoid ambiguity.

[P3] Requiring replacement of parts listed in Tables 2–5 per the "referenced ASB" without attaching the ASB could create compliance uncertainty for international operators who may not have immediate access to GE Aviation Czech service documents.

[P4] § 39.13(g)(1)(i) mandating replacement "during the next engine shop visit" unfairly penalizes low-utilization engines that may not have shop visits for many years; request an alternative flight-hour or cycle-based trigger.

[P4] The phrase "next engine shop visit" is ambiguous—commenters request the FAA define "engine shop visit" (e.g., removal from aircraft, major teardown, specific maintenance tasks) to ensure consistent application.

[P5] The 6,600 engine equivalent cycles threshold in § 39.13(g)(1)(ii) is unsupported by presented risk analysis in the preamble; operators request the FAA provide the safety data justifying the 6,600-cycle limit or revise to a risk-based threshold.

[P5] § 39.13(g)(1)(ii)'s reference to "engine equivalent cycles since new or since last overhaul" creates recordkeeping burdens for older engines with incomplete history; request guidance on acceptable methods to estimate cycles or an alternative compliance metric.

[P6] § 39.13(g)(1)(iii) ties compliance to Table 1 but those rows (P7–P10) appear duplicative and inconsistent (overlapping manufacture dates); ask FAA to reconcile manufacture date boundaries to avoid conflicting applicability.

[P7] Table 1 row 1 (§ 39.13(g) Table 1) imposes a 5-year compliance for engines manufactured on or before December 31, 2008, measured from release to service after last shop visit; operators request clarification whether the countdown begins from the most recent shop visit before the AD effective date or from the next shop visit.

[P7] Smaller operators with older fleets (engine MFG ≤ Dec 31, 2008) will face concentrated shop workload due to the 5-year deadline in Table 1 row 1 and request phased or priority scheduling assistance to avoid operational disruptions.

[P8] Table 1 row 2 establishes 10 years for engines manufactured Jan 1, 2009 or later that have never had a shop visit; this creates incentives to avoid shop visits to gain the longer compliance window—request the FAA close this loophole or provide anti-abuse language.

[P8] The distinction in Table 1 row 2 between engines "never subjected to an engine shop visit" and those with any shop visit creates recordkeeping verification burdens; request the FAA specify acceptable proof (e.g., maintenance logs, EASA/FAA records) and allow operator affidavits where records are missing.

[P9] Table 1 row 3 repeats a 5-year compliance for engines manufactured Feb 9, 2014 or before; since this overlaps with earlier rows, commenters ask for a consolidated table with non-overlapping date ranges and rationale for different cutoffs.

[P10] Table 1 row 4's 10-year compliance for engines manufactured Feb 10, 2014 or later appears to grant newer engines longer compliance times without clear safety justification; request the FAA provide data showing lower risk for newer manufacturing dates.

[P11] § 39.13(h)(1) prohibition on reinstalling P/Ns listed in Tables 2–5 after modification lacks an accommodation for parts recovered from salvage or used for training; propose allowing non-airworthy use or clearly permitting part marking and disposal methods.

[P11] The absolute ban in § 39.13(h)(1) on installing listed P/Ns on modified engines may create supply-chain disruptions for in-service spares pools; recommend a grandfathering allowance for parts already ordered or in transit at the AD effective date, with a limited-time installation permit if used to return an engine to service pending replacement.

[P12] § 39.13(h)(2) prohibits installation of listed P/Ns on engines manufactured on or after Sept 1, 2017 after the AD effective date; this retroactive prohibition on manufacturer-supplied parts needs coordination with part distributors and OEM warranty processes—request a compliance grace period for parts sold before the AD effective date.

[P12] The effective date cutoff of Sept 1, 2017 for manufacture-based prohibition may conflict with international certification schedules for engines assembled overseas; request explicit guidance for non-U.S. manufacturers and importers.

[P13] § 39.13(j)(1) authorizes the ECO Branch Manager to approve AMOCs, but centralizing discretion could delay urgent AMOC approvals; recommend delegating limited AMOC authority to DERs or regional FAA offices for quicker response.

[P14] The requirement in § 39.13(j)(1) to send AMOC requests to a principal inspector or local FSDO could be inefficient for operators without an assigned inspector (e.g., foreign operators); request explicit alternative routing and timelines for acknowledgement/decision.

[P15] The instruction in § 39.13(j)(1) to address direct submissions to the person in paragraph (k) lacks the specific name and contact details in this excerpt; request the rule include the point of contact name, title, address, and phone to avoid misrouting.

[P16] Permitting AMOC requests by email to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov is helpful, but the rule should require confirmation of receipt and provide expected response time windows (e.g., 30 days) to allow operational planning.

[P17] § 39.13(j)(2) requires notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC; operators request clarification whether "before" means prior to the first flight conducted under the AMOC, prior to parts installation, or prior to physical use of the modified component.

[P17] The obligation to notify the principal inspector prior to using an AMOC could cause delays if the principal inspector is unavailable; suggest allowing simultaneous notice and use with retroactive acknowledgement in urgent cases.

[P18] § 39.13(k)(2) permits public examination of the MCAI in Docket FAA–2017–0967 at regulations.gov, but many referenced technical data may be proprietary and missing from the docket; request FAA ensure all safety-critical MCAI material is publicly accessible or provide redacted summaries sufficient for compliance.

[P19] § 39.13(k)(3) allows viewing service information at the FAA Engine & Propeller Standards Branch, but access during business hours only and potential export control issues may impede foreign operators; request electronic access or a public copy in the docket.

[P20] 50 CFR Part 660 deadline (Feb 23, 2018) conflicts with FAA deadlines (Mar 12, 2018 & Mar 20, 2020) causing stakeholder confusion across agencies; request NOAA and FAA harmonize comment periods for related rules or clearly explain cross-agency interdependencies.

[P21] Allowing multiple submission methods under 50 CFR Part 660 ADDRESSES is appropriate, but the rule should specify whether identical submissions via multiple methods will be treated as single comments to avoid duplication.

[P22] Electronic submission instructions (www.regulations.gov) in 50 CFR Part 660 are fine, but the required steps are cumbersome for bulk attachments (technical data); request explicit guidance for submitting large technical appendices or proprietary attachments.

[P23] Mailing comments to NMFS is permitted (50 CFR Part 660) but the rule should clarify whether mailed submissions must be accompanied by electronic copies for docketing and expedite scanning times.

[P24] The warning that comments received after the comment period "may not be considered" is standard, but NMFS should commit to accepting late comments that raise new data or safety-critical information received within a reasonable cure period, especially if caused by systems outages.

[P25] Accepting anonymous comments (enter "N/A") is useful, but NMFS should clarify how it will weigh anonymous submissions and whether they will be used in regulatory impact analyses and stakeholder outreach.

[P26] 50 CFR 660.50(d) requirement that tribes request allocations in writing during the biennial process may disadvantage tribes that missed the window due to lack of notice; recommend NMFS provide direct outreach and allow late requests when justified.

[P27] The Secretary's obligation to develop tribal allocations "in consultation" and "as practicable with tribal consensus" lacks measurable standards; tribes seek a defined timeline, attendance protocols, and dispute resolution mechanisms to ensure meaningful consultation.

[P28] The FAA comment deadline of March 20, 2020 in (a) differs from earlier FAA deadlines listed elsewhere; please reconcile the multiple FAA comment deadlines and specify which applies to this AD.

[P29] Reiteration of the compliance obligation in (f) is redundant and could cause interpretive conflict with specific timing options in (g)(1); request consolidation and cross-references to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P30] (g)(1) requires replacement with parts identified in "Planning" ASB—commenters request the full ASB citation, part numbers, and whether any modified parts require additional airworthiness approvals (STC, major repair) before installation.

[P31] (g)(1)(i) "During the next engine shop visit" should explicitly permit operators to coordinate with maintenance providers to avoid duplicate shop events—request allowance to combine required replacements with other scheduled maintenance to reduce downtime.

[P32] (g)(1)(ii) referencing "applicable Airworthiness Limitations Section" as a timing option is appropriate, but the AD should explicitly state that the ALS timing supersedes table-based timing where more restrictive, or clarify precedence.

[P33] (g)(1)(iii) reliance on Table 1 compliance "in years after the effective date" needs clarity on how to compute fractional years and whether leap years or month/day calculations matter; request an explicit formula.

[P34] (h)(1) prohibition should include a process for returning inadvertently installed prohibited P/Ns to the manufacturer for traceability and disposal documentation to ensure chain-of-custody and reporting compliance.

[P35] (h)(2) forbids installation of listed P/Ns on engines manufactured on or after Sept 1, 2017; OEMs request transition guidance for their production lines, inventory control recommendations, and a window to update manufacturing instructions and distribution channels.

[P36] (j)(1) AMOC authority vested in the Manager, ECO Branch, should include published objective criteria for AMOC approval to increase transparency and predictability for applicants.

[P37] (j)(1) requiring AMOC requests to go to the principal inspector or local FSDO is problematic for foreign repair stations; request FAA to permit foreign repair stations to submit AMOC requests via the OEM or assigned principal inspector of the U.S. operator.

[P38] (j)(1) directing AMOC information to the person in paragraph (k)(1) without including that contact in the final rule could lead to mail/email misdirection; require the FAA to include a named contact with office address and phone in the rule text.

[P39] (j)(1) permitting email submissions to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov is helpful but raises cybersecurity and proprietary information concerns; request FAA provide secure file upload instructions or guidance on redaction of proprietary data.

[P40] (j)(2) requiring notice to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC should also require the FAA to issue written AMOC approvals with explicit limitations and start/end dates so operators know when they can implement changes.

Electronic submission instructions (www.regulations.gov) in 50 CFR Part 660 are fine, but the required steps are cumbersome for bulk attachments (technical data); request explicit guidance for submitting large technical appendices or proprietary attachments.
Mailing comments to NMFS is permitted (50 CFR Part 660) but the rule should clarify whether mailed submissions must be accompanied by electronic copies for docketing and expedite scanning times.

The warning that comments received after the comment period "may not be considered" is standard, but NMFS should commit to accepting late comments that raise new data or safety-critical information received within a reasonable cure period, especially if caused by systems outages.

Accepting anonymous comments (enter "N/A") is useful, but NMFS should clarify how it will weigh anonymous submissions and whether they will be used in regulatory impact analyses and stakeholder outreach.

50 CFR 660.50(d) requirement that tribes request allocations in writing during the biennial process may disadvantage tribes that missed the window due to lack of notice; recommend NMFS provide direct outreach and allow late requests when justified.

The Secretary's obligation to develop tribal allocations "in consultation" and "as practicable with tribal consensus" lacks measurable standards; tribes seek a defined timeline, attendance protocols, and dispute resolution mechanisms to ensure meaningful consultation.
The FAA comment deadline of March 20, 2020 in (a) differs from earlier FAA deadlines listed elsewhere; please reconcile the multiple FAA comment deadlines and specify which applies to this AD.

Reiteration of the compliance obligation in (f) is redundant and could cause interpretive conflict with specific timing options in (g)(1); request consolidation and cross-references to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

(g)(1) requires replacement with parts identified in "Planning" ASB—commenters request the full ASB citation, part numbers, and whether any modified parts require additional airworthiness approvals (STC, major repair) before installation.

(g)(1)(i) "During the next engine shop visit" should explicitly permit operators to coordinate with maintenance providers to avoid duplicate shop events—request allowance to combine required replacements with other scheduled maintenance to reduce downtime.

(g)(1)(ii) referencing "applicable Airworthiness Limitations Section" as a timing option is appropriate, but the AD should explicitly state that the ALS timing supersedes table-based timing where more restrictive, or clarify precedence.

(g)(1)(iii) reliance on Table 1 compliance "in years after the effective date" needs clarity on how to compute fractional years and whether leap years or month/day calculations matter; request an explicit formula.

(h)(1) prohibition should include a process for returning inadvertently installed prohibited P/Ns to the manufacturer for traceability and disposal documentation to ensure chain-of-custody and reporting compliance.

(h)(2) forbids installation of listed P/Ns on engines manufactured on or after Sept 1, 2017; OEMs request transition guidance for their production lines, inventory control recommendations, and a window to update manufacturing instructions and distribution channels.
(j)(1) AMOC authority vested in the Manager, ECO Branch, should include published objective criteria for AMOC approval to increase transparency and predictability for applicants.

(j)(1) requiring AMOC requests to go to the principal inspector or local FSDO is problematic for foreign repair stations; request FAA to permit foreign repair stations to submit AMOC requests via the OEM or assigned principal inspector of the U.S. operator.

(j)(1) directing AMOC information to the person in paragraph (k)(1) without including that contact in the final rule could lead to mail/email misdirection; require the FAA to include a named contact with office address and phone in the rule text.

(j)(1) permitting email submissions to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov is helpful but raises cybersecurity and proprietary information concerns; request FAA provide secure file upload instructions or guidance on redaction of proprietary data.

(j)(2) requiring notice to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC should also require the FAA to issue written AMOC approvals with explicit limitations and start/end dates so operators know when they can implement changes.

[P1] The definition of physical and biological features in §17.95(i)(2) is overly vague because it truncates the sentence and omits clear spatial boundaries for the "critical habitat area on San Juan Island," making it impossible to determine which parcels are included.

[P1] Conservation NGOs will request that the rule clarify the geographic extent of the "critical habitat area on San Juan Island" by providing maps, parcel identifiers, or legal descriptions to avoid uncertainty for landowners and managers.

[P1] Legal commenters will argue that the rule must specify the baseline date and the process used to delineate the critical habitat to satisfy the Administrative Procedure Act requirement for a reasoned explanation.

[P2] Private landowners and the San Juan County government will object that the requirement for areas to be "large enough" to allow patchy-population dynamics is subjective and lacks a quantified minimum area, creating regulatory uncertainty for land-use planning.

[P2] Developers and transportation agencies will request specific numeric thresholds (e.g., minimum patch size in hectares or distances between patches) for the "patchy-population dynamics" requirement so they can evaluate project impacts.

[P2] Conservation biologists will support the emphasis on open, treeless areas with short-statured forb- and grass-dominated vegetation but will ask the agency to include explicit reference to historic disturbance regimes (e.g., grazing, fire) that maintain those habitats.

[P2] Forestry interests will ask for clarification whether tree removal or canopy thinning to create "primarily treeless" conditions will be permitted within existing forested parcels that are otherwise designated as critical habitat.

[P3] Agricultural groups and private landowners will seek to confirm whether low- to medium-density larval host plants permit continued agricultural use (e.g., pasture, low-intensity haying) or whether such activities would constitute take or prohibited modification.

[P3] Pollinator advocates will request that the rule list the specific plant species included as acceptable larval hosts or, at minimum, publish an appendix with currently known host species to avoid misinterpretation.

[P3] Scientific commenters will ask the agency to provide empirical justification (citations/studies) for the May–July bud-and-bloom phenology window and whether climate change-induced phenological shifts would require adaptive updates to the rule.

[P3] Restoration practitioners will request guidance on acceptable planting densities for "low- to medium-density" host plant stands and monitoring criteria to demonstrate compliance with the provision.

[P4] Recreational groups and land managers will seek clarification on whether "adult nectar resources in bloom" includes nonnative or ornamental plantings (e.g., garden plantings) and whether such plantings can be used intentionally to provide nectar resources within critical habitat.

[P4] Property owners adjacent to critical habitat will request assurance that incidental planting of white-flowering, short-statured ornamental plants will not trigger regulatory restrictions or be construed as altering critical habitat.

[P4] Pollinator conservation NGOs will recommend that the agency explicitly include a broader list of nectar species known to be used by island marble butterflies and provide seasonal bloom calendars to ensure nectar availability across the flight period.

[P5] Farmers and ranchers will object that the obligation to keep "vegetation around larval host plants...undisturbed and be left standing long enough for diapause, pupation, and completion" could prohibit customary fall and early-spring mowing, grazing, and haying without defining allowable timing and intensity.

[P5] Agricultural extension services will request explicit seasonal timelines and allowable management windows (e.g., latest allowable mowing date) to reconcile agricultural operations with the requirement to leave vegetation standing for diapause and pupation.

[P5] Conservation scientists will ask the agency to define "sufficient" in terms of buffer width and vegetation structure (e.g., minimum 0.5 m height, 1–3 m buffer radius) around larval host plants to make enforcement and restoration planning practicable.

[P5] Livestock owners will request guidance on whether rotational grazing that temporarily removes vegetation around host plants during non-critical life stages is permitted, and whether exclosures or compensatory measures would satisfy the obligation.

[P6] Real estate and infrastructure stakeholders will welcome the exclusion of manmade structures but will request explicit examples and mapping criteria to determine when a parcel's developed footprint versus undeveloped remainder is excluded from critical habitat.

[P6] County assessors will ask for clarification about partial exclusions: whether the land underlying a building is excluded but an immediately adjacent lawn or road shoulder is included, and how the boundary is determined legally.

[P6] Legal advocates for private property rights will argue that excluding "manmade structures and the land they occupy as of the rule's effective date" should be expanded to include previously developed but currently unused structures to prevent retroactive restrictions.

[P6] Conservation groups will caution that the manmade-structure exclusion must not be used to de-designate adjacent natural habitat patches necessary for butterfly conservation and will request a statement that the exclusion does not apply to surrounding native vegetation required by P5.

[P1] Environmental consultants will request the rule include specific metrics for "physical and biological features" (e.g., soil types, elevation bands, microclimate parameters) to guide surveys and conservation planning for the island marble butterfly.

[P2] Military or emergency-response agencies operating on San Juan Island will request an exemption process when temporary alterations to topography or vegetation are necessary for public safety, with clear criteria and consultation procedures.

[P3] Nurseries and native-plant suppliers will ask whether propagation and sale of listed larval-host species for use within critical habitat will be regulated, and if permitting or certifications are required.

[P4] Homeowner associations will request clarification whether small garden patches of nectar-producing species are encouraged or regulated, and whether promotion of native nectar plantings could be part of compensatory mitigation.

[P5] Attorneys will note that the phrase "left standing long enough" is inherently subjective and ask the agency to adopt measurable endpoints (e.g., percent overwintering survival targets) to allow for objective compliance assessment.

[P6] Transportation agencies will ask how the exclusion of paved areas interacts with rights-of-way and utility easements where infrastructure corridors contain adjacent native vegetation that may function as critical habitat, requesting mapping and case examples.
