[P1] Industry commenters will argue that the blanket prohibition on separate OPPS payment for specified drugs and biologicals (except non-opioid surgical supplies) is overly broad and will disincentivize hospitals from stocking novel, high-cost biologics that legitimately require outpatient administration, risking patient access.

[P1] Clinical specialty societies will claim the exception for “non-opioid pain management drugs that function as a supply in surgery” is ambiguous and will lead to inconsistent billing because the rule does not define “function as a supply in surgery” or list qualifying products.

[P1] Hospital associations will assert the prohibition fails to account for drugs administered in observation stays or extended recovery where separate payment is clinically necessary, requesting carve-outs for infusion biologics and certain chemotherapy agents.

[P2] Health economists will request clarification and a calculation example for the “conversion factor equal to prior year updated as follows” language to ensure transparency and reproducibility of year-to-year rate setting.

[P3] Provider groups will object to setting the CY2009 update at zero percent as arbitrary, asking CMS to explain why a historical zero update remains appropriate for precedent and calculation continuity.

[P4] Patient advocates will ask CMS to justify using CPI-U for CY2010–CY2018 rather than a health-care specific price index, arguing CPI-U underestimates real medical input cost growth and harms ASC financial viability.

[P5] ASC trade groups will challenge using the hospital inpatient market basket for CY2019–CY2023 updates, contending inpatient cost structures differ materially from ASC operations and this will misalign payments with ASC costs.

[P6] Smaller ASCs will oppose reverting to CPI-U from CY2024 onward, stating CPI-U does not reflect wage and supply cost inflation relevant to surgical facilities, and request adoption of a health-sector or ASC-specific index.

[P7] ASCs and safety advocates will contest the 2.0 percentage-point reduction for failing ASC quality reporting standards for CY2014–CY2018 as punitive, arguing the reduction amount is arbitrary and disproportionately harms rural and small-volume ASCs that lack reporting infrastructure.

[P8] Legal experts will request CMS provide due process safeguards and an appeal mechanism before imposing the 2.0 percentage-point reduction for CY2019–CY2023, noting the provision ties payment reductions to administrative reporting compliance without clear procedural protections.

[P9] Equity-focused commenters will state the continued 2.0 percentage-point reduction for CY2024+ will exacerbate disparities by disproportionately impacting ASCs serving low-income or rural populations that struggle with reporting resources, and ask for mitigation measures or scaled penalties.

[P10] Policy analysts will ask CMS to publish the exact statutory productivity adjustment methodology and example calculations applied to CPI-U for CY2011–CY2018 to allow stakeholders to model impacts on conversion factors.

[P11] ASC operators will request CMS disclose the multifactor productivity inputs and weighting used when applying the statutory productivity adjustment to the hospital inpatient market basket for CY2019–CY2023, because unpublished assumptions can materially affect payments.

[P12] Industry commenters will seek clarity on the interaction between the statutory productivity adjustment and the 2.0 percentage-point reductions for CY2024+, specifically whether reductions are applied before or after productivity adjustments and how negative updates are handled.

[P13] Providers and hospitals will strongly object to the explicit permission that application of prescribed adjustments may yield negative updates (i.e., a decrease in payment rates compared to prior year), arguing CMS should cap decreases at zero to prevent service disruption.

[P14] Measure developers and quality advocates will support the requirement that CMS use the regular rulemaking process to remove ASCQR measures unless immediate safety concerns exist, but will request a defined timeline for that rulemaking to avoid long delays.

[P15] Hospitals and measurement bodies will request CMS to require publication of the weight or priority CMS gives to each factor listed in § 416.320(c)(2) when deciding to remove measures, to ensure transparent, consistent decisions.

[P16] Hospital quality directors will ask for clarification on the evidence standard and data sources CMS will use to determine a measure is “topped-out” among ASCs under § 416.320(c)(2)(i), including minimum sample sizes and risk adjustment expectations.

[P17] Patient outcome researchers will request CMS define metrics or thresholds for concluding a measure’s performance “does not result in better patient outcomes” under § 416.320(c)(2)(ii), and require empirical studies be cited in removal decisions.

[P18] Clinical societies will caution that removing measures because they “do not align with current clinical guidelines” (§ 416.320(c)(2)(iii)) may disadvantage emerging best practices that lack guideline incorporation; they request a process to evaluate timeliness of guidelines.

[P19] Quality advocates will support replacing setting-specific measures with more broadly applicable measures (§ 416.320(c)(2)(iv)) but request CMS demonstrate equivalence and validity before removal to avoid losing setting-specific patient-safety signals.

[P20] Public commenters will urge CMS to prioritize measures more proximal to patient outcomes (§ 416.320(c)(2)(v)) but to provide standards for “proximal” (e.g., time horizon, clinical significance) so removals are not subjective.

[P21] Researchers will request CMS require statistical evidence demonstrating stronger association with desired outcomes for any replacement measure (§ 416.320(c)(2)(vi)) and publish those validity analyses.

[P22] Hospital compliance officers warn that removing measures because their collection “leads to negative unintended consequences” (§ 416.320(c)(2)(vii)) requires careful documentation of consequence types and causality to prevent gaming claims.

[P23] Fiscal watchdog groups will demand CMS perform and publish cost-benefit analyses when invoking “costs outweigh benefits” (§ 416.320(c)(2)(viii)), including quantification of reporting burden, IT costs, and downstream clinical effects.

[P24] Measure developers will seek technical details on the two-part topped-out definition (§ 416.320(c)(3)), including the “specified test” referenced for percentile indistinguishability and how truncation for the variance is performed.

[P25] Statisticians will request the exact statistical test and alpha level CMS will use to judge whether 75th and 90th percentile performances are “statistically indistinguishable” (§ 416.320(c)(3)(i)), because results vary by method.

[P26] Analysts will ask CMS to justify and provide empirical support for choosing a truncated coefficient of variation threshold of ≤0.10 (§ 416.320(c)(3)(ii)) as the criterion for topped-out measures, and to consider alternatives.

[P27] Patient safety organizations will welcome the case-by-case assessment requirement (§ 416.320(c)(4)) but will request CMS explicitly prohibit removal based solely on performance improvement unless patient harm-risk is evaluated.

[P28] Labor unions and provider groups will request CMS explain how the CY2019 multifactor productivity adjustment and the 0.75 percentage point adjustment (§ 419.32(b)(1)(iv)(B)(10)) were calculated, and provide modeling showing net effect on hospital reimbursement.

[P29] Hospitals will raise operational concerns about the QualityNet registration requirement (§ 419.46(a)(1)), requesting CMS provide technical support timelines and exception/backup procedures for hospitals that experience registration system outages.

[P30] IT and security officers will point out that requiring identification and registration of a QualityNet security administrator (§ 419.46(a)(2)) imposes liability concentration; they will ask CMS to allow multiple administrators and backup designees.

[P31] Small hospitals will object that the requirement to “submit at least one data element” (§ 419.46(a)(3)) is vague and could be interpreted to mean minimal compliance is acceptable; they request CMS specify mandatory core data elements to standardize reporting.

[P32] Hospital associations will request CMS specify which previously adopted Hospital OQR measures are retained (§ 419.46(h)(1)) and commit to a published schedule for any proposed removals to allow hospitals time to adjust reporting systems.

[P33] Patient safety advocates will support immediate removal and notification for safety-concerning measures (§ 419.46(h)(2)) but will request CMS define “patient safety concerns” and require public posting of supporting evidence in the ListServ/QualityNet notice.

[P34] Hospitals will emphasize that the rule’s requirement to use regular rulemaking for non-safety removals (§ 419.46(h)(3)) must include minimum notice periods and comment windows to permit technical changes to EHRs and vendor software.

[P35] Quality measure stakeholders will ask CMS to clarify whether the same eight factors listed for Hospital OQR (§ 419.46(h)(3)(i)) mirror those used for ASCQR (and vice versa), and to harmonize factor definitions and removal processes across programs to reduce burden.

[P36] Hospital analysts will reiterate concerns about using the “topped-out” criteria (§ 419.46(h)(3)(i)(A) and (ii)) without specifying how often CMS will reassess measures for topped-out status and whether small-sample hospitals are shielded from spurious classification.

[P37] Clinical guideline organizations will ask CMS to ensure that measures are not removed simply because they are “not aligned with current clinical guidelines” (§ 419.46(h)(3)(i)(C)) when guideline bodies lag new evidence; they propose a supplemental evidence review process.

[P38] Measure stewards will request transparency on analytic methods and public release of datasets used to evaluate measure performance and remove measures under § 419.46(h)(3)(i)(D)-(F) (availability of broader/proximal/stronger measures).

[P39] Hospital CFOs will request guidance on the payment transition for items/services not meeting the ASC definition where payment will “generally” be made under the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule effective Jan 1, 2017 (§ 419.48(d)), asking CMS to list specific affected services and transitional billing codes.

[P40] Ambulatory surgery centers and physician groups will object to the Jan 1, 2019 effective date for Physician Fee Schedule payment for items/services not meeting paragraph (a)(2) (§ 419.48(e)) as creating billing confusion and request a joint crosswalk and education program before the date.

[P41] Legal commenters will argue that use of the term “generally” in §§ 419.48(d) and (e) creates uncertainty about exceptions and discretion; they request CMS specify the circumstances under which payments would not be made under the MPFS.

[P42] Rural hospitals will request phased implementation or hardship exemptions for conversion factor reductions and quality-reporting penalties (P2, P7–P9, P13) to avoid destabilizing critical access to surgical services in underserved communities.

[P43] Advocacy groups for chronically ill patients will ask CMS to create explicit exceptions to P1 for drugs and biologics that are clinically necessary for outpatient chronic disease management (e.g., biologic injectables) that do not fit the “supply in surgery” exception.

[P44] Health policy researchers will urge CMS to perform and publicly post distributional impact analyses showing how combined updates, productivity adjustments, and reporting penalties (P2, P7–P13, P28) affect provider types, regions, and patient access.

[P45] Privacy and security experts will request CMS include minimum security and privacy controls for the QualityNet security administrator role (§ 419.46(a)(2)), and protocols for credential transfer when administrators change employment.

Labor unions and provider groups will request CMS explain how the CY2019 multifactor productivity adjustment and the 0.75 percentage point adjustment (§ 419.32(b)(1)(iv)(B)(10)) were calculated, and provide modeling showing net effect on hospital reimbursement.

Hospitals will raise operational concerns about the QualityNet registration requirement (§ 419.46(a)(1)), requesting CMS provide technical support timelines and exception/backup procedures for hospitals that experience registration system outages.

Small hospitals will object that the requirement to “submit at least one data element” (§ 419.46(a)(3)) is vague and could be interpreted to mean minimal compliance is acceptable; they request CMS specify mandatory core data elements to standardize reporting.

Patient safety advocates will support immediate removal and notification for safety-concerning measures (§ 419.46(h)(2)) but will request CMS define “patient safety concerns” and require public posting of supporting evidence in the ListServ/QualityNet notice.

raw_output:
[P1] The comment deadline of January 28, 2021 is unreasonably short and should be extended to allow more meaningful public and industry input, particularly given complexities of the GTS software issue.

[P1] Industry stakeholders (airlines, MROs, OEMs) request a 60- to 90-day extension of the comment period to coordinate technical analyses and submit consolidated responses.

[P1] Small operators request an extension because they lack in-house regulatory staff to prepare detailed comments by January 28, 2021.

[P2] The rule repeats the same calendar date in two provisions (P1 and P2); the FAA should clarify whether the deadline is a postmark date, receipt date, or electronic submission date.

[P2] The AD should explicitly allow comments received after January 28, 2021 to be considered if they contain substantive technical data — the hard deadline could exclude valuable information.

[P3] The 12‑month compliance time to update GTS processor software to a version later than 3.13 is insufficient for operators who must coordinate with suppliers, obtain approvals, and schedule avionics shop visits.

[P3] Operators in remote regions and those with limited shop capacity request a two-tiered compliance schedule (e.g., 12 months for large operators, 18–24 months for small operators) or relief via AMOC.

[P3] Aircraft with heavy maintenance schedules should be allowed to perform the software update at the next C‑check without exceeding safety objectives; the rule should allow flexibility tied to scheduled maintenance.

[P4] The AD should define the "effective date" precisely (e.g., date of publication in the Federal Register) to remove ambiguity about the 12‑month clock start.

[P4] The FAA should permit credit for updates already completed to non-3.13 versions before the AD effective date and explicitly state how compliance dates apply in such cases.

[P5] The requirement that installed software "must not be 3.13 or earlier" lacks clarity about acceptable minor revisions (patches) — specify acceptable version numbers or build IDs rather than a cutoff of "3.13 or earlier."

[P5] The FAA should provide a list of approved GTS software versions (build numbers) that meet the AD, or incorporate by reference the supplier's release notes certifying compliance.

[P5] Manufacturers and software vendors request technical criteria or test evidence required to demonstrate that a version newer than 3.13 resolves the unsafe condition.

[P6] The provision allowing the Wichita ACO Branch Manager to approve AMOCs concentrates decision authority; commenters request clarification whether other FAA offices may also approve AMOCs for operators outside Wichita's geographic area.

[P6] Legal commenters ask for a statement that AMOC approvals will be made in writing and that denial reasons will be documented to allow for adjudication or appeal.

[P7] The requirement to follow 14 CFR 39.19 for AMOC requests is appropriate, but commenters request the FAA publish a template or checklist to expedite the submission and review process.

[P7] The AD should specify estimated FAA review timelines for AMOC requests to enable operators to plan compliance (e.g., 60 or 90 days).

[P8] The obligation to send AMOC requests to a principal inspector or local FSDO is reasonable, but the rule should permit electronic submission to a centralized FAA mailbox to reduce routing delays.

[P8] Some operators do not have an assigned principal inspector; the AD should include direct contact information (email/phone) for the Wichita ACO Branch to avoid misrouting.

[P9] The instruction to address direct submissions to the person identified in Related Information is fine, but commenters ask the FAA to publish the name and contact details in the AD text to prevent ambiguity.

[P9] Legal commenters request confirmation that submissions addressed directly to the certification office manager will be treated as timely if received by the AMOC deadline even if routing delays occur.

[P10] Requiring notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC may create operational delays; commenters request that the AD allow contemporaneous notification (e.g., within 48 hours of first use) when prior notice would disrupt operations.

[P10] Operators ask that the AD clarify what constitutes "notify" (written email, phone call, formal letter) and whether submission to an electronic tracking system satisfies the obligation.

[P10] Maintenance organizations point out that some AMOCs may be approved after an action has been performed under emergency circumstances; the rule should allow post‑use notification and ratification procedures for retroactive AMOCs.

[P11] The provision for notifying the local FSDO/CHDO if no principal inspector exists is reasonable, but commenters request that FAA publish contact info for FSDO/CHDO managers relevant to this AD.

[P11] Small operators who operate outside the continental U.S. request that the AD clarify which regional office they should contact as their local FSDO/CHDO may not cover international operations.

[P3] Safety advocacy groups request that the FAA justify the 12‑month compliance interval with risk analysis (e.g., probability of hazardous event with version 3.13) and publish the supporting data.

[P5] Cybersecurity advocates request that the AD include requirements to validate that newer software versions do not introduce new vulnerabilities and require evidence of cybersecurity testing.

[P3] Software vendors request allowance for staged rollouts and testing windows (e.g., install on a test aircraft or simulator first) before fleet-wide mandated updates.

[P6] Industry requests clarity on whether previously approved AMOCs for similar GTS software updates on other ADs will be accepted or need re‑submission under this AD.

[P1] Aviation labor groups request additional time to review the AD's operational effects on crew training, manuals, and procedures and thus an extension of the comment deadline.

[P5] The AD should specify whether third‑party field software loads (not provided by the OEM) are acceptable, and if so, what validation steps are required.

[P4] The FAA should provide transitional provisions for aircraft scheduled for decommissioning or sale within the 12‑month window to avoid undue burden.

[P7] Aviation legal experts recommend the FAA include an expedited AMOC process for operators who can demonstrate equivalent safety with documented test results to avoid unnecessary grounding.

raw_output:
[P1] The FAA's comment deadline of November 4, 2022 is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60–90 days to allow affected operators, repair stations, and labor unions sufficient time to prepare technical and economic comments.

[P1] Small operators and owner-operators will be unable to compile the necessary maintenance-hours and service-data comments by the November 4, 2022 deadline; the FAA should publish a 120-day comment period or reopen comments after issuing service information.

[P3] The requirement to "comply with all requirements of this AD within the specified compliance times" lacks clarity about how compliance times interact with scheduled maintenance events (e.g., calendar vs. TIS); the FAA should explicitly allow compliance at the next scheduled maintenance within the prescriptive TIS window.

[P3] Legal experts will comment that § 39.13(g) should clarify enforcement discretion if operators reasonably rely on maintenance intervals or inadvertent record gaps while making good-faith efforts to comply.

[P4] Requiring removal and replacement of v-band couplings without specifying approved replacement part numbers or manufacturer part data may create supply-chain issues; the AD should reference acceptable replacement coupling P/Ns or installation instructions.

[P5] The threshold of 500 hours TIS for mandatory removal is arbitrary and unsupported in the NPRM; request FAA provide data (failure rates vs. hours) that justify 500-hour limit.

[P5] Operators will comment that the initial removal-before-500-hours-for-<500-hours clause could force premature replacement for couplings with only a few hours remaining until 500 hours; ask for allowance to remove at first convenient maintenance event within the 500-hour limit.

[P6] Requiring immediate initial removal within 50 hours for couplings with ≥500 hours or unknown hours is impracticable for aircraft on worldwide operations with limited parts availability; ask FAA to allow inspections as the initial compliance option for aircraft with traceability issues instead of mandatory removal.

[P6] Maintenance recordkeeping systems often cannot determine hours on individual couplings; the FAA should allow use of conservative estimates or dispatch-level inspections rather than a hard 50-hour removal requirement when hours are unknown.

[P7] The alternative-of-inspections permission lacks clear reference to which specific inspection procedures (manufacturer SB) meet the requirements; commenters will request explicit incorporation by reference of inspection procedures and acceptance criteria.

[P8] Repeating the inspections every 6 months or 100 hours TIS, whichever occurs first, for up to 2 years may be burdensome and costly for general aviation owners; request extending intervals to 12 months or 200 hours TIS based on low-utilization safety data.

[P8] The 2-year inspection period cutoff is arbitrary; stakeholders will ask FAA to justify why inspections are limited to two years and what happens after two years for parts that pass inspections.

[P9] The requirement to remove couplings that fail any inspection "before further flight" may ground aircraft unexpectedly in remote locations; request allowance for temporary flight to a maintenance base under ferry permit and definition of acceptable ferry conditions.

[P10] Requiring the first visual inspection at the next annual inspection or within 12 months could delay detection of imminent failures for high-usage aircraft; recommend the FAA require inspection within 30 days for aircraft that accrue >100 hours per year.

[P11] The instruction that finding exhaust staining/sooting triggers removal and the k inspections is vague about the staining threshold; request clear photographic examples or objective criteria for what constitutes actionable staining.

[P12] The j(2) crack inspection criterion should specify crack size or location thresholds for mandatory replacement rather than "if there is a crack" which could be interpreted inconsistently.

[P13] The "looseness or separation" criterion needs measurable definitions (e.g., allowable play mm/inch at spot welds) to ensure consistent inspection results across mechanics and repair stations.

[P14] The "cupping/bowing/crowning" criterion references a figure, but the AD should include quantitative tolerances (millimeters of deformation) rather than only visual depiction to reduce subjectivity.

[P15] Inspecting "area opposite t-bolt for damage/distortion" without defining acceptable deformation tolerances will cause compliance inconsistency; propose specifying maximum allowable out-of-plane deformation.

[P16] Using a mirror to detect space between v-retainer segments is ambiguous — the AD should specify minimum detectable gap size or provide a go/no-go gauge or reference photos.

[P17] The torque check requirement (j(7)) must specify the torque value, torque procedure (e.g., in-lb/Nm, sequence), and acceptable tolerance; otherwise mechanics cannot determine "correct torque".

[P18] The statement that installing a new v-band coupling does not terminate repetitive inspections will increase life-cycle costs; request FAA provide an optional terminating action (e.g., installation of redesigned coupling P/N) or a documented service life.

[P19] The requirement to remove coupling for k inspections when j(1) or j(4) conditions are found could require complete disassembly and replacement of exhaust components — FAA should quantify typical downtime and provide allowance for scheduled maintenance coordination.

[P20] Specification to use crocus cloth and mineral spirits or Stoddard solvent should include warnings about potential damage to plated or coated couplings and authorized cleaning alternatives; request inclusion of acceptable substitutes and safety precautions.

[P21] The "if corrosion cannot be removed or there is pitting, remove and replace before further flight" provision should define "pitting" severity thresholds (depth, area) to distinguish minor surface etch from safety-critical pitting.

[P22] Requiring a 10X magnifier inspection is appropriate, but the AD should allow alternative NDT (dye penetrant or borescope) performed per approved procedures — request explicitly permitting equivalent inspection methods.

[P23] The straight-edge flatness gap limit of >0.062 inch lacks justification; operators request the basis for 0.062 inch and that the AD permit calibration/measurement guidance (straight edge length, measurement points).

[P24] The requirement to position the t-bolt at 12 o'clock for inspection could be impractical for some installations; request allowance to inspect in other orientations if the same inspection access is achieved.

[P25] The bend radii crack inspection should specify rolling or flex criteria and acceptable crack length threshold for replacement to avoid inconsistent judgment calls.

[P26] The inspection for damage from spreading opposite the t-bolt should be clarified with quantitative damage metrics (crease depth, bulge height) or photographic examples.

[P27] Allowing reinstallation if k(1) inspections pass is reasonable, but the AD should require documentation of the inspection and re-torque action in the permanent records and specify what paperwork is acceptable.

[P28] The reinstallation torque requirement must specify the torque value and method (calibrated torque wrench) and require documentation in the maintenance log for traceability.

[P29] The pre-reinstallation requirement to inspect for space between v-retainer segments should define acceptable gap width and require documentation that the inspector used a mirror or other method.

[P30] The mandate to remove if no space exists between segments next to the t-bolt before further flight may be overbroad; provide technical rationale why zero-gap is unsafe and allow engineering evaluation for borderline cases.

[P31] The prohibition on installing any used coupling (>0 hours TIS) during first two years unless it passes inspections is likely to create acute parts shortages for small operators; request temporary relief allowing installation of overhauled couplings with traceable inspection records.

[P31] Suppliers will note this ban effectively prevents use of serviceable used inventory and will increase costs; request an exemption for used couplings that have known, documented small hours and passing recent inspections.

[P32] Beginning two years after the AD, prohibiting installation of used couplings with >0 and <500 hours unless they pass inspections is redundant if adequate inspection procedures exist; commenters will ask FAA to harmonize this with existing PMA/overhaul approvals.

[P33] The prohibition on installing any coupling with 500+ hours after two years is effectively a service-life limit; request FAA provide a method for parts manufacturers to produce replacement couplings with an FAA-approved life extension or redesigned part acceptance.

[P33] Legal counsel will assert that the retrofit/installation prohibition after two years needs a regulatory economic analysis, as it imposes de facto retirements and could affect secondary-market aircraft values — request detailed cost-benefit analysis.

[P34] While the Manager may approve AMOCs, commentors will ask for faster, centralized AMOC processing and provision for pre-approved AMOCs for specific repair stations to avoid flight disruptions.

[P35] Requiring AMOC requests be sent to principal inspectors or local FSDOs may delay critical approvals for multistate operators; request an online AMOC portal or direct FAA regional contact list with SLA for responses.

[P36] The requirement to send AMOC information to the person in n(1) and email to AMOC@faa.gov should include secure document transfer procedures for proprietary data and specify expected review timelines.

[P37] The obligation to notify principal inspectors before using an approved AMOC should be modified to allow electronic notification within 24–48 hours for time-critical ferry flights or where inspector has no jurisdiction; require FAA to issue guidance on notification format.

[P11] Aviation consumer advocates will request the FAA to provide illustrative photos in the AD (or incorporated service info) of acceptable vs. unacceptable exhaust staining/discoloration to reduce inspection subjectivity.

[P17] Mechanics' associations will comment that no guidance is provided about torque re-check intervals after initial re-torque — recommend including a torque re-check at 25 flight hours or 10 cycles after re-torque.

[P8] For aircraft that fly less than 100 hours per year, the "whichever occurs first" rule makes the inspection interval effectively 6 months; suggest FAA allow alternative intervals scaled to utilization (e.g., annual for <200 hrs/yr aircraft).

[P18] Airworthiness authorities and repair stations will ask FAA to clarify whether installing a redesigned v-band coupling (manufacturer service kit) could terminate repetitive inspections and request inclusion of terminating action details.

[P6] Operators operating internationally request harmonization with EASA and other authorities; comment that the 50-hour initial removal requirement may conflict with foreign ADs and ask FAA to coordinate internationally.

[P23] Measurement tolerances (0.062 inch) should be given in metric units as well (millimeters) to avoid conversion errors in international maintenance shops.

[P7] Maintenance burden estimates are missing; stakeholders will request FAA to include detailed labor-hour and cost estimates for inspections, removals, and parts to comply with the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

[P21] Insurance providers may comment that mandatory replacements and inspection burdens will influence hull and liability premiums; request FAA to quantify expected reduction in incidents to justify premium impacts.

[P9] Commercial air carriers will request explicit language allowing ferry flights after failed inspection subject to FAA-approved special flight permits and clear criteria for granting such permits to avoid undue grounding.

[P31] Salvage and aircraft recyclers will ask whether couplings removed from scrapped aircraft are subject to the installation prohibitions and request guidance for disposition and documentation requirements.

[P2] The rule should clarify whether cumulative compliance actions taken under fleet-level maintenance programs count toward "unless already done" to avoid duplication of work when an operator has previously replaced or inspected couplings per manufacturer recommendations.

[P20] The AD's specification of cleaning materials should include environmental and disposal guidance (e.g., for Stoddard solvent) and allow use of less hazardous cleaners approved by the manufacturer.

[P1] The deadline in § 39.13(a) (April 2, 2018) is unreasonably short for stakeholders to prepare technically detailed comments and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow affected operators, repair stations, and labor groups to assess costs and safety impacts.

[P1] Providing a fixed calendar date (April 2, 2018) without describing receipt time zone, acceptable delivery methods, or confirmation procedures risks late or lost comments; the rule should clarify acceptable submission methods and that timely electronic submissions will be considered.

[P2] § 39.13(f) mandates compliance “within the specified compliance times” but does not allow for documented operational disruptions (e.g., lack of available maintenance windows or parts); commenters request explicit allowance for scheduling flexibility or phased compliance with FAA notification.

[P2] The obligation to comply “unless already done” lacks a recordkeeping requirement to prove prior completion; commenters ask the rule require documentation standards (work orders, logbook entries) acceptable as evidence of prior compliance.

[P3] § 39.13(g) incorporates Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin actions by reference but does not provide the full bulletin text in the NPRM, prejudicing meaningful comment; stakeholders request that the FAA publish the complete bulletin and any referenced service instructions with the rule.

[P3] Requiring performance “at the times specified” in the Boeing bulletin may create inconsistent applicability across fleets with different maintenance calendars; commenters recommend allowing calendar-based or flight-cycle-based alternatives with FAA approval.

[P4] § 39.13(h)(1) instructs use of the AD effective date where the bulletin references “original issue date,” which could shorten compliance windows for operators who received later revisions; commenters request that the FAA allow using the date the operator received the bulletin or the date of posting to the AD docket.

[P4] Using the AD effective date instead of the bulletin’s original issue date may create retroactive obligations and compliance uncertainty for parts already procured per earlier bulletin versions; legal commenters assert this could raise due-process and notice concerns and request clearer grandfathering language.

[P5] § 39.13(h)(2) prohibits contacting Boeing for repair instructions and instead mandates use of FAA-approved methods per paragraph (i); OEMs and repair stations object that this removes the efficient, established channel for technical guidance and could delay repairs — they request recognition that OEM-approved repairs, when documented, should remain acceptable.

[P5] Requiring FAA-approved repair methods where the bulletin directs contacting Boeing could overwhelm the FAA certification office and cause operational delays; commenters request that the rule explicitly permit using Boeing-approved methods when accompanied by a Boeing ODA approval or equivalent documented method.

[P6] § 39.13(i)(1) vests AMOC approval authority solely in the Manager, Los Angeles ACO Branch, which centralizes decision-making and may slow AMOC processing for operators outside the region; commenters recommend allowing geographically appropriate ACO managers or delegated ODA staff to approve AMOCs to speed resolution.

[P6] Industry stakeholders request that the rule provide objective criteria and target turnaround times for AMOC approvals under § 39.13(i)(1) to ensure timely safety-compliant relief, rather than leaving approval entirely to Manager discretion.

[P7] § 39.13(i)(1) requires submission of AMOC requests to principal inspectors or FSDOs per 14 CFR 39.19 but fails to specify the documentation format or technical substantiation required; commenters ask for a checklist of required technical analyses, substantiating data, and expected evaluation metrics.

[P7] Small operators and foreign repair stations may not have a principal inspector; the rule should clarify the appropriate point of contact and process to avoid misdirected AMOC requests and delay.

[P8] § 39.13(i)(1) instructs addressing direct submissions to the person identified in paragraph (j)(1), but the NPRM does not publish paragraph (j)(1) content in a convenient place; commenters request that the specific contact name, title, and mailing address be clearly included in the preamble and regulatory text.

[P9] § 39.13(i)(1) permits emailing AMOC requests to 9-ANM-LAACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov but does not specify security, file formats, or confirmation procedures; commenters request guidance on encrypted transmission for sensitive data, acceptable attachments (PDF, CAD), and confirmation of receipt.

[P9] Allowing email submission without specifying retention or public disclosure policy raises confidentiality concerns for proprietary repair methods; industry requests a process to submit proprietary attachments under protective treatment.

[P10] § 39.13(i)(2) requires notifying the principal inspector or FSDO manager before using an approved AMOC but does not set a timeline for such notification (e.g., prior to entry into service); commenters request the rule require notification at least 72 hours before use or immediate notification if prior notice is impracticable.

[P10] The obligation to notify a principal inspector “before using any approved AMOC” may be impractical for unscheduled on-wing repairs occurring outside regular office hours; stakeholders ask for an exception allowing post-action notification within a specified short time window (e.g., 24–48 hours) for emergency repairs.

[P11] § 39.13(i)(3) allows AMOCs approved by Boeing ODA for repairs/modifications, but the rule lacks standards for determining when an ODA approval “provides an acceptable level of safety”; commenters request explicit criteria or reference to existing ODA procedures to ensure consistency.

[P11] OEMs request explicit recognition that Boeing ODA approvals that are documented and traceable should be treated as presumptively acceptable, provided they meet the airplane certification basis and directly reference this AD, to avoid redundant FAA review.

[P12] § 39.13(i)(3) conditions AMOC/repair approval on meeting the airplane’s certification basis and explicitly referencing this AD, but does not explain how to handle changes in certification basis over time (e.g., later STCs or amendments); commenters ask for guidance on applying this standard to modified airplanes and STC holders.

[P12] Legal commenters note that requiring explicit reference to this AD in approvals may be administratively burdensome for generic repair methods; they suggest allowing AMA/ODA or FAA approvals that cite an equivalent identifying mechanism (e.g., AD docket number or service bulletin number) instead.

[P12] The requirement that the method/deviation “meet the certification basis of the airplane” lacks an explanation of acceptable means of showing compliance (analysis, tests, similarity to prior approvals); commenters request a clear list of acceptable substantiation methods and documentation templates.

[P5] Maintenance organizations warn that prohibiting contact with Boeing for certain instructions (per § 39.13(h)(2)) could create liability ambiguity between the FAA and OEMs; they request the FAA clarify liability and responsibility for repaired work when using FAA-approved alternatives.

[P3] Consumer/advocacy groups request that the AD include a monitoring and reporting obligation to the FAA after implementation of the Boeing bulletin actions to collect field data on effectiveness and any incidents post-repair.

[P1] Public interest groups note that the April 2, 2018 comment deadline predates the AD effective date and may have prevented meaningful public participation; they ask the FAA to withdraw and reissue the proposed AD with a fresh comment period if the deadline cannot be extended.

[P6] Aviation labor unions request that AMOC approvals consider workforce impacts (training, hours) and ask the FAA to consult labor representatives before approving AMOCs that change maintenance practices under § 39.13(i)(1).

[P1] The revised authority citation in Part 300 (33 U.S.C. 1321(d); 42 U.S.C. 9601–9657; E.O. 13626) is too narrow/does not include other statutory authorities the Agency relied upon in prior NPL actions—request inclusion of any additional statutes or executive orders relied upon to avoid legal challenge.

[P1] The authority citation as written contains a typographical truncation ("3 CFR,") that should be corrected to provide a complete citation to E.O. 13626 and the proper Federal Register reference.

[P2] Removing the Shpack Landfill entry from Appendix B Table 1 appears to be a full deletion of the site from the NPL; the preamble lacks the technical justification and supporting data for removal—request full risk assessment and documentation be appended to the docket.

[P2] The amendment removing Shpack Landfill may affect state and local responsibilities for future monitoring—request explicit statement in the rule text that clarifies who is responsible for long‑term monitoring after deletion.

[P3] Simply removing the state abbreviation "MA" for the Shpack Landfill without additional clarifying changes could create an ambiguous, orphaned entry in Table 1—request verification that the entire row is removed, not just the state code.

[P4] Removing the site name "Shpack Landfill" from Table 1 may create recordkeeping inconsistencies with other federal databases (CERCLIS/FINDS)—request cross‑database coordination and update plan be disclosed in the docket.

[P5] Removal of the location "Norton/Attleboro" from Table 1 could hinder public notice and access—request that any deletion be accompanied by a clear notice to the affected municipalities and local repositories.

[P6] The specified comment deadline of August 30, 2019 is inconsistent with other listed 30‑day comment periods in the preamble—request clarification and, if needed, an extension to a uniform minimum 60‑day comment period to allow affected communities adequate time.

[P7] The requirement to identify Docket ID EPA–HQ–SFUND–1986–0005 in submissions should explicitly state if multiple docket IDs apply when commenters wish to address more than one site—request guidance for multi‑site comments.

[P8] The prohibition on editing or removing comments once posted to Regulations.gov dissuades commenters from submitting sensitive updates—request that Regulations.gov provide a mechanism to withdraw or correct clerical errors within a short window (e.g., 48 hours).

[P9] EPA's permission to publish received comments in the public docket should explicitly state how personal contact information will be treated to protect privacy—request that EPA redact personal information upon request or provide instructions for submitting contact information separately.

[P10] The prohibition on submitting CBI electronically is unclear as to what format is acceptable for submitting CBI (paper only?)—request clear procedures and an address/method for secure submission of CBI to the docket.

[P11] Requiring a written comment as the official submission for multimedia submissions may disadvantage non‑English or visually impaired stakeholders—request allowance for multimedia to be considered the official comment if accompanied by a transcript or alternative format.

[P12] The obligation that the written comment include all points to be considered as official may prevent supplemental scientific data submissions after initial comment—request an allowance for substantive supplemental technical attachments within the comment period.

[P13] The prohibition on EPA considering materials located outside the primary submission channel is overly restrictive for large datasets—request an exception/process for linking to large datasets hosted on reputable data repositories and instructions for ensuring their accessibility.

[P14] The separate prohibition on submitting CBI via Regulations.gov or email repeats P10 and is unclear about encrypted file submissions sent by secure methods—request guidance on approved secure electronic methods (e.g., secure portal, SFTP).

[P15] EPA's recommendation to include contact information in electronic comments should be converted to a requirement to ensure EPA can clarify unreadable submissions—request that EPA require at minimum an email address for follow‑up rather than merely recommending it.

[P16] The exception noting EPA may be unable to consider unreadable comments places too much burden on the commenter—request EPA adopt a policy of contacting submitters whenever practicable before discarding a comment as unreadable, and publish steps taken to attempt contact.

[P17] The obligation that electronic files avoid special characters/encryption could preclude submission of valid scientific file formats—request a list of acceptable file types (e.g., PDF/A, CSV, TIFF) and an alternative secure submission process for encrypted files containing CBI.

[P22] The criterion concerning Fund‑financed responses requires documentation that no further Fund expenditures will be necessary—request a cost evaluation and contingency plan be provided in the docket.

[P23] Relying on an RI finding of “no significant threat” (criterion iii) requires transparency—request that the complete RI report and human health/ecological risk assessment be placed in the docket, not just summaries.

raw_output:
[P1] The proposed blanket statement amending Part 17 is overly vague and does not provide the regulatory text changes in full, making it impossible for stakeholders to assess the rule's full impacts on protections and enforcement.

[P2] The amendment process described in §17.11(h) lacks an explanation of the scientific basis and recovery criteria used to justify removing species from the list, violating the Administrative Procedure Act's requirement for reasoned decisionmaking.

[P3] Removing the "Bat, little Mariana fruit" from §17.11(h) (MAMMALS) appears to delist a species that still faces habitat loss on Guam and the Northern Marianas; the Service must provide recent population trend data and threat analyses before removal.

[P3] Industry commenters (e.g., development interests in the Marianas) will support removal of the little Mariana fruit bat only if the rule includes clear post-delisting monitoring and management commitments; the proposal lacks such conditions.

[P4] Removing multiple Hawaiian forest bird entries (Akepa, Akialoa, Creeper, Nukupuu, 'O'o, etc.) from §17.11(h) (BIRDS) seems to reflect extinction rather than recovery, and the rule fails to state that removal is due to extinction rather than recovery, which has distinct regulatory implications.

[P4] Hawaiian cultural and conservation groups will object that removing these bird species without discussion of genetic samples, museum specimens, and potential de-extinction research is premature and ignores cultural values tied to species names.

[P5] Delisting "Gambusia, San Marcos" and "Madtom, Scioto" from §17.11(h) (FISHES) may remove protections for small, localized populations; the proposal does not disclose whether critical habitat designations or recovery actions remain in place to prevent further declines.

[P6] Removing the listed clam species (Acornshell, southern; Blossom, green; tubercled, turgid, etc.) from §17.11(h) (CLAMS) risks extinguishing remaining genetic diversity — the Service must include justification and potential reclassification to a similar protective mechanism if warranted.

[P7] The removal of Phyllostegia glabra var. lanaiensis from §17.12(h) (FLOWERING PLANTS) lacks population survey data from Lanai and an explanation of whether extirpation or recovery is the basis for this action.

[P8] The amendment to §17.85(a) (pearlshell table and heading) that reduces "Seventeen" to "Fourteen" must include a reconciliatory table cross-reference; otherwise, it will create inconsistencies across the Code of Federal Regulations.

[P9] Replacing the word "Seventeen" with "Fourteen" in the heading of §17.85(a) (§17.85(a)(heading)) could mislead permittees and ESA practitioners unless the preamble identifies exactly which three species are removed and why.

[P10] Removing "tubercled blossom", "turgid blossom", and "yellow blossom" from the §17.85(a) table (pearly mussels) without providing updated recovery priority guidance will create uncertainty for restoration projects funded under existing recovery plans.

[P11] Changing the number '17' to '14' in §17.85(a)(1)(i) and (ii) and §17.85(a)(2)(iii) (P11–P13) could have cascading effects on formulas or thresholds referenced elsewhere; the Service must publish a matrix of all cross-references affected.

[P14] Amendment of §17.95 generally (P14) proposes many detailed revisions to the Mobile River Basin mussel entries without publishing the redline text of each change, preventing meaningful comment on altered regulatory text.

[P15] Removing "San Marcos Gambusia (Gambusia georgei)" from §17.95(e) is troubling because San Marcos springs are isolated and still subject to groundwater extraction threats; commenters request the Service justify that threats have been eliminated and provide monitoring commitments.

[P16] The revisions to §17.95(f) concerning "Eleven Mobile River Basin Mussel Species" (P16) appear to change the regulatory criteria for take prohibitions and exceptions but the proposal lacks a clear statement whether delisting, reclassification, or taxonomy changes motivate the revisions.

[P17] Revising the heading of the §17.95(f) mussel entry (P17) without explaining if species names or common names are being standardized could cause confusion for enforcement officers and permit applicants.

[P18] The proposed revision to §17.95(f)(1) introductory text (P18) may narrow or broaden the scope of exceptions to take — commenters demand a side-by-side comparison showing how permissive language is changing.

[P19] Changes to the introductory text of §17.95(f)(2)(i) (P19) could affect eligibility criteria for habitat conservation plans in the Mobile River Basin; local governments and utilities request explicit confirmation of any policy shifts.

[P20] Revising the table at §17.95(f)(2)(ii) (P20) without providing the table data in the proposed rule makes it impossible to assess impacts on permitted activities, mitigation ratios, or monitoring requirements.

[P21] The repeated edits to introductory texts and subparagraphs in §17.95(f)(2)(xiv) through (xxviii) (P21–P36) are highly granular; legal commenters will request the unabridged revised regulatory language and an explanation of whether these are purely editorial/taxonomic changes or substantive alterations to protections.

[P22] Several of the §17.95(f) subparagraph revisions (e.g., (xx)(B), (xxi)(B), (xxiii)(B), (xxvi)(B), (xxvii)(B), (xxviii)(B)) appear to modify conditions under which incidental take is allowed — conservation NGOs assert these changes could weaken safeguards unless justified by new science and accompanied by compensatory mitigation.

[P23] The Service has not provided regulatory impact analysis (RIA) or economic analysis estimating costs or savings to stakeholders from the mass removals and revisions; business groups request a full RIA per Executive Order requirements.

[P24] Tribes and state natural resource agencies will request consultation records; the proposal does not document government-to-government consultation regarding species that occur on tribal/state lands (e.g., Mobile River Basin mussels, Hawaiian birds).

[P25] Scientists will point out that removing species entries from the listing without designating post-delisting monitoring plans and funding sources increases the likelihood of extinction or unmonitored declines; the rule should include enforceable post-delisting monitoring.

[P26] The preamble must clarify whether removals reflect extinctions (i.e., species are gone) versus recovery; commenters representing museum and archival institutions urge clear labeling as "extinct" where applicable to preserve historical and cultural records.

[P27] The Service must ensure that removing species from these lists does not inadvertently nullify conservation grants, recovery plan obligations, or existing critical habitat protections; state conservation agencies express concern about loss of programmatic support.

[P28] The proposal's multiple textual numeric edits (17→14) raise concerns about clerical errors; regulated entities request a consolidated redlined regulatory text to verify no unintended changes to compliance obligations.

[P29] Environmental law practitioners note that the rule lacks description of how the Endangered Species Act's Section 4(a)(1) recovery criteria and Section 4(b)(1)(A) threats analysis were applied to each species removal; they request full species-specific analyses.

[P30] The Service should allow an extended comment period given the volume of affected species, numerous cross-references, and lack of full amended regulatory text in the notice.

[P31] Local conservation organizations in Ohio and Texas (for Scioto madtom, San Marcos gambusia, etc.) request that the agency publish all survey records, sampling methods, and dates used to conclude these fish species no longer require listing.

[P32] Commenters representing the aquaculture and aquarium trade warn that removing species like San Marcos gambusia may create regulatory ambiguity for captive populations and transport restrictions; the Service must clarify import/export and captive propagation rules post-removal.

[P33] The Service should explicitly state whether any of the proposed removals are attributable to taxonomic reclassification (e.g., lumping/splitting) rather than improved conservation status, and provide supporting peer-reviewed literature when taxonomic changes are the basis.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The proposed blanket statement amending Part 17 is overly vague and does not provide the regulatory text changes in full, making it impossible for stakeholders to assess the rule's full impacts on protections and enforcement.

The amendment process described in §17.11(h) lacks an explanation of the scientific basis and recovery criteria used to justify removing species from the list, violating the Administrative Procedure Act's requirement for reasoned decisionmaking.

Removing the "Bat, little Mariana fruit" from §17.11(h) (MAMMALS) appears to delist a species that still faces habitat loss on Guam and the Northern Marianas; the Service must provide recent population trend data and threat analyses before removal.

Industry commenters (e.g., development interests in the Marianas) will support removal of the little Mariana fruit bat only if the rule includes clear post-delisting monitoring and management commitments; the proposal lacks such conditions.

Removing multiple Hawaiian forest bird entries (Akepa, Akialoa, Creeper, Nukupuu, 'O'o, etc.) from §17.11(h) (BIRDS) seems to reflect extinction rather than recovery, and the rule fails to state that removal is due to extinction rather than recovery, which has distinct regulatory implications.

Hawaiian cultural and conservation groups will object that removing these bird species without discussion of genetic samples, museum specimens, and potential de-extinction research is premature and ignores cultural values tied to species names.

Delisting "Gambusia, San Marcos" and "Madtom, Scioto" from §17.11(h) (FISHES) may remove protections for small, localized populations; the proposal does not disclose whether critical habitat designations or recovery actions remain in place to prevent further declines.

Removing the listed clam species (Acornshell, southern; Blossom, green; tubercled, turgid, etc.) from §17.11(h) (CLAMS) risks extinguishing remaining genetic diversity — the Service must include justification and potential reclassification to a similar protective mechanism if warranted.

The removal of Phyllostegia glabra var. lanaiensis from §17.12(h) (FLOWERING PLANTS) lacks population survey data from Lanai and an explanation of whether extirpation or recovery is the basis for this action.

The amendment to §17.85(a) (pearlshell table and heading) that reduces "Seventeen" to "Fourteen" must include a reconciliatory table cross-reference; otherwise, it will create inconsistencies across the Code of Federal Regulations.

Replacing the word "Seventeen" with "Fourteen" in the heading of §17.85(a) (§17.85(a)(heading)) could mislead permittees and ESA practitioners unless the preamble identifies exactly which three species are removed and why.

Removing "tubercled blossom", "turgid blossom", and "yellow blossom" from the §17.85(a) table (pearly mussels) without providing updated recovery priority guidance will create uncertainty for restoration projects funded under existing recovery plans.

Changing the number '17' to '14' in §17.85(a)(1)(i) and (ii) and §17.85(a)(2)(iii) (P11–P13) could have cascading effects on formulas or thresholds referenced elsewhere; the Service must publish a matrix of all cross-references affected.

Removing "San Marcos Gambusia (Gambusia georgei)" from §17.95(e) is troubling because San Marcos springs are isolated and still subject to groundwater extraction threats; commenters request the Service justify that threats have been eliminated and provide monitoring commitments.

The proposed revision to §17.95(f)(1) introductory text (P18) may narrow or broaden the scope of exceptions to take — commenters demand a side-by-side comparison showing how permissive language is changing.

Changes to the introductory text of §17.95(f)(2)(i) (P19) could affect eligibility criteria for habitat conservation plans in the Mobile River Basin; local governments and utilities request explicit confirmation of any policy shifts.

Revising the table at §17.95(f)(2)(ii) (P20) without providing the table data in the proposed rule makes it impossible to assess impacts on permitted activities, mitigation ratios, or monitoring requirements.

[P1] The proposed Class E extension at Grayling Airport (extending upward from 700 ft within a 6.5‑mile radius and 2 miles either side of specified bearings) will impose new IFR procedures that could displace existing VFR traffic patterns; FAA should provide an aeronautical study showing expected changes to traffic flows and collision risk mitigation.

[P1] The 6.5‑mile radius and 2‑mile lateral corridor dimensions for the Grayling Class E area appear broader than similar rural Alaskan airports; FAA must justify these thresholds with operational data and identify why a smaller radius would be insufficient.

[P1] The text for P1 is truncated ("and that airspace 2 miles either side of"); commenters will request the complete bearing corridor descriptions and full legal description before the rule is finalized.

[P1] Local medevac and bush pilots need assurance that the new Class E designation will not create unnecessary delays or communication burdens; request an exception or streamlined VFR transition procedures for emergency medical flights into Grayling.

[P1] The proposed Class E upward-from-700‑ft designation may affect landowners’ use of their property for low-altitude agricultural aviation operations; FAA should analyze economic impacts on agricultural operators and include mitigation measures.

[P2] Removing Restricted Area R–2205 (Stuart Creek) could increase overflight by civilian aircraft in formerly restricted airspace; request an assessment of the safety and national security consequences of the removal and explanation of where impacted military activity will be relocated.

[P2] The rule provides no timeline or transition guidance for lifting R–2205; military and civilian users need a coordinated NOTAM and outreach plan so training and commercial operations can adjust safely.

[P3] The coordinates listed for R–2205A create complex polygon boundaries; request that FAA publish high-resolution geospatial files (KML/GEOJSON) and aeronautical charts so pilots and dispatchers can accurately plan around the new restricted area.

[P3] Commenters question whether the coordinate set for R–2205A overlaps with existing class E or special use airspace; request a map superimposing R–2205A on current airspace to identify conflicts and required lateral separations.

[P4] Designating R–2205A from surface to but not including 10,000 ft MSL will effectively close that vertical block to nonparticipating aircraft; stakeholders request clarification of permitted activities and coordination procedures for transient civil flights below 10,000 ft.

[P5] Limiting R–2205A active hours to 0700–1900 Monday–Friday with other times by NOTAM could create unpredictability for weekend users; recommend either fixed weekend hours or mandatory 24‑hour advance NOTAM issuance when activation is planned.

[P5] Civil operators request criteria for when the "other times by NOTAM" status will be invoked and a guarantee that late or last‑minute NOTAMs will not strand passengers or interfere with scheduled commercial flights.

[P6] Designation of FAA Fairbanks Approach Control as controlling agency for R–2205A places significant workload on that facility; request FAA staffing/automation assessments to ensure timely ATC responses and safe management during activations.

[P7] The Using Agency designation of USARAK (Commanding General, JBER) for R–2205A requires coordination between Army and FAA; request a Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) specifying procedures for activation, scheduling, and emergency access to the area.

[P8] The boundary coordinates for R–2205B appear to extend over populated or environmental sensitive areas; request environmental review and analysis of potential noise, wildlife disturbance, and socioeconomic impacts on local communities.

[P9] R–2205B’s surface-to-10,000‑ft vertical limits may interfere with general aviation cross-country routes; petitioners request published procedures for release of the area to civil traffic during active times and minimum advance notice requirements.

[P10] The same 0700–1900 Monday–Friday schedule for R–2205B fails to account for seasonal changes in daylight and training needs in Alaska; recommend a seasonal schedule or latitude-based adjustments and requirements for advance publication of schedules.

[P11] FAA Fairbanks Approach Control’s role for R–2205B should include an explicit requirement to coordinate with AK flight service stations and Aeronautical Information Services to ensure NOTAM dissemination to bush pilots who may not have data link services.

[P12] USARAK as the using agency for R–2205B must commit to minimizing civilian disruption; request limits on sortie rates, maximum allowable time-on-station, and public reporting of training usage hours.

[P13] The complex arc and coordinate descriptions for R–2205C increase the chance of charting errors; urge FAA to supply simplified textual descriptions and to verify that the boundaries do not create gaps or overlaps with adjacent restricted areas.

[P14] Surface-to-10,000 ft designation for R–2205C could impact aerial firefighting operations in the region which often operate at low altitudes; request guaranteed ingress/egress procedures and a priority access protocol for firefighting during wildfire season.

[P15] The NOTAM-driven status outside 0700–1900 Monday–Friday for R–2205C is insufficiently transparent; stakeholders ask for a public calendar of planned activations at least 30 days in advance when possible, and emergency activation limits.

[P16] Fairbanks Approach Control must have staffed contingency procedures (backup frequency, transfer of control) when R–2205C is activated; request documentation of those contingency processes.

[P17] USARAK should be required to publish contact points and activation schedules for R–2205C and to coordinate with local municipalities about training noise and safety buffers.

[P18] The R–2205D boundary that references the 4.7‑mile radius of Eielson AFB may create ambiguity if the base radius is later modified; request cross-reference language ensuring boundaries update if Eielson's radius changes, or require independent fixed coordinates.

[P19] R–2205D’s surface-to-10,000‑ft designation could conflict with civil instrument procedures into nearby airports; request an aeronautical procedures impact assessment and mitigation measures for affected approach/departure paths.

[P20] The 0700–1900 Monday–Friday activation window for R–2205D may not reflect actual training needs; ask for data showing why weekend or night activations are not necessary or for stricter limits on nighttime activations due to noise and safety concerns.

[P21] FAA Fairbanks Approach Control as controlling agency for R–2205D must ensure that general aviation flights crossing the area receive timely traffic advisories; request establishment of published routing or mandatory reporting points to facilitate coordination.

[P22] USARAK’s use of R–2205D should be limited by environmental protections around Eielson AFB (e.g., wildlife refuges); request environmental protections be explicitly incorporated into the using agency’s operating procedures.

[P23] The coordinate set for R–2205E appears nearly identical to others (A/E/B/F overlap concerns); request a consolidated map showing all R–2205 series areas to identify and resolve potential lateral and vertical overlaps.

[P24] Designating R–2205E from 10,000 ft MSL to FL310 restricts upper-altitude airspace commonly used by commercial and charter flights; airlines request analysis of rerouting impacts, fuel cost increases, and potential conflicts with IFR traffic flows.

[P25] The 0700–1900 Monday–Friday active times for R–2205E could intersect with peak airline cruise altitudes on certain flights; request scheduling constraints or limits on high-density activations during peak traffic hours.

[P26] FAA Fairbanks Approach Control must be required to deconflict R–2205E activations with adjacent military high‑altitude training areas; request inter-agency operational procedures and shared flight tracking during activations.

[P27] USARAK as using agency for R–2205E should delineate types of training (weapons release, supersonic, electronic warfare) intended for R–2205E and provide safety studies showing acceptable risk levels for overflight of nearby communities.

[P28] The boundaries for R–2205F overlap with R–2205B’s coordinates; request clarification of whether those areas are distinct vertically only or if the boundaries have been miscopied, and demand correction if duplicative.

[P29] R–2205F’s designation from 10,000 ft MSL to FL310 combined with other R–2205 upper blocks may create a continuous block up to FL310; request an airspace capacity analysis to ensure IFR traffic is not unduly constrained.

[P30] Activations of R–2205F during 0700–1900 Monday–Friday without predictable scheduling will hamper charter and cargo operators servicing rural Alaska; request that USARAK publish weekly activation schedules and provide at least 48 hours notice for changes.

[P31] Fairbanks Approach Control should be required to broadcast real-time status of R–2205F on appropriate VHF frequencies and on flight planning products used by GA pilots to avoid inadvertent incursions.

[P32] USARAK must commit to safety-of-flight reporting and incident transparency for R–2205F operations, including post-activation reports if any near-misses or deviations occur.

[P33] R–2205G coordinates and arcs seem to mirror R–2205C; request clarification and a consolidated depiction to avoid pilot confusion and possible triple-counting of restricted volumes.

[P34] The 10,000 ft MSL to FL310 vertical block for R–2205G may interfere with military training of other services and with transcontinental traffic; request inter-service coordination documentation showing deconfliction measures.

[P35] The Monday–Friday 0700–1900 time window for R–2205G should be limited further in proximity to local community events and special Use Airspace-sensitive periods; ask for a process to request temporary stand-downs for community activities.

[P36] Fairbanks Approach Control as controlling agency for R–2205G must have formal procedures to handle emergency releases of the area to civilian aircraft (medical flights, SAR); request explicit emergency access protocols.

[P37] USARAK’s designation as using agency for R–2205G should include noise abatement and wildlife impact mitigation plans given increased training activity near populated and ecologically sensitive areas.

[P38] The R–2205H boundary referencing the 4.7‑mile Eielson AFB radius lacks full coordinates in the proposal (truncated text); request the complete legal description, and urge that boundary definitions not rely on secondary references that could change.

[P39] R–2205H’s vertical limits (10,000 ft MSL to FL310) combined with nearby restricted areas may create stacked restrictions leaving narrow corridors for civil traffic; request traffic flow modeling and proposed alternative routes for civil IFR traffic.

[P40] The uniform activation times (0700–1900 Monday–Friday) across R–2205A–H do not account for tactical needs that may require short-duration activations outside those hours; recommend FAA require an after‑hours activation justification and stricter NOTAM requirements for nighttime activations.

[P41] Assigning Fairbanks Approach Control as the controlling agency across all R–2205 areas centralizes control but increases single-point-of-failure risk; request redundancy plans, including delegation to other facilities if Fairbanks is incapacitated.

[P42] USARAK listed as using agency for all R–2205 areas should be required to develop and publish a consolidated training plan, environmental assessment, and community outreach strategy explaining frequencies of use, types of activities, and mitigation measures.

[General] Many provisions reference activation "other times by NOTAM" without defining minimum lead times or notice reliability; commenters request a minimum 24‑ to 72‑hour notice standard for planned activations and limits on last-minute activations except for true emergencies.

[Legal] Several of the proposed restricted area vertical and lateral definitions risk overlapping with existing IFR airway and terminal airspace; request FAA legal review summary addressing compliance with airspace allocation statutes and procedures under 49 U.S.C. § 40103 and the Administrative Procedure Act.

[Environmental] The proposal lacks an environmental assessment (EA) or categorical exclusion determination for noise, wildlife, subsistence, and cultural impacts in rural Alaska; request that FAA prepare and circulate an EA and consult with affected tribes.

[Small Business] Small air taxi and tourism operators should be classified as small entities and receive regulatory flexibility; request an Economic Analysis detailing cost impacts (fuel, time, reroutes) and consideration of mitigation such as compensation or scheduling preferences.

[Charting] Request addition of the new Class E extension and all R–2205 areas to IFR/VFR sectional, terminal area charts, and FAA grafics, with publication timelines aligned to provide at least 90 days before effective dates.

[Enforcement] Ask FAA to clarify enforcement policy and procedures for inadvertent incursions into the restricted areas, distinguishing between willful violations and navigational errors caused by outdated charts or NOTAM latency.

[P1] The AD should clarify whether written, electronic, or docketed late comments received after September 9, 2022 will be considered, and provide a process for requesting an extension of the comment period.

[P2] Applying the AD to "all Boeing 777–200, –200LR, –300, –300ER, and 777F series airplanes, certificated in any category" is overbroad; the FAA should limit applicability to specific subconfigurations actually affected by the fastener/rib condition rather than all line numbers and variants.

[P2] The scope in paragraph (c) fails to identify whether freighter-converted 777s (post-delivery STC conversions) are included or excluded; commenters request explicit inclusion/exclusion of 777s modified by STC for freighter or other major modifications.

[P3] The requirement in paragraph (f) to "comply within the compliance times specified" is ambiguous because the AD references multiple compliance triggers (SB accomplishment, certificate date, AD effective date); FAA should provide a clear precedence rule for which compliance time applies if multiple are relevant.

[P4] Requiring "all applicable actions identified in the Boeing Alert Service Bulletin" (paragraph g) without FAA incorporation by reference of that exact revision creates legal uncertainty—request that the FAA incorporate Revision 6 by reference in the regulatory text or explicitly list each required action in the AD.

[P5] The mandatory installation of Teflon sleeves (paragraph g sub) may not be suitable for all affected fastener locations due to potential fuel compatibility or wear—operators request data on sleeve life, compatibility with fuel, and test results demonstrating long-term safety before mandating this installation.

[P5] Mandating Teflon sleeves without providing alternative approved materials denies operators flexibility; request that the AD allow equivalent materials proven by analysis or test as AMOCs, or provide Boeing-approved part numbers and procurement guidance.

[P6] The cap seal fastener requirement (paragraph g sub) lacks definition of "cap sealing" standards and acceptable materials; the AD should specify acceptable cap seal types, torque values, and inspection criteria to avoid inconsistent field application.

[P7] The detailed inspection obligation (paragraph g sub) does not define the required inspection method (e.g., borescope, eddy current, visual only) or the minimum training/certification for inspectors; operators request clarification of inspection technique acceptance criteria.

[P8] Requiring completion of corrective actions "prior to further flight" (paragraph g sub/paragraph 8) is operationally disruptive without prioritization tiers depending on severity; commenters ask for risk-based tolerances (e.g., ferry restrictions, operational mitigations) when immediate corrective actions require extended grounding.

[P9] The exception in (h)(1) that replaces references to the service bulletin revision date with the AD effective date may cause confusion; legal counsel requests a cross-reference table showing each replaced reference to avoid misinterpretation during maintenance and audit.

[P10] The illustrations clarification in (h)(2) (circle symbol 1 pointing to seven fasteners on the inboard side of rib no. 9) should be incorporated into the service bulletin drawings themselves; airlines and technicians need clear, corrected figures to avoid mislocation of required work.

[P11] Similar to P10, the interpretation provisions in (h)(3) and (h)(4) that map "7 locations" to specific fasteners risk inconsistency in field application; Boeing should issue corrected figures and the FAA should require operators to use the corrected figures rather than rely on textual interpretation in the AD.

[P13] The 60-day timeframe in paragraph (i) to revise maintenance/inspection programs is unduly short for operators with distributed program management and contractual third-party providers; request extension to 180 days to allow proper program reapproval and training.

[P13] The AD should clarify whether the AWL incorporation in paragraph (i) requires submission to the FAA for approval or merely incorporation into operator-maintained programs, and whether those revisions are subject to review during continuous airworthiness oversight.

[P14] The initial compliance time for ALI task 28–AWL–32 for L/Ns 1–503 (paragraph i(1)) creates a very long window (3,750 days) tied to SB action date; commenters request that the FAA justify the safety rationale for such a long interval and consider shorter intervals for high-utilization aircraft.

[P15] Similarly, the initial compliance time for L/Ns 504+ (paragraph i(2)) tied to certificate issuance (3,750 days) may lead to inconsistent fleet risk profiles; request risk analysis demonstrating acceptability of the 3,750-day period versus alternate periodic inspection intervals.

[P16] The AWL text change in (j)(1) that conditions Front Spar Bulkhead applicability on "Center Wing Tank Fuel Quantity Greater than 12,400 Gallons" should be accompanied by a method for operators to demonstrate which aircraft meet that threshold (e.g., configuration data, placard), as not all maintenance records reflect tank capacity.

[P17] The exclusion of 777F from paragraph 1.i.II per (j)(2) needs a rationale; cargo operators will request FAA/Boeing data showing why 777F is excluded and whether a compensating inspection is required for freighter structural differences.

[P18] The change in (j)(3) altering 1.i.III to "For 777F airplanes" (removing L/N limitation) raises concerns that earlier-production 777Fs may have different configurations—request clarity whether this expands or narrows applicability and the basis for that change.

[P19] The Rear Spar Bulkhead wording change in (j)(4) that ties applicability to center wing tank capacity (greater than 12,400 gallons) requires the FAA to provide guidance on how to determine tank capacity, and whether modifications or placards affect applicability.

[P20] The prohibition in paragraph (k) forbidding use of alternative actions, intervals, or CDCCLs after program revision unless approved as an AMOC is overly restrictive; industry requests that previously approved operator programs (with equivalent safety) be grandfathered for a transitional period while AMOCs are processed.

[P20] Requiring AMOC approval for any deviations (paragraph k) will create bottlenecks at the Seattle ACO—request delegation to regional ACOs or acceptance of Boeing ODA approvals (with FAA review) to streamline approvals consistent with safety.

[P21] The termination credit for AD 2017–11–14 provided in (l)(1) should be clarified to ensure that operators who have partially complied with prior ADs understand what records/documentation they must retain to demonstrate termination of the earlier AD obligations.

[P22] Similarly, the termination credit for AD 2021–24–12 in (l)(2) must specify record-keeping requirements and whether prior SB compliance substantiates termination without rework.
