[P24] The AMOC submission process (m)(1 procedure) requiring routing through principal inspectors may delay engineering AMOCs; request allowance for direct submission to the Seattle ACO with copy to the principal inspector to expedite technical reviews.

[P25] The requirement to notify principal inspectors before using an approved AMOC (m)(2) should be expanded to permit electronic notification and acceptance within a defined timeframe (e.g., 10 business days) to avoid operational delays.

[P26] Permitting Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs (m)(3) is helpful, but commenters request FAA oversight language requiring the ODA to provide documentation of compliance showing the AMOC meets the airplane’s certification basis prior to field use.

[P27] The condition that AMOC repair/modification deviations must meet the airplane's certification basis (m)(3 condition) is appropriate but ambiguous for legacy airplanes with multiple STCs—request that the FAA define how to determine the "applicable certification basis" when multiple STCs alter structure.

[P28] The requirement that AMOC approvals explicitly reference this AD (m)(3 condition) should be extended to require inclusion of the AD docket number and the specific paragraph(s) being replaced or altered, to avoid vague approvals.

[P4] The AD’s reliance on Boeing Alert Service Bulletin 777–57A0050, Revision 6 without making that service bulletin publicly available in the docket impedes independent review; request the FAA place the full SB Revision 6 and earlier revisions in the public docket.

[P7] The AD should include acceptance standards for "detailed inspections" such as crack size thresholds that require corrective action, to ensure consistent compliance and avoid disputes between operators and FAA inspectors.

[P8] For corrective actions required before further flight (paragraph g sub/paragraph 8), operators request explicit guidance on acceptable temporary repairs or operational limitations to allow safe repositioning if immediate permanent repair requires extended downtime.

[P13] The AD must state whether incorporation of the AWL into maintenance programs triggers mandatory training, habitability of inspection task cards, or modification of maintenance log templates—operators need clarity to budget for training and documentation changes.

[P14/P15] Operators request that the FAA provide a compliance time relief option tied to a utilization-based flight-cycle metric rather than a fixed 3,750-day/60-month schedule, because calendar-based intervals may not reflect actual fatigue accumulation on high-utilization aircraft.

[P20] Labor and pilot unions will want assurance that the prohibition on alternative CDCCLs does not prevent temporary operational mitigations (e.g., weight/fuel limitations) that reduce risk between inspections; request explicit allowance for operational restrictions approved by the principal inspector.

[P23] Legal commenters request confirmation that AMOC approvals under (m)(1) will be documented in the FAA's regulatory docket or otherwise posted publicly so that other operators can rely on established precedents.

[P26] Boeing and operators request explicit criteria for delegating AMOC authority to Boeing ODA (m)(3), including required submittal content, certification tests, and FAA monitoring to ensure consistent safety outcomes.

[P5/P6] MRO industry commenters ask for estimated labor-hour and parts-cost data (cost impact) associated with Teflon sleeve installation and cap sealing; without cost estimates, the economic impact on smaller operators cannot be evaluated in comments.

[P2/P16] Small cargo operators of 777F request transitional compliance relief or exemptions if their aircraft do not have center wing tanks exceeding 12,400 gallons, and request a clear method to demonstrate exemption status during ramp inspections.

[P3/P13] Airline fleet compliance planners request a sample compliance schedule template from the FAA showing how the various compliance triggers interact (SB action date vs. certificate issuance vs. AD effective date) to ensure fleet-wide consistent implementation.

[P9/P10] Maintenance technicians request a mandatory service bulletin errata sheet appended to the AD correcting all figure callouts and providing high-resolution, dimensioned drawings to avoid misidentification of the "7 locations."

[P20] Safety advocates oppose broad allowance of Boeing ODA AMOCs without enhanced FAA oversight, arguing that delegating approval to the manufacturer may create conflicts of interest; they recommend AMOC approvals by the FAA only.

[P21/P22] Operators request confirmation that accomplishment of the AD's actions will not create duplicative inspection requirements under other active ADs or service bulletins and ask for a consolidated compliance matrix to demonstrate termination interactions.

[P1] Industry commenter: The permission in §257.71(d) to submit an Alternate Liner Demonstration should be clarified to explicitly allow demonstrations for units constructed prior to a specific cutoff date (e.g., pre-1980) — the current text is vague about which legacy units qualify.

[P1] Environmental NGO: Allowing alternate liner demonstrations for units "constructed without a composite liner or alternate composite liner" risks legitimizing substandard liners; EPA should prohibit alternate liner approvals for any unit lacking a modern composite liner.

[P2] Public health group: The "reasonable degree of certainty" standard in §257.71(d) is undefined and too permissive; the rule must specify quantitative risk thresholds or modeling confidence intervals required to demonstrate compliance at the unit boundary.

[P2] Industry: The requirement to show no exceedances "at the unit boundary" should permit demonstration at multiple distances (e.g., 10 m beyond boundary) rather than only at the boundary, to reflect site-specific hydrogeology.

[P3] State regulator: The obligation to submit an application documenting eligibility prior to the demonstration (§257.71(d)) requires a standard application form and checklist; without it, submissions will be inconsistent and review burdensome.

[P4] Small utility operator: The requirement to meet deadlines in paragraph (d)(2) for both application and demonstration is administratively onerous — EPA should allow a phased submission schedule for small operators or extend deadlines.

[P5] Legal commenter: The statement that the Administrator or Participating State Director "will act" per paragraph (d)(2) is ambiguous about delegation and timelines; the rule should specify appeal rights and de novo review standards if the Participating State Director denies.

[P6] Industry consultant: The list of items required under §257.71(d)(1) should include a provision allowing a consolidated submission for multiple adjacent impoundments at the same facility to avoid duplicative work.

[P7] Industry: The requirement to submit a letter announcing intent to submit a demonstration (§257.71(d)(1)(i)) should specify required contents beyond location (e.g., contact person, planned timeline) — otherwise EPA will repeatedly request basic info.

[P7] Environmental NGO: A public notice requirement should be added when a facility submits the intent letter so nearby communities are aware before the demonstration is prepared.

[P8] Community group: The obligation to identify the specific impoundment (§257.71(d)(1)(i)) must require inclusion of geospatial coordinates and parcel/legal descriptions so residents can identify the exact unit.

[P9] Legal expert: The "specified evidentiary information (A–D)" referenced in §257.71(d)(1)(i) needs cross-references fixed — the proposal is poorly hyperlinked and could cause confusion in compliance.

[P10] Industry: Requiring that the unit be "in full compliance with this subpart except for §257.71(a)(1)(ii) and (iii)" (§257.71(d)(1)(i)(A)) effectively bars many legacy units; EPA should allow limited waivers for non-safety administrative compliance items.

[P11] Hydrogeologist: The demonstration that the monitoring well network is "sufficient to capture any releases" (§257.71(d)(1)(i)(B)) requires minimum numerical spacing standards or an acceptance criteria for spatial resolution; otherwise reviewers will apply inconsistent judgments.

[P11] Community group: The requirement to include well logs and borehole diagrams (§257.71(d)(1)(i)(B)) is good but must also require all historical well data be included, not just recent logs.

[P12] Statistician/industry: The requirement that monitoring data show "no indication" of adverse impacts and include statistical test rationale (§257.71(d)(1)(i)(C)) should specify acceptable statistical methods, significance levels, and handling of non-detects to avoid inconsistent approvals.

[P12] Environmental NGO: The allowance for facilities to argue no statistically significant increase is problematic when background concentrations are already near GWPS; the rule should require trend analyses and cumulative exceedance assessment, not just single-test non-significance.

[P13] Industry: The obligation to show compliance with location restrictions in §§257.60–257.64 (§257.71(d)(1)(i)(D)) must allow grandfathering for units predating those location rules, or provide a remediation schedule rather than immediate ineligibility.

[P14] Engineer association: The professional engineer certification (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)) must define minimum qualifications (e.g., licensed in the State where the unit is located and with demonstrated hydrogeologic experience) to ensure credibility.

[P15] Environmental NGO: The evidence standard in the certified package (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)) — "reasonable degree of certainty" again — should be elevated to "reasonable degree of scientific certainty" and require independent peer review prior to agency consideration.

[P16] Industry consultant: Requiring documentation of "data collection methods and justification for assumptions" (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)) is reasonable but should permit use of historical data if accompanied by validation studies; insistence on new sampling for every demonstration is unnecessary.

[P17] Hydrogeologist: The specified minimum lines of evidence (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)(A–B)) are appropriate, but EPA should allow supplemental lines of evidence (e.g., tracer tests, lysimeter data) to be used in place of or in addition to the minimum list.

[P18] Industry/environmental: The site-specific hydrogeologic characterization (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)(A)) must include guidance on depth of investigation and required number of boreholes per acre to avoid under-characterization.

[P19] Scientist: Hydraulic conductivity measurements from monitoring wells (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)(A)(1)) are unreliable if solely based on slug/pumping tests in screened wells; the rule should require supporting laboratory permeameter tests or specific in-situ test protocols to be described.

[P20] NGO/regulator: The requirement to collect subsurface samples around the perimeter at sufficient resolution (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)(A)(2)) needs a minimum spatial resolution standard (e.g., one borehole per 50 feet) or a performance-based criterion tied to heterogeneity metrics.

[P21] Industry engineer: Conceptual site models with cross-sections (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)(A)(3)) should require GIS shapefiles and CAD drawings in addition to static cross-sections so reviewers can re-evaluate the model interactively.

[P22] Academic geologist: The narrative description of geological history (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)(A)(4)) is useful but should be required to reference regional published stratigraphic and hydrogeologic studies, not just site anecdotes.

[P23] Public records advocate: Summaries of conceptual model data into "readable graphs or tables" (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)(A)(5)) must be provided in machine-readable formats (e.g., CSV) and included in the public docket.

[P24] Industry/hydrogeologist: The evaluation of infiltration potential through liners/soils (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)(B)) must allow use of predictive transport modeling (with documented parameters and uncertainty analysis) in lieu of extensive in-situ tests when access is limited.

[P24] NGO: Laboratory testing alone is insufficient to characterize liner performance over operational life; the rule should require aging tests, field performance monitoring, or conservative factors of safety in permeability assumptions.

[P25] Industry: The hard deadline to submit the initial application by April 2, 2020 (§257.71(d)(2)(i)) is obsolete (past date) and needs updating or transitional language for facilities that did not meet that date.

[P26] Legal/industry: The one-year deadline to submit the demonstration after the initial application (§257.71(d)(2)(i)) is unrealistic for complex sites; EPA should permit a project-specific schedule approved upon application acceptance.

[P27] Industry: The extension process for analytical limits (§257.71(d)(2)(i)) requires clearer standards for what constitutes "analytical limitations" and acceptable alternative timelines — otherwise requests will be inconsistently granted.

[P28] Industry/state: EPA's authority to request additional information during review (§257.71(d)(2)(ii)) should be bounded by a limit on the number and scope of follow-up requests and a maximum aggregate review timeline.

[P29] Facility operator: The tolling of the deadline to stop receiving waste upon submission of a complete application (§257.71(d)(2)(ii)) is appropriate; however, EPA should clarify that tolling extends only pending a final decision and not indefinitely during prolonged reviews.

[P30] Environmental attorney: The provision that incomplete submissions do not toll the deadline (§257.71(d)(2)(ii)) risks unfair denial based on technicalities; EPA should require an initial completeness determination and provide a cure period before tolling is denied.

[P31] Industry: The 60-day timeline to notify owner/operator of eligibility determination (§257.71(d)(2)(ii)) is too short given agency workloads; EPA should extend to 90 days or commit to expedited review only for complete, high-quality submissions.

[P32] Industry/regulator: During demonstration review (§257.71(d)(2)(iii)), EPA requesting "additional information as necessary" needs defined timelines for requests and for the facility's response to avoid open-ended reviews.

[P33] Facility operator: The tolling of the waste-receipt deadline upon submission of a complete demonstration package (§257.71(d)(2)(iii)) must be confirmed in writing by EPA; otherwise facilities may continue receiving waste without clear legal protection.

[P34] NGO: The rule allowing incomplete demonstrations not to toll deadlines (§257.71(d)(2)(iii)) creates a perverse incentive to submit borderline incomplete packages; EPA should provide clear completeness criteria and publicize them.

[P35] Public interest group: The 30-day public comment period following publication of a proposed decision on the agency website (§257.71(d)(2)(iv)) is too short for communities and technical reviewers; extend to 60 days and require direct notification to local stakeholders.

[P36] Industry: The 4-month limit for EPA decision after receiving a complete demonstration (§257.71(d)(2)(v)) is too aggressive for complex hydrogeologic reviews; allow up to 6 months with interim status notices.

[P41] Regulator/scientist: The requirement to perform intra-well analyses for assessment monitoring triggers (§257.71(d)(2)(vii)(A)) should specify acceptable statistical methods and frequency of analysis to detect trends early.

[P42] Public health NGO: The agency's stated authority to revoke authorization if evidence suggests potential exceedance (§257.71(d)(2)(vii)(A)) must be coupled with mandatory public notice and disclosure of the data prompting reevaluation.

[P43] Industry: The ongoing burden on the facility to demonstrate continued compliance (§257.71(d)(2)(vii)(B)) should be balanced by defined reporting intervals and clear metrics so facilities can plan monitoring budgets.

[P44] Legal/labor union: Allowing revocation of authorization "without further notice or process" (§257.71(d)(2)(vii)(B)) raises due process concerns; require at least an informal notice and an opportunity to cure before immediate revocation.

[P45] Industry: The closure-by-removal procedures (§257.102(c)) must allow staged removal and interim containment measures when immediate full removal is technically or economically infeasible.

[P46] Facility operator: The requirement to "complete all removal and decontamination activities during the active life" within paragraph (f) timeframes (§257.102(c)(1)) is unclear — EPA should specify the paragraph (f) deadlines or cross-reference them precisely.

[P47] Environmental NGO: "Removal and decontamination of all areas affected by CCR releases" (§257.102(c)(1)(i)) must be defined to include subsurface soil and groundwater impacted beyond the unit footprint, not just visible CCR.

[P48] Community: The obligation to document that groundwater monitoring concentrations do not exceed GWPS for Appendix IV constituents (§257.102(c)(1)(ii)) should require independent third-party sampling and confirmatory testing, not just owner/operator reports.

[P49] Industry: The requirement to obtain closure certification (§257.102(c)(1)(iii)) should specify the approving authority (EPA vs. Participating State) and whether the certification may be a state professional engineer sign-off.

[P50] Facility operator: The option to close by completing removal during active life and conducting groundwater corrective action in post-closure (§257.102(c)(2)) should allow financial assurance mechanisms to cover long-term corrective action costs.

[P51] Community: Completing removal except groundwater corrective action within paragraph (f) timeframes (§257.102(c)(2)(i)) risks leaving contaminated soils in place; EPA should require interim soil remediation where practicable.

[P52] Environmental engineer: The requirement to have remedy components in place and operating within paragraph (f) timeframes (§257.102(c)(2)(ii)) needs explicit milestones and enforcement triggers if milestones are missed.

[P53] Regulator: Requiring completion of groundwater corrective action per §257.104(g) during post-closure (§257.102(c)(2)(iii)) should include enforceable interim performance metrics and monitoring frequency to ensure progress.

[P54] Industry: The obligation to amend closure and post-closure care plans as necessary (§257.102(c)(2)(iv)) should permit administrative amendments without reapproval for minor changes (e.g., contact info) to reduce paperwork burden.

[P55] Facility operator: Requiring closure certification within paragraph (f) timeframes (§257.102(c)(2)(v)) must allow for phased certifications (e.g., interim and final) when corrective actions are ongoing.

[P56] Real estate/legal: Recording the deed notation (§257.102(c)(2)(vi)) within paragraph (f) timeframes needs standard sample language and a model form to ensure consistent public notice and title searches.

[P57] Industry: The alternative final cover design permission (§257.102(d)(3)(ii)) should explicitly recognize engineered evapotranspiration and other site-appropriate covers as presumptively acceptable if performance-equivalent.

[P58] Engineer group: Inclusion of the final cover design in the written closure plan (§257.102(d)(3)(ii)) is reasonable but the rule should require design-level drawings and specifications, not just conceptual descriptions.

[P59] Industry: Allowing CCR placement during closure if the written closure plan is approved (§257.102(d)(4)(i)) provides needed flexibility; EPA should further clarify acceptable CCR processing (e.g., stabilization) and testing required before placement.

[P60] Environmental NGO: The approved closure plan must demonstrate "no reasonable risk of adverse effects" (§257.102(d)(4)(i)) — EPA must define "reasonable risk" quantitatively and require independent review of the risk assessment.

[P61] Industry: The requirement that CCR volume placed will not exceed borrow material volume (§257.102(d)(4)(i)(A)) is unduly restrictive for sites where CCR can beneficially replace greater volumes of borrow due to lower density; allow mass- or function-equivalent demonstrations.

[P62] Operator: Demonstrating that closure time using CCR does not exceed time with soil/borrow (§257.102(d)(4)(i)(B)) is subjective; EPA should allow project schedules with documented assumptions and contingency allowances.

[P63] Regulator: The requirement that the CCR unit satisfy §257.64 requirements (§257.102(d)(4)(i)(C)) should specify which subsections apply when CCR is incorporated into the final cover.

[P64] Industry: The obligation to show continued compliance with §257.102 after additional CCR placement (§257.102(d)(4)(i)(D)) must permit adaptive management if monitoring later shows unforeseen issues.

[P65] Environmental scientist: Ensuring the final cover is "no more permeable than CCR placed during closure" (§257.102(d)(4)(i)(E)) seems backward — EPA should require the final cover to be less permeable than underlying CCR to limit infiltration.

[P66] Public health group: If an Appendix IV constituent exceeds detection (§257.102(d)(4)(i)(F)), EPA's requirement that additional CCR placement not adversely affect corrective action compliance must be stringent — require corrective action completion before permitting CCR use.

[P67] Industry: Submitting the closure plan including demonstrations to EPA before anticipated CCR use (§257.102(d)(4)(ii)(A)) should allow concurrent review and limited mobilization so work is not unreasonably delayed.

[P68] Legal/community: The prohibition on using the CCR-use exemption until approval (§257.102(d)(4)(ii)(A)) is appropriate; however, EPA must enforce the prohibition and require public notice of any approved exemptions.

[P69] Industry: The approving authority's timeline to notify owner/operator of approval or intent to disapprove within 3 months (§257.102(d)(4)(ii)(B)) should be suspended if the authority has requested supplemental information; allow tolling until complete response.

[P71] Industry: Requiring the notification to state the date closure was initiated (§257.102(g)(1)) is reasonable but the rule should allow specifying initiation dates for each impoundment stage for multi-phase projects.

[P72] PE organizations: The requirement that the notification include PE certification or approval for final cover design (§257.102(g)(1)) must specify acceptable alternative approvals (e.g., state agency approvals) where PE stamping is not recognized.

[P73] Industry/legal: Treating the notification as completed when placed in the facility operating record (§257.102(g)(1) & §257.105(i)(7)) is acceptable, but facilities should be required to also publicly post the notification on the facility website within a defined time (e.g., 7 days).

[P74] Owner/operator: The requirement to update prior notifications that omitted initiation dates within two months after the rule's effective date (§257.102(g)(2)) is burdensome if the effective date is not clearly published; EPA should provide a clear retroactivity date and grace period.

[P75] Industry: The exemption from deed notation requirements for closures under paragraph (c)(1) (§257.102(i)(4)) is appropriate but should be conditioned on independent verification that no residual contamination remains.

[P76] Environmental NGO: Requiring owners/operators to prepare specified notices and annual progress reports after closure per §257.102(l) is essential; EPA must ensure these reports are publicly accessible and timely.

[P77] Community group: Annual closure progress reports (§257.102(l)(1)) must include plain-language summaries and be translated into languages spoken by nearby residents for meaningful public participation.

[P78] Industry: The requirement to discuss which stage of closure is underway (§257.102(l)(1)(i)) should be standardized with defined stage descriptions (e.g., initial dewatering, CCR removal, cap construction) to improve comparability.

[P79] Facility: The obligation to include a closure schedule (§257.102(l)(1)(ii)) must allow for schedule revisions due to weather, supply chain issues, or permitting delays, with requirements to document reasons for delay.

[P80] Operator: Reporting "any problems experienced during closure" (§257.102(l)(1)(iii)) should be limited to material problems affecting schedule or environmental performance; trivial operational issues should not trigger enforcement.

[P81] Industry/state: The timing for the initial closure progress report by the first January 31 after the rule's effective date or after commencement (§257.102(l)(2)) should be clarified for facilities that began closure long before the effective date — allow an initial cumulative report.

[P82] Regulator: Requiring annual reports until closure completed as per paragraphs (f) and (h) (§257.102(l)(2)) needs an explicit definition of "closure completed" to avoid disputes about when reporting obligations end.

[P83] Industry: The exemption from post-closure care criteria for removal closures (§257.104(a)(2)) is appropriate but should require confirmatory groundwater monitoring for a minimum period (e.g., 5 years) to ensure no delayed impacts.

[P84] Community: The 30-year default post-closure care period (§257.104(c)(1)) may be insufficient for sites with long-term groundwater migration; EPA should allow site-specific determinations that extend beyond 30 years when warranted.

[P85] Industry/regulator: The requirement that units closed under §257.102(c)(2) conduct post-closure care consistent with paragraph (g) (§257.104(c)(3)) must specify monitoring frequency and maintenance tasks to avoid interpretive disputes.

[P86] Environmental NGO: Completing groundwater corrective action by demonstrating no exceedances of GWPS for Appendix IV constituents (§257.104(g)) is laudable but needs a clear protocol for re-sampling, statistical power, and independent verification before regulatory closure is granted.

[P88] Community: The condition that groundwater corrective action be complete and no exceedances remain (§257.104(h)(1)) should also require a 10-year institutional control and monitoring covenant before deed notation removal.

[P89] Legal: Requiring completion of notification of completion of post-closure care (§257.104(h)(2)) as a condition for removing deed notation must include public notice and a protest/comment period before removal.

[P90] Facility operator: Maintaining the notification of intent to initiate closure in the operating record (§257.105(i)(1)) is reasonable but EPA should allow centralized e-recording to reduce paper burdens.

parsed_claims.claim_text: Industry commenter: The permission in §257.71(d) to submit an Alternate Liner Demonstration should be clarified to explicitly allow demonstrations for units constructed prior to a specific cutoff date (e.g., pre-1980) — the current text is vague about which legacy units qualify.

Environmental NGO: Allowing alternate liner demonstrations for units "constructed without a composite liner or alternate composite liner" risks legitimizing substandard liners; EPA should prohibit alternate liner approvals for any unit lacking a modern composite liner.

Public health group: The "reasonable degree of certainty" standard in §257.71(d) is undefined and too permissive; the rule must specify quantitative risk thresholds or modeling confidence intervals required to demonstrate compliance at the unit boundary.

Industry: The requirement to show no exceedances "at the unit boundary" should permit demonstration at multiple distances (e.g., 10 m beyond boundary) rather than only at the boundary, to reflect site-specific hydrogeology.

State regulator: The obligation to submit an application documenting eligibility prior to the demonstration (§257.71(d)) requires a standard application form and checklist; without it, submissions will be inconsistent and review burdensome.

Small utility operator: The requirement to meet deadlines in paragraph (d)(2) for both application and demonstration is administratively onerous — EPA should allow a phased submission schedule for small operators or extend deadlines.

Legal commenter: The statement that the Administrator or Participating State Director "will act" per paragraph (d)(2) is ambiguous about delegation and timelines; the rule should specify appeal rights and de novo review standards if the Participating State Director denies.

Industry consultant: The list of items required under §257.71(d)(1) should include a provision allowing a consolidated submission for multiple adjacent impoundments at the same facility to avoid duplicative work.

Industry: The requirement to submit a letter announcing intent to submit a demonstration (§257.71(d)(1)(i)) should specify required contents beyond location (e.g., contact person, planned timeline) — otherwise EPA will repeatedly request basic info.
Environmental NGO: A public notice requirement should be added when a facility submits the intent letter so nearby communities are aware before the demonstration is prepared.

Community group: The obligation to identify the specific impoundment (§257.71(d)(1)(i)) must require inclusion of geospatial coordinates and parcel/legal descriptions so residents can identify the exact unit.
Legal expert: The "specified evidentiary information (A–D)" referenced in §257.71(d)(1)(i) needs cross-references fixed — the proposal is poorly hyperlinked and could cause confusion in compliance.

Industry: Requiring that the unit be "in full compliance with this subpart except for §257.71(a)(1)(ii) and (iii)" (§257.71(d)(1)(i)(A)) effectively bars many legacy units; EPA should allow limited waivers for non-safety administrative compliance items.

Hydrogeologist: The demonstration that the monitoring well network is "sufficient to capture any releases" (§257.71(d)(1)(i)(B)) requires minimum numerical spacing standards or an acceptance criteria for spatial resolution; otherwise reviewers will apply inconsistent judgments.
Community group: The requirement to include well logs and borehole diagrams (§257.71(d)(1)(i)(B)) is good but must also require all historical well data be included, not just recent logs.

Statistician/industry: The requirement that monitoring data show "no indication" of adverse impacts and include statistical test rationale (§257.71(d)(1)(i)(C)) should specify acceptable statistical methods, significance levels, and handling of non-detects to avoid inconsistent approvals.

Environmental NGO: The allowance for facilities to argue no statistically significant increase is problematic when background concentrations are already near GWPS; the rule should require trend analyses and cumulative exceedance assessment, not just single-test non-significance.

Industry: The obligation to show compliance with location restrictions in §§257.60–257.64 (§257.71(d)(1)(i)(D)) must allow grandfathering for units predating those location rules, or provide a remediation schedule rather than immediate ineligibility.

Engineer association: The professional engineer certification (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)) must define minimum qualifications (e.g., licensed in the State where the unit is located and with demonstrated hydrogeologic experience) to ensure credibility.

Environmental NGO: The evidence standard in the certified package (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)) — "reasonable degree of certainty" again — should be elevated to "reasonable degree of scientific certainty" and require independent peer review prior to agency consideration.

Industry consultant: Requiring documentation of "data collection methods and justification for assumptions" (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)) is reasonable but should permit use of historical data if accompanied by validation studies; insistence on new sampling for every demonstration is unnecessary.

Hydrogeologist: The specified minimum lines of evidence (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)(A–B)) are appropriate, but EPA should allow supplemental lines of evidence (e.g., tracer tests, lysimeter data) to be used in place of or in addition to the minimum list.

Industry/environmental: The site-specific hydrogeologic characterization (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)(A)) must include guidance on depth of investigation and required number of boreholes per acre to avoid under-characterization.

Scientist: Hydraulic conductivity measurements from monitoring wells (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)(A)(1)) are unreliable if solely based on slug/pumping tests in screened wells; the rule should require supporting laboratory permeameter tests or specific in-situ test protocols to be described.

NGO/regulator: The requirement to collect subsurface samples around the perimeter at sufficient resolution (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)(A)(2)) needs a minimum spatial resolution standard (e.g., one borehole per 50 feet) or a performance-based criterion tied to heterogeneity metrics.

Industry engineer: Conceptual site models with cross-sections (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)(A)(3)) should require GIS shapefiles and CAD drawings in addition to static cross-sections so reviewers can re-evaluate the model interactively.

Academic geologist: The narrative description of geological history (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)(A)(4)) is useful but should be required to reference regional published stratigraphic and hydrogeologic studies, not just site anecdotes.

Public records advocate: Summaries of conceptual model data into "readable graphs or tables" (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)(A)(5)) must be provided in machine-readable formats (e.g., CSV) and included in the public docket.

Industry/hydrogeologist: The evaluation of infiltration potential through liners/soils (§257.71(d)(1)(ii)(B)) must allow use of predictive transport modeling (with documented parameters and uncertainty analysis) in lieu of extensive in-situ tests when access is limited.

NGO: Laboratory testing alone is insufficient to characterize liner performance over operational life; the rule should require aging tests, field performance monitoring, or conservative factors of safety in permeability assumptions.

Industry: The hard deadline to submit the initial application by April 2, 2020 (§257.71(d)(2)(i)) is obsolete (past date) and needs updating or transitional language for facilities that did not meet that date.

Legal/industry: The one-year deadline to submit the demonstration after the initial application (§257.71(d)(2)(i)) is unrealistic for complex sites; EPA should permit a project-specific schedule approved upon application acceptance.

Industry: The extension process for analytical limits (§257.71(d)(2)(i)) requires clearer standards for what constitutes "analytical limitations" and acceptable alternative timelines — otherwise requests will be inconsistently granted.

Industry/state: EPA's authority to request additional information during review (§257.71(d)(2)(ii)) should be bounded by a limit on the number and scope of follow-up requests and a maximum aggregate review timeline.

[P1] The requirement to provide the Secretary of USDA a copy of any draft proposed rule (Section 25(a)(2)(A)) duplicates existing interagency consultation procedures and will create unnecessary paperwork without improving substance.

[P1] Requiring EPA to provide USDA every draft proposed rule could delay EPA’s internal deliberations by creating an expectation of formal agency-to-agency document sharing for routine rules that have no agricultural impacts.

[P2] The 60‑day advance delivery requirement is unworkable for time‑sensitive rulemakings (e.g., emergency or court‑ordered deadlines) and would force EPA to miss statutorily mandated timelines.

[P2] The 60‑day timing should be shortened for non‑agricultural rules or include an exception for emergency rulemakings; otherwise the requirement infringes on EPA’s ability to meet judicial and statutory deadlines.

[P3] The prohibition against public availability of draft proposed rules before EPA signs them will reduce transparency and hinder meaningful stakeholder engagement, particularly for regulated parties who need early notice.

[P3] Preventing public access to drafts until after EPA signs them effectively limits public participation and may violate FOIA principles and expectations of open rulemaking.

[P4] Restricting public access until after EPA signs the draft proposed rule creates a de facto internal review period that favors interagency negotiation over public scrutiny, disadvantaging non‑federal stakeholders.

[P5] The obligation to include USDA’s written comments and EPA’s responses in the Federal Register if comments are submitted within 30 days is ambiguous about the level of response required (summary vs. point‑by‑point); this should be clarified to avoid burdensome requirements.

[P5] Requiring inclusion of USDA comments and EPA’s response in the Federal Register could produce voluminous Federal Register entries and delay publication; the rule should allow incorporation by reference or summary rather than full insertion.

[P6] The 30‑day window for USDA to submit written comments on draft proposed rules is too short for complex technical rules where USDA may need to consult with stakeholders and produce substantive input.

[P7] Allowing EPA to proceed any time after the 30‑day period if USDA fails to comment effectively gives USDA a veto by delaying until it chooses to comment; conversely, the provision lacks a clear mechanism for EPA to proceed when USDA is nonresponsive in an urgent timeline.

[P7] The permission for EPA to sign after USDA’s 30‑day nonresponse should explicitly allow EPA to proceed immediately after 30 days to prevent indefinite delays.

[P9] Adding Chitosan (Poly‑D‑glucosamine), CAS 9012‑76‑4, to the §152.25(f)(1) table raises concerns from environmental health advocates about exempting this substance from certain regulatory requirements; commenters will request supporting data demonstrating safety.

[P9] Industry stakeholders supporting the Chitosan listing will comment that the chemical name and CAS are correct and that inclusion will clarify its exempted status, reducing labeling confusion.

[P10] The proposed table entry for Chitosan must specify the scope of the exemption (e.g., allowable formulations, application rates, and crop uses); without limits, the exemption could be misused.

[P10] The rule should clarify whether Chitosan is exempt only when used as an inert ingredient or also as an active pesticidal ingredient; current table entry is silent on this distinction.

[P11] The change to the Post‑Transition Table (§73.622(i)) removing channel 12 and adding channel 18 for Mesa, Arizona could cause technical interference and must be accompanied by engineering studies demonstrating no harmful overlap with adjacent markets.

[P11] Broadcaster commenters will request explanation of the technical basis and evidence of public interest benefits for moving Mesa from channel 12 to channel 18, including impact on viewers and equipment compatibility.

[P12] Deleting the channel 12 allotment for Mesa may strand existing licensees or planned service expansions; the rule should address transition protections for affected broadcasters.

[P13] Adding channel 18 at Mesa should be accompanied by an interference protection contour analysis and an explanation of how the change complies with FCC technical and international coordination obligations.

[P14] The requirement to provide USDA a copy of any draft final rule at least 30 days before signing (FIFRA 25(a)(2)(B)) may conflict with other statutorily required final‑rule deadlines and should include exceptions for exigent circumstances.

[P14] The 30‑day delivery requirement for draft final rules will create an additional pre‑publication hold that could be used to exert undue influence; procedural safeguards should be added to protect EPA’s independent decision‑making.

[P16] Prohibiting public access to draft final rules until after EPA signs them will prevent stakeholders from seeing proposed final regulatory language and preparing for compliance, raising fairness concerns.

[P18] Requiring EPA to include USDA’s written comments and EPA’s responses with the final rule if USDA comments within 15 days is vague about whether responses must be substantive and whether they must address every USDA point; clarify the standard.

[P18] The 15‑day window for USDA comment on draft final rules is unreasonably short for complex matters that may require interagency coordination and external consultation.

[P20] Allowing EPA to sign the final rule any time after USDA’s 15‑day nonresponse may not be sufficient protection against last‑minute USDA objections; conversely, it may allow EPA to finalize without meaningful agricultural input — the rule should set a firm deadline and default outcome.

[P3] Legal commenters will argue the restrictions on public access to drafts may conflict with the Administrative Procedure Act’s requirements for notice and comment and established norms for transparency in rulemaking.

[P5] Agricultural stakeholders will request that USDA’s comments, if included in the Federal Register, be accepted in redacted form if they contain confidential business information, and that EPA provide a method to handle CBI.

[P9] Environmental groups will request risk assessments and justification documentation be published supporting the decision to add Chitosan to the exemption table before the amendment is finalized.

[P11] Consumer‑advocacy organizations will request public notice and comment on the Mesa channel change because broadcast channel reallocations can affect public safety communications and emergency alerting.

[P1] Constitutional law experts will comment that mandatory pre‑sharing of drafts with USDA without simultanous public disclosure risks viewpoint discrimination and could be challenged under separation‑of‑powers principles if it results in substantive control by another agency.

[P2] States and local governments will request an exception to the 60‑day proposed‑rule notice when state or local interests are directly affected and require earlier notification to coordinate implementation.

[P13] Public interest groups will ask for a timeline and relocation assistance plan for viewers or low‑income households that may need equipment updates after Mesa’s channel reassignment.

[P10] Chemical manufacturers will seek confirmation that the label display name "Chitosan" must be used exactly as written and request flexibility for variant names (e.g., "Chitosan (derived from crustacean shells)") to avoid labeling conflicts.

[P6] The triggering condition that USDA must submit written comments within 30 days to obligate EPA to include those comments is unfair because it conditions inclusion on a strict format (written) and timeframe; allow phone or email initiation with follow‑up.

[P19] The 15‑day triggering condition for USDA comments on draft final rules should be extended to allow comprehensive interagency review; 15 days is not reasonable for complex or novel regulations.

[P16] FOIA advocates will request explicit language permitting release of drafts when required by FOIA requests, rather than an absolute prohibition on public access prior to EPA signing.

[P7] Industry trade associations will argue the rule should explicitly state that USDA’s failure to comment does not indefinitely delay EPA action and that EPA can proceed after 30 days to avoid regulatory uncertainty.

[P20] Administrative law scholars will request clarification whether the "may sign" language imposes a duty to wait or merely permits signing; ambiguity could lead to litigation over whether EPA unlawfully withheld final rules.

[P12] Broadcasters will request grandfathering provisions for any licensees operating under the channel 12 allotment and a clear timeline for operating authority changes to avoid service disruptions.

[P9] Organic farmers and certifiers will request confirmation that listing Chitosan does not affect organic certification standards and ask USDA and EPA to coordinate guidance.

[P5] Commenters will request that EPA include in the preamble an explanation of procedures for incorporating USDA comments into the administrative record and how conflicting agency positions will be reconciled.

[P3] Transparency advocates will recommend that any shared drafts to USDA be posted in parallel to a secure public docket with redactions only for legitimately protected material, rather than a blanket prohibition on public access.

[P18] Legal commenters will ask whether inclusion of USDA comments in the final rule could be interpreted as creating interagency veto power over final agency actions and request limiting language to preserve EPA’s final decision‑making authority.

[P1] The national permit authorization in § 111.2(b) is overly broad because it allows brokers to conduct customs business “throughout U.S. customs territory” without geographic limits or additional local registration requirements; industry commenters will request clarification on whether local port authorizations or port-specific rules still apply.

[P1] Trade associations will ask CBP to confirm that issuance of a national permit does not waive port-specific operational requirements (e.g., bonded warehouse access, port security credentials) and to describe interactions with existing port procedures.

[P2] Importer and consumer advocates will object to § 111.3(a)’s geographic restriction, arguing it is ambiguous for brokers who perform off-shore preparatory work (outside customs territory) and request an explicit definition of what constitutes “conducting customs business” inside vs. outside customs territory.

[P3] Small brokerages will complain that § 111.3(b) requiring a knowledgeable point of contact available “during and outside normal hours” creates an undue staffing and cost burden, and will request a narrower scope (e.g., on-call during declared CBP hours or a specified minimum coverage window).

[P4] Privacy advocates will request limits on the personal information required for the point-of-contact entry in the CBP-authorized EDI system under § 111.3(b) and demand safeguards on retention, access, and minimization of personal contact data.

[P5] Brokers in areas without reliable EDI access will request that § 111.3(b) and § 111.3(b) second clause allow alternative secure electronic submissions (e.g., email with encryption) rather than only “writing to the designated Center director,” and ask for defined timelines for CBP to acknowledge receipt.

[P6] New broker applicants will challenge § 111.12(a) requiring timely submission of the license application “after passing the exam,” asking CBP to specify the exact filing window (e.g., within 90 or 180 days) instead of leaving “timely” undefined.

[P7] Practitioners will request that CBP allow electronic completion of Form 3124 for § 111.12(a) (currently requiring Form 3124 execution) and clarify acceptance of electronic signatures to align with modern filing practices.

[P8] Applicants will ask CBP to waive or provide a reduced application fee under § 111.12(a) (referring to § 111.96(a)) for applicants from nonprofit or underserved communities or to offer an installment option for the fee.

[P9] Brokers planning to use trade or fictitious names will request a simplification of the § 111.12(a) requirement to “provide evidence of authority in each State” by allowing a centralized declaration plus state-specific updates only when a dispute arises, because obtaining multiple state certificates is burdensome.

[P10] Candidates will ask CBP to clarify the “3-year” deadline in § 111.12(a) for filing an individual license after passing the exam (P10) — specifically whether it is three calendar years, 36 months, and whether passing earlier versions of the exam counts toward the clock.

[P11] Legal commenters will caution that § 111.12(a)’s allowance for the Center director to request a copy of the exam pass notice and fingerprints may implicate privacy and background-check legal limits and request a data-protection statement and defined retention period for fingerprint records (P11).

[P12] Applicants will object to § 111.12(a) permitting rejection of incomplete applications (P12) without a cure period and request that CBP institute a 30-day cure opportunity to submit missing attachments or fees before rejecting and returning the application.

[P13] Procedural fairness advocates will ask CBP to require the Center director under § 111.14(b) to provide applicants with the recommendation and reasons submitted to the Executive Director so applicants can meaningfully respond to adverse findings (P13, P14).

[P14] Industry groups will request that § 111.14(c) (P15, P16) limit Executive Director-ordered further inquiry to discrete, time-limited fact-finding and require notice of scope and a defined deadline for applicant responses to avoid indefinite processing delays.

[P15] Applicants will request that § 111.15 include an explicit processing-time goal (e.g., 60–90 days) for issuance of a license once the Executive Director finds the applicant qualified and fees paid (P17), to promote predictability.

[P16] Commenters will ask that § 111.15 (P18) clarify delivery method and tracking obligations for licenses forwarded to designated Centers — specifically whether electronic delivery of license copies is acceptable and deemed effective notice.

[P17] Due process advocates will request that § 111.16(a) require that denial notices include not only reasons (P20) but also the factual basis, supporting documents, and citations to statutes/regulations relied upon, to allow meaningful appeals (P19, P20).

[P18] Applicants will recommend that § 111.17(a) extend the 60-day filing period (P22) to 90 days for submission of additional information or requests to appear after denial, to allow gathering of evidence and counsel consultation (P21, P22).

[P19] Legal commenters will advise that the 60-calendar-day deadlines in §§ 111.17(b) and 111.19(e)(1) (P24, P47) be clarified whether they are jurisdictional or subject-matter deadlines and request tolling provisions for extraordinary circumstances (e.g., natural disasters).

[P20] Applicants seeking national permits will request CBP clarify under § 111.19(a) whether national permit holders are required to maintain local branch registrations or pay additional local fees to transact in particular ports (P26).

[P21] Practitioners will seek clarification under § 111.19(b) (P27–P29) whether passage of the broker exam is sufficient for immediate national permit application or whether additional experience or principal-qualifier requirements apply.

[P22] Corporations applying for national permits will request that § 111.19(b)(2) and (b)(3) (P31, P32) allow equivalent foreign or multi-state corporate documents (e.g., foreign qualification affidavits) and permit electronic certified copies, not only original state-issued documents.

[P23] Brokers will ask CBP to define “responsible supervision and control” in § 111.19(b) (P28, P49) with clear staffing ratios, responsibilities, and examples of compliant supervision plans to avoid subjective enforcement under § 111.28.

[P24] Brokers will object to the detailed personnel data required in § 111.19(b)(6) and (b)(7) (P35, P36), including social security numbers and dates of birth (referred to in P64), as excessive and a privacy/security risk; they will ask CBP to permit partial identifiers or hashed identifiers in public-facing records.

[P25] Industry commenters will request that CBP provide a model supervision plan for § 111.19(b)(8) (P37) and limit proprietary-disclosure risk by allowing redaction of sensitive operational details in the public permit file.

[P26] Brokers will ask CBP to permit off-site record retention locations for § 111.19(b)(9) (P38) only if records are electronically accessible within a specified short time (e.g., 24–72 hours) and to define acceptable physical security standards for those locations.

[P27] Trade compliance consultants will request that the designated “knowledgeable employee responsible for broker-wide records maintenance and financial recordkeeping” in § 111.19(b)(10) (P39) be allowed to be a contracted third-party provider, with clear requirements for contractual responsibilities and CBP access.

[P28] Commenters will request that the fee-evidence requirement in § 111.19(b)(11) (P40) allow provisional filing with a later cure for fee payment confirmation rather than automatic rejection, to avoid unnecessary processing delays.

[P29] Brokers will request that § 111.19(d) (P41–P44) require the designated Center director to provide applicants with a written list of deficiencies and a reasonable cure period prior to forwarding a denial recommendation to Executive Director, instead of immediate denial.

[P30] Public-interest groups will support § 111.19(d)(45) requiring CBP to maintain a public alphabetical list of permitted brokers (P45), but will request that the list exclude sensitive personal data (SSNs, DOBs) and include whether the permit is active, suspended, or revoked.

[P31] Applicants denied a national permit will request that § 111.19(e)(1) (P46–P47) explicitly permit submission of additional evidence by electronic means and extend the 60-day timeframe to 90 days to align with comment on individual license appeals.

[P32] Legal commenters will request that § 111.19(e)(2) (P48) clarify appeal rights to the Court of International Trade, including whether administrative exhaustion is required and whether interim operational relief (stay) is available pending appeal.

[P33] Brokers will ask CBP to specify measurable criteria for “responsible supervision and control” in § 111.19(f) and § 111.28 (P49, P61–P62), including minimum numbers of licensed brokers per volume of transactions or per office square footage, to avoid arbitrary enforcement.

[P34] Cybersecurity experts will raise concerns about the 72-hour breach notification requirement in § 111.21(b) (P50), arguing the timeframe may be unrealistic for complex investigations; they will request a “72-hour initial notification” plus a 30-calendar-day forensic report, and safe-harbor language for good-faith reporting.

[P35] Brokers will request that § 111.21(d) (P51–P52) allow the designated records-responsible employee to be an outsourced records manager and call for clear rules on liability where outsourced employees provide incorrect contact info (given § 111.28(c) exception P68).

[P36] Brokers with multi-state operations will request that § 111.23(a) (P53) permit primary record storage physically outside customs territory if electronic copies are stored within customs territory and are immediately accessible, to reduce costs of duplicative storage.

[P37] Practitioners will highlight conflict between § 111.24 confidentiality prohibition (P54) and increasingly common regulatory information-sharing arrangements; they will request express authorization for disclosures to government partners with adequate confidentiality protections and specify processes for client consent.

[P38] Importers will request that § 111.24 exceptions (P55–P56) be expanded to allow broker disclosure to a client’s authorized third-party service providers (e.g., customs compliance counsel, freight forwarders) upon client-designated written authorization, with CBP-prescribed form for authorization.

[P39] Brokers will ask CBP to define “reasonably notice” in § 111.25(a) (P57) and to set a maximum notice period (e.g., 5 business days) for inspections to allow planning and ensure availability of records and staff for review.

[P40] International trade lawyers will request that the 30-calendar-day production requirement in § 111.25(b) (P59) include explicit exceptions for records located off-site or third-party custody and allow an agreed extension where CBP provides written justification for additional time.

[P41] Brokers will request harmonization of § 111.25(c) (P60) with part 163 timelines and methods, and suggest CBP publish cross-references and consolidated instructions to avoid inconsistent requests and duplicative production.

[P42] Small brokerage firms will ask CBP to clarify § 111.28(a)’s “sufficient number of licensed brokers” requirement (P62) with specific minimums (for example, one licensed broker per X employees, or per Y annual entries) to avoid unpredictable enforcement.

[P43] Privacy and civil-rights groups will object to the § 111.28(b)(1) requirement (P63–P64) that employee submissions include social security numbers and dates/places of birth, urging CBP to accept Employer Identification Numbers or other less-sensitive identifiers and to employ data-minimization and encryption.

[P44] Brokers will request CBP to permit an initial employee roster submission under § 111.28(b)(1) (P63) to be provisional and allow a 14-day cure period for missing or erroneous employee details before any enforcement action.

[P45] Practitioners will request that the 30-day update windows in §§ 111.28(b)(1)–(3) (P65–P67) be relaxed to 45 or 60 days to account for payroll cycles and HR processing time, especially for large brokers with frequent personnel changes.

[P46] Employers will ask CBP to specify acceptable methods for transmitting employee data securely to EDI under § 111.28, and to allow batch uploads rather than individual submissions to reduce administrative burden.

[P47] Brokers will rely on the § 111.28(c) (P68) non-liability exception and ask CBP to publish examples of “culpability” and standards of proof that would render a broker responsible for employee-provided inaccurate information.

[P48] Corporate brokers will request clarifications under § 111.28(e) (P69–P72) about the threshold for “ownership shares not publicly traded” and the timing and content required in immediate written notice of ownership changes, and ask for a 30-day cure period before CBP may object to new principals.

[P49] Broker organizations will ask CBP to define the term “reasonable period” (P71) given to brokers to remedy objections to new principals and to provide objective factors that CBP will consider in determining reasonableness.

[P50] Brokers will request that § 111.30(a) (P73–P76) require CBP to provide an automatic confirmation of address updates (EDI or written) and to specify penalties only for willful failures to update addresses rather than for inadvertent delays.

[P51] Commenters will ask CBP to clarify whether the 10-calendar-day update requirements in § 111.30(a) and (b) (P75–P77) begin on the date of the change or the date the broker becomes aware of the change.

[P52] Licensed individuals and entities will request that § 111.30(d)(1) (P79) allow biennial rather than triennial reporting or permit a simplified electronic affirmation for small-volume brokers to reduce compliance costs.

[P53] Individual brokers will request that § 111.30(d)(2)(i)(C) and (d)(2)(ii) (P82–P83) provide guidance on what constitutes “conduct that could lead to suspension or revocation” and whether past minor infractions must be disclosed, to reduce uncertainty and over-disclosure.

[P54] Entities will request that the triennial report templates in § 111.30(d)(3)(i) (P84) be standardized and made available in CBP-authorized EDI formats with instructions to ensure consistent filings and reduce rejection rates.

[P55] Practitioners will urge CBP to clarify whether § 111.32 prohibitions (P86–P87) on filing known false claims create any affirmative duty to investigate client-provided information prior to submission, and if so, to define the level of due diligence required.

[P56] Brokers will request explicit safe-harbor procedures under § 111.32’s reporting duty (P88) that protect brokers who terminate representation and report suspected client fraud in good faith from liability for breach of confidentiality claims.

[P57] Commenters will ask CBP to clarify § 111.36(c)(3) (P89) language requiring brokers to “obtain a customs power of attorney directly” — specifically whether electronic powers-of-attorney, third-party platforms, or general consultative representations satisfy the requirement and to provide a model form.

Privacy advocates will request limits on the personal information required for the point-of-contact entry in the CBP-authorized EDI system under § 111.3(b) and demand safeguards on retention, access, and minimization of personal contact data.

Brokers in areas without reliable EDI access will request that § 111.3(b) and § 111.3(b) second clause allow alternative secure electronic submissions (e.g., email with encryption) rather than only “writing to the designated Center director,” and ask for defined timelines for CBP to acknowledge receipt.

New broker applicants will challenge § 111.12(a) requiring timely submission of the license application “after passing the exam,” asking CBP to specify the exact filing window (e.g., within 90 or 180 days) instead of leaving “timely” undefined.

Practitioners will request that CBP allow electronic completion of Form 3124 for § 111.12(a) (currently requiring Form 3124 execution) and clarify acceptance of electronic signatures to align with modern filing practices.

Applicants will ask CBP to waive or provide a reduced application fee under § 111.12(a) (referring to § 111.96(a)) for applicants from nonprofit or underserved communities or to offer an installment option for the fee.

Brokers planning to use trade or fictitious names will request a simplification of the § 111.12(a) requirement to “provide evidence of authority in each State” by allowing a centralized declaration plus state-specific updates only when a dispute arises, because obtaining multiple state certificates is burdensome.

Candidates will ask CBP to clarify the “3-year” deadline in § 111.12(a) for filing an individual license after passing the exam (P10) — specifically whether it is three calendar years, 36 months, and whether passing earlier versions of the exam counts toward the clock.

Legal commenters will caution that § 111.12(a)’s allowance for the Center director to request a copy of the exam pass notice and fingerprints may implicate privacy and background-check legal limits and request a data-protection statement and defined retention period for fingerprint records (P11).

Applicants will object to § 111.12(a) permitting rejection of incomplete applications (P12) without a cure period and request that CBP institute a 30-day cure opportunity to submit missing attachments or fees before rejecting and returning the application.

Procedural fairness advocates will ask CBP to require the Center director under § 111.14(b) to provide applicants with the recommendation and reasons submitted to the Executive Director so applicants can meaningfully respond to adverse findings (P13, P14).

Industry groups will request that § 111.14(c) (P15, P16) limit Executive Director-ordered further inquiry to discrete, time-limited fact-finding and require notice of scope and a defined deadline for applicant responses to avoid indefinite processing delays.

Applicants will request that § 111.15 include an explicit processing-time goal (e.g., 60–90 days) for issuance of a license once the Executive Director finds the applicant qualified and fees paid (P17), to promote predictability.

Commenters will ask that § 111.15 (P18) clarify delivery method and tracking obligations for licenses forwarded to designated Centers — specifically whether electronic delivery of license copies is acceptable and deemed effective notice.

Due process advocates will request that § 111.16(a) require that denial notices include not only reasons (P20) but also the factual basis, supporting documents, and citations to statutes/regulations relied upon, to allow meaningful appeals (P19, P20).

Applicants will recommend that § 111.17(a) extend the 60-day filing period (P22) to 90 days for submission of additional information or requests to appear after denial, to allow gathering of evidence and counsel consultation (P21, P22).

Legal commenters will advise that the 60-calendar-day deadlines in §§ 111.17(b) and 111.19(e)(1) (P24, P47) be clarified whether they are jurisdictional or subject-matter deadlines and request tolling provisions for extraordinary circumstances (e.g., natural disasters).

Applicants seeking national permits will request CBP clarify under § 111.19(a) whether national permit holders are required to maintain local branch registrations or pay additional local fees to transact in particular ports (P26).

Practitioners will seek clarification under § 111.19(b) (P27–P29) whether passage of the broker exam is sufficient for immediate national permit application or whether additional experience or principal-qualifier requirements apply.

Corporations applying for national permits will request that § 111.19(b)(2) and (b)(3) (P31, P32) allow equivalent foreign or multi-state corporate documents (e.g., foreign qualification affidavits) and permit electronic certified copies, not only original state-issued documents.

Brokers will ask CBP to define “responsible supervision and control” in § 111.19(b) (P28, P49) with clear staffing ratios, responsibilities, and examples of compliant supervision plans to avoid subjective enforcement under § 111.28.

Brokers will object to the detailed personnel data required in § 111.19(b)(6) and (b)(7) (P35, P36), including social security numbers and dates of birth (referred to in P64), as excessive and a privacy/security risk; they will ask CBP to permit partial identifiers or hashed identifiers in public-facing records.

Industry commenters will request that CBP provide a model supervision plan for § 111.19(b)(8) (P37) and limit proprietary-disclosure risk by allowing redaction of sensitive operational details in the public permit file.

Brokers will ask CBP to permit off-site record retention locations for § 111.19(b)(9) (P38) only if records are electronically accessible within a specified short time (e.g., 24–72 hours) and to define acceptable physical security standards for those locations.

Trade compliance consultants will request that the designated “knowledgeable employee responsible for broker-wide records maintenance and financial recordkeeping” in § 111.19(b)(10) (P39) be allowed to be a contracted third-party provider, with clear requirements for contractual responsibilities and CBP access.

Commenters will request that the fee-evidence requirement in § 111.19(b)(11) (P40) allow provisional filing with a later cure for fee payment confirmation rather than automatic rejection, to avoid unnecessary processing delays.

Brokers will request that § 111.19(d) (P41–P44) require the designated Center director to provide applicants with a written list of deficiencies and a reasonable cure period prior to forwarding a denial recommendation to Executive Director, instead of immediate denial.

Public-interest groups will support § 111.19(d)(45) requiring CBP to maintain a public alphabetical list of permitted brokers (P45), but will request that the list exclude sensitive personal data (SSNs, DOBs) and include whether the permit is active, suspended, or revoked.

Applicants denied a national permit will request that § 111.19(e)(1) (P46–P47) explicitly permit submission of additional evidence by electronic means and extend the 60-day timeframe to 90 days to align with comment on individual license appeals.

Legal commenters will request that § 111.19(e)(2) (P48) clarify appeal rights to the Court of International Trade, including whether administrative exhaustion is required and whether interim operational relief (stay) is available pending appeal.

Brokers will ask CBP to specify measurable criteria for “responsible supervision and control” in § 111.19(f) and § 111.28 (P49, P61–P62), including minimum numbers of licensed brokers per volume of transactions or per office square footage, to avoid arbitrary enforcement.

Cybersecurity experts will raise concerns about the 72-hour breach notification requirement in § 111.21(b) (P50), arguing the timeframe may be unrealistic for complex investigations; they will request a “72-hour initial notification” plus a 30-calendar-day forensic report, and safe-harbor language for good-faith reporting.

Brokers will request that § 111.21(d) (P51–P52) allow the designated records-responsible employee to be an outsourced records manager and call for clear rules on liability where outsourced employees provide incorrect contact info (given § 111.28(c) exception P68).

Brokers with multi-state operations will request that § 111.23(a) (P53) permit primary record storage physically outside customs territory if electronic copies are stored within customs territory and are immediately accessible, to reduce costs of duplicative storage.

Practitioners will highlight conflict between § 111.24 confidentiality prohibition (P54) and increasingly common regulatory information-sharing arrangements; they will request express authorization for disclosures to government partners with adequate confidentiality protections and specify processes for client consent.

Importers will request that § 111.24 exceptions (P55–P56) be expanded to allow broker disclosure to a client’s authorized third-party service providers (e.g., customs compliance counsel, freight forwarders) upon client-designated written authorization, with CBP-prescribed form for authorization.

Brokers will ask CBP to define “reasonably notice” in § 111.25(a) (P57) and to set a maximum notice period (e.g., 5 business days) for inspections to allow planning and ensure availability of records and staff for review.

International trade lawyers will request that the 30-calendar-day production requirement in § 111.25(b) (P59) include explicit exceptions for records located off-site or third-party custody and allow an agreed extension where CBP provides written justification for additional time.

Brokers will request harmonization of § 111.25(c) (P60) with part 163 timelines and methods, and suggest CBP publish cross-references and consolidated instructions to avoid inconsistent requests and duplicative production.

Small brokerage firms will ask CBP to clarify § 111.28(a)’s “sufficient number of licensed brokers” requirement (P62) with specific minimums (for example, one licensed broker per X employees, or per Y annual entries) to avoid unpredictable enforcement.

Privacy and civil-rights groups will object to the § 111.28(b)(1) requirement (P63–P64) that employee submissions include social security numbers and dates/places of birth, urging CBP to accept Employer Identification Numbers or other less-sensitive identifiers and to employ data-minimization and encryption.

Brokers will request CBP to permit an initial employee roster submission under § 111.28(b)(1) (P63) to be provisional and allow a 14-day cure period for missing or erroneous employee details before any enforcement action.

Practitioners will request that the 30-day update windows in §§ 111.28(b)(1)–(3) (P65–P67) be relaxed to 45 or 60 days to account for payroll cycles and HR processing time, especially for large brokers with frequent personnel changes.

Employers will ask CBP to specify acceptable methods for transmitting employee data securely to EDI under § 111.28, and to allow batch uploads rather than individual submissions to reduce administrative burden.

Brokers will rely on the § 111.28(c) (P68) non-liability exception and ask CBP to publish examples of “culpability” and standards of proof that would render a broker responsible for employee-provided inaccurate information.

Corporate brokers will request clarifications under § 111.28(e) (P69–P72) about the threshold for “ownership shares not publicly traded” and the timing and content required in immediate written notice of ownership changes, and ask for a 30-day cure period before CBP may object to new principals.

Broker organizations will ask CBP to define the term “reasonable period” (P71) given to brokers to remedy objections to new principals and to provide objective factors that CBP will consider in determining reasonableness.

Brokers will request that § 111.30(a) (P73–P76) require CBP to provide an automatic confirmation of address updates (EDI or written) and to specify penalties only for willful failures to update addresses rather than for inadvertent delays.
Commenters will ask CBP to clarify whether the 10-calendar-day update requirements in § 111.30(a) and (b) (P75–P77) begin on the date of the change or the date the broker becomes aware of the change.

Licensed individuals and entities will request that § 111.30(d)(1) (P79) allow biennial rather than triennial reporting or permit a simplified electronic affirmation for small-volume brokers to reduce compliance costs.

Individual brokers will request that § 111.30(d)(2)(i)(C) and (d)(2)(ii) (P82–P83) provide guidance on what constitutes “conduct that could lead to suspension or revocation” and whether past minor infractions must be disclosed, to reduce uncertainty and over-disclosure.

Entities will request that the triennial report templates in § 111.30(d)(3)(i) (P84) be standardized and made available in CBP-authorized EDI formats with instructions to ensure consistent filings and reduce rejection rates.

Practitioners will urge CBP to clarify whether § 111.32 prohibitions (P86–P87) on filing known false claims create any affirmative duty to investigate client-provided information prior to submission, and if so, to define the level of due diligence required.

Brokers will request explicit safe-harbor procedures under § 111.32’s reporting duty (P88) that protect brokers who terminate representation and report suspected client fraud in good faith from liability for breach of confidentiality claims.

Commenters will ask CBP to clarify § 111.36(c)(3) (P89) language requiring brokers to “obtain a customs power of attorney directly” — specifically whether electronic powers-of-attorney, third-party platforms, or general consultative representations satisfy the requirement and to provide a model form.
