raw_output:
[P1] The April 15, 2019 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonable and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow stakeholders (airlines, MROs, labor groups, and suppliers) sufficient time to analyze the technical service bulletin and prepare substantive comments.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether electronic submissions (email) received on April 15, 2019 local time will be accepted, and state the time zone cutoff for the comment receipt deadline.

[P2] § 39.13(f) is vague about "the specified compliance times"; the AD should explicitly state whether compliance times are measured from the effective date of the AD or from the date of receipt of parts/approvals, to avoid inconsistent interpretation.

[P2] The phrase "unless already completed" in § 39.13(f) creates potential evidentiary disputes; the AD should specify acceptable documentation to prove prior compliance (e.g., method and sign-off by authorized inspector, reference to service bulletin revision).

[P3] The 120-day compliance requirement in § 39.13(g) for Group 1 airplanes in BASB 737–53A1362 is unworkably short for operators with limited docking capacity; FAA should allow phased compliance or extend to at least 180 days or provide relief for planned maintenance scheduling conflicts.

[P3] § 39.13(g) should permit use of previously performed inspections if they meet the same scope and were performed within a specified lookback period (e.g., 12 months), instead of blanket requiring actions within 120 days.

[P4] The timing requirements in § 39.13(h) for Groups 2–20 reference "applicable times specified" in the BASB but do not provide those intervals in the AD text; the FAA should incorporate or summarize the critical compliance intervals to reduce confusion.

[P4] Operators will likely request clarification whether calendar times or flight cycles/flight hours govern the "specified times" in § 39.13(h); the AD should explicitly state the units and how to count them.

[P5] The termination provision in § 39.13(i) (completion of part 13) should define acceptable variants of the modification and the required documentation to prove the modified locations are eligible for termination of repetitive open-hole eddy current inspections.

[P5] § 39.13(i) should clarify whether partial completion of part 13 on a frame (e.g., one side only) qualifies for termination of inspections for the modified locations only, and how to document such partial compliance.

[P6] Requiring use of the AD effective date under § 39.13(j)(1) instead of the service bulletin original issue date may penalize operators who complied with later service bulletin revisions; the AD should allow use of the service bulletin revision date if it provides a later, clearer compliance baseline.

[P6] The change in reference date in § 39.13(j)(1) could create grandfathering issues for inspections performed between the service bulletin issue date and the AD effective date; FAA should explicitly address acceptability of such interim actions.

[P7] § 39.13(j)(2) that forbids contacting Boeing as the sole source and requires FAA-approved methods is appropriate but needs a clear process and timeline for approval of Boeing-provided alternative repairs to avoid grounding aircraft awaiting approval.

[P7] The AD should allow use of Boeing ODA-approved repairs as an interim measure pending FAA approval, provided the ODA approval is submitted immediately to the FAA per a specified timeline (e.g., within 14 days).

[P8] The AMOC authority in § 39.13(k)(1) is delegated to the Manager, Los Angeles ACO Branch; commenters will request clarity on whether other FAA offices (e.g., AEG, AFS-300) can also approve AMOCs and the expected turnaround times for AMOC decisions.

[P8] Industry will request that the FAA publish standard criteria and examples for AMOC acceptance under § 39.13(k)(1) to ensure consistent decisions and predictable timelines.

[P9] Sending AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO under § 39.13(k)(1) is confusing for international operators whose principal inspectors are outside the U.S.; the AD should specify how foreign operators should route AMOC requests.

[P10] § 39.13(k)(1) requires addressing AMOC submissions to the person in paragraph (l)(2) if sent directly; commenters will request that the AD include that contact name and direct mailing address in the AD body to avoid misrouting.

[P11] Allowing email submission to 9-ANM-LAACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov under § 39.13(k)(1) is helpful, but the AD should state acceptable file formats, maximum file sizes, and confirmation procedures to ensure timely receipt and processing.

[P12] The pre-use notification requirement in § 39.13(k)(2) to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC may be operationally burdensome for large fleets; operators will request an option to notify within a specified period after first use (e.g., 48–72 hours) rather than prior notice.

[P12] § 39.13(k)(2) should clarify the content required in the notification to the principal inspector (e.g., AMOC reference number, affected tail numbers, scheduled date of use), to ensure consistent compliance.

[P13] Permitting Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to be used under § 39.13(k)(3) is beneficial, but the AD must require timely FAA oversight — specifically that Boeing ODA approvals be submitted to the FAA within a set period (e.g., 7–14 days) for recordation and audit.

[P13] Labor and safety advocates will request that § 39.13(k)(3) be revised to require FAA concurrence (not just Boeing ODA approval) for AMOCs that alter inspection intervals or structural repair methods, to maintain independent oversight.

[P14] The certification-basis requirement in § 39.13(k)(3) for AMOC approval should be clarified regarding parts and modifications introduced post-certification; commenters will ask how AMOC approvals address changed-product rules and possible need for supplemental type certificates.

[P14] Legal commenters will point out that requiring explicit reference to this AD in any AMOC approval (per § 39.13(k)(3)) may create administrative burden and recommend a standardized AMOC reference format to avoid inconsistent cross-referencing.

[P15] The strict RC obligation in § 39.13(k)(4)(i) that all RC-labeled steps and substeps must be performed should be balanced with practical maintenance realities; operators will request an allowance for minor administrative variances (e.g., different tooling callouts) that do not affect the safety outcome.

[P15] The AD should clarify whether tooling or procedural updates in the figures referenced by RC steps require separate AMOCs, as § 39.13(k)(4)(i) could be read to require AMOC approval for any illustrative change even if functionally equivalent.

[P16] The "RC Exempt" exception in § 39.13(k)(4)(i) needs clearer labeling in the service bulletin; commenters will ask Boeing to mark "RC Exempt" steps explicitly and consistently to avoid misapplication during maintenance.

[P17] Requiring AMOCs for any deviation to RC steps per § 39.13(k)(4)(i) could delay urgent repairs; industry will request an expedited AMOC review and temporary relief process for emergency deviations with post-facto AMOC submission.

[P17] Maintenance organizations will ask FAA to define what constitutes a "deviation" to RC steps (e.g., minor technique differences vs. substantive changes) so that AMOC requirements are applied consistently.

[P18] Allowing deviations from non-RC steps under § 39.13(k)(4)(ii) using operator programs is appropriate, but the AD must specify required recordkeeping and audit trails demonstrating that deviations did not impair the ability to perform RC steps.

[P18] The AD should confirm that standard acceptable methods under the operator's maintenance program include manufacturer-approved procedures and approved repair station methods, to avoid unnecessary AMOC requests for routine variations.

[P19] The condition in § 39.13(k)(4)(ii) that RC steps remain performable and the airplane can be returned to an airworthy condition should be accompanied by objective criteria for "performable" and "airworthy" (e.g., specific test or inspection acceptance criteria), to reduce subjective disputes.

[P19] Operators will seek clarification on who determines whether the airplane can be returned to an airworthy condition when deviating from non-RC steps — the principal inspector, certificate holder's accountable manager, or the certifying mechanic — and request a defined approval chain.

[P3] Structural repair stations and MROs will comment that the AD should provide expected parts lead times and any FAA-accepted suppliers list for parts required to perform the corrective actions within the 120-day window.

[P4] Smaller operators will request cost and burden estimates be included or updated in the preamble to justify the compliance intervals in § 39.13(h), in accordance with regulatory transparency best practices.

[P5] Aviation safety advocates will request that the termination of inspections in § 39.13(i) not be allowed without demonstration (e.g., nondestructive testing baseline) that the preventive modification fully mitigates the fatigue cracking risk.

[P7] Boeing and affected manufacturers will ask the FAA to explicitly permit use of Boeing Technical Instructions that the manufacturer deems necessary while FAA processes approval, to avoid operational disruptions — with a requirement to submit those instructions to the FAA within a tight timeframe.

[P8] International airworthiness authorities will likely request harmonization language indicating whether this AD and its AMOC processes are intended to satisfy parallel mandatory continuing airworthiness information (MCAI) in other jurisdictions.

[P9] Foreign-registered operators will request specific procedures for using their national civil aviation authority as the route for AMOC coordination under § 39.13(k)(1), including timing expectations.

[P11] Privacy and security commenters will ask the FAA to provide secure file-transfer alternatives for AMOC documents containing proprietary technical data, instead of only a public email address.

[P12] Labor organizations will request that notification to principal inspectors under § 39.13(k)(2) include coordination with workforce representatives when AMOCs affect routine maintenance scheduling or staffing levels.

[P14] Legal experts will request that the AD specify whether an AMOC approval that references the AD creates a regulatory obligation enforceable separate from the AD, to clarify compliance and enforcement scope.

[P15] Airlines will ask the FAA to allow consolidation of RC-identified repetitive tasks across fleet maintenance schedules when the RC steps are identical, to reduce duplicated downtime, subject to AMOC or principal inspector concurrence.

[P3] Commenters will request that the FAA provide sample inspection findings categories and allowable disposition actions (e.g., repair limits) in the AD or a referenced service document to standardize "on-condition" actions required within 120 days.

[P5] MROs will request that the AD state whether completion of part 13 performed per an earlier FAA-approved AMOC or per manufacturer's alternative that has FAA concurrence is acceptable for terminating inspections as described in § 39.13(i).

[P6] Consumer and passenger safety groups will ask the FAA to explain the safety rationale for substituting the AD effective date as the compliance trigger per § 39.13(j)(1), so the public can understand risk implications.

[P11] Commenters will request an acknowledgment/receipt mechanism and expected processing timeline for emailed AMOC submissions to the 9-ANM-LAACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov address to ensure transparency and planning.

[P17] Certification authorities and legal commenters will request that the FAA publish the expected documentation package required with an AMOC that seeks deviation from RC steps (engineering substantiation, stress analyses, test results), to avoid incomplete submissions.

[P1] The physical-examination requirement in § 274a.2(b)(1)(ii)(A) is impracticable for remote or multi-state employers who onboard employees telework­ing from different locations; the rule should clarify permissible technologies and cross-state procedures rather than leaving alternatives solely to the Secretary.

[P1] Requiring employers to ensure documents “appear genuine and relate to the individual” without objective standards creates legal uncertainty and increases liability exposure for employers; the rule should provide a non‑exhaustive list of acceptable indicators of genuineness and safe‑harbor procedures.

[P1] The provision should expressly permit inspection by trained third‑party agents (e.g., notaries, fingerprinting centers, employer‑authorized vendors) and define their required credentials, because many employers rely on vendors for document inspection.

[P1] The phrase “physically examine (or otherwise examine pursuant to an alternative procedure authorized by the Secretary…)” is ambiguous about whether employers may rely on employer‑developed remote verification processes pending Secretary authorization; commenters request explicit interim authorization or an expedited approval pathway.

[P2] The requirement to reverify “not later than the date work authorization expires” may create operational timing issues for short‑term and hourly workers hired under rolling authorization windows; the rule should clarify whether reverification may occur within a grace period before expiration.

[P2] Employers need clarification on whether receipt of a renewal application (e.g., a temporary extension receipt) satisfies reverification timing obligations and allows continued employment past the original expiration while the employee’s renewal is pending.

[P2] The rule should specify acceptable documentation for reauthorizations (e.g., USCIS receipts, updated EAD cards, updated foreign passport with visa) to reduce disputes about what constitutes adequate proof of continued work authorization.

[P3] The cross‑reference requiring compliance with (b)(1)(ii)(A) and (b)(1)(ix) during reverification duplicates burdens when alternative procedures are in effect; commenters request a single clear pathway for reverification under authorized alternative procedures to avoid conflicting requirements.

[P3] Form instructions should be revised to align explicitly with the option to use Secretary‑authorized alternative examinations during reverification; otherwise I‑9 guidance will remain inconsistent and lead to enforcement risk for employers using alternatives.

[P4] The Secretary’s discretion to authorize alternative examination procedures in § 274a.2(b)(1)(ix) is too broad; the rule should delineate criteria (privacy protections, fraud prevention measures, interoperability with DHS systems) and a public notice/response period before authorization.

[P4] Industry stakeholders support alternative procedures as necessary for modern hiring practices but request mandated uniform standards and certification for vendor solutions to ensure nationwide consistency and legal defensibility.

[P4] Employee‑privacy and civil‑liberties groups will demand that any authorized alternative procedure include strict limits on data collection, retention, and sharing; the rule should require a privacy impact assessment and data minimization standards before approval.

[P5] Authorizing alternatives “as part of a pilot program” is useful, but commenters request that pilots be required to publish evaluation metrics, duration, scope (size/industry/geography), and an independent assessment prior to scaling to all employers.

[P5] Small employers and rural employers should be included in pilot eligibility to assess impacts across employer sizes; the rule should prohibit pilots that only include large employers or tech firms.

[P6] The “equivalent level of security” standard in § 274a.2(b)(1)(ix)(B) is undefined; commenters request explicit security metrics (e.g., false acceptance rate, false rejection rate, encryption standards, identity‑proofing assurance levels) and an evidence‑based testing regimen.

[P6] Legal experts warn that without clear standards, courts and agencies will second‑guess Secretary determinations; the rule should require publication of the Secretary’s security determination and supporting technical evidence for public review.

[P7] Temporarily adopting alternative procedures during a declared public health or national emergency (§ 274a.2(b)(1)(ix)(C)) is reasonable, but the rule should require a sunset date, periodic review, and reporting to Congress to prevent indefinite continuation of emergency measures.

[P7] Public‑health advocates request that emergency authorizations explicitly include accommodations for vulnerable populations who may lack access to required technology for alternative examinations.

[P8] The employer obligation in § 274a.2(c)(1)(ii) to reverify upon finding expired authorization does not state required timing after discovery; commenters urge a clear deadline (e.g., within 3 business days of discovery) to provide operational certainty.

[P8] Employers request clarification on what constitutes “finding” expiration during inspection — whether a visual review of the I‑9 is sufficient or whether employers must verify expiration against government records before initiating reverification.

[P9] Requiring compliance with both (b)(1)(ii)(A) and (b)(1)(ix) during reverification creates a potential conflict if (b)(1)(ix) alternative procedures are not yet authorized for an employer; the rule should allow employers using currently authorized alternatives to rely on those alternatives for reverification.

[P9] The rule should explicitly state whether reverification may be completed remotely when authorized alternatives are in effect, and whether remote reverification requires employer retention of any additional documentation or logs.

[P10] The prohibition in § 274a.2(c)(1)(ii) that an individual “may no longer be employed” if reverification is not completed as required is harsh and could produce unintended terminations; commenters request a limited reinstatement period or conditional employment allowance pending prompt reverification notice.

[P10] Employment advocates and immigration attorneys warn that automatic termination for failure to reverify could disproportionately harm authorized workers who timely applied for renewal but lack documentation; the rule should explicitly protect workers with timely-filed renewals or provide a safe‑harbor.

[P10] Labor groups argue the employer‑liability focus should be balanced by protections for employees (e.g., notice and cure periods, ability to present documents within a prescribed timeframe) before ending employment for reverification noncompliance.

[P1/P9] Multiple commenters request that the rule include a clear audit trail requirement (dates, inspector identity, method of examination, copies or attestation of documents when lawful) to protect employers in compliance reviews, and specify permissible retention periods and redaction rules to protect sensitive data.

[P4/P5] Vendors and technology providers will request a streamlined, transparent approval process (including timelines and criteria) for becoming an approved alternative‑examination provider for purposes of (b)(1)(ix) and pilot programs under (b)(1)(ix)(A).

[P6/P3] Privacy and civil‑liberties organizations request that equivalence determinations include public interest balancing and a formal comment period before adoption, rather than leaving determinations solely to the Secretary’s internal judgment.

[P2/P8] Small businesses request model employer checklists, automated reminders, and access to low‑cost verification tools to meet reverification deadlines described in (b)(1)(vii) and (c)(1)(ii) without incurring disproportionate compliance costs.

[P1] The rule should explicitly prohibit employers from relying solely on employee attestations about document genuineness without physical or authorized alternative examination, to avoid ambiguous compliance practices.

[P3/P9] Legal commenters request that the agencies harmonize Form I‑9 instructions with the regulatory text to ensure that the form does not inadvertently require different actions than the regulation, particularly regarding authorized alternatives during reverification.

[P7] Public commenters request that any emergency alternative procedure adopted under (b)(1)(ix)(C) adhere to nondiscrimination obligations and not be used in a manner that increases disparate treatment of protected classes.

[P1] The May 5, 2022 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is arbitrary and unreasonable given the short public notice period; request extension of the comment period by at least 60 days to allow operators and suppliers to prepare technical comments and cost analyses.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether electronic postmark, courier receipt, or FAA receipt is controlling for the May 5, 2022 deadline; ambiguity could cause timely submissions to be rejected.

[P2] § 39.13(f) requires compliance "within the specified compliance times" but does not provide relief for unavoidable supply-chain delays (e.g., parts backorders); request insertion of a hardship extension procedure or explicit allowance for documented supply delays.

[P2] The obligation to comply "unless already done" lacks a clear recordkeeping requirement to demonstrate prior compliance; require that operators maintain traceable records and specify their form and retention period.

[P3] § 39.13(g) mandates performing all actions in the Boeing Requirements Bulletin "except as modified by paragraph (h)" but does not identify which operators’ bulletin revisions are acceptable; request that the AD explicitly reference the exact Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin revision and date to avoid confusion.

[P3] Requiring operators to perform "all applicable actions" per the Boeing bulletin without listing applicable airplane serial numbers or groups could create inconsistent interpretations; ask FAA to enumerate applicability by line number or group.

[P4] § 39.13(h) replaces the Boeing booklet's "original issue date" with the AD effective date for compliance times, but provides no transition guidance for operators that relied on the original bulletin schedule; request grandfathering or phase-in allowance so operators are not penalized if they followed the original bulletin schedule.

[P4] Using the AD effective date in place of Boeing's original issue date may shorten compliance windows unexpectedly; require FAA to recalculate and publish specific revised compliance dates for each compliance item rather than relying on substitution language.

[P5] § 39.13(i) terminates AD 2020–11–11 for a fleet only when "all affected airplanes in an operator's fleet" accomplish the actions, which could unfairly bind smaller carriers with mixed fleets; request clarification whether termination applies fleet-wide by operator certificate or by individual operator/owner and how to handle pooled/leased aircraft.

[P5] The provision that termination requires accomplishment on "all affected airplanes in an operator’s fleet" could incentivize delaying work on a single aircraft to prolong less burdensome requirements; suggest allowing termination on a per-operator-per-type basis or providing a mechanism to petition for partial termination.

[P6] § 39.13(j) outright prohibits installation of FQPU P/N 0320KPU01 on Group 1 airplanes as of the AD effective date but does not provide an approved replacement part number; request FAA to identify approved replacements or interim acceptable parts to avoid grounding or removal difficulties.

[P6] Banning installation "as of the effective date" with no grandfathering for parts already purchased but not yet installed could impose sunk-cost losses; request an exception allowing installation of already-purchased units if accompanied by a Safety Risk Assessment and traceability.

[P6] The prohibition on installing FQPU P/N 0320KPU01 does not define "install" in contexts of maintenance continuity (e.g., re-installing from one Group 1 airplane to another); request clarification to prevent inadvertent violations.

[P7] § 39.13(k)(1) delegates AMOC approval authority to the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch, but operators outside the Seattle region may find this geographic concentration inefficient; request that the FAA allow Regional Aircraft Certification Offices to grant AMOCs or provide expedited review timelines.

[P7] The rule should permit delegation of AMOC approval to authorized representatives or Designated Engineering Representatives (DERs) for minor deviations to reduce burden on the Seattle ACO and speed implementation.

[P8] § 39.13(k)(1) requires AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or responsible Flight Standards Office, which may create duplication if the same request must also go to the Seattle ACO manager; request explicit single-point submission instructions and confirmation procedures.

[P8] The obligation to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector fails to account for operators with multiple principal inspectors across regions; request guidance on routing when multiple inspectors have jurisdiction.

[P9] § 39.13(k)(1) requires direct submissions to the certification office manager “identified in paragraph (l)(1),” but paragraph (l)(1) is omitted or incomplete in the proposed text; ask FAA to correct this cross-reference and provide the contact name and address.

[P10] Permitting email to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is helpful, but § 39.13(k)(1) should also specify acceptable file formats, size limits, encryption requirements for sensitive data, and acknowledgement-of-receipt timelines.

[P11] § 39.13(k)(2) obligates operators to notify their principal inspector before using an approved AMOC but does not set a required timeframe for notification; recommend specifying a deadline (e.g., within 72 hours of first use) to ensure timely oversight.

[P11] The notification requirement lacks content requirements — it should state what information must be included (AMOC identifier, approved deviations, affected serial numbers, and dates of use) to be meaningful.

[P12] § 39.13(k)(3) allows AMOC-based repairs if approved by Boeing's authorized ODA, but this creates potential conflict of interest because Boeing both approves AMOC and benefits commercially; request FAA oversight requirements or bilateral review before accepting Boeing ODA approvals.

[P12] Relying on Boeing ODA approval for AMOC applicability may exclude operators or third-party repair stations from proposing viable solutions; suggest allowing other qualified design approval holders (e.g., other ODA organizations or DERs) to approve alternatives when Boeing cannot.

[P13] § 39.13(k)(3) conditions AMOC approvals on meeting the airplane’s certification basis and explicitly referencing this AD, but the rule does not detail how equivalence to certification basis will be demonstrated; request FAA to require a documented compliance matrix showing equivalence to each relevant certification requirement.

[P13] The requirement that AMOC approvals "must meet the certification basis of the airplane" is overly broad; ask FAA to specify whether previously-approved compliance findings for similar AMOCs will be accepted or whether a full recertification analysis is necessary.

§ 39.13(f) requires compliance "within the specified compliance times" but does not provide relief for unavoidable supply-chain delays (e.g., parts backorders); request insertion of a hardship extension procedure or explicit allowance for documented supply delays.

§ 39.13(g) mandates performing all actions in the Boeing Requirements Bulletin "except as modified by paragraph (h)" but does not identify which operators’ bulletin revisions are acceptable; request that the AD explicitly reference the exact Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin revision and date to avoid confusion.

[P1] CMS should clarify the phrase “at least as frequently as specified” in §414.8(b) to state explicitly that CMS will not reduce current coding cycle frequency below the minimums listed, to prevent future unilateral downgrades in frequency.

[P2] The bi-annual schedule for non-drug, non-biological items in §414.8(b)(1) is too infrequent for rapidly evolving technologies (e.g., digital therapeutics, new devices); request CMS allow for expedited ad hoc cycles when warranted.

[P3] The quarterly cycle requirement for drugs/biologics in §414.8(b)(2) should include guaranteed publication dates for each quarter’s decisions to improve industry planning and payer implementation.

[P4] §414.8(c) requires publishing application deadlines “on its website or otherwise” — commenters request that CMS commit to publishing deadlines on a single stable webpage and provide machine-readable calendar files (e.g., iCal/CSV) to ensure accessibility.

[P5] The “in or around January and June” deadlines for non-drug items in §414.8(c)(1) are vague; request precise calendar dates (e.g., January 15 and June 15) so applicants can reliably prepare submissions.

[P6] Similarly, §414.8(c)(2)’s “in or around January, April, June, and September” for drugs/biologics should specify exact submission deadlines or fixed-week deadlines (e.g., second Friday of month) to avoid ambiguity.

[P7] Under §414.8(d)(1), CMS must hold public meetings for notice/input — commenters request minimum advance notice (e.g., 30 days) and requirement for both virtual and in-person participation options to ensure broad stakeholder access.

[P8] For §414.8(d)(2), which mandates public meetings during each bi-annual coding cycle, stakeholders ask CMS to specify the number of meetings per cycle and to publish agendas and materials at least two weeks in advance.

[P9] §414.8(d)(3) requires public meetings for all non-drug code applications subject to e(3) delays — patient advocacy groups request that CMS not use e(3) routinely to avoid public meetings and require CMS to justify any omission in writing.

[P10] Under §414.8(d)(4), CMS limits public meetings for drug/biologics apps to certain circumstances — industry groups argue this narrows transparency and request that CMS hold public meetings for all drug/biologic applications unless a narrowly defined exemption applies.

[P11] §414.8(d)(4)(i) states a resubmitted application triggers a public meeting — commenters ask CMS to clarify whether the applicant may request a public meeting on first submissions and whether CMS will accommodate such requests.

[P12] For §414.8(d)(4)(ii), when CMS delays a decision and finds public input could assist, commenters request objective criteria for “program, policy, or implementation concerns” to limit arbitrary invocation of meetings.

[P13] §414.8(e)(1) requires preliminary recommendations be posted prior to meetings — commenters request a minimum posting window (e.g., 14 days before the meeting) and that recommendations include clear rationale and supporting evidence.

[P14] Under §414.8(e)(3)(i) permitting delays into subsequent cycles for complexity/significance, commenters urge CMS to define “complex” and “significant” and to require a maximum cumulative delay (e.g., one additional cycle) to avoid indefinite postponement.

[P15] The timelines in §414.8(e)(2) (six months for non-drug; three months for drugs) should be firm, not “approximately” — providers and manufacturers need firm deadlines to align contracting and billing systems.

[P16] §414.8(e)(2)(i)’s six-month target for non-drug final decisions is too long for items that impact patient care; request CMS expedite decisions to within 90–120 days for items designated as high-priority.

[P17] §414.8(e)(2)(ii)’s three-month target for drug final decisions should include penalties or reporting requirements if CMS misses the timeframe to ensure accountability.

[P18] Under §414.8(e)(3)(ii), allowing delay for resubmitted applications placed on public meeting agendas into a subsequent quarterly cycle could slow access; request caps on how many quarters such delays are permitted.

[P19] §414.8(e)(3)(iii) requires publication of delay decisions simultaneously with other recommendations — legal commenters request CMS include reasons for delay and an estimated new decision date in the publication.

[P20] The effective date provision §414.8(e)(4) (coding changes effective ~3 months after final decision) should include an exception for urgent patient-safety-related changes to take effect sooner (e.g., 30 days).

[P21] §414.9(a) requires timely/complete submissions to be considered — applicants request CMS publish a detailed completeness checklist and a pre-submission intake review option to reduce administrative declines.

[P22] Per §414.9(a) that CMS must decline incomplete/untimely applications, industry seeks clarification whether CMS will provide cure periods for minor administrative deficiencies (beyond the biosimilar 10-business-day rule).

[P23] §414.9(a) permits resubmission in a subsequent cycle — stakeholders request guaranteed feedback explaining why declined to support better resubmissions.

[P24] Under §414.9(a)(2)(i) requiring all specified information and administrative elements, commenters request CMS publish standardized templates for common documents (e.g., device descriptions, clinical evidence summaries).

[P25] §414.9(a)(2)(ii) requires FDA classification/marketing authorization documentation — device manufacturers ask for explicit guidance on acceptable alternative documentation for products with foreign approvals or FDA-exempt status.

[P26] For §414.9(a)(2)(iii), requiring evidence of U.S. market availability for non-drug items without marketing authorization, small manufacturers request a narrower definition of “available in the U.S. market” (e.g., distributor agreements or commercial sale) to avoid unfair exclusion.

[P27] The 10-business-day extension for biosimilars in §414.9(a)(3) is helpful, but commenters ask CMS to extend the policy to novel biologics that receive last-minute approvals and to allow an alternative electronic notice to trigger the extension.

[P28] §414.9(a)(3)(i) conditions the biosimilar extension on marketing authorization dated within the extension period — manufacturers request CMS accept date of FDA approval notice, not only the authorization letter date, to avoid technical denials.

[P29] Under §414.9(a)(3)(ii) requiring complete application by extension end, commenters request CMS provide interim acceptance confirmation to avoid uncertainty about whether the resubmitted package is considered complete.

[P30] §414.9(b)(1) allows up to two resubmissions — industry groups suggest increasing to at least three reevaluation resubmissions for complex products and request clarity whether each resubmission must wait a full cycle.

[P31] The requirement in §414.9(b)(1) that resubmissions be timely and complete should allow applicants to request expedited consideration of resubmissions that present new safety/efficacy information.

[P32] §414.9(b)(1)(i) obligates applicants to describe prior submissions — commenters urge CMS to provide a standardized form for this description to streamline reviewer evaluation.

[P33] §414.9(b)(1)(ii) requires copies of prior final decisions — legal commenters ask CMS to clarify whether redacted or annotated prior decisions are acceptable, and whether CMS will provide machine-readable copies.

[P34] §414.9(b)(1)(iii) requires applicants to explain disagreement with prior decisions — opponents caution that this could encourage adversarial submissions and request CMS provide examples of acceptable explanation formats and lengths.

[P35] §414.9(b)(2) mandates new significant information for second resubmissions — stakeholders ask CMS to define “significant new information” and provide examples (e.g., new RCT data vs. minor labeling changes).

[P36] The requirement in §414.9(b)(2)(i) that the new information “directly relates” to prior reasons could be interpreted narrowly; applicants request CMS allow novel evidence that reasonably addresses the decision rationale even if indirect.

[P37] §414.9(b)(2)(ii) asks applicants to explain how new information addresses prior reasons — commenters recommend CMS require a crosswalk table mapping old reasons to new evidence for transparency.

[P38] §414.9(b)(3) requires CMS to include resubmitted applications on a public meeting agenda — manufacturers ask for timeline guarantees (e.g., included in the next two scheduled meetings) to prevent indefinite deferral.

[P39] The prohibition in §414.9(b)(3)(i) barring resubmitted drug/biologic applications from being included in a public meeting or receiving a final decision in the same quarterly cycle they are submitted may cause delays — industry requests an exception for resubmissions that provide only administrative corrections.

[P40] Under §414.9(b)(3)(ii) permitting delay as described in §414.8(e)(3), commenters ask CMS to limit cumulative delays for resubmissions to one subsequent cycle unless extraordinary circumstances exist.

[P41] §414.10(b) permits adding, revising, discontinuing codes — stakeholders request clarity on required supporting documentation for revisions vs. new code requests to reduce inconsistent adjudications.

[P42] For §414.10(c), which lists evaluation sources including contractor evaluations and “any additional research,” commenters request that CMS disclose the identities and methodologies of third-party contractors and make underlying analyses available for public review.

[P43] Under §414.10(d)(1) CMS must determine whether factors are met before further evaluation — commenters ask CMS to publish rubrics or scoring criteria showing how it weighs each factor.

[P44] §414.10(d)(1)(i) requires non-appropriateness for other HIPAA code sets — clinical specialty societies request a formal process to arbitrate disputes where CPT vs. HCPCS inclusion is contested.

[P45] The “primarily medical in nature” test in §414.10(d)(1)(ii) is vague — commenters request objective criteria and examples to distinguish medical vs. non-medical products (e.g., wellness devices).

[P46] §414.10(d)(1)(iii) on FDA marketing authorization — device manufacturers ask CMS to explain how it treats products with conditional approvals, Limited Population Pathway, or EU approvals pending FDA approval.

[P47] For §414.10(d)(1)(iv) requiring a Medicare claims processing need, payers and providers request a clear definition and examples of what constitutes such a need (e.g., disparate billing practices, payment ambiguity).

[P48] §414.10(d)(2) requires evaluation even if some factors unmet when there is a claims processing need — stakeholders request CMS to define the evidentiary threshold (e.g., number of claims, provider complaints) to trigger evaluation under d(2).

[P49] The prohibition in §414.10(d)(3) against further evaluation when neither set of conditions is met may be too rigid; commenters request an appeal mechanism for applicants when CMS declines further evaluation under d(3).

[P50] §414.10(d)(4) requires determination of different clinical function or significant therapeutic distinction — manufacturers urge CMS to publish detailed case studies illustrating what meets these thresholds.

[P51] For §414.10(d)(4)(i) evaluating different clinical function, clinicians request CMS accept functional outcome measures and clinical practice guidelines as evidence, not only mechanism-of-action arguments.

[P52] §414.10(d)(4)(ii) on therapeutic distinction should clarify the required magnitude of benefit (e.g., effect size thresholds or absolute risk reductions) for items to qualify, to reduce subjectivity.

[P53] Under §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(1), using treatment for unresponsive/ineligible populations as evidence is appropriate, but CMS should require robust subgroup analyses to avoid overgeneralization from small cohorts.

[P54] §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(2) treating improved diagnostic ability as evidence if it affects management — diagnostics groups request CMS define what constitutes a meaningful change in management (e.g., change in treatment in X% of cases).

[P55] For §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(3)(i)’s reduction in significant adverse events, commenters ask CMS to require statistically significant and clinically meaningful reductions, and specify acceptable endpoints (mortality, major morbidity).

[P56] §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(3)(ii) on decreased subsequent interventions should require data on both short- and long-term follow-up to ensure reduced downstream care is durable.

[P57] The criterion in §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(3)(iii) on reductions in hospitalizations/visits should require quantitative thresholds (e.g., X% reduction) or comparative data against standard care.

[P58] §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(3)(iv) considering faster resolution or reduced length of stay should require demonstration of meaningful time savings that translate to cost or outcome improvements.

[P59] For §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(3)(v) improvements in activities of daily living, CMS should accept validated instruments (e.g., Barthel Index) and define minimally important differences.

[P60] §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(3)(vi) on improved quality of life needs acceptance of validated patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) and standards for clinically meaningful change.

[P61] §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(3)(vii) medication adherence as evidence should require objective measures (e.g., pharmacy refill data) and linkage to improved clinical outcomes.

[P62] §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(4) allowing consideration of the totality of information is appropriate, but CMS should provide guidance on how to weigh real-world evidence vs. randomized trial data.

[P63] §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(B) permitting consideration of subpopulation improvements is reasonable; patient groups ask CMS to require pre-specified subgroup hypotheses and not rely on post-hoc analyses alone.

[P64] §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(C) requiring determination without regard to disease prevalence is welcome for rare disease products, but CMS should provide examples to show how small-population benefits will be assessed.

[P65] §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(D) giving substantial weight to FDA Breakthrough Device designation is appropriate — request CMS explain how it will treat other expedited FDA pathways (e.g., PRIME, accelerated approval) comparably.

[P66] Under §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(E), applicants must provide sufficient information for therapeutic distinction — CMS should publish a required evidence checklist to reduce inconsistent submissions and rejections.

[P67] §414.10(d)(5)(i) mandates creation of a new HCPCS code if factors met and claims processing need exists — suppliers request CMS also consider transitional codes or temporary Q-codes when immediate unique identification is needed pending full code establishment.

[P68] The prohibition in §414.10(d)(5)(ii) against creating a new code when conditions not met should include a process by which applicants can request reconsideration or provide additional data rather than a final denial.

[P69] §414.10(d)(6) requires revising descriptors for minor distinctions — commenters ask CMS to publish proposed descriptor revisions for public comment before finalizing to avoid unintended billing impacts.

[P70] For §414.10(e)(1) evaluating drug/biologic requests, manufacturers request CMS clarify how it will handle combination products and products with multiple indications in assessing (i)-(iv).

[P71] §414.10(e)(2) requires considering statutory/regulatory payment rules — commenters request CMS publish how payment policy interacts with code decisions (e.g., J-code assignment effects on ASP+6% vs. other payment methodologies).

[P72] Under §414.10(e)(3) determining Part B payability and sourcing/classification under section 1847A, pharma companies ask for detailed examples showing classification outcomes and implications for billing and reimbursement.

[P73] §414.10(e)(4) requires CMS to decide add/revise/no action — stakeholders request timelines for each stage and the opportunity for applicants to withdraw or amend requests without penalty.

[P74] §414.10(e)(5) permits descriptors with drug amounts for smaller quantities to improve billing accuracy — payers request standardized unit descriptors (e.g., mg per code) and caps to prevent proliferation of too many granular codes that complicate claims processing.

[P75] §414.10(f) obligates CMS to revise descriptors where applicant revisions are better — applicants ask for an appeals process if CMS declines their proposed descriptor revision.

[P76] Under §414.10(g) discontinuing duplicative/obsolete codes is appropriate — stakeholders request CMS provide transition guidance, effective dates, and grandfathering provisions for legacy contracts and billing systems.

[P77] §414.10(h) requires CMS to state coding actions in final decisions — commenters ask that CMS include the full rationale, evidence considered, and any dissenting views to improve transparency.

[P78] §414.114(b)(1) requires benefit-category screening at cycle start — manufacturers request CMS allow applicants to request an early categorical review prior to full submission to avoid wasted application effort.

[P79] Under §414.114(b)(2) requiring preliminary payment determination if items fall into listed categories, commenters request CMS publish the methodology and rates used for preliminary determinations to allow meaningful public comment.

[P80] §414.114(b)(3) requires posting preliminary benefit and payment determinations about two weeks before the meeting — two weeks is insufficient for stakeholders to analyze complex payment proposals; request 30–45 days minimum.

[P81] §414.114(b)(4) mandates final determinations via program instructions after public consultation — stakeholders request that CMS publish proposed program instruction language for public comment before finalization.

[P82] §414.210(g)(1)(v) sets rural area fee schedules pre-April 1, 2021 to 110% of national average — states and rural providers request CMS assess impact analyses, as 110% may undercompensate high-cost rural providers; request an option to use local cost indices.

[P83] For §414.210(g)(2)(i) setting fee schedule amounts for non-contiguous areas as the greater of CBA averages or 110% national average for 2016–2020, commenters request CMS provide the underlying data and methodology used to compute those averages.

[P84] §414.210(g)(2)(i)(A) requires considering average single payment amounts for CBAs outside contiguous US — commenters urge CMS to ensure these CBAs have sufficient claim volumes to be statistically valid and to disclose sample sizes.

[P85] Under §414.210(g)(2)(i)(B) considering 110% of national average as the other candidate value, territories request CMS evaluate whether 110% adequately reflects higher operational/logistical costs and consider higher multipliers where justified.

[P86] §414.210(g)(2)(ii) prescribing a weighted sum for post-April 1, 2021 payments outside contiguous US is complex — comment that CMS must publish worked examples and a calculator to help providers understand payments.

[P87] The 50% of the greater of CBA average or 110% national average component in §414.210(g)(2)(ii)(A) could produce abrupt payment shifts; request CMS phase in changes over multiple years or allow provider appeals for severe adverse impacts.

[P88] §414.210(g)(2)(ii)(B) requires using 2015 area fee schedule amounts grown by update factors — commenters argue the 2015 baseline may be outdated and unfair to areas with structural cost changes; request CMS consider a more recent baseline or regional cost adjustments.

[P89] For §414.210(g)(2)(iii) applying a weighted sum for rural contiguous areas, rural hospitals and suppliers request CMS model impacts and allow alternative methodologies where 110% national average understates local costs.

[P90] The 50% of 110% national average component in §414.210(g)(2)(iii)(A) should allow for exceptions where national average calculations are skewed by outliers; request CMS include trimming or median-based measures.

[P91] §414.210(g)(2)(iii)(B) relying on 2015 area fee schedule amounts grown by statutory updates risks perpetuating past inequities; commenters request CMS allow for cost-of-living or wage adjustments in addition to statutory updates.

[P92] §414.210(g)(9)(vi) equalizing area fee schedules to adjusted payment amounts for services furnished on/after April 1, 2021 may create retroactive payment changes — providers request transitional protections and clear notice to avoid clawbacks.

[P93] §414.240(b)(1) benefit-category screening at cycle start — manufacturers of items that straddle DME and prosthetic categories request clearer criteria and examples to predict category outcomes.

[P94] Under §414.240(b)(2), preliminary payment determinations for items preliminarily found in listed categories should be accompanied by rationale and the data sources used so stakeholders can respond effectively at the public meeting.

[P95] §414.240(b)(3) posting preliminary determinations two weeks prior to meetings is insufficient; commenters request a minimum 30-day posting period with full supporting analyses and data.

[P96] §414.240(b)(4) requiring final determinations via program instructions after public consultation — encourage CMS to publish draft program instructions and allow a formal comment period before finalization to ensure stakeholder input is meaningful.

Under §414.9(a)(2)(i) requiring all specified information and administrative elements, commenters request CMS publish standardized templates for common documents (e.g., device descriptions, clinical evidence summaries).

§414.9(a)(2)(ii) requires FDA classification/marketing authorization documentation — device manufacturers ask for explicit guidance on acceptable alternative documentation for products with foreign approvals or FDA-exempt status.

For §414.9(a)(2)(iii), requiring evidence of U.S. market availability for non-drug items without marketing authorization, small manufacturers request a narrower definition of “available in the U.S. market” (e.g., distributor agreements or commercial sale) to avoid unfair exclusion.

The 10-business-day extension for biosimilars in §414.9(a)(3) is helpful, but commenters ask CMS to extend the policy to novel biologics that receive last-minute approvals and to allow an alternative electronic notice to trigger the extension.

§414.9(a)(3)(i) conditions the biosimilar extension on marketing authorization dated within the extension period — manufacturers request CMS accept date of FDA approval notice, not only the authorization letter date, to avoid technical denials.

Under §414.9(a)(3)(ii) requiring complete application by extension end, commenters request CMS provide interim acceptance confirmation to avoid uncertainty about whether the resubmitted package is considered complete.

§414.9(b)(1) allows up to two resubmissions — industry groups suggest increasing to at least three reevaluation resubmissions for complex products and request clarity whether each resubmission must wait a full cycle.
The requirement in §414.9(b)(1) that resubmissions be timely and complete should allow applicants to request expedited consideration of resubmissions that present new safety/efficacy information.
§414.9(b)(1)(i) obligates applicants to describe prior submissions — commenters urge CMS to provide a standardized form for this description to streamline reviewer evaluation.

§414.9(b)(1)(ii) requires copies of prior final decisions — legal commenters ask CMS to clarify whether redacted or annotated prior decisions are acceptable, and whether CMS will provide machine-readable copies.

§414.9(b)(1)(iii) requires applicants to explain disagreement with prior decisions — opponents caution that this could encourage adversarial submissions and request CMS provide examples of acceptable explanation formats and lengths.

§414.9(b)(2) mandates new significant information for second resubmissions — stakeholders ask CMS to define “significant new information” and provide examples (e.g., new RCT data vs. minor labeling changes).

The requirement in §414.9(b)(2)(i) that the new information “directly relates” to prior reasons could be interpreted narrowly; applicants request CMS allow novel evidence that reasonably addresses the decision rationale even if indirect.
§414.9(b)(2)(ii) asks applicants to explain how new information addresses prior reasons — commenters recommend CMS require a crosswalk table mapping old reasons to new evidence for transparency.

§414.9(b)(3) requires CMS to include resubmitted applications on a public meeting agenda — manufacturers ask for timeline guarantees (e.g., included in the next two scheduled meetings) to prevent indefinite deferral.

The prohibition in §414.9(b)(3)(i) barring resubmitted drug/biologic applications from being included in a public meeting or receiving a final decision in the same quarterly cycle they are submitted may cause delays — industry requests an exception for resubmissions that provide only administrative corrections.
Under §414.9(b)(3)(ii) permitting delay as described in §414.8(e)(3), commenters ask CMS to limit cumulative delays for resubmissions to one subsequent cycle unless extraordinary circumstances exist.
§414.10(b) permits adding, revising, discontinuing codes — stakeholders request clarity on required supporting documentation for revisions vs. new code requests to reduce inconsistent adjudications.

For §414.10(c), which lists evaluation sources including contractor evaluations and “any additional research,” commenters request that CMS disclose the identities and methodologies of third-party contractors and make underlying analyses available for public review.
Under §414.10(d)(1) CMS must determine whether factors are met before further evaluation — commenters ask CMS to publish rubrics or scoring criteria showing how it weighs each factor.
§414.10(d)(1)(i) requires non-appropriateness for other HIPAA code sets — clinical specialty societies request a formal process to arbitrate disputes where CPT vs. HCPCS inclusion is contested.
The “primarily medical in nature” test in §414.10(d)(1)(ii) is vague — commenters request objective criteria and examples to distinguish medical vs. non-medical products (e.g., wellness devices).

§414.10(d)(1)(iii) on FDA marketing authorization — device manufacturers ask CMS to explain how it treats products with conditional approvals, Limited Population Pathway, or EU approvals pending FDA approval.

For §414.10(d)(1)(iv) requiring a Medicare claims processing need, payers and providers request a clear definition and examples of what constitutes such a need (e.g., disparate billing practices, payment ambiguity).

§414.10(d)(2) requires evaluation even if some factors unmet when there is a claims processing need — stakeholders request CMS to define the evidentiary threshold (e.g., number of claims, provider complaints) to trigger evaluation under d(2).

The prohibition in §414.10(d)(3) against further evaluation when neither set of conditions is met may be too rigid; commenters request an appeal mechanism for applicants when CMS declines further evaluation under d(3).

§414.10(d)(4) requires determination of different clinical function or significant therapeutic distinction — manufacturers urge CMS to publish detailed case studies illustrating what meets these thresholds.

For §414.10(d)(4)(i) evaluating different clinical function, clinicians request CMS accept functional outcome measures and clinical practice guidelines as evidence, not only mechanism-of-action arguments.
§414.10(d)(4)(ii) on therapeutic distinction should clarify the required magnitude of benefit (e.g., effect size thresholds or absolute risk reductions) for items to qualify, to reduce subjectivity.

Under §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(1), using treatment for unresponsive/ineligible populations as evidence is appropriate, but CMS should require robust subgroup analyses to avoid overgeneralization from small cohorts.

§414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(2) treating improved diagnostic ability as evidence if it affects management — diagnostics groups request CMS define what constitutes a meaningful change in management (e.g., change in treatment in X% of cases).

For §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(3)(i)’s reduction in significant adverse events, commenters ask CMS to require statistically significant and clinically meaningful reductions, and specify acceptable endpoints (mortality, major morbidity).
§414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(3)(ii) on decreased subsequent interventions should require data on both short- and long-term follow-up to ensure reduced downstream care is durable.
The criterion in §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(3)(iii) on reductions in hospitalizations/visits should require quantitative thresholds (e.g., X% reduction) or comparative data against standard care.
§414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(3)(iv) considering faster resolution or reduced length of stay should require demonstration of meaningful time savings that translate to cost or outcome improvements.
For §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(3)(v) improvements in activities of daily living, CMS should accept validated instruments (e.g., Barthel Index) and define minimally important differences.
§414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(3)(vi) on improved quality of life needs acceptance of validated patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) and standards for clinically meaningful change.
§414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(3)(vii) medication adherence as evidence should require objective measures (e.g., pharmacy refill data) and linkage to improved clinical outcomes.
§414.10(d)(4)(ii)(A)(4) allowing consideration of the totality of information is appropriate, but CMS should provide guidance on how to weigh real-world evidence vs. randomized trial data.
§414.10(d)(4)(ii)(B) permitting consideration of subpopulation improvements is reasonable; patient groups ask CMS to require pre-specified subgroup hypotheses and not rely on post-hoc analyses alone.

§414.10(d)(4)(ii)(C) requiring determination without regard to disease prevalence is welcome for rare disease products, but CMS should provide examples to show how small-population benefits will be assessed.

§414.10(d)(4)(ii)(D) giving substantial weight to FDA Breakthrough Device designation is appropriate — request CMS explain how it will treat other expedited FDA pathways (e.g., PRIME, accelerated approval) comparably.

Under §414.10(d)(4)(ii)(E), applicants must provide sufficient information for therapeutic distinction — CMS should publish a required evidence checklist to reduce inconsistent submissions and rejections.

§414.10(d)(5)(i) mandates creation of a new HCPCS code if factors met and claims processing need exists — suppliers request CMS also consider transitional codes or temporary Q-codes when immediate unique identification is needed pending full code establishment.

The prohibition in §414.10(d)(5)(ii) against creating a new code when conditions not met should include a process by which applicants can request reconsideration or provide additional data rather than a final denial.

§414.10(d)(6) requires revising descriptors for minor distinctions — commenters ask CMS to publish proposed descriptor revisions for public comment before finalizing to avoid unintended billing impacts.
For §414.10(e)(1) evaluating drug/biologic requests, manufacturers request CMS clarify how it will handle combination products and products with multiple indications in assessing (i)-(iv).

§414.10(e)(2) requires considering statutory/regulatory payment rules — commenters request CMS publish how payment policy interacts with code decisions (e.g., J-code assignment effects on ASP+6% vs. other payment methodologies).

Under §414.10(e)(3) determining Part B payability and sourcing/classification under section 1847A, pharma companies ask for detailed examples showing classification outcomes and implications for billing and reimbursement.
§414.10(e)(4) requires CMS to decide add/revise/no action — stakeholders request timelines for each stage and the opportunity for applicants to withdraw or amend requests without penalty.

§414.10(e)(5) permits descriptors with drug amounts for smaller quantities to improve billing accuracy — payers request standardized unit descriptors (e.g., mg per code) and caps to prevent proliferation of too many granular codes that complicate claims processing.
§414.10(f) obligates CMS to revise descriptors where applicant revisions are better — applicants ask for an appeals process if CMS declines their proposed descriptor revision.

Under §414.10(g) discontinuing duplicative/obsolete codes is appropriate — stakeholders request CMS provide transition guidance, effective dates, and grandfathering provisions for legacy contracts and billing systems.
§414.10(h) requires CMS to state coding actions in final decisions — commenters ask that CMS include the full rationale, evidence considered, and any dissenting views to improve transparency.

§414.114(b)(1) requires benefit-category screening at cycle start — manufacturers request CMS allow applicants to request an early categorical review prior to full submission to avoid wasted application effort.

Under §414.114(b)(2) requiring preliminary payment determination if items fall into listed categories, commenters request CMS publish the methodology and rates used for preliminary determinations to allow meaningful public comment.

§414.114(b)(3) requires posting preliminary benefit and payment determinations about two weeks before the meeting — two weeks is insufficient for stakeholders to analyze complex payment proposals; request 30–45 days minimum.

§414.114(b)(4) mandates final determinations via program instructions after public consultation — stakeholders request that CMS publish proposed program instruction language for public comment before finalization.

§414.210(g)(1)(v) sets rural area fee schedules pre-April 1, 2021 to 110% of national average — states and rural providers request CMS assess impact analyses, as 110% may undercompensate high-cost rural providers; request an option to use local cost indices.

For §414.210(g)(2)(i) setting fee schedule amounts for non-contiguous areas as the greater of CBA averages or 110% national average for 2016–2020, commenters request CMS provide the underlying data and methodology used to compute those averages.

§414.210(g)(2)(i)(A) requires considering average single payment amounts for CBAs outside contiguous US — commenters urge CMS to ensure these CBAs have sufficient claim volumes to be statistically valid and to disclose sample sizes.

Under §414.210(g)(2)(i)(B) considering 110% of national average as the other candidate value, territories request CMS evaluate whether 110% adequately reflects higher operational/logistical costs and consider higher multipliers where justified.

§414.210(g)(2)(ii) prescribing a weighted sum for post-April 1, 2021 payments outside contiguous US is complex — comment that CMS must publish worked examples and a calculator to help providers understand payments.

The 50% of the greater of CBA average or 110% national average component in §414.210(g)(2)(ii)(A) could produce abrupt payment shifts; request CMS phase in changes over multiple years or allow provider appeals for severe adverse impacts.

§414.210(g)(2)(ii)(B) requires using 2015 area fee schedule amounts grown by update factors — commenters argue the 2015 baseline may be outdated and unfair to areas with structural cost changes; request CMS consider a more recent baseline or regional cost adjustments.

For §414.210(g)(2)(iii) applying a weighted sum for rural contiguous areas, rural hospitals and suppliers request CMS model impacts and allow alternative methodologies where 110% national average understates local costs.

The 50% of 110% national average component in §414.210(g)(2)(iii)(A) should allow for exceptions where national average calculations are skewed by outliers; request CMS include trimming or median-based measures.

§414.210(g)(2)(iii)(B) relying on 2015 area fee schedule amounts grown by statutory updates risks perpetuating past inequities; commenters request CMS allow for cost-of-living or wage adjustments in addition to statutory updates.

§414.210(g)(9)(vi) equalizing area fee schedules to adjusted payment amounts for services furnished on/after April 1, 2021 may create retroactive payment changes — providers request transitional protections and clear notice to avoid clawbacks.
§414.240(b)(1) benefit-category screening at cycle start — manufacturers of items that straddle DME and prosthetic categories request clearer criteria and examples to predict category outcomes.

Under §414.240(b)(2), preliminary payment determinations for items preliminarily found in listed categories should be accompanied by rationale and the data sources used so stakeholders can respond effectively at the public meeting.
§414.240(b)(3) posting preliminary determinations two weeks prior to meetings is insufficient; commenters request a minimum 30-day posting period with full supporting analyses and data.

§414.240(b)(4) requiring final determinations via program instructions after public consultation — encourage CMS to publish draft program instructions and allow a formal comment period before finalization to ensure stakeholder input is meaningful.

[P1] The September 9, 2019 comments due date is already past; the FAA must extend or reopen the comment period to allow meaningful stakeholder input on this AD.

[P1] Requiring FAA to receive comments by a fixed past date creates legal ambiguity; the rule should specify receipt or postmark dates and permit electronic submissions to ensure comments are accepted.

[P2] The applicability to all Boeing 757–200, –200PF, –200CB, and –300 series airplanes is overly broad; operators of specific ferry, cargo-converted, or special missions variants should be able to demonstrate non-applicability where systems/structures differ.

[P2] Certificated-in-any-category language could unintentionally capture museum, private, or restricted-category 757s that no longer operate in typical commercial service; the FAA should clarify or exempt non-operational or non-revenue aircraft.

[P3] The compliance obligation lacks specificity about what constitutes satisfactory completion; the AD should define acceptable evidence/documentation and recordkeeping standards to demonstrate compliance.

[P3] The AD should allow a defined grace period for operators waiting for parts, tooling, or training — a strict "must comply within specified times" without relief may cause operational disruptions.

[P4] The retained requirement to revise Section 9 within 36 months of June 30, 2006 is moot and confusing for a new AD; the FAA must reconcile legacy compliance dates with the current AD effective date.

[P4] Requiring incorporation of Subsection B of Boeing Document D622N001–9 without providing the document in the docket limits stakeholders' ability to assess burden; FAA should include the referenced document or fully describe the required revisions.

[P5] The 18-month deadline to revise maintenance/inspection programs to incorporate AWLs and CMRs is burdensome for small operators and foreign registry operators; FAA should provide phased compliance or extensions for operators with constrained resources.

[P5] The AD mandates incorporation of Boeing MPD Revision October 2018; operators and A&Ps need clarity whether later Boeing revisions or errata are acceptable without separate AMOC approvals.

[P6] Tying initial compliance timing to the MPD document or 18 months (whichever is later) could allow indefinite delays if MPD specifies a distant date; the AD should cap the MPD-specified dates to avoid excessive deferral.

[P6] The AD does not state whether MPD-specified times measured in flight cycles or flight hours are acceptable across jurisdictions; FAA should explicitly authorize operators to use their accepted timekeeping metrics.

[P7] Requiring unchanged tasks be done at MPD Revision October 2018 times may conflict with current operator-approved programs; FAA should permit retaining previously approved intervals where equivalency can be demonstrated.

[P7] The rule lacks guidance on how to handle previously extended intervals approved under other ADs or programs; will those approvals be invalidated by this AD's fixed MPD times?

[P8] The prohibition on alternative actions/intervals/CDCCLs after paragraph (g) is too restrictive and may prevent proven, safety-equivalent methods; FAA should allow alternatives subject to engineering substantiation and approval on a routine basis.

[P8] Requiring AMOC approval for any alternative creates a bottleneck at the Los Angeles ACO and prolongs operational impacts; FAA should delegate AMOC authority to principal inspectors or regional offices for routine equivalency cases.

[P9] The absolute ban on alternatives after paragraph (h) risks grounding aircraft that cannot meet the new tasks temporarily; FAA should include temporary relief provisions (e.g., limited extensions) for operators in hardship.

[P9] The prohibition may conflict with non-U.S. civil aviation authority approvals where national authorities have accepted different intervals; FAA should clarify harmonization with EASA/other CAAs to avoid duplicate approvals.

[P10] Terminating paragraph (g) upon accomplishment of paragraph (h) creates a confusing sequencing requirement; FAA should explicitly state whether operators may directly comply with (h) without first performing (g).

[P10] Operators who already complied with (g) years ago need clear documentation whether (h) requires rework or if (g) remains acceptable; the AD should add language on credit and record retention.

[P11] Concentrating AMOC approval authority in the Manager, Los Angeles ACO Branch, is inappropriate for a rule affecting operators worldwide; FAA should allow geographically appropriate certification office managers to approve AMOCs.

[P11] Legal experts will question whether delegating all AMOC authority to a single office is consistent with FAA policy and 14 CFR 39.19; the AD should cite the specific delegation authority and provide process transparency.

[P12] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO may conflict with operator organizational structures; FAA should permit submission through an operator's accountable manager or designated engineering representative.

[P12] The rule does not specify acceptable formats or timelines for AMOC responses from principal inspectors/FSDOs; stakeholders need assurance of predictable processing times.

[P13] Direct submissions to the certification office manager must include a named point of contact in paragraph (m)(1); without that name, this instruction is vague and could delay processing.

[P13] The AD should permit electronic upload to the FAA's established AMOC portal in addition to the named manager address to ensure timely receipt and tracking.

[P14] Emailing AMOC information to 9-ANM-LAACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov may create security/privacy issues for proprietary engineering data; FAA should provide secure file-transfer options and confirm receipt procedures.

[P14] The AD should clarify acceptable file formats and maximum attachment sizes for emailed AMOC requests to prevent rejections and processing delays.

[P15] Requiring notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC could create immediate operational hurdles when the inspector is unavailable; FAA should allow notification within a specified short timeframe (e.g., 48 hours) after using the AMOC.

[P15] The AD should clarify whether electronic notification (email) satisfies the notification requirement and whether confirmation from the inspector is required before implementation.

[P16] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs is reasonable, but the AD must require that Boeing document the authorization limited to the scope of the AD and provide copies of approvals to the operator and FAA for transparency.

[P16] Reliance on Boeing ODA approvals raises conflict-of-interest concerns; operators and third-party repair stations need assurance of impartial review and should be permitted to seek independent FAA review.

[P17] Requiring AMOC approvals to meet the airplane's certification basis may be difficult for older 757s with multiple supplemental type certificates; the FAA should provide a process for reconciling STCs in AMOC evaluations.

[P17] The requirement that approvals specifically reference this AD is fine, but FAA should publish a template for such references to avoid administrative rejections.

[P18] Automatically adopting AMOCs previously approved for AD 2001–20–12 and AD 2006–11–11 may inadvertently validate AMOCs that are no longer appropriate under the updated MPD Revision October 2018; FAA should review and reissue confirmations before automatic adoption.

[P18] Stakeholders need a list of the previously approved AMOCs that are being carried forward so operators can determine applicability; the AD should reference or include that list in the docket.
