[P1] The requirement that the certifying physician or allowed practitioner must "periodically review" the individualized plan of care is vague—stakeholders request a specified minimum review interval (e.g., every 30 days or every 60 days) to ensure regulatory clarity and consistent enforcement.

[P1] Home health agencies (HHAs) and clinicians will incur significant administrative burden from an undefined "periodic" review requirement; request that CMS include an exception for low-risk patients with stable conditions to allow annual reviews.

[P2] The obligation that the HHA "must be acting upon a plan of care that meets the requirements of this section for HHA services to be covered" should clarify whether retrospective coverage will be allowed when documentation deficiencies are corrected within a specified cure period.

[P2] Industry commenters request explicit guidance on what constitutes sufficient evidence that an HHA is "acting upon" the plan of care (e.g., visit notes linking to plan goals) to avoid inconsistent denials.

[P3] The cross-reference that the plan must "include the specified elements listed in subparagraphs (A)–(C)" should list those elements in full in the regulation text rather than relying on subparagraph references to reduce confusion.

[P4] Requiring identification of responsible disciplines and frequency/duration of all visits as well as items from § 484.60(a) duplicates existing requirements for home health aide plans and may create conflicting documentation obligations between HHA and hospice programs; request harmonization or explicit statement of precedence.

[P4] The inclusion of "frequency and duration of all visits" in the plan of care could force overly specific scheduling in cases where clinical flexibility is needed; request allowance for ranges or "as needed" with clinical justification.

[P5] The restriction that remote patient monitoring/telehealth services "may not substitute for ordered home visits" will hinder use of telehealth to safely reduce in-person visits during public health emergencies; request an emergency waiver mechanism.

[P6] Tying telecommunications services to "patient-specific needs identified in the comprehensive assessment" is appropriate, but CMS should clarify whether nurses conducting tele-visits may perform parts of the comprehensive assessment remotely and how to document that.

[P7] The prohibition on using remote/telecommunications services in place of an ordered home visit is unclear when the plan of care is changed contemporaneously (e.g., clinician orders a tele-visit instead of an in-person visit); request guidance on how plan amendments should be handled and documented.

[P8] Stating that remote/telecommunications services "cannot be considered a home visit for eligibility or payment" will disincentivize innovation and could create reimbursement gaps for medically appropriate remote care; request CMS to create a separate billing mechanism or rate for clinically equivalent tele-services.

[P9] The obligation to include "a description of how the technology use will help achieve the goals" is duplicative of care plan rationale and will increase documentation time; request a standardized template and examples to reduce burden.

[P10] Requiring that "all care provided must be in accordance with the plan of care" may not account for urgent, unanticipated clinical needs encountered during visits; request a provision allowing deviations in emergencies with post-hoc documentation and timely plan modification.

[P11] CMS permission for remote monitoring, TTY, and two-way audio-video is helpful, but the rule should explicitly permit use of commonly used commercial platforms that meet HIPAA/FTC security standards to avoid misinterpretation.

[P12] Limiting costs for equipment, setup, and related services to administrative costs (non-billable) will place financial burden on small HHAs and independent infusion suppliers; request permitting partial billing or a defined per-patient allowance for technology costs.

[P12] Clarify whether "administrative costs" can be recovered through the HHA consolidated cost report or whether suppliers must absorb those costs; request explicit cost-reporting instructions.

[P13] The prohibition on separately billing home visits solely for supplying/connecting/training on technology unless a skilled service is provided will discourage patient education that supports safe use of devices; request that training by a skilled professional (e.g., RN) be billable even if the primary purpose is device setup.

[P13] Define what constitutes a "skilled service" for purposes of allowing separate billing when technology setup/training occurs contemporaneously with a visit.

[P14] Excluding services covered under the home infusion therapy benefit from Medicare home health coverage is appropriate to avoid duplicate payments, but CMS should provide clear crosswalks and examples of services that are now exclusively under the home infusion benefit.

[P15] The permission allowing provision of drugs/biologics not covered under the home infusion definition to remain under Medicare home health should include a non-exhaustive list of examples and explain interaction with payer edits to prevent claim denials.

[P16] Requiring home infusion therapy suppliers to enroll consistent with § 424.68 and part 424 subpart P is reasonable; commenters request transitional enrollment timelines and grandfathering provisions for currently providing suppliers to avoid service disruption.

[P17] The definition of home infusion therapy supplier "must meet the listed requirements"—CMS should provide a compliance checklist and timeline for meeting newly articulated accreditation and enrollment criteria.

[P18] The requirement that suppliers "furnish infusion therapy to individuals with acute or chronic conditions requiring home infusion drugs" lacks specificity about minimum case volume or service mix; ask CMS to clarify whether isolated dispensing without administration meets the criterion.

[P19] Requiring 24/7 availability for safe and effective provision is burdensome for small suppliers; request clarification on the required response times, documentation of on-call coverage, and allowance for contracted after-hours arrangements.

[P20] The accreditation requirement by a Secretary-designated organization raises concerns about limited accreditor capacity and costs; request list of recognized accreditors, timelines for designation, and temporary alternative compliance pathways.

[P21] The dual requirement to be enrolled consistent with § 424.68 and part 424 subpart P may create circular dependencies; request CMS clarify sequencing and whether enrollment under other supplier types satisfies any portion during the transition.

[P22] Suppliers argue that the qualification-to-pay linkage is appropriate, but request CMS confirm whether existing Medicare suppliers who already bill infusion codes will be automatically transitioned or must re-enroll under a new supplier type.

[P24] The obligation to fully complete and submit Form CMS-855B to enroll is standard; request CMS permit electronic submission and allow temporary provisional enrollment while accreditation verification is completed.

[P25] Certifying on Form CMS-855B that the supplier "meets and will continue to meet" standards exposes organizations to aggressive revocation for inadvertent lapse; request a cure period for inadvertent noncompliance before enforcement.

[P26] Compliance with application fee requirements in § 424.514 could be cost-prohibitive for small suppliers; request fee waivers or reduced fees for rural and community-based suppliers.

[P27] The requirement to be currently and validly accredited by a CMS-recognized organization should include grandfathering for suppliers accredited by equivalent national accreditation bodies pending CMS recognition.

[P28] Compliance with § 414.1515 and all provisions of part 486, subpart I imposes hospital pharmacy-level requirements on small home infusion pharmacies; request risk-based application or scaled requirements for small-volume suppliers.

[P29] The limited categorical risk level screening under § 424.518 may not adequately assess clinical risk associated with home infusion suppliers; request CMS to apply full-level screening or require criminal background checks for key clinical staff.

[P30] Granting CMS authority to deny enrollment on listed grounds is expected; request CMS publish commonly used denial reasons and examples to enhance transparency and reduce unnecessary denials.

[P31] If failure to meet enrollment requirements is ground for denial, request CMS to allow provisional enrollment with conditions for suppliers actively seeking accreditation to prevent interruptions in patient access.

[P32] Inclusion of § 424.530 denial reasons as grounds for denial should be accompanied by a cross-reference table mapping each denial reason to typical supplier scenarios to improve clarity.

[P33] Permission to appeal enrollment denials under part 498 is essential; suggest CMS expedite appeals for suppliers whose denial would imminently disrupt patient care.

[P34] The continuing obligations upon and after enrollment are extensive; request a consolidated compliance manual and phased implementation schedule to allow suppliers to comply.

[P35] The continuing accreditation requirement (remain currently and validly accredited) is reasonable, but request CMS allow use of alternative compliance demonstrations (e.g., successful state surveys) when accreditors have long processing backlogs.

[P36] Requiring ongoing compliance with multiple cross-referenced provisions (this section, part 424 subpart P, § 414.1515, part 486 subpart I) could create contradictory obligations; request CMS to publish an integrated compliance matrix.

[P41] CMS's authority to revoke enrollment on specified grounds should be limited to material noncompliance; request that minor or technical violations be addressed through corrective action plans rather than immediate revocation.

[P42] Revocation for failure to meet accreditation requirements is reasonable, but CMS must provide a minimum notification period (e.g., 90 days) and an opportunity to remedy before revocation takes effect.

[P43] The broad noncompliance ground encompassing several parts could lead to automatic revocation for unrelated technical failures; request CMS require proximate causation between violation and patient safety risk before revocation.

[P49] Allowing appeal of revocation under part 498 is appropriate; request expedited interim billing rights during the appeal when revocation will disrupt ongoing patient therapy.

[P50] Identification of home infusion suppliers within the screening list (§ 424.518) is appropriate; request clarity on the specific screening level assigned and whether suppliers previously screened under DME or pharmacy categories will be re-screened.

[P51] Retrospective billing permission for listed entities (§ 424.521(a)) should specify the time limit (e.g., 12 months) and whether state licensure delays qualify as extenuating circumstances.

[P52] Duplicate listing of the plan of care establishment obligation across the document is confusing; recommend consolidation to a single clear regulatory statement.

[P55] Cross-referencing § 484.60(a) items that establish need may import requirements from the home health aide rule that are not applicable to all disciplines; request CMS to specify which § 484.60(a) items are relevant to skilled nursing and therapy services.

[P56] Requiring telecommunication-based services to be tied to needs identified in the comprehensive assessment is clinically appropriate, but CMS should clarify whether periodic reassessment may shift tele-services to in-person services and the documentation required.

[P57] The explicit prohibition that tele-services may not substitute for ordered home visits should permit clinician-directed modification of the plan when clinically appropriate, with contemporaneous documentation.

[P58] Prohibiting tele-services from counting as a home visit for eligibility/payment creates an incentive to prefer in-person visits even when telehealth would be equally effective; stakeholders request CMS to evaluate parity payment for certain tele-services.

[P59] The requirement to describe how technology will help achieve plan goals should be scaled for simple technologies (e.g., TTY) versus complex RPM devices to avoid disproportionate documentation burdens.

[P60] The "all care must be in accordance with the plan of care" obligation should explicitly permit scope-limited deviations (e.g., medication reconciliation changes) that are later reflected in an amended plan.

[P61] Designating technology costs as administrative only will disadvantage rural providers who lack capital; request allowance for capital depreciation or an administrative add-on payment.

[P62] The prohibition on billing separately for visits that only supply or train on technology could reduce patient safety if suppliers cannot bill; request an exception allowing billing when the training involves clinical instruction by a licensed clinician.

[P63] Excluding home infusion therapy benefit services from the home health benefit must include transition rules for patients mid-course whose coverage and provider responsibilities could otherwise be disrupted.

[P64] Clarify examples of "drugs and biologicals not covered under this definition" that remain eligible under home health, to avoid denials for borderline items.

[P65] The cross-reference in § 414.1505(c) tying payment eligibility to enrollment under § 424.68 and part 424 subpart P should include an effective date to allow suppliers to comply without sudden payment ineligibility.

[P66] The furnishing requirement (§ 424.68(a)(1)) could be read to require that the supplier both supply and administer infusions; request clarification that suppliers who coordinate but do not administer may still qualify under defined circumstances.

[P67] The 24/7 service expectation (§ 424.68(a)(2)) should be clarified to specify staffing levels and acceptable subcontracting, and to allow hosted call-center arrangements that ensure clinically appropriate response.

[P68] For the accreditation requirement (§ 424.68(a)(3)), request CMS to define minimum accreditation standards and provide flexibility for state-approved accreditation programs.

[P69] The enrollment consistency requirement (§ 424.68(a)(4)) should clarify whether multi-state suppliers must enroll in each state and how state licensure interacts with Medicare enrollment.

[P70] The payment qualification linkage (§ 424.68(b)) should specify whether existing Medicare billing privileges for current HCPCS infusion codes are sufficient evidence of qualification during a transition window.

[P71] For the enrollment requirements (§ 424.68(c)), request CMS to permit provisional enrollment for suppliers that have submitted applications and are awaiting accreditation verification to avoid patient access gaps.

[P72] The requirement to submit CMS-855B (§ 424.68(c)(1)(i)) should allow updated electronic forms and specify acceptable attachments proving accreditation and licensure.

[P73] Certifying ongoing compliance on CMS-855B (§ 424.68(c)(1)(ii)) must be accompanied by safe harbor language allowing correction of inadvertent noncompliance without automatic fraud referrals.

[P74] The application fee requirement (§ 424.68(c)(2)) could be financially punitive; request sliding-scale fees for rural and nonprofit suppliers.

[P75] Being "currently and validly accredited" (§ 424.68(c)(3)) at time of enrollment poses timing issues; request CMS permit conditional enrollment pending final accreditation within a defined deadline.

[P76] Compliance with § 414.1515 and part 486 subpart I (§ 424.68(c)(4)) may impose pharmacy sterile compounding and sterile handling obligations; request alignment with state pharmacy board standards and phased compliance.

[P77] The limited categorical risk screening (§ 424.68(c)(5)) should require background checks for clinical staff with direct patient contact; limited screening may not address patient safety concerns.

[P78] CMS's authority to deny enrollment (§ 424.68(d)(1)) should be exercised with transparent criteria and pre-decisional notice with opportunity to cure minor deficiencies.

[P80] If any applicable denial reason in § 424.530 applies (§ 424.68(d)(1)(ii)), suppliers request CMS to publish a digest of common § 424.530 scenarios and remedies to reduce inadvertent denial.

[P81] The appeal right under part 498 (§ 424.68(d)(2)) should include an expedited track for decisions that would otherwise terminate ongoing infusion therapy for patients.

[P82] Continuing obligations post-enrollment (§ 424.68(e)(1)) impose substantial compliance costs; request a one-year phase-in for routine reporting requirements and audits.

[P83] The accreditation maintenance requirement (§ 424.68(e)(1)(i)) should permit temporary lapses with documented remediation plans rather than immediate enrollment revocation.

[P84] Maintaining compliance with multiple regulations (§ 424.68(e)(1)(ii)) should be tied to materiality standards; request CMS limit enforcement to conditions that create patient harm.

[P89] CMS authority to revoke enrollment (§ 424.68(e)(2)) should require CMS to consider continuity of care and permit time-limited wind-down periods to transfer patients safely.

[P90] Revocation for failure to meet accreditation (§ 424.68(e)(2)(i)) should include a defined cure period (e.g., 60–90 days) and allow provisional certification where accreditors verify corrective action.

[P91] Revocation for noncompliance with listed provisions (§ 424.68(e)(2)(ii)) must require a showing of harm or imminent risk before immediate revocation; recommend graduated enforcement.

[P96] Applying revocation reasons from § 424.535 (§ 424.68(e)(2)(iii)) may capture administrative errors; request explicit examples of behaviors that would (and would not) lead to revocation.

[P97] The right to appeal revocation (§ 424.68(e)(3)) should include interim billing and service continuation rights to prevent interruption of essential ongoing infusion therapies during appeal.

[P98] The retrospective billing allowance (§ 424.521(a)) should specify the statutory time limit (e.g., within 12 months of service) and whether retroactive State licensure approvals qualify; request clarity to avoid claim denials.

[P99] Correcting the DATES section error is necessary; commenters urge CMS to confirm that the corrected effective and comment periods are publicly posted and to re-open the comment period if the date correction materially affected stakeholders' ability to comment.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement to increase the unadjusted Federal payment rate each year by the SNF market basket index (§413.337(d)(1)(v)) fails to account for regional cost variations and could undercompensate SNFs in high-cost areas; propose regionally adjusted indices or an outlier adjustment.

[P36] The annual automatic market-basket increase (§413.337(d)(1)(v) / §413.337(d)(1)(v) duplicate) may compound inaccuracies if the market basket itself is poorly specified; request transparent publication of the specific market-basket components and methodology used to calculate the percentage change.

[P2] Setting FY2018’s unadjusted Federal payment rate as only a 1% increase (§413.337(d)(1)(vi)) is insufficient given wage and input cost increases in 2017–2018; industry commenters will request increasing the FY2018 update to reflect actual cost growth or explaining the rationale for constraining to 1%.

[P37] The rule’s instruction to apply paragraphs (d)(2) and (d)(3) before the FY2018 1% update (§413.337(d)(1)(vi)) is unclear; request clarification and examples showing the order of application and numeric examples demonstrating how (d)(2)/(d)(3) alter the base prior to the 1% increase.

[P3] The 2.4% increase for FY2019 (§413.337(d)(1)(vii)) appears arbitrary relative to the FY2018 1% cap; request justification, supporting data, and whether FY2019’s figure reflects typographical error versus a policy decision.

[P38] If the FY2019 increase (§413.337(d)(1)(vii)) is applied after reductions or other adjustments, commenters seek a worked example to show interaction with paragraph (d)(2)/(d)(3) and with value-based reductions in §413.337(f).

[P4] The mandate to reduce the adjusted Federal per diem rate beginning Oct 1, 2018 and then apply a performance-based adjustment (§413.337(f)) effectively withholds funds up-front from all SNFs; industry groups will object and request that CMS instead apply only net neutral adjustments so providers are not cash-flow disadvantaged pending performance scoring.

[P39] The sequencing in §413.337(f) — reduce per diem then apply VBP adjustment — needs clarity on whether negative VBP scores can result in further reductions beyond the initial percent; legal commenters will request explicit caps and whether the combined reduction can create payments below cost.

[P5] Requiring that at least 60% of the reduction be redistributed as value-based incentive payments (§413.338(c)(2)(i)) raises concerns that 40% may be retained by CMS for unspecified uses; request a clear accounting of the full reduction, use of any non-redistributed portion, and statutory authority for any funds not returned to providers.

[P40] The obligation to increase the 60% pool "as appropriate" to account for low-volume SNFs (§413.338(c)(2)(i)) is vague; request a concrete methodology, trigger thresholds, and prospective notice to SNFs on how the pool will be adjusted.

[P6] The prohibition on awarding improvement points to SNFs with fewer than 25 eligible baseline stays (§413.338(d)(1)(iv)) will systematically disadvantage small and rural SNFs; comment recommending lowering the threshold (e.g., to 10 stays) or allowing proportional/continuous improvement scoring or statistical shrinkage methods.

[P41] The categorical cut-off of 25 stays (§413.338(d)(1)(iv)) likely violates equity principles and will drive consolidation; ask CMS to model the population of SNFs excluded and quantify financial impacts on rural providers.

[P7] Assigning low-volume SNFs a performance score that yields a VBP payment equal to the rate that would apply absent §413.337(f) (§413.338(d)(3)) appears to guarantee no net penalty for low-volume providers but may also block upside incentives; request clarification whether such SNFs can earn bonuses above neutral and how this interacts with the 60% pool.

[P42] The commitment to make low-volume SNFs whole (§413.338(d)(3)) requires funding sources — request explanation of whether additional funds reduce the pool available to larger SNFs or whether CMS will provide supplemental appropriations.

[P8] Allowing SNFs to request exceptions for months affected by extraordinary circumstances (§413.338(d)(4)(i)) is appropriate, but commenters will request a non-burdensome, expedited process for acute disasters (e.g., hurricanes) and clarity on retroactive payment adjustments.

[P43] CMS’s permission to grant exceptions (§413.338(d)(4)(i)) should include standardized criteria and timelines for decisions; stakeholders request maximum decision times and an appeals process for denied exception requests.

[P9] The dual permission that CMS may grant exceptions (§413.338(d)(4)(i) duplicate) without clear limits may lead to inconsistent treatment; request publication of precedent decisions and guidance on what constitutes “extraordinary circumstances.”

[P10] Requiring submission of exception requests by email to SNFVBPinquiries@cms.hhs.gov within 90 days (§413.338(d)(4)(ii)) may be impractical during disasters when electronic access is disrupted; suggest alternative submission methods (fax, mailed forms, regional MAC phone hotlines) and an extended filing window in declared disaster areas.

[P44] The 90-day filing deadline for extraordinary circumstances (§413.338(d)(4)(ii)) is too short for events that disrupt operations for months; request CMS to permit extensions when SNF facilities lack communications or to allow filing within 90 days after CMS makes communications feasible.

[P11] The timing condition requiring exception requests within 90 days (§413.338(d)(4)(ii) (timing)) is unduly rigid — legal advocates will request an exception for exceptions in declared federal disasters (FEMA) where documentation may only be available later.

[P12] The method condition obligating email submission (§413.338(d)(4)(ii) (method)) raises privacy and security concerns (PHI attachments) and may exceed some SNFs’ IT capacity; request secure upload portals or encrypted email channels and acceptance of paper submissions when necessary.

[P13] Requiring a completed Extraordinary Circumstances Request form and evidence (photos, media) (§413.338(d)(4)(ii) (content)) may be impossible for some events; suggest allowing attestation by facility leadership and accepting alternative forms of evidence (official disaster declarations, local public health notices).

[P14] The prohibition on CMS considering exception requests unless the SNF has fully complied with paragraph (d) requirements (§413.338(d)(4)(iii)) is circular and punitive — a facility affected by the extraordinary circumstance may be unable to comply; recommend that CMS waive compliance prereqs when the extraordinary circumstance directly impeded compliance.

[P45] Conditioning consideration of exception requests on prior full compliance (§413.338(d)(4)(iii) duplicate) could be challenged as arbitrary; legal commenters will ask CMS to define “full compliance” and permit good-faith efforts to be considered.

[P15] The obligation that an SNF must have fully complied with paragraph (d) before CMS will consider an exception (§413.338(d)(4)(iii) (SNF compliance)) lacks guidance on documentation of compliance; request CMS provide a checklist and allow attestation where records were destroyed or lost.

[P46] Requiring documentation of full compliance as a prerequisite for exception consideration (§413.338(d)(4)(iii) obligation) risks denying relief to SNFs that were most harmed; ask CMS to adopt a presumption of eligibility for exception requests tied to officially declared disasters.

[P16] CMS’s authority to grant exceptions without individual requests when an entire region is affected (§413.338(d)(4)(iv)) is necessary, but commenters request that CMS proactively publish affected SNF lists and the months covered and to provide automatic adjustments so facilities need not apply.

[P47] Permitting CMS to grant blanket exceptions for regions (§413.338(d)(4)(iv)) should require CMS to coordinate with state health departments and to publish criteria and notice in the Federal Register or CMS website to ensure transparency.

[P17] When CMS grants an exception, excluding readmission measure performance for affected months (§413.338(d)(4)(v)) is reasonable, but commenters request explanation of how the weighting and denominator adjustments will work and whether other measures will be similarly excluded.

[P48] The obligation to exclude only the readmission measure months when an exception is granted (§413.338(d)(4)(v)) may leave SNFs penalized on other measures affected by extraordinary events; request CMS allow exclusion of any measure demonstrably impacted, not only readmissions.

[P18] CMS’s permission to remove quality measures from the SNF QRP (§413.360(b)(3)) needs procedural protections; commenters will request advance notice, stakeholder comment opportunity, and public justification prior to removal.

[P49] The authority to remove measures (§413.360(b)(3)) should be constrained by defined thresholds for each criterion (e.g., what constitutes “so uniformly high”); request CMS publish quantitative thresholds and analyses used to support removals.

[P19] Removing a measure because performance is uniformly high (§413.360(b)(3)(i)) could prematurely eliminate important quality signals; urge CMS to ensure measures are truly saturated and to consider measure retargeting before removal.

[P50] The criterion that uniform high performance justifies removal (§413.360(b)(3)(i) duplicate) could incentivize gaming; recommend CMS examine variation across subpopulations (e.g., high-acuity vs low-acuity facilities) before removal.

[P20] The criterion to remove measures that don’t improve resident outcomes (§413.360(b)(3)(ii)) is appropriate but requires robust causal analysis; request publication of outcome linkage analyses and methodology for establishing lack of benefit.

[P51] Asking CMS to remove measures when they do not improve resident outcomes (§413.360(b)(3)(ii) duplicate) should include a stakeholder review and independent validation to guard against misclassification.

[P21] Removal for misalignment with clinical guidelines (§413.360(b)(3)(iii)) demands timely updates; request CMS to coordinate with clinical societies (e.g., AMDA) when assessing alignment and to publish rationale.

[P52] The “alignment with clinical guidelines” condition (§413.360(b)(3)(iii) duplicate) should account for lag time between guideline updates and measure revisions; ask for transition timelines before removal.

[P22] Removing a measure in favor of a more broadly applicable one (§413.360(b)(3)(iv)) should not reduce focus on SNF-specific quality issues; request evidence that the replacement measure adequately captures SNF performance and disparity impacts.

[P53] The criterion allowing removal when a broader measure exists (§413.360(b)(3)(iv) duplicate) could obscure SNF-specific nuances; propose that CMS pilot cross-setting measures before removing existing SNF measures.

[P23] The requirement to remove a measure if a more proximal measure is available (§413.360(b)(3)(v)) needs a clear definition of “proximal in time” and evidence that proximal measures are valid predictors of resident outcomes.

[P54] The “more proximal” criterion (§413.360(b)(3)(v) duplicate) could pressure CMS to favor short-term measures over meaningful long-term outcomes; request balanced consideration of both proximal and distal outcomes.

[P24] Removing measures more weakly associated with outcomes (§413.360(b)(3)(vi)) is sensible, but commenters request disclosure of the statistical thresholds and evidence used to judge association strength.

[P55] The “more strongly associated” criterion (§413.360(b)(3)(vi) duplicate) should include minimum effect sizes and confidence intervals; ask CMS to publish the analytic standards.

[P25] Allowing measure removal due to negative unintended consequences of collection or public reporting (§413.360(b)(3)(vii)) could be used to suppress transparency; request that CMS clearly define “negative unintended consequences” and require robust evidence before removal.

[P56] The condition about negative unintended consequences (§413.360(b)(3)(vii) duplicate) should exclude financial or reputational harms as sole grounds for removal; specify that resident safety and care quality must be central.

[P26] The cost-benefit ground for measure removal (§413.360(b)(3)(viii)) requires transparent accounting of both administrative burden and benefits; stakeholders request CMS publish cost estimates and benefit quantifications used to justify removals.

[P57] The "costs outweigh benefits" condition (§413.360(b)(3)(viii) duplicate) could permit removal of measures that are low-cost but high-value for subpopulations; ask CMS to include equity impact analyses.

[P58] Sending non-compliance notifications via QIES ASAP, USPS, or email from the MAC (§413.360(d)(1) methods) may still fail to reach facilities if contact data are outdated; request CMS mandate periodic confirmation of contact information and alternative notification channels.

[P28] Use of QIES ASAP for non-compliance notices (§413.360(d)(1) QIES ASAP) is acceptable but many small SNFs lack routine access; suggest CMS require that important notices also be sent by direct email and print.

[P29] Relying on USPS for non-compliance notices (§413.360(d)(1) USPS) may delay responses; commenters request that notice deadlines (for reconsideration) not start until electronic notice is also sent or until proof of receipt is established.

[P30] Email from the MAC as a notification method (§413.360(d)(1) email from MAC) should require authentication and anti-phishing guidance; ask CMS to standardize subject lines and sender addresses to reduce missed messages.

[P31] The 30-calendar-day reconsideration request period (§413.360(d)(1) permission) may be insufficient for facilities lacking legal staff; request extending reconsideration to 60 days and allowing requests by attestation pending submission of full documentation.

[P59] The reconsideration window of 30 days (§413.360(d)(1) permission duplicate) will disproportionately burden rural SNFs and those with limited administrative capacity; recommend deadline extensions and tolling when CMS’s notice was delivered only by mail.

[P32] CMS’s obligation to notify SNFs of final reconsideration decisions in writing (§413.360(d)(4)) should include reasoning and evidence relied upon; request full decision rationales and appeal instructions in the notification.

[P60] The requirement to notify reconsideration decisions via QIES ASAP, USPS, or MAC email (§413.360(d)(4) obligation) should require simultaneous posting on the Provider Enrollment Chain and Ownership System (PECOS) or CMS Portal for redundancy.

[P33] Using QIES ASAP to deliver final reconsideration decisions (§413.360(d)(4) QIES ASAP) risks non-receipt by facilities not monitored daily; propose CMS require an additional method (certified mail or confirmed email) for final adverse decisions.

[P34] Sending final reconsideration decisions by USPS (§413.360(d)(4) USPS) risks delay for time-sensitive appeals; ask CMS to allow reconsideration deadlines to be measured from the earliest of mailed date, email date, or QIES posting date.

[P35] Reliance on MAC email to send final decisions (§413.360(d)(4) email from MAC) needs assurances that MACs have adequate staff and consistent templates; request CMS create standard notification templates to reduce confusion.

[P58] The obligation to notify non-compliance through at least one method (§413.360(d)(1) / P58 duplicate) could lead to selective reliance on the slowest method; commenters request CMS require multi-modal (at least two) delivery methods for non-compliance notices.

[P40] The rule should require CMS to publish annual reconciliation reports detailing the reductions collected, amounts redistributed as VBP payments (at least 60%), how low-volume protections were funded, and distributions across SNFs to ensure transparency regarding §413.338(c)(2)(i).

[P5] Patient advocacy groups will ask whether the retained portion (up to 40%) of the reductions is being used to finance program administration or reallocated elsewhere, and demand statutory authority and budgetary accounting for any retained funds under §413.338(c)(2)(i).

raw_output:
[P1] The proposed division of the United States into 38 geographical units plus 1 importers unit (39 total) starting with 2023 nominations is arbitrary and lacks a clear statutory or empirical justification in the preamble; the agency should provide the data and criteria used to draw these unit boundaries and explain why a 39-unit structure is required.

[P1] Implementing the new unit divisions beginning with the 2023 nominations (appointments effective early 2024) does not provide sufficient lead time for potential nominees and stakeholders to adjust; request a delayed effective date of at least 12 months after final rule publication.

[P2] The rule requires Board member allocations by unit but does not explain the formula or population/production/import weighting used to determine the number of seats; the agency must publish the allocation methodology and supporting data.

[P2] Allocating fixed numbers of Board members to each unit without a statutory mechanism for periodic reapportionment will create representational distortions over time as production, population, or imports shift; the rule should include a schedule and criteria for periodic reapportionment (e.g., every 5 years tied to census/production data).

[P3] Assigning one Board member to Alabama (P3) may underrepresent Alabama producers relative to neighboring states if the allocation is based on outdated data; provide the state-level data that justify a single director for Alabama.

[P4] Arizona being allocated only one director (P4) could fail to reflect the state's producer base or import/export activity; the agency should explain how industry size, acreage, or producer counts were considered.

[P5] Arkansas being assigned two directors (P5) appears inconsistent with similarly sized states assigned more seats (e.g., Kansas with six); request justification for why Arkansas receives two directors versus other allocations.

[P6] Colorado receiving three directors (P6) may be disproportionate to on-the-ground production or stakeholder population; ask the agency to disclose the metrics used for Colorado’s allocation.

[P7] Florida’s allocation of two Board members (P7) incorrectly treats the state as homogeneous despite major regional differences in production and market; stakeholders from South Florida request either an additional seat or a multi-member at-large approach.

[P8] Georgia’s single director (P8) is likely insufficient given the state’s growing production and diversity of producers; the rule should allow for proportional adjustments or a petition process for additional representation.

[P9] Idaho’s allocation of three directors (P9) needs justification given Idaho’s comparatively small population but concentrated agricultural sectors; provide the data showing why Idaho merits three seats.

[P10] Illinois receiving one director (P10) appears low relative to other states with similar production levels; lack of transparency in the allocation undermines confidence in fairness.

[P11] Indiana’s single director (P11) may leave significant regional producer communities within the state without direct representation; recommend dividing the state into subunits or adding a second seat.

[P12] Iowa’s allocation of four directors (P12) should be explained with respect to the state's acreage and producer count; stakeholders request the underlying statistics used for this allocation.

[P13] Kansas assigned six directors (P13) seems disproportionately large compared to neighboring states; request disclosure of the metric (e.g., number of handlers, production volume) that produced this high allocation.

[P14] Kentucky’s two directors (P14) may not account for the state’s varied production systems; propose a review mechanism to reassess allocations if producer numbers increase.

[P15] Louisiana with one director (P15) could be underrepresented given unique coastal/southern issues; ask for explanation why Louisiana receives only a single seat.

[P16] Michigan’s single director (P16) will inadequately represent both large and small producers across the state; recommend either an additional seat or regional outreach to ensure statewide input.

[P17] Minnesota’s two directors (P17) allocation should be explained vis-à-vis similar Midwestern states; provide data on producer counts and production volumes used.

[P18] Mississippi with one director (P18) risks marginalizing producers in the northern vs. southern parts of the state; recommend a mechanism for regional alternation or additional representation.

[P19] Missouri’s allocation of four directors (P19) appears high relative to states with similar economic activity; request supporting data and the rationale for Missouri’s four seats.

[P20] Montana’s two directors (P20) allocation may not reflect low population density and sparse producers; agency should justify why Montana receives two seats rather than one.

[P21] Nebraska receiving seven directors (P21) is an extreme outlier and likely overrepresents the state; stakeholders from other Plains states will challenge the basis for seven seats and request recalculation.

[P22] New Mexico being assigned one director (P22) overlooks the state’s unique regional interests; request the opportunity to petition for an additional seat based on distinct production types.

[P23] New York’s single director (P23) allocation could fail to represent both upstate and downstate producers; recommend splitting representation or adding at-large seats for urban-proximate issues.

[P24] North Carolina’s single director (P24) may underrepresent the state’s extensive coastal and inland producer populations; request reassessment.

[P25] North Dakota’s two directors (P25) allocation needs clarification given North Dakota’s producer concentration and acreage; provide data supporting two seats.

[P26] Ohio with one director (P26) may not capture regional differences across the state; recommend additional outreach or an extra seat.

[P27] Oklahoma’s allocation of five directors (P27) is high relative to neighboring states; the agency should explain the variables that caused Oklahoma to receive five seats.

[P28] Oregon’s single director (P28) will have to represent highly diverse coastal and inland interests; request consideration of multi-member representation to avoid underrepresentation.

[P29] Pennsylvania’s single director (P29) seems insufficient to represent both agricultural and import-related stakeholders within the state; propose explanatory data.

[P30] South Dakota’s four directors (P30) allocation appears disproportionate and requires explanation of the counts used to assign four seats.

[P31] Tennessee’s two directors (P31) allocation should be justified with state-level production or handler data; lacking that, stakeholders will perceive arbitrary distribution.

[P32] Texas receiving thirteen directors (P32) creates an outsized influence on Board decisions; while Texas’s production may be large, the agency must disclose the exact metric producing 13 seats and consider caps to avoid dominance by a single state.

[P33] Utah’s one director (P33) allocation should be justified where geographic isolation and unique production types exist; the rule should explain why one seat suffices.

[P34] Virginia’s single director (P34) may not represent the state’s dual agricultural and import-related concerns; request clarification.

[P35] Wisconsin’s three directors (P35) allocation needs supporting data; stakeholders demand transparency on counts and whether processors or producers were weighted.

[P36] Wyoming’s single director (P36) fails to account for vast geography and sparse population; although small, the state may require special accommodation to ensure effective representation.

[P37] The Northwest multi-state unit combining Alaska, Hawaii, and Washington into a single seat (P37) will disenfranchise Alaska and Hawaii stakeholders because a single director cannot effectively represent three noncontiguous states with diverse interests; propose separate seats for each state or at least two seats for the unit.

[P38] The Northeast multi-state unit (Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Rhode Island, Vermont) being represented by a single director (P38) dangerously underrepresents nine states with highly varied markets; recommend dividing the unit or increasing seats to reflect constituent diversity.

[P39] The Mid-Atlantic multi-state unit composed of South Carolina and West Virginia receiving one seat (P39) is arbitrary, combining two states with different production profiles; stakeholders request individual seats or a clear rationale for combining them.

[P40] The Southwest multi-state unit (California and Nevada) assigned six directors (P40) may still underrepresent California’s sizable producer base despite the relatively high seat count; agency must provide state-level breakdown of how the six directors are distributed or elected and the data supporting 6 seats for the unit.

[P41] The Importers Unit being given seven directors (P41) overrepresents importers relative to domestic producers and raises potential conflicts of interest; request justification for seven seats and an explanation of how importers are defined and vetted to prevent undue industry capture.

[P41] Assigning seven directors to the Importers Unit (P41) without specifying eligibility criteria for importers (e.g., volume thresholds, registration) risks allowing large foreign-owned entities or non-producer intermediaries to dominate; require clear definitions and qualification criteria.

[P41] Allocating seven seats to importers could violate parity principles under the statute if domestic producer representation is intended to predominate; legal experts should analyze whether this allocation is consistent with the enabling statute.

[P37/P38] Creating multi-state units that group noncontiguous or regionally disparate states (P37, P38) will impair geographically precise representation and may conflict with statutory requirements for representative balance; recommend reconfiguring units to be contiguous and more homogeneous.

[P1/P2] The rule lacks a mechanism for addressing vacancies, resignations, or contested elections within newly defined units and assigned seat numbers; request adding procedural rules for interim appointments and special elections aligned with the new unit structure.

Implementing the new unit divisions beginning with the 2023 nominations (appointments effective early 2024) does not provide sufficient lead time for potential nominees and stakeholders to adjust; request a delayed effective date of at least 12 months after final rule publication.

The rule requires Board member allocations by unit but does not explain the formula or population/production/import weighting used to determine the number of seats; the agency must publish the allocation methodology and supporting data.

Allocating fixed numbers of Board members to each unit without a statutory mechanism for periodic reapportionment will create representational distortions over time as production, population, or imports shift; the rule should include a schedule and criteria for periodic reapportionment (e.g., every 5 years tied to census/production data).

Assigning one Board member to Alabama (P3) may underrepresent Alabama producers relative to neighboring states if the allocation is based on outdated data; provide the state-level data that justify a single director for Alabama.

Arizona being allocated only one director (P4) could fail to reflect the state's producer base or import/export activity; the agency should explain how industry size, acreage, or producer counts were considered.

Arkansas being assigned two directors (P5) appears inconsistent with similarly sized states assigned more seats (e.g., Kansas with six); request justification for why Arkansas receives two directors versus other allocations.
Colorado receiving three directors (P6) may be disproportionate to on-the-ground production or stakeholder population; ask the agency to disclose the metrics used for Colorado’s allocation.

Florida’s allocation of two Board members (P7) incorrectly treats the state as homogeneous despite major regional differences in production and market; stakeholders from South Florida request either an additional seat or a multi-member at-large approach.

Georgia’s single director (P8) is likely insufficient given the state’s growing production and diversity of producers; the rule should allow for proportional adjustments or a petition process for additional representation.

Idaho’s allocation of three directors (P9) needs justification given Idaho’s comparatively small population but concentrated agricultural sectors; provide the data showing why Idaho merits three seats.
Illinois receiving one director (P10) appears low relative to other states with similar production levels; lack of transparency in the allocation undermines confidence in fairness.
Indiana’s single director (P11) may leave significant regional producer communities within the state without direct representation; recommend dividing the state into subunits or adding a second seat.
Iowa’s allocation of four directors (P12) should be explained with respect to the state's acreage and producer count; stakeholders request the underlying statistics used for this allocation.

Kansas assigned six directors (P13) seems disproportionately large compared to neighboring states; request disclosure of the metric (e.g., number of handlers, production volume) that produced this high allocation.
Kentucky’s two directors (P14) may not account for the state’s varied production systems; propose a review mechanism to reassess allocations if producer numbers increase.
Louisiana with one director (P15) could be underrepresented given unique coastal/southern issues; ask for explanation why Louisiana receives only a single seat.
Michigan’s single director (P16) will inadequately represent both large and small producers across the state; recommend either an additional seat or regional outreach to ensure statewide input.
Minnesota’s two directors (P17) allocation should be explained vis-à-vis similar Midwestern states; provide data on producer counts and production volumes used.
Mississippi with one director (P18) risks marginalizing producers in the northern vs. southern parts of the state; recommend a mechanism for regional alternation or additional representation.
Missouri’s allocation of four directors (P19) appears high relative to states with similar economic activity; request supporting data and the rationale for Missouri’s four seats.
Montana’s two directors (P20) allocation may not reflect low population density and sparse producers; agency should justify why Montana receives two seats rather than one.

Nebraska receiving seven directors (P21) is an extreme outlier and likely overrepresents the state; stakeholders from other Plains states will challenge the basis for seven seats and request recalculation.
New Mexico being assigned one director (P22) overlooks the state’s unique regional interests; request the opportunity to petition for an additional seat based on distinct production types.
New York’s single director (P23) allocation could fail to represent both upstate and downstate producers; recommend splitting representation or adding at-large seats for urban-proximate issues.
North Carolina’s single director (P24) may underrepresent the state’s extensive coastal and inland producer populations; request reassessment.
North Dakota’s two directors (P25) allocation needs clarification given North Dakota’s producer concentration and acreage; provide data supporting two seats.
Ohio with one director (P26) may not capture regional differences across the state; recommend additional outreach or an extra seat.
Oklahoma’s allocation of five directors (P27) is high relative to neighboring states; the agency should explain the variables that caused Oklahoma to receive five seats.
Oregon’s single director (P28) will have to represent highly diverse coastal and inland interests; request consideration of multi-member representation to avoid underrepresentation.
Pennsylvania’s single director (P29) seems insufficient to represent both agricultural and import-related stakeholders within the state; propose explanatory data.
South Dakota’s four directors (P30) allocation appears disproportionate and requires explanation of the counts used to assign four seats.
Tennessee’s two directors (P31) allocation should be justified with state-level production or handler data; lacking that, stakeholders will perceive arbitrary distribution.

Texas receiving thirteen directors (P32) creates an outsized influence on Board decisions; while Texas’s production may be large, the agency must disclose the exact metric producing 13 seats and consider caps to avoid dominance by a single state.
Utah’s one director (P33) allocation should be justified where geographic isolation and unique production types exist; the rule should explain why one seat suffices.
Virginia’s single director (P34) may not represent the state’s dual agricultural and import-related concerns; request clarification.
Wisconsin’s three directors (P35) allocation needs supporting data; stakeholders demand transparency on counts and whether processors or producers were weighted.
Wyoming’s single director (P36) fails to account for vast geography and sparse population; although small, the state may require special accommodation to ensure effective representation.

The Northwest multi-state unit combining Alaska, Hawaii, and Washington into a single seat (P37) will disenfranchise Alaska and Hawaii stakeholders because a single director cannot effectively represent three noncontiguous states with diverse interests; propose separate seats for each state or at least two seats for the unit.

raw_output:
[P1] The deadline in § 39.13(a) (comments due June 21, 2021) is unreasonably short given the technical complexity of the AD; stakeholders need at least 60 additional days to prepare meaningful technical comments and cost analyses.

[P1] The AD should explicitly state whether electronic submissions received by midnight UTC on June 21, 2021 will be accepted; the current language risks excluding time-zone-affected commenters.

[P2] The applicability in § 39.13(c) listing only GE90–110B1 and GE90–115B engines is ambiguous — request clarification whether engines with FADEC MN4 identical hardware on other GE90 variants (or retrofit kits) are intended to be excluded or included.

[P2] Operators of GE90 engines not listed may still have FADEC units with MN4 microprocessors; the rule should require reporting or inspection to confirm whether unlisted engine models are truly unaffected.

[P3] § 39.13(f) requires compliance “within the specified compliance times” but does not provide clear mechanisms for operators to petition for extensions in operationally constrained situations (e.g., fleet dispatchability); request a defined process and criteria for short-term relief.

[P3] The provision should require the FAA to publish the “specified compliance times” within the AD text (or a short informative table); as written, it is unclear where to find the times and could lead to inconsistent interpretation.

[P4] § 39.13(g)(1) mandates replacement using an “approved overhaul procedure” but does not require documentation of the procedure used to be retained in the component record; request adding a mandatory recordkeeping requirement evidencing which approved procedure was used.

[P4] The AD should permit replacement during scheduled maintenance windows only and allow operators to consolidate replacements to minimize operational disruption; the current wording could force out-of-cycle shop visits.

[P5] § 39.13(g)(1)(i) requires replacement for MN4 with ≥10,500 CSN before 500 additional cycles — this short 500-cycle window is operationally burdensome for long-haul operators; request extension to at least 1,000 cycles or allowance to complete replacement at the next scheduled heavy maintenance visit within that period.

[P5] The threshold of 10,500 CSN appears arbitrary; provide technical justification and failure-rate data supporting the 500-cycle limit, and publish the risk analysis used to set this limit.

[P6] § 39.13(g)(1)(ii) directs replacement for MN4 with 5,000–10,499 CSN at the next shop visit or before 11,000 CSN — the dual triggers are confusing (next shop visit vs 11,000 CSN); recommend clear precedence (e.g., "whichever occurs first") and examples to avoid inconsistent compliance.

[P6] For MN4 units with between 5,000 and 10,499 CSN that are not scheduled for shop visit for many years (e.g., core-sparing programs), this requirement could leave long exposure; request an interim mandatory inspection or reporting requirement for these units.

[P7] § 39.13(g)(2) requires repeated replacement at the first shop visit after 5,000 CSN since last replacement but before 11,000 CSN — this creates ambiguity about whether shop visits occurring between 5,000 and 11,000 CSN must trigger replacement even if the shop visit is for unrelated FADEC maintenance; request clarification and examples for recurring timing.

[P7] The recurrent replacement at each shop visit after 5,000 CSN will materially increase life-cycle cost and teardown frequency; request the FAA to provide estimated incremental costs per engine and fleet-level economic impact analysis.

[P8] § 39.13(h) prohibits installing any FADEC with a main channel board that has had more than three MN4 replacements — this could render many existing spares unusable and create supply shortages; request phase-in or grandfathering for existing inventories until replacement microprocessors are available.

[P8] The prohibition should specify whether counting of “more than three” replacements applies to the main channel board serial number or per engine serial number; clarify inventory tracking requirements and acceptable evidence.

[P8] Legal comment: The outright installation prohibition may exceed the FAA’s authority if it effectively constitutes a retrofit mandate on spare parts; request legal justification or alternatives (e.g., labeling/spare-use restrictions).

[P9] § 39.13(i)(1) defines “approved overhaul procedure” but the list is limited; request adding a process to add other manufacturer-approved or FAA-approved procedures by amendment, to accommodate future acceptable methods.

[P10] § 39.13(i)(1)(i) permits FADEC International–approved procedures — industry requests clarity on how FADEC International approvals are verified by the FAA and whether third-party MRO approvals are acceptable.

[P11] § 39.13(i)(1)(ii) permits using GE Service Bulletin 73–0118 Rev 0 paragraph 3.A — request the AD reference the effective revision and date of the Service Bulletin explicitly, and allow incorporation by reference with full citation to avoid future ambiguity.

[P11] Provide a redline or summary of the actions in GE Service Bulletin 73–0118 in the AD to ensure operators without immediate access to GE documents can determine compliance obligations.

[P12] § 39.13(i)(2) defines FADEC component shop visit as induction into a repair facility for internal maintenance — clarify whether routine bench testing or software updates performed outside a repair induction qualify as a shop visit.

[P12] The definition should state whether preservation handling (e.g., shipping/inspection) counts as a shop visit; operators need precise triggers to avoid accidental noncompliance.

[P13] § 39.13(j)(1) grants the Manager AMOC authority — commenters support this but request publishing standard criteria the Manager will use to evaluate AMOC requests to ensure consistency and predictability.

[P13] Suggest adding a timeline requirement (e.g., FAA response within 60 days) for AMOC decisions to prevent operational delays caused by prolonged review.

[P14] § 39.13(j)(1) requires AMOC requests be sent to principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 — operators request an alternative electronic submission portal to streamline submissions and ensure auditable receipt.

[P15] § 39.13(j)(1) direct submission permission includes an email address (ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov) — request confirmation that emailed AMOC requests will be accepted as valid, specify acceptable file formats, and confirm security/confidentiality handling for proprietary attachments.

[P16] § 39.13(j)(2) requires notifying principal inspector before using an approved AMOC — operators request clarity on the notification content required (e.g., AMOC approval reference number, effective dates) and whether advance concurrence is required.

[P16] For international operators without an FAA principal inspector, the requirement to notify the manager of the local FSDO/CHDO may be impractical; request alternative procedures for foreign national aviation authorities to be notified.

[P17] The Airbus SNPRM DATES provision repeats the June 21, 2021 comment deadline — if multiple rulemakings share the same deadline, the FAA should extend to avoid simultaneous comment congestion; request consolidation or extensions.

[P17] The rule should explicitly confirm whether the SNPRM comment deadline is the same as the AD’s deadline and whether combined comments on both documents are acceptable.

[P18] The ADDRESSES permission to submit comments per 14 CFR 11.43/11.45 needs an explicit list of acceptable electronic portals (e.g., Regulations.gov) and instructions for submitting proprietary attachments under confidentiality claims; request clearer submission instructions.

[P18] Provide guidance on how to submit large technical appendices (test data, failure analysis) and whether the FAA will accept separate physical submissions to the docket if file-size limits are exceeded.

[General] The AD lacks a regulatory flexibility analysis addressing impacts on small air carriers and MRO shops; request the FAA to publish economic impacts, cost per replacement, and any small-entity considerations.

[General] Request the FAA to provide estimated lead times and supply availability for replacement MN4 microprocessors and for trained personnel to perform the approved overhaul procedures.

[General] Aviation safety advocacy comment: The FAA should publish the failure modes and safety risk assessment that led to these proposed replacement thresholds so the public can evaluate whether the mitigation is adequate.

[General] Legal/administrative comment: The AD should include an explicit effective date and a clarification whether the compliance schedule is measured from the effective date or the date of AD publication, to avoid interpretive disputes.

[P31] Limiting special early teal seasons to September 1–30 (P31) is inflexible given climate-driven shifts in migration timing; allow adaptive management and pilot variability in years where migration phenology changes.

[P35] Allowing a 5-day teal-wood duck season in lieu of early teal (P35) is useful flexibility, but the rule should require states to demonstrate that wood duck take under this option will not negatively affect wood duck populations.

[P37] Allowing a 4-day teal-only season adjacent to a 5-day teal-wood duck season (P37) could create enforcement complexity with back-to-back differing daily bag rules; require clear public notices and signage.

[P41] The prohibition on taking harlequin ducks (P41) should be accompanied by clear outreach to prevent accidental harvest and specify reporting mechanisms for incidental captures to inform conservation actions.

[P42] Allowing certain states to split seasons into three segments (P42) increases hunter confusion and enforcement complexity; require states to justify splits with demonstrable conservation or access benefits.

[P43] Multiple-zone options for states (P43) are administratively complex and require minimum standards for how zones are defined; otherwise there will be inconsistent protections across contiguous habitats.

[P44] Permitting some states to split each zone into three segments (P44) without reporting requirements risks unsustainable harvest; require mandatory post-season reporting to the Service to evaluate impacts.

[P45] The evaluation requirement for zones and split seasons (P45) is necessary but the 2021–25 timeframe is outdated/unenforceable; the rule should specify deadlines, methodologies, and independent review criteria for the evaluations.

[P46] Recommending identical seasons between adjoining zones (P46) without mandating harmonization may leave cross-border enforcement gaps; the Service should require cooperative agreements between states to ensure consistency.

[P47] Allowing powered craft to be used to shoot sea ducks in Sea Duck Areas (P47) raises safety and conservation concerns and may increase hunting efficiency to unsustainable levels; require strict boat-speed limits, gear restrictions, and justification based on local population status.

[P48] Requiring Sea Duck Areas to be designated by states under their regulations (P48) creates a loophole where important areas may remain undesignated; the Service should include a federal fallback designation process if states decline.

[P49] A 15-goose daily bag limit for special early Canada and cackling goose seasons (P49) is very high and could lead to rapid local depletion; recommend lower limits or spatial restrictions tied to population monitoring.

[P50] Extending shooting hours to half-hour after sunset during special early Canada/cackling goose seasons (P50) increases safety risks and may interfere with nocturnal migration; require local justification and nocturnal hunter safety measures.

[P51] Specifying dark goose seasons state- and zone-specifically (P51) is appropriate but the rule must require states to publish the referenced table in an accessible, consolidated federal document to avoid confusion.

[P52] A 107-day light goose season with a 25-bird daily bag and no possession limit (P52) could encourage overharvest or waste; require carcass utilization provisions and monitoring to ensure ethical take and population management goals.

[P53] The 50-day brant season with a two-brant daily limit (P53) may be too permissive in some staging areas; require area-specific assessments before allowing the full 50 days.

[P1] The July 17, 2017 comments due date is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60 days to allow operators, labor organizations, and small businesses sufficient time to evaluate technical impacts and prepare substantive comments.

[P1] The rule does not provide a mechanism for requesting an extension of the comments deadline; the FAA should publish a clear process and criteria for granting any deadline extensions.

[P2] The phrase "within the specified compliance times" in P2 is vague; commenters request that the AD explicitly list the compliance time windows (calendar time or flight cycles) to avoid enforcement ambiguity.

[P2] The rule should allow a temporary extension of compliance times for operators experiencing supply-chain issues or lack of qualified personnel, subject to AMOC approval, to prevent unnecessary grounding.

[P3] Requiring performance of "all applicable RC actions" per the Boeing service bulletin without specifying which airplanes or configurations are affected may impose unnecessary costs on operators with irrelevant configurations; the FAA should explicitly identify applicability by airplane serial numbers or configurations.

[P3] The AD requires performing RC actions "in accordance with" the service bulletin but does not address conflicts between the service bulletin and existing airline maintenance procedures; guidance is needed on resolving such conflicts.

[P4] Changing compliance timing references from "after the original issue of the service bulletin" to the AD effective date (P4) may impose shorter compliance windows than operators anticipated when initially planning work; the FAA should provide a transition allowance or grace period.

[P4] Retroactive calculation from the AD effective date unfairly penalizes operators who already scheduled work based on the service bulletin issuance date; FAA should grandfather prior planning and maintenance scheduling.

[P5] Requiring operators to use an FAA-approved AMOC instead of contacting Boeing for RC instructions (P5) could delay critical field fixes where Boeing has the most technical knowledge; the AD should permit interim compliance using Boeing instructions pending AMOC approval.

[P5] The prohibition on relying on Boeing contact instructions (P5) lacks an emergency exception for time-critical repairs; the FAA should allow time-limited use of Boeing-approved procedures when safety-critical and AMOC turnaround cannot meet the compliance time.

[P6] Limiting AMOC approval authority to the Manager, Los Angeles ACO (P6) centralizes decision-making and may create bottlenecks; FAA should authorize Regional ACOs or delegated offices to approve AMOCs to expedite approvals.

[P6] The rule should clarify whether existing delegated authorities (e.g., DERs or OEM ODAs) retain any concurrency in AMOC approvals to avoid confusion.

[P7] The requirement to submit AMOC requests to a principal inspector, local FSDO, or directly to the ACO manager (P7) could be interchangeable and unclear; provide a single, preferred submission pathway and a published timeline for FAA response.

[P7] The AD's option to email AMOC requests lacks secure submission guidance and raises confidentiality concerns for proprietary repair data; the FAA should provide secure submission methods.

[P8] The obligation to notify the principal inspector or local FSDO before using an approved AMOC (P8) could be operationally burdensome for international operators or ferry flights; allow notification within a reasonable timeframe (e.g., 72 hours) when immediate use is necessary.

[P8] The AD should specify what constitutes adequate notification and provide contact information or an electronic reporting mechanism to ensure compliance with P8.

[P9] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs for repairs (P9) is acceptable but must require FAA concurrence for safety-significant deviations; the AD should state that ODA approvals are effective only if the ODA is authorized by the Manager, Los Angeles ACO and FAA retains oversight.

[P9] The rule should require the ODA to provide complete technical substantiation and keep records of AMOCs for FAA audit to ensure transparency when using P9.

[P10] Requiring that AMOCs meet the airplane's certification basis and specifically reference the AD (P10) is appropriate, but FAA should publish the relevant certification basis reference(s) for affected models to reduce back-and-forth during AMOC processing.

[P10] The AD should clarify whether meeting the airplane's "certification basis" includes later, higher-level safety standards or only the original certification regulations applicable at type certification.
