[P1] The rule should clarify whether electronic comments submitted close to midnight on October 10, 2017 will be accepted, and provide the exact time zone for the deadline.

[P2] The reference to Boeing Alert Service Bulletin B787–81205–SB570030–00 to identify subject airplanes is vague; the AD should list affected serial/line numbers or provide a reproducible method for operators to determine applicability.

[P2] The AD's applicability in § 39.13(c) should explicitly state whether line numbers beyond those in the referenced service bulletin (e.g., production changes or later revisions) are included or excluded to avoid confusion.

[P3] § 39.13(f) requires compliance "within the specified compliance times" but does not state a mechanism for operators to request an extension for logistics reasons; the AD should specify allowance procedures or AMOC timelines for compliance time relief.

[P4] The requirement in § 39.13(g) to perform ultrasonic inspections and corrective actions "as specified" in the ASB lacks clarity on acceptable inspection equipment, personnel qualifications, and calibration requirements — the FAA should specify minimum NDI qualifications and equipment standards.

[P5] § 39.13(g) requires ultrasonic inspections of left and right upper wing stringers; the AD should specify whether the inspection must be by hands-on ultrasonic (contact) or if phased-array, immersion, or pulse-echo methods are acceptable.

[P6] Requiring operators to "do all applicable corrective actions in accordance with the Accomplishment Instructions" (§ 39.13(g)) without specifying approved deviations places undue reliance on Boeing's instructions; FAA should identify which corrective actions are FAA-approved or require AMOC.

[P7] Completing corrective actions "before further flight" (§ 39.13(g) & (j)(1)) may be operationally disruptive for passenger carriers; the AD should allow ferry or one-time flights under specific conditions with documented mitigations and a requirement to report such flights.

[P8] The repetitive inspection intervals in § 39.13(g)/(h) reference the ASB but do not appear in the AD text; the agency should include the exact intervals in the AD to avoid ambiguity and ensure enforceability.

[P9] § 39.13(h)(1) mandates revising operators' inspection/maintenance programs to incorporate AWL 57–AWL–13 but fails to define the AWL tasks' scope and detailed procedures; the AD should append or summarize the AWL tasks for operator clarity.

[P10] The initial compliance threshold in § 39.13(h)(1) of 24,000 flight cycles or 12 years is too long given the safety concern; commenters (safety advocacy groups) will request a shorter interval pending risk assessment data justifying the selected threshold.

[P11] Conversely, some operators will comment that the 24,000-cycle/12-year threshold (§ 39.13(h)(1)) is impractical for high-utilization aircraft and request the AD allow initial compliance based on flight hours or cycles since manufacture rather than cycles since ASB actions.

[P12] § 39.13(h)(2) requires specific line-number airplanes (10, 13, 15–19) to revise programs within 60 days; operators will request clarification whether this 60-day clock begins on AD issuance or AD effective date and request alignment with the global compliance timeline.

[P13] The initial compliance condition for the specified-line-number airplanes in § 39.13(h)(2) is ambiguous; commenters will seek explicit language whether "prior to the accumulation of 24,000 total flight cycles" is counted from delivery, entry-into-service, or another baseline.

[P14] § 39.13(i) prohibits alternative actions or intervals after paragraph (h) unless AMOC-approved; manufacturers and MROs will comment that the AMOC process is slow and ask for interim accepted alternatives (e.g., Boeing ODA approvals) to be explicitly authorized to avoid grounding impacts.

[P15] The preventive modification requirement in § 39.13(j) should have a stated window and clear parts/kit availability expectation; commenters will point out that supply-chain or scheduling delays could prevent timely compliance and seek relief provisions.

[P16] § 39.13(j)(1) duplicates inspection and corrective-action requirements already in paragraph (g); legal commenters will request consolidation to avoid confusion and to specify when the (g) repetitive inspections cease relative to j(1) completion.

[P17] Requiring corrective actions discovered under § 39.13(j)(1) to be completed before further flight (§ 39.13(j)(1)) will be protested by operators who need explicit permission for one-time ferry flights to reposition aircraft for maintenance, with prescribed operational mitigations.

[P18] § 39.13(j)(2) mandates performing the preventive modification per PART 3 of the ASB but does not identify parts, kits, labor hours, or necessary supplemental structural approvals—operators will ask that such implementation details and estimated labor/parts costs be provided.

[P19] The terminating effect in § 39.13(j) that ends repetitive inspections once modification is done must specify whether partial modifications (e.g., only one wing) terminate inspections for the entire airplane or only for modified areas.

[P20] § 39.13(k)(1) replaces references to "after Issue 001 date" with "after the effective date of this AD"; commenters will request confirmation that earlier compliance time calculations based on Issue 001 dates are grandfathered and not reset.

[P21] § 39.13(k)(2) allows RC repairs only with AMOC-approved Boeing instructions; legal and independent repair stations will object to delegating approval authority to Boeing and request that FAA-approved repair methods be explicitly allowed without Boeing involvement.

[P22] The AMOC authority in § 39.13(l)(1) concentrated in the Seattle ACO Branch manager could create bottlenecks; commenters will request multiple delegated FAA points or regional ACOs be listed to expedite AMOC approvals.

[P23] The submission process in § 39.13(l)(1)–(2) requiring sending AMOC requests per 14 CFR 39.19 to principal inspectors or local FSDOs is unclear about electronic submission timelines; operators will request an explicit email/portal and target review time (e.g., 30 days) for AMOC decisions.

[P24] § 39.13(l)(2) obligates notifying the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC; commenters will request that acceptance of notification be documented in writing by the FAA within a defined timeframe to provide legal certainty.

[P25] § 39.13(l)(3) permits use of AMOCs approved by the Boeing ODA but requires meeting the certification basis; non-Boeing repair stations will request clarity whether ODA approvals automatically satisfy FAA requirements or still require FAA concurrence.

[P26] The requirement in § 39.13(l)(3) that AMOC approvals "must specifically refer to this AD" is fine, but commenters will request a standard template to ensure consistent AMOC documentation for operators and auditors.

[P27] § 39.13(l)(4)(i) that RC-labeled steps must be performed is strict; commenters will ask for a definitive list of RC steps included in the ASB (with page/figure references) so operators can identify which steps require AMOC for deviation.

[P28] The "RC Exempt" exception in § 39.13(l)(4)(i) could be ambiguous in substeps; maintenance organizations will request an explicit printed list of RC Exempt substeps to avoid misinterpretation during maintenance.

[P29] The requirement that any deviation from RC steps needs prior AMOC approval (§ 39.13(l)(4)(i)) may be infeasible during in-service repairs at remote stations; commenters will request allowance for post-facto AMOC approvals with strict reporting and risk mitigation.

[P30] § 39.13(l)(4)(ii) allows deviation from non-RC steps without AMOC if RC steps remain performable and airworthiness is maintained, but does not define "accepted methods" — commenters will request that accepted methods be explicitly referenced (e.g., FAA ACs, Boeing SRMs).

[P31] The condition in § 39.13(l)(4)(ii) that RC steps must remain performable when deviating from non-RC steps should be supplemented with guidance on how to document and prove continued ability to perform RC steps for audit purposes.

[P32] The condition in § 39.13(l)(4)(ii) that the airplane be returned to an airworthy condition after deviation is tautological; legal commenters will propose adding objective acceptance criteria or inspections to demonstrate airworthiness following deviations.

[P33] The AD should include an economic analysis of costs to operators for the repeated ultrasonic inspections, corrective actions, preventive modification, and maintenance program revisions required in paragraphs (g)–(j) and (h) and invite comment on these cost estimates.

[P34] Labor unions and maintenance technician associations will comment that the AD requires specialized ultrasonic inspections and the FAA must ensure adequate training slots and certification routes are available to avoid creating an unqualified labor shortage.

[P35] International carriers and foreign civil aviation authorities will request clarification on how this FAA AD aligns with EASA or other CAAs' directives, and whether compliance with a foreign AD will be accepted as an AMOC for operators outside the U.S.

[P36] The AD should provide a compliance tracking/reporting mechanism (e.g., requirement to submit inspection and repair reports to FAA or Boeing) to aid post-implementation oversight; commenters will recommend specific reporting intervals and data fields.

[P37] Environmental and noise advocacy groups may request assessment of whether the preventive modification or repairs could have environmental impacts (e.g., adhesives, solvents) and demand inclusion of mitigation measures or disposal requirements.

[P38] Small operators will request relief or phased implementation schedules in recognition of limited maintenance capacity and to avoid unnecessary grounding or scheduling disruptions.

[P39] The AD must make clear whether temporary repairs or permanent repairs are required for corrective actions labeled as RC in the ASB; commenters will seek explicit acceptance criteria for temporary fix-to-fly vs. permanent repair.

[P40] The AD should clarify whether inspections and modifications are required on spare wings, test articles, or wings in storage; operators with parts inventories will request explicit applicability to non-installed components.

[P41] Legal commenters will ask that the AD explicitly state whether compliance with AWL 57–AWL–13 satisfies any existing maintenance program requirements or whether it creates a new independent mandatory program element.

[P42] The AD should allow operators to propose risk-based inspection intervals via AMOC if they can demonstrate equivalent or better safety (e.g., using fleet health monitoring); commenters will request explicit acceptance criteria for such risk-based proposals.

[P43] Boeing, MROs, and parts suppliers will comment that the AD needs to identify required parts/kits for the preventive modification, provide PN references, lead times, and whether Boeing will supply kits under warranty or service bulletins cost-sharing.

[P44] The AD should specify recordkeeping retention periods for the inspections, corrective actions, AMOCs, and maintenance program revisions required by § 39.13 to ensure compliance and auditability; commenters will propose a 3–5 year minimum.

[P1] The proposed automatic de-certification at final assessment for failing outcome measures §486.316(b) is too punitive and does not allow for remediation time; commenters will request a graduated enforcement approach (warning, corrective action plan, then de-certification).

[P1] The rule lacks clarity on the definition of “final assessment” timing and frequency; stakeholders will ask CMS to specify assessment dates and appeal windows to ensure due process.

[P1] Legal commentators will claim that de-certification based solely on outcome measures may violate procedural fairness principles unless CMS provides clear notice, benchmarking methodology, and an opportunity to cure before final decertification.

[P3] Labor and nonprofit OPOs will argue that a lifelong prohibition could be arbitrary and subject to legal challenge under administrative law and ask CMS to allow re-application after demonstrable remediation and third-party audit.

[P4] The requirement for competing OPOs to submit descriptive data about barriers, effects, corrective steps, and results lacks specificity about required data elements, formats, and verification; commenters will request a standardized template and data validation procedures.

[P4] Smaller OPOs will claim that the burden of preparing extensive narrative and data submissions to compete for an open area is disproportionate and will request proportionality or fee waivers/support for resource-limited OPOs.

[P4] Privacy advocacy groups will request explicit limits and guidance on protected health information in the required submissions, including de-identification standards and HIPAA compliance assurances.

[P5] Requiring OPOs to already meet outcome and certification requirements to be eligible to compete (§486.316(c)) effectively freezes out organizations working to improve performance; commenters will request allowance for conditional bids with time-bound improvement plans.

[P5] New or recently reorganized OPOs will point to §486.318(c)(3) (no 12 months data) and ask CMS to harmonize eligibility rules so entities without 12 months of data can still compete under supervised probationary status.

[P6] The requirement that competing OPOs must bid for the entire service area will be opposed by multi-state or geographically diverse OPOs and by transplant centers that value local expertise; commenters will request allowing partial-area bids or collaborative joint bids.

[P6] Rural stakeholders will argue that forcing bids for entire service areas could deter smaller OPOs from competing for remote counties, reducing local responsiveness; they will ask CMS to permit county- or hospital-cluster level bids.

[P7] Using OPTN-submitted data as the numerator (§486.318(a)(3)) raises concerns about timeliness, data quality, and potential reporting variability across OPOs; commenters will request data audits, standardization, and error-correction procedures before using OPTN data for enforcement.

[P7] Legal and technical commenters will request clarity on how discrepancies between OPTN data and OPO internal records or state death records will be reconciled and what appeals processes exist for data disputes.

[P8] The unspecified “parameters and requirements” for demonstrating success rates (§486.318(b)) are not detailed here; stakeholders will ask CMS to publish exact statistical formulas, minimum sample sizes, and adjustments for case mix or population differences.

[P8] Equity advocates will demand risk adjustment or stratification for donor demographics, hospital referral patterns, and population health to ensure outcome measures do not penalize OPOs serving higher-risk communities.

[P9] Setting the donation-rate threshold as the lowest rate among the top 25% in the prior 12 months (§486.318(b)(1)) may produce volatile thresholds and regional unfairness; commenters will request multi-year averaging or floor/ceiling limits to reduce volatility.

[P9] Smaller OPOs will argue that using a top-25% cutoff from a single 12-month period disadvantages small-volume OPOs with wide confidence intervals and ask for alternative thresholding (e.g., percentile over 3 years).

[P10] Similar to P9, commenters will challenge the transplant-rate threshold methodology (§486.318(b)(2)) and request adjustment for organ type mix, transplant center capacity, and inter-OPO sharing arrangements before applying thresholds.

[P11] The requirement to compute 95% confidence intervals using a one-sided test (§486.318(b)(3)) is statistically unusual and may increase false positives; statisticians will recommend two-sided intervals or justification for one-sided testing and sensitivity analyses.

[P12] Flagging OPOs whose upper one-sided 95% CI is below the threshold (§486.318(b)(4)) may identify OPOs with limited data rather than true underperformance; stakeholders will request minimum denominator thresholds before flagging to avoid penalizing low-volume OPOs.

[P12] OPOs will request that CMS apply shrinkage estimators or empirical Bayes methods to reduce overflagging of low-volume units and to account for statistical uncertainty more appropriately.

[P13] Annual assessments using the most recent 12 months of OPTN and state death certificate data (§486.318(c)(1)) may create timing mismatches due to death certificate reporting lags; commenters will request explicit data lag allowances and procedures for late-arriving data.

[P13] State vital records offices will request CMS coordinate with them on data access, timelines, and funding for expedited reporting if their data are being used for regulatory certification.

[P14] The obligation to meet §486.348(d)(3) actions if performance falls below measures before final cycle (§486.318(c)(2)) needs clarification on timelines, specific remedial actions, and whether external validation of improvement is required; commenters will ask for detailed corrective action plan requirements and independent oversight.

[P14] Advocacy groups will request transparency when an OPO is under remedial status, including public reporting and stakeholder input into improvement plans.

[P15] The exception that new service areas taken over after Jan 1 are not held accountable until 12 months of data exist (§486.318(c)(3)) is reasonable, but commenters will seek clarification on whether historical performance of the prior OPO will be considered and how shared historical data will be transferred.

[P15] Opposing commenters will argue this exception could incentivize strategic service-area transfers to avoid accountability and will ask for safeguards to prevent gaming (e.g., moratoria on transfers after notice of poor performance).

[P16] The requirement that each OPO have a process to review outcome-measure performance (§486.348(d)(1)) is appropriate but the rule lacks specificity on scope, frequency, staffing, and documentation; commenters will request minimum standards and auditability.

[P16] Labor groups will ask CMS to require involvement of clinical staff, community stakeholders, and patient representatives in the review process to ensure comprehensive oversight.

[P17] Mandating that the review process be continuous and improvement-focused (§486.348(d)(1)) could be interpreted variably; commenters will request a definition of “continuous” (e.g., quarterly reviews, monthly dashboards) and measurable performance improvement milestones.

[P17] Smaller OPOs will request flexibility in the frequency and intensity of continuous review commensurate with resources and volume, or federal support to implement continuous QI systems.

[P18] Requiring incorporation of outcome data into QAPI (§486.348(d)(2)) is reasonable, but commenters will request that CMS provide technical assistance materials, example QAPI plans, and clear expectations for documentation and reviewer qualifications.

[P18] Commenters will ask whether failure to incorporate outcome data into QAPI triggers immediate enforcement or whether it will be considered part of progressive remediation activities.

[P19] The requirement that OPOs identify opportunities and implement changes if outcome measures are statistically significantly below the top 25% at assessments before the final cycle (§486.348(d)(3)) needs clearer definitions of “statistically significantly below” (p-value threshold, one-sided vs two-sided), timelines for implementation, and evidence of effectiveness required.

[P19] OPOs will request that CMS allow use of qualified external consultants for remediation and that CMS specify acceptable evidence (process changes, intermediate outcomes) that will satisfy remedial obligations.

[P1/P3/P5] Several commenters will argue the combined effect of immediate decertification, permanent competition prohibition, and strict eligibility to re-compete creates a regulatory framework that risks reducing the number of experienced OPOs and could destabilize donation networks; they will ask CMS to model workforce and service-area impacts before finalizing.

[P7/P11/P12] Statisticians and academic researchers will request that CMS publish the full statistical code, simulation results, and sensitivity analyses showing expected false-positive and false-negative flagging rates under the proposed metrics to allow independent evaluation.

[P4/P6/P15] Hospital associations and transplant centers will request explicit coordination requirements in the solicitation process for open areas (including transition-of-care plans, existing hospital–OPO contracts, and patient notification) and ask CMS to permit partial-area awards or phased transitions to protect patient care.

[P9/P10/P14/P19] Equity and rural health advocates will request that CMS perform an equity impact analysis to ensure thresholds and enforcement do not disproportionately affect OPOs serving minority, low-income, or rural populations, and to require risk adjustment or mitigation strategies.

[P2/P3/P6] Legal commenters will request clearer appeals and post-decertification relief mechanisms, including a transparent auction/selection process for open areas, standards for choosing successor OPOs, and the right to seek injunctive relief to prevent sudden service interruptions.

[P8/P11/P12/P13] Multiple stakeholders will request pilot testing of the outcome measures and enforcement regime in selected regions prior to nationwide implementation, with results published and incorporated into final rulemaking.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement to mark every inspected-and-passed carcass at the time of inspection if it will be shipped into commerce is operationally infeasible for high-throughput establishments processing thousands of carcasses per hour; FSIS should provide a reasonable time window (e.g., within 2 hours) rather than “at the time of inspection.”

[P1] The rule lacks specificity about acceptable methods and dimensions for the “official inspection legend (including establishment number)” on carcasses shipped into commerce; industry requests clear technical specifications (size, placement, ink type, legibility standards) to ensure compliance consistency.

[P1] Requiring the mark “at the time of inspection” creates enforcement ambiguity when inspection and marking are separated by brief handling steps; FSIS should clarify whether automated in-line marking systems satisfy the “at the time” standard and whether electronic traceability can substitute a physical legend in some cases.

[P1] Small and very small establishments will face disproportionate compliance costs to modify workflows and acquire marking equipment to meet the “at the time of inspection” mandate; FSIS should include a delayed compliance timeline or exemptions for such establishments.

[P2] Permission to omit marking for carcasses to be further processed relies on establishments’ HACCP/SOPs but does not require FSIS review or approval of those procedures; consumer advocates request mandatory FSIS verification/approval of the HACCP/SOPs that govern unmarked carcasses to prevent abuse.

[P2] The phrase “appropriate procedures as part of HACCP/Sanitation SOPs or other prerequisite programs” is vague; industry requests explicit examples of acceptable controls (e.g., distinct tagging, electronic batch IDs, secure segregation protocols) that will satisfy FSIS.

[P2] Allowing unmarked passed carcasses for in-establishment further processing without real-time FSIS oversight could increase potential for diversion of unmarked meat into commerce; FSIS should require periodic audits and recordkeeping that allow tracing each unmarked carcass to the onward processed product.

[P3] The obligation that unmarked carcasses “are processed only within the slaughtering establishment” needs clarification on the geographic and ownership scope — does “processed only within” prohibit transfer between co-located establishments under common ownership or contract? FSIS should define terms like “establishment” and allow transfers under documented control procedures.

[P3] Enforcement will be challenging unless establishments must maintain contemporaneous logs showing that each unmarked carcass remained in-establishment; FSIS should require standardized log formats and retention periods (e.g., 12 months).

[P3] The rule should address whether temporary holds (e.g., for cooling, trimming) that occur in dispatched areas but within the same facility still count as “processed only within the slaughtering establishment” to avoid penalizing normal processing flows.

[P4] The absolute prohibition on unmarked carcasses leaving the establishment “for any reason” could prevent legitimate, FSIS-supervised transfers (e.g., to an affiliated processing facility for rendering or to a USDA lab for testing); FSIS should allow exceptions where FSIS control and custody are formally transferred and documented.

[P4] The rule lacks guidance on penalties for inadvertent departure of an unmarked carcass (e.g., during transportation error); stakeholders request an administrative correction pathway and proportional civil penalties rather than immediate criminal or shutdown actions.

[P4] Agricultural transporters and brokers need clarity about the point at which a carcass is considered to have “left the establishment” (loading dock vs. arrival at other facility); FSIS should define the threshold to avoid disputes and enforcement uncertainty.

[P5] Requiring unmarked and retained carcasses or parts to “remain under FSIS control” imposes significant FSIS resource burdens (personnel and holding space); FSIS should specify practical alternatives, such as bonded areas under establishment surveillance with FSIS verification instead of continuous FSIS custody.

[P5] The provision does not specify the form of “FSIS control” — whether physical custody, tagging, electronic lock, or FSIS presence is required; establishments need prescriptive guidance to implement compliant control measures.

[P5] The rule should set maximum time limits for how long FSIS will retain control of unmarked/retained parts before disposition (e.g., rework, condemn, rendering) to prevent indefinite holding that disrupts plant operations and product flow.

[P6] The obligation that establishments “make any corrections necessary to render the carcass or part eligible to bear the mark” needs clearer delineation of acceptable corrective actions (e.g., trimming, freezing, reinspection) and whether establishments may perform corrections under their own supervision or require FSIS presence.

[P6] Who determines when corrections are “sufficient” — the establishment or FSIS inspector? The rule should state that corrections require FSIS reinspection and sign-off before marking to prevent disputes about eligibility.

[P6] The policy should address responsibility and cost allocation when corrections are needed (e.g., if adulteration from establishment process caused the issue, can costs be charged to the establishment; if defect originated earlier, who pays for reinspection and storage?).

[P6] The rule does not specify recordkeeping for corrections made to render carcasses eligible; stakeholders request mandatory records documenting the defect, corrective action taken, personnel involved, and FSIS reinspection results, with a defined retention period.

[P2][P5] There is a regulatory gap: if an establishment claims it has “appropriate procedures” and unmarked carcasses remain under FSIS control, FSIS must be empowered to inspect and audit those procedures regularly. Commenters request periodic competency audits and public reporting of noncompliance instances.

[P1][P3][P6] Legal commenters note potential preemption and labeling law interactions if establishments later apply marks after corrections; the rule should harmonize with existing labeling and interstate commerce statutes to avoid litigation about misbranding or false inspection claims.

[P4][P5] Consumer safety groups recommend explicit chain-of-custody requirements and tamper-evident seals for any held unmarked carcasses to prevent intentional diversion and protect public health.

[P1] The requirement to include the establishment number in the inspection legend may raise confidentiality concerns for establishments that use establishment numbers as proprietary identifiers; FSIS should explain how those numbers are protected and whether alternative identifiers can be used in limited circumstances.

[P3] The rule fails to address how to handle mixed lots where parts from marked and unmarked carcasses are combined during further processing; FSIS should require segregation or clear product disposition rules to prevent commingling of unmarked-origin meat into marked-product lots.

[P5] For imported carcasses temporarily held in U.S. establishments, the “remain under FSIS control” requirement could conflict with customs and import regulations; FSIS should coordinate with CBP to clarify holding and control protocols for imports.

[P6] The lack of transitional guidance for establishments that discover they have already shipped unmarked carcasses into commerce by mistake means inconsistent remedial practices; FSIS should provide a required notification and recall framework for such incidents.

[P2] Smaller plants relying on HACCP flexibility fear FSIS will later reinterpret “appropriate procedures” narrowly; the rule should include a safe harbor list of procedures and a predictable approval process to avoid enforcement surprises.

[P1][P6] Meat processors and packers express concern that delayed marking for corrected carcasses will complicate downstream traceability systems that rely on immediate marking; FSIS should require linking marks to batch-level electronic records to maintain traceability.

[P4] The phrase “for any reason” in the prohibition is overbroad and may capture permitted movements such as emergency transfers to veterinary or laboratory facilities; FSIS should enumerate permitted exceptions with required documentation and notification procedures.

[P5] Labor unions note that increased FSIS control duties (e.g., monitoring retained carcasses) may require additional FSIS staffing and shift coverage; commenters urge FSIS to budget for additional inspectors or permit approved third-party custody under strict supervision.

[P3] The rule should require visual identifiers (e.g., color-coded tags) on unmarked carcasses to make it easy for all plant personnel and FSIS inspectors to identify items that cannot leave the slaughter establishment.

[P6] Environmental and waste management stakeholders ask for explicit disposal pathways for carcasses that cannot be corrected to bear the mark (e.g., condemned): clarify rendering, composting, or disposal requirements and who bears disposal costs.

[P1] The rule lacks an appeals process for establishments that are denied permission to mark a carcass as passed at inspection (for example, when an inspector deems a carcass ineligible); commenters request a defined, expedited administrative appeal mechanism.

[P2] Allowing reliance on “other prerequisite programs” beyond HACCP/SOPs could create inconsistent standards; FSIS should limit permissible programs to those that are documented and subject to FSIS verification to ensure uniform public health protection.

[P5] The requirement that retained carcasses stay under FSIS control until corrections are made could cause bottlenecks if FSIS reinspection scheduling is delayed; FSIS should commit to maximum reinspection response times (e.g., within 24 hours) to avoid undue accumulation of held product.

[P3][P6] Veterinary and public health experts ask for clarification on how disease-control holds (e.g., suspected zoonotic contamination) interact with this rule: must such carcasses remain under FSIS control even if subject to federal quarantine or investigation protocols?

[P1] Trade associations note the rule could affect export certification if marks are applied or reapplied after inspection; FSIS should coordinate with APHIS and trade partners to ensure export rules are not disrupted.

[P1] The May 27, 2020 receipt deadline is unreasonably short and does not provide sufficient time for affected stakeholders (local governments, industry, environmental NGOs) to prepare meaningful technical comments; EPA should extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] Requiring comments to be "received on or before May 27, 2020" rather than "postmarked by" unfairly excludes mailed comments delayed by postal service; EPA should accept comments postmarked by May 27, 2020.

[P2] Identification of the docket only by Docket ID No. EPA–R05–OAR–2019–0557 is insufficient; the NPRM should include alternative contact points and a general mailbox for administrative issues to avoid misplaced submissions.

[P2] Providing a single email address (aburano.douglas@epa.gov) creates a single point of failure and privacy concerns; EPA should provide a second backup email and a phone contact for receipt confirmation.

[P3] The requirement to follow Regulations.gov site instructions may disadvantage commenters unfamiliar with that platform; EPA should provide step-by-step guidance and a plain-language FAQ for first-time users.

[P3] Regulations.gov occasionally times out or rejects large file uploads; EPA should explicitly allow alternate submission methods (e.g., FTP or physical media) when the site fails to accept documents despite reasonable efforts.

[P4] Prohibiting edits or removals of submitted comments on Regulations.gov prevents commenters from correcting errors or withdrawing CBI inadvertently posted; EPA should permit limited post-submission edits or withdrawals within a reasonable window (e.g., 7 days) and provide a process for removal when sensitive information is posted.

[P4] The statement that comments cannot be removed conflicts with commenters' privacy and confidentiality rights; EPA must clarify procedures for redacting or removing personal data or inadvertently disclosed information.

[P5] The prohibition on electronically submitting CBI is vague and could chill submission of important data; EPA should provide clear instructions for submitting CBI (e.g., marking, segregating attachments) and an option for secure upload or encrypted email.

[P5] Telling commenters not to submit CBI electronically without specifying an alternative (e.g., physical submission or secure portal) is impractical; EPA must provide a secure mechanism (certified mail, secure file transfer) to accept CBI.

[P6] Requiring an accompanying written comment for multimedia submissions is reasonable, but EPA should specify accepted formats and maximum file sizes to avoid rejection of multimedia evidence.

[P6] EPA should clarify whether transcripts of audio/video are required, and whether captions or translations are needed for non-English multimedia.

[P7] Declaring the written comment as the "official comment" is appropriate, but EPA must make clear whether attachments (data files, spreadsheets) incorporated by reference will be treated as part of the official comment for record and FOIA purposes.

[P7] EPA should permit comments where the substantive points are included only in linked materials, provided the submission contains working links and instruction for accessing those materials; otherwise small file size limits may prevent full technical submissions.

[P8] EPA's discretion to publish comments raises privacy concerns; EPA should commit to removing personal contact information (home addresses, phone numbers, personal emails) before posting to the public docket.

[P8] NGOs and researchers may submit sensitive location-based data (e.g., private well locations) that should not be made public; EPA must define redaction policies prior to publication.

[P9] The rule's statement that EPA generally will not consider information located outside the primary submission is overly restrictive and could exclude large datasets hosted on cloud platforms; EPA should accept such materials if the primary submission contains a stable, permanent link and instructions for downloading.

[P9] EPA must create a process to accept and archive external datasets (e.g., on Data.gov) rather than refusing to consider them because they are hosted off-site.

[P10] Reliance on three complete consecutive years of quality-assured monitoring data may delay redesignation decisions in years with unusual events (e.g., wildfires, COVID-related emissions changes); EPA should allow consideration of exceptional events and alternative data analyses for borderline cases.

[P10] The requirement of three consecutive years could be unfair to areas that have rapidly improved air quality due to recent controls; EPA should permit provisional redesignation when robust modeling and mitigation commitments show durability.

[P11] The 0.075 ppm threshold for each monitor does not account for monitor siting biases; EPA should require assessments of representativeness and potential siting-induced measurement error before using design values for redesignation.

[P11] EPA should clarify whether the 0.075 ppm comparison uses rounding conventions and specify how fractional differences (e.g., exactly 0.0750) are handled to avoid interpretive disputes.

[P12] Data completeness criteria per 40 CFR part 58 may penalize monitors with instrument downtime due to maintenance; EPA should require WDNR to provide documentation and justification for any missing data and allow for approved data substitution methods where appropriate.

[P12] The rule should specify what procedures will be used to treat days with invalidated data due to exceptional events, and whether those days are excluded from completeness calculations.

[P13] The ≥90% average seasonal completeness and ≥75% in any season requirement may be unattainable for small or rural monitors; EPA should allow alternate completeness criteria or accept collocated monitors' data where appropriate.

[P13] EPA must specify how seasonal definitions are applied (calendar vs. meteorological seasons) and the handling of leap years.

[P14] The provision that certain attainment-related SIP submissions are no longer required once EPA finalizes an attainment determination could remove important planning safeguards; EPA should require states to continue development and periodic updating of substantive plans to ensure maintenance.

[P14] Legal commenters may argue that waiving SIP submission requirements conflicts with statutory obligations under the CAA unless explicitly authorized by Congress; EPA should provide legal justification and cite precedent.

[P15] The requirement that SIPs be adopted after "reasonable public notice and hearing" lacks specificity; EPA should define minimum notice periods and hearing accessibility standards (e.g., remote participation options).

[P15] Stakeholders will request that EPA require translated notices and outreach to affected environmental justice communities as part of "reasonable public notice."

[P16] Mandating "enforceable emission limitations" without guidance could create uncertainty for states about acceptable enforceability mechanisms; EPA should clarify whether state performance standards, consent decrees, and enforceable commitments qualify.

[P16] Industry commenters will request clear criteria for what constitutes an "enforceable" measure under the SIP to avoid future enforcement and planning uncertainty.

[P17] The obligation to establish monitoring systems should include funding and technical assistance commitments from EPA to states with limited resources; otherwise some states cannot meet monitoring expectations.

[P17] EPA should clarify the acceptable QA/QC procedures and whether low-cost sensor networks can supplement federal reference monitors for SIP purposes.

[P18] The required source permit program must be consistent with federal preemption principles; industry will request clear deadlines for state permit program updates and transitional relief where procedures differ from federal expectations.

[P18] EPA should provide guidance on whether title V permit programs satisfy the requirement for permitting new and modified sources under Section 110(a)(2)(3).

[P19] Requiring PSD and NSR provisions in the SIP may be duplicative of federal programs; states need clarity on how state rules interact with EPA's federal implementation and whether SIP provisions can be less stringent if federal PSD/NSR authorities remain.

[P20] The SIP obligations for stationary source control measures and monitoring/reporting should specify acceptable emission testing methods and reporting frequency to avoid inconsistent state practices.

[P21] Air quality modeling requirements should include standardized modeling platforms and documented inputs (emissions inventories, meteorology) to ensure comparability across submissions.

[P21] Environmental groups will request that EPA require transparency of modeling inputs and demand that models be peer-reviewed and publicly available.

[P22] The public participation requirement should mandate early engagement (pre-draft) and meaningful access for EJ communities, including translation, travel reimbursements for commenters, and remote testimony options.

[P22] Local agencies need a clear timeline for consultation and minimum timeframes to review draft rules before final adoption.

[P23] Requirements to address interstate pollution transport lack enforcement mechanisms; downwind states need assurance that EPA will require upwind states to adopt specific emission reduction measures and provide a predictable timeline.

[P23] Multi-state stakeholders will ask for use of modeled contribution thresholds and binding allocation of emission reduction obligations where significant contribution is demonstrated.

[P24] The three-year submission deadline from designations under Section 172(b) should be clarified for areas that have since been redesignated or had boundary changes; EPA should provide a safe-harbor for states with changed designations.

[P24] States will request flexibility or extensions in cases where data collection or legislative action delayed SIP submittal despite good-faith efforts.

[P25] The RACM requirement under 172(c)(1) needs guidance on how "reasonably available" is defined, especially regarding cost-effectiveness thresholds and technological feasibility; businesses want clear cost metrics.

[P25] Environmental advocates will insist that EPA require a transparent RACM screening process that documents rejected options and rationales, rather than perfunctory evaluations.

[P26] The obligation to consider RACT for existing sources may impose significant retrofit costs; EPA should issue clear RACT applicability thresholds and compliance timelines to allow industry planning.

[P26] Conversely, environmental groups will push EPA to ensure strict interpretation of RACT and to require adoption of the best available controls, not minimal technological options.

[P27] The comprehensive emissions inventory requirement should require public access to the underlying raw data and QA/QC procedures so third parties can validate the inventory.

[P27] States should be given federal funding or technical support to update emissions inventories to the required timeliness and accuracy.

[P28] Identifying allowable emissions for major new/modified sources requires clarity on baseline definitions and whether federally enforceable limits in permits can be used to cap potential-to-emit.

[P28] Industry will request that EPA provide guidance on how to treat fugitive emissions and aggregation rules when quantifying allowable emissions.

[P29] The SIP permit requirement for new/modified major stationary sources lacks guidance on permit processing timelines; regulated entities need assurance of timely permitting to avoid project delays.

[P29] EPA should clarify whether the federal PSD program will fill gaps for states that have not yet updated SIP permit programs.

[P30] The exception allowing redesignation without an approved Part D NSR program is acceptable only if the area provides legally enforceable contingency and maintenance measures; EPA should require a binding demonstration that maintenance will be sustained without part D NSR.

[P30] Legal commenters may argue that permitting states to be redesignated without approved NSR undermines statutory intent and could lead to increased emissions from new sources; EPA should promulgate strict conditions for this exception.

[P31] Section 172(c)(6)'s requirement for control measures necessary to achieve attainment must include enforceable timelines and quantitative emission reduction targets, not just aspirational language.

[P31] EPA should require interim milestones and measurable metrics for any control measures included under 172(c)(6).

[P32] The obligation to meet applicable provisions of section 110(a)(2) per 172(c)(7) should include an explicit list of which 110(a)(2) elements are considered "applicable" for purposes of nonattainment planning to avoid disputes.

[P33] Contingency measures under 172(c)(9) must be specific, enforceable, and capable of being implemented without further rulemaking; EPA should not accept vague "trigger" commitments.

[P33] Environmental groups will object to the NPRM's assertion (see P34) that 172(c)(9) contingency measures are irrelevant for redesignation, and request EPA to require contingency plans regardless of current monitored attainment to guard against future violations.

Providing a single email address (aburano.douglas@epa.gov) creates a single point of failure and privacy concerns; EPA should provide a second backup email and a phone contact for receipt confirmation.

The requirement to follow Regulations.gov site instructions may disadvantage commenters unfamiliar with that platform; EPA should provide step-by-step guidance and a plain-language FAQ for first-time users.

The statement that comments cannot be removed conflicts with commenters' privacy and confidentiality rights; EPA must clarify procedures for redacting or removing personal data or inadvertently disclosed information.

raw_output:
[P1] The November 26, 2018 comment deadline is unreasonably short and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow operators, OEMs, and unions sufficient time to analyze the technical and economic impacts of the AD.

[P1] The rule should provide an explicit time zone and receipt standard (e.g., received by 11:59 PM EDT) for the November 26, 2018 deadline to avoid disputes about late submissions.

[P2] The applicability in § 39.13(c) is ambiguous because it does not state whether engines installed on in-service aircraft and engines in storage are both included; clarify that the AD applies to both installed and stored engines with the listed blades.

[P2] The list of affected engine models in § 39.13(c) omits serial number ranges or production dates; request adding serial number, production batch, or fleet applicability criteria to avoid overbroad application to engines that never received the affected blades.

[P2] The phrase "when the listed 1st stage LPC blades are installed" lacks a reference to the specific Pratt & Whitney blade part numbers and approved revisions; require explicit P/N and S/N references to avoid misinterpretation.

[P3] The compliance obligation in § 39.13(f) should include a grandfathering clause for actions already performed in accordance with an FAA-approved alternative method of compliance (AMOC) to avoid double work.

[P3] § 39.13(f) must clarify whether "specified compliance times" include both initial and recurrent intervals described in (g), and confirm that operators may use their maintenance schedules to meet those times if earlier.

[P4] The initial TAI requirement in § 39.13(g)(1) should include clear acceptance/rejection criteria (e.g., defect sizing, disposition thresholds) rather than deferring entirely to an FAA-approved method.

[P5] The inspection trigger in § 39.13(g)(1)(i) that requires inspection at the next M-flange separation or before reaching 7,000 CSN is impractical for some operators who perform on-wing work cycles beyond typical M-flange separations; request alternative triggers tied to flight cycles or calendar time.

[P5] The 6,500 CSN threshold in § 39.13(g)(1)(i) appears arbitrary; provide supporting data and risk analysis demonstrating why 6,500 versus another threshold is appropriate.

[P6] The 500 flight cycle or 180-day window in § 39.13(g)(1)(ii) for blades ≥6,500 CSN or unknown cycles is operationally burdensome and may require unscheduled removals; propose allowing a single additional maintenance opportunity rather than an immediate corrective removal.

[P6] For blades with unknown CSN, § 39.13(g)(1)(ii) should permit use of trace-back procedures or engineering analysis to establish cycles instead of imposing the 500-cycle/180-day mandate.

[P7] The recurrent inspection requirement in § 39.13(g)(2) that mandates inspection at every M-flange separation when blades have ≥1,000 cycles since last TAI creates excessive shop visits for high-utilization fleets; suggest permitting TAI at alternate scheduled engine maintenance events when equivalent inspection access can be achieved.

[P7] The prohibition on any interval exceeding 6,500 cycles since last TAI in § 39.13(g)(2) is overly restrictive for engines in long-term storage or low-utilization buckets; allow a calendar-time cap for low-cycle engines or provide an AMOC path.

[P8] The requirement in § 39.13(g)(3) to remove and replace any blade that fails inspection before the next flight is operationally disruptive for aircraft scheduled for immediate flights; request allowance for limited ferry flights under strict conditions or temporary mitigation with continued monitoring.

[P8] Paragraph (g)(3) should specify what constitutes an "eligible part" for replacement (P/Ns, new vs. overhauled, life-limited part status) to avoid inconsistent interpretations across operators and repair stations.

[P9] Requiring FAA-approved methods for TAI and disposition in § 39.13(g)(4) without providing interim acceptable procedures or a timeline for approvals risks grounding aircraft while waiting for FAA responses; request that the AD list approved methods (e.g., PW ASB Revision No. 6) or allow approved industry-standard procedures until FAA approval is granted.

[P9] The AD should include an expedited process and SLA for FAA approval of TAI methods and dispositions, because current FAA review times can be months and will hamper compliance.

[P10] The credit allowance in § 39.13(h) for pre-effective-date TAI using PW ASB Revision No. 6 is too narrow; expand credit to include inspections done per equivalent industry-recognized procedures or prior FAA-approved AMOCs.

[P10] Require that operators submitting for credit per (h) must retain and make available supporting documentation (reporting format and retention period) — the AD is silent on required records.

[P11] The installation prohibition in § 39.13(i) banning blades with ≥1,000 cycles unless inspected effectively restricts the use of serviceable spares and may disrupt maintenance workflows; request a defined process to allow use of blades that have been inspected and properly documented without re-inspecting.

[P11] The 1,000-cycle installation threshold in § 39.13(i) is inconsistent with the thresholds in paragraphs (g)(1)(i) and (ii); provide a clear rationale or harmonize the thresholds across the AD.

[P12] The exception in § 39.13(i) that permits installation only if the blade passed the inspection required by paragraph (g)(1) is impractical because (g)(1) ties inspection timing to M-flange separations and CSN; request language allowing any FAA-approved TAI inspection meeting (g)(4) criteria to qualify.

[P13] Empowering the Manager, ECO Branch, to approve AMOCs per § 39.13(j)(1) centralizes authority and may create bottlenecks; recommend allowing regional FAA offices or delegated organizations (e.g., DERs) to approve AMOCs to accelerate decisions.

[P14] The requirement in § 39.13(j)(1) to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO is redundant with existing 14 CFR 39.19 procedures and could cause confusion; consolidate and clarify the AMOC submission channel.

[P15] The instruction in § 39.13(j)(1) about addressing information directly to the certification office manager per paragraph (k) is vague; specify the name, office address, and contact details in the AD to prevent misrouting.

[P16] Allowing email submission of AMOC requests per § 39.13(j)(1) is appropriate, but the AD should also permit secure uploads to FAA portals and require confirmation receipts to establish timeliness and completeness.

[P17] The notification requirement in § 39.13(j)(2) to inform the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC is impractical for emergency or time-critical AMOCs; provide an exception for immediate operational needs with retroactive notification within a defined short period (e.g., 48 hours).

[P17] Clarify in § 39.13(j)(2) whether notification to the local FSDO/CHDO manager must be written and retained, and specify the information content required for such notifications to ensure compliance and auditability.

[General] The AD lacks an estimate of the economic impact, labor hours, and parts costs for compliance; include a Regulatory Evaluation or Economic Analysis and a request for comments on cost assumptions.

[General] Provide sample TAI reporting forms and required data fields (blade P/N, S/N, CSN, date, inspector, disposition) to standardize compliance evidence across operators.

[Legal] Several provisions (e.g., FAA-approval requirement in (g)(4), centralized AMOC authority in (j)(1)) may raise due process concerns if approval timelines are not specified; recommend adding timelines and appeal processes for denials.

[Operational] Require coordination language for foreign civil aviation authorities (EASA, Transport Canada, etc.) to adopt harmonized compliance expectations to prevent conflicting directives for operators flying internationally.

[Safety Data] Request that FAA publish the underlying service difficulty reports, root cause analyses, and fracture mechanics data used to justify these inspection intervals to allow independent technical review.

[Implementation] Ask FAA to create a compliance grace period or temporary relief for operators with immediate operational constraints (e.g., humanitarian missions, military support) while ensuring mitigation steps are in place.

[P2] Environmental advocates will support §705.5 but request clarification that coverage includes PFAS present as unintended impurities, reaction byproducts, or degradation products in non-PFAS products, to avoid loopholes.

[P2] International trade groups will object that §705.5 could conflict with importers' obligations under other jurisdictions; they will request harmonization mechanisms and transitional relief for importers subject to foreign reporting requirements to avoid duplicate burdens.

[P3] Consumer product manufacturers will request that §705.10 allow reporting by upstream manufacturers on behalf of downstream users via consolidated submissions to reduce duplicative reporting and administrative burden.

[P4] §705.25's recordkeeping requirements should specify retention periods, format (electronic vs paper), and whether records must be kept in the U.S.; without these specifics, regulated parties face uncertainty about compliance costs and logistics.

[P4] Privacy and business confidentiality concerns: §705.25 must include guidelines on protecting sensitive commercial information, permissible redactions, and procedures for asserting and defending CBI claims to prevent unjustified disclosures.

[P4] Labor unions and workplace safety advocates will urge that §705.25 require record retention that supports worker right-to-know (e.g., access by employees and health professionals), not solely EPA enforcement, to aid occupational health monitoring.

[P2][P3] Manufacturers and importers will request phased implementation under §705.5 and §705.10 (e.g., high-volume PFAS first, low-volume and legacy PFAS later) to allow time to gather historic data and adapt IT systems.

[P3][P4] Legal commenters will ask for safe harbor provisions in §705.10 and §705.25 for good-faith reporting and recordkeeping errors submitted within a cure period rather than immediate civil penalties.

[P6][P7][P8][P9] Multiple stakeholders will ask EPA to publish a comprehensive guidance document with examples, flowcharts, and a pre-submission consultation mechanism to resolve ambiguous determinations about "intended for use by children."

[P1] The November 29, 2018 comment deadline in provision P1 is unreasonably short and should be extended to allow affected operators and labor unions sufficient time to prepare technical comments and cost analyses.

[P1] Request that the FAA provide an electronic portal and confirmation receipts for comments submitted before the November 29, 2018 deadline to avoid disputes about timeliness.

[P2] Provision P2's requirement to "comply within the specified compliance times" needs explicit allowance for supply-chain delays (parts, kit availability, or tooling) and should include an explicit hardship waiver process.

[P2] Operators request clarity about whether compliance times are measured in flight hours, cycles, or calendar days, and ask that the AD explicitly state the metric to avoid inconsistent operator interpretations.

[P3] Provision P3 requires performing all actions in the Boeing Requirements Bulletin "at the applicable times" — commenters ask the FAA to publish a matrix mapping each bulletin task to the AD's specific compliance time to reduce ambiguity.

[P3] Airlines and maintenance providers request clarification whether "all applicable actions" includes optional or alternative tasks listed in the bulletin (e.g., non-mandatory inspection intervals), and ask the FAA to list which bulletin actions are mandatory under this AD.

[P4] Using the AD's effective date in place of the bulletin's original issue date (P4) may create retroactive compliance obligations; request that the FAA specify the effective date explicitly and allow a minimum lead time (e.g., 30 days) after issuance before compliance is required.

[P4] Legal commenters note that substituting the AD effective date for the bulletin issue date could nullify service bulletin compliance histories used for maintenance planning; request guidance on how prior compliance performed against the bulletin’s original issue date will be credited.

[P5] P5 requires performing Boeing-directed alternative inspections/repairs before further flight but only if approved per paragraph (i). Commenters ask for a defined maximum response time for Boeing approvals and FAA disposition to avoid grounding aircraft awaiting approvals.

[P5] MRO organizations request that the rule allow use of industry-standard approved repair design organizations (not only Boeing) when an alternative inspection or repair is needed urgently, or provide interim permissive procedures pending FAA approval per (i).

[P6] The exception in P6 that exempts inspections in areas covered by existing FAA-approved repairs that extend three rows of fasteners may be unsafe if the existing repairs are older or poorly documented; request that the FAA require verification of repair integrity (e.g., non-destructive testing) before skipping inspections.

[P6] Structural repair stations request clarification of what constitutes documentation proving a repair "extends at least three rows of fasteners above and below" — ask for acceptable records formats and whether physical marking is required.

[P7] The obligation in P7 to continue damage tolerance inspections for existing repairs should specify the required inspection intervals and methods; commenters say without explicit intervals there will be inconsistent implementation across operators.

[P7] Labor organizations representing maintenance technicians request that the AD require those damage tolerance inspections be performed only by certificated personnel with specific training on the repair types, to ensure inspections are effective.

[P8] P8's requirement to perform inspections outside repaired areas "as specified" in the Boeing bulletin needs the FAA to publish any deviations the FAA expects to impose relative to the bulletin text; otherwise operators lack regulatory certainty.

[P8] General aviation operators request explicit upper bounds on inspection extent outside repaired areas (e.g., number of rivet rows or inches) to limit scope creep and unnecessary downtime.

[P9] Provision P9 vests AMOC approval authority in the Manager, Los Angeles ACO Branch; commenters from non-West Coast operators request clarity whether other ACO branches have delegated authority or whether centralization will significantly delay AMOC approvals.

[P9] Airlines request published target timelines and performance metrics for the LA ACO's processing of AMOCs to ensure predictable operational planning.

[P10] P10 requires AMOC requests be submitted to a principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19; commenters ask the FAA to also permit direct submission by certified repair stations and Boeing-authorized ODA organizations to streamline technical requests.

[P10] Safety advocates request that the rule mandate timely acknowledgement of AMOC submissions by the principal inspector or FSDO (e.g., within 7 calendar days) to reduce uncertainty.

[P11] Provision P11 instructs that AMOC information sent directly to the certification office manager must be addressed to the person in paragraph (j)(1); commenters request that the AD include the actual name and contact details or publish them concurrently to prevent misrouting.

[P11] Legal commenters ask whether failure to address the AMOC to the specific person named in (j)(1) could be deemed noncompliant; they request a non-waivable alternate procedure to avoid technical rejections.

[P12] Allowing AMOC information via the specified email (P12) is helpful, but commenters request confirmation that encrypted and secure transmission is permitted for proprietary repair data, and that receipt acknowledgment will be provided.

[P12] Commenters request clarification on file size limits, acceptable file formats, and whether attachments (e.g., CAD drawings, NDT reports) will be accepted via that email or require an alternative secure file-transfer method.

[P13] P13 requires notifying the principal inspector or FSDO manager before using an approved AMOC; operators ask for a clear timeline for that notification (e.g., "within 48 hours before implementing") and instructions on whether prior verbal notification is acceptable.

[P13] Pilots and operators request that the AD specify what information must be included in the notification to the principal inspector (AMOC reference, aircraft serial number, date of implementation) to standardize oversight.

[P14] P14 permits use of AMOCs approved by the authorized Boeing ODA for required repairs/modifications; labor safety groups are concerned that allowing OEM ODA approvals without additional FAA review shifts safety responsibility and request FAA concurrence or at least mandatory post-approval FAA oversight.

[P14] MRO and airline commenters support the use of Boeing ODA approvals for efficiency but ask that the AD require Boeing ODAs to document how the AMOC meets the airplane certification basis and provide those documents to the operator and FAA upon request.

[P15] Provision P15 requires that AMOC/repair methods meet the airplane's certification basis and that approvals specifically reference this AD; commenters request guidance on what constitutes sufficient demonstration that a method meets the certification basis, including required analyses, substantiation tests, and supporting data.

[P15] Legal and engineering commenters request the FAA to define the process if the airplane's certification basis is ambiguous or has evolved (e.g., later amendments), and whether equivalency to current standards is acceptable when original basis documents are unavailable.

[P6] Operators ask whether previously undocumented field repairs that appear to meet the "three rows of fasteners" criterion but lack FAA approval must undergo FAA approval before the inspection exemption applies.

[P5] Airlines request that the AD explicitly allow temporary ferry flights to a maintenance base under operational restrictions if an urgent Boeing-identified alternative inspection/repair cannot be approved before further flight, to avoid economic loss and passenger disruption.

[P3] Commenters request that the FAA include in the AD the full text or a complete copy of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 757–53A0111 RB dated May 21, 2018, as referenced, so that the AD can be fully evaluated without needing separate proprietary access.

[P1] Consumer and passenger advocacy groups request that the FAA reopen the comment period if substantive revisions are made after November 29, 2018, to ensure meaningful participation.

[P7] Structural repair stations request that the AD clarify whether damage tolerance inspections for existing repairs may be deferred to coincide with scheduled heavy maintenance to reduce operational impact, provided specified safety margins are met.

[P9] Some commenters warn that centralizing AMOC authority to one ACO manager may create a single point of failure and recommend delegating authority regionally to avoid approval bottlenecks.

[P12] Aviation cybersecurity experts ask whether the specified email address is monitored and protected from spoofing, and request publication of secure submission procedures to protect proprietary and safety-critical AMOC data.

[P15] Request that any AMOC approval explicitly include a duration or review period (e.g., annual revalidation) to ensure long-term compliance with the airplane certification basis and evolving safety data.

[P6] The compliance obligation "within the compliance times specified" lacks a consolidated compliance schedule table in the NPRM; provide explicit time windows (e.g., hours/cycles/calendar) for each affected engine group.

[P6] Legal commenters note that the AD must clearly state when the compliance times begin (e.g., effective date of AD vs. publication date) — please clarify.

[P7] Requiring either an independent inspection after each AGB handcranking pad cover reinstallation or insertion of that inspection into the maintenance program is ambiguous about whether both actions are required for some operators — clarify that one or the other suffices.

[P8] The independent inspection after reinstallation lacks objective acceptance criteria and a description of what constitutes "correct reinstallation" — provide a step-by-step inspection procedure, torque values, tolerances, or a referenced CFM inspection checklist.

[P8] Maintenance organizations request permission to use a suitably qualified technician (e.g., certifying mechanic vs. inspector) for the "independent inspection" and seek a definition of required qualifications and documentation requirements.

[P9] Adding the independent inspection to the approved continuous airworthiness maintenance program "prior to the next removal" is unworkable for engines where the cover has already been removed multiple times — request grandfathering for prior verified actions or allow immediate entry into the program at the next scheduled maintenance opportunity.

[P10] The mandatory terminating action relies solely on replacement of affected AGBs; commenters ask whether equivalent rework/engineering fixes (other than P/N change) approved by FAA/CFM could also serve as terminating actions and request explicit acceptance criteria.

[P11] For CFM56–3 engines, requiring replacement at the next engine shop visit or by December 31, 2026 is an excessively long calendar window for a safety-related AD—either justify the long phase-in with safety/risk analysis or accelerate the mandatory terminating date.

[P11] Operators ask the FAA to clarify whether scheduled shop visits that occur after 12/31/2026 but were booked before the AD effective date qualify for the "next shop visit" compliance or whether the calendar date controls.

[P12] For CFM56–7B engines (except 7B27A variants), the mandatory terminating date of December 31, 2024 is too soon for some international operators with constrained shop availability; request extension to allow coordinated fleet maintenance planning or provide credit for non‑US maintenance accomplished under equivalent regulatory approvals.

[P12] Several commenters request that the FAA permit phased replacement across the fleet (e.g., by tail number priority) and provide relief if a limited number of replacement AGBs are available, including temporary AMOCs to stagger compliance.

[P13] The definition of "engine shop visit" excludes many practical maintenance events; ask the FAA to clarify whether certain common events (e.g., borescope inspections requiring partial disassembly) count as a shop visit.

[P14] The exception excluding separations of flanges for transportation only is reasonable, but request language confirming required recordkeeping to demonstrate a separation was for transportation only.

[P15] The exception for separating flanges solely to replace the fan/propulsor should clarify whether concurrent transient maintenance (e.g., fastener checks) would convert the action into a shop visit — operators need clear bright-line rules.

[P16] The definition of "part eligible for installation" for CFM56–3 engines should list acceptable service bulletin numbers and revision levels explicitly, not just reference rework/reidentification generically.

[P17] Declaring that any AGB with a part number other than the listed ones is eligible could inadvertently permit known unsafe aftermarket or unauthorized parts — propose adding a requirement that "other" part numbers must be documented and traceable, or specifically listing approved successor P/Ns.

[P18] Accepting reworked and reidentified AGBs per the referenced CFM service bulletin requires FAA to publish the exact SB revision(s) and required inspections; commenters ask for incorporation by reference details and where to obtain non‑public CFM SBs.

[P19] The "part eligible for installation" definition for CFM56–7B engines needs to include clarity on rework performed outside CFM facilities and whether OEM authorization is required for reidentification to be accepted.

[P20] Similar to P17, permitting any AGB with a P/N other than the listed 340‑046‑503/504/505 to be eligible risks reinstallation of incompatible or counterfeit parts—request mandatory traceability, documentation, and OEM concurrence.

[P21] For CFM56–7B reworked AGBs, commenters request the FAA to include a validation path for field repairs (approved via AMOC) where the SB rework cannot be performed due to parts constraints.

[P22] Granting the ECO Branch manager authority to approve AMOCs is appropriate, but industry asks for an expedited AMOC review pathway for time-critical fleet-wide issues and for transparent timelines for FAA responses.

[P23] The required routing of AMOC requests through principal inspectors/FSDOs may cause delays; request allowance for direct submission from designated organizational designees (DGAs) or OEMs when accompanied by the operator's concurrence.

[P24] When submitting AMOC data directly to the certification office manager, commenters request confirmation of secure data transfer methods and acknowledgement receipt timelines.

[P25] Allowing AMOC requests via email to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov is helpful; request that the FAA also accept uploads through the FAA's AD docketing portal and provide an auto-acknowledgment with a tracking number.

[P26] The obligation to notify the principal inspector prior to using an approved AMOC is reasonable, but operators ask whether notification may be electronic and whether there is a required lead time before implementing the AMOC.

[P27] The FAA permitting view of referenced service information at a single physical location (Burlington, MA) is insufficient; request that the FAA require CFM and/or the FAA to make the service information available electronically, or provide copies to international authorities.

[P28] Removing AD 2013–26–01 and replacing it with this AD may create recordkeeping burdens; request the FAA clarify whether compliance with the previous AD satisfies any portions of the new AD and provide guidance on reconciling prior corrective actions.

[General] Small charter operators and non-U.S. carriers request explicit discussion of economic impacts, availability of replacement AGBs, and potential disruptions to operations, including a request for a regulatory flexibility analysis.

[General] Legal commenters request the FAA include rationale and safety risk assessment showing the likelihood of failure, incident history, and evidence supporting chosen compliance times and terminating actions.

[General] Maintenance providers request sample logbook entries, MEL allowances (if any), and recommended maintenance-task cards to standardize implementation of the independent inspection across operators.
