[P1] The requirement in §63.2984(a)(1) to maintain the 3-hour average oxidizer temperature at or above the performance-test established value is unworkable for facilities that have short-duration, frequent transient loads (e.g., frequent product changeovers) because a single brief, unavoidable dip could create a 3-hour block exceedance despite compliance intent.

[P1] Industry requests clarity on whether the 3-hour averaging period is rolling or fixed (calendar-aligned) and asks EPA to explicitly allow rolling 3-hour averages to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P1] Petitioners request an explicit allowance in §63.2984(a)(1) to use non-continuous thermal oxidizer monitoring data (e.g., validated redundant thermocouples) when primary temperature probes are offline for maintenance, without triggering a deviation.

[P2] (§63.2984(a)(4)) The provision requiring §63.8(f) Administrator approval to use alternative operating limits for non-thermal oxidizers is overly burdensome and will delay implementation; request a clear, expedited approval pathway and objective criteria for approval.

[P2] Small facilities and state agencies ask EPA to allow pre-approved alternative monitoring parameter sets for commonly used control devices (e.g., catalytic oxidizers, enclosed burners) rather than case-by-case §63.8(f) approvals.

[P3] Requiring inclusion of any approved alternative limits in the OMM plan (§63.2984(a)(4)) is reasonable but commenters request a template and examples to ensure consistent plan content across facilities and states.

[P4] (§63.2984(b)) The 1-hour deadline to "initiate corrective actions" after detecting an operating parameter deviation is too strict for remote operations or smaller plants without 24/7 staffing; request extension to 4 hours or allowance for virtual/remote corrective-action initiation where documented.

[P5] (§63.2984(b)) The phrase "completed in an expeditious manner as specified in the OMM plan" is vague; request that EPA define maximum corrective-action completion times or require OMM plans to include specific elapsed-time commitments for different deviation categories.

[P6] (§63.2984(e)) The mandatory capture and convey requirement referencing Industrial Ventilation procedures for formaldehyde emissions lacks specificity for unconventional oven designs (small batch ovens, mobile ovens); request alternative, performance-based capture criteria and explicit acceptance of engineering controls tailored to such designs.

[P7] (§63.2984(e)) Support for allowing Administrator-approved alternative capture/convey methods, but request an explicit list of acceptable alternative approaches or a clear approval checklist to reduce uncertainty and variation in approval decisions.

[P8] (§63.2985(b)) The compliance by startup or April 11, 2002 requirement for ovens constructed/reconstructed between May 26, 2000 and April 9, 2018 appears out-of-date and contradicts the rule's intent—request correction or explanation of these legacy dates and grandfathering consequences.

[P9] (§63.2985(d)) The requirement that ovens constructed or reconstructed after April 6, 2018 comply at startup or by the final rule publication date lacks a defined compliance date (placeholder "[DATE OF PUBLICATION]") — request EPA to specify a fixed compliance timeline (e.g., 180 days after final rule) and include transitional provisions.

[P10] (§63.2986(g)) The cross-reference to paragraphs (g)(1)-(3) without clear numbering in preamble makes it hard to interpret compliance milestones; request that EPA clearly restate the deadlines and transitional requirements in the final rule text.

[P11] (§63.2986(g)(1)) The requirement to "maintain continuous compliance" before [DATE 181 DAYS AFTER PUBLICATION] is confusing — commenters ask whether the 181-day period is a compliance grace period or a deadline to have written plans; request clarification and a uniform national effective compliance date.

[P12] (§63.2986(g)(2)) The obligation to "always operate and maintain any affected source ... in a manner consistent with safety and good air pollution control practices" is duplicative and may be interpreted to require additional unspecified control actions; request an explicit statement that this duty does not impose additional numeric emission reductions beyond applicable standards.

[P13] (§63.2986(g)(2) condition) Commenters (industry/legal) welcome the clarification that no further emission reduction is required once standard levels are achieved (P13), but ask EPA to add an example illustrating what constitutes "no further efforts" to avoid enforcement overreach.

[P14] (§63.2986(g)(3)) The requirement to develop a written SSM plan before the 181-day date creates burdens for small sources; request model SSM plan language and allow use of existing SSM plans that meet or exceed these requirements instead of requiring wholly new plans.

[P15] (§63.2992(b)) The cross-reference to §63.7(a)-(h) for performance testing may impose duplicative or conflicting requirements with other subparts; request EPA to clarify where §63.7 requirements differ from prior subpart tests and to harmonize schedules and methods.

[P16] (§63.2992(e)) Allowing the Administrator to specify "such conditions as...representative performance" creates potential for arbitrary directives; request objective criteria (e.g., typical production rate range, binder formulation, oxidizer load) to be published so permittees can plan tests.

[P17] (§63.2992(e) prohibition) The prohibition on performing performance tests during malfunctions is appropriate; however, request clarification on whether "malfunction" includes temporary control device ramp-up/down and how to document exclusion when these are inherent to normal operation.

[P18] (§63.2992(e)) The recordkeeping requirement to "include explanations showing test conditions represent normal operation" could expose proprietary operational details; request that EPA allow submission of non-confidential summaries and permit CBI protection for commercially sensitive process parameters.

[P19] (§63.2992(e)) Facilities request that the list of records to be made available to the Administrator upon request be limited to those "necessary to determine the conditions of performance tests" and that EPA define the minimum documentation required to avoid overly broad record demands.

[P20] (§63.2993 intro) Use of EPA Method 1 to select sampling ports is standard; however, commenters request allowance for modern stack configurations and CFD modeling to supplement physical port selection when Method 1 is impractical.

[P21] (§63.2993(b)) Requiring EPA Method 2 for volumetric flow is appropriate, but industry requests explicit acceptance of recent Method 2 alternatives or proven flow measurement technologies (e.g., ultrasonic flow meters) when validated per Appendix A procedures.

[P22] (§63.2993(c)) Requiring Method 3/3A for O2/CO2 is appropriate but request explicit allowance to use continuous analyzers that meet QA/QC criteria in lieu of extractive Method 3 when validated.

[P23] (§63.2993(d)) EPA Method 4 for moisture is standard; request clarification on acceptable frequency and whether continuous moisture monitors with documented QA/QC may substitute.

[P24] (§63.2993(e)) Mandating Methods 316, 318, or 320 for formaldehyde measurement may not reflect the state of the science and availability of labs; request EPA to accept equivalent validated methods and to publish certification criteria for lab methods.

[P25] (§63.2994(a)) The preparatory steps before performance testing are necessary but commenters request that EPA provide a checklist and minimum lead times (e.g., 30 days notice) to coordinate testing and lab scheduling.

[P26] (§63.2994(a)(1)) Requirement to install and calibrate all equipment before testing must recognize seasonal or long-lead calibration suppliers; request flexibility to use prior calibration records within a defined time window rather than on-site pre-test calibration in certain circumstances.

[P27] (§63.2994(a)(2)) Mandating a CMS quality control program and written procedures per §63.8(d)(1)-(2) is reasonable, but small facilities request a simplified template or tiered requirements proportionate to emission risk.

[P28] (§63.2994(a)(2)) Requiring retention of CMS written procedures for the life of the source is burdensome; request that retention be required only for 5 years after last applicability or until the source is permanently retired.

[P29] (§63.2994(a)(2)) The 5-year retention for superseded performance evaluation plans is excessive for small businesses; recommend reducing retention of superseded versions to 3 years consistent with many state records requirements.

[P30] (§63.2994(a)(2)) EPA's suggestion that a corrective action program "should" be included in the plan (recommended) should be made mandatory given its importance to demonstrate timely corrective actions and repeatability.

[P31] (§63.2994(a)(3)) The CMS performance evaluation per §63.8(e) is resource-intensive; request EPA to allow coordinated audits with state agencies to reduce duplicative oversight and to permit use of third-party accredited testers.

[P32] (§63.2996(a)) Monitoring frequencies in Table 1 are generally appropriate; however, requiring continuous monitoring of oxidizer temperature (Table 1 item 1) without explicit redundancy/backup requirements risks spurious violations due to single sensor failures—request a minimum redundancy requirement or allowance to use validated surrogate data during sensor downtime.

[P33] (§63.2996(b)) Excluding monitoring when using non-HAP binder is helpful, but commenters request a clear definition of "non-HAP binder" (i.e., thresholds for HAP content by weight) to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P34] (§63.2998 intro) The broad requirement to "maintain records per §63.10 procedures" should include explicit electronic recordkeeping standards and retention periods to align with CEDRI and state programs.

[P35] (§63.2998(a)) Because §63.10 cross-references are complex, commenters request a consolidated table in the final rule that maps each record type to retention period and format for ease of compliance.

[P36] (§63.2998(c)) Requiring recording of Table 1 parameters during HAP-containing binder use is reasonable, but commenters request explicit rounding/decimal requirements and acceptable units for reporting (e.g., lb/h to two decimal places).

[P37] (§63.2998(c)) If electing not to monitor during non-HAP binder periods, the requirement to record start/end dates/times is acceptable but should permit batch-level or shift-level entries rather than continuous timestamps to reduce administrative burden.

[P38] (§63.2998(e)) The placeholder for recording requirements "if an operating parameter deviation occurs before [DATE]" needs a defined effective date; commenters request a firm date and a statement whether pre-existing deviations prior to final rule publication must be retrospectively recorded.

[P39] (§63.2998(f)) Retaining SSM records specified in §63.6(e)(3)(iii)-(v) prior to the specified date is potentially duplicative—request EPA to allow use of existing SSM record formats and to harmonize retention periods with state rules.

[P40] (§63.2998(g)) The post-[180-day] requirement to record detailed failure information (date/time/duration; cause; estimates; corrective actions with timestamps) is onerous; industry asks EPA to allow aggregated monthly reporting for minor events and to limit the requirement for emission estimation to exceedances above a numeric threshold (e.g., >5% over limit).

[P41] (§63.2998(g)(1)) Recording date/time/duration for each failure is reasonable, but request clear guidance on how to treat intermittent sensor false-alarms (e.g., debouncing rules) so facilities are not required to record meaningless sub-minute failures.

[P42] (§63.2998(g)(2)) The requirement to "describe the cause" of each failure should be proportional; recommend tiers (known cause with root-cause analysis for major failures, preliminary cause statements for minor/short events).

[P43] (§63.2998(g)(3)) Requiring an estimate of pollutant emissions over limits and description of the estimation method for each failure will impose modeling or sampling costs; request EPA to allow use of conservative engineering emission factors or default estimation methods provided by EPA to standardize reporting.

[P44] (§63.2998(g)(4)) Mandating timestamps for initiation and completion of corrective actions is practical, but commenters seek clarification on whether automated control system logs are acceptable evidence and whether retrospective approximate timestamps are permitted when automated logging is unavailable.

[P45] (§63.2999(b)) The requirement to keep records "readily available" and "easily inspectable" is appropriate; request specific maximum retrieval times (e.g., within 3 business days) and acceptable electronic file formats to avoid disputes during inspections.

[P46] (§63.2999(c)) Allowing CEDRI electronic maintenance is helpful, but facilities need explicit instructions about which record types must still be maintained locally (e.g., original calibration certificates) vs. those that may be solely stored in CEDRI.

[P47] (§63.2999(c) condition) The rule's statement that electronic maintenance does not affect on-site availability requirements is potentially burdensome for facilities that rely primarily on cloud storage; request allowance for secure remote access during on-site inspections or acceptance of printed copies upon request.

[P48] (§63.3000(c)) Semiannual reporting frequency is reasonable; however, the mixture of quarterly reporting triggers before certain dates (P50) and semiannual thereafter creates complexity—request a single standard reporting cadence and clearer transition rules.

[P49] (§63.3000(c)(1)) The 30-day deadline to deliver or postmark semiannual compliance reports is strict for facilities that need to compile emission estimates for incidents; request extension to 45 days or allowance for an interim submission followed by a final within 90 days.

[P50] (§63.3000(c)(1) & P50) The requirement to begin quarterly reports "before [DATE 1 DAY AFTER PUBLICATION]" if you deviate from limits is unclear—commenters request EPA to clarify whether that creates retroactive quarterly reporting obligations and to provide a de minimis deviation threshold to avoid immediate quarterly reporting for trivial events.

[P51] (§63.3000(c)(1) exception) The elimination of quarterly reports after the publication date is welcomed, but states and enforcement agencies might still require quarterly updates; request EPA to coordinate with states to avoid conflicting reporting schedules.

[P52] (§63.3000(c)(4)) The requirement to include a statement of "no deviations" is reasonable but recommend a standard certification language and signer (e.g., responsible official) to ensure legality and consistency.

[P53] (§63.3000(c)(5)) The detailed reporting requirements for deviations occurring before the 181-day date are extensive; request EPA to provide an electronic reporting template and examples to minimize inconsistent submissions.

[P54] (§63.3000(c)(5)(i)) Requiring date/time/duration for each failure in semiannual reports is redundant with contemporaneous records; request allowance to reference previously submitted deviation logs rather than repeating the full dataset.

[P55] (§63.3000(c)(5)(ii)) The obligation to report CMS inoperative times excludes zero/high-level checks, but commenters ask EPA to define "inoperative" vs. "out-of-service for maintenance" to avoid misclassification.

[P56] (§63.3000(c)(5)(iii)) Reporting CMS out-of-control periods should be harmonized with §63.8(c)(8) content; commenters request EPA to explicitly allow reliance on manufacturer's alarm logs and third-party calibrator certificates to satisfy the §63.8(c)(8) documentation.

[P57] (§63.3000(c)(5)(iv)) The requirement to estimate emissions over limits for each affected equipment piece in semiannual reports is duplicative of P43; request default calculation methodologies from EPA and a de minimis cutoff to relieve burden for marginal exceedances.

[P58] (§63.3000(c)(5)(v)) Reporting timestamps of corrective actions and cause descriptions should be linked to the SSM plan actions; recommend EPA require facilities to include a reference to the SSM plan step taken rather than free-form narratives.

[P59] (§63.3000(c)(5)(vi)) Requiring total duration and percent operating time for failures may penalize intermittent processes; request clarity on how to compute percent operating time for facilities that operate in campaigns or for limited shifts.

[P60] (§63.3000(c)(5)(vii)) The breakdown of failure durations by cause categories is useful but the "known" vs "unknown" categories are ambiguous; ask EPA to provide definitions and examples for each cause category to improve consistency.

[P61] (§63.3000(c)(5)(viii)) The brief description of process units involved should have a standard minimum content (equipment ID, capacity, normal operating rate) to avoid superficial or inconsistent descriptions across facilities.

[P62] (§63.3000(c)(5)(ix)) The brief description of the continuous parameter monitoring system should specify required details (manufacture/model, calibration frequency, span/detection limits) rather than leave this open-ended.

[P63] (§63.3000(d)) The 60-day deadline to submit performance test results is tight when analytical labs require extended report turnarounds; request EPA to extend to 90 days or allow a one-time 30-day extension upon written request.

[P64] (§63.3000(d)(1)) Requiring use of EPA ERT-supported methods and CEDRI for certain tests will be challenging for tests using older methods; ask EPA to publish a current ERT-supported methods list at least 180 days before final rule compliance dates.

[P65] (§63.3000(d)(2)) For test methods not supported by ERT, the requirement to submit to the Administrator at the §63.13 address is fine but request allowance for modern electronic submittal to a designated state or EPA regional email to streamline reporting.

[P66] (§63.3000(d)(3)) The CBI submission procedure requiring physical CBI media to EPA CBI Office and a redacted file via CDX is procedurally confusing and costly; request EPA permit secure electronic CBI submission (SFTP or encrypted upload) to the CBI office and clarify timelines.

[P67] (§63.3000(e)) The cross-reference imposing §63.10(d)(5) reporting for SSM events before the 181-day date needs clarification regarding which events trigger reporting and whether previously reported events satisfy the requirement.

[P68] (§63.3000(f)) The "EPA system outage" claim option is useful but the required notification content (P70) is burdensome; request a short-form interim notification requirement (basic outage notice) with full details submitted within 15 days.

[P69] (§63.3000(f)) The requirement to submit the rationale tying the reporting delay to the EPA outage may require legal analysis; request EPA to accept operator attestations in good faith for minor delayed reports.

[P70] (§63.3000(f)) Facilities request EPA to publish an online, standardized outage claim form to ensure consistent submissions and faster EPA processing.

[P71] (§63.3000(g)) The force majeure claims process is reasonable but could be misused; request EPA to publish objective examples of qualifying force majeure events and provide maximum expected response times from EPA on claim acceptance.

[P72] (§63.3000(g)) The obligation to notify the Administrator "as soon as possible" when intending to assert force majeure needs a defined maximum timeframe (e.g., within 7 calendar days) to provide certainty.

[P73] (§63.3000(g)) Requiring description of measures taken to minimize delay during a force majeure event is appropriate; request EPA to acknowledge unavoidable delays where measures were impossible (e.g., road closures in disaster zones).

[P74] (§63.3000(g)) The Administrator's discretion to accept force majeure claims and extend deadlines introduces regulatory uncertainty; recommend EPA publish appeal/reconsideration procedures and average processing timelines for such claims.

[P75] (Table 1 item 1) Continuous monitoring of thermal oxidizer temperature with 15-minute and 3-hour block averages is appropriate, but request explicit allowed data validation/QA procedures (e.g., 3-hour averaging tolerance during probe calibration) and acceptance of redundant sensors.

[P76] (Table 1 item 2) Allowing OMM-specified frequencies for other parameters makes sense, but commenters request minimum frequencies for common parameters (e.g., binder flow, production rate) to ensure comparability across facilities.

[P77] (Table 1 item 3) The daily lb/h UF resin solids application rate calculation for each product is operationally burdensome where production is continuous and products change frequently; request allowance to report shift-level averages or batch totals and specify calculation methodology.

[P78] (Table 1 item 4) Recording free-formaldehyde content for each resin lot each operating day is reasonable, but commenters request recognition of supplier certificates of analysis as acceptable source documentation and allow entering supplier-provided lot-level values.

[P79] (Table 1 item 5) Measuring loss-on-ignition at least once per day per product could be impractical in small operations producing many small runs; request allowance to sample representative lots or to use supplier QC data when a certified supplier is used.

[P80] (Table 1 item 6) Recording the UF-to-latex ratio for each binder batch is feasible but for high-frequency small batches this is onerous; request allowance to record standard recipe identifiers and note deviations rather than full ratio logs for each batch.

[P81] (Table 1 item 7) Recording weight per square for each final mat product daily may duplicate existing quality control records; recommend EPA allow cross-reference to existing product QC records instead of duplicative entries.

[P82] (Table 1 item 8) Requiring average production rate per product each operating day is generally acceptable but commenters request clear instructions for products with variable production rates within a day (e.g., provide weighted average or separate entries).

[P83] (Table 1 footnote d / P33 / P83) The allowance to omit monitoring when using a non-HAP binder must be coordinated with suppliers and testing to verify non-HAP status; request EPA to define acceptable documentation (supplier certification, third-party analysis) and set minimum HAP content thresholds for qualification.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The requirement in §63.2984(a)(1) to maintain the 3-hour average oxidizer temperature at or above the performance-test established value is unworkable for facilities that have short-duration, frequent transient loads (e.g., frequent product changeovers) because a single brief, unavoidable dip could create a 3-hour block exceedance despite compliance intent.
Industry requests clarity on whether the 3-hour averaging period is rolling or fixed (calendar-aligned) and asks EPA to explicitly allow rolling 3-hour averages to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

Petitioners request an explicit allowance in §63.2984(a)(1) to use non-continuous thermal oxidizer monitoring data (e.g., validated redundant thermocouples) when primary temperature probes are offline for maintenance, without triggering a deviation.

(§63.2984(a)(4)) The provision requiring §63.8(f) Administrator approval to use alternative operating limits for non-thermal oxidizers is overly burdensome and will delay implementation; request a clear, expedited approval pathway and objective criteria for approval.

Small facilities and state agencies ask EPA to allow pre-approved alternative monitoring parameter sets for commonly used control devices (e.g., catalytic oxidizers, enclosed burners) rather than case-by-case §63.8(f) approvals.

Requiring inclusion of any approved alternative limits in the OMM plan (§63.2984(a)(4)) is reasonable but commenters request a template and examples to ensure consistent plan content across facilities and states.

(§63.2984(b)) The 1-hour deadline to "initiate corrective actions" after detecting an operating parameter deviation is too strict for remote operations or smaller plants without 24/7 staffing; request extension to 4 hours or allowance for virtual/remote corrective-action initiation where documented.

(§63.2984(b)) The phrase "completed in an expeditious manner as specified in the OMM plan" is vague; request that EPA define maximum corrective-action completion times or require OMM plans to include specific elapsed-time commitments for different deviation categories.

(§63.2984(e)) The mandatory capture and convey requirement referencing Industrial Ventilation procedures for formaldehyde emissions lacks specificity for unconventional oven designs (small batch ovens, mobile ovens); request alternative, performance-based capture criteria and explicit acceptance of engineering controls tailored to such designs.

(§63.2984(e)) Support for allowing Administrator-approved alternative capture/convey methods, but request an explicit list of acceptable alternative approaches or a clear approval checklist to reduce uncertainty and variation in approval decisions.

(§63.2985(b)) The compliance by startup or April 11, 2002 requirement for ovens constructed/reconstructed between May 26, 2000 and April 9, 2018 appears out-of-date and contradicts the rule's intent—request correction or explanation of these legacy dates and grandfathering consequences.

(§63.2985(d)) The requirement that ovens constructed or reconstructed after April 6, 2018 comply at startup or by the final rule publication date lacks a defined compliance date (placeholder "[DATE OF PUBLICATION]") — request EPA to specify a fixed compliance timeline (e.g., 180 days after final rule) and include transitional provisions.

(§63.2986(g)) The cross-reference to paragraphs (g)(1)-(3) without clear numbering in preamble makes it hard to interpret compliance milestones; request that EPA clearly restate the deadlines and transitional requirements in the final rule text.

(§63.2986(g)(1)) The requirement to "maintain continuous compliance" before [DATE 181 DAYS AFTER PUBLICATION] is confusing — commenters ask whether the 181-day period is a compliance grace period or a deadline to have written plans; request clarification and a uniform national effective compliance date.

(§63.2986(g)(2)) The obligation to "always operate and maintain any affected source ... in a manner consistent with safety and good air pollution control practices" is duplicative and may be interpreted to require additional unspecified control actions; request an explicit statement that this duty does not impose additional numeric emission reductions beyond applicable standards.

(§63.2986(g)(2) condition) Commenters (industry/legal) welcome the clarification that no further emission reduction is required once standard levels are achieved (P13), but ask EPA to add an example illustrating what constitutes "no further efforts" to avoid enforcement overreach.

(§63.2986(g)(3)) The requirement to develop a written SSM plan before the 181-day date creates burdens for small sources; request model SSM plan language and allow use of existing SSM plans that meet or exceed these requirements instead of requiring wholly new plans.

(§63.2992(b)) The cross-reference to §63.7(a)-(h) for performance testing may impose duplicative or conflicting requirements with other subparts; request EPA to clarify where §63.7 requirements differ from prior subpart tests and to harmonize schedules and methods.

(§63.2992(e)) Allowing the Administrator to specify "such conditions as...representative performance" creates potential for arbitrary directives; request objective criteria (e.g., typical production rate range, binder formulation, oxidizer load) to be published so permittees can plan tests.

(§63.2992(e) prohibition) The prohibition on performing performance tests during malfunctions is appropriate; however, request clarification on whether "malfunction" includes temporary control device ramp-up/down and how to document exclusion when these are inherent to normal operation.

(§63.2992(e)) The recordkeeping requirement to "include explanations showing test conditions represent normal operation" could expose proprietary operational details; request that EPA allow submission of non-confidential summaries and permit CBI protection for commercially sensitive process parameters.

(§63.2992(e)) Facilities request that the list of records to be made available to the Administrator upon request be limited to those "necessary to determine the conditions of performance tests" and that EPA define the minimum documentation required to avoid overly broad record demands.

(§63.2993 intro) Use of EPA Method 1 to select sampling ports is standard; however, commenters request allowance for modern stack configurations and CFD modeling to supplement physical port selection when Method 1 is impractical.

(§63.2993(b)) Requiring EPA Method 2 for volumetric flow is appropriate, but industry requests explicit acceptance of recent Method 2 alternatives or proven flow measurement technologies (e.g., ultrasonic flow meters) when validated per Appendix A procedures.
(§63.2993(c)) Requiring Method 3/3A for O2/CO2 is appropriate but request explicit allowance to use continuous analyzers that meet QA/QC criteria in lieu of extractive Method 3 when validated.
(§63.2993(d)) EPA Method 4 for moisture is standard; request clarification on acceptable frequency and whether continuous moisture monitors with documented QA/QC may substitute.

(§63.2993(e)) Mandating Methods 316, 318, or 320 for formaldehyde measurement may not reflect the state of the science and availability of labs; request EPA to accept equivalent validated methods and to publish certification criteria for lab methods.

(§63.2994(a)) The preparatory steps before performance testing are necessary but commenters request that EPA provide a checklist and minimum lead times (e.g., 30 days notice) to coordinate testing and lab scheduling.

(§63.2994(a)(1)) Requirement to install and calibrate all equipment before testing must recognize seasonal or long-lead calibration suppliers; request flexibility to use prior calibration records within a defined time window rather than on-site pre-test calibration in certain circumstances.

(§63.2994(a)(2)) Mandating a CMS quality control program and written procedures per §63.8(d)(1)-(2) is reasonable, but small facilities request a simplified template or tiered requirements proportionate to emission risk.

(§63.2994(a)(2)) Requiring retention of CMS written procedures for the life of the source is burdensome; request that retention be required only for 5 years after last applicability or until the source is permanently retired.

(§63.2994(a)(2)) The 5-year retention for superseded performance evaluation plans is excessive for small businesses; recommend reducing retention of superseded versions to 3 years consistent with many state records requirements.

(§63.2994(a)(2)) EPA's suggestion that a corrective action program "should" be included in the plan (recommended) should be made mandatory given its importance to demonstrate timely corrective actions and repeatability.

(§63.2994(a)(3)) The CMS performance evaluation per §63.8(e) is resource-intensive; request EPA to allow coordinated audits with state agencies to reduce duplicative oversight and to permit use of third-party accredited testers.

(§63.2996(a)) Monitoring frequencies in Table 1 are generally appropriate; however, requiring continuous monitoring of oxidizer temperature (Table 1 item 1) without explicit redundancy/backup requirements risks spurious violations due to single sensor failures—request a minimum redundancy requirement or allowance to use validated surrogate data during sensor downtime.

(§63.2996(b)) Excluding monitoring when using non-HAP binder is helpful, but commenters request a clear definition of "non-HAP binder" (i.e., thresholds for HAP content by weight) to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

(§63.2998 intro) The broad requirement to "maintain records per §63.10 procedures" should include explicit electronic recordkeeping standards and retention periods to align with CEDRI and state programs.
(§63.2998(a)) Because §63.10 cross-references are complex, commenters request a consolidated table in the final rule that maps each record type to retention period and format for ease of compliance.

(§63.2998(c)) Requiring recording of Table 1 parameters during HAP-containing binder use is reasonable, but commenters request explicit rounding/decimal requirements and acceptable units for reporting (e.g., lb/h to two decimal places).

(§63.2998(c)) If electing not to monitor during non-HAP binder periods, the requirement to record start/end dates/times is acceptable but should permit batch-level or shift-level entries rather than continuous timestamps to reduce administrative burden.

(§63.2998(e)) The placeholder for recording requirements "if an operating parameter deviation occurs before [DATE]" needs a defined effective date; commenters request a firm date and a statement whether pre-existing deviations prior to final rule publication must be retrospectively recorded.

(§63.2998(f)) Retaining SSM records specified in §63.6(e)(3)(iii)-(v) prior to the specified date is potentially duplicative—request EPA to allow use of existing SSM record formats and to harmonize retention periods with state rules.

(§63.2998(g)) The post-[180-day] requirement to record detailed failure information (date/time/duration; cause; estimates; corrective actions with timestamps) is onerous; industry asks EPA to allow aggregated monthly reporting for minor events and to limit the requirement for emission estimation to exceedances above a numeric threshold (e.g., >5% over limit).

(§63.2998(g)(1)) Recording date/time/duration for each failure is reasonable, but request clear guidance on how to treat intermittent sensor false-alarms (e.g., debouncing rules) so facilities are not required to record meaningless sub-minute failures.

(§63.2998(g)(2)) The requirement to "describe the cause" of each failure should be proportional; recommend tiers (known cause with root-cause analysis for major failures, preliminary cause statements for minor/short events).

(§63.2998(g)(3)) Requiring an estimate of pollutant emissions over limits and description of the estimation method for each failure will impose modeling or sampling costs; request EPA to allow use of conservative engineering emission factors or default estimation methods provided by EPA to standardize reporting.

(§63.2998(g)(4)) Mandating timestamps for initiation and completion of corrective actions is practical, but commenters seek clarification on whether automated control system logs are acceptable evidence and whether retrospective approximate timestamps are permitted when automated logging is unavailable.

(§63.2999(b)) The requirement to keep records "readily available" and "easily inspectable" is appropriate; request specific maximum retrieval times (e.g., within 3 business days) and acceptable electronic file formats to avoid disputes during inspections.

(§63.2999(c)) Allowing CEDRI electronic maintenance is helpful, but facilities need explicit instructions about which record types must still be maintained locally (e.g., original calibration certificates) vs. those that may be solely stored in CEDRI.

(§63.2999(c) condition) The rule's statement that electronic maintenance does not affect on-site availability requirements is potentially burdensome for facilities that rely primarily on cloud storage; request allowance for secure remote access during on-site inspections or acceptance of printed copies upon request.

(§63.3000(c)) Semiannual reporting frequency is reasonable; however, the mixture of quarterly reporting triggers before certain dates (P50) and semiannual thereafter creates complexity—request a single standard reporting cadence and clearer transition rules.

(§63.3000(c)(1)) The 30-day deadline to deliver or postmark semiannual compliance reports is strict for facilities that need to compile emission estimates for incidents; request extension to 45 days or allowance for an interim submission followed by a final within 90 days.

(§63.3000(c)(1) & P50) The requirement to begin quarterly reports "before [DATE 1 DAY AFTER PUBLICATION]" if you deviate from limits is unclear—commenters request EPA to clarify whether that creates retroactive quarterly reporting obligations and to provide a de minimis deviation threshold to avoid immediate quarterly reporting for trivial events.

(§63.3000(c)(1) exception) The elimination of quarterly reports after the publication date is welcomed, but states and enforcement agencies might still require quarterly updates; request EPA to coordinate with states to avoid conflicting reporting schedules.

(§63.3000(c)(4)) The requirement to include a statement of "no deviations" is reasonable but recommend a standard certification language and signer (e.g., responsible official) to ensure legality and consistency.

(§63.3000(c)(5)) The detailed reporting requirements for deviations occurring before the 181-day date are extensive; request EPA to provide an electronic reporting template and examples to minimize inconsistent submissions.

(§63.3000(c)(5)(i)) Requiring date/time/duration for each failure in semiannual reports is redundant with contemporaneous records; request allowance to reference previously submitted deviation logs rather than repeating the full dataset.

(§63.3000(c)(5)(ii)) The obligation to report CMS inoperative times excludes zero/high-level checks, but commenters ask EPA to define "inoperative" vs. "out-of-service for maintenance" to avoid misclassification.

(§63.3000(c)(5)(iii)) Reporting CMS out-of-control periods should be harmonized with §63.8(c)(8) content; commenters request EPA to explicitly allow reliance on manufacturer's alarm logs and third-party calibrator certificates to satisfy the §63.8(c)(8) documentation.

(§63.3000(c)(5)(iv)) The requirement to estimate emissions over limits for each affected equipment piece in semiannual reports is duplicative of P43; request default calculation methodologies from EPA and a de minimis cutoff to relieve burden for marginal exceedances.

(§63.3000(c)(5)(v)) Reporting timestamps of corrective actions and cause descriptions should be linked to the SSM plan actions; recommend EPA require facilities to include a reference to the SSM plan step taken rather than free-form narratives.

(§63.3000(c)(5)(vi)) Requiring total duration and percent operating time for failures may penalize intermittent processes; request clarity on how to compute percent operating time for facilities that operate in campaigns or for limited shifts.

(§63.3000(c)(5)(vii)) The breakdown of failure durations by cause categories is useful but the "known" vs "unknown" categories are ambiguous; ask EPA to provide definitions and examples for each cause category to improve consistency.

(§63.3000(c)(5)(viii)) The brief description of process units involved should have a standard minimum content (equipment ID, capacity, normal operating rate) to avoid superficial or inconsistent descriptions across facilities.

(§63.3000(c)(5)(ix)) The brief description of the continuous parameter monitoring system should specify required details (manufacture/model, calibration frequency, span/detection limits) rather than leave this open-ended.

(§63.3000(d)) The 60-day deadline to submit performance test results is tight when analytical labs require extended report turnarounds; request EPA to extend to 90 days or allow a one-time 30-day extension upon written request.

(§63.3000(d)(1)) Requiring use of EPA ERT-supported methods and CEDRI for certain tests will be challenging for tests using older methods; ask EPA to publish a current ERT-supported methods list at least 180 days before final rule compliance dates.

(§63.3000(d)(2)) For test methods not supported by ERT, the requirement to submit to the Administrator at the §63.13 address is fine but request allowance for modern electronic submittal to a designated state or EPA regional email to streamline reporting.

(§63.3000(d)(3)) The CBI submission procedure requiring physical CBI media to EPA CBI Office and a redacted file via CDX is procedurally confusing and costly; request EPA permit secure electronic CBI submission (SFTP or encrypted upload) to the CBI office and clarify timelines.

(§63.3000(e)) The cross-reference imposing §63.10(d)(5) reporting for SSM events before the 181-day date needs clarification regarding which events trigger reporting and whether previously reported events satisfy the requirement.

(§63.3000(f)) The "EPA system outage" claim option is useful but the required notification content (P70) is burdensome; request a short-form interim notification requirement (basic outage notice) with full details submitted within 15 days.

(§63.3000(f)) The requirement to submit the rationale tying the reporting delay to the EPA outage may require legal analysis; request EPA to accept operator attestations in good faith for minor delayed reports.
(§63.3000(f)) Facilities request EPA to publish an online, standardized outage claim form to ensure consistent submissions and faster EPA processing.

(§63.3000(g)) The force majeure claims process is reasonable but could be misused; request EPA to publish objective examples of qualifying force majeure events and provide maximum expected response times from EPA on claim acceptance.

(§63.3000(g)) The obligation to notify the Administrator "as soon as possible" when intending to assert force majeure needs a defined maximum timeframe (e.g., within 7 calendar days) to provide certainty.

(§63.3000(g)) Requiring description of measures taken to minimize delay during a force majeure event is appropriate; request EPA to acknowledge unavoidable delays where measures were impossible (e.g., road closures in disaster zones).

(§63.3000(g)) The Administrator's discretion to accept force majeure claims and extend deadlines introduces regulatory uncertainty; recommend EPA publish appeal/reconsideration procedures and average processing timelines for such claims.

[P1] The incorporation by reference of FAA Order 7400.11B dated August 3, 2017 creates legal uncertainty because it is an outdated document; the FAA should instead incorporate the most recent revision or publish the revision date and edition to be used.

[P1] Legal counsel: incorporating FAA Order 7400.11B by reference without providing full text in the docket could impede meaningful public review and may violate the Administrative Procedure Act unless copies are made readily available to the public.

[P1] Industry commenter: Pilots and operators need a clear crosswalk of changes between the previously incorporated order and the August 3, 2017 edition; the rule should include a summary of substantive changes to airspace designations to avoid operational confusion.

[P1] Safety advocacy group: The rule should explicitly state whether the incorporation includes any appendices, figures, or reporting points that have been modified, because those details directly affect navigation and safety.

[P2] Local government/airport authority: Designating a 4.6-mile radius Class D up to but not including 2,000 feet MSL at Castle Airport will impose new ATC requirements on local general aviation pilots; the FAA must provide data supporting the need for that specific radius and ceiling.

[P2] Business aviation operator: The proposed 4.6-mile radius and specified bearing segments may restrict efficient approaches and departures for business jets; request an analysis showing this configuration minimizes operational impacts while achieving safety goals.

[P2] Flight schools/GA pilots: The new Class D around Castle Airport will increase radio/ATC workload and costs for training flights; request an exemption or phased implementation for flight training operations or justification that training activity was considered.

[P2] Environmental/land-use group: The imposition of Class D could concentrate flight paths and increase noise in neighborhoods within the 4.6-mile radius; ask for a noise analysis and mitigation plan.

[P3] Local pilots: Making Class D airspace effective only via NOTAMs creates unpredictability; request that the rule specify minimum advance notice times for NOTAMs so pilots can plan accordingly.

[P3] Legal expert: Relying on NOTAMs to activate/deactivate the Class D may interfere with established airspace rights and complicate legal determinations (e.g., whether an operation was in controlled airspace); request clarification of legal status during NOTAM gaps.

[P3] Regional airlines/charter operators: Conditional activation via NOTAMs could cause dispatch and scheduling disruptions; ask the FAA to require coordination protocols between the airport operator and ATC to ensure predictable activation windows.

[P4] Chart users/pilots: Continuous publication of effective dates/times in the Chart Supplement is helpful, but the FAA should clarify whether Chart Supplement updates will show upcoming NOTAM-based activations and how far in advance they will be listed.

[P4] Safety advocate: Relying on Chart Supplement alone is insufficient because supplements are updated on a scheduled basis; request additional mechanisms (e.g., online portal) for timely updates of temporary recurring effective times.

[P5] GA community: Designating Class E beginning at 700 feet within a 7.2-mile radius may push VFR traffic into lower-level uncontrolled airspace closer to terrain or obstacles; request assessment of VFR traffic dispersal and collision risk.

[P5] Instrument flight operators: The 7.2-mile radius for Class E(700) should be justified by instrument approach procedures; request publication of the procedure reference or obstacle/terrain basis for that radius.

[P5] Agricultural aviation operators: A 7.2-mile Class E(700) could interfere with low-level agricultural operations; request either exclusionary corridors or coordination procedures for aerial application flights.

[P6] Casper general aviation community: Making Casper's Class D effective only by NOTAM may lead to safety gaps if NOTAMs fail to be disseminated correctly; request a requirement that the FAA publish standard hours or recurring schedules rather than ad hoc NOTAMs.

[P6] ATC labor union: Conditional activation increases controller staffing unpredictability; request the FAA coordinate with workforce planning and mandate minimum lead times for activation notices.

[P7] Chart/data users: Continuous publication of effective date/time for Casper in the Chart Supplement should include a history of recent NOTAM activations and anticipated schedule so operators can make informed decisions.

[P7] Legal/community advocate: The FAA should specify responsibility for ensuring Chart Supplement accuracy (e.g., which office inputs NOTAM-derived effective times) to prevent discrepancies between NOTAMs and the Chart Supplement.

[P8] Casper pilots/air ambulance services: Making Class E surface-area airspace effective only via NOTAM could affect emergency medical flights; request guaranteed immediate activation procedures or standby activation channels for emergency operations.

[P8] Safety analyst: Surface-area Class E that is NOTAM-activated may not be visible to older avionics or flight planning tools; request that the FAA ensure digital aeronautical data providers receive timely updates.

[P9] Flight planning/avionics industry: Requiring continuous publication in the Chart Supplement is inadequate for digital flight-planning services and FMS databases; ask that the FAA also provide machine-readable data feeds of the effective times.

[P9] Regulatory attorney: The rule should define the process and timeline for updating the Chart Supplement when NOTAM-established hours change, to ensure compliance with notice-and-comment obligations and operational certainty.

[P10] Atwater pilots: Repeating the NOTAM-only effectiveness for Atwater Class D raises the same predictability concerns; request the FAA define minimum notice periods, recurring schedules, or publish default hours when NOTAMs are not active.

[P10] Emergency responders: Unpredictable activation of Class D may hamper coordination for disaster response flights; request an exception or rapid-activation protocol for public safety operations.

[P11] Chart publishers/flight service providers: The FAA’s promise to continuously publish effective date/time in the Chart Supplement needs operational specifics: how frequently will the Chart Supplement be updated, and how will interim changes be communicated to third-party chart providers?

[P11] Policy watchdog: Continuous publication in the Chart Supplement does not eliminate the risk of conflicting information between NOTAMs and the Chart Supplement; request a requirement that NOTAMs and Chart Supplement entries be reconciled within a specified timeframe and that corrections be disseminated broadly.

[P11] Small business operator: The rule should require that changes to effective times be communicated to local stakeholders (airport tenants, flight schools, fixed base operators) in addition to NOTAM and Chart Supplement publication to avoid economic disruption.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement to assume an occupant mass of at least 86 kg (190 lb) is unreasonably high for average U.S. occupants and will overstate loads for many operators; ask FAA to justify basis and provide statistical data supporting 86 kg as the minimum design mass.

[P1] Using a single uniform occupant mass of 86 kg fails to account for child passengers and smaller adults and may force unnecessary heavy design margins; request allowance for alternate occupant mass assumptions for known child/infant seats or for aircraft limited to family operations.

[P1] Clarify whether the 86 kg occupant mass is per seated occupant or per crewmember with equipment; the provision lacks specificity about whether flightcrew clothing/equipment or passenger belongings are included.

[P2] The 1.33 factor of safety multiplied to inertia forces for attachments is ambiguous — request numerical examples and acceptable methodologies (load paths, factoring) for combined loads, especially for mixed analysis/test demonstrations.

[P2] Require clear test methods and pass/fail criteria for demonstrating the 1.33 safety factor (e.g., static pull tests, dynamic sled tests); without this, manufacturers will face inconsistent FAA interpretations.

[P2] The rule allows "analysis, tests, or both" but does not define when analysis alone is acceptable; request the FAA specify when physical testing is mandatory (e.g., novel materials, composite attachments) to ensure consistent safety levels.

[P3] The vague requirement to "give occupants a reasonable chance of avoiding serious injury" is subjective and legally uncertain; request quantitative injury criteria (e.g., HIC thresholds, injury probability targets) that designs must meet under the emergency landing inertia loads.

[P3] Provide definitions for "emergency landing conditions" (e.g., speed, descent rate, contact scenarios) and explicit scenarios the design must consider; without scenario definitions, compliance demonstrations will vary widely.

[P4] Requiring design to account for forward inertia of 6g is significant — request supporting data or references (accident/analysis) demonstrating 6g is a reasonable design basis for balloons; otherwise ask FAA to consider lower, scenario-based values or alternative loadcases.

[P5] Sideways inertia equal to 6g is extreme for lighter-than-air vehicles; request FAA to publish the derivation and consider differentiating between yaw/roll directions and occupant restraint effectiveness.

[P6] Downward inertia of 6g may double-count vertical landing loads with cushion/energy-absorbing seats; request guidance on how downward 6g interacts with seat energy absorbers and whether crashworthy seats can use reduced vertical g values.

[P7] The seat/support design obligation referencing the occupant mass and "maximum load factors" lacks clarity on combined load combinations (e.g., forward+downward, sideways+downward); ask FAA to specify required load combinations and load distribution factors.

[P7] Request explicit material and fatigue-life requirements for seat supports given repeated operations — current wording focuses on a single emergency event but neglects cyclic fatigue from normal operations.

[P8] Requiring an approved individual seat belt/harness for every seat is reasonable but raise concern about availability of certified harnesses sized for occupants exceeding 86 kg; ask FAA to allow use of harnesses that meet specified SAE/ISO standards and to list acceptable standards.

[P8] Clarify whether "approved" seat belts/harnesses must be FAA TSO-approved or may be shown compliant via equivalent foreign approvals or consensus standards; propose acceptance of recognized international approvals to avoid market barriers.

[P9] The prohibition on seat belts failing under specified load conditions requires precise definition of "failure"; request explicit acceptance criteria (load at which webbing tears, hardware yields, anchor pullout) and pass/fail metrics.

[P9] The requirement to consider "geometry of attachment and seat" is reasonable but lacks test fixtures and procedures; request FAA publish standard test rigs or reference standards (e.g., FAR 23/25 seat test procedures, 16 CFR) to ensure consistency.

[P10] The comments due date of August 9, 2018 is long past and inconsistent with the proposed rule date; request correction of the due date or, if this is a reissued action, explain why reopening comment period is not required.

[P10] If the due date is fixed, request extension of the comment period to allow stakeholders (manufacturers, operators, labor unions) time to perform technical analysis and economic impact assessments.

[P11] The general compliance obligation "within specified compliance times" is vague in absence of a clear compliance schedule; ask FAA to publish a consolidated compliance timetable and explain interactions with existing maintenance schedules.

[P12] The requirement to remove listed HPC rotor stage 2–5 spools per GE SB serial list is overly prescriptive and ties the AD to a specific manufacturer's service bulletin without incorporation by reference details; request FAA to incorporate the SB by reference or provide the full serial number list in the AD.

[P13] Removing spools with <4,500 CSN before they exceed 5,000 CSN imposes narrow operational windows that will disrupt scheduled rotations; request flexibility to coordinate removals with scheduled shop visits and allow a limited ferry operation to a maintenance facility.

[P13] Operators need clarification of how to calculate CSN accrual across time zones, maintenance logging conventions, and partially completed cycles; ask FAA to define "flight CSN" precisely and acceptable recordkeeping.

[P14] The 500-cycle removal window for spools with 4,500–4,999 CSN may create sudden fleet groundings; propose a risk-based prioritization or temporary repair/inspection option instead of mandatory removal within 500 cycles.

[P15] The 300-cycle window for spools 5,200–5,599 CSN is operationally disruptive for heavy operators; request that FAA permit conditional continued operation subject to enhanced NDT inspections and vibration monitoring until removal.

[P16] The 200-cycle window for 5,600–5,799 CSN may be economically punitive with limited safety gain vs. frequent inspections; ask FAA to provide probabilistic failure data supporting these thresholds or adopt a progressive inspection regime.

[P17] The 50-cycle window for 5,800–5,999 CSN is effectively immediate removal for many operators; request allowance for next scheduled engine shop visit within 50 cycles rather than strict removal at a specific flight, and compensation guidance if spares are insufficient.

[P18] Requiring removal before next flight for spools with >=6,000 CSN is a de facto grounding of affected engines; request transitional relief (e.g., temporary operational altitudes or weight limits) or FAA-provided on-site rapid replacements to avoid flight cancellations.

[P19] The second group removal before exceeding 8,200 CSN or before further flight lacks clarity about whether spools on listed serial numbers in paragraph (c)(2) are the same as in paragraph (c)(1); request cross-referencing and a consolidated serial list to avoid misinterpretation.

[P19] Provide a waiver path for emergency operations where replacement spools are not available (e.g., humanitarian flights), including criteria and maximum ferry distances.

[P20] The absolute prohibition on installing/reinstalling listed spools that exceed 5,000 CSN after the AD effective date may strand inventory of serviceable parts; request a grandfathering provision allowing reinstallation if the spool has been overhauled and passes defined borescope/NDT inspections.

[P20] Challenge the legal authority to prohibit installation of parts based solely on CSN when parts may be re-certified by overhaul — request FAA clarify whether certified overhaul facilities may return spools to service and under what conditions.

[P21] The ban on installing spools that exceed 8,200 CSN is vague as to whether the prohibition applies to spools that will exceed 8,200 CSN in service or only those already exceeding that CSN; request precise wording and examples.

[P21] Ask FAA to allow installation of affected spools for testing, ferry flights to maintenance, or crew training when subject to operational constraints (e.g., special flight permits) and with specific limitations.

[P22] The AMOC permission vested solely in the Manager, ECO Branch, FAA may bottleneck approvals; request delegation to regional offices or a fast-track process for low-risk AMOCs to avoid operational disruption.

[P22] Stakeholders request transparency — require FAA to publish criteria and precedent AMOCs and to commit to a defined turnaround time (e.g., 30 days) for AMOC decisions.

[P23] Routing AMOC requests through principal inspectors or FSDOs could duplicate reviews and slow responses; propose an electronic centralized submission and tracking portal with direct FAA certification-office reviews.

[P24] While emailing AMOC requests to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov is allowed, request confirmation of secure channels for proprietary data and acceptance of encrypted large attachments (e.g., test reports).

[P25] The notification requirement before using an approved AMOC could be burdensome for operators with many principal inspectors; ask FAA to allow a single corporate-level notification and provide guidance on timing and content of notifications.

[P25] Define what constitutes "using an approved AMOC" — does it include planned routine maintenance actions already scheduled or only new modifications; operators need clarity to avoid enforcement uncertainty.

[P3] Safety advocates will request that the FAA require post-landing occupant injury monitoring and accident data reporting specific to 6g design events, to validate the rule's effectiveness over time.

[P7] Labor groups representing maintenance technicians request clear training requirements and certification standards for personnel performing seat attachment tests and installations under the new requirements.

[P8] Accessibility advocates ask FAA to clarify whether the requirement for individual approved belts/harnesses includes options for persons with disabilities and to allow alternative restraint systems (e.g., multi-point harnesses, occupied restraint systems).

[P1] Insurance carriers may comment that assuming 86 kg as baseline will increase certification costs and premiums; request FAA to quantify expected cost impacts and required mitigation strategies.

[P12] Legal experts may challenge FAA's incorporation of manufacturer's serial-number lists without full public inclusion, arguing it limits public notice and creates enforcement ambiguity; request full inclusion of affected serial numbers in the preamble or AD text.

[P16] Manufacturers ask for a risk-based alternative allowing the use of life-limited part rework, uprated inspection intervals, or refurbishments with defined NDT acceptance criteria in place of mandatory removal windows.

[P17] Airlines operating international services request harmonization with EASA/other CAAs to prevent conflicting ADs on spool CSN thresholds; encourage FAA to coordinate and adopt consistent compliance schedules.

[P18] Maintenance organizations request adequate lead time to procure replacement spools and specialized tooling; ask the FAA to provide a grace period or staged implementation to prevent widespread capacity shortages.

[P13] Operators request clear credit provisions for spools already inspected per prior ADs or service bulletins — explicitly allow credit where equivalent inspections/repairs have already been performed.

[P2] Aerospace engineers request that the FAA define whether the 1.33 factor of safety applies to ultimate or limit load levels and whether fatigue life must be demonstrated at the factored loads.

[P9] Consumer safety groups request mandatory public disclosure of seat belt/harness failure modes found in compliance testing to inform ongoing standards improvements and consumer awareness.

[P4] Balloon operator associations point out that the inertia loadcases (6g in all axes) are modeled after fixed-wing crash scenarios and may not be applicable to lighter-than-air craft; urge FAA to develop balloon-specific dynamic models and occupant protection standards.

[P3] Request that the FAA require dummies or biofidelic restraint test devices representing a range of occupant sizes (including obese profiles over 86 kg) in certification tests to ensure harnesses perform across real-world anthropometrics.
