raw_output:
[P1] The May 10, 2021 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60 days to allow affected operators, manufacturers, and labor/advocacy groups time to review technical data and prepare substantive comments.

[P1] The rule fails to provide notice of where the full technical basis (service information, incident reports, inspection figures) is available; commenters need access to underlying data before the May 10, 2021 deadline.

[P2] § 39.13(f) requires compliance “within the specified compliance times” but does not clarify whether calendar vs. flight-hour time accumulation governs when different compliance actions become due for intermittent operators; request explicit guidance.

[P3] The requirement in § 39.13(g)(1) to determine total TIS of the main driveshaft before the next flight after the AD effective date is operationally disruptive for Part 91/135 operators that cannot ground aircraft; FAA should allow a 24–72 hour window to record TIS or permit a logbook/maintenance records check instead of grounding.

[P3] Legal commenters should note § 39.13(g)(1) could be read to require physical measurement rather than review of records; the provision must expressly permit determination via maintenance logs and timesheet records.

[P4] Under § 39.13(g)(1)(i), removing any driveshaft that will exceed 5,000 hours before it reaches the threshold could force removal in the middle of a multi-leg flight schedule; FAA should allow removal at the next scheduled maintenance event within X flight hours rather than “before exceeding.”

[P5] § 39.13(g)(1)(i) lacks exception language for aircraft with imminent ferry flights for safety of flight or emergency operations; propose adding a temporary ferry permit mechanism or AMOC pathway.

[P6] § 39.13(g)(1)(ii) mandates removal before further flight for driveshafts with 5,000 hours or more, which will strand aircraft and customers; FAA should specify acceptable replacement parts availability and an implementation window to avoid disruption.

[P7] The recurring removal requirement at § 39.13(g)(2) (remove before accumulating 5,000 TIS) effectively imposes a hard life limit on the current driveshaft P/Ns with no credit for refurbishment or overhaul; industry will request explicit allowance for life-extension via FAA-approved repair/overhaul programs or an AMOC path.

[P8] § 39.13(g)(3) requires removal of listed P/Ns within 25 hours TIS after the effective date but does not address how to handle aircraft located outside the U.S. within that time; international operators need clarification and possibly longer windows.

[P9] The 25-hour window in § 39.13(g)(3) is too short to obtain required tools, schedules, and parts in many remote locations; FAA should extend to 100 hours or allow removal at the next maintenance visit within 30 days.

[P10] § 39.13(g)(3)(i) requires inspection for broken/loose/missing hardware after removal, but the rule does not specify who is qualified to perform the inspection (A&P mechanic, repair station, manufacturer); request explicit qualification requirements.

[P11] The condition in § 39.13(g)(3)(i) to remove the driveshaft from service if broken or loose hardware is found is redundant with removal performed per (g)(3) and should be clarified as requiring replacement/repair before further flight rather than confusing duplication.

[P12] § 39.13(g)(3)(i) treats missing hardware differently (requires replacement) while broken/loose requires removal; commenters will request clarification on why missing hardware can be corrected in situ and whether torque/retorque or securement can be used instead of replacement.

[P13] § 39.13(g)(3)(ii) mandates visual inspection of torque stripes; commenters will ask FAA to define acceptable methods for detecting movement (e.g., magnification, markings photographs) and to allow retention of photographic evidence in the maintenance records.

[P14] The requirement in § 39.13(g)(3)(ii) to replace the driveshaft before further flight if any torque stripe movement is detected is overly strict; industry will request an allowance for re-torquing/retorquing and re-marking under an FAA-approved procedure rather than immediate replacement.

[P15] § 39.13(g)(3)(iii) requires visual inspection for fretting corrosion and defines red metallic particles as an indicator; material science experts will request clearer acceptance criteria (e.g., minimum particle counts, measurement of depth of fretting) to reduce subjectivity.

[P16] The cleaning/re-inspection requirement in § 39.13(g)(3)(iii) should specify approved cleaning agents/procedures and maximum allowed dwell times before the re-inspection to ensure consistent application across operators and repair stations.

[P17] The mandatory replacement before further flight for any fretting corrosion in § 39.13(g)(3)(iii) imposes a zero-tolerance standard; commenters will request a quantified damage tolerance level or allow repair per FAA-approved procedures when corrosion is superficial.

[P18] § 39.13(g)(3)(iv) refers to Figure 1 for allowable limits but the NPRM does not include a clear dimensioned table of allowable scratch, dent, and nick sizes; operators and repair stations need explicit numerical limits to determine repair vs replacement.

[P19] The cross-reference in § 39.13(g)(3)(iv) to a repair “per FAA-approved procedures” lacks a defined, expedited approval process; industry requests that FAA publish approved repair procedures or pre-authorize certain common repairs to avoid operational delays.

[P20] § 39.13(g)(3)(iv) requires replacement for cracks or damage exceeding limits “before further flight” — this will cause aircraft grounding; commenters request allowance for a single ferry flight to a maintenance facility under strict conditions and reporting.

[P21] The alignment inspection in § 39.13(g)(4) requires following TM paragraphs c–g but the proposed rule does not include the referenced TM or indicate how to obtain it; operators need the TM incorporated by reference or publicly posted.

[P22] § 39.13(g)(4) allows adjustment per TM paragraphs h–j for misalignment but does not state who is authorized to perform alignment adjustments; request specification that only qualified AMEs/repair stations may perform adjustments and require work to be logged.

[P23] § 39.13(g)(5) mandates inspections every 300 hours TIS with the driveshaft installed; small operators will comment that 300 hours may be too frequent or too infrequent depending on usage patterns and request risk-based interval justification or flight-cycle-based intervals.

[P24] The recurring 300-hour inspection interval in § 39.13(g)(5) lacks a grace period—operators want a ±10% or X-hour grace to enable scheduling maintenance without violating the AD inadvertently.

[P25] § 39.13(g)(5) requires performing multiple detailed inspections with the driveshaft installed; commenters will request clarity on downtime estimates and labor-hour burden for compliance (cost impact analysis requested).

[P26] § 39.13(g)(6) allows installation of KAflex P/N SKCP3303–1 as an optional terminating action but does not provide installation instructions, compatibility guidance, or parts availability; manufacturers/operators will request a parts/installation bulletin and lead-time estimate.

[P27] The cost-benefit analysis should consider that § 39.13(g)(6) voluntary terminating action will impose retrofit costs; industry will request FAA include estimated retrofit costs and certification status of the KAflex driveshaft.

[P28] § 39.13(h)(1) grants the Manager, DSCO Branch, FAA authority to approve AMOCs but does not guarantee timely processing; commenters request a required response timeframe (e.g., 60 days) for AMOC decisions to prevent prolonged operational uncertainty.

[P29] The AMOC submission procedure in § 39.13(h)(1) and (h)(1) request procedure appears duplicative; commenters request consolidation and clearer flowchart for where to send AMOCs depending on operator type and urgency.

[P30] § 39.13(h)(1) allows direct submission to the certification office manager when named in Related Information but the NPRM does not include that contact in the body; request that the Related Information and contact be explicit in the AD text.

[P31] The email option in § 39.13(h)(1) (9-ASW-190-COS@faa.gov) may not be secure for proprietary AMOC technical data; industry requests secure file transfer or encryption guidance and acknowledgement timelines.

[P32] § 39.13(h)(2) requires notifying the principal inspector or local FSDO/CHDO before using an approved AMOC but does not require written confirmation from the inspector; operators request written acceptance to avoid enforcement risk.

[P33] Legal commenters will argue that several “before further flight” mandates (e.g., P5, P9, P12, P15, P18, P20) could be interpreted to prohibit even single-ferry flights to maintenance when safety considerations make that unavoidable; request explicit ferry flight exception language subject to conditions.

[P34] Labor and mechanic associations will request training guidance and a training allowance, because the inspections (fretting corrosion, torque stripe movement, alignment checks) require specific skills not described in the rule.

[P35] Foreign registrants and operators will ask FAA to coordinate with EASA and other authorities, and to include ICAO-equivalent compliance guidance for aircraft outside U.S. jurisdiction given the short compliance times (25 and 300 hours).

[P36] The AD should require documentation of all inspections, cleaning actions, repairs, and replacements in the aircraft maintenance records with a specific wording template so FAA and operators have consistent records for enforcement and airworthiness.

[P37] Commenters will request that the FAA add an exception for driveshafts with documented prior modification or retrofits (e.g., earlier KAflex conversions or other FAA-approved life-limit changes) to avoid redundant removal/inspection.

[P38] Safety advocates will request that the FAA require reporting into the Service Difficulty Reporting system of any instances of fretting corrosion or torque stripe movement discovered, with a defined timeline (e.g., within 72 hours) to improve fleet-wide data collection.

[P39] The AD does not describe who bears the cost of component replacements or the acceptable sources for replacement parts; operators will request FAA guidance that only OEM or FAA-approved parts be used and whether warranty claims or cost relief is available.

[P40] The rule should explicitly state whether driveshafts removed per § 39.13(g)(3) and replaced with serviceable parts must be sent to the manufacturer for analysis, quarantine, or metallurgical inspection to identify root cause; commenters will ask for a return-to-manufacturer procedure.

[P41] Maintenance recordkeeping associated with recurring removals per § 39.13(g)(2) should include cumulative TIS tracking protocol for the driveshaft part numbers to prevent errors; request that the FAA provide a sample tracking form or mandate software fields.

[P42] Certification lawyers will note ambiguous cross-references to the Technical Manual paragraphs (c–j) and TM 55–1520–240–23; they will request the TM be incorporated by reference with a docketed copy to avoid interpretive disputes.

[P43] Operators will object that replacing driveshafts “before further flight” with no time for parts procurement can conflict with passenger-carrying obligations and suggest FAA allow a one-time extension when parts are not available within 24–72 hours, with restrictions.

[P44] The FAA should clarify whether the life limit in § 39.13(g)(2) applies to remanufactured or re-identified driveshafts that have had TIS counters reset or have been re-marked; commenters request prohibition on resetting time counters and guidance on part identity.

[P45] The AD lacks a clear definition of “main driveshaft” as applied to models or serial number ranges; operators request the AD list specific airplane/engine combinations and serial numbers affected to avoid over-application.

[P46] Commenters will request that the FAA provide an economic impact analysis specific to small operators and Part 135 operators showing estimated grounding days and replacement part costs caused by the “before further flight” and 25-hour removal requirements.

[P47] The FAA should allow an alternative interim inspection (e.g., borescope or dye-penetrant) for suspected fretting or cracking where visual inspection is inconclusive, rather than immediate replacement; commenters will request explicit allowance for such nondestructive evaluations via AMOC or in the AD.

[P48] The 300-hour recurrent interval in § 39.13(g)(5) should be tied to calendar time maximums (e.g., 6 months) for low-utilization aircraft to ensure inspections occur even if 300 hours are not reached; request addition of a 6-month maximum interval.

[P49] Commenters will ask FAA to define the term “edge dent” and provide minimum measurement methods (calipers, profilometry) in § 39.13(g)(3)(iv) so inspectors apply the same objective standard.

[P50] The AD should specify whether driveshaft installation after replacement requires a functional test flight or ground-run test and what those test parameters are; request FAA include test procedures and acceptance criteria.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The May 10, 2021 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60 days to allow affected operators, manufacturers, and labor/advocacy groups time to review technical data and prepare substantive comments.

The rule fails to provide notice of where the full technical basis (service information, incident reports, inspection figures) is available; commenters need access to underlying data before the May 10, 2021 deadline.

§ 39.13(f) requires compliance “within the specified compliance times” but does not clarify whether calendar vs. flight-hour time accumulation governs when different compliance actions become due for intermittent operators; request explicit guidance.

The requirement in § 39.13(g)(1) to determine total TIS of the main driveshaft before the next flight after the AD effective date is operationally disruptive for Part 91/135 operators that cannot ground aircraft; FAA should allow a 24–72 hour window to record TIS or permit a logbook/maintenance records check instead of grounding.

Legal commenters should note § 39.13(g)(1) could be read to require physical measurement rather than review of records; the provision must expressly permit determination via maintenance logs and timesheet records.

Under § 39.13(g)(1)(i), removing any driveshaft that will exceed 5,000 hours before it reaches the threshold could force removal in the middle of a multi-leg flight schedule; FAA should allow removal at the next scheduled maintenance event within X flight hours rather than “before exceeding.”
§ 39.13(g)(1)(i) lacks exception language for aircraft with imminent ferry flights for safety of flight or emergency operations; propose adding a temporary ferry permit mechanism or AMOC pathway.

§ 39.13(g)(1)(ii) mandates removal before further flight for driveshafts with 5,000 hours or more, which will strand aircraft and customers; FAA should specify acceptable replacement parts availability and an implementation window to avoid disruption.

The recurring removal requirement at § 39.13(g)(2) (remove before accumulating 5,000 TIS) effectively imposes a hard life limit on the current driveshaft P/Ns with no credit for refurbishment or overhaul; industry will request explicit allowance for life-extension via FAA-approved repair/overhaul programs or an AMOC path.

§ 39.13(g)(3) requires removal of listed P/Ns within 25 hours TIS after the effective date but does not address how to handle aircraft located outside the U.S. within that time; international operators need clarification and possibly longer windows.

The 25-hour window in § 39.13(g)(3) is too short to obtain required tools, schedules, and parts in many remote locations; FAA should extend to 100 hours or allow removal at the next maintenance visit within 30 days.

§ 39.13(g)(3)(i) requires inspection for broken/loose/missing hardware after removal, but the rule does not specify who is qualified to perform the inspection (A&P mechanic, repair station, manufacturer); request explicit qualification requirements.

The condition in § 39.13(g)(3)(i) to remove the driveshaft from service if broken or loose hardware is found is redundant with removal performed per (g)(3) and should be clarified as requiring replacement/repair before further flight rather than confusing duplication.

§ 39.13(g)(3)(i) treats missing hardware differently (requires replacement) while broken/loose requires removal; commenters will request clarification on why missing hardware can be corrected in situ and whether torque/retorque or securement can be used instead of replacement.

§ 39.13(g)(3)(ii) mandates visual inspection of torque stripes; commenters will ask FAA to define acceptable methods for detecting movement (e.g., magnification, markings photographs) and to allow retention of photographic evidence in the maintenance records.

The requirement in § 39.13(g)(3)(ii) to replace the driveshaft before further flight if any torque stripe movement is detected is overly strict; industry will request an allowance for re-torquing/retorquing and re-marking under an FAA-approved procedure rather than immediate replacement.

§ 39.13(g)(3)(iii) requires visual inspection for fretting corrosion and defines red metallic particles as an indicator; material science experts will request clearer acceptance criteria (e.g., minimum particle counts, measurement of depth of fretting) to reduce subjectivity.

The cleaning/re-inspection requirement in § 39.13(g)(3)(iii) should specify approved cleaning agents/procedures and maximum allowed dwell times before the re-inspection to ensure consistent application across operators and repair stations.

The mandatory replacement before further flight for any fretting corrosion in § 39.13(g)(3)(iii) imposes a zero-tolerance standard; commenters will request a quantified damage tolerance level or allow repair per FAA-approved procedures when corrosion is superficial.

§ 39.13(g)(3)(iv) refers to Figure 1 for allowable limits but the NPRM does not include a clear dimensioned table of allowable scratch, dent, and nick sizes; operators and repair stations need explicit numerical limits to determine repair vs replacement.

The cross-reference in § 39.13(g)(3)(iv) to a repair “per FAA-approved procedures” lacks a defined, expedited approval process; industry requests that FAA publish approved repair procedures or pre-authorize certain common repairs to avoid operational delays.

§ 39.13(g)(3)(iv) requires replacement for cracks or damage exceeding limits “before further flight” — this will cause aircraft grounding; commenters request allowance for a single ferry flight to a maintenance facility under strict conditions and reporting.

The alignment inspection in § 39.13(g)(4) requires following TM paragraphs c–g but the proposed rule does not include the referenced TM or indicate how to obtain it; operators need the TM incorporated by reference or publicly posted.

§ 39.13(g)(4) allows adjustment per TM paragraphs h–j for misalignment but does not state who is authorized to perform alignment adjustments; request specification that only qualified AMEs/repair stations may perform adjustments and require work to be logged.

§ 39.13(g)(5) mandates inspections every 300 hours TIS with the driveshaft installed; small operators will comment that 300 hours may be too frequent or too infrequent depending on usage patterns and request risk-based interval justification or flight-cycle-based intervals.
The recurring 300-hour inspection interval in § 39.13(g)(5) lacks a grace period—operators want a ±10% or X-hour grace to enable scheduling maintenance without violating the AD inadvertently.

§ 39.13(g)(5) requires performing multiple detailed inspections with the driveshaft installed; commenters will request clarity on downtime estimates and labor-hour burden for compliance (cost impact analysis requested).

§ 39.13(g)(6) allows installation of KAflex P/N SKCP3303–1 as an optional terminating action but does not provide installation instructions, compatibility guidance, or parts availability; manufacturers/operators will request a parts/installation bulletin and lead-time estimate.

The cost-benefit analysis should consider that § 39.13(g)(6) voluntary terminating action will impose retrofit costs; industry will request FAA include estimated retrofit costs and certification status of the KAflex driveshaft.

§ 39.13(h)(1) grants the Manager, DSCO Branch, FAA authority to approve AMOCs but does not guarantee timely processing; commenters request a required response timeframe (e.g., 60 days) for AMOC decisions to prevent prolonged operational uncertainty.

§ 39.13(h)(1) allows direct submission to the certification office manager when named in Related Information but the NPRM does not include that contact in the body; request that the Related Information and contact be explicit in the AD text.

§ 39.13(h)(2) requires notifying the principal inspector or local FSDO/CHDO before using an approved AMOC but does not require written confirmation from the inspector; operators request written acceptance to avoid enforcement risk.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement to submit a public notification plan with the permit application is unclear about permit renewals — commenters request explicit language that plan updates must be submitted with both new permit applications and renewals/major modifications to avoid ambiguity.

[P1] Municipal utilities with multiple permits across jurisdictions request clarification whether a single consolidated public notification plan may be submitted covering all CSO outfalls in the Great Lakes Basin or if a separate plan is required per permittee-permit.

[P2] The obligation to "describe any significant updates since the last plan submission" lacks a definition of "significant update"; commenters urge the Agency to define thresholds (e.g., changes to sign locations, notification protocols, measured vs. estimated volume methods) so permittees know what triggers reporting.

[P2] Small municipalities contend that requiring documentation of minor administrative changes as "significant updates" would be burdensome and request an exemption for clerical or contact information changes.

[P3] Environmental NGOs support the public-notification mandate but request that the rule require publication in multiple languages predominant in the community to ensure accessibility rather than leaving language choice to permittees.

[P4] Property owners and park authorities note that "where signage is feasible" is subjective; they request objective feasibility criteria (public access, safety, vandalism risk, right-of-way) and a formal process to document infeasibility determinations.

[P4] Transportation agencies and DOTs request clarity on liability and permittee obligations when signage placement is constrained by state roadway or right-of-way regulations — asking whether permits or easements will be needed and who pays for sign installation in such areas.

[P5] Local governments ask for flexibility to use municipal or brand logos in addition to the permittee name on signs and request confirmation that acronyms (e.g., "City of X") satisfy the "name" requirement.

[P6] Public health advocates request that the required sign language be standardized (model text) and scientifically reviewed (e.g., "Sewage may be present — avoid contact") to avoid confusing or downplaying health risks.

[P7] Concerned citizens and consumer advocates urge that sign contact information include an email address and website URL in addition to a telephone number, given declining landline access and the need for rapid electronic updates.

[P7] Legal commenters request clarification whether the NPDES permit number and outfall number are required to be posted for every outfall listed, and if so, how to handle composite outfalls or satellite systems without unique outfall identifiers.

[P8] Municipalities report that "periodic maintenance" needs specificity; they request minimum inspection intervals (e.g., quarterly, semi-annual) and allow an alternative risk-based inspection schedule approved by the Director.

[P9] Municipalities ask for a clear transition schedule and an explicit statement that pre-existing state-compliant signs are acceptable until replacement, including a requirement to inventory and report pre-existing signs when filing the plan.

[P10] Wastewater utilities contend that the 4-hour deadline to notify health departments and affected entities after "becoming aware" may be impractical during large storm events; they request extensions to 8 hours or an allowance to notify within 4 hours only for discharges confirmed by continuous monitoring.

[P10] Legal experts ask the Agency to clarify what constitutes "becoming aware by modeling, monitoring or other means" and whether early-warning models that predict a discharge trigger the 4-hour clock or only confirmed observations.

[P11] Utilities request guidance on the acceptable level of specificity for identifying the receiving waterbody (e.g., name and river mile, lake shoreline segment, GPS coordinates) to ensure consistency across jurisdictions.

[P12] Operators note that permitting an "area description" when multiple simultaneous locations discharge is necessary but ask the rule to require mapping conventions or GIS shapefile submission so the public can locate impacted areas accurately.

[P13] Sewage agencies ask the rule to specify timezone reference (e.g., local time or UTC) and precision for reported dates/times of commencement or awareness (to the nearest minute, hour) to avoid inconsistent reporting.

[P14] Public health departments request that the initial notice include expected duration estimates when discharges are ongoing, not only whether ended or ongoing, because duration affects exposure risk assessments.

[P15] Commenters ask that the "point of contact" include an on-call 24/7 phone number and escalation contacts for major events rather than a general office line that may be unattended outside business hours.

[P16] Utilities request an explicit exception to the 24-hour supplemental notice requirement when no volume estimate is available immediately, allowing submission within a reasonable additional timeframe (e.g., 48–72 hours) and an interim notice stating that detailed data is pending.

[P17] Municipalities request acceptable methodologies for estimating discharge volume (flow factors, model parameters) be enumerated or referenced to standard guidance to ensure reporting consistency.

[P17] Small jurisdictions with multiple outfalls ask for explicit permission to provide cumulative volume estimates for groups of nearby outfalls rather than per-outfall estimates, as the rule allows, and ask the Agency to define acceptable grouping criteria.

[P18] Utilities request clarity on whether "approximate end time" must be to the nearest minute, hour, or day and whether model-based end times are acceptable if monitoring is unavailable.

[P19] NGOs and public health groups support the 4-hour public notice to the public but urge inclusion of SMS/text alert requirements for subscribed users in affected areas to ensure timely reach.

[P19] Some municipalities argue that posting to a web page within 4 hours may be insufficient for people with limited internet access and request additional mandatory media (local radio, posted signs at parks) be explicitly required for high-use public access areas.

[P20] Recreational user groups request that notices identify not only the receiving waterbody name but also the precise affected reach (e.g., beach name, boat launch) to be actionable for users.

[P21] Boating associations request the rule require coordination with marine VHF radio channels or harbor-master notifications for immediate alerting of mariners in addition to electronic public notice.

[P22] Environmental lawyers recommend adding a requirement that public notices include simple health guidance (e.g., no swimming, avoid contact) and link to state/local health Department advisories rather than only raw facts about time/location.

[P23] Tribal governments request that notices explicitly indicate if tribal waters or treaty fishing areas are affected and require direct notification to tribal leadership and fishery managers within the same 4-hour window.

[P24] Public watchdog groups request that the electronic update within 24 hours include not just volume and end time but also any available pollutant concentration sampling results or an estimated health risk level.

[P25] Permittees ask the Agency to provide clear guidance on acceptable volume estimation precision (e.g., ±10%, ±20%) and acceptable rounding practices when reporting measured or estimated volumes to ensure uniform reporting.

[P25] Small systems without continuous flow meters request allowance to report model-based or historical-average estimates for volume if installing monitoring equipment is not economically feasible, and seek explicit grandfathering until they can equip outfalls.

[P26] Legal commenters ask whether the "unless already provided" clause for approximate end time in the electronic update refers specifically to earlier public notices or also to initial notices to health departments — they request consistent cross-referencing.

[P27] The May 1 annual notice deadline may conflict with local budgeting and reporting cycles for some agencies; commenters request the Agency allow an alternative date or a phased-in compliance year for the first reporting cycle.

[P27] Small utilities request an extended first-year deadline (e.g., 9–12 months after rule promulgation) for the initial annual notice to allow time to collect and quality-assure prior-year data.

[P28] Satellite system operators seek clarity whether the "copy to POTW operator" requirement creates any liability or operational obligations for the POTW receiving the copy and ask whether acknowledgement of receipt is required.

[P29] Public disclosure advocates request that the annual notice include direct links to the full public notification plan and historical annual notices online, not just information on availability.

[P30] Environmental groups request that the annual notice include GPS coordinates for each outfall and accessible maps so the public can identify locations rather than narrative descriptions.

[P31] Commenters urge the Agency to require per-event data in the annual notice in machine-readable form (CSV/JSON) rather than only narrative summaries to enable independent analysis of date, location, duration, and volume.

[P32] Concerned citizens note that dry weather discharges are often most concerning and request that the rule require immediate investigation reports be summarized in the annual notice, including root-cause analysis and corrective actions taken.

[P33] Public health officials ask that the "summary of available monitoring data" include microbial indicators (E. coli, enterococci) and priority pollutant results where available, rather than unspecified monitoring summaries.

[P34] Recreation and tourism stakeholders request that the annual notice link each CSO event to impacted public access areas and beaches with advisories or closures clearly marked to protect public health and local businesses.

[P35] Meteorological services and modeling experts request guidance on acceptable sources and siting for "representative rain gauge data" and clarification whether modeled precipitation (radar) is acceptable when gauge data is unavailable.

[P36] Commenters request that the annual notice point of contact include both a public information officer and an operations contact with phone/email to facilitate follow-up by the public and regulators.

[P37] Environmental advocates request that the annual summary of minimum controls and LTCP status include actual metrics (e.g., number of overflows reduced, percent capture, estimated pollutant load reduction) rather than qualitative descriptions.

[P38] Municipalities ask the rule to limit "key remaining milestones" to a manageable list and allow confidential treatment of sensitive contract/timetable details if disclosure would jeopardize procurement or security.

[P39] Communities request guidance on how to estimate "anticipated average annual number of CSO discharges after plan completion" (e.g., model scenarios, baseline years) and whether ranges/uncertainty bands are acceptable.

[P40] IT and reporting staff request detailed technical specifications and validation rules for the electronic reporting forms under 40 CFR 127 so agencies can integrate with existing DMR/SOER systems well before the first reporting cycle.

[P41] Public notification plan development: Small jurisdictions request a simplified template or model public notification plan to reduce administrative burden and ensure consistency across permittees.

[P42] Utilities ask for flexibility in the requirement to inform the public via bill mailings where some customers are not billed (e.g., municipal customers) and request alternative outreach methods be allowed and listed (e.g., utility bulletins, municipal newsletters).

[P43] The requirement to submit the plan within 6 months after final rule publication is potentially infeasible for small systems; commenters request a phased submission schedule based on population thresholds (e.g., <10,000 gets 12 months).

[P44] Municipalities request clarity on the required level of detail when identifying sign locations in the plan (e.g., photos, GPS coordinates, parcel IDs) and propose that a map attachment should suffice.

[P45] Public health stakeholders recommend that plan-required sign message descriptions include translations into commonly spoken local languages and plain-language health advisories vetted by health departments.

[P46] Commenters ask that signage maintenance protocols allow for adaptive frequency based on vandalism risk and seasonal impacts (e.g., winter snow coverage) and request that inspection intervals be adjustable after Director approval.

[P47] Tribes and downstream municipalities request a clear definition of "potentially affected" entities and a requirement that Tribes always be treated as potentially affected when in or downstream of the watershed, with direct written notification.

[P48] Public health departments support the requirement to summarize their comments but request that the plan also include demonstrable explanations of how health department recommendations were incorporated or reasoned responses if not adopted.

[P49] Other public entities request templates for documenting outreach efforts and a defined minimum timeframe for solicitation of comments (e.g., 30 days) so that the permittee's outreach is meaningful.

[P50] Health departments ask for a requirement that notification protocols include escalation thresholds for large-volume or untreated sewage events that trigger broader media outreach and temporary beach/boating closures.

[P51] Consumer groups request that the protocols for initial/supplemental public notice include use of social media, text alerts, and local media partnerships to maximize timely reach to affected populations.

[P52] Engineers and modelers request a clear list of acceptable flow-measurement technologies and minimum calibration/QA requirements; they also support the 5-year calibration interval for systems ≥75,000 but ask for definitions of calibration standards.

[P52] Smaller municipalities argue that the 5-year calibration mandate for populations ≥75,000 should be scaled for mid-sized communities (e.g., require calibration every 7 years for populations 25,000–75,000) to reflect resource constraints.

[P53] Commenters request that the plan must require that the annual notice be posted in machine-readable, searchable formats and archived for a minimum number of years (e.g., 10 years) on the permittee website.

[P54] Stakeholders want explicit minimum outreach steps required before plan submission (e.g., at least one public meeting, 30-day comment period, and direct notification to listed entities) rather than vague "seek input" language.

[P55] Local public health departments request that the rule require permittees to provide preliminary draft plans to health departments at least 45 days before formal submission to allow substantive input.

[P56] Health departments request specific collaborative tasks be codified (e.g., agreement on which discharges warrant public notification, thresholds by volume or duration) rather than open-ended "work with" language.

[P57] Tribal governments request explicit inclusion in paragraph (e)(1)(ii) that notification recommendations must consider tribal subsistence fishing and cultural uses and require direct tribal approvals for messaging affecting tribal resources.

[P58] Potentially affected public entities request mandatory written acknowledgment of receipt from each contacted entity so permittees can document outreach efforts in the plan.

[P59] Legal commentators ask that the "consider recommendations" obligation be clarified into a standard of reasonableness with documentation of how recommendations were considered and why they were or were not adopted.

[P60] Municipal associations support the discretionary extension authority for undue economic hardship but ask the rule to require a clear, objective standard and list of factors (budget shortfall, infrastructure damage, demonstrated inability to procure signs) that the Director may consider.

[P60] Consumer and environmental groups oppose overly broad extension authority and request that any extension be time-limited, publicly justified, and require enforceable interim measures to protect public health.

[P61] Commenters request a requirement that the Director's notification to the Regional Administrator include redacted financial information protections if communities provide sensitive proprietary economic data to demonstrate hardship.

[P62] Advocacy groups request that the Director's website notice for extensions include a summary of the justification and expected mitigation measures, not just community name and new dates, to preserve transparency.

[P63] Citizens ask that the posted notice of extensions remain on the Director’s website permanently (or archived) rather than removed at the new compliance date so there is an ongoing public record of extensions granted.

[P64] Industry groups request that permit language under §122.42(f) explicitly allow permittees to incorporate existing state/local public notification requirements if they meet or exceed the federal elements, to avoid duplication.

[P65] Legal commenters request that permits reference the exact subsection(s) of §122.38 to avoid inconsistency and to ensure that permit limits are enforceable and clearly tied to the regulatory text.

[P66] Permittees ask that the permit’s required signage information allow for use of QR codes on signs linking to up-to-date electronic information, rather than expecting static full disclosure on physical signs.

[P67] Utilities request that permittees be allowed to prioritize sign installation at high-use access points and provide alternative notification (e.g., temporary signs, boater advisories) for lower-use outfalls until budget allows full signage.

[P68] Commenters request that permit language specifying timing and content for notifications include standardized templates for initial and supplemental notices to ensure timely compliance and consistent public information.

[P69] Public communicators request the permit requirement for public notification content to mandate inclusion of clear health guidance and links to local health advisory pages instead of solely factual discharge details.

[P70] Technical staff ask for criteria for designating which CSO locations must be monitored for volume/duration (e.g., population served, history of overflows, proximity to public access) to ensure permits are practicable.

[P71] IT departments request explicit data formats, validation rules, and API endpoints for electronic submittal of the May 1 annual notice to allow automated uploads and reduce human error.

[P72] Environmental groups request that permit conditions explicitly require posting of the annual notice on a public portal and that the Director retain the authority to require additional disclosures if the public health risk is elevated.

[P73] Municipalities request that the electronic reporting requirement reference existing state e-reporting systems to avoid duplicative submissions and ask for coordination with state reporting timelines.

[P73] Compliance officers ask for safe-harbor provisions for reporting errors (e.g., corrected reports submission allowed within X days) to avoid punitive enforcement for initial inadvertent data inaccuracies.

Local governments ask for flexibility to use municipal or brand logos in addition to the permittee name on signs and request confirmation that acronyms (e.g., "City of X") satisfy the "name" requirement.

Public health advocates request that the required sign language be standardized (model text) and scientifically reviewed (e.g., "Sewage may be present — avoid contact") to avoid confusing or downplaying health risks.

Concerned citizens and consumer advocates urge that sign contact information include an email address and website URL in addition to a telephone number, given declining landline access and the need for rapid electronic updates.

Legal commenters request clarification whether the NPDES permit number and outfall number are required to be posted for every outfall listed, and if so, how to handle composite outfalls or satellite systems without unique outfall identifiers.

Municipalities report that "periodic maintenance" needs specificity; they request minimum inspection intervals (e.g., quarterly, semi-annual) and allow an alternative risk-based inspection schedule approved by the Director.

Municipalities ask for a clear transition schedule and an explicit statement that pre-existing state-compliant signs are acceptable until replacement, including a requirement to inventory and report pre-existing signs when filing the plan.

Wastewater utilities contend that the 4-hour deadline to notify health departments and affected entities after "becoming aware" may be impractical during large storm events; they request extensions to 8 hours or an allowance to notify within 4 hours only for discharges confirmed by continuous monitoring.

Legal experts ask the Agency to clarify what constitutes "becoming aware by modeling, monitoring or other means" and whether early-warning models that predict a discharge trigger the 4-hour clock or only confirmed observations.

parsed_claims.claim_text: Utilities request guidance on the acceptable level of specificity for identifying the receiving waterbody (e.g., name and river mile, lake shoreline segment, GPS coordinates) to ensure consistency across jurisdictions.

Operators note that permitting an "area description" when multiple simultaneous locations discharge is necessary but ask the rule to require mapping conventions or GIS shapefile submission so the public can locate impacted areas accurately.

Sewage agencies ask the rule to specify timezone reference (e.g., local time or UTC) and precision for reported dates/times of commencement or awareness (to the nearest minute, hour) to avoid inconsistent reporting.

Public health departments request that the initial notice include expected duration estimates when discharges are ongoing, not only whether ended or ongoing, because duration affects exposure risk assessments.

Commenters ask that the "point of contact" include an on-call 24/7 phone number and escalation contacts for major events rather than a general office line that may be unattended outside business hours.

Utilities request an explicit exception to the 24-hour supplemental notice requirement when no volume estimate is available immediately, allowing submission within a reasonable additional timeframe (e.g., 48–72 hours) and an interim notice stating that detailed data is pending.
Municipalities request acceptable methodologies for estimating discharge volume (flow factors, model parameters) be enumerated or referenced to standard guidance to ensure reporting consistency.

Small jurisdictions with multiple outfalls ask for explicit permission to provide cumulative volume estimates for groups of nearby outfalls rather than per-outfall estimates, as the rule allows, and ask the Agency to define acceptable grouping criteria.
Utilities request clarity on whether "approximate end time" must be to the nearest minute, hour, or day and whether model-based end times are acceptable if monitoring is unavailable.
NGOs and public health groups support the 4-hour public notice to the public but urge inclusion of SMS/text alert requirements for subscribed users in affected areas to ensure timely reach.

Some municipalities argue that posting to a web page within 4 hours may be insufficient for people with limited internet access and request additional mandatory media (local radio, posted signs at parks) be explicitly required for high-use public access areas.
Recreational user groups request that notices identify not only the receiving waterbody name but also the precise affected reach (e.g., beach name, boat launch) to be actionable for users.
Boating associations request the rule require coordination with marine VHF radio channels or harbor-master notifications for immediate alerting of mariners in addition to electronic public notice.

Environmental lawyers recommend adding a requirement that public notices include simple health guidance (e.g., no swimming, avoid contact) and link to state/local health Department advisories rather than only raw facts about time/location.

Tribal governments request that notices explicitly indicate if tribal waters or treaty fishing areas are affected and require direct notification to tribal leadership and fishery managers within the same 4-hour window.

Public watchdog groups request that the electronic update within 24 hours include not just volume and end time but also any available pollutant concentration sampling results or an estimated health risk level.

Permittees ask the Agency to provide clear guidance on acceptable volume estimation precision (e.g., ±10%, ±20%) and acceptable rounding practices when reporting measured or estimated volumes to ensure uniform reporting.

Small systems without continuous flow meters request allowance to report model-based or historical-average estimates for volume if installing monitoring equipment is not economically feasible, and seek explicit grandfathering until they can equip outfalls.

Legal commenters ask whether the "unless already provided" clause for approximate end time in the electronic update refers specifically to earlier public notices or also to initial notices to health departments — they request consistent cross-referencing.

The May 1 annual notice deadline may conflict with local budgeting and reporting cycles for some agencies; commenters request the Agency allow an alternative date or a phased-in compliance year for the first reporting cycle.
Small utilities request an extended first-year deadline (e.g., 9–12 months after rule promulgation) for the initial annual notice to allow time to collect and quality-assure prior-year data.

Satellite system operators seek clarity whether the "copy to POTW operator" requirement creates any liability or operational obligations for the POTW receiving the copy and ask whether acknowledgement of receipt is required.
Public disclosure advocates request that the annual notice include direct links to the full public notification plan and historical annual notices online, not just information on availability.
Environmental groups request that the annual notice include GPS coordinates for each outfall and accessible maps so the public can identify locations rather than narrative descriptions.

Commenters urge the Agency to require per-event data in the annual notice in machine-readable form (CSV/JSON) rather than only narrative summaries to enable independent analysis of date, location, duration, and volume.

Concerned citizens note that dry weather discharges are often most concerning and request that the rule require immediate investigation reports be summarized in the annual notice, including root-cause analysis and corrective actions taken.

Public health officials ask that the "summary of available monitoring data" include microbial indicators (E. coli, enterococci) and priority pollutant results where available, rather than unspecified monitoring summaries.

Recreation and tourism stakeholders request that the annual notice link each CSO event to impacted public access areas and beaches with advisories or closures clearly marked to protect public health and local businesses.

Meteorological services and modeling experts request guidance on acceptable sources and siting for "representative rain gauge data" and clarification whether modeled precipitation (radar) is acceptable when gauge data is unavailable.
Commenters request that the annual notice point of contact include both a public information officer and an operations contact with phone/email to facilitate follow-up by the public and regulators.

Environmental advocates request that the annual summary of minimum controls and LTCP status include actual metrics (e.g., number of overflows reduced, percent capture, estimated pollutant load reduction) rather than qualitative descriptions.

Municipalities ask the rule to limit "key remaining milestones" to a manageable list and allow confidential treatment of sensitive contract/timetable details if disclosure would jeopardize procurement or security.

Communities request guidance on how to estimate "anticipated average annual number of CSO discharges after plan completion" (e.g., model scenarios, baseline years) and whether ranges/uncertainty bands are acceptable.

IT and reporting staff request detailed technical specifications and validation rules for the electronic reporting forms under 40 CFR 127 so agencies can integrate with existing DMR/SOER systems well before the first reporting cycle.
Public notification plan development: Small jurisdictions request a simplified template or model public notification plan to reduce administrative burden and ensure consistency across permittees.

Utilities ask for flexibility in the requirement to inform the public via bill mailings where some customers are not billed (e.g., municipal customers) and request alternative outreach methods be allowed and listed (e.g., utility bulletins, municipal newsletters).

The requirement to submit the plan within 6 months after final rule publication is potentially infeasible for small systems; commenters request a phased submission schedule based on population thresholds (e.g., <10,000 gets 12 months).

Municipalities request clarity on the required level of detail when identifying sign locations in the plan (e.g., photos, GPS coordinates, parcel IDs) and propose that a map attachment should suffice.

Public health stakeholders recommend that plan-required sign message descriptions include translations into commonly spoken local languages and plain-language health advisories vetted by health departments.

Commenters ask that signage maintenance protocols allow for adaptive frequency based on vandalism risk and seasonal impacts (e.g., winter snow coverage) and request that inspection intervals be adjustable after Director approval.

Tribes and downstream municipalities request a clear definition of "potentially affected" entities and a requirement that Tribes always be treated as potentially affected when in or downstream of the watershed, with direct written notification.

Public health departments support the requirement to summarize their comments but request that the plan also include demonstrable explanations of how health department recommendations were incorporated or reasoned responses if not adopted.
Other public entities request templates for documenting outreach efforts and a defined minimum timeframe for solicitation of comments (e.g., 30 days) so that the permittee's outreach is meaningful.

Health departments ask for a requirement that notification protocols include escalation thresholds for large-volume or untreated sewage events that trigger broader media outreach and temporary beach/boating closures.

Consumer groups request that the protocols for initial/supplemental public notice include use of social media, text alerts, and local media partnerships to maximize timely reach to affected populations.

Engineers and modelers request a clear list of acceptable flow-measurement technologies and minimum calibration/QA requirements; they also support the 5-year calibration interval for systems ≥75,000 but ask for definitions of calibration standards.

Smaller municipalities argue that the 5-year calibration mandate for populations ≥75,000 should be scaled for mid-sized communities (e.g., require calibration every 7 years for populations 25,000–75,000) to reflect resource constraints.

Commenters request that the plan must require that the annual notice be posted in machine-readable, searchable formats and archived for a minimum number of years (e.g., 10 years) on the permittee website.

Stakeholders want explicit minimum outreach steps required before plan submission (e.g., at least one public meeting, 30-day comment period, and direct notification to listed entities) rather than vague "seek input" language.
Local public health departments request that the rule require permittees to provide preliminary draft plans to health departments at least 45 days before formal submission to allow substantive input.

Health departments request specific collaborative tasks be codified (e.g., agreement on which discharges warrant public notification, thresholds by volume or duration) rather than open-ended "work with" language.

Tribal governments request explicit inclusion in paragraph (e)(1)(ii) that notification recommendations must consider tribal subsistence fishing and cultural uses and require direct tribal approvals for messaging affecting tribal resources.
Potentially affected public entities request mandatory written acknowledgment of receipt from each contacted entity so permittees can document outreach efforts in the plan.

Legal commentators ask that the "consider recommendations" obligation be clarified into a standard of reasonableness with documentation of how recommendations were considered and why they were or were not adopted.

Municipal associations support the discretionary extension authority for undue economic hardship but ask the rule to require a clear, objective standard and list of factors (budget shortfall, infrastructure damage, demonstrated inability to procure signs) that the Director may consider.

Consumer and environmental groups oppose overly broad extension authority and request that any extension be time-limited, publicly justified, and require enforceable interim measures to protect public health.

Commenters request a requirement that the Director's notification to the Regional Administrator include redacted financial information protections if communities provide sensitive proprietary economic data to demonstrate hardship.

Advocacy groups request that the Director's website notice for extensions include a summary of the justification and expected mitigation measures, not just community name and new dates, to preserve transparency.

Citizens ask that the posted notice of extensions remain on the Director’s website permanently (or archived) rather than removed at the new compliance date so there is an ongoing public record of extensions granted.

Industry groups request that permit language under §122.42(f) explicitly allow permittees to incorporate existing state/local public notification requirements if they meet or exceed the federal elements, to avoid duplication.
Legal commenters request that permits reference the exact subsection(s) of §122.38 to avoid inconsistency and to ensure that permit limits are enforceable and clearly tied to the regulatory text.

Permittees ask that the permit’s required signage information allow for use of QR codes on signs linking to up-to-date electronic information, rather than expecting static full disclosure on physical signs.

Utilities request that permittees be allowed to prioritize sign installation at high-use access points and provide alternative notification (e.g., temporary signs, boater advisories) for lower-use outfalls until budget allows full signage.

Commenters request that permit language specifying timing and content for notifications include standardized templates for initial and supplemental notices to ensure timely compliance and consistent public information.

Public communicators request the permit requirement for public notification content to mandate inclusion of clear health guidance and links to local health advisory pages instead of solely factual discharge details.

Technical staff ask for criteria for designating which CSO locations must be monitored for volume/duration (e.g., population served, history of overflows, proximity to public access) to ensure permits are practicable.
IT departments request explicit data formats, validation rules, and API endpoints for electronic submittal of the May 1 annual notice to allow automated uploads and reduce human error.

Environmental groups request that permit conditions explicitly require posting of the annual notice on a public portal and that the Director retain the authority to require additional disclosures if the public health risk is elevated.
Municipalities request that the electronic reporting requirement reference existing state e-reporting systems to avoid duplicative submissions and ask for coordination with state reporting timelines.

Compliance officers ask for safe-harbor provisions for reporting errors (e.g., corrected reports submission allowed within X days) to avoid punitive enforcement for initial inadvertent data inaccuracies.

raw_output:
[P1] The September 20, 2021 postmark/receipt deadline is unreasonably short given the complexity of the proposed revisions; stakeholders need at least an additional 60 days to prepare substantive comments.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether comments that are mailed on September 20 but delivered after that date due to postal delay will be accepted, rather than treating postmark as the sole determinative factor.

[P2] Requiring electronic comments to be received by 11:59 p.m. ET on the closing date disadvantages commenters in other time zones and should allow receipt by 11:59 p.m. local time for the submitter or extend the window by 48 hours.

[P2] The provision should clarify whether partial uploads or upload errors received before 11:59 p.m. ET but completed only after will be accepted or whether an automated timestamp will control acceptance.

[P3] The September 3, 2021 deadline for written requests for a public hearing is too early and does not give potential hearing participants sufficient time to assess the proposal; hearing requests should be accepted through the close of the comment period.

[P3] The rule must state whether faxed, emailed, or electronic requests for a hearing constitute “in writing” and provide the specific address or email to which such requests should be sent.

[P4] The list of permitted submission methods should explicitly confirm that assisted submissions (e.g., filings by attorneys or third-party advocacy groups on behalf of individuals) are allowed and state any required authorization.

[P5] The regulations.gov submission instructions are vague regarding required docket identifiers; the rule should require commenters to include the docket number FWS–R1–ES–2020–0050 in the subject line to ensure proper docketing.

[P5] The rule should provide alternate electronic submission means for commenters who cannot use regulations.gov (e.g., direct email), rather than requesting the public only use the portal.

[P6] The mailing address for hard-copy submissions appears truncated in this excerpt; commenters need the complete mailing address and instructions about required labeling to ensure timely processing.

[P6] There should be guidance on whether hard-copy packages must be postmarked by the deadline or physically received by the Service by the deadline, and how courier deliveries are handled.

[P7] The Service’s request that commenters use only the specified methods could be read as limiting other reasonable submission channels; the agency should make clear that the listed methods are preferred but not exclusive if access barriers exist.

[P7] The rule should explicitly state accommodations for commenters with disabilities who cannot use the online portal or mail system and provide an alternative submission process.

[P8] Posting all comments on regulations.gov without redaction obligations raises serious privacy concerns; the Service should commit to redacting personal data by default or allow opt-out for sensitive information.

[P9] The statement that the Service will post personal information should be narrowed — personal information beyond name and city (e.g., phone numbers, email, home address) should not be posted without explicit consent.

[P9] The rule is inconsistent with privacy laws; the Service must publish a privacy impact assessment explaining how it will handle and protect personal data submitted with comments.

[P10] Allowing hardcopy submitters to request withholding of personal identifying information only by noting it at the top is insufficient — the Service should provide and require a standardized form or checkbox to request non-disclosure and explain limits to confidentiality.

[P10] The provision applies only to hardcopy submissions; equivalent protections should be provided for electronic submitters who request withholding of personal identifying information.

[P11] Posting all hardcopy submissions on regulations.gov could lead to indexing of sensitive attachments (e.g., resumes); the Service should state whether attachments will be published in full and whether file types or sizes are permitted.

[P12] While the Service will “consider all comments,” the rule should define the standard of consideration and commit to responding in the final rule to major themes and specific substantive objections raised by commenters.

[P12] The Service must publish a response-to-comments appendix in the final rule that identifies which comments led to any modifications and the factual/legal basis for accepting or rejecting them.

[P13] The exception that earlier comments to the August 11, 2020 proposal need not be resubmitted could cause confusion; the rule should list which topics/comments from that docket will carry forward and which must be resubmitted.

[P13] Legal and stakeholder groups request confirmation that previously submitted confidential or administrative records are preserved and will be considered even if not resubmitted.

[P14] Requiring parties who want March 1, 2021 comments reconsidered to resubmit is burdensome and may duplicate effort; the Service should automatically associate March 1 submissions with this docket unless the commenter withdraws consent.

[P14] The rule should specify whether resubmitted March 1 comments can reference the original docket entry rather than reattaching large datasets to avoid redundant submissions.

[P15] The requirement to include supporting information for scientific or commercial assertions is reasonable, but the Service must explain what level of documentation is required (e.g., peer-reviewed studies, raw data, methodologies).

[P15] The Service should commit to protecting proprietary commercial information submitted as supporting data and provide instructions for submitting confidential business information under FOIA exemptions.

[P16] Prohibiting consideration of comments that only state support or opposition could chill public participation — the Service should still consider such comments for gauging public sentiment and explicitly explain their limited weight in the decision.

[P16] The rule needs clear criteria for when a comment “merely states support or opposition” versus when it provides substantive reasoning; otherwise, the Service may arbitrarily disregard lay comments.

[P17] The request for comments from specific groups should include specific questions or topics of interest to guide input from agencies, Tribes, scientists, and industry.

[P17] The Service should provide Tribal governments with extended consultation timelines and dedicate government-to-government consultation sessions rather than a general call for comments.

[P18] Announcing hearings at least 15 days in advance may be inadequate for stakeholders who must arrange travel or schedule testimony; the Service should give at least 30 days’ notice for in-person hearings or 15+ for webinars.

[P18] The rule must clarify how testimony at hearings will be transcribed, archived, and incorporated into the administrative record.

[P19] Publishing hearing announcements in local newspapers is insufficient outreach in the digital era; the Service should require email notices to known stakeholders and postings on regional agency listservs.

[P19] The Service should specify which local newspapers will be used and require posting in Tribal newspapers or other media serving affected communities.

[P20] Webinars as the default hearing format are acceptable, but the Service must ensure platform accessibility (e.g., captioning, sign language interpreters) and provide instructions for registering and submitting remote oral comments.

[P20] The Service should state whether webinar attendees will be able to present oral comments live and how time will be allocated, as well as whether recordings will be posted to the docket.

[P21] The condition that final-rule changes be “reasonably anticipated” by the public is vague; the Service should define the standard for “reasonably anticipated” and provide examples of changes that would require supplemental notice.

[P21] If substantive, unanticipated changes are made, the Service should commit to a supplemental notice-and-comment period rather than incorporating them without further public input.

[P22] Basing changes on the “best scientific and commercial data available” requires transparency about data selection criteria and access to the datasets used; the Service should publish data and models used in decision-making.

[P22] The Service should commit to peer review of any new scientific analyses relied upon to make significant changes to critical habitat designation.

[P23] The requirement to explain factual basis and reasoning for changes should be operationalized by requiring a written justification in the preamble to the final rule that addresses major points raised in comments.

[P23] The Service must provide citations and the administrative record supporting any reversal of prior conclusions so that courts and stakeholders can review the rational connection.

[P24] The criteria for removing an area from designation (i.e., not meeting definition of critical habitat or exclusion benefits outweigh inclusion) must be accompanied by a detailed benefits-cost-style analysis and standards for what constitutes sufficient “benefits.”

[P24] The Service should clarify how it will weigh economic, national security, and other exclusion factors and whether the public can submit alternative valuations or evidence of benefits of inclusion.

[P25] The FAA designation of Class E surface airspace for Newton-City-County Airport with a 4.2-mile radius should be cross-referenced to ensure no conflict with critical habitat or other land-use restrictions in the surrounding area.

[P25] Local governments and airport operators should be allowed to comment on whether the specified coordinates and 4.2-mile radius interfere with existing flight procedures or local zoning; the rule lacks an interagency coordination discussion.

[P26] Designating Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet within a 6.7-mile radius may have implications for unmanned aircraft systems (drones); the FAA should clarify how this airspace change affects UAS operations and permitting.

[P26] The rule should include a chart or map with the Newton Airport airspace radii overlaid on land-use and protected habitat boundaries so stakeholders can assess impacts; textual coordinates alone are insufficient.
