[P1] The requirement in §60.105a(b)(2)(ii) to conduct performance evaluations "per §60.13(c) and Performance Specification 3" is vague about acceptable documentation and frequency; industry requests clarification that quarterly evaluations meet the obligation and that paper records are acceptable.

[P1] Performance Specification 3 was written for specific monitor technologies; requiring it for all CO2 and O2 monitors may be infeasible for non-reference sensors—request an explicit allowance for manufacturer-recommended verification procedures for newer sensor types.

[P2] Mandating EPA Method 3/3A/3B for relative accuracy evaluations of CO2 and O2 monitors will impose significant cost for small sources that use in-line non-extractive sensors; commenters request that equivalency testing or field calibration approaches be allowed for low-emission units.

[P2] Methods 3/3A/3B assume stack sampling access and probe traverses that are not possible for some existing stacks; the rule should specify modifications or alternatives where physical access is constrained.

[P3] Allowing ANSI/ASME PTC 19.10–1981 as an alternative to Method 3B is helpful, but the rule should spell out equivalency criteria—stakeholders request numeric acceptance thresholds and recordkeeping requirements for use of the ANSI method.

[P4] The obligation in §60.106a(a)(1)(iii) to follow §60.13(c) and Performance Specification 2 for SO2 monitor evaluations should clarify applicability to extractive versus in-situ SO2 technologies and whether Performance Specification 2 applies unchanged to newer CEMS designs.

[P5] Requiring Method 6 or 6C for SO2 evaluations will be burdensome where low-level detection is needed; small refineries and chemical plants ask for permission to use lower-flow sampling or updated methods (e.g., Method 6A/6B) or vendor calibration curves.

[P6] Allowing ANSI/ASME PTC 19.10–1981 as an alternative to Method 6 is welcome, but the provision lacks specificity on how to handle differences in method detection limits and quality assurance standards; request explicit guidance.

[P7] The permission in §63.643(c) to designate a process vent as a maintenance vent when used only during S/S/M/I is reasonable, but enforcement concerns exist—advocates request mandatory logging/auditing to prevent routine use being mischaracterized as maintenance.

[P8] The exception not to designate maintenance vents as Group 1/2 or include them in NOCS (§63.643(c)) could create unreported emission streams; public health groups request elimination of this exception or at minimum mandatory periodic reporting of aggregate maintenance vent emissions.

[P9] The obligation to comply with paragraphs (c)(1)-(3) for each maintenance vent by specified dates (unless extension requested) lacks clarity on which compliance dates apply to different facility classes; industry requests a compliance date table keyed to source categories.

[P10] §63.643(c)(1) requires removal of process liquids and depressurization prior to venting "as much as practical" — this subjective standard needs a clear, measurable definition or examples to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P11] §63.643(c)(1)(ii) mandates reducing pressure to ≤5 psig when LEL cannot be measured and prohibits active purging until LEL <10%; commenters representing operations argue that many systems cannot achieve ≤5 psig and request alternative safe pressure thresholds or allowed engineering controls.

[P11] Legal commenters note that the LEL thresholds (measure <10% before purging) conflict with some equipment design constraints and ask the agency to clarify applicability to low-vapor-pressure streams and to permit engineering judgements documented in MACT plans.

[P12] Allowing "<72 pounds of total VOC" in equipment before venting (§63.643(c)(1)(iii)) is arbitrary; operators request that the rule provide a calculation methodology (e.g., volume, vapor pressure, temperature inputs) for determining the 72-lb threshold and examples.

[P12] Environmental groups argue that the 72-lb threshold is too high and can permit large uncontrolled emissions; they request lowering the threshold or requiring notification when a maintenance vent will release ≥10 pounds VOC.

[P13] The special provision for pyrophoric catalyst equipment (§63.643(c)(1)(iv)) allowing an annual allowance up to 35% LEL across vents is insufficiently protective — safety and community health groups request that the agency require stricter limits and transparency about how the single annual allowance is allocated and tracked.

[P13] Industry operators of hydrotreaters/hydrocrackers request clarity on how the "one annual allowance up to 35%" is counted across multiple vents and whether method detection and recordkeeping (e.g., flow measurement) are required to substantiate the allowance.

[P14] The fallback allowing active purging if pressure reduced to ≤2 psig (§63.643(c)(1)(v)) may be technically infeasible for some pressurized equipment; stakeholders ask for explicit allowed purge gases, maximum purge flows, and monitoring requirements to avoid flaring or atmospheric release.

[P14] Safety engineers request confirmation that purging with inert gas (e.g., nitrogen) introduced at ≤2 psig does not create unsafe conditions for catalysts or downstream equipment and that permit conditions can specify purge procedures.

[P15] §63.644(c) forcing owners/operators with bypass-capable vent systems to comply with one of (c)(1)-(3) is reasonable, but companies request a clear definition of "bypass line that could reasonably divert" to avoid coverage of purely isolated emergency lines.

[P16] The prohibition on using bypass to divert vent streams to atmosphere or noncompliant devices (§63.644(c)) could criminalize short-term operational flexibility used during emergencies; industry requests an explicit emergency exception and required notification procedures when bypassing is used for immediate safety.

[P17] The requirement to install caps, blind flanges, plugs, or second valves for open-ended lines per §60.482–6 (¶63.644(c)(3)) may not be technically feasible for some process designs; operators request engineering alternatives (e.g., continuous monitoring with auto-shutdown) be allowed.

[P18] Requiring existing-source compliance with part 60 subpart VV and paragraph (b) (§63.648(a)) imposes substantial retrofitting obligations; small refiners request a small-source exemption or extended compliance schedule.

[P19] The new-source requirement to comply with subpart H (§63.648(a) second provision) needs clarification of the interplay with NSPS and PSD/NSR permitting to avoid duplicative or conflicting standards.

[P20] The alternative compliance election in §63.648(c) should include explicit crosswalk guidance and an approval mechanism from the permitting authority to avoid inconsistent interpretations by regional offices.

[P21] §63.648(j) obligations for PRDs in organic HAP service appear to apply broadly; manufacturers and legal advisors request clarity on scope (size, set pressure) and whether PRDs in intermittent/standby service are covered.

[P22] Counting specified indicators and automated devices as separate redundant prevention measures (§63.648(j)(3)(ii)(A)) is a positive flexibility, but the rule should define acceptable independence (e.g., independent power supplies, separate sensors) so that one failure cannot defeat redundancy.

[P23] Recognizing staged relief systems discharging initially to flare/closed vent as an acceptable prevention measure (§63.648(j)(3)(ii)(E)) requires clear performance criteria for the flare/closed vent (e.g., destruction efficiency, flare combustion stability) — request explicit numeric standards.

[P24] The requirement to determine and record total annual release events per PRD and those due to force majeure (§63.648(j)(3)(iv)) demands uniform counting rules; operators ask the agency to define what constitutes a "release event" (duration threshold, re-seating) and acceptable evidence for force majeure claims.

[P25] The prohibition in §63.648(j)(3)(v) that certain release events constitute violations except as in j(4)/(j)(5) requires more explicit cross-references to the listed exceptions; legal commenters ask for a consolidated table showing which events are violations and which are exempt.

[P26] The exception where all PRD releases are routed to closed vent/control/process/fuel gas (§63.648(j)(4)(i)) is sensible, but operators request clarity on required documentation and monitoring to demonstrate that "all releases" are indeed routed (e.g., continuous monitoring of pilot vents).

[P27] For pilot-operated PRDs routed to closed systems (§63.648(j)(4)(ii)), limiting compliance to j(1) and (2) for the pilot vent is acceptable, but the rule should require periodic integrity testing of pilot lines and recordkeeping to prove routing remains intact.

[P28] For balanced bellows PRDs routed to closed systems (§63.648(j)(4)(iii)), commenters request guidance on how to demonstrate routing (e.g., tagging, piping diagrams) and whether existing installations need retrofitting.

[P29] The obligation that closed vent systems and control devices meet §63.644 requirements (§63.648(j)(4)(iv)) requires harmonization of monitoring and leak detection schedules; industry asks for clarity to avoid duplicative surveillance.

[P30] Requiring flares receiving gas from PRD-connected fuel gas systems to comply with §63.670 after Jan 30, 2019 (§63.648(j)(4)(v)) may impose retrofit costs; operators request grandfathering for existing flares that meet equivalent state standards or an extended compliance timeline.

[P31] The NOCS submission within 150 days (§63.655(f)) is tight for complex facilities assembling multiple performance tests; commenters request flexibility to submit partial NOCS with a schedule for outstanding items or an allowance for a single consolidated submission within 180 days.

[P32] The special timing/format requirements for certain NOCS reports (§63.655(f)(6)) should be described explicitly in the preamble; states and permit writers need clear instructions to accept NOCS content in operating permit applications.

[P33] Providing multiple options for NOCS submission (operating permit app, amendment, separate submittal) (§63.655(f)) is helpful, but affected sources request an explicit statement that submission via state permitting portals satisfies the federal requirement.

[P34] The exception that prior-submitted information obviates a separate NOCS (§63.655(f)) needs specification of what constitutes "submitted before" (e.g., submitted to EPA, to state, or both) to avoid duplicate reporting.

[P35] Requiring the NOCS to include the method of compliance for each Group 1 storage vessel not in an emissions average (§63.655(f)(1)(i)(A)(1)) is reasonable but operators need templates or examples to ensure consistent presentation, particularly where control devices serve multiple vessels.

[P36] Mandating that NOCS state anticipated compliance date for vessels not yet complying (§63.655(f)(1)(i)(A)(2)) could encourage optimistic dates; industry requests allowance to revise dates via amendment without penalty if good-faith efforts are documented.

[P37] Requiring actual compliance dates in NOCS when vessels are complying (§63.655(f)(1)(i)(A)(3)) raises recordkeeping concerns for older vessels with incomplete historical records; commenters ask for guidance on acceptable substantiating documents.

[P40] Requiring one complete test report for each test method used in initial performance tests (§63.655(f)(2)) could produce large file sizes for ERT submissions; commenters request acceptance of compressed files and clear limits on attachments per submission.

[P42] Including CMS performance evaluation results in NOCS unless required electronically (§63.655(f)(4)) creates overlap with §63.655(h)(9); commenters ask for a single electronic submission route to avoid inconsistency.

[P44] Public interest groups argue the 72 lb/day threshold is too high and that all pilot vent releases should be reported to increase transparency, particularly near communities.

[P45] The periodic reporting requirements for maintenance vent releases exceeding limits (§63.655(g)(13)) are complex; commenters request templates for required data elements and sample calculations for determining whether a release meets the reporting threshold.

[P51] The force majeure assertion process for electronic submission failures (§63.655(h)(10)(ii)) requires clearer standards for what constitutes force majeure and the evidence required; operators and legal counsel request a checklist of acceptable documentation.

[P65] Industry commenters request that where the rule allows alternatives (ANSI/ASME methods, closed vent routing, alternative submission paths) the EPA provide templates, equivalency demonstration procedures, and a pre-approval process to limit regional enforcement variability.

[P66] Legal commenters warn that ambiguous terms used throughout (e.g., "as much as practical," "reasonably divert," "approved control device") create substantial compliance uncertainty and recommend substituting objective metrics or providing compliance examples in the final rule and guidance.

[P67] Small business groups request the EPA prepare a Small Entity Compliance Guide addressing practical implementation of the monitoring, reporting, and vent control requirements, including estimated costs and timelines.

[P1] Industry commenter: Requiring a valid ECT procedure code on all IPF claims is appropriate for billing integrity, but CMS should specify the exact list of acceptable ECT CPT/HCPCS/ICD-10-PCS codes and publish them in the preamble or an addendum to avoid adjudication delays.

[P1] Small IPF provider: The rule lacks guidance on how to handle legacy claims for ongoing courses of ECT that began before October 1 — request transition instructions and a grace period for claims submission correction without penalty.

[P1] Legal expert: CMS must clarify whether denial of payment for a missing/invalid ECT code constitutes a substantive condition of participation or only a claims processing issue, because hospitals may face different appeal rights.

[P1] Patient advocacy group: Requiring a single procedure code may not capture modalities or intensity (e.g., unilateral vs bilateral, number of stimuli) — request CMS allow reporting of secondary ECT procedure details for quality monitoring.

[P2] Hospital association: The statutory 2.0 percentage point reduction for failure to report quality data could disproportionately harm small IPFs; request flexibility such as corrective action windows or proportional penalties tied to the scope/length of nonreporting.

[P2] Quality measurement coalition: CMS should define what constitutes “failure to report” (complete absence vs partial/incomplete data) and provide safe-harbor for minor technical errors if data are otherwise submitted.

[P2] State Medicaid agency: The rule should clarify coordination between Medicare reductions and state payment methodologies if IPFs also participate in state-funded programs, to avoid double penalties.

[P3] IPF finance officer: Applying a 0.6% reduced update to the federal per diem without a clear methodological explanation creates budget uncertainty — request CMS provide the precise computation worksheet used to derive the FY2021 base rate.

[P3] Small rural IPF: The 0.6% reduction will squeeze margins further in thinly reimbursed facilities — ask CMS to exempt critical access or rural-designated IPFs from the reduced update or add a hardship waiver.

[P4] Provider billing director: CMS should publish the exact formula used to translate the 0.6% reduced annual update and the 0.9979 wage index budget neutrality factor into the per-treatment ECT payment to allow financial planning.

[P5] Medical coding association: The prohibition on reporting diagnoses that relate only to prior episodes is ambiguous — request explicit examples and ICD-10 coding scenarios demonstrating acceptable vs prohibited diagnosis reporting to ensure coder consistency.

[P5] Defense attorney/complaint: Prohibiting prior-episode diagnoses may impair risk adjustment fairness if prior conditions influence current treatment decisions — request an appeals process or allowance where prior diagnoses materially affect care.

[P6] Clinical society: The requirement that comorbid conditions must affect treatment or LOS to qualify for adjustment is subjective — request CMS define objective criteria (e.g., documented change in medication, therapy plan, or LOS extension) and acceptable documentation standards.

[P6] Audit/legal consultant: CMS should provide guidance on acceptable supporting documentation for comorbidity adjustments to reduce post-payment audit vulnerability; vague language increases recoupment risk.

[P7] Hospital coder: Limiting to one adjustment per comorbidity category may undercompensate for patients with multiple distinct manifestations within a category — request CMS to define categories explicitly and allow multiple adjustments when clinically justified.

[P7] Payer analyst: The one-adjustment-per-category rule is reasonable to prevent upcoding; request CMS publish the mapping of ICD-10 codes to comorbidity categories used for automated claims adjudication.

[P8] Medical records manager: Requiring up to 24 additional full ICD-10-CM codes may be burdensome for electronic health record interfaces — request CMS provide machine-readable claim field specifications and allow phased implementation.

[P8] Privacy advocate: Adding up to 24 additional diagnosis codes increases disclosure of sensitive behavioral health information on claims — request CMS issue guidance on confidentiality protections and minimum necessary principles for claims data.

[P9] Coding standards group: Requiring strict adherence to ICD‑10‑CM "code first" sequencing is consistent with coding guidance but CMS must publish examples for psychiatric principal diagnoses and common code-first pairings to reduce inconsistent sequencing across IPFs.

[P9] Clinician: Some psychiatric presentations involve overlapping etiologies where sequence is clinically debatable; request CMS allow clinical judgment documentation to supersede rigid code-first sequencing in ambiguous cases.

[P10] Hospital CFO: Denying MS‑DRG adjustment when a psychiatric principal diagnosis does not map to one of the 17 MS‑DRGs could produce significant revenue loss — request CMS provide a listing of diagnoses that will not map and the expected percentage impact, and propose an interim mapping for uncommon diagnoses.

[P10] Health policy researcher: CMS should clarify whether lack of MS‑DRG adjustment affects only psychiatric principal diagnoses or also affects secondary psychiatric-related MS‑DRG calculations.

[P11] Coding vendor: Updating IPF MS‑DRG definitions using FY2021 ICD‑10‑CM/PCS code sets on October 1, 2020 requires timely distribution of code mapping files — request CMS provide the updated IPF MS‑DRG lists and logic tables in machine-readable format at least 90 days before effective date.

[P11] Clinician-coder: Request a 6-month post-implementation audit moratorium or educational period for new mapping changes to reduce improper denials from unfamiliar code updates.

[P12] Industry association: Retaining current patient age adjustment factors may be reasonable short term, but CMS should commit to analysing age adjustment validity annually and publish supporting actuarial data showing the factors remain empirically justified for FY2021.

[P12] Elder advocacy group: Request CMS assess whether current age adjustments adequately account for increased complexity in older psychiatric patients (comorbidity burden, polypharmacy) and consider revising upward if not.

[P13] Hospital discharge planner: The variable per diem schedule declining through day 21 and constant thereafter may create perverse incentives to extend stays to reach the flat portion — request CMS evaluate behavioral incentives and monitor LOS trends.

[P13] Access advocate: The declining per diem could discourage necessary longer stays for complex psychiatric patients; ask CMS to publish analyses showing the schedule does not reduce access to longer inpatient treatment.

[P14] IPF with ED: Assigning a 1.31 day‑1 per diem for IPFs with a qualifying ED is appropriate, but CMS must clarify the definition of “qualifying emergency department” and provide objective criteria and documentation requirements.

[P14] Rural provider: Some facilities operate urgent psychiatric intake areas that are not full EDs — request a pathway for these sites to qualify for the 1.31 factor or for CMS to clarify exclusion criteria.

[P15] IPF without ED: The lower 1.19 day‑1 adjustment for IPFs without EDs may penalize freestanding psychiatric hospitals serving community needs — request CMS consider a midpoint factor or allow documentation of comparable intake services to qualify for a higher day-1 factor.

[P16] Provider association: Retaining the current variable per diem factors for FY2021 is administratively simple, but CMS should commit to reviewing per diem adequacy in light of pandemic-related cost shifts before finalizing.

[P17] Labor economist: Using the “best available Medicare data” for estimating per-day costs is vague — request CMS disclose the exact Medicare datasets and time periods used for wage index estimation and cost per day calculations.

[P17] Auditing firm: CMS should state how it validates the accuracy of Medicare data when estimating per-day costs and what recourse providers have if they identify data errors affecting their wage index.

[P18] State hospital association: Basing the IPF wage index on the concurrent pre‑floor, pre‑reclassified IPPS hospital wage index may not reflect IPF labor markets accurately — request CMS conduct sensitivity analyses comparing IPF-specific wage data versus hospital-based wage data.

[P18] Rural health advocate: Using the concurrent pre-floor, pre-reclassified index could disadvantage rural IPFs whose labor markets differ from acute hospitals; request CMS consider a rural adjustment or alternative data sources for rural labor markets.

[P19] Finance director: Increasing the labor-related share to 77.2% for FY2021 materially changes allocations — request CMS publish the labor share calculation steps, supporting data, and sensitivity analyses showing effects on facility-level payments.

[P19] Union representative: Raising the labor-related share appropriately reflects rising labor costs; request CMS ensure the increased labor share directly benefits front-line worker compensation and not only hospital margins.

[P20] State planning office: Adopting OMB Bulletin No.18‑04 delineations will change wage index areas—request CMS provide county-level mapping of old vs new CBSAs and a county lookup tool so IPFs can determine anticipated impacts.

[P20] Legal consumer: CMS must allow comment and transparency on how OMB delineation changes will interact with other CMS policies (reclassification, rural status), as automatic adoption may have unintended consequences.

[P21] Affected IPF: The proposed transition policy to mitigate negative impacts should include multi-year phase-ins, caps on annual wage index decreases, and an opt-in hardship waiver for institutions facing >5% net revenue loss.

[P21] Budget office: Any transition mitigation must be budget-neutral; ask CMS to provide the fiscal impact estimate of the transition policy and identify which providers would receive protection and which would not.

[P22] Rural hospital coalition: Treating Micropolitan Areas as rural is appropriate, but CMS should explicitly state how this reclassification will impact other rural payment adjustments and facility eligibility for rural programs.

[P22] Urban county official: Reclassifying micropolitan areas as rural for wage index calculations could understate urban labor costs in growing areas; request CMS provide a mechanism to revisit classification if area urbanizes.

[P23] County governments listed: Treating specified counties as rural may be inconsistent with local labor markets — request CMS publish the full list of counties and the analytic basis (commuting patterns, urbanization metrics) for reassigning them.

[P23] Labor union: Moving county wage data to rural calculations could reduce wages over time; request CMS model wage impacts by county and allow stakeholders to submit alternative data.

[P24] Metropolitan hospital: Including county wage data within newly assigned urban CBSAs may artificially inflate urban wage indices if those counties have atypically low wages; request CMS provide a transparent method and testing results showing minimal distortions.

[P24] State workforce agency: Ask CMS to allow state-provided wage surveys or comment period submissions if stakeholders believe county assignments to urban CBSAs misrepresent local wages.

[P25] Coding compliance officer: Removing 'site unspecified' codes where laterality exists is sensible, but CMS should provide mapping files showing which codes will be removed and crosswalks to assist EHR and billing system updates.

[P25] Rural clinician: Some clinical documentation initially uses unspecified codes; request CMS permit use of unspecified codes for a limited period during transition and accompanying coder education.

[P26] Coding advocacy group: The exception to removal because no new FY2021 ICD‑10 additions were site‑unspecified is fine, but CMS should state how future additions will be reviewed and give advance notice before batch removals.

[P26] Small vendor: Clarify whether the exception applies only to FY2021 additions or to any late code set updates published after the proposed rule was released.

[P27] Provider groups: Retaining FY2020 comorbidity adjustment factors may be appropriate, but CMS should publish the empirical validation demonstrating factors are still predictive for FY2021, especially given recent changes in treatment patterns.

[P27] Health services researcher: Request CMS release the regression models, coefficients, and datasets used to derive the comorbidity adjustment factors to allow independent replication.

[P28] Policy analyst: Incorporating relevant OMB bulletin updates into any final changes is reasonable, but CMS should commit to an explicit timeline for when such updates will be reviewed and how stakeholders will be informed.

[P28] State agency: Request clarification whether late OMB bulletins issued after the proposed rule but before the final rule will be automatically incorporated or require separate notice-and-comment.

[P29] Hospital CFO: Using unadjusted pre‑floor/pre‑reclassified IPPS wage index data for IPF calculations may transmit distortions from IPPS-specific policies — request CMS run parity analyses comparing wage indices computed with and without those pre-adjustments.

[P29] Legal expert: CMS should state whether IPFs may request reclassification or appeal assignments if they can show their assigned labor market area is not accurate under the CBSA framework.

[P30] City planner: Defining IPF labor market areas by OMB CBSAs may not reflect real employee commuting patterns in certain regions — request CMS allow alternative labor market definitions based on localized commuting data where justified.

[P30] Behavioral health association: CMS should publish the full list of CBSAs and which IPFs fall into which labor market areas, plus an appeals/reclassification procedure and timeline for providers to request changes.

raw_output:
[P1] The October 5, 2017 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonably short and should be extended to allow affected operators, unions, and independent MROs sufficient time to perform technical review and coordinate consolidated comments.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether comments must be received by midnight Eastern Time on October 5, 2017, or by the close of business in a different time zone.

[P2] Excluding line 1165 and subsequent from applicability (§ 39.13(c)) is ambiguous — commenters request justification and underlying fleet data showing why newer production line numbers are safe to exclude.

[P2] The provision § 39.13(c) does not explain how operators of mixed-fleet airplanes (some before and some after line 1165) should manage their maintenance programs; request explicit guidance.

[P3] § 39.13(f) requires compliance within specified times "unless already done" but fails to define acceptable evidence of prior compliance; commenters request documentation standards for proving prior compliance.

[P3] The AD should state whether previously performed work done to non-Boeing service bulletin standards qualifies as "already done" for the purpose of § 39.13(f).

[P4] The 24-month inspection timeline in § 39.13(g) is overly long and risks continued exposure to the identified unsafe condition; safety advocates request a shorter compliance interval (e.g., 6–12 months).

[P4] Conversely, some small operators and lessors will find 24 months financially or operationally burdensome; request allowance for staged compliance tied to scheduled heavy maintenance visits.

[P5] The maintenance-record review alternative in § 39.13(g) should specify what documents (work orders, invoices, component rosters) and what authentication (signatures, traceability) are acceptable for conclusively determining MOV actuator P/N.

[P5] Allowing record review in lieu of physical inspection without requiring an audit or traceability standard increases risk of incorrect part-number determination; require cross-check with physical tags or parts-traceability where records are incomplete.

[P6] § 39.13(g) requires further detail on the distinction between MA30A1017 and other actuators — commenters request a list of common alternate P/Ns that would trigger (g)(1) or (g)(2) actions to aid identification.

[P6] The rule should specify whether temporarily installed loaner actuators with different P/Ns constitute noncompliance and whether they must be replaced immediately.

[P7] Requiring installation of P/N MA30A1017 on all AIMS‑1 airplanes within 24 months (§ 39.13(g)(1)) may be cost-prohibitive for certain operators; request cost estimates and an economic impact analysis specific to small certificated operators.

[P7] The rule should permit installation during scheduled maintenance windows to minimize operational disruption rather than imposing a hard 24-month deadline for AIMS‑1 fleets.

[P8] For AIMS‑2, Blockpoint Version 16 or earlier (§ 39.13(g)(2)), the rule mandates actions within 24 months but does not provide a clear migration plan for operators with mixed software baselines; request explicit procedures for mixed-fleet software upgrades.

[P8] The AD should clarify whether software updates for AIMS‑2 Blockpoint are eligible for installation in-line during production-like maintenance or whether special configuration control steps are required.

[P9] § 39.13(g)(2)(i) mandates installing P/N MA30A1017 per Boeing SB 777–28A; commenters request that the AD explicitly allow equivalent parts approved under PMA or TSO when they meet the same specifications.

[P9] The rule should require Boeing to provide torque/installation procedures and any special tooling in the service bulletin; absence of such detail may lead to improper installations.

[P10] The alternative compliance option in § 39.13(g)(2)(ii) — installing AIMS‑2 Blockpoint Version 17A — should be expanded to permit equivalent FAA-approved software modifications from third-party suppliers, provided they meet the certification basis.

[P10] The AD should require Boeing to make AIMS‑2 Blockpoint Version 17A (and documentation) available at reasonable cost and provide a timeline for software distribution to operators.

[P11] The definition in § 39.13(g)(2)(ii) of "later-approved versions" tied to incorporation into the type design after the SB is overly narrow; commenters recommend allowing any FAA-approved replacement versions irrespective of incorporation timing, provided they maintain safety equivalence.

[P11] Legal commenters note that tying later-approved versions to type-design incorporation may create unnecessary constraints and recommend rewording to reference FAA approval under 14 CFR part 21 rather than type-design incorporation.

[P12] Requiring revision of the Airworthiness Limitations Section to add AWL 28–AWL–MOVA within 24 months after completing § (g) fleetwide (§ 39.13(h)) is ambiguous for multi-operator lessors — who is responsible when airplanes change operators during the 24-month period?

[P12] The directive to "incorporate figure 1 into the ALS" should specify whether figure 1 must be annotated in each airplane’s maintenance planning document or whether a single operator-level program revision suffices.

[P13] The condition in § 39.13(h) that the ALS revision must occur only after (g) actions are completed on all airplanes in the operator's fleet is impractical for large global operators undergoing continuous fleet transitions; request alternative language allowing per-airplane ALS updates as actions are completed.

[P13] The rule should clarify whether leased-in aircraft that are not under an operator's direct maintenance control are considered part of "operator's fleet" for the purposes of the sequencing requirement in § 39.13(h).

[P14] The prohibition in § 39.13(h) figure 1 against installing P/Ns MA30A1001 and MA20A2027 at specified positions is too absolute and does not provide an approved replacement parts list; operators request a list of allowed alternate P/Ns and a process to approve substitutes.

[P14] The prohibition fails to include procedures for verifying previous installations of the prohibited P/Ns during routine maintenance checks; recommend mandatory fleet-wide audit and reporting requirements.

[P15] The specification that the left engine fuel shutoff spar valve position is subject to the prohibition (§ 39.13(h) figure 1.1) needs clarity on whether this applies to inboard/outboard spar configurations or to all left-side positions on the spar.

[P15] Maintenance manuals and parts catalogs should be cross-referenced in the AD to avoid misinterpretation of the left-position designation.

[P16] Similarly, the right-engine fuel shutoff spar valve prohibition (§ 39.13(h) figure 1.2) requires precise definition of "right position" in relation to varying aircraft configurations and in-service modifications.

[P16] Operators request an illustration or coordinate reference system (e.g., left/right relative to fuselage centerline and forward/aft station) to ensure consistent compliance with the prohibition.

[P17] The termination clause (§ 39.13(i)) that accomplishing (g) and (h) terminates AD 2015–19–01 must include an explicit crosswalk showing which specific requirements of AD 2015–19–01 are superseded to avoid regulatory confusion.

[P17] Legal commenters request assurance that terminating AD 2015–19–01 will not inadvertently remove other unrelated safety requirements previously required by that AD.

[P18] The credit provision (§ 39.13(j)) for AIMS‑2 Blockpoint Version 17/17.1 installed before the effective date lacks documentation requirements to claim credit; request required evidence and an approval process.

[P18] Operators who installed 17/17.1 in production but not per the referenced SB need explicit instructions on how to demonstrate eligibility for credit under § 39.13(j).

[P19] Centralizing AMOC approval authority to the Seattle ACO Manager (§ 39.13(k)(1)) may create bottlenecks; request additional FAA offices be authorized to approve AMOCs or define expedited processing timelines.

[P19] Industry commenters request that AMOC authority be delegated to regional ACOs when workload warrants to avoid operational delays.

[P20] The AMOC submission procedures in § 39.13(k)(1) referencing 14 CFR 39.19 are acceptable but should also allow electronic submission through a secure FAA portal, not only email, to ensure traceability.

[P20] The rule should require the FAA to acknowledge receipt of AMOC requests within a defined time (e.g., 7 business days) and publish estimated processing times.

[P21] The requirement to notify the principal inspector before using any approved AMOC (§ 39.13(k)(2)) should allow alternative notification channels for foreign civil aviation authorities or operators without a U.S.-based principal inspector.

[P21] The provision should clarify whether notification must be prior to first use for each airplane or once per operator for the AMOC.

raw_output:
[P1] The FAA's January 7, 2020 comment deadline for the Airbus Helicopters AD is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60 days to allow affected operators, MROs, and unions adequate time to analyze technical data and prepare substantive comments.

[P1] The rule must clarify whether the "FAA must receive comments by January 7, 2020" deadline refers to postmark date, email timestamp, or receipt by the docket; ambiguity creates risk of rejected comments and should be fixed.

[P2] The compliance paragraph that states "You are responsible for performing each action required by this AD within the specified compliance time unless already done" is redundant but legally broad — it should expressly allow delegated MOUs (e.g., repair stations) to perform actions on behalf of the certificate holder and specify required recordkeeping.

[P2] The AD should specify acceptable recordkeeping/documentation required to demonstrate compliance with the "you are responsible" obligation (e.g., logbook entry format, work order references, and retention period).

[P3] The 110 hours time-in-service compliance window to remove sealing compound and inspect RH/LH rear attachment fitting screws is too short for operators with limited scheduled downtime; extend to at least 300 hours or provide a risk-based tiered schedule for business and emergency operators.

[P3] The AD's requirement to "remove the sealing compound and inspect each screw" lacks detail on allowable inspection methods (visual only vs. magnification, borescope) — the FAA should specify acceptable inspection techniques and minimal qualifications for the inspector.

[P3] The AD should define whether 110 hours TIS means flight hours since last overhaul/installation or since AD effective date and how partial hours are rounded; current language is ambiguous.

[P4] The condition "2 or less threads on each of the four screws; or 3 or more threads ... with H < 5 mm" that triggers sealing compound application is unclear about measurement tolerances — the rule must provide measurement method, acceptable instruments, and tolerances (e.g., ±0.1 mm).

[P4] Requiring only sealing compound (without replacement) when thread count is low (2 or fewer threads) may be a temporary mitigation insufficient to ensure long-term safety — FAA should require immediate replacement of affected screws/nuts or a recurring inspection interval.

[P5] The requirement to remove nuts and screws and measure screw length L "one-at-a-time in cross pattern" is operationally unclear — the AD must describe the precise cross pattern, torque states, and how to prevent misalignment or loss of preload during sequential removal.

[P5] The AD should permit removal and measurement by qualified repair stations and provide instructions for maintaining alignment and torque when reassembling after one-at-a-time removal; otherwise, repeated removals could create additional maintenance-induced damage.

[P6] The instruction to remove bent or corroded washers from service before further flight is appropriate, but the AD should provide acceptable replacement washer specifications (material, hardness, part number) and allowable sources to avoid supply bottlenecks.

[P7] The threshold L ≤ 59.3 mm triggers only a visual inspection for corrosion/cracks; this pass/fail criterion lacks non-destructive test (NDT) guidance — the FAA should require dye-penetrant or other NDT for suspect screws, especially where visual access is limited.

[P7] "Visually inspect the screw for corrosion and cracks" does not state inspector qualifications; the AD should specify required training or certification (A&P, inspector) and provide acceptance criteria (photographs/illustrations of acceptable/unacceptable conditions).

[P8] Replacing screws that show corrosion/cracks before further flight is necessary, but the AD must require use of specific approved part numbers and torque values for replacement screws and nuts to ensure consistent, airworthy repairs.

[P9] For screws with no corrosion/cracks, the AD requires re-installation with a new nut and sealant; this is ambiguous about whether the original washers may be reused if not bent/corroded — clarify acceptable reuse vs mandatory replacement of washers.

[P9] The AD must provide the specified sealant type, application method, and cure time needed before return to service; otherwise operators may use incompatible sealants that compromise safety.

[P10] Replacing the rear attachment fitting and its complete hardware when L > 59.3 mm is burdensome and costly — the FAA should provide cost/benefit analysis, alternative mitigations (e.g., calibrated shims or controlled re-machining), or a grace period to source parts.

[P10] The AD should specify approved replacement part numbers and whether field-modified fittings are permissible if certified data shows equivalent strength; currently the instruction to "replace" is vague and could result in part shortages and grounding.

[P11] Allowing the Manager, Safety Management Section to approve AMOCs centralizes authority; commenters request clarity on expected turnaround times and criteria the Manager will use to approve AMOCs to avoid operational delays.

[P12] The AMOC submission address lists a physical office and contact info but does not provide an electronic submission option for AMOCs; include an email/portal to streamline review and maintain auditable submissions.

[P13] The FAA's "suggestion" that operators notify their principal inspector before operating under an AMOC is too weak for Part 119 operators; the rule should make notification mandatory so oversight personnel are aware of deviations from standard procedures.

[P14] The Boeing AD comment deadline of December 23, 2019 conflicts with holiday staffing and is too short; extend the comment period 45–60 days to ensure stakeholders can perform required technical review.

[P15] The Boeing AD's general compliance clause repeating "unless already done" should require operators to provide documentation showing compliance date and method, including service bulletin revision, certifying inspector, and logbook entries.

[P16] The 60-month compliance window to perform replacements/installation/inspections per Boeing Service Bulletins is excessively long for parts subject to in-service failure modes; justify the schedule with probabilistic risk assessment or shorten it for high-utilization fleets.

[P16] The AD requires actions "in accordance with" Boeing Service Bulletin instructions but does not incorporate the service bulletin by reference in the regulation text — the FAA should incorporate the exact revision and make the SB publicly available in the docket.

[P17] The requirement for a general visual inspection of six override/jettison fuel pumps to determine bonding jumper braid type should define acceptance criteria and provide photographic examples of one-piece vs two-piece braid to prevent inconsistent determinations.

[P18] Allowing up to 60 months to replace one-piece braid bonding jumpers is too long given potential lightning/fuel ignition risks; require replacement within 12 months for commercial passenger operations.

[P19] Installing a second bonding jumper on applicable pumps is a generic statement; the AD must specify routing, connector/terminal specs, installation torque, and whether existing cable trays/clearances are sufficient.

[P20] The identical inspection requirement for two transfer/jettison pumps repeats the need for detailed acceptance criteria; the AD should require documentation of braid type in maintenance records for traceability.

[P21] The 60-month window to replace transfer/jettison pump one-piece braid jumpers should be reduced for aircraft in higher risk operations (e.g., known thunderstorm routes) or when the bonding jumper is subject to abrasion/age.

[P22] Installing a second bonding jumper on transfer/jettison pumps could create electrical bonding loops; the AD should require an electrical continuity/resistance test after installation to confirm intended bonding performance.

[P23] Replacing bonding jumpers on the APU fuel pump for all affected airplanes may drive parts shortages; the FAA must provide approved part numbers, supplier list, and allow phased compliance to avoid grounding due to parts unavailability.

[P23] The AD should require post-installation verification (e.g., continuity measurement, torque checks) for APU pump bonding jumper replacements to ensure workmanship and mitigating installation errors.

[P24] Requiring replacement of the electrical scavenge pump bonding jumper for Groups 1 and 2 airplanes demands definition of Group membership in the AD or cross-reference; current text assumes readers know groups which may be ambiguous.

[P24] The AD should provide rationale for differentiating Groups 1 and 2 from other groups and explain why Groups 3+ (if any) are not required to comply, including risk assessment data.

[P25] The authority for the Seattle ACO Branch Manager to approve AMOCs is fine, but the AD should permit delegation to Boeing's ODA for routine AMOCs to expedite operator compliance — currently delegation language appears elsewhere but should be explicit.

[P26] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to principal inspector or local FSDO may create inconsistent review; the FAA should centralize initial AMOC intake to the certification office to ensure consistent criteria and tracking.

[P27] The instruction to send direct submissions to the person identified in paragraph (j)(1) is opaque in the absence of paragraph (j)(1) text in the AD preamble; the AD should include full contact info in the main AMOC paragraph to reduce confusion.

[P28] The permission to email AMOC requests to 9–ANM-Seattle-ACO–AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is helpful, but the AD should also allow electronic signatures and encrypted transmissions for proprietary data.

[P29] The requirement to notify principal inspector/local FSDO before using an approved AMOC lacks timeline (how far in advance notification must be provided); specify a minimum notice period (e.g., 5 business days) and required content of the notification.

[P30] Allowing AMOCs approved by Boeing ODA to be used for required repairs provided they are approved by the Manager raises questions about independence and conflict of interest; require FAA concurrence or oversight in ODA approvals used as AMOCs.

[P31] Requiring AMOC repairs to meet the airplane's certification basis is reasonable but vague — the AD must specify acceptable substantiation (analysis, test data, structural substantiation) and level of documentation required for approval.

[P32] The requirement that any AMOC approval must specifically reference this AD should be clarified to require inclusion of the AD docket number and specific paragraph references to ensure the AMOC scope is clear.

[P3] The AD lacks provisions for sampling/representative inspections for fleets with many aircraft — allow initial sampling inspection with defined statistical confidence methods to reduce unnecessary labor for low-risk fleets.

[P16] The AD's dependence on Boeing Service Bulletins requires that Boeing make corrective revisions free of charge for avionics/structural ambiguities; FAA should require SBs be updated within 60 days if substantive comments are received.

[P10] The AD should include provisions for field approval of modified fittings when OEM parts are unavailable, including criteria for engineering approval and requirement for follow-up retrofit with OEM parts when available.

[P4] The measurement of "thread height H" should specify whether coating/paint is to be removed before measurement and whether damaged threads may be measured or require replacement without measurement.

[P7] For screws measured at or near the 59.3 mm threshold, the AD should require that measurements be taken to two decimal places and specify who is responsible for measurement accuracy to avoid disputes about compliance.

[P1] The requirement for States to submit "appropriate supporting information" consistent with Phase 2 of the 1997 Ozone Implementation Rule is vague; EPA should specify the exact data elements, formats, and analytical methods required to avoid inconsistent or incomplete SIP filings.

[P1] Industry commenters will request clarification that "appropriate supporting information" includes only information necessary to demonstrate RACT equivalence and not proprietary business data, and that EPA will protect confidential business information consistent with CAA procedures.

[P2] Environmental groups will assert that the rule's public notice requirement must include a minimum 30-day public comment period and require EPA to post state RACT SIP submissions and supporting materials on the EPA website to ensure meaningful public participation.

[P2] Small business associations will claim that the regulation should not require duplicative public notice when the state has already held public hearings under state law; EPA should allow coordination to avoid redundant processes.

raw_output:
[P1] The August 28, 2017 comments due date is unreasonable and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow affected operators and suppliers sufficient time to analyze the 777–53A0083 service bulletin and prepare substantive comments.

[P1] The rule violates APA notice-and-comment fairness because the comments period is shorter than typical FAA rulemakings for complex ADs; please provide justification for the expedited deadline or reissue with a longer comment window.

[P2] The compliance clause "within the specified compliance times" is ambiguous because the AD references multiple compliance intervals in the Boeing bulletin; the FAA should publish a consolidated table specifying exact compliance deadlines for each affected configuration.

[P2] There is no allowance for supply-chain or shop capacity delays to meet compliance times; the AD should include an explicit extension process or grace period when an operator cannot obtain parts or depot slots through no fault of its own.

[P3] Requiring operators to perform all actions labeled RC exactly as in Boeing Alert Service Bulletin 777–53A0083 without FAA-published clarifications could create conflicts with existing operator-approved maintenance programs; the FAA should identify which RC actions affect the type design and which are maintenance tasks.

[P3] The AD's reliance on Boeing's Accomplishment Instructions as incorporated by reference gives Boeing de facto rulemaking authority; the FAA must ensure full agency oversight and either include critical procedural text in the AD or publish FAA-approved clarifications.

[P4] Allowing PART 5 (cleaning and neutralization) to terminate repetitive inspections is reasonable, but the AD should require submission of test validation data demonstrating the long-term effectiveness of PART 5 before allowing it as an optional terminating action.

[P4] The AD does not specify recordkeeping or evidence requirements to demonstrate PART 5 was accomplished per the service bulletin; require operators to document PART 5 completion in maintenance records and report results to the FAA.

[P5] Interpreting "after the original issue date" as "after the effective date of this AD" will change compliance timing for certain tasks; the FAA should provide an explicit mapping table showing original bulletin timelines versus AD-effective-date timelines.

[P5] This substitution could create retroactive compliance obligations for work already performed between the bulletin original issue date and the AD effective date; the AD should explicitly exempt work already done in good faith before the AD became effective.

[P6] Replacing Boeing contact-based RC approval with an FAA-approved-AMOC-only process could slow necessary repairs; the FAA should permit use of Boeing-authorized ODA approvals as interim measures when they meet FAA standards.

[P6] The AD's requirement to use AMOCs instead of contacting Boeing for RC guidance lacks clarity about timeframe for FAA decisions; add a mandatory FAA response timeframe for AMOC requests to prevent operational delays.

[P7] Limiting AMOC approval authority to the Seattle ACO manager may bottleneck approvals for operators outside the Seattle region; permit delegated authority to other ACOs or allow ODA approvals that meet FAA criteria to streamline compliance.

[P8] Requiring AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 is duplicative if operators can submit directly to the Seattle ACO; the AD should clarify the preferred routing and whether simultaneous submissions are acceptable.

[P9] The requirement to address AMOC info to the person in paragraph (k)(1) is problematic because paragraph (k)(1) is not included in the public docket; provide the name/contact details in the NPRM or an accessible location to avoid misrouting.

[P10] Allowing AMOC submissions via the specified email is helpful, but the rule should require confirmation of receipt and an estimated processing timeline to allow operators to plan maintenance schedules.

[P11] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC could be impractical for operators without a designated principal inspector; the AD should allow electronic notification to the FAA maintenance program manager as an alternative.

[P12] Permitting Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs is appropriate, but the AD must require that Boeing ODA approvals be submitted to the FAA for recordkeeping and that the FAA reserve the right to review and rescind ODA approvals if safety standards are not met.

[P13] Requiring AMOC approvals to meet the airplane's certification basis and specifically reference this AD is appropriate, but the AD should prescribe the minimal documentation required to demonstrate compliance with the certification basis to expedite AMOC review.

[P14] The strict requirement that all RC steps, substeps, and figures be performed to comply with the AD leaves no margin for minor, safe-deviation or practical differences in shop processes; the FAA should allow minor procedural tailoring under an approved maintenance data system without full AMOC when safety is not affected.

[P15] The "RC Exempt" labeling exception is helpful but the AD should clarify the criteria used to designate a step as RC Exempt and require Boeing to justify any RC/RC Exempt designations in the service bulletin.

[P16] Requiring an AMOC for any deviation from RC steps, including figures, will create administrative burden and delay; the FAA should define what constitutes a "deviation" (e.g., substantive vs. editorial) and exempt minor editorial or typographical differences from AMOC requirements.

[P17] Allowing deviations to non-RC steps under an operator's maintenance/inspection program is appropriate, but the AD must require operators to assess and document that the deviation does not prevent completion of RC steps and does not alter the configuration that RC steps rely upon.

[P17] The AD should require operators who deviate from non-RC steps to submit periodic summaries to the FAA to ensure systemic deviations do not undermine the intent of the AD across the fleet.

[P3] The AD does not define "applicable times" from paragraph 1.E. of the Boeing bulletin clearly in the regulatory text; include explicit regulatory compliance time windows to eliminate reliance on the manufacturer document.

[P4] The AD should specify whether PART 5 must be performed by Boeing-authorized facilities, certified repair stations, or if operators may perform it in-house under their existing procedures.

[P6] The AD's prohibition on contacting Boeing for RC action approvals could conflict with existing contractual arrangements between operators and Boeing for technical support; include a grandfathering clause until contractual processes are updated.

[P7] The AMOC authority should explicitly include the ability to issue field approvals or temporary deviations for operators in remote locations where immediate compliance is necessary for safety-of-flight considerations.

[P11] The timing requirement to notify FAA before using an AMOC is vague; specify whether notification must occur before returning the aircraft to service and the acceptable time window for such notification.

[P10] The provided email address may not support secure transmission of proprietary repair data; the AD should permit secure upload portals or encrypted submissions and state data protection measures.

[P2] The phrase "unless already completed" for compliance is vague; operators need guidance on how to demonstrate completion (e.g., maintenance records, serviceable tag numbers) to the FAA to avoid enforcement uncertainty.

[P3] The AD should include a list of affected airplane serial numbers or line numbers to clarify the applicability of the Boeing service bulletin actions to specific aircraft.

[P4] For operators relying on PART 5 to terminate inspections, the AD should require a follow-up reporting requirement (e.g., 12- and 24-month inspections) to validate the terminating action's durability across environments and routes.

[P16] The requirement that deviations to RC steps require an AMOC could be interpreted to require AMOCs for minor tooling substitutions; clarify that known-equivalent tooling or processes previously accepted in operators’ maintenance programs do not require an AMOC.

[P13] Legal counsel notes that the requirement that AMOC approvals "must meet the certification basis" may be read to impose a retroactive design change obligation; the FAA should clarify that AMOC approvals need only demonstrate an acceptable level of safety relative to the existing certification basis.

[P1] The AD's comments deadline predates the expected publication date for the related service bulletin; stakeholders should be given the full service bulletin and any updated data before the comment period closes.

[P7] The AD should provide appeal or re-hearing procedures when the Seattle ACO manager denies an AMOC, including target response times and escalation paths.

[P12] The AD should clarify whether Boeing ODA approvals automatically become AMOCs or only if subsequently accepted by the FAA; ambiguity could lead to inconsistent implementation.

[P9] The AD must include the street/mailing address and telephone number of the Seattle ACO manager (paragraph k(1)) in the NPRM or final rule to ensure proper routing of direct submissions.

[P14] The AD should allow a process for emergency deviations to RC steps for safety-of-flight reasons, with retrospective AMOC submission allowed within a defined short period (e.g., 5 business days).

[P3] The AD should require the Boeing service bulletin to be incorporated by reference into the Federal Register citation so that operators have a single authoritative source for the mandatory actions.

[P5] Changing "original issue date" to "effective date of this AD" could unintentionally require compliance earlier than operators anticipated if the AD effective date is before planned maintenance; provide transition allowances.

[P10] The AD should allow submission of AMOC data through existing FAA portals (e.g., ADAMS) in addition to the email address to accommodate larger attachments and structured data formats.

[P1] The February 24, 2020 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is impractically short and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow operators, labor unions, and suppliers sufficient time to collect operational data and prepare detailed technical comments.

[P1] The rule violates the Administrative Procedure Act notice-and-comment expectations because the fixed past deadline (Feb 24, 2020) is impossible to meet now; FAA should reopen the comment period with a new future deadline.

[P2] Limiting applicability to only Boeing 737–900ER series airplanes in § 39.13(c) is overly narrow; other 737 variants may have identical MLG electrical connector configurations and should be included or the FAA should provide justification for excluding them.

[P2] The applicability provision does not clarify whether converted freighter 737–900ERs or other special configurations are included; FAA should state coverage for passenger-to-freighter conversions and other STC-modified airframes.

[P3] § 39.13(f) requires compliance within specified times "unless already done" but fails to define what constitutes adequate documentation of prior compliance; FAA should specify acceptable records and verification procedures.

[P4] The 12‑month action window in § 39.13(g) is arbitrary and may not account for seasonal deicing exposures; FAA should permit operators to phase inspections based on winter operations and present an alternative timeline for low-utilization aircraft.

[P5] The requirement in § 39.13(g)(1) to determine exposure by "reviewing airport deicing-fluid component data" is unclear about which party (operator, airport authority, or third-party contractor) bears primary responsibility; FAA should assign responsibility and require the airport to provide attestations.

[P5] Airport deicing-fluid component data may be proprietary or not maintained in a way accessible to carriers; FAA should prescribe acceptable sources and methods (e.g., invoices, supplier MSDS, airport records) for making the exposure determination.

[P6] Repeating the exposure-determination every 24 months under § 39.13(g)(1)(i) is insufficient for aircraft that operate seasonally at airports that recently switched to potassium-based fluids; FAA should require operators to re-check after any known supplier change or immediately after being notified by the airport.

[P7] The 90‑day window in § 39.13(g)(1)(ii) to perform the inspection after a determination of exposure is too long given the corrosion risk; FAA should shorten this to 30 days for aircraft that remain based at or frequently operate to airports using potassium formate/acetate.

[P8] The 24‑month recurring inspection interval in § 39.13(g)(1)(ii) and § 39.13(g)(2) may be inadequate for high-utilization airplanes operating in corrosive winter environments; FAA should allow risk‑based shorter intervals (e.g., 6–12 months) for such operators.

[P9] § 39.13(g)(2) requires detailed inspection per Boeing service bulletin but does not incorporate or attach the revision number or date of that bulletin; FAA should reference the exact service bulletin revision and effective date to avoid ambiguity.

[P9] Relying solely on the Boeing service bulletin in § 39.13(g)(2) could limit independent engineering judgments; FAA should allow equivalent procedures from other manufacturers or DER-approved procedures as AMOCs without unnecessary barriers.

[P10] The threshold in § 39.13(g)(2)(i) that permits cleaning for backshell corrosion ≤10% lacks a defined measurement methodology for "total backshell surface area corrosion," creating enforcement and compliance ambiguity; FAA should provide a quantitative measurement protocol and examples.

[P11] Requiring replacement within 30 days for corrosion >10% and <20% in § 39.13(g)(2)(ii) may be impractical for small operators without immediate spare parts; FAA should permit a temporary repair option with operational limitations while parts are sourced.

[P12] The requirement in § 39.13(g)(2)(iii) to replace connectors before further flight when corrosion is ≥20% will impose immediate AOG costs; FAA should allow a short, documented ferry authorization under strict conditions to reach maintenance facilities.

[P12] The "before further flight" mandate for ≥20% corrosion lacks consideration for life-safety vs. dispatch reliability distinctions; FAA should enumerate the specific safety hazards tied to ≥20% corrosion to justify immediate grounding.

[P13] Granting the Seattle ACO manager exclusive authority to approve AMOCs in § 39.13(h)(1) centralizes decision-making and may delay time-sensitive AMOC approvals for operators outside the Seattle region; FAA should allow regional FSDOs to concur or provide a streamlined national AMOC process.

[P14] The AMOC request routing requirement in § 39.13(h)(1) to principal inspectors or local FSDOs may be inconsistent with operators' existing points of contact; FAA should clarify how this interacts with existing continuous airworthiness management organization (CAMO) relationships.

[P15] Addressing direct submissions to the certification-office manager as required in § 39.13(h)(1) without providing the specific contact name or updated address in the AD text will cause confusion; FAA must publish the current contact details or a public web link.

[P16] Allowing email submissions to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov in § 39.13(h)(1) raises cybersecurity and privacy questions; FAA should specify secure file transfer procedures for proprietary technical data and confirm receipt/error handling.

[P17] The notification requirement in § 39.13(h)(2) to inform a principal inspector before using an approved AMOC may be duplicative where operators already have approvals recorded centrally; FAA should allow batch notifications or electronic registry entries to reduce administrative burden.

[P18] § 39.13(h)(3) permits Boeing ODA approvals of AMOCs for repairs but the provision requires the ODA approval to "reference this AD" and the airplane certification basis; this could create legal uncertainty about FAA oversight—FAA should clarify the FAA's review role and retention of authority.

[P19] The certification-basis requirement in § 39.13(h)(3) for AMOC approvals may preclude legacy airplanes with multiple amendments and special conditions; FAA should provide guidance on demonstrating equivalence to the certification basis for complex or modified airplanes.

[P20] § 39.13(h)(4) approving previously approved AMOCs for AD 2005–18–23 as valid for this AD could inadvertently import unsuitable relaxations or outdated methods; FAA should review those AMOCs case-by-case and publish which AMOCs apply and any limitations.

[P9] The AD does not require operators to report inspection findings or corrosion rates to FAA or Boeing; FAA should mandate reporting to build a safety database and permit trend analysis to determine whether the inspection intervals are adequate.

[P5] Requiring operators to rely on airport-supplied deicing composition data does not account for mixed-use airports where multiple deicing contractors operate; the AD should require per-event recordkeeping (e.g., service logs) demonstrating which fluid was applied to specific flights.

[P11] The 30‑day replacement window in § 39.13(g)(2)(ii) does not require parts stocking levels or provide an economic impact analysis for smaller carriers; FAA should consider grace periods or funding support for essential spares.

[P3] The phrase "unless already done" in § 39.13(f) should require that prior actions be performed in accordance with the same methods and standards as in this AD, and that documentation be submitted for FAA acceptance; otherwise operators may claim prior actions that are not equivalent.

[P7] § 39.13(g)(1)(ii) does not address airplanes that cannot be inspected within 90 days due to maintenance scheduling constraints; FAA should permit temporary mitigations (e.g., operational limitations) pending inspection.

[P10] Cleaning as remediation for ≤10% corrosion in § 39.13(g)(2)(i) should specify cleaning agents and post-cleaning corrosion inhibitor applications to prevent rapid recurrence.

The rule violates the Administrative Procedure Act notice-and-comment expectations because the fixed past deadline (Feb 24, 2020) is impossible to meet now; FAA should reopen the comment period with a new future deadline.

Limiting applicability to only Boeing 737–900ER series airplanes in § 39.13(c) is overly narrow; other 737 variants may have identical MLG electrical connector configurations and should be included or the FAA should provide justification for excluding them.

The applicability provision does not clarify whether converted freighter 737–900ERs or other special configurations are included; FAA should state coverage for passenger-to-freighter conversions and other STC-modified airframes.

§ 39.13(f) requires compliance within specified times "unless already done" but fails to define what constitutes adequate documentation of prior compliance; FAA should specify acceptable records and verification procedures.

Airport deicing-fluid component data may be proprietary or not maintained in a way accessible to carriers; FAA should prescribe acceptable sources and methods (e.g., invoices, supplier MSDS, airport records) for making the exposure determination.

Repeating the exposure-determination every 24 months under § 39.13(g)(1)(i) is insufficient for aircraft that operate seasonally at airports that recently switched to potassium-based fluids; FAA should require operators to re-check after any known supplier change or immediately after being notified by the airport.

The 90‑day window in § 39.13(g)(1)(ii) to perform the inspection after a determination of exposure is too long given the corrosion risk; FAA should shorten this to 30 days for aircraft that remain based at or frequently operate to airports using potassium formate/acetate.

The 24‑month recurring inspection interval in § 39.13(g)(1)(ii) and § 39.13(g)(2) may be inadequate for high-utilization airplanes operating in corrosive winter environments; FAA should allow risk‑based shorter intervals (e.g., 6–12 months) for such operators.

The requirement in § 39.13(g)(2)(iii) to replace connectors before further flight when corrosion is ≥20% will impose immediate AOG costs; FAA should allow a short, documented ferry authorization under strict conditions to reach maintenance facilities.

The "before further flight" mandate for ≥20% corrosion lacks consideration for life-safety vs. dispatch reliability distinctions; FAA should enumerate the specific safety hazards tied to ≥20% corrosion to justify immediate grounding.

Granting the Seattle ACO manager exclusive authority to approve AMOCs in § 39.13(h)(1) centralizes decision-making and may delay time-sensitive AMOC approvals for operators outside the Seattle region; FAA should allow regional FSDOs to concur or provide a streamlined national AMOC process.

The AMOC request routing requirement in § 39.13(h)(1) to principal inspectors or local FSDOs may be inconsistent with operators' existing points of contact; FAA should clarify how this interacts with existing continuous airworthiness management organization (CAMO) relationships.
