[P1] The requirement that the testing facility determine and document identity, strength, quality, and purity of each batch before study start is duplicative and will increase costs for contract testing labs that rely on sponsor-supplied characterization data.

[P1] The rule is unclear whether "before the study starts" permits characterization completed within a short window (e.g., 24–72 hours) prior to first use; please clarify acceptable timing to avoid operational disruption.

[P2] The exception allowing reliance on sponsor determinations lacks standards for the "verifying documentation" the sponsor must provide; specify minimum documentation (e.g., certificate of analysis, chain-of-custody, analyst signature, analytical method).

[P2] There is no requirement for independent verification by the testing facility when sponsor documentation comes from foreign or uncertified labs; require risk-based confirmatory testing when sponsor data are from labs without accreditation.

[P1] The provision does not address responsibility/resolution when sponsor documentation conflicts with the testing facility's own analysis; define which party bears the cost and the decision process for study continuation.

[P3] Requiring full refund to substituted charter participants regardless of timing (e.g., last-minute cancellations) could create severe financial exposure for charter operators; allow pro-rated refunds based on proximity to departure or nonrefundable costs.

[P4] The $25 administrative fee cap for non-European charters is arbitrary and fails to account for varying administrative costs across regions and booking channels; allow operators to charge a reasonable documented fee or index the cap to inflation.

[P3] The rule does not define "fully refund all monies that participant paid" — does this include ancillary fees (fuel surcharges, port fees, taxes)? Clarify which line items must be refunded.

[P4] The carve-out only for non-European charters is discriminatory and will distort competition; either apply the administrative fee allowance uniformly or provide justification for geographic differentiation.

[P5] Retaining reserve samples for studies over 4 weeks without regard to sample volume and storage capacity imposes onerous physical storage burdens on small labs; permit pooling strategies or minimum sample-size thresholds.

[P6] Mandating retention even when batches are prepared daily is impractical for high-throughput facilities producing many daily batches; allow alternative approaches such as rotating/reserve-of-records or targeted retention based on risk.

[P7] The term "sufficient sample to permit meaningful reanalysis" is vague; provide quantitative guidance (e.g., mg or mL per analysis type) or define criteria for "meaningful" to ensure consistent enforcement.

[P8] The dual requirement to retain for the period in §58.195 or the sample's useful life, whichever is shorter, may conflict with stability data uncertainties; require labs to document rationale and stability data supporting a shorter retention period.

[P9] Requiring storage conditions that "minimize deterioration" without definition will lead to inconsistent practices; provide acceptable storage condition ranges (temperature, humidity, light) or risk-based guidance.

[P10] While exhaustive stability studies are not required, the exception lacks a middle standard; request guidance on minimal stability testing or acceptance criteria that testing facilities should perform to justify storage conditions.

[P11] The inventory requirement to demonstrate test article accountability may duplicate existing custody tracking systems; allow use of validated electronic inventory systems and reduce redundant paper recordkeeping.

[P12] Documenting the initial amount and amount remaining after each mixture could be infeasible for continuous or automated mixing lines; allow batch-based or event-based recording methods with acceptance criteria.

[P13] The QA unit inspection list in §58.35(b)(3) is broad; define the frequency and scope of inspections to avoid open-ended obligations and to allow for risk-based inspection scheduling.

[P14] Deleting and reserving §58.113(b) (reserve-sample requirement) conflicts with other provisions in the proposal that reference reserve samples; reconcile the amendments so regulations are internally consistent.

[P15] Removing the phrase "samples of test or control article carrier mixtures" from §58.195(c) appears to shorten mandatory retention periods but leaves ambiguity about other sample types; clarify what sample categories remain subject to §58.195 retention.

[P14] The proposal to delete paragraph (b) of §58.113 without transitional guidance could invalidate ongoing studies' compliance plans; include grandfathering provisions or timelines for implementing the change.

[P16] The comment submission deadline of February 4, 1980 (historical date) appears erroneous or outdated; confirm the actual comment deadline and provide an extended period if needed for meaningful stakeholder input.

[P17] Requiring four copies of comments imposes an unnecessary burden and is environmentally wasteful in the digital era; accept electronic submissions as an alternative and eliminate the four-paper-copy requirement.

[P18] Allowing individuals only one copy but requiring organizations four copies is inconsistent; either accept electronic single submissions for all or explain rationales for differential copy requirements.

[P19] The instruction to include the Hearing Clerk docket number is reasonable, but the rule should provide an electronic docketing number and web instructions to facilitate correct identification.

[P20] Making submitted comments available for public inspection between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. weekdays at a physical location disadvantages remote stakeholders; provide online access and post comments on an official website to ensure transparency.

[P1] Legal commenters will question the division of responsibility between sponsor and testing facility; propose clearly assigning legal liability for mislabeled or nonconforming batches.

[P2] Industry requests a certification template for acceptable sponsor "verifying documentation" to harmonize submissions and speed reviews.

[P5] Animal welfare and clinical researchers express concern that eliminating reserve samples (per P14/P15) could impede investigation of adverse events; require retention of samples sufficient to perform root-cause analysis if safety issues arise.

[P7] Testing labs seek an appeals process or dispute resolution mechanism when regulators assert that retained samples are insufficient for reanalysis.

[P6] Small businesses request an exemption or simplified requirements for daily-prepared mixtures where identity can be ensured by continuous in-process controls.

[P9] Trade associations ask for an explicit statement that the "minimize deterioration" requirement does not mandate validated long-term stability studies for every matrix, only reasonable storage practices.

[P12] Some commenters will request electronic recordkeeping standards (audit trails, timestamps, and access controls) to satisfy the inventory and remaining-amount documentation requirements.

[P13] Professional QA organizations urge that inspections be limited to demonstration of compliance with written SOPs unless risk indicators warrant deeper review.

[P3] Consumer advocacy groups may argue that the full-refund requirement is necessary to protect passengers and should not be limited by operator-discretionary fees; recommend specifying that full refund includes all monies paid, including taxes and surcharges.

[P4] Charter operators note the $25 cap may be meaningless for high-dollar international substitutions; propose allowing a transparent actual-cost recovery option with documentation rather than a flat cap.

[P11] Academic labs request clarification whether transferred or destroyed test articles must be accounted for and by what documentation (e.g., disposal certificates).

[P15] Regulatory lawyers will ask for cross-references to be updated across the CFR to prevent orphaned citations after deletion of the phrase; request a full redline showing coordinated edits.

[P14] Enforcement officials will need interpretive guidance about whether the deletion of §58.113(b) reduces inspection priorities; request an FDA guidance document accompanying any final rule.

[P16] Public interest groups will request an extension of the comment period and public hearings in multiple regions to ensure broad participation.

[P17] Technology vendors offer that accepting electronic submissions would improve accessibility and request that the agency publish acceptable file formats and maximum file sizes.

[P1] Sponsors warn that duplicative testing by testing facilities when sponsor data exists will increase study start-up timelines; recommend allowing reliance with a documented risk assessment and spot checks.

[P2] International companies request that the rule explicitly accept internationally recognized certificates of analysis (e.g., ISO/IEC 17025 accredited labs) as satisfying sponsor verifying documentation.

[P8] Pharmaceutical manufacturers seek clarification on how to determine "useful life" for complex formulations and request permitted use of stability-indicating assay results to define useful life and retention periods.

[P1] The provision § 39.13(a) lacks clarity about whether comments submitted by mail that are postmarked by May 17, 2019 but received later will be accepted; request explicit statement that postmark date governs acceptance or that electronic submissions are permitted.

[P2] § 39.13(f) is vague about what constitutes “already completed” corrective actions — commenters request a definition or examples (e.g., actions completed per Service Bulletin X dated mm/dd/yyyy) to avoid inconsistent applicability.

[P2] The AD’s instruction in § 39.13(f) to perform the actions in (f)(1) and (f)(2) “if not already completed” creates recordkeeping burdens for operators; request that the FAA specify acceptable evidence of prior compliance (logbook entry, STC paperwork, manufacturer statement).

[P3] The 100 hours TIS compliance window in § 39.13(f)(1)(i) is too short and could impose operational disruptions on small operators and flight schools; request extending to 300 hours TIS or 90 days to allow scheduled maintenance.

[P3] § 39.13(f)(1)(i) does not state whether the removal must be performed by certificated repair stations or may be done by the owner/operator for its own aircraft; request clarification that certificated personnel requirements and any required certifications/tools are specified.

[P3] The work instruction referenced in § 39.13(f)(1)(i) is not included in the rule text; request that the FAA either include the full procedural steps in the AD or reference an accessible service document (with revision date and how to obtain it).

[P4] The requirement in § 39.13(f)(1)(ii) to update the AFM within 100 hours TIS lacks guidance on who is authorized to make AFM changes and whether these AFM inserts need FAA approval; request that FAA state whether the AFM revision is an owner/operator action and whether it must be submitted for FAA acceptance.

[P4] § 39.13(f)(1)(ii) does not specify if the AFM figures must be retained in the aircraft or whether a digital copy is acceptable; request permission for electronic AFM amendments and specify acceptable formats.

[P5] The prohibition in § 39.13(f)(2) banning installation of the left-hand rudder pedal gust lock mount “as of the effective date” appears retroactive for parts manufactured or stocked prior to the effective date; request clarification whether existing parts may be retained as spares or if they must be destroyed.

[P5] The blanket prohibition in § 39.13(f)(2) may negatively affect owners who rely on gust lock parts for other aircraft configurations; request an exception or process for obtaining approval to install the part for non-pilot-side or non-certified uses (e.g., display aircraft, ground-only use).

[P5] The rule in § 39.13(f)(2) does not specify enforcement mechanisms or whether previously issued PMA or TSO approvals are superseded; request FAA explain interplay with parts approvals and whether installation of existing PMA parts is prohibited.

[P6] § 39.13(g)(1) gives the Manager authority to approve AMOCs but does not commit to timelines for AMOC review and decision; industry requests an explicit maximum review time (e.g., 60 days) to avoid operational uncertainty.

[P6] The provision granting the Manager authority for AMOCs in § 39.13(g)(1) should be expanded to allow other field offices or delegated organizations to approve AMOCs in urgent cases; request additional delegation language for timeliness.

[P7] The requirement in § 39.13(g)(1) that AMOC requests follow 14 CFR 39.19 is appropriate but should include a summary of the key procedural elements (required contents, supporting data) to help submitters prepare complete requests.

[P8] § 39.13(g)(1) requires sending AMOC requests to a named FAA contact and physical address but omits secure electronic submission methods; request that FAA provide an email address and online portal to expedite AMOC processing and to preserve a clear date-stamped record.

[P1] The blanket prohibition in §17.43(g)(2) is overbroad because it fails to define the geographic scope of “persons subject to U.S. jurisdiction” with respect to activities occurring entirely outside the continental United States but within DPS ranges, creating ambiguity for researchers and international partners.

[P1] The regulation should clarify whether federally recognized tribes and their members acting on tribal land within the DPS ranges are “persons subject to U.S. jurisdiction” for purposes of §17.43(g)(2), to avoid unintended restrictions on tribal sovereign activities.

[P3] Prohibiting import/export per §17.21(b) without explicit language about scientific exchange will impede legitimate transboundary research collaborations; the rule should explicitly allow permit-authorized scientific transfers and clarify documentation requirements.

[P4] The cross-reference to §17.21(c)(1) for “take” does not define whether indirect habitat modifications (e.g., permitted water withdrawals upstream) constitute “take”; the rule should include examples or guidance on indirect and habitat-altering actions.

[P4] Industry commenters will object that reliance on §17.21(c)(1) without quantitative thresholds (e.g., number of individuals or area of habitat) creates regulatory uncertainty for landowners and project planners undertaking routine activities near streams.

[P5] The prohibition on possession of unlawfully taken specimens per §17.21(d)(1) should include a safe-harbor for previously held museum specimens or pre-existing captive collections with documentation, to avoid destruction or loss of scientific material.

[P6] Prohibiting interstate or foreign commerce in commercial activities (§17.21(e)) may inadvertently restrict businesses selling equipment or services used in stream management; the rule must clarify that commerce in tools or non-biological goods is not intended to be covered.

[P7] The sale/offer-for-sale prohibition per §17.21(f) lacks clarity about antique or historical specimens lawfully acquired prior to listing; stakeholders request a grandfathering provision or exemption for documented historical specimens.

[P8] Paragraph (g)(3) as the only listed exception is too narrow and places excessive discretionary power with the Service; stakeholders request criteria and timelines for Service approval to prevent arbitrary denials.

[P9] Permission via §17.32 permits is appropriate, but commenters will request a streamlined permit process and categorical permits for routine, low-risk activities (e.g., monitoring) to reduce administrative burden.

[P10] Allowing take under §17.21(c)(2)-(c)(4) is ambiguous for proponents of development because those provisions may include variably defined scientific or enhancement-of-survival takings; commenters request illustrative permitted actions and standardized mitigation requirements.

[P11] The allowance of take under §17.31(b) should specify whether incidental take permits under section 10 are available for private development projects within DPS ranges and what mitigation banking or conservation measures are acceptable.

[P12] The incidental-take permission (g)(3)(iv) is constructive, but commenters will demand quantified limits (e.g., maximum area disturbed or number of individuals affected) and mandatory reporting metrics for each approved activity.

[P13] For (g)(3)(iv)(A), forest management exceptions require Service-approval and “measures to minimize impacts” but lack minimum standards; timber and fire-management agencies request adoption of recognized best-management-practices and timelines for Service review to permit urgent wildfire-risk reduction projects.

[P13] Fire management agencies will contest the requirement that activities be “conducted under an established management plan” because emergency fuel reduction may be necessary before plans can be updated; they request an emergency-authorization pathway with after-the-fact Service notification.

[P14] (g)(3)(iv)(B) limits restoration-only exceptions to projects “specifically designed” for the frog and excludes restoration for other species unless Service-approved; conservation NGOs argue this is unduly restrictive and request a multi-species restoration allowance where measures benefit the frog.

[P14] Restoration practitioners request clarity on the approval process, criteria, and timelines for Service-approval of habitat restoration, and whether adaptive management modifications will require reapproval.

[P15] For (g)(3)(iv)(C), permitting cleanup of trespass cannabis sites is welcome, but growers’ advocates and landowners worry that the provision requires Service preapproval, which could delay removal; they request expedited approval procedures and clear definitions of “trespass” and “associated water diversion infrastructure.”

[P15] Law enforcement and landowners request indemnification language or liability protection for private actors who remove or remediate illicit cultivation sites pursuant to Service-approved activities to avoid legal exposure.

[P16] (g)(3)(iv)(D) allows removal of nonnative animals only in stream reaches “unoccupied” by the frog — fisheries managers and conservationists will ask for a clear, geographically explicit method to determine occupancy (e.g., survey window, protocols) to avoid paralysis of eradication efforts where nonnative predators threaten future recolonization.

[P16] Fishing industry and state wildlife agencies will object that restricting removals to unoccupied stream reaches could leave widespread predator populations unchecked; they request that eradication be permitted where potential or historical occupancy exists and where adaptive monitoring will prevent harm to frogs.

[P17] The possession exception per §17.21(d)(2) should be limited to documented, lawful prior possession with clear chain-of-custody requirements; commenters caution against criminalizing innocuous possession by hobbyists who lacked knowledge of listing status.

[P17] Legal experts note that cross-referencing §17.21(d)(2) without specifying proof burden creates evidentiary uncertainty for courts and enforcement; they request guidance on acceptable documentation to demonstrate lawful possession.

[P18] Regarding protests about protege firm size/status (I–105/I–obligations), small business advocates will argue that referring protests to the SBA is appropriate but request timelines for SBA resolution and appeal rights to prevent program delays.

[P19] The rule gives Directors authority to decide protests (I–106/I–obligation) about other eligibility aspects without specifying procedural safeguards; commenters request issuance of formal protest procedures, standard of review, and appeal mechanisms to ensure fairness.

[P20] The requirement to apply to the Mentor-Protege Program Director (I–105) should include a clear application checklist and maximum review period so potential mentors can plan participation; industry stakeholders request 60- to 90-day decision windows.

[P21] The requirement that agreements demonstrate contribution to DoD mission or fill a critical gap (I–106(g)) is subjective; prospective participants request objective evaluation criteria and examples of acceptable mission contributions to avoid arbitrary rejections.

[P22] Limiting program participation terms to no more than 2 years (I–107(k)) is too short for many capacity-building efforts; small businesses and mentors request a baseline 3-year standard or presumption of renewability to allow meaningful development.

[P23] The extension provision allowing up to an additional 3 years (I–107(k)) but requiring Director approval creates uncertainty; commenters request automatic one-year extensions upon good-faith progress and predefined benchmarks triggering discretionary extensions.

[P24] Requiring a justification showing “unusual circumstances” to extend beyond 2 years (I–107(k)) is vague; applicants request a non-exhaustive list of acceptable circumstances (e.g., multi-year certification timelines, regulatory delays) to avoid arbitrary denials.

[P25] Allowing termination for convenience or cause (I–111(f)) is standard, but industry stakeholders request notice-and-cure periods and compensation rules when termination for convenience disrupts ongoing investments under an agreement.

[P26] The enumerated considerations for termination for convenience (I–111(f)) are extremely broad (national security, funding); public commenters request that the Department publish threshold criteria and a non-exhaustive definition of “other considerations” to promote predictability.

[P27] Termination for cause requiring written findings (I–111(f)) should require those findings to be provided to the affected parties with an opportunity to respond before final termination where feasible; commenters request minimum procedural protections.

[P28] The provision that failure to provide adequate assurance of performance can be grounds for termination (I–111(f)) should define what constitutes “adequate assurance” and allow remedies or corrective action plans prior to termination.

[P29] Noncompliance with laws/regulations as grounds for cause (I–111(f)) should be tied to materiality; commenters request that only material or intentional legal violations justify immediate termination, with minor or inadvertent infractions addressed through corrective measures.

[P30] The conflicts-of-interest termination ground (I–111(f)) needs clearer guidance on disclosure obligations, mitigation, and a process to cure conflicts before termination, to protect collaborative partnerships that may involve complex corporate structures.

[P31] Default under any DoD contract as grounds for termination (I–111(f)) is overly broad because administrative or clerical defaults could trigger termination; commenters ask for a material breach standard and remediation periods.

[P32] Requiring DCMA to perform annual reviews (I–113) is reasonable, but DCMA must receive clear performance metrics and adequate funding/staffing to avoid cursory reviews; defense contractors urge the Department to commit resources and timelines for reviews.

[P33] The annual review requirement to verify semiannual report data (I–113) could create duplicative reporting burdens; mentor and protege firms request harmonization with existing federal reporting cycles and a single portal for submissions.

[P34] Verification that costs reimbursed to the mentor were “reasonably incurred” (I–113(a)) is subjective; mentors request a clear cost allowability standard, examples of reimbursable expenses, and an appeal process for disputed findings.

[P35] The obligation to verify accurate reporting of protege progress in employment, revenues, and DoD participation for five years post-expiration (I–113(b)) imposes long-term tracking burdens; small businesses request that the Department cover monitoring costs or limit the post-expiration reporting to three years.

[P1] Industry requests clarity on whether letters issued under §5.61(h) constitute final agency actions subject to judicial review, as ambiguity may affect enforcement risk for manufacturers relying on such letters.

[P2] The designation of the CFSAN Director in §5.61(h)(1) to issue below-threshold letters concentrates decisionmaking and could slow responses; FDA should allow delegated signatures from qualified designees or establish timeliness targets.

[P3] Authorizing the Director, Office of Premarket Approval (§5.61(h)(2)) but not mid-level reviewers to sign letters risks bottlenecks; trade associations will request that experienced office chiefs be permitted to sign.

[P4] The specification in §5.61(h)(3) of Division Directors raises separation-of-function concerns if those division personnel also conduct initial reviews; commenters will ask for conflict-of-interest safeguards and clear delegation protocols.

[P5] §25.22(a)(10) listing petition approvals as triggering an EA is burdensome for routine, low-risk exemptions under §170.39; small businesses will comment that an EA requirement in all these cases will impose significant cost and delay.

[P6] The mandatory format requirement in §25.31a(a) unduly restricts applicants' ability to submit concise, scientifically valid environmental information; commenters will request that the format be guidance-based rather than mandatory.

[P7] §25.31a(b)(1) requirement to include certain information when components ≤5% by weight lacks clarity on how to treat trace contaminants versus intentionally added components; regulators should define "component" and provide examples.

[P8] Stakeholders will request clarification in §25.31a(b)(1) about whether the ≤5% threshold applies per article, per formulation batch, or per migrating fraction; ambiguity could result in inconsistent EA submissions.

[P9] §25.31a(b)(2) triggers additional environmental information for surface-contact or repeated-use articles; manufacturers will argue this duplicates data already required in other sections and request cross-referencing or streamlining.

[P10] The exemption criteria in §170.39(a) are subjective in places (e.g., "present no other health or safety concerns"), inviting inconsistent application; public health advocates will ask FDA to define objective metrics and evidentiary standards.

[P11] §170.39(a)(1) requires that a substance "has not been shown to be a carcinogen" and addresses impurities by TD50 thresholds, but the proposed rule does not specify acceptable sources or study types for carcinogenicity determinations; commenters will request explicit guidance (GLP, peer-reviewed, weight-of-evidence).

[P12] Legal experts will challenge the TD50-based impurity threshold in §170.39(a)(1) as potentially inconsistent with current risk-assessment practice and request harmonization with EPA/ICH carcinogenicity metrics or clearer conversion guidance.

[P13] Consumer advocates will argue that §170.39(a)(2)(i)'s 0.5 ppb (1.5 μg/person/day) threshold is too permissive for vulnerable populations (infants, pregnant women) and request separate, lower thresholds or required margin-of-safety adjustments.

[P14] Food manufacturers will request explicit methods for estimating dietary concentrations under §170.39(a)(2)(i) (e.g., food consumption databases, assumptions about contact area and food types) to ensure consistent submissions.

[P15] The alternative pathway in §170.39(a)(2)(ii) that uses "<1% of the acceptable daily intake" for substances already regulated for direct addition is unclear about which ADI (current, original, or updated) applies; industry will request that FDA specify the ADI source and update procedure.

[P16] §170.39(a)(3)'s "no technical effect in or on the food" criterion is ambiguous for additives that serve a functional role in packaging but may incidentally alter sensory properties; package makers will request detailed examples and test methods to demonstrate lack of technical effect.

[P17] Environmental groups will challenge §170.39(a)(4)'s "no significant adverse impact on the environment" as vague and will demand that FDA adopt quantitative environmental fate and ecotoxicity screening criteria rather than a qualitative standard.

[P18] §170.39(b) reserving FDA's right to decline exemptions despite criteria being met is discretionary and could be used inconsistently; stakeholders will request enumerated specific public-health triggers and an appeals process beyond §10.33.

[P19] The obligation in §170.39(b) to explain reasons when declining an exemption is welcome, but commenters will ask that FDA specify the level of detail required in those explanations to enable meaningful responses (e.g., specific data gaps, risk estimates).

[P20] §170.39(c) requires multiple items in exemption requests; small companies will comment that the full set of required materials (composition, use conditions, exposure data, toxicology, environmental info) imposes disproportionate burdens and request an abbreviated pathway for de minimis exposures.

[P21] The chemical composition requirement in §170.39(c)(1) should clarify the level of detail (e.g., impurity profiles, CAS numbers, structural elucidation, stereochemistry); industry will ask for a template or checklist.

[P22] §170.39(c)(2) requiring detailed conditions of use (temperature, food type, contact duration, repeated vs. single use) lacks standardized categories; commenters will request a standardized form or examples to avoid inconsistent submissions.

[P23] §170.39(c)(3) obliging requesters to state which exemption basis they rely on (≤0.5 ppb or <1% ADI) needs guidance on borderline cases where both could plausibly apply, including instructions for dual-pathway submissions.

[P24] The dietary concentration data requirement in §170.39(c)(4) lacks clarity on acceptable modeling approaches, default assumptions, and uncertainty factors; risk assessors will request that FDA accept validated migration modeling (e.g., Cramer class, Fickian diffusion) with predefined assumptions.

[P25] §170.39(c)(4)(i) permits validated migration data under worst-case conditions but does not define "validated" nor the acceptable food simulants; commenters will request specified validation criteria, analytical limits, and a list of approved simulants.

[P26] The option in §170.39(c)(4)(ii) to use levels in manufacture is problematic because manufacturing input levels may not reflect migration into food; manufacturers will request guidance on how to convert input-use levels to dietary exposure estimates.

[P27] §170.39(c)(4)(iii) requires residual levels and, for repeat-use articles, lifetime contact estimates; industry will ask for a clear method to estimate lifetime contact and an agreed default contact surface-to-food mass ratios.

[P28] §170.39(c)(4)(iv) states that FDA will use validated detection limits when migration is non-detectable; analytical chemistry experts will comment that the rule must specify which LOQ/LOD conventions apply and how to account for method variability.

[P29] The encouragement in §170.39(c)(4)(v) to seek FDA guidance is positive, but stakeholders will request that FDA commit to timely, written pre-submission feedback with defined timelines to avoid project delays.

[P30] §170.39(c)(5) obligates submission of existing toxicological data on the substance and impurities; industry will request explicit minimum study types (e.g., genotoxicity battery, subchronic studies) and acceptance of read-across or QSAR in lieu of animal data.

[P31] Environmental commenters will request that §170.39(c)(6) explicitly require life-cycle analysis or downstream wastewater fate studies for substances likely to be released during use or disposal, as the abbreviated EA references may be insufficient.

[P32] §170.39(d) mandates submission to the Division of Petition Control (HFS-216) at an FDA address; commenters will ask for an option for electronic submission through a secure portal and confirmation timelines to modernize intake.

[P33] §170.39(e)'s requirement to notify requesters by letter about exemption status should specify whether electronic notification is acceptable and establish a statutory timeframe (e.g., 180 days) to prevent indefinite delays.

[P34] Maintaining a public list at the Dockets Management Branch (§170.39(e)) that includes company name, chemical name, specific use, and limitations is beneficial for transparency, but trade associations will object to forced disclosure of company identity for proprietary technologies and request alternative confidentiality protections.

[P35] The prohibition on including trade names (§170.39(e)) while listing company names and chemical identities may still enable reverse-engineering of proprietary products; companies will request that certain confidentially proprietary manufacturing details be exempted from public listing.

[P36] §170.39(e)'s requirement that FDA make the EA finding and supporting evidence available at the Dockets Management Branch per §25.41(b)(2) raises confidentiality concerns; commenters will request redaction rules for confidential business information (CBI) and sensitive analytical methods.

[P37] The permission in §170.39(f) to petition under §10.33 after denial is procedurally correct but duplicative; stakeholders will request a consolidated reconsideration process with specified timelines and an opportunity for an interlocutory meeting.

[P38] §170.39(g) allowing FDA to reconsider exemptions upon receipt of "significant new information" lacks definition of "significant"; regulated entities will ask for thresholds (e.g., new peer-reviewed studies showing >X-fold increase in risk) to prevent arbitrary reversals.

[P39] The obligation in §170.39(g) to notify original requesters of tentative decisions to revoke exemptions and to allow responses is appropriate, but commenters will request minimum response periods (e.g., 60–90 days) and a clear standard of evidence required to revoke the exemption.

[P40] §170.39(g)'s public display requirement for notifications and files at the Dockets Management Branch may expose confidential or proprietary data; companies will request an option to submit redacted public versions and a non-public confidential file.

[P41] The cross-references in §§171.8 and 174.6 exempting uses that meet §170.39 criteria and waiving the need for a food additive petition create regulatory parity, but petitioners will request assurance that exempted uses are treated equivalently across enforcement and compliance programs.

[P42] The exceptions in §§171.8 and 174.6 that no food additive petition is required for exempted uses may inadvertently create market entry loopholes if enforcement agencies implement different thresholds; stakeholders will request a harmonized federal guidance document.

[P43] §142.2(b)(1) and the electronic submission conditions (§142.2(b)(1)(i)-(iii)) enabling prearrival entry times could disadvantage importers lacking AMS participation; small importers will request grandfathering or an alternative prearrival submission mechanism.

[P44] The AMS-related conditions (§142.2(b)(1)(ii)-(iii)) are opaque about data security and liability for erroneous prearrival filings; customs brokers and carriers will request clarified responsibilities and error-correction procedures.

[P45] §141.68(a)(3) tying time of entry to merchandise arrival within port limits when documentation is pre-filed requires clarity on what constitutes "arrival within the port limits" (vessel mooring, pilot boarding, crossing a demarcation line); importers will request a precise definition to avoid disputes.

[P46] Practical commenters will seek harmonization between the new EA requirements (§25.22/25.31a) and the submission requirements under §170.39(c)(4)-(c)(6) to avoid duplicated studies and conflicting validation standards.

[P47] Legal commenters will request that FDA add an explicit savings clause confirming that reliance on an FDA-exempted letter or listing does not alter or waive other statutory obligations under FD&C Act or other environmental and consumer protection laws.

[P48] Public-interest groups will urge that the docketed public list (§170.39(e)) include a plain-language summary of the basis for exemption (key exposure estimates, toxicology conclusions) to help lay readers assess safety.

[P49] Analytical laboratories will request that FDA publish accepted analytical method validation criteria referenced across §25.31a and §170.39(c)(4)(i)-(iv), including minimum detection limits and proficiency testing expectations.

[P50] Small business commenters will ask for a reduced-fee or fee-exempt pathway for submitting exemption requests under §170.39(c), given the significant data and EA obligations that could otherwise deter innovation by smaller firms.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement to submit comments by July 16, 2018 is unreasonably short and does not provide sufficient time for affected operators and stakeholders to prepare technically informed comments on complex fuel-system changes.

[P1] The rule should explicitly state whether electronic submissions received after 11:59 PM ET on July 16, 2018 will be accepted if postmarked by that date to avoid confusion about deadline enforcement.

[P2] The phrase “within the specified compliance times” is vague; the AD must list the specific compliance times for each required action directly in the regulatory text rather than deferring to non-regulatory service information.

[P2] There is no grandfathering/provision for aircraft that are temporarily out of service; the AD should clarify how compliance times are calculated for aircraft in storage or undergoing major maintenance.

[P3] A 36‑month compliance window to revise operational documents is too long given the potential safety implications; the FAA should shorten the deadline to ensure immediate operational awareness and compliance.

[P3] The AD should permit interim operational directives (e.g., Flight Crew Notices) to be used pending the formal revision of manuals, and this authorization should be added to paragraph (g).

[P4] Requiring revision of the FAA‑approved Boeing Model 777 AFM 'Fuel System—Loading' section without specifying required approval workflow and turnaround times between operators and FAA designees will create inconsistent implementation; the AD should define approval timelines.

[P4] The AD should clarify whether the AFM revisions in paragraph (g)(1) require FAA re‑approval of the entire AFM or can be implemented via operator-approved AFM change processes under existing ODA/PMA authority.

[P5] The directive to revise the Weight and Balance Control and Loading Manual's 'Loading Limitations' section must specify whether each operator's company‑approved version or only the FAA‑approved master manual must be changed; ambiguity could delay compliance.

[P5] The AD should permit operators to incorporate the required text into electronic manuals and provide guidance on how electronic distribution satisfies the “revise” requirement.

[P6] The optional terminating actions in paragraph (h) reference multiple modifications (scavenge, jettison, electrical changes) but do not provide a clear scope or baseline configuration; the AD must enumerate which aircraft configurations are eligible for the terminating action.

[P6] The service bulletin referenced as the terminating action should be incorporated by reference in the AD or otherwise identified by exact revision/date to ensure operators know precisely which procedures qualify.

[P7] Requiring that all actions labeled 'RC' in the Boeing service bulletin be performed as a condition for credit is problematic if the service bulletin changes; the AD should lock the required RC steps to a specific revision and date.

[P7] The AD should allow composite compliance where an operator can use an FAA‑approved alternative procedure for an RC step when parts or tooling are unavailable, rather than forcing a full AMOC process.

[P8] Granting credit for previously performed work is appropriate, but the AD fails to define acceptable evidence/documentation for such credit; the rule should list the required records and means of verification.

[P8] The provision does not address credit for modifications accomplished under foreign approvals; the AD should explicitly state whether non‑U.S. approved service programs count for credit.

[P9] Concentrating AMOC approval authority with the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch, could create unnecessary bottlenecks; the rule should allow other designated FAA offices to approve AMOCs to improve responsiveness.

[P10] The requirement to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO may be redundant when sending directly to the Manager is permitted; the AD should clarify the preferred submission path and expected processing times.

[P11] Permitting AMOC requests via email is helpful but the AD should require confirmation of receipt and state the expected acknowledgement time to give applicants certainty.

[P12] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an AMOC lacks a time frame; the AD should specify how much advance notice is required (e.g., prior to first flight after modification) to avoid enforcement ambiguity.

[P13] Allowing Boeing ODA approvals to serve as AMOCs is appropriate, but the AD must require that Boeing provide a copy of any ODA‑approved AMOC to the FAA and the operator to ensure oversight and traceability.

[P14] Requiring that AMOC repairs meet the certification basis of the airplane without clarifying how differences due to later amendments to the certification basis will be handled is ambiguous; the AD should define whether the certification basis is that in effect at type certification or at the time of AMOC submission.

[P15] The requirement that AMOC approval specifically reference this AD is reasonable, but the AD should mandate inclusion of the AD number, effective date, and specific paragraph references in the AMOC documentation.

[P16] For service information containing RC steps, the AD should clarify whether inconsistencies between the service bulletin and the AD are resolved by the AD or the service bulletin to avoid confusion for maintenance personnel.

[P17] Requiring performance of all RC‑labeled steps, including figures, may inadvertently mandate non‑safety‑critical actions that are labeled RC for editorial reasons; the AD should require FAA concurrence before labeling steps as RC in revised service information.

[P18] The 'RC Exempt' carve‑out is useful, but the AD should define who may designate a step as 'RC Exempt' (Boeing vs FAA) and require the designation to be documented in the service bulletin revision referenced by the AD.

[P19] Requiring an AMOC for any deviation from RC steps could be unduly burdensome for minor deviations; the FAA should create a streamlined deviation approval process for de‑minimis variances that do not affect the safety benefit.

[P20] Allowing deviation from non‑RC steps under operator‑accepted methods without AMOC is appropriate, but the AD should require operators to document deviations in a formal maintenance record and make them available for FAA review.

[P21] The cross‑credit provision tying completion of the engine fuel feed system modification to AD 2002–16–15 routing requirements must specify how compliance with remaining provisions of AD 2002–16–15 will be verified and documented to avoid double-counting credit.

[P21] The listed eligible Groups (1–4, 7–14) reference Boeing Special Attention Service Bulletin 777–28–0082 Revision 1; the AD should include the date of that revision and a method to determine group membership unambiguously for mixed‑configuration fleets.

[P3] The AD should explicitly require operators to train flight crews on the revised AFM/ loading limitations within a specified time after the manual revision to ensure operational compliance.

[P4] The AFM text in figure 1 must be provided in the AD or incorporated by reference; otherwise operators cannot confirm that the AFM changes meet their national regulatory requirements or company procedures.

[P6] The scope of electrical changes “in the main equipment center” is not defined and could affect myriad systems; the FAA should supply a simplified list of circuits/components affected or require Boeing to annotate the service bulletin with affected harness/connector part numbers.

[P7] The RC-labeled requirement needs clarification about who may perform RC work — only certificated mechanics or also certified repair stations — and whether performance by foreign‑based repair stations is acceptable.

[P8] Credit for prior actions should be allowed only if the prior work was performed to the same level of detail as the RC steps; the AD should state that an inspection validating equivalence is required before accepting credit.

[P11] Emailing AMOC requests to the provided address raises cybersecurity and PII concerns; the FAA should provide guidance on secure transmission of proprietary technical data.

[P12] The AD should require operators to keep records of notifications to principal inspectors regarding AMOC usage and make them available to the FAA for audits.

[P14] The requirement that AMOC repairs meet the airplane certification basis may preclude pragmatic safety improvements that deviate from original certification assumptions; the AD should state how safety‑equivalent means of compliance will be evaluated.

[P20] The AD must clarify whether deviations from non‑RC steps that change Part 121/125/135 approved procedures require prior FAA approval under the certificates, not merely operator internal acceptance.

[P1] The option to submit Privacy Act access requests via a single "specified internet form" (§ 5.21(a)(2)) could disadvantage individuals without reliable internet access; the rule should explicitly preserve and publicize non-digital submission channels and response timelines for paper submissions.

[P1] The provision does not require DHS to maintain or publish the exact URL or location of the "specified internet form"; commenters should request that DHS publish and widely disseminate that URL and provide notice of any future URL changes.

[P2] Allowing component heads/designees to request records from other agencies for "authorized law enforcement purposes" (§ 5.21(c)) is overly broad; the rule lacks clear limits, definitions, or oversight of what constitutes an authorized purpose, risking mission creep and privacy intrusions.

[P2] The rule should require that inter-agency requests under subsection (b)(7) be logged with a standard justification, date, and supervisory approval to ensure accountability and enable auditing.

[P3] Treating all DHS components as a "single entity" for the (b)(1) exception (§ 5.21(d)) effectively eliminates intra-departmental privacy protections and could permit routine sharing of sensitive personal data across components without individual notice; commenters should request limits (e.g., need-to-know standard with recorded approvals).

[P3] The rule does not require any documentation or notification when (b)(1) intra-DHS disclosures occur; stakeholders should ask DHS to require written justifications and searchable logs for internal disclosures treated under the single-entity approach.

[P4] The obligation that components "retain their original authorities" during transition (§ 5.21(e)) is vague—commenters should request a timeline, clear criteria for what activities are preserved, and mechanisms to resolve conflicts between legacy authorities and the new central procedures.

[P5] Requiring requesters to send requests directly to field office addresses when records are held by field offices (§ 5.21(a) field office requests) will create confusion and delay for requesters who do not know where records are located; commenters should ask DHS to maintain a centralized intake option and to publish field office responsibilities and addresses.

[P6] Advising requesters to send CISA-held records requests to the DHS Privacy Office (§ 5.21(a)(4)) creates uncertainty: commenters should request clarification whether the DHS Privacy Office will forward or process CISA records and whether CISA retains discretion to respond.

[P7] The requirement to use the "most efficient and least costly method" to process requests (§ 5.21(d) fees processing) could be interpreted to favor automated redaction/denial over careful human review; commenters should ask DHS to define standards for "efficient" that protect accuracy and privacy.

[P8] Requiring payment of applicable fees "ordinarily" before providing copies (§ 5.21(d)) may create undue burdens on low-income requesters and conflict with statutory limits; commenters should request fee-waiver procedures and explicit exceptions for duplication fees in Privacy Act access requests.

[P9] The identity verification requirement (§ 5.21(e)) lacks alternatives for individuals who cannot provide traditional identity documentation; commenters should request that DHS accept reasonable alternative verification methods (e.g., in-person verification, video calls, agency records cross-check) and publish acceptable forms.

[P10] Mandating full name, address, date/place of birth, and citizenship/residency for verification (§ 5.21(e)) may be unnecessary and overbroad for many records requests; commenters should ask DHS to narrow required data to the minimum necessary and to explain retention/destruction of verification data.

[P11] Requiring notarized signatures or signatures under 28 U.S.C. 1746 (§ 5.21(e)) will be burdensome for many potential requesters, especially those overseas or low-income; commenters should ask DHS to accept unsworn electronic signatures or other reliable authentication methods and to confirm acceptance of electronic notarization.

[P12] Obliging third-party requesters to verify the subject's identity and provide consent or proof of death (§ 5.21(e) third-party verification) is appropriate in principle, but the rule fails to specify acceptable forms of consent or proof of death; commenters should request exemplars and flexibility for substitute documentation.

[P13] Permitting components to require "extra verification" from third parties (§ 5.21(e)) without specifying standards could lead to arbitrary denials; commenters should ask for objective criteria and an appeal process when additional verification is requested.

[P14] The duty to "charge fees" for Privacy Act or JRA requests (§ 5.21(b) Government-wide SORNs) may conflict with statutory provisions limiting fees for access to one's own records; commenters (consumer advocates and legal experts) should request DHS reconcile fee policy with the Privacy Act and provide fee schedules and waiver criteria.

[P15] Allowing submissions to the DHS Privacy Office by mail, online form, or fax (§ 5.21(b)) is good, but the rule should also require clear public guidance on when requesters should use component vs. Privacy Office submission routes and whether submissions to the Privacy Office create any delay compared to direct component submissions.

[P16] The Privacy Office's obligation to forward requests to the component most likely to maintain records (§ 5.21(b)) lacks timelines and accountability; commenters should ask for maximum forwarding timeframes and means for requesters to track forwarded requests.

[P17] Holding the component that first receives and possesses the record responsible for responding (§ 5.22(a)) could produce gamesmanship (e.g., routing requests to avoid obligations); commenters should request safeguards to prevent refusal-to-accept tactics and require prompt transfer if not the correct custodian.

[P18] The requirement to inform a requester if a component uses a different date to begin processing (§ 5.22(a)) is good, but the rule should specify what alternative dates are permissible and require explanation when a later date is used to prevent unfair delay.

[P19] Granting DHS discretion to administratively close requests or seek additional information (§ 5.22(a)) is ripe for abuse; commenters should request objective standards for closure, mandatory notice before closure, and an easy reinstatement process.

[P20] The obligation to send written notices for denials (§ 5.22(d)) should also require that denial notices be provided electronically if the requester used electronic submission and that denials provide enough detail to permit meaningful appeals.

[P21] Requiring denial letters to identify the responsible person, reasons, exemptions, and appeal instructions (§ 5.22(d)) is appropriate, but commenters should request that the rule mandate a standardized denial template and redaction rationale sufficient for judicial review.

[P22] When referring requests to other components/agencies (§ 5.22(e)), DHS must be required to provide the requester with a point of contact and expected decision timeline; otherwise referrals will create untracked delays.

[P23] Processing consultations and referrals based on the date of the first component's receipt (§ 5.22(f)) is fair, but commenters should request explicit maximum consultation timelines and penalties for unjustified inter-component delays.

[P24] Allowing components to make written agreements to avoid consultations/referrals for certain record types (§ 5.22(g)) risks carving out broad exemptions; commenters should ask DHS to require public disclosure of any such agreements and to limit them to clearly defined record categories with privacy safeguards.

[P25] Advising electronic communication to internet-capable requesters (§ 5.23(a)) should be coupled with express consent requirements and options for requesters who prefer paper; commenters should also ask DHS to ensure secure electronic channels and encrypt sensitive records in transit.

[P26] The requirement to acknowledge requests and assign tracking numbers if processing will exceed 10 working days (§ 5.23(b)) lacks penalties for noncompliance; commenters should request an SLA and public reporting on compliance with acknowledgement deadlines.

[P27] Including a brief description of the records sought in acknowledgements (§ 5.23(b)) is helpful, but DHS should also be required to include an estimated completion date and the assigned FOIA/Privacy Act case status.

[P28] Requiring acknowledgement to confirm the requester's agreement to pay fees (§ 5.23(b)) risks presuming consent for fees; commenters should request that DHS only consider fees accepted if the requester explicitly agrees and that fee estimates be provided in advance.

[P29] The 20 working day decision deadline (§ 5.23(c)) should apply equally to all components, and exceptions should be narrowly defined; commenters (especially civil liberties groups) should seek public reporting of instances where the FOIA-specified exceptions are invoked and the reasons for delay.

[P30] Notification in writing when a request is granted (§ 5.23(c)) should also require delivery of records in the requester's preferred medium (electronic where possible) and explicit redaction logs when partial grants are made.

[P31] Components must inform requesters of FOIA Public Liaison availability (§ 5.23(c)); commenters request that liaison contact information and escalation processes be provided in every acknowledgement and denial notice.

[P32] The obligation to assess classification and comply with part 7 when requests involve classified information (§ 5.24) should be supplemented with timelines and independent review for declassification decisions to prevent indefinite withholding.

[P33] Requiring consultation with the original classifier when records include derivatively classified information (§ 5.24) is appropriate, but commenters should insist on binding timelines for such consultations and documentation of the consultation outcome.

[P34] The prohibition on withholding information that no longer requires classification based on Privacy Act exemption (k)(1) (§ 5.24) is a positive safeguard; commenters request an affirmative duty to re-review legacy withheld material periodically and provide a process for requesters to challenge continued withholding.

[P35] The DHS OGC's role in ensuring part 7 compliance on appeals involving classified information (§ 5.24) should include an independent review path or the option to refer disputes to an external authority to avoid conflicts of interest.

[P36] Allowing appeals to the component Appeals Officer (§ 5.25(a)) is proper, but commenters should request that DHS publish appeal officers' contact information, decision precedents, and recusal policies for conflicts of interest.

[P37] The 90 working day deadline for submitting appeals (§ 5.25(a)) must be clarified as to whether it begins from the date of mailed denial receipt or postmark; commenters request tolling rules for mail delays and equitable relief for claimants with good cause.

[P38] Designating the DHS OGC as the authorized appeals authority (§ 5.25(b)) may concentrate power and create bias; commenters (legal experts) should request structural safeguards, publication of appeals standards, and the ability to escalate to an independent administrative tribunal.

[P39] Requiring Appeals Officers to consult the Chief Security Officer on classified appeals (§ 5.25(b)) risks insular decision-making; commenters should require that such consultations be documented in the appeal record and that appellants be notified when national security consultations influenced the decision.

[P40] The 20 working day timeframe for appeals decisions (§ 5.25(c)) is reasonable only if adequate resourcing exists; commenters request a statement of resources and contingency plans when decisions will exceed that period.

[P41] The exhaustion requirement that individuals must complete administrative appeals before seeking court review (§ 5.25(d)) should allow exceptions for extraordinary circumstances (e.g., irreparable harm); commenters request that DHS clarify when courts may be approached without exhaustion.

[P42] Allowing amendment requests to the component maintaining the record (§ 5.26(a)) is appropriate, but commenters request that DHS also permit centralized intake for amendment requests and publish processing timetables and contact points for common systems.

[P43] The 10 working day acknowledgment requirement for amendment/correction requests (§ 5.26(b)) should include content requirements (e.g., assigned tracking number, expected decision timeline) and remedies if not met.

[P44] Treating amendment requests as not received if fees are outstanding (§ 5.26(b)) unfairly penalizes individuals who may not be aware of fees; commenters should ask DHS to provide fee waivers, to notify requesters before deeming a request not received, and to allow cure periods.

[P45] Allowing appeals of amendment denials to the component Appeals Officer or DHS OGC (§ 5.26(c)) is fine, but commenters should request parallel timelines and transparency comparable to access appeals.

[P46] Permitting filing of a Statement of Disagreement after an amendment appeal denial (§ 5.26(d)) is valuable; commenters request that DHS provide standardized forms, guidance on length limits, and assistance for pro se individuals.

[P47] The limitation of Statements of Disagreement to "generally no longer than one typed page per disputed fact" (§ 5.26(d)) may be too restrictive for complex disputes; commenters request flexibility for complex records and an explicit mechanism to request additional space.

[P48] Requiring components to place the Statement of Disagreement in the system and mark the disputed record (§ 5.26(d)) is appropriate, but commenters should insist that DHS maintain a public index or searchable metadata indicating presence of such statements to inform future disclosures.

[P49] Obliging components to notify prior recipients within 30 working days of amendments (§ 5.26(e)) is good, but commenters point out the practical difficulty in identifying all prior recipients; they request clarification on "where an accounting was made or should have been made" and a safe-harbor standard.

[P50] Requiring that Statements of Disagreement be appended on disclosure and allowing components to append a concise rationale for denial (§ 5.26(e)) should include limits on the component's rationale length and a ban on additional substantive material that could prejudice the requester.

[P51] The prohibition on amending certain record categories (oath transcripts, court records, exempted systems) (§ 5.26(f)) is potentially overbroad—commenters request an exception where factual errors materially affect legal rights and a process for courts to order corrections.

[P52] Permitting accounting requests subject to JRA limitations (§ 5.27(a)) should require DHS to publish easily searchable accounting records (redaction-limited) and provide expedited processing for individuals alleging misuse.

[P53] The exception list for accountings (§ 5.27(b)) requires clearer guidance on how often DHS claims JRA or statutory exceptions; commenters request periodic public reporting of the frequency and types of exceptions invoked.

[P54] The obligation to preserve request-related correspondence and copies of requested records until authorized destruction (§ 5.28) should specify retention schedules and require that preservation holds be entered into any applicable records management system to prevent accidental disposal.

[P55] The prohibition on disposing of records subject to pending requests, appeals, litigation, or audit holds (§ 5.28) should include penalties for noncompliance and require components to certify preservation actions to the DHS Privacy Office.

[P56] Limiting fees for fully granted Privacy Act access requests to duplication costs (§ 5.29(a)) is consistent with the Privacy Act; commenters request DHS explicitly state how duplication costs are calculated, whether electronic delivery can be offered at no cost, and seek fee waiver criteria for indigent requesters.
