[P5] The provision that applicants "shall provide the information requested on the application form, including, but not limited to:" is overly broad—APHS should limit required data to what is necessary and provide a data‑minimization statement and justification for each requested item.

[P6] Requiring the applicant's name is reasonable, but the rule should allow use of trade names or DBAs in addition to legal names for multi‑site operations and partnerships.

[P7] Requiring "a valid mailing address through which the applicant can be reached at all times" is impractical; request modification to permit an email address or designated agent for service instead of constant physical reachability.

[P8] Requiring addresses for "all premises" where animals or records are kept could impose burdens on mobile exhibitors or transient operators; clarify whether temporary event locations or one‑time off‑site locations must be pre‑listed or can be reported via itinerary.

[P9] Requiring applicants to state the "anticipated maximum number of animals on hand at any one time" without guidance will lead to inconsistent licensing levels; provide a standard method for estimating peaks and allow for reasonable margins or seasonal variations.

[P10] The requirement for applicants to provide "records showing adequate knowledge and experience" for exotic/wild animals is vague—specify the types of records acceptable (e.g., certificates, references, training hours) and the standard used to evaluate "adequate."

[P11] The obligation that exhibitors disclose intent to exhibit off‑site on the application and supply itineraries under §2.126 raises confidentiality and security concerns; limit public disclosure and allow redaction of sensitive location details.

[P12] Mandatory disclosure of pleas or findings related to animal laws without context may deter applicants from honest disclosure; provide clear definitions of which offenses trigger denial and a process for rehabilitation or demonstrating fitness.

[P13] The $120 fee may be burdensome for small exhibitors or non‑profit educational groups; propose a reduced fee category or fee waiver/discount for low‑income or nonprofit applicants.

[P13] Requiring submission to the "appropriate Animal Care office" without listing those offices or permitting electronic submission is obsolete; permit online submission and payment to streamline the process.

[P14] Prohibiting a person from holding more than one license could disrupt multi‑facility corporations that previously held separate licenses per site; clarify whether the prohibition applies to individuals only or to entities and allow entity‑level licensing for multiple sites.

[P15] Treating any change in ownership, location, activities, or animals as invalidating a license is overbroad and disruptive; allow for administrative amendments for minor changes (e.g., moving within same county) and only require new licenses for substantive changes.

[P16] Requiring 90 days' advance notice and a new license before changes in name, address, management, substantial change in operations, or animals is impractical for emergency or unforeseen changes; allow shorter notice for certain changes and permit interim approvals.

[P17] Requiring written itineraries under §2.126 for all off‑site exhibits will be onerous for exhibitors that do many short shows; allow submission of itineraries seasonally or on rolling updates and permit electronic updates within a shorter timeframe.

[P18] Licensing animals in fixed increments of 50 lacks granularity and will impose unnecessary license costs on small operators with, for example, 10–20 animals; permit licenses authorizing exact numbers or smaller increments (e.g., 5 or 10).

[P19] The 50‑animal increment threshold will force many small dealers/exhibitors to pay for capacity they don't use; recommend proportional fees and authorization tiers based on actual anticipated max animals.

[P20] Requiring specific authorization for species subject to subparts D and E (wild/exotic) without clear species lists could lead to inconsistent interpretations; include a comprehensive list and process for adding species.

[P21] The catch‑all statement that licenses will be issued when conditions are satisfied is fine but needs transparent timelines and written standards for "satisfied" to prevent arbitrary denials.

[P22] Cross‑referencing compliance with §§2.2–2.3 as a condition for issuance is reasonable but these sections contain burdensome inspection requirements; suggest clarifying minimum standards and objective criteria for meeting §§2.2–2.3.

[P23] The fee payment clause permitting only certified/cashier's check, postal money order, or specified instruments discriminates against online/electronic payments; require acceptance of credit/debit/ACH payments.

[P23] Charging a $20 fee for returned checks is acceptable, but requiring certified/cashier's checks for subsequent payments after a bounced check is punitive; allow standard payment remedies without forcing cash‑only instruments.

[P24] The broad ground for denial/suspension/revocation for any failure to comply with the Act or regulations lacks proportionality; require APHIS to provide corrective action plans and graduated enforcement for minor infractions.

[P25] Requiring applicants to sign to acknowledge review and agreement to comply may be a legal formality, but APHIS should provide accessible summaries of key obligations and training resources to ensure meaningful understanding.

[P26] Requiring demonstration that premises, animals, and equipment comply with the Act at application time is reasonable, but the rule must define measurable standards and alternative compliance demonstrations for remote or mobile exhibitors.

[P27] Mandating inspections "during business hours or other mutually agreeable times" conflicts with §1.1's business hours definition and the need for timely inspections; require APHIS to offer reasonable scheduling options and respect event schedules.

[P28] Requiring APHIS pre‑license inspections before issuance is reasonable but APHIS should provide maximum timelines between application receipt and inspection (e.g., 30 days) to prevent undue delays.

[P29] The requirement to complete corrective measures identified at inspection without specifying reasonable cure periods is unfair; define timelines to cure deficiencies, with extensions for documented impediments.

[P30] Allowing only up to two re‑inspections and requiring they be requested within 60 days of the first inspection is restrictive—complex remediation may take longer; extend the 60‑day window or allow APHIS‑granted extensions.

[P31] Requiring appeals of third inspection findings to be received within 7 days of inspection report receipt is too short for applicants to prepare a meaningful appeal; extend the appeal window to at least 14 or 30 days.

[P32] The Deputy Administrator's obligation to issue a written response within 7 days of a timely appeal is laudable, but 7 days may not allow adequate review of complex documentation; allow 14 days or specify expedited versus standard timelines.

[P33] Forfeiture of the fee and a 6‑month prohibition on reapplying if an applicant fails to request reinspection or timely appeal is unduly punitive; require APHIS to provide clear written notice of reinspection and appeal deadlines before imposing such penalties.

[P34] The condition that no license will be issued until full compliance is shown is acceptable, but APHIS should allow conditional or provisional licenses with limited scope while minor deficiencies are cured.

[P35] Making licenses generally valid for 3 years is reasonable, but the rule should provide renewal notice timelines and renewal processing time targets to prevent gaps in licensure.

[P36] Allowing voluntary termination in writing is fine but require APHIS to acknowledge receipt and provide instructions for animal disposition and records retention upon termination.

[P37] The 120‑day temporary license for timely applicants with no documented noncompliances is helpful, but the criteria exclude applicants with prior minor noncompliances even if cured; consider allowing temporary licenses when prior issues were resolved.

[P38] Requiring submission of application before prior license expires to qualify for a temporary license is reasonable, but allow submission within a short grace period (e.g., 7 days after expiration) in extenuating circumstances.

[P39] The condition that no documented noncompliances during the prior period are allowed for a temporary license is overbroad—minor administrative noncompliances should not disqualify tenants; define "noncompliance" severity thresholds.

[P40] Allowing licenses to remain valid during expedited hearings protects due process, but the rule should clarify obligations during that time and whether activities may continue unchanged.

[P41] No refund of license fee if license ends early is punitive for applicants who face administrative error or are forced to close due to APHIS action; allow proportional refunds when termination is for reasons beyond licensee's control.

[P42] Requiring reinstatement applicants to follow new applicant procedures is reasonable, but permit streamlined reinstatement where the prior compliance record is good and only minor updates are needed.

[P43] The requirement to surrender invalid licenses and provide statements if lost is acceptable, but allow electronic notarized affidavits and afford a process to obtain replacement licenses without onerous delays.

[P44] Broad prohibition on individuals who participated in conduct causing suspension/revocation being licensed during the sanction period lacks specificity on the standard of "responsible for or participated in"; require proof and due process before disqualification.

[P45] Prohibiting suspended licensees from being licensed or registered in any manner "in his or her own name or in any other manner" is overbroad and could bar family members or unrelated employees; limit the prohibition to direct control or management roles and clarify when indirect ownership is disqualifying.

[P46] Barring entities in which a suspended person has a "substantial interest" from being licensed is vague—define "substantial interest" (percentage ownership, managerial control) to avoid chilling investment and employment.

[P47] Allowing suspended persons to apply in writing for reinstatement is positive, but the rule should establish objective criteria and timelines for reinstatement decisions to ensure fairness.

[P48] Permanent prohibition on licensing for revoked persons and entities they substantially interest may be necessary in severe cases but should allow for rehabilitation after an appropriate period and with demonstrated compliance measures.

[P49] The ban on transacting in animals during suspension or revocation should clarify exceptions for care, transport for veterinary care, or animal welfare transfers under APHIS supervision to avoid animal welfare harms.

[P50] The general prohibition against issuing licenses to applicants meeting listed disqualifiers needs a clear, accessible list of disqualifying actions and an opportunity to present mitigating evidence.

[P51] Denial for failure to comply with §§2.1–2.4 or nonpayment must include a cure period and notice before denial so applicants have an opportunity to remedy minor administrative defects.

[P52] Denying applicants for being "not in compliance" with the Act or regs without specifying which provisions they allegedly violate is unfair; require APHIS to cite specific noncompliances and provide an opportunity to cure.

[P53] Denying applicants who previously had licenses revoked/suspended should be qualified by the severity and recency of the prior action; an automatic bar is overly punitive if the applicant was a minor participant or remediation occurred.

[P54] Disqualifying applicants who previously "participated in activities" causing prior suspension/revocation lacks due process—APHS must require specific findings of culpability rather than mere association.

[P55] Denying applicants with convictions/findings related to animal cruelty within 3 years is reasonable for public protection, but the rule should specify which offenses trigger denial and allow individualized consideration and path to rehabilitation.

[P56] Allowing the Administrator to find applicants unfit after 3 years without standards is arbitrary; limit this authority to clearly defined circumstances and require written explanation and opportunity to rebut.

[P57] Denying licenses to applicants who would be operating in violation or circumvention of laws is appropriate, but APHIS should provide clear guidance on what constitutes "circumvention" and examples.

[P58] Denying based on false statements or records is necessary, but the rule should set a materiality standard—only falsehoods material to licensing eligibility should disqualify.

[P59] Granting applicants the right to request a hearing after denial is appropriate; clarify the applicable rules of practice and timelines for hearings.

[P60] Maintaining denial in effect until final decision is reasonable but applicants should be allowed an interim limited license in exceptional circumstances pending appeal to avoid undue hardship.

[P61] Allowing reapplication 1 year after denial is reasonable but APHIS should allow earlier reapplication upon demonstration of rehabilitation and corrected deficiencies with supervisory approval.

[P62] The criteria for expedited hearings are narrow (timely appeal, prior valid license, application received 90+ days before expiration); these thresholds will exclude many applicants deserving expedited review—broaden the eligibility criteria.

[P63] Requiring expedited hearing requests within 30 days of denial notice is acceptable but APHIS must ensure timely and reliable notice delivery methods so applicants are aware of the deadline.

[P64] Mandating the ALJ set an expedited hearing within 30 days of request is good but should allow scheduling flexibility for mutually agreeable dates and ensure adequate time for evidence preparation.

[P65] Requiring the ALJ to issue an initial decision within 30 days after the expedited hearing is ambitious for complex cases and may impair due process; extend to 45 days or allow a brief extension for complex factual records.

[P66] The rule that the applicant's license remains valid during expedited proceedings protects applicants but must clarify whether licensee may expand operations or must maintain status quo pending decision.

[P67] Prohibiting entities in which a denied applicant has substantial interest from licensing for 1 year is overly broad; define "substantial interest" and allow exceptions for unrelated managers or minority passive investors.

[P68] The prohibition on issuing licenses to circumvent prior enforcement orders is appropriate, but APHIS should provide examples of circumvention and a transparent review process to determine intent.

[P69] Allowing termination of licenses for reasons that would deny an application after a hearing is reasonable, but APHIS should require proportionality and consider corrective action plans before termination for minor offenses.

[P70] Requiring written appeals of inspection findings within 21 days is reasonable, but APHIS should accept electronic submissions and clarify standards for what constitutes a timely and sufficient appeal.

[P71] Publishing online lists of registered research facilities raises privacy and security concerns for sensitive research programs; APHIS should limit publicly posted data to facility name and city/state and allow redaction upon a showing of security risk.

[P72] Publishing lists of licensed/registered persons online could expose small businesses and individuals to harassment; limit public data to business name, license status, and city/state, and allow redaction of personal addresses and contact info.

[P73] Requiring continuous access to potable water for dogs is appropriate, but the exception "unless the attending veterinarian restricts access" is too vague—specify medical conditions that justify restriction and require documented veterinarian orders.

[P74] The provision allowing cats to be offered water at least twice daily for one hour if continuous access not provided is an unscientific minimum and may risk dehydration under some conditions; require continuous access as default and restrict intermittent access to documented veterinary or operationally necessary situations.

[P75] The specific minimum for cats (twice daily for one hour) is insufficient for multi‑cat housing or high‑temperature environments; require continuous access or more frequent offering, and mandate temperature‑based adjustments.

[P76] The water receptacle sanitation requirement is appropriate but references §3.11(b) without including sanitation frequency or standards; specify cleaning frequency and acceptable sanitizers to ensure enforceability.

[P77] Requiring a written veterinary care program signed by the attending veterinarian is sensible, but APHIS should provide a template and minimum content requirements so applicants know what is expected.

[P78] Requiring the attending veterinarian to visit all premises at least once every 12 months is too infrequent for large multi‑site operations or facilities with vulnerable animals; require risk‑based visit frequency and allow telemedicine visits for routine assessments.

[P79] Mandating annual complete physical exams for each dog may not be necessary for healthy adult dogs and would be burdensome for large kennels; allow veterinarians to set exam frequency based on risk and age, with minimum core preventive care documentation.

[P80] Requiring vaccinations and parasite control per a veterinarian‑approved schedule is appropriate, but the rule should specify core mandatory vaccines (e.g., rabies, distemper/parvo) and allow flexibility where local epidemiology differs.

[P81] The requirement for preventative grooming/hygiene "to ensure healthy and unmatted hair coats, properly trimmed nails, and clean and healthy eyes, ears, skin, and teeth" is subjective; provide objective standards and acceptable thresholds to reduce inconsistent enforcement.

[P82] Requiring maintenance of medical records and availability for inspection is reasonable, but APHIS must allow electronic records and provide data privacy protections for personally identifiable information.

[P83] Requiring identity details for each animal is reasonable but allowing group husbandry entries is appropriate; clarify minimum individual data elements that must be recorded for traceability.

[P84] The exception permitting routine husbandry for groups on a single record should be limited to homogeneous groups (same age, treatment status); define criteria for when group records are acceptable.

[P85] The detailed record requirement for identified problems is appropriate; however, APHIS should specify minimum retention periods for such records and allow redaction of proprietary medical notes where justified.

[P86] Requiring listing of all vaccines/treatments and dates is reasonable; require formats and retention periods to aid inspections and electronic reporting consistency.

[P87] Including dates and results of required or recommended tests is appropriate, but the term "recommended" is ambiguous—limit record retention obligations to required tests or those reasonably necessary for animal health.

[P88] Allowing lists of research facilities to be obtained from the Deputy Administrator on request is fine, but APHIS should publish the request procedure, expected turnaround time, and any fees.

[P89] Requiring lists of licensed/registered persons to be obtainable from the Deputy Administrator is appropriate, but APHIS should provide an online searchable database instead of manual requests and limit disclosure of sensitive contact details.

[P4] Requiring reporting of calibration results "whenever the dilution system is used" will create excessive paper/administrative burdens for frequently used mobile units; request allowance for electronic centralized records and periodic summary reporting.

[P4] The provision does not define the "specified calibration details" to be reported; EPA should list required fields (date, standard IDs, uncertainties, technician) to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P5] Requiring strict adherence to manufacturer's instructions for gas dilution system operation removes operator flexibility when manufacturer guidance is silent/obsolete; EPA should allow documented alternate procedures approved by the Administrator.

[P6] Making manufacturer's instructions and most recent calibration documentation available for inspection at the test site could be impractical for remote or continuous testing—request allowance for immediate electronic access (secure cloud) rather than physical copies.

[P6] The rule must clarify retention period for "most recent calibration documentation" and whether multi-year calibration histories must be onsite; propose 3-year electronic retention.

[P7] The 60-minute/0.85 dscm minimum per run (§60.46(b)(2)(i)) conflicts with other provisions requiring longer runs for certain sources; EPA should harmonize run durations across sections to avoid test invalidation.

[P7] Small sources and low-flow stacks may be unable to collect 0.85 dscm in 60 minutes without impacting isokinetic conditions; request performance-based exception where volume or time may be extended/shortened with Administrator approval.

[P8] Mandating average gas temperature of 160 ±5 °C in probe/filter holder (§60.46(b)(2)(i)) could cause volatilization or chemical changes in some particulate-bound species; request flexibility to use lower temperatures with demonstration that method performance is maintained.

[P9] The 120-minute/1.70 dscm minimum per run (§60.50Da(b)(1)(ii)(A)) will significantly increase test costs and field crew time for routine compliance tests; recommend allowing three 60-minute runs aggregated as equivalent.

[P9] There is no provision for interruption or restart protocols if a run cannot achieve 120 minutes (e.g., safety shutdown); request clear restart/void/sample salvage rules.

[P10] The optional language allowing heating "no greater than 160 ±5 °C" (§60.50Da) creates potential inconsistency with other mandatory 160 °C requirements; EPA should clarify when the option applies and whether lower target temps require approval.

[P11] Requiring continuous monitoring and maintenance of 160 ±5 °C during Method 5 runs (§60.46b(d)(4)) demands redundant sensors and increases instrument complexity; request allowance for periodic verification rather than continuous monitoring when data loggers are used.

[P12] The duplicate 160 ±5 °C requirement for Methods 5/5B (§60.45c(a)(5)) conflicts with Method 5 provisions that specify 120 °C in some contexts (Appendix A–3); EPA must reconcile the disparate temperature specifications to avoid contradictory obligations.

[P13] Requiring use of Method 5 to determine PM compliance (§60.58a(b)(3)) eliminates more modern alternative methods (e.g., Method 201A, sorbent-based CEMS) that may be equally accurate and less burdensome; EPA should allow validated alternatives or performance-based equivalency.

[P14] Mandating a 1.7 m3 (60 ft3) sample volume for each Method 5 run (§60.58a(b)(3)) is inconsistent with other sections that allow 0.9–1.70 dscm; EPA should harmonize required volumes across the rule.

[P15] The 160 ±5 °C heating requirement in §60.58a(b)(3) duplicates other heating specs and could conflict with Method 5's 120 °C filter exit temperature; the agency must clarify which temperature applies to which component of the train.

[P16] Requiring simultaneous O2 or CO2 measurement during each Method 5 run (§60.58a(b)(3)) will require additional analyzers and QA/QC burdens for sources that only report uncorrected concentrations; propose allowing stack flow determination methods that do not require continuous diluent measurement.

[P17] §60.293(f) references §60.296 methods for compliance but does not specify allowed deviations for specific furnace types; commenters ask EPA to provide crosswalk tables for which method parameters apply by source category.

[P18] The exception for certain glass melting furnaces to use Method 5 at 120 ±5 °C (§60.293(f) exception) is appropriate but needs clear criteria defining "modified processes" and fuel types to prevent inconsistent application.

[P19] Requiring Method 5 to measure particulate concentration and flow (§60.296(d)(2)) may be inappropriate for very hot, corrosive, or partially condensed effluents; propose permission to use validated extractive or nonextractive CEMS for such conditions.

[P20] The 60-minute/0.90 dscm minima in §60.296(d)(2) conflicts with the longer 120-minute/1.70 dscm requirement elsewhere; EPA must harmonize or explain why shorter runs are acceptable in some contexts.

[P21] Allowing probe/filter heating up to 177 ±5 °C (§60.296(d)(2) permission) is useful, but the exception referencing §60.293(e) is vague; EPA should explain interactions and provide a decision tree for allowable temperatures.

[P22] Allowing assumption of ambient CO2 equal to global monthly mean (Method 2B, 12.1) is inappropriate for local/regional studies where ambient CO2 can differ significantly; require measurement except where a reasoned justification demonstrates equivalence.

[P23] Method 5 requirement to collect PM isokinetically on a filter maintained at 120 ±5 °C (Appendix A–3, 2.0) conflicts with other provisions specifying 160 °C; EPA must harmonize filter temperatures across methods to avoid contradictory obligations and test invalidation.

[P23] Maintaining filter at 120 ±5 °C may not prevent volatilization for certain semi-volatile PM components at high stack temperatures; suggest allowing higher filter temperatures where justified by speciated PM studies.

[P24] Requiring borosilicate or quartz probe liners capable of 120 ±5 °C heating (Appendix A–3, 6.1.1.2) is unrealistic for stacks above 480 °C; comment requests clearer guidance on insulation and active heating requirements for high-temperature stacks.

[P25] Mandating quartz liners for stack temps 480–900 °C (Appendix A–3, 6.1.1.2) will significantly increase equipment costs and fragility; request allowance to use approved metal liners with protective coatings without Administrator approval as long as performance is documented.

[P26] The Administrator approval requirement to use liners above specified temps (permission) is discretionary and could introduce delays; propose a standardized qualification checklist for expedited approvals.

[P27] Allowing metal liners only with Administrator approval (Appendix A–3, Method 5) conflicts with other sections that prohibit metal liners (Method 8); EPA should reconcile liner material permissions across methods to avoid contradictory expectations.

[P28] Requiring heating systems that ensure sample gas exiting filter is 120 ±5 °C (Appendix A–3, 6.1.1.6) imposes substantial energy and equipment needs for field labs; suggest performance alternative—demonstrate target particle stability—rather than strict temp control.

[P29] Specifying ±3 °C accuracy for temperature sensors with tip in direct contact with sample gas (Appendix A–3, 6.1.1.7) may be unrealistic in harsh stacks; propose acceptable alternative sensor placements with correction factors and documented uncertainty.

[P30] Requiring sensor tip to protrude at least 1/2 inch into sample gas and allowing encasement in certain materials (Appendix A–3, 6.1.1.7) could cause probe damage or flow disturbance in small ducts; request dimension exceptions for small probe nozzles.

[P31] Mandating continuous monitoring and recording of filter temperature sensor during sampling (Appendix A–3, 6.1.1.7) creates large data retention burdens; recommend allowing summarized reports and retention aligned with existing QA/QC schedules.

[P32] Requiring a DGM capable of ±2% volume measurement (Appendix A–3, 6.1.1.9) excludes commonly used field dry gas meters with ±3–5% accuracy; propose allowing DGMs with documented calibration and uncertainty budget.

[P33] The permission to use alternative metering systems subject to Administrator approval (Appendix A–3, 6.1.1.9) is too vague; request defined performance criteria and an expedited approval pathway.

[P34] Mandating that metering systems allow periodic checks of isokinetic sampling when used with a pitot tube (Appendix A–3, 6.1.1.9) is technically unclear—need examples of acceptable check procedures and required frequency.

[P35] Maintaining isokinetic sampling within 10% and sample gas temp through filter at 120 ±5 °C during runs (Appendix A–3, 8.5) will be infeasible in fluctuating stacks; propose allowance for averaging or documenting transient excursions with corrective actions.

[P36] Method 5B requirement that probe liner and filter heating systems can maintain 160 ±5 °C (Appendix A–3, 6.1) will force expensive upgrades for labs historically operating at 120 °C; request grandfathering provision or phased compliance.

[P37] Keeping probe outlet and filter temperatures at 160 ±5 °C during sampling (Method 5B, 8.2) may cause loss of semi-volatile particulate material and bias results downward; ask EPA to permit lower temps where validated to preserve analytes.

[P38] Requiring data recorded on a sheet "such as Figure 5B–1" (Method 5B, 11.1) is prescriptive; allow equivalent electronic data capture formats provided they include all required fields.

[P39] Method 5B sample handling (oven drying at 160 ±5 °C for 6 hours, desiccate 2 hours, report to 0.1 mg) (Appendix A–3, 11.2.1) is very prescriptive and could conflict with lab capabilities; ask for tolerance for different ovens/conditions if demonstrated to produce equivalent weighings.

[P40] The rule's instruction to void samples when leakage occurred (Method 5B, 11.2.2) without specifying a validated correction method is overly punitive; request a list of Administrator-approved correction procedures and maximum allowable leak volumes.

[P41] Requiring weighing of spent silica gel to nearest 0.5 g (Method 5B, 11.2.3) is low precision compared with balances used for filter mass (0.1 mg); clarify rationale and consider harmonizing precision requirements.

[P42] The acetone evaporation and 24-hour desiccation and weighing to 0.1 mg (Method 5B, 11.2.4) is burdensome; recommend allowing validated solvent exchange/concentration methods or shorter desiccation when validated.

[P43] Guidance allowing paired-train oven temps within ±5 °C (Method 5I, 8.5.2.2) should explicitly allow use of a single oven with forced air to keep temps matched, to reduce equipment needs.

[P44] Requiring daily calibration procedures when samples are analyzed (Method 7, 10.1.2) is appropriate, but the rule should allow weekly calibration for analyzers with demonstrated stability and documented QA.

[P45] Method 7 optical/absorbance dilution provisions (11.3) are highly procedural; industry requests that EPA recognize validated labs that use automated spectrophotometers with equivalent QA rather than manual dilutions.

[P46] Requiring leak-free ground glass fittings when stack temp >210 °C (Method 8, 6.1.1.1) is unrealistic for field conditions where ground glass may seize; permit alternative non-contaminating fittings (e.g., PTFE unions) that provide equivalent leak performance.

[P47] Mandating button-hook or elbow probe nozzles (Method 8, 6.1.1.1) may be infeasible for narrow ducts and some source geometries; ask for allowance of alternative nozzle geometries with Administrator approval based on isokinetic equivalency demonstrations.

[P48] Prohibiting metal probe liners in Method 8 (Appendix A–4, 6.1.1.2) is inconsistent with allowances for metal liners in Method 5 and others; harmonize policy—allow corrosion-resistant metal liners when validated to prevent contamination.

[P49] Requirement that filter holder be placed between specified impingers and "do not heat it" (Method 8, 6.1.1.3) may promote condensation or leakage for high-water-content stacks; request an exception to preclude condensation when validated heated holders are needed.

[P50] The specified impinger tip configurations (Method 8, 6.1.1.4) are very prescriptive and may not be compatible with modern impinger designs; EPA should permit functionally equivalent modern impinger designs that meet capture efficiency criteria.

[P51] The 1 °C accuracy requirement for impinger effluent gas thermometers (Method 8, 6.1.1.5) is stricter than many field thermometers can reliably meet; allow ±2 °C where uncertainty is properly propagated.

[P52] Requiring recovery studies at each sampling point for Method 18 (Appendix A–6, 13.1(b)) is overly burdensome for sources with many sampling points; propose allowing representative recovery studies with statistical justification for grouped points.

[P53] Method 22 outdoor observation recordkeeping requiring wind speed/direction, sky condition, and sketches (Appendix A–7, 11.2.1) may risk privacy or proprietary information exposure when sketched process units are sensitive; request ability to submit redacted sketches or only coordinate references.

[P54] Allowing digital photography as alternative recordkeeping (Method 22, 11.2.1 permission) is helpful, but the rule should specify acceptable metadata (time, GPS) and image resolution to ensure evidentiary value.

[P55] Indoor observation recording requirements (Method 22, 11.2.2) requiring sketches of emission points may be impractical for complex facilities; propose use of pre-approved facility diagrams or GIS coordinates instead.

[P56] Permitting annotated digital photographs (Method 22, 11.2.3) is useful but the rule must specify acceptable annotation methods and file formats to avoid claims of image tampering.

[P57] Requiring "proper lighting, field of view and depth of field" for photos (Method 22, 11.2.3) is subjective; EPA should provide objective minimum image quality standards (resolution, exposure) and examples.

[P58] Requiring at least one photo from the observer's POV (Method 22, 11.2.3) may not capture the emission adequately; allow supplementary angles and permit omission if safety or access issues prevent such a photo.

[P59] Photo timing within about 15 minutes of observation (Method 22, 11.2.3) may be impractical for remote observations; allow a documented window (e.g., 30 minutes) when justified by operational context.

[P60] Retaining unaltered originals of altered/annotated photos (Method 22, 11.2.3) is reasonable, but the rule should allow secure digital versioning systems (hashing, audit trails) in lieu of physical originals.

[P61] Specifying HDPE or glass containers with Teflon screw cap liners for impinger samples (Method 26, 6.2.2) may not be compatible with certain solvent chemistries; allow alternative chemically compatible containers if documented and pre-approved.

[P62] Requiring same set of sampling tools as Method 5 for Method 26A (Appendix A–8, 6.2.1) can be redundant; suggest cross-referencing validated tool lists rather than full duplication of equipment lists.

[P63] Requiring Teflon liners in sample storage containers for Method 26A (Appendix A–8, 6.2.4) will increase costs and may not be necessary for all analytes; allow alternative lining materials with compatibility demonstration.

[P64] Requiring manufacturers to periodically select/test monitors per ASTM D6216–12 (PS1, 2.1) could conflict with existing QA programs; recommend harmonization with ISO/IEC calibration schemes and allow cross-recognized standards.

[P65] Requiring manufacturers to test every opacity monitor for conformance (PS1, 2.1) is overly burdensome and could delay shipments; permit statistically-based sample testing with traceable lot testing for high-volume manufacturers.

[P66] Obligating owners/operators to purchase monitors meeting ASTM D6216–12 including DAHS (PS1, 6.1) may be costly for small sources; propose phased compliance or allowance of functionally equivalent standards.

[P67] Mandating certificate of conformance from manufacturer at time of purchase (PS1, 8.1(1)) could be impractical for aftermarket or refurbished monitors; allow certificate issuance within a defined period after purchase if performance verified.

[P68] The three-point calibration error test requiring five nonconsecutive readings per attenuator (PS1, 8.1(3)(ii)) is specific but lacks tolerances for variability; request clarification of acceptance criteria and treatment of outliers.

[P69] Requiring verification per ASTM sections (PS1, 8.2(1)) binds compliance to a specific ASTM version; EPA should allow use of later ASTM revisions or equivalent standards without rule amendment.

[P70] Requiring verification of performance specs per ASTM section 7 (PS1, 8.2(2)) may impose specialized testing not available in regionally common labs; allow third-party certified labs and provide a list of acceptable testing providers.

[P71] Delivery of conformance report to owner/operator consistent with ASTM reporting (PS1, 8.2(3)) should be allowed electronically and must include a machine-readable summary of key metrics for easier integration with facility compliance systems.

[P72] Mandating that manufacturers start a quality program per ASTM section 8 (PS1, 9.0) could conflict with foreign manufacturers' quality systems (e.g., ISO); EPA should allow demonstration of equivalent quality systems such as ISO 9001.

[P73] Requiring opacity equipment to comply with ASTM D6216–12 design specs (PS1, 13.1) may exclude newer technologies (e.g., laser-based instruments) not contemplated by that ASTM; provide a mechanism to demonstrate equivalence for newer designs.

[P74] Mandating compliance with manufacturer's performance specs (PS1, 13.2) could lock in proprietary performance thresholds that are not independently verified; require independent verification of manufacturer claims.

[P75] The CEMS relative accuracy performance spec (PS2, 13.2) with percent limits tied to average emissions lacks clarity on calculation windows and data inclusion rules; EPA should specify averaging times, treatment of zeros, and minimum sample counts.

[P76] Requiring summary of calculations on a data sheet "similar to Figure 2.2" (PS3, 12.0) is prescriptive; allow electronic templates or equivalent summaries if all required metrics are present.

[P77] The CEMS RA requirement ≤20% of RM mean or alternate ≤1.0% O2 (PS3, 13.2) may be impossible to meet for low-emission sources where RM mean is near zero; propose relative accuracy criteria that consider absolute error thresholds for low-concentration ranges.

[P78] Daily internal drift checks for PM CEMS limited to ≤2% of response range (PS11, 13.1) are overly stringent relative to performance of optical PM monitors; suggest a higher drift limit or performance-based demonstration for equivalency.

[P79] Determining calibration drift separately for each ancillary monitor (PS11, 13.1) is technically sound but will increase testing complexity and cost; request consolidated drift protocols when ancillary monitors are co-located and share calibrations.

[P80] PS18 requirement that daily zero- and mid-level CD <5% of span for seven consecutive days (11.8.7) is operationally strict; propose allowing variability with documented corrective actions and re-test windows rather than outright test failure.

[P81] Allowing testing of interferent gases at lower concentrations if manufacturer provides scrubbing/limiting means (PS18, Table 1 note 1) is reasonable but requires objective criteria to evaluate manufacturer claims; request specific validation protocol and independent verification.

[P82] The prohibition against adding gases above 100% stack equivalent concentration during short path IP cell interference tests (PS18, Table 1 note 2) is unclear—EPA should define "stack equivalent concentration" and provide acceptable test concentration ranges for common interferents.

Allowing digital photography as alternative recordkeeping (Method 22, 11.2.1 permission) is helpful, but the rule should specify acceptable metadata (time, GPS) and image resolution to ensure evidentiary value.

Indoor observation recording requirements (Method 22, 11.2.2) requiring sketches of emission points may be impractical for complex facilities; propose use of pre-approved facility diagrams or GIS coordinates instead.
Permitting annotated digital photographs (Method 22, 11.2.3) is useful but the rule must specify acceptable annotation methods and file formats to avoid claims of image tampering.

Requiring "proper lighting, field of view and depth of field" for photos (Method 22, 11.2.3) is subjective; EPA should provide objective minimum image quality standards (resolution, exposure) and examples.

Requiring at least one photo from the observer's POV (Method 22, 11.2.3) may not capture the emission adequately; allow supplementary angles and permit omission if safety or access issues prevent such a photo.
Photo timing within about 15 minutes of observation (Method 22, 11.2.3) may be impractical for remote observations; allow a documented window (e.g., 30 minutes) when justified by operational context.

Retaining unaltered originals of altered/annotated photos (Method 22, 11.2.3) is reasonable, but the rule should allow secure digital versioning systems (hashing, audit trails) in lieu of physical originals.

Specifying HDPE or glass containers with Teflon screw cap liners for impinger samples (Method 26, 6.2.2) may not be compatible with certain solvent chemistries; allow alternative chemically compatible containers if documented and pre-approved.
Requiring same set of sampling tools as Method 5 for Method 26A (Appendix A–8, 6.2.1) can be redundant; suggest cross-referencing validated tool lists rather than full duplication of equipment lists.

Requiring Teflon liners in sample storage containers for Method 26A (Appendix A–8, 6.2.4) will increase costs and may not be necessary for all analytes; allow alternative lining materials with compatibility demonstration.

Requiring manufacturers to periodically select/test monitors per ASTM D6216–12 (PS1, 2.1) could conflict with existing QA programs; recommend harmonization with ISO/IEC calibration schemes and allow cross-recognized standards.

Requiring manufacturers to test every opacity monitor for conformance (PS1, 2.1) is overly burdensome and could delay shipments; permit statistically-based sample testing with traceable lot testing for high-volume manufacturers.

Obligating owners/operators to purchase monitors meeting ASTM D6216–12 including DAHS (PS1, 6.1) may be costly for small sources; propose phased compliance or allowance of functionally equivalent standards.

Mandating certificate of conformance from manufacturer at time of purchase (PS1, 8.1(1)) could be impractical for aftermarket or refurbished monitors; allow certificate issuance within a defined period after purchase if performance verified.

The three-point calibration error test requiring five nonconsecutive readings per attenuator (PS1, 8.1(3)(ii)) is specific but lacks tolerances for variability; request clarification of acceptance criteria and treatment of outliers.
Requiring verification per ASTM sections (PS1, 8.2(1)) binds compliance to a specific ASTM version; EPA should allow use of later ASTM revisions or equivalent standards without rule amendment.

Requiring verification of performance specs per ASTM section 7 (PS1, 8.2(2)) may impose specialized testing not available in regionally common labs; allow third-party certified labs and provide a list of acceptable testing providers.

raw_output:
[P1] The 18-month compliance deadline for existing sources (§49.4169(c)) is infeasible for many operators given permitting, engineering, and procurement lead times; EPA should extend to at least 36 months.

[P1] Shortening the compliance timeline will disproportionately burden small and independent operators who lack capital and staff to retrofit equipment within 18 months; EPA should provide phased compliance schedules or financial assistance.

[P2] The extension procedure (§49.4169(c) written request) lacks objective criteria and timelines for EPA action; commenters request clear standards for granting extensions and a required EPA decision timeline (e.g., 60 days).

[P2] EPA should allow extensions automatically when owners/operators can document supply-chain delays, equipment backlogs, or pending state/tribal permits rather than relying on discretionary approval.

[P3] Requiring new sources to comply “upon startup” (§49.4169(c)) is unclear as to whether startup means first production, first flowback, or first combustion; EPA must define “startup” precisely to avoid enforcement unfairness.

[P4] The requirement that new/modified true minor sources comply with §49.4173 when commencing construction after 30 days (§49.4169(c)) creates legal uncertainty about whether pre-construction activities trigger obligations; EPA should clarify the construction milestone.

[P5] The delegation request requirements for the Ute Indian Tribe (§49.4170(b)) are overly prescriptive and may conflict with tribal governance norms; EPA should allow equivalent tribal documentation in lieu of exact forms.

[P6] Requiring the delegation request to “identify the specific provisions” (§49.4170(b)(1)) could force tribes to foreclose future delegation expansion; EPA should permit a tribe to request delegation for classes of provisions or to amend later.

[P7] The legal statement requirement by tribal counsel (§49.4170(b)(2)) is legally intrusive and may expose tribal deliberations; EPA should permit an attestation from a tribal official rather than detailed legal analysis.

[P8] Requiring a statement that the Ute Indian Tribe is recognized by the Secretary of the Interior (§49.4170(b)(2)(i)) duplicates existing public records and could be simplified to a citation to DOI recognition documentation.

[P9] The demonstration that the Tribe “carries out substantial governmental duties” (§49.4170(b)(2)(ii)) mirrors §49.7(a)(2) but lacks guidance on acceptable evidence (e.g., codes, budgets); EPA should provide an evidentiary checklist to reduce back-and-forth.

[P10] Asking the Tribe to describe tribal laws granting authority to implement the rule (§49.4170(b)(2)(iii)) may reveal sensitive legal strategies; EPA should accept redacted summaries or attorney-privileged summaries.

[P11] The requirement to demonstrate adequate resources (§49.4170(b)(3)) lacks specificity on financial, technical, and staffing thresholds; EPA should state minimum staff/financial benchmarks or allow multi-year capacity-building plans.

[P12] The Delegation of Authority Agreement (§49.4170(c)(1)) becoming effective only when signed by both parties creates potential gaps—EPA should include an interim coordination mechanism so tribal oversight can begin on agreed elements pending final signature.

[P13] The clause allowing EPA to modify/revoke the Delegation Agreement after consultation (§49.4170(c)(2)) is too unilateral and could chill tribal acceptance; EPA should require written notice and a defined process with dispute resolution before revocation.

[P14] Publishing a Federal Register notice of delegation (§49.4170(d)) is welcome, but the rule should require EPA to publish the full Agreement text, not merely a notice, to ensure public transparency.

[P15] Requiring local newspaper announcements (§49.4170(d)) may be ineffective and costly; EPA should allow combined electronic notice (tribal websites, email lists) and a single local paper to satisfy the requirement.

[P16] The good-air-pollution-control-practices obligation (§49.4171(a)) is phrased as “to the extent practicable” which is subjective; EPA should provide sector-specific BACT/BACT-like guidance or benchmarks for what constitutes practicable design and maintenance.

[P17] The always-applicable obligation including startup, shutdown, and malfunction (§49.4171(a)) may subject operators to enforcement for unavoidable malfunctions; EPA should add a force majeure or affirmative defense provision and require written malfunction minimization plans.

[P18] The triennial inventory requirement beginning in 2017 (§49.4172(b)) is retroactive and impossible for operators who never submitted prior inventories; EPA must clarify that the first due inventory is the one described (due Oct 1, 2018) and offer alternatives for historic years.

[P19] Mandating inventories for PM10, PM2.5, SOx, NOx, CO, and VOC (§49.4172(c)) is burdensome for small sources lacking monitoring data; EPA should allow use of standard emission factors and tiered reporting based on source size.

[P20] Calculating emissions using “actual operating hours, product rates, and types of materials” (§49.4172(c)) may require recordkeeping not currently maintained; EPA should provide templates and accept best available data for initial inventories.

[P21] Requiring reporting of control equipment type and efficiency (§49.4172(d)) is reasonable but EPA must specify acceptable test methods to demonstrate efficiency (e.g., EPA test methods or manufacturer certifications).

[P22] The April 15 submission deadline (§49.4172(e)) following the inventory year (with first inventory due Oct 1, 2018) creates confusion; EPA should set consistent, non-retroactive start dates and align deadlines with fiscal cycles.

[P23] Mandatory electronic submission in a specified format (§49.4172(f)) could disadvantage operators without internet access or the exact software; EPA should provide alternate submission options and sample files for validation.

[P24] §49.4173(a) requiring compliance with both the FIP and Minor NSR could duplicate permitting and create conflicting requirements; EPA should harmonize provisions and clarify precedence when conflicts arise.

[P25] The statement that compliance with §49.4173(a) does not relieve obligations under other FIP sections (§49.4173(b)) is confusing and may subject operators to overlapping, redundant standards; EPA should cross-reference and reconcile overlapping requirements.

[P26] Exempting tanks subject to 40 CFR parts OOOO/OOOOa or 63 subpart HH (§49.4174(b)(1)) is appropriate but EPA should clarify interaction when only some tanks at a source are covered by those subparts.

[P27] The emergency tank exemption (§49.4174(b)(2)) requiring emptying within 15 days (§49.4174(b)(2)(ii)) is impractical in remote operations where removal of fluids may take longer; extend to 30 days or allow documented logistical exceptions.

[P28] Requiring emergency tanks to have a liquid level gauge (§49.4174(b)(2)(iii)) is reasonable, but EPA should accept equivalent technologies (e.g., sight glasses, GPS-based inventory systems) explicitly.

[P29] The binary choice to comply with either the 95% control per tank (c)(1) or the <4 tpy source-wide exemption (c)(2) (§49.4174(c)) may incentivize gaming throughput calculations to avoid controls; EPA should add anti-circumvention measures and independent verification.

[P30] The 95% continuous VOC reduction requirement per tank (§49.4174(c)(1)) is technologically feasible for many tanks but will be cost-prohibitive for low- throughput or intermittent tanks; EPA should allow performance-based alternatives or de minimis thresholds.

[P31] Requiring routing of all flashing, working, standing and breathing losses through closed-vent systems (§49.4174(c)(1)) is operationally challenging for tanks with frequent lifting of hatches; EPA should permit operational windows for safe hatch operation with immediate sealing procedures.

[P32] The option to recover 100% and recycle emissions (§49.4174(c)(1)(i)) is unrealistic; manufacturers cannot guarantee 100% capture—EPA should revise to “95–99% recovery” or allow demonstration of practical capture efficiency.

[P33] Requiring enclosed combustors or flares to achieve at least 95% reduction (§49.4174(c)(1)(ii)) and meet referenced operating sections may be infeasible at very low BTU flows; EPA should require minimum flow or heating value thresholds for safe, efficient flare operation.

[P34] The source-wide <4 tpy uncontrolled VOC threshold (§49.4174(c)(2)) is inconsistently applied across operators with seasonal throughput; EPA must clarify how seasonal spikes are treated and whether averaging can be seasonal rather than strictly monthly.

[P35] The 12-consecutive-month demonstration using monthly determinations (§49.4174(c)(2)) with calculations separated by at least 14 days (§49.4174(c)(2) & (42)) is confusing—EPA should provide a sample calculation protocol and explain the 14-day separation purpose.

[P36] Using “a generally accepted model or calculation methodology” (§49.4174(c)(2)) is vague; EPA should specify acceptable models (e.g., API, EPA AP-42, TANKS) and allow agreement on alternate methods by Region 8.

[P37] Basing monthly calculations on “average monthly throughput” (§49.4174(c)(2)(41)) could mask episodic peaks; EPA should require use of measured daily throughput if available or require conservative default emission factors.

[P38] The 30-day requirement to install 95% controls if monthly emissions ≥4 tpy (§49.4174(c)(2)) is too short for design, procurement, and installation; EPA should provide a longer compliance window (e.g., 120 days) or allow temporary mitigations.

[P39] Requiring covers for tanks when using control devices (§49.4174(c)(3)) is technically reasonable but the mandate to equip each tank with a cover that forms a continuous impermeable barrier (§49.4177(c)(1)) may not be achievable for certain tank designs; EPA should allow performance-based equivalence or engineering alternatives.

[P40] For floating roofs, the cross-reference to §60.112b and subpart Kb monitoring (§49.4174(c)(4)) is appropriate, but EPA should specify recordkeeping cadence and inspection frequencies for consistency across Regions.

[P41] Allowing removal of controls after 12 months if emissions maintained below thresholds (§49.4174(c)(5)) could incentivize removal to avoid maintenance costs; EPA should require notification, sampling, and a demonstration of sustained low emissions for an additional 12 months before permitting removal.

[P42] The alternative throughput-based condition allowing removal when source throughput <8,000 barrels (§49.4174(c)(5)(ii)) needs clarity whether this is per month, per year, or average monthly—EPA must define the timeframe for the 8,000-barrel threshold.

[P43] The glycol dehydration exemption (§49.4175(b)) for units subject to subpart HH is appropriate, but EPA should ensure consistent reporting so exempt units still appear in inventories to avoid data gaps.

[P44] The 95% control requirement for each glycol dehydration unit process vent (§49.4175(c)(1)) may not be achievable with existing dehydrators without major retrofit; EPA should allow alternative compliance methods (e.g., emission limits or work-practice standards).

[P45] The option to maintain a source-wide <4 tpy emissions rate instead of individual 95% controls (§49.4175(c)(2)) duplicates §49.4174(c)(2) and may allow sources to avoid best practices; EPA should require additional monitoring if using the <4 tpy route.

[P46] Pneumatic pump exemptions for those covered by subpart OOOOa (§49.4176(b)) are reasonable, but EPA must clarify when a pump moves in/out of subpart coverage (e.g., change in control status) and the transition timeline.

[P47] Requiring reevaluation of source-wide VOC emissions upon any modification (§49.4176(a)) could trigger a cascade of administrative burdens for de minimis changes; EPA should define what constitutes a modification that triggers reevaluation.

[P48] The 95% continuous reduction requirement for each pneumatic pump (§49.4176(c)(1)) may be cost-ineffective for intermittent or low-producing wells; EPA should allow low-emitters to qualify for the <4 tpy source-wide option with simplified monitoring.

[P49] The closed-vent system design requirement to have “no detectable emissions” demonstrated by fugitive emissions component monitoring (§49.4177(d)(3)) is unachievable if the monitoring method detection limit is higher than allowable emissions; EPA should specify detection limits and acceptable monitoring technologies.

[P50] Excluding low-leg drains, analyzer vents, and safety devices from bypass-device requirements (§49.4177(d)(4) exclusions) is necessary, but EPA must require documentation and engineering justifications to support those exclusions.

[P51] The requirement to install continuous flow indicators with alarms at bypass inlets (§49.4177(d)(4)(i)) may be technically challenging in remote cold climates where instruments freeze; EPA should allow alternative detection methods or instrument heaters.

[P52] Securing bypass valves with car-seals or lock-and-key (§49.4177(d)(4)(ii)) is an effective compliance measure but costly for large volumes of valves; EPA should allow electronic tamper-evident devices or SCADA interlocks as equivalent.

[P53] Exempting control devices regulated under federal subparts (§49.4178(b)) avoids duplication, but EPA should require cross-referencing so operators know which standard governs if multiple apply.

[P54] Mandating operators follow manufacturer operating instructions for combustors/flares (§49.4178(c)(1)) is sensible, but EPA should clarify which version of manufacturer instructions applies if updated after installation.

[P55] Requiring combustor/flares to be designed and operated to achieve 95% VOC reduction across expected flow/BTU ranges (§49.4178(c)(2)) should include explicit minimum BTU thresholds; otherwise, devices may be forced to operate outside safe parameters.

[P56] The continuous operation requirement to achieve 95% control efficiency (§49.4178(c)(3)) does not account for maintenance shutdowns; EPA should allow planned downtime when documented and require contingency controls.

[P57] The requirement that enclosed combustors be manufacturer-demonstrated models per an EPA-approved performance test (§49.4178(c)(5)(i)) could preclude field-proven retrofit devices; EPA should accept owner-performed validated demonstrations under an approved protocol.

[P58] Requiring performance testing by the owner/operator by the first annual report due date (§49.4178(c)(5)(ii)) is unclear about the test deadline and could impose high initial testing costs; EPA should set clear test windows and allow consolidated testing for multiple units.

[P59] The liquid knock-out, flash-back arrestor, pilot/ignition device, and continuous monitoring requirements (§49.4178(c)(6)(ii)-(v)) are technically sound but will increase capital/operating costs; EPA should provide a cost-effectiveness analysis and possible small-source exemptions.

[P60] The requirement for continuous monitoring/recording systems or SCADA connection to document pilot/ignition operation (§49.4178(c)(6)(v)) raises cybersecurity and data storage concerns; EPA should allow periodic manual log backups and define record-retention limits.

[P61] Maintaining combustors/flares in a leak-free condition and with no visible smoke (§49.4178(c)(6)(vi)-(vii)) are enforceable goals, but EPA must specify inspection frequency, repair timeframes, and acceptable monitoring methods.

[P62] Fugitive monitoring exemptions for sources covered by subpart OOOOa (§49.4179(b)) are appropriate, but EPA must ensure consistency of monitoring frequency and repair timelines between subparts to prevent regulatory gaps.

[P63] The Reservation-wide fugitive emissions monitoring plan requirement (§49.4179(c)(1)) shifts substantial compliance obligation to individual owners/operators to create a plan that is “Reservation-wide,” which may be unworkable without tribal leadership coordination; EPA should fund tribal planning or allow source-specific plans that meet minimum Reservation coordination standards.

[P64] The truncated requirement to perform initial monitoring of the collection of fugitive emissions components (§49.4179(c)(1)(i)) needs to be completed and specify timeframes, frequency, detection methods (OGI vs. Method 21), and repair deadlines.

[P65] Overall, the rule contains multiple cross-references to federal subparts and EPA sections without providing a consolidated compliance matrix for operators; EPA should publish a compliance guide with timelines, sample forms, and crosswalks to existing standards.

[P66] Legal commenters: Several provisions (e.g., retroactive inventory deadlines, ambiguous definitions of construction/startup/modification, and unilateral revocation of delegation) may raise due process concerns and could be subject to challenge unless EPA adds clearer standards and procedural protections.

The option to maintain a source-wide <4 tpy emissions rate instead of individual 95% controls (§49.4175(c)(2)) duplicates §49.4174(c)(2) and may allow sources to avoid best practices; EPA should require additional monitoring if using the <4 tpy route.

Pneumatic pump exemptions for those covered by subpart OOOOa (§49.4176(b)) are reasonable, but EPA must clarify when a pump moves in/out of subpart coverage (e.g., change in control status) and the transition timeline.

Requiring reevaluation of source-wide VOC emissions upon any modification (§49.4176(a)) could trigger a cascade of administrative burdens for de minimis changes; EPA should define what constitutes a modification that triggers reevaluation.

The 95% continuous reduction requirement for each pneumatic pump (§49.4176(c)(1)) may be cost-ineffective for intermittent or low-producing wells; EPA should allow low-emitters to qualify for the <4 tpy source-wide option with simplified monitoring.

The closed-vent system design requirement to have “no detectable emissions” demonstrated by fugitive emissions component monitoring (§49.4177(d)(3)) is unachievable if the monitoring method detection limit is higher than allowable emissions; EPA should specify detection limits and acceptable monitoring technologies.

Excluding low-leg drains, analyzer vents, and safety devices from bypass-device requirements (§49.4177(d)(4) exclusions) is necessary, but EPA must require documentation and engineering justifications to support those exclusions.

The requirement to install continuous flow indicators with alarms at bypass inlets (§49.4177(d)(4)(i)) may be technically challenging in remote cold climates where instruments freeze; EPA should allow alternative detection methods or instrument heaters.

Securing bypass valves with car-seals or lock-and-key (§49.4177(d)(4)(ii)) is an effective compliance measure but costly for large volumes of valves; EPA should allow electronic tamper-evident devices or SCADA interlocks as equivalent.
Exempting control devices regulated under federal subparts (§49.4178(b)) avoids duplication, but EPA should require cross-referencing so operators know which standard governs if multiple apply.

Mandating operators follow manufacturer operating instructions for combustors/flares (§49.4178(c)(1)) is sensible, but EPA should clarify which version of manufacturer instructions applies if updated after installation.

Requiring combustor/flares to be designed and operated to achieve 95% VOC reduction across expected flow/BTU ranges (§49.4178(c)(2)) should include explicit minimum BTU thresholds; otherwise, devices may be forced to operate outside safe parameters.

The continuous operation requirement to achieve 95% control efficiency (§49.4178(c)(3)) does not account for maintenance shutdowns; EPA should allow planned downtime when documented and require contingency controls.

The requirement that enclosed combustors be manufacturer-demonstrated models per an EPA-approved performance test (§49.4178(c)(5)(i)) could preclude field-proven retrofit devices; EPA should accept owner-performed validated demonstrations under an approved protocol.

Requiring performance testing by the owner/operator by the first annual report due date (§49.4178(c)(5)(ii)) is unclear about the test deadline and could impose high initial testing costs; EPA should set clear test windows and allow consolidated testing for multiple units.

The liquid knock-out, flash-back arrestor, pilot/ignition device, and continuous monitoring requirements (§49.4178(c)(6)(ii)-(v)) are technically sound but will increase capital/operating costs; EPA should provide a cost-effectiveness analysis and possible small-source exemptions.

The requirement for continuous monitoring/recording systems or SCADA connection to document pilot/ignition operation (§49.4178(c)(6)(v)) raises cybersecurity and data storage concerns; EPA should allow periodic manual log backups and define record-retention limits.

Maintaining combustors/flares in a leak-free condition and with no visible smoke (§49.4178(c)(6)(vi)-(vii)) are enforceable goals, but EPA must specify inspection frequency, repair timeframes, and acceptable monitoring methods.

Fugitive monitoring exemptions for sources covered by subpart OOOOa (§49.4179(b)) are appropriate, but EPA must ensure consistency of monitoring frequency and repair timelines between subparts to prevent regulatory gaps.

The Reservation-wide fugitive emissions monitoring plan requirement (§49.4179(c)(1)) shifts substantial compliance obligation to individual owners/operators to create a plan that is “Reservation-wide,” which may be unworkable without tribal leadership coordination; EPA should fund tribal planning or allow source-specific plans that meet minimum Reservation coordination standards.

The truncated requirement to perform initial monitoring of the collection of fugitive emissions components (§49.4179(c)(1)(i)) needs to be completed and specify timeframes, frequency, detection methods (OGI vs. Method 21), and repair deadlines.

Overall, the rule contains multiple cross-references to federal subparts and EPA sections without providing a consolidated compliance matrix for operators; EPA should publish a compliance guide with timelines, sample forms, and crosswalks to existing standards.

Legal commenters: Several provisions (e.g., retroactive inventory deadlines, ambiguous definitions of construction/startup/modification, and unilateral revocation of delegation) may raise due process concerns and could be subject to challenge unless EPA adds clearer standards and procedural protections.
