[P1] The blanket requirement in §63.6105(a) to be "in compliance ... at all times" is unworkable because it provides no allowance for brief unavoidable deviations during emergencies; we request clarification or a de minimis deviation allowance tied to documented emergency events.

[P2] The pre-compliance-date carve-out (P2) that allows SSM exceptions only prior to the specified date but not after creates regulatory uncertainty for sources transitioning compliance — EPA should harmonize the treatment of SSM across timelines or provide explicit transitional guidance.

[P3] §63.6105(a) (P3) requires compliance "at all times" after the specified date including during normal operational transients; suppliers request clarification that scheduled maintenance and normal short-duration operational adjustments are not enforcement violations if documented under §63.6155 recordkeeping.

[P4] §63.6105(b) (P4) requires operating/maintenance to minimize emissions "including during SSM" before the compliance date; industry comments that the phrase "including during SSM" conflicts with longstanding SSM enforcement policy and asks EPA to define acceptable practices and metrics for what constitutes "minimizing" during SSM.

[P5] §63.6105(c) (P5) obligates operation consistent with safety and pollution-control practices at all times after the compliance date, but does not define the interplay with occupational safety requirements; request explicit language establishing that compliance actions must not endanger personnel and that safety take precedence when necessary.

[P6] §63.6105(c) exception (P6) that owners are not required to make further reductions once standard levels are achieved could be interpreted to bar continuous improvement; environmental groups will comment that EPA should encourage or at least not discourage additional emission-reduction actions and should clarify that the provision does not preempt state or local more-stringent requirements.

[P7] The enforcement provision (P7) allowing the Administrator to base compliance determinations on "available information" including procedure/record reviews and inspections raises privacy and proprietary concerns — regulated entities request specificity about what documents may be requested and limits on scope to avoid fishing expeditions.

[P8] §63.6110(a) (P8) requires initial performance tests within 180 days after compliance date; commenters from small operators will request an extension or phased schedule for conducting costly initial tests, especially where multiple turbines or remote sites are involved.

[P9] §63.6110(a) condition (P9) concerning turbines previously under stay that must test within 180 days after the stay removal may be infeasible if the stay removal occurs during winter or maintenance seasons; request allowing scheduling flexibility tied to safe/representative operating periods.

[P10] §63.6120(b) (P10) mandates tests per Table 3; testing laboratories note that Table 3 references must align with available approved methods and request EPA to ensure testing method capacity exists nationally before compliance dates.

[P11] §63.6120(b) condition (P11) requiring tests to follow §63.7(e)(1) before the specified date conflicts with the simultaneous requirement to avoid testing during SSM; request clarification on how to reconcile test scheduling with SSM constraints and whether EPA will permit performance testing during controlled shutdowns for safety.

[P12] §63.6120(c) (P12) requiring tests at 100% ±10% load is infeasible for combined-cycle turbines operating most of the year at part load; industry requests allowance to test at representative steady-state operating load instead of strict high-load for turbines that never operate near 100%.

[P13] §63.6120(c) prohibition (P13) banning tests during startup/shutdown prior to the specified date could delay many initial tests because many plants only reach steady operation during certain hours; operators request an exemption allowing tests during controlled startups when representative and safe.

[P14] §63.6120(c) (P14) requiring tests to be "representative of the source's performance" after the date is vague — request EPA provide objective criteria (e.g., % load ranges, fuel composition windows) to determine representativeness and avoid subjective enforcement.

[P15] §63.6120(c) condition (P15) excluding startup/shutdown from representative testing raises concerns for turbines that routinely operate in cycling service — energy providers ask EPA to allow representative cycles to be defined for cycling units, including defined startup/shutdown segments when those are typical operation.

[P16] The absolute prohibition on testing during malfunctions (P16) lacks a definition of "malfunction" and could incentivize operators to claim malfunction to avoid unfavorable tests; legal commenters request a precise definition consistent with case law and prior EPA guidance and limits on use of malfunction claims.

[P17] §63.6120(c) (P17) requires recording process information and justification that test conditions represent normal operation; testing firms request a standardized template of required data elements and examples of acceptable justifications to ensure consistency.

[P18] §63.6120(c) (P18) requiring producers to provide records upon Administrator request needs a specified timeframe for production and protections for CBI — industry requests EPA to set a minimum response time (e.g., 30 days) and CBI handling procedures.

[P19] §63.6125(e) (P19) requires CMS quality control program with written procedures; smaller facilities will argue that the prescribed §63.8(d)(1)-(2) procedures are overly prescriptive and ask for scaled requirements based on CMS complexity and cost.

[P20] §63.6125(e) record retention (P20) mandating retention "for the life of the source" is unduly burdensome and legally uncertain; regulated entities request that retention be limited to a practicable period (e.g., 10 years) or until the source ceases to be subject to the subpart, and request guidance on handling facility ownership changes.

[P21] §63.6125(e) (P21) requiring keeping previous versions of a performance evaluation plan for 5 years after revision is reasonable, but commenters request clarity whether digital timestamps and version control systems satisfy the requirement.

[P22] §63.6125(e) recommendation (P22) that corrective action program "should" be included is vague — compliance officers request that EPA either make the corrective action program a mandatory element or provide a model corrective action plan template to reduce variability.

[P23] §63.6140(c) (P23) saying SSM deviations are not violations if operated per §63.6(e)(1)(i) prior to the specified date is helpful, but legal advocates will request that EPA make this SSM protection permanent and explicit beyond the pre-specified-date window to avoid a cliff.

[P24] §63.6150(a) (P24) requiring semiannual compliance reports for formaldehyde-limited turbines imposes a heavy administrative burden; smaller operators request allowance for annual reporting if no deviations occur or reduced reporting frequency for low-risk sources.

[P25] §63.6150(a) content requirement (P25) referencing paragraphs (a)(1)-(a)(5) is broadly stated; commenters request EPA to list the exact data fields and acceptable units/formats to facilitate automated reporting and reduce rejected submissions.

[P26] §63.6150(a) scheduling (P26) requires report submission by specified dates but allows Administrator-approved alternatives; states and permitting authorities request a process and timeline for obtaining such approvals to ensure coordination with state reporting cycles.

[P27] §63.6150(a) (P27) mandating that after the specified date all subsequent reports be submitted to EPA per paragraph (g) could conflict with state electronic reporting systems—state agencies request cross-acceptance or an option to submit jointly to EPA and state systems to avoid duplicate submissions.

[P28] §63.6150(a)(4) (P28) requiring specifics on each deviation prior to the specified date could force public disclosure of sensitive operational details; companies will request confidentiality protections and clear guidance on what qualifies as a deviation requiring reporting.

[P29] §63.6150(a)(5) (P29) the after-date requirement to report failures to meet standards in semiannual reports is duplicative of immediate notification obligations in other rules; commenters ask EPA to harmonize timing (immediate vs semiannual) and to allow semiannual aggregation unless the failure poses imminent public health risk.

[P30] §63.6150(a)(5)(i) (P30) requires reporting start date/time, duration, cause, and corrective action for each failure — companies note that root-cause analysis can take months; request provision to provide preliminary cause and corrective action and then submit a finalized root-cause report within a specified follow-up period (e.g., 90 days).

[P31] §63.6150(a)(5)(ii) (P31) requires estimated pollutant quantity over the limit and method used; sources request clear acceptable estimation methodologies and default emission factors to ensure consistency and defendability.

[P32] §63.6150(a)(5)(iii) (P32) requires monitor downtime reporting including unknown causes — CMS vendors request standardized definitions for downtime, repair initiation time, and whether short-term interruptions (e.g., <5 minutes) count as monitor downtime incidents.

[P33] §63.6150(a)(5)(iv) (P33) requiring total operating time reporting could be burdensome if reporting periods do not align with existing log systems — operators request allowance to use plant operating logs or SCADA exports and specify acceptable rounding conventions.

[P34] §63.6150(c) (P34) obligating annual reporting when landfill or digester gas equals or exceeds 10% gross heat input requires fuel tracking that many operators do not currently perform — affected parties request guidance on acceptable fuel sampling or mass-balance methods and allowance for quarterly instead of continuous tracking.

[P35] §63.6150(e) (P35) requiring reporting if distillate oil is used at the same major source imposes an administrative burden even when distillate use is incidental; request a threshold (e.g., >1% heat input) or de minimis exemption and clarity on how use is aggregated across multiple units at a site.

[P36] §63.6150(f) (P36) requiring submission of test results within 60 days after testing is short for third-party lab validation and CBI reviews; testing labs request a 90-day window or allowance for documented delays.

[P37] §63.6150(f)(1) (P37) mandating ERT-supported data formats could disproportionately impact tests using older methods or third-party labs not ERT-capable — request transitional compliance assistance, an EPA-provided conversion tool, or acceptance of current formats until labs upgrade.

[P38] §63.6150(f)(2) (P38) requiring attachment of non-ERT test results in ERT or alternate XML format and submission via CEDRI could force duplication; commenters request acceptance of PDF attachments for complex data files and a published schema example for XML.

[P39] §63.6150(f)(3) (P39) CBI filing procedure requiring a physical medium to the EPA CBI Office plus an electronic CBI-omitted file is burdensome and poses security risks — industry requests a secure electronic portal for encrypted CBI submissions certified to meet federal standards in lieu of physical media.

[P40] §63.6150(g) (P40) mandating use of CEDRI and meeting deadlines regardless of submission method may penalize parties whose internet connectivity failed; commenters request EPA adopt receipt-stamp rules (timestamp acceptance) and a backup electronic transfer protocol (e.g., secure FTP) accepted by EPA.

[P41] §63.6150(g) CBI (P41) duplicative physical/electronic submission requirement for CBI is unnecessary — legal commenters request EPA accept encrypted electronic submissions with certificates of CBI claims and rescind the physical media requirement.

[P42] §63.6150(h) (P42) allowing EPA system outage claims is useful but contested because burden is on the submitter to prove outage; stakeholders request that EPA publish outage logs and accept vendor/ISP outage records as supporting documentation.

[P43] §63.6150(h)(1) (P43) that the submitter must be "precluded" from access to CEDRI/CDX is vague — request definition of "precluded" (e.g., inability to connect, authentication failures) and whether localized outages (company network) qualify.

[P44] §63.6150(h)(2) (P44) limiting outage eligibility to outages within five business days before due date is too narrow if outages begin earlier or are intermittent; commenters ask for a longer window (e.g., 10 business days) or case-by-case flexibility.

[P45] §63.6150(h)(3) (P45) allowing planned outages to qualify for an outage claim could be abused — EPA should require that planned outages be communicated in advance and that the submitter demonstrate reasonable inability to use alternative submission methods.

[P46] §63.6150(h)(4) (P46) requiring prompt notification to Administrator when you know or should have known presumes regulated entities have constant monitoring of EPA systems; request clear timelines (e.g., within 2 business days) and an email/portal address for notifications.

[P47] §63.6150(h)(5) (P47) asking for detailed outage descriptions including access timestamps may require logging capability not available to small firms; EPA should accept attestation plus any available logs and not require exhaustive access logs.

[P48] §63.6150(h)(6) (P48) giving sole discretion to the Administrator to accept outage claims is too broad; commenters request an appeal or dispute process and publishable criteria EPA will use to evaluate outage claims.

[P49] §63.6150(h)(7) (P49) requiring submission "as soon as possible" after outage lacks a specific deadline; request a safe-harbor period (e.g., within 5 business days after outage resolution) to avoid ambiguous enforcement.

[P50] §63.6150(i) (P50) allowing force majeure claims for electronic reporting failures is appropriate, but the rule should define evidentiary standards and allow third-party certifications (e.g., from ISPs, emergency services) to support claims.

[P51] §63.6150(i)(1) (P51) restricting force majeure claims to events within five business days before due date is too constraining for events with lingering effects; stakeholders request that the window cover events occurring earlier if effects persist to the due date.

[P52] §63.6150(i)(2) (P52) requiring "prompt" notification for force majeure events needs a specified timeframe (e.g., within 2 business days of when submitter knew) and a designated email/contact to avoid uncertainty.

[P53] §63.6150(i)(3) (P53) requiring a written description and rationale for force majeure attribution may be burdensome for sudden disasters; request acceptance of initial short notification followed by fuller documentation within a reasonable period (e.g., 30 days).

[P54] §63.6150(i)(4) (P54) giving sole discretion to the Administrator to accept force majeure claims again raises fairness concerns; request publication of objective criteria and an appeal mechanism.

[P55] §63.6150(i)(5) (P55) obligation to report "as soon as possible" after force majeure overlaps with the "prompt notification" requirements — request EPA define timelines for final report submission (e.g., within 10 business days after event resolution).

[P56] §63.6155(a) (P56) record maintenance obligations are extensive; small entities request scaled recordkeeping requirements, safe-harbors for e-record formatting, and acceptance of automated system exports as compliant records.

[P57] §63.6155(a)(3) (P57) requiring records of SSM occurrences and durations prior to the specified date may conflict with previous guidance that limited SSM records — request harmonization with §63.6 and clarity on granularity (e.g., to the minute vs hour).

[P58] §63.6155(a)(4) (P58) requiring records of air pollution control equipment malfunctions prior to the specified date could penalize facilities for transient control device alarms; request a threshold for what constitutes a recordable malfunction (e.g., >30 minutes or causes exceedance).

[P59] §63.6155(a)(5) (P59) requiring records of all maintenance on air pollution control equipment is reasonable but resource-intensive; recommend EPA allow maintenance summaries and key maintenance logs rather than exhaustive parts-level documentation.

[P60] §63.6155(a)(6) (P60) after-date requirement to record startup date/time/duration and when source was subject to startup standard may be infeasible for units with frequent cycling; request allowance to record cumulative startup time per reporting period rather than each discrete startup event if start count is extremely high.

[P61] §63.6155(a)(7)(i) (P61) requiring recording of failure counts and for each failure date/time/cause/duration is onerous if there are many short transient exceedances; request aggregation rules for multiple very short failures (e.g., <5 minutes) or thresholds for reporting individual events.

[P62] §63.6155(a)(7)(ii) (P62) requiring estimates of quantities emitted over limits and methods used for each failure is technically challenging; request EPA publish default emission estimation protocols and allow use of emission factors and mass-balance methods.

[P63] §63.6155(a)(7)(iii) (P63) requiring record of actions taken to minimize emissions per §63.6105(c) and corrective actions to return to normal operation duplicates semiannual reporting; request acceptance of cross-referenced corrective action logs and permit-level CAPs as fulfilling this requirement.

[P64] §63.6155(d) (P64) permitting electronic maintenance of CEDRI-submitted records is helpful; commenters request EPA confirm acceptable file formats (PDF/A, CSV, XML) and maximum allowable file sizes and retention/back-up expectations.

[P65] §63.6155(d) (P65) despite permitting electronic records, requiring availability during on-site audits without specifying lead time is burdensome — request EPA require inspectors to provide reasonable notice (e.g., 24–48 hours) to permit retrieval of archived electronic records.

[P66] Table 1 formaldehyde limit (P66) of ≤91 ppbvd at 15% O2 is very stringent; industry requests EPA provide technical justification for the level, modeling of achievable compliance using current control technologies, and consideration of feasibility for existing turbines.

[P67] Table 1 startup allowance (P67) that limits idle/low-load and caps startup duration at 1 hour (simple) or 3 hours (combined) is unachievable for some turbines that require longer safe warm-up periods; turbine manufacturers and operators request extension of these caps or allowance for documented engineering-based longer startup periods.

[P68] Table 3 (P68) requiring initial and annual formaldehyde testing is costly and may duplicate credible continuous monitoring options; commenters request EPA accept validated CMS for formaldehyde (if available) in lieu of annual stack tests or allow biennial testing with CMS.

[P69] Table 3 test methods (P69) listing Test Method 320 or ASTM D6348–12e1 with Annex criteria may not be practical for some facilities; testing laboratories request EPA to include alternative validated methods and to update ASTM references to current versions.

[P70] Table 3 correction to 15% O2 dry basis (P70) is standard but operators whose combustor designs result in unusual oxygen levels request guidance on sampling and correction calculation when O2 deviates significantly from typical ranges.

[P71] Table 3 averaging (P71) requiring average of three one-hour runs could be problematic for turbines that cannot sustain steady operation for three hours due to dispatch; request allowance for three shorter runs (e.g., three 30-minute runs) or alternative statistical approaches endorsed by EPA.

[P72] Table 3 load window (P72) requiring testing within ±10% of 100% load conflicts with combined-cycle units operating at lower loads; request EPA permit testing at a defined "normal operating" load (e.g., the 90th percentile historical load) and provide a method to normalize results to the standard.

[P73] Table 3(b) port/traverse selection (P73) requiring Method 1/1A and sampling at control device outlet when used could be infeasible when stack geometry or access is limited; request EPA to accept engineered alternatives or to allow representative upstream sampling with correction factors if outlet access is unsafe.

[P74] Table 3(c) O2 measurement (P74) requiring Method 3A/3B or ANSI/ASME methods concurrently with testing may be challenging for some labs; request EPA to accept well-documented parametric O2 monitoring data correlated to Method 3A/3B as an alternative.

[P75] Table 3(d) moisture measurement (P75) required to correct to dry basis needs clearer guidance on acceptable moisture measurement frequency and methods for highly variable moisture content fuels (e.g., landfill gas) — request acceptance of continuous moisture monitoring or composite sampling approaches.

§63.6150(a)(5)(i) (P30) requires reporting start date/time, duration, cause, and corrective action for each failure — companies note that root-cause analysis can take months; request provision to provide preliminary cause and corrective action and then submit a finalized root-cause report within a specified follow-up period (e.g., 90 days).

§63.6150(a)(5)(ii) (P31) requires estimated pollutant quantity over the limit and method used; sources request clear acceptable estimation methodologies and default emission factors to ensure consistency and defendability.

§63.6150(a)(5)(iii) (P32) requires monitor downtime reporting including unknown causes — CMS vendors request standardized definitions for downtime, repair initiation time, and whether short-term interruptions (e.g., <5 minutes) count as monitor downtime incidents.

§63.6150(a)(5)(iv) (P33) requiring total operating time reporting could be burdensome if reporting periods do not align with existing log systems — operators request allowance to use plant operating logs or SCADA exports and specify acceptable rounding conventions.

§63.6150(c) (P34) obligating annual reporting when landfill or digester gas equals or exceeds 10% gross heat input requires fuel tracking that many operators do not currently perform — affected parties request guidance on acceptable fuel sampling or mass-balance methods and allowance for quarterly instead of continuous tracking.

§63.6150(e) (P35) requiring reporting if distillate oil is used at the same major source imposes an administrative burden even when distillate use is incidental; request a threshold (e.g., >1% heat input) or de minimis exemption and clarity on how use is aggregated across multiple units at a site.

§63.6150(f) (P36) requiring submission of test results within 60 days after testing is short for third-party lab validation and CBI reviews; testing labs request a 90-day window or allowance for documented delays.

§63.6150(f)(1) (P37) mandating ERT-supported data formats could disproportionately impact tests using older methods or third-party labs not ERT-capable — request transitional compliance assistance, an EPA-provided conversion tool, or acceptance of current formats until labs upgrade.

§63.6150(f)(2) (P38) requiring attachment of non-ERT test results in ERT or alternate XML format and submission via CEDRI could force duplication; commenters request acceptance of PDF attachments for complex data files and a published schema example for XML.

§63.6150(f)(3) (P39) CBI filing procedure requiring a physical medium to the EPA CBI Office plus an electronic CBI-omitted file is burdensome and poses security risks — industry requests a secure electronic portal for encrypted CBI submissions certified to meet federal standards in lieu of physical media.

§63.6150(g) (P40) mandating use of CEDRI and meeting deadlines regardless of submission method may penalize parties whose internet connectivity failed; commenters request EPA adopt receipt-stamp rules (timestamp acceptance) and a backup electronic transfer protocol (e.g., secure FTP) accepted by EPA.

§63.6150(g) CBI (P41) duplicative physical/electronic submission requirement for CBI is unnecessary — legal commenters request EPA accept encrypted electronic submissions with certificates of CBI claims and rescind the physical media requirement.

§63.6150(h) (P42) allowing EPA system outage claims is useful but contested because burden is on the submitter to prove outage; stakeholders request that EPA publish outage logs and accept vendor/ISP outage records as supporting documentation.

§63.6150(h)(1) (P43) that the submitter must be "precluded" from access to CEDRI/CDX is vague — request definition of "precluded" (e.g., inability to connect, authentication failures) and whether localized outages (company network) qualify.

§63.6150(h)(2) (P44) limiting outage eligibility to outages within five business days before due date is too narrow if outages begin earlier or are intermittent; commenters ask for a longer window (e.g., 10 business days) or case-by-case flexibility.

§63.6150(h)(3) (P45) allowing planned outages to qualify for an outage claim could be abused — EPA should require that planned outages be communicated in advance and that the submitter demonstrate reasonable inability to use alternative submission methods.

§63.6150(h)(4) (P46) requiring prompt notification to Administrator when you know or should have known presumes regulated entities have constant monitoring of EPA systems; request clear timelines (e.g., within 2 business days) and an email/portal address for notifications.

§63.6150(h)(5) (P47) asking for detailed outage descriptions including access timestamps may require logging capability not available to small firms; EPA should accept attestation plus any available logs and not require exhaustive access logs.

§63.6150(h)(6) (P48) giving sole discretion to the Administrator to accept outage claims is too broad; commenters request an appeal or dispute process and publishable criteria EPA will use to evaluate outage claims.

§63.6150(h)(7) (P49) requiring submission "as soon as possible" after outage lacks a specific deadline; request a safe-harbor period (e.g., within 5 business days after outage resolution) to avoid ambiguous enforcement.

§63.6150(i) (P50) allowing force majeure claims for electronic reporting failures is appropriate, but the rule should define evidentiary standards and allow third-party certifications (e.g., from ISPs, emergency services) to support claims.

§63.6150(i)(1) (P51) restricting force majeure claims to events within five business days before due date is too constraining for events with lingering effects; stakeholders request that the window cover events occurring earlier if effects persist to the due date.

§63.6150(i)(2) (P52) requiring "prompt" notification for force majeure events needs a specified timeframe (e.g., within 2 business days of when submitter knew) and a designated email/contact to avoid uncertainty.

§63.6150(i)(3) (P53) requiring a written description and rationale for force majeure attribution may be burdensome for sudden disasters; request acceptance of initial short notification followed by fuller documentation within a reasonable period (e.g., 30 days).
§63.6150(i)(4) (P54) giving sole discretion to the Administrator to accept force majeure claims again raises fairness concerns; request publication of objective criteria and an appeal mechanism.

§63.6150(i)(5) (P55) obligation to report "as soon as possible" after force majeure overlaps with the "prompt notification" requirements — request EPA define timelines for final report submission (e.g., within 10 business days after event resolution).

§63.6155(a) (P56) record maintenance obligations are extensive; small entities request scaled recordkeeping requirements, safe-harbors for e-record formatting, and acceptance of automated system exports as compliant records.

§63.6155(a)(3) (P57) requiring records of SSM occurrences and durations prior to the specified date may conflict with previous guidance that limited SSM records — request harmonization with §63.6 and clarity on granularity (e.g., to the minute vs hour).

§63.6155(a)(4) (P58) requiring records of air pollution control equipment malfunctions prior to the specified date could penalize facilities for transient control device alarms; request a threshold for what constitutes a recordable malfunction (e.g., >30 minutes or causes exceedance).

§63.6155(a)(5) (P59) requiring records of all maintenance on air pollution control equipment is reasonable but resource-intensive; recommend EPA allow maintenance summaries and key maintenance logs rather than exhaustive parts-level documentation.

§63.6155(a)(6) (P60) after-date requirement to record startup date/time/duration and when source was subject to startup standard may be infeasible for units with frequent cycling; request allowance to record cumulative startup time per reporting period rather than each discrete startup event if start count is extremely high.

§63.6155(a)(7)(i) (P61) requiring recording of failure counts and for each failure date/time/cause/duration is onerous if there are many short transient exceedances; request aggregation rules for multiple very short failures (e.g., <5 minutes) or thresholds for reporting individual events.

§63.6155(a)(7)(ii) (P62) requiring estimates of quantities emitted over limits and methods used for each failure is technically challenging; request EPA publish default emission estimation protocols and allow use of emission factors and mass-balance methods.

§63.6155(a)(7)(iii) (P63) requiring record of actions taken to minimize emissions per §63.6105(c) and corrective actions to return to normal operation duplicates semiannual reporting; request acceptance of cross-referenced corrective action logs and permit-level CAPs as fulfilling this requirement.

§63.6155(d) (P64) permitting electronic maintenance of CEDRI-submitted records is helpful; commenters request EPA confirm acceptable file formats (PDF/A, CSV, XML) and maximum allowable file sizes and retention/back-up expectations.

§63.6155(d) (P65) despite permitting electronic records, requiring availability during on-site audits without specifying lead time is burdensome — request EPA require inspectors to provide reasonable notice (e.g., 24–48 hours) to permit retrieval of archived electronic records.

Table 1 formaldehyde limit (P66) of ≤91 ppbvd at 15% O2 is very stringent; industry requests EPA provide technical justification for the level, modeling of achievable compliance using current control technologies, and consideration of feasibility for existing turbines.

Table 1 startup allowance (P67) that limits idle/low-load and caps startup duration at 1 hour (simple) or 3 hours (combined) is unachievable for some turbines that require longer safe warm-up periods; turbine manufacturers and operators request extension of these caps or allowance for documented engineering-based longer startup periods.

Table 3 (P68) requiring initial and annual formaldehyde testing is costly and may duplicate credible continuous monitoring options; commenters request EPA accept validated CMS for formaldehyde (if available) in lieu of annual stack tests or allow biennial testing with CMS.

Table 3 test methods (P69) listing Test Method 320 or ASTM D6348–12e1 with Annex criteria may not be practical for some facilities; testing laboratories request EPA to include alternative validated methods and to update ASTM references to current versions.

Table 3 correction to 15% O2 dry basis (P70) is standard but operators whose combustor designs result in unusual oxygen levels request guidance on sampling and correction calculation when O2 deviates significantly from typical ranges.

Table 3 averaging (P71) requiring average of three one-hour runs could be problematic for turbines that cannot sustain steady operation for three hours due to dispatch; request allowance for three shorter runs (e.g., three 30-minute runs) or alternative statistical approaches endorsed by EPA.

Table 3 load window (P72) requiring testing within ±10% of 100% load conflicts with combined-cycle units operating at lower loads; request EPA permit testing at a defined "normal operating" load (e.g., the 90th percentile historical load) and provide a method to normalize results to the standard.

Table 3(b) port/traverse selection (P73) requiring Method 1/1A and sampling at control device outlet when used could be infeasible when stack geometry or access is limited; request EPA to accept engineered alternatives or to allow representative upstream sampling with correction factors if outlet access is unsafe.

Table 3(c) O2 measurement (P74) requiring Method 3A/3B or ANSI/ASME methods concurrently with testing may be challenging for some labs; request EPA to accept well-documented parametric O2 monitoring data correlated to Method 3A/3B as an alternative.

Table 3(d) moisture measurement (P75) required to correct to dry basis needs clearer guidance on acceptable moisture measurement frequency and methods for highly variable moisture content fuels (e.g., landfill gas) — request acceptance of continuous moisture monitoring or composite sampling approaches.

[P1] The July 18, 2022 comment deadline is unreasonable and too short for international stakeholders and small operators to analyze technical data and prepare meaningful comments; extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] The AD does not provide sufficient notice of the effective date relative to the July 18, 2022 comment deadline; clarify when the AD becomes effective and ensure stakeholders have the full comment period before effectiveness.

[P2] The blanket statement to “comply within the specified compliance times” lacks clarity about which specific actions have what deadlines; require the AD to list explicit calendar dates or intervals for each required action rather than relying on cross-references.

[P3] The 90-day compliance time to revise the ALS and maintenance programs for all affected GEnx–1B engines is unduly burdensome for large fleets and MROs that must coordinate system updates, and should be extended to 180 days.

[P3] There is no transitional relief or phased compliance for operators with substantial numbers of affected engines; the AD should allow staged implementation tied to scheduled maintenance windows.

[P4] Table 1 life limits for spool P/N 2628M56G01 (stages 6–10 compressor rotor spool) appear to be lower than previously published service bulletin limits but no technical justification is provided in the AD; include the analysis and data supporting the reduced limits.

[P4] The AD does not state whether previously accumulated life on spool P/N 2628M56G01 will be grandfathered or how to recalculate life after modification; provide clear instructions for crediting time-in-service and shop visits.

[P5] Table 2 life limits for CDP seal P/N 2383M82P03 conflict with existing OEM maintenance instructions; reconcile any discrepancies and explicitly state precedence if the AD overrides manufacturer manuals.

[P5] There is no guidance for operators on how to handle seals removed for other reasons (e.g., repairs) with part P/N 2383M82P03 — clarify reinstallation limits and marking/traceability requirements.

[P6] Table 3 life limits for interstage seal P/N 2383M85P04 do not address life extension after approved repairs or overhaul; the AD should specify whether repair procedures can restore life or require part replacement.

[P6] The requirement to “insert the information in Table 3” into ALS lacks guidance on the exact ALS formatting and approved revision control process; provide a template and acceptable compliance documentation.

[P7] Table 4 life limits for HPT rotor stage 2 disk P/N 2383M86P02 could force premature retirements of scarce parts and disrupt spare pools; the FAA should allow temporary redistribution of life-limited part inventories until replenishment.

[P7] The AD fails to address how to handle disks that have accumulated cycles close to the new limit — require a mandatory inspection or risk assessment option before forced retirement.

[P8] The 90-day deadline for GEnx–2B ALS revisions burdens international operators with differing regulatory approval processes; extend compliance time or coordinate with foreign CAAs to avoid conflicting requirements.

[P9] Table 5 life limits for spool P/N 2628M56G01 on GEnx–2B models differ from GEnx–1B tables without explanation; provide engineering rationale for model-specific differences.

[P9] The AD does not clarify whether spools removed from GEnx–1B engines and installed on GEnx–2B engines (or vice versa) retain their life limits; include cross-model installation guidance.

[P10] Table 6 for CDP seal P/N 2383M82P03 lacks an inspection interval for early detection of wear; require an interim inspection task until parts are replaced at the new life limit.

[P10] Operators have concerns about supply chain capacity for replacement CDP seals P/N 2383M82P03; the FAA should coordinate with the manufacturer on parts availability and allow temporary extensions if parts are unavailable.

[P11] Table 7 life limits for interstage seal P/N 2383M85P04 should permit approved alternative inspection methods (e.g., borescope) to verify continued airworthiness instead of mandatory part retirement; request that the AD explicitly permit such AMOCs.

[P11] The AD is silent on recordkeeping requirements for these interstage seals — require explicit documentation standards (e.g., logbook entries, part-tagging) to ensure compliance audits are feasible.

[P12] Table 8 life limits for HPT rotor stage 2 disk P/N 2383M86P02 may conflict with life limits imposed by other ADs or manufacturer service documents — clarify regulatory hierarchy and how operators should resolve conflicts.

[P12] The AD should include an economic impact analysis of forced disk retirements (P/N 2383M86P02), including cost to airlines and effect on maintenance schedules and flight availability.

[P13] The prohibition on approving any alternative life limits after ALS revision effectively eliminates industry flexibility and could be arbitrary; restrict the prohibition only until the FAA has evaluated submitted AMOCs rather than a blanket ban.

[P13] The prohibition could conflict with internationally accepted maintenance program variances accepted by other civil aviation authorities; require coordination or recognition of equivalent foreign approvals.

[P14] Granting the Manager sole authority to approve AMOCs concentrates decision-making and may delay approvals; allow delegated or expedited AMOC review for routine, previously accepted methods.

[P14] The AD should specify objective criteria the Manager will use to evaluate AMOC requests to ensure predictability and fairness across applicants.

[P15] The requirement to route AMOC requests through a principal inspector or local FSDO will create bottlenecks and delays; permit direct submissions to the Manager in all cases with a requirement to copy the principal inspector.

[P15] The email address ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov may not be monitored for attachments over a certain size or sensitive proprietary information; provide secure submission options and acceptable formats for technical data.

[P16] Requiring notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC is vague about timing — specify whether notification must occur before the first use, within a set number of days, and what constitutes sufficient notice.

[P16] For operators without a principal inspector and where the local FSDO/CHDO manager is not readily available, the AD should allow notification through a centralized FAA portal to avoid operational delays.

[P2] There is no provision for temporary relief or ferry flights for aircraft that exceed revised life limits between scheduled maintenance; include emergency/operational exceptions with strict conditions.

[P3] The AD provides no coordination or harmonization language with EASA or other CAAs; request harmonization to prevent divergent requirements for multinational operators.

[P4] Legal counsel notes the AD does not state whether failure to revise ALS within 90 days is an independent violation or only a noncompliance if parts exceed limits; clarify legal consequences and enforcement policies.

[P5] Maintenance organizations request model ALS templates and example table insertions (for Tables 1–8) to ensure consistency across operators; the FAA should publish templates as part of the AD.

[P7] Request that the FAA allow credit for prior life reductions applied under earlier service bulletins, with a clear method to reconcile accumulated cycles/hours against new limits.

[P13] Clarify the scope of paragraph (h) exceptions referenced in the prohibition — commenters need to know what types of alternative life limit approvals are preserved, and under what conditions.

[P14] Request that AMOC decisions be published (redacted if necessary) in a timely public docket to provide precedent and technical guidance to other operators preparing similar requests.

[P1] Industry commenters will request clarification of what qualifies as an "official agency" for providing out-of-area service under the exception (e.g., state vs. local agencies, third‑party inspectors) to avoid disputes about who may actually perform services.

[P1] Trade associations will argue the rule should allow adjacent agencies to provide service on an ongoing basis when mutually agreed, not only under limited exceptions, to reduce operational disruptions for multi-state shippers.

[P2] Several commenters will request that the rule specify a required Service processing timeline (e.g., 48 hours) for exception requests, arguing that an undefined review period creates uncertainty and supply-chain delays.

[P3] Food-safety advocacy groups will ask the Service to publish clear examples and objective metrics for each enumerated instance (timely inability, nonuse, probe‑on‑barge, written waiver) to prevent arbitrary or inconsistent grants of exceptions.

[P6] Maritime operators and barge owners will request technical guidance on what constitutes a "probe inspection on a barge‑lot basis" (P6), including sampling plans, lot definitions, and chain‑of‑custody requirements.

[P7] Assigned and adjacent agencies will request a model written agreement template for the waiver process (P7) to standardize waivers and avoid legal disputes between agencies.

[P8] Applicants will ask the Service to clarify whether granting an exception for a single instance of untimely service (P8) automatically authorizes the gaining agency to issue official certificates, or whether additional approvals are needed per shipment.

[P9] Industry commenters will challenge the 6‑hour standard (P9) as unrealistic in many rural or maritime contexts and request extension to 8–12 hours, or an alternative standard based on travel distance or scheduled appointment windows.

[P9] Legal experts will request clarification whether the alternative "unable to provide results and certificate per §800.160(c)" standard requires physical issuance on premises or can be satisfied by electronic transmission.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement in § 91.1023(f) to ensure “appropriate parts” of the program manual are accessible to flight, ground, and maintenance personnel at all times is vague; commenters request a definition of “appropriate parts” (e.g., checklists, MELs, abnormal/emergency procedures) to avoid inconsistent implementation.

[P1] The obligation in § 91.1023(f) to make parts of the manual “accessible at all times while performing assigned duties” is ambiguous as applied to off-site or remote workers (e.g., remote dispatchers, contract maintenance at third‑party facilities); the rule should clarify whether remote electronic access meets the obligation.

[P1] Industry stakeholders will report that guaranteeing access “at all times” may be infeasible during system outages or situations with degraded connectivity; the rule should allow a contingency plan (e.g., cached/printed copies, backup devices) and permit temporary deviations when documented.

[P2] The § 91.1023(g) requirement that manual information be “displayed clearly and retrievable in English” lacks objective clarity about acceptable languages for personnel who are not native English speakers; unions and diversity advocates will request that the agency permit supplemental translations while preserving English as the authoritative text.

[P2] Small operators will comment that the retrievability requirement in § 91.1023(g) imposes burdens on legacy electronic systems and paper binders; they request an implementation timeline and acceptability criteria for “retrievable” (e.g., searchable PDFs, indexed binders).

[P3] The § 91.1025 obligation to display the date of last revision on each page of paper manuals is burdensome for large multi-volume manuals and may lead to frequent reprinting; commenters will ask for alternatives such as a revision control cover sheet with page-level versioning or use of revision bars instead of reprinting every page.

[P4] Requiring that electronic manuals display the date of last revision “in a way a person can immediately ascertain” under § 91.1025 is subjective; IT departments and legal counsel will request specific display requirements (e.g., top-right corner timestamp, persistent header/footer, ISO 8601 format) to avoid disputes about compliance.

[P5] The catch-all in § 91.1025 that the manual must include listed contents “unless the Administrator authorizes otherwise” is procedurally opaque; operators will ask for a formal waiver process with clear criteria and predictable timelines for authorization requests.

[P6] § 121.135(a) which mandates that each manual contain enumerated items should provide an Appendix cross-reference or template; major carriers will request explicit enumerations to ensure consistency across certificate holders and simplify audits.

[P7] The duplication of page-date requirements in § 121.135(a)(3) (paper) and electronic timing is redundant with other sections; commenters will request consolidation to reduce regulatory duplication and potential conflicts among compliance checks.

[P7] Air carriers will state that requiring date of last revision on each paper page in § 121.135(a)(3) will create a significant cost for carriers with high-frequency, iterative revisions (e.g., ops specifications, performance tables) and request allowance for stamped “controlled copy” processes or revision logs acceptable to inspectors.

[P8] § 121.139’s requirement that appropriate manual parts be accessible to flight, ground, and maintenance personnel “at all times while performing assigned duties” needs to explicitly include contract third‑party providers (e.g., ground handling, third‑party MROs) or specify transfer-of-knowledge obligations so certificate holders remain responsible.

[P9] The § 121.139 English-language retrievability requirement may conflict with international operations where manuals must be in other ICAO languages; international airlines will ask for an exception for required foreign-language supplements while keeping English as the master document.

[P10] § 125.71(f) mandating that manual info be “displayed clearly and retrievable in English” is unclear as to whether metadata, attachments, or linked external documents must also be in English; commenters will request clarification that only the core manual content must be English-retrievable, and linked third-party documents may remain in their original language if guidance is provided.

[P11] The § 125.73 requirement to display the date of last revision on each paper page is impractical for operators using standardized manufacturer manuals and AMM pages; commenters will request allowance to rely on manufacturer revision control or reference the manufacturer’s revision date instead of reformatting.

[P12] For § 125.73 electronic revision display, commenters in operations and IT will request standards for “immediately ascertainable” (e.g., persistent UI element, non-obscured by login) and note security concerns where displaying revision metadata could leak sensitive configuration info — ask for guidance balancing usability with security.

[P13] The content requirements in § 125.73 for manuals should be explicitly listed or cross-referenced in the NPRM; maintenance organizations and legal counsel will request the exact list to evaluate compliance costs and ensure no duplication/conflict with existing part 145 requirements.

[P14] § 135.21(f) accessibility obligations for flight, ground, and maintenance personnel should clarify applicability to single-pilot operations and fractional operators — commenters representing on‑demand operators will request scaled requirements for small operators.

[P15] The § 135.21(g) English retrievability mandate may create undue burdens on international charter operations; commenters will ask for an exception for materials that are adequately provided in the operator’s standard working language if English versions are available upon request.

[P16] The § 135.23 requirement that paper-format manuals display the date of last revision on each page will increase printing and distribution costs for commuter operators with frequent schedule/resume changes; these operators will request acceptance of a stamped “revision date” on a control page with page-level revision markings in lieu of full reprinting.

[P17] The electronic date-of-revision display requirement in § 135.23 is likely to conflict with common EFB and PDF viewers that suppress headers/footers on some displays; EFB vendors and operators will ask for technical specifications and a grace period to update platforms.

[P18] § 135.23’s mandated manual contents should allow incorporation by reference to existing regulatory-approved documents (e.g., FAA-approved training curricula, manufacturer procedures) to avoid duplication; commenters (operators, certificated trainers) will request explicit permission to incorporate by reference.

[P1] Legal commenters will argue that many of the accessibility and language requirements impose substantive operational changes that may conflict with collective bargaining agreements; they request consultation requirements before enforcement as to working conditions.

[P3] Safety advocates will support the page-level revision date requirement in paper manuals (§ 91.1025) as important for ensuring crew use of current procedures, but request enforcement provisions for instances where outdated pages are found in flight.

[P4] IT security experts will caution that requiring visible revision metadata in electronic manuals (§§ 91.1025,121.135,125.73,135.23) may create tamper-evidence needs; they will request guidance on cryptographic integrity, audit logs, and acceptable means to demonstrate authenticity beyond a visible date.

[P5] Small business representatives will request an economic impact analysis and a phased compliance schedule for all new manual content and display requirements (P5, P6, P13, P18), arguing that immediate compliance would impose disproportionate costs.

[P7] Aviation training organizations will request clarification whether training syllabi and records must be included in the manuals under the “required contents” sections (P5, P6, P13, P18), and if so, what confidentiality protections apply to personnel records.

[P8] International operators will ask that the rule explicitly permit the use of bilingual manuals where English is the primary retrievable language, to accommodate non-English-speaking flight crews while satisfying the “retrievable in English” requirement (P2, P9, P10, P15).

[P9] Human factors experts will request that “displayed clearly” (P2, P9, P10, P15) be defined with measurable typography and UI standards (font size, contrast, navigation steps) to ensure compliance is assessable and improves safety rather than just adding paperwork.

[P11] Compliance officers will ask whether historical revisions must remain accessible to demonstrate compliance or incident investigation needs, and whether the “date of last revision” display must show history or only the current revision (P3, P4, P7, P11, P12, P16, P17).

[P12] Commenters will request that the rule allow for localized deviation approvals where operational environments (e.g., austere airfields, international remote bases) make continuous access to electronic manuals unrealistic, and require the Administrator to provide written approvals rather than informal waivers (applies to P1, P8, P14).

[P13] Legal scholars will note potential preemption or conflict with existing FAA guidance and ACs on manual control and formatting; they request the agency harmonize this rule with existing Advisory Circulars and Order 8900.1 references to avoid contradictory inspector guidance (applies broadly across P1–P18).

[P14] Maintenance organizations will request explicit inclusion of standard maintenance documentation (work cards, inspection checklists, service bulletins) as “appropriate parts” that must be accessible under the maintenance accessibility provisions (P1, P8, P14).

[P15] Labor unions will insist that the rule require employers to provide equipment (e.g., EFBs, internet access, printed copies) at no cost to employees to meet the “accessible at all times” mandates (P1, P8, P14).

[P16] Consumer safety advocates will ask the FAA to require an audit trail or timestamped acknowledgement when personnel access updated manual sections to ensure personnel actually review critical revisions (applies to electronic display requirements in P4, P7, P12, P17).

[P17] Operators will request the FAA confirm that standard company procedures for controlled-distribution manuals (e.g., centralized revision control, master copy) satisfy the “display date on each page” requirement if the master includes clear pagination and revision identifiers (applies to P3, P7, P11, P16).

[P18] Commenters will ask the FAA to clarify enforcement expectations — whether inspectors will cite noncompliance for a missing date on a single page versus a systemic deficiency — and to provide a compliance checklist illustrating acceptable and non-acceptable examples for each provision (applies across P3–P4, P7, P11–P12, P16–P17).

[P19] Software vendors of EFB and manual management systems will request safe‑harbor technical specifications (API, UI, timestamp formats) from FAA to ensure their products can be certified as meeting the “immediately ascertainable” electronic date display requirement (applies to P4, P7, P12, P17).

[P20] Some commenters will request that the FAA permit the use of dynamic versioning (e.g., live-updated electronic manuals with a global revision identifier) in lieu of per-page revision dates, provided there is cryptographic proof of version and a clear user-visible timestamp (applies to P3–P4, P7, P11–P12, P16–P17).

The electronic date-of-revision display requirement in § 135.23 is likely to conflict with common EFB and PDF viewers that suppress headers/footers on some displays; EFB vendors and operators will ask for technical specifications and a grace period to update platforms.

§ 135.23’s mandated manual contents should allow incorporation by reference to existing regulatory-approved documents (e.g., FAA-approved training curricula, manufacturer procedures) to avoid duplication; commenters (operators, certificated trainers) will request explicit permission to incorporate by reference.

Legal commenters will argue that many of the accessibility and language requirements impose substantive operational changes that may conflict with collective bargaining agreements; they request consultation requirements before enforcement as to working conditions.

Safety advocates will support the page-level revision date requirement in paper manuals (§ 91.1025) as important for ensuring crew use of current procedures, but request enforcement provisions for instances where outdated pages are found in flight.

IT security experts will caution that requiring visible revision metadata in electronic manuals (§§ 91.1025,121.135,125.73,135.23) may create tamper-evidence needs; they will request guidance on cryptographic integrity, audit logs, and acceptable means to demonstrate authenticity beyond a visible date.

Small business representatives will request an economic impact analysis and a phased compliance schedule for all new manual content and display requirements (P5, P6, P13, P18), arguing that immediate compliance would impose disproportionate costs.

Aviation training organizations will request clarification whether training syllabi and records must be included in the manuals under the “required contents” sections (P5, P6, P13, P18), and if so, what confidentiality protections apply to personnel records.

International operators will ask that the rule explicitly permit the use of bilingual manuals where English is the primary retrievable language, to accommodate non-English-speaking flight crews while satisfying the “retrievable in English” requirement (P2, P9, P10, P15).

Human factors experts will request that “displayed clearly” (P2, P9, P10, P15) be defined with measurable typography and UI standards (font size, contrast, navigation steps) to ensure compliance is assessable and improves safety rather than just adding paperwork.

Compliance officers will ask whether historical revisions must remain accessible to demonstrate compliance or incident investigation needs, and whether the “date of last revision” display must show history or only the current revision (P3, P4, P7, P11, P12, P16, P17).

Commenters will request that the rule allow for localized deviation approvals where operational environments (e.g., austere airfields, international remote bases) make continuous access to electronic manuals unrealistic, and require the Administrator to provide written approvals rather than informal waivers (applies to P1, P8, P14).

Legal scholars will note potential preemption or conflict with existing FAA guidance and ACs on manual control and formatting; they request the agency harmonize this rule with existing Advisory Circulars and Order 8900.1 references to avoid contradictory inspector guidance (applies broadly across P1–P18).

Maintenance organizations will request explicit inclusion of standard maintenance documentation (work cards, inspection checklists, service bulletins) as “appropriate parts” that must be accessible under the maintenance accessibility provisions (P1, P8, P14).

Labor unions will insist that the rule require employers to provide equipment (e.g., EFBs, internet access, printed copies) at no cost to employees to meet the “accessible at all times” mandates (P1, P8, P14).

Consumer safety advocates will ask the FAA to require an audit trail or timestamped acknowledgement when personnel access updated manual sections to ensure personnel actually review critical revisions (applies to electronic display requirements in P4, P7, P12, P17).

Operators will request the FAA confirm that standard company procedures for controlled-distribution manuals (e.g., centralized revision control, master copy) satisfy the “display date on each page” requirement if the master includes clear pagination and revision identifiers (applies to P3, P7, P11, P16).

Commenters will ask the FAA to clarify enforcement expectations — whether inspectors will cite noncompliance for a missing date on a single page versus a systemic deficiency — and to provide a compliance checklist illustrating acceptable and non-acceptable examples for each provision (applies across P3–P4, P7, P11–P12, P16–P17).

Software vendors of EFB and manual management systems will request safe‑harbor technical specifications (API, UI, timestamp formats) from FAA to ensure their products can be certified as meeting the “immediately ascertainable” electronic date display requirement (applies to P4, P7, P12, P17).

Some commenters will request that the FAA permit the use of dynamic versioning (e.g., live-updated electronic manuals with a global revision identifier) in lieu of per-page revision dates, provided there is cryptographic proof of version and a clear user-visible timestamp (applies to P3–P4, P7, P11–P12, P16–P17).

raw_output:
[P1] Allowing Method 321 as an alternative performance test for initial compliance could undermine consistency across sources because Method 321 measures HCl in a different manner than paragraph (b)(6)(ii); request clarification comparing method detection limits, bias, and applicability to both new and existing sources.

[P1] Industry commenters will request explicit limits on when Method 321 may be used (e.g., only for sources with specific scrubber types or exhaust conditions) to avoid regulatory uncertainty about acceptability.

[P2] Requiring continuous HCl CPMS monitoring per (b)(6)(v)(A)-(G) imposes significant capital and operating costs; request a phased implementation schedule or allowance for using alternative monitoring technologies that meet equivalent data quality objectives.

[P2] Environmental NGOs will assert that continuous HCl CPMS monitoring is necessary and should be required at all affected sources without exceptions to ensure real-time protection of public health.

[P3] The requirement to perform compliance testing and HCl monitoring for both raw mill on and off conditions for inline raw mills is appropriate but needs specification of minimum durations and representative operating conditions for each mode to ensure comparability.

[P3] Kiln operators will comment that conducting tests in both mill-on and mill-off conditions doubles testing burden and may be impracticable during limited maintenance windows; they will request allowance to use validated surrogate data or historical operating distributions to set site-specific limits.

[P4] The obligation to take actions whenever the 30-kiln operating day HCl CPMS average exceeds the operating limit must be clarified to specify what actions are required, timeframes for corrective action, and whether excursions during startup/shutdown are excluded.

[P4] Legal commenters will note potential due process issues if the rule permits immediate enforcement solely on a 30-day average without opportunity for source-specific rebuttal or adjustment for known monitoring biases; request procedural protections.

[P5] Cross-referencing §§63.1349 and 63.7 for compliance demonstrations creates complexity; request a consolidated table in the final rule listing specific methods for each pollutant and scenario to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P6] The requirement to use the specified performance test methods in §63.1349(b)(3) for D/F initial compliance should explicitly state if alternative validated methods or updated methods issued after proposal are allowed with EPA approval.

[P7] Mandating separate initial performance tests with the raw mill on and off for inline raw mills should include allowance for combining data if variability is demonstrated to be statistically insignificant, to reduce repetitive testing.

[P8] The arithmetic averaging of three TEQ runs to determine compliance should be clarified whether non-detects are treated as zero or as the method detection limit, because this materially affects compliance calculations.

[P9] Requiring the system to be maintained within ±5% accuracy during the performance test per monitoring plan is overly stringent for some monitoring technologies; request allowance for ±10% or technology-specific accuracy bands, with justification.

[P10] If electing the total organic HAP limit in lieu of THC, the rule should clarify equivalency and how differences in sampling and analytical uncertainty between THC CEMS and organic HAP test methods will be reconciled for compliance.

[P11] The requirement to monitor and test kiln exhaust prior to reintroducing coal mill exhaust and of kiln exhaust diverted to coal mill needs defined minimum sampling durations and stabilization criteria to ensure representative results.

[P12] Aggregating emissions from all points to ensure they do not exceed §63.1343(b) limits should include guidance on temporal alignment of data (e.g., averaging periods and how to treat asynchronous monitoring data) to avoid double counting or gaps.

[P13] Allowing a BLDS in lieu of daily visible emissions testing is reasonable, but the compliance demonstration per §63.1350(f)(4)(ii) must be spelled out (performance criteria, calibration frequency) to prevent inconsistent implementation by permitting authorities.

[P14] Requiring a CMS to record temperatures for D/F compliance needs specification of sensor placement, response time, and calibration procedures to ensure temperature data are representative of D/F formation conditions.

[P15] For ACI systems, mandating a CMS for injection rate and §63.1350(h)(1) compliance is appropriate, but the rule must allow for validated mass-balance approaches where direct measurement is impracticable (e.g., multi-injector systems).

[P16] Conducting at least three runs per performance test is standard, but the rule should allow composite sampling or an expanded number of shorter runs for facilities that cannot sustain long single runs for operational or fuel supply reasons.

[P17] The minimum sample volume per run (2 dscm for new, 1 dscm for existing) should be re-evaluated for compatibility with lower-emission controls and detection capabilities; request option to use lower volumes if validated by method performance.

[P18] Calculating a time-weighted average of three consecutive runs should clarify how to weight runs when run durations differ or when the facility has intermittent kiln load changes during testing.

[P19] The permission not to measure PM in the impinger back half for Method 5/5I compliance is helpful, but permitting authorities should not be allowed to require it inconsistently; request that EPA provide objective criteria when back-half measurement can be required.

[P20] Requiring performance testing for inline raw mills in both mill-on and mill-off conditions duplicates P7 concerns; request incorporation of statistical equivalency testing to reduce redundant testing burden.

[P21] For comingled exhaust streams, testing with mill on and off is necessary; however, the rule must provide procedures for apportioning pollutant contributions when comingled streams include non-kiln sources (e.g., cooler, mill) to avoid unfair attribution.

[P22] Specifying that run average temperatures be included and averaged should also require reporting of temperature variability and how temperature excursions impacted emissions to afford transparent evaluation.

[P23] Operating a THC CEMS per §63.1350(i) is costly; request allowance for periodic stack testing as an alternative for small sources or sources with demonstrated low variability, or support funds/technical assistance for CEMS installation.

[P24] For scrubber-equipped sources, requiring Method 321 performance testing is appropriate, but commenters will ask for clarity on whether Method 321 must be used for both wet and dry scrubbers and whether wet sampling issues (e.g., condensation) are addressed.

[P25] The exception allowing qualifying CEMS per §63.1350(l)(1) to substitute Method 321 needs clearer criteria for CEMS qualification, including minimum data quality objectives, span requirements, and relative accuracy thresholds.

[P26] Using Equation 12 to calculate THC CEMS averages and average of three organic HAP runs needs definition of rounding rules, significant figures, and treatment of censored data to ensure consistency across reports.

[P27] Requiring separate performance tests in mill-on and mill-off conditions for inline kiln/raw mills (again reiterated) will be flagged by industry as a major compliance cost driver; request consolidation with P7/P20 comments and potential relief.

[P28] Calculating SO2 operating limits as a time-weighted average of mill-on and mill-off measurements requires clear guidance on determining the fraction of time the raw mill is on versus off (e.g., which historical period to use) and how to adjust for seasonal operations.

[P29] Using Equation 18 for SO2 and HCl averages must be accompanied by example calculations in guidance to prevent misapplication by permit writers and sources.

[P30] The D/F monitoring requirements and emissions monitoring plan under §63.1350(g) should permit electronic submission templates and provide a model plan to speed permitting and ensure consistency.

[P31] Requiring hourly reporting of a rolling 3-hour average temperature calculated from 180 one-minute averages is computationally specific — sources will request allowance to use the best available averaged data when minute-by-minute data gaps occur (e.g., due to data logger downtime), with clear gap-filling rules.

[P32] The obligation to calculate the 3-hour rolling average using all one-minute data available could penalize sources for transient data losses; request predefined data substitution or continuity rules (e.g., require ≥80% data availability for a valid rolling average).

[P33] Continuous THC monitoring per (j) is duplicative of P23 concerns; smaller facilities or those with low THC emissions should be allowed to petition for an alternative monitoring frequency based on risk assessment.

[P34] Requiring CEMS operation/maintenance per Procedure 1 QA is standard, but commenters will request harmonization between Procedure 1 and any more recent QA procedures (or allow equivalent state QA programs).

[P35] The emissions monitoring plan requirements should include an option for consolidated plans across multiple affected units at a facility to reduce administrative burden.

[P36] Restricting QA above-span data handling to three specified options may be inflexible; commenters will request allowance for additional QA approaches where validated by third-party audits or where newer instrumentation has different characteristics.

[P37] Weekly above-span linearity calibration introduced at the probe for Hg CEMS may be infeasible for some technologies or require on-site calibration gas infrastructure; request allowance for biweekly calibration with performance justification.

[P38] The ±10% success criterion for the weekly above-span challenge is stricter than typical QA tolerances for Hg CEMS; request harmonization with manufacturer and performance specification tolerances or provide staggered corrective actions.

[P39] The normalization of hourly average values exceeding span when CEMS response >±20% during the following week will create complex reporting burden and potential inaccuracies; suggest clearer examples and automated spreadsheet tools from EPA.

[P40] Requiring an above-span Hg reference gas introduction within 24 hours of two consecutive one-hour averages exceeding span is operationally burdensome; request extension to 72 hours to allow logistics for certified gas acquisition and safe introduction.

[P41] The requirement to normalize one-hour average stack gas values if above-span calibration exceeds ±20% could lead to retroactive adjustments affecting past compliance determinations; request clarification that normalization applies prospectively only or provide appeals process.

[P42] Limiting to one above-span calibration per 24-hour period may be too restrictive during troubleshooting; request allowance for additional calibrations documented with rationale without triggering enforcement presumptions.

[P43] Continuously calculating hourly mercury emissions from alkali bypass and coal mill exhausts requires reliable real-time flow and Hg concentration data; smaller facilities lacking flow metering should be allowed to use representative correlation factors with EPA approval.

[P44] Requiring HCl CEMS operation per PS15/PS18 is acceptable, but commenters will request confirmation that newer validated performance specifications may be used without formal rule amendment.

[P45] Applying Procedure 1 QA with RATA replaced by PS15 validation for HCl CEMS will require training and potentially new third-party QA vendors; request EPA-provided training materials and an implementation timeline.

[P46] Requiring Procedure 6 QA for PS18 HCl CEMS should be reconciled with Procedure 1 language to avoid conflicting QA obligations for facilities that can choose either PS.

[P47] Mandating Method 321 as the reference method for relative accuracy testing for any HCl CEMS ties future CEMS validation to a single reference method; commenters will request allowance for equivalent reference methods where Method 321 is impracticable.

[P48] Applying span and calibration requirements to HCl CEMS not under PS15/PS18 should include transitional compliance dates and clarity on acceptable span values for low-emission sources to avoid pushing instruments below their reliable detection ranges.

[P49] If choosing SO2 monitoring with scrubber/tray tower, continuous monitoring per §60.63(e)-(f) may duplicate HCl monitoring obligations; industry requests cross-referencing and opportunity to use one CEMS for both pollutants where technically feasible.

[P50] The requirement to inspect and take corrective action within 30 days for SO2 increases ≥10% and to re-test within 90 days or at next performance test is ambiguous about what constitutes adequate corrective action; request specification of minimum inspection steps and acceptable remedial timelines.

[P51] The semiannual summary report submission via CEDRI within 60 days is a reasonable reporting cadence, but commenters will request secure bulk upload options and testing of XML schema before the rule is finalized.

[P52] Allowing an alternate XML consistent with CEDRI schema once available is useful, but EPA should commit to publishing the schema and providing a validation tool and examples at least 120 days before enforcement.

[P53] If the subpart form isn't in CEDRI at due date, submitting to the Administrator's address per §63.13 is fine, but commenters will ask for a clear contact and confirmation procedure to avoid missed filings.

[P54] The 90-day deadline to begin using CEDRI after form availability may be too short for facilities with limited IT resources; request 180 days, particularly for small entities.

[P55] Requiring excess emissions and summary reports within 60 days regardless of submission method may be onerous when multiple tests/translations are needed; request allowance for one 30-day extension upon documented cause.

[P56] Including §63.10(e)(3)(vi) information in reports should be clarified with a checklist to ensure all required elements are submitted consistently.

[P57] Reporting all calculated 30-operating-day rolling averages from PM CPMS, HCl, Hg, THC, or Hg sorbent traps within 60 days imposes heavy data processing demands; request phased reporting (e.g., quarterly for first year) and standardized templates.

[P58] The 60-day deadline to submit initial performance test information after initial test should be extended to 90 days when third-party labs or stack test scheduling issues occur to avoid unintentional late submissions.

[P59] Submission of initial performance test data as recorded under §63.1349(a) must include machine-readable formats and raw data to allow EPA independent verification; request explicit list of required raw data elements.

[P60] Requiring submission of site-specific operating limits with sample calculations within 60 days post-test is reasonable but should permit confidential business information redaction where appropriate, with a non-redacted submission to EPA under CBI procedures.

[P61] The electronic submission of RATA and performance test data to CDX/ERT within 60 days may fail if ERT lacks pollutant listing; request contingency guidance and examples for transmittal to Administrator to avoid data loss.

[P62] Triggering excess emissions/CMS performance reports when downtime ≥10% in a reporting period is reasonable, but commenters request that the 10% threshold be calculated as percentage of scheduled operating time rather than actual operating time to avoid penalizing scheduled shutdowns.

[P63] Requiring reporting of each malfunction-caused failure to meet a standard in semi-annual reports is appropriate, but commenters will request clarity on what constitutes a "malfunction" versus planned maintenance and standardized definitions to reduce subjective reporting.

[P64] The requirement to include date, time, duration, cause, and total number of malfunction events in reports should also provide templates and examples for estimating unknown causes to ensure consistent disclosures.

[P65] For each malfunction event, requiring estimation of pollutant emissions over the limit and description of estimation methods may be technically challenging; request EPA-provided estimation methodologies and acceptance of engineering estimates with conservative assumptions.

[P66] The obligation to describe actions taken during malfunctions to minimize emissions per §63.1348(d) should be expanded to require documentation of training and preventative maintenance programs to demonstrate due diligence.

[P67] Maintaining daily clinker production rate records per §63.1350(d) is reasonable, but commenters will ask for clarification on acceptable rounding and whether short-term deviations affect reporting thresholds.

[P68] Limiting access to deposited electronic works at LOC facilities to authorized users is reasonable for rights protection, but public interest groups will request criteria for who qualifies as an "authorized user" and timeline for approval.

[P69] Allowing Library staff off-site access via secure connection should include security standards and audit logging requirements to ensure compliance with privacy and IP protection.

[P70] Limiting simultaneous access to two authorized LOC users per electronic work may unreasonably restrict legitimate research; academic and public interest commenters will request increasing or removing the two-user limit for works with low commercial value.

[P71] Prohibiting LOC from making electronic works publicly available without rightsholder permission will significantly limit public access to deposited materials; request that the rule allow anonymized or excerpted public access under fair use determinations.

[P72] Treating a group registration deposit as satisfying mandatory deposit for published newspapers is administratively efficient, but publishers' associations will request clarification on whether individual title metadata and pagination must be included to satisfy legal deposit requirements.
