[P1] The prohibition in §301.92(b) is overly broad because it could prohibit routine movement of non-host materials (e.g., office supplies, packaging) from regulated establishments, creating unnecessary burdens; the rule should explicitly exempt non-plant, non-soil items.

[P1] Industry will comment that §301.92(b) lacks clarity about who is the responsible "person" and whether transporters, carriers, or consignors are subject to criminal or civil penalties if they unknowingly move regulated articles from a regulated establishment.

[P1] Legal commenters will assert that §301.92(b) needs a safe-harbor for inadvertent, documented, emergency movements (e.g., evacuations, emergency animal feed) to avoid unreasonable liability.

[P2] State agriculture agencies will request clear criteria and timelines for how and when the Administrator will make quarantined area designations and publish them, to allow timely coordination with state actions.

[P2] Small-state stakeholders will argue the rule gives the Administrator too much discretion to designate entire States or portions as quarantined without transparent thresholds (e.g., number of confirmed detections), and request objective triggers be specified.

[P3] Several States and legal groups will oppose the condition allowing partial-State quarantines only when the State has intrastate restrictions "substantially the same" as federal rules, arguing this unlawfully conditions federal action on state law and could penalize states with different but effective approaches.

[P3] State agencies will request a definition or examples of what constitutes "substantially the same" intrastate movement restrictions to avoid inconsistent implementation and litigation.

[P4] Environmental NGOs will request that the Administrator must demonstrate, with epidemiological modeling or evidence, that designating less than the entire State will prevent interstate spread (not just a determination), and that that analysis be included in the administrative record.

[P4] Trade associations will argue that requiring a determination that partial designation "will prevent interstate spread" sets an impractically high standard—prevention cannot be guaranteed—and recommend language requiring a reasonable expectation of reducing interstate spread (not absolute prevention).

[P5] Nursery and shipping industry commenters will express concern that §301.92–3(a)(2) permits temporary designations by an inspector without prior notice to stakeholders, potentially disrupting commerce; they will ask for minimum notice periods or procedural protections before temporary designations take effect except in genuine emergencies.

[P6] Owners of affected properties will object that §301.92–3(a)(2) mandates only that a copy of the regulation and written notice be given, but does not require explanation of the factual basis, evidence, or appeals process; they request due-process protections and immediate access to test results.

[P7] Trucking firms and logistics groups will comment that §301.92–3(a)(2)'s requirement that interstate movement from temporarily designated areas comply with the subpart could cause instantaneous stoppages of transit traffic; they request explicit limited exceptions for through-traffic complying with §301.92–4(a)(2) conditions.

[P8] Agricultural stakeholders will request a firm deadline (e.g., 7 or 14 days) for the Administrator or inspector to either add a temporarily designated area to the official list or to terminate the temporary designation, as the phrase "as soon as practicable" is vague and harms business planning.

[P9] Property owners will request the rule require written notice of termination of a temporary quarantine to include the reasons and test data supporting termination, not merely notice that designation is terminated.

[P10] Nurseries and trade groups will request clear, published criteria and notice procedures for designating out-of-quarantine nurseries as regulated establishments under §301.92–3(b)(1), including whether a single positive environmental detection triggers designation.

[P10] Legal commenters will ask for appeal and reconsideration procedures for designations of out-of-quarantine nurseries as regulated establishments, and for transparency regarding the detection methods and lab accreditation used to support such designations.

[P11] Nursery associations will argue that the three-year consecutive inspection requirement to deregulate (§301.92–3(b)(2)) is excessive and propose reducing it to two years or allowing alternative evidence (e.g., negative bulk testing of irrigation water) to shorten the period.

[P11] Small nursery operators will request a streamlined, expedited deregulation pathway for small businesses where the cost of annual inspections imposes disproportionate economic hardship, possibly via approved private inspectors.

[P12] Trucking and parcel carriers will comment that the transit-without-stopping exception in §301.92–4(a)(2) is ambiguous about what constitutes "stopping" (e.g., mandatory weigh stations, driver rest breaks) and request explicit language exempting regulatory stops that do not involve unpacking or handling of regulated articles.

[P12] Carriers will also request confirmation that routine fuel stops where drivers stay in the vehicle qualify as permissible stops under §301.92–4(a)(2), to avoid citations.

[P13] Environmental testing labs will praise the allowance in §301.92–4(a)(2)(ii) but request that APHIS publish an expedited approval process and clear criteria for labs seeking compliance agreements and approval to receive soil samples for analysis.

[P13] Some commenters will note the provision could impede academic research by limiting movement of soil samples to only APHIS-approved labs under a compliance agreement and ask for research exemptions with appropriate biosafety assurances.

[P14] Laboratories will request the compliance agreement template referenced in §301.92–4(a)(2)(ii)(A) be published in the rulemaking record so applicants understand required biosafety, chain-of-custody, and disposal procedures before applying.

[P15] Labs and legal groups will request clarity in §301.92–4(a)(2)(ii)(B) about consequences for inadvertent noncompliance with a compliance agreement (e.g., cure periods, suspension vs. termination) to ensure due process.

[P16] Labs will request clear, objective APHIS approval criteria and reasonable timelines, as the requirement in §301.92–4(a)(2)(ii)(C) could create laboratory bottlenecks if approvals are slow.

[P17] Regulated establishments will request that §301.92–4(d) clarify whether compliance agreements must be site-specific or can cover multiple facilities under common ownership, to reduce administrative burdens.

[P17] Trade groups will ask APHIS to publish the standard form compliance agreement used for regulated establishments so businesses can plan and budget for compliance requirements before designation.

[P18] Nursery operators will request that the inspection and sampling protocol in §301.92–11(a)(1) cited in §301.92–5(a)(1)(iv)(A)(1) be detailed in guidance with sample sizes, sampling methods, and turnaround times to avoid inconsistent inspector determinations of "free of evidence."

[P19] Plant-health NGOs will argue that §301.92–5(a)(1)(iv)(A) allowing certificates if any one listed condition is met could allow lower-standard routes (e.g., minimal inspections) to substitute for rigorous testing, and request minimum combined inspection/testing standards for all certificate-eligible shipments.

[P20] Industry will ask that the alternative inspection protocol in §301.92–11(a)(2) referenced in §301.92–5(a)(1)(iv)(A)(2) be clearly defined and limited to situations when P. ramorum has been previously detected at the nursery, not used broadly to reduce oversight.

[P21] Consumer-safety advocates will challenge §301.92–5(a)(1)(iv)(A)(3) permitting shipments from nurseries with evidence of infestation if an inspector determines the nursery is abiding by its compliance agreement, arguing that presence of infestation should preclude general shipment except under strict conditions and traceability.

[P21] Legal commenters will request objective standards for an inspector's determination under §301.92–5(a)(1)(iv)(A)(3), and an appeal mechanism for nurseries disagreeing with the inspector's judgment.

[P22] Section §301.92–5(b)'s four-condition test for issuing certificates may be administratively burdensome; inspectors and regulated entities will request a checklist and timeline (e.g., sample test turnaround) so certificates can be issued without undue delay.

[P22] Associations of inspectors will ask for training, resources, and standardized forms to ensure consistent application of §301.92–5(b) across jurisdictions.

[P23] Nurseries in quarantined areas will request that the annual inspection/sampling/testing requirements in §301.92–11(a)(1) include notice periods and sampling windows to allow scheduling, and that APHIS publish expected sample numbers for planning.

[P24] Clarify in §301.92–11(a)(1)(i)(A) whether the "inspector" must be an APHIS employee or whether State-designated/third-party inspectors approved by APHIS can perform annual inspections.

[P25] The requirement in §301.92–11(a)(1)(i)(B) that APHIS determine a minimum number of plant samples "on a nursery-by-nursery basis" may be unpredictable; industry requests a published sampling formula (e.g., sample per unit area or per lot size) to allow cost estimation.

[P25] Small nurseries will request a cap or graduated scale on required sample numbers to prevent disproportionate disruption for small operations.

[P26] Nursery operators will object that §301.92–11(a)(1)(i)(B) obligates inspectors to consider fungicide programs but does not specify how fungicide history affects sampling intensity; they request explicit rules preventing over-penalization for legitimate integrated pest management.

[P27] The requirement to retain fungicide application records for 2 years (§301.92–11(a)(1)(i)(B)) raises privacy and proprietary concerns; nurseries request limits on the scope of records inspectors may access and assurances of confidentiality.

[P28] Laboratories and regulated entities request APHIS to publish the list of approved test methods referenced in §301.92–11(a)(1)(i)(C) and to allow emerging molecular methods pending validation to avoid long test turnaround times.

[P29] Stakeholders will ask that the authority in §301.92–11(a)(1)(i)(D) allowing inspectors to certify a nursery free of P. ramorum if all samples test negative specify the validity period of such certification and whether re-testing is required for each shipment.

[P30] The 30-day pre-shipment inspection window in §301.92–11(a)(1)(ii)(A) could be operationally infeasible for high-volume nurseries; industry will request extending the window (e.g., 45 or 60 days) or allowing validated sampling plans for frequent shipments.

[P31] Stakeholders will object to §301.92–11(a)(1)(ii)'s prohibition of shipment inspections for nurseries without a current annual certification, arguing it could create Catch-22s where certification is delayed yet shipments are needed; they request interim inspections or provisional certification processes.

[P32] Buyers and distributors will request clear documentation requirements under §301.92–11(a)(1)(ii)(A)(1) to prove "no symptomatic plants" were found, including inspector-signed forms to accompany shipments.

[P33] Inspectors and nurseries will request standardized sampling protocols for symptomatic findings per §301.92–11(a)(1)(ii)(A)(2) to clarify "one sample per symptomatic plant" and "one sample per regulated article in the same lot" and to avoid duplicative sampling.

[P34] Stakeholders will request timelines for test results and explicit rules about holding periods for shipments under §301.92–11(a)(1)(ii)(B), including permitted interim storage/segregation procedures while awaiting test results.

[P35] Operators of previously infected nurseries will request that the "at least twice annually" inspections in §301.92–11(a)(2)(i) be supplemented with risk-based criteria allowing more frequent inspections for high-risk operations and less frequent for those with demonstrated mitigation.

[P36] Water managers and nurseries will ask for clear testing methodologies, frequencies, and permissible remedial actions for irrigation water sampling under §301.92–11(a)(2)(ii), and for recognition of municipal water supplies with low risk.

[P37] Labs and regulated entities will request APHIS to provide a publicly available, time-bound approval and proficiency-testing program for labs used under §301.92–11(a)(2)(iii) to ensure consistent, timely results.

[P38] Concerned stakeholders will ask that the certification in §301.92–11(a)(2)(iv) be accompanied by written documentation of negative results and be entered into a publicly searchable registry to allow buyers to verify nursery status.

[P39] Small nurseries will comment that the three-consecutive-year clean-inspection rule (§301.92–11(a)(2)(iv)(3)) to revert to less-frequent inspections imposes long-term costs; they propose allowing alternate monitoring indicators (e.g., environmental sampling of irrigation water) to shorten the period.

[P40] Trade groups will request clarity in §301.92–11(a)(2)(v) about methods "specified in the compliance agreement" for deeming lots free of inoculum when positive environmental samples were found, including validated testing thresholds and retesting protocols.

[P41] Retailers and distributors will seek clarification that the "annual visual inspections" in §301.92–11(b)(1) may be performed by approved State or third-party inspectors, not strictly APHIS personnel, to increase inspection capacity.

[P42] Nurseries will ask for precise definitions of "symptomatic plants" and the methods for symptomatic identification to avoid inconsistent withholding of plants under §301.92–11(b)(2).

[P42] Operators will also request that the 2-meter radius containment rule for withholding plants (¶ b(2)) be replaced with a risk-based distancing approach or allow local mitigation measures (e.g., fungicide treatment) to avoid wholesale lot rejection.

[P43] Industry groups will request that the 1-year duration of inspector certification in §301.92–11(b)(3) be made flexible for low-risk nurseries with multi-year validated negative testing, to reduce administrative renewal costs.

[P44] Regulated establishments will ask that the "at least two annual inspections" requirement in §301.92–11(c)(1) include provisions for remote or targeted inspections when on-site access is limited (e.g., due to natural disasters).

[P45] Facilities will seek clear guidance on sampling scope in §301.92–11(c)(2), including whether growing media, containers, and shipping pallets are considered "other articles" and will request test frequency tied to risk factors.

[P46] Laboratories and legal experts will request that chain-of-custody, sample labeling standards, and sample retention times be specified for regulated-establishment samples under §301.92–11(c)(3) to ensure legal defensibility of results.

[P47] Buyer groups will request that inspector certifications under §301.92–11(c)(4) include machine-readable documentation (e.g., QR codes) linking to validated negative test results to facilitate commerce.

[P48] The rule's allowance in §301.92–11(c)(5) for shipping lots from establishments with positive samples only under compliance-agreement-specified methods raises concerns about transparency; commenters will request that the acceptable methods be defined in the regulation or published guidance and be subject to peer review.

[P1] The January 27, 2022 deadline for receipt of comments is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60 days to allow affected operators, unions, and third-party inspection providers to perform technical and cost analyses.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether comments submitted by mail, email, or through the FAA docket portal count as "received" on January 27, 2022, to avoid procedural rejections.

[P2] The phrase "unless already accomplished" in (f) is ambiguous and should be clarified to state whether prior actions taken under non-identical procedures (e.g., different service instructions) qualify as "already accomplished."

[P3] Requiring a flow path and mid-span ultrasonic inspection "before the next flight" for any blade with CSN > 0 is impracticable for many operators with multiple aircraft in service and should be adjusted to a realistic maintenance window (e.g., within 10 days or the next scheduled maintenance).

[P3] The requirement in (g)(1)(i) to follow the "referenced service bulletin" must identify the exact document number and revision incorporated by reference; otherwise operators cannot be certain what procedures are mandated.

[P4] The exemption for new fan blades with zero CSN is reasonable, but the rule fails to define how "new" is documented or verified—request explicit requirements for documentation in the logbook or certificate of conformance.

[P5] Requiring repetitive inspections for new blades (P5) without specifying initial interval start points creates confusion; the AD should state whether the first repetitive inspection for new blades is counted from delivery date, installation date, or first flight.

[P6] The requirement to use an "FAA-approved method" for TAI inspections in (g)(1)(ii) is vague; the AD should list acceptable TAI equipment and techniques or provide the process and expected time frame for obtaining FAA approval.

[P7] The before-next-flight TAI mandate for blades with ≥1,000 CSN and no prior TAI (g)(1)(ii)(A) will ground many aircraft immediately and may be unsafe for passenger operations; the FAA should allow limited ferry flights or provide express AMOC procedures to avoid wide disruptions.

[P7] The AD does not explain whether CSN is counted per blade serial number or per engine serial number; clarify how operators should determine which blades meet the "≥1,000 CSN" threshold.

[P8] The "1,000 FCs since last TAI" threshold in (g)(1)(ii)(B) requires precise maintenance recordkeeping; small operators may lack cycle-tracking systems accurate enough to comply—request the FAA provide acceptable recordkeeping standards or tolerance allowances.

[P9] The instruction in (g)(1)(ii)(C) to inspect blades with <1,000 CSN "before reaching 1,000 CSN" lacks a required lead time or buffer—operators need a clear compliance window (e.g., inspect at 950 CSN) to plan maintenance.

[P10] Similarly, (g)(1)(ii)(D) requiring TAI before reaching 1,000 FCs since last TAI should specify whether accumulated cycles are calendar day counted or flight cycle counted, and how cycles are to be documented.

[P11] The 275-FC interval for flow path UT inspections in (g)(2)(i) will significantly increase maintenance costs and downtime for high-utilization fleets; the FAA must provide an economic analysis and consider longer intervals or risk-based compliance options.

[P11] For (g)(2)(i), clarify whether partial-flight cycles (e.g., aborted takeoffs, engine starts without flight) count toward FCs for the 275-FC threshold.

[P12] The 550-FC mid-span UT interval in (g)(2)(ii) appears arbitrary relative to the 275-FC flow path interval; justify the scientific basis and provide data showing the damage progression that supports these specific intervals.

[P13] The 1,000-FC TAI repetitive interval in (g)(2)(iii) may be technically appropriate but should allow risk-based extension for blades that repeatedly pass UT and TAI with margin—request criteria for extending intervals via an AMOC.

[P17] The 10-day window in (h)(2) prior to flight for the hydraulic check is ambiguous—state whether the check must be performed within 10 days before the planned ferry flight or can be older if no flights occurred since.

[P19] Paragraph (i)(1) credit for Special Instruction No. 85F21 flows should specify which revision of that instruction is acceptable and whether deviations in acceptance criteria disqualify prior inspections for credit.

[P20] Paragraph (i)(2) credit for Special Instruction No. 130F–21 should require submission of records demonstrating that the exact paragraphs (1.a–c) were performed, to avoid disputes between operators and the FAA during compliance audits.

[P21] Paragraph (i)(3) credit for Revision A of Special Instruction No. 130F–21 should clarify whether inspections done to the original 130F–21 before the revision but with equivalent techniques are acceptable.

[P22] The AMOC authority delegation to the Manager, ECO Branch in (j)(1) is appropriate, but the AD should set expected timelines (e.g., 30–60 days) for AMOC decisions to avoid operational delays.

[P23] The AMOC submission routing requirements in (j)(1) requiring principal inspector, local FSDO, or email to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov create confusion—request a single centralized submission method and confirm receipt protocols.

[P24] The requirement in (j)(2) to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC lacks guidance on what documentation must be provided to the inspector and how quickly after approval notification must occur.

[P3] The AD does not address international operators or aircraft based outside the United States—request clarification on compliance obligations for non-U.S. operators and acceptance of foreign-approved inspection methods.

[P6] Requiring "FAA-approved" TAI methods without listing existing qualified laboratories or suppliers disadvantages smaller operators—request a list of known-approved providers or an expedited approval pathway for vendors.

[P11] The AD should include guidance on coordination of inspection intervals between engines on the same aircraft to avoid requiring duplicate inspections in short succession and unnecessary aircraft downtime.

[P14] The rule should require the FAA to provide a parts availability assessment, including inventory data for spare 1st-stage LPC blades, to justify the "replace before next flight" mandate.

[P15] Operator groups request an explicit exception to (h) for emergency medical flights or other public safety missions, subject to operational mitigation and FAA approval.

[P2] The AD should define whether scheduled maintenance actions performed under continuing airworthiness programs (e.g., OEM SB-compliant checks) constitute "compliance" for the purposes of paragraph (f).

[P13] The AD should allow data-driven extensions of the 1,000-FC TAI interval if operators gather and submit fleet inspection data showing low defect rates, via an AMOC pathway with clear evidentiary standards.

[P7] For blades near the 1,000-CSN threshold, require the FAA to permit a grace period of at least 3 flight cycles to position aircraft to maintenance facilities, provided conservative operational limitations are applied.

[P11] The AD must clarify how calendar time interacts with FC-based intervals for parked aircraft (e.g., aircraft in storage for months) — do inspections lapse on calendar basis or only on FC accrual?

[P5] For new blades, require manufacturers to provide an initial inspection report certifying baseline condition if they are to be exempt from the initial UT inspection per Note 1, thereby reducing operational risk.

raw_output:
[P1] The October 25, 2021 comments due date is impractical and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow operators, maintenance providers, and labor organizations sufficient time to review the referenced Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin and generate technical comments.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether electronic submissions received by 11:59 p.m. ET on October 25, 2021 will be accepted, and whether mailroom or courier delivery delays will be considered timely.

[P2] The applicability language is overbroad because it applies to "all" 757–200/–200PF/–200CB/–300 series airplanes without regard to configuration differences (e.g., specific line numbers, retrofits, or structural modifications); request narrowing applicability to aircraft with the affected lower frame fittings or having the identified part numbers/serials.

[P2] Operators that have incorporated certain supplemental type certificates (STCs) or Customer Modification Packages (CMPs) may be unnecessarily captured by this AD; FAA should add an exclusion for airplanes with STCs that alter the inspected structure or provide alternate means of compliance.

[P2] Clarify whether the applicability includes aircraft operated in foreign registry but maintained in the U.S., and whether foreign civil aviation authorities (CAAs) should be notified or allowed differing compliance schedules.

[P3] The compliance sentence is tautological and provides no relief for practical scheduling constraints; request explicit allowance for scheduling inspections within a maintenance window (e.g., within the next scheduled heavy maintenance) when safety is not compromised.

[P3] The AD must specify whether compliance times are calendar-based or flight-cycle-based where the referenced Boeing bulletin uses both metrics; ambiguity will cause inconsistent compliance.

[P4] Paragraph (g) incorporates actions by reference to the Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin but does not reproduce critical inspection thresholds, torque values, or part numbers; request that the AD include the critical compliance times and affected part numbers in the rule text for clarity and enforceability.

[P4] Reliance on the Boeing Accomplishment Instructions without FAA review of Boeing's service information raises potential safety and legal issues; request FAA justification for direct incorporation and confirmation that FAA certified the referenced Boeing documents for mandatory use.

[P5] The substitution of September 10, 2018 for the 'Original Issue date' may create confusion for operators using older or alternative revisions; request FAA to provide a version comparison table showing what changes are consequential between the original issue and Revision 2.

[P6] Using January 14, 2021 as the 'Revision 1 date' for compliance/time effectivity could disadvantage operators who relied on Revision 1 earlier; request clarification whether work performed between Revision 1 and the AD effective date is treated as compliant per paragraph (i)(2), and provide explicit cutoff language.

[P7] Making "the effective date of this AD" substitute for the 'Revision 2 date' may create circularity if operators must act before publication of the AD; request clarification of the AD effective date and whether any actions become mandatory immediately upon AD publication or only after an official effective date.

[P8] Requiring FAA-approved methods per paragraph (j) when Boeing directs contacting Boeing for repairs places an undue burden on operators in urgent maintenance situations; request that FAA pre-approve standardized repair schematics for commonly encountered damage or provide an expedited AMOC review timeline (e.g., 10 working days).

[P8] The AD should explicitly permit using Boeing-authorized repair data approved under the Boeing ODA (as suggested elsewhere), not require a separate paragraph (j) AMOC process for every instance, to avoid duplicative approvals and delay.

[P9] The credit provision excluding "open-hole high frequency eddy current inspections" is vague; request FAA to specify which exact inspections are excluded, and whether partial credit applies when prior work used equivalent NDT methods (e.g., ultrasonic).

[P9] Operators who performed prior actions under the July 14, 2017 bulletin should not be required to re-inspect if data records show compliance; request clear recordkeeping requirements and acceptance criteria for prior work to claim credit.

[P10] Paragraph (i)(2) credits Revision 1 actions but does not define acceptable differences between Revision 1 and Revision 2; request that FAA enumerate any divergence and state whether any operator-performed Revision 1 procedures now considered insufficient require rework.

[P11] Granting the Manager, Los Angeles ACO Branch, authority to approve AMOCs centralizes decision-making and may create bottlenecks for non-U.S. operators; request FAA provide alternative AMOC avenues (regional ACOs) or defined service levels for response times.

[P11] The AD should allow alternative AMOC approvers for foreign operators where the Los Angeles ACO does not have direct oversight, to avoid delays in implementing necessary repairs abroad.

[P12] The requirement to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or Flight Standards Office may be redundant when requests are routed via the Manager as allowed elsewhere; request clarification of the required routing hierarchy and whether emailing the FAA address satisfies this requirement.

[P13] The AD's instruction to address direct submissions to the person in Related Information should include a name, postal address, telephone, and secure file transfer instructions to ensure sensitive technical data can be transmitted and tracked.

[P14] Permitting AMOC requests by email to 9-ANM-LAACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov raises cybersecurity and data privacy concerns for proprietary Boeing data; request a secure portal or encrypted email procedures and confirm how proprietary markings will be treated.

[P15] Requiring notification of the principal inspector or Flight Standards Office before using an approved AMOC could delay urgent repairs; request that notification can be contemporaneous (within 48 hours) after commencing work when delay would adversely affect operations or introduce risk.

[P15] The AD should specify the content of the notification (AMOC reference number, work scope, location, contact) so principal inspectors receive consistent information.

[P16] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs to be used is appropriate, but the AD must require that ODA approvals explicitly reference this AD and include technical justification demonstrating equivalent level of safety; request FAA confirm documentation standards.

[P16] There is a potential conflict where Boeing ODA approvals may not satisfy foreign CAAs; request FAA to coordinate with EASA and other CAAs to ensure mutual acceptance of ODA-approved AMOCs for international operators.

[P17] Requiring that approved repairs meet the airplane's certification basis could be interpreted to prohibit practical repairs on older aircraft where showing conformance is difficult; request FAA guidance on acceptable means to show compliance with the certification basis for legacy airplanes.

[P17] The AD should require that AMOC approvals explicitly state the applicable amendments, type certificate data sheet references, and compliance showings so inspectors can verify conformity.

[P18] Accepting AMOCs from AD 2020–21–17 is appropriate, but the AD should list the specific AD 2020–21–17 AMOC identifiers that correspond to the new AD's provisions to avoid confusion about which AMOCs carry over.

[P18] Operators who relied on AD 2020–21–17 AMOCs should be given written confirmation that prior approvals remain valid and whether any conditions attached to the old AMOCs continue to apply under this AD.

[P4] The AD does not specify whether required repetitive inspections (if any) are mandated; request FAA to state whether the actions in the Boeing bulletin create one-time fixes or recurring inspection intervals.

[P8] The phrase "using a method approved in accordance with the procedures specified in paragraph (j)" should be clarified to permit temporary repairs (with follow-up permanent repair within a defined interval) to avoid aircraft AOG situations.

[P3] The AD should provide an explicit compliance clock start event (e.g., from the effective date of the AD, from receipt of the Boeing bulletin, or from the last inspection) to eliminate operator uncertainty.

[P2] Small cargo operators who operate 757–200PFs on thin margins need cost impact estimates; request FAA to provide cost-of-compliance analysis or regulatory flexibility allowances (phase-in or subsidy) for small operators.

[P4] The AD should explicitly identify the specific structural fasteners, frame numbers, and stringer/frame intersections to be inspected so maintenance planning can be accurate.

[P9] Labor unions representing maintenance technicians request that the FAA require training or qualification standards for personnel performing the specified inspections, particularly eddy current inspections, to ensure inspection quality.

[P14] The FAA should acknowledge receipt of emailed AMOC requests within 48 hours and post a public docket of AMOC approvals for transparency.

[P7] The use of "effective date of this AD" in (h)(3) should be defined (publication vs. legal effective date) to avoid operators mistakenly believing they must comply before the AD is legally effective.

[P1] Because the AD references a Boeing bulletin dated March 1, 2021, stakeholders request alignment of the comment period with the bulletin's publication so commenters can coordinate technical review; extend comment deadline accordingly.

[P8] For repairs requiring parts that may be backordered, the AD should allow use of temporary repairs and provide explicit maximum times before permanent repairs are required to avoid grounded aircraft.

[P11] Legal commenters note that delegation of AMOC approval to a single Manager may raise due process concerns; request FAA publish criteria that the Manager will use to evaluate AMOC requests to ensure consistent, transparent decisions.

[P3] Include a grandfathering exception for operators who have already performed equivalent procedures per accepted service bulletins prior to the AD effective date, with a process to document equivalency.

[P4] The retained AFM revision requirement to revise the Limitations section within 2 days after Jan 27, 2022 is retroactive and impossible to meet for operators who did not receive prior notice; either remove the retroactive date or allow a reasonable grace period from the AD effective date.

[P4] Explain whether the 2‑day AFM revision must be physically inserted into every paper AFM on each aircraft, whether electronic AFM (eAFM) updates are acceptable, and whether training records need updating.

[P5] The permission to comply by inserting figure 3 into the AFM should include exact formatting, scale, and legibility standards (font size, resolution) so inserted figures are uniformly readable across operator AFMs.

[P5] Clarify whether laminated inserts or temporary sleeves are permitted for the required figure insertion or whether only permanent AFM revisions are acceptable.

[P6] The new requirement targeting "non-radio altimeter tolerant airplanes" lacks a clear definition of "radio altimeter tolerant" and the criteria to determine whether an airplane qualifies; provide technical definitions or reference standards.

[P6] Require Boeing or the FAA to publish a model-by-model list identifying which serial numbers/configurations are non-radio altimeter tolerant so operators can determine applicability without interpreting avionics logs.

[P7] Clarify whether the June 30, 2023 deadline applies per-aircraft (from date of AD applicability on that aircraft) or globally — operators with continental fleets and different maintenance cycles need per-aircraft effective dates.

[P8] The allowance to comply by inserting figure 4 into the AFM should explicitly permit electronic distribution and recordkeeping (e.g., e-Revision control) and accept temporary placards if the official AFM revision cannot be completed within the timeframe.

[P9] The provision that incorporating paragraph (i)(1) terminates the paragraph (h) requirement is ambiguous about whether termination is automatic upon incorporation or requires formal notification to the FAA; request confirmation of automatic supersession.

[P9] Specify whether terminating paragraph (h) via incorporation of paragraph (i)(1) must be documented in aircraft records and whether operators must retain the superseded paragraph (h) material for a period.

[P10] Requiring removal of the paragraph (h) AFM revision "before further flight" after incorporating figure 4 is impractical and could create a regulatory gap during a maintenance event spanning multiple flights; allow removal at the next scheduled cockpit-bound maintenance action or within 7 days.

[P10] Clarify acceptable methods for "removal" — does this require physically excising pages, annotating the AFM, or can operators place an administrative note that the paragraph (h) content is superseded?

[P11] The split requirements for radio altimeter tolerant vs non-tolerant airplanes (paragraphs (i) and (j)) place a heavy compliance burden on mixed fleets; require a single harmonized AFM revision option or provide a compliance pathway for multi-configuration operators.

[P21] Accepting previously approved AMOCs for AD 2021–23–12 only through June 30, 2023 creates uncertainty for operators relying on those AMOCs beyond that date; state whether those AMOCs will be re-evaluated, extended, or must be re-submitted, and provide transition timelines.

[P21] Provide the technical rationale for limiting acceptance of AD 2021–23–12 AMOCs only through June 30, 2023 and explain what happens to operators who have ongoing operations that relied on those AMOCs after that date.

[P1] The requirement in § 80.590(a) to provide product transfer documents for each applicable fuel transfer will create significant operational burden for small fuel distributors who perform hundreds of daily transfers at terminals; the agency should allow consolidated batch documentation or electronic summaries rather than per-transfer paper documents.

[P1] The rule does not specify acceptable electronic formats or security standards for providing product transfer documents under § 80.590(a); commenters request explicit recognition of electronic manifests (e.g., EDI, ASTM, or API standards) and guidance on retention and authentication.

[P2] The mandated global marine fuel usage statement in § 80.590(a)(7)(viii) ("For use only in steamships or Category 3 marine vessels outside of an Emission Control Area (ECA), consistent with MARPOL Annex V") is ambiguous about which MARPOL Annex applies (Annex V addresses garbage) and should instead reference MARPOL Annex VI and the specific regulations for fuel sulfur and ECAs.

[P2] Requiring that exact usage statement on product transfer documents could expose suppliers to legal liability if downstream users misuse fuel; the agency should provide safe harbor language or a standardized abbreviated statement to reduce litigation risk.

[P3] § 80.602(a) backdates recordkeeping for global marine fuel to Jan 1, 2020, creating retroactive compliance obligations for producers and importers that may be impossible to meet; retroactive enforcement is unfair and the recordkeeping start date should be prospective from the final rule effective date.

[P3] The phrase "Beginning June 1, 2007, or June 1, 2006, if that is the first period credits are generated" in § 80.602(a) is confusing in the context of global marine fuel and should be clarified or removed so that stakeholders know which date applies to each fuel type.

[P4] § 80.602(a)(1) requires keeping copies of product transfer documents from §§ 80.590 and 80.591 but does not set a retention period; commenters ask EPA to specify a clear retention period (e.g., 5 years) consistent with other recordkeeping provisions.

[P4] The rule should permit storing copies of required product transfer documents electronically and offsite; the proposal lacks explicit permission and technical requirements for electronic storage, which creates uncertainty.

[P5] Requiring recording the location, date, time, and storage tank/truck ID for each sample (§ 80.602(a)(2)(i)) is operationally feasible for terminal-based sampling but will be burdensome and sometimes impossible for transient barge or shipboard sampling; the rule should allow reasonable alternatives for marine contexts.

[P6] § 80.602(a)(2)(ii) mandating names and titles of sampler and tester raises privacy and personnel-security concerns for small contractors; the agency should accept company identifiers and batch lab IDs in lieu of individual names.

[P7] The mandated recording of test results for sulfur content, including application of adjustment factors (§ 80.602(a)(2)(iii)), requires the rule to provide explicit formulas and examples for how to apply adjustment factors to avoid inconsistent reporting between laboratories.

[P8] § 80.602(a)(3) requires documenting actions taken to stop sale or distribution of noncompliant fuel, but provides no timeframe for corrective actions or required preventive steps; commenters request clear timelines and required content (root-cause analysis, corrective action plan) to ensure consistent enforcement.

[P9] The effective date for global marine fuel recordkeeping (§ 80.602 start Jan 1, 2020) is in the past; parties who have already disposed of records should be treated fairly and the EPA should state it will not seek penalties for pre-existing gaps if good-faith efforts are demonstrated.

[P10] § 80.602(b)(4)(i) requires including records pertaining to multiple fuel types (NRLM, NR, LM, global marine, ECA marine, heating oil) but does not define the boundaries between these categories or how blended products should be classified; EPA should provide clear definitions and examples for blended fuels.

[P11] § 80.598(a)(2)(i)(G) requires identifying exempt distillate fuels including global marine fuels in designation documentation; the proposal lacks a standardized code or label set that would enable industry to program designation systems—EPA should publish a required data dictionary.

[P12] § 80.598(b)(8)(iii) requires providing listed identification info for exempt distillate fuels as part of designation procedures, but the rule doesn't specify who is responsible at each transfer point (producer, importer, terminal operator, retailer); commenters urge EPA to allocate responsibilities precisely.

[P13] The broad exemption in § 80.605(a) for global marine fuel used in steamships or Category 3 vessels outside ECAs risks incentivizing mislabeling and sale into non-exempt markets; EPA should consider tightening eligibility or adding robust verification/chain-of-custody requirements.

[P14] § 80.605(b) conditions for exemption are numerous and complex; industry requests a consolidated checklist and template attestation form that suppliers can use to certify compliance with all conditions before claiming the exemption.

[P15] The sulfur limit in § 80.605(b)(1) set at 0.50 wt% (5,000 ppm) is higher than many international fuel specifications and could create health and environmental impacts in port communities if misused; environmental groups will oppose allowing fuel with such high sulfur except under tightly controlled circumstances.

[P15] Conversely, some small vessel operators contend the 0.50 wt% cap is too restrictive for existing refineries or remote bunkering operations and request an alternative compliance mechanism (e.g., documented scrubber use or onboard emissions controls) rather than a strict sulfur threshold.

[P16] § 80.605(b)(2) requires that exempt fuel be accompanied by § 80.590 product transfer documents; commenters ask EPA to explicitly allow consolidated batch paperwork for bunkering operations where one delivery fuels multiple vessels, as per international bunkering practices.

[P17] The designation requirement under § 80.605(b)(3) referencing § 80.598 lacks clarity on who must perform the designation and when (producer at refinery, importer at port, or bunker supplier at sale); commenters request a chain-of-custody model and liability allocation.

[P18] Requiring physical segregation of exempt fuel from non-exempt fuel throughout distribution (§ 80.605(b)(4)) is operationally impracticable at multi-product terminals that use shared pipelines and tanks; terminal operators request an allowance for use of dedicated bladders, time-based segregation with flushing protocols, or mass-balance accounting.

[P19] The prohibition in § 80.605(b)(5) against using exempt fuel in any equipment other than steamships or Category 3 marine vessels could be unenforceable without labeling and downstream checks; marine engine manufacturers and port authorities request explicit marking requirements at the dispenser and enforcement guidance.

[P20] § 80.605(c) makes fuel that fails exemption conditions subject to MVNRLM standards but does not clarify how jurisdictional enforcement and penalties will be applied when fuel crosses borders between vessels and shore; commenters want harmonization with Coast Guard and customs authorities.

[P21] The prohibition in § 80.605(c) on claiming exemption if § 80.602 recordkeeping is not met creates a strict liability standard that could penalize clerical errors; legal experts recommend a “cure period” or opportunity to correct recordkeeping deficiencies before loss of exemption and enforcement.

[P22] § 1042.145(k) permitting delays to Tier 4 for certain engines and vessels could undermine national air quality goals by allowing continued sale of higher-emitting engines; environmental NGOs will comment that EPA must justify emissions tradeoffs and include sunsets.

[P23] The power density threshold (>35.0 kW/liter and >40.0 kW/liter in later years) in § 1042.145(k)(1)(i) and (k)(2)(i) is overly technical and may be manipulable by manufacturers through minor design changes; commenters request EPA to require independent testing or third-party verification of power density claims.

[P24] The vessel total propulsion power caps (≤2,800 kW for MY2021 and ≤1,000 kW for MY2022–2023) in §§ 1042.145(k)(1)(ii) and (k)(2)(ii) could exclude many common commercial vessels; industry asks EPA to publish an exhaustive list of vessel types that would or would not qualify under these thresholds.

[P25] The vessel length thresholds (≤65 ft and ≤50 ft in §§ 1042.145(k)(1)(iii) and (k)(2)(iii)) appear arbitrary and do not correlate directly with emissions; commenters propose substituting thresholds tied to emissions potential or use-case (e.g., tonnage, service type).

[P26] Requiring vessels to qualify as uninspected under 46 CFR 2.01–7 (§§ 1042.145(k)(1)(iv) and (k)(2)(iv)) could exclude many small commercial vessels that are inspected but face the same installation constraints; stakeholders request EPA allow inspected vessels if they meet other qualifying criteria.

[P27] The speed requirement (max speed ≥ 3.0 * sqrt(L) in §§ 1042.145(k)(1)(v) and (k)(2)(v)) is an unconventional operational metric that will require manufacturers and owners to perform additional sea trials; the rule should allow documented design speed or manufacturer-rated speed as an alternative.

[P28] The hull material requirement in § 1042.145(k)(2)(vi) (fiberglass or other nonmetal hulls) unfairly disadvantages aluminum or steel small-vessel manufacturers and seems unrelated to emissions; commenters request EPA provide a technical justification or remove the hull material criterion.

[P29] § 1042.145(k)(3) requiring engines qualifying for the delay to be certified to Tier 3 standards is appropriate, but EPA should clarify whether previously certified Tier 3 engines with alternative deterioration factors remain eligible.

[P30] Allowing sub-600 kW configurations in the same engine family despite lower power density (§ 1042.145(k)(3) permission) could create loopholes for manufacturers to certify high-power configurations using favorable family averaging; commenters request strict family compliance demonstration and limits on inclusion.

[P31] The required label language in § 1042.145(k)(4) replaces the standard compliance statement with a Tier 3 compliance statement; commenters request sample label templates and clarification on whether additional consumer-facing language is required to prevent misuse.

[P32] § 1042.145(k)(4) label statement may negatively affect resale or financing of vessels if lenders or buyers view the label as indicating noncompliance with later standards; stakeholders request safe harbor language for secondary market transactions.

[P33] The procedure in § 1042.145(m) allowing vessel manufacturers to request Tier 4 exemptions beginning MY2024 is reasonable, but the process lacks clear timelines for EPA review and decisions; commenters request defined review periods (e.g., 90 days) and appeal procedures.

[P34] § 1042.145(m)(1) tying exemption requests to the criteria in §1042.145(k)(2) narrows eligibility; vessel manufacturers request a waiver path for vessels that meet most but not all k(2) criteria due to unique mission requirements.

[P35] The requirement in § 1042.145(m)(2) to submit a written exemption request to the Designated Compliance Officer should include a standard submission form and a secure electronic submission channel to avoid processing delays.

[P36] Requiring applicants to explain efforts to find Tier 4 certified engines and design efforts (§ 1042.145(m)(2)) could force disclosure of proprietary supplier search strategies; manufacturers ask EPA to allow confidential business information (CBI) redactions or summaries.

[P37] § 1042.145(m)(2) requiring the number of vessels needing exempt engines should specify the acceptable level of aggregation (per model year, per fleet, or lifetime) and whether estimates may be used; commenters request flexibility.

[P38] § 1042.145(m)(3) permits engine manufacturers to ship exempt engines only after a vessel manufacturer's approved written request is received, which may delay delivery and create supply chain complexities; commenters request a time-limited provisional shipping allowance for inventory already manufactured.

[P39] The exception in § 1042.145(m)(3) relaxing §1068.101(a)(1) prohibitions lacks clarity about cross-border sales and installations; manufacturers want clarification whether exempt engines can be exported or must remain in the U.S. market.

[P40] § 1042.145(m)(3)(i) requiring engines to comply with Tier 3 emissions per §1042.101 and §1068.265 needs EPA to clarify testing, certification, and in-use monitoring obligations for these engines when installed under the exemption.

[P41] § 1042.145(m)(3)(ii) restricting installation only in vessels consistent with paragraph (m) should require vessel-level documentation and post-installation certification to ensure engines are used only in approved vessels.

[P42] The noncompliance label statement required by § 1042.145(m)(3)(iii) is lengthy and could interfere with OEM labeling space and readability; EPA should permit an abbreviated standardized label and require distribution of a companion notice or manual insert.

[P43] The noncompliance label (§ 1042.145(m)(3)(iii)) may create liability for downstream installers who unknowingly install an exempt engine in an ineligible vessel; commenters request clear instructions and a registry of exempt engines to minimize accidental misuse.

[P44] § 1042.145(n) allowing assigned deterioration factors for certifying certain Tier 4 engines raises concerns that default multipliers (1.1 for NOx, 1.4 for HC/CO, additive 0.003 g/kW-hr PM) in § 1042.145(n)(3) may be inappropriate for some designs; engine manufacturers request a straightforward process and timelines for EPA approval of alternative factors.

[P45] The duration of eligibility for assigned deterioration factors through model year 2023 (§ 1042.145(n)(1)) and through 2025 (§ 1042.145(n)(2)) is inconsistent and may complicate product planning; commenters ask EPA to harmonize the dates or provide an explanation.

[P46] The rule’s demonstration standard for EPA to approve alternative deterioration factors (§ 1042.145(n)(3) permission) is vague; manufacturers request explicit data requirements (sample size, test cycles, statistical metrics) for approval.

[P47] § 1042.145(n)(3) default PM additive value of 0.003 g/kW-hr may be either too lenient or too strict depending on engine class; commenters request the ability to use measured deterioration data from in-use engines for more accurate certification.

[P48] § 1042.145(o) requiring a useful life of 10 years or 5,000 hours for certain Category 1 engines diverges from §1042.101(e) values and could impose longer warranty and monitoring requirements on manufacturers; industry requests alignment with existing useful-life conventions or compensation for extended responsibility.

[P49] The combination of exemptions, labeling, and recordkeeping across Parts 80 and 1042 creates complex compliance interplay; legal experts request EPA to publish comprehensive guidance, flowcharts, and example compliance pathways showing interactions between fuel exemptions and engine delays/exemptions.

[P50] Small businesses (fuel retailers, small boatyards, and small vessel manufacturers) will need compliance cost estimates; commenters request EPA to prepare and publish an economic impact analysis and provide temporary compliance assistance or phased implementation timelines.

[P51] Enforcement mechanisms and penalties for mislabeling or misuse of exempt global marine fuel (§ 80.605) and misuse of exempt engines (§ 1042.145(m)) are not described; stakeholders request clear enforcement policy, penalty ranges, and corrective-action procedures to ensure fair and predictable application.

[P52] The proposed rule should explicitly require coordination with the U.S. Coast Guard, Customs and Border Protection, and state environmental agencies for monitoring and enforcement of marine fuel segregation and exempt engine installation to avoid regulatory gaps.

Requiring recording the location, date, time, and storage tank/truck ID for each sample (§ 80.602(a)(2)(i)) is operationally feasible for terminal-based sampling but will be burdensome and sometimes impossible for transient barge or shipboard sampling; the rule should allow reasonable alternatives for marine contexts.

§ 80.602(a)(2)(ii) mandating names and titles of sampler and tester raises privacy and personnel-security concerns for small contractors; the agency should accept company identifiers and batch lab IDs in lieu of individual names.

The mandated recording of test results for sulfur content, including application of adjustment factors (§ 80.602(a)(2)(iii)), requires the rule to provide explicit formulas and examples for how to apply adjustment factors to avoid inconsistent reporting between laboratories.

§ 80.602(a)(3) requires documenting actions taken to stop sale or distribution of noncompliant fuel, but provides no timeframe for corrective actions or required preventive steps; commenters request clear timelines and required content (root-cause analysis, corrective action plan) to ensure consistent enforcement.

The effective date for global marine fuel recordkeeping (§ 80.602 start Jan 1, 2020) is in the past; parties who have already disposed of records should be treated fairly and the EPA should state it will not seek penalties for pre-existing gaps if good-faith efforts are demonstrated.

§ 80.602(b)(4)(i) requires including records pertaining to multiple fuel types (NRLM, NR, LM, global marine, ECA marine, heating oil) but does not define the boundaries between these categories or how blended products should be classified; EPA should provide clear definitions and examples for blended fuels.

§ 80.598(a)(2)(i)(G) requires identifying exempt distillate fuels including global marine fuels in designation documentation; the proposal lacks a standardized code or label set that would enable industry to program designation systems—EPA should publish a required data dictionary.

§ 80.598(b)(8)(iii) requires providing listed identification info for exempt distillate fuels as part of designation procedures, but the rule doesn't specify who is responsible at each transfer point (producer, importer, terminal operator, retailer); commenters urge EPA to allocate responsibilities precisely.

The broad exemption in § 80.605(a) for global marine fuel used in steamships or Category 3 vessels outside ECAs risks incentivizing mislabeling and sale into non-exempt markets; EPA should consider tightening eligibility or adding robust verification/chain-of-custody requirements.

§ 80.605(b) conditions for exemption are numerous and complex; industry requests a consolidated checklist and template attestation form that suppliers can use to certify compliance with all conditions before claiming the exemption.

The sulfur limit in § 80.605(b)(1) set at 0.50 wt% (5,000 ppm) is higher than many international fuel specifications and could create health and environmental impacts in port communities if misused; environmental groups will oppose allowing fuel with such high sulfur except under tightly controlled circumstances.

Conversely, some small vessel operators contend the 0.50 wt% cap is too restrictive for existing refineries or remote bunkering operations and request an alternative compliance mechanism (e.g., documented scrubber use or onboard emissions controls) rather than a strict sulfur threshold.

§ 80.605(b)(2) requires that exempt fuel be accompanied by § 80.590 product transfer documents; commenters ask EPA to explicitly allow consolidated batch paperwork for bunkering operations where one delivery fuels multiple vessels, as per international bunkering practices.

The designation requirement under § 80.605(b)(3) referencing § 80.598 lacks clarity on who must perform the designation and when (producer at refinery, importer at port, or bunker supplier at sale); commenters request a chain-of-custody model and liability allocation.

Requiring physical segregation of exempt fuel from non-exempt fuel throughout distribution (§ 80.605(b)(4)) is operationally impracticable at multi-product terminals that use shared pipelines and tanks; terminal operators request an allowance for use of dedicated bladders, time-based segregation with flushing protocols, or mass-balance accounting.

The prohibition in § 80.605(b)(5) against using exempt fuel in any equipment other than steamships or Category 3 marine vessels could be unenforceable without labeling and downstream checks; marine engine manufacturers and port authorities request explicit marking requirements at the dispenser and enforcement guidance.

§ 80.605(c) makes fuel that fails exemption conditions subject to MVNRLM standards but does not clarify how jurisdictional enforcement and penalties will be applied when fuel crosses borders between vessels and shore; commenters want harmonization with Coast Guard and customs authorities.

The prohibition in § 80.605(c) on claiming exemption if § 80.602 recordkeeping is not met creates a strict liability standard that could penalize clerical errors; legal experts recommend a “cure period” or opportunity to correct recordkeeping deficiencies before loss of exemption and enforcement.

§ 1042.145(k) permitting delays to Tier 4 for certain engines and vessels could undermine national air quality goals by allowing continued sale of higher-emitting engines; environmental NGOs will comment that EPA must justify emissions tradeoffs and include sunsets.

The power density threshold (>35.0 kW/liter and >40.0 kW/liter in later years) in § 1042.145(k)(1)(i) and (k)(2)(i) is overly technical and may be manipulable by manufacturers through minor design changes; commenters request EPA to require independent testing or third-party verification of power density claims.

The vessel total propulsion power caps (≤2,800 kW for MY2021 and ≤1,000 kW for MY2022–2023) in §§ 1042.145(k)(1)(ii) and (k)(2)(ii) could exclude many common commercial vessels; industry asks EPA to publish an exhaustive list of vessel types that would or would not qualify under these thresholds.

The vessel length thresholds (≤65 ft and ≤50 ft in §§ 1042.145(k)(1)(iii) and (k)(2)(iii)) appear arbitrary and do not correlate directly with emissions; commenters propose substituting thresholds tied to emissions potential or use-case (e.g., tonnage, service type).

Requiring vessels to qualify as uninspected under 46 CFR 2.01–7 (§§ 1042.145(k)(1)(iv) and (k)(2)(iv)) could exclude many small commercial vessels that are inspected but face the same installation constraints; stakeholders request EPA allow inspected vessels if they meet other qualifying criteria.

The speed requirement (max speed ≥ 3.0 * sqrt(L) in §§ 1042.145(k)(1)(v) and (k)(2)(v)) is an unconventional operational metric that will require manufacturers and owners to perform additional sea trials; the rule should allow documented design speed or manufacturer-rated speed as an alternative.

The hull material requirement in § 1042.145(k)(2)(vi) (fiberglass or other nonmetal hulls) unfairly disadvantages aluminum or steel small-vessel manufacturers and seems unrelated to emissions; commenters request EPA provide a technical justification or remove the hull material criterion.

§ 1042.145(k)(3) requiring engines qualifying for the delay to be certified to Tier 3 standards is appropriate, but EPA should clarify whether previously certified Tier 3 engines with alternative deterioration factors remain eligible.

Allowing sub-600 kW configurations in the same engine family despite lower power density (§ 1042.145(k)(3) permission) could create loopholes for manufacturers to certify high-power configurations using favorable family averaging; commenters request strict family compliance demonstration and limits on inclusion.

The required label language in § 1042.145(k)(4) replaces the standard compliance statement with a Tier 3 compliance statement; commenters request sample label templates and clarification on whether additional consumer-facing language is required to prevent misuse.

§ 1042.145(k)(4) label statement may negatively affect resale or financing of vessels if lenders or buyers view the label as indicating noncompliance with later standards; stakeholders request safe harbor language for secondary market transactions.

The procedure in § 1042.145(m) allowing vessel manufacturers to request Tier 4 exemptions beginning MY2024 is reasonable, but the process lacks clear timelines for EPA review and decisions; commenters request defined review periods (e.g., 90 days) and appeal procedures.

§ 1042.145(m)(1) tying exemption requests to the criteria in §1042.145(k)(2) narrows eligibility; vessel manufacturers request a waiver path for vessels that meet most but not all k(2) criteria due to unique mission requirements.

The requirement in § 1042.145(m)(2) to submit a written exemption request to the Designated Compliance Officer should include a standard submission form and a secure electronic submission channel to avoid processing delays.

Requiring applicants to explain efforts to find Tier 4 certified engines and design efforts (§ 1042.145(m)(2)) could force disclosure of proprietary supplier search strategies; manufacturers ask EPA to allow confidential business information (CBI) redactions or summaries.

§ 1042.145(m)(2) requiring the number of vessels needing exempt engines should specify the acceptable level of aggregation (per model year, per fleet, or lifetime) and whether estimates may be used; commenters request flexibility.

§ 1042.145(m)(3) permits engine manufacturers to ship exempt engines only after a vessel manufacturer's approved written request is received, which may delay delivery and create supply chain complexities; commenters request a time-limited provisional shipping allowance for inventory already manufactured.

The exception in § 1042.145(m)(3) relaxing §1068.101(a)(1) prohibitions lacks clarity about cross-border sales and installations; manufacturers want clarification whether exempt engines can be exported or must remain in the U.S. market.

§ 1042.145(m)(3)(i) requiring engines to comply with Tier 3 emissions per §1042.101 and §1068.265 needs EPA to clarify testing, certification, and in-use monitoring obligations for these engines when installed under the exemption.

The noncompliance label statement required by § 1042.145(m)(3)(iii) is lengthy and could interfere with OEM labeling space and readability; EPA should permit an abbreviated standardized label and require distribution of a companion notice or manual insert.

The noncompliance label (§ 1042.145(m)(3)(iii)) may create liability for downstream installers who unknowingly install an exempt engine in an ineligible vessel; commenters request clear instructions and a registry of exempt engines to minimize accidental misuse.

§ 1042.145(n) allowing assigned deterioration factors for certifying certain Tier 4 engines raises concerns that default multipliers (1.1 for NOx, 1.4 for HC/CO, additive 0.003 g/kW-hr PM) in § 1042.145(n)(3) may be inappropriate for some designs; engine manufacturers request a straightforward process and timelines for EPA approval of alternative factors.

The duration of eligibility for assigned deterioration factors through model year 2023 (§ 1042.145(n)(1)) and through 2025 (§ 1042.145(n)(2)) is inconsistent and may complicate product planning; commenters ask EPA to harmonize the dates or provide an explanation.

The rule’s demonstration standard for EPA to approve alternative deterioration factors (§ 1042.145(n)(3) permission) is vague; manufacturers request explicit data requirements (sample size, test cycles, statistical metrics) for approval.

§ 1042.145(n)(3) default PM additive value of 0.003 g/kW-hr may be either too lenient or too strict depending on engine class; commenters request the ability to use measured deterioration data from in-use engines for more accurate certification.

§ 1042.145(o) requiring a useful life of 10 years or 5,000 hours for certain Category 1 engines diverges from §1042.101(e) values and could impose longer warranty and monitoring requirements on manufacturers; industry requests alignment with existing useful-life conventions or compensation for extended responsibility.

The combination of exemptions, labeling, and recordkeeping across Parts 80 and 1042 creates complex compliance interplay; legal experts request EPA to publish comprehensive guidance, flowcharts, and example compliance pathways showing interactions between fuel exemptions and engine delays/exemptions.

Small businesses (fuel retailers, small boatyards, and small vessel manufacturers) will need compliance cost estimates; commenters request EPA to prepare and publish an economic impact analysis and provide temporary compliance assistance or phased implementation timelines.

Enforcement mechanisms and penalties for mislabeling or misuse of exempt global marine fuel (§ 80.605) and misuse of exempt engines (§ 1042.145(m)) are not described; stakeholders request clear enforcement policy, penalty ranges, and corrective-action procedures to ensure fair and predictable application.

The proposed rule should explicitly require coordination with the U.S. Coast Guard, Customs and Border Protection, and state environmental agencies for monitoring and enforcement of marine fuel segregation and exempt engine installation to avoid regulatory gaps.

[P1] The June 22, 2020 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonable and should be extended to allow affected operators and manufacturers sufficient time to analyze the technical rule and prepare meaningful comments.

[P1] Many small operators and third‑party vendors will not have been notified in time to meet the June 22, 2020 deadline; the FAA should reopen or extend the comment period to ensure equitable participation.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether electronic comments submitted before June 22, 2020 but not acknowledged will be considered timely; as written, § 39.13(a) creates uncertainty about receipt verification.

[P2] § 39.13(f)'s requirement to "comply with all requirements...within the specified compliance times" is overly rigid and does not allow for operational interruptions; the FAA should allow phased compliance or provide relief for operators with scheduling constraints.

[P2] The phrase "unless already complied with" in § 39.13(f) needs defining — operators need guidance on what documentation is acceptable to demonstrate prior compliance.

[P3] The 120‑day deadline to "install eligible EEC software" (§ 39.13(g)) is too short for fleetwide planning, procurement, testing, and installation, particularly for large commercial operators and international operators subject to multiple authorities.

[P3] § 39.13(g) should specify which EEC software versions are "eligible for installation" and provide a list or reference to approved software part numbers; otherwise operators cannot determine compliance.

[P3] There is no allowance in § 39.13(g) for required ground or flight testing after EEC software installation; the rule should require or permit phased validation and specify acceptable test procedures.

[P3] The rule must clarify whether third‑party maintenance organizations are authorized to install the EEC software within the 120‑day period under § 39.13(g), and what certification is required.

[P4] While § 39.13(i)(1) permits AMOC approval by the Manager, ECO Branch, FAA, it should also expressly allow delegated organizations (DARs) or manufacturers to propose AMOCs earlier in the process to expedite safe alternatives.

[P4] The provision in § 39.13(i)(1) that only the Manager, ECO Branch, may approve AMOCs could create bottlenecks; the FAA should publish expected turnaround times and criteria for approval.

[P5] § 39.13(i)(1) requires sending AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO, but does not clarify whether electronic submission to the principal inspector satisfies 14 CFR 39.19 — the rule should explicitly accept electronic submission methods.

[P5] The obligation in § 39.13(i)(1) to send AMOC requests to the "appropriate" principal inspector or FSDO is ambiguous for operators with multiple-designated principal inspectors; the FAA should provide guidance on which office has jurisdiction.

[P6] § 39.13(i)(1)'s instruction to address direct submissions to the person named in paragraph (j)(1) is incomplete as published; commenters object to the cross‑reference being truncated and request the rule be corrected to fully identify the addressee.

[P6] The rule should specify a physical and electronic address for direct AMOC submissions to the certification office manager (per § 39.13(i)(1) condition) so there is no confusion about where to send time‑sensitive requests.

[P7] Permitting AMOC requests via ANE–AD–AMOC@faa.gov (§ 39.13(i)(1)) is helpful, but the FAA must publish receipt confirmation procedures and expected processing times for email submissions to avoid claims of untimeliness.

[P7] The rule should allow alternative email addresses or web portal submissions for operators outside the ANE region; restricting to a single ANE email may delay AMOC processing for large multinational operators.

[P8] § 39.13(i)(2) requires notification of the principal inspector or local FSDO/CHDO manager before using an approved AMOC but does not specify the timeframe for such notification; commenters ask for a clear advance notice period (e.g., 48 or 72 hours).

[P8] The obligation in § 39.13(i)(2) to notify a principal inspector before using an AMOC could impede urgent safety actions; there should be an exception permitting immediate use followed by retroactive notification in emergency circumstances.

[P8] The rule should clarify the form of notification required by § 39.13(i)(2) (written, electronic, logging in maintenance records) and whether copies of the AMOC approval must be attached to aircraft records.

[P9] Allowing viewing of referenced service information at the FAA Airworthiness Products Section (§ 39.13(j)(2)) is useful, but the provision must also require the FAA to make that information available electronically for remote stakeholders and non‑local commenters.

[P9] The address in § 39.13(j)(2) (1200 District Avenue, Burlington) assumes physical access — international operators, lessors, and aftermarket vendors need downloadable copies and machine‑readable formats to evaluate compliance.

[general/legal] Several provisions (notably P1, P3, P5, P6) are vague or contain incomplete cross‑references; commenters request that the FAA correct typographical errors, fully identify persons/addresses in paragraph (j)(1), and republish the AD with clarified text before finalization.

[industry] Manufacturers and maintenance providers request a coordination period to finalize EEC software eligibility criteria and to publish a list of affected EEC part numbers and software release notes before the 120‑day installation requirement becomes mandatory.
