[P1] The requirement that "all new or revised DOE guidance documents" meet the content requirements in §1061.3(a) is overbroad and will unduly burden routine, technical, or internal guidance that does not affect the public; we request narrower scope or explicit exemptions for ministerial/internal-only documents.

[P2] §1061.3(a)(1) is redundant and potentially confusing: saying guidance must "comply with all applicable statutes and regulations" risks implying guidance itself creates new legal obligations; clarify that guidance must accurately reflect existing statutes/regulations rather than create independent legal duties.

[P3] The mandated "clear prominent declaration" in §1061.3(a)(2) is reasonable, but the rule should prescribe minimum formatting/placement standards (e.g., first page, font size) to ensure consistency and avoid litigation over what is "prominent."

[P4] §1061.3(a)(2)(i) requiring a statement that the document "does not have the force and effect of law" could confuse regulated parties when guidance interprets ambiguous statutory provisions; recommend adding language that guidance represents the agency's authoritative interpretation unless and until superseded by regulation or adjudication.

[P5] The exception clause referenced in §1061.3(a)(2)(ii) (authorization by law or contract) is truncated and unclear; the rule should explicitly define when guidance may be incorporated into contracts or authorized by law to avoid conflicting interpretations.

[P6] §1061.3(a)(2)(iii)'s promise that "DOE will not rely upon the document as an independent basis for an enforcement action" is ambiguous—does it preclude using guidance as evidence of knowledge or intent in enforcement? Clarify that DOE may not cite guidance as an independent legal basis but may consider it as interpretive context where relevant facts are in dispute.

[P7] The prohibition in §1061.3(a)(3) against mandatory wording unless describing statutory/regulatory requirements is vague—many interpretive recommendations legitimately use "must" to convey best practices; recommend allowing plain-language mandatory terms when accompanied by the declaration required in (a)(2).

[P8] The "directed solely to DOE personnel" exception in §1061.3(a)(3) (P8) lacks criteria to determine when a document "is not intended to have an impact on regulated parties"; request criteria or a certification process to avoid selective evasion of the wording prohibition.

[P9] §1061.3(a)(4) requires plain language; industry supports plain language but requests the rule exempt highly technical guidance where specialized terminology is necessary, or allow supplemental technical appendices to preserve precision.

[P10] The requirement to include the term "guidance" (§1061.3(a)(5)(i)) is minor but could produce awkward titles for documents that are jointly issued with other agencies; allow cross-references or joint-title exceptions.

[P11] §1061.3(a)(5)(iv) requiring specification of "activities and persons to which the guidance applies" could be interpreted to create a binding scope limitation; clarify that this is descriptive and not an exclusive limitation on DOE's enforcement or interpretation.

[P12] The requirement to cite the "relevant statute or regulation" (§1061.3(a)(5)(vii)) may be impossible in guidance that covers policy matters spanning multiple statutes; allow multiple citations or a range and permit hyperlinking to comprehensive lists.

[P13] §1061.3(b) mandating review by the Office of the Assistant General Counsel for Legislation, Regulation and Energy Efficiency could create bottlenecks and delay critical guidance; propose delegation to component legal offices with periodic centralized audits.

[P14] §1061.3(b)(1) directing reviewers to ensure compliance with EO 13891 as well as this part duplicates executive-order requirements and may constrain DOE discretion; request alignment language acknowledging other applicable internal review processes.

[P15] §1061.3(b)(2)'s requirement to obtain an Administrator determination of "significant" for every guidance risks inconsistent classifications and delay; request objective criteria or thresholds for "significant" to ensure predictable application.

[P16] §1061.3(b)(3)/§1061.3(c) that require coordination with OIRA for "significant" documents effectively subjects DOE guidance to OMB clearance processes not contemplated by statute; industry and states may oppose OMB's expanded role—request limiting OIRA coordination to guidance that has economically significant effects or affect other agencies.

[P17] The 30-day public comment period in §1061.3(c)(1) for "significant" guidance is insufficient for complex technical issues and for stakeholder groups requiring internal review; request a 60- or 90-day minimum or a tiered schedule based on complexity.

[P18] §1061.3(c)(2) requiring DOE to publicly respond to "major and relevant" comments is appropriate, but the rule should define "major and relevant" to avoid litigation over the adequacy of responses.

[P19] §1061.3(c)(3) requiring Secretary or component head approval prior to issuance of significant guidance centralizes authority and may politicize technical guidance; suggest allowing component heads to delegate approval to career officials in certain cases.

[P20] Requiring Administrator review under EO 12866 (§1061.3(c)(4)) for significant guidance could import cost-benefit analysis burdens onto interpretive documents; ask DOE to clarify when economic analysis is required and provide safe-harbor thresholds.

[P21] §1061.3(c)(5) mandating compliance with five Executive Orders (12866, 13563, 13609, 13771, 13777) may impose conflicting obligations (e.g., reducing regulatory burden vs. international regulatory cooperation); request guidance on resolving conflicts among EO requirements.

[P22] §1061.3(d) permits DOE to dispense with notice-and-comment for good cause but requires including the finding in the document (§1061.3(d) incorporation). Stakeholders will challenge both the scope of "good cause" and the sufficiency of a brief statement; demand a heightened justification standard and administrative record when skipping comment.

[P23] The categorical and exigent exceptions in §1061.3(e)(1)–(2) are too vague; request publication of any categorical exceptions and an annual report justifying their continued use to ensure transparency.

[P24] §1061.3(f)(1) requiring a single DOE web portal is supported for accessibility, but the rule needs to specify metadata, searchability, and machine-readable formats to make the portal usable by industry compliance systems.

[P25] §1061.3(f)(2) directing DOE to state on the portal that guidance is not legally binding is sensible, but the portal statement should also clarify how guidance interacts with contracts, grants, and cooperative agreements to avoid uncertainty.

[P26] §1061.3(g) deeming non-posted guidance "rescinded" is drastic and risks unintentionally rescinding longstanding operational guidance relied upon by regulated entities; require a phased approach, grandfathering, or notice before rescission.

[P27] The prohibition in §1061.3(g) against citing or relying on rescinded guidance except for historical facts is overly restrictive—DOE may need to rely on older guidance in active litigation or ongoing programs; allow limited temporary use where reliance interests exist until replacement guidance is issued.

[P28] §1061.3(g) creates significant legal uncertainty for regulated parties who have relied on guidance not yet posted on the portal; request an explicit non-retroactivity clause that rescission does not relieve parties of obligations or affect past compliance determinations.

[P29] §1061.4(a) allowing anyone to petition DOE to withdraw or modify guidance is positive, but the required addressing to a specific Assistant General Counsel and physical delivery methods (§1061.4(a)(1)–(3)) may disadvantage remote or under-resourced stakeholders; ensure electronic petitions via Guidance@hq.doe.gov are treated as timely and valid and publicize alternative submission supports.

[P30] The detailed petitioner identifying information in §1061.4(b)(1)–(4) (name, telephone, mailing, email) may deter anonymous or sensitive submissions; request the ability to submit petitions anonymously or with privacy protections in cases alleging misconduct.

[P31] §1061.4(b)(2)’s requirement to identify the specific guidance document is necessary but may be impractical where a petition concerns a family of cross-referenced documents; allow petitions to identify all applicable guidance by topic or citation range.

[P32] §1061.4(b)(3) requiring petitions to be signed may limit electronic filers; permit electronic signatures and clarify what constitutes an authorized representative.

[P33] The "should" provisions in §1061.4(c) that urge additional supporting information could be elevated to required elements for petitions to deter frivolous petitions; conversely, some nonprofits and small entities may lack resources—recommend a streamlined petition path for individuals and small entities.

[P34] §1061.4(c)(4) requiring technical/scientific data to support assertions may disadvantage procedural or legal challenges that do not hinge on technical data; clarify that legal or policy arguments without technical data are still valid petition bases.

[P35] §1061.4(d) obligating DOE to publish petitions in the Federal Register and allow comment is good, but the automatic publication requirement could expose confidential business information; ensure robust redaction procedures and timely CBI determinations per §1061.4(e).

[P36] §1061.4(d) allows DOE to waive notice-and-comment for petitions for good cause; stakeholders fear this could be abused to avoid scrutiny—require DOE to publish its good cause finding in the Federal Register contemporaneously and allow an expedited judicial review window.

[P37] §1061.4(e) requiring redacted copies for confidential treatment is consistent with FOIA rules, but the burden should not fall entirely on petitioners; DOE should offer guidance and confidentiality consultation and accept sealed CBI filings where necessary.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The requirement that "all new or revised DOE guidance documents" meet the content requirements in §1061.3(a) is overbroad and will unduly burden routine, technical, or internal guidance that does not affect the public; we request narrower scope or explicit exemptions for ministerial/internal-only documents.

§1061.3(a)(1) is redundant and potentially confusing: saying guidance must "comply with all applicable statutes and regulations" risks implying guidance itself creates new legal obligations; clarify that guidance must accurately reflect existing statutes/regulations rather than create independent legal duties.

The mandated "clear prominent declaration" in §1061.3(a)(2) is reasonable, but the rule should prescribe minimum formatting/placement standards (e.g., first page, font size) to ensure consistency and avoid litigation over what is "prominent."

§1061.3(a)(2)(i) requiring a statement that the document "does not have the force and effect of law" could confuse regulated parties when guidance interprets ambiguous statutory provisions; recommend adding language that guidance represents the agency's authoritative interpretation unless and until superseded by regulation or adjudication.

The exception clause referenced in §1061.3(a)(2)(ii) (authorization by law or contract) is truncated and unclear; the rule should explicitly define when guidance may be incorporated into contracts or authorized by law to avoid conflicting interpretations.

§1061.3(a)(2)(iii)'s promise that "DOE will not rely upon the document as an independent basis for an enforcement action" is ambiguous—does it preclude using guidance as evidence of knowledge or intent in enforcement? Clarify that DOE may not cite guidance as an independent legal basis but may consider it as interpretive context where relevant facts are in dispute.

The prohibition in §1061.3(a)(3) against mandatory wording unless describing statutory/regulatory requirements is vague—many interpretive recommendations legitimately use "must" to convey best practices; recommend allowing plain-language mandatory terms when accompanied by the declaration required in (a)(2).

The "directed solely to DOE personnel" exception in §1061.3(a)(3) (P8) lacks criteria to determine when a document "is not intended to have an impact on regulated parties"; request criteria or a certification process to avoid selective evasion of the wording prohibition.

§1061.3(a)(4) requires plain language; industry supports plain language but requests the rule exempt highly technical guidance where specialized terminology is necessary, or allow supplemental technical appendices to preserve precision.

The requirement to include the term "guidance" (§1061.3(a)(5)(i)) is minor but could produce awkward titles for documents that are jointly issued with other agencies; allow cross-references or joint-title exceptions.

§1061.3(a)(5)(iv) requiring specification of "activities and persons to which the guidance applies" could be interpreted to create a binding scope limitation; clarify that this is descriptive and not an exclusive limitation on DOE's enforcement or interpretation.

The requirement to cite the "relevant statute or regulation" (§1061.3(a)(5)(vii)) may be impossible in guidance that covers policy matters spanning multiple statutes; allow multiple citations or a range and permit hyperlinking to comprehensive lists.

§1061.3(b) mandating review by the Office of the Assistant General Counsel for Legislation, Regulation and Energy Efficiency could create bottlenecks and delay critical guidance; propose delegation to component legal offices with periodic centralized audits.

§1061.3(b)(1) directing reviewers to ensure compliance with EO 13891 as well as this part duplicates executive-order requirements and may constrain DOE discretion; request alignment language acknowledging other applicable internal review processes.

§1061.3(b)(2)'s requirement to obtain an Administrator determination of "significant" for every guidance risks inconsistent classifications and delay; request objective criteria or thresholds for "significant" to ensure predictable application.

§1061.3(b)(3)/§1061.3(c) that require coordination with OIRA for "significant" documents effectively subjects DOE guidance to OMB clearance processes not contemplated by statute; industry and states may oppose OMB's expanded role—request limiting OIRA coordination to guidance that has economically significant effects or affect other agencies.

The 30-day public comment period in §1061.3(c)(1) for "significant" guidance is insufficient for complex technical issues and for stakeholder groups requiring internal review; request a 60- or 90-day minimum or a tiered schedule based on complexity.
§1061.3(c)(2) requiring DOE to publicly respond to "major and relevant" comments is appropriate, but the rule should define "major and relevant" to avoid litigation over the adequacy of responses.

§1061.3(c)(3) requiring Secretary or component head approval prior to issuance of significant guidance centralizes authority and may politicize technical guidance; suggest allowing component heads to delegate approval to career officials in certain cases.

Stakeholders will challenge both the scope of "good cause" and the sufficiency of a brief statement; demand a heightened justification standard and administrative record when skipping comment.

[P1] The April 16, 2018 comment deadline in P1 is unreasonably short and does not provide sufficient time for stakeholders (airlines, MROs, labor unions, and foreign operators) to prepare technical comments; request an extension of at least 60 days.

[P1] The AD should clarify whether the April 16, 2018 due date is inclusive of mailed comments received by that date or only those timestamped in FAA electronic systems; request explicit acceptance rules for mailed, emailed, and hand-delivered comments.

[P1] The rule does not specify whether requests for extensions or petitions for late-filed comments will be considered; request that the FAA state a formal process for accepting late comments under extenuating circumstances.

[P2] The applicability in P2 referencing “as identified in the referenced service bulletin” is ambiguous—stakeholders need the exact effectivity (serial numbers, line numbers, or configuration codes) listed in the AD text, not only in the service bulletin.

[P2] Because P2 applies to Model 757–200, –200PF, –200CB, and –300 “certificated in any category,” the AD may inadvertently apply to aircraft used by government, cargo, or special-purpose operators; request a clear statement of any exclusions or tailored applicability for government/military-configured 757s.

[P2] Foreign-registered 757 operators require confirmation that P2’s applicability extends to their aircraft under FAA authority when operated into U.S. airspace; request cross-reference to ICAO/foreign authority coordination.

[P3] P3 requires compliance “within the specified compliance times” but does not restate the compliance time windows in the AD text; request that the AD include the critical compliance time(s) explicitly to avoid misinterpretation if the service bulletin is revised.

[P3] The AD should state whether compliance times in the service bulletin are calendar-based, flight-hour-based, or cycle-based; the absence of that distinction in P3 creates operational uncertainty for scheduling compliance.

[P4] P4 mandates performing all RC-designated actions in the Boeing Alert Service Bulletin but does not provide a mechanism for operators to document completion when the service bulletin is revised; request required forms or traceability requirements be specified.

[P4] The AD’s incorporation by reference of Boeing Alert Service Bulletin 75 (as cited) without also including any FAA-originated alternative procedures places excessive reliance on manufacturer documentation; request the FAA publish any FAA-approved deviations alongside the AD.

[P4] P4’s cross-reference to paragraph 1.E “Compliance” of the service bulletin may create conflicting compliance deadlines if future revisions renumber sections; request the AD specify the exact RC steps and table references to avoid reliance on future service bulletin layout.

[P5] The exception in P5 substituting the AD effective date for the service bulletin original issue date may disadvantage operators that already complied to the service bulletin’s original date; request clarification whether earlier compliance remains acceptable and how to document pre-effective-date actions.

[P5] The language in P5 could be read to retroactively shorten compliance timelines for operators who planned based on the service bulletin original issue date; request confirmation that the substitution will not impose shorter deadlines than originally intended.

[P6] P6 requires using an AMOC under paragraph (i) when the service bulletin directs contacting Boeing for RC actions; this shifts authority from the manufacturer to FAA but lacks specifics about expected AMOC content and review timelines — request required data elements and a 60-day FAA review target.

[P6] Requiring AMOCs instead of following Boeing contact procedures may disproportionately burden operators and Boeing ODA processes—suggest allowing documented Boeing-approved instructions as interim measures while an AMOC is processed.

[P7] P7 vests AMOC approval authority solely in the Manager, Los Angeles ACO Branch, which could create bottlenecks and geographic inequity for operators not based in the LA region; request simultaneous delegation options to other ACO branches or centralized e-approval to avoid delays.

[P7] Legal commenters should note P7 may conflict with established delegations under 14 CFR 39.19 in some regions; request FAA to clarify that existing delegations remain valid or to publish any changes to delegation authority.

[P8] P8 mandates sending AMOC requests to principal inspectors or local FSDOs per 14 CFR 39.19 but does not address digital submission standards (preferred file formats, security, attachments such as large engineering files); request guidance on acceptable electronic formats and maximum file sizes.

[P8] The requirement in P8 may impose inconsistent local practices if principal inspectors interpret 14 CFR 39.19 differently; request the FAA provide a standardized AMOC submission checklist to ensure uniformity.

[P9] P9 directs direct submissions to the person in paragraph (j)(1) but the AD does not reproduce that contact name or title within the public AD text provided; request that the AD include the full contact information to avoid misplaced or delayed submissions.

[P9] For international operators, P9’s single point of contact may not be practical due to time zone and language constraints; request an alternative international contact point or assurance of email processing for non-U.S. applicants.

[P10] P10 permits emailing AMOC information to 9-ANM-LAACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov but does not specify email security/formatting or confirm receipt procedures; request automated receipt acknowledgments and confirmation timelines.

[P10] Allowing email as in P10 is positive, but the AD should also permit secure file transfer for engineering drawings and large datasets; request inclusion of acceptable secure transfer mechanisms.

[P11] P11 requires notifying the principal inspector or FSDO manager before using an approved AMOC but does not state the minimum advance notice time; request a defined notice period (e.g., 72 hours) and the required notification content.

[P11] The AD should clarify whether verbal notification suffices under P11 or whether written notice is required; request specification that notification must be written and retained in records.

[P12] P12 allows using an AMOC-approved repair/modification if approved by an authorized Boeing ODA; this could permit manufacturer ODAs to approve AMOCs without FAA oversight — request clarity on the extent of Boeing ODA authority and FAA concurrence requirements.

[P12] Labor and safety advocacy groups may object under P12 that allowing Boeing ODA approvals could create conflicts of interest; request that the FAA require FAA concurrence or independent engineering review for ODA-approved AMOCs used for RC actions.

[P13] P13 requires that AMOC-approved repairs meet the airplane’s certification basis and specifically reference this AD, but does not specify how to demonstrate equivalency to the certification basis for legacy modifications; request guidance on acceptable substantiation methods and burden of proof.

[P13] Legal commenters should ask whether P13 requires reinterpretation of the original certification basis for older aircraft and, if so, how differences in previous amendments or exemptions will be handled.

[P14] P14 states that paragraphs (i)(4)(i) and (i)(4)(ii) govern compliance with RC-labeled steps but does not indicate how conflicts between the service bulletin text and AD text will be resolved; request a precedence clause that establishes AD text controls.

[P15] P15 mandating that all RC-labeled steps, substeps, and identified figures must be performed creates operational inflexibility for in-service repairs that may require slight deviations; request a streamlined AMOC pathway for minor deviations with short FAA review timelines.

[P15] Maintenance organizations will need clarity under P15 about recordkeeping for RC step completion (who signs, which forms), so request that the FAA specify acceptable logbook entries or electronic records.

[P16] P16’s RC Exempt carve-out may be insufficiently visible in the service bulletin; request the FAA require Boeing to clearly mark RC Exempt steps in the service bulletin and provide an index of exempted steps in the AD.

[P16] Some commenters may argue that P16 could be misinterpreted and want confirmation that “RC Exempt” labeling in revised service bulletins will be preserved and will not be treated as RC unless explicitly restated in a new AD.

[P17] P17’s blanket AMOC requirement for any deviations to RC steps may delay urgent in-service corrective actions; request allowance for a time-limited post-action AMOC filing in emergency situations (e.g., allow repairing deviation with immediate notification and filing within 5 business days).

[P17] Operators will need guidance on what constitutes a “deviation” under P17 (minor tolerance differences vs. substantive procedural changes); request FAA issue examples and thresholds that differentiate between reportable deviations and those requiring AMOCs.

[P18] P18 permits deviations from non-RC steps under the operator’s maintenance program but conditions that RC steps remain performable and the airplane can be returned to airworthy condition; request explicit criteria and documentation requirements for demonstrating that RC steps remain performable.

[P18] There is ambiguity in P18 about whether operators may rely on their SMS (safety management system) analyses to justify deviations from non-RC steps; request the FAA explicitly permit SMS-based risk assessments as part of the operator’s maintenance/inspection program justification.

[P6][P12] (combined) Several commenters will raise a legal concern that P6 and P12 together create overlapping approval pathways (contact Boeing vs. FAA AMOC vs. Boeing ODA approval) — request the FAA clarify the hierarchy and interactions among Boeing contact instructions, Boeing ODA approvals, and FAA AMOC approvals.

[P4][P14] (combined) The AD relies heavily on Boeing Alert Service Bulletin content while P14 states AD provisions govern RC steps — request the FAA include a redline or appendix summarizing the exact RC steps and any FAA modifications to the service bulletin to avoid conflicting interpretations.

[P3][P5] (combined) Request confirmation that operators who already completed actions per the Boeing bulletin prior to this AD’s effective date under the original service bulletin dates are in compliance and need not re-perform actions because P5 substitutes the AD effective date where the bulletin referenced original issue date.

[P7][P8] (combined) Small carriers and repair shops will request the FAA to permit direct submission and review of AMOCs via the FAA’s national AMOC portal rather than routing through principal inspectors or the LA ACO, to avoid local resource constraints and potential delays.

[P1] The broad prohibition in §17.46(d)(1) lacks a clear definition of “person subject to the jurisdiction of the United States,” creating uncertainty for non‑citizen landowners and contractors about whether they are covered.

[P2] §17.46(d)(1)(i)’s ban on import/export as cross‑referenced to §17.21(b) should explicitly clarify whether small, noncommercial transfers between private collectors or educational institutions are prohibited or allowed under any exemptions.

[P3] The prohibition in §17.46(d)(1)(ii) on “take” without further definition of incidental vs. purposeful take will criminalize routine land management activities unless the permitted take provisions are widely publicized and accessible.

[P4] §17.46(d)(1)(iii) should define “possession and other acts involving unlawfully taken specimens” to avoid penalizing bona fide possessors who obtained specimens prior to the effective date and did not know they were “unlawfully taken.”

[P5] §17.46(d)(1)(iv) prohibiting interstate or foreign commerce in commercial activity as per §17.21(e) may unintentionally restrict farmers and nursery operators who move soil or equipment interstate if the species is present in that soil; the rule should address contaminated soil/equipment.

[P6] The sale/offer for sale prohibition at §17.46(d)(1)(v) lacks a de minimis sales threshold; hobbyist sales under minimal value would be criminalized without an explicit small‑scale exemption.

[P7] §17.46(d)(2)(i) permitting activities by §17.32 permit requires clarification of the expected processing time and criteria so applicants can rely on obtaining permits before conducting time‑sensitive work.

[P8] The cross‑references in §17.46(d)(2)(ii) to §17.21(c)(2)–(c)(4) should be included verbatim or summarized to avoid confusion; stakeholders cannot assess risk without seeing the specific authorized types of take.

[P9] §17.46(d)(2)(iii) permitting take under §17.31(b) must specify whether emergency actions (e.g., disaster response after storms) qualify and the notification requirements for such take.

[P10] The incidental take allowance in §17.46(d)(2)(iv) is too vague about what documentation or take minimization measures landowners must keep to demonstrate compliance if questioned or inspected.

[P11] §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(A) permits Service or State agency conservation collection and propagation but omits requirements for transparency and public reporting of numbers collected, holding times, and disposition; advocates will request monitoring/reporting requirements.

[P12] The conservation exception in §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(A) should require genetic health and disease screening protocols before stocking or translocations to prevent spread of pathogens or genetic homogenization.

[P13] §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(B)(1) allowing maintenance within existing footprints fails to define “existing footprint” (e.g., does it include previously permitted temporary construction easements?), creating ambiguity for redevelopment projects.

[P14] The 100‑foot limit in §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(B)(2) for new structures near existing structures should be tied to parcel size and local zoning — on small lots this effectively prohibits reasonable infill; regulators should clarify applicability to subdivisions and mobile homes.

[P15] The footprint threshold “under 1,000 square feet” in §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(B)(2) appears arbitrary and may disproportionately impact affordable housing additions (accessory dwelling units); commenters will ask for exemptions or higher thresholds for housing needs.

[P16] §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(B)(3) permitting culvert installation only on parcels larger than one acre disadvantages small landowners and renters on smaller parcels who need drainage repairs; the rule should allow emergency culvert work regardless of parcel size.

[P17] The exclusion in §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(B)(3) for culverts “not part of housing developments” is ambiguous — it should clarify whether single‑lot home improvements in platted subdivisions qualify.

[P18] §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(B)(4) allowing platforms/boardwalks “if they allow sufficient sunlight to maintain herbaceous groundcover” lacks a measurable standard (e.g., percentage of canopy openness or light transmission) and will lead to arbitrary decisionmaking.

[P19] The 5% acreage disturbance cap in §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(B)(5) for nonmotorized paths on conservation easement lands does not specify how cumulative impacts across multiple projects are calculated or whether seasonal construction impacts count toward the 5%; conservation easement holders will request cumulative and temporal guidance.

[P20] §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(C)(1) permits forestry on secondary soils if state BMPs are followed, but does not specify which versions of BMPs apply or whether federal concurrence is needed; timber companies and environmental groups will request an explicit incorporated version and update procedures.

[P21] The allowance for prescribed burning in §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(C)(2) “when following state BMPs, guidelines, or permit conditions” lacks clarity about whether interstate differences in BMP rigor are acceptable; conservationists will request minimum federal standards.

[P22] §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(C)(3) herbicide application permission should require use of only products labeled for aquatic safety and specify buffer distances to waterways to prevent off‑target impacts to crayfish habitat.

[P23] The grandfathering in §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(C)(4) for agricultural operations established prior to January 3, 2018, is vague about what documentation proves establishment date and what level of “indirect impacts” are prohibited; farmers will request a clear, administrable definition and acceptable mitigation measures.

[P24] §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(D) utility actions requiring coordination with the local FWS office could unduly delay emergency repairs; utilities will request a fast‑track notification/approval timeline and criteria for emergency waivers.

[P25] The distinction in §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(D)(1) permitting ditch mowing outside critical habitat but requiring coordination inside (§D(2)) may create inconsistent mowing schedules across neighboring parcels; municipalities seek clear timing windows and standardized coordination procedures.

[P26] Coordination required by §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(D)(2) for ditch maintenance within critical habitat must include defined response times and written approval thresholds to avoid de facto moratoria.

[P27] §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(D)(3) allows culvert work if it “does not adversely affect, and instead improve or restore, the natural hydrology” but offers no metrics for “improve or restore”; engineers and conservationists will request hydrologic performance standards and monitoring requirements.

[P28] The requirement in §17.46(d)(2)(iv)(D)(4) for coordination for rights‑of‑way/powerline maintenance and directional boring should specify minimum notice periods and whether approvals can be verbal during emergencies.

[P29] §17.46(d)(2)(v) permitting possession of unlawfully taken wildlife per §17.21(d)(2) should clarify whether this applies to museum specimens, private collections, or animals in rehabilitation clinics and whether proof of lawful acquisition is required.

[P30] Making shapefiles available under §17.95(h)(4) via regulations.gov and field offices is positive, but the rule should require also providing a downloadable, georeferenced dataset and an easy‑to‑use web map to allow landowners to determine if they are in critical habitat.

[P31] The field office contact process under §17.95(h)(4) is insufficient; many landowners will not know which regional office to contact — the Service should provide a county‑level lookup tool and a single hotline/email for inquiries.

[P32] Legal commenters will note that several cross‑references (to §§17.21, 17.31, 17.32, etc.) create interpretive burdens and argue the final rule should incorporate or summarize the operative cross‑referenced provisions to satisfy notice‑and‑comment requirements.

[P33] Industry (construction, utilities) will claim the cumulative effect of the prohibitions and the multiple coordination requirements will increase project costs and timelines; they will request a categorical safe harbor or programmatic consultation to streamline compliance.

[P34] Environmental NGOs will argue that many permitted activities (forestry BMPs, herbicide use, culverts) lack required mitigation and monitoring commitments and that the exception language should require avoidance, minimization, and compensatory mitigation standards.

[P35] Local governments will request explicit coverage for routine public safety activities (e.g., road repairs, stormwater maintenance, emergency response) as permissible or eligible for an expedited permit pathway to avoid liability.

[P36] Recreational users will request clarification that noncommercial, low‑impact recreational activities (hiking, birdwatching) that may incidentally encounter Panama City crayfish are not treated as prohibited “take” absent willful harm.

[P37] Property rights advocates will challenge the rule’s application to preempt state and local ordinances, asking for an explicit statement about interplay with state land‑use laws and compensation mechanisms for regulatory takings.

[P38] Academic researchers will request streamlined permitting (§17.32) for nonlethal research, including multi‑year permits and standardized data‑sharing requirements to avoid repeated administrative burdens.

[P39] The rule should state enforcement priorities and penalties for violations referenced in P1–P6 so that stakeholders can assess legal risk; currently enforcement thresholds and penalty ranges are not provided in the cited text.

[P40] The rule should include a grandfathering clause or amnesty period for ongoing projects begun prior to publication to avoid penalizing developers who relied on prior regulatory expectations.

[P41] The “secondary soils” and “core soils” terminology used in several permissions (e.g., B5, C1) needs precise, map‑based definitions so landowners can determine whether their parcels qualify without repeated field determinations.

[P42] The Service should add a procedure for disputing field office determinations (e.g., coordination denials under D(2)/(4)) including an appeal timeline and independent review to protect stakeholders from arbitrary decisions.

[P43] The permit exceptions under §17.46(d)(2)(i) should specify criteria for when a §17.32 permit is required versus when the categorical exceptions apply, to reduce administrative uncertainty.

[P44] The rule should clarify whether mitigation banking or conservation crediting can be used to offset incidental take for permitted development activities under B and C, and if so, provide standards and approved banks.

[P45] The conservation exception A (collection, stocking, disposal/salvage) should require chain‑of‑custody documentation and veterinary oversight for any movement of live crayfish to reduce disease transfer and illegal trade.

[P46] Stakeholders will request timelines and public notice requirements for when the Service posts or updates the critical habitat shapefiles under §17.95(h)(4) so that changes do not surprise landowners mid‑project.

[P47] The rule should explicitly state whether private land conservation agreements (easements, safe harbor agreements) can be used to allow activities otherwise prohibited in P1–P6, and the process to enter such agreements.

[P48] Commenters will ask for examples or case studies illustrating how the 5% disturbance cap for paths (B5) is calculated in complex, irregularly shaped easements to ensure consistent application.

[P49] The rule must clarify whether temporary construction impacts (staging areas, temporary roads) count toward the 1,000 sq ft footprint and 5% disturbance limits, as that ambiguity could halt construction planning.

[P50] Tribal governments will request explicit recognition of Tribal sovereignty and a consultation mechanism when proposed activities affect lands or resources of interest to Tribes, which is not addressed in the cited provisions.

raw_output:
[P1] The November 15, 2019 comment deadline in § 39.13 new AD (a) is unreasonably short and should be extended to allow affected operators, suppliers, and labor representatives adequate time to analyze technical and economic impacts.

[P15] The duplicate comment deadline in 14 CFR Part 71 (DATES) specifying November 15, 2019 conflicts with later dates in the rule text (e.g., June 15, 2020) and creates confusion; the FAA should reconcile and clarify the single, correct deadline.

[P21] The June 15, 2020 comments due date provision conflicts with the November 15, 2019 deadlines (P1, P15); the FAA must correct which deadline applies and publish an extended period if necessary to avoid prejudicing stakeholders.

[P16] Requiring mailed comments to the Docket Operations physical address imposes an unnecessary burden on international commenters and small businesses; the FAA should emphasize and facilitate electronic submissions as the primary method.

[P17] Mandating that comments identify FAA Docket No. FAA–2019–0688 and Airspace Docket No. 18–AGL–25 at the beginning of submissions is overly prescriptive and could result in dismissal of substantive comments for formatting errors; the FAA should accept comments that clearly reference the docket anywhere in the submission.

[P19] The instruction to submit comments in triplicate to the Docket Management Facility is outdated given electronic filing capabilities and will impose paper-handling costs; the FAA should remove the triplicate requirement and accept single electronic or paper copies.

[P18] Although online submission is permitted, the regulations.gov portal should be explicitly stated as the preferred method and the FAA should ensure docket staff will accept comments emailed to technical contacts when the portal is unavailable.

[P2] The obligation to "comply with this AD within the specified compliance times" is vague without an explicit table of compliance deadlines in the AD text; the FAA should incorporate the exact compliance intervals (e.g., flight cycles or dates) into the regulatory text rather than relying solely on referenced service bulletins.

[P24] The repeated statement that operators must comply within specified compliance times unless already done (P24) is redundant and could be consolidated to reduce potential inconsistent interpretations across the AD.

[P22] The applicability provision listing Boeing 737–600/700/700C/800/900 series as identified in the requirements bulletin fails to list serial number ranges or configuration differences; the FAA should explicitly identify affected serial numbers and configuration limitations to prevent over- or under-inclusion.

[P23] The STC ST00830SE exception (that installation does not affect ability to accomplish actions) lacks detail on whether STC installations that change structure or wiring could affect inspection access or detection sensitivity; operators with STCs should be required to document compatibility rather than receive blanket exclusion from AMOC change-in-product requirements.

[P3] Requiring performance of all actions in the Boeing Accomplishment Instructions "except as provided in paragraph (h)" effectively delegates normative content to the manufacturer; the FAA should specify any non-mandatory manufacturer guidance and retain independent regulatory text for critical steps.

[P25] Requiring actions exactly per the referenced Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin without incorporating its specific revision into the regulatory text risks ambiguity when multiple revisions exist; the AD should reference a single revision by date and incorporate key steps into the AD.

[P26] The exception that "original issue date" should be read as the AD effective date (except in notes) (h)(1) could create unintended retroactive effects if operators relied on earlier bulletin issue-date compliance calculations; clarify transition provisions and provide grandfathering for actions done per earlier issue dates.

[P4] Using the AD effective date in place of the bulletin's "original issue date" for compliance calculations could shorten or lengthen compliance windows compared to manufacturer intent; FAA should model impacts and explain rationale in the preamble.

[P27] Paragraph (h)(2) directs that when the bulletin says "contact Boeing" for repair/alternative inspection, those actions must be performed using an FAA-approved method per paragraph (j), but paragraph (j) delegates approval to the Seattle ACO Manager and Boeing ODA; this could create circularity and impede timely corrective action—FAA must clarify an expedited approval pathway for on-wing repairs.

[P5] Requiring that repairs or alternative inspections that would otherwise be provided by Boeing must be done using a method approved per paragraph (i) may be impractical for non-Boeing repair stations and foreign authorities; FAA should permit equivalent approvals by EASA or other bilateral partners under a recognized process.

[P28] The credit-for-previous-actions provision that gives credit for actions done per the May 9, 2019 bulletin (P28) is helpful but omits explicit documentation requirements; FAA should specify records or logbook entries required to claim credit during audits.

[P29] The conditional credit provision for Option 2, Condition 4 (P29) forces additional external LFEC/HFEC inspections per Figure 4 without providing clear acceptance criteria; operators need explicit pass/fail thresholds and detailed procedures to avoid inconsistent findings.

[P30] The compliance threshold "before 15,000 total flight cycles" (i)(1) is overly blunt; the FAA should provide phased compliance or risk-based prioritization for high-utilization fleets that will reach 15,000 cycles sooner.

[P31] The alternative compliance deadline "within 6,000 flight cycles after the AD's effective date" (i)(2) combined with (i)(1) (do at later of) could extend the window to an unsafe length for certain high-cycle operators; FAA should state the actual maximum calendar time or provide an expedited requirement for high-risk airplanes.

[P32] Mandating performance of all on-condition actions in the Boeing bulletin (i) without independent FAA-specified acceptance criteria may allow inconsistent operator determinations of serviceability; the AD should include objective criteria for when on-condition sequences are required.

[P33] Authorizing the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch to approve AMOCs centralizes authority geographically and may disadvantage operators outside the Seattle ACO region; FAA should allow delegated ACO/branch managers or the local FSDO to approve AMOCs under standardized guidelines.

[P6] While the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch is authorized to approve AMOCs, the rule should also allow applicants to seek AMOCs from other FAA managers when operational circumstances make Seattle ACO an impractical point of contact.

[P34] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 could delay technical review if those offices lack resources; the FAA should permit direct submission to the certification office with concurrent notification to the principal inspector.

[P36] Allowing AMOC request information to be emailed to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is useful but raises cybersecurity and records-retention concerns; FAA should provide guidance on secure transmission and confirm email will constitute a filed AMOC request under 14 CFR 39.19.

[P10] The requirement to notify your principal inspector or local FSDO before using an approved AMOC may be administratively burdensome for operators that operate internationally where principal inspectors are not available; the FAA should permit notification to the local FAA representative at the principal place of business or to the managing office.

[P11] The permission that an approved AMOC may be used for repairs if approved by an authorized Boeing ODA conflates FAA authority with Boeing ODA approval; legal experts will comment that using a manufacturer ODA as a gatekeeper for AMOC effectiveness raises independence concerns — FAA must affirm its own approval and oversight role.

[P12] Conditioning AMOC acceptance on approval by a Boeing ODA "authorized by the Manager" (P12) limits options to Boeing-affiliated entities and may be challenged by third-party repair stations and airframers who lack Boeing ODA access; FAA should allow other qualified organizations to obtain authorization.

[P13] Requiring that any repair/modification meet the airplane's certification basis is appropriate, but operators need explicit instructions about how to handle changes in certification basis over time (e.g., later amendments); FAA should describe acceptable analysis methods and documentation for compliance.

[P14] The requirement that an AMOC approval "must specifically refer to this AD" is reasonable, but the FAA should allow a single AMOC approval covering multiple ADs where the repair/alteration addresses overlapping issues to reduce redundant approvals.

[P35] Direct submission to the certification office manager addressed to the person in paragraph (k)(1) assumes that contact is current; the FAA should provide an up-to-date contact list and alternative designees to prevent misdirected submissions.

[P37] Requiring notification to the principal inspector or FSDO manager "prior to using any approved AMOC" could delay scheduled maintenance; FAA should permit concurrent notification with the first use and require retrospective documentation when operationally necessary.

[P20] The "Comments Invited" permission to submit written data/views is standard, but the FAA should additionally invite public hearings or webinars for complex technical ADs to get verbal input from maintenance organizations and labor.

[P4/P26] The exception that the phrase "original issue date" is replaced by the AD effective date except in notes (h)(1/h)(26)) needs clarification on whether "notes" refer to FAA notes or manufacturer notes, as this distinction materially affects compliance timing.

[P40] The exclusion of airplanes with Option 2, Condition 4 from general credit (P40) needs justification and technical basis; operators who implemented Option 2, Condition 4 require an explanation of why their prior work does not satisfy the AD.

[P28/P29] The credit and conditional credit provisions should specify acceptable traceable records (workcards, inspection reports, signer qualifications) that demonstrate the prior LFEC/HFEC inspections were performed to the referenced standard.

[P31/P30] The rule should include an explicit inflation-adjusted or fleet-size–based cost estimate for complying within 15,000 cycles or 6,000 cycles, so stakeholders can assess economic impact and request relief where compliance imposes disproportionate burdens.

[P22] The applicability should explicitly state whether aircraft operated as part of governmental/military fleets are included or exempted, and whether foreign-registered airplanes operating to/from the U.S. are covered.

[P23] The claimed exception for STC ST00830SE that it "does not affect ability to accomplish actions" should be supported by Boeing analysis or FAA validation; otherwise operators with that STC may be unfairly presumed compliant while access or inspection fidelity is compromised.

[P3/P25] Delegation to Boeing's Accomplishment Instructions for "all actions" should be accompanied by FAA-adopted deviations or clarifications for steps that require FAA judgment, such as airworthiness-significant findings and disposition of damage.

[P11/P38/P39] The cross-references between paragraphs (i) and (j) for AMOC approval and Boeing ODA involvement are inconsistent in labeling and should be harmonized to avoid conflicting interpretations about who may approve and under what authority.

[P36] The email address provided for AMOC submissions should be mirrored by a phone/fax option and a confirmation-of-receipt mechanism so submitters know when the FAA has received an AMOC package.

[P2/P24/P4] The AD should explicitly state whether compliance actions accomplished before the AD's effective date per an AMOC or via foreign authority approvals are acceptable or require separate FAA concurrence.

[P32] The AD requires "all applicable on-condition follow-up actions" but does not provide an inspection interval for repeated on-condition monitoring after a no-find or repair; FAA should define repeat inspection intervals and criteria for terminating the inspection regime.

[P13] Stating that repair/modification methods must meet the airplane's certification basis requires that an acceptable means of compliance or equivalent-level-of-safety (ELOS) methodology be described or referenced to ensure uniform application.

[P21/P1] Given the multiple and conflicting comment deadlines, the FAA should reissue the NPRM with corrected dates and a fresh comment period to ensure procedural fairness and avoid challenges to the rulemaking process.

Requiring performance of all actions in the Boeing Accomplishment Instructions "except as provided in paragraph (h)" effectively delegates normative content to the manufacturer; the FAA should specify any non-mandatory manufacturer guidance and retain independent regulatory text for critical steps.

Requiring actions exactly per the referenced Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin without incorporating its specific revision into the regulatory text risks ambiguity when multiple revisions exist; the AD should reference a single revision by date and incorporate key steps into the AD.

The exception that "original issue date" should be read as the AD effective date (except in notes) (h)(1) could create unintended retroactive effects if operators relied on earlier bulletin issue-date compliance calculations; clarify transition provisions and provide grandfathering for actions done per earlier issue dates.

Using the AD effective date in place of the bulletin's "original issue date" for compliance calculations could shorten or lengthen compliance windows compared to manufacturer intent; FAA should model impacts and explain rationale in the preamble.

Paragraph (h)(2) directs that when the bulletin says "contact Boeing" for repair/alternative inspection, those actions must be performed using an FAA-approved method per paragraph (j), but paragraph (j) delegates approval to the Seattle ACO Manager and Boeing ODA; this could create circularity and impede timely corrective action—FAA must clarify an expedited approval pathway for on-wing repairs.

Requiring that repairs or alternative inspections that would otherwise be provided by Boeing must be done using a method approved per paragraph (i) may be impractical for non-Boeing repair stations and foreign authorities; FAA should permit equivalent approvals by EASA or other bilateral partners under a recognized process.

The credit-for-previous-actions provision that gives credit for actions done per the May 9, 2019 bulletin (P28) is helpful but omits explicit documentation requirements; FAA should specify records or logbook entries required to claim credit during audits.

The conditional credit provision for Option 2, Condition 4 (P29) forces additional external LFEC/HFEC inspections per Figure 4 without providing clear acceptance criteria; operators need explicit pass/fail thresholds and detailed procedures to avoid inconsistent findings.

The compliance threshold "before 15,000 total flight cycles" (i)(1) is overly blunt; the FAA should provide phased compliance or risk-based prioritization for high-utilization fleets that will reach 15,000 cycles sooner.

The alternative compliance deadline "within 6,000 flight cycles after the AD's effective date" (i)(2) combined with (i)(1) (do at later of) could extend the window to an unsafe length for certain high-cycle operators; FAA should state the actual maximum calendar time or provide an expedited requirement for high-risk airplanes.

Mandating performance of all on-condition actions in the Boeing bulletin (i) without independent FAA-specified acceptance criteria may allow inconsistent operator determinations of serviceability; the AD should include objective criteria for when on-condition sequences are required.

Authorizing the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch to approve AMOCs centralizes authority geographically and may disadvantage operators outside the Seattle ACO region; FAA should allow delegated ACO/branch managers or the local FSDO to approve AMOCs under standardized guidelines.

While the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch is authorized to approve AMOCs, the rule should also allow applicants to seek AMOCs from other FAA managers when operational circumstances make Seattle ACO an impractical point of contact.

Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 could delay technical review if those offices lack resources; the FAA should permit direct submission to the certification office with concurrent notification to the principal inspector.

Allowing AMOC request information to be emailed to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is useful but raises cybersecurity and records-retention concerns; FAA should provide guidance on secure transmission and confirm email will constitute a filed AMOC request under 14 CFR 39.19.

The requirement to notify your principal inspector or local FSDO before using an approved AMOC may be administratively burdensome for operators that operate internationally where principal inspectors are not available; the FAA should permit notification to the local FAA representative at the principal place of business or to the managing office.

The permission that an approved AMOC may be used for repairs if approved by an authorized Boeing ODA conflates FAA authority with Boeing ODA approval; legal experts will comment that using a manufacturer ODA as a gatekeeper for AMOC effectiveness raises independence concerns — FAA must affirm its own approval and oversight role.

Conditioning AMOC acceptance on approval by a Boeing ODA "authorized by the Manager" (P12) limits options to Boeing-affiliated entities and may be challenged by third-party repair stations and airframers who lack Boeing ODA access; FAA should allow other qualified organizations to obtain authorization.

Requiring that any repair/modification meet the airplane's certification basis is appropriate, but operators need explicit instructions about how to handle changes in certification basis over time (e.g., later amendments); FAA should describe acceptable analysis methods and documentation for compliance.

The requirement that an AMOC approval "must specifically refer to this AD" is reasonable, but the FAA should allow a single AMOC approval covering multiple ADs where the repair/alteration addresses overlapping issues to reduce redundant approvals.

Direct submission to the certification office manager addressed to the person in paragraph (k)(1) assumes that contact is current; the FAA should provide an up-to-date contact list and alternative designees to prevent misdirected submissions.

Requiring notification to the principal inspector or FSDO manager "prior to using any approved AMOC" could delay scheduled maintenance; FAA should permit concurrent notification with the first use and require retrospective documentation when operationally necessary.

The "Comments Invited" permission to submit written data/views is standard, but the FAA should additionally invite public hearings or webinars for complex technical ADs to get verbal input from maintenance organizations and labor.

/P26] The exception that the phrase "original issue date" is replaced by the AD effective date except in notes (h)(1/h)(26)) needs clarification on whether "notes" refer to FAA notes or manufacturer notes, as this distinction materially affects compliance timing.

The exclusion of airplanes with Option 2, Condition 4 from general credit (P40) needs justification and technical basis; operators who implemented Option 2, Condition 4 require an explanation of why their prior work does not satisfy the AD.

/P29] The credit and conditional credit provisions should specify acceptable traceable records (workcards, inspection reports, signer qualifications) that demonstrate the prior LFEC/HFEC inspections were performed to the referenced standard.

/P30] The rule should include an explicit inflation-adjusted or fleet-size–based cost estimate for complying within 15,000 cycles or 6,000 cycles, so stakeholders can assess economic impact and request relief where compliance imposes disproportionate burdens.

The applicability should explicitly state whether aircraft operated as part of governmental/military fleets are included or exempted, and whether foreign-registered airplanes operating to/from the U.S. are covered.

The claimed exception for STC ST00830SE that it "does not affect ability to accomplish actions" should be supported by Boeing analysis or FAA validation; otherwise operators with that STC may be unfairly presumed compliant while access or inspection fidelity is compromised.

/P25] Delegation to Boeing's Accomplishment Instructions for "all actions" should be accompanied by FAA-adopted deviations or clarifications for steps that require FAA judgment, such as airworthiness-significant findings and disposition of damage.

/P38/P39] The cross-references between paragraphs (i) and (j) for AMOC approval and Boeing ODA involvement are inconsistent in labeling and should be harmonized to avoid conflicting interpretations about who may approve and under what authority.
The email address provided for AMOC submissions should be mirrored by a phone/fax option and a confirmation-of-receipt mechanism so submitters know when the FAA has received an AMOC package.

/P24/P4] The AD should explicitly state whether compliance actions accomplished before the AD's effective date per an AMOC or via foreign authority approvals are acceptable or require separate FAA concurrence.

The AD requires "all applicable on-condition follow-up actions" but does not provide an inspection interval for repeated on-condition monitoring after a no-find or repair; FAA should define repeat inspection intervals and criteria for terminating the inspection regime.

Stating that repair/modification methods must meet the airplane's certification basis requires that an acceptable means of compliance or equivalent-level-of-safety (ELOS) methodology be described or referenced to ensure uniform application.

/P1] Given the multiple and conflicting comment deadlines, the FAA should reissue the NPRM with corrected dates and a fresh comment period to ensure procedural fairness and avoid challenges to the rulemaking process.

[P1] The requirement to mandate exactly the terms "net weight" or "net wt." is overly prescriptive and should allow equivalent common-language variants (e.g., "Net Wt." with different punctuation or lowercase) to reflect packaging design constraints and international labeling practices.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether pluralization or language translations are permitted (e.g., "net weights" or non-English translations) to accommodate multi-lingual packaging without risking noncompliance.

[P1] Industry stakeholder: Requiring "net weight" on small packages may conflict with limited label panel space; the rule should permit acceptable abbreviations beyond "net wt." for packages under a specified size.

[P1] Consumer advocacy: Mandating "net weight" benefits consumers by providing consistent terminology for comparing products; the agency should require the full phrase ("net weight") on larger packages and allow "net wt." on smaller ones.

[P2] The rule's allowance of "net contents" or "contents" for fluid measures is ambiguous — commenters request that the agency specify whether "Net Contents" must be capitalized or may appear in sentence case.

[P2] Industry comment: The terms "net contents" or "contents" may be confusing when packages contain multiple components (e.g., liquid + solids); guidance is needed on labeling mixed-content products (which provision applies).

[P2] Retailers selling refillable or concentrated liquids (e.g., detergents) request clarification whether the requirement applies to the volume before dilution or the volume as sold, and whether "contents" or "net contents" differs in legal meaning.

[P3] Legal experts: The cross-reference to § 381.128 should be explicitly reproduced or summarized here; otherwise, the instruction to use avoirdupois or liquid measure is vague and could lead to inconsistent enforcement.

[P3] Metric vs. customary: The rule does not address use of metric units (grams, liters) versus avoirdupois/pints; manufacturers need certainty whether metric-only labeling is permitted or whether dual units are required.

[P3] Small-business manufacturer: Expressing net quantity in avoirdupois weight can be problematic for imported products originally measured in metric — the agency should permit metric units or provide transition tolerance.

[P4] Consumer group: The exception in § 381.128 may create loopholes allowing less comprehensible units; the agency should disclose the exception criteria in the main provision to enable public review.

[P4] Industry/legal: Commenters request that § 381.128 be clarified to specify exactly which products qualify for exceptions (e.g., baby formula, pharmaceuticals) to avoid inconsistent application across product lines.

[P4] International trade stakeholders: If § 381.128 allows foreign measurement systems, the exemption should be clearly limited and include labeling that displays customary U.S. units prominently to avoid consumer confusion.

[P5] The phrase "general consumer usage" is vague and subjective; commenters request a definitional standard or examples (e.g., olive oil — liquid measure; peanut butter — weight) to guide compliance.

[P5] Manufacturers of viscous or semi-solid products (e.g., syrup, honey) note customer expectations vary regionally; the rule should require market research or objective criteria rather than an undefined "general consumer usage" test.

[P5] Retailers/packagers ask whether dual labeling (both weight and liquid measure) is permitted or required when consumer usage is ambiguous to ensure clear information and avoid enforcement risk.

[P5] Legal commenters: The provision should include a dispute-resolution mechanism or administrative guidance process for cases where a manufacturer and an enforcement agency disagree on whether "general consumer usage" indicates liquid measure or weight.

[P1/P2] Disability/accessibility advocates: The regulation should require standardized placement and legibility (font size) for "net weight"/"net contents" statements to ensure readability by visually impaired consumers; limiting terms alone is insufficient.

[P3/P5] Environmental/packaging groups: For products sold by count (e.g., shrimp by count but also weight), the rule should clarify interplay between count statements and the requirement to use weight or liquid measure when "general consumer usage" is mixed.

[P2/P4] Food safety organizations: For products sold in concentrate form requiring dilution, the rule should mandate that "net contents" reflect the product as packaged and include a clear statement if the prepared volume differs after consumer preparation.

[P1] Enforcement agencies: The rule should specify acceptable tolerances for typographical errors (e.g., missing period in "wt") and whether minor deviations will be treated as technical noncompliance.

[P3] Trade associations: For multipack packaging (e.g., six 8-oz bottles), the agency should provide explicit examples whether net quantity must be per unit, total, or both, and in what measures (avoirdupois vs. liquid).

[P5] Economists/industry: The government should permit market-based labeling (weight or volume) when both measures are commonly used, provided both measures are clearly shown, to avoid disadvantaging manufacturers with legacy packaging.
