[P1] The rule fails to define "reconstructed" clearly for purposes of determining the applicable compliance date in §63.4683(a), creating uncertainty for owners planning modifications and potential inconsistent enforcement.

[P1] Industry requests inclusion of a clear mechanism for notifying sources which of the three compliance-date categories (a)(1)-(3) applies to them, to avoid disputes about the applicable date.

[P2] Environmental groups will object that setting the default compliance date for sources with startup before May 28, 2003 to May 28, 2003 (§63.4683(a)(1)) provides no additional near-term emission reductions and is effectively a grandfathering clause.

[P2] Legal commenters will argue that the carve-out allowing certain "revised requirements" 180 days after final rule publication is vague because it does not specify which requirements are "revised," creating regulatory ambiguity and litigation risk.

[P3] Manufacturers and small facilities will comment that treating initial startup after May 28, 2003 as immediately subject to compliance as of startup (§63.4683(a)(2)) is retroactive and unfair for entities that started operations under a different regulatory expectation.

[P3] State permitting authorities will request clarification of the phrase "the date of initial startup" (§63.4683(a)(2))—whether it means first operation, first use of coating lines, or first day of revenue-producing operations.

[P3] Compliance consultants will note that the 180-day delayed compliance for certain revised requirements for startups between May 28, 2003 and May 16, 2018 (§63.4683(a)(2)) could create two sets of overlapping obligations and recommend specifying which requirements are delayed.

[P4] New facility developers will assert that making the compliance date the later of publication or startup for startups after May 16, 2018 (§63.4683(a)(3)) could cause unanticipated compliance costs for projects planned under prior rules and request a phase-in period.

[P4] States and legal experts will request that EPA include an exception for bona fide construction projects that commenced prior to the final rule publication but achieve startup after publication, to avoid unfair retroactivity.

[P5] Operators of existing sources will object that fixing the compliance date as three years after May 28, 2003 (§63.4683(b)) is moot and confusing for current compliance planning; suggest updating to a relative timeline from rule publication or allowing immediate applicability with a new transition schedule.

[P5] Environmental groups will challenge the blanket statement that "revised requirements" receive a 180-day compliance delay (§63.4683(b)), arguing this undermines the timeliness of health-protective controls and should be reduced or eliminated.

[P6] Coating manufacturers will request clarification of the phrase "applicable emission limits and related provisions in (a)(2)(i)-(iii)" (§63.4700(a)(2)) and ask for explicit cross-references to Table 3 to avoid interpretative conflicts.

[P6] Small-business trade associations will comment that the rule should allow alternative, less-burdensome compliance options for small or intermittent coating operations that cannot economically install add-on controls.

[P7] Facilities will object that the partial SSM (startup-shutdown-malfunction) exception prior to [DATE 181 DAYS AFTER PUBLICATION] (§63.4700(a)(2)(i)) is ambiguous as to what constitutes an SSM period and will request the inclusion of explicit SSM definitions and allowable durations.

[P7] Public health advocates will argue that allowing SSM exceptions even for a limited pre-effective period (§63.4700(a)(2)(i)) could cause localized health impacts and demand that compliance be required at all times without SSM exceptions.

[P8] Operators will seek clarification on the "specified exception for solvent recovery liquid-liquid material balances" in §63.4700(a)(2)(ii), requesting precise calculation procedures and recordkeeping requirements for that exception.

[P8] Compliance engineers will request clear performance metrics and monitoring frequency requirements for capture systems and add-on controls referenced in §63.4700(a)(2)(ii) to ensure enforceability.

[P9] Developers of new/reconstructed sources will ask EPA to allow a performance-based alternative to the prescriptive emission-rate-with-add-on-controls option in §63.4700(a)(3) for novel technologies not contemplated by the standard.

[P9] Legal commenters will request that EPA explicitly state whether the continuous obligations in (a)(3) apply from the date of startup or from the later publication date when both dates differ, to prevent conflicting interpretations.

[P10] Facilities will request an allowance for short, documented interruptions (e.g., maintenance) to the "continuous" compliance requirement in §63.4700(a)(3)(i), or at minimum explicit language recognizing planned maintenance windows.

[P10] Environmental groups will counter that "continuous" compliance (§63.4700(a)(3)(i)) must be strictly enforced with numeric monitoring and penalties to prevent any gaps in emission limits.

[P11] Operators will ask EPA to clarify the "specified exception for certain solvent recovery systems" in §63.4700(a)(3)(ii), including the technical criteria for which solvent recovery systems qualify.

[P11] Technical organizations will request that the rule include required minimum performance specifications (e.g., minimum capture efficiency or destruction removal efficiency) for add-on controls referenced in §63.4700(a)(3)(ii).

[P12] Trade associations will request more flexible work practice standards in §63.4700(a)(3)(iii) to accommodate different coating application methods and to allow equivalent practices proven to minimize emissions.

[P12] Compliance auditors will request that EPA specify what constitutes acceptable documentation to demonstrate continuous adherence to §63.4693 work practice standards.

[P13] Facility owners will challenge the requirement to operate and maintain equipment "at all times" per §63.6(e)(1)(i) prior to [DATE 181 DAYS AFTER PUBLICATION] (§63.4700(b)), requesting a definition of "operate" and allowance for routine maintenance and calibration downtime.

[P13] Labor groups will ask that the rule explicitly recognize safety and worker protection obligations when requiring operation and maintenance "in accordance with safety and good air pollution control practices" (§63.4700(b)), to prevent conflicts between safety protocols and emission minimization.

[P14] Industry trade groups will support the clarification in §63.4700(b) that operators are not required to reduce emissions beyond applicable standards, but will request further language that precludes mandatory retrofitting beyond what is required by the regulation.

[P14] Environmental advocates will argue that the explicit carve-out from a broader duty to minimize emissions (§63.4700(b)) undermines the Clean Air Act's goal to protect public health and should be narrowed to require continuous pursuit of additional feasible reductions.

[P15] Regulated entities will request that the Administrator be required to provide written notice and a reasonable opportunity to supplement monitoring records before making a compliance determination under §63.4700(b) (determination), to ensure fair process.

[P15] Legal commenters will note that reliance on "information available" (§63.4700(b) determination) without minimum evidentiary standards could lead to arbitrary enforcement; they request codification of acceptable monitoring data types and corrective procedures.

[P16] Existing sources required to develop an SSMP (§63.4700(d)) will request an extended timeline beyond 180 days to develop, train staff on, and implement comprehensive SSMPs, especially for small facilities with limited compliance staff.

[P16] Environmental organizations will request that EPA require public availability of SSMP summaries for affected sources so communities can evaluate preparedness for malfunctions and SSM events.

[P17] Operators will ask EPA to allow template SSMP procedures for startup, shutdown, and corrective actions (§63.4700(d) SSMP contents) that, if followed, constitute presumptive compliance to reduce administrative burden.

[P17] Safety experts will request that SSMP corrective action procedures (§63.4700(d)) explicitly integrate worker safety protocols and coordination with emergency responders.

[P18] Maintenance contractors will request that the SSMP requirement (§63.4700(d)) be limited to equipment reasonably expected to affect capture efficiency, and not extend to every ancillary piece of equipment, to reduce paperwork burden.

[P19] Facilities using the emission-rate-without-add-on-controls option will object to the monthly calculations requirement in §63.4710(c)(8)(ii) as overly burdensome and seek allowance for quarterly calculations for small operations.

[P19] Enforcement agencies will counter that monthly calculations (§63.4710(c)(8)(ii)) are necessary for timely detection of exceedances and recommend retention of the monthly frequency.

[P20] Operators will seek clarification in §63.4720(a)(6)(ii) on what "background supporting data" is excluded from submission and request safe-harbor language permitting submission when practicable to avoid disputes during audits.

[P20] Privacy/CBI-oriented commenters will insist that the rule explicitly permit withholding proprietary formulation data while still allowing submission of necessary calculation summaries as required by §63.4720(a)(6)(ii).

[P21] Facilities using the add-on controls option will ask for a streamlined deviation reporting pathway under §63.4720(a)(7) to prevent duplicative reports when deviations are corrected promptly.

[P21] Community advocates will argue that semiannual reporting for deviations (§63.4720(a)(7)) is insufficiently frequent to protect public health and request quarterly or monthly public disclosure of deviations.

[P22] Operators will request that the detailed information required in semiannual compliance reports for existing sources (A–N) under §63.4720(a)(7)(i) be consolidated or allowed in an electronic repository to reduce paper burden.

[P22] Legal commenters will challenge any requirement in §63.4720(a)(7)(i) that could be read to require disclosure of CBI in semiannual reports and ask EPA to clarify redaction and CBI submission procedures.

[P23] New/reconstructed source owners will request that the semiannual reporting deadlines in §63.4720(a)(7)(ii) be aligned with other federal and state reporting cycles to avoid duplicate reporting.

[P23] Environmental groups will request that the obligation in §63.4720(a)(7)(ii) to report deviations for new and existing sources include a public-facing summary to improve transparency.

[P24] Operators will ask EPA to define "compliance period" in §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(A) clearly (e.g., calendar month vs. 12-month rolling period) to avoid inconsistent reporting of start and end dates when the 12-month emission rate exceeded the limit.

[P24] Technical commenters will request example calculations and templates for identifying the "beginning and ending dates" of compliance periods for purposes of §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(A).

[P25] Sources will request that the "detailed calculations" required in §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(B) be allowed in electronic annexes rather than printed in semiannual reports, and that EPA accept summarized calculations when background data are voluminous.

[P25] Privacy-oriented commenters will reiterate that §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(B) explicitly permit omission of supplier proprietary data while still providing sufficient calculation summaries for EPA review.

[P26] Sources will request clear minimum content and format requirements for the "brief description" of the CPMS in §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(C) to ensure consistent enforcement and review.

[P26] Certification bodies will ask EPA to allow referencing CPMS manufacturer documentation in lieu of bespoke descriptions for §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(C).

[P27] Owners/operators will request clarification about what constitutes a "CPMS certification or audit" under §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(D) and acceptable evidence of such certification to be included in reports.

[P27] Third-party auditors will ask EPA to prescribe acceptable audit standards and auditor qualifications for CPMS certification dates reported under §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(D).

[P28] Facilities will argue that the requirement to list all dates and times each CPMS was inoperative (§63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(E)) is excessively granular and suggest allowing aggregated daily or hourly summaries instead.

[P28] Compliance attorneys will request explicit exemptions for routine zero and high-level checks in §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(E) be expanded to include other manufacturer-recommended calibration/check procedures.

[P29] Operators will request clearer guidance on the content of §63.8(c)(8) information that must accompany CPMS out-of-control event reports under §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(F) to ensure consistent reporting.

[P29] Enforcement attorneys will state that including §63.8(c)(8) information in §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(F) is appropriate and necessary for meaningful oversight and should be retained.

[P30] Owners/operators will request a de minimis threshold for reporting deviations from Table 3 operating limits and bypass events (§63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(G)), to avoid reporting trivial or momentary deviations caused by instrument noise.

[P30] Community groups will object to any de minimis threshold for §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(G), arguing that even short bypasses can lead to acute exposures and should be reported.

[P31] Facilities will request that the percent-of-operating-time calculation required in §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(H) allow use of reasonable estimates when precise operating time is difficult to determine, and request acceptable estimation methodologies.

[P31] Regulators will insist that §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(H) require verifiable records for operating time calculations to ensure accuracy of deviation percentage reporting.

[P32] Owners/operators will ask for a standard list of cause categories to be used when breaking down deviation durations by cause under §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(I), to promote consistency across reports.

[P32] Legal commenters will request guidance on acceptable methods to "estimate the quantity of each pollutant" exceeding limits during deviations (§63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(I)) and recommend EPA-provided estimation tools.

[P33] Sources will request that CPMS downtime summaries (§63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(J)) be permitted to be provided as aggregated daily totals rather than minute-by-minute logs to reduce burden.

[P33] Community health advocates will oppose aggregation for §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(J), asserting that detailed temporal information is necessary to correlate emissions with acute health events.

[P34] Operators will ask for safe harbor language that routine, documented minor changes to CPMS or equipment (described in §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(K)) need only be reported in the next scheduled semiannual report rather than immediately.

[P34] Environmental groups will demand that significant changes referenced in §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(K) trigger immediate public notice to affected communities.

[P35] Facilities will seek clarification on the level of detail required for "deviation from the work practice standards" (§63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(L)), and request that common corrective actions be listed as acceptable in the reporting template.

[P35] Compliance consultants will request example narratives and standardized codes for describing deviations and corrective actions under §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(L) to ensure uniform submissions.

[P36] Owners/operators will ask EPA to allow generalized cause descriptions when multiple minor deviations share a common cause in §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(M), rather than requiring a separate cause statement for each micro-event.

[P36] Legal experts will caution that vague cause statements under §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(M) could weaken enforcement and recommend EPA require root-cause analyses for major deviations.

[P37] Existing sources subject to SSM reporting (§63.4720(c)(3)) will request explicit definitions and thresholds for what constitutes an SSM reportable event and what minimal information is required, to avoid inconsistent state-by-state interpretations.

[P37] Community groups will request that SSM reports under §63.4720(c)(3) be made publicly available in near real-time to allow local residents and health departments to respond to potential exposures.

[P38] Owners/operators will request extension of the 60-day deadline for submitting performance test results (§63.4720(d)(1)) to 90 days in cases of complex testing or when confirmatory analyses are needed.

[P38] Enforcement officials will argue that 60 days (§63.4720(d)(1)) is already generous and should be strictly enforced to ensure timely corrective action.

[P39] Testing laboratories will request clarity on the acceptable file formats and metadata for ERT-supported performance test submissions (§63.4720(d)(1)(i)) and ask EPA to publish a technical specification document.

[P39] CBI proponents will request explicit procedures and timelines for EPA acknowledgement of physical-media CBI submissions per §63.4720(d)(1)(i), to ensure proprietary information is protected.

[P40] Laboratories using non-ERT methods will request an electronic submission pathway alternative to mailing physical reports to the Administrator under §63.4720(d)(1)(ii) to modernize reporting and reduce delays.

[P40] Legal commenters will request that §63.4720(d)(1)(ii) specify the address and contact for submissions to avoid misdirected reports and associated compliance disputes.

[P41] Small facilities will request a delayed mandatory start date for CEDRI submissions (§63.4720(d)(2)) beyond the one-year template-availability window to allow software integration and staff training.

[P41] IT vendors and EPA will be asked to provide test environments and batch-upload options for CEDRI to facilitate §63.4720(d)(2) compliance for large reporters.

[P41] Privacy advocates will request clear instructions on how CBI should be handled in CEDRI submissions required by §63.4720(d)(2), including encryption and access control standards.

[P42] Owners/operators will seek detail on what evidence is required to support an EPA system outage claim (§63.4720(d)(3)) and request objective criteria for Administrator acceptance to avoid discretionary denials.

[P42] EPA transparency advocates will request that the Administrator publish metrics on the number and disposition of outage claims accepted under §63.4720(d)(3).

[P43] Operators will request that force majeure provisions (§63.4720(d)(4)) include examples of acceptable events (e.g., natural disasters, cyberattacks) and objective documentation requirements to reduce discretionary determinations.

[P43] Legal commenters will ask for an appeals process or independent review for Administrator decisions denying force majeure or outage claims under §63.4720(d)(3)-(4).

[P44] Operators using the emission-rate-without-add-on-controls option will request allowance for electronic record summaries instead of maintaining voluminous monthly and 12-month calculation records (§63.4730(c)(3)) in paper form.

[P44] Enforcement agencies will request that §63.4730(c)(3) require retention of raw data (e.g., purchase receipts, batch records) behind the calculations for a minimum number of years to allow audits.

[P45] Facilities using emission-rate-with-add-on-controls will request that the records list in §63.4730(k) permit consolidated cross-cutting records for multiple coating lines to avoid duplicated paperwork.

[P45] EPA legal staff will caution that consolidation must preserve source-specific traceability to demonstrate compliance for each affected coating operation.

[P46] Operators of non-PTE capture systems will ask for a clear, step-by-step example of the data and documentation required to determine capture efficiency under §63.4730(k)(1)(v), including acceptable modeling approaches.

[P46] Testing professionals will request that EPA accept third-party verification of capture-efficiency data under §63.4730(k)(1)(v) and provide minimum qualifications for third-party testers.

[P47] Operators will request that records required by §63.4730(k)(1)(vi) for add-on control efficiency be permitted in electronic form and that redundant records submitted to state agencies satisfy federal retention requirements.

[P47] States will request coordination language to prevent divergent record retention requirements between federal §63.4730(k)(1)(vi) and state permitting rules.

[P48] Facilities will ask EPA to define the minimal data elements required to "show continuous compliance" with Table 3 operating limits (§63.4730(k)(2)(i)), and to permit summarized compliance logs for certain parameters.

[P48] Public health advocates will insist that complete, unabridged records be maintained for Table 3 limits to enable community oversight.

[P49] Owners/operators claiming PTE capture systems (§63.4730(k)(2)(ii)) will request clear test protocols and acceptable supporting documentation for showing Method 204 criteria were met and 100% capture efficiency was achieved.

[P49] Technical commenters will argue that claiming 100% capture efficiency should require periodic re-verification, not be a one-time demonstration as suggested in §63.4730(k)(2)(ii).

[P50] Operators of non-PTE capture systems will request transitional relief and staggered compliance dates for the data/documentation requirements under §63.4730(k)(2)(iii), due to the expense and logistics of extensive capture-efficiency testing.

[P50] Environmental groups will oppose delay of §63.4730(k)(2)(iii) requirements, arguing they are essential to ensure accurate accounting of fugitive emissions.

[P51] Testing labs will request clarification of acceptable TVH measurement methods and calibration procedures required for liquid-to-uncaptured-gas tests under §63.4730(k)(2)(iii)(A).

[P51] Owners/operators will ask EPA to allow surrogate measurement techniques when direct TVH measurement is technically infeasible under §63.4730(k)(2)(iii)(A), with a defined approval process.

[P52] Operators will request that inlet and escaped TVH measurement frequency and sampling locations be specified for gas-to-gas capture efficiency tests under §63.4730(k)(2)(iii)(B) to ensure consistent test protocols.

[P52] Testing professionals will recommend that EPA adopt standard QA/QC procedures for gas-to-gas tests under §63.4730(k)(2)(iii)(B) and include them in guidance.

[P53] Sources proposing alternative capture-efficiency protocols (§63.4730(k)(2)(iii)(C)) will ask EPA to publish a clear approval process and timeline for accepting alternative protocols under §63.4765(e).

[P53] Environmental NGOs will urge EPA to limit the use of alternative protocols to situations where standard methods are truly infeasible, to prevent gaming of capture-efficiency determinations.

[P54] Facilities will request that records of add-on control device performance tests (§63.4730(k)(2)(iv)(A)) be allowed in standard digital formats with machine-readable attachments to streamline review.

[P54] Testing labs will ask EPA to require that performance test records include raw data files (e.g., chromatograms) as an option under §63.4730(k)(2)(iv)(A).

[P55] Owners/operators will request a definition of "representative coating operation conditions" (§63.4730(k)(2)(iv)(B)) and examples of what would and would not constitute representativeness for the test.

[P55] Environmental groups will request that EPA require more frequent performance tests for add-on controls when coating operations have high variability to ensure representativeness.

[P56] Operators will ask for sample calculation templates acceptable to EPA for the data/calculations used to set operating limits and demonstrate compliance with Table 3 (§63.4730(k)(2)(v)).

[P56] Technical commenters will recommend that EPA require peer review of methods used to set operating limits under §63.4730(k)(2)(v) for novel control systems.

[P57] Facilities will request flexibility in documenting continuous implementation of work practice plans (§63.4730(k)(2)(vi)), such as use of checklists, photographs, or electronic logs, and ask EPA to accept multiple formats.

[P57] Community advocates will request that summaries of work practice plan implementation be made publicly available to help local stakeholders assess facility performance.

[P58] Industry will support allowing Method 24 or listed ASTM standards as alternatives (§63.4741(a)(2)) but will request that EPA allow other up-to-date voluntary consensus standards as they are developed without needing a rule amendment.

[P58] Standards organizations will request that EPA include a process for periodically updating the list of acceptable consensus standards in §63.4741(a)(2).

[P59] Coating formulators will request explicit acceptance criteria (e.g., precision, detection limits) for each ASTM alternative method listed in §63.4741(a)(2)(i)-(v) to ensure consistency across laboratories.

[P60] Operators will raise concerns that prioritizing ASTM D1475–90 results when density conflicts (§63.4741(b)(3)) may impose additional test costs; they request allowance to use supplier-certified densities when accompanied by a certification statement.

[P60] Consumer advocates will argue that relying on older ASTM versions (D1475–90) (§63.4741(b)(3)) is problematic and request that the rule reference the most recent ASTM standard edition rather than a 1990 version.

[P61] Operators will request permission to use modern, validated density test methods as substitutes for ASTM D1475–90 in §63.4741(c), given advances in test technology since 1990.

[P61] Legal commenters will ask EPA to clarify whether supplier-specified density data are acceptable for compliance in §63.4741(c) when test results are unavailable, and what documentation suffices.

[P62] Facilities will request that monthly density determinations under §63.4751(c) be allowed to use supplier certificates for low-volume or infrequently used materials, rather than monthly testing, to reduce costs.

[P62] Testing laboratories will request that EPA specify acceptable supplier data formats and required supporting documentation for densities reported under §63.4751(c).

[P63] Operators choosing the ASTM D6348–03 performance test alternative (§63.4751(i) intro) will ask EPA to allow use of later revisions of ASTM D6348 and provide a mechanism to accept updated standards.

[P63] Environmental groups will urge EPA to reserve the right to require the more stringent method among alternatives when public health concerns warrant.

[P64] Operators using the alternative compliance calculation (Equation 1A‑alt) (§63.4751(i)(1)) will request example worked calculations and validation datasets to ensure consistent application across sources.

[P64] Auditors will request that Equation 1A‑alt inputs be clearly defined, including units, rounding rules, and acceptable measurement uncertainty, to avoid inconsistent calculations.

[P65] Operators will request guidance on handling partial-month material usage and rounding conventions when calculating the 12‑month emission rate per Equation 3 (§63.4751(i)(2)).

[P65] Compliance consultants will recommend that EPA allow grace period averaging rules for the first 12‑month period to avoid penalizing new lines with atypical initial usage patterns.

[P66] Facilities will ask EPA to explicitly recognize and accept third-party laboratory reports and chain-of-custody documentation as sufficient records for the initial 12-month compliance demonstration required by §63.4751(i)(3).

[P66] Environmental groups will request that EPA require more stringent public disclosure for initial compliance demonstrations (§63.4751(i)(3)) to allow community verification.

[P67] Test method practitioners will request that the mandatory Test Plan Annex requirements in §63.4751(i)(4)(i) be updated to permit equivalent documented test plans where ASTM annex sections are inapplicable, with EPA approval.

[P68] Laboratories conducting ASTM D6348–03 tests will request clarification on acceptable corrective actions and retesting procedures when %R falls outside the 70–130% range in §63.4751(i)(4)(ii).

[P68] Operators will request that EPA allow a documented, method-specific justification for accepting %R values slightly outside 70–130% in exceptional circumstances, rather than always requiring test repetition per §63.4751(i)(4)(ii).

[P69] Sources will seek clarification in §63.4761(j)(3) on whether supplier-provided VOC/% volatile organic matter data can be used without further EPA approval as an alternative to Method 24 or ASTM methods.

[P69] Testing laboratories will ask EPA to publish an approval process and timeline for any "EPA-approved alternative" methods referenced in §63.4761(j)(3), to reduce uncertainty for method selection.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The rule fails to define "reconstructed" clearly for purposes of determining the applicable compliance date in §63.4683(a), creating uncertainty for owners planning modifications and potential inconsistent enforcement.
Industry requests inclusion of a clear mechanism for notifying sources which of the three compliance-date categories (a)(1)-(3) applies to them, to avoid disputes about the applicable date.

Environmental groups will object that setting the default compliance date for sources with startup before May 28, 2003 to May 28, 2003 (§63.4683(a)(1)) provides no additional near-term emission reductions and is effectively a grandfathering clause.

Legal commenters will argue that the carve-out allowing certain "revised requirements" 180 days after final rule publication is vague because it does not specify which requirements are "revised," creating regulatory ambiguity and litigation risk.

Manufacturers and small facilities will comment that treating initial startup after May 28, 2003 as immediately subject to compliance as of startup (§63.4683(a)(2)) is retroactive and unfair for entities that started operations under a different regulatory expectation.

State permitting authorities will request clarification of the phrase "the date of initial startup" (§63.4683(a)(2))—whether it means first operation, first use of coating lines, or first day of revenue-producing operations.

Compliance consultants will note that the 180-day delayed compliance for certain revised requirements for startups between May 28, 2003 and May 16, 2018 (§63.4683(a)(2)) could create two sets of overlapping obligations and recommend specifying which requirements are delayed.

New facility developers will assert that making the compliance date the later of publication or startup for startups after May 16, 2018 (§63.4683(a)(3)) could cause unanticipated compliance costs for projects planned under prior rules and request a phase-in period.

States and legal experts will request that EPA include an exception for bona fide construction projects that commenced prior to the final rule publication but achieve startup after publication, to avoid unfair retroactivity.

Operators of existing sources will object that fixing the compliance date as three years after May 28, 2003 (§63.4683(b)) is moot and confusing for current compliance planning; suggest updating to a relative timeline from rule publication or allowing immediate applicability with a new transition schedule.

Environmental groups will challenge the blanket statement that "revised requirements" receive a 180-day compliance delay (§63.4683(b)), arguing this undermines the timeliness of health-protective controls and should be reduced or eliminated.

Coating manufacturers will request clarification of the phrase "applicable emission limits and related provisions in (a)(2)(i)-(iii)" (§63.4700(a)(2)) and ask for explicit cross-references to Table 3 to avoid interpretative conflicts.

Small-business trade associations will comment that the rule should allow alternative, less-burdensome compliance options for small or intermittent coating operations that cannot economically install add-on controls.

Facilities will object that the partial SSM (startup-shutdown-malfunction) exception prior to [DATE 181 DAYS AFTER PUBLICATION] (§63.4700(a)(2)(i)) is ambiguous as to what constitutes an SSM period and will request the inclusion of explicit SSM definitions and allowable durations.

Public health advocates will argue that allowing SSM exceptions even for a limited pre-effective period (§63.4700(a)(2)(i)) could cause localized health impacts and demand that compliance be required at all times without SSM exceptions.

Operators will seek clarification on the "specified exception for solvent recovery liquid-liquid material balances" in §63.4700(a)(2)(ii), requesting precise calculation procedures and recordkeeping requirements for that exception.
Compliance engineers will request clear performance metrics and monitoring frequency requirements for capture systems and add-on controls referenced in §63.4700(a)(2)(ii) to ensure enforceability.

Developers of new/reconstructed sources will ask EPA to allow a performance-based alternative to the prescriptive emission-rate-with-add-on-controls option in §63.4700(a)(3) for novel technologies not contemplated by the standard.

Legal commenters will request that EPA explicitly state whether the continuous obligations in (a)(3) apply from the date of startup or from the later publication date when both dates differ, to prevent conflicting interpretations.

Facilities will request an allowance for short, documented interruptions (e.g., maintenance) to the "continuous" compliance requirement in §63.4700(a)(3)(i), or at minimum explicit language recognizing planned maintenance windows.
Environmental groups will counter that "continuous" compliance (§63.4700(a)(3)(i)) must be strictly enforced with numeric monitoring and penalties to prevent any gaps in emission limits.
Operators will ask EPA to clarify the "specified exception for certain solvent recovery systems" in §63.4700(a)(3)(ii), including the technical criteria for which solvent recovery systems qualify.

Technical organizations will request that the rule include required minimum performance specifications (e.g., minimum capture efficiency or destruction removal efficiency) for add-on controls referenced in §63.4700(a)(3)(ii).

Trade associations will request more flexible work practice standards in §63.4700(a)(3)(iii) to accommodate different coating application methods and to allow equivalent practices proven to minimize emissions.
Compliance auditors will request that EPA specify what constitutes acceptable documentation to demonstrate continuous adherence to §63.4693 work practice standards.

Facility owners will challenge the requirement to operate and maintain equipment "at all times" per §63.6(e)(1)(i) prior to [DATE 181 DAYS AFTER PUBLICATION] (§63.4700(b)), requesting a definition of "operate" and allowance for routine maintenance and calibration downtime.

Labor groups will ask that the rule explicitly recognize safety and worker protection obligations when requiring operation and maintenance "in accordance with safety and good air pollution control practices" (§63.4700(b)), to prevent conflicts between safety protocols and emission minimization.

Industry trade groups will support the clarification in §63.4700(b) that operators are not required to reduce emissions beyond applicable standards, but will request further language that precludes mandatory retrofitting beyond what is required by the regulation.

Environmental advocates will argue that the explicit carve-out from a broader duty to minimize emissions (§63.4700(b)) undermines the Clean Air Act's goal to protect public health and should be narrowed to require continuous pursuit of additional feasible reductions.

Regulated entities will request that the Administrator be required to provide written notice and a reasonable opportunity to supplement monitoring records before making a compliance determination under §63.4700(b) (determination), to ensure fair process.

Legal commenters will note that reliance on "information available" (§63.4700(b) determination) without minimum evidentiary standards could lead to arbitrary enforcement; they request codification of acceptable monitoring data types and corrective procedures.

Existing sources required to develop an SSMP (§63.4700(d)) will request an extended timeline beyond 180 days to develop, train staff on, and implement comprehensive SSMPs, especially for small facilities with limited compliance staff.
Environmental organizations will request that EPA require public availability of SSMP summaries for affected sources so communities can evaluate preparedness for malfunctions and SSM events.

Operators will ask EPA to allow template SSMP procedures for startup, shutdown, and corrective actions (§63.4700(d) SSMP contents) that, if followed, constitute presumptive compliance to reduce administrative burden.
Safety experts will request that SSMP corrective action procedures (§63.4700(d)) explicitly integrate worker safety protocols and coordination with emergency responders.

Maintenance contractors will request that the SSMP requirement (§63.4700(d)) be limited to equipment reasonably expected to affect capture efficiency, and not extend to every ancillary piece of equipment, to reduce paperwork burden.

Facilities using the emission-rate-without-add-on-controls option will object to the monthly calculations requirement in §63.4710(c)(8)(ii) as overly burdensome and seek allowance for quarterly calculations for small operations.
Enforcement agencies will counter that monthly calculations (§63.4710(c)(8)(ii)) are necessary for timely detection of exceedances and recommend retention of the monthly frequency.

Operators will seek clarification in §63.4720(a)(6)(ii) on what "background supporting data" is excluded from submission and request safe-harbor language permitting submission when practicable to avoid disputes during audits.

Privacy/CBI-oriented commenters will insist that the rule explicitly permit withholding proprietary formulation data while still allowing submission of necessary calculation summaries as required by §63.4720(a)(6)(ii).
Facilities using the add-on controls option will ask for a streamlined deviation reporting pathway under §63.4720(a)(7) to prevent duplicative reports when deviations are corrected promptly.

Community advocates will argue that semiannual reporting for deviations (§63.4720(a)(7)) is insufficiently frequent to protect public health and request quarterly or monthly public disclosure of deviations.

Operators will request that the detailed information required in semiannual compliance reports for existing sources (A–N) under §63.4720(a)(7)(i) be consolidated or allowed in an electronic repository to reduce paper burden.

Legal commenters will challenge any requirement in §63.4720(a)(7)(i) that could be read to require disclosure of CBI in semiannual reports and ask EPA to clarify redaction and CBI submission procedures.
New/reconstructed source owners will request that the semiannual reporting deadlines in §63.4720(a)(7)(ii) be aligned with other federal and state reporting cycles to avoid duplicate reporting.
Environmental groups will request that the obligation in §63.4720(a)(7)(ii) to report deviations for new and existing sources include a public-facing summary to improve transparency.

Operators will ask EPA to define "compliance period" in §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(A) clearly (e.g., calendar month vs. 12-month rolling period) to avoid inconsistent reporting of start and end dates when the 12-month emission rate exceeded the limit.

Facilities will argue that the requirement to list all dates and times each CPMS was inoperative (§63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(E)) is excessively granular and suggest allowing aggregated daily or hourly summaries instead.

Compliance attorneys will request explicit exemptions for routine zero and high-level checks in §63.4720(a)(7)(ii)(E) be expanded to include other manufacturer-recommended calibration/check procedures.

Environmental NGOs will urge EPA to limit the use of alternative protocols to situations where standard methods are truly infeasible, to prevent gaming of capture-efficiency determinations.
Facilities will request that records of add-on control device performance tests (§63.4730(k)(2)(iv)(A)) be allowed in standard digital formats with machine-readable attachments to streamline review.
Testing labs will ask EPA to require that performance test records include raw data files (e.g., chromatograms) as an option under §63.4730(k)(2)(iv)(A).

Owners/operators will request a definition of "representative coating operation conditions" (§63.4730(k)(2)(iv)(B)) and examples of what would and would not constitute representativeness for the test.
Environmental groups will request that EPA require more frequent performance tests for add-on controls when coating operations have high variability to ensure representativeness.
Operators will ask for sample calculation templates acceptable to EPA for the data/calculations used to set operating limits and demonstrate compliance with Table 3 (§63.4730(k)(2)(v)).
Technical commenters will recommend that EPA require peer review of methods used to set operating limits under §63.4730(k)(2)(v) for novel control systems.

Facilities will request flexibility in documenting continuous implementation of work practice plans (§63.4730(k)(2)(vi)), such as use of checklists, photographs, or electronic logs, and ask EPA to accept multiple formats.
Community advocates will request that summaries of work practice plan implementation be made publicly available to help local stakeholders assess facility performance.

Industry will support allowing Method 24 or listed ASTM standards as alternatives (§63.4741(a)(2)) but will request that EPA allow other up-to-date voluntary consensus standards as they are developed without needing a rule amendment.
Standards organizations will request that EPA include a process for periodically updating the list of acceptable consensus standards in §63.4741(a)(2).

Coating formulators will request explicit acceptance criteria (e.g., precision, detection limits) for each ASTM alternative method listed in §63.4741(a)(2)(i)-(v) to ensure consistency across laboratories.

Operators will raise concerns that prioritizing ASTM D1475–90 results when density conflicts (§63.4741(b)(3)) may impose additional test costs; they request allowance to use supplier-certified densities when accompanied by a certification statement.

Consumer advocates will argue that relying on older ASTM versions (D1475–90) (§63.4741(b)(3)) is problematic and request that the rule reference the most recent ASTM standard edition rather than a 1990 version.
Operators will request permission to use modern, validated density test methods as substitutes for ASTM D1475–90 in §63.4741(c), given advances in test technology since 1990.
Legal commenters will ask EPA to clarify whether supplier-specified density data are acceptable for compliance in §63.4741(c) when test results are unavailable, and what documentation suffices.

Facilities will request that monthly density determinations under §63.4751(c) be allowed to use supplier certificates for low-volume or infrequently used materials, rather than monthly testing, to reduce costs.

Operators choosing the ASTM D6348–03 performance test alternative (§63.4751(i) intro) will ask EPA to allow use of later revisions of ASTM D6348 and provide a mechanism to accept updated standards.
Environmental groups will urge EPA to reserve the right to require the more stringent method among alternatives when public health concerns warrant.

Operators using the alternative compliance calculation (Equation 1A‑alt) (§63.4751(i)(1)) will request example worked calculations and validation datasets to ensure consistent application across sources.

Facilities will ask EPA to explicitly recognize and accept third-party laboratory reports and chain-of-custody documentation as sufficient records for the initial 12-month compliance demonstration required by §63.4751(i)(3).

Sources will seek clarification in §63.4761(j)(3) on whether supplier-provided VOC/% volatile organic matter data can be used without further EPA approval as an alternative to Method 24 or ASTM methods.

raw_output:
[P1] The blanket application of all prohibitions and provisions in §§17.31 and 17.32 to the Neuse River waterdog (§17.43(f)(1)) is overly broad and will create regulatory uncertainty for routine landowners and local governments because it does not identify which specific prohibitions are most relevant to in-stream and riparian activities.

[P1] Legal commenters will note that cross-referencing entire sections (§§17.31 and 17.32) rather than listing tailored prohibitions could invite legal challenges for vagueness and will complicate compliance determinations for applicants seeking permits.

[P2] Conservation organizations will support the inclusion of narrowly drawn incidental-take exceptions but will request clarity on whether those exceptions are exhaustive or illustrative; the rule should state explicitly whether activities not listed remain presumptively prohibited.

[P2] Industry commenters (developers, utilities, DOTs) will request that the rule include an explicit process (e.g., concurrence letter or incidental take statement) for documenting when an incidental take falls within the exceptions to avoid discretionary enforcement.

[P3] State wildlife agencies will applaud the explicit exception for state-led restoration actions (§17.43(f)(2)(i)) but will request a clear definition of “species restoration efforts” to confirm that routine monitoring, genetic sampling, and removal of nonnative predators are covered.

[P3] Legal/administrative commenters will request that the rule define limits on broodstock collection (numbers, timing, location) or require that state restoration activities be conducted consistent with an approved conservation plan to prevent overcollection.

[P4] Environmental groups will question the criteria for channel restoration projects (§17.43(f)(2)(ii))—they will ask for objective standards or performance metrics (e.g., channel slope, substrate composition, frequency of pool–riffle sequence) to determine what constitutes “natural, physically stable, ecologically functioning” conditions.

[P4] Contractors and engineering firms will request that the rule permit use of temporary construction measures during channel restoration (e.g., cofferdams, temporary dewatering) without losing the incidental-take exception, and ask for explicit procedural steps to document post-project attainment of the stated stream conditions.

[P4] Local governments will ask for guidance on how the exception applies where restoration requires temporary impacts to occupied habitat and how long after project completion the reconnected habitat must persist to qualify.

[P5] Bridge/streambank repair contractors and municipalities will object to restrictions that limit bank stabilization methods to bioengineering (§17.43(f)(2)(iii)), seeking clarification about when engineered solutions (including limited riprap) are permissible due to public-safety or infrastructure protection concerns.

[P5] Conservation biologists will support the exception for bioengineering bank stabilization but request specific acceptable techniques and installation standards (e.g., live stake species, coir fiber log specifications, planting densities) so projects can be designed to meet the exception.

[P6] Road and bridge authorities will strongly object to the prohibition on relying solely on quarried rock, rock baskets, or gabions (§17.43(f)(2)(iii)), arguing that in high-energy reaches and where public safety/infrastructure are at risk, such techniques are necessary and should be allowed as part of hybrid designs.

[P6] Legal commenters will argue that an absolute prohibition on sole use of rip-rap/gabions may conflict with existing federal or state flood control standards and should allow for case-by-case waivers where bioengineering is inadequate.

[P7] Timber industry and private forest owners will support inclusion of silviculture/forest management exceptions (§17.43(f)(2)(iv)) but will request precise, practicable definitions of “highest standard” BMPs and how compliance will be demonstrated.

[P7] Environmental advocates will demand monitoring and enforcement mechanisms for the silviculture exception, arguing that voluntary BMP implementation without independent inspection or reporting will not prevent chronic habitat degradation.

[P8] Forest managers will request that §17.43(f)(2)(iv)(A) define the dimensions and composition of Streamside Management Zones (SMZs) required to meet the “highest standard” and ask whether setbacks differ by stream order or slope.

[P8] State forestry agencies will ask for alignment of the rule’s SMZ and stream crossing standards with existing state statutes and guidance to avoid conflicting obligations and redundant permitting.

[P9] Private landowners and certification program representatives will ask whether compliance with SFI/FSC/ATFS certification (mentioned in §17.43(f)(2)(iv)(B)) provides a safe harbor even if a particular harvest unit has incidental take, and whether interrupted or lapsed certifications affect eligibility for the exception.

[P9] Advocacy groups will point out that some certification programs have variable rigor; they will request that the rule specify minimum certification requirements or require third-party audits to qualify for the exception.

[P10] Property owners, transportation agencies, and utilities will express concern that §17.95(d)(3) excluding manmade structures and the land they occupy from critical habitat could be interpreted too narrowly or too broadly, asking for examples and a mapping protocol so they can determine whether particular structures are excluded.

[P10] Conservation lawyers will warn that excluding only the structures and the land they occupy may leave nearby modified lands functionally altered but still designated as critical habitat, creating enforcement and compensation issues for adjacent property owners.

[P11] Several stakeholders will welcome the availability of map coordinates at Regulations.gov (§17.95(d)(4)) but will request high-resolution GIS shapefiles and parcel overlays to enable accurate project planning and compliance.

[P11] Local planning departments will request that the rule provide contact names, email addresses, and telephone numbers for the “responsible field office” in addition to the general guidance directing them to 50 CFR 2.2 to speed information requests.

[P12] Small municipalities and private landowners will ask for an online interactive map and a formal process for appeal or correction of mapping errors, since reliance solely on paper maps or field office visits is burdensome and can delay projects.

[P13] Similar to P10, owners of developed waterfront property will ask for clarification of the exclusion of manmade structures from Carolina madtom critical habitat (§17.95(e)(3)), and whether ancillary areas (e.g., riprap toe, riparian yards) are included or excluded.

[P13] Environmental groups will caution that too broad an exclusion of “manmade structures and the land they occupy” for the Carolina madtom could create loopholes that exempt degraded habitats that are nonetheless essential for recovery.

[P14] Recreational users and NGOs will ask that the coordinates and plot points for the Carolina madtom maps (§17.95(e)(4)) be provided in multiple GIS formats (shapefile, GeoJSON) and that metadata include date, projection, and mapping scale to avoid misinterpretation.

[P15] Several commenters will request that field office contact information referenced in §17.95(e)(4) be consolidated into the rule preamble or an online appendix (rather than only at 50 CFR 2.2) to improve access and transparency for stakeholders seeking clarifications.

raw_output:
[P1] The comment deadline of November 13, 2017 is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60–90 days to allow affected operators, suppliers, and labor groups adequate time to evaluate costs and prepare technical comments.

[P1] The rule should provide clarification whether the November 13, 2017 deadline applies to supplemental or follow-up comments (e.g., after AMOC determinations) or only to initial submissions.

[P2] The applicability language referencing paragraphs (c)(1)–(c)(4) is too vague in this extract; commenters will request that the AD explicitly list affected Airbus models and serial number ranges in the preamble and regulatory text to avoid ambiguity.

[P2] Operators request inclusion of a mechanism to update the applicability remotely (e.g., via FAA notices) if additional serial numbers or derivative models are discovered after issuance.

[P3] The phrase “comply within the compliance times specified” lacks explicit tolerances for schedule conflicts (e.g., when an airplane is in heavy maintenance); commenters will request language permitting scheduling within the 35‑month window consistent with maintenance planning without penalty.

[P3] Legal commenters will argue that the AD must state whether noncompliance outside the specified times constitutes an immediate civil penalty exposure or whether enforcement discretion will be exercised for documented scheduling conflicts.

[P4] The 35‑month compliance window in § 39.13(g) is too long from a safety perspective for risk of fan cowl door failures; conversely, some operators will argue it is too short to schedule concurrent actions across global fleets and request alternative phased compliance options — the rule should justify the selected interval or allow staged compliance.

[P4] Stakeholders will request explicit guidance on whether the requirement to “accomplish concurrently the actions in (g)(1)–(g)(3)” precludes performing the actions on different maintenance visits when access or parts availability is limited.

[P5] Airlines and MROs will request technical clarification on the scope of “modify” for left/right FCDs with Old P/Ns — specifically, whether minor on-wing modifications are acceptable or whether removal and depot-level work is required.

[P5] Suppliers will request that table 1 be published in the AD (or referenced service bulletin be incorporated by reference) with full Old P/N/New P/N mapping; absence of the table in the rule text will lead to confusion and inconsistent compliance.

[P6] The placard installation requirement in (g)(2) lacks a diagram and exact placard text; commenters will request the required placard wording, dimensions, and fastening method to ensure standardization and avoid rework.

[P6] Cabin crews’ unions will request confirmation that placard placement (120 VU panel or coat stowage) will not interfere with emergency equipment stowage, accessibility, or crew procedures.

[P7] The re‑identification obligation in (g)(3) should specify acceptable marking methods (sticker, rivet tag, stenciling), permanence standards, and traceability to maintenance records to ensure long‑term compliance and auditability.

[P7] Maintenance organizations will request that re‑identification be allowed to be recorded in the ship’s log and component records as an alternative to physical re‑marking when doing so would not be practical.

[P8] The permission to replace Old P/N FCDs with New P/N FCDs as an acceptable means of compliance should clarify whether used/serviceable New P/N units from other aircraft are acceptable and whether they require new inspection or modification.

[P8] OEMs and parts-holders will request confirmation that installing New P/N FCDs as compliance does not create parts interchangeability issues with other maintenance procedures or warrantee implications.

[P9] The requirement that replacements follow instructions approved by the FAA Manager, EASA, or Airbus DOA creates administrative burden; commenters will request an established approval timeline and a presumptive acceptance of Airbus-approved instructions to expedite compliance.

[P9] Legal commenters will request clarification on the process and standards the FAA Manager will use to approve alternate instructions, to ensure decisions are predictable and transparent.

[P10] The allowance for Airbus modification 157517 in production to satisfy (g)(1) and (g)(3) should be expanded to permit retrofit of in‑service aircraft under the same modification instructions, with FAA acceptance, rather than limited to production only.

[P11] The condition that no Old P/N FCD be installed for acceptance of mod 157517 excludes aircraft that received partial fleet modifications; commenters will request guidance for mixed-configuration aircraft and for accepting production mods in retrofit contexts.

[P12] Allowing modifications 157519 or 157521 in production to satisfy (g)(2) should be clarified to permit retrofit installations and the AD should state whether post-production incorporation requires an STC or only operator work cards.

[P13] The prohibition in (k)(1) barring reinstallation of Old P/N FCDs on aircraft that had Old P/N FCDs as of the effective date is overly broad — commenters will ask for an exception for use of Old P/N parts temporarily during maintenance when New P/N parts are unavailable, provided an AMOC is in place.

[P13] Parts distributors will raise concerns that (k)(1) will make surplus Old P/N inventory unusable, causing economic loss; they will request a buy‑back or limited grandfathering provision.

[P14] The blanket prohibition in (k)(2) against installing any Old P/N on any airplane (even those that never had Old P/N installed) may be unnecessary and burdensome — operators will request clarification that the ban applies only to aircraft that have been modified under (g) or had Old P/Ns historically.

[P14] MROs will request an exception for use of Old P/N FCDs as temporary on-wing replacements pending installation of New P/Ns, provided additional inspections or mitigations are performed and documented.

[P15] Allowing installation of FCDs with part numbers approved after the AD effective date only for that airplane creates recordkeeping complexity; commenters will request that approvals be valid fleetwide once approved by the FAA Manager, EASA, or Airbus DOA.

[P16] The requirement that post-effective-date part numbers be approved by the FAA Manager, EASA, or Airbus DOA should explicitly permit approval via an established DOA approval process and specify timelines for agency review to avoid supply chain delays.

[P17] The obligation that installations follow modification instructions approved by the FAA Manager, EASA, or Airbus DOA should allow operators to use Airbus-issued service bulletins incorporated by reference without separate FAA approval, to streamline compliance.

[P18] Paragraph (m) granting credit for prior actions lacks specificity about acceptable documentary evidence; commenters will request a list of acceptable records (work orders, logbook entries, SB compliance forms) to receive credit.

[P18] Operators who complied using non‑identical but substantively equivalent service bulletin revisions will request explicit acceptance language and retroactive credit without requiring rework.

[P19] The AMOC authority to the FAA Manager is appropriate, but commenters will request a defined timeline (e.g., 60 or 90 days) for AMOC review and decision to prevent operational disruption.

[P19] Industry stakeholders will request clear criteria for AMOC approval, including acceptable data (test reports, engineering analyses) and whether previously approved AMOCs for similar ADs will be considered precedent.

[P20] Requiring AMOC requests be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO may impose unnecessary routing delay for international operators; commenters will request allowance for direct submission to the International Section for non‑U.S.-based fleets.

[P21] The requirement to address direct AMOC submissions to the person in paragraph (o)(2) is impractical without including that contact in the AD text; commenters will request that the named contact and contact information be published in the AD.

[P22] The option to email AMOC requests to 9-ANM-116-AMOC-REQUESTS@faa.gov is helpful but commenters will request that the AD also permit secure file transfer for large engineering packages and acknowledge electronic receipt within a set period.

[P23] Requiring operators to notify their principal inspector or local FSDO before using any approved AMOC is reasonable, but commenters will request a standard notification format and timeframe (e.g., within 48 hours) to ensure compliance clarity.

[P24] The mandate that corrective actions obtained from the manufacturer must be accomplished using a method approved by the FAA Manager, EASA, or Airbus DOA should clarify whether manufacturer-approved repair instructions accompanied by engineering data are sufficient or whether separate FAA approval is required.

[P24] Small operators will request expedited approval procedures for manufacturer corrective actions in cases of safety-critical items to avoid grounding aircraft during lengthy approvals.

[P25] The requirement that DOA approvals include the DOA-authorized signature should be expanded to accept digitally signed approvals in accordance with ICAO/EASA electronic signature guidance to avoid administrative delays.

[P25] Commenters will request that the AD explicitly recognize continuing airworthiness approval processes used by EASA and Airbus DOA so that dual signature requirements do not create duplication of approvals.

raw_output:
[P1] The proposed definition of critical habitat consisting solely of the listed physical or biological features is overly narrow and fails to account for landscape-level processes (e.g., riparian connectivity, floodplain dynamics) that are essential for candy darter conservation.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether adjacent upland areas that influence stream temperature and sediment inputs (e.g., riparian buffers) are included as part of the "physical or biological features" for critical habitat; omission will create enforcement gaps.

[P2] The provision to "maintain ratios or densities of nonnative species that allow candy darter populations to be maintained" is vague — the rule should specify numeric thresholds or monitoring protocols for nonnative species densities and identify which nonnative species are of concern.

[P2] Industry commenters will request an economic and practicability standard tied to any nonnative species management obligations, arguing the Service must consider costs before imposing controls on landowners for nonnative species removal.

[P2] Conservation groups will request that the rule prohibit introduction of known invasive species (e.g., specific crayfish or fish species) in designated habitat rather than relying on an ambiguous "ratios or densities" standard.

[P3] The requirement for "unembedded gravel and cobble substrate" needs measurable substrate stability and embeddedness criteria (e.g., percent surface area free of fine sediment, median grain size) to be enforceable.

[P3] Mining and dredging stakeholders will challenge the substrate provision as potentially precluding authorized gravel extraction or channel modification in designated reaches unless express exceptions or procedures for incidental take are defined.

[P3] Agencies responsible for permitting should be required to adopt best management practices for sediment control upstream to ensure substrate remains unembedded; the rule should state these expected actions.

[P4] The water quality provision is incomplete — it cuts off in the text ("e.g., pH, dissolved oxygen levels, tur") and must list the full parameters and quantitative criteria (specific pH range, minimum DO in mg/L, turbidity/STA) to provide legal certainty.

[P4] Municipal wastewater and stormwater permittees will request clear numeric water quality standards and seasonal temperature limits to know compliance requirements; otherwise the provision creates unbounded obligations.

[P4] Tribes and local governments will ask the Service to align the water quality criteria with existing state water quality standards and EPA criteria to avoid regulatory conflicts and duplicative monitoring.

[P5] The mandate for an "abundant, diverse benthic macroinvertebrate community" is commendable, but the rule must define "abundant" and "diverse" with specific indices (e.g., EPT richness, total density per m2) and monitoring frequency.

[P5] Agricultural stakeholders will request guidance on acceptable agricultural practices and buffers to support macroinvertebrate communities while allowing normal farming activities; without this, routine ag practices could face enforcement actions.

[P6] The requirement to "maintain adequate water quantity and flow velocities" requires quantifiable flow regimes (e.g., minimum base flows, peak flow limits, seasonal flow curves) so water managers and dam operators can plan operations accordingly.

[P6] Hydropower operators and water utilities will object to the lack of specified minimum instream flows and predictability of modifications; they request rule language that requires consultation and coordination before imposing flow restrictions.

[P6] The Service should clarify whether groundwater withdrawals that affect stream baseflows are regulated under this provision and whether water rights holders will be subject to new constraints.

[P7] The exclusion of "existing manmade structures and the land they occupy" is welcome for property owners but the rule must define "existing" (as of what date) to avoid retroactive inclusion of structures built after publication.

[P7] Transportation agencies will request explicit carve-outs for maintained roads, bridges, and associated rights-of-way where infrastructure is necessary, and a streamlined process for Federal actions that affect these structures.

[P7] Conservationists will warn that wholesale exclusion of lands with manmade structures could fragment critical habitat and undermine conservation if important riparian corridors contain small structures; propose narrower exclusions.

[P8] Making coordinates/plot points available online is useful, but the Service should ensure that the web resources are regularly updated, accessible (ADA-compliant), and accompanied by GIS shapefiles and metadata for use by practitioners.

[P8] Legal experts will note the rule should require publication-quality GIS files with coordinate reference system and datum stated (e.g., WGS84) to avoid mapping inconsistencies in implementation and permitting.

[P8] Some stakeholders will request that high-resolution map data not be publicly posted for certain sensitive reaches to prevent targeted vandalism or unauthorized access that could harm the candy darter or habitat.

[P9] The permission to obtain field office information via Service regional offices must include a clear list of responsible contacts and expect response timeframes; commenters will request a single point-of-contact for each designated reach.

[P9] Local governments and consultants will request that the Service provide templates for data requests and standardized protocols to streamline inquiries to field offices and avoid inconsistent responses.

[P1] Legal commentators will argue the rule must include a statement on how these physical/biological features were determined (scientific basis) and the record supporting inclusion or exclusion of specific reaches to satisfy Administrative Procedure Act requirements.

[P2] Scientists will request that monitoring and adaptive management triggers be defined: at what nonnative species density does the Service require management actions and what actions are acceptable.

[P3] Recreational users (anglers, paddlers) will ask whether substrate restoration projects (e.g., gravel augmentation) will be allowed and what permitting path will be used to implement habitat improvements within critical habitat.

[P4] Public health agencies will request clarity on whether chemical/physical parameters include contaminant thresholds (e.g., heavy metals, pesticides) and how those interact with existing Clean Water Act enforcement and NPDES permits.

[P5] Citizen scientists and NGOs will request funding or support commitments for macroinvertebrate monitoring to ensure data are available to evaluate compliance with the abundance/diversity requirement.

[P6] Climate change advocates will request that flow and temperature provisions include consideration of projected future climate conditions and require corridor protections to allow species to shift within the watershed.

[P7] Private landowners will request assurance that normal maintenance of excluded manmade structures (e.g., repaving roads, maintaining levees) will not trigger critical habitat modification consultations absent impacts to adjacent qualifying features.

[P8] Businesses and consultants will request that online coordinate data include a clear disclaimer and instructions on how to interpret boundaries for permitting and project planning to prevent inadvertent noncompliance.

[P9] Several commenters will request that the Service publish office hours, languages available, and whether site visits or in-person consultations are available to support stakeholders in understanding responsibilities under the rule.
