[P1] The requirement to always use the maximum value of any provided lead-content range (§143.12(b)) is overly conservative and will penalize manufacturers who reliably provide accurate ranges based on batch variability; EPA should allow use of a representative mean or median with appropriate documentation instead.

[P1] Using the maximum of a range will inflate calculated lead content for multi-component products and could improperly classify compliant products as noncompliant, causing unnecessary recalls and supply disruptions.

[P2] Requiring the maximum lead content of both coating and alloy when calculating component lead content (§143.12(c)) double-counts lead that may be non-contributory to potable water leaching and will create unrealistic compliance burdens.

[P2] The rule does not provide guidance on how to account for coatings that are not in contact with water or are fully encapsulated; EPA should allow exemptions or de minimis treatment for internal coatings that are protective and non-leaching.

[P3] Mandating use of the liner's maximum lead content in component calculations (§143.12(d)) fails to consider liners that are chemically bonded or non-leaching; request EPA permit testing for leachability rather than relying solely on composition maxima.

[P4] The broad prohibition on use of non-lead-free pipes, fittings, fixtures, solder, or flux in §143.13(a) lacks grandfathering for existing lawful installations and necessary maintenance, creating practical impossibilities for immediate repairs in older systems.

[P5] §143.13(a)(1) prohibiting use by any public water system is ambiguous as to whether it applies to homeowner-owned portions of the system (service lines on private property); EPA should clarify the boundary between public water system responsibilities and private property.

[P6] §143.13(a)(2) prohibition applying to “any plumbing in a residential or nonresidential facility providing water for human consumption” is too broad and may unintentionally cover industrial processes that use potable water for cooling or cleaning; recommend narrowing language or adding specified exceptions.

[P7] The exception for leaded joints to repair cast iron pipes (§143.13(b)) is appropriate but too narrowly worded — it should explicitly define “necessary” to avoid variable interpretations by enforcement agencies.

[P8] Conditioning full PWS grant allotments on state enforcement of §1417(a)(1) and §143.13 (§143.14) may coerce states before they have time to adopt implementing codes; EPA should include a reasonable compliance timeline and technical assistance funding.

[P8] The federal conditioning of grants on state code adoption (§143.14) could conflict with state law processes and create legal challenges under state sovereignty; recommend offering incentives rather than strict grant withholds.

[P9] The general prohibition on introducing non-lead-free pipes or fittings into commerce (§143.15(a)) lacks a clear mechanism for existing inventory sell-through; EPA should allow a transition sell-off period with recordkeeping.

[P10] The manufacturing/industrial processing exception in §143.15(a) is too vague — the rule needs a precise definition of “manufacturing or industrial processing” to prevent circumvention (e.g., labeling potable products as “industrial”).

[P11] §143.15(b) banning sellers (other than manufacturers) from selling non-lead-free solder or flux imposes strict liability on retailers who may unknowingly carry legacy stock; EPA should require reasonable notice periods and safe harbor if retailers act promptly to remove noncompliant items.

[P12] The labeling requirement for non-lead-free solder/flux in §143.15(c) is sensible, but the regulation should specify label size, contrast, and placement to ensure the “prominent” label standard is enforceable and uniform.

[P13] Conditioning allowed commerce of non-lead-free solders/flux on the label stating it is illegal to use for potable plumbing (§143.15(c)) may be ineffective because purchasers (e.g., DIY consumers) might ignore labels; EPA should require supply-chain controls or retailer training.

[P14] The exemptions in §143.16 for listed products are helpful, but the list in §143.16(b) and (c) appears incomplete (e.g., lacks certain commercial equipment); EPA should publish an exhaustive list or a clear petition process to add necessary items.

[P15] The “used exclusively for nonpotable services” condition (§143.16(a)) that products be “incapable of use” in potable services is unrealistically strict; many legitimately nonpotable products could be repurposed — EPA should instead require durable marking and contractual controls.

[P16] Requiring “clearly labeled” products as nonpotable (§143.16(a)(2)) is appropriate but the rule should define acceptable wording, language translations, and durability standards for labels to ensure long-term compliance.

[P17] Exempting toilets, bidets, urinals, and other items in §143.16(b) ignores evidence that some of these fixtures can be connected in atypical ways to drinking water systems; EPA should require those exempted items to be designed or marketed to prevent potable use when excluded.

[P18] The exemption for fire hydrants and service saddles (§143.16(b)) may pose a public health risk if hydrants are used as emergency drinking sources; recommend requiring alternative measures (e.g., adapters that are lead-free where likely to be used for potable water).

[P19] The exemption for clothes washing machines and sump pumps (§143.16(c)) is appropriate for nonpotable uses, but products marketed multifunctionally (e.g., emergency potable water collection) should be covered; EPA should require clear labeling and marketing restrictions.

[P20] The labeling deadline for products introduced into commerce (§143.17(a))—three years after publication or before introduction—creates market confusion and supply-chain disruption; recommend a phased approach tied to product categories and reasonable inventory depletion timelines.

[P21] §143.17(b)(1)’s rule that shrink wrap does not count as packaging for labeling may impose heavy costs on bulk suppliers who ship via standard industry packaging; EPA should permit durable exterior shipper labeling as an interim compliance option.

[P22] The marking requirements in §143.17(b)(2) that require indelible stamping or printing may be technically infeasible for certain materials (e.g., some plastics) or for parts produced in high-volume stamping lines; EPA should accept durable adhesive tags or embedded RFID marking as alternatives.

[P23] Permitting markings in non-visible locations when visible marking “will adversely impact visual appeal” (§143.17(b)(2)(ii)) is subjective and will invite inconsistent enforcement; EPA should define objective criteria for “adversely impact” and require an accompanying let-of-record explaining why.

[P24] The certification labeling content requirements (§143.17(c), §143.17(c)(1)-(2)) may conflict with third-party certifier branding rules and trademark licenses; EPA should coordinate with accreditors to ensure mutually acceptable labeling standards.

[P25] §143.18 requiring prominent labels on non-lead-free solder/flux lacks enforcement clarity — who is responsible for ensuring existing imported inventory bears these labels: importer, distributor, or retailer? The rule should specify liability.

[P26] The requirement that manufacturers/importers secure certification by an accredited third-party within three years (§143.19(a),(c)) could be infeasible given limited accreditation capacity and testing lab throughput; EPA should allow provisional self-certification while accreditation capacity scales up.

[P27] §143.19(b) mandating accredited third-party certification except for small manufacturers/importers may disadvantage mid-sized companies that cannot access accreditation but exceed the 100-employee threshold; recommend an intermediate pathway or expanded eligibility.

[P28] The 100-employee threshold for self-certification (§143.19(c)) is arbitrary; industry commenters will request use of revenue-based or production-volume criteria rather than employee count to determine eligibility.

[P29] Requiring self-certifying entities to post certificates on a U.S.-accessible web page (§143.19(d)(2)) disadvantages small manufacturers without U.S. web hosting and may impede foreign manufacturers who import via U.S. distributors; EPA should permit posting to a centralized EPA portal instead.

[P30] The certificate content requirements in §143.19(e) (contact info, product listing, verification method) raise confidentiality concerns for proprietary product models and supply-chain details; EPA must allow redaction of sensitive model-level data while still conveying compliance.

[P31] §143.19(e)(4)’s requirement to state how conformance was verified is vague and could require disclosure of proprietary laboratory methods and internal formulas; recommend allowing a high-level description and submission of detailed methods under CBI protections.

[P32] §143.19(f) requiring maintenance of certificates and supporting documentation at a U.S. primary place of business is burdensome for foreign manufacturers and small importers; EPA should allow documents to be maintained by the U.S. importer or a designated U.S. agent.

[P33] The list of acceptable supporting documentation examples (§143.19(f)) (e.g., schematic drawings and weighted average calculations) is helpful, but EPA should publish templates and calculation examples to ensure uniform submissions and avoid disputes.

[P34] §143.19(f) and (g) requiring documentation and certificate completion prior to introduction into commerce may be impractical for complex, multi-sourced products assembled in the U.S.; EPA should permit staged certification for assembled items where components are certified separately.

[P35] The Administrator’s wide discretion to request any information to determine compliance (§143.20(b)) without defined limits risks burdensome ad hoc demands; EPA should define scope, frequency limits, and appeal rights for information requests.

[P36] §143.20(b) requiring provision of requested information in a format “reasonably determined” by the Administrator is vague; stakeholders request defined acceptable electronic formats (PDF, CSV) and reasonable timeframes (minimum 30 days except in emergencies).

[P37] The enforcement provisions (§143.20(a)) referencing potential criminal penalties should be narrowed to require willful misconduct before criminal enforcement; otherwise, minor paperwork or labeling errors could trigger disproportionate sanctions.

[P38] Requiring comments to be submitted by May 17, 2017 (§62) is a past date and inconsistent with current rulemaking timelines; commenters request correction of all dated deadlines and clear current comment windows.

[P39] The mandated submission procedures to Regulations.gov with a specified Docket ID (§63-66) are fine, but EPA should provide alternative submission mechanisms for parties lacking internet access and clarify whether duplicate submissions to other dockets will be considered.

[P40] The prohibition on editing or removing comments on Regulations.gov (§66) raises privacy concerns for individuals who may inadvertently disclose personal data; EPA should allow redaction requests or correction mechanisms for personal information.

[P41] The rule’s public-docket publication permission (§67) requires assurance that CBI will never be published; EPA must clarify how it will screen docket submissions and handle redaction to protect confidential business information.

[P42] The prohibition on electronically submitting CBI (§68) is unrealistic in modern practice; EPA should provide secure upload mechanisms for CBI and clear instructions for how to submit confidential materials outside the public docket.

[P43] The requirement that multimedia submissions be accompanied by written comments (§69-70) is sensible, but EPA should define minimum written content length and acceptable multimedia file formats to facilitate review.

[P44] The rule’s statement that EPA generally will not consider comments located outside the primary submission system (§71) could result in loss of important stakeholder input posted on other industry platforms; EPA should allow cross-references and permit inclusion of materials hosted elsewhere if the primary submission contains a full copy.

[P45] Filing oppositions and replies by the specified April/May 2017 deadlines (§72-73) is impossible now; stakeholders request EPA update the procedural timetable and ensure adequate timeframes for petition oppositions and replies consistent with the Administrative Procedure Act.

[P46] The exemptions and exceptions scattered across §§143.13–143.16 and §143.15 create potential loopholes and inconsistent enforcement; stakeholders request a consolidated matrix of permitted/exempt products with illustrative use-cases.

[P47] The rule lacks clear testing protocols or accredited test methods for determining lead content and weighted average calculations referenced throughout (§143.12, §143.19); EPA should adopt standardized analytical methods (e.g., EPA-approved ICP-MS procedures) and provide guidance.

[P48] The required visible marking post-installation “where practical” (§143.17(b)(2)) is subjective; stakeholders request objective standards (e.g., marking must be visible without disassembly in X% of typical installations) to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P49] The requirement that self-certifying signatories be “responsible corporate officer” or similar (§143.19(d)(1)) may be unattainable for very small proprietorships or sole importers; EPA should permit authorized agents with notarized powers of attorney.

[P50] The rule does not address cost impacts or provide a Regulatory Flexibility Analysis for small businesses required to self-certify or obtain third-party certification; commenters will request EPA publish and consider an updated economic analysis and alternatives to minimize small business burdens.

Exempting toilets, bidets, urinals, and other items in §143.16(b) ignores evidence that some of these fixtures can be connected in atypical ways to drinking water systems; EPA should require those exempted items to be designed or marketed to prevent potable use when excluded.

The exemption for fire hydrants and service saddles (§143.16(b)) may pose a public health risk if hydrants are used as emergency drinking sources; recommend requiring alternative measures (e.g., adapters that are lead-free where likely to be used for potable water).

The exemption for clothes washing machines and sump pumps (§143.16(c)) is appropriate for nonpotable uses, but products marketed multifunctionally (e.g., emergency potable water collection) should be covered; EPA should require clear labeling and marketing restrictions.

The labeling deadline for products introduced into commerce (§143.17(a))—three years after publication or before introduction—creates market confusion and supply-chain disruption; recommend a phased approach tied to product categories and reasonable inventory depletion timelines.

§143.17(b)(1)’s rule that shrink wrap does not count as packaging for labeling may impose heavy costs on bulk suppliers who ship via standard industry packaging; EPA should permit durable exterior shipper labeling as an interim compliance option.

The marking requirements in §143.17(b)(2) that require indelible stamping or printing may be technically infeasible for certain materials (e.g., some plastics) or for parts produced in high-volume stamping lines; EPA should accept durable adhesive tags or embedded RFID marking as alternatives.

Permitting markings in non-visible locations when visible marking “will adversely impact visual appeal” (§143.17(b)(2)(ii)) is subjective and will invite inconsistent enforcement; EPA should define objective criteria for “adversely impact” and require an accompanying let-of-record explaining why.

The certification labeling content requirements (§143.17(c), §143.17(c)(1)-(2)) may conflict with third-party certifier branding rules and trademark licenses; EPA should coordinate with accreditors to ensure mutually acceptable labeling standards.

§143.18 requiring prominent labels on non-lead-free solder/flux lacks enforcement clarity — who is responsible for ensuring existing imported inventory bears these labels: importer, distributor, or retailer? The rule should specify liability.

The requirement that manufacturers/importers secure certification by an accredited third-party within three years (§143.19(a),(c)) could be infeasible given limited accreditation capacity and testing lab throughput; EPA should allow provisional self-certification while accreditation capacity scales up.

§143.19(b) mandating accredited third-party certification except for small manufacturers/importers may disadvantage mid-sized companies that cannot access accreditation but exceed the 100-employee threshold; recommend an intermediate pathway or expanded eligibility.

The 100-employee threshold for self-certification (§143.19(c)) is arbitrary; industry commenters will request use of revenue-based or production-volume criteria rather than employee count to determine eligibility.

Requiring self-certifying entities to post certificates on a U.S.-accessible web page (§143.19(d)(2)) disadvantages small manufacturers without U.S. web hosting and may impede foreign manufacturers who import via U.S. distributors; EPA should permit posting to a centralized EPA portal instead.

The certificate content requirements in §143.19(e) (contact info, product listing, verification method) raise confidentiality concerns for proprietary product models and supply-chain details; EPA must allow redaction of sensitive model-level data while still conveying compliance.

§143.19(e)(4)’s requirement to state how conformance was verified is vague and could require disclosure of proprietary laboratory methods and internal formulas; recommend allowing a high-level description and submission of detailed methods under CBI protections.

§143.19(f) requiring maintenance of certificates and supporting documentation at a U.S. primary place of business is burdensome for foreign manufacturers and small importers; EPA should allow documents to be maintained by the U.S. importer or a designated U.S. agent.

The list of acceptable supporting documentation examples (§143.19(f)) (e.g., schematic drawings and weighted average calculations) is helpful, but EPA should publish templates and calculation examples to ensure uniform submissions and avoid disputes.

§143.19(f) and (g) requiring documentation and certificate completion prior to introduction into commerce may be impractical for complex, multi-sourced products assembled in the U.S.; EPA should permit staged certification for assembled items where components are certified separately.

The Administrator’s wide discretion to request any information to determine compliance (§143.20(b)) without defined limits risks burdensome ad hoc demands; EPA should define scope, frequency limits, and appeal rights for information requests.

§143.20(b) requiring provision of requested information in a format “reasonably determined” by the Administrator is vague; stakeholders request defined acceptable electronic formats (PDF, CSV) and reasonable timeframes (minimum 30 days except in emergencies).

The enforcement provisions (§143.20(a)) referencing potential criminal penalties should be narrowed to require willful misconduct before criminal enforcement; otherwise, minor paperwork or labeling errors could trigger disproportionate sanctions.

Requiring comments to be submitted by May 17, 2017 (§62) is a past date and inconsistent with current rulemaking timelines; commenters request correction of all dated deadlines and clear current comment windows.

The mandated submission procedures to Regulations.gov with a specified Docket ID (§63-66) are fine, but EPA should provide alternative submission mechanisms for parties lacking internet access and clarify whether duplicate submissions to other dockets will be considered.

The prohibition on editing or removing comments on Regulations.gov (§66) raises privacy concerns for individuals who may inadvertently disclose personal data; EPA should allow redaction requests or correction mechanisms for personal information.

[P1] The October 8, 2021 comment deadline is unreasonable and precludes meaningful participation from affected small operators and labor organizations; extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] The rule fails to provide clear instructions for submitting late comments if technical problems occur before the October 8, 2021 deadline; add an electronic fallback and grace period.

[P2] The applicability language is incomplete—provision (c) truncates model list and does not specify serial number ranges or production blocks; clarify which serial numbers/production dates of CF34–10E variants are covered.

[P2] The AD should explicitly state whether engines installed on leased or repaired airframes, or engines with used/overhauled seals, are included; request clarity on applicability to engines with replacement stationary oil seals of unknown provenance.

[P3] The compliance clause lacks an explicit statement about whether compliance can be accomplished at the time of scheduled maintenance without additional inspections; clarify coordination with existing maintenance programs.

[P4] The initial visual inspection requirement does not define what constitutes a “visual inspection” (lighting, disassembly allowed, use of borescope, trained inspector qualifications); provide a detailed inspection procedure or reference an FAA/GE-approved procedure.

[P4] The AD does not state who is qualified to perform the initial visual inspection—certified mechanics, licensed repair stations, or other specified personnel; identify acceptable certifying authorities.

[P5] The threshold of 2,250 FHs for delayed inspection is arbitrary and unsupported by the NPRM—provide the data or analysis that justifies the 2,250 FH cutoff and the 2,350 FH hard limit.

[P6] Allowing 100 FHs after the effective date for seals with ≥2,250 FHs may create operational risk for high-utilization fleets; require immediate inspection at the next maintenance opportunity within 30 days rather than 100 FHs.

[P7] The repeat-inspection structure lacks guidance on recordkeeping for inspections and FH tracking; require operators to maintain a log entry format and retention period.

[P8] Repeating inspections every 750 FHs for 2,250–7,000 FH seals may be insufficient given potential progressive degradation; request data supporting the 750-FH interval and consider shortening to 500 FHs.

[P9] The 375-FH repeat interval for 7,001–10,000 FH seals may not account for variability in duty cycles (short sectors vs long sectors); require a cycle-based alternative or a risk-based adjustment for operators with high takeoff/landing cycles.

[P10] The 100-FH inspection interval for seals over 10,000 FHs could ground aircraft frequently and impose undue burden; propose an alternative of mandatory seal replacement at 10,000 FHs to eliminate repetitive inspections, or permit scheduling aligned with heavy maintenance visits.

[P11] Requiring immediate removal before further flight if Teflon material is found is operationally disruptive—allow a short, documented ferry flight to an approved maintenance base without passengers (beyond the five-cycle allowance) in extenuating circumstances, subject to FAA approval.

[P11] The AD does not define acceptable evidence of “Teflon material” in the strainer screen (size, particle composition); require laboratory confirmation versus visual identification to avoid unnecessary removals.

[P12] Mandating replacement before 10,000 FHs or within 500 FHs of the AD effective date, whichever is later, could force maintenance outside of scheduled checks; allow replacement to be performed at the next heavy maintenance visit within that interval and permit credit for recently installed eligible parts.

[P12] The combined “before 10,000 FHs or within 500 FHs after effective date, whichever is later” phrasing is confusing—clarify whether engines already beyond 10,000 FHs on the effective date must comply immediately or within 500 FHs.

[P13] The terminating action only covers two specific part numbers (B1316–00453 or B1316–01274); clarify whether other superseding/modified part numbers or OEM-reworked seals qualify as “eligible parts” and provide acceptable part number list or approval process.

[P13] The AD should allow use of equivalent parts approved by GE or an OEM repair station via AMOC, rather than limiting terminating action to specific part numbers; otherwise it may unnecessarily constrain available parts.

[P14] Requiring special flight permits to comply with paragraph (j)(1) creates ambiguity—specify the documentation and pre-flight inspections required to obtain such a permit.

[P15] The five-cycle non-revenue ferry flight permission is too restrictive for remote operators who may need longer transit times; allow ferry operations sufficient to reach the nearest qualified maintenance facility, subject to risk assessment and FAA approval.

[P15] The AD does not clearly state whether the five-cycle limit applies per engine or per flight; clarify whether multiple engines with findings are counted cumulatively and how cycles are calculated for ferry flights.

[P16] Requiring only essential flight crew and no passengers for ferry flights may be impractical for long repositioning flights that need relief crew; allow additional crew if safety dictates and with FAA concurrence.

[P17] The outright prohibition on passengers for ferry flights should include explicit carve-outs for essential non-revenue personnel (e.g., maintenance technicians needed to service the engine upon arrival) with FAA approval.

[P18] Mandating non-ETOPS operation for ferry flights could prevent necessary routing over oceanic or remote areas; request an alternative provision allowing ETOPS-like planning with mitigation measures and FAA concurrence when non-ETOPS routing is impossible.

[P19] The AMOC approval authority assigned to the ECO Branch Manager should be expanded to allow timely local relief by principal inspectors in urgent situations to avoid operational disruption.

[P20] Requiring AMOC requests to go through the requester’s principal inspector or local FSDO may delay approvals for foreign operators; allow foreign operators to submit AMOC requests through their national aviation authority or directly to the FAA certification office.

[P21] Directing AMOC submissions to the manager named in Related Information without providing contact details in the AD text will hinder timely compliance; include full contact information (name, phone, email) in the AD.

[P22] Permitting email submission to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov is helpful, but the AD should also allow secure file transfer for large engineering packages and require acknowledgment receipt timelines to ensure timely processing.

[P23] Requiring notification of the principal inspector or local FSDO before using an approved AMOC lacks timelines—specify how soon (e.g., within 48 hours) notification must be provided and what documentation must be forwarded.

[P23] The AD should clarify whether use of an approved AMOC must be recorded in the aircraft maintenance log and whether that record satisfies the notification requirement to the principal inspector.

[General legal] The AD does not include a regulatory flexibility analysis or cost estimate for small entities affected by mandatory inspections and replacements; publish a detailed cost-benefit and RFA analysis.

[General safety/data] The NPRM does not present the technical data or incident history (e.g., number of events, severity) supporting these compliance intervals and replacement requirements; include the underlying safety analysis for stakeholder review.

[General implementation] Provide an incorporation-by-reference (IBR) list of GE service bulletins or inspection procedures that define the strainer inspection method, including acceptable inspection tools and sample photos of Teflon debris.

[General international] The AD should harmonize with EASA and other authorities’ directives to avoid conflicting requirements for international operators; coordinate and adopt a common compliance schedule where possible.

[Industry practical] For operators who have already replaced seals under earlier service bulletins, allow credit and require documentation submittal rather than re-performing inspections.

[Maintenance cost] Provide an estimate of man-hours and part costs for the mandatory seal replacement before 10,000 FHs and any inspection labor to allow operators to budget and include in comments.

[Enforcement] Clarify enforcement policy for operators who miss an inspection interval by a small margin due to scheduling constraints—provide a cure period or grace allowance with required risk assessment rather than immediate grounding.

[Recordkeeping] Require standardized reporting of findings (Teflon presence, amount, photographs) to the FAA to support ongoing safety assessment and possible revision of inspection intervals.

[P1] The March 12, 2018 comment deadline in provision P1 is unreasonably short and does not allow sufficient time for affected operators, suppliers, and trade associations to perform technical review and coordinate consolidated responses; extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether the March 12, 2018 deadline applies to electronic and mailed submissions equally and provide an explicit time-of-day and time zone cutoff to avoid late-filing disputes.

[P2] Provision P2's cross-reference to "the compliance times specified" is vague; the AD should explicitly list each compliance time in the regulatory text rather than relying on other documents.

[P2] There is no grace period for operators that are between scheduled maintenance events; P2 should allow operators to incorporate required actions into the next scheduled maintenance visit within a reasonable window instead of forcing off-schedule maintenance.

[P3] The 42‑month inspection window in P3 is excessively long given the potential safety risk of defective fusible plugs; the FAA should shorten the inspection interval to 6–12 months or require immediate inspection for high-utilization aircraft.

[P3] Conversely, for small operators or operators with limited downtime, a 42‑month mandatory inspection may impose operational burdens; provide an option to perform inspections at the next scheduled heavy maintenance or within 18 months for smaller operators.

[P3] P3 lacks a clear definition of "effective date of this AD"; specify the exact calendar date or publication date to avoid confusion about when the 42‑month clock starts.

[P3] The provision P3 text appears truncated ("stamped with L"); the full lot stamping text must be provided (e.g., "stamped with Lot PA–21 or PA–22") to ensure inspectors can reliably identify affected parts.

[P4] Allowing record reviews as an alternative in P4 is reasonable, but the rule must specify what constitutes "conclusive" evidence in maintenance records (e.g., original part number, traceable invoice from manufacturer, installation log entry) to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P4] The AD should permit record review only if the records are original, verifiable, and include supplier lot/serial numbers; secondary or uncertified copies should not be accepted as "conclusive" per P4.

[P4] For older aircraft with missing or incomplete records, P4 should allow for a limited sampling physical inspection rather than forcing full replacement, to reduce cost and downtime.

[P5] P5 requires replacement before the next flight if an affected plug is found; this is operationally impracticable for some remote or international operations—allow replacement within 24–72 hours or before the next commercial passenger-carrying flight instead.

[P5] The AD should permit the use of temporary placarding or operational limitations if immediate replacement as required by P5 is not feasible, provided a flight risk assessment is performed and accepted by the principal inspector.

[P5] Clarify in P5 whether replacement parts must be FAA‑approved parts or may be identical OEM-design parts purchased through authorized distributors; specify acceptable part documentation.

[P6] The installation prohibition in P6 is appropriate, but it should include a grandfathering clause for parts installed on new production aircraft prior to the effective date, or at least clarify applicability to in‑stock inventory.

[P6] P6 should allow for documented transfer of affected plugs to non-flight uses (e.g., training, test rigs) so long as they are permanently tagged and not re-installed on aircraft.

[P6] The description in P6 references Lot PA–21 or PA–22; the AD should include a photo or diagram of the lot stamping location and alternative marking variations to avoid misidentification.

[P7] The AMOC authority in P7 is limited to the Manager, New York ACO Branch; commenters request clarification whether other FAA ODA holders or delegated authorities can submit AMOC proposals and whether the national Flight Standards division may provide final concurrence.

[P7] Provide expected processing timelines and criteria for AMOC approvals in P7; without timelines, operators cannot plan maintenance schedules around potential AMOC relief.

[P8] The requirement in P8 to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO may create unnecessary layers and delay; allow direct submission to the certification office with a copy to the principal inspector as an alternative.

[P9] P9 directs submissions to a specific Program Manager and address; commenters request an email submission option and an online portal to improve tracking and reduce mailing delays, and ask for confirmation that the listed contact information will be maintained.

[P9] The named contact in P9 should be accompanied by a backup contact or office mailbox in case of personnel changes; otherwise AMOC processing may be disrupted by turnover.

[P10] The obligation in P10 to notify the principal inspector or FSDO before using an AMOC needs a time window (for example, notify within 48 hours of implementation); otherwise operators will face ambiguity about when notification is required.

[P10] Clarify whether notification under P10 must include documentation of the AMOC approval and any operational limitations, and whether the notification must be submitted electronically or in writing.

[P11] The permission in P11 to view service information at the Renton address is insufficient for statewide or international stakeholders; require that the referenced service information be made electronically available (PDF) and free of charge.

[P11] Provide extended viewing hours or appointment procedures for the FAA Transport Standards Branch in P11; as written, access may be impractical for small operators without travel budgets.

[General] The AD text throughout appears to be truncated or contains typographical errors (e.g., P3 truncated stamp text); the FAA must issue a corrected supplemental notice before finalizing the AD to ensure legal certainty.

[Legal] Several provisions (P2, P5, P6) may conflict with existing 14 CFR parts regarding installation records and part approval; include a legal analysis or statement of regulatory compatibility to prevent enforcement conflicts.

[Industry] The economic impact of mandatory inspections, potential immediate replacements (P5), and prohibition of installations (P6) are not analyzed in the preamble; publish a Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis and quantify cost impacts on small entities.

[Safety Advocacy] Given that fusible plugs are a critical safety component, the FAA should require reporting of any discovered affected plugs to a central database to track prevalence, rather than merely requiring replacement as in P5.

[International Operators] The AD must clarify applicability to U.S.-registered aircraft only or foreign-registered aircraft operated into the U.S., and harmonize with EASA directives to avoid duplicate compliance; add cross-reference to international coordination.

The requirement in P8 to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO may create unnecessary layers and delay; allow direct submission to the certification office with a copy to the principal inspector as an alternative.

P9 directs submissions to a specific Program Manager and address; commenters request an email submission option and an online portal to improve tracking and reduce mailing delays, and ask for confirmation that the listed contact information will be maintained.
The named contact in P9 should be accompanied by a backup contact or office mailbox in case of personnel changes; otherwise AMOC processing may be disrupted by turnover.

The obligation in P10 to notify the principal inspector or FSDO before using an AMOC needs a time window (for example, notify within 48 hours of implementation); otherwise operators will face ambiguity about when notification is required.
Clarify whether notification under P10 must include documentation of the AMOC approval and any operational limitations, and whether the notification must be submitted electronically or in writing.

The permission in P11 to view service information at the Renton address is insufficient for statewide or international stakeholders; require that the referenced service information be made electronically available (PDF) and free of charge.
Provide extended viewing hours or appointment procedures for the FAA Transport Standards Branch in P11; as written, access may be impractical for small operators without travel budgets.

[General] The AD text throughout appears to be truncated or contains typographical errors (e.g., P3 truncated stamp text); the FAA must issue a corrected supplemental notice before finalizing the AD to ensure legal certainty.

[Legal] Several provisions (P2, P5, P6) may conflict with existing 14 CFR parts regarding installation records and part approval; include a legal analysis or statement of regulatory compatibility to prevent enforcement conflicts.

[Industry] The economic impact of mandatory inspections, potential immediate replacements (P5), and prohibition of installations (P6) are not analyzed in the preamble; publish a Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis and quantify cost impacts on small entities.

[Safety Advocacy] Given that fusible plugs are a critical safety component, the FAA should require reporting of any discovered affected plugs to a central database to track prevalence, rather than merely requiring replacement as in P5.

[International Operators] The AD must clarify applicability to U.S.-registered aircraft only or foreign-registered aircraft operated into the U.S., and harmonize with EASA directives to avoid duplicate compliance; add cross-reference to international coordination.

raw_output:
[P1] Industry commenters will argue that requiring the capitated contract to include Medicare cost‑sharing coverage (primary and acute care including Medicare cost‑sharing) creates significant actuarial and budget uncertainty for MA organizations without specifying how states will fund the Medicaid share of those cost‑sharing obligations.

[P1] Legal advocates will claim the provision is ambiguous about whether the obligation applies only to full‑benefit dual eligibles or also to partial duals, and request clarification that Medicare cost‑sharing coverage is required only for full‑benefit dual eligibles.

[P2] Nursing home operators and plans will contend that the 180‑day minimum nursing facility coverage per plan year is inflexible and could disincentivize community‑based LTSS by guaranteeing inpatient utilization; they will request an alternative metric tied to medical necessity rather than a fixed day count.

[P2] State Medicaid agencies will claim the mandated coverage of LTSS including at least 180 nursing facility days will impose unfunded mandate costs on state budgets and request that CMS provide actuarial guidance and federal financial participation assurances.

[P3] Behavioral health providers and mental health advocates will support the 2025 requirement to cover behavioral health services but request explicit definitions (scope, intensity, parity standards) and timelines for implementation resources and workforce development.

[P3] Behavioral health payers will request clarification whether the behavioral health coverage mandate requires inclusion of both inpatient and outpatient behavioral health, substance use disorder treatment, and whether carve‑outs to specialty managed behavioral health organizations remain permissible.

[P4] Home health agencies and plans will request clarity on how “home health services as defined in § 440.70” maps to Medicare versus Medicaid definitions, and whether differences in scope between programs create duplicate or conflicting obligations for plans.

[P4] Industry commenters will ask CMS to confirm whether home health services required beginning in 2025 include personal care services or just Medicare‑defined skilled nursing/home health, and whether states can limit scope by contract.

[P5] Durable medical equipment (DME) suppliers will request specification of which § 440.70(b)(3) DME categories are covered and whether plans must cover higher‑cost DME models without prior authorization, and they will seek clarification of repair/replacement rules and reimbursement rates.

[P6] Patient advocacy organizations will endorse aligned care management but request firm standards and measurable benchmarks for “aligned care management” and “specialty care networks” to ensure coordination is meaningful and not superficial.

[P6] Legal experts will warn that “aligned” care management is vague and may permit checkbox compliance; they will request CMS promulgate objective criteria (shared care plans, unified authorization processes, joint quality metrics) and require data‑sharing protocols and timetables.

[P7] MA organizations will oppose the “exclusively aligned enrollment” requirement starting 2025 as disrupting existing enrollment options for beneficiaries and assert it could reduce beneficiary choice; they will ask for transition flexibility or waiver options.

[P7] Consumer advocates will support exclusively aligned enrollment if it demonstrably improves coordination but request evidence‑based tracking and outcome reporting (e.g., hospitalizations, LTSS outcomes) before nationwide enforcement.

[P8] Plans and states will request clarification on what constitutes “entire service area” (county, state, MSA) and whether geographic access exceptions are allowable (rural counties with insufficient providers), asking for CMS waiver or phased implementation options.

[P8] Rural health providers will argue the mandate to cover the entire service area could force plans into uneconomic markets and request geographic exceptions or modified network adequacy standards for low‑population areas.

[P9] Industry commenters will ask for clarity on permissible contracting entities and whether management services organizations or separate corporate subsidiaries that are not legal parents can satisfy the parent/controlled entity requirement.

[P9] Legal commenters will warn the parent/controlled entity language could create anticompetitive consolidation incentives and request anti‑steering safeguards and transparency about related party arrangements.

[P10] Plans will request clarification whether the capitated contract must cover both LTSS and behavioral health concurrently or only one category depending on plan design, and seek guidance on minimum covered nursing facility days for the “highly integrated” standard.

[P10] States will request flexibility to choose which benefit (LTSS or behavioral health) to include under HIDE SNP contracts based on state priorities and fiscal capacity, and ask CMS to allow state‑specific tailoring.

[P11] Similar to P8, commenters will contend the requirement that HIDE SNP contracts cover an “entire service area” beginning 2025 is impractical for plans expanding incrementally and will request phased compliance timelines and exceptions for provider deserts.

[P12] Consumer advocates and legal groups will support MA plans tracking OOP maximums and notifications but request detailed requirements: frequency of notification, format, translations, and retroactive reconciliations to protect beneficiaries from ongoing balance billing.

[P12] Plans will object to the operational burden of real‑time tracking of accrued OOP across Medicare and Medicaid cost‑sharing and request CMS provide technical specifications, testing windows, and funding for system upgrades.

[P13] Similar to P12, stakeholders will ask CMS to harmonize tracking methods between the two different OOP maximum calculations in (f)(4) and (f)(5) and to clarify which applies to dual eligible subpopulations to avoid duplicative systems.

[P14] Emergency preparedness advocates will support ensuring access during disasters but request precise minimum benefit continuity standards (e.g., emergency prescriptions, dialysis, oxygen) and require reporting metrics and beneficiary notification obligations.

[P14] MA organizations will request temporal limits and liability protections for extraordinary costs incurred during declared emergencies and ask CMS to allow temporary modifications to network adequacy and prior authorization to preserve access.

[P15] Plans will argue the 30‑day continuation requirement after certain end‑of‑emergency conditions may be insufficient if supply chain or infrastructure disruptions persist longer; they will request that continuation be tied to objective recovery benchmarks rather than a fixed 30 days.

[P15] Consumer advocates will insist the 30‑day floor not be a ceiling and ask CMS to require plans to continue benefits until beneficiaries have meaningful access restored, with CMS oversight and escalation procedures.

[P16] Industry commenters will request clear notification timelines and content requirements for plans that cannot resume operations, including templates and whether notices to CMS substitute for notices to beneficiaries and states.

[P16] Legal commenters will request clarification on the consequences of notification (e.g., plan termination, enforcement actions) and due process rights for plans before adverse CMS actions are taken.

[P17] Providers and plans will seek clarification on who is authorized to conduct the comprehensive initial and annual health risk assessments (nurses, social workers, PCPs) and request standardized training/certification requirements.

[P17] Privacy advocates will request limitations on secondary uses of HRA data, requiring explicit beneficiary consent for sharing SDOH answers beyond care planning, and data security standards.

[P18] Plans and states will object to CMS specifying standardized questions via subregulatory guidance beginning 2024 without a formal rulemaking comment period, arguing this raises due process and notice‑and‑comment concerns.

[P18] Health IT vendors will request lead time and machine‑readable specifications for the CMS‑specified standardized questions so they can update assessment tools and EHR integrations before 2024.

[P19] Community‑based organizations will strongly support adding housing, food security, and transportation questions but urge CMS to require plans to have referral pathways and funding mechanisms to address identified needs, not merely screen.

[P19] Plans will request clarification on the required screening instruments (single question vs validated multi‑item screens), scoring thresholds, and whether affirmative responses trigger mandatory services or optional referrals.

[P20] Plans will object to contract-level verification of Medicaid eligibility as administratively duplicative where state enrollment files are integrated; they will request CMS to permit reliance on state eligibility feeds rather than separate plan verification.

[P20] Legal commenters will caution that inaccurate Medicaid eligibility verification could lead to wrongful disenrollment or benefit denials and request clear appeal and remediation procedures for beneficiaries.

[P21] Hospitals, SNFs, states, and plans will seek clarity on which “one group of high‑risk full‑benefit dual eligibles” is targeted, the definition of “high‑risk,” and whether the notification applies to all admissions or only certain diagnostic categories.

[P21] Hospitals will request standardized notification formats and electronic interfaces (e.g., ADT feeds) and reimbursement or cost offsets for building connectivity to multiple SNPs and state systems.

[P22] State Medicaid agencies will welcome the authority to set timeframes/methods for notifications but will request CMS technical assistance and templates to ensure compatibility with federal HIPAA and local systems.

[P22] Hospitals and providers will express concern about varying state notification requirements across states imposing multiple, potentially conflicting reporting obligations and ask CMS to set a national minimum standard.

[P23] Industry commenters will note that retaining ultimate responsibility after delegation is standard but will request CMS guidance on supervisory documentation requirements and limits on liability to avoid double exposure.

[P23] Legal commenters will suggest CMS require written delegation agreements with specific oversight metrics and periodic verification to demonstrate SNPs exercised adequate supervision.

[P24] Plans operating under the same parent organization claiming the paragraph (d)(1) exception will request a clear, objective test and documentation standards to qualify for the exception to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P24] Consumer advocates will oppose broad carve‑outs of notification requirements via parent‑organization exceptions and request safeguards to ensure beneficiaries still receive timely care coordination regardless of corporate structure.

[P25] MA organizations will object to CMS application/approval to limit MA contracts to a single state when the State requires it, citing administrative complexity; they will request streamlined application timelines and clearer standards for CMS approval.

[P25] State agencies will support the ability to require state‑specific contracts but ask CMS to define the scope of “limited to that State” and whether interstate provider networks serving border regions are permitted.

[P26] Plans and consumer advocates will endorse integrated Medicare‑Medicaid materials but request precise content and formatting standards, deadlines for implementation, and authority for states to require additional consumer‑facing disclosures.

[P26] Privacy advocates and legal experts will request safeguards ensuring that integrated materials do not disclose sensitive Medicaid information (e.g., LTSS authorization status) without beneficiary consent.

[P27] Stakeholders will request clarity on what “good faith work to collaborate” with States entails procedurally and timelines for CMS action after a State letter of intent, including published timelines for approval or denial.

[P27] States will ask for commitments on CMS staffing and resource allocation to ensure timely collaboration given existing CMS backlogs.

[P28] State Medicaid officials will request detailed HPMS access rules, audit logging, and whether access includes all modules (ratebook, model contract) and whether reciprocal access to State systems is required.

[P28] Industry and privacy advocates will object to broad HPMS access by states to proprietary plan data and request strict limits, data segmentation, and a requirement that states sign non‑disclosure agreements with defined penalties.

[P29] Plans will request clear appeal rights and notice before CMS terminates State HPMS access for alleged policy violations, and an opportunity for corrective action before termination.

[P29] State officials will warn that the threat of termination without clear objective standards may impede legitimate oversight and request an appeal/notice process.

[P30] Plans and auditors will support CMS–State coordination on audits but request protections against redundant or duplicative audits and clear rules for confidential treatment of proprietary plan audit findings.

[P30] Legal counsel will ask CMS to define how “coordination of audit schedules” will work practically and to require advance notice and instance‑based limits to protect operational stability.

[P31] MA organizations will raise operational concerns about establishing and maintaining enrollee advisory committees in each State, asking CMS to permit multi‑state committees or virtual formats to reduce burden.

[P31] Consumer and disability advocacy groups will support mandatory advisory committees but request strong representativeness requirements, minimum meeting frequency, and funding for outreach to hard‑to‑reach enrollees.

[P32] Advocates will request CMS define “reasonably representative,” including metrics (age, race/ethnicity, language, disability, geographic distribution), and require public disclosure of committee composition and meeting minutes.

[P32] Plans will request flexibility on committee composition where enrollment pools are small (rural or tribal areas) and ask for alternative mechanisms to solicit input.

[P33] Consumer groups will support committee advisory authority across affiliated managed care plans but request conflict‑of‑interest rules preventing parent organizations from overriding or limiting committee recommendations.

[P33] Industry will ask CMS to clarify the advisory committee’s authorities are nonbinding and to limit state or plan obligations to respond within set timeframes to committee recommendations.

[P34] Plans with CMS‑approved carve‑outs of LTSS will request clear, stable criteria for meeting the “minority/small‑part” carve‑out conditions and a streamlined reapproval process to avoid jeopardizing FIDE/HIDE SNP status.

[P34] Advocates will warn that allowing carve‑outs could undermine integration goals and request transparent public reporting of any carve‑outs and their impact on enrollee outcomes.

[P35] Similar to P34, behavioral health carve‑outs will prompt concern from mental health advocates that carve‑outs weaken integration; they will request strict limits, outcome monitoring, and beneficiary protections before CMS approves carve‑outs.

[P35] Plans will ask CMS to define the documentation and timeframes required to obtain and maintain carve‑outs for behavioral health services to ensure operational certainty.

[P36] New entrant MA organizations will assert that beginning 2024 network adequacy demonstration at application will slow market entry and request transition periods, grandfathering, or a phased approach tied to application types.

[P36] Consumer groups will support upfront network adequacy demonstrations but ask CMS to publish objective standards, allowable mitigations, and an expedited review process for underserved areas to promote access.

[P37] Applicants will challenge the 10‑point network credit rule as unclear (how points translate to scores) and request published scoring methodology, eligibility criteria for the credit, and appeals process if denied.

[P37] Plans receiving conditional approval will request CMS clarify what “fully compliant at the start of the contract year” means operationally and request reasonable cure periods rather than outright denials.

[P38] MA organizations will request clarification of how the 2023 HOS exception affects future measure clustering/thresholds and ask for advance notice on how measures will be treated in subsequent years to plan quality improvement activities.

[P38] Quality measurement advocates will ask for rationale and transparency for the temporary exception and seek assurance that data comparability and fairness across contracts will be preserved.

[P39] Applicants will object to CMS denying contract qualification based on prior 12‑month noncompliance even where corrective actions were completed and will request CMS to weigh remediation evidence and current compliance more heavily.

[P39] Legal commenters will ask for clear criteria and a proportionality standard to ensure denials are reserved for serious, ongoing noncompliance rather than minor past infractions.

[P40] Organizations will request examples and definitions for the (A‑E) criteria that trigger noncompliance points to reduce subjectivity and improve predictability in application reviews.

[P40] Plans will request an appeal process and independent review for findings that CMS regards as noncompliance during the review period.

[P41] MA organizations will critique the fixed point assignments (CAP=6, warning=3, notice=1) as arbitrary and ask for recalibration, transparency of thresholds that trigger denials, and an opportunity to offset points with remediation evidence.

[P41] Consumer advocates will support point‑based accountability but request that CMS publish point thresholds publicly and provide notice and an opportunity to correct prior to a disqualifying aggregation.

[P42] Organizations with reasonable cost contracts will argue the prohibition on accepting new enrollees under section 1876 reasonable cost contracts in areas where they seek to offer non‑D‑SNP MA plans is overly restrictive and may disrupt rural provider arrangements; they will seek exemptions or phase‑ins.

[P42] Legal experts will request clarification whether the prohibition applies only to new enrollments after the effective date and whether grandfathered arrangements are preserved.

[P43] Similarly, commenters will request clarity on corporate affiliation constructs in § 422.503(b)(5)(ii) to avoid unintended barriers to complex corporate structuring and legitimate affiliate arrangements.

[P44] MA organizations will request due process protections when CMS takes compliance actions under § 422.504(m), including required notice, opportunity to cure, and criteria for escalating actions.

[P44] Beneficiary advocates will request CMS prioritize beneficiary protection in selecting remedies and require corrective actions to include beneficiary remediation and monitoring.

[P45] Plans will request clearer definitions of “outlier performance” and whether CMS can act based on qualitative findings absent quantitative thresholds to avoid arbitrary enforcement.

[P45] Legal commenters will urge CMS to issue examples of conduct that would constitute noncompliance under the new language to ensure fair notice.

[P46] Plans will ask CMS to publish the weight assigned to each listed factor in deciding compliance actions and require CMS to afford plans a chance to submit mitigating evidence before a final decision.

[P46] Advocates will insist beneficiary harm should be the dominant factor and request public reporting of CMS’s analysis and rationale for major compliance decisions.

[P47] Industry commenters will request a formal timeline and process for each type of compliance action (notice, warning, CAP) including expected time for plan response and public disclosure rules.

[P47] Legal commenters will request appeal rights and independent review for corrective action plans imposed under the new authority.

[P48] Plans will complain that the CAP trigger language is broad and may result in frequent CAPs for complex operational issues; they will seek objective repeat/non‑remediation thresholds and proportional CAP scopes.

[P48] Consumer groups will support CAPs for repeated/unremedied noncompliance but request CMS require CAPs to include beneficiary remediation plans and periodic public progress reports.

[P49] Plans and advocates will request clarity on the “best interest” standard and CMS review criteria when moving enrollees between renewing and new/renewing D‑SNPs, including required beneficiary notice, consent, and appeal rights.

[P49] Legal commenters will insist that moving enrollees must not circumvent enrollee protections and that moves must preserve continuity of care, provider access, and prior authorizations.

[P50] Consumer advocates will expressly support the prohibition on moving enrollees between different contracts under the crosswalk exception and ask CMS to enforce strict limits to prevent plan shopping and beneficiary disruption.

[P50] Plans will ask for narrow exceptions (state‑mandated moves) to be clearly enumerated and processes standardized.

[P51] MA organizations will request operational guidance and beneficiary notification templates for state‑required creation of new MA contracts and the mechanics of moving enrollees to a D‑SNP‑only contract.

[P51] States will request the ability to require moves when it improves integration but ask CMS for expedited approvals and flexibility to ensure continuity.

[P52] Legal advocates will request clear timelines for scheduling in‑person and written opportunities to present evidence in integrated appeals, including minimum notice periods and accommodation requirements for disabled or remote enrollees.

[P52] Plans will ask for permissible formats (virtual, telephonic) to satisfy “in person” and instructions templates to ensure consistent implementation.

[P53] Beneficiary advocates will request CMS require advance notice in multiple languages and accessible formats when expedited cases limit time for presenting evidence.

[P53] Plans will ask CMS to allow compressed but fair timeframes for expedited cases and to define what constitutes “sufficient advance” notice.

[P54] Consumer advocates will welcome explicit party status for representatives but request CMS require documented proof of representation and safeguards against coercion or unauthorized representation.

[P54] Plans will ask for standardized forms and verification processes to confirm representative status quickly during integrated grievances/determinations.

[P55] Providers and assignees will request clear definitions of “appealable interest” and processes for establishing standing as a party in integrated reconsiderations, including confidentiality protections.

[P55] Plans will express concern about proliferation of third‑party appeals and ask CMS to limit standing to entities with documented financial or care responsibility.

[P56] Provider groups will request detailed prompt payment timelines, interest penalties, and dispute resolution pathways to ensure timely processing consistent with § 422.520.

[P56] Plans will request clarification on how prompt payment rules apply to integrated payments that include both Medicare and Medicaid funding streams and how responsibility is allocated.

[P57] Providers will strongly support accepting expedite requests from providers on behalf of enrollees (except for expedited payment requests) and ask CMS to define acceptable evidence to support expedites and safeguards against abuse.

[P57] Plans will request guidance on verifying provider authorization to request expedites and timelines to respond to such requests.

[P58] Plans will ask CMS to clarify the limited circumstances under which a 14‑day extension to reconsideration timeframes is allowed and require documentation standards to support extensions to prevent delay tactics.

[P58] Consumer advocates will oppose extensions that could delay beneficiary access and request that extensions be rare, well‑documented, and subject to CMS review.

[P59] Beneficiary advocates will request CMS require immediate service authorization within the shortest timelines (72 hours, 7 days, 30 days) and require notification to beneficiaries when services are authorized after appeal reversal, including retroactive coverage of incurred costs.

[P59] Providers will request clear billing instructions and timely payment obligations when plans must promptly provide/authorize disputed services following reversal.

[P60] Plans will request clarification on administrative timeframes in §§ 422.618 and 422.619 as applied to implementations of reversals by different adjudicative bodies to avoid conflicting deadlines.

[P60] Legal commenters will ask for mechanisms to coordinate timelines across federal and state adjudicative bodies to ensure consistent beneficiary protections.

[P61] Consumer advocates will request that website instructions for appointing representatives be prominent, accessible, available in multiple languages, and compliant with web accessibility guidelines (WCAG), not just included as a link.

[P61] Plans will request CMS provide standardized web text and the model CMS Appointment of Representative Form in machine‑readable formats and guidance on secure submission methods.

[P62] Consumer privacy advocates will applaud the prohibition on SSNs on ID cards but request guidance on alternative unique identifiers and data minimization practices to reduce fraud risk.

[P62] Plans will request clarification on the “specified timeline” for issuing ID cards to new enrollees, and whether temporary electronic cards suffice until physical cards are mailed.

[P62] Advocacy groups will request that ID cards include clear crisis contact numbers (24/7) and language/accessibility indicators for non‑English speakers, despite exclusion from translation requirements.

[P63] Plans will ask for precise operational thresholds and vendor timing to add languages that meet the 5% service area threshold to the MLI and request automated language determination methods to avoid errors.

[P63] Consumer rights groups will request that the MLI be required to be included in all communications where the beneficiary may need language support, not only some materials, and that electronic delivery include consent options.

[P64] Plans will request clarification and standardized text for the TPMO disclaimer and examples of acceptable verbal and electronic delivery to ensure consistent compliance.

[P64] TPMOs and marketing vendors will object to the “first minute” verbal requirement as impractical in many outreach settings and request alternative timing or audio scripting options.

[P65] MA organizations will request guidance on enforcing MA plan requirements against TPMOs that are not FDRs and liability limits where TPMOs refuse to comply or misrepresent information.

[P65] TPMO industry groups will request clear definitions of when a TPMO qualifies as an FDR and safe harbor procedures for transitioning TPMOs into FDR arrangements.

[P66] Plans will seek clarification on the scope of required TPMO disclosures of subcontractors and practical data security rules for recording full beneficiary calls, including retention periods and access controls.

[P66] TPMOs will argue monthly reporting of staff disciplinary actions is onerous and request that reporting be limited to incidents affecting beneficiary safety or regulatory compliance, with de‑identified summaries permitted.

[P66] Consumer advocates will support call recording and disciplinary reporting as important consumer protections but request CMS mandate secure storage, limited retention, and beneficiary access rights to recorded calls.

[P67] Lead‑generation vendors will request precise scripting and timing for disclosing that beneficiary information will be provided to a licensed agent and ask whether a consumer’s verbal consent at the point of lead gen is required.

[P67] Privacy advocates will demand affirmative consent requirements, limits on data sharing for lead generation, and an opt‑out mechanism so beneficiaries are not repeatedly solicited by licensed agents.

Plans operating under the same parent organization claiming the paragraph (d)(1) exception will request a clear, objective test and documentation standards to qualify for the exception to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

Consumer advocates will oppose broad carve‑outs of notification requirements via parent‑organization exceptions and request safeguards to ensure beneficiaries still receive timely care coordination regardless of corporate structure.

MA organizations will object to CMS application/approval to limit MA contracts to a single state when the State requires it, citing administrative complexity; they will request streamlined application timelines and clearer standards for CMS approval.

State agencies will support the ability to require state‑specific contracts but ask CMS to define the scope of “limited to that State” and whether interstate provider networks serving border regions are permitted.

Plans and consumer advocates will endorse integrated Medicare‑Medicaid materials but request precise content and formatting standards, deadlines for implementation, and authority for states to require additional consumer‑facing disclosures.

Privacy advocates and legal experts will request safeguards ensuring that integrated materials do not disclose sensitive Medicaid information (e.g., LTSS authorization status) without beneficiary consent.

Stakeholders will request clarity on what “good faith work to collaborate” with States entails procedurally and timelines for CMS action after a State letter of intent, including published timelines for approval or denial.
States will ask for commitments on CMS staffing and resource allocation to ensure timely collaboration given existing CMS backlogs.

State Medicaid officials will request detailed HPMS access rules, audit logging, and whether access includes all modules (ratebook, model contract) and whether reciprocal access to State systems is required.

Industry and privacy advocates will object to broad HPMS access by states to proprietary plan data and request strict limits, data segmentation, and a requirement that states sign non‑disclosure agreements with defined penalties.
Plans will request clear appeal rights and notice before CMS terminates State HPMS access for alleged policy violations, and an opportunity for corrective action before termination.
State officials will warn that the threat of termination without clear objective standards may impede legitimate oversight and request an appeal/notice process.

Plans and auditors will support CMS–State coordination on audits but request protections against redundant or duplicative audits and clear rules for confidential treatment of proprietary plan audit findings.
Legal counsel will ask CMS to define how “coordination of audit schedules” will work practically and to require advance notice and instance‑based limits to protect operational stability.

MA organizations will raise operational concerns about establishing and maintaining enrollee advisory committees in each State, asking CMS to permit multi‑state committees or virtual formats to reduce burden.

Consumer and disability advocacy groups will support mandatory advisory committees but request strong representativeness requirements, minimum meeting frequency, and funding for outreach to hard‑to‑reach enrollees.

Advocates will request CMS define “reasonably representative,” including metrics (age, race/ethnicity, language, disability, geographic distribution), and require public disclosure of committee composition and meeting minutes.
Plans will request flexibility on committee composition where enrollment pools are small (rural or tribal areas) and ask for alternative mechanisms to solicit input.

Consumer groups will support committee advisory authority across affiliated managed care plans but request conflict‑of‑interest rules preventing parent organizations from overriding or limiting committee recommendations.
Industry will ask CMS to clarify the advisory committee’s authorities are nonbinding and to limit state or plan obligations to respond within set timeframes to committee recommendations.

Plans with CMS‑approved carve‑outs of LTSS will request clear, stable criteria for meeting the “minority/small‑part” carve‑out conditions and a streamlined reapproval process to avoid jeopardizing FIDE/HIDE SNP status.
Advocates will warn that allowing carve‑outs could undermine integration goals and request transparent public reporting of any carve‑outs and their impact on enrollee outcomes.

Similar to P34, behavioral health carve‑outs will prompt concern from mental health advocates that carve‑outs weaken integration; they will request strict limits, outcome monitoring, and beneficiary protections before CMS approves carve‑outs.
Plans will ask CMS to define the documentation and timeframes required to obtain and maintain carve‑outs for behavioral health services to ensure operational certainty.

New entrant MA organizations will assert that beginning 2024 network adequacy demonstration at application will slow market entry and request transition periods, grandfathering, or a phased approach tied to application types.

Consumer groups will support upfront network adequacy demonstrations but ask CMS to publish objective standards, allowable mitigations, and an expedited review process for underserved areas to promote access.

Applicants will challenge the 10‑point network credit rule as unclear (how points translate to scores) and request published scoring methodology, eligibility criteria for the credit, and appeals process if denied.

Plans receiving conditional approval will request CMS clarify what “fully compliant at the start of the contract year” means operationally and request reasonable cure periods rather than outright denials.

MA organizations will request clarification of how the 2023 HOS exception affects future measure clustering/thresholds and ask for advance notice on how measures will be treated in subsequent years to plan quality improvement activities.
Quality measurement advocates will ask for rationale and transparency for the temporary exception and seek assurance that data comparability and fairness across contracts will be preserved.

Applicants will object to CMS denying contract qualification based on prior 12‑month noncompliance even where corrective actions were completed and will request CMS to weigh remediation evidence and current compliance more heavily.
Legal commenters will ask for clear criteria and a proportionality standard to ensure denials are reserved for serious, ongoing noncompliance rather than minor past infractions.
Organizations will request examples and definitions for the (A‑E) criteria that trigger noncompliance points to reduce subjectivity and improve predictability in application reviews.
Plans will request an appeal process and independent review for findings that CMS regards as noncompliance during the review period.

MA organizations will critique the fixed point assignments (CAP=6, warning=3, notice=1) as arbitrary and ask for recalibration, transparency of thresholds that trigger denials, and an opportunity to offset points with remediation evidence.

Consumer advocates will support point‑based accountability but request that CMS publish point thresholds publicly and provide notice and an opportunity to correct prior to a disqualifying aggregation.

Organizations with reasonable cost contracts will argue the prohibition on accepting new enrollees under section 1876 reasonable cost contracts in areas where they seek to offer non‑D‑SNP MA plans is overly restrictive and may disrupt rural provider arrangements; they will seek exemptions or phase‑ins.
Legal experts will request clarification whether the prohibition applies only to new enrollments after the effective date and whether grandfathered arrangements are preserved.
