raw_output:
[P1] The Comments Due Date of October 26, 2020 is unreasonable because it gives stakeholders (operators, MROs, unions, and foreign authorities) insufficient time to analyze technical data and prepare substantive comments; we request an extension of at least 60 days.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether comments received after October 26, 2020 will be considered if accompanied by a request for extension or supported by good cause; otherwise respondents may be unfairly excluded.

[P2] The phrase "within the specified compliance times" is vague without cross-referencing the specific calendar deadlines for each affected MMEL item; please publish an explicit compliance schedule by fleet and configuration.

[P2] The provision lacks a mechanism for temporary relief (e.g., ferry flights, maintenance scheduling) during compliance time windows; commenters request explicit temporary operational allowances or expedited AMOC procedures.

[P3] Prohibiting operation with any inoperative refuel valve secured open after 60 days is unduly prescriptive and does not account for operational realities (e.g., remote hubs, parts availability); request either a longer phase-in (e.g., 180 days) or allowances for documented logistics delays.

[P3] The 60-day prohibition applies broadly to all operators but does not consider differences between passenger, freighter, and military-derivative operations (e.g., 747-400LCF); request differentiated deadlines or an exception process for critical cargo operations.

[P3] The prohibition does not specify enforcement policy for flights that must depart within the 60-day window when replacement valves are unavailable; operators need clear guidance on enforcement discretion to avoid inadvertent violations.

[P4] Identifying MMEL items in paragraphs (h)(1)-(6) as affected by the prohibition is appropriate, but the AD fails to state whether existing MMEL dispatch reliefs that predate this AD are automatically superseded; request explicit language about the interaction with prior MMEL approvals.

[P5] For Model 747–100/–200/–300, restricting Pressure Fueling System MMEL items without providing retrofit or replacement part lead times will ground aircraft; request FAA coordination on parts distribution or a path for temporary operational relief.

[P6] MMEL Item 28–20 2) (Main Tank 1 and 4 Refueling Valves) — Commenters request technical justification (service difficulty reports, risk assessment) showing why these specific valves require prohibition rather than continued dispatch with limitations.

[P6] For MMEL Item 28–20 2), operators request clarity whether a single valve inoperative (e.g., only Tank 1) triggers the prohibition for the entire airplane or whether it applies only when valve(s) for a particular tank group are secured open.

[P7] MMEL Item 28–20 3) (Main Tank 2 and 3 Refueling Valves) — Airlines operating with legacy configurations need explicit instructions on acceptable maintenance actions (e.g., temporary lockouts, placarding) that would permit operation during the 60-day phase-in.

[P8] MMEL Item 28–20 4) (Center Tank Refueling Valves) — Cargo and ferry operations commonly rely on center tank fueling configurations; FAA should publish a risk-based analysis explaining why center tank valves are grouped with main tanks for a uniform prohibition.

[P9] MMEL Item 28–20 5) (Reserve Tank 1 and 4 Refueling Valves) — Request clarification of whether "reserve tank" nomenclature corresponds to operator-specific labeling; suggest adding part numbers or schematic references to avoid misinterpretation.

[P10] MMEL Item 28–20 6) (Reserve Tank 2 and 3 Refueling Valves) — Propose that the AD include acceptable interim maintenance procedures (e.g., chocking or mechanical tie-offs) that maintain fuel system safety without violating the prohibition.

[P11] For Model 747–400LCF (MMEL Item 28–21–1 1), second dispatch case), the AD singles out the second dispatch case; industry requests the FAA provide the full text of the referenced dispatch cases so operators can determine which configuration triggers the prohibition.

[P11] The 747–400LCF dispatch-case-specific prohibition may conflict with approved cargo conversion STCs; request coordination with conversion certificate holders (LOA/STC holders) and explicit guidance on STC interactions.

[P12] For Model 747–400 (MMEL Item 28–21–1 1), first dispatch case), operators ask whether the "first dispatch case" is the only affected case and whether earlier FAA-approved dispatch variances remain valid; request immediate publication of guidance to principal inspectors.

[P13] MMEL Item 28–21–01–01–01A (747–8 Refuel Valves) — 747-8 operators request analysis of fleet impact (number of affected aircraft, typical downtime) and recommended vendor lists for replacement valves.

[P14] For Model 767 (MMEL Item 28–21–01–01B, Fuel Shutoff Valves), 767 operators request clarification whether the prohibition applies to auxiliary/temporary shutoff valves installed under field modifications, or only to original-type valves listed in the MMEL.

[P15] For Model 767–2C/KC–46 (the listed Pressure Fueling System items), military/contract operators request confirmation the AD will not inadvertently invalidate existing DoD/contractual maintenance procedures; request a DoD coordination clause or special compliance considerations.

[P16] MMEL Item 28–21–01–01E (Main Tank Shutoff Valve Inoperative Open for 767–2C/KC–46) — The AD should specify whether redundant/main valve architecture (e.g., multiple independent shutoff valves per tank) affects whether the prohibition applies.

[P17] MMEL Item 28–21–01–01F (Center Tank Shutoff Valve Inoperative Open for 767–2C/KC–46) — Request that the FAA provide recommended inspection and testing protocols to demonstrate valve operability prior to the 60-day deadline.

[P18] The AMOC authority vested in the Seattle ACO Manager is appropriate, but operators outside the Seattle region need clarity on processing timeframes — propose a mandated 30-day FAA response time to AMOC requests to avoid operational delays.

[P19] The condition that AMOCs must be requested using 14 CFR 39.19 is standard; commenters ask the FAA to allow concurrent submission to both principal inspectors and the Seattle ACO to expedite consideration.

[P20] The instruction to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO is reasonable, but industry requests a clear escalation path and contact list for when those local offices are unfamiliar with these complex fueling-system AMOCs.

[P21] If sending AMOC information directly to the manager, the AD refers to paragraph (j) for the contact person but the proposed text does not include paragraph (j) in the docket excerpt; request that the final rule include the actual contact name, phone, and mailing address.

[P22] Allowing email submission to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is helpful, but commenters request confirmation of file size limits, accepted formats, and encryption/privacy protocols for proprietary repair data.

[P23] The requirement to notify the principal inspector or local FSDO before using an approved AMOC is appropriate, but the AD should define "notify" (written, electronic, timeframe prior to operation) to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P24] Allowing Boeing ODA approval for AMOCs for repairs/modifications is efficient, but commenters request documented criteria and required evidence for Boeing ODA approvals and clear FAA oversight/ratification steps to ensure impartiality.

[P25] The requirement that AMOC repairs meet the airplane's certification basis and explicitly reference this AD is necessary; however, the AD should provide guidance on how to handle airplanes with multiple certification baselines or amended Type Certificates.

[P25] The AD must clarify whether AMOCs approved by Boeing ODA require subsequent FAA concurrence when the AMOC impacts type-certification-level compliance (e.g., structural or systems changes).

[P3] Safety advocates will object that securing a valve "in the open position" is ambiguously defined; request precise operational definition (mechanical tie-off, software indication, physical placard) to avoid inconsistent compliance.

[P3] Legal commenters note that criminal or civil penalty exposure for violating the 60-day prohibition is unclear; request the FAA specify enforcement mechanisms and whether civil penalty actions will be stayed pending AMOC adjudication.

[P2] Small operators and Part 135 certificate holders request an explicit compliance relief mechanism for single-aircraft operators who cannot meet the 60-day deadline due to supply-chain constraints.

[P4] Airworthiness authorities from foreign jurisdictions (EASA, Transport Canada) will require harmonization; request FAA commit to sharing technical data and AMOC decisions to enable reciprocal acceptance.

[P6] MROs request that the AD include acceptable vendor repair or overhaul procedures and part-numbered service instructions to ensure field repairs meet certification-basis requirements for AMOCs.

[P13] 747-8 lessors request confirmation of lessor/lessee responsibilities for compliance costs and deadlines, and whether the prohibition affects lease returns or lease negotiations.

[P15] KC-46 operators note this AD could conflict with military mission-readiness needs; request DoD consultation and an exemption process for verified mission-critical flights under controlled conditions.

[P3] Insurance carriers may contend that operating with valves secured open increases hull and liability risk; request the FAA provide insurers with the risk analysis so premiums are not unfairly adjusted without justification.

[P22] Privacy/proprietary concerns: Manufacturers or MROs submitting AMOCs by email may need to transmit proprietary data; request FAA acceptance of secure file-transfer protocols and non-disclosure assurances.

[P24] Labor organizations (pilots, maintenance technicians) request that any AMOC allowing continued operation require specific maintenance procedure revisions, training, and documentation to protect safety and worker liability.

[P1] Public commenters will challenge retrospective application: if the AD's effective date precedes the comment deadline, operators cannot rely on the rule during the comment period; request clarification of effective date versus comment deadline.

[P2] The AD should explicitly state whether compliance actions performed before the AD’s effective date (but after publication) will be accepted as satisfying the requirement to “unless already accomplished.”

[P3] The AD must specify how to document an inoperative refuel valve that has been "secured open" for purposes of maintenance logs and operational dispatch records to provide auditability.

[P18] Aviation legal experts request that the AMOC approval letter template be published so applicants understand the scope, conditions, and limitations of approved AMOCs (duration, applicability to fleet, record-keeping requirements).

[P23] The requirement to notify the principal inspector "before using" an AMOC lacks a minimum notice period; request a defined advance-notice window (e.g., 48 hours) to allow inspectors to review and log AMOC use.

[P4] Consumer and environmental advocates may request that the FAA include in the AD an assessment of the environmental impact of any modifications or extra ferry flights caused by the 60-day prohibition.

[P6] For legacy 747s in storage or preservation, operators request guidance whether the prohibition applies during storage/status "inactive" periods or only during active operation.

raw_output:
[P1] The outright prohibition in § 60.5520(a) lacks any phase‑in or flexibilities for new entrants and could force immediate retirements of units that cannot meet the Table 1–3 limits without costly retrofits; EPA should include an interim compliance schedule or delayed effective date for units unable to comply on short notice.

[P1] The rule’s prohibition does not clarify enforcement discretion where exceedances result from emergency operations (e.g., black starts, reliability events); commenters request an explicit emergency exemption or force majeure provision.

[P2] The 910 kg CO2/MWh standard for newly constructed/reconstructed units ≤2,100 GJ/h in Table 3 is not achievable for many practical coal and biomass configurations and effectively bans new fossil steam capacity; EPA should justify the technical basis and consider technology‑specific limits.

[P2] The Table 3 standard for units ≤2,100 GJ/h fails to specify whether the metric is expressed on a gross or net basis in the default case (absent a successful petition under § 60.5520(c)), creating ambiguity for compliance calculations.

[P3] The 870 kg CO2/MWh standard for units >2,100 GJ/h in Table 3 is inconsistent with industry best practices for large coal and IGCC units and would require unproven or prohibitively expensive CCS for compliance; request economic impact analysis and alternative achievable levels.

[P3] Table 3’s multi‑tiered thresholds based on base load rating (2,100 GJ/h) may penalize slightly larger units due to a small breakpoint; request smoothing or a single scalable standard rather than a cliff at 2,100 GJ/h.

[P4] The Table 3 standard for units burning ≥75% coal refuse lacks clarity on how the 12‑month averaging of fuel composition is calculated and verified; EPA should require specified sampling frequencies and chain‑of‑custody fuel records.

[P4] The coal refuse standard appears more lenient (higher kg CO2/MWh) but does not account for increased local air pollutants or differences in heating value; request that EPA consider co‑pollutant limits or separate monitoring for refuse units.

[P5] The modified‑unit “best historical annual CO2 emission rate” approach for units ≤2,100 GJ/h could freeze in historically high emissions for poorly operated units and lacks a clear method for selecting the baseline year(s); the rule should specify remedy for missing or poor‑quality historical data.

[P5] The provision that unit‑specific limits “not more stringent than listed gross or net values” for modified units is vague about the interaction of gross vs net metrics; commenters request explicit default (gross or net) and transition rules.

[P6] For modified units >2,100 GJ/h, specifying a no‑more‑stringent limit of 870 kg CO2/MWh (gross) or 940 kg CO2/MWh (net) creates perverse incentives to claim net output credits; EPA must define precisely the components of net energy output (parasitic loads, station service, sales to grid vs onsite use).

[P6] The alternative limits for modified large units do not acknowledge measurement uncertainty in net output calculations; request inclusion of a de minimis allowance or measurement error margin.

[P7] The modified‑unit coal refuse alternative (1,000 kg gross /1,080 kg net) lacks data support and may incentivize co‑firing strategies to avoid stricter limits; EPA should require separate reporting of fuel mixes and ensure the standard does not encourage hazardous waste disposal via combustion.

[P8] The petition mechanism in § 60.5520(c) to use a net energy output‑based standard is welcome, but the proposed text does not provide timelines for EPA action on petitions; commenters request a specific decision deadline (e.g., 180 days) and process transparency.

[P8] The petition process places the burden fully on the owner/operator with no presumptive approval criteria; EPA should publish objective criteria for when a net‑based standard will be granted to avoid arbitrary denials.

[P9] Requiring compliance with the net energy output standard immediately upon grant (§ 60.5520(c) effect) could create operational disruption if permit modifications and monitoring systems lag; permit applicability should begin after permit modification is finalized.

[P10] Mandating that operating permits include monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting tied to net energy output (§ 60.5520(c)) is appropriate, but EPA must allow use of existing CAM/SIP/Title V provisions and specify acceptable monitoring technologies and sampling frequencies to avoid inconsistent permit conditions.

[P11] The automatic substitution that "gross or net energy output" means "net energy output" for petitioned units (§ 60.5520(c) term assignment) could inadvertently change other regulatory obligations beyond CO2 compliance (e.g., performance standards tied to gross output); EPA should limit the semantic change strictly to this subpart's calculations.

[P12] Requiring owners/operators who currently comply with net output standards to petition to revert to gross output (§ 60.5520(c) reversion) is an unnecessary administrative burden; EPA should allow unilateral reversion with notice and a short review period rather than a petition.

[P13] The combustion turbine exemption (§ 60.5525(d)(1)) is too broad if based only on qualifying criteria not restated here; stakeholders request explicit listing of qualifying criteria and an assessment of potential loopholes that would exempt high‑emitting turbines.

[P14] The fuel purchase recordkeeping requirement for exempt turbines (§ 60.5525) lacks minimum retention periods and required data fields (e.g., fuel origin, heating value, CO2 content); EPA should prescribe a minimum retention period (e.g., 5 years) and required record elements.

[P15] The 12‑operating‑month rolling average compliance period (§ 60.5525) is appropriate for smoothing variability, but the rule should clarify treatment of planned outages and low utilization months to prevent perverse incentives to reduce operation to avoid averaging effects.

[P16] The 30‑day timeline to make an initial compliance determination after the first 12‑month period (§ 60.5525(c)) may be infeasible for large fleets that require aggregate calculations and third‑party verification; extend to 60–90 days or allow a one‑time extension.

[P17] Reliance on Section 60.5555(c)(3)(i) to set the first operating month for Acid Rain Program units (§ 60.5525(c)(1)(i)) imposes cross‑referencing burdens and potential conflicts; EPA should reproduce the relevant rule text or provide an interpretative guidance document.

[P18] For non‑Acid Rain units, referencing § 60.5555(c)(3)(ii)(A) to determine the first operating month (§ 60.5525(c)(1)(ii)) similarly creates complexity; commenters request clarified examples and a flowchart for compliance start dates.

[P19] The rule’s treatment of EGUs that commenced commercial operation prior to Oct 23, 2015 (§ 60.5525(c)(2)(i)) depends on whether reporting was required earlier, creating legal uncertainty; industry requests a bright‑line rule for all pre‑2015 units with clear retroactive non‑applicability limits.

[P20] For EGUs with reporting requirements beginning on or after Oct 23, 2015 (§ 60.5525(c)(2)(ii)), the linkage to external reporting dates could produce gaming (delaying reporting to shift compliance start); EPA should use construction/operation dates rather than reporting trigger dates.

[P21] The rule lacks clarity on how newly covered modified/reconstructed EGUs determine the "first operating month" (§ 60.5525(c)(3)); request EPA to require notification to the permitting authority within 30 days of becoming subject and a standard start date (e.g., first month after notification).

[P22] Permitting monitoring at a common stack for multiple affected EGUs (§ 60.5535(f)) is reasonable for cost savings, but the requirement that the EGUs have “the same applicable standard” is ambiguous for units with different fuel blends or modified vs new designations; EPA should allow stack monitoring only where all units truly have identical standards and provide a certification procedure.

[P23] The requirement to sum hourly outputs of individual EGUs and report 'stack operating hours' (§ 60.5535(f)) will require new telemetry and synchronization across units; EPA must provide acceptable approaches for time‑synchronization and data reconciliation and allow use of reasonable data interpolation methods when outages occur.

[P24] For multiple stacks/ducts (§ 60.5535(g)) the rule requires separate hourly monitoring at each stack, which could be infeasible for large multi‑stack plants; EPA should allow representative monitoring plus validated allocation methods where stacks are physically similar.

[P25] The mandated compliance determination (sum CO2 divided by total gross/net output) (§ 60.5535(g)) does not address units with non‑continuous energy outputs (e.g., heat exported intermittently to district systems); EPA should provide methods to allocate fuel/energy outputs and avoid double counting.

[P26] The calculation procedures for 12‑month periods (§ 60.5540(a)) referencing non‑uniform fuels require clear guidance on handling variable fuel CO2 content, sampling frequency, and QA/QC protocols; otherwise compliance outcomes will be inconsistent across owners.

[P34] Mandating ASME PTC 46 for overall plant performance (§ 60.5580 alternative 2) could disadvantage smaller operators who lack resources to conduct ASME‑level testing; require EPA to accept vendor performance tests or manufacturer warranties where validated.

Table 3’s multi‑tiered thresholds based on base load rating (2,100 GJ/h) may penalize slightly larger units due to a small breakpoint; request smoothing or a single scalable standard rather than a cliff at 2,100 GJ/h.

raw_output:
[P1] The May 22, 2020 comment deadline in § 39.13(a) is unreasonable and should be extended because stakeholders need more time to collect serial-number and installation-date data from operators and MROs.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether comments submitted by email, fax, or mail on May 22, 2020 will be accepted as timely; the provision does not specify acceptable submission methods.

[P1] The FAA should provide an electronic docket number and web link in § 39.13(a) so commenters can confirm submission and view supporting documents before the May 22, 2020 deadline.

[P2] § 39.13(c) is ambiguous about applicability to aircraft certificated in multiple categories (e.g., experimental, light-sport, restricted); the AD should explicitly list included and excluded certification categories.

[P2] The AD should clarify whether governors installed on engines that were later re-certified on another airframe remain covered; the current text could be read to apply to any airframe that ever had the governor, creating enforcement confusion.

[P3] The reference in § 39.13(c)(1) to "table 2" and serial numbers 170061 through 180501 must include the full table or a direct incorporation-by-reference statement; otherwise operators cannot determine applicability.

[P3] The exclusion "excluding those listed in table 1" in § 39.13(c)(1) lacks clarity about whether table 1 refers to the same ASB or another document; that should be specified to avoid misidentifying compliant governors.

[P3] The serial number range 170061 through 180501 in § 39.13(c)(1) appears arbitrary; the FAA must provide data or risk analysis showing why that exact range is unsafe.

[P3] The rule should allow individual serial-number verification procedures (e.g., photos of nameplate) as acceptable evidence of whether a governor falls within the 170061–180501 range referenced in § 39.13(c)(1).

[P4] § 39.13(c)(2)'s coverage of models "with any serial number" if installed after Jan 31, 2017 is overbroad and will capture units that were manufactured to upgraded standards; the FAA must explain the basis for using installation date rather than manufacture date.

[P4] The AD should require operators to maintain installation-date records for McCauley governors because § 39.13(c)(2) makes applicability depend on installation date, and many older airframes lack precise installation records.

[P4] The phrase "installation date is unknown" in § 39.13(c)(2) effectively presumes noncompliance and will force widespread replacements; the FAA should allow trace evidence (work orders, logbooks) and a reasonable burden-of-proof standard rather than presumption.

[P5] The compliance time in § 39.13(f) (50 hours TIS or 24 months) is too short for small operators and repair stations to schedule replacements, especially given supply-chain constraints; FAA should extend to 100 hours TIS or 36 months.

[P5] The dual compliance threshold "50 hours TIS or 24 months, whichever occurs first" in § 39.13(f) disproportionately burdens low-utilization aircraft because 24 months may be inadequate for older parts sourcing; recommend "whichever occurs later."

[P5] The AD should permit replacement during scheduled overhauls or at the next maintenance event within 24 months, rather than a strict 50-hour TIS limit, to reduce operational disruption.

[P5] § 39.13(f) must state whether partial-time-in-service between start and effective date counts toward the 50 hours TIS compliance time for governors already in service.

[P6] The Note in § 39.13(f) exempting governors stamped with letter B is insufficiently precise — the AD must specify exact stamp location, font/size, and whether stamped on governor housing or nameplate to avoid inconsistent inspections.

[P6] The FAA needs to confirm the provenance of the "B" stamp in § 39.13(f) Note 1 and provide traceability records demonstrating that all "B"-stamped governors were inspected/modified to the requisite standard.

[P6] The AD should require operators to photograph and record the "B" stamp as proof of compliance and retain it in logbooks, otherwise enforcement will be inconsistent.

[P7] The definition in § 39.13(g) that a governor is eligible if it does not have an idler gear bearing marked "BA-59" is problematic because part-mark recognition is error-prone; recommend inclusion of bearing part numbers, manufacturer name, and acceptable alternate markings.

[P7] The rule does not address worn or illegible bearing markings; § 39.13(g) should provide guidance on how to treat governors whose idler gear bearing marking is unreadable.

[P7] The FAA should allow non-destructive testing or vendor verification as alternative means to establish eligibility under § 39.13(g) when the "BA-59" marking is missing or obscured.

[P8] The prohibition in § 39.13(h) on installing any McCauley governor that does not meet the "eligible for installation" definition should include an aviation maintenance technician (AMT) inspection standard and an affected parts tagging requirement to prevent inadvertent installations.

[P8] § 39.13(h) should provide an explicit grandfathering provision for governors installed prior to the AD effective date on new-production aircraft or during factory maintenance, otherwise manufacturers may face supply issues.

[P8] The AD's installation prohibition needs to specify penalties or enforcement approach; as written it's unclear how FAA inspectors should proceed when non-eligible governors are found.

[P9] The delegation in § 39.13(i)(1) that the Wichita ACO Branch manager may approve AMOCs centralizes authority and may delay responses; recommend allowing any FAA Designated Engineering Representative (DER) or the applicable ACO to approve time-limited AMOCs.

[P9] The rule should require the Manager to publish typical acceptable AMOCs or criteria to expedite common requests instead of leaving all to case-by-case decisions under § 39.13(i)(1).

[P10] The requirement in § 39.13(i)(1) to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO creates administrative burden for operators with multiple aircraft across districts; allow direct submission to the ACO with copies to the inspector.

[P10] The AD should provide clear timelines for FAA response to AMOC requests submitted per § 39.13(i)(1); without deadlines operators cannot plan compliance.

[P11] § 39.13(i)(1) referencing paragraph (l)(1) for the certification office manager's contact is incomplete in the provided text; the AD must include the name, address, and contact method in the final rule to ensure proper AMOC routing.

[P11] If the FAA expects electronic submission to the certification office manager referenced in § 39.13(i)(1), the AD must explicitly permit email and identify acceptable file formats.

[P12] The obligation in § 39.13(i)(2) to notify the principal inspector or local FSDO/CHDO before using an approved AMOC is vague about timing; it should require notification at least 48 hours before using the AMOC to allow local oversight.

[P12] § 39.13(i)(2) must state what information must be provided in the notification to the principal inspector or manager (e.g., AMOC reference number, aircraft N-number, scheduled operation) to ensure meaningful oversight.

[P12] The rule should clarify whether emergency use of an AMOC (e.g., in-flight diversion) qualifies for post-use notification under § 39.13(i)(2) and set a maximum delay for such notifications.

[P1] The requirement that all organizations "carry out eligible activities in accordance with all program requirements and other applicable requirements" is overly vague and could be used to impose additional, unstated administrative burdens on faith-based organizations; request clearer definitions of "all program requirements" and processes for dispute resolution.

[P1] Industry commenters will request clarification whether "reasonable religious accommodations" creates any specific procedural or documentation obligations for recipients or DHS, and ask for examples of what accommodations are considered "reasonable."

[P2] Civil liberties groups will urge that the prohibition against disqualifying faith-based organizations for being motivated by religion must explicitly prohibit indirect discrimination through overly burdensome neutrality tests or financial viability criteria that disproportionately exclude religious groups.

[P2] Legal commenters will request that DHS add an enforcement mechanism and remedies (e.g., administrative appeal, injunctive relief) when a faith-based organization claims it was improperly disqualified for religious motivation.

[P3] Nonprofit trade associations will seek clarification of what constitutes an impermissible "assurance or notice" and request a safe harbor list of acceptable standard program certifications that apply to all organizations.

[P3] State and local government recipients will ask whether they are prohibited from requiring certain documentation for compliance (e.g., proof of nondiscrimination policies) of faith-based organizations if those documents are not required of secular providers, and request guidance to reconcile this with state procurement rules.

[P4] Advocacy groups for beneficiaries will express concern that the requirement that restrictions apply "equally" could be interpreted to block necessary content restrictions (e.g., proselytizing bans) on faith-based providers; they will request explicit language that beneficiary-protection restrictions (such as prohibiting coercive proselytizing) remain enforceable.

[P5] Civil rights organizations will request concrete standards and monitoring requirements for "voluntary" participation in explicitly religious activities, including required written notices to beneficiaries and mechanisms to report coercion.

[P5] Faith-based providers will request flexibility on how to document voluntariness (e.g., verbal attestation vs. written consent) and request that DHS permit culturally appropriate forms of consent.

[P6] Legal experts will ask DHS to reconcile §19.4(c) with the Establishment Clause and practical grant compliance by specifying which explicitly religious activities are categorically prohibited when using DHS direct assistance.

[P6] Program administrators will request examples of program changes that would be required to comply with religious accommodation laws and ask for a compliance checklist for integrating religious accommodations with program rules.

[P7] Civil liberties commenters will ask for express protection against indirect exclusion via program performance metrics or eligibility criteria that, while neutral on face, effectively penalize religious exercise or affiliation.

[P7] State agencies will request clarification whether the prohibition applies to subcontractor selection or only to direct recipients, and whether intermediaries administering funds must follow the same non-disqualification rules.

[P8] Beneficiary advocates will oppose allowing mandatory attendance at "all activities that are fundamental to the program" without defining "fundamental," warning that this could permit compelled attendance at religious content if labeled as programmatic.

[P8] Faith-based service providers will support §19.5 as necessary to maintain program integrity and request DHS provide a non-exhaustive list of "fundamental" activities for common program types (e.g., job training, emergency shelter).

[P9] Small secular nonprofits will welcome the general non-requirement of 501(c)(3) status but request clarity on whether other tax statuses (e.g., fiscal sponsors, for-profit social enterprises) are eligible and under what conditions.

[P9] State attorneys general will ask DHS to clarify how the general rule interacts with statutory or state legal requirements that do require 501(c)(3) status for certain funding streams.

[P10] Applicants will request that DHS require every funding announcement that requires nonprofit status to include the exact statutory citation and sample acceptable documentation to reduce RFP ambiguity.

[P11] Legal commenters will insist that when tax-exempt status is required the solicitation must cite the specific statutory or regulatory authority authorizing that requirement and explain why it applies to this funding.

[P12] Civil liberties advocates will warn that allowing recipients to "engage in explicitly religious activities" could create Establishment Clause issues if those activities are intertwined with DHS-funded services and request strict limits and separation requirements.

[P1] The allowance to use a "line of oil or scum" or other physical indicators to determine the high tide line in § 328.3(c)(4) is vague and will produce inconsistent, non-scientific determinations across Corps districts.

[P1] The provision should require a clear hierarchy of methods (e.g., priority to recent tidal gage data, remote sensing, then physical indicators) rather than leaving the determination to unspecified "other suitable means."

[P1] Industry commenters will argue that reliance on ephemeral shore indicators like scum lines is impractical for permitting timelines and may force unnecessary delays or duplicative surveys.

[P1] Conservation groups will claim that using visible oil/scum lines as a legal boundary risks overlooking ecological high tide markers (vegetation changes, soil salinity) and could shrink protected intertidal areas.

[P1] Legal experts will assert that the phrase "in the absence of actual data" is ambiguous—rule should define what qualifies as "actual data" (timeframe, quality) to avoid arbitrary decisions.

[P2] Agricultural stakeholders will support § 328.3(c)(8) requiring EPA and the Corps to accept prior converted cropland (PCC) designations by USDA, arguing it reduces regulatory uncertainty for long-farmed land.

[P2] Environmental NGOs will object that automatic acceptance of USDA PCC designations removes necessary independent verification that lands currently function as aquatic resources and could exempt wetlands converted long ago from protection.

[P2] Legal commenters will recommend adding a process for EPA/Corps review or appeal of USDA PCC designations to ensure consistent Clean Water Act application and provide procedural safeguards.

[P2] Tribal governments will request that the rule require consultation with Tribes before accepting USDA PCC designations where tribal resources or treaty rights may be affected.

[P3] Assigning final authority to the EPA Administrator to determine abandonment of PCC without specifying review procedures (§ 328.3(c)(8)) centralizes power and may lack required procedural safeguards and transparency.

[P3] Farming associations will argue that EPA finality on abandonment determinations could create regulatory uncertainty if the agency reverses longstanding USDA PCC classifications without clear criteria.

[P3] Environmental law practitioners will request the rule include objective criteria, timelines, and opportunities for notice-and-comment or administrative appeal when the Administrator makes abandonment determinations.

[P4] The duplicate authorization to use physical indicators for the high tide line in § 110.1(3)(iv) across multiple sections risks inconsistent application; commenters will recommend harmonizing the language across parts and providing an explicit methodology appendix.

[P4] Coastal municipalities will warn that permitting reliance on "other suitable means" without standardized protocols will generate litigation and development delays in coastal permitting decisions.

[P5] Requiring EPA and the Corps to accept USDA PCC designations in § 110.1(3)(viii) could create interagency conflicts when USDA and EPA/Corps scientific assessments differ; commenters will request an interagency dispute-resolution mechanism.

[P6] Granting the EPA Administrator final authority over PCC abandonment in § 110.1(3)(viii) without defining "abandonment" invites arbitrary determinations; commenters will demand a statutory definition or regulatory criteria.

[P7] The high tide line determination permission in § 112.2(3)(iv) should expressly require documentation (photographs, GPS coordinates, assessor reports) when "physical indicators" are used so determinations are defensible.

[P7] Property owners will be concerned that ephemeral markers could be used retroactively to alter property rights or permit requirements; they will request a provision preventing retroactive boundary changes without notice.

[P8] Acceptance of USDA PCC designations in § 112.2(3)(viii) may conflict with state-level wetland protections; state environmental agencies will ask for coordination language to preserve more protective state classifications.

[P8] Small farmers will support acceptance of USDA PCC designations as lowering compliance burden, but will request clarity on whether any subsequent land-use changes could trigger reclassification.

[P9] Centralizing abandonment determination with the EPA Administrator in § 112.2(3)(viii) may violate the Administrative Procedure Act if decisions are made without opportunity for public participation; commenters will ask for procedural safeguards.

[P10] The permission to use physical indicators in § 116.3(3)(iv) must exclude contamination artifacts (e.g., petroleum sheens from upstream spills) from qualifying as the "line of oil or scum" to avoid misidentifying the high tide line.

[P10] Marine scientists will request that the rule require use of tidal datum references (e.g., mean high water) as the primary standard, with physical indicators only as last resort and with mandatory environmental corroboration.

[P11] Requiring EPA and the Corps to accept USDA PCC designations in § 116.3(3)(viii) without a sunset/clawback provision could permanently exempt lands that have reverted to wetland functions; commenters will demand a mechanism for reassessment if hydrology has changed.

[P11] Wetland conservation organizations will argue the rule should require field verification of USDA PCC designations in areas where recent aerial imagery or ground conditions suggest reversion to wetland.

[P12] Granting the EPA Administrator final authority to determine PCC abandonment in § 116.3(3)(viii) should include an independent scientific review requirement to prevent politicized decisions.

[P12] Civil liberties or property rights advocates will request explicit procedures for affected landowners to petition the Administrator's determination and obtain timely decisions to reduce business uncertainty.

[P12] Multiple commenters will point out the repeated replication of near-identical provisions across parts (P1/P4/P7/P10 and P2/P5/P8/P11 and P3/P6/P9/P12) increases the risk of inconsistent cross-references and request consolidation and harmonization across the rule.

[P1] The requirement to submit an annual report for each registered fuel showing additive concentration ranges and volume produced is overly burdensome for small fuel manufacturers and should include an exemption or scaled reporting threshold based on production volume.

[P1] The provision does not specify what constitutes “volume produced” (e.g., gallons manufactured, sold, or supplied into commerce); EPA should clarify the metric and whether blended fuels are reported by blender or refinery.

[P2] Mandating submission on EPA-provided forms by March 31 creates a narrow deadline that may conflict with corporate year-end audits; EPA should allow electronic submissions with a 60-day grace period or permit certified extensions.

[P3] The Oct 1–Dec 31 exception that waives reporting for the remainder of the year for late registrations could be exploited to delay reporting indefinitely by registering near October 1; EPA should require a prorated interim report regardless of registration date.

[P4] The 30-day notification timeframe for changes to multiple registration fields is unworkable for multinational manufacturers with complex supply chains; EPA should allow 60 or 90 days for non-safety-critical changes.

[P5] Requiring written notice to the Administrator within 30 days of changes to information in paragraphs (a)-(d) and (j) imposes an unclear standard for “written” (email, electronic portal, certified mail); EPA should specify acceptable submission methods and receipt confirmation.

[P6] Reliance on §79.5(b) for changes to paragraph (e) information lacks transparency; commenters request that EPA publish §79.5(b) procedures and timelines explicitly in the final rule.

[P7] The prohibition on representing additive registration as government endorsement is appropriate, but the rule’s broad wording could chill truthful communications (e.g., “registered with EPA”); EPA should allow neutral factual statements such as “registered under 40 CFR part 79” without implying endorsement.

[P8] Limiting the permission to advertise compliance with gasoline deposit control requirements only to additives that meet 40 CFR 1090.240 is reasonable, but the rule should require clear labeling language to avoid consumer confusion about performance claims.

[P9] The additional information required for gasoline deposit control additive registration substantially increases confidentiality concerns; EPA must adopt robust CBI protections and a clear process for redaction.

[P10] Requiring submission of the Lowest Additive Concentration (LAC) that meets 40 CFR 1090.240 may force disclosure of proprietary performance data; EPA should permit submission of ranges or confidential LAC values with CBI protection.

[P11] Requiring the specific deposit control test method from 1090.1395 is appropriate for comparability, but EPA should allow third-party test reports or accredited lab certifications in lieu of full method reporting.

[P12] Mandating a complete list of additive components with weight/volume percent risks disclosure of trade secrets; EPA should allow submission of confidential formulations or use CAS numbers with confidential masking and provide a clear CBI assertion process.

[P13] The requirement to use standard chemical names or structures is reasonable, but the burden of providing chemical structures for proprietary polymers may be excessive; allow use of unique identifiers with CBI safeguards and limited structural disclosure.

[P14] Requiring classification of detergent-active components into categories A–G may not accommodate novel chemistries; EPA should include an “Other” category and a petition process to add new categories.

[P15] The composition variability constraints under a single registration are vague about acceptable tolerances and testing evidence; EPA should provide quantitative examples and an approval pathway for multi-formulation registrations.

[P16] Prohibiting inclusion of detergent-active components not present during deposit control testing effectively bans post-test reformulation and may require repeat testing for minor substitutions; EPA should permit limited component substitutions if the manufacturer demonstrates equivalent activity.

[P17] Banning concentration ranges that permit efficacy at the lower bound to be less than demonstrated in testing could force narrow specification ranges that are impractical in commercial production; EPA should define acceptable statistical methods to relate test results to allowable concentration ranges.

[P18] Allowing sale of additives with higher detergent-active concentrations than reported is helpful, but EPA should require updated reporting when higher concentration products are marketed at scale to ensure LAC applicability remains valid.

[P19] Allowing variability of non-detergent-active components only if effectiveness is not reduced places the burden on manufacturers to prove a negative; EPA should clarify the evidence needed (e.g., bench tests, modeling) and acceptance criteria.

[P20] Treating carrier oils as detergent-active components unless manufacturer data show otherwise shifts the evidentiary burden to industry; EPA should provide clear scientific criteria and acceptable study designs to demonstrate non-enhancing behavior.

[P21] Requiring separate registrations for additive packages that do not meet composition variability requirements will increase administrative burden and costs; EPA should allow consolidated registrations with bounded variability and mandatory reporting when thresholds are exceeded.

[P22] Granting EPA authority to disqualify additives where variability could reduce effectiveness is necessary, but the rule lacks procedural safeguards (notice, opportunity to cure, appeal process); EPA should adopt due process steps prior to disqualification.

[P23] The exception allowing changes in minimum concentration from detergent blender modifications per 1090.1240 without new registration is appropriate, but EPA should specify documentation required to demonstrate modifications fall under this exception.

[P24] The requirement to identify reactant materials and acceptance criteria and to maintain documentation for EPA request creates supply-chain disclosure risks; EPA should permit manufacturers to submit supplier attestations or redacted documents with CBI protection.

[P25] Requiring that acceptance criteria be “those given to suppliers” may be untenable where multiple suppliers use different specifications; EPA should permit consolidated acceptance criteria and require manufacturers to document how supplier criteria map to manufacturer acceptance criteria.

[P26] Submitting Gel Permeation Chromatograph (GPC) data including calibration standard identity and characterizations imposes high analytical cost; EPA should allow accredited lab certification of GPC results and accept standardized reporting templates to reduce burden.

[P27] Providing extensive physical and compositional parameters for non-detergent-active carrier oils is technically justified, but EPA should limit reporting frequency (e.g., initial registration and significant change) rather than every annual report.

[P28] Measuring T10, T50, T90 and end boiling point per 1090.1350 is appropriate, but producers using alternative validated distillation methods should be allowed to submit equivalent data with EPA approval.

[P29] Requiring API gravity and viscosity reporting is reasonable; however, EPA should allow reporting in both SI and customary units and accept typical production ranges where individual batch testing is impractical.

[P30] The threshold of ≥0.5% by weight for reporting oxygen, sulfur, and nitrogen concentrations may be too high or too low depending on analytical uncertainty; EPA should clarify if this is an absolute or rounded threshold and the acceptable analytical methods.

[P31] The FTIR description and spectra requirement for additive packages and each detergent-active component may reveal proprietary fingerprints; EPA must accept redacted spectra, limit public disclosure, and permit use of hashed or reference spectra with CBI protections.

[P32] Requiring FTIR spectra from samples at or above reported lower-bound concentration values could force manufacturers to produce noncommercial-strength samples; EPA should accept spectra from representative commercial batches and allow composite sampling.

[P33] Mandating identification of physical parameters adequate for ID and QC is reasonable, but EPA should allow flexibility for novel products and provide a list of commonly accepted parameters to streamline compliance.

[P34] Requiring viscosity, density, and basic nitrogen as default parameters could be unnecessary for some additive chemistries; EPA should permit substitution upon justified request and expedite approval of substitutions.

[P35] The written request process to substitute parameters is bureaucratic; EPA should provide a standardized substitution request form with clear evaluation criteria and a guaranteed decision timeline.

[P36] EPA’s requirement to respond in writing and grant written approval before substitutions are effective is reasonable, but the rule must set a deadline (e.g., 60 days) for EPA’s response to avoid indefinite delays.

[P37] Requiring standardized measurement methods consistent with ASTM repeatability may not cover all analytical techniques; EPA should accept equivalent ISO or other consensus standards and permit labs to demonstrate method equivalence.

[P38] Limiting expected variability to five times the standard repeatability or specified percentages is overly prescriptive; manufacturers should be allowed to propose control limits based on statistical process control and historical production data.

[P39] Requiring prior written EPA approval for deviations from measurement or variability limits without specifying review timelines will create compliance uncertainty; EPA should establish an expedited review process with clear evidence requirements.

[P40] Allowing registration termination at a manufacturer’s request is appropriate, but EPA should require manufacturers to notify customers and downstream registrants within a defined period before termination to prevent market disruptions.

[P41] EPA’s authority to terminate registration for gasoline deposit control additives found noncompliant with 1090.240 must include clear notice, remedial timelines, and the ability to request re-testing or corrective action before termination.

[P42] Cross-requiring submission of reports from 40 CFR part 1090, subpart J duplicates reporting burdens; EPA should harmonize the forms and submission channels to prevent duplicate data entry.

[P43] The same comment applies to motor vehicle diesel reports under §79.33(c): harmonize requirements with 1090 subpart J and allow combined reporting.

[P44] The explicit preservation of state/local authority to regulate fuels/additives is appropriate, but EPA should clarify how federal registration interacts with state labeling or sale prohibitions to prevent conflicting compliance obligations.

[P45] The oxygenate “substantially similar” standard under section 211(f)(1) is vague; EPA should publish clear criteria and an administrative pathway for determinations to avoid litigation over “substantially similar” status.

[P46] The limit on separating RINs from renewable fuel volumes (per 80.1429(b)(9)) should be quantified in the rule text; commenters request explicit annual gallon-RIN caps and an explanation of how limits will be calculated and enforced.

[P47] Requiring obligated parties and exporters to provide 1090.805 registration information duplicates other registration systems; EPA should accept existing foreign registrations or recognized equivalency to avoid blocking trade.

[P48] RIN-generating foreign producers must provide 1090.805 information; EPA should provide a clear timeline and assistance for foreign entities to obtain required documentation and avoid supply disruptions.

[P49] Mandating EPA-issued company and facility identification numbers before generating any RINs is essential, but EPA must ensure a rapid onboarding process (e.g., online application with issuance within 10 business days) to avoid production delays.

[P50] Importers must obtain EPA company IDs before generating or owning RINs; EPA should allow retroactive issuance for imports occurring during the onboarding period to avoid penalizing importers for administrative delays.

[P51] The representative sampling requirement per 1090.1805 should include explicit sample size tables and tolerances to ensure consistent application across auditors and reduce disputes.

[P52] Requiring parties who will own RINs to provide 1090.805 info prior to ownership could be problematic for secondary market RIN traders; EPA should create different onboarding rules for traders versus producers.

[P53] The requirement that attest engagements be planned and conducted by an independent surveyor meeting 1090.55 standards is appropriate, but EPA should publish a list of pre-approved independent surveyors or qualification criteria to facilitate compliance.

[P54] Applying annual attest engagement requirements in 1090.1800 to subpart M increases audit burden; EPA should allow multi-year attest cycles for small producers with risk-based sampling.

[P55] Comparing reported product volumes with inventory reconciliation and non-renewable diesel production/import volumes may require proprietary sales data; EPA should permit aggregation or redaction in public reports and limit disclosure to EPA.

[P56] The requirement to select representative exported fuel sample batches and indicate whether exporters calculated advanced/cellulosic RVOs could expose confidential commercial strategies; EPA should limit public disclosure of such findings to protect competitive information.

[P57] Obtaining and retaining invoices, bills of lading, and other commercial documentation for representative samples is standard, but EPA should set retention periods and limits on EPA’s use of the data for enforcement beyond RFS program compliance.

[P58] Requiring attest auditors to be U.S.-licensed CPAs and U.S. citizens (80.1466(m)(6)(ii), 80.1467(h)(2)) is unduly restrictive for international companies and qualified foreign auditors; EPA should allow foreign-licensed CPAs and non-citizen auditors who meet competency and independence criteria, subject to EPA pre-approval.

[P59] The U.S.-citizenship requirement may violate trade agreements and unnecessarily narrows the pool of qualified auditors; EPA should instead require auditors to be authorized to practice in their jurisdiction and to demonstrate equivalence to U.S. CPA standards.

[P60] Requiring attest auditors to sign commitments containing specific provisions (80.1466(m)(6)(iii), 80.1467(h)(3)) is reasonable, but the rule should clarify the legal liability imposed on auditors and whether indemnity language is permissible.

[P61] Permitting independent third-party auditors to use representative sampling per 1090.1805 (80.1469(c)(5)) is sensible, but EPA should specify exclusions and minimum coverage percentages to ensure audit reliability.

[P62] The refueling inlet compatibility requirement (86.1810-17(j) and 1037.115(c)) that excludes nozzles ≥ 24 mm OD may create compatibility problems with legacy equipment and international nozzles; EPA should provide an extended compliance timeline for vehicle manufacturers and consider allowing adapters.

[P63] The nozzle dimension requirement may conflict with some aftermarket refueling systems and fuel dispensers in other countries; clarify applicability only to vehicles sold for use in the U.S. market and provide transition guidance for OEMs.

[P64] The numerous cross-references to 40 CFR 1090 series requirements across subparts create complexity; EPA should publish an integrated compliance guidance document and consolidated forms to reduce compliance costs.

[P65] Many obligations reference representative sampling “in accordance with 1090.1805” but do not define acceptable statistical methods for selecting representative samples; EPA should prescribe minimum randomization and confidence levels to avoid inconsistent audits.

[P66] The rule lacks explicit timelines for EPA review and response to submissions (registration data, substitution requests, independence approvals); commenters request statutory review deadlines and default approvals if EPA fails to act within set timeframes.

[P67] Multiple provisions require document submissions “upon request” without limiting the scope or frequency of requests; EPA should limit requests to reasonable intervals (e.g., once per compliance year) and require specificity to avoid fishing expeditions.

[P68] Several requirements could impose significant costs (analytical testing, GPC, FTIR, attest audits); EPA must include a thorough Regulatory Flexibility Analysis and consider phased compliance or financial assistance for small entities.

[P69] Confidential business information (CBI) protections are insufficiently described given the volume of proprietary data required (formulations, spectra, supplier information); EPA should define redaction procedures, timelines for CBI determinations, and penalties for improper disclosure.

[P70] The rule must clarify enforcement consequences, civil penalties, and remediation procedures for failures to submit reports or to comply with composition variability restrictions to allow entities to assess compliance risk.

[P71] Where EPA may terminate registrations (80.24(b)), the rule should allow a remedial period and specify criteria and evidentiary standards for termination, as well as an administrative appeal mechanism.

[P72] The interplay between RVO calculations for exporters and attest/audit sampling requirements is confusing; EPA should provide worked examples illustrating auditor findings, exporter calculations, and implications for RIN generation/separation.

[P73] For foreign renewable fuel producers required to obtain EPA company/facility IDs before generating RINs, EPA must allow electronic verification of foreign tax IDs or other national identifiers to expedite onboarding.

[P74] The requirement that auditors be independent under 1090.55 should explicitly prohibit financial relationships with the auditee during a defined look-back period (e.g., two years) to avoid conflicts of interest.

[P75] EPA should clarify whether blended fuels (e.g., biodiesel blends) require separate additive registrations per blend or whether single additive registrations covering multiple fuel types are acceptable under composition variability rules.

[P76] The rule should explicitly state how EPA will treat legacy registrations and grandfather existing products that were tested under previous procedures to avoid mandatory re-testing and market disruption.

[P77] Testing and reporting requirements tied to 40 CFR 1090 test methods assume availability of testing labs; EPA should authorize accredited third-party labs and publish an approved lab list or accreditation criteria.

[P78] Many provisions require selection of “representative samples” but do not address chain-of-custody requirements for samples; EPA should require documented chain-of-custody and provide acceptable templates.

[P79] The obligations in 80.1464 and related attest provisions create overlapping audit obligations for parties in the same supply chain; EPA should permit a single consolidated audit report recognized for multiple covered entities to reduce duplicate audit costs.

[P80] EPA should provide safe harbors for inadvertent minor reporting errors discovered and corrected in good faith (e.g., procedural correction window) to avoid punitive actions for minor administrative mistakes.

Reliance on §79.5(b) for changes to paragraph (e) information lacks transparency; commenters request that EPA publish §79.5(b) procedures and timelines explicitly in the final rule.

The prohibition on representing additive registration as government endorsement is appropriate, but the rule’s broad wording could chill truthful communications (e.g., “registered with EPA”); EPA should allow neutral factual statements such as “registered under 40 CFR part 79” without implying endorsement.

The requirement to use standard chemical names or structures is reasonable, but the burden of providing chemical structures for proprietary polymers may be excessive; allow use of unique identifiers with CBI safeguards and limited structural disclosure.
Requiring classification of detergent-active components into categories A–G may not accommodate novel chemistries; EPA should include an “Other” category and a petition process to add new categories.

The composition variability constraints under a single registration are vague about acceptable tolerances and testing evidence; EPA should provide quantitative examples and an approval pathway for multi-formulation registrations.

raw_output:
[P1] The provision allowing temporary FTE cap adjustments for displaced residents beginning July 1, 2011 is unclear whether it applies retroactively to closures that occurred between July 1, 2011 and the effective date of the final rule; request clarification and/or explicit retroactivity language.

[P1] Hospitals and IPFs will need guidance on how "temporary" is defined for the adjustment (maximum duration); propose specifying a default maximum duration (e.g., one program year, two years).

[P2] The eligibility condition limiting displaced residents to those from IPFs that closed on or after July 1, 2011 is arbitrary and may unfairly exclude residents displaced by earlier closures still undergoing training; request removing the date cutoff or providing an exception mechanism.

[P2] Advocacy groups representing displaced residents will object that the rule does not allow displaced residents from non-IPF psychiatric training programs (e.g., general hospital psychiatry rotations) to trigger adjustments; request expanding eligible sources.

[P3] The 60-day deadline to submit a request to the Medicare contractor after beginning to train displaced residents is unreasonably short for hospitals dealing with sudden closures; request extending to 120 days or adding a hardship waiver.

[P3] Legal commenters will ask whether failure to meet the 60-day filing deadline results in permanent ineligibility or whether late submissions will be accepted with justification; recommend adding a cure/late-submission process.

[P4] Requiring IPFs to identify which displaced residents "caused" it to exceed its cap is administratively vague—request clear methodology and examples for attributing which residents are counted as causing the cap exceedance.

[P4] Industry commenters will request that documentation standards (what records, attestation, signatures) for identifying displaced residents be specified to ensure consistent audits.

[P5] Requiring IPFs to "specify the length of time the adjustment is needed" without standards will invite inconsistent or overly long requests; recommend specifying default timeframes or maximum allowable durations and renewal procedures.

[P6] Permitting adjustments only where the closed IPF agrees to reduce its cap creates perverse incentives and potential bargaining between hospitals; request safeguards to prevent coercion or extortion and clarify whether the closed hospital's consent must be written and notarized.

[P6] Small hospitals and rural providers may be unable or unwilling to accept a cap reduction; request alternative mechanisms (e.g., CMS-administered temporary pool) to avoid penalizing receiving IPFs.

[P7] The condition that receiving IPFs must be training displaced residents is reasonable but silent on whether observational or temporary rotations count; request clarification on the minimum training commitment required (FTE percentage or months).

[P8] The duplicate 60-day submission requirement (for transfers from closed programs) compounds administrative burden; suggest harmonizing deadlines across P3/P8/P27/P33 to a single, practical timeframe.

[P9] Requiring documentation that identifies displaced residents from the closed program opens confidentiality/privacy issues—request guidance on permissible redaction and HIPAA-safe methods for sharing resident identities with Medicare contractors.

[P10] The obligation to "specify the duration" when combined with no renewal process could force repeated filings; ask CMS to define renewal processes, required supporting evidence, and timelines for extensions.

[P11] Requiring receiving IPFs to submit the closed hospital's FTE reduction statement within 60 days presumes the closed hospital will cooperate promptly; propose allowing the receiving IPF to submit its request with an attestation and a copy of its request to the closed hospital if the closed hospital fails to respond within the deadline.

[P12] The rule permits adjustments only if the closed hospital reduces its cap based on displaced residents per program year at time of closure—this could penalize closed hospitals that no longer have an active accreditation record or that dissolved records; ask CMS to accept alternative proof (e.g., residency program accreditation records, ACGME rosters).

[P13] Determining annual FTE reduction "based on the number of displaced residents who would have been training" invites speculative calculations for future program years; request instruction on acceptable methods (e.g., match lists, contractual rotation schedules) and whether fractional FTEs are allowed.

[P14] The 60-day deadline for closed hospitals to submit a signed, dated statement identifying displaced residents and reductions may be impossible when the closing entity has ceased operations; request a provision allowing former administrators or legal successors to file the statement.

[P14] Legal commenters will request a template for the required signed statement to ensure legal sufficiency and consistent processing by Medicare contractors.

[P15] The requirement that the hospital's statement affirmatively agree to a temporary reduction raises questions about whether agreement can be conditional or limited; request clarity on whether hospitals can limit reductions to specific program years or resident cohorts.

[P16] Identifying "displaced residents who were in training at closure" may exclude residents whose training was interrupted but who later resumed elsewhere; ask CMS to clarify treatment of residents on leaves or rotations at time of closure.

[P17] The requirement to identify receiving IPFs could create privacy concerns and potential resident choice restrictions; resident advocacy groups will request that residents' consent be required before listing their new training sites.

[P18] Specifying FTE cap reductions for applicable program years must account for residents who change training intensity or leave the profession; request guidance on mid-year adjustments for attrition, resignations, or early graduations.

[P19] Requiring facilities to provide CEO and QualityNet security official contact information (name, email, phone, mailing address) raises security/privacy concerns for named individuals; request allowing generic departmental contacts or a privacy-protected point of contact and specify protections against public disclosure.

[P19] Suggest adding an obligation that CMS safeguard this contact information and limit use to administrative communications to avoid spam or misuse.

[P20] The repeated permission language (duplicate of P1/P20) creates redundancy—request consolidation to reduce confusion and cross-references in the final regulatory text.

[P21] The condition referencing closures on or after July 1, 2011 is repeated elsewhere—request CMS explain the policy rationale for this specific cutoff and consider aligning with the effective date of program changes rather than an arbitrary historical date.

[P22] Repeated 60-day submission obligations across provisions need harmonization; request a single, standard submission timeline and a clear definition of "begins to train" (first day resident provides clinical services vs. orientation).

[P23] The documentation obligation to identify displaced residents "who caused it to exceed its cap" invites disputes in multi-hospital transfers where multiple displaced residents arrive across time; request a cumulative reporting method and tolerance for incremental exceedances.

[P24] The requirement to specify how long the adjustment is needed should include instructions on whether adjustments may be prorated for partial years; request explicit language on prorating adjustments for mid-year starts.

[P25] Reiterates P6; request CMS define terms such as "agrees to temporarily reduce" (written signed statement, regulatory filing) to avoid interpretive disputes.

[P26] Receiving IPFs required to provide closed hospital's FTE reduction statement may face delays when closed hospitals are bankrupt or in receivership; request that CMS accept court-appointed trustee affidavits or evidence from state licensing boards as substitutes.

[P27] The obligation to submit a request to Medicare Contractor within 60 days should include guidance on what constitutes evidence of the "beginning to train" displaced residents (payroll record, schedule, resident credentialing).

[P28] The documentation obligation to identify displaced residents should allow use of ACGME or NRMP records as acceptable evidence; request CMS list acceptable source documents.

[P29] Request CMS clarify whether "length of time the adjustment is needed" must match the closed hospital's reduction years, and whether receiving IPFs can request less than the full period.

[P30] The subpoena-like requirement to submit the closed hospital's FTE reduction statement could conflict with ongoing litigation or bankruptcy confidentiality; request an exception or protective order process.

[P31] Mandating that closed hospitals reduce their FTE cap based on displaced residents per program year risks permanently reducing the closed hospital's legacy caps and affecting future reopenings; request that reductions be explicitly temporary and reversible if the hospital reopens programs.

[P32] The methodology for determining yearly reduction "based on the number who would have been training" lacks standards for residents with nonstandard training (part-time, extended) — request CMS permit fractional FTE calculations and provide examples.

Hospitals and IPFs will need guidance on how "temporary" is defined for the adjustment (maximum duration); propose specifying a default maximum duration (e.g., one program year, two years).

The eligibility condition limiting displaced residents to those from IPFs that closed on or after July 1, 2011 is arbitrary and may unfairly exclude residents displaced by earlier closures still undergoing training; request removing the date cutoff or providing an exception mechanism.

Advocacy groups representing displaced residents will object that the rule does not allow displaced residents from non-IPF psychiatric training programs (e.g., general hospital psychiatry rotations) to trigger adjustments; request expanding eligible sources.

The 60-day deadline to submit a request to the Medicare contractor after beginning to train displaced residents is unreasonably short for hospitals dealing with sudden closures; request extending to 120 days or adding a hardship waiver.

Legal commenters will ask whether failure to meet the 60-day filing deadline results in permanent ineligibility or whether late submissions will be accepted with justification; recommend adding a cure/late-submission process.

Requiring IPFs to identify which displaced residents "caused" it to exceed its cap is administratively vague—request clear methodology and examples for attributing which residents are counted as causing the cap exceedance.
Industry commenters will request that documentation standards (what records, attestation, signatures) for identifying displaced residents be specified to ensure consistent audits.

Requiring IPFs to "specify the length of time the adjustment is needed" without standards will invite inconsistent or overly long requests; recommend specifying default timeframes or maximum allowable durations and renewal procedures.

Permitting adjustments only where the closed IPF agrees to reduce its cap creates perverse incentives and potential bargaining between hospitals; request safeguards to prevent coercion or extortion and clarify whether the closed hospital's consent must be written and notarized.
Small hospitals and rural providers may be unable or unwilling to accept a cap reduction; request alternative mechanisms (e.g., CMS-administered temporary pool) to avoid penalizing receiving IPFs.

The condition that receiving IPFs must be training displaced residents is reasonable but silent on whether observational or temporary rotations count; request clarification on the minimum training commitment required (FTE percentage or months).
