raw_output:
[P1] The broadcast-only notice requirement places undue burden on stakeholders without reliable VHF/HF reception; the rule should require additional notification methods (e.g., email lists, local marina postings) in addition to broadcast notices.

[P1] The provision does not specify the minimum lead time for the COTP’s broadcast notice before enforcement begins; commenters will request a required notice period (e.g., 24 or 48 hours) to allow mariners to plan.

[P2] The blanket prohibition on entering the regulated area without COTP authorization fails to define the authorization process or timelines; industry stakeholders will request a clear, predictable authorization procedure and contact point.

[P2] The rule lacks criteria for when the COTP will grant or deny entry; legal commenters will argue it must include objective standards to prevent arbitrary enforcement.

[P3] Restricting recreational vessels to only the Indiana side of the navigation channel discriminates against Ohio-based boaters and may conflict with state water jurisdiction; recreational boating associations will request equal access or reciprocal provisions.

[P4] The rule’s directive that recreational vessels “stay on the Indiana side” is ambiguous regarding lateral boundaries and enforcement; commenters will request precise latitude/longitude coordinates or marked buoys.

[P4] The provision does not address vessels crossing for safe navigation or emergency maneuvers; safety advocates will request a clear exception for emergency avoidance or other safety maneuvers.

[P5] The prohibition on anchoring or loitering in the navigation channel is reasonable for safety, but the rule should specify penalties and enforcement procedures to ensure proportionality.

[P6] The no-entry zone from MM 602.7 to MM 607.0 covers a substantial stretch without explaining the operational justification; commercial operators will demand evidence and risk assessment supporting the extent of the closed zone.

[P6] Barges, tow operators, and commercial traffic that routinely operate in MM 602.7–607.0 will be severely impacted; industry commenters will request exemptions or scheduled transit windows for commercial navigation.

[P7] The “slowest safe speed creating minimum wake” standard is too vague and subjective; commenters will request a defined speed limit (e.g., 5 knots) or measurable wake-height guidance.

[P7] Enforcement of minimum-wake speed requires measurement protocols; law enforcement and marinas will request guidance on how violations will be determined and documented.

[P8] Granting the COTP authority to terminate events or vessel operations “at any time” is overly broad; event organizers will request criteria, notice requirements, and appeal processes before termination powers are exercised.

[P9] Requiring all other persons/vessels to request permission without specifying the method, contact, or processing timeframe will create confusion; commenters will request the inclusion of contact information and standard response times.

[P10] Requiring EPA to maintain a guidance portal is supported, but commenters will ask for assurances that the portal will be searchable, machine-readable, and accessible (ADA-compliant).

[P11] The requirement to include all “active guidance documents” on the portal may create an administrative burden and delay timely guidance posting; program offices will request phased implementation or exceptions for high-volume administrative documents.

[P11] Declaring excluded documents “have no effect” could inadvertently nullify longstanding interpretive materials; legal commenters will request a grandfathering clause preserving reliance interests until reissuance on the portal.

[P12] The specified metadata requirements are useful, but commenters will request an indexable metadata schema (e.g., JSON-LD) and bulk download capability to facilitate regulatory compliance and public analysis.

[P13] The concise name requirement should include naming conventions to prevent duplicate/ambiguous titles; commenters will ask EPA to issue standardized naming rules.

[P14] Posting issuance dates is appropriate, but commenters will request that guidance also include an “effective date” if different from issuance.

[P15] The portal posting date must be recorded, and commenters will request an audit trail (timestamped revisions) so stakeholders can track changes over time.

[P16] The requirement for a unique EPA identifier is supported; commenters will request that identifiers be persistent (DOI-like) and used in cross-references across EPA systems.

[P17] Portal hyperlinks must link to machine-readable source documents (e.g., PDF/A or HTML) and all supporting materials; commenters will request that attachments are preserved and archived.

[P18] The portal’s topic/program/statute field should allow multiple tags and standard taxonomy to support cross-cutting guidance; commenters will ask EPA to adopt controlled vocabularies.

[P19] The “brief summary” must be standardized in length and format to prevent inconsistent summaries; commenters will suggest a 150–300 word limit and required keywords.

[P20] Requiring specific standard elements in each guidance document is reasonable, but commenters will note that small, operational guidance (e.g., internal or technical memoranda) may not practicably include all elements and request exemptions.

[P21] Mandating the word “guidance” in every document could be circumvented or cause redundancy; commenters will ask for flexibility allowing equivalent terminology if clearly labeled.

[P22] Specifying the issuing office is appropriate, but commenters will request clarity on multi-office or interagency guidance and how issuance is attributed.

[P23] Requiring a title is standard; commenters will request a format (e.g., Program: Short Title) to improve portal sorting and search.

[P24] The unique document identification number requirement must coordinate with existing EPA numbering systems; program offices will request transitional guidance.

[P25] Issuance date must be present; commenters will ask that revisions include both original issuance and revision dates to preserve history.

[P26] The “when practicable” qualifier for stating applicability could lead to inconsistent application and legal uncertainty; stakeholders will request objective criteria for when applicability must be specified.

[P27] Requiring statutory/regulatory citations is beneficial, but commenters will caution that some guidance synthesizes multiple authorities; EPA should allow citation of multiple statutes/regulations and explanatory notes.

[P28] The revision-identification requirement is important to track continuity; commenters will request cross-links to the prior guidance for transparency.

[P29] Requiring a short summary at the beginning is helpful; commenters will request a standard template (purpose, scope, applicability, contact).

[P30] The disclaimer that guidance lacks force of law is appropriate, but commenters will stress it must also explain the interplay with binding requirements and whether reliance on guidance will be considered in enforcement discretion.

[P31] Notifying the public when guidance is issued/modified/withdrawn via the portal is necessary, but commenters will request automated subscription/email alerts and RSS feeds to ensure stakeholders receive timely updates.

[P32] The prohibition on mandatory language is reasonable, but commenters will request clear exceptions and examples for when mandatory language is allowed (e.g., safety protocols).

[P33] Requiring regional concurrence from Headquarters will slow routine technical guidance; Regional offices will request an expedited concurrence process or thresholds for which guidance requires concurrence.

[P34] Seeking OIRA significance determinations may be administratively burdensome for routine guidance; commenters will request criteria defining which guidance qualifies for OIRA review.

[P35] Subjecting “significant guidance documents” to public comment is supported, but commenters will request a clear, narrow definition of “significant” to avoid over-inclusion.

[P36] The proposed 30-day public comment period for draft significant guidance is too short for complex technical guidance; industry and environmental NGOs will request at least 60 days for technical documents.

[P37] Requiring 30 days for comments on modifications/withdrawals is appropriate, but commenters will ask for exception handling when the modification is minor or purely administrative.

[P38] Posting draft significant guidance concurrently with the Federal Register notice is beneficial; commenters will request that all supporting technical datasets and analyses also be posted to allow meaningful review.

[P39] Requiring commenters to use methods specified in the Federal Register may limit participation; commenters will request multiple submission channels (regulations.gov, email, and mail) and accommodations for people without internet access.

[P40] Making all comments publicly available is supported, but commenters will request protections for confidential business information (CBI) and personally identifiable information (PII), and clear redaction procedures.

[P41] Publishing a Federal Register notice when issuance/modification/withdrawal is finalized is useful; commenters will request that the notice explain changes made in response to comments.

[P42] Requiring EPA to respond to “major” comments is ambiguous; commenters will request a definition of “major” and require that responses address substantive arguments, not just procedural summaries.

[P43] The limited exceptions to notice-and-comment are necessary for emergencies, but commenters will urge strict, narrowly defined criteria and mandatory retrospective review when exceptions are used.

[P44] Allowing EPA to bypass public comment under exigent circumstances risks overuse; stakeholders will request mandatory documentation and independent review when exigent circumstances are invoked.

[P45] The “good cause” exception language mirrors Administrative Procedure Act standards but could be abused; commenters will request that EPA define “impracticable,” “unnecessary,” and “contrary to the public interest” and require advance publication of the good-cause rationale.

[P46] The requirement to state the good-cause finding is necessary but should mandate publication in the Federal Register (not just the guidance document) and include a public explanation and opportunity for post-issuance comment.

[P47] Requiring a Presidentially-appointed official’s approval for each significant guidance document will create bottlenecks; commenters will request delegation authorities and defined timelines for approval to avoid paralysis.

[P48] Compliance with multiple Executive Orders is appropriate, but commenters will request clarification on how conflicting EO requirements are reconciled and which EO controls in case of inconsistency.

[P49] The $100 million annual-effects threshold for required economic assessment should be harmonized with OMB definitions; commenters will ask whether aggregated, multi-year, or market-mediated impacts count toward the threshold.

[P50] Economic analyses must account for impacts on small entities; small business groups will request required use of SBA size standards and regulatory flexibility analyses consistent with the RFA.

[P51] Allowing public petitions to modify/withdraw guidance is positive, but commenters will request transparency on petition handling and publication of petitions received.

[P52] The portal’s instructions for petitions must be detailed and user-friendly; NGOs and community groups will request templates and examples to facilitate meaningful petitions.

[P53] Allowing electronic or paper petitions is good; commenters will request clear deadlines, confirmation receipts, and tracking numbers for petitions.

[P54] The electronic submission link should accept common file formats and provide automatic acknowledgement; commenters will request an accessible, robust submission system with error-checking.

[P55] Accepting paper petitions is important for some stakeholders; commenters will request a mailing address and clarify postal receipt date counts as the filing date.

[P56] Required petition formatting elements may be overly prescriptive; community organizations with limited resources will request flexibility or a simplified petition option.

[P57] Requiring petitioner contact information is reasonable but commenters will request confidential contact options for whistleblowers and protections for petitioners from retaliation.

[P58] The heading requirement for petitions is bureaucratic; commenters will request that EPA accept petitions without the exact heading if substantive content is present.

[P59] Requiring content elements is sensible, but commenters will ask that EPA accept well-reasoned submissions that may lack specific formatting and not dismiss them solely for form.

[P60] Identification by title and unique identifier is necessary, but historical guidance without identifiers may be hard to reference; commenters will request an EPA-maintained crosswalk mapping legacy documents to identifiers.

[P61] Requiring statement of relief sought (modification vs withdrawal) is appropriate; commenters will ask that EPA clarify what types of modifications are appropriate via petition versus requiring formal rulemaking.

[P62] Requiring an explanation of the petitioner’s interest could disadvantage third-party public interest groups; commenters will request that EPA accept broad public-interest petitions without narrow standing requirements.

[P63] Requesting specification of exact text to be changed and suggested replacement text is useful for efficiency, but commenters will request that EPA still consider petitions that provide principled objections without drafting alternative text.

[P64] The rationale requirement is necessary; commenters will request that EPA provide guidance on evidentiary standards and acceptable types of supporting data.

[P65] Allowing incomplete petitions to be considered is fair, but commenters will ask for an initial intake process where EPA notifies petitioners of missing items and allows cure periods before deeming petitions deficient.

[P66] Treating properly formatted petitions filed by nonstandard methods as filed upon discovery is reasonable, but commenters will request time-stamping and notification to the submitter when EPA treats a submission as a petition.

[P67] The risk that documents lacking required elements will be treated as generic correspondence will chill public participation; commenters will request that EPA proactively identify potential petitions and contact authors before discounting them.

[P68] The 90-day response deadline is a tangible improvement, but commenters will ask that EPA commit to substantive responses (not merely procedural acknowledgments) within 90 days.

[P69] Allowing an extension only once for up to 90 days may be insufficient for complex petitions; commenters will request flexibility for exceptionally complex matters while requiring transparency and interim status updates.

[P70] The one-time extension cap is helpful for predictability, but commenters will request that EPA publish extension notices that explain reasons and provide a new decision date.

[P71] Consolidated responses to duplicative or mass petitions are efficient, but commenters will request that consolidated replies still address materially distinct points raised in subsets of petitions.

[P72] Excluding petitions that seek changes to statutes or promulgated rules is legally required, but commenters will request EPA clarify how petitioners seeking such changes will be redirected (e.g., to rulemaking docket) and ensure their concerns are not ignored.

raw_output:
[P1] The exception in §91.146(b) creates a loophole allowing passenger-carrying charity flights to avoid part 119 certification and part 120 drug/alcohol testing, undermining safety oversight for flights that carry paying passengers for nonprofit events.

[P1] Charitable and community event operators will be confused about what constitutes “for the benefit of” an event in §91.146(b), creating enforcement ambiguity and potential misuse to evade certification and testing requirements.

[P2] Requiring departure from an “adequate public airport or FAA-approved alternate location” (§91.146(b)(2)) is vague — the rule does not define “adequate,” leaving small community airports subject to inconsistent FAA interpretation.

[P2] The FAA-approval requirement for alternate locations in §91.146(b)(2) will impose an unreasonable administrative burden and delay for grassroots nonprofit organizers seeking to host impromptu or seasonal events.

[P3] The 30-passenger-seat and 7,500-pound payload cap in §91.146(b)(3) is inconsistent with other parts (e.g., §136.71(b)(1)) and creates an incentive to reconfigure aircraft seating or offload cargo to qualify for exceptions, undermining safety.

[P3] The 7,500-pound payload threshold in §91.146(b)(3) is lower than thresholds used elsewhere (e.g., §119.1(e)(7) 6,000 lbs and §136.71(b)(1)) and will create compliance complexity for operators whose aircraft hover near the limits.

[P4] Requiring a standard airworthiness certificate and compliance with subpart E (§91.146(b)(5)) is appropriate, but the rule fails to specify how FAA will verify ongoing airworthiness for transient or one-off charitable flights.

[P5] The pro rata reimbursement limitation in §91.146(b)(5) is insufficiently precise — the rule does not define allowable accounting methods or documentation required to substantiate “pro rata” costs, creating opportunities for abuse.

[P5] The reimbursement limitation (fuel, oil, airport costs, rental) in §91.146(b)(5) may still permit operators to receive de facto profit and thus effectively conduct common carriage without part 119 oversight; enforcement and auditing provisions are needed.

[P6] Mandating that management specifications include authorized deviations/exemptions (§91.1015(a)(9)) is reasonable, but the rule lacks procedures and timelines for updating those specifications when deviations are granted or rescinded.

[P7] Allowing the FAA to consider multiple factors (§110.2) when determining a “commercial air tour” is too discretionary and will result in inconsistent application across regions; the FAA should publish a prioritized list or binding criteria.

[P8] The broad exception to part 119 applicability in §119.1(e) for operations without common carriage may be exploited by operators who market flights as private while functioning as de facto common carriers.

[P9] Excluding nonstop commercial air tours from part 119 (§119.1(e)(2)) provided LOA compliance creates a two-tier system — LOA holders should still be subject to drug and alcohol testing and other safety requirements analogous to part 119 certificated operators.

[P10] The exception for powered-lift/rotorcraft construction operations (§119.1(e)(4)(v)) that covers transportation to/from sites lacks limitations and could be used to bypass part 119 for passenger transport under the guise of “transport to/from site.”

[P11] Excluding sightseeing hot-air balloon and glider flights from part 119 (§119.1(e)(5)) without additional safety or reporting requirements is risky given passenger operation variability and may reduce oversight of commercial sightseeing businesses.

[P12] The 25-statute-mile radius exception for powered-lift/rotorcraft in §119.1(e)(7) is arbitrary and could encourage operators to cluster routes just inside the limit to avoid certification, creating safety inconsistencies over slightly longer distances.

[P13] Limiting those excepted flights to no more than two passengers (§119.1(e)(7)(i)) is workable, but enforcement will be difficult without manifest or inspection requirements; operators could circumvent by rotating passengers.

[P14] Requiring standard-category certification and 100-hour inspections (§119.1(e)(7)(iii)) is appropriate but conflicts with §91.146(b)(3)’s seat/payload thresholds; the agency should harmonize these sections to reduce operator confusion.

[P15] The prohibition on carrying cargo (§119.1(e)(7)(vii)) lacks clarity on baggage allowance and passenger personal items; the rule should define “cargo” and set weight limits for carry-on items.

[P16] The Administrator’s obligation to issue an Operating Certificate for U.S. commercial operators not direct air carriers (§119.5(b)) needs clearer criteria and timelines to prevent delays that stall lawful operations.

[P17] Issuing Operating Certificates for nongenerally-carriage operations with 20+ seats or >=6,000 lb payload (§119.5(c)) will impose significant new compliance burdens on small operators that previously operated under more flexible rules; an implementation timeline and economic analysis are missing.

[P18] Requiring compliance with subpart C certification/specifications (§119.21(a)) for intrastate common carriage operators lacks transitional relief and may force small operators to suspend service while obtaining complex approvals.

[P19] Mandating part 125 compliance (§119.23(a)(2)) for certain non-common carriage operations will create operational and training costs that small corporate operators cannot absorb without grandfathering provisions.

[P20] The broad list of requirements for noncommon/private carriage for compensation (§119.23(b) intro) is vague about which specific sections apply, increasing legal risk for operators who may inadvertently omit compliance steps.

[P21] Requiring operations specifications to include authorized deviations/exemptions (§119.49(a)(12), (b)(12), (c)(11)) is sensible, but the rule should specify how deviations are displayed, updated, and made available to inspectors and the public.

[P25] The requirement that part 121 certificate holders have specified management personnel (§119.65) is appropriate, but the proposed rule lacks guidance on acceptable organizational structures for smaller carriers merging into part 121 operations.

[P26] Requiring a Chief Pilot for each category listed in §61.5(b)(1) (§119.65(a)(3)) could impose undue personnel burdens on small certificate holders that operate a single pilot type across multiple small subcategories.

[P27] The obligation to specify number and type of aircraft used (§119.65(b)(2)) may force frequent amendments for operators with dynamic fleets (charters, leased aircraft) — the rule should allow a range or rolling notification in lieu of constant amendments.

[P28] The ATP requirement and experience thresholds for Director of Operations (§119.67(a)) are overly prescriptive and will exclude otherwise-qualified managers with extensive non‑ATP operational experience, particularly from the helicopter and rotorcraft sectors.

[P29] Requiring three years supervisory/managerial experience in large aircraft in the last six years for Directors when large aircraft are used (§119.67(a)(1)) is unduly restrictive and ignores transferable experience from small aircraft operations.

[P30] Mandating three years PIC experience under parts 121/135 in large aircraft for Directors (§119.67(a)(2)) will disqualify industry professionals from airlines with different regulatory backgrounds (foreign operators, Part 91 turboprops) without offering equivalency standards.

[P31] Allowing experience in small aircraft to satisfy Director requirements when only small aircraft are used (§119.67(a)(3)) is beneficial, but the rule does not define “small” clearly, riskily relying on §61.5 references that may not align with operational realities.

[P32] The Chief Pilot ATP and rating requirement (§119.67(b)(1)) is appropriate for safety, but exceptions for experienced non-ATP pilots (e.g., highly experienced commercial pilots) should be permitted through a defined deviation process.

[P33] The three-year PIC experience requirement for Chief Pilots (§119.67(b)(2)) — particularly the presumption of large-aircraft experience under parts 121/135 — will disproportionately impact helicopter operators and small air tour companies that operate under part 91.

[P34] Requiring first-time Chief Pilots to have experience within the last six years (§119.67(b)(2)(i)) is reasonable, but the rule lacks clarity on acceptable career interruptions (medical leaves, military service) and how these affect recency.

[P35] The insistence that PIC experience be in the same category of aircraft the Chief Pilot will oversee (§119.67(b)(2)(iii)) is appropriate for oversight, but the rule does not account for mixed fleet operations where one Chief Pilot must cover multiple categories.

[P36] The Director of Maintenance requirement to hold A&P with both ratings (§119.67(c)(1)) is sound, but the one-year “returning aircraft to service” experience (§119.67(c)(2)) is vague — it does not define the depth or scope of the role required.

[P37] The supervisory experience requirement for the Director of Maintenance (§119.67(c)(3)) and the three-year options (§119.67(c)(4)) will be difficult for operators that outsource maintenance to third-party repair stations; the rule should allow documented oversight experience instead.

[P38] Requiring three years maintaining large aircraft (10+ seats) for Director of Maintenance (§119.67(c)(4)(i)) will exclude maintenance leaders from helicopter/small-aircraft sectors where relevant expertise exists; the FAA should provide alternative experience pathways.

[P39] Allowing repair station experience (§119.67(c)(4)(ii)) as an alternative is positive, but the rule fails to specify required certifications/ratings of the repair station and the nature of tasks that qualify as comparable experience.

[P40] The Chief Inspector A&P and three-year rating holding requirement (§119.67(d)(1)) is reasonable, but the three-year maintenance experience on different large types (§119.67(d)(2)) is onerous and will be hard to satisfy for operators of a single type.

[P41] Requiring one year supervisory maintenance experience in the same category for Chief Inspector (§119.67(d)(3)) may force hiring of additional senior personnel rather than allowing internal promotion, increasing costs for small carriers.

[P42] The deviation process in §119.67(e) that allows hiring persons who lack specified experience is positive, but the rule gives too much discretion to FAA managers without publishing objective criteria for “comparable experience.”

[P43] Granting deviations based on “size and scope” and intended qualifications (§119.67(e)) is sensible, but the lack of a defined appeals process or timeline for decisions risks arbitrary denials and operational disruption.

[P44] The FAA’s unilateral authority to terminate any deviation at any time (§119.67(e) termination) is too broad and could destabilize operations; the rule should require notice periods and opportunity to cure before termination.

[P45] The general obligation under part 125 (§125.23 intro) to follow the part’s requirements is fine, but the rule does not include grandfathering for existing private carriage operators currently operating larger aircraft without part 125 compliance.

[P46] Requiring operators to follow the most stringent requirement when subparts conflict (§136.1(a)) is appropriate for safety but may lead to overlapping compliance costs; the FAA should publish a deconfliction guidance matrix.

[P47] Allowing §119.51 procedures to amend LOAs (§136.3) is helpful, but the timeline and criteria for those amendments are not provided, which may delay operators’ needed changes for safety and scheduling.

[P48] Requiring operators meeting §136.71 criteria to comply with subpart D (§136.5) without a phased implementation schedule will impose immediate operational and financial burdens on air tour operators.

[P49] The life preserver exceptions in §136.9(b) are reasonable in limited circumstances but the phrase “power-off gliding distance” (§136.9(b)(2)) needs a specific definition or method of calculation to ensure consistent compliance.

[P50] The multiengine single‑engine climb-performance exception (§136.9(b)(3)) relies on AFM data but does not require periodic verification or logging of that performance capability under actual operating weights and environmental conditions.

[P51] Requiring floats or adequate inflatable flotation for rotorcraft over water beyond shoreline (§136.11(a)) is safety‑enhancing, but the standard for “adequate” inflatable systems and acceptable certification levels is not defined.

[P52] The requirement that the activation switch for flotation be on a primary flight control (§136.11(b)(1)) may be incompatible with some existing rotorcraft cockpit designs; retrofit timelines and acceptability of equivalent switch locations should be addressed.

[P53] Mandating that flotation systems be armed when over water and below AFM‑prescribed speeds (§136.11(b)(2)) is sensible but may conflict with operations that require different speed regimes; the rule should allow an operational risk assessment alternative.

[P54] The exceptions to flotation equipment when over water only during takeoff/landing or within gliding distance if occupants wear life preservers (§136.11(c)) are fine but enforcing continuous wear of life preservers from before takeoff (§136.11(c)(2)) will be difficult and burdensome to police.

[P55] The requirement to complete a rotorcraft performance plan before each flight (§136.13(a)) is appropriate, but the rule should specify recordkeeping duration, standard format, and audit procedures to ensure consistent implementation.

[P56] Requiring the PIC to review and comply with the performance plan on the day of flight (§136.13(a) PIC review) is good practice but the rule should allow for a signed electronic acknowledgment and define who is responsible for ensuring the plan’s currency.

[P57] The detailed performance plan content requirements (§136.13(a)(1)-(3)) are technically sound, but small operators need model templates and training to reasonably comply without incurring large administrative burdens.

[P58] Mandating operation outside the caution/warning areas of the height/velocity diagram (§136.13(b)) may be infeasible in certain confined area tours (canyon flights); the FAA should permit risk-assessed exceptions with documented mitigations.

[P59] Requiring PIC compliance with the plan except when necessary for safety (§136.13(c)) gives appropriate discretion, but the rule should require post-flight reporting when deviations occur for transparency and safety analysis.

[P60] The subpart D exception for part 121 with >30 seats or >7,500 lb payload (§136.71(b)(1)) is appropriate, but it underscores the need to harmonize numeric thresholds across the rule to avoid contradictory applicability determinations.

[P61] The exclusion of gliders and hot-air balloons from subpart applicability (§136.71(b)(2)) removes oversight for certain sightseeing operations; the FAA should require minimal safety standards and reporting for those operations.

[P62] The absolute prohibition on rotorcraft air tours beyond island shores in Hawaii (§136.75(a)) unless flotation or life preservers are provided may overly restrict beneficial tourism operations where risk is managed through other mitigations (e.g., route planning, rescue capability).

[P63] Requiring either amphibious/float-equipped rotorcraft with accessible flotation gear (§136.75(a)(1)) or that all occupants wear approved flotation gear (§136.75(a)(2)) is prudent, but the rule should clarify acceptable “approved” flotation gear standards and inspection intervals.

[P64] The preflight performance plan obligation for Hawaii rotorcraft air tours (§136.75(b)) duplicates §136.13 requirements — the FAA should harmonize the two and avoid redundant documentation.

[P65] The PIC compliance mandate with the performance plan for Hawaii air tours (§136.75(b)(2)) should allow for operational exigencies with a post-flight exception reporting requirement to collect safety data.

[P66] The height/velocity envelope operating limitation (§136.75(c)) is safety-focused, but enforcing compliance will require GPS/flight-data monitoring or mandatory pilot logs, which the rule does not require or fund.

[P67] The minimum altitude and distance prohibitions for Hawaii air tours (§136.75(d), (d)(1)-(2)) (1,500 feet above surface and 1,500 feet from persons/property) are stricter than many local practices; FAA should provide a process for route-specific waivers based on noise and safety studies.

[P68] Prohibiting flights below any federal statutory/regulatory altitude unless authorized (§136.75(d)(3)) is reasonable, but the rule should provide clear guidance on the application process and criteria for Administrator authorizations.

[P69] Requiring enhanced passenger briefings for Hawaii flights beyond shore (§136.75(e)-(e)(3)) is sensible, but the rule should standardize briefing language and permit prerecorded briefings supplemented by PIC confirmation to reduce variability.

[P70] The water-ditching, flotation use, and emergency egress briefing requirements (§136.75(e)(1)-(3)) impose additional preflight time and could lengthen boarding; the FAA should allow combined briefings with written materials or electronic acknowledgments.

[P71] Overall, the proposed rule contains numerous overlapping numeric thresholds (30 seats, 7,500 lb, 6,000 lb, 25 miles, 1,500 feet) that are inconsistent across sections; the FAA must harmonize thresholds and provide a single applicability chart to reduce ambiguity.

[P72] The rule frequently delegates broad discretion to FAA managers for deviations and approvals (§§91.146,119.67(e),119.5), but does not provide transparent criteria, timelines, or an appeal process, raising due process and regulatory predictability concerns.

[P73] Small businesses and community air tour operators will bear significant compliance costs (management, maintenance, performance planning, flotation equipment, training) that are not analyzed in the rulemaking economic impact statement; FAA should publish a quantified cost–benefit analysis and consider phased implementation.

[P74] Several provisions rely on Aircraft Flight Manual (AFM) data for performance determinations (§136.13,136.75), but many older airframes or supplemental type-certificated configurations lack AFM data for specific operations; the FAA should allow approved equivalent data and clear validation procedures.

[P75] The rule should include transitional grandfathering provisions for ongoing operations and set reasonable compliance timelines (12–24 months) for equipment retrofits (flotation systems, activation switches) and personnel qualification changes.

[P76] The FAA should require operators relying on exceptions (e.g., §91.146(b), §119.1(e) categories) to submit annual safety reports and make certain compliance documents available for inspection to prevent misuse of exceptions.

[P77] Legal commenters will note potential preemption and conflict issues between part 91 exceptions (§91.146) and part 119 applicability (§119.1), recommending the FAA include a cross-reference table and legal rationale for overlaps and prioritization.

[P78] Privacy and commercial confidentiality concerns arise if operations specifications must include authorized deviations/exemptions (§119.49 series); the FAA should allow redaction of proprietary business information while ensuring inspector access.

[P79] The rule should clarify record retention periods for performance plans, passenger briefings, deviation approvals, and proof of pro rata reimbursements (§91.146(b)(5), §136.13, §136.75) to enable audits and enforcement.

[P80] Air tour passenger safety advocates will request mandatory passenger seat restraints/armrests and life preserver stowage location standards tailored to sightseeing operations, which the proposed rule does not address.

Requiring the PIC to review and comply with the performance plan on the day of flight (§136.13(a) PIC review) is good practice but the rule should allow for a signed electronic acknowledgment and define who is responsible for ensuring the plan’s currency.

The detailed performance plan content requirements (§136.13(a)(1)-(3)) are technically sound, but small operators need model templates and training to reasonably comply without incurring large administrative burdens.

Mandating operation outside the caution/warning areas of the height/velocity diagram (§136.13(b)) may be infeasible in certain confined area tours (canyon flights); the FAA should permit risk-assessed exceptions with documented mitigations.

Requiring PIC compliance with the plan except when necessary for safety (§136.13(c)) gives appropriate discretion, but the rule should require post-flight reporting when deviations occur for transparency and safety analysis.

The subpart D exception for part 121 with >30 seats or >7,500 lb payload (§136.71(b)(1)) is appropriate, but it underscores the need to harmonize numeric thresholds across the rule to avoid contradictory applicability determinations.

The exclusion of gliders and hot-air balloons from subpart applicability (§136.71(b)(2)) removes oversight for certain sightseeing operations; the FAA should require minimal safety standards and reporting for those operations.

The absolute prohibition on rotorcraft air tours beyond island shores in Hawaii (§136.75(a)) unless flotation or life preservers are provided may overly restrict beneficial tourism operations where risk is managed through other mitigations (e.g., route planning, rescue capability).

Requiring either amphibious/float-equipped rotorcraft with accessible flotation gear (§136.75(a)(1)) or that all occupants wear approved flotation gear (§136.75(a)(2)) is prudent, but the rule should clarify acceptable “approved” flotation gear standards and inspection intervals.
The preflight performance plan obligation for Hawaii rotorcraft air tours (§136.75(b)) duplicates §136.13 requirements — the FAA should harmonize the two and avoid redundant documentation.

The PIC compliance mandate with the performance plan for Hawaii air tours (§136.75(b)(2)) should allow for operational exigencies with a post-flight exception reporting requirement to collect safety data.

The height/velocity envelope operating limitation (§136.75(c)) is safety-focused, but enforcing compliance will require GPS/flight-data monitoring or mandatory pilot logs, which the rule does not require or fund.

The minimum altitude and distance prohibitions for Hawaii air tours (§136.75(d), (d)(1)-(2)) (1,500 feet above surface and 1,500 feet from persons/property) are stricter than many local practices; FAA should provide a process for route-specific waivers based on noise and safety studies.

Prohibiting flights below any federal statutory/regulatory altitude unless authorized (§136.75(d)(3)) is reasonable, but the rule should provide clear guidance on the application process and criteria for Administrator authorizations.

Requiring enhanced passenger briefings for Hawaii flights beyond shore (§136.75(e)-(e)(3)) is sensible, but the rule should standardize briefing language and permit prerecorded briefings supplemented by PIC confirmation to reduce variability.

The water-ditching, flotation use, and emergency egress briefing requirements (§136.75(e)(1)-(3)) impose additional preflight time and could lengthen boarding; the FAA should allow combined briefings with written materials or electronic acknowledgments.

Overall, the proposed rule contains numerous overlapping numeric thresholds (30 seats, 7,500 lb, 6,000 lb, 25 miles, 1,500 feet) that are inconsistent across sections; the FAA must harmonize thresholds and provide a single applicability chart to reduce ambiguity.

The rule frequently delegates broad discretion to FAA managers for deviations and approvals (§§91.146,119.67(e),119.5), but does not provide transparent criteria, timelines, or an appeal process, raising due process and regulatory predictability concerns.

Small businesses and community air tour operators will bear significant compliance costs (management, maintenance, performance planning, flotation equipment, training) that are not analyzed in the rulemaking economic impact statement; FAA should publish a quantified cost–benefit analysis and consider phased implementation.

Legal commenters will note potential preemption and conflict issues between part 91 exceptions (§91.146) and part 119 applicability (§119.1), recommending the FAA include a cross-reference table and legal rationale for overlaps and prioritization.

The rule should clarify record retention periods for performance plans, passenger briefings, deviation approvals, and proof of pro rata reimbursements (§91.146(b)(5), §136.13, §136.75) to enable audits and enforcement.

Air tour passenger safety advocates will request mandatory passenger seat restraints/armrests and life preserver stowage location standards tailored to sightseeing operations, which the proposed rule does not address.

raw_output:
[P1] The October 4, 2019 deadline for receiving comments is unreasonably short and should be extended to allow broader stakeholder input, particularly from international operators and labor unions.

[P1] The rule’s requirement that the FAA “receive” comments by October 4, 2019 creates confusion about postmark vs. receipt; the FAA should accept comments postmarked by that date or clarify electronic timestamp rules.

[P2] The applicability language in §39.13(c) is too narrow/ambiguous because it references paragraphs (c)(1) and (c)(2) without listing part numbers and serial ranges; commenters request explicit model and serial-number detail to avoid uncertainty.

[P2] The AD should explicitly state whether special configurations, retrofits, and Supplemental Type Certificates (STCs) on listed 757/767 airplanes are included or excluded from applicability.

[P3] The phrase “within the compliance times specified” lacks specificity for some procedures (e.g., immediate vs. within 60 days); the FAA should include maximum allowable delays and clarification for in-service scheduling.

[P4] The 60-day window to perform the paragraph (g)(1) and (g)(2) AFM amendments is impracticable for large operators and maintenance providers; request extension to 180 days or allowance to implement via electronic AFM supplements.

[P5] Requiring amendment of the AFM Certificate Limitations chapter to include Figures 1–3 without specifying formatting and approval process will create administrative burden; request sample redline text and confirmation that a simple insert constitutes compliance.

[P5] The rule does not state whether AFM changes must be FAA-approved as a revision or may be operator-initiated via master minimum equipment list (MMEL)-type replacement; request clarification of approval pathway.

[P6] The requirement to revise the Operating Procedures chapter to include Figures 4–7 should permit incorporation by reference or temporary flight manual (TFM) placards; operators request acceptance of electronic quick-reference handouts as compliant.

[P7] The Figure 4 procedural steps to address excessive flight deck temperature do not account for single-pilot operations or reduced crew scenarios; request clarification that procedures are safe and practicable in all authorized crew compositions.

[P8] Mandating Trim Air Switch to OFF in Figure 4 could, in some configurations, cause unexpected thermal effects in passenger compartments; request validation data or an allowance for operator-specific deviation following testing.

[P9] The condition in Figure 4 requiring Pack Control Selectors to STBY-N if outlet air remains hot after one minute does not define “excessively hot” or provide temperature thresholds; request numeric temperature limits to guide crew action and reduce subjectivity.

[P10] The step to set the left pack control selector OFF after one minute (Figure 4) may create asymmetric pack operation and unexpected pressurization/temperature consequences; ask for flight test data demonstrating safety of single-pack shutdown under all load/altitude regimes.

[P11] The repeated step to set left pack control selector to AUTO (Figure 4) immediately after OFF is ambiguous and potentially contradictory; request editorial clarification of sequencing and timing.

[P12] The command to set the right pack control selector to OFF (Figure 4) could lead to total loss of conditioned air; ask the FAA to require guidance on how to sustain essential environmental controls for crew and avionics during this step.

[P13] The mandatory descent to 10,000 ft or minimum safe altitude within the procedure is operationally disruptive for long overwater or remote flights; request an alternative allowing diversion to nearest suitable airport when descent to 10,000 ft is impracticable.

[P14] Requiring both utility bus switches OFF to reduce heat sources may isolate critical systems (e.g., communications, navigation); operators request a list of specific systems that can be shed safely and guidance to prevent inadvertent loss of required instrumentation.

[P15] Mandating turning off all shoulder and foot heaters could affect passenger comfort and safety in cold conditions; request an exception for flights where external temperatures require heater operation to prevent frost, with appropriate monitoring.

[P16] The level-off airspeed requirement of “290 knots or greater” (Figure 4) is incompatible with airspace speed limits (e.g., below 10,000 ft or terminal area speed restrictions) and the 767 Freighter references a different speed; request reconciliation with FAA airspace speed limitations and clarification when this speed is permissible.

[P17] Requiring oxygen masks/regulators ON at 100% above 10,000 ft is inconsistent with standard operating practice thresholds (usually above 14,000 ft for crew); ask for justification and physiological evidence or request raising the threshold consistent with existing regulations.

[P18] The requirement to “Establish” crew communications is vague—does it mean interphone only, or include PA to cabin crew? Request explicit definition to ensure compliance and crew coordination.

[P19] The duplicate instruction to set left pack control selector OFF (Figure 4 and elsewhere) creates redundancy and potential confusion during an emergency checklist; recommend consolidating and clarifying the single required action and its intent.

[P20] The obligation to “manually depressurize and open the outflow valve” may conflict with structural/cabin safety in some flight regimes and with pressurization SOPs; request risk assessment and criteria for when manual depressurization is safe (e.g., overwater, passenger oxygen availability).

[P21] The 757 Passenger (Figure 5) procedures mirror the 767 freighter instructions but do not account for differences in avionics, pack layouts, or crew procedures between passenger and freighter; request airplane-specific validation data and allow for operator-specific minor adaptations proven by test.

[P22] The Figure 5 command to set Trim Air Switch OFF may degrade temperature control in occupied zones and create passenger discomfort or safety issues on long flights; request evidence that this step does not impair critical systems.

[P23] The Figure 5 condition that would set Trim Air to ON after one minute if outlet air remains hot is contradictory to the initial OFF step; request clarification of trigger conditions and timing for toggling between OFF and ON.

[P24] The mandated use of Pack Control Selectors STBY-N (Figure 5) may not be available on all STC-modified aircraft or different avionics versions; request allowance to achieve equivalent functionality via alternate controls and acceptance of AMOCs.

[P25] Switching left pack control selector OFF (Figure 5) without specifying minimum run times or cool-down durations risks cycling damage to the pack; request maintenance/operational guidance and limitations to prevent equipment harm.

[P26] Subsequent return of left pack control selector to AUTO (Figure 5) after OFF lacks timing guidance; request precise timing and temperature criteria for reversion to AUTO to prevent oscillatory control.

[P27] Turning right pack control selector OFF (Figure 5) could result in insufficient airflow to cabin or avionics cooling; ask for required monitoring and minimum safe time limits before landing or diversion once a pack is off.

[P28] The descent-to-10,000-ft requirement for Figure 5 again fails to consider remote oceanic segments and ETOPS operations; request specific provisions for ETOPS/remote operations and alternative mitigations to descent.

[P29] Turning off utility bus switches and all heaters (Figure 5) may disconnect emergency equipment (e.g., cargo fire detection/ suppression, lighting); request a prohibited-systems list or an alternate configuration that maintains fire/safety systems while reducing heat loads.

[P30] The consistent airspeed of 290 knots at level-off in Figure 5 conflicts with minimum maneuvering speeds in turbulence and with noise abatement procedures; request performance-based flexibility or lower-speed alternatives.

[P31] The combined actions required when level-off is above 10,000 ft (oxygen ON 100%, crew communications, left pack off, depressurize) create heavy simultaneous workload; recommend sequencing guidance and human factors assessment to ensure crews can complete steps safely.

[P32] The 767 Freighter procedure (Figure 6) assumes a main deck cargo environment without specifying cargo fire or hazardous materials considerations; request integration guidance with cargo fire response procedures and notification to loadmasters.

[P33] Setting Trim Air OFF (Figure 6) on 767 Freighters may not be feasible with certain freight container arrangements that depend on trim air for temperature-sensitive cargo; request an exception or cargo-specific guidance.

[P34] The step in Figure 6 that sets Trim Air ON and pack selectors to STBY-N after one minute is inconsistent with other steps that initially set Trim Air OFF; ask for explanation of rationale and clear decision criteria for switching states.

[P35] The sequence in Figure 6 that toggles left pack OFF then AUTO, and right pack OFF, contains conflicting timing; request a clarified, unambiguous sequential checklist with allowed time windows between actions.

[P36] The descent requirement to 10,000 ft (Figure 6) again poses operational problems for heavy freighters on oceanic legs; ask for ETOPS-compliant alternatives and the ability to use nearest diversion airport rather than strict altitude descent.

[P37] Turning off utility bus switches and all shoulder/foot heaters on a freighter (Figure 6) may disable pallet/consignment monitoring or special systems; request a list of non-sheddable systems and allowance for operator risk-assessed exceptions.

[P38] The Figure 6 instruction to “maintain airspeed of 290 knots or less” is different from the “290 knots or greater” requirement for other models; this inconsistency will confuse crews — request harmonization and justification for different speed prescriptions.

[P39] Requiring oxygen masks ON 100% and manual depressurization/open outflow valve at level-off above 10,000 ft (Figure 6) could endanger occupants or cause physiological issues; request medical justification and alternative thresholds consistent with oxygen system limitations.

[P40] While delegation to the Manager, Seattle ACO for AMOC approvals is helpful, stakeholders request clearer SLA timelines for AMOC adjudication (e.g., 60/90/120 days) to allow business planning.

[P41] The requirement to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 may be burdensome for multi-base carriers; request allowance for centralized submission via the certificate holder’s principal operations inspector and electronic tracking.

[P42] The requirement to address direct AMOC submissions to the person in paragraph (i) should name that person in the AD text to avoid routing delays; commenters request insertion of the contact name and office address in the rule.

[P43] The allowance to email AMOC requests to 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is useful but should be supplemented with a secure file-transfer option for large technical packages; request explicit acceptance of SFTP or other secure portals.

[P44] The requirement to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC creates potential delays in emergency use; request an exemption for immediate safety-of-flight AMOCs allowing retrospective notice within a specified short timeframe (e.g., 24–72 hours).

[P45] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs for repairs/modifications is reasonable, but the AD must require documentation of ODA approvals to be provided to the FAA and operators to ensure transparency; request mandatory filing of ODA AMOC approvals in AD compliance records.

[P46] The obligation that AMOC repairs meet the airplane’s certification basis and specifically reference this AD could be interpreted narrowly and block innovative fixes; recommend the FAA adopt a performance-based acceptance criteria and provide examples of acceptable certification-basis demonstrations.

[P1] The requirement that the listed regulatory provisions take effect immediately upon promulgation (§ 141.6(c)) is arbitrary and violates the Administrative Procedure Act because affected systems were not given a reasonable transition period to comply.

[P1] Immediate effectiveness of §§ 141.11(d); 141.21(a),(c),(i); 141.22(a),(e); 141.23(a)(3),(a)(4), (f); 141.24(e),(f); 141.25(e) will impose substantial unplanned administrative costs on small systems and should be delayed at least 12–24 months.

[P2] Setting the arsenic MCL effective three years after publication (§ 141.6(j) / § 141.62) is insufficient; commenters request a five-year implementation period to allow capital planning, financing, and construction of treatment facilities.

[P2] Conversely, public health advocacy groups may comment that a three-year delay for the arsenic MCL (§ 141.6(j)) is too long and urges an effective date within 12–18 months to protect vulnerable populations.

[P3] The staged compliance deadline that requires community water systems serving ≤10,000 to comply by 5 years after publication (§ 141.6(j)) is inconsistent with § 141.6(j) elsewhere and needs clarification about obligations for systems between 10,000 and 50,000 served.

[P3] Requiring smaller community water systems to meet the arsenic MCL by the listed staged dates without explicit funding or technical assistance constitutes unfunded federal mandate and violates the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act.

[P4] The 30-day reporting date for arsenic-related consumer confidence report and § 141.154(b) reporting after final rule publication (§ 141.6(j)) is unworkable because systems will not have finalized laboratory results, and EPA should allow at least 90 days.

[P4] Requiring § 141.154(b) reports only 30 days after publication (§ 141.6(j)) will produce inaccurate public communications; EPA should permit preliminary notice followed by a final CCR update after the first monitoring cycle.

[P5] Applying the sampling, monitoring, and reporting requirements to non-transient non-community systems as of the stated date (§ 141.6(j)) fails to provide for training and laboratory capacity and will likely cause widespread noncompliance.

[P5] The rule should include an explicit provision allowing short-term compliance extensions for non-transient non-community water systems that can demonstrate inability to obtain certified lab analysis in time for the stated date.

[P6] Requiring compliance with §§ 141.23(c)(9), 141.24(f)(15)(ii), 141.24(f)(22) and 141.24(h)(20) by the stated date (§ 141.6(k)) will strain State primacy agencies’ capacity; EPA must provide funding and a timeline for State rule adoption.

[P6] The compliance date structure in § 141.6(k) for monitoring and sampling frequencies lacks uniformity across contaminants and will cause confusion; EPA should harmonize effective dates and publish a compliance calendar.

[P7] Mandating that compliance analyses for the 0.05 mg/L arsenic MCL follow § 141.23(1) (§ 141.11(a)) is ambiguous because § 141.23(1) is not clearly cited; EPA must correct the citation to § 141.23(i) or the precise subsection.

[P7] The analytical and averaging methodologies required by § 141.23 for determining compliance at 0.05 mg/L (§ 141.11(a)) will disadvantage systems using point-of-entry devices unless the rule clarifies how POU/POE sample locations are treated.

[P8] Listing 0.05 mg/L as the MCL for CWS serving ≤10,000 until 5 years after publication (§ 141.11(b)) creates a two-tiered regulatory regime that may underprotect populations relying on smaller systems; EPA should apply the same MCL to all CWS simultaneously.

[P8] The temporary applicability period in § 141.11(b) for small systems is unclear about whether it supersedes state MCLs; EPA should clarify interaction with more stringent State standards.

[P9] Excluding non-transient non-community systems from §§ 141.23(c)(7),(8) and 141.62(b)(16) until the stated date (§ 141.11(b)) will create monitoring loopholes; EPA must justify the exclusion or remove it.

[P9] The differential application of sampling/monitoring provisions to NTNC systems (§ 141.11(b)) may conflict with the Safe Drinking Water Act’s requirements for non-community systems and should be reconsidered.

[P10] The requirement that new systems or systems with a new source show MCL compliance within a State-specified period (§ 141.23(c)(9)) leaves too much discretion to States and may allow inconsistent public health protection; EPA should specify maximum and minimum demonstration periods.

[P10] Allowing States to set the initial compliance demonstration period for new sources (§ 141.23(c)(9)) may lead to delays in detecting arsenic problems; EPA should require demonstration prior to starting service or within 30 days of operation.

[P11] Requiring adherence to State-specified initial sampling frequencies to demonstrate compliance (§ 141.23(c)(9)) is appropriate, but EPA must require States to adopt frequencies at least as stringent as the EPA guidance document to ensure comparability.

[P12] The routine and increased monitoring obligations (§ 141.23(c)(9)) must include explicit provisions for corrective action timelines when monitoring shows exceedances; currently the provision lacks enforceable remediation deadlines.

[P13] Permitting compliance averages to be based on fewer than required samples if some samples are missed (§ 141.23(i)(1)) will allow systems to avoid detection by under-sampling; EPA should require missed-sample substitution or re-sampling to achieve the required n.

[P13] The language in § 141.23(i)(1) should require systems to report missed samples and include those misses in enforcement determinations, rather than allowing average calculation based solely on collected samples.

[P14] Defining systems monitoring annually or less as out of compliance when contaminant levels exceed the MCL (§ 141.23(i)(2)) may be unfair where seasonal variability leads to transient exceedances; EPA should allow targeted follow-up sampling before declaring noncompliance.

raw_output:
[P1] The flat prohibition on any refunds of filing fees (§ 103.2(a)(1)) is arbitrary and unduly burdensome because it provides no relief if USCIS causes excessive delay, loses an application, or commits an adjudicative error that prevents adjudication.

[P1] Non‑refundability regardless of denial (§ 103.2(a)(1)) will discourage low‑income applicants from filing meritorious claims (e.g., asylum, VAWA) and creates a chilling effect that likely conflicts with statutory intents to ensure access to remedies.

[P2] Requiring fees at time of filing (§ 103.2(a)(1)) with no exception for indigent applicants or emergency filings will prevent access to benefits for those unable to pay upfront and conflicts with due process and equal protection principles.

[P2] The obligation to pay at filing (§ 103.2(a)(1)) should allow alternative timing or installment plans for complex filings (e.g., I‑485 family applications) or for applicants served by nonprofits collecting fees on behalf of clients.

[P3] The requirement that benefit requests be submitted with the "correct fee(s)" (§ 103.2(a)(7)(ii)(D)) is insufficiently defined — USCIS must publish a clear crosswalk and guidance for multi‑fee filings to avoid rejections for technical mismatches.

[P4] USCIS's policy to attempt to redeposit a returned payment once (§ 103.2(a)(7)(ii)(D)) is acceptable in principle but needs explicit notice to the payer upon first return and a specific timeframe for when the second attempt will occur.

[P5] Allowing USCIS to reject filings if a payment instrument is returned unpaid a second time (§ 103.2(a)(7)(ii)(D)) is overly punitive; USCIS should be required to provide notice and a cure period before rejection.

[P6] The prohibition on redepositing payments returned for reasons other than insufficient funds (§ 103.2(a)(7)(ii)(D)) is arbitrary — returned items for bank errors or truncated account numbers could be retriable; USCIS should retain discretion to redeposit after reasonable inquiry.

[P7] Permitting USCIS to reject payments and requests if the payment instrument is over one year old (§ 103.2(a)(7)(ii)(D)) unfairly penalizes filers who rely on legacy checks (e.g., remote communities) and should be tied to whether the instrument would still be honored, not solely the date.

[P8] Requiring USCIS to deliver secure ID documents only to the applicant unless they consent (§ 103.2(b)(19)(iii)(A)) may create delays for applicants who cannot be physically present at delivery addresses (e.g., detained persons, employers) — USCIS should allow verified designees without separate consent in documented circumstances.

[P9] Requiring designated agents or attorneys to provide ID and sign upon receipt of secure documents (§ 103.2(b)(19)(iii)(B)) is reasonable for security but needs clarity on acceptable forms of ID, procedures for remote pickup, and what happens if an agent is unavailable.

[P10] Permitting USCIS to accept fees payable to DOJ under certain conditions (§ 103.7(a)(1)) risks confusion and potential misdirection of funds; the rule should require a clear process and reporting reconciliation between DHS and DOJ.

[P11] Allowing payers to pay EOIR‑related fees to USCIS (§ 103.7(a)(1)) without clear mechanisms to ensure the payment results in filing before EOIR creates risk that payers will assume filing occurred when it has not (§ 103.7(a)(1) & (a)(1) condition).

[P12] The express condition that payment to USCIS does not constitute filing with EOIR (§ 103.7(a)(1)) is essential but must be accompanied by mandatory, contemporaneous written notice to the payer clarifying that filing still must be completed with EOIR.

[P13] DHS's obligation to provide receipts and to return any documents submitted with EOIR‑related fee payments (§ 103.7(a)(1)) is appropriate but needs a required timeline (e.g., within 7 business days) and format (electronic + physical) to prevent lost documents.

[P14] Requiring an extra $30 to cover DHS biometric collection and storage for certain EOIR‑related fees (§ 103.7(a)(2)) effectively acts as an add‑on charge and should be justified with a statutory cost analysis and waiver for indigent or vulnerable populations.

[P15] Allowing immigration judges or the Board to waive fees (§ 103.7(a)(3)) is appropriate, but the rule lacks standards for when waivers should be granted and an appeal mechanism if a waiver is denied.

[P16] The cross‑reference requiring payment of USCIS fees as laid out in 8 CFR part 106 (§ 103.7(b)) will cause confusion unless USCIS publishes an integrated, searchable fee table aligning provisions in part 103 and part 106.

[P17] Mandating remittances to the BIA be payable to the "United States Department of Justice" (§ 103.7(c)) is fine but the rule should accommodate electronic ACH/payment portal options to replace outdated paper remittance requirements.

[P18] Requiring DCL participants to pay the DCL system cost fee after approval but before use (§ 103.7(d)(1)(iv)) could delay program participation and should permit a short window post‑activation (e.g., 14 days) to submit the fee.

[P19] The obligation that approved participants pay separate DCL fees for individuals, families, and additional vehicles (§ 103.7(d)(1)) may be administratively burdensome; DHS should allow family consolidated billing and prorated fees for partial year participation.

[P20] Declaring DCL fees generally non‑refundable (§ 103.7(d)(1)(v)) is harsh — DHS should provide refund scenarios (e.g., lane closures, DHS cancellations, program denial after approval) and require DHS to publish refund policy details.

[P21] Permitting DHS to impose fees for biometric collection, background checks, identity verification, and biometric storage (§ 103.17) requires a cost justification and statutory authority citation; stakeholders will request a fee schedule and cost breakdown.

[P22] The obligation that biometric service fee requirements be specified in 8 CFR part 106 (§ 103.17) is appropriate, but USCIS must ensure fee notices are updated in parallel with benefit rule changes so filers are not rejected for outdated fees.

[P23] Allowing USCIS to reject benefit requests lacking required biometric fees (§ 103.17) should be tempered by a cure period or an opportunity to supplement payment within a defined timeframe prior to outright rejection.

[P24] Making genealogy request forms available electronically (§ 103.40(b)(1)) is positive but USCIS must also ensure accommodations (paper requests, assistance) for elderly or rural patrons without internet access.

[P25] Requiring separate genealogy request forms for each individual searched (§ 103.40(c)) imposes duplicative fees and administrative burden on family researchers; USCIS should allow batch or group requests with a single submission fee or discounted rate.

[P26] The requirement to include full name, DOB, and place of birth on genealogy requests (§ 103.40(c)(iii)) is reasonable but should allow alternative identifiers where such data are unknown (e.g., estimated birth years) and provide guidance on acceptable approximations.

[P27] Permitting optional additional information to improve search success (§ 103.40(d)) is sensible; commenters will request explicit examples and encouragement for submitters to provide alternate name spellings and travel dates.

[P28] Requiring requestors to identify records by certificate/A‑file/visa/registry numbers when requesting copies (§ 103.40(d)(i)-(C)) is necessary, but USCIS should accept sworn statements attesting inability to obtain those numbers and proceed with reasonable searches.

[P29] The obligation that requestors attach documentary evidence per instructions when requesting genealogy records (§ 103.40(e)(1)) should include a safe harbor for filings where records are not in petitioner's possession and permit documented affidavits instead.

[P30] Presuming subjects born over 100 years ago to be deceased (§ 103.40(e)(2)) is a reasonable default, but USCIS must provide an appeal/overturn mechanism for cases where evidence shows the subject might still be living (e.g., unusual longevity, island populations).

[P31] Requiring documentary evidence of death to obtain certain records (§ 103.40(e)(3)) is appropriate for privacy, but DHS must specify acceptable documents and provide alternatives (e.g., death index searches) where official documents are unavailable.

[P32] Allowing index search requests (§ 103.40(f)) is helpful; however, USCIS must commit to standard search scopes and include estimated processing times to set expectations for users.

[P33] Obliging USCIS to notify requestors of search results and provide electronic copies at no extra charge (§ 103.40(f)) is positive; commenters will ask for a guaranteed timeframe and an option for certified paper copies for legal use.

[P34] The broad requirement to submit fees with benefit requests in prescribed amount and manner (§ 106.1(a)) must be coordinated with fee exemptions and waivers — commenters will ask for clearer cross‑references to fee exceptions to avoid wrongful rejections.

USCIS's policy to attempt to redeposit a returned payment once (§ 103.2(a)(7)(ii)(D)) is acceptable in principle but needs explicit notice to the payer upon first return and a specific timeframe for when the second attempt will occur.

Allowing USCIS to reject filings if a payment instrument is returned unpaid a second time (§ 103.2(a)(7)(ii)(D)) is overly punitive; USCIS should be required to provide notice and a cure period before rejection.

The prohibition on redepositing payments returned for reasons other than insufficient funds (§ 103.2(a)(7)(ii)(D)) is arbitrary — returned items for bank errors or truncated account numbers could be retriable; USCIS should retain discretion to redeposit after reasonable inquiry.

Permitting USCIS to reject payments and requests if the payment instrument is over one year old (§ 103.2(a)(7)(ii)(D)) unfairly penalizes filers who rely on legacy checks (e.g., remote communities) and should be tied to whether the instrument would still be honored, not solely the date.

Requiring USCIS to deliver secure ID documents only to the applicant unless they consent (§ 103.2(b)(19)(iii)(A)) may create delays for applicants who cannot be physically present at delivery addresses (e.g., detained persons, employers) — USCIS should allow verified designees without separate consent in documented circumstances.

Requiring designated agents or attorneys to provide ID and sign upon receipt of secure documents (§ 103.2(b)(19)(iii)(B)) is reasonable for security but needs clarity on acceptable forms of ID, procedures for remote pickup, and what happens if an agent is unavailable.

Permitting USCIS to accept fees payable to DOJ under certain conditions (§ 103.7(a)(1)) risks confusion and potential misdirection of funds; the rule should require a clear process and reporting reconciliation between DHS and DOJ.

Allowing payers to pay EOIR‑related fees to USCIS (§ 103.7(a)(1)) without clear mechanisms to ensure the payment results in filing before EOIR creates risk that payers will assume filing occurred when it has not (§ 103.7(a)(1) & (a)(1) condition).

The express condition that payment to USCIS does not constitute filing with EOIR (§ 103.7(a)(1)) is essential but must be accompanied by mandatory, contemporaneous written notice to the payer clarifying that filing still must be completed with EOIR.

DHS's obligation to provide receipts and to return any documents submitted with EOIR‑related fee payments (§ 103.7(a)(1)) is appropriate but needs a required timeline (e.g., within 7 business days) and format (electronic + physical) to prevent lost documents.

Requiring an extra $30 to cover DHS biometric collection and storage for certain EOIR‑related fees (§ 103.7(a)(2)) effectively acts as an add‑on charge and should be justified with a statutory cost analysis and waiver for indigent or vulnerable populations.

raw_output:
[P1] The electronic-only submission requirement for certifications as of Dec 21, 2023 (§122.26(b)(15)(i)(C)) will impose undue hardship on small operators lacking internet access or adequate IT systems and should include an alternative paper-filing exception for demonstrated hardship.

[P2] The provision allowing permits or state law to require electronic reporting before the federal deadline (§122.26(b)(15)(i)(C) condition) creates legal uncertainty for permittees because it permits disparate earlier state deadlines without national coordination.

[P3] Requiring a signed certification to be submitted every five years to the NPDES permitting authority (§122.26(g)(1)(iii)) is too infrequent for fast-changing compliance conditions; EPA should consider a shorter interval or trigger-based re-certification.

[P4] The duplicate language that both requires five‑year signed certifications (§122.26(g)(1)(iii)) and simultaneously mandates electronic submission by Dec 21, 2023 could cause confusion where a physical signature is required but only electronic methods are accepted; guidance on acceptable electronic signature methods is needed.

[P5] The allowance that permits or state laws may require electronic reporting before the federal deadline (§122.26(g)(1)(iii) condition) could create conflicts with state privacy or data-protection laws; EPA should require coordination and preemption analysis.

[P6] The requirement that dischargers seeking general permit coverage must submit a Notice of Intent to the Director (§122.28(b)(2)(i)) without explicit provision for small operators to receive technical assistance will impede timely compliance and should be paired with outreach support.

[P7] The prohibition that a discharger failing to submit the required NOI is not authorized to discharge under the general permit (§122.28(b)(2)(i) prohibition) is harsh for inadvertent or clerical failures; EPA should include a short cure period or administrative relief process.

[P8] Requiring NOIs to be submitted electronically by Dec 21, 2023 (§122.28(b)(2)(i) electronic obligation) will disproportionately affect multi-site operators who manage many NOIs at once unless batch-upload and API capabilities are mandated.

[P9] The condition allowing states or permits to require electronic NOI submission prior to the federal deadline (§122.28(b)(2)(i) condition) could result in inconsistent compliance timelines across states that undermine national permit standardization.

[P10] The annual report obligation for first permit term permittees (§122.34(d)(3)) should explicitly clarify the start date and reporting period for new permits to avoid ambiguity about the "first permit term" reporting requirement.

[P11] The requirement to submit reports in years two and four in subsequent permit terms (§122.34(d)(3)) may not align with permit terms shorter than four years; EPA should clarify applicability for permits with non-standard term lengths.

[P12] Mandating electronic submission of §122.34(d)(3) reports as of Dec 21, 2023 (§122.34(d)(3) electronic) fails to account for small MS4s with limited IT budgets; EPA should allow deferrals or phased implementation for small jurisdictions.

[P13] Allowing permit or state law to require electronic reporting before the federal deadline for small MS4s (§122.34(d)(3) condition) risks creating inequitable burdens for municipalities depending on state approaches.

[P14] The obligation that required reports include multiple specified elements (§122.34(d)(3) content) must be accompanied by standardized templates and machine-readable formats to avoid variable interpretations and burdensome bespoke submissions.

[P74] Mandating that authorized programs share facility NAICS codes with EPA when approving permit coverage after June 12, 2021 (Appendix A Table 2 No. 3) implicates confidentiality and competitive harm for some facilities; allow protections or CBI redaction.

[P75] Requiring the NAICS primary indicator to be shared when approving permit coverage after June 12, 2021 (Appendix A Table 2 No. 3) could force facilities to publicly reveal proprietary primary-business determinations; provide guidance and CBI protections.

[P76] Allowing authorized programs to use the Waterbody Name data element to identify receiving waterbody or intake source (Appendix A Table 2 Permitted Feature Info permission) is useful, but EPA must standardize naming conventions (e.g., GNIS identifiers) to avoid inconsistent entries.
