raw_output:
[P1] The requirement that ASCs and their agents maintain a QualityNet account to submit web-based quality data is burdensome for small ASCs that lack IT staff and should be modified to allow alternative secure submission methods (e.g., secure FTP or HL7 interfaces).

[P1] Requiring agents of ASCs to maintain a QualityNet account creates liability and access-control issues when third-party vendors submit data on behalf of multiple ASCs; the rule should require role-based segregation and limits on cross-ASC data access.

[P2] Mandating that a QualityNet security administrator set up the account imposes an additional administrative burden and single point of failure for small facilities; CMS should permit delegated setup by an ASC executive or third-party vendor under documented authorization.

[P2] The rule is vague about qualifications, responsibilities, and background-check requirements for a QualityNet security administrator; commenters request CMS to specify minimum training, identity verification, and change-management procedures.

[P3] The provision allowing CMS to grant exceptions for extraordinary circumstances is too discretionary without defined criteria; stakeholders request CMS to publish the factors it will consider and an appeals process for denied exceptions.

[P4] The requirement that ASCs must follow QualityNet website procedures to request exceptions could be problematic when the website is inaccessible during the same extraordinary event; commenters request alternative submission channels (email, fax, phone) and retroactive submission allowances.

[P5] CMS reserving the right to grant exceptions without an ASC request raises due-process concerns; ASCs want notice and an opportunity to opt in or opt out of an automatically granted exception before it is applied to their reporting obligations.

[P6] The CY2018 multiproductivity and 0.75 percentage point adjustment is not adequately justified in the preamble; hospitals and industry groups will challenge the methodology and request CMS provide the underlying data and economic model used to set the multiproductivity factor.

[P6] Small and rural hospitals will be disproportionately affected by the multiproductivity and 0.75% reduction and request a rural adjustment or phase-in to avoid financial harm.

[P7] Requiring hospitals to complete and submit the online participation form in the specified circumstances without a paper alternative discriminates against facilities with limited internet access; CMS should provide hard-copy or assisted-submission options.

[P8] The condition that hospitals must submit the form if it has not previously been completed lacks guidance on how CMS will determine prior completion and what documentation hospitals must provide if records are lost; request clarification and a grace period.

[P9] Hospitals that previously withdrew from the program may have legitimate reasons for previous withdrawal (e.g., mergers); forcing re-enrollment without considering prior context could create administrative confusion—request exception pathways for merged or consolidated hospitals.

[P10] The requirement to submit the form when a hospital acquires a new CCN does not address complex ownership/management structures where a CCN transfer occurs mid-year; request transitional provisions to avoid duplicate reporting or gaps.

[P11] Requiring hospitals that share a CCN to complete one joint online participation form may be infeasible where multiple legal entities operate under a shared CCN; request that CMS allow separate attestations tied to individual operating entities while recognizing the shared CCN.

[P12] The obligation to submit the participation form before registering on QualityNet is an unnecessary sequencing restriction; hospitals should be allowed to register and then complete the form to streamline onboarding.

[P13] Requiring previously non-participating hospitals to begin submitting data starting with encounters in the first calendar quarter of the prior year is retroactive and administratively infeasible; request that CMS allow prospective submission starting the date of enrollment or provide a limited retrospective window with clear instructions.

[P14] Tying non-participating hospitals to data submission deadlines in paragraph (c)(2) without allowing a phased reporting schedule will overwhelm hospital staff; ask for a phased approach and clear calendar with reminders.

[P15] The exception authority for data submission deadlines is insufficiently transparent — CMS should define what constitutes “extraordinary circumstances,” provide examples (natural disaster, widespread cyberattack), and publish an expedited exception review timeline.

[P16] Requiring hospitals to follow QualityNet website submission procedures for exception requests disadvantages hospitals in the same events that cause the exception (e.g., network outages); request alternative submission mechanisms and retroactive exception filing.

[P17] CMS’s discretion to grant exceptions without hospital requests could create unequal treatment; request CMS to publish a list of affected hospitals when it grants such exceptions and allow an appeals process.

[P18] Selecting 450 hospitals at random plus 50 targeted hospitals for validation (total 500) will impose an unpredictable administrative burden; hospitals request advance notice of selection criteria, validation timelines, and an opportunity to prepare documentation.

[P19] Using failure of the prior year’s validation as a sole criterion for additional selection risks repeat punishment for hospitals that corrected past issues; request that CMS consider remediation actions and time since remediation before reselecting.

[P20] Selecting hospitals for validation if a measure value is >5 standard deviations from the mean is arbitrary and may capture legitimate outliers (specialized centers); request CMS to allow facilities to provide clinical justification and adjust thresholds to a more standard 3–4 SD or use robust outlier detection methods.

[P21] The 20% payment reduction for film X-ray services furnished in 2017 or later is arbitrary and creates sudden revenue loss for facilities that still rely on film due to clinical or regulatory constraints; request a longer phase-in, hardship exemptions, or funding support to transition to digital systems.

[P22] Payment reductions for computed radiography services by specified percentages fail to account for providers in rural or resource-poor settings who may not be able to upgrade immediately; request exemptions for facilities demonstrating financial hardship or certified replacement plans.

[P23] The 7% reduction for computed radiography X-ray services in CY2018–2022 lacks a cost-analysis justification; commenters demand CMS provide the cost-savings calculations and evidence supporting the specific percentage.

[P24] Increasing the computed radiography reduction to 10% in CY2023 and beyond will create planning uncertainty; request a re-evaluation mechanism tied to market adoption rates of digital radiography and periodic review of the percentage.

[P25] Requiring ASCs and agents to maintain QualityNet accounts may expose PHI to increased cybersecurity risk if CMS’s QualityNet platform is not certified to the latest standards; request CMS to publish security certifications, encryption standards, and incident response expectations.

[P26] The requirement that an ASC (or agent) establish a QualityNet security administrator should include clear procedures for administrator changes, emergency delegation, and multi-factor authentication; otherwise, ASCs risk being locked out and unable to meet reporting deadlines.

[P27] The exception authority in §416.310(d) references “extraordinary circumstances beyond the control of the hospital” but the provision applies to ASCs in other parts of the rule; request clarification whether the same exception standard applies to ASCs and hospitals and consistent terminology.

[P28] Allowing ASCs to request exceptions via QualityNet website procedures without alternative means is problematic during the same extraordinary event; request that CMS accept exception requests by direct email or phone with subsequent portal confirmation.

[P29] CMS granting exceptions to ASCs without a request could inadvertently waive reporting obligations and affect quality measurement comparability; stakeholders ask CMS to describe how it will document and publicize such discretionary exceptions to preserve transparency.

[P30] The requirement for hospitals to complete the online participation form when they haven’t previously completed it could be redundant for hospitals that already submit equivalent attestations elsewhere; request CMS allow cross-recognition of existing attestations to reduce duplicate reporting.

[P31] Hospitals that claim they never completed the form but CMS records indicate otherwise should have an expedited dispute-resolution process; request a mechanism for reconciling administrative record errors.

[P32] Hospitals that previously withdrew may have done so because of prior penalties or disputes; forcing automatic re-enrollment without considering those circumstances could reopen unresolved administrative claims — request CMS to coordinate re-enrollment with resolution of prior issues.

[P33] For hospitals acquiring a new CCN, the rule does not specify timing relative to payment determinations; request CMS define effective dates for reporting obligations tied to CCN change dates.

[P34] Requiring submission of the participation form before QualityNet registration could delay hospitals’ ability to set up users and testing; request CMS permit provisional registration to allow technical validation before final submission.

[P35] Requiring a single form for hospitals sharing a CCN may obscure variation in measure reporting across distinct hospital campuses; request guidance on how composite responses will be handled and how liability/penalties are assigned among participants.

[P36] The obligation that previously non-participating hospitals must submit initial data and adhere to deadlines should include technical assistance resources and a contact at CMS to reduce noncompliance caused by lack of guidance.

[P37] Requiring initial data starting with encounters from the first calendar quarter of the prior year could create retroactive compliance obligations that are impossible to meet; request CMS allow hospitals to submit from the quarter after they are notified of their obligation.

[P38] The requirement that nonparticipating hospitals follow submission deadlines in paragraph (c)(2) should be accompanied by a published, machine-readable calendar and automated reminders to help compliance.

[P39] The exception authority for hospitals lacks a requirement for CMS to provide written reasoned explanations when denying exception requests; request mandatory written determinations including factual basis and appeal rights.

[P40] The requirement that hospitals must follow QualityNet website submission requirements to request exceptions is impractical in disaster scenarios; request CMS to create a dedicated exception hotline and coordination with FEMA/state emergency officials.

[P41] CMS’s discretionary authority to grant exceptions without requests should be subject to oversight and reporting — request CMS publish a quarterly report listing all blanket or unilateral exceptions granted, the rationale, and list of affected providers.

[P42] Selecting 450 random hospitals plus 50 targeted for validation may produce biased samples if not stratified by hospital size, type, and region; request CMS stratify the random sample to ensure representative coverage and avoid overburdening particular hospital categories.

[P43] Using prior validation failure as a criterion for additional selection may unfairly penalize hospitals that had legitimate data issues resolved; request CMS set a time limit (e.g., only hospitals that failed in the prior 2 years) and allow demonstration of corrective action.

[P44] The >5 standard deviation threshold for outlier selection is opaque — commenters request CMS to publish the statistical methodology, whether measures are normalized, and whether adjustments are made for small-volume hospitals.

[P45] The 20% payment reduction for film X-ray services may contravene statutory limits or required notice periods for payment policy changes; legal commenters will request CMS to cite the statutory authority and compliance with notice-and-comment and anti-backsliding rules.

[P46] The phased percentage reductions for computed radiography do not account for hybrid services where computed radiography is part of a package; request clarity on how packaged services will be priced and whether reductions apply to entire bundled payments.

[P47] The 7% reduction for CY2018–2022 will require systems updates to billing and claims-processing systems; providers request a timeline and technical specifications for claim edits and system testing windows.

[P48] Increasing to 10% in CY2023+ demands advance notice well before CY2023 to allow capital planning; request CMS commit to publishing reaffirmation or modification of the percentage no later than one year before implementation.

[P49] Declaring that these payment reductions are not adjustments under section 1833(t)(2)(E) and are not budget-neutral raises legal and budgetary concerns; commenters ask CMS to explain the statutory interpretation and how this interacts with other Medicare payment-setting rules, and to provide a legal memorandum supporting the treatment.

raw_output:
[P1] Industry commenter: The proposed § 216.23(a) list is too narrow and omits several bulk drug substances routinely relied upon by 503A compounding pharmacists for patient-specific therapy; FDA should add a mechanism to request expedited additions to the list for substances with urgent clinical need.

[P1] Legal expert: The rule does not specify whether inclusion on § 216.23(a) creates any safe-harbor for interstate distribution limits under 503A; we request clarification that listing does not change statutory limits on distribution or create implicit approval.

[P1] Patient advocacy group: Inclusion of substances on § 216.23(a) without explicit indications or dosing guidance could lead to inconsistent compounding practices; FDA should require recommended uses, concentrations, and compounding conditions be published alongside the list.

[P1] State pharmacy board: The rule should clarify whether state-licensed pharmacists compounding with listed bulk drug substances remain subject to state formularies and recordkeeping requirements, to avoid regulatory conflict.

[P2] Dermatology society: Permitting Brilliant Blue G (Coomassie Brilliant Blue G–250) for compounding raises concerns because its dermatologic safety profile is not well established; FDA should require safety data or restrict use to investigational or limited clinical settings.

[P2] Industry/regulatory affairs: Brilliant Blue G is primarily used as a laboratory stain, not a therapeutic agent; FDA should explain the clinical use cases justifying its inclusion and provide sourcing and purity specifications to prevent misuse of laboratory-grade material in patients.

[P2] Toxicologist: Brilliant Blue G has potential systemic toxicity if used on compromised skin; the rule should limit its use to topical formulations only (if intended) and set maximum concentrations or require safety testing.

[P3] Pediatric advocacy group: Allowing cantharidin only for topical use is appropriate, but the rule must expressly prohibit pediatric use in children under a specified age or require weight-based dosing guidance to prevent accidental overexposure.

[P3] Immunology clinician: Cantharidin can cause severe blistering and scarring; FDA should require labeling warnings, standardized concentration limits, and provider training for compounding cantharidin products.

[P3] Legal expert: The “for topical use only” limitation lacks enforcement mechanisms—FDA should specify whether non-topical compounding with cantharidin would be a violation subject to action and how FDA will verify formulations.

[P4] Allergy advocacy group: Diphenylcyclopropenone (DPCP) is used in contact immunotherapy with documented risks of severe allergic reactions; FDA should require allergist oversight, informed consent templates, and contraindication guidance for compounded DPCP topical products.

[P4] Manufacturer/trade association: The chemical stability and impurity profile of DPCP vary by source; the rule should require compounding pharmacists to use bulk substance meeting specific pharmacopeial or certificate-of-analysis standards.

[P5] Cosmetic industry: N-acetyl-D-glucosamine is widely used in topical cosmeceuticals; permitting it for compounding without specifying permitted indications may blur lines between cosmetic and drug uses—FDA should clarify allowable therapeutic claims and compounding concentrations.

[P5] Dermatology researcher: Evidence for topical N-acetyl-D-glucosamine efficacy for medical dermatologic conditions is limited; FDA should publish the evidence base considered under § 216.23(c)(3) that justified inclusion or require post-market data collection.

[P6] Safety organization: Squaric acid dibutyl ester can be a strong sensitizer; limiting to topical use is insufficient—FDA should specify maximum concentration thresholds, patch-test protocols, and mandatory patient counseling.

[P6] Pharmacy compounding group: Some compounding pharmacies lack access to high-quality squaric acid dibutyl ester; the rule should permit use only when substance meets defined purity standards and include guidance on storage and handling due to potential irritancy.

[P7] Endocrinology/ENT clinicians: Thymol iodide topical use may interact with thyroid function or iodine-sensitive patients; FDA should require labeling regarding iodine exposure and contraindications for patients with thyroid disease.

[P7] Environmental health NGO: Thymol iodide manufacturing and disposal may pose environmental hazards; FDA should require compounding pharmacies to follow specific waste handling protocols.

[P8] Academic commenter: The description in § 216.23(b) that FDA “has determined that the listed substances will not be placed” on the list lacks transparency—FDA must provide the full rationale, including data and weighting of criteria from paragraph (c), for each excluded substance.

[P8] FOIA/legal group: For substances excluded under § 216.23(b), FDA should publish the evidence and peer-reviewed references used in the decision and provide a process for petitioning reconsideration.

[P9] Neurology clinicians: Oxitriptan is excluded but some practitioners use it off-label for depression/anxiety; FDA should explain safety or efficacy deficiencies that led to exclusion and whether compounding could still be considered under investigational protocols.

[P9] Patient advocate: Patients who rely on oxitriptan compounded formulations will lose access if excluded; FDA should allow a transitional period or provide alternative therapeutic recommendations.

[P10] Cognitive disorder advocacy: Piracetam exclusion will impact patients in certain countries using it for cognitive impairment; FDA should justify exclusion with evidence and consider narrow allowances for compassionate use in 503A settings under physician order.

[P10] Pharmacology expert: Piracetam has an ambiguous regulatory status in the U.S.; FDA should clarify whether exclusion is due to efficacy/safety concerns or because approved alternatives exist, and whether pharmacovigilance data were considered.

[P11] Ophthalmology society: Silver protein mild is often used in ophthalmic compounded products; excluding it raises patient care concerns—FDA should cite sterility/safety data and provide recommended alternatives or conditions for sterile compounding.

[P11] Sterile compounding pharmacist: If silver protein mild is excluded, FDA must clarify applicability to ophthalmic agents compounded under USP <797> and provide guidance on transitioning prescriptions to approved alternatives.

[P12] Dermatology/clinical researcher: Tranilast exclusion may affect dermatologic patients (e.g., keloids); FDA should disclose the evidence demonstrating lack of benefit or safety concerns, and whether topical tranilast formulations were considered separately.

[P12] Small compounding pharmacy: Many compounding prescriptions for tranilast are patient-specific; banning compounding of tranilast could disrupt care—FDA should permit case-by-case compounding under documented medical necessity.

[P13] Health policy group: The criteria in § 216.23(c) are appropriately broad but lack a transparent weighting scheme; FDA should state how it balances physical characterization, safety, evidence of effectiveness, and historical use when making inclusion/exclusion decisions.

[P13] Academic reviewer: The rule should require that FDA publish for each evaluated substance a summary table showing how each § 216.23(c) criterion was assessed and the sources used.

[P14] Chemist/trade group: Requiring consideration of physical and chemical characterization is appropriate—FDA should adopt specific minimum analytical standards (e.g., identity, purity, impurity profile) and acceptable analytical methods (HPLC, NMR) for bulk drug substances used in compounding.

[P14] Industry commenter: The rule should specify whether pharmacopeial monographs satisfy the physical/chemical characterization criterion and whether non-pharmacopeial substances must have a certificate of analysis from an approved vendor.

[P15] Safety/advocacy group: The “safety issues” criterion must explicitly include risks from impurities, degradation products, and interactions with excipients or packaging; FDA should require toxicological assessments and adverse event reporting for newly listed substances.

[P15] Risk management expert: FDA should require that safety considerations include dose-related adverse events and special-population risks (pediatrics, pregnant/lactating, renal/hepatic impairment) and provide guidance on label warnings.

[P16] Evidence-based medicine group: The “available evidence of effectiveness” standard is vague—FDA should define acceptable evidence (randomized controlled trials, observational studies, case series) and state whether historical use alone can justify inclusion.

[P16] Legal/clinical commenter: If no evidence exists, FDA should require post-marketing surveillance or a registry for compounded products containing the substance to monitor effectiveness and safety.

[P17] Historian/clinician: Considering historical use is appropriate, but FDA should weight recent high-quality peer-reviewed references more heavily than older anecdotal reports; the rule should state how FDA evaluates the quality of references.

[P17] Patient groups: For substances historically used for rare conditions, FDA should allow inclusion based on clinician consensus and case reports when randomized trials are impractical, with conditions for monitoring.

[P18] Patient safety/consumer advocate: Section 216.23(d) appropriately prohibits claims that compounded drugs are “FDA-approved” but the rule should clarify permitted language (e.g., “compounded following applicable law”) and require templates for compliant patient-facing statements.

[P18] Industry/legal commenter: The misbranding provision could chill truthful statements by pharmacists about FDA oversight; FDA should define clearly what constitutes a prohibited representation and provide safe-harbor examples for acceptable communications.

[P18] First Amendment/legal scholar: The rule should avoid overbroad restrictions on speech—provide illustrative examples of prohibited claims (e.g., “FDA-approved”) and permitted factual statements (e.g., “compounded by a licensed pharmacist”) to reduce litigation risk.

[P18] Enforcement NGO: FDA should outline enforcement priorities and penalties for misbranding representations under (d), and explain how it will investigate and respond to noncompliant claims by online pharmacies or manufacturers.

raw_output:
[P1] The minimum age requirement of 18 for pesticide handlers and early-entry workers is appropriate and should be retained to protect minors from hazardous exposure and long-term health risks.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether the 18-year-old minimum applies to both full-time and seasonal/temporary handlers and early-entry workers to avoid enforcement gaps.

[P2] The exemption for owners and immediate family members undermines the protective intent of the age limit and should be removed because family members can be equally vulnerable to pesticide exposure.

[P2] If the owner/immediate family exemption is retained, the rule must define "owner" (e.g., percentage of ownership) and "immediate family member" precisely to prevent loopholes and inconsistent application across states.

[P2] Allowing minors who are immediate family members to handle pesticides creates child labor and child welfare concerns and conflicts with state child labor laws; EPA should coordinate with DOL and state agencies.

[P3] Employers must be required to provide pesticide application information and safety data sheets (SDS) to designated representatives in a timely manner (e.g., within 24 hours) and the rule should specify delivery methods (electronic, paper, in-language).

[P3] The rule should require employers to document and retain records of when SDS and application information were provided to designated representatives to enable enforcement and audits.

[P4] Requiring employers to provide SDS and application information to any requesting worker/handler and to medical personnel is essential; however, the rule should define "request" (oral vs. written) and establish maximum response times.

[P4] The regulation should mandate that SDS and pesticide application information be provided in the worker's/handler's primary language when reasonably foreseeable to be other than English.

[P5] The AEZ requirements are critical for safety; the rule should specify measurement or buffer distances by application method (e.g., aerial, ground spray, airblast) so employers have clear, implementable standards.

[P5] The rule must clarify enforcement responsibilities for third parties and nonemployees (e.g., visitors, service workers) who enter AEZs and specify employer liability and required signage.

[P6] The obligation to keep workers and other persons out of treated areas should include explicit re-entry intervals based on label-specified restricted-entry intervals (REIs) and require employers to post REI information visibly.

[P6] The rule should require employers to provide PPE and decontamination facilities if inadvertent entry into treated areas is possible, rather than solely relying on exclusion.

[P7] The requirement that handlers suspend applications if persons are in the AEZ is reasonable, but EPA should provide guidance on what constitutes "immediate" suspension and any safe procedures for resuming applications.

[P7] The rule should address potential operational and crop-loss impacts of mandatory suspension and consider narrow, specified exemptions for emergencies (with strict notification and mitigation measures).

[P8] The cross-references to multiple CFR sections create complexity; EPA should publish a consolidated compliance checklist for regulated persons to ensure all obligations (training, records, postings) are understandable.

[P8] Given the breadth of obligations, EPA should offer a phased compliance timeline, compliance assistance materials, and a hotline for farmers and small businesses to reduce inadvertent violations.

[P9] Stakeholders note that many provisions became enforceable on January 2, 2017; EPA should confirm enforcement discretion for small entities that made good-faith efforts but could not meet deadlines and consider penalty mitigation.

[P10] The expanded poster content requirement coming into effect January 2, 2018 should include bilingual posters (English/Spanish) and templates downloadable from EPA to ease employer compliance.

[P10] EPA should clarify whether employers may display digital versions of the pesticide safety information display (e.g., on a locked tablet) and whether that satisfies the posting requirement.

[P11] The January 2, 2018 requirement that handlers suspend applications if others enter the AEZ duplicates P7 and should include guidance on notification systems (e.g., flags, radios) to prevent unnecessary suspensions.

[P12] The deferred effective date for expanded training content is appropriate, but EPA should set a firm timeline for completing rulemaking and publishing approved materials to avoid indefinite delay.

[P13] Allowing trainers to use either old or new EPA-approved materials until rulemaking concludes reduces confusion; EPA should ensure both versions are easily accessible online and indicate which topics differ.

[P14] Making expanded training mandatory 180 days after EPA publishes available materials is acceptable only if EPA commits to publishing clear trainer guidance, sample curricula, and assessment tools within a defined short timeframe.

[P14] The 180-day waiting period should be shortened (e.g., to 90 days) if EPA makes materials available with electronic distribution and training modules to accelerate worker protections.

[P15] The obligation to provide USDA Secretary a copy of any draft proposed rule at least 60 days before signing is consistent with FIFRA; EPA should document when it complied and provide the public a summary of USDA's input.

[P16] The 60-day timing specification must be adhered to; EPA should publish the date the draft was transmitted to USDA to demonstrate compliance with FIFRA Section 25(a)(2)(A).

[P17] The prohibition on public access to the draft regulatory document until EPA signs it reduces transparency; EPA should nonetheless publish a non-binding summary or hold stakeholder briefings during the USDA review period.

[P17] Legal experts will likely challenge withholding the draft from the public as inconsistent with principles of open government and administrative procedure; EPA should make redacted drafts available to stakeholders under confidentiality protections.

[P18] The obligation to include USDA's written comments and EPA responses with the proposed rule if submitted within 30 days is important for transparency; EPA should commit to including the full comments and responses in the docket.

[P19] The 30-day submission window for USDA to comment is tight; EPA should confirm when USDA received the draft to verify the adequacy of the comment period.

[P20] If USDA does not submit comments within 30 days and EPA signs the proposed rule afterward, stakeholders should be given a separate opportunity to review USDA-EPA communications or an explanation of why no USDA comments were received.

[P21] The rule should address the contingency where USDA fails to submit comments within 30 days but subsequently provides substantial input; EPA should commit to considering any late USDA comments and documenting the rationale for acceptance or rejection.

[P22] The August 21, 2019 comment deadline is reasonable only if EPA ensures wide dissemination of the proposed rule and provides at least one public listening session and materials in Spanish and other commonly used languages.

[P22] Given the complexity of the revised WPS, EPA should extend the comment period beyond August 21, 2019 (e.g., by 30–60 days) to allow farmers, small business owners, worker advocacy groups, and state agencies sufficient time to prepare substantive comments.

[P1] Agricultural employers and applicator associations will request clarity on enforcement mechanisms for the age restriction and whether criminal, civil, or administrative penalties will apply for employing under-18 handlers.

[P2] Small family farms will argue that the owner/immediate family exemption is necessary to preserve family farm operations and should be retained, but they will request an explicit safe-harbor certification process to document eligibility for the exemption.

[P3] Worker advocacy groups will demand that designated representatives include legally authorized guardians and community health advocates and that employers be prohibited from retaliating against workers who name representatives.

[P4] Medical associations will request that SDS and pesticide application information be provided immediately to emergency medical services by phone or electronic transmission when requested and that employers maintain a 24/7 point of contact.

[P5] Pesticide applicator groups will request precise definitions of "application exclusion zone" by equipment type and wind speed parameters to reduce uncertainty during operations.

[P6] State enforcement agencies will request model signage requirements (size, wording, pictograms) for treated areas and AEZ per P5/P6 to ensure consistency across jurisdictions.

[P7] Legal commenters will request that EPA clarify the interplay between these WPS requirements and state child labor laws, OSHA standards, and the Fair Labor Standards Act to avoid conflicting obligations.

[P8] Environmental and public health NGOs will urge EPA to close the owner/immediate family exemption loophole by at least requiring training and medical monitoring for exempt minors engaged in handling or early entry.

[P9] Farmworker unions will request that the rule expressly prohibit coerced consent for minors to work as handlers or early-entry workers and include enforcement mechanisms and whistleblower protections.

[P10] Industry commenters will request safe-harbor compliance guidance and compliance assistance funding for small and limited-resource farms to implement poster updates, training changes, and AEZ procedures.

[P11] University extension services will ask EPA to coordinate with state extension programs to develop and distribute approved training materials in multiple languages and formats (in-person, online, video).

[P12] Some commenters will request that EPA publish incident reporting requirements for any AEZ breaches or unauthorized entries during applications to facilitate surveillance and worker protection improvements.

[P13] Public commenters will request that EPA require employers to maintain records of all AEZ suspensions, including reason, duration, and any injuries/exposures, for a minimum retention period (e.g., 2–3 years).

[P14] Worker representatives will request that EPA require employers to post contact information for local medical facilities and poison control centers on the pesticide safety information display.

[P15] Agricultural labor contractors will ask for clarification whether the 18-year age limit applies to contractors’ employees and how liability is apportioned between contractors and farm operators.

[P16] Civil rights advocates will request demographic data collection requirements (age, language, employment status) for enforcement and to assess disproportionate impacts on immigrant or minority youth.

[P17] Insurance industry stakeholders will request guidance on how AEZ suspension requirements affect crop insurance claims and whether unavoidable suspensions constitute insurable loss events.

[P18] State agriculture departments will request transitional guidance on inspections and citations for violations that occurred between January 2, 2017 and the present, especially where training materials were in flux.

[P19] Some agricultural employers will request an exemption or limited exception for emergency pest-control situations (e.g., explosive outbreaks, invasive pests) that threaten crop viability, with strict notification and mitigation requirements.

[P20] Human rights organizations will request that EPA remove the public access prohibition (P17) or at minimum make redacted drafts available to community groups representing vulnerable workers during USDA review.

[P2] The 165 hours TIS compliance time in § 39.13(f)(1) is unreasonably short for large operators and small maintenance facilities that must coordinate parts, tooling, and scheduling across fleets; we request extension to a minimum of 300 hours TIS or a calendar alternative (e.g., 90 days) to ensure safe, practicable compliance.

[P2] The rule lacks an allowance for operators with low-utilization aircraft (e.g., emergency medical, offshore transport) who may not accrue 165 hours TIS within the intended safety window; request an alternative compliance metric based on calendar days (e.g., within 60 days after effective date) as an option.

[P3] § 39.13(f)(1)(i) requires a “visual inspection” for bend, twist, or breakage but provides no definition of accepted visual inspection standards (lighting, magnification, displacement tolerances); request incorporation by reference of an inspection standard or minimum acceptance criteria.

[P3] The provision does not specify training or qualification requirements for the inspector performing the control end fitting inspection; request that only certificated A&P mechanics with rotorcraft experience perform the inspection, or provide explicit qualification criteria.

[P3] The mandatory “replace with an airworthy fitting before further flight” language lacks guidance on acceptable replacement parts or part-number limitations; request clarification that only OEM or FAA-approved equivalent parts may be used and whether repaired fittings are acceptable.

[P4] The dye-penetrant inspection requirement in § 39.13(f)(1)(ii) lacks procedural details (penetrant type, dwell times, developer, acceptable crack length) and acceptance criteria for defects; request that the AD incorporate or reference the Eurocopter Alert Service Bulletin procedure or other industry standard NDT procedures.

[P4] The AD does not address environmental or contamination constraints for the dye-penetrant process (e.g., aircraft in service in remote locations where shop facilities are limited); request allowance for alternative NDT methods (eddy current, ultrasonic) if demonstrated equivalent.

[P4] Replacement “before further flight” for a cracked star support pin may not be logistically possible on off-site operations or during critical missions; request allowance to ferry the helicopter to a maintenance base under specific operational restrictions and with documented risk mitigation.

[P5] Mandating installation of exactly “three carbon fiber plies” to reinforce the stringer may be overly prescriptive if equivalent composite layups or alternative reinforcement designs provide equal or better strength; request performance-based language allowing alternative reinforcement validated by engineering analysis or STC.

[P5] The re-identification requirement after reinforcement references an accompanying service bulletin but the AD fails to include the exact re-identification marking, format, or data to be recorded in the logbook; request explicit re-identification text and logbook entry language to ensure uniform compliance.

[P5] The AD does not provide torque, bonding, or curing procedures for the composite plies nor curing environment controls; request inclusion of detailed installation instructions or explicit incorporation by reference of the Eurocopter service instructions.

[P6] The blanket prohibition in § 39.13(f)(2) on installing specific sliding door P/Ns after the AD effective date could ground aircraft awaiting spare doors and could create parts shortages; request a grace period for existing stock or an allowance to install the door if accompanied by a completed reinforcement and documentation.

[P6] The prohibition fails to address installed doors on leased aircraft that may be swapped between operators or returned to lessors; request clarification on documentation transfer requirements and responsibilities of lessors vs. lessees.

[P7] The exception in § 39.13(f)(2) relies on compliance with paragraph (f)(1)(iii) but does not specify who may perform the reinforcement (manufacturer, repair station, field approval); request clarification that FAA-certificated repair stations or the OEM must perform reinforcement unless performed under an approved AMOC.

[P8] Accepting prior compliance with AD 2014–12–12 as meeting paragraph (f)(1) obligations (per § 39.13(g)) is ambiguous because AD 2014–12–12 may not have included the same inspection zones or reinforcement; request a crosswalk table showing exactly which actions in AD 2014–12–12 satisfy each paragraph (f)(1)(i)–(iii).

[P8] The rule should require documentation demonstrating prior compliance with AD 2014–12–12 (work orders, logbook entries, parts tags) be available for FAA inspection; request explicit recordkeeping requirements for transferred compliance credit.

[P9] § 39.13(h)(1) allows AMOCs but funnels all proposals to a single named individual (David Hatfield) and a Fort Worth address; request additional, modern submission means (secure electronic portal) and a named office-level contact to avoid delay if the individual is unavailable.

[P9] The rule does not specify evaluation timelines for AMOC approval; stakeholders request a required FAA response time (e.g., 60 days) for AMOC decisions to enable operational planning.

[P10] Requiring AMOC proposals to be sent to a physical address and phone number in § 39.13(h)(1) may not be practical for international operators; request explicit permission to submit AMOC requests electronically (email or FAA portal) and to accept electronic signatures.

[P11] § 39.13(h)(2) “we suggest that you notify” principal inspectors prior to operating under an AMOC is advisory only and creates uncertainty about whether formal pre-approval/notification is required; request the AD be explicit that notification is mandatory and specify the content and timing of the notification.

[P1] The catch-all obligation in § 39.13(e) that operators are responsible for performing each action “within the specified compliance time” lacks an explicit allowance for exigent circumstances (e.g., parts shortages, weather); request a formal mechanism for requesting extensions beyond an AMOC for documented hardships.

[P1] The AD does not specify recordkeeping periods for documenting compliance with its obligations (inspections, replacements, reinforcements); request explicit retention periods (e.g., 2 years) and the required content of maintenance records.

[P12] Removing and reserving paragraphs (e)(4)(vi) and (ix) of 21 CFR § 2.125 (per § 2.125) eliminates “essential-use” designations without providing a rationale or transition plan for regulated parties; request an explanation of the regulatory impact and outreach to affected stakeholders before finalizing.

[P14] The repeated instruction to “remove and reserve” paragraphs (e)(4)(vi) and (ix) without publishing the full current text may create confusion about what specific products are affected; request that the agency publish the exact text being removed and a regulatory impact analysis.

[P15] Deleting paragraph (e)(4)(iii) from § 2.125 without cross-referencing consequential amendments elsewhere in CFR may create regulatory gaps or conflicts; request a comprehensive review and redline showing all consequential edits and citations to be updated.

[P13] The provision to “maintain the existing authority citation” for part 2 should include confirmation that no other statutory authorities (e.g., recent amendments to underlying statutes) affect the rulemaking; request the agency confirm that the authority citation is complete and cite any additional statutes relied upon.

[P5] Reinforcement with carbon fiber may affect crashworthiness, weight and balance, or door dynamics; request a required supplemental structural analysis and flight-test data to demonstrate no adverse effects on performance, certification basis, or occupant safety.

[P4] The AD’s inspection zones “Zone X and Zone Y in Figure 3” are referenced but the figure is not reproduced in the AD text; request that all referenced figures be included in the rule or explicitly incorporated by reference with location details.

[P6] The prohibition targets specific part numbers without addressing interchangeable part-number revisions or superseded P/Ns; request inclusion of a “P/N equivalency” clause that covers superseding or superseded part numbers listed in OEM parts catalogs.

[P2] The AD provides no funding or cost-estimate information for operators to prepare for compliance; request the FAA include an economic analysis and estimated per-aircraft cost for inspections, replacement pins, reinforcement kits, and downtime.

[P9] AMOC approval authority limited to “The Manager, Safety Management Group” may be interpreted narrowly; request delegation language allowing the Manager to delegate approval to qualified staff to ensure timely decisions.

[P3] The requirement to inspect both “upper and lower locking pin control rod end fittings” should specify whether symmetric inspection documentation is required for each side and how to handle simultaneous findings (e.g., if one fitting is damaged, must both be replaced).

[P5] “Re-identify the sliding door” is vague — request that re-identification include both a physical placard on the door and a maintenance entry specifying the reinforcement method, date, and technician signature to ensure traceability.

[P4] The AD’s requirement to “clean and dye penetrant inspect” may require disassembly of adjacent components creating additional hours beyond the inspection; request that the FAA quantify expected man-hours or allow declarative time-and-materials claims in the economic analysis.

[P6] The installation prohibition after the AD effective date could impact aftermarket suppliers and MRO inventories; request a phased implementation that allows suppliers to update inventory labeling and customers to confirm reinforcement before installation.

[P8] Accepting prior compliance with AD 2014–12–12 as meeting requirements could create legal uncertainty if earlier ADs were complied with under different AMOCs; request the AD require evidence that prior work was performed per the exact procedures referenced in this AD or an approved AMOC validating equivalence.

[P12] Removing essential-use designations under § 2.125 may affect domestic production and distribution chains for affected products; request stakeholder outreach and a 180-day transition period to allow affected parties to adjust processes.

The mandatory “replace with an airworthy fitting before further flight” language lacks guidance on acceptable replacement parts or part-number limitations; request clarification that only OEM or FAA-approved equivalent parts may be used and whether repaired fittings are acceptable.

The dye-penetrant inspection requirement in § 39.13(f)(1)(ii) lacks procedural details (penetrant type, dwell times, developer, acceptable crack length) and acceptance criteria for defects; request that the AD incorporate or reference the Eurocopter Alert Service Bulletin procedure or other industry standard NDT procedures.

The AD does not address environmental or contamination constraints for the dye-penetrant process (e.g., aircraft in service in remote locations where shop facilities are limited); request allowance for alternative NDT methods (eddy current, ultrasonic) if demonstrated equivalent.

Replacement “before further flight” for a cracked star support pin may not be logistically possible on off-site operations or during critical missions; request allowance to ferry the helicopter to a maintenance base under specific operational restrictions and with documented risk mitigation.

Mandating installation of exactly “three carbon fiber plies” to reinforce the stringer may be overly prescriptive if equivalent composite layups or alternative reinforcement designs provide equal or better strength; request performance-based language allowing alternative reinforcement validated by engineering analysis or STC.

The re-identification requirement after reinforcement references an accompanying service bulletin but the AD fails to include the exact re-identification marking, format, or data to be recorded in the logbook; request explicit re-identification text and logbook entry language to ensure uniform compliance.

The AD does not provide torque, bonding, or curing procedures for the composite plies nor curing environment controls; request inclusion of detailed installation instructions or explicit incorporation by reference of the Eurocopter service instructions.

The blanket prohibition in § 39.13(f)(2) on installing specific sliding door P/Ns after the AD effective date could ground aircraft awaiting spare doors and could create parts shortages; request a grace period for existing stock or an allowance to install the door if accompanied by a completed reinforcement and documentation.

The prohibition fails to address installed doors on leased aircraft that may be swapped between operators or returned to lessors; request clarification on documentation transfer requirements and responsibilities of lessors vs. lessees.

The exception in § 39.13(f)(2) relies on compliance with paragraph (f)(1)(iii) but does not specify who may perform the reinforcement (manufacturer, repair station, field approval); request clarification that FAA-certificated repair stations or the OEM must perform reinforcement unless performed under an approved AMOC.

Accepting prior compliance with AD 2014–12–12 as meeting paragraph (f)(1) obligations (per § 39.13(g)) is ambiguous because AD 2014–12–12 may not have included the same inspection zones or reinforcement; request a crosswalk table showing exactly which actions in AD 2014–12–12 satisfy each paragraph (f)(1)(i)–(iii).

The rule should require documentation demonstrating prior compliance with AD 2014–12–12 (work orders, logbook entries, parts tags) be available for FAA inspection; request explicit recordkeeping requirements for transferred compliance credit.

§ 39.13(h)(1) allows AMOCs but funnels all proposals to a single named individual (David Hatfield) and a Fort Worth address; request additional, modern submission means (secure electronic portal) and a named office-level contact to avoid delay if the individual is unavailable.
The rule does not specify evaluation timelines for AMOC approval; stakeholders request a required FAA response time (e.g., 60 days) for AMOC decisions to enable operational planning.

Requiring AMOC proposals to be sent to a physical address and phone number in § 39.13(h)(1) may not be practical for international operators; request explicit permission to submit AMOC requests electronically (email or FAA portal) and to accept electronic signatures.

§ 39.13(h)(2) “we suggest that you notify” principal inspectors prior to operating under an AMOC is advisory only and creates uncertainty about whether formal pre-approval/notification is required; request the AD be explicit that notification is mandatory and specify the content and timing of the notification.

The catch-all obligation in § 39.13(e) that operators are responsible for performing each action “within the specified compliance time” lacks an explicit allowance for exigent circumstances (e.g., parts shortages, weather); request a formal mechanism for requesting extensions beyond an AMOC for documented hardships.

The AD does not specify recordkeeping periods for documenting compliance with its obligations (inspections, replacements, reinforcements); request explicit retention periods (e.g., 2 years) and the required content of maintenance records.

Removing and reserving paragraphs (e)(4)(vi) and (ix) of 21 CFR § 2.125 (per § 2.125) eliminates “essential-use” designations without providing a rationale or transition plan for regulated parties; request an explanation of the regulatory impact and outreach to affected stakeholders before finalizing.

The repeated instruction to “remove and reserve” paragraphs (e)(4)(vi) and (ix) without publishing the full current text may create confusion about what specific products are affected; request that the agency publish the exact text being removed and a regulatory impact analysis.

Deleting paragraph (e)(4)(iii) from § 2.125 without cross-referencing consequential amendments elsewhere in CFR may create regulatory gaps or conflicts; request a comprehensive review and redline showing all consequential edits and citations to be updated.

The provision to “maintain the existing authority citation” for part 2 should include confirmation that no other statutory authorities (e.g., recent amendments to underlying statutes) affect the rulemaking; request the agency confirm that the authority citation is complete and cite any additional statutes relied upon.

Reinforcement with carbon fiber may affect crashworthiness, weight and balance, or door dynamics; request a required supplemental structural analysis and flight-test data to demonstrate no adverse effects on performance, certification basis, or occupant safety.

The AD’s inspection zones “Zone X and Zone Y in Figure 3” are referenced but the figure is not reproduced in the AD text; request that all referenced figures be included in the rule or explicitly incorporated by reference with location details.

The prohibition targets specific part numbers without addressing interchangeable part-number revisions or superseded P/Ns; request inclusion of a “P/N equivalency” clause that covers superseding or superseded part numbers listed in OEM parts catalogs.

The AD provides no funding or cost-estimate information for operators to prepare for compliance; request the FAA include an economic analysis and estimated per-aircraft cost for inspections, replacement pins, reinforcement kits, and downtime.

AMOC approval authority limited to “The Manager, Safety Management Group” may be interpreted narrowly; request delegation language allowing the Manager to delegate approval to qualified staff to ensure timely decisions.

The requirement to inspect both “upper and lower locking pin control rod end fittings” should specify whether symmetric inspection documentation is required for each side and how to handle simultaneous findings (e.g., if one fitting is damaged, must both be replaced).

“Re-identify the sliding door” is vague — request that re-identification include both a physical placard on the door and a maintenance entry specifying the reinforcement method, date, and technician signature to ensure traceability.

The AD’s requirement to “clean and dye penetrant inspect” may require disassembly of adjacent components creating additional hours beyond the inspection; request that the FAA quantify expected man-hours or allow declarative time-and-materials claims in the economic analysis.

The installation prohibition after the AD effective date could impact aftermarket suppliers and MRO inventories; request a phased implementation that allows suppliers to update inventory labeling and customers to confirm reinforcement before installation.

Accepting prior compliance with AD 2014–12–12 as meeting requirements could create legal uncertainty if earlier ADs were complied with under different AMOCs; request the AD require evidence that prior work was performed per the exact procedures referenced in this AD or an approved AMOC validating equivalence.

Removing essential-use designations under § 2.125 may affect domestic production and distribution chains for affected products; request stakeholder outreach and a 180-day transition period to allow affected parties to adjust processes.

[P1] The permission to use the APHIS Contingency Plan form (§2.38(l)(2) / §2.134(b)) should be clarified to state whether use of the form is mandatory or optional; as written “may use” creates uncertainty for compliance enforcement and inspections.

[P1] The rule should specify whether facilities that use their own contingency plan format instead of the APHIS form must include all fields/questions on the APHIS form; otherwise divergent formats could omit critical information.

[P1] Industry commenters will request that the APHIS Contingency Plan form be made publicly available in editable digital formats (fillable PDF and machine-readable XML/CSV) to reduce administrative burden.

[P1] Commenters seek clarification on record retention: if a facility uses the APHIS form, how long must the completed form be retained and where (on-site vs. electronic off-site backup)?

[P2] The obligation to “provide training for personnel” (§2.38(l)(3) / §2.134(c)) should define minimum training content, learning objectives, and acceptable documentation (e.g., sign-in sheets, LMS records) to ensure uniformity across facilities.

[P2] Labor and union groups will request that the rule require documentation of competency (e.g., short assessment or attestation) rather than mere attendance to verify personnel understand their roles.

[P3] The 60-day deadline for training current registrants (§2.38(l)(3)) is unrealistic for large facilities with high staff counts; commenters will ask for an extended compliance window (e.g., 120–180 days) or phased implementation.

[P3] Legal commenters will point out that “current registrants must complete training within 60 days of putting the contingency plan in place” is ambiguous when facilities revise plans multiple times — request clarification that the 60-day clock runs from initial plan enactment only.

[P4] The identical 60-day requirement for facilities registered after the effective-date trigger (P4) may impose immediate burdens on new registrants; industry will ask that training be allowed to be completed during the first routine orientation cycle rather than a hard 60-day deadline.

[P5] Requiring employees hired 30+ days before plan implementation to be trained “by the date the facility implements the contingency plan” (P5) may force mass training on short notice; commenters will request phased training schedules or a minimum notice period before implementation (e.g., 30 days).

[P6] The requirement to train employees hired less than 30 days before implementation or hired after within 30 days of their start date (P6) will be operationally burdensome for small operators and those with high turnover; commenters will request flexibility for remote/on-call employees or allowance for online training completion within 45–60 days.

[P6] Privacy and labor groups will request that the rule allow remote/online training to satisfy the 30-day requirement and specify acceptable modalities and standards (synchronous vs asynchronous).

[P7] The requirement to retrain employees within 30 days of any changes stemming from the annual review (P7) is vague about what constitutes a “change” — commenters will ask for a materiality threshold so only substantive changes (not minor wording edits) trigger retraining.

[P7] Facilities will request that entities be permitted to use targeted communications (email/email acknowledgement and updated SOPs) for minor changes instead of full formal training sessions within 30 days, to avoid duplicative training.

[P8] Duplicate permission provisions (§2.38(l)(2) and §2.134(b)) should be harmonized to avoid conflicting language; commenters will recommend cross-references and single-source guidance.

[P9] The obligation in §2.134(c) that dealers, exhibitors, intermediate handlers, and carriers provide training should explicitly identify who within those entities is responsible for training (e.g., named training coordinator) to avoid diffusion of responsibility.

[P9] Commenters representing carriers and transporters will request exemptions or modified requirements for short-term contracted personnel (e.g., courier drivers) who perform transient functions and for whom full facility-level contingency training may be impractical.

[P10] The 60-day completion requirement for current licensees and registrants (§2.134(c)) duplicates P3 and may create inconsistent compliance dates across categories (research vs. dealer/exhibitor); stakeholders will ask for uniform timelines across §2.38 and §2.134 or clear rationale for differences.

[P11] New licensees/registrants subject to the 60-day rule (P11) will request that training deadlines begin at issuance of license/registration rather than “putting the contingency plan in place,” to avoid confusion when the plan is created pre-licensure.

[P12] The mandate that employees hired ≥30 days before plan implementation be trained by implementation date (P12) should include a transition provision allowing staggered completion for employees on leave, temporary furlough, or remote assignments.

[P13] The 30-day training timeline for employees hired just before or after implementation (P13) penalizes employers with weekend or seasonal hiring peaks; commenters will ask that “30 days” be measured in business days or allow up to 45 calendar days.

[P14] The retraining requirement within 30 days of annual-review changes (P14) duplicates P7 and raises administrative cost concerns; commenters will request an option to combine retraining with routine annual refreshers to minimize operational disruption.

[P2] Animal welfare and public health advocates will request that training include specific modules on emergency notification procedures, zoonotic risk mitigation, and recordkeeping for reportable incidents, not just general “roles and responsibilities.”

[P2] Legal commenters will request that the rule define penalties or corrective actions for failure to provide training and clarify whether lack of documented training will be considered a per-se violation.

[P3] Small businesses and non-profit exhibitors will ask for a waiver or reduced training frequency for volunteer-only staff or for facilities with fewer than a specific threshold of employees (e.g., <10 employees).

[P1] The rule should allow facilities to pre-populate the APHIS form with standard institutional information and stamp “controlled copy” to reduce repetitive paperwork; commenters will request permission to maintain a master template and only update changed fields.

[P6] Training timing rules do not account for seasonal workers or temporary contractors; commenters representing seasonal industries will request explicit provisions for contingent workforce training or a limited-scope orientation covering only essential contingency roles.

[P7] The provision lacks minimum trainer qualifications — commenters will request that trainers be qualified (e.g., appointed safety officer, veterinary professional, or certified trainer) and that training materials be approved or validated.

[P9] Dealers and exhibitors will request clarity whether third-party contractors (e.g., cleaning crews, maintenance) who access areas with regulated animals are covered by the training requirement, and if so, whether a brief site-specific orientation suffices.

[P2] Data protection and privacy advocates will request that the rule limit personal data collected during training documentation and set retention/deletion requirements to protect employee privacy.

[P3] Commenters will seek grandfathering provisions or phased enforcement for facilities that already conduct similar training on different schedules, to avoid duplicate efforts and compliance penalties.

[P11] Accreditation bodies will request that completion of accredited training programs or existing certifications be explicitly accepted as satisfying the contingency-plan training requirements.

[P14] Commenters will ask for model training curricula and sample training records from APHIS to ensure consistent compliance and to reduce legal uncertainty during inspections.

[P1] The rule should state whether use of the APHIS form subjects facilities to additional audits or data collection by APHIS beyond the content of the form; stakeholders will ask for limits on federal use of submitted information.

[P6] Medical/occupational health stakeholders will request that training include protections and accommodations for employees with disabilities and that timelines allow for reasonable accommodations without penalty.

[P2] Commenters request clarity whether contractors who perform animal care under supervision count as facility personnel and therefore must receive full contingency training, or whether delegated task-specific training is acceptable.

[P12] Human resources and compliance officers will ask for sample language for employment contracts or job descriptions that integrate contingency-plan training obligations to ensure consistent implementation.

[P7] Commenters will request that APHIS define the “annual review” process (who conducts it, scope, recordkeeping) so triggers for retraining are clear and defensible during enforcement actions.

[P9] Transport industry commenters will request an exception or streamlined process for carriers who never hold custody of animals for more than 24 hours and operate under federal DOT rules, arguing duplicative regulation.

[P1] The blanket prohibition on entry into the safety zone (Monongahela River mile 28.0–30.0) is overly broad and will unreasonably restrict commercial barge traffic and towing operations that routinely transit this stretch; request carving out scheduled commercial transits or defined corridors.

[P1] The rule fails to define what constitutes "enter" or whether brief transits or crossings (versus mooring or anchoring) are treated the same; please clarify scope to avoid enforcement ambiguity.

[P1] Recreational boaters and kayak rental operators will be unable to reasonably operate without advance authorization; recommend an exemption or expedited authorization process for small recreational craft during published hours.

[P2] The permission authority vested in the COTP or a "designated representative" lacks standards or timelines for granting or denying requests, creating potential arbitrary or delayed decisions that harm commerce; require written criteria and maximum response times.

[P2] Industry groups request that the rule allow pre-authorized permits for repetitive, scheduled commercial users (e.g., pipeline inspection vessels, towboats) to minimize administrative burden.

[P3] Requiring all persons or vessels to "request permission" to enter the zone is vague about acceptable request channels (radio, phone, electronic); mandate specific communications protocols (VHF channel, phone number, online form) and hours of operation.

[P3] Tug and tow companies argue the requirement to request permission could be impossible during emergent navigational situations; request an explicit emergency exception allowing passage to avoid collisions or grounding, with post-incident notification.

[P3] The obligation to request permission imposes compliance costs on small businesses without notice of any fee structure; request economic analysis and consider a de minimis exemption for vessels under a certain length or horsepower.

[P4] The mandate that "all persons and vessels shall comply with the instructions of the COTP or a designated representative" lacks limits; commenters request that instructions be reasonable, necessary, and statutorily authorized and that there be an appeals or review mechanism for contested actions.

[P4] Legal advocates note that the provision gives sweeping discretionary power to "designated representatives" and request qualification, credentialing, and training requirements be specified to ensure lawful and non-discriminatory enforcement.

[P5] Relying on LNMs, BNMs, and MSIBs to inform the public is insufficient for timely notice to transient recreational boaters; request additional notice mechanisms such as signage at public launches, marina notifications, and cruise/charter operator advisories.

[P5] Coastal and river user organizations request minimum advance notice periods (e.g., 72 hours) for planned safety zone activations communicated via LNMs/BNMs, and immediate broadcast updates if timings change.

[P5] The proposed communications plan does not commit to language or accessibility accommodations (e.g., Spanish translations); request multilingual and accessible outreach to affected communities.

[P6] Environmental and wildlife advocates may argue that the MBTA prohibition is necessary and should be enforced in conjunction with the safety zone to prevent harm to migratory birds in the river corridor; propose adding explicit operational restrictions during nesting/migration season.

[P6] Industry commenters seek clarification on how MBTA prohibitions intersect with permitted activities in the safety zone, requesting safe harbor language for authorized activities that may unintentionally disturb migratory birds when undertaken pursuant to COTP authorization.

[P7] The rule's limitation of MBTA applicability "only to actions directed at migratory birds, their nests, or their eggs" could be interpreted as authorizing incidental take; environmental groups challenge this narrowing and request reconsideration, arguing it conflicts with statutory intent and may increase unmonitored bird mortality.

[P7] Legal experts note that limiting the MBTA to only directed actions may not align with judicial interpretations; request the agency provide legal justification and cite authoritative case law supporting this narrowing.

[P8] The explicit exception for incidental injury or mortality to migratory birds removes deterrents and mitigation obligations; conservation organizations demand that any acceptance of incidental take be conditioned on mandatory mitigation, monitoring, and reporting requirements.

[P8] Industry commenters supporting the incidental-take exception request a clear process for post-incident reporting, standards for what qualifies as "incidental," and a safe-harbor permitting mechanism to avoid civil liability when actions were authorized by the COTP and undertaken in good faith.

[P1/P3] Emergency responders and local governments request an interoperable notification and authorization process (e.g., pre-authorized emergency response credentials) so first responders can enter the safety zone without delay while still complying with the rule.

[P2/P4] Vessel operators request clarity about which officials may serve as "designated representatives" (name, rank, agency), their delegation authority, and scope of powers to issue instructions and permits, to prevent contradictory orders from different agencies.

[P5/P3] Commercial operators ask for a streamlined advance-notice permitting system (online permit portal) integrated with LNMs/BNMs so repeated users can obtain standing permissions and avoid repeated ad hoc requests.

[P1] Property owners and waterfront businesses request maps with precise GPS coordinates and lateral limits of the safety zone; the mile markers alone are insufficient for navigation and enforcement.

[P4] Maritime labor groups worry that the requirement to follow COTP instructions without exception could conflict with crew safety obligations and the COLREGS; request language preserving the primacy of collision avoidance and seafarer safety.

[P6/P8] Wildlife lawyers warn that permitting incidental take without a formal permitting framework may expose the government to litigation under other statutes (e.g., Endangered Species Act) and request an inter-agency review and NEPA/ESA analysis.

[P3/P2] Commercial fishing operators request an explicit exemption or a simplified authorization for licensed fishermen working within the zone to avoid economic harm.

[P5] Mariners request that BNMs be broadcast on standard VHF channels and at set intervals (e.g., every 4 hours) during active safety zone periods to ensure all transiting vessels receive notice.

[P1/P5] Tribal governments assert they were not consulted and request government-to-government consultation plus tribal-specific notice procedures given subsistence and cultural uses of the river near mile 28–30.

[P7/P8] Scientists ask the agency to publish the basis for asserting that incidental take is outside MBTA prohibitions, including citations to administrative precedent or legal opinions, to enable informed comment.

[P1] Small-tour operators request grandfathering for previously authorized river events or scheduled excursions that coincide with the safety zone, or at least transitional flexibility during the first year of implementation.

[P4] Civil liberties groups request recordkeeping requirements for COTP instructions (audio and written logs) and public access to enforcement records to ensure accountability for orders given under this authority.

[P2/P3] Shipping companies request that the rule include an expedited pre-clearance process for commercial tows subject to tight scheduling and lock transit windows on the Monongahela River.

[P6] Hunters and birdwatchers request clear guidance distinguishing lawful recreational observation from prohibited "pursuit" or "take" under the MBTA to avoid inadvertent criminal liability.

[P8] Animal welfare organizations request mandatory carcass collection, reporting, and necropsy protocols for any migratory bird mortality connected with authorized activity in the safety zone to monitor impacts.

[P1/P4] Local law enforcement requests procedural coordination language to allow municipal water patrols to enforce the zone under defined Memoranda of Understanding with the Coast Guard to ensure consistent enforcement.

[P5] The Coast Guard should commit to publishing a calendar of anticipated safety zone activations at least monthly, with updates to LNMs/BNMs, to help commercial planning and public awareness.

[P3] The rule should specify that requests for passage made via standard marine VHF on channel 16 or channel 22A satisfy the "request permission" requirement to avoid confusion.

[P7] If the agency intends to narrow MBTA applicability, it must explicitly state how this interacts with state wildlife protection laws, which may be broader; request coordination language to prevent regulatory gaps.

Legal advocates note that the provision gives sweeping discretionary power to "designated representatives" and request qualification, credentialing, and training requirements be specified to ensure lawful and non-discriminatory enforcement.

/P3] Commercial operators ask for a streamlined advance-notice permitting system (online permit portal) integrated with LNMs/BNMs so repeated users can obtain standing permissions and avoid repeated ad hoc requests.

/P8] Wildlife lawyers warn that permitting incidental take without a formal permitting framework may expose the government to litigation under other statutes (e.g., Endangered Species Act) and request an inter-agency review and NEPA/ESA analysis.
/P2] Commercial fishing operators request an explicit exemption or a simplified authorization for licensed fishermen working within the zone to avoid economic harm.
