raw_output:
[P1] The March 19, 2018 postmark deadline is unreasonably short for stakeholders needing to collect technical data and legal review; request extension of at least 60–90 days.  
[P1] The rule’s exclusive emphasis on postmark date creates confusion for electronic filers; clarify whether electronic submissions on Regulations.gov that show a timestamp after March 19, 2018 but were initiated before that date will be accepted.  
[P2] Requiring commenters to identify the correct docket number in a table is likely to cause misplaced comments if the table is long or confusing; require automatic docket assignment tools on Regulations.gov or allow docket identification in the body of submissions.  
[P2] The rule should specify a fallback procedure and contact for commenters who cannot find the appropriate docket number in the provided table.  
[P3] Requiring submission only at Regulations.gov disadvantages individuals and small community groups without reliable internet access; permit and clearly describe alternative paper submission methods and provide free assistance for electronic filing.  
[P3] The provision does not state whether email submissions are acceptable; clarify whether email is allowed as an alternative and, if not, explain the rationale.  
[P4] The prohibition on editing/removing comments after submission may chill participation when commenters discover inadvertent personal or confidential information; allow a limited window (e.g., 48 hours) to correct or withdraw submissions.  
[P4] The inability to remove comments raises privacy concerns for individuals who later realize they posted identifying or sensitive personal information; require a process for redaction or removal upon request.  
[P5] The blanket prohibition on submitting CBI electronically conflicts with commenters’ need to support claims with proprietary data; require a clear, secure mechanism and instructions for submitting CBI (e.g., encrypted uploads, CBI cover sheets).  
[P5] The provision does not define the process for designating material as CBI or the treatment of inadvertently disclosed CBI; include procedures for marking, segregating, and requesting removal of inadvertently posted CBI.  
[P6] Requiring multimedia submissions to include written comments is reasonable, but the rule should specify acceptable file formats and size limits for multimedia to ensure accessibility and successful uploads.  
[P6] Specify whether a link to hosted multimedia (e.g., YouTube) is acceptable in lieu of uploading large files, and how such links will be preserved in the docket.  
[P7] Declaring the written submission as the “official comment” could unfairly devalue oral or multimedia testimony from communities with low literacy; permit oral testimony to be treated as official if accompanied by a transcript.  
[P8] The statement that EPA may make comments publicly available should be expanded to explain redaction practices and timelines for public posting to protect personal data.  
[P8] Clarify whether the EPA will notify commenters before publishing their submissions in the public docket, especially for submissions containing potentially sensitive details.  
[P9] The refusal to consider content outside the primary submission is overly rigid for complex matters where supporting documents may reside in public repositories; allow the EPA to accept references to externally hosted materials if stable, cited, and accessible by docket ID.  
[P9] The rule should allow submission of supplemental materials located offsite (e.g., large datasets) with clear instructions and cross-references to the primary comment to avoid arbitrary exclusions.  
[P10] The requirement to use the Docket Center address for courier deliveries is fine but should include operating hours, contact person, and security procedures to avoid rejected deliveries.  
[P11] The USPS address requirement should include a specific mail-stop or attention line to reduce misrouting at the EPA Superfund Docket Center.  
[P12] Requiring in-person appointments to view docket documents limits access for the public and remote stakeholders; provide remote access options or extend free scanning/copying services.  
[P12] The EPA should publish the appointment scheduling process, including typical wait times, to avoid discouraging public review of docket materials.  
[P13] The provision permitting requests for copies should specify costs and turnaround times for copies from Headquarters or regional dockets.  
[P13] Require that EPA proactively publish key docket documents online to reduce the need for individual copy requests.  
[P14] Advising informal requests instead of formal FOIA is reasonable but should not prevent a requester from using FOIA if necessary; clarify the interplay and expected response times for informal requests.  
[P15] Restricting oversized maps to in-person viewing unfairly burdens remote stakeholders; require EPA to provide high-resolution digital scans upon request or establish regional viewing locations.  
[P16] The statement that Headquarters docket documents are available via Regulations.gov should explicitly list which types of documents will be posted and anticipated posting timelines.  
[P17] Requiring comments to be sent to EPA Headquarters via the ADDRESSES section may create inconsistent filing rules if regional dockets contain site-specific material; clarify whether regional submissions are accepted and how they will be routed.  
[P17] Provide explicit instructions for multi-site commenters about whether to submit one consolidated comment or separate comments per docket.  
[P18] Saying EPA will review all comments received during the comment period should be qualified to state that comments meeting the format and procedural requirements will be reviewed; otherwise it is misleading.  
[P19] Requiring that voluminous materials indicate specific relevance to HRS factors is practical, but EPA should provide a template for how to map report sections to HRS components to ensure submissions are considered.  
[P20] The promise not to consider large submissions not tied to HRS scoring risks arbitrary exclusion of important contextual evidence; define what constitutes “tied to HRS” and allow explanatory materials that set context.  
[P21] The requirement that comments specify which HRS component they affect is reasonable, but EPA should accept good-faith attempts by lay commenters and provide assistance or templates for identifying applicable components.  
[P22] The general refusal to reply to late comments should be tempered by exceptions for compelling circumstances (e.g., postal strikes, natural disasters); include a defined exceptions process.  
[P23] Guaranteeing consideration only for postmarked comments by the deadline unfairly penalizes electronic filers who cannot be “postmarked”; clarify equivalence between postmark and electronic timestamp and explicitly accept timely electronic submissions.  
[P24] Making public comments available on Regulations.gov “as received” must be accompanied by a moderation policy to prevent doxxing, libelous statements, and personal attacks from being published unredacted.  
[P25] The exception for copyrighted, CBI or restricted information should explain how EPA will notify commenters when it withholds publication and provide redacted versions instead.  
[P26] Requiring use of the search function and docket ID to find comments presumes digital literacy; provide direct links to docket search pages and instructions in plain language.  
[P27] The obligation to resubmit prior concerns if a site is later proposed is burdensome; EPA should link earlier submissions automatically to new proposals or allow commenters to reference previous docket numbers instead of resubmitting.  
[P28] The rule’s description that sites scoring high on the HRS “may” be listed lacks clarity about minimum procedural protections for affected communities; recommend explicit notice and community involvement requirements when a high HRS score is achieved.  
[P29] The 28.50 HRS threshold for NPL eligibility should be revisited — provide empirical justification or consider raising/lowering the threshold based on recent risk assessments.  
[P29] Clarify whether rounding rules apply to HRS scores (e.g., 28.495) and how tie-breaking is handled when scores are near 28.50.  
[P30] Allowing each state to select one top-priority site without an HRS score raises concerns about politicization; require transparency, public justification, and minimum documentation of the basis for each state priority.  
[P30] Specify whether the state’s single nomination is subject to public comment and whether EPA will apply any independent review before listing.  
[P31] The third mechanism to list without an HRS score is too vaguely described; detail the “specified conditions” and provide examples and procedural safeguards before invoking this mechanism.  
[P32] Relying on an ATSDR health advisory as a listing condition should require the advisory to be current and include a documented causal link to the release; specify what form and content of ATSDR advisory is sufficient.  
[P33] EPA’s determination that a release poses a “significant public health threat” needs definitional clarity and an evidentiary standard; provide criteria, thresholds, and documentation requirements.  
[P34] The anticipated cost-effectiveness standard comparing remedial versus removal authority is subjective; require a transparent cost-benefit analysis and public disclosure of the assumptions used.  
[P35] Stating that Trust Fund-financed remedial actions may be taken only after NPL placement should be clarified for emergent circumstances where immediate remedial action is needed before listing.  
[P36] The allowance to use other authorities, including CERCLA enforcement, should explain how these authorities interact with NPL listing decisions and whether enforcement actions can substitute for listing.  
[P37] EPA should provide a clear timeline and procedural steps for deletion from the NPL, including public notice and an opportunity for comment.  
[P38] The requirement to consult with states on deletions should be expanded to require public notice and involvement of potentially affected local communities and tribes.  
[P39] The deletion criterion that responsible parties have implemented all required actions needs a definition of “required” and a mechanism for independent verification by EPA or third parties.  
[P40] The criterion that all Superfund-financed responses are complete should include procedures for assessing whether long-term monitoring or operation & maintenance obligations remain and how they affect deletion.  
[P41] Declaring a site eligible for deletion based on an RI showing no significant threat requires transparent RI methods, peer review, and access to underlying data for public scrutiny.  
[P42] The eligibility rules for the Construction Completion List (CCL) should require that “construction complete” determinations be documented and subject to public notice prior to listing.  
[P43] Clarify whether partial construction completion at multi-operable-unit sites qualifies the entire site for the CCL or only the completed units.  
[P44] If EPA determines response action is non-construction (institutional controls), require documentation of enforceability, monitoring plans, and contingency actions before placing a site on the CCL.  
[P45] Using NPL deletion qualification as a CCL criterion creates circularity; define the relationship and sequencing between deletion and CCL listing to avoid premature CCL placement.  
[P46] Placing primary response obligations on federal agencies for federal facilities is appropriate but EPA’s role in preparing the HRS score and deciding placement must be transparent; require EPA to publish federal agency HRS data and allow public comment prior to listing decisions.

[P1] The November 29, 2021 comments due date is too short for affected operators and manufacturers to prepare meaningful technical comments, especially given pandemic staffing constraints; extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P16] Docket FAA–2021–0794 shares the same November 29, 2021 deadline; consolidating comment periods with different AD numbers creates confusion—align and clarify which docket governs comments or extend both deadlines.

[P17] The listed submission methods (Regulations.gov, fax, mail) are acceptable, but the FAA should explicitly confirm receipt timelines and provide a contact for confirmation to ensure timely filing by the deadline.

[P2] The compliance clause requiring adherence "within the specified times" lacks clarity about applicability to aircraft that have undergone recent maintenance—require inclusion of grandfathering language for actions already in-progress but not completed before the effective date.

[P3] Requiring performance of all actions labeled 'RC' per Boeing Alert Service Bulletin without providing the full service bulletin text in the docket deprives commenters of necessary detail; the FAA should include the complete Boeing Alert Service Bulletin 777–53A0075, Revision 2, in the public docket.

[P4] The substitution of the AD effective date for Revision 2 dates in the Service Bulletin could create inconsistencies for operators who performed actions based on prior revisions—require explicit cross-reference tables mapping original Revision 2 dates to the AD effective date for each affected airplane configuration.

[P5] The restriction that repairs specified as "contact Boeing" must be approved per paragraph (i) effectively prohibits operators from using other qualified repair sources; allow approved repair methods from other qualified design approval holders or authorized repair stations when they meet the certification basis.

[P6] Granting the Seattle ACO Branch Manager sole AMOC authority centralizes decision-making and could create bottlenecks; authorize regional ACO branches or delegated offices to approve AMOCs to expedite operator compliance.

[P7] Requiring AMOC requests to go through principal inspectors or Flight Standards Offices may delay review; permit direct submission to the Seattle ACO Branch for complex technical AMOCs and provide a clear processing timeline (e.g., 60 days).

[P8] The email address for AMOC requests lacks encryption/security guidance; require FAA to provide secure file transfer or encrypted email options for proprietary repair data.

[P9] The obligation to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC is vague regarding timing; define a specific notification window (e.g., 72 hours prior to use) and the required notification content.

[P10] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs for repairs conflates manufacturer approval with regulatory approval; require that AMOC approvals by a Boeing ODA be concurrently submitted to the FAA for acceptance and explicit reference to this AD prior to use.

[P11] The requirement that repair methods meet the airplane's certification basis and reference this AD is appropriate, but FAA should clarify the process for determining the certification basis for older variants or supplemental type certificates (STCs).

[P12] Mandating all RC steps and figures be performed exactly as written may be infeasible for operators with alternative tooling or inspection equipment; permit equivalent procedures when demonstrated to provide equal or greater safety, with a streamlined AMOC process.

[P13] The RC Exempt labeling exception should include examples and a clear definition to prevent inconsistent interpretations by operators and inspectors.

[P14] Requiring an AMOC to deviate from any RC-labeled substep could be overly burdensome for minor deviations (e.g., different fastener torque tools); allow designated deviations that do not affect safety-critical outcomes to be handled via maintenance release procedures with FAA notification.

[P15] The permission to deviate from non-RC steps under an operator’s maintenance program must be constrained by objective criteria; request FAA provide specific acceptance criteria for what constitutes returning the airplane to an airworthy condition without AMOC involvement.

[P18] The proposed mandatory replacement of BMS 8–39 urethane foam seals in specified areas lacks a quantified risk assessment (probability of failure, fire risk); request FAA include the safety analysis and data that justify mandatory replacement rather than inspection or monitoring.

[P18] The rule requires replacing BMS 8–39 foam but does not specify approved replacement materials or part numbers; require the AD to list acceptable replacement materials, their specifications, and any required qualification tests.

[P18] There is no cost estimate provided for the replacement of system tube/wire seals per airplane and for the U.S. fleet; require FAA to include detailed economic impact analysis, including labor hours, part costs, and aircraft downtime.

[P18] For in-service time-based compliance intervals in paragraph 1.E of the Service Bulletin, the AD should allow credit for previous seal replacements performed using FAA-acceptable materials and processes—clarify credit provisions.

[P5] The AD's instruction to contact Boeing for repair instructions without mandating a responsive timeline could delay operators; require Boeing (or FAA) to provide repair instructions within a specified time (e.g., 30 days) or allow interim safe measures.

[P3] The AD relies on Boeing Alert Service Bulletin 777–53A0075 Revision 2; operators need confirmation that incorporation by reference is permissible and instructions for obtaining any non-copyrighted portions of the bulletin at no charge.

[P6] The AMOC approval authority should be expanded to include the delegated FAA representatives in the operator's district to reduce delays for geographically dispersed operators.

[P10] The text allowing Boeing ODA approvals should specify the scope of their authority, documentation requirements, and the requirement to reference the AD number in ODA approvals to ensure traceability.

[P11] The phrase "meet the certification basis of the airplane" is ambiguous for DER-designed repairs or modifications—request FAA to provide guidance on how DER approvals interact with AMOC approvals for this AD.

[P12] Require the FAA to publish a list of all RC-labeled steps and figures extracted from the Service Bulletin in the AD preamble to avoid ambiguity about what constitutes RC work.

[P4] Replacing Revision 2 dates with the AD effective date could unintentionally shorten compliance times for certain SB-specified actions; request clarification that compliance intervals are preserved as originally intended or provide a rationale for any shortening.

[P1] Because the FAA mandates comments be received "by November 29, 2021" (not postmarked), request explicit clarification that electronic submissions must be timestamped by that date and provide guidance for cross-timezone submissions.

[P17] The ADR lacks an explicit mechanism for submitting proprietary or sensitive technical data to the docket; request FAA provide instructions for submitting confidential business information and how it will be protected.

[P9] The requirement to notify the principal inspector "before using any approved AMOC" should include exceptions for emergency situations or temporary deviations required for flight safety; define emergency notification procedures.

[P15] The allowance to deviate from non-RC steps per an operator’s maintenance program could result in inconsistent levels of compliance across operators; request FAA issue advisory guidance or acceptable means of compliance to harmonize practices.

[P18] The AD should include applicability by airplane serial numbers and configurations—currently it references "specified areas" but does not clearly identify affected line numbers, options, or equipment installations.

[P3] The AD exception referencing paragraph (h) is complex; recommend the FAA provide a consolidated compliance table in the AD summarizing required actions, compliance times, and any deviations from the Service Bulletin for clarity.

[P1] The June 19, 2017 comments due date is unreasonably short and will prevent smaller operators and public-interest NGOs from providing meaningful technical comments; extend to at least 60 days from publication.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether electronically postmarked comments received after June 19, 2017 but transmitted earlier will be accepted; otherwise stakeholders may lose the opportunity to comment due to delivery delays.

[P2] The exception for STC ST01518SE should explicitly state whether subsequent STC revisions or repair kits associated with STC ST01518SE remain covered, to avoid future ambiguity about AMOC requirements.

[P2] Industry requests documentation demonstrating that installation of STC ST01518SE has been validated across all affected 757 structural configurations before exempting those operators from the 'change in product' AMOC requirement.

[P3] The phrase "within the compliance times specified, unless already done" lacks specificity about record evidence required to prove inspections were "already done"; the AD should require retained maintenance records and specify acceptable forms of proof.

[P4] Paragraph (g) requires performing inspections in (g)(1)-(g)(3) but does not define responsibility between owner and operator for leased aircraft; clarify who is legally obligated to perform and certify the inspections.

[P5] The Zone 1 inspection requirement referencing paragraph (h) should clarify whether calendar-based compliance times (days) apply equally to all operators worldwide or only U.S.-registered airplanes.

[P6] The termination provision for Zone 1 inspections in (g)(1) should require submission of compliance data to the FAA or logging in the aircraft maintenance records to demonstrate the preventative modification or replacement has been accomplished.

[P7] The external sliding probe EC inspection method in (g)(1)(i) references Boeing service bulletin Part 1 but does not specify equipment calibration standards or technician qualification requirements; the AD should set minimum NDT qualifications and calibration procedures.

[P8] The external spot-probe medium-frequency EC inspection in (g)(1)(ii) must define probe frequencies, scan parameters, and acceptance criteria rather than relying solely on the Boeing service bulletin, which may be updated independently.

[P9] The trigger for Zone 2 inspections in (g)(2) includes "any crack" found in (g)(1) but does not differentiate based on crack size, orientation, or criticality; industry requests threshold criteria for when Zone 2 inspections are mandated.

[P10] The Zone 2 sliding probe EC inspection in (g)(2)(i) references Part 4 of the service bulletin but lacks a requirement to use OEM-approved tooling or to record probe dwell times; specify these to ensure inspection consistency.

[P11] The Zone 2 spot-probe inspection in (g)(2)(ii) should include a requirement to notify the FAA when recurring cracks are found across multiple airplanes to permit fleet-level risk assessment.

[P12] The termination of Zone 2 inspections through replacement (k)(2) should require that replaced panels be manufactured to at least the same fatigue life standard as the original or greater; otherwise replacement could reduce structural life expectancy.

[P13] Paragraph (g)(3) mandates Zone 3 inspections after certain triggers but does not define the personnel or facility environment required for effective eddy current inspections in Zone 3; require maintenance environment controls.

[P14] The external sliding probe EC inspection for Zone 3 in (g)(3)(i) should require documentation of probe serial numbers, calibration certificates, and technician sign-off to ensure traceability.

[P15] The Zone 3 spot-probe medium-frequency EC inspection in (g)(3)(ii) should clarify applicability to aircraft with corrosion or paint coating variables that can affect EC results; require surface prep standards.

[P16] The termination condition for Zone 3 inspections (replacement per k(2)) should specify acceptable alternative parts and any required recordation that the termination applies to that specific tail number.

[P17] The compliance timing scheme in (h) that requires doing the initial Zone 1 inspection within the latest of multiple thresholds is confusing; request a matrix example showing different scenarios (e.g., airplanes at 10,000 FC with prior inspections) for clarity.

[P18] The 15,000 flight cycle threshold in (h)(1) does not account for high-utilization operators or high-cycle short-duration flights; propose a flight-hour-based alternative or a combined cycle/hour metric.

[P19] The 620-flight-cycle window in (h)(2) after the most recent sliding probe EC inspection is too long for aircraft near fatigue limits; propose shortening to 180-300 flight cycles or adding risk-based criteria.

[P20] The 200-flight-cycle window in (h)(3) for spot-probe inspections after a recent spot-probe inspection should be harmonized with (h)(2); having two different intervals depending on method creates operational complexity.

[P21] The alternative initial window in (h)(4) of 200 flight cycles or 90 days (whichever is first) should include a provision allowing operators to bank cycles from maintenance programs so inspections can be scheduled during heavy maintenance visits.

[P22] Paragraph (i) requires repeated EC and detailed inspections after preventive modification but does not provide the interval values in the AD text; require that all repeat interval values from Boeing service bulletin table 4 be reproduced in the AD for legal clarity.

[P23] The repair-before-further-flight mandate in (j) for any cracking found is appropriate for safety but needs clarification on acceptable "method approved" channels — require explicitly that approval can be via FAA field office, Boeing ODA, or approved repair authority and specify timelines for approval.

[P24] The permission in (k)(1) that the preventative modification terminates Zone 1 inspections if performed before further flight after a (g)(1) inspection should be clarified to state whether operators may defer the modification and continue inspections instead.

[P25] The repair requirement in (k)(1) for high-frequency EC open-hole inspections demands an FAA-approved method but omits a maximum allowable downtime or access to interim measures; request inclusion of acceptable temporary repairs and their time limits.

[P26] The replacement permission in (k)(2) that terminates all Zone 1-3 inspections must require that replacement parts come with full traceability, material certifications, and equivalent or improved design life documentation.

[P27] Paragraph (l)(1) that measures service bulletin "after revision date" compliance times from the AD effective date may produce unintended longer or shorter intervals if SBs are revised; recommend instead fixing compliance times in the AD itself to avoid ambiguity.

[P28] The obligation in (l)(2) that operators must repair before further flight rather than contact Boeing when the SB directs contact is necessary, but the AD should require that FAA/ACO-approved repair methods be documented and published to avoid delays.

[P29] The credit for previous Zone 1 inspections in (m) should require that earlier inspections meet the same acceptance criteria and include sample reporting requirements to demonstrate equivalency; otherwise unsafe inspections could be grandfathered.

[P30] The authority for the ACO Manager in (n)(1) to approve AMOCs should be expanded to allow delegated authorities (e.g., regional ACOs) to avoid bottlenecks and speed safety improvements.

[P31] The AMOC request procedure in (n)(1) that mandates sending requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO is unnecessarily burdensome for international operators based outside the U.S.; allow direct submission to the ACO with a clear routing alternative.

[P32] The option in (n)(1)/(n)(2) to email AMOC requests to 9-ANM-LAACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is beneficial, but the AD should require acknowledgment of receipt within a specified timeframe (e.g., 10 business days) to avoid operational uncertainty.

[P33] The requirement in (n)(2) to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC lacks guidance for operators without a designated principal inspector — clarifying that notification to the local FSDO manager suffices would help.

[P34] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs in (n)(3) is helpful, but paragraph (n)(3) should mandate FAA concurrence or post-approval notification to the FAA to ensure government oversight of ODA approvals.

[P35] The certification-basis requirement in (n)(3) for Boeing ODA AMOCs to explicitly reference this AD is vague — require inclusion of the AD docket number and a statement of how the AMOC meets the airplane's certification basis.

[P36] The acceptance of prior AMOCs from AD 2011–01–15 in (n)(4) but revocation of extensions to initial compliance times may create legal uncertainty for operators who planned based on earlier AMOCs; provide a transition grace period to comply with shorter times.

[P37] The RC-step obligation in (n)(5)(i) that any deviation requires an AMOC is broadly worded and could prevent minor, non-safety-relevant optimizations; request a definition of "deviation" and a list of examples that would not require an AMOC.

[P38] The permission in (n)(5)(ii) to deviate non-RC steps under an operator's program should include a requirement to document deviations in the aircraft logbook and in the operator's maintenance program records to preserve airworthiness traceability.

[P39] The AD relies heavily on Boeing service bulletin content; request that the FAA include the referenced service bulletin parts or essential inspection acceptance criteria in the AD docket so that public commenters and operators can review the full requirements.

[P40] Legal counsel notes that several provisions (e.g., (l)(2), (n)(5)(i)) create obligations to act "before further flight" without defining timelines for FAA reviews or approvals; this may lead to groundings or operational disruptions and requires more precise process timelines.

[P41] Small Part 121/135 operators comment that the cumulative inspection burden (Zones 1-3 plus repeated intervals) will significantly increase maintenance man-hours and costs; request FAA cost-benefit analysis and potential relief measures or funding.

[P42] Labor unions request that the AD specify that eddy current inspections must be performed by certificated A&P mechanics or NDT technicians with defined training to protect worker safety and ensure inspection quality.

[P43] Maintenance providers request clarification whether inspections performed under NRC/foreign aviation authority approvals are acceptable in lieu of FAA approvals for U.S.-registered airplanes operating overseas.

[P44] A fleet operator requests that the AD allow phase-in scheduling of initial inspections across line numbers within a fleet over a short, defined window to avoid AOG peaks, with documentation to the FAA.

[P45] An aircraft lessor requests language clarifying that compliance records and proof of terminating modifications must be provided to subsequent lessees/transferees to avoid disputes at lease turn-in.

[P1] The proposed §146.152(d)(3) is vague where it says “subject to applicable State law” and fails to explain how federal and differing state discontinuation standards will be reconciled, creating regulatory uncertainty for multi-state issuers.

[P1] The clause in §146.152(d)(3) should require notice to enrollees and the State when an issuer claims a qualifying condition to avoid surprise network or product losses; the current provision contains no explicit notice requirement.

[P2] §146.152(d)(3)(i) appears to permit an issuer to avoid discontinuation rules by offering a product “considered the same,” but the rule lacks objective criteria to determine when a new product is “the same as a previously offered product,” inviting gaming by insurers.

[P2] Industry commenters will request specific equivalence metrics in §146.152(d)(3)(i) (e.g., identical network, formulary, metal level, actuarial value within +/-1%, and same premium tier) so issuers can confidently comply.

[P2] Consumer advocates will oppose any interpretation of §146.152(d)(3)(i) that allows minor plan design changes to qualify as the “same” product; they will demand that material differences (cost-sharing shifts, network reductions) disqualify the product.

[P3] §146.152(d)(3)(ii) conditions liability on subjecting the continuing product to rate review and “reasonably identifying” a discontinued product — the term “reasonably identify” is ambiguous and should be defined or replaced with a clear evidentiary standard.

[P3] State regulators will request that §146.152(d)(3)(ii) require documentation submitted with rate review to include a mapping table tying discontinued plan IDs to continuing plan IDs with explanations of differences.

[P3] Legal commenters will challenge whether linking discontinuation relief to federal rate review in §146.152(d)(3)(ii) may conflict with states that have different rate review processes or timelines.

[P4] §146.152(f)(3)(i) tying renewability to “same issuer or controlled group” may enable insurers to shift products to affiliate entities to avoid nonrenewal restrictions; commenters will ask for anti-avoidance language preventing form, not substance, reorganizations.

[P14] §153.320(a)(1) obligates HHS to publish risk adjustment methodology via rulemaking in advance of the benefit year; industry commenters will request minimum lead times and a predictable schedule (e.g., at least 180 days before open enrollment) for methodology publication.

[P16] Insurer commenters will ask HHS to provide a reconciliation timeline and interest/penalty rules for under- or over-payments under §153.610(f)(2).

[P17] §153.630(b)(7)(iii) mandates review of all relevant paid pharmacy claims beginning in the 2018 benefit year to validate enrollee health status — issuers will raise operational and privacy concerns and request phased implementation or scope-limiting language (e.g., only pharmacy claims relevant to validation codes).

[P17] Pharmacy benefit managers and issuers will seek clarification under §153.630(b)(7)(iii) about whether denied or reversed pharmacy claims are included and the timeframe for accessible pharmacy data retrieval.

[P18] The 15-calendar-day deadline in §153.630(d)(1) to confirm initial validation audit samples is unreasonably short given data gathering across vendors and will likely be infeasible for many issuers; commenters will request an extension to 30 or 45 days.

[P18] Legal commenters will note §153.630(d)(1) lacks specificity on the “manner set forth by HHS” and request HHS publish the required confirmation/discrepancy report format and secure transmission methods.

[P19] §153.630(d)(2)’s 30-day deadline to confirm second audit findings or file discrepancies may be inadequate for complex record retrieval or third-party vendor coordination; issuers will ask for a 60-day period and a tolling provision when records are with providers.

[P19] Auditors and issuers will request that §153.630(d)(2) permit iterative discussions before a formal discrepancy filing to reduce adversarial appeals and administrative burden.

[P20] §153.630(d)(3) grants appeal rights under §156.1220 — commenters will ask HHS to clarify timelines and evidentiary standards for these appeals and whether independent third-party review will be available to reduce perceived agency bias.

[P22] Under §155.200(f)(4)(i), requiring standardized premium calculation, payment, and collection processes may conflict with state-specific laws on premium payment mechanics; States will ask for explicit preemption or waiver language.

[P23] §155.200(f)(4)(ii) forcing QHP issuers to adhere to Federally-facilitated SHOP rate change timelines may disrupt existing state rate filing cycles; issuers will request alignment mechanisms or grandfather provisions.

[P24] Establishing minimum participation rates under §155.200(f)(4)(iii) could harm small employers; commenters will ask for flexibility or exemptions for small groups and transitional relief.

[P25] §155.200(f)(4)(iv)’s employer contribution methodology mandate may conflict with collective bargaining agreements and state insurance requirements; labor groups and employers will request carve-outs for bargained plans.

[P26] The annual employee open enrollment requirement in §155.200(f)(4)(v) should allow employers flexibility to align with existing corporate plans; commenters will request optional alignment periods and notice timelines to avoid administrative burdens.

[P27] §155.200(f)(4)(vi) requires effective date rules consistent with Federally-facilitated SHOP — employers will ask for clear rules on retroactive effective dates and for exceptions when delays are caused by employer action or vendor error.

[P28] Termination policy requirements in §155.200(f)(4)(vii) may conflict with state continuation or COBRA rules; commenters will request that the provision explicitly conform to state and federal continuation obligations.

[P29] §155.205(c)(2)(iii)(A) requires taglines by the first day of 2017 open enrollment — Exchanges and issuers will state that the timeline is unworkable and ask for a later compliance date with phased implementation for websites and printed materials.

[P30] The requirement in §155.205(c)(2)(iii)(A) to include language availability taglines in the top 15 LEP languages will be burdensome for small QHP issuers; commenters will ask for proportionality (e.g., top 5 languages for single-state small issuers).

[P30] Civil rights and LEP advocates will support the top 15 language threshold in §155.205(c)(2)(iii)(A) but request that HHS provide standardized, professionally translated taglines to ensure accuracy.

[P31] The aggregation permission in §155.205(c)(2)(iii)(A) may mask local LEP needs if Exchanges aggregate across states; community organizations will argue that local language outreach obligations should be preserved and that aggregation must not reduce services in particular states.

[P32] The issuer permission under §155.205(c)(2)(iii)(A) to aggregate LEP populations across controlled-group states could allow large issuers to avoid providing localized language support; consumer groups will request that issuers still be required to provide language services where they have significant enrollment.

[P33] Allowing compliance via a prominent link under §155.205(c)(2)(iii)(A) may be insufficient for non-English speakers who may not navigate the link; commenters will ask that full taglines be on the homepage text (not just behind a link) for accessibility.

[P34] §155.205(c)(2)(iii)(B) obligating agents/brokers to include taglines beginning in 2017 imposes training and system change costs; broker associations will request phased compliance and liability protection for inadvertent noncompliance.

[P35] Requiring agents/brokers to include top 15 LEP language taglines per §155.205(c)(2)(iii)(B) could be disproportionate for single-state brokers; commenters will ask for the same proportionality exceptions suggested for issuers.

[P36] The aggregation permission in §155.205(c)(2)(iii)(B) for multi-state agents/brokers risks under-serving LEP customers in high-need states; community groups will request that brokers still provide state-specific language assistance.

[P37] Alternative compliance by posting a prominent link for agents/brokers (§155.205(c)(2)(iii)(B)) is inadequate for low-literacy populations; advocates will request additional modalities (phone hotlines, text messages) to ensure LEP access.

[P38] Privacy and security commenters will insist that §155.220(c)(3)(i)(E) include encryption and secure storage standards for the ten-year retention to protect consumer data.

[P39] §155.220(c)(3)(i)(H) requiring display consistency with Federally-facilitated Exchange displays may stifle innovation by agents/brokers; industry will request a streamlined approval process for deviations rather than blanket prohibition without process.

[P40] Under §155.220(c)(3)(i)(I), the obligation to prominently display HHS information about APTC/CSR eligibility requires frequent updates; agents/brokers will ask HHS to provide a centralized, machine-readable feed to ensure consistent, up-to-date displays.

[P41] §155.220(c)(3)(i)(J) allowing consumers to select advance premium tax credit amounts requires clear consumer safeguards and UI design standards to prevent accidental over- or under-selection; consumer advocates will ask for required confirmations and plain-language explanations.

[P42] The requirement in §155.220(c)(3)(i)(K) to support post-enrollment activities should specify response timeframes and escalation processes so consumers are not left with unresolved enrollment issues.

[P43] §155.220(c)(3)(i)(L) mandating demonstration of operational readiness before using an agent/broker website to complete QHP selections should include explicit testing standards and an appeals process if HHS denies operational readiness.

[P44] §155.220(c)(3)(i)(M) authorizing immediate suspension of agent/broker access poses due process concerns; commenters will request notice, a cure period, and an expedited review process before suspension or at minimum immediate notification and right to remedy.

[P45] §155.220(4)(i)(E) requiring reporting of potential material breaches to HHS and State insurance departments should define “material breach” and establish timelines, confidentiality protections, and coordinated notification responsibilities to avoid duplicative reporting.

[P48] §155.230(d)(2) allowing electronic or standard mail notice elections requires clear consent and proof-of-delivery standards; commenters will request that Exchanges obtain explicit written consent from employers/employees for electronic notice and keep auditable records.

[P54] Allowing Exchanges under §155.330(e)(2)(iii)(B) to follow Secretary-published guidance as an alternative is useful, but commenters will ask that such guidance be published with ample notice and public comment opportunities.

[P55] §155.330(e)(2)(iii)(C) permitting Secretary-approved alternative procedures requires objective approval criteria (e.g., demonstration metrics) and timelines for HHS review so Exchanges can plan; commenters will request that approvals be time-limited and revocable.

[P1] The proposed definition of “reporting entity” in §402.1(c)(21) is ambiguous because it does not specify whether third‑party administrators (TPAs), stop‑loss carriers, or administrative service organizations for self‑funded plans are covered; clarify whether these intermediaries are subject to CMPs.

[P1] The rule lacks safe‑harbor language clarifying that inadvertent technical or system errors in the reporting transmission (e.g., file format errors) should not automatically be treated as report violations under §402.1(c)(21).

[P2] The 1‑year reporting deadline in §402.1(c)(21)(i) is unworkable for large employers and multiemployer plans that have delayed roster updates; request extension to 18–24 months or allowance for phased reporting for plans with >10,000 enrollees.

[P2] The provision §402.1(c)(21)(i) does not define “GHP coverage effective date” for mid‑year plan changes, COBRA, or retroactive enrollment — CMS should provide precise definitions and examples.

[P3] §402.1(c)(21)(ii) prohibiting contradictions during CMS recovery efforts is overly broad and could penalize entities that correct prior inadvertent reporting errors; request an affirmative right to amend prior reports without penalty if corrections are documented and submitted promptly.

[P3] The prohibition in §402.1(c)(21)(ii) should include an exception for cases where CMS guidance or requests reveal inaccuracies created by prior CMS interpretations; require CMS to accept corrected data without penalties in those instances.

[P4] The error‑rate standard in §402.1(c)(21)(iii) that triggers violation when exceeded in 4 of 8 consecutive reporting periods is arbitrary; request publication of the Secretary’s methodology and consideration of using a weighted or rolling average rather than a simple count.

[P4] The rule lacks specificity on how reporting “periods” are defined (monthly/quarterly/annual) for §402.1(c)(21)(iii); CMS should define reporting period length and the timing of submissions.

[P5] §402.1(c)(21)(iv)(A) exception that delays CMPs for two reporting periods after a policy/procedural change is insufficient for major system migrations; request extension to four reporting periods and allowance for documented implementation plans.

[P6] §402.1(c)(21)(iv)(B) condition that compliance with thresholds or exclusions avoids CMPs needs clear thresholds and examples; stakeholders need to know numeric tolerances and how exclusions apply before relying on the exception.

[P7] The definition of “applicable plan” in §402.1(c)(22) is unclear whether it includes self‑insured employers, insurers, and TPAs — request explicit list of covered actors and responsibilities.

[P8] The 1‑year reporting requirement in §402.1(c)(22)(i) from the TPOC date is unrealistic for complex settlements where plaintiffs change counsel or releases occur late; request extension to 18 months or tolling during active settlement disputes.

[P8] §402.1(c)(22)(i) does not address settlements with periodic payment structures where a TPOC is unclear; ask CMS to clarify treatment of structured settlements and the date that starts the reporting clock.

[P9] The prohibition in §402.1(c)(22)(ii) against contradicting prior NGHP reporting during recovery efforts should allow for good‑faith corrections when new information becomes available without automatically triggering penalties.

[P10] The error threshold cap “not to exceed 20%” in §402.1(c)(22)(iii) is extremely low for many NGHPs that rely on third‑party vendor matching; request graduated tolerances by plan size and complexity and require CMS to publish the tolerance level and calculation method.

[P10] The “4 out of 8” periods standard in §402.1(c)(22)(iii) should be replaced with a statistically validated approach; otherwise plans subject to seasonal variations could be unfairly penalized.

[P11] §402.1(c)(22)(iv)(A) Good‑faith effort exception is useful but the requirements are onerous and may not be sufficient to protect plans that legitimately cannot obtain MBIs/SSNs; propose accepting alternative proof such as attestation by counsel or claimant declarations.

[P12] The requirement in §402.1(c)(22)(iv)(A)(1) to communicate to the individual and their attorney about needing identifying information is reasonable but should allow electronic communications (email, secure portal) as sufficient in addition to mail.

[P13] The mandate in §402.1(c)(22)(iv)(A)(2) to make at least two mail requests and one phone/other contact is too prescriptive; require flexibility to use email, secure file transfers, or portal messages and allow documented single comprehensive outreach in certain documented circumstances.

[P14] §402.1(c)(22)(iv)(A)(3) conditions the CMP exception on a documented “no response” or written refusal to provide MBI/SSN; this will be difficult when claimants provide partial info or ambiguous replies — request that partial cooperation (e.g., providing last 4 digits) qualify if accompanied by documented attempts to get full info.

[P15] Documenting “efforts” per §402.1(c)(22)(iv)(A)(4) should require a specified log format and minimum data elements; otherwise enforcement will be arbitrary. CMS should publish example documentation templates.

[P16] §402.1(c)(22)(iv)(B) exception allowing CMP avoidance where NGHP meets reporting thresholds/exclusions should explicitly state whether small settlement exemptions or de minimis exemptions apply and set concrete thresholds.

[P17] §402.1(c)(22)(iv)(C) delay of CMPs for two reporting periods after a policy/procedural change again is insufficient for NGHPs implementing new claims systems; request CMS to allow a remediation plan with longer safe‑harbor when reasonable.

[P18] §402.105(b)(2) cross‑references to §1862(b)(7) obligations should expressly state how CMS will coordinate CMP assessments with state regulators to avoid duplicative penalties on the same conduct.

[P19] §402.105(b)(2)(i) penalizes late reporting measured from the later of GHP coverage effective date or Medicare entitlement; this “later of” rule could unfairly penalize for retroactive entitlement determinations — ask CMS to use the date the entity reasonably should have known the beneficiary was Medicare‑eligible.

[P20] The daily penalty calculation in §402.105(b)(2)(i)(A) based on the number of records submitted more than 1 year late is administratively complex and may double‑count days for multiple records; request CMS to clarify aggregation rules and provide examples.

[P21] The penalty amount up to $1,000/day per individual in §402.105(b)(2)(i)(B) is punitive and could produce catastrophic liabilities (exceeding $365,000 per beneficiary per year) for large employers over clerical errors; request lower per‑day amounts, caps tied to plan size, or a reasonableness standard.

[P22] §402.105(b)(2)(ii) prohibiting contradictions during recovery efforts duplicates §402.1(c)(21)(ii) and should include a cure period and an appeals process before penalties are assessed.

[P23] The calculation method in §402.105(b)(2)(ii)(A) that counts calendar days for failure to report updates lacks clarity on when the clock starts and stops; require CMS to define event triggers that start the counting period.

[P24] §402.105(b)(2)(ii)(B)’s $1,000/day per individual for failure to report updates is disproportionate for minor classification errors (e.g., wrong Medicare HICN vs. MBI); request tiered penalties based on severity and intent.

[P25] §402.105(b)(2)(iii) references Secretary‑established tolerances but caps them at 20 percent; stakeholders request CMS to publish the tolerances, statistical methodology, and an appeals mechanism.

[P26] The penalty basis in §402.105(b)(2)(iii)(A) relying on the “number of beneficiary records on the fourth submission” is vague — clarify whether partial corrections across submissions reset the count and how multiple submissions for the same beneficiary are handled.

[P27] §402.105(b)(2)(iii)(B) prescribes $1,000/day per individual for records exceeding tolerances; request proportionality safeguards and a maximum aggregate cap per plan year lower than $365,000 per beneficiary to prevent ruinous exposure.

[P28] §402.105(b)(3) applicable plan penalties under §1862(b)(8) should expressly state whether insurers that settle claims on behalf of NGHPs (e.g., guaranty funds) are treated as applicable plans or merely service providers.

[P29] §402.105(b)(3)(i) 1‑year TPOC reporting deadline should include a tolling provision when plaintiffs do not disclose settlement details, or when appeals could change the TPOC, to avoid unfair penalties.

[P30] The daily penalty calculation in §402.105(b)(3)(i)(A) should exclude weekends/holidays or provide an alternative “calendar day” clarification to ensure consistent computations.

[P31] §402.105(b)(3)(i)(B)’s cap of $365,000 per individual per year remains unacceptably high; recommend aligning maximum penalties with the gravity of misinformation (e.g., a $25,000 annual cap per individual).

[P32] §402.105(b)(3)(ii) contradicts the need for a correction mechanism; require CMS to allow NGHPs to amend prior reports during recovery efforts without penalty if done within a specified cure period and accompanied by documentation.

[P33] §402.105(b)(3)(ii)(A) calculation of penalty days for contradictions must clarify whether days prior to CMS notification count and whether plans can demonstrate reasonable cause to avoid counting earlier days.

[P34] §402.105(b)(3)(ii)(B) imposes up to $1,000/day with a $365,000 cap; request CMS to adopt a good‑faith compliance standard that reduces penalties for entities with robust compliance programs.

[P35] §402.105(b)(3)(iii) tiered penalties for exceeding error tolerances in 4 of 8 periods should require CMS to provide a written warning and technical assistance after the first and second exceedances before imposing monetary penalties.

[P36] §402.105(b)(3)(iii)(A) initial 25% of maximum penalty per beneficiary per day is not tied to harm and may be arbitrary; request that the initial penalty be a fixed monetary amount or percentage scaled by plan size and error magnitude.

[P37] §402.105(b)(3)(iii)(B) escalation by 25% increments up to the maximum lacks transparency — require CMS to publish the escalation schedule and examples of how the percentages translate to dollar amounts.

[P38] §402.105(b)(3)(iii)(C) reduction of penalties by 25% per compliant quarter presumes quarterly data; CMS should allow alternative remediation schedules for entities that report on a different cadence and provide an immediate reinstatement path when full compliance is demonstrated.

[P39] Table entry prohibitions in §102.3 (e.g., 1395m(k)(6), 1395m(l)(6)) regarding assignment‑related billing are duplicative of existing fraud statutes; request CMS to harmonize definitions of “knowingly and willfully” and clarify enforcement priorities to avoid double penalties.

[P40] The requirement in Table entry 1395y(b)(6)(B) to complete claim forms accurately about OHI availability (§102.3) imposes strict liability for errors by enrollees or providers; request a presumption of good faith when errors are promptly corrected.

[P41] The penalties in Table entries for failure to provide information identifying when GHP/NGHP is primary (§102.3 entries for 1395y(b)(7)(B)(i), 1395y(b)(8)(E)(i)) should not apply where the insurer has no practical way to know a payment is related to a Medicare beneficiary (e.g., anonymous litigation settlements); clarify knowledge and willfulness standards.

[P42] §102.3 Table entry 1395pp(h) refund timing obligations for DME suppliers lack clear timelines and conditions for complex return or repair situations; CMS should specify reasonable timelines and dispute resolution processes.

[P43] §102.3 entries for Medicare supplemental policy approval (1395ss(a)(2), (p)(8), (p)(9)(C)) impose federal penalties for state regulatory decisions; request CMS to coordinate with states and provide a safe harbor for insurers while awaiting state approvals.

[P44] Penalties associated with suspension/reinstatement obligations in §102.3 (1395ss(q)(5)(C)) should allow automated systems to handle suspensions and prevent penalties when actions are taken in good faith based on state Medicaid lists.

[P45] The requirement to publish a regular timeline for final regulations per Section 1871(a)(3)(A) (P52) is acceptable, but CMS should commit to publishing the methodology and criteria used to set timelines and to notify stakeholders when complex rules will take longer.

[P46] For the permission to extend timelines under Section 1871(a)(3)(B) (P53, P55), request that any extension beyond the original targeted date requires a public comment period on the justification and an estimate of the new publication date.

[P47] Section 1871(a)(3) prohibition on initial timelines exceeding three years (P54) should be interpreted to require CMS to update the public quarterly on progress toward final rules if initial timelines approach three years.

[P48] The permitted factors for varying timelines under Section 1871(a)(3)(B) (P56) should explicitly include resource constraints and interagency coordination problems, and CMS should publish a checklist of factors used to extend timelines.

[P49] The DATES extension to February 18, 2024 (P57) is now stale; request CMS to update the rule text and cross‑references to reflect the current state and avoid confusion for regulated entities about final rule timing.

[P50] Overall, the rule imposes severe per‑beneficiary per‑day penalties without a clear intent standard; request insertion of a “willful or knowing” culpability requirement and a reasonable cause/cure period before monetary penalties are assessed.

[P1] The rule’s statement that a PIP “qualifies for a FIFRA exemption only if it meets the criteria in paragraphs (a)–(d)” is ambiguous about who bears the burden of proof for meeting those criteria; industry requests explicit allocation that the developer bears the burden and must retain documentation for EPA inspection.

[P1] Environmental and public health groups will comment that allowing any broad exemption from FIFRA is inappropriate without mandatory independent safety testing and that § 174.21 should not permit exemptions that could avoid meaningful EPA risk assessment.

[P2] Farmers and seed companies will point out that § 174.21’s cross-reference to “all the requirements of FIFRA” creates uncertainty about which registration pathways and fees apply; commenters will request an explicit list or reference of which FIFRA sections (e.g., registration, labeling, worker protection) apply to non-exempt PIPs.

[P3] Trade associations will argue that requiring the pesticidal substance to satisfy at least one criterion in §§ 174.25–174.50 is acceptable only if those downstream criteria are clearly defined and not open-ended; they will request clarifying guidance or examples for borderline cases.

[P4] Food safety advocates will challenge § 174.21(b)’s two-prong approach (residues exempt in subpart W or not require a tolerance) as insufficiently protective and request that any PIP intended for food crops must undergo a mandatory tolerance assessment unless unequivocal evidence shows no residues.

[P5] Consumer advocacy groups will assert that § 174.21(c) mandating that inert ingredients be “listed as approved in subpart X” is inadequate because subpart X’s approval criteria are not described here; they will request that only inert ingredients evaluated for toxicity and dietary exposure be allowed and that the rule require public listing and review.

[P6] Small seed developers will note that § 174.21(d) conditions the exemption for “listed PIPs” on compliance with recordkeeping and eligibility procedures; they will request clarification which PIPs are “listed” and whether transitional provisions apply to legacy products.

[P7] Organic certification bodies will comment on § 174.25, arguing that exempting pesticidal substances from conventionally bred sexually compatible plants fails to address unintended compositional changes and should require compositional comparability testing against conventional counterparts.

[P8] Consumer groups will object to § 174.25(c)’s allowance of genetic transfer “only via conventional breeding” without defining “conventional breeding” (e.g., whether marker-assisted selection or protoplast fusion is included); they will request a clear regulatory definition.

[P9] Environmental NGOs will challenge § 174.26’s blanket exemption possibility for biotechnology-derived sexually compatible plants, arguing that biotechnology methods can have off-target effects and that exemption should not be permitted absent rigorous case-by-case assessment.

[P10] Industry biotech trade groups will support § 174.26(a) but request that the types of insertion and modification described be expanded to include modern genome editing techniques (e.g., base editing, prime editing) explicitly to avoid regulatory uncertainty.

[P11] Seed companies will request that § 174.26(a)(1)’s pathway “engineering a native gene into a non-genic location” include criteria for confirming identity (e.g., sequence identity thresholds, functional assays) so developers know what “identical” means.

[P12] Plant breeders will comment that § 174.26(a)(2)(i) permitting modification that changes expression level but not identity needs quantitative thresholds (e.g., fold-change limits) for “not higher” and specify acceptable measurement methods and tissues.

[P13] Food manufacturers will request that § 174.26(a)(2)(ii)’s allowance for producing a substance “identical to a native allele” require documentation of allele frequency and natural variation to justify identity claims and to assess allergenicity/ tox profile.

[P14] Legal experts will warn that § 174.26(a)(2)(iii) permitting combined modifications could create complex regulatory classification issues and request a decision tree or flowchart to determine when an event remains exempt versus requiring full FIFRA review.

[P15] Public health advocates will object that § 174.26(a)(2)(iv) allowing loss-of-function modifications could produce novel secondary metabolites or increased susceptibility to pests and therefore should trigger at minimum compositional and toxicity screening.

[P16] Several commenters will demand that § 174.26(b)’s restriction that expression must not be “higher or in different tissues/developmental stages” include precise numerical expression thresholds, specified comparator plants, validated assay methods, and statistical criteria for equivalence.

[P17] Industry will request that § 174.26(c)’s requirement that exemptions are not effective until “subpart E requirements have been satisfied” be clarified to specify which subpart E deliverables (data types and timelines) are required and whether EPA confirmation of completeness is needed.

[P18] Small growers and seed companies will complain that § 174.73’s five-year recordkeeping obligation will be onerous and request either a shorter retention period or an option to retain records electronically with clear templates to reduce administrative burden.

[P19] Compliance officers will propose that § 174.73(a) define the minimum content and format for the “documentation of the self-determination or EPA request and supporting documents” to avoid disputes over adequacy (e.g., required tables, sequence files, lab reports).

[P20] Legal commenters will request that § 174.73(b) include procedural details on how and within what timeframe EPA may request documentation, and protections against fishing expeditions (e.g., limits on frequency, scope, and confidentiality).

[P21] Developers will ask that § 174.90(a) clarify what qualifies as the “at least one” action required for exemption eligibility (self-determination vs. EPA confirmation) and whether administrative fees or waiting periods apply to each path.

[P22] Industry will support § 174.90(a)(1) but request explicit assurances that a valid self-determination will be treated as legally effective pending EPA review, with a defined timeline for EPA to challenge the determination to preserve business planning certainty.

[P23] Developers will note that § 174.90(a)(2) permitting EPA confirmation requests must include fee and timeline provisions; they will request a specified review deadline (e.g., 120 days) after which EPA must either confirm or refuse.

[P24] Administrative commenters will request that § 174.90(b) provide alternate submission mechanisms (secure electronic portal) in addition to the specified mailing address and that EPA commit to acknowledging receipt within a defined timeframe.

[P25] Startups will welcome § 174.90(c) allowing submission of both self-determination and EPA request but ask that the rule specify whether submitting both triggers simultaneous review or whether EPA will prioritize one path, to avoid duplicative work.

[P26] Civil liberties groups will request safeguards in § 174.90(d)(intro) to ensure EPA’s notification of intent to review and any follow‑up information requests are narrowly tailored and time-limited to avoid indefinite business uncertainty.

[P27] Developers and trade groups will demand that § 174.90(d) include an explicit appeals or dispute resolution process if EPA determines a PIP does not meet exemption criteria, including a timeline for corrective action before enforcement.

[P28] Legal commenters will assert that § 174.90(d)’s statement that noncompliant PIPs “may be considered...subject to enforcement” is vague and request specification of potential penalties, opportunity to cure, and whether actions already taken will be grandfathered.

[P29] Large seed companies will support § 174.90(e)(1) allowing extension to subsequent engineering into other varieties but request clarity on whether this applies across different registrants, contract farmers, and sublicensed varieties.

[P30] Breeders will urge clarification of § 174.90(e)(1)(i) about “identical substance without modifying regulatory regions” to define what constitutes a regulatory region and how to document absence of modifications (e.g., sequencing coverage depth).

[P31] Developers will ask § 174.90(e)(1)(ii) to define “targeting the same regulatory sequence resulting in NHEJ mutation” — specifically whether different NHEJ indel outcomes are allowed and what phenotypic and molecular evidence must be supplied.

[P32] Commenters will request that § 174.90(e)(1)(iii) include streamlined procedures and timelines for producing a new self-determination or EPA request for subsequent engineering events to avoid unnecessary market disruption.

[P33] Developers using the self-determination route will stress in comments that § 174.91 imposeable requirements must be practicable and request an example self-determination template and checklist corresponding to § 174.91(b) elements.

[P34] Industry will insist that § 174.91(a)’s requirement to submit the self-determination letter “prior to engaging in FIFRA-subject activities” be clarified with a bright-line definition of “engaging” (e.g., field testing, seed multiplication, commercial sales).

[P35] Commenters will request that § 174.91(b)’s list of content elements be harmonized with § 174.93(b) to avoid duplicative submissions and that EPA provide an electronic form that enforces required fields.

[P36] Corporate compliance officers will ask that § 174.91(b)(1) provide privacy protections for submitter contact information and clarify how EPA will handle confidential business information (CBI) claims associated with submitter identity.

[P37] Developers will request that § 174.91(b)(2) specify the exact “exemption-specific information” required (e.g., sequences, expression assays, tissue panels) and acceptable formats to ensure submissions are accepted as complete.

[P38] Legal commenters will request § 174.91(b)(2)(i) be updated to include examples or citations for how to choose the correct paragraph under §§ 174.26 or 174.541 to reduce mis-categorization risk.

[P39] Commenters will recommend revising § 174.91(b)(3) certification text to add a safe harbor limiting criminal liability for inadvertent errors in self-determination where the developer acted in good faith and promptly corrected mistakes.

[P40] Corporate counsel will request that § 174.91(b)(4) clarify who qualifies as an “authorized company representative” for signature purposes (e.g., officer level, delegated signatory) to avoid rejections.

[P41] Industry and rulemaking commenters will request that § 174.91(c) require written confirmation within a shorter, defined timeframe (e.g., 5 business days for mailed submissions) rather than 30 business days to reduce uncertainty.

[P42] Several commenters will note that § 174.91(d) making the exemption effective only after EPA confirms receipt is problematic because immediate electronic confirmation is deemed equivalent to written; they will ask EPA to state that electronic timestamped confirmations provide legal effect.

[P43] Developers requesting EPA confirmation under § 174.93 will ask for a formal pre-submission consultation option to resolve data adequacy questions before a formal submission to avoid cycles of deficiency requests.

[P44] Commenters will request that § 174.93(a) state clear consequences if EPA does not act on a confirmation request within a defined period (e.g., constructive approval or a status escalation process) to prevent indefinite delay.

[P45] Biotechnology firms will request that § 174.93(b) limit the scope of EPA’s “supporting documentation” requests to only information necessary to determine exemption eligibility and prohibit requests for unrelated proprietary R&D data.

[P46] Industry groups will ask that § 174.93(c) include an explicit timeline for EPA’s review (e.g., 180 days) and require EPA to provide a written deficiency notice with specific data requests and timelines for response.

[P47] Developers will request that § 174.93(d) clarify whether EPA’s written notification that an exempt status applies is subject to judicial review and whether the notification is a final agency action for court purposes.

[P48] Commenters will seek clarification in § 174.95 that documentation maintained under § 174.73 includes raw data (e.g., sequencing files) and request guidance on acceptable data standards and formats for sequences and expression data.

[P49] Botanists and registrants will support § 174.95(a)(1) but request that EPA accept cultivar-level identifiers in addition to genus and species and provide guidance on taxonomic updates or synonyms.

[P50] Commenters will urge that § 174.95(a)(2) require the developer to provide peer-reviewed evidence of sexual compatibility when derived from another species, and request criteria for acceptable evidence (crossing studies, fertility data).

[P51] Consumer safety groups will demand that § 174.95(b) require developers to provide quantitative exposure estimates and data demonstrating how breeding ensures safe toxin levels in food plants, not just descriptive statements.

[P52] Scientists will request that § 174.95(c)(1) specify acceptable sequence submission formats (e.g., FASTA), minimum sequencing coverage, and that sequence comparisons include nearest natural alleles and public database accession numbers.

[P53] Commenters will ask that § 174.95(c)(2) set explicit numeric equivalence limits for expression level comparisons and require tissue-by-tissue analysis with statistical methods prescribed for demonstrating non-expansion of expression.

[P54] Consumer advocacy groups will challenge § 174.508 for allowing tolerance exemptions for conventionally bred PIPs without mandatory residue monitoring and will request post-market residue surveillance requirements as a condition of exemption.

[P55] Food safety commenters will request a definition of “conventional breeding” in § 174.508(c) that excludes methods that might introduce foreign genetic material (e.g., protoplast fusion without segregation) and specify acceptable breeding techniques.

[P56] Public health advocates will insist that § 174.508(d)’s “not present in food at levels that are injurious” standard require a specified toxicological benchmark or reference dose and specify who bears the burden of proof.

[P57] Industry will support § 174.541’s parallel pathway for biotechnology-derived residues but request consistency with international standards (Codex, OECD) to avoid trade disruptions and duplicate testing.

[P58] Companies will request that § 174.541(a) explicitly include modern genome editing methods (base, prime editing) in the described insertion/modification methods to avoid interpretation that they are excluded.

[P59] Developers will request that § 174.541(a)(1) require criteria for proving “identical” pesticidal substance (e.g., amino acid sequence identity threshold, post-translational modifications assessment).

[P60] Food processors will seek that § 174.541(a)(2)(i) include quantitative thresholds for acceptable changes in production amount (e.g., fold-change limits) and require evaluation of processing effects on residues.

[P61] Public interest groups will request that § 174.541(a)(2)(ii) require disclosure of natural allele frequency and allergenicity/toxicity comparisons when claiming identity to a native allele.

[P62] Scientists will recommend that § 174.541(a)(2)(iii) include guidance on cumulative or synergistic effects when multiple modifications are combined and require at least tiered toxicology screening.

[P63] Health advocates will comment that § 174.541(a)(2)(iv) loss-of-function exemptions must still require compositional analysis because loss of a target protein can alter metabolic flux and generate novel compounds.

[P64] Consumer groups will demand that § 174.541(b) define “matching those in a sexually compatible plant” with precise tissue panels, developmental stages, and acceptable measurement variability to ensure tolerances are comparable.

[P65] Legal and industry commenters will ask that § 174.541(c) specify what “requirements in subpart E” must be satisfied, expected timelines, and whether EPA’s completeness determinations are appealable.
