raw_output:
[P1] The requirement to "maintain the Federal Register online and make it available on at least one GPO website" lacks specificity about uptime, accessibility standards (e.g., WCAG), and preservation of historical content; commenters request explicit minimum availability and accessibility metrics.

[P1] Industry commenters will request clarification whether mirrored or third-party sites beyond the GPO may be used to satisfy the "at least one" website requirement for redundancy and disaster recovery.

[P2] Commenters will ask the agency to specify acceptable methods under § 12.1(b) (e.g., online form, postal mail, fax, telephone) because leaving methods unspecified creates uncertainty for institutions without reliable email/web access.

[P3] Members of Congress and staff will seek assurance that email submission via the GPO website will provide authenticated delivery and chain-of-custody (timestamped receipts) for subscription requests; they may request a requirement that confirmations be issued.

[P4] Government offices and agencies will request clarification whether "current year or the upcoming year" subscriptions can be backdated or prorated for mid-year requests, and whether multi-year bulk subscriptions for agencies are permitted.

[P5] State and local government subscribers will object to automatic expiration at calendar year-end (§ 12.1(b)(2)(ii)) because it imposes administrative burden; they will request an option to pre-authorize renewal or multi-year subscriptions.

[P6] Libraries and long-term archives will challenge the prohibition on automatic renewal (§ 12.1(b)(2)(iii)) as counterproductive to continuity of service and request an opt-in automatic renewal mechanism or allowance for standing subscriptions.

[P7] Commenters will request that the rule require the GPO to publish clear, centralized notifications about procedures for requesting official copies or print subscriptions, with contact information and timelines, rather than merely listing locations where such notices "are available."

[P8] Stakeholders will request that the dedicated GPO official subscriptions website referenced in § 12.1(c)(1) include machine-readable subscription metadata (formats, prices, processing times) and an API for bulk requests by other government entities.

[P9] Libraries and FOIA advocates will ask for explicit confirmation that notifications on www.federalregister.gov (§ 12.1(c)(2)) will remain persistent and searchable and not be removed from the website front matter after a limited period.

[P10] Commenters will seek clarification about the phrase "front matter of the Federal Register daily issue" (§ 12.1(c)(3)) — specifically whether print front matter and online front matter are equivalent and how subscribers will be informed if front matter content is revised.

[P11] Several industry and legal commenters will object that the comment receipt date of February 12, 2021 (§ 39.13 AD para (a)) is obsolete or inconsistent with other deadlines in the document and request updated, consistent comment deadlines.

[P12] Operators and legal counsel will request clarification on the scope of applicability in § 39.13(c) — whether any Boeing 757 variants not explicitly listed but certificated under the same type certificate are covered, and how NB451 is singularly treated.

[P13] Operators will ask for more detailed definitions of "compliance times" in § 39.13(f) and request a range of acceptable compliance windows or relief for operators with maintenance scheduling conflicts.

[P14] Airlines will request that § 39.13(g) explicitly allow incorporation of equivalent procedures where the Boeing Requirements Bulletin references proprietary tooling or parts that may be backordered, i.e., a nexus for AMOCs without undue delay.

[P15] Legal commenters will request that the substitution in § 39.13(h)(1) of the AD effective date for "Revision 1/2 date" be clarified to prevent ambiguity when multiple revisions exist; they will recommend specifying the exact date string to be used.

[P16] For airplane NB451, the directive to "perform the Group 4 actions" (§ 39.13(h)(2)) will prompt requests for the precise list of Group 4 actions, associated parts lists, labor hours, and any differences from other groups — commenters seek attached technical detail.

[P17] Airlines and MRO providers will challenge the broad installation prohibition (§ 39.13(i)/(j)) on installing PSUs, life vest panels, or video panels without updated lanyards, arguing it could ground aircraft due to unavailability of updated assemblies and ask for a phased compliance schedule.

[P18] Suppliers will request clarity on whether aftermarket component manufacturers must certify that their PSUs/life vest panels/video panels include updated lanyard assemblies to be eligible for installation after the applicable times (§ 39.13(j)), and whether existing inventories are grandfathered.

[P19] Operators will point out an ambiguity between paragraphs (i)(1)/(i)(2) and (j)(1)/(j)(2) regarding the effective dates for the installation prohibition and request consolidated, unambiguous timing language for aircraft that had or lacked updated lanyards at the AD effective date.

[P20] Commenters will request that the AMOC approval authority in § 39.13(j)(1) be expanded beyond the Seattle ACO Manager to include other regional ACOs to speed approvals for operators outside the Seattle region.

[P21] Legal and industry commenters will request that the required procedure to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO per § 39.13(j)(1) be supplemented with an online submission portal and acknowledgement system to avoid lost paperwork and unclear receipt.

[P22] Operators will seek clarification on the mailing/addressing requirement in § 39.13(j)(1) when submitting AMOC information directly to the certification office manager — specifically, a contact name and physical address (it references paragraph (k)(1) but commenters will ask that the rule itself include the contact).

[P23] Commenters will express privacy and security concerns about permitting AMOC requests via the specified email address (§ 39.13(j)(1) email) and request data-protection requirements or encrypted submission options for sensitive technical data.

[P24] Operators will ask for a specific timeline for FAA response to AMOC requests (§ 39.13(j)(1)) and a de facto approval/denial timeline to prevent prolonged grounding while waiting for an AMOC decision.

[P25] Boeing and other commenters will support paragraph (j)(3) allowing Boeing ODA approval of AMOCs for repairs/mods, but will request clarification about the scope of the ODA's authority and whether such approvals supersede FAA regional procedures.

[P26] Certification authorities will request that the requirement that an AMOC meet the airplane's certification basis (§ 39.13(j)(3) condition) include a clear process for resolving conflicts where the original certification basis is unclear or multiple certification bases apply.

[P27] Multiple stakeholders will note the inconsistent comment deadlines listed (January 3, 2022 in § 39.13(a) and elsewhere February 12, 2021) and request a single, correct comment deadline be published and any previous dates removed to avoid confusion.

[P28] Airlines and unions will request relief or extension for compliance with the AD's deadlines (§ 39.13(f)/(g)) if supply chain disruptions delay acquisition of updated lanyard assemblies, asking for a waiver or interim operational mitigation (e.g., placarding) until parts are available.

[P29] Operators will ask that credit for actions done using Revision 1 (§ 39.13(i)) be broadened to include equivalent work done to the same safety standard by other approved providers, not only actions explicitly using Revision 1 of Boeing's bulletin.

[P30] VT Mobile Aerospace Engineering will likely comment in support of § 39.13(h)(2)/(h)(2 exception) that exempts certain modified 757–200s from lanyard installation, but request explicit recordkeeping and modification identification guidance to ensure operators can rely on the exception.

[P31] Maintenance organizations will ask for inclusion of detailed parts numbers, torque values, and step-by-step procedures referenced in the Boeing Requirements Bulletins to be incorporated by reference or appended to the AD for enforceability and clarity (§ 39.13(g)).

[P32] Commenters will request that the prohibition on installing affected panels without updated lanyards (§ 39.13(j)/(s) prohibitions) include a clear definition of "updated lanyard assembly" including part numbers and acceptable alternatives to avoid enforcement ambiguity.

[P33] Legal commenters will point out duplication and redundancy across provisions (§ 39.13 paragraphs repeated in P11–P44) and request consolidation to avoid conflicting obligations and ensure the final AD is concise and internally consistent.

[P34] Smaller operators and charter companies will request cost estimates and an economic impact analysis be included or updated in the preamble, arguing that compliance (lanyard parts, labor, grounding) could impose significant unquantified costs.

[P35] Safety advocacy groups will support the lanyard installation requirement but request the AD include explicit safety rationale and incident data justifying the urgency and scope of the prohibitions on installations without updated lanyards.

[P36] International operators will request clarification whether foreign-registered Boeing 757s operating internationally are subject to the AD's installation prohibitions and AMOC procedures and how bilateral agreements affect compliance.

[P37] Commenters will request that the FAA provide a clear grandfathering provision for spare parts inventories produced before the AD effective date to avoid waste and stranded inventory, specifying a sell-through period or labeling requirement.

[P38] Airlines will request temporary relief allowing installation of legacy panels with supplemental procedures (e.g., additional inspections, placarding) where updated lanyards are unavailable, pending AMOC approval, without violating the absolute prohibition in § 39.13(j).

[P39] Aviation insurers will request clarification on liability allocation for installations performed under AMOCs approved by the Boeing ODA per § 39.13(j)(3) — specifically whether insurer consent or notice is required when AMOCs alter configurations.

[P40] Industry standards bodies will request that the AD require updated lanyard assemblies to meet standardized performance and test criteria (e.g., tensile strength, fire resistance) and ask that those criteria be published or referenced.

[P41] Commenters will ask for an explicit mechanism and timeline for emergency AMOC processing for operators facing immediate safety issues or scheduled revenue flights, to prevent unnecessary cancellations.

[P42] Aircraft lessors will request guidance on responsibilities between lessor and lessee for compliance with the AD (installations, AMOCs, recordkeeping) and whether lessors must approve AMOC requests submitted by lessees.

[P43] Maintenance recordkeepers will request explicit instructions about how to document compliance with paragraph (g) and credit under paragraph (i), including forms or data fields to ensure auditability.

[P44] Commenters will request that the FAA publish the exact contact identified in paragraphs (k)(1)/(l)(1) within the AD text (name, phone, postal address) to remove ambiguity when directing AMOC submissions or correspondence.

[P45] Small repair stations will request training and certification guidance for technicians performing the required lanyard installations, including whether specialized certification or Boeing training is mandatory to meet the AD's requirements.

[P46] Commenters will recommend that the FAA allow temporary deviations for humanitarian or medical flights where immediate installation of updated lanyards is infeasible, with specified compensating measures to maintain safety.

[P47] Industry groups will request that the AD explicitly permit use of equivalent commercial-off-the-shelf lanyard assemblies that meet specified performance standards, rather than restricting installations to Boeing-specified parts only.

[P48] Aviation attorneys will request clarification of the interplay between the AMOC process (j/k) and other regulatory relief mechanisms under 14 CFR, e.g., exemptions or special flight permits, to avoid procedural conflicts.

[P49] Commenters will ask the FAA to publish a FAQ and implementation timeline for operators addressing common scenarios (e.g., mixed fleets, stored aircraft, spare part pools) to facilitate uniform compliance.

[P50] Public commenters will request translation or outreach to non-English-speaking operators and MROs worldwide to ensure understanding of the AD's requirements, deadlines, and AMOC procedures.

[P1] The January 22, 2019 deadline for submitting public comments is unreasonably short and will prevent meaningful participation by small operators and consumer advocacy groups that require more time to analyze the technical service letter.

[P1] The rule should extend the comments due date beyond January 22, 2019 to at least 60 days from publication to allow stakeholders sufficient time to prepare substantive comments.

[P1] The FAA must accept late comments submitted after January 22, 2019 when good cause is shown (e.g., stakeholders only recently received the referenced Rockwell Collins service information).

[P2] Requiring operators to determine CSU and FMC part numbers by referring to manufacturer or STC holder maintenance instructions is vague—specify how to resolve conflicts between manufacturer and STC documentation.

[P2] The rule should provide an alternative verification method (e.g., physical unit inspection or serial number cross-reference with FAA registry) when manufacturer or STC maintenance instructions are unavailable.

[P2] Note 1 should obligate manufacturers and STC holders to make the necessary maintenance instructions publicly accessible (e.g., via a download link) so operators can comply.

[P3] The phrase “within the compliance times specified” in (f) is ambiguous; the AD must list explicit calendar-based deadlines per operator class (e.g., commuter, large air carrier, part 135 operators).

[P3] There should be an exception for aircraft that have documented operational constraints preventing compliance within the specified times—provide an explicit temporary ferry or operational relief process.

[P4] The 12-month compliance time to disable automatic temperature compensation on the CSU is arbitrary; some commenters will request a shorter compliance time (e.g., 90–180 days) if data show a safety risk.

[P4] Conversely, smaller operators and low-utilization aircraft request extending the 12-month deadline to 18–24 months to accommodate maintenance scheduling and parts availability.

[P4] The AD must clarify whether disabling the temperature compensation requires software changes, hardware modification, or only a configuration change, and whether Rockwell Collins service letter steps affect warranty or avionics certification.

[P4] The AD should specify which personnel (e.g., certificated repair stations, DER-approved technicians) are authorized to perform the steps in the Rockwell Collins service letter to disable the feature.

[P4] The proposed step reference in P4 truncates at “(2”; provide the complete procedural reference and ensure the service letter revision number and date are cited to avoid confusion.

[P5] Requiring AFM limitations revision within 12 months without sample text or exact wording creates operational and legal uncertainty; the AD must include the exact language to be added to the AFM.

[P5] Operators request permission to insert the AFM limitation as an operator-specific temporary revision (e.g., via company bulletin) until the AFM can be formally reissued during scheduled maintenance.

[P5] The AD must confirm whether the AFM revision needs FAA approval or does it qualify as an operator-maintained limitation under existing AFM change procedures.

[P6] Centralizing AMOC approval authority in the Wichita ACO Branch Manager may create bottlenecks; industry requests allowing regional ACOs or the local FSDO to approve AMOCs for their certificate holders to reduce delays.

[P6] Commenters request clear criteria and expected decision timelines for the Wichita ACO Branch Manager to approve or deny AMOC requests to avoid operational disruption.

[P7] Requiring AMOC requests to be routed through the principal inspector or local FSDO may delay submissions; allow direct submission to the ACO with a courtesy copy to the principal inspector.

[P7] The AD should specify acceptable content and supporting data for AMOC requests (test data, risk assessment, leak-down data, etc.) to reduce back-and-forth and speed approvals.

[P8] If AMOC information is sent directly to the ACO manager, the AD must identify the specific name, mailing address, email, and fax number referenced in paragraph (j)(1) to ensure proper routing.

[P8] The rule should permit electronic submission of AMOC documentation (encrypted email or a secure portal) rather than relying on physical mail to the ACO manager.

[P9] The requirement to notify the principal inspector or local FSDO before using an approved AMOC is unclear about timing—is notification prior to first use required, or within a specified number of days after approval? Clarify the timeframe.

[P9] The AD must explain whether notification of AMOC use triggers additional surveillance or inspection by the principal inspector and whether that surveillance imposes costs on operators.

[P9] Provide a streamlined, standardized notification form or electronic reporting template for operators to use when notifying principal inspectors about AMOC use.

[P10] The permission to view service information at the FAA Small Airplane Directorate in Kansas City may not be practical for remote stakeholders; request that the FAA post the referenced service information on its public docket website.

[P10] Clarify whether viewing the referenced service information at the FAA office is by appointment only, and whether copies can be obtained electronically or in hard copy, and whether there will be any fee.

[P11] The contact information for Rockwell Collins appears truncated; provide a complete phone number, email, and a working web link for obtaining the service information.

[P11] Commenters request that Rockwell Collins be required to provide the service letter at no cost to operators and to make it available electronically to ensure timely compliance and review.

[P4][P5] The AD must specify whether disabling temperature compensation and revising the AFM are reversible actions, and whether re-enabling the feature in the future would require FAA approval or additional testing.

[P3][P4] State whether aircraft that have already implemented equivalent mitigations (e.g., aftermarket software fixes or CSU replacements) are considered “action already completed” under (f) or whether documentation must be submitted for verification.

[P2][P4] For aircraft modified by STC holders, require STC holders to issue service bulletins that reference the CSU/FMC RCPN and identify how to perform the disablement consistent with the STC, to avoid conflicts.

[P5] Pilot unions and safety advocates will request that the AFM revision include clear operational prohibitions (e.g., altitude or temperature operating limits) instead of vague informational notes to ensure crew compliance.

[Legal] The AD should include an explicit statement regarding the regulatory impact analysis (costs, number of affected aircraft, labor hours) for the requirements in P4 and P5 to satisfy the Administrative Procedure Act and inform commenters about economic impacts.

[Legal] Provide the legal basis for limiting AMOC approval to the Wichita ACO Branch Manager rather than allowing delegation consistent with 14 CFR 39.19 to other FAA authorities; justify the delegation decision.

[Small Business] Small repair stations and part 145 certificated facilities request an economic hardship exemption or phased compliance schedule for the 12-month requirements due to limited staff and competing mandatory maintenance.

[Safety Monitoring] Request that the FAA require reporting of anomalies or failures after disabling the temperature compensation (e.g., via service difficulty reports or AD follow-up) so the FAA can assess the effectiveness and unintended consequences.

[P4] Require a parts availability statement—if disabling the feature requires replacement components, the AD should provide lead times and allowable part numbers to prevent grounding.

[P5] Clarify whether the AFM limitation revision must be carried in both physical and electronic flight manuals and whether dispatch is allowed with a company minimum equipment list (MEL) entry referencing the temporary AFM limitation.

[P6][P9] Stakeholders request that the FAA publish a list of previously approved AMOCs for similar CSUs so applicants can reference existing approvals and streamline their requests.

[Formatting] Several provisions appear truncated (e.g., P4 shows “step 2” cut off); provide the complete AD text and referenced service information in the docket before final rulemaking to avoid ambiguous obligations.

[P2] Advocacy groups will point out that limiting federal BHP payments only to months of documented enrollment and eligibility could create coverage gaps for retroactive eligibility determinations and request explicit rules for retroactive payment for months later determined eligible.

[P2] State Medicaid/BHP administrators will request clarification on how mid-month enrollment and terminations are handled for payment—whether partial-month payments are permitted or payments must be pro-rated.

[P3] States and auditors will ask CMS to specify the exact data elements, formats, and retention periods required by the "CMS verification requirements," since the proposed text is too general to implement consistent IT and recordkeeping systems.

[P3] Privacy and consumer advocates will demand that CMS specify security and access controls for the auditable individual records required, including limits on redisclosure and retention to protect sensitive income data.

[P4] Legal commenters will note that duplicative language in P3 and P4 could be consolidated, and request CMS clarify any differences between the two obligations to avoid inconsistent state interpretations and enforcement.

[P4] State IT directors will request a phased compliance timeline and funding assistance for building systems to produce auditable individual-level quarterly snapshots, since creating and validating point-in-time records is resource-intensive.

[P5] States will request the proposed rule to list the "certain data" required under § 600.610 and provide data submission schemas, deadlines, and error-correction procedures so states can comply uniformly.

[P5] Health plans and actuaries will ask for transparency on how CMS will use submitted data under § 600.610 to calculate Secretarial determinations, including provision of reproducible calculation files or templates.

[P6] State administrators will argue that the obligation to "collect and validate" data under the BHP methodology needs clearer standards for validation (e.g., acceptable tolerance rates, validation methods, third‑party audits).

[P6] Small states and tribal commenters will request CMS allow reliance on existing state eligibility systems and verification processes rather than imposing new validation methods that duplicate work.

[P7] States will request clarification on submission mechanisms, file formats, frequency, and acknowledgement of receipt for the required data submission to CMS to avoid misunderstandings and late submissions.

[P7] Commenters will ask CMS to provide error handling and appeals processes if CMS rejects submitted data, including timelines for corrective submission without penalty.

[P8] QHP issuers and insurer associations will note the obligation to provide CSRs despite discontinued federal CSR payments increases their uncompensated cost and request explicit federal funding, reinsurance, or compensation mechanisms.

[P8] Legal and consumer advocates will argue that maintaining insurer CSR obligations without federal payments could raise premiums—request CMS model the premium impacts and consider transitional support or regulatory relief.

[P9] Insurers and consumer groups in densely populated urban areas will object to the permission process for serving sub-county areas as unduly restrictive and request CMS to publish clear criteria and a predictable timeline for approval of sub-county service areas.

[P9] Rural health advocates will support CMS oversight but request that CMS facilitate rather than block sub-county network configurations needed to tailor plans to rural service realities.

[P10] Health plans will object that requiring payment rate cells to be at least county-sized ignores market realities in very small or very large counties and request flexibility to define rate cells by metropolitan statistical area or other meaningful geographies.

[P10] States with large, diverse counties will ask CMS to allow creation of smaller-than-county rate cells in highly heterogeneous counties where provider networks and costs vary dramatically, subject to CMS approval.

[P11] Taxpayer advocacy groups will request that CMS coordinate the annual reconciliation under 26 U.S.C. 36B(f) with state processes to avoid duplicate reconciliations and inconsistent taxpayer notices.

[P11] Tax preparers and software vendors will ask CMS to provide the reconciliation algorithm, required data elements, and timeline well in advance to allow integration with tax filing systems and avoid taxpayer confusion.

[P12] Consumer advocates will ask for protections and notice requirements when underpaid APTC is identified and paid to taxpayers—requiring clear notice explaining why the payment occurred and whether it affects eligibility for other programs.

[P12] The IRS and tax administration commenters will request CMS coordinate with IRS systems and timelines to ensure payments to taxpayers are accurate and do not create tax filing complications.

[P13] Consumer rights groups will object to charging taxpayers additional tax for APTC overpayments without strong safeguards and propose limits, appeals rights, and clear advance notice before tax liability is assessed.

[P13] Legal experts will flag that any additional tax charge should be aligned with the statutory/regulatory limitations and request CMS publish enforcement protocols, statutory citations, and sample notices for affected taxpayers.

[P14] Consumer navigators and enrollment assisters will request clear operational guidance and Exchange IT flags to prevent erroneously treating BHP-eligible individuals as "qualified individuals" for QHP enrollment to avoid consumer confusion and improper subsidies.

[P14] States operating both BHP and Exchanges will seek clarification on how eligibility handoffs will occur and ask for standardized data exchanges and timely denials/redirects to prevent dual enrollment or coverage gaps.

[P15] Insurers and state regulators will request guidance on what constitutes acceptable "alternative methods" for including BHP standard plans in state risk‑sharing mechanisms, including actuarial equivalence tests and financial reporting requirements.

[P15] Risk-bearing entities will warn that excluding BHP enrollees from standard risk pools without clear alternative methods may destabilize markets and ask CMS to allow temporary transitional adjustments to risk pool calculations.

[P16] Actuaries and insurers will request CMS to publish the exact formula, data inputs, and treatment of age-rating and tobacco adjustments for calculating the Reference Premium so states can replicate PTC estimates reliably.

[P16] States will ask CMS to allow use of state-specific adjustments when calculating RP to account for state pricing practices and benefit design differences that affect premiums used to estimate PTC.

[P17] Commenters will seek clarity on how the second-lowest cost silver plan premium is identified across differing age ranges, whether plan variations by age banding are required, and how geographic rating areas interact with age ranges.

[P17] Consumer advocates will caution that relying on the second-lowest silver premium could understate costs for families if silver plan availability varies by age or region and request CMS model the distributional impacts on enrollee cost-sharing.

[P18] Tax experts will request CMS provide computational examples showing the PTC calculation as the lesser of enrolled premium and adjusted SLCSP minus contribution, including treatment of zero-premium plans, to avoid misapplication by states.

[P18] Software vendors implementing PTC calculations will ask for precise definitions of “enrolled plan premium” and “adjusted second-lowest silver premium,” including rounding rules and treatment of rebates, fees, and CSR loadings.

[P19] Hospital and provider associations will object to calculating BHP payments as if enrollees would have enrolled in QHPs, arguing this overstates PTC-equivalent amounts because BHP enrollees differ systematically from Exchange enrollees, and ask CMS to adopt empirically based adjustment factors.

[P19] Legal commenters will note that section 1331(d)(3)(A)(ii) may allow adjustment for realistic enrollment differentials and request CMS to permit state-level or demographic adjustments rather than a blanket assumption of identical enrollment behavior.

[P1] The deadline in § 39.13(a) (August 16, 2021) is already past; the FAA should withdraw or reissue the AD with a current comment period date to allow meaningful stakeholder participation.

[P1] If the FAA intends to rely on an August 16, 2021 comment close date, it should explain why reopening the comment period is not required under the Administrative Procedure Act given the elapsed date.

[P2] The applicability in § 39.13(c) references the Boeing requirement bulletin but does not list specific line numbers/serial ranges; operators need explicit line/serial number applicability to determine fleet impact.

[P2] The plain language should state whether all variations/configurations of Model 787–8/–9/–10 (e.g., freighter conversions, modified interiors) are included; otherwise, some operators cannot determine applicability.

[P3] § 39.13(f) mandates compliance "within the compliance times specified"; commenters request that the FAA publish those compliance intervals in the AD text (not just in the Boeing bulletin) to ensure enforceability and clarity.

[P3] Industry requests a grace period (e.g., 120 days) from AD effective date for scheduled maintenance planners to incorporate tasks; immediate compliance windows may conflict with existing maintenance schedules and reduce operational flexibility.

[P4] Requiring strict adherence to the Accomplishment Instructions in the Boeing bulletin (§ 39.13(g)) could improperly incorporate by reference proprietary manufacturer procedures without FAA elaboration; the FAA should include sufficient non-proprietary detail in the AD.

[P4] Maintenance providers without access to Boeing service materials may be unfairly disadvantaged; FAA should provide or facilitate access to the referenced Accomplishment Instructions or provide an FAA-approved public alternative.

[P5] The termination provision (§ 39.13(g)) that relies on actions identified as "terminating" in the Boeing bulletin should be clarified to state whether the terminating action applies fleetwide or only to the specific affected serial-numbered airplanes.

[P5] Operators request clarity on whether a terminating action performed per the bulletin on one landing gear leg terminates requirements for other legs or for other airplanes in the fleet.

[P6] § 39.13(h)(1) replaces the bulletin's "Issue 001 date" with the AD effective date; legal commenters note this could create ambiguity if Boeing revises the bulletin—FAA should explicitly state which revision(s) of the bulletin are approved and how later revisions are treated.

[P6] The AD should clarify whether future Boeing bulletin revisions automatically become incorporated or require separate FAA approval; otherwise operators may be uncertain which instructions are mandatory.

[P7] § 39.13(h)(2) requires AMOC approval when the bulletin instructs to contact Boeing for repair instructions; commenters say this imposes an unreasonable burden on operators who lack an ODA relationship with Boeing and request the FAA provide an alternate path for approved repairs by independent repair stations.

[P7] Legal/repair-station commenters request explicit timelines for FAA AMOC review of Boeing-provided repair instructions to avoid operational delays when repairs are necessary.

[P8] The mandated detailed and fluorescent penetrant inspection (FPI) for CONDITION 2 in § 39.13(h)(3) has no acceptance criteria in the AD; inspectors need clear defect definitions and disposition criteria to ensure consistent compliance and avoid unnecessary part removals.

[P8] The AD should specify inspector qualification/authorization requirements for performing the detailed and FPI (e.g., level II/III certs) to ensure inspection quality and legal enforceability.

[P9] § 39.13(i) allows termination of repetitive lubrication by revising the maintenance program to include CMR item 32–CMR–01, but commenters ask the FAA to publish the exact CMR text in the docket so operators can assess long-term maintenance/cost impacts before making program changes.

[P9] Labor/maintenance organizations request confirmation that incorporation of the CMR into the maintenance program does not waive other lubrication tasks in collective maintenance programs; FAA should clarify interaction with other tasks.

[P10] § 39.13(j) prohibits alternative actions/intervals once the maintenance program is revised unless an AMOC is approved; commenters say this rigid prohibition unduly restricts operator flexibility and request allowed temporary deviations for operational necessity with reporting requirements.

[P10] Legal commenters warn that forbidding alternatives without an AMOC may conflict with operators' authority under continuing airworthiness management systems to propose equivalent means of compliance; FAA should clarify criteria for temporary relief.

[P11] § 39.13(k) prohibits installing aluminum-nickel-bronze inner cylinder bushings at specified times but does not define whether this applies to shop stock parts, new-build installations, or parts used for training; suppliers request clarification to avoid inventory obsolescence.

[P11] Component manufacturers and MROs request an explicit grandfathering provision for parts ordered before the AD effective date to avoid economic loss.

[P12] Under § 39.13(k)(1), the prohibition applies after an aluminum-nickel-bronze bushing has been replaced with a copper-nickel-tin one; operators request clarification of acceptable installation records/evidence to demonstrate replacement date (logbooks, e-signatures, work order numbers).

[P12] The AD should specify whether partial replacement (one leg) triggers the prohibition for subsequent installations fleetwide or only for that specific MLG; ambiguity will create compliance divergence.

[P13] § 39.13(k)(2) applies the prohibition immediately for airplanes with copper-nickel-tin bushings as of the effective date; commenters ask FAA to explain the safety basis for immediately prohibiting aluminum-nickel-bronze installations on those airplanes.

[P13] Suppliers request a specific compliance timeline for retiring existing aluminum-nickel-bronze spares on airplanes that currently have copper-nickel-tin bushings to permit orderly supply chain adjustments.

[P14] The AMOC authority in § 39.13(l)(1) is limited to the Manager, Seattle ACO Branch; commenters from international operators and repair stations request clarification on delegation or reciprocal acceptance by non-Seattle FAA offices to avoid bottlenecks.

[P14] Industry asks for a published expected turnaround time for AMOC decisions by the Seattle ACO Branch to help plan maintenance windows.

[P15] § 39.13(l)(1) specifies routing AMOC requests to principal inspectors or Flight Standards Offices, but does not provide a complete mailing address for the "person in Related Information"; commenters request explicit contact details to avoid administrative rejections.

[P15] Operators request confirmation that electronic submissions to the provided email address satisfy statutory filing requirements and will be accepted as timely for compliance relief.

[P16] § 39.13(l)(2) requires notifying the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC; operators ask whether oral notification followed by written confirmation is acceptable and whether emergency use of an AMOC can proceed with retroactive notification.

[P16] Small operators request an allowance for notification via their Continuing Airworthiness Management Organization (CAMO) in lieu of a principal inspector when the operator does not have a designated PI.

[P17] § 39.13(l)(3) allows AMOC use if approved by the Boeing ODA; independent commenters and repair stations object that relying on the manufacturer's ODA for approval risks conflicts of interest and request FAA-only approvals or independent technical review.

[P17] The AD should require documented evidence that any Boeing ODA-approved AMOC has been reviewed and concurred with by the FAA, especially for structural repairs affecting certification basis.

[P18] § 39.13(l)(3) conditions AMOC approval on meeting the airplane's certification basis; commenters request the AD specify how differences in certification bases between variants (787–8/–9/–10) will be assessed and documented in AMOC approvals.

[P18] Legal commenters request that the FAA outline the evidence or analysis required to demonstrate that an alternative repair meets the original certification basis (fatigue analysis, testing, substantiation reports).

[P19] § 39.13(l)(3) requires any AMOC approval to specifically reference this AD; commenters ask the FAA to require that AMOC approvals also be recorded in the aircraft maintenance records to ensure traceability and enforceability during inspections.

[P19] Compliance auditors request that AMOC approvals include explicit expiration or review dates when they rely on assumptions that may change (materials, loads) so that safety does not depend on indefinite approvals without periodic reassessment.

[P1] The September 27, 2017 comment deadline is unreasonably short given the complexity of the Portland Cement NESHAP; stakeholders request a 60–90 day extension to allow time for data collection and coordination among affected facilities and state agencies.

[P1] EPA should confirm whether the September 27, 2017 deadline applies to all docket submissions (including supplemental technical attachments) or only to the primary written comment, and clarify procedures if additional time is needed for large file submissions.

[P2] Requiring submission via Regulations.gov may disadvantage small businesses or community groups without reliable internet access; EPA should allow alternative filing methods (mail or hand-delivery) with the same docket-identification requirement.

[P2] The instruction to identify comments by Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2017–0203 appears to contain a typographical error linking to the Office of Water rather than the Office of Air; EPA should confirm the correct docket ID for the Portland Cement NESHAP.

[P3] The prohibition on editing or removing comments after submission on Regulations.gov raises privacy and error-correction issues; EPA should permit commenters to correct clerical errors or redact sensitive personal contact information post-submission.

[P3] Legal experts note that the inability to withdraw a comment could deter participation from individuals who later learn they inadvertently disclosed confidential or harmful information; EPA should allow a limited withdrawal window or redaction mechanism.

[P4] Agencies’ permission to publish submitted comments to the public docket should be explicitly qualified to protect personally identifying information (PII) and phone numbers; EPA must describe redaction practices and whether submitters will be notified before publication.

[P4] Advocacy organizations request assurance that comments published to the public docket will not be repurposed by third parties for commercial solicitation and that EPA will not transfer contact information to unrelated parties.

[P5] The prohibition on electronically submitting Confidential Business Information (CBI) must be accompanied by clear instructions on how to submit CBI securely (e.g., mailed paper submission or encrypted submission) and how EPA will handle CBI claims.

[P5] Industry commenters request detailed guidance on what constitutes "CBI or other statutorily restricted information" in this context (e.g., emissions testing data, cost figures), including examples and the procedure for marking and segregating CBI submissions.

[P6] Requiring an accompanying written comment for multimedia submissions may be burdensome for stakeholders who rely on audio testimonies (non-English speakers or disabled persons); EPA should allow multimedia alone to be accepted if it contains full substantive comments, or provide accessible transcription services.

[P6] Community groups raising oral testimony at hearings should be allowed to submit audio-only files where transcription resources are unavailable; EPA should clarify acceptable formats, size limits, and whether subtitles or transcripts are required.

[P7] Stating that the written comment is the "official record" may discourage submission of important evidentiary multimedia content; EPA should clarify how multimedia will be indexed and used in the administrative record alongside the written comment.

[P7] Legal commenters request confirmation that attachments (data tables, technical reports) referenced in the written comment but uploaded as separate files will be considered part of the official record and will be retained and searchable in the docket.

[P8] The general prohibition against considering comments located outside the primary submission (e.g., on web/cloud links) is problematic for large datasets or interactive models; EPA should permit external hosting of large files with stable, permanent links and explicitly allow such content to be considered.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement in § 309.19(a) to conduct market hog sorting before ante-mortem inspection is operationally impractical for large harvest establishments that receive animals continuously and request clarification on where and by whom sorting must occur (on-farm, lairage, or within the plant receiving area).

[P1] Industry requests clarification whether temporary holding pens at the plant entrance qualify as the point "before ante-mortem inspection" so that sorting does not disrupt current receiving flows or require additional real estate.

[P1] Animal welfare advocates contend that pre-ante-mortem sorting by establishment employees risks harming animals if untrained staff perform medical triage and request that FSIS require veterinary oversight for sorting decisions.

[P2] Packers object that § 309.19(a) disposal mandate referencing paragraph (c) lacks specificity about timeframe and chain-of-custody—requesting explicit timelines and procedures to avoid regulatory uncertainty when disposing animals showing moribundity, CNS signs, or pyrexia.

[P2] Legal commenters assert that the disposal requirement for animals with CNS disorders could lead to over-classification and unnecessary waste; they request clear diagnostic criteria and examples to distinguish transient signs from conditions warranting disposal.

[P3] Small- and very small-establishment representatives say the written-procedure requirement in § 309.19(b) will impose disproportionate administrative burdens and request either model procedures, compliance templates, or an extended implementation timeline.

[P3] Worker-safety advocates recommend that written procedures in § 309.19(b) explicitly require training and competency documentation for personnel who identify sick market hogs to ensure consistent detection and protect workers.

[P4] HACCP consultants and inspectors note ambiguity in § 309.19(b) about whether the written procedures must be integrated within an existing HACCP plan or may be maintained as separate prerequisite programs—requesting clear language that allows flexibility while requiring cross-references.

[P4] Consumer groups request that incorporation of procedures into HACCP, sanitation SOPs, or another prerequisite program (P4) include a requirement that these procedures be subjected to HACCP verification and validation records accessible to FSIS.

[P5] Establishments ask for clarification in § 309.19(c) on what constitutes an acceptable "unique tag, tattoo, or similar device" for identifying sorted/condemned carcasses, and whether electronic tracking (RFID/barcodes) is permissible.

[P5] Food safety NGOs request that identification methods required by § 309.19(c) include tamper-evident features and require retention of identification records for the same one-year period required elsewhere (§ 310.18(e)) to ensure traceability.

[P6] Industry commenters say the mandate to "immediately denature all major portions of the carcass on-site" in § 309.19(c) is vague as to what constitutes "major portions" and request precise definitions to ensure uniform enforcement.

[P6] Small processors express concern that immediate on-site denaturation and disposal per 9 CFR part 314.3 may not be feasible during night operations or when rendering pickup is delayed; they request allowance for temporary refrigerated hold with FSIS notification.

[P7] Establishments subject to § 309.19(d) argue that daily recordkeeping of animals disposed by sorters prior to ante-mortem inspection duplicates other record systems and request harmonization with existing lot/receipt records to avoid redundant paperwork.

[P7] Privacy advocates request that records documenting disposed animals (P7) be limited to business-relevant information and that personal employee identifiers be exempted from routine FSIS review to protect worker privacy.

[P8] Industry legal counsel supports § 309.19(d) allowing FSIS review of records but requests clear limits on FSIS access (e.g., during normal business hours only) and a defined process for dispute resolution if FSIS challenges the records.

[P9] Producers and packers ask for a clear definition of "reason to believe" in § 309.19(e) for notifying FSIS about notifiable diseases to prevent over-reporting; they request objective criteria or a list of reportable clinical signs that trigger immediate notification.

[P9] Agricultural associations request explicit confidentiality protections for disease notifications under § 309.19(e) to avoid market disruption from premature public disclosure.

[P10] Establishments seeking to use NSIS under § 310.1(b)(3)(i) request detailed guidance on the "requirements in 9 CFR 309.19" they must meet, including sample templates and timelines for FSIS approval.

[P11] Some establishments request clarity about the waiver process under § 310.1(b)(3)(i) for non-market-hog swine to use NSIS under 9 CFR 303.1(h), including evaluation criteria and expected approval timelines to plan operations.

[P12] Multi-class swine slaughter facilities request further technical guidance on how to simultaneously operate NSIS for market hogs and traditional inspection for other swine classes (P12), including line separation, inspector staffing, and recordkeeping distinctions.

[P13] Consumer safety advocates note that § 310.1(b)(3)(ii) requiring traditional inspection when NSIS is not used could create inconsistent inspection levels network-wide and urge that FSIS publish criteria for when NSIS is appropriate vs. traditional inspection.

[P14] Establishments with one- or two-inspector configurations request a waiver or alternative for the mirror requirement in § 310.1(b)(3)(ii) §307.2(m)(6) citing physical space constraints and costs of installing compliant mirrors.

[P15] Food safety NGOs support § 310.18(c) written procedures to prevent contamination but request that the rule require periodic third-party verification or FSIS audits of those procedures rather than relying solely on establishment self-monitoring.

[P16] Small-plant operators request model contamination-prevention procedures for incorporation into HACCP or sanitation SOPs per § 310.18(c) to ensure compliance without unnecessary expense.

[P17] Microbiology labs and industry trade groups object to the prescriptive sampling "locations and frequencies" in § 310.18(c) without disclosure of the scientific basis; they request risk-based justification and potential flexibility for equivalent methods.

[P18] Larger establishments question the burden of collecting pre-evisceration and post-chill samples (P18) and request data on expected sample volumes, testing throughput, and associated costs; they request phased implementation for lab capacity buildup.

[P18] Very small and very low volume establishments request a clear definition and threshold criteria for what counts as "very small" or "very low volume" for applicability of the pre-evisceration exemption under § 310.18(c)(1).

[P19] Very small establishment associations say limiting their sampling to post-chill (P19) is reasonable but request that FSIS provide subsidized lab access or pooled sampling options to reduce per-sample costs.

[P20] Establishments ask for technical clarification in § 310.18(c)(1) on acceptable sampling technique—whether sponge or excision methods are required in all cases and whether composite samples are permissible for ham, belly, or jowl areas.

[P21] Industry requests that the alternative sampling-location provision (§ 310.18(c)(1)(iii)) clearly define the evidentiary standard ("definite improvement") and what types of data (historical, challenge studies, validation trials) FSIS will accept.

[P22] Academic microbiologists caution that the condition in § 310.18(c)(1)(iii)(A) requiring demonstrating improvement from alternative locations may be scientifically challenging and request that FSIS accept statistically powered equivalence studies rather than only improvement.

[P23] Compliance officers request that § 310.18(c)(1)(iii)(B)'s requirement that FSIS not disapprove in writing be revised to set a specific review timeframe (e.g., 90 days) so establishments are not left waiting indefinitely for FSIS response.

[P24] Establishments challenge proportional sampling in § 310.18(c)(2) as administratively complex and ask for concrete formulas or tables showing sample counts by weekly/annual production tonnage to facilitate compliance.

[P25] The specific frequency of "once per 1,000 carcasses, minimum once per week" (P25) may be overly burdensome for operations with low daily production variability; industry requests allowance to average production over a month for sampling frequency calculations.

[P26] Very small/very low volume establishments request clarity on when the June 1 start date for weekly sampling (P26) applies and ask for a transitional phase-in for the first year of compliance.

[P27] Small-plant advocates strongly support the permission in § 310.18(c)(2)(ii) for modifying sampling after 13 weekly controlled results but ask FSIS to define the statistical criteria for "effectively maintain[ing] process control."

[P28] HACCP consultants request additional detail on what constitutes an "integral part" of HACCP verification so an alternative sampling frequency (P28) will be acceptable and not subject to arbitrary FSIS disapproval.

[P29] Legal commenters seek assurance that acceptance of alternative frequencies under § 310.18(c)(2)(iii)(A) will not be applied retroactively to prior enforcement actions if FSIS later disapproves the alternative.

[P30] Establishments request that the "FSIS does not disapprove in writing" condition in § 310.18(c)(2)(iii)(B) include a fixed decision timeline and an appeal or reconsideration procedure if FSIS disapproves the proposed alternative frequency.

[P31] Public health groups endorse § 310.18(c)(2)(iv)'s mandate to sample at a frequency adequate for enteric pathogen control but request that the rule specify minimum pathogen targets and corrective-action thresholds (e.g., acceptable CFU levels) to ensure actionable results.

[P32] Industry expresses concern about record retention obligations in § 310.18(c)(2)(iv) and requests harmonization with other record retention schedules (e.g., FSIS QM records) to avoid inconsistent retention periods.

[P33] Establishments request templates and training resources for the pre-operational contamination-prevention procedures required by § 310.18(d) to reduce compliance costs and variability in implementation.

[P34] Food safety advocates request that sampling of food contact surfaces and cleaning water per § 310.18(d) explicitly include potable water sources and on-site well testing to address contamination sources beyond processing surfaces.

[P35] Small processors note that § 310.18(d)'s sampling frequency requirement for the pre-operational environment may be burdensome; they request a risk-based tiered frequency tied to prior violation history and production volume.

[P36] Industry requests that FSIS provide validated, standardized test methods and accredited labs list for microbial analysis referenced in § 310.18(d) to ensure consistency and defensibility of results.

[P37] Establishments request clarification that the test-result record retention referenced in § 310.18(d) and repeated in (c)(2)(iv) (P32, P37) may be combined into a single laboratory results file rather than multiple duplicative record sets.

[P38] Several commenters request that § 310.18(e)'s daily recordkeeping requirement be limited to key performance indicators (e.g., number of samples, positive detections, corrective actions) rather than full raw data to reduce administrative burden.

[P39] Industry supports § 310.18(e) allowing electronic records (P39) but requests that FSIS specify minimum electronic controls (audit trail, access controls, backup frequency) and acceptance standards for electronic signatures.

[P40] Privacy and commercial confidentiality advocates ask that the one-year record retention requirement in § 310.18(e) be extended to allow confidentiality protection of proprietary process-control data from FOIA disclosure except as necessary for food safety investigations.

[P41] Establishments note that complying with 9 CFR part 307 facility requirements (§ 310.26(a)) may necessitate capital investments for older plants and request a phased compliance schedule or cost-estimate guidance.

[P42] Facilities with two or fewer inspection stations object to the mandatory mirror at the carcass inspection station (§ 310.26(a)) on grounds of space and hygiene; they request an alternative technology allowance (camera systems) if they meet § 307.2(m)(6) performance.

[P43] Packinghouse associations ask for clear definitions and examples of "condemnable conditions" in § 310.26(b) to reduce inconsistent plant-level sorting and avoid unnecessary condemnations.

[P44] Establishments request that written procedures to remove carcasses with septicemia, toxemia, pyemia, and other conditions (P44) include standardized decision trees and photographic examples to ensure consistent identification.

[P45] HACCP auditors note the repeated requirement to incorporate carcass-removal procedures into HACCP or SOPs (P45) and ask FSIS to publish harmonized guidance about where such procedures should live within existing documentation to facilitate audits.

[P46] Worker-safety groups request that procedures in § 310.26(b) addressing sorting activities include ergonomic protections and specify that sorters receive occupational safety training given their close contact with sick or contaminated carcasses.

[P47] Industry groups welcome the line-speed exception in § 310.26(c) but request objective metrics for "effective process control" so they can document compliance and rely on the exemption without subjective IIC determinations.

[P48] Establishments operating under NSIS request procedural clarity about the process and timeframe for an IIC to order a line-speed reduction under § 310.26(c) and whether such reductions must be documented with specific findings.

[P49] Unions and worker advocates support § 310.26(c)(permission) that allows the IIC to reduce line speed but request that this authority include a requirement for written rationale and a post-action review with establishment management.

[P50] Establishments request guidance on what documentation is sufficient to show products meet the "ready-to-cook" definition in § 301.2 for the recordkeeping requirement in § 310.26(d)(1), including acceptable tests or process validations.

[P51] Industry legal counsel asks that FSIS limit off-site access to ready-to-cook documentation (§ 310.26(d)(1) & P51) to prevent undue disruption of proprietary business operations and require formal requests for remote records review.

[P52] Establishments request a standardized form to document daily numbers of animals disposed or condemned (§ 310.26(d)(2)) to ensure consistency in records subject to FSIS review and reduce dispute over counts.

[P53] Consumer advocates request that FSIS publish aggregated, de-identified summaries of disposition/condemnation data (from P52/P53) to enable independent public health research into disease trends without compromising individual establishment confidentiality.

[P54] Labor and public-health advocates support the annual attestation in § 310.27 (intro) for worker-condition monitoring but request that attestations be made available to FSIS inspection personnel and aggregated for public transparency on occupational health trends.

[P55] Worker groups request that § 310.27(a) explicitly prohibit production-based incentives or disciplinary policies that could deter reporting and require establishments to certify absence of such practices during attestation.

[P56] Multi-lingual facilities request that § 310.27(b)'s requirement to notify employees "in a manner and language that workers can understand" include a requirement to provide written materials in all languages regularly used by the workforce and fund translation services.

[P57] Employee safety advocates request that § 310.27(c) require establishments to document the frequency and results of routine monitoring of injury/illness logs and workers’ comp data and to include a corrective-action plan when trends indicate increased risk.

[P1] The rule lacks clarity on whether the 20% coinsurance applies to rental versus purchase of DME; commenters request explicit language distinguishing rental payments, capped rental periods, and purchase transactions to avoid double charging.

[P1] The provision does not clarify how customary charge is defined or calculated for DME under §409.50; stakeholders request CMS adopt a clear, auditable definition (e.g., Medicare allowed amount or median local payment) to avoid inconsistent beneficiary liabilities.

[P1] Home health agencies that supply DME as part of bundled services may face billing complexity and cash-flow disruption from shifting a portion to beneficiary coinsurance; industry asks CMS to allow consolidated billing and remittance processes to minimize administrative burden.

[P1] Advocacy groups request an explicit prohibition on balance billing beyond the 20% coinsurance for items furnished under Medicare home health to prevent surprise charges.

[P2] Imputing episode costs by national per‑15‑minute unit amounts (§484.240(d)) ignores regional wage and cost variation, disadvantaging agencies in high-cost areas; commenters urge CMS to incorporate geographic wage adjustment factors.

[P2] The methodology in §484.240(d) may misrepresent multi-disciplinary visits where concurrent services occur; providers request guidance on allocating overlapping 15‑minute units across disciplines to avoid double-counting or underpayment.

[P2] National per‑15‑minute unit amounts risk distorting payment accuracy when visit intensity varies; clinical stakeholders recommend CMS permit agency-specific or regional modifiers when supported by validated cost data.

[P3] Evaluating competing HHAs using a set of quality measures (§484.315(a)) without risk adjustment could penalize agencies serving higher-acuity, socioeconomically disadvantaged populations; commenters request risk adjustment and stratification by patient complexity.

[P3] The proposed quality measure set is not specified in the rule text; agencies request CMS publish the exact measures, numerators/denominators, and calculation specifications well before implementation to allow data validation.

[P3] Consumer advocates request inclusion of functional outcome and patient-reported outcome measures in the quality set under §484.315(a) to capture benefits meaningful to patients, not only process measures.

[P4] The permission to request recalculation under §484.335(a)(1) is subject to statutory limitations under section 1115A; legal commenters ask CMS to clarify how those statutory limitations will be applied and whether any calculations are categorically non-reviewable.

[P5] The 15-calendar-day deadline to submit recalculation requests (§484.335(a)(2)) is unreasonably short given agencies’ need to access, review, and validate posted HHA-specific information; industry requests extension to 30 or 45 days.

[P5] CMS should allow for an automatic extension of the 15-day recalculation request period in cases of CMS portal outages or cybersecurity incidents, with clear procedures to document and grant extensions.

[P6] Requiring provider name, service address, and CCN (§484.335(a)(3)(i)) is appropriate, but commenters request CMS allow submissions on behalf of a parent organization or management company with documentation, to accommodate agencies that use third-party consultants.

[P7] The mandate to specify which quality measure data or calculation is believed inaccurate (§484.335(a)(3)(ii)) is reasonable, but CMS must provide templates and examples of acceptable bases for recalculation to ensure uniformity and prevent frivolous or procedurally defective requests.

[P8] The contact information requirement (§484.335(a)(3)(iii)) should permit a designated external representative (e.g., legal counsel or third‑party data firm) to be listed, with a process for submitting proof of authorization.

[P9] Allowing additional documentary evidence (§484.335(a)(3)(iv)) is valuable, but CMS should specify acceptable file formats, maximum file size, and whether redacted documents are permitted to protect PHI and trade secrets.

[P10] The prohibition on including data that should have been filed by the submission deadline (§484.335(a)(3)(iv)) is excessively rigid; agencies that can demonstrate reasonable cause (e.g., technical failures) should be allowed to submit corrected data during recalculation, not just evidence of timely submission.

[P11] CMS’s review scope (§484.335(a)(4)) needs to include a commitment to provide detailed explanations of the “evidence and findings” relied upon, so agencies can meaningfully assess CMS’ rationale for recalculation outcomes.

[P12] The open-ended allowance for CMS to review “any other evidence” (§484.335(a)(4)) could enable consideration of post-hoc or irrelevant materials; providers request CMS set criteria for what constitutes relevant evidence and provide notice of any additional evidence considered.

[P13] The requirement that CMS provide written notification of recalculation findings (§484.335(a)(5)) should include a standardized results form that details changes to measures, scores, and payment adjustments, and the underlying computations for transparency.

[P14] Because recalculation decisions may be reconsidered (§484.335(a)(5)), stakeholders request CMS publish timelines for when reconsideration officials will render decisions to ensure finality before payment adjustments are applied.

[P15] The permission to request reconsideration of annual total performance score and payment adjustment percentage (§484.335(b)(1)) should explicitly confirm that a timely reconsideration request will suspend application of payment adjustments until final determination, to avoid retroactive financial harm.

[P19] Contact information for reconsideration (§484.335(b)(3)(iii)) should permit multiple points of contact and require CMS to confirm receipt to the listed contacts to avoid missed communications.

[P26] Stakeholders request CMS set binding timeframes for issuing the written determinations under §484.335(b)(5) (e.g., 60 days) to ensure agencies receive timely final decisions for budgeting and contracting purposes.

[P3] Patient advocacy organizations request transparency on public reporting tied to the quality measures in §484.315(a); they oppose using unadjusted measure comparisons in public rankings that could mislead consumers.

[P2] Health economists warn that using national per‑15‑minute unit amounts (§484.240(d)) may create incentives to fragment visits into 15‑minute billing units to maximize imputed episode costs; CMS should add anti-fraud safeguards and clear coding rules.

[P1] Small HHAs and rural providers will be disproportionately affected by the new 20% coinsurance (§409.50) because their payer mixes include more Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries; CMS should assess distributional impacts and consider mitigation.

[P1] The 250-hour airplane PIC/SIC-PIC combination requirement in §61.159(a)(5) is duplicative of existing experience requirements and will disproportionately burden new pilots seeking airline careers without demonstrable safety benefit.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether simulated flight time in a flight simulator or FSTD can count toward the 250-hour PIC/SIC-PIC requirement; as written it appears to exclude any simulators, which harms training flexibility.

[P1] The provision does not specify whether dual instruction received during PIC time (e.g., training PIC under instruction) counts as PIC hours; industry needs clarity to avoid inconsistent logbook acceptance.

[P2] The 100-hour cross-country requirement in §61.159(a)(5)(i)(A) is arbitrary and may be infeasible for pilots based in congested metropolitan areas where long cross-country sorties are operationally difficult.

[P2] Cross-country is undefined as to distance or point-to-point routing; the agency should adopt the 50-nautical-mile standard or specify minimum leg lengths to ensure uniform application.

[P3] The 25-hour night flight requirement in §61.159(a)(5)(i)(B) will be difficult to achieve in regions with limited night operations or seasonal darkness and could delay pilot progression unnecessarily.

[P3] The regulation should allow crediting night flight time obtained in simulators with night visual cues or in Part 142 training programs toward the 25-hour requirement for safety and training modernization.

[P4] §61.159(a)(5)(ii) allowing powered-lift horizontal flight time is appropriate, but the phrase “except as provided” is vague; the rule must specify which exceptions apply and how to document equivalency.

[P4] The permission to credit powered-lift horizontal flight time could create safety gaps if powered-lift types are significantly dissimilar to airplanes; the FAA should limit credit to proven equivalent aircraft types or require transition training.

[P5] The exception disallowing credit for those removed from flying status for lack of proficiency or disciplinary actions lacks due process details—commenters request a clear appeals process and definition of “disciplinary action involving aircraft operations.”

[P5] The prohibition on crediting powered-lift time for pilots removed for disciplinary reasons may be overbroad—disciplinary actions unrelated to flight competency (e.g., administrative misconduct) should not permanently bar crediting valid flight time.

[P6] The 1,000-hour requirement in §121.436(a)(3) for serving as PIC in Part 121 operations is a substantial increase for some carriers’ internal promotion pipelines and could create pilot shortages unless grandfathering or transition timelines are extended.

[P6] Legal commenters will argue the rule could exceed the FAA’s statutory authority if it effectively mandates hiring and promotion standards beyond safety justification; FAA should provide evidence linking 1,000 hours to safety outcomes.

[P7] Allowing 1,000 hours of SIC under Part 121 toward the PIC requirement (§121.436(a)(3) alternative 1) is reasonable, but the rule should specify whether SIC time accrued as a trainee under supervised training programs counts.

[P7] Carriers need clarification whether SIC time in Part 121 ferry flights, repositioning flights, or augmented flight operations qualify toward the 1,000-hour credit.

[P8] Crediting PIC time from §91.1053(a)(2)(i) operations (§121.436(a)(3) alternative 2) is beneficial, but the provision should define which 91.1053 operations qualify (e.g., fractional ownership vs. other high-minimum charters).

[P8] There is ambiguity whether single-pilot 91.1053 operations count; the alternative should be limited to operations that meet multi-crew standards comparable to Part 121 for safety equivalence.

[P9] Allowing PIC time under §135.243(a)(1) to count toward the 1,000 hours (§121.436(a)(3) alternative 3) helps career bridges from Part 135, but the FAA should confirm whether on-demand and commuter operations are equally creditable.

[P9] Operators express concern that without specifying aircraft types or operational complexity, some Part 135 PIC time (e.g., in small piston singles) may not prepare pilots for large Part 121 aircraft; restrictions or conversion training should be required.

[P10] The exemption for pilots who were PIC in Part 121 on July 31, 2013 (§121.436(a)(3) exception) creates a two-tier workforce and potential equal-protection issues; commenters request justification and a plan to avoid institutional inequities.

[P10] Labor groups will argue the grandfathering date is arbitrary; if retained, FAA should extend grandfathering to those with continuous service or offer a path via training/checking for late entrants.

[P11] Allowing up to 500 hours of military flight time to count (§121.436(c)) is appropriate, but the cap may unfairly penalize military pilots with substantial relevant experience; consider increasing the cap or allowing full credit with verification.

[P11] Military organizations request streamlining verification procedures for military logs to avoid administrative delays and ensure military PIC time is accepted promptly.

[P12] The condition that military time must be PIC in multiengine, turbine-powered, fixed-wing or powered-lift aircraft (§121.436(c)(1)) unfairly excludes relevant military rotary-wing or single-engine turbine experience that may be transferable; commenters ask for competency-based assessment instead of rigid type limitations.

[P12] Legal experts will note that the term “powered-lift” is not sufficiently defined in the military context; FAA must enumerate eligible military aircraft types to avoid inconsistent determinations.

[P13] Requiring that military flight time be obtained “in an operation requiring more than one pilot” (§121.436(c)(2)) excludes relevant single-pilot military missions that involve complex crew coordination and systems knowledge; propose evaluation by an approved alternative training pathway.

[P13] The multi-crew requirement may disproportionately impact helicopter and special-mission military pilots who typically operate single-pilot but gain high levels of systems and mission experience.

[P14] Crediting PIC flight time obtained under this part prior to July 31, 2013 (§121.436(d)) should be permitted, but the rule needs explicit guidance on acceptable documentation for pre-2013 logs and how carriers should verify them.

[P14] Senior pilots and unions will request that §121.436(d) include a transition timeline and clear process for ongoing carriers to incorporate pre-2013 PIC time without reopening closed personnel decisions.

[P1] Aviation training providers note the rule lacks guidance on documenting combined PIC and SIC-performing-PIC duties; specify acceptable logbook entries and instructor attestations.

[P2] Regional carriers argue the 100-hour cross-country requirement will force unnecessary ferry flights solely for logbook compliance, increasing costs and emissions; propose allowing simulated cross-country in FTDs or approved syllabus events.

[P3] Safety advocates may support the night requirement but request the FAA define night currency vs. night experience to avoid counting minimal night exposure as equivalent to night proficiency.

[P6] Small carriers warn that the 1,000-hour SIC/PIC mix could exacerbate pilot hiring bottlenecks and recommend a phased implementation (e.g., three-year phase-in) or temporary relief options.

[P11] Veteran advocacy groups ask for an appeals mechanism where military pilots denied full credit can undergo competency testing to obtain additional credit beyond the 500-hour cap.

[P5] Privacy advocates request limits on sharing disciplinary records if airlines are required to verify prior removals from flying status before permitting or denying crediting of time.

[P8] Legal commenters request consistency checks: if §61.159 and §121.436 overlap, the rule should reconcile which standard controls for pilots transitioning from general aviation to Part 121.

Labor groups will argue the grandfathering date is arbitrary; if retained, FAA should extend grandfathering to those with continuous service or offer a path via training/checking for late entrants.

Allowing up to 500 hours of military flight time to count (§121.436(c)) is appropriate, but the cap may unfairly penalize military pilots with substantial relevant experience; consider increasing the cap or allowing full credit with verification.
Military organizations request streamlining verification procedures for military logs to avoid administrative delays and ensure military PIC time is accepted promptly.
