[P1] The July 23, 2020 comments deadline is insufficiently long for international operators and affected MROs to collect fleet-wide inspection data and submit meaningful comments; extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] Small repair stations and independent shops lack the administrative resources to develop technical comments by July 23, 2020; FAA should allow a longer period or provide guidance documents to aid comments.

[P2] The applicability lists specific CF6 variants and serial numbers via service bulletin lists but does not clearly state whether engines with equivalent HPT disk part numbers but different serial-number formatting are included; clarify to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P2] The AD’s applicability cuts off mid-list (text appears truncated); the rule must include the complete model and serial-number lists or explicitly reference the full, dated service bulletins to avoid ambiguity.

[P2] The provision fails to state treatment for engines installed on non-U.S.-registered aircraft or on freezers/inventory; clarify whether spares and engines in storage are within applicability.

[P3] The compliance timing phrase “within the compliance times specified” is vague unless those compliance times are explicitly printed in the AD; include explicit calendar or cycle-based deadlines in the AD itself, not just in referenced service bulletins.

[P3] There is no grandfathering provision for inspections already performed using equivalent techniques prior to the AD effective date; add explicit language that inspections performed per approved methods before the effective date satisfy compliance.

[P4] Requiring ultrasonic inspection “at each piece-part exposure” is ambiguous for assemblies that may be exposed multiple times during a shop visit; define “piece-part exposure” precisely (e.g., removal from engine module, or disassembly to single-disk removal).

[P4] The AD mandates inspections per CF6–80C2 SB 72–1562 R04 but does not allow for equivalent non-proprietary inspection procedures; allow FAA-approved non-manufacturer procedures to prevent forced use of potentially costly SB-paid services.

[P4] There is no performance standard or minimum detectable crack size specified for the ultrasonic inspections; require the AD to state the crack-detection threshold or probe/technique acceptance criteria.

[P5] For CF6–80A HPT stage 2 inspections, the AD requires ultrasonic inspection at each piece-part exposure but does not account for engines used for short-term ferry flights where immediate disassembly is impractical; provide a time-limited alternative compliance path.

[P5] Operators will incur significant additional shop time and cost for the required inspections on CF6–80A engines; FAA should provide a cost-estimate analysis and consider phased implementation to reduce economic burden.

[P6] The blanket requirement to “replace the disk before further flight” if a crack is found does not permit temporary operational limitations or expedited repair/temporary life-limits; allow for confirmed non-propagating defect dispositioning or expedited repair options approved by FAA.

[P6] The AD does not define whether replacement with a serviceable disk requires a new life-limit or whether existing cycles transfer; clarify life-limit transfer and recordkeeping requirements when disks are replaced.

[P7] Removing the reporting requirements from the AD (paragraph h) undermines the FAA’s ability to gather fleet health data and assess AD effectiveness; reinstate mandatory reporting or require voluntary reporting with strong incentives.

[P7] If reporting is not required, the FAA should at minimum require submission of inspection findings when cracks are detected to support continued monitoring; otherwise safety data will be lost.

[P8] The designation of the Manager, ECO Branch as sole AMOC-approving authority may create bottlenecks; permit regional FAA certificate-holding district offices to approve routine AMOCs to expedite operator compliance.

[P8] The provision should require FAA to publish criteria for AMOC approval to ensure transparency and predictability for applicants seeking alternative inspection techniques.

[P9] Requiring AMOC requests to route through the principal inspector or local FSDO could delay time-sensitive relief; allow direct submission to the ECO Branch with concurrent notice to the principal inspector.

[P10] The AD references paragraph (k)(1) for the certification office manager contact but the proposed rule text does not include paragraph (k)(1); include the contact details in the AD to avoid confusion when sending direct submissions.

[P11] Allowing email submission of AMOC requests to ANE-AD-AMOC@faa.gov is helpful, but the AD should also permit secure file transfer for large attachments and specify acceptable file formats and maximum file sizes.

[P11] The AD should require an acknowledgement of receipt for emailed AMOC requests within a specified timeframe (e.g., 5 business days) to provide applicants certainty that their request is under review.

[P12] The requirement to notify the principal inspector or local FSDO manager before using an approved AMOC lacks a timeframe; specify whether notification must be prior to the first use or within an identified number of days after approval.

[P12] The AD should clarify the notification content and provide a standard form or electronic process to ensure consistent reporting when approved AMOCs are implemented.

[P4][P5] The AD depends heavily on specific service bulletins (CF6–80C2 SB 72–1562 R04 etc.) that may be updated; specify that compliance is required with the SB revision in effect on the AD effective date or allow later FAA-approved revisions.

[P2][P4] The AD does not address engines with repaired or reworked HPT disks; state whether disks repaired per FAA-approved repair methods are subject to the same inspection frequency and replacement requirements.

[P6] Requiring unconditional replacement before further flight will create supply-chain issues for spare disks; FAA should permit temporary grounded ferry operations to a maintenance base under strict limitations if replacement parts are not immediately available.

[P3] The AD should provide explicit compliance metrics (by flight cycles, flight hours, or calendar time) for first inspections after the AD effective date to remove ambiguity.

[P4] Specify qualifications and training requirements for ultrasonic inspection technicians (e.g., NAS 410 level) to ensure inspection consistency across operators and repair stations.

[P5] For leased aircraft and engines, clarification is needed on who is responsible for compliance costs (lessor or lessee) and notification duties; AD should address assignment of compliance responsibility.

[P7] The AD’s exclusion of reporting is inconsistent with previous GE CF6 ADs that required data collection; explain the rationale for removing reporting and provide alternative data collection mechanisms.

[P8] The AMOC authority should include a requirement for FAA to publish a log of approved AMOCs (redacted for proprietary data) to aid other operators and maintain transparency.

[P2] The AD must clarify applicability to CF6 engines modified with service bulletins that changed disk serial-number records to prevent erroneous aircraft grounding.

[P6] Require that replacement disks be traceable with clear documentation of part number, serial number, and life cycles; AD should mandate record retention period (e.g., 2 years or until next shop visit).

[P4] The AD should allow phased inspection intervals for low-utilization engines, tied to flight cycles instead of “piece-part exposure” which may not occur frequently on such engines.

[P1] Because the comment due date is in 2020 and this AD appears urgent, the FAA should publish an interim contact for expedited technical inquiries during the comment period to help stakeholders prepare substantive comments quickly.

[P1] The deadline in § 39.13(a) (FAA must receive comments by December 14, 2020) is insufficiently long for small operators and non‑profit advocacy groups to prepare meaningful technical or economic comments; the FAA should extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether the December 14, 2020 receipt date is a hard postmark/receipt date or whether comments sent by overnight mail or electronic submission received after that date will be considered; ambiguity will chill participation.

[P2] § 39.13(f) as written is vague about what constitutes "the specified compliance times"; the AD must explicitly state all compliance deadlines in the regulatory text rather than relying solely on service documents.

[P2] The statement in § 39.13(f) that affected persons "must comply with the AD within the specified compliance times unless already complied" fails to account for supply chain delays; there should be an allowance for documented delays in parts availability.

[P3] The 24‑month replacement period in § 39.13(g)(1) is arbitrary and either too long (from a safety advocate perspective) or too short (from an operator/manufacturer perspective); the FAA should provide and justify risk analysis that supports the 24‑month compliance window.

[P3] For operators with aircraft on seasonal or low utilization schedules, replacing GPS units within 24 months could be logistically disruptive and costly; the FAA should permit phased compliance tied to scheduled maintenance windows.

[P3] The rule lacks an estimate of the number of units affected and the replacement cost per unit; without that economic information, commenters cannot quantify the economic impact of the 24‑month requirement.

[P3] The mandate to replace P/N 822–2189–100 with P/N 822–2189–101 presumes immediate availability of P/N 822–2189–101; the FAA should require the manufacturer to certify production capacity and spare‑parts distribution before the AD becomes effective.

[P3] The AD should permit installation of functionally equivalent alternative GPS units certified to meet the same performance standards, rather than mandating a single P/N replacement, to promote competition and mitigate supply constraints.

[P4] The prohibition in § 39.13(g)(2) on installing P/N 822–2189–100 "as of the effective date" is overly broad and will prevent installation of serviced/recertified units that may be safe; the FAA should allow installation of rebuilt units that meet equivalent airworthiness standards or are covered by an approved STC.

[P4] The absolute installation ban in § 39.13(g)(2) could ground aircraft awaiting installation of the replacement unit if spares are not available; the FAA should include an exception for temporary ferry operations with operational mitigations.

[P4] The rule does not define "install" (e.g., whether reinstallation on the same aircraft after maintenance counts); ambiguity may create enforcement issues—clarify whether reinstalling the same P/N 822–2189–100 unit on the same aircraft after bench repair is prohibited.

[P5] Granting AMOC authority solely to the Wichita ACO Branch Manager in § 39.13(h)(1) centralizes decisionmaking and could create bottlenecks; the FAA should allow other appropriate FAA offices to grant AMOCs to expedite approvals.

[P5] The provision should specify a target turnaround time for AMOC decisions by the Wichita ACO Branch Manager to provide predictability for operators pursuing alternatives.

[P6] Requiring AMOC requests to be sent to the principal inspector or local FSDO per § 39.13(h)(1) may be inconsistent with the centralized AMOC authority in § 39.13(h)(1); the rule should clearly explain the routing process and who has final decision authority.

[P6] Small operators who do not have an assigned principal inspector may not know who to contact at the local FSDO; the FAA should publish contact points and an online submission mechanism for AMOC requests to reduce confusion.

[P7] § 39.13(h)(1) requires that if sending information directly to the certification office manager it must be sent to the person in paragraph (i)(1), but paragraph (i)(1) is truncated in the proposed text—this drafting error must be corrected to identify the named contact.

[P7] The rule should allow electronic submission directly to the certification office manager (specified in paragraph (i)(1)) and confirm email addresses/secure upload procedures to ensure timely receipt.

[P8] Requiring notification to the principal inspector or local FSDO manager before using an approved AMOC (§ 39.13(h)(2)) may create operational delays if the FAA does not process notifications promptly; the FAA should define what constitutes adequate notification (e.g., email with confirmation) and allow usage upon acknowledgement or after a specified period.

[P8] The obligation in § 39.13(h)(2) to notify before using an AMOC is unclear whether a documented electronic notification suffices or whether prior written FAA approval is required; the FAA should clarify that notification is informational and does not require prior concurrence.

[General/legal] The preemption and enforcement implications of prohibiting installation of P/N 822–2189–100 (§ 39.13(g)(2)) need to be analyzed relative to existing repair station approvals and manufacturer warranties; commenters request the FAA provide legal justification for excluding factory‑authorized repairs or refurbishments.

[General/industry] The AD should include a parts‑tracking requirement or a registry for replaced GPS units (P/N 822–2189–100) to ensure removed units are not improperly reintroduced into the fleet, given the absolute installation prohibition.

[General/safety] The FAA should publish the safety rationale and failure data that motivated the replacement mandate and installation prohibition so stakeholders can evaluate the necessity and proportionality of the requirements.

[General/cost] The FAA should include a regulatory flexibility analysis and an economic impact estimate showing cost per operator, aggregate industry cost, and availability of financial assistance or extensions for small businesses for compliance with P3 and P4.

[P1] The proposed exclusion of services performed by marriage and family therapists from Medicare coverage (§411.15(p)(2)(vi)) will reduce access to outpatient behavioral health care for Medicare beneficiaries who rely on MFTs in rural and underserved areas.

[P1] Excluding marriage and family therapists from Medicare coverage conflicts with state licensure scopes of practice that authorize independent MFTs to provide clinically necessary services, creating reimbursement gaps and continuity-of-care problems.

[P1] The rule does not explain how beneficiaries currently receiving MFT services would transition; CMS should provide a phased implementation or grandfathering for patients mid-course of therapy before enforcing the exclusion.

[P2] The exclusion of services performed by mental health counselors (§411.15(p)(2)(vii)) will disproportionately affect beneficiaries with mild-to-moderate mental health conditions who are typically treated by licensed professional counselors (LPCs), increasing emergency and higher-cost care downstream.

[P2] Mental health counselors (as defined in 1861(lll)(4)) are licensed and credentialed in many states to deliver psychotherapy; denying Medicare coverage for their services likely violates statutory intent to cover medically necessary services furnished by qualified professionals.

[P2] The rule offers no analysis of supply effects—removing Medicare payment for mental health counselors may worsen workforce shortages and increase wait times; CMS should include workforce impact data.

[P3] Requiring CMS to set the total amount available for VBP incentive payments at least 60% of the reduction to adjusted SNF PPS payments (§413.338(c)(2)(i)) could underfund incentive pools when payment reductions are modest, limiting program effectiveness unless CMS clarifies adjustment methodology.

[P4] Fixing the FY2023 total incentive amount at 60% of the reduction to adjusted SNF PPS payments (§413.338(c)(2)(i) FY2023) removes CMS discretion to increase incentives in response to implementation needs; commenters urge CMS to make the FY2023 pool flexible.

[P5] Beginning FY2027, mandating that CMS increase the incentive pool "as appropriate" to account for the Health Equity Adjustment (§413.338(c)(2)(i) FY2027) is vague—CMS should specify the formula and triggers for increases to ensure transparency and predictability.

[P6] Calculating a SNF Performance Score for SNFs that received extraordinary circumstance exceptions while excluding months affected (§413.338(d)(4)(v)) may create apples-to-oranges comparisons if peers did not receive exceptions; CMS should describe risk-adjustment or minimum denominator rules.

[P7] The multi-step calculation requirement for SNF performance scores starting FY2027 (§413.338(e)(3)) is complex; CMS must publish worked examples and technical specifications well before the reporting year so SNFs can validate their data.

[P8] Summing points across measures for each SNF (§413.338(e)(3)(i)) could overweight measures with different clinical importance; commenters request that CMS publish the weighting scheme and rationale for aggregating unweighted points.

[P9] Normalizing SNF point totals to a 0–100 scale (§413.338(e)(3)(ii)) may mask distributional effects; CMS should disclose the normalization formula, handling of ties, and whether missing measures reduce denominators.

[P10] Adding Health Equity Adjustment bonus points to the normalized total but capping at 100 (§413.338(e)(3)(iii)) could render HEA bonuses ineffective for already high-performing SNFs; commenters recommend allowing HEA to affect rank-ordering or tie-breaks rather than being fully subject to an absolute cap.

[P11] The phased validation timeline (§413.338(j))—starting SNFRM validation FY2023 and other claims-based measures FY2026—lacks transitional support; SNFs and MACs need clear audit instruments and sample selection criteria.

[P12] Requiring MACs to validate claims-reported SNFRM data beginning FY2023 (§413.338(j)(1)) imposes resource burdens on MACs and providers; CMS should provide funding or timing flexibility and publish error tolerance thresholds.

[P13] Quarterly PBJ audits beginning FY2026 (§413.338(j)(2)) will be administratively burdensome for SNFs and contractors; commenters request that CMS limit audit frequency in the first program year and provide an appeals process for audit findings.

[P14] Periodic MDS audits capped at 1,500 SNFs per year beginning FY2027 (§413.338(j)(3)) may result in uneven oversight across regions; commenters ask CMS to clarify selection methodology to avoid targeting small or rural SNFs disproportionately.

[P15] The Health Equity Adjustment calculation steps (§413.338(k)) require transparency—CMS should publish the formula, data sources for underserved multipliers, and how top-tier determinations are made to allow independent verification.

[P16] Assigning two HEA points for each measure where a SNF is top tier (§413.338(k)(1)) appears arbitrary; stakeholders request evidence that two points per measure appropriately incentivizes equity improvements versus other allocation levels.

[P17] Summing points to compute a measure performance scaler (§413.338(k)(2)) without normalization across measures with varying sample sizes risks bias; CMS should ensure that measures with small denominators do not unduly influence the scaler.

[P18] The process for calculating the underserved multiplier (§413.338(k)(3)) must account for socioeconomic and regional variation; advocates request an explicit definition of "underserved" and mechanisms to avoid penalizing SNFs serving very high-need populations.

[P19] Multiplying the performance scaler by the underserved multiplier to compute HEA bonus points (§413.338(k)(4)) could produce volatile bonuses; CMS should cap year-over-year HEA point changes and provide simulation tools for SNFs to estimate effects.

[P22] CMS approval criteria for survey vendors (§413.360(b)(2)(ii)) should be transparent and include appeal rights; potential vendors need clear timelines and published minimum business requirements to plan application submissions.

[P23] Requiring entities to be CMS-approved before administering or submitting resident satisfaction surveys (§413.360(b)(2)(ii) sentence 2) may disrupt ongoing contracts—CMS should allow a limited transitional period during which pending applicants can submit data under supervision.

[P24] The oversight requirement that vendors permit CMS site visits at vendor locations (§413.360(b)(2)(iii)) raises confidentiality and proprietary concerns; CMS should limit site visits to document review and remote inspections when the vendor demonstrates data security compliance.

[P28] Requiring 100% submission of NHSN-collected measures starting FY2023 (§413.360(f)(1)(iii)) places SNFs at the mercy of CDC system outages or interface problems; CMS should include contingency rules for technical failures and allow batch resubmissions.

raw_output:
[P1] The August 16, 2021 comment deadline is unreasonably short and should be extended by at least 60 days to allow affected operators, supply-chain vendors, labor unions, and safety advocacy groups adequate time to prepare technical and economic comments.

[P1] The notice lacks clear instructions for electronic submission formats and supporting documentation limits (e.g., file size, accepted file types); the FAA should clarify acceptable submission methods to avoid lost or rejected comments before the August 16, 2021 deadline.

[P1] Because the AD affects international operators and foreign regulatory authorities, the FAA should explicitly provide an extended comment period or consultation opportunity for foreign civil aviation authorities and non‑U.S. stakeholders who will be impacted.

[P2] The blanket obligation to "comply within the specified compliance times" fails to acknowledge practical constraints (parts availability, scheduled maintenance windows) and should permit temporary relief or staggered compliance schedules for operators with documented logistical constraints.

[P2] The rule should require the FAA to publish precise definitions of "specified compliance times" in the final rule; currently the phrase is vague and may lead to inconsistent enforcement across operators.

[P3] The 60‑month compliance window measured from April 8, 2019 effectively shortens compliance time for operators that acquired airplanes after that date; the FAA should allow the 60 months to be measured from the date of issuance of this AD or from airplane delivery to the operator.

[P3] Requiring all "applicable 'RC' actions" within 60 months without distinguishing between actions of differing complexity (simple inspection vs. structural modification) is burdensome; the FAA should stratify compliance times based on task complexity and risk.

[P3] The provision references a Boeing Service Bulletin but does not provide the revision number or ensure public availability; the FAA must incorporate by reference the exact SB revision or include the SB in the docket to permit meaningful comments and compliance planning.

[P3] The rule should clarify whether recurring RC actions (if any) are required only once within 60 months or on an ongoing basis; ambiguity could create compliance and enforcement issues.

[P4] The parts installation prohibition lacks an implementation grace period for legacy spare parts inventories; suppliers and MROs that hold PSUs and life vest panels acquired before the AD's effective dates may be unfairly barred from using legitimate spares unless a limited sell-through period is allowed.

[P4] The prohibition is overly broad by preventing installation "on any airplane" without specifying whether this includes non‑U.S.-registered aircraft undergoing maintenance in the U.S.; FAA should clarify territorial scope and applicability to foreign-registered aircraft receiving maintenance in the U.S.

[P4] The prohibition fails to define who has the duty to verify that a lanyard assembly has been "modified or re-identified" — installer, operator, or supplier — and what documentation or physical marking constitutes acceptable re‑identification.

[P5] Paragraph (h)(1)'s trigger — applying the installation prohibition "after the airplane has been modified or re-identified as required by paragraph (g)" — is circular and confusing: it appears to prevent installation until modification is completed, but then uses completion as the trigger for prohibition; FAA should reword to clarify the intended timing.

[P5] For airplanes without secondary retention features, the rule should allow installation of replacement PSUs or life vest panels with an approved alternate means (AMOC) while operators schedule the paragraph (g) actions, rather than an absolute prohibition tied to modification status.

[P6] Applying the installation prohibition immediately "as of the effective date of this AD" for airplanes already having secondary retention features installed is unnecessarily punitive — operators with compliant installations should be permitted to install parts that match existing installations; the FAA should limit the prohibition only to non‑conforming parts.

[P6] The AD should clarify whether previously installed PSUs/life vest panels with secondary retention features but lacking the specified identification require re‑identification, or whether the installation prohibition only applies to subsequent installations.

[P7] Granting the Seattle ACO Branch Manager authority to approve AMOCs centralizes decision authority and may delay approvals for operators outside the Seattle ACO's region; FAA should allow regional Flight Standards offices to approve AMOCs subject to coordination to expedite compliance.

[P7] The rule should set a mandatory FAA timeline (e.g., 60 or 90 days) for AMOC determinations to prevent indefinite delays and provide regulatory certainty for operators seeking alternatives.

[P8] Requiring AMOC requests to be routed through the principal inspector or responsible Flight Standards Office may create additional administrative burden and delay; the FAA should allow direct submission to the certification office with a copy to the principal inspector.

[P8] The provision does not address what constitutes a "principal inspector" for part‑time or contract maintenance organizations; the FAA should define the proper recipient for AMOC requests in such cases.

[P9] Direct submissions to the certification office manager must be allowed electronically and tracked; the rule should specify an official point of contact name and mailing address and require FAA to acknowledge receipt within a specified timeframe.

[P10] Email submission to the specified address is helpful, but the rule should require an automated confirmation of receipt, and specify required file formats, encryption guidance for proprietary data, and maximum attachment sizes to prevent lost materials.

[P11] The requirement to notify the principal inspector "before using any approved AMOC" is ambiguous as to timing (how far in advance) and method of notification; the FAA should require written notification at least 10 business days prior and allow electronic notification via the AMOC tracking system.

[P11] Small operators without assigned principal inspectors may find it difficult to comply with the notification requirement; the FAA should designate a clear alternative contact or centralized notification portal.

[P12] Allowing Boeing ODA approval for AMOC use on repairs risks conflict of interest; independent FAA concurrence or an independent third‑party review should be required when Boeing ODA approves AMOCs affecting structural modifications or flight‑safety items.

[P12] The provision should specify the scope of Boeing ODA authority (which specific AMOC types it may approve) and require transparent recordkeeping and public availability of ODA approvals used in lieu of FAA approvals.

[P13] Requiring that AMOC repairs/modifications meet the airplane's certification basis is appropriate, but the rule should clarify how changed certification basis from later ADs or STCs will be reconciled with AMOC approvals that reference earlier certification bases.

[P13] The stipulation that AMOC approvals "must specifically reference this AD" should be expanded to require inclusion of the AMOC approval number and any limitations or required inspections, to improve clarity for maintenance personnel and inspectors.

[P14] The automatic recognition of AMOCs approved for AD 2019–03–26 may be problematic if the Boeing Service Bulletin revision differs materially; the FAA should require re‑validation of prior AMOCs against the current SB revision rather than blanket acceptance.

[P14] The rule should publish a complete list of previously approved AMOCs for AD 2019–03–26 in the docket so operators can determine whether their previously approved AMOC applies to the corresponding SB provisions required by paragraph (g).

[P14] Legal commenters may assert that treating previous AMOCs as automatically applicable could contravene procedural requirements if the prior approvals were limited in scope; FAA should specify any scope or condition differences that would prevent automatic recognition.

Paragraph (h)(1)'s trigger — applying the installation prohibition "after the airplane has been modified or re-identified as required by paragraph (g)" — is circular and confusing: it appears to prevent installation until modification is completed, but then uses completion as the trigger for prohibition; FAA should reword to clarify the intended timing.

For airplanes without secondary retention features, the rule should allow installation of replacement PSUs or life vest panels with an approved alternate means (AMOC) while operators schedule the paragraph (g) actions, rather than an absolute prohibition tied to modification status.

Applying the installation prohibition immediately "as of the effective date of this AD" for airplanes already having secondary retention features installed is unnecessarily punitive — operators with compliant installations should be permitted to install parts that match existing installations; the FAA should limit the prohibition only to non‑conforming parts.

The AD should clarify whether previously installed PSUs/life vest panels with secondary retention features but lacking the specified identification require re‑identification, or whether the installation prohibition only applies to subsequent installations.

Granting the Seattle ACO Branch Manager authority to approve AMOCs centralizes decision authority and may delay approvals for operators outside the Seattle ACO's region; FAA should allow regional Flight Standards offices to approve AMOCs subject to coordination to expedite compliance.
The rule should set a mandatory FAA timeline (e.g., 60 or 90 days) for AMOC determinations to prevent indefinite delays and provide regulatory certainty for operators seeking alternatives.

Requiring AMOC requests to be routed through the principal inspector or responsible Flight Standards Office may create additional administrative burden and delay; the FAA should allow direct submission to the certification office with a copy to the principal inspector.

The provision does not address what constitutes a "principal inspector" for part‑time or contract maintenance organizations; the FAA should define the proper recipient for AMOC requests in such cases.

Direct submissions to the certification office manager must be allowed electronically and tracked; the rule should specify an official point of contact name and mailing address and require FAA to acknowledge receipt within a specified timeframe.

Email submission to the specified address is helpful, but the rule should require an automated confirmation of receipt, and specify required file formats, encryption guidance for proprietary data, and maximum attachment sizes to prevent lost materials.

The requirement to notify the principal inspector "before using any approved AMOC" is ambiguous as to timing (how far in advance) and method of notification; the FAA should require written notification at least 10 business days prior and allow electronic notification via the AMOC tracking system.

Small operators without assigned principal inspectors may find it difficult to comply with the notification requirement; the FAA should designate a clear alternative contact or centralized notification portal.

Allowing Boeing ODA approval for AMOC use on repairs risks conflict of interest; independent FAA concurrence or an independent third‑party review should be required when Boeing ODA approves AMOCs affecting structural modifications or flight‑safety items.

The provision should specify the scope of Boeing ODA authority (which specific AMOC types it may approve) and require transparent recordkeeping and public availability of ODA approvals used in lieu of FAA approvals.

Requiring that AMOC repairs/modifications meet the airplane's certification basis is appropriate, but the rule should clarify how changed certification basis from later ADs or STCs will be reconciled with AMOC approvals that reference earlier certification bases.

The stipulation that AMOC approvals "must specifically reference this AD" should be expanded to require inclusion of the AMOC approval number and any limitations or required inspections, to improve clarity for maintenance personnel and inspectors.

The automatic recognition of AMOCs approved for AD 2019–03–26 may be problematic if the Boeing Service Bulletin revision differs materially; the FAA should require re‑validation of prior AMOCs against the current SB revision rather than blanket acceptance.

The rule should publish a complete list of previously approved AMOCs for AD 2019–03–26 in the docket so operators can determine whether their previously approved AMOC applies to the corresponding SB provisions required by paragraph (g).

Legal commenters may assert that treating previous AMOCs as automatically applicable could contravene procedural requirements if the prior approvals were limited in scope; FAA should specify any scope or condition differences that would prevent automatic recognition.

[P1] The requirement that CE credit hours “must be obtained prior to qualifying as a laboratory director” is impracticable for candidates who obtain a director position contingent on completing CE within a short onboarding window; request either allowance for CE completion within a set post-appointment period (e.g., 90 days) or clarification on employers’ ability to hire conditionally.

[P1] Clarify what qualifies as CE “covering director responsibilities” — commenters request an explicit list of acceptable topics or approved CE providers and whether in-house training counts.

[P2] The restriction that director/supervisory experience must be obtained only in facilities that meet the definition of a laboratory and are not excepted under §493.3(b) will disqualify experienced supervisors from community clinics or mobile units that perform equivalent work; request recognition of equivalent supervisory experience in such settings.

[P3] The rule’s prohibition on counting training/experience gained in excepted facilities under §493.3(b) is overly narrow and will penalize personnel trained in federally funded research labs and public health emergency sites; request an exceptions process or competency-based alternative.

[P4] The proposed flat fee requirements for “issuance, renewal, change in certificate type, or reinstatement” impose significant cost burdens on small and rural laboratories with limited margins; request a tiered fee schedule or small-lab waivers.

[P5] The flat registration certificate fee that “includes issuing, collecting, and evaluating application test scope costs” is arbitrary without published fee amounts or cost breakdowns; request transparency on cost calculations and examples of fee amounts for small vs. large labs.

[P6] The waiver certificate fee that includes evaluating whether tests meet waived criteria risks duplicative review of FDA-cleared waived tests; request that CMS accept FDA categorization for waived tests to avoid redundant evaluation and reduce fees.

[P7] The PPM certificate fee that covers “evaluating whether the procedures meet PPM criteria” will deter clinics that rely on PPM tests; request clear definition of “PPM procedure criteria” and an inexpensive streamlined review for widely used PPM methods.

[P8] The accreditation certificate fee that includes accreditor program evaluation duplicates costs already borne by accrediting organizations; request an offset or credit for labs accredited by HHS-approved accreditors to avoid double charging.

[P9] The compliance certificate fee that funds “proficiency testing evaluation/monitoring” lacks specificity on how frequently PT will be evaluated and how those costs translate to fee amounts; request detailed methodology and examples.

[P10] Setting certificate fee amounts only every two years reduces HHS flexibility to respond to rapid cost changes; recommend annual, not biennial, fee-setting or interim adjustment authority.

[P11] Requiring CMS to publish fee adjustments and inflation adjustments biennially in the Federal Register is appropriate, but request advance notice (e.g., 90 days) before new fees take effect so labs can budget.

[P12] The biennial fee payment schedule is reasonable for cash flow, but some labs prefer annual billing; request optional annual installment payment plans without penalties.

[P13] Tying the fee owed to the “most recent Federal Register notice when their transaction is processed” creates unpredictability for applicants during notice publication windows; request that fee amounts be fixed at application receipt date or provide a grace period to allow applicants to withdraw without penalty if fees rise.

[P14] The provision that HHS notifies labs of applicable fees after processing their application may delay operations; request that fee estimates be provided at application submission and that any post-processing fee increases be limited.

[P15] Charging labs a fee to reissue revised certificates for clerical changes (e.g., address correction) is burdensome; request fee exemptions for administrative changes that do not alter certificate scope.

[P16] Requiring payment in full before issuance of a revised certificate will delay time-sensitive operations; request allowance for escrow or installment payments for minor revisions.

[P17] The additional fee for adding services to a compliance certificate only if §493.643(d)(2) requires it is ambiguous; request criteria and fee schedule for upgrades be published.

[P18] Charging a fee for replacement certificates (lost/stolen) penalizes labs for clerical issues; request minimal administrative fee and free electronic reissuance.

[P19] Requiring full payment before replacement certificate issuance may prevent labs from demonstrating licensure in urgent situations; request temporary issuance of an electronic attestation while payment is processed.

[P20] The program compliance determination fee imposed on labs subject to routine inspections places heavier burden on smaller labs that already pay compliance certificate fees; request reduced or capped fees for small-volume labs and a cost-justification analysis.

[P21] Exempting PPM, waiver, and accredited laboratories from the routine inspection fee is logical, but commenters request clarity on labs with mixed test menus that perform both waived and nonwaived testing and how exemptions apply proportionally.

[P22] Biennial assessment of program compliance fees may not match inspection timing for labs with off-cycle inspections; request proration or alignment with individual lab inspection schedules.

[P23] Assessing follow-up visit costs to compliance certificate labs when inspections find deficiencies is reasonable, but require clear caps, notice, and appeal rights before fees are billed.

[P24] Permitting revocation of a compliance certificate for failure to pay assessed follow-up visit fees raises due process and patient-safety concerns; request a graduated enforcement approach (payment plans, administrative appeal) before revocation.

[P25] Requiring fees for upgrade determinations (inspection, personnel evaluation, proficiency monitoring) when labs add services will discourage service expansion; request fee waivers for community health expansions or an affordability threshold.

[P26] The authority to revoke a certificate for failure to pay upgrade-related fees is disproportionate; request limits on revocation authority and mandatory notice plus cure period.

[P27] Assessing fees for complaint investigations, sanctions, or hearings only “when necessary” is vague; request objective criteria for when costs will be assessed and estimated hourly rates for staff time.

[P28] The exception that costs will not be imposed if a complaint is unsubstantiated or action overturned is appropriate but lacks specificity on reimbursement timelines; request timelines and interest on refunded amounts if previously collected.

[P29] Conditioning assessment of investigation/hearing fees on laboratory concession or ALJ ruling in favor of HHS improperly shifts litigation risk; request that HHS be required to demonstrate final determination of culpability before billing.

[P30] Revocation for failure to pay investigation/hearing costs creates perverse incentives for labs to contest findings; request alternative enforcement such as liens or payment plans, not immediate revocation.

[P31] Charging desk review fees when labs fail proficiency testing will financially punish labs already remediating deficiencies; request fee waivers for first-time or minor PT failures and transparency in desk review cost calculations.

[P32] Tying desk review fees to “actual resources and time” is fair but requires published hourly rates and caps to prevent excessive charges; request independent audit of billing.

[P33] The additional validation inspection fee for accredited labs “shared among accredited labs” duplicates accreditation costs and will be seen as double payment; request credit for existing accreditor validation activities or elimination of the shared fee.

[P34] Imposing a biennial shared validation inspection cost equal to 5% of comparable nonaccredited inspection costs is arbitrary; request justification for the 5% rate and an alternative formula tied to actual HHS validation activity.

[P35] Revoking accreditation for failure to pay shared validation inspection fees is punitive; request alternative sanctions and protections for accredited labs that dispute fee calculations.

[P36] Assessing additional fees for follow-up visits to accredited labs after deficient inspections is acceptable but should exclude costs already charged by accreditors; request coordination to avoid duplicate charges.

[P37] The revocation threat for failure to pay follow-up fees by accredited labs creates undue risk; request notice, ability to appeal, and payment plan options before revocation.

[P38] Billing approved State lab programs for Federal inspection costs, substantiated complaint investigations, and pro rata overhead imposes large burdens on State budgets; request cap, phased implementation, and consultation with States to align budgets.

[P39] The requirement that HHS or a designee notify labs in writing of fees and submission instructions (except approved State programs) is reasonable, but request electronic notice options and standardized invoice formats to streamline payments.

[P40] Withholding issuance of applicable certificates until fees are paid will interrupt patient care in situations of billing disputes; request temporary provisional certificates or escrow mechanisms to prevent service disruption.

[P41] Requiring HHS to estimate validation inspection costs in approved States at least every two years is good practice, but request that estimates be accompanied by detailed methodologies and opportunities for State comment before finalization.

[P42] Mailing approved States notice of fees and payment bank addresses is insufficient in the digital age; request secure electronic transmission and advance electronic invoicing.

[P43] Billing approved States for substantiated complaint investigations in their labs could discourage States from cooperating with HHS investigations; request shared-cost models or at least an appeals process for disputed substantiation.

[P44] Tying fee increases to a two-year compounded CPI–U may not reflect actual program cost drivers (e.g., personnel, travel); request use of a more relevant index or inclusion of a healthcare-specific inflation adjustment.

[P45] The across-the-board fee increase to cover shortfalls could lead to sudden, large increases in fees that disproportionately impact small labs; request phased increases, a reserve fund, and stakeholder review before applying shortfall-driven increases.

[P46] Rolling fee increases into future baselines will cause compounding and potentially runaway fee growth; request safeguards such as caps on annual increases and transparency on cumulative increases.

[P47] Publishing the fee increase calculation in the Federal Register is necessary but must include detailed spreadsheets and assumptions; request publication of the underlying financial model and opportunity for public comment prior to implementation.

[P48] The continuous monitoring and alert system requirement for specimen and reagent storage temperatures will impose significant equipment and maintenance costs on small labs; request allowance for validated periodic monitoring (with automated logging) where continuous systems are not feasible, or a phased compliance schedule.

[P48] Require specification of acceptable alarm parameters, notification timelines, and documentation standards so labs can implement consistent systems.

[P49] The mandate for written storage/retention policies “tailored to specimen type” is ambiguous; request model templates and minimum retention periods by specimen category.

[P50] The requirement that specimens be “readily retrievable” needs clarification about electronic vs. physical retrieval standards and acceptable retrieval timeframes; request a maximum retrieval time (e.g., within 15 minutes) be defined.

[P51] The emergency alternate storage plan requirement is reasonable but should permit shared community contingency agreements for rural labs; request allowance for third-party or regional backup storage providers.

[P52] Requiring method efficacy QC for immunologic reagents used in lymphocyte isolation adds technical burden; request specific performance metrics and acceptable QC frequencies to avoid over-testing.

[P53] The requirement for written criteria to determine when antigen and allele typing is required could lead to overtesting; request that criteria be evidence-based and allow clinician-ordered testing to supersede routine typing when clinically indicated.

[P54] The obligation to “reasonably attempt” to have monthly serum specimens for all potential transplant recipients is vague and operationally difficult; request definition of “reasonable effort” (e.g., documented contact attempts) and allowance for clinically justified exceptions.

[P55] Requiring written procedures and criteria for each crossmatch type and to specify crossmatch type on reports is appropriate but will necessitate report template changes; request a compliance timeline and examples of acceptable report language.

[P56] The detailed requirement to define which HLA antigens, alleles, and antibodies are to be tested will increase workload; request that labs be permitted to adopt standardized test panels endorsed by transplant societies.

[P57] Written criteria for assessing recipient alloantibody status must allow clinician judgment and rapid communication in urgent cases; request provisions for emergency exception workflows.

[P58] Ongoing assessment criteria for recipient antibody presence/absence should specify minimum monitoring frequency and circumstances that trigger additional testing to avoid arbitrary practices.

[P59] Requiring donors be serologically typed for HLA antigens identified in recipients “where applicable” needs clearer definitions of “applicable” to avoid inconsistent application between labs.

[P60] The written criteria for pre- and post-transplant confirmation testing must address timeframe requirements (e.g., within X hours/days) to support urgent transplants; request explicit time windows.

[P61] Mandating that donor and recipient test results be made available to the transplant team raises confidentiality and interoperability concerns; request standards for secure electronic transmission and turnaround time requirements.

[P62] The requirement that immunologic assessments rely on CLIA-certified laboratory test reports could exclude valuable research or specialty lab data; request procedures for validating and accepting external non-CLIA data where appropriate and documented.

[P63] Defining time limits between recipient testing and crossmatch must balance safety and logistics; request specific maximum intervals (e.g., crossmatch must be within 72 hours of recipient sample) and allowance for exceptions with documentation.

[P64] Specifying crossmatch type on the test report is reasonable but require standardized nomenclature to avoid confusion among transplant teams.

[P65] The obligation for transplant histocompatibility labs to have written policies specifying testing for each transplant type will burden smaller programs that perform low volumes of multiple transplant types; request streamlined policy templates and recognition of regional reference labs.

[P66] Requiring protocols addressing transplant type, donor type, and recipient risk status is clinically appropriate but request examples and a risk-stratification framework to standardize implementation.

[P67] Specifying types and frequencies of testing to support transplant protocols needs to be evidence-based; request that CMS reference transplant society guidelines as acceptable standards.

[P68] The requirement to have a process to obtain same-day recipient specimens and to document efforts when unable to obtain one is onerous for out-of-area recipients; request allowance for telemedicine-coordinated specimen collection or documented coordination with sending facilities.

[P69] The mandate to document all control procedures is appropriate; request electronic documentation templates and retention periods be specified to reduce recordkeeping burden.

[P70] The PPM laboratory director’s duty to evaluate and ensure testing personnel competency is reasonable, but evaluate frequency and acceptable evaluators (remote vs. onsite); request allowance for third-party competency assessments.

[P71] Including direct observation of routine patient test performance in competency evaluations may be infeasible for remote or decentralized testing sites; request allowance for video observation or periodic proficiency testing as alternatives.

[P72] Monitoring how tests are recorded and results reported as part of competency assessments is reasonable; request guidance on acceptable sampling sizes and frequency.

[P73] Requiring review of test results or worksheets for competency assessment needs specifics on sample sizes and the acceptable rate of review to make it practical.

[P74] Internal blind samples or external PT for competency evaluations may not be available for all PPM tests; request flexibility to allow equivalent methods (e.g., simulated samples, manufacturer QC) when PT is not available.

[P75] Assessing problem-solving skills as part of competency evaluations is subjective; request objective criteria and standardized assessment tools.

[P76] The semiannual competency evaluations in the first year then annual thereafter will increase administrative burden for labs with high turnover; request flexibility for frequency when staff have documented extensive prior experience.

[P77] The multiple qualification pathways for laboratory directors create complexity; request a consolidated, competency-based pathway that allows for equivalencies rather than rigid degrees/licenses.

[P78] The MD/DO with AP/CP board certification pathway is appropriate but may disadvantage rural clinics that cannot recruit such specialists; request allowance for remote medical directors with demonstrated competencies.

[P79] The pathway allowing MD/DO/DPod with ≥1 year directing/supervising nonwaived testing plus ≥20 CE hours is workable but the CE hour requirement should permit in-house directed CE and provide approved CE lists.

[P80] Grandfathering current moderate complexity directors is necessary; recommend clarifying that temporary gaps in service (e.g., medical leave) do not forfeit grandfathered status provided continuous service overall.

[P81] The requirement for laboratory directors to be on-site at least twice per year (minimum 4 months apart) may be insufficient for high-volume or complex labs; request risk-based on-site frequency requirements tied to lab complexity and performance.

[P82] Documentation of on-site visits and evidence of activities must specify minimum content to avoid inconsistent enforcement; request a standardized checklist of activities to be documented.

[P83] The technical consultant qualification pathways should allow teleconsultation from qualified consultants in other States when state licensure permits; request clarification on interstate telemedicine applicability.

[P84] Requiring MD/DO AP/CP certification for technical consultants in some pathways will limit available consultants; request inclusion of PhD-level experts with equivalent training for certain specialties.

[P85] The technical consultant pathway requiring ≥1 year lab training/experience in nonwaived testing in the specialty they cover should allow equivalent experience in regulated research/lab settings; request language permitting equivalent competency demonstration.

[P86] For blood gas analysis, allowing a bachelor’s degree plus ≥2 years blood gas experience is appropriate; request explicit acceptable degree fields and documentation standards for the experience.

[P87] Grandfathering technical consultants serving on the effective date is appropriate, but request clarification on requalification requirements if they leave and later return.

[P88] The multiple qualification pathways for testing personnel are complex and may be difficult for HR departments to interpret; request simplified flowcharts and examples for common staffing scenarios.

[P89] The high school diploma pathway with extensive documented training requires detailed training curricula to ensure consistency; request CMS-provided training modules or minimum hour requirements per competency area.

[P90] The blood gas personnel qualification allowing specified degrees plus required years of experience is workable but request flexibility for point-of-care blood gas testing performed under PPM with targeted competency verification.

[P91] The high-complexity laboratory director MD/DO with AP/CP certification pathway is reasonable; request transitional flexibility for labs in underserved areas to use qualified alternative directors temporarily.

[P92] The high-complexity director pathway allowing MD/DO/DPod with ≥2 years directing/supervising high complexity testing plus ≥20 CE hours should clarify whether prior experience in non-CLIA research labs counts toward the two-year requirement.

[P1] The rule’s allowance of a foreign passport plus Form I-94/I-94A with a valid endorsement as proof of employment authorization creates ambiguity about whether employers may accept electronic I-94 records; the provision should explicitly permit or prohibit electronic I-94s to avoid inconsistent employer practices.

[P1] The provision fails to define “valid endorsement” and whether endorsements issued by foreign consular officials or only DHS-issued endorsements qualify; clarify which issuing authorities are acceptable.

[P1] Stating that employment must “not be in conflict with the endorsement or its restrictions” is vague; the regulation should require employers to check and document the specific employer name and any employer-specific restrictions on the endorsement.

[P1] The text does not address how employers verify endorsements that are employer-specific incident to status (e.g., H-1B amendment situations); recommend adding procedures for verifying that the endorsement applies to the employing entity.

[P1] For individuals authorized to work only “incident to status,” accepting a passport plus I-94 could allow unauthorized work if employers misread restrictions; require employers to retain copies of both documents to demonstrate good-faith compliance.

[P2] The list of nonimmigrant classes authorized to work for a specific employer lacks clarity about subclasses and dependents (e.g., L-2, E-2 dependents); the rule should explicitly list dependent classes and any differing restrictions.

[P2] The phrase “subject to listed restrictions” provides insufficient guidance to employers about what restrictions are mandatory versus discretionary; include a clear, standardized table of employer obligations and allowed job functions.

[P2] The provision appears to authorize employment only by a “specific employer” but does not define whether successor employers after mergers/acquisitions are covered; include rules for change of employer, corporate restructures, and staffing through third-party contractors.

[P2] Industry stakeholders will be concerned that employer-specific authorization will increase E-Verify or I-9 audit exposure; request longer implementation timelines and transitional protections for employers relying on prior guidance.

[P3] Prohibiting DHS issuance of EADs to aliens in these employer-specific classes may disadvantage workers whose status changes or who need portable work authorization; suggest an exception allowing EADs when the alien demonstrates imminent loss of status and no continuing employer.

[P3] The prohibition on EAD issuance could conflict with existing INA provisions granting EADs to certain categories; request DHS to reconcile this prohibition with statutory eligibility and cite legal authority.

[P3] Legal advocates will challenge the lack of an administrative appeal or waiver process for individuals denied EADs due to being in employer-specific classes; propose adding an appeal mechanism or discretionary waiver.

[P4] Including section 212(d)(5) parolees as authorized to accept employment is beneficial, but the rule doesn’t define whether parolees need additional confirmation of work permission or a duration limit; require DHS to issue clear parole documentation specifying employment start/end dates and employer restrictions.

[P4] Humanitarian organizations will request that parolees be allowed to change employers without losing parole status, but the provision remains silent on portability; recommend explicitly permitting employer changes with DHS notification.

[P4] The rule should clarify whether parole for “significant public benefit” parolees are eligible for Social Security numbers and access to benefits; include guidance to agencies processing benefit eligibility.

[P5] The comment deadline of July 13, 2018 is outdated and inconsistent with current timelines in the preamble; request an updated, reasonable comment period of at least 60 days from publication and an extension for stakeholders requiring regulatory impact analysis.

[P5] Small businesses and advocacy groups will likely need an extension beyond July 13, 2018 to prepare detailed comments; request a 90-day extension and stakeholder outreach sessions.

[P6] Requiring use of procedures in 14 CFR 11.43 and 11.45 may be inappropriate for this DHS rulemaking; request DHS confirm that these DOT procedures apply or provide the correct federal rulemaking citation for submission procedures.

[P6] The provision should include accommodations for commenters with disabilities who cannot submit using standard electronic or mail channels; request alternative submission methods and confirmation of receipt.

[P7] Directing commenters to regulations.gov is appropriate, but the rule should require DHS to post a consolidated FAQ and comment guidance on regulations.gov to assist non-technical stakeholders in submitting effective comments.

[P8] Allowing fax submissions to 202-493-2251 may be obsolete and insecure; recommend removing fax as an accepted method or ensuring fax submissions receive the same processing and acknowledgement as electronic submissions.

[P9] The mail address specified is for DOT Docket Operations and may be incorrect for DHS rulemaking; request confirmation of the proper mail address and guarantee that mailed comments will be docketed promptly.

[P10] Limiting hand delivery to Monday–Friday 9 a.m.–5 p.m. to the specified room may hinder stakeholders in different time zones; propose accepting hand deliveries at other DHS facilities or providing longer delivery windows.

[P11] The instruction to view service information at the FAA Transport Standards Branch is inconsistent with a DHS regulation; clarify where service information relevant to this immigration/employment rule is stored and accessible.

[P12] The Proposed AD’s requirement for initial and repetitive special detailed inspections and corrective actions appears to apply to aircraft parts, which is unrelated to employment authorization provisions; request clarification of scope and correction if provisions were erroneously mixed from another rulemaking.

[P12] If the AD inspection requirements are intended, there is no estimate of inspection intervals, costs, or safety benefits; request a Regulatory Flexibility Analysis and economic impact statement detailing inspection frequency, labor hours, and cost to small entities.

[P12] The rule should include clear definitions of “detailed inspection,” “special detailed inspections,” and thresholds that trigger corrective actions to prevent inconsistent enforcement.

[P13] The provision allowing examination of the AD docket online is helpful, but the internet address is incomplete; require DHS to provide a fully qualified URL and ensure all supporting documents are uploaded in searchable text formats to facilitate public review.

[P13] Commenters will request that DHS provide downloadable datasets of redacted prior decisions and form examples to enable empirical analysis of how employer-specific work authorizations have been administered historically.

raw_output:
[P1] The June 22, 2020 comment deadline is already passed; the rule should either reopen the comment period or update the date to a current, reasonable deadline to allow meaningful stakeholder participation.

[P1] Requiring comments to be “received by June 22, 2020” without specifying receipt methods and time zone creates uncertainty; the FAA should clarify accepted submission methods (mail, email, docket portal) and the time zone for the deadline.

[P2] The compliance provision is unacceptably vague because it references “the compliance times specified” without summarizing those times in the AD; operators need explicit, consolidated compliance schedules in the AD text.

[P2] The AD should include grace periods or phased compliance for small operators and lessors who may face logistical or supply-chain delays in meeting the compliance times specified.

[P3] The 120-day requirement to install eligible EEC software is overly aggressive for operators with limited down-time windows; FAA should extend to at least 180 days or allow staged compliance tied to scheduled maintenance.

[P3] The AD does not define “eligible” EEC software or provide a list/clear criteria; this ambiguity exposes operators to enforcement risk and should be clarified by referencing specific software part numbers or service bulletin versions.

[P3] Requiring EEC software installation within 120 days imposes cost and scheduling burdens; the FAA should provide an estimate of expected costs and allow credits for previously-installed compatible software.

[P4] Granting sole AMOC approval authority to the ECO Branch Manager without clear delegation procedures may bottleneck requests; the FAA should clarify delegation and expected response timelines for AMOC applications.

[P5] Requiring AMOC requests to go to the principal inspector or local FSDO may be inefficient for operators without an assigned principal inspector; the AD should permit direct submission to the ECO Branch as an alternative.

[P6] The instruction about addressing AMOC information “to the person identified in paragraph (j)(1)” is incomplete/truncated and creates administrative uncertainty; the AD must include the full contact name, office address, and position.

[P7] Permitting email submissions to ANE–AD–AMOC@faa.gov is helpful, but the AD must state file format limits, maximum attachment size, and confidentiality handling for proprietary data.

[P8] The requirement to notify the principal inspector or FSDO before using an approved AMOC needs a clear timeline (e.g., within 24 hours or prior to the next flight) and method of notification; otherwise operators will not know when the notification must occur.

[P8] The AD should allow electronic notification (email or portal entry) as acceptable means to notify the principal inspector or FSDO, to accommodate large fleets and remote operations.

[P9] The duplicate comment due date provision for the Boeing AD repeating June 22, 2020 should be corrected; having identical past deadlines across multiple ADs without current applicability is confusing.

[P10] The Boeing AD’s reliance on “the compliance times specified” lacks transparency — the AD should explicitly state the 9-month inspection window and any follow-up intervals within the compliance paragraph, not only in the body.

[P11] The 9-month window to inspect the SOB slot for insufficient sealant may be too long for safety-critical fuel-sealing issues; safety advocates will request a shorter interval (e.g., 90 days) given potential fuel leak risks.

[P11] The AD’s mandate to “do all applicable investigative and corrective actions per Boeing MOM” without including or summarizing required steps forces operators to purchase or obtain the MOM; the AD should incorporate or append the required procedural steps.

[P11] Requiring corrective actions “before further flight” after detecting insufficient sealant is appropriate, but the AD must define acceptable temporary measures and limitations if immediate full repair would ground aircraft and threaten essential service.

[P12] Allowing deferred repair up to 10 days only if the center tank is empty and no fuel contamination exists is reasonable, but the AD should require periodic re-inspection within the 10-day deferral period to ensure no new contamination occurs.

[P12] The deferral exception tied to MEL procedures may be inconsistently applied across operators; the FAA should provide a standardized MEL relief form or example procedures to avoid regulatory ambiguity.

[P13] The AD’s explicit non-requirement to report inspection findings conflicts with service information requesting reports; operators and safety groups may prefer mandatory reporting to monitor fleet-wide trends — the FAA should reconsider and require de-identified reporting.

[P13] Removing the reporting requirement impedes FAA and manufacturer ability to track prevalence and recurrence; at minimum, an optional voluntary reporting channel with guidance should be established.

[P14] Concentrating AMOC approval authority in the Seattle ACO Branch Manager for the Boeing AD may create regional bottlenecks; the AD should authorize parallel review by delegated designees or specify expected processing times.

[P15] The requirement to send AMOC requests to the principal inspector or local FSDO per 14 CFR 39.19 should be harmonized with the Seattle ACO email option to prevent confusion about the correct routing.

[P16] The direct submission address referencing paragraph (l)(1) is incomplete in the published text; the AD must provide the full attention line and mailing address to satisfy FOIA/administrative requirements.

[P17] Allowing AMOC requests via 9-ANM-Seattle-ACO-AMOC-Requests@faa.gov is good but the AD should require confirmation of receipt and provide SLA target (e.g., response within 45 days) to help operators plan.

[P18] The requirement to notify the principal inspector or FSDO before using an approved AMOC lacks clarity on whether prior FAA inspection or concurrence is needed; the AD should state that notification does not require further FAA approval unless specified.

[P19] Permitting use of an AMOC approved by Boeing ODA is efficient, but the AD should require Boeing to document the ODA approval decision and make it available to the operator and FAA for audit.

[P20] Requiring that any AMOC repair/modification “meet the certification basis of the airplane” is appropriate but will often be difficult to demonstrate; the AD should offer guidance on acceptable methods to establish compliance with the certification basis (e.g., test data, analysis templates).

[P21] Requiring explicit reference to this AD in any AMOC approval is reasonable, but the AD should clarify whether single AMOC approvals can cover multiple ADs or multiple airplanes, to reduce administrative burden.

[P11] The AD does not define “general visual inspection” in objective terms (tools, access panels, lighting); the FAA should include the inspection definition or reference the general visual inspection definition used in other ADs.

[P3] The AD lacks any allowance for operators who already have a field-modified EEC with equivalent functionality but without an FAA-approved paperwork trail; the FAA should include a pathway to validate equivalency without full reinstallation.

[P7] The email address provided for AMOC requests (ANE–AD–AMOC@faa.gov) may not be secure for proprietary attachments; the FAA should provide secure file transfer options or explicit guidance on handling proprietary/confidential material.

[P11] The AD references Boeing MOM–MOM–20–0049–01B (R1) dated Jan 29, 2020, but does not indicate whether later revisions are acceptable; the AD should specify that only the referenced revision is required or allow later revisions if approved by the FAA.

[P12] The 10-day deferral may create operational confusion across international flights where local regulations differ; the FAA should coordinate with foreign authorities or provide clear instructions on how MEL deferrals apply to operations outside the U.S.

[P19] Allowing Boeing ODA approvals requires clear limits on ODA authority; the AD should specify whether an ODA approval is self-executing or still requires FAA notification/acceptance and audit rights.

[P20] The phrase “meet the certification basis” could be interpreted as requiring structural reanalysis for minor sealant repairs; the FAA should provide examples of acceptable minor repairs that do not trigger full certification-basis analysis.

[P13] By declining to require reporting, the FAA is depriving the public record of safety data; citizen groups will likely request at least an aggregated summary of inspection findings be published periodically.

[P3] The AD should include provisions for software rollback procedures in case the new EEC software causes unforeseen flight-control issues; operators need guidance and approval pathways for emergency deinstallation.

[P11] The AD should include a compliance credit for operators who have already performed detailed inspections of the SOB slot within a recent time window (e.g., past 6 months), to avoid redundant work.

[P5] The AD should explicitly permit third-party representatives (e.g., contracted maintenance organizations) to submit AMOC requests on behalf of operators to reflect real-world practices.

[P8] The AD should require the FAA to provide an experimental or temporary AMOC for essential operations where full compliance would otherwise ground aircraft for safety-critical routes (e.g., medevac), subject to strict conditions.

[P1] If the comment due date cannot be changed, the FAA should at least issue a notice extending the comment period and indicate why the past date remains in the preamble; otherwise the rulemaking record will be procedurally deficient.

[P11] The AD should quantify the acceptable variability for “insufficient sealant” (e.g., gap measurements, visual criteria) to avoid inconsistent inspection results among inspectors.

[P17] The Seattle ACO email address should include a backup or cc list (e.g., mailbox monitored by multiple staff) so that requests are not delayed due to single-person absence.
