[P1] The broad listing of “all other waters such as intrastate lakes, rivers, streams (including intermittent streams), mudflats, sandflats, wetlands, sloughs, prairie potholes” in §328.3(a)(3) is unacceptably vague and will create regulatory uncertainty for landowners and developers.

[P1] Environmental groups will support §328.3(a)(3)’s inclusion of intermittent streams and prairie potholes as likely necessary to protect downstream waters; excluding them would harm migratory birds and water quality.

[P2] §328.3(a)(3)(i)’s reliance on a “continuous surface connection” to include relatively permanent waters is ambiguous where seasonal surface expressions exist (e.g., ephemeral overflow channels); the rule should clarify whether intermittent seasonal connections meet this test.

[P2] State water agencies will request that “continuous surface connection” be defined quantitatively (e.g., percent of days per year or presence during a specified return period) to ensure consistent jurisdictional determinations.

[P3] §328.3(a)(3)(ii) uses “significantly affect the chemical, physical, or biological integrity” without a concrete significance threshold; industry commenters will argue this invites case-by-case determinations that are costly and unpredictable.

[P3] Conservation scientists will request that the rule provide prescriptive examples and standardized metrics (e.g., nutrient load reduction, habitat connectivity indexes) for demonstrating “significant effect.”

[P4] The tributary definition in §328.3(a)(5) as tied to paragraph (a)(1), (2), (4), or (6) creates dependency on other provisions that are not reproduced here—commenters will ask for an integrated definitions table to avoid interpretive confusion.

[P5] §328.3(a)(5)(i) includes “relatively permanent, standing or continuously flowing bodies of water” as tributaries; agricultural stakeholders will request guidance on whether man-made ditches that are seasonally flowing are captured.

[P5] Flood-control districts will argue that the phrase “relatively permanent” should exclude engineered drainage ditches and conveyances constructed for stormwater management to preserve local infrastructure management flexibility.

[P6] §328.3(a)(5)(ii)’s “alone or in combination with similarly situated waters…significantly affect” standard could impose regional cumulative-impact analyses on routine permitting; regulated parties will request clear screening distances or thresholds to avoid extensive regional studies.

[P7] §328.3(a)(7) treats wetlands adjacent to certain waters as waters of the U.S.; landowner groups will object to adjacency being applied across parcels without a clear delineation method, especially where legal property boundaries and roads separate features.

[P8] Under §328.3(a)(7)(i), wetlands adjacent to (a)(1), (2), or (6) are included — environmental advocates will support this broad adjacency rule as necessary to protect riparian functions and wildlife habitat.

[P9] §328.3(a)(7)(ii) includes wetlands adjacent to relatively permanent waters with continuous surface connection; regulators should clarify how “continuous surface connection” is measured in karst or subsurface-flow dominated landscapes.

[P9] Agricultural commenters will request an explicit exclusion for artificially irrigated lands that seasonally create a “connection” to relatively permanent waters but do not function hydrologically the same way as natural connections.

[P10] §328.3(a)(7)(iii)’s “alone or in combination with similarly situated waters significantly affect…integrity” test for adjacent wetlands duplicates the vagueness of other “significance” clauses and will produce litigation; commenters recommend a rebuttable presumption framework and objective criteria.

[P11] §328.3(a)(8)’s exclusion for waste treatment systems “designed to meet CWA requirements” may be interpreted too narrowly; wastewater utilities ask clarification that secondary treatment lagoons and engineered wetlands permitted under NPDES are excluded even if they have incidental surface connections.

[P11] Conversely, environmental groups will warn that the waste-treatment-system exclusion must not be used to exempt illicit or poorly designed treatment facilities that discharge contaminants to adjacent waters; propose oversight and enforceable design standards.

[P12] The exclusion of prior converted cropland in §328.3(a)(9) could incentivize removal of wetland protections through conversion; conservation organizations will ask for a clear date cutoff and documentation requirements to prevent retroactive conversions.

[P13] §328.3(a)(9) reserving EPA final authority over prior converted cropland determinations conflicts with USDA and NRCS practice — state agencies request a formal interagency coordination mechanism and timeline to prevent conflicting federal designations.

[P14] §328.3(d)’s permission to use physical indicators (line of oil/scum, continuous deposit) to determine the high tide line is practical but needs standardized protocols and training to ensure consistent application along varied shorelines.

[P15] The explicit exclusion of storm surges from the high tide line in §328.3(d) is appropriate, but coastal municipalities request guidance on how to handle exceptional events (e.g., sea level rise–related baseline shifts) when historical indicators are obscured.

[P16] §328.3(g) requires agencies to consider certain factors when assessing significant functional effects; environmental groups will support this multi-factor approach but urge that factors be treated as equally worthy rather than discretionary.

[P17] The requirement in §328.3(g)(1) to consider distance from a water of the United States lacks a defined distance threshold; agricultural and development stakeholders will request clear distance bands (e.g., 50 ft, 100 ft, 1,000 ft) to reduce uncertainty.

[P18] §328.3(g)(2) repeats consideration of distance from waters identified in (a)(1), (2), or (6); legal commenters will note this redundancy and suggest consolidating distance factors to avoid conflicting interpretations.

[P19] §328.3(g)(3) mandates consideration of hydrologic factors including shallow subsurface flow — hydrologists will request specific guidance on acceptable assessment methods and minimum data requirements (e.g., monitoring wells, tracers) for demonstrating subsurface connectivity.

[P20] §328.3(g)(4) obligates considering the size, density, and/or number of similarly situated waters; rural counties will warn that counting “similarly situated” waters regionally could expand jurisdiction beyond local expectations and ask for geographic scope limits (e.g., watershed or HUC scale).

[P21] §328.3(g)(5) requires considering climatological variables like temperature, rainfall, and snowpack; commenters from arid western states will request that climate-change projections not be used retroactively to expand jurisdiction on historic drylands without clear temporal limits.

[P22] §120.2’s directive that terms have the indicated meanings is appropriate but commenters will request that the rule include an integrated definitions index and cross-references to avoid duplicate or inconsistent definitions between parts 120 and 328.

[P23] Mirroring §328.3(a)(3), §120.2(a)(3) repeats broad categories of waters — regulatory commenters will flag the duplication and ask the agencies to harmonize language or explain why parallel definitions are necessary.

[P24] §120.2(a)(3)(i)’s “continuous surface connection” standard should be harmonized with §328.3’s identical provision; interagency legal counsel will request one controlling interpretive memorandum to prevent divergent applications.

[P25] The “significantly affect” language in §120.2(a)(3)(ii) repeats across parts and compounds uncertainty; industry will urge adoption of quantitative thresholds (e.g., percent contribution to downstream flow or pollutant loads) as a safe harbor.

[P26] §120.2(a)(5) defining tributaries identically to §328.3(a)(5) doubles opportunities for inconsistent application; state agencies will request model field protocols and checklists for determining tributary status.

[P27] §120.2(a)(5)(i) capturing “relatively permanent, standing or continuously flowing bodies” as tributaries lacks guidance on man-made alterations; commenters ask for explicit treatment of jurisdiction over channelized or piped streams.

[P28] §120.2(a)(5)(ii) again uses the cumulative-impact standard for tributaries — agricultural coalitions will argue that requiring regional analyses for routine farm maintenance is impractical and recommend a de minimis threshold for small features.

[P29] §120.2(a)(7) treating adjacent wetlands as jurisdictional will impose significant permitting burdens on landowners adjacent to non-wetland waters; county governments request an appeals process and expedited jurisdictional determinations.

[P30] §120.2(a)(7)(i) tying adjacency to (a)(1), (2), or (6) appears to assume readers know those categories — request explicit cross-references and examples (e.g., lakes, public waters, territorial seas).

[P31] §120.2(a)(7)(ii) should clarify if roads, berms, or levees that separate wetlands from relatively permanent waters preclude adjacency, to avoid asserting jurisdiction across artificial barriers.

[P32] §120.2(a)(7)(iii) calls for considering combinations of similarly situated waters to determine adjacency-based jurisdiction — developers will argue this invites speculative regional analyses and seek a presumption that adjacency is limited to contiguous hydrologic connection.

[P33] §120.2(a)(8)’s exclusion for waste treatment systems should explicitly exclude treatment wetlands and retention basins constructed under permits, and should describe when monitoring and maintenance obligations could negate the exclusion.

[P34] §120.2(a)(9) excluding prior converted cropland is necessary for agricultural certainty, but NRCS and landowners request a clear documentation standard (e.g., aerial photos, certification process) to establish prior conversion status.

[P35] §120.2(a)(9) asserting EPA’s final authority over prior converted cropland determinations will create interagency friction; USDA asks for a formal dispute-resolution process and timelines to prevent project delays.

[P36] §120.2(d)’s allowance of physical indicators for the high tide line is reasonable, but commenters request a requirement that determinations using these indicators be corroborated by a trained professional and documented with photos and GPS coordinates.

[P37] The exclusion of storm surges from the high tide line in §120.2(d) is sensible; coastal developers request clarification on how episodic overwash events that alter shoreline morphology are treated for future HTL determinations.

[P38] §120.2(g) repeating the multi-factor test is redundant with §328.3(g); state environmental departments recommend a single, uniform guidance document applicable across both parts to ensure consistent functional assessments.

[P39] §120.2(g)(1) requiring consideration of distance from a water of the United States should specify whether measured horizontal distance, flow-path distance, or catchment boundary distance applies; practitioners will otherwise apply inconsistent measures.

[P40] §120.2(g)(2) duplicative distance language will cause procedural inefficiency; legal commenters recommend streamlining to a single distance consideration tied to the nearest water identified in (a)(1), (2), or (6).

[P41] §120.2(g)(3)’s inclusion of shallow subsurface flow as a factor should be accompanied by standards for acceptable evidence (e.g., field indicators versus modeling) to avoid subjective determinations that are costly to defend.

[P42] §120.2(g)(4) requiring agencies to consider size, density, and number of similarly situated waters needs an operational definition of “similarly situated” (e.g., same hydrogeomorphic class, same watershed) to prevent arbitrary aggregation.

[P43] §120.2(g)(5) listing climatological variables is appropriate, but commenters from regions with high interannual variability request that agencies rely primarily on historical baselines rather than single anomalous years when making jurisdictional calls.

[P1] Industry commenter: The definition of covered facilities in §63.8681(a) is overly broad because it captures any facility that "is or is part of a major source" without clarifying whether minor processes colocated at a major source are intended to be regulated as separate affected sources; request clarification that only units meeting the definitions of asphalt processing or asphalt roofing manufacturing in §63 are covered.

[P1] Legal expert: The phrase "as defined in §63" in §63.8681(a) should cite the exact subsection(s) that define "asphalt processing facility" and "asphalt roofing manufacturing facility" to avoid interpretive ambiguity during permitting and enforcement.

[P2] State agency: The cross-reference in §63.8683(d) to notification schedules in §§63.8692 and 63.9(a)-(f) and (h) may create impossible timelines for small facilities; request additional implementation time or staggered deadlines for Tier 2/3 facilities.

[P3] Environmental NGO: §63.8685(a)’s requirement to "maintain continuous compliance" prior to the stated cutoff date is vague about monitoring frequency; request explicit statement that continuous means 24/7 monitoring where emission limits apply to ensure meaningful enforcement.

[P4] Industry: The pre-cutoff exception in §63.8685(a) allowing noncompliance during startup, shutdown, and malfunction (SSM) is too broad and could be abused; request tighter definition or mandatory SSM plans with demonstration that emissions are minimized during SSM prior to granting exception.

[P5] Environmental NGO: The removal of SSM exceptions after [DATE …] in §63.8685(a) is appropriate, but the rule should explicitly state that any emissions during "nonoperation" that nonetheless escape (e.g., leaks during maintenance) are not exempt and must be controlled.

[P6] Industry safety officer: §63.8685(b) requires operation and maintenance per §63.6(e)(1)(i) before the specified date; this cross-reference to general duty language conflicts with site-specific safety protocols — request confirmation that compliance actions will not require unsafe operating practices.

[P7] Industry: The post-date language in §63.8685(b) requiring operation "consistent with safety and good pollution-control practices" is ambiguous; request an explicit safe harbor describing what constitutes "good pollution-control practices" and how to reconcile with workplace safety and process constraints.

[P8] Legal commenter: §63.8685(b) stating that the duty to minimize emissions does not require further efforts beyond applicable standard should be clarified that it does not override state or local requirements that may be more stringent.

[P9] Industry: §63.8685(c) requires development of a written SSMP before the date; request sample SSMP templates and additional time (e.g., 12 months) to prepare detailed SSMPs given limited resources at smaller facilities.

[P10] Environmental NGO: The removal of SSMP requirement on and after [DATE …] in §63.8685(c) is concerning — removing mandatory SSM planning reduces public assurance that facilities will minimize emissions during non-routine events; recommend retaining SSMP requirement indefinitely.

[P11] Regulated facility: §63.8686(a) mandates initial performance tests within 180 days after each facility's compliance date; request allowance for extensions for facilities with seasonal shutdowns or supply chain delays that prevent testing within 180 days.

[P12] Industry: §63.8686(b) permits use of prior tests if Administrator approves; request presumption of approval where prior tests were conducted within the last 5 years, used the same control device, and were conducted under normal operating conditions to reduce administrative burden.

[P13] Testing laboratory: §63.8686(b)(3) requires that prior test's control device and process parameter values be used to demonstrate continuous compliance — request clarification whether marginal parameter deviations (±5–10%) disqualify prior tests or whether a tolerance band is acceptable.

[P14] Industry: The 5-year limit in §63.8686(b)(4) for prior tests is arbitrary; request extension to 7 years for low-throughput facilities that rarely change processes, or allow renewal upon demonstration that process and control device remain unchanged.

[P15] Testing group: §63.8687(b) requires tests under "normal operating conditions" and Table 3 conditions; ask EPA to provide an approved list of what constitutes normal operating conditions for common asphalt processes (throughput rates, temperatures) to ensure consistency.

[P16] Industry: §63.8687(b) prohibits using startup/shutdown/nonoperation conditions for performance testing; request explicit allowance to document representative operating ranges that include low-load operations for facilities that run intermittently.

[P17] Industry association: The prohibition on testing during malfunctions (§63.8687(b)) is reasonable but the rule should specify how to handle a situation where a malfunction is intermittent during the scheduled test window — i.e., allow rescheduling without penalty.

[P18] Testing labs/state agency: §63.8687(b) requires recording and justifying representativeness during tests; request standardized reporting forms and minimum data elements to streamline Administrator review.

[P19] Industry: §63.8687(b) obligates making test records available to the Administrator on request; suggest allowing electronic submission within a defined period (e.g., 10 business days) as an alternative to on-site review to reduce travel burdens.

[P20] Industry: §63.8688(f) allows installing a CEMS/COMS instead of CPMS if it meets referenced requirements; request clearer criteria and performance specifications for acceptable CEMS/COMS to avoid inconsistent approvals.

[P21] Compliance consultant: §63.8688(h) requires the monitoring plan to address specific topics but does not specify required detail level; request a template for the site-specific monitoring plan to ensure minimal acceptable content.

[P22] Industry: §63.8688(h)(1) requires O&M procedures per §63.8 subparts; ask EPA to confirm whether third-party maintenance (contractors) and their records satisfy this requirement, and specify acceptable frequency for preventive maintenance tasks.

[P23] Industry: §63.8688(h)(2) requires data QA procedures per §63.8(d); request explicit acceptable QA/QC metrics (e.g., calibration frequency, control charts) for CPMS and CEMS to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P24] Facility compliance officer: §63.8688(h)(3) requires recordkeeping/reporting per §§63.8693/63.8694 and §63.10; request consolidation allowances when facilities are already reporting similar metrics under state programs to prevent duplicate reporting.

[P25] Industry: §63.8689(b) requires establishing site-specific operating limits in Table 2 using referenced procedures; request clarification on whether limits set during performance tests can be revised later if process changes reduce emissions.

[P26] Manufacturer/industry: §63.8689(d) permits using manufacturer specs to set pressure drop limits for PM devices; request that EPA explicitly allow published manufacturer warranty performance curves or certified testing reports as acceptable documentation.

[P27] Industry: §63.8690(b) mandates continuous monitoring/collection whenever the source is operating before the date, except for limited exceptions; request clarification if brief process purges (<30 minutes) count as "operating" for monitoring continuity purposes.

[P28] Industry: §63.8690(b) allows exceptions for monitor malfunctions and QA/QC activities prior to the date; ask EPA to define maximum allowable duration for such exceptions before they are considered a recordkeeping violation.

[P29] Legal/industry: §63.8690(b) requires monitoring at all times after the date except nonoperation; request explicit guidance on the definition of "nonoperation" and whether maintenance that results in emissions qualifies for an exception.

[P30] Industry: §63.8691(a) requires demonstrating continuous compliance with operating limits in Table 2 and periodic tests; request allowance for averaging periods or alternative statistical approaches for low-frequency monitor data.

[P31] Industry: §63.8691(b) requires reporting all instances of noncompliance before the date and, after the date, excludes nonoperation deviations; request clarity whether temporary monitored exceedances when equipment is isolated but not producing emissions must be reported.

[P32] Legal expert: §63.8691(d) gives Administrator discretion to determine whether SSM deviations are violations before the date; request procedural safeguards (e.g., burden of proof, timelines) so facilities understand evidentiary requirements.

[P33] Industry: §63.8691(e) mandates periodic performance tests for each control device; request consolidation if multiple devices are identical and co-located so a representative test can satisfy requirements.

[P34] Existing facility: §63.8691(e)(1) requires first periodic test by specified date and every 60 months thereafter; request extension to 72 months for low-risk devices or small facilities to reduce compliance costs.

[P35] New source developer: §63.8691(e)(2) requires first periodic tests within 60 months after initial test or alternative demonstration; request clarification on how alternative demonstrations are documented and approved.

[P36] Industry: §63.8691(e)(3) allows testing within 60 days of resuming operations and no later than 180 days if source was not operating on scheduled date — recommend changing the outer limit to 90 days to ensure timelier verification.

[P37] Industry/state: §63.8692(a) requires numerous notifications by various deadlines; request EPA provide a compliance calendar or consolidated table listing specific deadlines by facility type to aid compliance planning.

[P38] Industry: §63.8692(e) requires submission of Notification of Compliance Status within 60 days after test completion; propose allowing 90 days for complex tests that require extensive QA/QC and lab analyses.

Legal expert: The phrase "as defined in §63" in §63.8681(a) should cite the exact subsection(s) that define "asphalt processing facility" and "asphalt roofing manufacturing facility" to avoid interpretive ambiguity during permitting and enforcement.

State agency: The cross-reference in §63.8683(d) to notification schedules in §§63.8692 and 63.9(a)-(f) and (h) may create impossible timelines for small facilities; request additional implementation time or staggered deadlines for Tier 2/3 facilities.

Environmental NGO: §63.8685(a)’s requirement to "maintain continuous compliance" prior to the stated cutoff date is vague about monitoring frequency; request explicit statement that continuous means 24/7 monitoring where emission limits apply to ensure meaningful enforcement.

Industry: The pre-cutoff exception in §63.8685(a) allowing noncompliance during startup, shutdown, and malfunction (SSM) is too broad and could be abused; request tighter definition or mandatory SSM plans with demonstration that emissions are minimized during SSM prior to granting exception.

Environmental NGO: The removal of SSM exceptions after [DATE …] in §63.8685(a) is appropriate, but the rule should explicitly state that any emissions during "nonoperation" that nonetheless escape (e.g., leaks during maintenance) are not exempt and must be controlled.

Industry safety officer: §63.8685(b) requires operation and maintenance per §63.6(e)(1)(i) before the specified date; this cross-reference to general duty language conflicts with site-specific safety protocols — request confirmation that compliance actions will not require unsafe operating practices.

Industry: The post-date language in §63.8685(b) requiring operation "consistent with safety and good pollution-control practices" is ambiguous; request an explicit safe harbor describing what constitutes "good pollution-control practices" and how to reconcile with workplace safety and process constraints.

Legal commenter: §63.8685(b) stating that the duty to minimize emissions does not require further efforts beyond applicable standard should be clarified that it does not override state or local requirements that may be more stringent.

Industry: §63.8685(c) requires development of a written SSMP before the date; request sample SSMP templates and additional time (e.g., 12 months) to prepare detailed SSMPs given limited resources at smaller facilities.

Environmental NGO: The removal of SSMP requirement on and after [DATE …] in §63.8685(c) is concerning — removing mandatory SSM planning reduces public assurance that facilities will minimize emissions during non-routine events; recommend retaining SSMP requirement indefinitely.

Regulated facility: §63.8686(a) mandates initial performance tests within 180 days after each facility's compliance date; request allowance for extensions for facilities with seasonal shutdowns or supply chain delays that prevent testing within 180 days.

Industry: §63.8686(b) permits use of prior tests if Administrator approves; request presumption of approval where prior tests were conducted within the last 5 years, used the same control device, and were conducted under normal operating conditions to reduce administrative burden.

Industry: §63.8687(b) prohibits using startup/shutdown/nonoperation conditions for performance testing; request explicit allowance to document representative operating ranges that include low-load operations for facilities that run intermittently.

raw_output:
[P1] The exemption in § 595.8(a) is too broad because it allows rental companies to "make inoperative" safety equipment (even if only temporarily) as long as the parts were originally installed in compliance with specified FMVSS provisions, creating potential safety risks for renters and other road users.

[P1] Rental industry commenters will claim the exemption is necessary and appropriate because it enables accessible rentals for people with disabilities without forcing permanent vehicle modification or expensive fleet segregation.

[P2] Disability advocates will assert that limiting the exemption to only FMVSS provisions listed in paragraph (d) (rather than all FMVSS) unfairly precludes some reasonable accommodations that require disabling other safety features, thereby reducing accessibility options.

[P2] Legal experts will note the rule lacks clarity about which FMVSS beyond 49 CFR 571.208 are covered or excluded, creating regulatory uncertainty and potential litigation; recommend a complete, enumerated list or cross-reference.

[P3] Consumer safety groups will object that the exemption's temporal limitation ("during the rental and reasonable time before and after") is vague—there is no defined "reasonable time" and the rule should specify hours or maximum days for installation/removal to prevent prolonged periods in which safety devices are inoperative.

[P3] Rental companies will argue the unspecified "reasonable time" is necessary because installation/removal time can vary by site and technician; prescriptive time limits would be impractical and hamper service to customers with disabilities.

[P4] Plaintiff attorneys and safety advocates will point out the labeling and documentation obligations in § 595.8(c), (e), and (f) are insufficiently robust to ensure accountability—there are no audit, reporting, or notification requirements to safety regulators when FMVSS parts are disabled.

[P4] Rental companies will claim the combination of required label plus renter-facing document and five-year record retention provides sufficient transparency and traceability, and that additional reporting would be burdensome and costly.

[P5] Medical equipment providers and adaptive equipment installers will request clarification that § 595.8(d)(1) permits disablement of knee bolster air bags only to the extent necessary to install specific hand controls, and that it does not allow disabling for unrelated modifications.

[P5] Safety engineers will warn disabling knee bolster air bags (49 CFR 571.208) even temporarily may materially affect occupant protection in frontal impacts and propose that the rule require documented risk assessment or OEM approval before disabling.

[P6] Advocacy groups will demand that the label specification (§ 595.8(e)) include additional safety information (e.g., the date modification was performed, installer name, and a telephone number for verification) beyond the single warning statement mandated.

[P6] Rental industry commenters will argue the required label text is adequate and that adding installation dates or installer details could violate privacy or create unnecessary administrative burdens.

[P7] Disability rights organizations will request that § 595.8(e)(1) require the label to be affixed in a standardized location (e.g., driver's sun visor or A-pillar) to ensure consistency and that accessible drivers can easily find the warning.

[P7] Rental companies will counter that requiring a single standardized location across diverse vehicle interiors may be impractical; the current "within the passenger compartment" requirement provides needed flexibility.

[P8] Road-safety advocates will claim § 595.8(e)(2) should explicitly require that the label not be placed on or near airbags, mirrors, or windshield areas where it could still present a hazard or indirectly obstruct safety systems.

[P8] Rental companies will respond that § 595.8(e)(2) already prohibits obstructing the driver's view, which reasonably covers such concerns; specifying every prohibited location is unnecessary.

[P9] Plaintiffs and safety analysts will object that the required warning statement in § 595.8(e)(3) is too limited and passive; it should additionally mention specific crash risks, instruct renters not to transport certain passengers (e.g., children) in affected seating positions, and advise on when the modification must be reversed.

[P9] Disability advocates will caution against warnings that are overly restrictive (e.g., blanket prohibition on carrying passengers) because they could stigmatize or unduly limit the mobility of people with disabilities.

[P10] Compliance auditors will note that § 595.8(e)(4) requires removal of the label when modifications are undone, but the rule lacks a verification procedure to ensure rental companies actually remove labels and do not re-rent mislabeled vehicles.

[P10] Rental companies will claim the removal requirement is straightforward and enforceable through existing fleet-control processes; additional verification steps would be duplicative.

[P11] Privacy advocates will raise concerns about the required document under § 595.8(f) containing personal or identifying information about renters (if any), and ask for limits to ensure only company/vehicle/modification data are retained.

[P11] Rental companies will likely argue that the required document (§ 595.8(f)) does not need renter personal data beyond what is already collected in the rental agreement and that record retention is standard business practice.

[P12] Consumer groups will assert that § 595.8(f)(1) must require that the document include timestamps for installation and removal, and clear signatures from the technician and renter acknowledging the modification and associated risks—current text does not require this.

[P12] Small rental operators will counter that mandatory technician signatures and timestamps will increase transaction time and staffing burdens, especially for single-location businesses.

[P13] Safety attorneys will argue § 595.8(f)(2)'s requirement to include the "physical address" of the rental company is ambiguous for national chains that operate through franchises or third-party managers; the rule should specify whether corporate headquarters, franchise location, or modification site address is required.

[P13] Franchise organizations will request an option to provide a central corporate contact and identification of the specific location that performed the modification to avoid conflicting address requirements.

[P14] Regulatory compliance officers will point out that the five-year retention period in § 595.8(f)(3) may be insufficient for investigating long-tail crash claims and recommend retention aligned with statute of limitations for personal injury claims (commonly longer than five years).

[P14] Small businesses will argue five years is a reasonable compromise balancing evidentiary needs and recordkeeping burdens; requiring longer retention would disproportionately burden small rental firms.

[P15] Enforcement practitioners will note § 595.8(f)(4) requires the document to identify the modified vehicle, but does not specify acceptable identifiers (VIN, license plate, fleet number); they will recommend mandating VIN plus license plate for unambiguous identification.

[P15] Rental industry representatives may support requiring VIN but object to additional identifiers like license plate (subject to change) or internal fleet IDs that may not be consistent for auditing across entities.

[P16] Consumer safety advocates will emphasize § 595.8(f)(5) must require precise identification of the specific FMVSS devices or design elements disabled (e.g., "driver knee bolster airbag, left side") rather than general references, to enable proper risk assessment and enforcement.

[P16] Legal commenters will request model language for identifying devices/elements to ensure consistent descriptions (e.g., reference to specific FMVSS clause and vehicle component name).

[P1] Public commenters will call for explicit liability protection or carve-outs — either for rental companies acting in good faith under this exemption or conversely for victims — as the rule as written is silent on whether temporary disablement changes civil liability exposure.

[P3] Accident victim advocates will demand the rule require rental companies to inform subsequent renters and maintenance staff via fleet management systems that an affected vehicle cannot be re-rented until restored and inspected.

[P6] Civil rights organizations will recommend that the label also include accessible-format requirements (high-contrast, large type, braille or NFC/link to audio) so renters with visual impairments can obtain the same safety information.

[P9] Child-safety advocates will specifically request the warning include an instruction that children should not occupy positions where an airbag has been disabled, or specify whether child seat use is affected by the modification.

[P5] Engineers and OEMs will urge the agency to require that any temporary disabling of an airbag be performed only by certified technicians following OEM-approved procedures, and that documentation include certification details.

[P4] Consumer protection groups will argue that the rule should require periodic compliance audits by the agency or third parties to ensure rental companies adhere to labeling, documentation, and restoration requirements.

[P2] Disability advocates will request that the rule allow exemptions for disabling FMVSS devices other than those listed in (d) if an accessible alternative is not reasonably available, subject to a documented hardship process, to prevent discriminatory denial of service.

[P7] Enforcement agencies will suggest adding a prohibition on placing the label where it could interfere with airbag deployment or occupant protection systems, not just obstruct the driver's view.

[P14] Tax and financial officers will warn that five-year document retention may create storage and privacy compliance costs; they will request safe-harbor electronic recordkeeping standards and options for secure deletion after retention period.

[P11] Data-security experts will ask the rule to specify security standards for electronic retention of documents (encryption, access controls) because retained records identify vehicles modified for disability accommodations and could be misused if breached.

[P15] Industry legal counsel will request an express allowance to use fleet management databases to satisfy the "clearly identifiable" vehicle documentation requirement to avoid duplicative paper records.

[P16] Consumer safety researchers will ask the agency to require collection and anonymized reporting of the number, type, and outcomes of temporary modifications to support future safety assessments and rulemaking.

raw_output:
[P1] The June 15, 2020 comment deadline is unreasonably short and should be extended to at least 60 days from publication to allow affected operators, manufacturers, labor unions, and safety advocates adequate time to prepare informed comments and data.

[P1] The provision's absolute phrasing "FAA must receive comments by June 15, 2020" creates confusion about whether comments postmarked or submitted electronically by that date are acceptable; clarify acceptable submission methods and time-zone cutoffs.

[P2] The compliance requirement to "comply within the specified compliance times" is vague because the AD does not clearly enumerate compliance time windows for subsequent recurring inspections or follow-up actions; specify exact intervals or inspection schedules.

[P2] The rule does not provide for operational hardships or scheduling conflicts for small operators to meet compliance times; include provision for temporary relief or phased compliance based on operational constraints.

[P3] The 60-day deadline to inspect assemblies or review records is overly burdensome for large fleets and parts located at multiple maintenance facilities; extend to 120 days or allow staggered inspections.

[P3] The rule fails to define who is an authorized inspector for physical inspections; specify required qualifications (e.g., A&P mechanic, certified technician) to ensure consistent determinations.

[P4] Allowing maintenance-record review in lieu of physical inspection only "if the serial numbers can be conclusively determined" is ambiguous; provide standards for what constitutes "conclusive" documentation and acceptable record types (electronic logs, OEM certificates).

[P4] Operators who rely on third-party records (leasing companies, lessors) should be explicitly permitted to obtain and use supplier/lessor records to satisfy the record-review option without requiring physical access to assets under lessor control.

[P5] The requirement to perform a "detailed gap-spacing inspection" per referenced service instructions lacks specificity in the AD text; incorporate or summarize the critical measurement threshold in the AD to avoid reliance on potentially unavailable service documents.

[P5] The AD does not address access to proprietary service instructions for independent repair stations and foreign operators; require FAA to make necessary inspection procedures publicly available or provide alternative equivalent methods.

[P6] Requiring parts marking actions "before further flight" if the gap is acceptable may impose unnecessary grounding for aircraft already scheduled for immediate operations; allow markings to be completed within a short deferred maintenance window (e.g., 5 days) provided placarding and temporary controls are used.

[P6] The AD does not specify who may perform parts marking (manufacturer, certified repair station, operator maintenance); clarify acceptable parties and documentation of marking completion.

[P7] Immediate removal "before further flight" of assemblies with unacceptable gap could create safety and operational disruption if spare serviceable assemblies are not available; require allowance for a ferry permit or allow a short-term relief to reposition spares under operational risk assessment.

[P7] The AD should require manufacturers to provide a supply plan or parts availability assessment to ensure operators can comply with immediate removal and replacement requirements without disproportionate impact.

[P8] Mandating replacement "before further flight" with a serviceable assembly lacks clarity on what qualifies as "serviceable" (e.g., newly manufactured, overhauled per specific SB); define serviceable and allow FAA-accepted equivalents.

[P9] The reporting requirement referencing accomplishment instructions should include explicit reporting fields and an electronic submission method; otherwise reporting will be inconsistent and burdensome.

[P10] The 30-day reporting window after inspection (if done on/after effective date) is too short for large operators to compile consolidated reports across multiple bases; extend to 60 days or permit staggered reporting.

[P11] Requiring reports within 30 days after the AD effective date for inspections done before the AD is impractical if inspections were piecemeal over a long prior period; allow reporting to be submitted in phased batches or extend the window.

[P12] Returning assemblies to the manufacturer within tight timelines may be cost-prohibitive and logistically difficult for international operators; allow returns to FAA-designated evaluation centers or approved repair stations with documented chain-of-custody.

[P13] The 30-day return requirement for assemblies found unacceptable on/after the effective date is too short for operators needing export/import clearances or quarantine; extend the timeframe or permit temporary storage/retention with mandatory preservation protocols.

[P14] Requiring return within 30 days for pre-effective-date findings could penalize operators who already quarantined parts; clarify whether operators may keep parts pending manufacturer instruction and whether costs for shipping/handling are reimbursable.

[P15] The prohibition on installing affected assemblies unless paragraph (i) completed effectively grounds aftermarket supply channels and could disrupt maintenance programs; allow installation if a documented inspection and mitigation (e.g., parts marking) is in place even when full paragraph (i) paperwork is pending.

[P15] The installation ban should include an exception for emergency replacement with an equivalent FAA-approved part or an AMOC that ensures temporary airworthiness pending full compliance.

[P16] The credit provision for previous actions is unduly narrow if it limits acceptable service information to specific versions; clarify that earlier revisions that accomplish equivalent inspections/actions are acceptable with operator documentation.

[P16] Require explicit guidance on how to document and demonstrate that previously performed actions meet the AD's requirements to qualify for credit, including acceptable evidence and FAA audit procedures.

[P17] The PRA prohibition language conflicts with the AD's mandatory reporting obligations in paragraph (j); reconcile the statements so operators understand whether reporting is voluntary or mandatory and ensure an OMB control number is provided.

[P18] Paragraph (m)'s assertion that responses are mandatory conflicts with the PRA prohibition; provide the OMB Control Number and the approved burden estimate, or amend the PRA statement to reflect compliance with PRA requirements.

[P19] Limiting AMOC approval authority to the New York ACO Branch manager without a clear timeline for decision could delay operations; require FAA to commit to a specific review timeframe (e.g., 60 days) for AMOCs.

[P20] The mandated routing of AMOC requests to principal inspectors or local FSDOs may be inefficient for international or certificate-holding overseas operators; allow direct electronic submission to the ACO Branch and provide a single point of contact for non-U.S. operators.

[P21] The requirement to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC needs an exception for Part 121/135 operators with multiple certificates and multiple principal inspectors; permit corporate-level notification procedures.

[P3] The AD does not address assemblies that have been re-serialized or re-marked; provide guidance on how to handle suspect serial numbers that may have been altered intentionally or unintentionally.

[P5] The AD lacks a risk-based prioritization for inspection of assemblies based on usage hours or exposure; recommend prioritizing aircraft with high flight hours or certain operational profiles to reduce safety risk.

[P9] The rule does not indicate whether the inspection and return reports will be publicly available or redacted; operators request confidentiality treatment for proprietary maintenance data and a clear FOIA/privilege policy.

[P7] There is no cost-assessment or economic impact analysis provided showing availability of replacement assemblies; request that FAA publish estimated costs and parts lead times to inform commenters.

[P15] The installation prohibition's scope is unclear whether it applies to spares in supplier inventory and consignments; clarify whether warehouse stock may be installed after in-house inspection or whether it is barred until FAA acceptance.

[P4] Maintenance-record reviews for vintage or legacy aircraft may lack serial numbers; allow alternative identification methods such as part-number cross-reference or lab testing rather than forcing physical removal.

[P19] The AMOC authority should explicitly include timelines and criteria for emergency AMOCs (short-term operational deviations) for aircraft in service with no immediate access to serviceable parts.

[P12] The AD should require the manufacturer to cover reasonable shipping costs and provide pre-paid shipping labels for returns to avoid imposing unexpected expenses on operators.

[P6] Parts marking might require downtime for aircraft and specialized tooling; justify why marking cannot be deferred to the next scheduled heavy maintenance event if the gap is acceptable.

[P11] The reporting deadlines should include provisions for electronic batch submission or API integration with FAA databases to reduce administrative burden.

[P17] The PRA paragraph should not be used to imply that failure to provide information will not be enforced; state the legal basis for mandatory reporting and any penalties explicitly to avoid confusion.

[P16] Allow credit for earlier inspections performed to equivalent international airworthiness directives (EASA or Transport Canada) and provide a streamlined acceptance process to prevent duplicate inspections.

[P3] The AD should allow use of non-destructive test equipment or photographic evidence for remote inspections when assemblies are inaccessible due to COVID-19 or travel restrictions.

[P8] Define protocol for procurement of "serviceable assembly" including approved suppliers, traceability paperwork, and whether reworked/overhauled parts from OEM-authorized repair stations qualify.

[P2] Include a provision allowing operators to request short-term extensions to compliance times in circumstances of demonstrated hardship, pending AMOC approval.

[P20] Provide a digital template and contact email/portal for AMOC requests to ensure timely and trackable submissions, rather than relying solely on postal addresses.

[P9] Specify whether incomplete or partial reports will be accepted with follow-up supplements, to accommodate operators who discover additional affected parts after initial submission.

[P14] Clarify whether returns of assemblies found unacceptable before the AD were already returned under earlier manufacturer programs, and if so, whether duplicate returns are required.

[P5] Require the FAA to publish the acceptable gap tolerance values in the AD text (numerical thresholds) rather than only in referenced service documents to ensure uniform enforcement.

[P21] Clarify whether notification to principal inspectors must be written, electronic, or verbal and what constitutes adequate proof of notification before using an AMOC.

The AD should require manufacturers to provide a supply plan or parts availability assessment to ensure operators can comply with immediate removal and replacement requirements without disproportionate impact.

Mandating replacement "before further flight" with a serviceable assembly lacks clarity on what qualifies as "serviceable" (e.g., newly manufactured, overhauled per specific SB); define serviceable and allow FAA-accepted equivalents.

The reporting requirement referencing accomplishment instructions should include explicit reporting fields and an electronic submission method; otherwise reporting will be inconsistent and burdensome.

The 30-day reporting window after inspection (if done on/after effective date) is too short for large operators to compile consolidated reports across multiple bases; extend to 60 days or permit staggered reporting.

Requiring reports within 30 days after the AD effective date for inspections done before the AD is impractical if inspections were piecemeal over a long prior period; allow reporting to be submitted in phased batches or extend the window.

Returning assemblies to the manufacturer within tight timelines may be cost-prohibitive and logistically difficult for international operators; allow returns to FAA-designated evaluation centers or approved repair stations with documented chain-of-custody.

The 30-day return requirement for assemblies found unacceptable on/after the effective date is too short for operators needing export/import clearances or quarantine; extend the timeframe or permit temporary storage/retention with mandatory preservation protocols.

Requiring return within 30 days for pre-effective-date findings could penalize operators who already quarantined parts; clarify whether operators may keep parts pending manufacturer instruction and whether costs for shipping/handling are reimbursable.

The prohibition on installing affected assemblies unless paragraph (i) completed effectively grounds aftermarket supply channels and could disrupt maintenance programs; allow installation if a documented inspection and mitigation (e.g., parts marking) is in place even when full paragraph (i) paperwork is pending.
The installation ban should include an exception for emergency replacement with an equivalent FAA-approved part or an AMOC that ensures temporary airworthiness pending full compliance.

The credit provision for previous actions is unduly narrow if it limits acceptable service information to specific versions; clarify that earlier revisions that accomplish equivalent inspections/actions are acceptable with operator documentation.

Require explicit guidance on how to document and demonstrate that previously performed actions meet the AD's requirements to qualify for credit, including acceptable evidence and FAA audit procedures.

The PRA prohibition language conflicts with the AD's mandatory reporting obligations in paragraph (j); reconcile the statements so operators understand whether reporting is voluntary or mandatory and ensure an OMB control number is provided.

Paragraph (m)'s assertion that responses are mandatory conflicts with the PRA prohibition; provide the OMB Control Number and the approved burden estimate, or amend the PRA statement to reflect compliance with PRA requirements.

Limiting AMOC approval authority to the New York ACO Branch manager without a clear timeline for decision could delay operations; require FAA to commit to a specific review timeframe (e.g., 60 days) for AMOCs.

The mandated routing of AMOC requests to principal inspectors or local FSDOs may be inefficient for international or certificate-holding overseas operators; allow direct electronic submission to the ACO Branch and provide a single point of contact for non-U.S. operators.

The requirement to notify the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC needs an exception for Part 121/135 operators with multiple certificates and multiple principal inspectors; permit corporate-level notification procedures.
The AD does not address assemblies that have been re-serialized or re-marked; provide guidance on how to handle suspect serial numbers that may have been altered intentionally or unintentionally.

The AD lacks a risk-based prioritization for inspection of assemblies based on usage hours or exposure; recommend prioritizing aircraft with high flight hours or certain operational profiles to reduce safety risk.

The rule does not indicate whether the inspection and return reports will be publicly available or redacted; operators request confidentiality treatment for proprietary maintenance data and a clear FOIA/privilege policy.
There is no cost-assessment or economic impact analysis provided showing availability of replacement assemblies; request that FAA publish estimated costs and parts lead times to inform commenters.

The installation prohibition's scope is unclear whether it applies to spares in supplier inventory and consignments; clarify whether warehouse stock may be installed after in-house inspection or whether it is barred until FAA acceptance.

Maintenance-record reviews for vintage or legacy aircraft may lack serial numbers; allow alternative identification methods such as part-number cross-reference or lab testing rather than forcing physical removal.
The AMOC authority should explicitly include timelines and criteria for emergency AMOCs (short-term operational deviations) for aircraft in service with no immediate access to serviceable parts.
The AD should require the manufacturer to cover reasonable shipping costs and provide pre-paid shipping labels for returns to avoid imposing unexpected expenses on operators.
Parts marking might require downtime for aircraft and specialized tooling; justify why marking cannot be deferred to the next scheduled heavy maintenance event if the gap is acceptable.
The reporting deadlines should include provisions for electronic batch submission or API integration with FAA databases to reduce administrative burden.
The PRA paragraph should not be used to imply that failure to provide information will not be enforced; state the legal basis for mandatory reporting and any penalties explicitly to avoid confusion.

Allow credit for earlier inspections performed to equivalent international airworthiness directives (EASA or Transport Canada) and provide a streamlined acceptance process to prevent duplicate inspections.
The AD should allow use of non-destructive test equipment or photographic evidence for remote inspections when assemblies are inaccessible due to COVID-19 or travel restrictions.
Define protocol for procurement of "serviceable assembly" including approved suppliers, traceability paperwork, and whether reworked/overhauled parts from OEM-authorized repair stations qualify.
Include a provision allowing operators to request short-term extensions to compliance times in circumstances of demonstrated hardship, pending AMOC approval.
Provide a digital template and contact email/portal for AMOC requests to ensure timely and trackable submissions, rather than relying solely on postal addresses.
Specify whether incomplete or partial reports will be accepted with follow-up supplements, to accommodate operators who discover additional affected parts after initial submission.
Clarify whether returns of assemblies found unacceptable before the AD were already returned under earlier manufacturer programs, and if so, whether duplicate returns are required.
Require the FAA to publish the acceptable gap tolerance values in the AD text (numerical thresholds) rather than only in referenced service documents to ensure uniform enforcement.
Clarify whether notification to principal inspectors must be written, electronic, or verbal and what constitutes adequate proof of notification before using an AMOC.

raw_output:
[P1] The requirement to “properly file in accordance with form instructions” is vague and could lead to denials for minor clerical errors; USCIS should publish a non-exhaustive list of curable vs. incurable filing deficiencies and allow cure periods.

[P1] Requiring “supporting documentation” without specifying minimum document types for common situations (e.g., job creation via TEA regional centers) will cause inconsistent adjudications; request issuance of detailed evidentiary checklists.

[P2] Allowing an alien to self-file is helpful, but the rule should clarify whether beneficiaries may file pro se when represented previously by counsel and how previously-submitted evidence can be reused.

[P3] Prohibiting transfer of a priority date to another alien will harm family-based planning and derivative investors in family office structures; request an exception for derivative family members listed on the original petition.

[P4] The prohibition on conferring a priority date to a later petition if conditional residence was obtained from the approved petition could unfairly penalize victims of fraud or error who were unaware; recommend allowing priority date retention where petition revocation resulted from actions of third parties (e.g., I-526 regional center operator fraud) and beneficiary demonstrates good faith.

[P5] Setting the standard investment minimum at $1,800,000 is a large increase from prior levels and will drastically reduce program access for many investors; request an economic impact analysis and transitional grandfathering for petitions filed within 12 months of final rule.

[P6] Automatic five-year CPI-U adjustments are reasonable, but indexing to cumulative CPI-U without caps could create abrupt increases in high-inflation periods; request inclusion of a maximum five-year increase cap (e.g., 10%) to prevent destabilizing jumps.

[P7] Rounding down to the nearest $100,000 reduces precision but creates large effective changes (e.g., a $1.79M index -> $1.7M); recommend rounding to the nearest $25,000 or $10,000 for fairness and to better reflect CPI changes.

[P8] DHS’s permission to update by technical amendment without notice-and-comment creates due-process concerns; request that substantive investment amount changes undergo notice-and-comment and that technical amendments be limited to clerical corrections only.

[P9] Establishing TEA minimum at $1,350,000 (75% of $1.8M) will still price out many investors in distressed areas; request retention of prior lower TEA thresholds or a multi-tiered TEA scale based on local median income/unemployment.

[P10] Tying the TEA amount automatically to 75% of standard amount every five years could amplify increases; recommend decoupling TEA adjustments from the standard amount and indexing TEA separately to local economic indicators.

[P11] Allowing DHS to update TEA amount via technical amendment similarly risks bypassing notice-and-comment; ask for requirement to publish proposed TEA levels with justification and allow stakeholder input.

[P12] Designating the high employment area minimum equal to standard $1,800,000 (no reduction) eliminates any premium for low-unemployment areas and may be unnecessary; ask DHS to justify parity with standard amount or to consider slightly lower thresholds for high-employment areas.

[P13] Automatic CPI-U adjustments for high-employment area amount without consideration of regional economic differences is arbitrary; recommend adjusting high-employment area amounts tied to region-specific cost-of-living indices or holding them constant absent specific justification.

[P14] Rounding high-employment adjustments to nearest $100,000 is too coarse and may create material increases for investments near thresholds; request finer rounding or caps on per-adjustment increases.

[P15] DHS updating high-employment amounts by technical amendment should require transparency and a public notice period; recommend at least 60 days’ notice before taking effect.

[P16] Allocating full-time positions solely to investors who based a petition on establishing the NCE could unfairly exclude investors relying on indirect job creation models (e.g., regional center projects); request explicit allowance for allocation among investors in pooled/regional-center investments where job creation methodology supports allocation.

[P17] The prohibition on allocating qualifying positions to non-natural persons or those not seeking EB-5 classification may inadvertently preclude lawful corporate arrangements (e.g., parent companies assigning jobs); request clarification that allocations among entities owned by investor-natural persons are permitted if consistent with job-creation evidence.

[P18] USCIS recognition of “reasonable agreements” among investors is welcome but undefined; request examples of acceptable agreements and a safe-harbor template for allocation agreements to reduce litigation.

[P19] USCIS authority to designate subdivisions as high unemployment areas should include an appeal or petition process for stakeholders to request designations or challenge boundaries; propose a formal petition process and timeline.

[P20] Requiring the designated subdivision to be composed of the census tract(s) where the NCE principally operates could disadvantage mobile or multi-site enterprises; request flexibility allowing a principal place of business plus contiguous tracts where substantial operations occur.

[P21] Allowing contiguous tracts to be included is positive, but the rule should set a maximum number of contiguous tracts or criteria to prevent artificially expanding TEA boundaries to capture lower unemployment tracts; request anti-manipulation safeguards.

[P22] The 150% national average weighted unemployment threshold lacks provision for using the most recent labor force data when national average changes rapidly; ask DHS to specify the data source(s), time frame, and handling of data lags.

[P23] Requiring customs/commercial entry documents to show property transferred from abroad may be infeasible for intangibles, intellectual property, or services; suggest alternate evidence standards (e.g., escrow records, contracts, valuations) and allow expert valuations in lieu of customs forms.

[P24] The managerial-control requirement for engagement in the NCE disadvantages passive investors in pooled investment models; request clarification that policy-making via limited partnership documents or board seats satisfies engagement and provide standards for passive vs. active roles.

[P25] The equity-holder evidence standard (organizational documents granting typical rights) should explicitly accept subscription agreements, operating agreements, or transferable membership interests as evidence and allow sworn affidavits when organizational documents are silent.

[P26] Evidence requirements for rural or high-unemployment classification are extensive; request a streamlined certification process for projects located within DHS-designated TEAs to reduce duplicative evidentiary burdens.

[P27] The rural area test requiring being outside MSAs and cities/towns of 20,000+ may be outdated due to changing commuting patterns; request consideration of commuter-shed, daytime population, or economic integration when determining rural status.

[P28] Using MSA/county/city averages to qualify as high-unemployment may cause inconsistent outcomes for tracts within heterogeneous MSAs; recommend preserving tract-level analysis (with aggregation rules) rather than defaulting to larger geographies.

[P29] Requiring boundary descriptions and “reliable methods” to obtain unemployment statistics without specifying acceptable data sources or methodology will cause denials; request a list of approved sources (BLS, ACS) and an approved statistical methodology or recognized third-party providers.

[P30] The obligation to provide reasons for denial is appropriate but should require detailed, itemized explainers for each missing or deficient piece of evidence to allow adequate opportunity to cure on appeal or motion to reopen.

[P31] Allowing appeals to the AAO is standard; however, appeals timelines and required fee waivers for humanitarian cases should be clarified—request fee waiver criteria for indigent petitioners.

[P32] The requirement to include the appropriate fee when filing for removal of conditions must include clear guidance on fee waivers or reductions for heirs of deceased investors or those in hardship—request extension of fee waiver eligibility for eligible derivatives.

[P33] The strict 90-day filing window before the second anniversary is unforgiving; request a grace period (e.g., 30 days) or clearer guidance on computation of the 90-day period, particularly where the anniversary falls on a weekend/holiday.

[P34] The proper-signature requirement should allow electronic signatures where permitted by law and clarify acceptability of notarized signatures executed abroad; request explicit acceptance of scanned signatures and e-signature platforms.

[P35] Automatic extension of conditional status upon receipt of a properly filed petition is essential; request clarification whether extension applies to travel and reentry (i.e., I-551 validity) and issuance of automatic temporary evidence for travel.

[P36] Allowing spouse and children to be included on the removal petition is helpful, but the rule should require guidance on documentation for derivatives who aged-out or married during the conditional period.

[P37] Requiring separate filings for spouse/child not included in the investor’s petition may be duplicative and costly; recommend permitting joint consolidated filings or waiving duplicate fees when family members file concurrently.

[P38] The permission for spouse/children to file after investor death is necessary; request clarification on deadlines and whether humanitarian parole or other relief is available while adjudication is pending.

[P39] Inclusion of aged-out children or former spouses should be clarified with examples of acceptable evidence to show continuous eligibility (e.g., school records, marriage/divorce decrees).

[P40] Automatic termination of status for failure to timely file is harsh; propose that USCIS implement notice reminders (electronic and postal) 120 and 60 days before the 90-day window opens and allow equitable tolling for service disruptions.

[P41] Requirement to send written notice of termination and NTA is necessary but must include a plain-language explanation of rights, remedies, and timelines; request standardized notice forms with translations for common languages.

[P42] The prohibition on appeals from termination decisions eliminates meaningful review; suggest reinstating limited administrative appeal rights or expedited motions to reopen before termination is final.

[P43] Allowing review during removal proceedings is insufficient when appeals are barred; require that petitions denied administratively be stayed pending removal proceedings or that an administrative reconsideration be available.

[P44] Placing the burden on the investor to prove timely filing by a preponderance in removal proceedings may disadvantage those with lost/delayed mail; request a rebuttable presumption in favor of timely filing if timely evidence (e.g., postal tracking, bank transactions) is presented.

[P45] USCIS discretion to accept late petitions for good cause is appropriate but should enumerate examples (illness, natural disaster, mailing disruptions) and provide a presumptive standard to reduce arbitrariness.

[P46] Restoration of status and cancellation of NTA if USCIS excuses a late petition before IJ jurisdiction is acceptable; request clear timelines for USCIS action to avoid prolonged uncertainty.

[P47] Allowing IJ termination upon joint motion after IJ jurisdiction vests is appropriate, but the rule should ensure that DHS cannot unreasonably withhold consent to joint motions; request criteria for DHS’s consent and a deadline for deciding such motions.

[P48] Eligibility of spouse/children to remove conditions after investor death should explicitly permit survivors to rely on investment evidence already submitted and waive fees when investor estate is insolvent.

[P49] USCIS review to determine interview waivers must be transparent; request publication of objective waiver criteria and an online status indicator for applicants to see whether their interview will be scheduled or waived.

[P50] The permissive interview waiver if paragraph (c)(1) met should list the exact documentary standards that satisfy c(1) (e.g., audited financials, source-of-funds documents) so petitioners know what triggers waiver.

[P51] The discretion to require interviews when not satisfied is broad; request procedural safeguards including advance notice of specific issues, ability to submit additional evidence before appearance, and telephonic/video interview options.

[P52] Requiring interviews at the office with jurisdiction over the enterprise location, investor residence, or adjudication location may impose travel burdens; request allowance for local USCIS office interviews, remote interviews, or community-based locations.

[P53] Automatic termination for failure to appear at a requested interview as of the second anniversary is an overly harsh sanction; propose that USCIS provide one reschedule opportunity before termination and require proving actual notice of the interview.

[P54] Written notice of termination and NTA issuance must include detailed reasons and evidence relied upon; request that USCIS include information on how to request a reschedule or to present supporting evidence and the contact for filing such requests.

[P55] The right to seek review in removal proceedings is important, but specialized expertise may be required; request provision of guidance to IJs on evaluating EB-5 investment evidence and recognition of non-traditional documentation.

[P56] Burden on investor to prove compliance with interview requirements by preponderance should be balanced by presumption of regularity for USCIS scheduling; recommend shifting initial burden to USCIS to show proper notice of interview.

[P57] Allowing written requests to reschedule or waive the interview is good; require clear deadlines (e.g., within 14 days of missed interview) and confirmation receipts from USCIS when such requests are filed.

[P58] The investor’s written request explaining reasons should allow supporting medical, travel, or emergency documents and acceptance of translations and certified copies from abroad; request a list of acceptable supporting documents.

[P59] USCIS discretion to find good cause to reschedule or waive is appropriate but should be exercised under published standards to avoid inconsistency; request enumerated examples and processing timelines for decisions.

[P60] Requirement to restore status and cancel NTA when USCIS waives the interview is fair; request that USCIS also provide retroactive employment and travel documentation if termination erroneously occurred.

[P61] When USCIS reschedules the interview, automatic restoration and NTA cancellation is necessary; request that USCIS provide interim work authorization documents and temporary I-551 evidence for travel if adjudication exceeds 90 days.

[P62] Offering opportunity to rebut derogatory information or evidence of illegally obtained funds is essential; request a defined process and minimal timeframes for investors to obtain forensic documents and legal counsel.

[P63] Allowing denial if investor cannot rebut illegal-funds evidence is appropriate, but the rule must require DHS to disclose sources and basis of derogatory information (subject to confidentiality concerns) so the investor can meaningfully respond.

[P64] Forwarding unrelated derogatory information to investigations for action is fine, but there should be safeguards to prevent indefinite investigatory delays that stall removal-of-conditions adjudication; request time limits for investigative referrals.

[P65] The requirement to approve when no unresolved derogatory information exists should include a presumption in favor of approval where documentation meets regulatory standards; request clearer timelines for approval after the interview.

[P66] Removing conditional status effective as of the second anniversary upon approval is retroactive; request clarification whether benefits (e.g., eligibility for federal programs, Social Security credits) accrue retroactively and guidance on how to correct past denials.

[P67] Written notice of approval should include all next steps, effective dates, and instructions for document surrender/issuance; ask DHS to standardize approval notices and provide digital copies for recordkeeping.

[P68] DHS may require biometrics for new PR cards; request that biometrics appointments be coordinated to minimize multiple visits and that mobile biometrics be available for incapacitated applicants.

[P69] Upon denial USCIS must provide written reasons and issue NTA; request that denials specify which documents were insufficient and give guidance on available relief other than removal proceedings (e.g., motions to reopen/reconsider).

[P70] Termination of PR status and derivatives’ status as of USCIS decision should allow a short administrative stay of enforcement (e.g., 30 days) to permit filing of motions or gathering of evidence before removal action commences.

[P71] Instructions to surrender PR card should allow surrender at a USCIS facility or by mail with receipt and provide a waiver for individuals who cannot return cards for compelling reasons (lost, destroyed, abroad).

[P72] Prohibiting appeals from denial removes an important procedural safeguard; recommend reinstatement of appeal rights to AAO for EB-5 program denials or at minimum a streamlined, expedited review process.

[P73] Allowing review in removal proceedings is not an adequate substitute for administrative appeal; removal proceedings are adversarial and burdensome—request preservation of administrative appeals to reduce immigration court backlog.

[P74] Placing the burden on USCIS in removal proceedings to prove that petition facts are untrue is appropriate; request explicit instruction to immigration judges that USCIS must produce contemporaneous adjudicative records and any expert analyses used in denial.

When USCIS reschedules the interview, automatic restoration and NTA cancellation is necessary; request that USCIS provide interim work authorization documents and temporary I-551 evidence for travel if adjudication exceeds 90 days.

Offering opportunity to rebut derogatory information or evidence of illegally obtained funds is essential; request a defined process and minimal timeframes for investors to obtain forensic documents and legal counsel.

Allowing denial if investor cannot rebut illegal-funds evidence is appropriate, but the rule must require DHS to disclose sources and basis of derogatory information (subject to confidentiality concerns) so the investor can meaningfully respond.

Forwarding unrelated derogatory information to investigations for action is fine, but there should be safeguards to prevent indefinite investigatory delays that stall removal-of-conditions adjudication; request time limits for investigative referrals.

The requirement to approve when no unresolved derogatory information exists should include a presumption in favor of approval where documentation meets regulatory standards; request clearer timelines for approval after the interview.

Removing conditional status effective as of the second anniversary upon approval is retroactive; request clarification whether benefits (e.g., eligibility for federal programs, Social Security credits) accrue retroactively and guidance on how to correct past denials.

Written notice of approval should include all next steps, effective dates, and instructions for document surrender/issuance; ask DHS to standardize approval notices and provide digital copies for recordkeeping.
DHS may require biometrics for new PR cards; request that biometrics appointments be coordinated to minimize multiple visits and that mobile biometrics be available for incapacitated applicants.

Upon denial USCIS must provide written reasons and issue NTA; request that denials specify which documents were insufficient and give guidance on available relief other than removal proceedings (e.g., motions to reopen/reconsider).

Termination of PR status and derivatives’ status as of USCIS decision should allow a short administrative stay of enforcement (e.g., 30 days) to permit filing of motions or gathering of evidence before removal action commences.

Instructions to surrender PR card should allow surrender at a USCIS facility or by mail with receipt and provide a waiver for individuals who cannot return cards for compelling reasons (lost, destroyed, abroad).

Prohibiting appeals from denial removes an important procedural safeguard; recommend reinstatement of appeal rights to AAO for EB-5 program denials or at minimum a streamlined, expedited review process.

Allowing review in removal proceedings is not an adequate substitute for administrative appeal; removal proceedings are adversarial and burdensome—request preservation of administrative appeals to reduce immigration court backlog.

Placing the burden on USCIS in removal proceedings to prove that petition facts are untrue is appropriate; request explicit instruction to immigration judges that USCIS must produce contemporaneous adjudicative records and any expert analyses used in denial.
