raw_output:
[P1] The requirement in §63.14 to publish a Federal Register document before enforcing an edition other than specified is impractical because it creates undue delay in enforcement actions when urgent public health risks arise.

[P1] EPA should clarify what constitutes sufficient publication in the Federal Register for alternate editions (full notice vs. short notice), otherwise regulated entities will face uncertainty.

[P2] Requiring that incorporated materials be “available to the public” when enforcing a different edition (§63.14) is vague; the rule should specify formats (free online PDF, physical copies) and access means to satisfy the requirement.

[P2] The obligation to make incorporated-by-reference materials available could conflict with third-party copyright restrictions; EPA must commit to providing free public access or obtain permissions.

[P3] §§63.2342(a) compliance scheduling for new/reconstructed affected sources lacks clarity on the trigger date for “commenced construction or reconstruction”; EPA should define whether permits, ground-breaking, or contract awards trigger the schedule.

[P3] Industry commenters will request a grace period longer than dates in §63.2342(a) to allow for procurement and retrofitting of control equipment for newly reconstructed sources.

[P4] The compliance schedule in §63.2342(b) for existing affected sources is onerous for small businesses and should include phased implementation or size-based exemptions.

[P5] The cross-reference in §63.2342(d) to notification requirements (§§63.2343 and 63.2382) is confusing—EPA should provide a consolidated timeline table in the preamble or regulatory text to avoid misinterpretation.

[P6] §63.2342(e) requiring compliance with a long list of discrete requirements by initial startup or specified dates imposes compliance complexity; EPA should allow consolidated compliance demonstrations or a single compliance window.

[P7] §63.2342(e)(1) referencing §63.2343(b)(4)-(7) for storage tanks not requiring control is ambiguous about applicability when tank service changes; EPA should require re-evaluation triggers when commodity changes occur.

[P8] §63.2342(e)(2) cross-references numerous sections and tables for existing tanks; owners may be unable to determine which specific provisions apply—request that EPA provide worked examples or applicability flowcharts.

[P9] The equipment leak requirements in §63.2342(e)(3) are extensive; EPA should provide a compliance template and allow use of existing LDAR (leak detection and repair) programs to avoid duplication.

[P10] Requiring fenceline monitoring per §63.2342(e)(4) by the schedule in §63.2342(f) will impose substantial capital and operational costs; EPA should perform and publish a cost-benefit analysis specific to fenceline options.

[P11] The flare-related obligations in §63.2342(e)(5) may conflict with state emergency response requirements; EPA should clarify precedence and allow temporary exemptions during bona fide emergency operations.

[P12] The miscellaneous requirements in §63.2342(e)(6) lump many disparate obligations together, increasing legal risk for noncompliance for minor infractions; consider splitting into prioritized phases.

[P13] §63.2342(e)(7) mandating performance testing in §63.2354(b)(6) by certain dates will be difficult to schedule due to seasonal process variability—EPA should allow windows for representative testing and retesting.

[P14] The parent provision §63.2342(f) referencing OLD operations and §63.2348 should explicitly state whether choosing fenceline monitoring affects other permitting or state rules to avoid conflicting requirements.

[P15] §63.2342(f)(1) requiring submission of modeling results, analytes, and action levels by specified deadlines or with permit applications creates duplicative burdens—facilities often already prepare similar materials for permits and should be allowed to reuse those submittals.

[P16] §63.2342(f)(2) obligating approval of modeling/analytes/action levels by a deadline is likely to overwhelm permitting authorities; EPA must provide timelines for agency review or deem submissions approved after a fixed period.

[P17] §63.2343(a) requirement that small tanks (<5,000 gal) comply with §63.2343(e) should be revised to exempt small tanks storing low-volatility commodities, which pose minimal emissions risk.

[P18] The documentation retention and availability requirement in §63.2343(a) for small tanks and certain transfer racks should specify retention periods and acceptable “suitable forms” (electronic formats, stamped site plans).

[P19] The permission in §63.2343(a) to use site plan or P&ID identification as documentation is helpful but should be limited to plans signed and dated by a responsible official to ensure accuracy.

[P20] §63.2343(b) imposing requirements for larger tanks not subject to control needs clearer definitions of “subject to this subpart” versus exemptions; regulated entities need a decision tree.

[P21] §63.2343(b)(4) monitoring of potential vapor leakage sources from fixed roof tanks per schedule is technically feasible, but EPA must clarify monitoring frequency for tanks with intermittent service.

[P22] The requirement in §63.2343(b)(4)(i) to use Method 21 within 90 days after initial fill and annually thereafter is acceptable for many operators but may be unduly frequent for tanks that consistently test non-detect; allow reduced frequency after repeated non-detects.

[P23] §63.2343(b)(4)(i)(A) daily calibration per Method 21 with specified gases increases costs for small operators; EPA should permit weekly calibration when monitoring frequency is monthly.

[P24] The end-of-day calibration drift assessment in §63.2343(b)(4)(i)(B) without adjusting readout is technically sound but needs clarity whether automated logging systems satisfy the requirement.

[P25] §63.2343(b)(4)(i)(C) mandating re-monitoring if calibration drift >10% could lead to large data gaps if instruments drift; EPA should allow immediate corrective action and documented rationale in lieu of full re-monitoring in certain cases.

[P26] The 500 ppmv leak threshold in §63.2343(b)(4)(ii) should be justified with health-based and control-technology rationale; environmental groups may argue it is too lenient and request a lower threshold.

[P27] §63.2343(b)(4)(iii) requiring repair or emptying within 45 days is reasonable, but regulators should allow alternative repair schedules for complex repairs provided interim mitigation is implemented.

[P28] The permission in §63.2343(b)(4)(iii) for two 30-day extensions is necessary, but EPA must limit extensions for repeated or chronic leaks and require corrective action plans.

[P29] §63.2343(b)(4)(iii) records for extension decisions (A)-(C) impose specific burdens; EPA should allow incorporation by reference to maintenance logs or work orders to avoid redundant paperwork.

[P30] Reporting requirements in §63.2343(b)(4)(iii) to include date of emptying/repair in compliance reports if beyond second extension should require certified dates and photographic or other evidence for enforcement certainty.

[P31] §63.2343(b)(4)(iii)(A) record content requirements for first extensions (defect description, alternative capacity documentation) are reasonable but need thresholds for what constitutes adequate “documentation.”

[P32] §63.2343(b)(4)(iii)(B) requiring documentation of unavailability of alternative storage for second extensions is potentially intrusive; EPA should permit a signed attestation by a responsible official instead of third-party proof.

[P33] Requiring the date of complete emptying per §63.2343(b)(4)(iii)(C) is acceptable; EPA should also specify acceptable evidence (manifests, pump-out records).

[P34] §63.2343(b)(5) periodic vapor pressure analyses to show annual average true vapor pressure below control thresholds using ASTM D6378–18a are technically specific, but facilities might not have testing access; EPA should allow third-party labs and clarify QA/QC requirements.

[P35] The specification in §63.2343(b)(5) to use a 4:1 vapor-liquid ratio and actual annual average temperature is precise; industry may comment that determining “actual annual average temperature” at tank top needs guidance on measurement protocol.

[P36] The requirement to maintain vapor pressure records per §63.2394 is fine but EPA should set explicit retention periods (e.g., 5 years) to reduce ambiguity.

[P37] §63.2343(b)(5)(i)/(ii) deadlines for initial and subsequent vapor pressure analyses every 60 months are acceptable, but EPA should allow extensions when supply chain or lab capacity constraints exist.

[P38] §63.2343(b)(6) requiring periodic HAP content analyses and prohibiting voluntary consensus standards or SDS uses is overly prescriptive; industry requests allowance to use certified supplier data sheets in combination with periodic lab verification to reduce costs.

[P39] The use of §63.2354(c) procedures for HAP analysis in §63.2343(b)(6) is acceptable, but EPA should publish an implementation guidance document and approved labs list.

[P40] The 60-month interval for HAP content analyses in §63.2343(b)(6)(i)/(ii) is long enough for stable commodities, but facilities that change feedstock frequently should be required to analyze upon each commodity change—EPA should define “significant change.”

[P41] §63.2343(b)(7)(i) applying (b)(1)-(6) to listed tank categories must include a complete list in the preamble; otherwise regulated parties cannot determine applicability.

[P42] The optional fenceline monitoring alternative in §63.2343(b)(7)(ii) is a valuable flexibility; however, EPA should quantify equivalence in emission reduction or public protection so facilities can make informed choices.

[P43] The permission in §63.2343(c)(1)(iii) to allow one report to satisfy multiple transfer racks reporting reduces administrative burden and should be explicitly allowed across all overlapping reporting obligations.

[P44] §63.2343(e) monitoring of small fixed roof tanks with vapor pressure >10.3 kPa must clarify how vapor pressure is measured for mixed or variable-content tanks.

[P45] The Method 21 monitoring onset and annual frequency in §63.2343(e)(1) is repetitive with larger-tank requirements; EPA should harmonize schedules to reduce duplicative monitoring.

[P46] Daily instrument calibration per §63.2343(e)(1)(i) may be unnecessary when monitoring is infrequent; EPA should allow calibration based on monitoring schedule (e.g., on the day of monitoring).

[P47] The end-of-day calibration drift assessment in §63.2343(e)(1)(ii) should be modified to allow alternate QA/QC procedures for continuous automated monitors.

[P48] §63.2343(e)(1)(iii) re-monitoring when drift exceeds 10% is appropriate, but EPA should permit use of corrective actions and statistical adjustment approaches in limited circumstances.

[P49] The 500 ppmv leak threshold in §63.2343(e)(2) for small tanks mirrors larger-tank thresholds; environmental justice advocates will likely push for a lower threshold based on health risk concerns.

[P50] The repair/emptying within 45 days in §63.2343(e)(3) may be infeasible for seasonal operations; EPA should allow seasonal exceptions tied to documented process schedules.

[P51] Two 30-day extensions permitted in §63.2343(e)(3) seem generous; community groups may argue that enforcement should require formal corrective action plans rather than repeated extensions.

[P52] The recordkeeping specifics in §63.2343(e)(3)(i)-(iii) are detailed; small operators request templates and allow electronic records to satisfy the requirements.

[P53] §63.2346(a) applicability criteria tied to tank capacity and Table 2/2b thresholds need clearer examples for borderline capacities and mixed-use tanks.

[P54] §63.2346(a)(1) requiring compliance with emission limits in Table 2/2b and paragraph (m) should include test methods tolerances and allow alternative monitoring means approved by the Administrator.

[P55] Routing emissions to fuel gas systems per §63.2346(a)(2) may be infeasible where fuel gas infrastructure is absent; EPA should allow vapor recovery to be routed to thermal oxidizers or other recovery systems as equivalent.

[P56] §63.2346(a)(4)(ii) requiring transport vehicles to have current U.S. DOT certifications is reasonable but EPA should clarify which specific DOT certifications are acceptable and how to document them.

[P57] The prohibition in §63.2346(a)(4)(iv) against relief devices opening during loading or diurnal breathing losses may create safety risks if over-pressurization occurs; operators need an exception for bona fide safety events.

[P58] Setting relief devices to no less than 2.5 psig per §63.2346(a)(4)(v) may be incompatible with some tank designs; the permission in §63.2346(a)(4)(v) to set lower values with rationale must be expanded to allow engineering justification rather than only notification.

[P59] The monitoring and record requirements for each relief valve in §63.2346(a)(4)(v)(A)-(C) will be burdensome for facilities with many valves; EPA should allow representative sampling or risk-based monitoring frequencies.

[P60] §63.2346(a)(5) changing applicability for tanks meeting Table 2b items 1–3 needs a phase-in schedule for existing tanks that require retrofits to comply with paragraphs (a)(1)-(4).

[P61] The fenceline monitoring alternative in §63.2346(a)(6) should include explicit criteria for when fenceline monitoring is considered “equivalent” to equipment-level controls to prevent backsliding.

[P62] §63.2346(b)(1)-(2) requirements for transfer racks referencing subpart SS need harmonization with existing subpart SS compliance deadlines and measurement methods.

[P63] §63.2346(c) LDAR applicability for components operating ≥300 hours/year may create perverse incentives to reduce recorded operating hours to avoid LDAR; EPA should provide anti-circumvention language.

[P64] §63.2346(d)(2) loading only into DOT-certified vehicles needs a mechanism for verifying certifications of third-party carriers and documenting temporary exceptions.

[P65] §63.2346(e) Table 3 operating limits for high throughput racks are prescriptive; EPA should allow performance-based demonstrations or equivalent-performance controls where Table 3 parameters cannot be met.

[P66] §63.2346(f) requiring Administrator approval to use TOC as a surrogate for organic HAP is reasonable, but the approval process must include clear criteria and time limits for agency review.

[P67] §63.2346(i) permitting opening safety devices when required to avoid unsafe conditions is necessary; EPA should require immediate notification and documentation of any safety-device openings to regulators and nearby communities.

[P68] The expiration of the safety device permission in §63.2346(i) three years after final rule publication (§63.2346(i) condition) is concerning—EPA must explain the rationale and provide transition options for facilities that rely on this safety flexibility.

[P69] §63.2346(k) directing venting-to-flare closed vent systems to comply with §63.2380 rather than other flare standards must ensure consistency with state flare rules and not create gaps in monitoring or testing.

[P70] The equipment leak re-structuring in §63.2346(l) that supersedes paragraph (c) and forces choice between (l)(1) and (l)(2) is confusing; EPA should allow a hybrid approach for complex facilities.

[P71] §63.2346(l)(1) maintaining traditional controls for components operating ≥300 hours/year is fine, but the rule should define how to treat components that cross the 300-hour threshold intermittently.

[P72] The option in §63.2346(l)(2) to elect fenceline monitoring instead of component-level LDAR is an important flexibility; however, EPA must provide decision tools and modeling criteria to demonstrate equivalency.

[P73] §63.2346(m) eliminating certain startup/shutdown/malfunction allowances for subparts H, SS, and UU requires further justification and may expose operators to noncompliance during events outside their control—petition to retain limited SSM affirmative defense.

[P74] The opt-in permission in §63.2348(a) to conduct fenceline monitoring for sources not required under §63.658 is valuable but EPA should provide incentives (e.g., compliance credits) for facilities that opt in.

[P75] §63.2348(a) mandatory boundary sampling and Methods 325A/325B requirement could be cost-prohibitive for small facilities; EPA should consider lower-cost monitoring tiers or phased implementation.

[P76] §63.2348(b) requirements to determine target analytes and action levels per (b)(1)-(5) place technical modeling burdens on facilities; EPA must provide standardized tools or funded assistance for small businesses.

[P77] §63.2348(b)(1) requirement to use EPA guidance to develop HAP emissions inventory and modeling is appropriate, but EPA should make the referenced guidance final and provide example inventories.

[P78] The condition in §63.2348(b)(1) setting the HAP emissions inventory at allowable emissions from all equipment under common control may overstate real-world emissions; industry will request the option to use actual emissions with supporting monitoring.

[P79] §63.2348(b)(1) obligating modeled allowable emissions to be adjusted for certain control requirements could double-count controls if permits already reflect those requirements; EPA should coordinate with permitting authorities to avoid inconsistency.

[P80] §63.2348(b)(2) requiring at least one target analyte is reasonable, but the requirement that analytes have a validated uptake rate (b)(2)(i) may restrict analyte selection; EPA should provide an expedited validation process.

[P81] The prohibition in §63.2348(b)(2)(ii) against using a HAP as an analyte unless its action level is ≥5× MDL is technically motivated, but may exclude low-level toxic HAPs of concern to communities; EPA should allow community-priority analytes with enhanced monitoring protocols.

[P82] §63.2348(b)(2)(iii) selecting the first analyte as the Table 1 HAP with highest annual allowable emissions favors facilities’ allowable emissions profile; communities may object and ask for cumulative risk consideration in analyte selection.

[P83] Legal commenters will assert that several cross-references (e.g., to table numbers, other subparts) risk circularity and ambiguity; EPA should provide clear, non-contradictory regulatory text and consolidated applicability tables.

[P84] Environmental justice advocates will likely comment that the rule’s fenceline monitoring provisions lack mandatory community notification and public access to fenceline data in near-real time.

[P85] Small business associations will submit comments requesting regulatory flexibility, phased compliance schedules, and reduced monitoring frequencies for low-risk tanks and transfer racks.

[P86] State air agencies will request clarity on primacy and delegation: whether states implementing more stringent standards can enforce alternate editions and how §63.14 publication interacts with state rulemakings.

[P87] Permitting authorities will comment that submission review timeframes for modeling and analyte approvals (§63.2342(f)(2)) must be codified or the backlog will prevent timely permitting decisions.

[P88] Trade associations will request that EPA allow the use of equivalent consensus standards or industry best practices in lieu of some specified methods (e.g., allow accredited lab methods for HAP content under §63.2343(b)(6) with EPA approval).

[P89] Compliance auditors will request clarification whether electronic recordkeeping systems meet the “suitable form” availability requirements in §63.2343(a) and related recordkeeping provisions.

[P90] Public health groups will demand that the 500 ppmv leak threshold be re-evaluated against acute exposure health benchmarks and request a lower action level or additional community exposure mitigations.

§63.2346(a)(4)(ii) requiring transport vehicles to have current U.S. DOT certifications is reasonable but EPA should clarify which specific DOT certifications are acceptable and how to document them.

The prohibition in §63.2346(a)(4)(iv) against relief devices opening during loading or diurnal breathing losses may create safety risks if over-pressurization occurs; operators need an exception for bona fide safety events.

Setting relief devices to no less than 2.5 psig per §63.2346(a)(4)(v) may be incompatible with some tank designs; the permission in §63.2346(a)(4)(v) to set lower values with rationale must be expanded to allow engineering justification rather than only notification.

The monitoring and record requirements for each relief valve in §63.2346(a)(4)(v)(A)-(C) will be burdensome for facilities with many valves; EPA should allow representative sampling or risk-based monitoring frequencies.
§63.2346(a)(5) changing applicability for tanks meeting Table 2b items 1–3 needs a phase-in schedule for existing tanks that require retrofits to comply with paragraphs (a)(1)-(4).
The fenceline monitoring alternative in §63.2346(a)(6) should include explicit criteria for when fenceline monitoring is considered “equivalent” to equipment-level controls to prevent backsliding.
§63.2346(b)(1)-(2) requirements for transfer racks referencing subpart SS need harmonization with existing subpart SS compliance deadlines and measurement methods.

§63.2346(f) requiring Administrator approval to use TOC as a surrogate for organic HAP is reasonable, but the approval process must include clear criteria and time limits for agency review.

§63.2346(k) directing venting-to-flare closed vent systems to comply with §63.2380 rather than other flare standards must ensure consistency with state flare rules and not create gaps in monitoring or testing.
The equipment leak re-structuring in §63.2346(l) that supersedes paragraph (c) and forces choice between (l)(1) and (l)(2) is confusing; EPA should allow a hybrid approach for complex facilities.
§63.2346(l)(1) maintaining traditional controls for components operating ≥300 hours/year is fine, but the rule should define how to treat components that cross the 300-hour threshold intermittently.

The option in §63.2346(l)(2) to elect fenceline monitoring instead of component-level LDAR is an important flexibility; however, EPA must provide decision tools and modeling criteria to demonstrate equivalency.

§63.2346(m) eliminating certain startup/shutdown/malfunction allowances for subparts H, SS, and UU requires further justification and may expose operators to noncompliance during events outside their control—petition to retain limited SSM affirmative defense.

The opt-in permission in §63.2348(a) to conduct fenceline monitoring for sources not required under §63.658 is valuable but EPA should provide incentives (e.g., compliance credits) for facilities that opt in.
§63.2348(a) mandatory boundary sampling and Methods 325A/325B requirement could be cost-prohibitive for small facilities; EPA should consider lower-cost monitoring tiers or phased implementation.

§63.2348(b) requirements to determine target analytes and action levels per (b)(1)-(5) place technical modeling burdens on facilities; EPA must provide standardized tools or funded assistance for small businesses.
§63.2348(b)(1) requirement to use EPA guidance to develop HAP emissions inventory and modeling is appropriate, but EPA should make the referenced guidance final and provide example inventories.

The condition in §63.2348(b)(1) setting the HAP emissions inventory at allowable emissions from all equipment under common control may overstate real-world emissions; industry will request the option to use actual emissions with supporting monitoring.

§63.2348(b)(1) obligating modeled allowable emissions to be adjusted for certain control requirements could double-count controls if permits already reflect those requirements; EPA should coordinate with permitting authorities to avoid inconsistency.

Environmental justice advocates will likely comment that the rule’s fenceline monitoring provisions lack mandatory community notification and public access to fenceline data in near-real time.
Small business associations will submit comments requesting regulatory flexibility, phased compliance schedules, and reduced monitoring frequencies for low-risk tanks and transfer racks.

Permitting authorities will comment that submission review timeframes for modeling and analyte approvals (§63.2342(f)(2)) must be codified or the backlog will prevent timely permitting decisions.

[P1] The requirement that the 2020 Board have exactly 10 members is arbitrary and may conflict with practical considerations if qualified nominees are unavailable; we recommend allowing a range (e.g., 8–10) rather than a fixed number.

[P1] Requiring a 10-member Board in 2020 creates transitional complexity compared to subsequent years and may increase administrative costs for that single year; propose harmonizing 2020 and later boards to the same size.

[P2] Mandating 8 members for every Board from 2021 onward is too rigid and could impede continuity if vacancies occur; allow temporary appointment of interim members or permit the Board to operate with a minimum quorum number lower than 8.

[P2] The flat 8-member rule does not account for differences in industry size or regional representation over time; suggest periodic review of optimal Board size based on industry metrics.

[P3] The composition rules as written lack clarity on tie-breakers and prioritization if nominations exceed seats in a category; request explicit procedures for resolving over-nominations.

[P4] Allocating 9 manufacturer seats for 2020 and 7 thereafter concentrates control with manufacturers and may marginalize importers and other stakeholders; propose reducing manufacturer majority or adding public interest seats.

[P4] The switch from 9 to 7 manufacturer members between 2020 and 2021 may create instability or unequal representation for ongoing Board initiatives; recommend grandfathering certain incumbent seats or staggering transitions.

[P5] Requiring five Southern manufacturers in 2020 and four thereafter may be unconstitutional if it effectively conditions federal participation on geographic origin; request legal analysis of geographic quotas’ compatibility with equal protection and commerce clause concerns.

[P5] The regional quota for the South could disadvantage manufacturers in other regions with high production but outside the “South” classification; propose basing seats on production volume or number of firms rather than a fixed regional count.

[P6] Allocating four (2020) and three (2021+) seats to "all other parts of the United States" is vague—does that encompass multiple regions with differing needs? The rule should define the regions or provide a mechanism to allocate among non-South areas fairly.

[P6] The small number of non-South seats may underrepresent significant manufacturing clusters in the Midwest and West; propose reallocating seats to reflect production distribution data.

[P7] Having exactly one importer member does not reflect the market share of imports for paper and paper-based packaging; stakeholders from the importing sector request that importer seats be proportionate to import volume (e.g., more than one seat).

[P7] The single importer seat could create conflict-of-interest issues if that importer is a large firm; propose allowing two importer seats or rotating importer representation to minimize dominance.

[P8] The requirement that subsequent nominations “follow the listed procedures” is fine but the rule lacks an appeals process for rejected nominations; include an appeals or reconsideration mechanism.

[P9] Outreach to manufacturers and importers that meet a 100,000 short ton threshold is overly narrow and will exclude small- and medium-sized enterprises that nonetheless have significant local impacts; recommend lowering the threshold or requiring outreach to all known stakeholders regardless of volume.

[P9] The 100,000 short ton threshold is arbitrary and lacks supporting data; request that the agency publish the empirical basis for choosing that threshold and consider a tiered outreach approach.

[P9] The outreach obligation does not specify format, timelines, or documentation standards—request explicit requirements (e.g., written notices, posted on agency website, certified mail) to ensure meaningful outreach and a record for compliance.

[P10] While manufacturers/importers may submit nominations, the rule does not state whether third-party nominations (e.g., trade associations) are allowed; clarify whether organizations may nominate individuals and whether self-nominations are permissible.

[P10] Permission for manufacturers and importers to submit nominations should include protections against coercion by employers; request confidentiality or an option to submit nominations anonymously until vetted.

[P11] Allowing nominees to provide a “short background statement” is vague—specify maximum length, required content (e.g., conflicts of interest, financial disclosures), and whether the statements will be made public.

[P11] The rule should require standardized background statements to enable fair comparison among nominees rather than allowing variable, potentially misleading submissions.

[P12] Allowing nominees to seek any vacant seats for which they qualify could produce strategic gaming (nominees applying across multiple categories); request limiting the number of seats an individual can seek simultaneously and clarifying priority rules.

[P12] The provision lacks a deadline for nominees to indicate which seats they seek, which could hamper timely appointment; require seat-selection by a specific date in the nomination cycle.

[P13] Requiring domestic manufacturers to manufacture in the region for which they seek nomination will exclude companies with national operations and complex supply chains; clarify how “manufacture in the region” is defined (e.g., percentage of production, facility location).

[P13] The regional manufacturing requirement may penalize firms with contract manufacturing or multi-site production; propose allowing demonstration of substantial operational presence (e.g., 25% of production) rather than strict single-region manufacture.

[P14] Permitting nominees who manufacture in both regions to choose one region could incentivize strategic selection to game regional balances; the rule should require disclosure of multi-region operations and potentially randomize or rotate such nominees’ regional seat assignments.

[P14] The provision should require nominees who select one region to commit publicly to advocate for that region’s interests, to avoid conflicts if their primary operations are elsewhere.

[P15] Allowing persons who are both manufacturers and importers to seek nomination as either creates potential conflicts of interest and dual representation; recommend clear disclosure requirements and a restriction preventing nominees from representing both interests simultaneously.

[P15] The rule should clarify whether an individual may be nominated in both capacities in the same cycle and, if so, how conflicts will be resolved.

[P16] Requiring the Board to submit nominations at least six months before the new term could be impractical given business cycles and nominee availability; propose shortening to 90 days or permitting exceptions for good cause.

[P16] The six-month deadline should include a provision for emergency or late nominations if unforeseen vacancies arise (e.g., resignations, disqualifications), with a fast-track appointment process.

[P17] Requiring the Secretary to select members from nominations submitted by the Board limits independent appointment authority; suggest allowing the Secretary to solicit outside nominations in cases of insufficient or non-representative nominations.

[P17] The rule should clarify whether the Secretary can reject an entire slate of nominations and request resubmission, and establish standards for such rejection to avoid arbitrary exercise of discretion.

[P18] Mandating a background questionnaire at nomination time is reasonable but the rule must specify the questionnaire’s scope, privacy protections, and whether information will be public; request limits on sensitive personal data and clear guidance on FOIA release.

[P18] The rule should permit nominees reasonable time to complete complex questionnaires (e.g., 30 days) and provide assistance or templates to ensure compliance.

[P19] The Secretary’s appointment based on representation rules in § 1222.40(b) requires transparency regarding how representation will be verified—request publication of appointment criteria and data used to determine representation.

[P19] If the Secretary must adhere strictly to the representation rules, there should be guidance on how to handle ties, insufficient qualified nominees in a category, or overlapping qualifications; propose fallback appointment rules.

[P20] Prohibiting two Board members from being employed by the same legal entity is appropriate to prevent concentration, but the rule should define “employed by” to include contractors, subsidiaries, and affiliated entities to prevent circumvention.

[P20] The prohibition should also address indirect control (e.g., family ownership, cross-directorships) that could effectively produce single-entity influence; recommend defining affiliated entities and applying the prohibition accordingly.

[P21] Allowing the Board to recommend modifications to nomination procedures is sensible, but the rule should require public notice and comment on the Board’s proposed modifications before submission to the Secretary to ensure stakeholder input.

[P21] The provision should set a deadline for the Secretary to respond to Board recommendations (e.g., 120 days) to prevent indefinite delay.

[P22] Requiring the Secretary to implement recommended modifications only through rulemaking could unreasonably slow needed procedural updates; propose allowing interim administrative adjustments via guidance followed by formal rulemaking.

[P22] The rule should clarify whether modifications must follow notice-and-comment rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act or whether an abbreviated process is acceptable, and whether emergency changes can be made faster.

[P1] The April 19, 2018 comment deadline is unreasonably short for international operators and manufacturers to compile technical data and coordinated joint comments; extend the comment period by at least 60 days.

[P1] The rule should clarify whether the April 19, 2018 date is the postmark date or actual receipt date for electronic and postal submissions to avoid inadvertent rejections.

[P2] The applicability language omits Boeing 737 NG sub-variants used in cargo conversions (e.g., 737–700C conversions to freighter); specify whether supplemental type certificated (STC) converted airplanes are included or excluded.

[P2] The AD should explicitly state whether leased aircraft certificated in other countries but operated under U.S. registry fall within the applicability to prevent confusion among lessors and operators.

[P3] The compliance clause needs clarification on whether calendar deadlines, flight-cycle thresholds, or flight-hour thresholds govern the "specified compliance times" — the AD should explicitly list the time-basis for each table entry.

[P3] There is no provision for extensions due to parts shortages or scheduled maintenance block planning; include an allowance or process for temporary relief without requiring an AMOC.

[P4] The inspection timing references Table 1/2/4/5 but the proposed rule fails to reproduce or summarize the table thresholds in the AD text; include the critical part-number-specific deadlines in the regulatory text.

[P4] The obligation in (g) lacks guidance on acceptable inspection methods and qualifications for personnel performing the part-number verification; require certified maintenance personnel or provide equivalent standards.

[P5] Allowing maintenance-records review in lieu of physical inspection is acceptable only if records are complete and traceable; the AD should define "conclusive" and require provenance (work order, signature, organization) to prevent fraudulent record claims.

[P5] The permission to use records should require cross-checking with part serial numbers and maintenance tags; otherwise, operators may inadvertently accept incorrect part-number entries.

[P6] The exception reference to paragraph (l) is buried and non-intuitive; the AD should restate the exception conditions in each affected paragraph for clarity and enforceability.

[P7] The repetitive lubrication intervals refer only to tables in the service bulletin; the AD should include a maximum allowable interval in the regulation to avoid ambiguity if the service bulletin is revised.

[P7] Lubrication must be performed using specified lubricants; the AD does not specify lubricant type or material specifications — require reference to the service bulletin or include part numbers to avoid incompatible products.

[P8] The phrase "not to exceed those specified" is vague without the actual numeric intervals; include explicit interval values (e.g., hours/cycles/months) in the AD.

[P9] Termination of lubrication after paragraph (j) modification assumes modification is permanent and effective; require documented proof (work package sign-off) and define acceptable paperwork to demonstrate termination eligibility.

[P10] The requirement for general visual inspections and "applicable lubrication" should define what constitutes a discrepancy and provide sample defect criteria to ensure uniform enforcement across operators.

[P10] The AD should allow incorporation of inspections into existing maintenance programs (e.g., MSG-3 or CAMP) and specify whether compliance inspections can be credited to scheduled maintenance tasks.

[P11] Repeat inspection intervals tied to a service bulletin revision are problematic because future revisions could change intervals; the AD should lock the intervals to the revision named or provide an FAA-approved alternative.

[P12] Requiring all corrective actions "before further flight" could ground aircraft for extended periods if parts or engineering approvals are needed; provide a risk-based allowance for ferry flights or limited operations with additional inspections and restrictions.

[P12] The AD must specify who is authorized to perform and sign off the required investigative and corrective actions (operator maintenance, Boeing ODA, repair station), and whether post-repair inspections require FAA concurrence.

[P13] Termination of repetitive inspections upon completion of paragraph (j) should require follow-up verification over a defined service life; otherwise, latent failures in the modification could go undetected.

[P14] The modification Work Package 3 lacks a cost estimate and parts availability analysis; operators need this information to budget and schedule fleet compliance — include an economic impact appendix.

[P14] Work Package 3 instructions should clarify whether structural modifications require inspection panels, jacking, or other heavy maintenance actions that affect scheduling and costs.

[P15] Stating that investigative/corrective actions must be done "at the time specified" is ambiguous; the AD should permit staged completion if safety is not compromised and define allowable sequencing.

[P16] The AD should require a post-modification inspection after a defined number of flight cycles to confirm that completion of Work Package 3 legitimately terminates repetitive actions.

[P17] Replacement of the forward trunnion pin housing assembly and associated seal/retainer/support ring may require proprietary parts; the AD should permit use of FAA-approved equivalent parts from independent suppliers if Boeing parts are unavailable.

[P17] The lubrication requirement after replacement references Work Package 4 but does not state whether initial lubrication counts toward the repetitive lubrication interval; clarify if replacement-triggered lubrication restarts interval counting.

[P18] Changing "after the Revision 2 date" compliance to be measured from the AD effective date may shorten or lengthen originally intended compliance windows; explain the rationale and quantify differences compared to the service bulletin schedule.

[P18] The exception in (l) could create conflicts with operators who already adopted Revision 2 compliance timing; require grandfathering or explicit transition instructions for earlier adopters.

[P19] The parts-installation prohibition is overly broad; it bars installing any MLG or trunnion assembly unless that assembly has already had modification/replacement done — clarify whether newly manufactured assemblies from Boeing shipped with the modification are exempt.

[P19] The prohibition does not address installation of new replacement assemblies under warranty or on ground maintenance in non-U.S. jurisdictions; provide an import/installation path with documentation requirements.

[P20] Credit for prior actions should be expanded to include equivalent procedures performed under approved AMOCs or other manufacturers' service instructions where the work provides an equivalent level of safety.

[P21] The list of accepted service bulletin revisions for credit needs to be exhaustive and include equivalent Boeing service bulletins that accomplish the same work but use different numbering — otherwise operators may be denied credit for valid prior work.

[P22] Credit for prior compliance should require submission of records to the FAA or principal inspector to avoid future enforcement disputes; the AD should specify what documentation is sufficient.

[P23] Granting AMOC authority to the Seattle ACO Branch Manager is appropriate, but the AD should provide estimated processing times and criteria to give operators predictability.

[P24] The requirement to send AMOC requests to a principal inspector or local FSDO may be inefficient for international operators; allow direct submission to the Seattle ACO with a courtesy copy to the principal inspector.

[P25] Directing AMOC communications to the person in paragraph (p)(1) is fragile if personnel change; include a generic office address and email as a stable routing alternative.

[P26] The provided email for AMOCs is helpful, but the AD must also accept encrypted submissions and large attachments via an FAA file-transfer mechanism; clarify acceptable electronic formats and security protocols.

[P27] Requiring notification to a principal inspector before using an approved AMOC may delay implementation in urgent safety cases; allow immediate use with prompt notification within a short window (e.g., 24–48 hours) for time-sensitive fixes.

[P28] Allowing Boeing ODA to approve AMOCs only if authorized by the Manager creates a single-point bottleneck; the AD should permit use of other authorized ODAs or approved engineering organizations where they can demonstrate equivalent competence.

[P29] Requiring Boeing ODA authorization from the Seattle ACO Branch for AMOC approval may exceed Boeing's authority and conflict with existing ODA delegations; clarify the scope and any transitional provisions.

[P30] The requirement that an AMOC meet the airplane's certification basis and explicitly reference this AD is appropriate, but the AD should specify whether novel compliance methods (e.g., new materials or analyses) require supplemental type certificates or conforming approvals.

[P31] Accepting prior AMOCs approved for AD 2016–18–01 is helpful, but the AD should provide a mapping table of which older approvals correspond to each new requirement to ease operator compliance verification.

The requirement for general visual inspections and "applicable lubrication" should define what constitutes a discrepancy and provide sample defect criteria to ensure uniform enforcement across operators.
The AD should allow incorporation of inspections into existing maintenance programs (e.g., MSG-3 or CAMP) and specify whether compliance inspections can be credited to scheduled maintenance tasks.

[P1] The phrase "reasonable grounds to suspect" in §1002.20(a) is vague and will create legal uncertainty for manufacturers about when reporting is required; request adoption of a clearer objective standard (e.g., "credible evidence of emission above regulatory limits" or "confirmed measurement showing radiation emission exceeding X").

[P1] Requiring manufacturers to "report all accidental radiation occurrences known or reported" without a de minimis threshold will overwhelm the agency and manufacturers with trivial reports (e.g., minor non-emissive incidents); propose a quantitative threshold for reportability (e.g., exposures above 5 mSv or device emissions exceeding specified performance limits).

[P2] Mandating electronic submission via CDRH eSubmitter or mail in §1002.20(b) will disadvantage small manufacturers and foreign firms unfamiliar with eSubmitter; request acceptance of alternate secure electronic formats (e.g., email or portal uploads) and translation/assistance for non‑U.S. firms.

[P2] The instruction to mark mailed reports "Report on 1002.20" is inadequate for secure handling and could delay processing; ask the Agency to provide a dedicated mailing address and reference code and to clarify handling/privacy procedures for mailed submissions.

[P3] §1002.20(b)(1) requires inclusion of "the nature of the accidental radiation occurrence" but does not define categories; industry requests a non‑exhaustive list of reportable nature types (e.g., unintended emission, containment breach, component failure) to standardize reporting.

[P4] Requiring the "location" of occurrence in §1002.20(b)(2) may raise confidentiality and security concerns, especially for critical infrastructure or sensitive military customers; propose allowing redaction or submission of facility identifiers via secure channels and permitting provision of general location descriptors when security is implicated.

[P5] §1002.20(b)(3) demands manufacturer, type, and model number "where known"; commenters request guidance on acceptable identifiers when aftermarket or third‑party components are involved (e.g., serial numbers, lot codes) and on obligations when identity is unknown.

[P6] §1002.20(b)(4) asks for "circumstances and causes" but offers no timeline or expectation for ongoing investigations; manufacturers request the ability to submit preliminary reports with available facts and supplement later when root‑cause analysis is complete.

[P7] The requirement in §1002.20(b)(5) to report "names of persons" if requested by the Director raises privacy and HIPAA concerns; health advocacy groups and manufacturers ask that the rule specify that personal identifiers will be requested only with a legal basis and that de‑identified data suffice for routine reports.

[P7] Request clarification whether contractors, service personnel, or bystanders are included in "persons involved, adversely affected, or exposed" in §1002.20(b)(5), and whether estimates are acceptable when exact counts are unavailable.

[P8] §1002.20(b)(6) obliges reporting "actions...taken by the manufacturer to control, correct, or eliminate the causes"; manufacturers request protection for proprietary corrective‑action plans (e.g., trade secret treatment) and a process for submitting redacted or validated summaries.

[P9] The catch‑all §1002.20(b)(7) "any other pertinent information" is overly broad and could be interpreted to require submission of confidential commercial information; suggest limiting to information reasonably related to public health/safety and allowing trade‑secret designations.

[P10] §1002.20(c)(1) cross‑references part 803 but does not explain prioritization when reporting obligations overlap; request explicit coordination rules to avoid duplicate submissions and clarify timelines when both regimes apply.

[P11] For §1002.20(c)(2), the two paths (subject to part 803 vs not) are confusing; manufacturers ask for flowchart-language and examples determining when part 803 applies, especially for products not traditionally regulated as medical devices.

[P12] The "immediately report" requirement in §1002.20(c)(2)(i) for incidents involving death or serious injury is ambiguous regarding exact timing (hours vs business days); industry and legal commenters request a defined timeframe (e.g., within 24 hours of knowledge) and provision for after‑hours reporting for the Director.

[P13] The quarterly summary option in §1002.20(c)(2)(ii) for non‑serious incidents requires "tracking and trending analysis" but lacks format and data-field specifications; both manufacturers and public‑health groups request standardized templates and minimum analytic requirements to ensure comparability.

[P13] Allowing aggregation of non‑serious incidents into quarterly reports per §1002.20(c)(2)(ii) could delay detection of systemic hazards; consumer advocates urge mandatory threshold triggers requiring immediate individual reporting if trend analysis shows increasing frequency or severity.

[P14] The exception in §1002.20 regarding incidents already reported under §1003.10 lacks a clear mechanism to avoid under‑reporting or double‑reporting; commenters recommend a mandatory cross‑reference field in either report to indicate whether an incident has been reported elsewhere.

[P15] §1010.4(b) requiring an original mailed copy for variance applications is burdensome and outdated; stakeholders request full electronic acceptance (e.g., e‑signature and e‑filing) and elimination of mailed originals to modernize submissions.

[P16] While §1010.4(b) permits electronic submission via Regulations.gov, the rule references a specific docket number (FDA–2013–S–0610) which may be outdated; request confirmation of current docket number(s) and addition of alternative electronic channels for large technical attachments.

[P17] §1020.30(d)(1) obliges assemblers who install certified components to file a report of assembly, potentially expanding regulatory burden to small contract assemblers; trade associations ask for exemptions for low‑volume assemblers or subcontractors and clear definitions of "assembler."

[P18] The affirmation requirement in §1020.30(d)(1) that manufacturer's instructions were followed or that components meet §§1020.30–1020.33 could be interpreted to impose strict liability on assemblers; assemblers request a safe‑harbor if they rely in good faith on supplier documentation and provide written notice to purchasers.

[P19] Requiring use of a form "prescribed by the Director" in §1020.30(d)(1) without providing the form in the rule or guidance creates compliance uncertainty; recommend publishing the prescribed form and allowing an interim period for adoption.

[P20] §1020.30(d)(1) demands assembler reports to be submitted to purchasers and State radiation agencies within 15 days; commenters request alignment with standard commercial timelines (e.g., 30 days) and clarification on submission method (electronic vs mail) and handling confidential business information.

[P21] The exception in §1040.10(a)(1) exempting uncertified laser components when incorporated into a certified electronic product lacks clarity about responsibility allocation between component sellers and final product manufacturers; component suppliers ask for clear contractual allocation language and limits on their recordkeeping burdens.

[P22] §1040.10(a)(1)(i)'s condition that the component be "sold to a manufacturer...for use as a component" could be exploited by third‑party sellers to evade compliance by labeling consumer‑facing replacement parts as "components"; consumer safety groups request anti‑circumvention provisions.

[P23] The requirement in §1040.10(a)(1)(ii)(A) that the laser be accompanied by a general warning and servicing instructions is insufficiently specific; request sample wording for the warning and minimum content for servicing instructions to ensure consistent safety communication.

[P24] §1040.10(a)(1)(ii)(B) requires labeling that the laser "does not comply with full product requirements," but that label may confuse downstream assemblers and end users; suggest standardized label language and placement specifications to avoid misinterpretation.

[P25] The prohibition in §1040.10(a)(1)(ii)(C) that the laser not be a "removable laser system" depends on the definition in (c)(2); commenters ask for more explicit examples of removable vs non‑removable systems to reduce disputes.

[P26] §1040.10(a)(1)(iii)(A) obliges manufacturers to register and list by type with specific technical fields (product name, model, laser medium/wavelength, name/address), but does not address proprietary technical information; request that commercially sensitive fields be eligible for confidentiality designation and secure handling.

[P27] The allowance in §1040.10(a)(1)(iii)(A) for eSubmitter submissions is positive, but small manufacturers report that eSubmitter often lacks capacity for bulk uploads; request batch registration features and API support.

[P28] §1040.10(a)(1)(iii)(B) requires maintenance and access to sales/shipping/distribution records identifying purchasers; this imposes heavy data retention and privacy obligations on sellers and downstream manufacturers; propose narrowing required fields or extending retention periods and clarifying circumstances under §1002.31 when records must be disclosed.

[P28] Civil liberties and privacy advocates express concern that §1040.10(a)(1)(iii)(B)'s requirement to identify purchasers by name and address could be misused or compromise customer privacy; request limits on disclosure and requirements for lawful requests and data minimization.

[P29] The applicability exceptions in §1040.10(a)(2) for manufacturers incorporating certified laser products into other products are complex; manufacturers request illustrative scenarios and a decision tool to determine whether their product is exempted.

[P30] §1040.10(a)(2)(ii) requires the incorporated laser product to be certified under §1010.2; commenters ask for guidance on certification timelines and whether pre‑existing inventories require retroactive certification.

[P31] The prohibition on "modified" incorporated laser products in §1040.10(a)(2)(iii) is vague because "modified" is defined elsewhere; request a clear list of modifications (mechanical, electrical, firmware) that would void the incorporation exception.

[P32] §1040.10(a)(2)(iv) requiring installation per original manufacturer's instructions could conflict with real‑world manufacturing integration needs; integrators ask for allowance to adapt installation methods when equivalent safety is demonstrated and documented.

[P33] §1040.10(a)(2)(v) obliges incorporating product manufacturers to provide user information required under paragraph (h); commenters request that the rule specify which party is responsible for future user warnings and post‑sale support to avoid gaps.

[P34] §1040.10(a)(2)(vi) mandates that labeling for the incorporated laser product comply with §§1010.3 and 1040.10(g) when removed; service organizations point out practical difficulty labeling internal components and request an alternative method (e.g., service decals or service manuals).

[P35] The service‑configuration labeling condition in §1040.10(a)(2)(vii) could be infeasible for complex assemblies serviced in the field; request flexibility allowing service technicians to access labeling via digital records or QR codes rather than physical labels.

[P36] §1040.10(a)(2)(viii) places distributor obligations (§§1002.40 and 1002.41) on manufacturers of incorporating products; stakeholders urge the Agency to clarify exactly which distributor obligations apply and to harmonize responsibilities to avoid duplicative compliance across supply chains.

[P1] The incorporation-by-reference approach in § 820.15 lacks clarity about which specific edition and year of ISO 13485 is incorporated; the rule should specify the exact edition to avoid ambiguity and litigation risk.

[P1] Construe-the-term provisions in § 820.15 effectively rewrite ISO 13485 language; the agency must provide a crosswalk showing every ISO clause affected and the regulatory text mapping to each ISO term to avoid inconsistent interpretations.

[P2] § 820.15(a) redefines "Organization" to mean "manufacturers" but fails to explain how contract manufacturers, suppliers, distributors, or single legal entities with multiple roles are treated; this creates compliance uncertainty for CMOs and OEMs.

[P2] The change in § 820.15(a) may unintentionally narrow responsibilities for organizations that perform post-market activities but are not 'manufacturers' as defined; FDA should clarify whether service organizations and sterilization/service providers are covered.

[P3] § 820.15(b) equating "safety and performance" with "safety and effectiveness" will create conflicts with ISO-derived quality processes focused on 'performance' metrics (e.g., life-cycle performance); request clarification on whether performance measures distinct from clinical effectiveness are still required.

[P3] The substitution in § 820.15(b) could inject a statutory standard ("effectiveness") into technical/process requirements intended by ISO; legal commenters should evaluate whether this alters statutory scope and requires public notice-and-comment beyond incorporation.

[P4] § 820.15(b) sentence preserving obligations to implement controls to assure "safety and effectiveness" is vague—what constitutes "reasonable" controls? The agency must define the expected level of control (risk-based, proportionate, etc.) or provide examples.

[P4] Requiring that “safety and performance” does not relieve manufacturers from implementing controls creates potential duplication with existing FDA device-specific requirements (e.g., performance testing); FDA should harmonize to avoid redundant obligations.

[P5] § 820.15(c) mapping "Validation of processes" to "process validation" could be read to import different definitions; the rule should explicitly include the definition of "process validation" used under this part to prevent inconsistent application.

[P6] § 820.35’s requirement to “obtain signatures and dates of approval on records and include specified information” duplicates ISO Clause 4.2.5 but adds unspecified additional elements—request that FDA publish a complete list of required signature types, electronic signature acceptance, and retention requirements.

[P6] The rule does not address electronic records and electronic signatures (e.g., 21 CFR Part 11) in § 820.35; manufacturers need guidance whether scanned signatures, electronic approvals, or audit trails satisfy the signature/date requirement.

[P7] § 820.35(a) imposes minimum complaint record content but omits thresholds for when a complaint must be recorded (e.g., consumer inquiries vs. complaints); FDA should align with existing complaint reporting thresholds (21 CFR Part 803) and clarify what constitutes a "complaint" for these records.

[P7] The requirement to record the complainant's name, address, and phone (§ 820.35(a)(4)) raises privacy concerns; FDA should permit redaction or alternative contact methods for anonymous reports and provide guidance on handling personal data consistent with privacy laws.

[P8] § 820.35(a)(1) mandating the device name may be problematic where products are provided under multiple trade names or in complex device families; agency should allow use of product codes or catalog numbers in addition to name.

[P9] § 820.35(a)(2) requiring the date the complaint was received needs clarification whether the “received” date is the date the manufacturer learned of the issue (e.g., via distributor) or the date the end-user complained; define which triggers the clock for complaint handling timelines.

[P10] § 820.35(a)(3) mandates recording UDI/UPC for applicable complaints, but many legacy devices lack UDIs; FDA should provide a phase-in period or alternative identifiers for devices placed on the market before UDI compliance.

[P11] § 820.35(a)(4) requiring complainant contact details could discourage reporting by clinicians or patients who fear retribution; suggest allowing pseudonymous reporting and detailing when contact information is necessary for follow-up.

[P12] § 820.35(a)(5) "nature and details of the complaint" is subjective—FDA should provide a standard complaint severity classification or a template to ensure consistent reporting across manufacturers.

[P13] § 820.35(a)(6) requiring recording of "any corrective action taken" should be limited to actions actually implemented, not preliminary assessments; specify timeframe for when corrective actions must be documented and whether CAPA plans suffice.

[P14] § 820.35(a)(7) requiring record of "any reply provided to the complainant" may conflict with confidentiality or legal privilege in certain investigations; FDA should allow redaction or indicate that legal-protected communications need not be recorded in full.

[P15] § 820.35(b) imposes servicerecord requirements without clarifying applicability to third-party service providers; contract service organizations should be explicitly covered or exempted and allocation of recordkeeping responsibilities between manufacturer and servicer clarified.

[P16] § 820.35(b)(1) requiring the device name for serviced devices is impractical when servicing multiple models in a device family; allow model number or serial number to meet the requirement.

[P17] § 820.35(b)(2) requiring UDI/UPC for servicing records again fails to account for legacy devices or devices without UDIs; propose grandfathering or alternative identifier options.

[P18] § 820.35(b)(3) requiring service date is reasonable but should allow capture of start and end dates for multi-day services and clarify time zone and format expectations.

[P19] § 820.35(b)(4) obligating identification of individual(s) who performed service raises privacy and liability concerns for independent contractors; permit identification by role or anonymized employee ID where legal restrictions apply.

[P20] § 820.35(b)(5) requiring the "service performed" needs to be defined—provide a taxonomy or code list to standardize entries and facilitate data aggregation for surveillance.

[P21] § 820.35(b)(6) requiring test and inspection data for servicing may impose heavy burdens for low-risk maintenance; FDA should make this proportional to risk or exempt routine, non-invasive servicing activities.

[P22] § 820.35(c) mandating UDI for each device or batch will impose significant recordkeeping burdens on small manufacturers and importers—request phased implementation and clarification on batch-level vs. unit-level UDIs for disposable devices.

[P22] The UDI recording requirement in § 820.35(c) may conflict with international suppliers using different identifier schemes; FDA should accept equivalent foreign identifiers and provide guidance for crosswalks.

[P23] § 820.35(d) permitting manufacturers to mark records “confidential” for FDA disclosure determinations needs stronger limits; without guidance, manufacturers may over-designate material and impede FOIA transparency—define criteria for confidentiality markings and require justifications.

[P23] The rule should state whether confidentiality markings asserted under § 820.35(d) bind FDA’s disclosure decisions or merely assist them; manufacturers need predictability about what will remain non-public.

[P24] § 820.45’s broader requirement to establish procedures for labeling and packaging operations duplicates existing ISO requirements but adds U.S.-specific elements; request harmonized guidance to avoid dual-compliance burdens.

[P25] § 820.45(a) requiring labeling/packaging be examined for accuracy "prior to release or storage" is ambiguous for continuous production lines and repackaging; clarify whether in-line sampling is acceptable and the acceptable sampling plans.

[P26] § 820.45(a)(1) mandating correct UDI/UPC on labeling/packaging again does not account for legacy or custom-labeled products; request transitional relief and guidance on UDI placement and format for small-package or multi-pack configurations.

[P27] § 820.45(a)(2) requiring expiration dates on labeling/packaging may not be applicable to non-expiring devices (e.g., most durable devices); allow the element to be recorded as "N/A" and specify when expiration is required.

[P28] § 820.45(a)(3) mandating storage instructions be present and accurate may impose burdens on devices sold through third-party distributors who repackage or relabel; clarify manufacturer responsibility vs. distributor obligations for storage instructions.

[P29] § 820.45(a)(4) requiring handling instructions be present could create liability for manufacturers for downstream handling by health facilities; recommend limiting obligation to provide accurate handling instructions to the extent known and foreseeable.

[P30] § 820.45(a)(5) requiring additional processing instructions to be present and accurate may be overbroad—define "additional processing" (e.g., sterilization at healthcare facility) and allocate responsibilities when downstream parties perform those processes.

[P31] § 820.45(b) documentation requirement referencing Clause 4.2.5 of ISO 13485 must clarify whether electronic release approvals satisfy documentation standards and whether signature/approval retention periods differ from other records.

[P32] § 820.45(c) requiring operations to be established/maintained to prevent errors and including immediate-before-use inspections could disrupt high-volume operations; request flexibility for risk-based sampling and acceptance criteria rather than mandatory 100% inspection immediately before use.

[P33] § 820.45(c) forcing inspection "immediately before use" may be impossible for devices used in manufacturing that are packaged months earlier; propose alternative language allowing inspection at the point of assembly or prior to sterile processing instead.

[P34] § 820.45(c) documentation of labeling inspections per ISO Clause 4.2.5 needs a clear record retention period and guidance on minimum documentation fields to avoid burdensome and inconsistent recordkeeping.

[P7] Patient advocacy groups will object that requiring complainant contact info (§ 820.35(a)(4)) will deter patient reports and recommend permitting anonymous reporting and protecting complainant privacy in records provided to FDA or third parties.

[P22] Small device manufacturers will request a small-entity compliance guide for UDI recording (§ 820.35(c)) and a multi-year phased implementation with de minimis recordkeeping thresholds for low-risk device classes.

[P15] Third-party service organizations and independent service engineers request explicit allocation of recordkeeping responsibility between servicer and manufacturer for § 820.35(b) records to avoid duplicative obligations and liability double-counting.

[P23] Transparency advocates will request that FDA publish its approach to resolving confidentiality markings (§ 820.35(d)) and require manufacturers to justify each confidentiality claim, with a penalty for frivolous over-designation.

[P4] Risk-management professionals will request that the phrase in § 820.15(b) regarding not relieving obligations be tied explicitly to established risk management standards (e.g., ISO 14971) to provide a clear compliance framework.

[P1] The comment deadline of May 23, 2023 is unreasonable and too short for operators and manufacturers to prepare meaningful technical comments, given the complexity of the AFM revisions and coordination needed.

[P1] Request to extend the comment period beyond May 23, 2023 to allow stakeholders (airlines, repair stations, avionics manufacturers, pilot unions) at least 60–90 days to analyze operational impacts and safety data.

[P2] The requirement to "comply within the specified compliance times" lacks clarity about what constitutes acceptable evidence of prior compliance ("unless already done"); the AD should define acceptable records and documentation to demonstrate prior completion.

[P2] The compliance clause should include a provision allowing relief or phased compliance for operators with scheduling conflicts or limited maintenance windows, otherwise it will cause operational disruptions.

[P3] The 2-day compliance timeframe after Jan 19, 2022 to revise the AFM Limitations Section is unworkable for many operators because it predates the AD effective date and does not account for delivery/receipt of the AD or company AFM revision processes.

[P3] Legal concern: Requiring action "within 2 days after Jan 19, 2022" appears retroactive; the FAA should clarify legal authority to mandate actions effective before stakeholders received notice.

[P4] Allowing compliance by simply inserting a copy of figure 4 into the AFM without requiring technical review or formatting guidance risks inconsistent presentations and possible omission of essential cross-references.

[P4] Request that the FAA provide an approved, ready-to-insert AFM page or a template of figure 4 in a standard format to ensure uniform implementation across operators.

[P5] The 2-day deadline for revising the Operating Procedures Section (figure 5) similarly is infeasible and creates operational risk by forcing rushed, unvetted procedural changes without training.

[P6] Inserting figure 5 into the AFM should require operators to provide pilot briefing and confirmation of pilot receipt; permit insertion alone is insufficient to ensure the procedures are understood and implemented.

[P7] The blanket division between "radio altimeter tolerant" and "non-radio altimeter tolerant" airplanes lacks a clear definition and verification method; the AD should specify how to determine and document "tolerance."

[P7] Request guidance on acceptable evidence (manufacturer statements, equipment lists, test reports) to demonstrate that an airplane is "radio altimeter tolerant" for purposes of compliance with paragraphs (i) and (j).

[P8] The June 30, 2023 deadline to revise the AFM Limitations for non-radio altimeter tolerant airplanes does not account for operators with restricted access to maintenance facilities; suggest a phased compliance schedule or extensions upon showing good cause.

[P9] Permitting compliance by inserting figure 6 is acceptable only if the FAA also issues a machine-readable, signed PDF of figure 6 so organizations can incorporate it accurately into their AFM systems.

[P10] The condition that incorporation of the (i)(1) AFM revision terminates the (h)(1) revision could create confusion during transition; the AD should state explicitly whether both revisions may be present temporarily and provide the required sequence of changes.

[P11] Requiring removal of the (h)(1) AFM revision "before further flight" after incorporation of figure 6 may be logistically impossible if the aircraft is in remote location; request allowance for removal at the next maintenance visit within a specified short period.

[P11] Clarify what "remove the AFM revision required by (h)(1)" entails — does it mean deleting the text, replacing with new pages, or annotating the AFM? Provide acceptable methods and documentation for removal.

[P12] The separate obligations for radio altimeter tolerant airplanes should include procedures for switching between operational statuses if an aircraft is modified or equipment is replaced after the compliance deadline.

[P13] The June 30, 2023 deadline for radio altimeter tolerant airplanes to revise Limitations to include figure 7 requires coordination with international operators whose AFMs must be simultaneously updated to meet other authorities' requirements; request harmonization with EASA timelines.

[P14] Inserting figure 7 into the AFM should be accompanied by driver and maintenance instructions if figure 7 imposes operational or maintenance restrictions; mere insertion may not inform maintainers how to comply.

[P15] The termination effect of incorporating (j)(1) on (h)(1) revision again creates potential gaps if operators misunderstand priority; request a clear matrix showing which revisions govern at each stage and examples.

[P16] The requirement to remove (h)(1) before further flight after incorporating figure 7 needs an exception for ferry flights required to reach a maintenance facility for AFM revision — request an explicit ferry flight provision.

[P17] The Manager's authority to approve AMOCs is standard, but commenters request published timelines for AMOC review and criteria for approval to avoid undue delays.

[P17] Request that the FAA publish a list of pre-approved AMOCs or frequently granted reliefs for common configurations to reduce backlogs.

[P18] Sending AMOC requests to the principal inspector may be impractical for operators that operate in multiple FSDOs; request permission to coordinate centrally with the manager to streamline AMOC processing.

[P19] The requirement to address direct submissions to the person in paragraph (m) should include contact details and an alternative if that person changes; request a durable contact mechanism.

[P20] Providing an email (AMOC@faa.gov) is helpful, but commenters ask for confirmation of receipt, expected processing time, and secure upload capability for sensitive engineering data.

[P21] Requiring notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC is reasonable, but the AD should allow notification within a specified short window (e.g., 72 hours) rather than prior to first use when immediate operational need is present.

[P21] Clarify whether the notification must be written and which information is required (AMOC approval number, effective date, affected aircraft) to ensure consistent compliance.

[P22] Extending AMOCs approved for AD 2021–23–12 to cover paragraph (h) until June 30, 2023 may inadvertently allow unsafe configurations beyond the original scope; request the FAA to list explicitly which AMOCs are extended and any limitations on their applicability.

[P22] Legal comment: Retroactive approval of previous AMOCs for new requirements may exceed the Manager's delegated authority without individualized technical review; request the FAA provide the technical basis for automatic acceptance.

[General] The AD contains multiple interrelated AFM revision requirements with overlapping deadlines and termination clauses; request the FAA provide a consolidated implementation guidance document, including sample AFM pages and a step-by-step compliance flowchart.

[General] Request an economic impact analysis showing cost estimates for AFM revisions, training, distribution, and administrative overhead for small operators and fractional ownership operations.

[General] Aviation labor groups request that FAA require operators to provide training and competency verification for flight crews when AFM operating procedures are revised under (h)(2), (i), or (j).

[General] Manufacturers request that the AD include precise revision control language (e.g., record-keeping requirements, revision numbers, and distribution lists) so inspectors can readily verify compliance.

[P1] The August 13, 2020 receipt deadline is unclear as to time zone; request EPA clarify the exact time (including time zone) by which comments must be received.

[P1] The single hard deadline of August 13, 2020 does not account for mail/backlog delays; request EPA accept comments postmarked by that date if submitted by mail or courier.

[P2] Requiring identification by Docket ID No. EPA–R03–OAR–2020–0157 creates risk of misfiling; request guidance on how to correct an incorrectly identified submission.

[P2] The specified email address (spielberger.susan@epa.gov) may expose individuals to privacy concerns; request confirmation of secure handling and an alternative encrypted submission method for sensitive but non‑CBI comments.

[P3] The requirement to follow Regulations.gov online submission instructions unfairly burdens commenters with disabilities unless the site meets accessibility standards; request EPA certify site accessibility and provide alternative submission means for persons with disabilities.

[P3] Regulations.gov often imposes file type/size limits; request EPA publish explicit permitted file formats and maximum sizes to avoid rejected submissions.

[P4] The prohibition on editing or removing comments after submission on Regulations.gov denies commenters the ability to remedy inadvertent disclosures or errors; request EPA allow comment withdrawal or editing within a reasonable timeframe (e.g., 48 hours).

[P4] Because Regulations.gov makes comments public and uneditable, the rule should explicitly allow commenters to request redaction of personal contact information after submission; request an established redaction process.

[P5] EPA's permission to publish comments regardless of submission method lacks clear criteria about redaction of personal data; request EPA adopt and publish a privacy redaction policy prior to posting comments.

[P6] The prohibition on submitting CBI electronically is too broad and may prevent legitimate technical data submission; request EPA provide secure electronic portals or encrypted email options for submitting CBI with instructions for marking CBI.

[P6] The rule truncates the prohibition text; request EPA publish the full text and examples of "legally restricted information" to avoid uncertainty among submitters.

[P7] Requiring multimedia submissions to include a written comment may disadvantage non‑English speakers or those with literacy barriers; request EPA accept multimedia as primary submissions when accompanied by a short description and provide translation support.

[P7] The obligation that multimedia must be accompanied by written comment should specify acceptable minimum content (e.g., summary of multimedia) to ensure consistent processing.

[P8] Declaring the written submission as the "official comment" could cause EPA to ignore substantive material contained only in the accompanying multimedia; request EPA commit to considering multimedia contents when accompanied by written notice.

[P9] The prohibition on linking to materials stored off the primary submission will preclude large datasets that exceed file size limits; request EPA explicitly permit hosted data repositories (with persistent links) and describe how EPA will access and consider them.

[P9] The phrase "generally will not consider" is vague; request EPA clarify circumstances under which external links will be considered and how to cite or submit large supplemental materials.

[P10] Contacting the listed person for alternative submission methods is necessary but may not be timely; request EPA publish multiple alternative contacts and an automated submission exception procedure for those with technical barriers.

[P11] The obligation to consider all timely comments lacks a statement about how late comments that raise novel issues will be handled; request EPA commit to documenting and responding to all substantive comments in the final action docket.

[P11] The provision does not explain how EPA will handle duplicate comments or mass‑filings; request EPA publish its approach to treating form letters and unique submissions in the public record.

[P12] Accepting comments submitted between the original close and re-opening could create confusion about which comments will be considered; request EPA define the exact interim dates and whether such comments will be treated as timely for both the original and reopened periods.
