raw_output:
[P1] The prohibition in § 357.1 is unconstitutionally vague because it refers to plants “taken… in violation of applicable Federal, Tribal, State, or foreign plant-protecting laws” without defining which foreign or Tribal laws are “applicable” to an importer, creating uncertainty for compliance and enforcement.

[P1] Industry commenters will state § 357.1 imposes strict liability on downstream commercial actors (buyers, receivers, transporters) for prior acts by foreign suppliers, and request a due-diligence defense or safe harbor to avoid penalizing actors who reasonably relied on supplier documentation.

[P1] Importers and carriers will argue the broad ban in § 357.1 could disrupt supply chains because a single minor paperwork error by a foreign supplier could render otherwise legal shipments unlawful; they will request a notice-and-cure procedure before enforcement.

[P1] Legal experts will contend the cross-reference to the Lacey Act in § 357.1 should clarify mens rea requirements (knowing, negligent, or strict liability) for each prohibited act to conform with constitutional due process and existing Lacey Act enforcement practice.

[P2] Trade associations will comment that the prohibition on submitting any false record (§ 357.1/§ 357.2 text) is overly broad as drafted and may criminalize innocuous clerical mistakes; they will request a materiality threshold (e.g., intentional or material misstatements only).

[P2] NGOs will support § 357.1’s ban on false records but urge the agency to specify that knowingly false declarations will carry enhanced penalties and that the rule should require public reporting of enforcement metrics.

[P3] Importers will request that § 357.3(a) declarations be allowed electronically via existing ACE/CBP channels and integrated with other import documentation to avoid duplicate filings and significant cost burdens.

[P3] Small businesses and artisan importers will comment that the declaration requirement in § 357.3(a) is burdensome and request an exemption or simplified streamlined form for low-risk small shipments.

[P3] Legal commenters will request clarification of who is the “person importing any plant” for purposes of § 357.3(a) — the owner of the goods, the customs broker, the consignee, or the carrier — and ask for liability allocation language.

[P4] Botanical industry groups will request an exception in § 357.3(a)(1) for processed botanical products where precise species identification is scientifically impracticable, allowing use of common names plus best-effort scientific IDs and documentation of due diligence.

[P4] Scientists will request that § 357.3(a)(1) allow for higher-level taxonomic designations (genus only, family) when species-level identification is not possible, along with prescribed testing or alternative procedures.

[P5] Importers will object that requiring a “description of the value” and “quantity including unit of measure” (§ 357.3(a)(2)) duplicates customs valuation data and could create inconsistencies; they request alignment with CBP declared value and harmonized units.

[P5] E-commerce platforms will highlight the compliance complexity for bundles or multi-component products where per-unit plant content value/weight is unclear and request guidance and simplified aggregation rules for § 357.3(a)(2).

[P6] Trade organizations will note that identifying the “country from which the plant was taken” (§ 357.3(a)(3)) is often infeasible for mixed-origin commodities and ask for flexibility to report “country of origin of the product” or “known sourcing countries” instead.

[P6] Environmental NGOs will urge that § 357.3(a)(3) require exporters to include provenance documentation (harvest permits, chain-of-custody) for high-risk species and origins, not just the country name.

[P7] Manufacturers of composite goods will request clearer guidance under § 357.3(b) about what constitutes a “plant product” vs. non-plant inputs and for examples of required supporting documentation for plant products.

[P7] Importers will ask § 357.3(b) to allow suppliers’ attestations or standardized supplier declarations to be submitted in lieu of detailed species-by-species documentation to reduce compliance burden.

[P8] Apparel and accessory industry groups will argue that § 357.3(b)(1)’s requirement to “list every species that may have been used” when composition varies is impractical for products (e.g., leather, wood-veneer mixes) composed of hundreds of possible species; they will ask for a risk-based alternative (list of probable species plus percent thresholds).

[P8] Legal commentators will say the “every species” requirement in § 357.3(b)(1) is impossible for recycled or blended materials and request allowance for “known or reasonably likely species” with supplier attestations and random testing.

[P9] Importers of commodities (e.g., botanicals, spices) will state § 357.3(b)(2)’s mandate to “list each possible source country” where species are commonly sourced from multiple countries will produce very long, low-value declarations and request limiting to “known” or “documented” source countries or a duty to provide likely sourcing regions only.

[P9] NGOs will support § 357.3(b)(2) as necessary to prevent laundering of illegally harvested plant material through ambiguous country designations, and will request verification requirements when multiple countries are listed.

[P10] Paper and packaging manufacturers will request clarification and an alternative method for § 357.3(b)(3)’s “average percent recycled content” reporting, arguing that averaging across paper grades and recycled streams is technically complex and proposing a standard calculation method.

[P10] Recycling industry commenters will point out § 357.3(b)(3) should permit default recycled-content values for common recycled paper grades or acceptance of mill certificates to avoid burdensome testing.

[P11] Retailers and importers will welcome § 357.4’s exceptions in principle but request simplified criteria and an automated worksheet to determine eligibility, arguing the current language is too complex for routine use.

[P11] Conservation groups will warn that § 357.4 exceptions risk being exploited as loopholes and will call for strict audits and denial of exceptions where chain-of-custody documentation is missing.

[P12] Consumer goods companies will request an explicit safe harbor in § 357.4(a) confirming that common corrugated and paper packaging (e.g., boxes, cushioning) is exempt even when marked or marketed as packaging material to avoid classification disputes.

[P12] Customs attorneys will note ambiguity in § 357.4(a) about “unless the packaging material itself is the item being imported” and ask for examples and objective tests to determine when packaging is “the item.”

[P13] Small importers and e-commerce sellers will argue the 5% weight threshold in § 357.4(b) is arbitrary and request that the agency raise it (e.g., to 10%) to reduce paperwork burdens for items with trivial plant content.

[P13] Environmental NGOs will oppose raising the threshold in § 357.4(b) and request the agency tighten it (e.g., lower than 5% or add product categories) to better capture harmful plant-sourced materials.

[P14] Manufacturers will point out the 2.9 kg per entry/unit limit in § 357.4(b) weight criterion is unclear — is it per shipment line, per SKU, per container? They will ask the agency to define “entry” and provide worked examples.

[P14] Trade groups will request the agency allow aggregation of plant material across an importer’s consolidated shipment for the § 357.4(b) weight threshold (2.9 kg) rather than applying the limit per product unit, to reflect commercial reality.

[P15] Importers will claim the alternative value/volume criteria in § 357.4(b) are unworkable because determining the “value” of plant material in a complex mixed product (≤10% of declared value) is speculative; they ask for acceptable valuation methodologies or presumption rules.

[P15] Small businesses will request that the 1 board foot per entry/unit standard in § 357.4(b) (value/volume alternative) be revised to reflect modern products — 1 board foot is irrelevant for many goods and causes compliance confusion.

[P16] Conservation advocates will support § 357.4(c) disqualifying products containing CITES-, ESA-, or State-listed plants from the paragraph (b) exception, but will ask the agency to clarify whether partial inclusion (trace amounts) triggers disqualification.

[P16] Industry groups will argue § 357.4(c) is overbroad if a tiny, incidental amount of listed species in a blended product disqualifies the entire product from the exception; they will ask for a de minimis threshold.

[P17] Importers of regulated timber or orchids will request precise implementation guidance for § 357.4(c)(1) CITES-listed materials, including whether a CITES permit submission can substitute for declaration or allow continued eligibility for other exceptions.

[P17] Legal experts will call for harmonization between § 357.4(c)(1) and existing CITES enforcement regimes to avoid duplicative permitting and prevent conflicting determinations.

[P18] Agricultural exporters will ask § 357.4(c)(2) to define whether domesticated cultivars derived from ESA-listed species are covered, and to provide criteria for when nursery-propagated stock is exempted from disqualification.

[P19] State regulatory agencies will request coordination protocols because § 357.4(c)(3) relies on diverse State conservation listings that vary widely; they will ask for a central searchable list and advance notice before relying on State lists for federal disqualification.

[P20] Importers will say the 3-business-day submission deadline in § 357.5 is impractical for complex supply chains where species identification and provenance verification take longer; they will ask for an extended period (e.g., 10 business days) or phased submission (initial notice then supplemental within 30 days).

[P20] Enforcement attorneys will warn that § 357.5’s tight 3-day timeline may encourage rushed, inaccurate declarations, increasing inadvertent violations; they recommend a reasonableness standard and cure period.

[P21] Nursery and horticulture associations will request that § 357.2(4) provide an appeal or clarification process before excluding a plant from categorical exclusions solely on a State list, to prevent sudden market disruptions from state-level listings.

[P21] Conservation groups will support § 357.2(4)’s exclusion of listed plants from categorical exclusions but ask the agency to include a mechanism to promptly update federal lists when new State or CITES listings change risk status.

[P22] Trade lawyers will ask § 357.2(4)(i) to clarify whether inclusion of a species in any CITES appendix, regardless of annotation or annotation exceptions, automatically removes categorical exclusions or whether specified CITES annotations must be considered.

[P22] Importers of CITES-annotated timber will seek explicit guidance on how § 357.2(4)(i) applies to annotated listings (e.g., parts and derivatives that are exempt), to avoid overbroad exclusion of benign products.

[P23] Agricultural stakeholders will request § 357.2(4)(ii) to distinguish between wild-caught/harvested specimens of ESA-listed species and cultivated/propagated specimens produced under valid permits so that nursery-propagated stock may still qualify for exclusions.

[P24] State wildlife agencies will urge the agency to coordinate before applying § 357.2(4)(iii) to ensure State lists used to disqualify categorical exclusions reflect current scientific assessments and provide standardized notification to federal authorities and stakeholders.

[P1] The requirement that the Service manage each listed experimental population and each reintroduction site "according to their respective management plans" (§17.84(g)(1)) is vague and lacks enforceable timelines, measurable objectives, and monitoring standards; commenters will request that each management plan be appended to the rule or that the rule specify minimum content (e.g., population viability targets, habitat metrics, monitoring frequency).

[P1] Environmental NGOs will assert that making management contingent only on "their respective management plans" grants the Service unfettered discretion and could permit rollbacks of protections if plans are weakened; they will ask for safeguards requiring public notice and comment before any substantive changes to those management plans.

[P1] State wildlife agencies will request clarification whether "manage according to their respective management plans" preempts or defers to state management authorities and will seek explicit language preserving coordination and delineating federal vs. state roles, responsibilities, and funding obligations.

[P1] Tribal governments will comment that management plans must include co-management provisions and tribal consultation requirements; they will request a specific obligation that plans incorporate Traditional Ecological Knowledge and tribal interests.

[P2] Private landowners and ranching associations will object that the obligation in §17.84(g)(6)(iv) to report anyone who "takes" a ferret in SWEPA to the Field Supervisor is ambiguous as to what constitutes "takes" (e.g., capture, observation, harassment) and will request a precise definition and a specified reporting timeframe (e.g., within 24–72 hours).

[P1] The February 21, 2017 comment deadline is unreasonably short and does not provide sufficient time for affected manufacturers, operators, and repair stations to analyze the technical impacts and prepare substantive comments.

[P1] The rule should include an extension mechanism or clearly state whether late-filed comments will be considered, because stakeholders may need more time due to holiday staffing and contract obligations.

[P2] The requirement to "follow the requirements of this AD within the specified compliance times" is redundant but could be interpreted to prohibit phased implementation; the agency should clarify whether staged compliance plans are acceptable.

[P2] The provision lacks clarity on whether compliance times can be adjusted via alternate inspection/maintenance programs under existing maintenance agreements; this should be expressly allowed or disallowed.

[P3] The requirement to remove all EEC software earlier than SCN 5B/I and install eligible software may impose significant operational downtime and costs; the FAA should provide an economic impact assessment and cost-recovery guidance.

[P3] The term "eligible EEC software" is undefined; commenters ask the FAA to provide a clear list of eligible software versions or a reference to the service bulletin that defines eligibility.

[P3] The rule does not specify responsibility for software upgrade costs (operator vs. OEM); the provision should state who bears labor, parts, and testing costs.

[P4] Requiring removal at the "next engine shop visit or prior to December 2018, whichever is earlier" will create a hard deadline that could force unscheduled shop visits and fleet disruptions; the FAA should allow coordination to minimize operational impact.

[P4] For engines listed in Figure 1, operators may have engines on long-term lease or in storage—clarify whether "next engine shop visit" includes planned long-term maintenance events outside typical intervals.

[P4] The December 2018 date may be technologically or logistically infeasible for some operators with limited shop capacity; propose alternative phasing or prioritization by utilization or risk.

[P5] The July 2024 deadline for engines not listed in Figure 1 is excessively long compared to the December 2018 date for listed engines; the differential treatment should be justified with safety risk data or harmonized.

[P5] Operators will have mixed fleets with engines on both schedules; the rule should permit a unified compliance plan and explain recordkeeping for mixed-compliance engines.

[P6] The installation prohibition after the AD effective date banning any software earlier than SCN 5B/I could prevent legacy support and necessary troubleshooting; request an exception allowing installation of older software for troubleshooting under controlled conditions.

[P6] The prohibition fails to address engines undergoing intermediate maintenance that inadvertently use older software; request incorporation of an allowance for emergency repairs or temporary reversion with notification.

[P6] The rule should specify enforcement consequences for inadvertent installations and outline corrective action procedures, rather than an absolute ban without guidance.

[P7] Granting the Manager authority to approve AMOCs centralizes discretion; commenters request transparency on criteria and timelines for AMOC review to ensure predictability.

[P7] Industry requests a standing AMOC template for common variations (e.g., alternate shop schedules) to streamline approvals and reduce FAA workload.

[P8] Requiring use of 14 CFR 39.19 procedures is appropriate but commenters ask the FAA to confirm whether electronic signatures and digitally submitted substantiation are acceptable under these procedures.

[P8] The rule should clarify expected supporting data for an AMOC per 14 CFR 39.19 (e.g., test results, risk assessments) to avoid back-and-forth and lengthy review times.

[P9] Allowing submission of AMOC requests via ANE–AD–AMOC@faa.gov is helpful, but commenters request acknowledgment timelines and a tracking number system so requesters can monitor progress.

[P9] Stakeholders request alternative submission methods (secure file transfer, postal mail with clear address) for proprietary data that cannot be emailed to a public inbox.

[P10] Requiring notification to the principal inspector or district manager before using an approved AMOC is reasonable, but the rule is truncated and does not specify the content, timing, or form of the notification—this must be clarified.

[P10] For operators without a principal inspector, notification to the "manager of the local flight standar[d]" is ambiguous; request clarification of the exact office/title and contact details.

[P10] The provision should allow prior notification via the same email used for AMOC requests when acceptable and provide a maximum timeline (e.g., 48 hours) before using the AMOC to ensure operational planning.

[P1] The rule does not indicate whether virtual docketing or comments submitted to associated rulemaking dockets (e.g., Docket No.) will be linked; request cross-referencing details to ensure comments are considered.

[P3] The AD lacks explicit reference to the service information (e.g., service bulletin number and revision) that details the installation procedure for the eligible EEC software; include exact references and parts/materials lists.

[P3] The AD should allow credit for earlier voluntary installations of SCN 5B/I-equivalent software implemented under approved service bulletins prior to the AD's effective date; state the documentation needed as compliance credit.

[P6] The prohibition could conflict with international maintenance practices and foreign repair station approvals; request harmonization language or recognition of equivalent approvals by EASA/other authorities.

[P7] The Manager's discretionary approval of AMOCs should include an appeals process or timeframe for FAA action (e.g., decisions within 60 days), to prevent undue operational delay.

[P2] The phrase "unless already accomplished" is vague about acceptable evidence—request specification of required documentation (work orders, shop visit reports, logbook entries) to prove prior compliance.

[P5] The July 2024 deadline should be reconsidered in light of potential equipment obsolescence; for certain low-utilization engines the upgrade may never be practical—request an alternative risk-based approach.

[P4] The "next engine shop visit" trigger could be ambiguous for engines undergoing on-wing repairs; define what constitutes a "shop visit" (module-level vs. complete engine teardown).

[P6] The prohibition after the AD's effective date should include an exception for installation of older software on engines not in revenue service (e.g., test cells, training units) with appropriate tagging/controls.

[P3] The AD does not address required post-installation testing or flight hours before return to service; request specification of functional tests, data recording, and acceptance criteria.

[P7] Small operators may lack resources to prepare full AMOC packages; request a streamlined AMOC pathway for low-complexity deviations (e.g., extended compliance windows) with reduced documentation requirements.

[P8] The rule should allow collaborative pre-submission meetings with the Aircraft Certification Office to discuss AMOCs to avoid wasted effort and speed approvals.

[P9] The email address provided is not encrypted; request guidance on submission of sensitive proprietary data and whether FAA will accept encrypted attachments or a secure portal.

[P10] The truncated text of P10 ("manager of the local flight standar") indicates an editorial error; request correction and full text disclosure to avoid compliance confusion.

[P1] The requirement that each and every material processed in an agricultural digester have at least 75% adjusted cellulosic content is infeasible for mixed-feed digesters and will force operators to discard or pre-sort low-cellulose inputs, increasing costs and waste.

[P1] Small farms and community digesters that rely on diverse feedstocks (manure, food waste, bedding) cannot meet the 75% adjusted cellulosic threshold for every individual material and will be effectively excluded from participation.

[P1] The phrase "each and every material" is ambiguous and overbroad — it should be clarified whether blended feedstocks are evaluated as combined streams or each ingredient separately.

[P1] The 75% adjusted cellulosic threshold lacks an explanation or scientific basis in the preamble; EPA should provide data demonstrating that 75% is necessary and achievable without harming digestor economics.

[P1] Enforcement of a per-material 75% requirement will create perverse incentives to avoid accepting high-nutrient, low-cellulose wastes (e.g., food waste), undermining organics diversion and greenhouse gas goals.

[P2] Limiting digestate to "only contain the leftovers that were unable to be completely converted to biogas" is vague and unenforceable; almost all digestate contains microbial biomass and transformation products — the rule should define allowable constituents and analytical thresholds.

[P2] The phrase "unable to be completely converted to biogas" is scientifically imprecise and could be interpreted to prohibit normal residuals (e.g., volatile solids) — EPA should specify percent volatile solids remaining or chemical oxygen demand limits.

[P2] Requiring digestate to be only leftovers could conflict with existing beneficial use practices (land application, soil amendment) and with state biosolids rules; EPA must reconcile with other regulatory frameworks.

[P3] The definition of "actual peak capacity" as 105% of the maximum annual volume is confusing and could be misread to allow inflation of capacity metrics; EPA should clarify calculation examples and rationale for the 105% multiplier.

[P3] Different time-base rules depending on construction date and fuels create complexity and potential inequity; the rule should explain why legacy facilities get different treatment and provide transition guidance.

[P4] For pre-December 19, 2007 facilities, basing actual peak capacity on the last five calendar years prior to 2008 is arbitrary and penalizes facilities that expanded operations after 2007; EPA should allow more recent historical data.

[P4] The provision does not account for facilities that were idle, mothballed, or changed ownership before 2008 — require a mechanism to use later years that reflect true capacity.

[P5] Paragraph (2) that uses any calendar year within the first three years after startup for facilities constructed after Dec 19, 2007 but before Jan 1, 2010 will advantage facilities that had unusually high early-year production; EPA should require averaging rather than permitting single-year cherry-picking.

[P5] The limitation to natural gas, biomass, or combined firing is unclear — the rule should specify treatment for facilities that subsequently switch fuel sources.

[P6] For "all other facilities" basing capacity on the five years prior to registration year is burdensome for new registrants with less than five years of operation; requiring use of any calendar year within first three years after startup should be extended to all new facilities.

[P6] The disparate approaches across P4-P6 may create opportunities for manipulation; EPA should require standardized rolling-average calculations (e.g., three-year rolling average) to prevent gaming.

[P7] The continuous measurement requirements impose significant capital and O&M costs without a demonstrated proportional benefit; EPA should include a cost estimate and allow tiered monitoring options for small generators.

[P7] The rule lacks calibration, QA/QC, data retention, and verification specifications for automated continuous measurement systems; EPA should include standards for sensor accuracy, maintenance, and auditability.

[P8] Requiring in-line GC meters to record at least once every 15 minutes may be insufficient to capture transient events for certain biogas quality parameters (e.g., H2S spikes) and should be justified or tightened.

[P8] The 15-minute interval for in-line GC may be technologically infeasible for many existing GC installations without hardware upgrades; EPA should allow alternative validated sampling protocols.

[P9] Mandating flow meters to record every 6 seconds will generate massive data volumes and may exceed data storage/telemetry capabilities for remote digesters; allow longer intervals or aggregated reporting for small facilities.

[P9] The 6-second interval is inconsistent with industry practice; EPA should accept industry standard averaging intervals (e.g., 1-minute) calibrated to meter type.

[P10] Requiring "all other meters" to record at least once every 2 seconds is excessively strict and will necessitate expensive instrumentation even where such granularity provides no compliance benefit.

[P10] The differentiations among meter types are unclear — EPA should list covered meter classes and provide technical rationale for the 2-second standard.

[P11] The requirement that records evidencing active management be "traceable to the land" is reasonable, but the rule needs examples of acceptable evidence and data retention periods to enable compliance.

[P11] The term "actively managed as agricultural land or fallow" lacks definition; EPA should define minimum management actions (e.g., tilling, planting, grazing) that qualify.

[P12] Accepting sales or purchase records tied to the land as proof is practical, but confidentiality concerns arise for small farmers — EPA should allow redacted or aggregated documentation.

[P12] Sales/purchase records may not exist for subsistence or tenant farmers; EPA should accept attestations or other forms of documentation in those cases.

[P13] Requiring a written agricultural management plan is appropriate, but the rule should specify minimum plan elements and acceptable formats to ensure consistency.

[P13] Farmers without formalized management plans will be disadvantaged; EPA should provide templates and technical assistance or accept producer attestations with follow-up audits.

[P14] Documented participation in government agricultural programs is a reasonable alternative, but many eligible landowners may not participate in such programs — EPA should permit other credible documentation.

[P14] The provision should clarify acceptable documentation types (e.g., program enrollment letters, payment records) and how to handle expired or intermittent participation.

[P15] Accepting certification program documentation is useful, but the rule should list recognized certification schemes or criteria to avoid ambiguity.

[P15] Some certification programs are costly to smallholders; EPA should allow equivalent third-party verification or phased compliance timelines.

[P16] Calculating annual volume by multiplying hourly permit output by 8,322 hours per year artificially assumes lower availability than continuous operation; EPA should use 8,760 hours or the statute-cited availability factor with justification.

[P16] The specific multiplier 8,322 hours/year is unexplained; EPA must justify this value (it equals 95% availability) or allow alternative baselines consistent with the permit's intended operating profile.

[P16] Facilities with seasonal operation will be disadvantaged by using hourly-rated capacity multiplied by 8,322 — EPA should permit seasonal adjustments or actual operating hours.

[P17] Requiring A–RIN verification by registered independent third-party auditors using an EPA-approved QAP is sensible, but the process for registering auditors and approving QAPs must be transparent and timely.

[P17] The rule should specify conflict-of-interest safeguards, auditor qualification criteria, and mechanisms for removal/suspension of auditors to protect A–RIN integrity.

[P17] The interim period verification requirement may create a bottleneck if insufficient auditors are registered; EPA should allow provisional approvals or recognize accredited auditors from other programs.

[P18] The B–RIN verification requirements cross-reference § 80.1469(b) but the proposed subsection appears incomplete; EPA must ensure the referenced QAP approval criteria are finalized and consistent.

[P18] The distinction between A–RIN and B–RIN verification regimes could be confusing to market participants; EPA should provide clear flowcharts and examples of which RINs fall into each category.

[P19] The requirement that PTD for certified non-transportation 15 ppm distillate fuel meet § 80.1453(e) is reasonable, but the rule should clarify cross-references and ensure § 80.1453(e) is consistent with this program.

[P19] Stakeholders need guidance on testing methods and documentation required to demonstrate PTD compliance; EPA should issue templates and approved test protocols.

[P20] Requiring biomass-based diesel intended for motor vehicle use to be registered under 40 CFR part 79 is appropriate, but the registration process is time-consuming — EPA should allow temporary compliance mechanisms for small producers.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The requirement that each and every material processed in an agricultural digester have at least 75% adjusted cellulosic content is infeasible for mixed-feed digesters and will force operators to discard or pre-sort low-cellulose inputs, increasing costs and waste.

Small farms and community digesters that rely on diverse feedstocks (manure, food waste, bedding) cannot meet the 75% adjusted cellulosic threshold for every individual material and will be effectively excluded from participation.
The phrase "each and every material" is ambiguous and overbroad — it should be clarified whether blended feedstocks are evaluated as combined streams or each ingredient separately.

The 75% adjusted cellulosic threshold lacks an explanation or scientific basis in the preamble; EPA should provide data demonstrating that 75% is necessary and achievable without harming digestor economics.

Enforcement of a per-material 75% requirement will create perverse incentives to avoid accepting high-nutrient, low-cellulose wastes (e.g., food waste), undermining organics diversion and greenhouse gas goals.

Limiting digestate to "only contain the leftovers that were unable to be completely converted to biogas" is vague and unenforceable; almost all digestate contains microbial biomass and transformation products — the rule should define allowable constituents and analytical thresholds.

The phrase "unable to be completely converted to biogas" is scientifically imprecise and could be interpreted to prohibit normal residuals (e.g., volatile solids) — EPA should specify percent volatile solids remaining or chemical oxygen demand limits.

Requiring digestate to be only leftovers could conflict with existing beneficial use practices (land application, soil amendment) and with state biosolids rules; EPA must reconcile with other regulatory frameworks.

The definition of "actual peak capacity" as 105% of the maximum annual volume is confusing and could be misread to allow inflation of capacity metrics; EPA should clarify calculation examples and rationale for the 105% multiplier.

Different time-base rules depending on construction date and fuels create complexity and potential inequity; the rule should explain why legacy facilities get different treatment and provide transition guidance.

For pre-December 19, 2007 facilities, basing actual peak capacity on the last five calendar years prior to 2008 is arbitrary and penalizes facilities that expanded operations after 2007; EPA should allow more recent historical data.
The provision does not account for facilities that were idle, mothballed, or changed ownership before 2008 — require a mechanism to use later years that reflect true capacity.

Paragraph (2) that uses any calendar year within the first three years after startup for facilities constructed after Dec 19, 2007 but before Jan 1, 2010 will advantage facilities that had unusually high early-year production; EPA should require averaging rather than permitting single-year cherry-picking.
The limitation to natural gas, biomass, or combined firing is unclear — the rule should specify treatment for facilities that subsequently switch fuel sources.

For "all other facilities" basing capacity on the five years prior to registration year is burdensome for new registrants with less than five years of operation; requiring use of any calendar year within first three years after startup should be extended to all new facilities.
The disparate approaches across P4-P6 may create opportunities for manipulation; EPA should require standardized rolling-average calculations (e.g., three-year rolling average) to prevent gaming.

The continuous measurement requirements impose significant capital and O&M costs without a demonstrated proportional benefit; EPA should include a cost estimate and allow tiered monitoring options for small generators.

The rule lacks calibration, QA/QC, data retention, and verification specifications for automated continuous measurement systems; EPA should include standards for sensor accuracy, maintenance, and auditability.

Requiring in-line GC meters to record at least once every 15 minutes may be insufficient to capture transient events for certain biogas quality parameters (e.g., H2S spikes) and should be justified or tightened.
The 15-minute interval for in-line GC may be technologically infeasible for many existing GC installations without hardware upgrades; EPA should allow alternative validated sampling protocols.

Mandating flow meters to record every 6 seconds will generate massive data volumes and may exceed data storage/telemetry capabilities for remote digesters; allow longer intervals or aggregated reporting for small facilities.
The 6-second interval is inconsistent with industry practice; EPA should accept industry standard averaging intervals (e.g., 1-minute) calibrated to meter type.
Requiring "all other meters" to record at least once every 2 seconds is excessively strict and will necessitate expensive instrumentation even where such granularity provides no compliance benefit.
The differentiations among meter types are unclear — EPA should list covered meter classes and provide technical rationale for the 2-second standard.
The requirement that records evidencing active management be "traceable to the land" is reasonable, but the rule needs examples of acceptable evidence and data retention periods to enable compliance.
The term "actively managed as agricultural land or fallow" lacks definition; EPA should define minimum management actions (e.g., tilling, planting, grazing) that qualify.
Accepting sales or purchase records tied to the land as proof is practical, but confidentiality concerns arise for small farmers — EPA should allow redacted or aggregated documentation.
Sales/purchase records may not exist for subsistence or tenant farmers; EPA should accept attestations or other forms of documentation in those cases.
Requiring a written agricultural management plan is appropriate, but the rule should specify minimum plan elements and acceptable formats to ensure consistency.
Farmers without formalized management plans will be disadvantaged; EPA should provide templates and technical assistance or accept producer attestations with follow-up audits.

Documented participation in government agricultural programs is a reasonable alternative, but many eligible landowners may not participate in such programs — EPA should permit other credible documentation.
The provision should clarify acceptable documentation types (e.g., program enrollment letters, payment records) and how to handle expired or intermittent participation.
Accepting certification program documentation is useful, but the rule should list recognized certification schemes or criteria to avoid ambiguity.
Some certification programs are costly to smallholders; EPA should allow equivalent third-party verification or phased compliance timelines.

Calculating annual volume by multiplying hourly permit output by 8,322 hours per year artificially assumes lower availability than continuous operation; EPA should use 8,760 hours or the statute-cited availability factor with justification.

The specific multiplier 8,322 hours/year is unexplained; EPA must justify this value (it equals 95% availability) or allow alternative baselines consistent with the permit's intended operating profile.
Facilities with seasonal operation will be disadvantaged by using hourly-rated capacity multiplied by 8,322 — EPA should permit seasonal adjustments or actual operating hours.

Requiring A–RIN verification by registered independent third-party auditors using an EPA-approved QAP is sensible, but the process for registering auditors and approving QAPs must be transparent and timely.
The rule should specify conflict-of-interest safeguards, auditor qualification criteria, and mechanisms for removal/suspension of auditors to protect A–RIN integrity.

The interim period verification requirement may create a bottleneck if insufficient auditors are registered; EPA should allow provisional approvals or recognize accredited auditors from other programs.
The B–RIN verification requirements cross-reference § 80.1469(b) but the proposed subsection appears incomplete; EPA must ensure the referenced QAP approval criteria are finalized and consistent.
The distinction between A–RIN and B–RIN verification regimes could be confusing to market participants; EPA should provide clear flowcharts and examples of which RINs fall into each category.

[P1] Industry commenter: CMS’s authority to reinstate enrollment without interruption (§417.460(c)(3)) should explicitly require HMO/CMPs to obtain written confirmation from CMS or the assigned third party before restoring services to prevent billing disputes.

[P1] Consumer advocate: The provision allowing CMS or an HMO/CMP to reinstate enrollment without interruption lacks a clear timeline for when benefits resume; commenters will request a specific maximum time (e.g., within 5 business days of approval) to avoid care gaps.

[P2] Legal expert: The 60‑calendar‑day deadline to submit a reinstatement request (§417.460(c)(3)) may be jurisdictionally challenged as unreasonably short for beneficiaries with cognitive impairments or limited notice; recommend extension to 120 days or inclusion of tolling provisions.

[P3] Disability rights group: The prohibition on multiple reinstatement requests within the same 60‑day period (§417.460(c)(3)) is unduly punitive for those who do not understand prior denials; request an exception for beneficiaries with documented cognitive disabilities.

[P4] Consumer advocate: The requirement to “show good cause for failure to pay” (§417.460(c)(3)) is vague — commenters ask CMS to define “good cause” with examples (medical emergency, hospitalization, natural disaster, administrative error) to ensure consistent adjudication.

[P5] Low‑income advocacy group: The obligation to pay all overdue amounts within 3 calendar months (§417.460(c)(3)) to reinstate enrollment is burdensome for low‑income beneficiaries; recommend allowing payment plans or waivers for those meeting hardship criteria.

[P6] Legal expert: Requiring a “credible statement” that nonpayment was due to circumstances beyond control (§417.460(c)(3)) is subjective; request CMS specify acceptable forms of corroboration (medical records, hospital discharge, employer letters) and prohibit reliance solely on staff discretion.

[P7] Patient rights organization: The HMO/CMP obligation to make a “serious effort” to resolve enrollee problems (§417.460(e)(2)) is insufficiently defined; commenters will ask CMS to enumerate minimum steps (number of attempted contacts, timelines, escalation procedures) that constitute a serious effort.

[P8] Consumer advocate: Including “attempted use” of internal grievance procedures (§417.460(e)(2)) as part of resolution efforts could be abused by plans; request that CMS require documentation that the enrollee was effectively assisted in using grievance processes, not merely informed of them.

[P9] Disability rights group: The requirement to provide “reasonable accommodations” for mental/cognitive conditions (§417.460(e)(2)) must include examples (extended deadlines, plain‑language notices, proxy assistance) and require training for plan staff to identify accommodation needs.

[P10] Consumer advocate: The obligation to inform individuals of the right to use grievance procedures via notices (§417.460(e)(7)) should require notices in multiple languages and accessible formats (large print, Braille, easy‑read, audio) and confirmation of receipt.

[P11] Civil rights group: Documentation obligations (§417.460(e)(4)) to record problems, efforts, and medical conditions raise HIPAA/privacy concerns; ask CMS to specify permitted data elements, retention periods, and safeguards to protect sensitive information.

[P12] Legal expert: Requiring dated copies of notices from paragraph (d)(2)(iv) to be submitted to CMS (§417.460(e)(4)) creates administrative burden; request CMS clarify the submission format (electronic upload standard), timeframe for submission, and whether redacted PHI is acceptable.

[P13] Consumer advocate: Requiring two notices before submitting a disenrollment request to CMS (§417.460(e)(7)) is positive but must specify delivery methods (certified mail, telephone, email, in‑person) and proof of delivery to protect beneficiaries.

[P14] Patient advocacy group: The restart requirement if disruptive behavior ceases and later resumes (§417.460(e)(7)) could permit indefinite delays; request a cap on how many times the process can be restarted within a year and clear definitions of “ceases” and “resumes.”

[P15] Consumer advocate: Waiting at least 30 days after the advance notice before sending the second notice (§417.460(e)(7)) should be coupled with required outreach during the 30‑day window (e.g., care manager contact) to offer remediation and supports for behavioral issues.

[P16] Legal expert: The second notice of intent to request disenrollment to CMS (§417.460(e)(7)) must include a clear explanation of appeal rights, timelines, and contact information for independent advocates; otherwise the notice may not meet due process standards.

[P17] Industry/MA plan: FI–SNP requirement to “own or have contractual arrangements with each institutionalized facility serving plan enrollees” (§422.2) is impractical in markets with many small facilities; request clarification that “contractual arrangement” can be limited to facilities with a threshold number of enrollees.

[P17] Nursing home association: The FI–SNP ownership/contract requirement (§422.2) may constitute anticompetitive vertical integration pressures; request a safe harbor allowing network agreements rather than ownership or exclusive contracts.

[P18] HI–SNP operators: Requiring HI–SNPs to meet FI–SNP and IE–SNP standards (§422.2) could create duplication/conflict between standards; ask CMS to provide an integrated compliance framework and transition period.

[P19] Specialty‑care provider group: Allowing C–SNPs to focus on a single severe chronic condition (§422.4(a)(1)(iv)(A)) is appropriate, but CMS should require explicit eligibility criteria and care standards to prevent narrow benefit designs that shift cost/risk.

[P20] MA organizations: The permission to offer C–SNPs focusing on multiple co‑morbid conditions upon CMS approval (§422.4(a)(1)(iv)(B)) needs transparent approval criteria and predictable timelines; request CMS publish evaluation metrics and a 90‑day decision standard.

[P21] Patient advocates: The rule that only one qualifying condition is needed for enrollment in grouped C–SNPs (§422.52(g)) may lead to enrollment of patients without substantial needs; request CMS ensure condition severity and care needs are documented, not just diagnostic codes.

[P22] MA plans: The obligation to reinstate enrollment when an individual cancels a new plan election within CMS timeframes (§422.60(h)) should specify how overlapping premiums and enrollment effective dates are reconciled to avoid double billing.

[P23] Consumer advocate: The 10‑calendar‑day requirement to notify members of reinstatement (§422.60(h)) should mandate that notice include effective date of reinstatement, retroactive coverage details, and contact information for disputes.

[P24] Disaster response NGOs: The SEP tied to emergency declaration dates (§422.62(b)(18)) is necessary, but CMS should allow flexible start dates for individuals displaced after the declaration and require widespread outreach in affected areas.

[P25] Legal expert: Defaulting an unidentified incident end date to one year after SEP start with a maximum SEP of 14 months (§422.62(b)(18)(i)) may be arbitrary; recommend CMS allow extensions based on ongoing local conditions and state declaration changes.

[P26] MA plan compliance officer: Documenting efforts to obtain missing information for disenrollment requests (§422.66(b)(3)(v)(A)) should include a required log format and retention period; ask CMS to provide a template to standardize enforcement.

[P27] Consumer advocate: The 10‑calendar‑day notice to the individual after receiving a disenrollment request (§422.66(b)(3)(v)(B)) must be required in plain language and accessible formats and include clear instructions on what additional information is needed.

[P28] Legal expert: Denying disenrollment requests if additional info is not received within specified timeframes (§422.66(b)(3)(v)(C)) could improperly trap beneficiaries; request that CMS allow extensions for good cause and require plans to notify the beneficiary that denial will occur if no response.

[P29] AEP enrollment counselor: The December 7 or 21‑day cutoff for AEP disenrollment requests (§422.66(b)(3)(v)(C)(1)) is confusing; ask CMS to harmonize deadlines and publish examples showing how the “whichever is later” rule applies in practice.

[P30] State consumer protection agency: The end‑of‑month or 21‑day rule for non‑AEP disenrollments (§422.66(b)(3)(v)(C)(2)) may disadvantage beneficiaries who submit requests late in the month; recommend extending the 21‑day period to 30 days for fairness.

[P31] Consumer advocate: Defining a disenrollment request as incomplete if missing info not received within the timeframe (§422.66(b)(6)) should require the plan to provide a written “incomplete” determination that explains missing elements and appeals process.

[P32] Consumer rights group: Written notices explaining the reason for planned disenrollment (§422.74(c)) must include evidence relied upon, the specific contractual or policy provision alleged to be violated, and instructions for submitting rebuttal materials.

[P33] Legal expert: Requiring the written disenrollment notice to be provided before submission to CMS (§422.74(c)(1)) is appropriate but CMS should specify minimum timing (e.g., at least 30 days before submission) so beneficiaries have meaningful opportunity to respond.

[P34] Patient advocates: Inclusion of the right to submit a grievance in the disenrollment notice (§422.74(c)(2)) is necessary but should also list independent external appeal options and contact information for state health insurance assistance programs.

[P35] Consumer advocate: Permitting reinstatement without interruption after premium nonpayment (§422.74(d)(1)(v)) is beneficial, but CMS should limit retroactive reinstatement liability for providers and clarify whether cost sharing applies retroactively.

[P36] Legal expert: The 60‑day deadline for reinstatement requests after premium nonpayment (§422.74(d)(1)(v)(A)) mirrors other provisions; request CMS consolidate and align these 60‑day rules and provide tolling for hospitalization or natural disasters.

[P37] Disability advocate: The prohibition on multiple requests for reinstatement during the same 60‑day period (§422.74(d)(1)(v)(B)) risks denying vulnerable beneficiaries who file duplicate requests due to confusion; request an exception for requests filed but lost by the plan or CMS.

[P38] Consumer group: Requiring showing good cause for failure to pay within the initial grace period (§422.74(d)(1)(v)(C)) should include a presumption of good cause for documented hospital stays or medically necessary institutionalizations during the grace period.

[P39] Low‑income advocacy group: Payment of overdue premiums within 3 months to reinstate (§422.74(d)(1)(v)(D)) should allow for income‑based payment plans and require MA organizations to assist beneficiaries in applying for subsidy programs.

[P40] Legal expert: The “credible statement” standard for justification of nonpayment (§422.74(d)(1)(v)(E)) is vague; recommend CMS define evidentiary thresholds and prohibit blanket denials based solely on absence of documentary proof when such proof is unavailable.

[P41] Consumer rights organization: The MA organization’s duty to make a serious effort and provide reasonable accommodations for mental/cognitive conditions (§422.74(d)(2)(iii)) should include mandatory training, documentation requirements, and audits for compliance.

[P42] Disability advocate: “Reasonable accommodations as determined by CMS” (§422.74(d)(2)(iii)) must be publicly listed with examples and a clear process for beneficiaries to request and appeal accommodation denials.

[P43] Patient advocacy group: Informing individuals of right to use grievance procedures via notices (§422.74(d)(2)(iii)) requires that notices also explain timeframes and that the organization will not seek disenrollment while a grievance is pending.

[P44] Consumer advocate: Documentation of behavior, organizational efforts, and extenuating circumstances (§422.74(d)(2)(iv)) should prohibit collection of non‑relevant medical or behavioral health records beyond what is necessary and require beneficiary consent for sensitive disclosures.

[P45] Legal expert: Allowing MA organizations to request permission to decline future enrollment by an individual (§422.74(d)(2)(iv)) raises due process issues; request CMS establish a transparent review process, standards for refusal, and rights to appeal CMS’s decision.

[P46] Consumer advocate: Requiring submission of beneficiary‑provided documentation to CMS (§422.74(d)(2)(iv)) should include protections so that plans cannot coerce beneficiaries into waiving privacy rights when providing evidence.

[P47] Compliance officer: Submitting dated copies of notices to CMS (§422.74(d)(2)(iv)) must include electronic submission standards and deadlines; ask CMS to provide an electronic portal and sample templates to reduce administrative errors.

[P48] Consumer advocate: Providing two notices before submitting the disenrollment request to CMS (§422.74(d)(2)(vii)) should require that at least one notice be personally delivered or confirmed by phone for high‑risk cases (behavioral health, cognitive impairment).

[P49] Patient rights group: Restarting the notice/process if disruptive behavior stops and later resumes (§422.74(d)(2)(vii)) could be manipulated to prolong disenrollment timelines; request CMS require objective incident thresholds (e.g., number/severity of incidents) before restarting.

[P50] Consumer advocate: The 30‑day waiting requirement after the advance notice before issuing the second notice (§422.74(d)(2)(vii)) should be accompanied by mandatory interventions (care planning, in‑home supports) during that period for beneficiaries with complex needs.

[P51] Legal expert: The second notice of intent to request disenrollment (§422.74(d)(2)(vii)) must include a clear statement that the MA organization will submit supporting documentation to CMS and advise beneficiaries how to submit rebuttal material directly to CMS.

[P52] MA plan: The requirement to disenroll and document basis when an individual permanently moves (§422.74(d)(4)(i)) needs clear guidance on acceptable proofs of permanent move (lease, utility bills, declarations) and how temporary relocations are handled.

[P53] Consumer advocate: Documentation of basis for disenrollment due to move (§422.74(d)(4)(i)) must not rely on third‑party address data without beneficiary confirmation; request beneficiary notice and ability to contest address determinations.

[P54] Legal expert: The 10‑day timing tied to confirmation of residence/temporary absence for issuing disenrollment notice (§422.74(d)(4)(iv)) is ambiguous; ask CMS to clarify triggers and require mailed notice plus verbal confirmation when possible.

[P55] SNP advocacy group: Providing at least 30 days advance notice when an enrollee loses special needs status (§422.74(d)(8)) is appropriate, but CMS should require outreach assistance to help enrollees find alternative plans suited to their needs.

[P56] Consumer advocate: The 10‑calendar‑day requirement to provide advance notice after learning of loss of special needs status (§422.74(d)(8)(i)) is too short for beneficiaries to gather documentation to prove continued eligibility; request 30 days.

[P57] Patient advocates: Advance notices that must include SEP eligibility, deemed continued eligibility, and consequences (§422.74(d)(8)(ii)) should be standardized in plain language and translated into multiple languages commonly spoken in the plan’s service area.

[P58] Consumer rights group: Sending the final involuntary disenrollment notice within 3 business days following the disenrollment effective date and before submitting to CMS (§422.74(d)(8)(iii)) risks beneficiaries missing opportunities to appeal; require that final notice include appeal instructions and that disenrollment be stayed while an appeal is pending.

[P59] Legal expert: Requiring final involuntary disenrollment notice to explain right to file a grievance (§422.74(d)(8)(iv)) is necessary but insufficient; recommend inclusion of timelines for filing and contact details for state/regional advocates.

[P60] Clinician association: Allowing MA organizations to create internal coverage criteria when external criteria are absent (§422.101(b)(6)) may lead to inconsistent access; request CMS limits on using internal criteria to restrict access and requirement for CMS review of such criteria.

[P61] Consumer advocate: Requirement to provide a publicly accessible summary of evidence for internal coverage criteria (§422.101(b)(6)(i)) must mandate posting in machine‑readable format and require notification to affected enrollees when criteria change.

[P62] Research organizations: The obligation to provide a list of sources used in internal coverage criteria (§422.101(b)(6)(ii)) should require full citations and links to studies, and require disclosure of unpublished data or manufacturer submissions.

[P63] Patient advocates: The mandated rationale explanation for internal coverage criteria (§422.101(b)(6)(iii)) should include how considerations like patient preferences, clinical heterogeneity, and social determinants were weighed.

[P64] Medical societies: The requirement that medical necessity determinations be based on coverage criteria, section 1862(a)(1) reasonableness, medical history, and medical director involvement (§422.101(c)(1)(i)) is appropriate but CMS should specify when medical director involvement is “appropriate” to avoid denial without clinical review.

[P66] Patient rights advocates: The prohibition on denying basic benefits based on coverage criteria not specified in paragraphs (b) or (c) (§422.101(c)(1)(i)(A) prohibition) should be enforced with penalties and public reporting for violations.

[P68] Provider organizations: Considering enrollee medical history, physician recommendations, and clinical notes (§422.101(c)(1)(i)(C)) must be documented in denial letters; request that plans be required to cite which elements were considered and why they were insufficient.

[P69] Physician groups: Involving the organization’s medical director when appropriate (§422.101(c)(1)(i)(D)) should be expanded to require clinical review by an independent specialty reviewer for complex denials and require documentation of their qualifications.

[P70] Hospitals/SNF providers: Permitting MA organizations to elect to provide posthospital SNF care without prior qualifying hospital stay (§422.101(c)(2)) is beneficial; recommend CMS incentivize plans to adopt this option and provide clear payment rules.

[P71] I–SNP operators: Contracts with long‑term care institutions must allow I–SNP staff access (§422.101(f)(2)(vi)); CMS should define reasonable notice and privacy protocols for access and require facility cooperation standards.

[P72] SNP operators: The MOC element and aggregate benchmark thresholds (50% per element; 70% aggregate) (§422.101(f)(3)(iii)) may be too rigid; request phase‑in, appeals for borderline scores, and transparency in scoring rubrics.

[P74] I/D‑SNP operators: The tiered approval durations based on aggregate scores (§422.101(f)(3)(iii)(B)) create instability; request softened cutoffs, remediation plans before downgrades, and clarity on how performance is remeasured.

[P75] MA organizations: Allowing one corrected resubmission for failed MOCs with 1‑year approval (§422.101(f)(3)(iii)(C)) is restrictive; request two resubmissions and that corrected resubmissions be eligible for longer approval if substantial improvements shown.

[P76] SNP legal counsel: Prohibiting implementation of MOC changes until NCQA approval and that no rescoring occurs during off‑cycle review (§422.101(f)(3)(iv)(D)) could prevent urgent clinical updates; recommend an expedited interim approval pathway for clinically necessary changes.

[P77] D/I–SNP compliance staff: The June 1–Nov 30 window for MOC updates/corrections (§422.101(f)(3)(iv)(A)) may not align with operational cycles; request flexibility or predefined off‑cycle submission windows for urgent updates.

[P78] SNP administrators: The requirement to submit off‑cycle updates when substantial changes occur (§422.101(f)(3)(iv)(B)) should include clear definitions of “substantial change” and examples to avoid inconsistent reporting.

[P79] SNP quality officer: Allowing a one‑time cure of off‑cycle MOC deficiencies between June 1 and Nov 30 (§422.101(f)(3)(iv)(G)) is helpful but CMS should specify timelines for cure and consequences for failure to cure.

[P80] Clinical trial advocates: The obligation that original Medicare covers routine costs and complication costs for MA enrollees in CMS‑approved trials (§422.109(e)(1)) is positive; commenters will request explicit notice requirements so enrollees know their coverage rights before enrolling.

[P81] Legal/consumer groups: The prohibition on charging MA enrollees traditional Medicare Part A/B deductibles for clinical trial coverage (§422.109(e)(2)) should be explicitly enforced with audit rights and penalties for plans that attempt to collect those deductibles.

[P82] MA plan actuary: Requiring MA plans to pay the difference between traditional Medicare cost‑sharing and plan in‑network cost‑sharing for clinical trial services (§422.109(e)(3)) raises potential fiscal impacts; request CMS guidance on accounting and reporting these adjustments.

[P83] Consumer advocates: Including enrollee in‑network cost‑sharing for clinical trial services in the plan’s MOOP calculation (§422.109(e)(4)) should prevent plans from excluding such costs; request monitoring and public reporting to ensure compliance.

[P84] Research/advocacy groups: Prohibiting prior authorization or impediments to participating in non‑plan‑sponsored Medicare‑qualified clinical trials (§422.109(e)(5)) should include enforcement language and examples of prohibited impediments (e.g., retroactive denials, site restrictions).

[P85] MA plans: The obligation to pay for routine care in CMS‑approved IDE Category A/B studies (§422.109(f)(1)) needs alignment with FDA/CMS timelines and definitions; ask CMS to clarify scope and billing rules to prevent disputes.

[P86] Device manufacturers: MA plans’ obligation to cover CMS‑approved Category B devices (§422.109(f)(2)) should include clear coding, prior authorization exceptions, and timetables for coverage determinations.

[P87] Consumer transparency advocates: The detailed provider network disclosure requirements (§422.111(b)(3)(i)) must be published in machine‑readable form, updated frequently (e.g., monthly), and include wait‑time estimates and telehealth capacity.

[P89] Patient groups: The “good faith effort” to notify enrollees of for‑cause provider terminations within required timeframes (§422.111(e)) must be defined (number of contact attempts, modalities) and audited for compliance.

[P90] Mental health advocates: For primary care or behavioral health provider terminations (§422.111(e)(1)(i)), requiring both written and telephonic notice is essential; request that plans also provide care coordination outreach to affected patients.

[P91] Consumer advocates: The 45‑calendar‑day advance notice for primary care/behavioral health terminations (§422.111(e)(1)(ii)) is reasonable but must include exceptions for emergent terminations that threaten patient safety and require immediate alternative arrangements.

[P92] Patient advocates: Notifying all enrollees who have ever been patients of a terminating primary care/behavioral health provider (§422.111(e)(1)(iii)) could be administratively burdensome; ask CMS to narrow to patients seen within the past 12 or 24 months to ensure relevancy.

[P94] Provider groups: The 30‑calendar‑day notice for specialty provider terminations (§422.111(e)(2)(ii)) should be aligned with contractual termination notice periods to prevent conflicting obligations.
