Consumer advocate: The requirement to “show good cause for failure to pay” (§417.460(c)(3)) is vague — commenters ask CMS to define “good cause” with examples (medical emergency, hospitalization, natural disaster, administrative error) to ensure consistent adjudication.

Low‑income advocacy group: The obligation to pay all overdue amounts within 3 calendar months (§417.460(c)(3)) to reinstate enrollment is burdensome for low‑income beneficiaries; recommend allowing payment plans or waivers for those meeting hardship criteria.

Legal expert: Requiring a “credible statement” that nonpayment was due to circumstances beyond control (§417.460(c)(3)) is subjective; request CMS specify acceptable forms of corroboration (medical records, hospital discharge, employer letters) and prohibit reliance solely on staff discretion.

Patient rights organization: The HMO/CMP obligation to make a “serious effort” to resolve enrollee problems (§417.460(e)(2)) is insufficiently defined; commenters will ask CMS to enumerate minimum steps (number of attempted contacts, timelines, escalation procedures) that constitute a serious effort.

Consumer advocate: Including “attempted use” of internal grievance procedures (§417.460(e)(2)) as part of resolution efforts could be abused by plans; request that CMS require documentation that the enrollee was effectively assisted in using grievance processes, not merely informed of them.

Disability rights group: The requirement to provide “reasonable accommodations” for mental/cognitive conditions (§417.460(e)(2)) must include examples (extended deadlines, plain‑language notices, proxy assistance) and require training for plan staff to identify accommodation needs.

Consumer advocate: The obligation to inform individuals of the right to use grievance procedures via notices (§417.460(e)(7)) should require notices in multiple languages and accessible formats (large print, Braille, easy‑read, audio) and confirmation of receipt.

Civil rights group: Documentation obligations (§417.460(e)(4)) to record problems, efforts, and medical conditions raise HIPAA/privacy concerns; ask CMS to specify permitted data elements, retention periods, and safeguards to protect sensitive information.

Legal expert: Requiring dated copies of notices from paragraph (d)(2)(iv) to be submitted to CMS (§417.460(e)(4)) creates administrative burden; request CMS clarify the submission format (electronic upload standard), timeframe for submission, and whether redacted PHI is acceptable.

Consumer advocate: Requiring two notices before submitting a disenrollment request to CMS (§417.460(e)(7)) is positive but must specify delivery methods (certified mail, telephone, email, in‑person) and proof of delivery to protect beneficiaries.

Patient advocacy group: The restart requirement if disruptive behavior ceases and later resumes (§417.460(e)(7)) could permit indefinite delays; request a cap on how many times the process can be restarted within a year and clear definitions of “ceases” and “resumes.”

Consumer advocate: Waiting at least 30 days after the advance notice before sending the second notice (§417.460(e)(7)) should be coupled with required outreach during the 30‑day window (e.g., care manager contact) to offer remediation and supports for behavioral issues.

Legal expert: The second notice of intent to request disenrollment to CMS (§417.460(e)(7)) must include a clear explanation of appeal rights, timelines, and contact information for independent advocates; otherwise the notice may not meet due process standards.

Industry/MA plan: FI–SNP requirement to “own or have contractual arrangements with each institutionalized facility serving plan enrollees” (§422.2) is impractical in markets with many small facilities; request clarification that “contractual arrangement” can be limited to facilities with a threshold number of enrollees.

Nursing home association: The FI–SNP ownership/contract requirement (§422.2) may constitute anticompetitive vertical integration pressures; request a safe harbor allowing network agreements rather than ownership or exclusive contracts.

HI–SNP operators: Requiring HI–SNPs to meet FI–SNP and IE–SNP standards (§422.2) could create duplication/conflict between standards; ask CMS to provide an integrated compliance framework and transition period.

Specialty‑care provider group: Allowing C–SNPs to focus on a single severe chronic condition (§422.4(a)(1)(iv)(A)) is appropriate, but CMS should require explicit eligibility criteria and care standards to prevent narrow benefit designs that shift cost/risk.

MA organizations: The permission to offer C–SNPs focusing on multiple co‑morbid conditions upon CMS approval (§422.4(a)(1)(iv)(B)) needs transparent approval criteria and predictable timelines; request CMS publish evaluation metrics and a 90‑day decision standard.

Patient advocates: The rule that only one qualifying condition is needed for enrollment in grouped C–SNPs (§422.52(g)) may lead to enrollment of patients without substantial needs; request CMS ensure condition severity and care needs are documented, not just diagnostic codes.

MA plans: The obligation to reinstate enrollment when an individual cancels a new plan election within CMS timeframes (§422.60(h)) should specify how overlapping premiums and enrollment effective dates are reconciled to avoid double billing.

Consumer advocate: The 10‑calendar‑day requirement to notify members of reinstatement (§422.60(h)) should mandate that notice include effective date of reinstatement, retroactive coverage details, and contact information for disputes.

Disaster response NGOs: The SEP tied to emergency declaration dates (§422.62(b)(18)) is necessary, but CMS should allow flexible start dates for individuals displaced after the declaration and require widespread outreach in affected areas.

Legal expert: Defaulting an unidentified incident end date to one year after SEP start with a maximum SEP of 14 months (§422.62(b)(18)(i)) may be arbitrary; recommend CMS allow extensions based on ongoing local conditions and state declaration changes.

MA plan compliance officer: Documenting efforts to obtain missing information for disenrollment requests (§422.66(b)(3)(v)(A)) should include a required log format and retention period; ask CMS to provide a template to standardize enforcement.

Consumer advocate: The 10‑calendar‑day notice to the individual after receiving a disenrollment request (§422.66(b)(3)(v)(B)) must be required in plain language and accessible formats and include clear instructions on what additional information is needed.

Legal expert: Denying disenrollment requests if additional info is not received within specified timeframes (§422.66(b)(3)(v)(C)) could improperly trap beneficiaries; request that CMS allow extensions for good cause and require plans to notify the beneficiary that denial will occur if no response.

AEP enrollment counselor: The December 7 or 21‑day cutoff for AEP disenrollment requests (§422.66(b)(3)(v)(C)(1)) is confusing; ask CMS to harmonize deadlines and publish examples showing how the “whichever is later” rule applies in practice.

State consumer protection agency: The end‑of‑month or 21‑day rule for non‑AEP disenrollments (§422.66(b)(3)(v)(C)(2)) may disadvantage beneficiaries who submit requests late in the month; recommend extending the 21‑day period to 30 days for fairness.

Consumer advocate: Defining a disenrollment request as incomplete if missing info not received within the timeframe (§422.66(b)(6)) should require the plan to provide a written “incomplete” determination that explains missing elements and appeals process.

Consumer rights group: Written notices explaining the reason for planned disenrollment (§422.74(c)) must include evidence relied upon, the specific contractual or policy provision alleged to be violated, and instructions for submitting rebuttal materials.

Legal expert: Requiring the written disenrollment notice to be provided before submission to CMS (§422.74(c)(1)) is appropriate but CMS should specify minimum timing (e.g., at least 30 days before submission) so beneficiaries have meaningful opportunity to respond.

Patient advocates: Inclusion of the right to submit a grievance in the disenrollment notice (§422.74(c)(2)) is necessary but should also list independent external appeal options and contact information for state health insurance assistance programs.

Consumer advocate: Permitting reinstatement without interruption after premium nonpayment (§422.74(d)(1)(v)) is beneficial, but CMS should limit retroactive reinstatement liability for providers and clarify whether cost sharing applies retroactively.

Legal expert: The 60‑day deadline for reinstatement requests after premium nonpayment (§422.74(d)(1)(v)(A)) mirrors other provisions; request CMS consolidate and align these 60‑day rules and provide tolling for hospitalization or natural disasters.

Disability advocate: The prohibition on multiple requests for reinstatement during the same 60‑day period (§422.74(d)(1)(v)(B)) risks denying vulnerable beneficiaries who file duplicate requests due to confusion; request an exception for requests filed but lost by the plan or CMS.

Consumer group: Requiring showing good cause for failure to pay within the initial grace period (§422.74(d)(1)(v)(C)) should include a presumption of good cause for documented hospital stays or medically necessary institutionalizations during the grace period.

Low‑income advocacy group: Payment of overdue premiums within 3 months to reinstate (§422.74(d)(1)(v)(D)) should allow for income‑based payment plans and require MA organizations to assist beneficiaries in applying for subsidy programs.

Legal expert: The “credible statement” standard for justification of nonpayment (§422.74(d)(1)(v)(E)) is vague; recommend CMS define evidentiary thresholds and prohibit blanket denials based solely on absence of documentary proof when such proof is unavailable.

Consumer rights organization: The MA organization’s duty to make a serious effort and provide reasonable accommodations for mental/cognitive conditions (§422.74(d)(2)(iii)) should include mandatory training, documentation requirements, and audits for compliance.

Disability advocate: “Reasonable accommodations as determined by CMS” (§422.74(d)(2)(iii)) must be publicly listed with examples and a clear process for beneficiaries to request and appeal accommodation denials.

Patient advocacy group: Informing individuals of right to use grievance procedures via notices (§422.74(d)(2)(iii)) requires that notices also explain timeframes and that the organization will not seek disenrollment while a grievance is pending.

Consumer advocate: Documentation of behavior, organizational efforts, and extenuating circumstances (§422.74(d)(2)(iv)) should prohibit collection of non‑relevant medical or behavioral health records beyond what is necessary and require beneficiary consent for sensitive disclosures.

Legal expert: Allowing MA organizations to request permission to decline future enrollment by an individual (§422.74(d)(2)(iv)) raises due process issues; request CMS establish a transparent review process, standards for refusal, and rights to appeal CMS’s decision.

Consumer advocate: Requiring submission of beneficiary‑provided documentation to CMS (§422.74(d)(2)(iv)) should include protections so that plans cannot coerce beneficiaries into waiving privacy rights when providing evidence.

Compliance officer: Submitting dated copies of notices to CMS (§422.74(d)(2)(iv)) must include electronic submission standards and deadlines; ask CMS to provide an electronic portal and sample templates to reduce administrative errors.

Consumer advocate: Providing two notices before submitting the disenrollment request to CMS (§422.74(d)(2)(vii)) should require that at least one notice be personally delivered or confirmed by phone for high‑risk cases (behavioral health, cognitive impairment).

Patient rights group: Restarting the notice/process if disruptive behavior stops and later resumes (§422.74(d)(2)(vii)) could be manipulated to prolong disenrollment timelines; request CMS require objective incident thresholds (e.g., number/severity of incidents) before restarting.

Consumer advocate: The 30‑day waiting requirement after the advance notice before issuing the second notice (§422.74(d)(2)(vii)) should be accompanied by mandatory interventions (care planning, in‑home supports) during that period for beneficiaries with complex needs.

Legal expert: The second notice of intent to request disenrollment (§422.74(d)(2)(vii)) must include a clear statement that the MA organization will submit supporting documentation to CMS and advise beneficiaries how to submit rebuttal material directly to CMS.

MA plan: The requirement to disenroll and document basis when an individual permanently moves (§422.74(d)(4)(i)) needs clear guidance on acceptable proofs of permanent move (lease, utility bills, declarations) and how temporary relocations are handled.

Consumer advocate: Documentation of basis for disenrollment due to move (§422.74(d)(4)(i)) must not rely on third‑party address data without beneficiary confirmation; request beneficiary notice and ability to contest address determinations.

Legal expert: The 10‑day timing tied to confirmation of residence/temporary absence for issuing disenrollment notice (§422.74(d)(4)(iv)) is ambiguous; ask CMS to clarify triggers and require mailed notice plus verbal confirmation when possible.

SNP advocacy group: Providing at least 30 days advance notice when an enrollee loses special needs status (§422.74(d)(8)) is appropriate, but CMS should require outreach assistance to help enrollees find alternative plans suited to their needs.

Consumer advocate: The 10‑calendar‑day requirement to provide advance notice after learning of loss of special needs status (§422.74(d)(8)(i)) is too short for beneficiaries to gather documentation to prove continued eligibility; request 30 days.

Patient advocates: Advance notices that must include SEP eligibility, deemed continued eligibility, and consequences (§422.74(d)(8)(ii)) should be standardized in plain language and translated into multiple languages commonly spoken in the plan’s service area.

Consumer rights group: Sending the final involuntary disenrollment notice within 3 business days following the disenrollment effective date and before submitting to CMS (§422.74(d)(8)(iii)) risks beneficiaries missing opportunities to appeal; require that final notice include appeal instructions and that disenrollment be stayed while an appeal is pending.

Legal expert: Requiring final involuntary disenrollment notice to explain right to file a grievance (§422.74(d)(8)(iv)) is necessary but insufficient; recommend inclusion of timelines for filing and contact details for state/regional advocates.

Clinician association: Allowing MA organizations to create internal coverage criteria when external criteria are absent (§422.101(b)(6)) may lead to inconsistent access; request CMS limits on using internal criteria to restrict access and requirement for CMS review of such criteria.

Consumer advocate: Requirement to provide a publicly accessible summary of evidence for internal coverage criteria (§422.101(b)(6)(i)) must mandate posting in machine‑readable format and require notification to affected enrollees when criteria change.

Research organizations: The obligation to provide a list of sources used in internal coverage criteria (§422.101(b)(6)(ii)) should require full citations and links to studies, and require disclosure of unpublished data or manufacturer submissions.

Patient advocates: The mandated rationale explanation for internal coverage criteria (§422.101(b)(6)(iii)) should include how considerations like patient preferences, clinical heterogeneity, and social determinants were weighed.

Medical societies: The requirement that medical necessity determinations be based on coverage criteria, section 1862(a)(1) reasonableness, medical history, and medical director involvement (§422.101(c)(1)(i)) is appropriate but CMS should specify when medical director involvement is “appropriate” to avoid denial without clinical review.

Provider groups: MA organizations must base determinations on coverage/benefit criteria (§422.101(c)(1)(i)(A)); request CMS ensure that plan‑developed criteria align with NCDs/LCDs and require reconciliation when conflicts occur.

Patient rights advocates: The prohibition on denying basic benefits based on coverage criteria not specified in paragraphs (b) or (c) (§422.101(c)(1)(i)(A) prohibition) should be enforced with penalties and public reporting for violations.

Clinicians: The obligation to consider reasonable/necessary under section 1862(a)(1) (§422.101(c)(1)(i)(B)) should include explicit guidance on how plans document and weigh functional outcomes and clinician input.

Provider organizations: Considering enrollee medical history, physician recommendations, and clinical notes (§422.101(c)(1)(i)(C)) must be documented in denial letters; request that plans be required to cite which elements were considered and why they were insufficient.

Physician groups: Involving the organization’s medical director when appropriate (§422.101(c)(1)(i)(D)) should be expanded to require clinical review by an independent specialty reviewer for complex denials and require documentation of their qualifications.

Hospitals/SNF providers: Permitting MA organizations to elect to provide posthospital SNF care without prior qualifying hospital stay (§422.101(c)(2)) is beneficial; recommend CMS incentivize plans to adopt this option and provide clear payment rules.

I–SNP operators: Contracts with long‑term care institutions must allow I–SNP staff access (§422.101(f)(2)(vi)); CMS should define reasonable notice and privacy protocols for access and require facility cooperation standards.

SNP operators: The MOC element and aggregate benchmark thresholds (50% per element; 70% aggregate) (§422.101(f)(3)(iii)) may be too rigid; request phase‑in, appeals for borderline scores, and transparency in scoring rubrics.
C–SNPs: A one‑year approval for a passing C–SNP MOC (§422.101(f)(3)(iii)(A)) is short; request multi‑year approvals (2–3 years) to allow programs time to implement and measure outcomes.

I/D‑SNP operators: The tiered approval durations based on aggregate scores (§422.101(f)(3)(iii)(B)) create instability; request softened cutoffs, remediation plans before downgrades, and clarity on how performance is remeasured.

MA organizations: Allowing one corrected resubmission for failed MOCs with 1‑year approval (§422.101(f)(3)(iii)(C)) is restrictive; request two resubmissions and that corrected resubmissions be eligible for longer approval if substantial improvements shown.

SNP legal counsel: Prohibiting implementation of MOC changes until NCQA approval and that no rescoring occurs during off‑cycle review (§422.101(f)(3)(iv)(D)) could prevent urgent clinical updates; recommend an expedited interim approval pathway for clinically necessary changes.

D/I–SNP compliance staff: The June 1–Nov 30 window for MOC updates/corrections (§422.101(f)(3)(iv)(A)) may not align with operational cycles; request flexibility or predefined off‑cycle submission windows for urgent updates.

SNP administrators: The requirement to submit off‑cycle updates when substantial changes occur (§422.101(f)(3)(iv)(B)) should include clear definitions of “substantial change” and examples to avoid inconsistent reporting.

SNP quality officer: Allowing a one‑time cure of off‑cycle MOC deficiencies between June 1 and Nov 30 (§422.101(f)(3)(iv)(G)) is helpful but CMS should specify timelines for cure and consequences for failure to cure.

Clinical trial advocates: The obligation that original Medicare covers routine costs and complication costs for MA enrollees in CMS‑approved trials (§422.109(e)(1)) is positive; commenters will request explicit notice requirements so enrollees know their coverage rights before enrolling.

Legal/consumer groups: The prohibition on charging MA enrollees traditional Medicare Part A/B deductibles for clinical trial coverage (§422.109(e)(2)) should be explicitly enforced with audit rights and penalties for plans that attempt to collect those deductibles.

MA plan actuary: Requiring MA plans to pay the difference between traditional Medicare cost‑sharing and plan in‑network cost‑sharing for clinical trial services (§422.109(e)(3)) raises potential fiscal impacts; request CMS guidance on accounting and reporting these adjustments.

Consumer advocates: Including enrollee in‑network cost‑sharing for clinical trial services in the plan’s MOOP calculation (§422.109(e)(4)) should prevent plans from excluding such costs; request monitoring and public reporting to ensure compliance.

Research/advocacy groups: Prohibiting prior authorization or impediments to participating in non‑plan‑sponsored Medicare‑qualified clinical trials (§422.109(e)(5)) should include enforcement language and examples of prohibited impediments (e.g., retroactive denials, site restrictions).

MA plans: The obligation to pay for routine care in CMS‑approved IDE Category A/B studies (§422.109(f)(1)) needs alignment with FDA/CMS timelines and definitions; ask CMS to clarify scope and billing rules to prevent disputes.

Device manufacturers: MA plans’ obligation to cover CMS‑approved Category B devices (§422.109(f)(2)) should include clear coding, prior authorization exceptions, and timetables for coverage determinations.

Consumer transparency advocates: The detailed provider network disclosure requirements (§422.111(b)(3)(i)) must be published in machine‑readable form, updated frequently (e.g., monthly), and include wait‑time estimates and telehealth capacity.

Consumer advocates: The obligation to notify enrollees of a contracted provider’s termination (§422.111(e)) should require plans to provide transition-of‑care options and honor existing authorizations for a reasonable period.

Patient groups: The “good faith effort” to notify enrollees of for‑cause provider terminations within required timeframes (§422.111(e)) must be defined (number of contact attempts, modalities) and audited for compliance.

Mental health advocates: For primary care or behavioral health provider terminations (§422.111(e)(1)(i)), requiring both written and telephonic notice is essential; request that plans also provide care coordination outreach to affected patients.

Consumer advocates: The 45‑calendar‑day advance notice for primary care/behavioral health terminations (§422.111(e)(1)(ii)) is reasonable but must include exceptions for emergent terminations that threaten patient safety and require immediate alternative arrangements.

Patient advocates: Notifying all enrollees who have ever been patients of a terminating primary care/behavioral health provider (§422.111(e)(1)(iii)) could be administratively burdensome; ask CMS to narrow to patients seen within the past 12 or 24 months to ensure relevancy.

Specialty provider organizations: For specialty provider terminations (§422.111(e)(2)(i)), written notice is appropriate; request clarity on whether email suffices and how to handle providers with high volumes of affected enrollees.
Provider groups: The 30‑calendar‑day notice for specialty provider terminations (§422.111(e)(2)(ii)) should be aligned with contractual termination notice periods to prevent conflicting obligations.

Consumer advocates: Notifying enrollees who are regular patients of a terminating specialty provider (§422.111(e)(2)(iii)) should define “regular basis” more precisely (e.g., 2 visits in past 6 months or ongoing treatment plan) and require plans to assist in finding replacement providers.

raw_output:
[P1] The rule is internally inconsistent because § 93.427(c)(1) requires the "M" mark on the right hip for steers/spayed heifers from Mexico, but § 93.427(e)(3)(i) requires the mark on the upper right front shoulder, creating legal uncertainty about the correct location.

[P1] Industry commenters will request clarification and harmonization between subsections so producers know whether to brand hip or shoulder; enforcement cannot rely on two conflicting placement requirements.

[P1] Legal experts will argue the conflict could render enforcement arbitrary and subject to challenge under the Administrative Procedure Act unless the agency issues an explanatory preamble or corrective amendment.

[P2] Producers will object that the 3–5 inch size requirement is too narrow and may be difficult to achieve consistently in field conditions, particularly for smaller animals or with certain branding methods.

[P2] Animal welfare organizations may comment that a 3–5 inch freeze or hot-iron brand could increase animal pain compared to smaller marks and request consideration of nonthermal alternatives or reduction in size.

[P2] Meat processors will note that the specified size may be unnecessary for carcass inspection visibility and propose allowing smaller marks if they remain legible on carcasses, or allowing electronic/labeled carcass tags as an alternative.

[P3] Ranchers and importers will assert that the requirement to place the top of the brand within 4 inches of the tailhead midline is impractical for animals with varying conformation (e.g., very fat or muscled cattle) and ask for an alternative tolerance zone or flexibility based on animal anatomy.

[P3] Veterinary groups will request that the rule allow authorized veterinarians to certify alternate placement when hip anatomy prevents the exact 4-inch placement to avoid repeated branding attempts that could harm the animal.

[P4] Stakeholders will point out that § 93.427(c)(1) states the 18-inch-from-anus guidance as a recommendation, not a requirement, causing confusion with the mandatory 4-inch midline rule; they will request the agency either makes it mandatory or removes the contradictory guidance.

[P4] Animal welfare advocates will express concern that recommending proximity to the anus could increase the risk of infection or contamination during slaughter and request sanitation protocols be specified if brands are applied in that region.

[P5] Consumer advocates and animal welfare groups will oppose the slaughter exemption (§ 93.429) if animals move through feedlots or holding facilities where marks inform traceback; they will request documentation requirements for exempted animals to prevent fraud.

[P5] Importers will support the slaughter exemption but request clear documentation (e.g., slaughter-only import permits) and procedures to ensure animals inadvertently diverted from slaughter remain traceable.

[P6] Meatpackers will request clearer standards for what constitutes "easily visible on the carcass before skinning," proposing objective visibility tests or photographic examples to eliminate inspector discretion.

[P6] Industry commenters will argue that some acceptable marking methods (e.g., freeze brand) can fade on carcasses and ask that the rule permit accompanying documentation (movement papers, electronic ID) to corroborate identity if carcass visibility is poor.

[P7] Small-scale producers will argue repeating the 3–5 inch requirement in § 93.427(e)(3)(i) for carcass marks is redundant and suggest consolidating size standards in one place to avoid conflicting interpretations.

[P7] Cattle breed associations will comment that certain coat colors (very dark or very light) affect legibility at the specified size and request allowance for larger marks or contrasting dyes for carcass visibility.

[P8] Livestock transporters and ranchers will object to requiring marks on the upper right front shoulder (per § 93.427(e)(3)(i)) because that placement can interfere with shoulder cuts and value at slaughter, and request relocation to a non-usual-cut area or to the hip as per c(1).

[P8] Animal welfare and husbandry groups will note that shoulder branding can be more painful or cause mobility issues and request that the agency prefer freeze-branding or nonthermal options if shoulder placement is maintained.

[P9] Several stakeholders will request that the rule explicitly permit scarring, ear notches, and electronic identifiers (RFID tags) as alternative "other methods" to accommodate modern identification practices and reduce animal welfare impacts.

[P9] Privacy/traceability advocates will insist that "other method" be defined to exclude temporary paints or washes and require methods to be permanent and tamper-resistant, with standards for acceptable technology.

[P10] Processors will request precise criteria for "easily visible on the live animal and on the carcass before skinning," such as minimum contrast, inspection distance, and lighting conditions, to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P10] Consumer safety groups will comment that visibility on carcass before skinning is insufficient for traceability after processing and ask for provisions requiring linkage between brands and official export/import records to ensure chain-of-custody.

[P1] Exporters and Mexican industry groups will request a transition period before enforcement to allow Mexican producers time to adopt the specific branding size, placement, and method standards.

[P2] Small-scale Mexican ranchers will comment that applying a 3–5 inch uniform brand may require new equipment and training, requesting financial or technical assistance to comply.

[P3] Enforcement agencies will ask for authority to accept pre-arrival inspection photographs showing correct placement when animals are to be imported at dispersed locations, to reduce port delays.

[P5] Customs attorneys will warn that the slaughter exemption could be misused to circumvent identification for animals intended for breeding or resale, and recommend documentation and audit provisions to prevent abuse.

[P6] Animal health authorities will request that brands be readable after refrigeration and during various carcass handling procedures, and ask the agency to test methods under typical processing conditions before finalizing the rule.

[P9] Veterinary associations will request that the rule specify training or certification standards for personnel applying brands to ensure marks are legible and applied humanely.

[P1] The requirement that all State, university, and private laboratories obtain APHIS approval before conducting any official testing is overly broad and will create undue delays during outbreaks when rapid testing by capable but unapproved labs could be critical.

[P1] The rule does not clarify whether routine surveillance or research testing that contributes to outbreak detection is considered “official testing,” creating uncertainty for university research labs about when APHIS approval is required.

[P2] Requiring applicants to comply with all requirements in § 71.22 without a clear, itemized checklist in the regulation itself is vague and may permit arbitrary denial; APHIS should publish a definitive checklist and allow phased compliance timelines.

[P3] The phrase “controlled conditions, appropriate instruments, and commensurate biosecurity” is vague; the regulation should specify minimum biosafety level (BSL) requirements, engineering controls, instrumentation standards, and acceptable biosecurity practices for each disease class.

[P3] Small or rural veterinary diagnostic labs lack funds to upgrade facilities to unspecified “controlled conditions” and will be excluded—there should be a proportionality or tiered standard based on risk and test type.

[P4] Allowing periodic, unannounced inspections using an APHIS checklist raises privacy and operational concerns; APHIS should limit inspections to reasonable hours and provide advance notice except in documented emergency situations.

[P4] The regulation should require APHIS to publish the inspection checklist and criteria in advance so labs know what will be inspected and can avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P5] “Quality system acceptable to APHIS” is subjective; APHIS must define minimum elements (document control, corrective actions, validation) or explicitly accept ISO/IEC 17025 as presumptively acceptable.

[P6] The permission to use recognized national/international quality systems is helpful but APHIS should explicitly list accepted standards (e.g., ISO/IEC 17025, CLIA for human labs where applicable, GLP) to avoid case-by-case uncertainty.

[P7] Inspectors’ review of quality system records could implicate proprietary or client-sensitive data; APHIS should limit review to records relevant to diagnostic quality and protect confidential business information.

[P8] Requiring all official tests to use APHIS-approved assay methods could slow adoption of new validated methods; APHIS should provide an expedited pathway for review and provisional approval of emergent assays during outbreaks.

[P9] Allowing NVSL/NAHLN SOPs and USDA-licensed kits is appropriate, but the rule should also explicitly accept peer-reviewed, validated methods from accredited reference labs to encourage innovation.

[P10] Limiting performance of official testing to individuals with APHIS-approved training and APHIS-administered proficiency tests may create bottlenecks—APHIS should accept equivalent training and proficiency assessments from recognized accreditation bodies.

[P11] Annual or APHIS-determined interval proficiency testing will impose costs and staffing burdens; APHIS must estimate costs and provide funding or fee waivers for public health labs with limited budgets.

[P12] Supervisory oversight by individuals “determined qualified by APHIS” is vague; the rule should specify minimum qualifications (degrees, years’ experience, certifications) or allow equivalent credentials certified by professional bodies.

[P13] Disease-specific reporting timelines set by APHIS could be burdensome if unpredictably changed; the rule should require APHIS to publish timelines with at least 30 days’ notice and to coordinate with State animal health officials.

[P14] Mandatory use of APHIS application forms and an agreement to meet all section obligations is reasonable, but APHIS should provide electronic submission capability and an estimated processing time to reduce administrative burden.

[P15] The permission to request inspection and training after a preliminary positive determination is useful; APHIS must publish estimated wait times for inspections/training to enable operational planning.

[P16] Providing a rationale for preliminary denials is necessary; APHIS should be required to include specific corrective actions and a timeline for reapplication to ensure fairness.

[P17] The appeal right under paragraph (j) is appropriate, but the rule should permit informal conferences or expedited appeals for denial decisions affecting outbreak response.

[P18] The NVSL Director’s sole authority to issue final approval centralizes decision-making; commenters request a defined timeframe for final approvals (e.g., 60 or 90 days) and an independent review if not acted upon.

[P19] Requiring reapplication at least 1 month before expiration or every 2 years may be administratively frequent for stable labs; extend renewal interval to 3–5 years for labs with good compliance records.

[P20] The need to submit APHIS-supplied renewal forms to the NVSL Director should allow electronic renewals and confirmation receipts; lack of this capability will create delays.

[P21] Requiring an approved lab to always employ at least one person with unexpired proficiency certification is reasonable for continuity, but APHIS should allow documented contingency plans (cross-training, MOUs with nearby labs) during short-term staff absences.

[P22] Mandating performance of a minimum number of tests as stipulated in APHIS guidance is potentially arbitrary; APHIS must publish the minimums by disease and provide scientifically justified thresholds and allowance for low-case prevalence periods.

[P23] Placing a lab on probation after failing minimum tests in one period could disproportionately penalize small-volume labs; probation should be accompanied by technical assistance and a remedial plan period before formal probation is imposed.

[P24] Allowing probationary labs to continue official testing risks quality degradation; probation should be accompanied by enhanced oversight, mandatory corrective actions, and reporting until compliance is demonstrated.

[P25] Declaring labs ineligible for renewal after two consecutive shortfalls without consideration of external causes (e.g., supply chain disruptions, regional outbreaks reducing sample flow) is unfair; APHIS should allow documented extenuating circumstances and alternative proficiency demonstration.

[P26] Granting the NVSL Director discretion to grant exceptions to minimum-test requirements is necessary but should be subject to published criteria and appealable decisions to prevent arbitrary denial of exceptions.

[P27] Suspending approval when labs undergo changes that impact quality is appropriate, but APHIS must provide clear definitions of what changes trigger suspension and a rapid pathway for temporary authorization under controlled conditions.

[P28] Examples of triggering changes (loss of approved personnel, relocation, utility-disrupting disasters) are useful; APHIS should require labs to report such changes within a defined short window (e.g., 72 hours) and provide interim guidance.

[P29] Prohibiting suspended labs from conducting official testing may create service gaps; APHIS should permit conditional authorization where mitigation measures (e.g., oversight by another approved lab) are in place.

[P30] Reinstatement after training, inspection, or corrective actions is sensible; APHIS must specify timelines and objective criteria for “successful” outcomes to prevent open-ended suspension.

[P31] Requiring resubmission of sections of application materials as required by the NVSL Director is vague; APHIS should specify which sections must be resubmitted for common suspension reasons to streamline reapproval.

[P32] Allowing the NVSL Director to rescind approval at any time for failure to meet obligations concentrates power without due process; commenters request additional procedural protections and independent review before rescission.

[P33] The NVSL Director’s notice explaining reasons for proposed removal must be detailed and include factual findings, references to the specific obligations violated, and corrective actions required.

[P34] Giving labs 30 days to respond before final removal may be insufficient for complex disputes; propose extending the response period to 45–60 days, or allow immediate interim measures pending a full response rather than immediate removal.

[P35] Appeal submissions must be permitted by electronic filing, and the regulation should clarify required content for appeals and provide contact information for the APHIS Administrator or designee.

[P36] APHIS’s commitment to respond to appeals within 60 days is positive, but the rule should state that failure to respond within 60 days results in automatic temporary relief (e.g., stay of probation/suspension) until APHIS acts.

[P4] State animal health agencies may object that the rule does not clarify coordination between APHIS inspections and State inspections, risking duplicative efforts and resource strain.

[P13] Laboratories and States request that APHIS publish all disease-specific reporting timelines and any changes in the Federal Register or on a publicly accessible website to ensure transparency.

[P11] Professional associations request that APHIS recognize proficiency testing done by external accredited providers (e.g., AAVLD, ISO proficiency programs) in lieu of APHIS-administered tests to reduce redundancy.

[P22] Small-animal and food-animal diagnostic labs ask for exemptions or reduced minimum-test requirements for low-prevalence diseases or for labs serving small populations, with options to demonstrate proficiency via inter-lab comparisons.

[P6] International diagnostic partners and export-oriented labs need assurance that recognized international quality systems (e.g., OIE standards) will be accepted to avoid trade disruptions.

[P8] Diagnostic manufacturers request a clear process and timeline for review and acceptance of new diagnostic kits to be included among APHIS-approved assay methods.

[P21] Workforce-constrained labs request an allowance for tele-supervision or electronic oversight by APHIS-qualified supervisors during temporary staffing shortages.

[P32] Constitutional and civil liberties groups may raise concerns about unannounced inspections’ implications for Fourth Amendment-type protections and request limits or warrants for certain intrusive inspections.

[P4] Accreditation bodies request that APHIS align inspection frequency and scope with existing accreditation cycles (e.g., AAVLD, ISO) to reduce duplication.

raw_output:
[P1] The May 23, 2023 comment deadline is unreasonable and insufficient for international operators, manufacturers, and labor groups to review technical attachments (figures 3–7) and submit coordinated responses; request extension of the comment period by at least 60–90 days.

[P1] The AD does not specify how commenters can obtain high-resolution or machine-readable copies of figures 3–7 referenced in the rule; request that the FAA provide downloadable, print-quality figures and any underlying data in the docket.

[P2] The compliance clause “within the specified compliance times unless already done” is vague; request clarification of whether earlier operator actions under AD 2022–04–05 satisfy each new paragraph automatically or whether documentation must be resubmitted.

[P3] Requiring AFM Limitations to be revised within 2 days after Feb 14, 2022 is retroactive and impossible for operators who received this AD after that date; request correction to use the effective date of the current AD (not the prior AD) or provide relief for late notice.

[P3] The 2-day compliance time for inserting figure 3 into AFMs is practically unachievable for large operators with many aircraft and distributed AFM inventories; request extension to at least 30 days or allowance to apply revisions during the next scheduled maintenance.

[P4] While insertion of figure 3 is permitted, the AD should allow electronic AFM updates or portable electronic flight bags (EFBs) as an acceptable method instead of only physical insertion; request explicit permission for EFB distribution and electronic marking of AFMs.

[P5] The 2-day requirement to revise Operating Procedures with figure 4 repeats the retroactivity problem; request that the FAA align these dates with the current AD issuance and provide a realistic compliance window for operators.

[P6] The permission to insert figure 4 does not state format/size/validation requirements; request specification that inserted figures must be legible, include revision/date stamps, and be logged in the aircraft records.

[P7] The distinction between “non-radio altimeter tolerant” and other classifications is not defined in the AD; request explicit definition criteria and a clear method for operators to determine which category their aircraft fall into.

[P8] The June 30, 2023 deadline to incorporate figure 5 for non-radio altimeter tolerant airplanes is insufficient for internationally registered aircraft that require home-state approval of AFM changes; request coordination time and extension to 120 days.

[P8] The AD should specify whether incorporation of figure 5 into operator MELs or company procedures is acceptable in lieu of changing the manufacturer’s AFM when operators use company-supplemented AFMs.

[P9] Allowing insertion of figure 5 into the AFM is fine, but the rule must allow a temporary placard or checklist alternative for aircraft that use standardized AFM books maintained by the manufacturer, pending permanent AFM revision.

[P10] Requiring removal of the paragraph (h)(1) AFM revision before next flight after incorporating figure 5 could create confusion and missed steps; request that the FAA allow a 24-hour grace period to complete the exchange and require logging of both revisions.

[P11] The AD mandates separate paths for radio altimeter tolerant airplanes but does not provide criteria or testing procedures to determine “tolerance”; request the FAA publish the technical standard or approved testing protocol.

[P12] The June 30, 2023 due date to insert figure 6 for radio altimeter tolerant airplanes is too close and does not account for fleet-wide coordination; request that compliance be aligned across subparagraphs and extended.

[P13] As with other figure insertions, inserting figure 6 should be allowed electronically (EFB) and via operator amendments to the quick reference handbook (QRH); request explicit permission and guidance.

[P14] The requirement to remove paragraph (h)(1) AFM revision before next flight after incorporating figure 6 may produce inconsistent AFM states across the fleet; request standardized administrative procedures and a model log entry for removal.

[P15] Requiring all affected airplane operators to perform actions in (k)(1) and (k)(2) may duplicate previous ADs without clear benefit; request that the FAA provide a table cross-referencing which airplanes are newly affected vs. already compliant under AD 2022–04–05.

[P16] The June 30, 2023 deadline for revising Operating Procedures to include figure 7 for all airplanes is arbitrary and may conflict with international continuing airworthiness rules; request synchronization with EASA and other authorities and extension.

[P16] The AD should clarify whether the Operating Procedures revision requires formal approval by the aircraft certification holder (Boeing) or can be implemented by operators under their operational control.

[P17] Permitting insertion of figure 7 does not address operators that use consolidated, company-level AFM supplements; request allowance for inclusion in the company operations manual or AFM supplement with cross-reference.

[P18] The obligation to remove the paragraph (h)(2) AFM revision before next flight after incorporating figure 7 creates operational risk if the removal is not coordinated; request a requirement to document the change in the aircraft maintenance log and to notify crewmembers by formal bulletin.

[P19] Granting the Manager authority to approve AMOCs is standard, but the AD should specify target response times for AMOC decisions (e.g., 30–60 days) to avoid operational delays; request a 45-day decision SLA.

[P20] The AMOC submission procedure should allow submission through designated FAA online systems and by the type certificate holder (Boeing) on behalf of multiple operators; request explicit acceptance of batch or consolidated AMOC requests.

[P21] Direct submittal to the person in paragraph (m) may not be feasible for international operators; request that the AD explicitly allow submissions through the U.S. principal inspector or the operator’s assigned FAA office without direct mailing to the person in (m).

[P22] Emailing AMOC information to AMOC@faa.gov is helpful, but the AD should require secure file transfer for large attachments and permit alternative filing for proprietary data; request FAA provide a secure upload portal and confirmation receipts.

[P23] Requiring notification to the principal inspector before using an approved AMOC could delay operations where rapid use is necessary; request that notification may be done within 24 hours after first use in emergency cases and that electronic notification satisfies the requirement.

[P24] Approval of AMOCs previously approved for AD 2021–23–12 only through June 30, 2023 creates a cliff that may strand operators who relied on those AMOCs; request automatic grandfathering of those AMOCs until the FAA reviews and either re-approves or issues alternate relief, or extend the date to provide time for re-evaluation.

[P25] Removing AD 2022–04–05 from § 39.13 without clear cross-reference to how remaining compliance is handled risks legal confusion; request the FAA include an explicit transition table showing how each requirement of the removed AD maps to the new AD.

[P26] Adding the new AD to § 39.13 for Boeing airplanes needs clarity on applicability by model, serial number, and modification status; request an explicit applicability list (Boeing models/series and serial ranges) and inclusion of post-production modifications that may change applicability.

[P3] Legal counsel: imposing retroactive compliance dates (Feb 14, 2022) may exceed the FAA’s rulemaking authority and could be challenged; request revision to ensure effective dates and compliance windows are forward-looking.

[P7] Pilot and labor groups: the AD imposes AFM/Operating Procedures changes without consulting pilot unions on human factors and training impacts; request human factors review and that changes be accompanied by required training guidance.

[P16] Maintenance/repair organizations: inserting procedures into the AFM may conflict with approved maintenance program items; request that the FAA coordinate with 145/147 organizations and allow incorporation via company maintenance manuals as appropriate.

[P8] International flag carriers: the June 30, 2023 deadline conflicts with some national aviation authority processes for AFM approval; request that the FAA accept foreign-authority-approved equivalents and provide an extended compliance window.

[P22] Privacy/FOIA: emailing AMOC requests to a public FAA email without guidance on sensitive security or proprietary information risks disclosure; request procedures for redacting or submitting sensitive attachments securely.

[P1] Small operators: the docket does not appear to include an economic analysis specific to small certificated operators for the administrative burden of manual AFM insertions; request a regulatory flexibility analysis and small-entity impact assessment.

[P12] Aerospace OEMs: the AD lacks technical justification explaining the differences in required limitations between radio altimeter tolerant and non-tolerant airplanes (figures 5 vs. 6); request the FAA publish the risk assessment and rationale.

[P10] Safety managers: requiring removal of earlier temporary AFM inserts before flight could lead to inadvertent loss of critical procedures during changeover; request a mandatory check and sign-off by maintenance release certifying both the insertion and removal actions.

[P24] Legal/operations: the AD should state whether AMOCs previously approved for AD 2021–23–12 are considered to satisfy any training or recordkeeping elements of the new AD beyond June 30, 2023, until renewed; request explicit continuity language.

[P4] Flight operations: the AD should permit use of revised Quick Reference Handbooks (QRH) with cross-references to AFM figures for immediate operational use, instead of only AFM insertion; request QRH allowance.

[P6] Airlines: require clarification whether the inserted figures require being signed and dated by a certificated person and recorded in the aircraft logbook as a revision per 14 CFR part 43 or company procedures.

[P21] International operators: provide a clear contact and escalation path for AMOC denial or delays, including appeal to higher FAA authorities or designated points of contact, to prevent prolonged grounding.

[P25] Consumers/advocates: removing the older AD without simultaneous public explanation could obscure earlier safety issues; request the FAA include a public summary explaining why AD 2022–04–05 is being removed and how safety is maintained.

[P26] Type certificate holders: require the FAA to coordinate with Boeing to issue an AFM revision bulletin or service letter to standardize the insert format and distribution; request mandatory manufacturer bulletin accompanying AD issuance.

Emailing AMOC information to AMOC@faa.gov is helpful, but the AD should require secure file transfer for large attachments and permit alternative filing for proprietary data; request FAA provide a secure upload portal and confirmation receipts.

Removing AD 2022–04–05 from § 39.13 without clear cross-reference to how remaining compliance is handled risks legal confusion; request the FAA include an explicit transition table showing how each requirement of the removed AD maps to the new AD.

International operators: provide a clear contact and escalation path for AMOC denial or delays, including appeal to higher FAA authorities or designated points of contact, to prevent prolonged grounding.

[P1] The requirement in §412.604(c) to complete a patient assessment instrument for every Medicare Part A fee-for-service admission or discharge since Jan 1, 2002 is retroactive and imposes recordkeeping burdens and potential liability for historical omissions; CMS should clarify whether enforcement will apply to pre-implementation periods or provide a safe-harbor.

[P2] Requiring IRFs to complete IRF-PAIs for Medicare Advantage patients under §412.604(c) starting Oct 1, 2009 creates inconsistent effective dates between payers that are confusing for billing and audit purposes; CMS should harmonize effective dates or explicitly explain transition rules.

[P3] The blanket expansion in §412.604(c)/P3 to require IRF-PAIs for all other patients regardless of payer beginning Oct 1, 2023 will substantially increase administrative workload and costs for IRFs without additional reimbursement; CMS must provide an implementation period, technical assistance, and funding or exclude non-Medicare payers.

[P4] §412.606(a) obligating use of the CMS IRF-PAI for Medicare Part A and C inpatients (P4/P51) lacks specificity about acceptable alternative validated instruments; providers request an allowance for certified third-party assessment tools that map to CMS data elements.

[P5] The Oct 1, 2023 universal-use requirement in §412.606(a)(1) (P5/P52) will require software upgrades and staff retraining; CMS should publish technical specifications and provide at least 12 months' notice plus testing windows before mandatory enforcement.

[P6] §412.606(b)(1) obligation that a "clinician" perform a comprehensive, standardized assessment (P6/P53) is vague about which licensed professions qualify as "clinician" — CMS should list acceptable clinician types (e.g., RN, PT, OT, physician) and whether trained non-licensed personnel may perform certain sections under supervision.

[P7] The duplicate statements across P7, P8, P54, P55 that require completion of the IRF-PAI for Part C and other payers create potential double-counting and compliance confusion; commenters request consolidation and clarity to avoid redundant regulatory language.

[P8] §412.610(a) and related provisions (P9/P56) require completion of the IRF-PAI covering a specified time period per schedule §412.610(c) but do not address situations with very short stays (e.g., same-day discharges); CMS should specify modified or abbreviated assessment requirements for stays under 24 or 48 hours.

[P9] Counting the first day of service as day one under §412.610(b) (P10) may force some admission assessments to be completed immediately upon admission even when clinically inappropriate; request flexibility allowing a clinician up to a specified number of hours (e.g., 24) to complete admission assessments.

[P10] §412.610(c) requirement to complete assessment at admission and discharge (P11/P57) lacks clear time windows for "discharge" assessments when patients are transferred or leave against medical advice; CMS should define maximum allowable time after cessation of IRF services for discharge assessment completion.

[P11] The definition of the assessment time period covering calendar days 1 through 3 in §412.610(c)(1)(i)(A) (P12) does not account for admissions that cross midnight or daylight-saving changes; CMS should clarify how to count calendar days for admissions late in the day.

[P12] The trigger in §412.610(c)(2)(ii)(B) that cessation of furnishing inpatient rehabilitation services requires a discharge assessment (P13) could be interpreted to require assessments for temporary interruptions (e.g., short medical transfers); CMS should clarify whether temporary transfers trigger discharge assessments or only permanent discharges.

[P13] §412.610(f) retention requirement (P14/P58) to maintain assessment data sets "in paper or readily producible electronic format" for production on request is overly prescriptive about format; commenters request CMS permit storage in certified electronic health record systems and clarify acceptable retrieval timeframes and security requirements.

[P14] Disparate retention periods—5 years for Part A (P15/P59), 10 years for Part C (P16/P60), and 5 years for other patients (P17/P61)—are administratively complex and may conflict with state law retention/privacy rules; CMS should harmonize retention periods or explain legal basis for longer Part C retention and compatibility with state requirements.

[P15] §412.614(a)/(b)(1) obligation to encode and electronically transmit complete, accurate IRF-PAI data to CMS (P18/P19/P62/P63) requires explicit data format, validation rules, and secure transmission standards; without published technical guidance and test environments, facilities face compliance risk and potential forfeitures.

[P16] The forfeiture consequences in §412.614(d)(2) for late Medicare Advantage (Part C) transmissions (P20/P64) are severe — permanently excluding Part C data from compliance calculations under §412.29(b)(1); commenters argue forfeiture should be applied proportionally or allow cure periods and administrative appeals before exclusion.

[P17] Similarly, §412.614(d)(3) forfeiture for late submissions for other payers (P21/P65) will discourage inclusion of non-Medicare data in compliance calculations; stakeholders request CMS adopt graduated sanctions, warning notices, and an opportunity to correct before data exclusion.

[P18] §412.614(e) grant of waiver discretion to CMS for extraordinary situations (P22/P66) is appropriate, but the rule’s language (P23/P67) that "only CMS" can determine extraordinariness without defined criteria is arbitrary; commenters request objective criteria, presumptive categories (e.g., natural disaster, major system outage), and an expedited review process.

[P19] The documentation requirement for waivers in §412.614(e) (P24/P68) is reasonable but should specify the form, timeline (how soon after the event documentation must be submitted), and what constitutes adequate evidence to avoid inconsistent denials.

[P20] §412.624(e)(1) wage index adjustment (P25/P69) based solely on facility location urban/rural status (P26/P70) may not capture sub-regional labor market differences; commenters from high-cost micropolitan areas request consideration of county-level or CBSA refinements.

[P21] The wage index decrease cap at 95% of prior year (§412.624(e)(1)(ii), P27/P71) is welcomed for stability, but CMS should explain how this interacts with budget-neutrality adjustments in §412.624(e)(1)(iii) (P28/P72) — commenters seek worked examples and transitional protections for facilities that still face large net payment reductions.

[P22] The budget-neutral wage adjustment mechanism in §412.624(e)(1)(iii) (P28/P72) could shift costs across providers unpredictably; commenters request CMS publish the methodology and the budget-neutral adjustment factor in advance so facilities can forecast revenue.

[P23] The teaching adjustment provisions (§412.624(e)(4)(i)-(E), P29-P35/P73-P78) rely on legacy cost report data and a base year ending Nov 15, 2004 (P33/P76); academic medical centers argue this base-year cap is outdated and penalizes programs that have legitimately expanded training since 2004 — request periodic re-evaluation or an upward adjustment mechanism.

[P24] The prohibition in §412.624(e)(4)(i)(B) against claiming resident time spent at another IRF or hospital (P32/P75) will disadvantage programs that use cross-coverage rotations essential for training; commenters ask CMS to permit limited pro-rated credit where significant training occurs and is documented.

[P25] Limiting FTE resident counts to numbers reported in the settled cost report for the base period (P33/P76) may disallow valid increases in trainee volume due to community needs; suggest an appeals process or verifiable exception path beyond the narrow new-program exception at (D).

[P26] The new-program exception (§412.624(e)(4)(i)(D)/(77)) that allows FTE adjustments only if training began after Nov 15, 2004 using §413.79(e)(1)(i) methodology is too narrow; academic programs that expanded existing specialties or merged programs after that date need clearer allowance and step-by-step guidance.

[P27] The interim nature of teaching adjustments (§412.624(e)(4)(i)(E)/(35)/(78)) tied to final cost report settlement creates cash-flow uncertainty; commenters request CMS accelerate reconciliation timelines or provide transitional payments to avoid financial stress during settlement lags.

[P28] The temporary FTE cap adjustment permission for displaced residents (P36/P79) is beneficial, but the 60-day submission deadlines in multiple subparts (P38/P42/P47/P81/P87) are impractical for complex transitions; commenters request extensions to 120 days or allowance for good-cause late filings.

[P29] §412.624(e)(4)(ii)(A)(1)/(80) requiring that displaced residents come from an IRF that closed on or after Oct 1, 2011 excludes residents displaced by program downsizing or mergers; commenters urge CMS to broaden eligibility to include bona fide displacements not strictly caused by closure.

[P30] The documentation and evidentiary standards for temporary FTE cap adjustments (P38/P43/P44/P81/P83) — including copies of closed hospital FTE reduction statements — may be difficult to obtain from closed entities; CMS should allow alternative evidence, sworn declarations, or contractor verification.

[P31] The requirement that a closed hospital itself submit a signed, dated FTE reduction statement within 60 days after displaced residents begin training elsewhere (P45-P47/P84-P85) is unworkable if the closed hospital no longer has administrators available; request that receiving IRFs be permitted to attest and supply corroborating documentation.

[P32] The rule does not explain how CMS will audit and verify transmitted IRF-PAI data used in wage index, teaching adjustments, or compliance metrics; commenters request a transparent audit protocol, timelines, and appeal rights to contest CMS data uses.

[P33] Small, rural IRFs will face disproportionate compliance costs from universal IRF-PAI requirements (P5/P52/P63) and annual retention/storage obligations (P14/P58-P61); request CMS provide a de minimis exemption for facilities below a patient-volume threshold or offer financial assistance/grants.

[P34] Patient privacy concerns: §412.610(f)/§412.614(b)(1) (P14/P63) require electronic transmission and retention of PAI data but lack explicit HIPAA-aligned data security and de-identification standards; commenters request CMS require encryption, access controls, and guidance on sharing with contractors.

[P35] The rule should clarify whether failure to include non-Medicare payer PAI data due to contractual limits with payers exempts the IRF from forfeiture under §412.614(d)(3) (P21/P65); insurers sometimes prohibit data sharing — CMS should coordinate with payers or limit penalties in such cases.

[P36] Legal commenters note potential conflict between the differentiated retention periods for Part C data (10 years) (P16/P60) and state-specific statutes of limitation or record-destruction laws; request CMS reconcile federal retention with applicable state requirements and liability exposure.

[P37] Vendors ask CMS to publish the exact machine-readable IRF-PAI schema, error codes, testing certification process, and a sandbox environment well in advance to avoid mass rejections and associated forfeitures under §412.614(d) (P15/P63/P66).

[P38] Quality advocates support broader collection of PAI data for all payers (P3/P50/P55) to improve outcomes measurement but urge CMS to publicly report de-identified aggregated metrics and provide risk adjustment methodology to prevent unintended penalization of providers treating more complex patients.

[P39] Enforcement fairness: commenters request CMS adopt a cure period (e.g., 30 days) and progressive enforcement for first-time late transmissions before applying data-use forfeiture under §412.614(d)(2)-(3) (P16/P17/P64/P65).

[P40] The regulation should specify whether paper PAI submissions are acceptable in emergencies or for providers without robust electronic systems, and how such submissions will be processed for compliance calculations (P13/P62).

[P41] Clarify whether the 95% wage-index floor (P27/P71) applies before or after budget-neutrality adjustments (P21/P22/P72) because its position will change the effective payment for many IRFs; request illustrative calculations.

[P42] Ask CMS to provide a hardship exemption process for facilities that experience prolonged IT vendor failures or cybersecurity incidents that prevent timely PAI transmission, beyond the narrow "extraordinary situation" waiver (P22/P66-P68).

[P43] Request clarification whether discharge assessments are required for patients who die during an IRF stay, and if so, what data elements are mandated and acceptable timelines (relates to P11/P57 and P13/P62).

[P44] Legal experts request CMS confirm that the rule does not expand CMS's authority to request IRF-PAI data for civil monetary penalty assessments unless separate regulatory authority is invoked, to prevent unintended uses of transmitted data.

[P45] Provider associations request CMS to delay enforcement of payer-neutral PAI requirements (Oct 1, 2023) (P3/P5/P50/P52) for at least 12 months beyond final rule publication to allow electronic health record vendors and facilities to comply.

[P46] Clarify whether rotating residents who split time across multiple sites may be credited proportionally across those sites for teaching adjustment purposes if supported by time logs, contrary to the prohibition on claiming time spent at another IRF for a single facility's adjustment (P31/P32/P75).

[P47] Hospitals that accept displaced residents under temporary FTE cap adjustments (P36-P41/P79-P83) request CMS to confirm that such temporary adjustments will not negatively affect their ability to add new residency slots in future years.

[P48] Request that CMS adopt a single uniform effective date across the PAI, transmission, retention, and wage/teaching provisions to reduce implementation complexity and allow coordinated compliance planning.

[P49] Small IRFs request clarification of whether subcontracted management companies can be held responsible for timely PAI submission and retention or whether liability remains with the IRF operator (affects P14/P18/P62-P63/P64-P65).

[P50] Comment that CMS should provide a centralized helpdesk and expedited adjudication process for waiver requests and temporary FTE cap adjustment requests to avoid inconsistent contractor-level adjudications (related to P22/P24/P36-P43/P81).
