[P1] The requirement that the Secretary appoint a five-member Board is arbitrary and lacks justification; commenters should request analysis showing why five members (rather than a larger or smaller number) is optimal for representation and decisionmaking.

[P1] Industry stakeholders will request that appointment processes and timelines be specified (e.g., nomination, vetting, and confirmation timelines) because §405.1845(a) gives no procedural detail on how appointments will be made.

[P1] Legal experts may claim the rule should specify conflict-of-interest standards, recusal obligations, and disclosure requirements for the five appointed Board members to avoid ethics concerns.

[P2] Trade associations representing hospitals and providers will object to the blanket requirement that all five members have knowledge of Medicare Part A provider payment, arguing it unduly narrows the candidate pool and excludes members with valuable health policy, public health, patient advocacy, or rural health expertise.

[P2] Patient advocacy groups will argue that the rule should explicitly permit at least one member with demonstrated expertise in patient rights or consumer advocacy in addition to technical Medicare payment knowledge, because the current text implicitly excludes such perspectives.

[P2] Commenters will request that the rule define "knowledge of Medicare Part A provider payment" (e.g., years of experience, types of prior roles, certifications) to ensure transparent, objective qualification criteria.

[P3] Certified public accountants' professional societies will support the CPA requirement but request clarification that the CPA may be licensed in any state and that equivalent certifications (e.g., international accounting credentials for U.S.-licensed practice) be accepted where appropriate.

[P3] Small hospital associations will request an exception permitting a health care financial officer with demonstrated Medicare Part A payment expertise to serve in lieu of a CPA if no CPA candidates with Medicare-specific experience are available.

[P4] Provider organizations will request clarification of "represent providers of services": whether it requires active/practicing providers, executives of provider organizations, or representatives from provider trade associations.

[P4] Nursing and allied health groups will object that requiring at least two provider-representative members could over-represent institutional interests and urge inclusion of at least one direct-care clinician (e.g., physician or nurse) to ensure clinical perspectives.

[P5] Hospital systems and boards will request that the Secretary publish the schedule of staggered initial term lengths when making appointments to provide predictability and avoid frequent turnover disrupting Board continuity.

[P5] Commenters will ask for a provision allowing members who take leaves of absence (e.g., medical or military) to have their terms tolled rather than counted against term limits, to avoid losing experienced members due to temporary absences.

[P6] Associations of former federal appointees will challenge the language permitting a Chairperson in a second or third consecutive term to serve up to four terms only while Chair, requesting clarification whether the extended term is automatic or requires re-designation and whether a Chair who loses the Chair designation must immediately vacate the extra-term seat.

[P6] Civil-society commenters will urge that the prohibition on serving more than three consecutive terms include an absolute cap (e.g., total years) to prevent de facto lifetime service through repeated reappointments.

[P6] Legal commenters will request clear definitions of "term" and rules for partial terms (if a member fills a vacancy mid-term) as to whether partial terms count toward consecutive-term limits.

[P7] Labor unions and provider groups will request that the Secretary publish the standards and process for "good cause" termination (notice procedures, opportunity to respond, and appeal rights) to protect due process for Board members.

[P7] Civil liberties advocates will insist on an independent review or appeal mechanism (e.g., administrative hearing) for any termination to avoid politicized removals.

[P8] Small independent hospitals will strongly support inclusion of buffer stock costs as an additional payment category but will request explicit definitions of "buffer stock" (what items qualify) and eligible cost categories to avoid inconsistent claims.

[P8] CMS auditors and fiscal intermediaries will request guidance on documentation standards and allowable supporting invoices for buffer stock costs to ensure consistent audit treatment.

[P9] Commenters will request that the rule clarify which hospitals qualify as "small, independent hospitals" (size thresholds, ownership criteria, affiliation limits) for §412.2(f)(11) to prevent inconsistent eligibility determinations.

[P9] Rural health advocates will request that the adjustment be available retroactively to cost reporting periods that experienced documented trauma to supply chains, not only to future periods.

[P10] Hospitals and auditors will request detailed instructions and worked examples on calculating average Medicare inpatient length of stay per §412.23(e)(3)(i), particularly addressing how transfers, same-day readmissions, and observation stays are treated.

[P10] Long-term care hospitals (LTCHs) will request clarification of whether psychiatric, rehabilitation, or observation days are included in "inpatient days" for the purpose of the average length-of-stay calculation.

[P11] Hospitals near the 25-day threshold will argue that requiring use of at least 5 months of prior data could produce unstable results for seasonal facilities and request a seasonal adjustment or alternative methodology for hospitals with documented seasonality.

[P11] Commenters will ask CMS to allow an appeal process or exception where hospitals can demonstrate that use of alternative months is more representative than the prior-6-month rule when the prior period was affected by anomalies (natural disaster, PHE).

[P12] Hospitals converting satellite/remote facilities into separate hospitals seeking LTCH status will request specific documentation templates and timelines for submission of discharges post-participation as required under §412.23(e)(4)(ii).

[P12] Commenters will request clarification whether discharges attributable to shared staffing or joint credentialing during the separation transition count toward the new hospital’s post-participation discharge history.

[P13] Rural hospital systems will request details on when and how the 5 months of discharge data from before separation must be submitted, and whether those months must be consecutive, and will ask how shared admissions between parent and satellite are allocated.

[P13] Commenters will recommend an allowance for additional months of pre-separation data when the five-month sample is affected by atypical events, to avoid misclassification.

[P14] Hospitals seeking LTCH classification will request precise definitions of "consecutive" months and whether short gaps due to data reporting lags or temporary closures interrupt the counting toward the 5 consecutive months requirement.

[P14] Commenters will urge CMS to publish an expedited review process for hospitals that meet the 6-month qualifying period so patient access is not delayed.

[P15] Hospital systems acquiring facilities will request clarification on the interplay of ownership change timing and cost reporting period boundaries to determine eligibility for exclusion from IPPS as an LTCH.

[P15] Medicare fiscal intermediaries will ask CMS to specify documentation needed to demonstrate continuous operation and continuous Medicare participation to support the post-ownership exclusion.

[P16] Manufacturers and provider groups will seek clarification of the base DRG payment comparison methodology and request worked examples demonstrating how the "lesser of two 75%-based calculations" is computed for gene therapies for sickle cell disease.

[P16] Patient advocates will support enhanced payment for high-cost gene therapies but request that CMS ensure payment timing aligns with clinical delivery to prevent provider cash-flow problems caused by large up-front therapy costs.

[P17] Hospitals and payers will request that CMS define "costs of the new medical service or technology" for the 75% calculation—specifically whether acquisition price, administration, monitoring, and follow-up care costs are included.

[P17] Pharmaceutical manufacturers will request that CMS permit inclusion of amortized therapy acquisition costs (e.g., for episodic high-cost therapies) in the cost calculation methodology.

[P18] Commenters will ask CMS to clarify the measurement of "the amount by which the costs of the case exceed the standard DRG payment" (gross costs vs. marginal/additional costs) used to compute the alternate 75% payment.

[P18] Hospitals will request guidance on documentation and audit trails demonstrating case costs that exceed the DRG payment, including vendor invoices, billing records, and clinical orders.

[P19] Providers will request that CMS publish the method and timing for estimating costs used to calculate the 75% estimated payment at discharge, including how to handle cases where final costs materially differ at settlement.

[P19] Commenters will urge inclusion of a reconciliation mechanism to ensure hospitals are reimbursed for underestimates, and not over-recover when estimates exceed final allowed costs.

[P20] Small and rural hospitals will request explicit criteria and documentation requirements for a hospital to be classified as Medicare-dependent, small rural (MDH), including any thresholds and periodic recertification requirements.

[P20] Commenters will ask whether prospective payment rate adjustments for MDH hospitals will be budget-neutral or funded separately and request impact analyses showing expected payment changes.

[P21] Osteopathic hospitals and rural referral center applicants will challenge the requirement of at least 3,000 discharges, arguing it is unduly high for many rural osteopathic facilities and will request alternative criteria (e.g., catchment-area population, referral patterns).

[P21] Legal commentators will ask CMS to clarify whether the 3,000-discharge threshold is counted during a single cost reporting period or over a rolling period and whether transfers and observation cases are included.

[P22] Small rural hospitals will question the continued use of the <200 discharges and >25 road miles standard for the FY 2005–2010 and post-2025 periods; they will request modernization of distance metrics (e.g., driving time or network availability) and updated discharge thresholds to reflect current rural demographics.

[P22] Commenters will ask CMS to reconcile overlapping eligibility periods (FY 2019–2024 rules vs. FY 2025 portions) and to publish guidance on which rule applies to ambiguous cost reporting periods.

[P23] Hospitals that fall between the thresholds will request clarity on the different miles and discharge tests across fiscal year windows and propose harmonizing the distance measurements (road miles) with modern mapping tools.

[P24] Hospitals eligible for low-volume adjustments will request confirmation that the additional 25% per Medicare discharge is applied before other adjustments and ask for examples showing final payment calculations.

[P24] Budget-constrained commenters will request CMS provide estimates of aggregate program costs associated with reinstating the 25% adjustment and any offsetting reductions elsewhere.

[P25] Providers and auditors will ask how historical 1983 dialysis sessions per week data will be validated and whether modern clinical practice changes justify updating the historical baseline for periods before Oct 1, 2024.

[P25] Commenters will note that reliance on 1983 session data is outdated and will ask CMS for justification and evidence that this historical figure remains representative for reimbursement purposes.

[P26] Dialysis providers will request clarification that calculating estimated weekly dialysis cost as "3 sessions/week times the ESRD PPS base rate" aligns with current clinical practice and will ask for transition rules to avoid sudden payment shocks.

[P26] Patient groups will express concern that assuming 3 sessions per week may undermine coverage for medically necessary more-frequent dialysis regimens and request a mechanism to reimburse for clinically indicated higher-frequency schedules.

[P27] Hospitals will seek a precise list of costs considered "directly related to renal dialysis services" for inclusion in the average cost calculation for periods before Oct 1, 2024, and request examples and audit documentation requirements.

[P27] Commenters will ask whether shared overhead or infection-control costs partially related to dialysis are excluded and seek guidance on allocation methods.

[P28] Providers will request that CMS publish the frequency and triggers for reviewing and adjusting the average dialysis cost in composite rate reimbursement reviews to enable forward planning.

[P28] Commenters will propose including a requirement that CMS publish results of such reviews and the rationale for any adjustments to promote transparency.

[P29] Teaching hospitals and academic medical centers will support the ability to use FTE slots in GME affiliation agreements beginning in the fifth year, but will request clear application, tracking, and portability rules to prevent double-counting or misuse.

[P29] Commenters will request examples showing how the five-year delay interacts with program start dates, transfers of residents, and joint training arrangements.

[P30] Hospitals concerned about uncompensated care will request CMS to explain the methodology for estimating interim uncompensated care payments based on the "average of the most recent three years of discharge data," including how outliers and pandemic years are weighted or excluded.

[P30] Safety-net hospitals will request accelerated interim payments or higher front-loaded interim amounts if historical data understate current uncompensated care due to recent increases in uninsured populations.

[P31] Small independent hospitals will support §412.113(g)(3) but request transition guidance and templates for claiming buffer stock adjustments for cost reporting periods beginning on/after Oct 1, 2024.

[P31] Commenters will ask whether hospitals that established buffer stocks before Oct 1, 2024 are eligible for adjustment for ongoing maintenance costs in subsequent periods.

[P32] Hospitals will ask CMS to define "estimated reasonable cost" (e.g., allowable cost categories, markup limits, depreciation rules) and to provide an audit protocol for buffer stock cost claims to limit future repayment risk.

[P32] Commenters will propose a capped per-hospital or per-bed buffer stock reimbursement formula or a standardized per-item cost schedule to simplify administration.

[P33] Hospitals will request clarity on the eCQM medical record sampling methodology, including sample size, selection method, and what constitutes "timely and complete" submission prior to FY2028.

[P33] Health IT vendors will ask CMS to define data element formats and transmission protocols tied to the 100% submission requirement to ensure interoperability and compliance.

[P34] Hospitals will request detailed explanation of how the 75% eCQM validation score for FY2028 and later will be calculated, including weighting of measures, handling of missing data, and whether site-level or system-level aggregation applies.

[P34] Commenters will ask for an appeals process and remediation pathway for hospitals that narrowly miss the 75% threshold, including opportunities for technical assistance.

[P35] Hospitals disputing CMS validation outcomes will request a specified evidentiary standard and deadline for reconsideration submissions and that CMS commit to providing the specific validation errors identified rather than a boilerplate conclusion.

[P35] Legal commenters will request CMS to permit submission of third-party attestations or independent audits along with the hospital's explanation in reconsideration requests.

[P36] Stakeholders will challenge the 45-day/7-day timing rule for requests for withdrawal as potentially conflicting with other appeal or administrative timelines and request harmonization with existing MGCRB procedures.

[P36] Commenters will ask CMS to clarify which date governs the 45-day period when filings are posted online and to extend the deadline where public inspection posting is delayed for reasons outside the requester’s control.

[P37] Applicants will request notice and cure opportunities if a termination request to MGCRB is filed late because of postal delays or system outages and recommend CMS adopt electronic filing with timestamp assurances.

[P37] Legal advocates will ask CMS to define extensions or equitable tolling provisions for the 45/7-day deadlines to prevent forfeiture of rights due to minor procedural delays.

[P38] Teaching hospitals absorbing displaced residents will request detailed guidance on the averaging methodology used when adding displaced FTE residents to the receiving hospital's count, including how partial years and mid-year transfers are handled.

[P38] Commenters will propose that displaced residents added to FTE counts be accompanied by funding or per-resident payment adjustments for the receiving hospital due to increased training costs.

[P39] Hospitals participating in GME affiliations will request detailed procedures and forms for using cap slots in affiliation agreements starting in year five, including documentation of slot transfers and duration limits.

[P39] Commenters will request CMS to clarify whether cap slots used in affiliation agreements are portable across multiple affiliations or permanently assigned to the receiving hospital.

[P40] Urban hospitals operating rural track programs will request clarification of how the rolling average is calculated for the rural track FTE limitation and whether attrition or leaves of absence affect the limit during the first 3 years.

[P40] Commenters will ask how the rule treats residents who split time between rural and urban sites in counting toward the rural track FTE limitation.

[P41] Hospitals will seek clarification of the term "prior to the start of the relevant cost reporting period" and request examples showing how to document the actual FTE number for calculation under §413.79(k)(2)(i)(B).

[P41] Commenters will ask CMS to allow corrections to the reported FTE number in case of clerical errors discovered after the reporting deadline, with an appeal or amendment process.

[P42] Hospitals will request clear instructions on compliance with §413.78(g) as applied to rural track FTE limitations for cost reporting periods beginning on/after Oct 1, 2022, and whether penalties apply for inadvertent over-reporting.

[P42] Commenters will ask for transitional relief if a hospital’s information systems cannot produce the required rolling-average data immediately.

[P43] Hospitals seeking increased FTE caps will request that CMS publish the application form, required supporting documentation, review timeline, and criteria used to determine whether statutory requirements are met for §413.79(q).

[P43] Commenters will propose allowing provisional increases pending final CMS approval when applications are timely submitted to avoid delays in resident recruitment for portions of cost reporting periods beginning July 1, 2026.

[P44] Hospitals will request that CMS specify the exact data elements and reporting frequencies for acute respiratory illness electronic reporting and provide burden estimates and timelines for system modifications.

[P44] Privacy advocates will request safeguards limiting the granularity of reported demographic data to prevent inadvertent patient identification and ensure HIPAA-compliant aggregation.

[P45] Hospitals will ask CMS to publish the Secretary-specified standardized format and frequency well in advance and to accept common interoperable formats (e.g., HL7 FHIR) rather than creating proprietary formats.

[P45] Health IT vendors will request a phased implementation timeline and test environment prior to mandatory reporting to ensure conformance with the Secretary-specified format.

[P46] Commenters will seek clarification about the scope of "limited demographic information" (which elements are required), and request minimum cell-size suppression rules to prevent re-identification.

[P46] Hospitals will request that CMS limit the required demographic elements to those essential for public health surveillance and explicitly prohibit collection of unnecessary patient identifiers.

[P47] Hospitals and CAHs will ask CMS to define thresholds that trigger the additional PHE reporting obligations (e.g., specific declarations or objective threat metrics) to avoid inconsistent activation of the mandate.

[P47] Supply-chain managers will request that requirements for reporting "supply and staffing shortages" include standard definitions (e.g., staffing FTE vacancy rates, PPE days-on-hand) to ensure comparability across facilities.

[P48] Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs) will request that CMS provide small-hospital-tailored reporting specifications and technical assistance given limited IT resources.

[P48] Rural health coalitions will ask CMS to provide funding or grants to help CAHs implement electronic reporting systems required under §485.640(d)(1).

[P49] CAHs will request the Secretary accept multiple common data exchange standards and offer a waiver or simplified reporting option for CAHs with fewer than X beds.

[P49] Commenters will request an extended implementation window (at least 12 months) and test periods to enable CAHs to comply with Secretary-specified formats and frequencies.

[P50] CAHs will request clear limits on required demographic data and minimum cell-size protections to preserve patient privacy in small communities.

[P50] Legal commenters will ask for explicit statement that CMS will not use demographic reporting for reimbursement or enforcement purposes absent a separate rulemaking.

[P51] CAHs will request clarity on the scope and timing of additional PHE reporting requirements and whether reporting obligations continue after a PHE ends (e.g., for after-action reporting).

[P51] Public health organizations will request that CMS coordinate reporting requirements with state public health departments to avoid duplicate reporting burdens.

[P52] Eligible professionals, hospitals, and CAHs subject to the Stage 3 meaningful use objective will request CMS to provide a detailed scoring rubric and examples showing how different activities translate into the 80-point requirement to avoid year-to-year uncertainty.

[P52] Small practices and rural providers will ask CMS to incorporate hardship exemptions or an alternative lower point threshold for providers with limited HIT capabilities to avoid penalizing under-resourced clinicians and facilities.

Commenters will propose allowing provisional increases pending final CMS approval when applications are timely submitted to avoid delays in resident recruitment for portions of cost reporting periods beginning July 1, 2026.

Hospitals will request that CMS specify the exact data elements and reporting frequencies for acute respiratory illness electronic reporting and provide burden estimates and timelines for system modifications.
Privacy advocates will request safeguards limiting the granularity of reported demographic data to prevent inadvertent patient identification and ensure HIPAA-compliant aggregation.

Hospitals will ask CMS to publish the Secretary-specified standardized format and frequency well in advance and to accept common interoperable formats (e.g., HL7 FHIR) rather than creating proprietary formats.
Health IT vendors will request a phased implementation timeline and test environment prior to mandatory reporting to ensure conformance with the Secretary-specified format.
Commenters will seek clarification about the scope of "limited demographic information" (which elements are required), and request minimum cell-size suppression rules to prevent re-identification.
Hospitals will request that CMS limit the required demographic elements to those essential for public health surveillance and explicitly prohibit collection of unnecessary patient identifiers.

Hospitals and CAHs will ask CMS to define thresholds that trigger the additional PHE reporting obligations (e.g., specific declarations or objective threat metrics) to avoid inconsistent activation of the mandate.

Supply-chain managers will request that requirements for reporting "supply and staffing shortages" include standard definitions (e.g., staffing FTE vacancy rates, PPE days-on-hand) to ensure comparability across facilities.
Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs) will request that CMS provide small-hospital-tailored reporting specifications and technical assistance given limited IT resources.
Rural health coalitions will ask CMS to provide funding or grants to help CAHs implement electronic reporting systems required under §485.640(d)(1).
CAHs will request the Secretary accept multiple common data exchange standards and offer a waiver or simplified reporting option for CAHs with fewer than X beds.
Commenters will request an extended implementation window (at least 12 months) and test periods to enable CAHs to comply with Secretary-specified formats and frequencies.
CAHs will request clear limits on required demographic data and minimum cell-size protections to preserve patient privacy in small communities.
Legal commenters will ask for explicit statement that CMS will not use demographic reporting for reimbursement or enforcement purposes absent a separate rulemaking.
CAHs will request clarity on the scope and timing of additional PHE reporting requirements and whether reporting obligations continue after a PHE ends (e.g., for after-action reporting).
Public health organizations will request that CMS coordinate reporting requirements with state public health departments to avoid duplicate reporting burdens.

Eligible professionals, hospitals, and CAHs subject to the Stage 3 meaningful use objective will request CMS to provide a detailed scoring rubric and examples showing how different activities translate into the 80-point requirement to avoid year-to-year uncertainty.

Small practices and rural providers will ask CMS to incorporate hardship exemptions or an alternative lower point threshold for providers with limited HIT capabilities to avoid penalizing under-resourced clinicians and facilities.

raw_output:
[P1] Industry commenter: The July 13, 2018 deadline to notify the contact person for testimony is unreasonably short and should be extended to at least 30 days from publication to allow companies to secure subject-matter witnesses and approvals.

[P1] Small business association: Requiring notification by a fixed date (July 13, 2018) without an alternative contingency (e.g., if the notice is published late) discriminates against small businesses with limited administrative capacity; propose a rolling notification or later deadline.

[P1] Environmental advocacy group: The rule should clarify whether the July 13, 2018 notification must include an outline of testimony and supporting materials; otherwise, late-submitted materials may be excluded unfairly.

[P2] Public interest organization: Equating written statements with oral comments is acceptable only if the agency provides guidance on formatting, length limits, and how weight will be assessed to ensure transparency.

[P2] Legal expert: The provision that written comments will be given "the same weight" as oral comments is vague and may be arbitrary in practice; request clarification of the criteria EPA will use to assign weight to comments to avoid arbitrary decision-making.

[P2] Individual citizen: If written comments are to be treated the same as oral comments, EPA should allow witnesses unable to attend the hearing to submit written statements during the hearing period and have them read into the record.

[P3] Industry compliance officer: The requirement that written comments must be received by the last day of the comment period should be paired with a clear time-of-day cutoff and time zone to avoid inadvertent late submissions.

[P3] State government: State agencies request confirmation whether simultaneous submission to state dockets is acceptable and whether EPA will consider late state submissions caused by internal review processes if they arrive immediately after the deadline.

[P4] NGO commenter: Extending the comment period to August 13, 2018 is helpful but insufficient given the complexity of the RFS volume calculations; request a minimum 60-day extension from publication instead.

[P4] Biofuels industry group: The extension to August 13, 2018 appears arbitrary; request EPA provide the rationale and, if analytical models or data sets are being shared late, further extend the period to permit meaningful review.

[P4] Labor union: Workers impacted by renewable fuel standards need more time to analyze workforce effects; ask EPA to extend the comment period beyond August 13, 2018 or hold additional stakeholder sessions.

[P5] Trade association: Mandatory identification of Docket ID EPA–HQ–OA–2018–0107 on Regulations.gov is fine, but EPA should also accept mailed submissions for stakeholders with limited internet access and clarify how mailed comments will be docketed.

[P5] Privacy advocacy group: Regulations.gov submissions are public; request EPA provide a clear process for redacting personal information and confirm whether docket staff will redact personally identifiable information upon request.

[P5] Small rural stakeholder: Some rural stakeholders lack reliable internet and may miss the Regulations.gov requirement; urge EPA to accept emailed submissions to the listed contact or to provide paper submission instructions.

[P6] Civil society commenter: The obligation to use online submission instructions is reasonable, but EPA must ensure those instructions accommodate file size limitations and provide alternatives for large data submissions (e.g., FTP or CD-ROM).

[P6] Technical commenter: Regulations.gov upload formats and metadata fields can corrupt complex attachments (e.g., spreadsheets); request that EPA accept native file formats and provide a checksum/confirmation receipt for submitted files.

[P7] Privacy-rights advocate: The prohibition on editing/removing comments after submission may deter submissions containing inadvertent personal data; request EPA implement a redaction or removal process for sensitive data or allow edits within a short cure period.

[P7] Legal commentator: Prohibiting removal or editing of comments prevents commenters from correcting factual errors and could chill participation; recommend a limited window (e.g., 7 days) during which commenters can correct or supplement their filings.

[P7] Industry compliance counsel: Given the prohibition on removal, EPA should permit follow-up supplemental comments to correct errors rather than leaving incorrect information permanently in the public docket.

[P8] Hearing participant: The EPA's ability to ask clarifying questions during oral presentations is appropriate, but the rule should limit questions to clarification only and prohibit cross-examination to protect presenters from adversarial questioning.

[P8] Academic commenter: EPA should publish the scope and types of clarifying questions that may be asked to avoid fishing expeditions and to allow presenters to prepare concise responses.

[P9] Consumer advocate: The provision that EPA will not provide responses during the oral hearing is problematic because real-time clarification may be necessary; recommend allowing brief Agency responses for clarification to avoid misinterpretation.

[P9] Procedural fairness expert: Not allowing EPA responses during the hearing may hinder interactive deliberation; request that EPA permit limited responses that do not preclude public comment rights.

[P10] Biofuel producers: Setting the 2019 cellulosic biofuel standard to 0.209% appears low relative to production capacity; request EPA to explain the data and methodologies used and consider raising the volume to reflect new commercial-scale projects.

[P10] Conservative/regulatory-relief group: The 0.209% cellulosic standard may overstate realistic supply and unduly burden obligated parties; recommend EPA publish the projected cellulosic volume in million gallons and the underlying assumptions.

[P10] Renewable fuels advocate: If 0.209% translates to a modest absolute volume, EPA should provide projected statutory waivers analysis and confirm whether this value will trigger hardship relief for obligated parties.

[P11] Biodiesel industry: The biomass-based diesel standard of 1.72% for 2019 is below industry expectations given recent production increases; request EPA to use the latest production data through June 2018 and raise the standard accordingly.

[P11] Refiners association: Increasing the biomass-based diesel requirement to 1.72% could raise compliance costs; request EPA provide a detailed cost impact analysis per gallon of gasoline and diesel and consideration of RIN price effects.

[P11] Environmental NGO: The 1.72% biomass-based diesel standard may not fully capture lifecycle greenhouse gas benefits of biodiesel feedstocks; request EPA to account for additional feedstocks and potential scalability in standard-setting.

[P12] Advanced biofuel producers: The advanced biofuel standard of 2.67% for 2019 underestimates projected available volumes from new facilities; ask EPA to publish facility-specific expected production and reconsider raising the percentage.

[P12] Agricultural group: The 2.67% advanced biofuel requirement may rely on feedstocks that compete with food; urge EPA to assess land-use and commodity price impacts before finalizing the standard.

[P12] State air agencies: Provide a regionally disaggregated projection showing how the 2.67% advanced biofuel standard will affect local air quality and infrastructure needs for blending.

[P13] Oil industry: The renewable fuel standard of 10.88% for 2019 imposes significant blending and compliance obligations; request EPA provide the equivalent volumetric target in billion gallons and the expected RIN bank drawdown.

[P13] Ethanol producers: The 10.88% RFS for 2019 is too low given current ethanol production capacity; EPA should increase the renewable fuel standard to reflect actual supply and support domestic biofuel markets.

[P13] Consumer group: EPA must analyze and disclose the impact of the 10.88% standard on fuel prices, vehicle compatibility (warranties for E15), and rural consumer fuel access before finalizing.

[P13] Legal analyst: The proposed percentages (P10–P13) appear precise but lack explanation of rounding conventions and whether these percentages are by energy content, by volume, or relative to total transportation fuel; request statutory basis and calculation methodology be published.

[P1] The obligation in § 84.5(b)(1)(i) is ambiguous about the timing when an importer of record "possesses" allowances — commenters will request clarification whether "possesses at the time they are required to submit reports" means possession at the pre-import EDI submission deadline (e.g., 14/5 days) or at the later quarterly reporting deadline under § 84.31.

[P1] Industry commenters will claim that requiring expenditure "at the specified timepoints" without clear sequencing between allowance possession, EDI pre-notification, and physical arrival creates operational infeasibility for just-in-time imports and will request a safe-harbor allowing expenditure within X days after arrival.

[P2] Many importers will object that the 0.1 allowance minimum per import (to one decimal place) will disproportionately penalize small, low-weight shipments (e.g., samples, lab-scale imports) and request either a de minimis exemption (e.g., shipments <1 kg) or aggregation of small shipments for allowance calculation.

[P2] Legal commenters will argue that forcing calculations to one decimal place with a minimum 0.1 allowance creates rounding and enforcement complexity, and recommend allowing calculations to at least two decimal places or specifying a standardized rounding rule to avoid under/over-reporting.

[P3] Stakeholders will challenge § 84.5(b)(1)(A) requiring year-of-arrival allowances where imports arrive near year-end (e.g., berth on Dec 31 but customs entry occurs in January), requesting clarification whether arrival, scheduled entry, or customs release governs the calendar year for allowance use.

[P3] Import/export practitioners will request an explicit exception for vessels delayed at sea and arriving after a planned year (e.g., force majeure), asking that allowance use be permitted in the year of customs entry rather than physical berthing to avoid double-counting or lost allowances.

[P4] Importers will protest the heel rule (§ 84.5(b)(1)(v)) that presumes 10% of container volume when heel is unmeasured, saying 10% is arbitrary and can overstate actual heel quantities for small-bore or valve-containing containers; ask EPA to require measurement within a reasonable time after arrival or permit lower default percentages based on container type.

[P4] Small businesses and logistics providers will note that measuring heels prior to import is often impossible and that expending allowances on a 10% assumption will create significant compliance costs; they will request an alternative of provisional reporting with post-arrival adjustment within Y days.

[P5] Industry will raise concerns that the certificate of analysis requirement for all imports under (b)(1)(i) or (v) (§ 84.5(b)(1)(vi)) is impractical where suppliers cannot provide accredited COAs in time, and will ask EPA to accept supplier declarations or batch traceability records as interim proof.

[P6] Foreign suppliers/exporters and port authorities will claim that § 84.5(b)(2) prohibition on landing bulk regulated substances unless a category in §84.5(b)(1) is met could result in denied berthing or seizure of cargo when administrative paperwork (e.g., EDI) is delayed; they request a short grace period (e.g., 48–72 hours) to remedy paperwork before prohibition is enforced.

[P6] Legal commenters will argue that the blanket prohibition lacks an emergency/force majeure exception (e.g., for safety, salvage, or contamination) and request explicit carve-outs for emergency response or contaminated shipments.

[P7] Trade associations will object to joint-and-several liability for all importers (§ 84.5(b)(3)), asserting this will unfairly expose brokers, freight forwarders, and incidental consignees who lack control over labeling/allowance possession; they will request liability limited to importer of record absent gross negligence or fraud.

[P7] Compliance officers will request that the rule require EPA to provide written notice and an opportunity to cure before pursuing joint-and-several enforcement against minor paperwork violations by one party among multiple importers.

[P8] Manufacturers will say § 84.5(d) limiting allowances to the calendar year of allocation will create mismatches with long-run production cycles and inventory management; they will request carryover provisions (e.g., X% carryforward) or auction mechanisms to reallocate unused allowances across years.

[P9] Market participants will argue that the prohibition on expending, transferring, or conferring allowances after December 31 (§ 84.5(d)) eliminates flexibility and may force artificial year-end transactions; commenters will ask for a short post-year administrative window to correct errors (e.g., until Jan 31) or permit transfers for transactions initiated before Dec 31.

[P10] Conversely, environmental NGOs will support § 84.5(d) permission to transfer allowances before the calendar year, but will request EPA require disclosure of pre-year transfers and anti-speculation measures to prevent stockpiling and market manipulation.

[P11] Container importers and distributors will state that the January 1, 2022 label prohibition (§ 84.5(i)(1)) is retroactive and unrealistic for existing stock; they will ask for a phased compliance timeline (e.g., 18–24 months) and an allowance for existing inventory to be sold with supplemental labels.

[P12] Packaging manufacturers will question the requirement that permanent labels be printed/affixed to the external surface (§ 84.5(i)(1)(i)), noting some containers (e.g., cylinders with welded-on placards or translucent shrink-wrap) cannot accommodate affixed labels; request alternative acceptable methods (e.g., durable tamper-evident sleeves).

[P13] Importers will contest the "readily visible and legible" standard (§ 84.5(i)(1)(ii)) as subjective and ask EPA to define measurable criteria (minimum font size, minimum contrast ratio, minimum readable distance) to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

[P14] Logistics companies will point out the weather-resistance obligation (§ 84.5(i)(1)(iii)) may be costly for temporary transit packaging; they will request that the weather-resistance standard apply only to final sale distribution containers and not to short-term transit overpacks or marine-grade stretch wrap.

[P15] Small distributors will object to the "contrasting background color" requirement (§ 84.5(i)(1)(iv)) as overly prescriptive given varied container colors and printing technologies, and will request an alternative requiring minimum color contrast metrics (e.g., WCAG contrast ratio) rather than a categorical mandate.

[P16] Shippers using overpacks will request clarification of the 20-point font requirement (§ 84.5(i)(1)(v)); they will ask whether that applies to all languages and whether 20-point is measured in points as printed (which varies by font), and request an equivalency (e.g., minimum x mm height).

[P17] Repackagers and supply chain actors will object to the absolute prohibition on label removal/tampering (§ 84.5(i)(1) prohibition), arguing that legitimate repackaging for retail sale may require label updates; they request a permitted process with documentation and re-labeling requirements rather than a blanket ban.

[P18] Repackagers other than the importer of record will criticize § 84.5(i)(2) prohibition on repackaging by anyone other than importer of record as impracticable where importers routinely contract third-party repackers; they will ask EPA to allow repackaging by third parties under a delegated-authority and documentation regime.

[P19] Repackagers will argue the alternative in § 84.5(i)(2)(i) requiring expenditure of allowances equal to full-cylinder HFC-23 equivalent to repackage is punitive and economically infeasible; they will request an alternative that allows repackaging with post-repackaging testing rather than immediate allowance surrender.

[P20] Repackagers and importers will prefer the § 84.5(i)(2)(ii) option allowing independent lab verification but will request EPA specify acceptable lab accreditation standards, acceptable sample sizes, and turnaround time allowances for testing to prevent shipment delays.

[P21] Producers, reclaimers, and repackagers will object to the pre-sale representative-sample testing prohibition (§ 84.5(i)(3)(i)) being too prescriptive, and will request flexibility to use validated quality systems (e.g., ISO 17025 labs, validated in-house methods), pooled sampling schemes, or risk-based testing frequencies.

[P22] Technical commenters will request more specificity for the required sampling/testing methodologies in § 84.5(i)(3)(i)/Table 1, arguing that some regulated substances and mixtures are not well-covered by the referenced methods (Appendix A/ AHRI/Method 18) and that EPA should publish method equivalency guidance and allow modern analytical techniques (e.g., GC×GC, FTIR) after validation.

[P23] HVAC and refrigerant industry groups will request an allowance in § 84.5(i)(3)(ii) for temporary distribution of older blends that do not meet Appendix A specifications for specified non-refrigerant uses (e.g., solvent, calibration gas) rather than an absolute prohibition.

[P24] Allocation recipients will seek clarity on § 84.9(b) notification timing and the process for disputing initial production allowance quantities issued by the Agency official, requesting a formal appeals / reconsideration timetable.

[P25] Large producers will contest the high-three-average (2011–2019) methodology in § 84.9(b)(1) as potentially inaccurate for entities that restructured, merged, or changed product mix since 2019; they will ask EPA to allow alternative baselines (e.g., 2017–2022) or an adjustment mechanism for structural changes.

[P26] Legal experts will flag antitrust and confidentiality concerns with § 84.9(b)(2)–(4) allocation method, requesting that EPA protect commercially sensitive data used in calculating percentage shares and provide anonymized aggregate disclosures only.

[P27] NGOs and climate advocates will support § 84.9(b)(3) subtraction of application-specific allowances from the production cap but will ask EPA to publish the list and quantities of application-specific allowances and the rationale to ensure transparency.

[P28] Companies will request that § 84.9(b)(4) specify how EPA will round fraction allowances when multiplying percentages by general pool amounts to avoid allocation disputes and to allow planning.

[P29] Entities anticipating consumption allowances under § 84.11(b) will request EPA to publish the notification schedule and the format of "separate notification" so recipients can plan corporate treasury and trading activities.

[P30] New market entrants will challenge § 84.11(b)(1) method of adjusting 2023 allocations and dividing by general pool proportions as disadvantaging true new entrants that had no 2023 allocation; they will seek a distinct carve-out and an equitable initial allocation procedure.

[P31] Importers with complex ownership will warn that § 84.11(b)(2) aggregation of related importers by corporate/common ownership could penalize decentralized trading affiliates and ask EPA to define aggregation thresholds and safe-harbor ownership percentages.

[P32] Entities with differing values under (b)(1) and (b)(2) will request written guidance and examples on the "higher of the values" rule (§ 84.11(b)(3)), including how EPA will handle tied values and how this interacts with mergers or acquisitions.

[P33] Small traders will request that § 84.11(b)(4) require EPA to provide pre-allocation notice of aggregated totals and percentage shares before finalizing allocations so entities can verify data and correct errors.

[P34] Entities will seek a clear explanation of what constitutes "application-specific allowances" subtracted in § 84.11(b)(5), including a list of eligible applications, quantities, and recipient identities to assess how much remains in the general pool.

[P35] Allocation recipients will request EPA to set a deadline and process for correcting misallocated consumption allowances (§ 84.11(b)(6)), including transfer procedures and compensation mechanisms where EPA error caused allocation shortfalls.

[P36] Applicants for additional consumption allowances (§ 84.17(a)) will say the required documentation list is overly burdensome and requests streamlined submission for routine, verified exporters (e.g., trusted exporter program) with reduced paperwork.

[P37] Exporters will flag § 84.17(a)(8) requirement for bill of lading and invoice showing net quantities and sale documentation as problematic when third-party logistics consolidate shipments; request allowance for consolidated documentation and clarifications on acceptable invoice formats.

[P38] Trade counsel will request clarification whether the HTS codes (§ 84.17(a)(9)) must be specific to each regulated substance or can be submitted as the generic HS code used by customs, and ask whether EPA will accept subsequent commercial corrections to HTS codes.

[P39] Applicants will ask whether internal transaction numbers (§ 84.17(a)(10)) can be substituted with other unique shipment identifiers (e.g., purchase order + invoice number) when internal numbering systems differ.

[P40] Exporters will ask whether "conveyance names" (§ 84.17(a)(11)) must be the shipping line vessel name or may be the forwarding company's booking reference, and whether small shipments moved by truck require carrier name only.

[P41] Maritime operators will request an explicit exemption in § 84.17(a)(12) for IMO numbers when not applicable (e.g., inland barges, domestic tugs) and ask EPA to accept other vessel identifiers where IMO is not issued.

[P42] Shipping lines and logistics providers will seek an exemption from § 84.17(a)(13) container-number requirement for LCL (less-than-container-load) consignments or bulk break-bulk shipments that are not containerized.

[P43] Several commenters will praise § 84.19(a)(5) allowing entities to expend allowances from related majority-owned entities without following procedures but will request clear definitions of "majority-owned" and documentation required to demonstrate the relationship.

[P44] Importers filing petitions per § 84.25(a)(1)(v) will request the proposed requirement to notify EPA of port/vessel/expected date before importation be extended to accommodate last-minute voyage changes and ask for an exception where changes are communicated within 48 hours of arrival.

[P45] Producers will request clarification on what qualifies as "transformation by the producer" in § 84.31(b)(2)(i) (e.g., chemical conversion, blending, repackaging) and whether transfers between related facilities require separate reporting if located within the same corporate entity.

[P46] Producers will seek a definition and verification standard for "destruction" in § 84.31(b)(2)(ii), including acceptable destruction technologies, certificates of destruction, and third-party verification where destruction occurs off-site.

[P47] Chemical manufacturers will request examples and boundaries for "process agent" use reporting in § 84.31(b)(2)(iii) to avoid requiring reporting for trace or incidental process agent uses below a materiality threshold.

[P48] Producers will ask EPA to specify what form the list of entities conferring application-specific allowances (§ 84.31(b)(2)(ix)) must take (e.g., legal names, EINs) and whether confidentiality can be claimed for commercial partners.

[P49] Producers will object to the requirement to maintain daily dated records and certify daily allowance expenditures (§ 84.31(b)(2)(x)/(b)(4)(xiv)), saying intraday production variability and ERP system limitations mean same-day certification is impractical; they will request allowance to record within 3 business days.

[P50] Producers will recommend clarifying whether the December 31 inventory reporting requirement (§ 84.31(b)(2)(xi)) is by produced substance specification or by finished product SKU, and whether tolerances are allowed for reconciliation.

[P51] Industry will object to the 45-day post-year-end emissions report deadline (§ 84.31(b)(3)), arguing it is too short given testing, QA/QC and third-party verification needs, and will request extension to 90 days or allowance for provisional submissions with final reports later.

[P52] Producers will request EPA clarify the exact list of hazardous air pollutants and substances to be reported under § 84.31(b)(3)(i) and (ii), and whether global warming potential-weighted reporting is required in addition to pounds.

[P53] Technical commenters will ask for guidance on how to attribute emissions to specific production lines and emission units (§ 84.31(b)(3)(ii)) in integrated facilities where materials and feedstocks move between lines.

[P54] Producers and reclaimers will request that the dated batch test record requirement (§ 84.31(b)(4)(xi)) allow digital records and scanned calibration logs, and ask EPA to specify acceptable file formats and retention/back-up standards.

[P55] Producers will challenge the requirement to record allowance date/quantity/type on the same day expended for production (§ 84.31(b)(4)(xiv)), arguing their accounting and ERP systems batch-process allocations and requesting a reasonable business-days window (e.g., 3–5 business days).

[P56] Importers will raise similar concerns about the same-day recording requirement for imports (§ 84.31(c)(1)(ix) and (c)(2)(xvii)), asserting customs release timing and EDI synchronization make same-day recording impossible in many cases and asking for a short compliance window.

[P57] Importers will request detailed technical specifications and test EDI schemas for the pre-import submissions required by § 84.31(c)(7), and ask EPA to provide an onboarding/testing period and API documentation.

[P58] Importers will argue that the 14-day marine / 5-day non-marine pre-import EDI deadlines (§ 84.31(c)(7)) are too short for shipments originating from distant suppliers and will request harmonization with CBP ACE timeframes (e.g., 24 hours for mass manifest) or a longer window (e.g., 21/7 days).

[P59] Trade groups will request clarification on what level of cargo description (§ 84.31(c)(7)(i)) is required (HS heading vs. specific chemical name) and whether CAS numbers suffice.

[P60] Importers will object that requiring net weight or heel-equivalent numbers (§ 84.31(c)(7)(ii)) when heels are unknown (using 10% assumption) will cause frequent post-arrival reconciliation needs; ask for a two-step reporting (estimated pre-import, final post-import reconciliation) process.

[P61] Containerized importers will request guidance on acceptable container-number formats for § 84.31(c)(7)(iii) submissions and whether multiple container numbers can be aggregated for consolidated shipments.

[P62] Maritime shippers will request explicit guidance about vessel naming conventions (§ 84.31(c)(7)(iv)) and whether "vessel name" may be the voyage number or shipping line service name in addition to the physical ship name.

[P63] Maritime industry will reiterate that IMO number (§ 84.31(c)(7)(v)) should be optional when not applicable and that alternate identifiers must be accepted for river barges or domestic carriers.

[P64] Importers will ask EPA to allow provisional gross weight or heel-equivalent gross weight (§ 84.31(c)(7)(vi)) in pre-import notices with mandatory post-arrival reconciliation rather than forcing importers to expend allowances on an estimated heel.

[P65] Commenters will ask the agency to specify exact units of measure accepted (§ 84.31(c)(7)(vii)) and whether EPA will convert between metric and imperial or require metric-only submissions.

[P66] Importers will request harmonization of "port of entry" (§ 84.31(c)(7)(viii)) with customs definitions (port of unlading vs. port of entry) and flexibility when cargo is transshipped.

[P67] Industry will request that "scheduled entry date" (§ 84.31(c)(7)(ix)) accommodate reasonable itinerary changes and allow updates without penalty when notified within 48–72 hours.

[P68] Commenters will ask whether HTS code requirements (§ 84.31(c)(7)(x)) require full 10-digit subheading or whether 6-digit HS is acceptable, and for guidance on mixtures and multi-component product classification.

[P69] Importers will request flexibility on HTS description (§ 84.31(c)(7)(xi)) allowing pre-populated customs description text rather than requiring bespoke descriptions for each submission.

[P70] Manufacturers and importers will ask how "country of origin" (§ 84.31(c)(7)(xii)) is determined for substances that are fractionally produced in multiple countries (e.g., chemical intermediates) and request guidance consistent with customs rules.

[P71] Entities will request the format and validation rules for importer name and importer number (§ 84.31(c)(7)(xiii)), including how third-party brokers should represent themselves versus the importer of record.

[P72] Consignees will ask whether the consignee entity name (§ 84.31(c)(7)(xiv)) may be a DBA and whether multiple consignees on a single container require separate entries.

[P73] Importers and formulators will challenge the requirement to submit CAS numbers and either ASHRAE designation or component percentages (§ 84.31(c)(7)(xv)), saying percentage breakdowns for proprietary blends are confidential; they will request a confidentiality regime or allow CAS + ASHRAE designation instead of percentages.

[P74] Entities importing for transformation or destruction (§ 84.31(c)(7)(xvi)) will request streamlined acceptance of non-objection notices issued under § 84.25 including electronic copies and cross-agency recognition (e.g., DOT/CBP letters).

[P75] Transhipment operators will ask for a clear definition and process to provide the confirmation required under § 84.31(c)(7)(xvii) and whether inland transits within the U.S. are treated the same.

[P76] Importers will request that EPA clarify acceptable formats and signatory requirements for the certificate of analysis (§ 84.31(c)(7)(xviii)) and whether lab accreditations are required.

[P77] Entities anticipating being importers of record but not yet allocated allowances (§ 84.31(c)(9)(i)) will ask EPA to clarify the consequences of failing to submit the Nov 15 information — whether it results in forfeiture of the right to be allocated allowances or triggers compliance enforcement.

[P78] Multinational corporations will flag privacy and competitive concerns with the requirement to list all subsidiaries (§ 84.31(c)(9)(ii)(A)) and will request protection for sensitive corporate structure information or the ability to submit redacted versions with justification.

[P79] Large corporate groups will seek clarity on the scope of entities to report under § 84.31(c)(9)(ii)(B) for commonly or majority-owned entities and whether minority-owned joint ventures are included.

[P80] Businesses using multiple DBAs will request guidance on what constitutes "alternative business names" (§ 84.31(c)(9)(ii)(C)) and whether trade names registered in different states must be separately listed.

[P81] Trade groups will ask how importer of record numbers (§ 84.31(c)(9)(ii)(D)) should be formatted and whether foreign importer IDs or customs broker IDs may be included for planning.

[P82] Entities will urge EPA to limit the granularity requested in § 84.31(c)(9)(ii)(E) about ownership percentages and allowances allocations among affiliates, citing competitive sensitivity and ask for an option to provide summary information or claim confidentiality.

[P83] Importers will ask for a practical update period for changes to submitted ownership/affiliate data (§ 84.31(c)(9)(iii)) when it requires board approvals or public filings, requesting a two-step update process with interim certification.

[P84] Trade associations will reiterate concerns about joint-and-several liability for any violation of pre-import reporting (§ 84.31(c)(10) & (11)) and ask EPA to limit liability where a party can show it exercised reasonable due diligence and relied in good faith on the importer of record.

[P85] Reclaimers will support § 84.31(i)(4)(i) requiring batch-by-batch analyses but will request EPA allow validated in-house labs (ISO/IEC 17025) and electronic submission of test summaries rather than full raw data for confidentiality and administrative efficiency.

[P86] Recyclers will request that the five-year transactional record retention requirement (§ 84.31(j)(3)(i)) be harmonized with other federal and state record retention rules (e.g., DOT, EPA hazardous materials) and allow electronic records with secure backups.

[P87] Recyclers will ask EPA to define the "quantity of the material" metric in § 84.31(j)(3)(i) (gross weight vs. net regulated-substance weight after recovery) to avoid reporting inconsistencies.

[P88] Recyclers and repackagers will request guidance on acceptable sample sizes and acceptance criteria for dated batch test records (§ 84.31(j)(3)(ii) and (k)(1)) and whether aggregated daily/weekly summaries are acceptable for high-volume operations.

[P89] Repackagers will ask for a phased compliance timeline to implement the dated batch test records requirement (§ 84.31(k)(1)) and for sample templates and electronic filing specifications.

[P90] Privacy and legal groups will request that EPA adopt safeguards and redaction standards for all commercially sensitive data submitted under §§ 84.9–84.31 and publish a clear FOIA/confidential business information process.

[P91] Several commenters (industry and legal) will request that EPA perform and publish a regulatory flexibility analysis and economic impact assessment quantifying compliance costs (labeling, testing, EDI systems, allowances) for small entities to support the final rulemaking record.

[P92] Trade groups will seek harmonization of definitions and timelines with CBP, DOT, and other agencies (e.g., ACE/ITDS), asking EPA to adopt existing customs identifiers and timelines to reduce duplicative reporting under § 84.31(c)(7).

[P93] Commenters will request that EPA create a transitional compliance program (e.g., warning-first enforcement, compliance assistance, pre-certification) for the first two years after implementation given the large operational changes required across the supply chain.

[P94] Legal commenters will ask EPA to state enforcement priorities and penalty frameworks for infractions under the new allowances and labeling regimes to provide predictability for industry actors.

[P95] Environmental NGOs will urge EPA to tighten some provisions — for example, reducing the 10% heel assumption to a lower default or requiring mandatory measurement — contending that overestimation undermines environmental integrity but also to ensure that the allowances regime prevents circumvention.

[P96] Academic and technical commenters will ask EPA to clarify metrics used for "exchange-value weighted" calculations throughout (§§ 84.5, 84.9, 84.11), request the specific exchange or price series to be used, and ask how volatility will be handled in allocation formulas.

[P97] Entities will request model forms, sample EDI messages, and an FAQ from EPA addressing every data element in § 84.31(c)(7)(i)-(xviii) and § 84.17(a)(8)-(13) to ensure consistent implementation.

[P98] Currency/financial officers will ask whether allowance transfers permitted before the calendar year (§ 84.5(d) permission) will be taxable events and request coordination with IRS guidance or an explicit non-tax statement.

[P99] International trading partners will request EPA coordinate allowance rules with foreign equivalency systems to avoid double regulation and to enable mutual recognition for accredited labs issuing certificates of analysis under § 84.5(b)(1)(vi).

[P100] Commenters will request EPA provide a binding compliance safe-harbor for good-faith attempts to comply with newly required documentation elements (e.g., internal transaction numbers, conveyance names, IMO numbers, container numbers) during the first 12 months after finalization.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The obligation in § 84.5(b)(1)(i) is ambiguous about the timing when an importer of record "possesses" allowances — commenters will request clarification whether "possesses at the time they are required to submit reports" means possession at the pre-import EDI submission deadline (e.g., 14/5 days) or at the later quarterly reporting deadline under § 84.31.

Industry commenters will claim that requiring expenditure "at the specified timepoints" without clear sequencing between allowance possession, EDI pre-notification, and physical arrival creates operational infeasibility for just-in-time imports and will request a safe-harbor allowing expenditure within X days after arrival.

Many importers will object that the 0.1 allowance minimum per import (to one decimal place) will disproportionately penalize small, low-weight shipments (e.g., samples, lab-scale imports) and request either a de minimis exemption (e.g., shipments <1 kg) or aggregation of small shipments for allowance calculation.

Legal commenters will argue that forcing calculations to one decimal place with a minimum 0.1 allowance creates rounding and enforcement complexity, and recommend allowing calculations to at least two decimal places or specifying a standardized rounding rule to avoid under/over-reporting.

Stakeholders will challenge § 84.5(b)(1)(A) requiring year-of-arrival allowances where imports arrive near year-end (e.g., berth on Dec 31 but customs entry occurs in January), requesting clarification whether arrival, scheduled entry, or customs release governs the calendar year for allowance use.

Import/export practitioners will request an explicit exception for vessels delayed at sea and arriving after a planned year (e.g., force majeure), asking that allowance use be permitted in the year of customs entry rather than physical berthing to avoid double-counting or lost allowances.

Importers will protest the heel rule (§ 84.5(b)(1)(v)) that presumes 10% of container volume when heel is unmeasured, saying 10% is arbitrary and can overstate actual heel quantities for small-bore or valve-containing containers; ask EPA to require measurement within a reasonable time after arrival or permit lower default percentages based on container type.

Small businesses and logistics providers will note that measuring heels prior to import is often impossible and that expending allowances on a 10% assumption will create significant compliance costs; they will request an alternative of provisional reporting with post-arrival adjustment within Y days.

Industry will raise concerns that the certificate of analysis requirement for all imports under (b)(1)(i) or (v) (§ 84.5(b)(1)(vi)) is impractical where suppliers cannot provide accredited COAs in time, and will ask EPA to accept supplier declarations or batch traceability records as interim proof.

Foreign suppliers/exporters and port authorities will claim that § 84.5(b)(2) prohibition on landing bulk regulated substances unless a category in §84.5(b)(1) is met could result in denied berthing or seizure of cargo when administrative paperwork (e.g., EDI) is delayed; they request a short grace period (e.g., 48–72 hours) to remedy paperwork before prohibition is enforced.

Legal commenters will argue that the blanket prohibition lacks an emergency/force majeure exception (e.g., for safety, salvage, or contamination) and request explicit carve-outs for emergency response or contaminated shipments.

Trade associations will object to joint-and-several liability for all importers (§ 84.5(b)(3)), asserting this will unfairly expose brokers, freight forwarders, and incidental consignees who lack control over labeling/allowance possession; they will request liability limited to importer of record absent gross negligence or fraud.

Compliance officers will request that the rule require EPA to provide written notice and an opportunity to cure before pursuing joint-and-several enforcement against minor paperwork violations by one party among multiple importers.

Manufacturers will say § 84.5(d) limiting allowances to the calendar year of allocation will create mismatches with long-run production cycles and inventory management; they will request carryover provisions (e.g., X% carryforward) or auction mechanisms to reallocate unused allowances across years.

Market participants will argue that the prohibition on expending, transferring, or conferring allowances after December 31 (§ 84.5(d)) eliminates flexibility and may force artificial year-end transactions; commenters will ask for a short post-year administrative window to correct errors (e.g., until Jan 31) or permit transfers for transactions initiated before Dec 31.

Conversely, environmental NGOs will support § 84.5(d) permission to transfer allowances before the calendar year, but will request EPA require disclosure of pre-year transfers and anti-speculation measures to prevent stockpiling and market manipulation.

Container importers and distributors will state that the January 1, 2022 label prohibition (§ 84.5(i)(1)) is retroactive and unrealistic for existing stock; they will ask for a phased compliance timeline (e.g., 18–24 months) and an allowance for existing inventory to be sold with supplemental labels.

Packaging manufacturers will question the requirement that permanent labels be printed/affixed to the external surface (§ 84.5(i)(1)(i)), noting some containers (e.g., cylinders with welded-on placards or translucent shrink-wrap) cannot accommodate affixed labels; request alternative acceptable methods (e.g., durable tamper-evident sleeves).

Importers will contest the "readily visible and legible" standard (§ 84.5(i)(1)(ii)) as subjective and ask EPA to define measurable criteria (minimum font size, minimum contrast ratio, minimum readable distance) to avoid inconsistent enforcement.

Logistics companies will point out the weather-resistance obligation (§ 84.5(i)(1)(iii)) may be costly for temporary transit packaging; they will request that the weather-resistance standard apply only to final sale distribution containers and not to short-term transit overpacks or marine-grade stretch wrap.

Small distributors will object to the "contrasting background color" requirement (§ 84.5(i)(1)(iv)) as overly prescriptive given varied container colors and printing technologies, and will request an alternative requiring minimum color contrast metrics (e.g., WCAG contrast ratio) rather than a categorical mandate.

Shippers using overpacks will request clarification of the 20-point font requirement (§ 84.5(i)(1)(v)); they will ask whether that applies to all languages and whether 20-point is measured in points as printed (which varies by font), and request an equivalency (e.g., minimum x mm height).

Repackagers and supply chain actors will object to the absolute prohibition on label removal/tampering (§ 84.5(i)(1) prohibition), arguing that legitimate repackaging for retail sale may require label updates; they request a permitted process with documentation and re-labeling requirements rather than a blanket ban.

Repackagers other than the importer of record will criticize § 84.5(i)(2) prohibition on repackaging by anyone other than importer of record as impracticable where importers routinely contract third-party repackers; they will ask EPA to allow repackaging by third parties under a delegated-authority and documentation regime.

Repackagers will argue the alternative in § 84.5(i)(2)(i) requiring expenditure of allowances equal to full-cylinder HFC-23 equivalent to repackage is punitive and economically infeasible; they will request an alternative that allows repackaging with post-repackaging testing rather than immediate allowance surrender.

Repackagers and importers will prefer the § 84.5(i)(2)(ii) option allowing independent lab verification but will request EPA specify acceptable lab accreditation standards, acceptable sample sizes, and turnaround time allowances for testing to prevent shipment delays.

Producers, reclaimers, and repackagers will object to the pre-sale representative-sample testing prohibition (§ 84.5(i)(3)(i)) being too prescriptive, and will request flexibility to use validated quality systems (e.g., ISO 17025 labs, validated in-house methods), pooled sampling schemes, or risk-based testing frequencies.

Technical commenters will request more specificity for the required sampling/testing methodologies in § 84.5(i)(3)(i)/Table 1, arguing that some regulated substances and mixtures are not well-covered by the referenced methods (Appendix A/ AHRI/Method 18) and that EPA should publish method equivalency guidance and allow modern analytical techniques (e.g., GC×GC, FTIR) after validation.

HVAC and refrigerant industry groups will request an allowance in § 84.5(i)(3)(ii) for temporary distribution of older blends that do not meet Appendix A specifications for specified non-refrigerant uses (e.g., solvent, calibration gas) rather than an absolute prohibition.

Allocation recipients will seek clarity on § 84.9(b) notification timing and the process for disputing initial production allowance quantities issued by the Agency official, requesting a formal appeals / reconsideration timetable.

Large producers will contest the high-three-average (2011–2019) methodology in § 84.9(b)(1) as potentially inaccurate for entities that restructured, merged, or changed product mix since 2019; they will ask EPA to allow alternative baselines (e.g., 2017–2022) or an adjustment mechanism for structural changes.

Legal experts will flag antitrust and confidentiality concerns with § 84.9(b)(2)–(4) allocation method, requesting that EPA protect commercially sensitive data used in calculating percentage shares and provide anonymized aggregate disclosures only.

NGOs and climate advocates will support § 84.9(b)(3) subtraction of application-specific allowances from the production cap but will ask EPA to publish the list and quantities of application-specific allowances and the rationale to ensure transparency.
Companies will request that § 84.9(b)(4) specify how EPA will round fraction allowances when multiplying percentages by general pool amounts to avoid allocation disputes and to allow planning.

Entities anticipating consumption allowances under § 84.11(b) will request EPA to publish the notification schedule and the format of "separate notification" so recipients can plan corporate treasury and trading activities.

New market entrants will challenge § 84.11(b)(1) method of adjusting 2023 allocations and dividing by general pool proportions as disadvantaging true new entrants that had no 2023 allocation; they will seek a distinct carve-out and an equitable initial allocation procedure.

Importers with complex ownership will warn that § 84.11(b)(2) aggregation of related importers by corporate/common ownership could penalize decentralized trading affiliates and ask EPA to define aggregation thresholds and safe-harbor ownership percentages.

Entities with differing values under (b)(1) and (b)(2) will request written guidance and examples on the "higher of the values" rule (§ 84.11(b)(3)), including how EPA will handle tied values and how this interacts with mergers or acquisitions.

Small traders will request that § 84.11(b)(4) require EPA to provide pre-allocation notice of aggregated totals and percentage shares before finalizing allocations so entities can verify data and correct errors.

Entities will seek a clear explanation of what constitutes "application-specific allowances" subtracted in § 84.11(b)(5), including a list of eligible applications, quantities, and recipient identities to assess how much remains in the general pool.

Allocation recipients will request EPA to set a deadline and process for correcting misallocated consumption allowances (§ 84.11(b)(6)), including transfer procedures and compensation mechanisms where EPA error caused allocation shortfalls.

Applicants for additional consumption allowances (§ 84.17(a)) will say the required documentation list is overly burdensome and requests streamlined submission for routine, verified exporters (e.g., trusted exporter program) with reduced paperwork.

Exporters will flag § 84.17(a)(8) requirement for bill of lading and invoice showing net quantities and sale documentation as problematic when third-party logistics consolidate shipments; request allowance for consolidated documentation and clarifications on acceptable invoice formats.

Trade counsel will request clarification whether the HTS codes (§ 84.17(a)(9)) must be specific to each regulated substance or can be submitted as the generic HS code used by customs, and ask whether EPA will accept subsequent commercial corrections to HTS codes.

Applicants will ask whether internal transaction numbers (§ 84.17(a)(10)) can be substituted with other unique shipment identifiers (e.g., purchase order + invoice number) when internal numbering systems differ.

Exporters will ask whether "conveyance names" (§ 84.17(a)(11)) must be the shipping line vessel name or may be the forwarding company's booking reference, and whether small shipments moved by truck require carrier name only.

Maritime operators will request an explicit exemption in § 84.17(a)(12) for IMO numbers when not applicable (e.g., inland barges, domestic tugs) and ask EPA to accept other vessel identifiers where IMO is not issued.

Shipping lines and logistics providers will seek an exemption from § 84.17(a)(13) container-number requirement for LCL (less-than-container-load) consignments or bulk break-bulk shipments that are not containerized.

Several commenters will praise § 84.19(a)(5) allowing entities to expend allowances from related majority-owned entities without following procedures but will request clear definitions of "majority-owned" and documentation required to demonstrate the relationship.

Importers filing petitions per § 84.25(a)(1)(v) will request the proposed requirement to notify EPA of port/vessel/expected date before importation be extended to accommodate last-minute voyage changes and ask for an exception where changes are communicated within 48 hours of arrival.

Producers will request clarification on what qualifies as "transformation by the producer" in § 84.31(b)(2)(i) (e.g., chemical conversion, blending, repackaging) and whether transfers between related facilities require separate reporting if located within the same corporate entity.

Producers will seek a definition and verification standard for "destruction" in § 84.31(b)(2)(ii), including acceptable destruction technologies, certificates of destruction, and third-party verification where destruction occurs off-site.

Chemical manufacturers will request examples and boundaries for "process agent" use reporting in § 84.31(b)(2)(iii) to avoid requiring reporting for trace or incidental process agent uses below a materiality threshold.

Producers will ask EPA to specify what form the list of entities conferring application-specific allowances (§ 84.31(b)(2)(ix)) must take (e.g., legal names, EINs) and whether confidentiality can be claimed for commercial partners.

Producers will object to the requirement to maintain daily dated records and certify daily allowance expenditures (§ 84.31(b)(2)(x)/(b)(4)(xiv)), saying intraday production variability and ERP system limitations mean same-day certification is impractical; they will request allowance to record within 3 business days.

Producers will recommend clarifying whether the December 31 inventory reporting requirement (§ 84.31(b)(2)(xi)) is by produced substance specification or by finished product SKU, and whether tolerances are allowed for reconciliation.
