[P1] The rule text inconsistently lists the same July 3, 2017 deadline for both Bombardier and Boeing ADs without clarifying whether extensions or staggered deadlines apply; clarify and harmonize comment deadlines.

[P2] Requiring compliance "within the specified compliance times" without incorporating explicit calendared dates for each affected fleet creates uncertainty for operators; the AD should specify absolute dates or clearly map service bulletin compliance tables to AD compliance times.

[P3] The 24‑month compliance window in paragraph (g) for performing inspections and modifications is excessive for safety-critical APU/hydraulic interferences; require earlier action (e.g., 90–180 days) for aircraft with higher utilization or known histories of chafing.

[P3] Conversely, the 24‑month compliance time may be infeasible for some small operators facing maintenance scheduling constraints and parts lead times; allow phased compliance tied to the next deep maintenance visit or provide an AMOC pathway with documented risk assessment.

[P4] Paragraph (g)(1) limits applicability to serial numbers 20003–20500 but does not state how operators should treat aircraft with serial numbers near those cutoffs or aircraft with re‑identified serial numbers; clarify applicability and provide a cross‑reference list.

[P4] Requiring compliance with Bombardier Service Bulletin 100–24–28 (subject to paragraph (h)) without incorporating the service bulletin by reference leaves ambiguity about acceptable deviations and inspection criteria; incorporate the service bulletin text or key required procedures into the AD.

[P5] The mandate to complete any repairs "before further flight" is operationally disruptive and may be impracticable without contingency allowances; allow ferry flight authorization under specific conditions (e.g., with operational limitations and documented risk mitigation) to permit repositioning for repairs.

[P6] Paragraph (g)(2) applies Bombardier Service Bulletin 350–24–003 to serial numbers 20501–20635 but does not account for mixed configuration differences between nearby serial numbers; require Bombardier to provide a configuration trace matrix to justify separate service instructions.

[P6] The AD requires modification "per Bombardier Service Bulletin 350–24–003" but the bulletin's mandated parts or kits may not be available within the 24‑month window; include a provisioning grace period or allow temporary mitigations approved via AMOC.

[P7] Requiring repairs found in paragraph (g)(2) to be done "before further flight" (same as P5) fails to consider possible limited-risk discrepancies that could be deferred to the next scheduled heavy maintenance with operational risk assessment; request a damage‑severity matrix to permit deferral in low-risk cases.

[P8] Paragraph (h) requires manufacturer‑approved repair methods or approval by Manager, New York ACO, or TCCA, but the burden and time required to obtain such approvals may ground aircraft; establish an expedited approval timeline and interim repair authorization procedures.

[P8] The requirement that Bombardier's TCCA DAO approvals "must include signature as required elsewhere" is vague — specify the required authorized DAO signature format and recordkeeping requirements to ensure legal validity.

[P9] Centralizing AMOC authority in the Manager, New York ACO may delay approval for operators based outside that jurisdiction; allow regional FAA ACOs or principal inspectors more explicit delegated authority to approve AMOCs to expedite operator requests.

[P10] The routing instructions for AMOC requests add procedural complexity; allow submission via secure electronic portal and permit acknowledgments with target review timeframes (e.g., 30 days) to improve transparency.

[P11] Requiring notification to the principal inspector or local FSDO "before using" an approved AMOC is unclear concerning timing—must notification occur 24 hours, 5 days, or immediately before the flight? Define a specific advance-notice period.

[P12] Mandating that corrective actions obtained from the manufacturer be approved by the Manager, New York ACO, TCCA, or Bombardier's TCCA DAO with DAO signature can create duplication; allow manufacturer corrective actions approved by TCCA DAO to be accepted unilaterally by FAA if mutually recognized to avoid redundant approvals.

[P13] The duplicate comment deadline for the Boeing AD (July 3, 2017) causes confusion if stakeholders wish to submit differentiated comments; clarify whether a single submission may address both ADs or if separate submissions are required.

[P14] Similar to P2, the Boeing AD's requirement to "comply within specified compliance times" references the service bulletin but does not state whether times are counted from the service bulletin date or the AD effective date for initial compliance—clarify to avoid inconsistent operator interpretations.

[P15] The stipulated HFEC inspection for Group 1 airplanes per Boeing Alert Service Bulletin 757–53A0101 lacks specific threshold crack sizes or acceptance criteria within the AD; incorporate or reference the exact crack dimensions or criteria that constitute a fail.

[P16] The requirement that corrective actions be done "before further flight" could ground aircraft for extensive structural repairs; allow for ferry permits under strict conditions with short-term operational limitations when immediate repair is not feasible.

[P17] The mandated repeat HFEC inspection intervals per the service bulletin should be set forth explicitly in the AD rather than by reference to avoid confusion when future revisions of the service bulletin change intervals; lock the required intervals to those in the cited revision or specify acceptable revision procedure.

[P18] Identification of material for STA 1380 inner chord per the service bulletin (paragraph h) requires access to manufacturer records that some operators may not possess; allow alternative acceptable means of compliance (e.g., material sampling or engineering substantiation) and specify acceptable documentation.

[P19] The exception for 2024–T42 material (no further action) assumes equivalence across production lots; require verification testing or traceable documentation to ensure that the identified 2024–T42 meets strength and chemistry requirements before exempting.

[P20] For 7075–T73 material, requiring HFEC inspections "before further flight" may be excessive if the identified area is inaccessible without heavy maintenance; permit a short window to perform inspections at the next maintenance opportunity with interim risk controls.

[P21] Requiring corrective actions for material 7075–T73 "before further flight" fails to consider the potential need for engineering design data for structural repairs; mandate availability timeframes for repair design packages or permit temporary repairs approved via AMOC.

[P22] The repeat inspection intervals for 7075–T73 must be resource‑feasible; request that Boeing provide fleet-level estimates of expected repeat inspection burdens and recommended interval adjustments for low-utilization aircraft.

[P23] Changing compliance times measured from the service bulletin's original issue date to the AD effective date (paragraph i(1)) may shorten operator timelines unexpectedly; require FAA to provide a clear conversion table showing original vs. AD effective dates for all affected compliance items.

[P24] When the service bulletin instructs operators to "contact Boeing for an RC action," the AD's requirement to repair before further flight using methods approved under paragraph (j) creates potential circularity and delay; permit repairs using FAA‑accepted temporary repair schemes when Boeing cannot respond within a defined short period.

[P25] Concentrating AMOC approval authority with the Manager, Los Angeles ACO for Boeing ADs may disadvantage operators outside the LA ACO region; permit delegation to principal inspectors for limited-scope AMOCs and establish maximum processing times.

[P26] The AMOC request routing that allows email submission should explicitly require secure transmission and include suggested templates and data fields (aircraft serial, operator, proposed method, substantiation) to accelerate review.

[P27] The requirement to notify the principal inspector or local FSDO "prior to using" an AMOC (j(2)) lacks a defined timeframe and could be interpreted to require in-person notification; specify acceptable notification methods and a minimum advance notice (e.g., 48 hours).

[P28] Allowing Boeing ODA approvals to be used as AMOCs (j(3)) is useful, but the AD should require Boeing to register and publish the specific ODA approvals referencing this AD in a public docket or operator portal for transparency.

[P29] The binding nature of steps labeled RC (j(4)(i)) requires that every RC-designated step be clearly marked in the service bulletin; if service bulletins do not explicitly label RC steps, require Boeing to issue revised documents with clear RC markings prior to AD effective date.

[P30] The permission in j(4)(ii) to deviate from non‑RC steps without AMOC should be accompanied by mandatory documentation and audit trail requirements in the operator's maintenance records to ensure compliance and facilitate oversight.

[P4] Industry commenters will request that the AD explicitly allow use of previously accomplished Bombardier Service Bulletin actions (if done to a specified revision) to be credited toward compliance to avoid redundant work.

[P6] Operators of aircraft in serial range 20501–20635 request clarification regarding aircraft assembled from kits or with replaced APU installations — whether such aircraft remain in the applicability and how to document compliance.

[P8] Legal counsel will challenge any requirement that forces operators to rely exclusively on manufacturer contact for repairs, arguing that regulatory oversight should permit operator‑developed repairs approved by FAA without mandatory manufacturer concurrence.

[P12] Maintenance providers request guidance on the acceptable format and content of manufacturer corrective action submissions to the Manager, New York ACO to standardize approval packages and reduce back-and-forth.

[P15] Labor unions representing maintenance technicians will request training guidance, certification requirements, and estimated task times for HFEC inspections to ensure safe work practices and adequate staffing.

[P17] Safety advocates will demand that the FAA quantify the risk reduction expected from the repeat inspection intervals and provide data justifying those intervals instead of deferring to Boeing's service bulletin alone.

[P23] Aviation insurers will request clarification that compliance measured from the AD effective date does not create retroactive liability for operators who followed the service bulletin on its original schedule; include a safe‑harbor statement for good-faith compliance.

[P5] International operators subject to TCCA oversight request clear coordination procedures when TCCA and FAA approval pathways differ, to avoid conflicting directives about "before further flight" repair approvals.

[P1] The March 26, 2018 comment deadline (P1) is unreasonably short and should be extended at least 60 days to allow affected operators and stakeholders to prepare technical comments and economic analyses.

[P1] Small carriers and individual technicians will not be able to submit meaningful comments by March 26, 2018 due to limited staffing; FAA should publish a notice extending the comment period or provide targeted outreach.

[P2] The phrase "within the compliance times specified" (P2) is vague because the AD references multiple timing tables; FAA should specify absolute calendar or flight-cycle limits in the regulatory text to avoid ambiguity.

[P2] The obligation in P2 must include an explicit grandfathering clause for operators who have initiated but not completed actions prior to the compliance deadline to avoid enforcement uncertainty.

[P3] Relying on the service bulletin's paragraph 1.E for inspection times (P3) improperly delegates substantive regulatory requirements to a manufacturer document; FAA should incorporate the specific intervals into the AD itself.

[P3] The AD should clarify which revision of the Aviation Partners Boeing Service Bulletin is mandatory; P3 cites Revision 1 but cross-references in other paragraphs use a different date—this creates compliance confusion.

[P4] The options for "Condition 1" (P4) allow repeated inspections or other actions, but the AD does not quantify acceptable crack growth rates or provide clear criteria for choosing between (g)(1)(i) and (g)(1)(ii); FAA must add decision criteria.

[P5] Requiring indefinite repeated HFEC inspections at the service bulletin intervals (P5) imposes potentially high recurring maintenance costs without a defined terminating action; FAA should require a terminating modification or set a maximum interval/final action.

[P6] Option (g)(1)(ii) (P6) mandates both a preventative modification and inspections but fails to specify acceptable parts, materials, or workmanship standards for the modification; FAA should reference detailed procedures or approved drawings.

[P7] The requirement to perform the preventative modification before further flight (P7) may be operationally infeasible for long-range or international flights; FAA should allow temporary flight restrictions or provide a flight-limitation protocol until modification can be accomplished.

[P7] Requiring modification "before further flight" (P7) without an allowance for ferry flight or minimum equipment list (MEL) procedures could ground aircraft unexpectedly; FAA should include narrow exceptions for one-time ferry flights to a maintenance base.

[P8] The post-modification inspection timing referenced in P8 again defers to the service bulletin (P8); FAA should specify the inspection interval in the AD and confirm whether the post-modification inspection is a terminating action.

[P9] The separate treatment of "Condition 2" (P9) is appropriate, but the AD does not define "Condition 2" within the regulatory text, relying instead on the service bulletin—this lacks the necessary regulatory clarity.

[P10] Requiring repairs per Part 2 of the service bulletin before further flight (P10) should be accompanied by a provision permitting temporary repairs under approved procedures to allow safe repositioning to a repair facility.

[P11] The follow-up HFEC inspection schedule after repair (P11) should include the number of required repeats and whether repeated non-detections after X cycles terminate the requirement; current language is indefinite.

[P12] Mandating repair of any crack before further flight (P12) is safety-justified but the AD's cross-reference to paragraph (j) for approved methods is circular; FAA should list acceptable repair methods or the criteria for approval to expedite compliance.

[P13] Modifying service-bulletin "after initial issue date" intervals to be relative to the AD's effective date (P13) may shorten intended compliance windows and increase burden; FAA should provide transitional relief or grandfathering for actions already scheduled.

[P14] Granting credit for actions performed under the earlier service bulletin for Group 2 airplanes (P14) is sensible, but the AD should require documentation evidencing the exact procedures performed to qualify for credit.

[P15] The AMOC authority vested in the Seattle ACO Manager (P15) should permit delegation to other ACOs to avoid bottlenecks; commenters request clear timelines for AMOC decision-making to prevent operational delays.

[P16] The procedural requirement to route AMOC requests through principal inspectors or local FSDOs or email (P16) should allow electronic submission through FAA's Docket System and require FAA to acknowledge receipt within a set timeframe.

[P17] The notification requirement before using an approved AMOC (P17) should be clarified to state whether written confirmation to the principal inspector is sufficient and to require FAA acknowledgement to avoid enforcement disputes.

[P18] Allowing Boeing ODA-approved AMOCs (P18) is useful, but the AD should require that Boeing's approval be filed with FAA or documented in the AMOC record to ensure traceability and oversight.

[P19] Requiring that AMOC repair/modification methods meet the airplane's certification basis (P19) could preclude time-limited or novel temporary fixes; FAA should clarify that time-limited AMOCs can be approved for safety as interim measures.

[P20] The requirement that all steps labeled "Required for Compliance" (RC) must be performed (P20) is appropriate, but FAA should publish an explicit list of RC steps in the AD to avoid reliance on an external service document that may be updated.

[P21] The "RC Exempt" exception (P21) could be abused if manufacturers overuse the label; FAA should set criteria limiting when "RC Exempt" may be applied and require justification in the service bulletin.

[P22] Requiring an AMOC for any deviation to RC steps (P22) is necessary for safety but imposes procedural burden for minor deviations (e.g., material substitutions); FAA should allow the principal inspector limited authority to approve minor deviations when safety is maintained.

[P23] Permitting deviations from non-RC steps by an operator's maintenance program (P23) is practical, but FAA must require operators to document deviations and rationale in their maintenance records to ensure auditability.

[P3] Several provisions (P3, P8, P11, P13) inconsistently reference service bulletin dates (April 1 vs April 11, 2017); FAA should correct these clerical inconsistencies to prevent compliance conflicts.

[P6] The AD should estimate the labor-hours and parts cost for the preventative modification (P6/P7) so commenters can assess economic impact; absence of cost information undermines the regulatory flexibility analysis.

[P12] Paragraph (j) approval route for repairs (P12) should include the timeframe for FAA to approve repair methods to avoid extended grounding of aircraft.

[P15] AMOC requests per 14 CFR 39.19 (P15) often require substantial supporting data; FAA should provide a template of required data to speed review and reduce repetitive requests.

[P14] The crediting provision for Group 2 airplanes (P14) should require operators to retain service records proving the earlier actions were identical in scope to those required by the AD.

[P2] Enforcement discretion guidance is needed explaining how FAA will treat minor paperwork or timing discrepancies when operators are actively working to comply within overlapping service bulletin and AD deadlines (P2).

[P7] The "before further flight" requirement for a preventative modification (P7) should specify whether approved deferred maintenance procedures or MEL entries can be used for airplanes operating outside the U.S.

[P18] Reliance on Boeing ODA approvals (P18) raises potential conflict-of-interest concerns; FAA should require independent verification or periodic audits of ODA-issued AMOCs used to comply with this AD.

[P20] The RC-step requirement (P20) should permit equivalent procedures demonstrably providing equal safety when supported by data, subject to AMOC, and FAA should expedite such AMOCs for common equivalent methods.

[P1] The proposed rule should clarify whether extensions to the comment period will be allowed upon request and whether late-filed, but substantive, comments will be considered.

[P1] The blanket prohibition in § 330.200(a) is overly broad and could unintentionally restrict low-risk academic research materials (e.g., dead/inactivated specimens, preserved slides) that pose no biosecurity threat; the rule should clarify exclusions for non-viable materials.

[P1] The prohibition lacks a clear definition of "associated articles" and risks encompassing common laboratory supplies and packaging; the agency should define the term to avoid regulatory uncertainty.

[P2] Requiring permits under § 330.200(a) without streamlined pathways will impose undue burdens on small research labs and universities that regularly import benign biological control organisms; APHIS should create a simplified, low-cost permit or declaration process for low-risk imports.

[P3] Cross-referencing "other APHIS regulations in 7 CFR chapter III" without specifying which parts apply creates compliance uncertainty; the rule should list or summarize relevant APHIS regulations that authorize movements to ensure consistency.

[P4] The exception for explicit exemptions in the subpart (§ 330.200(a)) is too vague — stakeholders need the full list of exceptions in the proposed rule text prior to finalization and an explanation of how exemptions will be granted or revoked.

[P5] The authority to rely on general permits (§ 330.200(a)) is useful, but the proposal provides no criteria or public-process requirements for issuing general permits; APHIS should specify the process, transparency requirements, and standard conditions for general permits.

[P6] The statement in § 330.200 that the Administrator may issue general permits under PPA section 7711 should include limits on scope (e.g., organism classes, quantities, containment levels) to prevent overly broad general authorizations that circumvent case-specific review.

[P7] Allowing APHIS to regulate additional types of biological control organisms case-by-case (§ 330.200(c)) creates retroactive compliance risk for entities currently working with organisms not presently regulated; APHIS should provide a predictable timeline and criteria for when case-by-case regulation would be applied.

[P7] The rule should require notice and a meaningful comment period before APHIS begins to regulate a new class of biological control organisms under the revised subpart, to allow affected stakeholders to prepare.

[P8] Exempting EPA-authorized microbial pesticides (§ 330.200(d)) risks regulatory gaps because EPA reviews focus on human and pesticide-related risks, not necessarily plant-pest risks; APHIS should retain oversight or at least a coordination review for EPA-authorized products with outdoor use.

[P8] The exemption for EPA experimental use permits (EUPs) and registered microbial pesticides could allow importation of organisms that still pose plant pest risks; APHIS should require notification and the ability to impose additional plant-health conditions even for EPA-authorized products.

[P9] Allowing import and interstate movement of some unregistered EPA-regulated microbial products without APHIS oversight (§ 330.200(d)) will create conflicting regulatory regimes and potential loopholes; APHIS should condition the exemption on EPA providing APHIS all application data and a plant-health risk assessment.

[P10] The list of permit types (§ 330.201(a)) is appropriate, but APHIS should publish standardized application forms and decision timelines for each permit type to reduce administrative burden and unpredictability for applicants.

[P11] Requiring individual import permit applicants to be 18+ and have a U.S. physical address (§ 330.201(a)(1)) could exclude legitimate foreign researchers collaborating with U.S. institutions; permit rules should allow sponsoring U.S. institutions to serve as the U.S. address and accountable party.

[P12] The corporate permittee requirement to maintain a U.S. office and designate an individual for service of process (§ 330.201(a)(1)) could bar foreign companies from conducting lawful research collaborations; APHIS should permit U.S.-based authorized agents to fulfill these functions.

[P13] The identical 18+ and U.S. address requirement for interstate movement permits (§ 330.201(a)(2)) may be unnecessary for shipments between accredited U.S. institutions; APHIS should allow institutional permits where the institution, not an individual, is the permit holder.

[P14] The corporate interstate permit requirement (§ 330.201(a)(2)) to maintain a U.S. address and designated service individual should explicitly allow third-party logistics providers or registered agents to satisfy the requirement.

[P15] Requiring individuals issued continued curation permits to be 18+ with a U.S. address (§ 330.201(a)(3)) may prevent graduate students and visiting scholars without permanent U.S. addresses from being permittees; APHIS should permit institutional sponsorship and responsible individual assignment instead.

[P16] The corporate continued curation permit condition (§ 330.201(a)(3)) to maintain a U.S. business office and designate an individual for service of process must clarify expectations for small nonprofits and museums that curate collections but lack a formal "business office"—allow mailing addresses or institutional contact information.

[P17] The requirement that applications be submitted via specified electronic methods or in writing (§ 330.201(b)) must include accessible, reliable electronic submission portals and alternatives for applicants without robust internet access; APHIS should commit to maintaining the portal and providing helpdesk support.

[P18] Stating that applications must be "complete" before evaluation (§ 330.201(c)) is reasonable, but APHIS should provide applicants with a detailed completeness checklist and a timeline for deficiency notices to avoid indefinite processing delays.

[P19] Advising submission at least 90 days in advance (§ 330.201(c)) is appropriate for many cases, but APHIS should provide an expedited review pathway for urgent research or pest-response movements with specific maximum review times (e.g., 15 business days).

[P20] APHIS' ability to share applications and proposed conditions with State/Tribal officials (§ 330.201(d)(1)) raises confidentiality concerns for proprietary research; the rule should require APHIS to protect trade secrets and confidential business information and to obtain applicant consent before disclosure, except where legally required.

[P21] The requirement that facilities be constructed and maintained to prevent dissemination (§ 330.201(d)(2)) lacks clear technical standards (e.g., biosafety levels, physical containment measures); APHIS should adopt or reference specific facility standards to ensure uniform enforcement.

[P22] Mandating applicants to provide all facility/site assessment information and allow inspections during normal business hours (§ 330.201(d)(2)) is reasonable, but APHIS must define "normal business hours," provide advance notice of inspections except in exigent circumstances, and ensure inspector credentials and limits on scope of inspection.

[P23] Denial of permit application for failure to provide information or allow inspections (§ 330.201(d)(2)) could be disproportionate; APHIS should require notice of deficiency and an opportunity to cure before outright denial.

[P24] Permitting movements deemed "highly unlikely" to result in introduction (§ 330.201(d)(3)) is appropriate, but the rule lacks the risk assessment methodology and thresholds APHIS will use to make that determination — APHIS should publish its risk criteria and models for public review.

[P25] Requiring applicants to agree in writing to permit conditions including authorizing unscheduled assessments in private residences (§ 330.201(d)(3)(i)-(iv)) raises Fourth Amendment and privacy concerns; APHIS should limit warrantless or unscheduled inspections of private residences and require judicial warrants or owner consent.

[P26] A three-year maximum permit validity period (§ 330.201(d)(3)) may be too short for long-term curatorial collections and breeding programs; APHIS should allow multi-year renewals with abbreviated reviews and set clear renewal timelines.

[P27] The obligation that permittees comply with all permit conditions and use organisms only as specified (§ 330.201(d)(3)) should include a process for requesting amendments to permits when legitimate changes in research needs arise, with defined review timelines.

[P28] Restricting use of organisms derived from a regulated parent organism to the parent's permitted intended use (§ 330.201(d)(3)) may unduly constrain downstream research (e.g., characterization or taxonomic work); APHIS should allow derivative research under notification or minor-modification procedures.

[P29] The definition that a permittee must comply with all permit provisions and the regulations (§ 330.100) is standard, but APHIS should require clear written notice of noncompliance allegations and a fair administrative appeal or correction process before penalties.

[P30] The requirement that the responsible individual be physically present during normal business hours at or near the permit-specified ultimate destination (§ 330.100) is impractical for remote or multi-site facilities; APHIS should allow designated alternates and permit remote supervision if adequate monitoring systems are in place.

[P31] Attributing acts or omissions of the responsible individual to the permittee (§ 330.100 / PPA sec. 7734) could result in unfair liability where the permittee has implemented adequate supervision; APHIS should include a defense for permittees who can show reasonable care and compliance systems.

[P32] The export coordination note (§ 330.201) is helpful but non-binding; APHIS should require applicants to certify that they have consulted with destination countries or provide a plan to ensure exports meet foreign phytosanitary requirements to avoid rejections and invasive species risks.

[P20] APHIS' plan to share applications with Tribal governments must include consultation requirements and respect Tribal sovereignty; Tribal nations should have the ability to opt in or out of notifications based on their own preferences.

[P21] The facility construction standard (§ 330.201(d)(2)) may disproportionately burden small museums, seed banks, and tribal repositories that cannot afford upgrades; APHIS should offer guidance, cost-sharing, or phased compliance timelines.

[P25] The requirement to authorize unscheduled assessments for private-residence containment without clear limits could chill citizen science and home-based curation; APHIS should prohibit unscheduled inspections of private residences unless there is probable cause and obtain consent or a warrant.

[P9] The interplay between EPA and APHIS jurisdiction (§ 330.200(d)) requires a formal memorandum of understanding (MOU) specifying data sharing, roles, and timelines; commenters request that APHIS publish the MOU before finalizing the rule.

[P5] The delegation of broad authority to the Administrator to issue general permits (§ 330.200(a), (discussion)) should be subject to notice-and-comment procedures for each general permit and periodic review to assess environmental outcomes.

[P18] APHIS' "complete application" standard should include metrics for completeness determinations and an applicant right to prompt reconsideration if APHIS erroneously deems an application incomplete.

[P24] The "highly unlikely" risk standard is inherently vague; APHIS should quantify acceptable risk thresholds (e.g., numerical likelihoods) or reference specific scientific criteria for permit issuance.

[P12] Requiring corporate permittees to designate an individual for service of process (§ 330.201(a)(1)) should allow foreign corporations to designate a U.S.-based registered agent; lack of this flexibility will impede international scientific collaboration.

[P16] The term "business office" for corporate continued curation permittees (§ 330.201(a)(3)) should be defined to include nonprofit institutional addresses and shared laboratory spaces used by multiple organizations.

[P22] APHIS should clarify whether inspections can include review of proprietary records, electronic data, or personnel files, and set limits to protect confidential business information during facility/site assessments (§ 330.201(d)(2)).

[P27] The rule should permit emergency deviations from permit-specified uses in pest-response situations (e.g., need to move organisms to contain an outbreak) with an after-the-fact notification requirement rather than denial or immediate sanction.

[P28] For organisms derived from regulated parents (§ 330.201(d)(3)), APHIS should define "derived" and provide examples (e.g., mutants, hybrids, cultured isolates) so permittees can determine when additional approvals are required.

[P11] The age requirement of 18+ for individual permittees (§ 330.201(a)(1)) should allow supervised minors in educational settings under an adult responsible individual's permit to facilitate STEM education programs.

[P26] APHIS should clarify renewal procedures and limits on cumulative years of permit validity if successive three-year permits are granted to avoid perpetual permits without review of long-term impacts.

[P20] When APHIS shares application information with States, the agency must provide a reconciliation process for conflicting state-imposed conditions to avoid duplicative or contradictory permit requirements.

[P31] The rule should limit strict liability for permittees regarding the acts of a responsible individual and instead require showing of intentional negligence for severe penalties, aligning with due process principles.

[P1] The two-year stay of § 60.5393a(b)–(c) will unlawfully delay compliance obligations that are necessary to reduce near-term methane emissions and should be shortened or justified with a quantified emissions impact analysis.

[P1] Industry commenters will request clarification whether the stay of §§ 60.5393a(b)–(c) applies to newly installed well sites as well as existing sites, and ask for explicit language stating applicability to new versus existing sources.

[P2] Operators will argue that exempting pneumatic pumps at well sites from § 60.5393a(d)–(e) for two years creates regulatory uncertainty for lease purchasers and lenders and request that the rule require disclosure of the temporary exemption in transfer documents.

[P2] Environmental groups will object that the exemption for pneumatic pumps is an unlawful loophole because pneumatic pumps are a major source of methane and VOC emissions; they will demand removal of the exemption or, at minimum, monitoring and recordkeeping requirements during the exemption period.

[P3] Commenters will request that the stay of § 60.5397a include an explicit statement that state and local requirements more stringent than the federal stay remain enforceable, to avoid preemption confusion.

[P3] Legal experts will assert that staying § 60.5397a for two years without a formal cost-benefit or substantive justification may violate the Administrative Procedure Act’s requirement for reasoned explanation and request the agency provide the administrative record supporting the stay.

[P4] Public health and environmental advocates will challenge the stay of § 60.5410a(e)(2)–(5) because those paragraphs likely contain monitoring and control requirements; they will request that the stay be rescinded or accompanied by interim protective measures.

[P4] Industry will request clarification on whether the stay of § 60.5410a(e)(2)–(5) affects obligations under related NSPS provisions or state implementation plans (SIPs), and ask for a cross-reference table showing interactions.

[P5] Operators will support § 60.5410a(e)(8) exempting pneumatic pump affected facilities at wells from (e)(6)–(7) for two years, but request an alternative compliance pathway (e.g., interim best management practices) to be codified during the exemption.

[P5] Environmental groups will oppose § 60.5410a(e)(8) as inconsistent with the statute’s purpose to control methane and VOCs and demand that the exemption include mandatory leak detection and reporting at a minimum.

[P6] Commenters will request specification of whether the stay of § 60.5410a(j) affects permit issuance, including Title V permit terms that reference paragraph (j), and ask the Agency to require permit writers to note the temporary suspension.

[P7] Industry groups will request that § 60.5411a’s obligation to “comply with the applicable requirements … for each cover and closed vent system” clarify what constitutes “applicable” requirements during overlapping stays and exemptions to avoid duplicative or conflicting obligations.

[P7] Environmental NGOs will argue that § 60.5411a should require electronic submission of compliance records for each cover/closed vent system to the EPA to ensure public transparency, and note that the proposed text lacks such a requirement.

[P8] Operators will ask for clarity on the scope of § 60.5411a(e) — whether the exemption of pneumatic pump affected facilities at well sites from paragraph (a) applies to all pneumatic pumps regardless of size, power source, or lease location.

[P8] Public interest commenters will request that even if pneumatic pumps are exempted under § 60.5411a(e), the rule require interim reporting of pump counts and locations so emissions can be estimated during the exemption period.

[P9] Industry will request clarification whether the stay of § 60.5411a(d) halts specific monitoring, recordkeeping, or design requirements, and urge the Agency to provide a compliance guide explaining which obligations remain operable.

[P9] States with delegated programs will request explicit guidance about state enforcement authority over § 60.5411a(d) requirements during the federal stay to avoid enforcement gaps.

[P10] Operators will ask that § 60.5415a(b)’s continuous compliance demonstration provisions include explicit flexibility for record-lag and downtime (e.g., force majeure, maintenance), and propose alternative language allowing reasonable delays in data submission.

[P10] Environmental groups will contend that exempting pneumatic pumps from compliance demonstration undermines the continuous monitoring framework and request that compliance demonstrations for pneumatic pumps be retained.

[P11] Commenters will seek clarification of the technical content of paragraphs (b)(1) and (b)(2) for centrifugal compressors — specifically what types of monitoring equipment, instrument accuracy, and data retention periods are required — because the proposed rule references them but does not enumerate measurement methods.

[P11] Legal commenters will request that the Agency explicitly state whether existing continuous monitoring system (CMS) performance standards apply to centrifugal compressors or whether new performance criteria will be promulgated.

[P12] Operators will support § 60.5415a(b)(4) exempting pneumatic pump affected facilities at well sites from (b)(3) for two years but request that the rule permit voluntary early compliance without penalty and provide a mechanism for crediting early reductions.

[P12] Environmental advocacy organizations will state that exempting pneumatic pumps from (b)(3) for two years will likely increase aggregate emissions and urge the Agency to require at minimum monthly leak inspections during the exemption.

[P13] Industry will request clarity on what obligations are suspended under the stay of § 60.5415a(h), including whether recordkeeping and reporting requirements are tolled, and ask for an explicit list of suspended subsections.

[P13] Public commenters will ask that the Agency analyze and disclose the projected emission increases resulting from suspending § 60.5415a(h) for two years.

[P14] Operators will seek detailed guidance on how to comply with § 60.5416a(a)–(c) for closed vent systems and covers at mixed-facility sites (storage vessels, compressors, pumps) and request standardized templates for inspection checklists and monitoring logs.

[P14] Environmental groups will request that § 60.5416a include minimum inspection frequencies and instrumentation accuracy requirements for closed vent systems to ensure inspections are meaningful.

[P15] Industry will request clarification of the scope of § 60.5416a(d) so they can identify which well-site pneumatic pumps are exempt from inspections and monitoring; they will also ask whether the exemption applies to oil versus gas wells.

[P15] States and tribes will warn that exempting inspections for pneumatic pumps at well sites may frustrate state/tribal monitoring programs and request that the Agency coordinate with them to maintain data collection during the exemption.

[P16] Regulated entities will request that § 60.5420a(b) annual report templates be published in machine-readable formats and that the Agency provide an electronic submission portal to avoid duplicative reporting burdens.

[P16] Environmental groups will argue that the required annual report elements in (b)(1)–(8) and (12) are insufficiently specific in the proposed text and demand that the Agency specify exact data fields, units, and acceptable supporting documentation.

[P17] Industry commenters will request extension of the 90‑day deadline for the initial annual report in § 60.5420a(b) to at least 180 days, arguing that the initial compliance period end may be followed by operational transitions that make a 90‑day submission impracticable.

[P17] States and legal commenters will caution that lengthening the initial report deadline could hinder EPA and state oversight and ask for evidence-based justification if the Agency considers extending the 90‑day timeline.

[P18] Operators will request flexibility in § 60.5420a(b) allowing subsequent annual reports to be tied to fiscal or permit cycles rather than exactly the same calendar date as the initial report, to reduce administrative burden.

[P18] Environmental groups will oppose shifting the due date away from a fixed annual schedule because it could make tracking compliance over time more difficult and ask the Agency to keep strict same-date annual reporting.

[P19] Industry will request that the procedure in § 60.5420a(b)(11) be published as a step-by-step template with examples of acceptable submissions and redaction rules for confidential business information (CBI).

[P19] Public interest groups will request transparency and public access to the annual reports filed under § 60.5420a(b), and ask the Agency to limit CBI claims and require standardized redaction protocols.

[P20] Operators will support the permission in § 60.5420a(b) to combine multiple facilities into one report but ask the Agency to permit aggregated reporting by basin or operator region instead of facility-by-facility submissions to reduce costs.

[P20] Environmental advocates will oppose aggregated reporting by basin or region unless such reports still contain facility-level data and GPS-located equipment lists to allow public accountability.

[P21] Industry will request formal acceptance that annual reports submitted with Title V reports satisfy § 60.5420a(b) by reference, and ask the Agency to issue compliance guidance confirming acceptable cross-referencing methods.

[P21] State permitting authorities will caution that relying on Title V reports may cause timing mismatches; they will request clearer rules to ensure both Title V and § 60.5420a(b) obligations are met without gaps.

[P22] Operators will request broader authority to agree with the Administrator to a common reporting schedule that could include multi-year cycles, as long as environmental outcomes are protected.

[P22] Environmental groups will object to any common scheduling that effectively extends reporting periods beyond annual frequency and insist the provision’s limitation (“does not extend the required reporting periods”) be strictly enforced and audited.

[P23] Industry will request clarifying definitions for “collection of fugitive emissions components at a well site” referenced in § 60.5420a(b)(13) to determine which component counts are exempted and which are reportable.

[P23] Environmental and public health commenters will object to exempting fugitive emission collections and pneumatic pumps under § 60.5420a(b)(13) for two years, arguing this will blind regulators and the public to leak trends during the stay.

[P24] Commenters will note that P24 duplicates P4 and request that the Agency consolidate and correct redundant stays of § 60.5410a(e)(2)–(5) for clarity and legal precision in the preamble and regulatory text.

[P24] Legal commentators will argue that repeating the same stay in multiple provisions increases risk of conflicting interpretations and ask the Agency to cross-reference rather than restate stays to avoid ambiguity.

[P25] Industry will request detail on which elements in § 60.5420a(b)(7), (b)(8), and (b)(12) are being stayed and whether those elements include quantification methods or specific data fields; they ask for a table showing suspended reporting fields.

[P25] Environmental groups will request modeling that quantifies the data loss to EPA from suspending (b)(7), (b)(8), and (b)(12) for two years, and demand that the Agency collect substitute summary-level data during the suspension.

[P26] Commenters will request specifics about which reporting or recordkeeping obligations are contained in § 60.5420a(c)(15)–(17) and why they were selected for a two-year stay, and will ask for the legal rationale for suspending those particular subsections.

[P26] Transparency advocates will recommend that any suspension of reporting subsections (c)(15)–(17) be accompanied by interim public dashboards or periodic disclosures so that stakeholders still have visibility into emissions trends during the suspension.

[P1] Small producers will request an explicit small-entity compliance assistance package and a safe-harbor certification process for demonstrating good-faith compliance once the stays and exemptions expire.

[P2] Indigenous and local community groups will demand that the Agency conduct cumulative impact assessments for communities near well sites before approving any multi-year exemptions for pneumatic pumps.

[P3] Technical commenters will request that the final rule include an explicit requirement that EPA publish an implementation timeline (milestones) during the two-year stay that details when guidance, test methods, and enforcement policies will be finalized.

[P4] Several commenters will urge that during the two-year stays the Agency require at minimum monthly self-certification and an interim emissions inventory from affected sources to mitigate the information gap created by the suspensions.

parsed_claims.claim_text: The two-year stay of § 60.5393a(b)–(c) will unlawfully delay compliance obligations that are necessary to reduce near-term methane emissions and should be shortened or justified with a quantified emissions impact analysis.

Industry commenters will request clarification whether the stay of §§ 60.5393a(b)–(c) applies to newly installed well sites as well as existing sites, and ask for explicit language stating applicability to new versus existing sources.

Operators will argue that exempting pneumatic pumps at well sites from § 60.5393a(d)–(e) for two years creates regulatory uncertainty for lease purchasers and lenders and request that the rule require disclosure of the temporary exemption in transfer documents.

Environmental groups will object that the exemption for pneumatic pumps is an unlawful loophole because pneumatic pumps are a major source of methane and VOC emissions; they will demand removal of the exemption or, at minimum, monitoring and recordkeeping requirements during the exemption period.

Commenters will request that the stay of § 60.5397a include an explicit statement that state and local requirements more stringent than the federal stay remain enforceable, to avoid preemption confusion.

Legal experts will assert that staying § 60.5397a for two years without a formal cost-benefit or substantive justification may violate the Administrative Procedure Act’s requirement for reasoned explanation and request the agency provide the administrative record supporting the stay.

Public health and environmental advocates will challenge the stay of § 60.5410a(e)(2)–(5) because those paragraphs likely contain monitoring and control requirements; they will request that the stay be rescinded or accompanied by interim protective measures.

Industry will request clarification on whether the stay of § 60.5410a(e)(2)–(5) affects obligations under related NSPS provisions or state implementation plans (SIPs), and ask for a cross-reference table showing interactions.

Operators will support § 60.5410a(e)(8) exempting pneumatic pump affected facilities at wells from (e)(6)–(7) for two years, but request an alternative compliance pathway (e.g., interim best management practices) to be codified during the exemption.

Environmental groups will oppose § 60.5410a(e)(8) as inconsistent with the statute’s purpose to control methane and VOCs and demand that the exemption include mandatory leak detection and reporting at a minimum.

Commenters will request specification of whether the stay of § 60.5410a(j) affects permit issuance, including Title V permit terms that reference paragraph (j), and ask the Agency to require permit writers to note the temporary suspension.

Industry groups will request that § 60.5411a’s obligation to “comply with the applicable requirements … for each cover and closed vent system” clarify what constitutes “applicable” requirements during overlapping stays and exemptions to avoid duplicative or conflicting obligations.

Environmental NGOs will argue that § 60.5411a should require electronic submission of compliance records for each cover/closed vent system to the EPA to ensure public transparency, and note that the proposed text lacks such a requirement.

Operators will ask for clarity on the scope of § 60.5411a(e) — whether the exemption of pneumatic pump affected facilities at well sites from paragraph (a) applies to all pneumatic pumps regardless of size, power source, or lease location.

Public interest commenters will request that even if pneumatic pumps are exempted under § 60.5411a(e), the rule require interim reporting of pump counts and locations so emissions can be estimated during the exemption period.

Industry will request clarification whether the stay of § 60.5411a(d) halts specific monitoring, recordkeeping, or design requirements, and urge the Agency to provide a compliance guide explaining which obligations remain operable.
States with delegated programs will request explicit guidance about state enforcement authority over § 60.5411a(d) requirements during the federal stay to avoid enforcement gaps.

Operators will ask that § 60.5415a(b)’s continuous compliance demonstration provisions include explicit flexibility for record-lag and downtime (e.g., force majeure, maintenance), and propose alternative language allowing reasonable delays in data submission.

Environmental groups will contend that exempting pneumatic pumps from compliance demonstration undermines the continuous monitoring framework and request that compliance demonstrations for pneumatic pumps be retained.

Commenters will seek clarification of the technical content of paragraphs (b)(1) and (b)(2) for centrifugal compressors — specifically what types of monitoring equipment, instrument accuracy, and data retention periods are required — because the proposed rule references them but does not enumerate measurement methods.

Legal commenters will request that the Agency explicitly state whether existing continuous monitoring system (CMS) performance standards apply to centrifugal compressors or whether new performance criteria will be promulgated.

Operators will support § 60.5415a(b)(4) exempting pneumatic pump affected facilities at well sites from (b)(3) for two years but request that the rule permit voluntary early compliance without penalty and provide a mechanism for crediting early reductions.

Environmental advocacy organizations will state that exempting pneumatic pumps from (b)(3) for two years will likely increase aggregate emissions and urge the Agency to require at minimum monthly leak inspections during the exemption.
